Initially created: 2025-12-17T09:24:56.991+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Annals of Guāngwǔ Dì, Part One, Upper Section
Shìzǔ Guāngwǔ Huángdì, personal name Xiù,
courtesy name Wénshú,
was from Càiyáng in Nányáng.
He was a ninth-generation descendant of Gāozǔ.
His lineage originated from Jǐngdì, who fathered Chángshā Dìng Wáng Fā.
Fā fathered Chōnglíng Jié Hóu Mǎi.
Mǎi fathered Yùlín Tàishǒu Wài.
Wài fathered Jùlù Dūwèi Huí.
Huí fathered Nándùn Lìng Qīn.
Qīn fathered Guāngwǔ.
Guāngwǔ became an orphan at the age of nine
and was raised by his uncle, Liáng.
He was seven *chǐ* and three *cùn* tall,
had handsome eyebrows and a beautiful beard,
a large mouth,
a prominent nose,
and a "sun-horn" forehead.
He was diligent in farming,
but his elder brother, Bóshēng, was fond of chivalry and hosting retainers.
Bóshēng often scoffed at Guāngwǔ's preoccupation with agriculture,
comparing him to Gāozǔ's elder brother, Zhòng.
(10) In the Tiānfèng era of Wáng Mǎng,
(11) he went to Cháng'ān
to study the *Shàngshū*
and generally grasped its main principles.
Towards the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
the empire suffered successive years of droughts and locust plagues,
and bandits arose everywhere.
In Dìhuáng 3rd year (22 CE),
Nányáng was ravaged by famine,
and many household retainers turned to petty thievery.
Guāngwǔ avoided officials in Xīnyě
and subsequently sold grain in Wǎn.
Lǐ Tōng and others from Wǎn used prophetic diagrams and texts to tell Guāngwǔ:
"The Liú clan will rise again,
and the Lǐ clan will serve as its aids."
Guāngwǔ at first dared not accept this,
but he thought to himself that his elder brother Bóshēng had long associated with daring men
and would certainly embark on a great undertaking.
Moreover, Wáng Mǎng's defeat and downfall were already portended,
and the empire was on the brink of chaos.
So he decided on a plan with them,
and thereupon purchased weapons and crossbows.
In the tenth month,
he and Lǐ Tōng’s cousin, Yì, and others, rose up in Jiē. He was twenty-eight years old at the time.
In the eleventh month,
a comet appeared in the Zhāng asterism.
Guāngwǔ then led his retainers back to Chōnglíng.
At this time, Bóshēng had already gathered a multitude and raised an army.
Initially,
the young men of the various clans were frightened,
and all fled and hid themselves,
saying,
"Bóshēng will kill us!"
But when they saw Guāngwǔ in his crimson robes and tall hat,
they were all astonished and exclaimed,
"Even the discreet and honest are doing this!"
Only then did they gradually feel at ease.
Bóshēng then recruited troops from Xīnshì and Pínglín,
and together with their leaders, Wáng Fèng and Chén Mù, attacked Chángjù to the west.
Guāngwǔ initially rode an ox,
but after killing the Xīnyě尉, he obtained a horse.
They advanced and massacred Tángzǐ Xiāng,
and also killed the Húyáng尉.
There was an unfair division of wealth and goods in the army,
which angered and resented the troops,
who wanted to turn and attack the Liú clan.
Guāngwǔ collected the belongings obtained by his clansmen
and gave them all to the soldiers,
who were then pleased.
They advanced and captured Jíyáng,
and fought Wáng Mǎng's Qiánduì Dàfū Zhēn Fù and
Zhǔzhèng Liángqiū Cì (10) at Xiǎocháng'ān.
(11) The Hàn army was severely defeated
and retreated to defend Jíyáng.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day, the first day of the first month of Gèngshǐ 1st year (23 CE),
the Hàn army again fought Zhēn Fù and Liángqiū Cì west of the Bǐshuǐ River,
decisively defeating them,
and beheading Fù and Cì.
Bóshēng also defeated Wáng Mǎng's Nàyán Jiāngjūn Yán Yóu and Zhìzōng Jiāngjūn Chén Mào at Yùyáng,
and advanced to besiege Wǎnchéng.
On the *xīnsì* day of the second month,
Liú Shènggōng was proclaimed Emperor,
Bóshēng was appointed Dàsītú,
and Guāngwǔ was appointed Tàicháng Piān Jiāngjūn.
In the third month,
Guāngwǔ, separately with other generals, campaigned in Kūnyáng, Dìnglíng, and Yǎn,
all of which surrendered.
They obtained many cattle, horses, and valuables,
and several hundred thousand *hú* of grain,
which were then transported to supply the forces besieging Wǎn.
When Wáng Mǎng heard of Fù and Cì's deaths
and the establishment of a Hàn Emperor,
he was greatly alarmed,
and dispatched Dàsītú Wáng Xún and Dàsīkōng Wáng Yì
with an army of a million soldiers,
including two hundred and twenty thousand armored troops.
In the fifth month,
they arrived in Yǐngchuān
and joined with Yán Yóu and Chén Mào.
Initially,
Guāngwǔ, on behalf of the Chōnglíng Marquis's family, had argued a case of overdue rent to Yán Yóu,
who had seen him and been impressed by his unusual qualities.
At this time,
those who surrendered from the besieged city to Yán Yóu reported that Guāngwǔ did not take wealth,
but only gathered troops and planned strategies.
Yán Yóu laughed and said,
"Is that the man with the handsome eyebrows and beard?
How can he be like this!"
Initially,
Wáng Mǎng had conscripted sixty-three schools of military strategists, numbering several hundred people, from across the empire,
and appointed them as military officials.
He selected and trained elite guards,
and recruited fierce warriors.
His banners and supply trains
stretched for a thousand *lǐ* without interruption.
At that time, there was a giant, Jùwúbà,
who was one *zhàng* tall
and ten *wéi* in girth,
whom Wáng Mǎng made a fort commander.
He also drove various fierce beasts,
such as tigers, leopards, rhinoceroses, and elephants,
to enhance their might.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties, there had never been such a grand display of military deployment.
Guāngwǔ, with a few thousand soldiers,
ambushed them at Yángguān.
When the generals saw the vast army of Wáng Xún and Wáng Yì,
they fled back,
galloping into Kūnyáng,
all terrified
and worried about their wives and children,
wanting to disperse and return to their respective cities.
Guāngwǔ debated, saying:
"Now our troops and grain are few,
while the external enemy is strong and numerous.
If we unite our strength to resist them,
we might achieve success.
If we wish to disperse,
it is impossible for us all to survive.
Moreover, Wǎnchéng has not yet been captured,
so it cannot come to our aid.
If Kūnyáng is broken,
in a single day,
all other divisions will also be destroyed.
Why do you not unite your hearts and courage to achieve fame and glory,
but instead wish to protect your wives, children, and possessions?"
The generals angrily said,
"How dare General Liú speak like this!"
Guāngwǔ smiled and rose.
Just then, a scout returned,
reporting that the main army was about to arrive north of the city,
with battle lines stretching for hundreds of *lǐ*,
their rear invisible.
The generals immediately said to one another,
"Let's invite General Liú again to plan."
Guāngwǔ again drew out the strategy for success and failure.
The generals, anxious and pressed,
all said,
"Yes."
At that time, there were only eight or nine thousand people in the city.
Guāngwǔ then ordered Chéngguó Shànggōng Wáng Fèng and Tíngwèi Dàjiāngjūn Wáng Cháng to remain and defend,
while he himself, at night, with Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn Zōng Tiāo
and Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn Lǐ Yì and eleven other riders, totaling thirteen horsemen,
(10) exited the city's south gate
to gather troops from outside.
At that time, Wáng Mǎng's army that had reached the city walls numbered nearly a hundred thousand,
and Guāngwǔ barely managed to get out.
(11) Upon reaching Yǎn and Dìnglíng,
he mobilized all the troops from the various camps.
However, the generals were greedy and reluctant to part with their wealth and goods,
wanting to keep a portion to guard.
Guāngwǔ said:
"If we defeat the enemy now,
our treasures will increase ten thousandfold,
(12) and great success can be achieved.
If we are defeated,
not even our heads will remain,
what wealth and goods will there be then!"
Only then did the crowd follow.
Yán Yóu persuaded Wáng Yì, saying:
“Kūnyáng City is small but strong.
Now the usurper is in Wǎn.
If we quickly advance with a large army,
they will certainly flee.
When Wǎn falls,
Kūnyáng will surrender on its own.”
Yì replied:
“In the past, as Hǔyá Jiāngjūn, I besieged Zhái Yì,
and was criticized for failing to capture him alive.
I was thus blamed and reprimanded.
Now, commanding a million troops,
if I encounter a city and cannot take it,
what would that be called?”
So, he besieged it with dozens of layers of troops,
set up hundreds of camps,
and used cloud-ladders over ten *zhàng* tall,
overlooking the city.
Flags and banners covered the fields,
dust and dirt reached the sky,
and the sound of gongs and drums could be heard for hundreds of *lǐ*.
Some dug tunnels,
and battering rams struck the city walls.
Massed crossbows fired relentlessly,
arrows fell like rain.
Inside the city, people drew water by carrying it from house to house.
Wáng Fèng and others begged for surrender,
but it was not granted.
Soon, Yì considered his achievement a matter of mere moments,
and his spirits were exceedingly high.
At night, a shooting star fell into his camp;
by day, clouds like collapsing mountains
fell over his camp,
scattering a foot above the ground.
All the officers and soldiers were demoralized.
On the *jǐmǎo* day of the sixth month,
Guāngwǔ advanced with his division.
He personally led over a thousand infantry and cavalry,
arrayed four or five *lǐ* ahead of the main army.
Soon, Yì also dispatched several thousand soldiers to engage in battle.
Guāngwǔ charged them,
beheading dozens.
The various divisions joyfully exclaimed:
“Liú Jiāngjūn usually shows fear before small enemies,
but now he is brave before a great enemy!
This is most remarkable.
Furthermore, he leads the charge.
We ask to assist the general!”
Guāngwǔ advanced again.
Soon, Yì’s troops retreated.
All the divisions joined to press the attack,
beheading hundreds, even thousands.
With repeated victories,
they pressed forward.
At this time, Bóshēng had already captured Wǎn three days prior,
but Guāngwǔ did not yet know.
So, he sent a false messenger with a letter to the city,
saying,
“The troops from Wǎn have arrived,”
and pretended to drop the letter.
Soon, Yì got it
and was displeased.
Since the various generals had already achieved several victories,
their courage grew stronger,
each capable of fighting a hundred.
Guāngwǔ then, with three thousand men determined to die,
charged through their central stronghold from the west side, along the water.
Soon, Yì’s formation was in disarray.
Taking advantage of their momentum, they routed them,
and then killed Wáng Xún.
The city also burst forth with drums and shouts,
striking the enemy’s main force.
Their thunderous cries shook heaven and earth.
Máng’s army was utterly routed.
Those who fled trampled over one another,
perishing for over a hundred *lǐ*.
Coincidentally, there was a great thunderstorm;
roof tiles all flew off,
and rain poured down like a deluge.
The Zhī Chuān River swelled immensely.
Even tigers and leopards trembled with fear.
Soldiers scrambled to cross,
and tens of thousands drowned.
The water ceased to flow.
Wáng Yì, Yán Yóu, and Chén Mào, with light cavalry, rode over the dead to cross the water and escape.
All their military supplies and baggage train were captured,
along with chariots, armor, and precious treasures,
too numerous to count.
It took months to collect them all,
and some of the remainder was burned.
Guāngwǔ then proceeded to capture Yǐngyáng.
At this time, Bóshēng was killed by Gēngshǐ.
Guāngwǔ rode from Fùchéng to Fènyù.
The Sītú’s officials and retinue greeted and offered condolences to Guāngwǔ.
Guāngwǔ found it difficult to engage in private conversation,
and merely deeply acknowledged his faults.
He never boasted of his achievements at Kūnyáng,
nor dared to observe mourning for Bóshēng.
He ate, drank, spoke, and laughed as usual.
Gēngshǐ was ashamed by this,
and appointed Guāngwǔ as Pòlǔ Dàjiāngjūn
and enfeoffed him as Wǔxìn Hóu.
On the *gēngxū* day of the ninth month,
the local magnates of Sānfǔ together executed Wáng Máng
and sent his head to Wǎn.
Gēngshǐ was about to make Luòyáng his northern capital.
He appointed Guāngwǔ as acting Sīlì Xiàowèi
and sent him ahead to organize and repair the palaces and government offices.
Thereupon, he appointed officials and subordinates,
drafted documents,
and oversaw investigations,
all according to the old regulations.
At that time, the officials and soldiers from Sānfǔ came east to welcome Gēngshǐ.
They saw that when the various generals passed,
they all wore caps
but dressed in women’s clothing,
with patterned embroidery on their sleeves.
None could help but laugh at them,
and some even ran away in fear.
However, when they saw the Sīlì’s officials and subordinates,
they were all overjoyed and could not contain themselves.
Some old clerks even shed tears, saying:
“We never expected to see the dignified bearing of a Han official again today!”
Because of this, all discerning people gave their hearts to him.
When Gēngshǐ arrived in Luòyáng,
he sent Guāngwǔ, as Pòlǔ Jiāngjūn, to act as Dàsīmǎ.
In the tenth month,
he, bearing the imperial credential, crossed the Yellow River northwards
to pacify and comfort the *zhōu* and *jùn*.
Wherever he went, in the various *bù* and *xiàn*,
he would meet with the officials of 2,000 *shí* salary, the chief officials, the Sānlǎo, and the government staff,
down to the junior clerks,
to investigate, dismiss, and promote,
just as a *zhōu* governor conducts an inspection tour.
He would immediately release prisoners,
abolish Wáng Máng’s harsh policies,
and restore the names of Han officials.
The officials and common people rejoiced,
vying to bring oxen and wine to welcome and entertain him.
He advanced to Hándān.
The former prince of Zhào Mù, Zǐ Lín,
said to Guāngwǔ:
“The Chìméi are now in Hédōng.
If we just divert water to flood them,
their million troops can be turned into fish.”
Guāngwǔ did not answer
and went to Zhēndìng.
Lín then falsely claimed that the diviner Wáng Láng was Zǐ Yú, son of Emperor Chéng.
In the twelfth month,
he enthroned Láng as the Son of Heaven,
making Hándān his capital,
and then sent envoys to demand the surrender of the various *jùn* and *guó*.
In the first month of the second year,
Guāngwǔ, seeing Wáng Láng's new power,
then went north to Jì to secure it.
Wáng Láng circulated a proclamation offering a reward of 100,000 households for Guāngwǔ,
and Liú Jiē, the former prince of Guǎngyáng,
raised troops in Jì to respond to Láng.
The city was in turmoil,
and people were startled and panicked, one after another,
saying that an envoy from Hándān was about to arrive,
and all officials of 2,000 dàn and below went out to welcome him.
Thereupon, Guāngwǔ hurried to hitch his carriage and turn south,
not daring to enter cities or towns day or night,
eating by the roadside.
When they reached Ráoyáng,
his officials and retinue were all short of food.
Guāngwǔ then declared himself an envoy from Hándān
and entered a relay station.
As the relay station official was serving food,
his followers, being hungry,
fought over it.
The relay station official, suspecting a deception,
then beat a drum dozens of times,
falsely announcing that the general from Hándān had arrived,
and all of Guāngwǔ's officials turned pale.
Guāngwǔ ascended his carriage, intending to flee;
but then, fearing he could not escape,
he slowly returned to his seat,
saying:
"Please invite the general from Hándān in."
After a long while, he drove away.
The people inside the relay station called out to the gatekeeper to close the gate.
The gate captain said:
"How can the world know who is who,
and yet close the gate on an elder?"
Thus, they were able to exit to the south.
Traveling day and night,
they endured frost and snow.
The weather was cold,
and their faces were all chapped.
When they reached the Hūtúo Hé,
[一０]there were no boats.
Just then, the river was frozen solid,
so they were able to cross.
[一一]Before they had finished crossing a few carriages, the ice broke.
They advanced to the west of Xiàbó city,
[一二]confused and not knowing where to go.
An old man in white clothing was by the roadside,
[一三]pointing and saying:
"Keep going!
Xìndū Jùn is loyal to Cháng'ān,
and it is eighty *lǐ* from here."
[一四]Guāngwǔ immediately hastened there,
and Xìndū *Tàishǒu* Rèn Guāng opened the gates to welcome him.
Shìzǔ then mobilized troops from nearby counties,
obtaining four thousand men,
and first attacked Tángyáng and Shì Xiàn,
forcing them all to surrender.
[一五]Wáng Mǎng's (Róng) [Chéng] *Zúzhèng* Pí Tóng also surrendered.
[一六]Moreover, Liú Zhí from Chāngchéng,
and Gěng Chún from Sòngzǐ,
[一七]each led their clansmen, children, and younger brothers,
occupying their respective counties and towns,
to serve Guāngwǔ.
Thereupon, he marched north to receive the surrender of Xiàqǔyáng,
[一八]and his forces gradually gathered,
with tens of thousands eager to join.
He then attacked Zhōngshān to the north,
capturing Lúnú.
Wherever he passed, he raised conscripted soldiers,
and sent proclamations to the border regions,
to jointly attack Hándān.
The commanderies and counties once again responded.
He attacked Xīnshì, Zhēndìng, Yuánshì, and Fángzǐ to the south,
all of which surrendered.
He then entered the territory of Zhào.
At this time, Wáng Láng's grand general Lǐ Yù was stationed at Báirén.
The Hàn army advanced without knowing this,
and their vanguard generals Zhū Fú and Dèng Yǔ were defeated by Yù,
losing their baggage and supplies.
Guāngwǔ, hearing of this from the rear,
collected Fú and Yǔ's scattered troops,
and fought Yù at Guōmén,
decisively defeating him,
and recovering all that had been lost.
Yù returned to hold the city,
but it could not be taken.
Therefore, Guāngwǔ withdrew his forces and captured Guǎng'ā.
At this time, Gěng Kuàng, the *Tàishǒu* of Shànggǔ, and Péng Chǒng, the *Tàishǒu* of Yúyáng,
each dispatched their generals Wú Hàn and Kòu Xún, among others, leading crack cavalry to assist in attacking Wáng Láng.
Gēngshǐ also sent *Shàngshū Púyè* Xiè Gōng to attack Láng.
Guāngwǔ then held a grand feast for his officers and soldiers,
and subsequently besieged Jùlù to the east.
Wáng Láng's defending general Wáng Ráo held firm,
and the city could not be taken for over a month.
Láng sent his generals Ní Hóng and Liú Fèng
leading tens of thousands of men to relieve Jùlù.
Guāngwǔ met them in battle at Nán,
beheading several thousand.
In the fourth month,
he advanced to besiege Hándān,
and after continuous battles, he broke through.
On the *jiǎchén* day of the fifth month,
he captured its city
and executed Wáng Láng.
He collected documents
and found several thousand memorials from officials and commoners who had colluded with Láng and slandered him.
Guāngwǔ did not examine them.
He gathered his generals and burned them,
saying:
"Let those with wavering loyalties feel secure."
Gēngshǐ sent a *Shìyùshǐ* with a *jié* to appoint Guāngwǔ as Xiāo Wáng,
ordering him to disband all his troops and proceed to the imperial residence.
Guāngwǔ declined, citing that Héběi was not yet pacified,
and did not accept the summons.
From this point, he began to waver in his loyalty to Gēngshǐ.
At this time, Cháng'ān's government was in chaos,
and the four directions were in rebellion.
Liáng Wáng Liú Yǒng established his command at Suīyáng,
Gōngsūn Shù proclaimed himself king in Bāshǔ,
Lǐ Xiàn declared himself king of Huáinán,
Qín Fēng styled himself King Chǔlí,
Zhāng Bù rose in Lángxié,
Dǒng Xiàn rose in Dōnghǎi,
Yán Cén rose in Hànzhōng,
Tián Róng rose in Yílíng,
all appointing generals and commanders,
invading and plundering commanderies and counties.
There were also other bandit groups known as Tóngmǎ, Dàróng, Gāohú, Chónglián, Tiějīng, Dàqiǎng, Yóulái, Shàngjiāng, Qīngdú, Wǔxiào, Bùxiāng, Wǔfān, Wǔlóu, Fùpíng, and Huòsuǒ,
each leading their divisions,
[一０]totaling several million people,
plundering everywhere.
Guāngwǔ intended to attack them and
first sent Wú Hàn north to mobilize troops from ten commanderies.
Yōuzhōu Mù Miáo Zēng did not comply,
so Hàn executed Zēng and mobilized his troops.
In autumn,
Guāngwǔ attacked the Tóngmǎ at Qiāo.
Wú Hàn led crack cavalry to rendezvous at Qīngyáng.
The bandits repeatedly challenged them,
but Guāngwǔ held his camp firmly;
when anyone went out to loot,
he would attack and seize them,
cutting off their supply lines.
After more than a month,
the bandits ran out of food
and fled under cover of night.
He pursued them to Guǎntáo
and decisively defeated them.
Before all the surrendered forces had been processed,
Gāohú and Chónglián arrived from the southeast
and joined the remaining Tóngmǎ forces.
Guāngwǔ again fought a major battle at Púyáng,
completely defeating and forcing them to surrender,
and enfeoffing their leaders as *lièhóu*.
The surrendered forces still felt uneasy,
but Guāngwǔ, understanding their intentions,
ordered them all to return to their camps and marshal their troops.
He then personally rode light cavalry to inspect their formations.
The surrendered men said to each other:
"Xiāo Wáng places his true heart in people's bellies,
how can we not dedicate our lives to him!"
From this, they all submitted.
He distributed all the surrendered men among his various generals,
and his forces consequently numbered several hundred thousand.
Thus, in Guānxī, Guāngwǔ was called
"Tóngmǎ Dì" (the Copper Horse Emperor).
The separate leader of the Chìméi, along with Dàróng and Qīngdú, numbering over a hundred thousand, were at Shèquǎn.
Guāngwǔ advanced and attacked them,
decisively defeating them,
and all their forces scattered and fled.
He sent Wú Hàn and Cén Péng to raid and kill Xiè Gōng at Yè.
The Qīngdú and Chìméi bandits entered Hángǔ Guān
and attacked Gēngshǐ.
Guāngwǔ then sent Dèng Yǔ leading six *píjiàng* (deputy generals) with troops to the west,
to take advantage of the chaos between Gēngshǐ and Chìméi.
At this time, Gēngshǐ had sent *Dàsīmǎ* Zhū Wěi and Wǔyīn Wáng Lǐ Yì, among others, to be stationed at Luòyáng.
Guāngwǔ also ordered Féng Yì to guard Mèngjīn to resist them.
In the first month of spring, the first year of Jiànwǔ,
Fāng Wàng from Pínglíng
proclaimed the former Rúzi Liú Yīng as Son of Heaven.
Gēngshǐ sent *Chéngxiàng* Lǐ Sōng to attack and execute him.
On the *jǐhài* day,
the Emperor arrived at Huái.
He dispatched Gěng Yǎn to lead the General of Strong Crossbows, Chén Jùn, to garrison Wǔshèjīn,
to guard the area east of Xíngyáng.
He ordered Wú Hàn to lead Zhū Yòu, the Grand Judge Cén Péng,
the Bearer of the Gilded Mace Jiǎ Fù,
the General Who Spreads Transformation Jiān Tán, and nine other generals
to besiege Zhū Wěi in Luòyáng.
On the *rénzǐ* day of the eighth month,
sacrifices were offered to the deities of the land and grain.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
sacrifices were made to Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, and Shìzōng at Huáigōng.
The Emperor then proceeded to Héyáng.
Tián Lì, the Prince of Lǐnqīu under Gēngshǐ, surrendered.
In the ninth month,
the Chìméi entered Cháng'ān,
and Gēngshǐ fled to Gāolíng.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Gēngshǐ, suffering from defeat, abandoned the city and fled,
his wife and children left naked,
wandering the roads.
I greatly pity them.
Now, I enfeoff Gēngshǐ as the Prince of Huáiyáng.
Any official or common person who dares to harm him
shall be guilty of treason."
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Zhuó Mào, formerly the Magistrate of Gāomì, was appointed Grand Tutor.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Zhū Wěi surrendered the entire city.
In the winter, on the *guǐchǒu* day of the tenth month,
the imperial carriage entered Luòyáng,
and the Emperor lodged at the Quèfēi Hall in the Southern Palace,
thereby establishing the capital.
Cén Péng was dispatched to attack the various bandits in Jīngzhōu.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day of the eleventh month,
the Emperor visited Huái.
Liú Yǒng proclaimed himself Son of Heaven.
On the *bǐngxū* day of the twelfth month,
the Emperor returned from Huái.
The Chìméi killed Gēngshǐ,
while Wěi Xiāo occupied Lǒngyòu,
and Lú Fāng rose in Āndìng.
The General Who Breaks the Captives, Shú Shòu, attacked the Wǔxiào bandits at Qǔliáng,
and was killed in battle.
In the second year, on the *jiǎzǐ* day, the first day of the first month of spring,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Grand Marshal Wú Hàn led nine generals to attack the Bùxiāng bandits east of Yè,
greatly defeating and subduing them.
On the *gēngchén* day,
the meritorious officials were all enfeoffed as marquises,
with the largest states comprising four counties,
and others varying accordingly.
An imperial edict was issued, stating:
"Human nature, having achieved sufficiency,
suffers from indulgence,
satisfying momentary desires,
and forgetting the principle of prudent punishment.
Considering that the generals' achievements are far-reaching and great,
and truly wishing them to be passed down endlessly,
they should be like one standing on the brink of a deep abyss,
like one treading on thin ice,
trembling with fear,
becoming more cautious each day.
As for those whose manifest achievements have not yet been rewarded,
whose names have not yet been established in the records,
the Grand Minister of the Guests shall promptly submit their names,
and I shall select and record them."
Doctor Dīng Gōng argued:
"Ancient emperors and kings enfeoffed lords no more than a hundred *lǐ* in extent,
thus it was advantageous for establishing lords,
taking the law from thunder,
strengthening the trunk and weakening the branches,
this was the way of governance.
Now, enfeoffing lords with four counties
does not conform to the established regulations."
The Emperor said:
"The ancient fallen states
all perished due to their lack of the Way;
I have never heard of a state perishing because its meritorious officials had too much land."
Thereupon, he dispatched court attendants to personally bestow the seals and ribbons,
and the proclamation stated:
"High, but not arrogant;
exalted, yet not perilous;
tempering extravagances and observing measures,
full, but not overflowing.
Respect this and be warned.
Pass it on to your children and grandchildren,
and for a long time be a bulwark of Han."
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Dèng Yè, Gēngshǐ's General Who Restored Han, and Yú Kuāng, General Who Aided Han, surrendered,
and both had their noble ranks restored.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
the High Temple was erected,
the altars of the land and grain were established in Luòyáng,
and the suburban altar was set up south of the city,
beginning to correctly establish the Fire Element,
with red being the revered color.
In this month,
the Chìméi burned the palaces of the Western Capital,
excavated the imperial tombs,
and plundered Guānzhōng.
The Grand Minister over the Masses Dèng Yǔ entered Cháng'ān,
and dispatched a registrar to present the spirit tablets of the eleven emperors,
and install them in the High Temple.
Yáng, the Prince of Zhēndìng, and Ràng, the Marquis of Línyì, conspired to rebel,
and the Former General Gěng Chún was dispatched to execute them.
On the *jǐyǒu* day of the second month,
the Emperor visited Xiūwǔ.
The Grand Minister of Works Wáng Liáng was dismissed.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Sòng Hóng, a Grandee Remonstrant, was appointed Grand Minister of Works.
The General of Agile Cavalry Jǐng Dān was dispatched to lead the General Who Conquers Barbarians Jì Zūn and one other general to attack the bandits in Hóngnóng,
defeating them,
and then Jì Zūn was sent to besiege Zhāng Mǎn, the bandit in Mánzhōng.
Péng Chǒng, the Administrator of Yúyáng, rebelled,
attacking Zhū Fú, the Governor of Yōuzhōu, at Jì.
Yán Cén proclaimed himself Prince of Wǔ'ān in Hànzhōng.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
the Emperor returned from Xiūwǔ.
On the *yǐwèi* day of the third month,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire,
and an imperial edict stated:
"Recently, there have been many wrongly imprisoned people,
and punishments have been excessively severe;
I greatly pity them.
Confucius said: 'If punishments are not just,
the people will not know where to put their hands and feet.'
Let the officials of two thousand *shí* and above, all grandees, doctors, and court counselors discuss and review the penal laws."
The Bearer of the Gilded Mace Jiǎ Fù was dispatched to lead two generals to attack Yǐn Zūn, Gēngshǐ's Prince of Yǎn,
defeating and subduing him.
The General of Valiant Cavalry Liú Zhí attacked the bandits in Mì,
and was killed in battle.
The General of the Tiger's Teeth Gài Yán was dispatched to lead four generals to attack Liú Yǒng.
In the summer, in the fourth month,
Yǒng was besieged at Suīyáng.
Sū Máo, a general of Gēngshǐ, killed Pān Jiǎn, the Administrator of Huáiyáng, and defected to Liú Yǒng.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the Emperor's uncle Liáng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Guǎngyáng,
his nephew Zhāng as the Prince of Tàiyuán,
Zhāng's younger brother Xīng as the Prince of Lǔ,
and Zhǐ, the legitimate son of the Marquis of Chūnlíng, as the Prince of Chéngyáng.
On the *gēngchén* day of the fifth month,
Shè, Gēngshǐ's Prince of Yuánshì, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Sìshuǐ,
Dé, the son of the former Prince Yáng of Zhēndìng, was made Prince of Zhēndìng,
and Jī Cháng, a descendant of the Zhou royal house, was made Duke of Zhōu Chéngxīu.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"If common people who have married off wives or sold children wish to return to their parents,
they shall be freely permitted to do so.
Anyone who dares to detain them
shall be punished according to the law."
On the *wùxū* day of the sixth month,
the Noble Lady Guō was established as empress,
and her son Qiáng as crown prince,
and a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
The ranks of the Gentlemen, Court Attendants, and attendant officials were each increased by one grade.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
the imperial kinsman Liú Zhōng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Zīchuān.
In the autumn, in the eighth month,
the Emperor personally led an expedition against the Wǔxiào.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
he arrived at Nèi Huáng,
and greatly defeated the Wǔxiào at Yīyáng,
subduing them.
The General of Light Cavalry Dèng Lóng was dispatched to relieve Zhū Fú,
and fought against Péng Chǒng at Lù,
where Lóng's army was defeated.
Gài Yán captured Suīyáng,
and Liú Yǒng fled to Qiáo.
The General Who Breaks the Captives Dèng Fèng rebelled at Yùyáng.
On the *rénxū* day of the ninth month,
the Emperor returned from Nèi Huáng.
The General of Agile Cavalry Jǐng Dān passed away.
Yán Cén greatly defeated the Chìméi at Dùlíng.
Guānzhōng suffered from famine,
and people resorted to cannibalism.
In the winter, in the eleventh month,
the Grand Judge Cén Péng was appointed General Who Conquers the South,
and led eight generals to attack Dèng Fèng at Dǔxiāng.
The remaining bandits of Tóngmǎ, Qīngdú, and Yóulái jointly enthroned Sūn Dēng as Son of Heaven in Shàngjùn.
Dēng's general Yuè Xuán killed Dēng,
and surrendered with his army of over fifty thousand men.
The General of Flank Guards Féng Yì was dispatched to replace Dèng Yǔ in attacking the Chìméi.
The Grandee Remonstrant Fú Lóng was sent with a credential to pacify Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu,
and persuade Zhāng Bù to surrender.
On the *wùwǔ* day of the twelfth month,
an imperial edict stated:
"Considering that the imperial kinsmen and marquises were deposed by Wáng Mǎng,
and their ancestral spirits have no place to return,
I greatly pity them.
They shall all have their former states restored.
If a marquis has already passed away,
let his lineage submit the names of his sons and grandsons to the Imperial Secretariat,
to be enfeoffed and appointed."
That year,
Gài Yán and others greatly defeated Liú Yǒng at the west of Pèi.
Initially,
at the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
drought and locusts afflicted the empire.
One jīn of gold could be exchanged for one hú of grain.
By this time, wild grains grew everywhere,
hemp and jute were particularly abundant,
and wild silkworms formed cocoons,
covering the mountains and hills.
People profited from these.
In the first month of spring of the third year, on the day of Jiǎzǐ,
Féng Yì, a general of the household, was made General-in-chief Who Conquers the West,
and Dù Mào was made General of Agile Cavalry.
Grand Minister of Works Dèng Yǔ and Féng Yì fought the Chìméi at Huíxī,
but Yǔ and Yì were defeated.
General Who Conquers Barbarians Jì Zūn subdued the barbarians of Mánzhōng,
beheading Zhāng Mǎn.
On the day of Xīnsì,
four ancestral temples were established for the late imperial father, the Lord of Nándùn, and his ancestors.
On the day of Rénwǔ,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
In the intercalary month, on the day of Yǐsì,
Grand Minister of Works Dèng Yǔ was dismissed.
Féng Yì fought the Chìméi at Xiáodǐ,
greatly defeating them.
The remaining forces moved south towards Yíyáng,
and the Emperor personally led an expedition against them.
On the day of Jǐhài,
he arrived at Yíyáng.
On the day of Jiǎchén,
he personally marshaled the six armies,
displaying a grand array of troops and horses.
Grand Marshal Wú Hàn's elite soldiers were at the front,
the central army was next,
and the Agile Cavalry and Martial Guard were arrayed on the left and right.
The Chìméi were terrified at the sight,
and sent envoys to surrender.
On the day of Bǐngwǔ,
the Chìméi ruler and his officials presented themselves with hands bound,
offering the imperial seal and sash of Gāo Huángdì.
An edict assigned them to the Commander of the City Gate.
On the day of Wùshēn,
he returned from Yíyáng.
On the day of Jǐyǒu,
an edict stated:
"Bandits have run rampant,
harming the common people.
Pénzi usurped the imperial title,
confusing and misleading the empire.
I raised troops to attack them,
and they immediately collapsed.
More than 100,000 men surrendered with bound hands,
and the imperial seal and sash of the previous emperor were returned to the imperial household.
All of this is due to the spirits of our ancestors,
and the strength of our warriors.
How could I alone enjoy such success!
Let a propitious day be chosen to sacrifice at the Gāo Temple,
and grant a noble rank to all eldest sons in the empire who are to succeed their fathers,
each one grade."
In the second month, on the day of Jǐwèi,
a sacrifice was offered at the Gāo Temple,
and the State-Transmitting Seal was received.
Liú Yǒng appointed Dǒng Xiàn as King of Hǎixī,
and Zhāng Bù as King of Qí.
Bù killed Grand Master of Imperial Advisers Fú Lóng and rebelled.
The Emperor proceeded to Huái.
Wú Hàn was dispatched with two generals to attack the Qīngdú at the west of Zhǐ,
greatly defeating and subduing them.
In the third month, on the day of Rén'yín,
Fú Zhàn, Chief Clerk to the Grand Minister of Works, was made Grand Minister of Works.
Péng Chǒng captured Jìchéng,
and Chǒng declared himself King of Yān.
The Emperor personally led an expedition against Dèng Fèng,
proceeding to Dǔyáng.
In the fourth month of summer,
Dèng Fèng was greatly defeated at Xiǎocháng'ān,
and was beheaded.
Féng Yì fought Yán Cén at Shànglín,
and defeated him.
Wú Hàn, with seven generals, fought Sū Máo, a general of Liú Yǒng, at Guǎngyuè,
and greatly defeated him.
General Hǔyá Gài Yán besieged Liú Yǒng at Suīyáng.
In the fifth month, on the day of Jǐyǒu,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
On the last day of the month, Yǐmǎo,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the sixth month, on the day of Rénxū,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
Gěng Yǎn fought Yán Cén at Ráng,
greatly defeating him.
In the seventh month of autumn,
General Who Conquers the South Cén Péng, with three generals, campaigned against Qín Fēng,
fighting at Líqiū,
greatly defeating him,
and capturing his general, Cài Hóng.
On the day of Gēngchén,
an edict stated:
"Officials below 600 dàn,
down to those with black seals of commandants and chancellors,
if they commit a crime, permission must be sought first.
Males aged 80 and above,
and 10 and below,
as well as women who are implicated,
unless they have committed acts against morality
or are specifically named in an imperial arrest warrant,
shall not be detained.
Those who require questioning shall be questioned on the spot.
Female convicts shall be hired out to work in the mountains and then sent home."
Gài Yán captured Suīyáng,
and apprehended Liú Yǒng.
Sū Máo and Zhōu Jiàn then established Liú Yǒng's son, Yú, as King of Liáng.
In the tenth month of winter, on the day of Rénshēn,
he proceeded to Chōnglíng,
sacrificed at the garden temple,
and then held a banquet at his old residence,
gathering with old friends and elders.
In the eleventh month, on the day of Yǐwèi,
he returned from Chōnglíng.
Zhāng Fēng, Administrator of Zhuójùn, rebelled.
That year,
Lǐ Xiàn proclaimed himself Emperor.
General of Xīzhōu, Kuí Xiāo, submitted a memorial.
General Jiànyì Zhū Yòu, with Jì Zūn, fought Yán Cén at Dōngyáng,
beheading his general, Zhāng Chéng.
In the first month of spring of the fourth year, on the day of Jiǎshēn,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
In the second month, on the day of Rénzǐ,
he proceeded to Huái.
On the day of Rénshēn,
he returned from Huái.
General of the Right Dèng Yǔ was dispatched with two generals to fight Yán Cén at Wǔdāng,
and defeated him.
In the fourth month of summer, on the day of Dīngsì,
he proceeded to Yè.
On the day of Jǐsì,
he further proceeded to Límpíng.
Grand Marshal Wú Hàn was dispatched to attack the Wǔxiào bandits at Jīshān,
greatly defeating them.
In the fifth month,
he further proceeded to Yuánshì.
On the day of Xīnsì,
he further proceeded to Lúnú.
General Who Conquers Barbarians Jì Zūn was dispatched with four generals to suppress Zhāng Fēng in Zhuójùn,
and beheaded Fēng.
In the sixth month, on the day of Xīnhài,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
In the seventh month, on the day of Dīnghài,
he proceeded to Qiáo.
General Who Captures Bandits Mǎ Wǔ and General of the Household Wáng Bà besieged Liú Yú at Chuíhuì.
Bēn Xiū, a general of Dǒng Xiàn, surrendered with the city of Lánlíng.
Xiàn then besieged it.
General Hǔyá Gài Yán, with General Píngdí Páng Méng, went to rescue Bēn Xiū,
but failed,
and Lánlíng was captured by Xiàn.
In the eighth month of autumn, on the day of Wùwǔ,
he further proceeded to Shòuchūn.
Grand Master Tàizhōng Huán Hú killed Liú Dù, Administrator of Línhuái.
Hú was executed for this.
General Yángwǔ Mǎ Chéng was dispatched with three generals to campaign against Lǐ Xiàn.
In the ninth month,
Xiàn was besieged at Shū.
In the tenth month of winter, on the day of Jiǎyín,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
Grand Tutor Zhuó Mào passed away.
In the eleventh month, on the day of Bǐngshēn,
he proceeded to Wǎn.
General Jiànyì Zhū Yòu was dispatched with two generals to besiege Qín Fēng at Líqiū.
In the twelfth month, on the day of Bǐngyín,
he further proceeded to Líqiū.
That year,
General Who Conquers the West Féng Yì fought Chéng Yān, a general of Gōngsūn Shù, at Chéncāng,
and defeated him.
In the first month of spring of the fifth year, on the day of Guǐsì,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
In the second month, on the day of Bǐngwǔ,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
General Who Captures Bandits Mǎ Wǔ and General of the Household Wáng Bà captured Chuíhuì.
On the day of Yǐchǒu,
he proceeded to Wèijùn.
On the day of Rénshēn,
Kǒng Ān, a descendant of Yīn, was enfeoffed as Lord Shàojiā of Yīn.
Péng Chǒng was killed by his servant,
and Yúyáng was pacified.
Grand Marshal Wú Hàn, with General Jiànwēi Gěng Yǎn, attacked the Fùpíng and Huòsuǒ bandits at Píngyuán,
greatly defeating and subduing them.
Gěng Yǎn was again dispatched with two generals to suppress Zhāng Bù.
In the third month, on the day of Guǐwèi,
Liáng, King of Guǎngyáng, was transferred to become King of Zhào,
and began to reside in his state.
General Píngdí Páng Méng rebelled,
killed Sūn Méng, Administrator of Chǔjùn, and defected east to Dǒng Xiàn.
General Who Conquers the South Cén Péng was dispatched with two generals to campaign against Tián Róng at Jīnxiāng,
greatly defeating him.
In the fourth month of summer,
there was a drought
and locusts.
The Grand General of Hexī, Dòu Róng, first sent envoys to present tribute.
On the day bǐngzǐ of the fifth month,
an imperial edict stated:
"The prolonged drought has harmed the wheat,
and the autumn sowing has not yet occurred.
I am deeply worried about this.
Could it be that corrupt officials have not been overcome,
and there are many wrongful cases in the prisons,
causing the common people to grieve and resent,
thus moving the weather?
Let the central government offices, the Sānfǔ, and the commanderies and kingdoms release their prisoners.
Those whose crimes do not warrant capital punishment should all be pardoned;
those currently serving sentences should be freed as commoners.
Strive to promote the gentle and good,
and remove the greedy and cruel.
Let each rectify their affairs."
In the sixth month,
Grand General Jiànyì Zhū Yòu captured Líqiū
and seized Qín Fēng.
However, Páng Méng and Sū Mào besieged Táochéng.
The Emperor then proceeded to Méng
and personally led a campaign against them.
He first marshalled his troops at Rèncchéng,
then advanced to relieve Táochéng,
and greatly defeated Méng and others.
In the autumn, on the day dīngchǒu of the seventh month,
he proceeded to Pèi
and sacrificed at Gāoyuán Miào.
An edict commanded the restoration of the imperial tombs in Xījīng.
He then proceeded to Húlíng
to campaign against Dǒng Xiàn.
He also proceeded to Fán,
then attacked Dǒng Xiàn at Chānglǜ
and greatly defeated him.
On the day jǐyǒu of the eighth month,
he proceeded to Tán.
Wú Hàn was left to attack Liú Yū and Dǒng Xiàn and others,
while the imperial carriage moved on to pacify Péngchéng and Xiàpī.
Wú Hàn captured Tán
and seized Liú Yū.
Hàn then besieged Dǒng Xiàn and Páng Méng at Qú.
In the winter, in the tenth month,
he returned,
proceeded to Lǔ,
and had the Grand Minister of Works sacrifice to Kǒngzǐ.
Gěng Yǎn and others battled Zhāng Bù at Línzī
and greatly defeated him.
The Emperor proceeded to Línzī,
then proceeded to Jù.
Zhāng Bù beheaded Sū Mào and surrendered,
and the Qí region was pacified.
The Imperial Academy was first established.
The imperial carriage returned to the palace,
proceeded to the Imperial Academy,
and bestowed gifts upon the Erudites and their disciples, each according to their rank.
On the day rén yín of the eleventh month,
the Grand Minister of Education, Fú Zhàn, was dismissed,
and the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Hóu Bà, became Grand Minister of Education.
In the twelfth month,
Lú Fāng proclaimed himself Emperor at Jiǔyuán.
Wěi Xiāo’s son, Xún, Grand General of Xīzhōu, entered to serve at court.
The Governor of Jiāozhǐ, Dèng Ràng, led the Grand Administrators of seven commanderies to send envoys bearing tribute.
An edict remitted corvée labor for Jìyáng for two years.
That year,
wild grains gradually decreased,
and cultivated land greatly expanded.

Collation Notes, Page 1, Line 3: From Jǐngdì shēng Chángshā Dìng Wáng Fā (Emperor Jǐng gave birth to Prince Dìng Fā of Chángshā). Liú Bīn's Dōng Hàn Shū Kān Wù (Corrections to the Eastern Hàn History) states that
"生" (shēng, gave birth to)
should be
"子" (zǐ, son).
Comment: The Jíjiě (Collected Explanations) quotes Huì Dòng's (惠棟) view,
stating that the Dōng Guān Jì Shìzǔ Jì (Records of the Eastern Lodge, Annals of Emperor Shìzǔ) says:
"Shìzǔ Guāngwǔ Huángdì (Emperor Guāngwǔ),
ninth-generation descendant of Gāozǔ (Emperor Gāo),
succeeded the lineage of Wén (Emperor Wén) and Jǐng (Emperor Jǐng),
descended from Chángshā Dìng Wáng Fā (Prince Dìng Fā of Chángshā),
and Prince Dìng gave birth to Chōnglíng Jié Hóu (Marquis Jié of Chōnglíng)."
This book clarifies itself;
Fàn Shì (范氏) merely changed the text, making the meaning obscure.
Page 1, Line 12: Originally belonged to Línglíng (Lěng) [Líng] Dào Xiàn (Línglíng Commandery's Língdào County). Changed based on the Jí Běn (Jí Edition).

Page 1, Line 12: The old city is (now) in [now] the east of Suí Zhōu Zǎoyáng Xiàn (Zǎoyáng County, Suí Prefecture). Changed based on Zhāng Dòu's (張钭) Dú Shǐ Jǔ Zhèng (Correction of Historical Readings).
Page 2, Line 1: Now (Chēn) [Guì] Zhōu Xiàn (Guìzhou County). Wáng Xiānqiān (王先謙) said it is now Guì Xiàn (Guì County) in Xún Zhōu Fǔ (Xúnzhou Prefecture),
which was Guì Zhōu Xiàn (Guìzhou County) during the Táng (唐) dynasty.
Writing
"郴" (Chēn)
is incorrect.
Now corrected accordingly.
Page 2, Line 5: Tíng Zhōng Gǔ Qǐ (Bones rose in the courtyard). Comment: The Diàn Běn (Palace Edition) and Jíjiě Běn (Collected Explanations Edition) have
"庭中" (tíng zhōng, in the courtyard)
written as
"中庭" (zhōng tíng, in the middle of the courtyard).
Page 2, Line 8: Wáng Mǎng 【Shǐ】 Jiàn Guó Liù Nián (Sixth year of Wáng Mǎng's Shǐ Jiànguó era). Supplemented based on the Kān Wù (Corrections).
Page 2, Line 15: Tiān Fèng Liù Xù Mǐ Zhī Huáng (Six Xù Mǐ Zhī Huáng of Tiānfèng). Comment: Zhāng Dòu (張钭) said that according to the Qián Shū (Former Han History),
"六" (liù, six)
should be
"七" (qī, seven).

Page 3, Line 10: Bèi Xīng Guāng Máng Duǎn Péng Rán (The comet's light was short and scattered). Comment: Yáo Fàn's (姚範) Yuán Chúntáng Bǐjì (Notes from Chúntáng Studio) states that the Wén Jì Wén Yǐng Zhù (文紀文穎注) in the Qián Shū (Former Han History) says:
"孛星光芒短，
其光四出蓬蓬孛孛也" (The comet's light was short, its light scattered out in all directions, like a péngpéng bóbo).
Therefore, the annotation here
"蓬然" (péng rán, scattered)
should have one more
"蓬" (péng)
character.
Page 3, Line 13: Wèi 【Wǔ Guān】 Wǔ Guān Guān Zhī (Referred to the official wearing the martial cap). Supplemented based on the Kān Wù (Corrections).

Page 4, Line 8: Gēngshǐ Yuán Nián Zhēngyuè Jiǎzǐ Shuò (First month, Jiǎzǐ day, new moon of the first year of Gēngshǐ). Zhāng Dòu's (張钭) Dú Shǐ Jǔ Zhèng (Correction of Historical Readings) and Huáng Shān's (黃山) Hòu Hàn Shū Jiào Bǔ (Corrections and Supplements to the Later Han History) both state that according to the following text
"二月辛巳" (Èryuè Xīnsì, second month, Xīnsì day),
the first month's Jiǎzǐ was not the new moon.
Now, according to the commentary: The first month of that year was Rénzǐ (壬子) new moon.
This might be an extra
"朔" (shuò, new moon)
character,
or
"甲子" (Jiǎzǐ)
is a corruption of
"壬子" (Rénzǐ).
Page 4, Line 11: Qián Shū Yuē (The Former Han History says). Comment: Zhāng Dòu (張钭) said that the quote from Qián Shū (Former Han History) is not the main text;
below
"書" (shū, book) there should be the two characters
"音義" (yīnyì, pronunciation and meaning).
Page 4, Line 13: Shǔ Nán 【Yáng】 Jùn (Belonging to Nányáng Commandery). Comment: Zhāng Dòu (張钭) said that
below
"南" (nán, south) there should be the character
"陽" (yáng).
Now supplemented accordingly.

Page 4, Line 13: Gù Chéng Zài Jīn Dèng Zhōu Nányáng Xiàn Nán (Zài) Yù Shuǐ Zhī Yáng (The old city is now south of Nányáng County, Dèngzhou, on the sunny side of the Yù River). Deleted based on the Diàn Běn (Palace Edition).

Page 5, Line 1: Dé Dìng Wǔ Hóu Jiā Chéng Yìn (Obtained the seal of the Household Administrator of Marquis Dìngwǔ). Comment: Shěn Jiābĕn's (沈家本) Hòu Hàn Shū Suǒ Yán (Miscellaneous Remarks on the Later Han History) states that the Qián Shū (Former Han History) has no
"定武" (Dìngwǔ);
it is unknown whether Bān (Bān Gù) omitted it,
or if the Dōng Guān Jì (Records of the Eastern Lodge) was mistaken.
Page 5, Line 8: 【Yǎn】 Yīn Yú Jiàn Fǎn (Yǎn, pronounced Yú Jiàn Fǎn). Supplemented based on the Jí Běn (Jí Edition) and Diàn Běn (Palace Edition).
Page 6, Line 8: Yù Fēn Liú Shǒu Zhī (Wanted to divide the garrison). Comment: The Tōngjiàn (Comprehensive Mirror) has
"留" (liú, garrison)
as
"兵" (bīng, troops).
Page 6, Line 13: (Zhào) 【Zhāo】 Rú Hǎibīn (Like the seashore). Changed based on the Diàn Běn (Palace Edition),
which matches Wáng Mǎng Zhuàn (Biography of Wáng Mǎng) in the Qián Shū (Former Han History).

Page 7, Line 4: Piàojì Dà Jiàngjūn Wǔdì Zhì Zì Huò Qùbìng Shǐ (The General of Agile Cavalry was established by Emperor Wǔ, starting with Huò Qùbìng). Comment: Qián Dàxīn's (錢大昕) Èrshí'èr Shǐ Kǎo Yì (Studies on the Discrepancies in the Twenty-Two Histories) states that Qùbìng (Qùbìng) was Piàojì Jiàngjūn (General of Agile Cavalry),
without the character
"大" (dà, grand).
Page 7, Line 11: Zhēng Gǔ Zhī Shēng Wén Shù Bǎi Lǐ (The sound of gongs and drums was heard for several hundred lǐ). Comment: Yuán Hóng's (袁宏) Hòu Hàn Jì (Records of the Later Han) has
"數百里" (shù bǎi lǐ, several hundred lǐ)
as
"數十里" (shù shí lǐ, several tens of lǐ).
The Yùlǎn (Imperial Readings) Volume 283 quotes the same.
Page 7, Line 12: Chéng Zhōng Fù Hù Ér Jí (People in the city carried household items to fetch water). Comment: The Yùlǎn (Imperial Readings) Volume 283 quotes
"戶" (hù, household)
as
"楯" (shǔn, shield).
Page 8, Line 7: Wèi Yíng Tóu Zhī Xīng Yě (Refers to the star Yíngtóu). Comment: The Yùlǎn (Imperial Readings) Volume 328 quotes
above
"謂" (wèi, refers) there is the character
"所" (suǒ).
Page 8, Line 8: Guāngwǔ Suì Yǔ Yíng Bù Jù Jìn (Guāngwǔ then advanced with the camp troops). Comment: Zhāng Wénhǔ's (張文虎) Shū Yì Shì Suí Bǐ (Notes from the Shū Yì Studio) states that
"營部" (yíng bù, camp troops)
is not a proper phrase;
the Tōng Diǎn (Comprehensive Canons) Volume 158 quotes
above
"營部" (yíng bù) there is the character
"諸" (zhū, all),
and the Tōngjiàn (Comprehensive Mirror) is the same.
"諸" (zhū) is indispensable.
The character
Page 9, Line 14: Xián Wàn Rén Yuē Jié (One who surpasses ten thousand people is called a hero). The Diàn Běn (Palace Edition) and Jíjiě Běn (Collected Explanations Edition) have
below
"賢" (xián, virtuous) the character
"過" (guò, surpass).
Comment: The Báihǔ Tōng Shèngrén Piān (Discourses in the White Tiger Hall, Chapter on Sages) has
"萬人曰傑" (wàn rén yuē jié, ten thousand people are called heroes).
Page 9, Line 15: Shàonián Zǐ Dì (Younger brothers and sons). Comment: The Qián Shū Mǎng Zhuàn (Biography of Wáng Mǎng in the Former Han History) has
"子" (zǐ, son)
as
"朱" (zhū).
The Diàn Běn (Palace Edition) is the same.
The Kǎo Zhèng (Textual Research) states that the Jiān Běn (Jiān Edition) has
and the Sòng Běn (Sòng Edition) has
"宋" (Sòng).
Page 10, Line 4: Zhì (Bǐ) Èr Qiān Shí (Ranked second thousand shí). Deleted based on the Qián Shū Bǎi Guān Gōng Qīng Biǎo (Table of Officials and Nobles in the Former Han History).
Comment: The Qián Shū (Former Han History) states:
"自司隸至虎賁、校尉秩皆二千石" (From the Sīlì (Director of Retainers) to the Hǔbēn (Tiger Warriors) and Xiàowèi (Commandant), all were ranked second thousand shí).
The character
"比" (bǐ, comparable)
here is likely a truncated
"皆" (jiē, all)
character, missing its lower half.
Page 10, Line 9: (Bìng) Yīn Qí Wù Fǎn (Bìng, pronounced Qí Wù Fǎn). Deleted based on the Kān Wù (Corrections).
Page 10, Line 10: Duō. Comment:
"ヅ" (duō)
was originally corrupted as
Directly corrected based on the Jí Běn (Jí Edition) and Diàn Běn (Palace Edition).
Page 11, Line 5: Zhū (Shì) Cáo 【Yuán】 Shǐ (All Cáo Yuánshǐ). The Kān Wù (Corrections) states that the text has an extra character
"事" (shì, affair).
Comment: The Bǎi Guān Zhì (Treatise on Officials) has
"諸曹掾史" (zhū cáo yuàn shǐ, all section heads and clerks).
Now corrected accordingly.
Page 11, Line 13: Dōng Guān Jì (Yuē) Lín Zuò Lín Zì (The Dōng Guān Jì says Lín (林) is written as Lín (臨)). Comment: Yú Wén Míng (于文明) added an extra character
"曰" (yuē, says);
now deleted.

Page 12, Line 13: Wáng Mǎng Hé (Róng) 【Chéng】 Zú Zhèng Pī Tóng Yì Jǔ Jùn Jiàng (Wáng Mǎng's Héróng (Pacifier of Barbarians) Military Commander Pī Tóng also surrendered with his entire commandery). Comment: Pī Tóng Zhuàn (Biography of Pī Tóng) has
"和戎" (Héróng)
as
"和成" (Héchéng).
Zhāng Dòu (張钭) said it should follow Pī Tóng Zhuàn.
Furthermore, Shěn Jiābĕn (沈家本) said that according to Pī Tóng Zhuàn,
"戎" (róng)
is written as
"成" (chéng).
The annotation quoting Dōng Guān Jì (Records of the Eastern Lodge) also has
"成" (chéng).
Only this biography is mistaken.
The Shuǐ Jīng Zhuó Zhāng Shuǐ Zhù (Commentary on the Turbid Zhāng River in the Water Classic) quotes it as
"和城" (Héchéng).
Chéng (城) and Chéng (成) are often used interchangeably in books.
Now corrected accordingly.
Also, comment: The Jí Běn (Jí Edition) has
"彤" (tóng)
as
"肜" (róng).
Page 13, Line 2: Xiàn Míng Shǔ Zhuó Jùn (County name, belonging to Zhuó Commandery). Comment: Zhāng Dòu (張钭) said that according to the Qián Zhì (Former Han Treatise),
Jì (薊) belonged to Guǎngyáng Guó (Kingdom of Guǎngyáng),
and the Xù Zhì (Continued Treatise) had it belonging to Guǎngyáng Jùn (Guǎngyáng Commandery).
Neither has the phrase
"屬涿郡" (shǔ Zhuó Jùn, belonging to Zhuó Commandery).
Page 15, Line 6: Yǒu 【Cháng】 Shì Cáo Shàngshū (There was a Chángshì Cáo Shàngshū (Secretary of the Chángshì Section)). Supplemented based on the Kān Wù (Corrections).

Page 16, Line 11: Jùn 【Míng】 Yǒu Lángyá Shān Gù Chéng 【Zài】 Jīn Hǎizhōu Qúshān Xiàn Dōng Běi (The commandery name is Lángyá Mountain. The old city is now northeast of Qúshān County, Hǎizhou). The Kān Wù (Corrections) states that below
"郡" (jùn, commandery) a character
"名" (míng, name) is missing,
and below
"城" (chéng, city) a character
"在" (zài, located) is missing.
Now supplemented accordingly.
Page 16, Line 15: Dà Róng Qú Shuài Fán Zhòng (Great Róng tribe leader Fán Zhòng). Comment: Gěng Yǎn Zhuàn (Biography of Gěng Yǎn) has
"故大肜渠帥重異" (gù dà róng qú shuài Zhòng Yì, former great Róng tribe leader Zhòng Yì).
Lǐ Zhù (Lǐ Xián's Commentary) states:
"重姓，
異名" (Zhòng is the surname, Yì is the given name).
This text has
"樊重" (Fán Zhòng),
which seems to be a corruption.
Page 17, Line 11: Zāng (Jīn) 【Jìng】 Yīn Zuò Yān (Zāng Jìng, pronounced Yān). Comment: The Jíjiě (Collected Explanations) quotes Huì Dòng's (惠棟) view,
stating that
"矜" (jīn)
should be
"競" (jìng).

The Suí Shū Jīngjí Zhì Fàn Hàn Yīn Xùn (Treatise on Classics and Bibliography in the History of the Suí Dynasty, Fàn's Han Pronunciation and Exegesis) has three volumes written by Chén Zōngdào (陳宗道) titled Zāng Jìng (臧競).
Now corrected accordingly.
Page 19, Line 5: Nǎi Qiǎn Wú Hàn Shuài Gěng Yǎn Chén Jùn Mǎ Wǔ Děng Shí Èr Jiāngjūn (Then sent Wú Hàn to lead Gěng Yǎn, Chén Jùn, Mǎ Wǔ, and other twelve generals). Comment:
"Twelve"
should be
"fourteen."
The collected commentaries cite Huì Dòng's 惠棟 explanation,

stating that the biography of Gěng Yǎn 耿弇 records Guāngwǔ 光武 dispatching Yǎn 弇 with Wú Hàn 吳漢, Jǐng Dān 景丹, Gài Yán 蓋延, Zhū Yòu 朱祐, Pī Tóng 邳彤, Gěng Chún 耿純, Liú Zhí 劉植, Cén Péng 岑彭, Jì Zūn 祭遵, Jiān Tán 堅鐔, Wáng Bà 王霸, Chén Jùn 陳俊, and Mǎ Wǔ 馬武, thirteen generals,
making fourteen including Yǎn 弇.
Page 21, Line 3: "Your servant hears that emperors should not be long vacant." Note: Lǐ Címíng's 李慈銘 *Hòuhànshū Zhájì* 後漢書札記 states that
"王" (wáng, king)
should be
"位" (wèi, position).
Page 22, Line 8: "East of the altar (temple)." According to *Kān Gǎo Bǔ Quē* 刊誧R.
Page 23, Line 6: "named [Liú 劉]." According to *Kān Wù Bǔ* 刊誤補.
Page 23, Line 8: "attacked Gēngshǐ's 更始 Dìngguó Gōng 定國公 Wáng Kuāng 王匡 at Ānyì 安邑." Note:
The character
"公" (gōng, duke)
was originally followed by the superfluous character
"主" (zhǔ, lord),
which is directly deleted according to the Jíběn 汲本 and Diànběn 殿本 editions.
Page 23, Line 12: "The general of the flanks, Zhū Yòu 朱祐, was made Grand General of Jianyi." Note: Wáng Xiānqiān 王先謙 stated that
"祐" (yòu)
should be
as detailed in the collation notes for the biography of Zhū Yòu 朱祐 below.
Page 24, Line 5: "Wèipíng 尉平." Note: Yán Shīgǔ's 顏師古 commentary in the *Qián Shū* 前書 reads
"Tíng 廷,
Píng 平."
Page 24, Line 10: "[Former] city is in present-day Púzhōu Léizé Xiàn 濮州雷澤縣 to the north." Note: Zhāng Sēnkǎi's 張森楷 collation notes state that
the character
"城" (chéng, city)
should be preceded by
"故" (gù, former),
which is now added accordingly.
Page 24, Line 15: "Its text says: 'Inform such-and-such official that [such-and-such].'" [Yun 云] added according to *Kān Wù Bǔ* 刊誤補.

Page 25, Line 3: "previously (Gāomì 高密) magistrate Zhuó Mào 卓茂 as Grand Tutor." Deleted according to the Diànběn 殿本 textual research citing Hé Zhuó's 何焯 explanation and the collected commentaries citing Qián Dàxīn's 錢大昕 explanation.
Note: Qián Shì 錢氏 stated that Mào 茂 served as magistrate in Mì 密, Hénán 河南,
not Gāomì 高密,
and the *Jì* 紀 contains the superfluous character
"高" (gāo).
Page 25, Line 4: "Zhuó 卓 was magistrate of Mì 密 during the time of Emperor Píng 平." Note: The collected commentaries cite Hé Zhuó's 何焯 explanation,
stating that
"卓" (zhuó)
should be changed to
"茂" (mào).
Page 27, Line 2: "Cài Zhì's 蔡質 *[Hàn] Diǎn Zhí Yí* 漢典職儀 says." [Hàn 漢] added according to *Kān Wù Bǔ* 刊誤補.
Page 27, Line 3: "It is a grass name." Note:
"草" (cǎo, grass)
was originally
"華" (huá, flower),
directly changed according to the Jíběn 汲本 and Diànběn 殿本 editions.
Page 27, Line 9: "Therefore, Emperor Yuán 元 was established as the ancestral temple." Note: *Kān Wù* 刊誤 states that in terms of generation,
Emperor Yuán 元 was Guāngwǔ's 光武 father,
not grandfather,
and the character
"祖" (zǔ, ancestor)
is incorrect.
Page 27, Line 15: "Geography: the various marquises enjoy offerings." Note:
"后" (hòu, marquis)
should be
"神" (shén, spirit),
which can be proven by the *Xù Zhì* 續志.
Page 28, Line 7: "Zhēndìng Wáng Yáng 真定王楊, Lín Yì Hóu Ràng 臨邑侯讓." Note: Qián Dàxīn 錢大昕 stated that in the biographies of Liú Zhí 劉植 and Gěng Chún 耿純,
"楊" (yáng)
is always written as
"揚" (yáng),
and in the biography of Gěng Chún 耿純,
"臨" (lín)
is written as
"林" (lín).

Page 28, Line 9 – Page 29, Line 2: "In the second month, on the *jǐyǒu* 己酉 day, he went to Xiūwǔ 修武. On the *xīnmǎo* 辛卯 day, he returned from Xiūwǔ 修武. In the third month, on the *yǐwèi* 乙未 day, a general amnesty was granted to the empire." *Jiào Bǔ* 校補 cites Hóng Liàngjí's 洪亮吉 explanation,
stating that *jǐyǒu* 己酉 and *xīnmǎo* 辛卯 are not in the same month,
and the two characters
"三月" (sānyuè, third month)
should be placed before
"辛卯" (xīnmǎo),
as Fàn Shǐ 范史 incorrectly inverted them.
Huáng Shān 黃山 stated that if the first day of the first month of this year was *jiǎzǐ* 甲子,
then *jǐyǒu* 己酉 of the second month would already be past the full moon,
and not only would there be no *xīnmǎo* 辛卯 in the second month,
but there also should not be an *yǐwèi* 乙未 in the third month.
Yuán Jìshū 袁紀書 records
"In the third month, on the *yǐyǒu* 乙酉 day, a general amnesty was granted to the empire,"
not
"乙未" (yǐwèi).
The numerous discrepancies in dates in Fàn Shū 范書 cannot be exhaustively listed;
since there are omissions in the record,
it is impossible to correct all of them.
Page 29, Line 14: "Therefore, the son of the former Zhēndìng Wáng Yáng 真定王楊, Dé 德, became Zhēndìng Wáng 真定王." The Jíběn 汲本 and Diànběn 殿本 editions have
"得" (dé)
as
Note: *dé* 得 and *dé* 德 were often interchangeable in ancient times.

Page 30, Line 2: "Emperor Chéng 成 enfeoffed Jī Yán 姬延 as Zhōu Chéngxīu Gōng 周承休公, and Cháng 常 was Yán's 延 descendant." Note: Shěn Jiābĕn 沈家本 stated that according to the *Qián Shū Ēnzé Hóu Biǎo* 前書恩澤侯表,
"延" (yán)
is written as
"延年" (yánnián),
and it is suspected that this note is missing the character
"年" (nián).
Cháng 常 was the fourth-generation descendant of Yánnián 延年.
However, the table states "later changed to Zhōu Chéngxīu Hóu 周承休侯," which differs from this.
Page 37, Line 1: "Now the surname is written as (bēn 賁) [Bēn 奔] with the sound (bēn)." Changed according to *Kān Wù* 刊誤.
Page 39, Line 16: "Fán 蕃 is pronounced pí." The Diànběn 殿本 edition has
"皮" (pí)
as
"反" (fǎn).
Note: Zhāng Sēnkǎi's 張森楷 collation notes state that the commentary to the *Qián Shū Dìlǐ Zhì* 前書地理志 cites Yīng Shào's 應劭 pronunciation as *pí*,
and also cites Bái Páo's 白裒 explanation,
saying that Chén Fán's 陳蕃 son was the Chancellor of Lǔ 魯,
and changed the reading to *pí*, etc., to confirm this.
However, Hú Sānsǐng 胡三省, based on the *Tōng Diǎn* 通典,
stated that
"皮" (pí)
is a mistake for
"反" (fǎn),
and there is no genuine *pí* pronunciation.
Modern scholars blindly trust Yīng's 應 explanation,
claiming that Fán 蕃 is interchangeable with Fān 番,
and Fān 番 and Pí 皮 are double-consonant,
which is incorrect.
Page 40, Line 15: "The former city is in present-day Shèngzhōu Yínchéng Xiàn 勝州銀成縣." The Jíběn 汲本 and Diànběn 殿本 editions have
"成" (chéng)
as
"城" (chéng).
Note: *chéng* 成 and *chéng* 城 were often interchangeable in ancient times.
Annals of Emperor Guāngwǔ, Part 1, Section 2.
In the spring of the sixth year, first month, on the *bǐngchén* 丙辰 day,
Chūnlíng Xiāng 舂陵鄉 was renamed Zhānglíng Xiàn 章陵縣.
Generation after generation, they were exempt from corvée labor,
comparable to Fēng 豐 and Pèi 沛, with no participation required.
On the *xīnyǒu* 辛酉 day,
an imperial edict stated:
"In recent years, floods, droughts, and locusts have caused disasters,
grain prices have soared,
and people are in distress.
We consider that the common people have no means to support themselves,
and feel compassion for them.
Command the commanderies and states with grain
to provide rations to the elderly, the orphaned, widows, the lonely, and those who are seriously ill, homeless, poor, and unable to sustain themselves,
according to the law.
The two-thousand-bushel officials should diligently tour and comfort them,
without allowing anyone to lose their livelihood."
Yángwǔ 將軍 Mǎ Chéng 揚武將軍馬成 and others captured Shū 舒
and apprehended Lǐ Xiàn 李憲.
In the second month,
Grand Marshal Wú Hàn 大司馬吳漢 captured Qú 朐
and apprehended Dǒng Xiàn 董憲 and Páng Méng 龐萌,
and the entire region east of the mountains was pacified.
The various generals returned to the capital,
where a banquet was held and rewards were bestowed.
In the third month,
Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 dispatched his general Rèn Mǎn 任滿 to invade Nánjùn 南郡.
In the summer, fourth month, on the *bǐngzǐ* 丙子 day,
he visited Cháng'ān 長安,
for the first time paying respects at Gāomiào 高廟,
and then performed rites at the eleven imperial tombs.
He dispatched the Grand General Hǔyá 虎牙 Gài Yán 蓋延 and seven other generals to attack Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 via the Lǒng 隴 road.
In the fifth month, on the *jǐwèi* 己未 day,
he returned from Cháng'ān 長安.
Kuí Xiāo 隗囂 rebelled,
and Gài Yán 蓋延 and others fought Xiāo 囂 at Lǒngdǐ 隴阺,
where the generals were defeated.
On the *xīnchǒu* 辛丑 day,
an imperial edict stated:
"All officials and people in Tiānshuǐ 天水, Lǒngxī 隴西, Āndìng 安定, and Běidì 北地
who were misled by Kuí Xiāo 隗囂,
and also the three commanderies (Sānfǔ 三輔) that suffered disaster from the Chìméi 赤眉
and committed unlawful acts,
from those deserving capital punishment downwards,
are all hereby pardoned and exempted."
In the sixth month, on the *xīnmǎo* 辛卯 day,
an imperial edict stated:
"The establishment of officials and setting up of offices
are for the sake of the people.
Now, the common people have suffered hardship,
and the household population has greatly diminished,
yet the number of government officials is still excessive.
Therefore, command the Chief Administrator of the Capital (Sīlì) 司隸 and the Provincial Governors (Zhōumù) 州牧
to each assess their respective jurisdictions
and reduce the number of officials.
For counties and states where there are insufficient personnel to appoint a chief official and which can be consolidated,
report to the two ministries of the Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sītú) 大司徒 and the Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sīkōng) 大司空."
Thereupon, memorials were submitted to consolidate over four hundred counties,
and the number of officials was reduced,
with only one-tenth remaining.
Liú Xīng 劉興, the Administrator of Dàijùn 代郡, attacked Jiǎ Lǎn 賈覽, a general of Lú Fāng 盧芳, at Gāoliǔ 高柳,
and was killed in battle.
Initially,
Wáng Diào 王調, a man from Lèlàng 樂浪, occupied the commandery and refused to submit.
In the autumn,
Wáng Zūn 王遵, the Administrator of Lèlàng 樂浪, was dispatched to attack him,
and the commandery officials killed Diào 調 and surrendered.
Li Tōng, the former General, was dispatched with two generals,
to battle Gōngsūn Shù's generals at Xīchéng,
and they defeated them.
In summer,
there were locusts.
In autumn, the ninth month, on the day of Gēngzǐ,
an amnesty was granted to those in Lèlàng involved in treasonous rebellion and capital offenses down to lesser crimes.
On the day of Bǐngyín, the last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day of Dīngchǒu,
an edict stated:
"My virtue is shallow and my perception unclear.
Bandits and rebels cause harm,
the strong bully the weak,
and the common people lose their homes.
The Shījīng says: 'The sun and moon announce misfortune,
not following their course.'
Perpetually I reflect on these faults,
and feel inner guilt.
Therefore, instruct the ducal ministers to each recommend one worthy and upright person;
all officials are to submit memorials,
without concealment or reservation;
and the supervising officials are to attend to their duties,
striving to adhere to laws and regulations."
In the eleventh month, on the day of Dīngmǎo,
an edict decreed that all officials and common people who had been enslaved during Wáng Mǎng's time and whose enslavement did not conform to old laws,
were to be freed as commoners.
In the twelfth month, on the day of Rénchén,
Dàsīkōng Sòng Hóng was dismissed.
On the day of Guǐsì,
an edict stated:
"Recently, military operations have not ceased,
and expenditures have been insufficient,
hence the one-tenth tax was implemented.
Now, soldiers are cultivating fields,
and grain reserves are gradually accumulating.
Therefore, order the commanderies and kingdoms to collect land rent at one-thirtieth of the harvest,
as per the old system."
Wěi Xiāo dispatched his general Xíng Xún to raid Fúfēng,
but Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn Féng Yì repelled and defeated him.
In this year,
the offices of Commandery Dūwèi were first abolished.
Hereditary Marquis were first sent to their states.
The Xiongnú sent envoys to offer tribute,
and a Zhōnglángjiàng was dispatched to return their greetings.
In the seventh year, spring, the first month, on the day of Bǐngshēn,
an edict ordered the Zhongdu officials, Sanfu, commanderies, and kingdoms to release prisoners;
those who had not committed capital offenses
were all to have their charges dropped without exception.
Existing convicts were released as commoners.
Those who had fled to escape punishment for crimes
were cleared by officials through written decree.
Another edict stated:
"The world regards extravagant burials as virtuous,
and simple funerals as vulgar.
This leads the wealthy to ostentation and extravagance,
and the poor to deplete their resources.
Laws cannot prohibit it,
and rites and righteousness cannot stop it,
until suddenly its faults are realized.
Proclaim to all under heaven
the meaning of simple burials and funerals for loyal ministers, filial sons, benevolent elder brothers, and respectful younger brothers."
In the second month, on the day of Xīnsì,
the office of Hùcáo Dūwèi was abolished.
In the third month, on the day of Dīngyǒu,
an edict stated:
"Now the state has numerous armies,
and many are elite and brave.
It is appropriate to temporarily dismiss the light chariots, cavalrymen, skilled officers, marines, and acting military officials,
and allow them to return to the ranks of commoners."
Gōngsūn Shù established Wěi Xiāo as Shuòníng Wáng.
On the day of Guǐhài, the last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
The emperor avoided the main hall,
ceased military activities,
and did not attend to affairs for five days.
An edict stated:
"My meager virtue has caused calamity,
and the rebuke is seen in the sun and moon.
Trembling with fear,
what more can I say!
Now I reflect on my transgressions,
hoping to dispel their ill effects.
Order the supervising officials to each attend to their duties,
upholding laws and regulations,
and benefit these common people.
All officials are to submit memorials,
without any concealment.
Those who submit letters
are not permitted to use the word 'sacred'."
In summer, the fourth month, on the day of Rénwǔ,
an edict stated:
"Recently, yin and yang have been in disorder,
and the sun and moon have been eclipsed.
If the hundred surnames have faults,
the blame rests with me alone.
A great amnesty is granted to all under heaven.
The Gōng, Qīng, Sīlì, and Zhōu Mù are each to recommend one worthy and upright person,
and send them to the Gōngchē,
and I shall personally examine them."
In the fifth month, on the day of Wùxū,
Li Tōng, the former General, became Dàsīkōng.
On the day of Jiǎyín,
an edict decreed that officials and commoners who had suffered famine and chaos, or had been captured and made slaves or concubines by the Qīng and Xú rebels,
if they wished to leave or stay,
were to be freely allowed.
Anyone daring to restrain them and prevent their return
would be dealt with according to the law for selling people.
This summer,
there were continuous heavy rains.
Wáng Cháng, Hàn Zhōngjiāngjūn, became Héngyě Dàjiāngjūn.
In the eighth month, on the day of Dīnghài,
Shào, the former King of Héjiān, was enfeoffed as King of Héjiān.
Wěi Xiāo raided Āndìng,
and Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn Féng Yì and Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Jì Zūn attacked and repelled him.
In winter,
Tián Sà, Shuòfāng Tàishǒu appointed by Lú Fāng,
and Qiáo Hù, Yúnzhōng Tàishǒu, each surrendered their commanderies.
In this year,
the offices of Chángshuǐ and Shèshēng Xiàowèi were abolished.
In the eighth year, spring, the first month,
Zhōnglángjiàng Lái Xī attacked and seized Luèyáng,
killing Wěi Xiāo's defending general and occupying the city.
In summer, the fourth month,
Sīlì Xiàowèi Fù Kàng died in prison.
Wěi Xiāo attacked Lái Xī,
but could not take the city.
In the intercalary month,
the Emperor personally led an expedition against Xiāo.
Dòu Róng, Héxī Dàjiāngjūn, led the five commandery governors to meet the imperial chariot at Gāopíng.
Lǒngyòu collapsed,
and Wěi Xiāo fled to Xīchéng.
Dàsīmǎ Wú Hàn and Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn Cén Péng were dispatched to besiege him;
the Emperor advanced to Shàngguī,
which did not surrender,
and ordered Hǔyá Dàjiāngjūn Gài Yán and Jiànwēi Dàjiāngjūn Gěng Yǎn to attack it.
Robbers and bandits in Yǐngchuān raided and plundered its subordinate counties,
and the garrison soldiers of Hédōng also rebelled,
causing unrest in the capital.
In autumn,
there were great floods.
In the eighth month,
the Emperor rushed eastward day and night from Shàngguī.
In the ninth month, on the day of Yǐmǎo,
the imperial chariot returned to the palace.
On the day of Gēngshēn,
the Emperor personally led an expedition against the Yǐngchuān bandits,
who all surrendered.
Zhāng Bù, Marquis of Ānqīu, rebelled and returned to Lángyá,
and Chén Jùn, Lángyá Tàishǒu, attacked and captured him.
On the day of Wùyín,
the Emperor returned from Yǐngchuān.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day of Bǐngwǔ,
the Emperor visited Huái.
In the eleventh month, on the day of Yǐchǒu,
the Emperor returned from Huái.
Gōngsūn Shù sent troops to relieve Wěi Xiāo,
and Wú Hàn, Gài Yán, and others returned their armies to Cháng'ān.
Tiānshuǐ and Lǒngxī again rebelled and returned to Xiāo.
In the twelfth month,
the King of Gāogōulí sent envoys to offer tribute.
This year there were great floods.
In the ninth year, spring, the first month,
Wěi Xiāo died of illness,
and his generals Wáng Yuán and Zhōu Zōng re-established Xiāo's son Chún as King.
Officials and common people from Yànmén were relocated to Tàiyuán.
In the third month, on the day of Xīnhài,
the office of Qīngjīn Zuǒxiàowèi was first established.
Gōngsūn Shù sent his generals Tián Róng and Rèn Mǎn to occupy Jīngmén.
In summer, the sixth month, on the day of Bǐngxū,
the Emperor visited Gōushì,
and ascended Huányuán.
Dàsīmǎ Wú Hàn was dispatched with four generals to attack Lú Fāng's general Jiǎ Lǎn at Gāoliǔ,
but the battle was unfavorable.
In autumn, the eighth month,
Zhōnglángjiàng Lái Xī was dispatched to supervise Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn Féng Yì and four other generals in attacking Wěi Chún in Tiānshuǐ.
Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn Dù Mào battled Jiǎ Lǎn at Fánzhì,
and Mào's army suffered a defeat.
In this year,
the Gūan Dūwèi were abolished,
and the office of Hùqiāng Xiàowèi was re-established.
In the tenth year, spring, the first month,
Dàsīmǎ Wú Hàn, with Bǔlǔ Jiāngjūn Wáng Bà and four other generals, attacked Jiǎ Lǎn at Gāoliǔ.
The Xiongnú sent cavalry to aid Lǎn,
and the generals fought them
and repelled them.
The Gāomiào in Cháng'ān was repaired.
In summer,
Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn Féng Yì defeated Gōngsūn Shù's general Zhào Kuāng in Tiānshuǐ,
and beheaded him.
Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn Féng Yì passed away.
In autumn, the eighth month, on the day of Jǐhài,
the Emperor visited Cháng'ān,
offered sacrifices at the Gāomiào,
and then performed rites at the eleven imperial mausoleums.
On the *wùxū* day,
the Emperor proceeded to Qían (汧).
Gāo Jùn (高峻), a general of Wěi Xiāo (隗囂), surrendered.
In winter, the tenth month,
Middle-ranking General Lái Xī (來歙) and others decisively defeated Wěi Chún (隗純) at Luòmén (落門).
His general, Wáng Yuán (王元), fled to Shǔ (蜀).
Chún (純) and Zhōu Zōng (周宗) surrendered,
and Lǒngyòu (隴右) was pacified.
The Xiānlíng Qiāng (先零羌) plundered Jīnchéng (金城) and Lǒngxī (隴西).
Lái Xī (來歙) led his generals to attack the Qiāng (羌) at Wǔxī (五谿),
and decisively defeated them.
On the *gēngyín* day,
the Emperor's carriage returned to the palace.
In this year,
Dìngxiāng (定襄) Commandery was abolished,
and its people were resettled in Xīhé (西河).
Sìshuǐ (泗水) King Shè (歙) passed away.
Zīchuān (淄川) King Zhōng (終) passed away.
In the eleventh year, spring, the second month, on the *jǐmǎo* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Of all beings created by Heaven and Earth, humans are the most precious.
Therefore, those who kill slaves
shall not have their punishment reduced."
【In the third month】 On the *jǐyǒu* day,
the Emperor visited Nányáng (南陽);
returning,
he visited Zhānglíng (章陵)
and offered sacrifices at the imperial tombs.
Chéngyáng (城陽) King Zhǐ (祉) passed away.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
the Emperor's carriage returned to the palace.
In the intercalary month,
General-in-chief Who Conquers the South, Cén Péng (岑彭), leading three generals, fought Gōngsūn Shù's (公孫述) generals Tián Róng (田戎) and Rèn Mǎn (任滿) at Jīngmén (荊門),
decisively defeating them
and capturing Rèn Mǎn (任滿).
General Who Manifests Might, Féng Jùn (馮駿), besieged Tián Róng (田戎) at Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Cén Péng (岑彭) then led his navy to attack Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述),
pacifying Bājùn (巴郡).
In summer, the fourth month, on the *dīngmǎo* day,
the office of Assistant Administrator of the Grand Minister of Works was abolished.
The Xiānlíng Qiāng (先零羌) plundered Líntáo (臨洮).
In the sixth month,
Middle-ranking General Lái Xī (來歙), leading General Who Spreads Martial Awe, Mǎ Chéng (馬成), defeated Gōngsūn Shù's (公孫述) generals Wáng Yuán (王元) and Huán Ān (環安) at Xiàbiàn (下辯).
Ān (安) sent an assassin to murder Middle-ranking General Lái Xī (來歙).
The Emperor personally led an expedition against Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述).
In autumn, the seventh month,
he arrived at Cháng'ān (長安).
In the eighth month,
Cén Péng (岑彭) defeated Gōngsūn Shù's (公孫述) general Hóu Dān (侯丹) at Huángshí (黃石).
General Who Assists Might, Zāng Gōng (臧宮), fought Gōngsūn Shù's (公孫述) general Yán Cén (延岑) at Chénshuǐ (沈水),
decisively defeating him.
Wáng Yuán (王元) surrendered.
The Emperor returned from Cháng'ān (長安).
On the *guǐhài* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Those who dare to brand or cauterize slaves
shall be judged according to the law,
and those who were branded or cauterized shall be emancipated as commoners."
In winter, the tenth month, on the *rénwǔ* day,
an imperial edict abolished the law regarding slaves injuring people with arrows in the marketplace.
Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述) sent an assassin to murder General-in-chief Who Conquers the South, Cén Péng (岑彭).
Mǎ Chéng (馬成) pacified Wǔdū (武都),
and with the assistance of Mǎ Yuán (馬援), the Administrator of Lǒngxī (隴西), defeated the Xiānlíng Qiāng (先零羌),
relocating them to Tiānshuǐ (天水), Lǒngxī (隴西), and Fúfēng (扶風).
In the twelfth month,
Grand Marshal Wú Hàn (吳漢) led his navy to attack Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述).
In this year,
the office of Shepherd of Shuòfāng (朔方) was abolished,
and Bìngzhōu (并州) was incorporated.
For the first time, it was decreed that provincial governors should no longer personally report to the court.
In the twelfth year, spring, the first month,
Grand Marshal Wú Hàn (吳漢) fought Gōngsūn Shù's (公孫述) general Shǐ Xìng (史興) at Wǔyáng (武陽),
and beheaded him.
In the third month, on the *guǐyǒu* day,
an imperial edict stated that all people from Lǒng (隴) and Shǔ (蜀) who had been captured and made slaves, and who brought their own lawsuits,
and whose cases had not yet been reported by judicial officials,
should all be emancipated as commoners.
In summer,
sweet dew fell in Nánxíngtáng (南行唐).
In the sixth month,
a yellow dragon appeared in Dōng'ē (東阿).
In autumn, the seventh month,
General Who Manifests Might, Féng Jùn (馮駿), captured Jiāngzhōu (江州),
and seized Tián Róng (田戎).
In the ninth month,
Wú Hàn (吳漢) decisively defeated Gōngsūn Shù's (公孫述) general Xiè Fēng (謝豐) at Guǎngdū (廣都),
and beheaded him.
General Who Assists Might, Zāng Gōng (臧宮), captured Fúchéng (涪城),
and beheaded Gōngsūn Huī (公孫恢).
Grand Minister of Works Lǐ Tōng (李通) was dismissed.
In winter, the eleventh month, on the *wùyín* day,
Wú Hàn (吳漢) and Zāng Gōng (臧宮) fought Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述) at Chéngdū (成都),
decisively defeating him.
Shù (述) was wounded
and died during the night.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Wú Hàn (吳漢) massacred Chéngdū (成都)
and exterminated Shù's (述) clan and Yán Cén (延岑) and others.
In the twelfth month, on the *xīnmǎo* day,
General Who Spreads Martial Awe, Mǎ Chéng (馬成), temporarily held the office of Grand Minister of Works.
In this year,
Zhāng Yóu (張遊), a barbarian chieftain from beyond the borders of Jiǔzhēn (九真), led his people to submit,
and was enfeoffed as the lord of Guīhàn Lǐ (歸漢里).
Jīnchéng (金城) Commandery was abolished and made subordinate to Lǒngxī (隴西).
The Cānláng Qiāng (參狼羌) plundered Wǔdū (武都).
Mǎ Yuán (馬援), the Administrator of Lǒngxī (隴西), attacked and subdued them.
An edict ordered border officials to defend if their strength was insufficient for battle,
and when pursuing captives or assessing the enemy, not to be bound by the law against delay.
General-in-chief Who Spreads Awe, Wáng Cháng (王常), passed away.
General-in-chief of Cavalry Dù Mào (杜茂) was dispatched with troops from various commanderies to establish garrisons on the northern border,
construct watchtowers,
and repair beacon fires.
In the thirteenth year, spring, the first month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
Grand Minister of Works Hóu Bà (侯霸) passed away.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Previously, I issued an edict to the commanderies and states
that exotic delicacies should not be presented to the court.
Even now, this has not ceased.
Not only does it involve the toil of preparation and selection,
but it also causes trouble and disturbance on the roads,
and the expenditure far exceeds what is necessary.
Let the Grand Cook no longer accept such offerings.
Issue a clear edict below that local products for presentation to the ancestral temples
shall continue as per the old system."
In the second month,
General Who Captures Barbarians, Mǎ Wǔ (馬武), was dispatched to garrison Hútuóhé (虖沱河) to prepare for the Xiōngnú (匈奴).
Lú Fāng (盧芳) fled from Wǔyuán (五原) into Xiōngnú (匈奴) territory.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Chángshā (長沙) King Xīng (興), Zhēndìng (真定) King Dé (得), Héjiān (河閒) King Shào (邵), and Zhōngshān (中山) King Mào (茂)
all inherited their titles as kings,
which does not conform to the principles of the classics.
