and the Tàicháng shall choose an auspicious day to make a ceremonial announcement to the ancestral temple.
Let all men in the empire be granted a noble rank,
two grades each;
Sānlǎo, Xiàotì, and Lìtián, three grades each;
wandering people without registered names who wish to be registered, one grade each.
The widowed, lonely, orphaned, childless, seriously ill, and poor who cannot support themselves shall be given grain,
three *hú* each;
Lang and attendant officials who have served for ten years or more,
ten bolts of silk.
Officials from Zhōng’èrqiānshí and Èrqiānshí down to Huángshòu,
who were demoted in rank and paid a ransom,
those from last year onwards shall all have their ransoms returned."
In the eighth month of autumn, on the day of Bǐngyín,
an order was issued that in Wǔwēi, Zhāngyè, Jiǔquán, Dūnhuáng,
and the dependent states of Zhāngyè,
prisoners whose right foot had been cut off or worse, and who were capable of military service,
should all be fully acquitted of their crimes
and report to the military camps.
In the eleventh month of winter,
Dòu Gù, the Fèngchē Dūwèi, Gěng Bǐng, the Fùmǎ Dūwèi, and Líu Zhāng, the Qí Dūwèi, were dispatched out of the Kūnlún Pass in Dūnhuáng,
to attack and defeat the Báishān barbarians by the Púléi Sea,
then entered Chēshī.
The office of Xīyù Dūhù and Wùjǐ Xiàowèi was first established.
That year,
Tiānshuǐ was renamed Hànyáng Commandery.
In the spring of the eighteenth year, in the third month, on the day of Dīnghài,
an edict stated:
"Let all fugitives in the empire
redeem themselves for crimes from death penalty downwards: for death penalty, thirty bolts of thin silk;
for crimes from cutting off the right foot to *kūnqián chéngdànchōng*, ten bolts;
for *wán chéngdàn* to *sīkòu*, five bolts.
Officials and commoners who have committed crimes not yet discovered,
if they report themselves upon the arrival of this edict,
shall pay half the ransom."
In the fourth month of summer, on the day of Jǐwèi,
an edict stated:
"Since spring,
timely rain has not fallen,
the winter wheat is damaged by drought,
and the autumn seeds have not been sown.
The administration has lost its balance,
and I am filled with anxiety and fear.
Let all men in the empire be granted a noble rank,
two grades each,
and wandering people without registered names who wish to be registered, one grade each.
The widowed, lonely, orphaned, childless, and seriously ill
who cannot support themselves shall be given grain,
three *hú* each.
Redress unjust cases,
and review minor prisoners.
Officials of two thousand *shí* salary shall separately pray to the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers.
In commanderies where there are famous mountains and great rivers capable of raising clouds and bringing rain,
the chief officials shall each purify themselves and offer prayers,
hoping to receive the benevolent downpour."
In the sixth month, on the day of Jǐwèi,
a comet appeared in Tàiwēi.
Yānqí and Qūcí attacked Chén Mù, the Xīyù Dūhù,
and annihilated all his forces.
The Northern Xiōngnú and the King of Chēshī Hòuwáng besieged Gěng Gōng, the Wùjǐ Xiàowèi.
In the eighth month of autumn, on the day of Rénzǐ,
the Emperor passed away in the front hall of the Eastern Palace.
He was forty-eight years old.
His dying edict forbade the construction of a sleeping temple,
and ordered his spirit tablet to be placed in a separate changing room of Empress Guāngliè.
The Emperor had initially constructed his longevity tomb,
decreeing that it should simply follow the natural flow of water,
with a stone sarcophagus twelve *chǐ* wide
and twenty-five *chǐ* long,
and no mound was to be raised.
After ten thousand years,
sacrifices should be offered by sweeping the ground,
with only a basin of water, dried meat, and dry provisions.
After a hundred days,
offerings should only be made quarterly,
with a few officials and soldiers stationed to provide sweeping and cleaning,
and no renovations of the path.
Anyone who dared to initiate any construction
should be dealt with according to the law for disrespecting the ancestral temple.
The Emperor strictly adhered to the Jiànwǔ system,
and no one dared to violate it.
The families of the imperial concubines
were not allowed to be enfeoffed as marquises or participate in governance.
Guàntáo Gōngzhǔ
sought a Lang official position for her son,
but it was not granted,
though she was given ten million cash.
He said to his ministers:
"Lang officials correspond to the constellations above,
and govern hundreds of *lǐ* below.
If they are not the right people,
then the common people will suffer disaster,
which is why it is difficult."
Therefore, officials were praised for their positions,
the people lived peacefully in their occupations,
those near and far submitted respectfully,
and the population thrived.
Commentary states: Míngdì excelled in legal administration,
with clear laws and regulations.
He sat in court late into the day,
and obscure grievances were surely addressed.
Internally and externally, there was no private favoritism,
and he showed no arrogance or self-importance.
He judged cases justly,
and was ranked twelve among previous dynasties.
Therefore, later commentators on affairs
all look to the governance of Jiànwǔ and Yǒngpíng first.
However, Zhōnglí Yì, Sòng Jūn, and their like
often spoke of his excessive astuteness,
could it be that his magnanimity was not yet superior enough?
Eulogy says: Xiǎnzōng grandly succeeded,
diligent and cautious.
With a wary heart and respectful virtue,
his governance was discerning, overcoming wickedness.
He ordered court ceremonies,
and simplified tomb mounds.
Always remembering abandoned rituals,
he humbled himself to follow the Way.
He ascended the platform to observe clouds,
and bowed to the elders at the academy.
He diligently contemplated imperial achievements,
adding glory to his cultivated father.
Biographies of Sùzōng Xiàozhāng Dì, Third Part
Sùzōng Xiàozhāng Huángdì, whose taboo name was Dá,
was Xiǎnzōng's fifth son.
His mother was Guìrén Jiǎ.
In the third year of Yǒngpíng,
he was established as Crown Prince.
He was lenient in his youth,
and fond of Confucian arts,
and Xiǎnzōng highly esteemed him.
In the eighteenth year, in the eighth month, on the day of Rénzǐ,
he ascended the imperial throne,
aged nineteen.
He honored the Empress as Empress Dowager.
On Rénxū,
Xiàomíng Huángdì was buried at Xiǎnjiélíng.
In the tenth month of winter, on the day of Dīngwèi,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
The people were granted noble ranks,
two grades each;
those who succeeded their fathers, and Xiàotì, and Lìtián, three grades each;
those without registered names and wandering people who wished to be registered, one grade each.
Ranks exceeding Gōngchéng could be transferred to one's son or a son of the same lineage.
The widowed, lonely, orphaned, childless, seriously ill, and poor who cannot support themselves were given grain,
three *hú* each.
An edict stated:
"I, with my meager self,
am entrusted above kings and marquises,
to govern myriad affairs.
Fearing to lose balance,
I am ever cautious and diligent,
unsure how to succeed.
I deeply reflect that a ruler who maintains established traditions
must appoint teachers and mentors.
Does not the Shī say: 'Without fault, without forgetfulness,
following the old rules'?
Xǐ, the acting Tàiwèi and Jiéxiāng Hóu, served three generations in office,
and is an elder statesman of the nation;
Róng, the Sīkōng,
has held his position for six years,
industrious and never slack.
Let Xǐ be Tàifù,
and Róng be Tàiwèi,
both concurrently overseeing the affairs of the Shàngshū.
'The great officials,
none are willing to serve day and night,'
is what the Xiǎoyǎ laments.
'If I err, you correct me;
do not outwardly comply,'
is the true meaning of chief ministers.
Let all lords and officials diligently consider their duties,
each contributing loyalty and sincerity,
to assist my inadequacy.
Instruct the four directions,
and let them know my intentions."
In the eleventh month, on the day *wùxū*,
Dìwǔ Lún (第五倫), the Administrator of Shǔjùn (蜀郡), became Sīkōng (司空).
An imperial edict ordered Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn (征西將軍) Gěng Bǐng (耿秉) to garrison Jiǔquán (酒泉).
Duàn Péng (段彭), the Administrator of Jiǔquán, was dispatched to rescue Wùjǐ Xiàowèi (戊己校尉) Gěng Gōng (耿恭).
On the last day of the month, *jiǎchén*,
there was a solar eclipse.
Consequently, [the emperor] avoided the main palace hall,
disbanded the military ceremonies,
and did not attend to affairs for five days.
An imperial edict ordered all officials to submit confidential memorials.
In the twelfth month, on the day *guǐsì*,
officials submitted a memorial stating:
“Xiàomíng Huángdì (孝明皇帝) possessed sagely virtue and pure integrity,
toiled diligently day and night,
personally wore washed clothes,
and had no extravagant food.
His benevolence reached the four quarters,
and distant peoples longed for his civilizing influence.
The Jiāoyáo (僬僥) and Dān'ěr (儋耳) [peoples]
came of their own accord to pledge allegiance at the frontier.
He conquered Guǐfāng (鬼方),
opened roads to the Western Regions,
and his awesome might and spiritual power spread widely,
with none failing to submit.
He worried for the common people,
and did not take pleasure in ruling the world.
He fully implemented the teachings of the Sānyōng (三雍),
and personally performed the rites of elder care.
He composed the Dēnggē (登歌),
rectified court music,
and extensively studied the Six Arts,
without ceasing day or night.
His wisdom was profound and insightful,
recorded in the charts and prophecies.
The influence of his utmost virtue
communicated with the gods and spirits.
His accomplishments shone throughout the four seas,
and his benevolent influence lasted for a thousand years.
Yet, he held deep humility,
claiming himself lacking in virtue,
and forbade the construction of a sleeping temple (cǐ miào 寢廟),
advocating for ground-swept sacrifices,
abolishing the daily sacrifice system,
and reducing the funeral rites.
Consequently, the spirit tablet was hidden in the separate dressing room of Guāngliè Huánghòu (光烈皇后).
When the world heard of this,
none were not mournful.
Your Majesty, being supremely filial and benevolent,
has upheld and followed these sacred virtues.
Your humble servants believe that the dressing room is outside the inner gate,
a distinct location.
It is fitting to honor the temple as Xiǎnzōng (顯宗).
Regarding the seasonal *dì* and *xiá* sacrifices,
they should be performed in Guāngwǔ (光武)'s hall.
All other regular sacrifices should revert to the dressing room,
and the Wǔdézhīwǔ (武德之舞) should be performed together,
following the precedent of Xiàowén Huángdì (孝文皇帝)'s *xiá* sacrifice at Gāomiào (高廟).”
The imperial decree stated:
“Granted.”
That year,
there was a cattle plague.
The capital and three provinces suffered a severe drought.
An edict ordered the cancellation of land taxes and fodder levies in Yǎnzhōu (兗州), Yùzhōu (豫州), and Xúzhōu (徐州),
and that existing grain be distributed to the poor.
In the first month of spring of Jiànchū (建初) first year,
an imperial edict was issued to the commanderies and states of the three provinces, stating:
“As spring begins the eastern agricultural work,
I fear that people may gradually receive rations,
and the frequent comings and goings may
hinder farming.
Therefore, each [commandery and state] shall accurately verify the truly impoverished,
calculate the amount to be lent, and give it to them.
For migrants wishing to return to their hometowns,
the commanderies and counties shall provide them with sufficient rations
to ensure their return,
and allow them to stop at official rest houses,
without requiring them to pay for lodging.
Chief officials shall personally oversee this,
so that no poor or weak individuals are overlooked or left behind,
and no petty officials or powerful magnates can exploit the situation through deceit or misconduct.
Once this edict is issued,
it must not be delayed.
Inspectors (Cìshǐ 刺史) shall clearly supervise and investigate those who are most derelict.”
On the day *bǐngyín*,
an imperial edict stated:
“In recent years, cattle have suffered much from disease and plague,
cultivated land has decreased,
grain prices are quite high,
and people have become displaced.
As spring begins the eastern agricultural work,
it is crucial to attend to these matters in a timely manner.
The Two Thousand *Dàn* officials should diligently encourage agriculture and sericulture,
and widely attract and comfort the people.
The *Gōng* (公) and various *Yǐn* (尹) officials
should each exert their sincerity,
and prioritize urgent human affairs.
Crimes not punishable by death
should await investigation after the autumn harvest.
Officials concerned should be careful and discerning in their selections,
promoting the gentle and good,
and dismissing the corrupt and cunning,
following the seasonal regulations,
and rectifying unjust cases.
‘The five teachings lie in leniency,’
a virtue praised in the imperial canons;
‘A pleasant and easygoing gentleman,’
lauded in the *Dàyǎ* (大雅).
Let this be proclaimed throughout the world,
so that my intentions are clearly known.”
Duàn Péng (段彭), the Administrator of Jiǔquán, attacked and
severely defeated Chēshī (車師).
The office of Wùjǐ Xiàowèi (戊己校尉) was abolished.
In the second month,
the Mán (蠻) people of Lǐzhōng (澧中) in Wǔlíng (武陵) rebelled.
In the third month, on the day *jiǎyín*,
there was an earthquake in Shānyáng (山陽) and Dōngpíng (東平).
On the day *jǐsì*,
an imperial edict stated:
“I, being without virtue,
have inherited this great enterprise,
and night and day I tremble with apprehension,
not daring to indulge in idleness or ease.
Yet, disasters and anomalies continue to appear,
corresponding to governmental affairs.
Not only am I unenlightened,
and my understanding of the Way grows daily shallower;
but also, selections are contrary to reality,
vulgar officials harm the people,
official duties are chaotic and wasteful,
and punishments are unjust.
How can I not be concerned!
In the past, Zhònggōng (仲弓) was a household retainer of the Jì (季) family,
and Zǐyóu (子游) was a minor magistrate of Wǔchéng (武城).
Confucius still instructed them on selecting worthy talents
and inquired about finding the right people.
It is clear that in governance, regardless of scale,
finding the right people is fundamental.
Indeed, selection from districts and villages
must be based on accumulated merit and service.
Today, Inspectors and Administrators fail to distinguish true from false,
and *Màocái* (茂才) and *Xiàolián* (孝廉) are numbered by the hundreds each year.
Since they are not truly capable,
it is utterly meaningless
to entrust them with governance.
Whenever I reflect on how earlier generations selected and presented scholars,
some rose from the fields
without being tied to aristocratic lineage.
When they spoke in memorials,
their writings were worthy of adoption;
when tested by achievements,
their governance showed extraordinary results.
With substance and refinement in good balance,
I greatly commend them.

Therefore, let the Tàifù (太傅), Sāngōng (三公), Zhōng'èrqiānshí (中二千石), Èrqiānshí (二千石), and the Administrators of commanderies and states each recommend one person who is *Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng* (賢良方正) and capable of speaking frankly and admonishing strongly.”
In the fifth month of summer, on the day *xīnyǒu*,
for the first time, *Xiàolián* and *Lángzhōng* (郎中) who were broad-minded and resourceful,
and fit to govern cities,
were appointed as Chiefs (*Zhǎng* 長) and Chancellors (*Xiāng* 相).
In the seventh month of autumn, on the day *xīnhài*,
an imperial edict granted the fields of the Shànglín (上林) imperial park to the poor.
In the eighth month, on the day *gēngyín*,
a comet appeared in Tiānshì (天市).
In the ninth month,
the Àiláo (哀牢) barbarians of Yǒngchāng (永昌) rebelled.
In the tenth month of winter,
the Wǔlíng (武陵) commandery troops attacked the rebellious Mán,
defeated and subjugated them.
In the eleventh month,
Fùlíng Wáng (阜陵王) Yán (延) conspired to rebel,
and was demoted to Fùlíng Hóu (阜陵侯).
In the third month of spring of the second year, on the day *xīnchǒu*,
an imperial edict stated:
“In recent years, the *yīn* and *yáng* have been out of balance,
and famine has repeatedly occurred.
I deeply ponder the former emperor’s original concern for the people,
whose edicts stated: ‘Do not harm wealth,
do not harm people.’
Indeed, he wished for the common people to abandon secondary pursuits and return to fundamental ones.
Yet now, honored relatives and close kin
are excessively extravagant without limit,
and their weddings, marriages, and funerals
are particularly ostentatious and presumptuous.
Officials have abandoned their duties
and none are willing to investigate or report.
According to the principles of the *Chūnqiū* (春秋),
the noble should govern the humble.
Now, starting from the Sāngōng (三公),
all should clearly investigate illegal activities
and assert their authority.
I, being in my weak冠 (guàn, 'cap-wearing age,' referring to coming of age),
do not know the hardships of farming.
My humble and limited understanding, like looking through a tube,
how can it illuminate even a corner?
Therefore, concerning regulations and systems that should be implemented,
those in charge should thoroughly establish prohibitions,
starting with the capital and then extending to all the provinces.”
On the day *jiǎchén*,
the troops garrisoned at Yīwúlú (伊吾盧) were withdrawn.
The common people and the Àiláo (哀牢) barbarians of the three commanderies—Yǒngchāng (永昌), Yuècuì (越巂), and Yìzhōu (益州)—attacked the Àiláo,
defeated and pacified them.
In the summer, fourth month, on the day *wùzǐ*,
an edict was issued to pardon over four hundred families who had been banished for involvement in affairs concerning Chǔ and Huáiyáng,
ordering them to return to their home commanderies.
On the day *guǐsì*,
an edict instructed the Chancellor of Qí to reduce the production of ice silk, square-hole gauze, and blown floss.
In the sixth month,
the Shāodāng Qiāng rebelled.
Háo Chóng, the Administrator of Jīnchéng, attacked them,
suffered a defeat,
and the Qiāng then raided Hànyáng.
In the autumn, eighth month,
Mǎ Fáng, the Acting General of Agile Cavalry, was dispatched to suppress them.
In the twelfth month, on the day *wùyín*,
a comet appeared in the Purple Palace constellation.
In the third year, spring, first month, on the day *jǐyǒu*,
ancestral sacrifices were performed in the Míngtáng.
After the rites were completed,
he ascended the Língtái
to observe the clouds and atmospheric phenomena.
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
In the third month, on the day *guǐsì*,
Noble Lady Dòu was established as empress.
Titles were bestowed,
each person receiving two ranks,
while the three elders (*sānlǎo*), filial and fraternal individuals (*xiàotì*), and diligent farmers (*lìtián*) received three ranks;
commoners without registered names and vagrants wishing to register each received one rank.
The widowed, lonely, orphaned, childless, seriously ill, and impoverished who could not sustain themselves were given grain,
five *hú* per person.
In the summer, on the day *jǐsì*,
the operation of the Shíjiù River canal in Chángshān was ceased.
Mǎ Fáng, the Acting General of Agile Cavalry, defeated the Shāodāng Qiāng at Líntáo.
In the intercalary month,
Bān Chāo, the Acting Cavalier Commandant of the Western Regions, attacked Gūmò
and thoroughly defeated them.
In the winter, twelfth month, on the day *dīngyǒu*,
Mǎ Fáng was appointed General of Agile Cavalry.
The Lóuzhōng Mán of Wǔlíng rebelled.
In this year,
Línglíng presented auspicious *zhī* grass.
In the fourth year, spring, second month, on the day *gēngyín*,
Grand Commandant Móu Róng died.
In the summer, fourth month, on the day *wùzǐ*,
Prince Qìng was established as Crown Prince.
Titles were bestowed,
each person receiving two ranks,
while the three elders (*sānlǎo*), filial and fraternal individuals (*xiàotì*), and diligent farmers (*lìtián*) received three ranks;
commoners without registered names and vagrants wishing to register themselves each received one rank.
The widowed, lonely, orphaned, childless, seriously ill, and impoverished who could not sustain themselves were given grain,
five *hú* per person.
On the day *jǐchǒu*,
Gù, King of Jùlù, was moved to become King of Jiānglíng;
Chàng, King of Rǔnán, was moved to become King of Liáng;
Bǐng, King of Chángshān, was moved to become King of Huáiyáng.
On the day *xīnmǎo*,
the imperial sons Kàng
and Quán were enfeoffed as King of Qiānchéng
and King of Píngchūn, respectively.
In the fifth month, on the day *bǐngchén*,
General of Agile Cavalry Mǎ Fáng died.
On the day *jiǎxū*,
Bāo Yù, Minister of Works, became Grand Commandant;
Huán Yú, Administrator of Nányáng, became Minister of Works.
In the sixth month, on the day *guǐchǒu*,
Empress Dowager Mǎ died.
In the autumn, seventh month, on the day *rénxū*,
Empress Míngdé was buried.
In the winter,
there was a great cattle plague.
In the eleventh month, on the day *rénxū*,
an edict stated:
"The three dynasties guided the people,
taking education as their foundation.
The Hàn, succeeding the tyrannical Qín,
praised and highlighted Confucian learning,
established the Five Classics,
and appointed Erudites for them.
Thereafter, scholars made diligent progress,
and though they claimed to inherit from their teachers,
they also formed separate schools of thought.
Emperor Xiàoxuān believed that as the sages were long past,
one could not be too broad in learning.
Thus, he established Erudites for the Greater and Lesser Xiàhóu versions of the *Shàngshū*,
and later also established the Jīng school of the *Yì*.
By the middle of the Jiànwǔ era,
Erudites were again appointed for the Yán and Yán schools of the *Chūnqiū*,
and the Greater and Lesser Dài schools of the *Lǐ*.
All these were intended to promote subtle learning
and broaden the arts of the Dao.
In the first year of Zhōngyuán, regarding the *Shàngshū*,
the numerous chapters and annotations of the Five Classics were considered troublesome,
and there was a discussion to reduce them.
By the first year of Yǒngpíng,
Chángshuǐ Commandant Dù
presented a memorial, stating,
'The great enterprise of the late emperor
should be carried out in due course.
We should have all the Confucians collectively rectify the meaning of the classics,
allowing scholars to somewhat help themselves.'
Confucius said, 'The neglect of learning
is my worry.'
He also said, 'To learn extensively and hold to one's purpose with earnestness,
to inquire with urgency and reflect on what is at hand—
therein lies benevolence.'
Alas,
strive diligently!"
Thereupon, the Grand Minister of Ceremonies,
generals, grand masters, erudites, counsellors, and palace attendants,
as well as various students and Confucians, gathered at the Báihǔ Temple
to discuss the agreements and differences in the Five Classics.
Wèi Yìng, Colonel-Director of the Five Official Bureaus, was ordered to pose questions on behalf of the Emperor,
and Chúnyú Gōng, Palace Attendant, presented the memorials.
The Emperor personally presided over and decided the matters,
following the precedent of Emperor Xiàoxuān's Gānlù-Shíqú discussions,
and compiled the *Báihǔ Yìzòu*.
In this year,
sweet dew descended in the two counties of Quánlíng and Táoyáng.
In the fifth year, spring, second month, on the first day *gēngchén*,
there was a solar eclipse.
An edict stated:
"I have recently lost my mother's sustenance,
and my transgressions are manifest to all.
Heaven has sent down an anomaly,
and a great change has followed.
Does not the *Shī* say: 'It is truly most shameful'?
Furthermore, the prolonged drought has damaged the wheat,
causing deep and bitter sorrow in my heart.
Let the high officials and all below
each recommend one person who speaks truthfully and remonstrates strongly, able to point out my faults.
Send them to the Privy Chariot office,
and I will personally review and question them.
Let those from remote places be prioritized,
and do not select the superficial and showy."
On the day *jiǎshēn*,
an edict stated:
"The *Chūnqiū* records 'no wheat seedlings,'
attaching great importance to it.
Last autumn the rain was not suitable,
and now it is again dry,
like a raging fire.
It is a year of misfortune without end,
yet preparations are insufficient.
My lack of virtue
has affected the three luminaries above,
causing me to tremble with anxiety,
my heart aching, my head throbbing.
The sage rulers of previous generations,
through extensive deliberation and consultation,
even when disaster descended,
always had responses like opening granaries and changing the winds.
Now I, the insignificant one,
am merely filled with sorrow.
Let the officials holding two thousand *shí* salary resolve unjust cases
and record those lightly imprisoned.
Pray to the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers,
and to the famous mountains capable of raising clouds and bringing rain,
hoping to receive the blessing of rain covering the whole empire before morning.
Be sure to show utmost reverence."
In the third month, on the day *jiǎyín*,
an edict stated:
"Confucius said, 'If punishments are not just,
then the people will not know where to put their hands and feet.'
Now, many officials are not good;
they act capriciously and follow their whims,
or they indict without cause,
coercing the innocent,
leading to self-inflicted deaths.
Such cases in a year are even more numerous than judicial executions,
which is truly not the intention of those who are parents to the people.
Let the relevant authorities deliberate on how to investigate and expose this."
The troops from the various commanderies of Jīng and Yù attacked and defeated the rebellious Lóuzhōng Mán of Wǔlíng.
In the summer, fifth month, on the day *xīnhài*,
an edict stated:
"I seek righteous scholars,
leaving my seat expectant of unusual talents.
Those who arrived first
each expressed their indignation and grievances,
and I have briefly heard the aspirations of you gentlemen.
I wish to place all of you by my side,
to consult you and accept your advice.
The Jiànwǔ edict also stated that
Yáo tested his officials through their duties,
not merely through their words and writings.
Currently, many external official positions are vacant,
and you can all be appointed to them."
On the day *wùchén*,
Grand Tutor Zhào Xǐ died.
In the winter,
the ritual music for welcoming the *qì* of the months began to be performed.
In this year,
Línglíng presented auspicious *zhī* grass.
Eight yellow dragons were seen at Quánlíng.
Bān Chāo, Acting Cavalier Commandant of the Western Regions, attacked Shūlè
and defeated it.
In the sixth year, spring, second month, on the day *xīnmǎo*,
Jīng, King of Lángyá, died.
In summer, the fifth month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
Zhào Wáng Xū passed away.
In the sixth month, on the day Bǐngchén,
Grand Commandant Bào Yù passed away.
On Xīnwèi, the last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Guǐsì,
Dèng Biāo, the Grand Minister of Agriculture, was appointed Grand Commandant.
In the seventh year, in spring, the first month,
Pèi Wáng Fǔ, Jìnán Wáng Kāng, Dōngpíng Wáng Cāng, Zhōngshān Wáng Yān, Dōnghǎi Wáng Zhèng, and Lángyé Wáng Yǔ came to court.
In summer, the sixth month, on the day Jiǎyín,
Crown Prince Qìng was deposed and made Qīnghé Wáng.
Imperial Prince Zhā was established as Crown Prince.
On Jǐwèi,
Guǎngpíng Wáng Xiàn was transferred to become Xīpíng Wáng.
In autumn, the eighth month,
wine was offered at Gāomiào,
and the Dì sacrifice was offered to Guāngwǔ Huángdì and Xiàomíng Huángdì.
On Jiǎchén,
an imperial edict stated:
"The 'Shū' says, 'Ancestors and forefathers come to visit,'
referring to the sacrifices of the wise.
I, a young and humble man,
of meager character,
reflect upon the profound affection of the former emperors.
The previous Dì sacrifice was performed
to fully express filial piety and respect.
I have come to understand the order of ancestral tablets,
and feel a connection to distant ancestors.
This year, the great ritual is performed again,
and with the seats of the former emperors present,
I am filled with sorrow and emotion.
Joyfully we welcome the spirits,
sorrowfully we see them off.
Though the deceased are as if present in the sacrifice,
the emptiness makes me unsure where to place my grief,
hoping they may partake.
Can it be that there are no reverent and harmonious officials,
or excellent ministers,
who can assist in my yearning?
Now, I grant the Dukes 400,000 cash,
the Ministers half of that,
and other officials and attendants a varying amount."
In the ninth month, on Jiǎxū,
the Emperor proceeded to Yǎnshī,
crossed Juǎnjīn to the east,
and arrived in Hénèi.
An imperial edict was issued, stating:
"The imperial carriage inspects the autumn crops,
observes the harvest,
and thus traverses the commandery borders.
All are elite cavalry traveling lightly,
without other baggage.
No one is permitted to arbitrarily repair roads or bridges,
stay far from cities,
send officials to greet the procession,
inquire about daily life,
or move in and out of the front and rear of the retinue,
creating disturbance.
Every action should be as simple and economical as possible;
the only concern is not being able to eat coarse grain and drink from a gourd.
Wherever we pass, we wish the poor and weak to benefit,
without violating this edict."
Then, Qíyuán was visited.
On Jǐyǒu,
the Emperor proceeded to Yè,
and bestowed rewards and entertained the administrators and magistrates of Wèijùn and below,
down to the Sanlǎo, menlán, and zǒuzú,
each receiving varying amounts of cash.
The officials and common people of Chángshān and Zhàoguó were rewarded,
and the rent and taxes of Yuánshì were remitted for three years.
On Xīnmǎo,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
An edict was issued, stating that prisoners throughout the empire whose crimes were punishable by death should have their sentences reduced by one degree,
and not be flogged,
but sent to border garrisons;
their wives and children could follow them,
and be registered at their location;
their parents and siblings who wished to accompany them were
freely permitted to do so;
those who did not arrive
were all to be judged as failing to contribute to military provisions.
For those who had committed particularly heinous crimes,
all were to be recruited and sent to the cāncóng (eunuch office);
female offenders were to undergo 'gōng' (punishment of women).
Prisoners sentenced to guǐxīn and báicàn or above
all had their original sentences reduced by one degree,
and were sent to the Sīkòu for forced labor.
Fugitives could redeem themselves: those guilty of capital crimes paid twenty rolls of plain silk;
those whose crimes ranged from losing the right foot to being tattooed, collared, and sentenced to grind grain or build walls paid ten rolls;
those whose crimes ranged from full-bodied laborers building walls to being sent to the Sīkòu paid three rolls;
officials and common people who had committed crimes not yet discovered,
but reported themselves upon the arrival of the edict,
paid half the redemption fee.
In winter, the tenth month, on Guǐchǒu,
the Emperor made a western inspection tour,
and proceeded to Cháng'ān.
On Bǐngchén,
a sacrifice was offered at Gāomiào,
and then rituals were performed at the eleven imperial mausoleums.
Envoys were dispatched to offer sacrifices to Tàishàng Huáng at Wànnián,
and to Xiāo Hé and Huò Guāng with a Zhōngláo sacrifice.
The Emperor then proceeded to Huáilǐ.
A bronze vessel,
shaped like a wine jar, was found on Qíshān
and presented.
A white deer was also captured.
The Emperor said:
"Above, there is no enlightened Son of Heaven;
below, there are no virtuous regional governors.
'If a man is not good,
he blames one side.'
Why then did this vessel come?"
The Emperor then proceeded to Chángpíng,
resided at Chíyáng Gōng,
traveled east to Gāolíng,
built boats on the Jīng River, and then returned.
Wherever the Emperor went,
officials and common people from the commanderies and counties were assembled,
rewarded, and entertained with music.
In the eleventh month,
an edict rewarded the administrators, magistrates, and clerks of Hédōng and below.
In the twelfth month, on Dīnghài,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
In this year,
the capital and the commanderies and kingdoms suffered from locusts.
In the eighth year, in spring, the first month, on Rénchén,
Dōngpíng Wáng Cāng passed away.
In the third month, on Xīnmǎo,
Dōngpíng Xiàn Wáng was buried,
and bestowed with a luánlù and lóngqí.
In summer, the sixth month,
a chieftain of the Northern Xiōngnú led his people to surrender at the border.
In winter, the twelfth month, on Jiǎwǔ,
the Emperor made an eastern inspection tour,
and proceeded to Chénliú, Liángguó, Huáiyáng, and Yǐngyáng.
On Wùshēn,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
An edict stated:
"The five classics have been analyzed,
and we are increasingly distant from the sages.
Fragmentary sentences and forgotten words
are contradictory and difficult to correct,
lest the subtle words of the former masters be completely lost and abandoned,
which would not be in line with upholding antiquity
and seeking the true Way.
Let the scholars select highly talented students
to study the Zuǒshì and Gǔliáng commentaries to the Chūnqiū,
the Gǔwén Shàngshū,
and the Máoshī,
to support these fading studies
and broaden the understanding of their different meanings."
In this year,
the capital and the commanderies and kingdoms suffered from locusts.
In the first year of Yuánhé, in spring, the first month,
Zhōngshān Wáng Yān came to court.
Barbarians from beyond the borders of Rìnán presented a live rhinoceros and white pheasants.
In the intercalary month, on Xīnchǒu,
Jìyīn Wáng Cháng passed away.
In the second month, on Jiǎxū,
an edict stated:
"Of the eight policies of a ruler,
food is the foundation.
Therefore, in ancient times, the work of plowing and planting was urgent,
and the effort of using plows and hoes was exerted,
to economize and store provisions
to prepare for disasters.
Thus, even if the harvest was poor, people did not show signs of hunger.
Since the cattle plague,
grain harvests have been continuously poor,
which is largely due to officials' teachings not being effective,
and the Inspectors and Two-Thousand-Picul officials not considering it their responsibility.
Let the commanderies and kingdoms recruit people without land who wish to move to other fertile areas,
and freely permit them to do so.
Upon arrival at their destination,
they shall be granted public land,
hired for farming,
rented seeds,
and loaned farm implements,
with no rent collected for five years,
and taxes waived for three years.
After this, if they wish to return to their hometowns,
they shall not be forbidden."
In summer, the fourth month, on Jǐmǎo,
Dōngpíng Kingdom was divided,
and Xiàn Wáng Cāng's son, Pàishēng, was enfeoffed as Lord of Xíng.
In the sixth month, on Xīnyǒu,
Pèi Wáng Fǔ passed away.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the day dìngwèi (丁未),
an imperial edict stated:
"The law says, 'Those who commit robbery are only to be subjected to flogging, caning, and standing.'
Also, decree B stipulates
that the length and number of lashings are fixed.
Since the major cases of sedition of the past,
torture and interrogation have been mostly cruel,
with methods like drilling and piercing,
causing extreme agony.
Reflecting on such pain and suffering,
my heart is moved with apprehension.
The Shū (書) says, 'Whipping is used for official punishment,'
how could it refer to such practices?
It is fitting that during the autumn and winter months, when legal cases are processed,
a clear prohibition against these methods be established."
In the eighth month, on the day jiǎzǐ (甲子),
Grand Commandant Dèng Biāo (鄧彪) was dismissed,
and Grand Minister of Agriculture Zhèng Hóng (鄭弘) became Grand Commandant.
On the day guǐyǒu (癸酉),
an imperial edict stated:
"My moral transformation is lacking,
and the administration of officials is out of harmony.
The common people are still unenlightened,
and crimes are committed by those below.
Banditry continues unabated,
and frontier towns and houses are not maintained.
Constantly reflecting on all affairs,
I ponder the core reasons,
wishing to work with all gentlemen
to promote this dao.
My heart is deeply troubled;
what means shall I use to express this?
Let the ninth year of Jiànchū (建初) be changed to the first year of Yuánhé (元和).
For those imprisoned in the commanderies, kingdoms, and central government offices, their sentences shall be reduced by one degree, short of death.
They shall not be caned,
but sent to frontier counties;
their wives and children may accompany them,
registered in their new locations.
Those who have committed crimes punishable by death
shall all be conscripted to the silk-moth house;
their women shall suffer palace punishment.
Prisoners sentenced to guǐxīn (鬼薪) or báicàn (白粲) or higher
shall all have their original sentences reduced by one degree,
and be sent to the Ministry of Justice for labor.
Fugitives shall be allowed to redeem themselves,
with varying scales."
On the day dīngyǒu (丁酉),
during the southern inspection tour,
an edict was issued that along the imperial route,
commanderies and counties were not permitted to set up provisions or displays.
The Grand Minister of Works was ordered to personally lead laborers to repair bridges.
Any official who sent envoys to welcome the Emperor
or inquired about his daily life
would be subject to dismissal, if they held a salary of two thousand bushels.
Grain was to be bestowed upon the widowed, orphaned, solitary, and those unable to support themselves,
five hù (斛) per person.
In the ninth month, on the day yǐwèi (乙未),
Prince Zhōng (忠) of Dōngpíng (東平) passed away.
On the day xīncǎo (辛丑),
the Emperor visited Zhānglíng (章陵),
offered sacrifices at the former residence and ancestral temple,
met old acquaintances of the imperial clan,
and bestowed rewards of varying amounts.
In the tenth month of winter, on the day jǐwèi (己未),
the Emperor proceeded to Jiānglíng (江陵),
and ordered the Administrator of Lújiāng (廬江) to offer sacrifices at the Southern Marchmount.
He also ordered the Administrators of Chángshā (長沙) and Línglíng (零陵) to offer sacrifices to King Dìng (定) of Chángshā, Marquis Jié (節) of Chōnglíng (舂陵), and Lord Fú (府) of Yùlín (鬱林).
Returning,
he visited Wǎn (宛).
In the eleventh month, on the day jǐchǒu (己丑),
the imperial carriage returned to the palace,
and rewards were bestowed upon the attendants according to their ranks.
In the twelfth month, on the day rénzǐ (壬子),
an imperial edict stated:
"The Shū (書) says: 'If the father is not benevolent,
the son is not respectful;
if the elder brother is not friendly,
the younger brother is not deferential;
they are not to be allowed to intermingle.'
In the past, during the great cases of seditious speech,
the reach was wide and far,
with one person's crime
leading to the proscription of three generations of relatives,
none of whom could wear a cap and tassel to serve in the imperial court.
If there are talented individuals who are thus rendered useless for life,
I greatly pity them,
for this is not what is meant by 'beginning anew' with them.
Therefore, all those previously proscribed for seditious acts
shall have their prohibitions entirely removed,
to make clear the path to avoiding blame,
but they are not to be allowed to serve in the imperial guard."
In the first month of spring of the second year, on the day yǐyǒu (乙酉),
an imperial edict stated:
"The decree says, 'Those who give birth to a child shall be granted exemption [from taxes or labor],
and shall not be counted for three years.'
Now, all pregnant women
shall be granted three hù (斛) of grain for prenatal care,
their husbands shall be exempted,
and shall not be counted for one year,
and this shall be established as a decree."
The Emperor also issued an edict to the Three Excellencies, saying:
"In the spring, when all things are born and nurtured,
and all myriad things sprout,
it is fitting to aid the burgeoning yang (陽) energy
to cultivate the seasonal things.
Let the relevant officials be ordered that cases not involving crimes punishable by death
shall temporarily not be investigated or examined,
and denunciations by officials or commoners shall not be heard or accepted,
in the hope of calming affairs and bringing peace to the people,
respectfully observing the qi (氣) of Heaven.
This shall revert to normal after the Autumn Equinox.
Common officials often feign external appearances,
seeming right but being wrong;
judging by human affairs, it pleases the ear,
but discussing it in terms of yin (陰) and yang (陽), it harms transformation.
I am deeply disgusted by this,
and greatly troubled by it.
Tranquil officials
are sincere and unadorned;
their daily achievements may seem insufficient,
but their monthly achievements are ample.
Like Liú Fāng (劉方), the Magistrate of Xiāngchéng (襄城),
officials and commoners alike say he causes no trouble.
Although he has not yet performed any extraordinary feats,
he is indeed very close to this ideal.
I have recently instructed officials of two thousand bushels to uphold leniency and clarity,
yet now wealthy scoundrels practice bribery below,
and corrupt officials pervert the law above,
causing the guilty to go unpunished and the innocent to be punished,
which is extremely rebellious.
To take harshness for discernment,
severity for clarity,
leniency for virtue,
and gravity for might—
if these four are allowed to flourish,
then resentment will arise among the people.
My imperial edicts have been issued numerous times,
and officials have thronged the roads,
yet administration has not improved,
and people are losing their positions.
Where does the fault lie?
Strive to remember the old decrees,
and fulfill my intent."
In the second month, on the day jiǎyín (甲寅),
the Sifèn Calendar (四分歷) was first adopted.
An imperial edict stated:
"Currently, the mountain and river spirits, and other gods who should be honored according to ritual,
have not yet all been appropriately sacrificed to.
Let there be a discussion on increasing and improving the collective sacrifices,
to pray for abundant years."
On the *bǐngchén* day,
the Emperor made an eastern tour of inspection (*xúnshǒu*).
On the *jǐwèi* day,
phoenixes gathered at Féichéng.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor plowed the fields at Dìngtáo.
An edict stated:
"The Sānlǎo
are revered for their age.
Filial piety and brotherly submission
are excellent conduct.
Hardworking farmers
are diligent laborers.
The state greatly commends them.
Let each be granted one bolt of silk,
to encourage agricultural work."
Envoys were dispatched to offer sacrifices to Táng Yáo at the Língtái altar in Chéngyáng.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
the Emperor proceeded to Tài Shān,
and offered a *chái* sacrifice to Dàizōng.
Thirty yellow swans came from the southwest,
passed over the sacrificial altar,
flew northeastward over the palace buildings,
soaring and descending.
The Emperor then proceeded to Fènggāo.
On the *rénshēn* day,
the Emperor offered the ancestral sacrifices to the Five Thearchs at the Míngtáng in Wènshàng.
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
sacrifices were announced and offered to the Two Ancestors and Four Zōngs,
and a great assembly of inner and outer officials was held.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
an edict stated:
"I have toured Dàizōng,
offered *chái* and *wàng* sacrifices to mountains and rivers,
and announced sacrifices at the Míngtáng,
to make manifest the achievements of the ancestors.
Therefore, the descendants of the two kings,
the progeny of the former sages,
the feudal lords of the east serving as guardians,
my paternal uncles and elder brothers,
my middle uncles and younger brothers,
my young sons and grandsons,
all officials and attendant ministers,
all sons of the imperial clan,
those from distant and desolate lands and the four frontiers,
north of the desert,
west of the Cōnglǐng mountains,
〔一０〕and those of the Màonái type,
〔一一〕who have traveled over mountains and waters,
〔一二〕and traversed rugged and perilous terrain,
have all swiftly come to the suburban altars,
〔一三〕to assist in the sacrifice.
The merits and virtues of the ancestors
have extended to my person.
I, the lone one, am empty and full of faults,
yet I have succeeded to the exalted and enlightened position,
〔一四〕and have performed the ablutions and presented the offerings,
feeling ashamed and reverently trembling.
Does not the *Shī Jīng* say: 'If the lord is blessed,
disorder will quickly cease'?
〔一五〕Since the Mandate of Heaven has been followed,
and its spiritual radiance is manifest,
〔一六〕I also wish to renew myself with the gentlemen and officials.
Let there be a great amnesty throughout the empire.
All who have committed crimes and are not supposed to receive amnesty
are hereby absolved.
Bó, Fènggāo, and Yíng
are exempted from this year's land tax and fodder."
On the *wùyín* day,
the Emperor proceeded to Jìnán.
〔一七〕In the third month, on the *jǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor proceeded to Lǔ,
and offered sacrifices at the tomb of Gōng Wáng of Dōnghǎi.
On the *gēngyín* day,
sacrifices were offered to Kǒngzǐ at Quèlǐ,
and to his seventy-two disciples.
Bóchéng Hóu and all the Kǒng clan's men and women were granted silk.
On the *rénchén* day,
the Emperor proceeded to Dōngpíng,
and offered sacrifices at the tomb of Xiàn Wáng.
〔一八〕On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
envoys were dispatched to offer sacrifices at the tombs of the Dìngtáo Tàihòu and Gōng Wáng.
〔一九〕On the *yǐwèi* day,
the Emperor went to Dōng'ē,
then ascended the Tàiháng Shān to the north,
reaching Tiānjǐng Guān.
〔二０〕In the fourth month of summer, on the *yǐsì* day,
a guest star entered Zǐgōng.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
the Emperor sacrificed at the ancestral temple,
〔二一〕and announced sacrifices at Gāomiào.
In the fifth month, on the *wùshēn* day,
an edict stated:
"Recently, phoenixes, yellow dragons, and divine birds have gathered successively in seven commanderies,
some commanderies seeing them twice,
and white ravens, divine sparrows, and sweet dew have frequently arrived.
According to ancestral precedents,
grace should be extended.
Let all officials in the empire be granted titles of nobility,
three ranks each;
the aged, widows, orphans, and the solitary be granted silk,
one bolt each.
The *Jīng* says:
'Do not insult the widowed and orphaned,
be kind to the solitary and helpless.'
Furthermore, let one hundred households of women in Hénán be granted cattle and wine,
and let the entire empire celebrate with a great feast for five days.
Let dukes and ministers and those below them be granted money and silk according to their respective ranks;
and the people of Luòyáng eligible for the feast be granted cloth,
one bolt per household,
and outside the city, three households share one bolt.
Let the current students of the Imperial Academy (Bóshì Yuán Dìzǐ) be granted cloth,
three bolts each.
Let each commandery and state recommend scholars accomplished in the classics (*míngjīng zhě*):
five persons if their population is over one hundred thousand,
three persons if less than one hundred thousand."
Lújiāng was renamed Liù'ān Guó,
and Jiānglíng was restored as Nánjùn.
Wáng Gōng of Jiānglíng was transferred to become Wáng of Liù'ān.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the *gēngzǐ* day,
an edict stated:
"The *Chūnqiū* writing 'the King' in the spring of each month
emphasizes the three orthodoxies,
and shows caution towards the three subtle beginnings.
The legal code states that spring begins in the twelfth month,
and does not permit reporting of prisoners then.
The *Yuèlìng* text after the winter solstice
contains passages about following the rising yang and assisting life,
but no policies about judging prisons or executing punishments.
I have consulted Confucian scholars,
and examined the classics,
and believe that the King's power to grant life or death
should align with the seasonal *qì*.
Therefore, let the laws be revised:
do not report prisoners for execution in the eleventh and twelfth months."
In the ninth month, on the *rénchén* day,
an edict ordered:
"The *tíngbù* where phoenixes and yellow dragons have been seen are exempted from two years of rent and taxes.
Furthermore, men are granted titles of nobility,
two ranks each;
those who first saw them are granted twenty bolts of silk,
those nearby three bolts,
the Grand Administrators (tàishǒu) thirty bolts,
the magistrates (lìng, cháng) fifteen bolts,
and the assistant magistrates (chéng, wèi) half of that.
The *Shī Jīng* says: 'Though I have no virtue to give you,
yet sing and dance.'
Other matters follow the precedent of granting titles."
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
Wáng Kāng of Jìnán and Wáng Yān of Zhōngshān were summoned to participate in the *zhēng* sacrifice.
In the eleventh month of winter, on the *rénchén* day,
the sun reached its southernmost point (winter solstice),
and the passes and bridges were first closed.
In the first month of spring of the third year, on the *yǐyǒu* day,
an edict stated:
"Indeed, he who rules over people
regards the people as parents,
having worries of compassion,
and teachings of loyalty and harmony,
and aid that is given with great effort.
Therefore, for infants without parents or relatives,
and those with children who cannot support them,
provide sustenance according to the law."
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
the Emperor made a northern tour of inspection (*xúnshǒu*);
Wáng Kāng of Jìnán, Wáng Yān of Zhōngshān, Wáng Xiàn of Xīpíng, Wáng Gōng of Liù'ān, Wáng Dǎng of Lèchéng, Wáng Bǐng of Huáiyáng, Wáng Shàng of Rènchéng, and Wáng Dìng of Pèi all accompanied him.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
the Emperor plowed the fields at Huái.
In the second month, on the day Rén-yín,
an edict was issued to the Grand Administrators and Chancellors of Chángshān, Wèijùn, Qīnghé, Jùlù, Píngyuán, and Dōngpíng Commanderies, stating:
"We believe that the system of imperial tours
serves to promulgate our teachings,
to ensure uniformity across distant lands,
and to resolve grievances.
Now, 'The four states are without proper governance,
and their good men are not employed.'
We set out on an imperial tour
wishing to personally understand their difficulties and ease.
Previously, we offered sacrifices at the imperial mausoleums,
then performed distant sacrifices to Huá and Huò mountains,
and erected a pyre on Dàizōng,
praying for blessings for the people.
Now we are going to perform rites at Chángshān,
then proceed north,
passing through Wèijùn,
and via Píngyuán.
Ascending and treading upon the dikes and embankments,
we inquired of the elders,
all of whom said, 'Before the Biàn Gate was constructed,
the deep areas became vast pools,
while the shallow areas were muddy quagmires.'
Reflecting on the former emperors' virtue in toiling for the people,
laying foundations for long-term plans,
and restoring Yǔ's grand enterprise,
their sagely deeds flowed widely,
even to the ends of the sea.
We are much ashamed that we have not been able to achieve the same.
The Monthly Ordinances state that
in early spring, one should carefully examine hills and lands for what is suitable.
Now, there is still much fertile land
that has not been reclaimed or cultivated.
Let all of it be distributed to the poor,
providing them with grain and seeds,
to ensure the full utilization of the land's potential,
and prevent idleness.
In all counties and towns we pass through,
permit half of this year's land tax to be remitted,
to encourage the efforts of the farmers."
On the day Yǐ-chǒu,
an edict was issued to the Palace Attendant Imperial Censor and the Minister of Works, stating:
"It is now spring.
In places we pass through, there must be no felling or killing of anything.
If carriages can be diverted,
divert them;
if outrider horses can be unharnessed,
unharness them.
The Odes say:
'Those dense reeds by the path,
let no cattle or sheep trample them.'
According to the Rites,
if a ruler fells a single plant or tree out of season,
it is called unfilial.
People know how to conform to men,
but do not know how to conform to Heaven.
Let this intention of Ours be clearly proclaimed."
On the day Wù-chén,
the imperial retinue proceeded to Zhōngshān,
and envoys were dispatched to offer sacrifices to the Northern Marchmount
and pass beyond the Great Wall.
On the day Guǐ-yóu,
the imperial retinue returned to Yuánshì,
and offered sacrifices to Guāngwǔ and Xiǎnzōng in the main hall of the county residence;
the next day, sacrifices were again offered to Xiǎnzōng in the Shǐshēng Hall,
all with music.
In the third month, on the day Bǐng-zǐ,
an edict ordered the Magistrate of Gāoyì to offer sacrifices to Guāngwǔ at the platform where he ascended the throne.
The corvée and taxes of Yuánshì were remitted for seven years.
On the day Jǐ-mǎo,
the imperial retinue proceeded to Zhào.
On the day Gēng-chén,
sacrifices were offered to Fángshān in Língshòu.
On the day Xīn-mǎo,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
Those accompanying the tour were granted rewards, each according to their rank.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Bǐng-yín,
Grand Commandant Zhèng Hóng was dismissed,
and Grand Minister of Agriculture Sòng Yóu became Grand Commandant.
In the fifth month, on the day Bǐng-zǐ,
Minister of Works Dìwǔ Lún was dismissed,
and Grand Coachman Yuán Ān became Minister of Works.
In autumn, the eighth month, on the day Yǐ-chǒu,
the imperial retinue proceeded to Ānyì
to inspect the salt lakes.
In the ninth month,
the imperial retinue returned from Ānyì.
In winter, the tenth month,
Běihǎi King Jī passed away.
The Shāodāng Qiāng rebelled
and plundered Lǒngxī.
In this year,
Bān Chāo, Protector General of the Western Regions, attacked and beheaded the King of Shūlè.
In the first year of Zhānghé, spring, the third month,
Fù Yù, Colonel Protector of the Qiāng, pursued and attacked the rebellious Qiāng
and died in battle.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Bǐng-zǐ,
an order was issued that prisoners in commanderies, kingdoms, and central government offices whose crimes merited death should have their sentences reduced by one degree
and be sent to garrison Jīnchéng.
In the sixth month, on the day Wù-chén,
Minister over the Masses Huán Yú was dismissed.
On the day Guǐ-mǎo,
Minister of Works Yuán Ān became Minister over the Masses,
and Minister of the Household Rèn Kuí became Minister of Works.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Guǐ-mǎo,
Qí King Huàng was found guilty
and demoted to Marquis of Wúhú.
On the day Rén-zǐ,
Huáiyáng King Bǐng passed away.
The Xiānbēi attacked and defeated the Northern Chányú
and beheaded him.
The Shāodāng Qiāng plundered Jīnchéng.
Liú Xū, Colonel Protector of the Qiāng, attacked them
and beheaded their chief.
On the day Rén-xū,
an edict stated:
"We have heard that the virtue of an enlightened ruler
initiates and inspires grand transformations,
promotes and harmonizes peace,
and casts its light across the six directions,
so that all humanity,
without exception, submits and follows,
benevolent winds soar beyond the seas,
and the thunder of might reaches the realm of spirits.
Only then does one respectfully perform bright sacrifices,
receive the blessings of the five fortunes,
and obtain the auspicious omens of submission.
We, with Our lack of virtue,
have received the magnificent legacy of Our ancestors.
Recently, phoenixes have repeatedly gathered,
qílín have arrived together,
sweet dew has descended at night,
auspicious grains have grown abundantly,
and various species of numinous ganoderma
have not ceased throughout the years.
Day and night, We reverently fear High Heaven,
unable to manifest the accomplishments of Our predecessors.
We now change the fourth year of Héyuán to the first year of Zhānghé."
In autumn,
an order was given that in this month, the elderly should be cared for,
walking sticks issued,
and congee and other foods provided.
In addition, two high-ranking elders should each be granted one bolt of cloth and silk,
to be used for fermented liquor and cheese.
Death row prisoners who violated the law before the amnesty on Bǐng-zǐ but were apprehended and imprisoned afterward,
shall all have their death sentences commuted,
not be flogged,
and be sent to garrison Jīnchéng.
In the eighth month, on the day Guǐ-yóu,
the imperial retinue began a southern tour.
On the day Rén-wǔ,
envoys were dispatched to offer sacrifices to Empress Zhāolíng in Xiǎohuáng Park.
On the day Jiǎ-shēn,
Rènchéng King Hú was summoned to Suīyáng.
On the day Wù-zǐ,
the imperial retinue proceeded to Liáng.
On the day Jǐ-chǒu,
envoys were dispatched to offer sacrifices at Pèigāo Grand Temple
and the Fēngfúyú Altar.
On the day Yǐ-wèi,
the imperial retinue proceeded to Pèi,
offered sacrifices at the mausoleum of Xiàn King,
and summoned Dōnghǎi King Zhèng for a meeting.
On the last day of Yǐ-wèi,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the ninth month, on the day Gēng-zǐ,
the imperial retinue proceeded to Péngchéng;
Dōnghǎi King Zhèng, Pèi King Dìng, and Rènchéng King Shàng all accompanied him.
On the day Xīn-hài,
the imperial retinue proceeded to Shòuchūn.
On the day Rén-zǐ,
an edict ordered that prisoners in commanderies, kingdoms, and central government offices whose crimes merited death should have their sentences reduced by one degree
and be sent to garrison Jīnchéng;
those who committed crimes punishable by exceptional death
were all to be recruited and sent to the silkworm chamber;
women were to be subjected to castration;
those imprisoned for crimes such as grand theft or white rice theft and above
were to have their sentences reduced by one degree
and be sent to the Ministry of Justice for labor.
Those who had fled were allowed to redeem themselves: twenty bolts of silk for death sentences,
seven bolts for crimes from amputation of the right foot to shaving of the head, neck-ironing, and forced labor as a city guard or pestle-pounder,
and three bolts for forced labor as a complete city guard to working for the Ministry of Justice;
officials and common people who had committed crimes but had not yet been discovered,
and who reported themselves upon the arrival of the imperial edict,
were to pay half of the redemption fee.
Fùlíng Marquis Yán was reinstated as Fùlíng King.
On the day Jǐ-wèi,
the imperial retinue proceeded to Rǔyīn.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Bǐng-zǐ,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
Wūlánchú and others of the Northern Xiōngnú surrendered with their forces.
In this year,
Bān Chāo, Protector General of the Western Regions, attacked Shāchē
and greatly defeated it.
The state of Yuèzhī sent envoys to offer húbá and shīzǐ.
In the second year, spring, the first month,
Jìnán King Kāng, Fùlíng King Yán, and Zhōngshān King Yān came to court.
In the second month, on the day Rénchén, the Emperor passed away in the Qián-diàn of Zhāngdé Palace,
aged thirty-three.
His final edict stipulated that no sleeping temple should be erected for him,
following the regulations of the previous emperor.
A commentary states: Wèi Wéndì said,
“Míngdì was meticulous,
Zhāngdì was a benign elder.”
Zhāngdì knew well that people were weary of Míngdì's harshness and severity,
so he acted with leniency and generosity.
Moved by Chén Chǒng's righteousness,
he abolished cruel punishments.
Deeply loving the common people,
he issued an edict on prenatal care.
He served the Empress Dowager Míngdé,
devoting himself to filial piety.
He partitioned renowned prefectures,
to elevate and establish his close relatives.
He equalized labor services and simplified taxes,
and the people benefited from his blessings.
Moreover, he embodied loyalty and magnanimity,
and adorned them with ritual and music.
Therefore, his vassal states were in harmony,
and his many lords showed virtue and humility.
To call him a benign elder,
is it not appropriate!
During his thirteen-year reign,
the auspicious signs reported by commanderies and states,
which matched the diagrams and texts, numbered in the hundreds of thousands.
Ah, how glorious!
A eulogy says: Sùzōng was majestic and dignified,
his nature was benevolent and gentle.
How profound was his imperial virtue,
truly embodying depth.
He patronized arts and literature,
and deliberated on laws and rituals.
He pondered and practiced the imperial way,
promoting this lasting grandeur.
Scholarly halls offered songs,
and military outposts stood empty of foes.
The climate was timely and propitious,
his governance peaceful and the people wealthy.
Annals of Xiàohé and Xiàoshāng, Chapter Four.
Emperor Xiàohé's personal name was Zhào,
he was Sùzōng's fourth son.
His mother, Consort Liáng,
was slandered by Empress Dòu,
and died of grief.
Empress Dòu adopted the Emperor as her own son.
In the seventh year of Jiànchū,
he was established as Crown Prince.
In the second month of the second year of Zhānghé, on the day Rénchén,
he ascended the imperial throne,
aged ten.
The Empress was honored as Empress Dowager,
and the Empress Dowager presided over the court.
In the third month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
Huáiyáng was renamed Chén-guó,
Chǔ-jùn was renamed Péngchéng-guó,
Xīpíng became Rǔnán-jùn,
and Liù'ān was restored as Lújiāng-jùn.
The posthumous edict moved Wáng Xiàn of Xīpíng to be Wáng of Chén,
and Wáng Gōng of Liù'ān to be Wáng of Péngchéng.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Emperor Xiàozhāng was buried at Jìnglíng.
On the day Gēngxū,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict stating:
“The late Emperor, with his sagely wisdom,
upheld the supreme virtues and essential ways of his ancestors,
bringing peace and tranquility to the realm,
and prosperity to all affairs.
Now, the Emperor is young,
and in mourning;
I shall assist him in governing.
Externally, there are great states and worthy kings serving as barriers,
and internally, there are dukes, ministers, and grand masters governing the court.
I shall receive their accomplishments with deference;
what cause for worry is there!
However, during a period of preserving established order,
there must be an inner assistant to participate in deliberations and judgments.
The Palace Attendant Dòu Xiàn,
my elder brother,
possesses both conduct and ability,
and is especially devoted in loyalty and filial piety.
He was highly regarded by the late Emperor
and personally received his final edict;
he should assist in this duty according to old regulations.
Dòu Xiàn steadfastly adheres to humility and deference,
his integrity cannot be compromised.
Now, providing for the two palaces
and guarding left and right,
his duties are already heavy;
he should not be burdened again with governmental affairs.
Therefore, the former Grand Commandant Dèng Biāo,
from a family of great merit,
whose three rejections made him even more esteemed,
to whom the whole empire attributes benevolence,
and who is the foremost among worthy men,
was praised and honored by the late Emperor,
who wished to promote transformation through him.
Now, Dèng Biāo is intelligent and robust;
he can be called a seasoned and venerable elder.
Let Dèng Biāo be appointed Grand Tutor,
bestowed the title Marquis within the Pass,
and oversee the affairs of the Masters of Writing.
All officials shall heed his command,
and I shall endeavor to focus on my inner position.
Alas!
May the various dukes strive to lead the multitude of officials,
each performing their duties,
cherishing and nurturing the common people,
and pacifying them with moderation and harmony,
thus fulfilling my intention.”
On the day Xīnyǒu,
the officials presented a memorial:
“Emperor Xiàozhāng greatly promoted grand endeavors,
his virtuous transformations universally permeated,
his concern was for the common folk,
and his thoughts lingered on agriculture.
His civilizing influence extended to distant customs,
his military might spread throughout the borders,
wherever there were human faces,
there was no thought but submission.
How majestic and expansive,
none can compare in greatness.
The Odes of Zhōu say: ‘How solemn are the clear temples,
reverent and harmonious are the august ministers.’
We request to honor his temple as Sùzōng,
and together advance the Dance of Martial Virtue.”
An imperial decree stated:
“Granted.”
On the day Guǐhài,
Wáng Xiàn of Chén, Wáng Gōng of Péngchéng, Wáng Dǎng of Lèchéng, Wáng Yǎn of Xiàpī, and Wáng Chàng of Liáng, began to proceed to their states.
In summer, in the fourth month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
they paid respects at the Gāo-miào.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
they paid respects at the Shìzǔ-miào.
On the day Wùyín,
an edict stated:
“In the past, Emperor Xiàowǔ brought about the punishment of the Hú and Yuè,
and thus temporarily seized the profits from salt and iron
to fund the expenses of his armies.
Since the Restoration,
the Xiongnú have not submitted,
and in the late Yǒngpíng era,
military campaigns were resumed.
When the late Emperor ascended the throne,
he endeavored to reduce labor services,
yet still thought deeply and far-sightedly,
not forgetting danger in times of peace.
He explored old regulations
and reinstated the collection of salt and iron
to guard against unforeseen events
and secure the borders.
However, many officials were not good,
often losing their opportune advantage,
thus violating the Emperor's intention.
The late Emperor regretted this,
and therefore left a final instruction to the commanderies and states to abolish the salt and iron prohibitions,
allowing the people to boil and cast,
paying tax to the county officials as before.
Let the Regional Inspectors and the Officials of Two Thousand Stone [dàn] be strictly instructed
to comply with the sagely decree,
to diligently promote virtuous transformation,
and to proclaim it throughout the realm,
so that my intention is clearly understood.”
In the fifth month,
there was a drought in the capital.
Huán Yù, the Shàofǔ of Chánglè Palace, was commanded to lecture inside the palace.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the day Yǐhài,
the Palace Attendant Dòu Xiàn was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry
to attack the Northern Xiongnú.
The kingdom of Ānxī sent envoys to present lions and fúbá (mythical beasts).
In the spring of the first year of Yǒngyuán, in the third month, on the day Jiǎchén,
it was first decreed that palace gentlemen who were appointed by edict could concurrently hold positions as Cán and Wèi,
with their rank equivalent to their original office.
In summer, in the sixth month,
General of Chariots and Cavalry Dòu Xiàn departed from Jīlù-sài,
General Dèng Hóng of Dùliáo departed from Guōyáng-sài,
and the Southern Chányú departed from Mǎnyí-gǔ.
They engaged the Northern Xiongnú in battle at Jīluò-shān,
and utterly defeated them.
They pursued them to Sīqú Bǐdī-hǎi.
Dòu Xiàn then ascended Yànrán-shān,
carved an inscription to commemorate his achievement, and returned.
The Northern Chányú sent his younger brother, the Right Wēnyúqúdī-wáng,
to present a tribute memorial.
In autumn, in the seventh month, on the day Yǐwèi,
Kuàijī Mountain collapsed.
In the intercalary month, on the day bǐngzǐ,
an edict stated:
“The Xiōngnú have rebelled
and caused harm for a long time.
Relying on the spiritual power of our ancestors,
our armies have achieved victory.
The vile enemies have been shattered;
their courts have been swept clean.
Conscription for service is no longer needed,
and the land for ten thousand lǐ is clear and tranquil.
This is not something I, a small and insignificant person, could have accomplished.
Let the relevant officials follow the old statutes,
make declarations of this achievement, and offer sacrifices,
to manifest these glorious deeds.”
In the ninth month, on the day gēngshēn,
Dòu Xiàn, General of Chariots and Cavalry, was made Grand General,
and Liú Shàng, Central Internuncio, was made General of Chariots and Cavalry.
In winter, the tenth month,
an order was issued to the commanderies and kingdoms for those sentenced to penal servitude to be transferred to work in military camps.
For those who had been exiled beyond the frontier,
even if their sentences were not yet completed,
all were pardoned and allowed to return to their fields and homes.
On the day gēngzǐ,
Yán, Prince of Fùlíng, passed away.
In this year,
there were nine major floods in the commanderies and kingdoms.
In the second year, spring, the first month, on the day dīngchǒu,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
In the second month, on the day rénwǔ,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the day jǐhài,
the offices of Commendatory Commandant of the Dependent States of Xīhé and Shàngjùn were re-established.
In summer, the fifth month, on the day gēngxū,
Tàishān Commandery was divided to form the Kingdom of Jìběi;
Lèchéng, Zhuōjùn, and Bóhǎi Commanderies were divided to form the Kingdom of Héjiān.
On the day bǐngchén,
Shòu, the Imperial Younger Brother, was enfeoffed as Prince of Jìběi;
Kāi was enfeoffed as Prince of Héjiān;
Shū was enfeoffed as Prince of Chéngyáng;
Cè, son of the late Prince Bǐng of Huáiyáng, was resealed as Prince of Chángshān.
Money and cloth were bestowed upon dukes, ministers, and below, down to subordinate clerks, each according to their rank.
On the day jǐwèi,
Vice-Colonel Yán Pán was dispatched to campaign against the Northern Xiōngnú,
and seized the territory of Yīwúlú.
On the day dīngmǎo,
Wújì, son of the late Prince Huǎng of Qí, was resealed as Prince of Qí;
Wēi, son of Prince Mù of Běihǎi, was resealed as Prince of Běihǎi.
The Former and Latter Kings of Chēshī both sent their sons to serve at court.
The Kingdom of Yuèzhī dispatched troops to attack Bān Chāo, Protector General of the Western Regions,
and Chāo defeated and subjugated them.
In the sixth month, on the day xīnmǎo,
Yān, Prince of Zhōngshān, passed away.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day yǐmǎo,
Grand General Dòu Xiàn moved out to garrison Liángzhōu.
In the ninth month,
the Northern Xiōngnú sent an envoy to declare submission.
In winter, the tenth month,
Acting Central Internuncio Bān Gù was dispatched to return the greetings of the Southern Chányú.
The Left Gǔlí King, Shīzi, was dispatched
out of Jīlù Pass,
to attack the Northern Xiōngnú north of Héyún,
and inflicted a great defeat upon them.
In the third year, spring, the first month, on the day jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor underwent the capping ceremony for adulthood.
Princes, dukes, generals, special advisors,
officials of the second thousand-picul rank, marquises, and descendants of the imperial clan residing in the capital and attending court were granted gold;
generals, grand masters, palace attendants, and retainers were granted silk.
The common people were granted noble ranks, millet, and silk, each according to their circumstances,
and there was a grand feast for five days.
In the commanderies and kingdoms, capital officials allowed those imprisoned for capital crimes to redeem themselves with silk;
down to those who had committed crimes against the state or were fugitives,
each according to their circumstances.
On the day gēngchén,
the common people of the capital were granted a feast,
and one bolt of cloth for every two households.
In the second month,
Grand General Dòu Xiàn dispatched Left Colonel Gěng Kuí out of Jūyán Pass,
to besiege the Northern Chányú at Jīnwēi Mountain,
and inflicted a great defeat upon them,
capturing his mother, the Yānzhī.
In summer, the sixth month, on the day xīnmǎo,
Princess Bǐyáng, mother of the Empress Dowager, was honored
as Grand Princess.
On the day xīnchǒu,
Zhǒng, Prince of Fùlíng, passed away.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day guǐwèi,
the imperial cortege journeyed to Cháng'ān.
An edict stated:
“The Northern Dí have been destroyed,
their eminent kings have submitted one after another,
and the various kingdoms of the Western Regions
have sent hostages and pledged allegiance.
Is this not due to the great achievements of our ancestors, who enlightened and brought forth brilliant glory?
Awake and asleep, I sigh
as I recall the former capital.
Therefore, let money and silk be bestowed upon officials from the two-thousand-picul rank and below, and the sanlǎo and official retinues in the places visited,
each according to their rank;
and for widows, widowers, orphans, the childless elderly, the seriously ill, and the poor who cannot sustain themselves, millet,
three hù per person.”
In the eleventh month, on the day guǐmǎo,
sacrifices were offered at the High Temple,
followed by ceremonies at the Eleven Imperial Tombs.
An edict stated:
“Among the meritorious officials of Gāozǔ,
Xiāo and Cáo were foremost,
and it was decreed that their lineage should not be extinguished through generations.
Cáo, the Minister, whose descendant was the Marquis of Róngchéng, had no heir.
When I looked from the east gate of Chánglíng,
I saw the mounds of these two ministers.
Reflecting on their distant loyalty,
I am always moved.
Loyalty and righteousness receiving favor
is common to ancient and modern times.
Let an envoy be dispatched to offer sacrifices with a middle-rank animal,
and let the Grand Master of Ceremonies seek out a suitable close relative to be adopted as heir,
to be enfeoffed once prosperity returns,
to manifest their achievements.”
In the twelfth month,
the offices of Protector General of the Western Regions, Cavalry Commandant, and Wǔjǐ Colonel were re-established.
On the day gēngchén,
upon returning from Cháng'ān,
the sentences of penal laborers who accompanied the imperial carriage were reduced by five months.
In the fourth year, spring, the first month,
Yúchújiàn, the Right Gǔlí King of the Northern Xiōngnú, declared himself Chányú,
and sought to surrender at the frontier.
Grand General Dòu Xiàn's Left Colonel Gěng Kuí was dispatched to present him with the seal and ribbon.
In the third month, on the day guǐchǒu,
Yuán Ān, Minister of Works, passed away.
In the intercalary month, on the day dīngchǒu,
Dīng Hóng, Grand Minister of Ceremonies, became Minister of Works.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day bǐngchén,
Grand General Dòu Xiàn returned to the capital.
In the sixth month, on the first day wùxū,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the day bǐngchén,
there were thirteen earthquakes in the commanderies and kingdoms.
Dòu Xiàn secretly plotted regicide.
On the day gēngshēn,
the emperor visited the Northern Palace.
An edict ordered the arrest of Guō Huáng, Colonel of Archers, a member of Dòu Xiàn's faction,
and his son Jǔ, Attendant at Court,
and Dèng Xí, Commandant of the Guards,
and Xí's younger brother Léi, Colonel of Infantry.
All were imprisoned and died.
An Imperial Messenger and Household Superintendent was sent
to confiscate Dòu Xiàn's Grand General's seal and ribbon.
Dòu Xiàn and his younger brothers Dǔ and Jǐng were sent to their respective kingdoms,
and all committed suicide upon arrival.
That summer,
there was a drought
and a locust plague.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day jǐchǒu,
Sòng Yóu, Grand Commandant, committed suicide due to his involvement with Dòu Xiàn's faction.
In the eighth month, on the day xīnhài,
Rèn Kuí, Minister of Works, passed away.
On the day guǐchǒu,
Yǐn Mù, Grand Minister of Agriculture, became Grand Commandant,
and was put in charge of the affairs of the Masters of Writing.
On the day dīngsì,
money and grain were bestowed upon dukes, ministers, and below, down to subordinate clerks, each according to their rank.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day jǐhài,
Liú Fāng, Court Supervisor, became Minister of Works.
In the twelfth month, on the day rénchén,
an edict stated:
“This year, the autumn harvest in the commanderies and kingdoms was damaged by drought and locusts.
Therefore, for those with damages of forty percent or more, do not collect land tax or fodder tax;
for those with lesser damages,
deduct them according to the actual situation.”
The Mán people of Wǔlíng, Línglíng, and Lǐzhōng rebelled.
The Shāodāng Qiāng plundered Jīnchéng.
In the fifth year, spring, the first month, on the day yǐhài,
sacrifices were offered to the Five Emperors at the Míngtáng,
followed by an ascent to the Língtái,
to observe meteorological phenomena.
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
On the day wùzǐ,
Kàng, Prince of Qiānchéng, passed away.
On the day xīnmǎo,
Wàansuì, the Imperial Younger Brother, was enfeoffed as Prince of Guǎngzōng.
In the second month, on the day wùxū,
an edict ordered the relevant officials to reduce the number of horses in the imperial stables inside and outside the capital, and in the various pastures of Liángzhōu.
From the capital, the detached palaces, fruit orchards, the Imperial Park, and Guǎngchéng Park were all temporarily granted to the poor,
who were allowed to gather and hunt freely,
without paying taxes.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
an edict stated:
"Last year's autumn wheat harvest was small,
and I fear the people may not have enough to eat.
Let the households and population numbers of those who are especially poor and unable to sustain themselves be reported.
Previously, when commanderies and kingdoms reported poor people,
they based their assessment on clothing, shoes, cauldrons, and sieves,
and the powerful and wealthy gained from this.
The edict was intended to ascertain the facts
and provide assistance,
but the chief officials failed to personally attend to it.
Instead, they repeatedly summoned and gathered people,
causing them to miss their farm work
and troubling the common folk.
If anyone commits such an offense again,
officials of two thousand *shí* salary and above shall be held accountable first."
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Grand Tutor Dèng Biāo passed away.
On the *wǔwǔ* day,
there was an earthquake in Lǒngxī.
In the third month, on the *wǔzǐ* day,
an edict stated:
"Selecting good talent
is the foundation of governance.
Distinguishing abilities and conduct
must rely on local communities.
However, when commanderies and kingdoms recommend officials,
they do not exercise discretion.
Therefore, the former emperor explicitly instructed those in charge
to test them in their positions
before they could be selected.
Furthermore, for those with exceptionally outstanding virtue and conduct
who do not require prior official experience,
their circumstances should be separately reported.
Since this was announced,
nine years have passed,
but officials of two thousand *shí* salary have not complied,
acting according to their own preferences.
The *Sīlì* and *Cìshǐ* have utterly failed to investigate this.
Now that a new amnesty has been granted,
this instruction is hereby re-emphasized.
Should anyone violate it hereafter,
their punishment will be made clear.
Those in office who do not concern themselves with selection,
and those who supervise and inspect who do not consider uncovering wrongdoing a responsibility,
are not limited to the provinces and commanderies.
Thus, many officials are not the right people for their posts.
The common people suffer from the harm of treachery and evil
because the laws are not enforced."
On the *gēngyín* day,
envoys were dispatched to tour among the poor,
to verify the displaced and destitute,
and to open granaries to distribute grain in over thirty commanderies.
In summer, fourth month, on the *rénzǐ* day,
Zhǒng's elder brother, Fáng, the Prince of Fùlíng, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Fùlíng.
In the sixth month, on the *dīngyóu* day,
three commanderies and kingdoms experienced hail.
In autumn, ninth month, on the *xīnyǒu* day,
Wànsuì, Prince of Guǎngzōng, passed away.
Having no son,
the kingdom was abolished.
Yúchújiān, the *Chányú* of the Xiongnu, rebelled.
Zhōnglángjiàng Rèn Shàng was dispatched to suppress and destroy him.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
commandery and county officials were ordered to encourage the people to store vegetables and other foods to supplement the five grains.
If any official lands had ponds,
the people were allowed to gather from them,
and no rent or taxes were to be collected for two years.
In winter, tenth month, on the *xīnwèi* day,
Grand Commandant Yǐn Mù passed away.
