the Commandant of Archers, Mǎ Rìdī, became Grand Commandant.
In the eighth month,
the Eight Colonels of the Western Garden were first established.
The Minister of Works Xǔ Xiāng was dismissed,
and the Minister of Education Dīng Gōng became Minister of Works.
The Minister of the Imperial Household, Liú Hóng of Nányáng, became Minister of Education.
The Commandant of the Guard Dǒng Chóng became General of Agile Cavalry.
In the ninth month,
the Southern Chányú rebelled,
and with the Baíbō bandits, plundered Hédōng.
The Colonel-Director Mèng Yì was dispatched to lead the Cavalry Commandant Gōngsūn Zàn to suppress the Yúyáng bandits Zhāng Chún and others.
In winter, the tenth month,
(On *rénwǔ*, a pagoda tree behind the imperial hall uprooted itself and stood upside down.) The Yellow Turbans of Qīng and Xú Prefectures rose again,
and plundered commanderies and counties.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the Emperor proclaimed himself
"Supreme General" (*Wúshàng Jiāngjūn*),
and displayed his troops at Pínglè Guān.
In the eleventh month,
the Liángzhōu bandit Wáng Guó besieged Chéncāng.
The General of the Right, Huángfǔ Sōng, went to relieve it.
The Colonel of the Lower Army, Bào Hóng, was dispatched to suppress the Gépí Yellow Turbans.
The Bǎnshǔn Mán of Bājùn rebelled.
The Detached Sima of the Upper Army, Zhào Jǐn, was dispatched to suppress and pacify them.
Gōngsūn Zàn battled Zhāng Chún at Shímén,
and thoroughly defeated him.
In this year,
inspectors (*cìshǐ*) were reformed,
and new governors (*mù*) were established.
In the sixth year, spring, the second month,
the General of the Left, Huángfǔ Sōng, thoroughly defeated Wáng Guó at Chéncāng.
In the third month,
the Governor of Yōuzhōu, Liú Yú, offered a reward for and executed the Yúyáng bandit Zhāng Chún.
The Colonel of the Lower Army, Bào Hóng, was imprisoned and died.
In summer, the fourth month, on the first day, *bǐngwǔ*,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Grand Commandant Mǎ Rìdī was dismissed,
and the Governor of Yōuzhōu, Liú Yú, became Grand Commandant.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
the Emperor passed away in the Jiādé Hall of the Southern Palace,
at the age of thirty-four.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
the Imperial Prince Biàn ascended the imperial throne,
at the age of seventeen.
The Empress was honored as Empress Dowager,
and the Empress Dowager presided over court affairs.
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire,
and the era name was changed to Guāngxī.
The Imperial Brother Xié was enfeoffed as King of Bóhǎi.
The General of the Rear, Yuán Wěi, became Grand Tutor,
and together with the General-in-Chief Hé Jìn, participated in managing the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.
The Colonel of the Upper Army, Jiǎn Shuò, was imprisoned and died.
In the fifth month, on the *xīnsì* day,
the General of Agile Cavalry, Dǒng Chóng, was imprisoned and died.
In the sixth month, on the *xīnhài* day,
Empress Xiàorén Dǒng passed away.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Emperor Xiàolíng was buried at Wénlíng.
There was rain.
In autumn, the seventh month,
King Zhōng of Gānlíng died.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Empress Xiàorén was reburied at Shènlíng in Héjiān.
King Xié of Bóhǎi was transferred and enfeoffed as King of Chénliú.
The Minister of Works Dīng Gōng was dismissed.
In the eighth month, on the *wùchén* day,
the Regular Palace Attendants Zhāng Ràng, Duàn Guī, and others killed the General-in-Chief Hé Jìn.
Thereupon, the Colonel-Director of the Imperial Guards, Yuán Shù, burned the Eastern and Western Palaces
and attacked the eunuchs.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
Zhāng Ràng, Duàn Guī, and others abducted the Young Emperor and the King of Chénliú, fleeing to the Déyáng Hall of the Northern Palace.
Wú Kuāng, a commander of Hé Jìn's forces, fought the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Hé Miáo, below the Zhūquè Gate,
and Hé Miáo was defeated and beheaded.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
the Intendant of the Capital, Yuán Shào, led troops to apprehend the false Intendant of the Capital, Fán Líng, the Mayor of Hénán, Xǔ Xiāng, and various eunuchs,
beheading them all, regardless of age.
Zhāng Ràng, Duàn Guī, and others again abducted the Young Emperor and the King of Chénliú, fleeing to Xiǎopíngjīn.
The Minister Lú Zhí pursued Zhāng Ràng, Duàn Guī, and others,
beheading several people,
while the rest threw themselves into the river and died.
The Emperor and King Xié of Chénliú walked several *lǐ* through the night, following flickering lights,
and found a commoner's open carriage,
which they both rode in.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
they returned to the palace.
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire,
and Guāngxī was changed to Zhāoníng.
The Governor of Bìngzhōu, Dǒng Zhuó, killed the Commander of the Guards, Dīng Yuán.
The Minister of Education Liú Hóng was dismissed,
and Dǒng Zhuó made himself Minister of Education.
In the ninth month, on the *jiǎxū* day,
Dǒng Zhuó deposed the Emperor as King of Hóngnóng.
It had rained since the sixth month,
continuing until this month.
A discussion states: The Qin Annals recounts how Zhào Gāo deceived the Second Emperor,
pointing to a deer and calling it a horse.
Zhào Zhōng and Zhāng Ràng likewise tricked Emperor Líng, preventing him from ascending to a high place for observation.
Thus it is known that those who bring about ruin arrive at the same end.
However, Emperor Líng, in his "spirit," was superior!
A eulogy states: Emperor Líng rode in a cart,
entrusting his body to eunuch villains.
The signs of ruin were fully prepared,
and the *Xiǎo Yǎ* was entirely lacking.
Deer in frost and dew,
thereby nested in the palace guards.
Annals of Emperor Xiàoxiàn, Ninth
Emperor Xiàoxiàn's given name was Xié,
the middle son of Emperor Líng.
His mother, Consort Wáng,
was harmed by Empress Hé.
In the sixth year of Zhōngpíng, fourth month,
the Young Emperor ascended the throne and
enfeoffed this Emperor as King of Bóhǎi,
then transferred his enfeoffment to King of Chénliú.
In the ninth month, on the *jiǎxū* day,
he ascended the imperial throne,
at the age of nine.
The Empress Dowager was moved to Yǒng'ān Palace.
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
Zhāoníng was changed to Yǒnghàn.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Dǒng Zhuó killed the Empress Dowager Hé.
Initially, an order was issued that there should be six each of the Palace Attendants and Palace Attendants of the Yellow Gates.
From the dukes and ministers down to the families of the Yellow Gates Attendants, one person per family was granted the title of Attendant,
to fill various posts previously held by eunuchs,
and to serve in the palace hall.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
the Grand Commandant Liú Yú was made Grand Minister of War.
Dǒng Zhuó made himself Grand Commandant,
and was granted ceremonial axes and imperial guards.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
the Grand Master of Remonstrance Yáng Biāo became Minister of Education.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the Governor of Yùzhōu, Huáng Wǎn, became Minister of Works.
Envoys were dispatched to offer condolences and sacrifices to the late Grand Tutor Chén Fān, General-in-Chief Dòu Wǔ, and others.
In winter, the tenth month, on the *yǐsì* day,
Empress Língsī was buried.
The Baíbō bandits plundered Hédōng.
Dǒng Zhuó dispatched his general Niú Fǔ to attack them.
In the eleventh month, on the *guǐyǒu* day,
Dǒng Zhuó made himself Chancellor of State.
In the twelfth month, on the *wùxū* day,
the Minister of Works Huáng Wǎn became Grand Commandant,
the Minister of Education Yáng Biāo became Minister of Works,
and the Minister of the Imperial Household Xún Shuǎng became Minister of Education.
The Commandant of Fúfēng was abolished,
and the Protectorate of Hàn'ān was established.
An imperial edict abolished the three era names Guāngxī, Zhāoníng, and Yǒnghàn,
reverting to the sixth year of Zhōngpíng.
In the spring, the first month of the first year of Chūpíng
, the states and commanderies east of the mountains raised armies to suppress Dǒng Zhuó.
On the day Xīnhài,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Dǒng Zhuó killed King Hóngnóng.
The Báibō bandits attacked Dōngjùn.
In the second month, on the day Yǐhài,
Grand Commandant Huáng Wǎn and Minister of the Masses Yáng Biāo were dismissed.
On the day Gēngchén,
Dǒng Zhuó killed the Commander of the City Gates, Wǔ Qióng, and the Commander of the Supervising Army, Zhōu Bì.
Guānglùxūn Zhào Qiān was appointed Grand Commandant,
and Grand Coachman Wáng Yǔn was appointed Minister of the Masses.
On the day Dīnghài,
the capital was moved to Cháng'ān.
Dǒng Zhuó forced the populace of the capital to all move west into the pass
, while he himself remained garrisoned at Bìguī Yuàn.
On the day Rénchén,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
In the third month, on the day Yǐsì,
the imperial carriage entered Cháng'ān
and arrived at Wèiyāng Gōng.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Dǒng Zhuó burned the palaces, temples, and homes in Luòyáng.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Dǒng Zhuó killed Grand Mentor Yuán Wěi and Grand Coachman Yuán Jī
, exterminating their clan.
In the summer, the fifth month,
Minister of Works Xún Shuǎng died.
In the sixth month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Zhǒng Fú was appointed Minister of Works.
Grand Herald Hán Róng, Lesser Treasurer Yīn Xiū, Chief Commandant of Retainers Húmǔ Bān
, Grand Artisan Wú Xiū, and Colonel of Yue Cavalry Wáng Guī were sent to pacify and settle Guāndōng.
Later, General of the Rear Yuán Shù and Administrator of Hénèi Wáng Kuāng each seized and killed them
, only Hán Róng escaped.
Dǒng Zhuó destroyed the wǔzhū coins
and minted smaller coins instead.
In the winter, the eleventh month, on the day Gēngxū,
the planets Saturn, Mars, and Venus converged in Wěi.
In this year
, officials submitted a memorial stating
that Emperors Hé, Ān, Shùn, and Huán had no merits or virtues
and should not be referred to as Zōng (ancestor),
and furthermore, Empresses Gōnghuái, Jìngyǐn, and Gōngmǐn were not of the main legitimate lineage
and should not be referred to as Hòu (empress);
they all requested to remove their honorific titles.
An imperial edict said:
"Granted."
Sūn Jiān killed the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Wáng Ruì
, and also killed the Administrator of Nányáng, Zhāng Zī.
In the spring, the first month of the second year, on the day Xīnchǒu,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
In the second month, on the day Dīngchǒu,
Dǒng Zhuó made himself Grand Preceptor.
Yuán Shù dispatched his general Sūn Jiān to battle Dǒng Zhuó's general Hú Zhěn at Yángrén
, and Zhěn's army was greatly defeated.
Dǒng Zhuó then excavated the imperial tombs in Luòyáng.
In the summer, the fourth month,
Dǒng Zhuó entered Cháng'ān.
In the sixth month, on the day Bǐngxū,
there was an earthquake.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
Minister of Works Zhǒng Fú was dismissed,
and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Chúnyú Jiā of Jǐnán was appointed Minister of Works.
Grand Commandant Zhào Qiān was dismissed,
and Grand Herald Mǎ Rìdī was appointed Grand Commandant.
In the ninth month,
the Chīyóu Banner was seen in Jiǎo and Kàng.
In the winter, the tenth month, on the day Rénxū,
Dǒng Zhuó killed Commandant of the Guards Zhāng Wēn.
In the eleventh month,
the Qīngzhōu Yellow Turbans attacked Tàishān
, and the Administrator of Tàishān Yīng Shào defeated them.
The Yellow Turbans then attacked Bóhǎi
, and Gōngsūn Zàn battled them at Dōngguāng
, again inflicting a great defeat.
In this year
, a person in Chángshā died and revived after a month.
In the spring, the first month of the third year, on the day Dīngchǒu,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
Yuán Shù dispatched his general Sūn Jiān to attack Liú Biǎo at Xiāngyáng
, and Jiān was killed in battle.
Yuán Shào and Gōngsūn Zàn battled at Jièqiáo
, and Zàn's army was greatly defeated.
In the summer, the fourth month, on the day Xīnsì,
Dǒng Zhuó was executed
, and his three clans were exterminated.
Minister of the Masses Wáng Yǔn recorded the affairs of the Masters of Writing
and managed the court administration,
sending envoy Zhāng Zhǒng to soothe and comfort Guāndōng.
The Qīngzhōu Yellow Turbans attacked and killed the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Liú Dài, at Dōngpíng.
The Administrator of Dōngjùn, Cáo Cāo, greatly defeated the Yellow Turbans at Shòuzhāng
, and they surrendered.
In the fifth month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
On the day Dīngwèi,
General Who Attacks the West Huángfǔ Sōng was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry.
Dǒng Zhuó's subordinate generals Lǐ Què, Guō Sì, Fán Chóu, Zhāng Jì, and others rebelled
and attacked the imperial capital.
In the sixth month, on the day Wùwǔ,
Cháng'ān city fell.
Grand Herald Zhǒng Fú, Grand Coachman Lǔ Xù, Grand Herald Zhōu Huàn
, Commander of the City Gates Cuī Liè, and Colonel of Yue Cavalry Wáng Qí all died in battle.
Over ten thousand officials and common people died.
Lǐ Què and the others all appointed themselves generals.
On the day Jǐwèi,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
Lǐ Què killed Inspector of the Capital Region Huáng Wǎn.
On the day Jiǎzǐ
, he killed Minister of the Masses Wáng Yǔn
, exterminating their clans.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
General of the Vanguard Zhào Qiān was appointed Minister of the Masses.
In the autumn, the seventh month, on the day Gēngzǐ,
Grand Commandant Mǎ Rìdī was appointed Grand Mentor
and recorded the affairs of the Masters of Writing.
In the eighth month,
Rìdī and Grand Coachman Zhào Qí were dispatched
, bearing imperial credentials, to soothe and comfort the empire.
General of Chariots and Cavalry Huángfǔ Sōng was appointed Grand Commandant.
Minister of the Masses Zhào Qiān was dismissed.
In the ninth month,
Lǐ Què appointed himself General of Chariots and Cavalry,
Guō Sì General of the Rear,
Fán Chóu General of the Right,
and Zhāng Jì General Who Guards the East.
Jì moved out to garrison Hóngnóng.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Minister of Works Chúnyú Jiā was appointed Minister of the Masses
, and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Yáng Biāo was appointed Minister of Works
, both recording the affairs of the Masters of Writing.
In the winter, the twelfth month,
Grand Commandant Huángfǔ Sōng was dismissed.
Grand Master of Splendid Happiness Zhōu Zhōng was appointed Grand Commandant
and participated in recording the affairs of the Masters of Writing.
In the spring, the first month of the fourth year, on the first day Jiǎyín,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
In the third month,
Yuán Shù killed the Inspector of Yángzhōu, Chén Wēn
, and occupied Huáinán.
The outer eaves of the Xuānpíng Gate in Cháng'ān collapsed on their own.
In the summer, the fifth month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
there was thunder without clouds.
In the sixth month,
there was a great wind in Fúfēng
and hail.
Huàshān collapsed and cracked.
Grand Commandant Zhōu Zhōng was dismissed
, and Grand Coachman Zhū Jùn was appointed Grand Commandant
, recording the affairs of the Masters of Writing.
The Qū Xuān bandits of Xiàpī declared themselves ruler of the world.
There was rain.
Imperial Censor Péi Mào was dispatched to investigate the imperial prisons
and pardon those lightly confined.
In the sixth month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
a "celestial dog" moved to the northwest.
In the ninth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
over forty Confucian scholars were tested.
The highest ranking were granted the position of Lángzhōng,
the next were Princely Palace Attendants,
and the lowest ranking were dismissed. An imperial edict said:
"Confucius lamented 'the lack of instruction'
; without instruction, what one knows is forgotten daily.
Now, elderly Confucians, over sixty years old
, leave their homelands
to seek food and resources
and cannot specialize in their profession.
They enter school as children
and return home empty-handed in old age
, forever relegated to the agricultural fields
, permanently cut off from honor and prospects.
I am deeply saddened by this.
Those who are dismissed according to regulations
are permitted to become Princely Palace Attendants."
In the winter, the tenth month,
ceremonies were held at the Imperial Academy.
The imperial carriage proceeded to the Yǒngfú City Gate
to observe the rites
, and various awards were given to academicians and below.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
A comet appeared in Tiānshì.
Minister of Works Yáng Biāo was dismissed
, and Grand Herald Zhào Wēn was appointed Minister of Works.
Gōngsūn Zàn killed Grand Marshal Liú Yú.
In the twelfth month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
there was an earthquake.
Minister of Works Zhào Wēn was dismissed
, and on the day Yǐsì
, Commandant of the Guards Zhāng Xǐ was appointed Minister of Works.
In this year
, King Róng of Lángyé died.
In the first year of Xīngpíng [194 CE], in spring, the first month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
a great amnesty was declared throughout the empire,
and the era name was changed to Xīngpíng.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Emperor came of age.
In the second month, on the day Rénwǔ,
the Emperor's late mother, Empress Wáng, was posthumously honored with the title Línghuái Hòuhòu.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
she was reinterred at Wénzhāo Líng.
On the day Dīnghài,
the Emperor personally ploughed the ceremonial field.
In the third month,
Hán Suì and Mǎ Téng battled Guō Sì and Fán Chóu at Chángpíng Guān.
Suì and Téng were defeated,
and the Left Colonel of the Internal Affairs, Liú Fàn, and the former Inspector of Yìzhōu, Zhǒng Shào, were killed in action.
In summer, the sixth month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
the four commanderies west of the Hé River in Liángzhōu were separated to form Yōngshì.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
there was an earthquake;
on the day Wùyín,
there was another earthquake.
On the last day of the month, Yǐsì,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Emperor retired to the main palace hall,
suspended military affairs,
and did not attend to governmental matters for five days.
There was a great plague of locusts.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Rénzǐ,
Grand Commandant Zhū Jùn was dismissed.
On the day Wùwǔ,
Grand Minister of Ceremonies Yáng Biāo became Grand Commandant,
and was given authority over the privy purse.
The Three Fǔ suffered a great drought,
lasting from the fourth month until this month.
The Emperor retired to the main palace hall to pray for rain,
and dispatched envoys to Luòyáng
to pardon those lightly imprisoned.
At this time, one hù of grain cost five hundred thousand [coins],
and one hù of beans or wheat cost two hundred thousand [coins].
People resorted to cannibalism,
and white bones lay piled up.
The Emperor ordered Palace Attendant Censor Hóu Wèn to distribute rice and beans from the Grand Granary
to make gruel for the starving,
but the number of deaths did not decrease after days.
The Emperor suspected the relief efforts were fraudulent,
so he personally measured and prepared gruel in front of his imperial seat
and realized it was not real.
He then sent Palace Attendant Liú Ài to reprimand the responsible officials.
Consequently, the Director of the Department of State Affairs and those below him all went to the imperial secretariat to apologize,
and submitted a memorial to arrest Hóu Wèn for investigation.
An imperial edict stated:
"I cannot bear to bring Wèn to justice yet;
he may be flogged fifty times."
After this,
many were saved.
In the eighth month,
the Qiāng of Fēngyì rebelled,
raiding the dependent counties.
Guō Sì and Fán Chóu attacked and defeated them.
In the ninth month,
mulberry trees bore fruit again,
allowing people to eat.
Minister of Works Chúnyú Jiā was dismissed.
In winter, the tenth month,
the city gate of Cháng'ān collapsed of its own accord.
Guard Commander Zhào Wēn was appointed Minister of Works,
and given authority over the Department of State Affairs.
In the twelfth month,
Āndìng and Fúfēng were separated to form Xīnpíng Commandery.
This year,
the Inspector of Yángzhōu, Liú Yáo, battled Sūn Cè, a general of Yuán Shù, at Qū'ā.
Yáo's army was defeated,
and Sūn Cè subsequently occupied Jiāngdōng.
Grand Tutor Mǎ Rìdī died in Shòuchūn.
In the second year, spring, the first month, on the day Guǐchǒu,
a great amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
In the second month, on the day Yǐhài,
Lǐ Jué killed Fán Chóu and then attacked Guō Sì.
In the third month, on the day Bǐngyín,
Lǐ Jué coerced the Emperor to go to his camp,
and burned the palace buildings.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
Noble Lady Fú was established as Empress.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
Guō Sì attacked Lǐ Jué,
and arrows reached the imperial presence.
On this day,
Lǐ Jué moved the Emperor to the northern stronghold.
There was a great drought.
In the fifth month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Lǐ Jué appointed himself Grand Marshal.
In the sixth month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
Zhāng Jì came from Shǎn to reconcile Jué and Sì.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Jiǎzǐ,
the imperial carriage returned eastward.
Guō Sì appointed himself General of Cavalry and Chariots,
Yáng Dìng as General of the Rear,
Yáng Fèng as General Who Rouses Righteousness,
Dǒng Chéng as General Who Pacifies and Assembles,
all accompanying the imperial carriage.
Zhāng Jì was appointed General of Swift Cavalry,
and returned to garrison Shǎn.
In the eighth month, on the day Jiǎchén,
the Emperor visited Xīnfēng.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Wùxū,
Guō Sì ordered his general Wǔ Xí to burn the lodging at the academy that the Emperor was staying at during the night,
threatening the imperial carriage.
Yáng Dìng and Yáng Fèng fought Guō Sì,
and defeated him.
On the day Rényín,
the Emperor visited Huáyīn,
and stayed overnight by the roadside to the south.
That night,
a red qi penetrated the Zǐ Gōng (Purple Palace constellation).
Zhāng Jì rebelled again,
and joined Lǐ Jué and Guō Sì.
In the eleventh month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì, and others pursued the imperial carriage,
and fought at Dōngjiàn.
The imperial army was defeated,
and Grand Master of Ceremonies Dèng Quán, Guard Commander Shìsūn Ruì, Minister of Justice Xuān Bō, Grand Steward Miáo Sì,
Colonel of Infantry Wèi Jié, Palace Attendant Zhū Zhǎn, and Colonel of the Shooting Archers Jǔ Jùn were killed.
On the day Rénshēn,
the Emperor visited Cáoyáng,
and stayed overnight in a field.
Yáng Fèng and Dǒng Chéng led the White Wave leaders Hú Cái, Lǐ Lè, Hán Xiān, and the Southern Xiōngnú Left Worthy King Qù Bēi,
who brought their armies to welcome and escort the Emperor.
They fought Lǐ Jué and others,
and defeated them.
In the twelfth month, on the day Gēngchén,
the imperial carriage finally advanced.
Lǐ Jué and others again pursued and attacked,
and the imperial army suffered a great defeat,
killing and capturing palace women.
Privy Treasurer Tián Fēn, Grand Minister of Agriculture Zhāng Yì, and others were all killed in action.
The Emperor advanced to Shǎn,
and crossed the Hé River at night.
On the day Yǐhài,
the Emperor visited Ānyì.
This year,
Yuán Shào dispatched his general Qū Yì to battle Gōngsūn Zàn at Bāoqīu.
Zàn's army was greatly defeated.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān [196 CE], spring, the first month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
sacrifices were offered to the Supreme Deity at Ānyì,
a great amnesty was declared throughout the empire,
and the era name was changed to Jiàn'ān.
In the second month,
Hán Xiān attacked Guard General Dǒng Chéng.
In summer, the sixth month, on the day Yǐwèi,
the Emperor visited Wénxǐ.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Jiǎzǐ,
the imperial carriage arrived in Luòyáng,
and the Emperor visited the former residence of Chief Palace Attendant Zhào Zhōng.
On the day Dīngchǒu,
sacrifices were offered to the Supreme Deity,
and a great amnesty was declared throughout the empire.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
the Emperor paid respects at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
In the eighth month, on the day Xīnchǒu,
the Emperor visited the Yáng'ān Palace in Nángōng.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
General Who Pacifies the State Zhāng Yáng was appointed Grand Marshal,
Hán Xiān as General,
and Yáng Fèng as General of Cavalry and Chariots.
At this time,
the palace buildings were all burned down,
and the hundred officials cleared away thorns [to find shelter],
leaning against walls.
Each province and commandery held strong armies,
but supplies did not reach [the capital].
The various officials were hungry and destitute,
and the gentlemen of the Department of State Affairs and those below them had to go out to forage for themselves,
some starving to death among the walls,
others killed by soldiers.
On the day Xīnhài,
General Who Guards the East Cáo Cāo personally took up the post of Colonel Director of Retainers,
and was given authority over the Department of State Affairs.
Cáo Cāo killed Palace Attendant Tái Chóng, Gentleman of the Department of State Affairs Féng Shuò, and others.
Guard General Dǒng Chéng was enfeoffed as General Who Supports the State, and Fú Wán and thirteen others were enfeoffed as marquises.
Jǔ Jùn was posthumously granted the title of Administrator of Hóngnóng.
On the day Gēngshēn,
the capital was moved to Xǔ.
On the day Jǐsì,
the Emperor visited Cáo Cāo's camp.
In the ninth month,
Grand Commandant Yáng Biāo and Minister of Works Zhāng Xǐ were dismissed.
In winter, the eleventh month, on the day Bǐngxū,
Cáo Cāo appointed himself Minister of Works,
and acted as General of Cavalry and Chariots.
All officials generally submitted to his authority.
In the second year, spring,
Yuán Shù declared himself Son of Heaven.
In the third month,
Yuán Shào declared himself Grand General.
In the fifth month of summer,
there was a locust plague.
In the ninth month of autumn,
the Hànshǔi overflowed.
That year there was a famine,
and people between the Jiāng and the Huái rivers cannibalized each other.
Yuán Shù killed Chén Wáng Chǒng.
Sūn Cè sent envoys to present tribute.
In the fourth month of summer of the third year,
Yèzhě Péi Mào was sent to lead Zhōnglángjiāng Duàn Wēi to suppress Lǐ Jué,
exterminating his three kin groups.
Lǚ Bù rebelled.
In the eleventh month of winter,
bandits killed Dàsīmǎ Zhāng Yáng.
On the Guǐyǒu day of the twelfth month,
Cáo Cāo attacked Lǚ Bù in Xúzhōu,
and executed him.
In the third month of spring of the fourth year,
Yuán Shào attacked Gōngsūn Zàn at Yìjīng,
and captured him.
Wèijiāngjūn Dǒng Chéng was made Chējìjiāngjūn.
In the sixth month of summer,
Yuán Shù died.
That year,
the positions of Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè and Yòupúshè were first established.
A woman from Wǔlíng died and revived after fourteen days.
In the first month of spring of the fifth year,
Chējìjiāngjūn Dǒng Chéng, Piānjiāngjūn Wáng Fú, and Yuèqíxiàowèi Zhǒng Jí received a secret edict to execute Cáo Cāo,
but the plot was exposed.
On the Rénwǔ day,
Cáo Cāo killed Dǒng Chéng and others,
exterminating their three kin groups.
In the seventh month of autumn,
Imperial Prince Fēng was enfeoffed as Nányáng Wáng.
On the Rénwǔ day,
Nányáng Wáng Fēng passed away.
On the Gēngwǔ day, the first day of the ninth month,
there was a solar eclipse.
An imperial edict ordered the Sāngōng to recommend two candidates of extreme filial piety,
and the Jiǔqīng, Xiàowèi, and Gùn and Guó Shǒuxiàng each to recommend one.
All submitted sealed memorials,
without holding anything back.
Cáo Cāo fought Yuán Shào at Guāndù,
and Shào was defeated and fled.
On the Xīnhài day of the tenth month of winter,
a comet appeared in Dàliáng.
Dōnghǎi Wáng Zhī passed away.
That year,
Sūn Cè died,
and his younger brother Quán inherited his remaining enterprise.
On the Dīngmǎo day, the first day of the (third) [second] month of spring of the sixth year,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the Gēngxū day of the fifth month of summer of the seventh year,
Yuán Shào passed away.
The Kingdom of Yútián presented trained elephants.
That year,
a man from Yuèsuí transformed into a woman.
On the Jǐsì day of the tenth month of winter of the eighth year,
the Gōngqīng first welcomed winter in the Northern Suburb,
and the Zǒngzhāng dance was once again performed with eight rows of dancers.
The office of Sīzhí was first established,
to supervise the central capital officials.
On the Wùyín day of the eighth month of autumn of the ninth year,
Cáo Cāo decisively defeated Yuán Shàng,
pacified Jìzhōu,
and personally assumed the role of Jìzhōumù.
In the tenth month of winter,
a comet appeared in Dōngjǐng.
In the twelfth month,
gold and silk were bestowed upon the Sāngōng and officials below them, each in varying amounts.
From then on, this was bestowed once every three years,
as a regular system.
In the first month of spring of the tenth year,
Cáo Cāo defeated Yuán Tán in Qīngzhōu,
and executed him.
In the fourth month of summer,
the Hēishān bandit Zhāng Yàn led his followers to surrender.
In the ninth month of autumn,
gold and silk were bestowed upon the poorest among the hundreds of officials, each in varying amounts.
In the first month of spring of the eleventh year,
a comet appeared in Běidǒu.
In the third month,
Cáo Cāo defeated Gāo Gàn in Bìngzhōu,
and captured him.
In the seventh month of autumn,
Wǔwēi Tàishǒu Zhāng Měng killed Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Hándān Shāng.
That year,
Xī, the son of the late Lángyá Wáng Róng, was established as Lángyá Wáng.
The eight kingdoms of Qí, Běihǎi, Fùlíng, Xiàpī, Chángshān, Gānlíng, Jì(yīn) [běi], and Píngyuán were all abolished.
In the eighth month of autumn of the twelfth year,
Cáo Cāo decisively defeated the Wūhuán at Liǔchéng,
and executed their Tàdùn.
On the Xīnmǎo day of the tenth month of winter,
a comet appeared in Qúnwěi.
On the Yǐsì day,
the Huángjīn bandits killed Jìnán Wáng Yùn.
In the eleventh month,
Liáodōng Tàishǒu Gōngsūn Kāng killed Yuán Shàng and Yuán Xī.
In the first month of spring of the thirteenth year,
Sītú Zhào Wēn was dismissed.
In the sixth month of summer,
the offices of Sāngōng were abolished,
and the positions of Chéngxiàng and Yùshǐ Dàfū were established.
On the Guǐsì day,
Cáo Cāo himself became Chéngxiàng.
In the seventh month of autumn,
Cáo Cāo marched south against Liú Biǎo.
On the Dīngwèi day of the eighth month,
Guānglùxūn Xī Lǜ became Yùshǐ Dàfū.
On the Rénzǐ day,
Cáo Cāo killed Tàizhōng Dàfū Kǒng Róng,
exterminating his kin group.
That month,
Liú Biǎo died,
and his youngest son Cóng was enthroned.
Cóng surrendered Jīngzhōu to Cáo Cāo.
On the Guǐwèi day, the first day of the tenth month of winter,
there was a solar eclipse.
Cáo Cāo attacked Sūn Quán with a naval force,
and Quán's general Zhōu Yú defeated him at Wūlín and Chìbì.
In the tenth month of winter of the fourteenth year,
there was an earthquake in Jīngzhōu.
On the Yǐsì day, the first day of the second month of spring of the fifteenth year,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the Gēngxū day of the ninth month of autumn of the sixteenth year,
Cáo Cāo fought Hán Suì and Mǎ Chāo at Wèinán,
Suì and the others were utterly defeated,
and Guānxī was pacified.
That year,
Zhào Wáng Shè passed away.
On the Guǐwèi day of the fifth month of summer of the seventeenth year,
Wèiwèi Mǎ Téng was executed,
exterminating his three kin groups.
On the Gēngyín day, the last day of the sixth month,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the seventh month of autumn,
the Wěishǔi and Yǐngshǔi overflowed.
There were locusts.
In the eighth month,
Mǎ Chāo broke through Liángzhōu,
and killed Cìshǐ Wéi Kāng.
On the Gēngxū day of the ninth month,
Imperial Prince Xī was enfeoffed as Jìyīn Wáng,
Yì as Shānyáng Wáng,
Cái as Jìběi Wáng,
and Dūn as Dōnghǎi Wáng.
In the twelfth month of winter,
a comet appeared in Wǔzhūhóu.
On the Gēngyín day of the first month of spring of the eighteenth year,
the Jiǔzhōu of Yǔ Gòng were restored.
On the Bǐngshēn day of the fifth month of summer,
Cáo Cāo established himself as Wèi Gōng,
and was granted the Nine Marks of Favor.
There was heavy flooding.
Zhào Wáng Guī was relocated and enfeoffed as Bólíng Wáng.
That year,
the Jìxīng, Zhènxīng, and Yínghuò planets all entered Tàiwēi.
Péngchéng Wáng Hé passed away.
In the nineteenth year,
in the fourth month of summer,
there was a drought.
In the fifth month,
there was rain and flooding.
Liú Bèi defeated Liú Zhāng,
and occupied Yìzhōu.
In the tenth month of winter,
Cáo Cāo sent general Xiàhóu Yuān to attack Sòng Jiàn at Páohǎn,
and captured him.
On the Dīngmǎo day of the eleventh month,
Cáo Cāo killed Empress Fú Shì,
and exterminated her kin group and the two Imperial Princes.
On the Jiǎzǐ day of the first month of spring of the twentieth year,
Guìrén Cáo Shì was established as Empress.
All men in the realm were granted one rank of nobility,
and those filial and brotherly, or diligent in farming, received two ranks.
Grains were bestowed upon the various princes, marquises, gongs, and qings below, each in varying amounts.
In the seventh month of autumn,
Cáo Cāo conquered Hànzhōng,
and Zhāng Lǔ surrendered.
On the Jiǎwǔ day of the fourth month of summer of the twenty-first year,
Cáo Cāo advanced his title to Wèi Wáng.
On the Jǐhài day, the first day of the fifth month,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the seventh month of autumn,
the Southern Chányú of the Xiōngnú came to court.
That year,
Cáo Cāo killed Lángyá Wáng Xī,
and the kingdom was abolished.
In the sixth month of summer of the twenty-second year,
Chéngxiàng Jūnshī Huá Xīn became Yùshǐ Dàfū.
In winter,
a comet appeared in the northeast.
That year, there was a great epidemic.
In the twenty-third year, in the first month, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
the Palace Assistant Minister, Gěng Jì, and the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Wéi Huǎng, raised an army to punish Cáo Cāo.
They did not succeed,
and their three kindreds were exterminated.
In the third month,
a comet appeared in the east.
In the twenty-fourth year, in the second month, on the *rénzǐ* day, the last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the fifth month of summer,
Liú Bèi captured Hánzhōng.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the *gēngzǐ* day,
Liú Bèi proclaimed himself King of Hánzhōng.
In the eighth month,
the Hàn River overflowed.
In the eleventh month of winter,
Sūn Quán captured Jīngzhōu.
In the twenty-fifth year, in the first month, on the *gēngzǐ* day,
Wèi King Cáo Cāo died.
His son, Pī, succeeded him.
In the second month, on the *dīngwèi* day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the third month,
the era name was changed to Yánkāng.
In the tenth month of winter, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
the Emperor abdicated,
and Wèi King Pī proclaimed himself Son of Heaven.
The Emperor was enfeoffed as Shānyáng Gōng,
with ten thousand households,
his rank superior to that of other kings,
he reported to the throne without addressing himself as a subject,
and received edicts without bowing.
He was allowed to use the Son of Heaven's carriages and robes for sacrifices to Heaven and Earth in the suburbs,
and his ancestral temples, ancestral rites, and seasonal sacrifices all followed the Hàn system.
His capital was in Zhuólù City in Shānyáng.
The four imperial princes who had been enfeoffed as kings
were all demoted to marquises.
The next year,
Liú Bèi proclaimed himself Emperor in Shǔ,
and Sūn Quán also proclaimed himself King in Wú.
Thus, the world was finally divided into three.
In the second year of Qīnglóng of Wèi, in the third month, on the *gēngyín* day,
Shānyáng Gōng died.
From his abdication to his death,
it was fourteen years.
He was fifty-four years old.
His posthumous title was Xiàoxiàn Huángdì.
In the eighth month, on the *rénshēn* day,
he was buried in Chánlíng with the rituals for a Hàn Son of Heaven,
and an Administrator and Assistant for the imperial tomb estate were appointed.
His Crown Prince died young.
His grandson, Kāng, reigned for fifty-one years,
and died in the sixth year of Tàikāng of Jìn.
His son, Jǐn, reigned for four years,
and died in the tenth year of Tàikāng.
His son, Qiū, reigned for twenty years,
and was killed by Hu bandits during the Yǒngjiā period.
The state was abolished.
Commentary says: The傳 (tradition/chronicle) states that the *dǐng* (tripod),
though small, is heavy;
therefore, it is treasured by the gods
and cannot be taken or moved.
That a person would carry it and rush [to abdicate]—
is this also the ultimate destiny of a declining era!
Heaven had long been weary of the Hàn virtue;
what fault then was there in Shānyáng!
Eulogy says: Xiàn was born in an unlucky time,
his person tossed by national turmoil.
Ending our four hundred years,
forever to be a guest of Yú.
Records of Empresses and Consorts, Part One, Chapter Ten
Before the Xià and Yīn dynasties,
the regulations for empresses and consorts
were briefly documented.
The Rites of Zhōu state that when a king established an empress,
there were three *fūrén* (ladies),
nine *pín* (concubines),
twenty-seven *shìfù* (court ladies),
and eighty-one *nǚyù* (female attendants),
to fulfill the inner court duties.
The empress presided over the inner palace,
sharing the status of the Son of Heaven.
The *fūrén* discussed matters of feminine rituals,
the nine *pín* managed the teaching of the four virtues,
the *shìfù* presided over mourning rites, sacrifices, and guests,
and the *nǚyù* served in the king's private chambers.
Offices were distributed and duties assigned,
each with their specific responsibilities.
Female scribes with vermilion brushes
recorded merits and faults.
Their residence had the instruction of tutors,
and their movements were accompanied by the jingle of jade pendants.
They recommended virtuous talents to assist the ruler,
and mourned for the virtuous and beautiful without indulging in their charms.
This is why they could promulgate the feminine virtues,
perfect the inner regulations,
ensure harmony in the private quarters,
and prevent impropriety.
Therefore, when King Kāng rose late,
the "Guān Jū" ode was composed as a remonstrance;
when Empress Xuān rose late,
Lady Jiāng requested to admit her transgression.
When the Zhōu court moved eastward,
the ritual order became fragmented.
Feudal lords acted presumptuously and unrestrainedly,
without fixed regulations.
Qí Huán Gōng had six concubines who were treated as wives,
Jìn Xiàn Gōng elevated a Róng woman to be his chief consort,
which ultimately led to the five sons causing chaos,
and the heir encountering difficulties.
By the Warring States period,
moral standards became even weaker.
People indulged their feelings and desires,
reversing the proper order of things,
leading to the destruction of states and loss of lives,
which were countless.
This was certainly due to neglecting ritual and disregarding precautions,
prioritizing beauty over virtue.
When Qín unified the realm,
it became overly arrogant.
The palace included the women from the seven states,
and ranks were divided into eight grades.
When Hàn arose,
it followed these titles,
but the system for women was unclear.
Gāo Zǔ's domestic affairs were unruly,
and Xiào Wén's bedchamber distinctions were blurred.
However, their selection and admission were still simple,
and adornments and playthings were modest.
After Wǔ and Yuán,
each generation increased extravagance,
to the extent that the Yètíng (inner palace) had three thousand women,
and fourteen additional ranks.
The omens of corrupting government by favored beauties
and the traces of foreign relatives causing disorder in the state
are detailed in previous histories.
When Guāng Wǔ restored the Hàn dynasty,
he carved away the ornate to return to simplicity.
Among the titles for the six palaces,
there were only the empress and *guìrén*.
The *guìrén* had a gold seal and purple ribbon,
and their emolument was no more than several tens of *hú* of grain.
Additionally, three ranks of *měirén*, *gōngrén*, and *cǎinǚ* were established,
all without official titles or ranks,
receiving only seasonal rewards and provisions.
Hàn law usually conducted a census in the eighth month,
dispatching a Grand Master of the Household together with the Yètíng Assistant and physiognomists,
to survey virtuous young girls in the villages of Luòyáng,
aged thirteen and above,
and under twenty,
who were beautiful and elegant,
and whose features matched the required auspicious appearance.
They were then brought back to the rear palace,
where their suitability was inspected,
and only then were they allowed to be presented to the emperor.
This was to ensure careful selection and admission,
and to thoroughly seek out virtuous and wise women.
Míng Dì dutifully followed his predecessor's directive,
and palace education was largely reformed.
When establishing empresses and concubines,
he always prioritized virtue.
There were no rumors of women interfering in politics,
nor any private granting of power,
which can be said to have rectified the prevailing abuses.
If he had then established prohibitions against imperial relatives,
compiled them into primary statutes,
and reformed the system of empresses and consorts,
leaving it as a legacy for future generations,
would that not have been excellent!
Although his own conduct was regulated,
the prevention of impropriety was not strict enough.
Therefore, from Xiào Zhāng onwards,
the practice of awarding based on beauty gradually returned,
favor and intimacy flourished,
and the distinction between the worthy and unworthy was forgotten.
From ancient times, although rulers were young and times were difficult,
the royal family often had problems.
It was always necessary to entrust matters to the Grand Chancellor,
and to seek out loyal and virtuous individuals.
Never was power exclusively given to women,
to wield the instruments of state.
Only when Qín Mǐ Tàihòu began to assume regency
did Ráng Hóu's power outweigh that of Zhāo Wáng,
and his household's wealth surpass that of the Yíng state.
The Hàn continued this error,
knowing the harm but not correcting it.
During the Dōngjīng (Eastern Hàn), the imperial line was repeatedly broken,
and power reverted to empresses.
Four emperors were installed from outside,
and six empresses presided over court.
None failed to make policies from behind the curtains,
and entrust affairs to their fathers and elder brothers,
grasping at child emperors to prolong their rule,
and suppressing bright and virtuous officials to monopolize their authority.
With heavy responsibilities and a long road,
the gains were deep but the disasters swift.
Their persons faced the mist and dew above the Yúntái,
while their families were chained and imprisoned below the jail.
Annihilations followed one after another,
carriages overturned continuously on the road.
Yet they rushed forward without ceasing,
until they were utterly consumed.
Ultimately, the great destiny declined,
and the divine treasure was lost.
What the Shī and Shū lamented,
was generally of the same ilk.
Therefore, their actions are examined and listed,
to form the Basic Annals of Empresses.
Although the successes and failures of their affairs differed,
those who held the official title [of empress]
are all listed in this chapter.
Those who were posthumously honored out of private favor,
and not formally revered at the time,
are appended to other sections when relevant.
〔一０〕As for relatives and separate matters,
they are each recorded in their respective biographies.
For others not mentioned elsewhere,
they are included in these Annals,
〔一一〕to continue the tradition of recording imperial relatives from the Xījīng (Western Hàn).
〔一二〕
Guāngwǔ's Guō Empress, personal name Shèngtōng,
was a native of Zhēndìng.
Her family was a prominent clan in the commandery.
Her father, Chāng,
relinquished land, houses, and property worth several million [cash] to his half-brother,
and the people of the state regarded him as righteous.
He served as a meritorious registrar in the commandery.
He married the daughter of Zhēndìng Gōng Wáng,
known as Guō Zhǔ,
who bore the Empress and her son Kuàng.
Chāng died early.
Although Guō Zhǔ was a royal daughter,
she was fond of propriety and frugal,
possessing the virtues of a mother figure.
In the spring of Gēngshǐ's second year (24 CE),
Guāngwǔ attacked Wáng Láng,
and reached Zhēndìng.
He then took the Empress as his concubine,
and she was favored.
Upon his enthronement,
she was made a noble lady (guìrén).
In Jiànwǔ's first year (25 CE),
she gave birth to the imperial prince Qiáng.
The Emperor admired Kuàng for his caution and prudence;
though only sixteen,
he was appointed Huangmen Shilang (Palace Attendant).
In the second year (26 CE),
the noble lady was established as Empress,
Qiáng was made Crown Prince,
and Kuàng was enfeoffed as Miánmán Hóu.
Due to the Empress's brothers becoming distinguished,
guests flocked to them.
Kuàng was humble and treated scholars courteously,
gaining considerable reputation.
In the fourteenth year (38 CE),
he was promoted to Chéngmén Xiàowèi (Commander of the City Gates).
Thereafter,
the Empress's favor gradually waned,
and she frequently harbored resentment.
In the seventeenth year (41 CE),
she was ultimately deposed as Zhongshān Wáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager of the Prince of Zhōngshān),
and her middle son, Yòuyì Gōng Fǔ, was advanced to be Zhōngshān Wáng (Prince of Zhōngshān),
with Chángshān Commandery added to the state of Zhōngshān.
Kuàng was transferred to a larger state,
and became Yáng'ān Hóu.
The Empress's maternal cousin Jìng,
as a Qí Dūwèi (Cavalry Commandant), had rendered meritorious service in campaigns,
and was enfeoffed as Xīnqī Hóu,
eventually rising to the post of Dōnghǎi Xiàng (Chancellor of Dōnghǎi).
Jìng's younger brother Kuāng was Fāgān Hóu,
and served as Tàizhōng Dàfū (Grandee Remonstrant).
The Empress's uncle Liáng
died early without sons.
His son-in-law, Chén Mào of Nányáng,
was enfeoffed as Nán Hóu due to imperial grace.
In the twentieth year (44 CE),
Zhōngshān Wáng Fǔ was again transferred to be Pèi Wáng (Prince of Pèi),
and the Empress became Pèi Tàihòu (Empress Dowager of Pèi).
Kuàng was promoted to Dàhónglú (Grand Herald).
The Emperor frequently visited his residence,
where he would gather high officials, nobles, and royal relatives for banquets.
The bestowed gold, money, and silk
were extraordinarily abundant,
and the capital nicknamed Kuàng's home "the gold mine."
In the twenty-sixth year (50 CE),
the Empress's mother Guō Zhǔ passed away.
The Emperor personally attended the mourning and funeral,
all officials gathered,
and an envoy was sent to retrieve Chāng's coffin
to be interred with Guō Zhǔ.
Chāng was posthumously granted the seal and ribbon of Yáng'ān Hóu,
with the posthumous title Sī Hóu.
In the twenty-eighth year (52 CE),
the Empress passed away
and was buried at Běimáng.
The Emperor pitied the Guō clan,
and decreed that Kuàng's son Huáng marry Princess Yùyáng,
and Huáng was appointed a Lang (Gentleman).
When Xiǎnzōng ascended the throne,
Kuàng, along with the Emperor's maternal uncles Yīn Shì and Yīn Jiù, were all made Tèjìn (Specially Advanced Officials),
frequently receiving rewards and gifts,
their favor and grace were equally profound.
The Yīn and Guō families were treated with equal respect
in every matter.
In Yǒngpíng's second year (59 CE),
Kuàng died.
The posthumous gifts were very generous,
and the Emperor personally attended the funeral,
bestowing the posthumous title Jié Hóu.
His son Huáng succeeded him.
In Yuánhé's third year (86 CE),
Sùzōng made a northern inspection tour,
passing through Zhēndìng.
He met with all the Guō family members,
who paid their respects and offered longevity greetings.
He invited them in for a very joyful banquet.
With grand sacrificial offerings, he honored Guō Zhǔ's tomb,
and bestowed ten thousand hú of grain
and five hundred thousand cash.
In the early Yǒngyuán period (89 CE),
Huáng was Chánglè Shàofǔ (Minor Controller of Chánglè Palace),
and his son Jǔ was Shìzhōng (Attendant at Court),
also serving as Shèshēng Xiàowèi (Commander of Archers).
When Dàjiāngjūn Dòu Xiàn was executed,
Huáng was implicated as Dòu Xiàn's son-in-law in a conspiracy of rebellion,
so both father and son were imprisoned and died.
Their family members were exiled to Hépǔ,
and those of their clan who were officials
were all dismissed.
Xīnqī Hóu Jìng initially served as a cavalry general,
and rendered meritorious service in campaigns.
He was appointed Dōnghǎi Xiàng.
He died during the Yǒngpíng era,
and his son Sōng succeeded him.
Sōng died,
and was posthumously implicated in the affair of Chǔ Wáng Yīng,
and his state was abolished.
In Jiànchū's second year (77 CE),
Zhāng Dì re-enfeoffed Sōng's son Qín as Yítíng Hóu.
Qín had no sons,
and his state was abolished.
Fāgān Hóu Kuāng
served as Tàizhōng Dàfū,
and died in Jiànwǔ's thirtieth year (54 CE).
His son Xūn succeeded him.
Xūn died,
and his son Jùn succeeded him.
In Yǒngpíng's thirteenth year (70 CE),
he was also implicated in the affair of Chǔ Wáng Yīng,
and lost his state.
In Jiànchū's third year (78 CE),
Jùn was re-enfeoffed as Guāndū Hóu.
He died
without sons,
and his state was abolished.
There were three Guō clan members who were enfeoffed as marquises,
and all their states were extinguished.
A discourse: The rise and fall of things,
the ebb and flow of emotions,
are naturally so.
But for those extreme instances of exaltation and decline, of departure and return,
must they be solely due to infatuation and delusion?
When one is close to the bedchamber,
receiving favor and affection,
even if their disposition is treacherous or their conduct superfluous,
there is nothing that is not considered virtuous.
But when affection shifts,
and intimate bonds are severed,
even if one's heart is kind and their appearance beautiful,
they increasingly appear ugly.
When love rises,
then the world is not vast enough to contain its loftiness;
when joy departs,
then the nine regions have nowhere to escape their fate.
This is truly what noble-minded individuals are engrossed in,
what rulers elevate and suppress,
and none can defy it.
Empress Guō, having suffered estrangement, was demoted,
and her resentment turned into a grievance,
yet she still received favor in a separate palace,
and her relatives by marriage were granted increased honor.
As for Dōnghǎi, he hesitated,
and his departure and acceptance were conducted with propriety,
so that later generations would not perceive any gap in the rise and fall, the advancement and retreat.
Is this not more glorious than antiquity!
Guāngliè Yīn Huánghòu, personal name Lìhuá,
was from Xīnyě, Nányáng.
Initially,
Guāngwǔ came to Xīnyě,
heard of the empress's beauty,
and was pleased in his heart.
Later, upon reaching Cháng'ān,
he saw the chariots and cavalry of the Zhí Jīnwú were very grand,
and thereupon sighed, saying:
"In officialdom, one should be a Zhí Jīnwú;
in marriage, one should marry Yīn Lìhuá."
In the sixth month of Gēngshǐ first year (23 CE),
he then took the empress into his household in Wǎn's Dāngchéng Lǐ.
At that time, she was nineteen years old.
When Guāngwǔ became Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and was about to travel west to Luòyáng,
he ordered the empress to return to Xīnyě.
When Dèng Fèng raised an army,
the empress's elder brother Shí became his general.
The empress followed her family to Yùyáng,
and stayed at Fèng's residence.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he ordered Attendant Fù Jùn to welcome the empress.
She, along with Húyáng, Níngpíng Zhǔ, and other palace women, all arrived in Luòyáng.
The empress was made a Guìrén.
The emperor, finding the empress's nature elegant, broad-minded, and benevolent,
wished to elevate her to a position of honor.
However, the empress firmly declined,
citing that the Guō clan had a son,
and she ultimately refused to accept it.
Therefore, Empress Guō was established instead.
In Jiànwǔ fourth year (28 CE),
she accompanied the expedition against Péng Chǒng,
and gave birth to Xiǎnzōng in Yuánshì.
In the ninth year (33 CE),
a bandit robbed and killed the empress's mother, Dèng Shì, and her younger brother, Xīn.
The emperor was greatly saddened by this,
and thereupon issued an edict to the Dà Sīkōng, saying:
"When I was humble and lowly,
I married into the Yīn clan.
Then, leading troops in battle,
we were separated.
Fortunately, we remained safe,
both escaping the tiger's maw.
Because the Guìrén possessed the beauty of a mother's virtue,
she ought to have been established as empress,
but she firmly declined, not daring to accept,
and was ranked among the concubines.
I admired her righteous humility,
and promised to enfeoff her younger brothers.
Before they could be granted titles and lands,
they encountered misfortune and calamity.
Mother and son shared the same fate,
causing sorrow in my heart.
The Xiǎo Yǎ says: 'When there is fear and apprehension,
it is only I and you.
When there is peace and joy,
you turn to me.'
The warnings of the poets,
how can one not be careful?
Let her father, Lù, be posthumously ennobled and given the posthumous title Xuān'ēn Āihóu,
and her younger brother Xīn be Xuānyì Gōnghóu.
Let her younger brother Jiù inherit the title of Āihóu.
When the coffin was in the hall,
I sent the Tàizhōng Dàfū to present the seal and sash,
as per the rites for a marquis in a state.
If her soul has spiritual power,
may it approve of this honor and glory!"
In the seventeenth year (41 CE),
Empress Guō Shì was deposed, and the Guìrén was established as empress.
An imperial edict was issued to the Sān Gōng, saying:
"The empress harbors resentment and ill will,
repeatedly violates imperial commands,
is unable to care for other children,
or instruct those of different households.
Within the palace,
she is like a hawk or a falcon.
She lacks the virtue of Guānjū,
but has the manner of Lǚ and Huò.
How can she be entrusted with young orphans,
or respectfully undertake the bright sacrifices?
Now, I dispatch Dà Sītú Shè
and Zōngzhèng Jí with credentials,
to present the empress's seal and sash.
Yīn Guìrén, from a humble village,
returned from her lowly state.
'Since I last saw her,
three years have passed.'
She is fit to serve in the ancestral temple,
and be the mother of all under heaven.
Let the relevant officials carefully examine the old codes,
and promptly confer the exalted title.
These unusual circumstances
are not a blessing for the state.
Do not offer longevity congratulations or felicitations."
The empress was respectful and frugal in her position,
had few frivolous tastes,
and did not enjoy jesting.
Her nature was benevolent and filial,
and she was often compassionate.
She lost her father at the age of seven;
though many decades had passed,
whenever she spoke of it, she never failed to shed tears.
The emperor, seeing this,
often sighed.
When Xiǎnzōng ascended the throne,
he honored the empress as Huáng Tàihòu.
In the winter of Yǒngpíng third year (60 CE),
the emperor accompanied the grand empress dowager to Zhānglíng.
Wine was served at the old residence,
and descendants of old friends from the Yīn and Dèng families
were all given rewards.
In the seventh year (64 CE),
she passed away,
having been on the throne for twenty-four years,
at the age of sixty.
She was interred with the emperor in Yuánlíng.
Emperor Míng was filial and affectionate by nature.
His remembrance and longing for her were endless.
In the first month of the seventeenth year (74 CE),
when he was due to visit Yuánlíng,
he dreamt that his late father and the grand empress dowager were as joyful as in life.
After waking,
he was so sad he could not sleep.
He immediately consulted the calendar,
and the next morning was an auspicious day.
He then led all officials and former guests to visit the mausoleum.
On that day,
sweet dew descended upon the trees of the mausoleum.
The emperor ordered all officials to collect it and offer it as a sacrifice.
After the assembly concluded,
the emperor bowed before his seat, leaning on the imperial couch,
and looked at the items in the grand empress dowager's cosmetic box.
He was moved to tears by sorrow,
and ordered that the cosmetics and furnishings be replaced.
All his attendants wept,
none able to look up.
Míngdé Mǎ Huánghòu, personal name withheld,
was the youngest daughter of the Fúbō Jiāngjūn, Yuán.
She lost her parents young.
Her elder brother Kèqīng, who was intelligent and bright, died young,
and her mother, Lìn Fūrén, was so grief-stricken that she became ill and disoriented.
At that time, the empress was ten years old,
managed family affairs,
and directed the servants.
Both inside and outside the household, people sought her advice and reported to her,
as if she were an adult.
Initially,
none of the families knew of this,
but later, when they heard,
they all marveled at it.
The empress once suffered a prolonged illness.
Her grand dame ordered a divination for her.
The diviner said:
"Although this girl shows signs of illness, she will become greatly honored.
The omen cannot be fully spoken."
Later, she also called a physiognomist to examine her daughters.
Upon seeing the empress,
he was greatly surprised and said:
"I will surely become a subject to this girl.
However, though she will be noble, she will have few children.
If she raises others' children, she will gain strength,
and they will surpass her biological offspring."
Initially,
when Má Yuán 馬援 campaigned against the Wǔxī Mán 五溪蠻,
he died in the army.
The Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng 虎賁中郎將 Liáng Sōng 梁松 and Huángmén Shìláng 黃門侍郎 Dòu Gù 竇固, among others, took the opportunity to slander him.
Because of this, the family's influence further declined,
and they were frequently oppressed and insulted by powerful nobles.
Later, his cousin Yán 嚴, unable to bear the grief and indignation,
reported to the Grand Matron (Tàitàifūrén 太太夫人) that she should break off the engagement with the Dòu 竇 family
and seek to have her daughter enter the Yètíng 掖庭 (Imperial Harem).
So, she submitted a memorial stating:
"My uncle Yuán 援, though his kindness was not repaid by others,
his wife and children alone received imperial grace and were spared.
They look up to Your Majesty
as heaven and as a father.
Since it is human nature to desire to live,
they naturally seek blessings.
I secretly hear that consorts for the Crown Prince and the various princes are not yet all selected.
Yuán 援 has three daughters:
the eldest is fifteen,
the next is fourteen,
and the youngest is thirteen.
Their appearance, complexion, and hair
are all above average.
They are all filial and careful,
gentle, serene, and courteous.
I wish for a physiognomist to be sent
to assess their suitability.
Should there be even one chance in ten thousand,
Yuán 援 would be immortal in the underworld.
Moreover, Yuán 援's maternal aunt and female cousins were all Jiéyú 婕妤 (Imperial Concubines) of Emperor Chéng 成帝.
They were buried at Yánlíng 延陵.
I, Yán 嚴, have been fortunate enough to receive grace and be reborn.
I hope that through the connection with my late aunt,
my daughter may fill a place in the imperial harem."
Because of this, the Empress (Hòu 后) was chosen to enter the Crown Prince's palace.
At that time, she was thirteen.
Serving Yīn Hòu 陰后 with reverence,
and interacting with her peers,
her decorum and conduct were thoroughly prepared,
and all, high and low, were pleased with her.
Thus, she gained favor and distinction,
always residing in the rear hall.
When Xiǎnzōng 顯宗 ascended the throne,
he made her a Guìrén 貴人.
At that time, Jǐa Shì 賈氏, the daughter of the Empress's former maternal elder sister, had also been selected and admitted,
and she gave birth to Sùzōng 肅宗.
Since the Empress had no children,
the Emperor ordered her to adopt him,
saying:
"One need not necessarily give birth to one's own child;
the only concern is that one's love and care might not be complete."
Thereupon, the Empress devoted herself to his upbringing,
toiling more intensely than a birth mother.
Sùzōng 肅宗, too, was naturally filial and sincere,
with an innate capacity for affection.
The mother and son shared loving kindness,
from beginning to end without the slightest estrangement.
The Empress often worried that the imperial succession was not yet extensive,
and she frequently sighed with concern,
recommending and promoting those around her
as if fearing she would not act quickly enough.
When any concubine received an imperial audience,
she would always offer comfort and acceptance.
If someone was frequently favored and promoted,
she would invariably enhance their generous treatment.
In the spring of the third year of Yǒngpíng 永平 (60 CE),
the officials proposed establishing the Chángqiū Gōng 長秋宮 (Empress's Palace),
but the Emperor had not yet expressed his opinion.
The Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu 皇太后) said:
"Mǎ Guìrén 馬貴人's virtue surpasses all in the imperial harem;
she is precisely the one."
So, she was established as Empress.
A few days before this,
she dreamt that countless small flying insects landed on her body,
then entered her skin and flew out again.
Having been formally installed in the inner palace,
she became even more humble and modest.
She was seven chǐ and two cùn tall,
with a square mouth
and beautiful hair.
She could recite the Yì 易 (Book of Changes)
and enjoyed reading the Chūnqiū 春秋 (Spring and Autumn Annals) and Chǔcí 楚辭 (Songs of Chu).
She was especially skilled in the Zhōuguān 周官 (Rites of Zhou) and the writings of Dǒng Zhòngshū 董仲舒.
She always wore coarse silk,
and her skirts had no elaborate borders.
On the first and fifteenth days of the month, when the various princesses came for court greetings,
they would see the Empress's robes were coarse and simple,
and mistakenly thought they were fine silk gauze.
Upon closer inspection,
they would laugh.
The Empress would explain:
"This silk is particularly suitable for dyeing,
which is why I use it."
None in the six palaces failed to sigh in admiration.
When the Emperor occasionally visited gardens, parks, or detached palaces,
the Empress would always warn him about wind, chill, dew, and mist,
her words sincere and complete,
often leading him to consider and choose carefully.
When the Emperor visited the Zhuólóng Zhōng 濯龍中,
and summoned all the Zhōng Hù 中戶,
the Prince of Xiàpī 下邳 and others were also present.
They requested to summon the Empress.
The Emperor smiled and said:
"This household is not fond of pleasure;
even if she comes, there will be no joy."
Thus, she rarely participated in recreational activities.
In the fifteenth year (72 CE),
the Emperor consulted maps
to enfeoff the imperial princes,
giving each half of the lands of the various states.
The Empress saw this and said:
"If the princes merely receive food revenues from a few counties,
is this not too parsimonious according to the regulations?"
The Emperor said:
"How can my sons be equal to the sons of previous emperors?
An annual allowance of twenty million (cash) is sufficient."
At that time, the Chǔ 楚 prison cases continued for years without end,
with prisoners implicating each other,
and a great many people were imprisoned.
The Empress, fearing widespread injustice,
mentioned it during a quiet moment,
feeling deep compassion.
The Emperor was moved and enlightened by her words.
He rose in the night and paced,
pondering her suggestion,
and ultimately granted many pardons and remissions.
Whenever generals presented reports or ministers debated difficult issues,
the Emperor often tested the Empress with them.
The Empress would always clarify the issues and address the principles,
each obtaining a fair understanding of the situation.
Whenever she attended to him,
she would invariably discuss matters of state,
offering many helpful suggestions and corrections,
yet never interfering with private family matters.
Therefore,
her favor and respect grew daily and remained constant throughout.
When the Emperor passed away,
and Sùzōng 肅宗 ascended the throne,
he honored the Empress as the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu 皇太后).
When the various noble ladies were to move to the Nángōng 南宮 (Southern Palace),
the Empress Dowager, feeling the sorrow of separation,
bestowed upon each prince a red ribbon of office,
and added an comfortable carriage drawn by four horses,
three thousand bolts of white Yuè 越 silk,
two thousand bolts of assorted silks,
and ten catties of gold.
She personally compiled the "Daily Record of Xiǎnzōng's 顯宗 Activities" (Xiǎnzōng Qǐjūzhù 顯宗起居注),
omitting her brother Fáng's 防 involvement in medical affairs.
The Emperor asked:
"My maternal uncle, the Huángmén 黃門 (palace eunuch), has been serving day and night for almost a year.
If he receives no special commendation,
and his diligence is not recorded,
is that not excessive?"
The Empress Dowager replied:
"I do not wish future generations to hear that the late emperor frequently favored the families of concubines,
therefore I have not recorded it."
In the first year of Jiànchū
the Emperor desired to enfeoff his maternal uncles,
but the Empress Dowager refused to allow it.
The following summer,
there was a great drought.
Those who spoke on current affairs thought this was due to not enfeoffing the imperial relatives by marriage.
The officials concerned thus presented a memorial,
stating that it was appropriate to follow the old statutes.
The Empress Dowager issued an edict saying:
"All who speak on current affairs merely wish to flatter me to gain favor.
In the past, the five marquises of the Wáng [Wáng] family were all enfeoffed on the same day,
yet at that time, a yellow mist filled the air, and there was no response of timely rain.
Furthermore, Tián Fén and Dòu Yīng,
favored and powerful, were arrogant and unrestrained;
the disaster of their downfall
is recounted by the world.
Therefore, the former Emperor was careful and cautious with his maternal relatives,
not allowing them to hold pivotal positions.
When his sons were enfeoffed,
it was only to half the size of the states of Chǔ and Huáiyáng.
He often said, 'My sons should not be equal to the sons of the former Emperor.'
How can the officials now wish to compare the Mǎ clan to the Yīn clan!
I am the mother of the world,
yet I wear coarse silk,
do not seek sweet food,
and my attendants wear only plain cloth,
without perfumed ornaments;
this is because I wish to lead by example.
I thought that when my relatives saw this,
they would be moved to self-restraint,
but they merely laugh and say, 'The Empress Dowager has always been fond of frugality.'
Previously, when I passed by the Zhuólóng Gate,
I saw my relatives' family members coming to inquire after my well-being,
their carriages like flowing water,
their horses like swimming dragons.
Their attendants wore green robes,
with perfectly white collars and sleeves.
Looking at my charioteer,
he was far inferior.
Therefore, I did not rebuke them in anger,
but merely cut off their annual expenses.
I hoped to silently shame their hearts,
but they remained complacent,
without any thought of worrying about the state or forgetting their families.
No one knows a minister better than the ruler,
how much more so one's relatives?
How can I betray the will of the former Emperor above,
and diminish the virtue of my ancestors below,
thereby re-invoking the disaster of the Western Capital's downfall!"
She steadfastly refused.
The Emperor, reading the edict, sighed sadly,
and again earnestly pleaded, saying:
"Since the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
the enfeoffment of maternal uncles as marquises
is like the enthronement of imperial princes as kings.
If Your Majesty sincerely maintains humility,
how can you alone deny favor to my three maternal uncles?
Moreover, the Grand Commandant of the Guards is advanced in years,
and the two Commandants of the Guards suffer from severe illnesses.
Should they unfortunately pass away,
it would cause me to bear a lifelong, deep-seated regret.
It is fitting to act while there is still a propitious time;
it must not be delayed."
The Empress Dowager replied:
"I have considered this repeatedly,
desiring to achieve a favorable outcome for both sides.
How could I merely wish to gain a reputation for humility,
and thus cause the Emperor to incur the criticism of not extending favor to his relatives?
In the past, Empress Dowager Dòu wished to enfeoff the brother of Empress Wáng;
Chancellor Tiáo Hóu stated that according to the agreement with Emperor Gāozǔ,
those without military merit
who were not of the Liú clan could not be enfeoffed as marquises.
Now, the Mǎ clan has no merit to the state;
how can they be equated with the Yīn and Guō clans, Empresses of the restoration?
I often observe that in wealthy and noble families,
when emoluments and positions are piled high,
it is like a tree that bears fruit twice,
its roots are bound to be damaged.
Furthermore, the reason people desire to be enfeoffed as marquises
is to offer sacrifices to their ancestors above,
and to seek warmth and sustenance below.
Now, for sacrifices, they receive treasures from all directions,
and for clothing and food, they receive surplus resources from the imperial treasury.
Is this not sufficient,
that they must acquire a county?
My calculations are thorough;
do not have any doubts.
The highest act of filial piety
is to bring peace to one's parents.
Now, we have repeatedly encountered calamities and anomalies,
grain prices have multiplied several times,
causing worry and fear day and night,
making it impossible to sit or sleep peacefully.
And yet you wish to prioritize the establishment of external enfeoffments,
going against the earnest wishes of your loving mother?
I am by nature stern and resolute,
with a resolute spirit within my breast;
you must not disobey.
If the yin and yang are harmonious,
and the borders are tranquil,
then you may pursue your wishes.
I merely wish to chew on sweets and play with my grandchildren;
I cannot concern myself with governance anymore."
At that time, a fire broke out due to an attendant in the household of Princess Xīnpíng,
spreading to the Northern Pavilion and rear palace.
The Empress Dowager considered it her own fault,
and was unhappy in her daily life.
When it was time to visit Yuánlíng,
she attributed it to her own laxity in security,
and was ashamed to face the imperial tomb,
thus she did not go.
Initially,
when the Grand Lady was buried,
her tomb mound was slightly elevated.
The Empress Dowager commented on it,
and her elder brother Liáo and others immediately reduced it.
For her relatives who showed humility, simplicity, and righteous conduct,
she would grant them kind words,
and reward them with wealth and positions.
If there was the slightest transgression,
she would first show a stern and solemn expression,
and then inflict punishment.
Those who displayed extravagant carriages and clothing that did not conform to the law and regulations
were immediately struck from the family register
and sent back to their home villages.
The carriages and cavalry of the Princes of Guǎngpíng, Jùlù, and Lèchéng were simple and unadorned,
without gold or silver ornaments.
The Emperor reported this to the Empress Dowager,
and the Empress Dowager immediately bestowed five million cash upon each of them.
Thus, those within and outside the court conformed to her influence,
and their attire became uniform.
The various families were in awe and fear,
even more so than during the Yǒngpíng era.
She then established a weaving workshop,
and raised silkworms in Zhuólóng,
often going to observe them,
taking it as recreation.
She often discussed affairs of state with the Emperor morning and evening,
as well as instructing the younger princes,
debating classical texts,
and recounting past events,
harmoniously throughout the day.
In the fourth year,
the world had abundant harvests,
and the four directions were peaceful.
The Emperor then enfeoffed his three maternal uncles, Liáo, Fáng, and Guāng, as marquises.
They all declined the honor,
wishing instead to accept the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
When the Empress Dowager heard this,
she said:
"The sages established teachings,
each having its own method, knowing that human natures cannot all be alike.
When I was young,
I only admired bamboo and silk (writings),
and my ambition disregarded life itself.
Now, though I am old,
I am again 'wary of acquisition';
thus, day and night I remain vigilant,
thinking of humbling myself.
I do not seek comfort in dwelling,
nor satisfaction in food.
I hope by this path
not to fail the former Emperor.
The reason I guided my brothers
to share this ambition
was to have no regrets
on the day I close my eyes.
How can it be that my elderly wish
is again not followed?
For ten thousand years, there will be long regret!"
Liáo and the others had no choice
but to accept the enfeoffment and then retire to their residences.
That year, the Empress Dowager fell ill.
She did not trust shamans, sorcerers, or minor physicians,
and repeatedly ordered an end to prayers and sacrifices.
In the sixth month,
she passed away.
She had reigned for twenty-three years,
and was over forty years old.
She was interred together with the Emperor at Xiǎnjié Líng.
Concubine Jiǎ was
a native of Nányáng.
At the end of Jiànwǔ, she was selected into the Crown Prince's palace.
In the second year of Zhōngyuán, she gave birth to Sùzōng,
but Xiǎnzōng regarded her as a mere concubine.
Since the Emperor was raised by the Empress Dowager,
he exclusively regarded the Mǎ clan as his maternal family.
Therefore, Concubine Jiǎ did not ascend to the highest position,
and her relatives of the Jiǎ clan received no favor or honor.
When the Empress Dowager passed away,
an edict was issued promoting Concubine Jiǎ to wearing a red ribbon,
granting her a carriage with four horses,
two hundred palace attendants from the Yǒngxiàng Palace,
twenty thousand bolts of assorted silk from the imperial treasury,
a thousand catties of gold from the Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and twenty million cash.
All historical records lack information about her later life,
hence her ultimate fate is unknown.
Zhāngdé Dòu Empress, personal name unknown,
was from Pínglíng, Fúfēng.
She was the great-granddaughter of Dà Sīkōng Róng.
Her grandfather was Mù,
and her father was Xūn.
Xūn died in a case,
details of which are in the biography of Dòu Róng.
Xūn married Princess Bǐyáng, daughter of Gōng Wáng Qiáng of Dōnghǎi.
The Empress was their eldest daughter.
After her family fell into ruin,
they frequently summoned physiognomists to inquire about their fortunes.
All who saw the Empress said she would attain great honor and nobility,
and that her appearance was not that of a concubine.
At six, she could write,
and her relatives all marveled at her.
In Jiànchū second year (80 CE),
the Empress and her younger sister were selected to enter and be presented at Chánglè Gōng.
Their movements were orderly,
and their demeanor was exceedingly dignified.
Sùzōng had previously heard of the Empress's talent and beauty,
and often questioned his imperial concubines and tutors about her.
When he saw her,
he found her truly beautiful,
and Mǎ Tàihòu also found her exceptional.
Consequently, she entered the Yè Tíng
and was presented at the Zhāngdé Diàn in Běi Gōng.
The Empress was quick-witted and agile,
giving her whole heart to serving,
and her praises were heard daily.
The next year,
she was established as Empress,
and her sister as a Guìrén.
In the seventh year (83 CE),
her father Xūn was posthumously ennobled and given the posthumous title Ānchéng Sī Hóu.
The Empress's favor and distinction were unique,
and she firmly controlled the inner palace.
Initially,
Guìrén Sòng gave birth to Crown Prince Qìng,
and Guìrén Liáng gave birth to Emperor Hé.
Since the Empress had no son,
she deeply resented and envied them,
often sowing discord with the Emperor,
gradually leading to their estrangement and suspicion.
She then falsely accused Guìrén Sòng of practicing evil charms and witchcraft,
leading Sòng to commit suicide.
Qìng was deposed as Qīnghé Wáng.
The account is in Qìng's biography.
Guìrén Liáng
was the daughter of Bāoqīn Mǐn Hóu Liáng Sǒng.
She lost her mother young
and was raised by her paternal aunt, Wǔyīn Cháng Gōngzhǔ.
At sixteen,
also in Jiànchū second year (80 CE), she and her middle sister were selected to enter the Yè Tíng as Guìrén.
In the fourth year (82 CE),
she gave birth to Emperor Hé.
The Empress adopted him as her own son.
She wished to solely promote her own maternal family and resented the Liáng clan.
In the eighth year (86 CE),
she fabricated a slanderous letter to implicate Sǒng.
Sǒng was executed for his alleged crime,
and the Guìrén sisters died of grief.
From then on, the palace women were terrified and silent,
and the Empress's favor grew daily.
When the Emperor died,
Emperor Hé ascended the throne,
honoring the Empress as Huáng Tàihòu.
The Huáng Tàihòu presided over the court.
She honored her mother, Princess Bǐyáng, as Cháng Gōngzhǔ,
and increased her income-producing fief by three thousand households.
Her elder brother Xiàn,
and younger brothers Dǔ and Jǐng,
all attained high positions and wealth,
and wielded great power.
Later, they secretly plotted rebellion.
In Yǒngyuán fourth year (92 CE),
their plot was discovered and they were executed.
In the ninth year (97 CE),
the Tàihòu died.
Before her burial,
Guìrén Liáng's sister Yì
submitted a memorial detailing the unjust death of Guìrén Liáng.
Tàiwèi Zhāng Pú, Sītú Liú Fāng, and Sīkōng Zhāng Fèn submitted a memorial,
proposing to follow the precedent of Guāngwǔ's demotion of Empress Lǚ Tàihòu,
to demote the Tàihòu's honorary title,
and not to inter her with the late emperor.
Many officials also submitted memorials.
The Emperor issued an imperial edict:
"Although the Dòu clan did not abide by the laws,
the Tàihòu always diminished herself.
I served her for ten years,
and deeply consider the greater principles of righteousness.
According to ritual,
there is no text for a subject or son to demote their superior.
My affection cannot bear to separate her,
and righteousness cannot bear to diminish her.
Reviewing previous generations, Shàngguān Tàihòu was also not demoted or deposed.
Let there be no further deliberation."
Thus, she was interred with the Emperor at Jìng Líng.
She reigned for eighteen years.
Because the Guìrén had suffered a cruel death
and her funeral rites were deficient,
the Emperor re-interred her at Chéngguāng Gōng,
conferring the posthumous title Gōnghuái Huánghòu,
and subsequently observing the mourning rites,
with all officials wearing plain white.
She was interred with her elder sister, Dà Guìrén, at Xī Líng,
with ceremonies comparable to Jìng Yuán.
Emperor Hé's Yīn Empress, personal name unknown,
was the great-granddaughter of Zhí Jīnwú Shí, the elder brother of Guāngliè Huánghòu.
The Empress was intelligent and wise from a young age,
and skilled in calligraphy and arts.
In Yǒngyuán fourth year (92 CE),
she was selected to enter the Yè Tíng.
Due to her close relation to the former Empress,
she was made a Guìrén.
She enjoyed exceptional favor.
In the eighth year (96 CE),
she was established as Empress.
After Héxī Dèng Empress entered the palace,
her favor gradually declined,
and she frequently harbored resentment.
The Empress's maternal grandmother, Dèng Zhū, frequently entered and exited the palace.
In the summer of the fourteenth year (102 CE),
there were rumors that the Empress and Zhū were jointly practicing witchcraft.
The matter was discovered,
and the Emperor then ordered Zhōng Chángshì Zhāng Shèn and Shàngshū Chén Bāo to conduct a joint investigation in the Yè Tíng prison.
Zhū and her two sons, Fèng and Yì, as well as the Empress's brothers Yì, Fǔ, and Chǎng, were implicated in interconnected statements,
accused of performing sacrifices and curses,
constituting great treason.
Fèng, Yì, and Fǔ died under interrogation in prison.
The Emperor sent Sītú Lǔ Gōng, bearing a scepter, to present a decree to the Empress,
taking back her imperial seals and ribbons.
She was moved to Tóng Gōng
and died of grief.
She reigned for seven years.
She was buried at Qiáng Chóng Bù.
Her father, Tèjìn Gāng, committed suicide.
Yì, Chǎng, and the Zhū family members were exiled to Bǐjǐng Xiàn, Rìnán.
All her relatives, both imperial and maternal, were dismissed from office and returned to their hometowns.
In Yǒngchū fourth year (110 CE),
Dèng Tàihòu issued an edict pardoning all exiled members of the Yīn clan, allowing them to return to their former commanderies,
and returning their assets, exceeding five million coins.
Héxī Dèng Empress, personal name Suí,
