was the granddaughter of Tàifù Yǔ.
Her father, Xùn, was Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi;
her mother, from the Yīn clan,
was the daughter of Guāngliè Huánghòu's cousin.
When the Empress was five years old,
the Tàifù's wife, who loved her,
cut her hair herself.
The wife, being old and with dim eyesight,
accidentally cut the Empress's forehead,
who endured the pain without a word.
Those around, seeing it, were surprised and asked her about it.
The Empress said:
"It is not that it doesn't hurt,
but Tàifūrén, out of compassion, cut my hair.
It would be difficult to hurt the old lady's feelings.
Therefore, I endured it."
At six, she could read historical texts,
and by twelve, she was proficient in the Shī and Lúnyǔ.
Whenever her elder brothers read classics and commentaries,
she would humbly ask them difficult questions.
Her ambition lay in classics and books,
and she did not inquire about household matters.
Her mother often criticized her,
saying:
"You don't practice needlework to provide clothes,
but instead busy yourself with study.
Are you going to become a Bóshì?"
The Empress was reluctant to disobey her mother's words,
so she performed women's tasks during the day
and recited classics in the evening.
Her family called her
"Zhūshēng."
Her father, Xùn, found her exceptional,
and consulted her on all matters, big or small.
In the fourth year of Yǒngyuán,
she was due to be selected and enter the palace,
but Dèng Xùn passed away.
The Empress Dowager wept day and night,
and for three years she ate no salt or vegetables.
She became emaciated and disfigured,
so much so that her relatives did not recognize her.
Later, she once dreamed of touching the sky,
which was vast and perfectly blue,
as if there were stalactites.
She looked up, gargled, and drank from them.
When she consulted a dream interpreter about this,
he said, "Yáo dreamed of climbing the sky,
and Tāng dreamed of reaching the sky and breathing from it.
These are all auspicious omens for sage kings,
and the good fortune is ineffable."
Another physiognomist, upon seeing the Empress Dowager, exclaimed,
"This is the physiognomy of Chéng Tāng!"
Her family secretly rejoiced but dared not declare it.
Her uncle, Dèng Gāi, said,
"I often hear that those who save a thousand lives
will have descendants who are enfeoffed.
My brother Dèng Xùn, as an Yèzhě,
was tasked with repairing the Shíjiù River,
saving thousands of lives each year.
The Way of Heaven is trustworthy;
our family will surely receive blessings."
Initially,
Grand Tutor Yǔ sighed, saying,
"I led an army of a million men,
yet I never wantonly killed a single person.
My descendants will surely rise to prominence."
In the seventh year,
the Empress Dowager was again selected, along with other noble daughters, to enter the palace.
She was seven feet two inches tall,
with a beautiful face and radiant appearance,
exceptionally different from the others.
Everyone around her was astonished.
In the winter of the eighth year,
she entered the Yè Tíng as a Guìrén,
then sixteen years old.
She was respectful, cautious,
and everything she did followed proper rules.
She served Empress Yīn
with apprehension day and night.
When interacting with her peers,
she always restrained herself and showed deference.
Even palace servants and laborers
received her kindness and consideration.
The Emperor deeply admired and loved her.
When the Empress Dowager fell ill,
the Emperor specifically allowed her mother and brothers to visit and attend to her medicine,
without restricting the number of days.
She said to the Emperor,
"The palace is of utmost importance,
yet allowing my family members to stay long within the inner chambers
would expose Your Majesty to criticism of favoritism,
and would bring upon this humble concubine the blame of being insatiable.
Such mutual harm to both above and below
is truly undesirable."
The Emperor said,
"Everyone considers frequent visits an honor,
but you, Guìrén, instead worry about it.
Your deep self-restraint and humility
are truly beyond reach."
Whenever there were banquets,
the other consorts and Guìrén competed to adorn themselves,
with shining hairpins and earrings,
and bright, fresh robes and skirts.
But she alone wore plain clothes,
her attire unadorned.
If her clothing happened to be the same color as Empress Yīn's,
she would immediately change it.
If they were to be presented together,
she dared not sit upright or stand prominently,
and when walking, she would bend her body in humility.
Whenever the Emperor asked her a question,
she would always hesitate and answer after Empress Yīn,
not daring to speak before her.
The Emperor, knowing her mental and physical strain,
sighed,
"The effort of cultivating virtue
is truly like this!"
Later, Empress Yīn gradually became estranged,
and whenever it was her turn to be with the Emperor,
she would always decline, citing illness.
At that time, the Emperor frequently lost imperial princes,
and the Empress Dowager worried about the lack of heirs.
She constantly shed tears and sighed,
and repeatedly selected and brought in talented women
to broaden the Emperor's options.
Empress Yīn, seeing the Empress Dowager's reputation for virtue growing daily,
did not know what to do,
and so resorted to witchcraft and curses,
intending to harm her.
The Emperor once became critically ill in bed,
and Empress Yīn secretly said,
"When I gain power, I will not allow any descendants of the surname Dèng to remain!"
When the Empress Dowager heard this,
she wept before her attendants and said,
"I served the Empress with utmost sincerity and devotion,
yet I did not receive her blessing,
and instead am about to incur heavenly wrath.
Although women do not have the duty to die with their husbands,
Zhōu Gōng personally offered his life for King Wǔ,
and the concubine Yuè Jī swore with her heart to die.
I will do so, first, to repay the Emperor's kindness,
second, to resolve the misfortune of my clan,
and third, to prevent the Yīn clan from receiving the reproach of being 'human swine'."
She then intended to drink poison,
but the palace attendant Zhào Yù firmly restrained her,
and then falsely claimed that an envoy had arrived,
saying the Emperor's illness had already improved.
The Empress Dowager believed it to be true
and stopped.
The next day,
the Emperor indeed recovered.
In the summer of the fourteenth year,
Empress Yīn was deposed for witchcraft and sorcery.
The Empress Dowager pleaded for her but could not succeed,
and the Emperor's affections then turned to her.
She increasingly claimed to be gravely ill,
keeping herself deeply secluded.
At that time, officials proposed establishing the Chángqiū Palace.
The Emperor said,
"The honor of the Empress
is equal to Our own;
she carries on the ancestral temple,
and is the mother of all under Heaven.
How can this be taken lightly!
Only Guìrén Dèng, whose virtue surpasses all in the inner court,
can be worthy of it."
By winter,
she was established as Empress.
She declined the position three times
before finally ascending.
She personally wrote a memorial to decline,
deeply explaining her meager virtue,
insufficient to fulfill the selection for a lesser ruler.
At this time,
various regions and states offered tributes,
competing to present rare and beautiful objects.
From the time she became Empress,
she ordered all such practices to be strictly forbidden,
and only paper and ink were provided annually.
The Emperor repeatedly wished to grant official titles and ranks to the Dèng family,
but she always tearfully pleaded with humility to decline,
thus her brother Dèng Zhì remained merely a Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiāng throughout the Emperor's reign.
In the first year of Yuánxīng,
the Emperor passed away.
His eldest son, the Prince of Píngyuán, was ill,
and the other imperial princes had died young,
numbering more than ten before and after,
with those born later always being secretly raised among the people.
Emperor Shāng was only a hundred days old when
she welcomed and enthroned him.
She was honored as Empress Dowager,
and the Empress Dowager held court.
After Emperor Hé's funeral,
all palace women were to return to their estates.
The Empress Dowager bestowed an edict upon Guìrén Zhōu and Guìrén Féng, saying:
"I and you, Guìrén, were matched in the inner court,
sharing joy as equals
for over ten years.
Not having received blessings,
the late Emperor departed early from the world.
My lonely heart is desolate,
with no one to look up to.
Day and night, I constantly reflect,
and sorrow arises within me.
Now, according to old regulations, you must return to your outer estates.
My grief intensifies with sighs;
how can the poem of 'Yànyàn'
express this?
You, Guìrén, are granted a royal qīnggài carriage,
a decorated lù carriage,
and one team of four horses each,
thirty *jīn* of gold,
three thousand bolts of assorted silks,
and four thousand *duān* of white Yuè cloth."
She also granted Guìrén Féng a royal red ribbon.
As she did not yet have a step-shake hairpin and jade pendants,
she was additionally granted one set of each.
At that time, having just suffered a great sorrow,
the prohibitions had not yet been established.
A casket of large pearls was lost from the palace.
The Empress Dowager thought
that if she interrogated and questioned,
there would surely be innocent people implicated.
So she personally reviewed the palace women,
observed their complexions,
and immediately they confessed.
Furthermore, there was Jíchéng, a favored attendant of Emperor Hé.
The imperial attendants jointly falsely accused Jíchéng of sorcery and witchcraft.
She was then sent to the Yèting for interrogation and questioning,
and the confession and evidence were clear.
The Empress Dowager considered that as an attendant to the previous emperor,
she had been treated with kindness,
and ordinarily had no malicious words,
yet now she was like this;
it was contrary to human nature.
She then personally called her in for a thorough re-examination,
and indeed, it was the imperial attendants who were responsible.
Everyone marveled and submitted,
considering her sagacious and discerning.
She often remarked that ghosts and spirits were difficult to verify,
and licentious sacrifices brought no blessings.
So she issued an edict to the relevant officials to abolish all祠官 (cíguān) that did not conform to ritual norms.
She also issued an edict pardoning and releasing all those who had committed "demon-evil" offenses since the Jiànwǔ era,
as well as those from the Mǎ and Dòu families who had been imprisoned.
All were restored to commoner status.
She reduced the extravagant and difficult-to-obtain items for imperial use, rare delicacies, and luxurious decorations from the Dàguān, Dǎoguān, Shàngfāng, and Nèizhě departments.
Unless it was for offerings to the imperial tombs and temples,
rice and millet were not to be specially selected;
only one meat meal per day, morning and evening, was allowed.
Previously, the annual expenses for the Dàguān and Tāngguān departments were nearly 200 million.
The Empress Dowager ordered them to stop,
and daily cut down on extravagant expenses.
From then on, it was only a few tens of millions.
As for the tributes from commanderies and kingdoms,
all were reduced by more than half.
All hawks and hounds in the Shànglín were sold off.
The embossed bronze vessels, nine-strand belts, and ceremonial daggers from Shǔ and Hàn
were no longer to be procured.
The number of painters was limited to thirty-nine types.

Furthermore, brocades and embroideries, fine silk, damask and crepe, gold and silver, pearls and jade, rhinoceros horn and ivory, tortoiseshell, carved and playful objects from the Yùfǔ, Shàngfāng, and Zhīshì
were all completely discontinued.
The stores of rice, dried provisions, firewood, and charcoal in the detached palaces and separate residences
were all ordered to be reduced.
She also issued an edict to the noble ladies in the various imperial gardens,
stating that if any of their palace women belonged to the imperial clan or were too frail or old to serve,
the garden overseers were to verify their names and submit them.
She personally went to the Zēngxǐ Guān in the Northern Palace to review and question them,
allowing them to leave or stay as they wished.
On that very day, five or six hundred people were dismissed and sent away.
When Emperor Shāng passed away,
the Empress Dowager decided on the plan to enthrone Emperor Ān,
and continued to preside over court affairs.
Due to successive great sorrows
and the people suffering from hard labor,
the secret treasures within Emperor Shāng’s Kānglíng Mausoleum
and all other works
were reduced and economized,
by nine-tenths.
She issued an edict to the Sīlì Xiàowèi, Hénán Yǐn, and Nányáng Tàishǒu, saying:
"Every time I review the foreign relatives and guests of previous dynasties,
who borrowed power and authority,
and were frivolous and reckless,
even to the point of corrupting public service
and causing suffering to the people,
the fault lies with the laxity of the enforcers of the law,
who did not immediately carry out their punishments.
Now, although Chēqí Jiāngjūn Zhì and others harbor respectful and compliant intentions,
their clan is vast,
and their in-laws are numerous.
Their guests are cunning and treacherous,
often infringing upon prohibitions and laws.
They must be strictly admonished and controlled,
and not be tolerated or protected."
From then on, when relatives committed crimes,
there was no favoritism.
The Empress Dowager pitied the disgraced Yīn clan.
She pardoned those who had been exiled and allowed them to return home,
and ordered the return of their assets, totaling over five million.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (107 CE),
she granted the title of Xīnyě Jūn to the Tàifūrén,
with ten thousand households providing for her bath-and-food-tax domain.
In the summer of the second year (108 CE),
there was a drought in the capital.
She personally visited Luòyáng Temple to review wrongful convictions.
There was a prisoner who had not actually committed murder but had been tortured into confessing falsely.
Frail and exhausted, he was brought in on a stretcher.
Fearing the officials, he dared not speak.
As he was about to leave,
he raised his head as if wanting to make an appeal.
The Empress Dowager observed and noticed this.
She immediately called him back and asked about his situation,
and fully uncovered the injustice.
Immediately, the Luòyáng Lìng was arrested and imprisoned, convicted of his crime.
Before she even returned to the palace,
heavy rain fell.
In the autumn of the third year (109 CE),
the Empress Dowager felt unwell.
Her attendants were anxious and fearful,
offering prayers and incantations,
wishing to take her place.
When the Empress Dowager heard of this,
she immediately reprimanded them angrily,
sternly ordering the Yèting Lìng and others
to merely apologize for faults and pray for blessings,
and not to utter ominous words.
According to old custom,
at the end of the year, the guards were to be feasted and dispatched,
and a grand exorcism (dànuó) was to be held to drive away epidemics.
The Empress Dowager, seeing the disharmony of yin and yang and the frequent military campaigns,
decreed that the feasts and gatherings should not include plays or music,
that the number of child exorcists for driving away epidemics should be halved,
and that all elephant and camel displays
should be abolished.
They would revert to the old ways in a year of plenty.
Since the Empress Dowager entered the imperial harem,
she studied classics and history under Cáo Dàjiā,
as well as astronomy and mathematics.
By day, she reviewed state affairs;
by night, she recited and read.
But she was troubled by errors,
fearing they would deviate from canonical regulations.
So she extensively selected scholars like Liú Zhēn and others, along with erudites, court gentlemen, and over fifty clerks from the four ministries,
to go to the Dōngguān to collate and verify historical records.
After the work was completed, it was submitted to the emperor,
and they were given varying amounts of ramie cloth.
She also ordered court eunuchs and close officials to study classics and histories at the Dōngguān,
to teach the palace women,
so that those around her would habitually recite them,
and morning and evening, they were numerous and orderly.
When Xīnyě Jūn passed away,
the Empress Dowager personally attended to her illness
until her very end,
grieving and weakening herself,
her actions exceeding the usual.
She was posthumously granted the red ribbon of a Cháng Gōngzhǔ, hidden treasures from the Eastern Garden, a jade burial suit, and an embroidered quilt,
and also three thousand bolts of cloth
and thirty million coins.
Zhì and others firmly declined the money and cloth, refusing to accept them.
She had the Sīkōng, bearing a scepter, oversee the funeral arrangements,
with rites comparable to those of Dōnghǎi Gōng Wáng,
and was given the posthumous title Jìng Jūn.
After the Empress Dowager’s period of deep mourning ended,
there was a prolonged drought.
The Empress Dowager personally visited Luòyáng for three consecutive days,
reviewed prisoners,
and released thirty-six condemned prisoners,
and eighty prisoners sentenced to *nài* (amputation).
The remaining prisoners had their death sentences reduced, from "right foot amputation and below" to "Sīkòu."
In the first month of the seventh year (113 CE),
she first entered the Tàimiào,
fasting for seven days,
and bestowed gifts upon the high officials and all civil and military officers, each in varying amounts.
On the day Gēngxū,
she visited the ancestral temple,
leading the imperial women and concubines to perform the rituals,
and together with the emperor, made joint offerings and personally presented them,
completing the ceremony before returning.
Thereupon, she issued an edict saying:
"All offerings of new flavors
are often out of season,
either unnaturally cultivated and ripened,
or sprouts dug up prematurely.
The flavor is not fully developed, and the growing things are cut short.
How can this be following the seasons and nurturing living things?
The tradition says, 'Do not eat out of season.'
From now on, all items to be offered at the imperial tombs and temples, and for imperial use,
must await their proper season before being presented."
In total, twenty-three kinds of items were eliminated.
Since the Empress Dowager began to preside over court,
there had been droughts and floods for ten years,
the four barbarian tribes invaded externally,
and bandits rose internally.
Whenever she heard of people starving,
she would sometimes stay awake all night,
and personally reduced her own consumption
to alleviate disasters and hardships.
Therefore, the empire was restored to peace,
and the years returned to abundance.
In the fifth year of Yuánchū
, Liú Yì
, Marquis of Píngwàng, believed that the Empress Dowager had performed many virtuous deeds
and wished for them to be recorded early.
He submitted a memorial to Emperor Ān, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the *Yì* records Fúxī and Shénnóng, and thus their imperial virtue is manifest;
the *Shū* describes Táng and Yú, and thus their imperial way is exalted.
Therefore, even the most sagacious and enlightened [sovereigns]
invariably had their accomplishments recorded on bamboo and silk
and their fame spread through pipes and strings.
I humbly consider that the August Empress Dowager embodies the disposition of a great sage
and the virtue of Heaven and Earth,
matching the footsteps of the concubines of Yú
and rivaling the achievements of Rèn and Sì.
Filial, fraternal, compassionate, and benevolent
—she is truly reverent and frugal,
cutting off the source of extravagance and excess,
and suppressing the omens of indulgence and desire.
She has rightly governed the inner court,
spreading her transforming influence throughout the four seas.
And during the periods of Yuánxīng and Yánpíng,
when the state had no heir,
she looked up at the celestial phenomena
and consulted human renown,
establishing Your Majesty as the ruler of all under Heaven,
bringing everlasting peace to the realm and tranquility to the four seas.
She also encountered floods and heavy rains,
and the eastern provinces suffered famine.
Extending her grace to the common people,
she saw officials crowding the roads [to seek relief].
With simple clothing and food,
she personally set an example for all beneath her,
reducing her own meals and unharnessing her chariots [to sell the horses]
to provide for the masses.
Her compassionate kindness
was like gazing upon her own infants.
She disciplined herself and acknowledged her faults,
promoting the humble and obscure.
She advocated for a government of harmony and peace,
continued broken lineages,
rewarded meritorious ministers,
and reinstated imperial clansmen.
She recalled exiled people
and abolished prohibitions and proscriptions.
If a policy was not beneficial and harmonious,
she would not consider it in her heart;
if an enactment was not based on old statutes,
she would not consult the court about it.
Her profound virtue overflows
and fills the universe;
and spreads to the eight directions.
The Huáxià rejoice in her transforming influence,
and the Róng and Dí are unified.
Her great accomplishments are manifest in the great Hàn,
and her profound kindness benefits all living beings.
Her towering achievements
can be heard but not equaled;
her boundless merits
can be praised but not fully described.
In ancient times, emperors and kings
placed historians at their left and right;
that there have always been records of the times.
Indeed, the Way has its easy and its difficult paths,
and governance has its advances and retreats.
If good governance is not described
while minor aberrations are immediately recorded,
this would be to hold Yáo and Tāng responsible for the calamities of great floods and severe droughts,
yet deny them the beauty of universal harmony bestowed by Heaven;
yet deny them the accomplishments of restoration and peace.
the two concubines of Yú
and the three mothers of the Zhōu royal house
faced internal family difficulties and
external disasters,
yet comprehensively managed the great administration
and operated the affairs of state,
It is fitting to order the historiographers to compile the 'Chánglè Gōng Zhù' (Records of the Chánglè Palace) and the 'Shèngdé Sòng' (Eulogy of Sacred Virtue),
to widely proclaim her glorious brilliance,
engrave her achievements on metal and stone,
make them visible as the sun and moon,
The Emperor assented to this.
In the sixth year,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict summoning over forty princes and princesses, male and female, aged five and above, from the princes of Jìběi and Héjiān, brothers of Emperor Hé.
She also summoned over thirty close relatives and descendants of the Dèng clan.
She had mansions opened for them,
where they were taught the classics,
and she personally supervised their examinations.
For those still young,
she appointed teachers and guardians,
and they entered the palace morning and evening,
where she caressed, nurtured, and instructed them,
showing them immense love and affection.
She then issued an edict to her elder cousin, Dèng Bào
, Magistrate of Hénán, and Dèng Kāng
, Commandant of Yùeqí, and others, saying:
"The reason I have brought in these children
and placed them in the academies
is truly because we now inherit the decline of a hundred kings,
and the customs of the time are shallow and superficial,
with artifice and deceit increasingly prevalent.
The Five Classics are decaying and incomplete;
if there is no transformation and guidance,
they will continue to decline.
Therefore, I wish to promote and honor the sacred Way
to rectify the corrupt customs.
Does the tradition not say: 'To eat one's fill all day,
without applying one's mind to anything—that is difficult!'
Nowadays, in this latter age, the noble and powerful families who enjoy emoluments,
wear warm clothes and eat fine food,
ride sturdy chariots and drive good horses,
but they face a wall in learning [are ignorant of scholarship]
and do not distinguish between good and bad.
This is precisely where misfortune and ruin originate.
During the Yǒngpíng era,
all the young marquises of the Four Clans were ordered to enter school,
in order to correct customs, stimulate the indolent,
and revert them to loyalty and filial piety.
My late father not only had his military exploits recorded on bamboo and silk,
but also used his cultivated virtue to educate his children and grandchildren.
Therefore, they were able to conduct themselves properly
and avoid falling into the net [of transgression].
If these children can emulate the splendid achievements of their ancestors
and recall the original intent of the imperial edict,
then that will be sufficient.
Strive hard!"
Dèng Kāng
felt fearful because the Empress Dowager had presided over the government for a long time
and pretended to be ill, not attending court.
The Empress Dowager sent a palace attendant to inquire about him.
At that time, many palace maids who entered and exited [the palace]
were capable of slandering or praising others,
and the older ones among them were all called 'Zhōngdàrén'.
The one sent was a former maid from Dèng Kāng's household,
who also referred to herself as 'Zhōngdàrén'.
When Kāng heard this,
he cursed her, saying:
"You came from my household; how dare you act like this!"
The maid was enraged
and returned to report that Kāng was feigning illness and had spoken disrespectfully.
The Empress Dowager then dismissed Kāng from his office,
sent him back to his native state,
and severed his family registration.
In the second month of the second year of Yǒngníng
, her illness gradually worsened.
She then rode in her palanquin to the front hall
to meet with the attendants and ministers,
and then proceeded north to the newly constructed palace for the Crown Prince.
Upon her return,
a general amnesty was issued throughout the empire,
and gifts of money and cloth were distributed in varying amounts to the noblewomen, princes, princesses, and officials of the various gardens.
An edict stated:
"I, being without virtue,
was entrusted as the mother of all under Heaven,
yet with meager fortune and disfavored by Heaven,
I suffered great sorrow early.
At the time of Yánpíng,
the realm was without a sovereign,
and the common people were in a dire situation,
as precarious as stacked eggs.
With diligent and arduous effort,
I dared not take pleasure in the imperial throne,
wishing above not to deceive Heaven or shame the former emperors,
and below not to betray the people or my original intention.
My sincere desire was to rescue and save the common people
to secure the Liú clan.
I told myself that by moving Heaven and Earth,
I would receive blessings and good fortune,
yet misfortunes and calamities, both internal and external,
have brought unceasing grief and pain.
Recently, due to debilitating illness and prolonged stagnation,
I have long been unable to attend the ancestral sacrifices.
I forced myself to ascend to the Yuánlíng mausoleum,
but this exacerbated my coughing and spitting blood,
leading to an irrecoverable state.
The great division between life and death
is beyond my control.
May the dukes, ministers, and all officials
strive to be utterly loyal and respectful
in assisting the court."
In the third month, she passed away.
She had reigned for twenty years,
and was forty-one years old.
She was interred with Emperor Hé at Shùnlíng.
A commentary states: Dèng Hòu (Empress Dèng) controlled the government throughout her life.
Edicts issued from her personally.
Her methods fell short of the excellence of previous administrations,
and she lacked the virtue of an enlightened ruler,
leading to the heir-apparent eyeing her askance,
bowing in reverence to an empty vessel.
Righteous scholars harbored resentment,
hanging their critiques on the Xiàngwèi gate.
To praise her as righteous
is surely a delusion!
However, after Jiànguāng,
the imperial power found its rightful owner,
yet then esteemed scholars were humiliated and killed,
and the party of corrupt relatives advanced.
The onset of decay
is evidenced by this.
Thus, one knows that those who wield power and attract slander,
what they rely on is not themselves;
those who burn with anxiety and worry about calamity,
what they strive for is solely the state.
Therefore, when Bān Mǔ made a single comment,
she retired from public life and closed her doors;
when her beloved niece committed a minor fault,
she shaved her head and begged forgiveness.
[一０]Could it be that Dù Gēn, facing execution,
had not yet revealed his true sincerity?
[一一]But the ox that treads on the field,
it has been deprived too much.
[一二]Ān Sī Yán Huánghòu (Empress Yán), personal name Jī,
was from Yíngyáng, Hénán.
Her grandfather Zhāng,
during the Yǒngpíng reign, served as Shàngshū.
He had two younger sisters who were Guìrén (Honored Ladies).
Zhāng was diligent and knowledgeable in old precedents.
After long service,
he should have been promoted to an important position,
but Xiǎnzōng considered him a relative of the Empress's family,
and ultimately did not employ him,
sending him out as a Bùbīng Xiàowèi (Colonel of Infantry).
Zhāng begot Chàng,
and Chàng begot the Empress.
The Empress possessed both talent and beauty.
In the first year of Yuánchū,
she was selected to enter the Yèting (Inner Palace),
and was greatly favored,
becoming a Guìrén.
In the second year,
she was established as Empress.
The Empress was possessive and jealous.
When the Emperor favored the palace lady Lǐ Shì,
who bore him the imperial son Bǎo,
she poisoned Lǐ Shì to death.
In the third year,
her father, Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) Chàng, was made Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi (Colonel of Chángshuǐ),
and enfeoffed as Běi Yíchūn Hóu,
with a fiefdom of five thousand households.
In the fourth year,
Chàng died,
and was posthumously named Wén Hóu.
His son Xiǎn succeeded him.
In the first year of Jiànguāng,
Dèng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager Dèng) died,
and the Emperor began to personally attend to state affairs.
Xiǎn and his younger brothers Jǐng, Yào, and Yàn were all made Qīngxiào (Ministers and Colonels),
commanding the imperial guards.
In the first year of Yán'guāng,
Xiǎn was further enfeoffed as Chángshè Hóu,
with a fiefdom of thirteen thousand five hundred households.
The Empress's mother Zōng was posthumously honored as Yíngyáng Jūn.
All of Xiǎn's and Jǐng's sons were still children,
and all were made Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Attendants).
With the Empress's favor flourishing,
and her brothers largely involved in court power,
the Empress then conspired with Dàchángqiū (Grand Chief Steward) Jiāng Jīng, Zhōngchángshì (Regular Palace Attendant) Fán Fēng, and others to slander Crown Prince Bǎo,
who was deposed as Jìyīn Wáng.
In the spring of the fourth year,
the Empress accompanied the Emperor on a trip to Zhānglíng.
The Emperor fell ill on the road,
and died in Yè Xiàn.
The Empress, her brothers Xiǎn and others, and Jiāng Jīng, Fán Fēng, and others conspired, saying:
"Now that the Emperor has passed away on the road,
and Jìyīn Wáng is within the palace,
if the high officials were to by chance establish him,
it would later become a great danger."
They then falsely claimed the Emperor was gravely ill,
and moved him into a sleeping carriage.
After traveling for four days,
they rushed back to the palace.
The next day,
they deceitfully sent Sītú (Minister of Works) Liú Xī to the suburban altars, ancestral temples, and altars of soil and grain,
to announce to Heaven and beg for a mandate.
That evening,
they then announced the Emperor's death.
The Empress was honored as Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager).
The Empress Dowager presided over court,
and appointed Xiǎn as Chēqí Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry) with the honors of Sānsī (Three Excellencies).
The Empress Dowager wished to monopolize state power for a long time,
and coveted establishing a young ruler. Together with Xiǎn and others, she decided on a plan within the forbidden palace,
welcoming Yī, the Běixiāng Hóu (Marquis of Běixiāng) and son of Jìběi Huì Wáng,
and establishing him as Emperor.
Xiǎn was jealous of Dàjiāngjūn (General-in-Chief) Gěng Bǎo,
whose position was honorable and power great, and whose prestige extended to the previous court.

So he subtly encouraged officials to impeach Bǎo and his faction, along with Zhōngchángshì (Regular Palace Attendant) Fán Fēng, Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng (Commandant of Tiger-Guards) Xiè Yùn, Yùn's younger brother Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) Dú, Dú's younger brother Dàjiāngjūn Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk of the General-in-Chief) Mì,
Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) Zhōu Guǎng, the Emperor's nurse Yěwáng Jūn Wáng Shèng, Shèng's daughter Yǒng, Yǒng's husband Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Attendant) Fán Yán, and others,
claiming they formed factions,
abused their authority,
probed into the forbidden palace,
and colluded with each other,
all committing great insolence.
Fēng, Yùn, and Guǎng were all imprisoned and died;
their families were exiled to Bǐjǐng.
Mì and Yán were spared death,
but were shaved and collared.
Bǎo was demoted to Zétíng Hóu,
sent to his fief,
and committed suicide.
Wáng Shèng and her son were exiled to Yànmén.
Thereupon, Jǐng was appointed Wèiwèi (Minister of the Guards),
Yào as Chéngmén Xiàowèi (Colonel of City Gates),
and Yàn as Zhífū Jīnwú (Bearer of the Gilded Halberd).
The brothers held crucial power,
wielding influence as they pleased.
The Young Emperor reigned for just over two hundred days and then fell gravely ill.
Xiǎn, his brothers, and Jiāng Jīng were all at his side.
Jīng drew Xiǎn aside and whispered:
"Běixiāng Hóu's illness is not getting better.
The succession to the throne should be decided soon.
Previously, we did not choose Jìyīn Wáng.
If we establish him now,
he will surely harbor resentment later.
Why not send for the various imperial princes early
and select one to install?"
Xiǎn thought this was correct.
When the Young Emperor died,
Jīng reported to the Empress Dowager,
who then summoned the princes of Jìběi and Héxián.
Before they arrived,
the Zhōnghuángmén (Inner Yellow Gate) Sūn Chéng conspired to kill Jiāng Jīng and others,
and established Jìyīn Wáng,
who became Shùn Dì (Emperor Shùn).
Xiǎn, Jǐng, Yàn, and their faction were all executed.
The Empress Dowager was moved to a detached palace,
and her family was exiled to Bǐjǐng.
The following year,
the Empress Dowager died.
She had reigned for twelve years,
and was interred with her husband in Gōnglíng.
The Emperor's mother, Lǐ Shì, had been buried north of Luòyáng city.
The Emperor initially did not know,
and no one dared to inform him.
After the Empress Dowager died,
his attendants informed him.
The Emperor was moved and saddened,
personally went to the burial site,
re-interred her with proper rites,
and bestowed upon her the honorary posthumous title Gōngmǐn Huánghòu,
burying her in Gōng Běi Líng.
A ceremonial document was placed in a golden casket,
and stored in the temple of Shìzǔ.
Shùnliè Liáng Huánghòu (Empress Liáng), personal name Nà,
was the daughter of Dàjiāngjūn (General-in-Chief) Shāng,
and a granddaughter of Gōnghuái Huánghòu's younger brother.
When she was born,
there was an auspicious omen of light.
In her youth, she was skilled in needlework
and enjoyed historical texts.
At nine, she could recite the Lúnyǔ (Analects),
and studied the Hán Shī (Han Poems), grasping their general meaning.
She often kept illustrations of exemplary women by her side,
to serve as her guide and warning.
Her father Shāng was deeply impressed,
and secretly told his younger brothers:
"Our ancestors completely saved Héxī,
and those they saved were countless.
Although they did not attain the highest positions,
their accumulated virtue will surely be rewarded.
If good fortune is to flow to our descendants,
perhaps it will arise through this girl?"
In the third year of Yǒngjiàn,
she and her maternal aunt were selected to enter the Yètíng,
she was then thirteen years old.
The physiognomist Máo Tōng saw the empress,
and was astonished.
He bowed twice and congratulated her, saying:
"This is what is called a 'sun-cornered and crescent-moon-like' countenance,
the utmost noble of physiognomies,
which your servant has never before seen."
The Grand Astrologer obtained the divination 'Shòufáng',
and also divined 'Kūn zhī Bǐ' from the Yì Jīng.
Thus, she was made a guìrén.
She was often especially favored to be with the Emperor,
and calmly declined to the Emperor, saying:
"Indeed, yang considers broad bestowal a virtue,
and yin considers non-exclusivity righteousness.
The locust produces a hundred offspring;
this is whence blessings arise.
I wish Your Majesty would consider the equalizing moisture of clouds and rain,
and recognize the orderly sequence of strung fish,
so that your humble concubine may be spared the burden of blame and slander."
Because of this, the Emperor held her in greater esteem.
In the spring of the first year of Yángjiā,
the officials concerned proposed establishing the Chángqiū Palace,
stating that since Shāng, Marquis of Chéngshì, was an empress's relative of the late Emperor,
and according to the righteousness of the Chūnqiū,
one should marry from a great state first,
Liáng Xiǎoguìrén was suitable to match the heavenly blessing
and rightfully occupy the position of the queen.
The Emperor agreed to it,
and so in the Shòu'ān Hall, he established the guìrén as Empress.
The Empress, being intelligent and sagacious from a young age,
deeply understood the successes and failures of previous generations.
Although she advanced through virtue,
she dared not harbor pride or exclusivity.
Whenever there were solar or lunar eclipses,
she would don plain clothes and seek out her faults.
In the first year of Jiànkāng,
the Emperor passed away.
The Empress had no sons.
Bǐng, the son of Meírén Yú Shì, was enthroned,
who became Emperor Chōng.
The Empress was honored as Empress Dowager,
and the Empress Dowager presided over the court.
Emperor Chōng soon passed away,
and Emperor Zhì was again enthroned,
but she still held the reins of government.
At that time, fierce bandits from Yáng and Xú harassed the prefectures and commanderies.
The Western Qiāng, Xiānbēi, and Rìnán Mányí attacked cities and plundered violently.
Taxes and levies were frequent and numerous,
and both officials and common people were exhausted.
The Empress Dowager toiled day and night,
trusted the virtuous,
and delegated responsibility to Tàiwèi Lǐ Gù and others.
She promoted loyal and good officials,
and strove to advocate frugality.
Many who were greedy and wicked
were punished or removed.
Troops were dispatched to suppress the rebels,
and the various bandits were eliminated.
Thus, the whole country was peaceful,
and the ancestral temples were secure.
However, her elder brother, Grand General Liáng Jì, poisoned Emperor Zhì,
monopolized power and was tyrannical,
and was jealous of and harmed loyal and good officials.
He frequently misled the Empress Dowager with perverse arguments,
and consequently enthroned Emperor Huán and executed Lǐ Gù.
The Empress Dowager was also overly fond of eunuchs,
granting many titles and favors,
which caused the common people to be disappointed.
In the spring of the first year of Hépíng,
she returned governmental authority to the Emperor.
The Empress Dowager's illness worsened severely,
so she was carried by imperial carriage to Xuāndé Hall,
where she met palace officials and her brothers of the Liáng clan.
An imperial edict stated:
"I have always had a 'knot of qi' in my chest.
Since recently,
swelling has been added,
hindering my eating and drinking.
I have gradually become critically ill,
causing both internal and external officials to worry and pray.
I privately estimate
that I am weakening day by day and night by night,
and will not be able to conclude my work with the various Dukes and high officials.
I assisted in establishing the holy heir,
but regret not being able to nurture him for long
and witness his beginning and end.
Now, I entrust the Emperor and my brothers, the Generals, to my loyal ministers.
May each of you exert yourselves."
Two days later, she passed away.
She had been in power for nineteen years,
and was forty-five years old.
She was interred with Emperor Shùn in the Xiànlíng tomb.
As for Meírén Yú Shì,
she was selected into the Yètíng at thirteen years old, as a daughter of a good family.
She also gave birth to Princess Wǔyáng Zhǎng.
Since the founding of the Hàn dynasty,
mothers [of emperors] had all been honored and favored.
Emperor Shùn had not yet bestowed a noble title upon the meírén,
and Emperor Chōng died young.
Grand General Liáng Jì held power,
and he disliked other clans,
so the Yú clan was suppressed and not elevated,
only referred to as
"Dàjiā"
and nothing more.
As for Fūrén Chén,
her family was originally from Wèijùn.
At a young age, she entered the palace of King Xiào with her singing and performing skills,
gained favor,
and gave birth to Emperor Zhì.
Also because of the Liáng clan,
she did not receive honor and favor.
In the fourth year of Xīpíng,
Xiǎohuángmén Zhào Yòu
and Yìláng Bēi Zhěng submitted a memorial, stating:
"According to the righteousness of the Chūnqiū,
a mother is honored by her son.
The grand ceremonies of the glorious Hàn dynasty
honor and elevate the mothers;
all those who are empresses' relatives
are granted favor.
Now, Dàjiā Yú, mother of Emperor Chōng,
and Fūrén Chén, mother of Emperor Zhì,
both gave birth to sagely emperors,
yet they have no titles.
Even humble officials and sons
still have the custom of posthumous grants.
How much more so for these two mothers who are still alive,
not receiving the order of elevation and distinction?
This does not follow the precedents of previous generations,
nor set an example for future generations."
The Emperor was moved by their words,
and so he appointed Dàjiā Yú as Xiànlíng Guìrén,
and Fūrén Chén as Bóhǎi Xiàowángfēi.
He ordered the Zhōngchángshì to hold the ceremonial staff and bestow the seal and cord,
and dispatched the Tàicháng to offer sacrifices with three animals at Xiànlíng, Huáilíng, and Jìnglǐng.
Empress Xiàochóng Yǎn, personal name Míng,
was a concubine (yìngqiè) of Yì, Marquis of Líwú,
and gave birth to Emperor Huán.
When Emperor Huán ascended the throne,
the following year,
he posthumously honored Yì as Emperor Xiàochóng,
and his tomb as Bólíng.
The Empress was made Bóyuán Guìrén.
In the first year of Hépíng,
when Empress Dowager Liáng passed away,
Empress Yǎn was then honored as Empress Xiàochóng at Bólíng.
The Sītú was dispatched to hold the ceremonial staff and present the imperial decree and seal,
bringing imperial carriages, garments,
and all necessary ritual objects.
Her palace was named Yǒnglè.
Officials such as Tàipú and Shàofǔ were appointed below her,
all following the precedents of the Chánglè Palace.
Furthermore, Hǔbēn and Yǔlín guards were established,
palaces were built,
and nine counties of Jùlù were designated as her private income-producing territory (tāngmùyì).
She was in position for three years,
and passed away in the second year of Yuánjiā.
Emperor Huán's younger brother, Shí, Prince of Píngyuán, was made the chief mourner.
She was interred with a painted cypress coffin from the Eastern Park, a jade casket, and funerary provisions for the mouth.
Her funeral rites and system followed those of Empress Gōnghuái.
The Sītú was sent with the ceremonial staff,
and the Dàchángqiū offered condolences and sacrifices.
A funerary gift of forty million cash
and forty thousand bolts of cloth was given.
The Zhōngyèzhě Púshè was in charge of the funeral arrangements,
and the Shìyùshǐ guarded the imperial ceremonial procession.
An edict commanded Bào, Prince of Ānpíng; Jiàn, Prince of Héjiān; Kūi, Prince of Bóhǎi;
and the two Eldest Princesses of Chángshè and Yìyáng,
along with the marquises of various states within three hundred lǐ,
and officials of the rank of Zhōng Èrqiānshí, Èrqiānshí, lìng, zhǎng, and xiāng,
to all attend the funeral.
The Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng was to complete the tomb mound and repair the ancestral temple,
and she was interred with Emperor Huán in Bólíng.
Empress Yìxiàn Liáng of Huán Dì, personal name Nǚyíng,
was the younger sister of Empress Shùnliè.
When the Emperor was first the Marquis of Líwú,
Empress Dowager Liáng summoned him,
wishing to arrange a marriage with the Empress.
Before the auspicious ceremony could take place,
Zhì Dì passed away,
and so the Emperor was enthroned.
The following year,
officials reported to the Empress Dowager, saying:
“The Spring and Autumn Annals record that the Queen was welcomed from Jì,
and while on the road, she was referred to as the Queen.
Now the younger sister of the General-in-Chief Jì
is worthy of inheriting the sacred virtue.
At the time of the marriage,
when the decree is issued and assembled,
it is appropriate to prepare the ritual documents
and promptly present the betrothal gifts.
Please instruct the Three Excellencies and the Grand Minister of Ceremonies to examine the rites.”
The report was approved.
Thus, everything followed the precedent of Emperor Xiàohuì's marriage to his empress.
The betrothal involved twenty thousand catties of gold,
and the presentation of wild geese, jade discs, chariots and horses, and bundles of silk,
all in accordance with ancient customs.
In the sixth month of the first year of Jiànhé, she first entered the Yè Tíng,
and in the eighth month, she was established as Empress.
At this time, the Empress Dowager held power, and Liáng Jì monopolized court affairs,
so the Empress alone received favor and affection;
those below her were not permitted to meet the Emperor.
The Empress relied on the influence of her elder sister and brother,
indulging in extreme luxury and extravagance.
Her palace chambers were intricately carved and beautiful,
her clothing and carriages were adorned with precious and splendid items,
and the craftsmanship and designs
surpassed those of previous eras by double.
However, after the Empress Dowager passed away,
her favor and affection gradually waned.
As the Empress had no children,
she secretly harbored resentment and jealousy.
Whenever palace women became pregnant,
few managed to carry to term.
Although the Emperor was coerced by Liáng Jì
and dared not express anger or blame,
his visits to her became increasingly rare.
In the second or third year of Yánxī,
the Empress died of sorrow and resentment.
She had been on the throne for thirteen years
and was buried in Yì Líng.
In that same year,
Liáng Jì was executed,
and Yì Líng was demoted to the tomb of a Guìrén.
Empress Dèng Měngnǚ of Huán Dì
was the daughter of Dèng Xiāng, who was the son of a paternal cousin of Empress Héxī.
Her mother, Xuān,
first married Xiāng
and gave birth to the Empress.
She later remarried Liáng Jì,
who was
the maternal uncle of Sūn Shòu, the wife of General-in-Chief Liáng Jì.
The Empress became an orphan at a young age
and lived with her mother,
thus taking on the surname Liáng.
Liáng Jì's wife, seeing the Empress's beauty,
brought her into the Yè Tíng during the Yǒngxīng period
as a Cǎinǚ,
and she became extremely favored.
The following year,
her brother Dèng Yǎn was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Nándùn
with the rank of Tèjìn.
Upon Yǎn's death,
his son Kāng succeeded him.
After Empress Yìxiàn passed away
and Liáng Jì was executed,
she was established as Empress.
The Emperor disliked the Liáng clan,
so he changed her surname to Bó,
and enfeoffed her mother Xuān as the Lady of Cháng'ān.
In the fourth year,
officials reported that the Empress was originally the daughter of the Administrator Dèng Xiāng
and it was inappropriate to change to another surname.
Thus, she reverted to the Dèng surname.
Dèng Xiāng was posthumously enfeoffed and granted the seals and ribbons of the Chējì Jiāngjūn, Marquis of Ānyáng.
Xuān and Kāng were re-enfeoffed with large counties,
Xuān as the Lady of Kūnyáng,
and Kāng as the Marquis of Bǐyáng.
Their rewards and gifts amounted to tens of millions.
Upon Xuān's death,
the funeral expenses, gifts, and burial ceremonies
all followed the old rites for an empress's mother.
Kāng's younger brother Tǒng inherited the title of Marquis of Kūnyáng
and the position of Shìzhōng;
Tǒng's paternal cousin Huì inherited the title of Marquis of Ānyáng
and became the Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiāng;
also, Tǒng's younger brother Bǐng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yùyáng.
All members of the clan were appointed as school officials or military commanders.
The Emperor had many concubines,
collecting five or six thousand palace women,
and including servants and attendants,
this number doubled.
However, the Empress, relying on her elevated status, was arrogant and jealous,
and she and the Emperor's favored Guō Guìrén frequently slandered each other.
In the eighth year,
an imperial edict deposed the Empress,
sending her to the bào shì (prison for imperial women),
where she died of sorrow.
She had been on the throne for seven years.
She was buried in Běimáng.
Her paternal cousin Wànshì, the Governor of Hénán, and Huì were all imprisoned and died.
Tǒng and others were also imprisoned in the bào shì,
deprived of their official ranks and titles,
returned to their original commanderies,
and their property was confiscated by the state.
Empress Dòu Miào of Huán Sī
was the granddaughter of a paternal cousin of Empress Zhāngdé.
Her father was Wǔ.
In the eighth year of Yánxī,
after Empress Dèng was deposed,
she was chosen and entered the Yè Tíng as a Guìrén.
That winter,
she was established as Empress,
but the Emperor's visits to her were very rare;
his favored ones were only Cǎinǚ Tián Shèng and others.
In the winter of the first year of Yǒngkāng,
when the Emperor was gravely ill,
he elevated Tián Shèng and nine other women to the rank of Guìrén.
When he passed away,
having no heir,
she became Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager presided over the court and decided on the succession,
establishing Hóng, the Marquis of Xièdútíng,
who became Líng Dì.
The Empress Dowager was always jealous and ruthless,
having accumulated anger towards Tián Shèng and others.
While Huán Dì's coffin was still in the front hall,
she killed Tián Shèng.
She also intended to execute all the Guìrén,
but the Central Regular Attendants Guǎn Bà and Sū Kāng earnestly admonished her,
and so she stopped.
At that time, her father, General-in-Chief Wǔ, planned to eliminate the eunuchs,
but the Central Regular Attendant Cáo Jié forged an imperial edict and killed Wǔ,
relocating the Empress Dowager to the Yúntái in the Nán Gōng,
and her family members were moved to Bǐjǐng.
Although the Dòu clan was purged,
the Emperor still recognized the Empress Dowager's contribution in supporting his enthronement.
On the first day of the tenth month of the fourth year of Jiànníng,
he led his officials to pay respects at the Nán Gōng,
personally offering her a toast for longevity.
The Palace Gate Chief Dǒng Méng
consequently frequently reported the Empress Dowager's grievances,
and the Emperor listened intently,
increasing her provisions and support more than before.
The Central Regular Attendants Cáo Jié and Wáng Fǔ resented Méng for assisting the Empress Dowager,
falsely accusing him of slandering the Yǒnglè Gōng.
Méng was consequently imprisoned and died.
In the first year of Xīpíng,
the Empress Dowager's mother died in Bǐjǐng,
and the Empress Dowager fell ill and passed away.
She was on the throne for seven years and was buried with the Emperor in Xuānlíng.
Empress Dǒng of Xiào Rén, personal name unknown,
was from Héjiān.
She was the wife of Cháng, the Marquis of Xièdútíng,
and gave birth to Líng Dì.
In the first year of Jiànníng,
when the Emperor ascended the throne,
Cháng was posthumously honored as Emperor Xiào Rén,
his tomb was called Shènlíng,
and she was designated as Shènyuán Guìrén.
After the Dòu clan was purged,
the following year,
the Emperor sent a Central Regular Attendant to welcome the Guìrén
and also summoned her elder brother Chǒng to the capital.
She was honored with the title of Empress Xiào Rén
and resided in the Jiádé Diàn of the Nán Gōng,
her palace being named Yǒnglè.
Chǒng was appointed Zhí Jīn Wú.
Later, because he falsely claimed to be acting on behalf of Empress Yǒnglè to seek favors,
he was imprisoned and died.
When Dòu Tàihòu passed away,
she began to participate in court politics,
causing the Emperor to sell offices and seek bribes,
personally collecting gold and money
until her halls and rooms were overflowing.
In the fifth year of Zhōngpíng,
her elder brother's son, Wèi Wèi Xiū Hóu Chóng,
was made Piàojí Jiāngjūn,
leading over a thousand soldiers.
Originally,
she personally raised the imperial prince Xié,
repeatedly urging the Emperor to establish him as crown prince.
However, Hé Huánghòu resented this,
and the Emperor passed away before a decision could be made.
When Hé Tàihòu presided over the court,
Chóng and the Grand General Jìn, the elder brother of Hé Tàihòu, contended for power and were mutually hostile.
She often wanted to interfere in state affairs,
but Hé Tàihòu always forbade and blocked her.
She, in anger and resentment, cursed, saying:
"You are now acting so arrogant,
relying on your brother, are you?
I will order the Piàojí to bring Jìn's head."
Hé Tàihòu heard this
and reported it to Jìn.
Jìn, together with the Sāngōng and his younger brother, Chējí Jiāngjūn Miáo, memorialized:
"Xiàorén Huánghòu sent the former Zhōng Chángshì Xià Yùn and Yǒnglè Tàipú Fēng Xǔ and others to collude with the commanderies and provinces,
extorting precious treasures and bribes from their locations,
all entering the Western Palace.
According to old precedents, a former empress (Fān Hòu) is not allowed to remain in the capital.
Her chariots and garments have regulations,
and her meals have grades.
We request that Yǒnglè Hòu be moved to her original state."
The memorial was approved.
Hé Jìn then raised troops to surround the Piàojí government office,
arrested Chóng,
who was stripped of his office and committed suicide.
She was worried and afraid,
fell ill, and died suddenly,
having been on the throne for twenty-two years.
The common people blamed the Hé clan.
Her coffin was returned to Hélián,
and she was buried together in Shènlíng.
Língdì's Sòng Huánghòu, whose personal name is not known,
was from Pínglíng, Fúfēng.
She was the great-grandniece of Sùzōng's Concubine Sòng.
In the third year of Jiànníng,
she was selected into the Yèting as a noble lady (guìrén).
The next year,
she was established as Empress.
Her father, Fēng,
was Zhí Jīnwú,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Bùqí Xiāng.
The Empress was not favored but occupied the principal position.
The palace had many favored concubines,
who conspired to slander and defame her.
Initially,
Zhōng Chángshì Wáng Fǔ unjustly executed Prince Lǐ of Bóhǎi and his consort, Lady Sòng,
who was the Empress's paternal aunt.
Fǔ feared that the Empress resented him,
so he and Tàizhōng Dàfū Chéng Ā conspired to fabricate a story that the Empress practiced sorcery and curses with forbidden methods.
The Emperor believed it.
In the first year of Guānghé,
he therefore issued an edict to confiscate her imperial seal and ribbon.
The Empress was confined to the Bàoshì (chamber of punishment)
and died of grief.
She was on the throne for eight years.
Her father and brothers were all executed.
All the Zhōng Chángshì and Xiǎo Huángmén within the palace gates,
pitying the innocent Sòng clan,
pooled their money and goods to collect and bury the deposed Empress and her father Fēng,
returning them to the Sòng clan's old graveyard at Gāomén Tíng.
Later, the Emperor dreamed that Huándì angrily said:
"What crime or fault did Empress Sòng commit,
that you listened to evil and wicked individuals
and caused her death?
Prince Lǐ of Bóhǎi was already demoted,
and then he was executed.
Now the Sòng clan and Lǐ are appealing to Heaven,
and Shàngdì is greatly enraged.
Your crime is beyond salvation."
The dream was extraordinarily vivid and clear.
When the Emperor awoke, he was afraid,
and asked Yǔlín Zuǒ Jiān Xǔ Yǒng
about the matter,
saying:
"What kind of omen is this?
Can it be averted?"
Yǒng replied:
"Empress Sòng personally shared with Your Majesty the responsibility of upholding the ancestral temples,
and acted as mother to all nations.
She held this position for a long time,
and the realm benefited from her influence,
with no known faults or wickedness.
Yet, you falsely listened to slanders and jealous words,
leading to the crime of an innocent person,
suffering extreme punishment,
and calamity reaching her family.
All your subjects and concubines in the world
are filled with resentment and sorrow.
Prince Lǐ of Bóhǎi
was the younger brother of Huándì by the same mother.
He governed his state and served his princedom,
never having committed any fault.
Your Majesty did not verify and investigate,
and thus he suffered his fate.
In the past, when Duke Jìn lost justice,
he also dreamed of a great vengeful spirit with disheveled hair touching the ground.
The ways of Heaven are clear and discerning;
ghosts and spirits cannot be deceived.
It is appropriate to rebury them together
to appease their wronged souls.
Restore the Sòng Empress's exiled family,
and reinstate Bóhǎi's former enfeoffment,
to dispel this calamity."
The Emperor could not adopt his advice
and soon also passed away.
Língsī Hé Huánghòu, whose personal name is not known,
was from Wǎn, Nányáng.
Her family was originally butchers,
and she was selected into the Yèting.
She was seven *chi* and one *cun* tall.
She gave birth to the imperial prince Biàn,
who was raised in the household of Shǐ Dàorén
and called Marquis Shǐ.
She was appointed a noble lady (guìrén),
and was greatly favored.
She was strong and jealous by nature;
no one in the inner palace dared not tremble before her.
In the third year of Guānghé,
she was established as Empress.
The next year,
her father Zhēn was posthumously honored as Chējí Jiāngjūn and Wǔyáng Xuāndé Hóu,
and her mother Xīng was enfeoffed as Wǔyáng Jūn.
At this time, Concubine Wáng was pregnant.
Fearing the Empress,
she took medicine to abort it,
but the fetus remained secure.
She also frequently dreamed of carrying the sun and walking.
In the fourth year,
she gave birth to the imperial prince Xié.
The Empress then poisoned the concubine to death.
The Emperor was greatly enraged
and wanted to depose the Empress,
but the eunuchs strongly pleaded for her, and he stopped.
Dǒng Tàihòu personally raised Xié,
who was called Marquis Dǒng.
Concubine Wáng
was from the state of Zhào.
Her grandfather, Bāo,
was Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiāng.
The concubine was beautiful in appearance,
intelligent and talented,
skilled in writing and accounting.
She was selected into the Yèting as a daughter of a respectable family according to the law.
The Emperor pitied Xié for losing his mother early
and also missed the concubine,
so he composed the "Fu of Recalling Virtue" and the "Ode to Gracious Demeanor."
In the sixth year of Zhōngpíng,
the Emperor passed away.
The imperial prince Biàn ascended the throne,
and the Empress was honored as Huáng Tàihòu.
The Empress Dowager presided over the court.
Her elder brother, the Grand General Jìn, wished to execute the eunuchs,
but was instead harmed by them.
Wǔyáng Jūn was also killed by rebellious soldiers.
Dǒng Zhuó, the Governor of Bìngzhōu, was summoned
and led troops into Luòyáng.
He oppressed the imperial court,
then deposed the young Emperor as Hóngnóng Wáng and enthroned Xié,
who became Xiàndì.
He helped Hóngnóng Wáng descend from the hall
and face north to declare himself a subject.
The Empress Dowager choked back tears,
and the assembled officials were filled with sorrow,
but none dared to speak.
Dǒng Zhuó also argued that the Empress Dowager had oppressed the Yǒnglè Palace,
leading to Dǒng Tàihòu's death from grief,
and had violated the rites between daughter-in-law and mother-in-law.
So he moved her to Yǒng'ān Gōng,
and then offered her poisoned wine,
murdering her.
She passed away,
having been on the throne for ten years.
Dǒng Zhuó ordered the Emperor to mourn her at Fèngcháng Tíng,
and the Gōngqīng all gathered in plain white clothes,
but it was not a proper funeral.
She was buried together in Wénzhāo Líng.
Initially,
when the Empress Dowager was newly established,
she was supposed to visit the temples of the two ancestors.
She wanted to fast,
but there were always unforeseen incidents.
This happened repeatedly,
and she ultimately could not accomplish it.
At the time, discerning individuals privately found this strange,
and later, the Hàn dynasty's fate was indeed ruined by the Hé clan.
The next year,
righteous troops from Shāndōng rose up in great numbers
to suppress Dǒng Zhuó's rebellion.
Dǒng Zhuó then placed King Hóngnóng in an upstairs chamber,
and ordered Lángzhōnglì Lǐ Rú to bring poison,
saying:
“Take this medicine;
it can ward off evil.”
The King said:
“I am not ill;
you wish to kill me!”
He refused to drink it.
He was forced to drink it,
and having no alternative,
he and his wife, Táng Jī, and his palace attendants held a farewell banquet.
As the wine circulated,
the King sang a sorrowful song:
“The Dao of Heaven is changing, how ill-fated am I! Forsaking the myriad chariots, I retreat to a mere fief.
Rebellious ministers persecute me, my life will not be extended;
I am about to leave you all and go to the mysterious depths!”
He then ordered Táng Jī to dance.
She raised her sleeves and sang:
“The Imperial Heaven collapses, the Empress Earth crumbles;
though I am an emperor, my life is cut short.
The paths of life and death diverge, from this point we part;
alas for my solitary state, my heart is grieved!”
Thereupon, tears streamed down, and she sobbed,
and all who were seated sighed with sorrow.
The King said to Jī:
“You are a king's consort;
you must not again become the wife of a common official or citizen.
Take care of yourself;
from this point, a long farewell!”
He then drank the poison and died.
He was eighteen years old at the time.
Táng Jī
was a native of Yǐngchuān.
When the King passed away,
she returned to her hometown.
Her father, Huìjī Tàishǒu Mào, wanted to marry her off,
but Jī swore she would not allow it.
When Lǐ Quē broke Cháng'ān,
he sent troops to raid Guāndōng
and captured Jī.
Lǐ Quē then wanted to take her as his wife,
but she firmly refused,
and never revealed her name.
Shàngshū Jiǎ Xǔ learned of this
and reported the situation to Xiàndì.
The Emperor was moved and saddened upon hearing it,
and issued an edict to welcome Jī,
placing her in the royal garden,
and sent a Shìzhōng holding a jié to formally appoint her as King Hóngnóng's consort.
In the second month of the first year of Chūpíng,
King Hóngnóng was buried in the former tomb of Zhōng Chángshì Zhào Zhōng,
and was posthumously given the title Huái Wáng.
The Emperor sought his mother, Wáng Měirén's, elder brother Bīn.
Bīn brought his wife and children to Cháng'ān,
and was bestowed a residence and land,
and appointed Fèngchē Dūwèi.
In the first year of Xīngpíng,
the Emperor came of age.
Officials proposed establishing the Chángqiūgōng.
The imperial edict stated:
“I was born with an ungenerous fate,
and have encountered disaster and chaos;
I have not yet been able to carry on the legacy of my predecessors
and glorify the old traditions.
My Imperial Mother passed away earlier,
and a burial site has not yet been determined;
the rites are incomplete,
and my heart is tied in knots.
During the three years of mourning,
it is generally not proper to speak of auspicious matters;
we should wait until after that.”
Thereupon, officials proposed posthumously honoring Wáng Měirén as Línghuái Huánghòu,
and reburying her in Wénzhāolíng,
with ceremonies comparable to those of Jìng and Gōng mausoleums.
Guānglù Dàfū, holding a jié, acted as Sīkōng to present the imperial seal and ribbon,
and Bīn and Hénán Yǐn Luò Yè performed the reburial.
Upon Bīn's return,
he was promoted to Zhí Jīnwú,
enfeoffed as Dūtíng Hóu,
and granted an income of five hundred households.
When he died of illness,
he was posthumously granted the seal and ribbon of Qián Jiāngjūn,
and a Yèzhě supervised his funeral arrangements.
His eldest son, Duān, inherited the title.
Xiàndì's Empress Fú, whose taboo name was Shòu,
was a native of Dōngwǔ, Lángyá,
and an eighth-generation descendant of Dà Sītú Zhàn.
Her father, Wán,
was profound and broad-minded;
he inherited the title of Bùqí Hóu
and married Huán Dì's daughter, Yáng'ān Gōngzhǔ,
and served as Shìzhōng.
In the first year of Chūpíng,
he followed the imperial carriage westward to Cháng'ān.
The Empress then entered the Yè Tíng as a Guìrén.
In the second year of Xīngpíng, she was established as Empress,
and Wán was promoted to Zhí Jīnwú.
Soon after, the Emperor returned eastward,
but Lǐ Quē and Guō Sì pursued and defeated the imperial retinue at Cáoyáng.
The Emperor then secretly crossed the river by night and fled,
and all the imperial consorts walked out of the camp.
The Empress carried several bolts of silk in her hands.
Dǒng Chéng ordered Fújié Lìng Sūn Huī to threaten her with a blade and seize them,
killing a nearby attendant,
whose blood spattered the Empress's clothes.
Upon arriving at Ānyì,
the imperial robes were torn and worn out,
and they had only dates and chestnuts for food.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān,
Wán was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
with ceremonies equivalent to the Three Excellencies.
Wán, knowing that the government was in the hands of Cáo Cāo,
and feeling self-conscious about his esteemed relatives,
then resigned his seal and ribbon,
was appointed Zhōngsàn Dàfū,
and soon after promoted to Túnqí Xiàowèi.
He died in the fourteenth year,
and his son Diǎn succeeded him.
From the imperial capital, Xǔ,
he merely held the throne.
The palace guard ④
were all members of Cáo Shì's party, old acquaintances, or relatives by marriage.
Counselor Zhào Yàn once presented to the emperor a policy for the times,
but Cáo Cāo detested it and killed him.
Many others, both inside and outside the court,
were executed.
Later, Cáo Cāo entered the palace to see the emperor on some matter.
The emperor, unable to restrain his indignation,
then said,
"If you can assist me,
that would be great;
otherwise,
I hope you would graciously release me."
Cáo Cāo's expression changed,
and he bowed and sought permission to leave.
According to old custom,
when the Three Excellencies led troops for an imperial audience,
the tiger guards would be ordered to hold their blades and stand beside them.
When Cáo Cāo left,
he looked left and right,
sweat streaming down his back,
and thereafter dared not attend court again.
Dǒng Chéng's daughter was a Guìrén.
Cáo Cāo executed Dǒng Chéng and sought to have the Guìrén killed.
The emperor pleaded repeatedly for the Guìrén because she was pregnant,
but he could not succeed.
The Empress thereafter became fearful,
and so wrote a letter to her father, Fú Wán,
describing Cáo Cāo's cruel oppression,
ordering him to secretly plan.
Fú Wán dared not act.
In the nineteenth year,
the matter was exposed.
Cáo Cāo was greatly enraged,
and consequently forced the emperor to depose the Empress.
He fabricated an edict that read:
"Empress Fú Shòu,
though of humble origin,
ascended to the pinnacle of honor
and presided over the inner palace
for two decades.
She possessed neither the virtue of Rèn and Sì
nor the fortune of careful self-cultivation.
Instead, she secretly harbored jealousy and malice,
concealing a treacherous heart,
making her unfit to receive Heaven's mandate
and serve the ancestors.
Now, the Grandee Secretary, Xī Lǜ, is sent with credentials and an imperial edict,
to retrieve her empress's seals and ribbons,
and for her to withdraw from the central palace
and move to another residence.
Alas, how lamentable!
Fú Shòu brought this upon herself,
yet not being brought to justice,
she is fortunate indeed."
He also appointed Shàngshūlìng Huà Xīn as Xī Lǜ's deputy,
who led troops into the palace to seize the Empress.
She closed the door and hid in the wall,
but Huà Xīn pulled her out.
At that time, the emperor was in the outer hall,
drawing Xī Lǜ to sit.
The Empress, with disheveled hair and bare feet, weeping as she passed, bade farewell, saying:
"Can I not live again?"
The emperor said:
"I also do not know when my life will end!"
He looked at Xī Lǜ and said:
"Xī Gōng,
is there such a thing in the world?"
Then he had the Empress taken to the "violent room" (prison),
where she died in confinement.
Her two born princes
were both poisoned to death.
The Empress had been on the throne for twenty years.
Over a hundred of her brothers and clan members died,
and nineteen people, including her mother Fú Yíng, were exiled to Zhuó Jùn.
Empress Xiànmù Cáo, whose taboo name was Jié,
was the second daughter of Wèi Gōng Cáo Cāo.
In the eighteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
Cáo Cāo presented his three daughters, Cáo Xiàn, Cáo Jié, and Cáo Huá, as ladies,
betrothing them with fifty thousand bolts of patterned silk and black and crimson fabrics.
The younger ones awaited their coming of age in their state.
In the nineteenth year,
they were all appointed Guìrén.
After Empress Fú was murdered,
the following year,
Cáo Jié was made Empress.
When the Wèi dynasty received the imperial abdication (shànràng),
an envoy was sent to request the imperial seals and ribbons,
but the Empress angrily refused to give them.
After several such attempts,
the Empress summoned the envoy,
personally rebuked him repeatedly,
and threw the seal under the carriage rail,
then with tears streaming down her face, said:
"Heaven will not bless you!"
None of those around dared to look up.
The Empress was on the throne for seven years.
After the Wèi clan was established,
the Empress was made the Lady of Shānyáng Gōng.
Forty-one years after that,
in the first year of Wèi Jǐng Yuán, she passed away,
and was interred with the emperor in Chánlíng,
with carriages, attire, and rituals all according to Hàn customs.
Commentary: In the Hàn dynasty, empresses did not have their own posthumous titles,
but were designated by the emperor's posthumous title.
Even when Empress Lǚ monopolized power
and Empress Shàngguān controlled the government,
they had no special titles.
During the Restoration (Zhōngxīng),
Emperor Míng first established the title of Guāngliè,
and thereafter, all empresses were matched with "Virtue" (dé).
Thus, regardless of their wisdom or foolishness, their superiority or inferiority,
they were indiscriminately grouped together,
hence Empresses Mǎ and Dòu both bore the title "Dé."
The only exceptions were the emperor's concubine mothers and the mothers of feudal kings who succeeded to the throne;
due to the great honor of posthumous veneration,
special titles were given to them,
such as Gōnghuái and Xiàochóng.
In the Chūpíng era,
Cài Yōng first posthumously rectified the title for Empress Héxī,
and subsequently, the titles for Ānsī, Shùnliè, and others
were all added in accordance.
Eulogy: The earth alone bears the heavy load,
the feminine is proper within.
The Odes praise the beautiful companion,
the Yi calls it 'the marrying maiden'.
The stately imperial beauties,
their chastity and virtue are observed.
May these wise and excellent women,
receive our heavenly bounty.
Governing from the orchid chambers,
propagating etiquette in the pepper house.
Some are said to rise by virtue,
others by fortunate advancement.
Their persons reach the greatest heights,
their clans gradually flourish like rivers.
Their brilliance rivals the sun,
their majesty parallels mountains.
Riding the rigid often faces obstacles,
treading the earth must be compliant.
Calamities gather from arrogance and excess,
blessings accord with chastity and trustworthiness.
Fortune extends to oneself,
whose fault is the cause of misfortune?
According to Hàn regulations,
all imperial daughters were enfeoffed as Xiàn Gōngzhǔ (county princesses),
with ceremonial attire similar to that of a Lièhóu.
Those of greater eminence
were additionally titled Cháng Gōngzhǔ (grand princesses),
with ceremonial attire similar to that of a feudal king.
The daughters of all kings were enfeoffed as Xiāng or Tíng Gōngzhǔ (town or pavilion princesses),
with ceremonial attire similar to that of a Xiāng or Tíng Hóu.
Emperor Sùzōng alone specially enfeoffed the daughters of Dōngpíng Xiànwáng Cāng and Lángxié Xiàowáng Jīng as Xiàn Gōngzhǔ.
Thereafter, the sisters of Emperor Ān and Emperor Huán were also enfeoffed as Cháng Gōngzhǔ,
like imperial daughters.
For imperial daughters enfeoffed as princesses,
their sons inherited their mother's enfeoffment as Lièhóu,
and all transmitted the state to their descendants.
Xiāng and Tíng enfeoffments,
however, were not hereditary.
Their official positions and ranks
are detailed in the 'Records of Official Posts' (Bǎiguān Zhì).
It is not necessary to list them separately,
thus they are appended at the end of the 'Records of Empresses' (Hòujì).
Imperial daughter Yìwáng,
in the fifteenth year of Jiànwǔ, was enfeoffed as Wǔyáng Chánggōngzhǔ,
and married Liáng Sōng, the Tàipú and Marquis of Yánlíng Xiāng.
Liáng Sōng was executed for slander.
Imperial daughter Zhōnglǐ,
in the fifteenth year, was enfeoffed as Nièyáng Gōngzhǔ,
and married Dòu Gù, the Dàhónglú and Marquis of Xiǎnqīn.
Emperor Sùzōng honored her as Cháng Gōngzhǔ.
Imperial daughter Hóngfū,
in the fifteenth year, was enfeoffed as Guǎntáo Gōngzhǔ,
and married Hán Guāng, the Fùmǎ Dūwèi.
Hán Guāng was executed for conspiring with Huáiyáng Wáng Yán in rebellion.
Imperial daughter Lǐliú,
in the seventeenth year, was enfeoffed as Yùyáng Gōngzhǔ,
and married Guō Huáng, the Chánglè Shàofǔ and Marquis of Yáng'ān.
Guō Huáng was executed for conspiring with Dòu Xiàn in rebellion.
Imperial daughter Shòu,
in the twenty-first year, was enfeoffed as Lìyì Gōngzhǔ,
and married Yīn Fēng, the heir of Xīnyáng Hóu.
Yīn Fēng murdered the princess
and was executed.
Imperial daughter Jī,
in the second year of Yǒngpíng, was enfeoffed as Huòjiā Chánggōngzhǔ,
and married Féng Zhù, the Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng and Marquis of Yángyì.

in the third year, was enfeoffed as Píngyáng Gōngzhǔ,
and married Féng Shùn, the Dàhónglú.
Imperial daughter Yíng,
in the third year, was enfeoffed as Lónglǜ Gōngzhǔ,
and married Gěng Xí, the Móupíng Hóu.
Imperial daughter Cì,
in the third year, was enfeoffed as Píngshì Gōngzhǔ.
Imperial Daughter Zhì,
in the third year, was enfeoffed as Qìnshuǐ Gōngzhǔ,
and married Dèng Qián, Marquis of Gāomì.
Imperial Daughter Xiǎojī,
in the twelfth year, was enfeoffed as Pínggāo Gōngzhǔ,
and married Dèng Fān, Marquis of Chāng'ān and Shìzhōng.
Imperial Daughter Zhòng,
in the seventeenth year, was enfeoffed as Jùnyí Gōngzhǔ,
and married Wáng Dù,
Huángmén Shìláng and Marquis of Rǎng.
Imperial Daughter Huì,
in the seventeenth year, was enfeoffed as Wǔ'ān Gōngzhǔ,
and married Lái Léng, son of the Marquis of Zhēngqiāng and Huángmén Shìláng.
Emperor Ān honored her as Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ.
Imperial Daughter Chén,
in the first year of Jiànchū, was enfeoffed as Lǔyáng Gōngzhǔ.
Imperial Daughter Xiǎoyíng,
in the first year, was enfeoffed as Lèpíng Gōngzhǔ.
Imperial Daughter Xiǎomín,
in the first year, was enfeoffed as Chéng'ān Gōngzhǔ.
Imperial Daughter Nán,
in the fourth year of Jiànchū, was enfeoffed as Wǔdé Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ.
Imperial Daughter Wáng,
in the fourth year, was enfeoffed as Píngyì Gōngzhǔ,
and married Féng Yóu, Huángmén Shìláng.
Imperial Daughter Jí,
in the fifth year of Yǒngyuán, was enfeoffed as Yīn'ān Gōngzhǔ.
Imperial Daughter Bǎo,

Imperial Daughter Chéng,
in the first year, was enfeoffed as Gòngyì Gōngzhǔ.
Imperial Daughter Lì,
in the first year, was enfeoffed as Línyǐng Gōngzhǔ.
She married Jiǎ Jiàn, Marquis of Jìmò and Shìzhōng.
Imperial Daughter Xīng,

Biographies of Liúxuán and Liúpénzǐ, Chapter 1:
Liúxuán, courtesy name Shènggōng,
was Emperor Guāngwǔ's (光武) paternal cousin.
When his younger brother was killed by others,
Shènggōng gathered followers to seek revenge.
His followers violated the law,
so Shènggōng evaded officials in Pínglín.
Officials then arrested Shènggōng's father and son, Zhāng.
Shènggōng feigned death,
sending someone to carry his "corpse" back to Chōnglíng.
The officials then released Zǐzhāng,
and Shènggōng subsequently went into hiding.
Towards the end of Wángmáng's reign,
famine struck the south.
The common people flocked into swamps,
digging up and eating duckweed,
and robbing each other.
Wángkuāng and Wángfèng of Xīnshì settled disputes,
and were consequently elevated as leaders,
with a following of several hundred people.
Then, various fugitives such as Mǎwǔ, Wángcháng, and Chéngdān went to join them.
Together, they attacked and plundered villages,
hiding in Lùlín,
and within a few months, their numbers swelled to seven or eight thousand.
In the second year of Dìhuáng,
the Governor of Jīngzhōu, a certain individual, dispatched twenty thousand conscripts to attack them.
Kuāng and others led their forces to meet the attack in Yúndù.
They greatly defeated the Governor's army,
killing several thousand people,
and captured all their supplies and equipment.
They then attacked and captured Jìnglíng.
Moving on, they attacked Yúndù and Ānlù,
abducted many women,
and returned to Lùlín.
Their numbers reached over fifty thousand,
and the prefectures and commanderies were unable to control them.
In the third year,
a great plague broke out,
killing almost half of them.
They then dispersed and left.
Wángcháng and Chéngdān moved west into Nánjùn,
calling themselves the Xiàjiāng forces.
Wángkuāng, Wángfèng, Mǎwǔ, and their associates Zhūwěi and Zhāng'áng
moved north into Nányáng,
calling themselves the Xīnshì forces: all proclaimed themselves generals.
In the seventh month,
Kuāng and others advanced to attack Suí,
but were unable to take it.
Chénmù and Liàozhàn of Pínglín
again gathered over a thousand people,
calling themselves the Pínglín forces,
to aid them.
Shènggōng then went to join Mù and others,
serving as an Aide-de-camp for their army.
At this time, Guāngwǔ and his elder brother Bóshēng also rose in Chōnglíng,
combining their forces with other divisions and advancing.
In the first month of the fourth year,
they defeated Zhēnfù, the Grandee of the Vanguard, and Liángqiūcì, the Minister of Dependent States, under Wángmáng,
beheading them.
Shènggōng was proclaimed Gēngshǐ Jiāngjūn.
Although their forces were numerous, they lacked unity.
The generals then jointly deliberated and enthroned Gēngshǐ as the Son of Heaven.
On the Xīnsì day of the second month,
an altar was set up on a sandy bank of the Yùshuǐ River,
and troops were paraded for a grand assembly.
Gēngshǐ ascended the imperial throne,
facing south,
and received homage from his officials.
Naturally timid and weak,
he was ashamed and perspired,
unable to speak even when raising his hand.
Then, a great amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire,
and the era name was established as Gēngshǐ Yuánnián.
All generals were appointed to positions.
His paternal cousin Liáng was made Guósānlǎo,
Wángkuāng was made Dìngguó Shànggōng,
Wángfèng was made Chéngguó Shànggōng,
Zhūwěi was made Dàsīmǎ,
Bóshēng was made Dàsītú,
Chénmù was made Dàsīkōng,
and the rest were all appointed as Jiǔqīng or generals.
In the fifth month,
Bóshēng captured Wǎn.
In the sixth month,
Gēngshǐ entered and made Wǎnéchéng his capital,
granting noble titles to all imperial clansmen and generals,
with over a hundred becoming marquises.
Gēngshǐ, fearing Bóshēng's prestige,
subsequently executed him,
appointing Liúcì, the Guānglùxūn, as Dàsītú.
Previously, Liúwàng, the former Zhōngwǔ Hóu, raised an army
and occupied Rǔnán.
At that time, Yányóu, Wángmáng's Nàyán Jiāngjūn, and Chénmào, the Zhìzōng Jiāngjūn, having been defeated at Kūnyáng,
went to him.
In the eighth month,
Wàng then proclaimed himself Son of Heaven,
appointing Yóu as Dàsīmǎ and
Mào as Chéngxiàng.
Wángmáng sent Tàishī Wángkuāng and Guójiàng Āizhāng to defend Luòyáng.
