Gēngshǐ dispatched Dìngguó Shànggōng Wángkuāng to attack Luòyáng,
and Xīpíng Dàjiāngjūn Shēntújiàn and Chéngxiàng Sījí Lǐsōng to attack Wǔguān.
The Sānfǔ region was shaken.
At this time, heroes and magnates throughout the realm enthusiastically responded,
all killing their governors and prefects,
proclaiming themselves generals,
using the Hàn (漢) reign title,
and awaiting imperial decrees.
Within ten days to a month,
this spread throughout the empire.
In Cháng'ān, forces rose and attacked the Wèiyāng Gōng.
In the ninth month,
Gōngbīnjiù of Dōnghǎi beheaded Wángmáng at Jiàntái,
seized the imperial seals and ribbons,
and sent his head to Wǎn.
Gēngshǐ was then in a casual setting at Huángtáng,
took and looked at it,
and happily said:
"If Máng hadn't been like this,
he would have been equal to Huòguāng and the like."
His favorite concubine, Lady Hán, smiled and said:
"If he hadn't been like this,
how could Your Majesty have obtained it?"
Gēngshǐ was pleased,
and then hung Máng's head in the market of Wǎnchéng.
In this month,
Luòyáng was captured,
Wángkuāng and Āizhāng were captured alive,
brought [to the capital],
and both were executed.
In the tenth month,
Gēngshǐ sent Fènwēi Dàjiāngjūn Liúxìn to attack and kill Liúwàng in Rǔnán,
and also executed Yányóu and Chénmào.
Gēngshǐ then moved his capital north to Luòyáng,
appointing Liúcì as Chéngxiàng.
Shēntújiàn and Lǐsōng sent the imperial carriage and ceremonial regalia from Cháng'ān,
and also dispatched eunuchs and attendants to respectfully welcome the relocation of the capital.
In the second month of the second year,
Gēngshǐ traveled west from Luòyáng.
At the initial departure,
Lǐsōng led the way.
His horse was startled and bolted,
crashing into the iron pillar [gate] of the North Palace;
all three horses died.
Originally,
when Wángmáng was defeated,
only the Wèiyāng Gōng was burned,
while the rest of the palaces and halls were completely undamaged.
Thousands of palace women
were arranged in the imperial harem.
From bells and drums, curtains and canopies, carriages and palanquins, vessels and clothing, the Grand Granary, the Armory, government offices, to markets and neighborhoods,
nothing had changed from before.
When Gēngshǐ arrived,
he resided in the Chánglè Gōng.
Ascending the front hall,
the officials and scribes were arranged in order in the courtyard.
Gēngshǐ was ashamed and embarrassed,
bowing his head and scraping the mat, not daring to look up.
When the later-arriving generals came,
Gēngshǐ asked how much plunder they had obtained,
causing the surrounding attendants and officials, who were long-serving palace functionaries,
to look at each other in astonishment.
Lǐ Sōng and Zhào Méng, from Jíyáng, persuaded Gēngshǐ,
saying that he should enfeoff all the meritorious ministers as kings.
Zhū Wěi argued against this,
believing that Emperor Gāozǔ's covenant
stated that no one not of the Liú clan should be made king.
Gēngshǐ then first enfeoffed members of the imperial clan: Grand General of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Liú Zhǐ was made King of Dìngtáo;
Liú Cì was made King of Àn; Liú Qìng was made King of Yān;
Liú Shè was made King of Yuánshì;
Grand General Liú Jiā was made King of Hànzhōng;
Liú Xìn was made King of Rǔyīn.
Afterward, he proceeded to establish Wáng Kuāng as King of Bǐyáng,
Wáng Fèng as King of Yíchéng,
Zhū Wěi as King of Jiāodōng,
Grand General of the Palace Guard Zhāng Áng as King of Huáiyáng,
Grand General of the Court of Judicial Review Wáng Cháng as King of Dèng,
Grand General of the Bearers of the Gilded Mace Liáo Zhàn as King of Ráng,
Shēntú Jiàn as King of Píngshì,
Minister of the Imperial Secretariat Hú Yīn as King of Suí,
Grand General of Heavenly Guiding Lǐ Tōng as King of Xīpíng,
Wŭwēi Zhōnglángjiàng Lǐ Yì as King of Wǔyīn,
Grand General of Waterways Chéng Dān as King of Xiāngyì,
Grand Minister of Works Chén Mù as King of Yīnpíng,
Grand General of Cavalry Sòng Tiāo as King of Yǐngyīn,
and Yǐn Zūn as King of Yǎn.
Only Zhū Wěi declined, saying:
"Your servant is not of the Liú lineage;
I dare not violate the established rule."
He then resigned and would not accept.
Thereupon, Wěi was moved to the position of Left Grand Marshal,
and Liú Cì was made Front Grand Marshal.
They were sent with Lǐ Yì, Lǐ Tōng, Wáng Cháng, and others to guard and pacify Guāndōng.
Lǐ Sōng was made Chancellor,
and Zhào Méng was made Right Grand Marshal,
together taking charge of internal affairs.
Gēngshǐ took Zhào Méng's daughter as a consort,
and she was much favored.
He then entrusted the government to Méng,
spending day and night drinking and feasting with women in the rear palace.
When his ministers wished to present matters,
he was always too drunk to receive them.
At times, as a last resort,
he would order a palace attendant to sit behind a curtain and speak with them.
The generals recognized that it was not Gēngshǐ's voice,
and when they emerged, they all complained, saying:
"Whether we succeed or fail is not yet known,
yet he indulges himself so recklessly!"
Consort Hán was particularly fond of wine.
Whenever she attended a drinking session,
and saw a regular attendant presenting a report,
she would immediately become angry and say:
"The Emperor is drinking with me right now;
is this the proper time to bring up affairs?"
She would stand up
and throw things.
Zhào Méng wielded exclusive power,
dispensing rewards and punishments himself.
When a court gentleman reported Méng's recklessness,
Gēngshǐ became angry
and drew his sword to strike him.
After this, no one dared to speak out again.
Méng privately resented a palace attendant,
had him seized and beheaded.
Gēngshǐ interceded on his behalf,
but Méng did not comply.
At that time, Lǐ Yì and Zhū Wěi were acting wantonly in Shāndōng,
while Wáng Kuāng and Zhāng Áng were violent and oppressive in Sānfǔ.
Those they appointed to official positions and granted noble titles
were all petty ruffians and merchants,
some even chefs and kitchen staff,
many wearing embroidered jackets, brocade trousers, short robes, and clogs,
cursing in the streets.
A saying circulated in Cháng'ān:
"Kitchen boy,
Zhonglangjiang.
Rotten sheep stomach,
Cavalry Commandant.
Rotten sheep head,
Marquis Within the Passes."
General-in-chief of the Army Lǐ Shú from Yùzhāng submitted a memorial advising:
"At this moment, the rebels have only just been suppressed,
and the imperial rule has not yet been fully implemented.
All officials and ministries should be cautious in their duties.
The Three Ducal Ministers correspond to the constellation Sāntái,
and the Nine Ministers encompass the rivers and seas;
thus, Heaven's work is carried out by men on its behalf.
Your Majesty's establishment of power,
though it relied on the influence of Xiàjiāng and Pínglín,
was merely a temporary measure for expediency,
and should not be applied once stability is achieved.
It is fitting to reform the institutions,
and again invite outstanding talents,
assigning titles according to ability
to rectify the imperial realm.
Now, the high positions of Ducal Ministers and Grandees are filled almost exclusively by military men,
and prominent posts in the Imperial Secretariat are all held by common soldiers.
They are of the caliber of village chiefs and bandit catchers,
yet they are entrusted with the responsibility of assisting and governing the state.
Names and instruments [of power] are
what the sages held in high regard.
Now, to bestow what is held dear upon the wrong persons,
and expect them to contribute greatly,
to promote transformation and achieve good governance,
is like climbing a tree to seek fish,
or ascending a mountain to gather pearls.
The people within the four seas, observing this,
have reason to doubt the duration of the Hàn dynasty.
Your servant does not harbor ill will or seek advancement;
I merely lament this course of action before Your Majesty.
To ruin good material and damage fine brocade
is something that requires utmost consideration.
May Your Majesty discard the past errors and absurdities,
and contemplate the excellence of King Wén of Zhōu and his array of talents."
Gēngshǐ was enraged,
and imprisoned Shú in the imperial jail.
After this, Guānzhōng became disaffected,
and the four quarters were resentful and rebellious.
When the generals went on campaigns,
each arbitrarily appointed governors and commandery administrators.
The prefectures and commanderies were intertwined and confused,
and people did not know whom to follow.
In the twelfth month,
the Chìméi entered Guānzhōng from the west.
In the first month of the third year,
Fāng Wàng from Pínglíng established the former Rúzi Liú Yīng as Emperor.
Initially,
Wàng, seeing Gēngshǐ's chaotic rule,
judged that he was bound to fail.
He said to Gōng Lín and others from Ānlíng:
"The former Duke of Dìng'ān, Yīng,
was the heir of Emperor Píng.
Although Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he was once a Hàn ruler.
Now everyone says that the true Liú clan
should receive the mandate again.
How about we work together to achieve this great accomplishment?"
Lín and others agreed.
They then found Yīng in Cháng'ān
and took him to Línjīng to establish him.
They gathered several thousand followers.
Wàng was made Chancellor,
and Lín was made Grand Marshal.
Gēngshǐ dispatched Lǐ Sōng with General Tǎonàn Sū Máo and others to attack and defeat them,
and they were all beheaded.
He also sent Sū Máo to resist the Chìméi in Hóngnóng,
but Máo's army was defeated,
and over a thousand men died.
In the third month,
he sent Lǐ Sōng to join Zhū Wěi in battling the Chìméi at Wùxiāng.
Sōng and the others suffered a crushing defeat;
their army was routed and fled,
with over thirty thousand dead.
At that time, Wáng Kuāng and Zhāng Áng were guarding Hédōng,
but they were defeated by Dèng Yǔ
and fled back to Cháng'ān.
Áng discussed with the generals, saying:
"The Chìméi are now close by, between Zhèng and Huàyīn,
and will arrive any moment.
Now we only have Cháng'ān;
our destruction is imminent.
It would be better to gather our troops, plunder the city to enrich ourselves,
then attack elsewhere,
return east to Nányáng,
and collect the forces of the King of Wǎn and others.
If the plan does not succeed,
we can just become bandits in the lakes and marshes again."
Shēntú Jiàn, Liáo Zhàn, and others all agreed,
and together they went in to persuade Gēngshǐ.
Gēngshǐ was angry and did not respond,
and no one dared to speak again.
When the Chìméi established Liú Pénzǐ,
Gēngshǐ sent Wáng Kuāng, Chén Mù, Chéng Dān, and Zhào Méng to garrison Xīnfēng,
and Lǐ Sōng's army to camp at Jù,
to resist them.
Zhāng Áng, Liáo Zhàn, Hú Yīn, Shēntú Jiàn, and others conspired with Grandee Secretary Kuí Xiāo,
planning to seize Gēngshǐ together on the day of Lìqiū during the *Chúfú* sacrifice,
to carry out their previous plan.
Palace attendant Liú Néngqīng learned of their plot
and reported it.
Gēngshǐ feigned illness and did not come out,
but summoned Zhāng Áng and the others.
Áng and the others all entered,
and he intended to execute them all.
Only Kuí Xiāo did not arrive.
Gēngshǐ hesitated,
and ordered Áng and the other four to wait outside in the temporary lodge.
Áng, along with Zhàn and Yīn, suspected a change of plans,
and immediately broke out.
Only Shēntú Jiàn remained,
and Gēngshǐ beheaded him.
Áng, Zhàn, and Yīn then gathered troops and plundered the eastern and western markets.
At dusk,
they burned the gates and entered,
fighting in the palace.
Gēngshǐ was utterly defeated.
The next morning,
with his wife and children and over a hundred chariots and cavalry,
he fled east to Zhào Méng in Xīnfēng.
Gēngshǐ, however, again suspected Wáng Kuāng, Chén Mù, Chéng Dān, and Zhāng Áng of plotting together.
So he summoned them all.
Mù and Dān arrived first,
and he immediately had them beheaded.
Wáng Kuāng, terrified,
led his troops into Cháng'ān
and joined Zhāng Áng and others.
Lǐ Sōng returned to Gēngshǐ
and, with Zhào Méng, attacked Kuāng and Áng inside the city.
After more than a month of continuous fighting,
Kuāng and the others were defeated and fled.
Gēngshǐ moved to live in the Chángxìn Gōng.
When the Chìméi reached Gāolíng,
Kuāng and the others welcomed them and surrendered,
then joined forces and advanced together.
Gēngshǐ defended the city
and sent Lǐ Sōng out to battle.
He was defeated,
and over two thousand people died.
The Chìméi captured Sōng alive.
At that time, Sōng's younger brother Fàn was a Gate Guard Commandant.
The Chìméi sent an envoy to tell him:
"Open the city gate,
and your brother will live."
Fàn immediately opened the gate.
In the ninth month,
the Chìméi entered the city.
Gēngshǐ fled alone on horseback,
exiting through the Chúchéng Mén.
The women followed behind, repeatedly calling out:
"Your Majesty,
you should dismount and bid farewell to the city!"
Gēngshǐ immediately dismounted and bowed,
then remounted and left.
Initially,
the Imperial Household Attendant Liú Gōng, because the Chìméi had enthroned his younger brother Pénzǐ,
had imprisoned himself in the imperial jail.
When he heard of Gēngshǐ's defeat,
he came out
and walked to Gāolíng,
stopping at a post station.
The Right Assistant Commandant Yán Běn
feared that Gēngshǐ would be killed by the Chìméi if he escaped.
He led his troops outside,
claiming to be a garrison guard, but in reality, he held him captive.
The Chìméi issued an order saying:
"Any 'Sage Duke' who surrenders
shall be enfeoffed as the King of Chángshā.
After twenty days,
he shall not be accepted."
Gēngshǐ sent Liú Gōng to request surrender.
The Chìméi sent their general Xiè Lù to receive him.
In the tenth month, Gēngshǐ followed Lù, baring his torso, to the Chánglè Gōng
and presented his imperial seal and ribbon to Pénzǐ.
The Chìméi made Gēngshǐ sit
in the courtyard,
intending to kill him.
Liú Gōng and Xiè Lù pleaded for him,
but could not succeed.
So they led Gēngshǐ out.
Liú Gōng chased after them, crying out:
"Your servant's strength is truly exhausted;
I beg to die first!"
He drew his sword, intending to commit suicide.
The Chìméi chiefs Fán Chóng and others immediately rushed to stop him.
Then they pardoned Gēngshǐ
and enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Wēiwēi.
Liú Gōng again pleaded earnestly,
and he finally succeeded in being enfeoffed as the King of Chángshā.
Gēngshǐ usually resided with Xiè Lù,
and Liú Gōng also protected him.
The Three Commanderies suffered from the Chìméi's tyranny
and all pitied Gēngshǐ.
But Zhāng Áng and others considered him a concern
and said to Lù:
"Now, many of the camp commanders want to usurp the Sage Duke.
If he is lost one day,
they will combine their forces and attack you,
which is the path to self-destruction."
Thereupon, Lù had his soldiers pasture horses with Gēngshǐ in the suburbs
and then ordered them to strangle him.
Liú Gōng went that night to collect and bury his body.
Guāngwǔ heard of it and was saddened,
issuing an edict to the Grand Minister of Works, Dèng Yǔ, to bury him at Bālíng.
He had three sons: Qiú,
Xīn,
Lǐ.
The following year, in the summer,
Qiú and his brothers and mother traveled east to Luòyáng.
The Emperor enfeoffed Qiú as the Marquis of Xiāngyì,
to maintain Gēngshǐ's ancestral sacrifices;
Xīn as the Marquis of Gǔshú;
and Lǐ as the Marquis of Shòuguāng.
Qiú was later transferred to be enfeoffed as the Marquis of Chéngyáng.
When Qiú died,
his son Xún succeeded him,
and was again transferred to be enfeoffed as the Marquis of Huòzé.
When Xún died,
his son Yáo succeeded him.
Commentary says: King Wǔ of Zhōu reviewed his troops at Mèngjīn,
then retreated and returned his army,
believing that Zhòu was not yet ready to be attacked.
At that time, there were things not yet achieved.
When the Hàn arose,
it drove a rabble of nimble and cunning commoners,
not even one ten-thousandth of the whole realm,
yet wherever its banners and flags reached,
and wherever its written decrees were disseminated,
none failed to lay down their spears and bow their heads,
vying to accept appointment and command.
This was not only due to the lingering affection for the Hàn,
but also indeed a confluence of fate.
Those who are at the head of power
rarely fail to seize opportunity.
Chén Shèng and Xiàng Yǔ had not yet risen,
let alone ordinary people!
Liú Pénzǐ was a native of Shì in Tàishān,
a descendant of Prince Zhāng of Chéngyáng Jǐng.
His grandfather Xiàn,
during Emperor Yuán's reign, was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Shì.
His father Méng succeeded him.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
the state was abolished,
and he therefore became a native of Shì.
In the first year of Tiānfēng,
in Hǎiqǔ, Lángyé, there was a Lǚ Mǔ
whose son was a county official.
He committed a minor offense,
and the magistrate sentenced him to death.
Lǚ Mǔ resented the magistrate
and secretly gathered retainers,
planning to seek revenge.
Her family had always been wealthy,
with assets of several million.
So she brewed more strong wine
and bought swords and clothing.
When young men came to buy wine,
she always gave it to them on credit.
If she saw someone in need,
she would lend them clothes,
without asking for much.
After several years,
her funds were gradually exhausted.
The young men wanted to repay her.
Lǚ Mǔ wept and said:
"The reason I was generous to you gentlemen
was not to seek profit,
but merely because the county magistrate was wicked
and unjustly killed my son.
I want to avenge him.
Would you gentlemen perhaps pity me?"
The young men admired her resolve
and had also received her kindness,
so they all agreed.
Among them, a brave warrior called himself the Fierce Tiger.
They then gathered several hundreds of people
and, with Lǚ Mǔ, entered the sea,
recruiting fugitives.
Their numbers reached several thousands.
Lǚ Mǔ declared herself a general
and led her troops back to attack and capture Hǎiqǔ.
She seized the county magistrate.
All the officials kowtowed and pleaded for the magistrate.
Lǚ Mǔ said:
"My son committed a minor offense,
which did not warrant death,
yet he was killed by the magistrate.
A killer should die.
Why do you plead for him?"
Then she executed him
and offered his head as a sacrifice at her son's tomb,
before returning to the sea.
Several years later,
Fán Chóng (樊崇) from Lángxié (琅邪) raised an army in Jǔ (莒).
His force numbered over a hundred men,
then moved into Tài shān (太山),
and he proclaimed himself Sānlǎo (三老).
At that time, Qīng (青) and Xú (徐) provinces suffered a great famine,
and bandits rose like swarms of bees.
All the bandits, seeing Fán Chóng's bravery and ferocity,
attached themselves to him.
Within a year, his numbers reached over ten thousand.
Páng Ān (逄安) from Fán Chóng's (樊崇's) own commandery,
and Xú Xuān (徐宣), Xiè Lù (謝祿), Yáng Yīn (楊音) from Dōnghǎi (東海),
each raised their own forces,
totaling several tens of thousands of men,
and again led them to join Fán Chóng (樊崇).
Together, they returned to attack Jǔ (莒),
but could not take it.
They then moved to plunder as far as Gūmù (姑幕),
and there attacked Wáng Mǎng's (王莽's) Tàntāng Hóu (探湯侯), Tián Kuàng (田況),
greatly defeating him,
and killing over ten thousand men.
They then marched north into Qīngzhōu (青州),
plundering and pillaging wherever they went.
Returning to Tài shān (太山),
they encamped at Nánchéng (南城).
Initially,
Fán Chóng (樊崇) and others became bandits out of destitution,
having no plans to attack cities or occupy territories.
As their numbers gradually grew,
they made an agreement among themselves: those who kill shall die,
and those who injure shall compensate for the wound.
They used verbal agreements as their regulations,
without written documents, banners, military divisions, or commands.
The most respected among them was called Sānlǎo (三老),
the next was Cóngshì (從事),
and the next was Zúshǐ (卒史).
They generally referred to each other as Jùrén (巨人).
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) dispatched Píngjūn Gōng (平均公) Lián Dān (廉丹) and Tàishī (太師) Wáng Kuāng (王匡) to attack them.
Fán Chóng (樊崇) and the others wanted to fight,
but feared their troops would get mixed up with Wáng Mǎng's (王莽's) forces,
so they all painted their eyebrows red to distinguish themselves.
Because of this, they were called Chìméi (赤眉) (Red Eyebrows).
The Chìméi (赤眉) then greatly defeated Lián Dān's (廉丹) and Wáng Kuāng's (王匡) armies,
killing over ten thousand men,
and pursued them to Wúyán (無鹽).
Lián Dān (廉丹) died in battle,
and Wáng Kuāng (王匡) fled.
Fán Chóng (樊崇) again led his army of over a hundred thousand,
and returned to besiege Jǔ (莒)
for several months.
Someone persuaded Fán Chóng (樊崇) saying:
"Jǔ (莒)
is the land of our ancestors;
how can you attack it?"
So, he lifted the siege and left.
At this time, Lǚ Mǔ (呂母) died of illness,
and her followers divided into the Chìméi (赤眉), Qīngdú (青犢), and Tóngmǎ (銅馬) factions.
The Chìméi (赤眉) then raided Dōnghǎi (東海),
and fought with Wáng Mǎng's (王莽's) Yípíng Dàyǐn (沂平大尹)
and were defeated,
with several thousand dead.
They then withdrew,
plundering Chǔ (楚), Pèi (沛), Rǔnán (汝南), and Yǐngchuān (潁川),
and returned to Chénliú (陳留).
They attacked and captured Lǔchéng (魯城),
and then moved to Púyáng (濮陽).
It happened that Gēngshǐ (更始) had established his capital in Luòyáng (洛陽),
and sent an envoy to accept Fán Chóng's (樊崇's) surrender.
Fán Chóng (樊崇) and others, hearing that the Hàn (漢) dynasty had been restored,
immediately left their troops,
and personally led over twenty of their chieftains
to follow the envoy to Luòyáng (洛陽) and surrender to Gēngshǐ (更始),
who enfeoffed them all as Lièhóu (列侯).
However, Fán Chóng (樊崇) and the others did not yet possess their granted territories,
and their remaining troops gradually began to desert and rebel.
So, they escaped back to their camp,
led their troops into Yǐngchuān (潁川),
and divided their forces into two divisions:
Fán Chóng (樊崇) and Páng Ān (逄安) formed one division,
and Xú Xuān (徐宣), Xiè Lù (謝祿), and Yáng Yīn (楊音) formed another division.
Fán Chóng (樊崇) and Páng Ān (逄安) attacked and captured Chángshè (長社),
then marched south to attack Wǎn (宛),
and beheaded the county magistrate.
Meanwhile, Xú Xuān (徐宣) and Xiè Lù (謝祿) also captured Yángzhái (陽翟),
led their forces to Liáng (梁),
and attacked and killed the Grand Administrator of Hénán (河南).
Although the Chìméi (赤眉) troops won several battles,
they were exhausted and weary of war,
and all day and night they wept sorrowfully,
longing to return east.
Fán Chóng (樊崇) and the others discussed it,
fearing that if the troops headed east, they would certainly disperse.
It would be better to attack Cháng'ān (長安) to the west.
In the winter of Gēngshǐ (更始) second year
(24 CE), Fán Chóng (樊崇) and Páng Ān (逄 Ān) went through Wǔguān (武關),
and Xú Xuān (徐宣) and others went through Lùhún Guān (陸渾關),
both routes entering simultaneously.
In the first month of the third year
(25 CE), they both arrived at Hóngnóng (弘農),
and repeatedly engaged and defeated Gēngshǐ's (更始's) generals.
Their forces then greatly gathered.
They divided their army into thirty camps,
each with ten thousand men,
and each camp appointed one Sānlǎo (三老) and one Cóngshì (從事).
They advanced to Huáyīn (華陰).
In the army, there was often a Qí (齊) shaman who would beat drums, dance, and offer sacrifices to Chéngyáng Jǐng Wáng (城陽景王)
to seek blessings and assistance.
The shaman wildly declared that Jǐng Wáng (景王) was greatly angered,
saying:
"You should serve the government;
why are you acting as bandits?"
Anyone who laughed at the shaman immediately fell ill,
causing panic in the army.
At this time, Fāng Wàng's (方望's) younger brother Yáng (陽), resenting Gēngshǐ (更始) for killing his elder brother,
reversed his position and said to Fán Chóng (樊崇) and the others:
"Gēngshǐ (更始) is chaotic and disorderly,
his decrees are not implemented,
which is why you generals have been able to reach this point.
Now you generals command an army of a million,
marching west towards the imperial city,
yet you have no title,
and are called a band of bandits.
This cannot last long.
It would be better to establish a member of the imperial clan,
and punish the unjust in the name of righteousness.
With this as your rallying cry,
who would dare not submit?"
Fán Chóng (樊崇) and the others thought this was sound,
and the shaman's pronouncements became even more severe.
When they reached Zhèng (鄭),
they discussed among themselves, saying:
"Now we are close to Cháng'ān (長安),
and the spirits are like this.
We should seek a member of the Liú (劉) clan and jointly enthrone him."
In the sixth month,
they then enthroned Pénzǐ (盆子) as emperor,
and he styled himself Jiànshì Yuánnián (建世元年).
Initially,
when the Chìméi (赤眉) passed through Shì (式),
they plundered Pénzǐ (盆子) and his two elder brothers Gōng (恭) and Mào (茂),
who were all in the army.
Gōng (恭) had studied the Shàngshū (尚書) when he was young
and generally understood its profound meaning.
When he followed Fán Chóng (樊崇) and others to surrender to Gēngshǐ (更始),
he was immediately enfeoffed as Shìhóu (式侯).
Because of his clear understanding of the classics and frequent pronouncements on affairs,
he was appointed Shìzhōng (侍中)
and accompanied Gēngshǐ (更shǐ) in Cháng'ān (長安).
Pénzǐ (盆子) and Mào (茂) remained in the army,
attached to the Yòu Xiàozúshǐ (右校卒史) Liú Xiáqīng (劉俠卿),
responsible for gathering fodder and herding cattle,
and were called "cattle officials" (Niú Lì).
When Fán Chóng (樊崇) and the others wished to establish an emperor,
they sought descendants of Jǐng Wáng (景王) in the army,
and found over seventy people.
Only Pénzǐ (盆子), Mào (茂), and the former Xī'ānhóu (西安侯) Liú Xiào (劉孝) were the closest relatives.
Fán Chóng (樊崇) and the others discussed, saying:
"We heard that ancient Sons of Heaven commanding armies were called Shang Jiāngjūn (上將軍)."
So, they wrote the characters "Shàng Jiāngjūn" (上將軍) on a slip of bamboo,
and also placed two blank slips in a box.
Then, north of Zhèng (鄭),
they set up an altar
and offered sacrifices to Chéngyáng Jǐng Wáng (城陽景王).
All the Sānlǎo (三老) and Cóngshì (從事) gathered before the altar,
with Pénzǐ (盆zǐ) and the other two standing in the center.
They drew the slips in order of age.
Pénzǐ (盆zǐ) was the youngest
and drew the inscribed slip last.
All the generals then proclaimed themselves his subjects and bowed.
Pénzǐ (盆zǐ) was fifteen years old at the time,
with disheveled hair and bare feet,
wearing tattered and mud-stained clothes.
Seeing everyone bow,
he was frightened and wanted to cry.
Mào (茂) told him:
"Hide the slip well."
Pénzǐ (盆zǐ) immediately bit off and discarded it,
and returned to rely on Liú Xiáqīng (劉俠卿).
Liú Xiáqīng (劉俠卿) made him a crimson unlined robe,
a half-red turban,
and straight-soled shoes,
and he rode in a canopy carriage with a large horse,
with red mudguards
and crimson trappings.
Yet, he still roamed with the cowherds.
Although Fán Chóng (樊崇) had risen due to his bravery and strength and was revered by the masses,
he was illiterate.
Hàn Yē (悍贗) the county jailer,
was well-versed in the Yì Jīng (易經).
So, they jointly pushed Xú Xuān (徐宣) to be Prime Minister (Chéngxiàng),
Fán Chóng (樊崇) as Grand Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Dàfū),
Páng Ān (逄Ān) as Grand Marshal of the Left (Zuǒ Dà Sīmǎ),
Xiè Lù (謝 Lù) as Grand Marshal of the Right (Yòu Dà Sīmǎ),
and from Yáng Yīn (楊 Yīn) downwards, all were made high-ranking ministers (Lièqīng).
When the army reached Gāolíng (高陵),
they allied with Gēngshǐ's (更始's) rebellious general Zhāng Áng (張卬) and others.
They then attacked the Dōngdū Mén (東都門) gate,
entered Cháng'ān (長ān) city,
and Gēngshǐ (更shǐ) came to surrender.
Pénzi resided in the Chánglè Gōng.
The generals met daily to discuss their merits,
shouting and clamoring in contention,
drawing swords and striking pillars,
unable to agree with one another.
The superintendents of the commanderies and counties of Sānfǔ sent envoys to offer tribute,
but the soldiers invariably plundered and seized it.
They also frequently captured and brutalized officials and common people,
so the populace fortified their walls
and consequently all resumed their strong defenses.
On Làyì (the sacrificial day at the end of the year),
Chóng and others held a grand celebration with music.
Pénzi sat in the main hall,
with Zhōnghuángmén (eunuchs) holding weapons behind him.
The gōngqīng (high officials) were all seated in rows in the hall.
Before the wine was served,
one of them produced a knife and brush to write a congratulatory address.
The others, who were illiterate, stood up and requested it,
each forming clusters
and turning their backs to one another.
Dàsīnóng Yáng Yīn drew his sword and cursed, saying:
"All you sirs are old laborers!
Today, the rites of sovereign and subject are being observed,
yet you are instead creating disorder!
Even children's play isn't like this!
You should all be killed!"
They then began to argue and fight,
and the soldiers, consequently, each climbed over the palace walls, cut down the gates,
and entered to plunder wine and meat,
killing and wounding each other.
Wèiwèi Zhūgě Zhì heard of this,
mobilized his troops,
and killed over a hundred people,
before order was restored.
Pénzi was terrified,
weeping day and night,
sleeping and waking only with the Zhōnghuángmén.
He could only observe from an elevated pavilion but heard nothing of external affairs.
At that time, there were still several hundred or a thousand palace women in the Yètíng.
Since Gēngshǐ's defeat,
they had been confined within the palace,
digging up turnip roots in the courtyard
and catching fish from the pond to eat.
Those who died were buried within the palace.
There were former musicians from the Gānquán shrine
who still played drums and danced,
their clothes bright and fresh.
They saw Pénzi, kowtowed, and said they were hungry.
Pénzi ordered the Zhōnghuángmén to give them rice,
several dòu (pecks) per person.
Later, when Pénzi left,
they all starved to death without leaving.
Liú Gōng saw the disorder among the Chìméi troops
and knew they were doomed to fail.
Fearing that he and his brother would both suffer disaster,
he secretly instructed Pénzi to return the imperial seal and sash,
and to practice words of resignation.
On the first day of the first month of Jiànwǔ Èr Nián (26 CE),
Chóng and others held a grand assembly.
Liú Gōng spoke first, saying:
"Gentlemen, you jointly established my brother as emperor.
Your virtue is indeed profound and generous.
He has been established for almost a year,
but the disorder has grown daily.
He is truly insufficient to accomplish anything.
I fear that even dying would be of no benefit.
I wish to retire as a commoner,
and seek out a worthy and wise person instead.
I only ask that you gentlemen consider this."
Chóng and others bowed and said:
"This is all our fault, Chóng and the others."
Gōng again earnestly requested it.
Someone said:
"Is this not a matter for Shìhóu?"
Gōng was terrified and stood up to leave.
Pénzi then got down from his couch, unbound the imperial seal and sash,
and kowtowed, saying:
"Now that a county official (emperor) has been established, we are still like bandits.
When officials and common people offer tribute,
it is invariably plundered and robbed.
This news has spread throughout the four directions,
and there is no one who does not resent it,
no longer trusting or supporting us.
This is all due to establishing the wrong person.
I beg to be allowed to retire (return my bones),
and make way for a worthy sage.
If you must kill Pénzi to satisfy your responsibilities,
there is no escape from death.
I sincerely hope you gentlemen will take pity on me!"
He then wept and sighed.
Chóng and the hundreds of others present at the assembly
were all moved to pity.
They all rose from their seats, prostrated themselves, and said:
"Your subjects are unworthy,
we have failed Your Majesty.
From now on,
we dare not be dissolute again."
Then they together embraced Pénzi
and belted him with the imperial seal and sash.
Pénzi cried out but could not refuse.
After the assembly dispersed,
they each closed their camps and guarded themselves.
The Sānfǔ region universally
proclaimed the Son of Heaven to be intelligent.
The common people rushed back to Cháng'ān,
and the markets and streets were almost full.
Twenty-odd days [after],
the Chìméi, coveting wealth,
again went out on a great rampage.
The grain in the city was exhausted,
so they collected and loaded up treasures,
then set fire to the palaces on a large scale,
and led their troops westward.
They passed by the Southern Suburbs shrine,
their chariots, armor, and horses were most fierce and flourishing,
their numbers were said to be a million.
Pénzi rode in a royal chariot,
drawn by three horses,
followed by several hundred cavalry.
They then turned from the Nánshān and plundered cities and towns.
They fought Gēngshǐ general Yán Chūn at Méi,
defeated Chūn,
and killed him,
then entered Āndìng and Běidì.
When they reached Yángchéng and Fānxū,
they encountered a great snowstorm.
The pits and valleys were all filled,
and many soldiers froze to death.
They then returned,
excavated various imperial tombs,
took their treasures,
and then defiled the corpse of Lǚ Hòu.
In all the tombs the bandits opened,
those interred in jade caskets were mostly as if alive,
which is why the Chìméi committed many acts of lewdness.
Dàsītú Dèng Yǔ was then in Cháng'ān.
He sent troops to attack them at Yùyí,
but was instead defeated by them.
Yǔ then withdrew to Yúnyáng.
In the ninth month,
the Chìméi re-entered Cháng'ān
and stopped at Guìgōng.
At that time, Yán Cén, a bandit from Hànzhōng, came out of Sànguān
and encamped at Dùlíng.
Páng Ān led over a hundred thousand men to attack him.
Dèng Yǔ, knowing that Páng Ān's elite troops were outside,
and that only Pénzi and the weak were left in the city,
personally went to attack them.
At that moment, Xiè Lù's relief forces arrived.
They fought a night battle in the streets,
and Yǔ's troops were defeated and fled.
Yán Cén and Gēngshǐ general Lǐ Bǎo combined their forces, numbering tens of thousands,
and fought Páng Ān at Dùlíng.
Cén and the others were utterly defeated,
with over ten thousand dead.
Bǎo then surrendered to Ān,
while Yán Cén gathered his scattered soldiers and fled.
Bǎo then secretly sent someone to tell Cén:
"You should try hard to return and fight.
I will rebel from within,
and we can join forces (form an external and internal pincer attack),
which can greatly shatter them."
Cén immediately returned and challenged them to battle.
Ān and others emptied their camp to attack him.
Bǎo, from the rear, pulled down all the Chìméi banners and flags,
and re-erected his own banners.
Ān and others, exhausted from battle, returned to their camp
and saw that all the banners were white.
They were greatly shocked and scattered in disarray,
throwing themselves into rivers and valleys.
Over a hundred thousand died.
Páng Ān escaped with several thousand men back to Cháng'ān.
At this time, there was a great famine in Sānfǔ.
People ate each other,
and cities and towns were all empty.
White bones covered the fields.
The survivors often gathered to form fortified camps,
each holding firm and not surrendering.
The Chìméi plundered but gained nothing.
In the twelfth month,
they then withdrew and returned eastward,
their numbers still over two hundred thousand,
but they scattered further along the way.
Guāngwǔ (光武) then dispatched the General Who Breaks Evils, Hóu Jìn (侯進), and others to garrison Xīn'ān (新安);
the General Who Establishes Might, Gěng Yǎn (耿弇), and others to garrison Yíyáng (宜陽),
dividing them into two routes,
to intercept their return path.
He instructed his generals, saying:
“If the bandits flee east,
you can lead the Yíyáng (宜陽) troops to rendezvous at Xīn'ān (新安);
if the bandits flee south,
you can lead the Xīn'ān (新安) troops to rendezvous at Yíyáng (宜陽).”
In the first month of the following year,
Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) crossed from north of the Yellow River,
and attacked the Chìméi (赤眉) at Hú (湖).
Yǔ (禹) was again defeated and fled,
and the Chìméi (赤眉) then exited the pass and headed south.
The General Who Conquers the West, Féng Yì (馮異), defeated them at Xiáodǐ (崤底).
When the Emperor heard this,
he personally went to Yíyáng (宜陽),
massing troops to intercept their escape route.
When the Chìméi (赤眉) suddenly encountered the large army,
they were shocked and knew not what to do.
They then sent Liú Gōng (劉恭) to beg for surrender,
saying:
“Pénzi (盆子) is leading a million troops to surrender;
how will Your Majesty treat them?”
The Emperor said:
“I will treat you by not killing you.”
Fán Chóng (樊崇) then led Pénzi (盆子) and Chancellor Xú Xuān (徐宣) and over thirty others, stripped to the waist, to surrender.
They handed over the Imperial Seal and ribbon,
the Gēngshǐ (更始) seven-foot precious sword, and one jade bi disc each.
The accumulated weapons and armor at the west of Yíyáng (宜陽) city
were as high as Mount Xióng'ěr (熊耳).
The Emperor ordered the county kitchens to provide food,
and the starving and exhausted masses,
over one hundred thousand people, all had their fill.
The next morning,
a grand display of soldiers and horses was arrayed overlooking the Luòshuǐ (洛水),
and Pénzi (盆子) and his officials were ordered to observe them in formation.
He said to Pénzi (盆子):
“Do you know you are to die?”
He replied:
“My crimes indeed deserve death,
but I still hope Your Majesty will pity and pardon me.”
The Emperor laughed and said:
“This boy is very clever;
none of the imperial clan are foolish.”
He then said to Chóng (崇) and the others:
“Are you not regretting your surrender?
I will now send you back to your camps to muster your troops,
beat your drums and attack each other,
to decide the victor.
I do not wish to force your submission.”
Xú Xuān (徐宣) and the others kowtowed and said:
“When we exited the Dōngdū (東都) Gate of Cháng'ān (長安),
we, ruler and subjects, deliberated and decided
to commit our lives to your sagely virtue.
The common people can share in the enjoyment of success,
but are difficult to plan with at the beginning;
hence, we did not inform the masses.
To be able to surrender today
is like leaving a tiger's mouth and returning to a kind mother.
We are truly joyful and happy,
and have no regrets.”
The Emperor said:
“You are truly 'the ringing in iron,
the excellent among ordinary people.'”
He further said:
“You generals have committed great lawlessness.
Wherever you passed, you annihilated the old and weak,
defiled the altars of earth and grain,
and dirtied wells and stoves.
However, you still have three good points: when you attacked and broke cities and towns,
spreading throughout the world,
you did not alter or change your original wives and women.
This is one good point.
When establishing a ruler, you were able to use a member of the imperial clan.
This is the second good point.
When other bandits established rulers,
in desperate situations, they all brought the heads of their rulers to surrender,
considering it their achievement.
You generals alone preserved your ruler intact and handed him over to me.
This is the third good point.”
He then ordered each to live with their wives and children in Luòyáng (洛陽),
granting each person one residence
and two qǐng of land.
That summer,
Fán Chóng (樊崇) and Páng Ān (逄安) plotted rebellion and were executed.
Yáng Yīn (楊音), when in Cháng'ān (長安),
had been treated kindly by King Zhào Liáng (趙王良),
and was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu (關內侯).
He returned to his hometown with Xú Xuān (徐宣),
and died at home.
Liú Gōng (劉恭) avenged Gēngshǐ (更始) by killing Xiè Lù (謝祿),
and then imprisoned himself.
He was pardoned and not executed.
The Emperor pitied Pénzi (盆子),
rewarding him generously
and appointing him a Langzhong (郎中) to the King of Zhào (趙).
Later, he fell ill and lost his sight.
He was granted land from the Yíngyáng Jūnshū (滎陽均輸) office,
to be used for shops,
and allowed to collect its taxes for life.
A eulogy states: “The Sagely Duke was unheard of,
loaning me wind and clouds.
Beginning with conforming to the calendar,
ending naturally in collapse and division.
The Chìméi (赤眉) brought chaos and disorder,
Pénzi (盆子) seized the tally.
Though he stole the imperial regalia,
he ate from the equalized tribute.”
Biographies of Wáng (王), Liú (劉), Zhāng (張), Lǐ (李), Péng (彭), and Lú (盧), Part Two
Wáng Chāng (王昌), also named Láng (郎),
was a native of Hándān (邯鄲) in Zhào (趙) Commandery.
He was originally a diviner and physiognomist,
skilled in observing stars and calendars.
He often believed that there was an aura of an Emperor in Héběi (河北).
At that time, Lín (林), son of King Zhào Mù (趙繆),
was fond of unusual calculations
and was a chivalrous figure in the region between Zhào (趙) and Wèi (魏),
having many connections with powerful rogues.
Láng (郎) was close friends with him.
Initially,
when Wáng Mǎng (王莽) usurped the throne,
someone in Cháng'ān (長安) claimed to be Zǐyú (子輿), son of Emperor Chéng.
Mǎng (莽) killed him.
Láng (郎), taking advantage of this, falsely claimed to be the true Zǐyú (子輿),
saying:
“My mother was a singer for Emperor Chéng.
She once fell down in the hall and collapsed.
After a moment, a yellow qi ascended from her body,
and it dissipated after half a day.
She then became pregnant and went to the imperial residence.
Empress Zhào (趙后) wanted to harm her,
but she secretly exchanged her child for another's,
and thus was able to survive.
When [Zǐ (子)] Yú (輿) was twelve years old,
Lǐ Mànqīng (李曼卿), a Langzhong (郎中) who recognized fate,
went with him to Shǔ (蜀).
At seventeen,
they reached Dānyáng (丹陽).
At twenty,
they returned to Cháng'ān (長安).
They journeyed through Zhōngshān (中山),
traveling between Yān (燕) and Zhào (趙),
awaiting the opportune moment.”
Lín (林) and the others became even more perplexed and swayed.
They then conspired with Lǐ Yù (李育) and Zhāng Cān (張參), great magnates of Zhào (趙) Commandery,
planning to jointly enthrone Láng (郎).
It happened that there was a rumor among the people that the Chìméi (赤眉) were about to cross the Yellow River.
Lín (林) and the others thereupon declared that the Chìméi (赤眉) were coming,
and enthroned Liú Zǐyú (劉子輿) to observe the public sentiment.
Many common people believed it.
In the twelfth month of the first year of Gēngshǐ [2 AD],
Lín and others led several hundred chariots and cavalry
into the city of Hándān at dawn.
They stopped at the royal palace
and enthroned Láng as Son of Heaven.
Lín was made Chancellor,
Lǐ Yù Grand Commander,
and Zhāng Cān General-in-Chief.
They dispatched generals and commanders
to conquer Yōu and Jì.
They issued a proclamation to the prefectures and commanderies, saying:
"An imperial edict to the provincial governors and commandery administrators: I,
the son of Emperor Xiàochéng, Zǐyú,
formerly encountered the calamity brought by the Zhào clan,
and was subsequently usurped and murdered by Wáng Mǎng.
Thanks to those who knew fate and protected my person,
I shed my form by the riverbank
and erased my tracks in Zhào and Wèi.
Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
offending Heaven.
Heaven's mandate supports Hàn,
therefore it caused Zhái Yì, the administrator of Dōngjùn, and Liú Xìn, the Marquis of Yánxiāng,
to raise troops and campaign,
moving between Hú and Hàn.
All under Heaven
know that I was hidden among men.
The various Liú from Nányuè
served as my vanguard.
I observed the celestial phenomena
and therefore rose here.
On the day Rénchén of this month, I ascended the throne in the Zhào palace.
Propitious energy permeated,
and rain fell in due season.
It is said that in governing a nation,
a son succeeding his father
is an immutable principle from ancient to modern times.
Liú Shènggōng does not yet know me,
so he temporarily holds the imperial title.
All who raise righteous armies
are helping me
and shall all be granted territories and enjoy prosperity for their descendants.
I have already ordered Shènggōng and Administrator Zhái
to immediately come with their meritorious officials to my temporary residence.
I suspect that the governors and high officials (two thousand piculs salary) were all appointed by Shènggōng,
and have not seen my obscurity.
Some may not know whether to leave or stay;
the strong rely on their power,
the weak are frightened and bewildered.
Now the common people are suffering,
more than half already.
I deeply lament this,
therefore I dispatch envoys to circulate this imperial edict."
Láng knew that the common people longed for Hàn,
and many were saying that Zhái Yì was not dead,
so he falsely claimed to be him
to meet popular expectations.
Thereupon, north of the State of Zhào
and west of Liáodōng,
all followed and submitted.
The following year,
Guāngwǔ, having received Láng's proclamation in Jì,
fled south to Xìndū.
He raised troops to conquer neighboring counties,
then attacked Bǎirén,
but could not take it.
Discussants thought that defending Bǎirén was not as good as pacifying Jùlù,
so Guāngwǔ led his troops northeast to besiege Jùlù.
Láng's administrator, Wáng Ráo, held the city,
and after several tens of days of continuous attacks, it was not overcome.
Gěng Chún persuaded him, saying:
"To long besiege Wáng Ráo
will exhaust the soldiers.
It is better, while our main army is fresh and sharp,
to advance and attack Hándān.
If Wáng Láng is already executed,
Wáng Ráo will surrender without a fight."
Guāngwǔ approved of his plan,
so he left General Dèng Mǎn
to guard Jùlù
and advanced his army to Hándān,
encamping north of its outer wall.
Láng repeatedly sallied out to fight but was unsuccessful,
so he sent his remonstrance minister, Dù Wēi, with a staff of authority to request surrender.
Wēi openly claimed that Láng was truly the surviving son of Emperor Chéng.
Guāngwǔ said:
"Even if Emperor Chéng were to be reborn,
he could not obtain the empire, much less one who falsely claims to be Zǐyú!"
Wēi requested a marquisate of ten thousand households.
Guāngwǔ said:
"Just being able to keep your body whole will suffice."
Wēi said:
"Although Hándān is humble,
by uniting our strength and holding it firmly,
we can still extend the days and months;
ultimately, it is not just for ruler and ministers to save their own lives."
Thereupon he departed.
[Thus] they attacked urgently,
and after more than twenty days,
Láng's Junior Tutor Lǐ Lì acted as a counter-spy,
opened the city gates to let in the Hàn troops,
and thus captured Hándān.
Láng fled in the night,
died on the road,
and was pursued and beheaded.
Liú Yǒng was
from Suīyáng, Liángjùn,
and was the eighth-generation descendant of Liáng Xiàowáng.
The kingdom was transmitted to his father Lì.
During the Yuánshǐ era,
Lì had illicit relations with Wèi Shì, the maternal family of Emperor Píng,
and was executed by Wáng Mǎng.
When Gēngshǐ ascended the throne,
Yǒng first went to Luòyáng
and was posthumously enfeoffed as King of Liáng,
with his capital at Suīyáng.
Yǒng heard that Gēngshǐ's government was chaotic
and thus held his state and raised troops.
He made his younger brother Fáng General-in-Chief Protecting the State,
and Fáng's younger brother Shàogōng Grandee Secretary,
enfeoffing him as King of Lǔ.
He then recruited various local heroes like Zhōu Jiàn from Pèi,
appointing them all as generals and commanders,
and conquered Jìyīn, Shānyáng, Pèi, Chǔ, Huáiyáng, and Rǔnán,
acquiring a total of twenty-eight cities.
He also sent an envoy to appoint Jiǎo Qiáng from Shānyáng, a bandit leader in Xīfáng, as General Roving and Attacking.
At this time, Dǒng Xiàn from Dōnghǎi raised troops and held his commandery,
and Zhāng Bù also pacified the Qí region.
Yǒng sent envoys to appoint Xiàn as General-in-Chief Aiding Hàn,
and Bù as General-in-Chief Assisting Hàn,
forming an alliance with them,
and thus exclusively occupying the east.
When Gēngshǐ was defeated,
Yǒng proclaimed himself Son of Heaven.
In the summer of the second year of Jiànwǔ [26 AD],
Guāngwǔ sent Tiger's Teeth General-in-Chief Gài Yán and others to attack Yǒng.
Initially,
Sū Mào from Chénliú served as Gēngshǐ's General for Suppressing Difficulties,
and with Zhū Wěi and others, guarded Luòyáng.
After Wěi surrendered to Hàn,
Mào also submitted.
Guāngwǔ then sent Mào to attack Yǒng together with Gài Yán.
They were not compatible in the army,
so Mào rebelled,
killed the administrator of Huáiyáng,
plundered several counties,
occupied Guǎnglè, and became Yǒng's vassal.
Yǒng made Mào Grand Commander and King of Huáiyáng.
Gài Yán then besieged Suīyáng,
and after several months,
captured it.
Yǒng fled with his family to Yú.
The people of Yú rebelled,
killing his mother and wife and children.
Yǒng fled to Qiáo with several tens of his subordinates.
Sū Mào, Jiǎo Qiáng, and Zhōu Jiàn combined their forces to rescue Yǒng,
but were defeated by Gài Yán.
Mào fled back to Guǎnglè,
and Qiáng and Jiàn followed Yǒng to take refuge in Húlíng.
In the spring of the third year [27 AD],
Yǒng sent envoys to enthrone Zhāng Bù as King of Qí
and Dǒng Xiàn as King of Hǎixī.
Thereupon, he sent Grand Commander Wú Hàn and others to besiege Sū Mào at Guǎnglè.
Zhōu Jiàn led his forces to rescue Mào.
Mào and Jiàn were defeated in battle,
abandoned the city, and returned to Húlíng,
while the people of Suīyáng rebelled, opened the city, and welcomed Yǒng.
Wú Hàn and Gài Yán and others combined their forces to besiege him.
When food in the city ran out,
Yǒng, Mào, and Jiàn fled to Cuō.
The generals pursued them closely.
Yǒng's general, Qìng Wú, beheaded Yǒng and surrendered,
and Wú was enfeoffed as a marquis.
Sū Mào and Zhōu Jiàn fled to Chuíhuì
and together enthroned Yǒng's son Yū as King of Liáng.
Jiǎo Qiáng returned to hold Xīfáng.
In the autumn of the fourth year [28 AD],
General Capturing Bandits Mǎ Wǔ and Cavalry Commandant Wáng Bà were sent to besiege Yū and Jiàn at Chuíhuì.
Sū Mào led five regiments of soldiers to relieve them.
Yū and Jiàn also sallied out with troops to fight Mǎ Wǔ and others,
but were unsuccessful.
Meanwhile, Jiàn's nephew Sòng rebelled
and closed the city gates to resist them.
Jiàn, Mào, Yū and others all fled.
Jiàn died on the road,
Mào fled to Xiàpéi to join Dǒng Xiàn,
and Yū fled to Jiǎo Qiáng.
In the fifth year [29 AD],
General of Agile Cavalry Dù Mào was sent to attack Jiǎo Qiáng at Xīfáng.
Qiáng and Liú Yū fled to Dǒng Xiàn.
At this time, General Quelling Barbarians Páng Méng rebelled,
then attacked and defeated Gài Yán,
led his troops to ally with Dǒng Xiàn,
proclaimed himself King of Dōngpíng,
and encamped north of Táoxiāng.
Páng Méng,
a native of Shānyáng.
Initially, he was a fugitive among the Jiàng兵 [troops] in Xiàjiāng.
When Gēngshǐ was enthroned,
he was appointed Jìzhōu Mù,
and led troops under Shàngshū Lìng Xiè Gōng,
together defeating Wáng Láng.
After Gōng's defeat,
Méng then surrendered.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Shìzhōng.
Méng was humble and compliant,
and greatly trusted and loved.
The Emperor often praised him, saying:
"One who can be entrusted with an orphan six chǐ tall,
and whose life is dependent on a hundred lǐ,
is Páng Méng."
He was appointed Píngdí Jiāngjūn,
and together with Gài Yán attacked Dǒng Xiàn.
At that time, imperial edicts were sent only to Yán and not to Méng,
Méng thought Yán had slandered him,
became suspicious,
and consequently rebelled.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he was furious,
and personally led an expedition to suppress Méng.
He wrote to his generals, saying:
"I always considered Páng Méng a pillar of the state,
would the generals not laugh at my words?
The old villain must be annihilated with his clan.
Let each of you sharpen your weapons and horses,
and meet at Suīyáng!"
When Xiàn heard that the Emperor was personally leading the campaign against Páng Méng,
he and Liú Yū, Sū Mào, and Jiǎo Qiáng left Xiàpī,
returned to Lánlíng,
and sent Mào and Qiáng to assist Méng,
combining their forces of thirty thousand,
to urgently besiege Táochéng.
The Emperor was then at Méng,
and hearing this,
he left behind his heavy baggage,
and personally led three thousand light cavalry,
and tens of thousands of infantry,
galloping day and night,
his army encamped at Rèncchéng,
sixty lǐ from Táoxiāng.
The next morning,
the generals requested to advance,
the rebels also arrayed their troops and challenged them to battle,
but the Emperor did not agree,
instead resting his soldiers and preserving their morale,
to blunt the enemy's spirit.
When those in the city heard the imperial carriage had arrived,
the morale of the populace became even firmer.
At that time, Wú Hàn and others were in Dōngjùn,
and a fast envoy was sent to summon them.
Méng and the others then used all their forces to attack the city,
for more than twenty days,
their troops were exhausted and could not take it.
When Wú Hàn and the generals arrived,
they led the entire army to advance on Táochéng,
and the Emperor personally engaged in fierce combat,
greatly defeating them.
Méng, Mào, and Qiáng abandoned their baggage and fled during the night,
Dǒng Xiàn then, with Liú Yū, gathered all their tens of thousands of troops and encamped at Chānglǜ,
and personally led his elite soldiers to resist Xīnyáng.
The Emperor first sent Wú Hàn to attack and defeat them,
Xiàn fled back to Chānglǜ.
Hàn advanced and held it,
Xiàn was afraid,
so he enticed the remaining bandits of the Wǔxiào, several thousand cavalry and infantry, to encamp at Jiànyáng,
thirty lǐ from Chānglǜ.
The Emperor arrived at Fān,
over a hundred lǐ from Xiàn's position.
The generals requested to advance,
but the Emperor did not agree,
knowing that the Wǔxiào would retreat due to lack of food,
he ordered them all to strengthen their defenses and await their exhaustion.
After a short while,
the Wǔxiào ran out of provisions,
and indeed withdrew.
The Emperor then personally oversaw,
attacking Xiàn from all four sides,
for three days,
again greatly defeating him,
all his troops scattered.
He sent Wú Hàn to pursue and attack them,
Jiǎo Qiáng surrendered with his troops,
Sū Mào fled to Zhāng Bù,
Xiàn and Páng Méng fled into Zēngshān.
After several days,
officials and soldiers heard that Xiàn was still alive,
and again gathered here and there,
obtaining several hundred cavalry,
and welcomed Xiàn into Tánchéng.
Wú Hàn and others again attacked and captured Tán,
Xiàn and Páng Méng fled to secure Qú.
Liú Yū did not know where to go,
and his soldier Gāo Hù beheaded him and surrendered,
the Liáng territory was completely pacified.
Wú Hàn advanced and besieged Qú.
The next year,
grain in the city was exhausted,
Xiàn and Méng secretly went out,
and raided Gànyú,
Lángyé Tàishǒu Chén Jùn attacked them,
Xiàn and Méng fled into the swamps.
At that time, Wú Hàn took Qúchéng,
and advanced to capture all their wives and children.
Xiàn then wept and apologized to his generals and soldiers, saying:
"Our wives and children have all been taken.
Alas!
I have long troubled you, sirs."
Then he led several tens of cavalry and left in the night,
intending to surrender via a secret path,
but Wú Hàn's Xiàowèi Hán Zhàn pursued and beheaded Xiàn at Fāngyǔ,
and Qín Líng, a person from Fāngyǔ, also beheaded Méng,
their heads were all sent to Luòyáng.
Hán Zhàn was enfeoffed as a Lièhóu,
and Qín Líng as a Guānnèihóu.
Zhāng Bù, courtesy name Wéngōng,
was a native of Bùqí, Lángyé.
When the Han army rose,
Bù also gathered several thousand people,
and attacked neighboring counties,
taking several cities,
styling himself Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn,
and thus occupied his home commandery.
Gēngshǐ sent Wèi Jùn Wáng Hóng as Lángyé Tàishǒu,
but Bù resisted him,
preventing him from advancing.
Hóng issued a proclamation,
enlightening officials and people to surrender,
and gained six counties including Gànyú,
gathering several thousand soldiers,
and fought Bù,
but was defeated.
At that time, Liáng Wáng Liú Yǒng, considering himself established by Gēngshǐ,
coveting Bù's strong infantry,
acted on his own authority to appoint Bù Fǔhàn Dàjiāngjūn and Zhōngjié Hóu,
overseeing Qīng and Xú two zhōu,
and commanding him to conquer those who did not obey,
Bù coveted the titles,
and thus accepted them.
He then mustered his troops at Jù,
appointed his younger brother Hóng as Wèijiāngjūn,
Hóng's younger brother Lán as Xuánwǔ Dàjiāngjūn,
and Lán's younger brother Shòu as Gāomì Tàishǒu.
He sent generals to campaign in Tàishān, Dōnglái, Chéngyáng, Jiāodōng, Běihǎi, Jǐnán, and Qí commanderies,
all of which surrendered.
Bù expanded his territory widely,
and his armed forces grew daily.
Wáng Hóng feared his troops would scatter,
so he went to meet Bù,
intending to persuade him with righteousness.
Bù arrayed a large army and brought Hóng in,
and angrily said:
"What fault did Bù have,
that you previously attacked him so severely!"
Hóng gripped his sword and said:
"The Tàishǒu received imperial orders,
while Wéngōng held troops to resist,
Hóng merely attacked a rebel,
how can you say it was severe!"
Bù fell silent,
after a long while,
he left his seat and knelt in apology,
then arranged music and offered wine,
treating Hóng with the courtesy of a distinguished guest,
and ordered Hóng to manage the commandery affairs.
In Jiànwǔ three years,
Guāngwǔ sent Guānglù Dàfū Fú Lóng with an imperial credential as envoy to Qí,
to appoint Bù as Dōnglái Tàishǒu.
Liú Yǒng heard that Lóng had arrived at Jù,
and immediately sent an envoy to establish Bù as Qí Wáng,
Bù immediately killed Lóng and accepted Yǒng's decree.
At that time, the Emperor was preoccupied with northern troubles at Yúyáng
and southern campaigns against Liáng and Chǔ.
Therefore, Bù was able to gather troops exclusively in Qí,
holding twelve commanderies.
When Liú Yǒng died,
Bù and others wanted to enthrone Yǒng's son, Yū, as Son of Heaven,
and declare themselves Duke of Dìnghàn,
establishing a full bureaucracy.
Wáng Hóng advised,
"King of Liáng, by virtue of his allegiance to the imperial court,
was able to win over many in Shāndōng.
Now to elevate his son will
surely create doubt among the populace.
Moreover, the people of Qí are often deceitful;
it would be advisable to consider this carefully."
Bù then ceased.
In the fifth year,
Bù heard the Emperor was about to attack him,
and appointed his general Fèi Yì as King of Jìnán,
garrisoning him at Lìxià.
In winter,
the Grand General of Establishing Martiality, Gěng Yǎn, defeated and beheaded Fèi Yì,
then advanced to capture Línzī.
Bù, believing Yǎn's forces to be small and far from home,
ripe for a single decisive attack,
led all his troops to attack Yǎn at Línzī.
Bù's army was utterly routed,
and he fled back to Jù.
The Emperor personally proceeded to Jù.
Bù retreated to defend Píngshòu,
and Sū Mào arrived with over ten thousand men to rescue him.
Mào rebuked Bù, saying,
"With the elite troops of Nányáng and Yán Cén's skill in battle,
Gěng Yǎn was still able to put them to flight.
Why did Your Majesty personally attack his camp?
Since you called for me,
could you not have waited?"
Bù said,
"Alas, alas,
there is nothing to be said."
The Emperor then sent an envoy to Bù and Mào,
promising to enfeoff as a marquis anyone who could behead the other and surrender.
Bù then beheaded Mào
and sent an envoy with his head to surrender.
Bù's three younger brothers, who were imprisoned in their respective locations,
were all pardoned.
Bù was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānqiū,
and later lived with his family in Luòyáng.
Wáng Hóng also came to Jù and surrendered.
In the eighth year, in summer,
Bù fled with his wife and children to Línhuái,
and with his brothers Hóng and Lán, sought to rally his former followers,
sailing into the sea.
The Administrator of Lángyá, Chén Jùn, pursued, attacked, and beheaded them.
Wáng Hóng was
the son of Wáng Mǎng's uncle, Píng'āu Hóu Tán,
and served as a Regular Palace Attendant during Emperor Āi's reign.
At that time, the favored minister Dǒng Xián was Grand Marshal,
enjoying great favor and power.
Hóng repeatedly remonstrated,
offending the Emperor.
When Emperor Āi was on his deathbed,
he entrusted the imperial seal and sash to Xián, saying,
"Do not give them to anyone rashly."
At that time, the state had no successor,
and there was widespread fear both within and outside the court.
Hóng reported to the Empress Dowager Yuán,
requesting to take them from Xián;
he then, carrying his sword, went to the rear hall of Xuāndé,
raised his hand, and shouted at Xián, saying,
"The imperial carriage has departed,
and the state's successor is not yet established.
You have received profound imperial grace;
you should be prostrating yourself and wailing.
Why do you hold onto the imperial seal and sash for so long, waiting for disaster to strike?"
Xián knew Hóng would surely kill him
and dared not refuse,
so he knelt and handed over the imperial seal and sash.
Hóng took them and presented them to the Empress Dowager,
and the court highly praised his courage.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he was jealous of Hóng
and sent him out to be Administrator of Dōngjùn.
Hóng, fearing execution,
always kept poison hidden in his sleeve.
When Mǎng was defeated
and the Hàn forces rose,
Hóng alone completely preserved Dōngjùn, with over three hundred thousand households,
and surrendered to Gèngshǐ.
Lǐ Xiàn was
a native of Xǔchāng, Yǐngchuān.
During Wáng Mǎng's time, he was a subordinate magistrate of Lújiāng.
At the end of Mǎng's reign,
the Jiāng River bandits Wáng Zhōugōng and others raised a force of over ten thousand,
attacking and plundering commanderies and counties.
Mǎng appointed Xiàn as a Partial General and Commandant of Lújiāng
to defeat Zhōugōng.
After Mǎng's defeat,
Xiàn held the commandery and defended himself.
In the first year of Gèngshǐ,
he proclaimed himself King of Huáinán.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ,
he then declared himself Son of Heaven,
established dukes, ministers, and a full bureaucracy,
and held nine cities,
with a force of over ten thousand.
In the fourth year, in autumn,
Guāngwǔ personally went to Shòuchūn
and dispatched the General of Martial Might, Mǎ Chéng, and others to attack Xiàn,
besieging Shū.
They reached Liùróng County and captured it.
Xiàn fled,
and his soldier Bó Yì
pursued, beheaded Xiàn, and surrendered.
Xiàn's wife and children were all executed.
Bó Yì was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yúpǔ.
Later, Xiàn's remaining followers, such as Chúnyú Lín, still gathered several thousand men,
garrisoned them at Qiánshān,
and attacked and killed the Magistrate of Ānfēng.
The Inspector of Yángzhōu, Ōuyáng Xī, sent troops but could not defeat them.
The Emperor considered attacking them.
Chén Zhòng, a native of Lújiāng and an official aide,
reported to Xī, requesting permission to persuade Lín to surrender;
thereupon, he rode a single carriage,
drawn by a white horse,
went and convinced them to surrender.
The people of Qiánshān collectively built a shrine for him,
calling him
"White Horse Aide Chén."
Péng Chǒng, courtesy name Bótōng,
was a native of Wǎn, Nányáng.
His father, Hóng,
served as Administrator of Yúyáng during Emperor Āi's reign.
He was imposing in appearance,
could drink and eat much,
and commanded authority on the border.
When Wáng Mǎng acted as regent,
executing those who did not submit to him,
Hóng, along with Hé Wǔ and Bào Xuān, were killed.
Chǒng served as a county official in his youth.
During the Dìhuáng era,
he was a clerk under the Grand Minister of Works
and followed Wáng Yì eastward to resist the Hàn army.
Upon reaching Luòyáng,
he heard that his full brother was among the Hàn forces,
feared execution,
and immediately fled with his fellow townsman Wú Hàn to Yúyáng,
where he stayed with his father's former subordinates.
When Gèngshǐ was enthroned,
he sent the Imperial Envoy Hán Hóng with a credential to pacify the northern provinces,
authorized to independently appoint officials of two thousand *shí* and below.
Hóng arrived at Jì,
and as Chǒng and Hàn were both old acquaintances from his home village,
they met with great joy.
He immediately appointed Chǒng as Partial General,
acting Administrator of Yúyáng,
and Hàn as Magistrate of Ānlè.
When Guāngwǔ pacified and comforted Héběi
and reached Jì,
he wrote a letter inviting Chǒng.
Chǒng prepared oxen and wine
and was about to go for an audience.
At this time, Wáng Láng falsely established himself,
sent proclamations to Yān and Zhào,
dispatched generals to pacify Yúyáng and Shànggǔ,
and urgently called up their troops.
Many in the northern provinces were doubtful
and wished to follow him.
Wú Hàn persuaded Chǒng to follow Guāngwǔ,
an account of which is in Hàn's biography.
At the same time, the Administrator of Shànggǔ, Gěng Kuàng, also sent his Chief Clerk, Kòu Xún, to Chǒng
to form an alliance and jointly submit to Guāngwǔ.
Chǒng then dispatched three thousand cavalry and infantry,
with Wú Hàn acting as Chief Clerk,
and also the Commandants Yán Xuān and Gài Yán, and the Magistrate of Húnú, Wáng Liáng,
to join forces with the Shànggǔ army and head south,
meeting Guāngwǔ at Guǎng'ā.
Guāngwǔ, acting under imperial authority, enfeoffed Chǒng as Marquis of Jiànzhōng
and bestowed upon him the title of Grand General.
They then besieged Hándān,
and Chǒng continuously transported provisions,
without interruption.
When Wáng Láng died,
Guāngwǔ pursued the Bronze Horses,
north to Jì.
Pǒng went to seek an audience,
priding himself on his achievements,
and his expectations were very high.
Guāngwǔ’s reception of him failed to satisfy him,
and because of this, he harbored resentment.
Guāngwǔ knew this,
and asked Zhū Fú, the Governor of Yōuzhōu.
Fú replied,
"Previously, when Wú Hàn led troops north,
His Majesty gave Pǒng the sword he wore,
and also relied on him as the host of the northern route.
Pǒng thought that upon arrival, he would surely be welcomed and greeted with a handshake,
and they would share joy and sit together.
Now that this is not the case,
he is disappointed."
Fú then said,
"When Wáng Mǎng was Zǎihéng,
Zhēn Fēng went in and out day and night to deliberate.
At the time, people said, 'The midnight guest
is Zhēn Chángbó.'
After Mǎng usurped the throne,
Fēng was dissatisfied,
and eventually was executed."
Guāngwǔ laughed heartily,
thinking it would not come to that.
When he ascended the throne,
Wú Hàn and Wáng Liáng,
who were sent by Pǒng,
both became Sāngōng,
but Pǒng alone received no promotion,
and became increasingly discontent and frustrated.
He sighed,
"My achievements warrant kingship;
if it's just this,
has His Majesty forgotten me?"
At this time, the northern commanderies were shattered,
but Yúyáng was relatively intact,
having old salt and iron officials.
Pǒng converted this into trading grain,
accumulating treasures,
and growing richer and stronger.
Zhū Fú and Pǒng were incompatible,
and Fú repeatedly slandered and framed him.
In the spring of Jiànwǔ 2nd year,
an imperial edict summoned Pǒng.
Pǒng suspected Fú was selling him out,
and submitted a memorial wishing to be summoned with Fú.
He also wrote to Wú Hàn, Gài Yán, and others,
strongly speaking of Fú's wrongful actions,
and firmly requested to be summoned together.
The Emperor did not allow it,
which made Pǒng even more suspicious.
Moreover, his wife was inherently strong-willed,
unable to endure suppression and humiliation,
and strongly advised him not to accept the summons.
Pǒng also consulted with his often trusted officials,
who all harbored resentment towards Fú,
and none advised him to go.
The Emperor sent Pǒng's adopted son, Hòu Lánqīng, to persuade him.
Pǒng then detained Hòu Lánqīng,
and subsequently raised troops to rebel.
He appointed generals and commanders,
and personally led over twenty thousand men to attack Zhū Fú in Jì,
while dividing troops to plunder Guǎngyáng, Shànggǔ, and Yòuběipíng.
He also considered that he and Gěng Kuàng both had significant achievements,
yet their favors and rewards were equally meager.
He repeatedly sent envoys to entice Kuàng,
but Kuàng refused,
and promptly executed his envoys.
In autumn,
the Emperor sent Yóují Jiāngjūn Dèng Lóng to rescue Jì.
Lóng's army was south of Lù,
Fú's army was in Yōngnú,
and they sent an officer to report the situation.
The Emperor read the dispatch,
and angrily said to the officer,
"Their camps are a hundred lǐ apart;
how can they possibly reach each other in time?
By the time you return,
the northern army will surely be defeated."
Pǒng indeed amassed troops by the river to resist Lóng,
and also separately dispatched three thousand light cavalry to attack his rear,
greatly defeating Lóng's army.
Fú was far away
and thus could not rescue them.
They withdrew and left.
The following spring,
Pǒng subsequently captured several counties in Yòuběipíng and Shànggǔ.
He sent envoys with beautiful women, silk, and colorful fabrics to bribe the Xiongnú,
seeking to establish a peaceful alliance.
The Chányú sent Zǔonán Jiāngjūn with seven or eight thousand cavalry,
who came and went as skirmishers to assist Pǒng.
He also allied with Zhāng Bù and the various chieftains of Fùpíng and Huòsuǒ in the south,
all forming sworn bonds and alliances.
He then attacked and captured Jì Chéng,
and declared himself King of Yān.
His wife often had bad dreams,
and frequently saw strange omens.
Diviners and qi-gazers all said that rebellion would arise from within.
Pǒng suspected that his adopted son, Hòu Lánqīng, had returned to Hàn as a hostage,
and therefore did not trust him.
He made him lead troops outside,
leaving no relatives within.
In the spring of the 5th year,
Pǒng was fasting
and alone in his private room.
Cāngtóu Zǐmì and two others, while Pǒng was asleep,
bound him to the bed.
They told the outside officials,
"His Majesty is observing a fast and isolation,
all officials are to rest."
They falsely claimed it was Pǒng's order,
and arrested and bound the servants and maids,
placing each in a separate location.
They also called his wife by Pǒng's command.
When his wife entered,
she was greatly alarmed.
Pǒng urgently shouted,
"Quickly prepare provisions for the generals!"
Thereupon, two servants led his wife to retrieve treasures,
leaving one servant to guard Pǒng.
Pǒng said to the guarding servant,
"You are a young lad,
whom I have always loved.
Now you are merely coerced by Zǐmì.
Untie me,
and I will give you my daughter Zhū in marriage,
and all the family's wealth will be yours."
The young servant wanted to untie him,
but looked outside the door
and saw Zǐmì listening to their conversation,
so he dared not untie him.
Then they collected gold, jade, clothing, and other items,
and brought them to Pǒng's place to pack.
They saddled six horses
and made his wife sew two silk bags.
After dusk,
they untied Pǒng's hand
and made him write a note informing the city gate general, saying,
"I am now sending Zǐmì and others to Hòu Lánqīng's place.
Quickly open the gate and let them out,
do not delay them."
Once the letter was written,
they immediately cut off Pǒng's and his wife's heads,
placed them in the bags,
and then, carrying the note, galloped out of the city.
They subsequently presented them at the imperial palace,
and Zǐmì was enfeoffed as Bùyì Hóu.
The next morning,
the palace gate did not open.
Officials climbed over the wall to enter,
and seeing Pǒng's corpse,
they were terrified.
His Shàngshū Hán Lì and others together established Pǒng's son, Wǔ, as king,
and made Hòu Lánqīng a general.
Guóshī Hán Lì cut off Wǔ's head
and surrendered to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Jì Zūn.
Pǒng's clan was exterminated.
Lú Fāng, courtesy name Jūnqī,
was a native of Sānshuǐ, Āndìng Commandery.
He lived in Zuǒgǔ.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
everyone in the realm longed for Hàn virtue.
Fāng thus fraudulently claimed to be Liú Wénbó, a great-grandson of Emperor Wǔ.
His great-grandmother, a sister of the Xiongnú Gǔlí Húnyé Wáng, became Emperor Wǔ's empress,
and bore three sons.
During the turmoil of Jiāng Chōng,
the crown prince was executed,
and the empress died for her involvement.
The middle son, Cìqīng, fled to Chánglíng;
the youngest son, Huíqīng, escaped to Zuǒgǔ.
General Huò established Cìqīng,
and summoned Huíqīng,
but Huíqīng did not come out,
and thus remained in Zuǒ Gǔ,
where he begot Sūnqīng.
Sūnqīng begot Wénbó.
He constantly used this story to deceive and mislead people in the Āndìng area.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
he and the Qiāng and Hú of the Sānshuǐ dependent state raised an army.
When Gēngshǐ arrived in Cháng'ān,
he summoned Fāng as a Qí Dūwèi,
and sent him to pacify the region west of Āndìng.
When Gēngshǐ failed,
the heroes of Sānshuǐ discussed together,
considering that Fāng was a descendant of the Liú clan,
and that he ought to succeed to the ancestral temple.
So they jointly established Fāng as Grand General and King of Xīpíng,
and sent envoys to Qīang and Xiōngnú to form a peace and kinship alliance.
The Chányú said:
“The Xiōngnú originally made an agreement with Hàn to be brothers.
Later, the Xiōngnú declined,
and Hūhánxié Chányú submitted to Hàn.
Hàn dispatched troops to protect him,
and he called himself a subject for generations.
Now Hàn is also in decline,
and a member of the Liú clan has come to submit to me.
I should also establish him,
and let him respectfully serve me.”
Then he sent Jùlín Wáng with several thousand cavalry to welcome Fāng.
Fāng, with his elder brother Qín and younger brother Chéng, entered Xiōngnú.
The Chányú then established Fāng as Hàn Dì.
He appointed Chéng as Grandee of the Household,
who led Hú cavalry back into Āndìng.
Initially,
Lǐ Xīng and Suí Yù from Wǔyuán,
Tián Sà from Shuòfāng,
Shí Wěi and Mǐn Kān from Dàijùn,
each raised troops and proclaimed themselves generals.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
the Chányú sent Wúlóu Qiěqú Wáng into the Wǔyuán pass,
to make peace and kinship with Lǐ Xīng and others,
informing Xīng that he wished Fāng to return to Hàn territory as emperor.
Wǔshì A Lǐ Xīng and Mǐn Kān led their troops to the Chányú’s court to welcome Fāng,
and together they entered the pass,
making Jiǔyuán Xiàn their capital.
They plundered and occupied Wǔyuán, Shuòfāng, Yúnzhōng, Dìngxiāng, and Yànmén, the five commanderies,
and appointed governors and magistrates,
and collaborated with the Hú troops,
harassing the northern border.
In the sixth year,
Fāng’s general Jiǎ Lǎn led Hú cavalry to attack and kill Liú Xīng, the Administrator of Dàijùn.
Later, Fāng executed his Wǔyuán Administrator Lǐ Xīng and his brothers for some matter,
and his Shuòfāng Administrator Tián Sà and Yúnzhōng Administrator Qiáo Hù, out of fear,
rebelled against Fāng,
and surrendered their commanderies.
Guāngwǔ ordered them to retain their original positions.
Later, Grand Marshal Wú Hàn and General-in-Chief of Cavalry Dù Mào repeatedly attacked Fāng,
but none were successful.
In the twelfth year,
Fāng and Jiǎ Lǎn together attacked Yúnzhōng,
but could not take it for a long time.
His general Suí Yù, who was left to guard Jiǔyuán,
intended to coerce Fāng into surrendering.
Fāng knew his wings were externally dependent and his core internally alienated,
so he abandoned his baggage,
and fled into Xiōngnú with more than ten horsemen.
His followers all returned to Suí Yù.
Yù then accompanied the envoy Chéng Xún to the imperial court.
Yù was appointed Administrator of Wǔyuán
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Juānhú;
Yù’s younger brother Xiàn was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔjìn.
In the sixteenth year,
Fāng again entered and resided in Gāoliǔ,
and together with Mǐn Kān’s elder brother Lín, sent envoys to request surrender.
So Fāng was established as King of Dài,
Kān as Chancellor of Dài,
and Lín as Grand Tutor of Dài.
They were bestowed 20,000 bolts of silk,
and then sent to harmonize and unite the Xiōngnú.
Fāng submitted a memorial expressing gratitude, saying:
“Your subject Fāng, due to the misfortune of being a descendant of the former emperor,
was abandoned on the borderlands.
When the altars of soil and grain suffered destruction under Wáng Mǎng,
it became the concern of the descendants
to jointly punish him.
Therefore, I allied with the Qiāng and Róng in the west,
and embraced the Xiōngnú in the north.
The Chányú did not forget the old virtue
and temporarily established me to provide assistance.
At that time, wars arose simultaneously,
occurring everywhere.
Your subject did not dare to be covetous,
but hoped to uphold the ancestral temple
and revive the altars of soil and grain.
That is why I usurped the imperial title for a long time,
for more than ten years;
my crime deserves ten thousand deaths.
Your Majesty's sagely virtue is lofty and enlightened;
personally leading all the wise,
the whole realm has submitted,
and your benevolence extends to different customs.
For the sake of being a distant relative,
You pardoned your subject Fāng's crime,
and further bestowed benevolent favor,
enfeoffing me as King of Dài,
to guard the northern frontier.
I have no means to repay this grave responsibility,
but I earnestly desire to harmonize and unite the Xiōngnú,
daring not to spare any effort,
nor to betray Your grace and pardon.
I respectfully offer the Emperor's jade seal,
and look forward to visiting the imperial court.”
An edict replied to Fāng, instructing him to come to court in Míngróng Xiàn.
That winter,
Fāng came to court,
reaching as far south as Chāngpíng.
There was an imperial decree to stop,
ordering him to come to court again the following year.
Fāng returned from the road,
anxious and fearful,
and then betrayed again,
thus revolting.
He and Mǐn Kān and Mǐn Lín attacked each other for months.
The Xiōngnú sent several hundred cavalry to welcome Fāng and his wife and children out of the pass.
Fāng remained in Xiōngnú for more than ten years
and died of illness.
Initially,
the Hú people of Āndìng Subordinate State were Fāng’s confederates,
and when Fāng was defeated,
the Hú people returned to their hometowns,
suffering greatly from county government corvée labor.
Among them was Bómǎ Shàobó,
who was naturally strong and courageous.
In the twenty-first year,
he led his tribesmen in rebellion,
allied with the Xiōngnú,
and gathered in Qīngshān.
Then the Senior Clerk of the General, Chén Xīn,
was sent to lead three thousand cavalry to attack him.
Shàobó then surrendered.
He was relocated to Jì Xiàn.
Commentary says: The traditions state,
“Great virtue will surely be worshipped for a hundred generations.”
Confucius said,
“Benevolence wins the multitude.”
Indeed, one who can win the hearts of the multitude
will not be forgotten for a hundred generations.
Considering the time of Gēngshǐ,
the lingering grace and residual achievements of the Liú clan—
how could heroes resist it?!
Thus, one knows how profound the leniency and benevolence of Gāozǔ and Xiàowén
were embedded in people’s hearts.
The people of Zhōu thought of Shàogōng,
loving his sweet pear tree;
how much more so their descendants!
Is this why the Liú clan received the Mandate again?!
As for these few individuals,
how could they have long-term plans for the state?!
They merely indulged in the chaos of the times,
wanting to act wantonly.
Yet, because they were attached to the imperial clan,
they could stubbornly endure for years.
Looking at their strategies,
they were indeed not enough to awe Hàn Zǔ
or awaken his heroic spirit.
A eulogy says: Heaven and earth were violently altered,
a multitude of dragons fought in the wilds.
Chāng and Fāng usurped deceptively,
Liáng and Qí continuously vied.
Chǒng relied on strong territories,
Xiàn was entangled in deep rivers.
Indeed, they were lawless,
and their generations entrusted to a divine land.
Biography of Wěi Xiāo and Gōngsūn Shù, Chapter Three.
Wěi Xiāo,
courtesy name Jìmèng,
was from Chéngjì in Tiānshuǐ.
In his youth, he served in the prefecture and commandery.
Wáng Mǎng’s Imperial Mentor, Liú Xīn, recommended Xiāo as a scholar.
After Xīn died,
Xiāo returned to his hometown.
His paternal uncle, Cuī,
was always a chivalrous and influential figure
who could win over the masses.
Hearing that Gēngshǐ had been established and Mǎng’s forces were repeatedly defeated,
he then plotted with his elder brother Yì, Yáng Guǎng from Shàngguī, and Zhōu Zōng from Jì
to raise troops in support of Hàn.
Xiāo tried to stop them, saying:
“Armaments
are instruments of ill omen.
What crime have our clans committed?!”
Cuī did not listen,
and then gathered several thousand people,
attacked Píngxiāng,
and killed Mǎng’s Protector-General of Róng, Dà Yǐn.
