Cuī, Guǎng, and others believed that to initiate an undertaking, a leader should be established to unify the masses.
They all said that Xiāo had always been famous
and fond of classics,
so they jointly acclaimed him as Grand General.
Xiāo declined but could not avoid it,
saying:
“My uncles and all you wise gentlemen underestimate this young fellow.
If you can truly follow my words,
then I dare to obey the command.”
Everyone said,
“Yes.”
As soon as Wēi Xiāo
had established himself, he dispatched an envoy to invite Fāng Wàng of Pínglíng,
to make him his military strategist.
When Wàng arrived,
he advised Xiāo, saying:
“Your Excellency wishes to follow Heaven and obey the people,
assisting the Hàn to rise.
However, the one who is now established is in Nányáng,
and Wáng Mǎng still occupies Cháng'ān.
Though you wish to use the name of Hàn,
in reality, you have received no mandate.
How then will you gain the trust of the masses?
You should immediately establish the high temple,
proclaim yourself a subject, and offer sacrifices.
This is what is called ‘teaching through divine ways,’
seeking assistance from both men and gods.
Moreover, rites have their augmentations and diminutions;
substance and refinement are not constant.
By clearing the ground and opening the foundation,
with thatched roofs and earthen steps,
you can achieve reverence and respect.
Even if the offerings are not fully complete,
the divine spirits will surely accept them.”
Xiāo followed his advice,
and thus erected a temple east of the city,
sacrificing to Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, and Shìzōng.
Xiāo and the others all declared themselves subjects and attended to the rites,
while the historian presented a jade disk and made the announcement.
When the prayer was finished,
an officer dug a pit in the courtyard,
led in a horse, wielded a knife,
presented a tray with a pig and a spade,
then slaughtered the animal and swore an oath.
It said:
“We, all thirty-one generals of this alliance,
of sixteen surnames,
sincerely accept the Dao of Heaven,
to assist and support the Liú clan.
If any harbor treachery,
may the enlightened spirits strike them down.
May Gāozǔ, Wénhuáng, and Wǔhuáng
cause them to lose their mandate,
their clan to suffer war,
and their families to be exterminated.”
An officer presented the blood-spade,
and the protector-general raised his hand, saluting the generals, saying:
“If the spade is not moistened with blood,
and the blood not tasted by mouth,
it is deceiving the divine spirits,
and the punishment will be as stated in the oath.”
Afterward, the blood was buried and the document added,
all according to ancient rites.
When the ceremony was finished,
a proclamation was sent to the commanderies and states, saying:
“Hàn is restored, year one, seventh month, Jǐyǒu day, first of the month.
On Jǐsì,
Senior General Wēi Xiāo, White Tiger General Wēi Cuī, Left General Wēi Yì, Right General
Yáng Guǎng, Manifest Might General Wáng Zūn, Cloud Banner General Zhōu Zōng, and others,
proclaim to the provincial governors, departmental supervisors, commandery chief wardens, chief controllers, grand administrators, administrators, cavalry
commanders, chief clerks, and commandery magistrates:
The former Marquis of Xīndū, Wáng Mǎng,
treated Heaven and Earth with insolence,
and acted contrary to the Dao and reason.
He poisoned and killed Emperor Xiàopíng,
and usurped his throne.
He falsely
claimed the mandate of Heaven,
fabricated auspicious writings,
deceived and misled the populace,
and angered the Lord on High.
He twisted and adorned texts,
calling them auspicious omens.
He toyed with the gods and spirits,
and sang praises
to disaster.
The bamboos of Chǔ and Yuè
are not enough to write down his evil deeds.
The whole world knows it clearly,
what everyone has heard and seen.
Now, we briefly list the major points,
to inform officials and commoners.
He confused and disturbed the heavenly arts,
and cited historical records.
In the past, Qín Shǐhuáng destroyed the system of posthumous titles,
wishing to number from one and two up to ten thousand generations.
Yet Mǎng decreed a calendar of thirty-six
thousand years,
claiming he himself would fulfill this span.
He followed the path of the perished Qín,
and pushed an infinite number.
This is his great crime of defying Heaven.
He built nine temples,
exhausting earthworks.
He dug up tombs in Hédōng,
and attacked and plundered burial mounds.
This is his great crime of defying Earth.
He cruelly
and wantonly exterminated the common people.
He implemented the 'burning and grating' punishments,
abolished laws suited to the times,
drenched people in strong vinegar,
and tore them apart with five poisons.
His decrees changed daily,
official titles monthly,
currency yearly,
leaving officials and commoners confused,
not knowing what to follow,
merchants and travelers in distress,
weeping in the marketplaces.
He established six
monopolies,
increased heavy taxes,
exploited the common people,
lavishly provided for himself,
allowed bribes to circulate,
with wealth flowing into the public coffers,
and corruption rampant from top to bottom,
without mutual supervision
or examination.
People were punished for possessing copper or charcoal,
confiscated into the Zōngguān,
with convicts accumulating,
hundreds of thousands of them,
artisans starved to death,
and Cháng'ān reeked.
After disturbing all
of Huáxià,
his mad heart grew even more perverse.
He attacked the powerful Hú in the north,
harassed the formidable Yuè in the south,
〔一０〕invaded the Qiāng and Róng in the west,
and plucked at the Huì and Mò in the east.
〔一一〕He caused all beyond the four borders
to become
a menace,
and the border commanderies,
the coasts of rivers and seas,
were swept clean of people.
〔一二〕Thus, those who perished in wars,
those ensnared by harsh laws,
those who died young from famine,
and those
affected by epidemics,
were counted in the millions.
The dead lay exposed without burial,
the living fled and scattered,
young orphans and women
wandered as captives.
This is his
great crime of defying humanity.
Mǎ Dǒngzhōng,
National Preceptor Liú Xīn,
and General of the Guards Wáng Shè,
all conspired for internal collapse;
Chief of Fate Kǒng Rén,
Chief of Advisers Yán Yóu,
and Minister of Rites Chén Mào,
led
their masses to surrender externally.
Now the armies east of the mountains, numbering over two million,
have already pacified Qí and Chǔ,
descended into Shǔ and Hàn,
secured Wǎn and Luò,
occupied Áocāng,
and defended Hángǔ.
Their powerful
commands have spread far and wide,
their influence proclaimed to the Central Peak.
They restore fallen states and continue broken lines,
enfeoff and settle all states,
follow the old institutions of Gāozǔ,
and cultivate the enduring virtues of Xiàowén.
Those who do not
obey,
will be pacified by military force.
Envoys are dispatched to the Four Barbarians,
restoring their titles.
Thereafter, the armies will return and disband,
sheathing bows and silencing drums.
A mandate will be issued to the common people,
that each
be at peace in their place,
so as to avoid the responsibility of failing the people.”
Xiāo then marshaled an army of 100,000,
and attacked and killed Chén Qìng, the Governor of Yōngzhōu.
He was about to attack Āndìng.
The Grand Administrator of Āndìng, Wáng Xiàng,
was the son of Wáng Mǎng's younger cousin, Tán, the Marquis of Píng'ā.
His prestige and influence alone could prevail within his commandery,
and none of the dependent counties rebelled.
Xiāo then sent a letter to Xiàng,
explaining the Mandate of Heaven,
repeatedly advising and showing him the way,
but Xiàng ultimately did not comply.
Thereupon, Xiāo advanced his troops and captured him,
displaying him to the populace,
and then executed him.
Āndìng completely surrendered.
Meanwhile, an army was also raised in Cháng'ān to execute Wáng Mǎng.
Xiāo then dispatched his generals to subjugate Lǒngxī, Wǔdū, Jīnchéng, Wǔwēi, Zhāngyè, Jiǔquán, and Dūnhuáng;
all of them submitted.
In the second year of Gēngshǐ's reign,
an envoy was sent to summon Xiāo, Cuī, Yì, and others.
As Xiāo was about to depart,
Fāng Wàng believed that Gēngshǐ's fate was uncertain,
and firmly tried to stop him,
but Xiāo did not listen.
Wàng then sent a letter excusing himself and left,
saying:
“You are about to establish the achievements of Yī and Lǚ,
and widely spread an unparalleled功.
However, the great undertaking has just begun,
and the heroes are not yet gathered.
As for me, Wàng, a person from a foreign land,
whose flaws have not yet been exposed,
I wished to first honor Guō Kuí,
and hoped to attract Yuè Yì.
Therefore, I respectfully accepted your great purpose,
and followed the trend without hesitation.
General, you honor the worthy with supreme virtue,
and broaden their counsel.
Every action brings success,
every move is appropriate.
Your foundation is already established,
and your great achievements are about to be gathered.
Now, the elite are all assembled,
their wings shoulder to shoulder.
I, Wàng, have no virtue of an elder,
yet I am presumptuously placed above other guests.
I am truly ashamed.
Although I harbor a firm personal integrity,
wishing to keep my departures and arrivals pure,
I truly will never betray my origins,
nor waver in my resolve.
Why so?
Fàn Lí, having achieved success for Gōujiàn,
traveled in a small boat on the Five Lakes;
Jiù Fàn, having made amends to Wéngōng,
also hesitated by the Hé River.
With the virtue of these two men,
whose names are inscribed in both states,
they still effaced their traces and confessed their errors,
asking for their lives and their freedom.
It is fitting that I, Wàng, should not exert myself.
This is probably appropriate.
I, Wàng, heard that in Wūshì there is a Mount Lóngchí,
with a small path leading south,
connecting with the Hàn River.
There are often extraordinary people by its side.
I will temporarily reside there,
to extensively seek the truth.”
“May the General strive hard.”
Xiāo and the others then arrived at Cháng'ān.
Gēngshǐ appointed him Right General,
and Cuī and Yì both retained their former titles.
That winter,
Cuī and Yì plotted to rebel and return home.
Xiāo feared being implicated in their misfortune,
and immediately reported the matter to Gēngshǐ,
whereupon Cuī and Yì were executed.
Gēngshǐ was moved by Xiāo's loyalty,
and appointed him Grandee Secretary.
The following summer,
the Chìméi entered the pass,
and the Sānfǔ region was in chaos.
News spread that Guāngwǔ had ascended the throne north of the Yellow River.
Xiāo immediately persuaded Gēngshǐ to return political power to Guāngwǔ's uncle, Guó, the Three Elders of Liáng,
but Gēngshǐ did not listen.
The generals wanted to coerce Gēngshǐ to return east,
and Xiāo also conspired with them.
When the matter was discovered,
Gēngshǐ sent an envoy to summon Xiāo.
Xiāo claimed illness and did not enter,
and instead gathered his retainers Wáng Zūn, Zhōu Zōng, and others, and marshaled troops to defend himself.
Gēngshǐ sent the Commander of the Guards, Dèng Yè,
to lead troops to surround Xiāo.
Xiāo closed the gates and resisted.
By dusk,
he broke through the encirclement,
and with several dozen horsemen, cut down the gates of Píngchéng at night,
fleeing back to Tiānshuǐ.
He again gathered his followers,
occupied his old territory,
and proclaimed himself Supreme General of Xīzhōu.
When Gēngshǐ was defeated,
the elders and gentry of Sānfǔ all flocked back to Xiāo.
Xiāo had always been humble, respectful, and fond of scholars,
humbling himself to welcome them and treating them as common friends.
He appointed Gǔ Gōng of Cháng'ān, who had been Grand Administrator of Pínghé under Wáng Mǎng,
as Grand Administrator of Zhǎngyě.
Fàn Qūn of Pínglíng was his teacher and friend.
Zhào Bǐng, Sū Héng, and Zhèng Xīng were his Sacrificial Officers.
Shēntú Gāng and Dù Lín were his Secretaries.
Yáng Guǎng, Wáng Zūn, Zhōu Zōng, as well as Xíng Xún of Píngxiāng, Wáng Jié of Āyáng, and Wáng Yuán of Chánglíng were his Grand Generals.
Dùlíng, Jīndān, and their ilk were his guests.
Because of this, his fame shook Xīzhōu,
and was heard of in Shāndōng.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Grand Minister of Works Dèng Yǔ marched west to attack the Chìméi,
stationing his troops at Yúnyáng.
Yǔ's subordinate general Fényīn led his troops to rebel against Yǔ,
marching west towards Tiānshuǐ.
Xiāo intercepted and attacked,
defeating him at Gāopíng,
and capturing all his baggage train.
Thereupon, Yǔ, acting on imperial authority, sent an envoy with a credential to appoint Xiāo as Grand General of Xīzhōu,
giving him independent control over the affairs of Liángzhōu and Shuòfāng.
When the Chìméi left Cháng'ān,
intending to march west into Lǒng,
Xiāo sent General Yáng Guǎng to meet and attack them,
defeating them.
He then pursued and defeated them again between Wūshì and Jīngyáng.
Since Xiāo had rendered service to Hàn,
and also received a noble title from Dèng Yǔ,
and appointed his trusted confidantes to positions,
many advisers urged him to establish diplomatic relations with the capital.
In the third year,
Xiāo then submitted a memorial to the court.
Guāngwǔ had long heard of his reputation,
and replied with extraordinary courtesy,
addressing him by his courtesy name,
using the etiquette accorded to a rival state,
thereby comforting and reassuring him generously.
At that time, Lǚ Wěi of Chéncāng commanded tens of thousands of troops,
and in communication with Gōngsūn Shù,
raided Sānfǔ.
Xiāo again sent troops to assist the General Who Conquers the West, Féng Yì, in attacking him,
driving Wěi away.
He then sent an envoy to report the situation.
The Emperor replied with a handwritten letter, saying:
“I admire your virtue and righteousness,
and wish to form a bond with you.
In ancient times, King Wén, though he controlled two-thirds of the realm,
still served Yīn.
However, a jaded horse and a blunt knife
cannot be forced.
Repeatedly receiving the praise of a Bólè,
a common fly's flight
does not exceed a few steps.
But relying on the tail of a thoroughbred,
it can surpass its kind.
Separated by bandits,
news has been infrequent.
General, your principled conduct,
supporting the weak and saving the endangered,
resisting Gōngsūn's troops in the south,
and defending against the chaos of the Qiāng and Hú in the north,
is why Féng Yì, on his western expedition,
was able to wander in Sānfǔ with merely a few hundred men.
Without the General's assistance,
Xiányáng would already have fallen into others' hands.
Currently, bandits in Guāndōng
are gathering in various places,
and our ambitions are far-reaching,
leaving us little leisure for many things.
We have not yet been able to lead an army to Chéngdū,
to contend with Ziyáng.
If Ziyáng reaches Hànzhōng and Sānfǔ,
I wish to rely on the General's troops and horses,
to face him with drums and banners.
If you would agree to this,
and we receive the blessings of Heaven,
it will be the time for wise strategists to allocate territories based on merit.
Guǎn Zhòng said: ‘My parents gave me birth,
but Bào Zǐ made me who I am.’
From now on,
let us correspond by handwritten letters,
and not be swayed by the words of outsiders who sow discord.”
Later, Gōngsūn Shù repeatedly dispatched troops to Hànzhōng,
and sent an envoy to bestow upon Xiāo the seal and sash of Grand Minister of Works and King Fú'ān.
Xiāo considered himself an equal of Shù,
and was ashamed to be his subject.
So he executed the envoy,
and dispatched troops to attack Shù,
repeatedly defeating Shù's army.
Because of this, the Shuǐ troops no longer ventured north.
At that time, the generals and commanders in Guānzhōng
repeatedly submitted memorials, stating that Shǔ could be attacked.
The Emperor showed them to Kuí Xiāo,
and then ordered him to campaign against Shǔ,
to prove his loyalty.
Kuí Xiāo then sent his Chief Clerk to memorialize,
strongly arguing that Sānfǔ was weak and isolated,
and that Liú Wénbó was on the border,
so it was not yet appropriate to plan for Shǔ.
The Emperor knew that Kuí Xiāo wanted to play both sides,
and did not wish for the unification of the empire.
Thereupon, he gradually curtailed the禮 (lǐ) shown to him
and rectified the etiquette between ruler and subject.
Initially,
Kuí Xiāo was on good terms with Lái Shè and Mǎ Yuán.
Therefore, the Emperor repeatedly sent Shè and Yuán as envoys to and fro,
urging him to come to court,
and promising him high titles.
Kuí Xiāo did not wish to go east,
and repeatedly sent envoys with deeply humble words,
saying that he had no merits or virtues,
and that he wished to retire to his village
after the four quarters were pacified.
In the fifth year (29 CE),
Lái Shè was again sent to persuade Kuí Xiāo to send a son to serve at court.
When Kuí Xiāo heard that Liú Yǒng and Péng Chǒng had both been defeated,
he then sent his eldest son, Xún, with Shè to the imperial court.
Xún was made Commander of Hu Cavalry
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Juānqiāng.
However, Kuí Xiāo's generals Wáng Yuán and Wáng Jié always believed that the outcome of the empire was still uncertain,
and did not wish to commit wholeheartedly to internal affairs.
Wáng Yuán then persuaded Kuí Xiāo, saying:
"In the past, when Gēngshǐ moved his capital west,
the four quarters responded,
and the world looked up to him,
calling it a time of great peace.
But it was destroyed overnight,
and Your Majesty almost had no place to settle.
Now, in the south there is Zǐyáng,
in the north there is Wénbó,
and throughout the rivers, lakes, seas, and mountains of Tài,
there are dozens of kings and dukes.
Yet you wish to follow the advice of scholars,
abandon the foundation of a thousand chariots,
and travel to a perilous state
in pursuit of complete safety?
This is following the track of an overturned carriage,
a plan that is impossible!
Currently, Tiānshuǐ is rich and prosperous,
with the strongest soldiers and horses.
We can gain Xihe and Shàngjùn in the north,
and the lands of Sānfǔ in the east.
Following the old traces of Qín,
we can make the Yellow River and mountains our boundaries.
Your servant asks to use a single ball of mud to seal Hángǔ Pass for Your Majesty in the east.
This is an opportunity of a myriad generations!
If this plan is not feasible,
then let us accumulate soldiers and horses,
hold the strategic passes and defend ourselves.
Let time pass,
await changes in the four quarters,
and even if we fail to become king,
our situation will still be sufficient to become a hegemon.
In short,
a fish cannot leave its deep pool;
if a divine dragon loses its power,
it will become like an earthworm."
Kuí Xiāo inwardly approved of Wáng Yuán's plan.
Although he sent his son as a hostage,
he still relied on his strategic advantage,
desiring to control his own region.
Therefore, wandering scholars and venerable elders
gradually began to leave him.
In the sixth year (30 CE),
Guāndōng was entirely pacified.
The Emperor, weary of incessant warfare,
and with Kuí Xiāo's son serving at court,
while Gōngsūn Shù was far away on the frontier,
then said to his generals:
"For now, we should put these two sons out of our minds."
He then repeatedly sent letters to Lǒng and Shǔ,
announcing warnings and blessings.
Kuí Xiāo's retainers and officials were mostly cultured scholars,
and whatever they presented
was recited by the gentry of the time.
Therefore, when the Emperor replied,
he paid particular attention to his words.
Kuí Xiāo again sent his envoy Zhōuyóu to the imperial court,
who first arrived at Féng Yì's camp.
Zhōuyóu was killed by enemies.
The Emperor sent Guard Commander Cháo Qī with treasures and silks to bestow upon Kuí Xiāo.
Cháo Qī was robbed in Zhèng,
and the valuables were lost.
The Emperor often praised Kuí Xiāo as a gentleman,
and was determined to win him over.
Hearing of these incidents, he sighed and said:
"It seems that things between me and Kuí Xiāo are not destined to succeed.
My envoy was killed,
and the gifts were lost on the way."
At that time, Gōngsūn Shù sent troops to invade Nánjùn.
The Emperor then ordered Kuí Xiāo to attack Shǔ from Tiānshuǐ,
intending to break his spirit.
Kuí Xiāo again memorialized:
"Báishuǐ is perilous and rugged,
and the plank roads are ruined."
He also set up many other obstacles.
The Emperor knew that he would ultimately not be of use,
and intended to attack him.
So he traveled west to Cháng'ān,
and sent General who Establishes Awe Gěng Yǎn and six other generals to attack Shǔ from the Lǒng Pass.
He first had Lái Shè deliver an imperial edict with a seal.
Kuí Xiāo became suspicious and fearful,
and immediately mustered his troops,
ordering Wáng Yuán to occupy Lǒngdǐ,
cut down trees to block the road,
and plot to kill Shè.
Shè managed to escape.
The generals fought with Kuí Xiāo,
suffered a great defeat,
and each retreated.
Kuí Xiāo then sent Wáng Yuán and Xún to invade Sānfǔ.
General who Conquers the West Féng Yì and General who Captures the Enemy Jì Zūn, among others, defeated them.
Kuí Xiāo then submitted a memorial of apology, saying:
"My officials and people, upon hearing of the sudden arrival of a large army,
were terrified and defended themselves.
I, Kuí Xiāo, was unable to restrain them.
Although there was great benefit in warfare,
I dared not abandon the principles of a loyal subject,
and personally pursued them to call them back.
In ancient times, Yú Shùn served his father;
when struck with a large staff, he fled,
but when struck with a small staff, he endured.
Although I am not agile,
how dare I forget this principle?
My present affairs
rest with the imperial court.
If granted death, I will die;
if punished, I will accept the punishment.
If I continue to receive your grace,
and am able to cleanse my heart anew,
my bones will not decay even in death."
The officials deemed Kuí Xiāo's words insolent
and requested the execution of his son, Xún.
The Emperor could not bear to do it,
and again sent Lái Shè to Qī,
bestowing a letter upon Kuí Xiāo that read:
"In ancient times, General Chái wrote to Hán Xìn, saying:
'Your Majesty is magnanimous and benevolent;
although vassal lords may have rebelled and later returned,
their titles and ranks are always restored,
and they are not punished.'
Because Kuí Xiāo is a cultured official who understands righteousness and principle,
I again bestow this letter.
To speak too deeply would seem disrespectful;
to speak too briefly would leave matters unresolved.
Now, if you submit yourself
and send your younger brother Xún back to the court,
then your titles and emoluments will be preserved,
and you will enjoy great and vast fortune.
I am almost forty years old,
and have been engaged in warfare for ten years.
I am weary of empty words and hollow rhetoric.
If you do not wish to comply,
do not reply."
Kuí Xiāo knew that the Emperor had seen through his deception,
and so he sent an envoy to declare himself a subject of Gōngsūn Shù.
The next year,
Gōngsūn Shù made Kuí Xiāo Prince of Shuòníng,
and sent troops back and forth
to support him.
In the autumn,
Kuí Xiāo led thirty thousand cavalry and infantry to invade Āndìng,
reaching Yīnpán.
Féng Yì led his generals to resist him.
Kuí Xiāo also ordered a separate general to descend from Lǒng
and attack Jì Zūn at Qī.
Neither of these campaigns was successful,
so he withdrew.
The emperor then ordered Lái Shè to write a letter to summon Wáng Zūn.
Zūn then, with his family, went east to the capital.
He was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū
and enfeoffed as Xiàngyì Hóu.
Zūn's courtesy name was Zǐchūn,
and he was a Bālíng native.
His father was the Tàishǒu of Shàngjùn.
Zūn was heroic and chivalrous in his youth,
possessing talent and eloquence.
Although he had raised an army with Kuí Xiāo,
he always harbored intentions of returning to the Hàn dynasty.
He once privately said to Lái Shè in Tiānshuǐ:
"The reason I exert myself and do not shun arrows and stones
is not for rank and position!
It is merely because people remember their former lord,
and my late father received great kindness from the Hàn dynasty.
I wish to repay but one ten thousandth of it."
He also frequently advised Xiāo to send a son to serve at court,
offering earnest and sharp counsel repeatedly,
but Xiāo did not comply.
Therefore, he left.
In the spring of the eighth year,
Lái Shè, following a mountain path, launched a surprise attack and captured Luèyáng city.
Xiāo was caught off guard,
fearing that a larger army would arrive.
He then sent Wáng Yuán to resist at Lǒngdǐ,
Xíng Xún to guard Fān Xū kǒu,
Wáng Mèng to block Jītóu Dào,
and Niú Hán to encamp at Wǎtíng.
Xiāo himself led his large army to besiege Lái Shè.
Gōngsūn Shù also dispatched his generals Lǐ Yù and Tián Yǎn to assist Xiāo in attacking Luèyáng.
The city was not taken for months.
The emperor then led his generals on a western expedition,
advancing into Lǒng from several routes,
and ordered Wáng Zūn, holding the jié, to oversee Dàsīmǎ Wú Hàn, who was left to garrison Cháng'ān.
Zūn knew that Xiāo was destined for defeat and destruction,
and having a former acquaintance with Niú Hán,
knew that he had intentions of returning to righteousness.
He conveyed this in a letter to him, saying:
"Zūn and King Kuí formed an alliance to serve the Hàn dynasty.
Having personally
experienced danger and trodden on death ground
dozens of times already.
At that time, west of Zhōuluò
there was no unified command,
so I devised a strategy for the king,
hoping to gather Guānzhōng in the east,
take Shàngjùn in the north,
and advance to serve the will of Heaven and man,
and retreat to punish the chaos of foreign tribes.
I repeatedly speculated and hoped that the holy Hàn would be restored,
and that we would bring Hélǒng to the old capital to return to the imperial court.
Since the birth of mankind,
among those who have served others,
none have had an opportunity more opportune than this.
Yet the king's officers and men,
a rabble dwelling in caves,
all clap their hands
and desire to make wicked plans.
The matters over which Zūn and Rúqīng argued day and night,
which nearly brought harm to ourselves,
were they but one thing?
The former plan was suppressed and rejected,
the later strategy was not followed;
that is why I sighed and clapped my wrist,
and boarded my chariot with tears streaming.
Fortunately, I received appointment and enfeoffment,
and was able to continue offering counsel.
Whenever matters of Xīzhōu were brought up,
I never dared forget Rúqīng's words.
Now the imperial carriage and the great army
are already on the road;
Wú and Gěng, valiant generals,
are gathered like clouds on all four borders.
Yet Rúqīng, with fleeing, scattered troops,
blocks strategic points
and confronts the main army's vanguard.
What do you think of this situation?
Indeed, the wise foresee danger and contemplate change;
the virtuous are mired but not sullied.
Thus, their achievements and fame are ultimately realized,
and their strategies succeed.
Therefore, Yí Wú was bound in shackles yet became prime minister of Qí;
Qíng Bù carried his sword and returned to Hàn.
Abandoning folly and embracing righteousness,
their achievements and fame were equally illustrious.
Now Rúqīng stands at a juncture of success or failure,
facing the vanguard of a mighty army;
this is truly terrifying.
You should make up your mind decisively
and consult with those who understand."
Hán received the letter,
pondered for more than ten days,
then thanked his officers and men,
and submitted to Luòyáng.
He was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū.
Thereupon, thirteen of Xiāo's great generals,
sixteen dependent counties,
and a host of over one hundred thousand men
all surrendered.
Wáng Yuán entered Shǔ to seek aid.
Xiāo, with his wife and children, fled to Xīchéng,
following Yáng Guǎng.
Meanwhile, Tián Yǎn and Lǐ Yù held Shàngguī.
An imperial edict was sent to Xiāo, saying:
"If you bind your hands and come in person,
father and son will meet,
and I guarantee no harm will come to you.
Gāo Huángdì said: 'If they come voluntarily,
the great ones will be made kings,
the small ones marquises.'
If you insist on being like Qíng Bù,
that is your own choice."
Xiāo ultimately did not surrender.
Therefore, his son Xún was executed.
Wú Hàn and Zhēngnán Dàjiàngjūn Cén Péng were ordered to besiege Xīchéng,
and Gěng Yǎn and Hǔyá Dàjiàngjūn Gài Yán were ordered to besiege Shàngguī.
The imperial carriage returned east.
After more than a month,
Yáng Guǎng died,
and Xiāo was in dire straits.
His great general Wáng Jié, who was separately at Róngqiū,
climbed the city wall and shouted to the Hàn army:
"Those who defend the city for King Kuí
will all die without a second thought!
I wish for all your armies to quickly withdraw;
I request to commit suicide to demonstrate this."
He then slit his own throat and died.
Several months later,
Wáng Yuán, Xíng Xún, and Zhōu Zōng, leading five thousand or more reinforcement troops from Shǔ,
arrived abruptly from a height.
They beat drums and shouted loudly, saying:
"An army of a million is about to arrive!"
The Hàn army was greatly startled
and had not yet formed their lines.
Yuán and the others broke through the encirclement,
fighting to the death,
and thus managed to enter the city
and escort Xiāo back to Jì.
Coincidentally, Wú Hàn and the others, having run out of provisions, withdrew.
Thereupon, Āndìng, Běidì, Tiānshuǐ, and Lǒngxī again revolted and returned to Xiāo.
In the spring of the ninth year,
Xiāo, ill and starving,
came out of the city to eat dried provisions,
and died of vexation and indignation.
Wáng Yuán and Zhōu Zōng enthroned Xiāo's youngest son, Chún, as king.
The following year,
Lái Shè, Gěng Yǎn, Gài Yán, and others attacked and broke Luòmén.
Zhōu Zōng, Xíng Xún, Gǒu Yǔ, Zhào Huī, and others surrendered with Chún.
Zōng, Huī, and the various Kuí family members were resettled east of the capital.
Chún, along with Xún and Yǔ, were resettled in Hóngnóng.
Only Wáng Yuán remained to serve as a Shǔ general.
When Fǔwēi Jiāngjūn Zāng Gōng defeated Yán Cén,
Yuán led his troops to Gōng and surrendered.
Yuán's courtesy name was Huìmèng.
Initially appointed Shàngcài Lìng,
he was promoted to Dōngpíng Xiàng.
He was imprisoned and died for failing to meet the land reclamation quota.
Niú Hán's courtesy name was Rúqīng,
and he was a Dídào native.
He possessed courage, strength, and talent,
and was a dominant figure on the frontier.
Upon his surrender,
Dàsītú Sīzhí Dù Lín and Tàizhōng Dàfū Mǎ Yuán both recommended him,
and he was appointed Hùqiāng Xiàowèi
and, with Lái Shè, pacified Lǒngyòu.
In the eighteenth year,
Chún, with several dozen horsemen among his retainers, fled into the lands of the Hú.
Upon reaching Wǔwēi,
he was captured
and executed.
The commentary says: Kuí Xiāo raised his banner and gathered his clan,
falsely using the authority of the divine.
His initial plans and actions
were enough to understand his disposition.
Ultimately, he was isolated in a corner,
situated between great powers.
Although Lǒngdǐ was narrow,
it did not possess the strategic advantage of "one hundred men holding against two hundred thousand."
With merely two paltry commanderies,
he resisted the overwhelming might of the imperial army,
to the extent that it exhausted the court's strategies
and depleted its levies,
and only after his death and the dispersal of his forces
was the situation settled.
This indicates that his way had something admirable,
which is why he attracted heroes from all quarters,
and why his officers would fight to the death without regret.
Indeed, when achievements are complete, reputation is evident;
when enterprises fail, discord arises.
To twist success into failure and then comment on it
is perhaps not yet heard of.
If Xiāo's destiny had aligned with the times
and his enemy had not been Heaven's will,
even if he were to be compared to the Xībó,
would there be much ridicule?
Gōngsūn Shù, courtesy name Zǐyáng,
was a native of Màolíng, Fúfēng.
During the reign of Emperor Āi,
he became a Lang based on his father's appointment.
Later, his father Rén was appointed as Hénán Dūwèi,
and Shù was assigned as Magistrate of Qīngshuǐ.
Rén, considering Shù to be young,
dispatched a clerk from his retinue to accompany him to his post.
After more than a month,
the clerk took his leave to return,
and reported to Rén, saying:
"Shù is not one who needs guidance."
Later, the Grand Administrator, seeing his capability,
had him concurrently administer five counties.
His governance was well-ordered,
and crime and theft did not occur.
The people of the commandery said there were spirits.
During Wáng Mǎng's Tiānfèng era,
he became the Commander of Dǎojiāng.
Residing in Línqióng,
he again earned a reputation for capability.
When Gēngshǐ was established,
local heroes each rose in their counties to respond to the Hàn.
Zōng Chéng from Nányáng called himself
"Hǔyá Jiāngjūn"
and entered to plunder Hànzhōng.
Then, a merchant, Wáng Cén, also raised troops in Luòxiàn,
calling himself
"Dìnghàn Jiāngjūn,"
and killed Wáng Mǎng's Yōngbù Mù to support Chéng.
Their forces totaled tens of thousands of men.
Shù heard of this
and sent envoys to welcome Chéng and others.
When Chéng and others arrived in Chéngdū,
they plundered and committed atrocities.
Shù was disgusted by this.
He summoned the local heroes of the county and said:
"The whole world suffers under the Xīn dynasty,
and has longed for the Liú clan for a long time.
Therefore, upon hearing of the Hàn general's arrival,
people rushed to welcome him along the roads.
Now, innocent common people have their wives and children seized,
and their homes burned.
These are bandits,
not righteous soldiers.
I wish to secure my commandery and defend myself,
awaiting the true lord.
Those of you who wish to join forces, stay;
those who do not wish to, may leave."
All the heroes kowtowed and said:
"We are willing to die for you."
Shù then sent someone to falsely claim to be a Hàn envoy from the east,
who bestowed upon Shù the seals and ribbons of Fǔhàn Jiāngjūn, Shǔjùn Tàishǒu, and concurrent Yìzhōu Mù.
He then selected over a thousand elite soldiers
and attacked Chéng and others to the west.
By the time they reached Chéngdū,
their forces numbered several thousand.
They then attacked Chéng
and thoroughly defeated him.
Chéng's general Yuán Fù killed Chéng
and surrendered with his forces.
In the autumn of the second year,
Gēngshǐ dispatched Zhùgōng Hóu Lǐ Bǎo and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Zhōng,
leading over ten thousand troops to campaign in Shǔ and Hàn.
Shù, relying on his formidable terrain and the allegiance of his people,
had ambitions of self-establishment.
He then sent his younger brother Huī
to Miánzhú to attack Bǎo and Zhōng,
soundly defeating and routing them.
Because of this, his prestige shook Yìbù.
Gōngcáo Lǐ Xióng persuaded Shù, saying:
"Currently, the four seas are in turmoil,
and common men speak recklessly.
General, you occupy a thousand li,
your territory rivals that of Tāng and Wǔ.
If you exert your awe-inspiring virtue to seize this heavenly opportunity,
the enterprise of a hegemon-king will be achieved.
You should change your title
to stabilize the common people."
Shù said:
"I too have considered this;
your words align with my intentions."
Thereupon, he declared himself King of Shǔ
and established his capital in Chéngdū.
The land of Shǔ was fertile and rich,
its military strength elite and formidable.
Many scholars and commoners from distant lands came to join him.
The lords and chiefs of Qióng and Zuǒ
all came to offer tribute.
Lǐ Xióng again persuaded Shù, saying:
"Currently, east of the mountains there is famine,
and people devour each other;
cities and towns are ruins, slaughtered by war.
The land of Shǔ has a fertile plain stretching a thousand li,
its soil is rich and productive.
The fruits it bears
satisfy without grain.
The industry of women's crafts
clothes the entire realm.
Famous timber and bamboo,
and an abundance of tools and weapons
are inexhaustible.
Moreover, there are the benefits of fish, salt, copper, and silver,
and the convenience of water transport.
To the north, it holds Hànzhōng,
blocking the passes of Bāo and Xié;
to the east, it guards Bājùn,
resisting the mouth of Hànguān.
Its territory spans several thousand li,
and its warriors number no less than a million.
When there is an advantage, it dispatches troops to seize territory;
when there is no advantage, it firmly defends and vigorously farms.
Down the Hàn River to the east, it spies on Qín territory;
following the Jiāng River to the south, it shakes Jīng and Yáng.
This is what is called utilizing the heavens and relying on the earth,
the capital for success.
Now, your majesty's fame
is known throughout the world,
but your title is not yet settled,
and ambitious individuals are hesitant.
You should immediately ascend to the great position
so that people from afar have someone to rely on and return to."
Shù said:
"Emperors and kings have their destiny;
how am I sufficient to bear it?"
Xióng said:
"Heaven's mandate is not constant;
the common people align with the capable.
The capable deserve it,
why does your majesty hesitate!"
Shù dreamt that someone said to him:
"The character for 'eight' (八) is divided,
with 'child' (子) and 'thread' (系);
twelve years is the limit."
Upon waking,
he said to his wife:
"Though noble, my reign will be short,
what about it?"
His wife replied:
"To hear the Way in the morning,
and die in the evening, is still acceptable,
how much more so twelve years!"
Coincidentally, a dragon appeared in his palace hall.
At night, it glowed.
Shù considered it an auspicious omen,
and consequently carved into his palm
the characters
"Gōngsūn Dì."
In the fourth month of Jiànwǔ first year,
he then declared himself Son of Heaven,
naming his dynasty Chéngjiā.
Its auspicious color was white.
He named his era Lóngxīng first year.
He appointed Lǐ Xióng as Dà Sītú,
his younger brother Guāng as Dà Sīmǎ,
and Huī as Dà Sīkōng.
He changed Yìzhōu to Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and Shǔjùn to Chéngdū Yǐn.
Rèn Guì of Yuèsuí also killed Wáng Mǎng's Dà Yǐn and occupied the commandery, then surrendered.
Shù then sent General Hóu Dān to open Báishuǐguān,
to guard Nánzhèng to the north.
He sent General Rèn Mǎn from Lángzhōng down the Jiāng River
to occupy Hànguān to the east.
Thus, he completely held the land of Yìzhōu.
Since the defeat of Gēngshǐ,
Guāngwǔ was preoccupied with affairs east of the mountains,
and had no time to campaign to the west.
Among the heroes of Guānzhōng, Lǚ Wěi and others often gathered tens of thousands of troops,
without knowing to whom they belonged.
Many went to join Shù,
and were all appointed as generals.
He then extensively built camps and fortifications,
arrayed chariots and cavalry,
trained in warfare and archery,
and amassed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and armor.
He stored grain in Hànzhōng
and built palaces in Nánzhèng.
He also constructed ten-story red towers and silk-covered boats.
He carved numerous seals for governors and grand administrators of the realm,
and appointed dukes, ministers, and all officials.
He sent Generals Lǐ Yù and Chéng Wū with tens of thousands of troops to emerge from Chéncāng
and campaign with Lǚ Wěi in Sānfǔ.
In the third year,
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Féng Yì attacked Wěi and Yù at Chéncāng,
soundly defeating them.
Wěi and Yù fled to Hànzhōng.
In the fifth year,
Yán Cén and Tián Róng were defeated by Hàn forces,
and both fled into Shǔ.
Yán Cén 嚴岑, courtesy name Shūyá 叔牙,
was a Nányáng 南陽 man.
At first, he rose up and occupied Hànzhōng 漢中,
then also gathered troops in Guānxī 關西.
Wherever he went, he was defeated and scattered.
He fled to Nányáng 南陽,
and managed to seize a few counties.
Tián Róng 田戎
was a Rǔnán 汝南 man.
He first raised an army in Yílíng 夷陵,
then plundered various commanderies and counties,
with a multitude of tens of thousands.
Yán Cén 嚴岑 and Tián Róng 田戎 both allied with Qín Fēng 秦豐,
and Qín Fēng 秦豐 gave both his daughters in marriage to them.
When Qín Fēng 秦豐 was defeated,
the two men consequently surrendered to Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述.
Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 appointed Yán Cén 嚴岑 as Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ 大司馬),
and enfeoffed him as King of Rǔníng 汝寧.
Tián Róng 田戎 was enfeoffed as King Yìjiāng 翼江.
In the sixth year (of Gōngsūn Shù's 公孫述 reign),
Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 dispatched Tián Róng 田戎 and General Rèn Mǎn 任滿 to exit Jiāngguān 江關,
and descend into the area between Línjǔ 臨沮 and Yílíng 夷陵,
to recruit their former followers,
intending thereby to seize the various commanderies of Jīngzhōu 荊州.
Ultimately, they could not succeed.
At this time,
Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 abolished copper coins
and introduced iron currency (tiě guān qián 鐵官錢).
The people's currency did not circulate.
A children's rhyme in Shǔzhōng 蜀中 said:
"Yellow ox, white belly;
Wǔzhū 五銖 (coins) shall return."
Enthusiasts secretly said that Wáng Mǎng 王莽 claimed
"Yellow,"
while Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 styled himself
"White."
The Wǔzhū 五銖 coins
were Hàn 漢 currency,
meaning that the empire would eventually return to the Liú 劉 clan.
Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 was also fond of creating prophecies, omens, and auspicious portents,
and falsely cited prophetic texts (chènjì 讖記).
He believed that Confucius (Kǒngzǐ 孔子), in composing the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū 春秋),
created the "red system" (chì zhì 赤制) and concluded the twelve dukes,
clarifying that the Hàn 漢 dynasty, up to Emperor Píng (Píng Dì 平帝), had twelve generations,
and its allotted reign was exhausted.
One clan could not receive the mandate twice.
He also cited the Lùyùnfǎ 錄運法, saying:
"Abolish the prosperous emperor,
establish Gōngsūn 公孫."
The Kuòdìxiàng 括地象 said:
"Emperor Xuānyuán 軒轅 received the mandate,
the Gōngsūn 公孫 clan shall grasp it."
The Yuánshénqì 援神契 said:
"Western Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守),
Yǐmǎo Jīn 乙卯金."
This meant that the Grand Administrator of the West, Yǐmǎo Jīn 乙卯金, would sever (the connection with) Mǎo Jīn 卯金.
According to the cycle of the Five Virtues (Wǔdé 五德),
Yellow succeeded Red, and White followed Yellow.
Metal occupies the West as the White Virtue (Báidé 白德),
and would replace the Wáng 王 clan,
thus obtaining its proper sequence.
He also claimed that the lines on his hand were unusual,
and that he had received an omen of a rising dragon (lóngxīng zhī ruì 龍興之瑞).
He frequently sent letters to the Central Plains (Zhōngguó 中國),
hoping to move the hearts of the multitude.
The Emperor (Liú Xuán 劉玄, i.e., Emperor Gèngshǐ 更始帝) was troubled by this,
and so wrote to Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述, saying:
"The prophecies say 'Gōngsūn 公孫,'
referring to Emperor Xuān (Xuān Dì 宣帝).
He who replaces the Hàn 漢 is 'dāng tú gāo 當塗高.'
Are you perhaps the person of 'gāo 高'?
And you again use palm lines as auspicious omens?
Why should Wáng Mǎng 王莽 be emulated?
You are not a treacherous minister or a rebellious son to me.
In times of crisis, everyone wants to do things for themselves,
how can it be counted?
Your days are already passing,
your wife and children are young.
You should make plans early
so that you can be free from worry.
The divine instrument (shénqì 神器) of the empire
cannot be contended for by force.
You should think three times."
He signed it
"Emperor Gōngsūn 公孫."
Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 did not reply.
The next year,
Kuí Xiāo 隗囂 declared himself a vassal to Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述.
Gōngsūn Shù's 公孫述 Cavalry Commandant (Qí Dūwèi 騎都尉) Jīng Hán 荊邯, a Pínglíng 平陵 man, seeing that the East was about to be pacified,
and that the army would soon turn westward,
advised Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述, saying:
"Military force is
the great instrument of emperors and kings,
which has never been abandoned throughout history.
In the past, when Qín 秦 lost its hold,
heroes and magnates rose simultaneously.
The Hàn Ancestor (Hànzǔ 漢祖, i.e., Liú Bāng 劉邦), having no precedent,
and no place to even stick an awl,
rose from the ranks of soldiers,
personally fighting with great effort,
and was defeated and exhausted multiple times.
Yet, the army would reassemble after defeat,
and fight again after healing.
Why?
Because to die advancing and achieve success
is better than to retreat and perish.
Kuí Xiāo 隗囂 encountered a opportune moment,
occupied Yōngzhōu 雍州,
with strong troops and attached loyalists,
his might extending east of the mountains (Shāndōng 山東).
When Emperor Gèngshǐ's 更始帝 government fell into chaos,
and he again lost the empire,
the multitudes craned their necks (in anticipation),
and the four directions disintegrated.
Kuí Xiāo 隗囂 failed to seize this opportune moment, push through the danger, and capitalize on his victory
to contend for the Mandate of Heaven.
Instead, he retreated, desiring to emulate the deeds of the Western Earl (Xībó 西伯, i.e., King Wén 文王 of Zhōu 周),
revering teachers of sentences and phrases,
befriending reclusive scholars,
sheathing weapons and resting spears,
and humbly serving the Hàn 漢,
sighing to himself that King Wén 文王 had returned.
This allowed the Hàn 漢 Emperor to relieve his worries about Guānlǒng 關隴,
and concentrate his efforts on campaigning in the East,
thus possessing three-quarters of the empire;
it made the heroes of the Western provinces (Xīzhōu 西州) all turn their hearts towards Shāndōng 山東.
If we send agents
to recruit those who are wavering,
then we will possess four-fifths;
if we raise an army in Tiānshuǐ 天水,
it will certainly lead to collapse.
Once Tiānshuǐ 天水 is settled,
we will possess eight-ninths.
Your Majesty, with the lands of Liángzhōu 梁州,
internally supporting the Son of Heaven (wàn shèng 萬乘),
and externally supplying the three armies,
the common people are distressed and weary,
unable to endure the imperial demands.
There will be a disaster of the Wáng 王 clan collapsing from within.
My foolish plan
is that we should act while the hopes of the empire are not yet extinguished,
and heroes can still be recruited.
Urgently, at this time, dispatch elite troops from within the country.
Order Tián Róng 田戎 to occupy Jiānglíng 江陵,
overlook the Chǔ 楚 region south of the Yangtze (Jiāngnán 江南),
build forts and hold them firmly.
Send manifestoes to Wú 吳 and Chǔ 楚,
and regions south of Chángshā 長沙 will certainly yield like grass in the wind.
Order Yán Cén 嚴岑 to advance from Hànzhōng 漢中,
pacify the Three Commanderies (Sānfǔ 三輔).
Tiānshuǐ 天水 and Lǒngxī 隴西 will submit willingly.
If this is done,
the whole world will be shaken,
and great benefits are hoped for."
Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 consulted his ministers.
Dr. Wú Zhù 吳柱 said:
"In ancient times, King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng 武王) attacked Yīn 殷.
He first paraded his troops at Mèngjīn 孟津.
Eight hundred feudal lords, without prior arrangement, spoke with one voice.
Yet, he still withdrew his army to await the Mandate of Heaven.
I have never heard of anyone, without assistance on his flanks,
wanting to dispatch an army a thousand *lǐ* (li 裡) away
to expand his territory."
Jīng Hán 荊邯 said:
"Today, the Eastern Emperor (Dōng Dì 東帝, referring to Liú Xuán 劉玄 or Liú Xiù 劉秀) has not an inch of land to his name,
yet he drives a mob (wūhé zhī zhòng 烏合之眾),
charges on horseback into the enemy,
and pacifies everywhere he goes.
If we do not quickly seize the moment and share in the achievement with him,
but instead sit and discuss the words of King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng 武王),
this is to imitate Kuí Xiāo 隗囂 in wishing to be the Western Earl (Xībó 西伯)."
Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 agreed with Jīng Hán's 荊邯 words
and wanted to mobilize all the northern garrison troops and eastern guest soldiers,
sending Yán Cén 嚴岑 and Tián Róng 田戎 out on two separate routes,
to join forces with the generals in Hànzhōng 漢中.
The people of Shǔ 蜀 and his younger brother Gōngsūn Guāng 公孫光 thought it inappropriate to empty the country to fight a thousand *lǐ* (li 裡) away,
deciding success or failure in a single move.
They strongly opposed it,
so Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 stopped.
Yán Cén 嚴岑 and Tián Róng 田戎 also repeatedly requested troops to achieve merits, but Gōngsūn Shù 公孫述 ultimately hesitated and did not listen.
His nature was harsh and meticulous,
observing small matters.
He dared to execute and kill without seeing the larger picture,
and liked to change the names of commanderies, counties, and official titles.
However, when he was young, he served as a郎 (láng),
and was familiar with the institutions of the Hàn house.
He would enter and exit with the emperor's ceremonial carriage (fǎjià),
with flags adorned with bells (luánqí) and cavalry bearing yak-tail banners (máoqí),
and a display of halberds on the imperial steps (bìjí),
before he was carried out of his private chambers (fángtà).
He also established his two sons as kings,
granting them several counties each in Jiānwéi and Guǎnghàn.
Many officials advised against this,
believing that success or failure was still uncertain,
and while the soldiers were exposed to hardship,
to immediately make the imperial princes kings
showed a lack of great ambition,
and wounded the hearts of the warriors.
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) did not listen.
Only those of the Gōngsūn (Gōngsūn) clan were allowed to hold office,
and because of this, all the high officials resented him.
In the eighth year [of Jiànwǔ],
the Emperor (Dì) sent his generals to attack Kuí Xiāo (Kuí Xiāo).
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) dispatched Lǐ Yù (Lǐ Yù) with over ten thousand men to rescue Kuí Xiāo (Kuí Xiāo).
Kuí Xiāo (Kuí Xiāo) was defeated,
and his army was also lost.
The people of Shǔ (Shǔ) were alarmed and disturbed upon hearing this.
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) was afraid,
and wished to calm the people.
Outside the city of Chéngdū (Chéngdū) was an old granary from the Qín (Qín) era.
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) renamed it Bái Dì Cāng (Bái Dì Cāng),
which had been empty since Wáng Mǎng (Wáng Mǎng).
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) then falsely sent people to spread rumors that Bái Dì Cāng (Bái Dì Cāng) was yielding grain like mountains.
The common people emptied the markets to go and observe it.
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) then convened a great assembly of his officials,
and asked:
"Did Bái Dì Cāng (Bái Dì Cāng) really yield grain?"
They all replied,
"No."
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) said:
"False rumors cannot be believed,
the report of Kuí (Kuí) King's defeat is like this."
Soon after, Kuí Xiāo's (Kuí Xiāo) general Wáng Yuán (Wáng Yuán) surrendered,
and Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) appointed him as a general.
The next year,
he sent Wáng Yuán (Wáng Yuán) and the Commander of the Army (lǐngjūn) Huán Ān (Huán Ān) to resist at Héchí,

and also dispatched Tián Róng (Tián Róng) and the Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sītú) Rèn Mǎn (Rèn Mǎn), and the Administrator of Nánjùn (Nánjùn) Chéng Fàn (Chéng Fàn) with troops to descend the Jiāngguān (Jiāngguān),
where they defeated the General who Awed the Barbarians (Wēilǔ Jiāngjūn) Féng Jùn (Féng Jùn) and others,
and captured Wū (Wū), Yílíng (Yílíng), and Yídào (Yídào),
then occupied Jīngmén (Jīngmén).
In the eleventh year,
the General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Dà Jiāngjūn) Cén Péng (Cén Péng) attacked them.
Rèn Mǎn (Rèn Mǎn) and the others were utterly defeated,
and Gōngsūn Shù's (Gōngsūn Shù) general Wáng Zhèng (Wáng Zhèng) beheaded Rèn Mǎn (Rèn Mǎn) and surrendered to Cén Péng (Cén Péng).
Tián Róng (Tián Róng) fled to hold Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu).
All the cities opened their gates and surrendered,
and Cén Péng (Cén Péng) then drove straight to Wǔyáng (Wǔyáng).
The Emperor (Dì) then wrote a letter to Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù),
explaining the consequences of misfortune and fortune,
to clarify the trustworthiness of his imperial word (dānqīng zhī xìn).
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) read the letter and sighed,
showing it to his trusted Grand Mentor (Tàicháng) Cháng Shǎo (Cháng Shǎo) and Grand Master of Ceremonies (Guānglùxūn) Zhāng Lóng (Zhāng Lóng).
Zhāng Lóng (Zhāng Lóng) and Cháng Shǎo (Cháng Shǎo) both urged him to surrender.
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) said:
"Rise and fall are matters of destiny.
How can there be an emperor who surrenders!"
His attendants dared not speak again.
The Colonel (Zhōnglángjiàng) Lái Xī (Lái Xī) urgently attacked Wáng Yuán (Wáng Yuán) and Huán Ān (Huán Ān),
and Huán Ān (Huán Ān) sent assassins to kill Lái Xī (Lái Xī);
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) later ordered Cén Péng (Cén Péng) to be assassinated.
In the twelfth year,

Gōngsūn Shù's (Gōngsūn Shù) brother Gōngsūn Huī (Gōngsūn Huī) and son-in-law Shǐ Xīng (Shǐ Xīng) were both defeated by the Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) Wú Hàn (Wú Hàn) and the General Who Assists with Awe (Fǔwēi Jiāngjūn) Zāng Gōng (Zāng Gōng),
and died in battle.
From then on, the generals and commanders were terrified,
and deserted day and night.
Although Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) executed their families,
he still could not stop it.
The Emperor (Dì) was determined to make him surrender,
so he issued an edict to Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù), saying:
"In recent years, imperial edicts have been repeatedly issued,
showing grace and trustworthiness,
so do not be suspicious because Lái Xī (Lái Xī) and Cén Péng (Cén Péng) suffered harm.
If you come now in due time,
your family will be safe;
if you remain deluded and do not understand,
throwing your flesh into the tiger's mouth,
how regrettable and lamentable!
The generals and commanders are weary,
the officers and soldiers long to return home,
and are not happy to be stationed for a long time.
Imperial edicts written by my own hand
are not to be had often;
I will not break my word."
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) ultimately had no intention of surrendering.
In the ninth month,
Wú Hàn (Wú Hàn) again defeated and beheaded his Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sītú) Xiè Fēng (Xiè Fēng) and the Commandant of the Guards (Zhí Jīnwú) Yuán Jí (Yuán Jí).
The Hàn (Hàn) army then advanced to Chéngdū (Chéngdū).
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) said to Yán Cén (Yán Cén):
"What should we do?"
Yán Cén (Yán Cén) replied:
"A man should seek life in the midst of death;
how can we just sit and be at our wits' end!
Wealth is easily gathered,
there is no need to be stingy."
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) then scattered all his gold and silk,
recruiting over five thousand dare-to-die soldiers,
assigning them to Yán Cén (Yán Cén) at Shìqiáo (Shìqiáo).
He falsely set up banners,
and beat drums to challenge them,
while secretly sending elite troops to the rear of Wú Hàn's (Wú Hàn) army,
attacking and defeating Wú Hàn (Wú Hàn).
Wú Hàn (Wú Hàn) fell into the water,
but managed to get out by clinging to a horse's tail.
In the eleventh month,
Zāng Gōng's (Zāng Gōng) army arrived at Xiánmén (Xiánmén).
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) looked at a divination book,
which said,
"The enemy will die beneath the city walls."
He was greatly pleased,
thinking that Wú Hàn (Wú Hàn) and the others would be the ones.
He then personally led tens of thousands of men to attack Wú Hàn (Wú Hàn),
and sent Yán Cén (Yán Cén) to resist Zāng Gōng (Zāng Gōng).
In the great battle,
Yán Cén (Yán Cén) was victorious three times in three engagements.
From dawn until noon,
the soldiers could not eat,
and were all exhausted.
Wú Hàn (Wú Hàn) then ordered brave men to charge them.
Gōngsūn Shù's (Gōngsūn Shù) troops fell into great disarray,
and he was stabbed through,
falling from his horse.
His attendants carried him into the city.
Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) entrusted his troops to Yán Cén (Yán Cén),
and died that night.
The next morning,
Yán Cén (Yán Cén) surrendered to Wú Hàn (Wú Hàn).
Wú Hàn (Wú Hàn) then exterminated Gōngsūn Shù's (Gōngsūn Shù) wife and children,
and utterly annihilated the Gōngsūn (Gōngsūn) clan,
and also executed Yán Cén's (Yán Cén) family.
He then let his soldiers plunder extensively,
and burned Gōngsūn Shù's (Gōngsūn Shù) palaces.
The Emperor (Dì) heard of this and was enraged,
condemning Wú Hàn (Wú Hàn).
He also rebuked Wú Hàn's (Wú Hàn)副將 (fùjiàng) Liú Shàng (Liú Shàng), saying:
"The city surrendered three days ago,
officials and people had submitted,
children and elderly mothers,
numbering in the tens of thousands,
and then suddenly the soldiers were allowed to burn and loot.
Hearing this makes one's nose run with sorrow!
Liú Shàng (Liú Shàng) is a descendant of the imperial clan,
and has served in official positions;
how could he bear to do this?
Looking up at heaven,
looking down at earth,
consider releasing a fawn or sipping its broth,
which of these two is benevolent?
This truly failed the righteousness of beheading a general and consoling the people!"
Originally,
Cháng Shǎo (Cháng Shǎo) and Zhāng Lóng (Zhāng Lóng) had urged Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) to surrender,
but he did not follow,
and both died of sorrow.
The Emperor (Dì) issued an edict posthumously granting Cháng Shǎo (Cháng Shǎo) the title of Grand Mentor (Tàicháng),
and Zhāng Lóng (Zhāng Lóng) the title of Grand Master of Ceremonies (Guānglùxūn),
and they were reburied with proper rites.
Those loyal and righteous gentlemen
were all commended and honored.
Chéng Wū (Chéng Wū) and Lǐ Yù (Lǐ Yù), for their talent and ability,
were both promoted and employed.
Thereupon, the people of the Western lands were all pleased,
and everyone pledged their loyalty.
Commentary states: In ancient times, Zhào Tuó (Zhào Tuó) enthroned himself in Pānyú (Pānyú),
and Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) also secretly claimed emperorship in Shǔ Hàn (Shǔ Hàn).
If we consider that they had no other special abilities,
and yet ended up failing,
was it because their territories were remote,
not yet reached by the transforming influence of the king?
Although Gōngsūn Shù (Gōngsūn Shù) was a Hàn (Hàn) official,
he had no support or resources,
but merely delighted in scholarly customs,
and thus was able to achieve his ambitions and plans.
His way was insufficient, but his ambition was excessive;
he could not seize opportunities to achieve merit,
but rather sat and adorned his outward appearance,
taking comfort in his own profundity and loftiness,
which is why Wú Qǐ (Wú Qǐ) was ashamed before Marquis Wèi (Wèi Hóu).
When he bade farewell to his subordinates,
and correctly judged the fate of rise and fall,
he was speaking of a different time than those who would bow their heads in surrender and offer jade.
Praise says: Gōngsūn (Gōngsūn) practiced officialdom,
Kuí Xiāo (Kuí Xiāo) gained scholars.
The mandate of Hàn (Hàn) had returned,
and the two corners were merely standing.
Heaven's will was against them,
and the rivers and mountains were unreliable.
Biographies of the Four Princes and Three Marquises of the Imperial Clan, Chapter Four
Qí Wǔwáng Yǎn, courtesy name Bóshēng,
was Gūangwǔ's eldest brother.
His nature was firm and resolute,
magnanimous and of great principle.
Ever since Wáng Mǎng usurped the Hàn dynasty,
he was often indignant,
harboring thoughts of restoring the imperial ancestral altars.
He did not concern himself with family business or property,
but rather devoted himself and spent his wealth
to associate with the eminent heroes of the realm.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
bandits rose in groups,
especially rampant in the south.
Bóshēng summoned the various heroes and discussed, saying:
"Wáng Mǎng is tyrannical and cruel,
the common people are scattered and broken.
Now, drought has persisted for years,
and military conflicts have risen everywhere.
This is also a time when Heaven intends his demise,
to restore the enterprise of Gāozǔ,
and establish a foundation for ten thousand generations."
All the assembled agreed with him.
Thereupon, he dispatched trusted retainers,
sending Dèng Chén to rise in Xīnyě,
while Gūangwǔ, Lǐ Tōng, and Lǐ Yì rose in Wǎn.
Bóshēng himself rallied the young men from Chūnlíng,
gathering seven or eight thousand people,
deployed his guests,
and styled himself Zhùtiān Dūbù.
He sent the imperial clansman Líu Jiā to entice the forces of Xīnshì and Pínglín, Wáng Kuāng and Chén Mù, etc.,
merged their armies and advanced,
massacring Chángjù and Tángzǐxiāng,
killing the Húyáng magistrate,
then captured Jíyáng,
and intended to attack Wǎn.
Upon reaching Xiǎocháng'ān,
they fought Wáng Mǎng's vanguard Grandee Zhēn Fù and Commander Liángqīu Cì.
At that time, there was a dense fog,
and the Hàn army suffered a great defeat;
his elder sister Yuán and younger brother Zhòng were both killed,
and dozens of his followers died.
Bóshēng again gathered his troops,
and returned to secure Jíyáng.
Fù and Cì, emboldened by their victory,
left their baggage train in Lánxiāng,
and led ten thousand elite troops south across the Huángchún River,
reaching the Pí River,
setting up camp between the two streams,
cutting off the rear bridge,
signaling that they had no intention of retreating.
Xīnshì and Pínglín, seeing the Hàn army repeatedly defeated,
and Fù and Cì's large army arriving,
each wished to withdraw.
Bóshēng was greatly troubled by this.
Coincidentally, five thousand men from the Xiàjiāng army arrived at Yíqīu.
He then went and persuaded them of the advantage of a united front,
and Xiàjiāng agreed.
The account is in the biography of Wáng Cháng.
Bóshēng then held a great feast for his soldiers,
and established an oath.
After three days of rest,
he divided his forces into six divisions,
secretly moved his troops during the night,
and launched a surprise attack to seize Lánxiāng.
They captured all their baggage train.
The next morning,
the Hàn army attacked Zhēn Fù from the southwest,
and the Xiàjiāng army attacked Liángqīu Cì from the southeast.
By mealtime,
Cì's formation collapsed,
Fù's army saw this and scattered and fled.
The Hàn army pursued them fiercely,
driving them back to the Huángchún River,
where over twenty thousand were beheaded or drowned.
Fù and Cì were then executed.
Wáng Mǎng's Nàyán General Yán Yóu and Zhìzōng General Chén Mào, hearing of Fù and Cì's defeat,
led their forces intending to occupy Wǎn.
Bóshēng then arrayed his troops and swore an oath to the masses,
burned their provisions,
smashed their cooking pots,
advanced with drums beating,
and encountered Yóu and Mào below Yùyáng,
fought,
and utterly defeated them,
beheading over three thousand.
Yóu and Mào abandoned their army and fled.
Bóshēng then advanced to besiege Wǎn,
styling himself Zhùtiān Dàjiāngjūn.
Wáng Mǎng had long heard of his reputation,
and was greatly terrified.
He offered a reward for Bóshēng: fifty thousand households as an estate,
one hundred thousand catties of gold,
and the rank of superior duke.
He ordered the official agencies in Cháng'ān and the rural townships throughout the realm to paint Bóshēng's image on their walls,
and shoot at it every morning.
After Fù and Cì died,
common people surrendered daily,
and the numbers reached over a hundred thousand.
The generals convened to discuss establishing a member of the Líu clan to satisfy the people's hopes,
and the heroes all inclined towards Bóshēng.
However, the generals of Xīnshì and Pínglín enjoyed unrestrained freedom,
feared Bóshēng's prestige and brilliance, but coveted the weakness of Shènggōng.
They first secretly decided to enthrone him,
then sent a rider to summon Bóshēng,
and presented their decision to him.
Bóshēng said:
"It is indeed a great virtue that all you generals wish to enthrone a member of the imperial clan.
However, in my humble and rustic opinion,
there are some points I do not agree with.
Now, the Chìméi have risen in Qīng and Xú,
numbering several hundred thousand.
If they hear that a member of the imperial clan has been enthroned in Nányáng,
I fear the Chìméi will also enthrone someone.
If this happens,
there will certainly be internal strife.
Wáng Mǎng is not yet destroyed,
but the imperial clansmen are already fighting each other;
this will create doubt throughout the realm and weaken our own power,
which is not the way to defeat Wáng Mǎng.
Moreover, those who first raise troops and proclaim themselves
rarely succeed in the end;
Chén Shèng and Xiàng Jí
are examples of this.
Chūnlíng is only three hundred *lǐ* from Wǎn,
and this is not enough to constitute a great achievement.
To hastily enthrone ourselves
and become a target for the realm,
allowing later generations to exploit our weaknesses,
is not a good strategy.
For now, let us simply declare ourselves kings to issue commands.
If the one the Chìméi enthrone is worthy,
we can lead our forces to follow him;
if they enthrone no one,
then after defeating Wáng Mǎng and subduing the Chìméi,
it will not be too late
to assume the honored title.
I urge you all to consider this carefully."
Many generals said,
"Excellent."
General Zhāng Áng drew his sword and struck the ground, saying:
"Doubt leads to no success.
Today's discussion
brooks no second opinions."
The masses all followed him.
After Shènggōng was enthroned,
Bóshēng was appointed Dàsītú,
and enfeoffed as Hànxìn Hóu.
Because of this, the heroes were disappointed,
and many were not convinced.
The rear division of Pínglín attacked Xīnyě,
but could not take it.
The magistrate of Xīnyě stood on the city wall and said:
"If we receive a single letter from Dàsītú Líu Gōng,
we are willing to surrender first."
When Bóshēng's army arrived,
they immediately opened the city gates and surrendered.
In the fifth month,
Bóshēng captured Wǎn.
In the sixth month,
Gūangwǔ defeated Wáng Xún and Wáng Yì.
From then on, the prestige of the brothers grew even greater.
The Gēngshǐ ruler and his ministers felt insecure,
and thus conspired to execute Bóshēng.
They then convened a grand assembly of all generals
to carry out their plan.
Gēngshǐ took Bóshēng's precious sword to examine it.
The Embroidered-Clad Imperial Censor Shēntú Jiàn then presented a jade *jué* (half-ring).
Gēngshǐ ultimately could not bring himself to act.
After the assembly was dismissed,
Bóshēng's maternal uncle Fán Hóng said to Bóshēng:
"During the Hongmen Banquet,
Fàn Zēng raised a *jué* to signal Xiàng Yǔ.
Given Jiàn's intention here,
could it be ill-omened?"
Bóshēng smiled and did not respond.
Earlier,
Lǐ Yì had flattered the esteemed generals of Gēngshǐ.
Gūangwǔ deeply suspected him,
and often warned Bóshēng, saying:
"This person cannot be trusted again."
But he did not accept it.
Bóshēng’s subordinate and kinsman, Liú Jì
frequently charged into battle, breaking through sieges
with courage unmatched in the three armies.
At that time, he was leading troops to attack Lǔyáng.
Hearing that Gēngshǐ had been established [as emperor],
he angrily said,
"The ones who originally raised an army for a great cause
were Bóshēng and his brothers.
What is Gēngshǐ doing now?"
Gēngshǐ and his ministers, hearing this, became wary of him.
Jì was appointed as Kàngwēi Jiàngjūn (General Who Resists Might),
but Jì refused to accept the appointment.
Gēngshǐ then, with several thousand soldiers and various generals,
first apprehended Jì,
intending to execute him.
Bóshēng strongly argued against it.
Lǐ Yì and Zhū Wěi then persuaded Gēngshǐ to arrest Bóshēng as well,
and on that very day, they killed him.
He had two sons.
In Jiànwǔ second year (26 CE),
his eldest son, Zhāng, was made King of Tàiyuán,
and Xīng was made King of Lǔ.
In the eleventh year (35 CE),
Zhāng was moved to become King of Qí.
In the fifteenth year (39 CE),
Bóshēng was posthumously honored with the title Qíwǔ Wáng (Martial King of Qí).
Zhāng was orphaned young.
Guāngwǔ, feeling pity for Bóshēng's unfinished achievements,
nurtured him with great affection and care.
Because Zhāng had become noble at a young age,
Guāngwǔ wished for him to become familiar with official duties.
Therefore, he was made acting magistrate of Píngyīn,
and later promoted to Administrator of Liáng Jùn.
He reigned for twenty-one years and then passed away,
posthumously named Āi Wáng (Sorrowful King).
His son, Yáng Wáng (Resplendent King) Shí, succeeded him.
In Jiànwǔ twenty-seventh year (51 CE),
Shí first went to his fief.
In the thirtieth year (54 CE),
Shí's younger brother, Zhāng, was enfeoffed as Hùxiá Bó Hóu.
In Yǒngpíng fourteenth year (71 CE),
Shí's two sons were enfeoffed as Xiāng Hóu (Marquis of a Township).
Shí reigned for twenty-four years and then passed away,
and his son, Huàng, succeeded him.
Hùxiá Bó Hóu Zhāng was good at discussing matters.
In the sixteenth year (73 CE),
along with the Fèngchē Dūwèi (Colonel of the Chariot Guards) Dòu Gù and others,
he went out to attack the Xiongnú.
Those who were promoted later often found fault with his abilities,
and he was frequently slandered.
He died during the Jiànchū period.
Sùzōng issued an edict praising him,
and his son, Tārén, was re-enfeoffed to continue his sacrifices.
Huàng and his younger brother, Lìhóu Gāng, and their mother, Tàijī Zōng, mutually slandered and accused each other.
In Zhānghé first year (87 CE),
the officials memorialized to strip Huàng and Gāng of their titles and reduce them to commoners,
and to exile them to Dānyáng.
The Emperor could not bear to do so
and issued an edict stating:
"I have heard that a ruler of men, when purifying his inner quarters,
has things he does not listen to.
The matriarch is honored as the little lady;
the palace guards are fully prepared;
when she goes out, there are adornments of carriages;
when she enters, there are secure windows and doors.
It is unlikely to be as the slanderers claim.
Huàng and Gāng have erred in their conduct
and have tainted the great human relationships.
Of the three thousand punishments of Fǔ Xíng,
none is greater than unfilial conduct.
I cannot bear to subject them to the full legal process.
Therefore, Huàng's title shall be demoted to Marquis of Wúhú,
and Gāng's households shall be reduced by three thousand.
Alas!
The youngsters do not exert themselves in the great Way,
but turn to legal disputes,
thereby causing their ancestral line to decline.
Let an usher be sent to collect Huàng and Tàijī's seals and ribbons."
Huàng reigned for seventeen years before his title was demoted.
After Huàng died,
his son, Wújí, succeeded him.
The Emperor, because Bóshēng had first initiated the great enterprise,
but his successors had been punished and deposed,
often felt sympathy for this.
At that time, Běihǎi also had no successor.
When he passed away,
he left an imperial edict to restore the two states.
In Yǒngyuán second year (90 CE),
Wújí was re-enfeoffed as King of Qí,
who was Hùiwáng (Benevolent King).
He reigned for fifty-two years and then passed away,
and his son, Qǐng Wáng (Tranquil King) Xǐ, succeeded him.
He reigned for five years and then passed away,
and his son, Chéng, succeeded him.
In Jiàn'ān eleventh year (206 CE),
the state was abolished.
The commentary states: The motivation and aspirations of a great man who rises up
are indeed far-reaching.
For Qíwǔ Wáng to greatly favor scholars,
how could it have been for the sake of mere chivalrous ruffians or low-ranking guests!
His consideration surely lay in establishing an ultimate legacy that matched heaven,
and he grieved that the Míngtáng (Hall of Light) was not worshipped.
As for his initiating the great plan,
amidst the sudden turmoil,
he first established trust with the enemy,
pardoning Cén Péng to demonstrate righteousness.
Such actions are enough to reveal his magnanimity.
High aspirations and far-reaching thoughts,
yet disaster struck from an unexpected quarter.
Alas!
The ancients took the bee and scorpion as a warning,
indeed fearing this.
The Shī (Odes) says:
"Be reverent, be reverent!
Destiny is not easily maintained!"
Běihǎi Jìng Wáng (Tranquil King) Xīng
was enfeoffed as King of Lǔ in Jiànwǔ second year (26 CE),
succeeding Guāngwǔ's elder brother, Zhòng.
Originally,
the Lord of Nándùn married a daughter of Fán Zhòng from the same commandery,
whose courtesy name was Tiándū.
Tiándū was gentle and compliant by nature.
From childhood,
she did not display her face or dress improperly outside her room,
and her clan respected her.
She gave birth to three sons and three daughters: the eldest son was Bóshēng,
the second was Zhòng,
the third was Guāngwǔ;
the eldest daughter was Huáng,
the second was Yuán,
the third was Bó Jī.
The Empress Mother died of illness during the initial uprising,
and her kinsman, Fán Jùgōng, collected her remains.
In Jiànwǔ second year (26 CE),
Huáng was enfeoffed as Húyáng Cháng Gōngzhǔ (Eldest Princess of Húyáng),
and Bó Jī as Níngpíng Cháng Gōngzhǔ (Eldest Princess of Níngpíng).
Yuán and Zhòng both died in Xiǎocháng'ān.
Yuán was posthumously titled Xīnyě Cháng Gōngzhǔ (Eldest Princess of Xīnyě).
In the fifteenth year (39 CE),
Zhòng was posthumously titled Qī Wáng (Equal King).
In that same year, Xīng was made acting magistrate of Gōushì.
He was a man of clear strategies,
good at listening to legal cases,
and greatly earned a good reputation.
He was promoted to Administrator of Hóngnóng,
where he also had good governance.
After serving for four years,
he submitted a memorial requesting to retire,
and was recalled to the capital
to attend court.
In the twenty-seventh year (51 CE),
he first went to his fief.
The following year,
because the state of Lǔ was added to Dōnghǎi,
Xīng was moved to become King of Běihǎi.
In the thirtieth year (54 CE), Xīng's son, Fù, was enfeoffed as Línyì Hóu.
In Zhōngyuán second year (57 CE),
Xīng's two other sons were enfeoffed as Xiàn Hóu (Marquis of a County).
Xiǎnzōng greatly valued Xīng.
Whenever there was an unusual political matter,
he would immediately send an express messenger to ask him.
He reigned for thirty-nine years and then passed away,
and his son, Jìng Wáng (Reverent King) Mù, succeeded him.
Mù was fond of learning in his youth,
thoroughly conversant with books and commentaries.
Guāngwǔ loved him,
and he was frequently invited and welcomed.
When Xiǎnzōng was in the Eastern Palace (i.e., Crown Prince),
he was especially favored and treated well,
attending to him inside to recite and chant,
and holding the reins for him outside.
In the early period of Zhōngxīng,
the prohibitions were still lax,
and Mù, by nature humble, respectful, and fond of scholars,
formed connections across a thousand *lǐ*.
From renowned scholars to venerable elders,
none failed to visit his gate,
and his reputation and standing consequently grew.
During the Yǒngpíng era,
the legal system became quite strict,
so Mù dismissed all guests
and indulged in music.
However, he was fond of reading by nature,
and constantly enjoyed it.
At the end of the year,
he sent a Zhōngdàfū to offer a jade *bì* and pay respects at court.
He summoned the officer and said to him:
"If the imperial court questions me,
what will the *dàfū* say in response?"
The envoy replied:
"Your Royal Highness is loyal, filial, benevolent, and kind,
respects the wise, and delights in scholars.
Though your servant is but an ant,
how dare I not speak the truth?"
Mù said:
"Alas,
you would endanger me!
These are the actions of my childhood, when I strove for advancement.
The *dàfū* should respond by saying that since I inherited my title,
my ambition has waned and I have become indolent,
taking pleasure in sights and sounds,
and being fond of dogs and horses."
The envoy received his orders and departed.
His ability to adapt like this was remarkable.
Initially,
when Jìngwáng passed away,
he gave all his wealth and property to his younger brothers.
Even the royal carriages, attire, and precious treasures, which were not permitted for Marquises of the Imperial Domain,
he considered them as their shares,
and then redeemed them with gold and silk.
Mù was skilled in writing,
composing dozens of essays, rhapsodies, and eulogies, including the *Chūnqiū Zhǐyì Zhōngshǐ Lùn*.
He was also good at historical writing,
and was regarded as a model by his contemporaries.
When he fell ill,
the Emperor dispatched horses, ordering him to compose ten letters in cursive script.
He passed away after holding his position for ten years.
His son, Āiwáng Jī, succeeded him.
In the eighteenth year of Yǒngpíng,
Jī's two younger brothers were enfeoffed as Xiànhóu,
and two other younger brothers as Xiānghóu.
In the second year of Jiànchū,
Jī's brother Yì was again enfeoffed as Píngwànghóu.
Jī passed away after holding his position for fourteen years,
without a son.
Sùzōng pitied him
and did not abolish his state.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán,
Hédì enfeoffed Mù's illegitimate son, Zhēnxiānghóu Wēi, as Běihǎiwáng,
to continue Mù's lineage.
After holding his position for seven years,
Wēi, not being Mù's son
and also being accused of slander,
was summoned in a caged cart to the Imperial Censorate,
and committed suicide on the way.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng again enfeoffed Mù's grandson, Shòuguānghóu Pǔ, as Běihǎiwáng,
who was Kǐngwáng.
In the second year of Yán'guāng,
Mù's youngest son was again enfeoffed as Tínghóu.
Pǔ passed away after holding his position for [seven] years.
His son, Gōngwáng Yì, succeeded him.
Yì passed away after holding his position for fourteen years.
His son, Kāngwáng, succeeded him,
but had no heir.
In the eleventh year of Jiàn'ān,
the state was abolished.
Initially,
Línyìhóu Fù was also fond of learning
and skilled in writing.
During the Yǒngpíng era,
whenever there were lectures or academic matters,
Fù was always put in charge.
He collaborated with Bān Gù and Jiǎ Kuí in compiling the history of the Hàn,
and Fù Yì and others all revered him.
Fù's son Táotú and his cousin Píngwànghóu Yì
both possessed talent and scholarship.
During the Yǒngníng era,
Empress Dowager Dèng summoned Yì and Táotú to the Dōngguān
to co-author, with the Yèzhě Púyè Liú Zhēn,
biographies of famous ministers and distinguished scholars from the Zhōngxīng period onwards.
Táotú also personally composed four pieces of rhapsodies, eulogies, letters, and treatises.
Zhào Xiàowáng Gǔ, courtesy name Cìbó,
was the paternal uncle of Guāngwǔ.
During Píngdì's reign, he was recommended as a Xiàolián
and served as the magistrate of Xiāo.
Guāngwǔ and his brothers became orphans at a young age,
and their affection was very deep.
When Guāngwǔ raised an army,
he informed Liáng of the matter.
Liáng was furious
and said:
"Your ambition and character are different from Bóshēng's.
Now our family is on the verge of ruin,
yet you conspire like this!"
Later, having no choice,
he followed the army to Xiǎocháng'ān.
The Hàn army suffered a great defeat,
and Liáng's wife and two sons were all killed.
When Gēngshǐ was enthroned,
he appointed Liáng as Guósānlǎo
and he followed Gēngshǐ into the Pass.
When Gēngshǐ was defeated,
Liáng heard that Guāngwǔ had ascended the throne
and fled to Luòyáng.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Liáng was enfeoffed as Guǎngyángwáng.
In the fifth year,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Zhàowáng,
and first went to his state.
In the thirteenth year,
he was demoted to Zhàogōng.
He came to court every few years.
In the seventeenth year,
he passed away in the capital.
He held his position for a total of sixteen years.
His son, Jiéwáng Xǔ, succeeded him.
In the thirtieth year of Jiànwǔ,
Xǔ's two sons were enfeoffed as Xiānghóu.
In the second year of Jiànchū,
Xǔ's ten sons were again enfeoffed as Tínghóu.
Xǔ passed away after holding his position for forty years.
His son, Kǐngwáng Shāng, succeeded him.
In the third year of Yǒngyuán,
Shāng's three younger brothers were enfeoffed as Tínghóu.
In the first year,
Shāng's four sons were enfeoffed as Tínghóu.
Shāng passed away after holding his position for twenty-three years.
His son, Jìngwáng Hóng, [succeeded him].
Hóng passed away after holding his position for twelve years.
His son, Huìwáng Gān, succeeded him.
In the fifth year of Yuánchū,
Gān's two younger brothers were enfeoffed as Tínghóu.
In that year,
the Chancellor of Zhào impeached Gān for secretly taking a concubine during his father's mourning period,
and also for leaving through the Sīmǎ Mén in plain white clothes.
As punishment, the county of Zhōngqiū was cut from his domain.
At that time, Lángzhōng Chéng Jiān of Nányáng, who had always possessed integrity and good conduct,
was appointed as Gān's tutor.
Jiān assisted him with rites and righteousness,
and Gān repented of his former misdeeds.
Jiān reported this to the emperor,
and the cut county was restored.
In the first year of Běnchū,
Gān's one son was enfeoffed as Tínghóu.
Gān passed away after holding his position for forty-eight years.
His son, Huáiwáng Yù, succeeded him.
After Yù passed away,
his son, Xiànwáng Shè, succeeded him.
After Shè passed away,
his son, Guī, succeeded him.
In the eighteenth year of Jiàn'ān, he was transferred and enfeoffed as Bólíngwáng.
After holding his position for nine years,
in the early days of Wèi, he was made Chóngdéhóu.
