Chéngyáng Gōngwáng Zhǐ, courtesy name Jùbó,
was the son of Chōnglíng Kānghóu Chǎng, a cousin of Guāngwǔ.
Chǎng's great-grandfather, Jiéhóu Mǎi,
was enfeoffed in Chōnglíng Township of Língdào as the son of Chángshā Dìngwáng,
and became Chōnglínghóu.
After Mǎi died,
his son, Dàihóu Xióngqú, succeeded him.
After Xióngqú died,
his son, Kǎohóu Rén, succeeded him.
Rén, finding the land of Chōnglíng to be low and damp,
with poisonous gases from the mountains and forests,
submitted a memorial requesting a reduction of his fief and relocation.
In the fourth year of Chūyuán of Yuándì,
he was transferred and enfeoffed in Báishuǐ Township of Nányáng,
still retaining Chōnglíng as the name of his state.
He then moved there with his cousin, Jùlù Dūwèi Huí, and other clan members to settle.
After Rén died,
his son, Chǎng, succeeded him.
Chǎng was modest and thrifty, and fond of righteousness.
He gave all the gold, treasures, and property from his father's time to his brothers.
The Inspector of Jīngzhōu reported his righteous conduct,
and he was appointed Lújiāng Dūwèi.
After about a year,
his cousin Ānzhònghóu Liú Chóng raised an army.
Wáng Mǎng, fearing and disliking the Liú clan,
summoned Chǎng to Cháng'ān,
and then dismissed him back to his state.
Formerly, during the reign of Píngdì,
Chǎng and Chóng both went to the capital, Jīngshī,
to assist in the sacrifice at Míngtáng.
Chóng saw that Wáng Mǎng would endanger the Hàn dynasty,
and privately said to Chǎng:
“The Duke of Ānhàn, Wáng Mǎng, monopolizes state power,
and none of the officials fail to comply.
The overthrow of the altars of soil and grain is imminent.
The Empress Dowager is advanced in years,
and the Son of Heaven is young and weak.
This is why Emperor Gāo partitioned and enfeoffed his sons and younger brothers,
it was precisely for this reason.”
Chǎng inwardly approved of this.
When Chóng’s plot failed,
Chǎng was afraid
and wished to form alliances and build a faction.
So he arranged for Zhǐ to marry the daughter of Dié Xuān, the Marquis of Gāolíng.
Just then, Dié Xuān’s younger brother, Dié Yì, raised troops, intending to attack Wáng Mǎng.
In Nányáng, Dié Xuān’s daughter was captured and killed,
and Zhǐ was implicated and imprisoned.
Chǎng then submitted a memorial apologizing for his fault,
and requested to lead his sons, younger brothers, and clansmen as vanguard soldiers.
Wáng Mǎng had just assumed regency,
and wished to comfort and pacify the imperial clan,
so he was not punished with execution.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
all the Liú clan members who were marquises were demoted to the rank of Zǐ,
receiving the emoluments of a Gūqīng.
Later, their titles were all stripped.
When Chǎng died,
Zhǐ was subsequently and especially dismissed,
and also prevented from holding office as an official.
Zhǐ, as the legitimate son of a former marquis,
was pure and honest in conduct,
and all the imperial clan respected him.
When Guāngwǔ raised an army,
Zhǐ and his brothers led one another to join the army.
Zhēn Fù, the Grandee of the Vanguard, seized all their family members and imprisoned them in Wǎn.
Zhǐ escaped alone and returned to defend Jíyáng.
Zhēn Fù then killed his mother, younger brothers, wife, and children.
When Gēngshǐ was enthroned,
he appointed Zhǐ as Tàicháng Jiāngjūn,
and he inherited the enfeoffment as Marquis of Chōnglíng.
He followed Gēngshǐ west into the pass,
and was enfeoffed as King of Dìngtáo.
He separately led troops to defeat Liú Yīng at Línjīng.
When Gēngshǐ surrendered to the Chìméi,
Zhǐ then traveled secretly and fled to Luòyáng.
At this time, among the imperial clan, only Zhǐ arrived first,
and Guāngwǔ was extremely pleased to see him.
In Jiànwǔ second year,
he was enfeoffed as King of Chéngyáng,
and granted an imperial carriage, imperial articles, chariots, horses, and clothing.
Chǎng was posthumously titled Kāng Hóu.
In the eleventh year,
Zhǐ fell ill.
He submitted the seal and ribbon of the King of Chéngyáng,
wishing to serve his ancestors’ sacrifices as a titled marquis.
The Emperor personally attended to his illness.
Zhǐ died
at the age of forty-three,
and was posthumously titled Gōng Wáng.
He never went to his kingdom,
but was buried at Běimáng, Luòyáng.
In the thirteenth year,
Zhǐ’s legitimate son Píng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Càiyáng,
to maintain Zhǐ’s sacrifices;
Píng’s younger brother Jiān was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāoxiāng.
Initially,
in Jiànwǔ second year,
the tombs of the imperial grandfather and imperial father were designated as Chānglíng,
and a tomb supervisor was appointed to guard them;
later it was changed to Zhānglíng,
and Chōnglíng was consequently made Zhānglíng County.
In the eighteenth year,
temples for Kǎo Hóu and Kāng Hóu were established,
comparable to imperial mausoleums,
and Sèfū were appointed.
An edict instructed Línglíng Commandery to offer sacrifices to the temples of Jié Hóu and Dài Hóu,
with five sacrifices in the four seasons and at the end of the year.
A Sèfū and an assistant official were appointed for each.
Píng was later implicated in illicit communication with various kings,
and his state was abolished.
In Yǒngpíng fifth year,
Xiǎnzōng re-enfeoffed Píng as Marquis of Jìnglíng.
Píng died,
and his son Zhēn succeeded.
Zhēn died,
and his son Yǔ succeeded.
Yǔ died,
and his son Jiā succeeded.
Shuǐshuǐ Wáng Shè, courtesy name Jīngsūn,
was Guāngwǔ’s paternal clan uncle.
Shè’s son Zhōng
and Guāngwǔ were very close in their youth.
When the Hàn army arose,
Shǐ and Tángzǐ
Zhōng lured and killed the Prefect of Húyáng.
When Gēngshǐ was enthroned,
Shè followed him into the pass
and was enfeoffed as King of Yuánshì,
while Zhōng became Shìzhōng.
When Gēngshǐ was defeated,
Shè and Zhōng fled east to Luòyáng.
In Jiànwǔ second year,
Shè was established as King of Shuǐshuǐ,
and Zhōng as King of Zīchuān.
In the tenth year,
Shè died.
His youngest son Chǎn was enfeoffed as Marquis of Tángxī
to carry on Shè’s lineage.
Zhōng grieved and mourned,
weeping for over twenty days,
and also died.
His eldest son Zhù was enfeoffed as Marquis of Qíl,
to carry on Zhōng’s sacrifices,
and Zhōng’s son Fèng was also enfeoffed as Marquis of Qǔyáng.
Shè’s paternal cousin Mào,
at eighteen years old,
when the Hàn army rose,
Mào styled himself Liú Shīzhí,
and also gathered a crowd between Jīng and Mì,
calling himself Yànxīn Jiāngjūn.
He captured Yǐngchuān and Rǔnán,
with a force of over 100,000 men.
After Guāngwǔ arrived at Hénèi,
Mào led his forces to surrender
and was enfeoffed as King of Zhōngshān.
In the thirteenth year,
all imperial clan members who were kings were demoted to marquises,
and Mào was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Ráng.
Mào’s younger brother Kuāng
also joined the Hàn army in its uprising.
In Jiànwǔ second year,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yíchūn.
He was humble and modest,
and during the Yǒngpíng era, he served as Zōngzhèng.
His son Fú succeeded,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Cháoyáng.
Fú’s younger brother Jiè A served as Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn during the Yǒngyuán era.
Fú’s lineage continued to his grandson Hù,
who had no sons,
and the enfeoffment was severed.
During the Yán’guāng era,
Hù’s paternal cousin Guī had a secret affair with Bórong, the daughter of Āndì’s wet nurse Wáng Shèng.
He then married Bórong,
and was able to inherit Hù’s enfeoffment as Marquis of Cháoyáng,
holding the position of Shìzhōng.
When Wáng Shèng was disgraced,
his noble rank was demoted to Tíng Hóu.
Ānchéng Xiàohóu Cì, courtesy name Zǐqín,
was Guāngwǔ’s paternal clan cousin.
His grandfather Lì was
the Administrator of Cāngwú.
Cì was orphaned young.
His elder brother Xiǎn avenged a grievance by killing someone,
and officials arrested and killed Xiǎn.
Cì and Xiǎn’s son Xìn sold their fields and residence,
together abandoning
their property,
recruiting retainers to avenge themselves on the officials.
They all became fugitives and went into hiding,
but returned after an amnesty.
When Bóshēng raised troops,
they followed him to attack various counties.
After Gēngshǐ was enthroned,
he appointed Cì as Guānglùxūn,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Guǎnghàn.
When Bóshēng was murdered,
Cì replaced him as Dàsītú,
leading troops to suppress Rǔnán.
Before it was pacified,
Gēngshǐ again appointed Xìn as Fènwēi Dàjiāngjūn,
to replace Cì in attacking Rǔnán,
and Cì went with Gēngshǐ to Luòyáng.
Gēngshǐ wanted to send a trusted general to pacify Héběi,
but did not know whom to appoint.
Cì said that among the various clan members, only Wénshú could be used,
but Dàsīmǎ Zhū Wěi and others thought it was not feasible.
Gēngshǐ was hesitant,
but Cì strongly urged him,
so he appointed Guāngwǔ as acting Dàsīmǎ,
and sent him with a staff of authority to cross the Yellow River.
On that day, Cì was appointed Chéngxiàng,
and ordered to enter the pass first
to repair the ancestral temples and palaces.
He returned to welcome Gēngshǐ to establish the capital at Cháng'ān,
enfeoffing Cì as King of Wǎn,
and appointing him as Qián Dàsīmǎ,
sending him with a staff of authority to pacify and govern Guāndōng.
In the second year, spring,
Cì went to his state in [name missing], leading six divisions of soldiers.
Later, when the Chìméi defeated Gēngshǐ,
the six divisions led by Cì also gradually dispersed and mutinied,
so he left Wǎn and sought refuge in Bǎoyáng.
Hearing that Guāngwǔ (光武) had ascended the throne,
he then went west to Wǔguān (武關),
to welcome Gēngshǐ's (更始) wife and children, intending to take them to Luòyáng (洛陽).
The Emperor praised and rewarded Zhōng (忠),
and in Jiànwǔ (建武) second year (26 CE),
enfeoffed him as Shènhóu (慎侯).
In the thirteenth year (37 CE),
his household and land were further increased,
and he was formally enfeoffed as Ānchénghóu (安成侯),
attending court by imperial invitation.
Because of the Emperor's special favor and trust,
he was treated with great intimacy and generosity,
frequently receiving private banquets,
and the Emperor sometimes visited his residence;
his favors and rewards were exceptionally unique.
He always distributed the bestowed gifts to his old friends and acquaintances,
without keeping any for himself.
The Emperor built him a tomb hall,
erected a memorial temple,
and appointed officials and soldiers
like those for Chōnglíng Xiàohóu (舂陵孝侯).
He died in the twenty-eighth year (52 CE).
His son Mǐn (閔) succeeded him.
In the thirtieth year (54 CE),
the Emperor again enfeoffed Mǐn's (閔) younger brother Sōng (嵩) as Báiniúhóu (白牛侯).
Due to involvement in the Chǔ (楚) incident,
their statements were implicated,
and the marquisate was abolished.
Mǐn (閔) died,
and his son Shāng (商) succeeded him,
transferred and enfeoffed as Báiniúhóu (白牛侯).
Shāng (商) died,
and his son Chāng (昌) succeeded him.
Initially,
Xìn (信) pacified Rǔnán (汝南) for Gēngshǐ (更始),
and was consequently enfeoffed as Rǔyīnwáng (汝陰王).
Xìn (信) then led troops to pacify Jiāngnán (江南),
occupying Yùzhāng (豫章).
When Guāngwǔ (光武) ascended the throne,
Zhāng Lóng (張隆), the Grand Administrator of Guìyáng (桂陽), defeated him.
Xìn (信) then went to Luòyáng (洛陽) and surrendered,
and was appointed Rǔyīnhóu (汝陰侯).
In Yǒngpíng (永平) thirteenth year (70 CE),
he was also implicated in the Chǔ (楚) incident, and his marquisate was abolished.
Chéngwǔ Xiàohóu (成武孝侯) Shùn (順), courtesy name Píngzhòng (平仲),
was a cousin of Guāngwǔ (光武) by clan.
His father, Qìng (慶),
was a full brother of Chōnglínghóu (舂陵侯) Chǎng (敞).
Shùn (順) and Guāngwǔ (光武) lived in the same neighborhood,
and were close friends in their youth.
When Gēngshǐ (更始) ascended the throne,
he appointed Qìng (慶) as Yānwáng (燕王),
and Shùn (順) as Hǔyá Jiāngjūn (虎牙將軍).
When Gēngshǐ (更始) surrendered to the Chìméi (赤眉),
Qìng (慶) was [killed] by mutinous soldiers.
Shùn (順) then secretly went to Guāngwǔ (光武),
and was appointed Grand Administrator of Nányáng (南陽).
In Jiànwǔ (建武) second year (26 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Chéngwǔhóu (成武侯);
his estate was the largest,
and his tax revenue was double that of other imperial clan families.
In the eighth year (32 CE),
he was sent to defeat the bandits of Liù'ān (六安),
and was consequently appointed Grand Administrator of Liù'ān (六安).
After several years,
the Emperor wanted to summon him,
but the officials and people petitioned to keep him.
He died in the eleventh year (35 CE).
The Emperor sent envoys to receive the funeral,
and personally attended to mourn.
His son Zūn (遵) succeeded him.
Due to illicit communication with various kings,
he was demoted to Duānshìhóu (端氏侯).
Zūn (遵) died,
and his son Yǎn (弇) succeeded him.
Yǎn (弇) died
without issue,
and the marquisate was abolished.
In Yǒngpíng (永平) tenth year (67 CE),
Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) visited Zhānglíng (章陵),
and recalling past favors,
enfeoffed three of Shùn's (順) nephews as Xiānghóu (鄉侯).
Initially,
Shùn's (順) uncle Hóng (弘)
married into the Fán (樊) clan,
who was the Imperial Mother's (皇妣) cousin.
She bore two sons: Mǐn (敏)
and Guó (國).
They stayed with their mother and Gēngshǐ (更始) in Cháng'ān (長安).
In Jiànwǔ (建武) second year (26 CE),
they went to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Guāngwǔ (光武) enfeoffed Mǐn (敏) as Gānlǐhóu (甘里侯),
and Guó (國) as Yìyánghóu (弋陽侯).
Mǐn (敏) was well-versed in the Classics and had good conduct.
In the early Yǒngpíng (永平) period,
he rose to the position of Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉).
Hóng's (弘) younger brother Liáng (梁)
was known for his chivalrous spirit.
In Gēngshǐ (更始) first year (23 CE),
he raised troops in Yùzhāng (豫章),
intending to pacify Jiāngdōng (江東),
and proclaimed himself
"Jiùhàn Dàjiāngjūn" (就漢大將軍),
but died suddenly of illness.
Shùnyáng Huáihóu (順陽懷侯) Jiā (嘉), courtesy name Xiàosūn (孝孫),
was a cousin of Guāngwǔ (光武) by clan.
His father, Xiàn (憲),
was a full brother of Chōnglínghóu (舂línghóu) Chǎng (敞).
Jiā (嘉) was orphaned young,
and had a benevolent and magnanimous nature.
Nándùn Jūn (南頓君) raised him as her own son.
Later, he studied in Cháng'ān (長安) with Bóshēng (伯升),
learning the Shàngshū (尚書) and Chūnqiū (春秋).
When the righteous army rose,
Jiā (嘉) followed Gēngshǐ (更始) in campaigns.
When the Han army was defeated at Xiǎocháng'ān (小長安),
Jiā's (嘉) wife and children were killed.
When Gēngshǐ (更始) ascended the throne,
he appointed him Piānjiāngjūn (偏將軍).
After Wǎn (宛) was captured,
he was enfeoffed as Xīngdéhóu (興德侯)
and promoted to Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍).
He attacked Yán Cén (延岑) at Guānjūn (冠軍)
and made him surrender.
When Gēngshǐ (更始) established his capital in Cháng'ān (長安),
he appointed Jiā (嘉) as Hànzhōngwáng (漢中王) and Fúwēi Dàjiāngjūn (扶威大將軍),
with a staff of authority to proceed to his state,
establishing his capital at Nánzhèng (南鄭),
with a multitude of several hundred thousand.
In Jiànwǔ (建武) second year (26 CE),
Yán Cén (延岑) rebelled again,
attacked Hànzhōng (漢中),
and besieged Nánzhèng (南鄭).
Jiā's (嘉) troops were defeated and fled.
Cén (岑) then secured Hànzhōng (漢中)
and advanced his troops to Wǔdū (武都),
where he was defeated by Gēngshǐ's (更始) Zhùgōnghóu (柱功侯) Lǐ Bǎo (李寶).
Cén (岑) fled to Tiānshuǐ (天水),
and Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述) sent his general Hóu Dān (侯丹) to take Nánzhèng (南鄭).
Jiā (嘉) gathered scattered soldiers,
obtaining several tens of thousands of men.
He appointed Bǎo (寶) as Prime Minister,
and from Wǔdū (武都) attacked Hóu Dān (侯丹) to the south.
He was unsuccessful,
and returned his army to Héchí (河池) and Xiàbiàn (下辨).
He then repeatedly engaged in battle with Yán Cén (延岑).
Cén (岑) led his forces north through Sànguān (散關),
reaching Chéncāng (陳倉).
Jiā (嘉) pursued and defeated him.
Gēngshǐ's (更始) Dèngwáng (鄧王) Liáo Zhàn (廖湛), with eighteen thousand Chìméi (赤眉) soldiers, attacked Jiā (嘉).
Jiā (嘉) fought them at Gǔkǒu (谷口)
and utterly routed them.
Jiā (嘉) personally killed Zhàn (湛),
and then arrived at Yúnyáng (雲陽) to obtain provisions.
Lǐ Bǎo (李寶) and others, hearing that Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) was campaigning in the west,
held their troops and defended themselves,
advising Jiā (嘉) to observe the outcome for a while.
When Guāngwǔ (光武) heard of this,
he told Yǔ (禹),
"Xiàosūn (孝孫) has always been prudent and good-natured,
and has been close and dear since childhood.
This must be the work of frivolous youths in Cháng'ān (長安) enticing him."
Yǔ (禹) immediately proclaimed the Emperor's will,
and Jiā (嘉) then went through Lái Xī (來歙) to meet Yǔ (禹) at Yúnyáng (雲陽).
In the third year (27 CE),
he arrived at Luòyáng (洛陽),
joined in the campaigns,
and was appointed Grand Administrator of Qiānchéng (千乘).
In the sixth year (30 CE),
he fell ill,
and submitted a memorial requesting to retire.
He was summoned to the capital.
In the thirteenth year (37 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Shùnyánghóu (順陽侯).
In the autumn,
Jiā's (嘉) son Qiáng (廧) was again enfeoffed as Huánglǐhóu (黃李侯).
In the fifteenth year (39 CE),
Jiā (嘉) died.
His son Cān (參) succeeded him.
Having committed a crime,
he was demoted to Nánxiānghóu (南鄉侯).
During the Yǒngpíng (永平) period,
Cān (參) served as Chéngmén Xiàowèi (城門校尉).
Cān (參) died,
and his son Xún (循) succeeded him.
Xún (循) died,
and his son Zhāng (章) succeeded him.
The encomium says: Qí Wǔ (齊武) was profound and heroic,
his righteous spear rode the wind.
Unexpectedly and unintentionally,
heavenly skill abandoned us.
Chéngyáng (城陽) allied early,
Zhào Xiào (趙孝) joined late.
The three marquises of Sìshuǐ (泗水),
some for grace, some for merit.
Biographies of Lǐ (李), Wáng (王), Dèng (鄧), Lái (來) Part Five.
Lǐ Tōng 字 Yuánzì,
was a native of Wǎn, Nányáng.
His family was known for its wealth and trade for generations.
His father, Shǒu,
was nine *chǐ* tall,
with an extraordinary appearance.
He was stern and resolute,
and managed his household as if it were an official court.
He initially served Liú Xīn,
was fond of astronomy, calendars, prophecies, and omens,
and became Wáng Mǎng's Zōngqīngshī.
Tōng also served as a Wǔwēijiāngjūn Cóngshì.
He was dispatched to serve as a Wūchéng,
and gained a reputation for competence.
Towards the end of Mǎng's reign,
the common people were distressed and resentful.
Tōng had long heard Shǒu speak of a prophecy which said:
"The Liú clan will revive,
and the Lǐ clan will assist it."
He secretly kept this in mind.
Moreover, his family was wealthy and free from worry,
and he was a prominent figure in his neighborhood.
Because of this, he was not content to be an official,
so he resigned and returned home.
When the forces of Xiàjiāng and Xīnshì arose,
Nányáng was in turmoil.
Tōng's younger cousin, Yì,
who also had a liking for such affairs,
discussed the matter with him, saying:
"Now the four quarters are in chaos,
the Xīn dynasty is about to fall,
and the Hàn will rise again.
Among the imperial relatives in Nányáng,
only Liú Bóshēng and his brothers are broadly benevolent and able to gather people.
We can conspire with them for a great enterprise."
Tōng smiled and said:
"That is what I had in mind!"
It so happened that Guāngwǔ was avoiding [officials] in Wǎn.
When Tōng heard this,
he immediately sent Yì to invite Guāngwǔ.
Guāngwǔ initially admired Tōng as a gentleman,
so he went to respond to his invitation.
When they met,
they talked for a whole day,
and shook hands with great joy.
Tōng then fully explained the matter of the prophetic texts.
Guāngwǔ was initially quite surprised,
and did not dare to accept it.
At that time, Shǒu was in Cháng'ān.
Guāngwǔ then subtly observed Tōng and said:
"If this is the case,
what about Zōngqīngshī?"
Tōng said:
"I have already made arrangements for that."
He then fully explained his plan.
Guāngwǔ, having deeply understood Tōng's intention,
then entered into an agreement with him,
finalized their plan,
and set a date for the trial of cavalry at the military review of the *Cáiguān*.
They intended to seize the former leader of the advance guard (*Qiánduì Dàfū*) and the commander of the rectifiers (*Shǔzhèng*),
and then use this to command the masses.
They then sent Guāngwǔ and Yì back to Chōnglíng
to raise troops in response.
He sent his cousin's son, Jì, to Cháng'ān
to report the matter to Shǒu.
Jì fell ill and died on the way.
Shǒu secretly learned of this
and wanted to escape and return.
He had always been good friends with Huáng Xiǎn, a native of his district.
At that time, Xiǎn was a Zhōnglángjiāng.
When he heard of it,
he said to Shǒu:
"Now the city gates are strictly guarded,
and your appearance is extraordinary.
How will you deal with this?
Why not go to the imperial court and surrender yourself?
Since the matter has not yet occurred,
perhaps you can avoid disaster."
Shǒu followed his advice
and immediately submitted a memorial offering to die.
Before the memorial was reported,
he remained below the palace gate.
When the matter was discovered,
Tōng managed to escape.
Mǎng heard of this
and then imprisoned Shǒu.
Huáng Xiǎn pleaded on his behalf, saying:
"Shǒu heard that your son was rebellious,
but did not dare to flee.
Shǒu believed in his own righteousness
and surrendered himself to the imperial palace.
Your minister, Xiǎn, is willing to serve as a guarantor for Shǒu and go east together
to persuade his son.
If he persists in his rebellion,
Shǒu will face north and cut his own throat
to atone for your great kindness."
Mǎng agreed to his words.
At this time, the advance guard again reported Tōng's uprising.
Mǎng was enraged
and wanted to kill Shǒu.
Xiǎn argued for him,
and consequently, both were executed,
and all of Shǒu's family in Cháng'ān were killed.
In Nányáng, Tōng's brothers and sixty-four members of his clan were also executed,
and all their bodies were burned in the Wǎn marketplace.
At that time, the Hàn army had also gathered in great force.
Tōng, Guāngwǔ, and Lǐ Yì met at Jíyáng,
and together they defeated the advance guard,
killing Zhēn Fù and Liángqiū Cì.
When Gēngshǐ was enthroned,
he appointed Tōng as Zhùguó Dàjiāngjūn and Fǔhàn Hóu.
He followed Gēngshǐ to Cháng'ān,
and was again appointed Dàjiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Xīpíng Wáng;
Yì was made Wǔyīn Wáng;
Tōng's cousin, Sōng, was made Chéngxiàng.
Gēngshǐ sent Tōng with a *jié* (credentials) to return and govern Jīngzhōu.
Tōng then married Guāngwǔ's younger sister, Bó Jī,
who became Níngpíng Gōngzhǔ.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he summoned Tōng to be Wèiwèi.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he was enfeoffed as Gùshǐ Hóu
and appointed Dàsīnóng.
Whenever the Emperor campaigned in the four directions,
he often ordered Tōng to remain in the capital,
to pacify the people,
repair palaces,
and establish schools.
In the spring of the fifth year,
he succeeded Wáng Liáng as Qiánjiāngjūn.
In the summer of the sixth year,
he led ten camps, including Pòjiān Jiāngjūn Hóu Jìn and Bǔlǔ Jiāngjūn Wáng Bà, to attack the bandits in Hànzhōng.
Gōngsūn Shù sent troops to rescue them.
Tōng and others fought them in Xīyù,
defeated them,
and returned to establish military colonies in Shùnyáng.
At this time, the world was largely settled.
Tōng considered avoiding honors and favors,
and memorialized the throne, pleading illness and requesting to retire.
An imperial edict was issued for the high officials and ministers to deliberate.
Dàsītú Hóu Bà and others said:
"Wáng Mǎng usurped the Hàn and
threw the world into chaos.
Tōng conceived the strategies of Yī Yǐn, Lǚ Shàng, Xiāo Hé, and Cáo Cān,
established great plans,
assisted the divine spirit,
and helped perfect the sagely virtue.
He sacrificed his family for the state,
forgot himself in serving his lord,
and had the righteousness of saving the imperiled and preserving the dying.
His achievements and virtues are the highest,
known throughout the realm.
Tōng, seeing the world settled,
humbly resigned from his position.
Truly, one should not forget danger in times of peace.
It is fitting that Tōng should remain in office while recovering from illness.
His desire to withdraw to his fiefdom
cannot be granted."
Thereupon, an edict ordered Tōng to diligently seek medical treatment
and attend to his duties when able.
In that summer,
he was promoted and appointed Dàsīkōng.
Tōng, as a commoner, initiated a righteous cause
and helped achieve a great undertaking.
Furthermore, due to Níngpíng Gōngzhǔ,
he was particularly cherished and highly regarded.
However, his nature was humble and deferential;
he always wanted to avoid power and influence.
He had always suffered from a wasting disease.
After becoming prime minister,
he pleaded illness and did not attend to affairs.
He repeatedly requested to retire for years,
but the Emperor always treated him with exceptional favor.
He was allowed to return to his residence to recover from illness while holding his public office,
but Tōng again firmly declined.
After two years,
he was finally permitted to surrender his Dàsīkōng seal and sash,
and was granted the special privilege of *Tèjìn* to attend court.
Officials submitted a memorial requesting the enfeoffment of the imperial princes.
The Emperor, moved by Tōng's initial proposal of the great plan,
on that very day enfeoffed Tōng's youngest son, Xióng, as Zhàolíng Hóu.
Whenever the Emperor visited Nányáng,
he always sent envoys to offer a grand sacrifice of an ox, a sheep, and a pig at Tōng's father's tomb.
He died in the eighteenth year,
and was given the posthumous title Gōng Hóu.
The Emperor and Empress personally attended the mourning
and funeral.
His son, Yīn, succeeded him.
When Yīn died,
his son, Dìng, succeeded him.
When Dìng died,
his son, Huáng, succeeded him.
When Huáng died,
his son, Shòu, succeeded him.
Lǐ Yì (李軼) was later killed by Zhū Wěi (朱鮪).
When Gēngshǐ (更始) was defeated,
Lǐ Sōng (李松) died in battle,
only Tōng (通) was able to end his life with honor.
During the Yǒngpíng (永平) reign,
Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) visited Wǎn (宛),
and issued an edict for all the Lǐ (李) family members and the imperial clan of Ānzhòng (安衆) to assemble and meet him.
They were all given rewards,
and bestowed with generous favor.
The commentary says: The Master said,
“Wealth and high station are what people desire.
If they are not obtained in the right way,
one should not abide in them.”
Did Lǐ Tōng (李通) know what was desired but not understand how to obtain it by the right way?
The Way of Heaven and destiny are
difficult for even the sages to speak of,
how much more so to conjecture about the subtle and obscure,
or to pursue the wild and unfounded blessings,
defiling and destroying one's own kin,
in order to achieve a unique merit!
In the past, Méng Gǔ (蒙穀), carrying books,
did not abandon Chǔ (楚) during its difficulties;
Jímò (即墨), serving Qí (齊),
righteously avenged Yān’s (燕) humiliation.
The choices and positions taken by them,
were they perhaps different from Tōng (通)’s?
Wáng Cháng (王常), courtesy name Yánqīng (顏卿),
was a native of Wǔyáng (舞陽) in Yǐngchuān (潁川).
At the end of Wáng Mǎng (王莽)’s reign,
he avenged his younger brother,
and fled to Jiāngxià (江夏).
After a long time,
he, along with Wáng Fèng (王鳳) and Wáng Kuāng (王匡), raised an army in the Lùlín (綠林) Mountains of Yúndù (雲杜),
gathering tens of thousands of people.
Cháng (常) was made a subordinate general,
and attacked neighboring counties.
Later, he, along with Chéng Dān (成丹) and Zhāng Áng (張卬), separately entered Lánkǒu (藍口) in Nánjùn (南郡),
and were called the Xiàjiāng (下江) forces.
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) sent Yán Yóu (嚴尤) and Chén Mào (陳茂) to attack and defeat them.
Cháng (常), Dān (丹), and Áng (卬) gathered the scattered soldiers and entered Lóuxī (蔞谿),
plundering between Zhōng (鍾) and Lóng (龍),
and their forces recovered.
They led their army to battle the Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州) at Shàngtáng (上唐),
where they decisively defeated him,
and then advanced north to Yíqiū (宜秋).
At this time,
the Hàn (漢) army, along with the Xīnshì (新巿) and Pínglín (平林) forces, were all defeated at Xiǎocháng'ān (小長安),
and each wished to disperse.
Bóshēng (伯升) heard that the Xiàjiāng (下江) army was at Yíqiū (宜秋),
and immediately went with Guāngwǔ (光武) and Lǐ Tōng (李通) to Cháng (常)’s camp,
saying:
“We wish to meet a worthy general from Xiàjiāng (下江)
to discuss important matters.”
Chéng Dān (成丹) and Zhāng Áng (張卬) jointly pushed Cháng (常) forward.
Bóshēng (伯升) met Cháng (常),
and persuaded him with the benefits of alliance.
Cháng (常) was greatly enlightened,
and said:
“Wáng Mǎng (王莽) usurped the throne and murdered,
cruelly oppressing the world.
The common people long for the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
which is why heroes are rising up everywhere.
Now the Liú (劉) clan is reviving,
and they are the true rulers.
I sincerely wish to devote myself to their service,
to assist in achieving a great accomplishment.”
Bóshēng (伯升) said:
“If the undertaking succeeds,
how dare I enjoy it alone!”
Then he and Cháng (常) formed a deep bond and departed.
Cháng (常) returned,
and fully explained it to Dān (丹) and Áng (卬).
Dān (丹) and Áng (卬), relying on their forces,
all said:
“Since we great men have risen,
we should each be our own master,
why should we be controlled by others?”
Cháng (常) alone in his heart returned to the Hàn (漢),
and gradually enlightened and persuaded his generals and commanders, saying:
“In the past, Chéng (成) and Āi (哀) declined and had no heir,
which allowed Wáng Mǎng (王莽) to take advantage and usurp the throne.
After he possessed the world,
his administration was harsh and cruel,
gradually losing the hearts of the people.
The people’s yearning for the Hàn (漢) has not been for just one day,
which is why we were able to rise because of this.
That which the people resent,
Heaven abandons;
that which the people long for,
Heaven grants.
To undertake a great endeavor, one must
act in accordance with the people’s will below,
and align with Heaven’s will above,
only then can success be achieved.
If one relies on strength and courage,
indulges in desires without restraint,
even if one gains the world,
one will surely lose it again.
Even with the power of Qín (秦) and Xiàng (項),
they were ultimately destroyed and overthrown,
how much more so now, when commoners gather in the wilderness?
To act in this way
is the path to extinction.
Now the various Liú (劉) families of Nányáng (南陽) have raised an army.
Observing those who came to discuss matters,
they all have profound plans and great foresight,
the talent of kings and dukes.
If we join with them,
we will surely achieve great success.
This is how 【Heaven】 helps us.”
Although the Xiàjiāng (下江) generals were stubborn and lacked much understanding,
they had always respected Cháng (常),
so they all bowed and said:
“Without General Wáng (王),
we would have nearly fallen into unrighteousness.
We humbly accept your instruction.”
They immediately led their troops to join the Hàn (漢) army, and the Xīnshì (新巿) and Pínglín (平林) forces.
Thereupon, all the various divisions united in spirit and strength,
their morale greatly boosted.
They then advanced together,
defeating and killing Zhēn Fù (甄阜) and Liángqiū Cì (梁丘賜).
When the generals discussed establishing a member of the imperial clan,
only Cháng (常) and the scholars and officials of Nányáng (南陽) agreed to establish Bóshēng (伯升),
but Zhū Wěi (朱鮪), Zhāng Áng (張卬), and others did not agree.
When Gēngshǐ (更始) was established,
Cháng (常) was appointed Tíngwèi (廷尉) and Dàjiàngjūn (大將軍),
and enfeoffed as Zhīmìng Hóu (知命侯).
He separately pacified Rǔnán (汝南) and Pèijùn (沛郡),
then returned to Kūnyáng (昆陽),
and together with Guāngwǔ (光武) defeated Wáng Xún (王尋) and Wáng Yì (王邑).
When Gēngshǐ (更始) moved his capital west to Cháng'ān (長安),
he appointed Cháng (常) to act as Governor of Nányáng (南陽),
giving him independent authority to issue orders for executions and rewards,
enfeoffing him as Dèng Wáng (鄧王),
with eight counties as his domain,
and bestowed upon him the surname Liú (劉).
Cháng (常) was naturally respectful and frugal,
and observed laws and regulations.
The people of the south praised him.
When Gēngshǐ (更始) was defeated,
in the summer of the second year of Jiànwǔ (建武),
Cháng (常) brought his wife and children to Luòyáng (洛陽),
and surrendered himself, exposing his upper body in submission.
Guāngwǔ (光武) saw Cháng (常) and was very pleased,
comforting him, saying:
“Minister Wáng (王), you have suffered much.
I often recall the past,
when we shared hardships and dangers together,
how could I ever forget it?
‘No coming, no going’—
surely you have not gone against our words of old?”
Cháng (常) kowtowed and replied:
“I received your great command,
and was able to entrust myself to Your Majesty’s service.
We first met at Yíqiū (宜秋),
and later converged at Kūnyáng (昆陽);
fortunately, relying on your divine military prowess,
we immediately forged a bond as strong as metal.
Gēngshǐ (更始) underestimated this foolish minister,
and entrusted me with the southern provinces.
During the disaster of the Chìméi (赤眉),
I lost heart and hope,
thinking that the world had again lost its order.
Hearing that Your Majesty ascended the throne in Héběi (河北),
my heart opened and my vision cleared.
Now that I am able to see your court,
I have no regrets even if I die.”
The Emperor laughed and said:
“I was merely jesting with you, Minister.
Now that I have seen you,
I am no longer worried about the south.”
Then he summoned the grandees, ministers, and generals to a great assembly,
and thoroughly explained to all the officials:
“Cháng (常), as a commoner, raised an army of righteousness,
and was clear in knowing the Mandate of Heaven,
which is why Gēngshǐ (更始) enfeoffed him as Zhīmìng Hóu (知命侯).
He and I met amidst the army,
and were especially close and kind to each other.”
He particularly added rewards,
appointed him Zuǒcáo (左曹),
and enfeoffed him as Shānsāng Hóu (山桑侯).
Later, the Emperor, during a grand assembly, pointed at Cháng and said to his ministers:
“This family, having led the various generals from Xiàjiāng to assist and protect the Hàn dynasty,
has a heart like gold and stone;
truly they are loyal subjects.”
On that day, Cháng was promoted to Mànxūn Dàjiāngjūn,
and sent south to attack Dèng Fèng and Dǒng Xīn,
with orders for all generals to be subordinate to him.
He was also ordered to lead an expedition north to Héxián and Yúyáng,
and pacify all the scattered garrisons.
In the autumn of the fifth year,
he attacked and captured Húlíng,
and then met the Emperor in Rènchéng,
consequently joining in the defeat of Sū Mào and Páng Méng.
Advancing to attack Xiàpī,
Cháng’s unit engaged in battle at the city gate,
fighting several times in one day.
The bandits retreated and fled into the city.
Cháng pursued them closely;
arrows rained down from the city walls.
The Emperor, with over a hundred cavalrymen, watched from a high position south of the city,
seeing Cháng fight with great strength.
He immediately dispatched a Zhōnghuángmén with an edict to order his withdrawal,
and then the bandits surrendered.
He also separately led Qí Dūwèi Wáng Bà to jointly pacify the bandits in Pèi Jùn.
In the spring of the sixth year,
he was recalled to Luòyáng.
The Emperor ordered his wife to welcome Cháng at Wǔyáng,
and he returned home to visit the ancestral tomb.
He then garrisoned Cháng’ān to the west,
to resist Kuí Xiāo.
In the seventh year,
an envoy was sent with an imperial seal and edict to immediately appoint Cháng as Héngyě Dàjiāngjūn,
with his position uniquely distinguished among the generals.
Cháng separately attacked and defeated Kuí Xiāo’s general Gāo Jùn at Cháonà.
When Xiāo sent his generals past Wūshì,
Cháng intercepted and defeated them.
He successively received the surrender of various camps and fortifications of the Bǎosài Qiāng,
pacifying them all.
In the ninth year,
he attacked the bandits of Nèihuáng,
defeating and subduing them.
Later, he garrisoned Gù’ān to the north,
to resist Lú Fāng.
In the twelfth year,
he died at his garrison post,
and was posthumously named Jié Hóu.
His son was Guǎng.
Thirty years later,
he was enfeoffed as Shíchéng Hóu.
In the fourteenth year of Yǒngpíng,
because of his involvement with the affair of Chǔ,
his marquisate was abolished.
Dèng Chén, courtesy name Wěiqīng,
was a native of Xīnyě, Nányáng.
His family served as officials of two thousand *dàn* for generations.
His father, Hóng,
was the Yùzhāng Dūwèi.
Chén initially married Guāngwǔ’s elder sister, Yuán.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng’s reign,
Guāngwǔ once went with his elder brother Bóshēng and Chén to Wǎn,
and feasted and conversed with Cài Shǎogōng of Ráng and others.
Shǎogōng, who was somewhat learned in prognostication texts,
said that Liú Xiù would become the Son of Heaven.
Someone asked:
“Is that the State Preceptor Liú Xiù?”
Guāngwǔ jokingly said:
“How do you know it’s not me?”
All those present laughed loudly,
but Chén alone was secretly pleased.
When Guāngwǔ and his family avoided officials in Xīnyě,
they lodged in Chén’s hut,
and were very close and affectionate.
Chén then said to Guāngwǔ:
“Wáng Mǎng is tyrannical and cruel;
he executes people in the height of summer.
This is the time when Heaven wills his destruction.
When we met in Wǎn earlier,
were you the only one who was supposed to fulfill the prophecy?”
Guāngwǔ smiled and did not answer.
When the Hàn army rose,
Chén led his retainers to gather at Jíyáng.
When the Hàn army was defeated at Xiǎocháng’ān,
many generals abandoned their families.
Guāngwǔ fled alone on horseback,
met his younger sister Bójī,
and they rode together.
Further ahead, he saw Yuán again,
and urged her to get on the horse.
Yuán waved her hand and said:
“Go!
I cannot save you;
there is no need for both of us to perish.”
Just then, pursuing soldiers arrived,
and Yuán and her three daughters were all captured.
The Hàn army retreated to hold Jíyáng,
and the Xīnyě magistrate defiled Chén’s residence
and burned his ancestral tombs.
His clan members were all furious,
saying:
“Our family is wealthy enough on its own,
why must we follow our wife’s family into a boiling pot?”
Chén, however, showed no resentment.
When Gēngshǐ was enthroned,
he appointed Chén as Piān Jiāngjūn.
He and Guāngwǔ surveyed the land in Yǐngchuān,
and together they rode out of Kūnyáng city at night
to defeat Wáng Xún and Wáng Yì.
He also separately brought Yángzhái and areas east of it under control,
reaching Jīng and Mì,
all of which surrendered.
When Gēngshǐ moved his capital north to Luòyáng,
he made Chén the Tàishǒu of Chángshān.
When Wáng Láng rebelled,
Guāngwǔ fled from Jì to Xìndū.
Chén also traveled incognito and met him below Jùlù,
volunteering to join in the attack on Hándān.
Guāngwǔ said:
“Wěiqīng, for you to follow me with just yourself,
is not as good as having a commandery serve as my host for the northern route.”
So he sent Chén back to his commandery.
When Guāngwǔ pursued the bandit groups of the Tóngmǎ and Gāohú in Jìzhōu,
Chén dispatched a thousand elite archers,
and also sent an uninterrupted supply of provisions to the army.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Chén as Fángzǐ Hóu.
The Emperor, deeply saddened by his sister’s death amidst the chaos of war,
posthumously enfeoffed and named Yuán as Xīnyě Jiéyì Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ,
and erected a temple for her west of the county.
He enfeoffed Chén’s eldest son, Fàn, as Wúfáng Hóu,
to oversee the sacrifices for the princess.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ,
Chén was summoned back to the capital.
He frequently attended banquets and audiences,
recounting old stories and happy times from their youth.
Chén calmly said to the Emperor:
“I finally accomplished it.”
The Emperor laughed heartily.
He followed the Emperor on a visit to Zhānglíng,
was appointed Guānglù Dàfū,
and was given the imperial insignia to supervise Zhíjīnwú Jiǎ Fù and others in pacifying the bandits of Shàolíng and Xīnxī.
In the fourth year,
he followed the Emperor on a visit to Shòuchūn,
and was left to garrison Jiǔjiāng.
Chén enjoyed his commandery duties,
and thus was again appointed Tàishǒu of Zhōngshān.
Officials and common people praised him,
and he was always ranked highest in Jìzhōu.
In the thirteenth year,
he was re-enfeoffed as Nán Hóu.
He entered the court for consultations,
and was again made Tàishǒu of Rǔnán.
In the eighteenth year,
when the Emperor made an inspection tour to Zhānglíng,
Chén was summoned to act as Tíngwèi.
He followed to Xīnyě,
where a lavish banquet was held.
He was rewarded with several tens of millions (of cash),
and then sent back to his commandery.
Chén initiated the construction of the Hóngxì Bēi irrigation system, irrigating several thousand *qǐng* of fields.
The soil of Rǔ was thus enriched,
and the abundance of fish and rice
flowed to other commanderies.
The next year,
he was permanently enfeoffed as Xīhuá Hóu,
and again summoned for court consultations.
He died in the twenty-fifth year,
and an imperial edict dispatched a Zhōngyèzhě with full princely retinue and rites
to invite the soul of Princess Xīnyě,
and she was interred with Chén at Běimáng.
The Emperor’s carriage and the empress personally attended the funeral and burial.
He was posthumously named Huì Hóu.
His youngest son, Táng, succeeded him,
and was later enfeoffed as Wǔdāng.
When Táng died,
his son Gù succeeded.
When Gù died,
his son Guó succeeded.
When Guó died,
his son Fú succeeded.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn, Fú died,
having no son,
and the marquisate was abolished.
Lái Xī, courtesy name Jūnshú,
was a native of Xīnyě, Nányáng.
His sixth-generation ancestor, Hàn,
was talented and strong.
During the reign of Wǔdì,
as Guānglù Dàfū, he assisted Lóuchuán Jiāngjūn Yáng Pú
in defeating Nányuè and Cháoxiǎn.
His father, Zhòng,
served as Jiàndàfū during the reign of Āidì,
and married Guāngwǔ’s great-aunt,
giving birth to Xī.
Guāngwǔ held him in great affection and respect,
and they often traveled to Cháng’ān together.
When the Hàn army rose,
Wáng Mǎng, considering Jiǎ Shè to be an external relation of the Liú clan,
arrested and imprisoned him.
His retainers jointly plotted to rescue him,
and he managed to escape.
When Gēngshǐ ascended the throne,
he appointed Shè as an official
and Shè followed him into Guānzhōng.
He frequently offered advice, but it was not adopted,
so he left due to illness.
Shè's younger sister was the wife of Liú Jiā, King of Hànzhōng.
Jiā sent someone to welcome Shè.
He consequently went south to Hànzhōng.
When Gēngshǐ was defeated,
Shè persuaded Jiā to submit to Guāngwǔ,
and thus he and Jiā together went east to Luòyáng.
When the Emperor saw Shè,
he was greatly pleased,
and immediately took off his own robes and gave them to him,
appointing him as Tàizhōng Dàfū.
At that time, the Emperor was particularly concerned about Lǒng and Shǔ,
and said exclusively to Shè:
"Now Xīzhōu has not yet submitted,
and Zǐyáng proclaims himself Emperor.
The roads are distant and difficult,
and the generals are currently occupied with Guāndōng.
I am thinking about a strategy for Xīzhōu,
but do not know whom to appoint.
What is your plan?"
Shè then volunteered, saying:
"Your servant once met Wěi Xiāo in Cháng'ān.
When that man first rose up,
he used 'Hàn' as his banner.
Now that Your Majesty's sagely virtue is flourishing,
your servant wishes to receive your mighty command,
and open up communication with him through sincere trust,
then Xiāo will surely surrender himself,
and the power of Shù, who is destined to perish,
will not be worth planning against."
The Emperor approved of this.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ
Shè first was sent as an envoy to Wěi Xiāo.
In the fifth year,
he again carried the imperial staff and accompanied Mǎ Yuán,
and then presented an imperial letter to Xiāo.
After he returned,
he went again to persuade Xiāo,
and Xiāo then sent his son Xún to accompany Shè as a hostage,
and appointed Shè as Zhōngláng Jiāng.
At this time, Shāndōng was mostly pacified,
and the Emperor planned to bring Wěi Xiāo's troops into his fold in the west,
and together attack Shǔ,
so he again sent Shè to convey his will.
Xiāo's general Wáng Yuán persuaded Xiāo,
raising many doubts and difficulties,
which caused him to hesitate for a long time and remain undecided.
Shè, being inherently firm and resolute,
became indignant and reproached Xiāo, saying:
"The state considers you to know right from wrong
and understand rise and fall,
hence it conveyed its intentions through a personal letter.
Your Excellency demonstrated loyalty and sincerity
by sending Bóchūn as a hostage;
this signified a relationship of trust between lord and subject.
Now you instead wish to follow the words of treacherous flatterers,
and plot for the extermination of your clan,
betraying your lord and abandoning your son,
and violating loyalty and trust?
The decision of fortune or misfortune
rests on this very day."
He wanted to stab Xiāo,
but Xiāo rose and went inside,
mustered his troops,
and was about to kill Shè.
Shè calmly held his staff and went to his carriage and departed.
Xiāo became even more enraged.
Wáng Yuán advised Xiāo to kill Shè,
and sent Niú Hán to lead troops to surround and guard him.
Xiāo's general Wáng Zūn remonstrated, saying:
"Your humble servant has heard that those who govern a state are careful with their reputation and authority,
and those who manage a family fear resentment and heavy misfortune.
If they are both careful with reputation and authority,
then their subordinates will obey their commands;
if they lightly incur resentment and misfortune,
then the family will suffer its calamity.
Now the general has sent his son as a hostage to Hàn,
but inwardly harbors other intentions;
his reputation and authority are already in reverse.
Outsiders are now discussing plotting against the Hàn envoy;
this is lightly incurring resentment and misfortune.
In ancient times, when states were at war,
an envoy would be allowed to pass between them.
This was to emphasize the gravity of war and the value of peace, rather than simply resorting to battle.
How much more so when he acts on the King's command and relies on a weighty hostage, yet is offended against?
Though Jūnshū has traveled far in a single carriage as an envoy,
he is also Your Majesty's maternal cousin.
Harming him will not diminish Hàn,
but will lead to the extermination of your clan.
In the past, Sòng seized a Chǔ envoy,
and consequently suffered the calamity of 'breaking bones for fuel and exchanging children for food.'
〔一０〕A small state could not be insulted,
how much less the lord of ten thousand chariots,
especially when it involves Bóchūn's life!"
Shè was a man of integrity and trustworthiness;
his words and actions were consistent.
When he traveled and persuaded,
everything could be verified,
and the gentry and officials of Xīzhōu all trusted and respected him,
many spoke on his behalf,
so he managed to escape and return east.
In the spring of the eighth year,
Shè and Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Jì Zūn attacked and captured Luèyáng.
Zūn fell ill on the way back,
and sent a detachment of elite troops with Shè,
totaling over two thousand men.
They cut down mountains and cooked their food,
passing through Fānxū and Huízhōng
directly to Luèyáng,
beheading Xiāo's defending general Jīn Liáng,
and then holding the city.
Xiāo was greatly alarmed and said:
"How divine is this!"
Then he mobilized tens of thousands of troops to besiege Luèyáng,
cutting down mountains and building dikes,
diverting water to flood the city.
Shè and his officers and soldiers held fast with grim determination,
and when their arrows were exhausted,
they tore down houses and cut wood to make weapons.
Xiāo attacked with all his might,
from spring to autumn,
his soldiers became exhausted.
The Emperor then massively dispatched troops from Guāndōng,
and personally led them up to Lǒng.
Xiāo's forces scattered and fled,
and the siege was lifted.
Thereupon, the Emperor held a grand banquet,
rewarding and honoring Shè,
who was seated above all the generals,
on a separate mat to their right.
Shè's wife was given a thousand bolts of silk.
An imperial edict ordered him to remain stationed in Cháng'ān,
and to oversee all the generals.
Shè then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Gōngsūn Shù used Lǒngxī and Tiānshuǐ as his shield,
thus he was able to prolong his life and temporarily survive.
Now that the two commanderies are pacified,
Shù's strategies and plans are exhausted.
It would be advisable to select more soldiers and horses,
and store up provisions and grain.
In the past, many of Zhào's generals were merchants,
and Gāodì rewarded them with heavy prizes.
Now that the western forces are broken,
the soldiers are weary and hungry.
If we recruit them with wealth and grain,
their numbers can be gathered.
Your servant knows that the state has many expenditures,
and resources are insufficient,
but there are times when it cannot be helped."
The Emperor approved of this.
Thereupon, a large amount of grain was transported,
and an edict ordered Shè to lead Zhēngxī Dàjiāngjūn Féng Yì, Jiànwēi Dàjiāngjūn Gěng Yǎn, Hǔyá Dàjiāngjūn Gài Yán, Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn Mǎ Chéng, and Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn Liú Shàng into Tiānshuǐ,
where they defeated Gōngsūn Shù's generals Tián Yǎn and Zhào Kuāng.
The following year,
they attacked and captured Luòmén.
Wěi Xiāo's adherents Zhōu Zōng and Zhào Huī, and the dependent counties of Tiānshuǐ, all surrendered.
Originally, during Wáng Mǎng's era,
many Qiāng barbarians rebelled,
but Wěi Xiāo attracted and embraced their chieftains,
thus gaining their service.
After Xiāo's demise,
the Wǔxī, Xiānlíng, and other tribes frequently committed raids,
all building moats and fortifications to defend themselves,
and the commanderies and prefectures could not suppress them.
Shè then extensively repaired siege equipment,
and led Gài Yán, Liú Shàng, and Tàizhōng Dàfū Mǎ Yuán, among others, to attack the Qiāng in Jīnchéng,
where they decisively defeated them,
beheading and capturing several thousand people,
and seizing over ten thousand cattle and sheep,
and hundreds of thousands of *hú* of grain.
He also defeated the bandits Fù Lìqīng and others in Xiāngwǔ.
Although Lǒngxī was pacified,
the people were hungry,
and refugees were seen everywhere.
Shè then emptied the granaries,
and transported provisions to various counties,
to relieve and support them,
whereupon Lǒngyòu became stable,
and Liángzhōu's communications were opened.
In the eleventh year,
Lái Xī, along with Gài Yán and Mǎ Chéng, advanced to attack Gōngsūn Shù’s generals Wáng Yuán and Huán Ān at Héchí and Xià [Biàn]
and captured them.
Taking advantage of the victory, they continued to advance.
The people of Shǔ were greatly alarmed
and sent assassins to stab Lái Xī.
Before he succumbed,
he urgently summoned Gài Yán.
When Yán saw Lái Xī,
he prostrated himself in sorrow,
unable to look up.
Lái Xī reprimanded Yán, saying:
"Hǔyá, how dare you act like this!
Now that I, your envoy, have been stabbed by assassins,
and cannot repay the nation,
I called you, Jùqīng,
to entrust you with military affairs.
Yet, you weep like a child!
Even with the blade in my body,
can I not command my troops to execute you?!"
Yán wiped away his tears and reluctantly rose,
receiving his instructions.
Lái Xī personally wrote a memorial, saying:
"Last night, after curfew,
I was wounded by an assailant,
who struck me in a vital spot.
I do not regret this for myself;
I truly regret that my service has been inadequate,
bringing shame upon the imperial court.
Governing the nation fundamentally relies on obtaining worthy individuals.
Tàizhōng Dàfū Duàn Xiāng
is upright and capable of responsibility.
I beg Your Majesty to examine this.
Furthermore, my brothers are unworthy
and I fear they may eventually incur guilt.
May Your Majesty pity them
and frequently provide guidance and instruction."
He threw down his brush, drew his blade, and died.
The Emperor was greatly astonished upon hearing this.
He read the memorial, wiping away tears,
and then bestowed a decree, saying:
"Zhōnglángjiāng Lái Xī
has fought in campaigns for many years,
pacifying Qiāng and Lǒng.
He worried for the nation and forgot his home;
his loyalty and filial piety are manifest.
He met his fate and was tragically killed!
Alas, how mournful!"
He sent the Tàizhōng Dàfū to posthumously appoint Lái Xī as Zhōnglángjiāng and confer upon him the seal and ribbon of the Zhēngqiāng Hóu,
with the posthumous title Jiéhóu.
An Yèzhě was dispatched to oversee the funeral arrangements.
When the coffin returned to Luòyáng,
the imperial carriage, in plain white mourning clothes, approached to offer condolences and attend the funeral.
Because Lái Xī had the merit of pacifying Qiāng and Lǒng,
the Dāngxiāng county of Rǔnán was changed to the state of Zhēngqiāng.
His son, Lái Bāo, inherited.
In the thirteenth year,
the Emperor commended Lái Xī’s loyalty and integrity,
and again enfeoffed Lái Xī’s younger brother, Lái Yóu, as Yíxī Hóu.
Lái Bāo’s son, Lái Líng,
married the daughter of Xiǎozōng, Princess Wǔ'ān.
Líng died young.
When Bāo died,
Líng’s son, Lái Lì, succeeded him.
The commentary states: The world called Lord Lái Jūnshū a man of great trustworthiness.
Indeed, when sent as an envoy between two nations,
how could one dislike deceptive strategies?
Yet, that he alone could be known for trustworthiness
was truly because his sincerity lay in ensuring the well-being of both parties
and not claiming personal credit for his achievements.
Lái Lì, whose courtesy name was Bózhēn,
inherited his title young.
As the son of a princess,
during the Yǒngyuán era,
he served as Shìzhōng,
supervising the Yǔlín Yòuqí.
In the third year of Yǒngchū,
he was promoted to Shèshēng Xiàowèi.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
he replaced Féng Shí as Zhíjīnwú.
In the first year of Yán'guāng,
Lái Lì’s mother was honored as a Cháng Gōngzhǔ.
In the second year,
Lái Lì was promoted to Tàipú.
The following year,
Zhōngchángshì Fán Fēng, along with Dàjiāngjūn Gěng Bǎo, Shìzhōng Zhōu Guǎng, Xiè Yùn, and others, conspired to falsely accuse Tàiwèi Yáng Zhèn.
Yáng Zhèn subsequently committed suicide.
Lái Lì said to Shìyùshǐ Yú Xǔ:
"Gěng Bǎo, relying on his kinship as a maternal uncle,
enjoys excessive favor and honor.
He does not remember to repay the nation's grace,
but instead allies with treacherous officials,
falsely accusing Lord Yáng,
and harming loyal and virtuous individuals.
Heaven's calamity will surely befall him soon."
Thereupon, he severed ties with Zhōu Guǎng and Xiè Yùn,
refusing to associate with them.
At that time, the crown prince was sick and uneasy,
and moved to the residence of Emperor Ān's wet nurse, the Lady of Yěwáng, Wáng Shèng.
The crown prince’s wet nurse, Wáng Nán, and the kitchen supervisor, Bǐng Jí, believed that Wáng Shèng’s residence, having been newly renovated,
violated earth taboos
and was not suitable for a long stay.
Wáng Shèng and her daughter, Wáng Yǒng, along with Dàchángqiú Jiāng Jīng and Zhōngchángshì Fán Fēng, Wáng Nán, Bǐng Jí, and others, engaged in mutual accusations.
Shèng and Yǒng then falsely accused Nán and Jí,
who were both imprisoned and died,
their families exiled to Bǐjǐng.
The crown prince missed Nán and others,
often sighing over them.
Jiāng Jīng and Fán Fēng feared future repercussions,
so they fabricated false accusations,
slandering the crown prince and the officials of the Eastern Palace.
The Emperor was enraged
and summoned the Gōngqīng and lower-ranking officials to a meeting to discuss his deposition.
Gěng Bǎo and others, following the imperial will,
all believed the crown prince should be deposed.
Lái Lì, along with Tàicháng Huán Yān and Tíngwèi Zhāng Hào, argued:
"The Classics state that
if one is not yet fifteen years old,
their grave faults are not attributed to them.
Moreover, regarding the schemes of Nán and Jí,
His Royal Highness may well have been unaware.
It is fitting to select loyal and virtuous guardians and tutors
to assist him with rites and righteousness.
The matter of deposition is weighty;
this is truly a decision that His Sacred Grace should carefully consider."
The Emperor did not comply,
and on that very day, deposed the crown prince as the King of Jìyīn.
At that time, the supervisor of the crown prince’s household, Xiǎo Huángmén Jí Jiàn, and Zhōngfù Gāo Fàn, and others
were all exiled to Shuòfāng without guilt.
Lái Lì then allied with Guānglùxūn Duì Fèng,
Zōngzhèng Liú Wěi,
Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng Xuē Hào,
Shìzhōng Lǘqiū Hóng, Chén Guāng, Zhào Dài, Shī Yán,
Tàizhōng Dàfū Zhū Chāng,
Dìwǔ Jié,
Zhōngsǎn Dàfū Cáo Chéng,
Jiànyì Dàfū Lǐ Yóu,
Fújié Lìng Zhāng Jìng,
Chíshū Shìyùshǐ Gōng Diào,
Yǔlín Yòujiān Kǒng Xiǎn,
Chéngmén Sīmǎ Xú Chóng,
Wèiwèi Shǒuchéng Yuè Wéi,
and more than ten others, including Chánglè and Wèiyāng Lìng Zhèng Ānshì,
all went to Hóngdū Mén to attest to the crown prince's innocence.
Gōng Diào, based on the law, clearly stated
that while Nán and Jí were guilty,
the crown prince should not be implicated.
The Emperor and his attendants were troubled by this,
and so he sent a Zhōngchángshì with an imperial decree to threaten the assembled officials, saying:
"Father and son are one body,
a natural heavenly disposition.
To sever this affection for righteousness
is for the sake of all under heaven.
Lái Lì, Duì Fèng, and others do not understand the great principles,
and instead join with petty men in clamor.
Outwardly they appear loyal and upright, but inwardly they hope for future favor.
To adorn falsehood and defy righteousness,
how can this be the proper conduct of serving a ruler?
The court has broadly opened the path for speaking out,
so for now, we shall temporarily pardon all;
but if you persist in your delusion and do not repent,
the punishments of the law will be clearly applied."
Those who remonstrated all turned pale.
Xuē Hào was the first to kowtow, saying:
"Indeed, it should be as the clear decree states."
Lái Lì was displeased
and publicly questioned Xuē Hào, saying:
"What did you say when we remonstrated together just now?
And now you go back on it?
How can a high minister, riding in the court carriage
and handling state affairs,
be so fickle?!"
Thereupon, the others gradually excused themselves,
but Lái Lì alone remained at the palace gate,
refusing to leave for days.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and thereupon dismissed Lái Lì and his brothers from their offices,
reduced their state revenues,
and forbade the princess from meeting them.
Lái Lì then secluded himself, not communicating with relatives,
and people at the time were filled with trepidation because of him.
When the emperor died,
Empress Dì Yán 閻太后 appointed Lì 歷 as Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng 將作大匠.
When Emperor Shùn 順帝 ascended the throne,
the court all acclaimed him a minister of the state,
so he was promoted to Wèiwèi 衞尉.
Dòu Fěng 祋諷, Liú Wěi 劉瑋, Lǘqiū Hóng 閭丘弘, and others had died earlier,
and their sons were all appointed Láng 郎;
Zhū Chāng 朱倀,
Shī Yán 施延, Chén Guāng 陳光, Zhào Dài 趙代, and others all became Gōngqīng 公卿,
and held positions;
the families of Wáng Nán 王男 and Bǐng Jí 邴吉 were summoned back to the Jīngshī 京師,
and richly rewarded;
Jí Jiàn 籍建, Gāo Fàn 高梵, and others were all notably promoted.
In Yǒngjiàn 永建元年,
Lì 歷 was appointed Chēqí Jiāngjūn 車騎將軍,
his younger brother Zhǐ 祉 was appointed Bùbīng Xiàowèi 步兵校尉,
and Chāo 超 was appointed Huángmén Shìláng 黃門侍郎.
In the third year,
his mother, the Cháng Gōngzhǔ 長公主, died,
and Lì 歷 claimed illness and returned to his residence;
after the mourning period ended,
he was reinstated as Dàhónglú 大鴻臚.
In Yángjiā 陽嘉二年,
he died in office.
His son Dìng 定 inherited.
Dìng 定 married Empress Ān's 安帝 younger sister, Princess Píngshì Cháng Gōngzhǔ 平氏長公主;
during Emperor Shùn's 順帝 time,
he served as Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng 虎賁中郎將.
When Dìng 定 died,
his son Hǔ 虎 inherited;
during Emperor Huán's 桓帝 time,
he served as Túnqí Xiàowèi 屯騎校尉.
His younger brother Yàn 豔,
courtesy name Jìdé 季德,
was fond of learning and associating with scholars from a young age.
He opened a school to teach students;
he held prominent positions from a young age;
during Emperor Líng's 靈帝 time,
he was twice promoted to Sīkōng 司空.
Eulogy says: Lǐ 李 and Dèng 鄧 were generous and wealthy,
leaving their homes to follow the prophecy.
Although Shàogōng 少公 gained trust,
Zōngqīng 宗卿 was not yet proven.
Wáng Cháng 王常 knew his destiny,
his功 was merely the emperor's thought.
The sincere Jūnshū 君叔,
his words were without blemish.
About to offer three victories,
forever dropping one sword.
Biography of Dèng Kòu 列傳第六 (Dèng Yǔ's 鄧禹 son Xùn 訓, grandson Zhì 騭; Kòu Xún's 寇恂 great-grandson Róng 榮)
Dèng Yǔ 鄧禹, courtesy name Zhònghuá 仲華,
was from Xīnyě 新野, Nányáng 南陽.
At thirteen,
he could recite the Shī 詩, and studied in Cháng'ān 長安.
At that time, Guāngwǔ 光武 also traveled to the Jīngshī 京師 to study.
Although Yǔ 禹 was young,
he recognized Guāngwǔ 光武 as an extraordinary person,
and so they became close.
After several years, he returned home.
When the Hàn 漢 army rose,
and Gēngshǐ 更始 was established,
many heroes recommended Yǔ 禹,
but Yǔ 禹 refused to follow.
When he heard that Guāngwǔ 光武 was pacifying Héběi 河北,
he immediately took his staff and crossed north,
catching up with him in Yè 鄴.
Guāngwǔ 光武 was very pleased to see him,
and said:
"I can personally grant titles and appointments.
You have come a long way;
do you wish to serve?"
Yǔ 禹 replied:
"I do not."
Guāngwǔ 光武 said:
"If so,
what do you wish to do?"
Yǔ 禹 said:
"I only wish that your honored lord's prestige and virtue extend throughout the Four Seas,
and that I, Yǔ 禹, may contribute a small measure
and have my merits recorded in history."
Guāngwǔ 光武 smiled,
and thereupon kept him to stay and chat privately.
Yǔ 禹 then advised:
"Although Gēngshǐ 更始 has made his capital in Guānxī 關西,
Shāndōng 山東 is not yet peaceful.
The Chìméi 赤眉, Qīngdú 青犢, and others,
number in the tens of thousands.
The Sānfǔ 三輔 are claiming titles,
gathering in groups everywhere.
Gēngshǐ 更始 has not yet suffered a setback,
but he does not make his own decisions;
his generals are all mediocre men who rose from obscurity,
interested in wealth and currency,
contending to use power and force,
only seeking their own satisfaction day and night.
There are none who are loyal, wise,
far-sighted, and deeply planning,
who wish to honor their lord and pacify the people.
The four directions are collapsing and splitting apart;
the situation is evident.
Although your honored lord has established the功 of a藩輔,
I fear he will have nothing established.
For the present plan,
nothing is better than to attract heroes,
endeavor to please the people's hearts,
establish the enterprise of Gāozǔ 高祖,
and save the lives of the myriad people.
For you, sir, to worry about the world,
it is not enough to stabilize it."
Guāngwǔ 光武 was greatly pleased,
and thereupon ordered his attendants to call Yǔ 禹 'General Dèng 鄧'.
He often stayed and lodged with him,
and discussed plans with him.
When Wáng Láng 王郎 started his uprising,
Guāngwǔ 光武 traveled from Jì 薊 to Xìndū 信都,
and sent Yǔ 禹 to gather troops,
obtaining several thousand men,
whom he ordered to lead himself,
and separately attack and capture Lèyáng 樂陽.
Following him to Guǎng'ā 廣阿,
Guāngwǔ 光武 lodged on the city tower,
unrolled a map,
and pointed to Yǔ 禹, saying:
"The prefectures and kingdoms of the world are like this;
now we have only just obtained one of them.
You previously said that with my worry, the world would not be enough to stabilize.
Why?"
Yǔ 禹 replied:
"At present, the realm is in chaos,
people long for an enlightened ruler,
like an infant yearns for its loving mother.
Those who rose in ancient times
depended on the depth of their virtue,
not on the size of their territory."
Guāngwǔ 光武 was pleased.
At that time, when appointing generals,
he often consulted Yǔ 禹;
whenever Yǔ 禹 recommended someone,
they always matched their talent,
and Guāngwǔ 光武 considered him to be a judge of character.
He sent him to lead cavalry separately,
and with Gài Yán 蓋延 and others, attack the Tóngmǎ 銅馬 at Qīngyáng 清陽.
Gài Yán 蓋延 and others arrived first,
fought unfavorably,
and returned to defend the city,
where they were besieged by the rebels.
Yǔ 禹 then advanced and fought with them,
defeating them,
and capturing their great general alive.
He followed Guāngwǔ 光武 in pursuing the rebels to Púyáng 蒲陽,
achieving great victories,
and the northern region was largely pacified.
When the Chìméi 赤眉 entered Guān 關 from the west,
Gēngshǐ 更始 sent Dìngguó Shànggōng 定國上公 Wáng Kuāng 王匡, Xiāngyì Wáng Chéng Dān 襄邑王成丹, Kàngwēi Jiāngjūn 抗威將軍 Liú Jūn 劉均, and other generals,
to divide and occupy Hédōng 河東 and Hóngnóng 弘農 to resist them.
The Chìméi 赤眉 assembled in great numbers,
and Wáng Kuāng 王匡 and others could not withstand them.
Guāngwǔ 光武 calculated that the Chìméi 赤眉 would surely defeat Cháng'ān 長安,
and wished to seize the opportunity to incorporate Guānzhōng 關中,
but was currently occupied with Shāndōng 山東.
Unsure whom to entrust,
he considered Yǔ 禹 profound and magnanimous,
so he entrusted him with the strategy for the western campaign.
He then appointed him Qián Jiāngjūn 護軍 with a staff of authority,
divided his elite troops of 20,000 men,
sent them west into Guān 關,
and ordered him to select his own subcommanders and others who could go with him.
Thereupon, he appointed Hán Xīn 韓歆 as Jūnshī 軍師,
Lǐ Wén 李文, Lǐ Chūn 李春, Chéng Lǜ 程慮 as Jìjiǔ 祭酒,
Féng Yīn 馮愔 as Jīnú Jiāngjūn 積弩將軍,
Fán Chóng 樊崇 as Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn 驍騎將軍,
Zōng Xīn 宗歆 as Chēqí Jiāngjūn 車騎將軍,
Dèng Xún 鄧尋 as Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn 建威將軍,
Gěng Xīn 耿訢 as Chìméi Jiāngjūn 赤眉將軍,
Zuǒ Yú 左于 as Jūnshī Jiāngjūn 軍師將軍,
and led them west.
In the first month of the first year of Jiànwǔ,
Yǔ, starting from Jīguān, was about to enter Hédōng.
The Hédōng Dūwèi guarding the pass did not open it.
Yǔ attacked for ten days,
breached it,
and captured over a thousand wagons of supplies.
He then besieged Ānyì,
but could not take it for several months.
Gēngshǐ's Dàjiāngjūn Fán Cān, with tens of thousands of men,
crossed Dàyáng, intending to attack Yǔ.
Yǔ sent his generals to intercept and attack them south of Xiè,
defeating them utterly,
and beheading Cān.
Thereupon Wáng Kuāng, Chéng Dān, Liú Jūn and others gathered an army of over one hundred thousand,
and again attacked Yǔ.
Yǔ's army was at a disadvantage,
and Fán Chóng was killed in battle.
As night fell,
the battle ended.
The army strategist Hán Xīn and the various generals, seeing that the military situation was already broken,
all urged Yǔ to leave by night.
Yǔ did not listen.
The next day, guǐhài,
Kuāng and the others did not venture out, as it was a "qióng rì" (exhausted day) of the "liù jiǎ" cycle.
Yǔ thus managed to reorganize his troops and marshall his forces.
The next morning,
Kuāng led his entire army out to attack Yǔ.
Yǔ ordered his army not to move recklessly;
when they reached the camp,
he then ordered his generals to beat their drums and advance simultaneously,
utterly defeating them.
Kuāng and the others all abandoned their armies and fled.
Yǔ led light cavalry in a swift pursuit,
capturing Liú Jūn, the Hédōng Tàishǒu Yáng Bǎo, and the Chíjié Zhōnglángjiàng Mí Qiáng,
and beheading them all.
He seized six jǐe (credentials),
five hundred seal cords,
and countless weapons.
Thus, Hédōng was pacified.
Acting on imperial authority, he appointed Lǐ Wén as Hédōng Tàishǒu,
and entirely replaced the prefects and chiefs of the dependent counties to govern and pacify them.
That month,
Guāngwǔ ascended the throne at Qū,
and sent an envoy with a jǐe to appoint Yǔ as Dàsītú.
The imperial edict read:
"An edict to the former Jiāngjūn Yǔ: You uphold loyalty and filial piety deeply,
and have consulted with Us in the strategizing tent,
deciding victory a thousand lǐ away.
Confucius said: 'Since I have had Huí,
my disciples have become daily closer.'
You have beheaded generals, broken armies,
and pacified Shānxī,
your meritorious achievements are especially prominent.
If the people are not affectionate,
and the five relationships are not cultivated,
you shall serve as Sītú,
respectfully spreading the five teachings.
The five teachings lie in leniency.
We now send the Fèngchē Dūwèi to bestow the seal and cord,
enfeoffing you as Énhóu,
with an income of ten thousand households.
Be reverent!"
Yǔ was then twenty-four years old.
He then crossed the Fén'yīn River,
and entered Xiàyáng.
Gēngshǐ's Zhōnglángjiāng Zuǒfǔ Dūwèi Gōngchéng Shè,
leading his tens of thousands of men,
together with the troops of Zuǒfēngyì, resisted Yǔ at Yá.
Yǔ again defeated and routed them.
And the Chìméi then entered Cháng'ān.
At this time, the Sānfǔ had suffered repeated defeats,
and the Chìméi left devastation wherever they passed.
The common people did not know where to turn.
Hearing that Yǔ had achieved victories alone while advancing with discipline,
they all carried and supported each other to welcome his army, like wind.
The number of surrendering people increased by thousands daily,
and his forces were said to number a million.
Wherever Yǔ stopped, he would halt his chariot and hold his jǐe,
to console and welcome them.
Elders and children,
with flowing hair and white heads,
filled the space beneath his chariot,
all felt grateful and joyful.
Thus, his fame shook Guānxī.
The Emperor admired him,
and frequently sent letters praising him.
All the generals and heroes urged Yǔ to attack Cháng'ān directly.
Yǔ said:
"No.
Although our forces are numerous now,
few are capable fighters.
We have no accumulated provisions in front of us,
nor any means of transport for supplies behind us.
The Chìméi have just captured Cháng'ān;
their wealth and resources are abundant,
and their sharp edge cannot yet be withstood.
Bandits gather together,
without plans for the whole day.
Even if their grain is plentiful,
with countless unexpected changes,
how can they hold out firmly?
The three commanderies of Shàngjùn, Běidì, and Āndìng,
have vast land and sparse population,
with abundant grain and livestock.
I shall temporarily rest our troops on the northern route,
acquire provisions and train soldiers,
to observe their weaknesses,
then we can plan."
Thereupon, he led his army north to Xúnyì.
Wherever Yǔ went,
he defeated the various camps and strongholds of the Chìméi's separate generals,
and the commanderies and counties all opened their gates and submitted.
Xīhé Tàishǒu Zōng Yù sent his son to present a dispatch and surrender.
Yǔ sent him to the capital.
The Emperor, seeing that Guānzhōng was not yet pacified,
and Yǔ had not advanced his troops for a long time,
issued an edict:
"Sītú,
you are like Yáo;
the fleeing bandits,
are like Jié.
The officials and people of Cháng'ān,
are anxious and without support.
You should advance and suppress them in due time,
pacify and comfort Xījīng,
and win the hearts of the people."
Yǔ still held to his previous intention,
and thus separately dispatched generals to attack the various counties of Shàngjùn,
further recruiting soldiers and transporting grain,
and returned to Dàyào.
He sent Féng Yīn and Zōng Xīn to guard Xúnyì.
The two men contended for power and attacked each other.
Yīn then killed Xīn,
and subsequently turned to attack Yǔ.
Yǔ sent an envoy to report this to the Emperor.
The Emperor asked the envoy:
"Who is Yīn's close confidant?"
The envoy replied:
"The Hùjūn Huáng Fáng."
The Emperor judged that Yīn and Fáng could not long remain harmonious,
and would inevitably come into conflict.
He then replied to Yǔ:
"The one who binds Féng Yīn,
will surely be Huáng Fáng."
He then sent Shàngshū Zōng Guǎng with a jǐe to receive their surrender.
More than a month later,
Fáng indeed seized Yīn,
and led his followers to confess their crime.
All of Gēngshǐ's generals, Wáng Kuāng, Hú Yīn (and Chéng Dān), etc., all came to Guǎng to surrender,
and returned east with him.
Upon reaching Ānyì,
they attempted to flee on the way,
and Guǎng beheaded them all.
Yīn reached Luòyáng,
was pardoned and not executed.
In the spring of the second year,
an envoy was sent to re-enfeoff Yǔ as Liánghóu,
with an income from four counties.
At this time, the Chìméi fled west to Fúfēng.
Yǔ then went south to Cháng'ān,
camped at Kūnmíng Chí,
and held a grand feast for his soldiers.
He led his generals in ritual purification and fasting,
selected an auspicious day,
performed rites and offered sacrifices at the Gāomiào (High Temple),
collected the spirit tablets of the eleven emperors,
and sent envoys to respectfully deliver them to Luòyáng.
He then inspected the imperial tombs and parks,
and appointed officials and soldiers to guard them.
Yǔ ēn led his troops to battle Yán Cén at Lántián,
but was unsuccessful,
and returned to gather provisions at Yúnyáng.
Liú Jiā, King of Hànzhōng, went to Yǔ ēn and surrendered.
Jiā's chancellor, Lǐ Bǎo, was arrogant and disrespectful,
so Yǔ ēn beheaded him.
Bǎo's younger brother gathered Bǎo's subordinates and attacked Yǔ ēn,
killing General Gěng Xīn.
Since Fèng Yīn's rebellion,
Yǔ ēn's prestige gradually declined,
and he also lacked food,
so those who had joined him dispersed.
Then the Chìméi returned to Cháng'ān.
Yǔ ēn fought them,
was defeated and fled,
reaching Gāolíng.
The soldiers were starving,
and all ate jujubes and wild vegetables.
The Emperor then summoned Yǔ ēn back,
issuing an edict that said:
"The Chìméi have no provisions;
they will naturally come eastward.
I will break a switch and flog them;
this is not for my generals to worry about.
You must not advance troops rashly again."
Yǔ ēn was ashamed that he had been entrusted with a task but had not succeeded.
He repeatedly engaged in battles with his starving troops,
but always met with defeat.
In the spring of the third year,
he and the General of Cavalry and Chariots, Dèng Hóng, attacked the Chìméi,
and were utterly defeated by them.
His forces all died or scattered.
The details are in the biography of Fény Yì.
He alone, with twenty-four cavalrymen, returned to Yíyáng,
and offered to return his seals of Grand Minister of Works and Marquis of Liáng to the Emperor.
An imperial edict ordered him to keep his marquisate seals.
A few months later,
he was appointed General of the Right.
Yán Cén, after his defeat at Dōngyáng,
then allied with Qín Fēng.
In the spring of the fourth year,
they again raided the area around Shùnyáng.
The Emperor dispatched Yǔ ēn to oversee the Restoring-Hàn General Dèng Yè and the Assisting-Hàn General Yú Kuāng,
who defeated Cén at Dèng.
Pursuing him to Wǔdāng,
they defeated him again.
Cén fled to Hànzhōng,
and his remaining followers all surrendered.
In the thirteenth year,
the realm was pacified.
All meritorious officials had their households and fiefs increased.
Yǔ ēn was formally enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāomì,
with the four counties of Gāomì, Chāng'ān, Yí'ān, and Chúnyú as his stipend.
The Emperor, considering Yǔ ēn's great achievements,
enfeoffed his younger brother Kuān as Marquis of Míngqīn.
Thereafter, the positions of General of the Left and Right were abolished,
and he was given the title of Special Advance, attending court.
Yǔ ēn was intelligent and cultured within,
with a sincere and complete conduct.
He was extremely filial to his mother.
After the realm was settled,
he always sought to distance himself from fame and power.
He had thirteen sons,
each of whom he taught a specific art.
He kept his household in order,
and raised and educated his sons and grandsons,
all of whom could serve as models for later generations.
He used his wealth from the state and fief,
but did not engage in profitable enterprises.
The Emperor respected him even more.
In the first year of Zhōngyuán,
he again served as Grand Minister of Works, accompanying the Eastern巡狩,
and performed the Fēng and Dài sacrifices.
When Xiǎnzōng ascended the throne,
considering Yǔ ēn's foundational achievements for the late emperor,
he appointed him Grand Tutor,
allowing him to face east when received in audience,
and showed him great respect and favor.
After a year or so,
he fell ill.
The Emperor repeatedly visited him to inquire about his condition,
and appointed two of his sons as Lang officials.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng,
at the age of fifty-seven, he passed away,
and was posthumously granted the title of Yuán Marquis.
The Emperor divided Yǔ ēn's fief into three states: his eldest son, Zhèn, became Marquis of Gāomì;
Xí succeeded as Marquis of Chāng'ān;
and Zhēn became Marquis of Yí'ān.
Yǔ ēn's youngest son, Hóng,
was good at strategy and planning.
During the Yǒngpíng reign,
he was appointed a minor marquis.
He was brought in to discuss frontier affairs,
and the Emperor, recognizing his ability,
appointed him Chief Clerk to the General Commanding Troops,
leading five battalions of soldiers to garrison at Yànmén.
During Sùzōng's time,
he served as General Crossing the Liao River.
In the Yǒngyuán reign,
he accompanied Grand General Dòu Xiàn in attacking the Xiongnú,
and performed meritorious service.
He was then recalled and appointed General of Cavalry and Chariots.
He pursued the rebellious Hú leader Fèng Hóu beyond the frontier,
but was imprisoned and died for delaying.
When Marquis of Gāomì, Zhèn, died,
his son, Gān, succeeded him.
Gān married Princess Qìnshuǐ, the Emperor's daughter.
In the fourteenth year of Yǒngyuán,
the incident of Empress Yīn's witchcraft was exposed.
Gān's cousin, Fèng, was executed as the Empress's maternal uncle,
and Gān was implicated,
leading to the abolition of his state.
In the first year of Yuánxīng,
Emperor Hé restored Gān to his original state,
and appointed him Attendant-in-Ordinary.
When Gān died,
his son, Chéng, succeeded him.
When Chéng died,
his son, Bāo, succeeded him.
Bāo married Princess Wǔyīn, Emperor Ān's younger sister,
and served as Minor Minister of the Treasury during Emperor Huán's reign.
When Bāo died,
his eldest son, Mǒu, succeeded him.
His youngest son, Chāng, inherited his mother's title as Marquis of Wǔyīn,
and was appointed Palace Attendant.
The successor of Marquis of Chāng'ān, Xí, was Fān.
He also married Princess Pínggāo, Emperor Xiǎnzōng's daughter,
and served as Attendant-in-Ordinary during Emperor Hé's reign.
The son of Marquis of Yí'ān, Zhēn, was Kāng,
who showed integrity in his youth.
His elder brother, Liáng, inherited the fief,
but had no heir.
In the sixth year of Yǒngchū,
Kāng was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Yí'ān.
At that time, those who were re-enfeoffed received half the rent of their former states.
Kāng, being a relative of the Empress Dowager,
uniquely received two-thirds of the rent.
As an Attendant Marquis,
he was appointed Commandant of Elite Cavalry.
Kāng, seeing that the Empress Dowager had long overseen court affairs,
and her clan was prosperous and numerous,
repeatedly submitted memorials to the Chánglè Palace, admonishing and arguing
that the imperial house should be strengthened,
and private power should be diminished.
His words were very earnest and heartfelt.
The Empress Dowager did not heed him.
Kāng felt fear in his heart.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
he excused himself from court on the pretext of illness.
The Empress Dowager sent an internal attendant to inquire about him.
At that time, many palace servants who went in and out
were able to praise or disparage others,
and among them, the elders all called themselves "Middle Adults".
The one sent was a former maid from Kāng's family,
who also referred to herself as "Middle Adult".
When Kāng heard this,
he scolded her,
saying:
"You came from my household;
how dare you act like that!"
The maid, resentful and angry,
returned and reported that Kāng was feigning illness and had spoken disrespectfully.
The Empress Dowager was furious,
and consequently dismissed Kāng from office,
sent him back to his state,
and removed him from the imperial clan registry.
When his cousin, Zhì, was executed,
Emperor Ān summoned Kāng to be Attendant-in-Ordinary.
When Emperor Shùn ascended the throne,
he was appointed Grand Coachman,
gaining a reputation for uprightness and integrity,
and was highly regarded at court.
He was dismissed due to illness,
and given the additional title of Special Advance.
He died in the third year of Yángjiā,
and was posthumously granted the title of Yì Marquis.
The encomium states: In times of change and adaptation,
when ruler and minister choose each other,
this is truly the crucial moment for undertaking affairs and planning beginnings.
Duke Dèng, carrying provisions and traveling on foot,
braved chaos to go to Guāngwǔ,
which can be said to be knowing where to converge.
Thereupon, he divided his army into two,
to overlook the passes west of the mountains,
to the extent that the passes and rivers resounded,
and people hastened to him as if returning home.
Although his achievements were not fully realized,
his principles were grand!
And when his prestige waned at Xúnyì,
and his troops scattered at Yíyáng,
