he shed his splendid imperial attire in the morning,
and resumed the attire of a marquis for the rest of the year.
With honor and disgrace intertwined, his subordinates showed no second thoughts;
with advancement and retreat used, his superior harbored no suspicion.
This made the virtue between ruler and minister
such that later generations could not glimpse any flaw between them.
Is this not the achievement of a gentleman!
Dèng Xùn (訓), styled Píngshū (平叔),
was the sixth son of Yǔ (禹).
From a young age, he had great ambitions
and did not like literary studies.
Yǔ (禹) often criticized him for this.
When Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) ascended the throne,
he was initially made a Lángzhōng (郎中).
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) was generous in bestowing favors upon scholars,
and many officials and gentry consequently attached themselves to him.
In the Yǒngpíng (永平) period,
he was tasked with managing the Hútúo (虖沱) and Shíjiù (石臼) Rivers,
from Dūlǜ (都慮) to Yángcháng (羊腸) Granary,
with the aim of making them navigable for transport.
The officials and people of Tàiyuán (太原) suffered from the forced labor,
and after successive years, nothing was achieved.
The transportation route passed through three hundred eighty-nine difficult passes,
and the number of those who drowned or died before and after was innumerable.
In Jiànchū (建初) 3rd year,
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) was appointed Yèzhě (謁者)
and sent to supervise the project.
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) carefully assessed and considered the situation,
knowing that such a great undertaking would be difficult to accomplish.
He then submitted a detailed report to the emperor.
Sùzōng (肅宗) followed his advice
and subsequently halted the project.
Instead, donkeys and carts were used for transport.
This saved expenses amounting to hundreds of millions each year
and saved the lives of several thousand laborers and soldiers.
The Taishou (太守) of Xiègǔ (楔W谷), Rèn Xīng (任興), wanted to execute the Chìshā Wūhuán (赤沙烏桓).
The Wūhuán (烏桓) harbored resentment and plotted rebellion.
An imperial edict ordered Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) to lead the Lìyáng (黎陽) garrison troops to station at Húnú (狐奴)
to prevent any uprising.
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) treated the border residents kindly,
and was thus welcomed by the Yōu (幽) region.
In the 6th year,
he was promoted to Hù Wūhuán Xiàowèi (護烏桓校尉).
Many former residents of Lìyáng (黎陽) brought their elderly and children,
happily following Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) to resettle on the border.
The Xiānbēi (鮮卑), hearing of his authority and benevolence,
all dared not approach south of the frontier.
In the 8th year,
Liáng Hù (梁扈), the son of Wǔyīn (舞陰) Princess, committed a crime.
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) was implicated for privately exchanging letters with Liáng Hù (梁扈),
and was summoned, dismissed, and returned to his hometown.
In Yuánhé (元和) 3rd year,
when the Lúshuǐ Hú (盧水胡) rebelled,
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) was appointed Yèzhě (謁者).
He traveled by imperial post to Wǔwēi (武威)
and was appointed Taishou (太守) of Zhāngyè (張掖).
In Zhānghé (章和) 2nd year,
Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi (護羌校尉) Zhāng Yū (張紆) lured and executed Míwú (迷吾) and other leaders of the Shāodāng Qiāng (燒當種羌).
Because of this, the various Qiāng (羌) were greatly angered
and plotted to avenge themselves.
The imperial court was concerned about this.
The Gōngqīng (公卿) recommended Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) to replace Zhāng Yū (張紆) as Xiàowèi (校尉).
The Qiāng (羌) were enraged
and consequently allied with each other, forming marriage ties,
exchanging hostages, and swearing oaths.
Their forces numbered over forty thousand,
intending to cross the river and attack Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) when the ice solidified.
Previously, the Xiǎoyuèzhī Hú (小月氏胡) were divided and resided within the frontier.
Those capable of fighting numbered two to three thousand cavalry,
all brave, strong, and wealthy.
Whenever they fought the Qiāng (羌),
they often defeated the many with the few.
Although they often played both sides,
the Hàn (漢) also sometimes made use of them.
At that time, Mítáng (迷唐), the son of Míwú (迷吾),
separately joined forces with the Wǔwēi (武威) branch of the Qiāng (羌), forming a force of ten thousand cavalry.
They arrived at the frontier,
but dared not attack Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) directly,
first wanting to coerce the Yuèzhī Hú (月氏胡).
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) held back and restrained the Yuèzhī Hú (月氏胡),
preventing them from fighting.
Those who deliberated all said that if the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) attacked each other,
it would be to the government's advantage,
using barbarians to fight barbarians,
and there was no need to prohibit or protect them.
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) said:
"That is not so.
Now Zhāng Yū (張紆) has lost trust,
and the various Qiāng (羌) are greatly agitated.
Regular garrison troops
number no less than twenty thousand,
and the cost of transport
has depleted the government treasury.
The officials and people of Liángzhōu (涼州)
have their lives hanging by a thread.
The reason why the various Hú (胡) have been difficult to win over
is entirely due to insufficient benevolence and trust.
Now, taking advantage of their urgent predicament,
if we treat them with virtue,
perhaps they can be of use."
He then ordered the city gates and the gates of their residential compounds to be opened,
and had all the Hú (胡) women and children driven inside,
with heavily armed guards protecting them.
The Qiāng (羌) looted nothing,
and also dared not approach the various Hú (胡),
so they consequently withdrew.
Because of this, the various Hú (胡) in Huángzhōng (湟中)
all said:
"The Hàn (漢) government always wanted us to fight each other,
but now Governor Dèng (鄧使君) treats us with benevolence and trust,
opening the gates to admit our wives and children,
truly like our own parents."
All were joyful and kowtowed, saying:
"We will obey whatever the Governor commands."
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) then fostered and raised several hundred brave young men among them,
making them his Yìcóng (義從) (righteous followers).
It was the custom of the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) to feel ashamed of dying from illness.
Whenever they were critically ill,
they would stab themselves with a blade.
When Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) heard of anyone gravely ill,
he would immediately detain and restrain them,
not giving them weapons,
and had doctors treat them.
More than one recovered,
and all, young and old, were moved and pleased.
Thereupon, he rewarded and bribed various Qiāng (羌) tribes,
encouraging them to invite and attract others.
Hàowú (號吾), the paternal uncle of Mítáng (迷唐), then brought his mother and eight hundred households of his people
to surrender from beyond the frontier.
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) then mobilized four thousand Qín (秦), Hú (胡), and Qiāng (羌) soldiers from Huángzhōng (湟中),
went beyond the frontier to ambush Mítáng (迷唐) in Xiěgǔ (寫谷),
beheading and capturing over six hundred people,
and obtaining over ten thousand horses, cattle, and sheep.
Mítáng (迷唐) then left Dàyú (大榆) and Xiǎoyú (小榆),
residing in the arduous Yángǔ (巖谷),
his forces completely scattered.
That spring,
Mítáng (迷唐) again wanted to return to his former lands to resume agriculture.
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) then mobilized six thousand men from Huángzhōng (湟zhōng),
ordering Changshi (長史) Rèn Shàng (任尚) to lead them.
They sewed leather to make boats,
placed them on rafts to cross the river,
and ambushed Mítáng's (迷唐) encampments and major chieftains,
killing and capturing many.
They then pursued the fleeing enemies.
Coincidentally, Rèn Shàng (任尚) and others were attacked by the Qiāng (羌) at night.
Thereupon, the Yìcóng Qiāng (義從羌) and Hú (胡) combined their strength and defeated them,
beheading over eighteen hundred enemies in total,
capturing two thousand living people,
and over thirty thousand horses, cattle, and sheep.
One tribe was almost completely annihilated.
Mítáng (迷唐) then gathered his remaining forces
and moved his encampment far away,
traveling over a thousand li to the west.
All the allied smaller tribes then deserted him.
Dōnghào (東號), the chieftain of Shāodāng (燒當), prostrated himself and surrendered, ready for death.
The rest all submitted and offered hostages at the frontier.
Thereupon, Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) received and welcomed those who came to pledge allegiance,
and his authority and trust became widely known.
He then disbanded the garrison troops,
ordering each to return to their respective commanderies.
Only two thousand enfeoffed criminals were retained,
divided for garrison farming,
cultivating land for the poor,
and repairing city walls and fortified villages.
In Yǒngyuán (永元) 2nd year, Dàjiàngjūn (大將軍) Dòu Xiàn (竇憲) led troops to garrison Wǔwēi (武威).
Dòu Xiàn (竇憲), knowing Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) was familiar with the strategies concerning the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡),
memorialized the emperor to let Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) accompany him.
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) had initially been close to the Mǎ (馬) clan,
and was not favored by the Dòu (竇) family.
When Dòu Xiàn (竇憲) was executed,
Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) therefore did not escape the misfortune.
Although Dèng Xùn (鄧訓) was tolerant and accommodating to the public,
he was very strict within his own household.
None of his brothers dared to be disrespectful.
When his sons came to see him,
he never granted them a seat or treated them with a warm demeanor.
In the winter of the 4th year,
he died in office at the age of fifty-three.
At that time,
officials, common people, Qiāng (羌), and Hú (胡) all cherished him.
Thousands would visit daily, morning and evening.
It was the custom of the barbarians that when their parents died,
they considered it shameful to weep with grief,
and would all ride horses and sing and shout.
Yet, upon hearing of Dèng Xùn's (鄧訓) death,
none did not roar and wail.
Some even cut themselves with knives,
and also stabbed and killed their dogs, horses, cattle, and sheep,
saying:
"Governor Dèng (鄧使君) is dead,
we too shall all die with him."
Former Wūhuán (烏桓) officials and soldiers all fled along the roads,
to the point of emptying the cities and fortified areas.
Officials tried to stop them,
and reported the situation to Xiàowèi (校尉) Xú Yǎn (徐傿).
Xú Yǎn (徐傿) sighed and said:
"This is righteousness."
Then he released them.
Consequently, every household built a shrine for Dèng Xùn (鄧訓),
and whenever there was illness,
they would pray there for blessings.
In the first year of Yuánxīng,
Emperor Hé, considering Xùn as the father of Empress Xùn,
sent an imperial messenger with a staff of authority to Xùn's tomb,
bestowing an imperial edict to posthumously enfeoff him,
and giving him the posthumous title Píngshòu Jìnghóu.
The Empress Dowager personally attended,
and all officials gathered.
Xùn had five sons: Zhì,
Jīng,
Kuī,
Hóng,
and Chāng.
Zhì, whose courtesy name was Zhāobó,
was early on invited to serve in the household of the Great General Dòu Xiàn.
When his younger sister became a Guìrén,
Zhì and his brothers were all appointed Lángzhōng.
When the Guìrén was enthroned,
she became Empress Héxī.
Zhì was promoted three times to Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng,
while Jīng, Kuī, Hóng, and Chāng were all Huángmén Shìláng.
Jīng died in office.
In the first year of Yánpíng,
Zhì was appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn, with the privilege of Yítóng Sānsī.
The title Yítóng Sānsī [儀同三司] began with Zhì.
Kuī was Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng,
and Hóng and Chāng were both Shìzhōng.
When Emperor Shāng passed away,
the Empress Dowager and Zhì and others determined the plan to enthrone Emperor Ān.
Kuī was promoted to Chéngmén Xiàowèi,
and Hóng to Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng.
After Emperor Hé's death,
Zhì and his brothers often resided within the forbidden palace.
Zhì, being modest, did not wish to remain long in the interior [palace],
and repeatedly requested to return to his residence.
After more than a year,
the Empress Dowager finally granted his request.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
Zhì was enfeoffed as Shàngcài Hóu,
Kuī as Yè Hóu,
Hóng as Xīpíng Hóu,
and Chāng as Xīhuá Hóu,
each with an income of ten thousand households.
Zhì, due to his merit in determining the succession,
had his enfeoffment increased by three thousand households.
Zhì and the others declined, but their refusal was not accepted.
They then evaded the messengers,
traversed mountains and valleys to the palace gate,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"We, your servants, are impure and insignificant,
with no discernible merit.
By virtue of being imperial relatives,
we encountered an enlightened era,
benefited from the residual light of the sun and moon,
and received the profound grace of clouds and rain.
We have collectively held prominent positions,
shining gloriously in our time.
Unable to promote goodness and beauty,
or assist in pure governance,
we are truly ashamed and fearful,
with no peace in our hearts.
Your Majesty possesses a naturally endowed disposition,
and embodies the virtues of benevolence and sageliness.
Having encountered an unfortunate state,
and repeatedly endured great sorrow,
you opened the wisdom of the sun and moon,
and acted with singular judgment,
establishing the imperial lineage
and reverently upholding the great ancestral line.
Your sacred policy was determined by divine will,
and your glorious achievements will endure eternally,
which is not even one-ten-thousandth attributable to us.
Yet, we are undeservedly praised,
and all enjoy great enfeoffments.
Having heard the imperial edict,
we are startled, ashamed, and terrified.
Reflecting on the warnings of past downfalls,
and considering our own situation,
we shiver without cold.
〔一０〕Although we, your servants, lack far-sighted deliberation,
we still possess a hope of caution and fear.
Our mother, brothers, and we [the imperial family] constantly admonish and encourage each other internally,
hoping to be upright,
reverent, and cautious,
to serve with one heart,
to uphold imperial grace above,
and to preserve our lives below.
Our commitment is etched in our bones,
to death there will be no second thought.
We would never dare to accept undeserved titles and territories,
thereby increasing our transgressions.
In distress and agitation,
we beg to make this plea, risking death."
The Empress Dowager did not listen.
Zhì repeatedly submitted memorials,
five or six times,
before she finally granted his request.
That summer,
the rebellious Qiāng tribes in the Liáng region agitated Xīzhōu,
causing concern at court.
Thereupon, an edict ordered Zhì to lead the Zǔoyòu Yǔlín, the Northern Army's five legions, and troops from various divisions to attack them.
The imperial carriage proceeded to Pínglè Guān to see him off.
Zhì camped in Hányáng to the west,
and sent the Zhēngxī Xiàowèi Rèn Shàng and the Cóngshì Zhōngláng Sīmǎ Jūn to battle the Qiāng,
who suffered a great defeat.
At that time, due to the weariness of transport and supply,
the common people suffered from forced labor.
In winter,
Zhì was recalled to return the army.
The court, for the sake of the Empress Dowager,
sent the Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng to welcome and appoint Zhì as Dàjiāngjūn.
When the army reached Hénán,
the Dàhónglú was sent to personally welcome him,
and the Zhōngchángshì brought oxen and wine to entertain him in the suburbs.
Princes, princesses, and others waited for him along the road.
Upon his arrival,
all officials gathered,
and he was bestowed with bolts of silk and riding horses.
His favor and prestige were顯赫,
shaking the capital and countryside.
At that time, suffering from the disasters of Yuán and Èr,
people were starved,
with corpses visible everywhere,
bandits rose in groups,
and the four Yi invaded.
Zhì and others promoted frugality,
abolished forced labor,
and advanced talented scholars from across the empire, such as Hé Xī, Duì Fèng,
Yáng Jìn, Lǐ Hé, and Táo Dūn, to positions at court.
They invited Yáng Zhèn, Zhū Chǒng, and Chén Chán to serve in their personal administration.
Consequently, the empire became peaceful again.
In the fourth year,
his mother, Lady Xīnyě, fell ill.
Zhì and his brothers all submitted memorials requesting to return to attend to her.
The Empress Dowager, considering Chāng to be the youngest [son]
and particularly outstanding in filial piety,
specially granted his request,
bestowing an comfortable carriage and four horses.
When Lady Xīnyě passed away,
Zhì and others again requested to step down from office to observe mourning.
Their memorials were submitted repeatedly,
and the Empress Dowager granted their request.
Upon returning to their private residences,
Zhì and others all resided near the tomb.
Chāng's extreme filial piety made him emaciated,
and was well-known at the time.
When the mourning period ended,
an imperial edict instructed Zhì to return to assist in court affairs,
and restored his former enfeoffment.
Zhì and others repeatedly kowtowed and firmly declined,
so it was stopped.
Thereupon, they all served as Fèngcháo Qǐng,
their status ranking below the Sāngōng,
but above Tèjìn and Marquises.
When there was a major deliberation,
they would proceed to the court hall
to consult with the Gōngqīng.
In the second year of Yuánchū,
Hóng died.
The Empress Dowager wore Qīcuī mourning clothes,
and the Emperor wore Sīmá,
both staying overnight at his residence.
Hóng had early on studied the Ōuyáng version of the Shàngshū,
and taught it to the Emperor within the forbidden palace.
Many scholars gravitated towards him.
When he first fell ill,
he left instructions to be buried in ordinary clothes,
without using brocade garments or jade caskets.
The officials proposed to posthumously grant Hóng the title Pàojì Jiāngjūn,
with the rank of Tèjìn,
and enfeoff him as Xīpíng Hóu.
The Empress Dowager, remembering Hóng's wishes,
did not add posthumous titles, ranks, or special garments,
but only bestowed ten million coins
and ten thousand bolts of cloth.
Zhì and others again declined to accept them.
An edict ordered the Dàhónglú, holding a staff of authority,
to immediately enfeoff Hóng's son Guǎngdé as Xīpíng Hóu at Hóng's funeral.
Before the burial,
officials again proposed to dispatch light chariots and cavalry from the Five Camps,
with rituals like those for Huò Guāng.
The Empress Dowager did not allow any of it,
but only permitted a white canopy and two riders,
with his disciples pulling the hearse.
Later, due to his importance as the Emperor's teacher,
the Dūxiāng of Xīpíng was separated and enfeoffed upon Guǎngdé's younger brother Fǔdé as Dūxiāng Hóu.
In the fourth year,
Jīng's son, Huángmén Shìláng Zhēn, was also enfeoffed as Yáng'ān Hóu,
with an income of three thousand five hundred households.
In the fifth year,
Kuī and Chāng successively died.
Both left instructions for simple burials,
and not to accept posthumous titles or gifts.
The Empress Dowager complied with both requests.
Thereupon, Kuī's son Guǎngzōng was enfeoffed as Yè Hóu,
and Chāng's son Zhōng as Xīhuá Hóu.
From his grandfather, Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹), instructing his descendants,
all followed laws and regulations,
deeply cautioned the Dòu (竇) clan,
inspected and restrained their kinsmen,
and kept their household quietly secluded.
Dèng Zhì's (鄧騭) son, Attendant-in-ordinary Dèng Fèng (鄧鳳),
once wrote a letter to Secretary-general Zhāng Kān (張龕),
recommending Erudite-of-the-Gentlemen Mǎ Róng (馬融) for a position in the imperial court.
Also, Colonel Rèn Shàng (任尚) once sent Dèng Fèng (鄧鳳) a horse.
Later, Rèn Shàng (任尚) was convicted of stealing military rations,
and was summoned in a caged cart to the Grand Judge.
Dèng Fèng (鄧鳳), fearing the matter would be exposed,
first confessed to Dèng Zhì (鄧騭).
Dèng Zhì (鄧騭), fearing the Empress Dowager,
then shaved his wife's head and Dèng Fèng's (鄧鳳) to apologize,
which was praised by all under Heaven.
In the first year of Jiànguāng (建光) (121 CE),
the Empress Dowager passed away.
Before the grand embalming,
the Emperor reinstated his former decree,
enfeoffing Dèng Zhì (鄧騭) as Marquis of Shàngcài (上蔡)
with the rank of Special Advanced Official.
The Emperor was known as intelligent in his youth,
but as he grew older, he was often lacking in virtue.
His wet nurse, Wáng Shèng (王聖), seeing that the Empress Dowager had long not returned power to him,
feared that there might be a deposition or replacement.
She often spied on the Emperor with the Central Yellow Gate attendant Lǐ Rùn (李閏).
When the Empress Dowager died,
some palace women who had previously been punished,
harboring resentment,
used this opportunity to falsely accuse Dèng Kuī (鄧悝), Dèng Hóng (鄧弘), and Dèng Chāng (鄧閶) of having first obtained precedents for deposing an emperor from Secretary Dèng Fǎng (鄧訪),
and conspiring to install Prince Dé (得) of Píngyuán (平原).
The Emperor heard this,
and was enraged.
He ordered the relevant authorities to accuse Dèng Kuī (鄧悝) and others of great treason and wickedness.

Consequently, Marquis Guǎngdé (廣德) of Xīpíng (西平), Marquis Guǎngzōng (廣宗) of Yè (葉), Marquis Zhōng (忠) of Xīhuá (西華), Marquis Zhēn (珍) of Yáng'ān (陽安), and Marquis Pǔdé (甫德) of Dūxiāng (都鄉) were all reduced to commoners.
As Dèng Zhì (鄧騭) was not involved in the conspiracy,
he was merely stripped of his Special Advanced Official rank
and sent back to his fief.
All his kinsmen were dismissed from office and returned to their old commanderies.
The properties, wealth, fields, and residences of Dèng Zhì (鄧騭) and others were confiscated.
Dèng Fǎng (鄧訪) and his family were exiled to a distant commandery.
Under coercion from the commandery and county officials,
Guǎngzōng (廣宗) and Zhōng (忠) both committed suicide.
Dèng Zhì (鄧騭) was then re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Luó (羅),
and Dèng Zhì (鄧騭) and his son Dèng Fèng (鄧鳳) both died of starvation.
Dèng Zhì's (鄧騭) younger cousins, Hénán (河南) Prefect Dèng Bào (鄧豹), General Who Crosses the Liao Dèng Zūn (鄧遵), Marquis of Wǔyáng (舞陽), and Grand Architect Dèng Chàng (鄧暢), all committed suicide.
Only Guǎngdé (廣德) and his brothers, as relatives of Empress Yán (閻后) through their mother, were allowed to remain in the capital.
Grand Minister of Agriculture Zhū Chǒng (朱寵) grieved that Dèng Zhì (鄧騭) had suffered calamity without guilt.
So he bared his torso and carried a coffin,
submitting a memorial to posthumously plead Dèng Zhì's (鄧騭) case, saying:
"I humbly believe that the virtuous and benevolent character of Empress Héxī (和熹皇后)
made her the 'Mother of Han.'
Her brothers were loyal and filial,
united in their concern for the nation.
The imperial ancestral temple had a master,
and the royal house relied on them.
Having accomplished their work, they withdrew from power,
ceding the nation and resigning their positions.
Among all imperial relatives throughout the ages,
none can compare with them.
They ought to have enjoyed the blessings of accumulated goodness and humility,
yet were unjustly framed by the sole words of palace women.
Their treacherous and glib tongues
overturned and disrupted the state.
Without any evidence to confirm the accusations,
and without proper investigation of the charges,
Dèng Zhì (鄧騭) and others were made to suffer this cruel injustice.
Seven members of one family
all lost their lives unnaturally.
Their remains scattered and adrift,
their aggrieved souls unable to return.
This defies Heaven and moves men,
causing the whole land to lose spirit.
It is fitting to reclaim their burial sites,
bestow favor upon their surviving orphans,
and maintain their blood sacrifices,
to appease their departed spirits."
Zhū Chǒng (朱寵) knew his words were harsh,
and voluntarily reported himself to the Grand Judge.
An imperial edict dismissed him from office and sent him back to his fields and village.
Many common people spoke out about the injustice against Dèng Zhì (鄧騭).
The Emperor's mind was somewhat enlightened.
He then reprimanded the provincial and commandery officials,
and Dèng Zhì (鄧騭) was reburied in his old tomb on Běimáng (北芒) in Luòyáng (洛陽).
All the high officials attended the funeral,
and none were not sorrowful.
An edict dispatched an envoy to offer sacrifices with a medium-sized animal.
All his cousins and brothers returned to the capital.
When Emperor Shùn (順帝) ascended the throne,
he remembered the Empress Dowager's benevolent instruction
and pitied Dèng Zhì's (鄧騭) innocence.
He then issued an edict to the Imperial Clan Court to restore the former Grand General Dèng Zhì's (鄧騭) kinsmen, both immediate and extended,
and decreed that their court audiences should be as before.
Dèng Zhì's (鄧騭) brothers' sons and twelve retainers were all appointed as Erudite-of-the-Gentlemen.
Zhū Chǒng (朱寵) was promoted to Grand Commandant
and Supervisor of the Affairs of the Masters of Writing.
Zhū Chǒng's (朱寵) courtesy name was Zhòngwēi (仲威),
and he was a native of Jīngzhào (京兆).
He was first invited to serve in Dèng Zhì's (鄧騭) administration,
and gradually rose to become Administrator of Yǐngchuān (潁川).
His governance was renowned.
When he was appointed Grand Commandant,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānxiāng (安鄉)
and treated with great honor.
Dèng Guǎngdé (鄧廣德) died young.
Dèng Pǔdé (鄧甫德) was again summoned and appointed Magistrate of Kāifēng (開封).
He studied and passed on his father's learning.
After his mother's death,
he did not pursue an official career.
Dèng Chāng's (鄧閶) wife, Lady Gěng (耿氏), was virtuous and principled.
Grieving the execution and deposition of the Dèng (鄧) clan,
and that her son Zhōng (忠) had died young,
she adopted Dèng Bào's (鄧豹), the Prefect of Hénán (河南), son as Dèng Chāng's (鄧閶) heir.
Lady Gěng (耿氏) taught him literature,
and he became known for his extensive learning.
During the Yǒngshòu (永壽) era (155-158 CE),
he collaborated with Fú Wújì (伏無忌) and Yán Dǔ (延篤) in writing books at the Eastern Library,
and rose to the official position of Colonel of the Garrison Cavalry.
Dèng Yǔ's (鄧禹) great-grandson Dèng Xiāng's (鄧香) daughter became Empress to Emperor Huán (桓帝).
The Emperor then re-enfeoffed General Who Crosses the Liao Dèng Zūn's (鄧遵) son Wànshì (萬世) as Marquis of Nánxiāng (南鄉),
and appointed him Prefect of Hénán (河南).
When the Empress was deposed,
Wànshì (萬世) was imprisoned and died.
The remaining kinsmen all returned to their old commanderies.
Since the Restoration, the Dèng (鄧) clan
had been favored and distinguished for generations.
There were twenty-nine Marquises in total,
two Dukes,
thirteen Grand Generals and below,
fourteen officials with salaries of two thousand *shi* or more,
twenty-two colonels,
forty-eight provincial governors and commandery administrators,
and countless others such as attendants-in-ordinary, generals, grandees, erudite-of-the-gentlemen, and court attendants.
No other family in the Eastern Capital could compare.
A commentary states: Among the imperial relatives of the Han dynasty,
from the Eastern and Western Capitals, there were over ten clans
who not only became arrogant and tyrannical to the extreme,
bringing disaster upon themselves,
but inevitably caused problems for later rulers,
leading to their downfall.
The reasons for this are explainable.
Why?
Their favor was not personally cultivated by the ruler,
yet their power preceded it.
Their personal ties were distant, yet their ceremonial status was high,
and they twisted their nature to scheme.
When new favor was bestowed,
their existing position already harmed it.
When their influence waned,
slander also overcame them.
How tragic!
Dèng Zhì (鄧騭) and his brother Dèng Kuī (鄧悝),
who delegated distant temporal authority
and loyally toiled for the royal house,
yet ultimately could not escape their fate.
This is why Yuè Yì (樂毅) wept and resigned from Yān (燕)!
Kòu Xún (寇恂), whose courtesy name was Zǐyì (子翼),
was a native of Chāngpíng (昌平) in Shànggǔ (上谷).
His family had been prominent for generations.
Kòu Xún (寇恂) first served as the merit officer of the commandery.
The Administrator Gěng Kuàng (耿況) highly esteemed him.
When Wáng Măng was defeated,
Gēngshǐ was enthroned.
He sent envoys to inspect the commanderies and states,
saying,
"Those who surrender first will have their titles and positions restored."
Kòu Xún, following Gěng Kuàng, went to welcome the envoy at the border.
Gěng Kuàng handed over his seal and ribbon,
and the envoy accepted it.
After one night, there was no sign of its return.
Kòu Xún led his troops and entered to see the envoy,
requesting it back.
The envoy refused to give it,
saying,
"I am an envoy of the Heavenly King.
Does the meritorious official wish to threaten me?"
Kòu Xún replied,
"I dare not threaten Your Excellency.
I am merely concerned that your plan is ill-considered.
Today, the empire is only just settled,
and the state's credibility has not yet been widely proclaimed.
Your Excellency holds the banner and carries the mandate,
coming to the four directions.
There is no commandery or state that is not craning its neck and pricking up its ears,
hoping to submit at the sound of your name.
Now you have just arrived in Shànggǔ and have already undermined the great trust,
discouraging the hearts that wish to submit,
and creating a rift for defection.
How then will you issue commands to other commanderies?
Furthermore, Administrator Gěng is in Shànggǔ,
having been cherished by officials and people for a long time.
If he is replaced now,
even if a worthy man is obtained, things will be unsettled at first;
if an unworthy man is obtained, it will only create more chaos.
For your sake,
nothing is better than restoring him to pacify the common people."
The envoy did not respond.
Kòu Xún shouted at his attendants to summon Gěng Kuàng by the envoy's order.
When Gěng Kuàng arrived,
Kòu Xún stepped forward, took the seal and ribbon, and fastened it to Gěng Kuàng.
The envoy, having no other choice,
then issued an imperial edict through his authority,
and Gěng Kuàng accepted it and returned.
When Wáng Láng rose,
he sent generals to campaign in Shànggǔ,
urgently demanding Gěng Kuàng to dispatch troops.
Kòu Xún and his subordinate, Mǐn Yè, jointly advised Gěng Kuàng, saying,
"Hándān has risen forcefully,
and it is difficult to trust or follow them.
In Wáng Măng's time,
the only one who was difficult was Liú Bóshēng.
Now we hear that Grand Marshal Liú Gōng,
Liú Bóshēng's younger brother by the same mother,
honors the worthy and is humble towards scholars,
and many scholars return to him.
He is someone we can attach ourselves to."
Gěng Kuàng said,
"Hándān is currently flourishing.
We lack the strength to resist them alone.
What should we do?"
Kòu Xún replied,
"Currently, Shànggǔ is complete and substantial,
with ten thousand cavalrymen ready to draw bows.
With the resources of the Jiāng commandery,
we can carefully choose our course of action.
I request to go east and make an alliance with Yúyáng,
uniting our hearts and gathering our forces.
Hándān is not worth worrying about."
Gěng Kuàng agreed with his words.
So he sent Kòu Xún to Yúyáng
to conspire with Péng Chǒng.
When Kòu Xún returned,
reaching Chāngpíng,
he launched a surprise attack on the Hándān envoy,
killed him,
seized his army,
and then, along with Gěng Kuàng's son Gěng Yǎn and others, went south and met Guāngwǔ at Guǎng'ā.
Kòu Xún was appointed General of the Household,
and given the title of Marquis Chéngyì.
He followed in defeating various bandits.
He frequently discussed plans with Dèng Yǔ,
who admired him.
Thus, Dèng Yǔ offered him ox and wine, and they became close friends.
Guāngwǔ pacified Hénèi in the south,
while Gēngshǐ's Grand Marshal Zhū Wěi and others strongly held Luòyáng with their large army.
Moreover, Bìngzhōu was not yet pacified.
Guāngwǔ found its defense difficult,
and asked Dèng Yǔ,
"Among the generals, who can be entrusted with guarding Hénèi?"
Dèng Yǔ replied,
"In the past, Gāozǔ entrusted Xiāo Hé with Guānzhōng,
and had no worries about the west,
thus he could concentrate his efforts east of the mountains,
and ultimately achieve his great undertaking.
Now, Hénèi is fortified by the river,
its population is prosperous,
it connects to Shàngdǎng in the north,
and is close to Luòyáng in the south.
Kòu Xún is fully equipped in both civil and military aspects,
possessing the talent to govern people and command armies.
None other than this man can be entrusted with this task."
So Kòu Xún was appointed Administrator of Hénèi,
and acted as Grand General.
Guāngwǔ said to Kòu Xún,
"Hénèi is complete and wealthy.
I will use this as my base to rise.
In the past, Gāozǔ left Xiāo Hé to guard Guānzhōng.
I now entrust Hénèi to you, Your Excellency.
Firmly hold it, transport supplies,
provide sufficient military provisions,
encourage and lead the soldiers and horses,
and prevent other armies
from crossing north. That is all."
Guāngwǔ then resumed his northern campaign against Yàn and Dài.
Kòu Xún sent letters to the subordinate counties,
training soldiers and practicing archery.
He cut down the bamboo from Qíyuán,
making over a million arrows,
reared two thousand horses,
collected four million hú of grain,
and transported it to supply the army.
Zhū Wěi heard that Guāngwǔ was in the north and Hénèi was isolated,
so he sent General Tǎonán Sū Máo and his deputy Jiǎ Qiáng, leading over thirty thousand troops,
to cross the Gǒng River and attack Wēn.
When the urgent letter arrived,
Kòu Xún immediately led his army and rushed out,
and also sent notices to the subordinate counties,
mobilizing troops to gather below Wēn.
All the military officials advised,
"Now the Luòyáng army is crossing the river,
continuously, one after another.
It is advisable to wait until all our armies have gathered
before we can sally forth."
Kòu Xún said,
"Wēn
is the defense screen of the commandery.
If Wēn is lost, the commandery cannot be defended."
So he galloped to its aid.
The next day, they engaged in battle.
At that time, General of the Household Féng Yì's relief force and the troops from various counties just arrived.
Soldiers and horses gathered from all four directions,
their banners covering the fields.
Kòu Xún then ordered his soldiers to ascend the city walls, beat drums, and shout,
loudly proclaiming,
"Liú Gōng's army has arrived!"
When Sū Máo's army heard this,
their formation stirred.
Kòu Xún seized the opportunity to launch a swift attack,
greatly defeating them.
He pursued them to Luòyáng,
and then beheaded Jiǎ Qiáng.
Thousands of Sū Máo's soldiers threw themselves into the river and died;
over ten thousand were captured alive.
Kòu Xún and Féng Yì crossed the river and returned.
From then on, Luòyáng was terrified,
and its city gates were closed during the day.
At that time, Guāngwǔ heard rumors that Zhū Wěi had defeated Hénèi.
A moment later, Kòu Xún's urgent letter arrived.
Guāngwǔ was overjoyed and said,
"I knew Kòu Zǐyì could be entrusted with the task!"
All the generals offered their congratulations,
and then urged him to accept the imperial title.
Thus, he ascended the throne.
At that time, military provisions were critically short.
Kòu Xún used carts and harnessed horses for continuous transport,
which never ceased,
so the Secretariat could allocate grain to all officials.
The Emperor repeatedly sent written messages to commend and inquire after Kòu Xún.
His fellow student, Dǒng Chóng from Máolíng, advised Kòu Xún, saying,
"The Emperor has newly ascended the throne,
and the four directions are not yet settled.
At this time, Your Excellency holds a great commandery,
winning the hearts of the people internally,
and defeating Sū Máo externally,
your might shaking neighboring enemies.
Your achievements and fame are widely known.
This is a time when slanderers will look askance and harbor resentment and malice.
In the past, Xiāo Hé, when guarding Guānzhōng,
heeded Bào Shēng's words, and Gāozǔ was pleased.
Now, those you lead
are all your kinsmen and brothers.
Should you not take those who came before as a warning mirror?"
Kòu Xún affirmed his words
and claimed illness, not attending to affairs.
The Emperor was about to attack Luòyáng,
and first arrived at Hénèi.
Kòu Xún requested to join the army.
The Emperor said,
"Hénèi cannot be left yet."
Kòu Xún repeatedly made strong requests,
but was not granted.
So he sent his nephew Kòu Zhāng and his sister's son Gǔ Chóng, leading elite cavalry, wishing to be the vanguard of the army.
The Emperor approved of this,
and appointed them both as Generals of the Household.
In Jiànwǔ second year (26 CE),
Kòu Xún was imprisoned for having a memorial submitted on his behalf, but was then pardoned.
At this time, Yǐngchuān men Yán Zhōng and Zhào Dūn gathered over ten thousand men,
and joined forces with Mì man Jiǎ Qī to become bandits.
Several months after Xún's pardon,
he was again appointed Administrator of Yǐngchuān,
and, together with General Who Breaks Treachery Hóu Jìn, attacked them.
After several months,
Jiǎ Qī's head was taken,
and the entire commandery was pacified.
Xún was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yōngnú,
with ten thousand households.
The Grand Master of Gilded Gate, Jiǎ Fù, was in Rǔnán.
One of his subordinate generals killed a man in Yǐngchuān,
and Xún arrested him and imprisoned him.
At that time, the state was still being established,
and those who committed crimes in military camps
were mostly tolerated.
But Xún executed him in the marketplace.
Jiǎ Fù considered this a disgrace
and sighed.
When he returned and passed through Yǐngchuān,
he said to his attendants:
"Kòu Xún and I are both marshals and generals,
but now I have been humiliated by him.
How can a true man harbor resentment without settling it?
When I see Xún today,
I will surely kill him with my own sword!"
Xún knew of his plan
and did not wish to meet him.
Gǔ Chóng said:
"I, Chóng,
am a general,
and I can wear a sword by your side.
Should there be an emergency,
I will be sufficient to handle it."
Xún said:
"No.
In the past, Lìn Xiàngrú, who did not fear the King of Qín, bowed before Lián Pō
for the sake of the state.
Even the small state of Zhào
had such righteousness.
How can I forget it?"
So he ordered the subordinate counties to prepare lavish provisions,
and store wine.
When the Grand Master of Gilded Gate's army entered the border,
each man received double rations.
Xún then went out to meet him on the road,
claiming illness, and returned.
Jiǎ Fù ordered his troops to pursue him,
but his officers and soldiers were all drunk,
so he simply passed by.
Xún dispatched Gǔ Chóng to report the situation to the Emperor.
The Emperor then summoned Xún.
When Xún arrived and was granted an audience,
Jiǎ Fù was already seated and
wished to rise and avoid him.
The Emperor said:
"The world is not yet settled.
How can two tigers privately fight?
Today, I will separate you."
Thereupon, they sat together in utmost harmony,
and then left in the same carriage,
forming a friendship as they departed.
Xún returned to Yǐngchuān.
In the third year (27 CE),
the Emperor sent an envoy to appoint him Administrator of Rǔnán.
He also sent General of Agile Cavalry Dù Mào with troops to assist Xún in suppressing the bandits.
The bandits were pacified,
and there was no trouble in the commandery.
Xún had always been fond of learning,
so he repaired the local schools,
taught students,
and invited a master of the Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū
to personally learn from him.
In the seventh year (31 CE),
he succeeded Zhū Fú as Grand Master of Gilded Gate.
The following year (32 CE),
he accompanied the imperial carriage to attack Wěi Xiāo.
However, bandits rose up in Yǐngchuān,
so the Emperor led the army back,
saying to Xún:
"Yǐngchuān is close to the capital
and must be pacified promptly.
Only you, my lord, can pacify it.
That you would leave your position among the Nine Ministers again to worry about the state is understandable."
Xún replied:
"The people of Yǐngchuān are impetuous and flighty.
Hearing that Your Majesty has traveled far over dangerous terrain
to deal with matters in Lǒng and Shǔ,
these reckless ruffians have seized the opportunity to cause mischief and lead people astray.
As soon as they hear the imperial carriage heading south,
the bandits will surely be terrified and surrender or die.
I wish to lead the vanguard wielding sharp weapons."
On that very day, the imperial carriage marched south.
Xún accompanied it to Yǐngchuān,
and all the bandits surrendered.
He was not, however, appointed Administrator of the commandery.
The common people blocked the road, saying:
"We beg Your Majesty to lend us Lord Kòu for one more year."
Therefore,
Xún was left in Chángshè
to stabilize and pacify officials and people,
and accept the remaining surrenders.
Initially,
Wěi Xiāo's general, Gāo Jùn of Āndìng,
commanded ten thousand troops
and occupied the First Peak of Gāopíng.
The Emperor sent Gentleman-in-Attendance Mǎ Yuán to persuade Jùn to surrender.
Thus, the Héxī road was opened.
Assistant Gentleman-of-the-Palace Lái Xī, acting under imperial authority, appointed Jùn as General Who Opens the Road
and enfeoffed him as Marquis Within the Passes.
Later, he was subordinate to Grand Marshal Wú Hàn
and jointly besieged Wěi Xiāo in Jì.
When Hàn's army retreated,
Jùn fled back to his old camp
and again assisted Wěi Xiāo in resisting at Lǒngdǐ.
After Wěi Xiāo's death,
Jùn occupied Gāopíng
and, fearing punishment, held out stubbornly.
General Who Establishes Might Gěng Yǎn, leading Grandee of the Palace Dòu Shì, Administrator of Wǔwēi Liáng Tǒng, and others, besieged him,
but could not take the city for a year.
In the tenth year (34 CE),
the Emperor entered Guān
intending to personally campaign against him.
Xún was accompanying the imperial carriage at the time
and remonstrated, saying:
"Cháng'ān, being centrally located,
is conveniently close.
Āndìng and Lǒngxī will surely be struck with fear.
This one place can calmly control the four directions.
Currently, the soldiers and horses are weary,
and are about to traverse dangerous terrain.
This is not secure for the Son of Heaven.
Last year in Yǐngchuān
can serve as a stern warning."
The Emperor did not heed him.
When the army advanced to Qǐan,
Jùn still refused to surrender.
The Emperor discussed sending an envoy to persuade him,
and said to Xún:
"You previously tried to stop me from this undertaking;
now you go for me.
If Jùn does not surrender immediately,
lead Gěng Yǎn and the other five battalions to attack him."
Xún, bearing the imperial edict, arrived at the First Peak.
Jùn sent his military adviser Huángfǔ Wén out to greet him,
but Wén's manner was arrogant and unyielding.
Xún was enraged
and was about to execute Wén.
The generals remonstrated, saying:
"Gāo Jùn has ten thousand elite troops,
mostly powerful crossbowmen.
He blocks the Lǒng road to the west
and has not surrendered for years.
Now, we wish to persuade him to surrender, but instead you are killing his envoy.
Is this not unacceptable?"
Xún did not respond,
and promptly beheaded him.
He sent Wén's deputy back to tell Jùn:
"Your military adviser was disrespectful
and has already been executed.
If you wish to surrender,
surrender quickly;
if not,
hold your ground firmly."
Jùn was terrified
and immediately opened the city gates and surrendered that very day.
All the generals congratulated Xún
and then asked:
"May we ask, why did killing his envoy lead to the surrender of his city?"
Xún said:
"Huángfǔ Wén was Jùn's confidant
and the one he relied on for advice.
Now that he came,
his words and manner were unyielding,
which meant he certainly had no intention of surrendering.
If I had spared him, Wén would have achieved his goal.
By killing him, Jùn lost his courage.
That is why he surrendered."
All the generals said:
"This is beyond our comprehension."
So Jùn was escorted back to Luòyáng.
Xún was well-versed in the classics and of upright conduct,
and his reputation was great in court.
The emoluments he received
he generously distributed to friends, old acquaintances, and his subordinate officers and soldiers.
He often said:
"I have achieved this through the gentlemen,
how can I enjoy it alone?"
People at the time regarded him as a true elder
and considered him to have the capacity of a prime minister.
He died in the twelfth year (36 CE),
and was posthumously named Wēi Marquis.
His son, Sǔn, succeeded him.
Xún's full brothers and his nephews and nieces on his sister's side, who were enfeoffed as marquises for military merit, totaled eight people.
This did not pass down to subsequent generations after their lifetime.
Initially, those who plotted with Kòu Mǐn (寇閔) were
Xún (恂) who repeatedly spoke to the emperor of their loyalty.
They were granted the noble rank of Guānnèi Hóu (關內侯),
and their highest office reached Liáoxī Tàishǒu (遼西太守).
In the thirteenth year [of Jiànwǔ, 37 CE],
Sǔn (損)'s elder half-brother, Shòu (壽), was again enfeoffed as Xiáo Hóu (洨侯).
Later, Sǔn (損) was transferred and enfeoffed as Fúliǔ Hóu (扶柳侯).
When Sǔn (損) died,
his son Lí (釐) succeeded him,
and was transferred and enfeoffed as Shāngxiāng Hóu (商鄉侯).
When Lí (釐) died,
his son Xí (襲) succeeded him.
Xún (恂)'s granddaughter was the wife of Dàjiàngjūn (大將軍) Dèng Zhì (鄧騭),
and because of this, the Kòu (寇) clan prospered during the Yǒngchū (永初) era.
Xún (恂)'s great-grandson was Róng (榮).
A commentary says: "It is rare for
joy and anger to be expressed appropriately."
Indeed, those who are joyful without being overbearing,
and angry while considering the difficulties [it may cause],
are perhaps only the *jūnzǐ* (君子)!
Confucius said:
"Bóyí (伯夷) and Shúqí (叔齊)
did not remember old grievances,
and their resentment was therefore rare."
This can be seen in Lord Kòu (寇).
Róng (榮) was famous in his youth,
and during the reign of Huán Dì (桓帝) served as Shìzhōng (侍中).
He was by nature proud and valued his own integrity,
associating with few people,
and because of this, he was harmed by those with power and favor.
Moreover, his cousin's son married the emperor's sister, Yìyáng Cháng Gōngzhǔ (益陽長公主),
and the emperor also sought his grandniece for the imperial harem,
which made those around him dislike him even more.
In the middle of the Yánxī (延熹) era,
he was consequently framed and sentenced to death,
and he and his clan were pardoned and returned to their ancestral commandery.
Officials, anticipating the imperial will,
harassed him with increasing severity.
Róng (榮), fearing he would not escape,
fled to the palace to plead his case.
Before he arrived,
Cìshǐ (刺史) Zhāng Jìng (張敬) pursued and impeached Róng (榮) for unauthorized departure from the border,
and an imperial edict was issued for his arrest.
Róng (榮) hid for several years,
and though an amnesty was declared,
he was not exonerated.
Having accumulated poverty and distress,
he wrote a memorial from hiding, saying:
"When people govern parents,
they first show compassion,
then authority;
first leniency,
then punishment.
From those who are old enough to have teeth [i.e., infants] upwards,
all receive beneficence.
Yet I and my brothers alone,
without guilt, have been slandered and attacked by ministers who wield sole power,
and conspired against by ‘green flies’ [sycophants].
Because of my marital ties to the imperial family,
they say I will pat their
backs,
usurp their positions,
remove their persons,
and seize their authority.
Thus, they fabricated flying memorials to incriminate me,
wishing to make me fall into a pit of ten thousand fathoms,
tread on the ground of certain death,
and cause Your Majesty to forget the benevolence of a compassionate mother
and unleash the wrath of the 'flying shuttle' [false accusation].
The Shàngshū (尚書), disregarding principles,
impeached me on false charges,
without verifying my offenses,
placed me under the severe
thorns [of the law],
and then reported my crime as established.
Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉) Féng Xiàn (馮羨), being sycophantic and conforming to the imperial will,
violated the imperial mandate,
and expelled me and others,
not allowing us to turn back.
I
fled back to my commandery,
without resentment even if I were to die there.
I truly fear that I might ultimately be devoured by jackals and wolves,
so I dared to risk death and wished to approach the palace,
to reveal my heart and liver,
and lay bare my innermost thoughts.
The Léi Bào (雷豹) and Luòyáng Lìng (洛陽令) Yuán Téng (袁騰) competed to be first,
as if rushing to an enemy.
Even after death,
they shave and destroy graves,
only not yet excavating the burial pit to exhume the corpse
and open the coffin to expose the remains
— that is all.
In ancient times, King Wén (文王) buried dry bones,
and Duke Liú (公劉) diligently cultivated the reeds;
the world praised their benevolence.
Now, cruel and flattering officials,
without the heart to mediate and be impartial,
disregard the harm to the innocent
and instigate false slanders,
wishing to ensure that the solemn court applies excessive punishment.
Therefore, I dared not violate the imperial majesty,
but hid myself in
the mountains and forests,
awaiting Your Majesty to open your divine and sagely ears,
enlighten your unique and discerning vision,
reject the slanders of traitors and villains,
cut off the words of the cunning and wicked,
save those who can be saved,
and rescue
those drowning in peril.
Unexpectedly, Your Majesty's lingering wrath does not abate with the spring and summer,
and your prolonged resentment does not diminish with the changing seasons.
Thus, envoys were dispatched via post-stations,
broadcasting messages far and wide,
with strict and harsh
measures of confiscation and exploitation,
more painful than frost and snow.
Nets were cast throughout the realm,
and traps set for ten thousand *lǐ* (里).
Those who pursue me exhaust human tracks,
and those who chase me extend their carriage wheels to the limit.
Even Chǔ (楚)'s bounty for Wǔ Yuán (伍員)
or Hàn (漢)'s
search for Jì Bù (季布)
could not surpass this.
If I exert my
strength,
if I stop, I will be annihilated;
if I move, I will become a captured fugitive.
If I live, I will be a destitute person;
if I die, I will be a wronged ghost.
The sky is vast, yet I have no means to cover myself;
the earth
is thick, yet I have no means to carry myself.
I tread on dry land, yet I have the worry of sinking;
I am far from cliffs, yet I have the fear of being crushed.
My sincerity is enough to move Your Majesty,
yet
the wise king is unwilling to comprehend.
If I had committed such grave and heinous crimes
as to deserve to be displayed in the wilderness,
and to be subjected to knives and saws,
Your Majesty should announce the charges against me
to resolve the doubts of the multitude.
I wish to enter the national gate,
sit upon the 'bone-stone' [place for punishment],
and have the three *huái* (槐) and nine *jí* (棘) [court officials] judge my crime.
However, the Chānghé (閶闔) gate has nine
layers,
and pitfalls are laid at every step.
Every move I make touches a snare,
every step I take is caught in a net.
There is no way for me to reach the presence of the Son of Heaven,
and no hope of ever being believed.
Alas.
The warmth turns cold;
spring constantly brings bitter winds,
and summer brings frost and hail.
Moreover, there have been successive years of great winds,
snapping and uprooting trees.
Wind is a command.
Spring and summer are the seasons to
bestow virtue,
to review cases, and to grant delays of execution.
I wish Your Majesty to reflect on the virtue of Emperor Yáo (帝堯)'s five teachings, which emphasized leniency,
and to aspire to the warning of King Chéng Tāng (成湯) to keep away from slanderers,
so as
to calm the winds and droughts,
and to quell disasters and warfare.
I have heard that the brave do not flee death,
and the wise do not add to their distress.
Indeed, I do not regret sacrificing my fading life for the enlightened court.
I wish to throw myself into
the waves of Xiāng (湘) and Yuán (沅),
to share the sorrow of Qū Yuán (屈原),
and sink into the rivers and lakes,
to mourn the grief of Zǐxū (子胥).
I am a descendant of meritorious officials,
born and raised in the imperial state.
I fear
that I alone would die holding resentment, buried in the belly of a river fish,
without being able to distinguish myself in the world.
I cannot bear the feeling of a fox dying with its head towards its hill [longing for home],
or the yearning of a wandering soul to know the way back.
I have
dared to provoke imperial wrath,
and violate imperial prohibitions,
prostrating myself before the Twin Towers [a part of the palace],
to present my bitter grievances.
After that, I will ascend the golden cauldron,
enter the boiling soup,
and be reduced to pulp beneath the scorching fire,
dying nine
times without regret.
I remember
the difficulty of Jùn Jǐng (浚井),
and that Shēn Shēng (申生) did not decline the slanders of the Jī (姬) clan.
How dare I forget this principle
and not perish myself to appease the anger of the enlightened court?"
I beg to offer my own body to atone for the grave offense.
I pray Your Majesty will spare my brothers' lives,
so that my family may have some survivors,
thereby glorifying Your Majesty's benevolent clemency.
I
express my feelings before death,
and my tears stream down as I write this memorial,
my tears of blood flow like a continuous stream.
The Emperor, upon reading the memorial, grew even more enraged,
and consequently executed Kòu Róng.
The Kòu clan consequently declined and fell into disuse.
A eulogy says: Yuán Hóu, with his profound strategies,
was made Sītú.
He brilliantly initiated the imperial plan,
and first established the Qín capital.
His achievements accomplished, he wisely concealed himself,
remaining quiet as if foolish.
Zǐ Yì guarded Wēn,
Xiāo Gōng was this,
connecting troops and transporting provisions,
thereby achieving great deeds.
He executed Wén and humbled Jiǎ.
He had both rigidity and flexibility.
Biography of Féng and Cén and Jiǎ, Chapter Seven.
Féng Yì, courtesy name Gōngsūn,
was a native of Fùchéng, Yǐngchuān.
He loved to read books,
and was thoroughly conversant with the *Zuǒshì Chūnqiū* and *Sūnzǐ Bīngfǎ*.
When the Hàn army rose,
Yì, as a prefectural clerk, supervised five counties,
and together with Miáo Méng, the magistrate of Fùchéng, defended the city,
resisting the Hàn for Wáng Mǎng.
Guāngwǔ campaigned in Yǐngchuān,
attacked Fùchéng but could not take it,
and encamped his troops in Jīnchē Township.
Yì secretly went out to a subordinate county
and was captured by the Hàn army.
At that time, Yì's elder cousin Xiào, and Dīng Chēn and Lǚ Yàn from the same commandery,
were all following Guāngwǔ.
They jointly recommended Yì,
who was summoned for an audience.
Yì said:
"Yì, a mere man,
is not enough to sway the balance of power.
I have an aged mother in the city.
I wish to return and hold the five cities
to demonstrate my loyalty and repay your kindness."
Guāngwǔ said:
"Excellent."
Yì returned,
and said to Miáo Méng:
"Currently, all the generals who have risen are brave men,
many are violent and unrestrained.
Only General Liú, wherever he goes, does not plunder.
Observing his words and actions,
he is no ordinary man;
we can pledge allegiance to him."
Miáo Méng said:
"Life and death are one's destiny.
I respectfully follow your plan."
When Guāngwǔ returned south to Wǎn,
the Gēngshǐ generals who attacked Fùchéng were more than ten groups, one after another,
but Yì held fast and did not surrender.
When Guāngwǔ became Sīlì Xiàowèi [Colonel Director of Retainers],
and passed through Fùchéng,
Yì and others immediately opened the gates and offered cattle and wine to welcome him.
Guāngwǔ appointed Yì as Zhǔbù [Chief Clerk]
and Miáo Méng as Cóngshì [Attendant Official].
Yì then recommended local men such as Diào Qī,
Shú Shòu, Duàn Jiàn, and Zuǒ Lóng.
Guāngwǔ appointed them all as clerks and historians,
and they followed him to Luòyáng.
Gēngshǐ repeatedly wanted to send Guāngwǔ to campaign in Héběi,
but all the generals considered it inadvisable.
At this time, Zuǒ Chéngxiàng [Left Chancellor] Cáo Jìng's son, Xǔ, was Shàngshū [Minister],
and father and son were influential.
Yì advised Guāngwǔ to cultivate strong ties with them.
When he crossed Héběi,
Xǔ played a helpful role.
Since Bóshēng's defeat,
Guāngwǔ dared not openly show his sorrow.
Whenever he was alone,
he would abstain from wine and meat,
and there would be traces of tears on his pillow and mat.
Only Yì would kowtow and gently console his grief.
Guāngwǔ stopped him, saying:
"Do not speak rashly."
Yì again took the opportunity to advise him, saying:
"The world has long suffered under the Wáng clan,
and has long yearned for the Hàn.
Now, Gēngshǐ's generals are violent and tyrannical,
plundering wherever they go.
The common people are disappointed
and have no one to rely on.
Now, you are solely entrusted with authority in this region;
you should implement benevolent policies.
Indeed, the chaos of Jié and Zhòu
reveals the achievements of Tāng and Wǔ.
People who have been hungry and thirsty for a long time
are easily satisfied.
You should immediately dispatch your officials
to tour the commanderies and counties,
to redress grievances,
and spread kindness."
Guāngwǔ accepted this.
Upon reaching Hándān,
he dispatched Yì and Diào Qī by post-carriage to comfort and inspect the subordinate counties,
record prisoners,
care for the poor and widowed,
and pardon those fugitives who presented themselves.
Secretly, he also listed the two-thousand-shi officials and chief administrators who were loyal to him or disloyal, and reported them.
When Wáng Láng rose,
Guāngwǔ rode swiftly southeast from Jì,
traveling day and night in crude shelters,
until he reached Wúlóu Pavilion in Ráoyáng.
The weather was bitterly cold then,
and everyone was hungry and exhausted.
Yì offered bean porridge.
The next morning,
Guāngwǔ said to his generals:
"Yesterday, I had Gōngsūn's bean porridge,
and both my hunger and cold were relieved."
When they arrived at Nángōng,
they encountered a great storm.
Guāngwǔ pulled his carriage into an empty house by the roadside.
Yì gathered firewood,
Dèng Yǔ lit the fire,
and Guāngwǔ dried his clothes by the stove.
Yì again offered wheat cakes and roasted rabbit haunches.
After this, he crossed the Hútuó River to Xìndū,
and sent Yì to separately gather troops from Hénèi.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Piān Jiāngjūn [Minor General].
He followed in defeating Wáng Láng,
and was enfeoffed as Yìng Hóu.
Yì was humble and not boastful.
When he met other generals on the road,
he would always pull his carriage aside to yield the way.
His movements and stops all had clear distinctions,
and in the army, he was known for his orderliness.
Whenever they stopped for quarters,
while other generals sat together discussing their merits,
Yì always stood alone beneath a tree.
The army called him
"General of the Great Tree."
After Hándān was defeated,
Guāngwǔ re-assigned the generals,
each with their specific duties.
All the soldiers said they wished to belong to the General of the Great Tree.
Guāngwǔ greatly admired him for this.
He separately defeated Tiě Qǐng in Běipíng,
and also subjugated the Xiongnú king Línqiūdùn,
and then followed in pacifying Héběi.
At that time, Gēngshǐ sent Wǔyīn Wáng Lǐ Yì, Lǐnqīu Wáng Tián Lì, Dà Sīmǎ Zhū Wěi, and Báihǔ Gōng Chén Qiáo
leading an army said to number 300,000,
together with Hénán Tàishǒu [Administrator of Hénán] Wǔ Bó, to defend Luòyáng.
Guāngwǔ was about to go north to campaign in Yān and Zhào.
Because Wèijùn and Hénèi alone had not experienced warfare,
and their cities were intact,
and granaries full,
he appointed Kòu Xún as Hénèi Tàishǒu,
and Yì as Mèngjīn Jiāngjūn [General of Mèngjīn],
to command the armies of the two commanderies along the river,
to combine forces with Xún,
to resist Zhū Wěi and others.
Yì then sent a letter to Lǐ Yì, saying:
"I have heard that a bright mirror is used to reflect one's form,
and past events are used to know the present.
In ancient times, Wēizǐ departed from Yīn and entered Zhōu;
Xiàng Bó betrayed Chǔ and returned to Hàn;
Zhōu Bó welcomed the King of Dài and deposed the Young Emperor;
Huò Guāng honored Xiàoxuān and廢 Chāngyì.
They all feared Heaven and knew fate,
seeing the omens of survival or demise,
and the affairs of rise and fall.
Thus, they were able to achieve success in their time
and establish their legacy for ten thousand generations.
If Cháng'ān could still be assisted,
extending its years and months,
then strangers would not be closer than kin,
nor the distant outweigh the near.
How could Jìwén dwell in a mere corner?
Now, Cháng'ān is in ruin and chaos,
the Chìméi are at the outskirts,
princes and marquises stir up trouble,
and high officials are estranged.
The order and discipline are broken,
the four quarters are disintegrating,
and different surnames are rising together.
Therefore, Xiāo Wáng traversed frost and snow,
managing affairs in Hébĕi.
Presently, heroes gather like clouds,
and the common people flock like the wind.
Even Bīn and Qí in their prime
cannot be compared to this.
If Jìwén can truly realize success and failure,
and promptly settle on a grand strategy,
comparing his merits to the ancients,
and turning disaster into fortune,
it is at this very moment.
If a fierce general drives his forces swiftly,
and a formidable army besieges the city,
even if there is regret,
it will be too late."
Initially,
Yì and Guāngwǔ were the first to conspire and make an agreement,
and they were especially close and loving.
But when Gèngshǐ was established,
they instead worked together to entrap Bóshēng.
Though he knew Cháng'ān was in danger,
Lǐ Yì wanted to surrender but was not at ease with himself.
So he replied to Yì's letter, saying:
"Yì originally conspired with Xiāo Wáng to establish Hàn,
making a pact of life and death,
and sharing the plan for glory or decline.
Now Yì holds Luòyáng,
and the General garrisons Mèngjīn.
Both occupy crucial positions,
a once-in-a-thousand-years opportunity.
We hope to achieve something as strong as cut metal.
I only wish to convey this deeply to Xiāo Wáng,
and offer my humble plan,
to assist the state and bring peace to the people."
After Yì sent this letter,
he no longer contended with Yì.
Therefore, Yì was able to advance north and attack Tiānjǐng Guān,
capturing two cities in Shàngdǎng.
[一０]Then he advanced south into Hénán, taking thirteen counties east of Chénggāo,
as well as various garrisons and settlements.
He pacified them all,
with over one hundred thousand surrendering.
Wǔ Bó led over ten thousand men to attack those who had rebelled.
Yì led his army across the river
and fought Bó at Shìxiāng Xià.
[一一]He greatly defeated and beheaded Bó,
capturing over five thousand heads.
Yì, meanwhile, kept his gates closed and offered no rescue.
Yì saw his trustworthiness and effectiveness,
and fully reported it to the throne.
Guāngwǔ therefore publicly displayed Yì's letter
[一二]to let Zhū Wěi know of it.
Wěi was enraged,
and subsequently sent someone to assassinate Yì.
Because of this, there was disunity within the city,
and many defected.
Wěi then dispatched Tǎonàn General Sū Máo with tens of thousands of men to attack Wēn,
while Wěi himself led tens of thousands of men to attack Píngyīn to tie down Yì.
[一三]Yì sent his Colonel-Protector of the Army (General) with troops
to join Kòu Xún in attacking Máo,
and they defeated him.
Yì then crossed the river to attack Wěi,
and Wěi fled.
Yì pursued him to Luòyáng,
circled the city once, and returned.
He sent a proclamation and a memorial,
and all the generals entered to congratulate him
and urged Guāngwǔ to ascend the imperial throne.
Guāngwǔ then summoned Yì to Guō
to inquire about the situation in the four quarters.
Yì said:
"The three kings have rebelled,
Gèngshǐ has been defeated and lost,
the world is without a master.
The concern for the ancestral temples
rests with Your Highness.
It is fitting to follow the public's opinion,
for the sake of the altars of soil and grain above,
and for the sake of the common people below."
Guāngwǔ said:
"Last night I dreamt I rode a red dragon to heaven.
When I awoke,
my heart was pounding."
Yì then descended from his mat and bowed twice in congratulation, saying:
"This is Heaven's mandate manifesting in your spirit.
Your pounding heart
is a sign of Your Highness's cautious and prudent nature."
Yì then, with the other generals, finalized the decision to bestow the exalted title.
In the spring of Jiànwǔ 2nd year,
Yì was formally enfeoffed as Yángxià Hóu.
He then led an attack on the bandits Yán Zhōng and Zhào Gēn in Yángzhái,
and defeated them.
An imperial edict ordered Yì to return home to visit his ancestral tomb,
and sent a Grand Master of the Household with beef and wine,
ordering the Grand Administrators and Commandants within a two-hundred-lǐ radius, and below, as well as his clan members, to gather there.
At that time, the Chìméi and Yán Cén were causing chaos in Sānfǔ.
The great clans in the commanderies and counties each commanded their own troops.
Dàsītú Dèng Yǔ could not pacify them.
So, Yì was sent to replace Yǔ to suppress them.
The imperial carriage saw him off to Hénán,
bestowing upon him a seven-foot sword used by the emperor.
The emperor commanded Yì, saying:
"Sānfǔ has suffered the chaos of Wáng Mǎng and Gèngshǐ,
compounded by the cruelty of the Chìméi and Yán Cén.
The common people are in dire straits,
with nowhere to turn for help.
This current campaign
is not necessarily about seizing territory or slaughtering cities,
but about pacifying and settling them.
The generals are not without bravery in battle,
but they are fond of plunder.
You are inherently capable of controlling your officers and soldiers;
remember to conduct yourself properly
so as not to cause hardship for the commanderies and counties."
Yì bowed his head and accepted the command,
then led his forces west.
Wherever he went, he established his prestige and trust.
Over ten groups of bandits in Hóngnóng, who called themselves generals,
all led their followers and surrendered to Yì.
Gōu Yǔ and the Chìméi met at Huáyīn.
They held each other off for over sixty days,
fighting dozens of engagements.
Gōu Yǔ captured their generals Liú Shǐ and Wáng Xuān, among others,
numbering over five thousand men.
In the spring of the third year [of Jiànwǔ],
the emperor sent an envoy to immediately appoint Gōu Yǔ as Grand General of the Expedition to the West.
Gōu Yǔ led the Chēqí General Dèng Hóng and others in their return.
They met Gōu Yǔ.
Yǔ and Hóng urged Gōu Yǔ to jointly attack the Chìméi.
Gōu Yǔ said,
"I have been resisting the bandits for several tens of days now.
Although I have repeatedly captured mighty generals,
their remaining forces are still numerous.
We can gradually win them over with kindness and trust;
it is difficult to defeat them with a sudden military strike.
The emperor has now ordered his generals to garrison at Mǐnchí to block them to the east,
while I strike them from the west.
Taking them in one swift action [this way],
this is a foolproof plan."
Yǔ and Hóng did not agree.
Dèng Hóng then fought a great battle that lasted the whole day.
The Chìméi feigned defeat,
abandoned their baggage train, and fled.
Their carts were all loaded with earth,
with beans covering the top.
The soldiers were hungry [from Gōu Yǔ's army]
and eagerly seized them.
The Chìméi turned back to attack Hóng,
and Hóng's army disintegrated in disorder.
Gōu Yǔ and Yǔ combined their forces to rescue him,
and the Chìméi retreated slightly.
Gōu Yǔ thought his soldiers were hungry and tired
and should rest for a while,
but Yǔ did not listen.
They fought again
and were greatly defeated,
with over three thousand dead or wounded.
Yǔ managed to escape back to Yíyáng.
Gōu Yǔ abandoned his horse and walked up Huíxī Bǎn,
returning to his camp with several men from his command.
He again fortified his position,
gathered his scattered troops,
and recruited several tens of thousands of garrisoned troops from various camps.
He arranged a date for a decisive battle with the bandits.
He sent brave men disguised in Chìméi uniforms
to lie in ambush by the roadside.
At dawn the next day,
the Chìméi sent ten thousand men to attack Gōu Yǔ's vanguard.
Gōu Yǔ barely dispatched troops to relieve them.
Seeing Gōu Yǔ's weak position,
the bandits then used all their forces to attack Gōu Yǔ.
Gōu Yǔ then unleashed his troops for a major battle.
By afternoon,
the bandits' morale waned.
The ambushing troops suddenly rose up.
Their clothes were mixed,
and the Chìméi could no longer distinguish [friend from foe].
Their forces then panicked and disintegrated.
Gōu Yǔ pursued and attacked them,
greatly defeating them at Xiáo Dǐ,
capturing eighty thousand men and women.
The remaining forces, over a hundred thousand strong,
fled east and surrendered at Yíyáng.
An imperial edict of commendation was sent to Gōu Yǔ, saying:
"The Chìméi have been broken and pacified.
The officers and soldiers have toiled hard.
Though you initially 'drooped your wings at Huíxī,'
you were ultimately able to 'flap your wings at Mǐnchí.'
This can be called 'losing at the eastern corner [of the sky]
and gaining at the mulberry and elm [sunset].'
We shall now discuss merits and rewards
to repay your great achievements."
Although the Chìméi had surrendered at that time,
numerous other bandits were still rampant: Yán Cén occupied Lántián,
Wáng Xīn occupied Xiàguī,
Fāng Dān occupied Xīnfēng,
Jiǎng Zhèn occupied Bālíng,
Zhāng Hán occupied Cháng'ān,
Gōngsūn Shǒu occupied Chánglíng,
Yáng Zhōu occupied Gǔkǒu,
Lǚ Wěi occupied Chéncāng,
Jué Hóng occupied Qiān,
Luò Yán occupied Zhōuzhì,
Rèn Liáng occupied Hù,
Rǔ Zhāng occupied Huáilǐ.
Each claimed the title of general,
commanding forces of over ten thousand at most,
and several thousand at least.
They attacked each other in turn.
Gōu Yǔ fought and marched,
camping his army in the Shànglínyuàn.
Yán Cén, having defeated the Chìméi,
proclaimed himself King Wǔ'ān,
appointed governors and prefects,
and sought to occupy Guānzhōng.
He led Zhāng Hán and Rèn Liáng to jointly attack Gōu Yǔ.
Gōu Yǔ defeated them,
beheading over a thousand.
All the garrisoned camps that had sided with Yán Cén came and surrendered to Gōu Yǔ.
Yán Cén fled to attack Xī.
Gōu Yǔ sent the Fùhàn General Dèng Yè and the Fǔhàn General Yú Kuāng to intercept Yán Cén,
greatly defeating him
and capturing his general Sū Chén and over eight thousand others.
Yán Cén then fled via Wǔguān to Nányáng.
At that time, the common people were starving,
and people were eating each other.
One jīn of gold could be exchanged for five shēng of beans.
Roads were cut off,
and supplies could not reach them.
The soldiers all subsisted on fruits and berries.
An imperial edict appointed Zhào Kuāng of Nányáng as Right Fúfēng,
to lead troops to assist Gōu Yǔ,
and also sent silk and grain.
Everyone in the army cried, "Long live!"
Gōu Yǔ's army grew in strength and provisions.
He then gradually executed and attacked the powerful local figures who defied his orders,
and liberally rewarded those who surrendered and performed meritorious deeds.
He sent all their leaders to the capital,
and dispersed their followers to return to their original occupations.
His prestige spread throughout Guānzhōng.
Only Lǚ Wěi, Zhāng Hán, and Jiǎng Zhèn sent envoys to surrender to Shǔ;
all the others were pacified.
The following year,
Gōngsūn Shù sent his general Chéng Yān,
with several tens of thousands of men, to join Lǚ Wěi and garrison at Chéncāng.
Gōu Yǔ and Zhào Kuāng met and attacked them,
greatly defeating them.
Chéng Yān retreated to Hànchuān.
Gōu Yǔ pursued and fought him at Jīgǔ,
defeating him again.
He then turned back and defeated Lǚ Wěi,
and many garrisons and surrendered troops joined him.
Thereafter, Shǔ repeatedly sent generals to make incursions,
but Gōu Yǔ always thwarted them.
He pacified the common people,
and redressed injustices.
In three years of campaigning,
he reached Shànglín.
Gōu Yǔ felt uneasy being away for so long,
and was not at ease.
He submitted a memorial expressing his longing for the imperial court,
wishing to be close to the emperor's inner circle.
The emperor did not permit it.
Later, someone submitted a memorial stating that Gōu Yǔ was acting as an autocrat in Guānzhōng,
had executed the Prefect of Cháng'ān,
and wielded immense power and authority.
The people were loyal to him,
calling him
"King Xiányáng."
The emperor had the memorial shown to Gōu Yǔ.
Gōu Yǔ was terrified and frightened.
He submitted a memorial expressing his apologies, saying:
"Your servant was originally a mere scholar.
I happened to encounter the beginning of this new dynasty,
filled a position in the ranks,
and received excessive imperial favor,
being appointed Grand General
and ennobled as Marquees of a Commandery.
I was entrusted with a regional command
to achieve minor merits,
all of which came from the strategies and deliberations of the state.
Your foolish servant could never have achieved them.
Your servant humbly reflects: when I followed imperial edicts in battle,
everything always went as desired.
When I made decisions based on my own private judgment,
I never failed to regret it.
The state's unique discerning wisdom
becomes ever clearer with time.
Then I realized that 'human nature and the Way of Heaven
are not to be learned by hearing.'
When military conflict first broke out,
in that tumultuous time,
heroes competed,
and thousands were bewildered.
Your servant, by chance,
entrusted myself to the sagacious and enlightened emperor.
Even amidst danger and confusion,
I dared not make excessive mistakes.
How much more so now that the empire is pacified,
with the exalted above and the humble below,
and the exalted rank and title I have received
are immeasurably high?
I sincerely hoped to maintain diligence and caution
and thus preserve myself from beginning to end.
Seeing the memorial shown to your servant,
I trembled with fear.
I humbly pray that the enlightened sovereign, knowing your servant's foolish nature,
would kindly allow me to present my case."
An imperial edict replied:
"The relationship between the general and the state
is that of lord and subject,
but our affection is like that of father and son.
What is there to doubt or suspect
that you should be afraid?"
In the sixth year, in spring,
Jǐng Yì went to the imperial capital.
He was granted an audience,
and the Emperor said to his ministers:
"This is my chief clerk from when I first raised an army.
He cleared the way for me,
and secured Guānzhōng."
After the audience,
he ordered a junior eunuch to bestow upon Jǐng Yì precious treasures, clothes, money, and silk.
An imperial edict stated:
"In the rush, there was no dòuzhōu at Lóutíng,
nor màifàn at the Hūtuó River.
This great kindness has long gone unrewarded."
Jǐng Yì bowed his head and expressed gratitude, saying:
"I have heard that Guǎn Zhòng said to Duke Huán: 'May Your Highness not forget the shooting of the hook,
and may your servant not forget the cage-cart.'
The state of Qí relied on this.
I now also wish that the state not forget the hardship in Héběi,
and this humble servant dares not forget the kindness of the jīchē."
Later, he was repeatedly summoned for banquets and audiences.
They finalized plans for attacking Shǔ,
and after staying for more than ten days,
Jǐng Yì's wife and children were ordered to return west with him.
In summer,
the generals were dispatched to ascend Lǒng,
but they were defeated by Wěi Xiāo.
Thereupon, an edict ordered Jǐng Yì's army to Xúnyì.
Before he could arrive,
Wěi Xiāo, emboldened by victory, sent his generals Wáng Yuán and Xíng Xún with over twenty thousand men to descend Lǒng.
He then separately dispatched Xíng Xún to take Xúnyì.
Jǐng Yì immediately rode with his troops,
intending to secure it first.
All the generals said:
"The barbarian troops are strong and have just won a victory;
we cannot contend with them.
We should halt the army in a favorable position,
and slowly consider our strategy."
Jǐng Yì said:
"The barbarian troops are at the border,
tempted by small gains,
and thus wish to penetrate deep.
If they obtain Xúnyì,
the Sānfǔ will be shaken,
which would be a great worry for me.
Indeed, 'the attacker has insufficient strength,
while the defender has more than enough.'
Now, if we first occupy the city,
we can await the exhausted while being at ease.
This is not a matter of contention."
He secretly went to the city, closed the gates,
and lowered his flags and silenced his drums.
Xíng Xún, unaware,
rushed towards it.
Jǐng Yì, taking advantage of his surprise,
suddenly beat the drums, raised the flags, and sallied forth.
Xíng Xún's army was shocked, disordered, and fled.
Jǐng Yì pursued and attacked them for tens of *lǐ*,
utterly defeating them.
Jì Zūn also took advantage of the situation and attacked the barbarians in Běidì. Thereupon, the chieftains of Běidì, such as Gěng Dìng,
all abandoned Wěi Xiāo and surrendered.
Jǐng Yì submitted a memorial detailing the situation,
not daring to boast of his own achievements.
Some generals wished to share his credit,
which troubled the Emperor.
Thereupon, he issued an imperial sealed letter stating:
"An edict to the Grand Marshal,
the Generals of Tiger's Teeth, Establishing Awe, Loyal to Hàn, Capturing Barbarians, and Martial Awe: The barbarian troops have poured down,
and the Sānfǔ are in alarm.
Xúnyì is in peril,
its downfall imminent.
The garrisons in Běidì
are holding their troops and observing.
Now, a single city has been preserved,
the barbarian troops have been repulsed,
causing Gěng Dìng and his ilk
to remember the righteousness between ruler and subject.
The achievements of the General who Conquers the West are like mountains,
yet he still considers them insufficient.
Mèng Zhīfǎn fleeing but bringing up the rear,
how is this different?
Now, I dispatch a Grand Master of the Middle to bestow medicine and coffins upon the wounded and deceased officers and soldiers of the General who Conquers the West.
The Grand Marshal and those below him shall personally condole the dead and inquire after the sick,
to uphold humility and yielding."
Thereupon, Jǐng Yì was ordered to advance his army to Yìqú,
and also to oversee the affairs of the Administrator of Běidì.
The Qīngshān Hú, numbering over ten thousand, surrendered to Jǐng Yì.
Jǐng Yì also attacked Jiǎ Lǎn, a general of Lú Fāng, and the Xiongnu Yùjiàn Rìzhú Wáng,
defeating them.
Shàngjùn and Āndìng all surrendered,
and Jǐng Yì again oversaw the affairs of the Administrator of Āndìng.
In the ninth year, in spring,
Jì Zūn died.
An edict ordered Jǐng Yì to assume the post of General who Conquers Barbarians,
and also to command Jì Zūn's camp.
When Wěi Xiāo died,
his generals Wáng Yuán and Zhōu Zōng and others again enthroned Xiāo's son, Chún,
still retaining troops and occupying Jì.
Gōngsūn Shù sent his general Zhào Kuāng and others to assist them.
The Emperor again ordered Jǐng Yì to oversee the affairs of the Administrator of Tiānshuǐ.
He attacked Kuāng and others for nearly a year,
and beheaded them all.
The generals jointly attacked Jì,
but could not take it.
They wished to withdraw for a rest,
but Jǐng Yì firmly held his ground,
always acting as the vanguard of the combined forces.
In the following year, in summer,
he attacked Luòmén with the other generals.
Before it was taken,
his illness recurred,
and he died in the army.
His posthumous title was Jié Hóu.
His eldest son, Zhāng, inherited the title.
In the following year,
the Emperor, mindful of Jǐng Yì's merits,
again enfeoffed Zhāng's younger brother, Xīn, as the Marquis of Xīxiāng.
In the thirteenth year,
Zhāng was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngmín,
with three counties as his stipend.
During the Yǒngpíng era,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Píngxiāng.
Zhāng died,
and his son, Pǔ, succeeded him.
Pǔ committed a crime,
and the marquisate was abolished.
In the sixth year of Yǒngchū,
Emperor Ān issued an edict stating:
"Indeed, benevolence does not abandon relatives,
and righteousness does not forget merit.
Restoring what was abolished, continuing what was cut off,
and extending goodness to descendants,
these are the ancient codes.
In the past, our Guāngwǔ received the mandate and brought about a revival,
expanding the sagely lineage,
spreading his influence across the four quarters,
manifesting himself to heaven and earth,
shining brilliantly for ten thousand generations.
His blessings and fortune flowed widely,
extending boundlessly.
I, a humble descendant,
think day and night,
recollecting the glorious achievements.
Consulting maps and records,
the twenty-eight meritorious generals of Jiànwǔ,
the tiger-like ministers who aided the mandate,
