whose records are attested by prophecies.
Indeed, Xiāo and Cáo were enfeoffed and their titles passed down,
continuing to this day.
How much more so for those not long past,
yet some even lack heirs for their sacrifices?
I am deeply saddened by this.
Therefore, let a list be made of the twenty-eight generals whose lineages have died out,
or whose marquisates were revoked due to crimes,
and whose descendants ought to succeed them.
Let their cases be separately presented.
This will reach even to Jǐngfēng,
manifesting their old virtues,
and highlighting these inherited merits."
Thereupon, Pǔ's son, Chén, was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Píngxiāng.
In the following year,
all those among the twenty-eight generals whose marquisates had been cut off
were re-enfeoffed.
Cén Péng, courtesy name Jūnrán,
was a native of Jíyáng, Nányáng.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
he served as the county magistrate of his home county.
When the Hàn army rose and attacked and took Jíyáng,
Péng led his family to flee to Zhēn Fù, the Grandee of the Vanguard.
Fù was angry that Péng could not hold his post,
and detained Péng's mother and wife,
ordering him to make achievements to redeem himself.
Péng led his retainers and fought with great effort.
When Zhēn Fù died,
Péng was wounded
and fled back to Wǎn,
where he jointly defended the city with Yán Yuè, the Second in Command of the Vanguard.
The Hàn army attacked for several months.
When food in the city ran out,
and people resorted to cannibalism,
Péng and Yuè surrendered the city.
All the generals wished to execute him,
but Dà Sītú Bóshēng said:
“Péng
is a great official of the commandery,
who held steadfast to his resolve.
This is his integrity.
Now that we are undertaking a great enterprise,
we should honor righteous gentlemen.
It would be better to enfeoff him,
to encourage those who come after him.”
Gēngshǐ then enfeoffed Péng as Guīdé Hóu,
and ordered him to serve under Bóshēng.
When Bóshēng met his demise,
Péng again became a Commandant under Dà Sīmǎ Zhū Wěi.
He followed Wěi in attacking Wáng Mǎng’s Yángzhōu Mù Lǐ Shèng,
killed him,
and pacified Huáiyáng Chéng.
Wěi recommended Péng as Huáiyáng Dūwèi.
Gēngshǐ dispatched Lìwēi Wáng Zhāng Áng and General Yáo Wěi to garrison Huáiyáng.
Wěi rebelled
and attacked and drove off Áng.
Péng led troops to attack Wěi
and defeated him.
He was promoted to Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
At that time, Liú Mào of Chōnglíng raised an army
and conquered Yǐngchuān.
Péng could not take up his post,
so he led his several hundred subordinates to follow his fellow townsman Hán Xīn, the Hénèi Tàishǒu.
When Guāngwǔ campaigned in Hénèi,
Xīn suggested holding the city in defense,
but Péng stopped him and he did not listen.
Shortly after, Guāngwǔ arrived at Huái,
and Xīn, under duress, welcomed him and surrendered.
Guāngwǔ knew his previous plan
and was greatly enraged.
He arrested Xīn, placed him under a drum,
and was about to execute him.
He summoned Péng for an audience,
and Péng took the opportunity to advise him, saying:
“Now that the Chìméi have entered Guān,
Gēngshǐ is in peril.
Powerful ministers are indulging themselves,
falsely claiming imperial decrees and edicts.
The roads are blocked,
and the four quarters are rising in swarms.
Numerous heroes are competing for power,
and the common people have no one to whom to pledge allegiance.
I secretly heard that Your Majesty pacified Hébĕi
and established the royal power in Chǔ. A This is truly Heaven assisting the Hàn,
and a blessing for all gentlemen.
I was fortunate to be spared by Sītú Gōng,
but before I could repay his kindness,
I was suddenly afflicted with misfortune,
a perpetual regret in my heart.
Now I have encountered Your Majesty again;
I wish to dedicate myself to your service.”
Guāngwǔ accepted him profoundly.
Péng then said that Hán Xīn, being a prominent man from Nányáng,
could be utilized.
So Xīn was pardoned
and made Dèng Yǔ’s military advisor.
Gēngshǐ’s Dà Jiāngjūn Lǚ Zhí was leading troops to garrison Qíyuán,
and Péng persuaded him to surrender.
Thereupon, Péng was appointed Cìjiān Dà Jiāngjūn,
and ordered to supervise all the camps,
entrusted with the staff he always carried,
and followed in pacifying Hébĕi.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
Péng was appointed Tíngwèi,
his title of Guīdé Hóu remained as before,
and he acted as Dà Jiāngjūn.
Together with Dà Sīmǎ Wú Hàn,
Dà Sīkōng Wáng Liáng,
Jiànyì Dà Jiāngjūn Zhū Yòu,
Yòujiāngjūn Wàn Xiū,
Zhíjīnwú Jiǎ Fù,
Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Liú Zhí,
Yánghuà Jiāngjūn Jiān Xún,
Jīshè Jiāngjūn Hóu Jìn,
Piānjiāngjūn Féng Yì, Jì Zūn, Wáng Bà, and others,
he besieged Luòyáng for several months.
Zhū Wěi and others held firm and refused to surrender.
The Emperor, knowing that Péng had once been Wěi’s Commandant,
ordered him to go persuade him.
Wěi was on the city wall,
and Péng was below the wall.
They greeted each other and conversed happily as if in normal times.
Péng then said:
“In the past, I was privileged to serve and attend you,
and was recommended and promoted by you.
I have always thought of how to repay your kindness.
Now the Chìméi have already taken Cháng’ān,
Gēngshǐ has been overthrown by the Sān Wáng,
the Emperor has received the Mandate,
pacified Yān and Zhào,
and completely possesses the lands of Yōu and Jì.
The people are loyal,
and wise talents gather like clouds.
He personally leads a great army
to attack Luòyáng.
The affairs of the world
are destined to proceed thus.
Although you hold the city firmly,
what are you waiting for?”
Wěi said:
“When Dà Sītú was killed,
I was complicit in the plan,
and I also advised Gēngshǐ not to send Xiāowáng to campaign in the north.
I truly know my sins are deep.”
Péng returned
and fully reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
“He who undertakes great affairs
does not dwell on petty grievances.
If Wěi surrenders now,
his official rank and title can be preserved,
let alone punishment?
The Yellow River is here;
I will not go back on my word.”
Péng again went to tell Wěi.
Wěi lowered a rope from the city wall and said:
“If you truly mean it,
you can climb up with this.”
Péng quickly grabbed the rope, intending to go up.
Wěi saw his sincerity
and immediately agreed to surrender.
Five days later,
Wěi led light cavalry to Péng.
He turned and ordered his subordinate generals:
“Hold fast and wait for me.
If I do not return,
you gentlemen should lead the great army directly up Huányuán
and return to Yǎn Wáng.”
Then, with his hands bound in front,
he went with Péng to Héyáng.
The Emperor immediately untied his bonds,
granted him an audience,
and again ordered Péng to send Wěi back to the city that night.
The next morning,
he led all his troops out to surrender.
Wěi was appointed Píngdí Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Fúgōu Hóu.
Wěi,
a native of Huáiyáng,
later became Shàofǔ,
〔一０〕and his enfeoffment was passed down for generations.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ [26 CE],
Péng Yì was sent to attack Jīngzhōu,
capturing Shēnzì, Yè, and over ten other cities.
At this time, the southern regions were particularly chaotic.
Qín Fēng, a native of Nánjùn, occupied Líqiū,
proclaimed himself King Chǔ Lí,
and had acquired twelve counties.
Dǒng Xīn rose up in Dǔxiāng;
Xǔ Hán rose up in Xìng;
and furthermore, various generals of the Gèngshǐ Emperor each held forces and occupied cities in Nányáng.
The Emperor dispatched Wú Hàn to attack them,
but Wú Hàn's army committed many acts of aggression and violence wherever they went.
At this time, Dèng Fèng, General Who Breaks the Captives, had returned to Xīnyě for an audience.
Angered by Wú Hàn's plundering of his hometown,
he thereupon rebelled,
defeated Wú Hàn's army,
seized their supplies,
garrisoned and occupied Yùyáng,
and allied with the other bandits.
In autumn,
Péng Yì conquered Xìng,
and Xǔ Hán surrendered.
Péng Yì was promoted to General-in-Chief Who Conquers the South.
The Emperor again dispatched Zhū Yòu, Jiǎ Fù, and Gěng Yǎn, General-in-Chief Who Establishes Might;
Wáng Cháng, General Who Is Loyal to Hàn;
Guō Shǒu, General Who Inspires Awe;
Liú Hóng, General of Elite Cavalry;
and Liú Jiā and Gěng Zhí, Major Generals,
to join forces with Péng Yì to suppress Dèng Fèng.
They first attacked Dǔxiāng,
but Dèng Fèng's general led over ten thousand men to rescue Dǒng Xīn.
Both Dǒng Xīn and Dèng Fèng had elite troops from Nányáng,
and though Péng Yì and the others attacked them,
they could not overcome them for months.
In the summer of the third year [27 CE],
the Emperor personally led an expedition south.
When he reached Yè,
Dǒng Xīn's detached general, leading several thousand men, blocked the road,
preventing the imperial chariots and cavalry from advancing.
Péng Yì swiftly attacked
and decisively defeated them.
When the Emperor arrived at Dǔyáng,
Dèng Fèng fled back to Yùyáng under cover of night,
and Dǒng Xīn surrendered.
Péng Yì, together with Gěng Yǎn, Jiǎ Fù, Fù Jùn, General Who Commands Crossbowmen, and Zāng Gōng, Commandant of Cavalry, pursued Dèng Fèng to Xiǎocháng'ān.
The Emperor personally led his generals into battle
and decisively defeated him.
Dèng Fèng, cornered,
then surrendered.
The Emperor pitied Dèng Fèng as a former meritorious official,
and moreover, the conflict had been instigated by Wú Hàn,
so he wished to fully pardon him.
Péng Yì and Gěng Yǎn advised, saying:
"Dèng Fèng betrayed our grace and rebelled,
exhausting the army for a year,
causing Jiǎ Fù to be wounded,
and Zhū Yòu to be captured.
After Your Majesty arrived,
he showed no repentance or desire to do good,
but rather engaged in battle personally,
surrendering only after his army was defeated.
If Dèng Fèng is not executed,
there will be no means to deter evil."
Thereupon, he was beheaded.
Dèng Fèng was
the nephew of Dèng Chén, Marquis of Xīhuá.
The imperial carriage returned,
and Péng Yì was ordered to lead Fù Jùn, Zāng Gōng, Liú Hóng, and over thirty thousand other men south to attack Qín Fēng.
They captured Huángyóu.
Qín Fēng and his chief general, Cài Hóng, resisted Péng Yì and the others at Dèng,
and they could not advance for several months.
The Emperor was surprised and reproached Péng Yì.
Fearing this, Péng Yì
then marshaled his troops and horses at night,
issued orders throughout the army,
commanding them to attack Shāndū to the west the next morning.
He then loosened the captives they had taken,
allowing them to escape
and report this to Qín Fēng.
Qín Fēng immediately led his entire army west to intercept Péng Yì.
Péng Yì then secretly led his troops across the Miǎn River,
attacked Qín Fēng's general Zhāng Yáng at Ātóushān,
and decisively defeated him.
He cut down trees and cleared a path through the valleys,
striking directly at Líqiū,
and defeated the various garrisoned troops.
Qín Fēng was greatly alarmed upon hearing this,
and rushed back to relieve them.
Péng Yì and the generals established a camp relying on the Eastern Mountain.
Qín Fēng and Cài Hóng attacked Péng Yì at night,
but Péng Yì had already prepared for them,
and sent out troops to counterattack.
Qín Fēng was defeated and fled,
and Cài Hóng was pursued and beheaded.
Péng Yì was again enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔyīn.
Qín Fēng's chancellor Zhào Jīng died, and Wú Chéng surrendered.
He was appointed General Who Establishes Hàn
and together with Péng Yì besieged Qín Fēng at Líqiū.
At this time, Tián Róng, who held a multitude of followers at Yílíng,
heard that Qín Fēng was besieged,
and fearing that a large army was approaching,
wished to surrender.
However, his wife's elder brother, Xīn Chén, advised Tián Róng, saying:
"Currently, heroes from all four directions each occupy commanderies and states.
Luòyáng is but the size of a palm;
it would be better to hold our forces and observe the changes."
Tián Róng replied:
"With the strength of King Qín [Fēng],
he is still besieged by the General Who Conquers the South.
How much more so for me?
The plan to surrender is decided."
In the spring of the fourth year [28 CE],
Tián Róng then left Xīn Chén to guard Yílíng,
and personally led troops along the river, up the Miǎn River, stopping at Líqiū.
He set a date to surrender,
but Xīn Chén later stole Tián Róng's treasures
and surrendered to Péng Yì first by a secret path,
and sent a letter to persuade Tián Róng.
Tián Róng suspected he would surely betray him,
and thus dared not surrender,
but instead allied with Qín Fēng.
Péng Yì sent troops to attack Tián Róng,
and after several months,
decisively defeated him.
His chief general, Wǔ Gōng, went to Péng Yì and surrendered,
and Tián Róng fled back to Yílíng.
The Emperor visited Líqiū to commend the army,
and enfeoffed over a hundred meritorious officers and soldiers of Péng Yì.
Péng Yì attacked Qín Fēng for three years,
beheading over ninety thousand people.
Qín Fēng's remaining troops were barely a thousand,
and the food in the city was almost exhausted.
The Emperor, seeing Qín Fēng weakening,
ordered Zhū Yòu to take over Péng Yì's guard,
and sent Péng Yì and Fù Jùn south to attack Tián Róng.
They decisively defeated him,
then captured Yílíng,
and pursued him to Zǐguī.
Tián Róng, with several tens of horsemen, fled into Shǔ,
and all his family members, wives, and tens of thousands of soldiers were captured.
Péng Yì, intending to attack Shǔ-Hàn,
found the river valleys narrow,
and the treacherous waters made transport difficult.
He left Fēng Jùn, General Who Inspires Awe, to garrison Jiāngzhōu;
Tián Hóng, Commandant, to garrison Yílíng;
and Lǐ Xuán, Army Commander, to garrison Yídào.
He himself led his troops back to garrison Jīnxiāng,
which was a strategic point in Jīngzhōu.
He informed and announced to the various barbarian tribes
that those who surrendered would have their rulers and chiefs presented for enfeoffment.
Earlier,
Péng Yì had been on good terms with Dèng Ràng, Administrator of Jiāozhǐ.
He wrote to Dèng Ràng, explaining the might and virtue of the state,
and also dispatched Major General Qū Chōng to issue a proclamation to the south of the Jiāng River,
circulating imperial edicts.

Thereupon, Dèng Ràng, along with Hóu Dēng, Administrator of Jiāngxià; Wáng Táng, Administrator of Wǔlíng; Hán Fú, Chancellor of Chángshā; Zhāng Lóng, Administrator of Guìyáng; Tián Xī, Administrator of Línglíng; Dù Mù, Administrator of Cāngwú; and Xī Guāng, Administrator of Jiāozhǐ,
collectively sent envoys to offer tribute,
and all were enfeoffed as marquises.
Some even sent their sons to lead troops to assist Péng Yì in his campaigns.
Thus, the treasures from south of the Jiāng River began to circulate.
In the winter of the sixth year [30 CE],
Péng Yì was summoned to the capital.
He was frequently invited to banquets and audiences,
and was generously rewarded.
He then returned south to Jīnxiāng.
There was an imperial edict for him to visit his home and ancestors' tombs,
and the Grand Palace Secretary would inquire about the Grand Lady's well-being on the first and fifteenth of each month.
In the eighth year [32 CE],
Péng Yì led his troops to follow the imperial carriage and conquer Tiānshuǐ,
and together with Wú Hàn, besieged Kuí Xiāo at Xīchéng.
At this time, Lǐ Yù, a general of Gōngsūn Shù, led troops to rescue Kuí Xiāo,
garrisoning Shàngguī.
The Emperor left Gài Yán and Gěng Yǎn to besiege him,
while the imperial carriage returned east.
The Emperor sent a letter to Péng Yì, saying:
"If both cities fall,
you can then lead troops south to attack the Shǔ barbarians.
People suffer from insatiability;
having pacified Lǒng,
I again covet Shǔ.
Each time I dispatch troops,
my hair turns white."
Péng Yì then dammed the Gǔ River to flood Xīchéng.
Before the city was submerged by more than a丈,
Kuí Xiāo's generals Xíng Xún and Zhōu Zōng arrived with relief troops from Shǔ,
allowing Kuí Xiāo to escape back to Jì.
The Hàn army ran out of food,
burned their supplies,
and led their troops down from Lǒng.
Gài Yán and Gěng Yǎn also retreated with them.
Kuí Xiāo sent out troops to attack the rear of the various camps.
Péng Yì formed the rearguard,
thus enabling the generals to preserve their entire force and return east.
Péng Yì returned to Jīnxiāng.
In the ninth year,
Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述) dispatched his generals Rèn Mǎn (任滿), Tián Róng (田戎), and Chéng Fàn (程汎),
who led tens of thousands of men on rafts down the Jiāngguān (江關) pass.
They defeated Féng Jùn (馮駿), Tián Hóng (田鴻), Lǐ Xuán (李玄) and others.
They then captured Yídào (夷道) and Yílíng (夷陵),
and occupied Jīngmén (荊門) and Hǔyá (虎牙).
They built pontoon bridges and fighting towers across the river,
set up clustered stakes to block the waterway,
and established camps on the mountains
to resist the Hàn (漢) forces.
Péng (彭) attacked them several times,
but without success.
Thereupon, he equipped several thousand direct-advance tower-ships and assault ships with shielded oars.
In the spring of the eleventh year,
Péng (彭), along with Wú Hàn (吳漢), Zhūlǔ Jiāngjūn Liú Lóng (誅虜將軍劉隆), Fǔwēi Jiāngjūn Zāng Gōng (輔威將軍臧宮), and Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn Liú Xīn (驍騎將軍劉歆),
mobilized troops from Nányáng (南陽), Wǔlíng (武陵), and Nánjùn (南郡).
They also summoned provision-carrying oarsmen from Guìyáng (桂陽), Línglíng (零陵), and Chángshā (長沙).
In total, there were over sixty thousand men
and five thousand cavalry,
all converging at Jīngmén (荊門).
Wú Hàn (吳漢) considered that the oarsmen from the three commanderies consumed too much grain,
and wished to dismiss them.
Péng (彭), believing the Shǔ (蜀) forces to be strong,
thought they could not be sent away,
and submitted a memorial detailing the situation.
The Emperor replied to Péng (彭), saying:
"The Grand Marshal is accustomed to using infantry and cavalry
and is not skilled in naval warfare.
The matter at Jīngmén (荊門)
depends entirely on the Duke who Pacifies the South."
Péng (彭) then ordered a recruitment within the army for those willing to attack the pontoon bridge,
promising a supreme reward for the first to ascend.
Thus, Junior General Lǔ Qí (魯奇) answered the call and came forward.
At that time, a fierce wind raged.
Qí's (奇) ship went upstream against the current,
directly towards the pontoon bridge,
but the clustered stakes prevented it from leaving.
Qí (奇) and his men fought with desperate determination, leveraging the situation,
and then used flying torches to set it ablaze.
The furious wind intensified the fire,
and the bridge towers collapsed and burned.
Péng (彭) then led his entire army forward with the wind,
sweeping aside all opposition.
The Shǔ (蜀) forces fell into great disarray,
and several thousand drowned.
Rèn Mǎn (任滿) was beheaded,
Chéng Fàn (程汎) was captured alive,
while Tián Róng (田戎) escaped and took refuge in Jiāngzhōu (江州).
Péng (彭) recommended Liú Lóng (劉隆) to be Administrator of Nánjùn (南郡),
and he himself, leading Zāng Gōng (臧宮) and Liú Xīn (劉歆), marched directly into Jiāngguān (江關),
ordering the army not to plunder.
Wherever they passed,
the common people brought cattle and wine to welcome and entertain them.
Péng (彭) met with the elders
and told them that the Great Hàn (大漢) sympathized with Bāshǔ (巴蜀) for having been long subjected to tyranny,
and had therefore raised an army for a distant expedition
to punish the guilty
and eliminate harm for the people.
He politely refused their cattle and wine.
The common people were all greatly pleased
and eagerly opened their gates to surrender.
An imperial edict appointed Péng (彭) as Administrator of Yìzhōu (益州),
and for any commanderies he captured,
he was to act as Administrator.
When Péng (彭) arrived at Jiāngzhōu (江州),
he considered Tián Róng (田戎) to have abundant provisions,
making it difficult to capture quickly.
He left Féng Jùn (馮駿) to guard it,
and himself led his troops, capitalizing on the advantage, directly to Diànjiāng (墊江).
He attacked and captured Píngqǔ (平曲),
seizing hundreds of thousands of *shi* of grain.
Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述) sent his generals Yán Cén (延岑), Lǚ Wěi (呂鮪), Wáng Yuán (王元), and his younger brother Huī (恢) with all their troops to resist at Guǎnghàn (廣漢) and Zīzhōng (資中).
He also dispatched General Hóu Dān (侯丹) with over twenty thousand men to resist at Huángshí (黃石).
Péng (彭) then deployed many feinting troops,
sending Guardian of the Army Yáng Xī (楊翕) and Zāng Gōng (臧宮) to resist Yán Cén (延岑) and others.
He himself divided his forces, floated down the river back to Jiāngzhōu (江州),
then ascended the Dūjiāng (都江)
to launch a surprise attack on Hóu Dān (侯丹),
utterly defeating him.
He then marched day and night, covering more than two thousand *li* at double speed,
directly capturing Wǔyáng (武陽).
He sent elite cavalry to Guǎngdū (廣都),
which was dozens of *li* from Chéngdū (成都).
Their momentum was like a storm,
and wherever they went, people scattered.
Initially,
when Shù (述) heard that the Hàn (漢) troops were at Píngqǔ (平曲),
he had dispatched a large army to intercept them.
But when Péng (彭) reached Wǔyáng (武陽),
bypassing to the rear of Yán Cén's (延岑) army,
Shǔ (蜀) was shocked.
Shù (述) was greatly alarmed and,
striking the ground with his staff, exclaimed:
"What kind of divine being is this!"
The place where Péng (彭) encamped was called Péngwáng (彭亡) ("Péng's Demise").
Hearing this, he disliked it
and wished to move,
but it was already dusk.
A Shǔ (蜀) assassin, pretending to be a runaway slave seeking surrender,
stabbed and killed Péng (彭) that night.
Péng (彭) first broke Jīngmén (荊門),
then marched directly to Wǔyáng (武陽).
He maintained strict military discipline,
not harming even an autumn hair.
The King of Qiónggǔ (邛穀) Rèn Guì (任貴), hearing of Péng's (彭) prestige and trustworthiness,
sent envoys from thousands of *li* away to surrender.
At that time, Péng (彭) had already died.
The Emperor gave all of Rèn Guì's (任貴) offerings to Péng's (彭) wife and children,
and posthumously honored him as Zhuàng Hóu (壯侯).
The people of Shǔ (蜀) mourned him
and built a temple for him in Wǔyáng (武陽),
where they sacrificed to him annually.
His son Zūn (遵) inherited the title
and was transferred to be enfeoffed as Xìyáng Hóu (細陽侯).
In the thirteenth year,
the Emperor, mindful of Péng's (彭) achievements,
again enfeoffed Zūn's (遵) younger brother Huái (淮) as Gǔyáng Hóu (穀陽侯).
Zūn (遵) served as Commandant of Cavalry in the Yǒngpíng (永平) era.
When Zūn (遵) died,
his son Kàng (伉) succeeded.
When Kàng (伉) died,
his son Shí (嵵) succeeded.
In the third year of Yuánchū (元初),
he lost his state due to an incident.
In the first year of Jiànguāng (建光),
Emperor Ān (安帝) re-enfeoffed Shí (嵵) as Xìyáng Hóu (細陽侯).
During Emperor Shùn's (順帝) reign, he served as Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
When Shí (嵵) died,
his son Xī (熙) succeeded
and married Princess Nèyáng (涅陽長公主), Emperor Ān's (安帝) younger sister.
In his youth, he served as Attendant and Commander of the Tiger Guards,
and many in court praised his ability.
He was promoted to Administrator of Wèijùn (魏郡),
where he invited reclusive talents
to participate in governance,
bringing about transformation through non-action.
After serving for two years,
the common people sang of him:
"If I have brambles and thorns,
Lord Cén (岑) cuts them down.
If I have crop pests,
Lord Cén (岑) stops them.
Dog barks do not startle us;
hair grows under our feet (i.e., we are undisturbed and at peace).
Full of food, beating our bellies,
how can we know of disaster?
I rejoice that I was born,
and solely came across this time.
How excellent is Lord Cén (岑)!
Alas, how glorious!"
When Xī (熙) died,
his son Fú (福) succeeded,
serving as Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
Jiǎ Fù (賈復), courtesy name Jūn Wén (君文),
was from Guānjūn (冠軍), Nányáng (南陽).
In his youth, he loved learning
and studied the *Shàngshū* (尚書).
He served Lǐ Shēng (李生) of Wǔyīn (舞陰).
Lǐ Shēng (李生) regarded him as extraordinary
and told his disciples:
"Jia Jun's (賈君) appearance and ambition are thus,
and he is diligent in his studies;
he is an instrument for a general or prime minister."
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) reign,
he served as a county clerk.
While transporting salt from Hédōng (河東),
he encountered bandits.
More than ten others like him all abandoned their salt,
but Fù (復) alone returned it intact to the county.
The county praised his trustworthiness.
At that time, soldiers from Xiàjiāng and Xīnshì rose in rebellion.
Jiǎ Fù also gathered several hundred men at Yǔshān,
styling himself a general.
When Gēngshǐ was established,
Jiǎ Fù led his troops to pledge allegiance to Hàngzhōngwáng Liú Jiā,
who appointed him as a commandant (xiàowèi).
When Jiǎ Fù saw that Gēngshǐ's government was in chaos
and his generals were unrestrained,
he advised Jiā, saying:
"I have heard that those who sought to emulate the achievements of Yáo and Shùn but could not reach them
were Tāng and Wǔ;
those who sought to emulate the achievements of Tāng and Wǔ but could not reach them
were Huán and Wén;
those who sought to emulate the achievements of Huán and Wén but could not reach them
were the Six States;
those who established the rules of the Six States,
wishing to maintain them securely but could not,
were the ones who lost the Six States.
Now, the Hàn dynasty is experiencing a revival,
and Your Majesty, as a relative, serves as a bulwark.
The world is not yet settled, yet you would wish to securely hold what you possess.
Is it not possible that what you possess cannot be held?"
Jiā said:
"Your words are profound,
but this is not my responsibility.
Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) Liú Gōng is in Héběi;
he will surely be able to put your plan into effect.
Just take my letter and go."
Jiǎ Fù then bid farewell to Jiā,
took the letter, crossed the river northward,
and reached Guāngwǔ at Bǎirén.
Through Dèng Yǔ, he was granted an audience.
Guāngwǔ was impressed by him,
and Yǔ also praised him for possessing the qualities of a commander.
Thereupon, Jiǎ Fù was appointed as the General Who Breaks Captives (Pòlǔ Jiāngjūn), overseeing bandits.
Jiǎ Fù's horse was weak,
so Guāngwǔ unhitched his left outrider and bestowed it upon him.
The officials believed that Jiǎ Fù, as a newcomer, liked to bully and belittle his peers,
and proposed appointing him as the commandant of Guō.
Guāngwǔ said:
"Commander Jiǎ possesses the might to break a thousand li.
I am about to entrust him with important duties;
you must not arbitrarily remove him."
When Guāngwǔ arrived at Xìndū,
he made Jiǎ Fù a Major-General (Piān Jiāngjūn).
After taking Hándān,
he was promoted to Commander of the Capital Garrison (Dūhù Jiāngjūn).
He followed in attacking the Qīngdú bandits at Shèquǎn.
The great battle lasted until midday,
and the enemy lines were firm, refusing to yield.
Guāngwǔ sent for Jiǎ Fù, saying:
"The officers and soldiers are all hungry;
perhaps they should have breakfast first."
Jiǎ Fù replied:
"First break them,
then eat."
Thereupon, he donned his armor, was the first to ascend,
and wherever he advanced, everything collapsed.
The bandits then fled in defeat.
All the generals admired his bravery.
He also fought the Wǔxiào to the north at Zhēndìng,
inflicting a great defeat upon them.
Jiǎ Fù sustained severe wounds.
Guāngwǔ was greatly alarmed, saying:
"The reason I do not allow Jiǎ Fù to lead a separate army
is because he is reckless in battle.
As expected,
I almost lost my famous general.
I heard his wife is pregnant.
If it's a girl,
my son will marry her;
if it's a boy,
my daughter will marry him.
I will not let him worry about his wife and children."
Jiǎ Fù's illness soon recovered,
and he caught up with Guāngwǔ at Jì.
They met with great joy.
A great banquet was held for the officers and soldiers,
and Jiǎ Fù was made to sit in front.
He attacked the Yè bandits,
defeating them.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
Jiǎ Fù was appointed Marshal-Protector (Zhí Jīnwú)
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Guànjūn.
He first crossed the river to attack Zhū Wěi at Luòyáng,
and fought with Báihǔ Gōng Chén Qiáo,
repeatedly defeating and subduing him.
In Jiànwǔ second year (26 CE),
his fiefs of Ráng and Cháoyáng counties were increased.
Gēngshǐ's King of Yǎn, Yǐn Zūn, and other great generals in the south had not yet surrendered.
The Emperor summoned his generals to discuss military matters.
For a long time, no one spoke,
and he pondered for a while.
Then he struck the ground with a document and said:
"Yǎn is the strongest,
Wǎn is second.
Who will attack them?"
Jiǎ Fù boldly replied:
"I request to attack Yǎn."
The Emperor smiled and said:
"With Marshal-Protector attacking Yǎn,
what more do I have to worry about!
The Grand Marshal should attack Wǎn."
Accordingly, he sent Jiǎ Fù, along with Cavalry Commandant (Qí Dūwèi) Yīn Shí and General of Swift Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn) Liú Zhí, south across Wǔshè Jīn to attack Yǎn,
defeating them repeatedly.
After more than a month,
Yǐn Zūn surrendered,
and all his territory was secured.
He then led east to attack Gēngshǐ's Grand Administrator of Huáiyáng, Bào Sì.
Bào Sì surrendered,
and all the dependent counties were settled.
That autumn,
he attacked Zhàolíng and Xīnxī in the south,
pacifying them.
In the spring of the following year,
he was promoted to General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn),
and separately attacked the Chìméi between Xīnchéng and Miǎnchí,
repeatedly defeating them.
He met the Emperor at Yíyáng,
and the Chìméi surrendered.
Jiǎ Fù participated in campaigns and expeditions,
never suffering a defeat,
and often broke through encirclements and relieved critical situations with other generals,
personally sustaining twelve wounds.
The Emperor, seeing Jiǎ Fù's daring deep thrusts,
rarely sent him on distant expeditions,
but admired his bravery and resolve,
often keeping him close.
Therefore, Jiǎ Fù had fewer achievements commanding a single front.
Whenever the generals discussed their achievements and boasted,
Jiǎ Fù never said a word.
The Emperor would always say:
"As for Lord Jiǎ's achievements,
I know them myself."
In the thirteenth year (37 CE),
he was formally enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiāodōng,
with emoluments from Yùzhì, Zhuàngwǔ, Xiàmì, Jìmò, Tǐng (Hú), and Guānyáng,
a total of six counties.
Jiǎ Fù knew that the Emperor desired to lay down weapons
and cultivate civilian virtues,
not wishing for meritorious officials to maintain private armies in the capital.
So, he and High Chancellor (Gāomì Hóu) Dèng Yǔ together renounced their armor and weapons,
and focused on Confucian studies.
The Emperor deeply approved of this,
and subsequently disbanded the Left and Right Generals.
Jiǎ Fù, as a marquis, returned to his private residence,
and was granted the special title of Special Advancement (Tèjìn).
Jiǎ Fù was a person of firm and straightforward character,
possessing great integrity.
After returning to his private residence, he shut his gates and cultivated an air of solemn dignity.
Zhū Yòu and others recommended Jiǎ Fù as suitable for prime minister,
but the Emperor was currently holding the Three Excellencies (Sān Gōng) accountable for administrative matters,
so meritorious officials were generally not employed.
At this time, among the marquises, only the Marquises of Gāomì, Gùshǐ, and Jiāodōng
participated with the grandees in discussing important national affairs;
their favor and treatment were exceedingly generous.
In the thirty-first year (55 CE), he died,
and was given the posthumous title of Gāng Hóu.
His son Zhōng succeeded.
When Zhōng died,
his son Mǐn succeeded.
In Jiànchū first year (76 CE),
he was implicated in falsely accusing his mother of murder,
and his marquisate was abolished.
Sùzōng re-enfeoffed Jiǎ Fù's youngest son Hán as Marquis of Jiāodōng,
and Hán's younger brother Zōng as Marquis of Jìmò,
each with one county.
When Hán died,
his son Yù succeeded.
When Yù died,
his son Cháng succeeded.
Zōng, courtesy name Wǔrú,
had a reputation for integrity and conduct in his youth,
and possessed great intelligence and strategy.
He was initially appointed as a Gentleman (Lángzhōng),
gradually promoted,
and during the Jiànchū era, he became Grand Administrator of Shuòfāng.
In the past, internal commandery migrants residing in the border regions
were mostly poor and weak,
serving as servants to local residents
and unable to become officials.
Zōng promoted those among them who were capable of holding office,
having them participate in selections with border officials,
and rotating them to oversee each other
to expose corruption.
Some were even appointed as chief magistrates based on their merit,
so each was willing to give their utmost.
The Xiōngnú feared him
and dared not enter the pass.
He was summoned to serve as Commandant of Chángshuǐ.
Zōng was proficient in both classical scholarship and strategy.
Whenever there was a banquet or audience,
he was often made to discuss matters with Minor Treasurer (Shàofǔ) Dīng Hóng and others in the Emperor's presence.
In Zhānghé second year (88 CE), he died,
and the imperial court mourned and regretted his passing.
His son Cān succeeded.
Cān died,
his son Jiàn succeeded.
In the first year of Yuánchū (107 CE),
he married Princess Línyǐng, daughter of Emperor Hé.
The princess simultaneously received revenue from Yǐngyīn and Xǔ,
making a total of three counties,
comprising tens of thousands of households.
At that time, Empress Dowager Dèng's favor and honor were at their peak,
so Jiàn was appointed Shìzhōng,
and during Emperor Shùn's reign, he became Guānglùxūn.
The commentary says: Among the generals and commanders who achieved merit and fame during the Restoration, there were many.
Only Cén Péng and Féng Yì established a reputation for governing a region,
from Hángǔ Pass to the west,
and Fāngchéng Mountains to the south,
the achievements of these two generals
were truly great.
Such as Féng [Yì]'s and Jiǎ [Fù]'s lack of boasting,
and Lord Cén [Péng]'s righteousness and trustworthiness,
these were enough to inspire the entire army and win over enemies,
thus enabling them to successfully complete great undertakings
and ultimately preserve their good fortune.
Formerly, Emperor Gāozǔ feared the name Bǎirén,
and avoided it in order to preserve his good fortune;
Zhēngnán abhorred the place named Péngwáng,
but he remained there, thereby generating disaster.
Could it be that human foresight inherently possesses both clarity and confusion,
or is it destiny that causes things to be so?
An encomium states: In Yángxià, the master's victory
was truly due to his harmonious virtue.
The salt official of Jiāodōng,
who conquered the bandits of Wǎn in the south.
His marvelous vanguard shocked the enemy,
and his far-sighted plans aided the state.
Textual Notes: Page 639, line 4: Rǔzhōu Jíchéng Xiàn also has Fùchéng. Annotation: Jíjiě quotes Shěn Qīnhán's explanation,
stating that the Fùchéng in Rǔzhōu Jíchéng Xiàn
is the Chénggōng of Pèijùn mentioned in the former gazetteer,
not Fùchéng.
The note is mistaken.
Page 639, line 12: Duàn Jiàn. Annotation: The original text
is everywhere mistakenly written as
which has been directly corrected.
Henceforth, not all such instances will be pointed out.

Page 640, line 9: Jìng, whose courtesy name was Zǐqī, was a native of Shānyáng. He later died in the disaster of the Chìméi. See the Former History. Annotation: Shěn Jiābĕn said that according to the Former History, there is no mention of Cáo Jìng. The biography of Shènggōng also has no Left Chancellor.
The two characters

Biographies of Wú Gài (吳蓋), Chén Zāng (陳臧), Eighth Section
Wú Hàn (吳漢), courtesy name Zǐyán (子顏), was from Wǎn (宛) in Nányáng (南陽).
His family was poor, and he served the county as a Tíngzhǎng (亭長).
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) reign,
he committed a crime with his retainers
and then fled to Yúyáng (漁陽).
Lacking resources,
he made a living by trading horses,
traveling between Yān (燕) and Jì (薊),
and wherever he went, he befriended local heroes.
When Gēngshǐ (更始) was enthroned, he sent an envoy, Hán Hóng (韓鴻), to inspect Héběi (河北).
Someone said to Hóng (鴻):
"Wú Zǐyán (吳子顏) is an extraordinary man; he can be consulted on affairs."
Hóng (鴻) summoned Hàn (漢) to an audience,
was very pleased with him,
and then, by imperial decree, appointed him as Ānlè Lìng (安樂令).
At that time, Wáng Láng
arose, perturbing and confusing the northern prefectures.
Wú Hàn had long heard that Guāngwǔ was a benevolent elder
and wished only to pledge his loyalty to him.
So he persuaded Grand Administrator Péng Chǒng, saying:
"The mounted troops of Yúyáng and Shànggǔ
are renowned throughout the world.
Why don't you combine the elite forces of these two commanderies,
join Lord Liú, and attack Hándān?
This would be an achievement for this moment."
Péng Chǒng thought this was a good idea,
but his subordinates all wanted to align with Wáng Láng,
and Chǒng could not overrule them.
Wú Hàn then excused himself and left,
stopping at an outer pavilion.
He contemplated how to trick the masses,
but knew not what to do.
He saw a man on the road who resembled a scholar,
so Wú Hàn sent for him,
provided him with food,
and asked him what he had heard.
The scholar then spoke of where Lord Liú had passed,
and how he was welcomed by commanderies and counties;
and that the one who had assumed the imperial title in Hándān
was truly not of the Liú clan.
Wú Hàn was greatly pleased.
He immediately forged a letter from Guāngwǔ
and dispatched a proclamation to Yúyáng,
sending the scholar to present it to Péng Chǒng,
instructing him to recount everything he had heard.
Wú Hàn followed shortly after.
Péng Chǒng was deeply convinced.
Thereupon, he sent Wú Hàn to lead troops to combine forces with the generals of Shànggǔ and march south.
Wherever they went, they attacked and killed Wáng Láng's generals and commanders.
When he met Guāngwǔ in Guǎng'ā,
Wú Hàn was appointed as Piān Jiāngjūn.
After Hándān was captured,
he was granted the title Jiàncè Hóu.
Wú Hàn was honest and unrefined,
unable to express himself articulately in haste.
Dèng Yǔ and many other generals knew this,
and repeatedly recommended him.
When he obtained an audience,
he was trusted and favored,
and often stayed close to the emperor.
When Guāngwǔ was about to launch an expedition to Yōuzhōu,
he summoned Dèng Yǔ at night
and asked who could be sent to lead it.
Dèng Yǔ said:
"I have recently spoken with Wú Hàn many times.
He is courageous, fierce, and possesses wisdom and strategy;
few generals can match him."
Guāngwǔ immediately appointed Wú Hàn as Dà Jiāngjūn,
with the imperial insignia, to go north and mobilize ten commanderies' mounted troops.
Miáo Zēng, the provincial governor of Yōuzhōu appointed by Gēngshǐ, heard of this,
secretly disciplined his troops,
and ordered the various commanderies not to respond to the call.
Wú Hàn then led twenty horsemen and galloped ahead to Wúzhōng.
Miáo Zēng, thinking Wú Hàn was unprepared,
came out to meet him on the road.
Wú Hàn immediately signaled his cavalry,
seized Zēng, executed him,
and took over his army.
The northern prefectures were struck with awe and dread;
no cities or towns failed to submit at his approach.
He then mobilized all their troops,
led them south,
and met Guāngwǔ in Qīngyáng.
When the generals saw Wú Hàn returning,
with a very impressive force of soldiers and horses,
they all said:
"Will he be willing to divide his troops with others?"
When Wú Hàn arrived at the headquarters,
and submitted the troop roster,
all the generals requested many soldiers for themselves.
Guāngwǔ said:
"Just now you feared he wouldn't share,
but now why are your requests so numerous?"
All the generals felt ashamed.
Initially,
Gēngshǐ had sent Shàngshū Lìng Xiè Gōng to lead six generals to attack Wáng Láng,
but they could not defeat him.
When Guāngwǔ arrived,
they jointly pacified Hándān.
However, Xiè Gōng's subordinate generals engaged in looting and did not obey orders,
which Guāngwǔ deeply resented.
Although they were both in Hándān,
they divided the city and occupied separate quarters.
Nevertheless, Guāngwǔ always found ways to reassure and comfort him.
Xiè Gōng was diligent in his duties,
and Guāngwǔ often praised him, saying:
"Shàngshū Xiè is truly an official."
Therefore, Xiè Gōng did not suspect him.
Later, Xiè Gōng led his army of several tens of thousands
back to garrison at Yè.
At that time, Guāngwǔ was attacking Qīngdú to the south,
and he said to Xiè Gōng:
"I am pursuing the bandits at Shèquǎn
and will surely defeat them.
Yóulái, who is in Shānyáng,
will certainly be startled and flee.
If you, with your power and might,
attack these scattered remnants,
you will surely capture them."
Xiè Gōng said:
"Excellent."
After Qīngdú was defeated,
Yóulái indeed fled north to Lónglǜ Shān.
Xiè Gōng then left Dà Jiāngjūn Liú Qìng and Wèijùn Grand Administrator Chén Kāng to guard Yè,
and personally led his generals to attack Yóulái.
Desperate bandits fight to the death,
and their vanguard was irresistible.
Xiè Gōng was then greatly defeated,
with several thousand dead.
Taking advantage of Xiè Gōng's absence,
Guāngwǔ sent Wú Hàn and Cén Péng to assault his city.
Wú Hàn first ordered a skilled orator to persuade Chén Kāng, saying:
"I have heard that the wisest do not remain in danger hoping for luck,
the moderately wise can turn danger into achievement,
and the utterly foolish stay in danger and self-destruct.
The arrival of danger and destruction
depends on the path one chooses,
and one must not fail to examine it.
The capital is now in chaos,
and the four quarters are in turmoil;
this is what you have heard.
King Xiāo's army is strong, his soldiers loyal,
and Héběi has pledged allegiance;
this is what you have seen.
Xiè Gōng has secretly betrayed King Xiāo
and outwardly lost the hearts of the people;
this is what you know.
You now hold a lonely and perilous city,
awaiting the disaster of destruction.
You will have no righteousness to uphold,
and no integrity to achieve.
It is better to open the gates and admit the army,
turning disaster into fortune,
avoiding the defeat of the utterly foolish,
and gaining the merit of the moderately wise.
This is the best strategy."
Chén Kāng assented.
Thereupon, Chén Kāng arrested Liú Qìng and Xiè Gōng's wife and children,
and opened the gates to admit Wú Hàn and others.
When Xiè Gōng returned from Lónglǜ to Yè,
unaware that Chén Kāng had already rebelled,
he lightly entered the city with several hundred horsemen.
Wú Hàn's ambush troops seized him,
and personally struck and killed Xiè Gōng.
His followers all surrendered.
Xiè Gōng's courtesy name was Zǐzhāng,
and he was a native of Nányáng.
Earlier,
his wife knew that Guāngwǔ was displeased with him
and often warned Xiè Gōng, saying:
"You and Lord Liú have long been at odds,
yet you believe his empty words
and do not prepare for it;
you will ultimately be controlled."
Xiè Gōng did not heed her,
and thus met with disaster.
When Guāngwǔ attacked the various bandits in the north,
Wú Hàn often led five thousand mounted troops as the vanguard,
repeatedly being the first to climb and break through enemy lines.
After Héběi was pacified,
Wú Hàn and the generals presented the imperial seals and documents,
and requested the assumption of the imperial title.
Upon Guāngwǔ's accession,
Wú Hàn was appointed Dà Sīmǎ
and re-enfeoffed as Wǔyáng Hóu.
In the spring of Jiànwǔ second year (26 CE),
Wú Hàn led Dà Sīkōng Wáng Liáng,
Jiànyì Dà Jiāngjūn Zhū Yòu,
Dà Jiāngjūn Dù Mào,
Zhí Jīnwú Jiǎ Fù,
Yánghuà Jiāngjūn Jiān Tán,
Piān Jiāngjūn Wáng Bà,
Qí Dūwèi Liú Lóng, Mǎ Wǔ, Yīn Shí,
and together they attacked the Tánxiāng bandits by the Zhāng Shuǐ River east of Yè,
decisively defeating them,
with over a hundred thousand surrendering.
The Emperor sent an envoy with an imperial decree to formally enfeoff Wú Hàn as Guǎngpíng Hóu,
granting him the four counties of Guǎngpíng, Chìzhāng, Qǔzhōu, and Guǎngnián.
He again led the generals to attack the bandits such as Lí Bóqīng in the western mountains of Yè,
and then Xiūwǔ in Hénèi,
completely destroying all their fortified camps.
The imperial carriage personally went to console and reward them.
Wú Hàn was again sent to advance troops into Nányáng,
attacking the cities of Wǎn, Nièyáng, Lí, Ráng, and Xīnyě,
all of which were captured.
He led his troops south,
and fought Qín Fēng by the Huángyóu Shuǐ River,
defeating him.
He also, with Piān Jiāngjūn Féng Yì, attacked Zhāng Wén and other Wǔlóu bandits at Chāngchéng,
and then attacked the Tóngmǎ and Wǔfān bandits at Xīn'ān,
defeating them all.
Míng collected K,
and led the Grand General Who Establishes Might, Gěng Yǎn, and the Grand General Who Has Tiger's Fangs, Gài Yán,
to attack the Qīngdú at Zhǐxī,
utterly defeating and making them surrender.
He also led the Grand General of Agile Cavalry, Dù Mào, and the General of Strong Crossbows, Chén Jùn, and others,
to besiege Sū Mào at Guǎngyuè.
Liú Yǒng's general Zhōu Jiàn separately recruited and gathered over 100,000 men
to relieve Guǎngyuè.
The Hàn general, with light cavalry, met and fought them,
but was unsuccessful,
fell from his horse, injuring his knee,
and returned to camp.
Jiàn and others then joined forces and entered the city.
The generals said to Hàn:
"A formidable enemy is before us, and you, my lord, are injured and confined to bed;
the morale of the troops is fearful."
Hàn then indignantly wrapped his wound and rose,
slaughtered oxen to feast his soldiers,
and ordered the army, saying:
"Though the enemy's numbers are many,
they are all marauding bandits,
'who do not yield to each other in victory
and do not save each other in defeat';
they are not those who uphold loyalty and die for righteousness.
Today is the season for enfeoffment!
All you gentlemen, strive diligently!"
Thereupon, the soldiers were enraged and spurred on,
each man doubling his spirit.
The next morning,
Jiàn and Mào led out troops to surround Hàn.
Hàn selected elite soldiers from four divisions, such as the Huángtóu Wúhé,
and over 3,000 Wūhuán cavalry,
advanced with beating drums.
Jiàn's army utterly collapsed
and fled back into the city.
Hàn pressed forward in pursuit,
fighting to enter the gates together,
utterly defeating them.
Mào and Jiàn broke out and fled.
Hàn left Dù Mào, Chén Jùn, and others to guard Guǎngyuè,
and personally led troops to assist Gài Yán in besieging Liú Yǒng at Suīyáng.
After Yǒng died,
both cities surrendered.
The following year,
he again led Chén Jùn and the Former General, Wáng Liáng,
to defeat the Wǔxiào bandits at Línpíng,
pursuing them to Jīshān in Dōngjùn,
where he utterly defeated them.
To the north, he attacked the Zhǎngzhí of Qīnghé and the Wǔlǐ bandits of Píngyuán,
pacifying them all.
At that time, five families in Gé Xiàn jointly drove out the magistrate
and occupied the city in rebellion.
The generals vied to attack it,
but Hàn did not allow it,
saying:
"Those who caused Gé to rebel
are all the magistrate's fault.
Those who dare to lightly risk advancing troops will be executed."
He then issued a dispatch to the commandery,
ordering the arrest of the magistrate,
and sent someone to apologize to those within the city.
The five families were greatly pleased
and immediately led each other to surrender.
The generals then submitted,
saying:
"To take a city without battle
is beyond the reach of the common man."
In winter,
Hàn led the Grand General Who Establishes Might, Gěng Yǎn, and the General Zhōng, Wáng Cháng, and others,
to attack the Fùpíng and Huòsuǒ bandits at Píngyuán.
In the spring of the following year,
the bandits, with over 50,000 men, attacked Hàn's camp by night.
The army was alarmed and in disarray,
but Hàn lay steadfastly still,
and after a while, calm was restored.
That very night, he dispatched elite troops out of the camp to launch a surprise attack,
utterly defeating their forces.
He then pursued and suppressed the remaining factions,
reaching Wúyán,
and then advanced to attack Bóhǎi,
pacifying them all.
He also participated in the campaign against Dǒng Xiàn,
besieging Qúchéng.
In the spring of the following year,
Qú was captured,
and Xiàn was beheaded.
This matter has been seen in the biography of Liú Yǒng.
The east was entirely pacified,
and the army returned in triumph to the capital.
Coincidentally, Kuí Xiāo rebelled.
In summer,
Hàn was again sent to garrison Cháng'ān in the west.
In the eighth year,
he followed the emperor's carriage to Lǒng,
and then besieged Kuí Xiāo at Xīchéng.
The Emperor ordered Hàn, saying:
"The armored soldiers from the various commanderies merely consume provisions.
If they desert,
it will demoralize the troops.
They should all be dismissed."
Hàn and the others were eager to combine forces and attack Xiāo,
so they could not dismiss them.
Provisions daily diminished,
officials and soldiers were exhausted,
and many deserted.
When Gōngsūn Shù's relief forces arrived,
Hàn subsequently retreated in defeat.
In the spring of the eleventh year,
he led the Grand General Who Conquers the South, Cén Péng, and others to attack Gōngsūn Shù.
When Péng broke through Jīngmén
and advanced rapidly into Jiāngguān,
Hàn remained at Yílíng,
equipped exposed oar-powered boats,
and led Nányáng soldiers and 30,000 recruited soldiers from Shǔ Xíng upstream along the river.
Coincidentally, Cén Péng was killed by an assassin,
and Hàn took command of his army as well.
In the spring of the twelfth year,
he fought Gōngsūn Shù's generals Wèi Dǎng and Gōngsūn Yǒng at Yúfú Jīn,
utterly defeating them,
and then besieged Wǔyáng.
Shù sent his son-in-law, Shǐ Xīng, leading 5,000 men to relieve it.
Hàn met and attacked Xīng,
completely annihilating his forces,
and then entered the territory of Jiànwéi.
All the counties defended their cities.
Hàn then advanced to attack Guǎngdū,
capturing it.
He sent light cavalry to burn the bridges of Chéngdū,
and all the small cities east of Wǔyáng surrendered.
The Emperor admonished Wú Hàn
saying: "Chéngdū
's population of over one hundred thousand
is not to be underestimated.
You must firmly hold Guǎngdū,
wait for them to attack,
and not contend with them directly.
If they dare not come,
you, sir, should move your camp to press them;
only when their strength is exhausted can you strike."
Wú Hàn, seizing the advantage,
personally led over twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to press Chéngdū.
He camped ten-odd *lǐ* from the city,
blocking the north bank of the river,
and built a pontoon bridge.
He ordered his deputy, General Wǔwēi Líu Shàng,
to lead over ten thousand men and encamp on the south bank of the river,
about twenty *lǐ* away.
The Emperor, hearing this, was greatly astonished,
and reproached Wú Hàn
saying: "I have given you countless instructions,
how could you act so recklessly when faced with the situation?
You have not only lightly advanced deep into enemy territory,
but also encamped separately from Líu Shàng.
Should there be an emergency,
you will not be able to support each other.
If the rebels send troops to tie you down,
and attack Líu Shàng with their main force,
when Shàng is defeated,
you too will be defeated.
If no harm has yet come,
quickly lead your troops back to Guǎngdū."
Before the imperial edict arrived,
Gōngsūn Shù indeed sent his generals Xiè Fēng and Yuán Jí to lead over one hundred thousand troops,
divided into more than twenty camps,
and all sallied forth to attack Wú Hàn.
He also sent another general with over ten thousand men to intercept Líu Shàng,
preventing him from providing aid.
Wú Hàn engaged in a great battle for a day,
but his army was defeated,
and he retreated into his fortifications.
Xiè Fēng then surrounded him.
Wú Hàn then summoned his generals and encouraged them, saying:
"We, together with all of you, have overcome dangerous obstacles,
fought battles for a thousand *lǐ*,
achieved many captures and beheadings everywhere,
and thus penetrated deep into enemy territory,
reaching their city walls.
But now, both Líu Shàng and I are besieged in two separate locations.
Our forces are not connected,
and the disaster is immeasurable.
I wish to stealthily lead our army to Líu Shàng on the south bank of the river,
and combine our forces to resist them.
If we can unite our hearts and strength,
and each man fights for himself,
a great victory can be achieved;
if not,
there will surely be no survivors from our defeat.
The turning point between success and failure
rests on this one action."
All the generals said,
"Yes."
Thereupon, they feasted the soldiers and fed the horses,
closed their camps and did not sally forth for three days.
Then they erected many banners,
kept the smoke and fires burning,
and at night, with gags in their mouths, led their troops to join forces with Líu Shàng.
Xiè Fēng and others were unaware.
The next day,
they divided their troops to resist on the north bank of the river,
and personally led the attack on the south bank.
Wú Hàn engaged them with all his forces,
from dawn to dusk,
and greatly defeated them,
beheading Xiè Fēng and Yuán Jí,
and capturing over five thousand armored heads.
Thereupon, he led his troops back to Guǎngdū,
leaving Líu Shàng to resist Gōngsūn Shù,
and fully reported the situation,
deeply reproaching himself.
The Emperor replied:
"Your return to Guǎngdū
is most appropriate.
Gōngsūn Shù will surely not dare bypass Líu Shàng to attack you, sir.
If he first attacks Shàng,
you, sir, can march with all your infantry and cavalry from Guǎngdū, fifty *lǐ* away, to his aid;
you will arrive just when he is in dire straits,
and will certainly defeat them."
From then on, Wú Hàn fought Gōngsūn Shù between Guǎngdū and Chéngdū,
winning eight battles out of eight,
and subsequently stationed his army in its outer city.
Gōngsūn Shù personally led tens of thousands of men out of the city for a great battle.
Wú Hàn sent Commandant Gāo Wǔ and Táng Hán to lead tens of thousands of elite troops to strike them.
Gōngsūn Shù's army was defeated and fled.
Gāo Wǔ pursued and stabbed Gōngsūn Shù,
killing him.
This event is already detailed in the biography of Gōngsūn Shù.
The next day, the city surrendered,
and Gōngsūn Shù's head was sent to Luòyáng.
In the first month of the following year,
Wú Hàn mustered his troops and sailed down the river.
Upon reaching Wǎn,
an imperial edict ordered him to visit his home and ancestral tombs,
and bestowed upon him twenty thousand *hú* of grain.
In the fifteenth year,
he again led General Yángwǔ Mǎ Chéng and General Bǔlú Mǎ Wǔ north to attack the Xiōngnú,
relocating over sixty thousand people from Yànmén, Dàijùn, and Shànggǔ
to settle east of Jūyōng and Chángshān Pass.
In the eighteenth year,
Shǐ Xīn, the Prefect of Shǔjùn, rebelled in Chéngdū,
proclaiming himself Grand Marshal,
and attacked Grand Administrator Zhāng Mù.
Zhāng Mù scaled the city wall and fled to Guǎngdū.
Shǐ Xīn then issued a proclamation to the commanderies and counties.
Yáng Wěi from Dàngqú and Xú Róng from Qúxú, among others,
raised several thousand troops each to respond to him.
The Emperor, knowing that Shǐ Xīn had previously served as Cén Péng's Commandant and
was skilled in military affairs,
therefore dispatched Wú Hàn to lead Líu Shàng and Grand Master of the Palace Zāng Gōng with over ten thousand men to suppress him.
Wú Hàn entered Wǔdū,
then mobilized troops from Guǎnghàn, Bā, and Shǔ commanderies to besiege Chéngdū.
After more than a hundred days, the city fell,
and Shǐ Xīn and others were executed.
Wú Hàn then went downstream on a raft along the river to Bājùn.
Yáng Wěi, Xú Róng, and others panicked and dispersed.
Wú Hàn executed over two hundred of their chieftains,
relocated several hundred families of their partisans to Nánjùn and Chángshā, and returned.
Wú Hàn was by nature resolute and strong.
Whenever he participated in campaigns,
before the Emperor felt at ease,
he would always stand on one foot.
When generals saw that a battle array was disadvantageous,
many would become anxious and fearful,
losing their usual composure.
Wú Hàn, however, remained self-possessed and resolute,
methodically sharpening his weapons and equipment,
and inspiring his officers and soldiers.
At that time, the Emperor sent someone to observe what the Grand Marshal was doing.
The person returned and reported that he was busy preparing for battle and attack.
The Emperor then sighed,
saying: "Wú Gōng is quite capable,
as formidable as an enemy state!"
Whenever he was ordered to lead an army,
he would receive the imperial edict in the morning,
and immediately set off in the evening,
never taking a day to prepare.
Therefore, he could always fulfill his duties
and conclude his life with功名.
When in court,
he was meticulous and honest,
evident in his demeanor.
Once, Wú Hàn was away on campaign,
and his wife and children behind bought land and property.
When Wú Hàn returned,
he reproached them, saying:
"The army is on campaign,
and officers and soldiers are in want;
why buy so much land and houses?"
He then distributed all of it among his brothers and extended family.
In the twentieth year,
Wú Hàn fell gravely ill.
The imperial carriage personally visited him,
asking what he wished to say.
He replied:
"Your humble servant is ignorant and knows nothing,
I only wish Your Majesty would be careful not to grant pardons lightly."
Upon his death,
an imperial edict expressed sorrow and compassion,
and bestowed upon him the posthumous title of Zhōng Hóu.
The five garrisons of the Northern Army, light chariots, and armored soldiers were dispatched to attend his funeral,
following the precedent of Grand General Huò Guāng.
His son, the Marquis Āi Chéng, succeeded him,
but was killed by a slave.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Wú Hàn's marquisate was divided into three states: Chéng's son Dàn was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Quānyáng
to continue Wú Hàn's line;
Dàn's younger brother Xū
was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhúyáng;
and Chéng's younger brother Guó was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīncài.
Dàn died
without a son,
and his state was abolished.
In the eighth year of Jiànchū,
Xū was relocated and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Píngchūn
to continue Wú Hàn's line.
Xū died,
and his son Shèng succeeded him.
Previously,
Wú Hàn's elder brother Wèi served as a general,
died in battle while on campaign,
and Wèi's son Tóng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānyáng.
Because of Wú Hàn's great achievements, the Emperor
again enfeoffed his younger brother Xī as the Marquis of Bāoqīn.
There were a total of five marquises from the Wú family.
Previously,
Yúyáng Commandant Yán Xuān,
together with Wú Hàn, met Guāngwǔ at Guǎng'ā.
Guāngwǔ made him a General of the Household,
and enfeoffed him as the Marquis of Jiànxìn.
The commentary says: Wú Hàn (吳漢) had, since the Jiànwǔ (建武) era,
always held the position of a high-ranking duke,
and throughout his life, enjoyed the trust and affection of the emperor.
This was probably due to his simple and strong character.
Confucius said,
"The firm, the enduring, the simple, and the modest are near to virtue."
Was this not Wú Hàn's (吳漢) way?
In the past, Chén Píng (陳平) was suspected because he had too much wisdom,
while Zhōu Bó (周勃) was trusted because of his simple and loyal nature.
If benevolence and righteousness are not enough to inspire affection,
then the wise are suspected for their excess,
and the simple are trusted for their insufficiency.
Gài Yán (蓋延), whose courtesy name was Jùqīng (巨卿),
was a native of Yúyáng (漁陽) and Yàoyáng (要陽).
He was eight *chǐ* (尺) tall
and could draw a bow of three hundred *jīn* (斤).
The border regions valued strength and bravery,
and Gài Yán (蓋延) was known for his vigor.
He served as a clerk in various commanderies and an attendant in the provincial administration,
performing his duties effectively wherever he was.
Péng Chǒng (彭寵) was the Administrator,
and he appointed Gài Yán (蓋延) as Camp Commandant,
acting as Protector of the Army.
When Wáng Láng (王郎) rose in rebellion,
Gài Yán (蓋延) and Wú Hàn (吳漢) conspired to submit to Guāngwǔ (光武).
When Gài Yán (蓋延) arrived at Guǎng'ā (廣阿),
he was appointed General of the Household,
and titled Marquis of Jiàngōng (建功侯).
He followed Guāngwǔ (光武) in pacifying Héběi (河北).
When Guāngwǔ (光武) ascended the throne,
he made Gài Yán (蓋延) General of Tiger's Teeth.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ (建武)
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānpíng (安平).
He was sent south to attack Áocāng (敖倉),
then advanced to attack Suānzǎo (酸棗) and Fēngqiū (封丘),
all of which he captured.
That summer,

he supervised the Commandant of the Mounted Escort, Mǎ Wǔ (馬武), the Commandant of Cavalry, Liú Lóng (劉隆), the Commandant of the Protector of the Army, Mǎ Chéng (馬成), and the General of the Household, Wáng Bà (王霸), among others, in a southern expedition against Liú Yǒng (劉永).
First, they attacked and captured Xiāngyì (襄邑),
then advanced to take Máxiāng (麻鄉),
and then besieged Liú Yǒng (劉永) at Suīyáng (睢陽).
After several months,
they collected all the wild grain
and entered the city at night by scaling the walls.
Liú Yǒng (劉永) was terrified
and led his troops out through the east gate.
Gài Yán (蓋延) pursued and attacked,
utterly defeating them.
Liú Yǒng (劉永) abandoned his army and fled to Qiáo (譙).
Gài Yán (蓋延) advanced and attacked,
capturing Xuē (薛),
and beheaded its Administrator of Lǔ Jùn (魯郡).
Péngchéng (彭城), Fúyáng (扶陽), Zhùqiū (杼秋), and Xiāo (蕭) all surrendered.
He also defeated Liú Yǒng's (劉永) Administrator of Pèi Jùn (沛郡),
and beheaded him.
Liú Yǒng's (劉永) generals Sū Máo (蘇茂), Jiǎo Qiáng (佼彊), Zhōu Jiàn (周建), and others, with over thirty thousand men,
came to Liú Yǒng's (劉永) aid
and jointly attacked Gài Yán (蓋延).
Gài Yán (蓋延) fought them west of Pèi (沛),
utterly routing them.
Liú Yǒng's (劉永) army was in disarray,
and more than half fled, drowning.
Liú Yǒng (劉永) abandoned the city and fled to Húlín (湖陵),
while Sū Máo (蘇茂) fled to Guǎngyuè (廣樂).
Gài Yán (蓋延) then pacified Pèi (沛), Chǔ (楚), and Línhuái (臨淮),
repaired the temple of Gāozǔ (高祖),
and appointed local officials, sacrificial priests, and musicians.
In the third year,
Suīyáng (睢陽) rebelled again, welcoming Liú Yǒng (劉永).
Gài Yán (蓋延) again led his generals to besiege it for one hundred days,
collecting its wild grain.
Liú Yǒng (劉永) ran out of food
and broke out, fleeing.
Gài Yán (蓋延) pursued and attacked,
seizing all his baggage train.
Liú Yǒng (劉永) was killed by his own general,
and Liú Yǒng's (劉永) younger brother, Fáng (防), surrendered the city.
In the spring of the fourth year,
Gài Yán (蓋延) again attacked Sū Máo (蘇茂) and Zhōu Jiàn (周建) at Qí (蘄),
then advanced and fought Dǒng Xiàn (董憲) at Liúxià (留下),
defeating them both.
He then led General Páng Méng (龐萌) (who was called Píng Dí (平狄) or 'Pacifier of the Di') to attack Xīfáng (西防),
capturing it.
He again pursued and defeated Zhōu Jiàn (周建) and Sū Máo (蘇茂) at Péngchéng (彭城).
Sū Máo (蘇茂) and Zhōu Jiàn (周建) fled to Dǒng Xiàn (董憲).
Dǒng Xiàn's (董憲) general Bēn Xiū (賁休) surrendered Lánlíng (蘭陵) city.
When Dǒng Xiàn (董憲) heard of this,
he personally besieged Bēn Xiū (賁休) from Tán (郯).
At that time, Gài Yán (蓋延) and Páng Méng (龐萌) were in Chǔ (楚),
and they requested to go and rescue him.
The emperor commanded:
"You should go directly and strike Tán (郯),
and then Lánlíng (蘭陵) will certainly be relieved."
Gài Yán (蓋延) and the others, considering Bēn Xiū's (賁休) city to be in danger,
first went to its aid.
Dǒng Xiàn (董憲) met them in battle and feigned defeat.
Gài Yán (蓋延) and the others pursued him as he retreated,
and then broke through the siege and entered the city.
The next day,
Dǒng Xiàn (董憲) sent out a large army to encircle them.
Gài Yán (蓋延) and the others were afraid
and hastily broke out and fled,
then went to attack Tán (郯).
The emperor admonished them, saying:
"My previous intention was for you to go directly to Tán (郯)
because it would be unexpected.
Now that you have fled,
the enemy's plan is already established.
How can the siege be relieved?"
When Gài Yán (蓋延) and the others reached Tán (郯),
they indeed could not conquer it,
and Dǒng Xiàn (董憲) then captured Lánlíng (蘭陵),
killing Bēn Xiū (賁休).
Gài Yán (蓋延) and the others went back and forth, intercepting and attacking Dǒng Xiàn's (董憲) detached generals between Péngchéng (彭城), Tán (郯), and Pī (邳).
There were sometimes several engagements a day,
and they achieved considerable success.
The emperor, considering Gài Yán (蓋延) to be reckless and penetrating too deeply,
repeatedly warned him in letters.
When Páng Méng (龐萌) rebelled,
he attacked and killed the Administrator of Chǔ Jùn (楚郡),
and led his army to attack and defeat Gài Yán (蓋延).
Gài Yán (蓋延) fled,
crossed the Sì Shuǐ (泗水) to the north,
destroyed his boats and oars,
and broke the bridges,
barely escaping.
The emperor personally led an expedition to the east,

summoning Gài Yán (蓋延) to meet at Rènchéng (任城) with the Grand Marshal Wú Hàn (吳漢), General of Han's Loyalty Wáng Cháng (王常), General of the Vanguard Wáng Liáng (王梁), General who Captures the Barbarians Mǎ Wǔ (馬武), and General who Attacks the Barbarians Wáng Bà (王霸), among others,
to suppress Páng Méng (龐萌) at Táoxiāng (桃鄉).
They also jointly participated in the campaign against Dǒng Xiàn (董憲) at Chānglǜ (昌慮),
both of whom were defeated and pacified.
In the spring of the sixth year,
he was sent to garrison Cháng'ān (長安).
In the ninth year,
when Kuí Xiāo (隗囂) died,
Gài Yán (蓋延) attacked the various garrisons and settlements of Jiēquán (街泉), Lüèyáng (略陽), and Qīngshuǐ (清水) in the west,
all of which he pacified.
In the eleventh year,
he and Colonel Lái Xī (來歙) attacked Héchí (河池).
Before capturing it,
he withdrew due to illness,
and was appointed Left Fengyì,
retaining his generalship.
In the thirteenth year,
his fief was increased to ten thousand households.
In the fifteenth year,
he passed away in office.
His son Fú (扶) succeeded him.
When Fú (扶) died,
his son Cè (側) succeeded him.
In the thirteenth year of Yǒngpíng (永平),
Cè (側) was implicated in a conspiracy to rebel with his maternal uncle Wáng Píng (王平),
was executed,
and his marquisate was abolished.
In the seventh year of Yǒngchū (永初),
Empress Dowager Dèng (鄧) re-enfeoffed Gài Yán's (蓋延) great-grandson Huī (恢) as Marquis of Lútíng (蘆亭).
When Huī (恢) died,
his son Suí (遂) succeeded him.
Chén Jùn (陳俊), whose courtesy name was Zǐzhāo (子昭),
was a native of Xī'è (西鄂) in Nányáng (南陽).
In his youth, he served as a subordinate official in the commandery.
When Gēngshǐ (更始) was established,
Liú Jiā (劉嘉), a member of the imperial clan, was made Grandee Secretary General,
and Chén Jùn (陳俊) became his Chief Clerk.
When Guāngwǔ (光武) campaigned in Héběi (河北),
Liú Jiā (劉嘉) sent a letter recommending Chén Jùn (陳俊).
Guāngwǔ (光武) appointed him Commissioner for Pacification.
From attacking the Bronze Horses (Tóngmǎ) at Qīngyáng,
he advanced to Púyáng,
and was appointed General of the Strong Crossbows (Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn).
He fought the Five Squads (Wǔxiào) at Āncì.
Jùn dismounted,
personally engaged in close combat,
and wherever he attacked, he was sure to break through.
He pursued the fleeing enemy for more than twenty *lǐ*,
beheaded their leader, and returned.
Guāngwǔ looked on and sighed, saying,
"If all commanders fought like this,
what worries would we have!"
The Five Squads retreated into Yúyáng,
plundering as they went.
Jùn advised Guāngwǔ, saying,
"We should send light cavalry ahead of the bandits,
and instruct the common people to fortify their walls,
to cut off their food supply.
Then we can exterminate them without fighting."
Guāngwǔ approved of this,
and dispatched Jùn to lead light cavalry to ride ahead of the bandits.
He saw those whose defensive walls were strong and intact,
and ordered them to hold firm;
those who were scattered in the fields,
he consequently plundered.
When the bandits arrived and found nothing,
they consequently scattered and were defeated.
When the army returned,
Guāngwǔ said to Jùn,
"The one who confounded these barbarians,
General, was your strategy."
When he ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Jùn as a Marquis (Lièhóu).
In the spring of Jiànwǔ 2nd year (26 CE),
he attacked the Kuāng bandits,
and captured four counties.
He was then enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīnchǔ.
He then attacked Dùnqiū,
and three cities surrendered.
In that autumn,
Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ) Wú Hàn, acting on imperial authority, appointed Jùn as Grand General of the Strong Crossbows (Qiángnǔ Dàjiāngjūn),
and separately attacked the Jīnmén and Báimǎ bandits in Hénèi,
defeating them all.
In the 4th year (28 CE),
he was transferred to campaign in Rǔyáng and Xiàng,
and also captured Nánwǔyáng.
At this time, many local strongmen in Tàishān gathered their forces and allied with Zhāng Bù.
Wú Hàn advised the Emperor, saying,
"Only Chén Jùn can pacify this commandery."
Thereupon, Jùn was appointed Administrator of Tàishān (Tàishān Tàishǒu),
and acted as Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn).
Zhāng Bù heard of this,
and sent his general to attack Jùn.
They fought at Yíngxià,
and Jùn decisively defeated him.
He pursued them to Jìnán,
and captured over ninety seals and ribbons.
He gradually attacked and took control of various counties,
thus pacifying Tàishān.
In the 5th year (29 CE),
he, along with Grand General who Establishes Awe (Jiànwēi Dàjiāngjūn) Gěng Yǎn, jointly defeated Zhāng Bù.
This event is recorded in Yǎn's biography.
At that time, Lángyá was not yet pacified.
Thus, Jùn was transferred to become Administrator of Lángyá (Lángyá Tàishǒu),
and retained his general's authority as before.
The people of Qí (territory) had long heard of Jùn's reputation.
Upon his entry into the territory,
all bandits disbanded.
Jùn led troops to attack Dǒng Xiàn at Gànyú,
then advanced to defeat Sūn Yáng, the bandit of Qú,
and pacified the area.
In the 8th year (32 CE),
Zhāng Bù rebelled,
returning to Lángyá.
Jùn pursued and punished him,
beheading him.
The Emperor praised his achievements,
and issued an edict granting Jùn sole authority to campaign in Qīng and Xú provinces.
Jùn comforted the poor and weak,
commended the righteous,
and restrained military officials,
preventing them from interfering with the commanderies and counties.
The common people sang his praises.
He repeatedly submitted memorials requesting
to be allowed to bravely attack Lǒng and Shǔ.
The imperial reply stated:
"The eastern provinces have just been pacified,
which is the achievement of the Grand General.
The areas by the sea and the 'slippery' lands of Huáxià,
are places where bandits reside.
The state considers this a grave concern.
Please continue to exert yourself in pacifying and comforting them."
In the 13th year (37 CE),
his fief was increased,
and he was permanently enfeoffed as Marquis of Zhù'ā.
The following year,
he was summoned to attend court.
He died in the 23rd year (47 CE).
His son Fú inherited the title,
and was transferred to be enfeoffed as Marquis of Qíchūn.
When Fú died,
his son Zhuānzhū inherited.
When Zhuānzhū died,
his son Dǔ inherited.
Zāng Gōng, courtesy name Jūnwēng,
was a native of Jiá, Yǐngchuān.
In his youth, he was a county *tíngzhǎng* (village head) and a *yóujiào* (patrol officer).
Later, he led his retainers and joined the Xiàjiāng army as a *xiàowèi* (captain).
Consequently, he followed Guāngwǔ in campaigns.
Many generals praised his bravery.
Guāngwǔ observed that Gōng was diligent and spoke little,
and greatly trusted and accepted him.
Upon reaching Héběi,
he was made a Partial General (Piānjiāngjūn),
and followed in defeating numerous bandits,
often breaching enemy formations and repelling them.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he was made Attendant at the Palace (Shìzhōng) and Commandant of Cavalry (Jì Dūwèi).
In Jiànwǔ 2nd year (26 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chéng'ān.
The following year,
he led elite cavalry with General who Conquers Bandits (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn) Jì Zūn to attack Gēngshǐ's generals Zuǒ Fáng and Wéi Yán
at Nèyáng and Lì,
and they all surrendered.
In the 5th year (29 CE),
he led troops to campaign in Jiāngxià,
attacking Dàixiāng, Zhōngwǔ, and Zhúlǐ,
and all were captured.
The Emperor sent a Grand Master of the Palace (Tàizhōng Dàfū)
with an imperial staff to appoint Gōng as General who Assists Awe (Fǔwēi Jiāngjūn).
In the 7th year (31 CE),
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Qīsī.
He attacked Liángjùn and Jìyīn,
and pacified them all.
In the 11th year (35 CE),
he led troops to Zhōnglú,
and garrisoned Luòyuè.
At this time, Gōngsūn Shù's generals Tián Róng and Rèn Mǎn were resisting Grand General who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn) Cén Péng at Jīngmén.
Péng and others had several unfavorable engagements.
The Yuè people planned to rebel and join Shǔ.
Gōng had few troops,
and was unable to control them.
Just then, several hundred carts of supplies from a subordinate county arrived.
That night, Gōng secretly ordered the city gate's threshold to be sawn off.
He had the sound of the carts turn around and go in and out until dawn.
The Yuè scouts heard the continuous sound of carts,
and that the threshold was cut,
and they told each other that a large Han army had arrived.
Their chiefs then brought cattle and wine to entertain the army camp.
Gōng arranged his troops in a grand assembly,
slaughtered the cattle and poured out the wine,
and feasted, rewarded, and comforted them.
The Yuè people were consequently pacified.
Gōng, with Cén Péng and others, defeated Jīngmén,
then separately went to Chuíquèshān,
opened a path to Zǐguī,
and reached Jiāngzhōu.
Cén Péng captured Bājùn,
and sent Gōng to lead 50,000 surrendered soldiers
up the Fúshǔi to Píngqǔ.
Gōngsūn Shù's general Yán Cén had amassed troops at Chénshǔi.
At this time, Gōng's forces were numerous but had little food,
and supplies did not arrive.
Moreover, the surrendered soldiers all wanted to scatter and rebel,
and the commanderies and counties again fortified themselves,
watching for success or failure.
Gōng wanted to withdraw,
fearing they would revolt against him.
It happened that the Emperor sent an imperial envoy with troops to Cén Péng.
There were seven hundred horses.
Gōng falsely invoked an imperial order to take them to augment his own forces,
and advanced day and night,
displaying many banners,
ascending mountains and shouting battle cries,
with infantry on the right and cavalry on the left,
dragging boats alongside,
their shouts shaking the mountains and valleys.
Cén did not expect the Han army to arrive so suddenly.
He climbed the mountain to observe them,
and was greatly terrified.
Gōng then attacked,
and decisively defeated him.
More than ten thousand people were beheaded or drowned,
and the river flowed turbid because of it.
Yán Cén fled to Chéngdū,
and all his forces surrendered,
all their soldiers, horses, and treasures were captured.
From then on, he pursued the fleeing enemy, capitalizing on his victory,
and those who surrendered numbered in the tens of thousands.
The army reached Píngyáng Xiāng,
where the Shǔ general Wáng Yuán surrendered with his troops.
They advanced and captured Miánzhú,
then broke Fúchéng,
beheading Gōngsūn Shù’s younger brother, Huī.
They then attacked and captured Fán and Pí.
Altogether, they seized five official tallies [jié]
and one thousand eight hundred seals and ribbons.
At this time, the Grand Marshal, Wú Hàn, also pressed his advantage, leading his camp to approach Chéngdū.
Gōng successively captured major cities,
his troops and banners were extremely magnificent.
He then rode his soldiers into the Xiǎoluò Guōmén gate,
passed by the Chéngdū city walls,
reached Wú Hàn’s camp,
and held a grand feast with wine.
Hàn was very pleased to see him,
and said to Gōng:
“General, you just passed by the enemy's city,
displaying your awe-inspiring power,
sweeping like the wind and shining like lightning.
However, cornered foes are unpredictable.
When returning to your camp, I wish you would take another route.”
Gōng did not comply,
and returned by the same route;
the rebels dared not approach him.
He advanced his army to Xiánmén
and, together with Wú Hàn, annihilated Gōngsūn Shù.
The Emperor, seeing Shǔ land newly pacified,
appointed Gōng as Grand Administrator of Guǎnghàn.
In the thirteenth year [of the Jiànwǔ reign],
his fief was increased,
and he was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zá.
In the fifteenth year,
he was summoned back to the capital [Jīngshī]
to serve at court as a 列侯 (lièhóu, marquis of a subordinate rank),
and was formally enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lánglíng.
In the eighteenth year,
he was appointed Grand Master of the Household [tàizhōng dàfū].
In the nineteenth year,
the disciples of the sorcerers Wéi Sì, Dān Chén, Fù Zhèn, and others,
again spread seditious rumors and gathered together,
entering Yuánwǔchéng,
abducting officials and commoners,
and styling themselves generals.
Thereupon, Gōng was dispatched to lead the Northern Army and several thousand men from the Líyáng camp to besiege them.
The rebels had ample grain and food,
and after several attacks, the city could not be taken,
resulting in casualties among the soldiers.
The Emperor summoned the high ministers [gōngqīng] and feudal kings [zhūhóuwáng] to inquire about a strategy.
They all said,
“It is advisable to increase the rewards for capture.”
At that time, Xiǎnzōng, as the King of Dōnghǎi,
alone replied:
“These sorcerers have abducted people;
their power cannot last long.
There must be those among them who regret and wish to escape.
However, the outer encirclement is tight,
preventing their escape.
It would be advisable to loosen the siege slightly
to allow them to flee.
Once they flee, a single village head [tíngzhǎng] would be enough to capture them.”
The Emperor assented to this
and immediately ordered Gōng to withdraw the siege and loosen the pressure on the rebels.
The rebel forces dispersed,
and Chén and Zhèn, among others, were then beheaded.
Upon Gōng’s return,
he was promoted to Colonel of the City Gates [chéngmén xiàowèi],
and later transferred to Left Commander of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household [zuǒ zhōnglángjiàng].
He attacked the Wǔxī rebels,
reached Jiānglíng,
and made them surrender.
Gōng, being cautious, trustworthy, and simple,
was therefore always entrusted with important tasks.
Later, the Xiongnú suffered from famine and plague,
and began to quarrel among themselves.
The Emperor asked Gōng about this.
Gōng said,
“I wish to lead five thousand cavalry to achieve merit.”
The Emperor smiled and said,
“One who is always victorious
is difficult to consult with about the enemy;
I will consider this myself.”
In the twenty-seventh year,
Gōng, together with the Marquis of Yángxū, Mǎ Wǔ, submitted a memorial, saying:
“The Xiongnú are greedy for profit
and lack propriety and trustworthiness.
When in distress, they bow their heads;
when at peace, they invade and plunder.
The border regions suffer from their poisonous pain,
and the central states worry about their incursions.
Now the barbarians’ people and livestock are dying of plague,
and drought and locusts have ravaged the land.
Their strength, weakened by plague,
is not equal to one commandery of the central states.
Their lives, spanning ten thousand *lǐ*,
are suspended upon Your Majesty.
Such good fortune will not come again,
and opportunities are easily lost.
How can we cling to civil virtue and neglect military affairs?
Now, dispatch generals to the frontier,
and offer generous rewards for capture.
Inform and instruct Gāogōulí, Wūhuán, and Xiānbēi to attack their left flank,
and mobilize the four commanderies of Héxī,
Tiānshuǐ, and Lǒngxī, along with the Qiāng and Hú, to strike their right flank.
If this is done,
the northern barbarians will be annihilated
in no more than a few years.
Your humble servants fear that Your Majesty’s benevolence and compassion will prevent action,
and that your strategists will be hesitant,
thereby preventing an everlasting inscription of merit from being established in this sagely era.”
The imperial edict replied:
“The records of Huángshí Gōng state,
‘The soft can control the hard;
the weak can control the strong.’
Softness is virtue;
hardness is villainy.
Weakness is the aid of benevolence;
strength is the accumulation of resentment.
Therefore, a virtuous ruler
enjoys with the people what he enjoys;
a virtueless ruler
enjoys only for himself what he enjoys.
He who enjoys with the people will have lasting joy;
he who enjoys for himself will perish soon.
He who abandons near plans for distant ones
toils without merit;
he who abandons distant plans for near ones
rests and achieves his goal.
An easy administration produces many loyal officials;
a toilsome administration produces many chaotic people.
