Therefore, it is said that he who strives to expand his territory will become desolate;
he who strives to expand his virtue will become strong.
He who maintains what he possesses is secure;
he who covets what others possess will be destroyed.
A destructive administration,
even if successful, will eventually fail.
Now, the state lacks good governance,
calamities and anomalies do not cease,
the common people are terrified,
and no one feels safe.
How then can we again desire to engage in distant affairs beyond the borders?
Confucius said: ‘I fear Jìsūn’s worries
are not in Zhuānyú.’
Moreover, the northern Dí are still strong,
and reports of garrisoning fields and maintaining vigilance
are often inaccurate.
If we could truly use half of all under heaven to destroy the great bandits,
would that not be our ultimate wish?
But if it is not the right time,
it is better to let the people rest.”
From then on, no general dared to speak of military affairs.
Gōng died in the first year of Yǒngpíng,
and was posthumously named Mǐnhóu.
His son Xìn succeeded him.
When Xìn died,
his son Zhèn succeeded him.
When Zhèn died,
his son Sōng succeeded him.
In the fourth year of Yuánchū,
Sōng lived separately from his mother,
and the marquiseship was abolished.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
Empress Dowager Dèng re-enfeoffed Sōng’s younger brother Yóu as the Marquis of Lánglíng.
A commentary says: The undertaking of the restoration [zhōngxīng]
was indeed arduous.
However, the enemies were not as strong as Qín or Xiàng,
and the people inherently longed to attach themselves to the Hàn.
Though some bore seals and wore ribbons,
straddling commanderies and counties,
with different names and strange titles,
forming groups of thousands,
they were still not enough to be compared to the achievements of the highest heroes.
As for the time when the region west of the mountains was pacified,
and awe was cast over all under heaven,
the Róng and Jié lost their courage,
and the various chieftains squandered their remaining might.
This was truly an opportune moment for ambitious and martial hearts,
a time for those with foresight to wield arms.
Zāng Gōng, Mǎ Wǔ, and their like,
stroked their swords and clapped their hands,
their ambitions soaring north of Yīwú.
Guāngwǔ, having carefully considered Huángshí Gōng’s words,
preserved Báosāng,
closed the Jade Gate [Yùmén] in rejection of tribute from the Western Regions [Xīyù],
and used humble words and gifts to treat Xiongnú envoys.
His preventative intentions were indeed profound.
How could he suffer the distress of the Píngchéng siege
or endure the humiliation of the Qíng Wáng’s encampment?
A eulogy says: Wú Gōng was fierce and strong,
truly a soaring dragon.
He swept away all evildoers like lightning,
and moved like the wind through Bā and Liáng.
Hǔyá was mighty and powerful,
achieving merit at Suīyáng.
Gōng and Jùn were serene and composed,
they too were soaring eagles.
Biography of Gěng Yǎn, Ninth [chapter] (younger brother Guó, Guó’s son Bǐng, Bǐng’s younger brother Kuí, Guó’s son Gōng)
Gěng Yǎn, courtesy name Bózhāo,
was a native of Máolíng, Fúfēng.
His ancestors, during the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
were moved from Jùlù as officials receiving two thousand dàn of grain.
His father, Kuàng,
courtesy name Xiáyóu,
became a lang (gentleman-in-waiting) by mastering the classics.
He studied the Lǎozi with Wáng Mǎng’s younger cousin Jí under Mr. Ānqiū.
Later, he became the Shuòdiào Liánsài.
Yǎn was fond of learning in his youth
and mastered his father's profession.
He often saw the commandery commandant test cavalrymen,
setting up flags and drums,
and practicing galloping and archery.
From this, he became fond of matters of generalship.
When Wáng Mǎng was defeated
and Gēngshǐ was enthroned,
many generals who seized territory
frequently arrogated power,
constantly replacing commandery administrators and magistrates.
Kuàng, considering himself appointed by Mǎng,
felt uneasy.
At this time, Yǎn was twenty-one years old,
so he bade farewell to Kuàng and presented a memorial to Gēngshǐ,
also bringing tribute
to secure their position.
Upon reaching Sòngzǐ,
they encountered Wáng Láng, who falsely claimed to be Zǐyú, son of Emperor Chéng,
raising an army in Hándān.
Yǎn's subordinates Sūn Cāng and Wèi Bāo conspired with him on the road, saying:
"Liú Zǐyú is the legitimate heir of Emperor Chéng.
If we don't go to him,
where are we going by traveling far?"
Yǎn pressed his sword and said:
"Zǐyú is a worthless rebel;
he will eventually become a captive.
When I reach Cháng'ān,
I will present to the court the use of soldiers and horses from Yúyáng and Shànggǔ.
Then, returning via Tàiyuán and Dàijùn,
in a matter of dozens of days,
I will send out elite cavalry to crush these rabble
as easily as breaking dry rot.
Seeing that you gentlemen don't know where to go or stay,
your families will not last long."
Cāng and Bāo did not obey,
and consequently defected to Wáng Láng.
Yǎn heard on the road that Guāngwǔ was in Lúnú,
so he galloped north to meet him.
Guāngwǔ kept him and appointed him a subordinate official.
Yǎn then persuaded the Protector of the Army, Zhū Yòu,
to ask for permission to return and raise troops
to pacify Hándān.
Guāngwǔ smiled and said:
"This young fellow actually has great ambitions!"
He then repeatedly summoned him, bestowing favor and comfort.
Yǎn consequently followed Guāngwǔ north to Jì.
Hearing that Hándān's forces were approaching,
Guāngwǔ intended to return south,
and summoned his officials to discuss.
Yǎn said:
"Now that the enemy forces are coming from the south,
we cannot go south.
The Administrator of Yúyáng, Péng Lǒng,
is your fellow townsman;
the Administrator of Shànggǔ
is my father.
If we mobilize these two commanderies,
with ten thousand cavalrymen,
Hándān is not worth worrying about."
Guāngwǔ's confidant officials all refused,
saying:
"Even in death, one faces south.
How can we go north into a trap?"
Guāngwǔ pointed at Yǎn and said:
"This is my host for the northern route."
At that time, Jì was in turmoil,
so Guāngwǔ fled south,
and his officials scattered.
Yǎn went to Chāngpíng to join Kuàng,
and then persuaded Kuàng to send Kòu Xún east to make an agreement with Péng Chǒng,
each raising two thousand elite cavalry
and one thousand infantry.
Yǎn, together with Jǐng Dān, Kòu Xún, and the Yúyáng army, combined forces and marched south.
Along the way, they attacked and slew over four hundred of Wáng Láng's grand generals, nine ministers, and commandants.
They captured one hundred twenty-five seals and ribbons,
two tallies,
beheaded thirty thousand,
and pacified a total of twenty-two counties in Zhuōjùn, Zhōngshān, Jùlù, Qīnghé, and Héjiān.
They then met Guāngwǔ at Guǎng'ā.
At this time, Guāngwǔ was attacking Wáng Láng,
and rumors spread that the forces from the two commanderies were coming for Hándān,
causing everyone to be afraid.
Soon after, they all went to the camp to report.
When Guāngwǔ saw Yǎn and the others,
he was pleased
and said:
"You must share this great achievement with the gentry of Yúyáng and Shànggǔ."
He then appointed them all as pìanjiāngjūn (partial generals),
and sent them back to command their troops.
Kuàng was additionally appointed Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General) and Xīngyì Hóu (Marquis of Spreading Righteousness),
allowed to appoint his own subordinate officers.
Yǎn and the others then followed in the capture of Hándān.
At that time, Gēngshǐ summoned Zhào Yǒng, the Administrator of Dàijùn,
but Kuàng persuaded Yǒng not to answer the summons,
but to go to Guāngwǔ.
Guāngwǔ sent Yǒng back to his commandery.
When Yǒng returned north,
Zhāng Yè, the Magistrate of Dài, rebelled by occupying the city,
and invited the Xiōngnú and Wūhuán for aid.
Guāngwǔ appointed Yǎn's younger brother Shū as Fùhú Jiāngjūn (General Who Restores the Hu),
and sent him to attack Yè,
defeating him.
Yǒng was then able to resume his commandery.
At that time, over two hundred thousand of the Wǔxiào bandits ravaged Shànggǔ to the north.
Kuàng and Shū repeatedly attacked and defeated them,
and all the bandits retreated.
Gēngshǐ, seeing Guāngwǔ's prestige growing daily,
felt suspicion and worry among his ruler and ministers,
so he sent an envoy to appoint Guāngwǔ as Xiāo Wáng,
ordering him to disband his army and return to Cháng'ān with the generals who had achieved merit.
He sent Miáo Zēng as Yōuzhōu Mù (Governor of Yōuzhōu),
Wéi Shùn as Shànggǔ Tàishǒu (Administrator of Shànggǔ),
and Cài Chōng as Yúyáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Yúyáng),
all heading to the northern region.
At this time, Guāngwǔ was residing in the Hándān palace,
sleeping during the day in Wēnmíng Diàn.
Yǎn entered, went to the foot of the bed, and requested a private audience,
then said:
"Now Gēngshǐ has lost proper governance,
his ruler and ministers are debauched,
generals are arrogating commands within the capital region,
and royal relatives are running rampant within the capital.
The Son of Heaven's commands
do not go beyond the city gates,
and local governors and administrators
arbitrarily change their positions.
The common people do not know whom to follow,
and scholars dare not feel secure.
They plunder wealth,
and seize women.
Those with gold and jade
do not return alive.
The common people beat their breasts,
longing once more for Mǎng's court.
Furthermore, dozens of groups like the Tóngmǎ and Chìméi,
each numbering hundreds of thousands,
are beyond the sagely duke's ability to manage.
Their defeat will not be long in coming.
You first began your enterprise in Nányáng,
defeating an army of a million;
now you have pacified Héběi,
occupying a land of heavenly abundance.
By campaigning righteously,
your commands are met with instant response,
and the world can be pacified by merely circulating a proclamation.
The world is of utmost importance and
cannot be allowed to fall into the hands of another surname.
I hear envoys have come from the west,
wishing to disband the army;
this must not be obeyed.
Now many officers and soldiers have died.
I wish to return to Yōuzhōu
and raise more elite troops
to accomplish this great plan."
Guāngwǔ was greatly pleased,
and then appointed Yǎn as Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General),
sending him with Wú Hàn to raise troops from the ten commanderies of Yōuzhōu in the north.
When Yǎn arrived at Shànggǔ,
he arrested Wéi Shùn and Cài Chōng and executed them;
Hàn also executed Miáo Zēng.
Thereupon, all the Yōuzhōu troops were mobilized,
and led south.
They followed Guāngwǔ in defeating the Tóngmǎ, Gāohú, Chìméi, and Qīngdú,
and also pursued the Yóulái, Dàqiāng, and Wǔfān at Yuánshì.
Yǎn always commanded the elite cavalry as the vanguard of the army,
always breaking and driving them away.
Guāngwǔ, pressing his advantage, fought on the Shuǐshuǐ,
but the desperate bandits
fought to the death.
At that time, the troops were exhausted and defeated,
and were utterly routed and fled,
encamping at Fányáng,
where they regrouped after several days.
The bandits also retreated,
and were pursued to Róngchéng, Xiǎoguǎngyáng, and Āncì,
where they were repeatedly defeated in battle.
Guāngwǔ returned to Jì,
and again sent Yǎn with Wú Hàn, Jǐng Dān, Gài Yán, Zhū Yòu, Pī Tóng, Gěng Chún, Liú Zhí, Cén Péng, Jì Zūn, Jiān Tán, Wáng Bà, Chén Jùn, and Mǎ Wǔ, thirteen generals,
to pursue the bandits to Lùdōng
and Pínggǔ.
In two battles,
they beheaded over thirteen thousand,
and then relentlessly pursued them to the area between Wúzhōng and Tǔyín in Yòuběipíng,
returning only after reaching Jùnmí.
The bandits scattered into Liáoxī and Liáodōng,
some being plundered and attacked by the Wūhuán and Mò people,
almost entirely wiped out.
Guāngwǔ was enthroned.
He appointed Yǎn as Grand General Establishing Awe.
Together with Grand General of Cavalry Jǐng Dān and General of Strong Crossbows Chén Jùn, he attacked the rebels of Yànxīn at Áocāng,
defeating and pacifying them all.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Hǎozhì.
He held the two counties of Hǎozhì and Měiyáng as his fief.
In the third year,
Yán Cén came out from Wǔguān and attacked Nányáng,
capturing several cities.
Dù Hóng of Ráng led his followers to join Cén.
Yǎn fought Cén and his forces at Ráng,
thoroughly defeating them,
beheading over three thousand men,
capturing alive over five thousand of their officers and soldiers,
and obtaining three hundred seals and sashes.
Dù Hóng surrendered.
Cén fled with a few horsemen to Dōngyáng.
Yǎn followed the Emperor to Chōnglíng.
There, he saw the Emperor and personally requested permission to go north to rally the unmobilized troops from Shànggǔ,
stabilize Péng Chǒng in Yúyáng,
capture Zhāng Fēng in Zhuójùn,
then return to reclaim Fùpíng and Huòsuǒ,
and finally march east to attack Zhāng Bù,
thereby pacifying the Qí region.
The Emperor admired his ambition,
and therefore granted his request.
In the fourth year,
an imperial edict ordered Yǎn to advance and attack Yúyáng.
Yǎn, whose father Jù was stationed in Shànggǔ,
and who had originally shared the same merits as Péng Chǒng,
and whose brothers were not in the capital,
became suspicious,
not daring to advance alone.
He submitted a memorial requesting to go to Luòyáng.
The edict replied:
“General, your entire clan has risen for the nation,
breaking through enemy lines wherever you marched,
your achievements are particularly outstanding.
What suspicion or doubt do you have,
that you wish to be recalled?
Moreover, you are to jointly garrison Zhuójùn with Wáng Cháng,
diligently contemplating strategies.”
Kuàng, hearing of Yǎn's request to be recalled,
also felt uneasy.
He sent his younger brother Shū to serve at court.
The Emperor approved of this,
and promoted Kuàng to be the Marquis of Yúmí.

Then he ordered Yǎn, along with Grand General Establishing Righteousness Zhū Yòu, Han Loyal General Wáng Cháng, and others, to attack more than ten camps of bandits in Wàngdū and Gù'ān's Western Mountains,
defeating them all.
At this time, General Quelling Barbarians Jì Zūn was garrisoned at Liángxiāng,
and General of Valiant Cavalry Liú Xǐ was garrisoned at Yángxiāng,
to resist Péng Chǒng.
Chǒng sent his younger brother Chún to lead over two thousand Xiongnu cavalry,
while Chǒng himself led tens of thousands of troops,
dividing them into two routes to attack Zūn and Xǐ.
The Hu cavalry passed through Jūndū,
and Shū launched a surprise attack, shattering their forces,
and beheading two Xiongnu kings.
Chǒng then retreated.
Kuàng and Shū again attacked Chǒng,
capturing Jūndū.
In the fifth year,
Chǒng died.
The Son of Heaven commended Kuàng's achievements,
sending the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with a retinue to welcome Kuàng.
He was bestowed a grand mansion
and honored with attendance at court.
Shū was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Móupíng.
Yǎn was sent with Wú Hàn to attack the rebels of Fùpíng and Huòsuǒ in Píngyuán,
completely defeating them,
with over forty thousand surrendering.
Then an imperial edict ordered Yǎn to advance and attack Zhāng Bù.
Yǎn gathered all the surrendered soldiers,
organized them into units,
appointed officers,
and led by Cavalry Commandant Liú Xīn and Administrator of Tàishān Chén Jùn, marched his troops eastward,
crossing the river from Cháoyángqiáo.
Zhāng Bù heard of this,
and sent his Grand General Fèi Yì to station troops at Lìxià,
also dividing his forces to garrison Zhù'ā,
and separately arraying dozens of camps at Tàishān Zhōngchéng to await Yǎn.
Yǎn crossed the river and first attacked Zhù'ā.
He attacked the city from dawn,
and by mid-morning captured it.
He intentionally left one corner of the encirclement open,
allowing its inhabitants to flee back to Zhōngchéng.
The people of Zhōngchéng, hearing that Zhù'ā had fallen,
were greatly terrified,
and consequently abandoned their fortifications and fled.
Fèi Yì sent his younger brother Gǎn to defend Jùlǐ.
Yǎn advanced his troops to first threaten Jùlǐ,
ordering many trees to be felled,
and spreading rumors that they would be used to fill the moats.
After several days,
a surrenderer reported that Yì had heard of Yǎn's intention to attack Jùlǐ,
and planned to come to its aid.
Yǎn then issued strict orders for his army to quickly prepare siege equipment,
and announced to all units
that in three days they would exert full strength to attack Jùlǐ City.
Secretly, he loosened the bonds of some captives,
allowing them to escape.
These escapees reported Yǎn's planned date to Yì,
and indeed, on that day, Yì personally led over thirty thousand elite troops to relieve it.
Yǎn rejoiced,
and said to his generals:
"The reason I prepared siege equipment
was to lure Yì here.
Now that he has come,
it is exactly what I wanted."
He immediately divided three thousand men to guard Jùlǐ,
and personally led his elite troops up the ridges and slopes,
fighting from a high position,
completely defeating them,
and personally beheading Yì in battle.
Afterward, he collected the heads and displayed them to the people within Jùlǐ City.
The city residents were panic-stricken,
and Fèi Gǎn fled with all his forces back to Zhāng Bù.
Yǎn again collected their stores,
and unleashed his troops to attack all those who had not yet surrendered,
pacifying over forty camps,
thus stabilizing Jìnán.
At this time, Zhāng Bù's capital was Jù,
and he sent his younger brother Lán to lead twenty thousand elite troops to defend Xī'ān,
while the various commandery administrators collectively held Línbō with over ten thousand men,
forty *lǐ* apart.
Yǎn advanced his army to Huàzhōng,
situated between the two cities.
Yǎn observed that Xī'ān City was small but strong,
and moreover Lán's troops were elite,
while Línbō, though great in name, was actually easy to attack.
So he ordered all his commanders
that in five days they would attack Xī'ān.
Lán heard of this,
and kept watch day and night.
On the appointed night, at midnight,
Yǎn ordered all his generals to eat their meals in the field,
and arrive at Línbō City by dawn.
Army Protector Xún Liáng and others argued against this,
believing it would be better to attack Xī'ān quickly.
Yǎn said:
"Not so.
Xī'ān heard I intended to attack it,
and has been preparing day and night;
Línbō, being attacked unexpectedly,
will surely be startled and in disarray.
If I attack it, I will certainly take it in one day.
Once Línbō is taken, Xī'ān will be isolated,
Zhāng Lán and Bù will be cut off,
and Lán will surely flee again.
This is what is meant by 'striking one and gaining two.'
If we first attack Xī'ān,
and fail to take it quickly,
our troops will be bogged down against a strong city,
and casualties will surely be many.
Even if we could take it,
Lán would lead his army back to Línbō,
combining forces and strength,
observing our strengths and weaknesses.
We would be deep in enemy territory,
with no supply lines behind us,
and within ten days,
we would be exhausted without even fighting.
What you all say
does not seem appropriate."
Thereupon, he attacked Línbō,
taking it in half a day,
and occupying its city.
Zhāng Lán, hearing [this, was greatly] terrified,
and then led his forces to flee back to Jù.
Gěng Yǎn then commanded his army not to plunder Jù,
but to wait until Zhāng Bù arrived before taking it,
in order to provoke Bù.
Bù heard this and laughed loudly, saying:
"With more than 100,000 troops from Yóulái and Dàtóng,
I immediately attacked and defeated them in their camps.
Now Dà Gěng's army is fewer than theirs,
and all are tired and weary.
What is there to fear?!"
So, with his three younger brothers Lán, Hóng, and Shòu, and the former Dàtóng leader Zhòng Yì and other soldiers,
numbering 200,000,
he arrived east of the great city of Línzī,
preparing to attack Gěng Yǎn.
Gěng Yǎn had previously gone out to the Zī River,
where he met Zhòng Yì.
His light cavalry wanted to charge,
but Gěng Yǎn feared damaging their morale
and preventing Bù from advancing.
So he feigned weakness to inflate Bù's confidence,
then withdrew to the small city,
arraying his troops within.
Bù, full of confidence,
directly attacked Gěng Yǎn's camp.
He engaged in battle with Liú Xīn and others.
Gěng Yǎn ascended the ruined terrace of the royal palace to observe,
and seeing Xīn's forces engaged,
he personally led his elite troops in a flanking assault on Bù's formation beneath the east wall,
thoroughly defeating them.
A flying arrow struck Gěng Yǎn's thigh;
he cut it out with his saber,
and his attendants were unaware.
The battle ceased at dusk.
The next morning, Gěng Yǎn again marshaled his troops and marched out.
At this time, the Emperor was in Lǔ,
and hearing that Gěng Yǎn was under attack by Bù,
he personally went to relieve him,
but had not yet arrived.
Chén Jùn said to Gěng Yǎn:
"The Jù rebels' army is strong;
we should temporarily close the camp and rest the soldiers,
awaiting His Majesty's arrival."
Gěng Yǎn said:
"The imperial carriage is about to arrive.
As a loyal subject, I should prepare oxen and wine to entertain the officials.
Would I instead leave the rebels for my lord and father to deal with?"
So he led out his troops for a great battle.
From dawn until dusk,
he again utterly defeated them,
killing and wounding countless.
The ditches in the city were all filled.
Gěng Yǎn knew Bù was trapped and would retreat,
so he had already placed his left and right wings in ambush to await him.
At the hour of Rén Dìng (around 9-11 PM),
Bù indeed withdrew.
The ambush troops rose and attacked,
pursuing them to the Jùmèi River.
For eighty or ninety *lǐ*, corpses lay connected,
and they captured over two thousand wagons of supplies.
Bù returned to Jù,
and his brothers each divided their troops and dispersed.
A few days later,
the imperial carriage arrived at Línzī to personally inspect the army,
and all the officials gathered.
The Emperor said to Gěng Yǎn:
"In the past, Hán Xìn broke Lìxià to establish his base.
Now the general has attacked Zhù'ā to begin his career.
These are both on the western border of Qí,
and your achievements are comparable.
But Hán Xìn attacked those who had already surrendered,
while the general alone defeated formidable enemies.
Your achievement is thus more difficult than Hán Xìn's.
Furthermore, Tián Héng boiled Lì Shēng alive.
When Tián Héng surrendered,
Emperor Gāo issued an edict to the Commandant of the Guards not to seek revenge.
Zhāng Bù previously also killed Fú Lóng.
If Bù comes to surrender,
I will instruct the Grand Minister of Works to release his resentment.
These matters are also similar.
General, you proposed this great strategy in Nányáng,
often thinking it was difficult to achieve,
but those with resolve will eventually succeed!"
Gěng Yǎn then pursued Bù again.
Bù fled to Píngshòu,
then bared his torso and carried an axe and chopping block to the camp gate.
Gěng Yǎn sent Bù to the imperial residence
and then garrisoned his troops to occupy the city.
He erected the flags and drums of the twelve commanderies,
ordering Bù's soldiers to gather under the flags according to their commandery.
There were still over 100,000 people,
and more than 7,000 wagons of supplies.
All were dismissed and sent back to their hometowns.
Gěng Yǎn again led his troops to Chéngyáng,
pacifying the remaining factions of the Wǔxiào.
[一０] The land of Qí was completely pacified.
He then returned triumphantly to the capital.
In the sixth year,
he resisted Wěi Xiāo in the west,
stationing troops at Qī.
In the eighth year,
he followed the Emperor to Lǒng.
The next year,
he and the Colonel Láixí divided forces to suppress the garrisons and strongholds of Āndìng and Běidì,
all of which submitted.
Gěng Yǎn pacified a total of forty-six commanderies,
sacked three hundred cities,
and never suffered a setback.
In the twelfth year,
Kuàng fell ill,
and the imperial carriage often personally visited him.
Again, his younger brothers Guǎng and Jǔ were both made Colonels.
All six of Gěng Yǎn's brothers wore "green and purple" (high official robes),
attending to his medical care,
which was considered a great honor at the time.
When Kuàng died,
he was posthumously granted the title Liè Hóu.
His youngest son, Bà, inherited Kuàng's peerage.
In the thirteenth year,
Gěng Yǎn's household income was increased,
and he was granted the seal and ribbon of Grand General,
then retired,
serving as a marquis by special summons to court.
Whenever there were differing opinions from the four quarters,
he was summoned to be consulted for strategy.
At the age of fifty-six,
he died in the first year of Yǒngpíng,
and was posthumously named Mǐn Hóu.
His son Zhōng succeeded him.
Zhōng, as a Cavalry Commandant, attacked the Xiongnu at Tiānshān,
achieving merit.
When Zhōng died,
his son Féng succeeded him.
When Féng died,
his son Liáng succeeded him,
also named Wújìn.
During the Yánguāng era,
he married Princess Púyáng, Emperor Ān's sister,
and reached the position of Palace Attendant.
When Liáng died,
his son Xié succeeded him.
When Marquis Yúmí, Bà, died,
his son Wénjīn succeeded him.
When Wénjīn died,
his son Xǐ succeeded him.
When Xǐ died,
his son Xiǎn succeeded him,
serving as Left Supervisor of the Imperial Guards.
When Xiǎn died,
his son Yuán succeeded him.
He married Princess Chángshè, Emperor Huán's sister,
and served as Administrator of Hédōng.
Later, Cáo Cāo executed the Gěng clan,
only Yuán's grandson Hóng survived.
When Marquis Mòupíng, Shū, died,
his son Xí succeeded him.
He married Princess Lónglǜ, Emperor Xiǎnzōng's daughter.
When Xí died,
his son Bǎo succeeded him.
Bǎo's younger sister became the consort of King Xiào of Qīnghé.
When Emperor Ān ascended the throne,
he honored King Xiào,
and his mother became Empress Xiàodé,
while the consort became Grand Noble Lady of Gānyuán.
The Emperor, considering Bǎo's importance as his maternal uncle,
made him supervisor of the Left Cavalry of the Imperial Guards,
reaching the position of Grand General.
However, he became entangled with palace favorites
and, with the Regular Palace Attendant Fán Fēng, the Emperor's wet nurse Wáng Shèng, and others, they slandered and deposed the Crown Prince, making him King of Jìyīn,
and also framed and ruined Grand Commandant Yáng Zhèn.
Critics resented this.
Bǎo's younger brother Chéng inherited the princess's peerage as Marquis of Línlǜ,
and reached the position of Palace Attendant.
When Emperor Ān died,
Empress Dowager Yán, seeing that Bǎo and others clung to favorites
and jointly committed misdeeds,
dismissed Bǎo and Chéng by imperial decree.
Both were demoted to Marquis of a Pavilion
and sent back to their fiefs.
Bǎo committed suicide on the way,
and his state was abolished.
The Grand Noble Lady repeatedly pleaded for the Gěng clan.
In the third year of Yángjiā,
Emperor Shùn then reinstated Bǎo's son Jī as Marquis of Mòupíng,
and made him Palace Attendant.
Héng was made Marquis of Yángtíng,
and Chéng was made Colonel of the Imperial Guards.
Afterwards, when the Noble Lady died,
Grand General Liáng Jì demanded the Noble Lady's treasures from Chéng,
but could not obtain them.
Jì was enraged,
and hinted to the officials to propose stripping him of his enfeoffment.
Chéng was terrified,
and fled to Ráng.
Several years later,
Jì tracked him down
and executed his entire family of more than ten people.
The commentary states: When Huái Yīn [Hán Xìn] discussed Xiàng Wáng with the court,
he accurately assessed the potential for success,
and thus knew that Gāo Zǔ's [Liú Bāng] ancestral temple would prevail.
Gěng Yǎn, in his strategy for Hé Běi [Hebei],
and his decisive plan for Nán Yáng [Nanyang],
also saw that Guāng Wǔ's [Liú Xiù] enterprise would succeed.
However, after Gěng Yǎn personally conquered and secured all of Qí,
he received no further inch of merit.
How could he not feel regret?
Perhaps the times and circumstances
were insufficient to accommodate him?
Serving as a general for three generations
was avoided by Daoists,
yet the Gěng clan accumulated fame and merit through successive generations until their end.
Could it be that their use of military force aimed to stop killing with killing?
How is it that they alone could achieve such prosperity!
Gěng Guó, courtesy name Shū Lǜ,
first entered service in the fourth year of Jiàn Wǔ [28 CE],
and Guāng Wǔ appointed him as a Huáng Mén Shì Láng [Yellow Gate Attendant-in-Waiting].
He responded to questions from the emperor's left and right,
and the emperor considered him capable,
promoting him to Shè Shēng Xiào Wèi [Colonel of Archers].
In the seventh year [31 CE],
the Shè Shēng office was abolished,
and he was appointed Fù Mǎ Dū Wèi [Commander of the Imperial Steeds].
When his father Kùang died,
Gěng Guó was next in line to inherit.
He submitted a memorial stating that his late marquis father had favored his youngest son, Bà,
and firmly expressed his refusal to inherit,
which the emperor permitted by edict.
Later, he successively served as magistrate of Dùn Qiū, Yáng Zhái, and Shàng Cài,
and was praised by officials and common people wherever he served.
He was summoned to serve as Wǔ Guān Zhōng Láng Jiāng [Gentleman of the Five Bureaus].
At this time, the Wū Huán and Xiān Bēi frequently raided the outer borders.
Gěng Guó had long had strategies,
and frequently spoke on border affairs;
the emperor valued him.
When the Xiōng Nú Áo Jiān Rì Zhú Wáng Bǐ proclaimed himself Hū Hán Yé Chán Yú,
he approached the frontier and declared vassalage,
wishing to defend against the northern barbarians.
The matter was sent down to the senior ministers.
The deliberators all believed that the empire had only recently been settled,
and Zhōng Guó was empty and weak.
The true intentions of the Yi Dí [barbarians] were difficult to ascertain,
and thus they should not be permitted.
Gěng Guó alone said:
"Your subject believes it is proper to accept them according to the precedent of Xiào Xuān [Emperor Xuān]'s time,
allowing them to defend against the Xiān Bēi in the east,
and resist the Xiōng Nú in the north,
to rally the four barbarians,
and restore the frontier commanderies,
so that there will be no alarm of a wide-open frontier,
this is a strategy for eternal peace."
The emperor followed his counsel,
and thus established Bǐ as the Southern Chán Yú.
Consequently, the Wū Huán and Xiān Bēi protected the frontier and defended themselves,
the northern barbarians fled far away,
and Zhōng Guó had fewer incidents.
In the twenty-seventh year [51 CE],
he replaced Féng Qín as Dà Sī Nóng [Grand Minister of Agriculture].
He also memorialized that a Dù Liáo Jiāng Jūn [General Who Crosses the Liao],
and left and right Xiào Wèi [Colonels], should be established,
to be stationed in Wǔ Yuán to prevent defections.
He died in office in the first year of Yǒng Píng [58 CE].
Xiǎn Zōng [Emperor Míng] later recalled Gěng Guó's words,
and subsequently established a Dù Liáo Jiāng Jūn,
and left and right Xiào Wèi,
as he had proposed.
Gěng Guó had two sons: Bǐng
and Kuí.
Gěng Bǐng, courtesy name Bó Chū,
had a magnificent physique,
with a waist measuring eight *wéi* [a large circumference].
He was well-versed in books and records,
could explain Sī Mǎ's art of war,
and was especially fond of the strategies of generals.
He was appointed as a Láng [Gentleman] due to his father's position,
and frequently submitted memorials on military affairs.
He often argued that Zhōng Guó was wasting resources,
the frontier was not peaceful,
and the problem lay solely with the Xiōng Nú.
To use war to end war
was the way of a great king.
Xiǎn Zōng already had aspirations for a northern expedition,
and secretly approved of his words.
During the Yǒng Píng era,
he was summoned to the imperial palace,
where he was questioned about the opportune strategies he had previously submitted,
and was appointed Yè Zhě Pú Shè [Attendant of the Imperial Secretariat],
thus gaining the emperor's trust and favor.
Whenever the senior ministers convened,
Gěng Bǐng was always brought before the emperor,
who consulted him on border affairs,
and his advice often pleased the emperor.
In the fifteenth year [72 CE],
he was appointed Fù Mǎ Dū Wèi.
In the sixteenth year [73 CE],
with Qín Péng, a Qí Dū Wèi [Cavalry Commander], as his deputy,
he, along with Fèng Chē Dū Wèi [Commander of the Imperial Chariots] Dòu Gù and others, jointly attacked the Northern Xiōng Nú.
The barbarians all fled,
and they returned without a battle.
In the summer of the seventeenth year [74 CE],
an edict ordered Gěng Bǐng and Dòu Gù to combine their forces, fourteen thousand cavalry,
and again march out to Bái Shān to attack Chē Shī.
Chē Shī had a Later King and a Former King;
the Former King was the son of the Later King,
and their courts were separated by over five hundred *lǐ*.
Dòu Gù considered the road to the Later King distant,
the valleys deep,
and the soldiers suffering from the cold,
and wished to attack the Former King.
Gěng Bǐng argued for first going to the Later King,
believing that by concentrating their forces on the root,
the Former King would naturally submit.
Dòu Gù's plan was undecided.
Gěng Bǐng rose decisively and said:
"I request to go first."
Thereupon he mounted his horse,
and led his troops north,
the rest of the army had no choice
but to advance.
They looted extensively,
beheading several thousand,
and capturing over ten thousand horses and cattle.
The Later King Ān Dé was terrified,
and came out with several hundred cavalry to welcome Gěng Bǐng.
However, Dòu Gù's Sī Mǎ [Military Advisor], Sū Ān, wished to secure the full credit for Dòu Gù,
and immediately galloped to tell Ān Dé:
"Among the noble Han generals, there is only the Fèng Chē Dū Wèi,
the emperor's brother-in-law,
ennobled as a Tōng Hóu [Marquis of Penetration],
you should surrender to him first."
Ān Dé then turned back,
and instead ordered his generals to welcome Gěng Bǐng.
Gěng Bǐng was greatly enraged,
donned his armor and mounted his horse,
and led his elite cavalry directly to Dòu Gù's encampment.
He said:
"The King of Chē Shī has surrendered,
but has not arrived yet.
I request to go and hang his head."
Dòu Gù was greatly alarmed and said:
"Stop for now,
you will ruin the matter!"
Gěng Bǐng said in a stern voice:
"Receiving a surrender is like facing an enemy."
Then he galloped towards Ān Dé.
Ān Dé was frightened,
ran out of the gate,
took off his cap, and embraced the horse's legs to surrender.
Gěng Bǐng brought him to Dòu Gù.
The Former King also submitted,
thus Chē Shī was pacified, and they returned.
In the autumn of the following year [75 CE],
Sù Zōng [Emperor Zhāng] ascended the throne,
and appointed Gěng Bǐng as Zhēng Xī Jiāng Jūn [General Who Conquers the West].
He was sent to inspect the border regions of Liáng Zhōu,
to comfort and reward the Qiāng and Hú tribes who protected the frontier,
and advanced to station troops in Jiǔ Quán to rescue the Wù Jǐ Xiào Wèi [Colonels of the Western Regions].
In the first year of Jiàn Chū [76 CE],
he was appointed Dù Liáo Jiāng Jūn.
He served for seven years,
and the Xiōng Nú harbored goodwill and trust towards him.
He was summoned to serve as Zhí Jīn Wǔ [Bearer of the Gilt Mace],
and was greatly trusted and esteemed.
Whenever the emperor toured the commanderies and states or visited palaces and temples,
Gěng Bǐng always led the imperial guard to escort him.
Three of his sons were appointed as Láng.
In the second year of Zhāng Hé [88 CE],
he was again appointed Zhēng Xī Jiāng Jūn,
to assist Chē Qí Jiāng Jūn [General of Chariots and Cavalry] Dòu Xiàn in attacking the Northern Xiōng Nú,
and greatly defeated them.
This event is also covered in Dòu Xiàn's biography.
Gěng Bǐng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Měi Yáng.
His fief had three thousand households.
Gěng Bǐng was brave and resolute by nature, and simple in his affairs.
When on campaign, he always donned armor and rode in front.
When resting, he did not set up complex encampments,
but he sent out distant scouts,
and was clear about his pledges.
When an alarm occurred,
his army formation was immediately complete,
and his soldiers were all willing to die for him.
In the second year of Yǒng Yuán [90 CE],
he replaced Huán Yú as Guāng Lù Xūn [Minister of the Imperial Household].
He died in the summer of the following year [91 CE],
at the age of over fifty.
He was granted a vermilion coffin and a jade suit,
the director of works dug his tomb,
he was granted drum and wind instruments for the procession,
and over three hundred knights from the Five Regiments escorted his funeral.
His posthumous title was Huán Hóu.
When the Xiōng Nú heard of Gěng Bǐng's death,
the entire nation cried out,
some even cutting their faces until blood flowed.
His eldest son, Chōng, succeeded him.
When Dòu Xiàn was defeated,
because he was a partisan of the Dòu clan,
his marquisate was abolished.
Chōng’s highest office was Tài shǒu of Hàn yáng.
His great-grandson, Jì,
had a fine reputation in his youth.
He was appointed to the Ducal Prefecture,
and Cáo Cāo held him in great respect and awe.
He gradually rose to the position of Shǎo fǔ.
Jì, believing that Cáo Cāo was about to usurp the Hàn dynasty,
in the twenty-third year of Jiàn’ān,
conspired with the Dà yī lìng Jí Ké
and the Chéng xiàng Sī zhí Wéi Huàng (or Wéi Yè) to raise troops to execute Cáo Cāo.
They failed,
and his three kindreds were exterminated.
At that time, many prominent families among the gentry suffered misfortune and destruction due to Jì.
Kuí’s courtesy name was Dìng gōng.
In his youth, he was resolute and spirited.
At the beginning of Yǒng yuán,
he served as the Jiǎ Sī mǎ for Chē qí jiāng jūn Dòu Xiàn.
He campaigned north against the Xiōng nú,
and was promoted to Chē qí dū wèi.
In the third year,
Dòu Xiàn again sallied out to Hé xī.
He appointed Kuí as Dà jiāng jūn Zuǒ xiào wèi.
Leading eight hundred elite cavalry,
he rode out through the Jū yán pass,
raced directly to the Northern Chányú’s court,
and at Jīn wēi shān, he beheaded the Yān zhī, famous kings, and over five thousand others.
The Chányú escaped with only a few riders,
and Kuí captured all their Xiōng nú treasures, wealth, and livestock.
He returned after having gone five thousand *lǐ* from the frontier,
a distance never before reached by a Hàn army.
Consequently, Kuí was enfeoffed as Sù yì hóu.
At that time, the Northern Chányú’s younger brother, the Zuǒ lù lí wáng Yú chú jiàn, declared himself Chányú,
with a following of over twenty thousand men from eight tribes.
He came to reside by the sea at Pú lèi,
and sent envoys to surrender at the frontier.
Kuí was appointed Zhōng láng jiāng,
and entrusted with the staff of authority to guard him.
When Dòu Xiàn was defeated,
Kuí was also dismissed from office and stripped of his noble rank and land.
Later, he was again appointed Cháng shuǐ xiào wèi,
then made Wǔ yuán tài shǒu,
and promoted to Liáo dōng tài shǒu.
In the first year of Yuán xīng,
the Mò people raided the commandery’s borders.
Kuí pursued and attacked them,
beheading their chieftain.
In the third year of Yǒng chū,
the Southern Chányú Tán rebelled.
Kuí was ordered to lead Xiān bēi and troops from various commanderies to garrison Yàn mén,
and together with Chē qí jiāng jūn Hé Xī, to attack him.
Hé Xī designated Kuí as the vanguard,
and sent his Sī mǎ Gěng Pǔ and Liú Zhǐ with two thousand men to advance with Kuí.
Upon reaching the former city of the tributary state,
the Chányú sent Aò jiàn Rì zhú wáng with over three thousand men to block the Hàn forces.
Kuí personally attacked their left flank,
and ordered the Xiān bēi to attack their right.
The barbarians were defeated and fled.
Kuí pursued and beheaded over a thousand,
killed six of their famous kings,
and captured over a thousand yurts, chariots, and heavy equipment,
along with a great number of horses, livestock, and captives.
Many of the Xiān bēi horses were emaciated and sick,
so they rebelled and left the frontier.
Kuí could not advance alone.
For not pursuing them thoroughly,
he was demoted and transferred to be Yún zhōng tài shǒu.
Later, he was promoted to act as Dù liáo jiāng jūn.
Kuí was brave and spirited,
and frequently encroached upon and insulted [the] Xiōng nú Zhōng láng jiāng Zhèng Jiǎn.
In the first year of Yuán chū,
he was summoned and imprisoned for this offense,
sentenced to a reduced death penalty,
and flogged two hundred times.
During Jiàn guāng,
he was again appointed Dù liáo jiāng jūn.
At that time, the Xiān bēi attacked and killed Yún zhōng tài shǒu Chéng Yán,
and besieged Wū huán xiào wèi Xú Cháng at Mǎ chéng.
Kuí, with Yōu zhōu cì shǐ Páng Cān, rescued them,
pursued the barbarians out of the frontier, and returned.
Later, he was dismissed due to an offense [against the law],
and died at home.
Gōng, courtesy name Bó zōng,
was the son of his younger brother Guǎng.
He was orphaned young.
He was generous and had great strategic vision,
possessing the talent of a general.
In the winter of the seventeenth year of Yǒng píng,
Qí dū wèi Liú Zhāng went to attack Chē shī,
and requested Gōng to be his Sī mǎ.
Together with Fèng chē dū wèi Dòu Gù and his cousin Fù mǎ dū wèi Bǐng, he defeated and subjugated them.
When the Western Regions Dū hù and Wù jǐ xiào wèi were first established,
Gōng was made Wù jǐ xiào wèi,
stationed at Jīn pú chéng in the territory of the Later King,
and Yè zhě Guān Chǒng was made Wù jǐ xiào wèi,
stationed at Liǔ zhōng chéng in the territory of the Former King.
Each garrison consisted of several hundred men.
When Gōng arrived at his post,
he sent a proclamation to the Wū sūn,
displaying the might and virtue of the Hàn.
The Dà Kūn mí and others were all joyful,
sent envoys to offer famous horses,
and presented the *bó jù* given to the princess during Xuān dì’s reign,
expressing their desire to send a son to serve at court.
Gōng then dispatched envoys with gold and silk
to welcome their hostage prince.
In the third month of the following year,
the Northern Chányú sent Zuǒ lù lí wáng with twenty thousand cavalry to attack Chē shī.
Gōng sent a Sī mǎ with three hundred soldiers to rescue them,
but they encountered many Xiōng nú cavalry on the way
and were all wiped out.
The Xiōng nú then defeated and killed the Later King Ān dé,
and attacked Jīn pú chéng.
Gōng fought on the city walls,
applying poison to his arrows.
He conveyed a message to the Xiōng nú, saying:
“The Hàn arrows are divine;
those wounded by them will surely experience something unusual.”
Then he fired powerful crossbows.
When the barbarians were struck by the arrows,
they saw their wounds festering,
and were greatly alarmed.
Just then, a violent storm broke,
and he attacked them during the rain,
killing and wounding many.
The Xiōng nú were terrified,
saying to each other:
“The Hàn soldiers are divine,
truly fearsome!”
So they withdrew.
Gōng, seeing that Shu lèi chéng had a ravine nearby that could be fortified,
in the fifth month,
led his troops to occupy it.
In the seventh month,
the Xiōng nú again came to attack Gōng.
Gōng recruited several thousand men to rush forward as vanguards,
and the barbarian cavalry scattered and fled.
The Xiōng nú then dammed the ravine beneath the city.
Gōng dug a well fifteen *zhàng* deep within the city but found no water.
His officers and soldiers were parched and exhausted,
so they squeezed horse dung to extract its liquid and drank it.
Gōng sighed, looking up:
“I hear that in ancient times, the Èr shī jiāng jūn drew his sword and pierced a mountain,
and a flying spring gushed forth.
Now, the Hàn’s virtue is divine and luminous,
how can it be exhausted?”
Then he straightened his clothes, bowed twice towards the well,
and prayed for his officers and soldiers.
A moment later,
a spring of water burst forth,
and everyone cheered, “Long live!”
He then ordered his officers and soldiers to splash water to show the barbarians.
The barbarians were caught off guard,
believing it to be a divine miracle,
and so they retreated.
At that time, Yān qí and Qīu cí attacked and annihilated Dū hù Chén Mù,
and the northern barbarians also besieged Guān Chǒng at Liǔ zhōng.
Just then, Xiǎn zōng died,
reinforcements did not arrive,
and Chē shī rebelled again,
attacking Gōng together with the Xiōng nú.
Gōng invigorated his troops and drove them away.
The Later King’s wife, a descendant of Hàn people,
often secretly informed Gōng of the barbarians’ plans
and provided him with provisions.
After several months,
food ran out and they were in dire straits,
so they boiled armor and crossbows,
and ate their sinews and leather.
Gōng treated his soldiers with sincerity, sharing life and death,
thus none harbored disloyal thoughts,
though they gradually died off,
with only dozens remaining.
The Chányú knew Gōng was in distress
and wanted to force his surrender.
He again sent an envoy to entice Gōng, saying:
“If you surrender,
you will be enfeoffed as Bái wū wáng,
and given a daughter in marriage.”
Gōng then lured the envoy onto the city wall,
personally struck and killed him,
and roasted him on the city wall.
The barbarian officials and subordinates saw this,
cried out, and left.
The Chányú was greatly enraged,
and reinforced his troops to besiege Gōng,
but could not capture the city.
Diáo Qī
with the courtesy name Cìkuàng, was from Jiá, Yǐngchuān.
He was eight *chǐ* and two *cùn* tall,
with an exceptionally striking appearance,
and was dignified and awe-inspiring.
His father, Měng,
was the Grand Administrator of Guìyáng.
When Měng died,
Qī observed the mourning rites for three years,
which the local villagers praised him for.
When Guāngwǔ campaigned in Yǐngchuān,
he heard of Qī's ambition and righteousness,
so he summoned him and appointed him Clerk of the Bandit Section (Zéi Cáo Yuàn).
He followed Guāngwǔ in pacifying Jì.
At that time, Wáng Láng's proclamation arrived in Jì,
and the people of Jì rose in arms to support Láng.
Guāngwǔ quickly set out in his carriage,
but the common people gathered to watch,
filling the road with clamor,
blocking his way so he could not proceed.
Qī rode his horse, brandishing his *jǐ* (halberd),
and, glaring fiercely, shouted to those around him,
The crowd all scattered.
When they reached the city gate,
the gate was already closed.
They attacked it and broke through.
Upon reaching Xìndū,
Qī was appointed Deputy General (Pí Jiàng),
and, along with Fù Kuān and Lǚ Yàn, was placed under Dèng Yǔ's command.
They pacified the surrounding counties
and also mobilized soldiers from Fángzi.
Yǔ considered Qī capable,
and solely promoted him to General of the Vanguard (Piān Jiāngjūn),
giving him two thousand soldiers,
while Kuān and Yàn each had several hundred.
When Yǔ returned and reported this situation,
Guāngwǔ greatly approved.
He sent Qī to separately pacify Zhēndìng and Sòngzi,
and to attack and capture Lèyáng, and Féilěi.
He followed in attacking Wáng Láng's generals Ér Hóng and Liú Fèng at Jùlù.
Qī was the first to ascend and breach the enemy lines,
personally killing over fifty people.
He sustained a wound to his forehead,
but covered it and fought again,
thus thoroughly defeating them.
When Wáng Láng was destroyed,
Qī was appointed General of the Tiger's Teeth (Hǔyá Dà Jiāngjūn).
Then, finding an opportune moment, he spoke to Guāngwǔ, saying:
"The region north of the Yellow River (Héběi),
borders the frontier passes.
Its people are accustomed to warfare
and are known for their bravery and skill.
Now Gēngshǐ has lost control of the government,
and the imperial authority is in peril.
The whole country (hǎinèi) has no one to turn to.
If Your Excellency (Míng Gōng) occupies the strongholds of the rivers and mountains,
commands elite troops,
and acts in accordance with the desire of all people to return to the Hàn,
then who in the world would dare not follow?"
Guāngwǔ smiled and said:
"Are you trying to advance my cause?"
At that time, several hundred thousand Bronze Horse (Tóngmǎ) bandits entered Qīngyáng and Bópíng.
Qī and the other generals met and attacked them.
After several unfavorable engagements,
Qī then fought with his back to the water,
killing and wounding many.
Just then, Guāngwǔ's reinforcements arrived,
and they thoroughly defeated the bandits,
pursuing them to Guǎntáo,
where all of them surrendered.
He followed in attacking the Green Colts (Qīngdú) and Red Eyebrows (Chìméi) at Shèquǎn.
The bandits attacked Qī's baggage train,
so Qī returned to engage them,
personally killing and wounding dozens of people.
He sustained three wounds,
but fought with renewed vigor,
and routed them.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
Qī was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānchéng,
with a fiefdom of five thousand households.
At that time, bandits from Tánxiāng and Wǔlóu entered Fányáng and Nèihuáng.
Moreover, several prominent clans in Wèi Jùn repeatedly rebelled,
and Gēngshǐ's general Zhuó Jīng
was plotting to lead them in a rebellion against Yèchéng.
The Emperor appointed Qī Grand Administrator of Wèi Jùn,
and acting Grand General.
Qī mobilized the prefectural troops to attack Zhuó Jīng,
defeated him,
and beheaded over six hundred people.
Jīng fled into the mountains,
and Qī pursued and beheaded dozens of his officers,
and captured Jīng's wife and children.
He advanced to attack Fányáng and Nèihuáng,
again beheading several hundred people,
and the prefectural border became peaceful.
The superintendent of bandits, Lǐ Xióng,
was a prominent figure in Yèchéng.
Xióng's younger brother, Lù, plotted to rebel and welcome Tánxiāng into the city.
Someone reported this to Qī,
but Qī did not respond.
After three or four reports,
Qī finally summoned Xióng and questioned him.
Xióng kowtowed and confessed,
offering to die with his elderly mother.
Qī said:
"If being an official is not as enjoyable as being a bandit,
you may return home with your elderly mother and go to Lù."
He ordered an officer to escort him out of the city.
Xióng went and found Lù,
and brought him to the west gate of Yèchéng.
Lù, overwhelmed by shame and gratitude,
committed suicide to apologize to Qī.
Qī sighed in admiration,
and buried him with due ceremony,
then restored Xióng to his former position.
Thereupon, everyone in the prefecture respected his authority and trustworthiness.
In the fifth year of Jiànwǔ
(29 CE), the Emperor visited Wèi Jùn,
and appointed Qī Grand Master of Remonstrance (Tàizhōng Dàfū).
He followed the Emperor back to Luòyáng,
and was again appointed Commandant of the Guard (Wèiwèi).
Qī highly valued good faith and integrity.
From the time he became a general,
he never plundered
those who surrendered.
When in the imperial court,
he was concerned for the country and loved his sovereign.
If there was anything he found unsatisfactory,
he would certainly risk offending the Emperor's countenance to remonstrate.
The Emperor once lightly ventured out with Qī in a close-by gate,
and Qī prostrated himself before the carriage, saying:
"Your subject has heard the ancient and modern warnings
that unforeseen changes arise.
I sincerely do not wish Your Majesty (Bìxià) to frequently make private excursions."
The Emperor turned his carriage around because of this.
He died in the tenth year (34 CE).
The Emperor personally oversaw his dressing and enshrouding,
and posthumously bestowed upon him the seal and sash of Commandant of the Guard and Marquis of Ānchéng,
with the posthumous title Zhōnghóu (Loyal Marquis).
His son, Dān, succeeded him.
Dān's younger brother, Tǒng, was then enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiànpíng.
Later, Dān was transferred to be enfeoffed as Marquis of Gélíng.
When Dān died,
his son, Shū, succeeded him.
When Shū died,
his son, Yǔ, succeeded him.
When Yǔ died,
his son, Cài, succeeded him.
Wáng Bà
with the courtesy name Yuánbó, was from Yǐngyáng, Yǐngchuān.
His family had for generations favored literary studies and law.
His father was the Chief Clerk for Judicial Cases (Juécáo Yuàn) in the prefecture,
and Bà also served as a prison official in his youth.
He often felt indignant and was unhappy with official duties,
which his father found remarkable.
He was sent west to study in Cháng'ān.
When the Hàn army rose,
Guāngwǔ passed through Yǐngyáng.
Bà led his retainers to request an audience,
saying:
"General, you are raising a righteous army.
I secretly do not presume to measure myself,
but I am eager for your prestige and virtue,
and wish to join your ranks."
Guāngwǔ said:
"I have dreamt of worthy gentlemen
to achieve great enterprises together.
How could there be two opinions on this!"
So, he followed in attacking and defeating Wáng Xún and Wáng Yì at Kūnyáng,
then returned to his hometown for a rest.
When Guāngwǔ became the Colonel-Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi),
he passed through Yǐngyáng.
Bà asked his father for permission,
wishing to follow.
His father said:
"I am old now
and not fit for military campaigns.
You go,
and exert yourself!"
Bà followed him to Luòyáng.
When Guāngwǔ became Grand Minister of War (Dà Sīmǎ),
he appointed Bà as Secretary of Merit Affairs (Gōngcáo Lìshǐ),
and he followed him across the Yellow River (Héběi).
Dozens of retainers who followed Bà
gradually left.
Guāngwǔ said to Bà:
"All those from Yǐngchuān who followed me have departed,
but you alone remain.
Keep striving!
Strong winds test the sturdy grass."
When Wáng Láng 王郎 rose in rebellion,
Guāngwǔ 光武 was in Jì 薊.
Wáng Láng sent a proclamation offering a reward for Guāngwǔ’s capture.
Guāngwǔ ordered Bà 霸 to go to the market to recruit men,
intending to attack Wáng Láng.
The market people all burst into laughter,
raising their hands to jeer at him.
Bà returned ashamed and embarrassed.
Guāngwǔ immediately rode south to Xiàqǔyáng 下曲陽.
It was rumored that Wáng Láng’s troops were behind them,
and all his followers were afraid.
When they reached the Hūtú Hé 虖沱河,
a scout returned to report that the river water was slushy,
there were no boats,
and it was impassable.
The officials and subordinates were greatly alarmed.
Guāngwǔ ordered Bà to go and inspect it.
Bà, fearing to alarm the multitude,
wanted to go forward temporarily,
but was blocked by the water.
Upon returning, he falsely reported:
“The ice is solid and passable.”
The officials and subordinates were all pleased.
Guāngwǔ smiled and said:
“The scout indeed spoke falsely.”
They then proceeded.
By the time they reached the river,
the river ice had also frozen solid.
He then ordered Bà to oversee the crossing.
Before a few riders had finished crossing, the ice broke.
Guāngwǔ said to Bà:
“That my multitude was safe and managed to cross and escape,
is due to your effort.”
Bà replied in humble thanks:
“This is Your Excellency’s ultimate virtue
and the aid of the divine spirits.
Even the omen of King Wǔ’s 武王 white fish
could not surpass this.”
Guāngwǔ said to his officials and subordinates:
“Wáng Bà 王霸’s expediency in handling affairs
is surely a heavenly omen.”
He made him Commander of the Army (jūnzheng 軍正)
and ennobled him as Marquis of the Interior (guānnèihóu 關內侯).
After reaching Xìndū 信都,
he dispatched troops to attack and capture Hándān 邯鄲.
Bà pursued and decapitated Wáng Láng,
obtaining his seal and ribbon.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wángxiāng 王鄉.
He followed in pacifying Héběi 河北,
often sharing a camp with Zāng Gōng 臧宮 and Fù Jùn 傅俊.
Bà alone was good at comforting his officers and soldiers;
for those who died, he removed his own clothes to shroud them,
and for the wounded, he personally cared for them.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
because Bà understood military affairs and loved his soldiers,
and could be solely entrusted with responsibility,
he was appointed General of the Household (piānjāngjūn 偏將軍),
also leading the troops of Zāng Gōng and Fù Jùn,
while Gōng and Jùn were made Cavalry Commanders (qídūwèi 騎都尉).
In Jiànwǔ 建武 second year (AD 26),
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Fùbō 富波.
In the autumn of the fourth year (AD 28),
the Emperor visited Qiáo 譙,
and sent Bà with the General Who Captures Bandits (bǔlǔ jiāngjūn 捕虜將軍) Mǎ Wǔ 馬武 to campaign eastward against Zhōu Jiàn 周建 at Chuíhuì 垂惠.
Sū Mào 蘇茂, leading five thousand Five-Battalion troops (wǔxiào bīng 五校兵), came to rescue Zhōu Jiàn,
and first sent elite cavalry to intercept and attack Mǎ Wǔ’s army’s provisions.
Mǎ Wǔ went to rescue them.
Zhōu Jiàn led troops out from the city to launch a pincer attack on Mǎ Wǔ.
Mǎ Wǔ, relying on Bà’s support,
did not fight with full effort,
and was defeated by Sū Mào and Zhōu Jiàn.
Mǎ Wǔ’s army fled past Bà’s camp,
shouting for help.
Bà said:
“The bandit forces are strong;
if we go out, both will be defeated.
Just do your best.”
He then closed the camp and fortified the walls.
The army officials all argued against this.
Bà said:
“Sū Mào’s troops are elite and sharp,
and their multitude is also great.
My officers and soldiers are fearful,
and the Capturer of Bandits and I rely on each other.
If the two armies are not united,
this is a path to defeat.
Now, if we close the camp and hold firm,
showing no intention of mutual support,
the bandits will surely advance lightly, riding on their victory;
with the Capturer of Bandits having no rescue,
his fighting will naturally intensify twofold.
In this way,
when Sū Mào’s multitude is exhausted,
we can take advantage of their weakness
and then be able to conquer them.”
Sū Mào and Zhōu Jiàn indeed brought out all their forces to attack Mǎ Wǔ.
After fighting for a long time,
dozens of brave men in Bà’s army, such as Lù Rùn 路潤, cut their hair and asked to fight.
Bà knew that the soldiers’ morale was high,
so he opened the rear of the camp
and sent out elite cavalry to attack their rear.
Sū Mào and Zhōu Jiàn, attacked from front and rear,
were surprised, thrown into disarray, and fled in defeat.
Bà and Mǎ Wǔ each returned to their camps.
The bandits again gathered their forces and challenged them to battle.
Bà remained steadfastly in his camp, not going out,
and was entertaining his soldiers with music and dance.
Sū Mào rained arrows into the camp,
hitting a wine jar in front of Bà,
but Bà sat calmly and did not move.
The army officials all said:
“Sū Mào was already defeated the other day;
he is easy to attack now.”
Bà said:
“Not so.
Sū Mào’s auxiliary troops have come from afar,
and their provisions are insufficient.
Therefore, he frequently challenges us to battle,
hoping for a quick, decisive victory.
Now, by closing the camp and resting our soldiers,
it is what is called ‘subduing the enemy without fighting,’
which is the supreme excellence.”
Since Sū Mào and Zhōu Jiàn could not provoke a battle,
they withdrew and returned to their camp.
That night,
Zhōu Jiàn’s nephew Sòng 誦 rebelled,
closing the city gates against them.
Sū Mào and Zhōu Jiàn fled,
and Sòng surrendered the city.
In the spring of the fifth year (AD 29),
the Emperor sent a Grand Master of the Palace (tàizhōngdàfū 太中大夫) with an imperial credential (jí 節) to appoint Bà as General Who Campaigns Against Bandits (tǎolǔ jiāngjūn 討虜將軍).
In the sixth year (AD 30),
he was stationed to establish military agricultural colonies in Xīn'ān 新安.
In the eighth year (AD 32),
he was stationed in Hángǔ Guān 函谷關.
He attacked the bandits of Xíngyáng 滎陽 and Zhōngmóu 中牟,
and pacified them all.
In the ninth year (AD 33),

Bà, along with Wú Hàn 吳漢, Grand General of Horizontal Fields (héngyě dàjiāngjūn 橫野大將軍) Wáng Cháng 王常, Grand General Who Establishes Righteousness (jiànyì dàjiāngjūn 建義大將軍) Zhū Yòu 朱祐, and General Who Crushes Treachery (pòjiān jiāngjūn 破姦將軍) Hóu Jìn 侯進, totaling over fifty thousand men,
attacked Lú Fāng’s 盧芳 generals Jiǎ Lǎn 賈覽 and Mǐn Kān 閔堪 at Gāoliǔ 高柳.
The Xiōngnú 匈奴 sent cavalry to assist Lú Fāng,
and Wú Hàn’s chariots encountered rain,
making the battle disadvantageous.
Wú Hàn returned to Luòyáng 洛陽,
ordering Zhū Yòu to be stationed in Chángshān 常山,
Wáng Cháng in Zhuōjùn 涿郡,
and Hóu Jìn in Yúyáng 漁陽.
An imperial edict appointed Bà as Administrator of Shànggǔ 上谷,
continuing to lead the stationed troops as before,
to capture and attack the Hú 胡 barbarians,
without being restricted by the commandery borders.
The following year (AD 34),
Bà again, with Wú Hàn and four other generals, totaling sixty thousand men, marched out from Gāoliǔ to attack Jiǎ Lǎn.
An imperial decree ordered Bà and Chén Xīn 陳訢, Administrator of Yúyáng, to lead troops as the vanguard of all armies.
The Xiōngnú Left Southern General (zuǒ nán jiāngjūn 左南將軍) led several thousand cavalry to rescue Jiǎ Lǎn.
Bà and the others fought continuous battles below Píngchéng 平城,
defeating them,
and pursued them out of the pass,
decapitating several hundred.
Bà and the generals returned and entered Yànmén 鴈門,
meeting with the Grand General of Agile Cavalry (piàojì dàjiāngjūn 驃騎大將軍) Dù Mào 杜茂 to jointly attack Lú Fāng’s general Yǐn Yóu 尹由 at Guō 崞 and Fánzhì 繁畤,
but did not succeed.
In the thirteenth year (AD 37),
his enfeoffment households were increased,
and he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiàng 向.
At this time,
Lú Fāng had allied his troops with the Xiōngnú and Wūhuán 烏桓,
and bandit raids were particularly frequent,
causing distress along the border.
An imperial decree ordered Bà to lead over six thousand convicted laborers (shǔxíngtú 薥刑徒),
with Dù Mào, to construct the Fēihú Dào 飛狐道,
piling stones and spreading earth,
building up beacon towers and barriers,
for over three hundred *li* from Dài 代 to Píngchéng.
In total, he fought dozens or hundreds of large and small battles with the Xiōngnú and Wūhuán,
and was quite knowledgeable about border affairs.
He frequently submitted memorials proposing that a peace and kinship alliance should be established with the Xiōngnú,
and also suggested that provisions could be transported via the Wēn Shuǐ 溫水,
to save the labor of land transport.
All his proposals were implemented.
Later, the Southern Chányú 南單于 and Wūhuán surrendered,
and the northern border became peaceful.
Bà served in Shànggǔ for over twenty years.
In the thirtieth year (AD 54),
he was definitively enfeoffed as Marquis of Huáilíng 淮陵.
In Yǒngpíng 永平 second year (AD 59),
he was dismissed due to illness,
and died several months later.
His son Fú 符 succeeded him,
and was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dài 軑.
When Fú died,
his son Dù 度 succeeded him.
Dù married Princess Jùnyí 浚儀, daughter of Emperor Xiǎnzōng 顯宗,
and served as a Yellow Gate Gentleman (huángmén láng 黃門郎).
When Dù died,
his son Xīn 歆 succeeded him.
Jì Zūn, courtesy name Dìsūn,
was a native of Yǐngyáng, Yǐngchuān.
In his youth, he loved the classics.
His family was wealthy,
but Zūn was respectful and frugal,
wearing poor clothes.
After his mother's death,
he carried earth to build her tomb.
Once, he was bullied by a local official,
so he gathered retainers and killed him.
Initially,
the county thought he was gentle,
but later they all feared him.
When Guāngwǔ defeated Wáng Xún and others,
he returned and passed through Yǐngyáng.
Zūn, as a county official, frequently sought an audience.
Guāngwǔ admired his appearance and demeanor,
and appointed him as a Staff Officer for the Imperial Secretariat.
He followed the campaign to Héběi
and served as the Army Market Administrator.
When one of the attendants in his quarters violated the law,
Zūn personally killed him.
Guāngwǔ was enraged
and ordered Zūn's arrest.
At that time, the Chief Clerk Chén Fù advised,
"Your Excellency always desires that all armies be orderly.
Now, Zūn upholds the law without evasion;
this shows that your commands are being followed."
Guāngwǔ then pardoned him
and appointed him as the General Who Investigates and Punishes Evil.
He told the generals,
"You must be wary of Jì Zūn!
He even killed one of my own attendants for violating the law,
so he certainly won't show partiality to you gentlemen."
Soon after, he was appointed as a General of the Vanguard
and followed in pacifying Héběi.
For his accomplishments, he was enfeoffed as a Marquis.
In the spring of the second year of Jiànwǔ (26 AD),
he was appointed General Who Conquers Barbarians
and was formally enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǐngyáng.

Together with the General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry Jǐng Dān, the General-in-Chief Who Establishes Righteousness Zhū Yòu, the General of Hàn Loyalty Wáng Cháng, the Cavalry Commandant Wáng Liáng, Zāng Gōng, and others, he entered Jīguān
and marched south to attack the bandits in Hóngnóng, Yànxīn, and Bóhuá Mánzhōng.
A crossbow bolt struck Zūn's mouth,
piercing through and causing blood to flow.
Seeing Zūn wounded, the troops
began to retreat.
Zūn shouted to stop them,
and the soldiers all fought with double their usual bravery,
thus greatly defeating the enemy.
At that time, Zhāng Mǎn, a bandit from Mánzhōng in Xīnchéng,
had gathered forces in a dangerous defile, causing harm to people.
An imperial edict ordered Zūn to attack him.
Zūn cut off his supply lines.
Mǎn repeatedly challenged him to battle,
but Zūn held fast to his fortifications and did not go out.
Then, the remaining bandits from Yànxīn and Bóhuá rejoined Mǎn,
and they successfully attacked and captured Huòyángjù.
Zūn then divided his troops, attacked them, defeated them, and forced their surrender.
In the spring of the following year,
Zhāng Mǎn was starving and exhausted.
The city was taken,
and he was captured alive.
Initially,
Mǎn had offered sacrifices to Heaven and Earth
and proclaimed that he would become king.
After being captured,
he sighed,
"The prophecies misled me!"
He was then executed,
and his wife and children were wiped out.
Zūn led his troops south to attack Dèng Fèng's younger brother, Zhōng, at Dùyǎn,
and defeated him.
At that time, Zhāng Fēng, the Administrator of Zhuó Commandery, seized the envoy and raised an army in rebellion,
proclaiming himself Grand General Wúshàng,
and allied with Péng Chǒng.
In the fourth year (28 AD),
Zūn, along with Zhū Yòu, the General-in-Chief Who Establishes Martial Might Gěng Yǎn, and the General of Valiant Cavalry Liú Xǐ, collectively attacked him.
Zūn's troops arrived first
and fiercely attacked Fēng.
Mèng Yì, Fēng's Chief Clerk of Meritorious Service, seized Fēng and surrendered.
Initially,
Fēng was fond of esoteric arts,
and a Daoist had told him that he would become Son of Heaven.
He wrapped a stone in a five-colored pouch and tied it to Fēng's elbow,
claiming that there was an imperial seal within the stone.
Fēng believed him
and thus rebelled.
When he was captured and about to be executed,
he still said,
"There is an imperial seal in the stone on my elbow."
Zūn had it hammered open,
and Fēng then realized he had been tricked.
He looked up at the sky and sighed,
"I will die without regret!"
All the generals withdrew and returned,
but Zūn received an imperial edict to remain garrisoned at Liángxiāng to resist Péng Chǒng.
He then dispatched his Protector of the Army Fù Xuán to raid Péng Chǒng's general Lǐ Háo at Lù,
greatly defeating him
and beheading over a thousand men.
They confronted each other for over a year,
and Zūn repeatedly blunted Péng Chǒng's advance,
leading many of his confederates to surrender.
After Péng Chǒng's death,
Zūn advanced and pacified his territory.
In the spring of the sixth year (30 AD),

an imperial edict ordered Zūn, along with the General-in-Chief Who Establishes Martial Might Gěng Yǎn, the General-in-Chief of Tiger's Teeth Gài Yán, the General of Hàn Loyalty Wáng Cháng, the General Who Captures Barbarians Mǎ Wǔ, the General of Valiant Cavalry Liú Xīn, and the General Who Exerts Martial Power Liú Shàng, to campaign against Gōngsūn Shù from Tiānshuǐ.
The army reached Cháng'ān.
At that time, the imperial carriage also arrived.
However, Wěi Xiāo did not want the Hàn army to ascend Lǒng
and offered excuses to dissuade them.
The Emperor summoned the generals to deliberate.
They all said,
"We can temporarily extend Wěi Xiāo's deadline by a few months
and increase the enfeoffments of his generals and commanders
to cause his forces to disperse."
Zūn said,
"Wěi Xiāo has harbored treachery for a long time.
If we now lay down our arms and delay,
it will only deepen his cunning schemes,
and Shǔ will increase its vigilance and defenses.
It is definitely better to advance directly."
The Emperor agreed with him
and then sent Zūn as the vanguard.
Wěi Xiāo sent his general Wáng Yuán to resist at Lǒngchí.
Zūn advanced and attacked,
defeating him
and pursuing him to Xīn Guān.
When the other generals arrived,
they fought with Wěi Xiāo
and were all defeated,
retreating down Lǒng.
An edict then ordered Zūn's army to garrison at Qiān,
Gěng Yǎn's army at Qī,
and the General-in-Chief Who Conquers the West Féng Yì's army at Xúnyì.
Grand Marshal Wú Hàn and others returned to garrison at Cháng'ān.
From then on, Zūn repeatedly frustrated Wěi Xiāo.
These events are already described in the Biography of Féng Yì.
In the autumn of the eighth year (32 AD),
he again followed the imperial carriage up Lǒng.
After Wěi Xiāo was defeated,
the Emperor returned east, passing through Qiān.
He visited Zūn's camp,
comforted and entertained the soldiers,
and had court music and dances performed.
It was late at night before they concluded.
At that time, Zūn was ill,
and an edict granted him a heavy mattress
and covered him with the imperial canopy.
He was again ordered to advance and garrison below Lǒng.
When Gōngsūn Shù sent troops to rescue Wěi Xiāo,
Wú Hàn, Gěng Yǎn, and others all fled back,
but Zūn alone remained and did not retreat.
In the spring of the ninth year (33 AD),
he died in the army.
Zhūn 遵 was a man of integrity, frugality, and circumspection.
He exercised self-restraint and dedicated himself to public service.
All rewards and grants were invariably distributed to his soldiers.
His household had no private wealth.
He wore trousers of deerskin,
slept under a cloth quilt,
and his wife's skirt had no added trim.
The Emperor valued him greatly for these reasons.
When he passed away,
the Emperor was exceptionally grieved.
When Zhūn's 遵 coffin arrived at Hénán 河南 County,
an imperial edict commanded all officials to first gather at the mourning site.
The Emperor, in plain clothes, personally attended,
weeping with profound sorrow from afar.
On his return, as he passed the city gate,
and his (Zhūn's 遵) chariots and cavalry,
his tears could not be stopped.
After the funeral rites were completed,
he again personally offered a sacrifice of a grand ox,
following the precedent of Emperor Xuān 宣 attending to Huò Guāng 霍光.
An edict commanded the Dàchángqiū 大長秋, Yèzhě 謁者, and Hénányǐn 河南尹 to oversee the funeral arrangements,
and the Dàsīnóng 大司農 to provide the expenses.
The Erudite Fàn Shēng 范升 submitted a memorial,
praising Zhūn 遵 retrospectively, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the Former Kings, in their governance,
honored what was good and banished what was evil.
In ancient times, Gāozǔ 高祖, being a great sage,
showed deep foresight.
He conferred ranks and allotted lands,
sharing merit with his subordinates,
registering meritorious officials,
and extolling their virtues.
While alive, they were honored with special rites:
when presenting reports, their names were not used,
and they did not hasten upon entering the palace.
Upon their deaths, their noble titles and fiefs were preserved,
so their lines would never be cut off for generations,
with red-script iron certificates
passed down through endless ages.
This indeed was the great virtue of the mighty Hàn 漢, fostering generosity towards subordinates, securing the people, and ensuring longevity,
which allowed it to endure for more than ten generations,
and hundreds of years,
to be restored after decline,
and continued after interruption.
Your Majesty, having received the Mandate with supreme virtue,
first illuminated the Way of Hàn 漢,
praised and ranked your assistants,
and bestowed fiefs and rewards upon meritorious ministers,
thereby matching the example of your ancestors.
The General who Conquers the Barbarians, Marquis of Yǐngyáng 潁陽, Zhūn 遵,
unfortunately died prematurely.
Your Majesty, with your benevolent grace,
was deeply moved and saddened by this,
traveling afar to meet his coffin in Hénán 河南.
The sorrow of your profound grief
was manifested in your sacred person.
The expenses for the funeral
were provided by the county office,
and his wife and children received countless
generous gifts.
The care for the dead surpassed that for the living,
and the generosity for the deceased exceeded that for the living.
Correcting customs and inspiring transformation,
this shines brilliantly like the sun and moon.
In ancient times, when a minister was ill, the lord visited;
when a minister died, the lord grieved.
[一０] This was a profound demonstration of virtue.
Such practices have long been neglected.
But with Your Majesty,
these rites have been revived,
moving all subordinates,
so none fail to strive for self-improvement.
Your servant secretly observed Zhūn 遵 in his conduct, accumulating good deeds,
and exhausting his loyalty to the state.
In the north, he pacified Yúyáng 漁陽;
in the west, he resisted Lǒng 隴 and Shǔ 蜀.
He was the first to ascend the heights,
and deeply captured Luèyáng 略陽.
When the main army retreated,
he alone defended the difficult terrain.
[一二] He controlled the soldiers' hearts,
not transgressing the laws.
The local officials and people
were unaware of the presence of an army.
[一三] His pure reputation was known throughout the realm,
and his incorruptibility was renowned in his time.
Whatever rewards he received
were all given to his officers and soldiers.
He owned no extravagant clothes,
and his household had no private wealth.
His elder brother, Wǔ 午, of the same mother, knowing Zhūn 遵 had no son,
married a concubine and sent her to him.
Zhūn 遵, however, sent someone to refuse her,
believing that as he held a significant office for the state,
he dared not plan for his personal life or consider the continuation of his lineage.
Before his death, he left instructions for his coffin to be transported by ox-cart,
and to be buried simply in Luòyáng 洛陽.
When asked about family matters,
he remained silent until the end.
His burden was heavy, his path long;
he only ceased upon death.
[一四] As a general, Zhūn 遵
selected his officers based entirely on Confucian principles.
At banquets with wine and music,
he invariably had elegant songs and played the game of 'pitch pot.'
[一五] He also proposed establishing a successor for Kǒngzǐ 孔子
and memorialized to appoint Grand Masters for the Five Classics.
Even amidst military campaigns,
he did not forget sacrificial rites,
and can be called one who
loved propriety and delighted in music, upholding the good Way even unto death.
According to ritual,
one has a noble title while alive,
and an posthumous title upon death.
Noble titles distinguish high and low,
and posthumous titles clarify good and evil.
Your servant humbly believes it is fitting, upon Zhūn's 遵 demise,
to discuss and recount his many achievements,
carefully examine the laws of posthumous titles,
and thus complete the ritual.
[一六] This would manifest the state's ancient and earnest regulations,
serving as a model for future generations."
The Emperor then sent Shēng's 升 memorial to the dukes and ministers.
At the burial,
the Emperor again personally attended,
bestowing upon him the seal and sash of a General and Marquis,
a red-wheeled carriage for officials,
and armored soldiers to form a procession for the funeral.
[一七] He was given the posthumous title of Chéng Hóu 成侯.
After the burial,
the Emperor again personally visited his tomb,
meeting with his wife and household.
Afterwards, at court assemblies,
the Emperor would often sigh and say:
"How can I find a minister as concerned for the state and devoted to public service as Jì Zhēnglǔ 祭征虜?"
Zhūn 遵 was remembered in this manner.
[一八]
He had no son,
so his marquisate was abolished.
His elder brother, Wǔ 午,
reached the rank of Grand Administrator of Jiǔquán 酒泉.
His cousin was Róng 肜.
Róng's 肜 courtesy name was Cìsūn 次孫.
He was orphaned early,
and was known for his extreme filial piety.
During a period of chaos throughout the land,
when there were no cooking fires in the wilderness,
he alone remained by his parents' tomb.
Whenever bandits passed by,
seeing him still young but possessing great integrity,
they were all astonished and felt pity for him.
In the early days of Guāngwǔ 光武, owing to Zhūn 遵,
Róng 肜 was appointed Huángmén Shìláng 黃門侍郎,
always remaining by the Emperor's side.
When Zhūn 遵 died without a son,
the Emperor, regretting and grieving this,
appointed Róng 肜 as the Chief of Yǎnshī 偃師,
instructing him to live near Zhūn's 遵 tomb
and offer sacrifices four times a year.
Róng 肜 possessed strategic ability.
After five years in office,
the county had no bandits,
and his administration was ranked first.
He was promoted to Magistrate of Xiāngbēn 襄賁.
At that time, not all commanderies and states in the empire had yet been pacified,
and in Xiāngbēn 襄賁, bandits openly roamed in broad daylight.
Upon Róng's 肜 arrival,
he executed and crushed the corrupt and cunning,
eradicating their factions.
Within a few years,
Xiāngbēn's 襄賁 administration was clean.
Imperial edicts encouraged him,
his rank was increased by one grade,
and he was given one hundred bolts of fine silk.
At that time,
the Xiōngnú, Xiānbēi, and Chìshān Wūhuán allied and grew strong,
frequently invading the frontier, killing and plundering officials and common people.
The imperial court was concerned about this,
and therefore increased the border troops,
with several thousand men in each commandery.
Generals were also dispatched to garrison the outposts.
The Emperor considered Róng to be capable.
In the seventeenth year of Jiànwǔ,
he was appointed Grand Administrator of Liáodōng.
Upon arrival, he drilled his troops
and expanded scouting efforts.
Róng possessed great courage and strength,
able to draw a bow of three hundred *jīn*.
Whenever the barbarians encroached upon the frontier,
he always served as the vanguard for his soldiers,
and repeatedly defeated and repelled them.
In the autumn of the twenty-first year,
over ten thousand Xiānbēi cavalry raided Liáodōng.
Róng led several thousand men to meet and attack them,
personally donning armor and charging into the enemy ranks.
The barbarians fled in great disarray,
more than half of them drowning in the water.
He then pursued them beyond the frontier.
The barbarians, in their desperation,
abandoned their weapons and scattered, naked.
More than three thousand heads were cut off,
and several thousand horses were captured.
From then on, the Xiānbēi were terrified,
fearing Róng and not daring to peer into the frontier again.
Róng, observing that the three barbarian tribes were allied
and constantly causing border troubles,
in the twenty-fifth year,
sent out calls to the Xiānbēi,
showing them financial benefits.
Their great protector Piānhé
sent envoys to offer tribute,
wishing to submit.
Róng comforted, accepted, and rewarded them,
and they gradually became close adherents again.
Other tribes, such as Mǎnlí and Gāogōulí,
subsequently flocked to the frontier in succession,
offering sable furs and fine horses.
The Emperor always doubled their rewards.
Later, the chieftains of Piānhé’s settlement all returned to allegiance,
wishing to offer their services.
Róng said:
"If you truly wish to achieve merit,
you should return and attack the Xiōngnú;
only by cutting off and presenting their heads will you be trusted."
Piānhé and others looked up to heaven and pointed to their hearts, saying:
"We will definitely render service!"
They immediately attacked the Xiōngnú's Zuǒzhìzī department,
beheading over two thousand and presenting their heads at the commandery.
Thereafter, they attacked each other year after year,
always presenting heads and receiving rewards.
From then on, the Xiōngnú declined,
and there were no border incursions or alarms.
The Xiānbēi and Wūhuán both came to the court to pay tribute.
Róng was of a sincere, steadfast, and resolute character,
and his physique and appearance surpassed the ordinary.
He treated the barbarian tribes with kindness and trust,
and they all feared and loved him,
thus securing their utmost loyalty.
Initially,
the Chìshān Wūhuán frequently harassed Shànggǔ,
causing border troubles.
Imperial edicts offered rewards
and severely criticized the provinces and commanderies
for being unable to suppress them.
Róng then encouraged Piānhé
and sent him to suppress them.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng,
