Piānhé defeated Chìshān,
beheaded their leader,
and presented his head to Róng.
The lands beyond the frontier were struck with awe.
Róng’s formidable reputation
spread throughout the north.
From Wǔwēi in the west
to Xuántú and Lèlàng in the east,
all the barbarians came to pledge allegiance,
and there was no more conflict in the wild.
Consequently, all border garrisons were disbanded.
In the twelfth year,
he was summoned to serve as Grand Coachman.
Róng had been in Liáodōng for nearly thirty years,
and had no change of clothes.
Emperor Xiǎnzōng not only praised his achievements
but also admired Róng's simple and frugal lifestyle.
On the day of his appointment,
he was granted one million coins,
three horses,
clothing, blankets, swords,
down to household items—
nothing, great or small, was left unprovided.
Every time the Emperor saw Róng,
he would often sigh with admiration, considering him worthy of great responsibility.
Later, when he accompanied the Emperor on an eastern inspection tour,
passing through Lǔ,
they sat in Confucius's lecture hall.
The Emperor looked around, pointed to Zǐlù's room, and said to his attendants:
"This is the Grand Coachman's room.
The Grand Coachman
is my protector against insult."
In the sixteenth year,
Róng, as Grand Coachman, was ordered to lead over ten thousand cavalry with Xìn, the Left Worthy King of the Southern Chányú, to attack the Northern Xiōngnú,
with a rendezvous set at Zhuóxié Mountain.
Xìn had an initial grudge against Róng.
After traveling over nine hundred *lǐ* beyond Gāoquè Pass,
he found a small mountain
and falsely claimed it to be Zhuóxié Mountain.
Róng arrived but saw no barbarians, so he returned.
He was imprisoned and dismissed for delaying and being cowardly.
Róng was by nature calm, resolute, and inwardly serious.
He resented being deceived and having achieved no merit.
Several days after his release from prison,
he vomited blood and died.
Before his death, he told his son:
"I have received profound imperial grace,
but my mission was not accomplished,
and no slight achievement was made.
My death is truly a matter of shame and regret.
It is unjust to receive rewards without merit.
After my death,
you should meticulously list all the gifts I received,
personally go to the military garrisons,
and risk your life on the front line
to fulfill my wish."
After his death,
his son Féng submitted a memorial fully detailing his father’s last words.
The Emperor had always highly esteemed Róng
and was about to employ him again.
Hearing this, he was greatly astonished,
summoned Féng to inquire about his father’s illness,
and sighed in lament for a long time.
The Wūhuán and Xiānbēi remembered Róng without end.
Whenever they came to the capital for court tribute,
they would always pass by his tomb to pay respects,
looking up to heaven and wailing before leaving.
The officials and people of Liáodōng erected a shrine for him
and offered sacrifices four times a year.
After Róng was buried,
his son Cān went to see Dòu Gù, the Commandant of Chariots,
followed the army to attack Chēshī, achieved merit,
and was gradually promoted to Grand Administrator of Liáodōng.
During the Yǒngyuán era,
the Xiānbēi invaded the commandery.
Cān was held responsible for the defeat,
imprisoned, and died.
Many of Róng's descendants became border officials,
and all gained renown.
A commentary states: Jì Róng's martial integrity was firm and upright,
and his actions were steady and weighty.
Even those like Marquis Tiáo and Rángjū
could not surpass him.
Moreover, when he governed the remote frontier,
his policies transformed the unruly customs.
Border people requested talismans to establish trust,
and the Hu and Mò tribes presented heads outside the city.
He even managed to have drums lie silent at border posts,
and signal fires extinguished on the distant defenses for nearly thirty years.
The ancients' saying,
"It takes a generation to achieve benevolence,"
is it not true?
Yet, due to a single fault,
he was led to resentment and indignation.
Alas,
the pitfalls of strict adherence to law!
Eulogy: Qí inspired Yānmén;
Bà iced Húhé.
Jì Zūn delighted in ritual;
facing battle, he sang elegantly.
Róng resisted in Liáozuǒ;
the border court cherished harmony.

Biographies of Rèn, Lǐ, Wàn, Pī, Liú, Gěng, Chapter 11 (Rèn Guāng zǐ Wěi)
Rèn Guāng, courtesy name Bóqīng,
was a native of Wǎn, Nányáng.
From a young age, he was loyal and honest,
and was loved by his fellow villagers.
Initially, he served as a xiāngsèfū
and a county official.
When the Hàn army reached Wǎn,
soldiers, seeing Rèn Guāng's bright cap and attire,
ordered him to take off his clothes,
intending to kill him and seize them.
It happened that Liú Cì, the Guānglùxūn, arrived at that moment.
Seeing Rèn Guāng's dignified appearance,
he saved his life.
Rèn Guāng then led his followers to join Liú Cì,
serving as Ānjí Yuàn.
He was appointed Piān Jiāngjūn
and, with Shìzǔ, defeated Wáng Xún and Wáng Yì.
When Gēngshǐ arrived in Luòyáng,
he appointed Rèn Guāng as Xìndū Grand Administrator.
When Wáng Láng arose,
all the commanderies and states surrendered to him,
but Rèn Guāng alone refused.
He then, with Commandant Lǐ Zhōng, Magistrate Wàn Xiū,
Merit Officer Ruǎn Kuàng, Officer of the Five Bureaus Guō Táng, and others,
united in heart to hold firmly to the city.
A court clerk, holding Wáng Láng's proclamation,
came to the府 (prefectural office) to report to Rèn Guāng.
Rèn Guāng had him executed in the marketplace,
to warn the populace,
and dispatched four thousand elite soldiers to defend the city.
In the spring of Gēngshǐ's second year,
Shìzǔ returned from Jì,
bewildered and not knowing where to go.
He heard that Xìndū alone was resisting Hándān for Hàn,
so he immediately rushed there.
Rèn Guāng and the others, holding an isolated city,
feared they could not preserve it whole.
When they heard Shìzǔ had arrived,
they were greatly pleased.
The officials and common people all cheered "Long live!"
and immediately opened the gates.
Rèn Guāng, with Lǐ Zhōng and Wàn Xiū, led his subordinates to welcome and pay respects.
Shìzǔ entered the guesthouse
and said to Rèn Guāng:
"Bóqīng,
our current power is weak.
What do you think of us entering the city together, amidst the troops of Chéngtóu Zǐlù and Lì Zǐdōu?"
Shìzǔ asked.
Rèn Guāng replied:
"That is not advisable."
Shìzǔ said:
"Your troops are few.
What do you propose?"
Rèn Guāng said:
"We can recruit desperate soldiers,
and go out to attack nearby counties.
If any do not surrender,
let them be plundered at will.
People are greedy for wealth,
so soldiers can be attracted and gathered."
Shìzǔ followed his advice.
He appointed Rèn Guāng as Left Grand General,
and enfeoffed him as Wǔchéng Hóu.
He left Zōng Guǎng of Nányáng to manage the affairs of Xìndū Grand Administrator,
and had Rèn Guāng lead his troops to follow him.
Rèn Guāng then drafted many proclamations saying:
"Grand Marshal Liú Gōng, with a million troops from Chéngtóu Zǐlù and Lì Zǐdōu, is coming from the east
to attack all the rebel barbarians."
He sent cavalry to rush to the border of Jùlù.
When the officials and common people received the proclamations,
they spread the word to each other.
Shìzǔ then, with Rèn Guāng and others, entered the border of Tángyáng at dusk,
making the cavalry each carry torches,
filling the marsh.
The blazing light illuminated heaven and earth,
and the entire city was shocked, terrified, and panicked.
They surrendered that very night.
Within ten days,
the army greatly increased in strength.
They then attacked cities and towns,
and subsequently sacked Hándān.
Then, Shìzǔ sent Rèn Guāng back to his commandery.
Chéngtóu Zǐlù was
a person from Dōngpíng,
whose surname was Yuán,
given name Zēng,
and courtesy name Zǐlù.
He raised an army with Liú Xǔ of Féichéng at Lúchéngtóu,
hence his troops were called
"Chéngtóu Zǐlù."
Yuán Zēng styled himself
"Dū Cóngshì,"
and Liú Xǔ styled himself
"Xiào Sānlǎo."
They plundered the area between the Hé and Jǐ rivers,
and their followers reached over two hundred thousand.
When Gēngshǐ was established,
Yuán Zēng sent envoys to surrender.
Yuán Zēng was appointed Dōnglái Grand Administrator,
and Liú Xǔ was appointed Jìnán Grand Administrator.
Both acted as Grand Generals.
That year,
Yuán Zēng was killed by his own general,
and the multitude elected Liú Xǔ as their leader.
Gēngshǐ enfeoffed Liú Xǔ as Zhùguó Hóu,
and ordered him to disband his troops and return to his native commandery.
Lì Zǐdōu was
a person from Dōnghǎi.
He raised an army in his hometown,
and raided the border between Xú and Yǎn.
His followers numbered sixty to seventy thousand.
When Gēngshǐ was established,
Lì Zǐdōu sent envoys to surrender,
and was appointed Xúzhōu Shepherd.
He was killed by his own subordinates,
and the remaining partisans regrouped,
meeting with various bandits in Bùxiāng.
They were then called Bùxiāng.
Dǒng Cìzhòng, the chief of Bùxiāng, initially rose in Chípíng,
then crossed the Hé river into Wèijùn and Qīnghé.
He joined with Wǔxiào,
and their followers numbered over one hundred thousand.
In Jiànwǔ's first year,
Shìzǔ entered Luòyáng,
and sent Grand Marshal Wú Hàn and others to attack Bùxiāng.
In the spring of the following year,
they were greatly defeated and surrendered.
That year,
Rèn Guāng was further enfeoffed as Ālíng Hóu,
with a food allotment of ten thousand households.
In the fifth year,
he was summoned to the capital
to attend court.
He died that winter.
His son, Rèn Kuí, succeeded him.
Later, Ruǎn Kuàng became Nányáng Grand Administrator,
and Guō Táng became Hénán Yǐn.
Both were renowned for their ability.
Rèn Kuí, courtesy name Zhònghé,
was fond of Huáng-Lǎo (Huang-Lao philosophy) in his youth,
pure, quiet, and with few desires.
The salary and emoluments he received
he often used to assist his clan members
and to care for orphans and the widowed.
Xiǎnzōng, hearing of this,
promoted him to attend court,
transferred him to Left Supervisor of the Yǔlín (Imperial Guard),
then Commander of the Hǔbēn (Imperial Guard),
and again transferred him to Commandant of Chángshuǐ.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
he respected and loved Rèn Kuí greatly,
often praising his conduct,
and appointed him Minister of Works.
Since Jiànwǔ, the Minister of Works had always been concurrently held by an imperial attendant.
It was not until Rèn Kuí that a genuine appointment was made.
In Jiànchū's fifth year,
he was transferred to Grand Coachman.
In the eighth year,
he replaced Dòu Gù as Minister of the Imperial Household.
In all his positions, he was praised.
In Zhānghé's first year,
he was appointed Minister of Public Works.
Rèn Kuí was righteous and cultivated within himself,
not seeking fame,
but was respected by the world for his profound steadfastness.
When Hédì ascended the throne,
Grand General Dòu Xiàn held power,
monopolizing authority and favor.
All internal and external court officials were terrified.
At that time, Dòu Xiàn attacked the Xiōngnú,
and state expenses were burdensome.
Rèn Kuí memorialized proposing Dòu Xiàn's recall,
submitting ten such memorials in succession.
He alone, with Minister of Education Yuán Ān, united their efforts,
maintained their firm and upright stance,
and offered blunt and direct criticisms,
without any evasion or concealment.
His words are recorded in the biography of Yuán Ān.
In Yǒngyuán's fourth year, he passed away.
His son, Rèn Tún, succeeded him.
The Emperor, reminiscing about Rèn Kuí's loyalty,
promoted Rèn Tún to Commandant of Infantry,
and transferred his enfeoffment to Xīyáng Hóu.
Rèn Tún died,
and his son, Rèn Shèng, succeeded him.
Rèn Shèng died,
and his son, Rèn Shì, succeeded him,
transferred his enfeoffment to Běixiāng Hóu.
Lǐ Zhōng, courtesy name Zhòngdū,
was a native of Huáng in Dōnglái.
His father was Gāomì Commandant.
In the Yuánshǐ era, Lǐ Zhōng became a郎 (Gentleman) through his father's appointment.
Among the dozens of people in his department, Lǐ Zhōng alone was praised for his good conduct and discipline.
During Wáng Mǎng's time, he served as Head of Xīnbó County,
and everyone in the commandery respected and trusted him.
When Gēngshǐ was established,
he sent envoys to tour the commanderies and states,
and immediately appointed Lǐ Zhōng to the office of Commandant.
Lǐ Zhōng then, with Rèn Guāng, jointly served Shìzǔ,
who appointed him Right Grand General
and enfeoffed him as Wǔgù Hóu.
At that time, Shìzǔ personally removed the sash and seal he wore and gave it to Lǐ Zhōng,
and then proceeded to attack and subdue the subordinate counties.
When they reached Kǔxíng,
Shìzǔ gathered his generals
and asked about the wealth they had acquired.
Only Lǐ Zhōng alone had plundered nothing.
Shìzǔ said:
"I wish to grant a special gift to Lǐ Zhōng.
Do any of you gentlemen have any objections?"
He then bestowed upon him the great black horse he was riding and embroidered clothing.
Zhōng advanced and besieged Jùlù,
but had not yet taken it.
Wáng Láng sent generals to attack Xìndū.
The prominent local gentry of Xìndū, Mǎ Chǒng and others, opened the city gates and let them in.
They seized the Administrator, Zōng Guǎng, and Zhōng’s mother and wife,
and then had Zhōng’s relatives call out to him.
At that time, Mǎ Chǒng’s younger brother served as a Commandant under Zhōng.
Zhōng immediately summoned him,
and rebuked him for betraying his benevolence and turning over the city,
then slew him with a weapon.
All the generals were alarmed and said:
“Your family is in their hands;
to kill his brother,
how fierce!”
Zhōng said:
“If I were to let the rebels go unpunished,
then I would have two minds.”
Shìzǔ heard of this and praised him,
saying to Zhōng:
“Now my army is formed.
General, you may return to rescue your aged mother, wife, and children.
You should personally recruit officials and commoners who can retrieve their family members,
and I will grant them ten million cash
to come and take from me.”
Zhōng said:
“Having received the great benevolence of the enlightened lord,
I wish to exert myself in service,
and truly dare not look back at my family.”
Shìzǔ then sent Rèn Guāng to lead troops to rescue Xìndū.
Rèn Guāng’s troops scattered and surrendered to Wáng Láng on the way,
and he returned without accomplishing anything.
Coincidentally, the general sent by Gēngshǐ attacked and captured Xìndū,
and Zhōng’s family was saved.
Shìzǔ then sent Zhōng back
to act as Administrator,
where he gathered the prominent local gentry of the commandery who had sided with Hándān
and executed several hundred people.
When Rèn Guāng returned to the commandery,
Zhōng then reverted to being a Commandant.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ
he was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhōngshuǐ,
with a fief of three thousand households.
In the same year,
he was summoned and appointed as the Commandant-in-Chief of the Five Bureaus (Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng),
and followed in pacifying Páng Méng, Dǒng Xiàn, and others.
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to Administrator of Dānyáng.
At this time, the realm had just been pacified;
in the south, along the coast, the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
many held onto their troops and occupied territory.
When Zhōng arrived at the commandery,
he recruited and conciliated those who surrendered;
those who did not submit were all executed,
and within ten days to a month, all was pacified.
Zhōng, noting that the Yuè customs in Dānyáng were not fond of learning,
and that wedding ceremonies
were inferior to those in Zhōngguó,
thereupon established schools,
practiced rites and decorum,
and held village drinking ceremonies in spring and autumn.
He selected and employed scholars learned in the classics,
and the commandery looked up to and admired him.
Cultivated land increased greatly,
and within three years, over fifty thousand displaced persons were registered.
In the fourteenth year,
the Three Ducal Ministers recommended him as the foremost in the empire,
and he was promoted to Administrator of Yùzhāng.
He left office due to illness,
and was summoned to the capital.
In the nineteenth year,
he died.
His son Wēi succeeded.
After Wēi died,
his son Chún succeeded.
In the ninth year of Yǒngpíng,
due to his mother killing Chún’s uncle,
the fief was abolished.
In the seventh year of Yǒngchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng re-enfeoffed Chún as the Marquis of Qíntíng.
After Chún died,
his son Guǎng succeeded.
Wàn Xiū, courtesy name Jūnyóu,
was a native of Máolíng, Fúfēng.
During the time of Gēngshǐ,
he served as the Magistrate of Xìndū,
and together with Administrator Rèn Guāng and Commandant Lǐ Zhōng, they defended the city.
They welcomed Shìzǔ
and he was appointed as a Brigadier-General (Piānjiāngjūn)
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zàoyì.
After Hándān was defeated,
he was appointed as General of the Right,
and followed in pacifying Héběi.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Huáilǐ.
Together with Jiān Tán, General of Yanghua, he attacked Nányáng,
but fell ill before conquering it,
and died in the army.
His son Pǔ succeeded,
and was transferred and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xuánshì.
After Pǔ died,
his son Qīn succeeded,
and was transferred and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Fúliǔ.
After Qīn died,
he had no sons,
and the fief was abolished.
In the seventh year of Yǒngchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng restored the enfeoffment of Xiū’s great-grandson Fēng as the Marquis of Qǔpíngtíng.
After Fēng died,
his son Chì succeeded.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn,
Chì died,
had no sons,
and the fief was abolished.
In the second year of Yánxī,
Emperor Huán restored the enfeoffment of Xiū’s great-great-grandson Gōng as the Marquis of Méndétíng.
Pī Tóng, courtesy name Wěijūn,
was a native of Xìndū.
His father, Jí,
was the Administrator of Liáoxī.
Tóng initially served as the Governor (Zúzhèng) of Héchěng under Wáng Mǎng.
When Shìzǔ campaigned in Héběi,
arriving at Xiàqǔyáng,
Tóng surrendered the city.
He was reappointed as Administrator,
and remained there for several days.
When Shìzǔ went north to Jì,
and Wáng Láng’s forces rose,
he sent his generals to secure territories.
Wherever they went, every county welcomed them,
except Héchěng and Xìndū, which held firm and did not surrender.
Tóng heard that Shìzǔ had returned from Jì,
having lost his army,
and wished to reach Xìndū.
He first sent his Chief Clerk (Wǔguān Yuán) Zhāng Wàn and Inspector (Dūyóu) Yǐn Suí,
selecting over two thousand elite cavalry,
to meet Shìzǔ’s army on the road.
Tóng soon met Shìzǔ at Xìndū.
Although Shìzǔ had the assistance of the two commanderies,
his troops were not yet assembled.
Many advisers suggested that he should rely on the Xìndū troops to escort him,
and return west to Cháng’ān.
Tóng addressed the court, saying:
“The words of the advisers are all incorrect.
The officials and commoners have long yearned for the Hàn and sung praises of it.
Therefore, when Gēngshǐ assumed the honored title, the empire responded,
and the Three Fǔ regions cleared palaces and roads to welcome him.
When a single man takes up a halberd and shouts loudly,
generals a thousand *lǐ* away will abandon their cities and flee,
and the captives will prostrate themselves and surrender.
Since ancient times,
there has never been such a moving of people and things.
Furthermore, the soothsayer Wáng Láng,
using a false name and relying on circumstances,
assembled a motley crowd,
and thus shook the lands of Yān and Zhào.
How much more so for the enlightened lord, who raises the armies of two commanderies,
and proclaims the might of a responding empire!
If you attack, what city will not be conquered?
If you fight, what army will not be subdued?
To abandon this now and return,
would not only mean losing Héběi in vain,
but would certainly further alarm the Three Fǔ,
diminishing your authority and prestige.
This is not a sound plan.
If the enlightened lord no longer has the intention of campaigning,
then even the troops of Xìndū will be difficult to gather.
Why?
Once the enlightened lord goes west,
the people of Hándān city will not be willing to abandon their parents
and turn their backs on their city lord
to escort you a thousand *lǐ*;
their dispersal and flight are certain.”
Shìzǔ approved of his words and stayed.
On that day, Tóng was appointed General of the Rear (Hòu Dàjiāngjūn),
remaining Administrator of Héchěng,
and was ordered to lead troops at the front.
By the time they reached Tángyáng,
Tángyáng had already defected to Wáng Láng.
Tóng sent Zhāng Wàn and Yǐn Suí ahead to enlighten the officials and commoners.
Shìzǔ arrived at night,
and they immediately opened the gates and welcomed him.
He led his troops to defeat the bandit Bái Shē at Zhōngshān.
From then on, he constantly followed in battles and attacks.
Xìndū again rebelled and went over to Wáng Láng.
The Xìndū King appointed by Láng arrested Tóng’s father, younger brother, wife, and children,
and had them write letters to Tóng, saying:
“Those who surrender will be enfeoffed with titles;
those who do not will have their clan exterminated.”
Tóng wept and replied:
“One who serves his lord cannot consider his family.
That Tóng’s relatives have been able to remain safe in Xìndū until now
is due to the grace of Lord Liú.
The lord is currently striving for the affairs of the state;
Tóng cannot again think of private matters.”
Coincidentally, the general sent by Gēngshǐ attacked and captured Xìndū,
Láng’s army was defeated and fled,
and Tóng’s family was spared.
When Hándān was captured,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔyì.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Língshòu,
and acted as Grand Minister of Works.
When the Emperor entered Luòyáng,
Tóng was appointed Grandee Secretary,
and after more than a month, transferred to Minor Treasury.
He was dismissed that year.
He was again made Left Scribe Attendant,
and often followed in campaigns.
In the sixth year,
he went to his state.
When Tóng died,
his son Tāng succeeded him.
In the ninth year,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Lèlíng.
In the nineteenth year,
Tāng died,
and his son Mǒu succeeded him.
Having no son,
the state was abolished.
In the first year of Yuánchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng re-enfeoffed Tóng's grandson Yīn as Marquis of Píngtíng.
When Yīn died,
his son Chái succeeded him.
Initially,
Zhāng Wàn and Yǐn Suí, along with Tóng, welcomed Shìzǔ,
and were all appointed Generals of the Household.
They also followed in campaigns.
Wàn was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chóngpíng,
and Suí as Marquis of Píngtái.
The commentary says: Generally, those who speak of accomplished deeds
are easily distinguished by their prominent achievements;
those who strategize at the outset of affairs
are difficult to clarify due to the subtlety of their principles.
This is indeed a comparison of circumstances and traces,
which ought to be thoroughly examined.
If the strategist wanted to use the forces of the two commanderies,
and propose the strategy of entering the pass,
abandoning an accomplished enterprise
to face the unpredictable,
and the sovereign had not yet awakened,
while the advisors were uniformly of the same view,
then Pī Tóng's court discussion
was indeed a critical moment!
The saying goes,
"One word can revive a nation,"
and this is close to it.
Liú Zhí, courtesy name Bóxiān,
was a native of Chāngchéng, Jùlù.
When Wáng Láng rose,
Zhí, with his younger brother Xǐ and cousin Xīn,
led their clan and retainers,
gathered several thousand soldiers, and occupied Chāngchéng.
Hearing that Shìzǔ was returning from Jì,
they opened the gates to welcome Shìzǔ.
Zhí was appointed General of Agile Cavalry,
and Xǐ and Xīn were appointed Generals of the Household,
all becoming marquises.
At that time, Liú Yáng, King of Zhēndìng, had raised an army to join Wáng Láng.
With over a hundred thousand troops,
Shìzǔ sent Zhí to persuade Yáng,
and Yáng consequently surrendered.
Shìzǔ then stayed in Zhēndìng,
and took Guō Hòu as his empress.
The empress was Yáng's niece,
and thus this connection was made.
Then, with Yáng and the generals, they held a banquet in the Guō clan's Qīlǐ village house.
Yáng played the zhù for entertainment,
and this allowed them to advance their troops to capture Hándān,
and subsequently pacify Héběi.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Zhí was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Chāngchéng.
He was killed in battle while suppressing the bandits of Mìxiàn.
His son Xiàng succeeded him.
The Emperor ordered Xǐ to take command of Zhí's camp,
and he was again appointed General of Agile Cavalry,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Guānjīn.
When Xǐ died,
Xīn was again appointed General of Agile Cavalry,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Fúyáng.
Xǐ and Xīn followed in campaigns,
and [their titles] were both passed down to their descendants.
Xiàng was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dōngwǔyáng.
He died,
and his son Shù succeeded him.
In the fifteenth year of Yǒngpíng,
he was implicated in the conspiracy of Chǔ Wáng Yīng,
and his state was abolished.
Gěng Chún, courtesy name Bóshān,
was a native of Sòngzǐ, Jùlù.
His father, Ài,
was the Administrator of Jìpíng under Wáng Mǎng.
Chún studied in Cháng'ān,
and was subsequently appointed Advisor.
When Wáng Mǎng was defeated,
and Gēngshǐ was established,
Wǔyīn Wáng Lǐ Yì was sent to persuade various commanderies and states to surrender.
Chún's father, Ài, surrendered,
and returned to be the Administrator of Jìnán.
At that time, Lǐ Yì's brothers were in power,
exercising exclusive control over their regions,
and there were many retainers and persuaders.
Chún repeatedly sought an audience but could not be admitted.
After a long time, he was finally granted an audience,
and then persuaded Yì, saying:
"Your Highness, with the bearing of a dragon and a tiger,
has encountered a time of wind and clouds.
You have risen swiftly,
and within a month, your brothers are called kings.
However, your virtue and trustworthiness are not heard among scholars and commoners,
and your achievements and contributions have not been applied to the populace.
Your favors and emoluments have suddenly appeared,
which is what the wise fear.
Even those who are constantly cautious and self-endangered
still fear not seeing their end,
let alone those who are naturally self-satisfied
and can achieve success?"
Yì was surprised by him,
and also because he was a prominent family in Jùlù,
he consequently, acting under imperial authority, appointed him Cavalry Commandant,
gave him a tally,
and ordered him to pacify Zhào and Wèi.
Just then, Shìzǔ crossed the river and reached Hándān.
Chún immediately sought an audience,
and Shìzǔ received him warmly.
Upon returning, Chún
saw that the officers and their military regulations were unlike those of other generals,
so he sought to form a bond,
offering horses and several hundred bolts of silk.
When Shìzǔ went north to Zhōngshān,
he left Chún in Hándān.
When Wáng Láng rebelled,
Shìzǔ rode southeast from Jì.
Chún, with his cousins Xīn, Sù, and Zhí, together led their clan and retainers,
over two thousand people,
with all the old and sick carried on wooden vehicles following them,
to welcome him at Yù.
Chún was appointed Front General,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Gěngxíang.
Xīn, Sù, and Zhí were all appointed Generals of the Household,
and sent to be in the vanguard with Chún.
They captured Sòngzǐ,
and then followed in attacking and taking Qǔyáng and Zhōngshān.
At this time, many commanderies and states had surrendered to Hándān.
Chún feared that his clan might harbor different intentions,
so he sent Xīn and Sù back to burn their dwellings.
Shìzǔ asked Chún why,
and he replied:
"I humbly observe that Your Excellency arrived in Héběi with a single carriage,
without stored wealth
or substantial rewards and sweet inducements
to gather people.
You merely embraced them with grace and virtue,
which is why the soldiers and populace gladly attached themselves.
Now Hándān has established itself,
and the northern provinces are in doubt.
Although my entire clan has pledged allegiance,
and the old and weak are on the march,
I still fear that half of my kinsmen and retainers may not be of the same mind.
Therefore, I burned our houses
to cut off any hope of turning back."
Shìzǔ sighed.
When they arrived at Xiāo,
Shìzǔ stayed in the relay station.
The prominent Xiāo family, Sū Gōng, rebelled by opening the city gates and admitting Wáng Láng's general Lǐ Yùn.
Chún perceived this beforehand,
led his troops to meet and fight Yùn,
and utterly defeated and killed him.
He followed in pacifying Hándān,
and then defeated the Bronze Horse bandits.
At that time, the Chìméi, Qīngdú, Shàngjiāng, Dàtóng, Tiějìng, and Wǔfān, totaling over one hundred thousand people, were all in Shèquǎn.
Shìzǔ led his troops to attack them.
Gěng Chún’s army was in front,
several *lǐ* away from the main camp.
Suddenly, the bandits attacked Gěng Chún at night,
shooting arrows into the camp like rain.
Many soldiers died or were wounded.
Gěng Chún commanded his troops,
holding fast and not moving.
He selected two thousand brave men ready to die,
each carrying a strong crossbow,
and each equipped with three arrows.
He had them silently advance, holding their gags,
and circle around to the bandits' rear.
With a unified shout and clamor,
their powerful crossbows all fired at once.
The bandits were startled and fled.
Gěng Chún pursued and attacked them,
thus defeating them.
He sent a swift horseman to report to Shìzǔ.
The next morning, Shìzǔ and his generals arrived at the camp,
and, comforting Gěng Chún, said:
“Were you troubled last night?”
Gěng Chún replied:
“By the awesome virtue of the Bright Lord,
we were fortunate to survive completely.”
Shìzǔ said:
“A large army should not be moved at night,
which is why I did not come to your aid.
Army camps are constantly moving forward and retreating;
your entire clan cannot all reside within the army.”
Thereupon, he appointed Gěng Jí, a member of Gěng Chún’s clan, as the Magistrate of Púwú,
and ordered him to bring all his relatives to live there.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he enfeoffed Gěng Chún as the Marquis of Gāoyáng.
He attacked Liú Yǒng in Jìyīn,
and then took Dìngtáo.
Initially,
Gěng Chún followed in the attack on Wáng Láng,
but fell from his horse and broke his shoulder.
When the ailment flared up,
he returned to Huái Palace.
The Emperor asked,
“Which of your brothers can be employed?”
Gěng Chún recommended his cousin Gěng Zhí.
Thus, Gěng Zhí was appointed to lead Gěng Chún’s camp,
while Gěng Chún still served as a former general.
At that time, Liú Yáng, the King of Zhēndìng, again created a *chènwěi* (prophetic text) saying:
“After Chì Jiǔ,
the goitrous Yáng will be the lord.”
Liú Yáng suffered from goiter,
and wished to use this to deceive the populace,
communicating with the bandits of Miánmàn.
In the spring of Jiànwǔ 2nd year (AD 26),
the Cavalry Commandant Chén Fù and the Guerrilla General Dèng Lóng were sent to summon Liú Yáng.
Liú Yáng closed the city gates,
not allowing Chén Fù and the others in.
Then, (the Emperor) again sent Gěng Chún, bearing a *jié* (credentials),
to proclaim an amnesty in Yōu and Jì provinces,
and wherever he passed, to comfort and console the kings and marquises.
He secretly instructed Gěng Chún, saying:
“If you see Liú Yáng,
then arrest him.”
Gěng Chún, with over a hundred of his officers and horsemen, met Chén Fù and Dèng Lóng in Yuánshì.
Together they went to Zhēndìng,
and stayed at the relay station.
Liú Yáng claimed illness and did not pay his respects.
Considering Gěng Chún to be from the imperial clan in Zhēndìng,
he sent an envoy with a letter to Gěng Chún,
desiring to meet him.
Gěng Chún replied:
“As an imperial envoy seeing kings, marquises, governors, and prefects,
I cannot visit first.
If you wish to meet in person,
you should come to the relay station.”
At that time, Liú Ràng, the Marquis of Línyì, Liú Yáng’s younger brother, and his cousin Xì
each commanded over ten thousand soldiers.
Liú Yáng, relying on his strong forces and seeing Gěng Chún’s tranquil demeanor,
immediately went with his officials to meet him,
with his brothers leading light troops outside the gate.
Liú Yáng entered to see Gěng Chún.
Gěng Chún received him with courtesy and respect,
then invited his brothers inside.
Once they all entered,
Gěng Chún closed the gate and executed them all,
then commanded his troops and emerged.
Zhēndìng was terrified,
and no one dared to make a move.
The Emperor pitied Liú Yáng and Liú Ràng, as their conspiracy had not yet materialized,
and enfeoffed their sons,
restoring their former states.
Gěng Chún returned to the capital,
and then personally requested, saying:
“Your servant is a descendant of a family of officials.
Fortunately, I encountered the restoration of the Great Hàn
and the reception of the mandate by the sagely Emperor.
I have held the position of a general,
and been granted the title of a marquis.
The empire is largely settled;
your servant has no further ambitions.
I wish to try governing a commandery,
and exert my full effort to prove myself.”
The Emperor smiled and said:
“You have already mastered the military,
do you now wish to cultivate literary arts as well?”
Thereupon, he appointed Gěng Chún as the Administrator of Dōngjùn.
At that time, Dōngjùn was not yet pacified.
Gěng Chún held office for several months,
and bandits and thieves became peaceful.
In the 4th year (AD 28),
an imperial edict ordered Gěng Chún to lead troops to attack Fàn Jīng, the Administrator of Dōngpíng under Gěngshǐ.
Fàn Jīng surrendered.
He then attacked the bandits in Tàishān, Jìnán, and Píngyuán,
and pacified them all.
He resided in Dōngjùn for four years.
At one point, the Magistrate of Fāgān committed a crime.
Gěng Chún investigated and impeached him,
surrounding and guarding him.
Before the impeachment was approved,
the magistrate committed suicide.
Gěng Chún was dismissed for this,
and served at court as a marquis.
He then followed in the attack on Dǒng Xiàn.
As the retinue passed through Dōngjùn,
thousands of common people, old and young, followed the imperial carriage, weeping.
They said,
“We wish to have Lord Gěng back again.”
The Emperor said to the dukes and ministers:
“Gěng Chún was young and only wore armor as a military officer!
Could his governance of a commandery cause him to be remembered like this?”
In the 6th year (AD 30),
he was officially enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngguāng.
Gěng Chún declined and requested to go to his state.
The Emperor said:
“Emperor Wén told Zhōu Bó, ‘The Chancellor is someone I respect.
You shall lead the marquises on my behalf to their states.’
It is the same now.”
Gěng Chún accepted the edict and departed.
Upon reaching Yè,
he was granted ten thousand *hú* of grain.
When he arrived at his state,
he consoled the bereaved and inquired about the sick.
The people loved and respected him.
In the 8th year (AD 32),
bandits rose in groups in Dōngjùn and Jìyīn.
The Grand Minister of Works Lǐ Tōng and the General Who Sweeps the Wilds Wáng Cháng were sent to attack them.
The Emperor, considering Gěng Chún’s prestige and trustworthiness to be well-established in the Wèi region,
sent an envoy to appoint him Grand Master of the Palace,
and had him join the main army in Dōngjùn.
When Dōngjùn heard that Gěng Chún had entered the border,
over nine thousand bandits all came to Gěng Chún to surrender.
The main army returned without fighting.
An imperial edict again appointed him Administrator of Dōngjùn.
Officials and common people alike were pleased and submitted.
In the 13th year (AD 37),
he died in office.
His posthumous title was Chéng Hóu.
His son, Gěng Fǔ, succeeded him.
Gěng Zhí later became General Who Assists in Awe,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Wǔyì.
Gěng Sù reached the position of Administrator of Dàijùn,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Suíxiāng.
Gěng Xīn was the General of Chìméi,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhùwǔ.
He followed Dèng Yǔ on the western expedition,
and died in battle at Yúnyáng.
In total, four members of his clan were enfeoffed as marquises,
three as marquises within the passes,
and nine as officials of two thousand *dàn* salary.
Gěng Fǔ was later transferred and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jǔxiāng.
In Yǒngpíng 14th year (AD 71),
because his clan member Gěng Shè was implicated in statements made by Yán Zhōng from Chǔ,
his state was abolished.
In Jiànchū 2nd year (AD 77),
Sùzōng remembered Gěng Chún’s achievements,
and re-enfeoffed Gěng Fǔ’s son, Gěng Xū, as the Marquis of Gāotíng.
When Gěng Xū died
without an heir,
the Emperor again enfeoffed Gěng Xū’s younger brother, Gěng Téng.
When he died,
his son, Gěng Zhōng, succeeded him.
When Gěng Zhōng died,
his grandson, Gěng Xù, succeeded him.
The encomium says: Rèn and Pī understood the opportune moment,
and opened their city gates.
The army returned in an orderly fashion;
the two administrators relied on them.
Gěng Chún and Gěng Zhí bravely took action,
leading soldiers to aid in inspiring awe.
Biographies of Zhū, Jǐng, Wáng, Dù, Mǎ, Liú, Fù, Jiān, Mǎ, 12th Chapter.
Zhū Yòu,
courtesy name Zhòngxiān, was a native of Wǎn in Nányáng.
Orphaned young,
he returned to his maternal relatives, the Liú clan of Fùyáng.
He frequently traveled to Chōnglíng,
where Shìzǔ and Bóshēng both held him in high regard.
When Bóshēng was appointed Dàsītú,
he made Yòu his Hùjūn.
When Shìzǔ became Dàsīmǎ
and attacked Héběi,
he again made Yòu Hùjūn.
Yòu was always favored and trusted,
and lodged within the camp.
While attending a banquet, Yòu
casually remarked:
“Cháng’ān is in political chaos.
You have the appearance of a 'sun-cornered' face,
this is Heaven's mandate.”
Shìzǔ said:
“Summon the officer to arrest the Hùjūn!”
Yòu then dared not speak again.
Following the campaign in Héběi,
he often fought bravely and broke through enemy lines.
He was made Piānjiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Ānyáng Hóu.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Jiànyì Dàjiāngjūn.
In Jiànwǔ second year
(26 CE), he was re-enfeoffed as Dǔyáng Hóu.
In winter,
he attacked Dèng Fèng with other generals at Yùyáng.
Yòu’s army was defeated
and he was captured by Fèng.
The next year,
when Fèng was defeated,
he bared his torso and surrendered through Yòu.
The Emperor reinstated Yòu to his position and generously comforted and rewarded him.
He was sent to attack Xīnyě and Suí,
and pacified them all.
After Yán Cén’s defeat at Ráng,
he allied with Qín Fēng’s general Zhāng Chéng.
Yòu led Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn Jì Zūn and fought them at Dōngyáng,
dealing them a great defeat.
Zhāng Chéng was beheaded on the battlefield.
Yán Cén was defeated and fled back to Fēng.
Yòu recovered ninety-seven seals and ribbons.
He advanced and attacked Huángyóu,
forcing its surrender,
and was rewarded with thirty jīn of gold.
In the fourth year
(28 CE), he led Pòjiān Jiāngjūn Hóu Jìn and Fǔwēi Jiāngjūn Gěng Zhí to replace Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn Cén Péng in besieging Qín Fēng at Líqiū.
They defeated Qín Fēng’s general Zhāng Kāng at Càiyáng
and beheaded him.
The Emperor personally came to Líqiū
and sent Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Lǐ Yóu with an imperial edict to persuade Fēng to surrender.
Fēng responded with insults
and refused to surrender.
The imperial carriage returned,
and Yòu was instructed on strategy.
Yòu exerted his full effort in attacking.
The next summer,
the city was in dire straits,
and Fēng brought his mother, wife, and nine children to surrender bare-chested.
Yòu sent Fēng in a caged cart to Luòyáng,
where he was executed.
Dàsīmǎ Wú Hàn impeached Yòu for violating the imperial edict by accepting the surrender
and neglecting his duty as a commander.
The Emperor did not punish him.
Upon Yòu’s return,
he joined Qí Dūwèi Zāng Gōng in attacking Yán Cén’s remaining partisans, the bandits of the three counties of Yīn, Cuó, and Zhúyáng,
and pacified them all.
Yòu was honest and straightforward,
and esteemed Confucian learning.
Leading troops and masses,
he accepted many surrenders,
taking the pacification of cities and towns as his priority,
not seeking credit for taking heads.
He also forbade his officers and soldiers from plundering the common people,
but his troops enjoyed unrestrained behavior,
and many resented him for this.
In the ninth year
(33 CE), he was stationed at Nánxíngtáng to resist the Xiōngnú.
In the thirteenth year
(37 CE), his fief was increased,
and he was officially enfeoffed as Gélì Hóu,
with a stipend of seven thousand three hundred households.
In the fifteenth year
(39 CE), he went to the capital,
submitted his Dàjiāngjūn seal and ribbons,
and remained there to attend court functions.
Yòu memorialized that in ancient times, ministers who received enfeoffment
were not given princely ranks,
and suggested that all kings be changed to gōng.
The Emperor immediately implemented this.
He also memorialized that the Sāngōng should
all remove the character
“Dà”
from their titles, in accordance with the classics.
Later, his suggestion was followed.
When Yòu first studied in Cháng’ān,
the Emperor visited him.
Yòu did not greet him immediately
but first ascended the lecture hall.
Later, when the imperial carriage visited his residence,
the Emperor laughed and said:
“Surely the host will not leave me to lecture, will he?”
Because of their long-standing friendship,
he frequently received rewards and gifts.
In the twenty-fourth year
(48 CE), he died.
His son, Shāng, succeeded him.
When Shāng died,
his son, Yǎn, succeeded him.
In Yǒngyuán fourteenth year
(102 CE), he was implicated in his cousin Bó’s involvement in witchcraft against the Empress Yīn, his maternal granddaughter,
and was demoted to commoner.
In Yǒngchū seventh year
(113 CE), Empress Dowager Dèng re-enfeoffed Yǎn’s son Chōng as Gélì Hóu.
Jǐng Dān,
courtesy name Sūnqīng, was a native of Lìyáng in Fēngyì.
He studied in Cháng’ān when young.
During Wáng Mǎng’s reign, he was nominated for the Four Qualities.
Dān was appointed Gùdé Hóuxiàng for his eloquence,
and was praised for his administrative abilities.
He was promoted to Shuòdiào Liánsài Fù’èr.
When Gēngshǐ was established,
he sent envoys to patrol Shànggǔ.
Dān and Liánsài Gěng Kuàng surrendered
and he was reinstated as Shànggǔ Zhǎngshǐ.
When Wáng Láng rose,
Dān and Kuàng conspired to resist him.
Kuàng sent Dān with his son Yǎn and Kòu Xún, among others, to lead troops south to Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ met Dān and the others
and laughed, saying:
“The generals and commanders in Hándān often say that I raised troops from Yúyáng and Shànggǔ.
I just casually agreed,
but who would have thought that these two commanderies truly came for me!
I shall share this glory with all you gentlemen.”
Dān was appointed Piānjiāngjūn
and given the title Fèngyì Hóu.
He followed in attacking Wáng Láng’s generals Ér Hóng and others at Nán.
Láng’s troops engaged,
and the Hàn army retreated.
Dān and others launched a charge with their elite cavalry,
greatly defeating them.
They pursued the fleeing enemy for over ten lǐ,
leaving dead and wounded everywhere.
Upon Dān’s return,
Shìzǔ said to him:
“I have heard that elite cavalry are the finest troops in the world.
Now I have seen them fight.
Can words express this joy?”
He then followed the campaign in Héběi.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
based on an oracle, he appointed Píngdí Jiāngjūn Sūn Xián as acting Dàsīmǎ.
The assembly was displeased with Xián.
An edict was issued to nominate suitable candidates for Dàsīmǎ.
Among the officials, only Wú Hàn and Dān were recommended.
The Emperor said:
“General Jǐng is a great general from the northern region,
he is indeed the right person.
However, General Wú has the merit of formulating great strategies,
and also executed Miáo Yōuzhōu and Xiè Shàngshū.
His achievements are greater.
The old system allowed the office of Piàojì Jiāngjūn to be concurrent with Dàsīmǎ.”
Thus, Wú Hàn was made Dàsīmǎ,
while Dān was appointed Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn.
In Jiànwǔ second year
(26 CE), Dān was officially enfeoffed as Lìyáng Hóu.
The Emperor said to Dān:
“Now, the former kingdoms east of the pass,
though composed of several counties,
none exceed Lìyáng, an estate of ten thousand households.
As the saying goes, ‘Wealth and honor not returned to one’s hometown
are like wearing embroidered clothes at night.’
Therefore, I have enfeoffed you with this.”
Dān bowed his head in thanks.
In autumn,

he joined Wú Hàn, Jiànwēi Dàjiāngjūn Gěng Yǎn, Jiànyì Dàjiāngjūn Zhū Yòu, Zhíjīnwú Jiǎ Fù, Piānjiāngjūn Fēng Yì, Qiángnǔ Jiāngjūn Chén Jùn, Zuǒ Cáo Wáng Cháng, Qí Dūwèi Zāng Gōng, and others in defeating the Wǔxiào bandits at Yìyáng,
capturing their force of fifty thousand men.
Around this time, the Shǎn bandit Sū Kuàng attacked and captured Hóngnóng,
taking the郡守 (Jùnshǒu) alive.
Dān was ill at the time,
but the Emperor, considering him an old general,
wanted him to forcefully take up the county’s affairs.
So he summoned him late at night
and said:
“The bandits are pressing close to the capital.
Just having your revered presence,
even if lying down, will be enough to pacify them.”
Dān dared not refuse,
and, despite his illness, accepted the appointment.
Upon leading his camp to the county,
he died after more than ten days.
Zǐ Shàng 嗣 [sì],
he was transferred and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yúwú.
When Shàng died,
his son Bāo 嗣 [sì].
When Bāo died,
his son Lín 嗣 [sì].
He had no son,
and the state was extinguished.
In the seventh year of Yǒngchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng enfeoffed Bāo's younger brother Jù as the Marquis of Jiāntíng.
Wáng Liáng, whose courtesy name was Jūnyán,
was a native of Yúyáng (or Ānyáng).
He served as a commandery official.
The Grand Administrator Péng Chǒng appointed Liáng as the Prefect of Húlú,
and together with Gài Yán and Wú Hàn, he led troops south and met Shìzǔ at Guǎng'ā.
He was appointed Pīanjiāngjūn.
After Handān was taken,
he was granted the noble title of Guānnèihóu.
He followed in pacifying Héběi,
and was appointed Prefect of Yěwáng.
Together with Kòu Xún, the Grand Administrator of Hénèi, he resisted Luòyáng in the south
and guarded Tiānjǐng Pass in the north.
Zhū Wěi and others dared not send out troops,
and Shìzǔ attributed this success to Liáng.
When he ascended the throne,
there was a discussion about selecting a Dàsīkōng.
The Chìfú Fú said,
"Wáng Liáng is to preside over the guard and act as Xuánwǔ."
The Emperor considered that Yěwáng was the place where the guard was transferred,
Xuánwǔ was the name of the water god,
and the Dàsīkōng was the official in charge of water and earth.
Therefore, he promoted and appointed Liáng as Dàsīkōng,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Wǔqiáng.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he joined Dàsīmǎ Wú Hàn and others in attacking Bùxiāng.
An imperial edict ordered that all military matters be subject to the Dàsīmǎ,
but Liáng still dispatched troops from Yěwáng.
The Emperor, considering that he did not obey the imperial edict,
ordered him to stop in his current county.
However, Liáng again advanced his troops as he saw fit.
The Emperor was greatly angered
by Liáng's repeated defiance of orders,
and dispatched Shàngshū Zōng Guǎng, holding the imperial credential, to the army to execute Liáng.
Guǎng could not bear to do so,
and instead sent him to the capital in a caged cart.
Upon his arrival,
he was pardoned.
More than a month later,
he was appointed Zhōnglángjiàng,
and acted as Zhíjīnwú.
He guarded Jī Pass in the north,
attacked a detachment of Chìméi,
and made them surrender.
In the spring of the third year,
he moved to attack the Wǔxiào,
pursued them to Xìndū and Zhàoguó,
defeated them,
and pacified all their garrisons and gatherings.
In winter,
an envoy was dispatched with the imperial credential to appoint Liáng as Qiánjiāngjūn.
In the spring of the fourth year,
he attacked Féichéng and Wényáng,
and captured them.
He advanced and, with Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn Dù Mào, attacked Jiǎo Qiáng and Sū Mào between Chǔ and Pèi,
capturing Dàliáng and Nièsāng.
Mǎ Wǔ, the Bǔlú Jiāngjūn, and Wáng Bà, the Pīanjiāngjūn, also advanced along separate routes.
In over a year, they completely pacified the area.
In the fifth year,
he followed in relieving Táochéng,
defeated Páng Méng and others.
Liáng fought with exceptional bravery,
and was appointed Grand Administrator of Shānyáng,
to pacify the newly surrendered,
while still leading troops as before.
Several months later, he was summoned to the capital
to replace Ōuyáng Xī as Hénányǐn.
Liáng dug a canal to divert the Gǔ River to flow beneath the city of Luòyáng,
and to the east to drain the Gǒng River.
However, when the canal was completed, the water did not flow.
In the seventh year,
officials impeached and reported him.
Liáng was ashamed and afraid,
and submitted a memorial requesting to retire.
An imperial edict was then issued, stating:
"Liáng previously led troops in campaigns,
and many praised him as worthy,
hence he was promoted to govern the capital.
He proposed to dig a canal,
to benefit the people,
but his efforts were flawed,
and he achieved no success.
The common people complained and criticized,
and talkers were noisy.
Although granted leniency,
he still maintained humility and sought to retire.
'A gentleman helps others achieve their good intentions,'
therefore, let Liáng be the Grand Administrator of Jìnán."
In the thirteenth year,
his fief was increased,
and he was officially enfeoffed as Marquis of Fùchéng.
In the fourteenth year,
he died in office.
His son Yǔ 嗣 [sì].
When Yǔ died,
his son Jiānshí 嗣 [sì].
Jiānshí was implicated in his father Yǔ's and younger brother Píng's conspiracy to rebel with Prince Yīng of Chǔ,
and was executed in the marketplace.
His state was abolished.
Dù Mào, whose courtesy name was Zhūgōng,
was a native of Guànjūn, Nányáng.
Initially, he joined Guāngwǔ in Héběi,
and served as Zhōngjiān Jiāngjūn,
often following in campaigns.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Dàjiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Lèxiāng.
He attacked the Wǔxiào in Zhēndìng in the north,
and advanced to receive the surrender of Guǎngpíng.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Kǔxíng.
Together with Zhōnglángjiàng Wáng Liáng, he attacked the Wǔxiào bandits in Wèijùn, Qīnghé, and Dōngjùn,
completely pacifying all their camps and strongholds,
and accepting the surrender of over thirty of their generals holding imperial credentials.
The three commanderies became peaceful,
and roads were open.
The next year,
an envoy was dispatched with the imperial credential to appoint Mào as Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn,
and he attacked Pèijùn,
capturing Máng.
At that time, Xīfáng rebelled again,
and welcomed Jiǎo Qiáng.
In the spring of the fifth year,
Mào led Bǔlú Jiāngjūn Mǎ Wǔ in an attack on Xīfáng,
and captured it after several months.
Qiáng fled to Dǒng Xiàn.
After the east was pacified,
in the seventh year,
an edict ordered Mào to lead his troops north to garrison and farm in Jìnyáng and Guǎngwǔ,
to guard against Hú invaders.
In the ninth year,
together with Guō Liáng, the Grand Administrator of Yànmén, he attacked Yǐn Yóu, a general of Lú Fāng, at Fánzhì.
Fāng's general Jiǎ Lǎn led over ten thousand Hú cavalry to relieve him.
Mào fought,
but his army was defeated,
and he retreated into Lóufán City.
At that time, Lú Fāng occupied Gāoliǔ,
and allied with the Xiōngnú,
frequently raiding border inhabitants.
The Emperor was troubled by this.
In the twelfth year,
he dispatched Yèzhě Duàn Zhōng to lead the auxiliary forces from various commanderies to assist Mào,
to guard the northern border.
He then mobilized border troops to build watchtowers [tínghòu]
and repair beacon fires.
He also dispatched transported gold, silk, and floss to supply the soldiers,
and also bestowed them upon the border inhabitants.
Officials' carriages and hats were seen continuously.
Mào also established military agricultural colonies,
with donkey carts transporting supplies.
Previously,
Jiǎ Dān, Huò Kuāng, Jiě Shèng, and others from Yànmén were captured by Yǐn Yóu.
Yóu made them generals
and together they guarded Píngchéng.
When Dān and others heard of Fāng's defeat,
they conspired to kill Yóu and went to Guō Liáng.
Liáng reported the situation,
and they were all enfeoffed as lièhóu.
An edict ordered the transported gold and silk to be given to Mào's and Liáng's military officials and the surrendered people of Píngchéng.
From then on, Lú Fāng's cities and towns gradually surrendered.
Liáng executed the powerful and prominent clans such as the Xún family,
and pacified the weak and common people.
Within a few weeks, Yànmén was almost pacified,
and Fāng then fled into the Xiōngnú territory.
The Emperor promoted Liáng's son to Zhōngláng,
to serve as an imperial bodyguard.
Liáng, whose courtesy name was Gōngwén,
was a native of Yòuběipíng.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
with robust strength.
Although a military general,
he was well-versed in classics,
and possessed much wisdom and strategy,
especially knowledgeable about border affairs,
and was famous in the north.
Initially,
Zhū Fú, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu, appointed him as Bīngcáocuàn.
He had achievements in attacking Péng Chǒng,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guǎngwǔ.
In the thirteenth year,
Mào's fief was increased,
and he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiū.
In the fifteenth year,
he was impeached for cutting off military provisions of silk
and causing military officials to commit murder.
He was dismissed from office,
his household and fief were reduced,
and he was officially enfeoffed as Marquis of Cānqúxiāng.
In the nineteenth year,
he died.
Zǐyuán 嗣,
In the fourteenth year of Yǒngpíng,
he was implicated in a conspiracy to rebel with Dōngpíng Wáng and others,
his punishment was reduced by one degree from death,
and his state was abolished.
In the seventh year of Yǒngchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng re-enfeoffed Máo's grandson Fèng as Ānlè Tínghóu.
Mǎ Chéng, courtesy name Jūnqiān,
was a native of Jíyáng, Nányáng.
In his youth, he served as a county official.
When Shìzǔ campaigned in Yǐngchuān,
he appointed Chéng as Ānjí Yuàn,
and later transferred him to serve as Prefect of Jiá.
When Shìzǔ campaigned in Hébĕi,
Chéng immediately [⿱𠫓廾]官步負
and caught up with him at Púyáng.
Shìzǔ appointed Chéng as a Qímén,
and he followed him in his campaigns.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
Chéng was twice promoted to Hùjūn Dūwèi.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
he was appointed Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn,
and supervised Zhūlǔ Jiāngjūn Liú Lóng, Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn Sòng Dēng, and Shèshēng Xiàowèi Wáng Shǎng.
He raised troops from the four commanderies of Kuàijī, Dānyáng, Jiǔjiāng, and Lù'ān to attack Lǐ Xiàn.
At that time, the Emperor visited Shòuchūn,
set up an altar,
and sent them off with ancestral rites.
They advanced and besieged Xiàn at Shū,
ordering all generals to dig deep trenches and build high ramparts.
Xiàn challenged them several times,
but Chéng firmly held his defenses and did not sortie.
He held the siege for over a year.
By the spring of the sixth year,
food in the city was exhausted,
so they attacked it.
They subsequently sacked Shū,
beheaded Lǐ Xiàn,
pursued and attacked his confederates,
and completely pacified the Jiāng-Huái region.
In the summer of the seventh year,
he was enfeoffed as Píngshū Hóu.
In the eighth year,
he accompanied the Emperor in defeating Kuí Xiāo,
and Chéng was appointed Tàiwèi of Tiānshuǐ,
retaining his generalship as before.
In winter,
he was recalled to the capital.
In the ninth year,
he replaced Lái Xī as Shǒu Zhōngláng Jiāng,
and led Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn Liú Shàng and others to defeat Héchí,
thus pacifying Wǔdū.
The following year,
Dàsīkōng Lǐ Tōng was dismissed,
and Chéng was appointed acting Dàsīkōng,
residing in the office as if he were the true incumbent.
Several months later, he was again appointed Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn.
In the fourteenth year,
he was stationed at Chángshān and Zhōngshān to guard the northern frontier,
and also commanded the camp of Jiànyì Dàjiāngjūn Zhū Yòu.
He also replaced Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn Dù Mào in repairing the defensive barriers,
from Xīhé to Wèiqiáo,
from Héshàng to Ānyì,
from Tàiyuán to Jǐngxíng,
and from Zhōngshān to Yè.
He built fortifications everywhere,
and erected beacon towers,
one every ten *lǐ*.
After five or six years in this post,
the Emperor, recognizing Chéng's diligence,
recalled him to the capital.
Many border residents submitted petitions requesting his return,
so Chéng was again sent back to his station.
When the Southern Chányú secured the frontier,
and the north was peaceful,
he was appointed Zhōngshān Tàishǒu,
returned his general's seals and cords,
and continued to command the stationed troops as before.
In the twenty-fourth year,
he led an expedition south to attack the Mán rebels of Wǔxī,
but achieved no success,
and returned his Tàiwèi's seals and cords.
In the twenty-seventh year,
he was formally enfeoffed as Quánjiāo Hóu,
and went to his fief.
He died in the thirty-second year.
His son Wèi succeeded.
When Wèi died,
his son Xiāng succeeded,
and was transferred to be enfeoffed as Jílíng Hóu.
When Xiāng died,
his son Fēng succeeded.
When Fēng died,
his son Xuán succeeded.
When Xuán died,
his son Yì succeeded.
When Yì died,
his son Chǒu succeeded,
but lost his state due to a crime during the reign of Huán Dì.
In the second year of Yánxī,
the Emperor re-enfeoffed Chéng's great-great-grandson Chāng as Yìyáng Tínghóu.
Liú Lóng, courtesy name Yuánbó,
was a member of the imperial clan of Ānzhòng Hóu from Nányáng.
During Wáng Mǎng's regency,
Lóng's father Lǐ and Ānzhòng Hóu Chóng raised an army to execute Wáng Mǎng.
The plot was discovered,
but Lóng, being less than seven years old,
was spared.
When he grew up,
he studied in Cháng'ān.
Gēngshǐ appointed him Qí Dūwèi.
He returned home for a visit,
and brought his wife and children to Luòyáng.
Hearing that Shìzǔ was in Hénèi,
he immediately caught up with him at Shèquǎn,
and was appointed Qí Dūwèi.
He and Féng Yì jointly resisted Zhū Wěi, Lǐ Yì, and others.
Yì then killed Lóng's wife and children.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he was enfeoffed as Kàngfù Hóu.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Zhūlǔ Jiāngjūn,
and suppressed Lǐ Xiàn.
After Xiàn was pacified,
Lóng was sent to establish military colonies at Wǔdāng.
In the eleventh year,
he served as Nánjùn Tàishǒu.
After more than a year,
he returned his general's seals and cords.
In the thirteenth year,
his fief was increased,
and he was re-enfeoffed as Jìnglíng Hóu.
At this time,
much of the cultivated land in the empire was not accurately reported,
and the household registers and ages varied.
In the fifteenth year,
an edict was issued to the prefectures and commanderies to investigate the matter,
but many of the Inspectors and Grand Administrators were unfair,
some favoring the powerful and wealthy,
and exploiting the weak,
causing the common people to grumble and complain,
blocking roads and crying out.
At that time, each commandery sent envoys to report on affairs.
The Emperor saw a document from an official of Chénliú with writing on it.
He looked at it
and it said:
"Yǐngchuān and Hóngnóng can be questioned,
but Hénán and Nányáng cannot be questioned."
The Emperor questioned the official about the reason,
but the official refused to admit it,
insisting he found it on Chángshòu Street.
The Emperor was enraged.
At that time, Xiǎnzōng, then Dōnghǎi Gōng,
was twelve years old,
and spoke from behind the curtain:
"The official received orders from his commandery,
and probably wanted to compare the cultivated land."
The Emperor said:
"If that is the case,
why did he say Hénán and Nányáng cannot be questioned?"
He replied:
"Hénán is the imperial capital,
with many close ministers.
Nányáng is the Emperor's hometown,
with many close relatives.
Their fields and residences exceed regulations,
and cannot be used as a standard."
The Emperor ordered the Hǔbēn Jiāng to question the official.
The official then truly confessed,
just as Xiǎnzōng had said.
Thereupon, he sent an inspector to verify,
and fully understood the deceit.
The following year,
Lóng was arrested and imprisoned,
and more than ten of his associates all died.
The Emperor, considering Lóng a meritorious minister,
specifically spared him and reduced him to a commoner.
The following year,
he was re-enfeoffed as Fúyào Xiānghóu,
and as Zhōngláng Jiāng, he assisted Fúbō Jiāngjūn Mǎ Yuán in attacking the Mán barbarians Zhēng Cè and others in Jiāozhǐ.
Lóng separately defeated them at Jìnxīkǒu,
captured their leader Zhēng Èr,
beheaded over a thousand,
and accepted the surrender of over twenty thousand people.
Upon his return,
he was re-enfeoffed with a larger state,
as Chángpíng Hóu.
When Dàsīmǎ Wú Hàn died,
Lóng was appointed Piàojì Jiāngjūn,
and acted as Dàsīmǎ.
Lóng Fèng guarded himself by the law.
He served for eight years,
then returned his general's seal and ribbon,
and retired.
He was granted oxen to raise,
ten *hú* of fine wine,
and served at court as a marquis by noble rank.
Thirty years later,
he was formally enfeoffed as Shèn Hóu.
In the second year of Zhōngyuán,
he died,
and was posthumously named Jìng Hóu.
His son Ān succeeded him.
Fù Jùn, courtesy name Zǐwèi,
was a native of Xiāngchéng in Yǐngchuān.
When Shìzǔ campaigned through Xiāngchéng,
Jùn, as the county *tíngzhǎng*, welcomed the army.
He was appointed as a Colonel.
Xiāngchéng seized his mother, younger brother, and clan,
and exterminated them all.
He participated in defeating Wáng Xún and others,
and was made a Partial General.
He separately attacked Jīng and Mì,
and defeated them.
He was sent back to Yǐngchuān
to collect and bury his family.
When Shìzǔ campaigned against Héběi,
Jùn, with more than ten retainers, pursued him north,
reaching him in Hándān.
He presented himself,
and Shìzǔ ordered him to lead the Yǐngchuān troops,
constantly accompanying him on campaigns.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Jùn as a Court Attendant.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he was enfeoffed as Kūnyáng Hóu.
In the third year,
Jùn was appointed General of Massed Crossbows,
and with the General-in-Chief Who Conquers the South, Cén Péng, he defeated Qín Fēng.
He then led troops to campaign in Jiāngdōng,
and Yángzhōu was completely pacified.
In the seventh year,
he died,
and was posthumously named Wēi Hóu.
His son Chāng succeeded him,
and was transferred to be enfeoffed as Wúhú Hóu.
During the Jiànchū period,
he suffered the loss of his mother,
and thereupon submitted a memorial,
stating that his state was poor and he did not desire the enfeoffment.
He begged for fifty thousand *qián*
and to be a Guānnèi Hóu.
Sùzōng was angry,
demoted him to Guānnèi Hóu,
and ultimately did not grant him the money.
In the seventh year of Yǒngchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng re-enfeoffed Chāng's son Tiě as Gāozhì Tínghóu.
Jiān Tán, courtesy name Zǐjí,
was a native of Xiāngchéng in Yǐngchuān.
He served as a county and commandery official.
When Shìzǔ campaigned against Héběi,
someone recommended Tán,
and he was summoned for an audience.
Because of his administrative ability,
he was appointed Chief Clerk.
He was also appointed Partial General,
and followed in pacifying Héběi.
He separately attacked and defeated Dàqiāng at Lúnú.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Tán General Who Spreads Civilization,
and enfeoffed him as Qiáng Hóu.
He attacked Luòyáng with the other generals,
and Zhū Wěi's separate general guarding the eastern city became a double agent,
privately agreeing with Tán to open the Upper East Gate at dawn.
Tán and the General-in-Chief Who Establishes Righteousness, Zhū Yòu, entered with the morning court,
and fiercely fought Wěi beneath the arsenal,
killing and wounding many.
They did not cease until breakfast,
and Zhū Wěi thereupon surrendered.
He also separately attacked Nèihuáng,
and pacified it.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
with the Right General Wàn Xiū, he campaigned through the counties of Nányáng.
Then, Dǒng Xīn from Dǔxiāng rebelled at Wǎncchéng,
and captured the Administrator of Nányáng, Líu Lín.
Tán then led his army to Wǎn,
selected daring commandos, and ascended the city wall himself at night.
They cut open the gate and entered,
and Xīn then abandoned the city and fled back to Dǔxiāng.
Dèng Fèng rebelled again at Xīnyě,
and attacked and defeated Wú Hàn.
At this time, Wàn Xiū had died of illness,
and Tán was isolated and cut off.
He resisted Dèng Fèng in the south,
and faced Dǒng Xīn in the north.
For a year, the roads were blocked,
and supplies did not arrive.
Tán ate vegetables,
and shared hardships with his soldiers.
In every emergency,
he would be the first to face arrows and stones,
sustaining three wounds to his body.
Because of this, he was able to preserve his troops.
When the Emperor campaigned in Nányáng,
and defeated Xīn and Fèng,
he appointed Tán as Left Chief Clerk,
constantly accompanying him on campaigns.
In the sixth year,
he was formally enfeoffed as Héféi Hóu.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he died.
His son Hóng succeeded him.
When Hóng died,
his son Fú succeeded him.
When Fú died,
his son Yǎ succeeded him.
Mǎ Wǔ, courtesy name Zǐzhāng,
was a native of Húyáng in Nányáng.
In his youth, he avoided enemies
and lived as a sojourner in Jiāngxià.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
the three elders of Jìnglíng and Xīyáng raised an army in the commandery's border region.
Wǔ went and joined them,
later entering the Lùlín army,
and then joined forces with the Hàn army.
When Gēngshǐ was enthroned,
he appointed Wǔ as a Gentleman.
He joined Shìzǔ in defeating Wáng Xún and others,
and was appointed General Who Shakes Awe.
He and the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Xiè Gōng, jointly attacked Wáng Láng.
When Shìzǔ captured Hándān,
he invited Gōng and Wǔ to a grand feast,
intending to plot against Gōng,
but did not succeed.
After the feast,
he alone ascended Cóngtái with Wǔ,
and leisurely said to Wǔ:
"I have the elite cavalry from Yúyáng and Shànggǔ.
I want to let you lead them.
What do you think?"
Wǔ replied:
"I am inept and lack strategy."
Shìzǔ said:
"General, you have led for a long time and
are skilled in military matters.
How can you be compared to my clerks and scribes!"
Wǔ thereupon gave him his loyalty.
When Xiè Gōng was executed,
Wǔ rode swiftly to Shèquǎn and surrendered.
Shìzǔ was very pleased to see him,
and placed him by his side.
Whenever he feasted his generals,
Wǔ would always rise and pour drinks before him,
and Shìzǔ found this amusing.
He again ordered Wǔ to lead his troops to Yè,
but Wǔ bowed his head and declined, saying he did not wish to.
Shìzǔ admired his sincerity even more,
and thereupon he followed him in attacking various bandits.
When Shìzǔ attacked Yóulái, Wǔfān, and others,
and was defeated at Shènshuǐ,
Wǔ alone brought up the rear,
and returned to break through the formation,
thus preventing the bandits from pressing close.
Advancing to Āncì and Xiǎoguǎngyáng,
Wǔ always served as the vanguard,
fighting valiantly without peer.
The other generals all followed his lead,
and thus they defeated the bandits,
pursuing them thoroughly to Pínggǔ and Jùnmí before returning.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Wǔ as a Court Attendant and Colonel-Protector of Cavalry,
and enfeoffed him as Shāndū Hóu.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
he, with the General of Tiger's Teeth Gài Yán and others, attacked Líu Yǒng.
Wǔ separately attacked Jìyīn,
subduing Chéngwǔ and Chǔqiū,
and was appointed General Who Captures Barbarians.
The following year,
Páng Méng rebelled,
and attacked Táochéng.
Wǔ engaged him first,
and defeated him;
at that time, the imperial carriage arrived,
and Méng then fled in defeat.
In the summer of the sixth year,
he, with the General-in-Chief Who Establishes Awe Gěng Yǎn, attacked Wěi Xiāo to the west.
The Hàn army was at a disadvantage
and retreated down the Lǒng.
Xiāo pursued fiercely,
so Wǔ selected elite cavalry to form the rear guard.
He donned armor and wielded a *jǐ*, rushing to attack,
killing several thousand people.
Xiāo's troops then retreated,
and the various armies were able to return to Cháng'ān.
In the thirteenth year,
his邑 was increased,
and he was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Shū.
He led troops north to garrison Xiàqǔyáng
to defend against the Xiōngnú.
Having been found guilty of killing a military official,
he received an imperial edict to take his wife and children to his fief.
Mǎ Wǔ went to Luòyáng
and offered his general's seal and sash,
whereupon five hundred of his households were cut,
and he was permanently enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yángxū,
and remained in the capital to attend court.
Later, the Emperor held a banquet with his meritorious officials and feudal lords,
and leisurely remarked:
"If you gentlemen had not met with this opportune time,
how far do you estimate your titles and emoluments would have reached?"
Dèng Yǔ, the Marquis of Gāomì, was the first to reply:
"As a youth, I studied,
so I could have been a Commandery Academician-Doctor."
The Emperor said:
"Why are your words so humble?
You are a son of the Dèng clan,
with a disciplined character and upright conduct.
Why would you not be a Senior Clerk?"
The others replied in turn,
and when it came to Mǎ Wǔ,
he said:
"With my martial prowess,
I could be a warden-officer supervising bandits."
The Emperor laughed and said:
"Let's not make you a bandit,
just reaching the rank of a village head
would be sufficient."
Mǎ Wǔ was a heavy drinker,
open-minded and outspoken.
When drunk, he would openly criticize his colleagues in front of the Emperor,
discussing their merits and faults
without any reservations.
The Emperor deliberately indulged him,
taking pleasure in his antics.
Although the Emperor controlled his meritorious officials,
he was always able to show leniency
and pardon their minor mistakes.
When rare delicacies were contributed from distant regions,
he would first distribute them all to the marquises,
leaving nothing for the imperial kitchen.
When they achieved merit,
he would promptly increase their邑 and bestow rewards,
but he did not appoint them to administrative posts.
Thus, they all preserved their fortunes and emoluments,
and none were ever executed or condemned.
In his twenty-fifth year,
Mǎ Wǔ, as a Colonel, led troops to attack the Mán and Yí of Wǔlíng.
Upon his return,
he surrendered his seal and sash.
At the beginning of Xiǎnzōng's reign,
the Western Qiāng raided Lǒngyòu,
destroying armies and killing generals.
The court was troubled by this,
so Mǎ Wǔ was again appointed General Who Captures Barbarians,
with Colonel Wáng Fēng as his deputy,
and together with Imperial Inspector Dòu Gù and Right Auxiliary Commandant Chén Xīn,
he led Wūhuán, Líyáng Camp, recruits from the Sānfǔ,
Qiāng and Hú soldiers from various commanderies in Liángzhōu, and pardoned criminals,
totaling forty thousand men, to attack them.
Upon reaching Hàowěi in Jīnchéng,
they fought the Qiāng,
beheading six hundred men.
They also fought in Luòdū Valley,
where they were defeated by the Qiāng,
with over a thousand dead.
The Qiāng then led their forces and withdrew beyond the frontier.
Mǎ Wǔ pursued them again to Dōnghán and Xīhán,
severely defeating them,
beheading four thousand six hundred men,
capturing one thousand six hundred prisoners,
and the rest either surrendered or dispersed.
Mǎ Wǔ returned triumphantly to the capital,
and his邑 was increased by seven hundred households,
making a total of one thousand eight hundred households.
In the fourth year of Yǒngpíng,
he passed away.
His son Mǎ Xù succeeded him.
Due to his elder brother Bóyì's involvement with Yán Zhōng, a confederate of Prince Yīng of Chǔ, in a rebellion,
his fief was abolished.
In the seventh year of Yǒngchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng re-enfeoffed Mǎ Zhèn, Mǎ Wǔ's grandson, as the Marquis of Liáotíng.
When Zhèn died,
his son Cè succeeded him.
A commentary states: The twenty-eight generals of the Restoration
were believed by earlier generations to correspond to the twenty-eight constellations,
but this is not thoroughly substantiated.
Nevertheless, all were able to inspire the gathering of wind and clouds,
exert their wisdom and courage,
and were called "supporters of the Mandate."
They were also men of ambition and ability.
Critics often faulted Guāngwǔ for not appointing meritorious officials to administrative posts,
thereby leaving their eminent talents and great achievements
unused.
However, if one considers his deep planning and far-reaching calculations,
there must have been a reason for this.
If the kingly way has already declined,
and it has descended to hegemonic virtue,
it is still possible to appoint only the capable,
and arrange the meritorious and worthy in due order,
like Guǎn and Xí who successively rose in Duke Huán's era,
and Xiān and Zhào who were simultaneously listed in Duke Wén's court;
this can be called comprehensive understanding.
Since Qín and Hàn,
generations have relied on military power,
and those who assisted the royal fortunes
were all military men who rose from humble origins.
There were also sellers of silk, dog butchers, and other cunning and slippery characters,
some were rewarded with cities,
or entrusted with positions like Āhéng (chief minister).
Thus, when power is equal, discord arises;
when strength is matched, rebellion erupts.
Xiāo and Fán were still imprisoned,
and Xìn and Yuè eventually met dismemberment and execution.
Is this not true?
From this time onwards,
up to Emperor Xiàowǔ,
the chief ministers for five generations
were all dukes and marquises.

Therefore, Guāngwǔ, learning from past mistakes,
held the ambition to correct the wrongs.

If this is applied

the harm is too great.
Being strictly righteous would mean losing loyal old friends;
bending principles would mean violating imperial laws;
selecting based on virtue does not guarantee great merit;
appointing based on effort does not mean the person is necessarily worthy;
appointing them jointly makes it difficult to satisfy the various minds;
and placing them side by side ensures the detrimental effects are not far off.

while strict laws and profound regulations
demanded accountability from administrative officials.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
there were over a hundred marquises.
As for those few prominent figures,
they participated in state affairs,
sharing responsibility for both good and bad outcomes.
ensuring the completeness of their fiefs and emoluments,
and all ended up extending their fame and blessings to their descendants.
In the past, Liú Hóu believed that Gāozǔ exclusively employed his old acquaintances like Xiāo and Cáo.
easily leads to the error of private favoritism,
while impartial treatment for all
will certainly broaden the path for recruiting the worthy.
Is this not the case?
During the Yǒngpíng era,
Emperor Xiǎnzōng, remembering the meritorious officials of the previous generation,
had the twenty-eight generals painted on the Cloud Terrace in the Southern Palace.
Outside of these, there were also Wáng Cháng, Lǐ Tōng, Dòu Róng, and Zhuó Mào,
making a total of thirty-two people.
Therefore, following their original order, they are listed at the end of this chapter
to record the sequence of the meritorious officials.

Grand Tutor, Marquis of Gāomì, Dèng Yǔ; Governor of Zhōngshān, Marquis of Quánjiāo, Mǎ Chéng; Grand Minister of War, Marquis of Guǎngpíng, Wú Hàn; Magistrate of Hénán, Marquis of Fùchéng, Wáng Liáng; Left General, Marquis of Jiāodōng, Jiǎ Fù; Governor of Lángyá, Marquis of Zhù'ā, Chén Jùn; General Who Establishes Might, Marquis of Hǎozhì, Gěng Yǎn; General of Cavalry, Marquis of Cānjù, Dù Mào; Bearer of the Golden Mace, Marquis of Yōngnú, Kòu Xún; General Who Accumulates Crossbows, Marquis of Kūnyáng, Fù Jùn; General Who Conquers the South, Marquis of Wǔyáng, Cén Péng; Left Aide, Marquis of Héfèi, Jiān Xún; General Who Conquers the West, Marquis of Yángxià, Féng Yì; Governor of Shànggǔ, Marquis of Huáilíng, Wáng Bà; General Who Establishes Righteousness, Marquis of Gé, Zhū Yòu; Governor of Xìndū, Marquis of Ālíng, Rèn Guāng; General Who Captures Barbarians, Marquis of Yǐngyáng, Jì Zūn; Governor of Yùzhāng, Marquis of Zhōngshuǐ, Lǐ Zhōng; General of Cavalry, Marquis of Lìyáng, Jǐng Dān; Right General, Marquis of Huáilǐ, Wàn Xiū; General of Tiger's Teeth, Marquis of Ānpíng, Gài Yán; Grand Master of Ceremonies, Marquis of Língshòu, Pī Tóng; Commandant of the Guards, Marquis of Ānchéng, Diāo Qī; General of Swift Cavalry, Marquis of Chāngchéng, Liú Zhí; Governor of Dōngjùn, Marquis of Dōngguāng, Gěng Chún; General Who Sweeps the Wilds, Marquis of Shānsāng, Wáng Cháng; Colonel of the City Gates, Marquis of Lánglíng, Zāng Gōng; Grand Minister of Works, Marquis of Gùshǐ, Lǐ Tōng; General Who Captures Barbarians, Marquis of Yángxū, Mǎ Wǔ; Grand Minister of Works, Marquis of Ānfēng, Dòu Róng; General of Cavalry, Marquis of Shèn, Liú Lóng; Grand Tutor, Marquis of Xuāndé, Zhuó Mào.
Eulogy: The Emperor's achievements were ponderous,
preserving the merits of the capable.
The multitude of lords came,
swiftly aiding our war chariots.
Graceful like dragons,
they accompanied the bright light and soared together.
Biography of Dòu Róng, Chapter 13 (His disciple Gù, great-grandson Xiàn, great-great-grandson Zhāng)
Dòu Róng 字 Zhōugōng,
was a native of Pínglíng, Fúfēng.
His seventh-generation ancestor, Guǎngguó,
was the younger brother of Empress Xiàowén,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhāngwǔ.
Róng's great-great-grandfather,
during the reign of Emperor Xuān, moved from Chángshān as an official earning two thousand shí.
Róng was orphaned early.
During Wáng Mǎng's regency,
he served as Sīmǎ of the Qiángnǔ general,
attacked Zhái Yì in the east,
then returned to attack Huáilǐ,
and was enfeoffed as the Baron of Jiànwǔ for his military achievements.
His younger sister was a concubine of the Grand Sīkōng, Wáng Yì.
His family resided in Cháng'ān,
mingled with the powerful and noble,
and associated with local heroes and magnates,
earning a reputation for chivalry.
However, he served his mother and elder brother,
and cared for his younger brother,
cultivating virtue within his household.
Towards the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
when bandits rose in Qīng and Xú,
Grand Tutor Wáng Kuāng
invited Róng to be an auxiliary general,
and they jointly campaigned eastward.
When the Hàn army rose,
Róng again followed Wáng Yì and was defeated at Kūnyáng.
He returned to [Cháng'ān.
The Hàn army] advanced rapidly into the pass.
Wáng Yì recommended Róng,
who was appointed Bōshuǐ General,
granted a thousand catties of gold,
and led troops to Xīnfēng.
After Mǎng's defeat,
Róng surrendered his army to Grand Sīmǎ Zhào Méng of Gēngshǐ,
who appointed him Xiàowèi.
Méng highly esteemed him,
and recommended Róng to be the Administrator of Jùlù.
Róng saw that Gēngshǐ had just been established,
the east was still in turmoil,
and did not wish to leave the pass.
Furthermore, his great-great-grandfather had once been the Administrator of Zhāngyè,
his granduncle had been the Protector of the Qiāng,
and his cousin had also been the Administrator of Wǔwēi.
For generations, his family had been in Hexi,
and he understood its customs and people.
He alone said to his brothers:
"The security or danger of the world is yet unknown.
Hexi is rich and prosperous,
with the river as its stronghold.
The elite cavalry of Zhāngyè Commandery, numbering ten thousand,
if there is a sudden emergency,
we can cut off the river fords,
sufficient to defend ourselves.
This is a place for a remnant to survive."
His brothers all agreed.
Róng then went to see Méng daily,
declining Jùlù,
planning to go to Hexi.
Méng spoke to Gēngshǐ on his behalf,
and he was then appointed Commandant of Zhāngyè Commandery.
Róng was greatly pleased,
and immediately took his family west.
Upon arrival,
he gathered and befriended the heroes,
and conciliated the Qiāng and Hú,
greatly winning their favor.
Hexi unanimously submitted to him.
At this time, the Administrator of Jiǔquán, Liáng Tǒng, the Administrator of Jīnchéng, Kù Jūn,
the Commandant of Zhāngyè, Shǐ Bāo,
the Commandant of Jiǔquán, Zhú Zēng, and the Commandant of Dūnhuáng, Xīn Róng,
were all outstanding talents from the commanderies and prefectures.
Róng developed close friendships with all of them.
When Gēngshǐ was defeated,
Róng discussed with Liáng Tǒng and others, saying:
"Now the world is in chaos,
and we don't know where to turn.
