Hexi is isolated among the Qiāng and Hú;
if we don't unite our hearts and exert our strength,
we cannot defend ourselves.
If our power is equally matched,
we also have no one to lead us.
We should elect one person as the Grand General,
jointly secure the five commanderies,
and observe the changing times."
Once the deliberation was settled,
they each humbly declined,
but all agreed that because Róng's family had served as officials in Hexi for generations,
and he was respected by all,
they nominated Róng to act as Grand General of the five commanderies of Hexi.
At this time, the Administrator of Wǔwēi, Mǎ Qī, and the Administrator of Zhāngyè, Rèn Zhòng, were both isolated and without allies.
So, they jointly sent a letter to inform them.
The two immediately relinquished their seals and left.
Thereupon, Liáng Tǒng was made Administrator of Wǔwēi,
Shǐ Bāo Administrator of Zhāngyè,
Zhú Zēng Administrator of Jiǔquán,
Xīn Róng Administrator of Dūnhuáng,
and Kù Jūn Administrator of Jīnchéng.
Róng resided in the commandery,
retaining his position as Commandant as before,
and appointed aides to supervise the five commanderies.
The people of Hexi were simple and honest,
and Róng's administration was also lenient and harmonious.
Superiors and subordinates were close,
and the region was peaceful and prosperous.
They trained soldiers and horses,
practiced archery,
and maintained vigilance with beacon fires.
When the Qiāng and Hú encroached on the frontier,
Róng would personally lead and rescue them with the various commanderies,
all acting according to a precise plan,
and they always defeated them.
Thereafter, the Xiōngnú were deterred,
rarely invading again,
and the Qiāng and Hú settled within the border were all overawed and submitted.
Refugees from Āndìng, Běidì, and Shàngjùn, fleeing disaster and famine,
flocked to him ceaselessly.
Róng and the others heard remotely of Guāngwǔ's enthronement,
and inwardly wished to turn eastward,
but Hexi was too remote,
and they could not communicate directly.
At that time, Wěi Xiāo first proclaimed the Jiànwǔ reign title,
and Róng and the others accepted his calendar.
Xiāo granted them all general's seals and cords.
Xiāo outwardly conformed to popular sentiment,
but harbored different intentions.
He sent the eloquent scholar Zhāng Xuán to persuade Hexi, saying:
"Gēngshǐ's enterprise was established,
but soon perished.
This is proof that a single family will not rise twice.
If you now choose a lord,
and immediately attach yourselves to him,
once you are constrained,
you will lose your power.
Should danger arise later,
even regret will be too late.
Now heroes are competing,
and the victor is undecided.
You should each hold your own territory,
and ally with Lǒng and Shǔ.
At best, you can be like the Six States;
at worst, you won't fall below Wèi Tuó."
Róng then convened the heroes and various administrators for a discussion.
Among them, the wise ones all said:
"The Hàn inherited the destiny of Yáo,
and its mandate is prolonged.
Now the emperor's surname and title appear in diagrams and writings.
From previous generations, scholars knowledgeable in astronomy and Daoist arts, such as Gǔ Zǐyún and Xià Héliáng,
have clearly stated that Hàn has the auspicious signs of receiving the mandate again.
This has been spoken of for a long time.
Therefore, Liú Zǐjùn changed his name,
hoping to fulfill that prophecy.
And at the end of Mǎng's reign,
the Daoist Xīmén Jūnhuì said that Liú Xiù would become the Son of Heaven,
and then conspired to establish Zǐjùn.
When the plot was discovered, he was killed.
He went out and told the observing common people: 'Liú Xiù is truly your lord.'
All these recent events are clearly evident,
and wise men all see them.
Besides speaking of the Mandate of Heaven,
let us also discuss it in terms of human affairs: There are several claimants to the imperial title now,
but Luòyáng has the largest territory,
the strongest armed forces,
and the clearest decrees.
Observing the prophecies and examining human affairs,
other families can probably not compare."
The administrators of the various commanderies had their own retainers and guests,
some with similar opinions, some with different.
Róng was cautious and thorough,
and ultimately decided to turn eastward.
In the summer of the fifth year,
he sent Chief Clerk Liú Jūn to present a letter and offer horses.
Previously,
the emperor (Dì) heard that Hexī (Héxī) was prosperous and wealthy,
and its territory adjoined Lǒng (Lǒng) and Shǔ (Shǔ).
He constantly wished to entice it to pressure Xiāo (Xiāo) and Shù (Shù).
He also sent an envoy to send Róng (Róng) a letter.
The envoy met Jūn (Jūn) on the way,
and immediately returned with him.
The emperor (Dì) was exceedingly delighted to see Jūn (Jūn).
After the formalities and feasting were over,
he then sent him back,
bestowing upon Róng (Róng) an imperial letter saying:

"An imperial edict to the Acting General-in-Chief of the Five Commanderies of Hexī (Héxī) and Commandant of the Dependent States: I commend your efforts in guarding and defending the five border commanderies.
Your soldiers and horses are elite and strong,
your granaries and treasuries are well-stocked,
and the common people are prosperous and wealthy.
Externally, you have repelled the Qiāng (Qiāng) and Hú (Hú),
and internally, the hundred surnames enjoy blessings.
Your prestige and virtue are widely heard,
and I eagerly await you with an open mind.
The roads are blocked and obstructed,
how can this vexation ever cease!
The letter and horses presented by your chief clerk (zhǎngshǐ) have all arrived,
and I deeply appreciate your profound intentions.
Now, Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu) has Gōngsūn Zǐyáng (Gōngsūn Zǐyáng),
and Tiānshuǐ (Tiānshuǐ) has General Guī (Guī) (Wěi Xiāo).
As Shǔ (Shǔ) and Hàn (Hàn) are currently attacking each other,
the power rests with the general.
A single step, left or right,
will have significant consequences.
From this perspective,
how can there be a limit to my desire to treat you generously!
All matters are as seen by your chief clerk (zhǎngshǐ),
and as known by the general.
Kings rise and fall in succession,
a thousand years meet once.
If you wish to establish Huán (Huán) and Wén (Wén) (Huan-Wen style hegemony),
and assist the humble state,
you should diligently strive to complete your meritorious work;
if you wish to divide the realm into a three-way standoff,
forming horizontal alliances (liánhéng) and vertical alliances (hézòng),
you should also decide in due time.
The world is not yet unified,
and you and I are in distant regions,
not states that seek to devour each other.
Those who deliberate now
will surely have the plan of Rèn Xiāo (Rèn Xiāo) imitating Wèi Tuó (Wèi Tuó) in controlling seven commanderies.
A king has divided lands,
but no divided people.
It is merely a matter of suiting one's own affairs.
I now bestow upon the general two hundred jīn (jīn) of gold.
You may speak whenever it is convenient."
Consequently, Róng (Róng) was appointed Pastor (Mù) of Liángzhōu (Liángzhōu).
When the imperial letter arrived,
Hexī (Héxī) was all astonished,
believing that the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) had clear insight over ten thousand *lǐ* (lǐ),
comprehending the scheme
of gathering support.
Róng (Róng) immediately sent Jūn (Jūn) again to submit a memorial, saying:
"Your servant Róng (Róng) humbly reflects on himself,
fortunate enough to have been associated with the late empress's (xiānhòu) lineage,
receiving grace as an imperial relative (wàiqī),
with two thousand *dàn* (dàn) (high-ranking official) across generations.
In my own person,
I have again filled a place in the ranks,
temporarily serving as a general,
holding a corner of the realm.
To offer my service is easy to say,
to offer my loyalty is easy to do.
A letter is insufficient to fully express my utmost sincerity,
therefore, I have sent Liú Jūn (Liú Jūn) to verbally convey my deepest feelings.
I consider myself to have laid bare my heart,
without the slightest concealment.
Yet the imperial letter greatly praises the two lords of Shǔ (Shǔ) and Hàn (Hàn),
the power of a three-way standoff,
and the strategies of Rèn Xiāo (Rèn Xiāo) and Wèi Tuó (Wèi Tuó).
I secretly feel pain and sorrow.
Although your servant Róng (Róng) is ignorant,
I still know the juncture of benefit and harm,
and the distinction between compliance and rebellion.
How can one betray the true old lord,
and serve treacherous and false individuals;
abandon the integrity of loyalty and steadfastness,
and undertake acts of overthrow;
overturn an established foundation,
and seek profit without hope?
Even if these three things were asked of a madman,
he would still know what to abandon and what to follow.
How then could I alone use my heart in such a way!
I respectfully send my younger brother of the same lineage, Yǒu (Yǒu), to the imperial court,
to verbally convey my humble sentiments."
Yǒu (Yǒu) reached Gāopíng (Gāopíng)
when Xiāo (Xiāo) rebelled.
The road was cut off,
so he galloped back.
Róng (Róng) then sent his Cavalry Commander (sīmǎ) Xí Fēng (Xí Fēng) to secretly deliver a letter.
The emperor (Dì) again sent Xí Fēng (Xí Fēng) to bestow letters upon Róng (Róng) and Yǒu (Yǒu),
in which he very thoroughly consoled and encouraged them.
Róng (Róng), having deeply understood the emperor's (Dì) intentions,
then wrote to Wěi Xiāo (Wěi Xiāo), rebuking him, saying:
"I humbly observe that the general's state is wealthy and his administration well-governed,
and his soldiers are loyal and attached.
In a time of personal difficulty and crisis,
when the state was in an unfavorable situation,
you maintained your integrity without wavering,
serving the imperial court (běncháo).
Later, you sent Bóchūn (Bóchūn)
to commit himself to the state,
and his sincerity, without doubt,
was demonstrated thereby.
This is why I and others admired your noble righteousness,
and wished to serve under the general:
it was precisely for this reason.
Yet in a fit of anger and vexation,
you changed your integrity and altered your plans,
with lord and subject disputing,
and superiors and inferiors engaging in battle.
Abandoning success,
creating difficulty,
departing from righteousness,
and engaging in perverse schemes—
what took a hundred years to accumulate,
is destroyed in a single morning.
Is this not regrettable!
Perhaps those in charge were greedy for功 (gōng) and made plans,
leading to this.
I secretly lament this!
At present, the terrain of Xīzhōu (Xīzhōu) is constrained,
and its people and soldiers are scattered.
It is easy to assist others,
but difficult to establish oneself.
If you lose your way and do not turn back,
hearing the right path yet remaining deluded,
then you will either not unite with Zǐyáng (Zǐyáng) to the south,
or enter with Wénbó (Wénbó) to the north.
[One Zero] Indeed, to engage in empty alliances and easily confront the powerful,
relying on distant aid while underestimating nearby enemies,
[One One] I do not see the benefit in this.
I have heard that the wise do not endanger the multitude to undertake affairs,
and the benevolent do not violate righteousness to achieve merit.
Now, to oppose the great with the small,
how is this for the multitude?
[One Two] To pursue merit for oneself,
how is this for righteousness?
[One Three] Moreover, you initially served the imperial court (běncháo),
bowing your head and facing north—
this was the integrity of a loyal minister.
[One Four] And when you sent Bóchūn (Bóchūn),
you shed tears bidding him farewell—
this was the kindness of a loving father.
Suddenly to betray this,
what will you say to your officials and soldiers?
To endure and destroy it,
what will you say to your son who remains?
[One Five] Since the uprising began,
there have been continuous mutual attacks,
cities and walls have all become ruins,
and living people have been abandoned in ditches and ravines.
Those who survive now
are either remnants of the sword,
or orphaned refugees.
To this day, the wounded bodies have not healed,
and the sounds of weeping are still heard.
Fortunately, the celestial fortune has slightly turned,
yet the general has again compounded the disaster.
This means that chronic ailments cannot fully recover,
and young orphans will again be displaced.
Such sorrow,
is especially pitiable and grievous,
to speak of it makes one's nose ache!
[One Six] Even ordinary people cannot bear it,
how much less a benevolent person!
I have heard that being loyal is very easy,
but achieving what is appropriate is truly difficult.
[One Seven] To cause great trouble for others,
and incur resentment with virtue,
[One Eight] I know that I will incur blame with these words.
My humble offering,
I only ask the general to examine."
Xiāo (Xiāo) did not accept it.
Róng (Róng) then, together with the five commandery administrators (tàishǒu), vigorously trained their troops and horses,
and submitted a memorial requesting a military campaign date.
The Emperor greatly praised and admired him,
and then bestowed upon Róng the Wàishǔ Tú (外屬圖) and the Tàishǐ Gōng Wǔ Zōng (太史公五宗), Wàiqī Shìjiā (外戚世家),
and Wèiqí Hóu Lièzhuàn (魏其侯列傳).
The edict in reply said:
"Every time I recall the imperial maternal relatives,
Emperor Xiàojǐng (孝景皇帝) came from the Dòu (竇) clan.
King Dìng (定王),
son of Emperor Jǐng (景帝),
is my ancestor.
In the past, one word from Wèiqí (魏其)
rectified the succession.
Chángjūn (長君) and Shàojūn (少君) respectfully served their teachers,
cultivated their virtuous character,
and passed it down to their descendants.
This is due to the divine spirit of the Empress Dowager
and Heaven assisting Hàn (漢).
The letter written from Tiānshuǐ (天水) containing the general's repudiation of Wěi Xiāo (隗囂)
pierces to the bone.
Rebellious ministers, seeing it,
would surely tremble and be ashamed;
loyal ministers would feel a pang in their noses and shed tears;
righteous gentlemen would be enlightened as if awakened from blindness.
Without loyalty and sincerity,
who could achieve such a thing?
How could one of meager virtue be capable of it!
Xiāo (囂) knew he had lost the support of Héxī (河西),
and that calamity would soon befall his clan.
He wished to sow discord and division
to confuse the loyal hearts,
and turn them against each other,
thus accomplishing his treachery.
Moreover, the hundred officials in the capital,
not understanding the true intentions of the state and the general,
were apt to adopt falsehoods,
and engage in exaggerated and baseless talk,
causing the loyal and filial to be disappointed,
and spreading rumors contrary to the truth.
The coming of praise and slander
is never without cause;
one must not fail to consider this.
Now the bandits east of the pass are settled,
the great army should now fully advance west.
General, do you rally your might and prestige
to meet the appointed time."
Róng (融), upon receiving the edict,
immediately led the governors of the various commanderies and their troops into Jīnchéng (金城).
Originally,
during the Gēngshǐ (更始) era,
the Xiānlíng Qiāng (先零羌) led by Fēng Hé (封何) and other tribes killed the Administrator of Jīnchéng (金城)
and occupied his commandery.
Wěi Xiāo (隗囂) sent envoys to bribe and give gifts to Fēng Hé (封何),
and formed an alliance with him,
wishing to mobilize his forces.
Róng (融) and others, taking advantage of the army's sortie,
advanced and attacked Fēng Hé (封何),
greatly defeating him,
beheading over a thousand,
and capturing ten thousand cattle, horses, and sheep,
and tens of thousands of hú (斛) of grain.
They then displayed their might along the river,
awaiting the imperial carriage.
At that time, the main army had not yet advanced,
so Róng (融) then withdrew.
The Emperor, seeing Róng's (融) proven loyalty,
praised him even more.
An edict commanded the Yòu Fúfēng (右扶風) to repair Róng's (融) father's tomb
and offer a grand sacrifice (tàiláo, 太牢).
He frequently dispatched light envoys
to deliver rare delicacies from all directions.
Liáng Tǒng (梁統) then sent someone to assassinate Zhāng Xuán (張玄),
and subsequently severed ties with Xiāo (囂),
all resigning their provisional general seals and ribbons.
In the summer of the seventh year,
Zhú Zēng (竺曾), Administrator of Jiǔquán (酒泉), killed someone to avenge his brother and left his post.
Róng (融), by imperial authorization, appointed Zēng (曾) as Wǔfēng Jiāngjūn (武鋒將軍),
and replaced him with Xīn Róng (辛肜).
In autumn,
Wěi Xiāo (隗囂) dispatched troops to raid Āndìng (安定).
The Emperor intended to personally lead a western campaign against him,
and first set a rendezvous time with Róng (融).
But it rained,
the roads were cut off,
and Xiāo's (囂) troops had already retreated,
so the campaign was halted.
When Róng (融) reached Gūzāng (姑臧),
he received an edict to disband and return.
Róng (融) feared that the main army would not advance for a long time,
and therefore submitted a memorial saying:
"Wěi Xiāo (隗囂) heard that the imperial carriage was coming west,
and that I, Róng (融), was descending from the east.
His officers and men were agitated,
and he planned not to fight for now.
Xiāo's (囂) generals, such as Gāo Jùn (高峻), all wished to greet the grand army,
but later heard that the campaign was halted,
and Jùn (峻) and others again became doubtful.
Xiāo (囂) spread rumors that there was trouble in the east,
and the powerful figures in Xīzhōu (西州) again sided with him.
Xiāo (囂) also summoned Gōngsūn Shù's (公孫述) generals
and ordered them to guard Tūmén (突門).
I, Róng (融), am isolated and weak,
caught in between.
Although I rely on your divine power,
I should be swiftly rescued and aided.
If the state presses from the front,
and I, Róng (融), press from the rear,
using urgency alternately,
and supporting each other from head to tail,
Xiāo's (囂) position will be squeezed,
unable to advance or retreat.
He will surely be defeated.
If the army does not advance early,
and holds doubts for too long,
then externally the enemy will grow,
and internally weakness will be shown.
This will again give slanderous villains an opportunity,
which I secretly worry about.
May Your Majesty please have pity!"
The Emperor greatly appreciated this.
In the summer of the eighth year,
the imperial carriage went west to campaign against Wěi Xiāo (隗囂).
Róng (融) led the administrators of five commanderies and tens of thousands of Qiāng (羌) and Lǔ Xiǎoyuèzhī (虜小月氏) infantry and cavalry,
with over five thousand baggage carts,
and met the main army first at Gāopíng (高平).
Róng (融) first sent an attendant to inquire about the proper protocol for meeting.
At that time, armies were being raised in succession,
and generals and the Three Dukes (sāngōng, 三公) crisscrossed paths,
some turning their backs to the envoy and conversing privately.
The Emperor heard that Róng (融) had first inquired about etiquette,
and greatly praised him,
announcing it to all officials.
He then held a grand banquet,
granted an audience to Róng (融) and others,
and treated them with exceptional courtesy.
He appointed his younger brother Yǒu (友) as Fèngchē Dūwèi (奉車都尉),
and his cousin Shì (士) as Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫).
They then advanced together,
Xiāo's (囂) forces were routed,
and all cities and towns surrendered.
The Emperor highly regarded Róng's (融) achievements,
and issued an edict to enfeoff Róng (融) as Ānfēng Hóu (安豐侯) with the four counties of Ānfēng (安豐), Yángquán (陽泉), Liǎo (蓼), and Ānfēng (安風).
His brother Yǒu (友) was enfeoffed as Xiǎnqīn Hóu (顯親侯).
Then, in order, the various generals and commanders were enfeoffed: Wǔfēng Jiāngjūn (武鋒將軍) Zhú Zēng (竺曾) as Zhùyì Hóu (助義侯),
Wǔwēi Tàishǒu (武威太守) Liáng Tǒng (梁統) as Chéngyì Hóu (成義侯),
Zhāngyè Tàishǒu (張掖太守) Shǐ Bāo (史苞) as Bāoyì Hóu (襃義侯),
Jīnchéng Tàishǒu (金城太守) Kù Jūn (厙鈞) as Fǔyì Hóu (輔義侯),
and Jiǔquán Tàishǒu (酒泉太守) Xīn Róng (辛肜) as Fúyì Hóu (扶義侯).
After the enfeoffments were completed,
the imperial carriage returned east,
and Róng (融) and others were all sent back west to their garrisons.
Róng (融), seeing that both he and his brother had received titles
and had long exclusively commanded a region,
feared for his own safety
and repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to be replaced.
The imperial edict in reply said:
"I and the general are like left and right hands.
Why do you repeatedly show humility and modesty,
and not understand my intentions?
Exert yourself to govern the soldiers and people,
and do not separate from your divisions."
When Lǒng and Shǔ were pacified,
an imperial edict commanded Dòu Róng, along with the grand administrators of the five commanderies, to report to the capital.
His officials, retainers, and guests followed him,
with over a thousand carriages,
and horses, oxen, and sheep covering the fields.
When Dòu Róng arrived,
he went to the gates of Luòyáng city,
and presented his seal and cord as the Shepherd of Liángzhōu, Commander of the Protectorate of Zhāngyè, and Marquis of Ānfēng.
An imperial edict then sent an envoy to return his marquisate seal and cord.
He was granted an audience
and seated among the feudal lords.
The rewards, favors, and honors
stirred the entire capital.
After several months,
he was appointed as the Shepherd of Jìzhōu.
Ten-some days later,
he was again promoted to Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sīkōng).
Dòu Róng considered himself not an old minister;
having suddenly entered the court
and surpassed the meritorious officials.
Whenever he was summoned for an audience,
his demeanor and words were excessively humble and respectful.
The Emperor, for this reason, became even more affectionate and close to him.
Dòu Róng was cautious
and for a long time felt uneasy.
He repeatedly declined his rank and position,
and through the court attendant Jīn Qiān, conveyed his utmost sincerity.
He also submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant Dòu Róng is fifty-three years old.
I have a son who is fifteen,
whose nature is dull and slow.
Your servant Dòu Róng teaches and guides him in the classics day and night,
not allowing him to observe astronomy
or read prognostication texts.
I sincerely wish him to be respectful and prudent in his duties,
and to cautiously follow the proper path.
I do not wish him to have talent,
much less inherit cities and vast territories,
and enjoy a former feudal princely state!"
He then again requested a private audience,
but the Emperor did not grant it.
Later, after court was dismissed,
he lingered behind the seats.
The Emperor knew he wished to decline,
so he ordered his attendants to escort him out.
On another day during an audience,
the Emperor welcomed Dòu Róng and said:
"The other day I knew you wished to resign your post and return to your land,
so I commanded you, being hot, to make yourself comfortable.
Now that we meet,
we should discuss other matters;
you must not speak of that again."
Dòu Róng dared not repeat his request.
In the twentieth year,
the Grand Minister of Education (Dà Sītú) Dài Shè was imprisoned for bribery, as a person he had recommended had stolen gold.
The Emperor, considering the three grand ministers shared responsibilities,
reluctantly issued a decree to dismiss Dòu Róng.
The next year,
he was given the special rank of Grandee Remonstrant (Tèjìn).
In the twenty-third year,
he replaced Yīn Xīng in performing the duties of Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi),
retaining his special rank.
He also concurrently held the position of Grand Architect (Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng).
His younger brother Yǒu became Commandant of the City Gates (Chéngmén Xiàowèi),
so both brothers commanded imperial guards.
Dòu Róng again begged for his bones to be retired,
and was immediately granted money and silk,
and the Grand Provisioner sent rare delicacies.
When Yǒu passed away,
the Emperor, pitying Dòu Róng's old age,
sent a Regular Palace Attendant (Zhōng Chángshì) and a Palace Usher (Zhōng Yèzhě) directly into his private chambers to forcibly offer him wine and food.
Dòu Róng's eldest son, Mù,
married Princess Nèihuáng
and succeeded Yǒu as Commandant of the City Gates.
Mù's son, Xūn,
married Princess Bǐyáng, daughter of Prince Gōng of Dōnghǎi, Liú Qiáng.
Yǒu's son, Gù,
also married Princess Nièyáng, a daughter of Guāngwǔ.
When Xiǎnzōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Dòu Róng's cousin's son, Lín, as Commandant Protector of the Qiāng (Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi).
The Dòu clan had one Grand Minister,
two marquises,
three princesses,
and four officials of the two-thousand-picus rank,
all at the same time.
From grandfather to grandson,
their official residences and mansions faced each other in the capital,
with thousands of slaves and maidservants.
Among relatives and meritorious officials, none could compare with them.
In Yǒngpíng second year
Lín was executed for a crime;
the details are in the biography of the Western Qiāng.
warning him with the misfortunes of Dòu Yīng and Tián Fěn.
Dòu Róng, terrified, begged for his bones to be retired.
An edict ordered him to return to his mansion to recuperate.
After a year or so,
The Emperor thereupon repeatedly issued edicts severely reprimanding Dòu Róng,
and was granted cattle for sustenance
and a jar of wine.
Dòu Róng had been in the imperial guard for over ten years;
he was old,
and his sons and grandsons were dissolute
and often violated the law.
Mù and others then associated with frivolous people,
entrusted matters to commanderies and counties,
and interfered with government affairs.
Because his enfeoffment was in Ānfēng,
he wished for his in-laws to all occupy the former state of Liù'ān.
He then falsely claimed an imperial edict from Empress Dowager Yīn,
ordering Liú Xū, Marquis of Liù'ān, to dismiss his wife,
and then gave him his own daughter in marriage.
In the fifth year,
Xū's wife's family submitted a memorial reporting the situation.
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and consequently dismissed all of Mù's and others' official positions.
All members of the Dòu clan who were palace attendants or minor officials, along with their families, returned to their native commanderies.
Only Dòu Róng remained in the capital.
When Mù and the others reached Hángǔ Pass in the west,
an edict ordered them all to be recalled.
It happened that Dòu Róng passed away
at the age of seventy-eight.
He was posthumously honored as Marquis Dài,
and was granted very generous funeral provisions.
The Emperor believed Mù was unable to maintain proper conduct
and yet possessed great wealth
and lived in a grand mansion.
He always ordered one palace usher to supervise his household.
After several years,
the usher reported that Mù and his son, having lost their power,
frequently uttered resentful words.
The Emperor ordered them to return to their native commandery with their families.
Only Xūn remained in the capital as the husband of Princess Bǐyáng.
Mù was imprisoned for bribing a minor official in the commandery
and was confined.
He and his son Xuān both died in Pínglíng prison.
Xūn also died in Luòyáng prison.
After a long time,
an edict ordered Dòu Róng's夫人 (fūrén - wife/lady) and one young grandson to reside in the Dòu family residence in Luòyáng.
In the fourteenth year,
Xūn's younger brother Jiā was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānfēng,
with a fief of two thousand households,
to continue Dòu Róng's lineage.
At the beginning of Emperor Hé's reign,
he served as Minister Steward (Shàofǔ).
When Xūn's son, Grand General Xiàn, was executed,
Jiā was dismissed and returned to his state.
When Jiā died,
his son Wànquán succeeded him.
When Wànquán died,
his son Huìzōng succeeded him.
Wànquán's younger brother Wǔ
has a separate biography.
The commentary states: Dòu Róng first gained renown for his heroism and chivalry,
rising from the midst of chaos
to fill a gap in the heavens.
He then transformed into the honored status of a prince and marquis,
and ultimately held the position of a minister or grand councilor.
This is the mark of one who seeks merit and pursues power.
Yet, when his rank and position were full,
he even distanced himself from power and favor,
seeming sincerely unable to do otherwise—
what wisdom this was!
I have often carefully pondered the demeanor of this man;
although his methods for governing the state are not much to speak of,
his decorum in advancing and retreating is indeed commendable.
Gù (固), courtesy name Mèngsūn (孟孫),
while young, was appointed Yellow Gate Attendant Officer because he married a princess.
He enjoyed reading historical texts,
was fond of military strategy,
and was prominent in wielding power.
In the first year of Zhōngyuán (中元) (56 CE),
he inherited his father Yǒu's (友) title, Marquis of Xiǎnqīn (顯親).
When Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Commander of the Household,
overseeing the Yǔlín (羽林) guards.
Later, for the transgression of his cousin Mù (穆),
he was dismissed and remained at home for more than ten years.
At that time, the empire was at peace.
The Emperor wished to emulate Emperor Wǔ's (武帝) deeds,
to attack the Xiōngnú (匈奴),
and open up the Western Regions.
Because Gù (固) was well-versed in frontier affairs,
in the winter of the fifteenth year (72 CE),
he was appointed Grand Master of Chariots,
with Cavalry Commandant Gěng Zhōng (耿忠) as his deputy,
and Palace Attendant and Master of the Imperial Household Gěng Bǐng (耿秉) as Grand Master of the Imperial Stable,
and Qín Péng (秦彭) as his deputy.
All of them were assigned assistants and chief clerks,
and dispatched to garrison Liángzhōu (涼州).
The following year (73 CE),
Gù (固) and Zhōng (忠) led twelve thousand cavalry of armored soldiers from Jiǔquán (酒泉), Dūnhuáng (敦煌), and Zhāngyè (張掖), as well as Lúshuǐ Qiānghú (盧水羌胡),
and advanced from Jiǔquán (酒泉) Pass.
Gěng Bǐng (耿秉) and Qín Péng (秦彭) led ten thousand recruited soldiers from Wǔwēi (武威), Lǒngxī (隴西), Tiānshuǐ (天水), and Qiānghú (羌胡), and advanced from Jūyán (居延) Pass.

Furthermore, Grand Minister of Agriculture Jì Róng (祭肜) and General Who Crosses the Liao Wú Táng (吳棠) led eleven thousand cavalry of Qiānghú (羌胡) from Hénán Běidì (河南北地) and Xīhé (西河), and soldiers of the Southern Chányú (南單于), and advanced from Gāoquē (高闕) Pass.

Cavalry Commandant Lái Miáo (來苗) and Colonel Protector of the Wūhuán (烏桓) Wén Mù (文穆) led eleven thousand cavalry of soldiers from Tàiyuán (太原), Yànmén (鴈門), Dàijùn (代郡), Shànggǔ (上谷), Yúyáng (漁陽), Yòuběipíng (右北平), Dìngxiāng (定襄) Commanderies, and Wūhuán (烏桓) and Xiānbēi (鮮卑), and advanced from Píngchéng (平城) Pass.
Gù (固) and Zhōng (忠) reached Tiānshān (天山),
attacked King Hūyǎn (呼衍王),
beheading over a thousand.
King Hūyǎn (呼衍王) fled,
and they pursued him to Púléihǎi (蒲類海).
[一０] They left officials and soldiers to garrison Yīwúlú (伊吾盧) city.
[一一] Gěng Bǐng (耿秉) and Qín Péng (秦彭) crossed over six hundred *li* of desert,
reaching Sānmùlóushān (三木樓山).
[一二] Lái Miáo (來苗) and Wén Mù (文穆) reached the Xiōngnú (匈奴) River.
The captives all fled,
and nothing was gained.
Jì Róng (祭肜) and Wú Táng (吳棠) were dismissed as commoners for failing to reach Zhuóxiéshān (涿邪山).
At that time, of all the generals, only Gù (固) had achieved merit,
and his rank was raised to Special Advanced.
The following year (74 CE),
he again sallied from Yùmén (玉門) to attack the Western Regions.
An imperial edict commanded Gěng Bǐng (耿秉) and Cavalry Commandant Liú Zhāng (劉張) to relinquish their credentials and be subordinated to Gù (固).
[一三] Gù (固) then decisively defeated Báishān (白山)
and received the surrender of Chēshī (車師).
The details are fully recorded in the biography of Gěng Bǐng (耿秉).
Gù (固) served on the frontier for several years,
and the Qiānghú (羌胡) submitted to his kindness and trustworthiness.
[一四]
When Sùzōng (肅宗) ascended the throne (75 CE),
because the princess was diligent, upright, and benevolent,
and had been highly esteemed for generations,
she was given the additional title of Grand Princess,
and her stipend was increased by three thousand households.
Gù (固) was recalled to replace Wèi Yīng (魏應) as Grand Minister of the Court.
The Emperor, knowing his familiarity with frontier affairs,
consulted him frequently.
In the third year of Jiànchū (建初) (78 CE),
in recognition of his previous merits,
his stipend was increased by thirteen hundred households.
In the seventh year (82 CE),
he replaced Mǎ Fáng (馬防) as Minister of the Imperial Clan.
The following year (83 CE),
he again replaced Mǎ Fáng (馬防) as Minister of the Guards.
Gù (固) held high positions for a long time,
was highly respected and honored.
His rewards, stipends, and salaries
accumulated to enormous wealth,
yet he was humble and frugal by nature,
loved people, and was generous,
for which scholars praised him.
He died in the second year of Zhānghé (章和) (88 CE),
and was posthumously titled Marquis Wén (文侯).
His son, Biāo (彪),
reached the rank of Colonel of Archers,
but died before Gù (固).
Having no son,
the fief was abolished.
Xiàn (憲), courtesy name Bódù (伯度).
His father Xūn (勳) was executed,
and Xiàn (憲) was orphaned young.
In the second year of Jiànchū (建初) (77 CE),
his younger sister was established as empress,
and Xiàn (憲) was appointed Gentleman,
gradually promoted to Palace Attendant and Colonel of the Tiger Guards.
His younger brother, Dǔ (篤),
was appointed Yellow Gate Attendant Officer.
The brothers were favored and trusted,
both serving in the imperial palace.
Their rewards accumulated,
and their favor and prestige grew daily.
Even the families of the kings, princesses, Yīn (陰), and Mǎ (馬),
all feared them.
Xiàn (憲), relying on the influence of the inner palace,
audaciously requested to seize the Qìnshuǐ (沁水) Princess's gardens and fields for a low price.
The princess, compelled by fear,
dared not contend.
Later, when Sùzōng (肅宗) was traveling and passed by the gardens,
he pointed and asked Xiàn (憲) about them.
Xiàn (憲) secretly gestured to prevent anyone from answering.
When the matter was later discovered,
the Emperor was furious.
He summoned Xiàn (憲) and severely reprimanded him, saying:
"Reflect deeply on your past transgression!
When you seized the princess's gardens and fields,
how was that better than Zhào Gāo (趙高) pointing to a deer and calling it a horse?
Thinking about it for a long time makes one frightened.
In the Yǒngpíng (永平) period,
I often ordered Yīn Dǎng (陰黨), Yīn Bó (陰博), and Dèng Dié (鄧疊) to mutually investigate each other,
which is why none of the powerful relatives dared to violate the law.
Yet the imperial edicts repeatedly
spoke of the land and houses of my maternal relatives.
Now, even a noble princess is unjustly dispossessed;
how much more so the common people!
The state regards Xiàn (憲) as a lone chick or a rotten rat!"
Xiàn (憲) was greatly terrified.
The Empress changed into mourning clothes and offered deep apologies,
and only after a long time was he pardoned,
and ordered to return the fields to the princess.
Although his crime was not punished,
he was also not entrusted with important responsibilities.
When Emperor Hé (和帝) ascended the throne (88 CE),
the Empress Dowager held court.
Xiàn (憲), as Palace Attendant,
managed confidential matters internally
and issued imperial edicts externally.
Sùzōng's (肅宗) dying wish was for Dǔ (篤) to be Colonel of the Tiger Guards.
Dǔ's (篤) younger brothers Jǐng (景) and Guī (瓌) were both Regular Palace Attendants.
Thus, all the brothers held crucial positions.
Xiàn (憲), considering former Grand Commandant Dèng Biāo (鄧彪) to be righteous and humble,
respected by the late emperor,
and benevolent and amenable,
therefore honored him,
appointing him Grand Tutor,
and ordered all officials to submit to his authority.
Whatever he enacted,
he would outwardly have Biāo (彪) memorialize,
and inwardly report to the Empress Dowager.
There was nothing that was not approved.
Furthermore, Colonel of Cavalry Huán Yù (桓郁),
whose family had been imperial teachers for generations,
was humble and self-restrained by nature.
Therefore, he memorialized to recommend him,
asking that he be allowed to teach classics within the forbidden palace.
Thus, both internal and external factions were in harmony,
and no doubts or dissensions arose.
Xiàn (憲) was resolute and impetuous by nature,
avenging every grudge, no matter how small.
Initially,
during the Yǒngpíng (永平) period, Palace Attendant Hán Yū (韓紆) had once investigated his father Xūn's (勳) imprisonment.
Xiàn (憲) then ordered his retainers to kill Yū's (紆) son,
and offered his head as a sacrifice at Xūn's (勳) tomb.
Chāng (暢), Marquis of Dūxiāng (都鄉), a son of Qí Shāng Wáng (齊殤王),
came to mourn the national grief.
Chāng (暢) had always behaved depravedly,
and, together with Infantry Colonel Dèng Dié (鄧疊), a relative, frequently visited the capital.
Through Dié's (疊) mother Yuán (元), he gained access to the Chánglè (長樂) Palace
and found favor with the Empress Dowager,
receiving an imperial edict summoning him to the Shàngdōng Mén (上東門).
Xiàn (憲) feared that Chāng (暢) would gain favor
and divide his authority in the palace.
He sent retainers to assassinate Chāng (暢) within the guard station,
and then blamed Chāng's (暢) younger brother, Lìhóu (利侯) Gāng (剛).
He then had the Imperial Censor and the Inspector of Qīngzhōu (青州) jointly investigate Gāng (剛) and others.
When the truth was later discovered,
the Empress Dowager was enraged
and confined Xiàn (憲) in the inner palace.
Dòu Xiàn feared execution,
so he requested to attack the Xiongnú to atone for his death.
At this time, the Southern Chányú requested troops for a northern expedition,
so Dòu Xiàn was appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry),
with a golden seal and purple ribbon.
His subordinates were organized according to the Sīkōng (Minister of Works).
Zhí Jīn Wú (General-in-Chief of the Guards) Gěng Bǐng was appointed as his deputy.
He dispatched the Wǔ Xiào (Five Regiments) of the Northern Army,
the cavalry from Líyáng, Yōngyíng, and the twelve frontier commanderies,
as well as Qiāng and Hú soldiers, to exit the pass.
The following year,
Dòu Xiàn and Gěng Bǐng each led four thousand cavalry, along with the Southern Xiongnú Zuǒ Gǔlí Wáng (Left Wise King) Shīzi's
ten thousand cavalry, out of Shuòfāng via Jīlù Sài (Jīlù Pass).
The Southern Chányú Tún Túhé
led over ten thousand cavalry out of Mǎnyí Gǔ (Mǎnyí Valley).
Dùliáo Jiāngjūn (General Who Crosses the Liao) Dèng Hóng
and eight thousand Qiāng and Hú volunteer cavalry from the frontier,
along with Zuǒ Xián Wáng (Left Worthy King) Ān'guó's ten thousand cavalry, exited Wúyáng Sài (Wúyáng Pass).
All met at Zhuōxié Shān (Zhuōxié Mountain).
Dòu Xiàn divided and dispatched Fù Xiàowèi (Deputy Commandant) Yán Pán, Sīmǎ (Chief Clerk) Gěng Kuí, and Gěng Tán, leading Zuǒ Gǔlí Wáng Shīzi and Yòu Hūyǎn Wáng (Right Hūyǎn King) Xūzī and others,
with over ten thousand elite cavalry,
to fight the Northern Chányú at Jīluò Shān (Jīluò Mountain).
They thoroughly defeated him,
the barbarian forces collapsed,
and the Chányú fled.
They pursued and attacked the various tribes,
eventually reaching Sīqú Bǐdí Hǎi (Sīqú Bǐdí Sea).
They beheaded over thirteen thousand enemy combatants, from famed kings downwards,
and captured over a million live captives, horses, cattle, sheep, and camels.
[一０]At this, Wēndúxū, Rìzhú, Wēnwú, Fúqú Wáng Liǔdí, and other eighty-one tribes, leading their people, surrendered.
Before and after, there were over two hundred thousand people.
Dòu Xiàn and Gěng Bǐng then ascended Yànrán Shān (Yànrán Mountain),
more than three thousand _lǐ_ from the pass.
They carved a stone to record their achievements,
commemorating the might and virtue of Han.
They ordered Bān Gù to compose an inscription, which read:
In the seventh month of autumn, the first year of Yǒngyuán,
there was the Han Imperial Maternal Uncle, Chējì Jiāngjūn Dòu Xiàn.
He diligently assisted the sagacious and enlightened emperor,
and ascended to aid the imperial house.
He was received into the great
court,
and was pure and brilliant.
Then, with Zhí Jīn Wú Gěng Bǐng,
he fulfilled his duty and surveyed the region,
managing troops in Shuòfāng.
Commandants like eagles soaring,
soldiers like dragons and tigers,
these
assembled the six armies.
Together with the Southern Chányú, the Eastern Wūhuán, the Western Róng, Dī and Qiāng marquises, kings, and chiefs,
there were thirty thousand valiant cavalry.
The vanguard was lightly armed,
the long spears were in four divisions,
the supply wagons covered the roads,
thirteen thousand carriages in total.
They arrayed the Eight Battle Formations,
governing with divine might.
Their dark armor shone in the sun,
their crimson banners
dyed the sky.
Then they surmounted Gāoquē,
descended Jīlù,
passed through deserts and salt flats,
crossed the Great Desert.
They beheaded Wēnyú to anoint the drums,
and stained the blades with the blood of Shīzhú.
[一０]Thereafter,
the four detachments swept across,
like shooting stars and sweeping comets.
For ten thousand _lǐ_ it was desolate,
without a single remaining bandit in the wilderness.
Thus, the territories of the chieftains were extinguished.
They turned their banners and returned.
They consulted historical records and maps,
thoroughly
surveying its mountains and rivers.
They then crossed Zhuōxié,
straddled Ānhóu,
rode over Yànrán,
stepped on the settlements of Mòdú,
and burned the dragon court of Lǎoshàng.
[一一]This was to avenge the long-held grievances of Gāo and Wén,
and to glorify the profound spirits of the imperial ancestors.
Below, it was to secure and strengthen future generations,
expand and open up the national territory,
and manifest the heavenly renown of Great Han.
[一二]This is what is called
one effort
for long-lasting ease,
a temporary expense for eternal peace.
[一三]Thus, they sealed the mountain and carved the stone,
proclaiming the supreme virtue in an inscription.
How brilliant the royal army, conquering the wild frontiers!
Destroying the violent oppressors beyond the seas!
How vast and distant, stretching across the earth's boundaries!
Sealing the divine mound, erecting a lofty stele!
Glorifying the Emperor's reign, enduring for ten thousand generations!
Dòu Xiàn then led his army back.
He dispatched Jūn Sīmǎ (Army Chief Clerk) Wú Sì and Liáng Fèng,
bearing gold and silk, to present to the Northern Chányú,
proclaiming the national might,
with troops following behind them.
At that time, there was internal strife among the barbarians.
Wherever Wú Sì and Liáng Fèng went,
they persuaded people to surrender.
Before and after, over ten thousand people surrendered.
They finally reached the Chányú by the Western Sea,
proclaimed the nation's power and trustworthiness,
and delivered the imperial gifts.
The Chányú bowed his head and received them.
Liáng Fèng then persuaded him that he should follow the example of Hū Hánxié,
for the benefit of protecting his state and pacifying his people.
The Chányú was delighted,
and immediately took his people and returned with Liáng Fèng.
Upon reaching Sīqú Hǎi (Sīqú Sea),
he heard that the Han army had already entered the pass,
so he dispatched his younger brother, Yòu Wēnyú Dí Wáng (Right Wēnyú Dí King), to offer tribute and serve at court,
accompanying Liáng Fèng to the imperial palace.
Because the Chányú did not come himself,
Dòu Xiàn memorialized to send his attendant brother back.
The Southern Chányú, from north of the desert, sent an ancient cauldron to Dòu Xiàn,
with a capacity of five _dǒu_.
An inscription on its side read:
"Zhòng Shānfǔ's cauldron,
may his myriad generations of descendants forever keep and use it."
Dòu Xiàn then presented it to the emperor.
An imperial edict ordered a Zhōngláng Jiāng (Gentleman of the Palace) holding a _jié_ (imperial staff) to immediately proceed to Wǔyuán to appoint Dòu Xiàn as Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General),
and to enfeoff him as Wǔyáng Hóu (Marquis of Wǔyáng),
with a fief of twenty thousand households.
Dòu Xiàn firmly declined the enfeoffment,
and was granted a document allowing him to do so.
Formerly, the Dàjiāngjūn's position was below the Sāngōng (Three Excellencies),
and his subordinates were organized according to the Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant).
Dòu Xiàn's power and authority shook the court.
The Gōngqīng (Dukes and Ministers) sought to please him,
and memorialized that Dòu Xiàn's rank should be below the Tàifù (Grand Tutor)
but above the Sāngōng.
His Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk) and Sīmǎ (Chief Clerk) would have the rank of Zhōng Èrqiān Shí (Central Two Thousand Piculs),
and his two Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Attendant Gentlemen of the Palace) would have six hundred piculs.
Ranks below these were also increased.
He returned to the capital with his army.
Thereupon, granaries and treasuries were opened widely,
and officers and soldiers were rewarded.
The sons of the Èrqiān Shí (Two Thousand Piculs) officials from various commanderies who had accompanied him on the expedition
were all appointed as Tàizǐ Shèrén (Attendants to the Crown Prince).
At this time, Dòu Dú was Wèiwèi (Commander of the Guards),
Dòu Jǐng and Dòu Guī were both Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant), Fèngchē (Charioteer), and Fùmǎ Dūwèi (Commandant of the Imperial Equerries).
The four families competed to build mansions,
exhausting the finest craftsmen.
The following year,
an imperial edict stated:
"Dàjiāngjūn Dòu Xiàn,
who campaigned last year,
conquered and destroyed the Northern Dí,
was granted titles and rewards by the court,
but firmly declined to accept them.
It is an old custom for imperial maternal relatives
to receive noble titles and land.
Therefore, enfeoff Dòu Xiàn as Guànjūn Hóu (Marquis of Guànjūn),
with a fief of twenty thousand households;
Dòu Dú as Yǎn Hóu (Marquis of Yǎn);
Dòu Jǐng as Rǔyáng Hóu (Marquis of Rǔyáng);
and Dòu Guī as Xiàyáng Hóu (Marquis of Xiàyáng),
each with six thousand households."
Dòu Xiàn alone did not accept the enfeoffment,
and then led troops to garrison Liángzhōu,
with Shìzhōng Dèng Dié acting as Cēngxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the West) as his deputy.
The Northern Chányú, because Han had returned his attendant brother,
again dispatched Chēxié Chú Wáng and others to approach Jūyán Sài (Jūyán Pass),
wishing to enter court and request an imperial envoy.
Dòu Xiàn memorialized to dispatch Dàjiāngjūn Zhōng Hùjūn (Grand General's Central Protector of the Army) Bān Gù, acting as Zhōngláng Jiāng,
with Sīmǎ Liáng Fèng, to welcome him.
It happened that the Northern Chányú was defeated by the Southern Xiongnú,
was wounded, and fled.
Bān Gù returned from Sīqú Hǎi.
Dòu Xiàn, seeing the Northern barbarians were weak,
then wished to destroy them.
The following year,
he again dispatched Yòu Xiàowèi (Right Commandant) Gěng Kuí, Sīmǎ Rèn Shàng, Zhào Bó, and others to lead troops to attack the Northern barbarians at Jīnwēi Shān (Jīnwēi Mountain).
They thoroughly defeated them,
capturing a great many.
The Northern Chányú fled,
and his whereabouts were unknown.
Dòu Xiàn, having pacified the Xiongnú,
his prestige greatly flourished.
He took Gěng Kuí, Rèn Shàng, and others as his claws and teeth,
and Dèng Dié, Guō Huáng as his confidants.
Men like Bān Gù and Fù Yì
were all placed in his personal secretariat,
to manage literary affairs.
Many Inspectors, Administrators, and Magistrates came from his门.
Zhì Shòu, the Director of the Palace Writers, and Yuè Huī both, by clashing with his wishes,
successively committed suicide.
Because of this, court officials trembled with fear,
and complied with his directives at first wind.
Meanwhile, Dòu Dú was promoted to Special Advanced Official,
gaining the right to nominate officials,
and was treated with the same courtesies as the Three Ducal Ministers.
Dòu Jǐng became Chief Commandant of the Capital,
and Dòu Guī became Superintendent of the Imperial Clan.
Their power and prominence were immense,
shaking the capital.
Although all were arrogant and unrestrained,
Jǐng was particularly so.
His servants and household cavalry relied on their power and influence,
to oppress common people,
forcibly seize property,
usurp criminals,
and abduct women.
Merchants closed their doors,
as if avoiding bandits.
The officials in charge were timid,
none daring to report him.
The Empress Dowager heard of it,
and sent an Usher to dismiss Jǐng from his office,
appointing him as a Special Advanced Official to attend court.
Dòu Guī had loved the classics since childhood,
and was frugal and self-disciplined.
He was sent out as Administrator of Wèi Jùn,
and later moved to be Administrator of Yǐngchuān.
The Dòu family, father and sons, brothers, all occupied prominent positions,
filling the court.
His uncle Dòu Bà was Commander of the City Gates,
Bà's younger brother Dòu Bāo was Grand Architect,
Bāo's younger brother Dòu Jiā was Prefect of the Palace,
and there were over ten others who were Court Attendants, Generals, Grand Masters, or Palace Gentlemen.
Having borne heavy responsibilities, Dòu Xiàn
became even more overbearing.
In the fourth year,
Dèng Dié was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ráng.
Dié, along with his younger brother Dèng Lěi, Commander of Infantry, and their mother Yuán,
as well as Dòu Xiàn's son-in-law Guō Jǔ, Commander of the Archer-Guards,
and Jǔ's father Guō Huáng, Prefect of Chánglè,
all formed a close alliance.
Yuán and Jǔ both entered and exited the forbidden palace freely,
Jǔ gaining the favor of the Empress Dowager,
and together they plotted murder.
The Emperor secretly knew of their scheme,
and decided with his favored Palace Regular Attendant Zhèng Zhòng to execute them.
As Dòu Xiàn was outside the capital,
fearing he might cause rebellion out of dread,
the Emperor held back for a time.
When Dòu Xiàn and Dèng Dié returned to the capital with their armies,
an imperial edict ordered the Grand Herald to hold a credential and welcome them in the suburbs,
bestowing gifts upon the military officials according to their rank.
Once Xiàn and the others arrived,
the Emperor proceeded to the Northern Palace,
and issued an edict to the Chief Commandant of the Capital and the five Colonels to lead troops to garrison the Southern and Northern Palaces,
close the city gates,
and arrest Dié, Lěi, Huáng, and Jǔ.
All were imprisoned and executed,
and their families were exiled to Hépǔ.
An Usher-Director was dispatched to seize Dòu Xiàn's seal and ribbon as Grand General,
and he was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Guànjūn.
Dòu Xiàn, Dú, Jǐng, and Guī were all sent to their respective fiefs.
Out of consideration for the Empress Dowager, the Emperor
did not wish to explicitly execute Dòu Xiàn,
but chose strict and capable officials to supervise him.
When Dòu Xiàn, Dú, and Jǐng arrived at their fiefs,
they were all compelled to commit suicide.
All clan members and retainers who had served as officials under Dòu Xiàn were dismissed and returned to their native prefectures.
As Dòu Guī had always been self-disciplined,
he was not forced to die.
The next year, for giving out grain to poor people,
he was moved to be enfeoffed as Marquis of Luó,
and was not allowed to have officials or subjects.
Originally,
when Empress Dòu slandered the Liáng family,
Dòu Xiàn and others were involved in the plot.
In the tenth year of Yǒngyuán,
Liáng Táng and his brothers,
returning from exile in Jiǔzhēn,
passed through Chángshā.
They compelled Dòu Guī to commit suicide.
Later, when Empress Dowager Héxī Dèng presided over the court,
in the third year of Yǒngchū,
an edict commanded all Dòu family members who had previously returned to their native prefectures, along with Wànquán, Marquis of Ānfēng, to return to the capital.
Wànquán's youngest son was Zhāng.
Commentary states: Wèi Qīng and Huò Qùbìng, relying on the strong armies of the Hàn,
fought the Xiongnú for years,
consuming more than half of the nation's resources,
yet they did not truly defeat the cunning barbarians.
Later generations still praised them as good generals.
Was it not because they ended their lives with honor?
Dòu Xiàn led an army of Qiāng, Hú, and border auxiliaries,
and in one campaign cleared the northern frontier,
even pursuing the fleeing enemy beyond Jīluò,
watering his horses at Bǐdí.
He inscribed stone and dedicated cauldrons,
reporting his achievements to the ancestral temple.
His merits and accomplishments,
taken together, far surpassed those before him.
Yet later generations do not praise him.
This is because of his later transgressions.
This is why base conduct
is so detested by gentlemen.
Those few obtained their positions merely through the bedchamber,
not by seeking out obscure talents,
or selecting and promoting them.
When Wèi Qīng was a sick servant,
and General Dòu was regretting his errors,
they were too busy exerting themselves,
and had no dawn to sing.
How could they have expected to carve out rich lands,
and enjoy exalted titles?
Dōngfāng Shuò said,
"If used, they become tigers;
if not used, they become mice."
It is true.
Judging by this,
how can a scholar with brilliant talent buried in the dust
be withstood?
Zhāng's courtesy name was Bóxiàng.
He loved learning in his youth,
and had literary talent.
He was friends with Mǎ Róng and Cuī Yuàn,
and they recommended each other.
During the Yǒngchū period,
the Three Fǔ regions were afflicted by Qiāng rebels.
Zhāng fled to the eastern states for refuge,
making his home in Wàihuáng.
He lived in poverty,
with a thatched hut and simple food,
personally working hard to support his parents.
Yet he never stopped lecturing and reading.
Dèng Kāng, the Grand Coachman,
heard of his reputation
and invited him to associate.
Zhāng refused to go,
which made Kāng respect him even more.
At that time, scholars referred to the Eastern Lodge as the "Old Man's Storehouse"
and the Daoist "Penglai Mountain."
Kāng then recommended Zhāng to enter the Eastern Lodge as a Collator.
At the beginning of Emperor Shùn's reign,
Zhāng's daughter, aged twelve,
was able to compose essays.
She was chosen for the Imperial Harem for her talent and beauty,
and was favored,
becoming a Noble Lady alongside Empress Liáng.
Zhāng was promoted to Commander of the Feathered Forest Guard,
and then transferred to Colonel of Cavalry.
Zhāng was humble towards scholars
and welcomed his peers,
earning great renown.
At this time, both the Liáng and Dòu families were powerful,
each having their own retainers.
Many caused trouble between them.
Zhāng treated them with sincerity,
and thus avoided misfortune.
The Noble Lady died young.
The Emperor constantly grieved for her,
and ordered the imperial historians to erect a stele to commemorate her virtues.
Zhāng himself composed the inscription.
After the Noble Lady's death,
the Emperor's respectful treatment of him did not wane.
In the fifth year of Yǒnghé,
he was promoted to Prefect of the Palace.
In the second year of Hàn'ān,
he was transferred to Grand Herald.
In the first year of Jiànkāng,
Empress Liáng governed as regent.
Zhāng resigned,
and died at home.
His second son, Dòu Táng,
was exceptionally talented,
and rose to the position of Commander of the Fierce Tiger Guards.
Eulogy says: Earnest Ānfēng,
also praised for his talent and might.
He held the Hé Yòu,
and returned with his allegiance to the diagram.
Mèngsūn made the borders clear,
campaigning north and opening the west.
Dòu Xiàn truly emptied the desert,
sending distant troops to Jīnshān.
He heard the reed pipes at the Dragon Court,
and carved stone at Yànrán.
Though his cauldron was broken,
the imperial prestige was proclaimed.
Biography of Mǎ Yuán, Chapter 14 (Son Liáo, Son Fáng, Nephew Yán, Grandson Lèng)
Mǎ Yuán [馬援], courtesy name Wényuān [文淵],
was a native of Máolíng [茂陵], Fúfēng [扶風].
His ancestor Zhào Shē [趙奢] was a general of Zhào [趙],
and was titled Mǎfú Jūn [馬服君].
His descendants therefore took Mǎ [馬] as their surname.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ [武],
his family, as officials earning two thousand *dàn* [石], moved from Hándān [邯鄲] to Máolíng.
His great-grandfather Tōng [通],
was enfeoffed as Chónghé Hóu [重合侯] for his merits,
but was implicated in his elder brother Hélúo’s [何羅] rebellion
and executed.
Thus, Mǎ Yuán’s [馬援] family was not prominent for two generations.
Mǎ Yuán’s [馬援] three elder brothers, Kuàng [況], Yú [余], and Yuán [員],
all possessed talent and ability,
and during Wáng Mǎng’s [王莽] time, all held positions of two thousand *dàn* [石].
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] was orphaned at twelve,
and had great ambitions from a young age.
His elder brothers regarded him as extraordinary.
He once studied the *Qí Shī* [齊詩],
but felt he could not adhere to the exact wording and phrases.
So he bid farewell to Kuàng [況],
wishing to go to the border regions to farm and herd.
Kuàng [況] said:
“You possess great talent,
and will mature late.
A skilled artisan does not show people his uncarved wood.
Just follow your inclinations.”
Soon after, Kuàng [況] died.
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] observed mourning for a full year,
not leaving the burial site;
he respectfully served his widowed sister-in-law,
not wearing a cap or entering the house.
Later, he became a Dūyóu [督郵] of the commandery.
He was sending a prisoner to the Sīmìng Fǔ [司命府].
The prisoner had committed a serious crime,
but Mǎ Yuán [馬援] took pity on him and released him.
He then fled to Běidì [北地].
When an amnesty was granted,
he stayed there to herd livestock.
Many guests and retainers gathered around him,
and he eventually had several hundred households under his command.
He then traveled between Lǒng [隴] and Hàn [漢],
often saying to his guests:
“A man of ambition,
when in poverty, should become firmer;
when old, should become stronger.”
He settled down to farm and herd,
eventually owning several thousand head of cattle, horses, and sheep,
and tens of thousands of *hú* [斛] of grain.
Then he sighed, saying:
“In accumulating wealth and property,
what is valued is the ability to give and relieve distress.
Otherwise, one is merely a slave to money.”
So he distributed all his wealth among his brothers, relatives, and old friends,
wearing only a sheepskin coat and leather breeches himself.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng’s [王莽] reign,
armies rose in all directions.
Wáng Mǎng’s [王莽] younger cousin, the Grand General Wèi [衛將軍] Lín [林], widely recruited heroes and talents.
He then appointed Mǎ Yuán [馬援] and Yuán Shè [原涉] from the same county as his aides,
and recommended them to Wáng Mǎng [王莽].
Wáng Mǎng [王莽] made Yuán Shè [原涉] the Zhènrón Dàyǐn [鎮戎大尹],
and Mǎ Yuán [馬援] the Xīnchéng Dàyǐn [新成大尹].
When Wáng Mǎng [王莽] was defeated,
Mǎ Yuán’s [馬援] elder brother Yuán [員], who was then the Zēngshān Liánlǜ [增山連率],
left his commandery with Mǎ Yuán [馬援],
and again sought refuge in Liángzhōu [涼州].
When Emperor Shìzǔ [世祖] ascended the throne,
Yuán [員] first went to Luòyáng [洛陽].
The Emperor sent Yuán [員] back to his commandery,
where he died in office.
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] remained in Xīzhōu [西州].
Wěi Xiāo [隗囂] greatly respected him,
appointing Mǎ Yuán [馬援] as Suídé Jiāngjūn [綏德將軍],
and consulting him on strategies.
At this time, Gōngsūn Shù [公孫述] declared himself emperor in Shǔ [蜀].
Wěi Xiāo [隗囂] sent Mǎ Yuán [馬援] to observe him.
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] and Gōngsūn Shù [公孫述] had lived in the same neighborhood
and were on good terms.
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] expected that upon arrival they would clasp hands and rejoice as in former times,
but Gōngsūn Shù [公孫述] grandly arrayed his palace guards
to usher Mǎ Yuán [馬援] in.
After they bowed to each other and completed the rites,
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] was sent out to his guest quarters.
Gōngsūn Shù [公孫述] then had a plain cloth tunic
and a Jiāoràng Guān [交讓冠] made for Mǎ Yuán [馬援],
and assembled all his officials in the ancestral temple,
setting up a seat for his old acquaintance.
Gōngsūn Shù [公孫述] rode in a carriage with phoenix banners and yak-tail standards,
with guards shouting to clear the way,
bowing deeply as he entered.
He held a very grand banquet for his officials and retainers,
wishing to bestow upon Mǎ Yuán [馬援] the title of Marquis and Grand General.
All the guests were pleased to stay,
but Mǎ Yuán [馬援] enlightened them, saying:
“The outcome of the struggle for the world is yet undecided.
Gōngsūn Shù [公孫述] does not stop eating to welcome men of worth,
and plan with them for success or failure.
Instead, he concerns himself with superficial appearances,
like a wooden dummy.
How can such a man long detain the talents of the world?”
He then declined and returned,
telling Wěi Xiāo [隗囂]:
“Zǐyáng [子陽] is merely a frog in a well,
vainly exalting himself.
It would be better to focus your attention on the east.”
In the winter of the fourth year of Jiànwǔ [建武] (28 CE),
Wěi Xiāo [隗囂] sent Mǎ Yuán [馬援] with a letter to Luòyáng [洛陽].
When Mǎ Yuán [馬援] arrived,
he was granted an audience in the Xuāndé Diàn [宣德殿].
Emperor Shìzǔ [世祖] greeted Mǎ Yuán [馬援] with a smile, saying:
“You have wandered between two emperors.
Seeing you now fills me with great shame.”
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] prostrated himself and apologized,
then said:
“In the world today,
it is not only the lord who chooses his ministers,
but the minister also chooses his lord.
I am from the same county as Gōngsūn Shù [公孫述],
and we were on good terms in our youth.
When I previously went to Shǔ [蜀],
Gōngsūn Shù [公孫述] had guards with pikes before admitting me.
Now I have come a long way.
How does Your Majesty know I am not an assassin or a villain,
yet you treat me with such simplicity?”
The Emperor again smiled and said:
“You are no assassin,
but merely a persuader.”
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] said:
“The world has turned upside down,
and those who usurp titles are countless.
Now that I have seen Your Majesty,
your broad and magnanimous character,
which matches that of Gāozǔ [高祖],
I know that the true Emperor has a distinct nature.”
The Emperor greatly admired him.
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] accompanied the Emperor south to Líqiū [黎丘],
and then to Dōnghǎi [東海].
Upon their return,
he was made a Dàizhào [待詔].
The Emperor sent Grand Master Tàizhōng [太中大夫] Lái Xī [來歙] with an imperial envoy's staff to escort Mǎ Yuán [馬援] back west to Lǒngyòu [隴右].
Wěi Xiāo [隗囂] slept and rose with Mǎ Yuán [馬援],
asking him about rumors from the east and the successes and failures of the capital.
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] told Wěi Xiāo [隗囂]:
“When I was at court,
the Emperor granted audiences to several tens of people,
and each time we met for conversation,
from dusk until dawn.
His talent, wisdom, courage, and strategy
are unmatched.
Moreover, he is open and sincere,
hiding nothing,
broad-minded and with great principles,
much like Emperor Gāo [高帝].
His learning is extensive,
and in matters of governance and eloquent debate,
he is unparalleled in previous generations.”
Wěi Xiāo [隗囂] asked:
“How do you compare him to Emperor Gāo [高帝]?”
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] replied:
“He is not as good.
Emperor Gāo [高帝] had no fixed preferences;
the present Emperor favors official matters,
acts always according to regulations,
and does not enjoy drinking.”
Wěi Xiāo [隗囂] was displeased,
saying:
“According to your words,
is he then inferior?”
Nevertheless, he generally trusted Mǎ Yuán [馬援],
and thus sent his eldest son Xún [恂] as a hostage.
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] then took his family and returned with Xún [恂] to Luòyáng [洛陽].
After several months, he had no other official duties.
Mǎ Yuán [馬援] considered that the three Fǔ [輔] regions had vast and fertile land,
and that his retainers were very numerous.
So he submitted a memorial requesting to establish military colonies in the Shànglín Yuàn [上林苑].
The Emperor granted his request.
At this time, Kuí Xiāo, following Wáng Yuán’s plan,
became even more suspicious and hesitant.
Mǎ Yuán repeatedly sent letters to rebuke and reason with Xiāo.
Xiāo resented Mǎ Yuán for betraying him,
and receiving the letters only increased his anger.
Subsequently, he dispatched troops to resist Hàn.
Mǎ Yuán then submitted a memorial, saying:
“I, Mǎ Yuán, reflecting on having committed myself to the enlightened court,
and serving Your Majesty,
originally had no recommendation from a senior official
or assistance from those around me.
If I do not speak for myself,
how can Your Majesty hear of it?
To be in a high position yet unable to make people humble,
or to be in a low position yet unable to make people proud,
or to have a grievance against someone yet be unable to cause them trouble –
this is what I find shameful.
Therefore, I dare to risk offending and violating taboos,
and at the risk of death, present my true feelings.
I and Kuí Xiāo
were originally true friends.
Initially,
when Xiāo sent me east,
he said to me: ‘I originally intended to side with Hàn.
I wish for you to go and observe it.
If it is acceptable in your opinion,
then I will wholeheartedly commit.’
When I returned,
I reported with a sincere heart,
truly intending to guide him towards good,
not daring to deceive him with injustice.
But Xiāo harbored treacherous intentions himself,
like a thief hating his master,
and the feelings of resentment and malice were thus directed at me.
If I do not speak,
then there is no way for this to reach Your Majesty.
I beg to be allowed to go to Your Majesty’s temporary residence,
to fully present my strategies for eliminating Xiāo,
to empty my heart,
express my humble plans,
and then retire to the fields.
Then I will die without regret.”
The Emperor then summoned Mǎ Yuán to discuss strategy,
and Mǎ Yuán fully explained his plans.
Consequently, the Emperor dispatched Mǎ Yuán to lead five thousand élite cavalry,
to travel back and forth persuading Xiāo’s generals such as Gāo Jùn and Rèn Yǔ,
as well as the Qiāng chieftains,
explaining the consequences of their actions,
thereby breaking up Xiāo’s supporters.
Mǎ Yuán also wrote a letter to Xiāo’s general Yáng Guǎng,
to make him understand and persuade Xiāo,
saying:
“Chūn Qīng, are you well?
Since our last parting in Jì Nán,
there has been no news or messenger.
I returned to Cháng’ān some time ago,
and have since stayed in Shàng Lín.
I secretly observe that the four seas are now settled,
and the myriad people are of the same mind.
Yet Jì Mèng remains defiant and rebellious,
setting an example for the world.
I constantly fear that the people within the seas will grind their teeth,
and wish to dismember each other.
Therefore, I send this letter with deep affection,
to express my compassionate plan.
Then I heard that Jì Mèng blamed me,
and listened to Wáng Yóu Wēng’s flattering and perverse words,
believing that everything west of Hán Gǔ
could be settled with a mere lift of his foot.
Looking at it now,
how has it turned out?
I recently arrived in Hé Nèi,
and visited Bó Chūn.
I saw his servant Jí returning from the west,
who said that Bó Chūn’s younger brother Zhòng Shū, upon seeing Jí,
wanted to ask if Bó Chūn was well,
but eventually could not speak,
crying day and night,
rolling in the dust.
He also spoke of the indescribable sorrow of their family.
An enemy can be stabbed but not defiled.
When I heard this,
I could not help but weep.
I have always known Jì Mèng to be filial and loving,
surpassing Zēng Shēn and Mǐn Sūn.
If he is filial to his parents,
how can he not be kind to his children?
How can his children be carrying the ‘three wooden yokes’
while he acts wildly and recklessly,
bringing upon himself the fate of being ‘divided like a soup’
Jì Mèng himself used to say that the reason he maintained his army
was to protect the land of his parents and preserve their tombs.
He also said that he merely wanted to treat scholars and officials generously.
Yet now, what he wishes to preserve, he will destroy and lose;
what he wishes to protect, he will ruin and damage;
what he wishes to treat generously, he will instead treat meagerly.
Jì Mèng once shamed Zǐ Yáng and
did not accept his title.
Now, he wants to join Lù Lù and attach himself to him?
How will he manage to save face?
If he is again demanded heavy hostages, where will he find his son and master to provide them?
In the past, Zǐ Yáng alone wished to treat you as a king,
but Chūn Qīng rejected him.
Now that he is old,
does he instead wish to bow his head and eat from the same trough with mere boys,
shouldering and squeezing into the court of his enemies?
〔一０〕What harm is it for a man to drown rather than be trapped and wander?
〔一一〕Now the state holds deep regard for Chūn Qīng.
It would be advisable to have Niú Rú Qīng and the other esteemed elders and important figures
jointly persuade Jì Mèng.
If the plan is not accepted,
then one can truly leave with regret.
Previously, I unrolled a map of the land
and saw that there are one hundred and six commanderies and states under Heaven.
How can he wish to use his small two states to contend against the hundred and four of Zhū Xià?
Chūn Qīng serves Jì Mèng,
outwardly observing the duty between lord and subject,
and inwardly having the bond of friendship.
If it is a matter of lord and subject,
one should certainly remonstrate and contend.
If it is a matter of friends,
one should encourage and advise.
〔一三〕How can one know that it will lead to no success,
yet merely wilt and hold one’s tongue,
crossing one’s hands and following the clan to destruction?
〔一四〕To make a plan now is still good.
If it goes beyond this,
it will lose its flavor.
〔一五〕Moreover, Lái Jūn Shū is a trustworthy gentleman in the world,
and the court values him.
His intention is earnest,
always speaking solely for Xī Zhōu.
I have discussed with the court,
and they particularly wish to establish trust in this matter,
〔一六〕and will certainly not break the promise.
I cannot stay long;
I wish for a swift reply.”
Guǎng ultimately did not reply.
In the eighth year,
the Emperor personally marched west to attack Xiāo,
reaching Qī.
Many generals believed that with the importance of the imperial army,
it was not advisable to penetrate deep into dangerous terrain,
and the decision was still hesitant and undecided.
Just then, Mǎ Yuán was summoned.
He arrived at night,
and the Emperor was greatly pleased.
He led him in
and presented all the generals’ opinions to him for consideration.
Mǎ Yuán then explained that Kuí Xiāo’s generals and troops were in a state of collapse,
and that an advance of the army would inevitably lead to victory.
He also, before the Emperor,
piled rice to form mountains and valleys,
drawing and illustrating the terrain,
showing the routes for all the armies to advance and retreat,
analyzing every twist and turn,
making it clearly understandable.
The Emperor said:
“The enemy is within my grasp!”
The next morning,
the army advanced to Dì Yī,
and Xiāo’s forces were utterly routed.
In the ninth year,
Mǎ Yuàn was appointed Grandee Remonstrant (Tàizhōng Dàfū),
and assisted Lái Xī in supervising the generals who pacified Liángzhōu.
Since the end of Wáng Mǎng’s reign,
the Western Qiāng had plundered the borders,
and then settled within the frontier,
with many of Jīnchéng Commandery’s dependent counties falling into their hands.
Lái Xī memorialized, saying that Lǒngxī was being ravaged,
and no one but Mǎ Yuàn could stabilize it.
In the eleventh year, in summer,
an imperial edict appointed Mǎ Yuàn as Administrator of Lǒngxī (Lǒngxī Tàishǒu).
Mǎ Yuàn then dispatched three thousand infantry and cavalry
to attack and defeat the Xiānlíng Qiāng at Líntáo,
beheading several hundred and
capturing over ten thousand horses, cattle, and sheep.
More than eight thousand Qiāng who had been guarding the passes surrendered to Mǎ Yuàn.
Various tribes, numbering in the tens of thousands,
gathered and plundered,
resisting at the Hàoqǐn Ài (浩亹隘) Pass.
Mǎ Yuàn and General Wǔwǔ (Yángwǔ Jiāngjūn) Mǎ Chéng attacked them.
The Qiāng then moved their wives, children, and baggage train to obstruct the Yǔnwú Gǔ Valley.
Mǎ Yuàn stealthily took a hidden path
and surprised their camp.
The Qiāng were greatly alarmed and broken,
and again moved far away to the Tángyì Gǔ Valley.
Mǎ Yuàn again pursued and attacked them.
The Qiāng led their elite troops to gather on the northern mountain.
Mǎ Yuàn arrayed his army facing the mountain,
while dispatching several hundred cavalry to circle around and raid their rear.
Under cover of night, they set fires
and beat drums, shouting loudly.
The barbarians then suffered a great defeat,
with over a thousand heads being taken in total.
As Mǎ Yuàn’s forces were few,
he could not pursue them exhaustively.
He gathered their grain, provisions, and livestock and returned.
Mǎ Yuàn was struck by an arrow that pierced his shin.
The Emperor sent an imperial edict to commend him,
and bestowed several thousand head of cattle and sheep.
Mǎ Yuàn distributed all of them to his guests.
At this time,
the court officials, considering the area west of Pòqiāng in Jīnchéng
to be remote and infested with bandits,
discussed abandoning it.
Mǎ Yuàn memorialized, stating:
“West of Pòqiāng, many cities are intact and strong,
easily defensible.
Their land is fertile
and irrigation flows freely.
If the Qiāng are allowed to remain in Huángzhōng,
they will cause endless harm,
and cannot be allowed to stay.”
The Emperor agreed with him.
Thereupon, an edict was issued to the Administrator of Wǔwēi (Wǔwēi Tàishǒu),
ordering all the displaced people of Jīnchéng to return.
More than three thousand households returned,
each to their former settlements.
Mǎ Yuàn requested that chief officials be appointed for them,
city walls be repaired,
fortified outposts be erected,
irrigated fields be opened,
and farming and herding be encouraged.
The commandery people were content with their livelihoods.
He also sent the Qiāng chieftain Yáng Fēng to persuade the Qiāng outside the passes,
who all came to establish friendly relations.
Furthermore, regarding the Dī people of Wǔdū who had betrayed Gōngsūn Shù and surrendered,
Mǎ Yuàn memorialized to restore all their marquises, kings, lords, and chiefs,
and granted them seals and ribbons.
The Emperor fully complied with this.
Then Mǎ Chéng's army was disbanded.
In the thirteenth year,
the Cānláng Qiāng of Wǔdū, along with various tribes outside the passes, became bandits,
killing chief officials.
Mǎ Yuàn led over four thousand men to attack them.
Upon reaching Dīdào County,
the Qiāng were on the mountain.
Mǎ Yuàn's army occupied strategic ground,
cutting off their water and fodder,
and did not engage in battle.
The Qiāng then became exhausted and desperate.
Several tens of thousands of households of chieftains fled out of the passes,
and over ten thousand men of various tribes all surrendered.
Thus, Lǒngyòu became peaceful and quiet.
Mǎ Yuàn made an effort to cultivate kindness and trust,
treating his subordinates with generosity,
and entrusting officials with their duties,
only overseeing the general framework.
Guests and old friends
filled his gate daily.
Whenever various clerks reported on external affairs,
Mǎ Yuàn would say:
“This is the duty of the Aide or Clerk (chéng, yuàn).
Why bother me with it?
Please pity this old man,
and let me roam freely.
If powerful clans oppress common people,
or cunning Qiāng wish to rebel,
these are matters for the Administrator.”
Once, in a neighboring county, there was a case of revenge.
Officials and common people were alarmed, saying the Qiāng had rebelled,
and the populace fled into the city.
The Prefect of Dídào came to his gate,
requesting to close the city and dispatch troops.
Mǎ Yuàn, who was drinking with guests at the time,
laughed loudly and said:
“How dare those barbarian scoundrels attack us again?
Tell the Prefect of Dídào to return and guard his residence.
Those who are truly frightened and anxious
can hide under their beds.”
Later, things gradually settled,
and the commandery admired him.
After serving for six years,
he was recalled to serve as Colonel of the Tiger’s Might (Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng).
Initially,
when Mǎ Yuàn was in Lǒngxī, he submitted a memorial
proposing that Wǔzhū coins should be cast as before.
The matter was sent down to the Three Ducal Ministries (Sānfǔ),
which memorialized that it was not yet permissible.
The matter was then shelved.
When Mǎ Yuàn returned,
he requested the former memorial from the ducal offices,
which contained more than ten objections.
He then provided explanations for each point
and resubmitted a detailed memorial.
The Emperor followed his advice,
and the empire benefited from its convenience.
Since Mǎ Yuàn's return to the capital,
he was frequently granted audiences.
He had distinct beard and hair,
and his eyebrows and eyes were like a painting.
He was skilled in presenting arguments and responding to questions,
and particularly good at narrating past events.
Whenever he spoke of the elders of Sānfǔ,
down to the young people of the villages,
all were worthy of attention.
From the Crown Prince and various kings who attended to listen,
none failed to lend an ear and forget their weariness.
He was also good at military strategy.
The Emperor often said,
“Fúbō's military discussions
are in accord with my intentions,”
and whenever there was a plan,
it was never not adopted.
Initially,
Wé Sǐ (維汜) from Juǎn (卷)
made deceptive claims of divinity,
and had several hundred disciples.
He was executed for his crimes.
Later, his disciples Lǐ Guǎng (李廣) and others declared that Wé Sǐ had transformed into a god and was immortal,
thereby deceiving and deluding the common people.
In the seventeenth year,
they gathered their followers
and attacked and captured Wǎnchéng,
killing Liú Mǐn (劉閔), the Marquis of Wǎn.
They declared themselves
“Great Master of Nányuè” (Nányuè Dàshī).
An attendant (yèzhě), Zhāng Zōng (張宗), was dispatched with several thousand troops to suppress them,
but he was again defeated by Lǐ Guǎng.
Thereupon, Mǎ Yuàn was ordered to mobilize troops from various commanderies,
totaling over ten thousand men,
to attack and defeat Lǐ Guǎng and his followers,
and beheaded them.
Furthermore, the Jiāozhǐ woman Zhēng Cè and her younger sister Zhēng È rebelled.
They attacked and captured their commandery.
The Mányí of Jiǔzhēn, Rìnán, and Hépǔ all responded to them,
raiding more than sixty cities south of the ridge.
Zhēng Cè declared herself king.
Thereupon, an imperial edict appointed Mǎ Yuán as Fúbō Jiāngjūn,
with Fúlè Hóu Liú Lóng as his deputy,
to oversee the Lóuchuán Jiāngjūn Duàn Zhì and others in attacking Jiāozhǐ from the south.
When the army reached Hépǔ, Duàn Zhì fell ill and died.
An imperial edict ordered Mǎ Yuán to take command of his troops as well.
He then advanced along the coast,
cutting a path through the mountains for over a thousand *lǐ*.
In the spring of the eighteenth year (of Jiànwǔ),
the army reached Làngpó Shàng [Lake],
and fought the rebels.
They defeated them,
beheading several thousand,
and receiving the surrender of over ten thousand.
Mǎ Yuán pursued Zhēng Cè and her group to Jīnxī,
defeating them repeatedly.
The rebels then scattered and fled.
In the first month of the following year,
Zhēng Cè and Zhēng È were beheaded,
and their heads were sent to Luòyáng.
Mǎ Yuán was enfeoffed as Xīnxī Hóu,
with an estate of three thousand households.
Mǎ Yuán then slaughtered oxen and poured wine,
to feast and reward his soldiers.
He calmly said to his officials and subordinates:
"My younger cousin, Shǎoyóu, often lamented my passionate ambition,
saying: 'A man living in this world
needs only enough clothing and food,
to ride in a simple carriage,
and drive a slow horse,
to be a commandery clerk,
guard ancestral tombs,
and be called a good person by his鄉 *xiāng* [village] and里 *lǐ* [neighborhood];
that is enough.
Seeking excess
only brings oneself hardship.'
When I was between Làngpó and Xīlǐ,
before the barbarians were eliminated,
with floods below and mist above,
and the poisonous *qì* intensely steaming,
I looked up to see flying kites flapping and falling into the water.
Lying there, I recalled Shǎoyóu's words from his lifetime.
How could I achieve that (simple life)?
Now, relying on the strength of the scholar-officials,
having received great imperial favor,
I, in my unworthiness, precede you gentlemen in wearing the golden seal and purple ribbon.
I am both pleased and ashamed."
The officers and soldiers all prostrated themselves, shouting "Long live!"
Mǎ Yuán led over two thousand large and small warships,
and more than twenty thousand soldiers,
to attack the remaining rebels of Jiǔzhēn, such as Dū Yáng,
from Wúgōng to Jūfēng.
They killed and captured over five thousand people,
and Jiàonán was completely pacified.
Mǎ Yuán memorialized that Xīyú County had thirty-two thousand households,
and its distant border was over a thousand *lǐ* from the imperial court.
He requested it be divided into Fēngxī and Wànghǎi counties.
This was granted.
