Wherever Mǎ Yuán passed, he built city walls for commanderies and counties,
and dug canals for irrigation,
to benefit the people.
He memorialized over ten matters where the Yuè laws contradicted the Hàn laws,
and clarified the old regulations with the Yuè people to restrain them.
Thereafter, the Luòyuè followed the precedents set by General Mǎ.
In the autumn of the twentieth year,
the army returned to the capital,
but fourteen or fifteen tenths of the military officials and soldiers had died from malaria and epidemics.
Mǎ Yuán was granted one armored carriage,
and his rank in court audiences was among the Nine Ministers.
Mǎ Yuán was fond of riding,
and skilled at distinguishing famous horses.
In Jiāozhǐ, he obtained a Luòyuè bronze drum,
which he cast into a horse model,
and presented upon his return.
He then memorialized, saying:
"In traversing the sky, none is like the dragon;
in traversing the earth, none is like the horse.
Horses are the foundation of weaponry and armor,
and of great use to the state.
In times of peace, they distinguish the order of noble and humble;
in times of change, they assist in overcoming difficulties both near and far.
In ancient times, there was Qíjì,
who could travel a thousand *lǐ* in a day.
Bólè saw him and
recognized him clearly without confusion.
In recent times, there was Xīhé Zǐyú,
who also understood the art of horse physiognomy.
Zǐyú transmitted it to Xīhé Yí Chángrǔ;
Chángrǔ transmitted it to Màolíng Dīng Jūndū;
Jūndū transmitted it to Chéngjì Yáng Zǐā.
I, your servant Mǎ Yuán, once studied under Zǐā,
receiving the bone methods for physiognomy of horses.
Examined in practice,
they invariably prove effective.
I, your humble servant, believe that hearing is not as good as seeing,
and watching a shadow is not as good as observing the form itself.
If one now wishes to represent it on a living horse,
the bone methods are difficult to fully convey,
and cannot be passed on to later generations.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Dōngmén Jīng, a skilled horse physiognomist,
cast a bronze horse model and presented it.
An imperial edict ordered the horse to be placed outside Lǔbān Mén,
and Lǔbān Mén was then renamed Jīnmǎ Mén.
I, your servant, have respectfully relied on the methods of Yí Shì,
the mouth and teeth methods of Bó Shì,
the lips of Xiè Shì,
and the body methods of Dīng Shì,
combining these several schools' bone physiognomy to create this model."
The horse was three *chǐ* five *cùn* high,
and four *chǐ* five *cùn* in girth.
An imperial edict ordered it to be placed below Xuāndé Diàn,
to serve as a model for famous horses.
Originally,
when Mǎ Yuán's army returned,
and was about to arrive,
many old acquaintances came to welcome and congratulate him.
Mèng Jì of Pínglíng,
known for his strategizing,
congratulated Mǎ Yuán at the gathering.
Mǎ Yuán said to him:
"I expected some good words from you;
why do you act like everyone else?
Previously, Fúbō Jiāngjūn Lù Bódé opened up and established seven commanderies,
but was only enfeoffed with a few hundred households.
Now, I have done minor work,
yet am unworthily granted a large county.
With shallow merit and rich reward,
how can it last long?
What advice do you, honored sir, have to help me?"
Mèng Jì replied:
"I am not so wise."
Mǎ Yuán said:
"At present, the Xiōngnú and Wūhuán are still disturbing the northern frontier.
I wish to volunteer to attack them.
A man should die in the borderlands,
and be buried wrapped in horsehide.
How can one die in bed, in the hands of children and women?"
Mèng Jì replied:
"Indeed, a valiant warrior should be like this."
About a month after his return,
it happened that the Xiōngnú and Wūhuán raided Fúfēng.
Mǎ Yuán, seeing that the Sānfǔ region was being disturbed,
and the imperial tombs were endangered,
requested to go, and was granted permission.
From the ninth month he was in the capital,
and in the twelfth month he again went out to garrison Xiāngguó.
An imperial edict ordered all officials to see him off.
Mǎ Yuán said to Huángmén Láng Liáng Sōng and Dòu Gù:
"Generally, for people to be noble,
they must be able to endure being humble.
If you gentlemen wish never to be humbled again,
you must hold yourselves firmly in high positions.
Strive to remember my humble words."
Liáng Sōng later indeed suffered disaster due to his excessive nobility,
and Dòu Gù also narrowly escaped.
In the autumn of the following year,
Mǎ Yuán led three thousand cavalry out of Gāoliǔ,
patrolling the barriers and fortresses of Yànmén, Dàijùn, and Shànggǔ.
When the Wūhuán scouts saw the Hàn army arrive,
the barbarians scattered and left.
Mǎ Yuán returned without having gained anything.
Mǎ Yuán once fell ill,
and Liáng Sōng came to visit him.
Liáng Sōng alone bowed by the bedside,
but Mǎ Yuán did not respond.
After Liáng Sōng left,
his sons asked:
"Liáng Bósūn is an imperial son-in-law,
and highly respected at court.
Below the dukes and ministers, there is no one who does not fear him.
Why did you, Father, alone not show him proper courtesy?"
Mǎ Yuán said:
"I am a friend of Liáng Sōng's father.
Though he is noble,
how can he lose his proper place in seniority?"
Liáng Sōng resented him for this.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the Wǔwēi General, Liú Shàng, attacked the Mányí of the Wǔlíng Wǔxī.
He penetrated deeply,
but his army was lost.
Mǎ Yuán thereupon requested to go again.
He was then sixty-two years old,
and the emperor, pitying his age,
did not grant permission.
Mǎ Yuán pleaded, saying:
"Your servant can still don armor and mount a horse."
The emperor ordered him to be tested.
Mǎ Yuán steadied himself in the saddle and looked around,
to show that he was still capable.
The emperor laughed and said:
"How hale and hearty this old man is!"
So he sent Mǎ Yuán to lead Zhongláng Jiāng Mǎ Wǔ, Gěng Shū, Liú Kuāng, Sūn Yǒng, and others,
with forty thousand recruited soldiers from twelve commanderies and convicts from Shǔ, to campaign against Wǔxī.
At night, Mǎ Yuán bid farewell to those seeing him off,
saying to his friend, Yèzhě Dù Yīn:
"I have received great kindness.
My years are pressing, and my remaining days are few,
and I constantly fear not being able to die in the service of the state.
Now I have obtained my wish,
and I will close my eyes content.
But I am afraid that the children of gentlemen, whether serving by my side
or working with me,
are truly difficult to get along with;
this alone vexes me."
The following spring,
the army reached Línxiāng [Xiàn],
and encountered rebels attacking the county.
Mǎ Yuán met them in battle
and defeated them,
beheading and capturing over two thousand people.
They all scattered and fled into the bamboo forests.
Initially,
when the army reached Xiàjùn,
there were two routes to enter.
From Hútóu, the road was short but the water dangerous;
from Chōng, the road was flat but the transport distant.
The emperor initially had doubts about this.
When the army arrived,
Gěng Shū wanted to take the Chōng route,
but Mǎ Yuán believed that it would waste provisions daily,
and that it was better to advance to Hútóu,
seizing its throat,
whereupon the Chōng rebels would break themselves.
He reported this to the emperor,
and the emperor followed Mǎ Yuán's plan.
In the third month,
they advanced and encamped at Hútóu.
The rebels held the high ground and defended the pass.
The current was swift,
and the boats could not ascend.
It happened to be extremely hot.
Many soldiers died of plague,
and Mǎ Yuán also fell ill,
and became severely debilitated.
He dug a chamber into the riverbank
to avoid the scorching heat.
Whenever the rebels ascended the perilous heights and beat drums and shouted,
Mǎ Yuán would drag his feet to observe them.
Those around him, pitying his valiant spirit,
all shed tears for him.
Gěng Shū wrote to his elder brother, Hǎozhì Hóu Gěng Yǎn, saying:
"Earlier, I submitted a memorial that we should first attack Chōng.
Although provisions would be difficult to transport, the soldiers and horses could be fully utilized,
and the tens of thousands of soldiers were eager to be the first to fight.
Now at Hútóu, we cannot advance at all,
and the masses are vexed and dying.
This is truly regrettable.
When we first arrived at Línxiāng,
the rebels unexpectedly came forward themselves.
If we had attacked them at night,
we could have wiped them out.
Fúbō [Jiāngjūn] is like a Hú merchant from the Western Regions,
stopping whenever he reaches a place.
Because of this, we suffered a loss.
Now, indeed, there is plague,
all as I predicted."
Gěng Yǎn received the letter
and reported it to the throne.
The emperor then sent Hǔbēn Zhongláng Jiāng Liáng Sōng by swift post to rebuke Mǎ Yuán,
and to take over as supervisor of the army.
Coincidentally, Mǎ Yuán died of illness.
Liáng Sōng, who harbored long-standing resentment,
then took advantage of the situation to incriminate him.
The emperor was furious
and posthumously recalled Mǎ Yuán's seal and ribbon as Xīnxī Hóu.
Earlier,
Mǎ Yuán's nephews Yán and Dūn were both fond of criticizing and debating,
and associated with frivolous knights-errant.
When Mǎ Yuán was in Jiāozhǐ,
he sent a letter home to admonish them, saying:
"I want you to hear of others' faults
as you hear your parents' names;
your ears may hear,
but your mouths may not speak of them.
To be fond of discussing the strengths and weaknesses of others,
and to wantonly affirm or deny established laws,
this is what I detest most.
I would rather die than hear that my descendants have such conduct.
You know how deeply I detest this,
and the reason I speak of it again
is like arranging a skirt and tying a sash,
reiterating the admonitions of parents,
to make sure you do not forget them.
Lóng Bógāo is honest, prudent, and cautious,
with no careless words.
He is humble, restrained, and frugal,
incorruptible, fair, and awe-inspiring.
I love and respect him,
and wish you would imitate him.
Dù Jìliáng is heroic and chivalrous, fond of righteousness,
grieving with others' sorrows,
and joyful with others' joys.
He loses nothing whether among the pure or the impure.
When his father died, he summoned guests,
and people from several commanderies all arrived.
I love and respect him,
but I do not wish you to imitate him.
If you imitate Bógāo and fail,
you will still be a cautious and diligent scholar,
which is like carving a swan but failing, yet still resembling a duck.
If you imitate Jìliáng and fail,
you will fall into being a frivolous person of the world,
which is like drawing a tiger but failing, and instead resembling a dog.
Even now, Jìliáng's reputation is still uncertain.
Commandery governors gnash their teeth upon arriving in office,
and the provincial and commandery authorities speak of it.
I often feel a chill in my heart because of it,
which is why I do not wish my descendants to imitate him."
Jìliáng's given name was Bǎo.
He was from Jīngzhào [Jùn],
and at the time served as Yuèqí Sīmǎ.
An enemy of Bǎo submitted a memorial,
accusing Bǎo
"of acting frivolously,
disordering groups and deluding the masses.
Fúbō Jiāngjūn, from ten thousand li away, sent a letter home to admonish his nephews,
yet Liáng Sōng and Dòu Gù associate with him,
and will propagate his frivolity and falseness,
disrupting and disordering all of Zhūxià."
When the memorial was submitted,
the emperor summoned Liáng Sōng and Dòu Gù to rebuke them,
showing them the accusation and Mǎ Yuán's admonition letter.
Liáng Sōng and Dòu Gù prostrated themselves, their heads bleeding,
and were spared punishment.
An imperial edict dismissed Bǎo from office.
Bógāo's given name was Shù.
He was also from Jīngzhào [Jùn].
He served as Shāndū Zhǎng,
and from this was promoted to Tàishǒu of Línglíng.
Originally,
when Mǎ Yuán was in Jiāozhǐ,
he regularly consumed Coix seeds,
which enabled him to lighten his body and reduce desires,
thus overcoming the miasma.
The Coix seeds in the south were large.
Mǎ Yuán wanted to use them as seeds,
and when the army returned,
he loaded a cart with them.
At the time, people thought these were rare treasures from the southern lands,
and the powerful and influential all desired them.
Mǎ Yuán was then in imperial favor,
so no one reported it.
After he died,
there were those who submitted memorials slandering him,
claiming that what he had brought back
were all bright pearls and rhinoceros horns.
Mǎ Wǔ and Yúlíng Hóu Hóu Yù and others
all spoke of this in their memorials,
and the emperor became even more angry.
Mǎ Yuán's wife and children were terrified
and dared not return the body to the ancestral burial ground,
but merely bought a few mǔ of land west of the city for burial.
No guests or old friends dared to offer condolences.
Yán and Mǎ Yuán's wife and children bound themselves with straw ropes
and went to the palace gate to plead guilty.
The emperor then brought out Liáng Sōng's letter to show them.
Only then did they know the charges against them.
They submitted memorials to appeal their injustice,
six times in total,
their words extremely mournful and earnest,
and only then was Mǎ Yuán allowed to be buried.
Furthermore, Zhū Bó, a former Yúnyáng Lìng from the same commandery, went to the palace gate and submitted a memorial, saying: "Your servant has heard that royal virtue and sagely governance
do not forget the achievements of others,
and, recognizing one good quality,
do not demand perfection in all.
Thus, Gāozǔ pardoned Kuǎtōng and buried Tián Héng with royal rites,
and the high officials were thereby enlightened
and none doubted themselves.
Indeed, when a great general is abroad,
and slanderous words are within,
minor faults are immediately recorded,
but great merits are not considered.
Truly,
is what the state holds in caution.
Therefore, Zhāng Hán (章邯) feared public opinion and fled to Chǔ (楚);
the Yān (燕) general held Liáo (聊) and refused to surrender.
How could they willingly plan for their downfall?
They grieved that clever
words could harm their kind.
Among the powerful,
without a single word of support nearby,
to rush into a deep abyss,
and enter a tiger's mouth,
how could they consider the consequences?
How could they know that they would be entrusted with the mission to secure seven commanderies,
and obtain the fortune
of being enfeoffed as a Marquis?
Eight years later,
the imperial carriage marched west to attack Wěi Xiāo (隗囂).
The national strategy was uncertain,
and the various camps had not yet gathered.
[Mǎ Yuán (馬援)] offered a proposal for a progressive advance,
and ultimately conquered Xīzhōu (西州).
When
Wú Hàn (吳漢) descended upon Lǒng (隴),
the path to Jì (冀) was cut off,
and only Dídào (狄道) held firm for the state.
The soldiers and common people were starving and exhausted,
their lives hanging by a thread.
Yuán (援) was sent west with an imperial edict,
to pacify the border
populace.
He then gathered heroes and outstanding figures,
enlightened and enticed the Qiāng Róng (羌戎),
his plans like a gushing spring,
his momentum like a turning wheel.
He then saved those in urgent distress,
preserved cities
on the brink of collapse,
marched with a full army,
supplied his troops from the enemy,
and Lǒng (隴) and Jì (冀) were largely pacified.
Yet he alone guarded an empty commandery,
his military movements always successful,
his advances always victorious.
He struck down
the Xiānlíng (先零),
entering the mountain valleys.
Fiercely enraged, he fought with all his might,
and an arrow pierced his shin.
He also marched to Jíāo Zhǐ (交阯),
where the land had much miasma.
Yuán (援) bade farewell to his wife and children,
without a heart
of regret.
He then slew and annihilated Zhēng Cè (徵側),
and pacified the entire province.
Later, he campaigned south again,
immediately capturing Línxiāng (臨鄉).
His army had already achieved its objective,
but he died before completing it.
Though the officials and soldiers
suffered from illness,
Yuán (援) did not remain safe alone.
Indeed, some establish merit through prolonged war,
while others meet defeat through haste;
deep penetration is not necessarily an advantage,
and not advancing is not necessarily a fault.
How could human nature enjoy being long besieged in a desperate place,
unable to return alive?
Mǎ Yuán (馬援) served the imperial court for twenty-two years.
He went north beyond the frontier and the deserts,
and south across rivers and seas.
He braved harmful
miasma,
and died in military service.
His name was extinguished, his title revoked,
and his estate not passed on.
The realm did not know his faults,
and the populace had not heard his slanders,
until he suddenly encountered the words
of common men,
and was unjustly subjected to slander and defamation.
His family shut their doors,
and his burial did not return to his ancestral tomb.
Grievances and animosities arose simultaneously,
and his relatives trembled in fear.
The deceased could not clear his name,
and the living
could not plead his case.
I secretly grieve for this.
How can he still be doubted over grain and money?
One who possesses the loyalty of Kǒng Fǔ (孔父) yet cannot escape slander,
this is what Zōu Yáng (鄒陽) lamented.
The *Shī* (詩) says:
"Take
those slanderers,
and throw them to wolves and tigers.
If wolves and tigers do not eat them,
throw them to the far north.
If the far north does not receive them,
throw them to Hào (昊) (Heaven)."
This means wishing to let Heaven
judge their evil.
May Your Majesty reflect on the words of a humble scholar,
and not let a meritorious minister harbor resentment in the underworld.
I have heard that according to the principles of the *Chūnqiū* (春秋),
crimes are pardoned
for meritorious service;
in the sacrifices of the sage kings,
ministers have five kinds of righteousness.
As for Yuán (援),
he is one who diligently served until death.
I wish for the high officials to deliberate on Yuán's (援) merits and faults,
whether to terminate
or continue [his lineage],
to satisfy the expectations of the realm.
Bó's (勃) courtesy name was Shūyáng (叔陽).
At twelve years old, he could recite the *Shī* (詩) and *Shū* (書).
He often visited Yuán's (援) elder brother Kuàng (況).
Bó (勃) wore a square-collared robe,
could walk with measured steps,
and his words were elegant and refined.
Yuán (援), who only moderately understood writing,
was flustered upon seeing him.
Kuàng (況) understood his feelings,
and poured wine to comfort Yuán (援), saying:
"Zhū Bó (朱勃) is a small vessel that matures quickly;
his wisdom is limited to this.
Eventually, he will have to learn from you,
do not fear him."
Before Zhū Bó (朱勃) was twenty,
the Yòu Fúfēng (右扶風) requested him to serve as acting magistrate of Wèichéng (渭城).
When Yuán (援) became a general
and was enfeoffed as a marquis,
Bó's (勃) position did not exceed that of a county magistrate.
Although Yuán (援) later became prominent,
he always treated Bó (勃) with old kindness and looked down on him,
yet Bó (勃) grew more personally devoted to him.
When Yuán (援) met with slander,
only Bó (勃) could remain loyal until the end.
When Sùzōng (肅宗) ascended the throne,
he posthumously bestowed two thousand *hú* (斛) of grain upon Bó's (勃) son, Gǔ (穀).
Originally,
Yuán's (援) niece's husband, Wáng Pán (王磐), courtesy name Zǐshí (子石),
was the son of Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) cousin, Rén (仁), Marquis of Píng'ā (平阿).
After Mǎng's (莽) defeat,
Pán (磐), possessing great wealth, lived in his native land.
He was a man of integrity and valued scholars, and was generous with his wealth,
becoming famous in the Jiānghuái (江淮) region.
Later, he traveled to the capital,
and became good friends with Wèi Wèi (衞尉) Yīn Xīng (陰興), Dà Sīkōng (大司空) Zhū Fú (朱浮), and Qí Wáng Zhāng (齊王章).
Yuán (援) told his sister's son Cáo Xùn (曹訓):
"The Wáng (王) family
is a fallen clan.
Zǐshí (子石) should seclude himself and maintain his integrity,
but instead he travels among the elders of the capital,
acting on his impulses,
often offending others.
His downfall is inevitable."
A little over a year later,
Pán (磐) was indeed implicated with Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉) Sū Yè (蘇鄴) and Dīng Hóng (丁鴻),
and died in the Luòyáng (洛陽) prison.
And Pán's (磐) son Sù (肅) again frequented the Northern Palace and the residences of princes and marquises.
Yuán (援) told Sīmǎ (司馬) Lǚ Zhǒng (呂种):
"The first year of Jiànwǔ (建武)
is known as the grand restoration of the empire.
From now on,
the realm will surely grow more peaceful day by day.
My only worry is that the various imperial sons are all growing strong,
yet the old precautions have not been established.
If they frequently associate with guests,
then great imprisonments will arise.
You all must be cautious!"
When Empress Guō (郭) died,
there were those who submitted memorials,
believing that Sù (肅) and others from punished families,
whose guests caused trouble through their affairs,
might lead to the rebellions of Guàn Gāo (貫高) and Rèn Zhāng (任章).
The Emperor was enraged,
and ordered the commanderies and counties to arrest all guests of the princes.
They implicated one another,
and thousands died.
Lǚ Zhǒng (呂种) also suffered from this misfortune.
At the moment of his death, he sighed:
"General Mǎ (馬) truly was a divine man!"
In the early Yǒngpíng (永平) era,
Yuán's (援) daughter was made Empress.
Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) had portraits of famous ministers and generals of the Jiànwǔ (建武) era painted in the Yúntái (雲臺),
but because of the imperial concubine's (椒房) status,
Yuán (援) alone was not included.
Dōngpíng Wáng Cāng (東平王蒼) observed the paintings,
and said to the Emperor:
"Why is there no painting of Fúbō Jiāngjūn (伏波將軍) (General Who Calms the Waves)?"
The Emperor smiled and did not speak.
By the seventeenth year,
Yuán's (援) wife died,
and then his burial mound was repaired and planted,
and an ancestral hall built.
In the third year of Jiànchū (建初),
Sùzōng (肅宗) sent the Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng (五官中郎將) with a ceremonial staff to posthumously honor him,
bestowing on Yuán (援) the posthumous title of Zhōngchéng Hóu (忠成侯).
Mǎ Yuán's four sons were: Mǎ Liào,
Mǎ Fáng,
Mǎ Guāng,
and Mǎ Kèqīng.
Mǎ Kèqīng was precocious from a young age.
When he was six years old,
he was able to converse with the various dukes
and specialized in responding to guests.
Once, a criminal on the run, guilty of a capital offense, came to visit.
Mǎ Kèqīng hid so that no one would know.
Outwardly, he appeared slow-witted, but inwardly, he was profound and perceptive.
Mǎ Yuán found him very extraordinary,
considering him a vessel for a general or a minister,
and thus used "Kèqīng" as his courtesy name.
After Mǎ Yuán died,
Mǎ Kèqīng also died young.
The commentary states: Mǎ Yuán gained fame throughout the Three Fǔ,
roaming and serving two emperors.
When he established his integrity and formed his strategies,
to serve the ruler of his time,
he harbored the ambition of shouldering the tripod (i.e., holding high office),
which was indeed a rare opportunity of a thousand years.
However, his warning others about misfortune
was wise,
yet he could not protect himself from slander and fault-finding.
Could it be that in matters of achievement and fame,
this is simply the way things are?
If self-interest is not involved
when planning affairs, then one is wise;
if considerations are not selfish
when judging righteousness, one will be resolute.
If one can truly turn the wisdom used to observe external things inward to examine oneself,
then if applied to others, one can be forgiving;
if used to reflect on one's own feelings, one will also be clear.
Mǎ Liào's courtesy name was Jìngpíng.
While young, he became a Gentleman through his father's merits.
After Empress Míngdé was established,
Mǎ Liào was appointed Left Supervisor of the Feathered Forest and Commandant of the Tiger-Guards.
When Emperor Xiǎnzōng died,
he received the dying imperial edict to manage the palace gates,
and subsequently replaced Zhào Xǐ as Commandant of the Guards.
Emperor Sùzōng greatly respected him.
At that time, the Empress Dowager personally practiced frugality,
and her affairs were conducted simply.
Mǎ Liào, fearing that this excellent endeavor might not last,
submitted a memorial to the Chánglè Palace to encourage the completion of virtuous governance,
saying:
"Your servant has examined previous imperial edicts,
which state that the people's destitution
arises from the world's emphasis on extravagance.
Therefore, Emperor Yuán dismissed palace officials,
Emperor Chéng wore plain clothes,
and Emperor Āi abolished the Music Bureau.
However, excessive spending did not cease,
leading to decline and disorder,
because the common people follow deeds, not words.
Indeed, to change policies and transform customs,
there must be a fundamental root.
The傳 *Zhuàn* says: 'When King Wú liked swordsmen,
the people mostly had sword scars;
when King Chǔ liked slender waists,
many in the palace starved to death.'
A Cháng'ān saying goes:
'If those in the city like high topknots,
those in the four quarters raise theirs a foot high;
if those in the city like broad eyebrows,
those in the four quarters extend them to half their forehead;
if those in the city like wide sleeves,
those in the four quarters use a whole bolt of silk.'
These words, though seemingly a jest,
cut to the heart of the matter.
Not long after the previous regulations were established,
they gradually ceased to be implemented.
Although officials sometimes failed to enforce the law,
it was largely due to laxity beginning in the capital.
Now, Your Majesty personally wears thick silk
and discards ornate decorations,
a practice you are accustomed to,
issuing from your sacred nature.
This truly accords with Heaven's will above
and complies with the people's hopes below.
No greater
and more immense fortune exists than this.
Although Your Majesty has attained this naturally,
you should still diligently strive for it,
emulating the lofty virtue of Emperor Tàizōng
and guarding against the failures of Emperors Chéng and Āi to endure.
The *Yì* says: 'If one does not constantly maintain one's virtue,
one will sometimes encounter shame.'
If this matter can truly be completed once,
then the four seas will sing of your virtue,
your fame will permeate heaven and earth,
[一０]the spirits and deities will be moved,
and it can be engraved on metal and stone.
How much more so for practicing benevolent intentions,
how much more for issuing commands!
I wish that this memorial be placed beside your seat,
to serve as the sound of a blind musician reciting at night."
[一一]The Empress Dowager deeply accepted his advice.
Whenever there was a major discussion in the court,
she would consult him.
Mǎ Liào was honest, cautious, and circumspect by nature,
not coveting power, influence, or fame.
He devoted himself to offering loyal advice,
not caring about praise or criticism.
Officials repeatedly cited old precedents
and memorialized to enfeoff Mǎ Liào and others.
After repeatedly declining and being unable to refuse,
in the fourth year of Jiànchū,
he finally accepted the enfeoffment as Marquis of Shùnyáng,
and was granted the special privilege of entering his residence.
Whenever there were rewards,
he would always decline them, not daring to accept,
and the capital praised him for this.
His son, Mǎ Yù,
was a Commandant of Infantry.
After the Empress Dowager died,
the Mǎ clan lost its influence.
Mǎ Liào was lenient and easygoing by nature,
and could not properly discipline his sons and grandsons.
Mǎ Yù then submitted a letter of resentment and slander.
Furthermore, Mǎ Fáng and Mǎ Guāng were extravagant
and fond of forming factions and associates.
In the eighth year,
officials memorialized to dismiss Mǎ Yù,
and sent Mǎ Liào, Mǎ Fáng, and Mǎ Guāng to their enfeoffments.
Mǎ Yù followed Mǎ Liào back to his state,
and died from being beaten in an investigation.
Later, an imperial edict recalled Mǎ Liào to the capital.
In the fourth year of Yǒngyuán,
he died.
Emperor Hé, considering Mǎ Liào to be the uncle of the previous emperor,
lavished funeral gifts and condolences upon him.
An envoy offered sacrifices,
and royal princesses attended the funeral.
He was given the posthumous title Marquis Ān.
His son, Mǎ Zūn, inherited the title,
and was transferred to be enfeoffed as Marquis of Chéngxiāng.
When Mǎ Zūn died,
he had no son,
and the state was abolished.
In the third year of Yuánchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng enfeoffed Mǎ Liào's grandson, Mǎ Dù, as Marquis of Yǐngyáng.
Mǎ Fáng's courtesy name was Jiāngpíng.
In the twelfth year of Yǒngpíng,
he and his younger brother Mǎ Guāng both became Yellow Gate Attendants.
When Emperor Sùzōng ascended the throne,
Mǎ Fáng was appointed Commandant,
and gradually promoted to Commandant of the City Gates.
In the second year of Jiànchū,
the Qiāng tribes of Jīnchéng and Lǒngxī who guarded the frontier all revolted.
Mǎ Fáng was appointed Acting General of Chariots and Cavalry,
with Gěng Gōng, Commandant of Chángshuǐ, as his deputy.
He led thirty thousand soldiers from the five camps of the Northern Army and the archers from various commanderies to attack them.
When the army reached Jì,
the Qiāng chieftain Bùqiáo and others besieged the Commander of the Southern Commandery in Líntáo.
Mǎ Fáng wanted to rescue them,
but the road to Líntáo was treacherous,
making it impossible for chariots to advance abreast.
Mǎ Fáng then separately dispatched two Sīmǎ leading several hundred cavalrymen,
dividing them into front and rear armies.
They set up a large camp more than ten *lǐ* from Líntáo,
erecting many banners and standards,
and spreading word that a large army would advance at dawn.
When the Qiāng scouts saw this,
they galloped back, reporting that the Han army was too strong to resist.
The next morning, the Han troops advanced with drums and shouts,
and the Qiāng barbarians fled in panic.
They were then pursued and defeated,
with over four thousand heads taken or prisoners captured,
thus relieving the siege of Líntáo.
Mǎ Fáng opened the way with kindness and trust,
and all the Shāodāng tribes surrendered.
Only Bùqiáo and twenty thousand others remained in the Wàngqǔ Valley, southwest of Líntáo.
In the twelfth month,
the Qiāng again defeated Gěng Gōng's Sīmǎ and the Chief Clerk of Lǒngxī in Héluó Valley,
with several hundred casualties.
The following spring,
Mǎ Fáng dispatched Sīmǎ Xià Jùn to lead five thousand men along the main road towards their front,
and secretly sent Sīmǎ Mǎ Péng to lead five thousand men through a narrow path to strike their vital center.
He also ordered Chief Clerk Lǐ Diào and others to lead four thousand men to encircle their west.
The three columns attacked simultaneously,
defeating them again,
killing or capturing over a thousand men,
and seizing over a hundred thousand cattle and sheep.
The Qiāng retreated,
but Xià Jùn pursued them and was in turn defeated.
Mǎ Fáng then led his troops to engage them in battle at Suǒxī,
and defeated them again.
Bùqiáo, pressed hard,
led over ten thousand of his tribesmen to surrender.
An imperial edict summoned Mǎ Fáng back,
appointing him General of Chariots and Cavalry,
while retaining his position as Commandant of the City Gates.
Dòu Fáng’s貴寵 (imperial favor and high position) was at its height,
and he sat separately from the Jiǔqīng.
Dòu Guāng was transferred from Cavalry Commandant (Yuèqí Xiàowèi) to Superintendent of the Capital Gates (Zhíwú Jīnwū).
Four years later,
Dòu Fáng was enfeoffed as Yǐngyáng Hóu,
and Dòu Guāng as Xǔ Hóu.
The two brothers each received six thousand households.
Dòu Fáng, because Emperor Xiǎnzōng was ill,
participated in medical care.
He also pacified the Western Qiāng,
and his fief was increased by one thousand three hundred and fifty households.
He repeatedly submitted memorials to resign his positions,
but was granted the title of Tèjìn (Special Advanced Official) and allowed to reside at home.
When the Empress Dowager passed away,
the following year,
Dòu Fáng was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglùxūn),
and Dòu Guāng was appointed Minister of the Guard (Wèiwèi).
Dòu Fáng frequently offered opinions on state affairs,
many of which were adopted.
That winter, the twelve-month迎氣樂 (music for welcoming the qi of the seasons) was first implemented,
which Dòu Fáng had proposed.
His son, Dòu Jù,
was appointed Cavalry Commandant (Chángcóng Xiǎohóu).
In the first month of the sixth year,
as Dòu Jù was due for his capping ceremony,
he was specially appointed as Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng).
Emperor Sùzōng personally presided over the ceremony on the platform below Zhāngtái Palace,
where tripods and sacrificial vessels were arranged,
and he personally oversaw the capping.
The following year,
Dòu Fáng again requested to resign due to illness,
and an imperial edict bestowed upon him the fields and residence of the former Zhōngshān Wáng,
and he was allowed to reside at home as a Tèjìn.
Dòu Fáng and his brother were wealthy and influential.
Each had over a thousand slaves,
assets amounting to hundreds of millions,
and they bought fertile and beautiful land in the capital.
They also built grand residences and pavilions,
with connecting galleries overlooking the roads,
extending across the streets.
They gathered many musicians and entertainers,
whose melodies rivaled those of the suburban temples.
Guests flocked to them,
from all four directions.
Several hundred people, such as Dù Dú of Jīngzhào,
living in their household.
Many Inspectors (Cìshǐ), Administrators (Shǒu), and Magistrates (Lìng) came from their family.
They generously provided relief to their local communities during seasonal festivals,
and none of their old acquaintances were left unprovided for.
Dòu Fáng also raised many horses and livestock,
and levied taxes on the Qiāng and Hú.
The Emperor was displeased by this,
and repeatedly issued reprimands and orders,
so much so that the prohibitions and restraints were very thorough.
As a result, their power and influence gradually diminished,
and their guests also dwindled.
In the eighth year,
due to his nephew Dòu Yù’s resentful slanders,
the officials memorialized that Dòu Fáng and his brother Dòu Guāng were extravagant and presumptuous,
corrupting the sacred transformation.
They were all dismissed and sent to their fiefs.
As they were about to depart,
an edict stated:
“My maternal relatives,
the entire family, are all being sent to their fiefs.
There will be no one to assist in the sacrifices to the empresses and emperors at the imperial ancestral temples during the four seasons,
which greatly grieves me.
Let Xǔ Hóu (Dòu Guāng) retain his fields and residence,
and the officials are not to request their forfeiture,
to comfort my feelings of Wèiyáng.”
Dòu Guāng was cautious and meticulous in his conduct.
When his mother died, he grieved excessively.
The Emperor especially loved him for this,
and he was reinstated as Tèjìn.
His son, Dòu Kāng,
was a Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng).
In Yǒngyuán two years,
Dòu Guāng became Grand Coachman (Tàipú),
and Dòu Kāng became Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
When Dòu Xiàn was executed,
Dòu Guāng was implicated for his close association with him,
and was again dismissed and sent to his fief.
Later, Dòu Xiàn’s slave falsely accused Dòu Guāng of conspiring with Dòu Xiàn in rebellion.
Dòu Guāng committed suicide,
and his family was sent back to their home commandery.
His home commandery then killed Dòu Kāng.
Dòu Fáng and his nephew Liáo Zǐzūn were both implicated and exiled to Dānyáng.
Dòu Fáng was made Zhaíxiāng Hóu,
with a limited annual tax income of three million,
and was not allowed to employ officials or commoners.
Later, Dòu Fáng, due to the humid and low-lying climate south of the Yangtze,
submitted a memorial requesting to return to his home commandery.
Emperor Hé granted his request.
In the thirteenth year,
he died.
His son, Dòu Jù, succeeded him,
and later became Colonel of the Long Water (Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi).
In Yǒngchū seven years,
Empress Dowager Dèng issued an edict for the descendants of Mǎ (Dòu Fáng’s maternal clan, likely a typo for Dòu here, but following instruction to not correct or comment) to return to the capital,
and to attend seasonal gatherings as before.
Dòu Guāng’s son, Dòu Lǎng, was again enfeoffed as Héxiāng Hóu.
Yán Yán’s courtesy name was Wēiqīng.
His father, Yán Yú,
was Governor of Yángzhōu during Wáng Mǎng’s time.
Yán Yán was orphaned young,
and enjoyed sword fighting and was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
Later, he followed Mǎ Yuán,
and studied with Yáng Tàibó of Píngyuán,
devoting himself to the Féndiǎn classics.
He was able to master the Zǔoshì variant of the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū Zuǒshì),
and also read extensively from various schools of thought.
Thus, he befriended outstanding and virtuous individuals,
and the prominent figures in the capital all admired his extraordinary talent.
He served as Supervisor of Documents (Dūyóu) in the commandery.
Mǎ Yuán often consulted with him on plans,
and entrusted him with family affairs.
His younger brother, Yán Dūn,
courtesy name Rúqīng,
was also famous.
After Mǎ Yuán died,
Yán Yán and Yán Dūn both returned to Ānlíng and resided in Jùxià.
The Sānfǔ praised their righteous conduct,
calling them
“The Two Qīng of Jùxià.”
After Empress Míngdé was established,
Yán Yán closed his doors and kept to himself,
still fearing causing suspicion or criticism.
He then moved to Běidì,
cutting off all visitors.
In Yǒngpíng fifteen years,
the Empress commanded him to move to Luòyáng.
Emperor Xiǎnzōng summoned him for an audience,
and Yán Yán’s replies were serene and elegant.
The Emperor was greatly impressed,
and issued an edict for him to stay at Rénshòutà,
where he, along with the Collators (Jiàoshūláng) Dù Fǔ and Bān Gù, jointly compiled the annotated records of Jiànwǔ.
He often discussed state affairs with imperial relatives and close kin, such as Línyì Hóu Liú Fù,
and was greatly favored.
Later, he was appointed Chief Clerk to a General (Jiāngjūn Zhǎngshǐ),
leading three thousand soldiers from the Five Bureaus of the Northern Army (Běijūn Wǔxiàoshì) and the Feathered Forest Imperial Guards (Yǔlín Jìnbīng).
He was stationed at Měijì in Xīhé,
to protect the Southern Chányú,
and was permitted to appoint Sīmǎ and Cóngshì.
Governors (Mùshǒu) paid him homage and respect,
treating him as a general.
The Emperor ordered Yán Yán to pass through the Imperial Armory (Wǔkù),
and sacrifice to Chīyóu.
The Emperor personally ascended the Ègé pavilion,
to observe his troops.
People at the time considered this an honor.
When Sùzōng肅宗 ascended the throne,
Yán嚴 was summoned and appointed as Shìyùshǐ Zhōngchéng侍御史中丞.
His son, Zhuān鱄, was appointed as a Láng郎,
ordered to encourage learning in the palace.
That winter,
there was an eclipse of the sun, a disaster.
Yán嚴 submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your servant has heard that the sun is the chief of all yang forces,
and an eclipse is a sign of yin encroaching.
The Shū書 says: ‘Do not neglect the various officials;
Heaven's work, men shall do it in its stead.’
This means that the king acts on behalf of Heaven to manage officials.
Therefore, performance is evaluated, and promotions and demotions are made,
to clarify rewards and punishments.
If those without merit are not demoted,
then yin will flourish and overwhelm yang.
Your servant observes that currently, Cìshǐ刺史 and Tàishǒu太守, who preside over provinces and command prefectures,
do not diligently serve and devote themselves to the state.
Instead, the supervising inspectors are biased and partial,
taking and giving as they please.
If someone is aligned with them, they are exalted as exceptionally outstanding;
if not, they are subjected to legal penalties.
They do not immediately lower their heads and cover their ears,
but rather seek wealth and bribes.
Currently, Zhū Pú朱酺, Cìshǐ刺史 of Yìzhōu益州; Ní Shuō倪說, Cìshǐ刺史 of Yángzhōu楊州;
Yǐn Yè尹業, Cìshǐ刺史 of Liángzhōu涼州, and others,
each time they conducted evaluations,
there were always deaths (among those they investigated),
and their selections were not genuine,
yet they have never been demoted or punished.
This allows subordinates to wield arbitrary power.
According to custom,
when provinces and commanderies recommend officials in memorials,
the Sīzhí司直 should investigate their competence to correct false or true reports.
Now, stricter oversight should be implemented,
following the former regulations.
In the past, the Chéngxiàng丞相 and Yùshǐ御史 personally managed their duties.
Only Bǐng Jí丙吉, due to old age, was lenient
and did not prosecute officials for their crimes.
Since then, the prime minister's office has made this a common practice,
colluding to protect each other,
thereby fostering an undeserved reputation.
[一０]Some, even before understanding their duties,
are immediately transferred.
This truly deviates from the original intention of establishing offices and bestowing emoluments.
It is fitting to command all departments to rectify themselves,
each held responsible for their tasks.
Those recommended by provinces and commanderies
must be the right persons.
If their reports are not truthful,
they should be dealt with according to law.
The Zhuàn傳 says: ‘The highest virtue is to win over the people with leniency;
next to that, nothing is better than severity.
Thus, when fire is fierce, people look upon it with awe;
when water is yielding, people treat it with familiarity and playfulness.
Those who govern should temper severity with leniency,
and leniency with severity.’
[一一]If this is done,
control and governance will have a proper standard,
and disasters will dissipate.”
[一二]When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor accepted his words and dismissed Pú酺 and others from their offices.
In the first year of Jiànchū建初 (76 CE),
he was promoted to Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng五官中郎將,
and his three sons were appointed as Láng郎.
Yán嚴 repeatedly recommended worthy and capable individuals,
and clarified cases of injustice,
many of which were accepted and used.
He again served as Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng五官中郎將, acting as Chánglè Wèiwèi長樂衞尉.
In the second year (77 CE),
he was appointed Tàishǒu太守 of Chénliú陳留.
When Yán嚴 was about to take up his post,
he spoke to the Emperor, saying:
“Previously, Xiǎnqīn Hóu顯親侯 Dòu Gù竇固 mistakenly led the late emperor to deploy troops to the Western Regions,
establishing the Yīwúlú Yíng屯 garrison,
which caused trouble and expense without benefit.
Furthermore, Dòu Xūn竇勳 was executed, and his family should not be allowed near the capital.”
At this time, Xūn’s勳 daughter was the Empress,
and the Dòu竇 clan was favored.
Some listeners who overheard Yán’s嚴 words
reported them to Dòu Xiàn竇憲 and his brothers,
whereupon he lost the favor of the powerful and influential.
Upon arrival at his post, Yán嚴
made clear rewards and punishments,
and exposed wickedness,
making the commandery peaceful and orderly.
At that time, rumors in the capital said that bandits were coming from the east.
The common people fled,
frightening each other.
The various commanderies were in a panic,
each reporting the situation.
Yán嚴 investigated and found the rumors to be false,
and alone made no preparations.
An imperial edict was sent asking about the situation,
with messengers stationed along the road.
Yán嚴 steadfastly maintained there were no bandits,
and later things turned out as he said.
He governed the commandery for four years,
and was implicated for colluding with Zōngzhèng宗正 Liú Yì劉軼, Shǎofǔ少府 Dīng Hóng丁鴻, and others.
He was summoned and appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū太中大夫;
after more than ten days,
he was promoted to Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng將作大匠.
In the seventh year (82 CE),
he was again dismissed due to an incident.
Thereafter, being resented by the Dòu竇 clan,
he never held office again.
When the Emperor passed away,
and Empress Dowager Dòu竇 presided over the court,
Yán嚴 retired to his home to protect himself,
educating his sons and grandsons.
In the tenth year of Yǒngyuán永元 (98 CE),
he died at home,
aged eighty-two.
His younger brother, Dūn敦,
reached the office of Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng虎賁中郎將.
Of Yán’s嚴 seven sons,
only Xù續 and Róng融 were famous.
Xù續, courtesy name Jìzé季則,
could understand the Lúnyǔ論語 at seven,
mastered the Shàngshū尚書 at thirteen,
and studied the Shī詩 at sixteen.
He extensively read various classics
and was skilled in Jiǔzhāng Suànshù九章筭術 (The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art).
During the reign of Shùndì順帝,
he served as Hùqiāng Xiàowèi護羌校尉,
and was promoted to Dùliáo Jiāngjūn度遼將軍,
wherever he served, he was praised for his authority and benevolence.
Róng融 has his own biography.
Léng棱, courtesy name Bówēi伯威,
was a grand-nephew of Yuán援.
He was orphaned young
and lived with his elder cousin Yì毅, sharing their livelihood,
with affection like that between full siblings.
When Yì毅 died without sons,
Léng棱 observed a heart-mourning for three years.
During the Jiànchū建初 era (76-84 CE),
he served as a Gōngcáo功曹 in the commandery
and was recommended as Xiàolián孝廉.
When the Mǎ馬 clan fell from power,
Sùzōng肅宗, recognizing Léng’s棱 righteous conduct,
summoned him and appointed him Yèzhě謁者.
In the first year of Zhānghé章和 (87 CE),
he was promoted to Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu廣陵太守.
At that time, grain was expensive and the people were starving.
He memorialized to abolish the salt official positions
to benefit the common people,
relieved the poor and weak,
lightened taxes,
and restored reservoirs and lakes,
irrigating over twenty thousand qǐng頃 of fields.
Officials and common people carved a stone inscription to praise him.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán永元 (90 CE),
he was transferred to Hànyáng Tàishǒu漢陽太守,
where he was known for his dignity and strictness.
When Dàjiāngjūn大將軍 Dòu Xiàn竇憲 garrisoned Wǔwēi武威 in the west,
Léng棱 often provided military expenses,
imposing levies on the common people.
When Xiàn憲 was executed,
Léng棱 was implicated and punished.
Several years later,
there were many fierce bandits in the Jiānghú江湖 region,
so Léng棱 was made Dānyáng Tàishǒu丹陽太守.
Léng棱 dispatched troops to ambush and attack them,
capturing and exterminating them all.
He was transferred to Kuàijī Tàishǒu會稽太守,
where his governance also had a good reputation.
He was transferred to Hénèi Tàishǒu河內太守.
During the Yǒngchū永初 era (107-113 CE),
he was implicated in a matter and punished,
dying at home.
The encomium says: Fúbō伏波 delighted in achievements,
from Jì冀 and Lǒng隴.
He pacified Luòyuè駱越 in the south,
and slaughtered Shāorǒng燒種 in the west.
Years had flowed by,
but his heroic spirit remained strong.
As his brilliant virtue ascended,
his family's fortune flourished.
Liáo廖 lacked the three paths,
and Fáng防 then grew arrogant and overbearing.
Zhuō Lǔ Wèi Liú Lièzhuàn Dì Shíwǔ卓魯魏劉列傳第十五 (Lǔ Gōng Dì Pī魯恭弟丕)
Zhuō Mào卓茂, courtesy name Zǐkāng子康,
was a native of Wǎn宛 in Nányáng南陽.
His father and grandfather both reached the position of Jùnshǒu郡守.
Mào茂,
during the reign of Yuándì元帝, studied in Cháng'ān長安,
serving Doctor Jiāng Shēng江生,
learning the Shī詩, Lǐ禮, and calendrical calculations.
He thoroughly mastered his teacher's methods
and was known as a learned scholar.
He was by nature broad-minded, benevolent, respectful, and loving.
His fellow villagers and old acquaintances,
even if their conduct and abilities differed from Mào’s茂,
all loved and admired him with delight.
Initially, he was appointed as a clerk in the Prime Minister's office.
He served Kǒng Guāng,
who praised him as a venerable elder.
One time, while he was traveling,
someone recognized his horse.
Mào asked,
"How long has it been since you lost your horse?"
He replied,
"More than a month."
Mào had owned the horse for several years
and knew in his heart that this was mistaken,
but he quietly unharnessed it and gave it to him,
pulled his cart away,
and looked back, saying,
"If it is not your horse,
please return it to me at the Prime Minister's office."
Another day,
the horse's owner found his lost horse elsewhere,
so he went to the office to return the horse,
bowing his head in apology.
Such was Mào's nature, disinclined to dispute.
Later, he was recommended for his Confucian scholarship and appointed as a Shìláng,
serving in the Huángmén.
He was then promoted to Mì-lìng.
He toiled earnestly,
treating people as his own children.
He promoted good deeds and instructed,
uttering no harsh words.
Officials and common folk loved him and could not bear to deceive him.
Someone once reported that a local Tíngzhǎng had received gifts of rice and meat.
Mào dismissed his attendants and asked him,
"Did the Tíngzhǎng ask you for it?
Or did you have a matter to entrust to him, for which he accepted it?
Or did you, in ordinary times, give it to him out of kindness?"
The man said,
"I just gave it to him."
Mào said,
"You gave it, and he accepted it.
Why do you speak of it?"
The man said,
"I have secretly heard that a wise and enlightened ruler
makes people unafraid of officials
and officials do not take from people.
Now I am afraid of officials,
which is why I gave it to him.
Since the official finally accepted it,
I came to report it."
Mào said,
"You have become a mean person.
The reason why humans are superior to birds and beasts
is that they possess benevolence and love,
and know how to respect and serve one another.
Even elderly neighbors still send gifts,
which is how human society fosters intimacy,
let alone between officials and the people?
Officials, however, should not take advantage of their power to forcefully demand things.
In general, human beings,
living together in groups,
therefore have rules, rites, and righteousness by which to interact.
If you alone do not wish to cultivate these,
can you fly far away
and not live among people?
The Tíngzhǎng has always been a good official.
To send him gifts seasonally
is proper etiquette."
The man said,
"If this is the case,
why does the law forbid it?"
Mào smiled and said,
"Laws establish major principles;
rites follow human emotions.
If I instruct you with rites,
you will surely have no complaints or ill will.
If I govern you by law,
where will you put your hands and feet?
Within a single household,
minor matters can be debated,
major ones can lead to death.
Go home and reflect on this!"
Thereupon, the man accepted his instruction,
and the officials felt his kindness.
Initially,
when Mào arrived in the county,
he made some changes,
and the officials and people laughed at him.
Those who heard of it in neighboring cities all scorned his incompetence.
Hénán Jùn appointed a different governor,
but Mào showed no resentment,
managing affairs as usual.
After several years,
his moral transformation became widespread,
and nothing was picked up from the roads.
During the reign of Píng-dì,
there was a great locust plague throughout the land.
More than twenty counties in Hénán were afflicted,
but the locusts did not enter Mì Xiàn's borders.
The Dūyóu reported this,
but the Grand Administrator did not believe it.
He went out himself to inspect,
and seeing it, he was convinced.
At this time, Wáng Mǎng held power.
He established six assistants for the Dàsīnóng,
to encourage agriculture and sericulture.
Mào was promoted to Jīngbùchéng.
Old and young from Mì wept as they saw him off.
When Wáng Mǎng became acting emperor,
Mào was dismissed due to illness and returned to his commandery.
He often served as a Ménxià Yuàn Jìjiǔ,
but refused to serve as a functional official.
When Gēngshǐ was established,
Mào was appointed Shìzhōng Jìjiǔ.
He followed Gēngshǐ to Cháng'ān,
but realizing Gēngshǐ's government was chaotic,
he requested to retire due to old age.
At that time, Guāngwǔ had just ascended the throne,
and first sought out Mào.
Mào went to Héyáng to meet him.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued saying:
"The former Mì-lìng Zhuó Mào
disciplined himself and cultivated his character,
maintaining pure and firm principles.
He is truly capable of what others cannot do.
Indeed, one whose name is renowned throughout the world
should receive the world's great rewards.
Thus, King Wǔ, after executing Zhòu,
sealed the tomb of Bǐ Gān
and honored the dwelling of Shāng Róng.
Now, Mào is appointed Tàifù,
enfeoffed as Bāodé Hóu,
with a stipend of two thousand households,
and granted a mat, staff, carriage, and horses,
one set of robes,
and five hundred catties of floss silk."
Mào's eldest son, Róng, was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū,
and his second son, Chóng, was made Zhōngláng,
serving in the Huángmén.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
he passed away.
He was granted a coffin, outer coffin, and burial ground,
and the emperor, in plain clothes, personally attended his funeral.
His son Chóng inherited his title,
and was transferred and enfeoffed as Fànhuāng Hóu.
His official career reached Dàsīnóng.
After Chóng died,
his son Chēn inherited the title.
After Chēn died,
his son Xīn inherited the title.
After Xīn died,
his son Lóng inherited the title.
In the fifteenth year of Yǒngyuán,
Lóng died without a son,
and the fief was abolished.
Initially,
Mào, along with Kǒng Xiū from the same county, Cài Xūn from Chénliú, Liú Xuān from Ānzhòng, Gōng Shèng from Chǔ Guó, and Bào Xuān from Shàngdǎng—six like-minded individuals—
did not serve during Wáng Mǎng's time,
and their names were highly regarded at the time.
Xiū, courtesy name Zǐquán,
in the early reign of Āi-dì,
served as the administrator of Xīndū.
Later, when Wáng Mǎng took power,
Xiū resigned his office and returned home.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he sent an envoy with black and crimson silks and bundles of cloth
to invite Xiū to be Guóshī.
Xiū then vomited blood, feigned illness,
and shut his door, isolating himself.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he sought out the descendants of Xiū and Xūn,
and bestowed grain upon them to honor and make them prominent.
Liú Xuān, courtesy name Zǐgāo,
a cousin of Ānzhòng Hóu Chóng,
knowing that Wáng Mǎng would usurp the throne,
changed his name and surname,
and, carrying classics, hid himself in the remote wilderness.
He only emerged in the early Jiànwǔ period.
Guāngwǔ then appointed Xuān to inherit the title of Ānzhòng Hóu.
Gōng Shèng's son, Cì, was promoted to be Shànggǔ Tàishǒu.
The affairs of Shèng and Bào Xuān are in the previous book.
The affairs of Xūn are in the biography of his great-grandson, Yōng.
A commentary states: In the early Jiànwǔ period,
when powerful heroes were causing disturbances,
their roars echoing continuously,
and walled cities were seen everywhere,
this was indeed a time of constant urgency and insufficient resources.
Zhuó Mào, a humble minor official,
without any other remarkable abilities,
was already over seventy years old at the time,
yet he was the first to be invited to serve,
with lavish words and heavy rites.
How was this different from the rulers of Zhōu and Yān honoring dwellings and establishing residences?
Thereupon, many guests, filled with indignation and aspiring to righteousness,
crossed barriers,
abandoned their families,
and came to knock on the golden gates.
Indeed, a generous nature and broad-mindedness are close
to benevolence;
being wronged and not retaliating is akin to forgiveness.
Following this path,
how could resentment and regret arise?
Lǔ Gōng 魯恭, courtesy name Zhòngkāng 仲康,
was a man from Pínglíng 平陵 in Fúfēng 扶風.
His ancestors descended from Lǔ Qǐnggōng 魯頃公.
When Lǔ 魯 was destroyed by Chǔ 楚,
they moved to Xiàyì 下邑,
and thus adopted the surname.
For generations, his family served as officials receiving a salary of two thousand dàn 石.
During the reigns of Emperor Āi 哀 and Emperor Píng 平,
they moved from Lǔ 魯.
His grandfather, Kuāng 匡,
during Wáng Mǎng's 王莽 time,
served as Xīhé 羲和.
He was known for his strategies
and was called
“Zhìnáng 智囊” (meaning "Wisdom Bag").
His father, [name omitted in original text],
at the beginning of the Jiànwǔ 建武 era,
served as the Grand Administrator of Wǔlíng 武陵,
and died in office.
At that time, Gōng 恭 was twelve years old,
and his younger brother Pī 丕 was seven.
They wailed and mourned day and night without ceasing.
He refused all condolences and gifts from the commandery,
and returned home to observe mourning,
his adherence to the rites surpassing that of an adult.
The local villagers considered him extraordinary.
At fifteen,
he and his mother and Pī 丕 all lived in the Grand Academy,
studying the Lǔ Shī 魯詩 (Lu Recension of the Book of Odes).
He lectured and recited behind closed doors,
cutting himself off from worldly affairs.
Both brothers were praised by the various Confucian scholars,
and many students eagerly sought to study under them.
The Grand Commandant Zhào Xǐ 趙憙 admired their ambition,
and every year sent his son to offer them wine and provisions,
but they always declined.
Gōng 恭 pitied Pī 丕 for being young
and wished for his brother to achieve fame first,
so he feigned illness and did not take office.
The commandery repeatedly invited him with rites,
but he respectfully refused.
His mother compelled him to go,
and Gōng 恭, having no choice, traveled west,
and consequently stayed in Xīnfēng 新豐 to teach.
At the beginning of the Jiànchū 建初 era,
Pī 丕 was recommended as "Upright and Forthright."
Gōng 恭 then began to serve as a commandery official.
The Grand Tutor Zhào Xǐ 趙憙 heard of this and invited him.
Emperor Sùzōng 肅宗 gathered various Confucian scholars at the Báihǔ Guān 白虎觀 (White Tiger Hall),
and Gōng 恭 was specifically summoned for his profound understanding of the classics
to participate in the discussions.
Xǐ 憙 again recommended Gōng 恭 for his direct speech.
He awaited appointment at the Gōngchē 公車 (Office of Public Carriages)
and was appointed Magistrate of Zhōngmóu 中牟.
Gōng 恭 governed purely by moral transformation,
without resorting to harsh punishments.
When litigant Xǔ Bó 許伯 and others disputed land,
successive magistrates were unable to resolve the matter.
Gōng 恭 justly arbitrated the right and wrong,
and they all withdrew and blamed themselves,
stopping their farming to yield to each other.
A village chief borrowed an ox from someone and refused to return it.
The ox owner sued him before Gōng 恭.
Gōng 恭 summoned the village chief,
ordering him repeatedly to return the ox,
but he still refused.
Gōng 恭 sighed, saying,
“This means that moral transformation is not effective.”
He wanted to resign his seal and ribbon and leave.
The clerks wept and jointly persuaded him to stay,
and the village chief then felt ashamed and remorseful,
returned the ox,
and went to prison to accept punishment.
Gōng 恭 pardoned him and did not prosecute.
Consequently, officials and common people trusted and obeyed him.
In the seventh year of Jiànchū 建初 (82 CE),
locusts damaged crops in the commanderies and kingdoms.
They bordered Zhōngmóu 中牟 like dog's teeth,
but did not enter it.
Yuán Ān 袁安, the Governor of Hénán 河南, heard of this
and doubted its truth,
so he sent his official known for kindness and leniency, Féi Qīn 肥親, to investigate.
Gōng 恭 walked through the fields with him,
and they both sat under a mulberry tree.
A pheasant passed by
and stopped nearby.
There was a young boy nearby.
Qīn 親 said,
“Boy, why don't you catch it?”
The boy said,
“The pheasant is just about to raise its chicks.”
Qīn 親 rose in astonishment
and took his leave of Gōng 恭, saying,
“The reason I came
was to observe your administration.
Now, the insects do not cross your border—
this is one anomaly;
your transformation reaches birds and beasts—
this is a second anomaly;
a mere youth possesses a benevolent heart—
this is a third anomaly.
To stay longer
would only disturb a worthy man.”
He returned to the prefectural office
and fully reported the situation to Ān 安.
That year,
auspicious grain grew directly in front of Gōng's 恭 seat in the courtyard.
Ān 安 then submitted a memorial reporting the situation,
and the emperor was surprised by it.
At that time, an imperial edict ordered all officials to recommend "Worthies and Upright, Forthright Men."
Gōng 恭 recommended Wáng Fāng 王方, a famous scholar from Zhōngmóu 中牟.
The emperor immediately summoned Fāng 方 to the Gōngchē 公車,
treating him with the same deference as those recommended by the grand ministers,
and Fāng 方 was appointed to the position of Attendant Censor.
Gōng 恭 served in office for three years.
The province recommended him as exceptionally outstanding.
He then suffered his mother's death and left office,
and the officials and people missed him.
Later, he was appointed Palace Assistant Censor.
At the beginning of Emperor Hé's 和帝 reign,
there was a discussion about sending the General of Chariots and Cavalry Dòu Xiàn 竇憲 and the General who Attacks the West Gěng Bǐng 耿秉 to attack the Xiongnu 匈奴.
Gōng 恭 submitted a memorial of remonstrance, saying: Your Majesty diligently applies your sacred thoughts,
fasting daily,
concerned about military campaigns,
truly desiring to stabilize the northern border,
eliminate harm for the people,
and establish a plan for ten thousand generations.
Your servant has considered this alone,
and does not yet see its convenience.
The plans for the altars of soil and grain and
the lives of ten thousand people
rest upon a single action.
In recent years,
autumn harvests have been poor,
people's food is
insufficient,
storehouses are empty,
and the state has no reserves.
We have just suffered a great sorrow (the death of the emperor's father),
and people are filled with fear.
Your Majesty embodies the virtue of a great sage
and practices the utmost filial
conduct,
completing the three years of mourning (liàngyīn 諒陰),
listening to the chief minister.
The common people are disappointed,
for three seasons they have not heard the sound of the imperial retinue's advance and clear-the-way calls,
and none are without longing and anxiety,
as if they have
sought something and not found it.
Now, in the prime month of spring,
to launch a military campaign,
disturbing the entire realm
to deal with the Rong and Yi barbarians,
is truly not how to bestow favor upon the Central Plains,
change the reign title and rectify the seasons,
from within to without.
of error, how much more so for humans?
Thus, he who loves people will surely receive heavenly reward.
Therefore, he who loves people will surely receive heavenly reward.
In the past, King Tài 太王 valued human lives and left Bīn 豳,
thus gaining the protection of Heaven.
As for the Rong 戎 and Dí 狄,
they are the deviant qi of the four directions.
Squatting and sprawling,
they are no different from birds and beasts.
If they were to intermingle with the Central Plains,
they would disrupt the heavenly qi
and defile
good people.
Therefore, the system of the sage kings
was merely to keep them loosely restrained and not cut them off.
Then yin and yang will be in harmony above,
auspicious winds and timely rains
will cover distant lands,
and the Yi 夷 and Dí 狄 will arrive, having their interpreters repeatedly translate.
The Yì Jīng 易經 says: 'If one has sincerity filling a jar,
in the end, there will be other
good fortune.'
This means that if sweet rain fills my jar,
sincerity will bring good fortune.
Indeed, he who overcomes others by virtue prospers;
he who overcomes others by force perishes.
Now
the Xiongnu 匈奴 have been defeated by the Xiānbēi 鮮卑,
their distant remnants residing west of the Shǐhóu River,
thousands of li 里 from the frontier.
To wish to take advantage of their emptiness and exhaustion,
to profit from their weakness,
is not where righteousness
comes from.
Previously, Grand Coachman Jì Róng 祭肜 went far beyond the frontier,
but ultimately did not see a single Hu 胡 barbarian, and his troops were already exhausted.
The disaster at Báishān 白山
was continuous like a thread,
The Dūhù
and the dead soldiers piled up like mountains.
To this day, they suffer from its grievous poison.
The hearts of the orphaned and widowed, filled with sorrow, have not yet ceased.
When a benevolent person considers this,
they take it
as a lesson.
How then can one again wish to follow in their footsteps,
disregarding the difficulties?
Now, conscription has just begun,
but the Dàsīnóng's provisions are insufficient.
Envoys are on the road,
dividing into sections
to urge things on,
with superiors pressuring inferiors.
The distress among the people is already severe.
The Sānfǔ, Bìng, and Liáng regions have had little rain,
wheat roots are withered and scorched,
and cattle deaths are increasing daily.
This
is proof that it does not accord with Heaven's will.
The officials and common people,
all say it is impossible.
How can Your Majesty alone, based on one person's plan,
sacrifice the lives of ten thousand people,
and not heed
their words?
Observing Heaven's will above,
and discerning the people's aspirations below,
is sufficient to know the success or failure of an undertaking.
Your minister fears that the Central Kingdom will cease to be the Central Kingdom;
how can it be merely about the Xiōngnú
then?
May Your Majesty preserve your sagely grace,
and grant respite to the soldiers,
to accord with Heaven's will.
After this, he was appointed as Lǔshī Bóshì.
From then on, the scholars of his family tradition flourished daily.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
and was frequently summoned for banquets and audiences,
where he was asked about gains and losses,
and awarded with generous gifts and special favors.
He was promoted to Lè'ān Xiàng.
At that time, there were many bandits in the eastern provinces,
gangs of them attacked and robbed,
and all the commanderies suffered from them.
When Gōng arrived,
he greatly increased bounties and rewards,
and showed kindness and trustworthiness.
Their leader, Zhāng Hàn, and others, led their followers to surrender.
Gōng memorialized to appoint Hàn as Bó Chāng Wèi.
The rest then captured and attacked each other,
and he completely pacified them,
bringing peace to the province and commanderies.
In the ninth year of Yǒngyuán,
he was summoned and appointed Yìláng.
In the eighth month,
during the celebration of the zhòu wine,
a purification ceremony was held at Zhāngtái.
An imperial edict ordered the Xiǎohuángmén to specifically lead Gōng forward.
That night, he was appointed Shìzhōng,
and ordered to ride in the imperial carriage,
receiving very warm greetings and inquiries.
In winter,
he was promoted to Guānglùxūn.
His selections were clean and fair,
and no noble relatives in the capital could corrupt his rectitude.
In the thirteenth year
he replaced Lǚ Gài as Sītú.
In the fifteenth year,
he accompanied the emperor on his southern inspection tour to Nányáng.
His son Fǔ was appointed Lángzhōng,
and was granted permission to ride in the imperial carriage with the emperor, as a Fùmǎ.
At that time, his younger brother Pī was also a Shìzhōng.
Brothers and father and son were all prominent in the court.
Later, he was dismissed from office due to an incident.
When Emperor Shāng ascended the throne,
Gōng was appointed Chánglè Wèiwèi.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
he again replaced Liáng Wěi as Sītú.
Initially,
at the end of Emperor Hé's reign,
an edict was issued that during the wheat harvest, minor punishments should be leniently reviewed,
but the provinces and commanderies preferred to govern with harsh scrutiny,
and consequently, executed judgments in mid-summer.
Gōng submitted a memorial admonishing: Your minister humbly observes the imperial edict,
which respects the seasons,
worries about the myriad people,
and seeks to promote harmony,
stating that for crimes not deserving of death,
examinations should be deferred.
To promote the gentle and good,
to dismiss the greedy and cruel,
and to follow the seasonal commands,
is to assist benevolent virtue,
to accord with the Vast Heaven,
to bring about harmony,
and to benefit the common people.
The origin of the matter,
the transformation of promoting the good and dismissing the cruel,
was misused by summoning farmers in mid-summer,
detaining them for questioning and examination,
with endless delays.
The Sīlì, who presides over the capital,
is a model for the four directions,
yet recently, in the spring months, they divided into various departments,
claiming to comfort and entice the poor,
but without any true compassion,
troubling the commanderies and counties,
with inspections and examinations that are not
urgent.
Arresting one person,
the crime extends to ten or more.
This goes against the seasonal qi above,
and harms agriculture below.
According to the Yì (Book of Changes), in the fifth month, the Gòu hexagram is active.
The classic states:
"The sovereign, by
issuing orders, instructs the four directions."
This means that the ruler, on the day of the summer solstice,
issues orders to stop travelers in the four directions,
to assist the subtle yin.
Even travelers are stopped
then,
how much more so arresting, summoning, and torturing people,
depriving them of their time!
In recent years, floods and droughts have damaged crops,
and people are hungry and wandering.
Now it is early summer,
the beginning of all grains,
a time when yang qi nourishes and fosters.
Since the third month,
the yin cold has not warmed,
and things that should transform and change have not received the harmonious qi.
The Yuèlìng states:
"In early summer, minor punishments are carried out,
and those lightly imprisoned are released.
If autumn commands are exercised, then bitter rains will frequently come,
and the five
grains will not ripen."
It also states:
"In mid-summer, serious prisoners are confined,
and their food is increased.
If autumn commands are exercised, then plants and trees will wither,
and people will suffer from epidemics."
To carry out minor punishments
means that their light offenses have already been corrected,
and they are not to be kept imprisoned for long,
thus they are released at the appropriate time.
Your humble servant believes that the current system for early summer
should follow this
edict,
and the final judgments and examinations of cases
should all be decided at the beginning of autumn,
to accord with the seasons,
and nurture all living things,
then Heaven and Earth will be in harmony,
and punishments will be clear.
Initially,
during the reign of Sùzōng,
all judgments were made before the winter solstice.
Thereafter, various differing opinions were debated.
Empress Dowager Dèng decreed that all officials below the Gōngqīng should meet to discuss,
and Gōng's discussion and memorial stated: The qi of yin and yang,
support each other in their operations,
and their activation and functions
each have their season.
If they are not in their proper time,
then things will be harmed accordingly.
Although the rulers
differed in their emphasis on simplicity or refinement,
this principle remains unchanged,
and the governance of the four seasons
is carried out uniformly.
The Yuèlìng,
though created during the Zhōu dynasty,
is based on the seasonal cycle of summer.
Its changes are only in the calendar, clothing colors, sacrifices, imperial titles, and implements.
Therefore it is said:
"The Yīn inherited the Rites of Xià,
and the Zhōu inherited the Rites of
Yīn.
What was added or subtracted is knowable."
The Yì states:
"Hidden dragon, do not act."
This means that in the eleventh and twelfth months, the yang qi is hidden,
and has not yet become active.
Although it
warms and nourishes all things,
nurturing their roots,
yet the predominant yin is above,
the earth is frozen and water turns to ice,
the yang qi is obstructed and isolated,
closing up to form winter.
Therefore it is said:
"Treading on frost,
“Solid ice,
is when the *yīn* first congeals.
Following its course,
it reaches solid ice.”
This means that in the fifth month, a faint *yīn* begins to rise,
and by the eleventh month, solid ice forms.
By conforming to Heaven’s will
and aligning with the nature and destiny of things,
universal harmony is achieved.
However, since the changes and reforms,
the harvests have not been abundant,
grain prices have constantly been high,
and the people have not been peaceful or secure.
Minor officials
who are not aligned with the national interest
often, upon reaching the eleventh month, would obtain criminals deserving of death,
and without questioning right or wrong,
would immediately execute them.
Even with doubtful cases,
there was no further review or correction.
If
even one man sighs in despair,
the Kingly Way is impaired;
how much more so when it is the multitude?
In the *Yìjīng*, the eleventh month says:
“The *jūnzǐ* thereby deliberates on lawsuits and delays executions.”
Doubtful cases should be thoroughly examined according to the law,
and capital punishments
should only be decided in the winter months.
If *lìchūn* falls in the twelfth month,
prisoners should not be reported as usual.
Gōng was again in public office,
and selected and promoted many outstanding scholars,
dozens of whom became high ministers and commandery governors.
However, among the elders and prominent families,
some were not recommended,
leading to resentment.
Gōng heard of this
and said:
“That learning is not practiced
is my concern.
Do not the scholars have local recommendations?”
In the end, nothing was said.
Gōng was by nature humble and reserved;
his memorials and discussions adhered to the classics,
and he secretly provided beneficial advice.
However, he never flaunted himself,
and thus was not known for his rigid uprightness.
After three years,
he was dismissed due to old age and illness.
Six years later,
at the age of eighty-one,
he died at home.
His two sons were made *láng*.
The eldest son, Qiān,
served as the Grand Administrator of Lǒngxī
and had a notable reputation and achievements.
Qiān’s son, Xù,
rose to the office of Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud.
He followed Emperor Xiàn westward into the passes
and conspired with Grand Minister over the Masses Wáng Yǔn to jointly execute Dǒng Zhuó.
When Lǐ Quē entered Cháng’ān,
Xù and Yǔn were both killed.
Pī, whose courtesy name was Shūlíng,
was profound and studious by nature,
diligently and tirelessly pursuing knowledge.
He therefore cut off social interactions
and did not respond to customary greetings.
Scholars and friends often criticized him for this,
but Pī was pleased and content with himself.
He then became proficient in the Five Classics
and taught the *Lǔ Shī* and *Shàngshū*,
becoming a renowned Confucian scholar of his time.
Later, he returned to his commandery
and served as Inspector and Registrar.
The generals he served
all treated him as a teacher and friend.
In the first year of Jiànchū,
Emperor Sù issued an edict to recommend worthy and upright individuals.
Grand Minister of Agriculture Liú Kuān recommended Pī.
At that time, over a hundred people submitted policy proposals,
but only Pī was ranked highly.
He was appointed Erudite Discussant
and later transferred to be Magistrate of Xīnyě.
After serving for a full year,
he was ranked first in the provincial assessment
and promoted to Inspector of Qīngzhōu.
His focus was on recognizing the virtuous and sagacious
and being cautious with punishments.
In the seventh year,
he was imprisoned and judged by the Minister of Justice for an offense.
In the first year of Yuánhé, he was summoned
and twice promoted,
appointed Chancellor of Zhào.
There were often over a hundred disciples and students who came to him.
People east of the passes called him
“Lǔ Shūlíng, who revived the Five Classics.”
Prince Shāng of Zhào once wanted to avoid illness
and moved to live in the academy.
Pī stopped him and would not allow it.
The Prince then submitted a memorial stating his case,
and an imperial edict was sent to Pī.
Pī memorialized, saying:
“Your servant has heard from the rites
that feudal lords die in the main hall,
and great officers die in the principal chamber.
Life and death are fated;
there is no precedent for escaping them.
The academy transmits the Way of the Five Emperors
and is where the rites, music, and teachings of the former kings are cultivated.
For the Prince to want to abandon and obstruct it to widely host banquets
is something that cannot be permitted.”
The edict followed Pī’s words,
and the Prince was thus intimidated by him.
Afterwards, when the Emperor made an inspection tour to Zhào,
Pī was specially granted an audience,
questioned on the classics and commentaries,
and richly rewarded.
He served for six years,
and auspicious omens repeatedly appeared;
officials and commoners highly respected him.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán,
he was transferred to be Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn.
In both commanderies, Pī
repaired and opened irrigation systems for the people,
and the populace became prosperous.
He frequently recommended and advanced reclusive and famous scholars.
The following year,
he was appointed Grand Administrator of Chénliú.
After serving for three full years,
he was later impeached for not accurately reporting aid to the poor
and was summoned to the Minister of Justice for judgment.
In the eleventh year, he was again summoned
and twice promoted to Palace Grandee.
At that time, Attendant Censor Jiǎ Kuí recommended Pī, stating that his knowledge of the Dao and arts was profound
and that he ought to be entrusted with responsibility.
Emperor Hé, during a court assembly,
summoned various Confucian scholars for an audience.
Pī, along with Attendant Censor Jiǎ Kuí and Minister of the Imperial Secretariat Huáng Xiāng, debated several matters.
The Emperor approved of Pī’s explanations.
After the court session,
he was specially bestowed with a cap, headscarf, shoes, socks, and a set of robes.
Pī then submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your servant, being foolish and stubborn,
has been prominently placed in a high position.
Though my vigor is diminished like that of an old dog or horse,
I was presumptuously granted an audience
and engaged in debate before Your Majesty.
I did not clarify anything distinctively,
and the bestowal of clothing
is truly an excessive honor.
Your servant has heard that those who expound on the classics
transmit the words of their former teachers,
not originating from themselves,
and thus must not yield to one another.
If there is yielding, the Way will not be clear,
just as a compass, square, scales, and steelyard cannot be distorted.
Those who question must clarify their evidence,
and those who explain must strive to establish their meaning.
Superficial and useless words should not be presented,
so that profound thought is not exhausted, and the Dao and its methods become clearer.
For those whose methods differ,
let each explain their own school’s methods,
and broadly observe their meanings.
Let us examine the intentions of the poets,
investigate the beginning and end of the *Yǎ* and *Sòng*,
illuminate the mutual admonitions of Shùn, Yǔ, and Gāoyáo,
reveal what Duke of Zhōu and Jīzǐ presented,
observe human culture,
and thereby transform the world.
Your Majesty has broadly accepted sincere advice to open up the four ears of wisdom;
do not let humble commoners be punished for their words.
You have already recognized recluses to seek benevolent and worthy individuals;
do not let those in remote obscurity be overlooked.”
In the thirteenth year,
he was transferred to be Attendant Censor,
then dismissed.
In the second year of Yǒngchū,
an edict ordered the high officials to recommend scholars who were diligent in Confucian studies.
General-in-Chief Dèng Zhì recommended Pī,
who was twice promoted,
again becoming Attendant Censor and Left Commandant of the Household,
and for a second time, one of the Three Elders.
In the fifth year,
at the age of seventy-five,
he died in office.
Wèi Bà, whose courtesy name was Qiáoqīng,
was a native of Jùyáng, Jìyīn.
His family was known for their rites and righteousness for generations.
Bà lost his parents young,
and his brothers lived together;
the local community admired their harmony and concord.
During the Jiànchū reign,
he was nominated as xiàolián.
He was promoted eight times.
During Emperor Hé's reign, he served as the Administrator of Jùlù.
He governed with simplicity, generosity, and forgiveness.
When his subordinates had faults,
he would first instruct them on their mistakes.
Only if they did not change would he dismiss them.
When officials slandered and accused each other,
Bà would always praise the strengths of other officials,
never mentioning their shortcomings.
Those who spoke felt ashamed,
and the slandering and lawsuits ceased.
In the sixteenth year of Yǒngyuán (104 CE),
he was summoned and appointed as Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng.
