The following year,
Emperor Hé passed away,
and he oversaw the construction of Shùnlíng.
At that time, it was deep winter and the ground was frozen.
The imperial envoy urged on the work,
frequently punishing county officials to pressure Bà.
Bà merely comforted and consoled them,
never harshly reprimanding them.
Instead, he would acknowledge their hard work, saying:
“Your being humiliated is the Dàjiàng’s fault.”
All the officials were grateful,
and worked twice as hard.
In the first year of Yánpíng (106 CE),
he succeeded Yǐn Qín as Tàicháng.
The following year,
he retired due to illness,
and was appointed Guānglù Dàfū.
In the fifth year of Yǒngchū (111 CE),
he was appointed Chánglè Wèiwèi.
Due to illness, he requested to resign,
and was again appointed Guānglù Dàfū,
dying in office.
Liú Kuān, courtesy name Wénráo,
was a native of Huáyīn, Hóngnóng.
His father, Qí,
served as Sītú during Emperor Shùn's reign.
Once, when Kuān was traveling,
a man who had lost his ox
approached Kuān's carriage and claimed the ox within it.
Kuān said nothing,
unhitched his carriage, and walked home.
A short while later,
the claimant found his ox and returned the other,
bowing his head and apologizing:
“I am ashamed to have wronged an elder;
please punish me as you see fit.”
Kuān said:
“Things sometimes resemble each other,
and errors can easily occur.
I am fortunate that you bothered to return it;
why apologize for it?”
The people of the province admired his lack of contention.
During Emperor Huán's reign,
he was invited by the Dàjiāngjūn.
He was promoted five times, reaching Sītú Chángshǐ.
At that time, there was an earthquake in the capital,
and he was specially questioned.
After two more promotions,
he was sent out to serve as the Xiàng of Dōnghǎi.
In the eighth year of Yánxī (165 CE),
he was summoned and appointed Shàngshū Lìng,
then promoted to Nányáng Tàishǒu.
He served in three commanderies,
being gentle, benevolent, and very forgiving.
Even in urgent situations,
he never spoke harshly or showed an angry face.
He often believed that
“if people are regulated by punishment,
they will avoid it but have no shame.”
When his subordinates committed faults,
he would only punish them with a reed whip,
merely to show disgrace,
never inflicting severe pain.
If there was meritorious work,
he would attribute it to his subordinates.
If abnormal phenomena or disasters occurred,
he would take responsibility and blame himself.
Whenever he traveled through counties and stopped at post stations,
he would always invite the jǐjiǔ of the academy and private scholars to hold classics and discuss them.
When he saw elders, he would comfort them with words about farming and village life.
He encouraged young people with lessons on filial piety and brotherly respect.
People were moved by his virtue and improved their conduct,
changing daily.
At the beginning of Emperor Líng's reign,
he was summoned and appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū,
serving as lecturer in the Huáguāng Diàn.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
and gifted a set of robes.
He was transferred to Túnqí Xiàowèi,
promoted to Zōngzhèng,
and transferred to Guānglù Xūn.
In the fifth year of Xīpíng (176 CE),
he succeeded Xǔ Xùn as Tàiwèi.
Emperor Líng was quite fond of learning and arts.
Whenever he granted Kuān an audience,
he would always have him lecture on the classics.
Once, Kuān fell asleep in his seat after drinking.
The Emperor asked:
“Is the Tàiwèi drunk?”
Kuān looked up and replied:
“Your subject dares not be drunk;
it is merely that the responsibility is heavy and the duties great,
so my heart is as if drunk with worry.”
The Emperor valued his words.
Kuān was simple and fond of wine,
and disliked washing.
This became a proverb in the capital.
Once, when he had guests,
he sent a servant to buy wine.
The servant delayed for a long time
and returned very drunk.
The guests found it intolerable
and cursed him, saying:
“You beast!”
A moment later, Kuān sent someone to check on the slave,
fearing he might commit suicide.
He turned to his attendants and said:
“This is a human being;
to curse him as a beast,
what greater insult is there?
Therefore, I fear he might die.”
His wife, wishing to test if Kuān could be angered,
waited for the day of the imperial assembly.
After he had fully dressed,
she had a maidservant present him with meat soup,
and deliberately spill it on his court robes.
The maid quickly gathered it,
but Kuān's expression did not change.
He slowly said:
“Did the soup scald your hand?”
Such was his temperament.
He was known throughout the realm as an elder.
Later, he was dismissed due to a solar eclipse.
He was appointed Wèiwèi.
In the second year of Guānghé (179 CE),
he again succeeded Duàn Jiǒng as Tàiwèi.
He held office for three years,
and was dismissed due to celestial anomalies.
He was again appointed Yǒnglè Shǎofǔ,
and promoted to Guānglù Xūn.
For his prior counsel regarding the evil plots of the Yellow Turbans,
which he reported to the emperor,
he was enfeoffed as Lùxiāng Hóu with six hundred households.
He died in the second year of Zhōngpíng (185 CE),
at the age of sixty-six.
He was posthumously granted the seal and ribbon of Chēqí Jiāngjūn,
given the rank of Tèjìn,
and posthumously named Zhāoliè Hóu.
His son, Sōng, succeeded him,
and his highest office was Zōngzhèng.
The encomium says: Zhuó and Lǔ were sincere and honest,
their hearts filled with virtue.
Their benevolence moved even insects,
and their love extended to fetuses and eggs.
Kuān and Bà, in their governance,
were also praised for their gentleness and leniency.
Biographies of Fú, Hóu, Sòng, Cài, Féng, Zhào, Móu, Wéi – Chapter 16 (Fú Zhàn, courtesy name Zǐlóng)
Fú Zhàn, courtesy name Huìgōng,
was a native of Dōngwǔ, Lángyá.
His ninth-generation ancestor, Shèng,
courtesy name Zǐjiàn,
was the so-called Fú Shēng of Jìnán.
Zhàn's great-great-grandfather, Rú,
during Emperor Wǔ's reign,
stayed as a guest teacher in Dōngwǔ,
and consequently settled there.
His father, Lǐ,
was a famous Confucian scholar of his time.
He taught the *Shī Jīng* to Emperor Chéng,
and served as Gāomì Tàifù,
establishing his own distinct school of learning.
Zhàn was filial and fraternal by nature.
From a young age, he inherited his father's profession,
teaching several hundred students.
During Emperor Chéng's reign,
he became a Bóshì Dìzǐ through his father's position.
He was promoted five times,
and during Wáng Mǎng's time, he served as Xiùyī Zhífǎ,
sent to supervise major criminals,
and was promoted to Hòuduì Shǔzhèng.
When Gēngshǐ (更始) was established,
he was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Píngyuán (平原).
At that time, as soldiers suddenly rose up,
the world was in turmoil,
but Zhàn (湛) alone remained calm,
continuing his teaching without interruption.
He said to his wife and children:
"If a single harvest fails,
the ruler of the state reduces his meals;
now all the people are hungry,
how can we alone be full?"
So they shared coarse food,
and he distributed all his salary to aid his hometown,
receiving over a hundred visiting families.
At that time, a subordinate supervisor (Ménxiàdū 門下督) who was known for his strength
plotted to raise troops for Zhàn (湛).
Zhàn (湛) disliked his misleading the masses,
so he immediately arrested and beheaded him,
displaying his head in the city walls
to show the common people.
As a result, officials and commoners trusted and looked up to him,
and the commandery became peaceful.
The entire region of Píngyuán (平原)
was preserved by Zhàn (湛).
When Guāngwǔ (光武) ascended the throne,
knowing Zhàn (湛) to be a renowned scholar and veteran official,
he wanted him to take on important internal duties,
so he summoned him to be appointed Shàngshū (尚書),
tasking him with establishing the old regulations.
At that time, Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sītú 大司徒) Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) was campaigning westward in Guānzhōng (關中).
The Emperor, considering Zhàn (湛)'s talent suitable for a prime minister,
appointed him as Sīzhí (司直),
acting as Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sītú).
Whenever the imperial carriage went on an expedition,
Zhàn (湛) was always left to guard the capital,
managing all the various officials.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ (建武) (27 CE),
he succeeded Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) as Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sītú),
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yángdū (陽都).
At that time, Péng Chǒng (彭寵) rebelled in Yúyáng (漁陽).
The Emperor wanted to personally lead an expedition against him.
Zhàn (湛) submitted a memorial remonstrating, saying:
"Your servant has heard that King Wén (文王), upon receiving the Mandate of Heaven to campaign against five states,
would first consult his kinsmen,
then deliberate with his ministers,
and additionally consult the milfoil and tortoise shells,
to determine the course of action.
Thus, his plans succeeded,
his divinations were auspicious,
and his battles were victorious.
The Odes (Shī 詩) say: 'The Lord said to King Wén (文王),
Consult your hostile states,
And your brothers,
With your hooks and supports,
And your spears,
To attack Chóngyōng (崇庸).'
When the state of Chóng (崇) defended its city,
he retreated first and then attacked,
thereby valuing human life
and waiting for the opportune moment to act.
Thus, he obtained two-thirds of the empire.
Your Majesty inherited the extreme chaos of the age,
received the Mandate and became Emperor,
restoring the brilliance of your ancestors.
Over four years,
you annihilated the settlements of Bùxiāng (ブ鄉),
controlled the Five Corps (Wǔxiào 五校),
subdued the Bronze Horses (Tóngmǎ 銅馬),
defeated the Red Eyebrows (Chìméi 赤眉),
and executed those like Dèng Fèng (鄧奉)—
these are not insignificant achievements.
Now the capital is empty and depleted,
resources are insufficient.
We are unable to pacify those nearby yet want to attend to border affairs;
furthermore, the land of Yúyáng (漁陽)
is adjacent to the Northern Di (Běidí 北狄),
and the cunning captives, being in distress,
will certainly seek their help.
Moreover, the counties and towns Your Majesty would pass through
are especially impoverished.
Families who plant wheat
are mostly in the cities and towns.
Upon hearing that government troops are coming,
they will have already harvested it.
A large army traveling over two thousand li
will exhaust its soldiers and horses,
and transporting provisions will be difficult and obstructed.
Now, Yǎn (兗), Yù (豫), Qīng (青), and Jì (冀),
the central regions of the country,
are plagued by bandits who run rampant,
and they have not yet submitted to transformation.
East of Yúyáng (漁陽),
originally a frontier defense,
the land adjoins foreign barbarians,
and its tributes and taxes are meager.
Even in times of peace,
it relied on internal commanderies,
how much less now, in its desolate state,
is it worth prioritizing?
Yet Your Majesty forsakes the near for the distant,
abandons the easy for the difficult.
The four quarters are filled with doubt and alarm,
and the common people are fearful.
This is truly what perplexes your servant.
I again wish Your Majesty would consider afar King Wén's (文王) prudence in using troops and broad deliberation,
and think nearby of the appropriateness of past and future campaigns,
consulting your officials
to allow them to express their utmost humble sincerity,
adopting their strengths,
and selecting from them with your sagely consideration,
making the central realm your concern."
The Emperor read his memorial,
and ultimately did not personally lead the campaign.
At that time, the bandit Xú Yìqīng (徐異卿) and others,
numbering over ten thousand, occupied Fùpíng (富平).
Repeated attacks failed to dislodge them.
They only said,
"We wish to surrender to Grand Minister Sītú (司徒) Fú Gōng (伏公)."
The Emperor, knowing Zhàn (湛) was trusted and respected in Qīng (青) and Xú (徐) provinces,
sent him to Píngyuán (平原).
Xú Yìqīng (徐異卿) and his followers immediately surrendered that very day,
and were escorted to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Though Zhàn (湛) was in chaotic times,
he always adhered to cultured virtues,
considering rites and music the foundation of governance and transformation,
which could not be abandoned even in adversity.
That year, he submitted a proposal to implement the village drinking ceremony (Xiāngyǐnjiǔlǐ 鄉飲酒禮),
which was subsequently put into practice.
That winter,
the Emperor personally led a campaign against Zhāng Bù.
Fú Zhàn was left to guard the capital.
At that time, a winter sacrifice was offered at the High Temple (gāo miào).
The Administrator of Hénán (hénán yǐn) and the Colonel Director of Retainers (sīlì xiàowèi) argued in the temple.
Zhàn did not report them,
and was consequently dismissed from his post.
In the sixth year,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Bùqí (bùqí hóu),
with an estate of 3,600 households,
and sent to his domain.
Later, Dù Shī (dù shī), the Administrator of Nányáng (nányáng tàishǒu), submitted a memorial recommending Zhàn, saying:
“Your servant has heard that Táng (táng) and Yú (yú) flourished through their trusted ministers,
and King Wén (wén wáng) found peace through his many scholars.
Therefore, the Shī Jīng (shī jīng) extols ‘numerous and dignified,’
and the Shū Jīng (shū jīng) says ‘excellent indeed!’
Your servant Shī (shī) has humbly observed the former Grand Minister over the Masses (dà sī tú) and Marquis of Yángdū (yángdū hóu), Fú Zhàn (fú zhàn),
who, from his youthful adherence to propriety,
has been without blemish.
He is sincerely faithful and fond of learning,
upholding the good Way even unto death.
In classics, he is a teacher to others;
in conduct, he is an exemplar.
Previously, in Hénèi (hénèi) and Cháogē (cháogē), and when he resided in Píngyuán (píngyuán),
officials and common people feared and loved him,
and emulated his example.
Though he encountered times of turmoil,
he did not fall prey to the calamities of war,
but held fast to his principles with gravitas,
possessing an unshakeable will.
Your Majesty deeply understood his abilities
and elevated him to the weighty position of a chief minister.
All the worthy and the common people
looked up to his virtue and integrity.
However, a minor transgression led to his dismissal,
and he has not been reinstated for a long time.
This is regretted by those who are discerning,
and grieves the scholars.
Your servant is deeply saddened by this.
Zhàn (zhàn) is majestic in appearance,
a glory to the nation;
in wisdom, strategy, and foresight,
he is a fount for the court.
From his youth, he set his ambitions,
and in old age, he has not declined.
He is truly capable of assisting the imperial house,
and his reputation is sufficient to enlighten distant peoples.
In ancient times, feudal lords were selected and promoted to be dukes and ministers,
wherefore the four quarters turned their heads
and looked up to the capital.
A minister who is a pillar of the state
should occupy a position of assistance and guidance,
[一０]entering and exiting the Forbidden Gate
to mend deficiencies and remedy omissions.
Your servant Shī (shī) is foolish and inept,
not capable of discerning the talent of a chief minister.
Yet, harboring my humble thoughts,
how dare I not exhaust myself?
Previously, when your servant was a Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (shìyù shǐ),
I submitted a sealed memorial,
stating that Zhàn (zhàn) is public-spirited, honest, and kind to subordinates,
with clear distinctions between what he likes and dislikes.
He comes from generations of Confucian scholars,
has always held a good reputation and trustworthiness,
is proficient in classics and exemplary in conduct,
and is well-versed in state governance.
He is especially suited for close attendance
to offer counsel at Your Majesty’s side.
According to the old system, the nine provinces had five clerks (shàngshū),
making it two men per commandery.
[一一]Zhàn (zhàn) could be appointed to replace one.
This was somewhat criticized by those in charge.
But your servant Shī (shī), having received deep imperial favor,
believes that what I say genuinely benefits the nation.
Even if I die, I would have no regrets,
thus I again overstep my duties and risk offense to make this known.”
In the thirteenth year, in the summer,
he was summoned.
The Secretariat (shàngshū) was ordered to choose a day for his appointment.
Before he could take office,
he suffered heatstroke during a banquet with the Emperor
and died.
He was granted secret funerary articles.
The Emperor personally offered condolences and sacrifices,
and sent an envoy to escort the funeral and construct his tomb.
He had two sons: Lóng (lóng)
and Xī (xī).
Xī (xī) inherited the peerage.
When he died,
his son Guāng (guāng) succeeded.
When Guāng (guāng) died,
his son Chén (chén) succeeded.
Chén (chén) was humble and respectful, benevolent to all,
and especially devoted to learning.
His granddaughter became a noble lady (guìrén) of Emperor Shùn (shùn dì),
and he was granted the honor of attending court (fèng cháoqǐng),
holding the title of Specially Advanced (tèjìn).
When he died,
his son Wújì (wújì) succeeded,
also inheriting the family scholarship.
He was learned in many subjects and widely knowledgeable.
During the reign of Emperor Shùn (shùn dì),
he served as Attendant at the Yellow Gates (shìzhōng) and Colonel of Agile Cavalry (túnqí xiàowèi).
In the first year of Yǒnghé (yǒnghé),

an imperial edict commanded Wújì (wújì), along with Counselor-Remonstrant Huáng Jǐng (huáng jǐng), to collate the Five Classics, the Hundred Schools of Thought, and arts and techniques in the Imperial Library (zhōngshū).
During the Yuánjiā (yuánjiā) period,
Emperor Huán (huán dì) again ordered Wújì (wújì), Huáng Jǐng (huáng jǐng), Cuī Shí (cuī shí), and others to collaboratively compile the Hàn Jì (hàn jì).
He also personally collected ancient and modern texts,
deleted superfluities, and compiled essential matters,
naming it Fú Hóu Zhù (fú hóu zhù).
When Wújì (wújì) died,
his son Zhì (zhì) succeeded,
whose highest office was Grand Minister of Agriculture (dàsī nóng).
When Zhì (zhì) died,
his son Wán (wán) succeeded,
who married Princess Yáng'ān (yáng'ān cháng gōngzhǔ), daughter of Emperor Huán (huán dì).
His daughter became Empress Xiàoxiàn (xiàoxiàn huánghòu).
Cáo Cāo (cáo cāo) killed the empress
and exterminated the Fú (fú) clan,
and the marquisate was abolished.
Originally,
from Fú Shēng (fú shēng) onward,
the family passed down classical learning,
maintaining quietude and freedom from contention,
hence the Eastern Region called them
“Fú bù dòu” (fú bù dòu)
— “Fú the Non-Contender.”
Lóng’s (lóng) courtesy name was Bówén (bówén).
From a young age, he established his reputation through integrity.
He served as a Commandery Supervisor of Posts (jùn dūdóu).
In the second year of Jiànwǔ (jiànwǔ),
he went to Huái (huái) Palace,
where Emperor Guāngwǔ (guāngwǔ dì) treated him with great cordiality.
At that time, Zhāng Bù’s (zhāng bù) brothers each commanded strong armies,
occupying the Qí (qí) region.
Lóng (lóng) was appointed Grand Master of the Household (tàizhōng dàfū),
bearing a staff of authority as an envoy to Qīng (qīng) and Xú (xú) provinces,
to persuade commanderies and states to surrender.
Lóng (lóng) issued a proclamation, saying:
“Formerly,
the treacherous minister Wáng Mǎng (wáng mǎng)
murdered the emperor and usurped the throne.
The imperial clan raised an army
to eliminate the chaos and punish Mǎng (mǎng).
Thus, the common people supported the establishment of a sagely Duke (shèng gōng)
to preside over the ancestral temples.
However, he employed treacherous ministers
and slaughtered the virtuous.
The Three Kings (sān wáng) rebelled,
and bandits ran rampant,
defying the will of Heaven,
and eventually he was harmed by the Red Eyebrows (chìméi).
Heaven aided Hàn (hàn),
and a sagely wise one arose in due time.
Your Majesty, with divine martial prowess, arose,
controlling the many with few.
Thus, Xún (xún) and Yì (yì), with an army of a million,
were scattered at Kūnyáng (kūnyáng).
Wáng Láng (wáng láng), with the entire army of Zhào (zhào),
collapsed at Hándān (hándān).
Dàtóng (dàtóng) and Gāohú (gāohú) vanished at the sight of the banners.
Tiějìng (tiějìng) and the Five Colonels (wǔ xiào) were all utterly crushed.
King Liáng (liáng wáng) Liú Yǒng (liú yǒng),
fortunately possessing imperial clan lineage,
was granted the title of Marquis and King.
Yet, not knowing contentment,
he sought his own downfall and abandonment,
then enfeoffed marquises and appointed administrators,
creating fraudulent rebellion.
Now, the General of Tiger’s Teeth (hǔyá dàjiāngjūn) has an encampment of 100,000,
has already captured Suīyáng (suīyáng),
and Liú Yǒng (liú yǒng) has fled,
his family already exterminated.
These are things you gentlemen have heard.
If you do not plan for yourselves now,
what good will regret do later?”
Upon hearing this, the bandits of Qīng (qīng) and Xú (xú) were terrified.
The six colonels, including Zhuó Suǒ (zhuó suǒ) and the General of the Right (yòushī láng), immediately all surrendered.
Zhāng Bù (zhāng bù) sent an envoy with Lóng (lóng)
to the imperial court to submit a memorial,
offering abalone.
That winter,
[Lóng] was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness ([Guānglù Dàfū]).
He was again sent on a mission to [Bù],
traveling east with the newly appointed governors ([Mùshǒu]) and Commandants ([Dūwèi]) of [Qīngzhōu].
An imperial edict instructed [Lóng] to directly appoint magistrates ([Lìngzhǎng]) and lower officials.
[Lóng] welcomed and pacified [Bù]'s followers,
and many surrendered.
The Emperor praised his achievements,
comparing him to [Lì Shēng].
[Bù] was immediately appointed Grand Administrator ([Tàishǒu]) of [Dōnglái],
and [Liú Yǒng] also sent an envoy to declare [Bù] the King of [Qí].
[Bù] coveted the royal title
and hesitated, unable to decide.
[Lóng] enlightened and advised him, saying:
"Emperor [Gāozǔ] made a covenant with the empire:
none but those of the [Liú] clan shall be made kings.
You can only hope to become a marquis of ten thousand households."
[Bù] wanted to keep [Lóng] to jointly defend the two commanderies,
but [Lóng] refused,
requesting to return and report.
[Bù] then seized [Lóng] and accepted [Yǒng]'s enfeoffment.
[Lóng] sent a secret messenger to submit a memorial, saying:
"Your servant [Lóng], having failed in his mission,
was seized by a fierce rebel.
Although in distress,
I did not hesitate to lay down my life.
Moreover, the officials and people know that [Bù] has rebelled
and their hearts are not with him.
I pray that you advance troops in a timely manner,
and not be concerned about your servant [Lóng].
It is my greatest wish
to live to return to the imperial court
and receive punishment from the appropriate authorities.
If I should perish at the hands of the rebels,
may my parents, siblings, and elders burden Your Majesty.
May Your Majesty, the Empress, and the Crown Prince eternally enjoy all the nations,
boundless as heaven."
When the Emperor received [Lóng]'s memorial,
he summoned [Fú Zhàn], weeping, and showed it to him, saying:
"[Lóng] can be called a man of [Sū Wǔ]'s integrity.
I regret that I did not first grant him leave and he hastily requested to return!"
Five years later,
[Zhāng Bù] was pacified,
and the imperial carriage went to [Běihǎi].
An edict ordered [Lóng]'s younger brother, [Hán], to collect [Lóng]'s remains,
providing a coffin and burial expenses.
A Grand Master of Central Affairs ([Tàizhōng Dàfū]) was sent to escort the funeral.
An edict ordered a tomb to be built in [Lángyá],
and his son [Yuàn] was appointed Gentleman of the Palace ([Lángzhōng]).
[Hóu Bà], courtesy name [Jūnfáng],
was from [Mì], [Hénán].
His paternal cousin, [Yuān],
was a talented and eloquent eunuch
who held office during Emperor [Yuán]'s reign,
assisting [Shí Xiǎn] and others in managing the Central Secretariat ([Zhōngshū]),
and was known as the Grand Regular Attendant ([Dà Chángshì]).
During Emperor [Chéng]'s reign,
[Bà] was appointed Gentleman of the Palace for the Crown Prince ([Tàizǐ Shèrén]).
[Bà] was dignified, serious, and awe-inspiring in appearance.
His family had thousands of gold pieces,
but he did not engage in business.
He was devoted to learning
and studied under [Fáng Yuán], the Grand Administrator of [Jiǔjiāng],
specializing in the [Gǔliáng] Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals ([Gǔliáng Chūnqiū]),
and served as [Yuán]'s chief lecturer ([Dūjiǎng]).
At the beginning of [Wáng Mǎng]'s reign,
[Chén Chóng], the Grand Supervisor of Five Mandates ([Wǔwēi Sīmìng]), recommended [Bà] for his virtuous conduct,
and he was promoted to Chief ([Zǎi]) of [Suí] County.
The county's borders were vast,
extending to the [Jiāng] and [Hú] rivers,
and many fugitives became bandits.
When [Bà] arrived,
he immediately investigated and executed the tyrannical and cunning,
and dispatched men to capture the mountain bandits.
The county became peaceful.
He was twice promoted to Enforcer of Laws and Investigator of Treachery ([Zhífǎ Cìjiān]),
inspecting and investigating those in positions of power
without any hesitation or fear.
Later, he became Grand Administrator ([Dàyǐn]) of [Huáipíng],
and gained a reputation for competent governance.
When [Wáng Mǎng]'s regime collapsed,
[Bà] secured and defended himself,
ultimately preserving the entire commandery.
In the first year of [Gēngshǐ]'s reign,
an envoy was sent to summon [Bà].
The common people, old and young, wept and clung to each other,
blocking the envoy's carriage,
some even lying in the road.
All said:
"We beg to keep Lord [Hóu] for another year."
The people even warned nursing mothers not to raise their children,
saying, "If Lord [Hóu] leaves,
they will surely not survive."
The envoy, fearing that if [Bà] were summoned,
[Línhuái] would surely fall into chaos,
dared not hand over the sealed decree,
and reported the full situation.
Coincidentally, [Gēngshǐ] was defeated,
and the roads became impassable.
In the fourth year of [Jiànwǔ],
Emperor [Guāngwǔ] summoned [Bà] to meet the imperial carriage in [Shòuchūn],
and appointed him Director of the Imperial Secretariat ([Shàngshū Lìng]).
At that time, there were no existing precedents,
and the court had few veteran officials.
[Bà], being thoroughly familiar with old customs,
collected forgotten documents,
and memorialized to implement the good governance and legal systems of previous generations that were beneficial at the time.
All of these were put into practice.
The edicts of leniency issued every spring
and the implementation of the orders for the four seasons
were all initiated by [Bà].
The following year,
he succeeded [Fú Zhàn] as Grand Minister of Works ([Dà Sītú])
and was enfeoffed as a Marquis within the Passes ([Guānnèi Hóu]).
In office, he was discerning, upheld righteousness,
and served the public faithfully without deviation.
In the thirteenth year,
[Bà] passed away.
The Emperor deeply mourned and cherished him,
personally attending the condolence.
An edict stated:
"Only [Bà] accumulated good deeds and remained pure.
He served for nine years.
According to the old system of the [Hàn] dynasty,
on the day a Chancellor ([Chéngxiàng]) was appointed,
he was enfeoffed as a ranked marquis.
Because Our military forces were exposed
and meritorious officials had not yet been enfeoffed,
and out of loyalty to Our ministers' principles,
We did not wish to bypass them
to bestow titles,
and he abruptly passed away.
Alas, how sad!"
Thereupon, [Bà] was posthumously enfeoffed and given the posthumous title Marquis [Zéxiāng] of Sorrow ([Zéxiāng Āihóu]),
with an estate of 2,600 households.
His son, [Yù], succeeded him.
The officials and people of [Línhuái] jointly established a shrine for him,
offering sacrifices four times a year.
[Hán Xīn], the Grand Administrator of [Pèijùn], succeeded [Bà] as Grand Minister of Works.
[Xīn], courtesy name [Wēngjūn],
was from [Nányáng].
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of [Fúyáng]
for his meritorious service in campaigns.
He was fond of speaking frankly,
without concealment or taboo,
which the Emperor often could not tolerate.
Once, during a court assembly,
he heard the Emperor reading letters exchanged between [Wěi Xiāo] and [Gōngsūn Shù].
[Xīn] remarked:
"All rulers of fallen states possessed talent;
[Jié] and [Zhòu] also had talent."
The Emperor was greatly angered,
considering it a provocation.
[Xīn] also testified that the year would bring famine and disaster,
pointing to heaven and drawing on the ground,
speaking with extreme bluntness and severity.
He was dismissed from office and returned to his village.
The Emperor was still displeased
and again sent an envoy to deliver an edict reprimanding him.
The Colonel Director of Retainers ([Sīlì Xiàowèi]) [Bāo Yǒng] earnestly pleaded on his behalf but could not succeed,
and [Xīn] and his son, [Yīng], ultimately committed suicide.
[Xīn] had always enjoyed a high reputation,
and his death was not for a crime he committed.
The public was largely dissatisfied.
The Emperor then posthumously granted money and grain
to ensure a proper burial.
Later, [Ōuyáng Xī] of [Qiānchéng] and [Dài Shè] of [Qīnghé] successively served as Grand Minister of Works,
but both were imprisoned and died for their involvement in affairs.
Since then, it became difficult for high ministers to hold the position of Chancellor.
Thereafter, [Cài Mào] of [Hénán] 【Nèi】, [Yù Kuàng] of [Jīngzhào], and [Féng Qín] of [Wèijùn]
all died in office.
[Kuàng], courtesy name [Wénbó],
was intelligent and quick-witted.
He served as Grand Administrator of [Chénliú],
transforming people through his virtuous conduct.
He was promoted to Minister of Works ([Sītú]),
and died after four years.
[Yù] was later transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of [Yúlíng],
and during the [Yǒngpíng] era, he concurrently served as Grand Coachman ([Tàipú]).
When [Yù] died,
his son, [Jiàn], succeeded him.
When [Jiàn] died,
his son, [Chāng], succeeded him.
Sòng Hóng, courtesy name Zhòngzǐ,
was a native of Cháng'ān in Jīngzhào.
His father, Sòng Shàng,
served as shàofǔ during Emperor Chéng's reign.
When Emperor Āi ascended the throne,
Sòng Shàng, for not aligning himself with Dǒng Xián,
defied and offended, and was punished.
Hóng was gentle and compliant in his youth.
During the reigns of Emperors Āi and Píng, he served as shìzhōng.
During Wáng Mǎng's time, he was gònggōng.
When the Chìméi rebels entered Cháng'ān,
they sent an envoy to summon Hóng.
Being compelled and having no choice,
he traveled to Wèiqiáo Bridge
and threw himself into the water.
His family rescued him,
and he then feigned death to escape.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
Hóng was summoned and appointed tài zhōng dàfū.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ
he replaced Wáng Liáng as dàsīkōng
and was enfeoffed as Xúnyì Hóu.
The rent and stipends he received he distributed to support his nine generations of relatives,
and his household had no assets.
He was praised for his integrity.
He was later transferred and enfeoffed as Xuānpíng Hóu.
The Emperor once asked Hóng about men of vast learning.
Hóng then recommended Huán Tán of Pèiguó, saying his talent and learning were extensive,
almost matching Yáng Xióng and Liú Xiàng and his son.
Thereupon, Tán was summoned, appointed yìláng, and made gěishìzhōng.
Whenever the Emperor held a banquet,
he would have Tán play the qín,
enjoying its complex melodies.
Hóng heard of this and was displeased,
regretting his recommendation.
Waiting for Tán to leave the inner court,
Hóng sat in his official robes in his residence
and sent an officer to summon him.
When Tán arrived,
Hóng did not offer him a seat but admonished him, saying:
"The reason I recommended you
was to have you assist the state with virtue and morality.
But now you repeatedly introduce Zhèng music to disrupt the Yǎ and Sòng,
which is not loyal or upright.
Can you reform yourself?
Or shall I impeach you according to the law?"
Tán bowed his head in apology,
and after a long while, Hóng dismissed him.
Later, at a grand assembly of ministers,
the Emperor had Tán play the qín.
Tán, seeing Hóng,
lost his usual composure.
The Emperor was puzzled and asked about it.
Hóng then left his seat, removed his cap, and apologized, saying:
"The reason Your servant recommended Huán Tán
was hoping he could guide Your Majesty with loyalty and integrity.
Yet he has made the court indulge in Zhèng music.
This is Your servant's fault."
The Emperor's expression changed, and he apologized,
telling Hóng to resume his attire.
Thereafter, Tán was no longer ordered to serve as gěishìzhōng.
Hóng promoted over thirty worthy men, including Fēngyì and Huán Liáng,
some of whom eventually became gōngqīng.
Once, when Hóng was granted an audience at a banquet,
there was a new screen in the imperial seat area,
depicting virtuous women.
The Emperor repeatedly looked at it.
Hóng, with a stern expression, said:
"I have not seen anyone who loves virtue as much as they love beauty."
The Emperor immediately had it removed.
He smiled and said to Hóng:
"When one hears what is righteous, one obeys.
Is that acceptable?"
Hóng replied:
"Your Majesty advances in virtue.
Your servant cannot but rejoice."
At that time, the Emperor's elder sister, Húyáng Gōngzhǔ, was newly widowed.
The Emperor discussed court officials with her,
subtly observing her inclinations.
The Princess said:
"Sòng Gōng's dignified bearing and virtuous character
are unmatched by any minister."
The Emperor said:
"I am considering it."
Later, when Hóng was summoned for an audience,
the Emperor had the Princess sit behind a screen,
and then said to Hóng:
"The proverb says that the noble easily change friends,
and the rich easily change wives.
Is this human nature?"
Hóng said:
"Your servant has heard that friends made in poverty and lowliness should not be forgotten,
and a wife who shared hardship should not be dismissed from the house."
The Emperor looked at the Princess and said:
"The matter will not come to pass."
Hóng served in his position for five years.
He was impeached for fabricating charges against the Tàishǒu of Shàngdǎng,
and was dismissed to his residence.
He died several years later,
without a son,
and his marquisate was abolished.
Hóng's younger brother, Sòng Sōng,
was known for his strong and resolute filial piety.
He rose to the rank of Hénán Yǐn.
Sōng's son, Sòng Yóu,
during the Yuánhé period, served as tàiwèi.
He was impeached for siding with Dòu Xiàn,
dismissed to his home commandery,
and committed suicide.
Yóu had two sons: Sòng Hàn
and Sòng Dēng.
Sòng Dēng is found in the Rú Lín Zhuàn.
Sòng Hàn, courtesy name Zhònghé,
was known for his upright conduct in the classics.
He was recommended as màocái
and rose through four promotions to Tàishǒu of Xīhé.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn,
he served as Dōngpíng Xiàng and Dùliáo Jiāngjūn,
establishing a reputation for integrity
and becoming known for his authority and benevolence.
He was promoted to tàipú,
but pleaded illness and requested to retire.
He was appointed tài zhōng dàfū
and died.
The imperial decree stated:
"Tài zhōng dàfū Sòng Hàn
was pure and unblemished,
upright and without crookedness.
Previously, in the frontier regions,
he commanded the military,
winning over the various tribes,
and achieved nothing but excellent results.
War chariots were put away,
and the border people enjoyed peace.
We recognized his achievements
and elevated him to the Nine Ranks.
Due to illness, he retired and declined,
holding firm to his principles.
We intended to grant him the Three Excellencies,
but he passed away before it could happen.
The court grieves and laments,
deeply saddened by this.
Does the Shī Jīng not say: 'Swiftly achieving military merit,
you are thereby granted blessings'?
Let the jiāngxiàng and dàfū attend his funeral,
and bestow an additional one hundred thousand coins,
and while he is in his coffin,
let the full white silk and lamb be used for purity."
His son, Sòng Zé,
courtesy name Yuánjǔ,
served as Yānlíng Lìng
and also had a good reputation.
He promoted Wéi Zhù of the same commandery and Fǎ Zhēn of Fúfēng,
and was praised for his discerning judgment of people.
When Zé's son was ten years old,
he was shooting a crossbow with a servant.
The servant's bowstring broke, and an arrow flew out,
accidentally hitting and
killing him instantly.
The servant kowtowed and begged for punishment.
Zé investigated and pardoned him.
Xún Shuǎng of Yǐngchuān greatly admired this,
and people at the time also approved.
The commentary says: After the Restoration,
many held the positions of Tái and Xiàng, wielding overall authority.
Those who gained fame through their office,
was it not by prioritizing long-term achievements over minor considerations?
Thus, when Huì Gōng was in a critical situation,
he was concerned with the rites of archery in the countryside.
When Jūnfáng entered the court,
he first proposed lenient decrees.
Indeed, a broad-minded instrument has no immediate practical use;
a long path leads to distant achievements.
This is what the aspiring and benevolent consider fundamental.
If a gentleman achieves through this,
it is indeed valuable;
if he fails through this,
it is also a gain.
Sòng Hóng stopped the complex melodies
and warned against licentious beauty.
Does this not align with the spirit of Guān Jū?
Cài Mào, courtesy name Zǐlǐ,
was a native of Huái in Hénèi.
During the reigns of Emperors Āi and Píng, he gained prominence for his classical learning.
He was summoned to be tested as a bóshì.
In his policy proposal, he elaborated on disasters and anomalies,
and was promoted with high marks to yìláng,
then transferred to shìzhōng.
When Wáng Mǎng assumed regency,
he resigned due to illness,
and did not serve in Wáng Mǎng's court.
At that time, the world was in turmoil.
Máo was always on good terms with Dòu Róng,
so he sought refuge with him.
Róng wished to make him the Administrator of Zhāngyè,
but he firmly declined;
whatever provisions and supplies he was given,
he only took what was sufficient for his household.
Later, he was summoned to court together with Róng,
and was again appointed Yìláng.
He was twice promoted to Administrator of Guǎnghàn,
where he was praised for his administrative achievements.
At that time, many guests of the Yīn clan in the commandery violated official prohibitions,
but Máo would always investigate and prosecute them,
without any evasion.
It happened that Dǒng Xuān, the Prefect of Luòyáng, impeached Húyáng Gōngzhǔ.
The Emperor initially became angry and had Xuān arrested,
but later pardoned him.
Máo admired Xuān's integrity and uprightness,
and wished to make the court prohibit the excesses of the imperial relatives.
So he submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that promoting transformation and establishing instruction
must come from advancing the good;
and bringing peace to the country and its people,
nothing is greater than administering justice against evil.
Your Majesty's sagely virtue has arisen,
and has twice revived the great mandate.
Since your ascension,
the four seas have been peaceful.
It is indeed fitting to rise early and sleep late,
and not rest even when there is rest.
However, lately, families of imperial relatives and consorts
have frequently, relying on their favor and power,
violated official prohibitions,
killing people without being put to death,
and injuring people without being prosecuted.
I fear that the measuring line will be abandoned and not used,
and the axes will be discarded and not lifted.
Recently, a slave of Húyáng Gōngzhǔ killed someone in the Western Market,
and yet rode in the same carriage with the princess,
entering and exiting the palace.
His crime was evaded for days,
and the wronged soul was not avenged.
Dǒng Xuān, the Prefect of Luòyáng,
with unwavering integrity,
dared to confront the princess and punish the wicked.
Your Majesty, without first clarifying the matter,
summoned him, intending to flog him.
When Xuān first incurred Your Majesty's wrath,
the capital listened intently;
but when he received a pardon,
the world watched with wide eyes.
Now,
the maternal relatives are arrogant and extravagant,
and their guests are dissolute and unruly.
It is appropriate to instruct the relevant authorities to investigate and prosecute their wicked crimes,
so that righteous officials may forever fulfill their duties,
to satisfy the dissatisfaction of those near and far."
Guāngwǔ accepted it.
In the twentieth year of Jiànwǔ,
he succeeded Dài Shè as Sītú.
In office, he was clean, frugal, and diligent.
In the twenty-third year, he died in office,
at the age of seventy-two.
He was granted a catalpa coffin from the Eastern Garden,
and a very generous funeral endowment.
When Máo was first in Guǎnghàn,
he dreamed he was sitting in a grand hall,
and at the highest point there were three ears of grain.
Máo leaped to take them,
and got the middle ear,
but then lost it again.
He asked his chief clerk, Guō Hè, about it.
Hè rose from his seat and congratulated him, saying:
"A grand hall
is an image of the palace and government office.
Grain at the highest point
is the highest emolument for a minister.
Taking the middle ear
signifies the position of the Sāntái.
In characters, '禾失' (hé shī) combines to form '秩' (zhì - rank, emolument).
Although it says 'lost it',
it is precisely how you will attain rank and emolument.
There is a vacancy in the high official positions;
you will fill it."
Within ten days or a month, Máo was summoned to court,
and then appointed Hè as his aide.
Hè's courtesy name was Qiáoqīng,
and he was from Luò (yáng).
His paternal grandfather, Jiānbó,
and his father, Yóujūn,
both cultivated a pure integrity
and did not serve Wáng Mǎng.
Hè was skilled in clarifying laws.
He was successively promoted,
and in the Jiànwǔ era, he served as Shàngshūlìng.
He was in office for six years,
thoroughly familiar with precedents,
and provided much correction and benefit.
He was appointed Cǐshǐ of Jīngzhōu.
He was granted an audience and bestowed with gifts,
receiving exceptionally high favor and honor.
Upon arriving at his post,
he had outstanding administrative achievements.
The common people found him convenient,
and sang:
"Our virtuous and enlightened Guō Qiáoqīng,
loyal and upright, brings peace to the court and to all."
Xiǎnzōng on his inspection tour reached Nányáng,
and particularly sighed in admiration,
bestowing upon him the robes of a Sāngōng,
with embroidered patterns and a ceremonial crown with dangling strings of beads.
He was ordered, when conducting his tour, to remove the curtains from his carriage,
so that the common people might see his appearance and attire,
to highlight his virtue.
Wherever he passed,
officials and people pointed him out to each other,
and none did not consider it an honor.
In the fourth year of Yǒngpíng,
he was summoned to be appointed Hénányǐn,
and was praised for his integrity and tranquility.
He died in office after three years.
An imperial edict expressed sorrow and regret,
granting him one carriage
and 400,000 coins.
Féng Qín, courtesy name Wěibó,
was from Fányáng, Wèijùn.
His great-grandfather, Yáng,
served as Administrator of Hóngnóng during Emperor Xuān's reign.
He had eight sons,
all of whom became officials receiving salaries of two thousand *dàn*.
People between Zhào and Wèi honored him,
calling him
"Myriad-stone Lord."
His brothers were all physically imposing and robust,
but only Qín's paternal grandfather, Yǎn,
was less than seven *chǐ* tall.
He was constantly ashamed of his short stature and plain appearance,
fearing his descendants would resemble him.
So he arranged for his son, Kàng, to marry a tall wife.
Kàng begot Qín,
who was eight *chǐ* three *cùn* tall.
At eight years old, he was good at calculation.
Initially, he served as the Registrar for the Administrator Diāo Qī.
He was praised for his high competence.
Qī often accompanied Guāngwǔ on military campaigns,
and entrusted all administrative matters to Qín.
Qín's fellow county-men, Féng Xún and others, raised an army to support Guāngwǔ,
but before their plan succeeded, they were betrayed by local magnates like Jiāo Lián.
Qín then led his elderly mother, brothers, and clansmen to seek refuge with Qī.
Qī treated them all as his trusted confidants,
and recommended Qín to Guāngwǔ.
Initially, he was not employed,
but later he was appointed Lángzhōng,
and served in the Secretariat.
Because of his plans and suggestions regarding military provisions,
and his diligence in his duties,
he gradually gained trust and recognition.
Each time he was granted an audience,
the Emperor would look to his attendants and say:
"What an excellent official!"
Consequently, he was made responsible for matters concerning the enfeoffment of feudal lords.
Qín assessed and ranked merits and achievements by their importance and severity,
and the distance and proximity of territories,
and the richness or barrenness of land,
ensuring no one overstepped their bounds,
and everyone was satisfied and submitted.
From then on, the system of enfeoffment and peerage
was not settled without Qín.
The Emperor increasingly considered him capable,
and ordered him to generally oversee all matters of the Secretariat.
Sītú Hóu Bà recommended the former Prefect of Liáng, Yán Yáng.
Yáng was known for his criticisms and discussions,
and the Emperor had always disliked him.
Upon seeing Bà's memorial,
he suspected some impropriety,
and became furious.
He granted Bà an imperial letter, saying:
"How can high mountains and dark abysses be joined?
Once the yellow axe descends, there will be no place to hide.
Do you wish to test the law with your own body,
or to sacrifice your life to achieve benevolence?"
He sent Qín to deliver the imperial decree to the Sītú's mansion.
When Qín returned,
he explained Bà's original intention,
and elucidated the circumstances and reasoning.
The Emperor's anger gradually subsided,
and he appointed Qín as Shàngshū Púyè.
He served for fifteen years,
and was granted the title Guānnèihóu for his diligence and hard work.
He was promoted to Shàngshūlìng,
appointed Dàsīnóng,
and three years later promoted to Sītú.
Previously, many of the Sāngōng had been found guilty and dismissed.
Dì Xián Qín
wished for them to end their lives well,
and so, during a banquet, he casually admonished them, saying:
“Zhū Fú was disloyal to his lord above
and oppressed his colleagues below.
He ultimately suffered slander to this day;
whether he lives or dies, whether he experiences fortune or misfortune, is still unknown.
Is this not regrettable!
When a minister is banished and punished,
even if additional rewards, gifts, and funeral offerings are bestowed later,
they are not enough to compensate for a life of invaluable worth.
Loyal ministers and filial sons
should observe the former generations
as a mirror and a warning.
If one can be utterly loyal to the state
and serve the sovereign with unwavering devotion,
then one’s titles and rewards will illuminate the present age,
and one’s achievements and fame will be ranked among the immortal.
How can one not strive for this!”
Qín became even more respectful, cautious, and utterly loyal,
and was renowned for his dedication to duty.
Qín’s mother was eighty years old.
Whenever they met,
an imperial edict instructed her not to bow,
and the charioteer was ordered to help her ascend the hall.
The Emperor would then turn to his various princes and princesses and say,
“This is the mother
who enabled Qín to be honored and favored.”
Such was the extent of his closeness and respect.
In the first year of Zhōngyuán,
he passed away.
The Emperor mourned and regretted his loss,
sending an envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and bestowing imperial burial garments,
with additional funeral gifts.
Qín had seven sons.
His eldest son, Zōng Sì,
became the Dūwèi of Zhāngyè Shǔguó.
His middle son, Shùn,
married Princess Píngyáng,
and eventually became Dà Hónglú.
In the eighth year of Jiànchū,
Shùn’s middle son, Fèn, inherited the title of Zhǔjué and became Marquis of Píngyáng.
He passed away
without a son.
In the seventh year of Yǒngyuán,
an imperial edict reinfeoffed Fèn’s elder brother, Jìng, the Yǔlín Yòujiān, as Marquis of Píngyáng,
to maintain the princess’s ancestral sacrifices.
Fèn’s younger brother, Yóu,
a Huángmén Shìláng,
married Princess Píng'ān.
When Jìng died,
his son Mǎo succeeded him.
Mǎo served as Shìzhōng during the Yán'guāng era.
When he died,
his son Liú succeeded him.
Zhào Xǐ, courtesy name Bóyáng,
was a native of Wǎn in Nányáng.
In his youth, he possessed integrity.
His paternal cousin was murdered
without leaving a son.
Xǐ, at fifteen,
constantly sought to avenge him.
He then took up arms and gathered followers,
later proceeding to seek revenge.
However, his enemies were all sick,
and none could resist him.
Xǐ felt that avenging a killing by taking advantage of illness
was not the act of a benevolent person,
and so he released them and left.
He turned to his enemies and said,
“If you recover,
stay far away from me.”
All his enemies lay there, beating themselves.
Later, when they recovered from their illness,
they all tied themselves up and went to Xǐ.
Xǐ refused to see them,
and eventually killed them.
When Gēngshǐ ascended the throne,
the powerful Lǐ clan of Wǔyīn held their city and refused to surrender.
Gēngshǐ sent Zhùtiān Jiàngjūn Lǐ Bǎo to induce their surrender,
but they refused,
saying,
“We have heard that the Zhào clan of Wǎn has an orphaned grandson, Xǐ,
who is renowned for his trustworthiness and righteousness,
and we wish to surrender to him.”
Gēngshǐ then summoned Xǐ.
Xǐ was not yet twenty.
After an audience,
Gēngshǐ laughed and said,
“How can a young, inexperienced calf
carry heavy loads and travel far?”
He immediately appointed him Lángzhōng,
acting as Piān Jiàngjūn,
and sent him to Wǔyīn.
The Lǐ clan then surrendered.
Xǐ then advanced into Yǐngchuān,
attacking all those who would not submit,
traversed the Rǔnán region,
and returned to Wǎn.
Gēngshǐ was greatly pleased,
and said to Xǐ,
“You are truly a promising young horse from a renowned lineage.
Strive diligently!”
At this time, Wáng Mǎng dispatched Wáng Xún and Wáng Yì to lead troops out of the pass.
Gēngshǐ then appointed Xǐ as Wǔwēi Piān Jiàngjūn,
sending him to assist the various generals in resisting Xún and Yì at Kūnyáng.
When Guāngwǔ defeated Xún and Yì,
Xǐ was wounded,
but had distinguished himself in battle.
Upon his return, he was appointed Zhōnglángjiàng
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒnggōng.
When Gēngshǐ was defeated,
Xǐ was besieged by Chìméi troops.
In his desperate situation,
he climbed over roofs and fled,
along with dozens of friends, including Hán Zhòngbó,
carrying the young and weak,
crossing mountains and obstacles,
and directly exiting Wǔguān.
Zhòngbó, seeing his wife’s beauty,
feared that strong and violent men might assault her,
and that he himself would suffer harm as a result,
so he wanted to abandon her on the road.
Xǐ angrily rebuked him and refused to allow it.
He then smeared mud on Zhòngbó’s wife’s face,
placed her on a deer cart,
and personally pushed it.
Whenever they encountered bandits on the road,
who might attempt to force or abduct her,
Xǐ would describe her symptoms of illness,
and thus they were able to escape.
Upon entering Dānshuǐ,
they encountered Gēngshǐ’s relatives,
all naked, barefoot, and covered in mud and ashes,
starving and too weak to proceed.
Xǐ was moved to sorrow and compassion by the sight.
He gave them all his packed silk and provisions,
and then
protected them and guided them back to their hometown.
At this time, Dèng Fèng rebelled in Nányáng.
Xǐ had always been on good terms with Fèng,
and repeatedly sent him letters sharply admonishing him.
However, slanderers then claimed that Xǐ was conspiring with Fèng,
and the Emperor became suspicious.
When Fèng was defeated,
the Emperor obtained Xǐ’s letters
and exclaimed in surprise,
“Zhào Xǐ is truly a man of integrity!”
He immediately summoned Xǐ,
granted him an audience,
bestowed upon him a saddled horse,
and ordered him to await further instructions at Gōngchē.
At that time, Jiāngnán had not yet submitted,
and roads were impassable.
Xǐ was appointed Shǒu Jiǎnyáng Hóuxiàng.
Xǐ refused to accept troops,
and traveled alone in a single cart to Jiǎnyáng.
The officials and common people were unwilling to let Xǐ in.
Xǐ then explained and exhorted them,
calling out to the prominent figures in the city
and demonstrating the state’s power and trustworthiness.
Their leader then opened the gates, bound himself, and surrendered,
and from this, all the camps and strongholds submitted.
The Jīngzhōu Mù memorialized that Xǐ was capable of governing a difficult region,
and an edict appointed him Pínglín Hóuxiàng.
He attacked the various bandits
and pacified those who had already surrendered,
bringing peace to the counties and towns.
Later, he was appointed Huáilìng.
The powerful Lǐ Zǐchūn had previously been Lángyé Xiàng,
and was unscrupulous and monopolistic,
causing distress to the people.
Upon Xǐ’s arrival,
he heard that two of Zǐchūn’s grandsons had committed murder, and the matter had not yet been discovered.
He immediately investigated their illicit acts thoroughly,
arrested and interrogated Zǐchūn,
and the two grandsons committed suicide.
Dozens of people in the capital pleaded for him,
but Xǐ ultimately refused to listen.
At this time, Zhào Wáng Liáng was critically ill and nearing his end.
The Emperor personally visited the king
and asked what he wished to say.
The king said,
“I have always been close to Lǐ Zǐchūn.
Now he has committed a crime,
and Huáilìng Zhào Xǐ intends to kill him.
I beg for his life.”
The Emperor replied,
“Officials uphold the law;
the law cannot be bent.
Tell me something else you wish.”
The king had nothing more to say.
After he passed away,
the Emperor, recalling his feelings for Zhào Wáng,
pardoned and released Zǐchūn.
That year,
Zhào Xǐ was promoted to Grand Administrator of Píngyuán.
At that time, Píngyuán had many bandits.
Zhào Xǐ, together with various commanderies, pursued and captured them.
Their leaders were beheaded,
and thousands of their remaining followers were liable to punishment.
Zhào Xǐ submitted a memorial, saying,
"Evil should stop with the perpetrators themselves.
They can all be relocated to commanderies near the capital."
The Emperor followed his advice,
and so they were all moved to Yǐngchuān and Chénliú.
Thereupon, he promoted and employed those with righteous conduct,
and eliminated the treacherous and wicked.
Later, a great locust plague struck Qīngzhōu;
upon entering Píngyuán's border, they would all die.
The harvests were abundant year after year,
and the people sang songs about him.
In the twenty-sixth year,
the Emperor gathered his maternal relatives for a banquet.
They were very joyful,
and the various ladies each came forward and said,
"Zhào Xǐ is truly righteous and benevolent.
When we encountered the Red Eyebrows leaving Cháng'ān,
we were all rescued and saved by Zhào Xǐ."
The Emperor greatly praised this.
Later, Zhào Xǐ was summoned to become Grand Coachman.
When granted an audience, the Emperor said to him:
"You are not only protected by heroes,
but women also cherish your kindness."
He was generously rewarded.
In the twenty-seventh year,
he was appointed Grand Commandant [Tàiwèi]
and granted the title of Marquis within the Passes [Guānnèi Hóu].
At that time, the Southern Chányú submitted as a vassal,
and the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi all came to pay tribute at court.
The Emperor ordered Zhào Xǐ to manage border affairs,
and to plan for long-term stability.
Zhào Xǐ submitted a memorial recommending the restoration of various border commanderies,
and the two provinces of Yōu and Bìng were thus pacified.
In the thirtieth year,
Zhào Xǐ submitted a memorial arguing for the Fēngshàn sacrifices [Fēngshàn]
and the rectification of the three Yōng rites.
In the first year of Zhōngyuán,
he accompanied the Emperor in the Fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài [Tàishān].
When the Emperor died,
Zhào Xǐ received the imperial will [yízhào]
and managed the funeral rites.
At this time, the vassal kings were all in the capital.
Since Wáng Mǎng's usurpation and chaos,
the old regulations no longer existed.
The Crown Prince and the Prince of Dōnghǎi, etc., mingled and shared the same seats,
and the imperial institutions were disorderly.
Zhào Xǐ then straightened his countenance,
held his sword across the palace steps,
and helped the various kings descend,
thereby clarifying the distinctions of rank.
At that time, officials and attendants of the vassal states entered and exited the palace [gōngshěng]
without distinction from the hundred officials.
Zhào Xǐ then presented a memorial requesting that the Ujhyer [Yèzhě] escort and guard them,
assign them to reside in other counties,
and order all kings to return to their residences,
only allowing them to enter for morning and evening audiences.
He rectified the rituals,
and strictly guarded the gates,
creating solemnity both inside and out.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiéxiāng [Jiéxiāng Hóu].
In the spring of the third year,
he was dismissed for failing to truthfully investigate the matter of Xuē Xiū, the Chancellor of Zhōngshān.
That winter,
he replaced Dòu Róng as Minister of the Guards [Wèiwèi].
In the eighth year,
he replaced Yú Yán to act as Grand Commandant [Tàiwèi],
residing in the office as if truly appointed.
Later, he suffered the sorrow of his mother's death.
He submitted a memorial requesting permission to perform the mourning rites himself,
but Xiǎnzōng did not permit it.
He sent an envoy to release him from his mourning clothes,
and bestowed generous rewards and favor.
Zhào Xǐ internally managed the palace guard [sùwèi],
and externally served as prime minister,
maintaining his integrity and standing firm at court,
never once being remiss.
When the Emperor died,
he again managed the funeral affairs,
serving the late Emperor a second time,
and the rites were properly carried out.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor [Tàifù]
and supervised the affairs of the Masters of Writing [shàngshū].
Seven of his sons were promoted to be Gentlemen [láng] or clerks.
His eldest son, Dài,
served as an attendant at the Yellow Gate [Huángmén].
In the fifth year of Jiànchū,
Zhào Xǐ fell ill.
The Emperor personally visited him.
Upon his death,
the imperial carriage went to offer condolences.
He was eighty-four years old at the time.
His posthumous title was Zhèng Hóu.
His son, Dài, succeeded him.
He rose to the position of Commandant of Cavalry [Yuèqí Xiàowèi].
During the Yǒngyuán era,
he served as deputy to Liú Shàng, the General Who Attacks the West [Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn], in attacking the Qiāng.
He was imprisoned for an offense,
fell ill, and died.
Hé Dì took pity on him,
bestowing secret treasures, money, and cloth.
He was posthumously granted the seal and ribbon of Commandant of Cavalry and Marquis of Jiéxiāng.
His son, Zhí, succeeded him.
He rose to the position of Commandant of Infantry [Bùbīng Xiàowèi].
When Zhí died,
his son, Shú, succeeded him.
He had no son,
and the marquisate was abolished.
Móu Róng, courtesy name Zǐyōu,
was a native of Ānqīu, Běihǎi.
He was widely learned in his youth,
and taught the Great Xiàhóu version of the Book of Documents [Shàngshū].
His disciples numbered several hundred,
and his reputation was known throughout the province and local communities.
As a xiàocái recommended by the Minister of Works [Sītú], he became Magistrate of Fēng.
After serving for three years,
there were no lawsuits in the county,
and he was considered the best in the province and commandery.
Fàn Qiān, the Minister of Works, recommended Móu Róng as loyal, upright, and impartial,
with pure and complete conduct,
and suitable for service at court.
He also submitted an account of his conduct.
In the fifth year of Yǒngpíng,
he entered the capital to replace Bāo Yù as Colonel Director of Retainers [Sīlì Xiàowèi].
He rectified many matters,
and all the officials respected and feared him.
In the eighth year,
he replaced Bāo Xián as Grand Herald [Dà Hónglú].
In the eleventh year,
he replaced Guīyáng Hóng as Grand Minister of Agriculture [Dà Sīnóng].
At this time, Xiǎnzōng was diligently managing all affairs of state.
The high officials frequently held court meetings,
and on each occasion, Móu Róng was invited to deliberate on government affairs [zhèngshì]
and resolve lawsuits.
Móu Róng was learned in the classics and highly talented,
skilled in discussion and debate.
The court all admired his ability;
the Emperor often sighed in praise,
considering him capable of being a prime minister.
The following year,
he replaced Fú Gōng as Minister of Works [Sīkōng].
His actions were dignified and weighty,
and he perfectly embodied the decorum of a high minister.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
considering Móu Róng an esteemed minister from the previous reign,
he replaced Zhào Xǐ as Grand Commandant [Tàiwèi],
and collaborated with Zhào Xǐ in overseeing the affairs of the Masters of Writing [shàngshū].
He died in the fourth year of Jiànchū.
The imperial carriage personally attended his funeral.
At that time, Móu Róng's eldest son, Lín, had returned to his hometown.
Because his other sons were young and weak, the Emperor
ordered the Grand Commandant's clerks to teach them etiquette and proper conduct,
and bestowed generous gifts and favors.
He also granted burial land near Xiǎnjiéling,
and appointed Lín as a Gentleman [láng].
Wéi Biāo, courtesy name Mèngdá,
was a native of Pínglíng, Fúfēng.
His great-grandfather, Xián,
was Chancellor [chéngxiàng] during the reign of Emperor Xuān.
His grandfather, Shǎng,
was Grand Marshal [Dà Sīmǎ] during the reign of Emperor Āi.
Wéi Biāo's filial piety was pure and profound.
When his parents died,
he mourned and wasted away for three years,
not leaving his mourning hut.
After the mourning period was over,
he was emaciated and skeletal, a changed man.
He recovered after several years of medical treatment.
He loved learning and was widely read,
and was elegantly called a Confucian master.
At the end of the Jiànwǔ era,
he was recommended as a xiàolián [xiàolián]
and appointed as a Gentleman of the Interior [lángzhōng].
He resigned due to illness
and returned to teaching.
He was content in poverty and delighted in the Way [dào],
indifferent to advancement.
Among the Confucians of the Sānfǔ, none did not admire and look up to him.
Xiǎn Zōng heard of Biāo's reputation.
In the sixth year of Yǒngpíng (63 CE),
he was summoned and appointed as a Yèzhě,
granted a carriage, horses, and clothing.
He was promoted three times to Wèi Jùn Tàishǒu.
Sù Zōng ascended the throne,
and he was dismissed due to illness.
He was summoned to be Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng and Chánglè Wèiwèi.
He frequently presented political strategies,
always advocating for leniency and generosity.
Later, he submitted a memorial requesting to retire due to old age ("begging for his bones"),
and was appointed Fèngchē Dūwèi,
with a salary of Zhōng Èrqiānshí.
The rewards and imperial favor
were equal to those given to relatives.
In the seventh year of Jiànchū (82 CE),
the imperial carriage made a western inspection tour (Xī Xún Shòuhu),
and Biāo, acting as Tàicháng, followed.
He was frequently summoned
and asked about the old affairs of the Sānfǔ,
rituals, and customs.
Biāo then proposed:
"Now that we are touring the old capital in the west,
it would be fitting to trace and record the meritorious officials of Gāozǔ and Zhōngzōng,
to honor and make known their former achievements,
and to record their descendants."
The emperor accepted this.
When they reached Cháng'ān,
an imperial edict was issued to the Jīngzhào Yǐn and Yòu Fúfēng to seek out the descendants of Xiāo Hé and Huò Guāng.
At that time, Huò Guāng had no direct descendants,
so only Xiāo Hé's youngest grandson, Xióng, was enfeoffed as Cuózé Hóu.
As Cáo Cān's descendant, Cáo Zhàn, had already been enfeoffed as Píngyáng Hóu in the second year of Jiànchū (77 CE),
he was therefore not mentioned again.
Biāo was then generously bestowed with money, rare delicacies, and food,
and sent home to Pínglíng to visit his ancestral tomb.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Dàhónglú.
At this time, many who presented memorials
spoke of how the provincial and commandery recommendations were not based on merit,
hence officials became increasingly lax in their duties and administrative affairs were neglected,
with the blame lying with the provinces and commanderies.
An imperial edict was issued for the Gōngqīng and court ministers to discuss this.
Biāo submitted a deliberation, saying:
"I humbly observe Your Majesty's enlightened edict,
that you worry and toil for the common people,
bestowing grace upon selection,
striving to obtain the right persons.
Indeed, the state's paramount task is to select the worthy,
and the worthy prioritize filial conduct.
Confucius said: 'One who serves their parents filially can transfer that loyalty to their lord.'
Therefore, when seeking loyal ministers, one must look among the households of filial sons.
Rarely can individuals combine all talents and conduct.
Thus, Mèng Gōngchuò excelled over Zhào Wèi Lǎo,
but could not serve as Dàfū of Téng and Xuē.
Loyal and filial people
have a fundamentally generous heart;
harsh and strict officials
have a fundamentally narrow heart.
The reason the Three Dynasties could act with integrity
lies in how they were refined.
Scholars should prioritize talent and conduct,
and not purely rely on family background.
However, the key
lies in the selection of the Èrqiānshí.
If the Èrqiānshí are worthy,
then all recommendations will select the right persons."
The emperor deeply accepted this.
Biāo, seeing that the world had inherited the bureaucratic practices of two emperors,
where many considered harshness as ability,
and furthermore, that officials were appointed and selected for positions
not necessarily based on talent,
and also observing that the height of summer had much cold,
submitted a memorial, remonstrating:
"I have heard that the foundation of governance and transformation
must follow the Yīn and Yáng.
I humbly observe that since the beginning of summer,
it has been cold when it should be hot.
This is probably due to overly harsh punishments
and the commanderies and provinces not adhering to seasonal regulations.
Farmers are pressed with their tasks, but harsh officials seize their time;
taxes are collected as per regular levies, but corrupt officials cut off their wealth.
These are the major afflictions.
If one wishes to expedite people's important tasks,
one must first remove their afflictions.
The pivotal center of the empire
lies with the Shàngshū.
How can the selection of Shàngshū
not be taken seriously?
Yet recently, many have been promoted to this position directly from the ranks of Lángguān.
Although they are familiar with legal texts
and skilled in repartee,
their meticulousness is a minor cleverness,
and they are generally without great ability.
It is proper to select those who have previously served as provincial governors and have established reputations.
Although they may be slow in their advancements and retreats,
and sometimes fall short,
they are sincerely dedicated to public service
and meticulous in their duties.
One should consider the quick and sharp responses of the嗇夫 (sèfū, a minor official)
and deeply reflect on the achievements of Jiàng Hóu (Zhōu Bó), who was earnest and not eloquent.
In the past, when the Chǔ prison cases arose on a large scale,
Sīlìshǐ were appointed to assist the Láng officials.
However, they were mostly petty individuals
who were fond of illicit gains.
Now, since simplicity is desired,
they can all be abolished.
Furthermore, the position of Jiànyì (remonstrance official)
should employ just and upright scholars,
individuals of comprehensive talent, candidness, and integrity,
who can be beneficial to the court.
Currently, some are appointed Dàfū from among those who are merely summoned for examination.
Also, when Yùshǐ are transferred externally,
they often take charge of provinces and commanderies.
Both these positions should have their incumbents clearly selected
and held accountable for their performance.
As for the Èrqiānshí who have served for a long time
and are considered convenient and reassuring by the officials and common people,
they should be given increased rank and generous rewards,
and not be rashly moved.
I pray for Your Majesty's holy consideration."
The memorial was presented,
and the emperor accepted it.
In the spring of the second year of Yuánhé (85 CE),
during the eastern inspection tour (Dōng Xún Shòuhu),
Biāo, acting as Sītú, accompanied the tour.
Upon his return,
he requested retirement due to illness.
The emperor sent a Xiǎo Huángmén and a Tàiyī to inquire about his illness,
bestowing food upon him.
Biāo then declared himself critically ill.
In the summer of the second year of Zhānghé (88 CE),
an imperial edict was issued by a Yèzhě, stating:
"Biāo, a descendant of generals and ministers,
has diligently cultivated himself and disciplined his conduct,
rising from his local district
and serving in various positions for many years.
He has been afflicted with a serious illness
and has repeatedly requested to retire.
As you are now of old age,
you cannot be further burdened.
I fear that the duties are too intricate and fragmented,
and would cause further harm.
Therefore, return the seal and sash of Dàhónglú.
A Tàizǐ Shèrén is to be sent to the Zhōngzàng Fǔ
to receive a grant of two hundred thousand coins."
In the first year of Yǒngyuán (89 CE),
he passed away.
An edict was issued to the Shàngshū:
"The late Dàhónglú Wéi Biāo
committed no transgression while in office.
Just as we were planning to employ him,
he suddenly passed away.
Grant him two hundred thousand coins,
one hundred bolts of cloth,
and three thousand hù of grain."
Biāo was pure, frugal, and fond of giving.
His salary and grants were distributed among his clan,
leaving no surplus wealth in his household.
He authored twelve chapters,
titled Wéi Qīngzǐ.
His clan nephew was Yì.
Yì's courtesy name was Jìjié.
His great-great-grandfather Xuánchéng
served as Céngxiàng during the reign of Yuán Dì.
Originally,
Biāo alone moved to Fúfēng,
so Yì was still considered a native of Jīngzhào Dùlíng.
His elder brother was Shùn,
courtesy name Shúwén,
and he was the Píngyú Lìng.
He had a high reputation.
His second elder brother was Bào,
courtesy name Jìmíng.
He was repeatedly invited to serve in ducal administrations
but always left due to some matter.
Sītú Liú Kǎi again invited him,
saying:
"Because you are so quick to accept and decline positions,
your rank and title have not advanced.
The year is almost over,
and we are to select Yùshǐ.
I intend to recommend you;
will you stay here for a while?"
Bào replied:
"My dog-and-horse years are declining,
and my traveling strength is already weak.
I admire your profound grace,
and thus cannot bring myself to refuse.
However, I suffer from dizziness and chronic illness,
and cannot endure a long wait.
I dare not accept the private recommendation."
Then
he rose barefoot and left.
Kǎi pursued him,
but he went straight away without looking back.
When Ān Dì made his western inspection tour,
he was summoned and appointed Yìláng.
Yì was famous along with his two elder brothers in his youth.
He first served in the provincial and commandery administration.
The Grand Tutor, Huán Yān, invited him to manage complicated affairs,
and he became the Chief of Guǎngdū,
and the Magistrate of Gānlíng and Chén two counties.
His administration was very successful;
government offices had no outstanding matters,
and prisons were empty.
He repeatedly submitted memorials to Emperor Shùn,
advocating for adherence to classical principles,
evaluating achievements and demoting or promoting officials,
and summoning renowned scholars
to greatly establish these systems.
He also sharply criticized those around the emperor
and disparaged the Dòu clan.
His words had no effect,
and he was long suppressed without promotion.
He resigned his post due to the mourning period for his elder brother, Shùn.
When later invited to serve in the Duke's residence,
he did not accept.
The people of Guǎngdū erected a temple for him while he was still alive.
When he died,
the officials and common people of the three counties mourned for Yì,
as if they had lost a parent.
Bào Zǐzhù,
courtesy name Xiūmíng.
He was renowned in his youth for his classical learning and conduct,
and he did not answer calls from the province or commanderies.
The General-in-Chief, Liáng Jì, invited him,
but he did not accept.
In the second year of Yánxī (159 CE),
Emperor Huán summoned him with full ceremony via the imperial carriage,
but upon reaching Bālìng,
he claimed illness and returned home,
then entered Yúnyáng Mountain
to gather herbs and did not return.
Officials reported him for punishment,
but the emperor specially pardoned him.
An imperial edict again instructed the Magistrate of Jīngzhào to earnestly persuade him with courtesy,
but Zǐzhù still did not accept the summons.
When Emperor Líng ascended the throne,
the Regular Palace Attendant, Cáo Jié, seeing that Chén Fān and the Dòu clan had been executed
and there was much resentment throughout the realm,
wished to gain prestige by favoring worthy scholars of the time.
He informed the emperor, who appointed Zǐzhù as the Administrator of Dōnghǎi in his home.
The imperial edict was so pressing
that he had no choice
but to untie his headcloth and go to the commandery.
His administration relied on stern punishments,
and he was impeached by those he had punished,
resulting in his being sentenced to serve in the Left School.
Moreover, his second wife was arrogant and interfered with governance,
causing him to lose his reputation.
He eventually returned home,
but was harmed by wicked people.
Recluses considered this a disgrace.
An appreciation states: Zhàn and Bà established their merits,
thereby pacifying two regions.
The people of Huái longed for them,
and the Xú bandits were compelled to surrender.
Hóng truly embodied foresight,
and Rén did not forget his roots.
Xǐ's administration had many achievements,
and Biāo Ming managed with moderation.
Móu Gōng was direct with the Emperor,
and died in high office.
Biographies of Xuān, Zhāng, the two Wángs, Dù, Guō, and Wú, Chapter Seventeen.
Xuān Bǐng, courtesy name Jùgōng,
was a native of Yúnyáng, Fēngyì Commandery.
In his youth, he cultivated lofty principles,
becoming renowned in the Three Fǔ.
During the reigns of Emperors Āi and Píng,
he saw the Wáng clan seize power and monopolize governance,
encroaching upon the imperial clan,
and signs of rebellion emerging.
He then retreated into deep mountains,
and though the province and commanderies repeatedly summoned him,
he always claimed illness and did not serve.
When Wáng Mǎng became Chancellor-Regent,
he invited him, but he did not respond.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he again sent envoys to summon him,
but Bǐng steadfastly claimed illness.
When Gēngshǐ ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be a Household Counselor.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (25 CE),
he was appointed Imperial Censor-in-Chief.
Emperor Guāngwǔ issued a special edict that the Imperial Censor-in-Chief, the Colonel-Director of Retainers, and the Grand Secretary
should meet together and each sit on his own mat,
thus the capital nicknamed them
"The Three Solo Sitters."
The following year,
he was promoted to Colonel-Director of Retainers.
He focused on upholding general principles,
simplifying harsh details,
and all officials respected him.
Bǐng was naturally frugal,
always wore clothes and slept under a quilt of coarse cloth,
and ate vegetables from earthenware.
The emperor once visited his residence
and, seeing this, sighed and said:
"The two Gōngs of Chǔ State
are not as good as Xuān Jùgōng of Yúnyáng."
He immediately bestowed upon him cloth, silk, curtains, and miscellaneous items.
In the fourth year (28 CE),
he was appointed Grand Administrator of the Secretariat.
Whatever salary he received,
he would use to support his relatives.
For those who were orphaned or weak,
he distributed land,
leaving himself with no personal savings.
In the sixth year (30 CE),
he died in office.
The emperor lamented and cherished him,
and appointed his son Biāo as a Gentleman.
Zhāng Zhàn, courtesy name Zǐxiào,
was a native of Pínglíng, Fúfēng Commandery.
He was solemn and fond of propriety;
his every movement and stillness had rules.
Even when in his secluded room,
he would meticulously maintain his appearance.
Even when with his wife and children,
he was like a strict lord.
When in his hometown,
he spoke thoughtfully and with a serious demeanor,
and the Three Fǔ regarded him as a model.
Some people called Zhàn hypocritical and deceitful,
and Zhàn, hearing this, laughed and said:
"Indeed I am deceitful.
Everyone else deceives for evil,
but I alone deceive for good.
Is this not acceptable?"
During the reigns of Chéng and Āi,
he served as a Two Thousand Pic salary official.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
he successively held the posts of Administrator and Commandant.
In the early Jiànwǔ period,
he was the Prefect of Zuǒ Fēngyì.
In his commandery, he cultivated classical rites
and established regulations,
and his governance and moral transformation were widely implemented.
Later, he requested leave to return to Pínglíng,
and would walk upon seeing the entrance to the temple.
His Chief Clerk advanced and said:
"Your Excellency's position is honorable and your virtue weighty;
you should not demean yourself."
Zhàn said:
"According to rites,
one dismounts when passing a public gate,
and bows in the carriage when passing a royal carriage.
Confucius was deferential when in his hometown.
One should perform rites fully
in the land of one's parents.
What do you mean by demeaning myself?"
In the fifth year (29 CE),
he was appointed Minister of the Household.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ presided over court,
he sometimes showed signs of idleness,
and Zhàn would immediately offer remonstrance about his mistakes.
He always rode a white horse,
and whenever the emperor saw Zhàn,
he would say,
"The white horse is coming, and he will remonstrate again."
In the seventh year (31 CE),
he requested retirement due to illness,
and was appointed Grand Master of Guanglu,
succeeding Wáng Dān as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince.
After Empress Guō was deposed,
he claimed illness and did not attend court,
and was appointed Grand Master of the Household,
residing in the guardhouse of the Central East Gate.
Thus, people at the time called him "Lord of the Central East Gate."
The emperor frequently sent inquiries and bestowed gifts.
Later, after the Grand Administrator of the Secretariat, Dài Shè, was executed,
the emperor forcefully compelled Zhàn to replace him.
When Zhàn arrived at the court hall,
he lost control of his bladder,
and then declared his illness was severe,
unable to resume his duties at court,
and was consequently dismissed.
Several years later,
he died at home.
Wáng Dān, courtesy name Zhònghuí,
was a native of Xiàguī, Jīngzhào.
During the reigns of Emperors Āi and Píng,
he served in the provincial and commandery administrations.
During Wáng Măng’s time,
he was repeatedly summoned but did not report for duty.
His family owned thousands of gold pieces,
and he lived in seclusion, cultivating his aspirations,
and enjoyed giving generously to those in need.
Every year during the farming season,
he would load wine and food into a cart and go to the fields,
seeking out diligent workers and commending them.
Those who were lazy and negligent,
ashamed that they had not earned Dān’s recognition,
all redoubled their efforts and spurred themselves on.
The villagers followed suit,
leading to prosperity.
For those who were frivolous, cunning, dissolute, and abandoned their work, causing trouble,
he would enlighten their fathers and elder brothers,
and have them reprimanded and punished.
For those who passed away, he would provide funeral contributions,
and personally oversee the arrangements.
Whenever anyone suffered a bereavement,
they would wait for Dān to handle it,
