and this became a custom among the villagers.
After more than ten years of this practice,
his transforming influence was widely felt,
and the local customs became virtuous.
Dān’s nature was upright and pure,
and he detested evil and oppressive powerful individuals.
At that time, Chén Zūn, the Administrator of Hénán and from the same commandery,
was a great hero of Guānxī.
When a friend of his lost a parent,
Zūn oversaw the funeral arrangements,
and provided very generous contributions.
Dān then carried a bolt of plain silk,
displayed it before the host,
and said:
“This silk of mine,
comes from a loom.”
Zūn heard this and showed a look of shame.
Considering himself famous,
he wished to befriend Dān,
but Dān refused to agree.
It happened that former General Dèng Yǔ was campaigning westward in Guānzhōng,
and the army provisions were scarce.
Dān led his clan to contribute two thousand *hú*
of wheat. Yǔ recommended Dān to be appointed Left Fengyì,
but he claimed illness and did not attend to affairs,
and was allowed to return home.
Later, he was summoned to be Tutor of the Crown Prince.
At that time, Grand Minister of Works Hóu Bà wished to befriend him,
and when Dān was summoned,
he sent his son Yù to greet him on the road.
Yù welcomed him and bowed before his carriage.
Dān dismounted and returned the bow.
Yù said:
“My father wishes to befriend you,
why do you bow to me?”
Dān said:
“Jūnfáng (Hóu Bà) said this,
but Dān has not yet agreed to it.”
A schoolmate of Dān’s son lost a parent.
His home was in Zhōngshān.
The son informed Dān that he wished to go and offer condolences.
He gathered companions and was about to set off,
but Dān became angry and flogged him,
ordering him to send silk as an offering instead.
Someone asked for the reason.
Dān said:
“The difficulty of friendship
is not easily spoken of.
The world praises Guǎn and Bào,
and next are Wáng and Gòng.
Zhāng and Chén ended in disaster,
Xiāo and Zhū had a rift at the end,
thus one knows that those who preserve it intact are few.”
People of the time admired his words.
Initially, a guest had recommended a scholar to Dān,
who then selected him.
Later, the person he had selected was implicated in a crime,
and Dān was dismissed from office because of it.
The guest was ashamed, feared, and cut off contact,
but Dān never said anything.
Soon after, he was again summoned to be Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
He then called the guest and said:
“By cutting off contact yourself,
how lightly you regard Dān!”
He did not set a meal for him as punishment,
but treated him as before.
Later, he resigned from his position
and died at home.
Wáng Liáng, courtesy name Zhòngzǐ,
was a native of Lánlíng, Dōnghǎi.
In his youth, he loved learning
and studied the Xiahou Recension of the *Shàngshū*.
During Wáng Măng’s time,
he feigned illness and did not serve,
teaching over a thousand students.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Grand Marshal Wú Hàn summoned him,
and he responded to the call.
In the third year,
he was summoned and appointed Counselor Remonstrant.
He frequently offered loyal advice,
and advanced and withdrew according to propriety,
so the court respected him.
He was promoted to Administrator of Pèi Commandery.
Upon reaching Qí County,
he claimed illness and did not go to the prefectural office.
All the officials and subordinates followed him there.
Liáng then submitted a petition stating his severe illness,
requesting to retire.
He was summoned and appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance.
In the sixth year,
he replaced Xuān Bǐng as Director of the Grand Minister of Works.
In office, he was respectful and frugal.
His wife and children did not enter the official residence,
using cloth quilts and earthenware.
At that time, Bào Huī, a clerk of the Grand Minister of Works, went to Dōnghǎi on business,
and visited his home.
Liáng’s wife, wearing a cloth skirt, was dragging firewood
back from the fields.
Huī said:
“I am a clerk of the Grand Minister of Works,
and have come to deliver a message,
I wish to see your lady.”
The wife said:
“I am she.
I am sorry, officer,
there is no message.”
Huī then dismounted and bowed,
sighing as he returned.
Those who heard of it all praised him.
Later, he returned home due to illness.
After one year, he was again summoned.
Upon reaching Xíngyáng,
his illness was severe and he could not proceed.
So he visited a friend.
The friend refused to see him,
saying:
“Without loyal advice or extraordinary strategies to achieve high positions,
why do you bother to travel back and forth so eagerly?”
And so he rejected him.
Liáng was ashamed.
Thereafter, when repeatedly summoned,
he always claimed illness.
An imperial edict offered him black and red silk as a betrothal gift (for office),
but he still did not respond.
Later, Emperor Guāngwǔ visited Lánlíng,
and sent an envoy to ask about Liáng’s suffering illness.
He was unable to speak or reply.
An edict exempted his descendants from local corvée labor,
and he died at home.
Commentary states: Indeed, those who profit from benevolence may borrow benevolence to pursue profit;
those who embody righteousness do not seek to embody it but are naturally aligned with righteousness.
Jì Wénzǐ’s concubine did not wear silk,
and the people of Lǔ regarded it as a beautiful story.
Gōngsūn Hóng personally wore cloth quilts,
but Jí Àn ridiculed him for being deceitful.
The facts are not so different, yet praise and criticism are distinct.
Why is this?
Is it perhaps the difference between embodying it and profiting from it?
Xuān Bǐng and Wáng Liáng held important positions,
and Bǐng embraced plainness,
while Liáng’s wife carried firewood.
It can be said that their conduct exceeded frugality.
Yet, the people of their time praised their purity,
and rulers esteemed their integrity.
Was this not because they were sincere in their approach!
The saying goes: ‘If words are trusted equally,
then trust precedes the words;
if orders are obeyed equally,
then sincerity is beyond the orders.’
Is this not so!
Zhāng Zhàn disdained the reproach of being affected or fake,
thus he was not fake.
Wáng Dān found the path of maintaining friendships difficult,
thus he understood friendship.
Dù Lín, courtesy name Bóshān,
was a native of Màolíng, Fúfēng.
His father, Yè,
was the Inspector of Liáng Province during the reigns of Emperors Chéng and Āi.
Lín was fond of learning and profound in his youth.
His family already possessed many books,
and his maternal relatives, Zhāng Sǒng and his son, delighted in literary accomplishments.
Lín studied under Sǒng,
becoming extensively learned and widely read,
and was at the time called a "thorough scholar."
Initially, Dù Lín served as a commandery clerk.
When Wáng Mǎng was defeated,
and bandits arose,
Dù Lín, with his younger brother Chéng, and Fàn Qūn and Méng Jì from the same commandery,
took their weak dependents and sought refuge in Héxī.
On the road, they encountered several thousand bandits.
The bandits then plundered their wealth,
stripped them of their clothes,
and drew their blades, intending to kill Dù Lín and the others.
Méng Jì looked up and said:
“I wish to speak one word before I die.
General, do you know of the gods of Heaven?
The Chìméi (Red Eyebrows) army numbered a million,
sweeping all before them,
yet they were cruel and unjust,
and ultimately met with utter defeat.
Now, General, with an army of a few thousand,
you wish to emulate the deeds of a hegemon and a king,
but instead of practicing benevolence and kindness, you follow the path of a overturned carriage.
Do you not fear Heaven?”
The bandits then released them,
and all escaped the calamity.
Wěi Xiāo had long heard of Dù Lín’s ambition and integrity,
and deeply respected and treated him well,
appointing him as Píng of Chúshū.
Later, Dù Lín cited illness and asked to leave,
declining the salary and provisions.
Wěi Xiāo again wanted to force him to rise,
but Dù Lín then claimed severe illness.
Although Wěi Xiāo still held expectations for him,
he decided to show him leniency,
and thus issued an order saying:
“Dù Bóshān is someone whom the Son of Heaven cannot make a minister,
and whom feudal lords cannot befriend.
Indeed, Bó Yí and Shū Qí were ashamed to eat the millet of Zhōu.
For now, let him hold the position of a teacher and friend,
and await the opening of the Dao,
to allow him to follow his aspirations.”
Although Dù Lín was constrained by Wěi Xiāo,
he never compromised his integrity.
In the sixth year of Jiànwǔ,
his younger brother Chéng died,
and Wěi Xiāo then permitted Dù Lín to take the corpse east to his homeland.
After sending him off, Wěi Xiāo regretted it,
and ordered the assassin Yáng Xián to intercept and kill him at Lǒngdǐ.
Yáng Xián saw Dù Lín personally pushing a deer cart,
carrying his brother’s corpse,
and sighed, saying:
“In this present age,
who can practice righteousness?
Although I am a humble person,
how can I bear to kill a righteous scholar!”
Thereupon, he fled.
Guāngwǔ heard that Dù Lín had returned to Sānfǔ,
and then summoned him and appointed him as Shìyùshǐ.
He was granted an audience,
and questioned about the classics, old acquaintances, and affairs of the Western Region.
The emperor was very pleased with him,
and bestowed upon him a carriage, horses, and clothing.
The court officials knew that Dù Lín was employed due to his reputation and virtue,
and greatly respected and feared him.
The literati and high-ranking officials in the capital
all praised his extensive knowledge.
Zhèng Xīng of Hénán and Wèi Hóng of Dōnghǎi, among others,
were all expert in ancient learning.
Zhèng Xīng had once studied under Liú Xīn.
When Dù Lín met him,
he happily said:
“It is certainly harmonious that Dù Lín has met Zhèng Xīng and the others.
If Wèi Hóng were to meet Dù Lín,
he would even benefit from him.”
When Wèi Hóng met Dù Lín,
he was silently convinced.
Xú Xún of Jǐnán,
who had initially studied under Wèi Hóng,
later all changed to receive Dù Lín’s teachings.
Earlier, Dù Lín had obtained a scroll of the *Gǔwén Shàngshū* (Ancient Text Book of Documents) written in lacquer in Xīzhōu.
He always treasured it,
and even when he encountered calamity and distress,
he held it close and never let it leave his side.
He brought it out to show Wèi Hóng and the others, saying:
“I, Dù Lín, have been wandering amidst war and chaos,
always fearing that this classic would be lost.
Who would have thought that Wèi Zǐ of Dōnghǎi and Xú Shēng of Jǐnán would again be able to transmit it?
This Dao will ultimately not fall to the ground.
Although the ancient text does not conform to current affairs,
I hope you gentlemen will not regret what you have studied.”
Wèi Hóng and Xú Xún respected it even more,
and thus the ancient text began to circulate.
The following year,
there was a great discussion on the system of suburban sacrifices.
Many believed that just as Zhōu sacrificed to Hòujì,
Hàn should sacrifice to Yáo.
An imperial edict was again issued for the high ministers to deliberate.
The deliberators unanimously agreed,
and the emperor also concurred.
Only Dù Lín believed that the rise of the Zhōu dynasty
was due to Hòujì,
while the Hàn enterprise arose independently,
its achievements not stemming from Yáo.
The ancestral precedents
should be followed.
It was decided to follow Dù Lín’s proposal.
Later, he succeeded Wáng Liáng as Dàsītú Sīzhí.
Dù Lín recommended Fàn Qūn, Zhào Bǐng, Shēntú Gāng from the same commandery, and Niú Hán from Lǒngxī, among others.
All were promoted and employed,
and many scholars gravitated towards him.
In the eleventh year,
the office of Sīzhí was abolished,
and Dù Lín replaced Guō Xiàn as Guānglùxūn.
Internally, he attended to the palace guard,
and externally, he supervised the three bureaus.
He was thorough, diligent, and cautious,
and his selections were considered fair.
Whenever there were imperial gentlemen who were fond of learning,
he would entice and encourage them,
and his hall was full morning and evening.
In the fourteenth year,
the various ministers submitted a memorial, saying:
“In ancient times, corporal punishments were severe,
and thus people feared laws and decrees;
now, the constitution and laws are lenient,
and so evil acts cannot be stopped.
It is appropriate to increase prohibitions and restrictions,
to prevent their source.”
An imperial edict was sent down to the high ministers.
Dù Lín submitted a memorial, stating:
“Indeed, when human emotions are frustrated and humiliated,
the spirit of righteousness and integrity is diminished;
when legal restrictions are numerous,
the conduct of seeking mere escape flourishes.
Confucius said: ‘If you lead them with governmental regulations,
and keep them in order with punishments,
the people will try to avoid punishment but will have no sense of shame.
If you lead them with virtue,
and keep them in order with propriety,
they will have a sense of shame and moreover will become good.’
The enlightened kings of antiquity,
with profound insight and foresight,
always acted with magnanimity,
not seeking to multiply prohibitions.
The Five Punishments of Zhōu
did not exceed three thousand.
When the great Hàn first arose,
it carefully considered gains and losses,
thus breaking the square to make it round,
carving into simplicity,
abolishing harsh governance,
and establishing a looser net.
The whole country rejoiced,
and people cherished broad virtue.
As time went on,
it gradually expanded,
splitting hairs to find fault,
and endlessly slandering and deceiving.
The giving of fruit, peaches, vegetables, and roots,
was accumulated to constitute embezzlement;
minor matters, though not hindering righteousness,
were deemed grave offenses.
Thus, the state had no incorruptible scholars,
and families had no perfect conduct.
Consequently, laws could not prohibit,
and decrees could not stop,
superiors and inferiors evaded each other,
and the harms became ever deeper.
Your foolish subject believes that the old system should be adhered to,
and not be changed.”
The emperor followed his advice.
Later, the Crown Prince Qiáng requested to abdicate,
and was enfeoffed as the King of Dōnghǎi.
Therefore, officials for his staff were carefully selected,
and Dù Lín was made his Royal Tutor.
He followed the imperial carriage on the southern inspection tour.
At that time, various royal tutors were frequently summoned,
but many were engaged in social activities,
and could not answer the summons;
only Dù Lín maintained caution and diligence,
and would always appear when summoned.
Although the others were not reprimanded,
Dù Lín alone received special rewards.
He further declined to accept them,
and the emperor respected him even more.
The following year,
he replaced Dīng Gōng as Shàofǔ.
In the twenty-second year,
he again became Guānglùxūn.
Shortly thereafter,
he replaced Zhū Fú as Dàsīkōng.
He was broad-minded and widely accomplished,
and was praised as a competent prime minister.
He died the following year,
and the emperor personally attended the funeral and sent off the coffin.
His son Qiáo was appointed as a Láng.
The imperial edict stated:
“The descendants of dukes and marquises
must be restored to their initial positions;
the descendants of worthy individuals
should govern cities and towns.
Let Qiáo be made the Chief of Dànshuǐ.”
The discussion states: When one relies on power and strength for self-defense,
if one's strength wanes, one's life is endangered;
when one uses deceit for self-benefit,
if one's deceit is exposed, one's path is constrained;
but when loyalty, sincerity, earnestness, and respect are practiced,
even the uncivilized (Mán-Mò) will follow them,
it is truly because the power of virtue moves all things profoundly.
Therefore, when Zhào Méng harbored loyalty,
an ordinary man achieved his benevolence;
when Dù Lín practiced righteousness,
a brave warrior sacrificed his life.
The *Yì Jīng* says,
"Those whom others help [because of] (trust/faith)"
is not a lie.
Guō Dān, courtesy name Shàoyīng,
was a native of Ráng, Nányáng.
His father, Zhì,
was the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng during Emperor Chéng's reign,
and had a reputation for integrity.
Dān was orphaned at seven,
and was careful and filial.
His stepmother pitied him,
sold clothes for him,
and bought him property.
Later, he followed a teacher to Cháng'ān.
When he bought a permit to enter Hángǔ Pass,
he sighed emotionally, saying:
"If Dān does not ride in an envoy's carriage,
he will never leave this pass."
After arriving in the capital,
he often acted as a master lecturer,
and all scholars respected him.
The Grand Marshal Yán Yóu invited Dān,
but he declined due to illness.
Wáng Mǎng also summoned him,
whereupon he and other students fled to Běidì.
In the second year of Gēngshǐ,
the Three Dukes recommended Dān for his talent and ability,
and summoned him to be an Advisor Remonstrant.
He was given a staff of authority and sent back to Nányáng
to pacify and gather those who surrendered.
Dān had been away from home for twelve years;
he indeed rode a high carriage out of the pass,
just as he had wished.
When Gēngshǐ was defeated,
all the generals returned to Guāngwǔ,
and were granted titles and fiefs;
Dān alone held Píngshì and did not surrender,
mourning Gēngshǐ,
wearing sackcloth and showing full sorrow.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he secretly fled,
wearing worn clothes and traveling incognito,
traversing dangerous terrain,
seeking to visit Gēngshǐ's wife and children,
returning the imperial staff and seal to them,
and then returning to his hometown.
The Grand Administrator Dù Shī invited him to be the Chief Clerk (Gōngcáo),
but Dān recommended an elder from his hometown to take his place and left.
Shī then sighed, saying:
"In ancient times, when enlightened kings promoted reform,
ministers (qīngshì) yielded their positions.
Now, the Chief Clerk (Gōngcáo) recommends a worthy man;
this can be called ultimate virtue.
He ordered Dān's deeds to be compiled and recorded in the Yellow Hall,
to serve as a future model."
In the thirteenth year,
the Grand Marshal Wú Hàn summoned and appointed him to a high rank.
He was twice promoted to Governor of Bìngzhōu,
where he was praised for his integrity and fairness.
He was transferred to be the Colonel-Protector of the Xiongnú,
and then promoted to Left Fēngyì.
In the third year of Yǒngpíng,
he replaced Lǐ Xīn as Minister of Works (Sītú).
In court, he was upright, honest, and just,
and was equally renowned and friendly with Hóu Bà, Dù Lín, Zhāng Zhàn, and Guō Jí.
The following year,
he was dismissed for being unable to substantiate his investigation of Dèng Róng, the Grand Administrator of Lǒngxī.
In the fifth year,
he died at home,
at the age of eighty-seven.
Fàn Qiān, the Prefect of Hénán, known for his integrity,
replaced him as Minister of Works (Sītú).
Qiān, courtesy name Zǐlú,
was a native of Pèiguó.
Initially, he served as the Grand Administrator of Yúyáng,
where he used his wisdom and strategy to secure the border,
and the Xiongnú dared not cross into the territory.
When he became a high official,
he owned only a few acres of land
and no more than one *qǐng* of fields,
which he further yielded to his elder brother's son.
His wife once said to him:
"You have four sons but no place to stand an awl.
You should save some of your salary
to create an inheritance for future generations."
Qiān replied:
"I hold the position of a great minister; if I accumulate wealth and seek profit,
how can I set an example for future generations!"
He died in office after four years,
leaving no property in his home.
Later, Xiǎnzōng, during a court assembly, asked his ministers about Guō Dān's family's current situation.
The Imperial Clan Court Director (Zōngzhèng) Liú Kuāng replied:
"In the past, Sūn Shú'áo served as prime minister of Chǔ,
his horses were not fed grain,
his wife did not wear silk,
and his descendants were eventually granted the fief of Qǐnqiū.
Dān served as a governor of commanderies and states,
and entered the court as one of the Three Dukes,
yet his family had no inheritance,
and his descendants are in poverty."
The Emperor then sent a mission to Nányáng to seek out his heirs.
His eldest son, Yǔ,
rose to the office of Grand Administrator of Chángshān.
His youngest son, Jì,
was the Chancellor of Zhào.
Wú Liáng, courtesy name Dàyí,
was a native of Línzī, Qíguó.
Initially, he was a county official.
On New Year's Day, he and the clerks entered to offer congratulations.
The Chief of the Gate Guards (Ménxià Yuàn) Wáng Wàng raised a cup to offer longevity,
flatteringly praising the Grand Administrator's virtues.
Liáng, from his seat below, indignantly stepped forward and said:
"Wàng is a sycophantic and wicked person,
his flattery is shameless.
I request that you do not accept his cup."
The Grand Administrator composed himself and stopped.
When the banquet concluded,
he transferred Liáng to be Chief Clerk (Gōngcáo);
but Liáng was ashamed to gain advancement through speech,
and ultimately refused to present himself.
At that time, the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn) Prince Cāng of Dōngpíng heard of him and invited him,
appointing him as Chief of the Western Office (Xīcáo).
Cāng greatly respected and loved him,
and submitted a memorial recommending Liáng, saying:
"I have heard that what a state values most
is certainly the obtainment of worthy men;
among acts of repaying kindness,
none is greater than recommending scholars.
I humbly observe that my subordinate, the Chief of the Western Office (Xīcáo Yuàn) Wú Liáng of Qíguó,
is fundamentally honest and firm,
public-spirited, upright, incorruptible, and scrupulous.
He practices frugality, is content in poverty,
and maintains his integrity until old age;
he also studies the *Shàngshū*,
is thoroughly learned in its teachings,
has served as an Erudite,
and his conduct is a model for all.
He is fit to serve in the imperial guard
to assist the sagely government.
I, Cāng, am already excessively favored and honored,
and my responsibilities are deep and great.
I secretly admire the righteousness of Gōngshū Tóng rising together [with his lord],
and fear the crime of Zāng Wén stealing a position.
I dare to offer my foolish and ignorant opinion,
violating strict prohibitions."
Xiǎnzōng showed this to the Dukes and Ministers, saying:
"Previously, I saw Liáng on official business;
his hair and beard were white,
and his attire was very imposing.
To recommend worthy men and assist the state
is the duty of a prime minister.
Xiāo Hé recommended Hán Xìn,
erected an altar and bowed to him,
without further examination.
Now, let Liáng be an Imperial Gentleman (Yìláng)."
During the Yǒngpíng era,
the imperial carriage was making a short excursion,
and the Marquis of Xìnyáng, Yīn Jiù, presumptuously intruded into the forbidden imperial guard.
The Director of the Imperial Stables (Chēfǔ Lìng) Xú Kuāng hooked Yīn Jiù's carriage,
and arrested the charioteer and sent him to prison.
An imperial edict reprimanded Kuāng,
whereupon Kuāng tied himself up.
Liáng memorialized, saying:
"The Marquis of Xìnyáng, Yīn Jiù, relying on his status as an imperial relative,
violated the imperial procession.
He showed no courtesy as a subject,
which is a great disrespect.
Kuāng upheld the law and maintained righteousness,
but was instead subjected to trial.
I fear that the sagely transformation will be obscured by this."
Although the Emperor pardoned Kuāng,
he still demoted Liáng to be the Prefect of Jíqiū.
Later, he was promoted to Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works (Sītú Zhǎngshǐ).
Whenever important matters were debated,
he would always base his arguments on the classics,
never trying to conform to the imperial will or popular custom
to gain temporary fame.
Later, he was dismissed for an incident.
He was again appointed Imperial Gentleman (Yìláng),
and died in office.
Chéng Gōng
, whose courtesy name was Shǎozǐ, was a native of Gūmù in Lángxié.
He was orphaned young,
and at eight years old, he herded pigs for others.
A local scholar named Xú Zǐshèng
taught the *Chūnqiū Jīng* to several hundred students.
Gōng rested beneath his hut
and delighted in his work,
so he went to listen to the scriptures.
He then asked to stay as a student
and gathered firewood for the other students.
He endured hardship for several years
and studied diligently without tiring.
Once the classics were clear to him,
he returned home to teach.
When the world fell into chaos,
he led his students to take refuge in Hànzhōng.
Later, he went with his wife and children to Mount Méngyīn
and dedicated himself to farming.
When his grain was about to ripen,
someone claimed it as their own.
Gōng did not dispute with him,
but gave it to him and left.
From this, his reputation became known.
The Three Dukes repeatedly invited him,
but he declined them all.
During the Yǒngpíng reign,
he was summoned to the imperial carriage.
The Emperor visited the Pìyōng,
summoned Gōng, appointed him as a Bóshì,
and promoted him to Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng.
He frequently offered loyal advice,
discussed governance,
and his arguments were incisive.
Court officials feared his integrity,
and his fame spread to the Xiōngnú.
At that time, the Northern Chányú sent an envoy requesting to see Gōng.
Xiǎnzōng ordered him to tidy himself up,
but Gōng replied:
"The barbarians are dazzled by fame,
they do not recognize substance.
My appearance is ugly,
and cannot be shown to those from afar.
It would be better to select someone with a dignified appearance."
The Emperor then appointed Dàhónglú Wèi Yīng to replace him.
In the seventeenth year,
he was appointed Shìzhōng Jìjiǔ.
In the first year of Jiànchū,
he passed away.
Sùzōng praised and lamented him
and bestowed upon him burial land.
His wife submitted a petition requesting to bury him in his hometown,
and was further granted three hundred thousand cash.
Zhèng Jūn,
whose courtesy name was Zhòngyú, was a native of Rènchéng in Dōngpíng.
In his youth, he enjoyed the writings of Huáng-Lǎo.
His elder brother was a county official
and often accepted gifts.
Jūn repeatedly advised him to stop,
but he did not listen.
So Jūn divested himself to become a laborer.
After more than a year,
he earned money and silk,
and returned to give it to his brother.
He said:
"Things can always be reacquired,
but if you are an official and convicted of corruption,
you will be cast aside for life."
His brother was moved by his words
and subsequently became honest and incorruptible.
Jūn was fond of righteousness and sincere,
supporting his widowed sister-in-law and orphaned nephew
with utmost kindness and propriety.
He often claimed illness at home
and did not respond to invitations from the province or commandery.
The commandery governor desired to compel his presence
and ordered the county magistrate to cunningly lead him to his gate.
Upon arrival,
he ultimately could not be swayed.
Jūn then became a sojourner in Púyáng.
In the third year of Jiànchū,
Sītú Bào Yù invited him,
and later he was recommended for straight speech,
but he did not respond to any of these.
In the sixth year,
he was specially summoned by the imperial carriage,
then promoted twice to Shàngshū.
He frequently offered loyal advice,
and Sùzōng respected him greatly.
Later, he requested to retire due to illness,
was appointed Yìláng,
and granted leave to return home.
He then claimed his illness was severe,
and the Emperor bestowed upon him clothes and a hat.
In the first year of Yuánhé,
an imperial edict was issued to the Lújiāng Táishǒu and Dōngpíng Xiàng, stating:
"Yìláng Zhèng Jūn
has always maintained his integrity and been content in poverty,
modest, frugal, and orderly.
Formerly, in a position of trust,
he retired due to illness,
steadfastly adhering to goodness,
and remains diligent in his old age.
Furthermore, the former Ānyì Lìng Máo Yì
personally practiced humility and yielding,
and declined recent summons due to illness.
His pure and incorruptible conduct
is praised as benevolent in the eastern region.
Does not the *Shū* say: 'Displaying constancy is
auspicious indeed!'
Therefore, grant Jūn and Yì each one thousand *hú* of grain.
Regularly, in the eighth month, the chief officials shall visit and inquire after them,
bestowing sheep and wine,
to highlight these extraordinary deeds."
The following year,
when the Emperor made an eastern tour and passed through Rènchéng,
he visited Jūn's residence
and ordered that he be granted the salary of a Shàngshū for the rest of his life.
Thus, people at the time called him
"the White-Robed Shàngshū."
During the Yǒngyuán reign,
he died at home.
Zhào Diǎn,
whose courtesy name was Zhòngjīng, was a native of Chéngdū in Shǔjùn.
His father, Jiè,
served as Tàiwèi.
When Huán Dì ascended the throne,
Jiè was enfeoffed as Chútíng Hóu for his role in establishing the imperial succession.
Diǎn, when young, was steadfast in his conduct and lived simply.
He studied the classics extensively,
and students came from afar to him.
In the early Jiànhé period,
the Four Dukes submitted memorials recommending him.
He was summoned and appointed Yìláng,
lecturing within the Forbidden Palace,
and was twice promoted to Shìzhōng.
At that time, the Emperor wished to expand the Hóngchí Lake.
Diǎn remonstrated, saying:
"The Hóngchí Lake already irrigates
nearly a hundred *qǐng*,
yet you still wish to expand and deepen it.
This is not how to uphold the self-restraint of Táng and Yú,
nor to follow the people-loving ways of Xiàowén."
The Emperor accepted his words and stopped.
When his father died,
he inherited the enfeoffment.
He was sent out as the Tàishǒu of Hóngnóng,
then transferred to Yòu Fúfēng.
He lost his office due to an official matter,
then was summoned and appointed Chéngmén Xiàowèi,
transferred to Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng,
promoted to Shàofǔ,
and then transferred to Dàhónglú.
At that time, many imperial relatives were enfeoffed without merit.
The officials were displeased but none dared to remonstrate.
Diǎn alone memorialized, saying:
"To reward without merit
discourages those who toil.
It shames those above and humiliates those below,
disturbing the order of things.
Moreover, Gāozǔ swore
that only meritorious officials should be enfeoffed.
It is fitting that all such titles and territories be abolished
to preserve the old institutions."
The Emperor did not follow.
A short while later,
he was transferred to Tàipú,
then promoted to Tàicháng.
Whenever there were ominous portents or controversial issues in court,
he was consulted.
Diǎn would respond based on the classics,
without any equivocation.
Whenever he received rewards,
he would distribute them to the poor among his students.
Later, for remonstrating against the imperial will,
he was dismissed from office and sent to his fief.
When the Emperor passed away,
it was forbidden for enfeoffed princes and marquises to attend the funeral.
Diǎn said with emotion:
"I rose from humble clothing
to a high position.
Even birds like crows return food to their parents in gratitude;
how much more so should a scholar!"
So he relinquished his seal, ribbon, and tally to the county
and rushed to the capital.
The province, commandery, and the Dàhónglú all sought to punish him,
but the ministers and numerous officials praised Diǎn's righteousness,
memorializing to request that he be allowed to redeem himself with rent.
The imperial edict permitted it.
He was twice promoted to Chánglè Shàofǔ and Wèiwèi.
The ministers again memorialized that Diǎn was a diligent scholar and broadly learned,
and should serve as the Imperial Preceptor.
Coincidentally, he died of illness,
and an envoy was sent to mourn and offer sacrifices.
Empress Dòu again sent an envoy to additionally bestow a seal and ribbon,
and he was given the posthumous title Xiàn Hóu.
Diǎn Xiōng, Zǐqiān,
Qiān's younger brother Wēn,
successively served as Sān Gōng.
Qiān's courtesy name was Yànxìn.
In the first year of Chūpíng,
he replaced Huáng Wǎn as Tàiwèi.
When Xiàndì relocated the capital to Cháng'ān,
he appointed Qiān as acting Chēqí Jiāngjūn
to lead the vanguard.
The following year, he fell ill and was dismissed.
He then became Sīlì Xiàowèi.
The Chēshī king's hostage son was favored by Dǒng Zhuó,
and frequently broke the law.
Qiān arrested and executed him.
Dǒng Zhuó was furious,
and killed the Dūguān Cóngshì,
but he had always respected and feared Qiān,
so he did not punish him.
He was transferred to become Qián Jiāngjūn,
and sent to attack the Báibō bandits.
He achieved success,
and was enfeoffed as Pí Hóu.
Lǐ Quē killed Sītú Wáng Yǔn,
and Qiān again replaced Yǔn as Sītú.
He was dismissed due to illness after several months,
and was appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
He died that year,
and was posthumously named Zhōng Hóu.
Wēn's courtesy name was Zǐróu.
He first served as Jīngzhào (Jùn) Céng.
He sighed and said:
"A true man should soar like an eagle;
how can he lie low like a hen!"
So he abandoned his office and left.
During a year of great famine,
he distributed his family's provisions to aid the poor and starving,
saving over ten thousand people.
When Xiàndì moved the capital west,
Wēn served as Shìzhōng,
and traveled with the imperial carriage to Cháng'ān.
He was enfeoffed as Jiāngnán Tíng Hóu,
and replaced Yáng Biāo as Sīkōng.
He was dismissed.
After a short while,
he again became Sītú,
and recorded Shàngshū affairs.
At that time, Lǐ Quē and Guō Sì were fighting each other.
Lǐ Quē plundered the forbidden palace,
and abducted the emperor to Běi Wū,
isolating him from outside and inside.
Lǐ Quē had always suspected Wēn of not being on his side,
so he confined Wēn in the stockade,
and also wanted to move the imperial carriage to Huángbái Chéng.
Wēn wrote a letter to Lǐ Quē, saying:
"You previously claimed to avenge Dǒng Gōng,
but in reality, you massacred and trapped the royal city,
and killed high officials.
This cannot be spoken of in every household and seen by every family in the empire.
Now you are quarreling with Guō Sì over a small grudge,
creating a monumental enmity.
People are in extreme misery,
each unable to make a living.
If you do not change your ways,
it will lead to disaster and chaos.
The imperial court has repeatedly issued clear edicts,
wishing to bring about a reconciliation.
The emperor's orders are not carried out,
and his authority and grace diminish daily.
Yet you still want to move the imperial carriage,
and go to an inappropriate place again.
This is truly what this old man does not understand.
In the *Yìjīng*,
one mistake is an 'overstep,'
a second is 'wading,'
but if you do not change after three,
you will 'destroy your head,'
which is inauspicious.
It would be better to reconcile quickly,
and withdraw your troops to your garrisons.
This would secure the emperor above,
and protect the common people below.
Would this not be extremely fortunate?"
Lǐ Quē was furious,
and wanted to send people to kill Wēn.
Lǐ Quē's younger cousin Yìng,
who was Wēn's former subordinate,
advised against it for several days,
and thus Wēn was spared.
Wēn followed the imperial carriage to Xǔ.
In the thirteenth year of Jiàn'ān,
he appointed Cáo Cāo's son Pī as his subordinate.
Cáo Cāo was angry,
and impeached Wēn for appointing the sons of loyal officials,
claiming the selection was not genuine,
and Wēn was dismissed from office.
He died that year,
aged seventy-two.
The eulogy states: Xuān and Zhèng, the two Wángs,
maintained their integrity and uprightness.
Dù Lín adhered to antiquity,
Zhāng Zhàn was dignified and solemn.
Diǎn was dismissed for righteousness,
Gōng was exalted for virtue.
Dàyí with white hair,
was seen as a model prince.
Shàoqīng aspired to officialdom,
and ultimately rode in a high carriage.
Huán Tán and Féng Yǎn, Biographies, Part One of Eighteen
Huán Tán, courtesy name Jūnshān,
was a native of Péiguó Xiāng.
His father served as Tàiyuè Lìng during Chéngdì's reign.
Tán, through his father's privilege, became a Láng.
He consequently developed a fondness for music,
and was skilled at playing the guqin.
He was broadly learned and well-versed,
studying all five classics extensively,
interpreting their profound meanings
without dwelling on mere phrases and sentences.
He was capable in writing,
especially fond of ancient studies,
and frequently debated and clarified doubts with Liú Xīn and Yáng Xióng.
He had a natural fondness for entertainment,
was simple and unconcerned with formal deportment,
but enjoyed criticizing and disparaging common scholars.
Because of this, he often faced opposition.
During the Ài and Píng reigns,
his position did not exceed Láng.
Fù Huánghòu's father, Kǒngxiāng Hóu Yàn, was deeply fond of Tán.
At this time, Gāo'ān Hóu Dǒng Xián was favored,
and his younger sister became Zhāoyí.
The Empress was becoming increasingly alienated,
and Yàn was silently discontent.
Tán advised him, saying:
"In the past, Wǔdì wanted to establish Wèi Zǐfū,
and secretly sought out the faults of Chén Huánghòu.
Chén Hòu was eventually deposed,
and Zǐfū was ultimately established.
Now, Dǒng Xián is most beloved, and his younger sister is especially favored.
There is a danger of a 'Zǐfū transformation.'
How can one not be worried?"
Yàn was startled,
and said:
"Indeed,
what should be done?"
Tán said:
"Punishments cannot be applied to the innocent,
and evil cannot overcome righteous people.
Scholars gain the emperor's favor through talent and wisdom,
while women seek the master's affection through charm and allure.
The Empress is young,
and rarely experiences difficulties.
She might be tempted to employ doctors and shamans,
seeking external magical arts.
This must be guarded against.
Furthermore, as a revered imperial in-law, you frequently host guests,
which will inevitably be perceived as leveraging your influence,
and invite criticism and discussion.
It would be better to dismiss your retainers,
and earnestly maintain humility.
This is the way to cultivate oneself, rectify one's family, and avoid calamity."
Yàn said,
"Excellent."
So he dismissed his regular guests,
and informed the Empress,
following Tán's warning.
Later, Dǒng Xián indeed influenced Tàiyī Lìng Zhēn Qīn,
making him seek out faults in the Fù clan.
Consequently, the Empress's younger brother, Shìzhōng Xǐ, was arrested.
The imperial prison found no evidence,
so he was released.
Thus, the Fù clan remained intact during Àidì's time.
When Dǒng Xián became Dà Sīmǎ,
he heard of Tán's reputation
and wished to associate with him.
Tán first submitted a letter to Xián,
explaining the art of assisting the state and preserving oneself,
but Xián could not adopt it,
so they did not communicate.
During Wáng Mǎng's regency, usurpation, and regicide,
the scholars of the empire
all competed to praise his virtues and beauty,
and fabricated auspicious signs to curry favor.
Tán alone maintained his integrity,
remaining silent.
Wáng Mǎng made him Zhǎnglè Dàfū.
When Gēngshǐ was established,
he was summoned and appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he summoned Tán as a consultant (dàizhào).
Tán submitted a memorial discussing affairs of state, but it did not align with the emperor's wishes,
so he was not employed.
Later, Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sīkōng) Sòng Hóng recommended Tán,
who was appointed Palace Assistant (yìláng) and Consultant (gěishìzhōng).
He then submitted a memorial presenting what was appropriate for the current administration,
saying: Your servant has heard that the rise and fall of a state
depend on its governance;
the success or failure of governance
stems from its assistants.
If the assistants are virtuous and enlightened,
then outstanding men fill the court,
and the administration aligns with
the needs of the world.
If the assistants are not enlightened,
then discussions lose their timeliness,
and actions often result in errors.
Rulers of states
all wish to promote good governance and establish virtue,
yet if the path of governance is not
in order,
it is because their definition of "virtuous" differs.
In the past, King Zhuāng of Chǔ asked Sūn Shú'áo:
"I have not yet grasped what constitutes a proper national policy."
Shú'áo
replied:
"A nation's proper policy
is something that the multitude dislikes.
I fear Your Majesty may not be able to establish it."
The King said:
"Is not establishing it solely the ruler's responsibility,
or also the minister's?"
He replied:
"The ruler
is arrogant towards scholars,
saying, 'Without me, scholars have no way to attain wealth and honor.'
Scholars are arrogant towards the ruler,
saying, 'Without scholars, the ruler has no way to be secure and survive.'
Some rulers may lose their state without realizing it,
and some scholars
may suffer hunger and cold without advancing.
If ruler and minister are not in harmony,
then the national policy cannot be established."
King Zhuāng said:
"Excellent.
I wish for you, my prime minister, and all the grandees to jointly establish the national
policy."
Indeed, good governance
observes the customs and then applies education,
examines shortcomings and then establishes preventative measures.
Authority and virtue alternate in ascendance,
and civil and military means are used in succession.
Only then can governance be adjusted to the times,
and restless people can be pacified.
In the past, Dǒng Zhòngshū said,
"Governing a state is like playing a zither;
if it is out of tune, one must loosen and re-string it."
However, re-stringing is difficult
to implement,
and those who oppose the multitude perish.
Thus, Jiǎ Yì was banished for his talent,
and Cháo Cuò died for his wisdom.
Although there are capable individuals in the world, none dare to speak out
for fear of past events.
Indeed.
Establishing officials and appointing administrators
is to govern the myriad people.
Setting rewards and instituting punishments
is to distinguish good from evil.
When wicked people are punished,
then good people receive blessings.
Currently, if people injure
or kill each other,
even if the culprits have been executed according to the law,
private feuds are formed,
and descendants seek revenge.
Later resentments deepen previous ones,
leading to the destruction of families and lineages,
yet this is praised by custom as bravery and strength.
Therefore, even
the timid and weak
are forced to engage in such acts.
This is allowing people to settle matters themselves, without laws or prohibitions.
Now, it is fitting to clearly reaffirm the old ordinances:
If, after an official execution has been carried out,
there are still private acts of injury or killing,
even if the individual responsible flees,
their entire family shall be exiled to the frontier.
Those who inflict injury
shall receive a punishment two degrees more severe than usual,
and shall not be allowed to pay a ransom (gù shān) to atone for their crime.
If
this is done,
then grudges will naturally dissolve,
and banditry will cease.
This will also curb mergers and acquisitions, and foster integrity and shame.
Currently, wealthy merchants and great traders
often lend out money and goods.
Children from middle-class families
become their guarantors and servants,
toiling and running errands like retainers,
and their tax collections rival the income of feudal lords.
Consequently, many people emulate them,
eating without tilling,
even to the point of indulging in excessive luxury
to please their senses.
Now, it should be ordered
that merchants and traders mutually expose each other.
If wealth is not acquired through one's own labor,
it shall all be confiscated as ill-gotten gains and given to the informer.
If this is done,
then one will devote oneself to one's own efforts,
not daring to give goods to
others.
With few undertakings and limited strength,
they will certainly turn their efforts to farming.
When fields are cultivated,
grain harvests will be abundant, and the land's potential will be fully realized.
Fabricating charges leads to a judgment where one is almost equated with death.
This is like opening two gates for punishment.
Now, it should be ordered that those who understand righteousness and are well-versed in laws
review and standardize the penalty ratios,
unifying the legal system.
These shall be proclaimed to the commanderies and states,
and old statutes shall be abolished.
If this is done,
the empire will know its direction,
and there will be no unjust or excessive cases in prisons.
At this time, the Emperor largely believed in prophetic texts (chèn),
often using them to resolve doubts.
Moreover, rewards were too meager,
and the world was not settling down in a timely manner.
Tán again submitted a memorial, saying: Your servant previously presented humble words,
but did not receive a reply to the imperial edict.
Overcome with indignation,
I risk death to present them again.
The strategies of foolish men
are beneficial to the path of governance
because they align with human
hearts and grasp the principles of affairs.
Indeed, human nature tends to neglect immediate matters and value strange tidings.
Observing the writings of the former kings,
they all take benevolence, righteousness, and the righteous path as their foundation,
not strange or fabricated matters.
Indeed, the Way of Heaven and destiny
are difficult for even sages to speak of.
From Zǐgòng downwards,
none could hear of them,
let alone shallow
scholars of later generations,
who could possibly comprehend them!
Currently, various clever, petty, and artful individuals
are adding to books and illustrations,
falsely claiming prophetic texts (chèn jì),
to deceive the greedy and wicked,
and mislead
the ruler.
How can they not be suppressed and kept away!
Your servant Tán humbly heard that Your Majesty utterly rejected the alchemical arts (huángbái zhī shù) of the fangshi,
which was truly enlightened;
yet now
you wish to listen to and accept prophetic texts (chèn jì).
How is this not a mistake!
Although these matters sometimes coincide,
it is like divination or odd-even numbers.
Your Majesty should listen with clear understanding,
express your sacred
will,
dismiss the crooked theories of petty individuals,
expound the true meaning of the Five Classics (wǔjīng),
disregard the vulgar sayings that are all alike,
and carefully consider the refined plans of insightful people.
As for the bandits from all directions who have not yet completely surrendered,
this is because the strategies are not yet perfect.
Your servant Tán humbly observes that when Your Majesty employs troops,
those who surrender
receive no substantial rewards
to entice them with grace,
and sometimes their property is plundered and seized.
Consequently, military leaders and chieftains
each develop suspicions,
and their factions remain connected,
not disbanding for months and years.
The ancients had
a saying:
"Everyone knows that taking is taking,
but no one knows that giving is taking."
If Your Majesty can truly lightly bestow titles and heavily award rewards,
sharing them with your officers,
then
What could be summoned but not arrive?
What could be explained but not be resolved?
What could be faced but not open?
What could be campaigned against but not be conquered?
If this were the case,
then the narrow could become broad,
the slow could become fast,
the lost would return to existence,
and the forgotten would be regained.
Afterward, an imperial edict convened a discussion on the location of the Língtái.
The emperor said to Tán,
"I want to decide this [with] prognostication scrolls.
What do you think?"
Tán was silent for a long time,
then said,
"Your servant does not read prognostication scrolls."
The emperor asked the reason,
and Tán again strongly stated that prognostication scrolls were not classical texts.
The emperor was furious and said,
"Huán Tán disregards the sages and has no law!
He shall be taken down and executed!"
Tán kowtowed until his head bled,
and after a long while, he was finally pardoned.
He was sent out as the commander of the Liù'ān Commandery.
He was restless and unhappy,
fell ill on the road, and died,
at the age of over seventy.
Initially,
Tán authored twenty-nine chapters discussing contemporary affairs,
titled Xīnlùn.
He presented the book to the throne,
and Shìzǔ praised it.
One chapter, Qíndào, was unfinished,
so Sùzōng ordered Bān Gù to complete it.
He authored twenty-six chapters of fu, leì, shū, and zòu.
In the Yuánhé period,
Sùzōng made an eastern inspection tour.
When he reached Pèi,
he sent an envoy to offer sacrifices at Tán's tomb,
which the local villagers considered an honor.
Féng Yǎn, courtesy name Jìngtōng,
was a native of Dùlíng, Jīngzhào.
His grandfather, Yěwáng,
was Grand Master of Ceremonies during Yuán Dì's reign.
Yǎn was extraordinarily talented as a child;
at nine years old,
he could recite the Shī Jīng,
and by twenty, he was thoroughly versed in all books.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
many dukes recommended him,
but Yǎn declined to serve.
At that time, military uprisings erupted throughout the land.
Mǎng sent Gēngshǐ general Lián Dān to suppress the eastern regions.
Dān appointed Yǎn as his aide,
and they traveled together to Dìngtáo.
Mǎng sent a follow-up edict to Dān, saying:
"The granaries are empty,
the treasuries are bare.
It is time to be angry!
It is time to fight!
As a general bearing a heavy national responsibility,
if you do not sacrifice yourself in the field,
there will be no way to repay gratitude or fulfill your duty."
Dān was terrified.
That night, he summoned Yǎn
and showed him the letter.
Yǎn then advised Dān, saying:
"Your servant has heard that success through compliance
is the greatest way;
and achieving merit through defiance
is what strategy values.
Therefore, one aims for success,
regardless of the means;
one considers the greater good,
and does not cling to minor details.
In the past, Féng Chǒufù shielded his lord and enabled him to drink,
and was praised by the feudal lords.
Zhèng Jìzhòng established Tū and ousted Hū,
ultimately regaining his position,
and was lauded in the Chūnqiū.
Indeed, to exchange death for life,
and existence for annihilation,
is the way of the gentleman.
To go against popular opinion,
yet preserve the state and oneself,
is the foresight of the wise.
Thus, the Yì Jīng says: 'When exhausted, one changes;
when changed, one is unimpeded;
when unimpeded, one endures.
Therefore, heaven assists him;
auspicious,
nothing is not beneficial.'
But to know it is impossible yet insist on proceeding,
destroying armies and slaughtering multitudes,
with no benefit to the lord,
and on the day of one's death,
to be deemed unrighteous by one's time—
the wise do not do it,
the brave do not undertake it.
Moreover, your servant has heard,
do not delay when the time is right.
Zhāng Liáng, whose family served Hán for five generations,
struck Qín Shǐhuáng at Bólàng,
his courage surpassing Bēn and Yù,
his fame higher than Tài Shān.
Your general's ancestors
were loyal subjects of Hàn.
[一０]With the rise of the Xīn dynasty,
the heroes and outstanding talents did not join it.
Now, the realm is in chaos,
and people cherish the virtue of Hàn
even more than the poets longed for Zhào Gōng,
cherishing his sweet pear tree—
how much more so his descendants?
What people sing and dance about,
Heaven will surely follow.
[一一]Currently, for your general's plan,
nothing is better than garrisoning a large commandery,
pacifying the officials and soldiers,
sharpening their integrity.
Within a hundred lǐ,
cattle and wine are granted daily,
receiving heroic and outstanding men,
seeking loyal and wise counsel,
securing the hearts of future generations,
awaiting the changes of alliances,
promoting the benefits of the state,
and eliminating harm for the myriad people.
Then fortune and emolument will flow endlessly,
and meritorious achievements will be eternally inscribed.
How can this compare to your army being annihilated in the central plains,
your body left as fertilizer on the wild grass,
[一二]your achievements failing and your name lost,
bringing shame upon your ancestors?
The sage transforms misfortune into blessing,
the wise scholar turns defeat into success.
I wish that you, My Lord, would plan deeply and not follow the common ways."
Dān could not follow his advice.
Advancing to Suīyáng,
Yǎn again advised Dān, saying:
"Indeed, I have heard that the discerning see the formless,
the wise deliberate on the unsprouted.
How much more so for what is clear and evident?
[一三]All troubles arise from what is overlooked;
calamities emerge from the minute.
[一四]Defeat cannot be regretted;
the opportunity cannot be lost.
Gōngsūn Yāng said: 'One who acts superior to others
will be condemned by his generation;
one who has unique insights
will be regarded as a burden by others.'
[一五]Thus, believing in mediocre opinions
breaks plans of gold and stone;
[一六]adopting contemporary conduct
loses high and brilliant virtue.
Indeed, resolution is the master of wisdom;
doubt is the servant of affairs.
[一七]Time does not come again;
My Lord, do not hesitate a second time."
Dān did not listen.
He then advanced to Wúyán
and died in battle with the Chìméi.
[一八]Yǎn then fled to Hédōng.
[一九]
In the second year of Gēngshǐ,
he dispatched the Minister of the Secretariat, Bào Yǒng, to act as Grand General,
to pacify and unite the North.
Yǎn then used a strategy to advise Yǒng, saying:
Therefore, lord and minister both prosper,
achievements and fame are both established,
inscribed on metal and stone,
so that their good name is never forgotten.
Now, your servant is fortunate to encounter days of leniency and enlightenment,
and is about to face a time
for candid words.
How dare I remain silent and avoid blame,
without exhausting my sincerity?
The barbarians
along the frontier are being defeated by the Northern Dí,
campaigning thousands of lǐ away,
exhausting troops for years.
The entangled disaster is unresolved,
the warfare unceasing,
penal laws growing
harsher,
and levies becoming heavier.
Parties of powerful factions
strike horizontally from without,
while ministers of the various offices
are greedy and cruel within.
The common people are miserable,
hunger and cold arriving simultaneously.
Fathers
Sons wandered away,
husbands and wives were separated,
villages turned into ruins,
fields became overgrown,
plagues raged,
and calamities arose one after another.
Thus, on the
rivers and lakes,
and by the seas and Mount Dài,
winds surged and waves boiled,
trampling and destroying one another.
People from all directions
lay with their brains splattered on the ground.
The number of dead
was more than half.
The poison of calamity
penetrated
to the bone marrow.
Common men and women
were all filled with resentment and anger.
The emperor, with his sagely virtue and divine might,
rose like a dragon and soared like a phoenix.
He led the multitudes of Wǎn and Yè,
and commanded the scattered
troops,
shedding blood at Kūnyáng,
and marching swiftly to Wǔguān.
He broke an army of a million,
and crushed the armies of the Nine Tigers.
〔一０〕His thunder shook the four seas,
and he swept across the land.
〔一一〕He eliminated
disorder and rebellion,
and annihilated the lawless.
Within one year,
the realm was greatly pacified.
He continued the glorious achievements of Gāozǔ,
and restored the interrupted work of civil and martial rule.
The altars of soil and grain were restored,
and the fiery essence
shone anew.
His virtue surpassed all previous times,
and his accomplishments were unparalleled.
〔一二〕The people of the world naturally believed that having left the usurper Wáng Mǎng
and joined the sagely Hàn,
they should receive its blessings and rely on its aspirations.
To bestow grace
and spread virtue
should have been easy and pervasive,
like flying a feather with a strong wind.
〔一三〕However, the various generals plundered and looted,
acting contrary to ethics and logic.
〔一四〕They killed people's
fathers and sons,
and took their wives and daughters.
They burned their homes
and seized their property.
The hungry ate raw meat,
and the cold were naked and barefoot.
〔一五〕Their grievances were deep, their hopes shattered,
with nowhere to turn for succor.
Now,
the Grand General, with his clear and pure virtue,
holds the authority of the Grand Envoy.
He presides over the administration of the three armies.
He provides for and comforts the people of Bìngzhōu,
and his sincerity of kindness and love
is bestowed upon the populace.
His lofty
reputation
is heard among all scholars.
Therefore, those who crane their necks and stand on tiptoe in expectation
are not merely one person.
Moreover, the Grand General's task
is not merely to maintain integrity in his
conduct
and cultivate his heart.
〔一六〕It is to establish the great enterprise of the state
and achieve the primal accomplishments for Heaven and Earth.
In ancient times, King Xuān of Zhōu was merely a lord who brought about a restoration,
and Duke Huán of Qí
was merely a hegemonic and powerful ruler.
Yet, they had Shēn Bó, Zhào Hǔ, Yí Wú, and Jí Fǔ
who eliminated their pests and bandits,
〔一八〕and secured their territories.
How much more so for the Hàn dynasty, spanning ten thousand *lǐ*,
where the Illustrious Emperor is bringing about a restoration,
and the Grand General acts as its pillar and beam?
This truly cannot be neglected.
〔一九〕
The troops under the General's command are no more than a hundred *lǐ*,
constantly guarding cities,
and endlessly fighting battles.
Weapons soar like clouds,
and the common people are terrified.
How can you be complacent
and not worry deeply?
Now, the land of Bìngzhōu
is bordered on the east by famous passes,
and pressed on the north by strong Hú tribes.
The annual harvest is unique,
and the people are well-resourced.
This is a land of four battles,
a field for offense and defense.
If the unexpected occurs,
how will we respond?
Therefore it is said,
"If virtue is not accumulated beforehand,
people will not be used.
If preparations are not made in advance,
it will be difficult to respond to sudden events."
Now, the lives
of the living
depend on the General.
The General's reliance
must be on good talent.
It is advisable to replace those unfit for office,
and select worthy and capable individuals anew.
Indeed, even in a village of ten households,
there must be loyal
and trustworthy people.
If the right people are truly found
to uphold the Grand General's sagacity,
even people from the mountains and marshes
will all be moved by your virtue
and happily offer their services.
Then, select elite
and sharp soldiers,
and mobilize garrison troops.
Once the three armies are in order,
and weapons and armor are complete,
assess the abundance of the land,
observe the benefits of its springs,
devise methods for
agricultural colonies,
and practice the teachings of warfare and archery.
Then, your imposing reputation will spread far and wide,
and the people will live in peace.
If you guard Tàiyuán,
and pacify Shàngdǎng,
winning the hearts of the people,
and establishing famous and worthy
good assistants,
then even if there are no changes in the realm,
it will be enough to make your reputation manifest.
If an event arises one day,
you can achieve great accomplishments.
May the Grand General open the brightness of the sun and moon,
and develop the thoughts of a deep abyss.
Observe the discussions of the Six Classics,
consider the strategies of Sūn Wǔ,
examine the right and wrong of all opinions,
and clarify the good and bad of all scholars,
so as to surpass the achievements of
Zhōu Nán
and establish the legacy of the sweet pear tree,
causing your accomplishments to extend for a thousand years,
and your wealth and honor to be passed down endlessly.
How could the strategies of Yī and Wàng
add anything more than this!
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he sent Zōngzhèng Liú Yán to attack Tiānjǐng Pass.
He fought with Tián Yì for more than ten engagements,
but Yán could not advance.
Yì's mother, younger brother, wife, and children
were captured by Yán.
Later, Yì heard that Gēngshǐ was defeated,
so he sent an envoy to Luòyáng to present jade and horses.
He was immediately appointed Grand Administrator of Shàngdǎng.
He then sent envoys to summon Yǒng and Yǎn.
Yǒng, Yǎn, and others were suspicious and unwilling to surrender,
and resented Yì for betraying their previous agreement.
Yǎn then sent a letter to Yì, saying:
"The Three Kings have betrayed,
the Chìméi have endangered the state.
The world stirs like ants,
and the altars of soil and grain are overthrown.
This is the day for loyal ministers to achieve merit,
and the autumn for ambitious scholars to ride forth.
Bóyù was selected and appointed with a tally,
and solely governs a large commandery.
Now, the land of Shàngdǎng
has the security of four strongholds,
bordered on the east by three passes,
and serving as a screen for the state in the west.
How
can you hand it over to aid a strong enemy,
open the heart of the realm,
and lend a blade to your foe?
Is this not lamentable!
Qū Jǐ,
did not change his words;
Xiè Xī guarded Chéng,
threatened by Jìn and Lǔ,
but did not lose his city.
Judging from this,
internally there was no disaster of a noose around the neck,
Outwardly, there is no benefit like that of Táo Lái,
and one is subjected to the reputation of a traitor,
enduring the shame of a surrendered city.
I secretly feel ashamed for your attendants.
Moreover, Zhū Shùqí stole a city and betrayed his lord
to secure great profit;
it is said that even though he was base, he was certainly recorded.
Jǔ Móuyí sought sustenance through land,
and his name was not extinguished.
Therefore, a true man, when he acts, considers propriety;
when he behaves,
he considers righteousness.
There has never been one who defied these principles and was able to preserve both his body and name.
For Bóyù's deep consideration,
nothing is better than to share sentiments and exert effort with Bào Shàngshū,
displaying a loyal and steadfast
spirit,
and establishing achievements that surpass the age.
If, due to the ties and burdens of your esteemed parents,
you can relinquish your position and commit your life,
submitting to Shàngshū,
then great righteousness will be complete,
and the enemy will alleviate
their resentment.
Above, it will not diminish your responsibility as an imperial delegate;
below, it will be sufficient to save the lives of your elders and children.
You can raise your brows and speak grandly,
without shame before the world.
But if you covet the authority of Shàngdǎng
and cling
to the substance of the whole state,
Yǎn fears that Bóyù will certainly harbor the anxieties of Zhōu and Zhào,
and Shàngdǎng will again suffer the calamity of previous years.
In the past, Yàn Píngzhòng heeded Yánlíng's admonition
and ultimately
avoided the disaster of Luán Gāo.
Sūn Línfù violated Mùzǐ's warning
and thus fell into lifelong evil.
〔一０〕I believe that when Bóyù hears these sincere words,
he will surely
be deeply moved,
and unless he fortifies the city and holds it firmly,
he will spur his horse and not look back.
〔一一〕Saints turn misfortune into blessing;
wise scholars achieve victory through defeat.
I wish
you to exert yourself in these times,
and not conform to common ways.
Like gold and stone,
it is acceptable to seek longevity and avoid death.
Now, the span of a hundred years,
no one has yet been able to reach;
between old age and youth,
how much difference is there?
If indeed the former court
were still in existence,
and loyalty and righteousness could be established,
even if one's elderly parents were executed
and one's wife and children were cruelly divided,
that would be Yì's wish.
Recently,
the cunning bandits of Shàngdǎng
besieged the city with a great army,
and two groups of righteous soldiers
entered and occupied Jǐngxíng.
Yì's relatives broke through the enemy's encirclement
and resisted and attacked Zōngzhèng,
testing
their wisdom and courage themselves,
not that they were unable to contend.
It is truly known that the former court was harmed by soldiers,
and the new emperor's Sītú has already pacified the three Fǔ;
Lǒngxī and Běidì responded like a wind.
These matters are as clear
as the sun and moon traversing the sky,
and the rivers and seas encompassing the earth,
which are not sufficient to compare.
Life and death are fated;
wealth and honor are in heaven.
The survival or destruction of the world
is truly destiny.
Even if Yì sacrifices himself,
what can he do about fate?
If we perish,
who will establish righteousness?
My elderly mother is detained,
and I am obligated to remain for her.
Yet you urge me with greed for power,
and entice me to spur my horse,
suppressing my desire for gain,
insisting that I will not
look back.
How foolish!
Yì is thirty years old,
has held the position of minister,
and by nature has few desires;
his disposition disdains worldly affairs.
Moreover, now that my position is exalted and my life is in danger,
my wealth is great and my fate is precarious,
even a common person understands this,
why doubt a gentleman?
Jūngcháng and Jìngtōng
displayed their banners and hung their sashes,
appointing themselves.
Gài Zhòngyóu made his disciples ministers,
and Kǒngzǐ criticized him for deceiving Heaven.
Jūngcháng occupied two provinces
and one commandery,
yet Hédōng betrayed the state,
and his troops did not enter Zhì;
Shàngdǎng was besieged,
but he did not glimpse Dàgǔ;
Zōngzhèng approached the border,
but none could come to their aid.
Military might was humbled,
national power daily diminished,
the Three Kings betrayed,
Chìméi harmed the lord,
yet we did not see him hasten with double marching speed
to the rescue,
like Mò Dí winding cocoons to save Sòng,
or Shēn Bāoxū rubbing his heels raw to preserve Chǔ,
or the Wèi woman rushing home to mourn her brother.
After the lord's death for a year,
no one knew his settled place,
only vain hopes and baseless talk,
indulging in vulgar and narrow views.
If one cannot serve the living,
how can one serve the dead?
If one does not know how to be a minister,
how can one know how to be a lord?
Is it that you are tired of being a subject and son,
and wish to be
a ruler and father?
If you wish to shake Tàishān and sway Běihǎi,
and the matter fails, endangering your life,
you will then remember Yì's words.
The emperor resented Yǎn and others for not arriving in time,
but Yǒng was able to redeem his fault by establishing merit,
and was subsequently appointed,
while Yǎn alone was dismissed.
Yǒng said to Yǎn:
"In the past, Gāozǔ rewarded Jì Bù's fault
and executed Dīng Gù for his merit.
Now we encounter an enlightened ruler,
what is there to worry about?"
Yǎn replied:
"It is recorded that
there was a man who propositioned his neighbor's wife.
He propositioned the elder,
and the elder cursed him.
He propositioned the younger,
and the younger reciprocated.
Later, after her husband died, he married the elder one.
Someone asked him: 'Was it not she who cursed you?'
He said: 'From others' perspective, they desire me to reciprocate,
but from my perspective, I desire her to curse me.'
Heaven's will is hard to know,
but human principles are easy to uphold.
A minister who upholds principles,
what does he fear from death?"
Soon after,
the emperor appointed Yǎn as Qǔyáng lìng.
He executed notorious bandits like Guō Shèng
and received the surrender of over five thousand people.
His merit deserved enfeoffment,
but due to slander,
the reward was not bestowed.
In the sixth year of Jiànwǔ, there was a solar eclipse,
and Yǎn submitted a memorial enumerating eight matters: The first was to manifest civil virtue,
the second to praise military achievements,
the third to restore former merits,
the fourth to attract outstanding talents,
the fifth to clarify likes and dislikes,
the sixth to simplify laws and decrees,
the seventh to differentiate ranks and salaries,
and the eighth to pacify the borders.
After the memorial was submitted,
the emperor was about to summon him for an audience.
Previously,
when Yǎn was Lángmèng zhǎng,
he had, due to a crime, brought down the prominent family of Lìnghú Lüè.
At this time, Lüè was Sīkōng zhǎngshǐ,
and he slandered him to Shàngshū lìng Wáng Hù and Shàngshū Zhōu Shēngfēng, saying:
"The reason Yǎn seeks an audience
is to discredit you."
Hù and others feared this,
and immediately worked together to obstruct him,
so Yǎn was unable to enter.
Later, Wèi Yù Yīn Xīng and Xīnyáng Hóu Yīn Jiù became prominent due to their status as imperial relatives.
They held Yǎn in deep respect,
and Yǎn consequently became associated with them.
Because of this, he was invited by various princes
and soon became a Sīlì Cóngshì.
The emperor, having learned from the imperial relatives and their retainers in the Western Capital,
punished them all according to the law.
The most serious cases resulted in death or exile,
while others faced demotion and dismissal.
Yǎn was thus implicated,
and once went to prison of his own accord.
He was granted amnesty and not questioned.
He returned to his old commandery in the west,
shut his gate and protected himself,
not daring to communicate with old friends and relatives again.
Féng Yǎn Zhuàn, Part Two of Eighteen
At the end of Jiànwǔ,
he submitted a memorial, stating: "I humbly recall Gāozǔ's strategy and Chén Píng's counsel:
to criticize them is to alienate,
to praise them is to draw near.
With Wéndì's sagacity and Wèi Shàng's loyalty:
to constrain him by law leads to guilt,
to treat him with virtue leads to merit.
Later, in recent generations,
Dǒng Zhòngshū spoke of morality and virtue,
but was envied by Gōngsūn Hóng.
Lǐ Guǎng displayed valor against the Xiōngnú,
but was obstructed by Wèi Qīng.
This is what loyal ministers constantly shed tears over.
I, Yǎn, consider myself a humble and lowly official,
having
no recommendation from those unaware of my worth above me,
nor any persuasion like Féng Táng's below me.
I lack Dǒng Shēng's talent
and am short of Lǐ Guǎng's influence.
Yet I wish to escape slanderous mouths
and resolve grudges and suspicions.
Is this not difficult
indeed!
I dare not deviate from the path to seek timely advantage,
nor harbor treacherous schemes when serving my lord,
nor have thoughts of plunder when leading troops.
Wèi Yù Yīn Xīng
was respectful, cautious, and meticulous,
internally
cultivating and restraining himself,
and externally keeping clear of suspicion.
Therefore, I dared to associate with him.
Xīng knew of my poverty
and often wanted to provide for my livelihood.
But I considered myself lacking in the 'three benefits' talent
and did
not dare to accept a position of 'three detriments.'
I firmly declined and did not accept.
Formerly, during Gēngshǐ's reign,
I held the authority over goods and wealth in Tàiyuán,
living amidst turmoil and urgency.
I held office and drew
salary for over twenty years,
yet my wealth diminished annually,
and my living situation became poorer day by day.
My home had no store of cloth or silk,
and when I went out, I had no ornate carriage or horse.
Now I encounter a time of clarity and enlightenment,
an era
for disciplined conduct and diligent action,
yet enemies rise in droves,
and criticisms spread across the world.
Indeed, it is easy for the rich and noble to do good,
but difficult for the poor and lowly to achieve merit.
I, a distant
official of the fields,
have no hope of reaching the exalted palace gates.
Trembling with fear, I present myself
to atone for my faults.
Yǎn did not achieve his ambitions,
so he retired and composed phú.
He also wrote of himself, saying: Féng Zǐ believes that a man of virtue
is not like a dull jade,
nor like a rigid stone.
Like wind rising and clouds gathering,
now a dragon, now a snake,
he soars with the Way
and changes with the times.
How could he cling to one principle?
When employed, he acts;
when dismissed, he withdraws.
His advance and retreat have no fixed master,
his bending and stretching have no constant form.
Therefore, it is said:
'He has
law and no law, taking action according to the times;
he has measure and no measure,
associating or separating with things.'
He constantly strives for the essence of morality and virtue,
not seeking worldly fame.
He is broad-minded towards minute
and trivial rituals
and disregards mundane human affairs.
He corrects his person and walks a straight path,
calmly pursuing his aspirations.
He once favored unconventional strategies,
but the times could not heed
his plans.
He sighed deeply,
lamenting his misfortune.
He remained long in a minor official post,
unable to express what was in his heart.
He suppressed his feelings and curbed his principles,
his heart distressed and his spirit
sorrowful.
Indeed, a family that hews ice
does not profit from raising chickens and pigs;
a minister in charge of stockpiles
does not engage in market trade.
Moreover, having held office and drawn salary for over twenty
years,
my wealth has diminished,
and my living situation has become poorer.
The gentleman's service
is solely to practice his Way.
Those who are preoccupied with current affairs cannot elevate their virtue;
those who seek
for themselves cannot accomplish their goals.
[(一０)] He left and returned home,
again traveling as a sojourner in the commanderies and prefectures.
The more he pursued office,
the poorer his family became,
eventually suffering the calamity of hunger and cold
and the misfortune of losing his eldest son.
In this region,
the terrain is high and expansive,
wide and accessible in all directions.
To the south, one gazes at Lí Shān;
to the north, it connects to Jīng and Wèi rivers;
to the east, it overlooks the Hé and Huà mountains,
the sunny side of Lóngmén,
the road to the three Jìn states.
To
the west, one looks back at Fēng and Hào,
the hills of Zhōu and Qín,
and the ruins of palaces and observatories.
He could see a thousand *lǐ* afar,
surveying the old capital,
and so he settled there.
He retired and lived
in seclusion.
Indeed, loyal ministers sigh as they pass old ruins,
and filial sons lament upon entering their old homes.
Each time he thought of his ancestors,
who displayed great virtue in the past
and bequeathed a grand legacy
for posterity,
he grieved that due to the calamity of the times,
their tombs were overgrown and neglected,
and the spring and autumn sacrifices
could not be arranged according to seniority.
With age declining and the year drawing to a close,
he lamented his lack of achievement.
He intended to cultivate the fertile
fields in the west,
increase production,
practice filial piety,
build ancestral temples,
and broaden ancestral sacrifices.
Thereafter, he would close his gate and devote himself to studying morality and virtue,
perusing the discourses of Kǒng and Lǎo,
hoping to attain the blessings of Sōng and Qiáo.
He ascended
mountain slopes,
climbed high ridges,
let his spirit roam the universe,
and cast his gaze across the eight directions.
He surveyed the forms of the mountains and rivers of the nine provinces,
recalled the customs of success and failure
in ancient times,
lamented the decline of the Way
and the fragmentation of virtue.
Indeed, observing its end necessarily reveals its beginning;
thus, we preserve the person and extol their Way.
He mapped out the nine
wilds,
managed the five mountains,
and had a profound desire to ascend to the clouds.
[(一０)] So he composed a *phú* to encourage himself,
naming the piece 'Xiǎn Zhì'.
Xiǎn Zhì means
to illuminate
the essence of civilized transformation
and to reveal profound and subtle thoughts.
Its words are:
"Jīng.
I passed the flying *lián* and sighed;
I ascended Píngyáng and felt sorrow.
I grieve over the treacherous customs of the age,
and mourn the inconstancy of likes and dislikes."
Forsaking the balance and weights, I measure with my heart;
Following the winds and waves, I soar.
In a world of chaos, flowing after power and gain,
People embrace the like and envy the different.
I, alone, am upright and admire
antiquity;
How can I be liked by the people of this age?
They undermine the established doctrines of the ancient sages,
And the noble conduct of worthy men.
They disregard the precious beauty of morality,
And strive for the pleasures of wealth
and indulgence.
They abandon the main road and wander astray,
Treading the dark and obscure paths of lesser virtue.
Truly, this confounds the common folk;
Who can perceive the formless?
I act with integrity and straightforwardness, though it leads to fault,
Such as those of my predecessors.
Reflecting within, I feel no shame,
So I hold firm to my resolve and do not change.
〔一０〕I rejoice in my generation's connection to Táng Yú,
Yet grieve over the worries and hardships of my life.
Let me vent my indignation and express my feelings,
So as to dispel these sorrowful thoughts.
〔一一〕The past cannot be grasped,
And the future cannot
be anticipated.
I lament not being appreciated in my lifetime,
And wish for a swift departure, but there is no way.
〔一二〕
I gaze upon the steep heights,
Listening to the sound of the Jīng and Wèi rivers' waves.
I look back at Hóngmén with a sigh,
Grieving for my orphan's early demise.
Why is Heaven's mandate not pure?
Indeed, it is born of my own sins.
I mourn the innocent suffering of the truly good,
Bearing this regret into the underworld.
Alas, my thoughts are not far-reaching;
How can failed endeavors
be regretted?
Even if I were to die nine deaths and not sleep,
I fear that my remaining misfortune might recur.
Tears stream down like gathering rain,
Emotions surge forth like parting clouds.
My heart is stifled and entangled,
My spirit is suppressed and inwardly sorrowful.
The sun sets,
And life fleetingly passes by, not staying.
Ashamed of my unfinished accomplishments,
I retreat to the wilderness and live in obscurity.
In the past, Yī Yǐn served Tāng,
And was only trusted after seventy persuasions.
Gāo Táo fished at Léi Zé,
And was only recognized through Yú Shùn.
Lacking the encounters of these two men,
I embrace loyalty and integrity, but cannot be understood.
I lead my wife
and children in farming,
Concealing my virtues and not boasting.
Hán Lú is restrained and not unleashed,
Qíjì is bridled and not tested.
I alone am impassioned and look far ahead,
Not understood by ordinary people.
I disdain Wèi Cì's accumulation of wealth,
And highly value what Yán Huí admired.
I value the great achievements of my ancestors,
Therefore I seek to accomplish
on this path.
Following the succession of the four seasons,
And discerning the influences of the five elements,
I examine what grows in the forests and mountains,
And taste what springs from the waters.
I practice
the fundamental occupation of Shénnóng,
And adopt the extraordinary strategies of Xuānyuán.
I pursue the遗teachings of Zhōu Qì,
And surpass the unique path of Fàn Lǐ.
I ascend Lǒng Shān to gaze afar,
Distantly surveying the eight wildernesses.
Winds and waves arise together,
My heart is dejected, and my sorrow increases.
I behold the vastness of the Hé and Huà rivers,
And gaze upon the old states of Qín and Jìn.
I resent Fēng Tíng's failure to succeed,
And lament Qù Jí's confusion.
I visit my old home,
Traversing the famous cities of Sòng and Chǔ.
I grieve that the many lords are no longer worshipped,
And lament that the various states have become ruins.
I gallop across the central plain, ascending and descending,
The path winding and full of difficulties.
I discuss the common theories of the sages and philosophers,
My mind is full of thoughts and turmoil.
Though the path of Heaven is the same,
The policies of emperors and kings differ.
Yáo and Shùn were glorious and magnanimous,
Yǔ brought peace and then revolutionized.
Day and night I ponder deeply,
Ending in doubt and profound uncertainty.
Gāoyáng is so far and ancient,
Who in this world can discuss this with me?
I question Xià Qǐ at Gān Zé,
Grieving the initial decline of the imperial order.
I praise the virtue carried by Chéng and Kāng,
And sing
the songs of Nán Fēng.
I recall the peace of Táng Yú,
And bow to Jì and Qì as companions.
Their descendants flourish and branch out,
Until Tāng and Wǔ rise
mightily.
In antiquity, the Three Sovereigns were pure,
But in every latter age, calamity intensified.
I mourn Xià Jié at Nán Cháo,
And weep for Yīn Zhòu at Mù Yě.
Yī
Yǐn was summoned to Bó Jiāo,
And Lǚ Wàng was honored at Fēng Zhōu.
