Their achievements shine as brightly as the sun and moon,
Their fame contends with the Three Kings.
I observe the subtle,
Grieving that the kingly way is about to collapse.
I extoll the flourishing virtue of Zhōu Táng,
And gather the expedient achievements of Huán Wén.
I resent the calamities encountered in the Warring States period,
And detest the overbearing
power of ministers.
I denounce Chǔ Zǐ at Nán Yǐng,
And capture Zhào Wǔ at Jū Liáng.
I admire loyalty and trustworthiness for saving the times,
And despise treacherous schemes and wrongful acts.
I appoint Shēn Shū in Chén and Cài,
And capture Xún Xī in Yú Yí.
I execute Lí Chú, who misled the sage,
And punish Zāng Cāng, who slandered the wise.
I banish Zǐ Fǎn to Péng
Chéng,
And ennoble Guǎn Zhòng at Yí Yí.
I detest the proliferation of warfare,
And suffer from the emergence of attacks and conquests.
I condemn Sūn Wǔ to Wǔ Hú,
And execute Bái Qǐ
at Cháng Píng.
I abhor the complexity and cunning that disrupt the world,
And detest the vertical and horizontal alliances that corrupt customs.
I banish Sū Qín to Huán Shuǐ,
And imprison Zhāng Yí in Guǐ Gǔ.
I purify the decline of moral transformation,
And establish severe and strict punishments.
I burn Shāng Yāng's legalist methods,
And incinerate Hán Fēi's theories.
I rebuke Shǐ Huáng's tyranny,
And cast Lǐ Sī to the four borders.
He abolished the laws of the former kings,
And his calamity was excessive and vast.
I draw upon the ancient sages to establish the mean,
Correcting the arrogance
and extravagance of the two rulers.
I feast Nǚ Qí at Jiàng Tái,
And honor Jiāo Jǔ at Zhāng Huá.
〔一０〕I display the brilliant radiance of morality,
Correcting the dwindling customs of a declining age.
I praise
Sòng Xiāng at Hóng Gǔ,
And recognize Jì Zhá at Yán Líng.
〔一一〕I gather the essence of benevolence and wisdom,
To stir the decadent trends of chaotic states.
I observe Zhèng Qiáo at Zhēn Wěi,
And visit Yàn Yīng at Yíng Qiū.
〔一二〕The sun dims as dusk approaches,
I alone am troubled and confused.
Why is Jiǔ Zhōu so vast,
Yet I am lost
and do not know north from south?
〔一三〕I harness white dragons and gallop forth,
Riding on emerald clouds and wandering freely.
I seek Bó Yí for guidance,
And become even
clearer with Wù Guāng.
〔一四〕I call upon Zǐ Gāo in the wilderness,
And meet Bó Chéng to settle my thoughts.
I admire the virtue and beauty of true men,
Lingering and not departing.
〔一五〕My heart contemplates.
Hesitant yet not tranquil,
I wait for the swirling wind to wander leisurely.
Seeking where Shàn Juǎn resides,
I met Xǔ Yóu at Fùshǔ.
I reined my chariot at Jīyáng,
and
fed my horses by the Yǐnghǔ.
Hearing profound words, I understood,
and returned to my old dwelling.
〔一六〕
In the azure sea,
I reared white tigers on Jīnshān.
Carving rock into a dwelling,
I relied on Gāoyáng to cultivate immortality.
Divine phoenixes soared over Hóngyá,
and Xuánwǔ
lurked in Yīngmíng.
Lying in a vermilion tower, I gazed in all four directions,
gathering the splendid flowers of the three-season herb.
I collected the grand virtues of former cultivators,
displaying the glorious achievements of the past.
Donning Qǐ Jì’s beautiful robes,
I heralded Qū Yuán’s spiritual fragrance.
My tall cap was lofty,
my long pendant flowing.
I drank the clear
nectar of the six sweet wines,
and ate the luxuriant blooms of the five auspicious fungi.
Mingling mǐwú,
I assembled magnolias and xīnyí.
Their light was abundant and dazzling,
their fragrance rich and wonderfully beautiful.
Their splendid blossoms burst forth luxuriantly,
but time
fleeted, unnoticed and unvalued.
It is not that I regret my own hardship,
but I pity the withered state of all beauty.
My spirit wandered in the great abode,
upholding an unfathomable and constant disposition.
Dwelling in purity and tranquility to nourish my will,
this is truly what my heart delights in.
The mountains were lofty, reaching to the sky,
the forests dark and luxuriant.
Luan birds soared, seeking their
flock,
deer cried mournfully, seeking their companions.
I recited ancient and modern texts to dispel my thoughts,
and observed the sages and worthies to calm myself.
I admired Kǒng Qiū for knowing his destiny,
and Dà Lǎo
for valuing the profound.
Which is more precious, virtue or the Way?
Which is dearer, fame or self?
Dwelling idly by hills and valleys,
I guarded solitude to preserve my spirit.
Zhūang Zhōu fished,
declining the prominent position of minister.
The gentleman of Yúlíng irrigated his garden,
resembling a perfect man.

and

When Xiǎnzōng ascended the throne,

Yǎn married a woman from Běidì, the Rèn clan, as his wife.
She was fierce and jealous,

However, he had great ambition

He often exclaimed with indignation:

He lived in poverty in his old age,

His writings included a fu, a lei, an ming, a shuo, a wenjiao, a degao, a shenqing,

Sùzōng greatly valued his writing.
His son was Bào.
Bào, courtesy name Zhòngwén,
was twelve years old

His stepmother hated him,
and once, while Bào was asleep at night,
she tried to poison him.
Bào escaped and was saved.
He served her with even greater diligence,
but his mother's hatred grew deeper.
People at the time praised his filial piety.
When he grew up, he loved Confucian studies
and taught poetry and the Chunqiu at Lìshān.
The villagers coined a saying about him:
"Féng Zhòngwén is refined in virtue and the Way."
He was recommended as Xiaolian,
appointed Shangshū Láng,
and was loyal and diligent without slackening.
Whenever he submitted a memorial and it had not yet been replied to,
he would often prostrate himself in the provincial office,

Sùzōng heard of this and commended him,
sending a Huangmén to cover Bào with a quilt,
ordering him not to disturb him.
Because of this, he often received awards.
At that time, the Western Regions were being pacified.
Because Bào possessed talent and strategy,
he was appointed Héxī Fù Xiàowèi.
At the beginning of Hédì's reign,
he repeatedly spoke on border affairs,
proposing the re-establishment of the Wùjǐ Xiàowèi,
and that the city-state kingdoms should resume their former duties.
He was promoted to Wǔwēi Tàishǒu.
After serving for two years,
Héxī praised him,
and he was again summoned to serve as Shangshū.
In the fourteenth year of Yǒngyuán,
he died in office.
The commentary states: Indeed, the noble rely on their power to be arrogant towards others,

Such is the general rule.
Are these two men not so?
Féng Yǎn's allusion to the analogy of choosing a wife

When marrying a wife, everyone knows to choose one who will not malign oneself,

Why?
Is it not that it is easy to counter jealousy,
but difficult to pardon a sense of righteousness?
Although Guāngwǔ gained from Bào Yǒng,
he still lost with Féng Yǎn.
Thus,
righteous straightforwardness was suppressed in the past,
and upholding integrity will likewise be greatly hindered in the future.
Alas!
A eulogy says: The discussions were not prophetic,
Yǎn pledged allegiance late.
The Way was not mutually planned,
devious times led to shared failure.
He possessed superior talent,
but had minor honor and a low rank.

In the seventh year of Jiànwǔ,

Thus, there will be no neglected strategies,

A sage does not consider his unique insights to be enlightenment,

Those who comply with others prosper;

Xiāo did not accept his advice.
Gāng arrived [at the capital]

Guāngwǔ once wished to go on an excursion,

At that time, many officials, both inside and outside the court,

Gāng always offered strong remonstrance,

Bào Yǒng, courtesy name Jūncháng,
was a native of Túnliú, Shàngdǎng.
His father, Xuān,
served as Sīlì Xiàowèi during the reign of Emperor Āi,
and was killed by Wáng Mǎng.
Yǒng had high aspirations and conduct from a young age,
and studied the *Ōuyáng Shàngshū*.
He was extremely filial to his stepmother.
His wife once scolded a dog in front of his mother,
and Yǒng immediately divorced her.
He initially served as the county Gōngcáo.
Wáng Mǎng, because Xuān had not supported him,
wanted to eradicate his descendants.
The Dūwèi Lù Píng, anticipating Mǎng's unspoken wishes,
intended to harm Yǒng.
The Grand Administrator Gǒu Jiàn protected him,
summoned him to be an official,
and always kept him within the prefecture office.
Yǒng, consequently, frequently presented to Jiàn strategies for restoring the Hàn dynasty
and eliminating the usurpers.
Jiàn often warned Yǒng, saying:
“Jūncháng, if your affairs are not kept secret,
calamity will knock at your door.”
Yǒng was deeply moved by his words.
When Jiàn died,
he personally escorted the coffin back to Fúfēng.
Lù Píng then arrested Yǒng's younger brother, Shēng.
When the Grand Administrator Zhào Xīng arrived,
he heard of this and sighed, saying:
“I received the Hàn's land and authority,
but could not uphold my principles,
while Bào Xuān died for them.
How can I harm his son?”
He ordered the county to release Shēng,
and reappointed Yǒng as Gōngcáo.
At that time, there was someone falsely claiming to be an attendant staying in a post-house,
and Xīng wanted to visit him.
Yǒng suspected it was a fraud,
and remonstrated, but Xīng did not listen and went out.
Xīng then drove his carriage towards the post-house.
Yǒng drew his ceremonial knife and cut across the horse's chest,
stopping it.
A few days later,
Wáng Mǎng's imperial edict indeed arrived, ordering the arrest of the false claimant,
and Yǒng became famous because of this.
He was recommended as Xiùcái,
but did not accept.
In the second year of Gēngshǐ, he was summoned.
He was twice promoted to Shàngshū Púyè,
acting as Dàjiāngjūn,
holding the *jié* and leading troops,
to pacify and stabilize Hédōng, Bīngzhōu, and Shuòbù.
He was granted authority to appoint his own subordinate generals,
and to implement military law immediately.
When Yǒng arrived in Hédōng,
he attacked the Qīngdú,
and decisively defeated them.
Gēngshǐ enfeoffed him as Zhōngyáng Hóu.
Although Yǒng was a general,
his carriages and clothes were simple and worn,

At that time, the Chìméi harmed Gēngshǐ,
and the routes to Sānfǔ were cut off.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he dispatched Jiànyì Dàfū Chǔ Dàbó,
holding the *jié*, to summon Yǒng to the imperial residence.
Yǒng was suspicious and did not comply,
but instead arrested and detained Dàbó,

Once he learned that Gēngshǐ had indeed perished,
he held a mourning ceremony,
released Dàbó and others,

disbanded all his troops,

The Emperor saw Yǒng

“Where are your troops?”
Yǒng left his seat and kowtowed, saying:
“Your subject served Gēngshǐ
but could not ensure his safety.
I am truly ashamed to seek wealth and honor through his troops,
so I have dismissed them all.”
The Emperor said:
“Your words are grand!”
but was not pleased.
At that time, the attack on Huái had not yet succeeded.
The Emperor said to Yǒng:
“I have been attacking Huái for three days, but the troops have not taken it.
The regions east of the pass fear and respect you.
You can, for now, take your old acquaintances and go to the city wall to persuade them.”
He immediately appointed Yǒng as Jiànyì Dàfū.
Upon reaching Huái,
he persuaded the Grand Administrator of Hénèi, who had been appointed by Gēngshǐ,

The Emperor was greatly pleased

Subsequently, he encountered his mother's mourning period,

In the eleventh year of Jiànwǔ,

The Emperor's uncle, Liáng, the Prince of Zhào, was of noble kinship and great importance.

Huī was also upright and did not flinch from the powerful.

Yǒng, while inspecting a district, reached Bálíng.
His road passed by Gēngshǐ's
tomb. He turned his chariot into the path.
His attendants advised him to stop.
Yǒng said:
"Having served him as a subordinate,

Even though he incurred guilt,

He then dismounted, bowed,
wept with full sorrow, and departed.
Westward, he reached Fúfēng

When the Emperor heard of this,

He asked his high officials:

Zhāng Zhàn, the Grand Master of the Palace (Tàizhōng Dàfū), replied:

Later, Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sītú) Hán Xīn was implicated in an incident.
Yǒng pleaded strongly for him but failed,

He was sent out as Chancellor of Dōnghǎi.

When Yǒng reached
Chénggāo,
an imperial edict appointed him Governor of Yǎn Province (Yǎnzhōu Mù),

He served for three years
and then died of illness.
His son was Yù.
The commentary says: Bāo Yǒng upheld righteousness towards his former lord;
this showed he could serve a new lord.
He was ashamed to receive favor with his multitude;
this showed he could receive great favor.
If those who speak are sincere,
yet those who hear do not understand,
is it that the pleasure of seeking advancement
is easily accepted with emotion,
while the offense of upholding righteousness
is difficult to accept with reason?
Truly, one who can abandon profit to follow the Way,
and stand firm to follow righteousness,
is a model gentleman.
Yù's courtesy name was Wénquán.
He studied his father's teachings from a young age,
giving lessons as a guest in Dōngpíng.
At the beginning of Jiànwǔ,
there were dangerous bandits in the Tàiháng Mountains.
The Administrator Dài Shè, hearing that Yù was Bāo Yǒng's son
and possessed wisdom and strategy,
went to meet him
and asked him to be appointed Chief of Gāodū.
Yù agreed
and then attacked the various bandits,
executing their leaders.
The roads were opened,
and he became known for this.
Later, he was Chief of Bǐyáng,
governing with benevolence and love,
and his territory was peaceful and clean.
The Inspector of Jīng Province (Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ) reported him to the throne.
After two promotions,
in the first year of Zhōngyuán,
he was appointed Colonel Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
An imperial edict ordered Yù to go to the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū)
to draft a proclamation for Fēng Hú to surrender.
Guāngwǔ sent a Yellow Gate Attendant (Xiǎo Huángmén) to ask Yù if he found anything strange.
He replied:
"I have heard that in historical practice, official documents do not include surnames,
and also that the Grand Minister of Works (Sītú) issues public declarations.
I find it strange that the Sīlì should issue a document with his surname attached."
The Emperor responded:
"I specifically wanted the world to know that the son of a loyal minister has again become Sīlì."
While in office, Yù
upheld the law and maintained righteousness,
showing his father's character.
In the fifth year of Yǒngpíng,
he was dismissed
for a fire-fighting incident.
Later, he was appointed Administrator of Rǔnán.
The commandery had many reservoirs and ponds,
which broke down year after year,
with annual expenses often exceeding thirty million.
Yù then proposed constructing square wooden beams and stone sluices.
The water was always abundant,
irrigating twice as much land,
and the people became prosperous.
In the seventeenth year,
he replaced Wáng Mǐn as Grand Minister of Works (Sītú).
He was granted money, silk, various utensils, and curtains,
and his son was appointed a Gentleman (Láng).
In the first year of Jiànchū,
there was a great drought,
and grain was expensive.
Sùzōng summoned Yù and asked:
"The drought is severe;
how can we dispel this disaster?"
He replied:
"I have heard that when a sage governs a nation,
achievements are seen in three years.
Your Majesty has just ascended the throne,
and the penal policies have not yet taken full effect.
If there are mistakes or gains,
how can we expect extraordinary results?
However, when your servant was previously in Rǔnán,
managing the affairs of Chǔ,
there were over a thousand prisoners,
and I fear not all of them fully deserved their punishment.
The late Emperor's edict stated
that when a major prison case arises,
more than half are wronged.
Moreover, those who have been exiled are separated from their kin,
and their lonely souls are not offered sacrifices.
If one person sighs in grief,
the king's governance is diminished.
It would be appropriate to restore all exiled families,
abolish imprisonment,
revive the fallen, and continue the interrupted,
so that the living and the dead all find their proper place.
If this is done,
harmonious qi can be achieved."
The Emperor accepted his words.
In the fourth year,
he replaced Móu Róng as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
In the sixth year,
he passed away
at the age of over seventy.
Zǐ Dé,
cultivated his ambition and integrity,
gained a reputation,
and was successively appointed as the Grand Administrator of Nányáng.
At that time, there were many famines,
but Nányáng alone was prosperous and bountiful.
The officials and common people loved and respected him,
calling him "Divine Father."
At that time, the prefectural school had long been abandoned.
Dé therefore repaired and rebuilt the transverse halls,
prepared sacrificial vessels, robes, and crowns,
and performed rites and played music.
He also respectfully entertained the venerable elders of the state
and hosted banquets for the various scholars.
Among the common people who observed,
none were not persuaded and convinced.
He held office for nine years,
was summoned and appointed Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sī nóng),
and died in office.
His son, Áng,
courtesy name Shūyǎ,
possessed filial piety, righteousness, and integrity.
Initially,
when Dé was afflicted with illness for several years,
Áng knelt and attended by his side,
not loosening his clothes or belt.
When it came to mourning,
he was emaciated for three years,
only able to walk with support.
After the mourning period ended,
he secluded himself by the tomb,
not involving himself in worldly affairs.
He was nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián),
and invited to the ducal palace,
but repeatedly summoned, he did not come.
He died at home.
Zhì Yùn, courtesy name Jūnzhāng,
was a native of Xīpíng, Rǔnán.
At the age of twelve, he lost his mother
and observed mourning beyond the customary rites.
When he grew up,
he studied the *Hán Shī* and Yán's *Chūnqiū*,
and was skilled in astronomy and calendrical calculations.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
when bandits and rebels rose en masse,
Yùn looked up and observed the celestial phenomena,
sighing and saying to his friends:
"Currently, the planets Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars are all within the Hán divisions of Yì and Zhěn constellations,
departing and then returning.
Hàn will certainly receive the Mandate again,
and blessings will return to the virtuous.
If there is someone who follows Heaven and devises a plan,
they will surely achieve great success."
At that time, Zuǒduì Dàfū Lù Bìng had always favored scholars.
Yùn persuaded him, saying:
"Currently, Heaven displays omens;
the wise prosper by them,
the foolish perish by them.
In the past, Yī Yǐn sold himself to assist Shāng,
establishing merit and preserving the people.
I, Yùn, presumptuously and immodestly,
dare to follow in Yī Yǐn's footsteps,
responding to the changes between Heaven and humanity.
If you, Illustrious Sir, do not doubt and reject me,
I can help achieve Heavenly virtue."
Bìng was impressed by him
and had him appointed as an official.
Yùn did not present himself,
saying:
"In the past, King Wén extracted Lǚ Shàng from the banks of the Wèi River;
Gāozōng respectfully treated Fù Yuè in the rocky abode;
Duke Huán took Guǎn Zhòng from the arrow-wound.
Thus, they were able to establish great achievements
and accomplish grand merits.
I have never heard of a teacher and minister (Shī Xiàng Zhòngfù)
who could be an ordinary official.
One who does not observe Heaven cannot plan for the distant future.
If you do not entrust a swift horse with a heavy responsibility,
the swift horse will also bow its head, wrap its hooves, and depart."
So he did not accept the appointment.
Traveling west to Cháng'ān,
he then submitted a memorial to Wáng Mǎng, saying:
"Your servant has heard that Heaven and Earth value their people
and cherish their creatures.
Therefore, they operate the celestial mechanisms,
suspend the sun and moon,
contain the primordial and embrace the singular,
and create and mold all categories of beings,
manifesting signs for the ages,
with plans and records pre-established.
The Hán dynasty's longevity is long.
Kǒng is the red control.
It does not allow the foolish and deluded
to harm people and disrupt the times.
The wise comply to achieve virtue;
the foolish resist to incur harm.
The divine implements have a destiny
and cannot be obtained in vain.
High Heaven sends warnings,
wishing to enlighten Your Majesty,
to allow you to assume the position of a minister,
and turn disaster into fortune.
The Liú clan enjoys Heaven's eternal mandate.
If Your Majesty follows the ebb and flow of their rise and decline,
taking it from Heaven
and returning it to Heaven,
this may be called knowing destiny.
If you do not plan early,
you will not escape the charge of usurping the throne.
Moreover, Yáo and Shùn did not take the Heavenly manifestation for themselves;
thus, they abdicated the empire.
Why should Your Majesty covet what is not a Heavenly manifestation and burden yourself?
Heaven is Your Majesty's stern father;
Your servant is Your Majesty's filial son.
A father's teaching cannot be abandoned;
a son's remonstrance cannot be rejected.
May Your Majesty pay careful attention."
Mǎng was greatly enraged
and immediately had him arrested and imprisoned in the imperial prison,
impeaching him for high treason.
However, as Yùn's claims were based on classical texts and prophecies (jīngchèn),
it was difficult to harm him immediately.
He ordered his eunuchs and close officials to threaten Yùn,
ordering him to declare himself mad and deluded,
unaware of what he had said.
Yùn, however, glared and cursed, saying:
"What I presented are all astronomical observations and the will of the sages;
they are not things a madman could concoct."
He was then imprisoned until winter.
He was released due to a general amnesty,
and then fled south to Cāngwú with Zhèng Jìng from the same commandery.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ,
he again reached Lújiāng,
where he coincidentally met the General of Massed Crossbows (Jīnnǔ Jiāngjūn), Fù Jùn, who was campaigning eastwards in Yángzhōu.
Jùn had long heard of Yùn's reputation
and therefore respectfully invited him,
appointing him as Chief Clerk for Leading Troops (Jiāngbīng Chángshǐ)
and entrusting him with military administration.
Yùn then swore to the troops, saying:
"Do not ambush people when they are unprepared,
or push people into distress.
You must not sever people's limbs,
expose their corpses,
or release lewd women."
However, Jùn's soldiers still plundered tombs and exposed bodies,
robbing the common people.
Yùn remonstrated with Jùn, saying:
"In the past, King Wén could not bear exposed bones,
and King Wǔ would not exchange the empire for the life of a single person.
Therefore, they were able to gain the response of Heaven and Earth
and defeat the innumerable army of Shāng.
How can the general not emulate King Wén,
but instead violate the prohibitions of Heaven and Earth,
greatly harming people and things,
even abusing withered corpses,
thereby incurring the wrath of the spirits?
If you do not now apologize to Heaven and change your policies,
you will not be able to preserve your life.
I wish the general would personally lead his soldiers
to collect the wounded and bury the dead,
and weep for those you have brutalized,
to show that this was not the general's original intention."
Jùn complied with this.
The common people were pleased and submitted,
and all places he advanced against surrendered.
In the seventh year,
Jùn returned to the capital,
and Shàng deliberated on him.
Yùn was ashamed to gain a position through military merit,
so he resigned and returned to his hometown.
The county magistrate humble himself and showed great respect,
inviting him to be his Ménxià Yuán.
Yùn's friend, Dǒng Zǐzhāng,
had a father who was earlier killed by a fellow villager.
When Zǐzhāng fell ill
and was near death,
Yùn went to visit him.
As Zǐzhāng was dying,
he looked at Yùn,
sighed, and could not speak.
Yùn said:
"I know you are not grieving over your destiny,
but lamenting that your enemy has not been avenged.
While you were alive,
I worried but did not act;
now that you are gone,
I will act and no longer worry."
Zǐzhāng merely looked at him with his eyes.
Yùn immediately rose,
led his retainers to intercept the enemy,
took his head, and showed it to Zǐzhāng.
Upon seeing it, Zǐzhāng breathed his last.
Yùn then went to the county office
and confessed his deed.
The magistrate responded to him,
and Yùn said:
"To avenge a friend is the private matter of an official.
To uphold the law impartially
is the duty of a ruler.
To wrong the ruler to save one's life
is not the integrity of a subject."
He hurried out to enter prison.
The magistrate, barefoot, chased after Yùn,
but could not catch him.
So he went personally to the prison,
drew his blade and pointed it at himself to demand of Yùn,
"If you do not come out with me,
I dare to prove my sincerity with death."
Yùn, thus compelled, came out,
and then left due to illness.
After a long time,
the Grand Administrator Ōuyáng Shè invited him to be his Gōngcáo.
In Rǔnán's old custom,
in the tenth month, there was a feast,
and counties within a hundred *lǐ* would all bring oxen and wine to the prefecture for banqueting.
At that time, after the banquet ceremony,
Shè instructed:
"The western Dūyóu, Yáo Yán,
is naturally loyal and upright,
and inherently public-spirited and impartial.
He crushes villains
and governs effectively without harshness.
Today, with all you scholars,
I will discuss Yán's merits,
and make them known at court.
The Grand Administrator respectfully praises his excellence,
and provides oxen and wine to nourish his virtue."
The Zhǔbù read the instruction,
and the Hùcáo led Yán to receive the gifts.
Yùn, from his lower seat, sadly stepped forward and said:
"The Chief of Justice raises his goblet
to confess your crimes
and apologize to Heaven.
Upon examination, Yán's character is greedy and corrupt,
outwardly upright but inwardly cunning.
He forms factions to scheme evil,
deceives superiors, and harms people,
causing disorder wherever he goes,
and resentment and treachery arise together.
Your Excellency treats evil as good,
and your subordinates, who should be upright, follow the crooked.
This shows neither a worthy ruler
nor worthy subjects.
I, Yùn, dare to bow twice and present this goblet."
Shè's face turned pale with shame,
and he did not know what to say.
The Ménxià Yuán, Zhèng Jìng, stepped forward and said:
"A ruler is enlightened and his ministers are upright.
The Gōngcáo's words are sharp,
which is Your Excellency's virtue.
How can you not accept the goblet?"
Shè's mood eased a little,
and he said:
"Indeed, it is my fault.
I respectfully accept the goblet."
Yùn then removed his cap and bowed, saying:
"In ancient times, Yú Shùn assisted Yáo,
and the Four Evils were all subdued.
Slanderous words were not used,
and partiality was not practiced.
Thus, he was able to be a true assistant,
and the Emperor had songs of praise.
I, Yùn, am disloyal,
as my partiality is evident.
With jackals and tigers in government,
I have fallen into slander
and also exposed what I said.
[一０]There is no greater crime.
Please arrest me and Yán,
to clarify what is good and evil."
Shè said:
"This would only aggravate my error."
[一一]So he dismissed the banquet without finishing.
Yùn returned to the prefecture,
claiming illness,
and Yán also withdrew.
Zhèng Jìng, who had always been close to Yùn,
seeing his words had offended Shè,
invited him to leave,
saying:
"You openly criticized Yáo Yán at court,
but the lord did not accept it.
Although Yán has left now,
he will surely return.
A straightforward heart without concealment
is indeed the way of the Three Dynasties.
However, those whose paths differ do not conspire together.
I cannot bear to see you in danger of not being tolerated by your lord.
Why not leave?"
Yùn said:
"Mèng Kē considered it loyalty to urge a ruler to do what he could not,
and treason to measure what a ruler could not do.
I, Yùn, have already urged him.
To obstruct the ruler at court
while possessing righteousness,
and yet not die for one's duty,
is a crime.
If Yán withdraws and I also leave,
it would not be right."
Jìng then alone hid in Yìyáng Shān.
After several months,
Shè indeed recalled Yán.
Yùn then left,
joined Jìng,
and enjoyed fishing and hunting,
staying for several tens of days.
Yùn's ambition was to serve in government,
so he sighed deeply,
and said to Jìng:
"Heaven creates outstanding talents
for the benefit of humanity.
Birds and beasts cannot be in the same flock as humans.
Will you follow me to be like Yī, Lǚ?
Or will you be like Cháo, Xǔ,
and consider Yáo and Shùn as elders?"
Jìng said:
"I am content.
Initially, I followed your steps to 重華 (Chónghuá) in the southern wilds,
and thought I would return as Sōngzǐ.
Now I am fortunate to preserve my body and uphold my lineage,
[一０]return to serve my ancestors,
and fully pursue knowledge and the Dao.
[一一]Although I do not serve in government,
to apply my principles for good governance
is also to govern.
[一二]I am old,
how can I follow you?
You should strive to rectify your nature and destiny,
and not exhaust your spirit to harm your life."
Yùn then bid farewell and left.
Jìng, whose courtesy name was Cìdū,
had a pure will and transcended the world.
Guāngwǔ repeatedly summoned him, but he did not appear.
[一三]Yùn then became a sojourner in Jiāngxià, teaching.
The commandery recommended him as Xiàolián,
and he became the guardian of the Upper Eastern City Gate.
The Emperor once went hunting.
When the imperial carriage returned at night,
Yùn blocked the gate and did not open it.
The Emperor ordered his attendants to show his face through the gate crack.
Yùn said:
"The firelight is too far away."
Thus, he did not accept the order.
The Emperor then turned and entered through the Eastern Middle Gate.
The next day,
Yùn submitted a memorial, advising:
"In the past, King Wén dared not indulge in hunting,
as he worried about the myriad people.
But Your Majesty hunts far in the mountains and forests,
continuing night into day.
What about the altars of the land and grain and the ancestral temples?
To 'fight a tiger barehanded or cross a river without a boat'
is a warning against recklessness
that this humble servant secretly worries about."
When the memorial was presented,
he was bestowed with a hundred bolts of cloth,
and the guardian of the Eastern Middle Gate was demoted to Cānfēng Wèi.
Later, Yùn was ordered to instruct the Crown Prince in the *Hán Shī*,
lecturing in the palace hall.
When Empress Guō was deposed,
Yùn then said to the Emperor:
"Your servant has heard that the affection between husband and wife
cannot be obtained by a father from his son,
how much less can your servant obtain it from Your Majesty?
This is what your servant dares not speak of.
Nevertheless,
I pray Your Majesty consider the pros and cons of this matter,
lest the empire have cause to discuss the future of the state."
The Emperor said:
"Yùn is good at putting himself in others' shoes to gauge his lord,
knowing that I would never act out of personal preference and lightly regard the empire."
After the empress was deposed,
Crown Prince Yì felt uneasy.
Yùn then advised the Crown Prince, saying:
"To long remain in a precarious position
would be to violate the path of filial piety above,
and approach danger below.
In the past, Gāozōng was an enlightened ruler,
Jífǔ a worthy minister,
yet when a slight issue arose,
a filial son was banished.
According to the principles of the *Chūnqiū*,
the mother is ennobled by her son.
Your Highness should, through your attendants and the other imperial princes, acknowledge your transgression and withdraw,
to provide for your mother,
thereby illustrating the sagely teaching
of not forsaking one's birth mother."
The Crown Prince followed this advice,
and the Emperor eventually consented.
Yùn was twice promoted to be the Administrator of Chángshā.
Prior to this, there was a filial son in Chángshā, Gǔ Chū,
who, after his father's death, had not yet buried him.
When a neighbor's house caught fire,
Chū prostrated himself on the coffin,
using his body to shield it from the fire,
and the fire was extinguished because of him.
Yùn recognized his extraordinary deed
and recommended him first.
Later, for an offense, he was demoted to Chief of Mángcháng,
then dismissed and returned home.
He moved to another area to teach,
and authored eight chapters of books.
He died of illness.
His son was Shòu.
Shòu, courtesy name Bókǎo,
was skilled in writing,
and renowned for his integrity and ability.
He was nominated as *xiàolián* (filial and incorruptible),
and gradually promoted to Inspector of Jìzhōu.
At that time, many commanderies within Jìzhōu were enfeoffed to various princes,
whose retainers were unrestrained
and generally lacked self-discipline.
Shòu investigated them,
showing no leniency.
He ordered his subordinate officials to reside specifically in the princely states,
and also moved the office of the Supervising Inspector outside the princely palaces.
Any misstep in their actions,
he would immediately dispatch a rider to report it and submit memorials denouncing the princes' crimes and impeaching their tutors and chancellors.
Consequently, the princely states were awed and fearful,
and all became compliant.
After three years in office,
Jìzhōu was pacified.
He was thrice promoted to Minister of the Secretariat.
Whenever there was a doubtful matter in court,
he often had a private audience.
Sùzōng marveled at his wisdom and strategy,
and promoted him to Grand Administrator of Jīngzhào.
The commandery had many powerful and influential families,
and rampant wrongdoing went unchecked.
The Three Auxiliaries had long heard of Shòu in Jìzhōu,
and all were shaken with fear,
each restraining themselves,
not daring to offend.
Although Shòu was awe-inspiring,
he treated his subordinates with sincerity,
who all wished to serve him to the death,
and none dared to deceive him.
He was dismissed for official business.
He was again summoned to be Assistant Minister of the Secretariat.
At this time, Grand General Dòu Xiàn, through the favor of his imperial relation,
wielded power that overshadowed the empire.
Xiàn once sent a protégé with a letter to Shòu,
requesting a favor.
Shòu immediately sent him to imperial prison.
Before and after, he submitted memorials denouncing Xiàn's arrogance and indulgence,
citing Wáng Mǎng as a warning to the state.
At this time, Xiàn was campaigning against the Xiongnú,
and the whole country supplied their expenses.
Meanwhile, Xiàn and his younger brothers Dǔ and Jǐng all built grand mansions,
living luxuriously and unlawfully,
which the common people resented.
Shòu, seeing the state treasury empty
and the military campaigns ongoing,
took advantage of a court assembly to criticize Xiàn and his brothers,
speaking with a stern voice and solemn expression,
his words exceedingly sharp.
Xiàn was enraged,
and framed Shòu for buying public land and slander,
sending him to officials for execution.
The Imperial Censor Hé Chǎng submitted a memorial defending him, saying:
"Your servant has heard that sagely kings open the four gates,
open the four ears (listen widely),
extend the path for honest words,
issue edicts that do not avoid prohibitions,
erect flags for daring remonstrance,
listen to folk songs on the roads,
and have seven remonstrating ministers
to reflect upon themselves,
to examine and understand governance,
and whenever they violate the hearts of the people,
they immediately reform,
thus heaven and man respond in unison,
transmitting blessings endlessly.
Your servant humbly observes that Minister of the Secretariat Zhì Shòu was seated at the platform,
discussing with other ministers the attack on the Xiongnú,
and his words were deemed excessive,
and that he submitted a memorial requesting to buy public land,
and was consequently imprisoned and interrogated for great disrespect, facing execution.
Your servant, in his humble opinion, believes that Shòu, as a close minister entrusted with confidential matters,
has the duty to rectify and save.
If he were to remain silent,
his crime would deserve execution.
Now Shòu has defied the multitude to uphold righteous discussion,
to secure the imperial ancestral temple;
how could this be out of private interest?
Furthermore, in court discussions of ordinary affairs,
disputing what is permissible or not,
even during the flourishing eras of Táng and Yú,
and the prosperous times of the Three Dynasties,
it was still said that 'straightforward speech leads to prosperity,'
and slander was not considered a crime.
Requesting to buy public land
is a minor human fault,
which can be tolerated and overlooked.
If Shòu is executed,
your servant fears that the empire will believe the state arbitrarily punishes the loyal and upright,
harming harmony,
and offending yin and yang.
The reason your servant dares to violate the solemn authority,
not shrinking from annihilation,
and risking death to speak foolishly,
is not for Shòu.
A loyal minister exhausts his duty,
taking death as his return.
Though your servant does not know Shòu,
I surmise he would gladly accept it.
Indeed, I do not wish for Your Sacred Dynasty to carry out the punishment for slander,
thereby harming the gentle transformation,
blocking loyal and upright speech,
and leaving behind endless criticism.
Your servant Chǎng has mistakenly involved himself in confidential matters,
speaking inappropriately.
My crime is clear,
and I should be thrown into prison,
to perish before Shòu;
ten thousand deaths would be insufficient."
When the memorial was presented,
Shòu's death sentence was commuted,
and he was sentenced to exile in Hépǔ.
Before he departed,
he committed suicide,
and his family was allowed to return to their hometown.
Eulogy says: Bào Yǒng hesitated,
but later returned to righteousness.
His will was fulfilled, his integrity complete;
first lamentation, then celebration.
Shēntú answered strategy,
Zhì Yùn submitted memorials.
With the Way, one is upright even if straightforward;
without the Way, one is not foolish.
Biography of Sū Jìng and Yáng Hòu, Part 1 of 20
Sū Jìng, courtesy name Bókùang,
was from Pínglíng, Fúfēng.
During Emperor Píng's reign,
Jìng became a scholar-official (*bóshì*) lecturing on the *Yì* and presiding over sacrificial rites for the books.
He was skilled in diagrams and prognostication texts,
and able to comprehend the teachings of various schools.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
he, along with Líu Xīn and others, collectively managed the collation of books,
and was appointed Commandant of Dàijùn.
At that time, the Xiongnú were causing disturbances,
and the northern border suffered greatly from their calamity.
Jìng eventually maintained the integrity of his commandery.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Administrator of Dàijùn,
and tasked with fortifying the frontiers to resist the Xiongnú.
In the winter of Jiànwǔ's fifth year,
Lú Fāng had largely seized the northern commanderies.
The Emperor sent General Piānjiāngjūn Suí Dì to garrison Dàijùn.
Jìng was gravely ill,
handed over his troops to Dì,
and went to the capital to apologize.
He was appointed Palace Attendant,
but after several months,
he was dismissed due to illness.
Initially,
Yán Cén’s defender-general, Dèng Zhòngkuàng, holding troops, occupied Yīnxìan of Nányáng and became a bandit.
Liú Xīn’s nephew, Gōng, was his chief strategist.
Jìng was then in Nányáng,
and wrote to Gōng, enlightening him, saying:
“From the time we became close,
I have not been able to distance myself from you.
I have heard that a gentleman pities those of his own kind and grieves for those who are unfortunate.
No one, neither foolish nor wise,
fails to first avoid harm and then seek profit,
first
to establish one's resolve and then seek fame.
In the past, Zhì Guǒ, seeing Zhì Bó’s overextension of military power that would inevitably lead to ruin,
therefore changed his name and fled far away.
Chén Píng knew that Xiàng Wáng was abandoned by Heaven,
so he gave his
allegiance to Gāo Zǔ.
These were all the epitome of wisdom.
I hear that you previously bent your principles for a time,
and paid homage to Yán Yá.
Only later did you awaken
and cultivate your virtue.
How much more can
the sons of former generations
achieve?
You are in Yīnzhōng,
a land rich in worthy scholars.
If, even for a moment,
you were to study and examine differences,
measure them against diagrams and books,
and gauge
them against human affairs,
then gains and losses, advantages and disadvantages,
would be clear before your eyes.
Why do you bear the burden of rebellion
and not shed the name of stubbornly clinging to evil?
How
is this contrary
to the Way of a gentleman?
Holding territory with troops,
one can plan for more than mere hopes.
Some say that the Sage King has not yet revealed himself,
so one should observe the changing times,
lean on the strong, attach oneself to the great,
and look around while preserving oneself.
Are these two arguments
truly
so?
Kǒng Qiū concealed the classics,
which were for the Hàn’s red imperial authority.
The profound mysteries were hidden in a dark chamber,
the words obscure, but the meaning clear.
Moreover, the element of fire succeeded Yáo;
though it might be dim, it will certainly
be bright.
Bearing the mandate of accumulated generations,
holding the boundless imperial tally,
though the Wáng clan seized the opportunity to usurp,
they ultimately suffered great execution,
their branches dismembered, their bodies dissolved,
and their clan slaughtered and exterminated.
Is this not its effect?
Heaven therefore watches and hesitates,
concerned for the descendants of Hàn.
If those who argue do not base themselves on Heaven,
and consult
the Sages,
but merely let themselves be bewildered by Shī Kuàng’s miscellaneous matters,
and if persuaders write books
that disturb the great Way,
how can they be trusted?
Looking at the omens,
the planet Zhèn Xīng circled the Heavenly Street,
and Suì Xīng did not leave Dī and Fáng.
It is believed that all such omens
pertain to the state.
Calamities are not set forth in vain;
they all correspond to their respective celestial divisions,
each having its own domain.
Now, Fáng and Xīn are the divisions of Sòng,
which is Dōnghǎi.
Wěi is the division of Yān,
which is Yúyáng.
Dōnghǎi’s Dǒng Xìan was confused and had not surrendered.
Yúyáng’s Péng Kǒng was rebellious and held troops.
The imperial majesty was enraged,
and commanded generals to conquer them.
Therefore, Yíng Huò responded to this,
and Xìan and Kǒng received
calamity.
Since the end of Wáng Xīn’s demise, Tàibái and Chén Xīng
have been losing their regular movements and calculations,
up until now.
Sometimes they guard Dōngjǐng,
sometimes they vanish into Yǔlín,
sometimes they wander around the feudal
screens,
sometimes they hesitate in the imperial palace,
sometimes they cross the sky and become bright,
sometimes they hide and sink for a long time,
sometimes they are faint and dim,
sometimes they shine brilliantly north and south,
sometimes they wax and wane to form a hook,
sometimes they are defiant and unchecked.
All these are auspicious signs of a great cleansing and elimination,
and omens of the Sage Emperor responding to the tally.
Rebellious ministers and errant sons
are constantly intermingled,
pointing and speaking falsely,
misleading each other through transmission.
From this perspective,
how can astronomical observations be followed strictly?
Qīu
was the capital of Qín Fēng.
At that time, the moon entered Bì.
Bì is the Heavenly Net,
which presides over snaring lawless rulers.
Therefore, when Wǔ Wáng was about to attack Zhòu,
he made a sacrifice to Bì,
seeking help from Heaven.
