to fully express what I have to say.
More than ten days later,
he again submitted a memorial, saying: I, your servant, humbly observe that Tài Bái (太白) entered the northern sky for several days
and then reappeared in the east.
This portends a major military conflict,
with Zhōngguó (中國) weakening
and the four Yi (夷) becoming strong.
I have also calculated
that Yínghuò (熒惑) should appear now but is hidden,
indicating
an imminent conspiracy.
All this is due to the many unjust cases in prisons
and the execution of loyal officials.
The Dégxīng (德星) has remained guarding the enforcement of law
also for this reason.
Your Majesty should heed the will of Heaven,
investigate and redress wrongful incarcerations,
reduce the punishments for Liú Kǎ (劉カ) and Chéng Gā (成ガ),
and posthumously recognize the descendants of Lǐ Yún (李雲), Dù Zhòng (杜衆), and others.
Gōng Chóng's (宮崇) presented divine texts
were primarily based on revering Heaven and Earth and conforming to the Five Phases,
and also contained methods for strengthening the nation and extending progeny.
Their language was easy to understand,
and they were consistent with the classics.
However,
Shùndì (順帝) did not implement them,
which is why the imperial line did not flourish,
and Xiàochōng (孝沖) and Xiàozhì (孝質) had short reigns in successive generations.
Thus, people like Shēn Xiū (申休), Sòng Wàn (宋萬), Péng Shēng (彭生), and Rèn Bǐ (任鄙) emerged during that time.
Yīn Zhòu (殷紂) loved beauty,
and Dájǐ (妲己) was born.
Yè Gōng (葉公) loved dragons,
and a real dragon
roamed his courtyard.
Now, the Huángmén Chángshì (黃門常侍),
who are people marked by heavenly punishment,
are loved and favored by Your Majesty,
receiving double the usual imperial favor.
If the succession is still unsettled,
is it not because of this?
The Tiānguān Huànzhě (天官宦者) star is not in the Zǐgōng (紫宮) but in the Tiānshì (天市),
clearly
indicating they should serve as administrators of markets and neighborhoods.
Now they instead occupy the position of Chángbó (常伯),
which is truly not the will of Heaven.
Your Majesty's desires are not curbed,
and punishments exceed reason.
Since you deviate from the Way,
how can you receive blessings?
Some say Lǎozǐ (老子) entered the Yi (夷) lands and became Fútú (浮屠).
Fútú (浮屠)
did not stay three nights under a mulberry tree,
not wishing to be long-bound by affections;
this is the utmost purity.
When heavenly deities sent him a beautiful woman,
Fútú (浮屠) said:
"This is merely a leather bag containing blood."
And he did not even glance at her.
His adherence to unity was thus,
and he was able to achieve enlightenment.
Now, Your Majesty indulges in beautiful women,
the most exquisite in the world,
and enjoys rich foods and fine drinks,
the most
sumptuous flavors in the world.
How can you wish to emulate Huáng-Lǎo (黃老)?
When the memorial was submitted,
an edict was immediately issued to summon [Xiāng] Kǎi (楷) to the Shàngshū (尚書) to inquire about the situation.
Kǎi (楷) said:
"I, your servant, have heard that in ancient times there were originally no eunuch officials.
At the end of Wǔdì's (武帝) reign,
when he was advanced in years
and frequently visited the imperial harem,
they were first established.
Later, they were gradually given more responsibilities,
and by Shùndì's (順帝) time,
they became exceedingly numerous and powerful.
Now Your Majesty ennobles them,
ten times more than before,
and to this day there is no successor.
Is it solely because of your fondness for them that this has happened?"
The Shàngshū (尚書) reported his reply,
and an imperial edict was issued to the relevant authorities for judgment.
The Shàngshū (尚書) then submitted a memorial by imperial decree, stating:
"The office of eunuch
was not established in recent times.
In the early Hàn (漢), Zhāng Zé (張澤) was a Dà Yèzhě (大謁者),
assisting Jiàng Hóu (絳侯) in executing Zhū Lǚ (諸呂);
Xiàowén (孝文) employed Zhào Tán (趙談) to ride in his chariot,
and his descendants prospered.
Kǎi (楷) did not speak with proper reason,
nor did he clearly articulate important matters,
but rather analyzed words to break laws,
violated the classics and arts,
borrowed from stars,
falsely invoked divine spirits,
fabricated private opinions,
and deceived the emperor and misrepresented affairs.
We request that he be handed over to the Sīlì (司隸)
to be judged according to law and imprisoned in Luòyáng (洛陽)."
The Emperor, though Kǎi's (楷) words were vehement,
considered them to be based on astronomical phenomena and constant patterns,
and thus did not execute him,
treating it like a Sīkòu (司寇) judging a legal case.
Earlier,
during Shùndì's (順帝) reign,
Gōng Chóng (宮崇) from Lángxié (琅邪) came to the imperial palace
and presented 170 rolls of divine texts his master Gān Jí (干吉) had obtained at Qūyáng Quánshuǐ (曲陽泉水).
All were bound in light blue-white silk with vermillion dividers and green headings and vermillion eyes,
and were called the Tàipíng Qīnglǐng Shū (太平清領書).
Its teachings were based on Yīnyáng (陰陽) and the Five Phases,
and contained many sayings of shamans and spirit-mediums.
The authorities memorialized that Chóng's (崇) offering was specious and unorthodox,
and so it was confiscated and stored.
Later, Zhāng Jiǎo (張角) acquired some of these texts.
When Língdì (靈帝) ascended the throne,
he considered Kǎi's (楷) memorial to be correct.
Tàifù (太傅) Chén Fān (陳蕃) recommended him for his uprightness,
but he did not accept the appointment.
His鄉里 (xiānglǐ) revered him,
and whenever a Tàishǒu (太守) arrived,
they would always pay respects and invite him.
During the Zhōngpíng (中平) era,
he was summoned along with Xún Shuǎng (荀爽) and Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) as a Bóshì (博士),
but he did not go,
and died at home.
The commentary says: The ancients had a saying:
"Those who speak well of Heaven
will certainly have it verified among humans."
And Zhāng Héng (張衡) also said:
"Astronomy, calendar calculations,
Yīnyáng (陰陽) divination,
these are what should be urgently attended to now."
Láng Yǐ (郎顗) and Xiāng Kǎi (襄楷) were able to look up at the sky and examine the earth,
referencing human affairs,
and when fortune and misfortune, auspiciousness and inauspiciousness corresponded,
their teachings derived from them were also clear.
This is how the arts of the Dao (道) could benefit their time,
and what later generations should take as a lesson.
However, their flaw was a fondness for shamanism,
which is why a Jūnzǐ (君子) would not devote their whole mind to it.
Eulogy says: Zhònghuán's (仲桓) skill was profound,
he was sought out repeatedly with simple carriages.
Sū Jìng (蘇竟) sent flying memorials,
clearing our old shadows.
Xiāng (襄) and Láng's (郎) warnings of disaster
truly stemmed from indulgent governance.
Biographies of Guō Dù, Kǒng Zhāng, Lián Wáng, Sū Yáng, Jiǎ Lù (郭杜孔張廉王蘇羊賈陸列傳第二十一)
Guō Jí (郭伋), courtesy name Xìhóu (細侯),
was a native of Màolíng (茂陵) in Fúfēng (扶風).
His great-great-grandfather Jiě (解),
was known for his chivalry during Wǔdì's (武帝) reign.
His father Fàn (梵),
served as Tàishǒu (太守) of Shǔjùn (蜀郡).
Jí (伋) showed integrity and ambition from a young age.
During the Āi (哀) and Píng (平) reigns, he was invited to the Dàsīkōng (大司空) office,
and after three promotions, became Yúyáng Dūwèi (漁陽都尉).
During Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) time, he was Shànggǔ Dàyǐn (上谷大尹),
and was then promoted to Bìngzhōu Mù (并州牧).
When Gēngshǐ (更始) was newly enthroned,
the Sānfǔ (三輔) region was repeatedly plagued by military incursions,
the people were terrified,
and powerful clans and influential families
each gathered followers to protect their strongholds,
none willing to be the first to submit.
Gēngshǐ (更始) had long heard of Jí's (伋) reputation,
so he summoned him and appointed him Zuǒ Fēngyì (左馮翊),
tasking him with pacifying the people.
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
he appointed him Yōngzhōu Mù (雍州牧),
then transferred him twice to become Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令),
and he frequently offered loyal counsel and remonstrances.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ
The next year,
after Péng Chǒng (彭寵) was defeated,
he was transferred to become the Grand Administrator of Yúyáng.
As Yúyáng had already been devastated by Wáng Mǎng’s (王莽) rebellion,
and further by Péng Chǒng’s defeat,
many of its people were treacherous and wicked,
and bandits and rebels were rampant.
When Jí (伋) arrived,
he demonstrated sincere rewards
and executed the ringleaders,
and the bandits dispersed.
At that time, the Xiōngnú (匈奴) frequently raided the commandery borders,
and the frontier people suffered greatly.
Jí (伋) reorganized and disciplined his soldiers and horses,
and devised strategies for offense and defense.
The Xiōngnú (匈奴) feared and dreaded him, keeping their distance,
and dared not re-enter the pass,
allowing the people to live peacefully.
After five years in office,
the population had doubled.
Later, bandits arose in great numbers in Yǐngchuān,
and in the ninth year,
he was summoned and appointed as the Grand Administrator of Yǐngchuān.
When he was granted an audience to bid farewell,
the Emperor comforted him, saying:
"A worthy and capable Grand Administrator
is not far from the imperial city.
The river irrigates nine lǐ,
and I hope the capital will also receive blessings.
Although you are skilled at pursuit and capture,
the mountain paths are treacherous,
and in a direct fight, you are but a single warrior.
You should be very cautious."
When Jí (伋) arrived at the commandery,
he recruited and appeased the mountain bandits Zhào Hóng (趙宏) from Yángxià (陽夏)
and Shào Wú (召吳) from Xiāngchéng (襄城), numbering several hundred people.
They all surrendered to Jí (伋) with their hands tied
and were all sent back to resume farming.
He then impeached himself for acting without imperial decree,
but the Emperor praised his strategy
and did not fault him.
Later, Zhào Hóng (趙宏), Shào Wú (召吳), and their confederates, hearing of Jí’s (伋) prestige and trustworthiness,
came from as far as Jiāngnán (江南),
or from Yōu (幽) and Jì (冀),
all unexpectedly surrendering,
a continuous stream.
In the eleventh year,
the Inspectorate of Shuòfāng (朔方) was abolished and its territory attached to Bìngzhōu (并州).
The Emperor, considering that Lú Fāng (盧芳) occupied the northern lands,
then transferred Jí (伋) to be the Governor of Bìngzhōu (并州).
He passed through the capital to express his gratitude,
and the Emperor immediately granted him an audience,
and also summoned the Crown Prince and various kings for a day-long banquet and conversation,
bestowing carriages, horses, clothing, and other valuables.
Jí (伋) then spoke about the selection and appointment of various officials,
suggesting that the nation’s wise and outstanding individuals should be chosen,
and that Nányáng (南陽) people should not be exclusively employed.
The Emperor accepted his advice.
Jí (伋) had previously served in Bìngzhōu (并州)
and had established a reputation for kindness and virtue.
When he later entered the border,
wherever he went in counties and towns,
old and young would hold hands,
coming to greet him on the roads.
He inquired about the people’s suffering wherever he passed,
and sought out venerable and outstanding individuals,
treating them with the ceremony of stools and staffs,
and consulting with them on political matters morning and evening.
When he first began his inspection tour,
upon reaching Měijì (美稷) in Xīhé (西河),
hundreds of children,
each riding a bamboo horse,
greeted him on the road.
Jí (伋) asked,
"Children, why have you come from so far?"
They replied:
"We heard that the Inspector has arrived,
and we are delighted,
so we came to welcome you."
Jí (伋) expressed his thanks.
When his duties were completed,
the children again escorted him outside the city walls,
asking,
"On what day will the Inspector return?"
Jí (伋) instructed his Chief Clerk
to calculate the day and tell them.
When he returned from his inspection tour,
one day earlier than scheduled,
Jí (伋), not wanting to break his promise to the children,
stayed overnight in a rural pavilion,
waiting until the appointed day to enter.
At this time, the court frequently nominated Jí (伋) for the position of Grand Minister of Works (Dà Sīkōng).
However, the Emperor, considering the ongoing threat from Lú Fāng (盧芳) in Bìng (并) commandery
and the instability with the Xiōngnú (匈奴),
wished for him to remain in his post for a long time,
and thus did not recall him.
Jí (伋) knew that Lú Fāng (盧芳) was a long-standing rebel
and difficult to subdue quickly by force.
He constantly kept the beacon fires well-maintained
and clearly offered rewards
to sow discord among the rebels.
Lú Fāng's (盧芳) general Suí Yù (隋昱) then conspired to force Lú Fāng (盧芳) to surrender to Jí (伋),
whereupon Lú Fāng (盧芳) fled into Xiōngnú (匈奴) territory.
Jí (伋), being old and ill, submitted a memorial requesting to retire.
In the twenty-second year,
he was summoned and appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance (Tàizhōng Dàfū),
granted a residence,
as well as curtains, money, and grain
to furnish his household.
Jí (伋) immediately distributed all of it among his relatives and nine degrees of kin,
leaving nothing for himself.
He died the following year,
at the age of eighty-six.
The Emperor personally attended his mourning,
and granted him burial land.
Dù Shī (杜詩), courtesy name Jūngōng (君公),
was a native of Jí (汲) in Hénèi (河內).
From a young age, he possessed talent
and served as an Administrative Officer (Gōngcáo) in the commandery,
earning a reputation for fairness.
During the Gēngshǐ (更始) reign,
he was appointed to the Grand Marshal’s (Dà Sīmǎ) office.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
within a year he was promoted three times to Imperial Censor (Shì Yùshǐ)
and brought stability to Luòyáng (洛陽).
At that time, General Xiāo Guǎng (蕭廣) allowed his soldiers to run rampant,
committing atrocities among the common people,
causing panic.
When Dù Shī (杜詩) admonished him and he did not change,
Dù Shī (杜詩) consequently executed Xiāo Guǎng (蕭廣)
and reported the situation.
Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) summoned him,
bestowed upon him jǐjǐ (棨戟) (a type of ceremonial halberd),
and again sent him to Hédōng (河東),
where he executed and brought to submission the rebel Yáng Yì (楊異) and others.
When Dù Shī (杜詩) arrived at Dàyáng (大陽),
he heard that the rebels intended to cross north.
He immediately, with his Chief Clerk, urgently burned their boats,
organized the commandery troops,
and led a charge with light cavalry to attack,
beheading Yáng Yì (楊異) and others,
thus eliminating the rebels.
He was appointed Magistrate of Chénggāo (成臯),
and after three years in office,
his governance was exceptionally outstanding.
He was promoted twice, first to Commander (Dūwèi) of Pèi (沛) commandery,
then transferred to Commander of Rǔnán (汝南),
and was praised for his good governance wherever he served.
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to Grand Administrator of Nányáng (南陽).
He was frugal by nature and his administration was pure and peaceful.
He established his authority by executing violent offenders
and was skilled in strategy,
saving the people from excessive labor.
He invented the water-powered trip hammer (shuǐpái),
which was used to cast farm tools.
It required little effort
but yielded great results,
and the common people found it very convenient.
He also repaired and managed reservoirs and ponds,
expanding cultivated land,
making every household in the commandery prosperous.
People at the time compared him to Shào Xìnchén (召信臣),
thus Nányáng (南陽) had a saying:
"First there was Father Shào (召),
then Mother Dù (杜)."
Dù Shī (杜詩), considering himself to have achieved little,
and feeling uneasy staying long in a large commandery,
sought to yield his position to meritorious officials,
and so he submitted a memorial which read: "Your Majesty, by perfecting Heaven’s work
and accomplishing a great enterprise,
you have laid down arms and cultivated culture,
and the many commanders have returned to their posts.
The whole country is in harmony,
and countless generations will receive blessings.
The world is extremely
fortunate.
Only the Xiōngnú (匈奴) have not yet understood your sagely virtue,
insulting the two frontiers
and oppressing the Central Plains.
The border people are depleted
and cannot defend themselves.
Your servant fears that even if the brave and fierce generals are diligent,
they may not yet be able to put away their armor and sheathe their bows.
Indeed, to toil ceaselessly leads to resentment;
to labor without rest also leads to resentment.
A resentful army
is difficult to expect achievement from again.
Your servant
humbly observes the feelings of the generals
and the expectations of the meritorious officials,
who hope to rest their feet in the inner commanderies,
and then take up arms and carry out orders,
without resentment.
Your servant foolishly believes that
"Victory in war lies in harmony, not in numbers."
Although Your Majesty cares for the northern frontier,
you should also be quite sparing in its use.
In ancient times, Tāng Wǔ (湯武) excelled at managing their forces,
hence they had no resentful
or fierce armies.
Your Majesty has raised armies for thirteen years;
the generals and commanders are harmonious,
and the soldiers are disciplined.
Now, if dukes, ministers, and commandery governors are allowed to emerge from the military camps,
then the generals and commanders will exert themselves;
if the soldiers who return
are treated like those in the imperial guard,
then the warriors will multiply a hundredfold.
Why is this?
The empire is now at peace,
everyone values their lives,
and from the great ministers downwards,
all cherish their peaceful homes.
If their merits are not rewarded and their efforts are not encouraged,
there will be no means to persuade them.
Your Majesty should truly vacate several commanderies
to await the returning
officials who have completed their campaigns,
and repeatedly bestow generous rewards
upon those who have served long.
If this is done,
the troops stationed and guarding the borders
will compete and forget death;
the officials manning the walls and defending the passes
will not shirk their
toil.
Then the beacon fires will burn brightly,
and the defense and battles will be firm and solid.
The governance of a sagely king
must always follow the hearts of the people.
Now, to indiscriminately employ the foolish and meager,
thereby thwarting the hopes of meritorious officials,
is truly inappropriate.
Having received great grace,
my (managing) [mù (牧)] and nurturing have been inadequate,
my service ineffective,
and I have long usurped my position and salary,
causing meritorious officials to harbor resentment.
I am truly filled with awe and trepidation.
In the eighth year,
I submitted a memorial requesting
to avoid meritorious service,
but Your Majesty's exceptional grace
did not permit my retirement.
I, Shī (詩), have received particularly profound grace;
it is my duty not to recklessly make a false request.
Truly, I cannot suppress my utmost desire;
I wish to resign from a large
commandery
and accept a small position.
When I am older [chǐ (齒) means age],
and my strength is capable of managing arduous affairs,
if I, Shī (詩), can truly be of assistance,
then I will again accept a high position,
and even if it means dividing the jade tablet and conferring a title,
I will
not decline it.
I beg Your Majesty to show compassion!
Shī (詩) has always enjoyed recommending the worthy,
and frequently advanced well-known scholars such as Liú Tǒng (劉統) of Qīnghé (清河) and Dǒng Chóng (董崇), the Chief of Lǔyáng (魯陽).
Initially,
the legal restrictions were still simple,
and troops were dispatched merely by imperial rescript;
there was no tiger tally for authentication.
Shī (詩) memorialized, saying:
"I have heard that 'troops are the inauspicious implements of the state,'
which the Sages treat with caution.
According to the old system, when troops were dispatched,
it was always with a tiger tally;
for other levies and deployments,
a bamboo tally sufficed.
The two halves of the tally, when joined,
served as a great token of trust,
thereby clearly manifesting the state's command
and maintaining its solemn authority.
Lately, when troops are dispatched,
only imperial rescripts are used,
or sometimes imperial edicts.
If there were treacherous individuals committing fraud,
there would be no way to detect it.
I humbly believe that as military campaigns are still ongoing
and bandits and captives are not yet exterminated,
when conscripting troops from commanderies and kingdoms,
there should be greater caution.
Tiger tallies should be established
to prevent all avenues for treachery.
In the past, the Duke of Wèi (魏),
whose prestige overshadowed neighboring states,
still had to borrow a military tally
to relieve Zhào (趙) from siege.
If not for the enmity of Rú Jī (如姬),
his achievement would not have been manifest.
There are matters that are troublesome yet cannot be simplified,
and costly yet unavoidable;
this refers precisely to such situations."
When the memorial was presented,
it was adopted.
Although Shī (詩) was stationed outside,
he dedicated his heart to the court,
offering upright words and good strategies
as occasions arose.
He governed for seven years,
and his administration and reforms were widely implemented.
In the fourteenth year,
he was summoned to court on account of sending retainers to avenge his brother,
but he died of illness
before arriving.
The Colonel-Director of Retainers, Bào Yǒng (鮑永), memorialized that Shī (詩) was poor and had no land or dwelling,
and had nowhere for his funeral.
An imperial edict ordered his funeral to be held at the commandery residence
and bestowed a thousand bolts of silk.
Kǒng Fèn (孔奮), courtesy name Jūn Yú (君魚),
was a native of Màolíng (茂陵) in Fúfēng (扶風).
His great-grandfather, Bà (霸), served as a Palace Attendant during the reign of Yuán Dì (元帝).
When Fèn (奮) was young, he studied the *Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn* (春秋左氏傳) under Liú Xīn (劉歆).
Xīn (歆) praised him,
saying to his disciples:
"I have already received instruction from Jūn Yú (君魚)."
During the chaos of Wáng Mǎng (王莽),
Fèn (奮), along with his aged mother and young brother, avoided the conflict in Hexī (河西).
In the fifth year of Jiànwǔ (建武),
the Grand General of Hexī (河西), Dòu Róng (竇融), invited Fèn (奮) to be appointed as Aide to the Chief Clerk
and concurrently serve as Prefect of Gūzàng (姑臧).
In the eighth year,
he was granted the title of Marquis within the Passes.
At that time, the empire was in turmoil,
but Hexī (河西) alone was peaceful.
Gūzàng (姑臧) was known as a wealthy city,
trading with the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡) peoples,
and its markets flourished four times a day.
Whoever held the position of county magistrate there
would invariably accumulate vast wealth within a few months.
Fèn (奮) served for four years,
but his personal wealth did not increase at all.
He was filial and diligent in serving his mother;
though he lived frugally himself,
he spared no effort in providing her with rare delicacies.
He personally led his wife and children
to partake in coarse vegetable fare.
At that time, the empire was not yet settled,
and many scholars did not uphold moral integrity.
However, Fèn (奮) vigorously practiced purity and incorruptibility,
which was mocked by many.
Some thought that being in a position of "fat and cream,"
yet unable to enrich himself,
only increased his hardship.
Having established his integrity,
Fèn (奮)'s governance was characterized by benevolence and fairness.
The Grand Administrator, Liáng Tǒng (梁統), deeply respected and treated him with deference,
not treating him as a mere subordinate.
He would always greet him at the main gate
and invite him in to see his mother.
After Lǒng (隴) and Shǔ (蜀) were pacified,
the administrators and magistrates of Hexī (河西) were all summoned.
Their wealth, with carriages linked together,
stretched across rivers and marshes.
Only Fèn (奮) had no assets,
traveling the road in a single carriage.
The officials and common people of Gūzàng (姑臧), as well as the Qiāng (羌) and Hú (胡), said to one another:
"Prefect Kǒng (孔) is incorruptible, benevolent, and virtuous;
the entire county has received his grace.
How can we let him leave now
without jointly repaying his kindness?"
They then collectively levied cattle, horses, artifacts, and goods worth over ten million
and escorted him for several hundred *lǐ* (里).
Fèn (奮) merely thanked them
and accepted nothing.
Upon reaching the capital,
he was appointed as Commandant of Wǔdū (武都) Commandery.
At that time, the remaining bandits of Lǒngxī, Wěi Mào and others, attacked the government office at night,
brutally killing the commander of the commandery.
Fèn, fearing the bandits, pursued them relentlessly.
They then seized his wife and children,
intending to hold them as hostages.
Fèn was already fifty years old,
and had only one son,
but he never looked back or hesitated,
and so exerted all his strength to suppress them.
The officials and common people were moved by his righteousness,
and all redoubled their efforts.
The commandery had many Dī people,
who were accustomed to the mountains and valleys.
Their great chieftain, Qí Zhōngliú,
was trusted and respected by the Dī groups.
Fèn then encouraged and led Zhōngliú and others to intercept and raid the bandits,
working together to be their vanguard.
The bandits, in distress and fear, were cornered,
so they pushed Fèn's wife and children to the front of their army,
hoping he would retreat.
But he attacked them even more fiercely,
and consequently captured and annihilated Mào and the others.
Fèn's wife and children were also killed by them.
Shìzǔ issued an imperial edict praising him,
and appointed him as the Grand Administrator of Wǔdū.
Fèn, since he was an Assistant Administrator,
had already been held in high regard.
When he was appointed Grand Administrator,
the entire commandery reformed its conduct.
He governed with clear judgment,
discerning good and detesting wrong.
When he saw someone with fine virtues,
he loved them as kin;
as for those without principles,
he resented them as enemies.
The commandery called his rule "pure and peaceful."
His younger brother, Qí,
studied in Luòyáng.
Fèn, believing Qí, being well-versed in the classics, would surely hold office,
fell ill and left his post,
observing a frugal life in his hometown,
and died at home.
Qí was extensively knowledgeable in the classics,
and authored the Chūnqiū Zuǒ Shì Shān.
Fèn later had a son, Jiā,
who reached the office of Colonel of the Gate Guards,
and authored the Zuǒ Shì Shuō.
Zhāng Kān, courtesy name Jūnyóu,
was a native of Wǎn in Nányáng,
and belonged to a prominent clan in the commandery.
Kān was orphaned early,
and yielded several million in inherited wealth from his deceased father to his elder brother's son.
At sixteen,
he studied in Cháng'ān,
possessing noble aspirations and rigorous conduct.
All the scholars called him
"the Sacred Youth."
When Shìzǔ was still a commoner,
seeing Kān's aspirations and integrity,
he often praised him.
Upon his ascension to the throne,
the Zhonglang Jiang Lái Xī recommended Kān,
who was summoned and appointed Lang Zhōng,
and was thrice promoted to Yèzhě.
He was sent to transport tribute silk and cloth,
and also commanded seven thousand cavalry,
to join the Grand Marshal Wú Hàn in attacking Gōngsūn Shù.
En route, he was retroactively appointed Grand Administrator of Shǔjùn.
At that time, Hàn's army had only seven days' provisions left,
and secretly prepared boats to retreat.
Kān heard of this,
and swiftly went to see Hàn,
persuading him that Shù would surely be defeated,
and a strategy of retreating was inappropriate.
Hàn followed his advice,
and then feigned weakness to provoke the enemy.
Shù indeed came out himself
and died in battle beneath the city walls.
After Chéngdū was captured,
Kān was the first to enter and occupy the city,
inspecting the treasury and stores,
collecting its treasures,
and meticulously reporting them in detail,
not taking even a single hair for himself.
He comforted and pacified the officials and common people,
and the people of Shǔ were greatly pleased.
After two years in the commandery,
he was recalled and appointed Colonel of Cavalry.
Later, he led the camp of the General of Agile Cavalry, Dù Mào,
and crushed the Xiōngnú at Gāoliǔ,
then was appointed Grand Administrator of Yúyáng.
He captured and struck down the cunning and corrupt,
and his rewards and punishments were unfailingly credible,
so officials and common people were all happy to serve him.
The Xiōngnú once invaded Yúyáng with ten thousand cavalry.
Kān led several thousand cavalry to rush and attack them,
thoroughly defeating them,
and the commandery's borders became peaceful.
He then opened over eight thousand qǐng of rice fields in Húnú,
encouraging the people to cultivate them,
thus achieving prosperity.
The common people sang:
"Mulberry trees have no extra branches,
wheat ears have bifurcated spikes.
Zhāng Jūn governs,
and our joy is boundless."
He served for eight years,
and the Xiōngnú dared not violate the frontier.
The Emperor once summoned the record-keepers from various commanderies,
asking about their local customs and the competence of previous and current commandery heads.
Fán Xiǎn, the clerk from Shǔjùn, stepped forward and said:
"Zhāng Kān, the Grand Administrator of Yúyáng, when he was in Shǔ in the past,
was benevolent and kind to his subordinates,
and his authority could suppress evildoers.
When Gōngsūn Shù was defeated before,
treasures were piled up like mountains;
the things he could have taken
would have enriched ten generations,
yet on the day Kān left his post,
he rode in a broken-axle cart,
with only a cloth quilt for his possessions."
The Emperor heard this,
and sighed for a long time,
then appointed Xiǎn as the Chief of Yúfù.
Just as Kān was being summoned,
he unfortunately died of illness.
The Emperor deeply lamented and regretted this,
issued an edict of praise,
and bestowed one hundred rolls of silk.
Lián Fàn, courtesy name Shūdù,
was a native of Dùlíng in Jīngzhào,
a descendant of Zhào General Lián Pō.
At the rise of Hàn,
because the Lián clan was a prominent family,
they moved from Kǔxíng.
Generations served as commandery governors on the frontier,
or were buried in Xiāngwǔ, Lǒngxī,
and thus settled there.
His great-grandfather, Bāo,
was the Right General during the Chéng-Āi period.
His grandfather, Dān,
was the Grand Marshal and Governor of the Yōng Department during Wáng Mǎng's time.
Both were renowned in previous generations.
Fàn's father encountered chaos and disaster,
and died as a sojourner in Shǔhàn.
Fàn consequently drifted and lived in Xīzhōu.
When Xīzhōu was pacified,
he returned to his hometown.
At fifteen,
he bade farewell to his mother and went west to retrieve his father's remains.
Zhāng Mù, the Grand Administrator of Shǔjùn,
an old subordinate of Dān, then offered Fàn a large sum of money for his journey.
Fàn accepted none of it,
and with a guest, carried his father's coffin on foot back to Jiāměng.
The boat carrying the coffin struck a rock and sank.
Fàn embraced and held onto the coffin,
and both sank into the water.
The crowd, moved by his righteousness,
hooked and retrieved him,
and after treatment, he barely escaped death.
Mù heard of this,
and again dispatched an envoy to pursue Fàn with the previous travel funds.
Fàn again steadfastly refused.
After returning to bury his father and completing the mourning period,
he went to the capital to study,
serving the Erudite Xuē Hàn.
The two commanderies of Jīngzhào and Lǒngxī successively invited and summoned him,
but he refused all.
At the beginning of Yǒngpíng,
Dèng Róng, the Grand Administrator of Lǒngxī, formally offered to make Fàn his Chief Clerk,
but Róng was then impeached by the province.
Fàn knew the accusation was difficult to resolve,
and wished to help him by extraordinary means,
so he feigned illness and asked to leave.
Róng did not understand his intention
and greatly resented him.
Fàn then went east to Luòyáng,
changed his name,
and sought to serve as a prison guard in the Court of Judicial Review.
Not long after,
Róng was indeed summoned and imprisoned.
Fàn then got to attend him closely,
devotedly offering comfort and assistance.
Róng was surprised that his appearance resembled Fàn but did not expect it,
and said to him:
"Why do you resemble my former Chief Clerk so much?"
Fàn rebuked him, saying:
"Are you confused and disoriented by your predicament?"
The conversation then ceased.
Róng, imprisoned and ill,
was accompanied and cared for by Fàn.
Even after his death,
Fàn never revealed his identity.
He personally drove the carriage to transport the coffin to Nányáng
and left only after the burial was complete.
Later, he was appointed to a ducal office.
It so happened that Xuē Hàn (薛漢) was executed for his involvement in the affairs of Chǔ Wáng (楚王).
His old friends and disciples dared not look upon him.
Fàn (范) alone went to collect and inter him.
The officials reported this.
Xiǎn Zōng (顯宗) was greatly enraged,
summoned Fàn (范),
and interrogated him, saying:
"Xuē Hàn (薛漢) conspired with Chǔ Wáng (楚王)
to sow chaos throughout the realm.
Fàn (范), as a ducal clerk,
did not align himself with the imperial court,
but instead collected and interred a criminal.
Why is this?"
Fàn (范) kowtowed and said:
"Your servant is foolish and dull-witted.
I believed that Hàn (漢) and the others had all been executed,
and could not bear the sentiments of a teacher and student.
My crime deserves ten thousand deaths."
The Emperor's anger gradually subsided.
He asked Fàn (范):
"Are you a descendant of Lián Pó (廉頗)?
Are you related to the Right General Bāo (襃) and Grand Marshal Dān (丹)?"
Fàn (范) replied:
"Bāo (襃)
was your servant's great-grandfather;
Dān (丹)
was your servant's grandfather."
The Emperor said:
"No wonder your ambition and courage are so great!"
Thereupon, he pardoned him.
From this, he gained renown.
He was recommended as a Mào Cái (茂才).
A few months later,
he was twice promoted to become Administrator of Yún Zhōng (雲中).
At that time, the Xiōngnú (匈奴) made a large incursion into the frontier,
and beacon fires were reported daily.
According to custom,
if more than five thousand barbarians entered,
a dispatch would be sent to neighboring commanderies.
The officials wanted to transmit a circular to seek aid,
but Fàn (范) would not allow it.
He personally led his soldiers to resist them.
The barbarian forces were strong, and Fàn's (范) troops were no match.
As night fell,
he ordered his soldiers to each bind two torches together,
creating three heads of fire,
and arrayed them like stars in the camp.
The barbarians, seeing many fires from afar,
thought that Han (漢) reinforcements had arrived,
and were greatly alarmed.
They intended to retreat at dawn.
Fàn (范) then ordered his army to eat a field ration,
and in the morning, he advanced to engage them.
He beheaded several hundred,
and the barbarians trampled over each other,
with over a thousand dead.
From then on, they dared not approach Yún Zhōng (雲中) again.
Later, he successively served as Administrator of the two commanderies of Wǔ Wēi (武威) and Wǔ Dū (武都).
He adapted to local customs and guided them,
each time achieving appropriate governance.
During the Jiàn Chū (建初) period,
he was promoted to Administrator of Shǔ Jùn (蜀郡).
The local custom valued literary debate
and enjoyed finding fault with each other.
Fàn (范) always encouraged simplicity and sincerity,
and did not tolerate petty and superficial discussions.
Chéng Dū (成都) was rich in people and goods,
and houses were densely packed.
The old regulations prohibited night work for the people
to prevent fire disasters,
but people concealed their activities,
and fires occurred daily.
Fàn (范) then abolished the old regulations,
only strictly requiring the storage of water.
The common people found this convenient
and sang:
"Lián Shú Dù (廉叔度),
why did you come so late?
No fire ban,
the people work in peace.
I used to have no trousers, now I have five."
After several years in Shǔ (蜀),
he was dismissed due to a legal transgression and returned to his hometown.
The Lián (廉) family had always lived on the frontier.
They owned extensive fields,
and accumulated wealth and grain,
all of which Fàn (范) used to relieve his relatives and friends.
When Sù Zōng (肅宗) passed away,
Fàn (范) rushed to Jìng Líng (敬陵).
At that time, Yán Lín (嚴麟), a clerk from Lú Jiāng (廬江) Commandery, was presenting a memorial to mourn the nation,
and they met on the road.
Lín (麟) was riding a small cart;
the road was deep, and his horse died.
He could not proceed.
Fàn (范) saw this and felt pity,
ordering one of his accompanying riders to dismount and give his horse to Lín (麟),
then departed without telling him.
After Lín (麟) completed his task,
he did not know where the horse had gone,
so he followed its tracks to inquire.
Someone told Lín (麟):
"The former Administrator of Shǔ Jùn (蜀郡), Lián Shú Dù (廉叔度),
likes to help those in extreme poverty.
Now, on his way to the national mourning,
it must have been him."
Lín (麟) had also heard of Fàn's (范) reputation,
and believed it to be true.
He immediately led the horse to Fàn's (范) gate,
thanked him, and returned it.
The world admired his righteousness,
yet he relied on the Grand General Dòu Xiàn (竇憲),
and this was a source of criticism.
He died at home.
Initially,
Fàn (范) and Luò Qìng Hóng (洛慶鴻) were sworn brothers,
and people at the time said:
"Before, there were Guǎn (管) and Bào (鮑);
after, there are Qìng (慶) and Lián (廉)."
Hóng (鴻) was generous and upright,
and rose to the positions of Administrator of Láng Yá (琅邪) and Kuài Jī (會稽) commanderies,
wherever he served, he left extraordinary achievements.
A commentary states: Zhāng Kān (張堪) and Lián Fàn (廉范) both established their names through their chivalrous spirit.
Observing their rescue of the imperiled and distressed,
and their facing of danger,
there is much to admire.
Kān's (堪) handling of wealth,
and Fàn's (范) forgetting of his good deeds,
are also sufficient to demonstrate sincerity and move others.
As for Gāo Zǔ's (高祖) summoning of Luán Bù (欒布),
and Míng Dì's (明帝) summoning of Lián Fàn (廉范),
their anger served to stir their ambition,
and the threat of execution further prolonged their favor.
To be able to change upon hearing righteousness
is truly what a ruler's way should uphold;
however, the crux of human sentiment and reason
also involves the feeling of opening and obstruction.
Wáng Táng (王堂), courtesy name Jìng Bó (敬伯),
was a native of Qī (郪), Guǎng Hàn (廣漢).
Initially, he was recommended as a Guāng Lù Mào Cái (光祿茂才),
and was promoted to Magistrate of Gǔ Chéng (穀城),
where his governance left a notable mark.
During the Yǒng Chū (永初) period,
the Western Qiāng (西羌) raided Bá Jùn (巴郡),
becoming a plague to the people.
An imperial decree ordered the Zhong Lang Jiang (中郎將) Yǐn Jiù (尹就) to attack and suppress them,
but he failed for years.
The Three Excellencies recommended Táng (堂) for his efficient administration,
and he was appointed Administrator of Bá Jùn (巴郡).
Táng (堂) rapidly deployed troops to engage the bandits,
beheading over a thousand barbarians.
Bā (巴) and Yōng (庸) became peaceful,
and the officials and people erected shrines for him during his lifetime.
The Inspector Zhāng Qiáo (張喬) memorialized his administrative ability,
and he was promoted to Right Fú Fēng (右扶風).
Ān Dì (Emperor An) western tour.
His wet nurse Wáng Shèng and the palace attendant Zhōng Chángshì Jiāng Jīng, among others, all requested to be assigned to Táng,
but Táng did not use them.
His clerk (yuàn [shǐ]) strenuously advised against this,
but Táng said:
“I have received the nation's grace;
how can I pander to the powerful and favored
and die clinging to that! ”
That very day, he sent his family members home
and closed his door, feigning illness.
Indeed, there were those who slandered Táng,
but then the Emperor collapsed,
and Jiāng Jīng and others were all executed.
Táng was praised for upholding righteousness.
In the second year of Yǒngjiàn
he was summoned to be Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng.
Four years later,
he was demoted to Yìláng (Counselor) for official matters.
He was again appointed Lǔ Xiàng (Chancellor of Lu),
and his administration was simple and unified,
such that for several years there were no lawsuits.
He was promoted to Rǔnán Tàishǒu (Administrator of Runan),
where he sought out talent and treated scholars with courtesy,
not acting arbitrarily.
He then instructed his clerks (yuàn [shǐ]), saying:
“The ancients toiled in seeking worthy men
and rested in employing them.
Thus, their transforming influence was pure above,
and affairs were well-ordered below.
As for setting precedents for the court,
and reviewing and verifying talent and duties,
I entrust this to Gōngcáo Chén Fān.
As for rectifying government, managing affairs,
and picking up what is missed and patching what is deficient,
I entrust this to Zhǔbù Yìng Sì.
I hope to follow the principle of 'seeking substance by name'
and 'observing effect from words'. ”
From then on, he sincerely sought what was appropriate,
no longer issuing arbitrary instructions,
and the commandery was well-governed.
At that time, Dàjiāngjūn Liáng Shāng and Shàngshūlìng Yuán Tāng,
because their requests for patronage were not fulfilled,
both resented him.
Later, brigands from Lújiāng burst into Yìyáng territory.
Táng commanded his troops to pursue and suppress them,
and they immediately dispersed.
However, Liáng Shāng and Yuán Tāng still used this opportunity to report to the court that Táng had been remiss in his duties,
and he was dismissed and returned home.
He died at the age of eighty-six.
His will stipulated a simple burial,
with a tile coffin.
His son, Zhì,
was pure in conduct and did not serve in office.
His great-grandson, Shāng,
was appointed Shǔjùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Shu Commandery) by Yìzhōu Mù Liú Yān,
and had a reputation for good governance.
Sū Zhāng, courtesy name Rúwén,
was a native of Pínglíng, Fúfēng.
His eighth-generation ancestor, Jiàn,
was Yòujiāngjūn (General of the Right) during the reign of Wǔ Dì (Emperor Wu).
His grandfather, Chún,
courtesy name Huán Gōng,
had a high reputation.
He was strong-willed and outspoken, holding firm to praise and criticism.
Scholars and friends alike feared him,
even saying among themselves:
“When we see Sū Huán Gōng,
we fret over his lecturing and reproaching people,
but when we don't see him,
we miss him.”
The Sānfǔ region called him
“the great man.”
During the Yǒngpíng era,
he served under Fèngchē Dūwèi Dòu Gù's army,
and gained merit by attacking the Northern Xiōngnú and Chēshī,
for which he was enfeoffed as Zhōnglíng Xiānghóu (Marquis of Zhongling Township).
His highest official position was Nányáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Nanyang).
Sū Zhāng was learned from a young age
and skilled in writing.
During Ān Dì's (Emperor An's) reign,
he was recommended as a Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng (Worthy and Upright scholar),
and his policy proposals earned him a high grade, making him
an Yìláng (Counselor).
He frequently pointed out gains and losses,
and his words were very direct.
He was sent out as Wǔyuán Lìng (Magistrate of Wuyuan).
At that time, there was a famine,
and he immediately opened the granaries,
saving over three thousand households.
During Shùn Dì's (Emperor Shun's) reign,
he was promoted to Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (Inspector of Jizhou).
An old friend of his was Qīnghé Tàishǒu (Administrator of Qinghe), and Sū Zhāng, while on inspection, investigated his corruption.
He then invited the Administrator,
prepared wine and food for him,
and spoke cheerfully of their lifelong friendship.
The Administrator joyfully said:
“Everyone has one heaven;
I alone have two heavens.”
Sū Zhāng said:
“Tonight, Sū Rúwén drinking with an old friend
is private affection;
tomorrow, the Jìzhōu Cìshǐ investigating affairs
is public law.”
He then formally prosecuted him for his crimes.
Within the province, everyone knew Sū Zhāng was impartial,
and were awe-struck by his reputation.
He was transferred to Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ (Inspector of Bingzhou).
Because he suppressed powerful magnates,
he displeased the emperor
and was dismissed.
He lived in seclusion in his hometown,
not associating with contemporary society.
Later, he was summoned to be Hénán Yǐn (Governor of Henan),
but he did not accept.
At that time, the empire was declining daily,
and the people suffered greatly.
Commentators praised Sū Zhāng as having the talent to govern the nation,
but the court was unable to reuse him.
He died at home.
His elder brother's great-grandson was Bùwéi.
Bùwéi, courtesy name Gōngxiān.
His father, Qiān,
first served as a commandery Dūyóu (Inspector).
At that time, Lǐ Gǎo of Wèi Jùn was Měiyáng Lìng (Magistrate of Meiyang),
and he was in communication with Zhōng Chángshì Jù Yuàn.
He was corrupt and tyrannical, afflicting the people.
Previous inspectors feared his powerful connections
and dared not investigate him.
When Qiān arrived,
he investigated and found his corruption,
and he was sentenced to be sent to the Left Labor Camp.
Qiān was successively promoted to Jīnchéng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Jincheng),
and then resigned from the commandery and returned to his hometown.
According to Han law,
magistrates who were dismissed or resigned
were not allowed to go to the capital without an imperial summons.
However, Qiān later privately went to Luòyáng.
At that time, Lǐ Gǎo was Sīlì Xiàowèi (Colonel Director of Retainers).
He arrested Qiān, interrogated and tortured him,
and he died in prison.
Lǐ Gǎo then mutilated his corpse
to avenge his old grudge.
Bùwéi was eighteen years old at the time.
He had been summoned to the Gōngchē (imperial carriage),
but when he heard of Qiān's murder,
Bùwéi carried his father's corpse back to his hometown,
buried it without interring it,
looked up to heaven and sighed:
“What kind of man was Wǔ Zǐxú alone!”
He then hid his mother in the Wǔdū mountains,
changed his name,
and used all his family wealth to recruit swordsmen.
He ambushed Lǐ Gǎo among the imperial tombs,
but failed.
Coincidentally, Lǐ Gǎo was promoted to Dàsīnóng (Minister of Agriculture).
At that time, the Right Ordnance Bureau's fodder storage was beneath the northern wall of the temple.
Bùwéi and his relatives secretly entered the storage.
They dug a tunnel at night
and hid during the day.
After a month of this,
they finally reached Lǐ Gǎo's bedchamber,
emerging from under his bed.
He caught Lǐ Gǎo in the lavatory,
and so he killed his concubine and a small child instead,
leaving a letter before departing.
Lǐ Gǎo was greatly alarmed and frightened.
He then spread thorns in his room
and laid boards on the ground.
He moved nine times in one night,
and even his family did not know his whereabouts.
Whenever he went out,
he always carried a sword and halberd with him
and was guarded by brave men.
Bùwéi knew Lǐ Gǎo was prepared,
so he traveled day and night,
directly to Wèi Jùn.
He dug up Lǐ Gǎo's father Fù's tomb,
cut off Fù's head,
and offered it as a sacrifice at his own father's grave.
He also displayed it in the market, saying
“This is the head of Lǐ Jūnqiān's father.”
Lǐ Gǎo hid and dared not speak,
but he voluntarily resigned from his position
and returned to his hometown,
privately sealing up his father's tomb and coffin.
He sought to capture Bùwéi,
but could not find him for over a year.
Filled with indignation and grief,
he fell ill, vomited blood, and died.
Bù Wéi was later pardoned and returned home,
then he began to rebury [the corpse],
and observe the mourning rites.
Many literati-officials ridiculed him for excavating a tomb,
and blaming a dry skeleton,
which was not in accord with ancient principles.
Only Hé Xiū of Rènchéng compared him to Wǔ Yuán.
Guō Línzōng of Tàiyuán heard of this and commented, saying:
"Although Zǐxū (Wǔ Yuán) was said to be fleeing for his life,
he was employed by powerful Wú,
relied on the might of Hélǘ,
and took advantage of a rash and fierce multitude,
to avenge his grievance in the old capital Yǐng.
Yet, in less than a morning,
he merely flogged the tomb and desecrated the corpse
to vent his fury,
ultimately failing to personally execute the [then] ruler in revenge.
How could this compare to Sū Zǐ, who stood alone and solitary,
without reliance or resources,
against a powerful enemy with strong backing,
who held the position of one of the Nine Ministers,
with city walls like a heavenly barrier,
and palace offices deeply secluded,
where dust could not pass,
and mist and dew could not reach?
Bù Wéi, harming himself and burning with anxiety,
emerged from a hundred deaths,
defying strict prohibitions,
and inviting calamity upon his clan.
Although he did not succeed [in killing him],
his act of revenge was already profound.
Moreover, by dismembering the body and severing the head,
he inflicted poison upon the living,
causing Gǎo to harbor resentment and knot up,
and not reach his destined end,
as if borrowing the hands of spirits to kill him.
His strength was merely that of a common man,
but his achievement was as great as a state of a thousand chariots.
Compared to Yuán,
is he not superior?"
The commentators thereupon esteemed him.
Later, Grand Tutor Chén Fān summoned him,
but he did not respond,
serving instead as the Commander of Five Bureaus for the commandery.
Initially,
Zhāng Huàn of Hóngnóng was friendly with the Sū clan,
while Duàn Jiǒng of Wǔwēi had always been on good terms with Gǎo.
Later, Huàn and Jiǒng had a falling out.
When Jiǒng became the Inspector of Sīlì,
he respectfully summoned Bù Wéi.
Bù Wéi feared him
and claimed illness, not attending.
Jiǒng, already having accumulated resentment towards Huàn,
became angry.
He then retrospectively condemned Bù Wéi's previous act of revenge against Gǎo,
believing that Gǎo had impeached and punished Qiān's matter,
and was subsequently retaliated against and executed.
A ruler's command is like heaven,
but Bù Wéi held a grudge against it.
He also ordered a man from Cháng'ān to accuse Bù Wéi of bringing many guests to seize his maternal uncle's property,
and then sent his aide Zhāng Xián and others to his home to kill him.
He first gave poison to Xián's father, saying:
"If Xián fails to get Bù Wéi,
you may drink this."
When Xián arrived in Fúfēng,
the governor of the commandery made Bù Wéi present his card and welcome Xián.
Immediately, Bù Wéi was arrested,
and his entire household of over sixty people were all executed.
The Sū clan consequently declined and was destroyed.
When Duàn Jiǒng was executed by Yáng Qiú,
the world regarded it as the revenge for the Sū clan.
Yáng Xù, courtesy name Xīngzǔ,
was a native of Píngyáng, Tàishān.
His ancestors for seven generations were officials of two thousand *shí* or military commanders.
His grandfather, Qīn,
was the Inspector of Sīlì during Emperor Ān's reign.
His father, Rú,
was the Grand Minister of Ceremonies during Emperor Huán's reign.
Xù, as the descendant of a loyal minister, was appointed a Gentleman.
After leaving office,
he was summoned to the Grand General Dòu Wǔ's residence.
When Wǔ was defeated,
Xù was implicated in the partisan proscription,
imprisoned for over ten years,
and lived in quiet seclusion.
When the partisan proscription was lifted,
he was again summoned to the Grand Commandant's residence,
and after four promotions, became the Administrator of Lújiāng.
Later, the Yellow Turban bandits from Yángzhōu attacked Shū,
burning cities and towns.
Xù mobilized all men aged twenty and above in the county,
making them all carry weapons and form ranks.
The younger and weaker ones
were all made to carry water to extinguish the fires.
Tens of thousands of people gathered,
and fighting with all their might,
they decisively defeated them,
and the commandery became peaceful.
Later, bandits like Dài Fēng from Ānfēng rebelled,
and Xù again defeated them,
beheading over three thousand,
and capturing the leaders alive.
The remaining followers were pardoned as commoners,
given farming tools,
and made to engage in agriculture.
In the third year of Zhōngpíng (186 CE),
Zhào Cí, a soldier from Jiāngxià, rebelled,
killed Qín Jié, the Administrator of Nányáng,
and captured six counties.
Xù was appointed Administrator of Nányáng.
When he was about to enter the commandery,
he dressed simply and traveled informally,
accompanied by a single servant boy.
He observed and toured the counties,
collecting popular sentiments,
before finally advancing.
He already knew in advance the integrity or corruption of the magistrates,
and whether the officials and common people were good or evil.
The entire commandery was astonished,
and everyone was struck with awe.
He then dispatched troops and, together with Wáng Mǐn, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, attacked Cí,
beheaded him,
and obtained over five thousand heads.
The remaining bandits in the subordinate counties all surrendered to Xù.
Xù reported to the throne on their behalf,
pardoning their associates.
Once the bandits were pacified,
he proclaimed governing policies,
inquiring into the people's sufferings and benefits,
and the hundred surnames rejoiced and submitted.
At that time, powerful and influential families often indulged in luxury and extravagance.
Xù deeply detested this
and always wore worn-out clothes, ate simple food,
and had dilapidated carriages and horses.
His Administrator's Assistant once presented him with fresh fish.
Xù accepted it and hung it in his courtyard.
Later, the Assistant offered it again.
Xù then brought out the previously hung fish to deter his intention.
Later, Xù's wife and son Mì came together to the commandery residence.
Xù closed the gate and did not let them in.
His wife then took Mì and left.
His belongings consisted only of a cloth quilt, worn-out sheets,
and several *hú* of salt and wheat.
He then instructed Mì, saying:
"I serve myself in this way;
how can I provide for your mother?"
He made them both return home.
In the sixth year (189 CE),
Emperor Líng wanted to appoint Xù as Grand Commandant.
At that time, those appointed to the Three Excellencies
all had to pay ten million in ritual money to the Eastern Garden,
and the emperor's envoys were sent to supervise this,
named
"Left Outriders."
Wherever they went,
they were always welcomed with respectful greetings
and given lavish gifts.
Xù then made the envoy sit on a simple mat
and held up his worn-out robe to show him,
saying:
"What I possess
is only this."
The Left Outrider reported this,
and the Emperor was displeased,
and thus he did not ascend to the ducal position.
However, he was summoned to be Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
Before he could take office,
he fell ill and died,
aged forty-eight.
His dying words were for a simple burial
and to refuse funerary gifts.
According to old regulations,
a two-thousand *shí* official who died in office received a funerary gift of one million.
His Administrator's Assistant, Jiāo Jiǎn, followed Xù's prior wishes
and accepted nothing.
An imperial edict praised him
and ordered the Administrator of Tàishān to give the funerary money from the government to Xù's family.
Jiǎ Cóng, courtesy name Mèngjiān,
was a native of Liáochéng, Dōngjùn.
He was nominated as Filial and Incorrupt,
and after two promotions, became the Magistrate of Jīng,
where he had a record of good governance.
Formerly, Jiāozhǐ Commandery produced many treasures.
Bright pearls, kingfisher feathers, rhinoceros horns, elephant tusks, tortoise shells, rare spices, and beautiful timbers
were all naturally abundant.
Previous governors were mostly not upright in their conduct.
They curried favor with powerful nobles above
and secretly accumulated bribes below.
Once their wealth and accounts were full,
they would seek to be transferred to another post.
Therefore, the officials and common people resented and rebelled.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng (184 CE),
the garrison in Jiāozhǐ rebelled,
seizing the governor and the Administrator of Hépǔ.
They proclaimed themselves
“Zhùtiān Jiāngjūn” (General Who Holds Up Heaven).
Emperor Língdi specially ordered the Three Ducal Ministers to carefully select capable officials.
The responsible officials recommended Cóng to be the Governor of Jiāozhǐ.
When Cóng arrived at the province,
he investigated the reasons for their rebellion.
They all said that the levies were too heavy,
and the common people were all impoverished and destitute.
The capital was far away,
and there was nowhere to appeal for justice.
The people could not make a living (suffer),
so they gathered as bandits.
Cóng immediately issued a notice,
instructing everyone to settle down with their property and occupations.
He recruited and pacified the scattered and dispossessed,
remitting corvée labor and taxes.
He executed the bandit leaders who were the greatest harms,
and selected upright officials to provisionally govern the various counties.
Within a year, peace was restored,
and the common people were settled.
People sang a song in the streets about it, saying:
"Jǐa Fù came late,
making me rebel first.
Now that we see peace and order,
officials dare not eat."
He served for three years,
and was ranked highest among the thirteen provinces.
He was summoned and appointed as Yìláng (Consultant Remonstrant).
At that time, the Yellow Turban Rebellion had just been suppressed.
After the ravages of war,
the commanderies and counties imposed heavy taxes,
leading to corruption.
An imperial edict ordered the removal of unfit governors and Two-Thousand-Picul officials
and the selection of new, upright, and capable officials.
Cóng was then appointed Governor of Jìzhōu.
According to old custom,
the post-carriage, drawn by three horses,
with a red curtain hanging down,
would be sent to welcome the new governor at the provincial border.
When Cóng reached the province,
he ascended the carriage and said:
"A governor should look far and listen widely,
investigating good and evil.
Why should he hang a curtain to conceal himself?"
He then ordered the charioteer to lift it.
The hundred cities heard of this and
were naturally awed and shaken.
Those who had committed transgressions,
hearing the news, relinquished their official seals and left.
Only Dǒng Zhāo of Jìyīn, the Prefect of Yǐngtáo, and Huáng Jiù of Liángguó, the Prefect of Guānshui, remained at their posts to await Cóng.
Thus, the provincial border was entirely pacified.
When Emperor Língdi died,
Grand General Hé Jìn memorialized Cóng as Dùliáo Jiāngjūn (General Who Crosses the Liao River),
and he died in office.
Lù Kāng, courtesy name Jìníng,
was a native of Wú Commandery in Wú.
His grandfather Xù
is mentioned in the "Biographies of Recluses".
His father Bāo
had noble aspirations and conduct,
and was repeatedly summoned but did not respond.
Kāng served the commandery in his youth,
and was praised for his righteousness and integrity.
Governor Zāng Mín nominated him as Màocái (Flourishing Talent),
and he was appointed Prefect of Gāochéng.
The county was located on the frontier.
According to old regulations,
one person from each household had to provide a bow and crossbow to guard against unforeseen events,
and was not allowed to travel.
When a new senior official arrived,
they would invariably mobilize the people to repair the city walls.
When Kāng arrived,
he dismissed everyone,
and the common people were greatly pleased.
He governed with kindness and trust,
and bandits also ceased their activities.
The province and commanderies reported his achievements.
In the first year of Guānghé (178 CE),
he was promoted to Administrator of Wǔlíng,
then transferred to govern the two commanderies of Guìyáng and Lè'ān,
and was praised wherever he served.
At that time, Emperor Língdi wanted to cast bronze figures,
but the national treasury was insufficient.
So he issued an edict to levy taxes on farmland,
collecting ten coins per *mǔ*.
However, recently, there had been droughts and floods damaging crops,
and the common people were suffering from poverty.
Kāng submitted a memorial advising against it, saying:
"Your servant hears that the sage kings governed the world,
valuing the love of the people.
They reduced corvée and lightened taxes,
to bring peace to the world;
they removed complexities and embraced simplicity,
to promote ease and straightforwardness.
Thus, all the people followed their transformation,
and spiritual beings responded to their virtue.
In later generations, declining rulers,
indulged in extreme extravagance,
making endless creations,
and establishing numerous systems,
causing hardship to those below,
to satisfy their temporary desires.
Thus, the common people sighed and groaned,
and *yīn* and *yáng* were disturbed.
Your Majesty, with your sacred virtue, has inherited the mandate of Heaven,
and should promote a prosperous transformation.
Yet, suddenly an edict was issued,
levying a land tax per *mǔ*,
to cast bronze figures.
Upon reading it, I am dismayed,
my heart aches, and I lose my sense of purpose.
The *Book of Rites* says: 'Taxing one-eleventh,
Zhōu called it *chè*.
*Chè* means to pass through,
meaning its laws and regulations can be passed down through ten thousand generations.'
Therefore, when Duke Xuān of Lǔ taxed land by the *mǔ*,
locust plagues arose;
when Duke Āi increased taxes,
Confucius disapproved of it.
How can one gather and seize the people's property
to construct useless bronze figures;
abandon sage warnings,
and personally tread the path of doomed kings!
It is said in the *Zuǒzhuàn*: 'When a ruler acts, it must be recorded.
If it is recorded but not lawful,
what will later generations have to narrate?'
Your Majesty should pay careful attention and examine,
correct errors and follow goodness,
to quell the hopes of resentment among the myriad people."
When the memorial was presented,
eunuchs within the court slandered Kāng, saying that he invoked fallen states
to compare with the sagely and enlightened ruler,
which was greatly disrespectful.
He was summoned in a caged cart to the Grand Judge's court.
Imperial Censor Líu Dài presided over the investigation of his case.
Dài presented a memorial to explain and clarify,
and he was cleared and returned to his hometown.
He was again summoned and appointed as Yìláng.
At that time, the Lújiāng bandit Huáng Ráng and others, allied with the Mán (barbarians) of Jiāngxià, numbered over a hundred thousand,
attacking and capturing four counties.
Kāng was appointed Administrator of Lújiāng.
Kāng clearly set out rewards and punishments,
defeated Ráng and his group,
and the remaining factions all surrendered.
The Emperor praised his achievements,
and appointed Kāng's grandson Shàng as Lángzhōng (Gentleman).
When Emperor Xiàndi ascended the throne,
the world was in great chaos.
Kāng bravely sent Filial and Incorrupt officials and accountants to present tribute to the imperial court.
An imperial edict commended his efforts,
and he was given the title Zhōngyì Jiāngjūn (General of Loyalty and Righteousness),
with a stipend equivalent to Two-Thousand-Picul officials.
At that time, Yuán Shù was stationed with troops at Shòuchūn.
His divisions were starving.
He sent envoys to request the transport of military provisions and weapons.
Kāng, considering him a rebel,
closed the city gates and refused access.
He inwardly prepared for battle,
intending to resist him.
Shù was greatly enraged,
and sent his general Sūn Cè to attack Kāng,
surrounding the city with several layers of troops.
Kāng held firm in defense.
Officials and soldiers who had previously been granted leave
all returned secretly and hurried back,
climbing the city walls at night to enter.
He withstood the enemy for two years
before the city fell.
A little over a month later,
he fell ill and died,
at the age of seventy.
His clan of over a hundred people
suffered from famine and distress,
and nearly half of them died.
The imperial court commiserated with his steadfast loyalty,
and appointed his son Jùn as Lángzhōng.
His youngest son Jì
served the Wú state as Administrator of Yùlín,
was widely learned and governed well,
and was praised at the time.
As a young boy, he once paid respects to Yuán Shù,
and was the one who hid tangerines and dropped them on the ground,
and was famous for this.
An encomium states: Jí pastured the northern frontier,
faith established in a childish and dim-witted lord.
Shī guarded the southern Chǔ,
and the people composed ballads.
Fèn rode alone in a single chariot,
capable of driving a broken-shafted carriage.
Fàn gained his friends,
Táng served as an excellent assistant.
The two Sū were vigorous and ardent,
Yáng and Jiǎ were honest and capable.
Jì Níng resisted the plan,
and the city fell to the assault ram.
Biography of Fán Hóng and Yīn Shí, Chapter 22 (Hóng's son Chóu, his great-grandson Zhǔn, Shí's younger brother Xīng)
Fán Hóng, courtesy name Míqīng,
was a native of Húyáng, Nányáng Commandery,
and the maternal uncle of Emperor Shìzǔ.
His ancestor was Zhōu Zhòng Shānfǔ,
who was enfeoffed in Fán,
and thus took Fán as his surname.
He became a prominent local gentry.
His father, Zhòng,
courtesy name Jūnyún,
was skilled in farming for generations
and fond of commerce.
Zhòng was gentle and benevolent by nature,
and had strict rules.
Three generations shared property,
and the children and grandchildren showed reverence morning and evening,
always as if in a public household.
In managing his family's property and industry,
nothing was wasted.
He assigned tasks to servants and slaves,
each according to their suitability,
thus enabling everyone, from top to bottom, to work together with concerted effort.
Their wealth and profits doubled each year,
to the extent that they opened and expanded over three hundred qǐng of farmland.
The houses they built
all had multiple halls and high pavilions,
with irrigation ditches and canals.
They also had fish ponds and livestock,
providing whatever was requested.
He once desired to make implements
and first planted catalpa and lacquer trees.
People at the time ridiculed him,
but after years accumulated,
they all became useful,
and those who had laughed at him then all sought to borrow them.
His wealth reached millions,
yet he generously assisted his clan
and extended kindness to his local community.
His maternal grandsons, the Hè family brothers, quarreled over property.
Zhòng was ashamed of this,
and used two qǐng of land to resolve their angry dispute.
The people in the county praised his goodness
and elected him as one of the Sānlǎo.
He died at over eighty years old.
He had privately lent several million [cash] to people,
and in his will, he ordered the burning and destruction of the contracts.
Those indebted, upon hearing this, were all ashamed
and rushed to repay him,
but his sons followed his command
and ultimately refused to accept it.
Hóng had aspirations and integrity from a young age.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
righteous armies rose.
Liú Bóshēng and his clan cousin Cì led troops to attack Húyáng,
but the city defenders did not surrender.
Cì's younger sister was Hóng's wife.
Húyáng therefore arrested and imprisoned Hóng's wife and children,
ordering Hóng to go out and persuade Bóshēng.
Hóng then stayed and did not return.
The military commander of Húyáng wanted to kill his wife and children.
The chief officials and others discussed among themselves, saying:
"Fán Zhòng and his son
are known throughout the community for their etiquette, righteousness, kindness, and virtue.
Even if they are guilty,
their punishment should come later."
Coincidentally, the Hàn army grew stronger day by day,
and Húyáng became panicked.
They dared not kill them
and thus they escaped.
When Gēngshǐ was established,
he wanted to appoint Hóng as a general.
Hóng kowtowed and declined, saying:
"A scholar is not skilled in military affairs."
He eventually obtained permission to return home
and, with his clan and relatives, built a camp to defend themselves.
Over a thousand families of old and weak people sought refuge with him.
At that time, the Chìméi bandits plundered Tángzǐ Township,
massacring many,
and intended to attack Hóng's camp.
Hóng sent people with cattle, wine, rice, and grain
to reward and give to the Chìméi.
The Chìméi elders had heard of Hóng's benevolence and generosity
and all exclaimed:
"Lord Fán has always been good,
and now he treats us like this.
How can we attack him?"
They led their troops away
and thus averted the bandit calamity.
When Emperor Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Hóng as Guānglù Dàfū,
a position of special distinction,
second only to the Sāngōng.
In the fifth year of Jiànwǔ [29 CE],
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chángluó.
In the thirteenth year [37 CE],
his younger brother Dān was enfeoffed as Marquis of Shèyáng,
his elder brother's son Xún as Marquis of Xuánxiāng,
and his clan elder brother Zhōng as Marquis of Gēngfù.
In the fifteenth year [39 CE],
Hóng was definitively enfeoffed as Marquis of Shòuzhāng.
In the eighteenth year [42 CE],
the Emperor went south to sacrifice at Zhānglíng.
Passing through Húyáng,
he sacrificed at Zhòng's tomb,
posthumously ennobling and bestowing the honorific title of Jing Marquis of Shòuzhāng,
and erecting a temple in Húyáng.
Whenever the imperial carriage toured the south,
it would often visit his tomb,
bestowing generous rewards and holding grand assemblies.
Hóng was humble, gentle, cautious, and circumspect by nature,
and did not seek advancement improperly.
He often admonished his sons, saying:
"When wealth and high status are overflowing,
there has never been anyone who could maintain them to the end.
It is not that I dislike glory and power,
but the Heavenly Way dislikes excess and favors humility.
The noble relatives of previous generations are all clear warnings.
To preserve one's body and complete oneself,
is this not joyful!"
Whenever there was a court assembly,
he would arrive early,
bow down and wait for the proceedings,
only rising when the time came.
The Emperor heard of this
and often ordered the imperial guards to inform him only when the court was about to convene,
not allowing him to arrive early.
Hóng would personally write
and then destroy the drafts of any suggestions or criticisms of gains and losses he submitted.
He would destroy the drafts.
When the court inquired,
he dared not answer in public.
His clan was influenced by his transformation
and never broke the law.
The Emperor greatly esteemed him.
When he became seriously ill,
the imperial carriage came to visit,
staying overnight,
and asked what he wished to say.
Hóng prostrated himself and stated:
"Without merit, I enjoy a large enfeoffment.
I sincerely fear that my descendants will not be able to preserve this immense grace,
making my soul and spirit ashamed and burdened in the Yellow Springs.
I wish to return Shòuzhāng
and be enfeoffed with a small village."
The Emperor was saddened by his words
but ultimately did not grant it.
In the twenty-seventh year [51 CE],
he passed away.
He left instructions for a simple funeral,
using nothing extra,
believing that once the coffin was interred,
it should not be seen again,
for if it decayed,
it would wound the heart of a filial son.
He wished to be buried in the same tomb but different chambers as his wife.
The Emperor approved his will
and showed it to his officials by written decree,
saying:
"If I do not follow the wishes of the Marquis of Shòuzhāng today,
I will have no way to demonstrate his virtue.
Furthermore, after I die,
I wish for this to be a model."
He was granted ten million cash,
ten thousand bolts of cloth,
bestowed the posthumous title of Gōng Marquis,
and presented with an official seal and ribbon.
The imperial carriage personally accompanied the funeral.
His son Chóu inherited his title.
The Emperor lamented Hóng incessantly,
and further enfeoffed his youngest son Mào as Marquis of Píngwàng.
There were altogether five marquises in the Fán family.
The next year,
Chóu's younger brother Wěi and seven clan brothers were granted a total of fifty million cash.
A discussion states: Formerly, King Qǐngxiāng of Chǔ asked Lord Yánglíng:
"What kind of wealth does a junzi possess?"
He replied:
"He lends to people without expecting repayment for their ingratitude,
feeds people without making them serve or labor for him,
his relatives love him,
and the multitude praises him."
Indeed, Fán Zhòng's act of burning contracts and settling disputes,
is it not close to the wealth of a junzi?
To distribute land according to the Way of Heaven,
to fill granaries to uphold propriety and moderation,
to obtain resources through rational transformation,
this can also be applied to governance.
What difference is there
between this and being loved and revered?
Fán Yóu, courtesy name Zhǎngyú,
was prudent and had a paternal demeanor.
He was exceedingly filial to his stepmother,
and when she died,
his grief was beyond the prescribed rites.
He became emaciated and could not support himself.
Shìzǔ (Emperor Guāngwǔ) often sent a Central Huángmén to deliver gruel morning and evening.
When the mourning period ended,
he studied the Gōngyáng and Yán clans' commentaries on the Chūnqiū with attendant Dīng Gōng.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
the prohibitions were still lax.
As the various kings grew up,
they each invited guests and retainers.
Because Fán Yóu was an imperial relative by marriage,
they vied to recruit him.
However, Fán Yóu maintained his purity and integrity,
and did not engage in any associations.
When the affair of Péi Wáng Fǔ occurred,
many imperial relatives and noble youths were arrested.
Fán Yóu was spared because he was not involved.
When the emperor (Guāngwǔ) passed away,
Fán Yóu served as Fùtǔ Xiàowèi.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng (58 CE),
he was appointed Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi.
He participated with the Gōngqīng in formulating the rituals for suburban sacrifices,
and used chèn prophecies to rectify divergent interpretations of the Five Classics.
Zhōu Zé of Běihǎi and Chéng Gōng of Lángyá were both great scholars from within the realm.
Fán Yóu regarded them as teachers and friends and brought them to court.
He submitted a memorial stating that when commanderies and kingdoms selected Xiàolián,
they often chose young men capable of repaying kindness,
while experienced elders and great worthies were often discarded.
He proposed that commanderies and kingdoms should be ordered to select and employ talented individuals.
He also argued that capital punishments should be carried out in autumn,
in accordance with the seasonal氣.
Xiǎnzōng (Emperor Míng) adopted both proposals.
In the second year (59 CE),
the state of Shòuzhāng was merged into Dōngpíng Wáng's territory,
and Fán Yóu was transferred and enfeoffed as Yān Hóu.
Later, Guǎnglǐng Wáng Jīng committed a crime.
The emperor (Míng) grieved over this close relative,
and ordered Fán Yóu and Yǔlín Jiān Rèn Kuí of Nányáng to jointly handle the case.
When the matter was concluded,
they presented a memorial requesting Jīng's execution.
They were summoned to Xuānmíng Diàn,
where the emperor angrily said:
"You, my lords, because he is my brother,
wish to execute him.
If he were my son,
would you dare to do so?!"
Fán Yóu looked up and replied:
"The world is Gāo Dì's (Emperor Guāngwǔ's) world,
not Your Majesty's world.
The principle of the Chūnqiū states,
'A ruler's kin may not rebel;
if they rebel, they shall be executed.'
Thus, Zhōu Gōng executed his brother,
and Jì Yǒu poisoned his elder brother.
The classics and commentaries greatly approve of this.
We, your ministers, considering Jīng to be your mother's brother,
and knowing Your Majesty's compassionate heart,
and profound empathy,
therefore dared to make this request.
If he were Your Majesty's son,
we, your ministers, would simply carry out the execution ourselves."
The emperor sighed for a long time.
Fán Yóu became even more renowned for this.
Later, his younger brother, Wěi, sought to marry his son Shǎng to Jìngxiāng Gōngzhǔ, the daughter of Chǔ Wáng Yīng.
Fán Yóu heard of it and stopped him,
saying:
"During the Jiànwǔ era,
our family enjoyed great honors and favors,
with five marquises in one clan.
At that time, a high official suggested
that our daughters could marry kings,
and our sons could marry princesses.
But because excessive favor leads to misfortune,
we did not do so.
Moreover, you have only one son,
how can you abandon him to Chǔ?"
Wěi did not comply.
In the tenth year (67 CE),
Fán Yóu died.
He received generous posthumous gifts and funeral offerings,
and was granted the posthumous title Āi Hóu.
The emperor (Míng) sent the junior Huángmén Zhāng Yīn to inquire about his dying words.
Previously, the prefecture of Hénán had lost official funds,
and many officials responsible for the deficit
were sentenced to death or exile,
thus passing the responsibility to others
to compensate for the loss.
Local officials used this as an opportunity for corruption,
which Fán Yóu always detested.
Additionally, Yěwáng annually presented sweet wine and cream,
which always disturbed the people,
and officials profited from it.
Fán Yóu wished to memorialize for the abolition of both,
but he was ill and unable to do so.
When Yīn returned,
he reported everything.
The emperor (Míng) read it and sighed with sorrow,
ordering
that both requests regarding the two commanderies be followed.
His eldest son Sī inherited the title,
and his second sons Chēn and Fàn were appointed Láng.
Later, when the Chǔ affair came to light,
the emperor (Míng) remembered Fán Yóu's prudence and integrity,
and also heard that he had stopped Wěi's marriage.
Thus, his various sons were not implicated.
Fàn, courtesy name Wéngāo,
served as a Láng for over twenty years,
and the three bureaus admired his solemn discretion.
He gave all his wealth, over twenty million (coins), to his orphaned brother's son.
He rose to the position of Dàhónglú.
When Sī died,
his son Shí inherited.
When Shí died,
his son Jiàn inherited.
When Jiàn died,
he had no son,
and the marquisate was abolished.
In the first year of Yǒngníng (120 CE),
Empress Dowager Dèng re-enfeoffed Jiàn's younger brother Pàn.
When Pàn died,
his son Shàng inherited.
Initially,
Fán Yóu edited and codified the chapters and sentences of the Gōngyáng and Yán clans' commentaries on the Chūnqiū.
The world called it
"Fán Hóu's Scholarship,"
and he taught over three thousand students.
His disciples Lǐ Xiū of Yǐngchuān and Xià Qín of Jiǔjiāng
both became Sāngōng.
Qín, courtesy name Bózōng,
served as magistrate of the two prefectures of Jīng and Wǎn,
and as Grand Administrator of Línglíng.
Wherever he served, his administrative ability was praised.
During the reign of Emperor Ān,
he rose to the position of Sītú.
Zhǔn, courtesy name Yòulíng,
was a great-grandson of the same clan as Hóng.
His father, Ruì,
was fond of Huáng-Lǎo teachings,
and was pure, serene, and had few desires.
Zhǔn, in his youth, strove to cultivate his conduct,
and studied Confucian arts.
He ceded his family's wealth of several millions to his orphaned elder brother's son.
In the fifteenth year of Yǒngyuán (103 CE),
Emperor Hé visited Nányáng.
Zhǔn was the Commandery Gōngcáo.
He was summoned for an audience,
and the emperor admired him,
appointing him Lángzhōng.
He returned to the palace with the imperial carriage,
and was specially appointed Shàngshū Láng.
When Empress Dowager Dèng held court,
Confucian learning declined.
Zhǔn then submitted a memorial, stating:
..."Illustrious teachers and masters.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ received the mandate and began the restoration,
the various heroes collapsed and caused disturbances,
with banners strewn across the fields.
Fighting campaigns in the east and west,
he had no leisure to rest.
Yet, he still laid down his
weapons to discuss the arts,
and rested his horses to discourse on the Way.
Reaching Emperor Xiàomíng,
who possessed the appearance of heaven and earth,
and used the brightness of the sun and moon,
he examined with his own heart all the myriad affairs of government.
Yet, he still devoted
his feelings to the classical texts,
and let his thoughts wander among the classics and arts.
Whenever a feast or archery ceremony concluded,
he would sit upright and lecture himself,
while all the scholars listened.
The four quarters rejoiced.
