and the events of
Juéxiàng
are truly not worth mentioning (in comparison).
He also summoned many famous scholars
to fill ritual offices,
such as Zhào Xiào of Péiguó and Chéng Gōng of Lángyá.
Some were sent home
to their villages
in comfortable carriages with four-horse teams;
others,
in splendid robes and wide belts,
followed and were seen in the ancestral temple.
The rest, who excelled in classical studies,
were distributed throughout the court and temples.
Thus, the court had many excellent white-haired individuals
and aged elders.
Whenever there was a banquet,
they would engage in joyful discussions and debates,
seeking to improve governance and transformation.
Listening carefully to their various words,
it was like the ringing of jade.
Those at court advanced and..."

Both great and small followed the transformation,
harmonious and admirable.
The feathered forest guards at the palace gates, clad in armor,
all became conversant with the Xiàojīng.
The Bóshì and
Láng,
when one opened the gate,

The transformation originated from the sagely person,
spreading even to the uncivilized regions,
where the Xiōngnú sent Yīzhīzīwáng Dàchēqǐqú to come and
study.
The eight directions were tranquil and clear,
with no disturbances above or below.
Therefore, commentators always praised the flourishing era,
unanimously speaking of Yǒngpíng.
He resigned.
Clerical officials abandoned laws to learn slander and deception,
sharpening the points of their knives,
to cut through the gravity of legal penalties,
their virtue shallow and customs meager,
leading to
harshness.
In the past, Empress Dòu of Xiàowén had a fondness for Huáng-Lǎo,
and the transformation of tranquility and purity spread during the reigns of Jǐng and Wǔ.
Your foolish servant believes that a clear edict should be issued,
to widely seek out the
hidden talents,
bringing forth those from caves and mountains,
favoring and promoting the refined scholars.
If there are any like Xiào or Gōng,
they should be summoned to the Gōngchē,
to await the Sacred Emperor's time for lectures and studies.
The Gōngqīng should each recommend those well-versed in the classics
and descendants of old Ru scholars,
advancing their ranks and positions,
so they may continue their work.
Also, summon the scribes from the commanderies and states,
to make them read the laws and ordinances.
If this is done,
those who crane their necks will see something new daily,
and those who cock their ears will hear something new monthly.
I humbly wish that Your Majesty would promote and follow the way of advancing undertakings of the former emperors.
Zhǔn was transferred a second time to be Yùshǐzhōngchéng.
At the beginning of Yǒngchū,
there were consecutive years of floods, droughts, and other calamities,
many commanderies and states suffered from hunger and distress.
Zhǔn submitted a memorial, saying: Your servant has heard that the tradition says:
"When there is hunger but no reduction, this is called too much,
and the calamity is water."
The Chūnqiū Gǔliáng Zhuàn says:
"When the five grains do not grow,
it is called a great
invasion.
For a great invasion,
all officials are prepared but not restrained,
and all spirits are prayed to but not sacrificed to."
From this, it can be said that
the regulation and harmony of yin and yang
truly lies in
frugality.
Although the court is toiling for the common people,
and matters are being simplified,
the officials in charge
have not yet complied.
Establishing transformation and achieving good governance
proceeds from near to far.
Therefore, the Shī
says,
"The capital is reverent and solemn,
the four quarters take it as their model."
Now, we can first order the Taìguān, Shàngfāng, Kǎogōng, and Shànglín Chí and other offices
to genuinely reduce unnecessary
items,
and the five bureaus should adjust and reduce the number of officials in the capital city who are performing work.
If this is done,
the transformation will reach the four directions,
and people's toil will be lessened.
Following the annual custom,
envoys bearing credentials were sent to comfort and pacify.
Those who were particularly distressed and impoverished
were resettled in the fertile commanderies of Jīng and Yáng.
This would both save the cost of transportation
and allow the people to settle
in their respective places.
Although there is currently a military campaign in the west,
the urgent needs of the eastern states should be prioritized.
If envoys are sent with the Èrqiānshí to adjust matters as needed,
leaving all wealthy people
to guard their old homes,
and relocating the especially poor with provisions for clothing and food,
this would truly be a parental strategy.
I wish that Your Majesty would submit my words to the Gōngqīng for impartial deliberation.
In the fifth year,
he was transferred to be the Taìshǒu of Hénèi.
At that time, the Qiāng repeatedly invaded the commandery borders.
Zhǔn immediately led troops to suppress and expel them,
and repaired the fortified villages,
his prestige and reputation spread widely.
After serving for three years,
he was summoned due to illness,
and was transferred three times to become Shàngshūlìng,
being familiar with old customs,
he was then appointed to important positions.
In the third year of Yuánchū,
he replaced Zhōu Chàng as Guānglùxūn.
In the fifth year,
he died in office.
Yīn Shí, courtesy name Cìbó,
was a native of Xīnyě, Nányáng,
and the elder maternal brother of Empress Guāngliè.
His ancestors originated from Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng's seventh-generation descendant, Xiū,
moved from Qí to Chǔ,
and became the Grand Master of Yīn,
thus adopting the surname Yīn.
Between the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
his family first settled in Xīnyě.
When Liú Bóshēng raised an army of righteousness,
Shí was then studying in Cháng'ān.
Hearing of it,
he abandoned his studies and returned,
leading over a thousand of his sons, younger brothers, clan members, and retainers to go and see Bóshēng.
Bóshēng then appointed Shí as Xiàowèi.
In the first year of Gēngshǐ,
he was promoted to Piānjiàngjūn,
and followed in the attack on Wǎn,
separately bringing Xīnyě, Yùyáng, Dùyǎn, Guànjūn, and Húyáng to surrender.
In the second year,
Gēngshǐ enfeoffed Shí as Yīndé Hóu,
and acted as Dàjiàngjūn.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
Guāngwǔ sent an envoy to welcome Noble Lady Yīn from Xīnyě,
and also summoned Shí.
Shí arrived with the Noble Lady,
was appointed Qídūwèi,
and re-enfeoffed as Yīnxiāng Hóu.
In the second year,
his fief was increased due to his military achievements in conquest.
Shí kowtowed and declined, saying:
"The world has just been settled,
and there are many generals and commanders who have made contributions.
Your servant relies on his connection to the Imperial Harem,
and yet my title and fief are increased.
This cannot be shown to the world."
The Emperor greatly admired him,
and appointed him Guāndūwèi,
to guard Hángǔ.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
but resigned due to his mother's mourning.
In the fifteenth year,
he was definitively enfeoffed as Yuánlù Hóu.
When Xiǎozōng was established as Crown Prince,
Shí was appointed Zhíjīnwǔ,
to assist and guide the Eastern Palace.
Whenever the Emperor toured the commanderies and states,
Shí always remained to guard the capital,
and was entrusted with the imperial guard.
In court, he would speak frankly with righteous proposals,
but when conversing with guests,
he never touched upon state affairs.
The Emperor respected him greatly,
often pointing to Shí to admonish his noble relatives,
and to encourage those around him.
All the officials and scribes Shí employed were chosen for their wisdom,
such as Yú Tíng, Fù Kuān, Xuē Yīn, etc.,
many of whom rose to become Gōngqīng and Xiàowèi.
When Xiǎozōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Zhíjīnwǔ,
with the rank of Tèjìn.
In the second year of Yǒngpíng,
he died,
and was posthumously granted his original official seal and ribbon,
with the posthumous title Zhēn Hóu.
His son Gōng succeeded him.
When Gōng died,
his son Huáng succeeded him.
In the seventh year of Yǒngchū,
he was murdered by a slave,
leaving no son,
and the fief was terminated.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
Empress Dowager Dèng enfeoffed Huáng's younger brother Shū as successor.
When Shū died,
his son Wěi succeeded him.
Gōng's younger brother Gāng's daughter became Empress of Hé Dì,
and Gāng was enfeoffed as Wúfáng Hóu,
with the rank of Tèjìn.
His three sons, Yì, Fǔ, and Chǎng,
were all Huángmén Shìláng.
The Empress was deposed due to witchcraft accusations.
Gāng committed suicide.
Fǔ died in prison.
Yì and Chǎng were exiled to Rìnán.
Shí's younger brother was Xīng.
Yīn Xīng
Yīn Xīng, whose courtesy name was Jūnlíng, was the younger brother of Empress Guāngliè.
He was a man of great physical strength.
In the 2nd year of Jiànwǔ (26 CE),
he was appointed Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Attendant),
and then acting Qímén Púyè (Commander of the Palace Guard),
commanding the armored cavalry.
He participated in various campaigns,
pacifying various commanderies and states.
Whenever Yīn Xīng accompanied Emperor Guāngwǔ,
he would always carry a small parasol
to shield the emperor from wind and rain,
and he himself would walk through mud,
leading the Qímén (Palace Guard).
Wherever Emperor Guāngwǔ went,
Yīn Xīng would first enter and clear the palace.
He was greatly trusted and favored.
Although he enjoyed giving to guests,
his gate was free of ruffians.
He was not on good terms with Zhāng Zōng from the same commandery and Xiānyú Pǒu from Shànggǔ,
but knowing their usefulness,
he still praised their strengths and promoted them.
His friends Zhāng Sì and Dù Qín, with whom he was close,
he considered showy and lacking substance;
he only privately bestowed wealth upon them,
but never spoke on their behalf. For this reason, the world praised his loyalty and fairness.
His residence was merely functional,
just enough to shelter from wind and rain.
In the 9th year (33 CE),
he was promoted to Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant)
and granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu (Marquis within the Pass).
Later, the Emperor summoned Yīn Xīng,
intending to enfeoff him,
and placed the seal and ribbon before him.
Yīn Xīng firmly declined, saying:
"Your servant has not achieved the merit of being first to ascend the ramparts or break through the enemy lines,
yet several members of my family have simultaneously received titles and lands.
This would cause the people of the world to be disappointed and resentful,
and would truly be excessive.
Your servant has received immense favor and grace from Your Majesty and the Guìrén (Empress).
My wealth and status are already at their peak,
and cannot be further increased.
I sincerely do not desire it."
The Emperor admired Yīn Xīng's humility
and did not force his will.
The Guìrén asked him for his reason.
Yīn Xīng said:
"Does the Guìrén not read the historical records?
'A dragon that has soared too high will have cause for regret.'
The families of imperial in-laws often fail to know when to be modest and retire.
They wish to marry their daughters to marquises and kings,
and marry their sons to princesses.
My foolish heart truly feels uneasy about this.
Wealth and status have their limits;
people should know when they have enough.
Excessive extravagance will only invite ridicule from observers."
The Guìrén was touched by his words,
and greatly humbled herself,
never again seeking positions for her relatives.
In the 19th year (43 CE),
he was appointed Wèiwèi (Commander of the Guards),
and also assisted in guiding the Crown Prince.
In the summer of the following year (44 CE),
the Emperor suffered a severe dizzy spell.
The Empress then had Yīn Xīng lead the Shìzhōng (Palace Attendants)
to receive the Emperor's dying instructions in the Guǎngshì of Yúntái.
When the Emperor's illness recuperated,
he summoned Yīn Xīng,
intending to appoint him Dàsīmǎ (Grand Marshal) in place of Wú Hàn.
Yīn Xīng kowtowed and wept,
firmly declining, saying:
"Your servant dares not spare himself,
but it would truly diminish Your Sacred Virtue;
I cannot presumptuously accept it."
His sincerity came from his heart,
moving those around him,
and the Emperor eventually consented.
In the 23rd year (47 CE),
he passed away
at the age of thirty-nine.
Yīn Xīng had always been at odds with his cousin Sōng,
yet he respected his gravity and influence.
When Yīn Xīng was gravely ill,
the Emperor personally visited him
and asked him about state affairs and the competence of his officials.
Yīn Xīng bowed his head and said:
"Your servant is too foolish to know.
However, I humbly observe that Councillor Xí Guǎng and Usher Yīn Sōng
both possess profound moral conduct and discernment,
surpassing the dukes and ministers."
After Yīn Xīng's death,
the Emperor remembered his words
and subsequently promoted Xí Guǎng to Guānglù Xūn (Minister of the Imperial Household);
Yīn Sōng became Zhōngláng Jiàng (Commander of the Gentlemen of the Household)
and supervised the Yǔlín (Feathered Forest imperial guards) for over ten years,
gaining favor for his prudence and diligence.
When Emperor Xiǎnzōng ascended the throne,
Yīn Sōng was appointed Chánglè Wèiwèi (Commander of the Chánglè Guards),
and then promoted to Zhí Jīnwú (Bearer of the Golden Spear).
In the 1st year of Yǒngpíng (58 CE), an imperial edict stated:
"The late Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant), Wèiwèi (Commander of the Guards), and Guānnèi Hóu (Marquis within the Pass) Yīn Xīng
commanded the imperial guards
and participated in pacifying the empire.
He should have been conspicuously enfeoffed with titles for his military achievements,
and also, according to the standard for maternal uncles,
he should have received imperial favor.
Yet Yīn Xīng consistently declined,
content to reside in his neighborhood.
He assisted and guided Us,
possessing the uprightness of Zhōu Chāng.
At home, he was benevolent and filial,
having the conduct of Zēngzǐ and Mǐnzǐ.
It is unfortunate that he died young,
and We are deeply saddened by this.
The descendants of a worthy man
should be given special distinction.
Therefore, Yīn Xīng's son Qìng is to be enfeoffed as Marquis of Tóngyáng in Rǔnán,
and Qìng's younger brother Bó as Marquis of Qiáng."
Bó's younger brothers Yuán and Dān were both Láng (Gentlemen).
Qìng yielded all his fields, residences, and wealth to Yuán and Dān.
The Emperor, seeing Qìng's righteous yielding,
promoted him to Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Attendant).
When Qìng died,
his son Qín succeeded him.
In the 5th year of Jiànchū (80 CE),
Yīn Xīng's wife passed away.
Emperor Sùzōng sent the Wǔguān Zhōngláng Jiàng (Commander of the Gentlemen of the Five Bureaus) with a ceremonial staff to Yīn Xīng's tomb to bestow an edict,
posthumously honoring Yīn Xīng as Yì Hóu (Marquis Yì).
When Qín died,
his son Wànquán succeeded him.
When Wànquán died,
his son Guì succeeded him.
Yīn Xīng's younger brother Jiù
succeeded his father's title as Xuān'ēn Hóu (Marquis of Xuān'ēn),
later re-enfeoffed as Xīnyáng Hóu (Marquis of Xīnyáng).
Yīn Jiù was skilled in discussion,
surpassing all court officials,
but his nature was rigid,
so he did not gain popular praise.
When Emperor Xiǎnzōng ascended the throne,
Yīn Jiù was appointed Shǎofǔ (Minister of the Lesser Treasury)
with the rank of Tèjìn (Special Advanced Rank).
Yīn Jiù's son Fēng married Princess Líyì.
The Princess was proud and jealous,
and Fēng was also irritable and impatient.
In the 2nd year of Yǒngpíng (59 CE),
he killed the Princess,
and was executed.
His parents were implicated,
and both committed suicide,
and their marquisate was abolished.
The Emperor, out of consideration for his maternal uncle's family,
did not carry out the full extent of the punishment.
There were four marquises from the Yīn clan in total.
Originally,
the Yīn clan generations worshipped Guǎn Zhòng,
referring to him as
"Xiàng Jūn" (Minister-Lord).
During Emperor Xuāndì's time,
a man named Yīn Zǐfāng,
who was extremely filial and benevolent,
was cooking breakfast on the Làyì (Winter Solstice festival) when the Stove God appeared.
Yīn Zǐfāng bowed twice and received blessings.
He had a yellow goat in his household,
which he then used to offer sacrifice.
From that time onward,
he rapidly became immensely wealthy,
owning over seven hundred qǐng of land,
with carriages, horses, and servants
comparable to a regional lord.
Yīn Zǐfāng often said,
"My descendants will certainly become powerful and great."
Indeed, by the third generation, they greatly prospered.
Therefore, later generations always offered sacrifices to the stove on Làyì,
and presented yellow goats.
Eulogy: Powerful clans are prone to collapse,
and empresses' families often face ruin.
The Fán clan generations were steadfast,
and the Yīn clan also guarded against extravagance.
Humble and cautious descendants,
passed down the turtle seals and inherited the purple robes.
Biographies of Zhū Fú, Féng Yì, Yú Yán, Zhèng Xīng, Zhōu Dà Second, Twenty-Third
Zhū Fú, whose courtesy name was Shūyuán,
was a man from Xiāo, Pèiguó.
Initially, he followed Emperor Guāngwǔ as Dàsīmǎ Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk to the Grand Marshal),
then promoted to Piān Jiāngjūn (Minor General),
and followed in the defeat of Hándān.
Emperor Guāngwǔ dispatched Wú Hàn to execute Miáo Zēng, the Gēngshǐ Emperor's Governor of Yōuzhōu,
and then appointed Zhū Fú Dà Jiāngjūn (General-in-Chief) and Yōuzhōu Mù (Governor of Yōuzhōu),
guarding Jìchéng,
and subsequently pacified the northern frontier.
In the 2nd year of Jiànwǔ (26 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Wǔyáng Hóu (Marquis of Wǔyáng),
receiving revenues from three counties.
Gèng Fú, while young, possessed talent and
greatly wished to foster a reputation for integrity,
and win the hearts of scholars.
He summoned and appointed famous elders from the prefecture, such as Wáng Cén of Zhuōjùn,
to serve as his subordinates.
He also brought in former officials of two-thousand-dàn rank from Wáng Mǎng's time,
and placed them all in his administration.
He then heavily drew upon the granaries of various commanderies,
to provide for their wives and children.
Péng Chǒng, the Administrator of Yúyáng, believing that the empire was not yet settled
and that armies were still rising,
thought it inappropriate to appoint too many officials
as it would deplete military resources.
He did not obey Gèng Fú's orders.
Gèng Fú, by nature arrogant and quick-tempered, and full of self-importance,
was quite displeased.
He then used harsh language to denounce Péng Chǒng.
Péng Chǒng was also stubborn and headstrong,
and, proud of his achievements,
their mutual resentment grew.
Gèng Fú secretly reported that Péng Chǒng had sent an officer to fetch his wife but not his mother,
that he had accepted bribes,
killed a friend,
accumulated a large number of soldiers and grain,
and that his intentions were unfathomable.
Péng Chǒng, having already harbored deep resentment,
heard [this],
became enraged,
and raised an army to attack Gèng Fú.
Gèng Fú sent a letter to reprove him,
saying:
"It is like the state of Zhèng.
To act expediently to relieve urgent situations,
both are for the sake of the country.
If you suspect that Gèng Fú slandered you,
why not go to the imperial court and state your case yourself,
instead of planning for the extermination of your clan?
The imperial court's benevolence towards
Bótōng [Péng Chǒng]
has been profound.
It entrusted you with a large commandery,
and invested you with authority and military power.
Your position is that of a pillar of the state,
and the sentiment towards you is as close as to one's own children and grandchildren.
Even an ordinary man's concubine's
mother could sacrifice her life for a single meal.
How can someone who wears three seals of office,
and holds sway over a great state,
disregard kindness and righteousness,
and harbor rebellious intentions?
Bótōng,
when you speak with officials and common people,
what face will you have?
When you walk, bow, and rise,
what demeanor will you show?
When you sit or lie down and ponder,
what will be in your heart?
When you look into a mirror at your reflection,
how will you compose your eyebrows
and eyes?
When you undertake actions and achieve merits,
how will you be a human being?
Alas, that you abandon the good name of a fine reputation,
and concoct the rebellious schemes of owls and vultures!
You discard the blessings and good fortune that would pass down through generations,
and invite
the great disaster of ruin and defeat!
You speak highly of the Way of Yáo and Shùn,
but cannot control the nature of Jié and Zhòu.
To live as a laughingstock of the world,
and die as a foolish ghost—
is this not sorrowful?
You waged war,
thinking your achievements were unsurpassed in the world.
Once, in Liáodōng, there was a pig
that gave birth to a white-headed piglet.
Finding it unusual, someone intended to present it to the court.
On the way to Hédōng,
he saw that all the pigs were white.
He returned, filled with shame.
If your achievements were to be discussed at court,
you would be like that Liáodōng pig.
Now you are foolish and presumptuous,
comparing yourself to the Six States.
In the time of the Six States,
their power
was each mighty,
expanding their territories by thousands of lì,
and possessing nearly a million victorious soldiers.
Therefore, they could hold their ground and resist each other
for many years and generations.
How many lì is the empire today?
How many cities in the various commanderies?
How can
your mere Yúyáng
incur the wrath of the Son of Heaven?
This is like a person by the riverbank carrying a handful of earth to block Mèngjīn—
it merely shows how little he understands his own limitations!
In times of prosperity,
you listen to the misguided counsel of a haughty wife within,
and trust the flattering words of treacherous scoundrels without.
This will long be a wicked example for all later rulers,
and an eternal warning for meritorious officials—
surely you will
go astray!
He who pacifies the realm has no private enemies.
Do not let past events lead you astray.
I implore you to consider your elderly mother and young brother.
In all your undertakings, do not do anything that causes pain to those who are close to you,
and brings joy to those who are your enemies."
At this time, the two commanderies were rebellious,
and the northern regions were filled with anxiety and fear.
Gèng Fú believed that the Son of Heaven would personally lead an army to suppress them,
but instead, only Yóují Jiāngjūn Dèng Lóng was sent to secretly assist Gèng Fú.
Gèng Fú became fearful,
believing that the Emperor was neglecting the enemy
and would not be able to save him.
He then submitted a memorial, saying:
"In the past, Chǔ and Sòng were states
and both were feudal lords.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ, because Sòng seized his envoy,
then launched an army in a fit of rage.
The Duke's son of Wèi, mindful of the commitment to a friend,
braved the sharp edge of powerful Qín.
Chǔ and Wèi did not have the great righteousness of upholding or correcting official duties.
King Zhuāng merely acted out of anger to assert his strength,
and the Duke's son established his credibility with a single word.
Now Péng Chǒng has rebelled,
and Zhāng Fēng has turned traitor.
I thought Your Majesty would surely abandon other matters
and destroy them promptly.
But after months have passed,
there has been no news.
To surround a city and not rescue it,
to allow rebellious captives to go unpunished and not suppress them—
I am truly bewildered.
In the past, Gāozǔ, with his sage martial prowess,
even after the empire was settled,
still personally led expeditions,
never resting in peace.
Although Your Majesty has begun a great enterprise,
and the realm is not yet unified,
you alone indulge in leisure
and disregard the northern frontier.
The common people are distraught,
with no one to rely on.
How can Sānhé and Jìzhōu
be sufficient to pass down to future generations?
Now the autumn harvest is ripe,
but it is again plundered by Yúyáng.
Zhāng Fēng is crazy and perverse,
his treacherous faction grows daily,
resisting for years,
tiring out officials and soldiers.
Lice breed in their armor,
and bows and crossbows cannot be stored.
All above and below are anxious,
looking to each other for rescue and protection,
aspiring to Your Majesty's grace of life. "
The imperial edict replied:
"Last year, the Chìméi rebels rampaged in Cháng'ān.
I calculated that without grain, they would surely head east,
and indeed, they came and surrendered.
Now, I estimate that these rebellious captives
cannot long maintain their power,
and surely there will be those among them who will kill each other internally.
Our military provisions are not yet sufficient,
so we must wait for the next wheat harvest."
Inside Gèng Fú's city, grain ran out,
and people resorted to cannibalism.
Coincidentally, Gěng Kuàng, the Administrator of Shànggǔ, sent cavalry to rescue Gèng Fú,
and Gèng Fú was then able to escape.
Southward, upon reaching Liángxiāng,
his own military commander rebelled and blocked him.
Gèng Fú feared he would not escape,
so he dismounted and stabbed his wife to death,
barely escaping with his life.
The city surrendered to Péng Chǒng.
Shàngshū Lìng Hóu Bà reported that Gèng Fú had thrown Yōuzhōu into chaos,
created the conditions for Péng Chǒng's crime,
needlessly exhausted the army,
and failed to die for his loyalty,
therefore his crime deserved execution.
The Emperor could not bear to do it,
and instead appointed Gèng Fú to replace Jiǎ Fù as Zhíjīnwú,
and transferred his enfeoffment to Fùchéng Hóu.
Later, Zhāng Fēng and Péng Chǒng both suffered defeat on their own.
The emperor considered that many Two-Thousand-Pīk officials and chief magistrates were not competent
for their positions. If there was
a minor transgression,
they were invariably dismissed, causing frequent changes and much disruption,
leaving the common people unsettled.
In the sixth year, there was an unusual solar eclipse,
and Fú Yī because of this submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the sun is the revered master of all yang,
and represents the position of the ruler above.
All who hold office and govern the people,
who administer commanderies and preside over counties,
are considered yang and superior,
noble and senior.
If the yang and superior are not clear,
and the noble and senior are insufficient,
then the Three Luminaries are agitated,
and a sign is shown to the ruler.
The 'Five Canons' record the policies of the state,
and the 'Great Plan' details the texts on omens and anomalies.
All of these illuminate the Way of Heaven,
thereby foretelling future events.
Your Majesty, out of compassion, has ensured that the people within the seas, having recently escaped calamity and poison,
are protected and nurtured,
allowing them to recover and breathe.
Yet now, many officials who govern the people
are not performing up to standard.
If they slightly deviate from what is reasonable and practical,
they are immediately dismissed.
Is this not a clear distinction of black and white?
However, even in the flourishing age of Yáo and Shùn,
officials were still evaluated three times.
When the Great Hàn arose,
meritorious service was also accumulated;
officials served for long periods,
supported in their old age in office,
even their children and grandchildren were named,
and thus became family clans.
At that time, how could all official duties
have been perfectly managed?
And would not those who debated
have been clamorous?
It was thought that the work of Heaven and Earth cannot be accomplished in haste,
and difficult undertakings require accumulation over time.
But recently, governors and administrators have been frequently replaced,
with new ones taking over from the old,
tiring themselves out on the roads.
Upon examination, their time in office is short,
not enough to clearly demonstrate their abilities.
Yet severe strictures are imposed,
and people feel insecure,
each looking out for themselves,
with no peace of mind.
Officials in charge sometimes exploit minor grudges to pursue private enmities,
eagerly seeking faults
to ingratiate themselves with the emperor.
The Two-Thousand-Pīk officials and chief magistrates, pressured by impeachments and denunciations,
and fearing criticism and ridicule,
thus compete to fabricate and deceive,
in order to gain empty reputations.
These are all responses to the agitation of the myriad yang
and the deviation of the sun and moon from their proper course.
Indeed, things that grow too quickly inevitably wither prematurely,
and achievements completed too suddenly are quickly ruined.
To destroy long-standing enterprises
and create hastily completed achievements
is not a blessing for Your Majesty.
The empire is not for use for a single moment,
and peace within the seas is not the work of a single day.
May Your Majesty set your mind on what lies beyond the years,
and look for transformation after a generation.
The world would be truly fortunate."
The emperor sent his proposal down for discussion,
and many ministers agreed with Fú Yī.
From then on, the replacement of governors and administrators was considerably simplified.
According to the old system,
when a provincial governor reported that a Two-Thousand-Pīk official or chief magistrate was unfit for office,
the matter was first submitted to the Three Dukes.
The Three Dukes would then send their subordinates to investigate and verify,
and only then would dismissal follow.
The emperor at that time valued clear discernment,
and no longer entrusted these matters to the Three Ducal Ministries,
but instead gave authority to the impeaching and investigating officials.
Fú Yī again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty is pure and brilliant, adhering to simplicity,
and following the rites without deviation.
From the imperial clan's various kings to the maternal relatives of the empress,
all abide by the rules and regulations,
without the reputation of forming factions.
Some even ride ox-carts,
on par with commoners.
This indeed shows that laws and regulations are orderly,
and none below can wield arbitrary power.
Examining the actual situation,
it ought to be peaceful and harmonious,
yet unusual calamities are still seen.
Could this be without reason?
The Way of Heaven is trustworthy and sincere;
it must not be ignored.
I humbly observe that Your Majesty, displeased that previously the imperial authority was not enforced
and subordinates usurped state power,
has since ascending the throne
not used the old system,
trusting the impeaching officials
and diminishing the role of the chief ministers.
As for any impeachment or report,
dismissal or retirement is immediately imposed;
re-investigation does not involve the Three Ducal Ministries,
and accusations and condemnations are not subjected to thorough scrutiny.
Your Majesty considers the envoys as your confidants,
and the envoys consider their subordinates as their eyes and ears.
This means that the impartiality of the Shangshū
is decided by minor officials.
Therefore, the subordinates are harsh and demanding,
each acting as if they are capable.
Moreover, private sentiments allow some to excel,
while likes and dislikes influence appointments.
All compete to spread empty rumors
to seize temporary advantages.
Thus, those who are guilty are not genuinely convinced,
while those who are innocent are falsely accused by empty documents.
This cannot be maintained through periods of prosperity and decline,
nor bequeathed to future kings.
Indeed, when matters accumulate over time, officials naturally become important.
When officials are at ease, the people naturally become tranquil.
The 'Traditions' say: 'If there are two intercalary months in five years,
the Way of Heaven is then complete.'
If even the spiritual power of Heaven and Earth
takes five years to complete its transformation,
how much more so for the way of humans!
Your servant Fú Yī, though foolish and dull-witted,
cannot bear to restrain my earnestness.
I wish Your Majesty would give careful thought to appointments that govern vast territories,
and carefully examine memorials based on biased reports."
In the seventh year,
he was transferred to become Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud.
Fú Yī also thought that since the national academy was flourishing,
the selection of Erudites should be broadened,
so he submitted a letter, saying:
"The Grand Academy
is the palace of rites and righteousness,
the origin from which education and transformation arise.
Your Majesty respects the ancient sages
and has set your mind on ancient classics.
Even though palaces are not yet adorned,
and military campaigns have not yet ceased,
you first established the Grand Academy,
and advanced the building of lateral dormitories.
Recently, the imperial carriage personally visited to observe and feast,
intending to propagate the transformation of universal harmony
and to demonstrate the encouragement of progress.
Upon examination, the office of Erudite
is the grand teacher of the empire,
ensuring that the words of Confucius are transmitted without interruption.
In former affairs,
when testing Erudites,
extensive efforts were always made to seek out and carefully select candidates,
ranging from the imperial domain
to the four directions.
Thus, those widely versed in the classics were chosen,
only the worthy were promoted,
scholars were diligent and encouraged,
and near and far alike admired them.
I humbly heard the imperial edict to test five more people,
but only those currently in Luòyáng City are to be chosen.
Your servant fears that from now on,
there will be something missed.
Seeking candidates only in close proximity
may not be exhaustive,
and scholars from the four directions
will have nothing to encourage or delight them.
The fundamental purpose of examinations
is to find genuine talent.
There is no fixed deadline
that prevents reaching distant places.
Moreover, all those summoned for testing
are dispatched by themselves;
there is no additional expense or trouble for the state.
The saying goes: 'If the Central States lose their rites,
seek them in the wilderness.'
Your servant Fú Yī has fortunately been allowed to discuss diagrams and prophecies,
and thus dares to overstep his duties."
The emperor approved of this.
In the twentieth year,
he succeeded Dòu Róng as Grand Minister of Works.
In the twenty-second year,
he was dismissed for abusing imperial favors.
In the twenty-fifth year,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīnxī.
The Emperor considered Fúlíng's (浮陵) behavior to have ridden roughshod over his peers,
and constantly harbored resentment,
but regretting his capabilities,
could not bear to punish him.
During the Yǒngpíng (永平) era,
someone anonymously accused Fú (浮) of misconduct.
Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) was furious,
and granted Fú (浮) death.
Fán Chóu (樊鯈), the Commandant of Chángshuǐ (長水), said to the Emperor:
"Táng Yáo (唐堯) was a great sage.
The common people found their place,
yet he still allowed the four villains to leisurely remain in prison,
thus appeasing the hearts of all within the seas.
He made everyone in the world aware,
and only then did he punish them.
Although Fú's (浮) misdeeds are clear,
they have not yet reached the ears of all people.
It is proper to refer the case to the Grand Minister of Justice,
and clearly reveal the facts."
The Emperor also regretted his decision.
Commentary says: Wú Qǐ (吳起) discussed his achievements with Tián Wén (田文),
and Tián Wén (田文) fell short in three aspects.
Zhū Mǎichén (朱買臣) challenged Gōngsūn Hóng (公孫弘) with ten strategies,
and Hóng (弘) could not answer a single one.
In the end, Tián Wén (田文) became the prime minister of Wèi (魏),
and Gōngsūn (公孫) presided over Hàn (漢).
Truly, they knew that the position of prime minister had its own specific nature.
Therefore, Zēngzǐ (曾子) said:
"There are three things the junzǐ (君子) values in the Way;
as for the matters of sacrificial vessels, the appropriate officials are responsible."
Yet Guāngwǔ (光武) and Míngdì (明帝) personally delighted in official affairs,
and even used this to evaluate and scrutinize the Three Ducal Ministers.
Consequently, these individuals sometimes erred, and the customary courtesies diminished,
leading to burdens of execution, dismissal, interrogation, and humiliation.
To hold officials responsible for their faults
to such an extent,
recalling Jiǎ Shēng's (賈生) discourse,
is it not excessive!
Zhū Fú (朱浮)'s ridicule of the abuses of harsh scrutiny and haste
was correct,
but how could they be considered the words of an elder!
Féng Fáng (馮魴), courtesy name Xiàosūn (孝孫),
was a native of Húyáng (湖陽) in Nányáng (南陽).
His ancestors were a branch family of Wèi (魏),
who were granted the fief of Féngchéng (馮城),
and thus took Féng (馮) as their clan name.
When Qín (秦) destroyed Wèi (魏),
they relocated to Húyáng (湖陽),
becoming a prominent clan in the commandery.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) reign,
chaos and rebellion erupted everywhere.
Fáng (魴) then gathered guests,
recruited heroes,
built a camp,
to await a lord to serve.
At this time, Yú Dūwèi (虞都尉), a prominent family in Húyáng (湖陽), rebelled and raised an army.
He previously had a grudge against Shēntú Jì (申屠季) from the same county,
and had killed Jì's (季) brother,
planning to exterminate Jì's (季) clan.
Jì (季) fled to Fáng (魴).
Fáng (魴) was taking Jì (季) back to his camp
when they encountered Dūwèi's (都尉) younger cousin Chángqīng (長卿),
who intended to seize Jì (季).
Fáng (魴) shouted at Chángqīng (長卿):
"Although Jì (季) and I have no prior acquaintance,
when a worthy man is in distress and seeks refuge,
I must bear the responsibility for him with my life.
What are you saying?"
So, they returned together.
Jì (季) bowed and said:
"I have been saved by your grace,
and even death cannot repay it.
I have oxen, horses, and valuables;
I wish to present them all to you."
Fáng (魴) put on a stern expression and said:
"My elderly parents and young siblings are all in the bandit-held city.
Today, as we are together,
I have no other concerns.
Why speak of valuables?"
Jì (季) was ashamed and dared not speak again.
From then on, Fáng (魴) was respected and trusted by the county and townships,
and thus was able to hold his camp and secure himself.
At that time, the world was not yet settled,
and many men from all directions held military power and made false claims.
Only Fáng (魴) maintained his integrity
and possessed strategic skill.
Guāngwǔ (光武) heard of him and praised him.
In the third year of Jiànwǔ (建武) (27 CE),
he was summoned to the Emperor's temporary residence,
met at Yúntái (雲臺),
and appointed Magistrate of Yú (虞).
As a ruler, he dared to execute,
and was known for his authority and trustworthiness.
He was promoted to Magistrate of Jiá (郟).
Later, when the imperial carriage went west to campaign against Kuí Xiāo (隗囂),
bandits rose up in Yǐngchuān (潁川).
Yán Bāo (延襃) and others, a group of over three thousand bandits from Jiá (郟),
attacked and surrounded the county office.
Fáng (魴) led his seventy or so officials and soldiers
in fierce fighting for several days.
Their crossbow arrows ran out,
the city fell,
and Fáng (魴) then fled.
The Emperor heard that commanderies and kingdoms had rebelled,
and immediately rushed to Yǐngchuān (潁chuān).
Fáng (魴) went to the Emperor's temporary residence.
The Emperor inspected the battle site,
recognized Fáng's (魴) fierce fighting,
and praised him, saying:
"This is a brave magistrate!
Wherever there are bandits to suppress,
do not be constrained by provinces or commanderies."
Bāo (襃) and others, hearing of the Emperor's arrival,
all shaved their heads,
carried axes and blocks,
and led their followers to request punishment.
The Emperor pardoned them temporarily,
and sent Fáng (魴) to persuade various settlements to surrender.
The county was pacified,
whereupon an edict ordered Bāo (襃) and his group to be returned to Fáng (魴) for execution.
Fáng (魴) rebuked them and was about to apply military law.
They all kowtowed and said:
"Today we receive our punishment,
and will die with no regrets."
Fáng (魴) said:
"Since you know to repent your faults and submit to your crimes,
I will now pardon you all.
You are permitted to return to farming and sericulture,
and serve as the magistrate's eyes and ears."
They all cried out "Long live!"
At this time, whenever there were bandits,
they were invariably reported by Bāo (襃) and his group.
None dared to stir up trouble,
and the county borders were peaceful.
In the thirteenth year (37 CE),
he was promoted to Grand Administrator of Wèijùn (魏郡).
In the twenty-seventh year (51 CE),
he was appointed Grand Coachman by exceptional merit, replacing Zhào Xǐ (趙憙).
In the first year of Zhōngyuán (中元) (56 CE),
he accompanied the Emperor on the eastern imperial sacrifice to Dàizōng (岱宗),
acting as Superintendent of the Imperial Guards.
Upon his return,
he replaced Zhāng Chún (張純) as Minister of Works,
and was granted the title of Marquis within the Pass.
In the second year (57 CE),
the Emperor passed away.
Fáng (魴) was sent to oversee the construction of Yuánlíng (原陵) with an imperial staff,
and was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Yángyì Township,
with an income of three hundred fifty households.
In the fourth year of Yǒngpíng (永平) (61 CE),
he was implicated in the severe examination of Dèng Róng (鄧融), Grand Administrator of Lǒngxī (隴西),
and for permitting corrupt officials to act.
He was dismissed from office and stripped of his title and territory.
In the sixth year (63 CE),
Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) visited Lǔ (魯),
and Fáng (魴) again acted as Superintendent of the Imperial Guards.
In the seventh year (64 CE),
he replaced Yīn Sōng (陰嵩) as Commandant of the Capital.
Fáng (魴) was naturally solemn, strict, and just.
While in office, he repeatedly offered loyal advice,
much of which was accepted and implemented.
In the fourteenth year (71 CE),
an edict restored his title and territory.
The following year (72 CE),
the Emperor made an eastern tour of the commanderies and kingdoms,
and Fáng (魴) was left to guard the Southern Palace.
In the third year of Jiànchū (建初) (78 CE),
he requested retirement due to old age and illness.
Sùzōng (肅宗) granted it.
That winter, he became a Wu Gēng (五更),
and an edict summoned Fáng (魴) to attend the New Year's court and take his place among the marquises.
In the second year of Yuánhé (元和) (85 CE),
he died,
at the age of eighty-six.
His son Zhù (柱) succeeded him.
Zhù (柱) married Xiǎnzōng's (顯宗) daughter, Princess Guà Jiā (獲嘉長公主).
In his youth, he served as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
and was known for his reverence, solemnity, humility, and frugality.
He rose to the position of Grand Architect.
After Zhù (柱) died,
his son Dìng (定) succeeded him,
and his highest office was Commandant of the Feathered Forest.
When Dìng (定) died,
he had no sons,
and his marquisate was abolished.
Dìngdì Shí,
inherited his mother, Princess’s, enfeoffment as Marquis of Huòjiā,
and also served as Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng).
He was gradually promoted to Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi).
He was able to please those of his time,
and was favored by Emperor Ān.
The Emperor once visited his residence,
stayed and drank for about ten days,
and bestowed upon him one sword with a dappled rhinoceros scabbard, one ceremonial knife,
one purple and artemisia-patterned ribbon,
and one jade split-ring (jué).
His son, Shì, was appointed Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Shìláng),
and Shì’s two younger brothers were both Gentlemen (Lángzhōng).
Since the military chaos of the Yǒngchū era,
the rents and salaries of kings and marquises were often insufficient.
Therefore, a special imperial edict was issued to supplement Shí with rent and taxes from other counties,
so that it would be as per the old limits,
yielding 30,000 hu of grain annually,
and 40,000 cash.
He was promoted to Minister of the Household (Guānglùxūn),
and then replaced Yáng Zhèn as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
When the Marquis of Běixiāng was established,
Shí was promoted to Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
and together with the Grand Commandant from Dōnglái, Liú Xǐ, he participated in recording the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū).
After Emperor Shùn was established,
both Shí and Xǐ were dismissed due to their partisan associations with Yán Xiǎn, Jiāng Jīng, and others,
and returned to the position of Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi).
When he died,
his son Dài succeeded him.
When Dài died,
his younger brother Chéng succeeded him
and served as Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi).
Shí’s younger brother, Guāng,
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yángyì by imperial edict during the reign of Emperor Hé.
Also because of Shí’s favor,
he rose to the official position of Colonel of the City Gates (Chéngmén Xiàowèi).
When he died,
his son Sù succeeded him
and served as Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Shìláng).
Yú Yán, courtesy name Zǐdà,
was from Dōnghūn, Chénliú.
When Yán was first born,
there was an object above him, like a bolt of white silk,
which then ascended to heaven.
The diviners considered this auspicious.
When he grew up,
he was eight *chǐ* and six *cùn* tall,
with a waist ten *wéi* in circumference,
and possessed the strength to lift a tripod.
In his youth, he served as Head of Hùyǒu Pavilion (Hùyǒu Tíngzhǎng).
At that time, Wáng Mǎng’s noble lady, Lady Wèi,
allowed her guests to run wild.
Yán led his clerks and soldiers to break into her house to arrest them.
Because of this, he incurred resentment,
and thus his position did not rise.
His nature was honest and simple,
not constrained by minor details,
nor did he have a reputation in his local village.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng’s reign,
the world fell into great chaos.
Yán often wore armor,
protected his relatives,
and defended against bandits.
Many relied on him for their safety.
Yán’s niece was an infant,
and her mother was unable to keep her alive,
abandoning her in a ditch.
Yán heard her cries,
and out of compassion, took her in
and raised her to adulthood.
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
he served in the office of the Commandant of the Capital (Zhí Jīn Wú Fǔ)
and was appointed Magistrate of Xìyáng (Xìyáng Lìng).
Every year during the seasonal festivals of Fúlào,
he would temporarily release prisoners and those held in custody,
allowing each to return home.
They were all moved by his kindness and virtue,
and returned as scheduled.
There was a prisoner who fell ill at home;
he had himself transported to prison.
Upon arrival, he died.
Yán led his subordinate clerks and historians,
and performed a funeral outside the gate.
The common people were moved and pleased by this.
Later, he resigned from office and returned to his hometown.
The Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) Fù Zōng heard of Yán’s reputation
and invited him to be appointed Registrar (Gōngcáo).
Zōng was extravagant by nature;
his carriages, clothes, and implements
were often immoderate.
Yán admonished him, saying:
"In the past, Yàn Yīng assisted Qí,
yet his deer-skin robe was not whole; Jì Wénzǐ served as Prime Minister of Lǔ,
yet his concubines did not wear silk.
Few have erred through frugality."
Zōng was displeased,
and Yán immediately resigned and retired.
After a while,
Zōng was indeed punished for his extravagance,
and as he was about to face execution,
he wiped away tears and sighed, saying:
"I regret not having followed the advice of Registrar Yú Yán!"
Emperor Guāngwǔ heard of this and was impressed by him.
In the 20th year, during his eastern tour,
he passed through Xiǎohuáng,
where the mausoleum of Emperor Gāo’s mother, Empress Zhāolíng, was located.
At that time, Yán was a Commander of the Postal Service (Bù Dūyóu).
An edict summoned him for an audience,
and the Emperor inquired about the mausoleum’s affairs.
Yán’s demeanor and conduct were composed,
and his bowing and salutations were remarkable.
He knew the exact number of trees and stumps in the mausoleum,
and was quite familiar with the rituals for sacrificial vessels and victims.
The Emperor praised him
and ordered Yán to follow his retinue to Lǔ.
On their return, passing through the gate of Fēngqiū city,
the gate was small
and could not accommodate the emperor’s feather-canopied carriage.
The Emperor was angry
and ordered the Attending Imperial Scribe (Shìyùshǐ) to be flogged.
Yán thereupon dismounted and took the blame,
attributing the fault to the Commander of the Postal Service.
His words were stirring and emotional,
moving the Emperor’s heart,
who then issued a proclamation saying:
"For the sake of Yú Yán, the Commander of the Postal Service of Chénliú,
the Imperial Scribe’s punishment is remitted."
Yán accompanied the imperial carriage westward to the border of the commandery,
and was granted money, a sword, a belt, and a ceremonial knife before returning to his commandery.
From then on, his reputation greatly flourished.
In the 23rd year,
the Minister of Works (Sītú) Yù Kuàng invited him to serve.
At the New Year’s court audience,
the Emperor saw and recognized Yán,
and sent a Grandee of the Yellow Gate (Xiǎohuángmén) to inquire about him.
On that very day, he was summoned and appointed Commandant of the Public Carriages (Gōngchē Lìng).
The following year,
he was promoted to Magistrate of Luòyáng (Luòyáng Lìng).
At this time, the Yīn clan had a guest named Mǎ Chéng,
who often committed crimes of theft.
Yán arrested and interrogated him.
The Yīn clan repeatedly interceded;
each time a letter was received, two hundred strokes of the bamboo rod were added to Mǎ Chéng’s punishment.
Then, Marquis of Xìnyáng Yīn Jiù
complained to the Emperor,
slandering Yán for many unjust accusations.
The Emperor then personally visited the roadside inn
and personally reviewed the prisoners.
Yán arranged the cases that could be argued in the east,
and those without merit in the west.
Mǎ Chéng then turned and tried to move to the east.
Yán stepped forward and seized him,
saying:
"You are a great pest to the people,
long relying on the city and its altars,
unafraid of being smoked out or burned down.
Now your interrogation is not yet complete;
you should face the full extent of the law!"
Mǎ Chéng cried out loudly, claiming injustice.
A palace guard (Bìjǐ Láng) pierced Yán with his *jǐ* (halberd),
shouting at him to let Mǎ Chéng go.
The Emperor knew that Yán was impartial
and said to Mǎ Chéng:
"You have violated the law of the state;
you brought this upon yourself!"
He commanded him to be quickly taken away.
A few days later, Mǎ Chéng was executed.
Thereafter, the imperial relatives restrained themselves,
none daring to violate the law.
After three years in the county,
Yán was promoted to Grand Administrator of Nányáng (Nányáng Tàishǒu).
In the early Yǒngpíng era,
there was a Registrar of Xīnyě (Xīnyě Gōngcáo) named Dèng Yǎn.
As an imperial relative and minor marquis, he often participated in court audiences,
and his appearance and demeanor
surpassed others.
Emperor Xiǎozōng observed him,
and turning to his attendants, said:
"My own appearance,
how could it compare to this man!"
He specially bestowed upon him a carriage, horses, and clothes.
Yán believed that although Dèng Yǎn possessed a fine appearance, he lacked substance,
and never accorded him special courtesy.
Since the Emperor had favored him,
he issued an edict commanding Dèng Yǎn to present himself at the palace as the Registrar of Nányáng.
Upon arrival,
he was appointed Gentleman (Lángzhōng)
and promoted to Commandant of Xuánwǔ (Xuánwǔ Sīmǎ).
Dèng Yǎn did not observe his father’s mourning period while in office.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he sighed, saying:
"'To know men is to be wise;
even the sage emperors find this difficult.'
How true are these words!"
Dèng Yǎn, ashamed, withdrew,
and from then on, Yán was considered discerning.
After three years,
Zhēng was appointed Grand Commandant, replacing Zhào Xǐ.
Eight years later,
he replaced Fàn Qiān as Minister of Education.
He held positions in the two highest government offices successively
for over ten years without distinguished achievements.
When King Yīng of Chǔ plotted rebellion,
Yīn Shì wished to slander him.
She sent someone privately to inform Yán of Chǔ's plot.
Yán, considering Yīng to be a close relative of the imperial family,
did not believe his words.
He also wanted to dismiss Gōngsūn Hóng, an aide of Yōuzhōu,
on the grounds that Hóng was in contact with the King of Chǔ, but then stopped.
He did not report any of this.
When Yīng's affair was discovered,
an imperial edict severely rebuked him,
and Yán subsequently committed suicide.
His family was extremely poor,
and his descendants could not escape cold and hunger.
Yán's great-great-grandson was Fàng,
courtesy name Zǐzhòng.
In his youth, he was a disciple of Grand Commandant Yáng Zhèn.
When Zhèn was slandered and committed suicide,
at the beginning of Emperor Shùn's reign,
Fàng went to the imperial court to appeal and clear Zhèn's name,
thus becoming renowned.
During Emperor Huán's reign, he served as a Secretary.
For his meritorious proposal to execute Grand General Liáng Jì, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng.
Later, he became Minister of Works,
but was dismissed due to floods.
He detested eunuchs by nature,
and was thus framed by them.
At the beginning of Emperor Líng's reign,
he was executed along with Lǐ Yīng, the Commander of the Chánglè Palace, and others, due to the partisan faction incident.
Zhèng Hóng, courtesy name Jùjūn,
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His paternal great-uncle, Jí,
served as Protector-General of the Western Regions during Emperor Xuān's reign.
Hóng was a village elder in his youth.
When Administrator Dìwǔ Lún toured the region in spring,
he saw Hóng and was deeply impressed by his exceptional qualities.
He summoned Hóng to serve as an Inspector,
and recommended him as Filial and Incorrupt.
Hóng's teacher was Jiāo Kuàng, the Administrator of Hédōng from the same commandery.
When King Yīng of Chǔ's plot of rebellion was discovered,
Kuàng was implicated through a minor connection.
Kuàng was arrested
and died of illness on the road.
His wife and children were imprisoned in the imperial jail
and tortured for consecutive years.
Scholars and old friends, fearing implication,
all changed their names
to escape the disaster.
Hóng alone shaved his head and carried an axe and a chopping block,
went to the imperial court to submit a memorial,
pleading for Kuàng's innocence.
Emperor Xiǎnzōng understood,
and immediately pardoned his family.
Hóng personally escorted Kuàng's coffin and his wife and children back to their hometown,
thus gaining renown.
He was appointed Magistrate of Zōu,
and his governance was benevolent and compassionate,
earning the people's praise for their recovery and relief.
He was promoted to Administrator of Huáiyáng.
After four further promotions,
at the beginning of Jiànchū,
he became Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
According to old regulations,
Secretaries of the Imperial Secretariat, upon completion of their term, were appointed as county magistrates, clerks, assistant magistrates, or sub-magistrates.
Hóng submitted a memorial arguing that although the office of the Secretariat was esteemed,
the rewards were meager.
When it came to opening appointments,
many were unwilling to take them.
He requested that Secretaries be appointed as magistrates of 1,000 *shi* of grain,
and clerks as magistrates.
The Emperor followed his advice.
All of Hóng's previous proposals that benefited imperial governance
were recorded in the Southern Palace
as precedents.
He was sent out to serve as Chancellor of Píngyuán,
then recalled and appointed Palace Attendant.
In the eighth year of Jiànchū,
he replaced Zhèng Zhòng as Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Previously, the tribute and transport from the seven commanderies of Jiāozhǐ
all came from Dōngyě,
traveling by sea.
The winds and waves presented difficulties and dangers,
causing frequent shipwrecks.
Hóng proposed opening the mountain passes of Línglíng and Guìyáng.
These were then cleared and made accessible,
and have since become regular routes.
In his two years in office,
he saved three hundred million in expenditure.
At that time, the empire suffered from drought,
there were alarms on the borders,
and people had insufficient food,
yet the national treasury was overflowing.
Hóng again proposed that tributes should be reduced
and corvée labor expenses cut,
to benefit the hungry people.
The Emperor acceded to his proposal.
In the first year of Yuánhé,
he replaced Dèng Biāo as Grand Commandant.
At that time, Dìwǔ Lún, whom Hóng had recommended, was appointed Minister of Works,
ranking below Hóng.
At every court audience on the first day of the month,
Hóng would bow deeply and humble himself.
When the Emperor inquired and understood the reason,
he allowed the placement of mica screens
to separate their positions,
which thereafter became a precedent.
In his four years in office,
he impeached Secretary Zhāng Lín for flattering Palace Attendant Dòu Xiàn
and for his habitually corrupt conduct.
He also reported Yáng Guāng, the Magistrate of Luòyáng,
who was a client of Xiàn,
for his greed and cruelty in office,
stating that neither was fit for their positions.
When the memorial was submitted,
an official who was an old acquaintance of Guāng
informed him.
Guāng reported this to Xiàn,
and Xiàn impeached Hóng for leaking secret affairs of state.
The Emperor interrogated and reproached Hóng,
and ordered him to surrender his seal and sash.
Hóng went personally to the Grand Judge's office,
but an imperial edict ordered his release.
He then requested to retire,
but this was not granted.
When he became critically ill,
he submitted a memorial expressing his gratitude
and also detailing Dòu Xiàn's shortcomings.
The Emperor read the memorial
and sent a physician to examine Hóng's illness,
but by the time he arrived, Hóng had already died.
Before his death, he returned all bestowed gifts,
and ordered his wife and children to wear coarse caps and plain clothes, and to be buried in a plain coffin,
and to return to their hometown.
Zhōu Zhāng, courtesy name Cìshú,
was a native of Suí, Nányáng.
He first served in the commandery as Chief of Merit.
At that time, Grand General Dòu Xiàn was dismissed
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Guànjūn, returning to his domain.
Zhāng accompanied the Administrator on his spring inspection tour to Guànjūn.
The Administrator still wished to pay a visit to Xiàn.
Zhāng remonstrated, saying:
“Today, you are on an official spring inspection.
How can you transgress protocol for a private meeting?
Moreover, Xiàn, a relative of the imperial family by marriage,
whose power once overshadowed the imperial court,
has been relegated to a feudal state.
His future misfortune or fortune is hard to gauge.
As a Prefect who has received the imperial tally, a minister
with heavy responsibilities over a thousand *li*,
how can your every action
be taken lightly?”
The Administrator did not listen and
proceeded to get into his carriage.
Zhāng stepped forward, drew his saber, and cut the traces of the horses,
thus stopping him.
When Xiàn was later executed,
many officials, from dukes and ministers downwards, were implicated and punished for their associations with him.
The Administrator was fortunate to escape punishment,
and thereafter held Zhāng in high regard.
He was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt,
and after six promotions, became Commandant of the Five Offices.
In the first year of Yánpíng,
he became Minister of the Household.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
Dài Wèi Bà was appointed Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
That winter,
Dài Yǐn Qín was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
At this time, the Permanent Attendants Zhèng Zhòng and Cài Lún and others all held power and participated in government.
Zhōu Zhāng frequently offered direct criticism.
Initially,
when Emperor Hé died,
Empress Dowager Dèng, believing that Imperial Prince Shèng suffered from a chronic illness
and was unfit to serve in the ancestral temple,
desired Emperor Shāng, who was still an infant,
and adopted him as her own son.
Therefore, she enthroned him,
and made Shèng the Prince of Píngyuán.
When Emperor Shāng died,
the officials, believing that Shèng's illness was not chronic,
unanimously favored him.
The Empress Dowager, having not enthroned him before,
feared future resentment,
and so she enthroned Yòu, the son of Prince Xiào of Qīnghé, Emperor Hé's elder brother.
This was Emperor Ān.
Zhāng, seeing that the hearts of the people were not attached,
secretly plotted to close the palace gates,
execute General of Cavalry Dèng Zhì and his brothers, as well as Zhèng Zhòng and Cài Lún,
coerce the Imperial Secretaries,
depose the Empress Dowager in the Southern Palace (Nángōng),
demote the Emperor to a king of a distant state,
and enthrone Prince of Píngyuán [Shèng].
The plot was discovered,
Shèng was dismissed from his post by imperial decree,
and Zhāng committed suicide.
His family had no surplus wealth;
his sons changed their clothes and left,
eating only every other day.
The luận (commentary) states: Kǒngzǐ said,
"One may associate with them in establishing,
but not in exercising expediency."
Expediency,
is acting contrary to the norm.
To undertake things contrary to the norm,
one must rely on an extraordinary conjunction of circumstances,
so that one's actions are without error or recklessness,
and one's ambition is achieved and reputation preserved.
Zhōu Zhāng, whose person was not entrusted with the auspicious diagram of a true ruler,
and whose virtue lacked the hopes of the myriad people,
faced a ruler without a flaw to separate him from Heaven,
and a land with an already stable situation.
Yet he conceived a plan difficult to achieve,
and hoped for success in a matter utterly impossible.
Is this not perverse?
If the ruler's capacity were easily open to lower counsel,
then even a mere measuring basket could claim the Heavenly mandate,
and madmen and base officials would also exert themselves.
Mèng Kē said:
"If one has the heart of Yī Yǐn, it is permissible;
if one does not have the heart of Yī Yǐn, then it is usurpation."
Alas,
may people in the future take heed!
The zàn (eulogy) says: Zhū (Mù) stabilized the northern region,
inciting immense favor.
Fáng (Jǐn) submitted his wife,
extending kindness to returning prisoners.
Zhèng (Zhòng) and Dòu (Xiàn) were resentful rivals,
each becoming the other's enemy.
Zhōu Zhāng rebelled against the Way,
with small wisdom but grand schemes.
Biography of Liáng Tǒng, Chapter 24 (Sons Sōng, Sǒng; great-grandson Shāng; great-great-grandson Jì)
Liáng Tǒng, courtesy name Zhòngníng,
was a native of Wūshì, Āndìng.
Liáng Yì'ěr, a grandee of Jìn,
was his ancestor.
Tǒng's great-great-grandfather Zǐdū
moved from Hédōng to Běidì.
Zǐdū's son, Qiáo,
moved to Màolíng with wealth of ten million.
Towards the end of Emperors Āi and Píng's reigns,
he returned to Āndìng.
Tǒng was by nature resolute and fond of law.
He first served in the commanderies and provinces.
In the second year of Gēngshǐ,
he was summoned and appointed Zhonglang Jiang,
tasked with pacifying and stabilizing Liángzhōu,
and appointed Administrator of Jiǔquán.
When Gēngshǐ was defeated,
and the Chìméi entered Cháng'ān,
Tǒng, along with Dòu Róng and other commandery administrators, raised troops to defend their borders,
and planned to jointly establish a commander.
Initially, by order of rank,
all jointly nominated Tǒng.
Tǒng firmly declined, saying:
"In the past, Chén Yīng did not accept the title of king
because he had an aged mother.
Now, I have respected elders at home,
and my virtue is shallow and ability meager.
I am truly insufficient to take on such a role."
So they jointly nominated Róng as Grand General of Héxī,
and Tǒng was instead made Administrator of Wǔwēi.
His governance was strict and fierce,
and his authority extended to neighboring commanderies.
In the fifth year of Jiànwǔ,
Tǒng and others each sent envoys, accompanying Dòu Róng's Chief Clerk Liú Jūn, to the imperial court to offer tribute,
wishing to present themselves at the imperial residence.
An imperial edict conferred upon Tǒng the title General Xuāndé.
In the summer of the eighth year,
Emperor Guāngwǔ personally campaigned against Kuí Xiāo.
Tǒng, Dòu Róng, and others led troops to meet the imperial carriage.
After Xiāo was defeated,
Tǒng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Chéngyì.
His biological elder brother Xún and cousin Téng were both made Marquises within the Pass (Guānnèi Hóu).
Téng was appointed Commandant of Agriculture (Diǎnnóng Dūwèi) of Jiǔquán,
and all were sent back to Héxī.
In the twelfth year,
Tǒng and Róng alike went to the capital.
As ranked marquises, they attended court.
Tǒng was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāoshān,
appointed Grand Master of the Palace (Tàizhōng Dàfū),
and his four sons were appointed as Lang.
While at court, Tǒng
frequently proposed advantageous policies.
Believing that the laws were too lenient,
and that corruption among the lower ranks could not be overcome,
he suggested that punishments should be made more severe
to conform to old statutes.
He then submitted a memorial stating: "Your subject humbly observes that Emperors Yuán and Āi lightened the penalty for capital offenses by one hundred and twenty-three matters;
those who personally killed others were reduced by one degree from the death penalty.
From then on,
this became a regular standard.
Thus, people lightly transgress the law,
and officials easily kill.
This is their intention.
Punishments are based on what is appropriate,
and should not be arbitrarily lightened.
Therefore, the Five Emperors had punishments of exile, extermination, banishment, and execution;
the Three Kings had capital punishment and
flesh-carving laws.
Hence, Kǒngzǐ said,
'The benevolent must be brave,'
and also said,
'To manage wealth, rectify words,
and prohibit people from wrongdoing is called righteousness.'
Emperor Gāo received the mandate
to punish tyranny,
pacify the world,
and establish laws and statutes,
which were truly appropriate.
Emperor Wén was generous and gentle,
and encountered a peaceful and stable era.
He only abolished the mutilating punishments
and the law of collective responsibility;
all other matters followed the existing rules,
without reforming old regulations.
Emperor Wǔ lived during a time when China was flourishing,
with abundant financial resources.
He launched distant campaigns,
and military expeditions frequently
arose.
Háo Jié violated prohibitions,
and corrupt officials manipulated the law.
Therefore, he increased the severity of penalties for harboring criminals
and established laws concerning informed complicity
to break up factions
and deter concealment.
Emperor Xuān
was intelligent and upright,
governing all under Heaven.
His officials upheld the constitution,
without any shortcomings.
He followed earlier statutes,
and the world acclaimed his governance.
However, when Emperors Āi and Píng succeeded to the throne,
and had
only been in power for a short time,
their judgments were still few.
Chancellor Wáng Jiā lightly made arbitrary alterations,
reducing and abolishing the established laws and old covenants of the former emperors.
Within a few years,
more than a hundred such matters occurred,
some inconvenient to governance,
some not satisfying the people's hearts.
I respectfully present those most harmful to the body politic in the attached memorial.
principles.
May Your Divine Sagacity clearly observe,
weigh the gains and losses,
issue an edict to the relevant officials,
carefully select the best,
establish unchangeable statutes,
and implement laws for all time.
The world would be exceedingly fortunate."
Liáng Tǒng
again submitted a memorial, saying: "The officials consider what I have said
to be impracticable.
Upon reviewing my memorial,
I did not advocate for severe punishments.
I humbly believe that from Gāo Dì
up to Xiào Xuān,
their implementations
were mostly in line with the Classics and commentaries.
It is fitting to compare these matters with current affairs,
and verify them with antiquity.
If we follow former precedents,
nothing is difficult to change.
I cannot but express my utmost wish
to be granted an audience,
or to discuss with the Palace Secretariat and close ministers,
and verbally explain the essentials."
The Emperor ordered the Palace Secretariat to inquire about the situation.
Liáng Tǒng replied: "I have heard that sagacious emperors and enlightened kings,
established punishments.
Therefore, even in the flourishing era of Yáo and Shùn,
the Four Fiends were still executed.
The Classic states:
'Heaven punishes the guilty,
with five penalties and five uses.'
It also states:
'Thus regulate the hundred clans in the fairness of punishment.'
Kǒng Zǐ said:
'If punishments are not fair,
then people will not know where to place their hands and feet.'
'Fairness' (zhōng)
means
neither light nor severe.
The executions in the Spring and Autumn period
did not spare relatives,
this was to prevent disaster and quell chaos,
and to ensure the safety of the common people.
How could there be no
benevolent love and grace,
but rather to value cutting off the path of cruelty and harm?
The number of judgments decreased.
By the time of Chūyuán and Jiànpíng,
over a hundred articles of punishment were reduced,
yet banditry progressively increased,
reaching tens of thousands annually.
Recently, the Sānfǔ
were rampant,
with gangs rising up in unison,
even burning Máolíng,
with the fire visible from Wèiyāng.
Thereafter, bandits from Lǒngxī, Běidì, and Xīhé,
crossed provinces and traversed commanderies,
connecting over ten thousand
lǐ,
attacking and seizing armories,
robbing and plundering officials and common people.
Imperial edicts were issued to suppress them,
but they were not captured for years.
At this time, it was thought that there were no difficulties in the empire,
and the common people were peaceful and secure,
yet the power of the mad and cunning
still reached such a point.
This was all due to unfair punishments,
making it easy for foolish people to transgress."
He selected the worthy ministers Kǒng Guāng, Shī Dān and others for discussion.
Later, he was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng,
and then enfeoffed as the Marquis of Fēnglíng Xiāng.
Liáng Tǒng also achieved good governance in the commandery;
officials and common people both feared and loved him.
He died in office.
His son Sōng succeeded him.
Sōng, courtesy name Bó Sūn,
was a Gentleman when young.
He married Gūangwǔ's daughter, Princess Wǔyīn Zhǎng.
He was twice promoted to Commandant of the Rapid as Tigers.
Sōng was widely versed in the Classics,
and well-versed in ancient affairs.
Together with other scholars, he restored the Míngtáng, Pìyōng, suburban sacrifices, and the rites of Fēngshàn.
He often participated in discussions,
and his favor was unmatched.
When Gūangwǔ died,
he received an imperial edict to assist in governance.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng,
he was promoted to Grand Coachman.
Sōng repeatedly sent private letters to solicit favors from commanderies and counties.
In the second year,
this was discovered and he was dismissed from office.
He then harbored resentment.
In the winter of the fourth year,
he posted a slanderous flying letter.
He was imprisoned and died,
and his marquisate was abolished.
His son Hù,
later, as a cousin of Empress Gōnghuái,
during the Yǒngyuán reign,
was promoted to Palace Attendant,
and successively held positions as Minister and Colonel.
He was gentle, respectful, modest,
and also deeply learned in poetry and classics.
During the Yǒngchū reign,
he served as Minor Supervisor of Chánglè.
Sōng's younger brother was Sǒng.
Sǒng, courtesy name Shū Jìng,
studied Mèng's Changes from a young age,
and could teach by the age of twenty.
Later, due to his brother Sōng's affair,
he and his younger brother Gōng were both exiled to Jiǔzhēn.
After arriving in the southern lands,
he traveled through the Jiāng and Hú,
crossed the Yuán and Xiāng.
He was moved by the tragic fates of Zǐ Xū and Qū Yuán, who drowned innocently.
So he composed the "Dàosāo Fù",
tied it to a black stone and sank it.
Later, Xiǎnzōng issued an edict allowing him to return to his home commandery.
Sǒng shut his door and cultivated himself,
finding joy in classical texts.
He authored several chapters,
titled "Qī Xù".
Bān Gù saw it and praised it, saying:
"Kǒng Zǐ wrote the Spring and Autumn Annals and rebellious ministers and treacherous sons feared;
Liáng Sǒng wrote 'Qī Xù' and those who usurped positions and lived idly felt ashamed."
He was naturally generous
and did not engage in industry.
His elder sister-in-law, Princess Wǔyīn, provided for all the Liáng family,
with order for close and distant relatives.
She particularly esteemed and respected Sǒng,
and even his clothes, food, and utensils
were specially augmented.
Sǒng distributed all of it to his relatives,
leaving nothing for himself to wear.
Sǒng grew up in the capital,
and did not enjoy his native land.
He felt proud of his talent,
but was depressed and discontent.
He once climbed to a high place and looked into the distance,
sighing and saying:
"A true man living in the world,
should be enfeoffed as a marquis in life,
and receive temple offerings in death.
If not so,
living in seclusion can nourish one's aspirations,
and poetry and classics are sufficient for self-amusement.
The duties of a province or commandery
are merely tiresome."
Later, numerous invitations for appointments arrived,
but he did not accept any of them.
He had three sons and three daughters.
Sùzōng took two of his daughters,
both becoming Guìrén.
The younger Guìrén gave birth to Hé Dì.
Empress Dòu adopted him as her son,
and the Liáng family privately celebrated.
Later, the Dòu family heard of this,
fearing that the Liáng clan would gain influence
and ultimately harm them.
In the eighth year of Jiànchū,
they then slandered and killed the two Guìrén,
and implicated Sǒng and others in a charge of grave rebellion.
An imperial edict ordered Zhèng Jù, the Grand Administrator of Hànyáng, to investigate Sǒng's crime.
He died in prison,
and his family was again exiled to Jiǔzhēn.
The statements implicated Princess Wǔyīn,
who was exiled to Xīnchéng,
and guarded by envoys.
Palace affairs were secret,
and no one knew that Hé Dì was born to a Liáng.
In the ninth year of Yǒngyuán
Dòu Tàihòu passed away.
Sōngzi Hù sent his paternal cousin
to present a memorial to the Sānfǔ,
arguing that according to the old customs of the Hàn imperial house,
the mother of the emperor should be greatly honored.
Yet, Liáng Guìrén, who had personally raised His Sacred Majesty,
had not received an honorable title.
He requested that the matter be discussed.
Tàiwèi Zhāng Pú summoned him to interrogate him about the facts.
Later, he was granted an audience
and explained the situation of the memorial.
The Emperor was deeply moved and wept for a long time,
saying,
"What do you think about this, Sir?"
Pú replied,
"The principle of the Chūnqiū
is that a mother becomes honored through her son.
Since the rise of Hàn,
no imperial mother has failed to be greatly distinguished.
Your humble servant believes it is fitting to bestow an honorable title
to comfort her sacred spirit,
and to record and honor her maternal uncles,
to clarify the bonds of kinship."
The Emperor wept sadly, saying,
"Who but you would think of this for me!"
At this time, Guìrén's elder sister, Fán Diào's wife Yì, who lived in Nányáng,
submitted a memorial to plead her case, saying,
"My full sister, Guìrén,
previously served in the imperial harem
and received great favor from the late emperor,
being fortunate enough to be cherished.
Heaven bestowed its mandate,
and she gave birth to a sagely and enlightened one.
However, she was slandered by Dòu Xiàn and his brothers,
causing my father Sǒng to die unjustly in prison,
his bones unburied.
My elderly mother and orphaned younger siblings
were banished thousands of miles away.
Only I was left behind,
hiding in the wilderness,
constantly fearing for my life,
with no way to make myself known.
Now, I have encountered Your Majesty's divine and sacred reign,
personally governing all affairs,
where all things find their proper place.
Xiàn and his brothers, being treacherous and wicked,
have already received their deserved punishment,
everyone receiving their due.
I am able to breathe again,
wiping my eyes to see anew,
and thus dare to risk death to present myself before Heaven.
I have heard that when Tàizōng ascended the throne,
the Bó clan received honor;
when Xuāndì succeeded to the lineage,
the Shǐ clan revived.
Although my family has kinship with Bó and Shǐ,
we alone have received no lingering grace as maternal relatives,
which truly grieves me.
My father, having been wronged,
cannot be brought back to life,
and my mother is over seventy years old,
while my younger brother Táng and others
are in a remote and distant land,
their fate unknown.
I beg that Sǒng's decayed bones be collected,
and that my mother and younger brother be allowed to return to their home commandery.
Then your benevolence will surpass Heaven and Earth,
and both the living and the dead will be fortunate to rely on it."
The Emperor read the memorial and was moved to understanding.
He then ordered the Zhōngchángshì and Yètíng Lìng to investigate.
Yì's account was confirmed to be true and accurate,
so she was granted an audience,
where she fully explained the situation.
Yì was then kept in the palace
for several months before being allowed to leave.
She was rewarded with clothes, bedding, money, silks, a residence, and servants.
Within ten days to a month,
her assets accumulated to tens of millions.
Yì had always possessed virtuous conduct,
and the Emperor loved her even more,
bestowing upon her the title of Liáng Fūren.
Fán Diào was promoted to Yǔlín Zuǒjiān.
Diào
was the great-grandson of Guānglù Dàfū Hóng's elder brother.
Thereupon, Gōnghuái Huánghòu was posthumously honored.
That winter,
an imperial edict was issued to the Sāngōng and Dàhónglú, saying:
"There is no greater filial piety than honoring the exalted and cherishing one's kin;
their meaning is one.
The Shījīng says: 'My father begat me,
my mother nurtured me,
they soothed me, they fed me,
they brought me up, they raised me,
they watched over me, they cared for me,
they clasped me to their bosom when I went out and in.
I wish to repay their kindness,
but it is as boundless as the vast heavens.'
I dare not initiate new customs,
but look to former generations.
Tàizōng and Zhōngzōng
indeed had old customs
of posthumously bestowing titles upon their maternal grandfathers,
to strengthen the bonds of kinship.
Therefore, the father of the Empress Dowager, Sǒng, shall be posthumously enfeoffed and given the posthumous title Bāoqīn Mǐnhóu,
on par with Língwén, Shùnchéng, and [Enchéng] Hóu.
If his soul has consciousness,
may he rejoice in this esteemed honor,
this noble rank and prominent vestment,
to comfort his mother's heart."
A Zhōngyèzhě was dispatched with Yì and Hù
to ceremoniously go west and welcome Sǒng's remains,
to be re-interred in the capital.
He was granted an Eastern Park painted coffin, a jade casket, and burial clothes and shrouds.
A tomb was built beside Gōnghuái Huánghòu's mausoleum.
The Emperor personally attended the funeral procession,
and all officials were present.
Sǒng's wife and children were summoned back.
His son Táng was enfeoffed as Lèpíng Hóu,
Táng's younger brother Yōng as Chéngshì Hóu,
and Yōng's younger brother Zhái as Dānfù Hóu.
Each was granted five thousand households,
all holding the rank of Tèjìn.
They received rewards of residences, servants, carriages, horses, weapons, crossbows, and miscellaneous goods totaling tens of millions,
their favor and treatment shining brightly in their era.
All members of the Liáng clan, both immediate and extended, were appointed as Láng or Yèzhě.
Táng rose to the position of Dàhónglú,
and Yōng to Shǎofǔ.
After Táng's death,
his son Ānguó inherited the title.
During Yán'guāng's reign, he served as Shìzhōng,
but was dismissed from office due to an offense,
and all Láng and Lì of the Liáng clan were also dismissed.
