Shāng, courtesy name Bóxià,
was Yōng's son.
As a youth, he was appointed Lángzhōng due to his status as an imperial relative,
and then promoted to Huángmén Shìláng.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn,
he inherited his father's title as Chéngshì Hóu.
In the third year,
Shùndì selected Shāng's daughter and his younger sister to enter the Yèting,
and Shāng was promoted to Shìzhōng and Túqí Xiàowèi.
In the first year of Yángjiā,
his daughter was enthroned as Empress,
and his younger sister became Guìrén.
Shāng's rank was elevated to Tèjìn,
his territory was further increased,
and he was bestowed an armored carriage with a team of four horses.
That same year, he was appointed Zhí Jīnwú.
In the second year,
his son Jì was enfeoffed as Xiāngyì Hóu,
but Shāng modestly declined.
In the third year,
Shāng was appointed Dàjiāngjūn,
but he feigned illness and did not rise.
In the fourth year,
Tàicháng Huán Yān was sent to deliver the imperial decree and officially appoint him at his residence.
Shāng then proceeded to the palace to accept the mandate.
The following year,
his wife, Lady Yīn, passed away.
She was posthumously honored as Kāifēng Jūn,
and granted a seal and ribbon.
Liáng Shāng, deeming himself a member of the imperial clan by marriage, held a high position.
He always maintained humility and gentleness,
emptying himself to advance the worthy.
He appointed Jù Lǎn from Hànyáng and Chén Guī from Shàngdǎng as his subordinates,
and Lǐ Gù and Zhōu Jǔ as his Attendants in the Central Bureau (Cóngshì Zhōngláng).
Consequently, the capital was unanimously
praising him as an excellent assistant,
and the Emperor entrusted him greatly.
Whenever there was a famine,
he would transport rent-grain to the city gates
to distribute to the poor and starving,
without publicizing his benevolence.
He strictly managed his family,
never abusing his power or influence to violate the law.
However, his nature was cautious and weak, lacking decisive authority,
and he was somewhat indulgent towards the eunuchs.
Because the Lesser Yellow Gate (Xiǎohuángmén) Cáo Jié and others held power in the court,
he sent his sons, Jì and Bùyí, to befriend them.
Nevertheless, the eunuchs, resentful of Shāng's favor and trust,
instead sought to entrap him.
In the fourth year of Yǒnghé (139 CE),
the Regular Palace Attendant (Zhōngchángshì) Zhāng Kuí and Qú Zhèng,
the Administrator of Inner Department (Nèizhělìng) Shí Guāng,
the Administrator of Imperial Workshops (Shàngfānglìng) Fù Fú,
and the Chief Commandant of Servants (Púshè) Dù Yǒng conspired,
and together slandered Shāng and the Regular Palace Attendants Cáo Téng and Mèng Bēn,
claiming they intended to summon all the imperial princes
to plot the deposition and establishment of an emperor.
They requested to arrest Shāng and the others and investigate their crimes.
The Emperor said:
“The Grand General and his sons are my close relatives,
and Téng and Bēn are my beloved.
There can be no such thing;
you are just jealous of them.”
Kuí and the others, knowing their words were not heeded,
and fearing reprisal,
then issued a forged imperial edict to arrest Téng and Bēn in the palace offices.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor was enraged,
and ordered the eunuch Lǐ Xī to quickly summon Téng and Bēn and release them,
and to arrest Kuí and the others,
who were all executed.
The accusations implicated many, including high-ranking officials.
Shāng, fearing that many innocent people would be wronged,
then submitted a memorial, saying:
“According to the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
merit belongs to the commander-in-chief,
and guilt stops at the principal culprits.
Thus, rewards are not excessive,
and punishments are not indiscriminate.
This is how the Five Emperors and Three Kings all achieved peace and prosperity.
I humbly hear that in the examination of the Regular Palace Attendant Zhāng Kuí and others,
their testimonies have implicated many.
When a major imprisonment begins,
the innocent are numerous;
if death-row prisoners are detained for a long time,
small matters become big.
This is not the way to welcome harmony,
or to achieve stable governance and transformation.
It is appropriate to conclude it quickly
to stop the vexation of arrests.”
The Emperor then accepted it,
and the punishment was limited to those directly involved.
In the autumn of the sixth year (141 CE),
Shāng fell seriously ill.
He ordered his son Jì and others, saying:
“I, being unworthy,
have enjoyed much fortune.
In life, I had no means to assist the court;
in death, I must not deplete the imperial treasury.
Things like grave clothes, food for the mouth, jade caskets, and pearls
are of no benefit to rotting bones.
For the myriad officials to be troubled and busy,
filling the roads with splendor,
only adds to the dust and grime.
Although it is called ritual,
there is also consideration for the times.
Currently, the borders are uneasy,
and bandits have not ceased.
How can I further burden the state?
After my last breath,
carry me to the tomb-house
and immediately perform the funeral rites.
Adorn me with clothes of the time,
all old clothes;
do not make new ones.
Once the coffin is prepared, open the tomb;
once the tomb is opened, bury me immediately.
Offerings of food should be as if I were alive;
do not use three sacrificial animals.
Filial sons skillfully follow their father's will;
you should not disregard my words.”
When he died,
the Emperor personally attended the mourning.
His sons wished to follow his instructions,
but the court did not permit it.

They were bestowed with red burial vessels from the Eastern Park (Dōngyuán Zhūshòu Qì), silver-inlaid items (Yínlòu), yellow cedar planks (Huángcháng), a jade casket (Yùxiá), and twenty-eight kinds of miscellaneous items,
two million cash,
and three thousand bolts of cloth.
The Empress was given five million cash
and ten thousand bolts of cloth.
At the burial,
he was posthumously granted light chariots and armored warriors,
and given the posthumous title Zhōnghóu (Loyal Marquis).
The Empress Dowager personally saw him off,
and the Emperor went to Xuānyáng Tíng
to gaze at the carriages and cavalry.
His son Jì succeeded him.
Jì's courtesy name was Bózhuó.
He had "eagle shoulders and jackal eyes" (yīnjiān cháimù),
with piercing, shifting gaze (dòngjīng duànyán),
muttering with his mouth and speaking with his tongue (kǒuyín shéyán),
barely capable of writing and calculation.
In his youth, as a distinguished relative,
he indulged in unrestrained pleasure.
He was fond of alcohol,
and skilled at archery (wǎnmǎn), flicking (tán),
the game of *ge wu* (gégǔ),
the game of *liubo* (liùbó),
kickball (cùjú),
and the game of "guessing money" (yìqián zhī xì).
He also liked keeping hawks and chasing dogs,
racing horses and fighting cocks.
Initially, he was a Yellow Gate Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng),
then transferred to Attendant (Shìzhōng),
Chief Commandant of Tiger Warriors (Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng),
Commandant of Elite Cavalry (Yuèqí), and Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi),
and Commandant of the Gilded Effigies (Zhí Jīnwú).
In the first year of Yǒnghé (136 CE),
he was appointed Administrator of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn).
Jì was tyrannical and unrestrained in office,
committing many illegal acts.
Lǚ Fàng, the Administrator of Luòyáng, a close guest of his father Shāng,
often spoke to Shāng about Jì's shortcomings.
Shāng reproached Jì about it,
whereupon Jì immediately sent men to assassinate Fàng on the road.
Fearing that Shāng would find out,
he shifted the suspicion to Fàng's enemies,
and requested that Fàng's brother Yǔ be made Administrator of Luòyáng
to apprehend them,
resulting in the extermination of Fàng's clan relatives and guests, over a hundred people.
Shāng died but had not yet been buried,
when Emperor Shùn appointed Jì as Grand General,
and his younger brother Bùyí, who was an Attendant (Shìzhōng), as Administrator of Hénán.
When the Emperor died,
Emperor Chōng was still in swaddling clothes.
The Empress Dowager presided over the court,
and decreed that Jì, along with Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Zhào Jùn and Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Lǐ Gù, participate in recording affairs of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Shì).
Although Jì declined to accept,
his extravagance and tyranny became even more severe.
Emperor Chōng also died,
and Jì enthroned Emperor Zhì.
The Emperor was young but intelligent,
aware of Jì's arrogance and overbearing nature.
One day, while holding court with his ministers,
he pointed at Jì and said:
“This is an overbearing general.”
Jì heard this
and deeply resented it,
so he ordered his attendants to put poison into a cake,
and the Emperor died that very day.
He then enthroned Emperor Huán,
and wrongly killed Lǐ Gù and the former Grand Commandant Dù Qiáo.
The empire lamented and feared,
as recounted in the Biography of Lǐ Gù.
In the first year of Jiànhé (147 CE),
Jì's fief was increased by thirteen thousand households.
The Grand General's office was expanded to recommend "high-grade and flourishing talents" (gāodì máocái),
and his staff doubled that of the Three Excellencies.
His brother Bùyí was also enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǐngyáng,
and Bùyí's brother Méng as Marquis of Xīpíng,
and Jì's son Yìn as Marquis of Xiāngyì,
each with ten thousand households.
In the first year of Hépíng (150 CE),
Jì's fief was again increased by ten thousand households,
making a total of thirty thousand households including previous grants.
Zǎi Xuān (宰宣) of Hóngnóng (弘農), naturally sycophantic and wicked,
wished to ingratiate himself with Jì (冀).
He then memorialized that the Grand General had the merits of Duke of Zhōu (周公),
and since his sons were already enfeoffed,
then his wife should be made an邑君 (yìjūn, “Lady of the Fief”).
An imperial edict then enfeoffed Jì's (冀) wife, Sūn Shòu (孫壽), as Xiāngchéng Jūn (襄城君, “Lady of Xiāngchéng”),
also receiving rents from Yángzhái (陽翟),
with an annual income of fifty million (cash).
She was additionally bestowed a scarlet sash,
on par with an elder princess.
Shòu (壽) was beautiful and adept at creating captivating looks:
she would draw her eyebrows in a sorrowful manner (愁眉, chóuméi),
make a pouting lip (嗁, tí),
wear a "fallen horse" bun (墯馬髻, duòmǎjì),
take a "broken waist" walk (折ェ步, zhéěbù),
and smile with exposed teeth (齲齒笑, qǔchǐxiào),
all to enchant and bewitch.
Jì (冀) also changed the regulations for carriages and attire,
creating a "flat-top screen carriage" (平上軿車, píngshàngpíngchē),
a "high turban" (埤幘, pízé),
a "narrow cap" (狹冠, xiáguān),
a "folded-up kerchief" (折上巾, zhéshàngjīn),
a "body-enclosing fan" (擁身扇, yǒngshēnshàn),
and a "fox-tail single garment" (狐尾單衣, húwěidānyī).
Shòu (壽) was naturally jealous and overbearing,
and capable of controlling Jì (冀),
who greatly pampered and feared her.
Initially,
her father Shāng (商) presented a beautiful woman, Yǒu Tōngqī (友通期), to Emperor Shùn (順帝).
Tōngqī (通期) committed a minor offense,
and the Emperor returned her to Shāng (商).
Shāng (商) dared not keep her and married her off.
Jì (冀) immediately sent retainers to abduct Tōngqī (通期) back.
When Shāng (商) died,
Jì (冀) was observing mourning,
and secretly lived with her west of the city.
Shòu (壽), observing Jì (冀) leave,
took many of her servants (倉頭, cāngtóu)
and forcibly brought Tōngqī (通期) back,
cut her hair, scraped her face,
and flogged her.
She intended to submit a memorial reporting the affair.
Jì (冀) was terrified,
and bowed his head repeatedly, begging Shòu's (壽) mother.
Shòu (壽) then reluctantly ceased.
Jì (冀) still continued his private affair with her,
and she gave birth to a son, Bóyù (伯玉),
whom he hid and dared not reveal.
Shòu (壽) soon found out,
and sent her son Yìn (胤) to exterminate Yǒu's (友) clan.
Jì (冀) feared Shòu (壽) would harm Bóyù (伯玉),
and always kept him hidden in a secret chamber.
Jì (冀) loved his household slave Qín Gōng (秦宮),
who rose to the position of Grand Granary Prefect (太倉令, Tàicāng Lìng),
and was allowed to enter and exit Shòu's (壽) residence.
Whenever Shòu (壽) saw Gōng (宮),
she would dismiss her attendants,
under the pretext of discussing matters,
and then engage in a private affair with him.
Gōng (宮) was favored both by Jì (冀) and Shòu (壽),
and his power and authority greatly increased;
inspectors (刺史, cìshǐ) and officials receiving two thousand dàn (二千石, èrqiānshí) of salary all came to pay their respects and take leave of him.
Jì (冀), acting on Shòu's (壽) words,
dismissed and deprived many members of the Liáng (梁) clan who held positions,
outwardly displaying humility,
but in reality promoting Sūn's (孫) family and relatives.

More than ten people, falsely using names, became Imperial Attendants (侍中, Shìzhōng), Ministers (卿, Qīng), Colonels (校尉, Xiàowèi), Commandery Governors (郡守, Jùnshǒu), and chief magistrates (長吏, zhǎnglì).
All were greedy, corrupt, brutal, and lecherous.
Each sent private retainers to register wealthy individuals in affiliated counties,
accusing them of other crimes,
imprisoning and torturing them,
forcing them to pay money to redeem themselves.
Those with little property were even punished with death or exile.
Sūn Fèn (孫奮), a scholar from Fúfēng (扶風), was wealthy but stingy.
Jì (冀) took the opportunity to send him a team of horses as a gift,
and then borrowed fifty million cash from him.
Fèn (奮) gave him thirty million.
Jì (冀) was furious,
and then reported to the commanderies and counties,
claiming Fèn's (奮) mother was his household slave (守臧婢, shǒuzāngbì),
and accused her of stealing ten measures of white pearls and a thousand catties of purple gold and fleeing.
He then arrested and tortured Fèn's (奮) brothers,
who died in prison,
and confiscated all their property, totaling over one hundred and seventy million (cash).
As for the levies from the four directions,
and seasonal tributes,
the best items were first delivered to Jì (冀);
the imperial carriage then received the next best.
Officials and commoners carrying goods to seek office or plead for pardon
were seen endlessly on the roads.
Jì (冀) also sent agents beyond the frontier,
communicating with foreign countries,
widely seeking exotic goods.
Along the roads,
he dispatched people to seize (妓)【伎】women and attendants.
His agents also used their power to act violently and oppressively,
abducting and raping women,
and beating officials and soldiers,
causing resentment and hatred everywhere.
Jì (冀) then built grand mansions,
and Shòu (壽) also built a residence directly across the street,
exhausting timber and earth,
competing with each other in extravagance.
The halls and bedchambers all had hidden and deep inner rooms (陰陽奧室, yīnyángàoshì),
with connecting rooms and winding doors.
Pillars and walls were carved,
and enhanced with bronze and lacquer;
windows all had fine silk screens and green lattice (綺疎青瑣, qǐshūqīngsuǒ),
painted with clouds and immortal spirits.
Terraces and pavilions were interconnected,
overlooking each other;
flying bridges and stone steps
spanned waterways.
Gold, jade, pearls,
and rare treasures from distant lands
filled the storage rooms.
They brought famous "sweat-blood" horses from afar.
He also extensively opened parks and gardens,
excavating earth to build mountains,
with nine slopes over ten li,
resembling the two Xiáo (二崤) passes,
with deep forests and sheer ravines,
as if natural,
where strange birds and tamed beasts
flew and roamed.
Jì (冀) and Shòu (壽) jointly rode in a covered carriage,
with a feather canopy,
decorated with gold and silver,
touring the interior of the mansion,
accompanied by many singing and dancing girls,
ringing bells and playing pipes,
singing drunkenly along the path.
Sometimes this would continue day and night,
to indulge in pleasure.
Guests arriving at the gate could not enter,
and all had to beg the gatekeepers for entry,
the gatekeepers accumulated thousands of gold.
He also greatly expanded his forest parks,
which were restricted like those of the imperial family,
extending west to Hóngnóng (弘農),
east to the border of Xíngyáng (滎陽),
south to the extreme of Lǔyáng (魯陽),
and north reaching the Hé (河) and Qí (淇) rivers,
encompassing mountains and marshes,
extending far to hills and wilderness,
its perimeter
almost a thousand li.
He also built a rabbit park west of Hénán (河南) city,
stretching for dozens of li,
mobilizing laborers from affiliated counties
to build and repair towers and observatories,
which took several years to complete.
He issued proclamations everywhere,
ordering the capture of live rabbits,
and marking their fur as identification.
Anyone who violated this
was punished with death.
Once, a Hú (胡) merchant from the Western Regions,
unaware of the prohibitions,
mistakenly killed a rabbit.
Word spread,
and over ten people were executed as a result.
Jì's (冀) two younger brothers once secretly sent people to hunt in Shàngdǎng (上黨).
Jì (冀) heard of it and arrested their retainers,
killing over thirty people at once,
with no survivors.
Jì (冀) also built a separate residence west of the city
to harbor criminals and fugitives.
Sometimes he took good people
and made them all slaves,
amounting to several thousand individuals,
calling them
"self-sold people."
In the first year of Yuánjiā,
the Emperor, considering Jì's meritorious service in supporting his enthronement,
wished to bestow upon him extraordinary honors.
Thereupon, he convened a grand assembly of dukes and ministers
to jointly deliberate on the appropriate rituals.
Consequently, the relevant authorities proposed that Jì, when entering the court, should not hasten,
be allowed to wear his sword and shoes into the hall,
and his name should not be called out during audience salutations,
his ceremonial treatment equaling that of Xiāo Hé;
he should be granted all remaining households from Dìngfáo and Chéngyáng as additional enfeoffments, forming four counties,
equaling Dèng Yǔ;
and he should be rewarded with gold, money, slaves, silk, chariots, horses, clothes, and a grand mansion,
equaling Huò Guāng: to distinguish his preeminent achievements.
At every court assembly,
he was to sit separately from the Sāngōng.
He would enter the court once every ten days
to handle the affairs of the Shàngshū.
This was announced throughout the realm
to serve as a law for all generations.
However, Jì felt that the proposed honors were meager,
and he was displeased.
He monopolized power and authority,
his ruthless and arbitrary conduct accumulated daily.
No matter how important or trivial the state affairs,
none were decided without consulting him.
The palace guards and close attendants
were all people he had personally appointed.
He knew every minute detail of the Emperor's daily life within the forbidden palace.
When officials were promoted or summoned,
they would first go to Jì's gate with a memorial to express gratitude,
before daring to proceed to the Shàngshū.
Wú Shù from Xiàpī was appointed as the magistrate of Wǎn.
When he left for his post, he bid farewell to Jì.
Jì's retainers were spread throughout the county,
and they entrusted their requests to Shù.
Shù replied:
"Corrupt and destructive petty individuals
could be found in every household, deserving execution.
General, with the weighty influence of the imperial consort's family
and occupying the position of supreme commander,
it would be appropriate for you to promote the virtuous and good
to fill vacancies in the court.
Wǎn is a major metropolis,
a haven for scholars.
Since I was granted an audience,
I have not heard you praise a single elder,
but rather you entrust many matters to unsuitable people.
This is truly something I dare not hear!"
Jì remained silent and displeased.
When Shù arrived at the county,
he immediately executed dozens of Jì's retainers who had harmed people.
Because of this, Jì harbored deep resentment against him.
Later, when Shù was appointed Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
he took leave of Jì before departing.
Jì prepared wine for him,
and then poisoned him.
Shù left,
and died in his carriage.
The Administrator of Liáodōng, Hóu Měng,
initially did not pay his respects upon appointment.
Jì used another pretext
and had him summarily executed.
At that time, Yuán Zhù of Rǔnán, a Lángzhōng,
was nineteen years old.
Seeing Jì's tyrannical behavior,
he was overcome with indignation,
and thus went to the palace to submit a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that Kǒng Ní sighed that the phoenix did not arrive,
and the River did not produce the Diagram,
lamenting his own humble status
and inability to bring them forth.
Now, Your Majesty holds a position that can bring them forth,
and also possesses the qualities to do so.
Yet, harmonious qi has not responded,
and the virtuous and foolish are out of order.
This is due to the transfer of power to influential ministers
and the obstruction between those above and below.
The operation of the four seasons
shows that once achievements are complete, one should retreat.
High titles and generous favors
rarely fail to bring disaster.
Now, the Grand General's position is at its peak and his achievements are complete;
he could serve as a supreme warning.
He ought to follow the ritual of 'hanging up the carriage'
and recline in peace, nourishing his spirit.
The traditions say: 'When a tree bears too much fruit,
its branches damage its core.'
If he does not curb and diminish his excessive power,
he will not be able to preserve himself.
Those around me, hearing my words,
will glare and grind their teeth.
Your servant, having been singled out from my youth,
therefore dares to disregard taboos.
In ancient times, Shùn and Yǔ warned each other not to be like Dān Zhū.
The Duke of Zhōu warned King Chéng not to be like King Zhòu of Yīn.
I humbly request that the crime of slander be abolished
to open the mouths of all under heaven."
The memorial was presented to the Emperor.
Jì heard of it and secretly sent men to arrest Zhù.
Zhù then changed his name,
and later feigned illness and death.
He fashioned a figure out of straw
and purchased a coffin for a funeral procession.
Jì, having investigated and learned of the deception,
secretly apprehended him
and had him flogged to death,
concealing the matter.
Liú Cháng of Guìyáng, a student and a renowned scholar of his time,
was formerly close to Zhù.
Jì summoned him and appointed him a petty clerk to humiliate him.
At that time, Hǎo Jié and Hú Wǔ of Tàiyuán
were both known for their bold and profound discussions,
and were good friends with Zhù.
Previously, Jié and others had jointly submitted a memorial to the Three Ducal Offices
recommending eminent scholars from throughout the country,
but did not visit Jì.
Jì harbored anger over this
and also suspected them of being Zhù's confederates.
He ordered the Zhōngdūguān to issue a warrant to arrest and kill all those who had previously submitted the memorial.
Consequently, Hú Wǔ's family was executed,
with over sixty people dying.
Jié initially fled,
but knowing he could not escape,
he had himself carried in a coffin and presented a memorial at Jì's gate.
After the memorial was delivered,
he took poison and died.
Thus, his family was spared.
When Jì was executed, an imperial edict ordered that Zhù and others be sacrificed to with proper rites.
Jì's cruel jealousy
was all of this nature.
Bùyí enjoyed classical texts
and treated scholars well.
Jì secretly resented this.
Through the Zhōngchángshì Bái Dì,
he had Bùyí transferred to the position of Guānglùxūn.
He also hinted to the public to jointly recommend his son Yìn as the Administrator of Hénán.
Yìn, also known as Húgǒu,
was sixteen years old at the time.
His appearance was very ugly;
he could not properly wear a hat and belt.
Those who saw him on the road
all laughed at him with disdain.
Bùyí, ashamed of the animosity between the brothers,
consequently resigned his position and returned to his residence,
and, with his younger brother Méng, kept their doors shut and lived in seclusion.
Jì did not want them to associate with guests,
so he secretly sent people in disguise to their gate
to record those who came and went.
Mǎ Róng, the Administrator of Nánjùn, and Tián Míng, the Administrator of Jiāngxià,
upon their initial appointments, passed by and visited Bùyí.
Jì hinted to the provincial and commandery authorities to frame them on other charges,
and both were shaven, flogged, and exiled to Shuòfāng.
Róng stabbed himself but did not die.
Míng died on the road.
In the second year of Yǒngxīng,
Bùyí's son Mǎ was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yǐngyīn,
and Yìn's son Táo as the Marquis of Chéngfù.
Jì's family, before and after, saw seven members enfeoffed as marquises,
three as empresses,
six as imperial concubines,
two as grand generals,
seven women (wives and daughters) granted fiefs and titles of 'Jūn',
and three men who married princesses.
The remaining ministers, generals, administrators, and commandants numbered fifty-seven.
He held office for over twenty years,
reaching the pinnacle of power and prosperity,
his authority extending throughout the court and beyond.
All officials looked askance,
none daring to disobey his commands.
The Son of Heaven respectfully maintained his position and was unable to personally intervene in affairs.
The Emperor was already displeased with him.
In the first year of Yánxī,
the Grand Astrologer Chén Shòu, through the Xǐaohuángmén Xú Huáng,
reported anomalies and an eclipse,
attributing the blame to the Grand General.
Jì heard of this
and hinted to the magistrate of Luòyáng to arrest and interrogate Shòu.
Shòu died in prison.
The Emperor's anger was sparked by this.
Initially,
Dèng Xiāng’s wife, Xuān, a woman from the Yètíng, bore a daughter named Měng.
When Xiāng died,
Xuān remarried Liáng Jì.
Liáng Jì
was the maternal uncle of Jì’s wife, Shòu.
Shòu introduced Měng into the Yètíng;
she gained favor
and became a Guìrén.
Jì then wanted to acknowledge Měng as his own daughter to solidify his position,
so he changed Měng’s surname to Liáng.
At that time, Měng’s elder sister’s husband, Bǐng Zūn, was an Yìláng.
Jì feared that Zūn would thwart Xuān’s intentions,
so he hired assassins in Yǎncéng
and had Zūn murdered.
He also wanted to kill Xuān.
Xuān’s house was in Yánxīlǐ,
next to that of the Zhōng Chángshì Yuán Shè.
Jì sent assassins to climb onto Shè’s roof,
intending to enter Xuān’s house.
Shè became aware of this,
beat a drum to gather the crowd and informed Xuān.
Xuān rushed in to report it to the Dì,
who became enraged.
He then conspired with the Zhōng Chángshì Shàn Chāo, Jù Yuàn, Táng Héng, Zuǒ Kuàng, Xú Huáng, and others, five men in total, to execute Jì.
The account is in the Biography of the Eunuchs.
Jì was suspicious of Chāo and the others,
so he sent the Zhōng Huángmén Zhāng Yùn to stay overnight in the palace
to prevent any sudden changes.
Jù Yuàn ordered his officers to arrest Yùn,
claiming he had entered from outside without authorization,
intending to plot a rebellion.
The Dì then went to the front hall,
summoned the various Shàngshū,
and exposed the matter.
He ordered the Shàngshū Lìng Yǐn Xūn to take the jié and command the chéngláng and those below them to wield weapons and guard the palace gates,
collecting all official seals and tallies and sending them to the palace.
He ordered the Huángmén Lìng Jù Yuàn to lead the Zǒuyòukuàizōu,
Hǔbēn, Yǔlín, Dōuhòu Jiànjí Shì,
amounting to over a thousand men,
and together with the Sīlì Xiàowèi Zhāng Biāo, to surround Jì’s residence.
He ordered the Guānglù Xūn Yuán Xū
to take the jié and seize Jì’s Dà Jiāngjūn seal and ribbon,
and he was re-enfeoffed as Bǐjǐng Dōuxiāng Hóu.
Jì and his wife Shòu both committed suicide that very day.
All his sons, including Hénán Yǐn Yìn, his uncle Túnqí Xiàowèi Ràng,
and his close relatives Wèiwèi Shú, Yuèqí Xiàowèi Zhōng, Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi Jí, and others,
all the Liáng family members and the Sūn family's relatives, both paternal and maternal, were sent to the imperial prison.
Without regard for age, all were executed in the marketplace.
Bùyí and Méng had died earlier.
Tens of others, including Gōngqīng, Lièxiào, Cìshǐ, and Èrqiānshí, who were implicated, died.
Over three hundred former officials and guests were dismissed.
The court was emptied.
Only Yǐn Xūn, Yuán Xū, and the Tíngwèi Hándān Yì remained.
At this time, the matter erupted from within;
messengers raced back and forth.
The Gōngqīng lost their composure;
official bureaus and marketplaces were in an uproar.
It took several days for order to be restored,
and there was no one among the common people who did not celebrate.
Jì’s wealth and goods were confiscated.
The provincial government sold them off,
totaling over three hundred million cash,
which was used to fill the imperial treasury
and reduce the empire's taxes by half.
His imperial parks and hunting grounds were distributed
to provide livelihoods for the poor.
Those who had contributed to Jì’s execution were recorded and rewarded.
Shàngshū Lìng Yǐn Xūn and dozens of others were ennobled.
Commentary says: During the reign of Shùndì,
Liáng Shāng was praised as a worthy chief minister.
Was it because he held such a high position
yet was able to maintain his integrity and caution until the end?
A chief minister moves the central pivot of government,
responding to the harmony between Heaven and man.
If he acts in accordance with the Dào, it is easy to promote good governance;
if he deviates from his duties, it is difficult to manage affairs.
Shāng held the power to reverse the course of Heaven
during a period of decline and weakness,
yet in reforming the court and alleviating suffering, he failed to employ superior strategies.
The sounds of distress
were widely rumored among the people.
Although his granaries were full,
how did that avert the calamity of starvation?
Speaking of his final actions,
they did not resolve the criticism of merely holding office in name.
Moreover,
he inclined towards wicked officials,
and transferred favor to a cruel successor,
leading to the ruin of his family and harm to the state.
How could this have been merely accidental!
Eulogy says:
Héxī aided Hàn,
and the succession was also determined.
Praising kin with hidden resentment,
ascending high with repeated sighs.
Shāng regretted his excessive gentleness,
Jì then indulged in chaos.
Biography of Zhāng, Cáo, and Zhèng, Chapter Twenty-Five
Zhāng Chún, courtesy name Bórén,
was a native of Dùlíng, Jīngzhào.
His great-great-grandfather, Ānshì, served as Dà Sīmǎ Wèijiāngjūn during the reign of Xuāndì
and was enfeoffed as Fùpíng Hóu.
His father, Fàng, served as Chéngdì’s Shìzhōng.
Chún inherited the noble title and territory in his youth.
During the reigns of Āidì and Píngdì, he was Shìzhōng.
During Wáng Mǎng’s time, he reached the rank of Lièqīng.
When the usurper seized power,
many lost their titles and lands.
Chún, due to his uprightness and adherence to principles,
preserved his former fief.
In the early Jiànwǔ period,
he was among the first to come to the imperial court,
thus he was able to recover his state.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū
and sent to lead the Yǐngchuān cavalry to pacify and settle the Jīng, Xú, and Yáng regions,
supervising the transport of supplies
and overseeing the camps of various generals.
Later, he again led troops to establish military agricultural settlements in Nányáng
and was promoted to Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiāng.
The relevant authorities memorialized,
stating that non-imperial clan Lièhóu should not have their states restored.
Guāngwǔ Dì said:
“Zhāng Chún has served as an imperial guard for over ten years.
He should not be abolished.
He shall be re-enfeoffed as Wǔshǐ Hóu,
receiving half of the Fùpíng fief.”
Chún served in court throughout his career,
and was thoroughly versed in historical precedents.
In the early Jiànwǔ period,
many old regulations were lacking,
and whenever there was a doubtful matter,
he would always be consulted.
From the suburban temples, ancestral shrines, marriage, capping, mourning rites, and other ceremonies,
he corrected and established many things.
The Emperor held him in great esteem,
and appointed Chún as concurrent Colonel of the Huángmén [Hǔbēn] Guard.
He was frequently granted audiences,
sometimes even three or four times in a single day.
Chún believed that the ancestral temples had not yet been settled,
and the order of generations was out of sequence.
In the nineteenth year,
he and the Grand Coachman, Zhū Fú, jointly presented a memorial, stating:
"Your Majesty rose from the common people,
cleansed the world,
suppressed the violent rebels,
and continued the legacy of your ancestors.
We humbly believe that according to the records of the classics,
and the sentiments of the people,
although the reality is that you initiated a new foundation,
your reign is nominally a restoration.
It is fitting to honor the former emperors [Xiān dì]
and respectfully carry out their sacrifices.
Since Emperor Yuán,
the ancestral temples have honored and sacrificed to Emperor Gāo as the ancestor who received the mandate,
Emperor Xiàowén as Tàizōng,
and Emperor Xiàowǔ as Shìzōng,
all according to the old system.
Furthermore, four generations of private temples [qīn miào] have been established,
tracing upwards from the Lord of Nándùn [Nándùn Jūn] to the Marquis Jié of Chōnglíng [Chōnglíng Jié Hóu].
According to the rites,
one who becomes the successor to another becomes their son;
having served the main lineage,
one then demotes their private relatives.
Now, when performing the Dì and Xiá sacrifices in the Gāo Temple,
and arranging the order of generations,
the four generations of Chōnglíng
are placed alongside emperors,
the humble alongside the exalted,
which does not conform to the spirit of the rites.
Supposing Wáng Mǎng had not been encountered,
and the national succession had no heir,
and Your Majesty was sought out among the imperial clan to continue the line,
how could you then care for private relatives
and violate the ritual system?
In the past, Emperor Gāo received the mandate himself,
and did not rely on the Tàishàng
[Emperor]; Emperor Xuān, as a grandson, succeeded his grandfather,
and dared not prioritize his private relatives.
Therefore, when a temple was established for his father,
only his ministers attended the sacrifices.
Your humble servant believes that the current private temples should be abolished,
to follow the old precedents of these two emperors [Èr Dì].
We wish for this matter to be submitted to the relevant officials to broadly collect their opinions."
The edict was sent to the grandees [gōng qīng].
The Grand Minister of Works, Dài Shè, and the Grand Minister of Agriculture, Dòu Róng,
deliberated, saying:
"It is fitting to replace the current private temples with the four generations of the five emperors Xuān, Yuán, Chéng, Āi, and Píng.
Emperors Xuān and Yuán should be honored as ancestors and fathers,
and may be personally offered sacrifices.
For Emperor Chéng and below,
the relevant officials shall conduct the ceremonies.
A separate temple for the Imperial Father should be established for the Lord of Nándùn.
Sacrifices therein shall extend up to the Marquis Jié of Chōnglíng,
with ministers attending the sacrifices,
thereby clarifying the respect for the exalted [zūn zūn zhī jìng]
and the affection for relatives [qīn qīn zhī ēn]."
The Emperor approved.
At this time, the ancestral temples were not yet fully prepared.
From Emperor Yuán upwards,
sacrifices were offered at the Gāo Temple in Luòyáng.
From Emperor Chéng downwards,
sacrifices were offered at the Gāo Temple in Cháng'ān.
As for the four generations of Nándùn,
sacrifices were offered wherever they resided.
The following year,
Chún replaced Zhū Fú as Grand Coachman.
In the twenty-third year,
he replaced Dù Lín as Grand Minister of Agriculture.
While in office, he emulated the conduct of Cáo Cān,
striving for non-interference,
and selected and appointed clerks and scribes [yuán shǐ] who were
all renowned great Confucian scholars.
The following year,
the Upper Yáng Canal was excavated,
diverting the Luò River for transport,
which benefited the populace.
In the twenty-sixth year,
an imperial edict to Chún stated:
"The Dì and Xiá sacrifices
have not been performed for a long time.
'If rites are not observed for three years,
the rites will surely be ruined;
if music is not performed for three years,
the music will surely collapse.'
You should refer to the classics
and formulate their regulations in detail."
Chún memorialized, saying:
"According to the rites,
the Xiá sacrifice is performed once every three years,
and the Dì sacrifice once every five years.
The Spring and Autumn Annals commentary states: 'What is the great Xiá sacrifice?
It is a combined sacrifice.'
The spirit tablets of both destroyed and extant temples are brought up,
and they are collectively offered food at the Grand Ancestor's temple,
repeated every five years.
The old Han system performed the Xiá sacrifice once every three years,
with the spirit tablets of destroyed temples collectively offered food at the Gāo Temple,
but the spirit tablets of extant temples were never collectively sacrificed to.
In the fifth year of Yuánshǐ,
the temples of various kings, dukes, and marquises assembled,
and the Dì sacrifice was performed for the first time.
Eighteen years prior, when the emperor personally visited Cháng'ān,
this rite was also performed.
The Rites explain that with one leap month every three years,
the cosmic energies are moderately prepared;
with two leap months every five years,
the cosmic energies are fully prepared.
Therefore, the Xiá sacrifice is performed once every three years,
and the Dì sacrifice once every five years.
The word 'Dì' means 'to discern' [dì],
meaning to discern and establish the order of generations, and the distinctions of exalted and humble.
The Dì sacrifice is performed in the fourth month of summer;
summer is when the yang energy is ascendant
and yin energy is subordinate,
hence it rectifies the meaning of exalted and humble.
The Xiá sacrifice is performed in the tenth month of winter;
winter is when the five grains are ripe,
things are complete, and rites are fulfilled,
hence it is a gathering for food and drink.
This ceremony has been abandoned
for eight years now.
I suggest it be carried out according to the rites,
and a decision made in due course."
The Emperor agreed,
and from then on, the Dì and Xiá sacrifices were established.
At this time, the Southern Chányú [Nán Chányú] and the Wūhuán had submitted,
the borders were peaceful,
the common people had recently put aside warfare,
and the harvests were good year after year,
with every family well-supplied and every person content.
Chún believed that the establishment of the Pìyōng by the sagely kings [shèng wáng]
was for the purpose of promoting ritual and righteousness,
instructing those who were already prosperous.
He then examined the Seven Canonical Prognostications [Qī Jīng Chèn], diagrams of the Míngtáng,
ancient records of the Pìyōng from Héjiān, the system of the Tàishān Míngtáng from Emperor Xiàowǔ's time,
and the discussions during Emperor Píng's reign,
intending to fully memorialize on them.
Before he could submit it,
the Erudite Huán Róng happened to memorialize that the Pìyōng and Míngtáng should be established.
The memorial was sent to the Three Dukes [Sān Gōng] and the Grand Minister of Ceremonies [Tàicháng],
and Chún's opinion agreed with Róng's.
The Emperor then assented.
Thirty years [after he was enfeoffed],
Chún submitted a memorial proposing the Fēngshàn sacrifices,
stating:
"Since ancient times, those who received the mandate and became emperors,
at the height of a prosperous reign,
invariably performed the Fēngshàn sacrifices,
to announce their achievements.
The 'Lè Dòng Shēng Yí' says: 'Govern people with elegance,
and customs are formed by odes.'
During the flourishing period of Zhōu,
between the reigns of Chéng Wáng and Kāng Wáng,
the suburban sacrifices, the Fēng sacrifices, and the Shàn sacrifices
are all evident.
The 'Shū' says, 'In the second month of the year,
the Son of Heaven makes an eastern tour of inspection,
arriving at Dàizōng,
and performs the chái sacrifice,'
which is the meaning of Fēngshàn.
Your servant humbly observes that Your Majesty received the mandate to restore the dynasty,
pacified the chaos within the seas,
restored the ancestral order,
and comforted and preserved the myriad people.
The empire is vast and clear,
all experiencing a new birth.
Your grace and virtue spread like clouds,
Your beneficence falls like rain.
The common people are at peace,
and the Yi and Di barbarians admire Your righteousness.
The 'Shī' says: 'Receiving blessings from Heaven,
the four quarters come to offer congratulations.'
Now, it is the year of Shèntí,
Cānglóng Jiǎyín,
and virtue resides in the eastern palace.
It is fitting to seize this propitious time,
follow the precedents of the Tángdì,
continue the work of Xiàowǔ,
and in the second month, make an eastern tour of inspection,
perform the Fēng sacrifice on Dàizōng,
to manifest the restoration,
engrave Your meritorious deeds,
restore the ancestral lineage,
repay the celestial deities,
perform the Shàn sacrifice on Liángfù,
and worship the terrestrial deities.
This will transmit the throne to Your descendants,
a foundation for ten thousand generations."
In the first year of Zhōngyuán [150 CE],
the Emperor made an eastern tour to Dàizōng.
He appointed Chún as Shì Yùshǐ Dàfū to accompany him,
and presented the old rites of the Yuán Fēng sacrifices and the inscription for the stone tablet.
In the third month,
he passed away.
His posthumous title was Jiéhóu.
His son Fèn inherited the title.
Fèn's courtesy name was Zhìtōng.
His father Chún,
on his deathbed, instructed his jiāchéng, saying:
"This Sīkōng had no accomplishments at the time,
yet was undeservedly granted a noble rank and territory.
As for the property of one who has died,
do not discuss transmitting it to the nation."
Fèn's elder brother Gēn
suffered from an illness when young.
Guāngwǔ issued an edict for Fèn to inherit the title.
Fèn cited Chún's last instructions,
and firmly refused to accept.
The Emperor, seeing Fèn defy the succession,
ordered him arrested and imprisoned.
Fèn, terrified,
then assumed the fief.
In the fourth year of Yǒngpíng [61 CE],
he returned to his state according to regulation.
Fèn was fond of learning in his youth,
was frugal, and acted righteously.
He often shared and reduced his rental income,
to assist and relieve his clan relatives.
Though he sometimes faced extreme shortages,
his giving and generosity never ceased.
Seventeen
Fèn came to court to offer congratulations on the Emperor's birthday.
He was granted an audience in Xuānpíng Diàn.
His responses were in accord with the Emperor's will.
Xiǎnzōng was impressed by his talent,
and appointed him Shìcíhóu.
In the first year of Jiànchū [76 CE],
he was appointed Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng,
then transferred to Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng,
and promoted to Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi.
In the seventh year [82 CE],
he became Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng.
In the first year of Zhānghé [87 CE],
he was dismissed.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán [89 CE],
he was again appointed Chéngmén Xiàowèi.
In the fourth year [92 CE],
he was promoted to Chánglè Wèiwèi.
The next year [93 CE],
he replaced Huán Yù as Tàicháng.
In the sixth year [94 CE],
he replaced Liú Fāng as Sīkōng.
At that time, the year saw drought disasters,
and prayers for rain went unanswered.
He then submitted a memorial stating:
"In recent years, harvests have been poor,
and people suffer from hunger and scarcity.
Now, there is another prolonged drought,
the autumn crops are not yet established,
the yang energy is almost exhausted,
and time is pressing.
Indeed, the state takes the people as its foundation,
and the people take grain as their life.
This is the most urgent matter of governance,
and the gravest concern.
Your servant's gratitude for Your grace is particularly profound;
I have received a position beyond my capabilities.
Morning and night, I am filled with anxiety and fear.
My written memorials cannot fully express my heart.
I wish to present my memorial directly to the Zhōng Chángshì."
He was immediately granted an audience,
and verbally presented the urgent political needs of the time.
The next day,
Hé Dì summoned the Tàiwèi and Sītú to visit the Luòyáng prison,
reviewed the prisoners,
and arrested Chén Xīn, the Luòyáng Lìng.
Immediately, there was heavy rain for three days.
Fèn was honest and upright in office,
with no other extraordinary achievements.
In the ninth year [97 CE],
he was dismissed due to illness.
At home, he submitted a memorial stating:
"What the sages praise,
the most essential aspect of the way of governance,
lies fundamentally in Rítuals and Music.
The Five Classics all converge on this,
and the utility of Rítuals and Music is particularly urgent.
Confucius said: 'For regulating superiors and governing the people,
nothing is better than Rítuals;
for transforming customs and changing practices,
nothing is better than Music.'
He also said: 'Those who transform the empire through deference and yielding,
this refers to Rítuals and Music.'
The way of the former kings,
Rítuals and Music can be said to have flourished.
Confucius said to Zǐxià: 'Rítuals cultivate the external,
Music controls the internal.
Qiu has done his part!'
He also said: 'If Rítuals and Music do not flourish,
then punishments will not be just;
if punishments are not just,
then the people will not know where to place their hands and feet.'
Your servant believes that Hàn should establish Rítuals and Music.
Therefore, the sage virtue of the former emperors
repeatedly issued edicts,
lamenting the collapse and disruption,
but the many Confucian scholars failed to comprehend,
and their opinions were often contradictory.
Your servant's family has served in high office for generations,
yet the great ceremonies remain unfixed.
I secretly worry about this,
and it affects my sleep and meals.
Your servant's dog-and-horse years are coming to an end;
I sincerely hope to see the establishment of Rítuals and Music before I die."
In the thirteenth year [101 CE],
he was again summoned and appointed Tàicháng.
He again submitted a memorial, stating:
"Hàn should reform and establish Rítuals and Music,
as clearly stated in the maps and documents.
A king transforms through establishing rules and instituting Rítuals,
and composes Music when his achievements are complete.
I humbly list three differing opinions regarding Rítuals and Music,
and wish for them to be submitted to the relevant officials,
to be considered and settled in due time.
In the past, Emperor Xiàowǔ and Emperor Guāngwǔ performed the Fēngshàn sacrifices and announced their accomplishments,
but Rítuals and Music were not fixed,
and the matters did not align.
The former emperor already issued an edict to Cáo Bāo;
now Your Majesty need only uphold and complete it,
just as Zhōu Gōng deliberated and adjusted the ways of Wén Wǔ,
not creating them himself.
There is truly no doubt.
Long-held excessive humility
causes the great undertaking of Hàn not to be completed in a timely manner.
This is not how to manifest the merits and virtues of the ancestors,
establish the foundation of grand peace,
or serve as a model for future generations."
Although the Emperor approved of this,
he still did not implement it.
That winter,
he was again dismissed due to illness.
The following year,
he died at home.
Zǐ Fǔ 嗣.
He served as Jīnchéngmén Hóu.
After Fǔ died,
his son Jí succeeded.
In the third year of Yǒngchū,
Jí died
without issue,
and the state was abolished.
From the time that Zhāodì enfeoffed Ānshì,
down to Jí,
the state was transmitted for eight generations,
passing through usurpations and disturbances,
yet for two hundred years
it was never condemned or deposed.
No other enfeoffed lord could compare.
Cáo Bāo, courtesy name Shūtōng,
was a native of Xuē in Lǔguó.
His father, Chōng,
upheld the rites of the Qìng clan.
During the Jiànwǔ era, he served as a Bóshì,
and accompanied the emperor on his巡狩 to Dàizōng.
He established the rites for the Fēngshàn sacrifices.
Upon his return,
he received an edict to deliberate on the establishment of the seven suburban altars, the three Yōng ceremonies, the grand archery ritual, and the rites for nourishing the elderly.
When Xiǎnzōng ascended the throne,
Chōng submitted a memorial, saying:
“The Hàn dynasty has received the mandate a second time,
and still has the matter of the Fēngshàn sacrifices to attend to.
However, the rituals and music are fractured and incomplete,
and cannot serve as a model for future generations.
The Five Emperors did not follow each other's music,
and the Three Kings did not inherit each other's rituals.
The Great Hàn [should] establish its own rituals,
to serve as an example for a hundred generations.”
The emperor asked:
“How should the rituals and music be established?”
Chōng replied:
“The Hétú Kuòdì Xiàng says: ‘In the era of Hàn, ritual and music, cultured and refined, shall emerge.’
The Shàngshū Xuánjī Qín says: ‘When Emperor Hàn emerges,
his virtue shall be pervasive, and he shall create music,
naming it Yǔ.’”
The emperor approved of this
and issued an edict saying:
“For now, let us rename the office of Tàilèguān to Tàiyǔyuè,
and its songs and compositions
shall await a superior man.”
He then appointed Chōng as Shìzhōng.
Chōng wrote commentaries and debated difficulties,
and thus the Qìngshì Xué was established.
Bāo was devoted in his youth,
possessing great magnanimity.
From a young age, he inherited Chōng’s profession,
being broadly learned and clear-minded,
especially fond of ritual matters.
He often felt that the court's institutions were incomplete,
and admired Shūsūn Tōng for establishing the Hàn rituals and ceremonies.
Day and night he diligently studied,
pondering and concentrating,
holding writing implements in his arms when sleeping,
and reciting documents when walking.
When an idea came to him,
he would forget where he was going.
He was initially recommended as Xiàolián,
then twice promoted to Yǔ Lìng.
He governed people with ritual
and transformed customs with virtue.
At that time, five robbers from another commandery entered the borders of Yǔ.
The officials apprehended them.
Mǎ Yán, the Tàishǒu of Chénliú, heard of this and fiercely detested them,
secretly instructing the county to kill them.
Bāo ordered his officials, saying:
“One who takes a human life,
Heaven will also take his.
Gāoyáo did not impose the death penalty for robbery,
and Guǎn Zhòng, encountering robbers, promoted them to public office.
Now, to obey the instruction and kill them
is to go against Heaven’s will
and to follow the prefecture's intention;
the punishment for this would be severe.
If I can preserve these men’s lives and suffer the consequences myself,
that is what I wish.”
So he did not have them killed.
Yán impeached Bāo for being weak and indecisive,
and he was dismissed from office and returned to the commandery,
serving as Gōngcáo.
Bāo was appointed Bóshì.
It so happened that Sùzōng desired to establish Rítuè and Yuán Hé
in the second year issued an edict saying:
“The Hétú states: ‘When the Red Nine convene, there will be prosperity;
in the tenth generation, there will be glory;
in the eleventh, there will be revival.’
The Shàngshū Xuánjīqián states: ‘He recounted Yáo’s governance of the world,
established Rítuè,
and followed the culture of Táng.’
I, a young and humble man,
am entrusted with the end of this cycle.
How can I continue the revival,
exalt and expand the achievements of my ancestors,
and benevolently aid the common people?
The Dìmìng Yàn states: ‘He followed Yáo’s virtue
and set the period to establish the image.’
Moreover, the steps of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors,
though superior or inferior, followed different paths.
How much more so I, who am dull and ignorant,
and unable to bear such a responsibility.
Though I wish to follow them,
there is no way for me to do so.
Whenever I see the diagrams and writings,
I feel ashamed in my heart.”
Bāo knew the emperor’s intention to initiate new creations,
and thus submitted a memorial, saying:
“In ancient times, when the Sages received the mandate and became kings,
none failed to establish rites and compose music
to manifest their merits and virtues.
Achievements led to the composition of music,
and transformative governance led to the establishment of rites.
This was to rectify worldly customs,
attract auspicious omens,
and enable the myriad people to receive blessings from August Heaven.
Now, August Heaven has bestowed blessings,
and auspicious omens have arrived in abundance.
The signs for creation
are more profound than words.
It is fitting to establish cultural regulations
and complete the Hàn Rítuè,
thereby grandly manifesting the splendid virtues of our ancestors.”
The memorial was sent down to the Tàicháng.
Tàicháng Cháo Kān believed that it was a great undertaking for a whole generation,
not something Bāo could decide,
and therefore it should not be approved.
The Emperor knew that his officials were constrained
and difficult to cooperate with in initiating new ventures.
The court's ritual statutes
should be promptly established.
The following year, he again issued an edict, saying:
“I, due to my lack of virtue,
have received the grand legacy of my ancestors.
Recently, phoenixes have repeatedly gathered,
and qilins and dragons have arrived together.
Sweet dew has fallen at night,
and auspicious grains have abundantly grown.
Such phenomena as the red grass
have been recorded by the historians.
I, day and night, revere and fear,
yet upwardly I have nothing to manifest the achievements of my predecessors,
and downwardly I have nothing to adequately respond to these spiritual omens.
Hàn inherited the remnants of Qín,
and rites were broken and music collapsed.
Moreover, following old customs,
it is not yet something to be observed and reviewed.
If there is anyone who understands its principles,
let each exert their abilities.”
Bāo read the edict
and sighed, saying to the scholars:
“In the past, Xī Sī praised Lǔ,
and Kǎo Pǔ sang of Yīn.
Indeed, it is the beauty of a subject’s conduct
to, by righteousness, make his sovereign illustrious, and to exhaust his loyalty to manifest his lord.
When it comes to benevolence, one should not yield.
Why should I decline?!”
Therefore, he submitted another memorial,
fully explaining the essence of rites and music,
and the intention to reform them.
Bāo was appointed Shìzhōng.
He accompanied the emperor on a southern tour.
Upon his return,
the matter was sent down to the Sāngōng.
Before a memorial could be presented,
an edict summoned Xuánwǔ Sīmǎ Bān Gù,
〔一０〕to inquire about the appropriateness of reforming and establishing the ritual system.
Gù said:
“Many scholars in the capital
are capable of explaining rites.
It would be advisable to broadly gather them
to jointly discuss the pros and cons.”
The Emperor said:
“The proverb says, ‘If you build a house by the roadside,
it won’t be finished in three years.’
Those who convene to discuss rites
are called ‘a crowd in dispute,’
〔一一〕they mutually raise doubts and differences,
and the brush cannot be put down.
In the past, when Yáo composed Dàzhāng,
one Kuí was enough.”
〔一二〕In the first month of the first year of Zhānghé,
Bāo was summoned to Jiādé Mén.
The Xiǎohuángmén was ordered to carry the twelve chapters of Shūsūn Tōng’s Hàn Yí,
which Bān Gù had submitted,
and the emperor instructed Bāo, saying:
“These regulations are scattered and brief,
and many do not conform to the classics.
〔一三〕Now, they should be corrected according to the rites,
so they can be implemented.
Apply your utmost effort in compiling and composing them at Nángōng and Dōngguān.”
Having received the command,
Bāo then arranged the ritual matters in order,
following the old statutes,
and incorporating texts from the Wǔjīng and chèn jì.
He compiled and arranged the systems for the beginning and end of capping, marriage, auspicious and inauspicious events, from the Son of Heaven to commoners,
resulting in one hundred and fifty chapters.
These were written on bamboo slips two chi and four cun long.
In the twelfth month of that year, he submitted them.
The Emperor, knowing that consensus was difficult to achieve among the various opinions,
merely accepted them,
and did not again order the relevant officials to review and present them.
Soon after, the Emperor died,
and Hè Dì ascended the throne.
Bāo then wrote commentaries for them.
The Emperor subsequently introduced the new rites with two chapters.
Bāo was promoted to Jiān Yǔlín Zuǒqí.
〔一四〕In the fourth year of Yǒngyuán,
he was transferred to Shèshēng Xiàowèi.
Later, Tàiwèi Zhāng Pú, Shàngshū Zhāng Mǐn and others memorialized that Bāo had compiled the Hàn Rítuè,
thereby disrupting the sacred arts,
and deserved punishment.
Though the Emperor shelved their memorial,
the Hàn Rítuè was ultimately not implemented.
While Bāo was Shèshēng,
there were over a hundred unburied coffins in the barracks.
Bāo personally inspected them
and inquired about the reasons.
The officials replied:
“Most of these are people who died without heirs since the Jiànwǔ era,
and thus could not be buried.”
Bāo was saddened
and bought empty land for them,
burying all those without owners,
and setting up sacrifices for them.
He was transferred to Chéngmén Xiàowèi and Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng.
At that time, there was an epidemic.
Bāo visited the sick,
provided medicine,
and managed the gruel,
saving many lives.
In the seventh year,
he was sent out as Hénèi Tàishǒu.
At that time, there was a great drought in spring and summer,
and grain prices soared.
Upon Bāo’s arrival,
he reduced officials and combined duties,
removed corrupt and cruel individuals,
and abundant rain fell several times.
That autumn brought a great harvest,
the common people had enough,
and all the refugees returned.
Later, he was dismissed for falsely reporting disasters.
After a while, he was summoned,
transferred twice,
and again became Shìzhōng.
Bāo was learned and knowledgeable about ancient matters,
and was considered the patriarch of scholars.
In the fourteenth year,
he died in office.
He authored twelve chapters of Tōngyì,
one hundred and twenty chapters of Yǎnjīng Zálùn,
and also transmitted forty-nine chapters of the Lǐjì,
teaching over a thousand students,
and the Qìng Shì learning subsequently spread throughout the world.
An argument states: In the early Hàn dynasty, when the world was newly settled,
the imperial regulations were unwritten.
Shúsūn Tōng largely adopted the rites from the classics
and selectively incorporated Qín laws.
Although he adapted to circumstances and observed the times,
and thus remedied the prevailing dilapidation,
the exemplary institutions of the former kings were largely lacking.
This is why people like Jiǎ Yì, Zhòngshū, Wáng Jí, and Liú Xiàng
were unable to cease their indignation and sighs.
With the far-sighted plans and brilliant virtues of Wén and Xuān,
which ultimately none could employ,
it is evident that when viewed from the perspective of Yān,
there was much left undone.
Xiàozhāng often spoke of the former kings,
and vigorously initiated new undertakings,
specifically commissioning ritual officials
to compile and establish national laws.
These were indeed matters of grand and abundant virtue.
However, the endeavor was cut short by Heaven's calculations,
and the proposals were discarded due to heterodox views.
Thus, this Way ultimately fell again.
The Three Kings did not inherit rites from one another,
and the Five Emperors did not share the same music.
This is why Xián and Jīng had different melodies,
and Zhōngdū differed greatly.
Moreover, as the workings of things shift and change,
and human emotions and circumstances undergo myriad transformations,
institutions cannot keep pace with their flowing changes,
and fixed standards are insufficient to define their flourishing growth.
This is indeed what rulers of the world ought to modify and supplement.
Furthermore, music is no longer Kúi or Xiāng,
yet new sounds arise to replace it.
Laws are no longer those of Gāo or Sū,
yet regulations are frequently changed.
〔一０〕Why then is there only suspicion
when it comes to revising and mending old texts?
〔一一〕Rites, oh rites!
How can it be so?
〔一二〕
Zhèng Xuán, courtesy name Kāngchéng,
was a native of Gāomì, Běihǎi.
His eighth-generation ancestor, Chóng,
was a Shàngshū Púyè during the reign of Emperor Āi.
As a youth, Xuán was a village magistrate.
Whenever he had leave,
he would constantly go to the academic institutions.
He did not enjoy being an official,
and his father often became angry with him,
but could not stop him.
Thus, he went to the Imperial Academy to study,
and apprenticed himself to Dìwǔ Yuánxiān of Jīngzhào,
first becoming proficient in Jīng's Yì, Gōngyáng Chūnqiū, Sāntǒng Lì, and Jiǔzhāng Suànshù.
He also studied Zhōuguān, Lǐjì, Zuǒshì Chūnqiū, Hánshī, and Gǔwén Shàngshū under Zhāng Gōngzǔ of Dōngjùn.
Believing there was no one in Shāndōng worth asking,
he then traveled west into Guān,
and through Lú Zhí of Zhuójùn,
served Mǎ Róng of Fúfēng.
Mǎ Róng had over four hundred disciples,
with more than fifty advanced students.
Mǎ Róng was habitually proud and distinguished.
While Xuán was under his tutelage,
he was unable to meet him for three years,
so Mǎ Róng had his advanced disciples teach Xuán.
Xuán studied day and night,
never showing laziness or weariness.
It happened that Mǎ Róng gathered his students to discuss and examine the charts and weft texts.
Hearing that Xuán was skilled in calculations,
he summoned him to meet him on the upper floor.
Xuán then took the opportunity to question him on various doubtful points,
and after finishing his questions, he took his leave and returned.
Mǎ Róng sighed deeply and said to his disciples,
"Now that Zhèng Shēng is leaving,
my Way will move eastward."
After his studies,
Xuán returned to his hometown more than ten years later.
His family was poor.
He worked as a tenant farmer in Dōnglái,
and several hundreds or thousands of students followed him.
When the Partisan Prohibitions arose,
he, along with Sūn Sōng and over forty others from the same commandery, were all banned from office.
He then secluded himself to pursue his studies of the classics,
shutting his door and not going out.
At that time, Hé Xiū of Rènchéng was fond of the Gōngyáng school,
and consequently wrote Gōngyáng Mòshǒu,
Zuǒshì Gāohuāng,
and Gǔliáng Fèijí.
Xuán then 'unblocked the obstinacy' (fā mòshǒu),
'applied needles to the vital points' (zhēn gāohuāng),
and 'raised the afflicted from their illness' (qǐ fèijí).
Hé Xiū saw this and sighed, saying,
"Kāngchéng has entered my chamber,
taken my spear,
and attacked me with it!"
Initially,
after the Zhongxing period,
Fàn Shēng, Chén Yuán, Lǐ Yù, and Jiǎ Kuí debated the ancient and modern schools.
Later, Mǎ Róng responded to Liú Guī, the Administrator of Běidì, and Xuán responded to Hé Xiū.
Their arguments were profound and thorough,
and thus the ancient learning became clear.
At the end of Emperor Líng's reign,
the partisan prohibitions were lifted.
Dà Jiāngjūn Hé Jìn heard of Xuán and invited him to serve.
As Hé Jìn held great power and influence, the provinces and commanderies
dared not defy his will.
Thus, they coerced Xuán,
who had no choice but to go to him.
Hé Jìn provided him with a stool and staff,
treating him with great respect.
Xuán did not accept the court robes,
but met him wearing a common scarf.
He fled after one night.
He was sixty years old at the time,
and several thousands of disciples, such as Zhào Shāng from Hénèi, came from distant places.
Later, Hou Jiangjun Yuán Wěi memorialized to have him appointed as Shìzhōng,
but he did not go due to his father's mourning.
Guóxiàng Kǒng Róng deeply respected Xuán,
and even went barefoot to his door.
He instructed the county of Gāomì to specially establish a village for Xuán,
saying:
"In ancient Qí, 'Shìxiāng' (Scholar's Village) was established,
and Yuè had 'Jūnzǐjūn' (Gentlemen's Army);
both were meant to honor worthy individuals.
Master Zhèng is fond of learning and truly possesses bright virtue.
In the past, Tàishǐgōng, Tíngwèi Wúgōng, and Yèzhě Púyè Dènggōng
were all famous officials of Hàn.
Also, among the Four White-Haired Elders of Nánshān, there were Yuángōng and Xiàhuánggōng,
who concealed their brilliance and hid their splendor,
and whose nobility was praised by the world,
all being addressed as 'Gōng'.
Therefore, 'Gōng' is a proper title for benevolent and virtuous individuals,
not necessarily limited to the Sānshì Dàfū.
Now, Master Zhèng's village should be called 'Zhènggōng Xiāng'.
In the past, Yúgōng of Dōnghǎi had only one virtue,
yet he still admonished his villagers to broaden their gates and entrances.
How much more so with the virtue of Zhènggōng,
who should not lack a road for four horses!
His gate entrance should be widened
to allow high carriages to pass,
and be named 'Tōngdé Mén'."
Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) moved the capital to Cháng'ān (長安).
The Grandees and Ministers recommended Xuán (玄) to be the Chancellor of Zhào (趙).
The roads were cut off, so he did not arrive.
When the Yellow Turbans (黃巾) raided Qīngbù (青部),
he took refuge in Xúzhōu (徐州).
Táo Qiān (陶謙), the Governor of Xúzhōu (徐州), received him with the courtesy due to a teacher and friend.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān (建安) (196 CE),
he returned from Xúzhōu (徐州) to Gāomì (高密).
On the way, he encountered tens of thousands of Yellow Turban (黃巾) rebels.
Seeing Xuán (玄), they all bowed,
and agreed not to enter the county's borders.
Later, Xuán (玄) suffered from a severe illness.
Reflecting on his life,
he wrote a letter to admonish his son, Yì'ēn (益恩), saying:
"My family was formerly poor.
I was not tolerated by my parents and younger siblings.
I left the lowly position of a clerk
to travel and study in the capitals of Zhōu (周) and Qín (秦),
and journeyed through the regions of Yōu (幽), Bīng (并), Yǎn (兗), and Yù (豫).
I had the good fortune to meet influential people in office
and great reclusive scholars.
Those who achieved success all followed and presented their hands [in greeting],
and from them I received knowledge.
Thus, I extensively researched the Six Arts (六蓺)
and broadly read commentaries and records.
From time to time, I glimpsed the profound mysteries of esoteric texts and prognostications.
When I was over forty,
I returned to provide for my parents,
leasing land to sow and cultivate,
to enjoy the mornings and evenings.
I encountered eunuchs who seized power,
and was imprisoned due to the party proscriptions.
Fourteen years passed,
and then I received an amnesty decree.
I was recommended as a 'Talented and Upright Man of the Way' (賢良方正有道)
and appointed to the staff of the Grand General and the Three Ministers (三司).
The Public Carriage (公車) summoned me twice,
my name was listed alongside others,
to become a Prime Minister early.
However, those several gentlemen,
with their admirable virtue and great refinement,
were truly capable royal ministers,
and thus deserved to be ranked first.
I considered myself
unfit for such a role.
I only wished to elaborate on the fundamental principles of the Former Sages
and to rectify the discrepancies among the Hundred Schools (百家).
I also hoped to exert all my talent,
and so I declined the command.
Then, the Yellow Turbans (黃巾) caused havoc,
and like floating duckweed, I drifted north and south,
before returning to my home region.
This year,
I am already seventy.
My physical condition has long been in decline,
and I still make mistakes.
According to the rites and canons,
it is fitting that I hand over family affairs.
Now I declare my old age to you,
and entrust you with all matters.
I will live in quiet retirement to nurture my nature,
and ponder deeply to complete my work.
Unless it is to receive a command from the ruler of the state,
to inquire about the worries of relatives,
to show respect at ancestral tombs,
or to observe nature in the fields,
how could I ever lean on my staff and go out the door?
All family matters, great and small,
you shall henceforth manage.
Alas, you are a solitary man,
with no siblings to rely on.
Strive to seek the way of a noble person,
study diligently without ceasing,
be respectful and cautious in your demeanor,
to approach those of virtue.
Eminent reputation is established among colleagues and friends,
and virtuous conduct is built upon one's own resolve.
If you achieve renown,
it will also bring honor to your ancestors.
How can you not ponder this deeply?
How can you not ponder this deeply?
Although I have no lineage of official robes and caps,
I have the high virtue of yielding high office.
I am content with the merit of my discussions and commentaries,
hoping not to bring shame to future generations.
What I am most vexed about in my final years
is merely that the tombs of my deceased parents are not yet completed,
and the numerous books I cherished have mostly rotted away,
so I could not have them copied and finalized in the ritual hall
to pass on to suitable persons.
The sun is setting in the west,
how can this be accomplished?
My family is now somewhat better off than in the past;
work hard and seize the opportune moment,
do not worry about hunger or cold.
Be frugal in food and drink,
and simple in clothing.
If you are temperate in these two things,
it will still leave me with few regrets.
If you neglect and forget these words,
then so be it!"
At that time, Grand General Yuán Shào (袁紹) commanded the armies in Jìzhōu (冀州).
He sent an envoy to invite Xuán (玄).
When the guests assembled,
Xuán (玄) arrived last,
and was ushered to the seat of honor.
He was eight *chǐ* (尺) tall,
could drink one *hú* (斛) of wine,
had beautiful eyebrows and bright eyes,
and a warm and imposing demeanor.
Many of Shào's (紹) guests were heroes and outstanding individuals,
all possessing talent and eloquence.
Seeing Xuán (玄) as a scholar,
they did not initially consider him a broad-minded person.
They competed in presenting various heterodox theories,
with a hundred schools of thought arising.
Xuán (玄) debated and responded appropriately,
revealing knowledge beyond their questions,
and all learned things they had never heard before.
No one failed to sigh in admiration and submit.
At that time, Yìng Shào (應劭) of Rǔnán (汝南) also sought refuge with Shào (紹).
He then praised himself, saying:
"How about Yìng Zhōngyuǎn (應中遠), the former Administrator of Tàishān (泰山), calling himself your disciple, facing north?"
Xuán (玄) smiled and said:
"At Zhòngní's (仲尼) (Confucius') gate, disciples were tested by the Four Subjects (四科);
followers like Huí (回) and Cì (賜) were not known by their official ranks."
Shào (劭) showed a look of shame.
Shào (紹) then recommended Xuán (玄) as a *Màocái* (茂才),
and memorialized him as Left Gentleman of the Household (左中郎將),
but he accepted neither.
The Public Carriage (公車) summoned him to be Grand Minister of Agriculture (大司農),
and provided him with an *ānchē* (安車) (comfortable carriage).
Local officials along his route were to greet and send him off.
However, Xuán (玄) pleaded illness and requested to return home.
In the spring of the fifth year (200 CE),
he dreamt that Kǒngzǐ (孔子) (Confucius) told him:
"Arise,
arise!
This year is the *chén* (辰) year.
Next year is the *sì* (巳) year."
After he awoke,
he combined it with a prognostication text,
and knew that his life was destined to end.
Soon after, he fell ill.
At that time, Yuán Shào (袁紹) and Cáo Cāo (曹操) were in a standoff at Guāndù (官度).
Shào (紹) ordered his son, Tán (譚), to send an envoy to compel Xuán (玄) to join the army.
Having no choice,
he traveled while ill to Yuánchéng (元城) County.
His illness became critical, and he could not proceed.
He died in the sixth month of that year,
at the age of seventy-four.
His dying wish was for a simple burial.
More than a thousand people, from commandery governors downwards, who had once been his students,
attended the funeral wearing mourning clothes.
His disciples collectively compiled Xuán's (玄) answers to his students' questions on the Five Classics,
creating eight chapters of *Zhèng Zhì* (鄭志), modeled after the *Lúnyǔ* (論語) (*Analects*).

All of Xuán's (玄) annotations included the *Zhōu Yì* (周易), *Shàngshū* (尚書), *Máo Shī* (毛詩), *Yílǐ* (儀禮), *Lǐjì* (禮記), *Lúnyǔ* (論語), *Xiàojīng* (孝經), *Shàngshū Dàchuán* (尚書大傳), *Zhōnghòu* (中候), and *Qiánxiànglì* (乾象歷).
He also wrote *Tiānwén Qīzhènglùn* (天文七政論), *Lǔlǐ Dìxiáyì* (魯禮禘祫義), *Liùyìlùn* (六蓺論), *Máo Shī Pǔ* (毛詩譜), *Bó Xǔ Shèn Wǔjīng Yìyì* (駮許慎五經異義), and *Dá Lín Xiàocún Zhōulǐ Nán* (荅臨孝存周禮難).
In total, these works amounted to over a million words.
Xuán (玄)'s style in commentaries and instructions was substantial,
and some well-versed scholars criticized it for being verbose.
However, regarding his thorough mastery of the classics and commentaries,
he was renowned as a pure Confucian scholar,
and scholars in Qí (齊) and Lǔ (魯) revered him as their patriarch.
Among his disciples, Xī Lǜ (郗慮) of Shānyáng (山陽) became Grandee Remonstrant (御史大夫);
Wáng Jī (王基) of Dōnglái (東萊) and Cuī Yǎn (崔琰) of Qīnghé (清河) became famous in the world.
Also, Guó Yuān (國淵) and Rèn Jiǎ (任嘏) of Lè'ān (樂安)
were both young boys at the time.
Xuán (玄) called Yuān (淵) a "national talent" (國器)
and said Jiǎ (嘏) possessed moral virtue.
He also discerned and promoted many others,
and they all turned out as he predicted.
Xuán (玄) had only one son, Yì'ēn (益恩).
When Kǒng Róng (孔融) was in Běihǎi (北海),
he recommended Yì'ēn (益恩) as a *Xiàolián* (孝廉).
When Róng (融) was besieged by the Yellow Turbans (黃巾),
Yì'ēn (益恩) rushed to his aid and died in the calamity.
Yì'ēn (益恩) left behind an unborn child.
Xuán (玄), seeing that the child's hand pattern resembled his own,
named him Xiǎotóng (小同).
A commentary states: Since the Qín dynasty burned the Six Classics,
the sagely writings perished into dust.
When the Hàn dynasty arose,
various scholars somewhat restored the classical texts;
by the Eastern Capital period,
scholars also each formed their own schools of thought.
However, those who adhered to the texts
rigidly clung to what they had received;
different interpretations proliferated,
mutually attacking and provoking each other.
This consequently led to the Classics having several schools,
each school having several interpretations.
Some commentaries and annotations sometimes even exceeded a million words,
making students toil hard but achieve little,
and later generations confused, unable to find the correct path.
Zhèng Xuán encompassed the great canons,
gathered all schools,
cut out prolixities and falsehoods,
and revised and corrected omissions and errors.
From then on, scholars generally knew where to turn.
My grandfather, Lord Yùzhāng, often examined the classical interpretations of former Confucians,
and excelled beyond Zhèng Xuán,
always believing that even the disciples of Zhòngní could not surpass him.
When he taught students,
he exclusively used Zhèng's family methods, it is said.
An encomium says: The Fùpíng lineage,
continued the family through generations.
Bórén was the first to return,
rectifying our national sacrifices.
Xuán's definitions were divergent,
praised cultivation of rites but lacked them.
Confucius's writings were thus clarified,
but the Hàn dynasty's commentaries were interrupted.
Biographies of Zhèng, Fàn, Chén, Jiǎ, and Zhāng, Number Twenty-Six
Zhèng Xīng, courtesy name Shàogàn,
was a native of Kāifēng, Hénán.
In his youth, he studied the Gōngyáng Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Later, he excelled at the Zuǒ Commentary,
consequently applying profound thought
to thoroughly understand its purport,
and all his peers took him as their teacher.
During the Tiānfèng reign,
he brought his disciples to follow Liú Xīn in expounding upon important principles.
Liú Xīn admired Xīng's talent,
and ordered him to compile regulations, commentaries, and explanations of commentaries,
as well as to collate the Sāntǒng Calendar.
When Gēngshǐ was enthroned,
he appointed Sīzhí Lǐ Sōng to act as Prime Minister.
Lǐ Sōng first entered Cháng'ān,
and appointed Xīng as Chief Clerk,
ordering him to return and respectfully escort the moving of the capital.
All of Gēngshǐ's generals were from east of the mountains,
and all advised him to stay in Luòyáng.
Xīng persuaded Gēngshǐ, saying:
"Your Majesty rose from Jīngchǔ,
your authority and policies have not yet been implemented.
Yet, as soon as you established your reign title,
heroes and outstanding figures west of the mountains vied to punish Wáng Mǎng,
opening the passes and welcoming you in the suburbs—
why is this?
This is because the world jointly suffered from the tyrannical government of the Wáng family,
and yearned for the former beneficence of Gāozǔ.
Now, if you do not pacify them for long,
your subject fears that the common people will become alienated,
and bandits will rise again.
The Spring and Autumn Annals records 'Qí Xiǎobái entered Qí',
without calling him marquis,
because he had not yet paid respects at the ancestral temple.
Now, those who advise wish to first pacify the Chìméi and then enter the Pass.
This is to not understand the root and contend over the branches.
I fear that the state's stronghold will shift to Hángǔ Pass,
and even if you reside in Luòyáng,
how can you rest peacefully?"
Gēngshǐ said:
"I have decided to go westward."
He appointed Xīng as Grand Master of Remonstrance,
ordering him to stabilize Guānxī and the three provinces of Shuòfāng, Liáng, and Yì.
Upon his return, he was appointed Inspector of Liáng Province.
At that time, there were rebels in Tiānshuǐ,
who attacked and killed the Administrator of the commandery.
Xīng was dismissed due to this incident.
At that time, the Chìméi entered the Pass,
and the eastern route was impassable.
Xīng thereupon went west to Wěi Xiāo.
Wěi Xiāo courteously invited him with an open mind,
but Xīng was ashamed to yield to him,
feigning illness and not rising.
Wěi Xiāo prided and flattered himself,
always thinking that the Western Earl had reappeared.
He then discussed with his generals establishing himself as king.
Xīng heard of this and persuaded Wěi Xiāo, saying:
"A commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals says: 'A mouth that does not utter loyal and trustworthy words is dumb;
an ear that does not listen to the harmony of the five notes is deaf.'
Recently, when the generals gathered,
perhaps no loyal and trustworthy words were uttered?
And Your Great General's listening,
perhaps it was partial and failed to discern?
In the past, King Wén inherited a legacy of accumulated virtue,
and in addition possessed sagely wisdom.
Even though he controlled two-thirds of the empire,
he still served the Yīn dynasty.
When King Wǔ ascended the throne,
eight hundred feudal lords, without prior consultation, gathered together,
and all said, 'Zhòu can be attacked!'
Yet King Wǔ, because he did not yet know the Mandate of Heaven,
returned his troops and waited for the opportune moment.
Even Gāozǔ, when campaigning and attacking for many years,
still used the title Duke of Pèi when leading his army.
Now, though your excellent virtue is brilliant,
you do not have the ancestral Zhōu's blessings through generations;
though your might and strategy are formidable,
you do not yet have the achievements of Gāozǔ.
To wish to undertake an inappropriate action
is to clearly invite calamity and disaster.
Is this not impermissible?
I only ask, General, that you observe this."
Wěi Xiāo ultimately did not declare himself king.
Later, he widely established official positions
in order to exalt himself.
Xīng again advised Wěi Xiāo, saying:
"Now, the titles of Colonel, Grand Master of the Central Court, and officials with imperial credentials are all instruments of a king,
not something a subject should appoint.
Confucius said: 'Only instruments and names
cannot be lent to others.'
That which cannot be lent to others
also cannot be bestowed by one on others.
It offers no real advantage,
but harms your reputation.
This is not the way to honor your superior."
Wěi Xiāo was troubled by this and stopped.
