When Wěi Xiāo sent his son Xún to serve at court,
and Xún was about to depart,
Xīng used Xún to request to return and bury his parents.
Wěi Xiāo did not grant this, but instead moved Xīng's residence
and increased his rank and courtesies.
Xīng entered and saw Wěi Xiāo, saying:
"Previously, encountering the rebellion of the Chìméi,
and as an old acquaintance of the General,
I therefore dared to entrust myself to your eminent virtue.
Fortunately, I received the grace of your protection,
and again managed to preserve my life.
I have heard that the way of serving one's parents is:
when they are alive, serve them with rites;
when they are dead, bury them with rites;
sacrifice to them with rites.
I diligently attend to this,
and dare not neglect it.
Now, because my parents are not yet buried,
I request to retire.
If you, by increasing my rank and moving my residence,
again detain me,
this would be using my parents as bait.
This is extremely disrespectful!
General, why would you employ such a person?"
Wěi Xiāo said:
"Am I, Wěi Xiāo, then not worthy enough to keep you for that reason?"
Xīng said:
"General, you occupy the territory of seven commanderies,
command the masses of the Qiāng and Hú tribes,
and thus support the current court.
No one's virtue is greater than yours,
and no one's might is heavier.
If I stay here, I would be an envoy acting on your authority;
if I enter the court, I will surely be a minister forming a tripod with others.
I, Xīng,
am one who follows convention.
I dare not live in deep seclusion.
By relying on the General to seek advancement,
I do not worry about not achieving it;
by relying on the General to seek entry into court,
why worry about not being close (to the emperor)?
This plan of Xīng's is not against the General's intentions.
I, Xīng, truly made this request for my parents,
and it cannot be stopped.
I wish to leave my wife and children behind and return alone to bury them.
General, what then is there to suspect?"
Wěi Xiāo said:
"Excellent."
He promptly prepared provisions for him,
and then ordered him to go east together with his wife and children.
This was the sixth year of Jiànwǔ.
Palace Censor Dù Lín, who had previously resided with Xīng in Lǒngyòu,
thereupon recommended him, saying:
"I humbly observe that Zhèng Xīng of Hénán
holds firmly to righteousness,
is devoted to and delights in the Books of Poetry and History,
loves antiquity and has extensive knowledge.
When faced with doubts, he is not confused,
and possesses the virtues of Gōngsūn Qiáo and Guān Shèfù.
He is fit to attend the imperial court
and manage affairs of secrecy.
In the past, Zhāng Zhòng served in Zhōu,
diligently assisted King Xuān,
and the poets were pleased and rejoiced.
I beg Your Majesty to listen carefully and investigate a little,
to aid in your myriad tasks."
Thereupon, he was summoned to be Grand Master of the Central Court.
in the last month of the third lunar month,
there was a solar eclipse.
Xīng thereupon submitted a memorial, saying: The *Chūnqiū* records that when Heaven acts contrary to the seasons, it is a disaster;
when Earth acts contrary to its nature, it is an omen of evil;
when humans act contrary to virtue, it is a rebellion.
When there is rebellion, omens of evil and disasters arise.
Since last year,
punishments
have appeared repeatedly.
I suspect that those in charge have considerable shortcomings.
According to the *Chūnqiū*: "In the seventeenth year of Zhāo Gōng, in the sixth month of summer, on the *jiǎxū* day of the new moon,
there was a solar eclipse."
The commentary says: "When the sun has passed its due time but has not yet arrived,
and the three luminaries suffer disaster,
then the hundred officials reduce their allowances,
the ruler does not hold court,
he avoids and moves for a time,
music is played and
drums are beaten,
prayers are offered with offerings,
and historians offer pronouncements."
the pure *qián* (Heaven) principle is dominant,
and *yīn* energy has not yet begun to operate,
so this disaster is particularly severe.
If the state lacks good
governance,
then punishments will be seen in the sun and moon.
The coming of transformations and misfortunes
must not be taken lightly.
The crucial point lies in following the will of the people
and selecting suitable individuals for positions.
suitable but still employed him;
this was him bending his own sagacity
to follow the will of the people.
Qí Huán returned to power and appointed Guǎn Zhòng as prime minister,
and Jìn Wén returned to his state and entrusted Xí Hú;
this
was not being selfish with their own interests,
but selecting suitable individuals for positions.
but it is not decided in time.
Rumors circulate on the roads,
all saying,
"The court wants to employ meritorious officials."
If meritorious officials are employed, then human positions will be mistaken.
I wish Your Majesty would emulate Táng and Yú above,
and observe Qí and Jìn below,
to perfect the virtue of bending oneself to follow the multitude,
and to achieve the meritorious deed of your officials yielding to the virtuous.
The moon is the celestial symbol for officials;
if the ruler is too harsh and hasty, then his subordinates become anxious and pressured,
hence the swift movement.
In the first month of this year, there was abundant frost;
since then,
it has generally been cold days.
This
is also the punishment for haste and fault.
Heaven treats a virtuous and sagely ruler
like a kind father treats a filial son;
it repeatedly and earnestly admonishes,
wishing for him to change his governance.
Therefore, disasters and transformations appear
repeatedly;
this is indeed a blessing for the state.
Now, Your Majesty is highly intelligent, but your officials are anxious and pressured.
You should contemplate a policy of gentleness and restraint,
and give attention to the laws of the *Hóngfàn*,
extensively
gather broad counsel,
and accept the strategies of your subordinates.
The Emperor once asked Xīng about the suburban sacrifices,
saying,
"I wish to decide it by *chèn* texts,
what do you think?"
Xīng replied,
"I do not advocate *chèn* texts."
The Emperor angrily said,
"You do not advocate *chèn* texts,
do you disapprove of them?"
Xīng, in fear, said,
"There are things in books that I have not studied,
but I do not disapprove of anything."
The Emperor's anger then subsided.
Xīng frequently spoke about government affairs,
adhering to the classics and upholding righteousness.
His writings were gentle and elegant.
However, because he was not skilled in *chèn* texts, he could not be fully employed.
In the ninth year,
he was sent to supervise the Zhēngnán and Jīnú camps in Jīnxiāng.
At that time, the General who Conquers the South, Cén Péng, was assassinated.
Xīng took command of his camp,
and then, with Grand Marshal Wú Hàn, attacked Gōngsūn Shù.
After Shù died,
an imperial edict ordered Xīng to remain stationed in Chéngdū.
A short while later,
a palace censor impeached Xīng for privately buying slaves and maids while on imperial mission.
He was demoted to Magistrate of Liánsháo.
At that time, after years of rebellion and chaos,
the commanderies and counties were desolate and barren.
Xīng was just about to build city walls,
and restore rituals and education to civilize them,
when he was dismissed due to this incident.
Xīng loved ancient learning,
especially excelling in *Zuǒshì* and *Zhōuguān*.
He was skilled in calendrical calculations.
From Dù Lín, Huán Tán, Wèi Hóng, and others of their kind,
none failed to consult him.
People of that era who spoke of *Zuǒshì* often traced their lineage to Xīng.
However, Jiǎ Kuí transmitted his father's teachings,
hence the schools of Zhèng and Jiǎ.
Xīng left Liánsháo,
and afterwards did not re-enter officialdom.
He taught as a guest in Wénxiāng.
The Three Ducal Ministers repeatedly invited him, but he refused to respond,
and died at home.
His son was Zhòng.
Zhòng, courtesy name Zhòngshī.
At the age of twelve,
he studied the *Zuǒshì Chūnqiū* under his father.
He devoted himself to learning,
understood the *Sāntǒng Lì*,
and authored the *Chūnqiū Nánjì Tiáolì*.
He was also proficient in the *Yì* and *Shī* classics,
and was well-known in his time.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
the Crown Prince and Liú Jīng, the King of Shānyáng,
through the Central Commandant of Tiger-Bane, Liáng Sōng, sent silk as a betrothal gift to invite Zhòng,
wishing to discuss righteousness,
and to grant him access in and out of the palace.
Zhòng said to Sōng,
"The Crown Prince is the heir apparent;
there is no principle of external relations.
The Hàn dynasty has old prohibitions,
and vassal kings should not privately communicate with guests."
He thus declined the invitation.
Sōng then subtly hinted to Zhòng
that "the wishes of a superior
cannot be defied."
Zhòng replied,
"Violating prohibitions and incurring guilt
is not as good as upholding righteousness and dying."
The Crown Prince and Jīng heard this and were impressed,
and did not force him.
When the Liáng clan's affair failed,
many guests were implicated,
but only Zhòng was not tainted by the accusations.
In the early years of [Yǒngpíng],
he was appointed to the office of Sīkōng.
As an erudite scholar of the classics, he served as a Gěishìzhōng.
He was twice promoted to Yuèqí Sīmǎ,
and then remained a Gěishìzhōng.
At this time, the Northern Xiongnu sent envoys to seek a peace alliance.
In the eighth year,
Xiǎnzōng dispatched Zhòng, bearing imperial credentials, as an envoy to the Xiongnu.
When Zhòng arrived at Běitíng,
the barbarians wished to compel him to bow.
Zhòng refused to yield.
The Chányú was greatly enraged,
and besieged and imprisoned him,
denying him water and fire,
hoping to coerce Zhòng into submission.
Zhòng drew his sword and swore an oath to himself.
The Chányú, fearing him, desisted,
and instead sent an envoy to return to the capital with Zhòng.
The court debated whether to send another envoy to reciprocate.
Zhòng submitted a memorial, advising:
"Your servant humbly hears that the reason the Northern Chányú seeks to draw Han envoys
is to alienate the Southern Chányú's people
and to firm up the resolve of the Thirty-six Kingdoms.
Moreover, it is to proclaim Han's peace alliance,
boast to neighboring enemies,
cause those in the Western Regions who desire to convert to waver in hesitation,
and make those who long for their homeland despair of China.
Once a Han envoy arrives,
he becomes arrogant and overconfident.
If another is sent,
the barbarians will surely believe they have achieved their scheme,
and their ministers who had opposed the plan will no longer dare to speak.
If this happens,
the Southern court will be destabilized,
and the Wūhuán will become disaffected.
The Southern Chányú has long resided in Han territory,
fully understanding the situation and circumstances.
If they were to completely disintegrate,
they would immediately become a frontier menace.
Fortunately, there are now the troops of Dùliáo displaying their might on the northern frontier.
Even if we do not reciprocate,
they would not dare to cause trouble."
The Emperor did not heed him,
and again dispatched Zhòng.
Zhòng then submitted another statement:
"Your servant previously served as an envoy and did not bow to the Xiongnu.
The Chányú was angry and resentful,
hence he sent troops to besiege your servant.
Now that I am again bearing the imperial command,
I will surely be humiliated and oppressed.
Your servant truly cannot bear to hold the great Han's credentials and bow alone to those clad in felt and fur.
If the Xiongnu were to succeed in subduing your servant,
it would diminish the might of the great Han."
The Emperor did not listen.
Zhòng had no choice.
Once he set out,
he repeatedly submitted memorials from the road, firmly arguing his case.
An edict severely reprimanded Zhòng,
recalled him, and had him imprisoned at the Tíngwèi.
He was later pardoned and returned home.
Afterward, when the Emperor saw Xiongnu visitors,
he inquired about Zhòng's dispute with the Chányú over protocol.
They all said that it was widely known among the Xiongnu that Zhòng was spirited and brave,
surpassing even Sū Wǔ.
He was then recalled and appointed Jūnsīmǎ,
and sent with Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng Mǎ Liáo to attack Chēshī.
Upon reaching Dūnhuáng,
he was appointed Zhōnglángjiàng,
and made Protector of the Western Regions.
It happened that the Xiongnu were threatening Chēshī
and besieging the Wùjǐ Xiàowèi.
Zhòng dispatched troops to rescue them.
He was promoted to Wǔwēi Tàishǒu,
and conscientiously strengthened border defenses,
so the barbarians dared not invade.
He was promoted to Zuǒfēngyì,
and his administration gained renown.
In the sixth year of Jiànchū,
he replaced Dèng Biāo as Dàsīnóng.
At this time, Sùzōng debated re-establishing the salt and iron monopolies.
Zhòng advised against it, deeming it impossible.
Edicts repeatedly and severely reprimanded him,
even leading to his impeachment,
but Zhòng held firm and would not change his stance.
The Emperor did not comply.
In office, he was known for his integrity and uprightness.
Later, he received an imperial edict to compile the nineteen chapters of the "Spring and Autumn Annals."
In the eighth year,
he died in office.
His son, Ānshì,
also inherited the family profession,
serving as the Chánglè and Wèiyáng Jiùlìng.
During the Yán'guāng era,
Emperor Ān deposed the crown prince as Jìyīn Wáng.
Ānshì, along with Tàicháng Huán Yān and Tàipú Lái Lì, among others, jointly argued for justice and remonstrated.
When Emperor Shùn was enthroned,
Ānshì had already passed away.
He was posthumously granted money and silk,
and his son Liàng was appointed Láng.
Zhòng's great-grandson, Gōngyè,
has his own biography.
Fàn Shēng, courtesy name Biànqīng,
was a native of Dàijùn.
He was orphaned young
and lived with his maternal grandparents.
At nine, he mastered the Lúnyǔ and Xiàojīng.
When he grew older,
he studied Liángqiū Yì and Lǎozǐ,
and taught younger students.
Wáng Mǎng's Dàsīkōng, Wáng Yì, appointed Shēng as a Yìcáoshǐ.
At that time, Mǎng frequently launched military campaigns,
and taxes and levies greatly increased.
Shēng then sent a memorandum to Yì, saying:
"Your servant has heard that a child not causing concern to their parents is filial,
and a subordinate not criticizing their ruler is loyal.
Now, everyone praises the court as sagacious,
and all say the Duke is discerning.
Truly, the discerning see all,
and the sagacious hear all.
Yet today, the affairs of the world,
clear as the sun and moon,
and resounding as thunder,
are said by the court to be unseen,
and by the Duke to be unheard.
Then, to whom shall the common people cry out to Heaven?
If the Duke believes these things are right and does not speak,
then his error is small;
if he knows but follows orders,
then his error is great.
There is no way for the Duke to escape either of these two,
and it is fitting that the world places blame upon the Duke.
The court's utmost concern is that distant peoples are not submissive,
but your servant's grave worry is that those nearby are displeased.
Now, every action is contrary to the times,
and every matter is contrary to the Way.
We rush along the tracks of overturned chariots,
and test the boiling water after the deed is done.
The later the emergence, the more astonishing;
the later the deployment, the more dreadful.
It is springtime, the beginning of the year,
yet distant campaigns are launched.
Wild vegetables are insufficient,
fields are barren and uncultivated,
grain prices soar,
a hù reaching several thousand coins.
Officials and commoners are plunged into a fiery abyss,
they are no longer the nation's people.
If this continues,
then the Hú and Mò will guard the passes,
and the bandits of Qīng and Xú will be within the imperial curtains.
Your servant has one word
that can resolve the world's desperate situation
and relieve the common people's distress.
It cannot be put in writing;
I beg to be granted an audience
to fully express my thoughts."
Although Yì assented to his words,
he ultimately did not employ them.
Shēng claimed illness and requested to retire,
but Yì did not permit it,
ordering him to travel by post-chaise as an envoy to Shàngdǎng.
Shēng then joined forces with the Han army
and remained, not returning.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Guāngwǔ summoned him to Huáigōng,
appointed him Yìláng,
and promoted him to Bóshì.
He submitted a memorial, declining, saying:
"Your servant, along with Bóshì Liáng Gōng and Shānyáng Tàishǒu Lǚ Qiāng, both cultivate the Liángqiū Yì.
Both ministers are advanced in age,
and their classical learning is profoundly clear.
Yet, your servant has not retired in time
and stands alongside Gōng.
I deeply understand Qiāng's learning,
yet I am unable to surpass it.
I am ashamed and indebted to these two elders,
and have no face in the world.
To recite without practicing,
to know without speaking,
I cannot open my mouth to be a teacher of men.
I wish to decline the position of Bóshì to defer to Gōng and Qiāng."
The Emperor did not permit it,
but consequently respected him more,
frequently summoning him for audiences.
Whenever there was a major deliberation,
he would always be consulted.
The Grand Secretary (Shàngshū Lìng) Hán Xīn (韓歆) submitted a memorial,
wishing to establish Erudites (Bóshì) for the Fèi Shì Yì (費氏易) and Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū (左氏春秋).
An imperial edict was issued to deliberate on this proposal.
In the first month of the fourth year,
the imperial court's high officials (gōngqīng), grandees (dàfū), and Erudites
met at Yúntái (雲臺).
The Emperor said:
"Doctor Fàn (范博士) may step forward and speak clearly."
Shēng (升) rose and replied:
"The Zuǒ Shì (左氏) does not take Kǒng Zǐ (孔子) as its ancestor,
but originates from Qiū Míng (丘明).
The transmission from teacher to student
has no verifiable lineage.
Furthermore, it was not recognized by previous emperors,
so there is no reason for it to be established."
Thereupon, he debated with Hán Xīn (韓歆) and the Grand Master of Remonstrance (Tàizhōng Dàfū) Xǔ Shū (許淑) and others,
only ceasing at midday.
Shēng (升) withdrew and then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that if the ruler does not study the past,
he has no means to receive Heaven's mandate;
if ministers do not recount the old ways,
they have no means to serve their lord.
Your Majesty laments the deficiencies in scholarship,
exerts your mind on the classics and arts,
and desires broad knowledge,
hence divergent theories compete to advance.
Recently, an official requested the establishment of Erudites for the Jīng Shì Yì (京氏易);
the multitude of subordinates and officials
were unable to uphold what is correct.
Once Jīng Shì (京氏) was established,
Fèi Shì (費氏) felt resentment and expectation.
The Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū (左氏春秋), by analogy,
also hoped for establishment.
If Jīng (京) and Fèi (費) are adopted,
next will be Gāo Shì (高氏).
Among the Chūnqiū (春秋) schools,
there are also Zōu (騶) and Jiá (夾).
If the Zuǒ Shì (左氏) and Fèi Shì (費氏) are allowed to establish Erudites,
Gāo Shì (高氏), Zōu (騶), and Jiá (夾),
and other strange and unusual branches of the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng),
will all again seek establishment.
Each will have their own positions,
leading to discord and contention.
To follow them would be to deviate from the Dao (Dào);
not to follow them would be to lose popular support.
I fear Your Majesty will surely grow weary of listening.
Kǒng Zǐ (孔子) said: 'Learn broadly, but restrain it with propriety,
and you will not rebel against it.'
Indeed, to learn without restraint
will surely lead to rebellion against the Dao (Dào).
Yán Yuān (顏淵) said: 'Broaden me with culture,
and restrain me with ritual.'
Kǒng Zǐ (孔子) may be called one who knows teaching,
and Yán Yuān (顏淵) may be called one who excels in learning.
Lǎo Zǐ (老子) said: 'In learning the Dao (Dào), one diminishes daily.'
'Diminish' is similar to 'restrain.'
He also said: 'Cease learning, and you will have no worries.'
This means to cease peripheral learning.
Now, the two schools of Fèi (費) and Zuǒ (左)
have no foundational masters,
and contain many contradictions and anomalies.
Previous emperors
had doubts about this,
hence even though Jīng Shì (京氏) was established,
it was immediately abolished.
A dubious path cannot be followed;
a dubious matter cannot be undertaken.
The creation of the Shī (詩) and Shū (書) [classics]
dates back a long time.
Kǒng Zǐ (孔子) still travelled and observed widely,
until he understood the Mandate of Heaven.
Returning from Wèi (衞) to Lǔ (魯),
he then rectified the Yǎ (雅) and Sòng (頌) odes.
Now Your Majesty has newly founded the empire;
the guiding principles are not yet settled.
Although academic offices are established,
there are no disciples.
The Shī (詩) and Shū (書) are not lectured upon,
rituals (lǐ) and music (yuè) are not cultivated.
To propose the establishment of Zuǒ (左) and Fèi (費) [Erudites]
is not an urgent matter of governance.
Kǒng Zǐ (孔子) said: 'To attack heterodox doctrines,
that is indeed harmful.'
The commentary says: 'Transmit what is doubtful as doubtful,
transmit what is credible as credible,
and the Dao (Dào) of Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜) will endure.'
I wish Your Majesty would doubt what previous emperors doubted,
and believe what previous emperors believed,
to demonstrate a return to the roots
and show that you do not act unilaterally.
The reason affairs under Heaven are diverse
is because they do not unify.
The Yì (易) says: 'The movements under Heaven
are constant in their unity.'
It also says: 'Rectify the root,
and all things will be in order.'
The root of the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng) began with Kǒng Zǐ (孔子).
I respectfully submit fourteen errors of the Zuǒ Shì (左氏)."
At that time, those who raised difficulties argued that the Grand Historian (Tàishǐ Gōng) frequently cited the Zuǒ Shì (左氏).
Shēng (升) again submitted a memorial stating that the Grand Historian (Tàishǐ Gōng) contradicted the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng),
misrepresented Kǒng Zǐ's (孔子) words,
and listed thirty-one reasons why the Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū (左氏春秋) should not be recorded.
An edict was issued to send this down to the Erudites (Bóshì).
Later, Shēng (升) was accused by his divorced wife,
imprisoned,
then released,
and returned to his hometown.
During the Yǒngpíng (永平) era,
he served as the Magistrate (Lìng) of Liáochéng (聊城),
was dismissed for an incident,
and died at home.
Chén Yuán (陳元), courtesy name Chángsūn (長孫),
was a native of Guǎngxìn (廣信), Cāngwú (蒼梧).
His father, Qīn (欽),
was skilled in the Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū (左氏春秋),
served Jiǎ Hù (賈護) of Líyáng (黎陽),
and, while contemporary with Liú Xīn (劉歆), established his own school.
Wáng Mǎng (王莽) learned the Zuǒ Shì (左氏) scholarship from Qīn (欽),
and appointed Qīn (欽) as General of Weariness and Difficulty (Yànnán Jiāngjūn).
Yuán (元) inherited his father's profession in his youth,
and provided textual explanations and commentaries for it.
He devoted himself diligently to profound thought,
to the point of not communicating with his fellow villagers.
By virtue of his father's appointment, he became a Gentleman (Láng).
In the early Jiànwǔ (建武) era,
Yuán (元), along with Huán Tán (桓譚), Dù Lín (杜林), and Zhèng Xìng (鄭興), were all revered by scholars.
At that time, there was a discussion about establishing Erudites (Bóshì) for the Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn (左氏傳).
Fàn Shēng (范升) memorialized that the Zuǒ Shì (左氏) was shallow and trivial,
and should not be established.
Yuán (元) heard of this,
and thereupon went to the palace to submit a memorial, saying: "Your Majesty, by bringing order out of chaos and restoring correctness,
employing both civil and military means,
deeply laments the confusion and mix-up in the classics and arts,
and the intermingling of truth and falsehood.
Each morning, when attending court,
you consistently summon your ministers to discuss
the sagely Dao (Dào).
Knowing that Qiū Míng (丘明) was a great sage
and personally received instruction from Kǒng Zǐ (孔子),
while the Gōngyáng (公羊) and Gǔliáng (穀梁) commentaries were transmitted in later generations,
you therefore issued an edict to establish the Zuǒ Shì (左氏),
widely inquiring about its pros and cons,
showing that you do not
act unilaterally,
but exhaustively consult your subordinates.
Now, those who argue are immersed in what they have learned,
clinging to old knowledge,
stubbornly adhering to words of hollow transmission,
using them to contradict the Dao (Dào)
of actual events personally witnessed.
The Zuǒ Shì (左氏), being a solitary school with few adherents,
was thus overshadowed by heterodox schools.
Indeed, the most perfect music does not suit the ears of the multitude,
hence Bó Yá (伯牙) broke his zither strings;
the most precious treasure
does not appeal to the tastes of the multitude,
hence Biàn Hé (卞和) wept blood.
Zhòngní (仲尼) possessed sagely virtue,
yet was not tolerated by his age,
let alone the remaining writings on bamboo and silk.
That it should be rejected by those who follow the common trend
is indeed
fitting.
If not for Your Majesty's supreme sagacity,
who could discern it?
What they say
contradicts itself repeatedly;
they cut off small passages,
profane subtle phrases,
take slight differences in years
and gather them into huge errors,
overlook trivial omissions
and point to them as great
faults.
They pick out flaws and expose weaknesses,
concealing its immense beauty.
This is what is called,
'small arguments destroy speech,
and small words destroy the Dao (Dào).'
Shēng (升) and others also said:
'Previous emperors did not
consider the Zuǒ Shì (左氏) a classic,
and therefore did not establish Erudites (Bóshì);
later rulers should follow this precedent.'
Your servant, in my humble opinion, believes that if a later ruler must follow whatever previous emperors did,
then Pán Gēng (盤庚) should not
have moved to Yīn (殷),
Zhōu Gōng (周公) should not have constructed Luòyì (洛邑),
and Your Majesty should not be enthroned in Shāndōng (山東).
In the past,
Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武) favored the Gōngyáng (公羊) [Commentary],
while Crown Prince Wèi (衞)
favored the Gǔliáng (穀梁) [Commentary].
An imperial edict commanded the Crown Prince to study the Gōngyáng (公羊),
and not to study the Gǔliáng (穀梁).
When Emperor Xiàoxuān (孝宣) was among the people,
he heard that Crown Prince Wèi (衞) favored the Gǔliáng (穀梁)."
Thus, he studied it alone.
When he ascended the throne,
he wrote the "Shíqú Lùn" (石渠論) and the Gǔliáng (穀梁) school flourished.
To this day, it coexists with the Gōngyáng (公羊) school.
This shows that the Former Emperor and the Later Emperor each had
their own establishments,
and it was not necessary for them to follow each other.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"For the pure black (satin caps)
and the frugal (silk caps),
I follow the majority."
However, when it came to bowing down to the lower step,
he went against it.
Indeed, a clear-sighted person sees uniquely
and is not confused by crimson and purple;
a keen listener hears uniquely
and is not mistaken by clear and turbid tones.
Thus, Lí Zhū (離朱) was not swayed by clever illusions to shift his gaze,
and Shī Kuàng (師曠) was not easily moved by new sounds to change
his hearing.
Currently, military conflicts have largely subsided,
and warfare has mostly ceased.
It is time to devote thought to the sacred arts,
and attend to refined scholarship.
If we adopt Kǒngzǐ's principle of bowing at the lower step,
and follow the profound and sacred unique insight
of the intent,
distinguish clearly between black and white,
establish the Zuǒ Shì (左氏) commentary,
resolve the accumulated doubts of the former sages,
and cleanse the accumulated confusions of scholars,
so that the foundation may be passed down for ten thousand generations,
and later generations will no longer have doubts,
then the world will be truly fortunate.
old grievances;
If the words do not conform to the classics,
or the events are not substantiated by ancient records,
then I shall retire and accept severe punishment.
Even the day of my death
would be a year of my birth.
Yuán (元) was famous for his high talent,
and was appointed to Sīkōng (司空) Lǐ Tōng's (李通) office.
At that time, Dàsīnóng (大司農) Jiāng Fēng (江馮) submitted a memorial, saying,
"It is fitting to order the Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉) to supervise and inspect the Three Ducal Ministers."
The matter was referred to the Three Ducal Ministers' offices.
Yuán (元) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your minister has heard that those who serve as teachers to emperors are sages,
and those who serve as guests to emperors are hegemons.
Therefore, Wǔ Wáng (武王) treated Tàigōng (太公) as his teacher,
and Qí Huán (齊桓) treated Yí Wú (夷吾) as his Zhongfù (仲父).
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said: 'All officials generally heed the Zǒngzǎi (冢宰).'
In recent times, Gāo Dì (高帝) showed great courtesy to the Xiangguó (相國),
and Tàizōng (太宗) granted power to the Zǎifǔ (宰輔).
However, during the demise of the Xīn (新) dynasty under Wáng Mǎng (王莽),
who encountered the decline of the Hàn (漢) dynasty,
he exclusively controlled the reins of government,
and usurped the empire by stealth.
He flattered himself,
and distrusted his ministers.
He stripped the public assistants of their duties,
and diminished the authority of the prime ministers.
He considered reporting shortcomings as enlightenment,
and exposing wrongdoings as righteousness.
He even allowed servants to accuse their masters,
and sons to betray their fathers and elder brothers.
The net of laws was dense and severe,
and grand ministers had nowhere to move their hands or feet.
Yet, he could not prevent Dǒng Zhōng's (董忠) plot,
and was himself disgraced by the world.
Therefore, the ruler's trouble lies in self-pride,
not in proud ministers;
the fault lies in self-reliance,
not in relying on others.
Thus, Wén Wáng (文王) had the toil of 'daily receiving guests',
and Zhōu Gōng (周公) held to the courtesy of 'spitting out food to receive guests'.
We have not heard of them advocating reporting shortcomings,
or diligently supervising.
Currently, the four directions are still disturbed,
and the empire is not yet unified.
The common people are watching and listening,
all ears and eyes.
Your Majesty should cultivate the sacred canon of civil and military affairs,
and inherit the legacy virtues of your ancestors.
You should labor your mind for humble scholars,
and humble yourself to treat worthy individuals.
It is truly not appropriate to let officials inspect the names of the ducal ministers."
The Emperor followed his advice,
and issued his decree.
After Lǐ Tōng (李通) was dismissed,
Yuán (元) was again appointed to Sītú (司徒) Ōuyáng Shè's (歐陽歙) office.
He frequently presented proposals concerning current advantageous affairs and the rituals of the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
but the Emperor could not adopt them.
He left due to illness,
and being old,
died at home.
His son, Jiān Qīng (堅卿),
was skilled in writing.
Jiǎ Kuí (賈逵), courtesy name Jǐngbó (景伯),
was a native of Pínglíng (平陵), Fúfēng (扶風).
His ninth generation ancestor, Yí (誼),
was the Grand Tutor to the King of Liáng (梁王) during the reign of Wén Dì (文帝).
His great-grandfather, Guāng (光),
was the Grand Administrator of Chángshān (常山).
During the reign of Xuān Dì (宣帝), he moved from Luòyáng (洛陽) as an official receiving two thousand dàn (石) of grain.
His father, Huī (徽),
studied the Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū (左氏春秋) from Liú Xīn (劉歆),
and also studied the Guóyǔ (國語) and Zhōu Guān (周官).
He also studied the Gǔwén Shàngshū (古文尚書) from Tú Yùn (塗惲),
and the Máoshī (毛詩) from Xiè Mànqīng (謝曼卿).
He composed "Zuǒ Shì Tiáolì" (左氏條例) in twenty-one chapters.
Kuí (逵) fully inherited his father's learning.
By the time he was a young man, he could recite the Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn (左氏傳) and the original texts of the Five Classics.
He taught the Dà Xiàhóu Shàngshū (大夏侯尚書).
Although he belonged to the ancient text school,
he was also conversant with the theories of the five Gǔliáng (穀梁) schools.
From childhood,
he was always in the Imperial Academy,
and knew nothing of worldly affairs.
He was eight feet two inches tall.
The scholars made a saying about him:
"Jiǎ Chángtóu (賈長頭) never stops asking questions."
He was kind and generous,
with much wisdom and thought,
and was uninhibited with great principles.
He was especially clear on the Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn (左氏傳) and the Guóyǔ (國語),
for which he wrote "Jiěgǔ" (解詁) in fifty-one chapters.
During the Yǒngpíng (永平) era,
he submitted a memorial offering it.
Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) valued his book,
copied it, and stored it in the secret library.
At that time, divine sparrows gathered in the palace buildings and official residences.
Their crown feathers had five colors.
The Emperor found this unusual,
and asked Línyì Hóu (臨邑侯) Liú Fù (劉復).
Fù (復) could not answer,
and recommended Kuí (逵) as being knowledgeable and widely informed.
The Emperor then summoned Kuí (逵)
and questioned him.
He replied:
"In the past, when Wǔ Wáng (武王) completed his father's work,
the Yuèzhǔo (鸑鷟) gathered at Qí (岐).
When Xuān Dì (宣帝) brought the Róngdí (戎狄) into submission with his might,
divine sparrows continuously gathered.
This is an omen of the submission of the Hú (胡) people."
The Emperor ordered the Lántái (蘭臺) to provide him with writing implements,
and had him compose the "Shénquè Sòng" (神雀頌).
He was appointed as a Láng (郎),
and worked with Bān Gù (班固) to proofread secret books,
answering questions at court.
When Sùzōng (肅宗) ascended the throne,
he showed favor to Confucian arts,
and especially liked the Gǔwén Shàngshū (古文尚書) and the Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn (左氏傳).
In the first year of Jiànchū (建初),
an edict ordered Kuí (逵) to lecture in the Běi Gōng Báihǔ Guān (北宮白虎觀) and Nán Gōng Yúntái (南宮雲臺).
The Emperor approved of Kuí's (逵) explanation,
and had him present the major principles of the Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn (左氏傳) that surpassed the other two commentaries.
Kuí (逵) then fully itemized and memorialized, saying: "Your minister respectfully selects thirty especially clear and prominent points from the Zuǒ Shì (左氏).
These are all the proper principles for rulers and ministers,
and the guiding principles for fathers and sons.
The remaining points that are similar to the Gōngyáng (公羊) constitute seven or eight
out of ten,
or have minor textual differences,
which do not harm the overall structure.
As for figures such as Jì Zhòng (祭仲), Jì Jì (紀季), Wǔ Zǐxū (伍子胥), and Shū Shù (叔術),
the Zuǒ Shì's (左氏) principles are deeper in regards to the ruler
and father,
while the Gōngyáng (公羊) tends more towards expediency.
Their differences are indeed very great,
yet the injustice has accumulated for a long time,
and no one has been willing to clarify it.
book.
During the Jiànpíng (建平) era,
Shìzhōng (侍中) Liú Xīn (劉歆) wished to establish the Zuǒ Shì (左氏),
but did not first publicly discuss its major principles.
Instead, he lightly transferred the Tàicháng (太常),
relying on its superior principles,
and criticized and suppressed the various
Confucian scholars.
The Confucian scholars harbored internal resentment,
and collectively opposed him.
Xiào'āi Huángdì (孝哀皇帝) was unwilling to go against the popular sentiment,
and therefore sent Xīn (歆) out as the Grand Administrator of Hénèi (河內).
From then on, the Zuǒ Shì (左氏) was attacked,
and became a severe enemy.
When Guāngwǔ Huángdì (光武皇帝) came to power,
he boldly displayed his unique insight,
and revived the Zuǒ Shì (左氏) and Gǔliáng (穀梁).
However, the early masters of these two schools did not understand the prophecies and omens,
and thus
they were abandoned midway.
All that which preserves the Way of the Former Kings
lies in bringing peace to the ruler and governing the people.
Now, the Zuǒ Shì (左氏) exalts the ruler and father,
and humbles the minister and son,
strengthening the core
weak branches,
exhorting good and deterring evil,
most clear and incisive,
most straightforward and compliant.
Moreover, the three dynasties had different systems,
with gains and losses adapting to the times.
Therefore, the former emperor (Xiào Míng Dì 孝明帝) extensively surveyed various schools,
each adopting what was suitable.
For the Yì 易, there were Shī 施 and Mèng 孟,
and then Liángqīu 梁丘 was re-established.
For the Shàngshū 尚書, there was Ōuyáng 歐陽,
and then the greater and lesser Xiàhóu 夏侯 were re-established.
The differences among the three commentaries (of the Chūnqiū 春秋) today are
likewise.
Furthermore, none of the Five Classics scholars could use the diagrams and prophecies to prove that the Liú 劉 clan was descended from Yáo 堯,
but the Zuǒ Shì 左氏 alone had clear text.
All Five Classics scholars said that Zhuānxù 顓頊 succeeded Huángdì 黃帝,
and thus Yáo 堯 could not be of the fire virtue.
The Zuǒ Shì 左氏 held that Shǎohào 少昊 succeeded Huángdì 黃帝,
which is what the diagrams and prophecies called Dì Xuān 帝宣.
If
Yáo 堯 could not be of fire,
then Hàn 漢 could not be red.
What he (Jiǎ Kuí 賈逵) elucidated
provided truly numerous supplements and benefits.
He pursued knowledge
like one who diligently toils morning and evening,
devoting his mind to the Six Arts (liù yì 六藝),
investigating subtle mechanisms,
and examining everything thoroughly.
If one further attends to and studies the neglected,
to broaden the sage's insight,
perhaps
nothing will be left out or lost.
Jiǎ Kuí's 賈逵 mother was often ill.
The emperor wished to grant extra favors,
but because the usual allowances for proofreaders were many,
he specifically gave 200,000 cash,
and sent Yǐngyáng Hóu 潁陽侯 Mǎ Fáng 馬防 to deliver it.
He (the emperor) told Mǎ Fáng 馬防:
"Jiǎ Kuí's 賈逵 mother is ill.
This son (Jiǎ Kuí 賈逵) has no external human affairs (to earn money),
and if he is frequently impoverished, he will follow the sons of Gūzhú 孤竹 to Shǒuyáng Shān 首陽山."
Jiǎ Kuí 賈逵 often told the emperor that the ancient text of the Shàngshū 尚書 corresponded with the commentaries of the classics and the explications of the Éryǎ 爾雅.
An imperial edict ordered him to compile the similarities and differences between the Ōuyáng 歐陽, greater and lesser Xiàhóu 夏侯 versions of the Shàngshū 尚書 and the ancient text.
Jiǎ Kuí 賈逵 collected them into three volumes,
and the emperor praised them.
He was again ordered to compile the differences between the Qí 齊, Lǔ 魯, and Hán 韓 versions of the Shī 詩 and the Máo 氏 (Máo Shī 毛詩).
He also composed a commentary on the Zhōuguān 周官.
Jiǎ Kuí 賈逵 was promoted to Wèishì Lìng 衞士令.
In the eighth year (of Yǒngyuán 永元),
an edict was issued for all scholars to select highly talented students
to study the Zuǒ Shì 左氏, Gǔliáng Chūnqiū 穀梁春秋, ancient text of the Shàngshū 尚書, and Máo Shī 毛詩.
From this, these four classics then circulated in the world.
All the disciples and students selected by Jiǎ Kuí 賈逵 were appointed as Láng 郎 of the Qiānchéng Wángguó 千乘王國,
receiving instruction morning and evening at the Huángmén Shǔ 黃門署.
Scholars all looked upon them with joy and admiration.
When Hédì 和帝 ascended the throne,
in the third year of Yǒngyuán 永元 (A.D. 91),
Jiǎ Kuí 賈逵 was appointed Zuǒ Zhōngláng Jiàng 左中郎將.
In the eighth year (A.D. 96),
he was again made Shìzhōng 侍中,
and concurrently held the position of Qí Dūwèi 騎都尉.
He served inside the imperial tent (as an advisor)
and concurrently headed the nearby Secretarial Bureau (Mìshū Jìn Shǔ 祕書近署),
and was greatly trusted and relied upon.
Jiǎ Kuí 賈逵 recommended Sīmǎ Jūn 司馬均 of Dōnglái 東萊 and Rǔ Yù 汝郁 of Chén Guó 陳國.
The emperor immediately summoned them,
and both received preferential treatment.
Sīmǎ Jūn's 司馬均 courtesy name was Shàobīn 少賓.
He was content in poverty and fond of learning,
living in seclusion and teaching,
not responding to official invitations.
His sincerity and integrity were known throughout the commandery and villages.
When villagers had disputes,
they would always make an oath by Shàobīn 少賓,
and those who were in the wrong would never dare to speak.
He rose to the position of Shìzhōng 侍中,
but due to old age and illness, he requested to retire.
The emperor granted him the emolument of a Dàfū 大夫,
and he returned to his home village.
Rǔ Yù's 汝郁 courtesy name was Shúyì 叔異.
He was by nature benevolent and filial.
After his parents passed away,
he then lived in seclusion in the mountains and marshes.
Later, he was repeatedly promoted to Lǔ Xiàng 魯相 (Chancellor of Lǔ).
He transformed (the people) with virtue and teaching,
and the hundred surnames praised him.
Eight or nine thousand households of displaced people returned.
Jiǎ Kuí's 賈逵 writings on the meanings and explications of classics and commentaries, as well as his arguments and debates, amounted to over a million words.
He also composed nine pieces in total: poems (shī 詩), eulogies (sòng 頌), laments (lěi 誄), letters (shū 書), linked pearls (liánzhū 連珠), and drinking games (jiǔlìng 酒令).
Scholars revered him,
and later generations called him a comprehensive scholar (tōngrú 通儒).
However, he was not attentive to minor details,
and people of his time somewhat criticized him for this,
hence he did not reach high office.
He died in the thirteenth year of Yǒngyuán 永元 (A.D. 101),
at the age of seventy-two.
The imperial court grieved and lamented,
and appointed his two sons as Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人.
The論 (Commentary) says: The scholarship of Zhèng 鄭 and Jiǎ 賈
prevailed for several hundred years,
and thus became the standard for all scholars,
which was not without reason.
Huán Tán 桓譚 was banished for not being skilled in divination,
Zhèng Xìng 鄭興 barely escaped with humble words,
but Jiǎ Kuí 賈逵, able to reconcile and artfully elaborate,
was the most distinguished and honored.
That rulers of the age used this to judge scholarship
is truly tragic!
Zhāng Bà's 張霸 courtesy name was Bóráo 伯饒.
He was a native of Chéngdū 成都 in Shǔjùn 蜀郡.
When he was a few years old, he knew filial piety and deference.
Even when entering, leaving, eating, and drinking,
he naturally conformed to ritual.
The villagers called him
"Zhāng Zēngzǐ 張曾子."
At seven, he mastered the Chūnqiū 春秋.
He then wished to proceed to the other classics.
His parents said,
"You are young and not yet able."
Zhāng Bà 張霸 said,
"I (ráo 饒) am capable of doing it."
Therefore, his courtesy name was
"Ráo 饒."
Later, he went to Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi 長水校尉 Fán Yóu 樊鯈 to study Yán Shì Gōngyáng Chūnqiū 嚴氏公羊春秋,
and then extensively read the Five Classics.
Students Sūn Lín 孫林, Liú Gù 劉固, Duàn Zhù 段著, and others admired him.
Each bought a residence near him
to pursue their studies.
He was recommended as Xiàolián 孝廉 and served as Guānglù Zhǔshì 光祿主事.
Gradually promoted,
during the Yǒngyuán 永元 era, he became Huìjī Tàishǒu 會稽太守.
He memorialized for the appointment of local recluses Gù Fèng 顧奉 and Gōngsūn Sōng 公孫松.
Gù Fèng 顧奉 later became Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu 潁川太守,
and Gōngsūn Sōng 公孫松 became Sīlì Xiàowèi 司隸校尉,
both achieving renown.
Other individuals with accomplishments and good conduct
were all promoted and employed.
Within the commandery, people eagerly strived for virtuous conduct and integrity,
and those who studied classics numbered in the thousands.
On the roads, only the sound of recitation could be heard.
Initially,
Zhāng Bà 張霸 felt that Fán Yóu's 樊鯈 abridgment of the Yán Shì Chūnqiū 嚴氏春秋 still contained too many superfluous words.
So he further reduced it to 200,000 words,
and renamed it Zhāng Shì Xué 張氏學.
When Zhāng Bà 張霸 first arrived in Yuè 越 (Huìjī 會稽),
the bandits had not yet dispersed,
and the commandery was not peaceful.
He then issued a proclamation offering rewards,
clearly stating the reliable rewards and punishments.
The bandits then surrendered and pledged allegiance,
without the need for soldiers' efforts.
A children's rhyme said:
"Break my halberd,
abandon my spear,
bandits are gone,
officials all rest."
After three years in office,
he told his clerks and officials:
"The grand administrator (tàishǒu 太守) rose from a humble background
to the position of commandery administrator.
However, when the sun reaches its zenith, it begins to set;
when the moon is full, it begins to wane.
Lǎozǐ 老子 said: 'One who knows contentment is not disgraced.'"
Then he submitted a resignation due to illness.
Later, he was summoned,
and after four promotions, he became a Shìzhōng.
At that time, Dèng Zhì, the Queen's brother and Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng,
was powerful and highly esteemed at court.
Hearing of Bà's reputation and conduct,
he wished to befriend him.
However, Bà hesitated and did not respond,
and everyone laughed at him for not understanding the times.
Later, when he was about to become a Wǔgēng,
he fell ill and died,
aged seventy.
He left an edict to his sons, saying:
"In ancient times, Yán Zhōu was sent as an envoy to Qí.
When his son died in Yíng and Bó,
he buried him by the roadside in a ditch,
and thus he was interred there.
Now the road to Shǔ is difficult and distant;
it is not fitting to return to the ancestral tomb.
You may bury me here,
just enough to conceal my hair and teeth.
Strive for quick decay,
fulfilling my original intention.
In a person's life,
one should only show awe and respect to others.
If unkindness is shown to you,
simply accept it."
His sons followed his command
and buried him in Liáng County, Hénán,
and subsequently made their home there.
Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng Zhái Pú and other scholars and disciples compiled a record of his conduct,
and he was posthumously granted the title Xiànwén.
His middle son was Kǎi.
Kǎi, courtesy name Gōngchāo,
was skilled in Yán Shì Chūnqiū and the Gǔwén Shàngshū.
He always had a hundred disciples.
Guests admired him,
and even old scholars from his father's generation
all came to his door.
Carriages and horses filled the streets;
there was no place for his followers to stop.
Households of Huángmén and high-ranking relatives
all built lodgings along the alleys
to profit from passing visitors.
Kǎi, disliking this situation,
would always move to avoid them.
His family was poor and had no means of livelihood,
so he often rode a donkey cart to the county to sell medicine.
When he had enough to provide food,
he would return to his village.
The Sīlì recommended him as a Màocái,
and he was appointed Magistrate of Chánglíng,
but he did not take up the post.
He lived as a recluse in the mountains of Hóngnóng,
and scholars followed him,
making his dwelling place like a market.
Later, a Gōngchāo Market appeared south of Mount Huáyīn.
He was repeatedly invited by the Five Bureaus
and nominated as Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng,
but he did not accept.
In the first year of Hàn'ān,
Emperor Shùn specially issued an imperial edict to the Hénán Yǐn, saying:
"The former Magistrate of Chánglíng, Zhāng Kǎi, emulates Yuán Xiàn in his conduct,
and his integrity rivals that of Yí and Qí.
He disdains wealth and delights in lowliness,
hiding his tracks in secluded thickets.
His noble aspirations are firm and unyielding,
standing out uniquely from the common crowd.
Previously, when he was summoned,
he hesitated and did not arrive.
Could it be that those in charge were accustomed to routine
and insufficient in showing deference to the virtuous,
making it difficult for him to advance?
The commandery should promptly send him off with due ceremony."
Kǎi again claimed illness and did not arrive.
He was fond of Daoist arts
and could create a five-lǐ fog.
At that time, Péi Yōu from Guānxī could also create a three-lǐ fog,
but considering himself inferior to Kǎi,
he sought to learn from him.
Kǎi avoided him and refused to meet him.
When Emperor Huán ascended the throne,
Yōu then used his fog to commit banditry.
When the matter was discovered, he was interrogated
and implicated Kǎi, saying he had learned the art from him.
Kǎi was imprisoned in the Tíngwèi Zhàoyù
for two years,
during which he constantly recited classics
and wrote a commentary on the Shàngshū.
Later, as there was no evidence in the case,
he was pardoned and returned home.
In the third year of Jiànhé,
an edict was issued to summon him with an ānchē and full ceremony,
but he declined, citing severe illness and did not go.
At seventy,
he died at home.
His son was Líng.
Líng, courtesy name Chǔchōng,
rose to the rank of Shàngshū.
During the Yuánjiā era,
at the New Year's court assembly,
Dàjiāngjūn Liáng Jì entered the palace hall wearing a sword.
Líng shouted at him to leave
and ordered the Yǔlín and Hǔbēn to disarm Jì.
Jì knelt and apologized,
but Líng did not respond.
He immediately impeached Jì,
requesting the Tíngwèi to judge his crime.
An imperial edict allowed him to redeem himself with one year's salary,
and all officials were awed.
Initially,
Jì's younger brother Bùyí, as Hénán Yǐn,
had nominated Líng as Xiàolián.
Bùyí resented Líng's impeachment of Jì,
and therefore said to him:
"My nominating you in the past
was simply a way to punish myself."
Líng replied:
"My lord did not consider me unworthy
and mistakenly promoted me.
Now I uphold public justice
to repay your private kindness."
Bùyí showed a look of shame.
Líng's younger brother was Xuán.
Xuán, courtesy name Chǔxū,
was profound and talented in strategy,
but due to the turbulent times, he did not enter officialdom.
Sīkōng Zhāng Wēn repeatedly invited him with ceremony,
but could not persuade him.
In the second year of Zhōngpíng,
Wēn, as Chējì Jiāngjūn, set out to suppress the Liáng Province bandits Biān Zhāng and others.
Before his departure,
Xuán, wearing coarse clothes and a hemp belt from his rural dwelling,
met and advised Wēn, saying:
"Bandits are rising like clouds across the empire,
is it not because the Huángmén Chángshì are without principle?
I hear that the Zhongguìrén and officials from the Gōngqīng downwards are to see you off at Pínglè Guān.
My lord holds immense authority over the empire
and grasps the crucial command of the six armies.
If, during the banquet, when the wine is flowing,
you sound the gongs and drums,
array your formations,
summon the Jūnzhèng to seize and execute the guilty,
then lead your troops back to garrison the Dūtíng,
and successively eliminate the palace eunuchs,
you would relieve the empire from its inverted hanging,
and satisfy the grievances and hatred of all within the seas.
Afterward, openly employ virtuous and loyal recluses,
and then Biān Zhāng and his ilk would be as easily managed as if they were in the palm of your hand."
Wēn was greatly shocked upon hearing this,
unable to respond.
After a long while, he said to Xuán:
"Chǔxū,
it is not that I dislike your words,
but I fear I cannot carry them out.
What then?"
Xuán then sighed and said:
"If the matter is carried out, it will be a blessing;
if not, it will be a calamity.
Now I bid you a long farewell."
He immediately raised medicine to drink it.
Wēn stepped forward and grasped his hand, saying:
"You are loyal to me,
but I cannot employ you;
this is my fault.
Why must you act so?
Moreover, words spoken and heard
—who will know them now?"
Xuán then left
and lived as a recluse in the Lǔyáng mountains.
When Dǒng Zhuó took power,
he heard of him
and invited him to be his Yuán,
and recommended him as Shìyù Shǐ,
but he did not accept.
Dǒng Zhuó pressed him with military force,
and he was compelled to reluctantly set out.
He reached Lún Shì
and died on the way due to illness.
A eulogy states: In the Middle Ages, among Confucian families,
Jiǎ and Zhèng were renowned scholars.
Many rushed to this one man,
competing to show respect at his felt tent.
Shēng and Yuán upheld the classics,
their interpretations differing in emphasis.
Bà valued knowing when to stop,
declining association with powerful relatives.
Gōngchāo was skilled in arts,
and his dwelling became a market.
Biographies of Huán Róng and Dīng Hóng, Chapter Twenty-seven.
Huán Róng, courtesy name Chūnqīng,
was a native of Lóngkàng, Péi Jùn.
In his youth, he studied in Cháng'ān,
practicing the Ouyáng version of the Shàngshū.
He served the Erudite Zhū Pǔ of Jiǔjiāng.
Impoverished and without resources,
he often worked as a hired laborer to support himself.
He was diligent and never tired,
and for fifteen years he did not glance back at his family garden.
He did not return until Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne.
When Zhū Pǔ died,
Róng rushed to Jiǔjiāng for the funeral,
carrying earth to build his teacher's grave.
He then stayed to teach,
with several hundred disciples.
After Mǎng's defeat,
the world was in chaos.
Róng embraced his classics and fled with his disciples into mountain valleys.
Though often hungry and distressed, he never stopped lecturing.
Later, he again taught as a guest between Jiāng and Huái.
In the nineteenth year of Jiànwǔ [43 CE],
at over sixty years old,
he was first recruited into the Grand Minister of Works' office.
At that time, Xiǎnzōng had just been made crown prince.
Seeking scholars proficient in the classics,
they promoted Róng's disciple Hé Tāng of Yùzhāng to Colonel of the Tiger Guard,
to instruct the crown prince in the Shàngshū.
Shìzǔ casually asked Tāng
who his original teacher was.
Tāng replied,
"I served Huán Róng of Pèi Guó."
The Emperor immediately summoned Róng
and ordered him to expound on the Shàngshū.
He praised him highly,
appointed him as a Remonstrance Official,
and bestowed upon him one hundred thousand cash,
ordering him to enter and instruct the crown prince.
At every court assembly,
Róng was ordered to expound on the classics before the grandees and ministers.
The Emperor praised him,
saying,
"How I regret meeting you so late!"
When the position of Erudite Ouyáng became vacant,
the Emperor wished to appoint Róng.
Róng kowtowed and declined, saying,
"My classical learning is shallow;
I am not as good as my fellow disciples, the Gentleman Péng Hóng and the Supervisor of Yángzhōu Gāo Hóng."
The Emperor said,
"Very well,
go,
you are fitting."
He then appointed Róng as an Erudite,
and appointed Hóng and Hóng as Remonstrance Officials.
The imperial carriage visited the Grand Academy,
where all the Erudites debated and challenged each other before the Emperor.
Róng, dressed in scholarly robes,
was gentle, respectful, and cultivated,
articulating the meaning of the classics clearly.
He always prevailed with courtesy and humility,
never winning by length of argument.
No other scholar could match him.
He received special rewards.
He also ordered the students to play elegant music and strike the chime stones,
only dismissing them at the end of the day.
Later, when Róng attended court in the courtyard,
the Emperor ordered rare fruits to be bestowed.
All who received them carried them in their bosoms,
but Róng alone raised his hands to hold them and bowed.
The Emperor laughed, pointed at him, and said,
"This is a true scholar!"
Because of this, he was even more revered and honored,
and was often allowed to stay overnight in the crown prince's palace.
After five years,
Róng recommended his disciple Hú Xiàn of Jiǔjiāng to serve as lecturer.
Only then was Róng allowed to leave,
entering only once in the morning.
Róng once fell ill.
The crown prince sent his tutor day and night to inquire about his illness,
bestowing rare delicacies, curtains, and servants,
saying,
"Should anything unfortunate happen,
do not worry about your family."
Later, he recovered
and resumed his duties as lecturer.
In the twenty-eighth year,
at a grand assembly of all officials,
the Emperor asked who could be the crown prince's tutor.
The assembled ministers, anticipating the Emperor's wishes,
all said that Yīn Shí, the crown prince's maternal uncle and Marquis of Yuánlù, who held the Golden Mace, would be suitable.
The Erudite Zhāng Yì, with a serious expression, said,
"Does Your Majesty establish the crown prince
for the Yīn clan?
Or for the empire?
If for the Yīn clan,
then Marquis Yīn is suitable;
if for the empire,
then it is fitting to use the empire's worthy talents."
The Emperor praised him,
saying,
"The purpose of appointing a tutor
is to assist the crown prince.
Now, the Erudite does not hesitate to correct Us;
how much more so the crown prince!"
He immediately appointed Yì as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince
and Róng as Junior Tutor,
bestowing upon him a covered carriage and a riding horse.
Róng held a grand assembly of his disciples,
displaying his carriage, horse, and official seals and ribbons,
saying,
"What I have received today
is the result of diligent study of the ancients.
How can one not strive?"
When the crown prince's classical studies were completed,
Róng submitted a memorial of thanks, saying,
"I have been fortunate to attend in the imperial presence,
holding the classics for many years,
yet my wisdom and learning are shallow
and cannot add one ten-thousandth.
Now, His Imperial Highness the Crown Prince, with his brilliant wisdom,
is thoroughly enlightened in the meaning of the classics,
and surveys ancient and modern times.
No heir apparent or co-ruler has been able to be so dedicated and widely learned.
This is truly a blessing for the state,
and a great fortune for the empire.
My teaching mission is complete;
all knowledge resides in the crown prince.
I respectfully send my subordinate Fàn to bow twice and return to the Dao."
The crown prince replied in a letter, saying,
"As a child,
I studied the Dao for nine years,
but the principles and teachings were unclear,
and I understood nothing.
Indeed, the Five Classics are vast,
and the words of the Sages are profound and distant.
Unless one possesses the utmost excellence in the world,
how can one participate in this?
How much less can I, with my unworthiness,
dare to receive your instructive command.
In ancient times, there were teachers who bade farewell to their disciples;
some, having attained a thorough understanding of the classics and elucidated chapters and verses,
and others, having left their homes and yearned for their native places,
sought to take leave of their teachers.
Now, I am ranked among the lowest
and dare not refuse.
I wish you to take care of your health, eat more,
and cherish your precious body."
In the thirtieth year,
he was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies.
When Róng first faced difficulties,
he and his kinsman Huán Yuánqīng endured hunger together,
yet Róng never ceased lecturing and reciting.
Yuánqīng scoffed at Róng, saying,
"You just torment yourself with effort;
when will this ever be useful?"
Róng smiled and did not reply.
When he became Grand Master of Ceremonies,
Yuánqīng sighed, saying,
"I am a farmer's son;
how could I have known that learning could be so beneficial!"
When Xiǎnzōng ascended the throne,
he honored Róng with the禮 of a teacher,
and showed him great closeness and respect,
appointing his two sons as Gentlemen.
Róng, being over eighty years old,
considered himself old and infirm,
and repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement,
but was always given additional rewards.
The imperial carriage once visited the Grand Master of Ceremonies' office,
where Róng was ordered to sit facing east,
with a small table and staff provided.
All officials, from the General of Agile Cavalry, Prince Cāng of Dōngpíng, downwards,
and several hundred of Róng's disciples were assembled.
The Son of Heaven personally held the classics,
and each time he spoke, he would say,
"Our Great Master is here."
After the event concluded,
all the provisions from the Grand Storehouse were bestowed upon the Grand Master of Ceremonies' household.
Such was his grace and courtesy.
In the second year of Yǒngpíng [59 CE],
when the three academies were first completed,
Róng was appointed Wǔ Gēng.
After every Grand Archery Ceremony and ceremony for honoring the elders,
the Emperor would invite Róng and his disciples to ascend the hall,
holding the classics and personally lecturing to them.
Róng was then enfeoffed as Marquis of Guānnèi,
with an income of five thousand households.
Whenever Huán Róng fell ill,
Dì would send emissaries to inquire about his well-being.
Officials from the Tàiguān and Tàiyī departments constantly passed each other on the road.
When his condition became critical,
he submitted a memorial to express gratitude for the emperor's favor
and offered to return his titles and estates.
Dì visited his home to inquire about his health,
dismounting from his carriage upon entering the street.
He held a scripture and advanced,
caressing Huán Róng and shedding tears.
He bestowed upon him an an upholstered mat, bed curtains, a sword, and clothing.
After a long while, he departed.
From then on, the princes, generals, and grandees who came to inquire about his illness
dared not ride their carriages to the gate
but all bowed below the bed.
When Huán Róng died,
Dì personally changed his clothes,
attended the mourning rites, and saw him off at the funeral.
He bestowed a burial ground on the sunny side of Shǒushān.
Two of his nephews were appointed to positions of four hundred shí,
and eight of his chief disciples were appointed to positions of two hundred shí.
Many of his other followers rose to the ranks of gōngqīng.
His son, Yù, succeeded him.
The commentary says: Zhāng Yì fiercely criticized Yīn Hóu,
thereby attaining a high position.
His bold words challenged the multitude,
and his righteousness moved the sagacious empress,
showing that his integrity was more than sufficient.
If one word could earn a reward,
men of noble aspirations would feel ashamed.
If one accepted a title without yielding,
it would inspire poets to sing.
Yet, Yì, in the court debate, relied on his powerful relatives
and considered himself perfectly virtuous.
Was it perhaps that he thought his integrity was insufficient?
In the past, Yuè Yáng ate his son,
and though he achieved merit, he was suspected.
Xībā released the fawn,
and by his transgression, he became a tutor.
Truly, distinguishing between benevolence and deceit
is rooted in their true nature.
If rulers can observe with this understanding,
then truth and falsehood will be nearly discernible.
Yù, courtesy name Zhòng'ēn, was, in his youth, appointed a láng due to his father's influence.
He was magnanimous and diligent in his studies,
inheriting his father's scholarly tradition.
He taught the Shàngshū,
and his disciples often numbered in the hundreds.
When Huán Róng died,
Yù was due to inherit the title.
He submitted a memorial to yield it to his nephew, Fàn.
Xiǎozōng did not permit it,
so he reluctantly accepted the封,
giving all the rent income to Fàn.
Dì, because Yù was the son of his former teacher
and showed礼让,
held him in great affection and esteem.
He often stayed in the palace to discuss the classics and books,
and the emperor consulted him on matters of governance.
Gradually, he was promoted to Shìzhōng.
Dì personally compiled chapters and sentences of the Wǔjiā Yàoshuō,
and ordered Yù to proofread and finalize it in the Xuānmíng Diàn,
serving concurrently as Shìzhōng and Jiān Hǔbēnzào Lángjiàng.
In the fifteenth year of Yǒngpíng,
he was appointed to instruct the huáng tàizǐ in the classics.
He was promoted to Yuèqí Xiàowèi.
An imperial edict instructed the Tàizǐ and various kings to each offer congratulations and pay their respects.
Yù frequently offered loyal advice,
much of which was accepted and adopted.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
Yù requested leave due to his mother's mourning.
An imperial edict allowed him to perform the mourning rites while still holding the position of Shìzhōng.
In the second year of Jiànchū,
he was promoted to Túnqí Xiàowèi.
When Hédì ascended the throne,
being young in years,
Shìzhōng Dòu Xiàn, relying on the prominence of his maternal relatives,
wished for the young emperor to somewhat engage in classical studies.
He submitted a memorial to the Huáng Tàihòu, saying:
"The Lǐjì says: 'The mandate of All Under Heaven
rests with the Son of Heaven;
the excellence of the Son of Heaven
is perfected by what he studies.
When learning grows with wisdom,
then one is sharp and not indolent;
when transformation is perfected with the heart,
then the Middle Way becomes like one's nature.
In ancient times, when Chéngwáng was young,
still in swaddling clothes,
Zhōugōng was in front,
Shǐ Yì was behind,
Tàigōng was on the left,
and Zhàogōng was on the right.
He stood in the middle listening to court,
upheld by four sages.
Thus, there were no forgotten plans,
and no mistaken actions.'
Xiàozhāo Huángdì ascended the throne at the age of eight.
When the great ministers assisted in governance,
they also selected renowned Confucians like Wéi Xián, Cài Yì, and Xiàhóu Shèng to enter and instruct him,
thereby completing his sacred virtue.
Recently, in the first year of Jiànchū,
Zhāng Pú, Wèi Yìng, and Shào Xùn also lectured within the forbidden palace.
Your humble servant observes that Your Majesty,
endowed with a natural disposition,
should gradually be taught.
Yet, you only face your close minor officials
and have not heard the classic principles.
In the past, Wǔ Gèng Huán Róng
personally served as the imperial tutor.
His son, Yù,
from his youth, upheld and esteemed learning,
continuing his father's scholarly tradition.
Therefore, he twice entered as Xiàowèi to instruct the late emperor.
Father and son served in the forbidden palace,
spanning four generations.
Now, he is white-haired, fond of rites,
and his conduct and study are profoundly complete.
Furthermore, Zōngzhèng Liú Fāng,
a model of the imperial clan,
is skilled in the Shī Jīng,
praised by the late emperor.
It is fitting to order Yù and Fāng to both enter and teach,
to elevate this court
and brightly display the great transformation."
Consequently, Yù was promoted to Chánglè Shàofǔ
and again entered to lecture.
After a short while,
he was transferred to Shìzhōng Fèngchē Dūwèi.
In the fourth year of Yǒngyuán,
he replaced Dīng Hóng as Tàicháng.
The following year,
he died of illness.
Yù taught two emperors;
his imperial favor and affection were profound.
His rewards and grants amounted to hundreds of millions,
making him prominent in his time.
His disciples Yáng Zhèn and Zhū Chǒng
both rose to the rank of Sāngōng.
Originally,
Huán Róng received from Zhū Pǔ a forty-thousand-word chapter and sentence commentary,
which was verbose and lengthy,
often exceeding its actual content.
When Huán Róng entered to instruct Xiǎozōng,
it was reduced to twenty-three thousand words.
Yù further edited and finalized it into twelve thousand words.
From this, there came to be the Huán Jūn's larger and smaller Tàicháng chapter and sentence commentaries.
His son Pǔ succeeded him,
and the title was passed down to his great-grandson.
Yù's middle son, Yān,
was able to continue his family's scholarship through the generations.
His grandson Luán and great-grandson Bīn
were both renowned.
Yān, courtesy name Shúyuán, was, in his youth, appointed a láng due to his father's influence.
He was skilled in classics and steadfast in conduct,
and gained a reputation.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
he entered to instruct Āndì.
He was promoted three times to Shìzhōng Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
In the Yǒngníng era,
when Shùndì was established as huáng tàizǐ,
Yān was made Tàizǐ Shàofù.
After more than a month,
he was promoted to Tàifù.
He requested leave due to his mother's mourning.
He was permitted to perform the mourning rites as a Dàfū.
After more than a year,
an imperial edict ordered an emissary to bestow cattle and wine,
divest him of his mourning attire,
and immediately appoint him Guānglù Dàfū.
He was promoted to Tàicháng.
At this time, the deposed huáng tàizǐ became Jìyīn Wáng.
Yān, along with Tàipú Lái Lì and Tíngwèi Zhāng Hào, remonstrated,
but they could not succeed.
The details are fully recorded in the biography of Lái Lì.
When Shùn Dì ascended the throne,
Yān was appointed Grand Tutor (Tàifù),
and along with Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Zhū Chǒng, concurrently managed the affairs of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Shì).
Yān again entered the forbidden palace to lecture on the classics.
During an imperial banquet,
he suggested that the Three Dukes (Sāngōng) and the Secretariat (Shàngshū) should be invited to participate in state affairs.
The emperor followed his advice.
Because Yān had previously upheld integrity in court discussions,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yángpíng.
He firmly declined and did not accept.
After overseeing affairs for three years,
he was dismissed for appointing officials who had been banned (jìngù).
He was again appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū).
In the second year of Yángjiā (133 CE),
he replaced Lái Lì as Grand Herald (Dàhónglú).
A few days later,
he was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
In the fifth year of Yǒnghé (140 CE),
he replaced Wáng Gōng as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
In the first year of Hàn'ān (142 CE),
he was dismissed due to a solar eclipse.
The following year,
he died at home.
Several hundred disciples passed on his teachings,
with Huáng Qióng and Yáng Cì being the most prominent and esteemed.
Yān's grandson was Diǎn.
Diǎn, courtesy name Gōngyǎ,
again transmitted his family's scholarship,
teaching the *Book of Documents* (Shàngshū) in Yǐngchuān,
with several hundred students.
He was nominated as Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián) and appointed Gentleman (Láng).
Not long after,
the Chancellor (Guóxiàng) Wáng Jí was executed for a crime,
and his former friends and relatives dared not approach.
Diǎn alone [⿱𠫓廾]官 collected and arranged for his burial,
observed mourning for three years,
carried earth to build his tomb,
and erected a shrine for him,
fulfilling all rites before leaving.
He was invited to the office of Grand Minister of Works (Sītú) Yuán Wěi,
was recommended as Superior Grade (Gāodì),
and appointed Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Shìyùshǐ).
At this time, the eunuchs held power,
but Diǎn, in his official duties, showed no evasion.
He often rode a piebald horse,
and the capital feared and dreaded him,
giving rise to the saying:
"Halt, halt!
Make way for the piebald horse Imperial Censor."
When the Yellow Turban rebels rose in Xíngyáng,
Diǎn was dispatched to supervise the army.
After the rebels were defeated,
he returned,
but because he offended the eunuchs, his reward was withheld.
He remained an Imperial Censor for seven years without promotion,
and was later reassigned as a Gentleman (Láng).
When Líng Dì died,
General-in-Chief (Dàjiāngjūn) Hé Jìn held power.
Diǎn participated in his consultations,
and was thrice promoted to Gentleman of the Feathered Forest (Yǔlín Zhōnglángjiāng).
When Xiàn Dì ascended the throne,
the Three Dukes (Sāngōng) memorialized that Diǎn had previously conspired with Hé Jìn to execute the eunuchs,
and although the effort did not succeed,
his loyalty and righteousness were brilliantly evident.
An imperial edict appointed one member of his family as a Gentleman (Láng)
and bestowed 200,000 cash.
Following the westward journey to the passes,
he was appointed Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
and granted the title of Marquis of the Interior (Guānnèi Hóu).
When the imperial carriage established its capital in Xǔ,
he was promoted to Minister of the Household (Guānglù Xūn).
In the sixth year of Jiàn'ān (201 CE),
he died in office.
Luán, courtesy name Shǐchūn,
was a disciple of Yān.
From a young age, he maintained strict integrity,
wearing simple robes and eating plain food,
seeking no excess.
Because the world was corrupt,
and many officials in the provinces and commanderies were not suitable,
he felt it shameful to serve.
When he was over forty years old,
the Prefect (Tàishǒu) Xiàng Miáo, who had a good reputation,
nominated Luán as Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián),
and he was promoted to Magistrate of Jiāodōng.
Immediately upon his arrival in office, Miáo died.
Luán promptly resigned his post and rushed to mourn,
completing three years of mourning before returning.
Those between the Huái and Rǔ rivers highly esteemed his righteousness.
Later, he served as Magistrate of Yǐwú and Jí counties,
and earned great renown.
All the high officials recommended him,
and he was again summoned (or appointed) as Consultant (Yìláng).
He submitted five proposals: to recommend worthy talents,
to carefully select and appoint them,
to dismiss sycophantic favorites,
to reduce imperial parks and preserves,
and to lighten labor services and taxes.
His memorial was presented to the emperor,
but it offended the palace eunuchs,
so it was not considered.
He was dismissed due to illness.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng (184 CE),
at the age of seventy-seven,
he died at home.
His son was Yè.
Yè, courtesy name Wénlín,
also named Yán,
especially cultivated firm integrity.
His aunt was the wife of Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Yáng Cì.
When Luán first died,
his aunt returned home to mourn.
As she was about to arrive,
she stopped at a post-house,
arranged and adorned her retinue before entering.
Yè inwardly disapproved of this.
When his aunt offered condolences,
he said nothing at all,
only wept aloud.
Yáng Cì sent an official to offer sacrifices,
and arranged for the county to provide sacrificial items.
Yè refused to accept them.
Later, whenever he went to the capital,
he never stayed at the Yáng family residence.
His upright obstinacy was like this.
His guests and followers
all revered his character and conduct,
and he never accepted even a single meal from others.
He served as Administrator (Gōngcáo) of a commandery.
Later, he was nominated as Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián), Erudite (Yǒudào), Upright (Fāngzhèng), and Abundant Talent (Màocái).
All Three Dukes (Sāngōng) invited him,
but he did not respond to any of them.
In the Chūpíng era (190-193 CE),
the world was in chaos.
He sought refuge in Kuàijī,
then traveled by sea to Jiāozhǐ.
The Yue people were influenced by his integrity,
so much so that there were no disputes in the villages.
He was falsely accused by wicked people,
and subsequently died in prison in Hépǔ.
Bīn, courtesy name Yànlín,
was the elder grandson of Yān's brother.
His father, Lín,
courtesy name Yuánfèng,
showed talent and wisdom early on.
At the beginning of Huán Dì's reign,
he was a Consultant (Yìláng),
and entered the forbidden palace to give lectures.
Because of his uprightness, he offended those around the emperor,
and was sent out as Magistrate of Xǔ,
but was dismissed due to illness.
When his mother died,
Lín was overcome by grief,
and died before the mourning period was complete,
at the age of forty-one.
His writings included twenty-one pieces of stelae inscriptions (bēi), eulogies (lěi), encomiums (zàn), discourses (shuō), and letters (shū).
Bīn was as famous as Cài Yōng in his youth.
He was first nominated as Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián) and appointed Gentleman of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Láng).
At that time, Fēng Fāng, the son-in-law of the Regular Palace Attendant (Zhōngchángshì) Cáo Jié, was also a Gentleman (Láng).
Bīn cultivated his strong principles,
and was on good terms and friendly with the Left Senior Secretary (Zuǒ Chéng) Liú Xīn and the Right Senior Secretary (Yòu Chéng) Dù Xī.
He never attended any banquets with Fāng.
Fāng deeply resented this,
and therefore openly declared that Bīn and others were a "wine faction."
The matter was sent to the Director of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng) Liú Měng.
Liú Měng had always been friendly with Bīn and others,
and did not report their actions correctly.
Cáo Jié was furious,
and impeached Liú Měng,
accusing him of forming a faction,
requesting his arrest and imprisonment in the imperial jail.
Those in court were chilled by this.
Liú Měng, however, maintained his composure.
He was released within ten days,
but was dismissed from office and banned from public service.
Bīn was thus ruined.
In the first year of Guānghé (178 CE),
he died at home,
at the age of forty-six.
All scholars mourned him.
His writings included seven discourses (shuō) and three letters (shū).
Cài Yōng and others jointly discussed and prefaced his aspirations,
all agreeing that Bīn excelled others in four ways:
his early wisdom was fully developed,
he was exceptionally bright;
his scholarship was excellent and his writing elegant,
he was thoroughly accomplished;
he did not seek salary through improper means,
his integrity was absolutely lofty;
he declined high positions and followed humble ones,
his conduct was pure.
They then jointly erected a stele and composed an encomium for him.
Liú Měng
was a person from Lángyá.
During the reign of Emperor Huán, he served as Zōngzhèng.
Due to his upright character, he was not tolerated,
and so he resigned and returned home.
When Emperor Líng ascended the throne,
Grand Tutor Chén Fān and General-in-Chief Dòu Wǔ assisted in government,
and he was again summoned for service.
A论 (commentary) says: The Fú clan, from the Eastern and Western Hàn dynasties, successively became renowned scholars,
thereby obtaining noble ranks and positions.
During the restoration (Eastern Hàn), the Huán clan became particularly prominent.
From Huán Róng to Huán Diǎn,
the world honored their teachings.
Fathers, sons, and brothers successively served as imperial tutors,
and those who received their instruction all became ministers (qīng xiàng),
illustrious in their time.
Confucius said:
“Ancient scholars studied for themselves;
modern scholars study for others.”
Those who study for others
rely on reputation to manifest themselves;
those who study for themselves
follow their heart to understand the Way.
How could Huán Róng, whose family was honored for generations,
have been studying for himself?
Dīng Hóng, courtesy name Xiàogōng,
was a native of Dìnglíng, Yǐngchuān.
His father, Dīng Lín,
courtesy name Yòuchūn,
served as the Magistrate of Yǐngyáng at the end of Wáng Mǎng’s reign.
When Emperor Shìzǔ campaigned in Yǐngyáng,
the city of Yǐngyáng held out and would not surrender.
Dīng Lín persuaded its magistrate,
and they both surrendered together.
Emperor Shìzǔ was greatly pleased
and generously rewarded him,
appointing Dīng Lín as a Piānjiāngjūn (partial general),
who then followed him on his campaigns.
Dīng Lín led troops to cross the Yellow River first,
sending proclamations to various commanderies and states,
attacking camps and seizing territory,
subduing twenty-one counties in Hénán, Chénliú, and Yǐngchuān.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ (25 CE),
he was appointed Grand Administrator of Hénán.
When rewarding meritorious officials,
the Emperor ordered each to state what they desired.
All the generals requested prosperous cities and beautiful counties,
but only Dīng Lín wished to be enfeoffed in his hometown.
Someone asked Dīng Lín,
“Everyone wants a county;
why do you alone seek a township?”
Dīng Lín replied,
“In the past, Sūn Shú’áo instructed his son
that when receiving an enfeoffment, they must seek barren and remote land.
Now, my achievements are meager,
so to receive a township is already quite generous.”
The Emperor followed his wish,
enfeoffing him as Marquis of Xīn’ān Township in Dìnglíng,
with an income of five thousand households.
Later, he was transferred to be enfeoffed as Marquis of Língyáng.
At thirteen, Dīng Hóng
studied the Ouyáng Shàngshū (Ouyang’s Book of Documents) under Huán Róng.
Within three years, he mastered the text and its commentaries,
excelling in debates.
He became a Dūjiǎng (chief lecturer),
and thus devoted himself diligently and sharply to his studies,
traveling as a commoner with his belongings on his back,
not shying away from journeys of a thousand lǐ.
Initially,
when Dīng Lín followed Emperor Shìzǔ on campaigns,
Dīng Hóng lived alone with his younger brother Dīng Shèng,
pitying Dīng Shèng for being young and sharing their cold and bitter existence.
When Dīng Lín passed away,
Dīng Hóng was to inherit the marquisate.
He submitted a memorial to cede the peerage to Dīng Shèng,
but it was not approved.
After the burial,
he hung his mourning clothes and cap in the tomb shed and fled,
leaving a letter for Dīng Shèng which said:
“Hóng is greedy for classical texts
and disregards kindness and righteousness.
While young, I followed my teacher;
while my parents lived, I did not provide for them;
when they died, I did not perform the mouth-feeding ritual.
May Imperial Heaven and my ancestors
not grant their protection and aid.
I have contracted a severe illness,
making me unfit for the茅土 (Máo tǔ, symbol of enfeoffment).
Previously, I submitted a report on my illness,
wishing to decline the title for Zhònggōng (Dīng Shèng).
My memorial was left unanswered,
and I am pressured to inherit the title.
I hereby release myself
to seek good doctors.
If I do not recover,
I will eternally return to the ravines.”
