Initially, Dīng Hóng and Bāo Jùn from Jiǔjiāng had studied under Huán Róng together,
and were very good friends.
When Dīng Hóng abandoned his marquisate,
he met Bāo Jùn in Dōnghǎi,
and feigned madness, pretending not to recognize him.
Bāo Jùn then stopped him and reproached him, saying:
“In ancient times, Bó Yí and Wú Zhá exercised their judgment in times of chaos,
thus they could express their aspirations.
According to the meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
one should not neglect the affairs of the state for family matters.
Now you, for private brotherly affection, sever the foundation established by your father that should not be extinguished.
Can this be called wisdom?”
Dīng Hóng was enlightened and realized his error,
shedding tears and sighing.
He then returned to his fief
and opened his gate to teach.
Bāo Jùn also submitted a memorial praising Dīng Hóng’s scholarly attainments and noble conduct.
Emperor Xiǎnzōng greatly admired him.
In the tenth year of Yǒngpíng (67 CE), an imperial edict summoned him.
Upon Dīng Hóng’s arrival, he was immediately granted an audience.
He expounded on the chapter “Wén Hóu Zhī Mìng” (The Mandate to Marquis Wén),
and was bestowed with imperial robes and a sash,
receiving provisions from the Gōngchē (Bureau of Imperial Carriages),
and was treated with the same courtesies as the Bóshì (Erudites).
Soon after,
he was appointed Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant).
In the thirteenth year,
he concurrently held the position of Shèshēng Xiàowèi (Colonel of Archer-Brave).
In the fourth year of Jiànchū (79 CE),
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Lǔyáng Township.
Emperor Sùzōng ordered Dīng Hóng, along with Wáng Xiàn of Guǎngpíng, and various scholars like Lóu Wàng, Chéng Fēng, Huán Yù, and Jiǎ Kuí,
to debate and settle the differences and similarities of the Five Classics at the Báihǔ Guān (White Tiger Hall) in the Northern Palace.
He made Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng Wèi Yīng preside over the questioning and debate on behalf of the Emperor,
and Shìzhōng Chúnyú Gōng presented the findings.
The Emperor personally presided over and made the final decisions.
Dīng Hóng, with his superior talent,
was the clearest in his arguments and debates.
The scholars praised him,
and the Emperor frequently lauded him.
People at the time exclaimed:
“There is no equal to Dīng Xiàogōng in the palace!”
He received numerous rewards and gifts,
and was promoted to Xiàoshū (Compiler),
and then succeeded Chéng Fēng as Shàofǔ (Minister of the Lesser Treasury).
From then on, his followers grew,
with thousands arriving from distant places.
Liú Kǎi from Péngchéng, Bā Mào from Běihǎi, and Zhū Chāng from Jiǔjiāng all became ministers (gōng qīng).
In the third year of Yuánhé (86 CE),
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Mǎtíng Township.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Tàicháng (Grand Minister of Ceremonies).
In the fourth year of Yǒngyuán (92 CE),
he succeeded Yuán Ān as Sītú (Minister of Works).
At this time, Empress Dowager Dòu oversaw the government,
and her brothers, Dòu Xiàn and others, wielded great power.
Taking advantage of a solar eclipse, Dīng Hóng
submitted a memorial, which said: Your servant has heard that the sun is the essence of Yang,
maintaining its substance without deficiency;
it is the symbol of the ruler.
The moon is the essence of Yin,
waxing and waning with regularity;
it is the manifestation of the minister.
Therefore, a solar eclipse
signifies
that a minister oversteps the ruler,
Yin overshadows Yang.
When the moon is full but not wanting,
it signifies that those below are arrogant and overbearing.
In the late decline of the Zhōu dynasty,
relatives like Huángfǔ monopolized power externally,
their factions
grew strong,
usurping the power of the sovereign.
Thus, there were solar and lunar eclipses.
Hence, the Shī (Book of Odes) says:
“In the tenth month’s conjunction,
on the first day, Xīn-mǎo,
the sun was eclipsed,
truly a
great disgrace.”
The Spring and Autumn Annals record thirty-six solar eclipses
and thirty-two instances of regicide.
Changes do not occur without reason,
each corresponds to its kind.
Indeed, authority should not be delegated,
and sharp weapons
should not be lent to others.
Looking back at ancient times
and closely observing the rise of the Hàn,
the calamities of collapse and danger
all stemmed from this.
Thus, the Sān Huán monopolized Lǔ,
the Tián clan usurped Qí,
and the Liù Qīng divided Jìn.
The various Lǚ seized power,
and the imperial succession was nearly altered.
At the end of the Āi and Píng reigns,
the ancestral temples lacked sacrificial offerings.
Therefore, even one with the kinship of Zhōu Gōng,
but without
his virtue,
should not wield his power.
When presenting a petition,
one requests to be received and waits for a reply.
Even if one bears the tally and seal,
and has received an imperial edict from the Grand Secretariat,
one dares not leave immediately.
For long waits, it can be up to several tens of days.
Turning one's back on the royal court
and facing private gates –
this is
when the Emperor's authority is diminished,
and the power of subordinates flourishes.
When human morality is perverse below,
its effects are seen in heaven.
Even if there are hidden schemes,
the gods illuminate their true nature,
displaying portents as warnings
to inform
the ruler.
Recently, the moon has been full before its proper phase,
and has not risen after the full moon.
This indicates that ministers are arrogant and overbearing, turning their backs on the ruler,
claiming all achievements and acting independently.
Your Majesty has not yet deeply awakened to this,
thus Heaven
has repeatedly shown warnings.
It is truly fitting to be awed and fearful,
to guard against disaster.
The Shī Jīng says:
"Revere Heaven's wrath,
and dare not be idle or indulgent."
If you rectify governance and examine yourself,
stopping troubles in their incipient
stages,
then evil omens will vanish,
harm will be removed, and blessings will gather.
No one fails to overlook the minute,
which then leads to the massive.
Compassion makes one unable to instruct,
righteousness makes one unable to cut off.
After the events have passed,
it becomes a clear mirror of what was to come.
Your humble servant believes that
officials holding external posts,
who rely on powerful factions,
and are obsequious and flattering
to gain favor,
should be subjected to universal execution.
Recently, the Grand General has been on campaign
twice,
his might shaking the provinces and commanderies.
None have failed to levy taxes and extort from officials and commoners,
and send envoys to offer tribute.
Although the Grand General claims not to accept them,
the goods are not returned to their owners.
The officials under his command have
nothing to fear or dread,
acting lawlessly,
and not submitting to punishment for their crimes.
Therefore, the greedy and cunning throughout the empire
compete to become corrupt officials,
the common people sigh with grief,
and resentment fills their hearts.
Your humble servant has heard that Heaven cannot
but be firm;
if not firm, the three luminaries will not shine brightly.
A king cannot but be strong;
if not strong, the regional governors will act with impunity.
It is fitting to take advantage of this great upheaval
to reform governance and rectify
mistakes,
to appease Heaven's will.
At that time, large commanderies with five or six hundred thousand people nominated two filial and incorrupt officials (xiào lián),
while small commanderies with two hundred thousand people, even those with barbarian tribes, also nominated two.
The Emperor considered this unequal,
and submitted it to the high ministers for discussion.
Dīng Hóng, along with Sīkōng Liú Fāng, submitted a memorial, stating:
"Regarding the criteria for population ratios,
there should be grades.
When barbarians are mixed in,
they should not be counted.
From now on, commanderies and kingdoms with a population of two hundred thousand shall nominate one xiào lián annually,
four hundred thousand two,
six hundred thousand three,
eight hundred thousand four,
one million five,
and one million two hundred thousand six.
Those with less than two hundred thousand shall nominate one every two years,
and those with less than one hundred thousand one every three years."
The Emperor adopted this.
In the sixth year,
Dīng Hóng died,
and was granted posthumous honors beyond the usual rites.
His son Zhàn succeeded.
After Zhàn died,
his son Fú succeeded.
After Fú died,
his son Xià succeeded.
The commentary states: Kǒngzǐ said,
"Tàibó thrice yielded the empire,
yet the people found nothing to praise him for."
Mèngzǐ said,
"Those who heard of Bó Yí's character,
the greedy became incorrupt,
and the timid became resolute."
If Tàibó yielded the empire to avoid Zhōu,
and Bó Yí led his pure heart to leave the state,
neither truly made a 'yield'.
Therefore, Tàibó is praised for his supreme virtue,
and Bó Yí for being a worthy person.
Later generations heard of their yielding and admired their character,
pursuing their names but misunderstanding their essence,
which led to the encouragement of strange conduct and mistaken giving and taking.
As for Dèng Biāo and Liú Kǎi,
they yielded to their younger brothers to attain righteousness,
making their brothers accept inappropriate offices while they themselves gained a greater reputation.
In terms of righteousness, was this not rather shallow?
When a jūn zǐ speaks,
it is not merely to make his principles clear,
but to enlighten those in the world who are about to awaken;
when he acts,
it is not merely to cultivate his own virtue,
but to instruct those in the world who are about to move.
How can one not be careful about what one's words and actions encourage or obstruct!
Examining Dīng Hóng's heart,
was it rooted in loyalty and love?
How then did he finally awaken and follow righteousness?
He was different from those several people who seemed to pursue fame.
The eulogy says: The five watches waited for questions,
answering like a tolling bell.
Carriages lined the courtyard,
ceremonial etiquette filled the hall.
Solemn was the Emperor's rule,
embracing classics to follow.
Dīng Hóng was respectful and cautious,
yielding without pretense.
His profound discussions at Báihǔ,
his deep words on solar eclipses.
Biography of Zhāng Fǎ, Téng Fēng, and Yáng Liè, Chapter 28
Zhāng Zōng, courtesy name Zhūjūn,
was a native of Lǔyáng, Nányáng.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
he served as a junior official in Yángquán township of the county.
When Wáng Mǎng was defeated,
and righteous armies rose,
Zhāng Zōng led three or four hundred people from Yángquán to raise an army and seize territory,
advancing west to Cháng'ān.
Gēngshǐ appointed Zhāng Zōng as a partial general.
Zhāng Zōng saw Gēngshǐ's government was chaotic,
and so he took his family and retainers to settle in Ānyì.
When Dà Sītú Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) campaigned west,
he pacified Hédōng (河東).
Zhāng Zōng (張宗) went to Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) and surrendered.
Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) heard that Zhāng Zōng (張宗) was habitually resourceful and full of stratagems,
so he memorialized to appoint him as Piān Jiāngjūn (偏將軍, General of the Household).
Dèng Yǔ's (鄧禹) army reached Xúnyì (栒邑).
The Chìméi (赤眉) large host was about to arrive.
Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) thought Xúnyì (栒邑) was not defensible,
and wished to lead his forces forward to a stronger city,
but many of the men feared being pursued by the bandits
and dreaded being the rearguard.
Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) then wrote the names of his generals on bamboo slips,
assigned their front and rear positions,
mixed them up in a casket,
and ordered each to draw one.
Zhāng Zōng (張宗) alone refused to draw,
saying:
"Life and death are fated.
How could Zhāng Zōng (張宗) shirk difficulty and seek ease?!"
Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) sighed and said to him:
"General, you have relatives and dependents in the camp.
How can you not consider them?"
Zhāng Zōng (張宗) said:
"I have heard that if one soldier exerts his full strength,
a hundred men cannot stop him;
if ten thousand men are determined to die,
they can advance unhindered.
I now command several thousand troops,
to receive the great power.
Why must we necessarily fail?"
Thus, he remained to be the rearguard.
After the other camps had withdrawn their troops,
Zhāng Zōng (張宗) spurred on his soldiers,
strengthened his fortifications,
and confronted them to the death.
When Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) reached the front county,
he deliberated, saying:
"With General Zhāng's (張宗) troops,
to face an army of a million,
is like throwing a small amount of snow into boiling water.
Although they may wish to exert themselves,
their situation is unsustainable."
So he dispatched two thousand infantry and cavalry to return and meet Zhāng Zōng (張宗).
As Zhāng Zōng (張宗) led his troops and had just set out,
the Chìméi (赤眉) suddenly arrived.
Zhāng Zōng (張宗) fought them,
repelled them,
and only then was able to return to camp.
At this, all the generals admired his bravery.
When they returned to Cháng'ān (長安),
Zhāng Zōng (張宗) led elite soldiers at night to raid the Chìméi (赤眉) in the city.
He was struck by a spear that pierced his shoulder blade,
and then continued to attack various encampments and strongholds,
where he was struck by a stray arrow.
Both times he nearly died.
When Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) was recalled from his campaign,
Guāngwǔ (光武) appointed Zhāng Zōng (張宗) as Jīngfǔ Dūwèi (京輔都尉),
leading crack cavalry to jointly attack the various encampments and strongholds in Guānzhōng (關中) with Zhēngxī Dà Jiāngjūn Fēng Yì (征西大將軍馮異).
They defeated them,
and he was promoted to Hénán Dūwèi (河南都尉).
In Jiànwǔ (建武) year six (30 CE),
the office of Dūwèi (都尉) was abolished.
He was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫).
In year eight (32 CE),
bandits rose in groups in Sāngzhōng (桑中), Yǐngchuān (潁川).
Zhāng Zōng (張宗) led troops to attack and pacify them.
Later, bandits from Qīng (青) and Jì (冀) provinces gathered in mountains and marshes.
Zhāng Zōng (張宗), as Yèzhě (謁者), supervised the troops of various commanderies to suppress and pacify them.
In year sixteen (40 CE),
bandits again rose in Lángyá (琅邪) and Běihǎi (北海).
Zhāng Zōng (張宗) supervised the troops of the two commanderies to suppress them.
He set out strategies,
clearly offered rewards,
and completely routed them.
At this, the bandit groups in Pèi (沛), Chǔ (楚), Dōnghǎi (東海), and Línhuái (臨淮) feared his might,
and several thousand people were captured and beheaded by their own kind,
causing Qīng (青) and Xú (徐) provinces to tremble.
Later, he was promoted to Lángyá Xiàng (琅邪相, Administrator of Langya).
His administration favored severity and fierceness,
and he dared to kill and punish.
In Yǒngpíng (永平) year two (59 CE),
he died in office.
Fǎ Xióng (法雄), courtesy name Wénqiáng (文彊),
was a man from Méi (郿) in Fúfēng (扶風),
a descendant of Qí Xiāngwáng Fǎ Zhāng (齊襄王法章).
When Qín (秦) destroyed Qí (齊),
his descendants dared not use the surname Tián (田),
and thus took Fǎ (法) as their clan name.
During the time of Xuāndì (宣帝),
they relocated to Sānfǔ (三輔),
and for generations served as officials earning two thousand *dàn* of grain.
Fǎ Xióng (法雄) initially served as Gōngcáo (功曹) in the commandery,
was invited to the office of Tàifù Zhāng Yǔ (太傅張禹),
who recommended him as a high-ranking talent,
and he was appointed Píngshì Zhǎng (平氏長, Magistrate of Pingshi).
He was skilled in governance,
and good at exposing hidden treachery,
so banditry rarely occurred.
Officials and common people feared and loved him.
Nányáng Tàishǒu Bāo Dé (南陽太守鮑得) reported his administrative achievements,
and he was promoted to Wǎnlíng Lìng (宛陵令, Magistrate of Wanling).
In Yǒngchū (永初) year three (109 CE),
sea bandits Zhāng Bólù (張伯路) and others, numbering over three thousand,
wore red turbans,
and scarlet robes,
calling themselves
"generals,"
plundered the nine coastal commanderies,
and killed officials of the two thousand *dàn* rank, magistrates, and chiefs.
Initially,
Shìyùshǐ Páng Xióng (侍御史龐雄) was dispatched to supervise the provincial and commandery troops to attack them.
Zhāng Bólù (張伯路) and his followers requested to surrender,
but soon gathered again.
The following year,
Zhāng Bólù (張伯路) again, with Liú Wénhé (劉文河) of Píngyuán (平原) and over three hundred others, called themselves
"envoys."
They attacked Yàncì (厭次) city,
killed the chief official,
then moved into Gāotáng (高唐),
burned government offices,
released prisoners.
All the ringleaders called themselves
"generals,"
and jointly paid respects to Zhāng Bólù (張伯路).
Zhāng Bólù (張伯路) wore a five-beamed cap
and a seal and ribbon.
His followers grew increasingly strong.
Then Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Wáng Zōng (御史中丞王宗) was dispatched, holding a staff of authority, to mobilize troops from various commanderies in Yōu (幽) and Jì (冀) provinces,
totaling tens of thousands of men.
Fǎ Xióng (法雄) was then summoned to be Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ (青州刺史, Inspector of Qingzhou),
to join forces with Wáng Zōng (王宗) to suppress them.
After continuous battles, they defeated the bandits,
beheading or drowning several hundred people.
The rest fled.
They recovered a large amount of weapons and valuables.
Just then, an imperial amnesty arrived,
but the bandits still had their military armor and weapons,
and dared not surrender.
At this, Wáng Zōng (王宗) convened the Inspector and Grand Administrators to deliberate.
All thought they should continue the attack.
Fǎ Xióng (法雄) said:
"Not so.
Weapons
are instruments of ill omen;
war
is a dangerous undertaking.
Bravery cannot be relied upon,
and victory is not certain.
If the bandits take boats and sail out to sea,
deep into distant islands,
attacking them will not be easy.
Since there is an amnesty,
we can temporarily withdraw our troops,
to comfort and entice their hearts.
The situation will surely lead to their dispersal,
and then we can plan for them.
This way, they can be pacified without battle."
Wáng Zōng (王宗) approved of his words,
and immediately withdrew the troops.
The bandits heard and were greatly pleased,
and returned the people they had plundered.
However, the troops of Dōnglái (東萊) commandery alone had not yet disarmed,
which again alarmed the bandits.
They fled to Liáodōng (遼東),
settling on a sea island.
In the spring of year five (111 CE),
lacking food,
they again plundered Dōnglái (東萊).
Fǎ Xióng (法雄) led the commandery troops to attack and defeat them.
The bandits escaped back to Liáodōng (遼東).
The people of Liáodōng (遼東), led by Lǐ Jiǔ (李久), jointly attacked and pacified them.
Thus, the provincial borders became peaceful.
Whenever Fǎ Xióng (法雄) traveled through his jurisdiction,
he would interrogate prisoners,
observe their expressions,
and often discern the truth from falsehood.
Chief officials who did not uphold the law all resigned their seals and left.
He served in the province for four years.
He was then promoted to Grand Administrator of Nánjùn.
His rulings in trials were few,
and the population increased.
The commandery was bordered by the Jiāng and Miǎn Rivers,
and also had the Yúnmèng marsh.
In the Yǒngchū period,
there was much violence from tigers and wolves.
The previous Grand Administrator had offered rewards and recruited people to hunt and capture them,
but many more were harmed as a result.
Xióng then issued a letter to the subordinate counties, saying:
"Tigers and wolves in the mountains and forests
are like people living in cities.
In ancient times, during periods of perfect governance,
fierce beasts did not cause disturbance,
all because of widespread benevolence and trustworthiness,
and kindness extending even to birds and animals.
Although I, the Grand Administrator, am not virtuous,
how could I forget this principle?
Upon receiving this notice,
you are to destroy all traps and snares;
do not senselessly hunt in the mountains and forests."
After this, the tiger menace gradually ceased,
and the people found peace.
He served in the commandery for several years,
and each year there was a bountiful harvest.
He died in office during the Yuánchū period.
His son, Zhēn,
is mentioned in the Yìrén Zhuàn.
Téng Fǔ, courtesy name Shūfǔ,
was a native of Jù, Běihǎi.
He first served in the province and commandery,
and was gradually promoted to Magistrate of Zhuó.
He possessed both civil and military talents.
The Grand Administrator, recognizing his ability,
entrusted him with commandery duties,
and he concurrently administered six counties.
His governance was well-ordered and clear,
and his affection flowed to the people.
He served for seven years,
during which lost items were not picked up from the roads.
At the end of Emperor Shùn's reign,
bandits rose up en masse in Yáng and Xú provinces,
persisting for years.
In the first year of Jiànkāng,
Fàn Róng and Zhōu Shēng of Jiǔjiāng, among others, gathered and rebelled,
stationing themselves at Lìyáng,
becoming a major scourge on the Jiāng and Huái regions.

The court dispatched Imperial Censor Zhōngchéng Féng Gǔn to lead troops and oversee the Provincial Inspector of Yángzhōu, Yǐn Yào, and the Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng, Dèng Xiǎn, in suppressing them.
Yào and Xiǎn's armies were defeated,
and they were killed by the bandits.
Furthermore, Xú Fèng and Mǎ Miǎn of Yīnlíng, among others, again raided commanderies and counties,
killing and plundering officials and commoners.
Fèng wore a crimson robe
and a black sash,
calling himself
"Wúshàng Jiāngjūn" (Supreme General).
Miǎn wore a leather cap and yellow clothes,
and carried a jade seal,
calling himself
"Huángdì" (Yellow Emperor).
They built camps in the mountains of Dāngtú.
They then established an era name
and appointed various officials.
They dispatched a separate commander, Huáng Hǔ, who attacked and captured Héféi.
The following year,
Zhāng Yīng and other bandits from Guǎnglíng again gathered several thousand people and rebelled,
occupying Guǎnglíng.
The imperial court widely sought generals and commanders.
The Three Excellencies recommended Fǔ for his civil and military talents,
and he was appointed Commandant of Jiǔjiāng.
Together with Colonel Zhàoxù, he assisted Féng Gǔn, joining tens of thousands of provincial and commandery troops to suppress them.
They also extensively offered rewards and recruitment,
with varying amounts of money and fiefs.
Empress Dowager Liáng, fearing that the multitude of bandits would consolidate
and that the generals would be unable to control them,
further deliberated dispatching Grand Commandant Lǐ Gù.
Before he could depart,
Fǔ and others advanced and attacked,
routing them greatly.
They beheaded Mǎ Miǎn, Fàn Róng, Zhōu Shēng, and one thousand five hundred others.
Xú Fèng then led his remaining followers to attack and burn Dōngchéng County.
Xiè Ān of Xiàpī responded to the recruitment,
leading his relatives to set an ambush for Fèng,
and beheaded him.
Ān was enfeoffed as Marquis of Píngxiāng,
with three thousand households.
Fǔ was appointed Colonel,
and oversaw affairs in Yáng and Xú provinces.
Fǔ again advanced and attacked Zhāng Yīng,
beheading and capturing over a thousand people.
Zhào Xù was impeached for cowardice and for not advancing,
as well as for falsely exaggerating the number of enemy heads.
He was recalled and executed in the marketplace.
Furthermore, Huá Mèng, a bandit from Lìyáng, called himself
"Hēidì" (Black Emperor),
attacked Jiǔjiāng,
and killed the Grand Administrator.
Fǔ, capitalizing on his victory, advanced and attacked,
defeating them.
He beheaded Mèng and three thousand eight hundred others,
and captured over seven hundred people,
with countless cattle, horses, and valuables.
Thus, the southeast was completely pacified,
and he returned triumphantly.
Fǔ was appointed Left Fēngyì,
and one of his sons was appointed as a Gentleman.
Fǔ distributed all his rewards
among his subordinates.
His nature was upright and straightforward;
he did not associate with influential figures,
which caused resentment among the eunuchs.
When his merits were to be recognized and he was due for enfeoffment,
Grand Commandant Hú Guǎng, who was then recording the affairs of the Secretariat,
acting on imperial instruction, submitted a memorial to dismiss Fǔ,
which caused widespread resentment throughout the realm.
He died at home.
Féng Gǔn, courtesy name Hóngqīng,
was a native of Dàngqú, Bājùn.
In his youth, he studied the Chunqiu and Sīmǎ's military strategies.
His father, Huàn,
was the Provincial Inspector of Yōuzhōu during Emperor Ān's reign.
He strongly disliked evildoers
and frequently punished their crimes.
At that time, Yáo Guāng, the Grand Administrator of Xuántú, also lacked popular support.
In the first year of Jiànguāng,
those who resented them forged an imperial edict condemning Huàn and Guāng,
and granted them "Ōudāo" (suicide daggers).
They also ordered Páng Fèn, the Commandant of Liáodōng, to swiftly execute the sentence.
Fèn immediately beheaded Guāng and arrested Huàn.
Huàn intended to commit suicide,
but Gǔn, suspecting something unusual in the imperial edict,
stopped Huàn, saying:
"My lord, while in the province,
you were determined to eliminate evil,
and there was truly no other reason for this.
It must be wicked people fabricating this,
planning to unleash their malicious poison.
I beg you to appeal the matter yourself;
it is never too late to accept punishment."
Huàn followed his advice
and submitted a memorial to protest his innocence.
It was indeed the work of forgers,
and Fèn was summoned and punished for his crime.
However, Huàn died of illness in prison.
The emperor pitied him
and bestowed upon Huàn and Guāng one hundred thousand cash each,
appointing their sons as Gentlemen of the Palace.
Gǔn thus became famous.
His family was wealthy and fond of giving,
providing relief to the poor and needy,
and was cherished and supported by his province and hometown.
He was first recommended as Xiàolián,
and after seven promotions, became Commandant of the Dependent State of Guǎnghàn.
He was then summoned and appointed Imperial Censor Zhōngchéng.
At the end of Emperor Shùn's reign,
Gǔn was given a staff of authority to oversee military affairs in the various commanderies of Yángzhōu.
Together with Colonel Téng Fǔ, he defeated the multitude of bandits,
and was promoted to Grand Administrator of Lǒngxī.
Later, the Xiānbēi raided the border,
and Gǔn was appointed Grand Administrator of Liáodōng.
He pacified them through persuasion and gathered them,
and the barbarians all dispersed.
He was summoned and appointed Metropolitan Commandant of Jīngzhào,
then transferred to Inspector of the Capital Region.
Wherever he served, he established his authority through strict penalties.
He was promoted to Court Minister, then Grand Master of Ceremonies.
At that time, the Mán of Chángshā were raiding Yìyáng,
gathering and accumulating for a long time.
By the fifth year of Yánxī,
their numbers had greatly increased.
Then the Mán bandits of Línglíng also responded to them,
forming a combined force of over twenty thousand men.
They attacked and burned cities and towns,
killing and injuring high-ranking officials.
Furthermore, the Mán and Yí of Wǔlíng all rebelled,
raiding the area around Jiānglíng.
Liú Dù, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, and Lǐ Sù, the Administrator of Nánjùn, both fled to Jīngnán,
and both perished.
Thereupon, Gǔn was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry,
leading over one hundred thousand troops to suppress them.
An imperial edict instructed Gǔn, saying:
"The Mán and Yí have been troubling the Huá (Chinese) for a long time,
and have not been suppressed.
They have each burned down capital cities,
and trodden upon government officials.
The generals and officials of the provinces and commanderies,
these ministers who died in their posts,
have fled one after another,
without even looking back.
This is truly a shameful thing to speak of.
The General has always possessed prestige and ferocity,
which is why you have been promoted to command the six armies.
In previous generations, Chén Tāng, Féng, and Fù, and their like,
with few attacked many,
and the Xī (tribes) of Zhìzhī, Yèláng, and Lóulán
had their heads hung in the capital streets.
Wèi and Huò campaigned in the north,
their achievements recorded in bronze and stone.
All these are things the General has thoroughly studied.
Now, if not for the General,
who could restore these former glories?
The appropriate way to advance,
the strategies for the present time,
the General will decide.
Matters beyond the capital,
will no longer be internally controlled.
We have already commanded the relevant officials to bid you farewell at the national gate.
Does not the Shī say: 'Advance our tiger ministers,
roaring like a fierce tiger,
spread out along the Huái riverbanks,
then seize the ugly captives.'
General, you must strive! "
At that time, there was famine throughout the land,
and the imperial treasury was completely empty.
Whenever a military expedition was launched,
the salaries of high-ranking officials were often reduced,
and taxes and levies of kings and marquises were borrowed.
Among the generals previously dispatched,
eunuchs frequently framed them for depleting military funds,
and many were punished.
Gǔn was by nature upright and direct,
and did not engage in bribery.
Fearing he would be targeted,
he submitted a memorial, saying:
"If power allows for treachery,
then Bó Yí could be doubted;
if it is simply said there is no suspicion,
then Dào Zhí could be trusted.
Therefore, when Lè Yáng presented his achievements,
Marquis Wén showed him a slanderous letter.
I request that one Palace Regular Attendant supervise military expenditures."
Shàngshū Zhū Mù memorialized that Gǔn, by expressing suspicion about finances,
had lost the decorum of a high minister.
An imperial edict ordered no impeachment.
When Gǔn's army reached Chángshā,
the bandits heard of it,
and all went to Yíngdào to surrender.
He then advanced to attack the Mán and Yí of Wǔlíng,
beheading over four thousand,
and receiving the surrender of over one hundred thousand people.
Jīngzhōu was pacified.
An imperial edict granted him one hundred million coins,
but he firmly declined to accept.
He returned to the capital with his troops,
attributing his success to the Attending Official of the Secretariat, Yīng Fèng,
and recommending him for the post of Colonel-Director of Retainers.
He then submitted a memorial requesting to retire.
The court did not permit it.
The supervising envoy, Zhāng Chǎng, acting on the instructions of the eunuchs,
memorialized that Gǔn had two maidservants dressed in military attire accompanying him,
and had also arbitrarily erected a stone tablet in Jiānglíng to record his achievements,
requesting that he be handed over to officials for investigation.
Shàngshūlìng Huáng Jùn debated this in a memorial,
believing that the offense had no legal basis,
and should not be investigated.
Coincidentally, the Chángshā bandits rose again,
attacking Guìyáng and Wǔlíng.
Because Gǔn's army had returned and the bandits had resurfaced,
he was dismissed from his post.
After a short while,
he was appointed Grand Builder,
and then transferred to be the Governor of Hénán.
He memorialized,
"According to old precedents,
the children and younger brothers of palace officials should not hold positions as provincial or commandery chiefs,"
but the Emperor did not accept this.
He was again appointed Grand Judge.
At that time, Shàn Qiān, the Administrator of Shānyáng, was imprisoned for an offense.
Gǔn investigated and caused his death.
Qiān
was the younger brother of the former General of Chariots and Cavalry, Shàn Chāo.
The palace officials, forming a faction,
then jointly slandered and falsely accused Gǔn.
He was condemned, along with Lǐ Yīng, the Colonel-Director of Retainers, and Liú Yòu, the Grand Minister of Agriculture, to be sent to the Left Repair Shop.
Yīng Fèng submitted a memorial to clear Gǔn and the others,
and they were released.
Later, he was appointed Colonel of Cavalry,
and again Grand Judge,
and died in office.
Gǔn's younger brother Yǔn
was pure and upright and had filial conduct.
He was capable in managing the Imperial Secretariat
and skilled in calendrical calculations.
He was appointed Colonel for Pacifying Captives,
and died at home.
Dù Shàng, courtesy name Bó Píng,
was a native of Húlù, Shānyáng.
His family was poor,
and he did not cultivate scholarship or conduct,
nor was he recommended by his local community.
Faced with continuous poverty,
he became a field overseer for Hóu Lǎn, a eunuch from the same commandery.
He managed to become a meritorious official for the commandery,
was appointed Gentleman,
and then appointed Magistrate of Shàngyú.
His governance was strict and severe,
and he was clear in exposing wickedness,
so officials and common people called him "divine and brilliant."
He was transferred to be Magistrate of Wén'ān.
He encountered a time of widespread epidemic,
high grain prices, and starving people.
Shàng opened the granaries to provide relief,
and arranged rescue for the sick,
and the common people were saved by him.
At that time, Zhū Mù, the Inspector of Jìzhōu, was on tour
and found Shàng to be very extraordinary.
In the fifth year of Yánxī,
thieves from Chángshā and Línglíng, numbering seven or eight thousand,
proclaimed themselves
“generals”
and entered Guìyáng, Cāngwú, Nánhǎi, and Jiāozhǐ.
The Inspector of Jiāozhǐ and the Administrator of Cāngwú fled at the mere sight of them,
and both commanderies were lost.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Shèng Xiū was dispatched to recruit soldiers and suppress them,
but he could not overcome them.
Over six hundred men from Ài County in Yùzhāng,
who had answered the call to enlist but did not receive their promised rewards,
became resentful
and revolted.
They burned down the counties in Chángshā Commandery,
raided Yìyáng,
killed the county magistrate,
and their numbers gradually swelled.
Yèzhě Mǎ Mù was again dispatched
to supervise the Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Liú Dù, in attacking them.
The army was defeated,
and Mù and Dù fled.
Emperor Huán issued an edict to the Duke-Ministers to nominate a replacement for Liú Dù.
Shàngshū Zhū Mù recommended Dù Shàng,
who was promoted from Yòuxiào Lìng to Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Shàng personally led his troops,
sharing their toil and rest,
and widely recruited various indigenous Mán Yí peoples.
He clearly set forth rewards
and advanced to attack,
greatly defeating them.
Tens of thousands surrendered.
The long-standing bandit chieftains in Guìyáng, Bǔ Yáng and Pān Hóng, feared Shàng’s might and prestige,
and moved into the mountain valleys.
Shàng pursued them for several hundred *lǐ*,
then entered Nánhǎi,
destroyed their three strongholds,
and acquired many treasures.
However, the followers of Yáng, Hóng, and others were still numerous.
Shàng wanted to attack them,
but his soldiers, having grown wealthy,
had no fighting spirit.
Shàng calculated that if he delayed, they would not fight,
but if he pressed them, they would surely flee.
So he declared that Bǔ Yáng and Pān Hóng had been bandits for ten years,
skilled in attack and defense,
and that his current forces were too few,
making it difficult to advance.
He would have to wait until all the troops dispatched by the various commanderies arrived,
and then they would unite their strength to attack.
He issued an order to the army
to freely engage in hunting.
The soldiers rejoiced,
and all, great and small, went hunting together.
Shàng then secretly ordered his trusted retainers to covertly burn their camps,
destroying all their accumulated treasures.
When the hunters returned,
none could help but weep.
Shàng consoled each person,
and deeply blamed himself,
then said:
“The wealth and treasures of Bǔ Yáng and others are enough to enrich several generations.
You gentlemen simply did not unite your strength!
The small loss we suffered
is not worth minding!”
Hearing this, the multitude was filled with indignation.
Shàng ordered them to feed their horses and eat their fill,
and the next morning,
they went directly to the bandit strongholds.
Yáng, Hóng, and others, considering their defenses strong,
no longer made preparations.
The officers and men, emboldened,
then greatly defeated and pacified them.
Shàng campaigned for three years,
and all the bandits were settled.
In the seventh year,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yòuxiāng,
and promoted to Administrator of Guìyáng.
The following year,
he was summoned back to the Jīngshī.
At that time, the Jīngzhōu soldiers under Zhū Gài and others,
having been on military duty for a long time
and not receiving sufficient rewards,
became resentful
and revolted again.
Together with the Guìyáng bandits Hú Lán and over three thousand others, they again attacked Guìyáng,
burning down counties.
The Administrator Rèn Yìn abandoned the city and fled,
and the bandit forces then grew to tens of thousands.
They then attacked Línglíng.
The Administrator Chén Qiú held firm and repelled them.
Thereupon, Shàng was made Zhōngláng Jiàng,
and led twenty-six thousand infantry and cavalry from Yōu, Jì, Líyáng, and Wūhuán to rescue Qiú.
He also joined with the Administrator of Chángshā, Kàng Xú, and others to raise troops from the various commanderies.
Combining their forces, they attacked,
greatly defeating them.
They decapitated Hú Lán and others, numbering three thousand five hundred heads,
and the remaining bandits fled to Cāngwú.
An imperial edict awarded Shàng a million cash,
and others received varying amounts.
At that time, Kàng Xú and Shàng were both renowned generals
who frequently achieved meritorious service.
Xú, courtesy name Bóxú,
was a native of Dānyáng.
His hometown praised his courage and wisdom.
He was first appointed acting Magistrate of Xuānchéng,
and moved all the top-knotted, bird-speaking people from the deep forests and distant swamps to reside under the county administration.
Thereafter, there were no more bandits within the territory.
Later, he served as a detached commander (Búbù Sīmǎ) under Zhōngláng Jiàng Zōng Zī,
attacking the Tàishān bandits Gōngsūn Jǔ and others.
He defeated and pacified them,
斬decapitating over three thousand heads,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wūchéng Dōngxiāng with five hundred households.
He was promoted to Dūwèi of Tàishān,
and bandits fled at the mere mention of him.
When he was in Chángshā,
all the long-standing bandits were pacified.
He died in office.
Emperor Huán issued an edict posthumously increasing Xú’s enfeoffment by five hundred households,
making a total of one thousand households.
Shàng was again made Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Shàng saw that the remnants of Hú Lán’s faction had fled south to Cāngwú,
and fearing he would be held accountable,
he falsely reported that Cāngwú bandits had entered Jīngzhōu territory.
Thereupon, the Inspector of Jiāozhǐ, Zhāng Pán, was summoned to the Tíngwèi.
His case had not yet been properly adjudicated
when he was granted amnesty and released.
Pán refused to leave prison,
instead holding firmly to his shackles and restraints.
The prison officials said to Pán:
“Heaven’s grace is boundless, yet you will not leave,
how can this be?”
Pán then made his own detailed statement, saying:
“Previously, the Chángshā bandit Hú Lán caused trouble in Jīngzhōu,
and his remnants scattered into Jiāozhǐ.
I personally donned armor,
traversed dangers and overcame obstacles,
attacked the vicious villains,
and cut down and exterminated their chieftains.
The rest all fled like birds and went into hiding,
returning to Jīngzhōu.
Inspector Dù Shàng, fearing that I would speak first,
and terrified of culpability,
secretly submitted a memorial slandering me.
I hold the position of a regional governor,
serving as a claw and tooth of the state,
yet I have been wronged by Shàng
and suffer punishment in prison.
Indeed, matters have truth and falsehood,
and the law has right and wrong.
I am truly innocent;
the amnesty has nothing to remove for me.
If I endure this to simply escape,
I will forever bear the shame of being wronged and humiliated,
living as a corrupt official,
and dying as a disgraced ghost.
I beg that Shàng be summoned to the Tíngwèi,
to face me and clarify right and wrong,
which will be sufficient to reveal the truth.
If Shàng is not summoned,
I will bury my bones in this cell,
and will never leave falsely,
accepting this injustice without resistance.”
The Tíngwèi submitted his statement,
and an imperial edict summoned Shàng to the Tíngwèi.
He exhausted his arguments and was found guilty,
but was pardoned due to his previous merits.
Pán, courtesy name Zǐshí,
was a native of Dānyáng,
known for his integrity,
and ended his career as Administrator of Lújiāng.
Shàng later became Administrator of Liáodōng.
Several months later,
the Xiānbēi led troops to attack Shàng.
He fought with them,
defeated them,
and the Róng Dí feared him.
At the age of fifty,
in the ninth year of Yánxī,
he died in office.
Yáng Xuán, courtesy name Jīpíng,
was a native of Wūshāng in Kuàijī.
His great-great-grandfather, Mào,
was originally from Hédōng.
He followed Guāngwǔ on campaigns
and became General Wēikòu,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīnyáng Township in Wūshāng.
During the Jiànwǔ era, he moved to his fief.
The title was inherited for three generations,
but due to a crime, the fief was abolished.
Thus, the family settled there.
His father, Fú,
was the Inspector of Jiāozhǐ,
known for his administrative ability.
His elder brother, Qiáo,
served as a Shàngshū.
He possessed a magnificent and beautiful appearance
and frequently submitted memorials on state affairs.
Emperor Huán loved his talent
and decreed that he marry a princess.
Qiáo firmly refused, but was not listened to.
Thereupon, he closed his mouth and refused to eat,
dying seven days later.
Xuán was initially nominated as Xiaolián.
He was gradually promoted,
and during Emperor Líng's reign, he became the Grand Administrator of Línglíng.
At this time, cunning bandits from Cāngwú and Guìyáng gathered,
attacking commanderies and counties.
The bandits were numerous, while Xuán's forces were weak,
causing the officials and people to be anxious and fearful.
Xuán then specially prepared several dozen horse-drawn chariots,
filling cloth bags with lime and placing them on the chariots,
and tying cloth ropes to the horses' tails.
He also prepared war chariots,
specifically equipped with bows and crossbows,
and set a date for a decisive battle.
He ordered the horse-drawn chariots to go first,
and with the wind, scatter the lime.
The bandits were unable to see.
Then, he set fire to the cloth.
As the cloth burned, the horses were startled,
charging into the bandit formation.
Following this, he ordered the rear chariots to fire bows and crossbows indiscriminately,
and gongs and drums to thunder.
The gangs of bandits were scattered and broken like waves.
Countless were pursued, wounded, and beheaded.
Their leaders were decapitated,
and the commandery territory was pacified.
Zhào Kǎi, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
falsely accused Xuán, claiming he had not personally defeated the bandits
but had falsely claimed the credit.
Xuán and Kǎi memorialized against each other.
Kǎi had partisans to assist him,
so Xuán was summoned in a caged cart.
The restrictions were strict,
leaving him no means to defend himself.
So he bit his arm to draw blood,
writing a memorial on his clothing,
detailing the circumstances of defeating the bandits
and Kǎi's false accusations.
He secretly ordered a relative to present it to the imperial court.
An imperial edict pardoned Xuán,
and he was appointed Yìláng.
Kǎi, on the contrary, suffered the punishment for falsely accusing others.
Xuán was promoted three times to become the Grand Administrator of Bóhǎi,
wherever he served, he had exceptional policies.
He was dismissed due to an incident.
Later, Zhāng Wēn, the Director of the Department of State Affairs, specially recommended him,
and he was summoned and appointed Shàngshū Púyè.
He requested retirement due to illness
and died at home.
The commentary says: After Ānshùn,
the imperial prestige gradually weakened.
Robbers and bandits proliferated,
arising from cracks [in governance].
Those who plundered people and stole cities were ceaseless month after month,
and those who falsely claimed imperial titles numbered in the tens.
Some relied on divine omens,
others fraudulently donned imperial robes.
Yet, among their principal leaders and chiefs,
none were ever heard of as truly formidable.
Nevertheless, they filled the four suburbs with their ramparts [or occupied the four directions],
sending out urgent orders from beginning to end.
As for these several generals,
they all exerted their efforts and diligently thought,
achieving merit through their toil.
However, the rewards of "brilliant wind" [imperial commendation] were not clearly distinguished,
and words of calumny mutually affected them.
From this, one can deduce
that the path of governance is difficult to escape [such problems].
The eulogy says: Zhāng Zōng and Pí Yǔ,
dared to stand firm and resist.
Jiāng, Huái, Hǎi, Dài,
were ravaged and blocked by bandits.
Who could clear them?
Xióng, Shàng, Gǔn, Fǔ.
Xuán was able to use stratagem,
and it can be said he revived the army.
Biographies of Liú, Zhào, Chúnyú, Jiāng, Liú, Zhōu, Zhào, Chapter 29.
Confucius said:
"Indeed, there is no greater filial piety than revering one's father;
and no greater reverence for one's father than correlating him with Heaven.
The Duke of Zhōu was such a man."
Zǐlù said:
"Alas, poverty!
Alive, there is nothing to nourish [parents];
dead, there is nothing to bury [them with]."
The Master said:
"Eating coarse vegetables and drinking water
is also filial piety."
Now, bells and drums are not the root of music,
yet the instruments cannot be removed;
three kinds of sacrificial animals are not the essence of utmost filial piety,
yet providing for parents cannot be neglected.
To preserve the instruments and forget the root is the straying of music;
to tune the instruments to harmonize the sound is the completion of music.
To over-emphasize providing for parents at the expense of conduct is the burden of filial piety;
to cultivate oneself to achieve official salary is the greatest way to provide for parents.
Therefore, speaking of being able to provide greatly,
the sacrifices to the Duke of Zhōu
received offerings from within the Four Seas.
Speaking of providing with righteousness,
Zhòngyóu's coarse vegetables
were sweeter than the sacrificial animals of the eastern neighbor.
Indeed, those who are troubled by the meagerness of coarse vegetables and water,
and seek official positions to provide for their parents,
they do so out of shame for their parents' situation.
Those who preserve sincerity and fulfill their conduct,
whose filial piety accumulates and whose salary becomes abundant,
these are the ones who can provide with righteousness.
During the Central Revival,
Máo Yì of Lújiāng had integrity in his youth.
His family was poor,
and he was praised for his filial conduct.
Zhāng Fèng of Nányáng admired his reputation
and went to visit him.
After they were seated, a prefectural summons happened to arrive,
appointing Yì as a magistrate.
Yì received the summons and went inside,
his face showing joy.
Fèng,
being a man of high aspirations,
held him in low esteem in his heart,
regretted coming,
firmly refused [to stay longer] and left.
When Yì's mother died,
he resigned from office and observed mourning.
He was repeatedly invited by government offices,
and served as a county magistrate,
always acting with propriety in taking up and leaving office.
Later, he was recommended as Xiánliáng,
and summoned by the Gōngchē,
but he never went.
Zhāng Fèng sighed, saying:
"Indeed, worthy men cannot be fathomed.
His joy on that day
was actually for the sake of his parents.
This is probably what is meant by,
'When the family is poor and parents are old,
one does not choose an office to serve in.'"
During the Jiànchū era,
Emperor Zhāng issued an edict praising and honoring Yì,
bestowing a thousand hú of grain.
Each eighth month, the senior officials were to inquire about his well-being,
and additionally bestow sheep and wine.
He died peacefully at home.
During the reign of Emperor Ān,
Xuē Bāo (Mèngcháng) of Rǔnán,
who was fond of learning and devoted to conduct,
lost his mother
and was known for his extreme filial piety.
When his father married a stepmother, she hated Bāo.
He was separated and driven out,
but Bāo cried day and night,
unable to leave,
even to the point of being beaten and flogged.
Having no other choice,
he built a hut outside the house.
He would enter in the morning to sprinkle and sweep,
but his father, angered,
again drove him away.
He then built a hut at the village gate,
never ceasing his duties morning and evening.
After more than a year,
his parents felt ashamed and allowed him to return.
Later, he observed the six-year mourning period,
his grief exceeding what was customary.
Afterwards, his younger brothers sought to divide the property and live separately.
Bāo could not stop them,
so he divided his property in half.
He took the elderly servants,
saying:
"They have served with me for a long time;
you cannot make them work."
He took the desolate and neglected fields and dwellings,
saying:
"These are what I managed in my youth;
my heart is attached to them."
He took the dilapidated and broken utensils,
saying:
"These are what I have always used for food and clothing;
my body and mouth are accustomed to them."
His younger brothers repeatedly squandered their wealth,
but he always provided relief.
During the Jiànguāng era,
he was specially summoned by gōngchē (the Imperial Courier Service).
Upon his arrival,
he was appointed Shìzhōng.
Bāo was by nature tranquil and humble;
he claimed illness and refused to take office,
begging to be allowed to die at home.
An imperial edict granted him leave to return,
with honors equivalent to Máo Yì.
He died of old age
at over eighty years old.
Such men,
who act with utmost sincerity,
whose actions are true to their hearts and move others,
and thereby achieve fame, receive emoluments, and are accorded礼,
can truly be said to have practiced filial piety.
The righteous deeds of several lords, such as Jiāng Gé and Liú Bān,
are also of this spirit.
Their deeds are compiled and recorded in this chapter.
Liú Píng, courtesy name Gōngzǐ,
was a native of Péngchéng, Chǔjùn.
His original name was Kuàng;
Emperor Xiǎnzōng later changed it to Píng.
During Wáng Mǎng's time, he served as a prefectural official,
and was appointed Magistrate of Zāiqiū.
His administration and teaching were greatly effective.
Thereafter, whenever a subordinate county faced serious bandits,
Píng was assigned to govern it,
and wherever he went, order was restored.
Because of this, the entire prefecture praised his ability.
During the Gēngshǐ era,
the world was in chaos,
and Píng's younger brother Zhòng was killed by bandits.
Later, bandits suddenly arrived again.
Píng supported and attended his mother,
fleeing for their lives.
Zhòng's posthumous daughter was just one year old.
Píng carried Zhòng's daughter and abandoned his own son.
His mother wanted to go back and retrieve the son,
but Píng would not allow it,
saying:
"I cannot save both.
Zhòng's lineage must not be cut off."
So he left without looking back,
and he and his mother hid together in the wilderness.
One morning, Píng went out to find food.
He encountered starving bandits
who were about to boil him.
Píng kowtowed and said:
"This morning, I am seeking vegetables for my elderly mother.
My mother depends on Kuàng for her life.
I wish to return first,
feed my mother,
and then come back to die."
He then wept.
The bandits, seeing his extreme sincerity,
took pity on him and let him go.
Píng returned,
and after feeding his mother,
he informed her, saying:
"I made a promise to the bandits just now.
It would be unrighteous to deceive them."
He then returned to the bandits.
Everyone was greatly astonished
and said to each other:
"We have always heard of courageous men,
but only now have we seen one.
Go, son!
We cannot bear to eat you."
Thus, he was spared.
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
Páng Méng, the General who Pacified the Di, rebelled in Péngchéng
and attacked and defeated the Administrator Sūn Méng.
Píng was again a prefectural official at that time.
He braved the white blades and lay on Méng's body,
suffering seven wounds.
Exhausted and unaware of what he was doing,
he cried out, pleading:
"I wish to take the place of the Prefect."
The bandits then lowered their weapons and stopped,
saying:
"This is a righteous man.
Do not kill him."
They then dispersed and left.
Méng was severely wounded and fainted.
After a while, he revived
and asked for a drink, being thirsty.
Píng tilted his wound to pour out blood and gave it to him to drink.
A few days later, Méng eventually died.
Píng then bandaged his wounds
and helped escort Méng's coffin
to his home county.
Later, he was recommended as Xiàolián
and appointed Jǐyīn Jùnchéng.
The Grand Administrator Liú Yù greatly esteemed him
and entrusted him with the affairs of the prefecture,
submitting a memorial to recommend Píng.
It happened that Píng encountered his father's death and left office.
After the mourning period was over,
he was appointed Magistrate of Quánjiāo.
His administration was benevolent and compassionate,
and the common people cherished him.
Some voluntarily increased their contributions to taxes,
while others reduced their age for conscription.
When the Inspector and Grand Administrator toured the region,
there were no prisoners in the jails.
People felt they had found their proper place
and knew not what to ask.
They merely issued imperial edicts and departed.
Later, he was dismissed due to illness.
In the early Xiǎnzōng era,
Zhōnglí Yì, the Shangshū Púyè, submitted a memorial recommending Píng, as well as Wáng Wàng of Lángyá and Wáng Fú of Dōnglái, saying:
"Your servant secretly observes that Wáng Wàng of Lángyá, Liú Kuàng of Chǔguó, and Wáng Fú of Dōnglái
are all seventy years old,
of tranquil and indifferent disposition.
Wherever they reside,
the villages are transformed by them.
They cultivate themselves and practice righteousness,
and should be in attendance at court.
Your servant is truly unworthy of knowing men,
but I secretly admire the principle of recommending worthy gentlemen and advancing the virtuous."
Upon the submission of the memorial,
an edict was issued to summon Píng and others,
and they were specially granted money for travel expenses.
Upon arrival, they were all appointed Yìláng
and frequently granted audiences.
Píng was twice promoted to Shìzhōng.
In the third year of Yǒngpíng,
he was appointed Zōngzhèng
and frequently recommended famous scholars like Chéng Gōng and Xún Rèn.
He held office for eight years.
Due to old age and illness, he submitted a memorial requesting to retire,
and died at home.
Wáng Wàng (王望), courtesy name Cíqīng (慈卿),
served as a guest official in Kuàijī (會稽).
He was transferred from Imperial Counselor to Inspector of Qīngzhōu (青州),
and had great prestige.
At that time, the commanderies suffered from drought,
and the people were destitute.
Wàng was touring his department
when he saw over
five hundred starving people,
walking naked and eating grass.
He felt pity and sorrow for them,
and so, acting on his own authority, he disbursed grain from local stores
to provision them
and made them coarse clothes.
When the matter was concluded, he submitted a report.
The Emperor, seeing that Wàng had not first requested permission,
displayed his memorial to all officials
for detailed discussion of his offense.
At that time, the high officials and ministers all considered Wàng to have acted on his own authority,
and that there were established laws for such actions.
Zhōnglí Yì (鍾離意) alone said:
"In ancient times, Huá Yuán (華元) and Zǐ Fǎn (子反),
good ministers of Chǔ (楚) and Sòng (宋),
did not await their ruler's command
to bring peace to their two states,
and the 'Spring and Autumn Annals'
considers this a beautiful tale.
Now, Wàng, cherishing righteousness and forgetting his offense,
acted benevolently without yielding.
If we strictly apply the law,
disregarding his original intention,
it will contradict the sagely court's aim of loving and nurturing the people."
The Emperor praised Yì's opinion
and pardoned him without punishment.
Wáng Fú (王扶), courtesy name Zǐyuán (子元),
was a native of Yè (掖).
In his youth, he cultivated virtuous conduct.
He resided as a guest in Bùqí (不其) county, Lángyá (琅邪),
and the villages where he stayed were transformed by his virtue.
The Chancellor of the state, Zhāng Zōng (張宗), invited him
but he did not respond.
When Zhāng Zōng wanted to compel him to come,
he took his staff and returned to his hometown.
He was repeatedly invited
but steadfastly feigned illness and did not rise.
Grand Tutor Dèng Yǔ (鄧禹) invited him,
but he did not go.
Later, he was appointed Imperial Counselor.
At an audience,
he appeared humble and as if he could not speak.
However, his nature was profound and upright;
he could not be swayed by unrighteousness,
and the people of his time held him in high regard.
During the Yǒngpíng (永平) reign,
Liú Fù (劉復), Marquis of Línyì (臨邑),
wrote a "Panegyric on Han Virtue,"
which highly praised Fú as a distinguished minister.
Zhào Xiào (趙孝), courtesy name Chángpíng (長平),
was a native of Qí (蘄) in Pèiguó (沛國).
His father, Pǔ (普),
was General of Field Crops during Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) time,
and appointed Xiào as a Gentleman.
Whenever he returned home,
he always wore white clothes and carried his own burden on foot.
Once, returning from Cháng'ān (長安),
he wished to stop at a post station.
The station master, having heard in advance that Xiào would pass by,
and expecting an esteemed guest,
swept and cleaned in preparation.
When Xiào arrived,
he did not identify himself,
and the master refused to let him in.
He then asked:
"I heard that General of Field Crops' son is coming from Cháng'ān.
When will he arrive?"
Xiào replied:
"He will arrive soon."
Thereupon, he left.
When the world fell into chaos
and people resorted to cannibalism,
Xiào's younger brother, Lǐ (禮), was captured by hungry bandits.
When Xiào heard of it,
he immediately bound himself and went to the bandits,
saying:
"Lǐ has been starving for a long time and is emaciated;
he is not as fat and well-fed as I am."
The bandits were greatly astonished
and released them both,
saying:
"You may go home for now and bring back some dried rice."
Xiào searched but could not obtain any,
so he returned to inform the bandits,
offering himself for cooking.
The crowd found him extraordinary
and therefore did not harm him.
His fellow villagers
admired his righteousness.
He was invited to serve by the provinces and commanderies,
but his acceptance or refusal always conformed to propriety.
He was nominated as Filial and Incorrupt,
but did not accept.
During the Yǒngpíng (永平) reign,
he was invited to the Grand Commandant's office.
Xiǎozōng (顯宗) had long heard of his conduct,
and issued an edict appointing him Grand Master of Remonstrance,
then promoted him to Imperial Household Grandee,
and again to Commandant of Chánglè (長樂) Palace Guards.
He also summoned his younger brother Lǐ (禮) to be Imperial Household Aide.
Lǐ also conducted himself with humility and modesty,
similar to Xiào.
The Emperor admired the profound conduct of the brothers
and wished to honor and distinguish them,
so he decreed that Lǐ should visit the Commandant of Palace Guards' office once every ten days,
and the Grand Provisioner would send supplies
for them to enjoy each other's company to the fullest.
After several years,
Lǐ passed away.
The Emperor ordered Xiào to escort the funeral procession with officials for burial.
Over a year later,
he was again granted leave as Commandant of Palace Guards and returned home,
where he died.
Xiào had no sons,
so Lǐ's two sons were appointed Gentlemen.
At that time, there was Wáng Lín (王琳), courtesy name Jùwèi (巨尉), in Rǔnán (汝南),
who lost his parents when he was just over ten years old.
Subsequently encountering great chaos,
with the people fleeing,
only Lín and his brother remained by the tomb hut,
weeping incessantly.
His younger brother, Jì (季),
encountered the Chìméi (赤眉) bandits
and was about to be eaten.
Lín bound himself
and pleaded to die before Jì.
The bandits took pity and released them,
whereby his name became famous in the villages.
Later, he was invited to the Grand Minister of Works' office,
recommended scholars, and then retired.
Wèi Tán (魏譚), courtesy name Shàoxián (少閒), from Lángyá (琅邪),
was also captured by hungry bandits at that time.
Dozens of his peers were all bound
and were to be cooked in turn.
The bandits saw that Tán seemed conscientious and honest,
so they uniquely ordered him to manage the cooking,
but bound him again every evening.
Among the bandits was a chieftain named Yícháng Gōng (夷長公),
who especially pitied Tán.
He secretly untied his bonds
and said:
"You all are supposed to be eaten.
Hurry and leave from here."
Tán replied:
"I am cooking for you gentlemen
and always get leftovers,
while the others eat grass and weeds.
It is better to eat me."
Yícháng Gōng (夷長公) considered him righteous,
and after explaining to the others, released them,
and all were able to escape together.
During the Yǒngpíng (永平) reign, Tán became House Administrator for a noble family.
Also, Ér Méng (兒萌), courtesy name Zǐmíng (子明), from Qíguó (齊國),
and Chē Chéng (車成), courtesy name Zǐwēi (子威), from Liángjùn (梁郡),
two brothers, were both captured by the Chìméi (赤眉) bandits.
When they were about to be eaten,
Méng and Chéng kowtowed,
begging to take each other's place.
The bandits also took pity and released both.
Chúnyú Gōng (淳于恭), courtesy name Mèngsūn (孟孫),
was a native of Chúnyú (淳于) in Běihǎi (北海).
He was skilled at explaining the Daodejing,
and was pure, tranquil, and unconcerned with fame.
His family owned mountain fields and fruit trees,
and if anyone encroached or stole,
he would always help them gather the harvest.
When he saw someone stealing his grain,
Gōng, mindful of their shame,
would hide in the grass,
and only rise after the thief had left.
The villages were transformed by his example.
In Wáng Mǎng's final years,
famine and war arose.
Gōng's older brother, Chóng, was about to be executed by bandits.
Gōng pleaded to take his place,
and both were spared.
Later, Chóng died,
and Gōng raised his orphaned children,
teaching them diligently.
If they did not follow his methods,
he would instead use a staff to whip himself,
to make them understand,
and the children, ashamed, would correct their mistakes.
When the banditry first occurred,
the common people ceased farming and sericulture.
Gōng alone always diligently worked the fields.
His fellow villagers tried to stop him, saying:
"Times are chaotic,
life and death are uncertain,
why needlessly exhaust yourself?"
Gōng replied:
"Even if I gain nothing,
how would it harm others?"
He continued tilling and weeding without stopping.
Later, the zhōu and jùn repeatedly summoned him,
but he did not respond.
He then lived in seclusion, cultivating his aspirations,
hiding in the mountains and marshes.
His every action and conduct
strictly adhered to ritual and propriety.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
the jùn nominated him as Xiàolián,
and the Sīkōng offered him a position,
but he did not accept any of them.
He went into hiding as a recluse in Qiánzōu Mountain in Lángyé,
and remained there for several decades.
In the first year of Jiànchū,
Sùzōng issued an edict commending Gōng's upright conduct,
notifying the jùn to bestow twenty bolts of silk upon him,
and sending for him to come to the gōngchē (imperial carriage),
appointing him as Yìláng.
He was granted an audience for the entire day,
where he was consulted on matters of governance.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng Qí Dūwèi,
and treated with great respect.
The worthy and virtuous persons he recommended
were all summoned and employed.
When he advanced to the court and presented his political views,
they were all based on morality and virtue.
Whenever the Emperor spoke with him,
he never failed to praise him.
In the fifth year,
he fell gravely ill.
Imperial envoys frequently visited to inquire about his health,
and he died in office.
An imperial edict praised and lamented him,
bestowed a thousand hú of grain,
and erected a stone stele to honor his village gate.
His son, Xiào, was appointed as Tàizǐ Shèrén.
Jiāng Gé, courtesy name Cìwēng,
was from Línzī in Qíguó.
He lost his father young,
and lived alone with his mother.
When the world fell into chaos
and bandits arose everywhere,
Gé carried his mother and fled from danger.
He endured numerous hardships and perils,
often foraging to support her.
He frequently encountered bandits.
Some would try to abduct him and take him away,
but Gé would always weep and beg for mercy,
stating that he had an elderly mother.
His tone and words were sincere and earnest,
enough to move people.
Because of this, the bandits could not bear to harm him,
and some even pointed out routes to avoid soldiers,
thus allowing both of them to survive the calamities.
Gé then traveled as a sojourner to Xiàpī,
impoverished and barefoot.
He worked as a laborer to support his mother,
providing everything she needed
without fail.
In the last years of Jiànwǔ,
he returned to his hometown with his mother.
Every year, at the appointed time,
the xiàn would conduct a census.
Gé, considering his mother elderly,
did not wish to disturb her.
He himself would pull the cart by the shafts,
without using oxen or horses.
Because of this, the villagers called him
"Jiāng Jùxiào" (Jiāng the Great Filial Son).
The Tàishǒu once summoned him with full ceremony,
but Gé declined due to his mother's old age.
When his mother passed away,
his profound grief nearly destroyed him.
He often slept prostrate in a grave-side hut,
and after the mourning period,
he could not bear to remove his mourning clothes.
The Jùnshǒu sent an chéngyuàn to have him remove his mourning clothes,
and then invited him to become an official.
In the early Yǒngpíng era,
he was recommended as Xiàolián and appointed Láng,
then assigned as Chǔ Tàipú.
After more than a month,
he impeached himself and left.
King Yīng of Chǔ sent his officials in a rush to pursue him,
but he refused to return.
He again sent a Zhōngfù with gifts,
but Gé declined to accept them.
Later, he repeatedly responded to summons from the Sāngōng,
but always left.
In the early Jiànchū era,
Tàiwèi Móu Róng recommended him as Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng,
and he was twice promoted to Sīkōng Zhǎngshǐ.
Sùzōng greatly revered and honored him,
promoting him to Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng.
At every court assembly,
the Emperor always had Hǔbēn Guards assist him,
and when he advanced to bow,
the Emperor always saluted him with his eyes.
When he was ill and unable to attend court,
the Tàiguān would send him wine and food,
his favor and indulgence were extraordinary.
At this time, the powerful relatives in the capital, Wèiwèi Mǎ Liào and Shìzhōng Dòu Xiàn, admired his conduct,
and each presented letters and extended courtesies.
Gé did not respond to or accept any of them.
The Emperor heard of this and esteemed him even more.
Later, he submitted a memorial requesting to retire,
and was transferred and appointed as Jiànyì Dàfū,
granted leave to return home,
and subsequently pleaded illness, claiming to be gravely ill.
During the Yuánhé era,
the Son of Heaven, recalling Gé's virtuous conduct,
issued an imperial edict to the Qí Xiàng, saying:
"Jiànyì Dàfū Jiāng Gé,
previously returned home due to illness.
How is his current health?
Filial piety
is the foremost of all virtues,
the beginning of all good deeds.
Whenever the state contemplates men of noble aspirations,
it never fails to think of Gé.
The xiàn is to bestow a thousand hú of current grain upon 'Jùxiào,'
and the senior officials are to visit and inquire after him every eighth month,
bringing sheep and wine,
until the end of his life.
Should any misfortune befall him,
sacrifice to him with a zhōngláo."
Because of this,
the title
"Jùxiào"
spread throughout the land.
When he died,
an edict again bestowed a thousand hú of grain.
Liú Bān, courtesy name Bóxīng,
was the great-great-grandson of Xuāndì.
Xuāndì enfeoffed his son Xiāo in Chǔ,
who was known as Xiàowáng.
Xiàowáng begot Sīwáng Yǎn,
Yǎn begot Wáng Yū,
and Yū begot Bān.
From Xiāo to Bān,
they accumulated benevolence and righteousness,
and for generations had a reputation for integrity,
with Yū being especially kind and compassionate.
He lost his mother early.
His full brother, Yuánxiānghóu Píng, was still young,
and Yū personally raised him,
always sleeping, waking, and eating with him.
Even when he became an adult,
he never left his side.
When Píng died of illness,
Yū wept and vomited blood,
and died a few months later.
Originally,
Yū inherited the royal enfeoffment.
However, he happened to live when Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
and was deposed as a commoner.
He then settled his family in Péngchéng.
Bān was orphaned at several years old,
and lived alone with his mother.
When Wáng Mǎng was defeated
and the world fell into chaos,
his Tàifūrén heard that Gēngshǐ had ascended the throne,
and so she took Bān and fled together to Cháng'ān.
When Gēngshǐ was defeated,
she again moved about with Bān amidst the warfare,
traveling west over Lǒng,
and eventually drifting to Wǔwēi.
Although Bān was still young,
he was devoted to cultivating himself,
lecturing and reciting without slackening.
His mother and maternal uncles,
thinking that they were stranded in a remote region,
with uncertain life and death,
believed it was not appropriate for him to exert himself so much,
and repeatedly tried to enlighten Bān,
but Bān still did not change his ways.
In the 8th year of Jiànwǔ,
Wēi Xiāo was defeated,
and the Hexi region was finally opened up.
Bān immediately took his family east to Luòyáng
to study classics with his teacher.
The following year,
Guāngwǔ issued an edict,
enfeoffing Bān as Marquis of Ziqīu,
to maintain the sacrifices to Xiàowáng,
and dispatched him to his state.
Later, as his state became subordinate to the King of Chǔ,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Zhùqīu.
In the 19th year,
when the emperor was touring Pèi,
he issued an edict asking about the conduct and abilities of the marquises in the commandery.
The Grand Administrator recommended Bān, stating that his conduct was exemplary
and that he was a mentor to the other marquises.
The Emperor heard this and praised him,
and then bestowed upon Bān an official ribbon,
one million coins,
and two hundred bolts of silk.
In the 20th year,
he again met with the imperial carriage in Pèi,
and subsequently followed it back to Luòyáng.
He was given grain and sundry items,
and kept as a Marquis Attending Sacrifices.
In the 1st year of Yǒngpíng,
as his state became subordinate to Pèi,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Marquis of Jūcháo,
and again followed the other marquises to his state.
Several years later,
Gūan Xún, the Inspector of Yángzhōu, recommended Bān, stating that while in his state, he spoke no untoward words,
and committed no hateful acts;
he deserved to be honored and distinguished.
Xiǎnzōng praised him.
In the 10th year,
Bān was summoned to act as the Supervisor of the Masters of the Imperial Guard (Zhí Jīnwú),
and accompanied the Emperor to Nányáng.
Upon his return, he became Marquis of Cháo.
The following year,
he also served as Colonel of the Cavalry (Túnqí Xiàowèi).
At that time, the five colonel positions were prominent but not demanding,
and their offices and residences were spacious,
their carriages and attire splendid,
and all their artisans' needs were met.
Thus, many imperial kinsmen and trusted confidantes held these posts.
Whenever the Emperor toured the commanderies and states,
Bān always led the cavalry from Chángshuǐ in attendance.
The Emperor once wanted to establish the Ever-Normal Granaries,
and many of the high officials and ministers debated, mostly finding it convenient.
Bān countered, saying:
"The Ever-Normal Granaries outwardly bear the name of benefiting the people,
but inwardly they actually oppress and exploit the common folk.
The powerful gentry use them to commit illicit acts,
and the common people cannot obtain fairness.
It is not convenient to establish them."
The Emperor then stopped the plan.
At this time, an edict was issued prohibiting the people from engaging in two occupations.
Also, due to a cattle plague in the commanderies and states,
envoys were sent to promote intercropping and increased cultivation.
However, the subordinate officials' inspections were superficial and often missed the truth,
and the common people suffered from this.
Bān submitted a memorial, saying:
"The commanderies and states, by official prohibition of two occupations,
even prevent those who own fields from fishing and hunting.
Currently, the commanderies along rivers and lakes generally produce little silk and mulberry.
The people rely on fishing and gathering to supplement their livelihoods,
and they do so during the idle months of winter and spring,
which does not interfere with agricultural work.
Moreover, the benefits of fishing and hunting
clear pests from fields,
aid in grain production,
and have nothing to do with two occupations.
Furthermore, due to cattle plague and floods and droughts in the commanderies and states,
the cultivated land has greatly decreased.
Therefore, an edict commanded intercropping
to increase the acreage,
for the sake of the people.
However, officials measure the land
with the desire to report more than before,
even counting uncultivated areas as taxable land.
It would be advisable to reiterate the command to the Inspectors and the Two-Thousand-Picul officials,
to ensure they thoroughly investigate the facts.
Anyone who falsely increases the reported acreage
should be punished with the same crime as those who seize land."
The Emperor followed all his suggestions.
Upon Sùzōng's ascension to the throne,
Bān was made Chief Steward of Chánglè.
In the 2nd year of Jiànchū,
he was promoted to Minister of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng).
When Bān'92]s wife passed away,
he received generous funeral gifts and contributions,
as well as burial land beneath Xiǎnjiélíng.
Bān, while in office, often spoke on matters of governance.
His care and protection of his nine generations of kin
and his righteous conduct
were especially prominent,
and people of his time praised him.
At the age of sixty,
he died in the 3rd year of Jiànchū.
His son, Xiàn, succeeded him.
After Xiàn's death,
his son, Zhòng, succeeded him.
Xiàn's elder brother was Kǎi.
Kǎi, courtesy name Bóyù,
was supposed to inherit Bān's title,
but he ceded it to his younger brother Xiàn,
and fled to avoid the enfeoffment.
After a long time,
during the Zhānghé era,
officials submitted a memorial requesting to abolish Kǎi's state.
Sùzōng admired his righteousness
and granted him special leniency,
but Kǎi still did not come forth.
After more than ten years,
in the 10th year of Yǒngyuán,
officials again submitted the request.
The Palace Attendant Jiǎ Kuí then submitted a memorial, stating:
"Confucius said, 'If one can govern the state with propriety and deference,
what difficulty will there be in managing affairs of government?'
I humbly observe that Kǎi, the heir of the late Marquis of Jūcháo, Liú Bān,
has always shown filial piety and fraternal devotion,
is humble and pure,
ceded his enfeoffment to his younger brother Xiàn,
and has kept himself hidden and distant.
The officials do not appreciate his desire for good deeds,
but rather bind him by conventional law.
I fear this is not conducive to promoting the spirit of yielding and deference,
nor to achieving a broad and tolerant transformation.
In previous generations, Wéi Xuánchéng, Marquis of Fúyáng,
and more recently Dīng Hóng, Marquis of Língyáng, and Dèng Biāo, Marquis of Méng,
all declined their titles due to their noble conduct and purity of character,
and we have not heard of them being demoted or stripped of their honors.
Instead, they all rose to the rank of the Three Ducal Ministers.
Now Kǎi admires these former exemplary individuals,
possessing the integrity of Bóyí.
He ought to receive compassion and forgiveness,
to preserve his former merits,
and thereby enhance the virtue-exalting beauty of the imperial court."
Hé Dì accepted this,
and issued an edict saying:
"Kǎi, the heir of the late Marquis of Jūcháo, Liú Bān,
was to inherit Bān's title,
but claimed his father's dying wish,
ceded the state to his younger brother Xiàn,
and fled for seven years,
his resolve growing ever firmer.
Indeed, the royal law esteems goodness
and perfects the virtues of others.
Therefore, let Xiàn succeed to the title.
This is an exceptional circumstance and should not be taken as a precedent for the future."
Then Kǎi was summoned,
appointed as a Gentleman (Láng),
and gradually promoted to Palace Attendant.
When Kǎi entered court,
no one in office failed to admire his conduct.
He was promoted to Colonel of the Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi).
In the 13th year,
he was promoted to Minister of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng),
then relieved of his post.
He was again appointed Palace Attendant,
and promoted to Colonel of the Long Water (Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi).
In the 1st year of Yǒngchū,
he replaced Zhōu Zhāng as Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
Kǎi's nature was earnest and old-fashioned;
he valued reclusive scholars,
and whenever there was a recommendation or summons,
he would always prioritize hermits.
His discussions were principled,
and his words and demeanor were lofty and refined.
In the 6th year (of Yǒngchū),
he replaced Zhāng Mǐn as Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
In the 2nd year of Yuánchū,
he replaced Xià Qín as Minister of Education (Sītú).
Under the old system,
the Gōngqīng (Grandees), Erqiānshí (Officials of Two Thousand Piculs), and Cìshǐ (Inspectors) were not allowed to observe the three-year mourning period.
Consequently, many officials, both inside and outside the court, abandoned mourning rituals.
During the Yuánchū reign,
Empress Dèng issued an edict stating that chief officials and those below who did not observe mourning for their parents
would not be permitted to govern cities or participate in elections.
At that time, someone submitted a memorial suggesting that Mùshǒu (Governors and Administrators) should be subject to the same regulations.
The edict was sent down to the Gōngqīng,
and those who deliberated thought it was inconvenient.
Kǎi alone argued:
“The reason the imperial edict institutes rules for mourning garments
is to promote virtuous transformation and elevate customs,
thereby extending the path of filial piety.
Now, the Cìshǐ is the exemplar of an entire province,
and the Erqiānshí is the teacher of a thousand *lǐ*;
their duty is to clarify matters for the common people
and propagate fine customs.
They should especially respect ritual institutions
and lead by example.
But the deliberators do not trace the origin of the matter,
and when it comes to Mùshǒu, they say it is inappropriate.
This is like muddling the source and hoping the stream will be clear,
or bending the form and wanting the shadow to be straight.
It cannot be achieved.”
The Empress Dowager adopted his view.
At that time, Rèn Shàng, the Zhēngxī Xiàowèi (Colonel of the Western Expedition), was summoned and convicted for illicit gains.
Shàng had once served as a deputy to the Dà Jiàngjūn (General-in-Chief) Dèng Zhì.
Dèng Zhì protected him,
and the Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) Mǎ Yīng and the Sīkōng (Minister of Works) Lǐ Hé, seeking to please Dèng Zhì,
did not first request approval
but unilaterally lifted Shàng’s *zānggù* (punishment of imprisonment and disbarment).
Kǎi refused to participate in the discussion.
Later, the Shàngshū (Secretariat) investigated the matter,
and both high officials received censure and blame.
The court praised Kǎi for this.
He served for five years.
In the first year of Yǒngníng (120 CE),
he claimed illness and submitted a memorial to resign from office.
