An imperial edict generously granted his request,
bestowing an additional 300,000 cash
and allowing him to return home to support his family with the salary of an official of a thousand *pǐ*.
The Hénán Yǐn (Administrator of Hénán) regularly sent sheep and wine in the eighth month of each year.
At this time, Emperor Ān had just begun to personally handle state affairs.
Many in the court praised Kǎi’s virtue,
so the Emperor sent someone to inquire about his health
and bestowed lavish rewards.
When Mǎ Yīng was removed from office,
the Shàngshū Chén Zhōng submitted a memorial recommending Kǎi, saying:
“I have heard that the Sāngōng (Three Ducal Ministers) above are like the celestial steps,
and below they resemble mountains and peaks.
They are the limbs and backbone of the sovereign,
standing like a tripod in office,
harmonizing *yīn* and *yáng*,
regulating and instructing the five virtues,
evaluating merits and assessing talents
to arrange the various officials.
They are not bewildered in fierce winds,
nor confused by torrential rains.
No position is more weighty than this.
But now the highest office is vacant,
and its occupant has not yet been discussed.
I have secretly ranked the various high officials
and compiled public opinions,
all commending the Tàicháng (Grand Master of Ceremonies) Zhū Cháng and the Shǎofǔ (Privy Treasurer) Xún Qiān.
My father, Chǒng,
formerly held the Sīkōng position,
and Cháng and Qiān were both his subordinates,
so he fully knew their abilities.
Cháng is skilled at explaining the classics but is narrow-minded in his approach,
while Qiān is stern, firm, and upright but weak in literary arts.
I humbly observe the former Sītú (Grand Minister over the Masses) Liú Kǎi,
who is profound, weighty, and sagacious,
with comprehensive virtue and integrity.
He humbly yielded titles and lands,
granting prosperity to his younger brother.
He embodies the spirit of 'floating clouds' (detachment from worldly affairs)
and possesses a vast, noble spirit.
He has served in two high offices repeatedly,
and his every action conformed to propriety.
He resigned due to illness,
keeping a low profile in his neighborhood,
content in simplicity, reflecting on purity.
His advancements and retreats were all measured.
All officials regard him as a model,
and the entire realm looks up to him with admiration.
In the past, Kǒng Guāng and Shī Dān,
and more recently Dèng Biāo and Zhāng Pú,
all left the position of prime minister
and were later reappointed to higher offices.
It is truly fitting to select and refine the exceptionally outstanding
to satisfy public expectations.”
Upon the submission of the memorial,
an edict summoned Kǎi and appointed him Tàiwèi.
At the beginning of Emperor Ān’s reign,
Shūnsūn Guāng, the Qīnghé Xiàng (Chancellor of Qīnghé), was convicted of corruption
and subsequently had his *gù* (disbarment) extended for two generations,
the affliction reaching his sons.
At this time, Fàn Bīn, the Jūyán Dūwèi (Commander of Jūyán), again committed the crime of corruption.
An edict was sent down to the Sāngōng and Tíngwèi (Minister of Justice) for deliberation.
The Sītú Yáng Zhèn, Sīkōng Chén Bāo, and Tíngwèi Zhāng Hào deliberated to follow Guāng’s precedent.
Kǎi alone believed
that “the principle of the *Chūnqiū* states:
‘Reward the good to their descendants;
punish the wicked only to their person.’
This is to encourage people toward good.
The *Shàngshū* says:
‘For severe penalties, be lenient; for light penalties, be severe.’
Now, if we impose *jìngù* (disbarment and punishment) on the descendants of corrupt officials,
treating a light offense as severe,
it may implicate good people.
This is not the intention of the former kings in detailing punishments.”
An edict stated:
“The Tàiwèi’s deliberation is correct.”
He served for three years,
and due to illness, he requested to retire.
After a long delay, his request was granted,
and the Hénán Yǐn was ordered to present gifts as before.
More than a year later,
he died at home.
An edict dispatched an envoy to oversee the funeral arrangements,
bestowing precious artifacts from the Eastern Garden,
and a thousand bolts of cloth.
His youngest son, Mào,
courtesy name Shúshèng,
also loved propriety and humility.
He successively held financial positions,
and during Emperor Huán’s reign, he became Sīkōng.
At that time, Lǐ Yīng, the Sīlì Xiàowèi (Colonel Director of the Retainers), and others were convicted,
and Chéng Yǔ, the Nányáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Nányáng), and Liú Huáng, the Tàiyuán Tàishǒu (Administrator of Tàiyuán), were imprisoned and sentenced to death.
Mào, along with the Tàiwèi Chén Fán and Sītú Liú Jǔ, jointly submitted a memorial to defend them.
The Emperor was displeased,
and officials, acting on his implied will, impeached the Sāngōng.
Mào was subsequently dismissed.
During the Jiànníng reign,
he was again appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū (Grandee Remonstrant),
and he died in office.
Zhōu Pán, courtesy name Jiānbó,
was a native of Ānchéng in Rǔnán,
and a kinsman of the hermit Xiè.
His grandfather, Yè,
served as the Tiānshuǐ Tàishǒu (Administrator of Tiānshuǐ) at the beginning of the Jiànwǔ reign.
Pán traveled to the capital in his youth,
studying the Ancient Text *Shàngshū*, the *Hóngfàn Wǔxíng* (Grand Norm of the Five Phases), and the *Zuǒshì Zhuàn*.
He loved ritual and had good conduct;
he spoke nothing outside of the *Diǎn Mú* (Canons and Counsels).
All scholars honored him.
He lived in poverty, supporting his mother,
and his frugal life was insufficient.
Once, while reciting the poem *Rúfén*, he reached its final stanza,
sighed deeply,
then removed his leather belt and sought an appointment as Xiàolián (Filial and Incorrupt).
At the beginning of Emperor Hé’s reign,
he was appointed Yèzhě (Court Gentleman),
and then made Zhǎng (Chief) of Rènchéng.
He was promoted to magistrate of Yángxià and Chónghé,
successively governing three cities,
and in all of them, he implemented benevolent governance.
Later, missing his mother,
he resigned his office
and returned to his hometown.
When his mother died,
his grief was so intense that he almost wasted away.
After the mourning period ended,
he built a hut beside her tomb.
He taught disciples, often numbering a thousand.
The Gōngfǔ (Ducal Administrations) made three attempts to recruit him,
each time with a special summons for his virtue.
Pán said to a friend:
“In the past, Fāng Huí and Zhī Fù nurtured their spirit and harmony by being frugal,
and did not let glory or gain disturb their way of life.
My mother has passed away;
what purpose would it serve to follow worldly things?”
Thus, he did not respond.
In the first year of Jiànguāng (121 CE),
at the age of seventy-three,
he gathered his students on New Year’s Day
and lectured all day.
Then he instructed his two sons, saying:
“Earlier today, I dreamt I saw my former teacher, Master Dōnglǐ,
lecturing with me in the innermost chamber of the underworld.”
After a moment, he sighed deeply:
“Is my time almost up?
If my life ends,
let a paulownia coffin be sufficient to encase my body,
and an outer coffin be sufficient to encase the inner coffin.
Let my body be arrayed and sealed in the shroud,
and washed clothes and a simple cloth headscarf be used.
Prepare bamboo slips two feet and four inches long,
copying one chapter of the *Yáo Diǎn*,
along with a knife and a writing brush,
and place them before the coffin,
to signify not forgetting the Way of the Sages.”
On the full moon day of that month,
he suddenly passed away without illness.
Scholars believed he knew his destiny.
Pán Tóng-jùn's Cài Shùn,
courtesy name Jūnzhòng,
was also known for his extreme filial piety.
Shùn was orphaned young
and cared for his mother.
Once, when he went out to gather firewood,
a guest suddenly arrived.
His mother, seeing Shùn had not returned,
bit her finger.
Shùn immediately felt a stirring in his heart,
threw down his firewood and rushed home,
kneeling to ask the reason.
His mother said:
"An urgent guest came,
and I bit my finger to alert you."
His mother lived to ninety
and died of old age.
Before she could be buried,
a fire broke out in the village.
The fire was about to reach their house.
Shùn embraced and lay on the coffin,
wailing and crying out to Heaven.
The fire then skipped over and burned other houses,
and Shùn's alone was spared.
The Grand Administrator, Hán Chóng, summoned him to be Libationer of the Eastern Gate (Dōnggé Jìjiǔ).
His mother had been afraid of thunder all her life.
After her death,
whenever there was a thunderstorm,
Shùn would always circle the tomb and weep,
saying:
"Shùn is here."
Chóng heard of this,
and every time there was thunder, he would dispatch a carriage and horses to the grave site.
Later, Grand Administrator Bào Zhòng recommended him as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate (Xiàolián),
but Shùn could not bear to leave the tomb,
and so he did not take up the post.
At eighty years old,
he died at home.
Zhào Zī, courtesy name Wénchǔ,
was a native of Yān in Dōng-jùn.
His father, Chàng,
was an Erudite (Bóshì).
Zī was orphaned young
and was known for his filial conduct.
The province and commandery summoned him and recommended him as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate,
but he did not take up any of the posts.
In the first year of Yánxī (158 CE),
the Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sīnóng), Chén Qí, recommended Zī for his extreme filial piety and upright conduct,
and he was subsequently promoted to Erudite.
At the beginning of Emperor Líng's reign (168 CE),
Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Chén Fán and General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Dòu Wǔ were executed by eunuchs.
Zī then feigned illness and left.
The Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Yáng Cì specifically invited him,
allowing him to wear a special cap (shìjīn) and enter and exit freely,
and invited him to discuss and deliberate.
He was recommended as an Eminent Scholar (Gāodì)
and successively promoted to Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng.
Due to illness, he was dismissed and returned home,
personally leading his sons and grandsons in farming for their sustenance.
One night, robbers came to plunder them.
Zī, fearing his mother would be frightened,
went to the gate first to meet the robbers,
and then invited them to a meal,
apologizing, saying:
"My old mother is eighty,
and sick and needs care.
We are poor,
with no provisions for morning or evening.
I beg you to leave some clothes and grain."
He asked for nothing from his wife or children's remaining belongings.
The robbers were all ashamed and sighed,
kneeling and departing, saying:
"Our actions were disgraceful;
we have violated a virtuous person."
After speaking, they rushed out.
Zī pursued them to give them some items,
but did not catch them.
From this, his fame increased.
He was summoned and appointed Counselor (Yìláng),
but he declined due to illness and did not arrive.
Imperial edicts severely reprimanded him,
and the province and commandery sent him off with due ceremony,
repeatedly, two or three times.
He had no choice but to answer the summons.
He was again appointed Chancellor of Dōnghǎi (Dōnghǎi Xiàng).
On his way to assume office,
he passed through Xíngyáng.
The Magistrate of Dūnhuáng, Cáo Gǎo,
who had been Zī's former Filial and Incorrupt candidate,
met him on the road to pay respects.
Zī did not stop for him.
Gǎo escorted him to the next post station,
but could not catch up, seeing only his dust.
He said to his Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù):
"Master Zhào's reputation is great.
If he passes through our territory and I don't see him,
I will surely be laughed at by the world!"
He immediately threw down his seal and sash,
and pursued him to Dōnghǎi.
After paying his respects to Zī,
he resigned and returned home.
This shows how much he was valued by the people of his time.
Zī was honest and frugal in office.
He received his emolument calculated by the day.
The powerful factions feared his thrift and moderation.
After three years in office,
he requested to resign due to illness,
and was appointed Yìláng.
He struggled with his illness in the capital.
As he approached his end,
he instructed his former subordinates Zhū Qí and Xiāo Jiàn,
to provide a simple, plain coffin,
and to line it with yellow earth,
wishing for it to quickly decay,
and soon return to the earth.
He forbade his descendants from altering this.
Then he left a letter enjoining his son Yìn, saying:
“Among all living beings,
that which has life must ultimately end.
This is the constant course of Heaven and Earth,
the ultimate law of nature.
Therefore, enlightened and sagacious people,
observing this nature of life,
regard existence and demise as night and day,
and life and death as morning and evening.
Thus, when they are alive, they do not seek amusement,
and when they pass away, they feel no sorrow.
When one passes away,
the primordial essence leaves the body,
the pure soul disperses,
returning to its origin,
reverting to nothingness.
Once vanished and collapsed,
it merges back with the earth and dust.
As earth is a [gòng] thing,
how can it have emotions?
Why then should one try to regulate its thickness or thinness,
or adjust its dryness or wetness?
It is merely because of the sentiment of the living,
who cannot bear to see the destruction of the form,
that the custom of covering bones and burying bodies arose.
The Yì says: ‘In ancient times, those who buried the dead
wrapped them in brushwood,
and interred them in the wilderness.
Later sages replaced this with coffins and outer coffins.’
The creation of coffins and outer coffins
began with Huángdì.
From the time of Táo Táng,
down to Yú and Xià,
simplicity and plainness were still valued,
using either pottery or wood.
It was not until the Yīn people that additions were made.
The Zhōu dynasty followed this,
combining the systems of the two preceding eras.
They further added the adornment of wall screens,
the ceremony of banners and inscriptions,
the rituals of summoning and covering,
the timing for temporary storage and burial sites,
the system of multiple layers of coffins and outer coffins,
〔一０〕and the number of clothes and shrouds for successive coverings.
〔一一〕These matters became troublesome and detrimental to practicality,
the items were fragmented and difficult to prepare.
Nevertheless, official ranks differed by grade,
and the noble and humble were distinguished.
From Chéng and Kāng onwards,
these regulations gradually went astray.
By the time of the Warring States,
they gradually declined,
〔一二〕laws and standards deteriorated,
and the high and low became intermingled and presumptuous.
Ultimately, this led to the Jìn Hóu requesting an underground tunnel for his tomb,
〔一三〕the Qín Bó practicing human sacrifice in burial,
〔一四〕the Chén Dàfū erecting three-doored timber structures,
and the Sòng Sīmǎ creating lavish stone outer coffins.
〔一五〕When it came to the tyrannical Qín,
they abandoned the Way and discarded virtue,
abolishing the systems of the Three Dynasties,
and instituting depraved and heterodox laws.
The national treasury was squandered on the Three Springs,
manpower exhausted for the Lì tomb,
precious objects buried in the dirt,
and craftsmanship expended on the tomb.
〔一六〕Since the beginning of human civilization,
the evils of extravagant funerals
have never been like this.
Even though Zhòngní vigorously clarified the Zhōu rites,
〔一七〕and Mòzǐ strove for the ancient Way,
they still could not prevent it.
〔一八〕Therefore, the scholars of Huáxià
competed in ostentation,
violating the essence of ritual,
attending to its superficialities,
pursuing its splendor,
and [gòng] its substance,
exhausting family wealth
to participate in these activities.
They neglected the living and focused on the dead,
abandoned those they supported to practice extravagant funerals.
〔一九〕How could this be the intention of the sages who instituted the rites?
The Records say:
‘Though there are rites for mourning,
grief is paramount.’
It also says: ‘For mourning, rather than being easy, it is better to be sad.’
But now it is not so;
combining inner and outer coffins
is considered filial piety,
and abundant wealth and multiple shrouds
are used to show compassion.
〔二０〕These are things I do not accept.
Of old, when Shùn was buried at Cāngwú,
his two consorts did not follow him.
〔二一〕How could there be a convention for reunion or a place for permanence?
Even sage rulers and enlightened kings were like this,
let alone ordinary people,
for whom the rites do not extend so far.
Ancient people reunited when times were suitable,
〔二二〕and parted when times were not.
〔二三〕Their actions and stillness accorded with ritual,
and they acted appropriately in all matters.
Wángsūn was buried naked,
〔二四〕and Mòyí exposed his corpse;
〔二五〕they both understood the nature of things,
and valued rapid transformation.
When Liáng Bólúan's father died,
he rolled up a mat and buried him;
when he himself died, his body was not returned.
〔二六〕Did these gentlemen lack profound affection for their kin,
or disregard the way of loyalty and filial piety?
Moreover, I am crude and ignorant,
lacking virtue and diligence.
My humble intention is clear within,
my aspiration is to emulate
the ancients above,
and below not to be blamed.
This must be carried out,
do not give rise to doubts or differences.
I fear that you will be weary of what you see,
and shun what you hear discussed,
and thus surely wish to alter the burial
and go against my will.
Therefore, I have widely drawn from ancient sages,
and recently examined current practices,
to enlighten your hearts.
I only wish to make a pit,
just large enough for a coffin and outer coffin.
Once the coffin arrives, bury it immediately.
〔二八〕Let there be no mound on the level ground.
Do not divine for auspicious dates and times,
do not set up offerings at the burial,
do not linger by the grave,
and do not raise a mound or plant trees.
Alas, my child,
strive for this!
I have no more words to say!”
Zhū Qí and Xiāo Jiàn escorted the coffin home.
〔二九〕His son Yìn could not bear to see his father's body merge with the earth
and wanted to alter the burial.
Qí and Jiàn persuaded him with Zī's dying instructions.
〔三０〕Thus, he complied.
At the time, people praised Zī as enlightened and perceptive.
An eulogy says: Gōngzǐ and Chángpíng,
faced bandits and yielded their lives.
Chúnyú was benevolent and fraternal,
famous for his 'great filial piety'.
Jūcháo loved to study,
and thus inherited family emoluments.
Bóyù hesitated and pondered,
following the footsteps of Gūzhú.
Wénchǔ valued a simple end,
wishing for rapid decay in burial.
Zhōu could move his parents,
conserving his spirit to nourish good fortune.
Biān Biāo's Liezhuan, Part 30, Volume I (from Dōngdū Zhǔrén onwards, it is divided into Volume II).
Bān Biāo, courtesy name Shúpí,
was a native of Fúfēng Ānlíng.
His grandfather Kuàng
served as Yuèjí Xiàowèi during the reign of Chéngdì.
His father Zhì
served as Guǎngpíng Tàishǒu during the reign of Āidì.
Bān Biāo's nature was profound and he loved antiquity.
When he was over twenty years old,
Gēngshǐ was defeated,
and the Sānfǔ region fell into great chaos.
At that time, Kuí Xiāo commanded a multitude in Tiānshuǐ,
so Biao took refuge with him.
Xiāo asked Biao, saying:
"In the past, when the Zhōu dynasty fell,
the Warring States contended,
the realm was divided,
and it took several generations to settle.
Do you think that the affairs of vertical and horizontal alliances will rise again today?
Or will the Mandate be received and new prosperity emerge,
centered on one person?
I wish for you to try and discuss this."
He replied:
"The rise and fall of Zhōu
were very different from Hàn.
In ancient Zhōu, there were five grades of nobility,
and the feudal lords managed the government.
The roots were already weak,
while the branches and leaves were strong,
thus in its decline, there were affairs of vertical and horizontal alliances.
This was the natural course of events.
Hàn followed the Qín system,
establishing commanderies and counties.
The ruler held sole authority,
and ministers had no hundred-year grip on power.
By the time of Chéngdì,
power was lent to the imperial relatives by marriage.
Āi and Píng had short reigns,
and the imperial succession was broken three times.
Thus, the Wáng clan gained power,
and then usurped the imperial title.
The danger arose from above,
and the harm did not reach below.
Therefore, after the usurpation,
the whole world sighed with longing.
Within more than ten years,
the interior and exterior were disturbed,
and distant and near regions all rose up.
Those claiming titles gathered like clouds,
all proclaiming the Liú clan,
without prior consultation, but with the same words.
Currently, the heroes who control regions
do not possess the inherited enterprises of the Seven States.
Yet the common people sing praises,
longing for and looking up to Hàn virtue.
This is already evident."
Xiāo said:
"Your words about the circumstances of Zhōu and Hàn are acceptable;
as for merely seeing that foolish people are accustomed to recognizing the Liú clan's surname and title,
and therefore saying that the Hàn house will revive,
that is shortsighted.
In the past, when Qín lost its deer,
Liú Jì chased and tethered it.
Did the people of that time already know Hàn?"
Biao was displeased by Xiāo's words,
and also lamented the difficulties of the time.
So he wrote the *Wángmìnglùn*,
believing that Hàn virtue inherited from Yáo,
and possessed the auspicious mandate.
The rise of a king's reign
was not achieved by deceit or force.
He wished to move Xiāo with it,
but Xiāo never understood.
So Biao withdrew to Héxī.
Dòu Róng, the Grand General of Héxī, appointed him as an aide,
and treated him with deep respect,
interacting with him as a teacher and friend.
Biao then advised Róng to serve Hàn,
and to unite Xīhé to resist Kuí Xiāo.
When Róng was summoned back to the capital,
Guāngwǔ asked:
"Who participated in preparing the memorials you submitted?"
Róng replied:
"They were all done by my aide, Bān Biāo."
The Emperor had long heard of Biao's talent,
so he summoned him for an audience,
appointed him as a Màocái for Sīlì,
and made him Magistrate of Xú.
He was dismissed due to illness.
Later, he was repeatedly invited by the Three Dukes,
but always declined.
Since Biao was highly talented and fond of writing,
he devoted himself to historical records.
During the time of Wǔdì,
Sīmǎ Qiān compiled the *Shǐjì*.
From the Tàichū era onwards,
it was incomplete and not recorded.
Later, enthusiasts occasionally collected contemporary events,
but these were mostly crude and vulgar,
insufficient to continue his work.
Biao then continued to collect neglected incidents from previous histories,
and broadly incorporated unusual accounts,
composing dozens of chapters for a *Hòuzhuàn* (Later Tradition).
He then weighed and considered previous histories,
and criticized and corrected their merits and demerits.
His brief discussion states:
He said,
"The *Táo Wù* of Chǔ,
the *Shèng* of Jìn,
and the *Chūnqiū* of Lǔ,
are all one thing."
During the time of Dìng and Āi,
the Lǔ gentleman Zuǒ Qiūmíng collected and compiled
their texts,
composing thirty chapters of *Zuǒshì Zhuàn*.
He also compiled differences and similarities,
titled *Guóyǔ*,
in twenty-one chapters.
From then on, the affairs of *Shèng* and *Táo Wù* became obscured,
while
only *Zuǒshì* and *Guóyǔ* became prominent.
There were also records from the time of Huángdì down to the Chūnqiū period, concerning emperors, kings, dukes, marquises, ministers, and grandees,
titled *Shìběn*,
in fifteen chapters.
After the Chūnqiū period,
the Seven States contended,
and Qín unified the various states,
then there was the *Zhànguócè* in thirty-three chapters.
When Hàn arose and pacified the realm,
Lù Jiǎ, a Grand Master of the Palace, recorded
the achievements of the time,
composing the *Chǔ Hàn Chūnqiū* in nine chapters.
In the reign of Xiàowǔ,
Sīmǎ Qiān, the Grand Historian, adopted from *Zuǒshì* and *Guóyǔ*,
abridged *Shìběn* and *Zhànguócè*,
and based on
the events of Chǔ and Hàn and the various states,
from Huángdì above,
to the capture of the Qílín below,
composed *Běnjì*, *Shìjiā*, *Lièzhuàn*, *Shū*, and *Biǎo*, totaling one hundred thirty chapters,
with ten
chapters missing.
The records by Qiān,
from Hàn Yuán to Wǔ, cease,
that is his achievement.
As for collecting classics and gathering traditions,
and dispersing the affairs of the Hundred Schools,
much is superficial and brief,
not as good as their originals.
He strove to make broad knowledge and extensive recording his merit,
but his discussions are shallow and not profound.
In his discussion of scholarship,
he elevates Huáng-Lǎo and disparages
the Five Classics;
in his preface to 'Treatise on Money-Makers',
he belittles benevolence and righteousness and shames poverty;
in his account of knight-errants,
he disparages upholding integrity and values popular achievements.
These are his great failings that harm the Dao,
and for which he incurred the punishment of extreme penalty.
However, he excels at describing and narrating events and principles.
He is clear but not flowery,
simple but not crude.
His literary quality and substance are well-matched,
truly the talent
of a good historian.
If only Qiān had followed the normative words of the Five Classics,
and accorded with the saints' judgments of right and wrong,
his work might have approached perfection.
That
by which we know antiquity,
and by which later generations observe the past,
is the eyes and ears of the sages.
Sīmǎ Qiān titled his accounts of emperors as *Běnjì*,
and accounts of dukes and marquises who passed on their states as *Shìjiā*,
and accounts of ministers and gentry who rose uniquely as *Lièzhuàn*.
Moreover, he advanced Xiàng Yǔ and Chén Shè while dismissing Huáinán and Héngshān.
His intentions are detailed and intricate,
but his arrangements are not consistent.
As for
Qiān's writings,
they gather from ancient and modern times,
and penetrate classics and traditions,
reaching extreme breadth.
With one person's intellect,
the text is heavy and thoughts are numerous,
so his book contains many omissions,
and still has superfluous words,
often inconsistent.
For example, when describing Sīmǎ Xiāngrú,
he mentions his commandery and county,
and records his courtesy name.
But for people like Xiāo, Cáo, and Chén Píng,
as well as Dǒng Zhòngshū
and his contemporaries,
he does not record their courtesy names,
or mentions their county but not their commandery.
Perhaps he did not have time for this.
Now, in these later chapters,
I will carefully examine the facts,
and standardize
writings
did not become family histories,
only annals and biographies.
The biography says:
"Slaying the historian to reach the ultimate truth,
being even-tempered and upright,
is the meaning of the Chūnqiū."
Biāo returned to serve under Sìtú Yù Kuàng.
At that time, the Dōnggōng was newly established,
and all the kingdoms of the princes were opened,
but their officials were not yet fully appointed,
and tutors and guardians were largely absent.
Biāo submitted a memorial, saying:
"Qí
cannot be without Qí speech.
Constantly dwelling with evil people,
one cannot be without doing evil,
just as one born and raised in Chǔ
cannot be without Chǔ speech."
Therefore,
the Sages carefully consider with whom they associate,
and are cautious about what they habituate themselves to.
In ancient times, when Chéng Wáng was a child,
when he went out, there were Zhōu Gōng, Shào Gōng, Tàishǐ Yì;
when he came in,
there were Dà Diān, Hóng Yāo, Nán Gōng Kuò, Sǎn Yí Shēng.
Before and after, to his left and right,
there was no one who violated ritual.
Therefore, on the day Chéng Wáng ascended the throne,
the world was tranquil and
peaceful.
This is why the Chūnqiū says:
"Love your child by teaching them the path of righteousness,
and do not let them fall into wickedness.
Arrogance, extravagance, debauchery, and idleness
are the sources of wickedness."
The Shī Jīng says:
"He bequeathed his descendants
counsel,
thereby tranquilizing and protecting his sons."
This speaks of Wǔ Wáng's counsel left to his descendants.
Xiàng, Wáng Bǎo, Xiāo Wàngzhī, and Zhōu Kān and their like,
with their literary talent and Confucian scholarship, safeguarded and instructed the Dōnggōng and those below.
Without exception, their character was highly esteemed and pure,
and their virtue perfected.
Now, although the imperial heir apparent and the various princes
have entered school and studied since childhood,
cultivating ritual and music,
their tutors and ministers have not yet found worthy talents,
and many official positions are lacking compared to the old regulations.
It is appropriate to broadly select famous Confucians
who possess gravity, wisdom, and competence in governance,
to serve as Tàizǐ Tàifù.
For the Dōnggōng and the various princely states,
all official positions should be filled.
Furthermore, according to the old system,
the Crown Prince was granted an income from ten
counties,
had a Zhōu Guard with crossed halberds,
and attended court once every five days.
He would then sit in the eastern chamber
to examine the imperial meals.
On non-court days,
the servants and Zhōngyǔn would daily inquire
and nothing more.
This made clear that he should not be lightly treated,
thereby expanding their reverence.
Later, he investigated Sìtú Lián, who was the magistrate of Wàngdū,
and the officials and common people loved him.
In the 30th year of Jiànwǔ,
at the age of fifty-two,
he died in office.
His collected works included nine pieces of fù, lùn, shū, jì, and memorials.
He had two sons: Gù
and Chāo.
Chāo has a separate biography.
The论曰 (Disquisition Says): Bān Biāo, with his erudite scholarship and superior talent,
amidst turmoil and danger,
did not overstep propriety in his actions,
did not deviate from correctness in his words,
did not seek rapid advancement in office,
and did not defy others in his integrity.
He displayed his literary brilliance to enrich the national canon,
and maintained his humble position without complaint.
He might have considered that the world's fortunes were not yet flourishing,
so that it was not a matter of being ashamed of his humble position.
How firm was his adherence to the Way and his tranquil detachment!
Gù, courtesy name Mèngjiān.
At nine years old,
he was able to compose essays and recite poetry and rhapsodies.
When he grew up,
he extensively studied all records,
and thoroughly investigated the words of the Nine Schools and Hundred Schools.
He had no fixed teachers for his studies,
did not engage in textual exegesis of sentences,
but grasped the general principles.
His nature was broad and tolerant,
and he did not exalt himself above others by his talent,
which led other scholars to admire him.
In the early years of Yǒngpíng,
Dōngpíng Wáng Cāng, being a close relative, was appointed Piàojì Jiāngjūn to assist in governance.
He opened his eastern chamber
to welcome heroes.
At that time, Gù was just coming of age,
and he submitted a letter to Cāng, saying:
"What is recorded in the Shī Jīng and Shū Jīng
has never seen three such [generations] as this."
The biography says:
"There must be extraordinary people
before there can be extraordinary events;
there must be extraordinary events

I am fortunate to be born in an era of peace and clarity,
to be among the last to see and hear.
Privately, like an ant,
I secretly observe the affairs of the state.
I sincerely admire the General for taking on a thousand-year responsibility,
treading in the footsteps of the former Sages,
embodying a grand and virtuous disposition,
occupying a high and prominent position.
You are broadly familiar with all matters,
and ardently devoted to the Six
Arts.
Your heart distinguishes right from wrong,

You gather the words of even a madman,

talents.

You aim to broadly gather worthy talents,

freely moving in the imperial court,
his brilliant name proclaimed in the present age,

Huī is
a talent of this generation.
Jīngzhào Jìjiǔ Jìn Féng,

He loves antiquity and delights in the Dao,

His virtuous conduct is
that of ancient people,

Fúfēng Yuàn Lǐ Yù,

He resides as a guest in Dùlíng,

He reviews the old and learns the new,

He is honest, pure, and upright,

complete.
Even the famous Confucians of previous generations,

It is fitting to let him examine and continue [the classics],

Jīngzhào Dūyóu Guō Jī,

His achievements in political affairs

If he can meet with an enlightened time,

Liángzhōu Cóngshì Wáng Yōng,

An imperial edict was sent to the commandery,

Its poems say:
When Sùzōng 肅宗 was fond of literature,
Bān Gù 班固 consequently gained even more favor.
He frequently entered the imperial palace to read,
sometimes for consecutive days and nights.
Whenever the emperor went on an inspection tour,
Bān Gù 班固 would offer *fù* 賦 and eulogies.
When there was a major deliberation in the court,
the emperor would send Bān Gù 班固 to question the high officials,
who would then debate before him.
The rewards and imperial favor were extremely generous.
Bān Gù 班固, considering his talent and skill were comparable to those of the second generation of famous scholars,
yet his position was no more than a *láng* 郎 (gentleman-in-waiting),
felt like Dōngfāng Shuò 東方朔 and Yáng Xióng 揚雄 who wrote about themselves.
Believing he was not living in the times of Sū Qín 蘇秦, Zhāng Yí 張儀, Fàn Ju 范雎, or Cài Zé 蔡澤,
he wrote the "Bīn Xì" 賓戲 to express his thoughts.
Later, he was promoted to Xuánwǔ Sīmǎ 玄武司馬.
The Son of Heaven convened all the Confucians to discuss the Five Classics,
and composed the "Bái Hǔ Tōng Dé Lùn" 白虎通德論,
ordering Bān Gù 班固 to compile its content.
At that time, the Northern Chányú 北單于 sent envoys to offer tribute,
seeking to establish a peace and kinship alliance.
The emperor issued an edict to consult his officials.
Some of the debaters thought,
"The Xiongnú 匈奴 are a deceitful nation,
without any sincere desire to submit.
They only fear the might of Hàn 漢,
and are pressed and deterred by the Southern captives,
hence they hope for a renewed alliance
to secure their disloyal and rebellious factions.
If we send envoys now,
we might lose the goodwill of the Southern captives,
and fulfill the cunning scheme of the Northern Dí 狄,
which is unacceptable."
Bān Gù 班固 argued:
"I humbly reflect that
since the rise of Hàn 漢,
throughout the ages and years,
wars have entangled the foreign tribes,
especially concerning the Xiongnú 匈奴.
The methods of pacification and control
have not been uniform.
Sometimes it was to cultivate culture to bring them into harmony,
sometimes to use military force to conquer them,
sometimes to humble ourselves to accommodate them,
and sometimes to make them submit as vassals.
Although the strategies of yielding and asserting have been inconstant,
varying with the times,
yet there has never been a refusal to engage
or a failure to interact with them.
Therefore, since the era of Jiànwǔ 建武,
the old traditions were revived,
and heavy envoys were repeatedly dispatched,
succeeding one another,
until the end of that period,
when contact was temporarily broken.
In the eighth year of Yǒngpíng 永平,
the re-establishment of communication was again debated.
And the court contention lasted for days,
with differing opinions swirling,
many emphasizing the difficulties,
few speaking of the ease.
The former emperor, with his sagely virtue and farsightedness,
looking both forward and back,
eventually decided to dispatch envoys again,
following the precedent of previous generations.
From this, it can be inferred
that there has never been an era where communication was neglected and not maintained.
Now, Wūhuán 烏桓 has come to the imperial court,
bowing before the interpreter;
Kāngjū 康居 and Yuèzhī 月氏
have arrived from afar;
the Xiongnú 匈奴 have splintered,
and their famous kings have surrendered.
Three parties have submitted
not through military might.
This is truly a sign that the state is connected to divine wisdom and natural order.
Your humble servant believes it is appropriate to follow precedent,
and again dispatch envoys.
At best, this can continue the assemblies of distant peoples from Wǔfèng 五鳳 and Gānlù 甘露;
at worst, it will not lose the meaning of Jiànwǔ 建武 and Yǒngpíng 永平's loose rein policy.
Let the barbarian envoys come again,
and then send our envoys once.
This will both clarify that the Central Kingdom's principle lies in loyalty and trustworthiness,
and also let them know that the sacred dynasty's rites and righteousness are constant.
How
can we anticipate treachery and show suspicion, alienating their good intentions?
Severing ties, we do not know its benefit;
maintaining ties, we have not heard of its harm.
If later the Northern barbarians gradually grow strong
and are able to create turmoil,
and we then seek to resume communication,
what will it achieve?
It is better to use the present opportunity to bestow favor,
as a strategy for the long term."
Bān Gù 班固 also composed the "Diǎn Yǐn Piān" 典引篇,
describing the virtues of the Hàn 漢 dynasty.
He believed that Sīmǎ Xiāngrú's 司馬相如 "Fēng Shàn" 封禪 was ornate but not classical,
and
Yáng Xióng's 揚雄 praise of the Xīn 新 dynasty
was classical but not true.
He implicitly considered his own work to have achieved the right balance.
Its text says:
Complete.
The initial mandate of the human lords,
the beginning of the five virtues,
was the same as in the primordial chaos,
amidst the profound obscurity.
Surpassing cords and exceeding notches,
silent and without pronouncements,
their lineage
cannot be traced or connected.
As for those who had clan names and titles,
who continued Heaven's work and expounded upon it,
none did not open their era at the head of the Great Hào's 太昊 imperial beginning.
How lofty and remote!
Their
records can still be obtained and studied.
In the ages thereafter,
transforming divinely,
they held light but did not yet shine.
Shùn 舜 inherited and abdicated to Yú 虞,

Jì 稷 and Xiè 契 flourished in their tasks,
leading to Chéng Tāng 成湯 and Wǔ Wáng 武王.
Once the ministers had completed their cycles,
Heaven then attributed the merit to the original head,
about to bestow it upon the Hàn
Liú 劉 clan.
Permitting them to succeed the chaotic end of the Three Dynasties,
and encounter the calamity of the soaring dragon's misfortune,

Therefore,
Heaven first commanded the Profound Sage,

Even the preceding sages Gāo Yáo 皋陶, Kuí 夔, Yī Yǐn 伊尹, and Duke of Zhōu 周旦's diligent assistance,

Thus, Gāo Zǔ 高祖 and Guāngwǔ 光武, the two sages,

without

it was.
It was.
Both initiated their paths from one deficiency,

diligently serving the people for generations,
ruling as hegemons of the regions.
They rode upon the prestige of their granted mandate, the crimson bow
and yellow axe,
to chastise Wéi 韋, Gù 顧, Lí 黎, and Chóng 崇 for their defiance.
Reaching the three and five illustrious ones of Huáxià 華夏,
when the capital moved to Hào 鎬 and Bó 亳,
they then turned their backs to the north,
like tigers scattering
their troops,
annihilating the celestial capital.
Therefore, righteous scholars consider it grand but not substantial,
and military praise is not fully exhausted,
showing a shameful lack of virtue. Is this not so?
Nevertheless, how solemn

Unanimously pure and luminous,
thereby venerating ancestors,

How

Their grand outline had constant principles,

their brilliant splendor shining brightly and unchangingly.
re-illuminated,

Thus, the achievements of establishing the three powers and ascending to manifest glory,

Hàn dynasty.
Its path reached the point of intertwining heaven and earth,
encompassing the three luminaries,

where natures and categories follow their principles,
and all things
prosper,
and this has been so for a long time.
Qiān,
cautious and diligent,
belittling what is established and suppressing what is settled,
dared not discuss creation.
Yet, the matters of rectifying the calendar, dismissing the colors, and honoring guests and overseers are brilliantly proclaimed throughout the realm,
but the ritual
officials, the literati, and the scholars who gather in groups to deliberate with profound insight do not transmit the vestiges of the ancestors.
Though it is said they are careful and cautious,

The heavenly principles ensure that
the transformation of profound harmony and clear distinctions is pervasive.
Touring to pacify the common people,

Performing burnt offerings, burials, and sinking sacrifices,

complete.
Therefore, the Fènghuáng arrive to display their presence, gathering the feathered tribes at Guānwèi,
the horned beasts with fleshy horns and furry bodies are tamed in the outer park,
the black-patterned, white-bodied animals are placated in the suburbs,
the yellow-glowing,

rare beasts and divine birds,
those that correspond to omens and
records,

and daily within the imperial domains,

In ancient times, the Jī (dynasty) merely had events concerning white pheasants, vermillion
crows, black millet, and yellow *ru* grass,
and yet rulers and ministers changed countenance,
and those on their left and right rushed about,
dignified and reverent,
majestic and grand.
This was surely to manifest solemn reverence,
and to receive the blessings of cherished hopes.
It was also to honor the civil and military,
to bequeath peace to later generations,

How could it be for personal gain that such exclusive words were uttered?
If that is the case, to accept
it,

to fulfill its path,
to open the metal-bound chests in the reverent library,

Indeed.
To follow the mandate and establish systems,

and occupies

Looking forward and backward,

From the most ancient times,
down to the present,
there have been seventy-
four authors.

Why should I alone be found lacking now?
Yuán,
scrutinized the thickets of benevolence and righteousness,
hoping for the arrival of the primordial tally.
Having already received the wise words of the many lords,
and also thoroughly considered the profound thoughts of the five *yóu*,
it will connect myriad generations,
radiate vast brilliance,
brandish magnificent flames,
fan the lingering winds,
and spread fragrant achievements,
growing newer with time,
and inexhaustible in use.
How vast is the great law of the supreme heaven,
