How grand, how majestic!
How majestic, how grand!
Gù subsequently resigned from office due to his mother's death.
At the beginning of Yǒngyuán,
Grand General Dòu Xiàn led an expedition against the Xīongnú.
He appointed Gù as Zhōnghùjūn,
and consulted with him.
The Northern Chányú, hearing that the Hàn army had set out,
sent an envoy to the Jūyán Pass,
desiring to follow the precedent of Hūhánxié,
to have an audience with the Son of Heaven,
and requested a grand envoy.
Xiàn memorialized and sent Gù, acting as Zhōnglángjiàng,
with several hundred cavalry to go out of Jūyán Pass with the Xīongnú envoy to welcome him.
At that time, the Southern Xīongnú suddenly attacked and defeated the Northern Court.
Gù reached Sīqúhǎi,
and hearing of the chaos among the Xīongnú,
turned back.
When Dòu Xiàn was defeated,
Gù was consequently dismissed from office.
Gù did not educate his sons,
and many of his sons did not follow the laws and regulations,
which troubled the officials and common people.
Initially,
Zhǒng Jīng, the magistrate of Luòyáng, once traveled,
and Gù's slave interfered with his carriage and cavalry.
The officer struck him and shouted at him.
The slave, being drunk, cursed.
Jīng was greatly angered,
but feared Xiàn and dared not act,
harboring resentment in his heart.
When Dòu's retainers were all arrested and investigated,
Jīng consequently arrested and imprisoned Gù,
who then died in prison.
He was sixty-one years old at the time.
An imperial edict condemned Jīng,
and punished the responsible officials.
Gù's writings, including Diǎnyǐn, Bīnxì, Yìngjī, poems, rhapsodies, inscriptions, laments, eulogies, letters, essays, records, treatises, deliberations, and six-character verses,
totaled forty-one extant pieces.
Commentary says: Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù, father and son,
their discussions on the works of history and records,
their great principles are clearly manifested.
Commentators all praise these two men as possessing the talent of excellent historians.
Qiān's writing is direct and his facts precise,
while Gù's writing is comprehensive and his facts detailed.
As for Gù's narration of events,
it is neither overly embellished nor
overly assertive,
comprehensive yet not disorderly,
detailed yet structured,
making readers diligently engaged and never weary.
Truly, he was able to achieve fame.
Biāo and Gù criticized Qiān,
believing that his judgments of right and wrong deviated considerably from those of the sages.
However, their discussions often condemned those who died for their principles,
denied the upright,
and did not consider sacrificing one's life for benevolence as beautiful,
thus making them treat benevolence and righteousness lightly,
and disparage adherence to principles even more.
Gù lamented that Qiān, despite his vast knowledge and extensive learning,
could not escape extreme punishment through wisdom;
yet he himself also fell into great calamity,
wisdom reached him but he could not uphold it.
Alas,
this is why the ancients debated even the minutiae!
Eulogy says: The two Bān, possessing literary talent,
fashioned the imperial records.
Comparable to the good Qiān and Dǒng,
and combining the elegance of Qīng and Yún.
Biāo understood the imperial mandate,
while Gù was lost in worldly strife.
Biographies of Dìwǔ, Zhōnglí, Sòng, and Hán, Chapter Thirty-One (Dìwǔ Lún's great-grandson Zhǒng, Sòng Jūn's nephew Yì)
Dìwǔ Lún, courtesy name Bóyú,
was a native of Chánglíng, Jīngzhào.
His ancestors were of the Zhū Tián clan of Qí.
Many of the Zhū Tián moved to Yuánlíng,
hence they took their surname based on their sequence.
Lún was upright and righteous in his youth.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
bandits arose,
and his clan and villagers competed to join them.
Lún, however, relied on dangerous terrain to build strongholds and stockades.
Whenever bandits appeared,
he would inspire his men,
drawing strong bows and holding them fully drawn to resist them.
Groups like the Tóngmǎ and Chìméi, numbering dozens of times,
were all unable to overcome him.
Lún first went as a camp leader to Xiānyú Bāo, the Administrator of the Commandery.
Bāo saw him and was struck by his uniqueness,
appointing him as an official.
Later, Bāo was demoted to Magistrate of Gāotáng due to an incident.
As he was leaving,
he grasped Lún's arm and bid farewell, saying:
"I regret that we met so late."
Lún [Lún] later became the xiāngsèfū [xiāngsèfū] in his village.
He equalized corvée and taxes,
resolved grievances,
and gained the people's favor.
Believing he had been an official for a long time without achieving success,
he then took his family to sojourn in Hédōng [Hédōng],
changed his name and surname,
calling himself Wáng Bóqí [Wáng Bóqí].
He transported salt back and forth between Tàiyuán [Tàiyuán] and Shàngdǎng [Shàngdǎng].
Wherever he went, he would clear away filth before leaving,
and on the roads, he was called a Dàoshì [Dàoshì].
His relatives, friends, and old acquaintances knew not his whereabouts.
Several years later,
Xiānyú Bāo [Xiānyú Bāo] recommended him to Yán Xīng [Yán Xīng], the Jīngzhào Yǐn [Jīngzhào Yǐn].
Xīng [Xīng] immediately summoned Lún [Lún] to be his zhǔbù [zhǔbù].
At that time, the coinage in Cháng'ān [Cháng'ān] was often counterfeit and skillfully made.
So, Lún [Lún] was appointed Dūzhùqián Yuàn [Dūzhùqián Yuàn],
overseeing the markets of Cháng'ān [Cháng'ān].
Lún [Lún] standardized weights and measures,
corrected bushels and pecks.
There was no corruption or distortion in the markets,
and the common people were pleased and submitted.
Whenever he read an imperial edict,
he would often sigh and say:
"This is a sagely ruler!
One meeting would settle it."
His peers laughed at him, saying:
"Even your current lord does not listen to you,
how can you move the Son of Heaven?"
Lún [Lún] replied:
"I have not yet met someone who understands me;
our paths are different, that is all."
In the 27th year of Jiànwǔ [Jiànwǔ] (51 CE),
he was nominated as xiàolián [xiàolián],
and appointed Yī Gōngzhǎng [Yī Gōngzhǎng] of Huáiyáng Guó [Huáiyáng Guó],
following the king to his state.
Guāngwǔ [Guāngwǔ] summoned and met him,
finding him very extraordinary.
In the 29th year (53 CE),
he followed the king to the capital.
As part of the official retinue, he had the opportunity to be received.
The Emperor questioned him on matters of governance.
Lún [Lún] thereupon responded on the principles of governance,
and the Emperor was greatly pleased.
The next day,
he was specially summoned again,
and they conversed until evening.
The Emperor jokingly asked Lún [Lún]:
"I hear that when you were an official, you flogged your father-in-law,
and that you would not even accept a meal from your older cousin.
Is there any truth to this?"
Lún [Lún] replied:
"I have married three wives, all of whom had no fathers.
I suffered greatly from famine and chaos when young,
and truly dared not wrongly accept food from others."
The Emperor burst into laughter.
When Lún [Lún] left,
an edict appointed him Fúyí Zhǎng [Fúyí Zhǎng].
Before he reached his post,
he was again appointed Huìjī Tàishǒu [Huìjī Tàishǒu].
Although he held a two-thousand-dàn [dàn] salary position,
he personally cut fodder to feed his horses,
and his wife cooked the meals.
From his salary, he barely kept enough for one month's rations;
the rest he sold cheaply to the poor and weak among the people.
The custom in Huìjī [Huìjī] was rife with excessive sacrifices [yínsì] [yínsì] and a fondness for divination.
The people often sacrificed oxen to the gods,
and the common people's wealth was thereby depleted.
Those who ate beef themselves but did not offer it in sacrifice
were said to fall ill and, before dying, first bellow like oxen.
Previous commandery administrators had not dared to prohibit this.
When Lún [Lún] arrived at his post,
he issued a letter to the subordinate counties,
instructing the common people.
As for the shamans and祝 [zhù] who relied on spirits and gods to deceive and frighten ignorant people,
he investigated and prosecuted them all.
If anyone slaughtered oxen without authorization,
officials immediately imposed punishment.
Initially, the people were quite afraid,
and some made curses or false statements,
but Lún [Lún] investigated them with even greater strictness.
Subsequently, these practices ceased entirely,
and the common people became secure.
In the 5th year of Yǒngpíng [Yǒngpíng] (62 CE),
he was summoned back due to legal issues.
The old and young clung to his carriage and knocked on his horse,
weeping and following him.
He could barely travel a few *lǐ* [lǐ] a day,
unable to advance.
Lún [Lún] then feigned stopping at a post station,
secretly departing by boat.
When the crowd found out,
they pursued him again.
When he arrived at the Tíngwèi [Tíngwèi] (Court of Judicial Review),
over a thousand officials and commoners submitted petitions and waited at the palace gate.
At this time, Xiǎnzōng [Xiǎnzōng] was reviewing the case of Liáng Sōng [Liáng Sōng],
and there were also many who pleaded for Sōng [Sōng].
The Emperor was troubled by this,
and issued an edict to the Gōngchē [Gōngchē] (Superintendent of Public Carriages) that no more petitions for the Liáng [Liáng] family or the Huìjī Tàishǒu [Huìjī Tàishǒu] should be received.
It happened that the Emperor visited the Tíngwèi [Tíngwèi] to record prisoners,
and Lún [Lún] was therefore pardoned and returned to his fields and home.
He personally tilled the fields,
not associating with people.
Several years later,
he was appointed Dàngqú Lìng [Dàngqú Lìng].
He notably promoted the village assistant Xuán Hè [Xuán Hè].
Hè [Hè] later became the governor of the two commanderies of Jiǔjiāng [Jiǔjiāng] and Pèi [Pèi],
renowned for his incorruptibility and purity.
Wherever he served, his transforming influence spread,
and he ultimately ended his career as Dàsīnóng [Dàsīnóng].
Lún [Lún] served for four years,
then was promoted to Shǔjùn Tàishǒu [Shǔjùn Tàishǒu].
The land of Shǔ [Shǔ] was fertile and rich,
and its officials and people were wealthy and substantial.
Many of the yuánshǐ's [yuánshǐ's] families possessed assets amounting to tens of millions,
all riding in splendid carriages and spirited horses,
achieving prominence through their wealth.
Lún [Lún] thoroughly selected those who were well-off and sent them back,
instead choosing poor, orphaned individuals with integrity and good conduct to fill official positions.
Thereupon, bribery and corruption were suppressed and eliminated,
and administrative duties were properly managed.
Many of the officials he recommended rose to be Jiǔ Qīng [Jiǔ Qīng] or Èrqiānshí [Èrqiānshí],
and he was considered a good judge of character at the time.
After serving for seven years,
when Sùzōng first ascended the throne,
he was promoted from a distant commandery
to replace Móu Róng as Sīkōng.
The Emperor, on account of Empress Míngdé,
highly honored his maternal uncle Mǎ Liáo,
and his brothers all held official posts.
Liáo and others spared no effort in forming connections,
and gentlemen of rank vied to flock to them.
Lún, fearing the imperial relatives were becoming too powerful,
wished to have the court curb their influence,
and submitted a memorial saying:
"Your servant has heard that the loyal do not conceal and avoid,
and the upright do not shy away from harm.
Unable to suppress my humble and timid nature,
I brave death to present myself.
The Shū Jīng says: 'Ministers shall not make awe or fortune for themselves,
for it will be harmful to your house
and disastrous to your state.'
The Zhuàn says: 'A grand master shall have no extra-territorial connections
nor gifts of dried meat.'
In recent times, Empress Guāngliè,
though her familial affection was heavenly and profound,
still eventually sent Yīn Jiù back to his fief,
and exiled and dismissed the retainers of Yīn Xīng;
after that, the families of Liáng and Dòu
each had illegal doings,
and when Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he ultimately executed many of them.
From then on, there were no more powerful imperial relatives in Luòzhōng,
and all requests for favors through letters were cut off.
He also likened the empress's relatives to this:
'To toil for gentlemen
is not as good as to serve the state;
one cannot wear a basin on one's head and look up at the sky simultaneously,
as two tasks cannot be performed at once.'
Your servant always carved this into my 'five viscera' [heart]
and wrote it on my sash.
But now, those who discuss affairs
again speak of the Mǎ family.
I secretly hear that Wèiwèi Liáo, with three thousand rolls of cloth,
and Chéngmén Xiàowèi Fáng, with three million cash,
privately aided the gentry of the Sānfǔ,
and whether known or unknown,
none were left unprovided for.
I also hear that on Làyì, they gave each of those in Luòzhōng five thousand cash,
and Yuèqí Xiàowèi Guāng,
for Làyì, used three hundred sheep,
four hundred hú of rice,
and five thousand catties of meat.
Your servant foolishly believes this does not conform to the classics,
and in trepidation, dares not fail to report it.
Your Majesty may wish to be generous to them,
but you should also consider how to keep them safe.
Your servant speaks this now,
sincerely desiring to be loyal to Your Majesty above,
and to preserve the empress's family below,
and hopes for your consideration."
Later, when Mǎ Fáng became Chējì Jiāngjūn
and was about to lead an expedition against the Western Qiāng,
Lún again submitted a memorial saying:
"Your servant foolishly believes that noble imperial relatives may be enfeoffed as marquises to enrich them,
but should not hold official posts to be entrusted with duties.
Why?
To bind them with laws would harm affection,
to favor them out of kinship would violate the constitution.
I humbly hear that Mǎ Fáng is now to embark on a western campaign.
Your servant, considering the Empress Dowager's benevolence
and Your Majesty's extreme filial piety,
fears that any minor incident might make it difficult to maintain affection.
I hear that Fáng requested Dù Dǔ to be his Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
and bestowed much wealth and silk upon him.
Dǔ was dismissed by his hometown
and resided as a guest in Měiyáng;
his younger sister is the wife of a Mǎ family member,
and relying on this, he engaged in illicit dealings.
The local county magistrate, troubled by his lawlessness,
arrested and tried him.
Now that he has come to Fáng's side,
those who discuss affairs are all suspicious and surprised,
let alone his being appointed a Cóngshì;
I fear this might invite criticism of the court.
It is now appropriate to select worthy and capable individuals to assist him;
Fáng should not be allowed to select people himself again,
as this would damage the prestige of the mission.
If I harbor any thoughts,
how dare I not make them known?"
Neither was taken into consideration or adopted.
Although Wǔ Lún 伍倫 was stern and upright,
he often detested the harshness of corrupt officials.
When he became one of the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng 三公),
it coincided with an Emperor (Dì 帝) who was a benevolent ruler.
There were repeatedly good policies,
so he submitted a memorial praising and extolling them,
and thereby used it to encourage the virtues of the times,
saying:
"Your Majesty (Bìxià 陛下), since ascending the throne,
has personally embodied natural virtue,
and adopted a gentle and serene demeanor.
With magnanimity, you govern those below.
In the four years that have passed,
last year you executed six corrupt and cruel Inspectors (Cìshǐ 刺史) and officials of the two-thousand-bushel rank (Èrqiānshí 二千石).
These were all discerned by your clear sagacity,
not something the multitude of your subordinates could achieve.
However, although edicts are always issued with leniency and harmony, the urgency of governance is not eased,
and while efforts are made to promote frugality, extravagance does not cease.
The fault lies in the corruption of the times,
and the failure of your subordinates to live up to expectations.
Guāngwǔ 光武, inheriting the aftermath of Wáng Mǎng 王莽,
largely governed with severity and fierceness.
Later generations followed suit,
and thus it became the prevailing custom.
Those recommended by the commanderies and states
are mostly officials skilled in administration but of vulgar character,
and there are few broad-minded selections to meet Your Majesty's requirements.
Liú Yù 劉豫, the Magistrate (Lìng 令) of Chénliú 陳留,
and Sì Xié 駟協, the Magistrate of Guānjūn 冠軍,
both with their harsh and severe dispositions,
govern the people and administer their territories.
They are solely intent on plundering and killing,
and strive for harshness and cruelty.
Officials and common people alike are distressed and resentful,
and none do not detest them.
Yet, those who debate today mistakenly consider them capable,
going against the will of Heaven (Tiān 天)
and losing the meaning of the classics.
This truly cannot be treated with insufficient caution.
Not only should Yù 豫 and Xié 協 be impeached,
but also those who recommended them ought to be censured.
If only a few benevolent and worthy individuals are promoted to hold office in the current administration,
not many,
then customs will naturally transform.
Your subject once read historical records
and knew that the Qín 秦 dynasty perished due to its harshness and severity.
I also personally witnessed Wáng Mǎng 王莽 destroy himself through draconian laws.
Therefore, my earnest and repeated exhortations
are truly based on this.
Furthermore, I hear that the various imperial princes (wáng zhǔ 王主) and noble relatives (guì qī 貴戚)
are arrogant and extravagant beyond measure.
If this is so in the capital (Jīngshī 京師),
how can it serve as an example for distant regions?
Thus it is said: 'If one's own person is not upright,
even if one issues commands, they will not be followed.'
Those who teach by example are followed;
those who teach by words are disputed.
When Yin (Yīn 陰) and Yang (Yáng 陽) are in harmony, the year is bountiful;
when ruler (jūn 君) and minister (chén 臣) are of one mind, transformation is achieved.
All Inspectors (Cìshǐ 刺ǐ) and Grand Administrators (Tàishǒu 太守) and below,
who are appointed or dismissed in the capital (Jīngshī 京師) or pass through Luòyáng 洛陽,
should all be summoned for an audience.
Opportunities can then be taken to broadly inquire about the four directions,
and also to observe their character.
As for those who submit memorials on affairs but whose suggestions are not suitable,
they should simply be sent back to their hometowns and villages.
It is inappropriate to excessively show joy or anger,
in order to demonstrate magnanimity.
Your subject's humble opinions are not worth adopting."
When the various Mǎ 馬 family members were disgraced and returned to their states,
and the Dòu 竇 clan began to gain prominence,
Lún 倫 again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your subject, with his empty and insignificant nature,
holds the responsibility of assisting and advising.
My innate disposition is dull and timid,
but my position is exalted and my rank is heavy.
Constrained by great righteousness,
I strive to exhort myself.
Even if I were to face a hundred deaths,
I would not dare to choose my ground,
let alone when I personally encounter an era of critical words!
Now, inheriting the failings of a hundred kings,
people still value artifice and skill,
and all flock to deviant paths,
unable to uphold integrity.
I humbly observe that Dòu Xiàn 竇憲, the Commander (Zhōnglángjiàng 中郎將) of the Agile Cavalry (Hǔbēn 虎賁),
a relative of the Empress's (Jiāofáng 椒房) family,
controls the imperial guards (jìn bīng 禁兵).
He enters and exits the imperial apartments (shěng tà 省闥),
is in the prime of his life and possesses noble aspirations,
humble and fond of goodness.
This is truly his way of befriending and associating with worthy men.
However, those who enter and exit among the noble relatives
are mostly individuals with flaws and those who have been subject to imperial prohibitions and restrictions.
There are particularly few who adhere to restraint and are content with poverty.
Unambitious scholars and officials instead engage in mutual patronage and influence-peddling,
congregating at his gate.
The combined breaths can blow away a mountain, and gathered mosquitoes form a thunderous sound.
This is where arrogance and dissipation originate.
Those who discuss matters in the Three Commanderies (Sānfǔ 三輔)
even say that since restrictions are imposed on noble relatives,
they should also be purified by noble relatives,
just as one cures a hangover with wine.
Crooked and dangerous individuals who pursue power
truly ought not to be associated with.
[一０] Your humble subject wishes that Your Majesty (Bìxià 陛下) would instruct the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng 中宮) to sternly order Xiàn 憲 and others to close their doors and guard themselves,
and not promiscuously associate with scholars and officials,
to prevent problems before they arise,
and to consider matters while they are still formless,
so that Xiàn 憲 may forever preserve his good fortune and emoluments,
and ruler and minister may enjoy harmonious relations,
without the slightest crack.
This is your subject's utmost wish."
Lún 倫 served the public with utmost devotion and integrity.
When speaking on affairs, he never wavered or held back.
When his sons sometimes tried to dissuade him,
he would immediately scold and send them away.
When officials and others presented memorials or offered suggestions for expediency,
he would also seal and submit them all,
so impartial was he.
His nature was honest and sincere,
and he had little literary embellishment.
In office, he was known for his integrity and purity.
People of his time compared him to Gòng Yǔ 貢禹 of the previous dynasty.
However, he lacked reserve,
and did not maintain a dignified demeanor,
and was thus looked down upon for this.
Someone once asked Lún 倫,
saying:
"Does Your Excellency have any private biases?"
He replied:
"In the past, someone offered me a thousand-li horse.
Although I did not accept it,
whenever the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng 三公) were to make selections,
I could not forget it in my heart,
yet I ultimately never used it.
My elder brother's son was often ill;
I would visit him ten times in one night,
and then return and sleep peacefully.
When my own son was ill,
although I did not personally check on him, I could not sleep all night.
In such cases,
how can it be said that I have no private biases?"
He repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to retire due to old age and illness.
In the third year of Yuánhé 元和 (86 CE),
an edict was issued to dismiss him,
allowing him to receive the salary of a two-thousand-bushel official for the rest of his life.
He was additionally granted five hundred thousand cash
and one residential compound.
He died several years later,
at the age of over eighty.
An imperial edict granted him secret funerary items, clothes, bedding, money, and silk.
His youngest son, Xié 頡, succeeded him,
and served as Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu 太shǒu) of Guìyáng 桂陽, Lújiāng 廬江, and Nányáng 南陽 in succession.
He was praised wherever he served.
When Shùndì 順帝 was deposed as Crown Prince (Tàizǐ 太子),
Xié 頡 was a Grand Master of Remonstrance (Tàizhōng Dàfū 太中大夫),
and together with the Grand Coachman (Tàipú 太僕) Lái Lì 來歷 and others, stood at the palace gate to strongly protest.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Grand Architect (Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng 將作大匠),
and died in office.
Lún's 倫's great-grandson was Zhǒng 種.
The commentary states: Wǔ Lún 伍倫 was stern and rigid in his principles,
not a genial and mild-mannered scholar.
Examining his memorials and proposals,
he earnestly emphasized broad-mindedness and generosity.
Was this perhaps to correct the abuses of harshness and severity?
Ancient people wore bowstrings (xián 弦) and leather (wéi 韋) as reminders,
which is similar to this.
However, a superior person (jūnzǐ 君子) does not indulge excessively to usurp his superiors,
nor is he so frugal as to oppress his subordinates.
How could one, presiding over a thousand li, equate oneself with herdsmen and stableboys?
If this was not an act of over-correction,
then it cannot be described as balanced and harmonious.
Zhǒng's 種's courtesy name was Xīngxiān 興先.
From a young age, he cultivated a resolute will and righteousness.
As an official,
he gained renown in the various commanderies and provinces.
In the Yǒngshòu 永壽 period (155-158 CE),
as an aide (yuàn 掾) to the Minister of Works (Sītú 司徒), he was dispatched as an imperial envoy (qīng zhào shǐ 清詔使) to Jìzhōu 冀州.
He investigated disasters,
and impeached and brought charges against Inspectors (Cìshǐ 刺史) and officials of the two-thousand-bushel rank (èrqiānshí 二千石) and below.
Many were punished or dismissed,
and dozens of officials fled their posts.
Upon his return,
he was commended for his excellent service as an envoy
and appointed Minister (Xiàng 相) of Gāomì Hóu 高密侯.
At this time, bandits formed gangs in Xú 徐 and Yǎn 兗 provinces.
Gāomì 高密 was on the border of these two provinces,
so Zhǒng 種 extensively stored grain
and diligently motivated his officers and soldiers.
When the bandits heard of this, they were all deterred.
Drums and clappers remained silent (no alarms were raised).
Returning refugees,
numbered several thousand families within a year.
Due to his capability, he was transferred to become Minister (Xiàng 相) of Wèi 衞.
Guān Wǔ [第五種] was transferred to be the Intendant of Yǎnzhoū [兗州].
Shàn Chāo's [單超] (a Chángshì [常侍]) nephew, Kuāng [匡], was the Administrator of Jìyīn [濟陰].
Relying on his power, he was greedy and unrestrained.
Guān Wǔ [第五種] wanted to arrest him,
but did not know whom to send.
He happened to hear that his subordinate, Wèi Yǔ [衞羽], was always upright and resolute.
So he summoned Wèi Yǔ [衞羽] and fully informed him of the situation.
He said:
"I hear you are not afraid of the powerful and oppressive.
I now wish to entrust you with an important matter.
What do you say?"
Wèi Yǔ [衞羽] replied:
"I wish to try my hand at one decisive action."
Wèi Yǔ [衞羽] left,
then immediately galloped to Dìngtáo [定陶].
He closed the gates and arrested over forty of Kuāng's [匡] guests, retainers, and close officials.
Within six or seven days,
he uncovered embezzlements totaling fifty or sixty million.
Guān Wǔ [第五種] immediately impeached Kuāng [匡],
and also included an indictment against Shàn Chāo [單超].
Kuāng [匡], in desperation,
sent an assassin to stab Wèi Yǔ [衞羽].
Wèi Yǔ [衞羽], sensing the treachery,
arrested and bound the assassin,
and obtained full details of the plot.
The province was shaken with fear,
and the imperial court praised this.
At this time, the bandits of Tàishān [太山], Shúxūn Wújì [叔孫無忌] and others, were violent and rampant throughout the region;
the provincial and commandery authorities were unable to suppress them.
Wèi Yǔ [衞羽] advised Guān Wǔ [第五種], saying:
"Zhōngguó [中國] has been peaceful,
and the people have forgotten war for a long time.
However, Tàishān [太山] is rugged and dangerous,
and the bandits and ruffians are not controlled.
Even if we had elite troops now,
it would be difficult to deploy them against the enemy.
I request to go and persuade them to surrender."
Guān Wǔ [第五種] respectfully agreed.
Wèi Yǔ [衞羽] then went,
fully explaining the advantages and disadvantages,
and Shúxūn Wújì [叔孫無忌] immediately led his gang of over three thousand people to surrender.
Shàn Chāo [單超], having harbored resentment for a long time,
then used this matter to implicate Guān Wǔ [第五種],
who was eventually exiled to Shuòfāng [朔方].
Shàn Chāo's [單超] maternal grandson, Dǒng Yuán [董援], was the Administrator of Shuòfāng [朔方],
and treated Guān Wǔ [第五種] with anger.
Initially,
when Guān Wǔ [第五種] was Minister of Wèi [衞相],
he considered his Menxiàyuán [門下掾] Sūn Bīn [孫斌] to be virtuous,
and treated him well.
When Guān Wǔ [第五種] was to be exiled,
Sūn Bīn [孫斌], having fully learned of Shàn Chāo's [單超] plot,
then said to his friends, Lǘ Zǐzhí [閭子直] of the same county and Zhēn Zǐrán [甄子然] of Gāomì [高密]:
"Indeed, a thief hates his master;
this has been an old saying.
Lord Dìwǔ [第五使君] is about to be cast into a remote land,
and Shàn Chāo's [單超] external relative is the Administrator of that commandery.
One who is in danger is easily overthrown;
it is cause for a chill in one's heart.
I am now going to pursue the Lord,
hoping to save him from this disaster.
If I succeed in bringing the Lord back,
I will entrust him to you."
The two said:
"You should go!
This is also our wish."
Thereupon, Sūn Bīn [孫斌], leading some chivalrous retainers, pursued Guān Wǔ [第五種] day and night.
They caught up with him in Tàiyuán [太原],
blocked the dangerous path, and killed the escorting officials.
He then dismounted and gave his horse to Guān Wǔ [第五種],
while Sūn Bīn [孫斌] himself walked alongside.
They traveled over four hundred *lǐ* [里] in one day and one night,
and thus managed to escape and return.
Guān Wǔ [第五種] hid at the residences of the Lǘ [閭] and Zhēn [甄] families for several years.
Then Zāng Mín [臧旻], a subordinate of Xúzhōu [徐州], submitted a memorial pleading for him, saying:
"Your subject has heard that a scholar who endures the humiliation of death
must have a plan to accomplish something.
Thus, Jì Bù [季布] humbled himself to Zhū Jiā [朱家],
and Guǎn Zhòng [管仲] acted inappropriately toward Shào Hū [召忽].
These two ministers, who could have died but did not,
were not clinging to life for a moment,
nor coveting a meager existence,
but rather concealed their intelligence and abilities,
considered their strategies,
hoping to seize an opportune moment to achieve something.
Eventually, they met with Gāo Dì's [高帝] establishment of his enterprise and
Qí Huán's [齊桓] rise as hegemon.
Their past fugitive actions were overlooked,
their enmity of shooting the hook was pardoned.
They were elevated from among prisoners,
and their advice for assisting the state was trusted.
Their meritorious achievements were passed down for a hundred generations,
and their stories as ruler and minister are recorded in books.
If these two rulers had held grudges over minor faults,
then these two ministers would have died like dogs and horses,
their names submerged in ditches and ravines.
How then could they have demonstrated their ability to rectify past mistakes
and established their extraordinary and profound strategies?
I humbly observe that the former Intendant of Yǎnzhoū [兗州], Dìwǔ Zhǒng [第五種],
was outstanding and self-reliant.
In his home region, he was free from suspicion of bribery,
and in the imperial court, he never lacked words of righteous counsel.
His nature abhorred evil,
and he was publicly upright and unbending.
Therefore, those who discuss the clear and lofty consider Dìwǔ Zhǒng [第五種] to be supreme,
and those who list upright gentlemen place Dìwǔ Zhǒng [第五種] first.
The meaning of the Spring and Autumn Annals [春秋] is to
select people for their strengths,
disregard their shortcomings,
record their small good deeds,
and overlook their major transgressions.
The crime for which Dìwǔ Zhǒng [第五種] was condemned was public theft by bandits,
for which he was not yet fully rehabilitated.
The offense led to his summons and exile,
but it was not a great evil.
In ancient times, Yú Shùn [虞舜], serving his parents,
would flee when struck with a large staff.
Therefore, Dìwǔ Zhǒng [第五種]'s escape
was to preserve his life,
hoping for the path of Zhū Jiā [朱家]
to manifest the opportune moment of Jì Bù [季布].
I wish that Your Majesty would not withhold even a moment's grace,
lest Dìwǔ Zhǒng [第五種] carry the regret of his loyalty into the ground."
Shortly after, an amnesty was granted,
and he died at home.
Zhōnglí Yì [鍾離意], courtesy name Zǐ'ā [子阿],
was a native of Shānyīn [山陰] in Kuàijī [會稽].
In his youth, he served as a Dūyóu [督郵] for the commandery.
At that time, a Tíngzhǎng [亭長] in a subordinate county had accepted wine and gifts from someone.
The commandery office recorded this case for investigation.
Zhōnglí Yì [鍾離意] returned the record,
and entered to speak with the Administrator, saying:
"The Spring and Autumn Annals [春秋] prioritize internal over external affairs.
The Shī [詩] says, 'Be a model to your wife,
and thereby manage your household and state.'
This clarifies that the foundation of governance and transformation
proceeds from the near to the far.
We should now first purify the internal affairs of the commandery,
and for now overlook the minor transgressions in distant counties."
The Administrator greatly admired him,
and subsequently entrusted him with county affairs.
In Jiànwǔ [建武] fourteen years (38 CE),
Kuàijī [會稽] suffered a great plague,
with tens of thousands of deaths.
Zhōnglí Yì [鍾離意] alone personally and secretly attended to the sick,
providing medicine and care.
Many in his district were saved.
He was recommended as Xiàolián [孝廉] (Filial and Incorrupt),
and after two promotions,
he was invited to the residence of the Dàsītú [大司徒], Hóu Bà [侯霸].
An imperial edict ordered the transportation of convicts to Hénèi [河內].
It was winter and very cold,
and the convicts were ill and unable to travel.
When passing through Hóngnóng [弘農], Zhōnglí Yì [鍾離意] immediately instructed the subordinate county to make clothes for the convicts.
The county, having no choice, provided them,
and then memorialized the situation.
Zhōnglí Yì [鍾離意] also fully reported it.
Guāngwǔ [光武] received the memorial,
showed it to Hóu Bà [侯霸],
and said:
"How kind-hearted is the clerk you sent?
He is truly a good official!"
Zhōnglí Yì [鍾離意] then, along the way, unbound the convicts' shackles,
allowed them to pass as they wished,
and set a deadline for them to arrive together,
and none violated it.
He returned,
and was dismissed due to illness.
Later, he was appointed Magistrate of Xiáqiū.
There was a clerk named Fǔ Jiàn.
He stole within the county.
Yì privately questioned him.
Jiàn kowtowed and confessed his crime.
Yì could not bear to inflict punishment.
He sent him home for an extended leave.
Jiàn's father heard of this.
He prepared a feast for Jiàn.
He said:
"I have heard that unprincipled rulers maim people with blades.
Principled rulers carry out executions with righteousness.
Your crime,
is destiny."
Thereupon, he ordered Jiàn to take poison and die.
Twenty-five years later,
he was transferred to become Magistrate of Tángyì.
A man from the county, Fáng Guǎng, avenged his father.
He was imprisoned.
His mother died of illness.
Guǎng wept and refused to eat.
Yì felt pity and sorrow for him.
So he allowed Guǎng to return home,
so that he could prepare for the funeral and burial.
The Chief Clerk and all his subordinates argued against this.
Yì said:
"The blame will fall on me alone.
It is not right to implicate my subordinates."
Thereupon, he sent him.
After Guǎng had buried his mother,
he indeed returned to prison.
Yì secretly reported the circumstances to the authorities.
Guǎng was ultimately sentenced to a reduced penalty, short of death.
When Emperor Xiǎnzōng ascended the throne,
he was summoned to be a Shàngshū.
At that time, the Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, Zhāng Huī,
was impeached for embezzling a thousand catties of gold.
He was summoned back and subjected to the law.
His assets were cataloged and submitted to the Dàsīnóng.
An imperial edict ordered them to be distributed among the officials.
Yì received pearls and jades.
He cast them all onto the ground and did not bow in gratitude for the imperial gift.
The Emperor was surprised and asked him the reason.
He replied:
"I have heard that Kǒngzǐ endured thirst rather than drink from Dàoquán spring.
Zēng Shēn turned his carriage back from Shèngmǔ gate.
They loathed their names.
These are treasures tainted by corruption.
I truly dare not accept them with a bow."
The Emperor sighed in admiration and said:
"How pure are the words of the Shàngshū!"
Thereupon, he instead bestowed upon Yì three hundred thousand coins from the imperial treasury.
He was transferred to become Shàngshū Púyè.
The imperial carriage frequently visited Guǎngchéng Yuàn.
Yì believed that hunting led to neglecting governance.
He often stood by the imperial carriage, remonstrating against pleasure-seeking and hunting trips.
The Son of Heaven would immediately return to the palace.
In the summer of the third year of Yǒngpíng, there was a drought,
yet a grand construction of the Běigōng was underway.
Yì went to the palace gate, removed his cap, and submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly observe that Your Majesty, seeing the slight drought at this time,
is worried about the common people.
You have descended from the main hall.
and personally taken responsibility.
Yet, in recent days, despite dense clouds,
there has been no significant rain.
Is it perhaps that there are aspects of governance that have not yet aligned with the will of Heaven?
In the past, when Chéng Tāng encountered a drought,
he blamed himself with six points, saying:
'Is my governance not temperate?
Do I cause people hardship?
Are my palaces overly magnificent?
Are female attendants' intercessions too prevalent?
Is bribery widespread?
Are slanderous individuals flourishing?'
I humbly observe the grand construction of the Běigōng.
People are losing their farming season.
This is what is meant by 'palaces being overly magnificent'.
Since ancient times, it is not the smallness or narrowness of palaces that has been a problem.
But rather the worry that the people are not at peace.
It is advisable to halt the construction for now,
in order to respond to the will of Heaven.
Your servant Yì, with the talent of a common man,
possesses no accomplishments or abilities.
I have long enjoyed a high salary.
and been promoted to serve as a close minister.
Recently, I received generous gifts.
Joy and fear are mixed.
Overwhelmed by my foolish bluntness and anxious thoughts,
my crime deserves ten thousand deaths."
The Emperor issued an imperial edict in reply, saying:
"Tāng cited six matters.
The fault lies with one person (myself).
Your cap and shoes,
do not give them up.
Recently, Heaven has sent down a drought.
Dense clouds have gathered several times.
I am sorrowful and ashamed.
hoping to obtain a favorable response.
Therefore, I have distributed prayers and supplications.
observing the winds and clouds.
I pray to the north at the Míngtáng.
and establish a Yúchǎng to the south.
Now, I have also ordered the Dàjiàng to stop the construction of all palaces.
and to reduce anything not urgent,
hoping to avert disaster and condemnation."
The edict thereupon apologized to the Dukes, Ministers, and all officials.
And then, timely rain fell.
At that time, an imperial edict granted silk to the surrendered barbarians.
A Shàngshū handled the matter,
mistakenly writing "one hundred" instead of "ten."
The Emperor saw the Sīnóng's report.
and was greatly enraged.
He summoned the Lángjiàng and flogged him.
Yì then entered and kowtowed, saying:
"A mistake or error
is something common people can accept.
If the transgression is due to negligence or disrespect,
then my rank is high,
and my crime is severe.
The Láng's rank is low,
and his crime is light.
The fault lies entirely with your servant.
Your servant should be punished first."
Thereupon, he removed his clothes and prepared for the rod.
The Emperor's anger subsided.
He ordered Yì to put his cap back on and spared the Láng.
The Emperor's nature was narrow-minded and suspicious.
He liked to demonstrate his wisdom by secretly discovering things through his informants.
Thus, dukes, ministers, and high officials were frequently slandered.
Close ministers, from Shàngshū downwards, were even dragged around.
He once, angered by an affair, struck the Láng Yuè Sōng with a staff.
Sōng ran and hid under the bed.
The Emperor was extremely angry.
and fiercely said:
"Láng, come out!
Láng, come out!"
Sōng said:
"The Son of Heaven should be majestic and dignified.
The feudal lords should be brilliant and splendid.
I have never heard of a ruler personally rising to strike a Láng."
The Emperor pardoned him.
No one in the court was not terrified.
They all vied to be severe and strict.
to avoid being punished and reprimanded.
Only Yì alone dared to remonstrate and contend.
He frequently sealed and returned imperial edicts.
and always intervened to save subordinates from their mistakes.
At that time, there were continuous strange occurrences.
Yì again submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly reflect that Your Majesty personally practices filial piety.
cultivates and clarifies classical scholarship.
performs suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth.
reveres ghosts and spirits.
worries about the common people.
and works tirelessly with your mind.
Yet, the weather is not harmonious.
The sun and moon are not bright.
Springs overflow.
and cold and heat deviate from their seasons.
The fault lies with your ministers, who are unable to propagate transformational influence and manage their duties.
and instead make harshness and severity their custom.
Officials kill innocent people.
one after another without ceasing.
Officials have no mutual affection.
and civil servants have no harmonious aspirations.
Even among kin, there is mutual harm.
and maliciousness runs deep.
This offends and goes against the harmonious energy.
leading to heavenly disasters.
The common people can be won over by virtue.
but are difficult to subdue by force.
The essential way of the ancient kings
was for the people to live in harmony.
Thus, they could bring about peace in the world.
disasters would not arise.
and turmoil would not occur.
The poem 'Lù Míng' certainly speaks of feasting and enjoyment.
because when the hearts of men and spirits are in accord,
then the weather is harmonious.
I wish Your Majesty would extend your sacred virtue.
manage the myriad affairs of state.
issue edicts to the relevant officials.
be cautious with human lives.
ease punishments.
follow the seasonal energies.

Although the Emperor could not put his advice into practice,
he nevertheless knew Yì's utmost sincerity.
It was also for this reason that Yì could not stay long.
He was sent out to become Chancellor of Lǔ.
Later, when Déyáng Diàn was completed,
all officials gathered.
The Emperor thought of Yì's words.
and said to the Dukes and Ministers:
"If Shàngshū Zhōnglí were here,
this hall would not have been built."
Yì Shì governed for five years.
He used love and beneficence to transform the people,
and many became prosperous.
He died in office after a long illness.
His dying words were to memorialize the emperor, stating that an age of peace and prosperity
was difficult to transform quickly,
and that there should be a little more leniency.
The Emperor was moved and saddened by his sentiment,
and issued an edict expressing his lament,
granting him 200,000 *qián*.
Yào Sōng was
a man from Hénèi.
His nature was simple and loyal.
Poor, he became a Gentleman (láng).
He often stood alone on the *tái* (terrace),
without a blanket,
using his arm as a pillow,
and eating husks and bran.
The Emperor often entered the *tái* at night,
always saw Sōng,
and asked him the reason.
He greatly praised him.
From then on, an imperial edict ordered the Grand Steward (tàiguān) to grant the Director of the Imperial Secretariat (shàngshū) and below morning and evening meals,
provide curtains, blankets, black robes,
and two attendant clerks.
Sōng rose to the office of Grand Administrator (tàishǒu) of Nányáng.
Sòng Jūn, courtesy name Shūxiáng,
was a man from Ānzhòng, Nányáng.
His father, Bó,
was the Commandant of the Five Offices (wǔguān zhōnglángjiàng) at the beginning of the Jiànwǔ era.
Jūn became a Gentleman (láng) through his father's privilege
at the age of fifteen.
He was fond of the classics and histories.
On every rest day,
he would receive instruction from erudites (bóshì).
He mastered the *Shī* and *Lǐ* classics
and was skilled in debate.
When he was over twenty,
he was appointed Magistrate (zhǎng) of Chényáng.
The local custom was to have few scholars and to believe in shamans and ghosts.
Jūn established schools for them
and prohibited illicit sacrifices.
Everyone felt at peace with this.
He resigned from office due to the mourning for his grandmother
and taught as a guest instructor in Yǐngchuān.
Later he became a Gentleman Attendant (yèzhě).
It happened that the Wǔlíng barbarians rebelled
and besieged General Wǔwēi Líu Shàng.
An edict ordered Jūn to take a post-carriage and mobilize 3,000 men from Jiāngxià for a rapid mission to rescue him.
By the time he arrived, Shàng had already perished.
It happened that General Fúbō Mǎ Yuán arrived.
The Emperor then ordered Jūn to supervise the army,
advancing with the generals,
but the rebels resisted, preventing their advance.
When Mǎ Yuán died in the campaign,
many soldiers suffered from warm, damp diseases,
and more than half died.
Jūn, fearing that the army would not return,
then discussed with the generals, saying:
"Now the road is long and the soldiers are sick;
we cannot fight.
What if we temporarily exercise authority to induce their surrender?"
All the generals prostrated themselves and dared not respond.
Jūn said:
"When a loyal minister is outside the borders,
if there is something that can bring peace to the state,
he may act on his own authority."
So he feigned an imperial edict, appointing Fúbō's Cavalier (sīmǎ) Lǚ Zhǒng as Magistrate (zhǎng) of Yuánlíng.
He ordered Zhǒng to carry the imperial decree into the barbarian camp,
informing them of imperial grace and trust,
while he arrayed his troops behind him.
The barbarians were struck with terror
and together beheaded their great chieftain and surrendered.
Thereupon, Jūn entered the rebel camp,
dispersed their forces,
sent them back to their respective commanderies,
appointed chief officials for them, and then returned.
Before Jūn arrived,
he first impeached himself for the crime of feigning an imperial edict.
Guāngwǔ commended his achievements,
welcomed him with gifts of gold and silk,
and ordered him to visit his home and ancestral tombs.
Thereafter, whenever there were different opinions from the four quarters,
he often consulted him.
He was promoted to Prefect (lìng) of Shàngcài.
At that time, a subordinate in the government office
prohibited people from holding extravagant funerals.
Jūn said:
"Exceeding regulations in funerary rites
is a minor transgression.
Now, there are unrighteous people
who have not yet been transformed;
to punish exceeding the rites immediately
is not the priority of governance."
He ultimately refused to implement it.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator (tàishǒu) of Jiǔjiāng.
The commandery had many fierce tigers,
which frequently troubled the people.
Traps and snares were often set through recruitment, but there were still many injuries.
Upon Jūn's arrival,
he issued a notice to the subordinate counties, saying:
"Tigers and leopards are in the mountains;
turtles and alligators are in the water.
Each has its proper place.
Moreover, the presence of fierce beasts in the Jiāng and Huái regions
is like the presence of chickens and pigs in the northern lands.
Now, if they are harming the people,
the fault lies with corrupt officials,
and to laboriously mobilize for their capture
is not the fundamental concern for the people.
Therefore, strive to remove corrupt and greedy officials,
and think of promoting the loyal and good.
All traps and snares should be removed,
and the system of quotas abolished."
Thereafter, it was rumored that the tigers migrated eastward across the Jiāng River together.
In the first year of Zhōngyuán (56 CE),
Shānyáng, Chǔ, and Pèi suffered from many locusts.
Those that flew to the borders of Jiǔjiāng
always dispersed to the east and west.
Because of this, his reputation spread far and wide.
Jùnxīu county had the two mountains, Táng and Hòu.
The people jointly worshipped them,
and the many shamans consequently took the sons and daughters of the common people to be "public consorts" (gōngyú),
changing them annually.
Afterward, they dared not marry,
and previous Grand Administrators and Prefects dared not prohibit it.
Jūn then issued a directive saying:
"From now on,
those who 'marry the mountain' shall all marry into the shamans' families,
and shall not disturb good commoners."
Thereupon, the practice ceased.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng (58 CE),
he was promoted to Chancellor (xiàng) of Dōnghǎi.
After five years in the commandery,
he was removed from office for a legal transgression
and taught as a guest instructor in Yǐngchuān.
However, the officials and people of Dōnghǎi missed Jūn's benevolent transformation
and composed a song for him.
Several thousand people went to the palace gate to petition for his return.
Xiǎnzōng, recognizing his ability,
in the seventh year (64 CE),
summoned him and appointed him Director of the Imperial Secretariat (shàngshūlìng).
Whenever there were conflicting opinions,
most of his coincided with the Emperor's will.
Jūn once edited and cut out questionable matters.
The Emperor believed it to be a trick
and was greatly enraged,
arresting the Gentlemen (láng) and having them bound and interrogated.
All the Directors of the Imperial Secretariat (shàngshū) were terrified
and kowtowed, confessing their guilt.
Jūn, looking stern, said:
"A loyal minister upholds righteousness
and has no divided loyalty.
If one fears authority and loses rectitude,
even if I die,
I will not change my resolve."
A lesser eunuch (xiǎohuángmén) nearby
entered and reported it fully.
The Emperor admired his unyielding nature,
immediately ordered the release of the Gentlemen,
and promoted Jūn to Superintendent of the Capital (sīlì xiàowèi).
Several months later,
he was sent out as Grand Administrator (tàishǒu) of Hénèi,
where his governance and transformation were widely successful.
Jūn once fell ill.
The common people and elders prayed for him
and inquired about his well-being morning and evening.
Such was the love the people had for him.
Due to his illness, he memorialized to request his dismissal.
An imperial edict appointed his son Tiáo as Attendant of the Crown Prince (tàizǐ shèrén).
Jūn, supporting himself, went to the palace gate to express his gratitude.
The Emperor sent a middle eunuch (zhōnghuángmén) to inquire about his health
and kept him there to recover.
When the position of Minister over the Masses (sītú) became vacant,
the Emperor, considering Jūn capable of serving as prime minister,
summoned him and personally checked on his illness,
ordering two grooms to support him.
Jūn bowed and said:
"Heaven has punished me for my sins,
and my suffering is deeply severe.
I can no longer serve in the imperial presence!"
Then he shed tears and declined.
The Emperor was greatly saddened,
summoned Tiáo to assist Jūn out,
and granted him 300,000 *qián*.
Jūn was naturally tolerant and moderate,
disliking intricate legal procedures.
He often believed that if officials were magnanimous and lenient,
even if they were corrupt and indulgent,
there would still be no harm.
But as for those who were harsh and scrutinizing,
even if they themselves were honest and law-abiding,
their cunning and shrewdness in cutting back and exploiting
would inflict suffering upon the common people,
leading to disasters and displacement.
When he was a Shàngshū,
he constantly wanted to prostrate himself and argue against this,
but because the times were very strict and severe,
he dared not present his views.
Later, the Emperor heard his words and felt a belated sorrow for him.
In the first year of Jiànchū (76 CE),
he died at home.
His nephew was Yì.
Yì's courtesy name was Bózhì.
His father, Jīng,
taught the Shàngshū with the Great Xiàhóu commentary,
and rose to Liáodōng Tàishǒu.
Yì inherited his father's profession in his youth.
During Xiǎnzōng's reign, he was nominated as Xiàolián,
and because his responses in audience accorded with the Emperor's will,
he was promoted and appointed Āyáng Hóuxiàng.
During the Jiànchū era,
he was summoned to be a Shàngshū.
Sùzōng was by nature benevolent and kind,
and his affection for relatives was deep.
Thus, his paternal uncles, the two kings of Jìnán and Zhōngshān, frequently came to court,
and received special favor and grace.
All his paternal cousins were also kept in the capital,
not dispatched to their respective states.
Yì believed that as subjects, one should uphold proper decorum,
and it was inappropriate to exceed rites and bestow excessive favor.
So he submitted a memorial, advising:
"Your Majesty is supremely filial and benevolent,
with profound affection and love.
Considering Kāng, the King of Jìnán, and Yān, the King of Zhōngshān, as elder brothers of the late Emperor,
they have specially received favored treatment.
Your sacred heart is deeply attached,
unable to bear their separation.
In recent years, they have attended court audiences
and been detained in the capital for long periods,
honored with the status of paternal uncles,
and treated with the rites of family members.
Their carriages enter the palace gates,
they take their seats without bowing,
you share your delicacies and reduce your own meals,
and bestow generous rewards.
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu, possessing the virtue of a sage,
achieved the功 of bringing about great peace,
and only then did the King address him as 'paternal uncle'
and bestow upon him gifts of silk.
Now, Kāng and Yān are fortunate to, as collateral relatives, enjoy the revenue of large states.
Upon Your Majesty's ascension,
you abolished their former transgressions,
restored what had been curtailed,
and expanded their income to other counties.
Men and women, young and old,
all received titles and fiefs.
Their favor and grace exceed the regulations,
and the respect shown is excessive.
According to the principles of the Chūnqiū,
all paternal uncles and cousins are without exception subjects.
This is to distinguish between the honored and the humble,
to strengthen the trunk and weaken the branches.
Your Majesty's virtuous achievements are grand and flourishing,
and you should serve as a model for ten thousand generations.
It is improper to diminish the order of superior and inferior with private affection,
and lose the proper relationship between ruler and subject.
Furthermore, the six kings, including Xiàn, the King of Xīpíng,
all have wives, children, and established households,
with a full complement of officials and retainers.
They ought to proceed to their feudal states promptly
to establish foundations for their descendants.
Yet their residences face each other,
and they have long lingered in the capital.
The lavishness of their marriages
surpasses that of the imperial court itself,
and the multitude of their servants and horses
fills the city.
They are arrogant, extravagant, and presumptuous in imitation,
with favor and emoluments far exceeding what is due.
Now, the lands of these various states
are all fertile,
with mild climates,
and roads that are easy and near.
There are fixed dates for court visits and tributes,
so travel is not difficult.
It is fitting to overcome your sentiments of reluctance
and sever affection with righteousness,
to dispatch Kāng and Yān, each to return to his feudal state,
and order Xiàn and the others to proceed quickly at an opportune time,
to satisfy the expectations of the populace."
The Emperor accepted his advice.
In the second year of Zhānghé (88 CE),
the Xiānbēi defeated the Northern Xiōngnú,
and the Southern Chányú, taking advantage of this, requested troops for a northern expedition,
intending to return to their former territory.
At that time, Empress Dowager Dòu was regent,
and deliberations were held to accede to his request.
Yì submitted a memorial, stating:
"The Róngdí are separated from China by a great distance,
dwelling in the desolate north,
divided by the desert.
They disregard rites and righteousness,
having no distinction between high and low.
The strong become paramount,
while the weak submit.
Since the rise of the Hàn,
there have been numerous campaigns,
but what was gained
never compensated for the harm.
Emperor Guāngwǔ personally endured the difficulties of warfare,
and deeply understood the clear principles of Heaven and Earth.
Therefore, he took advantage of their surrender,
keeping them under loose control and raising them.
The border people were able to live,
and labor and toil ceased,
for over forty years now.
Now, the Xiānbēi respectfully comply,
slaying and capturing tens of thousands.
China reaps great achievements without effort,
and the common people are unaware of their toil.
The achievements of the Hàn's rise
are at their peak in this regard.
The reason for this is
that the barbarians attack each other,
without harming the Hàn army.
Your subject observes that the Xiānbēi's invasion of the Xiōngnú
is precisely out of greed for plunder,
and attributing merit to the sacred court
is truly due to their desire for rich rewards.
Now, if we allow the Southern barbarians to return to their northern court,
we will inevitably have to restrain the Xiānbēi.
If the Xiānbēi lose their desire for violent plunder externally
and have no rewards for their merits internally,
their wolf-like greed
will surely become a border menace.
Now, the Northern barbarians have fled west
and request peace and kinship.
It is advisable to use their allegiance
as an external defense.
No majestic undertaking
could surpass this.
If we mobilize troops and expend resources
to satisfy the Southern barbarians,
we will lose the superior strategy without effort,
and abandon security for danger.
This truly cannot be permitted."
It so happened that the Southern Chányú ultimately did not move north.
He was promoted to Sīlì Xiàowèi.
In the early Yǒngyuán era,
General-in-Chief Dòu Xiàn and his brothers were powerful and favored.
Dèng Dié, Colonel of Infantry, Wáng Diào, Governor of Hénán, Lián Fàn, former Grand Administrator of Shǔjùn, and other partisans
frequented Dòu Xiàn's residence,
abusing their power and indulging in excesses.
Yì consistently investigated and impeached them,
without any hesitation.
Because of this, he had a rift with the Dòu clan.
In the second year (90 CE),
he died of illness.
His grandson, Jù,
served as Sīkōng during the reign of Emperor Líng.
Hán Láng, whose courtesy name was Bóqí,
was a man from Xuē, Lǔguó.
Three days after his birth,
he encountered chaos in the land;
he was abandoned in thorns.
After several days, the fighting ceased,
and his mother went to look for him.
He was still breathing,
so she took him back and raised him.
When he grew up,
he loved classical studies
and was widely conversant with books and commentaries,
teaching the Shàngshū.
He was nominated as Xiàolián.
During the Yǒngpíng reign,
he was appointed as an usher and served as an imperial censor.
Together with the various subordinate officials of the Three Bureaus, he investigated the Chǔ case involving Yán Zhōng and Wáng Píng.
Their confessions implicated Gěng Jiàn, the Marquis of Suìxiāng; Zāng Xìn, the Marquis of Lánglíng; Dèng Lí, the Marquis of Hùzé; and Liú Jiàn, the Marquis of Qǔchéng.
Jiàn and the others testified that they had never met Zhōng or Píng.
At that time, Xiǎnzōng was extremely angry,
and all the officials were terrified.
All those implicated
were universally condemned,
with no one daring to show mercy based on the facts.
Hán Láng was distressed by their injustice,
so he tried to question Zhōng and Píng separately about Jiàn and the others' physical appearances,
but the two were so flustered that they couldn't answer.
Hán Láng knew they were lying,
so he memorialized that Jiàn and the others were innocent
and had been solely slandered by Zhōng and Píng,
suspecting that many innocent people throughout the empire were similarly treated.
The Emperor then summoned Hán Láng
and asked,
"If Jiàn and the others are truly as you say,
why did Zhōng and Píng implicate them?"
Hán Láng replied,
"Zhōng and Píng knew that their crimes were heinous,
so they made many false accusations,
hoping to justify themselves."
The Emperor said,
"If that is the case,
and the four marquises are innocent,
why did you not report this sooner,
and why were they kept imprisoned for so long after the case was concluded?"
Hán Láng replied,
"Although I found them innocent in my investigation,
I feared that there might be others within the empire who would expose their alleged treachery,
so I did not dare to report it immediately."
The Emperor angrily cursed him, saying,
"You officials are equivocating!
Seize him and take him away!"
As his attendants were about to lead him away,
Hán Láng said,
"I beg to speak one more word before I die.
I, your humble servant, dare not deceive you;
I only wish to aid the state."
The Emperor asked,
"Who collaborated with you on this memorial?"
He replied,
"I know I am destined for extermination of my clan,
so I dared not implicate others.
I sincerely hoped that Your Majesty would awaken to the truth.
I observed that those involved in interrogating prisoners
all agreed that great evils and wickedness
should be universally abhorred by subjects,
and that it is better to condemn them than to release them,
to avoid future blame.
Thus, interrogating one implicates ten,
and interrogating ten implicates a hundred.
Moreover, when the dukes and ministers gather in court,
and Your Majesty asks about successes and failures,
they all kneel and declare
that according to old customs, great crimes bring disaster upon nine generations,
but Your Majesty's great benevolence
limits it only to the person themselves,
which is a great blessing for the empire.
However, when they return home,
though they speak no words,
they look up at the roof and sigh secretly,
all knowing there are many injustices,
but no one dares to contradict Your Majesty.
What I now present
is truly something I will not regret, even in death."
The Emperor's anger subsided,
and he issued an edict releasing Hán Láng.
Two days later,
the Emperor himself went to the Luòyáng prison to review the prisoners,
and released over a thousand people.
Later, Píng and Zhōng died in prison,
and Hán Láng then imprisoned himself.
A general amnesty was issued,
and he was relieved of his office.
He was again recommended as xiàolián (filial and incorrupt).
During the Jiànchū reign,
Sùzōng convened a grand assembly of officials.
Hán Láng came forward to express his gratitude.
An edict acknowledged Hán Láng's loyal counsel to the late Emperor
and appointed him as Magistrate of Yì.
After more than a year,
he was promoted to Magistrate of Jìyáng.
He resigned from office due to his mother's mourning.
The common people remembered him with affection.
In the first year of Zhānghé,
the Emperor made an eastern inspection tour
and passed through Jìyáng.
The Three Elders and local officials submitted a memorial praising Hán Láng's former governance.
When the Emperor arrived in Liáng,
he summoned Hán Láng for an audience,
and ordered the Three Bureaus to recommend him for office.
Thus, he was recruited by the Sītú's (Minister of Works) office.
During the Yǒngyuán reign,
he was twice promoted to Administrator of Qīnghé.
He was dismissed due to legal issues.
In the third year of Yǒngchū,
Grand Commandant Zhāng Yǔ recommended Hán Láng as a Doctor (bóshì).
He was summoned to the public carriage,
but died during the journey.
He was then eighty-four years old.
Commentary says: Zuǒ Qiūmíng said,
"The words of a benevolent person,
how widely beneficial they are!"
A single word from Yàn Zǐ prompted the Marquis of Qí to lighten punishments.
Such as Zhōnglí Yì's direct plea for correction,
and Hán Láng's open debate against unjust imprisonment,
how sincere
is the feeling of a benevolent person!
Indeed, uprightness rooted in loyalty and sincerity is not devious,
and rooted in remonstrance and debate, it is incisive.
The foundation of these two men was received from Heaven,
thus their words were trusted and their aspirations realized.
Eulogy says: Bóyú and Zǐ'ā,
corrected excesses and eliminated harshness.
They were pure in office,
and rectified the Emperor from extravagance.
Sòng Jūn achieved governance,
prohibiting these demonic sacrifices.
Birds and insects feared his virtue,
and the people requested relief from illness.
Yì Míng honored the venerable,
and sacrificed affection to protect the imperial clan.
For the trembling people of Chǔ,
Lord Hán provided their fate.
Biography of the Ten Princes of Guāngwǔ, Part 32

Guāngwǔ Emperor had eleven sons: Empress Guō gave birth to Liú Qiáng, Prince Gōng of Dōnghǎi; Liú Fǔ, Prince Xiàn of Pèi; Liú Kāng, Prince Ān of Jìnán; Liú Yán, Prince Zhì of Fùlíng; and Liú Yān, Prince Jiǎn of Zhōngshān.
Consort Xǔ gave birth to Liú Yīng, King of Chǔ.
Empress Guāngliè gave birth to Xiǎnzōng; Liú Cāng, Prince Xiàn of Dōngpíng; Liú Jīng, Prince Sī of Guǎnglíng; Liú Héng, Duke Huái of Línhuái; and Liú Jīng, Prince Xiào of Lángxié.
Liú Qiáng, Prince Gōng of Dōnghǎi.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
his mother, Lady Guō, was established as Empress,
and Liú Qiáng was made Crown Prince.
After seventeen years, Empress Guō was deposed,
and Liú Qiáng was constantly uneasy and unsettled.
He repeatedly used his attendants and other princes to express his sincere wish
to be granted a feudal state.
Guāngwǔ could not bear to,
and hesitated for several years
before finally agreeing.
In the nineteenth year,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Dōnghǎi.
In the twenty-eighth year,
he proceeded to his state.
The Emperor considered that Liú Qiáng's deposition was not due to his own fault,
and that his departure and assumption of office were conducted with propriety.
Therefore, he was generously granted a large enfeoffment.
He also governed the commandery of Lǔ,
totaling twenty-nine counties.
He was bestowed with tiger guards and feathered standards,
and his palace was equipped with bells and stands,
mimicking the imperial carriage.
Upon arriving in his state, Liú Qiáng
repeatedly submitted memorials requesting to return Dōnghǎi.
He also used the Crown Prince to firmly decline.
The Emperor did not allow it,
but deeply praised and admired him,
and displayed Liú Qiáng's memorial to the dukes and ministers.
Initially,
King Gōng of Lǔ was fond of palaces
and built the Língguāng Hall,
which was very magnificent.
It still existed at that time,
so an edict commanded Liú Qiáng to establish his capital in Lǔ.
In the first year of Zhōngyuán, he came to court,
followed the Emperor to perform the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Dài,
and remained in the capital.
In the spring of the following year,
the Emperor passed away.
In winter,
he returned to his state.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng,
Qiáng fell ill.
Xiǎnzōng sent a Zhōng Chángshì and a Gōudùn Lìng to take imperial physicians by post-horse to attend to his illness.
An imperial edict ordered Pèi Wáng Fǔ, Jìnán Wáng Kāng, and Huáiyáng Wáng Yán to go to Lǔ.
When he passed away,
on his deathbed, he submitted a memorial of thanks, saying:
"Your subject has received grace to be counted among the regional princes,
specially granted two states.
My palaces, rituals, and music
are all exceptionally splendid,
grand and immeasurable,
yet I have offered no recompense.
Furthermore, I have not conducted myself carefully,
suffering from illness for consecutive years,
causing concern to the imperial court.
The Empress Dowager and Your Majesty pity your subject Qiáng,
deeply moved within,
repeatedly sending envoys, imperial physicians, and masters of various arts and techniques,
arriving continuously.
Your subject reflects on this profound grace,
not knowing what to say.
Your subject examines himself inwardly,
his strength is weak and failing,
growing worse day by day.
I shall never again hope to see the palace court,
or serve beneath the imperial canopy.
I have failed in repaying this immense grace,
carrying this regret to the Yellow Springs.
My life has been cut short and I am weak and solitary,
and I have again caused worry to the Empress Dowager and Your Majesty.
I am truly saddened and truly ashamed.
My son, Zhèng,
is a small man.
If he were to presumptuously succeed me,
it would certainly not be beneficial to preserve him.
I sincerely wish for the Eastern Sea Commandery to be returned.
Your celestial grace has shown pity and compassion,
on account of your subject having no sons,
to make your subject's three daughters minor marquises.
This has long been your subject's plan.
Now the empire has newly suffered great sorrow.
I only ask Your Majesty to increase your care for the Empress Dowager
and frequently offer her meals.
Your subject Qiáng is weak and failing,
and cannot express his full thoughts.
I wish to bid farewell to all the other princes;
I did not expect never to see them again."
The Son of Heaven read the letter with grief and sorrow.
He went with the Empress Dowager to Jīnmén Tíng to express his lament.
He dispatched a Dà Sīkōng, holding the imperial credential, to oversee the funeral arrangements,
with a Dà Hónglú as deputy,
and the Zōngzhèng and Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng to supervise the funeral rites.
He bestowed extraordinary honors,
including the Shēnglóng banner, Máotóu banner, Luánlù carriage, Lóngqí banner, and one hundred Hǔbēn guards.

An edict ordered Chǔ Wáng Yīng, Zhào Wáng Xǔ, Běihǎi Wáng Xīng, Guǎntáo Gōngzhǔ, Bǐyáng Gōngzhǔ, and all relatives from the four prominent clans in the capital, along with the minor marquises, to attend the funeral.
The Emperor, reflecting on Qiáng's deep commitment to humility and frugality,
did not wish for a lavish burial to go against his wishes.
Thereupon, he specially decreed to Zhōng Chángshì Dù Cén and the tutor and administrator of Dōnghǎi:
"The Prince was humble, reverent, and fond of rituals,
concluding his life with virtue.
The items for his funeral
must adhere to simplicity and frugality.
Clothes sufficient to cover the body,
a thatch carriage, and pottery vessels,
items reduced from the standard,
to manifest the Prince's extraordinary and independent spirit.
The Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng shall remain to construct the mausoleum and temple."
Qiáng reigned for eighteen years,
and was thirty-four years old.
His son, Jìng Wáng Zhèng, succeeded him.
Zhèng was licentious and had poor conduct.
Later, when Zhōngshān Jiǎnwáng passed away,
Zhèng went to Zhōngshān to attend the funeral,
and privately took Jiǎnwáng's concubine, Lady Xú.
He also secretly welcomed a woman dismissed from the imperial harem.
The Yùzhōu Cìshǐ and Lǔ Xiàng submitted a memorial requesting Zhèng be executed.
An imperial edict then reduced his territory by Xuē Xiàn.
He reigned for forty-four years and passed away.
His son, Qǐng Wáng Sù, succeeded him.
In the sixteenth year of Yǒngyuán,
twenty-one of Sù's younger brothers were all enfeoffed as marquises.
Sù was humble and frugal by nature,
following the regulations of Gōngwáng.
During the Yǒngchū period,
as the Western Qiāng had not yet been pacified,
he offered twenty million cash.
During the Yuánchū period,
he again offered ten thousand bolts of fine silk,
to assist with state expenses.
Empress Dowager Dèng issued an edict praising and accepting his offering.
He reigned for twenty-three years and passed away.
His son, Xiào Wáng Zhēn, succeeded him.
In the second year of Yǒngjiàn,
Zhēn's two younger brothers, Mǐn and Jiǎn, were enfeoffed as xiānghóu.
Zhēn and his younger brother, Zhēng Xiānghóu Jiǎn, both had virtuous conduct.
When their mother died,
they both vomited blood and were emaciated with grief.
When it came to wearing the dyed white mourning clothes,
the brothers recalled that when their father died,
they were young,
and their mourning rituals were incomplete.
Therefore, they again observed the full mourning rites.
Zhēn was honest, generous, and kind by nature.
He often distributed his stipends and salaries to relieve his uncles and cousins.
Guó Xiàng Jí Bāo reported this in detail,
and Shùndì admired it,
issuing an edict to the Dà Jiāngjūn, the Sān Gōng, and the Dà Hónglú, saying:
"Dōnghǎi Wáng Zhēn, with the尊(dignity) of a close regional prince,
inherited the princely title at a young age,
receiving abundant blessings,
having known no hardships.
Yet he has been able to restrain himself and follow ritual,
with natural filial piety and reverence.
He served his parents with utmost love,
and exhausted his sorrow at their funerals.
He lowered his demeanor to that of a commoner,
sleeping on straw and using a clod of earth for a pillow for three years.
He is harmonious with his brothers,
and supports the orphaned and weak.
His filial piety is utterly complete,
and his benevolence and righteousness are widely manifest.
I greatly commend him.
Indeed, promoting good and encouraging virtuous customs
is paramount for the state.
In the past, Dōngpíng Xiàowáng Chǎng and his brothers practiced filial piety,
mourning their mother according to ritual,
and were granted an increase in households.
The *Shī* says: 'Forever filial,
remembering these imperial ancestors.'
Now, I increase Zhēn's fief by five thousand households,
and Jiǎn's by five hundred households,
to splendidly expand their territories,
in reward for their virtue."
He reigned for thirty-one years and passed away.
His son, Yì Wáng Zhī, succeeded him.
In the fourth year of Chūpíng,
he sent his son Wǎn to Cháng'ān to present a memorial.
Xiàndì enfeoffed Wǎn as Wènyáng Hóu,
and appointed him Píngyuán Xiàng.
Zhī reigned for forty-four years and passed away.
His son, Xiàn, succeeded him.
Twenty years later,
when Wèi received the abdication,
he was made Chóngdé Hóu.
Pèi Xiàn Wáng Fǔ,
in the fifteenth year of Jiànwǔ, was enfeoffed as Yòuféngyǐ Gōng.
In the seventeenth year,
Empress Guō was deposed as Empress Dowager of Zhōngshān.
Thus, Fǔ was transferred to be Zhōngshān Wáng,
also taking the income of Chángshān Commandery.
In the twentieth year,
he was again transferred to be enfeoffed as Pèi Wáng.
At that time, the prohibitions were still loose,
and all the princes were in the capital,
competing to cultivate a good reputation
and vie for the respect of guests from all directions.
Shòuguāng Hóu Liú Lǐ,
Gēngshǐ's son, was favored by Fǔ.
Lǐ resented Liú Pénzǐ for harming his father.
Through Fǔ, he gathered followers
and retaliated by killing Pénzǐ's elder brother, the former Shì Hóu Gōng.
Fǔ was implicated and imprisoned in the imperial jail,
but was released after three days.
From then on,
many guests of the princes suffered penalties,
and all followed the laws.
In the twenty-eighth year,
he proceeded to his state.
In the second year of Zhōngyuán,
Fǔ's son Bǎo was enfeoffed as Pèi Hóu.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng,
Bǎo's younger brother Jiā was enfeoffed as Tóng Hóu.
Fǔ was dignified and strict, with proper regulations.
He enjoyed the classics,
and was skilled at explaining the Jīng's *Yì*, *Xiàojīng*, *Lúnyǔ Zhuàn*, and prognostications.
He wrote *Wǔjīng Lùn*,
which was then called *Pèi Wáng Tōnglùn*.
In his state, he was cautious and disciplined,
consistent from beginning to end,
and was called a wise prince.
Xiǎnzōng respected him greatly,
and frequently bestowed rewards upon him.
He reigned for forty-six years and passed away.
His son, Xī Wáng Dìng, succeeded him.
In the second year of Yuánhé,
twelve of Dìng's younger brothers were enfeoffed as xiānghóu.
Dìng reigned for eleven years and passed away.
His son, Jié Wáng Zhèng, succeeded him.
In the first year of Yuánxīng,
two of Zhèng's younger brothers were enfeoffed as xiànhóu.
Zhèngdì reigned for fourteen years and then died.
His son, King Xiào (廣) Guǎng, succeeded him.
He had a chronic illness.
Emperor Ān (安) ordered Guǎng's (廣) grandmother, Zhōu (周), to manage the royal household affairs.
Zhōu (周) was righteous and adhered to propriety.
During the Hàn Ān (漢安) period, she died.
Emperor Shùn (順) issued an edict saying:
"The Grand Lady Zhōu (周), grandmother of the King of Pèi (沛),
maintained a pure and cautious heart,
guiding the King with benevolence."
He dispatched the Grand Master of Guanglù (光祿大夫) to bestow upon her a consort's seal and ribbon as a posthumous honor.
Guǎng (廣) reigned for thirty-five years and then died.
His son, King Yōu (幽) Róng (榮), succeeded him.
He reigned for twenty years and then died.
His son, King Xiào (孝) Cóng (琮), succeeded him.
He died.
His son, King Gōng (恭) Yào (曜), succeeded him.
He died.
His son, Qì (契), succeeded him.
When Wèi (魏) received the abdication,
he was made the Marquis of Chóngdé (崇德).
Yīng (英), King of Chǔ (楚),
was enfeoffed as the Duke of Chǔ (楚公) in the fifteenth year of Jiànwǔ (建武).
In the seventeenth year, his noble rank was raised to King.
In the twenty-eighth year, he went to his state.
His mother, Lady Xǔ (許), was not favored,
so Yīng's (英) state was the poorest and smallest.
In the thirtieth year,
the two counties of Qǔlǜ (取慮) and Xūchāng (須昌) from Lín’huái (臨淮) were added to the state of Chǔ (楚).
Since Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) was Crown Prince,
Yīng (英) had always uniquely attached himself to the Crown Prince,
and the Crown Prince especially loved him.
When the Crown Prince ascended the throne,
Yīng (英) frequently received rewards and gifts.
In the first year of Yǒngpíng (永平),
Yīng’s (英) maternal cousin, Xǔ Chāng (許昌), was specially enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lóngshū (龍舒).
In his youth, Yīng (英) enjoyed knight-errantry
and associated with retainers.
In his later years, he became fond of Huáng-Lǎo (黃老) philosophy,
studying and practicing the asceticism and sacrifices of Buddhism (浮屠).
In the eighth year,
an imperial edict ordered that all those condemned to death throughout the empire could redeem themselves with silk.
Yīng (英) dispatched his Lángzhōnglìng (郎中令) to present thirty bolts of yellow and white silk to the state chancellor, saying:
"Residing as a vassal,
my faults and evils have accumulated.
Rejoicing in the great benevolence,
I present this silk
to redeem my transgressions."
The state chancellor reported this.
The imperial edict replied:
"The King of Chǔ (楚) recites the subtle words of Huáng-Lǎo (黃老),
and venerates the benevolent shrines of Buddhism (浮屠).
Having purified himself for three months,
he has sworn an oath to the gods.
What doubt or suspicion
could there be for regret?
Return the ransom,
to aid in the grand feast for the Upāsaka (伊蒲塞) and Śramaṇa (桑門)."
This was then circulated among the tutors of the various states.
Afterward, Yīng (英) extensively associated with geomancers and Daoist practitioners,
making golden turtles and jade cranes,
inscribing texts to serve as auspicious omens.
In the thirteenth year,
a man named Yān Guǎng (燕廣) reported that Yīng (英), along with Yúyáng (漁陽) Wang Píng (王平), Yán Zhōng (顏忠), and others, were creating diagrams and texts
with rebellious intentions.
The matter was sent down for investigation.
The officials memorialized that Yīng (英) had gathered villains,
created diagrams and prophecies,
arbitrarily appointed official ranks,
and established nobles, lords, generals, and officials of two thousand dàns (二千石),
which was greatly rebellious and unlawful.
They requested his execution.
The Emperor, out of family affection, could not bear it,
so he deposed Yīng (英)
and exiled him to Jīng (涇) county in Dānyáng (丹陽),
granting him a tax-exempt household of five hundred families (湯沐邑).
He sent the Grand Chamberlain (大鴻臚) with a retinue to escort him,
allowing all musicians and servants to follow him,
permitting him to ride in a covered carriage,
carry weapons and crossbows,
hunt on the road,
and enjoy himself to his heart's content.
His sons and daughters who were enfeoffed as marquises or lords
retained their stipends as before.
The Grand Empress Dowager of Chǔ (楚) was not required to surrender her seals and ribbons,
and remained in the Chǔ (楚) palace.
The next year,
Yīng (英) reached Dānyáng (丹陽)
and committed suicide.
He had been on the throne for thirty-three years,
and his state was abolished.
An imperial edict dispatched the Grand Master of Guanglù (光祿大夫) with a retinue to offer condolences and sacrifices,
granting funeral gifts according to regulations,
additionally bestowing a marquis's seal and ribbon,
and burying him in Jīng (涇) with the rites of a vassal king.
A Zhonghuángmén (中黃門) was sent to care for his wife and children.
