All Chǔ (楚) officials and attendants who had not participated in the conspiracy were released.
An imperial edict was issued to Grand Empress Dowager Xǔ (許), saying:
"When the state first heard of the Chǔ (楚) affair,
it hoped it was not true.
Now that the reality is known,
I am filled with grief and distress.
I wished to pardon and preserve the King's life,
allowing him to complete his natural lifespan,
but the King did not consider the Grand Empress Dowager
and ultimately could not save himself.
This is fate,
and there is nothing to be done!
May the Grand Empress Dowager care for the young and weak
and force herself to eat and drink.
All the Xǔ (許) family wished for the King's wealth and honor,
which is human nature.
I have already ordered the authorities
to release those who were involved in the conspiracy
and allow them to settle their homes."
Thereupon, Yān Guǎng (燕廣) was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhéjiān (折姦).
The Chǔ (楚) prison case thus lasted for several years,
with confessions leading to more arrests.
From the imperial relatives in the capital, the nobles, the local officials, and the prominent families in the provinces and commanderies, as well as the investigating officials,
those who flattered and implicated others,
thousands were executed or exiled.
In the fifteenth year,
the Emperor visited Péngchéng (彭城)
and saw Grand Empress Dowager Xǔ (許) and Yīng's (英) wife and children in the inner palace.
He wept bitterly,
moving those around him.
In the second year of Jiànchū (建初),
Sùzōng (肅宗) enfeoffed Yīng's (英) son, Zhǒng (种), as the Marquis of Chǔ (楚),
and his five younger brothers were all made marquises.
However, none were allowed to appoint chancellors or officials.
In the third year of Yuánhé (元和),
Grand Empress Dowager Xǔ (許) died.
Again, the Grand Master of Guanglù (光祿大夫) was dispatched with a retinue to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and then stayed to oversee the funeral arrangements,
granting five million cash in funeral gifts.
An official (謁者) was also sent to prepare the royal retinue to welcome Yīng's (英) coffin,
reburying him in Péngchéng (彭城).
The King was granted a red ribbon, a feather canopy, and splendid decorations,
according to the ceremony for a successor king.
He was posthumously enfeoffed
and given the posthumous title of King Lì (厲) of Chǔ (楚).
In the first year of Zhānghé (章和),
the Emperor visited Péngchéng (彭城)
and met Yīng's (英) wife and six sons,
bestowing generous gifts upon them.
Afterward, Zhǒng (种) was transferred to be enfeoffed as Marquis of Liù (六).
He died,
and his son Dù (度) succeeded him.
Dù (度) died,
and his son Jū (拘) succeeded him,
passing on the state to subsequent generations.
Kāng (康), King Ān (安) of Jìnán (濟南),
was enfeoffed as the Duke of Jìnán (濟南公) in the fifteenth year of Jiànwǔ (建武).
In the seventeenth year, his noble rank was raised to King.
In the twenty-eighth year, he went to his state.
In the thirtieth year,
six counties from Píngyuán (平原)—Zhù’ē (祝阿), Āndé (安德), Cháoyáng (朝陽), Píngchāng (平昌), Xīyīn (隰陰), and Chóngqiū (重丘)—were added to the state of Jìnán (濟南).
In the second year of Zhōngyuán (中元),
Kāng's (康) son Dé (德) was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngwǔchéng (東武城).
Kāng (康) did not adhere to laws and regulations in his state,
and associated with retainers.
Afterward,
someone submitted a memorial accusing Kāng (康) of attracting corrupt and cunning individuals from the provinces and commanderies, such as Yúyáng (漁陽) Yán Zhōng (顏忠) and Liú Zǐchǎn (劉子產),
and of frequently giving them silk,
examining diagrams and texts,
and plotting rebellion.
The matter was sent down for investigation,
and the officials presented a memorial.
Xiǎnzōng (顯宗), due to family affection,
could not bear to thoroughly investigate the matter to its conclusion,
but merely reduced his territory by five counties: Zhù’ē (祝阿), Xīyīn (隰陰), Dōngcháoyáng (東朝陽), Āndé (安德), and Xīpíngchāng (西平昌).
In the 8th year of Jiànchū,
Sùzōng restored the lands that had been cut off,
and Kāng consequently accumulated much wealth,
greatly repairing his palaces and residences.
His slaves and maids numbered 1,400,
his stable horses 1,200,
and his private fields 800 qīng.
He was extravagant and indulgent,
and his pleasure excursions were without restraint.
At the beginning of Yǒngyuán,
the state tutor Hé Chǎng submitted a memorial to admonish Kāng, saying:
"I have heard that it is the principle for feudal lords
to moderate their activities and be prudent in their measures,
and only then can they preserve their altars of soil and grain
and harmonize their people.
Your Royal Highness, by virtue of being a close relative,
enjoys the emoluments of a feudal lord.
You ought to promulgate governmental decrees
and clarify your statutes and laws.
Your comings and goings, your advances and retreats,
should have a set timing and measure.
Your carriages and horses, your attendants and servants,
should be categorized and ranked.
Yet now, your slaves, maids, and stable horses each number over a thousand,
increasing useless mouths
to devour your own resources.
The palace maids are confined and isolated,
losing their natural dispositions,
and disrupting the harmonious qi.
Furthermore, you have built many inner residences,
violating prohibitions and restrictions,
spending tens of thousands,
yet the work is still not half done.
For when ornamentation is excessive, the substance is neglected;
when wood dominates, people perish.
These are not ways to uphold rites, serve the emperor,
and transmit boundless blessings.
Therefore, Chǔ built the Zhānghuá Palace and met with misfortune;
Wú built Gūsū and was destroyed.
Jǐng Gōng had a thousand teams of horses,
but the people had nothing to praise.
Now, you frequently tour various residences,
day and night without moderation.
This is also not the way to prevent calamities before they occur,
or to 'approach the deep and tread on thin ice.'
I wish Your Royal Highness would cultivate humility and frugality,
follow ancient regulations,
reduce the number of slaves and maids,
decrease the number of riding horses,
renounce the wealth from private fields,
and moderate your pleasure excursions.
Conduct your daily life according to rites,
then Chǎng would dare to feel at ease and secure himself.
May Your Royal Highness deeply consider my foolish words."
Kāng had always respected Hé Chǎng,
and although he showed no resentment or displeasure,
he was ultimately unable to change.
He reigned for 59 years and then passed away.
His son, Jiǎnwáng Cuò, succeeded him.
When Cuò was Crown Prince,
he was fond of Kāng's drummer and dancer, Sòng Rùn.
He sent the physician Zhāng Zūn to summon her, but Zhāng Zūn was unsuccessful.
Cuò became enraged
and personally stabbed Zhāng Zūn to death with a sword.
The Chancellor of the State reported this,
but an imperial edict ordered that the case not be prosecuted.
In the 11th year of Yǒngyuán,
seven of Cuò's younger brothers were enfeoffed as marquises.
Cuò reigned for six years and then passed away.
His son, Xiàowáng Xiāng, succeeded him.
In the 2nd year of Yǒngchū,
four of Xiāng's younger brothers were enfeoffed as marquises.
Xiāng was a man of earnest conduct
and fond of classics and books.
Initially,
his uncle Dú had committed a crime and could not be enfeoffed,
and Yù, Marquis of Xīpíngchāng, lost his marquisate due to legal transgressions.
Xiāng then submitted a memorial, proposing to divide his noble rank and territory to enfeoff Dú's son Wán and Yù's son Sōng,
who were both made marquises.
Xiāng reigned for 20 years and then passed away.
He had no son,
so his state was abolished.
In the 1st year of Yǒngjiàn,
Shùndì established Cuò's son, Fǔyánghóu Xiǎn, as successor,
who became Līwáng.
He reigned for three years and then passed away.
His son, Dàowáng Guǎng, succeeded him.
In the 5th year of Yǒngjiàn,
Guǎng's younger brother Wén was enfeoffed as Marquis of Lèchéngtíng.
Guǎng reigned for 25 years.
In the 1st year of Yǒngxīng, he passed away.
He had no son,
so his state was abolished.
Dōngpíng Xiànwáng Cāng
was enfeoffed as Duke of Dōngpíng in the 15th year of Jiànwǔ.
In the 17th year, his peerage was raised to King.
Cāng was fond of classics and books from a young age,
and naturally possessed intelligence and thoughtfulness.
He had a handsome beard
and a waist measuring eight *wéi*.
Xiǎnzōng greatly loved and respected him.
Upon ascending the throne,
he appointed Cāng as General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn),
and established a staff of 40 Chief Clerks and officials,
whose rank was above the Three Excellencies.
In the 1st year of Yǒngpíng,
two of Cāng's sons were enfeoffed as county marquises.
In the 2nd year,
the five counties of Shòuzhāng and Xūchāng from Dōngjùn,
and Nánpíngyáng, Tuó, and Húlíng from Shānyáng, were added to the State of Dōngpíng.
At this time, it had been over thirty years since the restoration,
and there was peace throughout the land.
Cāng believed that with the world pacified,
it was time to reform rites and music.
Thus, he deliberated with the dukes and ministers to determine the system for caps, robes, and chariots for the Northern and Southern Suburbs,
as well as the number of "ascending songs" and "eight-row dances" for the temple of Guāngwǔ.
The details are recorded in the Treatises on Rites and Music, and Carriages and Robes.
Whenever the Emperor went on an inspection tour,
Cāng always remained to guard,
serving and protecting the Empress Dowager.
In the spring of the 4th year,
the imperial carriage made a short excursion
to view the city mansions.
Soon after, it was heard that a grand hunt would be conducted in Hénèi.
Cāng immediately submitted a memorial in remonstrance, saying:
"Your servant has heard the seasonal regulations:
in the height of spring, during agricultural work,
one does not gather crowds to undertake major projects.
The tradition says: 'If hunting is not restricted to a single night's stay,
if food and drink are not offered to others,
if comings and goings are not restrained,
then trees will not grow straight or curved (as they should).'
This means violating the spring regulations.
Your servant knows that the imperial carriage's current outing
is intended to be simple and economical,
and that the officials and people everywhere recite the virtues of Gāntáng.
Nevertheless,
actions not in accordance with ritual
are not suitable for demonstrating to the four directions.
I only wish that Your Majesty, while traveling in the countryside,
would observe the crops,
stroll leisurely and aimlessly,
and then return without extending your stay.
Wait until autumn and winter,
then display your majestic power,
organize the imperial equipage,
prepare a full escort,
and set up feathered banners.
The *Shī* says: 'How solemn and dignified their demeanor,
which is the corner of virtue.'
Your servant, unable to contain his indignation,
has personally written this memorial,
begging to come to your current location
and fully express his utmost sincerity."
The Emperor read the memorial
and immediately returned to the palace.
Cāng was at court for several years,
making many significant contributions,
but he considered himself a close relative assisting in governance,
and as his prestige grew daily,
he felt uneasy.
He submitted a memorial to resign from his post, saying:
“Your servant, Cāng, is weary and incompetent,
especially due to Your Majesty’s benevolent protection.
At home, I received the kindness of guidance,
and at court, I was honored with titles and appointments.
Edicts praised my virtues,
broadcasting them throughout the four seas,
elevating a talent like one carrying firewood
to the stature of a gentleman’s vessel.
Even an ordinary commoner,
still does not forget the kindness of a single basket of food;
how much more so for your servant, occupying the position of prime minister,
a kinsman of the same spirit!
I ought to expose my bones in the wilderness
and set an example for all officials.
However, my foolish and stubborn nature,
compounded by chronic illness,
makes me truly ashamed to be like one riding an empty carriage,
disgracing the position of an assisting general,
and risking the condemnation of the poet’s ‘three hundred scarlet sashes.’
Now the realm is tranquil,
and there are no alarms in the remote regions.
This is a time to follow the supreme virtue of non-action.
Civil officials can still be consolidated and reduced,
and military positions are even less suitable for establishment.
In ancient times, Xiàng was enfeoffed in Yǒubí,
but not entrusted with governance.
This was truly due to profound love,
unwilling to expose his faults and wickedness.
That which is not forgotten from past events
serves as a teacher for future events.
Since the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
no imperial kinsmen have held positions among the high ministers.
May Your Majesty consider the compassionate care of Emperor Yú for his younger half-brother,
and uphold the old institutions,
ultimately maintaining generous kindness.
I beg to return my seal and sash as General of Agile Cavalry,
and retire to my feudal state.
I hope to receive your compassionate consideration.”
The Emperor issued a gracious edict, not consenting.
After that, he repeatedly petitioned to resign,
his words very sincere and urgent.
In the fifth year,
he was finally permitted to return to his state,
but not to relinquish his seal and sash as general.
The Commander of Agile Cavalry was made Grand Tutor of Dōngpíng,
his clerk was made a Palace Gentleman,
and his records clerk was made a Royal Household Gentleman.
An additional fifty million cash and
one hundred thousand bolts of cloth were bestowed upon him.
In the winter of the sixth year,
the Emperor visited Lǔ
and summoned Cāng to return with him to the capital.
The following year,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
After the burial,
Cāng then returned to his state,
and was specially granted five hundred palace women and slaves,
two hundred fifty thousand bolts of cloth,
and precious jewels, attire, and implements.
In the eleventh year,
Cāng and other kings paid their respects at the capital.
After more than a month,
he returned to his state.
The Emperor personally saw him off to his palace,
feeling sorrowful and nostalgic.
He then sent an envoy with a handwritten edict to the Grand Tutor of his state, saying:
“After our farewell,
I sat alone, unhappy.
I then got into my carriage to return,
leaning on the armrest and sighing.
Looking into the distance, I feel eternally moved,
which truly burdens my heart.
Reciting ‘Cǎishú,’
my sighs only increase.
A few days ago, I asked the King of Dōngpíng what he found most joyful in his home life.
The King said that doing good was the greatest joy.
His words are very profound
and truly accord with the essence of things.
Now I send nineteen seals for various marquises.
All the King’s sons aged five years and above who can walk and bow
should be allowed to wear them.”
In the spring of the fifteenth year,
the Emperor made an imperial tour to Dōngpíng,
bestowing upon Cāng fifteen million cash
and forty thousand bolts of cloth.
The Emperor showed Cāng the “Basic Annals of Guāngwǔ” he had compiled,
whereupon Cāng presented a “Praise for Guāngwǔ’s Reception of Heaven’s Mandate and Restoration.”
The Emperor was very pleased with it,
and because of its elegant and classical style,
he specially ordered the校書郎 Jiǎ Kuí to provide commentary and exegesis for it.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
he honored Cāng with even greater respect and courtesy than in previous reigns;
no other kings could compare.
In the first year of Jiànchū,
there was an earthquake,
and Cāng submitted proposals for timely reforms.
His matters were kept within the palace.
The Emperor replied with a letter, saying:
“On Bǐngyín, the three proposals for timely reforms you submitted,
I personally read them,
repeatedly several times.
My mind was opened and my eyes enlightened,
and I was suddenly awakened from my bewilderment.
Recently, officials submitting reports
also mentioned similar ideas,
but their wisdom was shallow and limited,
sometimes considering them possibly correct,
but then worrying they might be wrong.
Why?
Calamities and anomalies descend
in response to governance.
Now, after the change of era name,
years of famine and wandering people—
these are caused by my own lack of virtue and its resonance.
Moreover, the severe drought in winter and spring
affected an especially wide area.
Although I internally blamed myself,
I did not know what to decide.
Upon receiving your profound strategies,
my mind was quickly relieved.
Does not the ‘Shī’ say: ‘
my heart was filled with anxiety;
Now that I have seen the gentleman,
my heart is at peace.”’
I will contemplate your excellent advice
and implement it sequentially,
hoping to receive blessed responses.
To manifest gratitude for your supreme virtue,
I specially bestow upon you five million cash.”
Later, the Emperor wished to establish towns and cities for Yuánlíng and Xiǎnjiélíng.
Cāng heard of this
and immediately submitted a memorial in remonstrance, saying:
“I humbly hear that towns and cities are to be established for the two imperial tombs.
Your servant previously considered this merely rumor,
doubting its veracity.
Recently, I ordered my attendant Gǔ Bà to inquire about the illness of the Princess of Nièyáng,
and upon his return,
I learned that an imperial edict had already been issued.
I secretly observe that Emperor Guāngwǔ personally practiced frugality,
deeply understood the distinction between beginning and end,
and diligently and earnestly
spoke about burial regulations.
Therefore, when constructing the tomb site,
he fully followed the classical traditions,
issuing an edict saying, ‘Do not construct a mountain tomb,
let the ponds merely have flowing water.’
Emperor Xiàomíng, with great filial piety, did not deviate,
but respectfully continued the practice.
As for his own constructions,
they were especially frugal and simple.
The beauty of his humble virtue
was at its peak then.
Your foolish servant believes that the rise of tomb garden-cities
began with the powerful Qín dynasty.
In ancient times, people did not even wish for their burial mounds to be conspicuous;
how much less to build surrounding cities
and establish walled capitals!
This would violate the sacred intentions of the former emperors above,
and create useless works below,
needlessly expending state resources
and disturbing the populace.
This is not the way to achieve harmony
or pray for abundant years.
Moreover, speaking from the perspective of auspicious and inauspicious popular beliefs,
it is also not desirable to needlessly repair or construct burial mounds
or undertake new projects.
Examining ancient laws, it does not conform;
considering current circumstances, it displeases the people;
seeking auspiciousness, no blessings are yet seen.
Your Majesty possesses the supreme nature of Yǒuyú,
and deeply contemplates your ancestors.
However, I fear that the excessive proposals of those around you
might burden your sacred heart.
Your servant Cāng truly laments that the pure virtues of the two emperors
will not be fully expressed for endless generations.
I only ask for your compassionate consideration.”
The Emperor followed his advice and stopped.
From then on, whenever there was a doubtful policy in court,
an imperial envoy would be sent to consult him.
Cāng responded with his whole heart,
and all his suggestions were accepted and put into practice.
In the third year,
the Emperor hosted a feast for the imperial guards in the Nán-Gōng.
He then accompanied the Empress Dowager to tour the Yè-Tíng's ponds and pavilions,
and reviewed the late Empress Yīn's old clothes and artifacts.
He was deeply moved with sorrow,
and ordered that one set of each of her five seasonal garments be kept,
along with fifty chests of her regularly used clothes.
The rest were distributed among the various kings, princesses, and their descendants residing in the capital, each receiving a different amount.
He specifically wrote to Cāng and Liáng-Yé Wáng Jīng, saying:
"The zhōng-dà-fū, acting as envoy,
personally heard of your activities.
How can I ever praise this enough!
Years and months rush by,
the mausoleum becomes increasingly distant.
My lonely heart is filled with sorrow.
How can this be endured!
Recently, I feasted the imperial guards in the Nán-Gōng
and then reviewed her old clothes and belongings.
I heard from my teacher: 'When the objects remain,
but the person is gone,
sadness arrives without words.'
This is truly so.
With your filial and fraternal virtues,
how could it be otherwise?
Now I send one false hair bun and one silk headscarf of Empress Guāng-Liè,
and one chest of her clothes.
You may look upon them from time to time
to comfort your longing, like the 'Kǎi-Fēng' and 'Hán-Quán' poems.
I also wish to let future generations of descendants see the style of the former empress's clothes.
Now, the Kǒng clan in Lǔ-Guó
still possesses the chariot, cap, and shoes of Zhòng-Ní.
The more illustrious one's virtue, the farther one's spiritual radiance extends.
As for Emperor Guāng-Wǔ's artifacts and clothing,
they were already distributed to various states in Zhōng-Yuán second year,
so they are not being sent again.
Additionally, I am sending a horse from Wǎn,
whose blood emerges from a small hole above its front shoulder.
I often heard Emperor Wǔ sing of the 'heavenly horse'
sweating red.
Now I personally see it is so.
Recently, the rebellious captives are still stationed,
and generals are outside the capital.
My worries are restless and anxious.
I have not found peace and leisure.
I wish that you, O King, will cherish your spirit
and increase your offerings.
I long for your honest words and earnest admonitions
as if parched with thirst."
In the winter of the sixth year,
Cāng submitted a memorial requesting an audience.
In the first month of the following year,
the Emperor granted his request.
He specially bestowed fifteen million cash for travel expenses,
while other kings received ten million each.
Considering Cāng would traverse through cold and dew,
the Emperor dispatched an yè-zhě to bestow a sable coat,
and provisions of rare fruits and delicacies from the tài-guān.
He also had the Dà-Hóng-Lú Dòu Gù hold a staff and welcome him at the suburban outskirts.
The Emperor personally toured the residence,
pre-arranging curtains and beds.
There was nothing lacking in money, silk, or artifacts.
An imperial edict was issued saying:
"[The Lǐ-Yún states that] a paternal uncle returning to pay respects is like returning to one's own state;
the Shī-Yún states that a paternal uncle establishes your eldest son.
This shows the utmost respect.
In the past, Chancellor Xiāo was not even called by his name,
to honor his loyalty and sagacity.
How much more so for one who combines both kinship and high尊 (honor)?
Therefore, the four kings of Pèi, Jì-Nán, Dōng-Píng, and Zhōng-Shān,
let all their names not be used."
When Cāng arrived,
he ascended the hall and bowed,
and the Son of Heaven personally returned the salute.
Thereafter, when other kings entered the palace,
they were always welcomed by carriage,
and only disembarked upon reaching the inner palace chambers.
Cāng felt that he received excessive favor beyond protocol,
and his heart was not at ease.
He submitted a memorial declining, saying:
"I have heard that the noble have their constant dignity,
and the humble have their graded status;
the high and low are arranged in order,
and superiors and inferiors proceed according to reason.
Your Majesty's utmost virtue is widely extended,
and you lovingly care for your kin.
You have already granted the honor of attending court,
placing me a cubit away from the imperial presence.
Yet you personally humble your most noble self,
descending in protocol to your subject.
Each time you grant an audience,
you rise from your seat and change your demeanor;
the Empress personally bows.
These acts exceed conventional ceremonies.
Your subject is fearful and trembling,
truly ill at ease.
Every time we meet,
I am timid and do not know how to act.
This is not how to display to your subordinates
and reassure your subjects."
The Emperor read the memorial and sighed,
praising and valuing him even more.
According to old rites,
all daughters of kings were enfeoffed as xiāng-zhǔ.
But for Cāng alone, his five daughters were enfeoffed as xiàn-gōng-zhǔ.
In the third month,
the Dà-Hóng-Lú presented a memorial requesting that the kings be sent back to their states.
The Emperor specially detained Cāng,
bestowing upon him secret writings, paintings of immortals, and secret Daoist methods.
Until the eighth month, after the drinking of zhòu was complete,
the officials again memorialized to send Cāng off,
and only then did the Emperor permit it.
He personally wrote an edict to Cāng, saying:
"Kinship is Heaven-given nature,
and truly, proximity or distance does not determine closeness or alienation.
However, seeing one's face often
deepens affection for former times.
Considering your long toil, O King,
and your desire to return and rest,
I wanted to endorse the Dà-Hóng-Lú's memorial,
but I could not bear to put pen to paper.
Then I entrusted it to the xiǎo-huáng-mén;
my heart was lingering and reluctant,
and I was too sorrowful to speak."
Thereupon, the imperial carriage escorted him,
and they parted with tears.
He was again bestowed with imperial carriages and attendants,
precious chariots and horses,
and money and cloth amounting to hundreds of millions.
When Cāng returned to his state,
he fell ill.
The Emperor swiftly dispatched famous physicians
and xiǎo-huáng-mén to attend to his illness.
Envoys with their caps and canopies were ceaseless on the road.
He also set up post-horses for a thousand lǐ
to relay inquiries about his well-being.
He passed away in the first month of the following year.
An edict commanded the zhōng-fù
to seal and compile Cāng's memorials, writings, records, rhapsodies, eulogies, seven-character poems, unusual characters, and songs from the Jiàn-Wǔ era onwards,
and collect and review them all.
He dispatched the Dà-Hóng-Lú holding a staff,
the Wǔ-Guān-Zhōng-Láng-Jiàng as his deputy to supervise the funeral,
and six officials from the Jiāng-Zuò-Shǐ.
He ordered the xiǎo-hóu of the Four Surnames and the various kings and princesses to all gather at Dōng-Píng to attend the mourning.
He bestowed a total of one hundred million cash and
ninety thousand bolts of cloth.
At the burial,
the eulogy read:
"On the jǐ-mǎo day of the third month of the eighth year of Jiàn-Chū,
the Emperor says: Ah, O King, so illustrious,
who diligently served the royal house,
personally received the mandate,
and was renowned in former generations.
You went forth to act as a regional protector,
carefully cultivating bright virtue,
observing rituals without transgression,
your reputation reaching below.
Alas, Hao-Tiān is unmerciful,
not repaying supreme benevolence.
It has cast aside Me, the lonely one,
who, morning and night, am solitary,
without a fitting end.
Now, I command the officials to bestow a luán-lù carriage with horses,
a dragon banner with nine streamers,
and a hundred tiger warriors
to escort the King on his journey.
If not for our model King,
who else could separate from this?
If your soul has spiritual power,
may it preserve this honor and glory.
Alas, how sorrowful!"
He reigned for forty-five years.
His son, Huái-Wáng Zhōng, succeeded him.
The following year,
the Emperor divided the state of Dōng-Píng to enfeoff Zhōng's younger brother Shàng as Rèn-Chéng-Wáng,
and the other five sons as liè-hóu.
Zhōnglì (Shí) hōng in his first year,
and his son, Xiào Wáng Chǎng, succeeded him.
In Yuánhé (元和) 3rd year,
the emperor made an eastern inspection tour,
visiting Dōngpíng (東平) Palace.
The emperor, recalling Cāng (蒼) with emotion,
said to his sons:
"I think of the man
when I arrive at his hometown;
his place is still there,
but the man is gone."
Thereupon, tears streamed down, wetting his lapels.
He then visited Cāng's (蒼) mausoleum,
where he arranged húbì (虎賁) guards, luánlù (鸞輅) carriages, and lóngqí (龍旂) banners
to display his honor.
He offered a tàiláo (太牢) sacrifice,
personally bowed at the sacrificial altar,
cried to the fullest extent of his grief,
and bestowed an imperial sword before the tomb.
Previously,
when Cāng (蒼) returned to his kingdom,
Dīng Mù (丁牧) and Zhōu Xǔ (周栩), officials under the驃騎 (piàojì) general at the time, seeing Cāng's (蒼) respect for worthy men and his humility towards scholars,
could not bear to leave him.
So, they became dàfū (大夫) in the royal household,
serving the grandfather and grandson for several decades.
When the emperor heard of this,
he summoned them both for an audience.
Feeling pity for their prolonged stagnation,
and also wishing to praise Cāng's (蒼) virtues,
he immediately promoted them both to yìláng (議郎).
Mù (牧) rose to Qí Xiàng (齊相),
and Xǔ (栩) became Shàngcài Lìng (上蔡令).
In Yǒngyuán (永元) 10th year,
Cāng's (蒼) grandson Liáng (梁) was enfeoffed as Jīnyáng Tínghóu (矜陽亭侯),
and Chǎng's (敞) six younger brothers were made lièhóu (列侯).
Chǎng (敞) was extremely filial during his mother's mourning.
Guó Xiàng (國相) Chén Zhēn (陳珍) submitted a report on his conduct.
In Yǒngníng (永寧) 1st year,
Empress Dowager Dèng (鄧) increased his household stipend by five thousand families,
and also enfeoffed two more of Cāng's (蒼) grandsons as tínghóu (亭侯).
Chǎng (敞) died after reigning for forty-eight years,
and his son, Qǐng Wáng Duān (頃王端), succeeded him.
Duān (端) died after reigning for forty-seven years,
and his son Kǎi (凱) succeeded him.
After forty-one years of his reign,
Wèi (魏) received the abdication,
and he was made Chóngdé Hóu (崇德侯).
The commentary states: Confucius said,
"To be poor and yet without flattery,
to be rich and yet without arrogance,
is not as good as being poor and yet joyful,
or rich and yet loving ritual."
As for Dōngpíng Xiàn Wáng (東平憲王),
he can be called one who loved ritual.
As for his departure from close relatives,
and leaving his mother and empress dowager,
how could he have wished to merely establish a reputation for conduct while forgetting kinship and abandoning righteousness?
Perhaps, if one's position is doubtful, a rift arises;
if troubles accumulate close by, the loss is great.
This is what the wise lament.
Alas!
To distance oneself to preserve loyalty,
to release burdens to achieve filial piety,
how could that have been the intention of Xiàn Wáng (憲王)?
Dōnghǎi Gōng Wáng (東海恭王) was humble and knew when to desist;
"To be Wú Tàibó (吳太伯),
is that not acceptable?"
Rènchéng Xiào Wáng Shàng (任城孝王尚)
was enfeoffed in Yuánhé (元和) 1st year,
receiving the three counties of Rènchéng (任城), Kàngfù (亢父), and Fán (樊).
He died after eighteen years of reign, and his son, Zhēn Wáng Ān (貞王安), succeeded him.
In Yǒngyuán (永元) 14th year,
his mother's brother Fú (福) was enfeoffed as Táoxiāng Hóu (桃鄉侯).
In Yǒngchū (永初) 4th year,
Fú's (福) younger brother Kàng (亢) was enfeoffed as Dāngtú Xiānghóu (當塗鄉侯).
Ān (安) was frivolous, greedy, and miserly by nature,
frequently going out in plain clothes
to observe the kingdom.
He took official carriages, horses, swords,
down to the rice and meat of the guards,
all without payment.
In Yuánchū (元初) 6th year,
Guó Xiàng (國相) Xíng Hóng (行弘) submitted a memorial requesting his deposition.
Emperor Ān (安) could not bear to do so,
and redeemed his crime with one-fifth of his annual rent.
Ān (安) died after nineteen years of reign,
and his son, Jié Wáng Chóng (節王崇), succeeded him.
During Emperor Shùn's (順) reign,
the Qiāng (羌) barbarians frequently rebelled,
and Chóng (崇) consistently submitted money and silk to assist with border expenses.
When the emperor died,
he again submitted three million coins to assist with the mausoleum expenses,
which the imperial court praised but did not accept.
He died after thirty-one years of reign,
having no son,
and the kingdom was extinguished.
In Yánxī (延熹) 4th year,
Emperor Huán (桓) established Bó (博), the son of Héxián Xiào Wáng (河閒孝王) (Gōng [恭] as) Cānhù Tínghóu (參戶亭侯), as Rènchéng Wáng (任城王),
to continue the sacrifices to him.
Bó (博) was filial; during his mother's mourning, he observed the rites properly,
and his enfeoffment was increased by three thousand households.
He died after thirteen years of reign,
having no son,
and the kingdom was extinguished.
In Xīpíng (熹平) 4th year,
Emperor Líng (靈) again established Tuó (佗), the (son of) Xīnchāng Hóu (新昌侯) (son) [Jiàn (建)] of Héxián Zhēn Wáng (河閒貞王) (Xùn [遜]), as Rènchéng Wáng (任城王),
to continue the line of Xiào Wáng (孝王).
After forty-six years of his reign,
Wèi (魏) received the abdication,
and he was made Chóngdé Hóu (崇德侯).
Fùlíng Zhì Wáng Yán (阜陵質王延)
was enfeoffed as Huáiyáng Gōng (淮陽公) in Jiànwǔ (建武) 15th year.
In the 17th year, his peerage was advanced to king,
and in the 28th year, he proceeded to his kingdom.
In the 30th year,
four counties from Rǔnán (汝南) – Chángpíng (長平), Xīhuá (西華), Xīnyáng (新陽), and Fúlè (扶樂) – were added to the kingdom of Huáiyáng (淮陽).
Yán (延) was arrogant and extravagant by nature, and severe and fierce towards his subordinates.
During the Yǒngpíng (永平) period,
someone submitted a memorial accusing Yán (延) and his consort's brother Xiè Yǎn (謝弇) and his elder sister Gǔantáo Zhǔ (館陶主)'s husband Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉) Hán Guāng (韓光) of recruiting villains,
creating diagrams and prophecies,
and performing sacrifices and curses.
The matter was investigated.
Guāng (光) and Yǎn (弇) were killed,
and many of those implicated
died or were exiled.
The officials memorialized requesting Yán's (延) execution.
Xiǎnzōng (顯宗), considering Yán's (延) crime less severe than that of Chǔ Wáng Yīng (楚王英),
specially granted him clemency,
transferring him to be Fùlíng Wáng (阜陵王),
receiving two counties.
After Yán (延) was transferred,
he frequently harbored resentment.
During the Jiànchū (建初) period,
there was another accusation that Yán (延) and his son Fáng (魴) were plotting rebellion.
The officials memorialized requesting he be summoned in a caged cart to the imperial prison of the Tíngwèi (廷尉).
Sùzōng (肅宗) issued an edict saying:
"The king previously committed great treason,
his crimes are particularly heinous,
akin to Guǎn (管) and Cài (蔡) of Zhōu (周),
and Huáinán (淮南) of Hàn (漢).
The Classics have righteous principles,
and the laws have clear punishments.
The late emperor, unable to bear the affection for relatives,
twisted the great law,
and bore the king's transgression,
leaving all his subordinates bewildered.
Now the king has shown no repentance,
his rebellious heart unchanged,
his treacherous plot collapsing from within,
revealed by his own son Fáng (魴).
This is truly not what the imperial court desires to hear.
I am heartbroken with sadness,
and cannot bear to subject the king to the law.
Now I demote his peerage to Fùlíng Hóu (阜陵侯),
receiving one county.
Those who suffer this fate
bring it upon themselves.
Alas, a warning!"
He pardoned Fáng (魴) and others from investigation of their crimes,
and assigned one Yèzhě (謁者) to supervise Yán's (延) kingdom,
forbidding communication with officials and commoners.
In Zhānghé (章和) 1st year,
he toured Jiǔjiāng (九江),
and sent a letter to Yán (延), requesting him to meet the imperial carriage at Shòuchūn (壽春).
The emperor saw Yán (延) and his wife and children,
and felt pity and sadness for them.
He then issued an edict saying:
"In ancient Zhōu (周), there were eighteen hundred enfeoffments,
and the Jī (姬) surname occupied half,
thereby stabilizing the royal house.
I traveled south,
looking out over the Huái (淮) and the sea,
my thoughts on Fùlíng (阜陵),
and thus met the marquis.
The marquis's spirit is withered,
his physique not as it was.
Observing him fills me with emotion, both joy and sorrow.
Now I restore his peerage as Fùlíng Wáng (阜陵王),
increasing his enfeoffment by four counties,
making a total of five counties with the previous one."
As Fùlíng (阜陵) was low and damp,
he relocated his capital to Shòuchūn (壽春).
He was further granted ten million coins,
ten thousand bolts of cloth,
one ānchē (安車) carriage,
and his consort and various sons each received different rewards.
The following year, he entered the court.
He died after fifty-one years of reign,
and his son, Shāng Wáng Chōng (殤王沖), succeeded him.
In Yǒngyuán (永元) 2nd year,
an edict was issued to completely delete all previous memorials regarding Yán (延).
Chōng died in the second year of his reign,
without an heir.
Emperor Hédi then re-enfeoffed Chōng's elder brother, Fáng,
who became King Qǐng.
In the eighth year of Yǒngyuán,
Fáng's twelve younger brothers were enfeoffed as marquises of xiāng and tíng.
Fáng died after reigning for thirty years.
His son, King Huái, Huī, succeeded him.
In the third year of Yán'guāng,
Huī's five brothers were enfeoffed as marquises of xiāng and tíng.
Huī died after reigning for ten years.
His son, King Jié, Dài, succeeded him.
In the second year of Yángjiā,
Dài's elder brother, Biànqīn, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Bótíng.
Dài died after reigning for fourteen years,
without a son,
and the state was abolished.
In the first year of Jiànhé,
Emperor Huán established Biànqīn, Marquis of Bótíng, as Huī's successor,
and he became King Gōng.
He died after reigning for thirteen years.
His son, King Xiào, Tǒng, succeeded him.
He died after reigning for eight years.
His son, Shè, was established as king.
He died during the Jiàn'ān period,
without a son,
and the state was abolished.
Jīng, King Sī of Guǎnglíng,
was enfeoffed as Duke of Shānyáng in the fifteenth year of Jiànwǔ,
and his title was advanced to King in the seventeenth year.
Jīng was by nature harsh, impulsive, and prone to harming others,
possessing talent but fond of legalistic methods.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ passed away,
and the grand funeral cortege was in the front hall,
Jīng wept without sorrow,
but instead composed a secret letter,
sealed it with a square bottom,
and had a servant in dark clothes falsely claim it was a letter from Guō Kuàng, the Grand Minister of the Court and maternal uncle of Qiáng, King of Dōnghǎi, to Qiáng, saying:
"Your Highness has committed no offense,
yet you have been unjustly dismissed and degraded,
and some of your brothers have even been bound and imprisoned.
The Empress Dowager lost her position
and resided separately in the Northern Palace;
then, in her old age,
she was banished to the distant frontier.
The whole realm grieves deeply for this,
and those who witness it are moved to tears.
When the Empress Dowager's coffin was in the hall,
the officials of Luòyáng sequentially arrested and executed guests,
even to the point where three corpses lay in one family's hall.
How painful this is!
Now, with the realm in mourning,
bows and crossbows are set up with great readiness.
Recently, Liáng Sōng instructed the Tiger Lieutenant historian, saying: 'If an official acts opportunistically and is criticized,
do not be constrained by anything;
it is hard to obtain a marquessate again.'
The palace attendants secretly lament this,
sighing with a chill in their hearts for Your Highness.
Now, everyone in the realm is vying to carve out and harm Your Highness to achieve merit.
Is there any limit to this?
If you combine the forces of the two states,
you can gather a million men.
With Your Highness as their leader,
advancing with drums beating, irresistible,
success would be easier than breaking an egg on Mount Tài,
lighter than four horses carrying a wild goose feather.
This is the army of Tāng and Wǔ!
This year, the Xuānyuán star has a white aura.
Astrologers and those who delight in such matters
all say that a white aura signifies mourning,
and Xuānyuán represents the position of the empress.
Moreover, Tàibái has appeared early in the west;
by the Wǔ hour, troops will surely rise.
Furthermore, the Crown Prince star is black in color;
by the Chén day, it will inevitably turn red.
Indeed, black signifies illness,
and red signifies warfare.
Your Highness, strive diligently to complete this task!
Emperor Gāozǔ rose from a village head,
and His Majesty arose from Báishuǐ.
How much more so Your Highness, His Majesty's eldest son,
and former co-ruler!
On the one hand, to seek the success of affairs under heaven,
on the other, to wash away the shame of being disgraced and to avenge your deceased mother.
Sincerity, when applied,
can open even metal and stone.
[一０] You should be autumn frost,
not a caged lamb.
[一一] Even if you wished to be a caged lamb,
could you still achieve it?
[一二] I have secretly heard many physiognomists say Your Highness is noble,
destined for the imperial position.
When a ruler dies,
even common folk become bandits
hoping for something;
how much more so Your Highness!
However, a sovereign who has received the Mandate
is established by Heaven
and cannot be conspired against.
The new emperor, however,
was placed by man;
the strong takes precedence.
I wish Your Highness would follow the aspirations of Emperor Gāozǔ and His Majesty,
[一二] and not be like Fúsū and Jiānglǘ, crying out to Heaven."
[一三] Qiáng was terrified upon receiving the letter,
immediately seized its messenger,
sealed the letter, and sent it to the emperor.
Emperor Xiǎnzōng, considering Jīng to be his maternal younger brother,
kept the matter secret,
and sent Jīng to reside in the Hénán Palace.
At that time, the Western Qiāng revolted.
Jīng, dissatisfied with his situation,
hoped that the realm would be alarmed and change due to the Qiāng.
He secretly summoned an astrologer to consult with him.
When the emperor heard of this,
he transferred Jīng's enfeoffment to King of Guǎnglíng
and sent him to his state.
Later, Jīng again summoned a physiognomist and said:
"My appearance resembles that of the late emperor.
The late emperor gained the realm at thirty;
I am also thirty now.
Can I raise troops?"
The physiognomist went to the authorities and reported him.
Jīng was terrified
and imprisoned himself.
The emperor again extended grace,
did not fully investigate the matter,
and issued an edict that he should not be subject to officials or common people,
only receiving rent as before,
and ordered the chancellor and commandant to guard him diligently.
Jīng still did not change.
Afterwards, he employed a shaman to perform sacrifices and utter curses.
The relevant officials impeached him,
requesting his execution.
Jīng committed suicide.
He died after reigning for twenty-nine years.
The emperor felt pity and sorrow for him,
granting him the posthumous title of King Sī.
Fourteen years later,
Jīng's son, Yuánshòu, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guǎnglíng,
wore the king's seal and ribbons,
and received revenue from Jīng's former state's six counties.
Three of Yuánshòu's younger brothers were also enfeoffed as xiāng marquises.
The following year,
the emperor made an eastern tour of inspection
and summoned Yuánshòu and his brothers to assemble at Dōngpíng Palace,
where he bestowed upon them imperial clothing and artifacts.
He also took the imperial princes' carriages and horses
and gave them all to them.
In the seventh year of Jiànchū,
Emperor Sùzōng issued an edict for Yuánshòu and his brothers to join the other kings in court at the capital.
Yuánshòu died.
His son, Shāng, succeeded him.
Shāng died.
His son, Tiáo, succeeded him,
and the state was passed down through later generations.
Héng, Duke Huái of Línhuái,
was established in the fifteenth year of Jiànwǔ.
He died before his title could be advanced to king,
without a son,
and the state was abolished.
Yān, King Jiǎn of Zhōngshān,
was enfeoffed as Duke of Zuǒyì in the fifteenth year of Jiànwǔ,
and his title was advanced to King in the seventeenth year.
Yān, being the youngest son of Empress Dowager Guō,
alone remained in the capital.
In the thirtieth year,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as King of Zhōngshān.
In the winter of the second year of Yǒngpíng,
the kings came to assemble at Bìyōng.
After the affairs were concluded and they returned to their fiefs,
an edict ordered Yān to proceed to his state along with them,
accompanied by Tiger Lieutenant cavalry.
Yān submitted a memorial declining this,
to which Emperor Xiǎnzōng replied:
"Whenever feudal lords leave the capital,
they must be fully prepared with attendants.
Therefore, at the meeting of Jiágǔ,
the Sīmǎ accompanied them.
Now, each of the five states will have one hundred official cavalry,
advancing in order before you.
They are all northern Hu cavalry,
skilled in weaponry and archery.
Their bows do not fire in vain;
their arrows always hit the mark.
Indeed, where there is civil administration, there must be military preparation;
this is to emphasize the importance of the feudal office.
Let Your Highness not decline."
The emperor, due to Empress Dowager Guō's partiality towards Yān,
especially bestowed favor and grace upon him,
allowing him alone to travel to and from the capital.
In the fifteenth year,
Yān's concubine, Hán Xù, committed an offense.
Yān strangled her to death.
The chancellor of the state impeached him,
and he was penalized by having Ānxiǎn county cut off from his fief.
During the Yuánhé period,
Emperor Sùzōng again returned Ānxiǎn to Zhōngshān.
He reigned for fifty-two years.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán, he died.
From the Restoration until the time of Hèdì,
when imperial princes were first enfeoffed and then died,
they were all bestowed with thirty million *qián*
and thirty thousand bolts of cloth.
When a reigning prince died,
they were bestowed with ten million *qián* and ten thousand bolts of cloth.
At this time, Empress Dowager Dòu was regent,
and Dòu Xiàn and his brothers wielded great power.
The Empress Dowager and Xiàn, etc.,
were from Dōnghǎi,
and thus were friendly with Yān and placed great importance on the rites,
adding a grant of one hundred million *qián*.
An imperial edict ordered the princes of Jìnán and Dōnghǎi to both attend.
A great construction project was undertaken to repair his tomb,
opening a spirit path.
Thousands of tombs of officials and commoners were flattened,
with over ten thousand workers involved.
They requisitioned cypress, *huángcháng* timber, and various other woods from Chángshān, Jùlù, and Zhuō Jùn.
As these three commanderies could not supply enough,
they again conscripted thousands of laborers and transporters from other prefectures and commanderies.
In total, the levies and requisitions affected six provinces and eighteen commanderies.
The scale of this system was unmatched by any other state.
His son, Prince Yí Xiàn, succeeded him.
In the fourth year of Yǒngyuán,
Xiàn's eleven younger brothers were enfeoffed as marquises.
Xiàn reigned for twenty-two years and died.
His son, Prince Xiào Hóng, succeeded him.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
Hóng's two younger brothers were enfeoffed as marquises of a pavilion.
Hóng reigned for twenty-eight years and died.
His son, Prince Mù Chàng, succeeded him.
In the sixth year of Yǒnghé,
Chàng's younger brother Jīng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Nánxiāng.
Chàng reigned for thirty-four years and died.
His son, Prince Jié Zhì, succeeded him.
He had no son,
and the state was abolished.
Jīng, Prince Xiào of Lángxié,
was enfeoffed as Duke of Lángxié in the fifteenth year of Jiànwǔ.
In the seventeenth year, his noble rank was promoted to king.
Jīng was by nature respectful and filial,
and fond of classical studies.
Xiǎnzōng particularly loved and favored him,
bestowing gifts and grace upon him in an extraordinary way,
beyond comparison with others.
In the second year of Yǒngpíng,
Gài, Nánwǔyáng, and Huá from Tàishān,
along with Chāngyáng, Lúxiāng, and Dōngmóu from Dōnglái — six counties in total — were added to Lángxié.
In the fifth year,
he proceeded to his state.
When Empress Guāngliè died,
the Emperor gave all of the Empress Dowager's bequeathed gold, treasures, and valuables to Jīng.
Jīng's capital was Jǔ.
He delighted in building palaces and residences,
exhausting all his skill and artistry.
The walls and architectural belts of his halls and pavilions were all decorated with gold and silver.
He frequently submitted poems, rhapsodies, and eulogies praising the Emperor's virtue.
The Emperor praised their beauty
and sent them to the imperial historians.
Within Jīng's state, there was a temple to Prince Jǐng of Chéngyáng,
which officials and commoners worshipped.
The deity repeatedly delivered messages,
stating that there were many inconveniences within the palace.
Jīng submitted a memorial requesting to move his palace to Kāiyáng,
exchanging Huá, Gài, Nánwǔyáng, Hòuqīu, and Gànyú, five counties,
for Kāiyáng and Línyí of Dōnghǎi.
Sùzōng granted his request.
He reigned for thirty-one years and died.
He was buried at Jíqīu Guǎngpíngtíng in Dōnghǎi.
An imperial edict ordered that the pavilion be detached and appended to Kāiyáng.
His son, Prince Yí Yǔ, succeeded him.
In the seventh year of Jiànchū,
Yǔ's thirteen younger brothers were enfeoffed as marquises.
In the first year of Yuánhé,
two grandsons of Prince Xiào were enfeoffed as marquises.
Yǔ reigned for twenty years and died.
His son, Prince Gōng Shòu, succeeded him.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
Shòu's eight younger brothers were enfeoffed as marquises.
He reigned for seventeen years and died.
His son, Prince Zhēn Zūn, succeeded him.
In the second year of Yánguāng,
Zūn's four younger brothers were enfeoffed as marquises of a township.
Zūn reigned for eighteen years and died.
His son, Prince Ān Jù, succeeded him.
In the fifth year of Yǒnghé,
Jù's three younger brothers were enfeoffed as marquises of a township.
Jù reigned for forty-seven years and died.
His son, Prince Shùn Róng, succeeded him.
In the first year of Chūpíng,
he sent his younger brother Miǎo to Cháng'ān to present a memorial and tribute.
The Emperor appointed Miǎo as Grand Administrator of Jǐujiāng
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Yángdū.
Róng reigned for eight years and died.
The state was abolished.
Initially,
when Miǎo arrived in Cháng'ān,
he highly praised Cáo Cāo, the Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn, for his loyalty to the Emperor.
Cāo owed this favor to Miǎo.
In the eleventh year of Jiàn'ān,
Róng's son, Xī, was re-established as king.
He was in office for eleven years,
and was implicated in a plot to cross the river,
was executed,
and the state was abolished.
The encomium says: Guāngwǔ's ten sons,
their lands were granted, and they were divided as kings.
Xiàn of Pèi was revered for his integrity,
Yīng of Chǔ was exiled.
Yán already resented and cursed,
Jīng also harbored discontent.
Jìnán plotted secretly,
Lángxié was arrogant and dissolute.
Zhōngshān and Línhuái
died young without renown.
Dōngpíng loved goodness,
and resigned from his position as chancellor.
Prince Gōng was humble and courteous,
truly one who yielded three times.
Biographies of Zhū Huī and Lè Hán, Chapter 33 (Zhū Huī, Sūn Mù)
Zhū Huī, courtesy name Wénjì,
was a native of Wǎn in Nányáng.
His family had for generations been officials.
Huī was orphaned young,
and possessed ambition and decisiveness.
At thirteen,
Wáng Mǎng was defeated,
and the world was in chaos.
He and his maternal relatives fled from the countryside into Wǎnchéng.
On the way, they encountered a band of bandits
who, with drawn blades, robbed the women
and plundered their clothes and belongings.
His cousins and guests were all terrified,
prostrating themselves on the ground, not daring to move.
Huī drew his sword and stepped forward, saying:
"All possessions may be taken,
but my mothers' clothes cannot be taken.
Today is the day Zhū Huī dies!"
The bandits saw how young he was,
admired his spirit,
and laughed, saying:
"The young boy brandishes a knife."
They then left him and departed.
Originally,
Guāngwǔ and Huī's father, Cén, had studied together in Cháng'ān,
and had an old acquaintance.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne, he inquired about Cén,
who had by then already died.
So, he summoned Huī and appointed him as a *Láng*.
Huī soon left due to illness
and completed his studies at the Imperial Academy.
He was by nature dignified and strict;
his every action was in accordance with propriety,
and all scholars praised his noble character.
In the early years of Yǒngpíng,
Xiǎnzōng's maternal uncle, Yīn Jiù, the Marquis of Xīnyáng, admired Zhū Huī's virtue.
He personally went to call upon him,
but Huī avoided him and refused to meet.
Yīn Jiù then sent his household steward to convey his regards,
but Huī simply closed his gate and refused to receive him.
When Yīn Jiù heard this,
he sighed and said:
"He is a man of principle;
do not deprive him of his integrity."
Later, when Huī was a county official,
the Grand Administrator Ruǎn Kuàng once wanted to buy Huī's maid.
Huī refused to comply.
When Ruǎn Kuàng died,
Huī generously presented gifts to his family.
Some people criticized this,
but Huī said:
"Previously, Lord Ruǎn sought something from me,
which is why I dared not obey his command,
for I truly feared that I would contaminate the lord with wealth.
Now that I am sending gifts,
it demonstrates that I am not motivated by stinginess."
The General of Agile Cavalry, Prince Cāng of Dōngpíng, heard of this and invited him,
treating him with great respect.
On the morning of the first day of the first month,
Cāng was to attend court to offer felicitations.
According to custom,
the Lesser Minister would provide the jade disc.
At this time, Yīn Jiù was the Minister of the Prefecture,
and being noble and arrogant,
his subordinates did not follow the law.
Cāng was seated in the court hall,
and time was almost up,
but the jade disc could not be obtained.
He looked at his aides and said:
"What should we do?"
Huī saw the Chief Clerk of the Lesser Minister holding a jade disc,
and immediately went to deceive him, saying:
"I have often heard of the jade disc but never seen one;
please let me have a look."
The Chief Clerk handed it to Huī,
and Huī immediately called an archival clerk to present it.
The Chief Clerk was greatly alarmed,
and quickly reported it to Yīn Jiù.
Yīn Jiù said:
"Zhū, the aide, is a righteous gentleman;
do not ask for it back."
Another jade disc was then used for the court ceremony.
After Cāng had left,
he summoned Huī and said:
"Just now, do you consider yourself equal to Lìn Xiàngrú?"
The Emperor heard of this and greatly admired him.
When he was about to make an imperial tour to Cháng'ān,
wishing to strengthen the guards,
he appointed Huī as the Commandant of Palace Guards.
He was twice promoted to Grand Administrator of Línhuái.
Huī loved integrity and principle;
those he selected and promoted
were all men of strict conduct.
For those who sought to avenge grievances,
and whose actions violated regulations for the sake of righteousness,
he sought to find justice for them,
and many were saved.
As for prisoners whose actions were unrighteous,
they would immediately collapse and die.
Officials and common people both feared and loved him,
singing a song for him that went:
"Strong and upright, always achieving,
that is Zhū Jì of Nányáng.
Officials fear his authority,
and the people cherish his kindness."
After several years,
he was dismissed due to a legal infraction.
Huī was stern as an official,
and was feared by his superiors,
often being impeached wherever he served.
After leaving Línhuái,
he secluded himself in the countryside,
wearing plain clothes and eating simple food,
not associating with the local community.
His鄉黨 (xiāngdǎng, local community) criticized his aloofness.
In the Jiànchū period,
Nányáng suffered a great famine,
and rice cost over a thousand coins per shí (stone).
Huī dispersed all his family assets
to distribute among his impoverished and weak relatives and old acquaintances in the village,
and his clan and community all looked up to him.
Originally,
Zhāng Kān, a man from Huī's same county, was renowned for his reputation.
He once saw Huī at the Imperial Academy
and highly esteemed him,
treating him as a friend.
He then grasped Huī's arm and said:
"I wish to entrust my wife and children to you, Master Zhū."
Huī, considering Kān an elder and a prominent figure,
raised his hand but dared not respond.
Thereafter, they never met again.
When Kān died,
Huī heard that his wife and children were impoverished,
and so he personally went to visit them
and generously provided relief.
Huī's youngest son, Xié, was puzzled and asked:
"Father did not become friends with Kān, and they never interacted in their lives;
your sons are secretly puzzled by this."
Huī said:
"Kān once spoke words of a true friend;
I believed in them in my heart."
Huī also had a good friendship with Chén Yī from the same commandery.
Yī died early,
leaving behind a posthumous son named Yǒu.
Huī always pitied him.
When Sītú Huán Yú became the Grand Administrator of Nányáng,
he summoned Huī's son, Pián, to be an official.
Huī declined on behalf of Pián and recommended Yǒu.
Huán Yú sighed
and subsequently summoned Yǒu.
His righteousness and integrity were like this.
In the Yuánhé period,
Sùzōng made an imperial tour.
He instructed the Grand Administrator of Nányáng to inquire about Huī's well-being,
and summoned him to be appointed Shàngshū Púyè.
Within the year, he was promoted to Grand Administrator of Tàishān.
Huī submitted a memorial requesting to remain in the central government,
and the emperor granted his request.
He then submitted proposals for opportune policies,
presenting confidential matters,
which were deeply appreciated and accepted.
The imperial edict in reply said:
"To make up for deficiencies in the public service,
without staining one's pure and upright character,
this is indeed an excellent and virtuous gentleman.
Vulgar officials merely conform,
agreeing with intentions and complying superficially;
when advancing, they have no courageous will to speak frankly,
and when retreating, they have no thought of reflection.
This problem has existed for a very long time.
What you have said now
is precisely what I desired.
You must strive hard!"
At that time, grain was expensive.
The expenditure of the *xiàn guān* was insufficient,
and the court was worried about it.
The *Shàngshū* Zhāng Lín submitted a memorial, saying:
“The reason grain is expensive
is because money is cheap.
All money should be sealed,
and only cloth and silk should be collected as rent,
to facilitate transactions throughout the realm.
Furthermore, salt
is essential for eating.
Although expensive,
people cannot do without it.
The government should manage it itself.
It is also advisable to take advantage of the coming and going of *shàngjì lì* from Jiāozhǐ and Yìzhōu
to purchase rare treasures
and collect their profits.
This is what was called *jūnshū* during the reign of Emperor Wǔ.”
Thereupon, an imperial edict instructed all *shàngshū* to deliberate on it.
Huī memorialized, arguing that Lín's proposal was impractical,
and the matter was consequently shelved.
Later, others who presented matters again reiterated Lín's previous proposal,
believing it to be truly beneficial to the state.
The Emperor assented to it,
and an edict was issued for its implementation.
Huī again solely memorialized, saying:
“According to the Kingly Regulations,
the Son of Heaven does not speak of 'having or not having,'
the feudal lords do not speak of 'much or little,'
and those who live on official salaries do not contend for profit with the common people.
Now, the *jūnshū* method is no different from commercial trading.
If salt profits go to the government,
then the common people will be impoverished and resentful.
If cloth and silk are collected as rent,
then officials will commit much corruption and theft.
This is truly not something a wise ruler should implement.”
The Emperor ultimately considered Lín's and others' words to be correct.
When he received Huī's repeated deliberation,
he became enraged
and severely reprimanded all the *shàngshū*.
Huī and others all imprisoned themselves.
After three days,
an imperial edict ordered their release.
It said:
“The state is pleased to hear differing opinions.
An old man commits no offense.
The imperial edict was merely heard,
why did you imprison yourselves?”
Huī then claimed to be gravely ill
and refused to sign any further deliberations.
The *Shàngshū Lìng* and others below were terrified
and said to Huī:
“Now that we have just been reprimanded,
how can you claim illness?
The misfortune will not be small!”
Huī said:
“I am eighty years old.
Having received grace to be in a position of confidentiality,
I ought to repay it with my life.
If I know something is unfeasible in my heart but merely conform to the imperial will and echo others,
I would betray the duty of a minister and subject.
Now, with nothing to hear or see,
I await death.”
Thereupon, he closed his mouth and spoke no more.
The *shàngshū* did not know what to do,
so they jointly impeached Huī.
The Emperor's anger subsided
and he shelved the matter.
A few days later,
an edict sent a *zhíshì láng* to inquire about Huī's well-being,
the *tàiyī* to examine his illness,
and the *tàiguān* to bestow food.
Huī then arose to express his gratitude,
and was again granted 100,000 *qián*,
100 rolls of cloth,
and 10 garments.
Later, he was promoted to *Shàngshū Lìng*.
Due to old age and illness, he requested to retire.
He was appointed *Qí Dūwèi*
and granted 200,000 *qián*.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne,
Dòu Xiàn campaigned north against the Xiongnú,
and Huī again submitted a memorial of remonstrance.
Shortly thereafter,
he died of illness.
His son, Jié,
cultivated Confucian arts,
and reached the position of *Chén Xiàng* during the reign of Emperor Ān.
Jié's son was Mù.
Mù's courtesy name was Gōngshú.
At five years old,
he was already known for his filial piety.
When his parents were ill,
he would not eat or drink,
resuming normalcy only after their recovery.
When he grew up, he was devoted to learning,
eagerly lecturing and reciting.
Sometimes, when his thoughts were deep,
he would unconsciously lose his clothes and cap,
stumbling into pits and banks.
His father often considered him stubbornly foolish,
almost to the point of not knowing how to count horse's hooves.
Mù only became more refined and diligent.
He was first nominated as *xiàolián*.
Towards the end of Emperor Shùn's reign,
bandits rose en masse in Jiānghuái,
and the *zhōu* and *jùn* were unable to suppress them.
Someone advised the *Dàjiāngjūn* Liáng Jì, saying:
“Zhū Gōngshú possesses both civil and military talents,
a rare scholar in the realm.
If he were made a chief strategist,
the bandits would be easily pacified.”
Jì had also long heard of Mù's reputation,
so he invited him,
entrusted him with military affairs,
and held him in great trust and regard.
When Emperor Huán ascended the throne,
and Empress Dowager Shùnliè held court,
Mù, seeing Jì's influential and prominent position,
hoped that he could support the imperial house.
Thus, he invoked omens of disaster
and sent a written remonstrance to exhort Jì, saying:
“Your humble servant Mù considers that next year, the *dīnghài* year,
the *xíngdé* will align with the *qián* position,
which is the 'dragon battle' convergence in the *Yìjīng*.
Its text says: 'The dragons battle in the wild,
their path is exhausted.'
This means the *yáng* path will prevail and the *yīn* path will fail.
This year, in the ninth month, the weather was gloomy and obscured,
and the five positions and four seasons consecutively lost their proper *qì*.
This mutually clarifies the situation.
Indeed, the path of good belongs to *yáng*,
and the path of evil belongs to *yīn*.
If one rectifies and upholds *yáng*,
and crushes evil kinds,
then blessings will follow.
Mù is inadequate in all matters,
but his only passion is learning.
What I have transmitted and received from my teacher
can sometimes be put to the test.
I wish the General would slightly observe my foolish words,
and advocate for the admission of various Confucians,
and personally befriend the loyal and upright,
and sever ties with the indulgent,
and devote his mind to the public court,
and cut off private desires,
and broadly seek out the worthy and capable,
and distance himself from the flattering and wicked.
A ruler cannot afford not to learn.
He should gradually imbue his heart with the harmonious ways of heaven and earth.
It is appropriate to select and appoint teachers and lecturers for the Emperor,
obtaining cautious, loyal, sincere, and礼-abiding gentlemen.
The General should enter with them,
participate in exhorting and teaching,
and emulate the wise and follow the ancients.
This is like leaning on Mount Nán and sitting on a flat plain;
who can overturn it!
This summer,
the moon eclipsed the Fáng constellation.
Next year there will be a minor calamity.
It is advisable to swiftly execute the treacherous ministers who are hated and poisoned by the world,
to avert disaster and misfortune.
The positions of *Yìláng* and *Dàfū*
were originally for recognizing scholars of Confucian arts and noble conduct.
Now, many are not the right people;
among the *jiǔ qīng*,
there are also those who are unsuitable for their roles.
May the General please observe this.”
He also recommended Zhǒng Gǎo and Luán Bā, among others.
The following year, Yán Wěi plotted to enthrone King Sǔn of Qīnghé,
and two yellow dragons appeared in Pèiguó.
Jì had no scholarly knowledge,
so he took Mù's
“dragon battle”
words as a verification.
Thereupon, he requested Gǎo to be *Cóngshì Zhōngláng*,
recommended Bā to be *Yìláng*,
and nominated Mù as *Gāodì*
to be *Shì Yùshǐ*.
At that time, Zhào Kāngshú Shèng, from the same *jùn*,
lived in seclusion on Mount Wǔdāng,
living a pure and quiet life, not serving in office,
and teaching classics and commentaries.
Mù, then fifty years old,
sent a letter styling himself as his disciple.
When Kāng died,
he mourned him as his teacher.
His reverence for virtue and emphasis on the Dao
was admired by his contemporaries.
He often felt the shallowness of his era,
and admired and valued sincerity and earnestness.
So he wrote the *Chónghòu Lùn*.
Its text says: “The decline of customs
has a history.
Therefore, Zhòngní sighed, saying:
‘When the Great Dao was practiced,
I was not part of it.’
This grieved him."
it is.
Now, the Dào
takes All-under-Heaven as one,
what is with others is as if it were with oneself.
Therefore, if one's actions deviate from the Dào, shame arises in the heart;
this is not fear of Yì;
if one's deeds deviate
from Lǐ, a sense of failure binds the will;
this is not dread of Lǐ.
Hence, acting according to one's nature is called the Dào,
and achieving one's innate nature is called Dé.
After Dé and nature are lost,
then Rén and Yì are valued.
This is why when Rén and Yì arose, Dào and Dé declined,
and when Lǐ and Fǎ flourished, purity and simplicity scattered.
Therefore, Dào and Dé consider Rén and Yì as shallow,
and purity and simplicity
consider Lǐ and Fǎ as robbers.
What was esteemed in the middle ages
was already considered shallow in antiquity,
how much more so what is shallower than this!
In the past, Zhòngní did not lose his old affection for Yuán Rǎng,
and Chǔ Yán did not bear to expose the flaw at the Jué Yīng incident.
From this perspective,
the Dé of the sages and worthies was profound.
Lǎo Shì's
classic says:
"A great person dwells in the thick, not in the thin;
resides in the fruit, not in the flower.
Therefore, they reject the latter and take the former."
There are times when shallowness exists, yet profundity
is bestowed;
actions may err, yet kindness is used.
Thus, one who covers up others' faults
follows the Dào of profundity;
one who remedies others' errors
performs an act of generosity.
In the past,
Mǎ
Yuán clearly illuminated this Dào,
which can be considered Dé.
He admonished his nephews, saying:
"I wish you all to hear of others' faults as you hear your parents' names.
The ear may hear,
but the mouth must not speak."
These words are essential.
In the distant past, sages and worthies practiced it in antiquity;
more recently, Bǐng Jí and Zhāng Zǐrú implemented it in the Hàn court.
Thus,
they were able to spread their illustrious reputation for a hundred generations,
transmitting an enduring legacy.
Is this not excellent!
Their goodness.
All those in the distant past were like this;
how can they be praised!
All of these types
not only deviate from the Dào of a Jūnzi,
but will also lead to the disaster
of endangering oneself and implicating one's family.
Alas!
Those who practice it do not realize its perils,
and so harm arises without their being aware of it.
This being so,
there is yet another difference.
People all see
it but cannot change themselves.
Why?
Those eager for advancement rush forward without looking back;
those who are glorious and noble are proud of themselves and do not rely on others;
the wise do not engage with the foolish;
the wealthy do not
relieve the poor;
chaste scholars are isolated and unpitied;
worthy individuals are in distress and unsupported.
Hence, Tián Fén, by virtue of his prominence, obtained the gold of Ān Guó;
Chúnyú, by his noble influence, brought forth the words
of Fāng Jìn.
Even with the conduct of Hán and Zhái,
as renowned prime ministers of Hàn,
they still could not uplift a single poor worthy,
or recommend a single isolated scholar,
how much less
those beneath them!
This is why Qín Xī and Shǐ Yú were exclusively named in the past,
with no successors afterward.
Therefore, when the times are profound and customs are good,
even petty people adhere to
righteousness;
profit cannot tempt them.
When the times are adverse and customs are shallow,
even Jūnzi act perversely;
Yì cannot stop them.
Why?
Those who advanced first have gone and will not
return;
those who come later merely follow customs and pursue them.
This is why superficial splendor thrives and loyalty and trust wane;
harshness and meanness abound and purity and sincerity are rare.
This is why the Gǔ Fēng contains
the lament
of "abandoning
me,"
and the Fá Mù has
the sorrow
of "birds singing!"
If the two prime ministers were to rectify their failures,
appreciate the uprightness of Hán Léng,
value the generosity of Bǐng and Zhāng,
and disdain the slander of current customs,
then the Dào would be abundant and achievements great,
reputation would be prominent and one's person
honored,
bearing imperishable Dé,
and spreading an enduring renown.
Only then [hòu] would one know that shallowness is insufficient,
and profundity is abundant.
The former will decay
with plants and trees,
the latter will endure with metal and stone.
How can they be spoken of in the same year,
or discussed on the same day? "
Mù also wrote the Jué Jiāo Lùn,
which was also a work to rectify the times.
Liáng Jì 驕暴不悛,
the court and populace groaned in bitterness.
Mù, as his former subordinate,
feared his accumulation of transgressions would invite disaster,
so he again presented a memorial to admonish him, saying:
"Ancient enlightened rulers
surely had ministers who assisted them in virtue,
and officials who offered admonishment and counsel.
Even down to implements,
they inscribed successes and failures,
to prevent oversight.
Thus, the ruler had the correct path,
and the ministers had the correct road;
following it was like ascending a hall,
and violating it was like rushing into a ravine.
Now, you, enlightened General, have the veneration of Shēnbó,
and your position is foremost among all dukes.
If you perform good deeds for a day,
the world will attribute benevolence to you;
if you act wickedly for a morning,
the four seas will be overturned.
Recently,
officials and the common people are equally destitute,
and moreover, floods and insects have caused harm.
The expenses of various offices in the capital have increased,
and imperial edicts for levies sometimes reach ten times the usual amount.
Each official says that the government lacks ready funds,
and all must extract from the people,
flogging and flaying,
forcefully ensuring sufficiency.
Public taxes are already heavy,
and private extortions are even deeper.
Governors and chief officials,
many of whom are not chosen for their virtue,
greedily accumulate without satiety,
treating people like captives.
Some die under the whip and rod,
while others commit self-harm due to urgent demands.
Furthermore, the plundering of the populace
is all attributed to your esteemed residence.
This has caused the General to incur the resentment of the world,
the officials and people to feel bitter and poisoned,
and sighs and lamentations to fill the roads.
In the past, Qín's government was troublesome and harsh,
causing the people to collapse like crumbling earth.
Chén Shèng raised his arm and gave a single cry,
and the world boiled over.
Yet, the fawning ministers
still said it was peaceful.
They concealed evil and did not reform,
eventually leading to destruction.
At the end of Yǒnghé,
the national order was somewhat diminished,
and popular hopes were largely lost.
Only four or five years passed,
yet wealth was depleted, households scattered,
and the common people became disloyal.
Followers of Mǎ Miǎn took advantage of the weakness and rose up,
and in the area between Jīng and Yáng, a great calamity almost formed.
[一０]Fortunately, with Empress Shùnliè's initial clean and quiet administration,
and concerted efforts from within and without,
it was barely suppressed and pacified.
Now, the common people are distressed,
suffering more than during Yǒnghé.
Internally, this is not something that can be tolerated with a benevolent and loving heart;
externally, it is not a state-guarding strategy that can ensure long-term peace.
Indeed, generals and prime ministers, as great ministers,
are like integral parts of the head of state.
They ride together in the same carriage,
and cross the river in the same boat.
If the carriage overturns or the boat capsizes,
they truly share the misfortune.
How can one abandon enlightenment for ignorance,
tread on danger and feel self-content,
[一一]when the ruler is isolated and the times are difficult,
and yet not care for him!
You should promptly replace those governors and prefects who are not suitable,
reduce expenses for residences, gardens, and ponds,
and refuse all offerings from commanderies and kingdoms.
Internally, this will clarify your own position;
externally, it will resolve people's doubts.
It will prevent corrupt officials from having any support,
and allow investigative ministers to fully use their eyes and ears.
Once the laws and standards are established,
both near and far will be pure and unified.
Then, your person, General, will be respected and your deeds prominent,
and your virtue will shine boundlessly.
The Way of Heaven is clear and discerning;
no words are untrustworthy.
I humbly beg your consideration."
Jì did not accept it,
and his indulgence and recklessness increased daily.
He even bribed his attendants,
colluded with eunuchs,
and appointed his sons, younger brothers, and retainers to important posts in provinces and commanderies.
Mù again presented a memorial with extreme remonstrance,
but Jì never understood.
He replied in a letter, saying:
"In that case,
is there nothing at all good about me?"
Though Mù's words were sharp,
he was not severely punished.
In the first year of Yǒngxīng,
the river overflowed,
sweeping away and harming hundreds of thousands of households.
The people suffered from famine,
and migrated along the roads.
Robbers were particularly numerous in Jìzhōu.
Therefore, Mù was promoted to Inspector of Jìzhōu.
There were three eunuchs from that province who were Zhōngchángshì,
and they all sent summons to meet Mù.
Mù detested them and refused to meet them.
When the chiefs and magistrates of Jì's prefectures heard that Mù had crossed the river,
more than forty of them resigned their seals and left.
When he arrived,
he impeached officials in various commanderies,
to the extent that some committed suicide.
Using his authority and strategic expediency,
he executed all the bandit leaders.
He impeached and accused powerful and influential figures,
some of whom died in prison.
There was a eunuch, Zhào Zhōng, whose father died,
and he returned to Ānpíng for the burial.
He presumptuously used yúzhuó, jade caskets, and effigies.
Mù heard of this and
ordered the commandery to investigate.
The officials, fearing his strict fairness,
then opened the tomb and broke open the coffin,
exposing the corpse,
and arrested his family members.
The Emperor heard and was greatly angered,
summoning Mù to the Tíngwèi,
and sentencing him to penal labor in the Zuǒxiào.
Liú Táo and several thousand other students from the Tàixué went to the palace gate and presented a memorial defending Mù, saying:
"We humbly observe that the convicted penal laborer, Zhū Mù,
in his public concern for the nation,
upon his appointment to the province,
was determined to eliminate wickedness.
It is indeed because the Chángshì are honored and favored,
and their fathers, elder brothers, and sons are spread throughout the provinces and commanderies,
competing to act like tigers and wolves,
devouring the common people.
Therefore, Mù deployed the net of Heaven,
patched its gaps,
and ensnared the disastrous culprits,
to satisfy the will of Heaven.
Consequently, the palace officials collectively harbored hatred and animosity,
slanderous accusations frequently arose,
and malicious plots repeatedly occurred,
culminating in his severe punishment and sentence
to penal labor in the Zuǒxiào.
All intelligent people under Heaven
consider Mù to be diligent like Yǔ and Jì, yet subjected to the harshness of Gòng and Gǔn.
If the deceased have knowledge,
then Emperor Táng would be enraged on Chóngshān,
and Chónghuá would be vexed in Cāngmù.
Currently, the inner officials and close attendants
secretly hold the reins of state,
wielding royal authority,
and uttering imperial decrees.
When they dispense rewards, they make starving slaves richer than Jì Sūn;
when they issue commands, they turn Yī and Yán into Jié and Zhí.
Yet Mù alone stood firm,
disregarding personal harm.
It is not that he disliked glory and preferred disgrace,
or disliked life and preferred death,
but merely that he was moved by the failure of the royal order to govern,
[一０]fearing that the net of Heaven had been lost for too long.
Thus, he dedicated his heart to worry,
making profound plans for the emperor.
We, your subjects, wish to tattoo our foreheads and shackle our feet,
[一一]to take Mù's place in penal labor."
The Emperor reviewed the memorial
and then pardoned him.
Zhū Mù stayed at home for several years.
Many of the high officials at court recommended him,
so he was summoned and appointed as Shàngshū.
Zhū Mù had long harbored deep resentment towards the eunuchs,
and when he was in the imperial secretariat,
working with them day and night,
he was determined to eliminate them.
So he submitted a memorial which stated:
"According to Han precedents,
the Zhōngchángshì (Central Regular Attendants) were selected from among scholarly gentlemen.
After the Jiànwǔ era,
however, only eunuchs were used.
Since the Yánpíng era,
their power and prestige have gradually increased,
wearing the ornaments of marten tail and cinnabar,
occupying the office of Chángbó (Regular Elder),
the affairs of the imperial court,
all passed through their hands.
Their influence filled the realm,
their favor and wealth were limitless.
Their children and relatives
all received honorable appointments,
hence their extravagance, arrogance, and excess
could not be restrained.
Wicked and cunning individuals without integrity
flattered them to obtain official positions,
while those who relied on their power and indulged in their favor
preyed upon the common people,
impoverishing the whole empire,
and exhausting the humble folk.
Your foolish subject believes they should all be dismissed,
and the former practices restored,
following the old regulations,
selecting instead pure and upright scholars from the realm,
who understand the principles of state,
to fill their positions.
Then Your Majesty can become a ruler like Yáo and Shùn,
and all officials will become ministers like Jì and Xiè,
