and the myriad people will be bathed in your sagely transformation."
The Emperor did not accept this.
Later, Zhū Mù, during an audience,
verbally repeated:
"Your subject has heard that according to the old customs of the Han imperial house,
one Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and one Zhōngchángshì were appointed,
to oversee the affairs of the Shàngshū,
and one Huángmén Shìláng (Yellow Gate Remonstrance Official),
to transmit memorials and edicts,
all of whom were from established families.
Since Empress Dowager Héxī, as a female ruler, assumed regency,
and did not meet with high officials,
eunuchs were then appointed as Chángshì,
and Xiǎohuángmén communicated with the two palaces.
Since then,
their power has overshadowed the ruler,
and impoverished the empire.
They should all be dismissed,
and learned elders and venerable scholars widely selected,
to participate in state affairs."
The Emperor was angry
and did not respond.
Zhū Mù prostrated himself and refused to rise.
The attendants had him removed,
and after a long time, he hurried away.
From then on, the palace eunuchs frequently used various pretexts to issue edicts slandering him.
Zhū Mù was naturally rigid,
and feeling frustrated,
not long after,
his pent-up anger caused a carbuncle to erupt.
In the sixth year of Yánxī (163 CE),
he died
at the age of sixty-four.
Having served as an official for several decades,
he ate simple food and wore plain clothes,
with no surplus wealth in his home.
The high officials jointly memorialized that Zhū Mù had upheld integrity and was loyal and pure,
reverent and meticulous in confidential matters,
and had adhered to the good Way until death.
He deserved to be honored and praised.
An imperial edict was issued, commending him,
and posthumously appointing him Yìzhōu Tàishǒu.
His writings, including discourses, policies, memorials, instructions, letters, poems, records, and satires,
totaled twenty chapters.
Earlier, when Zhū Mù was in Jìzhōu,
all those he appointed were virtuous and respected elders,
many of whom became high officials or provincial and commandery administrators.
His son, Zhū Yě,
had a reputation for integrity in his youth,
and served as Hénányǐn.
Originally,
when Zhū Mù's father died,
Zhū Mù and other scholars, after consulting ancient principles,
gave him the posthumous title Zhēnxuān Xiānshēng.
When Zhū Mù himself died,
Cài Yōng and his disciples together recounted his conduct,
and gave him the posthumous title Wénzhōng Xiānshēng.
A discourse states: Zhū Mù observed how favoritism caused injury to righteousness,
and partisan factions corrupted customs.
Determined to suppress the selfishness of cliques,
he wrote the treatise on "severing friendships."
Cài Yōng believed Zhū Mù was upright but solitary,
and therefore wrote the treatise on "righteous friendships" to broaden his perspective.
Indeed, Kǒngzǐ said,
"In befriending superiors, one is not obsequious;
in befriending inferiors, one is not disrespectful,"
and also said,
"Yàn Píngzhòng was good at befriending people."
Zǐxià's disciples also asked Zǐzhāng about friendship.
Thus, the Yì Jīng speaks of
the meaning of "cutting metal" (i.e., strong friendship),
and the Shī Jīng records
songs of "feasting with friends."
As for friends who gather for literary pursuits and assist in benevolence,
those who are upright, sincere, and widely learned,
they are always beneficial.
And those who wear plain clothes and share a carriage (i.e., humble and intimate friends),
or who help each other adjust their hats and tie their sashes (i.e., assist in official promotion),
they foster deep affection.
These are indeed the proper ways of making friends.
As for the retainers of Tián, Dòu, Wèi, and Huò,
[footnote] and the guests of Lián Pō and Zhái Gōng,
[footnote] their advancement was due to power,
and their departure due to decline or estrangement.
Furthermore, there were the passionate deeds of Zhuān Zhū and Jīng Qīng,
[footnote] and the self-sacrifice of Hóu Shēng and Yù Zǐ.
[footnote] Their emotions were driven by gratitude,
and their lives were made light for righteousness.
All these individuals changed their hearts based on benefit or harm,
or cultivated integrity due to kindness.
These are not the fundamentals of true friendship,
and thus one cannot speak of the origin of gains and losses in such cases.
Zhū Mù, merely because friendship was partially incomplete,
consequently rejected the pursuit of like-minded individuals;
and seeing the abuses caused by partisan cliques,
he forgot the meaning of gaining friends.
[footnote] Cài Yōng's words about him being upright but solitary,
how true they are!
The ancients who were good at making friends are well-documented.
In the early Han, Wáng Yáng, Gòng Yǔ, Chén Zūn, and Zhāng Sǒng were praised.
[footnote] In the middle period, there were Lián Fàn, Qìng Hóng, Chén Zhòng, and Léi Yì.
Yuè Huī, courtesy name Bóqí,
was from Chánglíng, Jīngzhào.
His father
was a county official,
and offended the magistrate,
who arrested and intended to execute him.
Yuè Huī, at the age of eleven,
constantly prostrated himself at the temple gate,
weeping day and night.
The magistrate heard of it and took pity on him,
immediately releasing his father.
When he grew up, Yuè Huī loved classical studies,
and served the Erudite Jiāo Yǒng.
When Jiāo Yǒng became the Tàishǒu of Hédōng,
Yuè Huī followed him to his post,
staying indoors, diligently reciting texts,
and not socializing with others.
Later, Jiāo Yǒng was investigated for an incident,
and all his disciples were implicated and imprisoned for corruption.
Yuè Huī alone was conspicuously untainted by the law,
and thus dedicated himself to becoming a renowned scholar.
His nature was honest and upright, resolute and independent;
if someone's conduct did not align with his own,
no matter how noble, he would not associate with them.
Yīnyíng Hóu Yīn Jiù repeatedly sent gifts and invited Yuè Huī,
but Yuè Huī absolutely refused to respond.
Later, he served as an official in his home commandery.
When the Tàishǒu was executed for breaking the law,
his former associates dared not visit him,
but Yuè Huī alone attended the funeral and observed mourning,
for which he was prosecuted and found guilty.
Upon returning,
he again served as Gōngcáo.
He was impartial in selections
and would not accept any recommendations.
Yáng Zhèng of the same commandery repeatedly publicly slandered Yuè Huī,
but later Yuè Huī nominated Yáng Zhèng's son as Xiàolián,
which led to the local community respecting him.
He was appointed to Sīkōng Mó Róng's staff.
At that time, Dìwǔ Lún, the Tàishǒu of Shǔjùn, replaced Mó Róng as Sīkōng.
Yuè Huī, being from the same commandery as Dìwǔ Lún,
refused to stay,
and instead recommended Dù Ān of Yǐngchuān before retiring.
Many high officials admired his conduct,
and repeatedly invited him,
but he refused them all.
Later, he was summoned and appointed as a Counsellor (Yìláng).
At that time, the General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn), Dòu Xiàn, was campaigning against the Xiongnú.
Kuī repeatedly submitted memorials to remonstrate,
and the imperial court praised his loyalty.
He entered office as Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Púyè).
At this time, Wáng Diào, the Prefect of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn), and Lǐ Fù, the Magistrate of Luòyáng (Luòyáng Lìng), were close friends with Dòu Xiàn,
and were given free rein.
Kuī impeached and reported Diào and Fù,
and also implicated the Colonel Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
In all his impeachments and recommendations,
he showed no回避 (huíbì) favoritism,
which displeased the imperial relatives.
Xiàn's younger brother, Gūi, the Marquis of Xiàyáng (Xiàyáng Hóu), wanted to visit Kuī,
but Kuī refused to receive him.
The Xiàn brothers were unrestrained,
and resented him for not attaching himself to them.
His wife often remonstrated with Kuī, saying:
"In ancient times, people accommodated themselves to avoid harm;
why must you invite resentment with your words?"
Kuī sighed and said:
"How can I bear to merely consume and stand in the court without contributing?!"
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial which stated:
"Your servant has heard that the failures of all kings
resulted from power shifting to subordinates.
When great ministers govern the state,
it is always their excessive influence that causes calamity.
I respectfully recall the late emperor,
whose sagely virtue was not long-lasting,
and who prematurely abandoned the myriad states.
Your Majesty is young in years,
and has inherited the great enterprise.
It is not appropriate for the maternal uncles to interfere with the proper affairs of the royal house,
thereby displaying partiality to the world.
The classics say: 'When Heaven and Earth deviate from their course,
all things are prematurely harmed.
When ruler and ministers lose their proper order,
the myriad people suffer calamity.'
If political errors are not remedied,
their ultimate consequences are unfathomable.
The current propriety dictates
that those above should cut themselves off with righteousness,
and those below should withdraw themselves with humility.
This way, the four maternal uncles can long preserve the glory of their titles and territories,
and the Empress Dowager will forever be free from the worry of shaming the ancestral temple.
This is truly the best policy."
The memorial was submitted but not heeded.
At that time, Empress Dowager Dòu was regent,
and Emperor Hé had not yet personally attended to all state affairs.
Kuī, seeing that his intentions could not be carried out,
then feigned illness and requested to retire.
An imperial edict granted him money,
and the imperial physicians examined his illness.
Kuī recommended Guō Jūn from Rèncchéng and Gāo Fèng from Chéngyáng,
and then claimed to be critically ill.
He was appointed Commandant of Cavalry (Qí Dūwèi).
He submitted a memorial declining and expressing gratitude, saying:
"I have repeatedly received great favors,
but have no means to repay them.
That governance should be in the hands of great officers is what Kǒngzǐ abhorred;
that hereditary ministers should hold power is what the Spring and Autumn Annals warned against.
The sages' earnest concerns
were not empty words.
In recent times, the wealthy and powerful maternal relatives
have inevitably fallen due to arrogance and excess.
Now, Your Majesty longs for the mountain tombs [of your ancestors],
and has not yet attended to governmental affairs;
your maternal uncles are greatly favored,
and their power extends throughout the realm.
If they cannot restrain themselves,
punishment will surely befall them.
My life is drawing to a close;
before death, I exhaust my foolishness,
hoping only that you will pay attention."
An edict allowed him to relinquish his seal and ribbon,
and so he returned to his hometown.
Dòu Xiàn thereupon instigated the commanderies and districts to coerce and threaten him,
and Kuī subsequently drank poison and died.
Several hundred disciples, wearing mourning clothes, followed his bier,
and the common people mourned him deeply.
Later, when the Dòu clan was purged,
the emperor first began to attend to affairs personally.
Kuī's students, Hé Róng and others, submitted a memorial setting forth Kuī's loyalty and integrity,
and his son Jǐ was appointed as a Gentleman (Lángzhōng).
Hé Chǎng, courtesy name Wéngāo,
was a native of Pínglíng, Fúfēng.
His ancestors were originally from Rǔyīn.
His sixth-generation ancestor, Bǐgān,
studied the Book of Documents (Shàngshū) with Cháo Cuò.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ, he served as Chief Justice (Tíngwèi Zhèng),
at the same time as Zhāng Tāng.
Tāng was strict in applying the law, while Bǐgān was committed to benevolence and leniency.
He frequently argued with Tāng;
although he could not always prevail,
he nonetheless saved thousands of lives.
Later, he was promoted to Commandant of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Dūwèi),
and consequently moved to Pínglíng.
Chǎng's father, Chǒng,
served as Commandant of Qiānchéng during the Jiànwǔ era.
He was dismissed due to illness,
and subsequently lived in reclusion, not serving.
Chǎng's character was upright and just.
Believing that his principles did not align with the times,
he often claimed illness and refused to respond whenever summoned.
During the Yuánhé era,
he was invited by the office of Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Sòng Yóu.
Yóu treated him with exceptional respect.
Chǎng's discussions and opinions were profound,
always referring to fundamental principles,
and he corrected many things.
Minister of Works (Sītú) Yuán Ān also deeply respected him.
At this time, the capital and the four directions repeatedly saw strange and unusual birds, beasts, plants, and trees,
which commentators regarded as auspicious omens.
Chǎng was well-versed in the classics and commentaries,
and skilled in astronomy.
He deeply disapproved of these occurrences.
He then spoke to the two dukes (Yóu and Ān), saying:
"Auspicious signs appear in accordance with virtue,
and calamities arise due to governance.
Thus, when the jackdaws came to nest,
Duke Zhāo faced the calamity of Gānhóu;
when a qílín was captured in the western hunt,
Kǒngzǐ had the omen of the twin pillars' funeral.
When a sea bird avoided the wind,
Zāng Wén-Zhòng sacrificed to it,
and the noblemen criticized him.
Now, strange birds fly over the palace eaves,
and unusual plants grow by the courtyard's edge.
These cannot be left unexamined."
Yóu and Ān were struck with fear and dared not respond.
Not long after, Emperor Sùzōng passed away.
At that time, the Dòu clan [Dòu shì] held exclusive power.
The imperial relatives by marriage were extravagant,
and their rewards exceeded regulations.
The granaries and treasuries were emptied.
Chǎng [Chǎng] presented a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the principle of serving one's lord
is to think of exhausting one's loyalty when advancing,
and to think of rectifying one's errors when retreating.
Reviewing past lords and ministers throughout history,
none failed to wish to transform the age,
and leave a legacy for eternity.
Yet, among ten thousand, there was not one peaceful and harmonious reign.
This is probably because sagely lords and virtuous ministers could not meet each other.
Now, the state upholds the brilliant and magnificent Way,
and you, Minggōng [Mínggōng], possess a tranquil and pure virtue.
With lord and minister in harmony,
the whole world is united.
The transformation to peace and order
is hoped for in this present time.
Kǒngzǐ [Kǒngzǐ] said: 'If anyone were to employ me,
in three years there would be great success.'
Now, Minggōng [Mínggōng] has been in office,
coming and going for two full cycles.
It is proper to restrain oneself,
to respond to the aspirations of the four seas.
According to the Rites,
if even one grain crop fails,
one should reduce one's attire and simplify one's meals.
If the world suffers scarcity,
one should act as if one caused it.
However, in recent years, there have been floods and droughts,
and people have had no harvest.
The border regions of Liángzhōu [Liángzhōu]
have suffered severe calamities in every household.
Men are exhausted from battle,
and wives and daughters toil in transportation.
The old, young, orphaned, and widowed
sigh and cling to each other.
Furthermore, the central regions and interior commanderies
are utterly depleted, both publicly and privately.
This is truly a time for reduced meals and frugality.
Yet, the imperial benevolence covers and supports all,
and rewards and gifts are excessive.
It is heard that for the winter grants alone,
from court officials upwards,
and down to dukes, ministers, kings, and marquises,
they have gone so far as to empty the treasuries
and deplete the national resources.
Upon examination, the expenses of the public coffers
all come from the strength of the common people.
When an enlightened ruler bestows gifts,
there should be a system of grades and regulations.
When loyal ministers receive rewards,
there should also be a limit.
Thus, Yǔ [Yǔ] of Xià [Xià] received a dark jade tablet,
and Zhōugōng [Zhōugōng] received a bundle of silks.
Now, Minggōng [Mínggōng] holds a high position and heavy responsibility,
with deep obligations and great burdens.
Upwards, you should rectify the governmental system;
downwards, you should bring peace and security to the multitude.
How can you merely be empty and without error!
You should first rectify yourself to lead those below,
return the gifts you have received,
and then enumerate gains and losses,
memorialize for kings and marquises to return to their states,
abolish the prohibitions on imperial parks,
curtail unnecessary expenses,
and relieve the poor and orphaned.
Then, benevolence and grace will flow downwards,
the common people will be joyful and contented,
and Heaven, being sagacious and clear-sighted,
will surely give a prompt response.
This would make the common people sing your praises,
and historians record your virtues.
How could this merely be comparable to Zǐwén [Zǐwén] avoiding emoluments
or Gōngyí [Gōngyí] declining meals!"
Yóu [Yóu] did not use his advice.
At that time, Liú Chàng [Liú Chàng], Prince of Qí Shāng [Qí Shāng] and Marquis of Dūxiāng [Dūxiāng], had hurried to mourn the national sorrow,
but his memorial had not been answered.
The侍zhōng [shì zhōng] Dòu Xiàn [Dòu Xiàn] then ordered men to assassinate Chàng [Chàng] within the guards at the city gate,
and the principal culprit was not established.
Chǎng [Chǎng] again advised Yóu [Yóu], saying:
"Liú Chàng [Liú Chàng] was a close relative of the imperial clan,
a feudal lord of the 'mao' and 'tu' lands.
He came to mourn the great sorrow,
and his memorial awaited a response.
He was personally in the military guard,
yet this cruel act occurred.
The officials who received Xiàn's [Xiàn] orders
did not arrest the culprits.
The traces are unclear,
and the principal culprit is not established.
I, Chǎng [Chǎng], am counted among your trusted advisors,
and my duty is to oversee the criminal investigations.
Thus, I wish to personally go to the place where the incident occurred
to investigate the matter.
However, the two departments believe that according to precedent, the Three Dukes do not deal with thieves and bandits.
In the past, Chén Píng [Chén Píng], born in an era of warfare,
still understood the duties of a prime minister.
He said, 'Externally, bring peace to the four barbarians;
internally, soothe the feudal lords,
so that each minister and grandee finds his proper place.'
Now, the officials of the two departments do not deeply consider the great principles,
but are misled by what they have heard.
They openly indulge villains,
and hold no one accountable.
May Minggōng [Mínggōng] exercise your unique insight and wisdom,
be clear and without doubt.
I, Chǎng [Chǎng], cannot bear what I have witnessed,
and request to submit the case independently."
Yóu [Yóu] then granted permission.
When the two departments heard that Chǎng [Chǎng] was going,
they all sent their principal officers to accompany him.
Thereupon, he investigated and fully obtained the facts,
and the capital praised his righteousness.
He was promoted with high marks and appointed Shìyùshǐ [Shìyùshǐ].
At that time, Dòu Xiàn [Dòu Xiàn] was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry.
A large army was dispatched to attack the Xiōngnú [Xiōngnú].
The emperor also issued an edict ordering envoys to build grand residences for Xiàn's [Xiàn] younger brothers, Dǔ [Dǔ] and Jǐng [Jǐng].
Construction and labor were extensive,
and the common people suffered greatly.
Chǎng [Chǎng] submitted a memorial to admonish, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the Xiōngnú [Xiōngnú] have long been rebellious and perverse.
The siege of Píngchéng [Píngchéng]
and the shame of the insulting letter—
these two disgraces
are what ministers and sons would sacrifice their lives for and surely die for.
Gāozǔ [Gāozǔ] and Empress Lǚ [Lǚ hòu] endured their anger and suppressed their resentment,
letting it pass and not punishing them.
I humbly consider that the Empress Dowager possesses the conduct of a sagely mother,
and Your Majesty embodies a tranquil demeanor.
The Xiōngnú [Xiōngnú] have not committed a crime of rebellion,
and the Hàn [Hàn] court has no shameful disgrace.
Yet, in the flourishing spring, when eastern farming commences,
a great labor project is initiated,
causing resentment among the multitude,
all harboring displeasure.
Moreover, you are again building and repairing grand mansions for Wèiwèi [Wèiwèi] Dǔ [Dǔ] and Fèngchē Dūwèi [Fèngchē Dūwèi] Jǐng [Jǐng],
spanning streets and blocking neighborhoods.
Although your servant is a person of limited capacity,
I genuinely feel surprised and perplexed,
thinking that Dǔ [Dǔ] and Jǐng [Jǐng], being close and noble officials,
should be models for all officials.
Now, with numerous armies on the march,
the court is anxious,
the common people are suffering,
and the state treasury is empty,
yet grand mansions are hastily erected,
adorning them with precious items.
This is not how to establish a virtuous legacy
and demonstrate an enduring example.
It is fitting to halt the laborers for now,
focus solely on the northern border,
and relieve the people's distress."
The memorial was submitted but not heeded.
Later, he was appointed Shàngshū.
He again submitted a sealed memorial, saying:
"Truly, a loyal minister, worried for the world,
offends the stern countenance of his lord,
criticizes powerful officials,
even to the point of sacrificing his life and destroying his family, and yet still does it.
Why is this?
The righteousness between ruler and minister is weighty,
and there are times when one has no choice.
I have humbly observed past events:
the dangers and chaos of a state,
the impending misfortunes of a family,
all have their origins,
plainly and easily known.
In the past, Zhèng Wǔjiāng's favoritism towards Shúdùan,
Wèi Zhuānggōng's indulgence of Zhōuyù,
loving them but failing to teach them,
ultimately led to their violent deaths.
From this perspective,
to love one's child thus
is like feeding him poison when he is hungry,
which is precisely how one harms him.
I humbly observe that Dàjiāngjūn Dòu Xiàn,
at the beginning of his great mourning,
the Gōngqīng successively memorialized,
desiring him to manage state affairs.
Dòu Xiàn deeply insisted on humility and retreat,
firmly declined the high position,
sincerely and diligently,
speaking with profound earnestness,
and when the world heard of it,
none were not pleased and joyful.
Now, barely a year has passed,
the great rites are not yet concluded,
yet suddenly there is a change in the middle,
and the brothers monopolize the court.
Dòu Xiàn wields the heavy responsibility of the three armies,
while Dòu Dǔ and Dòu Jǐng collectively control the power of the palace guards,
and they cruelly exploit the common people,
are extravagant and overbearing,
execute the innocent,
and act wantonly for their own pleasure.
Today, opinions are fiercely agitated,
all saying that Shúdùan and Zhōuyù have been reborn in Hàn.
I observe that the Gōngqīng harbor conflicting thoughts,
unwilling to speak forthrightly,
thinking that if Dòu Xiàn and his brothers have a loyal and diligent will,
then they themselves will receive the merit of Jífǔ praising Shēnbó;
if Dòu Xiàn and his brothers fall into crime and guilt,
then they will themselves emulate Chén Píng and Zhōu Bó in yielding to Lǚ Hòu's power.
They ultimately do not worry about the fortune or misfortune of Dòu Xiàn and his brothers.
Your subject Chǎng, in my humble capacity,
sincerely wishes to devise a plan that ensures peace for both,
to cut off its continuous spread,
to block its gradual seepage,
so that above, the Huáng Tàihòu does not lose the title of Wénmǔ,
and Your Majesty avoids the criticism of the 'Oath at Quán,'
and below, Dòu Xiàn and his brothers may long preserve their blessings.
However, the plans of servants and concubines,
even if they secure the master above
and preserve the mistress below,
still do not escape severe anger.
〔一０〕Your subject humbly reflects that for generations my ancestors have received grace,
down to my eighth generation.
〔一一〕Furthermore, though I am foolish and untalented,
within a decade,
I have successively held prominent positions,
and been close to the imperial presence.
Whenever I recall the profound kindness,
I instantly forget my own life.
Though I know that speaking out will surely lead to extermination,
I brave death to speak my mind
because I truly cannot bear to witness this calamity with my own eyes and remain silent to preserve myself.
Fùmǎ Dōuwèi Dòu Guī,
though still young,
possesses the loyalty of not concealing.
He has repeatedly requested to withdraw himself,
wishing to restrain his family's power.
He can be consulted for advice;
listening to and following his intentions
would truly be a supreme plan for the ancestral temple
and a blessing for the Dòu clan."
Hé Chǎng frequently offered blunt remonstrances,
speaking of the faults of the Dòu brothers,
and Dòu Xiàn and his brothers deeply resented him.
At that time, Jìnán Wáng Kāng was extremely honorable and arrogant.
Dòu Xiàn then memorialized to send Hé Chǎng out as Jìnán Tàifù.
When Hé Chǎng arrived in the state,
he assisted Jìnán Wáng Kāng with principles of righteousness,
and repeatedly cited laws and regulations to remonstrate and correct him.
Kāng respected and treated him courteously.
After more than a year,
he was promoted to Rǔnán Tàishǒu.
Hé Chǎng detested sophisticated officials who sought contemporary fame through harshness,
so he governed with leniency and harmony during his tenure.
On Lìchūn Day,
he would always summon the Dūyóu back to the府,
and send out scholarly high officials to inspect the subordinate counties,
highlighting those who were filial, fraternal, and righteous in conduct.
He also reviewed unjust cases,
judging them according to the principles of the Chūnqiū.
Because of this, there were no complaints in the commandery,
and the common people were transformed by his kindness and etiquette.
Those who had left home
all returned to care for their parents,
observed mourning rites,
and were willing to yield property to each other, numbering about two hundred people.
He established officials for rites
and did not employ clerks.
He also repaired the old Qú channel in Tóngyáng.
The common people benefited from it,
and cultivated land increased by over thirty thousand qǐng.
Officials and commoners together carved a stone inscription,
praising Hé Chǎng's achievements and virtues.
When the Dòu clan fell,
the supervising authorities memorialized that Hé Chǎng's son was close friends with Xiàyáng Hóu Dòu Guī,
and he was dismissed from office for this reason.
In Yǒngyuán twelve, he was again summoned,
and three times promoted to Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng.
He often resented and detested Zhōngchángshì Cài Lún,
and Cài Lún deeply held a grudge against him.
In Yuánxīng one,
Hé Chǎng, due to the solemnity of the ancestral temple rites,
feigned illness and did not observe purification.
Later, Dèng Huánghòu went to the tomb of Tàifù Dèng Yǔ.
Hé Chǎng rose and joined the officials.
Cài Lún then memorialized that Hé Chǎng had feigned illness,
and he was found guilty and punished.
He died at home.
The commentary says: At the time of Yǒngyuán,
the Son of Heaven was young and weak,
the Tàihòu presided over the court,
and the Dòu clan, relying on the power of their influential relatives,
was on the verge of a Lǚ-Huò upheaval.
Fortunately, the virtue of Hàn had not yet declined,
and the ministers were still loyal.
Yuán and Rèn, two righteous gentlemen, stood firm in court,
while the likes of Lè and Hé debated beneath the pillars.
Thus, they were able to assist the young ruler
in suppressing the oppressive machinations of the treacherous.
Otherwise,
the state would have been in peril.
Among the Dòu clan,
only Hé Chǎng could have been spared,
yet he was dismissed specifically because his son associated with the wrong people,
and was not granted a high position.
What a pity,
it was a mistake indeed!
The eulogy says: Zhūshēng received the trust,
truly not deviating from righteousness.
Gōngshú and Píliáng,
sincerely accepted clear advice.
Severing ties, facing friends,
exalting extravagance and falsity.
Hui boldly slandered himself,
Chǎng was no auspicious omen.
Always speaking of the state's oppression,
willingly accepting strong falsehoods.
Biographies of Dèng, Zhāng, Xú, Zhāng, Hú No. 34
Dèng Biāo, courtesy name Zhìbó,
was from Xīnyě, Nányáng,
and a kinsman of Tàifù Dèng Yǔ.
His father, Dèng Hán,
was enfeoffed as Méng Hóu at the beginning of the restoration for his achievements,
and rose to Bóhǎi Tàishǒu.
Dèng Biāo cultivated his will from a young age
and practiced filial piety.
After his father died,
he ceded the fief to his half-brother Jīng Fèng.
Xiǎnzōng highly esteemed his integrity
and issued an edict granting permission.
Later, he served in provinces and commanderies,
was appointed to the ducal household,
and was five times promoted to Guìyáng Tàishǒu.
In Yǒngpíng seventeen,
he was summoned to the capital as Tàipú.
After several years,
he mourned his stepmother,
resigning due to illness and requesting to retire.
An edict appointed him Guānglù Dàfū to perform the mourning rites.
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Fèngchē Dōuwèi,
and promoted to Dàsīnóng.
A few months later,
he replaced Bào Yù as Tàiwèi.
Dèng Biāo was pure and upright in office,
serving as a model for all officials.
After serving for four years,
he requested retirement due to illness.
In Yuánhé one,
an edict granted his dismissal,
and he was bestowed with three hundred thousand cash,
receiving the salary of a two-thousand-dàn official for the rest of his life.
An edict also ordered the Tàicháng to send sacrificial meat from the ancestral temple quarterly,
and the Hénán Yǐn to send an assistant to inquire about his well-being,
always presenting a sheep and wine on the first day of the eighth month.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne,
Biāo was appointed Grand Tutor,
and given charge of the affairs of the Secretariat.
He was granted the title of Marquis of Guānnèi.
At the beginning of the Yǒngyuán era,
the Dòu clan monopolized power and acted arrogantly.
Many in the court remonstrated and debated,
but Biāo merely cultivated his own conduct in office,
unable to correct anything.
He once also impeached and secured the dismissal of Zhōu Yū, the Imperial Censor-in-chief.
Yū had previously displeased the Dòu clan,
so Biāo was somewhat criticized for this,
though at the time, people honored him for his courtesy and deference.
When the Dòu clan was purged,
due to old age and illness, he requested to resign from his pivotal post.
An imperial edict granted him cattle and wine for his upkeep and permitted it.
In the spring of the fifth year,
he died in office.
The Son of Heaven personally attended his mourning.
Zhāng Yǔ, courtesy name Bódá,
was a native of Xiāngguó, Zhàoguó.
His grandfather Kuàng's clan sister was the consort of the imperial great-grandfather.
He frequently traveled to Nándùn
and met Guāngwǔ.
When Guāngwǔ was Grand Marshal,
he passed through Hándān.
Kuàng, then a county official,
requested an audience with Guāngwǔ.
Guāngwǔ was greatly pleased
and said,
"Have I now found my maternal great-uncle?"
He then took him north with him,
and upon arriving at Gāoyì,
appointed him Magistrate of Yuánshì.
He was promoted to Administrator of Zhuōjùn.
Later, he became the Pass Commander of Chángshān.
When the Chìméi attacked the pass city,
Kuàng died in battle.
His father, Xīn,
initially fled due to avenging a wrong.
Later, he served as Chancellor of Huáiyáng
and eventually died as Magistrate of Jí.
Yǔ was a man of earnest and frugal character.
When his father died,
the officials and people of Jí contributed several million in funeral gifts,
but he accepted none of it.
He also gave his fields and residences to his paternal uncle,
and stayed elsewhere himself.
In the eighth year of Yǒngpíng,
he was recommended as Xiàolián and gradually promoted.
During the Jiànchū era,
he was appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu.
When he was to cross the river to inspect the region,
people in the central plains all believed the Jiāng River had the spirit of Zǐxū,
making it difficult to cross.
When Yǔ was about to cross,
his officials strongly urged him not to, but he did not listen.
Yǔ sternly said,
"If Zǐxū has a spirit,
knowing my ambition is to investigate and rectify wrongs and grievances,
how could he endanger me?"
Thus,
he paddled across.
He traveled through counties and districts,
reaching even the most remote and secluded places,
personally recording prisoners,
and clarifying many cases.
Officials and commoners rarely saw imperial envoys,
and the people were filled with joy,
so their grievances, virtues, good and evil deeds,
all were reported to him.
In the second year of Yuánhé,
he was transferred to Inspector of Yǎnzhōu,
and also gained a reputation for integrity and fairness.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Chancellor of Xiàpéi.
To the north of Xú County was Púyángpō,
with many good fields nearby,
but they were abandoned and uncultivated.
Yǔ had a sluice gate opened,
connecting and directing irrigation,
thereby creating several hundred qǐng of ripe fields.
He encouraged and led officials and commoners,
lent them seeds and provisions,
personally exerted effort,
and thus achieved a great harvest.
Over a thousand impoverished households from neighboring commanderies migrated to him,
their dwellings connecting one after another,
forming a market below.
In later years, over a thousand qǐng were cultivated,
and the people enjoyed a comfortable livelihood.
The Chief Clerk, Dài Rùn,
was a former aide to the Grand Commandant,
whose influence stirred the entire commandery.
When he committed a minor offense,
Yǔ ordered him to personally report to the prison in Xú,
and then applied the law correctly.
From the Chief Secretary downwards,
none were not awed and subdued.
In the sixth year of Yǒngyuán,
he entered the court as Grand Minister of Agriculture,
and was then appointed Grand Commandant.
Emperor Hé showed him great respect.
In the fifteenth year,
when the emperor traveled south to offer sacrifices at the imperial ancestral temples and gardens,
Yǔ, as Grand Commandant, concurrently served as Commander of the Guards, remaining behind to guard the capital.
Upon hearing that the imperial carriage was to proceed to Jiānglíng,
he believed it was unwise to risk such a distant journey,
and sent an urgent memorial to remonstrate.
The imperial reply stated:
"The sacrifices and visits being concluded,
We were to pay respects to the great Jiāng River to the south.
Having received your memorial,
We will turn Our carriage back at Línhàn and return."
When the emperor returned from his tour,
Yǔ received special rewards.
In the first year of Yánpíng,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor,
and given charge of the affairs of the Secretariat.
Empress Dowager Dèng, considering that Emperor Shāng was an infant,
desired a senior minister to reside within the Forbidden City.
Thus, she decreed that Yǔ reside in the palace,
provided with curtains, bedding, and cushions,
with the Imperial Kitchen providing meals morning and evening.
He would return to his residence once every five days.
Each time he had an imperial audience,
he was specially announced,
and sat separately from the Three Ducal Ministers.
Yǔ memorialized, saying:
"During this period of profound mourning and quietude,
it is not appropriate to regularly conduct affairs in the imperial parks and gardens.
The empty lands of Guǎngchéng and Shànglín
should temporarily be leased to the poor."
The Empress Dowager followed his advice.
When Emperor Ān ascended the throne,
Yǔ repeatedly reported illness and begged to resign.
An imperial edict dispatched a Young Yellow Gate official to inquire about his illness,
bestowing a bull,
ten hú of wine,
and urging him to take up residence at home.
Money, cloth, swords, and clothing
were sent to him in succession.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
for his service in establishing the new emperor, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānxiāng,
with a fief of one thousand two hundred households,
and was enfeoffed on the same day as Grand Commandant Xú Fáng and Minister of Works Yǐn Qín.
In that autumn,
due to bandits, floods, and heavy rains, Fáng and Qín were dismissed by imperial decree.
Yǔ, feeling uneasy,
submitted a memorial begging to retire.
He was then reappointed Grand Commandant.
In the fourth year,
when the Lady of Xīnyě fell ill,
the Empress Dowager and the imperial carriage visited her residence.
Yǔ, together with Minister of the Masses Xià Qín and Minister of Works Zhāng Mǐn, jointly submitted a memorial stating:
"The Lady of Xīnyě is unwell,
and the imperial carriage has stayed overnight for several consecutive days.
We, your servants, are truly and secretly apprehensive.
We have heard that when a king travels, security measures are set up in advance;
when he stops, halberds are crossed;
the path is cleared before he proceeds,
and the chamber is cleared before he enters;
he does not lodge in detached palaces.
This is to emphasize the importance of the imperial guard.
Your Majesty embodies the utmost filial piety,
personally inquiring about medicine and remedies.
Though your affection springs from within,
to reside long outside the palace,
leaving all officials exposed and staying out,
causes uneasiness among those who discuss it.
It is advisable to return to the palace for now,
first for the sake of the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain,
and then for the myriad states and common people."
After three such submissions,
they strongly argued,
and only then did the emperor return to the palace.
Later, consecutive years of disasters and famine occurred,
and the imperial treasury was empty.
Yǔ submitted a memorial requesting to contribute three years of his rent and taxes
to assist the commanderies and states with loans and provisions.
An imperial edict granted his request.
In the fifth year,
he was dismissed by imperial decree due to disharmony between yin and yang.
In the seventh year,
he died at home.
An imperial envoy offered condolences and sacrifices.
His younger son, Yào, was appointed Gentleman.
His eldest son, Shèng, inherited his title.
Xú Fáng, courtesy name Yèqīng,
was a native of Zhì, Péiguó.
His grandfather Xuān
was a Grand Master of Learning,
who taught the Yì Jīng to Wáng Mǎng.
His father Xiàn
also inherited Xuān's profession.
Fáng Shǎo (防少) practiced the scholarship of his father and grandfather.
During the Yǒngpíng (永平) era,
he was nominated as xiàolián (孝廉),
and appointed Láng (郎).
Fáng Shǎo (防少) possessed a dignified and solemn appearance,
and his responses were admirable.
Xiǎnzōng (顯宗) found him extraordinary,
and specially appointed him Shàngshū Láng (尚書郎).
His duties involved central and vital affairs,
which he handled with thoroughness, caution, and reverence.
He served two emperors,
and never made a mistake.
During Emperor Hé's (和帝) time,
he was gradually promoted to Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉),
then left to become Wèijùn Tàishǒu (魏郡太守).
In the tenth year of Yǒngyuán (永元) (98 CE),
he was promoted to Shǎofǔ (少府) and Dàsīnóng (大司農).
Fáng Shǎo (防少) was diligent and astute in government affairs,
leaving his mark wherever he served.
In the fourteenth year (102 CE),
he was appointed Sīkōng (司空).
Fáng Shǎo (防少) believed that because the Wǔjīng (五經) had existed for a long time,
the Sages' intentions were difficult to understand,
and it would be beneficial to create commentaries (zhāngjù 章句)
to enlighten later students.
He submitted a memorial, stating:
“Your servant has heard that the Shī (詩), Shū (書), Lǐ (禮), and Yuè (樂) [classics]
were established by Kǒngzǐ (孔子);
the illumination of their chapters and sentences [with commentaries]
began with Zǐxià (子夏).
Thereafter, various schools analyzed them,
each having different interpretations.
When Hàn (漢) succeeded the chaotic Qín (秦) dynasty,
the classics were abolished and lost.
Their original texts barely survived,
and some lacked commentaries.
Bits and pieces were collected,
and the 'enlightened classics' (míngjīng 明經) were established,
broadly drawing upon Rú (儒) scholarship,
and setting up the Tàixué (太學).
As Kǒng Shèng (孔聖) was already distant,
his subtle principles were on the verge of being lost.
Therefore, fourteen schools of Bóshì (博士) were established,
and the rankings of Jiǎ (甲) and Yǐ (乙) were set up [for examinations],
to encourage scholars.
This was to show people what was good and bad,
and to correct faults and embrace goodness.
I have observed that when the Tàixué (太學) tests Bóshì Dìzǐ (博士弟子),
they all explain according to their own ideas,
not following the established school traditions,
and privately tolerate and conceal each other's faults,
opening a path for corruption.
Whenever there is a policy examination,
disputes and lawsuits arise,
discussions are confused and erroneous,
and they mutually fault each other.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said, ‘I transmit but do not innovate,’
and also said, ‘I am still fortunate enough to have seen cases where the historian would leave a blank.’
He disapproved of historians who, being ignorant of something, were unwilling to leave it blank.
Now, without relying on established commentaries, people wantonly engage in far-fetched interpretations,
considering adherence to teachers as unrighteous,
and their own interpretations as correct reasoning,
thereby disrespecting the Way and its teachings,
and establishing a popular trend.
This is truly not the original intention of the imperial edicts' sincere selections.
To abandon shallowness and follow loyalty
is the constant path of the three generations,
and to specialize in and strive for the fundamentals
is what Rú (儒) scholarship prioritizes.
Your servant believes that for the Bóshì (博士) and Jiǎ (甲) and Yǐ (乙) policy examinations,
they should adhere to the commentaries of their own schools,
and open fifty difficult questions to test them.
Those who provide more explanations should be ranked highest,
and those who cite clear texts should be considered to have superior interpretations.
If they do not follow their former teachers,
and their interpretations conflict with each other,
〔一０〕all should be rectified as incorrect.
For each of the Wǔjīng (五經), the top six persons should be selected.
The Lúnyǔ (論語) should not be subject to policy examinations by shooting arrows.
Although what has been lost may have been so for a long time,
this measure can still somewhat rectify it.”
〔一一〕An imperial edict was issued to the gōngqīng (公卿),
and all followed Fáng Shǎo's (防少) proposal.
In the sixteenth year (104 CE),
he was appointed Sītú (司徒).
In the first year of Yánpíng (延平) (106 CE),
he was promoted to Tàiwèi (太尉),
and, together with Tàifù (太傅) Zhāng Yǔ (張禹),
participated in managing the affairs of the Shàngshū (尚書).
He frequently received rewards and gifts,
and was greatly favored.
When Emperor Ān (安帝) ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Lóngxiāng Hóu (龍鄉侯) for his role in establishing the succession.
His fief amounted to one thousand one hundred households.
In the same year, due to natural disasters and banditry, he was dismissed by imperial edict
and returned to his domain.
Fáng Shǎo (防少) was the first of the Sāngōng (三公) to be dismissed by imperial edict due to natural disasters.
When Fáng Shǎo (防少) died,
his son Héng (衡) was supposed to succeed him,
but he ceded the enfeoffment to his younger brother Chóng (崇).
After several years,
having no alternative,
he then went to claim the noble rank.
Zhāng Mǐn (張敏), courtesy name Bódá (伯達),
was a native of Mò (鄚), Héjiān (河閒).
In the second year of Jiànchū (建初) (77 CE),
he was nominated as xiàolián (孝廉).
After four promotions,
in the fifth year (80 CE),
he became Shàngshū (尚書).
During the Jiànchū (建初) era,
there was a case where someone insulted another's father,
and the son killed him.
Sùzōng (肅宗) pardoned his death sentence and commuted it.
Thereafter, this was used as a precedent.
At that time, the discussion was finally settled,
establishing it as a 'law of mild insult' (qīngwǔ zhī fǎ 輕侮之法).
Zhāng Mǐn (張敏) debated against this, saying:
“The law of mild insult
was merely an exceptional act of grace by the former emperor,
not an established statute or regulation.
Decisions regarding life and death
should follow the rhythm of nature,
like the four seasons of heaven,
which bring both life and death.
If we open up mutual tolerance and forgiveness
and establish it as a fixed law,
this would be intentionally creating seeds of evil
and fostering loopholes for crime.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said, ‘The people can be made to follow it,
but cannot be made to understand it.’
According to the meaning of the Chūnqiū (春秋),
a son who does not avenge his father
is not a son.
Yet, the law does not reduce the punishment for this,
because the path of mutual killing must not be opened.
Now, those who claim righteousness receive reductions,
while those who kill wantonly have varying punishments,
allowing officials who uphold the law to employ cunning and deceit,
which is not the way to guide towards the principle of
‘not contending when in disgrace.’
Moreover, the precedents of mild insult
have proliferated,
leading to four or five hundred categories,
with cases mutually referencing each other,
only increasing the severity,
making it difficult to hand down for ten thousand generations.
Your servant has heard a teacher say: ‘To remedy over-refinement, nothing is better than simplicity.’
Thus, Emperor Gāo (高帝) abolished complicated and harsh laws,
and established the three-article covenant.
If there are imperial edicts from Jiànchū (建初)
that have altered ancient practices,
they can be sent down to the Sāngōng (三公) and Tíngwèi (廷尉) to remove their弊 (bì) evils.”
The proposal was shelved and not considered.
Zhāng Mǐn (張敏) again submitted a memorial, stating:
“Your servant Mǐn (敏), having received grace,
was specially promoted.
What my foolish mind does not understand,
and what my confused thoughts cannot comprehend,
I truly dare not simply follow the majority opinion.
Your servant has observed that Kǒngzǐ (孔子) handed down the classics,
and Gāoyáo (臯陶) created laws.
Their original intentions,
at their root,
were all to prohibit people from doing wrong.
I do not understand how the law of mild insult will prohibit anything.
It certainly cannot prevent mutual mild insults,
but instead opens a path for mutual killing,
and officials who uphold the law will again tolerate their crookedness.
Some debaters say: ‘Fair laws should prioritize life.’
Your servant foolishly believes that among the natures of heaven and earth,
only humanity is most valuable.
A murderer must die;
this was a universal system across the three dynasties.
Now, wanting to pursue life,
you instead open a path to killing.
If one person does not die,
the whole world suffers harm.
The records say: ‘If one benefits and a hundred are harmed,
people will abandon their cities and towns.’
Indeed, spring brings life and autumn brings death;
this is the constant way of heaven.
If one plant withers in spring, it is a disaster;
if one plant blossoms in autumn, it is an anomaly.
A king inherits from heaven and earth,
follows the four seasons,
emulates the sages,
and adheres to the classics and laws.
I pray Your Majesty pays attention to the common people,
examines the advantages and disadvantages,
and broadly seeks fair opinions.
The empire would be extremely fortunate.”
Emperor Hé (和帝) followed his advice.
In his ninth year,
he was appointed Sīlì Xiàowèi.
After serving for two years,
he was promoted to Rǔnán Tàishǒu.
He was honest and not bothersome,
his punishments were fair and just,
and he had a reputation for good governance.
He was dismissed for an incident.
In the first year of Yánpíng,
he was appointed Yìláng,
and then again promoted to Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
During the first year of Yǒngchū,
he was summoned and appointed Sīkōng.
While in office, he merely upheld the law.
After serving for three years,
he requested retirement due to illness,
but it was not granted.
In the spring of the sixth year,
during the grand archery ceremony,
he collapsed in his accompanying position,
and so he was dismissed by imperial decree.
Because his illness worsened,
he died at home.
Hú Guǎng, courtesy name Bóshǐ,
was a native of Huáróng, Nánjùn.
His sixth-generation ancestor, Gāng,
was pure, noble, and principled.
During the reign of Emperor Píng,
the Grand Minister over the Masses, Mǎ Gōng, invited him to serve.
When Wáng Mǎng assumed regency,
Gāng removed his official robes and cap,
hung them at the gate of the prefecture office, and left.
He then fled to Jiāozhǐ,
hiding among butchers' stalls.
After Mǎng's defeat,
he returned to his hometown.
His father, Gòng,
was the Commander of Jiāozhǐ.
Guǎng was orphaned and poor when young,
and personally endured household hardships.
When he grew up,
he joined his peers and entered the commandery as a minor official.
Fǎ Xióng, the Tàishǒu, had a son named Zhēn,
who came from home to visit his father.
Zhēn was quite skilled at judging people.
It happened that at the end of the year, it was time for nominations,
and Xióng instructed Zhēn to help him find talented individuals.
Xióng then held a grand gathering of officials,
and Zhēn secretly observed them from behind a window.
He then pointed to Guǎng and reported to Xióng,
who subsequently nominated him as Xiàolián.
Upon arriving in the capital,
he was tested on his memorials,
and Emperor Ān declared Guǎng to be the best in the realm.
Within ten days, he was appointed Shàngshū Láng,
and after five promotions, he became Shàngshū Púyè.
Emperor Shùn wished to establish an empress,
but there were four favored noble ladies,
and he did not know whom to choose.
He proposed to draw lots
to let the spirits determine the selection.
Guǎng, along with Shàngshū Guō Qián and Shǐ Chǎng, submitted a memorial remonstrating:
"We humbly observe that the imperial decree regards the establishment of an empress as a great matter,
and out of humility, Your Majesty does not wish to decide unilaterally,
intending to rely on divining sticks
to resolve doubts with spiritual guidance.
In the records of books
and the precedents of our ancestors,
this has never occurred.
Relying on spirits and divination
does not necessarily guarantee selecting the virtuous;
even if the right person is found,
it is still not a selection based on virtue.
Indeed, outstanding qualities appear naturally,
and one who is destined to rule has distinct marks.
It is proper to consult good families,
and carefully seek out those with virtue.
If virtues are equal, choose by age;
if ages are equal, choose by appearance.
Consult the classics
and decide with imperial wisdom.
Government decrees are like sweat,
once issued, they cannot be retracted.
Once an imperial edict is issued,
it shapes the four directions.
Our duty is to collect forgotten advice,
and our concern and responsibility are profound.
Therefore, with anxious hearts,
we presumptuously present this to Your Majesty."
The Emperor followed their advice,
and because Lady Liáng Guìrén was from a good family,
she was decided upon and established as empress.
At that time, Shàngshū Lìng Zuǒ Xióng proposed to reform the system of recommendation and selection,
limiting candidates to those aged forty and above,
testing scholars on classical learning,
and civil officials on their memorials.
Guǎng, again with Chǎng and Qián, submitted a memorial refuting this,
saying:
"Your servants have heard that a ruler's virtue lies in comprehensive observation and broad discernment,
and a minister's loyalty lies in presenting what is advisable and rejecting what is not.
The classics record consulting on doubts,
and seeking counsel from high ministers;
the Odes praise our ancestors,
who consulted even reapers.
When the state has major policies,
it must deliberate on previous teachings
and seek advice from venerable elders.
Thus, there are no miscalculations in planning,
and no errors in actions.
We humbly observe that Shàngshū Lìng Zuǒ Xióng proposes that commandery-recommended Xiàolián
must all be aged forty and above,
with scholars tested on classical texts,
and civil officials tested on memorials and petitions.
Although Your Majesty has already approved this,
we are again permitted to participate in the discussion.
We humbly consider the gravity of imperial commands,
recorded in the classics,
which should be manifest like the sun and moon,
and firm as metal and stone,
leaving a legacy for a hundred kings,
and enduring for ten thousand generations.
The Odes say: 'Heaven is hard to trust;
it is not easy to be a king.'
How can one not be cautious!
Indeed, selection should be based on talent,
without rigid restrictions.
The strategies of Lìu Qí did not come from classical learning;
The governance of Zhèng and Ā did not necessarily rely on memorials.
Gān and Qí achieved prominence
though their age differed from the prime of life;
Zhōng and Jiǎ made their names
while still in their youth.
The Hàn Dynasty inherited from Zhōu and Qín,
also drawing upon Yīn and Xià,
following ancestral virtues and mastering the classics,
while incorporating elements of the Hegemons' ways.
Sage rulers and virtuous ministers
brought about good governance through the generations,
and the system of tribute and recommendation was never altered.
Now, based on the words of one minister,
old regulations are abrogated.
Its benefits are unclear,
and the populace is not pleased.
Rectifying wrongs and changing constants
are grave matters of governance,
and should not be decided without consulting the Three Dukes
or deliberating with the high ministers.
If this matter is implemented,
and subsequently those who discuss it disagree,
disagreement would cause the court to lose its advantage,
while agreement would mean the imperial word has already been enacted.
We, your foolish servants, believe that it should be announced to all officials,
to gather their agreements and disagreements,
and then select the better option,
carefully adopting the most suitable course.
We dare to offer this blind advice,
presumptuously violating imperial prohibitions.
We beg Your Majesty to accept it." The Emperor did not follow it.
At that time, there was a vacant position in Jìchénliú Commandery.
Shàngshū Shǐ Chǎng and others recommended Hú Guǎng.
They said:
"We have heard that virtue is used to honor the worthy,
and rank is used to establish affairs.
'Clearly testing by merit,'
is praised in the Diǎn Mó (Canon of Yao and Shun),
and 'five robes and five insignia,'
are instituted by Heaven's order.
This is why ministers exert their loyalty,
and rulers abundantly bestow their favor,
selecting those who do not deviate from virtue,
and the populace forgets their own deaths.
We humbly observe that Shàngshū Púyè Hú Guǎng
embodies truth and follows rules,
is humble and gentle,
widely learned and knowledgeable,
probing into profundities and exhausting principles.
The profound intricacies of the Six Classics,
and the old statutes and precedents,
nothing has he not examined.
He is gentle but not transgressing,
cultivated and yet courteous.
His nature is loyal and upright,
worrying about the public as if it were his own family.
He does not boast of his abilities,
nor does he flaunt his achievements.
He is diligent and circumspect,
his conduct without blemish or oversight.
He toils diligently day and night,
for more than ten years,
his heart not looking outward,
his ambition not seeking advancement improperly.
We humbly believe that Hú Guǎng, as Shàngshū,
has toiled laboriously for a long time.
His stepmother is old,
and since he has received your esteemed attention,
he should be tested with a position a thousand *lǐ* away,
to bring stability to a regional state.
Chénliú is a nearby commandery,
and the office of Grand Administrator is now vacant.
Hú Guǎng's talent and strategy are profound and abundant,
capable of resolving complex issues.
We wish to include him in the selection,
to bring order to the decadent customs,
and make those who are upright and good,
have someone to look up to and be encouraged by."
Hú Guǎng managed confidential affairs for ten years,
then was appointed Grand Administrator of Jìyīn,
but was dismissed for falsely recommending officials.
He was again appointed Grand Administrator of Rǔnán,
and then entered the court as Dà Sīnóng.
In the first year of Hàn'ān,
he was promoted to Sītú.
When Emperor Zhì died,
he replaced Lǐ Gù as Tàiwèi,
overseeing the affairs of the Shàngshū.
For his role in establishing Emperor Huán on the throne,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yùyáng Ānlè Xiāng.
He resigned due to illness.
He was again appointed Sīkōng,
and then retired due to old age.
Soon after, he was recalled with the title of Tèjìn and appointed Tàicháng,
then promoted to Tàiwèi,
but was dismissed due to a solar eclipse.
He was again appointed Tàicháng,
and then Tàiwèi.
In the second year of Yánxī,
Grand General Liáng Jì was executed.
Hú Guǎng, along with Sītú Hán Yǎn and Sīkōng Sūn Lǎng, were implicated for failing to guard the palace.
All were reduced one rank in punishment from death,
stripped of their titles and lands,
and demoted to commoners.
Later, he was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū and Tàicháng.
In the ninth year,
he was again appointed Sītú.
When Emperor Líng ascended the throne,
he participated in overseeing the affairs of the Shàngshū with Tàifù Chén Fān,
and was restored to his former marquisate.
He requested to resign due to illness.
Coincidentally, Chén Fān was executed,
and Hú Guǎng replaced him as Tàifù,
continuing to oversee affairs as before.
At that time, he was eighty years old,
but his mental and physical strength were still vigorous.
His stepmother was still living,
and he attended to her morning and evening.
He had no armrests or staffs nearby,
and did not refer to himself as old.
When his mother passed away,
he mourned her with utmost grief,
observing the rites without fault.
His nature was gentle, cautious, and simple,
always speaking humbly and showing respectful demeanor.
He was well-versed in matters of state,
and clearly understood court regulations.
Although he lacked the forthright and blunt style,
he often provided beneficial corrections to deficiencies.
Thus, a proverb in the capital said:
"If myriad affairs are not handled, ask Bóshǐ;
for moderation in the world, there is Duke Hú."
However, his joint decision with Lǐ Gù on the succession plan was not entirely sound,
and his marriage alliance with the Central Regular Attendant Dīng Sù,
led to criticism and slander at the time.
He was in high public office for over thirty years,
serving six emperors.
He was treated with great courtesy and trust.
Whenever he resigned due to illness,
or was dismissed and returned to his fields and home,
he never remained there for a full year
before being promoted again.
In total, he served as Sīkōng once,
Sītú twice,
Tàiwèi thrice,
and also as Tàifù.
Those he recommended and appointed
were all renowned scholars of the realm.
He, along with his former subordinates Chén Fān and Lǐ Xián,
all became San Sī (Three Excellencies).
Chén Fān and the others, whenever there was a court assembly,
would claim illness to avoid Hú Guǎng.
People at the time considered this an honor for Hú Guǎng.
He died at the age of eighty-two
in the first year of Xīpíng.
The Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng was sent with a credential to present the posthumous title of Tàifù and the seal and ribbon of the Marquis of Ānlè Xiāng.
He was granted a coffin made of *zǐ* wood from the Eastern Garden,
and an emissary oversaw the funeral arrangements.
A burial plot was bestowed near the Yuán Líng (Imperial Mausoleum).
His posthumous title was Wéngōng Hóu,
and one person from his family was appointed Lángzhōng.
His former subordinates, numbering several hundred, from Gōng, Qīng, Dàfū, Bóshì, and Yìláng downwards,
all wore mourning attire at the coffin,
from his death until his burial.
Since the founding of the Hàn dynasty,
the prosperity of a subject
had never been like this.
Originally,
Yáng Xióng, based on the *Yú Zhēn*, composed the "Twenty-five Official Precepts for Twelve Provinces."
Nine of these precepts were lost.
Later, Cuī Yīn of Zhuō Commandery, and his son Cuī Yuàn, along with Liú Táotú, Marquis of Línyì, augmented it with sixteen chapters.
Hú Guǎng further added four chapters,
the writing of which was very classical and beautiful.
He then compiled and arranged all the headings,
and provided explanations for them,
naming it "Bǎiguān Zhēn" (Precepts for all Officials),
totaling forty-eight chapters.
His other works, including poems, *fù*, inscriptions, eulogies, precepts, laments, and various commentaries,
totaled twenty-two chapters.
In the sixth year of Xīpíng,
Emperor Líng, recalling past virtues,
ordered portraits of Hú Guǎng and Tàiwèi Huáng Qióng to be painted within the palace.
He commanded Yìláng Cài Yōng to compose a eulogy for them.
The 論 (Disquisition) states: The responsibility of office is grave for a person,
and losing one's life completely is a great matter.
To cherish one's emolument and plan for survival
is the constant sentiment of an official;
to prudently assess one's abilities and join the ranks
is the usual way for one to enter public service.
To bend to external things is to lose oneself,
to be straightforward in one's will is to offend society.
To decline a difficulty is to go against righteousness,
to cling to one's principles is to lose one's life.
In sum,
following the straight path is easy to adhere to,
but a treacherous road is difficult to manage.
Therefore, the ancients were clear and cautious about the portion they received,
at the juncture of divergent paths.
If one's will and conduct are not swayed by external things,
and one does not prioritize one's survival when facing life,
what could later generations criticize?
The ancients warned against comfort and ease,
could this refer to these several dukes?
The 贊 (Appraisal) says: Dèng and Zhāng served as Tàifù,
with neither blame nor praise.
Mǐn was upright and adhered to regulations,
preventing discussions on words and phrases.
Duke Hú was mediocre,
adorning his feelings with a respectful demeanor.
Though court regulations were handled,
adherence to righteousness was sometimes bent.
Biographies of Yuán Ān, Zhāng Yǔ, Hán Yǎn, and Zhōu Xié, Chapter Thirty-Five.
Yuán Ān, courtesy name Shàogōng,
was a native of Rǔyáng, Rǔnán.
His grandfather, Yuán Liáng,
was skilled in the Mèng clan's *Yì* (Book of Changes).
During the reign of Emperor Píng, he was recommended as an *míngjīng* (erudite of classics)
and served as Tàizǐ Shèrén.
In the early Jiànwǔ period, he reached the position of Magistrate of Chéngwǔ.
Ān ēn studied with Liáng Xué when he was young.
He was a serious and imposing person,
and was respected in his home province.
He first served as a Gōngcáo in a county.
He was sent with a document to an Cóngshì.
The Cóngshì then used Ān ēn to deliver a letter to the magistrate.
Ān ēn said:
"Public affairs have their own postal service;
a private request is not something a Gōngcáo should carry."
He refused to accept it,
and the Cóngshì was afraid and stopped.
Later, he was recommended as Xiàolián,
and appointed as Zhǎng of Yīnpíng and Lìng of Rènchéng.
Officials and people in those places feared and loved him.
In the thirteenth year of Yǒngpíng (70 CE),
Chǔ Wáng Yīng conspired to rebel.
The matter was sent down to the commanderies for investigation.
The following year,
the three highest ministers recommended Ān ēn as capable of handling difficult cases,
and he was appointed Tàishǒu of Chǔjùn.
At that time, thousands of people were implicated and imprisoned by Yīng's confessions.
Xiǎnzōng was extremely angry,
and the officials pressed the cases severely,
forcing confessions through torture,
and a great many people died.
When Ān ēn arrived at the commandery,
he did not enter the yamen.
He first went to examine the prisons,
and for those whose guilt was not clearly proven,
he itemized and reported them for release.
The Fǔchéng, Yuánshǐ, and all the clerks prostrated themselves and argued,
believing that he was conniving with a rebel,
and would be equally guilty under the law,
which was unacceptable.
Ān ēn said:
"If there is anything improper,
the Tàishǒu himself will bear the consequences,
and it will not affect you."
Then he separately presented a detailed memorial.
The Emperor was enlightened and understood,
and immediately replied, granting permission,
allowing over four hundred families to be released.
After more than a year,
he was summoned to be Hénán Yǐn.
His administration was known for its strictness and clarity,
yet he never interrogated anyone for corruption.
He often said:
"All who study to become officials,
the ambitious aspire to be prime minister,
the less ambitious hope to be provincial governors.
To condemn people in a virtuous age,
is something the Yǐn cannot bear to do."
Those who heard this were all moved and encouraged themselves.
He served for ten years,
and the capital was orderly,
his reputation esteemed by the imperial court.
In the eighth year of Jiànchū (83 CE),
he was promoted to Tàipú.
In the second year of Yuánhé (85 CE),
Mèng Yún, the Tàishǒu of Wǔwēi, submitted a memorial:
"The Northern Xiongnu have already made peace,
yet the southern tribes again go to raid and plunder.
The Northern Chányú thinks that Han is deceiving them,
and plans to invade the border.
It would be appropriate to return their captives
to appease them."
The Emperor ordered all officials to discuss in the imperial court.
The Gōngqīng all said that the "barbarians" were deceitful,
and their demands insatiable.
Once they got the captives,
they would again boast arrogantly,
so it should not be granted.
Ān ēn alone said:
"The Northern Xiongnu sent envoys to offer peace,
and those who captured border inhabitants
immediately returned them to Han.
This clearly shows their awe of our power,
and that they did not violate the agreement first.
Yún, as a high minister guarding the border,
should not be faithless to the Rong and Di.
Returning them would show the Middle Kingdom's generosity,
and allow the border people to live in peace.
This is truly beneficial."
Sītú Huán Yú changed his opinion and agreed with Ān ēn.
Tàiwèi Zhèng Hóng and Sīkōng Dìwǔ Lún both resented this.
Hóng then spoke loudly to incite Yú, saying:
"Those who say the captives should be returned
are all disloyal."
Yú reprimanded him in court.
Lún and Dàhónglú Wéi Biāo both changed their expressions,
and the Sīlì Xiàowèi impeached them.
Ān ēn and others all offered their seals and sashes in apology.
Sùzōng issued an edict in reply, saying:
"Long-standing discussions are often stagnant,
each with their own opinions.
However, affairs are decided by discussion,
and policies are settled by the multitude.
To argue and contend with good humor
is the proper decorum.
To remain silent and suppress one's thoughts
is not a blessing for the court.
Why do you blame yourselves and apologize so deeply?
Each of you should resume your duties."
The Emperor ultimately followed Ān ēn's proposal.
The following year,
he succeeded Dìwǔ Lún as Sīkōng.
In the first year of Zhānghé (87 CE),
he succeeded Huán Yú as Sītú.
When Hé Dì ascended the throne,
Empress Dowager Dòu oversaw the court.
Her brother, Chēqí Jiāngjūn Dòu Xiàn, attacked the Xiongnu in the north.
Ān ēn, along with Tàiwèi Sòng Yóu, Sīkōng Rèn Kuí, and the Nine Ministers, went to the imperial court and submitted a memorial to remonstrate,
believing that since the Xiongnu had not invaded the border,
it was to no purpose to labor the army and travel far,
depleting national resources,
and seeking glory thousands of miles away,
which was not a plan for the state.
Their memorials were submitted repeatedly but always suppressed.
Sòng Yóu became fearful,
and then dared not sign the proposals again,
and the other ministers gradually withdrew.
Only Ān ēn and Rèn Kuí steadfastly upheld justice,
even going so far as to remove their hats in court and argue strenuously ten times.
The Empress Dowager did not listen.
Everyone was worried and afraid for them,
but Ān ēn remained calm and resolute.
After Dòu Xiàn had left,
his brothers, Wèiwèi Dù and Zhíjīnwú Jǐng, each wielded excessive power.
Publicly in the capital, they used their retainers to block roads and rob people of their property.
Jǐng also presumptuously sent messengers on post-horses to issue documents to various border commanderies,
to dispatch elite cavalry and those skilled in riding and archery with talent and strength.
The three commanderies of Yúyáng, Yànmén, and Shànggǔ each sent officials to lead and escort them to Jǐng's residence.
The relevant authorities were fearful and deterred,
none daring to speak.
Ān ēn then impeached Jǐng for presumptuously mobilizing border troops,
alarming and misleading officials and people.
He stated that the Two-Thousand-Picul officials who obeyed Jǐng's documents without waiting for imperial tallies
should be subjected to obvious punishment.
He also memorialized that the Sīlì Xiàowèi and Hénán Yǐn were fawning upon powerful relatives,
failing in their duty to serve with integrity,
and requested their dismissal and prosecution.
All these were suppressed and went unanswered.
Xiàn and Jǐng became increasingly arrogant,
planting their relatives, partisans, and retainers in famous cities and large commanderies,
all of whom levied taxes on officials and people,
and exchanged bribes.
The remaining provinces and commanderies
also followed suit, looking to them for direction.
Ān ēn and Rèn Kuí impeached various Two-Thousand-Picul officials,
and also over forty others who were implicated, demoted, or dismissed.
The Dòu clan greatly resented this.
However, Ān ēn and Kuí were known for their high moral conduct,
so there was no way to harm them yet.
At that time, Dòu Xiàn 竇憲 again garrisoned Wǔwēi 武威.
The following year,
the Northern Chányú 北單于 was defeated by Gěng Kuí 耿夔,
fleeing to Wūsūn 烏孫.
The land north of the frontier was empty,
and the remaining tribes did not know where they belonged.
Dòu Xiàn 日竇憲 daily boasted of his achievements,
wishing to curry favor with the Northern barbarians.
Thereupon, he memorialized to establish the surrendered Zuǒ Lùlí Wáng Ātóng 左鹿蠡王阿佟
as the Northern Chányú 北單于,
and appointed a Zhōnglángjiàng 中郎將 to lead and protect him,
following the precedent of the Southern Chányú 南單于.
The matter was sent down for discussion by the Gōngqīng 公卿.
Tàiwèi Sòng Yóu 太尉宋由, Tàicháng Dīng Hóng 太常丁鴻, Guānglùxūn Gěng Bǐng 光祿勳耿秉, and ten others debated and agreed that it should be permitted.
Ān 安 and Rèn Kuí 任隗 submitted a memorial,
believing that
"Guāngwǔ 光武's policy of recruiting and welcoming the Southern barbarians
was not intended for permanent peace in the interior,
but merely a temporary calculation
to defend against the Northern Dí 狄."
"Now that the northern desert is settled,
the Southern Chányú 南單于 should be ordered to return to his northern court,
and also lead the surrendered multitude.
There is no reason to again establish Ātóng 阿佟,
thereby increasing state expenditure."
Zōngzhèng Liú Fāng 宗正劉方 and Dàsīnóng Yǐn Mù 大司農尹睦 agreed with Ān's 安 proposal.
The memorial was submitted,
but it was not decided in time.
Ān 安 feared that Dòu Xiàn's 竇憲's plan would be carried out,
so he personally submitted a sealed memorial saying:
"Your servant has heard that achievements are difficult to plan,
and cannot be foreseen;
but matters are easy to judge,
clear and without doubt.
I humbly believe that the original reason why Emperor Guāngwǔ 光武 established the Southern Chányú 南單于
was for the policy of pacifying the south and settling the north.
His benevolence and virtue were fully provided,
so the Xiōngnú 匈奴 consequently split,
and the frontiers were without trouble.
Emperor Xiàomíng 孝明 continued the former intention,
not daring to let it fall,
and grandly ordered generals
to attack the lands north of the frontier.
Up until the beginning of Zhānghé 章和,
over a hundred thousand people surrendered.
Those who debated wished to place them along the frontier,
eastward to Liáodōng 遼東.
Tàiwèi Sòng Yóu 太尉宋由 and Guānglùxūn Gěng Bǐng 光祿勳耿秉 both thought that it would displease the Southern Chányú 南單于,
and was unacceptable.
The former emperor followed their advice.
Your Majesty has continued this great enterprise,
greatly expanding the territory.
The Great General has marched far to attack,
sweeping through the Northern Court.
This truly proclaims the brilliance of the ancestors,
and establishes immense merit.
It is fitting to consider the end carefully,
to perfect the beginning.
I humbly recall the Southern Chányú Túns 屯 settlement;
his late father led his people to submit to virtue,
and since receiving grace,
it has been over forty years.
Three emperors have accumulated
this inheritance for Your Majesty.
Your Majesty should deeply follow the will of the predecessors,
and accomplish their work.
Furthermore, Tún 屯 was the first to propose the great strategy,
completely emptying the Northern barbarians.
To stop and not consider this,
and instead establish a new surrendered one,
for the sake of a temporary plan,
goes against the rules of three generations,
loses trust with those who have been nurtured,
and establishes someone who has no merit.
Sòng Yóu 宋由 and Gěng Bǐng 耿秉 actually know the old discussion,
yet they wish to turn their backs on the former benevolence.
Indeed, words and actions are the pivot of a junzi 君子,
and rewards and punishments are the principles of governing a state.
The Analects say: 'If one is loyal and trustworthy in speech,
and earnest and respectful in conduct,
even in Mán Mò 蠻貊 lands, one will be able to proceed.'
If now we lose trust with one Tún 屯,
then the hundred barbarian tribes will not dare to pledge their allegiance again.
Moreover, the Wūhuán 烏桓 and Xiānbēi 鮮卑 have recently killed the Northern Chányú 北單于.
It is human nature
to fear one's enemies.
If we now establish his brother,
then the two barbarian tribes will harbor resentment.
Soldiers and food can be abandoned,
but trust cannot be forsaken.
Furthermore, according to Han history,
the annual expenditure for the Southern Chányú 南單于 was over 190 million,
and for the Western Regions, 74.8 million.
Now the Northern Court is even further away,
and its expenses will be more than double.
This would exhaust the entire empire,
and is not the essence of a sound strategy."
The edict ordered discussion on this.
Ān 安 again debated and refuted Dòu Xiàn 竇憲.
Dòu Xiàn 竇憲 was impetuous and relied on his power,
his words were arrogant and slanderous,
even defaming Ān 安,
citing the precedent of Guāngwǔ 光武 executing Hán Xīn 韓歆 and Dài Shè 戴涉.
Ān 安 remained unyielding.
Dòu Xiàn 竇憲 eventually established Yòu Lùlí Wáng Yú Chújiān 右鹿蠡王於除鞬, a surrendered Xiōngnú 匈奴, as Chányú 單于.
Later, he indeed rebelled,
precisely as Ān 安 had predicted.
Ān 安, seeing that the Son of Heaven was young and weak,
and the empress's relatives held power,
never failed to sigh and shed tears
whenever he attended court or spoke with the Gōngqīng 公卿 about state affairs.
From the Son of Heaven to the high officials, all relied on him.
In the spring of the fourth year,
he passed away,
and the court deeply mourned his loss.
A few months later,
the Dòu 竇 clan was defeated,
and the Emperor began to personally manage all affairs.
Recalling the integrity of those who had previously debated, whether crooked or upright,
he appointed Ān's 安 son, Shǎng 賞, as Láng 郎.
He dismissed Sòng Yóu 宋由 by imperial edict,
made Yǐn Mù 尹睦 Tàiwèi 太尉,
and Liú Fāng 劉方 Sīkōng 司空.
Yǐn Mù 尹睦,
a native of Hénán 河南,
died in office.
Liú Fāng 劉方,
a native of Píngyuán 平原,
was later dismissed for an offense and returned home,
where he committed suicide.
Originally,
when Ān's 安 father died,
his mother sent Ān 安 to search for a burial site.
On the way, he met three scholars,
who asked Ān 安 where he was going.
Ān 安 told them the reason,
and the scholars pointed to a spot,
saying,
"If you bury him here,
your descendants will be high officials for generations."
In a moment, they disappeared,
and Ān 安 found this strange.
Thereupon, he buried his father in the designated place,
and thus his family prospered for generations.
Ān's 安 sons, Jīng 京 and Chǎng 敞, were the most famous.
Jīng 京 had the courtesy name Zhòngyù 仲譽.
He mastered the Mèng 孟 family's *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes),
and wrote thirty thousand words for his *Nán Jì* 難記.
He was initially appointed Lángzhōng 郎中,
gradually promoted to Shìzhōng 侍中,
then went out to serve as Shǔjùn Tàishǒu 蜀郡太守.
His son Péng 彭,
courtesy name Bóchǔ 伯楚.
In his youth, he inherited his father's profession,
and successively served as Guǎnghàn Tàishǒu 廣漢太守 and Nányáng Tàishǒu 南陽太守.
In the early years of Emperor Shùn 順,
he became Guānglùxūn 光祿勳.
When he governed Qīng 清,
his officials wore coarse robes and ate rough food,
and he ended his career as Yìláng 議郎.
Shàngshū Hú Guǎng 尚書胡廣 and others later memorialized his purity and integrity,
comparing him to Gòng Yǔ 貢禹 and Dìwǔ Lún 第五倫 of previous dynasties.
He did not receive prominent posthumous honors,
which was lamented by all at the time.
Péng's 彭 younger brother, Tāng 湯,
courtesy name Zhònghé 仲河,
inherited the family scholarship in his youth.
Scholars praised his integrity,
and he held many prominent positions.
In the early years of Emperor Huán 桓, he served as Sīkōng 司空,
and for his participation in deliberating and finalizing the succession, he was enfeoffed as Ānguó Tínghóu 安國亭侯,
with an income of five hundred households.
He was successively promoted to Sītú 司徒 and Tàiwèi 太尉,
and was dismissed by imperial edict due to natural disasters.
After his death,
he was posthumously granted the title Kānghóu 康侯.
Tāng's 湯 eldest son, Chéng 成, was Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiāng 左中郎將.
He died young,
and his second son Féng 逢 inherited.
Féng 逢, courtesy name Zhōuyáng 周陽,
was known at the time for being a benevolent and trustworthy person,
as a descendant of a family that had produced three high officials for generations.
When Emperor Líng 靈 was enthroned, Féng 逢, as Tàipú 太僕, participated in the deliberations,
and his fief was increased by three hundred households.
Later, he served as Sīkōng 司空,
and died in the position of Zhí Jīnwǔ 執金吾.
The court, considering that Féng 逢 had once served as Sānlǎo 三老,
treated him with exceptional courtesy,
bestowing upon him a special edict with a pearl-painted secret instrument,
and twenty-six items of pearls and jade to be placed in his mouth.
They sent the Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng 五官中郎將 with a ceremonial staff to convey the edict,
presenting him with the seal and sash of a Chējì Jiāngjūn 車騎將軍,
conferring upon him the title Tèjìn 特進,
and posthumously naming him Xuānwén Hóu 宣文侯.
His son Jī 基 inherited,
and rose to the position of Tàipú 太僕.
Féng's younger brother, Kuí,
had held prominent official positions since youth.
He became a Sāngōng before Féng.
At that time, Yuán Shè, a Zhōng Chángshì,
who was of Kuí's clan,
was powerful at court.
Because Féng and Kuí came from generations of prime ministers,
Yuán Shè elevated them, using them as external support.
Hence, the Yuán clan was distinguished and favored by the world,
and immensely wealthy and extravagant,
unlike other noble families.
At the beginning of Emperor Xiàn's reign,
Kuí was a Tàifù.
Chéng Zǐshào and
Féng Zǐshù
have their own biographies.
Dǒng Zhuó, angered that Shào and Shù had betrayed him,
then executed Kuí and Shù's elder brother Jī, along with twenty or more men and women.
Chǎng, whose courtesy name was Shūpíng,
was taught the Yì Jīng in his youth.
Through his father's influence, he became a Tàizǐ Shèrén.
During Emperor Hé's time,
he successively held positions as Jiāngjūn, Dàfū, and Shìzhōng,
then went out to be Dōngjùn Tàishǒu,
and was later summoned to be Tàipú and Guānglùxūn.
In the third year of Yuánchū,
he replaced Liú Kǎi as Sīkōng.
The following year,
