he was dismissed for his son's communication with Shàngshū Láng Zhāng Jùn,
leaking confidential court information.
He was dismissed by imperial edict.
Chǎng was upright and unyielding, never flattering the powerful.
He displeased the Dèng clan,
and subsequently committed suicide.
Zhāng Jùn
was from Shǔjùn.
He was talented
and, along with his elder brother Kān, was a Shàngshū Láng.
Young and ambitious,
he saw that Láng Zhū Jǐ and Dīng Shèng's conduct was not proper,
and wanted to impeach them.
When the two heard this,
they became afraid.
They enlisted Láng Chén Chóng and Léi Yì to intercede with Jùn,
but Jùn refused to listen.
So they secretly bribed a Shìshǐ
to find Jùn's faults.
They found a private letter he had sent to Chǎng's son.
They then sealed and reported it to the throne.
All were imprisoned
and sentenced to death.
From prison, Jùn dictated a memorial to a prison official, pleading his case.
By the time the memorial was presented, Jùn's sentence had already been finalized.
As the Tíngwèi was about to lead him out of Gǔmén
for execution,
Empress Dowager Dèng issued an edict to send a swift rider, commuting his sentence to a lesser punishment.
Jùn, using a pseudonym, submitted a memorial of gratitude, saying:
"I, your subject, ungrateful and faithless,
have brought upon myself this severe punishment.
My emotions were severed, my intentions ceased,
with nothing left to hope for.
The Tíngwèi summoned me and sent me off;
the blade
was before me,
the coffin and shroud behind me.
My spirit soared,
my form already withered.
Your Majesty's sacred grace,
remembering that I was once close,
recognizing my appearance,
pitying my eyes,
you reserved your attention and consideration,
and specially granted a thorough review.
The hearse returned,
white bones regained flesh,
opening the coffin and uncovering the inner coffin,
I arose to see the light of day.
Heaven and Earth, my parents, could give birth to me, Jùn,
but they could not bring me, Jùn, back to life after being condemned to death.
Your Majesty's virtue surpasses Heaven and Earth,
your grace is heavier than that of parents.
Truly, even if I, Jùn, were to shatter my bones
and my whole clan were to perish,
it would not repay one ten-thousandth.
I, Jùn, am a convict
and am not permitted to present memorials.
However, I cannot suppress the joy of escaping death and embracing life,
my surprise and delight,
as I presumptuously present this memorial."
At the time, everyone pitied his writing.
The court, because of this, lightened Chǎng's crime and concealed the manner of his death,
burying him with the rites of a Sāngōng
and restoring his official title.
His son was Xū.
Xū later rose to Guānglùxūn.
At that time, Dàjiāngjūn Liáng Jì held sway at court,
and everyone, inside and outside, flattered him.
Only Xū and Tíngwèi Hándān Yì maintained their integrity.
When Emperor Huán executed Jì,
he sent Xū, holding the imperial credential, to seize Jì's seals and ribbons.
The details are fully recounted in the Biography of Liáng Jì.
Hóng, whose courtesy name was Xiàfǔ,
was Péng's grandson.
From a young age, he cultivated his conduct,
enduring hardship and maintaining his integrity.
His father, Hè,
was the Xiàng of Péngchéng.
Hóng went to visit him,
changing his name and surname, traveling on foot without companions.
Upon arriving at the government office gate,
the officials did not allow him to enter for several days.
Coincidentally, his mother's nursemaid came out
and, seeing Hóng, was surprised.
She went in and told the madam,
who then secretly called him in.
After a while, he took his leave.
Hè sent a carriage to see him off,
but Hóng claimed dizziness and refused to ride,
returning
without anyone in the commandery knowing.
When Hè died in the commandery,
Hóng and his brothers went to escort the funeral procession.
They refused all funeral gifts and contributions,
wearing mourning clothes and holding the coffin,
braving the cold and dew.
Their appearance was gaunt and withered,
and their hands and feet bled.
All who saw them were moved to sorrow.
After the mourning period,
he was repeatedly summoned, invited, and recommended,
but he declined them all.
He lived in humble dwellings,
making farming and study his occupation.
His paternal uncles Féng and Kuí were both noble and prosperous
and often sent him gifts,
but he accepted none.
Hóng saw that the times were dangerous and chaotic,
while his family was wealthy and flourishing.
He often sighed to his brothers, saying:
"The blessings and prosperity of our ancestors
cannot be maintained by the virtue of later generations.
Instead, they compete in extravagance
and contend for power in troubled times.
This is precisely like the three Xì of Jìn!"
At the end of Yánxī,
when the party proscription was about to begin,
Hóng scattered his hair and withdrew from the world,
intending to disappear into the deep forests.
As his mother was old and it was not proper to flee far,
he built an earthen chamber,
surrounded by a wall in his courtyard,
without a door,
receiving food and drink only through a window.
Each morning, he would bow to his mother from inside the chamber, facing east.
His mother, missing Hóng,
would sometimes go to visit him.
When his mother left,
he would immediately close himself off again.
None of his brothers, wife, or children could see him.
When his mother died,
he did not observe the proper mourning rites or set up a spirit tablet.
At the time, no one could name his actions;
some thought him a mad scholar.
He remained hidden for eighteen years.
When the Yellow Turbans rose,
attacking and seizing commanderies and counties,
the common people scattered in alarm,
but Hóng continued reciting classics, unmoved.
The bandits agreed among themselves not to enter his village.
People from the local gentry came to Hóng to seek refuge,
and all were spared.
At the age of fifty-seven,
he died in his earthen chamber.
His two younger brothers, Zhōng and Hóng,
were both slightly inferior to Hóng in integrity and conduct.
Zhōng, whose courtesy name was Zhèngfǔ,
was a friend of Fàn Pāng from the same commandery.
They were both implicated in the party proscription and later released.
Their story is in the Biography of Pāng.
During the Chūpíng period,
he became the Xiàng of Pèi,
arriving at the post in a reed carriage,
and was known for his purity and clarity.
When the world fell into great chaos,
Zhōng abandoned his office
and stayed as a guest in Shàngyú, Kuàijī.
Upon seeing Tàishǒu Wáng Láng's retinue so meticulously arrayed,
he disliked it in his heart
and feigned illness, isolating himself.
Later, when Sūn Cè conquered Kuàijī,
Zhōng and others sailed south to Jiāozhǐ.
When Emperor Xiàn established his capital in Xǔ,
Zhōng was summoned to be Wèiwèi.
Before he arrived,
he died.
Hóng, courtesy name Shàofǔ,
was ashamed of his family's noble and influential connections,
so he changed his name,
traveled on foot to his teacher's gate,
and did not respond to recruitment.
He died at home.
Zhōng's son, Bì,
served as a student deliberator for the commandery's office.
When the Yellow Turbans rose,
Bì followed Grand Administrator Zhào Qiān to attack them.
The army was defeated,
and Bì, along with Gōngcáo Fēng Guān and seven others, protected Zhào Qiān with their bodies,
all dying in battle.
Zhào Qiān thus escaped.
An imperial edict declared the residences of Bì and others
the "Seven Sages."
As for Fēng Guān,
he possessed integrity and resolve.
He was due to be nominated as Xiàolián,
but deeming his elder brother's reputation and position not yet prominent,
he was ashamed to accept it first.
So he claimed to suffer from a "wind-sickness,"
rendering him mute.
When a fire broke out in Guān's house,
he calmly went out to avoid it,
enduring it without speaking.
Several years later,
his brother was nominated,
whereupon Guān claimed to have recovered and served in the commandery.
The commentary says: Chén Píng had many secret plots,
yet it was known that his descendants would surely decline;
Bǐng Jí had hidden virtues,
and Xiàhóu Shèng knew that he and his descendants would be enfeoffed.
Ultimately, Chén Zhǎng was not enfeoffed as a marquis,
while Bǐng Chāng continued his state.
Though there are dissimilarities,
it is not possible to refute this;
the general trend is indeed so.
Between Yuán Gōng and the Dòu clan,
he showed affection for the imperial house,
upholding righteousness and elegance,
and could be called a paragon among royal ministers.
And when he administered the Chǔ prison case,
he never interrogated anyone for corruption,
his benevolence being sufficient to extend to later generations.
Is it not fitting
that his descendants flourished?
Zhāng Pú, courtesy name Mènghóu,
was a native of Xìyáng, Rǔnán,
and a descendant of Zhào Wáng Zhāng Áo.
Áo's son, Shòu,
was enfeoffed in Chíyáng township, Xìyáng.
Later, he was stripped of his title,
and settled there.
When Pú was young, he studied the *Shàngshū* under his grandfather Chōng,
and was able to transmit his teaching.
He also served Grand Astrologer Huán Róng.
He worked diligently and tirelessly,
gathering hundreds of disciples.
In the ninth year of Yǒngpíng (66 CE),
Xiǎnzōng established a school in the Nángōng for the young marquises of the Four Clans,
and appointed Five Classics masters.
Pú taught the *Shàngshū*,
frequently lecturing before the emperor.
Because his discussions and critiques met the emperor's expectations,
he was appointed as a Lang,
granted a carriage, horses, and clothing,
and then ordered to instruct the Crown Prince.
Pú was an honest and straightforward man,
adhering to classical principles.
During his lectures to the emperor,
he frequently offered correcting advice,
and was respected for his strictness.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
he promoted Pú to Shìzhōng and Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng.
A few months later,
he was sent out as Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn.
Pú, believing he had served closely at court,
did not understand why he was being sent out,
and was displeased.
He submitted a memorial, stating:
"Your foolish servant, relying on his classical learning, served at Your Majesty's side.
Having held no other post since youth,
I am unfamiliar with administrative law.
To presumptuously be entrusted with a commandery,
and administer affairs over a thousand *lǐ*,
will surely incur the fault of betraying imperial grace and disgracing the position.
I privately believed
that I would not be sent out of the capital.
I hoped to receive continued favor,
and be entrusted with a minor office,
where I would not avoid reporting
what officials found unsettling or what I saw and heard,
whether good or bad."
The imperial edict replied:
"The *Classic* says: 'Though the body is outside,
the heart does not leave the royal house.'
To govern a commandery and oversee the people
is an even greater way to repay your loyalty.
The good and the bad must be reported,
regardless of distance.
You are now granted three hundred thousand cash for travel expenses;
proceed to your post immediately."
Although Pú was a scholar,
he had a resolute and decisive character.
Upon arrival, he promoted brave and righteous men,
and challenged powerful bullies.
In Cháng'ān, there was a case of someone killing a bandit.
Pú immediately investigated it,
opining that even if a magistrate or chief accepted bribes,
it did not warrant death.
As for bandits, they were all hungry, cold, and hired laborers;
why should the law be applied so harshly to them?
A commandery clerk, Wáng Qīng,
whose grandfather Wēng,
had raised an army with former Grand Administrator Zhái Yì to attack Wáng Mǎng.
When Zhái Yì was defeated,
the remaining troops all surrendered,
but Wēng alone held his ground and fought valiantly.
Wáng Mǎng then burned him to death.
His father, Lóng,
served as Dūwèi Gōngcáo in the early Jiànwǔ era.
Qīng was a minor clerk.
He accompanied his father and the Dūwèi on a tour of the counties.
They encountered bandits on the road.
Lóng protected the Dūwèi with his body,
and died in the calamity.
Qīng was also pierced by an arrow in the throat,
making his voice hoarse and difficult.
Previous commandery administrators, seeing Qīng's physical impairment,
were ultimately unable to promote him.
When Pú saw him,
he sighed, saying:
"How can there be a family of such loyalty and righteousness, yet their services go unrewarded?"
He then promoted Qīng to the important position of Yòucáo,
and submitted a memorial recommending Qīng, citing three generations of his family's loyalty unto death,
deserving of special distinction.
The memorial was sent to the Three Dukes,
and Qīng was subsequently recruited by the Sīkōng.
After Pú was sent out,
the emperor, whenever he saw the tutors of the various princes,
would often say:
"Zhāng Pú, when he previously attended my lectures,
frequently offered counsel and corrections,
earnestly and sincerely,
stemming from a true heart.
He can be said to possess the demeanor of Shǐ Yú."
In the second year of Yuánhé (85 CE),
the emperor made an eastern tour and visited Dōngjùn.
He summoned Pú, his disciples, and the commandery and county clerks and officials to assemble in the courtyard.
The emperor first adopted the respectful manner of a student,
and had Pú lecture on a chapter of the *Shàngshū*.
Afterward, he resumed the etiquette of ruler and minister.
Rewards and gifts were exceptionally generous,
and everyone benefited.
Pú served for fifteen years.
At the beginning of Hédì's reign (88 CE),
he was transferred to be Grand Administrator of Wèijùn.
A native of the commandery, Zhèng Jù, was then Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and impeached Dòu Jǐng, the Zhí Jīn Wú, leading to his dismissal.
Jǐng later regained his position
and sent his aide Xià Měng to privately thank Pú, saying:
"Zhèng Jù is a petty man;
I was unjustly wronged by him.
I hear his son is an official,
indulging in wild excesses.
Taking just one of his men
would be enough to startle a hundred."
Pú was greatly angered.
He immediately arrested Měng and imprisoned him,
and sent a dispatch to the Zhí Jīn Wú's office,
suggesting that Měng, harboring a grudge against Zhèng Jù's son,
had falsely claimed to speak on Jǐng's behalf
to exact personal revenge.
Coincidentally, an amnesty decree for crimes was issued,
and Měng was then released.
Soon after,
Pú was summoned to serve as Hénán Yǐn.
Dòu Jǐng's household members again injured a market guard.
The officers arrested them,
but Jǐng, in a rage,
sent five hundred of his police cavalry, Hóu Hǎi and others, to beat and injure the market inspector.
Pú's subordinate officer Yáng Zhāng and others thoroughly investigated,
established Hǎi's crime,
and had him exiled to Shuòfāng.
Jǐng was resentful.
He then sent a letter summoning Zhāng and six others to become Zhí Jīn Wú officials,
intending to take revenge through this means.
Zhāng and the others, in fear,
reported to Pú,
and wished to confess to a fabricated crime
to decline Jǐng's summons.
Pú immediately reported the situation to the throne.
Empress Dowager Dòu issued an edict in reply:
"From now on,
when the Zhí Jīn Wú summons officials,
none are to be sent."
When the Dòu clan was defeated,
Pú then submitted a memorial, saying:
“I am truly foolish and
do not grasp the greater scheme of things.
I believe that although the Dòu clan has incurred their guilt,
their crimes and punishments have not yet been clearly established.
Later generations will not see the facts of their deeds,
but will only hear of their execution.
This is not a way to display the national laws
for posterity.
It would be appropriate to send the matter to the legal officials
and let it be judged fairly by the empire.
When Xiàn and others were favored and powerful,
the officials scrambled to fawn over them, fearing to be left behind,
all saying that Xiàn had received the trust of the deathbed command
and harbored the loyalty of Yī and Lǚ.
They even compared Lady Dèng to Wénmǔ.
Now that severe authority has been exercised,
everyone says they deserve death,
no longer considering their past and present
or examining the fairness of the matter.
I humbly observe that Xiàyáng Hóu Guī
has always maintained loyalty and goodness.
Previously, in conversations with me,
he always expressed a desire to serve with utmost devotion.
He restrained his guests
and never violated the law.
I have heard that the royal administration's punishment of close relatives
has the principle of three pardons,
which is neither too lenient nor too harsh.
Now, those who deliberate wish to select a severe and capable minister for Guī,
fearing that if he is pressed too hard,
he will surely not be spared entirely.
It would be appropriate to grant some leniency and pardon
to uphold abundant virtue.”
Emperor Hé was moved by Pú’s words,
and transferred Guī's fief,
sending him to his state only.
In the fifth year of Yǒngyuán (93 CE),
Pú was promoted to Tàipú.
A few months later,
he replaced Yǐn Mù as Tàiwèi.
He repeatedly submitted memorials asking to retire due to illness,
recommending Xú Fáng, the Administrator of Wèijùn, to succeed him.
The Emperor did not permit it,
and sent a Zhōnghuángmén to inquire about his illness,
adding precious delicacies
and granting 300,000 cash.
Pú then claimed to be critically ill.
At that time, his son Fān was serving as a Láng and侍講 (shìjiǎng).
The Emperor then ordered a Xiǎohuángmén to instruct Fān, saying:
“The Yin and Yang are out of harmony,
and countless people are suffering.
The court expects you, Duke, to ponder over gains and losses,
and be of one heart with the state.
Yet you feign illness to cleanse yourself
and seek to leave this heavy responsibility.
Who then will share my worries and burdens?
This is not to expect you to ‘break metal.’
The Sītú is truly ill,
the Sīkōng is old.
You, Duke, should humble yourself
and not reveal this instruction.”
Pú, in fear, went to the palace gate to apologize,
and returned to his duties.
Although Pú held a public office,
his father often lived in the countryside.
Whenever Pú was promoted,
his father would visit the capital once.
Once, his father came to visit Pú,
and it happened to be a seasonal festival.
The high officials and ministers, having concluded court,
all went to Pú's residence to offer wine and wish him longevity,
enjoying themselves throughout the day.
Everyone celebrated and admired this.
When his father died
and was buried,
an imperial edict dispatched an envoy with cattle and wine to release him from mourning.
Later, on an matter, Pú met with the Sīlì Xiàowèi Yàn Chēng at the court hall.
Pú casually said to Chēng:
“The officials appointed by the three departments
are mostly not the right people.”
When Chēng returned,
he immediately memorialized asking the three departments to verify their subordinate officials.
Pú had spoken privately
and did not expect Chēng to memorialize it;
he harbored deep resentment.
They met again to apologize at the palace gate.
Pú then reproached Chēng.
Chēng's reply was disobedient,
Pú became angry
and publicly reprimanded him.
Chēng then impeached Pú for having resentful words.
The Son of Heaven, considering Pú to be the former emperor's tutor,
issued an edict for high officials, Erudites, and court ministers to hold a conference.
Sītú Lǚ Gài memorialized that Pú, holding the position of one of the Three Ducal Ministers,
knew the decorum of the public court,
but instead of holding his breath and bowing to await an imperial command,
he became indignant and spoke loudly,
reproaching the imperial envoy.
This could not be shown to the four distant regions.
Thereupon, he was dismissed from office.
Pú returned to his village,
dismissed his students,
and closed his door to visitors.
Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiāng Hé Chǎng and many other memorialists defended Pú's public loyalty,
and the Emperor also greatly esteemed him.
In the sixteenth year (104 CE),
he was again appointed Guānglùxūn.
A few months later,
he replaced Lǔ Gōng as Sītú.
He died more than a month later.
The imperial carriage, in plain white, came to offer condolences,
granting land for his tomb
and gifts, with favor and honor exceeding other ministers.
When Pú was critically ill,
he instructed his sons, saying:
“The Xǐanjié Líng swept the ground and offered open-air sacrifices,
desiring to lead the empire in frugality.
As one of the Three Ducal Ministers,
since I could not promulgate the king's transforming influence
and make officials and common people follow the regulations,
how can I not strive for economy and moderation?
Do not erect a shrine hall;
you may build a covered veranda,
and offer sacrifices beneath it, that is all.”
His great-grandson Jì
was fond of Confucian studies,
and during the Guānghé era, reached the position of Sīkōng,
but was dismissed due to illness.
When he died,
Emperor Líng, out of old favor, posthumously granted him the title of Chējì Jiāngjūn and the seal and ribbon of a Guānnèihóu.
In that year,
in recognition of Jì's meritorious service as shìjiǎng,
his son Gēn was enfeoffed as Cáiyáng Xiānghóu.
Jì's younger brother Xǐ
became Sīkōng during the Chūpíng era.
Hán Léng, courtesy name Bóshī,
was a native of Wǔyáng, Yǐngchuān.
He was a descendant of Gōnggāo Hóu Tuī Dāng.
His family was for generations a prominent clan in the local area.
His father Xún
was the Administrator of Lǒngxī during the Jiànwǔ era.
Léng was orphaned at the age of four,
and was known for his filial piety and brotherly affection in raising his younger mother-side brother.
When he grew up,
he distributed several million in remaining wealth from his deceased father to his cousins,
and the local people esteemed him even more.
Initially, he served as Gōngcáo of the commandery.
The Administrator Gě Xìng suffered a stroke
and was too ill to attend to government affairs.
Léng secretly acted on Xìng's behalf,
for two years, ensuring no violations occurred.
Xìng's son once issued an instruction wanting to appoint an official.
Léng refused to obey,
and then allowed those who resented the son to report it.
The matter was sent down for investigation.
The officials, because Léng had concealed Xìng's illness
and unilaterally managed the commandery's duties,
consequently banned him from office.
Emperor Xiǎnzōng knew of his loyalty,
and later issued an edict specifically pardoning him.
Because of this, he was summoned for appointment,
and after five promotions, became Shàngshūlìng.
He was simultaneously praised for his talent along with Púshè Zhì Shòu and Shàngshū Chén Chǒng.
Emperor Sùzōng once bestowed swords upon the various Shàngshū,
but only these three men were specially given precious swords,
with their names personally inscribed by the Emperor:
“Hán Léng's Chǔ Lóngyuān,
Zhì Shòu's Shǔ Hànwén,
Chén Chǒng's Jìnán Zhuīchéng.”
At the time, commentators explained this thus:
Léng was profound and resourceful,
hence he received Lóngyuān;
Shòu was insightful and eloquent,
hence he received Hànwén;
Chǒng was honest and unadorned,
his goodness not outwardly displayed,
hence he received Zhuīchéng.
When Emperor Hè 漢和帝 ascended the throne,
Shìzhōng 侍中 Dòu Xiàn 竇憲 sent assassins to murder Cháng 暢, the Marquis of Dūxiāng 都鄉侯 and son of Qí Shāng Wáng 齊殤王, at the Upper East Gate (Shàngdōngmén 上東門).
The officials, fearing Dòu Xiàn 竇憲,
all cast suspicion on Cháng’s 暢 brothers.
An imperial edict dispatched the Shìyùshǐ 侍御史 to Qí 齊 to investigate the matter.
Léng 棱 submitted a memorial, arguing that since the murderer was in the capital,
it was inappropriate to neglect the near and inquire into the distant,
fearing it would become a laughingstock for treacherous ministers.
Empress Dowager Dòu 竇太后 was enraged
and severely reprimanded Léng 棱,
but Léng 棱 stubbornly adhered to his view.
When the matter came to light,
it turned out exactly as he had said.
Dòu Xiàn 竇憲, in panic,
petitioned the Empress Dowager to allow him to lead an expedition against the Northern Xiongnú 北匈奴 to atone for his crime.
Léng 棱 again submitted a memorial in remonstrance,
but the Empress Dowager did not comply.
When Dòu Xiàn 竇憲 achieved merit
and returned as Grand General (Dàjiàngjūn 大將軍),
his prestige shook the world.
He was again sent out to garrison Wǔwēi 武威.
At the time, the Emperor was going west to offer sacrifices at the imperial tombs (yuánlíng 園陵),
and an edict ordered Dòu Xiàn 竇憲 to meet the imperial carriage in Cháng’ān 長安.
When Dòu Xiàn 竇憲 arrived,
officials from the Shàngshū 尚書 downwards debated whether they should bow to him
and prostrate themselves, shouting "Long live!" (Wànsuì 萬歲).
Léng 棱, with a stern expression, said:
“Indeed, when associating with superiors, one should not be obsequious;
when associating with inferiors, one should not be disrespectful.
There is no ritual precedent for a subject to shout 'Long live!'”
Those who were debating were all ashamed and stopped.
Shàngshū Zuǒchéng 尚書左丞 Wáng Lóng 王龍 privately presented a memorandum to Dòu Xiàn 竇憲 with an offering of an ox and wine.
Léng 棱 impeached Wáng Lóng 王龍,
who was condemned to serve as a fortress laborer (chéngdàn 城旦).
While in court, Léng 棱 repeatedly recommended virtuous officials such as Yìng Shùn 應順, Lǚ Zhāng 呂章, and Zhōu Yū 周紆,
all of whom were famous at the time.
When the Dòu 竇 clan fell,
Léng 棱 presided over the investigation of their case,
thoroughly pursuing their partisans
and not resting for several months.
The Emperor, considering that he worried for the state and forgot his home,
bestowed upon him three hundred bolts of cloth.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Nányáng 南陽,
with special permission to pass by his home and visit his ancestral tombs (shàngzhǒng 上冢).
His fellow villagers considered this an honor.
Léng 棱 exposed thieves and bandits,
and the commandery trembled in fear;
his administration was known for its strictness and fairness.
After several years,
he was summoned to the capital to become Grand Coachman (Tàipú 太僕).
In the winter of the ninth year,
he replaced Zhāng Fèn 張奮 as Minister of Works (Sīkōng 司空).
He died the following year.
His son, Fǔ 輔,
reached the position of Chancellor of Zhào 趙相 during the reign of Emperor Ān 漢安帝.
Léng’s 棱 grandson, Yǎn 演,
served as Grand Administrator of Dānyáng 丹陽 during the reign of Emperor Shùn 漢順帝,
and his administration had a reputation for capability.
During the reign of Emperor Huán 漢桓帝, he became Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒).
When Grand General (Dàjiàngjūn 大將軍) Liáng Jì 梁冀 was executed,
Yǎn 演 was implicated for factional alignment and convicted.
His sentence was reduced from death,
and he was sent back to his home commandery.
Later, he was again summoned and appointed Colonel Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi 司隸校尉).
Zhōu Róng 周榮, courtesy name Píngsūn 平孫,
was a native of Shū 舒 in Lújiāng 廬江.
During the reign of Emperor Sù 漢肅宗,
he was recommended for his mastery of the classics (míngjīng 明經)
and appointed to the staff of Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒) Yuán Ān 袁安.
Yuán Ān 袁安 frequently discussed matters with him
and highly valued him.
When Yuán Ān 袁安 impeached Dòu Jǐng 竇景 and contended with Dòu Xiàn 竇憲 regarding the establishment of the Northern Chányú 北單于,
all the drafts were prepared by Zhōu Róng 周榮.
Xú Yǐ 徐齮, a client of the Dòu 竇 clan and an aide to the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi 太尉), deeply resented Zhōu Róng 周榮
and threatened him, saying:
“You are the trusted advisor to Duke Yuán 袁公,
impeaching the Dòu 竇 clan.
The Dòu 竇 clan has fierce warriors and assassins throughout the city.
Be careful!”
Zhōu Róng 周榮 replied:
“I, Róng 榮, am an orphan from Jiāng-Huái 江淮.
I have received great kindness from the late emperor
and have served as an official in two cities.
Now I am again serving as an official.
Even if I am harmed by the Dòu 竇 clan,
I will gladly accept it.”
Therefore, he often instructed his wife and children
that if he were to suddenly meet with an unforeseen calamity,
they should not perform the funeral rites,
hoping that his humble, decaying body might awaken the imperial court.
When the Dòu 竇 clan fell,
Zhōu Róng 周榮 gained fame from this.
He was promoted from Magistrate of Yǎn 郾 to Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令).
He was then sent out as Grand Administrator of Yǐngchuān 潁川.
Because of a legal transgression,
he was to be imprisoned,
but Emperor Hè 漢和帝, mindful of Zhōu Róng’s 周榮 loyalty and integrity,
demoted him to Magistrate of Gòng 共令.
After more than a year,
he was again appointed Grand Administrator of Shānyáng 山陽.
In every commandery and county he governed,
he was praised and recorded.
Due to old age and illness, he requested retirement
and died at home.
An edict specially granted him two hundred thousand coins
and appointed his son Xìng 興 as a Gentleman (Lángzhōng 郎中).
Xìng 興 had a good reputation in his youth.
During the Yǒngníng 永寧 era,
Shàngshū 尚書 Chén Zhōng 陳忠 submitted a memorial recommending Xìng 興, saying:
“Your servant humbly believes that in ancient times, when emperors issued decrees,
their words were always grand and refined,
and their language warm and beautiful,
passed down to later generations
and recorded in classics and scriptures.
Thus, Kǒng Ní 孔尼 (Confucius) admired the literary accomplishments of Táng 唐 and Yú 虞
and followed the rich culture of the Zhōu 周 dynasty.
Your servant secretly observes that Guānglù Láng 光祿郎 Zhōu Xìng 周興’s
filial piety and fraternal affection
are evident within his family,
and his pure and upright aspirations
are known throughout his home province.
He has accumulated knowledge of ancient and modern times,
is well-versed in many things,
and has examined
the chapters of the Sānfén 三墳
and the records of the Wǔdiǎn 五典, omitting nothing.
His literary compositions
are worthy of admiration and study.
The Shàngshū 尚書 transmit imperial commands
and act as the king's voice.
Your servants are ignorant and dim-witted,
and many of the gentlemen are vulgar literati,
with few elegant talents.
Whenever we draft imperial edicts
to be promulgated internally and externally,
we often seek help from each other,
or, being unable, act on our own free will,
with language often crude and rigid.
Xìng 興, with his extraordinary abilities,
is left to live among his peers,
which is truly regrettable.”
An edict then appointed Xìng 興 as Shàngshū Láng 尚書郎.
He died.
Xìng’s 興 son was Jǐng 景.
Jǐng’s 景 courtesy name was Zhòngxiǎng 仲饗.
He was appointed to the staff of Grand General (Dàjiàngjūn 大將軍) Liáng Jì 梁冀
and gradually promoted to Inspector of Yùzhōu 豫州 Cìshǐ 刺史 and Grand Administrator of Hénèi 河內.
He was fond of worthies and loved scholars,
always fearing that he would not be timely enough in selecting talents and recommending good people.
Every year at the time of seasonal change,
he would invite recommended officials to the rear hall
to feast with him.
After several such gatherings,
he would send them off.
The gifts he gave
were always abundant.
Afterward, he would select their fathers, elder brothers, and sons and younger brothers
for particularly distinguished treatment.
He often said:
“Ministers and their sons are bound by the same thread;
how can I not be generous?”
Before this, Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒) Hán Yǎn 韓演, while in Hénèi 河內,
was utterly impartial.
When an official was recommended and about to depart,
he would only say a single word of farewell,
and his benevolence did not extend to their families.
He said:
“It is sufficient that I have recommended you;
how can I let it benefit the entire household?”
Thus, contemporary commentators debated these two men.
Jǐng 景 was later summoned to the capital to become Grand Architect (Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng 將作大匠).
When Liáng Jì 梁冀 was executed,
Jǐng 景 was dismissed from office and forbidden from public service due to his former association with him.
However, the court, recognizing Jǐng’s 景 consistent loyalty and uprightness,
soon after
reappointed him Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令).
He was promoted to Grand Coachman (Tàipú 太僕) and Grand Master of Ceremonies (Wèiwèi 衛尉).
In the sixth year,
he replaced Liú Chǒng 劉寵 as Minister of Works (Sīkōng 司空).
At that time, eunuchs appointed people and their family members, filling many official positions.
When Jǐng 景 first took office,
he and Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi 太尉) Yáng Bǐng 楊秉 impeached numerous treacherous and cunning individuals.
More than fifty people, from generals to governors,
were dismissed.
This even implicated the Chief Regular Attendants (Zhōngchángshì 中常侍) Fángdōng Hóu Lǎn 封東侯覽 and Dōngwǔyáng Hóu Jù Yuán 東武陽侯具瑗,
both of whom were dismissed.
Everyone in the court praised him.
He served for two years
before being dismissed due to an earthquake (attributed to Heaven's disapproval).
After more than a year,
he again replaced Chén Fān 陳蕃 as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi 太尉).
He died in the first year of Jiànníng 建寧 (168 CE).
Because of his prior participation in deliberating and establishing Emperor Líng 漢靈帝,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānyáng Xiāng 安陽鄉侯.
His eldest son, Chóng 崇, succeeded him
and reached the position of Chancellor of Gānlíng 甘陵相.
Zhōng Zǐ-Zhōng
had held various posts since his youth,
and was successively promoted to Dàsīnóng.
Zhōng’s son, Huī,
had previously served as Luòyáng Lìng,
but had resigned and returned home.
The brothers were fond of entertaining guests,
and were influential in the Jiāng-Huái region.
Whenever they went out, they were always accompanied by more than a hundred carriages.
When the Emperor passed away,
Huī heard that the capital was unstable,
and came to visit Zhōng.
Dǒng Zhuó heard about this and was displeased,
so he sent soldiers to seize and kill the brothers.
Zhōng later succeeded Huángfǔ Sōng as Tàiwèi,
and concurrently held the office of Lù Shàngshūshì.
He was dismissed due to natural disasters.
He later served as Wèiwèi,
and accompanied Xiàndì on his eastward return to Luòyáng.
The encomium states: Yuán Gōng was steady and reliable,
truly dedicated to what he upheld.
Remembering only virtue,
his descendants received favor for generations.
Mèng Hóu was learned and broad,
attending to imperial pronouncements behind the curtain.
Léng and Róng served their lord,
their aspirations like the sparrowhawk and sparrow.
Biographies of Guō and Chén, Chapter 36 (Guō Gōng, his disciple Zhèn; Chén Chǒng, his son Zhōng)
Guō Gōng, courtesy name Zhòngsūn,
was a native of Yángzhái, Yǐngchuān.
His family had been officials for generations.
His father, Hóng,
was skilled in the laws of Xiǎo-Dù.
Tàishǒu Kòu Xún appointed Hóng as Juécáo Yuàn,
and he judged cases for thirty years,
applying the law fairly.
Those whose cases Hóng had decided,
harbored no resentment afterward.
Within the commandery, he was compared to Dōnghǎi Yú Gōng.
He died at the age of ninety-five.
Gōng began learning his father's profession in his youth,
lecturing to several hundred disciples.
Later, he became a commandery official,
and was appointed to the ducal mansion.
During the Yǒngpíng era,
Fèngchē Dūwèi Dòu Gù led an expedition against the Xiōngnú,
with Qí Dūwèi Qín Péng as his deputy.
Péng, while in a separate encampment, unilaterally executed a man according to the law.
Gù memorialized that Péng had acted without authorization,
and requested his execution.
Xiǎnzōng then summoned the Gōngqīng and court officials to assess the crime.
Gōng, being knowledgeable in law,
was summoned to participate in the deliberation.
All present agreed with Gù's memorial,
but Gōng alone said:
"According to the law,
Péng was permitted to execute him."
The Emperor said:
"On military expeditions,
a Xiàowèi is entirely subordinate to the commander.
Since Péng did not possess the symbolic axe and halberd,
how could he unilaterally kill someone?"
Gōng replied:
"Being entirely subordinate to the commander
refers to being within the main army division.
Now Péng commanded a separate army as an independent general,
which is different from that situation.
Military matters require immediate action;
it is not permissible to first consult the commander-in-chief.
Furthermore, the Hàn system considers the official ceremonial halberd as the symbolic axe and halberd.
Legally, this does not constitute a crime."
The Emperor followed Gōng's advice.
There was also a case where brothers jointly committed murder,
but the culpability had not been definitively assigned.
The Emperor, believing the elder brother failed to instruct the younger,
therefore ordered the elder brother to receive a heavier sentence and commuted the younger brother's death penalty.
Zhōng Chángshì Sūn Zhāng mistakenly announced the imperial decree,
stating that both would receive heavier sentences.
The Shàngshū memorialized that Zhāng had falsified an imperial decree,
and his crime was punishable by execution.
The Emperor again summoned Gōng to question him.
Gōng replied,
"Zhāng should be fined."
The Emperor said:
"Zhāng falsified an imperial decree, leading to a killing.
How can he merely be fined?"
Gōng said:
"Laws distinguish between intentional and unintentional acts.
Zhāng's error in transmitting the order
was unintentional;
unintentional errors are treated lightly in the law."
The Emperor said:
"Zhāng is from the same county as the prisoner;
I suspect it was intentional."
Gōng said:
"'The Zhōu road is like a grindstone,
straight as an arrow.'
'A gentleman does not anticipate deceit.'
Your Majesty's law should emulate Heaven;
punishments cannot be bent by personal conjecture."
The Emperor said:
"Excellent."
Gōng was promoted to Tíngwèi Zhèng,
but was dismissed due to legal infractions.
After three further promotions,
in the third year of Yuánhé (86 CE),
he was appointed Tíngwèi.
Gōng's family had managed legal affairs for generations;
his priority was clemency and fairness.
When he took charge of the judicial office,
in judging cases and sentencing,
he often showed leniency and forgiveness.
He then compiled a list of forty-one serious articles of law that could be treated lightly and submitted it to the throne.
All of these measures were implemented
and recorded in the statutes.
In the first year of Zhānghé (87 CE),
a general amnesty was granted to all prisoners in the empire for crimes committed before the丙zǐ day of the fourth month, reducing death sentences by one degree,
and commuting corporal punishment.
They were to be sent to Jīnchéng.
However, the text did not cover fugitives who had not yet been discovered.
Gōng submitted a sealed memorial, stating:
"The sagely grace in reducing death sentences and sending people to guard the borders
is out of regard for human life.
Currently, there are countless thousands of fugitives who committed capital crimes.
Since the amnesty,
many have been arrested,
but the imperial decree does not cover them,
and all of them must be re-tried.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty's grace extends to all, forgiving and pardoning everyone;
those with death sentences and lesser crimes have all received a new lease on life,
yet arrested fugitives alone do not partake in this benevolence.
I propose that
those who committed capital crimes before the amnesty and were imprisoned after it
should all be exempted from corporal punishment and sent to Jīnchéng,
to preserve human lives and benefit the border."
Sùzōng approved,
and immediately issued an edict of amnesty.
Gōng's legal interpretations and recommendations
saved many lives.
In the sixth year of Yǒngyuán (94 CE),
he died in office.
His son, Yǐn,
was also skilled in law,
and rose to Nányáng Tàishǒu,
where his administration left a notable record.
His disciple was Zhèn.
Zhèn, courtesy name Huánzhōng,
diligently pursued his family's profession from a young age.
He was appointed to the Tàiwèi's mansion,
and after two promotions, became Shàngshū during the Yán'guāng era.
When Zhōng Huángmén Sūn Chéng executed Zhōng Chángshì Jiāng Jīng and others and installed the King of Jìyīn,
Zhèn led the Yǔlín soldiers to attack and kill Wèiwèi Yán Jǐng,
thus achieving a great accomplishment.
This event is recorded in the "Biography of Eunuchs."
After two more promotions, he became Shàngshū Lìng.
The Tàifù and Sān Gōng memorialized that Zhèn had bravely faced drawn blades,
personally slaying traitorous officials,
annihilating the corrupt faction,
and thereby bringing peace to the imperial ancestral temple.
His merit was comparable to Liú Zhāng,
and he deserved a distinguished title and land
to encourage loyalty and integrity.
Consequently, Zhèn was enfeoffed as Dìngyǐng Hóu,
with an estate of two thousand households.
He was appointed Hénán Yǐn,
then transferred to Tíngwèi,
but was dismissed.
In the fourth year of Yǒngjiàn (129 CE),
he died at home.
An imperial edict granted him burial land.
His eldest son, Hè, was to inherit the peerage,
but he yielded it to his younger brother, Shí, and fled.
After several years,
an imperial edict commanded the Dàhónglú to order the provinces and commanderies to pursue him.
Hè had no choice
but to come out and accept the enfeoffment.
After several promotions,
he again reached Tíngwèi.
After Hè's death,
Shùndì, remembering Zhèn's achievements,
issued an edict posthumously bestowing on Zhèn the title Zhāowǔ Hóu,
and on Hè the title Chéng Hóu.
Hè's younger brother, Zhēn,
also rose to Tíngwèi due to his legal acumen.
Zhèn's disciple, Xǐ,
diligently mastered his family's profession from a young age,
and was also fond of Confucian studies,
gaining a good reputation.
During the Yánxī era, he also served as Tíngwèi.
In the second year of Jiànníng (169 CE),
he replaced Liú Chǒng as
Tàiwèi.
Xǐ's son, Hóng,
rose to Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and was enfeoffed as Chéng'ān Xiāng Hóu.
From Guō Hóng onwards,
for several generations, the Guō clan all passed down legal knowledge.
Among their descendants, one person reached the rank of Gōng,
seven were Tíngwèi,
three were Hóu,
over twenty were Cìshǐ, Èrqiānshí, Shìzhōng, or Zhōnglángjiàng,
and very many were Shìyùshǐ, Zhèng, Jiān, or Píng.
During Emperor Shùn's reign,
Wú Xióng Jìgāo from Hénán, a Tíngwèi,
was known for his clear understanding of the law
and fair judgment of cases.
He started as an orphan official
and rose to the position of Sītú.
When Wú Xióng was young, his family was poor.
His mother died,
and he buried her in a place where people would not normally build a mound,
choosing that spot for her burial.
He arranged the funeral quickly
without consulting auspicious days or times.
Physicians and sorcerers all said that his clan would be exterminated,
but Wú Xióng paid no heed.
Later, his son Xīn and grandson Gōng
were Tíngwèi for three generations,
becoming a famous legal family.
Originally,
during Emperor Sù's reign,
Zhào Xīng from Xiàpī, the Sīlì Xiàowèi, also disregarded taboos and prohibitions.
Whenever he entered an official residence,
he would immediately repair and renovate the buildings,
moving openings and altering structures,
thus deliberately violating superstitions.
Yet his family's ranks and emoluments
only grew more abundant and prosperous.
He rose to the position of Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
His son, Jùn,
was a Tàifù
and renowned for his talent and capability.
His grandson, Ānshì,
was the Lǔ Xiàng.
Three generations all served as Sīlì;
at the time, their prominence was much praised.
During Emperor Huán's reign,
there was a Chén Bójìng in Rǔnán.
When he walked, he would take careful, measured steps;
when he sat, his knees would be perfectly aligned.
When scolding dogs or horses,
he would never use the word "death."
If his eyes saw something,
he would not eat its meat.
If he heard ill omens on the road,
he would unharness his carriage and stop.
If he encountered a "return taboo" on his way back,
he would lodge in a village inn.
As he grew old, he became idle and stagnant,
never rising beyond being recommended as Xiàolián.
Later, he was implicated when his son-in-law became a fugitive official.
The Tàishǒu Shào Kuí was enraged and killed him.
People at the time who disregarded taboos
often cited this as proof.
Commentary says: Zēngzǐ said:
"If the superior loses the Way,
the people have long been scattered.
If one truly understands their situation,
then one should commiserate with pity and not rejoice."
Indeed, if one does not rejoice upon understanding the situation, then a compassionate heart is employed.
If a compassionate heart is employed, then one can be entrusted with the task of distinguishing right from wrong.
When worthy gentlemen judge cases,
must they not be guided by this principle?
Guō Gōng started as a clerk,
and whether cases were minor or major, he always investigated them thoroughly.
When examining his fair sentencing and meticulous judgments,
were they not perhaps akin to "not rejoicing"?
Thus, by putting oneself in others' shoes to discuss matters,
and setting aside appearances to grasp the true situation,
it is perhaps through this that legal families are able to extend their prosperity through generations!
Chén Chǒng, courtesy name Zhāogōng,
was a native of Xiáo, Pèiguó.
His great-grandfather, Xián,
served as Shàngshū during the reign of Emperors Chéng and Āi, specializing in laws and ordinances.
During Emperor Píng's reign,
Wáng Mǎng assisted in governance
and extensively changed the Hàn system.
Xián secretly disapproved of this.
When Wáng Mǎng, on account of Lǚ Kuān's incident, punished those who did not support him, such as Hé Wǔ and Bào Xuān,
Xián sighed and said:
"The Yìjīng says: 'A gentleman sees the subtle beginning and acts,
not waiting until the end of the day.'
I can depart now!"
He immediately requested to resign, pleading old age.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he summoned Xián to be Zhǎngkòu Dàfū,
but Xián refused, feigning illness.
At that time, his three sons, Cān, Fēng, and Qīn, were all in office.
He ordered them all to resign their posts,
and father and sons returned together to their hometown.
They closed their doors and did not go out,
still observing the Hàn imperial ancestral rites.
When people asked why,
Xián said:
"Did my ancestors know the Wáng family's rites?"
Later, Wáng Mǎng again summoned Xián,
who then claimed his illness was critical.
Thereupon, he collected all his family's law books and documents
and hid them in the walls.
Xián was benevolent and compassionate by nature,
and often warned his descendants:
"When discussing laws for others,
one should lean towards leniency.
Even if there is a profit of a hundred gold,
be careful not to engage in heavy penalties with others."
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
Qīn's son, Gōng, was Tíngwèi Zuǒjiān
but died early.
Gōng had a son, Chǒng,
who was well-versed in the family profession.
In his youth, he served as a provincial and commandery official,
and was invited to the office of Sītú Bào Yù.
At this time, the officials in the Three Ducal Ministries especially valued socializing,
considering it noble not to attend to official duties.
Chǒng often disagreed with this,
and alone diligently applied himself to public affairs,
frequently presenting Bào Yù with current expedient measures.
Bào Yù highly regarded his ability
and transferred him to be Cícáo,
in charge of all lawsuits in the realm.
His judgments
never failed to satisfy the public.
At that time, lawsuits under the Sītú
sometimes dragged on for decades,
and cases were mixed and complicated,
easily leading to unfair leniency or severity,
allowing corrupt officials to exploit opportunities.
Chǒng compiled seven scrolls of legal precedents for Bào Yù,
categorizing and arranging all judgments
according to their types.
Bào Yù submitted them to the emperor,
and thereafter, the Ducal Ministries adopted them as law.
After three transfers,
at the beginning of Sùzōng's reign,
he became Shàngshū.
At that time, following the precedents of the Yǒngpíng era,
administrative governance was still strict and severe,
and the Shàngshū's decisions were generally inclined towards severity.
Chǒng, believing that the emperor had just ascended the throne,
should reform the harsh customs of the previous era.
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial which stated:
“Your servant has heard that in the governance of the former kings,
rewards were not excessive,
and punishments were not abusive.
If it could not be avoided,
it was better to be excessive than abusive.
Thus, Emperor Táng Yáo's canon states:
‘For unwitting offenses and disasters, grant amnesty.’
The Duke of Zhōu composed a warning:
‘Do not mishandle the common lawsuits.’
Bó Yí's canon states:
‘Revere the five punishments,
to complete the three virtues.’
From this, it can be said that
the governance of the sages and worthies
regarded penal law as paramount.
In the past, the judgment of cases was strict and clear,
thereby deterring and punishing wickedness.
Once wickedness is pacified,
it must be supplemented with leniency.
Your Majesty, upon ascending the throne,
has followed this principle,
repeatedly issuing edicts to all officials,
greatly promoting peace and harmony.
However, the officials in charge
have not fully followed and complied;
their application of penal laws
is still severe and harsh.
Those who judge cases are eager for the pain of cruel flogging and torture;
those who enforce the law are troubled by the writings of slanderous deceit and excessiveness.
Some even exploit public authority for private gain,
indulging in their power and influence.
Indeed, governing is like tuning a qín and sè:
if the thick strings are too taut, the thin strings will break.
Therefore, Zǐgòng criticized Zāngsūn's harsh laws,
and praised Zhèng Qiáo's benevolent governance.
The Shī states: ‘Neither rigid nor soft,
govern with ease.’
Currently, Your Majesty's sagely virtue fills and pervades
heaven and earth.
[一０]It is fitting to uphold the way of the former kings
and abolish troublesome and harsh laws.
Lighten floggings and beatings
to benefit all living beings;
perfect and expand supreme virtue
to conform to the will of Heaven.”
The Emperor respectfully accepted Chǒng's words,
and thereafter always inclined towards leniency and generosity in his affairs.
Subsequently, he issued an edict to the officials
to abolish drilling and stabbing and other cruel penalties,
[一一]to loosen prohibitions on ominous and evil practices,
and to abolish more than fifty cases of forced interpretations and appeals,
establishing them as permanent regulations.
[一二]After this, the people's customs became peaceful,
and there were frequent auspicious signs.
According to Han old practice, the reporting of judicial cases involving severe penalties
always took place throughout the three winter months.
At that time, the Emperor first changed it to only the tenth month at the beginning of winter.
In the second year of Yuánhé,
there was a drought.
The Commander of Chángshuǐ, Jiǎ Zōng and others memorialized,
believing that the failure to complete judicial cases during the three winter months
resulted in weak yin energy
and excessive yang energy,
thereby causing calamities and drought;
the fault lay in this.
The Emperor referred their statement to the Gōngqīng for discussion.
Chǒng submitted a memorial stating:
“At the winter solstice,
yang energy begins to sprout.
Therefore, in the eleventh month, there is the corresponding growth of orchids, shègān, yún, and lì.
The seasonal ordinance says: ‘All living things are flourishing;
maintain physical forms peacefully.’
Heaven regards it as the beginning of the year;
Zhōu regards it as spring.
In the twelfth month, yang energy rises and connects;
pheasants crow and chickens lay eggs.
Earth regards it as the beginning of the year;
Yīn regards it as spring.
In the thirteenth month, yang energy has already arrived;
Heaven and Earth have already mingled;
all myriad things emerge;
hibernating insects begin to stir.
Humans regard it as the beginning of the year;
Xià regards it as spring.
The three subtle principles are established and revealed,
thereby connecting the three successions.
Zhōu uses the Celestial Primal,
Yīn uses the Terrestrial Primal,
Xià uses the Human Primal.
If executions are carried out at this time,
then both the Yīn and Zhōu New Year's Day would be stained with blood,
which does not conform to human sentiment
and does not accord with the will of Heaven.
The Yuèlìng states: ‘In the first month of winter,
expedite judicial punishments,
leave no crimes pending.’
This clearly indicates that major punishments must be completed by the beginning of winter.
It also states: ‘In the [middle] month of winter,
the body desires tranquility,
affairs desire stillness.’
If one descends with awe and anger,
it cannot be called tranquility;
if one carries out major executions,
it cannot be called stillness.
Those who debate all say: ‘The cause of the drought
is the fault of changing the laws.’
Your servant believes that Yīn and Zhōu did not judge cases according to the three subtle principles
yet achieved peace and prosperity through transformation,
without disasters.
Before Yuánhé,
the three winter months were always used,
yet floods and droughts
often caused suffering.
From this, it can be said that
disasters arise from other causes,
not from changing the laws.
Qín adopted oppressive governance,
carrying out executions in all four seasons.
When the holy Hàn first rose,
it changed to simplicity and ease.
Xiāo Hé drafted the laws,
judging prisoners in the last month of autumn,
both avoiding the month of Lìchūn,
[一０]but not accounting for the proper times of Heaven and Earth,
and the springs of the two kings,
which was indeed quite a deviation.
[一一]Your Majesty, having probed the obscure and analyzed the subtle,
truly adheres to the mean,
[一二]correcting centuries of error,
and establishing merits for eternity.
[一三]Above, there is reverence in welcoming and following;
below, there is the grace of upholding the subtle.
[一四]It accords with the texts of the Chūnqiū
and aligns with the intent of the Yuèlìng.
[一五]This sacred accomplishment and splendid deed
should not be doubted midway.”
After the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor accepted it
and subsequently did not change the practice again.
Chǒng was meticulous by nature,
often saying that the duty of a minister
was to not be heedless and reckless.
While he was in a pivotal position,
he dismissed his disciples
and refused close friends,
attending only to public affairs.
The court valued him.
Empress's younger brother, the Attendant (Shìzhōng) Dòu Xiàn,
recommended Zhēndìng Prefect Zhāng Lín to be Shàngshū.
The Emperor asked Chǒng about him.
Chǒng replied,
“Although Lín possesses talent,
his conduct has always been greedy and corrupt.”
Dòu Xiàn deeply resented Chǒng because of this.
Lín was eventually employed
but was later convicted for corruption.
When the Emperor passed away,
Dòu Xiàn and others held power.
They often held a grudge against Chǒng,
and therefore reported to the Empress Dowager,
ordering him to take charge of the funeral arrangements,
intending to punish him for any mistake.
The Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng) Bāo Dé, who had always respected Chǒng,
persuaded Dòu Xiàn's younger brother, the Marquis of Xiàyáng, Dòu Guī, saying:
“Chén Chǒng served the late emperor,
and was deeply trusted and relied upon.
Therefore, he remained in the imperial secretariat for a long time,
and his rewards and gifts were exceptional.
Now, if he does not receive the reward for his loyalty and ability,
but is judged for trivial matters,
it would truly harm the virtue of an assisting government that tolerates and forgives.”
Dòu Guī also admired worthy men
and deeply agreed with him.
Therefore, Chǒng was able to be appointed as the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Tài Mountain.
Later, he was transferred to become the Administrator of Guǎnghàn.
In Xīzhōu, powerful families engaged in widespread land grabbing,
and many officials were corrupt and greedy.
Lawsuits numbered in the hundreds daily.
When Chǒng arrived,
he conspicuously employed able officials like Wáng Huàn and Tán Xiǎn,
making them his trusted advisors.
The number of lawsuits decreased daily,
and the commandery became clear and solemn.
Previously, to the south of Luò Xiàn city,
whenever there was overcast weather and rain,
cries were often heard from within the official residence,
persisting for several decades.
Chǒng heard about this and doubted its cause,
so he sent an official to investigate.
Upon his return, the official reported:
"During times of decline and disorder,
many people died here,
and their bones were not buried.
Perhaps they are still there?"
Chǒng was deeply moved and sighed with compassion,
immediately ordering the county to collect and bury all the remains.
From then on, the crying sounds ceased.
When Dòu Xiàn became Grand General and campaigned against the Xiōngnú,
all officials from the imperial court down to the commanderies and kingdoms, without exception, sent their subordinates' sons and younger brothers to offer gifts.
However, Chǒng, along with Zhāng Chēn of Rǔnán, the Chancellor of Zhōngshān,
and Yīng Shùn, the Chancellor of Dōngpíng,
upheld righteousness and did not yield.
Later, Emperor Hé heard of this
and promoted Chǒng to Grand Minister of Agriculture,
Zhāng Chēn to Grand Coachman,
and Yīng Shùn to Left Protector of the Capital.
In the sixth year of Yǒngyuán (94 CE),
Chǒng replaced Guō Gōng as Minister of Justice.
His nature was benevolent and compassionate.
As a judicial official,
he frequently deliberated on difficult cases,
often personally drafting memorials,
always adhering to the classics,
and striving for leniency and forgiveness.
The Emperor consistently followed his advice,
saving a great many lives.
The practice of harsh and intricate legal interpretations
was somewhat mitigated by him.
Chǒng also reviewed and collated the laws and statutes,
removing those that exceeded the Fǔ Xíng.
He said:
"Your minister has heard that the Rítual Classics number three hundred,
with three thousand rules of decorum;
thus, the Fǔ Xíng has two hundred capital punishments
and three thousand lesser punishments.
What ritual rejects,
punishment embraces;
a transgression of ritual leads to punishment,
they are mutually indicative.
Currently, the laws and statutes prescribe six hundred and ten death penalties,
one thousand six hundred and ninety-eight penalties of mutilation,
and two thousand six hundred and eighty-one penalties of redemption or lighter.
Those that exceed the Fǔ Xíng number one thousand nine hundred and eighty-nine,
comprising four hundred and ten capital punishments,
one thousand five hundred mutilation punishments,
and seventy-nine redemption punishments.
The Chūnqiū Bǎo Qián Tú states: 'A king reforms the laws once every three hundred years.'
Since the founding of the Hàn dynasty,
three hundred and two years have passed,
and edicts and regulations have gradually increased,
with an infinite number of clauses.
Moreover, there are three schools of law,
each with differing interpretations.
It is advisable to order the Three Excellencies and the Minister of Justice to standardize the laws and statutes.
Those that accord with the classics and are reasonable
should allow for two hundred capital punishments,
and two thousand eight hundred mutilation and redemption punishments,
totaling three thousand.
All other regulations should be deleted,
to align with ritual,
making it easy for all people to understand and observe,
thereby achieving the beauty of 'no need for punishments,'
and transmitting it limitlessly."
Before it could be implemented,
he was implicated and found guilty of an imperial prison official colluding with a prisoner.
An imperial edict specifically pardoned his punishment,
and he was appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was promoted to Grand Herald.
Chǒng served in two commanderies and as three high ministers;
wherever he served, he left a mark
and was highly praised at the time.
In the sixteenth year of Yǒngyuán (104 CE),
he replaced Xú Fáng as Minister of Works.
Although Chǒng was proficient in law,
he also thoroughly understood the classics;
his memorials and deliberations were gentle and refined,
and he was known as a capable minister.
He died in office after three years.
Yǐn Qín of Nányáng, the Grand Minister of the Court, replaced him as Minister of Works.
Qín, whose courtesy name was Shúliáng,
had a strong character and loved learning.
He lived in seclusion away from others,
with thorns growing at his gate;
people at the time esteemed his integrity.
Later, for his role in establishing Emperor Ān,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Fútíng,
with five hundred households.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (107 CE),
due to rain damage to the crops,
he was dismissed by decree and returned to his fief.
He died of illness,
without a son,
and his fief was abolished.
Chǒng's son was Zhōng.
Zhōng, whose courtesy name was Bóshǐ, was recruited to the Office of the Minister over the Masses in the Yǒngshǐ era (107-113 CE).
He was successively promoted three times to Assistant Minister of Justice,
gaining renown for his talent.
Liú Kǎi, the Minister over the Masses, recommended Zhōng as being thoroughly conversant with the law
and suitable for confidential matters.
Thereupon, he was promoted to Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
and assigned to manage the departments of the Three Excellencies.
Zhōng, considering that his family had specialized in criminal law for generations,
devoted himself to being lenient and thorough.
Initially,
when his father Chǒng was Minister of Justice,
he memorialized for the removal of Hàn laws that exceeded the Fǔ Xíng,
but it was not implemented,
and after Chǒng's dismissal, it was abandoned.
However, harsh laws gradually proliferated,
and people could not bear them.
Zhōng generally followed Chǒng's intentions,
memorializing twenty-three articles
as precedents for adjudicating cases,
to eliminate the abuses of requesting and questioning judgments.
He also memorialized for the abolition of the silk-worm chamber punishment;
the lifting of the three-generation prohibition from office for corrupt officials;
allowing those who killed in a fit of madness to receive a lighter sentence;
and permitting mothers, sons, or brothers to die in place of each other,
pardoning the one who was substituted.
All these matters were implemented.
When Empress Dowager Dèng died,
Emperor Ān began to personally attend to court affairs.
Zhōng believed that at the beginning of his reign,
it was appropriate to discreetly seek out talented individuals
to promote and assist in moral transformation.
He frequently recommended recluses and upright scholars such as Féng Liáng, Zhōu Xiè, Dù Gēn, and Chéng Yìshì.
Consequently, imperial carriages were dispatched to courteously invite Liáng, Xiè, and others.
Later, there were successive calamities and unusual phenomena,
and an imperial edict called for the recommendation of men of integrity.
The Three Excellencies, high officials, and all functionaries each submitted sealed memorials.
Zhōng, seeing that the imperial edict had opened the way for remonstrance,
feared that those who spoke out would be overly vehement,
and might not be tolerated.
Therefore, he submitted a memorial to preemptively broaden the Emperor's understanding.
He said:
"Your minister has heard that benevolent rulers emulate the vastness of mountains and marshes,
accepting candid and direct counsel;
loyal ministers exhaust their honest remonstrations,
not fearing the harm of unpleasant words.
Thus, Emperor Gāozǔ overlooked Zhōu Chāng's comparison of him to Jié and Zhòu;
Emperor Xiàowén praised Yuán Àng's jibe about him being a pig-like emperor;
Emperor Wǔ accepted Dōngfāng Shuò's correction in the Xuānshì Chamber;
and Emperor Yuán tolerated Xuē Guǎngdé's extreme self-injuring remonstrance.
In the past, Duke Píng of Jìn asked Shú Xiàng: 'What is the greatest calamity for a state?'
He replied: 'If great ministers enjoy high emoluments but do not remonstrate to the fullest,
and minor officials fear punishment and dare not speak,
and the sentiments of the lower ranks do not reach above,
this is the greatest calamity.'
The Duke said: 'Good.'
Thereupon, he issued an order stating: 'I wish to promote good;
if anyone has a petition that is not passed up,
the crime is punishable by death.'
Now, Your sagacious edict exalts the virtue of Gāozōng,
demonstrates the sincerity of Sòng Jǐng,
attributes fault to yourself,
and seeks advice from all officials.
Those who speak out, seeing Dù Gēn, Chéng Yìshì, and others recently commended and recorded,
and prominently listed in the two official departments,
will surely respond to the wind and echo the call,
vying to be candid and direct.
If their counsel is brilliant and their strategies unique,
they should be immediately adopted.
If their insights are narrow,
and they make unwarranted criticisms,
even if their words are bitter and unpleasant to the ear,
and lack factual basis,
they should still be treated with gentleness and tolerance,
to demonstrate the virtue of a sagacious court that tolerates all opinions.
If there are men of integrity
whose answers during questioning are superior,
they should be considered,
and specially promoted by one rank,
to broaden the path for direct speech."
After the memorial was presented,
an imperial edict appointed Shī Yán of Pèi Guó, a man of integrity and high caliber, as Imperial Household Grandee.
Yán later rose to the position of Grand Commandant.
The regular attendants Jiāng Jīng and Lǐ Rùn, among others, were all made marquises
and together held positions of power.
The Emperor also loved and trusted his foster mother, Wáng Shèng,
whom he enfeoffed as Yěwáng Jūn.
Zhōng harbored internal fear and discontent but dared not remonstrate.
So he wrote the essay "On the Gentleman of the Court" to satirize,
but the text is long and thus not included here.
Since the Emperor's ascension to the throne,
there had been frequent encounters with the hardships of the Yuán’èr era.
The common people fled and dispersed,
and bandits rose everywhere.
Commanderies and counties covered up for each other,
none willing to expose the truth.
Zhōng alone worried about this
and submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the light is the beginning of the heavy,
and the small is the source of the great.
Thus, a dike collapses from an anthill,
and qi leaks from a needle's point.
Therefore, the discerning are cautious about the minute,
and the wise recognize the subtle signs.
The Book says: 'The small must not be left unpunished.'
The Odes say: 'Do not indulge deceitful followers,
so as to guard against the wicked.'
This is to uphold the root and eliminate the branches,
a deep consideration.
Your servant has observed that since the first year of the era,
banditry has erupted repeatedly,
attacking outposts and plundering,
causing much injury and death.
If house-breakers are not prohibited,
it leads to violent robbers;
if violent robbers are not stopped,
they become organized marauders;
if organized marauders form groups,
they will certainly engender great villainy.
Therefore, the provisions for fugitives
are urgent in the laws,
to the extent that providing passage or food
leads to the death penalty.
Yet recently,
no one considers this a concern.
Prefectural and commandery supervisors are negligent,
and chief officials' defenses are not strict.
All wish to gain empty reputations,
fearing to admit to banditry.
Even when something is discovered,
they do not strive to clarify it.
Some even unleash their power and arbitrary anger,
causing innocent people to fall.
Others are forced to huddle with their neighbors,
collecting funds among themselves.
Or they follow officials in pursuit,
bustling about on the roads.
Because of this, households attacked by bandits
dare not report it.
Neighbors and fellow villagers
pressure each other,
some even paying out private wealth
to compensate for what was lost.
Only those cases that are conspicuously evident and cannot be hidden
are then revealed.
This gradual decline
will eventually become a custom.
The punishment for brigands
all stems from this.
[一０] The case of Zhāng Bólù of Bóhǎi two years ago
can serve as a grave warning.
The track of an overturned carriage
is not far away.
Losing control at the end,
one must seek the source.
It is fitting to review and augment the old statutes
to prevent future occurrences.
Henceforth, if violent robbers are discovered by a superior official or by another commandery or county,
upon the first incident,
all subordinate officials shall be punished according to law.
[一一] The commandant shall be demoted one rank,
and the magistrate and chief shall redeem their guilt with three months' salary;
upon the second incident,
the commandant shall be dismissed,
and the magistrate and chief demoted one rank;
upon the third incident or more,
the magistrate and chief shall be dismissed.
It would be appropriate to compile articles of law,
formulate them into an imperial edict,
and strictly instruct the regional inspectors
to rigorously investigate and punish.
I hope to supplement leniency with severity,
striking fear into evildoers.
Recently, in late summer, there was intense heat,
but the seasons were out of balance.
[一二] Cold air came out of season,
and waters surged abnormally.
Heaven's sending of anomalies
must have its reasons.
Those virtuous scholars who have been recommended
should be questioned on the state's policies,
the errors in royal affairs,
and the reasons for the ineffectiveness of the warm qi.
I hope for candid words
to heed Heaven's warning."
In the third year of Yuánchū, an edict was issued
allowing high officials to observe a three-year mourning period,
returning to their posts after the mourning concluded.
Zhōng thereupon memorialized, saying:
"Emperor Xiàoxuān's old decree stipulated that
those serving in military garrisons or working for county government,
whose paternal grandparents died less than three months prior,
should all be exempt from corvée labor,
allowing them to arrange burials.
I request that this system be followed."
The Empress Dowager assented.
Later, during the Jiànguāng era,
the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Zhù Fěng,
and Imperial Secretariat attendant Mèng Bù, among others, memorialized,
believing that
"Emperor Xiàowén established the ritual regulations,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ abolished the custom of leave for mourning.
This set a pattern for ten thousand generations
and truly cannot be changed.
It is fitting to revert to the old practice of Jiànwǔ."
Zhōng submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard from the Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety) that
it begins with loving one's parents
and culminates in sorrow and grief.
From the Son of Heaven above
to the common people below,
regardless of status or rank,
the meaning is one.
Parents and child
share the same vital essence but different breaths,
one body but divided.
It is three years before they are released from the embrace.
The former sages, in accordance with human nature, established this observance,
ordaining a twenty-five-month mourning period.
This is why in the Spring and Autumn period, when a minister had a major mourning,
the ruler would not call at his gate for three years.
Although Mǐn Zǐ wore mourning clothes and served
to attend to public difficulties,
he later resigned his position
to fulfill his private obligations.
Thus it was said, 'The ruler ordered him wrongly;
the minister acted ritually.'
When the Zhōu dynasty declined,
ritual institutions were disordered.
The person who wrote the Lù'é poem lamented, saying: 'The jar is empty,
this is the shame of the pitcher.'
This means that for oneself not to be able to complete the filial path
is also the shame of those above.
When Gāozǔ received the mandate,
Xiāo Hé established the system.
There was a provision for high officials to take leave for mourning,
which accorded with the principle of expressing sorrow.
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
having just emerged from great chaos,
all state policies
tended towards simplicity and ease.
High officials could not take leave for mourning,
and all departments, seeking salary and thinking of private gain,
few observed the three-year mourning period
to repay the kindness of their parents' nurturing.
The principles of ritual and righteousness
were truly diminished.
The rise of the Great Hàn,
though inheriting a period of decline and decay,
gradually implemented
the institutions of the former kings.
Thus, the plowing of the sacrificial field
originated with Emperor Xiàowén;
the recommendation of filial and incorrupt officials
began with Emperor Xiàowǔ;
the rites of suburban sacrifice
were established during Yuán and Chéng;
the order of the Three Yǒng
was completed by Xiǎnzōng;
[一０] and high officials observing full mourning
was perfected by Your Majesty.
[一一] No holy accomplishment or beautiful deed
surpasses this.
Mencius said: 'Treat your elders as elders, and extend it to the elders of others;
treat your young as young, and extend it to the young of others,
then the world can be turned in your palm.'
[一二] Your servant wishes that Your Majesty look north from on high,
and with the thoughts of Gānlíng,
measure the hearts of your subjects and children,
then all within the seas will find their proper place."
[一三] The eunuchs found this inconvenient,
ultimately shelving Zhōng's memorial and following the proposal of Fěng and Bù,
which was then recorded in the statutes.
Zhōng, due to his long service,
was promoted to Púyè.
At that time, the Emperor often sent Huángmén Chángshì and the imperial envoy Bórong to and from Gānlíng.
Bórong, presuming upon imperial favor, became arrogant and unruly.
Wherever he passed through prefectures and states, none failed to welcome him with ritual obeisances.
Moreover, continuous heavy rains lasted for a long time,
the Yellow River waters overflowed,
and the common people were agitated.
Zhōng submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that if a position is not filled by the right person,
then all affairs will not be prosperous;
if all affairs are not prosperous,
then there will be gains and losses in governance;
if there are gains and losses in governance,
then yin and yang will be moved,
and portents and anomalies will appear as responses.
Your Majesty always attributes calamities to yourself,
and does not blame your ministers.
Your ministers, accustomed to your grace,
do not consider themselves at fault.
Therefore, the will of Heaven has not been attained,
and successive disasters frequently arrive.
In the regions of Qīng and Jì, excessive rains have flooded the rivers.
Along the shores of Xú and Dài, seawater has overflowed.
In Yǎn and Yù, locusts and their larvae proliferate.
In Jīng and Yáng, the rice harvest is meager.
In the two provinces of Bìng and Liáng, the Qiāng and Róng tribes are rebellious.
Added to this, the common people lack sufficiency,
and the imperial treasury is empty.
From west to east,
looms will soon be bare.
I have heard that among the five affairs of the Great Plan,
the first is 'mien'.
Mien is shown with reverence,
reverence creates solemnity.
If mien is damaged, it leads to madness,
and results in persistent rain.
In the Spring and Autumn period, great floods
were all due to the ruler's deportment not being harmonious,
his governance not being strict,
his ministers being disrespectful,
and favored relatives monopolizing power.
The yin qi becomes strong and abundant,
and the yang cannot control it,
hence the excessive rains.
Your Majesty, being unable to personally offer filial piety at the imperial temples and gardens,
frequently dispatches imperial envoys to convey respects to Gānlíng.
Red chariots and lined horses
are seen continuously on the roads.
This can be called utmost filial piety.
However, I secretly hear that wherever the envoy passes,
his authority and power are awe-inspiring,
shaking the commanderies and counties.
Kings, marquises, and officials of two thousand dàns even prostrate themselves before Bórong's chariot,
their demeanor overstepping the bounds,
equaling that of a sovereign.
Senior officials, terrified, reproach themselves,
or some flatter themselves wickedly,
mobilizing people to repair roads,
renovate post stations,
set up numerous provisions,
and impose unlimited levies and corvée.
[一０] The old and weak follow one another,
amounting to tens of thousands.
Bribes and gifts to his servants
number hundreds of bolts of silk.
They collapse and sigh,
all beating their chests.
The relatives of the uncle in Héjiān,
[一一] the venerable imperial mausoleums in Qīnghé,
[一二] all humiliatingly bow down before Bórong's chariot.
and high ministers who hold imperial seals,
Your Majesty does not inquire,
surely believing that Your Majesty wishes it to be so.
Bórong's prestige is greater than Your Majesty's,
and Your Majesty's authority rests with servants and concubines.
The occurrence of water disasters
must stem from this.
In the past, Hán Yān, presuming upon the privilege of a second chariot,
was given the mission to inspect on horseback;
Jiāngdū mistakenly offered a single bow,
and Yān suffered the punishment of the executioner's knife.
[一三] I wish that the enlightened ruler would strictly uphold the dignity of the Heavenly Sovereign,
establish the proper position of the celestial yang,
[一四] and for all official duties, great and small,
appoint virtuous and capable individuals.
It is not appropriate to again allow female envoys to interfere with the myriad affairs of state.
Closely examine those around you,
lest there be the treachery of Shí Xiǎn's leaks;
[一五] for the Shàngshū and Nàyán,
lest there be the deceit of Zhào Chāng's slanders;
[一六] for the Gōngqīng and high ministers,
lest there be the patronage of Zhū Bó's favoritism;
[一七] and for external relatives and close kin,
lest there be Wáng Fèng's schemes to harm the merchants.
[一八] If state affairs are solely determined by imperial decree,
and royal matters are always decided by yourself,
then those below cannot coerce those above,
and ministers cannot interfere with the sovereign.
Then persistent rains and great floods will surely cease,
[一九] and the myriad anomalies from all four quarters cannot cause harm."
The memorial was submitted but not heeded.
At that time, the authority of the Three Ducal Offices was light,
and crucial matters were exclusively entrusted to the Shàngshū.
Yet, whenever calamities and misfortunes occurred,
the Ducal Offices were promptly dismissed and reproached.
Zhōng believed this was not the old practice of the state
and submitted a memorial to remonstrate, saying:
"I have heard that 'the ruler employs ministers with propriety,
and ministers serve the ruler with loyalty.'
Therefore, the Three Dukes are called the Chief Ministers,
and the king treats them with special reverence.
When riding in a carriage, he descends;
when seated, he rises for them.
When entering, they participate in discussions and deliberate on state affairs;
when leaving, they supervise and correct right and wrong.
According to the old customs of the Hàn dynasty,
whatever the Chancellor requested,
there was nothing that was not granted.
Today's Three Dukes,
though bearing the name, lack the substance.
Elections, punishments, and rewards
are all determined by the Shàngshū.
The Shàngshū are relied upon,
having greater authority than the Three Dukes.
Since the reign of Emperor Líng,
this trend has long been established.
My loyal heart is always uniquely unsettled,
hence when facing matters, I am fearful and trembling,
not daring to invent or initiate anything from a small perspective.
Nor do I try to please my colleagues
by erroneously smoothing out established principles.
Yet slanders and reproaches are heard daily,
and my crime deserves ten thousand deaths.
Recently, Sīkōng Chén Bǎo was dismissed due to an earthquake.
Now, with current calamities,
there is again a desire to severely reprimand the Three Dukes.
In the past, Emperor Xiàochéng, when a baleful star guarded the Heart constellation,
shifted the blame to the Chancellor,
and ordered Bēnlì to persuade Fāng Jìn.
Fāng Jìn took the blame himself,
but ultimately did not receive the blessings of Heaven,
merely betraying Sòng Jǐng's sincerity.
Thus, it is clear that the distinction between right and wrong
has a clear conclusion.
Moreover, the Shàngshū, in deciding affairs,
