often deviate from old practices.
Penal laws are without precedent,
deceit and fraud are prioritized.
The language is harsh and ugly,
contrary to the imperial constitution.
It is proper to examine their intentions,
reject them, and not listen.
This would accord with national norms above,
prevent abuse of power below,
set squares and circles by compasses and rulers,
and weigh light and heavy by scales.
This is truly the state's established code
and a law for ten thousand generations."
Zhōng's intention was always to praise and elevate high ministers
and treat subordinates with propriety.
When any of the Nine Ministers fell ill,
he sent envoys to inquire,
and bestowed money and cloth.
These were all proposals Zhōng had submitted.
After a short while,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Lìng.
In Yánguāng third year (124 CE),
he was appointed Sīlì Xiàowèi.
He corrected the internal officials, imperial relatives by marriage, and their guests.
Those in favor feared him
and did not wish Zhōng to be in the inner court.
The next year,
he was sent out as the Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià,
but was again retained and appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
He then fell ill and died.
Initially,
Tàiwèi Zhāng Yǔ and Sītú Xú Fáng wanted to jointly memorialize with Zhōng's father Chǒng to posthumously ennoble Dèng Xùn, the Commandant of the Qiāng, father of Empress Héxī.
Chǒng, arguing that his ancestors had no precedent for such a memorial,
contended for several days but could not prevail,
and so followed the counsel of the two ducal offices.
When Xùn was posthumously granted an enfeoffment and谥号, Yǔ and Fáng again agreed with Chǒng to send their sons to pay respects to Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng Dèng Zhì.
Chǒng did not comply,
and Zhì held a grudge against him.
Therefore, Zhōng did not achieve his ambitions under the Dèng clan.
When Zhì and others were defeated,
many commoners harbored resentment against them.
Zhōng, however, repeatedly submitted memorials to expose and confirm their wickedness,
and subsequently impeached Dàsīnóng Zhū Chǒng.
When Emperor Shùn was deposed as太子,
several famous ministers, such as Láilì and Zhù Fěng, stood at the palace gate to strongly remonstrate.
At that time, Zhōng was Shàngshū Lìng,
and together with other Shàngshū, they again impeached and memorialized against them.
When Emperor Shùn ascended the throne,
Sīlì Xiàowèi Yú Xǔ subsequently memorialized about Zhōng's and others' transgressions.
People of the time criticized him for this.
A commentary states: When Chén Gōng 陳公 served as a judicial official, he deliberated on cases and delayed executions.
When he assisted the young ruler, he was upright and did not overstep his authority or seek undue favor.
He can be said to have possessed the qualities of a prime minister.
Zhōng 忠 was able to follow his example,
and was also nearly as discerning and cautious in applying punishments, not allowing cases to linger in prison.
However, his allowing madmen to kill people,
and opening up the possibility for fathers and sons, or brothers, to die in place of each other,
was a great error.
In this way, wicked people often benefited from good fortune,
while good people constantly suffered their misfortunes in their stead,
leaving them at a loss whether to advance or retreat.
A eulogy states: Chén 陳 and Guō 郭 presided over justice;
people relied on their fairness.
They compassionately tended to the deceased,
personally deciding with empathy.
Zhōng 忠 used meticulous care,
with prescribed limits for adding or removing.
Bestowed upon his descendants,
they would be both dukes and ministers.
Biographies of Bān 班 and Liáng 梁, Chapter Thirty-Seven
Bān Chāo 班超, courtesy name Zhòngshēng 仲升,
was a native of Pínglíng 平陵 in Fúfēng 扶風.
He was the youngest son of Biao 彪, the magistrate of Xú 徐.
He was a man of great ambition,
and did not bother with minor details.
However, he was inwardly filial and diligent;
at home, he always worked hard
and was not ashamed of toil or disgrace.
He was eloquent
and widely read in books and histories.
In the fifth year of Yǒngpíng 永平 (62 CE),
his elder brother Gù 固 was summoned to be a compiler in the Imperial Library.
Chāo 超 and his mother followed him to Luòyáng 洛陽.
Their family was poor,
so Chāo often worked as a hired scribe for officials to support his family.
After enduring long hardship,
he once stopped his work, threw down his brush, and sighed, saying:
"A true man with no other strategic aspirations
should still emulate Fù Jièzǐ 傅介子 and Zhāng Qiān 張騫 in achieving merit in foreign lands,
to attain a marquessate.
How can one long be occupied with mere brushes and inkstones?"
Those around him all laughed at him.
Chāo 超 said:
"How can you youngsters understand the ambition of a brave man!"
Later, he went to a physiognomist,
who said:
"My lord,
you are merely a common scholar now,
but you are destined to be enfeoffed as a marquis thousands of *lǐ* away."
Chāo 超 asked about his features.
The physiognomist pointed and said:
"You have a swallow's jaw and a tiger's neck,
flying and eating meat;
this is the physiognomy of a marquis of ten thousand *lǐ*."
After some time,
Xiǎnzōng 顯宗 asked Gù 固,
"Where is your younger brother?"
Gù 固 replied,
"He writes documents for officials,
receiving payment to support our aged mother."
The Emperor then appointed Chāo 超 as an official in the Imperial Library.
Later, he was dismissed from office due to an incident.
In the sixteenth year (73 CE),
the Grand Charioteer Dòu Gù 竇固 led an expedition to attack the Xiōngnú 匈奴.
He appointed Chāo 超 as Acting Sīmǎ 司馬,
leading troops to strike a separate blow against Yīwú 伊吾.
They fought at Púlèi Hǎi 蒲類海,
beheading and capturing many before returning.
Dòu Gù 竇固 considered him capable,
and sent him along with his subordinate Guō Xún 郭恂 on a mission to the Western Regions.
When Chāo 超 arrived in Shànshàn 鄯善,
Guǎng 廣, the King of Shànshàn 鄯善, offered Chāo 超 extremely generous hospitality and respect.
Later, he suddenly became distant and negligent.
Chāo 超 said to his subordinates:
"Do you not sense that Guǎng's 廣 courtesy has diminished?
This must be because a Xiōngnú 匈奴 envoy has arrived,
and he is hesitant, not knowing whom to follow.
A wise man discerns what is yet to sprout,
let alone what is already manifest!"
He then summoned a Hu 胡 attendant and feigned a question, saying:
"The Xiōngnú 匈奴 envoy arrived several days ago;
where is he now?"
The Hu 胡 attendant, greatly alarmed,
confessed everything.
Chāo 超 then detained the Hu 胡 attendant,
gathered all thirty-six of his officers and men,
and drank with them.
When the wine was flowing freely,
he incited them, saying:
"You and I are together in this remote region,
wanting to accomplish great deeds
to seek wealth and honor.
Now, the barbarian envoy arrived just a few days ago,
and King Guǎng's 廣 hospitality has already ceased;
if Shànshàn 鄯善 were to seize our group and send us to the Xiōngnú 匈奴,
our bones would long be food for jackals and wolves!
What should we do about it?"
His subordinates all said:
"We are now in a place of peril and death;
our lives and deaths are yours to command, Sīmǎ 司馬."
Chāo 超 said:
"One cannot enter the tiger's den
without obtaining its cub.
The current plan is
to attack the barbarians by night with fire,
so they won't know our numbers,
and will certainly be greatly terrified,
allowing us to wipe them out.
If we eliminate these barbarians,
Shànshàn 鄯善 will lose its nerve,
and our mission will be accomplished!"
The group said:
"We should discuss this with the aide."
Chāo 超 angrily said:
"Good or ill will be decided today!
The aide is a civilian official;
upon hearing this, he will surely be afraid and leak the plan.
We would die without renown;
this is not the way of brave men!"
The group said:
"Good!"
In the early night,
he led his officers and men to rush to the barbarian camp.
It happened to be a very windy night.
Chāo 超 ordered ten men to hold drums and hide behind the barbarian quarters,
instructing them:
"When you see the fire ablaze,
you must all beat the drums and shout loudly."
The rest of the men all held weapons and crossbows, ambushing at the gates.
Chāo 超 then, with the wind, started a fire,
and from front to back, drums sounded and shouts rang out.
The barbarian host was startled and in chaos.
Chāo 超 personally killed three men in hand-to-hand combat,
and his officers and soldiers killed the envoy and his followers, over thirty heads.
The remaining hundred or so people were all burned to death.
The next day, he returned to inform Guō Xún 郭恂.
Xún 恂 was greatly astonished,
and then his expression changed.
Chāo 超 understood his meaning,
raised his hand and said:
"Even though you, aide, did not go,
how could Bān Chāo 班超 dare to claim this merit alone?"
Xún 恂 was then pleased.
Chāo 超 then summoned King Guǎng 廣 of Shànshàn 鄯善,
showed him the heads of the barbarian envoys,
and the entire kingdom was terrified.
Chāo 超 enlightened and appeased them,
and consequently received a prince as a hostage.
He returned and reported to Dòu Gù 竇固.
Gù 固 was greatly pleased,
and fully reported Chāo's 超 accomplishments,
also requesting a new envoy to be selected for the Western Regions.
The Emperor admired Chāo's 超 integrity,
and issued an edict to Gù 固, saying:
"If an official is like Bān Chāo 班超,
why not send him instead of selecting another?
Now appoint Chāo 超 as Jūn Sīmǎ 軍司馬,
and let him continue his previous achievements."
Chāo 超 again received the mission.
Dòu Gù 竇固 wanted to increase his troops,
but Chāo 超 said:
"I wish to lead only the thirty or so men I originally had; that will be enough.
If there are unforeseen circumstances,
more troops would only be a burden."
At this time, Guǎngdé 廣德, the King of Yútián 于窴, had recently attacked and conquered Shāchē 莎車,
thus dominating the southern route,
and the Xiōngnú 匈奴 had sent an envoy to supervise his kingdom.
When Chāo 超 went west,
he first arrived in Yútián 于窴.
Guǎngdé's 廣德 hospitality was very lukewarm.
Moreover, it was their custom to believe in shamans.
The shaman said:
"The gods are angry—why do you wish to align with Hàn 漢?
The Hàn 漢 envoy has a dun-colored horse;
quickly request it to sacrifice to me."
Guǎngdé 廣德 then sent an envoy to Chāo 超 to request the horse.
Chāo 超 secretly understood the situation,
promised to agree,
but ordered the shaman to come and retrieve the horse himself.
A short while later,
the shaman arrived.
Chāo 超 immediately beheaded him and sent his head to Guǎngdé 廣德,
then excused himself and returned it.
Guǎngdé 廣德 had long heard that Chāo 超 had executed the barbarian envoy in Shànshàn 鄯善,
and was greatly terrified.
He immediately attacked and killed the Xiōngnú 匈奴 envoy and surrendered to Chāo 超.
Chāo 超 richly rewarded the king and his subordinates,
and then garrisoned and pacified the region.
At that time, Jiān, the king of Qiūcí, had been installed by the Xiōngnú,
and relying on the barbarian's might,
he occupied the Northern Route.
He attacked and destroyed Shūlè,
killed its king,
and installed Dōutí, a Qiūcí native, as the king of Shūlè.
In the spring of the following year,
Chāo reached Shūlè by an unfrequented path.
Ninety *lǐ* from Pántuó City, where Dōutí resided,
he sent his officer, Tián Lǜ, ahead to demand his surrender.
Chāo instructed Lǜ, saying:
"Dōutí is not originally of the Shūlè lineage,
and the people of the state will surely not obey him.
If he does not surrender immediately,
you may seize him."
When Lǜ arrived,
Dōutí saw Lǜ as weak and insignificant,
and had no intention of surrendering.
Lǜ, taking advantage of his unpreparedness,
advanced and seized and bound Dōutí.
His attendants, caught off guard,
were all startled and fled.
Lǜ galloped back to report to Chāo,
who immediately proceeded there,
summoned all the Shūlè generals and officials,
explained to them the wicked behavior of Qiūcí,
and then installed Zhōng, the nephew of the former king, as king.
The people of the state were greatly pleased.
Zhōng and his officials all requested to kill Dōutí,
but Chāo did not consent,
wishing to demonstrate his authority and trustworthiness;
he released and sent him away.
Shūlè, from this, formed an enmity with Qiūcí.
In the eighteenth year,
the Emperor died.
Yānqí, taking advantage of the great mourning in the Central Kingdom,
attacked and annihilated the Protector-General Chén Mù.
Chāo was isolated and without support,
while Qiūcí and Gūmò repeatedly sent troops to attack Shūlè.
Chāo defended Pántuó City,
forming a defensive line with Zhōng,
but his soldiers and officers were few,
and they resisted for over a year.
When Sùzōng first ascended the throne,
because Chén Mù had recently been annihilated,
fearing that Chāo, being isolated and in danger, could not maintain his position,
he issued an edict recalling Chāo.
When Chāo began his return journey,
the entire state of Shūlè was filled with sorrow and fear.
Its commander, Lí Yǎn, said:
"The Han envoy is abandoning us;
we will surely be destroyed by Qiūcí again.
I truly cannot bear to see the Han envoy leave."
Thereupon, he cut his own throat with a knife.
When Chāo returned to Yútián,
the king, marquises, and others below him all wept, saying:
"We rely on the Han envoy as we would on our parents;
you truly cannot leave."
They clung to Chāo's horse's legs,
preventing him from proceeding.
Chāo, fearing that Yútián would ultimately not allow him to go east,
and also wishing to fulfill his original aspiration,
then returned to Shūlè.
The two cities of Shūlè, after Chāo's departure,
had again surrendered to Qiūcí,
and had allied themselves with Wèitóu.
Chāo captured and executed the rebels,
attacked and defeated Wèitóu,
killing over six hundred people,
and Shūlè was pacified again.
In Jiànchū third year,
Chāo led one myriad troops from Shūlè, Kāngjū, Yútián, and Jūmí to attack Shíchéng in Gūmò,
defeating it
and beheading seven hundred men.
Chāo, wishing to pacify all the states by this means,
then submitted a memorial requesting troops.
He said:
"I humbly observe that the late Emperor wished to open the Western Regions,
and therefore attacked the Xiōngnú in the north
and sent envoys to foreign countries in the west.
Shànshàn and Yútián immediately turned to and embraced our civilization.
Now Jūmí, Shāchē, Shūlè, Yuèzhī, Wūsūn, and Kāngjū again desire to submit,
wishing to join forces to destroy Qiūcí
and open the Han route.
If Qiūcí is taken,
then only one percent of the Western Regions will remain unsubdued.
I humbly reflect that,
as a humble officer,
I sincerely wish to follow Gǔ Jí in dedicating my life in a distant land,
hoping perhaps to emulate Zhāng Qiān, who gave himself to the wilderness.
In antiquity, Wèi Jiàng, a grandee of a feudal state,
was still able to harmonize and unite various Róng tribes.
How much more so can I, serving with the might of the Great Han,
not accomplish a single act with a leaden blade?
Previous generations of strategists all said that conquering the Thirty-Six States
was known as severing the right arm of the Xiōngnú.
Now, among the states of the Western Regions,
from where the sun sets,
none have failed to embrace our civilization;
great and small are joyous,
and their tribute offerings are unceasing.
Only Yānqí and Qiūcí alone remain unsubmissive.
Previously, I, with thirty-six officials, was sent as an envoy to distant lands,
and encountered all manner of hardships.
Since I began my solitary defense of Shūlè,
five years have passed.
The dispositions and conditions of the Hu and Yí,
I have somewhat come to know.
When asked about the size of their walled cities,
they all say, 'Relying on Han is like relying on Heaven.'
From this, one can deduce
that the Cōnglíng Pass can be opened,
and if Cōnglíng is open, then Qiūcí can be attacked.
It is now fitting to appoint Bái Bà, the hostage prince of Qiūcí, as its king,
and send him with several hundred cavalry and infantry,
to join forces with the various states.
Within a year or so,
Qiūcí can be captured.
Using barbarians to attack barbarians
is the best strategy.
I observe that the lands of Shāchē and Shūlè are fertile and vast,
with abundant grass and pastures,
not comparable to the areas around Dūnhuáng
and Shànshàn.
[一０] Troops can be supplied without expenditure from the Central Kingdom, and food will be self-sufficient.
Furthermore, the two kings of Gūmò and Wēnsù
were specifically installed by Qiūcí.
[一一] Since they are not of the same lineage,
they mutually resent each other's oppression.
Their situation will inevitably lead to surrender or rebellion.
If these two states come to surrender,
then Qiūcí will be broken by itself.
I wish that Your Majesty would consider my memorial
and examine the course of action.
Should there be a one in ten thousand chance of success,
what regret would there be in death?
I, Chāo, though insignificant,
have been especially favored by divine spirits.
I secretly hope that I will not perish prematurely,
but live to see the Western Regions pacified,
and Your Majesty raise the cup of ten thousand years,
[一二] presenting your achievements at the ancestral temple,
spreading great joy throughout the world."
[一三] When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor, knowing that his endeavor could succeed,
considered providing troops.
Xú Gàn of Pínglíng, who had always shared Chāo's aspirations,
submitted a memorial expressing his wish to offer himself to assist Chāo.
In the fifth year,
Gàn was appointed acting Sīmǎ,
leading one thousand disciplined convicts and voluntary followers to join Chāo.
Earlier, Shāchē, believing that Han troops would not venture out,
had surrendered to Qiūcí,
and Fānchén, the commander of Shūlè,
had also rebelled.
Coincidentally, Xú Gàn arrived,
and Chāo, together with Gàn, attacked Fānchén,
decisively defeating him,
beheading over a thousand,
and capturing many alive.
Having defeated Fānchén, Chāo
wished to advance and attack Qiūcí.
Since Wūsūn's army was strong,
it was advisable to leverage its power.
He then submitted a report, saying:
"Wūsūn is a great state,
with one hundred thousand archers.
Therefore, Emperor Wǔ married a princess to them,
and up to Emperor Xuān,
their service was ultimately secured.
Now, an envoy can be sent to invite and comfort them,
to combine forces with them."
The Emperor accepted this.
In the eighth year,
Chāo was appointed General of the Vanguard,
and was granted imperial drums, trumpets, and banners.
Xú Gàn was appointed Army Commander,
and a separate envoy, Wèi Hòu Lǐ Yì, was sent to escort the Wūsūn envoys,
bestowing brocade upon the great and small Kūnmí and others.
Lǐ Yì 始 (shǐ) arrived at Yútián,
when he encountered Gūzī attacking Shūlè.
Frightened, he dared not advance,
and so he submitted a memorial stating that achievements in the Western Regions could not be made.
He also vehemently slandered Chāo, saying he 'embraced his beloved wife,
held his beloved son,
and enjoyed comfort in foreign lands,
with no thought of returning home.'
Chāo heard of this
and sighed, saying:
"I am not Zēng Shēn, yet I am slandered three times over;
I fear I shall be suspected by those of my time."
Thereupon he sent his wife away.
The Emperor, knowing Chāo's loyalty,
sternly rebuked Yì, saying:
"Even if Chāo embraces his beloved wife
and holds his beloved son,
there are more than a thousand men who long to return home.
How could they all be of the same mind as Chāo?"
He ordered Yì to go to Chāo and receive his instructions.
The imperial edict instructed Chāo:
"If Yì is suitable for an external post,
then keep him as an assistant."
Chāo immediately dispatched Yì to escort the Wūsūn princely hostage back to the capital.
Xú Gàn said to Chāo:
"Yì previously slandered you personally
and sought to undermine the Western Regions.
Why don't you now, in accordance with the imperial edict, keep him
and send another official to escort the princely hostage?"
Chāo said:
"How vulgar is such a statement!
Because Yì slandered Chāo,
I now send him away.
If one examines oneself and finds no fault,
why heed others' words?
To keep him out of personal satisfaction
would not be the act of a loyal subject."
The following year,
he again dispatched acting Commander Hé Gōng (gōng) and three others, leading eight hundred soldiers, to Chāo.
Chāo then mobilized troops from Shūlè and Yútián to attack Shāchē.
Shāchē secretly sent envoys to Shūlè King Zhōng,
luring him with great profit.
Zhōng then rebelled and sided with them,
entrenching himself in Wūjí City to the west.
Chāo then installed his own Household Supervisor, Chéng Dà, as King of Shūlè,
and mobilized all those who had not rebelled to attack Zhōng.
After half a year,
Kāngjū sent elite troops to assist him,
and Chāo was unable to take the city.
At this time, Yuèzhī had recently married into the Kāngjū royal family,
and they were close.
Chāo then sent an envoy with much brocade and silk to the King of Yuèzhī,
ordering him to instruct the King of Kāngjū.
The King of Kāngjū then withdrew his troops,
seized Zhōng, and returned to his country.
Wūjí City then surrendered to Chāo.
Three years later,
Zhōng persuaded the King of Kāngjū to lend him troops,
and returned to occupy Sǔnzhōng.
He secretly plotted with Gūzī
and sent an envoy to feign surrender to Chāo.
Chāo knew of his treachery inwardly but outwardly pretended to agree.
Zhōng was greatly pleased
and immediately rode with a light cavalry escort to Chāo.
Chāo secretly assembled his troops to await him
and prepared a banquet with music.
As the wine circulated,
he shouted at his officers to seize Zhōng and behead him.
Then he attacked and routed Zhōng's forces,
killing over seven hundred men.
The Southern Route was thus completely opened.
The following year,
Chāo mobilized twenty-five thousand troops from Yútián and other kingdoms
and again attacked Shāchē.
The King of Gūzī sent his Left General to mobilize fifty thousand troops from Wēnsù, Gūmò, and Wèitóu to assist them.
Chāo summoned his generals, officers, and the King of Yútián to deliberate, saying:
"Our forces are now too few to contend.
The best plan is for each of us to disperse.
Yútián will go east from here,
and the Chief Clerk will also return west from here.
We should wait for the sound of the night drum to depart."
He secretly loosened the ropes of the captured prisoners.
The King of Gūzī heard of this and was greatly pleased,
personally taking ten thousand cavalry to block Chāo on the western border,
while the King of Wēnsù led eight thousand cavalry to intercept Yútián on the eastern border.
Chāo, knowing that the two barbarian forces had departed,
secretly summoned his various divisions to assemble their troops.
At cockcrow, they swiftly advanced to the Shāchē camp.
The Hú were greatly startled, confused, and fled.
Chāo's forces pursued and decapitated over five thousand heads,
and captured a large amount of their horses, livestock, and valuables.
Shāchē then surrendered,
and Gūzī and the others consequently retreated and dispersed.
From this, his prestige shook the Western Regions.
Initially,
Yuèzhī had once assisted Hàn in attacking Chēshī and achieved merit.
In this year, they offered tribute of precious treasures, fúbá (mythical beasts), and shīzǐ (lions),
and then requested a Hàn princess.
Chāo refused and sent their envoy back,
which caused resentment.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán,
Yuèzhī sent its Vice-King, Xiè, leading seventy thousand troops to attack Chāo.
Chāo's forces were few,
and all were greatly terrified.
Chāo explained to his soldiers, saying:
"Although the Yuèzhī forces are numerous,
they have come thousands of *lǐ* (li) over the Cōng Líng (Cōnglíng) mountains.
Without transport,
why should we worry?
We only need to gather grain and hold fast to our defenses.
They will surrender from hunger and exhaustion themselves;
it will not take more than a few tens of days to decide it."
Xiè then advanced and attacked Chāo,
but could not take the city.
He also raided for provisions but gained nothing.
Chāo estimated that their food would soon run out
and that they would surely seek help from Gūzī.
So he sent several hundred soldiers to intercept them on the eastern border.
Xiè indeed sent cavalry carrying gold, silver, pearls, and jade to bribe Gūzī.
Chāo's ambush troops intercepted and attacked them,
killing them all.
He brought the heads of their envoys to show Xiè.
Xiè was greatly shocked
and immediately sent an envoy to plead for mercy,
wishing to return alive.
Chāo released him.
Yuèzhī was greatly awed by this,
and thenceforth offered annual tribute.
The following year,
Gūzī, Gūmò, and Wēnsù all surrendered.
Chāo was then appointed Protector-General,
and Xú Gàn was made Chief Clerk.
Bái Bà was appointed King of Gūzī,
and Military Commander Yáo Guāng was sent to escort him.
Chāo and Guāng together coerced Gūzī to depose its King Yóu Lìduō and enthrone Bái Bà,
and then had Guāng escort Yóu Lìduō back to the capital.
Chāo resided in Gūzī's Tāgān City,
and Xú Gàn was stationed in Shūlè.
Of the Western Regions, only Yānqí, Wēixū, and Wèilí, which had previously overthrown the Protector-General,
harbored double minds;
the rest were all pacified.
In the autumn of the sixth year,
Chāo then mobilized seventy thousand troops from Gūzī, Shànshàn, and eight other kingdoms,
as well as one thousand four hundred officers, soldiers, and merchants, to campaign against Yānqí.
When his army reached the border of Wèilí,
he sent an envoy to explain to Yānqí, Wèilí, and Wēixū, saying:
"The Protector-General has come
to pacify and govern the three kingdoms.
If you wish to correct your past mistakes and turn towards goodness,
you should send your dignitaries to welcome him.
Kings, marquises, and others will be rewarded,
and when the matter is concluded, he will return.
Now, the King is bestowed with five hundred bolts of colored silk."
King Guǎng of Yānqí sent his Left General Běi Jiānzhī to offer cattle and wine to welcome Chāo.
Chāo confronted Jiānzhī, saying:
"Although you are a Xiongnú princely hostage,
you now hold the reins of national power.
The Protector-General himself has come,
yet the King did not welcome him in a timely manner.
This is all your fault."
Some advised Chāo that he should simply kill him.
Chāo said:
"That is beyond your comprehension.
This man's power outweighs that of the King.
If we kill him now before entering his country,
it will only make them suspicious
and cause them to fortify their defenses.
How could we then reach their city walls?"
Thereupon, he gave gifts and sent him away.
Guǎng then, with his dignitaries, welcomed Chāo at Wèilí,
offering precious items.
The state of Yānqí had the danger of a reed bridge.
Guǎng then cut off the bridge,
not wishing the Hàn army to enter the state.
Chāo instead advanced and crossed from another path.
On the last day of the seventh month,
he arrived at Yānqí,
twenty *lǐ* from the city,
and set up camp in a large marsh.
Guǎng, caught by surprise,
was greatly afraid,
and thus wished to drive all his people into the mountains for protection.
Yuán Méng, the Left Marquis of Yānqí, had previously been a hostage in the capital.
He secretly sent an envoy to inform Chāo of the matter.
Chāo immediately executed the envoy,
showing that he did not trust him.
He then arranged a grand meeting of the kings of the various states,
and loudly announced that he would bestow generous rewards.
Thereupon, Guǎng, the King of Yānqí, Fàn, the King of Wèilí, and thirty others, including the Běi Jiānzhī, led their people to meet Chāo.
Fùjiǔ, the Chancellor of their state, and seventeen others, fearing execution,
all fled into the sea,
and the King of Wēixū also did not arrive.
Once seated,
Chāo angrily interrogated Guǎng, saying:
"Why has the King of Wēixū not arrived?
For what reason did Fùjiǔ and the others flee?"
He then shouted at his officers and soldiers to seize Guǎng, Fàn, and the others, and executed them in the old city of Chén Mù,
sending their heads to the capital.
He then unleashed his troops to plunder,
beheading over five thousand people,
capturing fifteen thousand living people,
and over three hundred thousand horses, livestock, cattle, and sheep.
He then established Yuán Méng as the King of Yānqí.
Chāo stayed in Yānqí for half a year,
comforting and pacifying them.
Thus, over fifty states in the Western Regions all offered hostages and submitted to the interior.
The following year,
an imperial edict stated:
"In the past, the Xiōngnú alone dominated the Western Regions,
raiding Héxī,
and at the end of Yǒngpíng,
city gates were closed during the day.
The late Emperor deeply pitied the border populace suffering from banditry and harm,
and so commanded generals to attack the right flank,
conquer Báishān,
approach Púlèi,
and capture Chēshī.
The walled states trembled and responded,
thus opening up the Western Regions
and establishing the Protector-General.
However, Shùn, the King of Yānqí, and his son Zhōng, alone plotted rebellion and defiance,
relying on their treacherous terrain,
annihilating the Protector-General
and also the officials and soldiers.
The late Emperor valued the lives of the common people
and was reluctant to initiate military campaigns,
therefore he sent Military Commandant Bān Chāo to pacify the region west of Yútián.
Chāo then crossed the Cōnglíng,
reached Xiándù,
operating for twenty-two years,
and all submitted.
He replaced their kings
and pacified their people.
Without moving the Central Plains,
without troubling the soldiers,
he achieved harmony with distant barbarians,
united the hearts of different customs,
and brought down heavenly punishment,
wiping away an old disgrace,
and avenging the generals and soldiers.
The *Sīmǎ Fǎ* says: 'Rewards should not exceed a month,
to let people quickly see the benefits of good deeds.'
Therefore, Chāo is hereby enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dìngyuǎn,
with a thousand households."
Chāo, considering himself to have been in a distant region for a long time,
and being old, yearned for his homeland.
In the twelfth year,
he submitted a memorial saying:
"Your servant has heard that Tàigōng was enfeoffed in Qí,
and after five generations, was buried in Zhōu;
a fox dies with its head facing its hill,
and a Dài horse longs for the wind.
Zhōu and Qí are both within a thousand *lǐ* of the Central Plains,
how much more so for one in a far-off, distant land?
How can a humble servant not have the longing of a Dài horse for the wind and a fox for its hill?
The customs of the barbarians
fear the strong and insult the old.
Your servant Chāo's teeth are worn out like those of a dog or horse,
and I constantly fear that as I age,
I will suddenly collapse and die,
leaving my lonely spirit abandoned.
Sū Wǔ remained among the Xiōngnú for nineteen years;
now your servant is fortunate enough to carry a banner and wear the golden and silver seals of the Protector of the Western Regions.
If I were to die of old age in my military post,
I would indeed have no regrets,
but I fear that later generations might call your servant 'one who perished in the Western Regions.'
Your servant does not dare to hope to reach Jiǔquán Commandery,
but only wishes to enter the Yùmén Pass alive.
Your servant is old, sick, and feeble,
and ventures to speak blindly despite facing death.
I respectfully send my son Yǒng to accompany the tribute and enter the pass.
While your servant is still alive,
let Yǒng witness the Central Plains with his own eyes."
And Chāo's younger sister Zhāo, wife of Cáo Shòu of the same commandery, also submitted a petition on Chāo's behalf, saying:
"It is truly exceptional,
not something a humble servant should receive.
When Chāo first set out,
he was resolved to sacrifice his life,
hoping to achieve a small功,
to prove his effectiveness.
Then came the disaster of Chén Mù,
and the roads were cut off.
Chāo, alone, turned and tossed in distant lands,
explaining to the various states,
and relying on their troops.
Whenever there was a battle,
he would always be the first to charge,
his body covered in
wounds,
not fearing death.
Thanks to Your Majesty's divine power,
he was able to prolong his life in the desert,
now for thirty years.
Separated from his flesh and blood,
they no longer
recognize each other.
The people he accompanied at that time
have all passed away.
Chāo is the oldest,
now almost seventy.
He is frail, old, and sick,
his hair has no black left,
both his hands
are numb,
his ears and eyes are not keen,
and he can only walk with a cane.
Though he wishes to exhaust his strength
to repay the imperial grace,
he is pressed by the twilight of his years,
his teeth worn out like those of a dog or
horse.
The nature of the barbarians
is rebellious and insulting to the old,
and Chāo will soon be in the grave.
If he is not replaced for a long time,
I fear it will open a source of treachery
and give rise to rebellious thoughts.
Yet
the *qīng* and *dàfū* all think superficially,
none willing to think long-term.
If there is a sudden incident,
Chāo's strength and energy will not be able to follow his will,
which would then harm the state's achievements over generations,
and waste the efforts of a loyal minister who gave his all.
This would truly be painful.
Therefore, Chāo, from ten thousand *lǐ* away, has sincerely expressed
his suffering and urgency,
stretching his neck and looking forward,
for three years now,
yet has not received
consideration.
To win the hearts of all nations,
one should not abandon the ministers of small states,
how much more so for Chāo, who holds the rank of Marquis?
Therefore, I dare to risk death to plead for Chāo,
to beg for Chāo's remaining years.
If he can return alive,
and again see the imperial court,
it will ensure the state forever has no worries about distant labor,
the Western Regions no sudden anxieties,
and Chāo will long enjoy the grace of King Wén burying old bones,
and Zǐ Fāng pitying the old.
The *Shī* says:
'The people are weary;
they can now have a little peace.
Be kind to this Central Plains,
to pacify the four quarters.'
Chāo has written a letter to
his wife, bidding farewell,
fearing they will never see each other again.
I truly grieve that Chāo, in his prime, dedicated his loyalty and filial piety in the desert,
only to be abandoned to die in the wilderness when old and weary.
This is truly lamentable
and pitiable.
If he is not rescued and protected,
and Chāo eventually suffers an unexpected mishap,
I hope that Chāo's family may receive the pardon previously granted at the pleas of Zhào Mǔ and Wèi Jī.
Your ignorant and foolish servant
does not understand the great principles,
and has violated taboos."
When the memorial was presented,
the Emperor was moved by her words,
and so summoned Chāo back.
Bān Chāo (班超) was in the Western Regions for thirty-one years.
In the eighth month of the fourteenth year, he arrived in Luòyáng (洛陽),
and was appointed as Shèshēng Xiàowèi (射聲校尉).
Bān Chāo (班超) had always suffered from a pectoral and hypochondriac illness,
and upon his arrival,
his condition worsened.
The Emperor sent a Zhōnghuángmén (中黃門) to inquire about his illness,
and bestowed medicine upon him.
He died in the ninth month of that year,
at the age of seventy-one.
The imperial court grieved for him,
and an envoy was sent to offer condolences and sacrifices,
bestowing a very generous funeral endowment.
His son, Bān Xióng (班雄), succeeded him.
Initially,
when Bān Chāo (班超) was summoned back,
Rèn Shàng (任尚), the Wùjǐ Xiàowèi (戊己校尉), was appointed as Dūhù (都護).
He was to take over from Bān Chāo (班超).
Rèn Shàng (任尚) said to Bān Chāo (班超):
"You, Sire, have been in foreign lands for over thirty years,
and this humble person now presumptuously succeeds you.
The responsibility is heavy, but my understanding is shallow.
It would be appropriate for you to offer some instruction."
Bān Chāo (班超) replied:
"I am old and have lost my wisdom.
You, Sir, are destined for great office.
How could Bān Chāo (班超) compare to that?
If I absolutely must,
I would like to offer some foolish words.
The officials and soldiers beyond the Great Wall
are not originally filial sons or obedient grandsons;
they have all been banished to border garrisons due to crimes and transgressions.
The barbarians harbor the hearts of birds and beasts;
they are difficult to nurture and easy to offend.
Now, your temperament is severe and urgent;
where the water is too clear, there are no big fish.
If you examine governance too meticulously, you will not achieve harmony with those below.
It would be better to be relaxed and simple,
to overlook minor faults,
and only to grasp the general principles."
After Bān Chāo (班超) left,
Rèn Shàng (任尚) privately said to his close associates:
"I thought Lord Bān (班) would have some extraordinary strategies;
but what he said was quite ordinary."
After Rèn Shàng (任尚) had been there for several years,
the Western Regions rebelled,
and he was summoned back due to his faults,
just as Bān Chāo (班超) had warned.
Bān Chāo (班超) had three sons.
The eldest son, Bān Xióng (班雄),
was successively promoted to Túnqí Xiàowèi (屯騎校尉).
When the rebellious Qiāng (羌) raided the Sānfǔ (三輔),
an imperial edict ordered Bān Xióng (班雄) to lead five battalions of troops to garrison Cháng'ān (長安),
and he was appointed Jīngzhàoyǐn (京兆尹).
When Bān Xióng (班雄) died,
his son Bān Shǐ (班始) succeeded him.
Bān Shǐ (班始) married the daughter of the King Xiào (孝) of Qīnghé (清河), Princess Yīnchéng (陰城).
The Princess was Emperor Shùn's (順) paternal aunt,
and she was arrogant, extravagant, and promiscuous.
She lived with her favorite paramour behind curtains,
and would summon Bān Shǐ (班始) to enter,
making him lie beneath the bed.
Bān Shǐ (班始)'s anger accumulated,
and in the fifth year of Yǒngjiàn (永建),
he drew his blade and killed the Princess.
The Emperor was greatly enraged,
and Bān Shǐ (班始) was cut in half at the waist,
and all his relatives by the same mother were executed in the marketplace.
Bān Chāo (班超)'s youngest son was Bān Yǒng (班勇).
Bān Yǒng (班勇), courtesy name Yíliáo (宜僚),
showed his father's demeanor from a young age.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (永初),
the Western Regions rebelled,
and Bān Yǒng (班勇) was appointed Jūnsīmǎ (軍司馬).
He went out from Dūnhuáng (敦煌) with his elder brother Bān Xióng (班雄),
to receive the Dūhù (都護) and the armored soldiers of the Western Regions, and returned.
Consequently, the office of Dūhù (都護) was abolished.
Thereafter, the Western Regions were cut off from Hàn (漢) officials for over ten years.
In the sixth year of Yuánchū (元初),
Cáo Zōng (曹宗), the Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng (敦煌), dispatched his Chief Clerk Suǒ Bān (索班) with over a thousand men to garrison Yīwú (伊吾).
The Former King of Chēshī (車師) and the King of Shànshàn (鄯善) both submitted to Suǒ Bān (索班).
A few months later,
the Northern Chányú (單于) and the Later Division of Chēshī (車師) attacked and annihilated Suǒ Bān (索班),
then advanced to rout the Former King,
and seized control of the Northern Route.
The King of Shànshàn (鄯善) was in distress
and sought help from Cáo Zōng (曹宗).
Cáo Zōng (曹宗) therefore requested to dispatch five thousand troops to attack the Xiongnú (匈奴),
to avenge the disgrace of Suǒ Bān (索班),
and thereby recover the Western Regions.
Empress Dowager Dèng (鄧太后) summoned Bān Yǒng (班勇) to the imperial court for a discussion.
Previously, many of the dukes and ministers believed that it was appropriate to close the Yùmén Guān (玉門關),
thus abandoning the Western Regions.
Bān Yǒng (班勇) submitted his argument:
"In the past, Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武) was concerned about the strength of the Xiongnú (匈奴),
who had united all the barbarians,
and were pressing against our border defenses.
Therefore, he opened up the Western Regions,
to separate their allies.
Commentators believed this was seizing the Xiongnú (匈奴)'s treasury
and severing their right arm.
During Wáng Mǎng (王莽)'s usurpation,
his demands were insatiable,
and the Hú Yí (胡夷) were resentful and bitter,
thus they revolted.
When Guāngwǔ (光武) rose again,
he did not yet attend to foreign affairs,
so the Xiongnú (匈奴) relied on their strength
to control various states.
By the time of Yǒngpíng (永平),
they attacked Dūnhuáng (敦煌) twice,
and the city gates of the various commanderies west of the river
were closed during the day.
Emperor Xiàomíng (孝明) deeply considered the temple strategy,
and thus ordered his brave ministers
to campaign in the Western Regions.
Therefore, the Xiongnú (匈奴) retreated far away,
and the border regions achieved peace.
By Yǒngyuán (永元),
none did not submit internally.
Recently, due to the Qiāng (羌) rebellion,
the Western Regions were again cut off,
and the Northern Lǔ (虜) then sent demands to the various states,
to collect their overdue taxes,
to set high prices,
and to strictly enforce deadlines.
Shànshàn (鄯善) and Chēshī (車師) both harbored resentment,
and longed to serve Hàn (漢),
but had no way to do so.
The reason why there were occasional rebellions previously
was due to improper administration
which then became detrimental to them.
Now, Cáo Zōng (曹宗) is merely shamed by the previous defeat,
wishing to avenge the Xiongnú (匈奴),
but he has not investigated past military campaigns
and has not considered what is appropriate for the current situation.
Indeed, to seek glory in distant lands
has one in ten thousand chance of success.
If war drags on and calamities multiply,
regret will be too late.
Moreover, the national treasury is not yet full,
and the army has no reserves.
This would be showing weakness to distant barbarians
and exposing our shortcomings to the world.
Your humble servant believes this should not be allowed.
Previously, Dūnhuáng (敦煌) Commandery had three hundred garrisoned troops;
it is now appropriate to restore them.
It is also appropriate to re-establish a Deputy Commandant for Protecting the Western Regions,
stationing him in Dūnhuáng (敦煌),
as was the practice in Yǒngyuán (永元).
Furthermore, it is appropriate to send a Chief Clerk for the Western Regions with five hundred men to garrison Lóulán (樓蘭).
This would block the routes to Yānqí (焉耆) and Qiūcí (龜茲) to the west,
strengthen the morale of Shànshàn (鄯善) and Yútián (于窴) to the south,
defend against the Xiongnú (匈奴) to the north,
and be close to Dūnhuáng (敦煌) to the east.
This would indeed be convenient."
Shàngshū asked Yǒng,
"Now, if a Fù Xiàowèi is established,
what would be the benefit?
Also, what are the pros and cons of stationing a Chángshǐ at Lóulán?"
Yǒng replied,
"In the late Yǒngpíng era,
we first opened communication with the Western Regions.
Initially, a Zhōnglángjiàng was sent to reside in Dūnhuáng,
and later a Fù Xiàowèi was established in Chēshī.
This was both to regulate the Hu barbarians
and to prevent Han people from encroaching.
Thus, the foreign tribes were won over,
and the Xiōngnú feared our might.
Now, Shànshàn King Yóu Huán,
a Han descendant through his mother,
would surely die if the Xiōngnú were to succeed.
Even though these people are like birds and beasts,
they know to avoid harm.
If we station troops at Lóulán,
it will be sufficient to attract their allegiance.
I believe this would be beneficial."
Chánglè Wèiwèi Tán Xiǎn, Tíngwèi Qímǔ Cān, and Sīlì Xiàowèi Cuī Jù objected, saying,
"The reason the imperial court previously abandoned the Western Regions
was because they were of no benefit to Zhōngguó and the expenses were difficult to sustain.
Now Chēshī has already submitted to the Xiōngnú,
and Shànshàn cannot be trusted.
Should they suddenly turn against us,
can Bān Jiāng guarantee that the northern barbarians will not harm the border?"
Yǒng replied,
"Zhōngguó now appoints Zhōumù
to suppress the cunning villains and bandits in the commanderies and counties.
If a Zhōumù can guarantee that no bandits will arise,
then I, your servant, would also pledge my life to guarantee that the Xiōngnú will not harm the border.
Now, by opening up the Western Regions, the power of the barbarians will surely weaken.
When the power of the barbarians weakens, their threat will diminish.
Which is better: to return their treasuries
and mend their severed arms?
Now, we establish a Xiàowèi to defend and soothe the Western Regions,
and appoint a Chángshǐ to attract and appease the various states.
If we abandon them and do not establish this presence,
then the hopes of the Western Regions will be cut off.
After their hopes are cut off,
they will submit to the northern barbarians,
and the commanderies along the border will suffer hardship.
I fear that the city gates of Héxī will again have to be closed by day as a warning.
If we do not now expand the virtue of the imperial court,
but instead restrict the expenses of garrisons,
and if the northern barbarians then flourish,
how can this be a long-term strategy for securing the border?"
Tàiwèi's subordinate Máo Zhěn objected, saying,
"If a Xiàowèi is established now,
then the Western Regions will send envoys one after another,
making insatiable demands.
If we grant them, the expenses will be difficult to bear;
if we do not, we will lose their allegiance.
Should they suddenly be pressured by the Xiōngnú,
they will again seek rescue,
which would entail great effort."
Yǒng replied,
"Suppose we now surrender the Western Regions to the Xiōngnú,
and they show kindness and virtue to the Great Han,
and do not raid us; then that would be acceptable.
If not,
then they would use the rich tribute from the Western Regions
and their numerous soldiers and horses
to harass the border regions.
This would be enriching the wealth of our enemies
and increasing the power of the violent barbarians.
Establishing a Xiàowèi is to propagate our might and spread our virtue,
to secure the inward-looking hearts of the various states,
and to sow doubt in the Xiōngnú's covetous intentions,
without the concern of financial expenditure depleting the nation.
Moreover, the people of the Western Regions have no other demands;
those who come to us
only seek provisions.
If we now refuse them,
they will inevitably submit to the north.
If the barbarians combine their forces to invade Bìng and Liáng,
then Zhōngguó's expenses will not be limited to a thousand billion.
Establishing this post is truly beneficial."
Thereupon, Yǒng's proposal was followed.
Three hundred garrison soldiers were restored to Dūnhuáng Commandery,
and a Fù Xiàowèi of the Western Regions was established to reside in Dūnhuáng.
Although this restrained the Western Regions,
they were still unable to send troops to garrison outside.
Afterward, the Xiōngnú indeed repeatedly invaded and raided with Chēshī,
and Héxī suffered greatly.
In the summer of Yánguāng second year (123 CE),
Yǒng was again appointed Chángshǐ of the Western Regions,
leading five hundred soldiers to garrison Liǔzhōng.
In the first month of the following year,
Yǒng arrived at Lóulán.
Because Shànshàn had submitted,
he was specially awarded three ribbons.
However, Qiūcí King Bái Yīng was still suspicious and had not yet submitted.
Yǒng persuaded him with kindness and trustworthiness,
and Bái Yīng then led Gūmò and Wēnsù to bind themselves and surrender to Yǒng.
Yǒng then dispatched their infantry and cavalry, over ten thousand men, to the former royal court of Chēshī,
and drove away the Xiōngnú Yīlí King at Yīhé Gǔ.
He recovered more than five thousand people from the Former Division,
and thus the Former Division began to reopen communication.
He returned
to establish military colonies at Liǔzhōng.
In the autumn of the fourth year (125 CE),

Yǒng dispatched six thousand cavalry from Dūnhuáng, Zhāngyè, and Jiǔquán, as well as soldiers from Shànshàn, Shūlè, and the Former Division of Chēshī, to attack the King of the Later Division, Jūn Jiù.
He thoroughly defeated him.
They captured over eight thousand heads and prisoners,
and over fifty thousand horses and livestock.
Jūn Jiù and the Xiōngnú envoy with credentials were captured,
brought to the place where Suǒ Bān had been killed, and executed,
to avenge that humiliation.
Their heads were sent to the capital.
In Yǒngjiàn first year (126 CE),
the former prince of the Later Division, Jiātè Nú, was re-established as king.
Yǒng also sent a separate commander to execute the King of Dōngqiěmí,
and re-established one of his kinsmen as king.
Thus, the six states of Chēshī were all pacified.
That winter,
Yǒng dispatched troops from the various states to attack the Xiōngnú Hūyǎn King.
Hūyǎn King fled,
and his more than twenty thousand followers all surrendered.
The Chányú's cousin was captured,
and Yǒng had Jiātè Nú personally execute him,
to seal the rift between Chēshī and the Xiōngnú.
The Northern Chányú personally led over ten thousand cavalry into the Later Division,
reaching Jīnqiě Gǔ.
Yǒng sent acting Sīmǎ Cáo Jùn to rush to their rescue.
The Chányú retreated,
and Jùn pursued and executed his nobleman Gǔdū Hóu.
Thus, Hūyǎn King then moved his residence to the banks of Kūwú Hé.
After this, there were no more barbarian traces in Chēshī,
and all the walled cities were secure.
Only Yānqí King Yuán Mèng had not yet submitted.
In the second year (127 CE),
Yǒng petitioned to attack Yuán Mèng.
Thereupon, Dūnhuáng Tàishǒu Zhāng Lǎng was sent to lead three thousand soldiers from the four commanderies of Héxī to reinforce Yǒng.
He then dispatched over forty thousand soldiers from the various states,
dividing the cavalry into two routes to attack them.
Yǒng took the southern route,
Lǎng took the northern route,
agreeing to arrive at Yānqí at the same time.
However, Lǎng had previously committed a crime
and wished to gain merit to redeem himself.
So he arrived at Juélí Guān ahead of schedule,
sent his Sīmǎ to lead troops to fight ahead,
capturing over two thousand heads and prisoners.
Yuán Mèng, fearing execution,
sent an envoy to surrender.
Zhāng Lǎng directly entered Yānqí to accept the surrender and returned.
Yuán Mèng ultimately refused to appear bound,
only sending his son to the imperial court to offer tribute.
Lǎng thus escaped execution.
Yǒng, for being late,
was summoned and imprisoned,
then dismissed.
Later, he died at home.
Liáng Jǐn, courtesy name Bówēi,
was a native of Yìjū, Běidì.
His father, Fěng,
served as a governor of provinces.
In Yǒngyuán first year (89 CE),
Chējì Jiāngjūn Dòu Xiàn led an expedition against the Xiōngnú.
Fěng was appointed Jūnsīmǎ
and ordered to first carry gold and silks to the Northern Chányú,
proclaiming the nation's might and virtue.
More than ten thousand people submitted to him.
Later, he was punished for displeasing Dòu Xiàn,
shaved his head and was exiled to Wǔwēi.
The Tàishǒu of Wǔwēi, following orders, killed him.
After the Dòu clan was exterminated,
Emperor Hé, knowing that Fěng had been falsely accused by Dòu Xiàn,
summoned Jǐn
and appointed him Lángzhōng.
Jǐn had courage,
and was always magnanimous and fond of glory.
Initially, he served as a Sīmǎ under Chējì Jiāngjūn, Dèng Hóng.
After further promotion,
in the first year of Yánpíng (106 CE), he was appointed Fù Xiàowèi of the Western Regions.
When Jǐn arrived at Héxī,
it happened that the various kingdoms of the Western Regions had rebelled,
attacking Dūhù Rèn Shàng in Shūlè.
Shàng sent a memorial requesting aid.
An imperial edict ordered Jǐn to lead five thousand Qīang and Hú cavalry from the four commanderies of Héxī to rush to his aid.
Before Jǐn arrived, Shàng had already been relieved.
It happened that Shàng was recalled,
and Qí Dūwèi Duàn Xǐ was appointed Dūhù,
while Xīyù Chángshǐ Zhào Bó became Qí Dūwèi.
Xǐ and Bó guarded Tāgān City.
Tāgān City was small,
and Jǐn thought it could not be held securely.
So, he cunningly persuaded the King of Qiūcí, Bái Bà,
to let him enter and jointly defend his city.
Bái Bà agreed.
His officials and people strongly advised against it,
but Bái Bà did not listen.
Once Jǐn entered,
he sent his generals to urgently summon Xǐ and Bó.
Their combined forces numbered eight or nine thousand men.
The officials and people of Qiūcí all rebelled against their king,
and joined tens of thousands of soldiers from Wēnsù and Gūmò in revolt,
together besieging the city.
Jǐn and the others sallied forth to fight,
and utterly defeated them.
After continuous fighting for several months,
the Hú forces were defeated and fled.
Taking advantage of the victory, they pursued and attacked,
beheading over ten thousand enemies in total,
capturing several thousand people,
and tens of thousands of camels and livestock.
Qiūcí was then pacified.
However, the roads were still obstructed,
and official dispatches could not pass through.
After more than a year,
the imperial court was concerned about this.
The senior officials and ministers who deliberated thought that the Western Regions were remote and distant,
and frequently rebelled.
The expenses for officials and soldiers stationed there for garrison farming
were endless.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (107 CE),
the Dūhù was consequently abolished.
Qí Dūwèi Wáng Hóng was dispatched to lead troops from Guānzhōng to escort Jǐn, Xǐ, Bó, and the garrison farming officials and soldiers from Yīwúlú and Liǔzhōng.
In the spring of the second year (108 CE),
they returned to Dūnhuáng.
It happened that the various Qiāng rebelled,
and the imperial court greatly mobilized forces to attack them in the west.
An imperial edict ordered Jǐn to stay and provide support for the various armies.
Jǐn arrived at Rìlè in Zhāngyè.
Over ten thousand Qiāng from various tribes attacked the observation posts,
killing and plundering officials and people.
Jǐn advanced his troops to attack,
and utterly defeated them.
Taking advantage of the victory, he pursued them to Zhāowǔ.
The captives then scattered and fled,
only twelve or thirteen out of a hundred able to escape.
Upon arriving at Gūzāng,
over three hundred great Qiāng chieftains surrendered to Jǐn.
He appeased them and sent them back to their original lands,
and the four commanderies of Héxī were once again peaceful.
Jǐn received an imperial edict to be stationed in Jīnchéng.
Upon hearing that the Qiāng had turned to raid Sānfǔ,
and were approaching the imperial mausoleums,
he immediately led his troops to attack them,
fighting continuously at Wǔgōng Měiyáng Pass.
Jǐn was wounded in battle,
but disregarded it,
repeatedly breaking and routing them.
He recovered all the captured people who had been plundered,
and seized a great many horses, livestock, and valuables.
The Qiāng then fled in disarray.
The imperial court commended him,
repeatedly sending sealed letters to commend and encourage him,
entrusting him with affairs in the west,
and ordering him to coordinate the various armies.
In the winter of the third year (109 CE),
the Southern Chányú and the Wūhuán chieftains all rebelled.
Dà Sīnóng Hé Xī was appointed to act as Chējì Jiāngjūn,
with Zhōngláng Jiāng Páng Xióng as his deputy,
leading the soldiers of the Yǔlín Wǔxiào camps,
and mobilizing over twenty thousand troops from ten frontier commanderies.
Additionally, Liáodōng Tàishǒu Gěng Kuí led his Xiānbēi tribesmen to jointly attack them,
and Jǐn was appointed to act as Dùliáo Jiāngjūn.
Páng Xióng and Gěng Kuí jointly attacked the Xiōngnú Àojiān Rìzhú Wáng,
and defeated him.
The Chányú then personally led his forces to besiege Zhōngláng Jiāng Gěng Zhǒng at Měijì.
After several months of continuous fighting,
the attacks became increasingly urgent.
Zhǒng dispatched a message requesting aid.
In the first month of the following year (110 CE),
Jǐn led over eight thousand men to rush to his aid.
Upon reaching the former city of Shǔguó,
he engaged in battle with the Xiōngnú Zuǒ Jiāngjūn and the Wūhuán chieftain,
defeating and beheading their leaders,
killing over three thousand people,
capturing their wives and children,
and seizing a great many valuables.
The Chányú then personally led seven or eight thousand cavalry to meet and attack him,
besieging Jǐn.
Jǐn donned his armor and charged,
breaking through wherever he went.
The captives then retreated to Hǔzé.
In the third month,
Hé Xī's army arrived at Mánbó in Wǔyuán,
and he fell severely ill,
unable to advance.
He sent Páng Xióng, Jǐn, and Gěng Zhǒng with sixteen thousand infantry and cavalry to attack Hǔzé.
They gradually advanced their camps.
The Chányú was terrified,
and sent the Zuǒ Àojiān Rìzhú Wáng to Jǐn to beg for surrender.
Jǐn then grandly arrayed his troops to receive him.
The Chányú removed his cap, went barefoot,
bound his hands, and kowtowed,
offering hostages.
It happened that Xī died in the army.
Jǐn was then appointed Dùliáo Jiāngjūn.
Páng Xióng returned to become Dà Hónglú.
Xióng,
a native of Bājùn,
possessed courage and strategy,
and was known as a famous general.
The following year (111 CE),
Āndìng, Běidì, and Shàngjùn were all ravaged by Qiāng bandits.
Grain was expensive, and people became refugees,
unable to sustain themselves.
An imperial edict ordered Jǐn to mobilize frontier troops to escort the Tàishǒus of the three commanderies,
and have their officials and people relocate to the Fúfēng region.
Jǐn immediately dispatched Yōugūtú Núl, the nephew of the Southern Chányú, to lead troops to escort them.
After they returned,
Jǐn, considering Tú Núl's efforts in escorting their families,
presumptuously granted him the seal and ribbon of a Qiāng Hóu.
For this unauthorized action,
he was summoned, imprisoned,
and convicted.
The following year (112 CE),
Xiàoshū Láng Mǎ Róng submitted a memorial defending Jǐn and Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi Páng Cān.
An imperial edict pardoned their punishment.
The account is in the biography of Páng Cān.
It happened that the rebellious Qiāng raided Sānfǔ,
and bandits arose in Guānzhōng.
Jǐn was appointed Yèzhě,
and ordered to lead troops to attack them.
Upon reaching Húxiàn,
he fell ill and died.
Hé Xī, courtesy name Mèngsūn,
was from Chénguó.
He had great ambition from a young age.
During the Yǒngyuán period (89-105 CE),
he served as Yèzhě.
He was eight feet five inches tall,
skilled at presenting a dignified appearance.
When announcing obeisance in the palace hall,
his voice resonated all around.
Emperor Hé admired him,
and promoted him to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
successively serving as Sīlì Xiàowèi and Dà Sīnóng.
When he was in the army and nearing his death,
he left instructions for a simple burial.
He had three sons: Lín,
Jǐn,
and Fù.
Lín and Jǐn both possessed administrative ability.
Fù was exceptionally talented but died young.
Lín's son, Héng,
served as Shàngshū,
and was known for his uprightness.
He was imprisoned for defending Lǐ Yīng and others,
dismissed from office,
and remained in his home.
Commentary: When governance is peaceful, civil virtue is employed,
and military strategists have no opportunity to display their strength and abilities.
Thus, in the Hàn dynasty, there were many who, full of indignation and courage,
competed to sacrifice themselves among the barbarians to achieve fame and glory.
There were many such individuals.
Zhài Róng and Gěng Bǐng initiated the power against the Xiōngnú;
Bān Chāo and Liáng Jǐn exerted their strategies in the Western Regions.
They ultimately succeeded in achieving fame,
enjoyed their noble ranks,
offered their accomplishments to the ancestral temple,
and inscribed their merits for posterity.
They were also ambitious men of their time.
Eulogy: Dìngyuǎn was magnanimous,
devoting his efforts to the far west.
He traversed the Cōng and Xuě mountains,
making Lóngshā seem close by.
Jǐn, too, was indignant,
and bravely took on responsibility.
Biographies of Yáng, Lǐ, Zhái, Yīng, Huò, Yuán, Xú, Thirty-eighth
Yáng Zhōng, whose courtesy name was Zǐshān,
was a native of Chéngdū, Shǔjùn Commandery.
At thirteen,
he became a minor official in the commandery.
The Grand Administrator admired his talent
and sent him to the capital to study,
where he specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
During the reign of Xiǎnzōng,
he was summoned to the Lántái Terrace
and appointed Collator of Books (Jiàoshūláng).
In the first year of Jiànchū (76 CE),
there was a great drought and grain was expensive.
Yáng Zhōng believed that the prisons of Guǎnglíng, Chǔ, Huáinán, and Jìnán
had tens of thousands of exiles,
who were moreover stationed in remote, desolate regions.
Officials and common people were resentful and neglected.
So he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard, 'Good deeds benefit one's descendants,
while evil deeds cease with one's own person.'
This is the constant principle of a hundred kings,
an unchanging way.
Qín's government was cruel and severe,
contrary to the heart of Heaven.
If one person committed a crime,
it extended to three generations of their family.
Gāozǔ pacified the rebellion
and enacted three simple laws.
Tàizōng was supremely benevolent
and abolished the practice of seizing families.
The myriad people were greatly relieved,
experiencing a new lease on life.
His beneficence reached even insects,
and his merits will endure for myriad generations.
Your Majesty's sagely ancestor
extended his virtue to all four quarters.
Now, with the continuous drought in recent years,
and epidemics still raging,
Your Majesty personally practices frugality,
extensively inquiring about shortcomings and successes.
Even the prosperity of the Three Dynasties
could not surpass this.
Your servant covertly examines the changes of floods and droughts in the Spring and Autumn Annals,
which all correspond to sudden urgency
and a failure of benevolence to flow downwards.
Since the Yǒngpíng era,
there have been repeated major legal cases.
The responsible officials rigorously investigated,
leading to mutual implication.
Torture and unjust accusations were rampant,
and families were exiled to the borders.
In addition, there was the northern campaign against the Xiōngnú
and the opening of the Thirty-Six States in the west.
Years of military service
and burdensome transport expenses followed.
Furthermore, there are remote garrisons at Yīwú, Lóulán, Chēshī, and Wùjǐ.
The people long for their homeland
and their resentment gathers at the frontiers.
The Classic says: 'Those who settle in their homeland and value their dwellings
are called the multitudes.'
In ancient times, when the Yīn people were moved to Luòyì,
they still harbored resentment and longing.
How much more so when they depart from the fertile richness of the central lands
to be cast into barren and desolate extremities?
Moreover, the south is hot and humid,
with miasmic poisons arising everywhere.
The distressed and suffering people
are enough to move Heaven and Earth
and alter the balance of Yin and Yang.
May Your Majesty give careful consideration and examine this,
to save the common people."
After the memorial was presented,
Sùzōng referred his petition.
The Minister of Works (Sīkōng), Díwǔ Lún, also agreed with Yáng Zhōng's view.
However, the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Móu Róng, the Minister of Education (Sītú) Bào Yù, and Collator of Books (Jiàoshūláng) Bān Gù, among others, challenged Díwǔ Lún,
arguing that since the policies had been in effect for a long time,
a filial son should not alter his father's way.
What the former emperor had established
should not be changed.
Yáng Zhōng again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Qín built the Great Wall,
with numerous public works.
Húhài did not reform this,
and consequently lost the empire.
Therefore, Emperor Xiàoyuán abolished the commandery of Zhūyá,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ cut off relations with the Western Regions states,
not valuing scales or fins over our clothing.
When Duke Wén of Lǔ destroyed the Quántái Terrace,
the Spring and Autumn Annals criticized him, saying, 'His ancestor made it, and he destroyed it;
it would have been better not to reside there.'
This was because it caused no harm to the people.
When Duke Xiāng established three armies,
Duke Zhāo abolished them.
The superior man praised his return to antiquity,
believing that not abolishing them would have harmed the people.
[一０] Now, the campaign at Yīwú
and the garrison at Lóulán
have been prolonged and the men have not returned.
This is not the will of Heaven."
The emperor agreed with him,
allowing the exiles to return
and entirely disbanding the border garrisons.
Yáng Zhōng further stated:
"Emperor Xuān extensively summoned scholars
to discuss and establish the Five Classics at the Shíqúgé Pavilion.
At present, there are few affairs in the empire,
and scholars are able to complete their studies.
However, the followers of fragmented sentences
are damaging the grand structure.
It would be appropriate to follow the precedent of Shíqúgé,
setting an eternal model for future generations."
Thereupon, an edict was issued for the scholars to discuss and examine similarities and differences at the Báihǔguān Pavilion.
At that time, Yáng Zhōng was imprisoned for a certain matter.
Doctor (Bóshì) Zhào Bó, Collator of Books (Jiàoshūláng) Bān Gù, Jiǎ Kuí, and others,
knowing Yáng Zhōng deeply understood the Spring and Autumn Annals
and possessed extensive and unique knowledge,
submitted a memorial requesting his release.
Yáng Zhōng also submitted a memorial to defend himself.
He was released the same day
and was thus able to participate in the Báihǔguān discussions.
Later, he received an imperial edict to abridge the Grand Historian's (Tàishǐgōng) work to over 100,000 words.
At that time, the Empress Dowager's brother, the Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi) Mǎ Liáo,
was discreet and self-controlled,
but failed to instruct his sons.
Yáng Zhōng was on good terms with Mǎ Liáo
and sent him a letter of admonition, saying:
"Your servant has heard that the people of Yáo and Shùn
could be enfeoffed house by house;
the people of Jié and Zhòu
could be executed house by house.
Why is this?
Yáo and Shùn established preventive measures for them,
while Jié and Zhòu displayed arrogance and extravagance.
The Odes say: 'How pure is the white silk,
it is dyed by what it touches.'
The supremely wise and the utterly foolish
are said to be unchangeable;
but those of moderate disposition
depend on education and transformation.
The Spring and Autumn Annals, when recording the killing of a crown prince's mother's brother,
directly states that 'the ruler greatly detested him,'
implying fault in the lack of instruction.
According to the rites,
when a ruler's son reaches eight years old,
a Junior Tutor (Shàofù) is appointed for him
to teach him writing and calculation,
to open his intelligence;
at fifteen, a Grand Tutor (Tàifù) is appointed
to teach him the Classics,
to guide his aspirations.
Since the Hàn dynasty arose,
the feudal princes did not exert themselves in teaching and admonishing,
often violating prohibitions.
Hence, they suffered the disaster of lost states
and lacked praise for virtue.
Now, your position is exalted and respected,
and the whole empire looks up to you.
How can you not be cautious, as if approaching a deep abyss or treading on thin ice,
taking this as the utmost warning!
The Yellow Gate Attendants (Huángménláng) are young,
with vigorous blood and qi.
They lack the humility and deference of an elder brother,
and instead associate with frivolous, cunning, and immoral guests.
If they are indulged and not admonished,
and allowed to act according to their nature,
reflecting on past examples,
it is enough to make one's heart turn cold.
Your Lordship should truly take approaching a deep abyss and treading on thin ice as a warning."
Mǎ Liáo did not accept it.
His son, Yù, later suffered for slandering the county government,
and Mǎ Liáo was sent back to his fief.
Yáng Zhōng's elder brother, Fèng, was a county official.
When the Grand Administrator Lián Fàn was investigated by the province,
he sent Fèng to visit Yáng Zhōng.
Yáng Zhōng spoke on Lián Fàn's behalf,
and consequently was exiled to Běidì.
When the emperor made an eastern inspection tour,
phoenixes and yellow dragons gathered simultaneously.
Yáng Zhōng praised these auspicious omens,
recounting the grand achievements of the ancestors
in fifteen chapters.
He presented them to the throne,
and an edict granted his return to his former commandery.
He authored twelve chapters of the Spring and Autumn External Commentary
and revised and finalized the sentences and chapters into 150,000 words.
In the twelfth year of Yǒngyuán (100 CE),
he was summoned and appointed Langzhong,
but died of illness.
Lǐ Fǎ 字 Bó dù,
a native of Nánzhèng, Hànzhōng.
He was broadly knowledgeable in many books,
and his nature was upright and principled.
In the 9th year of Yǒngyuán during Emperor Hé's reign,
he responded to the examination for "Xianliang Fangzheng" (Virtuous and Upright) by submitting a policy paper,
and was appointed Bóshì (Erudite).
He was promoted to Shìzhōng and Guānglù Dàfū.
After more than a year,
he submitted a memorial, believing that the court administration was overly meticulous and fragmented,
deviating from the precedents of Yǒngpíng and Jiànchū;
that the eunuchs held too much power,
and the empress's relatives were excessively favored.
He also criticized the historians for not recording events truthfully,
fearing that in later generations, discerning individuals,
when examining merits and assessing virtues,
would surely find them incredible.
For having expressed unpalatable views,
he was handed over to the relevant authorities
and dismissed as a commoner.
He returned to his hometown
and secluded himself.
His old acquaintances, scholars, occasionally visited him.
During their conversations,
they asked him about the reasons for his not aligning with the emperor's wishes,
but Fǎ never answered.
When his friends pressed him persistently,
Fǎ said:
"Can a common man serve a ruler effectively?
If one is constantly worried about losing one's position,
there is nothing one will not stoop to.
Mèngzǐ said: 'Indeed, a benevolent person is like an archer:
he rectifies himself before shooting.
If he shoots and does not hit the mark,
he does not blame those who surpassed him,
but simply seeks the cause within himself.'"
After eight years at home,
he was summoned and appointed Yìláng and Jiànyì Dàfū.
He spoke frankly and forcefully,
without changing his former ways.
He was appointed as Rǔnán Tàishǒu,
where his administration was renowned.
Later, he returned to his hometown
and died at home.
Zhái Pú, 字 Zǐchāo,
was a native of Luò, Guǎnghàn.
His family had transmitted the Book of Odes for four generations.
Pú was fond of Lǎozi,
and particularly skilled in prognostic charts (túwěi), astronomy, and calendrical calculations.
Because he avenged his maternal uncle,
he was sentenced to exile in Rìnán,
but he fled to Cháng'ān
and worked as a diviner and physiognomist.
Later, he herded sheep in Liángzhōu.
He returned after a general amnesty.
He served in the commandery,
then was summoned and appointed Yìláng,
and promoted to Shìzhōng.
At that time, there was a vacancy for the position of Shàngshū.
An imperial edict ordered officials of Dàfū rank and above, with salaries of 600 dàn or more, to be tested on political affairs, astronomy, and Daoist arts,
and the one with the highest score would be appointed.
Pú, confident in his high abilities,
yet wary of the former Tàishǐ Lìng Sūn Yì,
feared that Yì might be chosen first.
So he went to visit Yì.
After sitting down,
he spoke of nothing in particular,
but only wept profusely and lingered.
Yì found this strange and asked him about it.
Pú said:
"The prognostic charts speak of a Hàn 'bandit' named Sūn Dēng,
who, by virtue of his talent and wisdom, will be harmed by central officials.
Observing your physiognomy,
it seems you might be that person.
Pú, having received your kindness,
is merely saddened by your impending misfortune!"
Yì, anxious and fearful,
feigned illness and did not take the test.
Because of this, Pú ranked first in the examination
and was appointed Shàngshū.
At that time, Emperor Ān had just begun to handle state affairs personally.
He remembered with gratitude his grandmother, the noble consort Sòng,
and conferred titles upon all her family members.
Also, his maternal uncle Gěng Bǎo and the empress's brothers Yán Xiǎn and others all wielded great power.
Pú submitted a memorial, advising: "Your servant has heard that Wēizǐ feigned madness and departed from Yīn,
and Shūsūn Tōng abandoned Qín and returned to Hàn.
They did not estrange themselves from their rulers willingly,
but the times made it impossible.
Your servant bears extraordinary
favors,
and is fortunate to live under a reign where frank speech is not taboo.
How dare I merely follow suit to receive favor,
and live heedlessly under heaven and on earth?
I humbly submit that Your Majesty, having received Heaven's mandate and assumed the throne,
is experiencing a period of Middle
Revival.
You ought to establish the accomplishments of Great Peace,
yet I have not heard of the means to achieve such transformation.
Indeed, distant examples are hard to discern;
please allow me to illustrate with recent events.
In the past, the favor bestowed upon the Dòu and Dèng families
shook
the four directions.
They held multiple offices and heavy insignia,
amassed gold and accumulated goods,
even to the extent of contemplating usurpation of the divine instruments of power,
and altering the state.
Was this not due to their exalted position and extensive influence,
which led to such
disasters?
But when their downfall came,
their heads bowed to the ground,
wishing to be mere piglets—
how could that be granted!
Indeed, when acquiring wealth has no gradual process, loss is sudden and violent;
when receiving titles is not by the proper way,
calamity is swift.
Currently, the favored relatives of the empress
have power equal to that of creation itself;
since the time of Emperor Yuán of Hàn,
there has been no equal.
Your Majesty's benevolence and grace are indeed comprehensive,
extending to the nine kindred.
However, emoluments are leaving the public coffers,
and governance is shifting to private households.
If the overturned cart is followed again,
how can there not be collapse?
Yet, the court officials in their positions
are unwilling to speak righteously,
but rather flatter and criticize, mutually assisting and attaching themselves.
Your servant fears that if authority and power are delegated externally,
it will be very difficult to reclaim them.
Once a tiger's wings are spread,
it cannot be controlled.
Therefore, Confucius said:
'If pearls are thrown into the marsh,
who can avoid
picking them up?'
Lǎozi said:
'The sharp weapon of the state
must not be displayed to others.'
These are the most critical
warnings for safety and danger,
and profound
strategies for the state.
Jiǎn,
the emperor said:
'I am merely the guardian of the nation's wealth;
how can I use it indiscriminately?'
Until the grain in the granaries rotted and became inedible,
and the strings of coins decayed and could not be
counted.
Now, since the beginning of this reign,
not much time has passed,
yet expenses and rewards are already immeasurable.
The nation's wealth is collected
and accumulated in the homes of those without merit.
The national treasury is depleted
and exhausted,
and the people and resources are ravaged and injured.
Should an unforeseen event occur,
you will again have to heavily tax the populace,
and when resentment and rebellion arise,
danger and chaos will be imminent.
Róng,
who heard righteous words,
on the first day he ascended the throne,
the whole world felt enlightened,
signifying that his laws and institutions were already well-established.
Now, Your Majesty has the venerable status of King Chéng but lacks the ministers
who assisted the young king.
Even if you wish to promote harmony and prosperity,
and bring about great peace,
how can it be achieved?
Since last year,
disasters and condemnations have been frequent:
the earth has cracked, heaven has collapsed,
and high shores have become valleys.
If one cultivates oneself with fear and trepidation,
calamity can be turned into fortune;
if one treats Heaven's warnings with lightness and disrespect,
then the harm will be even deeper.
May Your Majesty personally exert yourself in caring for the people,
delve deeply into thought,
strive to seek out loyal and upright ministers,
punish and distance the party of sycophants,
reduce the extravagance of the imperial palace,
respect the importance of Heaven's titles,
curtail the pleasures of desires,
and abandon the fondness for private banquets.
Let the imperial records and maps
be displayed at your left and right,
keeping in mind how lost states fell,
and observing how founding kings succeeded.
Then disasters may be averted,
and abundant harvests may be ushered in."
In the third year of Yán'guāng (124 CE),
he was sent out as the Administrator of Jiǔquán.
Over a thousand Qīng riders from Dūnhuáng rebelled and plundered the commandery's border.
Pú went to attack them,
beheading nine hundred.
The Qīng forces were almost entirely wiped out,
and his prestige greatly increased.
He was promoted to Jīngzhàoyǐn.
When Emperor Shùn ascended the throne,
he was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū),
then promoted to Grand Artisan (Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng).
He reduced expenditures,
saving forty to fifty million [cash] annually.
Repeatedly, due to natural disasters and anomalies,
he made many corrections.
Because of this, powerful and influential officials collectively slandered Pú and Grandee Secretary Gāotáng Zhī, among others, alleging they engaged in illicit influence peddling and patronage.
He was sentenced to a reduced death penalty, which meant returning home.
Later, another memorial accused Pú of having previously conspired to rebel with Zhāng Kǎi of Hénán and others.
He was arrested and brought to the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi).
When Dù Zhēn and others submitted memorials defending him,
the matter was clarified and he was acquitted.
He died at home.
He authored twelve chapters of commentary, "Yuánshén Gōumìng Jiěgǔ".
Initially,
when Pú was Grand Artisan,
he memorialized, saying:
"Emperor Xiàowén first established a 'Doctor of One Classic' (Yī Jīng Bóshì);
Emperor Wǔ extensively gathered all the books in the realm;
and Emperor Xiānlùn discussed the Six Classics at the Shíqú Pavilion.
Scholars flourished,
with tens of thousands of disciples.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ first rose,
lamenting their desolation and neglect,
he built the Imperial Academy (Tàixué) doctors' residences and internal and external lecture halls.
Students filled the alleys,
making it a gathering place for the whole country.
During Emperor Míng's time, the Bìyōng was first completed.
Wishing to demolish the Imperial Academy,
Grand Commandant Zhào Xǐ believed that both the Imperial Academy and Bìyōng should be preserved.
Thus, both have been transmitted to this day.
But recently, they have fallen into disrepair,
even becoming places for gardens, foraging, and pasturage.
It is appropriate to repair them again,
to attract and advance later scholars."
The Emperor followed his advice.
After Pú was dismissed,
the Imperial Academy was indeed rebuilt,
and its rooms were expanded.
Scholars erected a stele in Pú's honor at the academy.
Yīng Fèng, courtesy name Shìshú,
was a native of Nándùn, Rǔnán.
His great-grandfather, Shùn,
courtesy name Huázhòng,
served as Administrator of Hénán and Grand Artisan during Emperor Hé's reign.
He was public-spirited, honest, and disciplined,
and insightful in governance.
He had ten sons,
all talented and learned.
His second son, Dié,
was Administrator of Jiāngxià.
Dié begot Chēn,
who was Administrator of Wǔlíng.
Chēn begot Fèng.
Fèng was intelligent from a young age.
From childhood to adulthood,
whatever he encountered,
he could memorize.
When reading, he could take in five lines at once.
As an Assistant Judge (Juécáo Shǐ) for the commandery,
he toured forty-two counties,
recording hundreds or thousands of prisoners.
Upon his return,
the Administrator questioned him thoroughly.
Fèng verbally recounted the names of the accused and incarcerated,
as well as the details and severity of their cases,
omitting nothing.
People of the time marveled at this.
He authored "Hànshū Hòuxù",
which recorded many events.
Grand General Liáng Jì recommended him as a Mào Cài.
Previously,
the Wǔlíng Mán, under Zhān Shān, numbering over four thousand, had rebelled,
captured the county magistrate,
