and remained entrenched for years.
An imperial edict was issued for the Grand Ministers (Gōngqīng) to deliberate.
The Four Bureaus (Sì Fǔ) recommended Fèng as capable of being a commander.
In the first year of Yǒngxīng (153 CE),
he was appointed Administrator of Wǔlíng.
Upon arrival, he offered comfort and conciliation,
and Zhān Shān and his followers all surrendered and dispersed.
Thereupon, he promoted schools,
and elevated the humble,
his governance being praised for transforming customs.
He was dismissed due to an official matter.
During the Yánxī period (158-167 CE),
the Wǔlíng Mán again plundered and caused unrest in Jīngzhōu.
General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn) Féng Gǔn, knowing Fèng had prestige and kindness,
and was respected by the barbarians,
memorialized to request his participation in the expedition.
He was appointed Palace Assistant Imperial Clerk (Cóngshì Zhōngláng).
Fèng diligently devised strategies,
and after the rebels were defeated and the army disbanded,
Gǔn attributed the success to Fèng,
and recommended him as Colonel Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
He investigated and exposed wrongdoing,
without sparing powerful relatives,
and gained a reputation for strictness.
When Empress Dèng fell from favor,
and Lady Tián was favored,
Emperor Huán considered making her empress.
Fèng, considering the Tián clan to be humble and lowly,
and therefore unsuitable to be elevated to the empress's position,
submitted a memorial remonstrating, saying:
"Your servant has heard that when Zhōu married a Dì woman,
King Xiāng was forced to reside in Zhèng;
when Hàn established Fēi Yàn,
Emperor Chéng's lineage became extinct.
The importance of the empress mother
is the cause of rise and fall.
It is fitting to consider what is sought by the 'Guān Jū' ode,
and avoid what is forbidden by the five prohibitions."
The Emperor accepted his words
and ultimately established Empress Dòu.
When the 'Partisan Prohibitions' (Dǎngshì) arose,
Fèng, with a sigh, retired due to illness.
He mourned Qū Yuán,
and thus felt sorrow for himself,
writing "Gǎn Sāo" in thirty chapters,
tens of thousands of words.
Many high officials recommended him,
but he died of illness.
His son was Shào.
Shào, courtesy name Zhòngyuǎn,
was devoted to learning from a young age,
and widely read and knowledgeable.
During Emperor Líng's reign, he was recommended as a Xiàolián,
and appointed as a clerk (yuán) to General of Chariots and Cavalry Hé Miáo.
In the second year of Zhōngpíng,
the Hàn Yáng bandits Biān Zhāng and Hán Suì, with the Qiāng and Hú, became brigands,
invading the Three Fǔ to the east.
At that time, the Chēqí Jiāngjūn Huángfǔ Sōng was dispatched to suppress them in the west.
Sōng requested to enlist three thousand Wūhuán.
The Běijūn Zhōnghòu Zōu Jìng submitted a memorial, stating:
“The Wūhuán are numerous but weak;
it is advisable to recruit Xiānbēi.”
The matter was sent down to the Four Fǔ.
The Dà Jiāngjūn Yuàn Hán Zhuó deliberated,
believing
“Wūhuán troops are few,
and they have been hereditary enemies with the Xiānbēi.
If the Wūhuán are deployed,
the Xiānbēi will certainly attack their homes.
When the Wūhuán hear of this,
they will withdraw their troops and return to rescue them.
Not only will this provide no practical benefit,
but it will also demoralize the three armies.”
Zōu Jìng lives close to the border,
and is thorough in understanding their deceptions.
“If Jìng is ordered to recruit five thousand Xiānbēi light cavalry,
it will surely be effective in defeating the enemy.”
Shào refuted this, saying:
“The Xiānbēi are separated by the desert to the north,
living in nomadic groups like dogs and sheep,
without a sovereign leader,
or permanent dwellings.
Their nature is greedy and violent,
they do not adhere to trustworthiness or righteousness.
Thus, they frequently violate the barriers and fortifications,
and there is never a year of peace.
Only when they come to the border markets
do they become submissive.
They merely desire China’s precious goods,
not out of fear of our might or admiration of our virtue.
Once their goal is achieved and their needs are met,
they immediately turn into a menace.
This is why the imperial court keeps them external and does not incorporate them,
this is precisely the reason.
Previously, when the Xiongnú rebelled,
the Dùliáo Jiāngjūn Mǎ Xù and Wūhuán Xiàowèi Wáng Yuán raised over five thousand Xiānbēi cavalry.
Moreover, the Wǔwēi Tàishǒu Zhào Chōng also led Xiānbēi to suppress the rebellious Qiāng.
The number of enemy captured and beheaded
was not worth mentioning.
Instead, the Xiānbēi went too far,
committing many illegal acts.
If restrained by military regulations,
they would become resentful and rebellious;
if control was slightly relaxed,
they would plunder and destroy.
They robbed residents,
pillaged merchants and travelers,
devoured people's cattle and sheep,
and seized people's soldiers and horses.
Having received many rewards,
they refused to leave,
and furthermore wanted to buy iron with goods.
When the border generals did not permit this,
they gathered silk and cloth, intending to burn it.
The border generals were terrified,
fearing their rebellion,
and offered apologies and appeasements,
not daring to refuse or disobey.
Now, the cunning bandits are not yet eliminated,
and the Qiāng are a great menace.
If a mistake is made,
how can it be rectified?
Your servant humbly believes that we should recruit those Qiāng and Hú from Lǒngxī who are good and not rebellious,
selecting their elite and brave,
and increasing their substantial rewards.
The Tàishǒu Lǐ Cān is calm and resourceful,
and will surely be able to encourage them to fight to the death.
We should consider strategies for gradual suppression,
and not expect immediate results in haste.”
Hán Zhuó then argued back and forth with Shào.
Thereupon, an imperial edict summoned all officials to a grand assembly in the imperial court,
and they all followed Shào's proposal.
In the third year,
he was promoted to the highest rank,
and moved twice.
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Tàishān Tàishǒu.
In the second year of Chūpíng,
three hundred thousand Yellow Turban rebels entered the commandery.
Shào organized and led his civil and military officials to repeatedly fight the bandits,
beheading several thousand in total,
capturing over ten thousand prisoners, old and weak,
and two thousand carts of supplies.
The bandits all retreated,
and the commandery became peaceful.
In the first year of Xīngpíng,
the former Tàiwèi Cáo Sōng and his son Dé, coming from Lángxié into Tàishān,
Shào sent troops to welcome them.
Before they arrived,
the Xúzhōu Mù Táo Qiān, who had long resented Cáo Sōng's son Cāo for repeatedly attacking him,
sent light cavalry to pursue Sōng and Dé,
killing them within the commandery's borders.
Shào, fearing punishment from Cāo,
abandoned the commandery and fled to the Jìzhōu Mù Yuán Shào.
Originally,
during the reign of Emperor Ān, Yǐn Cì from Héxián and Shǐ Yù from Yǐngchuān were both sentenced to death for murder.
Cì’s elder brother Chū and Yù’s mother Jūn both went to the official court to beg to die in their stead,
and consequently hanged themselves and died.
The Shàngshū Chén Zhōng, believing the crimes were doubtful and should be treated leniently,
proposed to spare Cì and Yù.
Shào later refuted this,
insisting on strict adherence to the law,
there were those who could be spared.
His argument stated: The Shàngshū says
“Heaven has ranks and rites,
the five services and five chapters.
Heaven punishes the guilty,
with five punishments and five applications.”
And Xún Qīng also said
“The basis for establishing
punishments
is to prohibit violence and wickedness,
and to curb their extremes.
All titles, official ranks, rewards, commendations, punishments, and prestige
are to be aligned accordingly,
so that they correspond to their reality.”
If virtue does not match one’s position,
ability does not suit one’s office,
rewards do not compensate for merits,
and punishments do not fit crimes,
there is no greater misfortune.
Those who kill die,
those who injure are punished—
this is the established rule of a hundred kings,
the perfected statute of law.
When Gāozǔ entered the Pass,
although he still simplified the law,
the death penalty for murderers
was not leniently reduced.
Indeed, when the times are orderly,
punishments are severe;
when the times are chaotic, punishments are lenient.
The Shū says
“punishments are sometimes light, sometimes heavy,”
this refers to that.
Jūn was foolish and narrow-minded,
recklessly throwing herself to death.
In the past, Zhào Hū died for Zǐ Jiū during his difficulties,
yet Confucius said
“he died in a ditch,
and no one knew him.”
Zhāo Shì’s
father was not mistaken in his harshness,
thus he could take his own life.
Bān Gù also said
“it is not as good as Zhào Mǔ using her finger to save her clan.”
The biography says
“when servants and concubines feel
indignant and commit suicide,
it is not because they are righteous and brave,
but simply because they lack foresight.”
Indeed, punishments, deterrence, and imprisonment
are akin to Heaven’s thunderous destruction and slaughter;
gentleness, kindness, and
benevolence
are like Heaven’s procreation and nurturing.
Therefore, if a single blade of grass withers in spring, it is a calamity;
if a single tree blossoms in autumn, it is an anomaly.
Now, to kill the innocent
Chū and Jūn,
and to spare the deserving-of-death Cì and Yù—
is this not like withering in spring and blossoming in autumn?
Chén Zhōng did not understand the essence of establishing punishments,
but believed in temporary benevolence,
and thus broadly cited the eight considerations for seeking leniency.
Are relatives, old friends, the worthy, the capable, those with merit, the noble, the diligent, and guests
applicable to the crimes of Cì and Yù?
If however, one decides
based on human sentiment,
and determines guilt by examining intentions,
this is seeking life,
not that substitution of death can bring life.
To corrupt the law and disorder the government,
how can such regret be remedied?
Shào wrote thirty refutation memorials in total,
all of this kind.”
He also abridged the penal codes and regulations to form the Hànyí,
which he presented in the first year of Jiàn'ān.
He said:
"Of the great affairs of state,
none is more important than records.
Records are for
resolving doubts,
clarifying right and wrong,
ensuring that rewards and punishments are appropriate,
and truly achieving impartiality,
so that future generations may take them as a perpetual guide.
Thus, when Jiāoxī's Dǒng Zhòngshū retired due to old age and illness,
whenever there was a governmental deliberation at court,
the Grand Judge Zhāng Tāng was frequently dispatched to his humble abode
to inquire about its merits and demerits.
Thereupon, Dǒng Zhòngshū compiled 'Two Hundred and Thirty-Two Cases for Deciding Lawsuits Based on the Chunqiu,'
always using the Classics for comparison,
speaking in detail.
The rebellious minister Dǒng Zhuó
overturned the royal house;
the statutes and precedents were burned,
leaving not a single trace.
Since the beginning of the world,
there has been no such cruelty.
Now, the Imperial Carriage has moved eastward,
inspecting Xǔdū,
having escaped peril and difficulty;
its destiny is renewed.
Your servant, whose family has received favors for generations,
with abundant glory and fortune,
humbly without considering my own measure,
desiring to contribute even a little,

has thus compiled the original chapters and sentences of the penal code, old precedents from the Shàngshū, regulations from the Grand Judge's office, principles for deciding cases, the Sītú's official records, edicts from the Five Bureaus,
and two hundred and fifty chapters of 'Judgments from the Chunqiu.'
I have removed repetitions
and refined their style.
I have also collected thirty chapters of 'Disputed Deliberations,'
categorized by type,
totaling eighty-two items.
Of these, twenty-five are found in the 'Hànshū,'
and four in the 'Hànjì';
all have been abridged and polished
to preserve their original essence.
As for the twenty-sixth,
I have broadly selected from the rare and extraordinary gentlemen of antiquity and modernity,
whose writings are brilliant
and whose virtues are admirable.
As for the twenty-seventh,
these are my own creations.
How dare I claim that they necessarily conform to the true path?
Yet, my heart is indignant,
so I merely present them as an expedient.
Formerly, the people of Zhèng took a dried mouse for a jade,
selling it to Zhōu;
the foolish man of Sòng also treasured an ordinary stone,
wrapping it in ten layers of silk.
Those who saw it covered their mouths and laughed silently;
we, the literati,
are perhaps like them.
Zuǒshì indeed said, 'Though there be silk and hemp from Jī and Jiāng,
one does not discard withered sedges and rushes,'
for they serve to supplement scarcity.
〔一０〕Therefore, I dare to reveal my crude talent,
placing it at the end of the wise.
Although it is insufficient to govern the state
and promote universal harmony,
I hope it may be observed
and enlighten the sagely ear.
May Your Majesty, during moments of leisure from the myriad affairs of state,
turn Your thoughts to examining it."
Xiàndì approved of it.
In the second year,
an edict appointed Shào as the Military Counselor and Commandant for Yuán Shào.
At that time, the capital had just been moved to Xǔ,
old regulations were submerged,
and records were rare.
Shào sighed with emotion
and then compiled what he had heard,
writing 'Stories of Han Official Rites and Ceremonies.'
All court institutions
and official protocols
were largely established by Shào.
Earlier,
when his father, Fèng, was Sīlì,
he issued orders to all governmental offices, commanderies, and kingdoms
to each submit encomia for their predecessors' portraits.
Shào then compiled their names,
recording them in 'Records of Noteworthy People.'
He also discussed contemporary events,
writing 'Collection of Middle Han Prefaces.'
He authored 'Fēngsú Tōng'
to differentiate categories of things and names,
and explain popular doubts of the time.
Although its style was not classical,
later generations admired his extensive knowledge.
He authored a total of one hundred and thirty-six chapters.
He also compiled commentaries on the 'Hànshū,'
all of which were transmitted in his time.
He later died in Yè.
His disciples, Yáng and Qú,
were both known for their literary talent.
In the early days of the restoration,
there was a woman named Yìng'ū,
who had four sons and was widowed.
She saw a divine light illuminating the altar,
and when she investigated,
she found gold.
Thereafter, her sons pursued official careers and studies,
all having talent and fame,
and the family prospered through seven generations until Yáng.
Huò Xǔ, courtesy name Shúzhì,
was from Yè in Wèijùn.
In his youth, he was a student,
versed in the Classics.
Someone falsely accused Xǔ's maternal uncle, Sòng Guāng, to the Grand General Liáng Shāng,
claiming he had forged official documents.
Sòng Guāng was consequently imprisoned in the Luòyáng Imperial Prison
and severely tortured.
Xǔ, then fifteen years old, presented a memorial to Shāng, saying: "General, your boundless benevolence,
pities my uncle Guāng's unjust entanglement.
Previously, your gracious instruction promised to consider a fair judgment;
though the matter has not yet been definitively settled by officials,
I have already received the attention
and hearing of divine wisdom.
Heaven and Earth
truly hear your virtuous words.
I am secretly elated
and privately rejoice.
I have heard that the principle of the 'Chunqiu' is to
determine guilt by intent
and pardon deeds
by punishing the intention.
Therefore, Xǔ Zhǐ, though he murdered his lord, was not punished;
Zhào Dùn was recorded for abetting a villain.
This is how Zhòngní laid down the royal law,
and what the Hàn dynasty ought to follow
from earlier traditions.
The 'Zhuàn' says:
'Human hearts are different,
just like their faces.'
This refers to the shapes of large and small, hollow and full, ugly and beautiful,
as well as the form of noses, eyes, various orifices,
and hair;
none are identical.
Differences in feelings are
between firmness and softness, haste and ease, arrogance and respect.
However, regarding pursuing gain and avoiding harm,
fearing death and loving life,
these are alike.
As Xǔ and Guāng are kin,
there is a duty to conceal for each other;
my words about his injustice
may not necessarily be believed.
Let me rather discuss the logic from the perspective of human sentiment.
What name
would one wish for a forged document?
Even if there are doubts,
one should seek what is convenient and safe.
How could one risk deadly calamity
to resolve a trivial matter?
It is like curing hunger with aconite
or quenching thirst with poison;
before entering the intestines and stomach,
it has already choked the throat.
How could one do such a thing!
In the past, the filial woman of Dōnghǎi was wronged innocently;
her spirit moved and caused
Heaven
to respond with drought.
Guāng's offense,
his intent being understandable,
yet he has stood before the palace gate for years
and has still not been judged.
His cries of grief at the gate of the Purple Palace,
and tears of blood beneath the Two Watchtowers,
harm harmony and bring about disaster,
causing even greater harm.
All cases that have been granted amnesty
should not be re-investigated.
If clearly guilty criminals
can still receive imperial grace,
how
can one who is falsely accused without evidence
not receive justice?
This would be to pardon actual crimes
and inflict punishment for false accusations.
Is this impartiality and fairness?
Illustrious General,
your virtue is profound and your position exalted;
you are second to none among your subjects.
Your words and actions move Heaven and Earth,
your every move shifts yin and yang.
If you can truly pay attention,
and understand clearly,
you will surely have the high gate of Yú Gōng's

When Xiàndì moved the capital to Xǔ,
[Yuán] Qiú was summoned as Court Steward (Tíngwèi).
He was supposed to proceed to the capital,
but on the way, he was seized by Yuán Shù,
who bestowed upon him the rank of Grand Ducal Minister (Shànggōng).
Qiú then sighed, saying:
"What kind of people were Gōng Shèng and Bào Xuān?
I must die upholding my integrity!"
Shù dared not pressure him.
When Shù died and his army was defeated,
Qiú obtained the stolen state seal.
When he returned to Xǔ,
he presented it [to the emperor]
and also surrendered the seals and ribbons of the two commanderies, Rǔnán and Dōnghǎi, which he had previously been granted.
Sītú Zhào Wēn said to Qiú:
"You suffered such great difficulties,
yet you still kept this [seal]?"
Qiú replied:
"In the past, Sū Wǔ was trapped among the Xiōngnú,
but he did not abandon his seven-chi staff of office.
How much more so this square-inch seal?"
Later, he was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng),
and, holding the imperial staff, he was sent to appoint Cáo Cāo as Chancellor (Chéngxiàng).
Cāo offered to yield the chancellorship to Qiú,
but Qiú dared not accept it.
He died in office.
The "Treatise" (Lùn Yuē) says: Sūn Yì was resented for his lofty intelligence
and fell victim to a deceptive plot;
Zhái Pú relied on cunning to gain access,
but ended with blunt remonstrance.
Could it be that natural intelligence inherently has its completeness and partiality,
and the crucial points of priority and subsequence differ in measure?
The Yìng family had seven generations of talent and renown,
with Fèng and Shào excelling in literary composition.
In terms of compiling writings and records,
and distinguishing various kinds of knowledge,
though it is called a minor path,
there are also admirable aspects.
Yán and Qiú were eloquent and correct in their responses,
yet did not commit the error of offending their superiors.
This is indeed a case where one cannot cease to make pronouncements.
The "Eulogy" (Zàn Yuē) says: Yáng Zhōng and Lǐ Fǎ,
were renowned in Huáyáng.
The two Yìngs were truly discerning,
also distinguished in Rǔfén.
Zhái Pú deceived Yì,
Huò Xū pleaded for his maternal uncle.
Yán could denounce the emperor,
and Qiú likewise opposed the empress.
Biographies of Wáng Chōng, Wáng Fú, and Zhòngcháng Tǒng, Chapter 39
Wáng Chōng, courtesy name Zhòngrèn,
was from Shàngyú, Kuàijī.
His ancestors had migrated there from Yuánchéng, Wèijùn.
Chōng was orphaned young,
and his hometown praised his filial piety.
Later, he went to the capital [Luòyáng]
and studied at the Imperial Academy (Tàixué),
learning from Bān Biāo of Fúfēng.
He enjoyed extensive reading but did not confine himself to specific phrases.
His family was poor and had no books,
so he often wandered through the markets of Luòyáng,
reading the books for sale.
He could memorize whatever he saw at a glance,
thus becoming widely conversant with the sayings of all schools and a hundred masters.
Later, he returned to his hometown
and lived in seclusion, teaching.
He served the commandery as Gōngcáo (Record Keeper),
but left due to frequent disagreements over his remonstrances.
Chōng enjoyed discourse and argument.
Initially, his ideas seemed strange and heterodox,
but ultimately, they were logical and truthful.
Believing that common scholars adhered to texts [too rigidly]
and often missed their true meaning,
he closed his door, pondered deeply,
and abstained from rituals of celebration and mourning.
He placed knives and brushes in every window and wall.
He wrote the Lùnhéng in eighty-five chapters,
over 200,000 words,
explaining similarities and differences among things
and correcting the doubts and uncertainties of his time.
Dǒng Qín, the Inspector (Cìshǐ), invited him to serve as an Attendant Official (Cóngshì),
then transferred him to Chief Secretary (Zhìzhōng),
but he resigned and returned home.
His friend Xiè Yíwú, also from his commandery, wrote a memorial recommending Chōng's talent and learning.
Sùzōng issued a special edict to summon him by imperial carriage (Gōngchē Zhēng),
but he was ill and did not go.
As he approached seventy,
his will and strength declined,
so he wrote sixteen chapters of the Yǎngxìngshū (Book on Nourishing Nature),
moderating his desires
and guarding his spirit.
During the Yǒngyuán era,
he died at home.
Wáng Fú, courtesy name Jiéxìn,
was from Línjìng, Āndìng.
From a young age, he loved learning
and possessed strong principles.
He was good friends with Mǎ Róng, Dòu Zhāng, Zhāng Héng, Cuī Yuàn, and others.
The custom in Āndìng was to despise children born of concubines,
and Fú had no powerful maternal relatives,
so he was looked down upon by his fellow villagers.
Since the Hè and Ān eras,
the world valued official careers,
and those in power recommended and promoted each other.
However, Fú alone remained upright and did not conform to the customs,
and thus he was unable to advance.
His aspirations were suppressed and resentful,
so he lived in seclusion and wrote over thirty chapters of books,
to criticize the successes and failures of his time.
He did not wish to make his name widely known,
so he called his work Qíanfū Lùn (Discourses of a Recluse).
Its aim was to expose contemporary shortcomings,
and chastise human nature.
It is sufficient to observe the customs and governance of that era through it.
Here are five of its chapters.
The chapter Guìzhōng (Honoring Loyalty) says: The one whom emperors and kings revere is Heaven.
The one whom August Heaven loves and nurtures is man.
Now, ministers receive heavy responsibilities from their ruler,
and shepherd what Heaven
loves.
How can they not bring peace and benefit to them,
or nurture and save them?
Therefore, a junzi (noble person) who assumes office thinks of benefiting the people,
and one who attains high position thinks of advancing the worthy.
Thus, those in high
positions are not resented by those below,
and those in front are not hated by those behind.
The Shū (Classic of History) says,
"Heaven's work, let man carry it out."
Kings emulate Heaven in establishing officials.
Therefore, enlightened rulers dare not
bestow offices for private gain,
and loyal ministers dare not accept them without merit.
Stealing a person's wealth is called theft,
how much more so is it to steal Heaven's office for personal gain!
If one commits a crime against a person,
punishment is surely inflicted.
How much more so if one offends Heaven,
can there be no blame?
Ministers of the five [dynasties],
who served their rulers with the Way,
their benevolence reached even the plants and trees,
and their kindness covered the entire
land.
Therefore, their blessings and prosperity flowed abundantly,
and their lineage lasted for a hundred generations.
Ministers of later generations [Jiéshì Zhī Chén]
flattered their lords,
did not think of obeying Heaven,
and relied solely on killing and punishment.
Bái Qǐ
and Méng Tián
were considered meritorious by Qín,
but deemed villains by Heaven;
Xīfū [Yǎn] and Dǒng Xián
were considered loyal by their lords,
but deemed thieves by Heaven.
The Yì (Classic of Changes) says:
"When virtue is slight but position
honored,
and wisdom is small but plans are great,
few avoid misfortune."
Therefore, if virtue does not match [one's position],
its calamity will surely be severe;
if ability does not match [one's position],
its disaster will surely be great.
Indeed, for those who usurp
positions,
Heaven takes away their discernment.
Even if they possess the capacity for clear insight
and aspirations for benevolence and righteousness,
once they attain wealth and nobility,
they turn their backs on relatives, abandon old friends,
lose their original heart,
alienate blood
relatives and befriend sycophants,
slight wise friends and favor dogs and horses.
They would rather see ten thousands of strings of coins rot,
than lend a single coin to someone.
They know full well that grain is rotting in the granaries,
but will
not lend a single dòu to someone.
Their relatives complain at home,
and common people slander them on the roads.
Those who came before them failed because of this,
yet those who follow contend to imitate them.
This is truly lamentable.
Cháng Shī (Constant Failures):
Rulers often have constant faults.
Infants are often sick
from being overfed;
noble ministers are often afflicted by calamity
from being over-favored.
Too much breastfeeding causes illness,
too much wealth
That those who become wealthy and powerful become arrogant and diseased,
those who love their children harm them,
and those who pamper their ministers destroy them,
are not few.
Those who suffer the ultimate punishment
are even known to die as servants in deep dungeons,
or be executed with a knife in
the city.
Are these not those who have no merit towards Heaven
and cause harm to people?
Birds use mountains as a base and build their nests upon them;
fish find springs too shallow and bore
holes within them.
What ultimately ensnares them is the bait.
Powerful relatives desire auspicious dwellings and thus give them grand names;
they wish their gates to be strong and thus construct iron pivots.
Yet, what
ultimately causes their downfall
is not the lack of prohibitions or the rotting of gate pivots,
but rather their constant pursuit of wealth and their arrogant transgressions.
They are in danger,
yet they plot for the security of Mount Tài;
they live like morning dew,
yet they aspire to achievements that will last for generations.
Is this not foolish?
Is this not foolish?
The "Fúchǐ Piān" (篇) says: Rulers take the four seas as their home
and the myriad people as their children.
If one man does not farm,
the world suffers from his hunger;
if one woman does not weave,
the world suffers from
her cold.
Now, the common custom is to abandon fundamental agriculture
and pursue commerce.
Cattle, horses, carriages, and palanquins
block the roads.
Idlers engage in crafts,
filling the cities.
Those who attend to fundamentals
are few,
while those who live idly are many.
"The city of Shāng is grand and stately,
a model for the four quarters."
Now, observing Luòyáng,
those engaged in secondary industries are ten times more numerous than farmers,
and idle tricksters are ten times more numerous
than those in secondary industries.
This means that if one man farms,
a hundred people eat from it;
if one woman raises silkworms,
a hundred people wear from it.
If one person supports a hundred,
who can sustain it?
Throughout the hundred commanderies
and thousand counties of the realm,
with tens of thousands of cities and towns,
most are like this.
If the fundamentals and secondary pursuits cannot adequately support each other,
how can the people avoid hunger and cold?
If hunger and cold arrive together,
how can the people avoid
evil and rebellion?
If evil and rebellion proliferate,
how can officials avoid severity and cruelty?
If severity and cruelty are frequently applied,
how can the common people avoid sorrow and resentment?
If there are many who are sorrowful and resentful,
then inauspicious omens
will arrive in unison.
If the common people are destitute
and Heaven sends down calamities,
then the state is in danger.
Instruct them and guide them,
be cautious of small things and prevent their budding,
to cut off their wickedness.
Therefore, the Yì (易) praises moderation as a system,
which does not harm wealth
nor injure the people.
The "Qīyuè" (七月) poem
teaches the young
and old,
ending and then beginning anew.
From this perspective,
people indeed cannot be allowed to act unrestrainedly.
matter.
Able-bodied men do not wield ploughs and hoes,
but instead carry pellets and slingshots,
holding hands and roaming the mountains for pleasure.
Some are fond of taking earth to make pellets and selling them,
which is insufficient to ward off bandits
from outside,
and insufficient to deter rats and sparrows within.
Others make clay carts, tile dogs, and other playthings,
to cleverly deceive children.
All of these are useless.
They dance to serve spirits,
deceiving and misleading the common people,
and bewildering the wives and daughters of the populace.
Families that are weak and sick,
full of worry and indignation,
are easily frightened.
They are made to rush
at opportune moments,
leaving their proper homes,
struggling by the roadside,
harmed by wind and cold,
profited from by wicked people,
and targeted by bandits.
Some even suffer increased misfortune and heavy visitations,
leading to death,
yet they do not realize they have been deceived and misled by shamans,
but instead regret having worshipped the spirits too late.
This is the height of delusion and absurdity.
They cut various threads
to tie around their wrists;
or cut silk and gauze
to sew into banners.
Each expends a hundred bolts of plain silk,
and works a thousand times harder,
breaking open prisons for falsity,
to make
difficult things easy,
and idly consume fine grains,
wasting precious days.
Forests cannot supply wildfires,
and rivers and seas cannot fill a leaky cup;
both should be prohibited.
The royal regulations
were indeed excessive.
Moreover, their attendants, charioteers, servants, and maids
all wore patterned ribbons and colorful brocades,
embroidered silks and fine damasks,
Gézǐ (葛子) from Yuè (越),
and fine linen from
bamboo tubes.
Rhinoceros horn, ivory, pearls, and jade,
amber, tortoiseshell,
rock carvings and intricate decorations,
gold and silver inlay,
reaching the utmost in luxury and extravagance,
constantly outdoing each other in display.
When they marry,
their carriages stretch for several li,
crimson canopies line the roads,
mounted slaves and child attendants
flank the wheels and lead the procession.
The wealthy compete to surpass each other,
while the poor are ashamed of their inability to keep up.
The cost of a single feast
destroys a lifetime's livelihood.
In ancient times, one could only wear fine silk and ride carriages and horses by imperial decree;
though we cannot revert to antiquity now,
it is fitting that the common people should roughly follow the system of Emperor Xiàowén.
They used cypress for outer coffins [guǒ] and
paulownia wood for inner coffins [guān],
with hemp fabric for bindings,
not reaching the springs below,
nor leaking stench above.
From the Middle Ages onwards,
they gradually used woods like catalpa,梓 (zǐ), huái (槐), bǎi (柏), chún (杶), and chū (樗),
each according to the local timber,
using glue and lacquer
to make them sufficiently strong and
serviceable,
and that was all.
Now, the powerful relatives in the capital
insist on having
yǔ (檽) and zǐ (梓) wood from Jiāngnán and Yùzhāng wood.
Even in remote, inferior lands,
they compete to imitate this.
Yǔ (檽), zhāng (樟), and Yùzhāng wood
come from extremely distant places.
They are felled in high mountains,
drawn
out from deep valleys,
enter the sea, travel along the Huái (淮) River,
go against the Hé (河) River, and ascend the Luò (洛) River.
Artisans carve them,
which takes months,
requiring many people to move them,
many oxen to transport them.
They weigh a thousand
catties,
requiring the labor of ten thousand men,
and extend east to Lèlàng,
west to Dūnhuáng,
wasting labor and harming agriculture over ten thousand li of land.
In ancient times, there were tombs but no mounds;
in the Middle Ages, mounds
and not exalted.
Kǒng Ní 喪母 (Kǒng Ní lost his mother),
the tomb was four *chǐ* high.
It collapsed in the rain,
and his disciples asked to repair it.
The Master wept and said:
“In ancient times, tombs were not repaired.”
Later,
Lǐ also died,
and he had a coffin but no outer coffin (*guǒ*).
Wén Dì was buried in Zhǐyáng,
Míng Dì was buried south of Luò,
none of them interred jewels and treasures,
nor did they raise grand tumuli.
Although their tombs were humble,
their virtue was the highest.
Now, in the capital, noble relatives
and powerful families in the commanderies and counties,
while alive, do not enjoy the utmost care,
but upon death, their funerals are grand.
Some even have golden shrouds and jade caskets,
and coffins of *nǔ zǐ pián* wood,
burying
many treasures, effigies, carriages, and horses.
They build massive tombs,
plant extensive pine and cypress trees,
and construct huts and ancestral halls,
striving for extravagance and luxury.
Considering the mausoleums of Hào and Bì,
and the tombs
south of the city,
Zhōu Gōng was not disloyal,
and Zēng Zǐ was not unfilial.
They believed that honoring the ruler and loving one’s father
did not lie in accumulating wealth,
and that enhancing one’s reputation and exalting one’s parents
had nothing to do with carriages and horses.
In the past, Jìn Líng Gōng levied heavy taxes for his carved walls,
and the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals) considered him to be an unworthy ruler [Bù Jūn].
Huá Yuán and Lè Jǔ gave Wén Gōng a lavish burial,
and the *jūnzǐ* (gentlemen) considered them to be unworthy
ministers [Bù Chén].
How much more so for the various officials and commoners?
How can they dare to be extravagant and exceed their superiors,
going beyond the Way of Heaven?
The *Shí Gòng Piān* (Chapter on Real Contributions) says: “A state rises through the virtuous,
and declines through the obsequious;
a ruler is secure through the loyal,
and endangered through the sycophantic.”
This is a common saying from ancient to modern times,
and is known by all.
However, as for declining states
and endangered rulers,
whose succession is unbroken,
is it truly that there are no loyal, trustworthy, and upright scholars at that time?
It is truly because their Way cannot be put into practice.
Indeed, within ten paces,
there must be luxuriant
grass;
in a village of ten households,
there must be loyal and trustworthy people.
Therefore, in the chaos of Yīn, there were three benevolent men;
in the small state of Wèi, there were many *jūnzǐ*.
Now, given the vast territory of the great Hàn,
the numerous
scholars and common people,
the clear and bright court,
and the rectitude of those above and below,
yet there are no good officials,
and no worthy ministers.
Is this because there are no wise men at this time?
It is truly because the method of selecting
them deviates from reality.
Indeed, those who aspire to the Way are few,
while those who chase after popular customs are many.
Therefore, factions use their private connections,
abandoning reality and pursuing superficiality.
Those who recommend scholars
no longer rely on their
true character,
or measure their talents and conduct,
but merely create false reputations
and arbitrarily fabricate merits.
Roughly calculating those recommended,
it amounts to nearly two hundred per year.
When examining their outward appearance,
their virtue matches Yán [Huí] and [Rǎn] [Yǒu],
but upon detailed investigation of their abilities,
few are even average.
All are busy getting promoted,
mutually recommending
and advancing each other.
Indeed, what is valued in a scholar is their utility;
one need not demand perfection.
Thus,
though the Four Friends were excellent,
they could not perfectly encompass each other's abilities;
the Three Benevolent Men, though equally devoted,
did not act in exactly the same way.
Gāo Zǔ's assistants,
emerged from the fallen Qín;
Guāng Wǔ obtained his scholars,
also
from the tyrannical Mǎng.
How much more so in times of great peace,
how can it be said there are no scholars!
One polishes jade with a stone,
washes gold with salt,
cleans silk with fish,
and launders cloth with ash.
Indeed, there are things that by being humble can manage the noble,
and by being ugly can transform the beautiful.
The wise
take advantage of strengths and avoid weaknesses,
thereby achieving their accomplishments.
Now, if the recommendation of scholars were truly based on reality,
even if there were minor flaws,
one should not force adornment.
Whether one appears or withdraws, speaks or remains silent,
each should act according to their
own way.
Then, figures like Xiāo, Cáo, Zhōu, and Hán,
why would they not be brought forth?
And types like Wú, Dèng, Liáng, and Dòu,
could be eagerly awaited.
Kǒng Fūzǐ said:
“If one has not considered
it,
what remoteness is there?”
The *Ài Rì Piān* (Chapter on Cherishing the Day) says: “The reason a state is a state
is because it has people.
The reason people are people
is because they have grain.
The reason grain is abundant
is because
there is human labor.
The reason labor can be established
is because of daily effort.
In a well-governed state, the days are relaxed and long,
so its people are at leisure and have surplus energy;
in a chaotic
state, the days are rushed and short,
so its people are burdened with tasks and lack energy.
‘Relaxed and long’
does not mean Xīhé travels slowly,
but rather that the ruler is enlightened and the people are peaceful, with surplus
energy.
‘Rushed and short’
does not mean the divisions of time are reduced,
but rather that those above are ignorant and those below are chaotic,
lacking energy.
Kǒng Fūzǐ said:
‘Once they are numerous, enrich them;
once they are rich,
then educate them.’
Therefore, propriety and righteousness arise from abundance,
while theft and robbery originate from poverty;
abundance arises from ample leisure,
while poverty originates from lacking days [for labor].
The sages
profoundly understood that labor is the foundation of the people
and the basis of the state.
Therefore, they made efforts to reduce corvée labor,
to make people cherish their days.
Thus, Yáo commanded Xīhé
to respectfully follow the vast heavens
and reverently bestow
the times upon the people.
During the reign of Míng Dì,
the *gōngchē* (Imperial messengers) refused to accept memorials on 'inauspicious' days.
The emperor heard of this and was puzzled, saying:
‘The people abandon farming and sericulture,
traveling far to reach the court,
and yet are further
restricted by taboos.
Is this the intention of governing?’
Thereupon, he abolished that system.
Now, [Jīn] when wronged people look up hoping to appeal,
the local officials [Lìng Zhǎng] act as if they are divine
and keep them at a distance.
The common people abandon farming and sericulture to rush to the government offices,
successively filling the roads.
They cannot be admitted except in the morning or evening,
and cannot be seen without a strong connection.
Some wait for days
or even months,
gazing at each other;
some turn to neighbors for help,
providing food and engaging in discussions.
When the year's labor is thus lost,
will there not be those in the world who suffer hunger?
The verdicts
are often unjust and distorted;
there is a reason for this.
If one's reasoning is straight, one relies on uprightness and does not bend;
if one's case is distorted, one uses flattery to offer bribes.
Not bending means no
showing favor to officials,
giving bribes, and thus being shown partiality in the law.
If a case is reversed,
the official should be implicated.
Because the official should be implicated,
they are forced to twist the case in court.
With the weak commoners having few allies,
and facing powerful officials in court,
how can they not be wronged?
The words of the Xiàncheng (縣丞) official
will therefore align with them.
If a case is reversed,
the Xiàn (縣)
should also be implicated.
Because the Xiàn (縣) should be implicated,
they will push the case up to the Jùn (郡).
With the insignificance of one commoner,
and litigating against an entire Xiàn (縣),
how can their justice be upheld?
If a case is reversed,
the Jùn (郡) will also be implicated.
Because the Jùn (郡) is implicated,
they will push the case up to the Zhōu (州).
With the insignificance of one commoner,
litigating against an entire Jùn (郡),
how can their case
be won?
Since justice is not forthcoming,
they then travel far to the Gōngfǔ (公府).
The Gōngfǔ (公府) again cannot investigate,
and instead prolongs it with days and months.
The poor and weak have no means to endure for
a single旬 (xún) (ten-day period),
while the strong and rich can last for a thousand days.
If litigation is like this,
what injustice can be rectified?
Upright individuals harbor resentment and are not believed,
while cunning officials indulge in corrupt
practices and are not punished.
This is why commoners are easily oppressed and suffer,
and why there is so much hardship and poverty in the world.
Of the people,
those whose official matters are interconnected,
and who inspect and contend with each other,
can number one hundred thousand daily.
If one person has a case,
two people are involved in managing it;
this means three hundred thousand people daily
abandon their work.
Calculated at the rate of an average farmer,
this means three million people suffer hunger annually.
If so, from where will banditry be eliminated,
and how will great peace
arise?
The Shī (詩) says:
"None are willing to think of the chaos,
who is without parents?"
If the people are not sufficient,
with whom will the ruler be sufficient?
How can one not reflect!
How can one not reflect
indeed!
The Shù Shè Piān (述赦篇) says: All who treat illness
must understand the deficiency and excess of the脉 (mài) (pulse),
and where the氣 (qì) is blocked,
and only then prescribe a remedy;
thus, illness can be cured and life prolonged.
Those who govern
a country
must first know what the people suffer,
and where disaster originates,
and only then establish prohibitions;
thus, wickedness can be stopped and the country can be at peace.
Today, what harms upright commoners most
severely
is nothing greater than frequent amnesties and redemptions.
If amnesties and redemptions are frequent,
then wicked people prosper and good people are harmed.
How can this be made clear?
Indeed, diligent and cautious people,
who themselves do not
tread on wrongdoing,
and furthermore, those who are honest officials,
not fearing the powerful and overbearing,
are all slandered by the party of treacherous and cunning individuals,
because they know that amnesties are not far off.
Among good and upright
gentlemen
who are wronged and can reach the palace court to clear their name,
there are countless few;
among these few who get an audience,
not one in a hundred;
and among those who face the Shàngshū (尚書)
but are sent away empty-handed,
there are six or seven out of ten.
As for those frivolous and wicked individuals,
who have already fallen into crime and law,
their vengeful families hope for their execution,
to vent their accumulated anger,
but
they are instead all completely pardoned and released,
allowing wicked people to gather boastfully and make a racket,
old bandits to conceal their loot and pass by the door,
filial sons to see their enemies and be unable to avenge,
and those who suffered robbery to see
their stolen goods and dare not reclaim them.
There is no pain greater than this!
Indeed, nurturing weeds harms the crops,
and favoring the wicked harms the good people.
The Shū (書) says:
"Wénwáng (文王) established punishments,
executing these without pardon."
The former
kings established laws and punishments,
not because they liked to injure human flesh,
or cut short human lives;
they valued deterring wickedness and punishing evil,
and removing harm from people.
Therefore, the classics state,
"Heaven's mandate favors
virtue,
with five robes and five chapters;
Heaven punishes the guilty,
with five punishments and five uses";
the Shī (詩) censures,
"They deserved to be punished,
but you instead released them."
In ancient times, only
the ruler who first received the mandate,
who succeeded to a period of great chaos,
with bandits and wicked individuals
difficult to control by law,
could not but issue one amnesty,
to start anew with the people,
nurture all
the commoners,
and achieve great transformation.
It was not to foster wickedness and preserve guilt,
or to indulge heavenly evils.
Indeed, people of wicked nature,
the wolves of the people,
even if they receive the grace of pardon,
will ultimately have no change of heart.
They are released from heavy shackles in the morning,
only to return to prison in the evening.
Even strict and clear-sighted magistrates
cannot make them stop.
Why is this?
All who dare to commit great wickedness
must
have talents surpassing the masses,
and be able to curry favor with superiors.
They often disperse wealth obtained illicitly,
offering it with flattering words,
to drive each other on,
if not for the incorruptibility and uprightness of Dìwǔ Gōng (第五公),
who would not be swayed?
Many commentators say:
"If there are no amnesties for a long time, then wickedness will flourish and officials will not be able to control it.
It is advisable to frequently grant
pardons to break them up."
This does not clearly understand the root cause of political disorder,
nor does it discern the origin of blessings and misfortunes.
Later, the Dùliáo Jiāngjūn (度遼將軍) Huángfǔ Guī (皇甫規) resigned his office and returned to Āndìng (安定).
A fellow villager, who had obtained the position of Yànmén Tàishǒu (雁門太守) through bribery,
also left his post and returned home.
He sent a calling card to visit Guī (規).
Guī (規) was lying down and did not go out to meet him.
After the man entered, Guī (規) asked:
"Did you enjoy eating goose when you were in Yànmén (雁門) before?"
A moment later,
it was announced that Wáng Fú (王符) was at the gate.
Guī (規) had long heard of Fú's (符) reputation,
and was startled, hastily getting up,
his clothes not even belted,
slipping on his sandals, he went out to greet him,
taking Fú's (符) hand and returning,
sitting together,
and enjoying himself immensely.
People at the time made a saying:
"To see a two-thousand-dàn official
is not as good as one scholar."
Meaning the value of a scholar's morality and principles.
Fú (符) ultimately did not serve in office,
and died at home.
Zhòngcháng Tǒng
(courtesy name Gōnglǐ) was a native of Gāopíng, Shānyáng Commandery.
In his youth, he loved learning
and widely studied books and records,
excelling in literary composition.
At over twenty years old,
he traveled and studied in the regions of Qīng, Xú, Bìng, and Jì.
Many of those he befriended found him extraordinary.
Gāo Gàn, the Inspector of Bìng Province
and nephew of Yuán Shào,
was inherently noble and renowned.
He recruited scholars from all directions,
and many flocked to him.
Tǒng visited Gàn,
who treated him well
and consulted him on current affairs.
Tǒng said to Gàn:
"You have grand ambition but lack grand talent.
You are fond of scholars but cannot select the right people.
This is a profound warning for you."
Gàn, being inherently self-important,
did not heed his words,
so Tǒng departed.
Not long after,
Gàn rebelled with Bìng Province,
eventually leading to his defeat.
The scholars of Bìng and Jì all found Tǒng extraordinary because of this.
Tǒng's nature was unconventional
and he dared to speak directly.
He did not concern himself with minor details,
and his speaking and silence were unpredictable.
People at the time sometimes called him a "mad scholar."
Whenever he was summoned by a province or commandery,
he would always claim illness and not attend.
He constantly believed that those who served emperors and kings
sought to establish themselves and gain fame,
but fame does not last forever,
and human life is easily extinguished.
To live leisurely and contentedly
could bring self-enjoyment.
He wished to settle in a clear and expansive place
to indulge his aspirations,
discussing it thus:
"If one has good fields and spacious dwellings,
backed by mountains and facing streams,
with canals and ponds encircling them,
and bamboo and trees all around.
A courtyard and garden built in front,
an orchard planted behind.
Boats and carriages suffice to replace the difficulty of walking,
and servants suffice to relieve the labor of the four limbs.
To support parents with exquisite meals,
and for wives and children to be free from hardship.
When good friends gather,
one sets out wine and delicacies to entertain them;
on auspicious times and good days,
one slaughters a lamb or pig to offer them.
Wandering in the garden plots,
playing in the flat woods,
washing in clear water,
chasing cool breezes,
fishing for swimming carp,
shooting high geese.
Reciting poetry beneath the Wǔyú altar,
singing and returning to the high hall.
Calming the spirit in the inner chambers,
contemplating Lǎo Zǐ's profound void;
breathing in essence and harmony,
seeking the semblance of a perfect being.
With a few enlightened individuals,
discussing the Dao and expounding on texts,
looking up and down at the two luminaries,
intricately examining people and things.
Playing the elegant melodies of the Southern Winds,
performing the wondrous tunes of Qīngshāng music.
Roaming freely above the world,
looking disdainfully at the space between heaven and earth.
Not subject to the demands of the time,
eternally preserving the span of one's life.
If it is like this,
then one can ascend to the heavens
and go beyond the universe.
Why envy those who enter the gates of emperors and kings!"
He also wrote two poems
to express his aspirations.
The lyrics say:
Galloping on wind without feet.
Drooping dew forms a curtain,
the sky forms a canopy.
Dew and mist as a meal,
the nine suns replace candles.
Constant stars are like shining pearls,
morning glow moistens jade.
Within the six
directions,
indulge the heart's desires.
Human affairs can be forsaken,
why be constrained?
It depends on me.
Send sorrow to the heavens,
bury worries beneath the earth.
Abandon and scatter the Five Classics,
extinguish the Fēng and Yǎ.
The hundred schools are fragmented,
please commit them to fire.
Elevate one's aspirations to mountain
dwellings,
let the mind wander to the left of the sea.
Primordial energy as a boat,
a gentle breeze as a rudder.
Soaring in the clear void,
indulging freely and gracefully.
Shàngshū Lìng Xún Yù heard Tǒng's name,
was impressed by him,
and recommended him as a Shàngshū Láng.
Later, he participated in Prime Minister Cáo Cāo's military affairs.
Whenever he discussed ancient and modern times or contemporary customs and practices,
he would constantly express indignation and sigh.
He then wrote a treatise titled "Chāng Yán,"
comprising thirty-four chapters
and over a hundred thousand words.
In the year Emperor Xiàn abdicated,
Tǒng died,
aged forty-one.
His friend Miáo Xí of Dōnghǎi often praised Tǒng's talent and literary skill as worthy of succeeding Dǒng, Jiǎ, Liú, and Yáng of the Western Jīng period.
Now, we have briefly selected beneficial political excerpts from his book,
and recorded them here.
The "Lǐ Luàn Piān" says: Those heroes who are destined by Heaven
have never initially held a share of the empire.
Without a share of the empire,
therefore wars and conflicts arise.
At this
time,
they all falsely assume Heaven's authority,
wrongfully seize states,
and wield armed forces to contend with me in talent and wisdom,
and compete with me in courage and strength to determine supremacy,
not knowing when to advance or retreat,
misleading the
empire.
They are innumerable.
Those who contend in knowledge all fail,
those who contend in strength all lose.
Their forms cannot resist further,
their power is insufficient to contend further,
and only then do they submit their necks and willingly accept
my reins and halter.
Perhaps some were once my superiors,
or once my equals,
or once enslaved me,
or once imprisoned
me.
Their resentment is deep,
they curse and scheme inwardly,
hoping for my failure
to revive their former ambitions.
How could they willingly accept this as their final
lot in life?
When sons and grandsons are nurtured,
the empire will be at peace,
and all will return their hearts to me.
The hearts of heroes are then extinguished,
the aspirations of scholars and common people are settled.
Nobility has a constant house,
and honor rests in
one person.
At such a time,
even a person of the lowest intellect, if in charge,
can still make their benevolence equal to Heaven and Earth,
and their majesty comparable to ghosts and spirits.
Violent winds and swift thunderbolts
are insufficient to describe their
wrath;
the spring sun and timely rain
are insufficient to illustrate their favor;
Zhōu and Kǒng, even thousands,
would have no one to contend with in sagacity;
Bēn and Yù, even millions,
would have no one to unleash their
courage against.
These foolish rulers, their descendants,
seeing that no one in the empire dares to defy them,
consider themselves as indestructible as Heaven and Earth.
They then indulge in their private desires,
giving free rein to their perverse
lusts.
Rulers and ministers openly engage in debauchery,
upper and lower classes share in evil.
Their eyes are filled with spectacles of wrestling,
their ears with the music of Zhèng and Wèi.
Indoors, they indulge in women;
outdoors, they
rush to hunting.
They neglect all government affairs,
destroy people and things,
spreading wantonly and endlessly,
reaching no extreme.
Those they trust and love are all fawning flatterers.
of people;
those who were favored, noble, prominent, and wealthy,
were all from the households of empresses, consorts, concubines, and maidservants.
It was like making hungry wolves guard the kitchen,
and starving tigers herd penned pigs,
eventually boiling the fat
of the world
and hewing the marrow from living people.
Resentment and malice became unbearable,
calamities and rebellions arose simultaneously,
Zhōngguó was in turmoil,
the four barbarian tribes invaded and rebelled,
the state crumbled and disintegrated
and was gone
in a single day.
Those who formerly were our nurtured descendants,
are now all our blood-drinking enemies.
As for those who, when fortune shifted and power departed,
still did not awaken
to it,
was it not that wealth and nobility gave rise to inhumanity,
and indulgence led to mental illness?
Survival and destruction alternate because of this,
and political order and chaos repeatedly cycle from this;
this is the great immutable law
of Tiāndào.
It is far worse;
how could it not be so?
Since the rise of Hàn,
those who, having started as ordinary registered commoners,
rose to become lords over others through their wealth and power,
have been countless throughout the ages.
While
upright and pure scholars,
merely suffer hardship amidst thorns and thistles,
without benefiting or harming the customs.
The mansions of powerful families,
had hundreds of interconnected buildings;
their fertile fields filled the plains;
their slaves numbered in thousands of groups;
their dependents were in the tens of thousands.
Boats and carts for trade,
circulated throughout the four directions;
their hoarded stores and accumulated wealth,
filled the capital city.
Rare treasures and precious goods,
their immense mansions could not contain;
their horses, cattle, sheep, and pigs,
the mountains and valleys could not hold.
Charming boys and beautiful concubines,
filled their elegant chambers;
singers, dancers, courtesans, and musicians,
were arrayed
in their inner halls.
Guests waited to be seen and dared not leave;
carriages and horsemen crossed paths but dared not advance.
