Biography of the Eight Princes of Xiào Míng, Chapter 40
The Xiào Míng Emperor had nine sons: Consort Jiǎ gave birth to Emperor Zhāng;
Consort Yīn gave birth to Liáng Jié Wáng Chàng;
the mothers of the remaining seven princes are not recorded in this book.
Qiān Chéng Āi Wáng Jiàn
was enfeoffed in the third year of Yǒng Píng.
He died the following year.
He was young and had no son,
so his principality was abolished.
Chén Jìng Wáng Xiàn
was enfeoffed as Guǎng Píng Wáng in the third year of Yǒng Píng.
In the third year of Jiàn Chū,
officials memorialized to send Xiàn, along with Jù Lù Wáng Gōng and Lè Chéng Wáng Dǎng, to their respective principalities.
Sù Zōng was deeply affectionate
and could not bear to be separated from his imperial brothers,
so he kept them all in the capital.
The following year,
based on the geographic maps,
the households of all principalities were made equal,
with an annual tribute of eighty million [cash] each.
Xiàn was widely read in the classics
and possessed dignity.
He lectured and debated with various scholars at the Bái Hǔ Diàn.
In the seventh year,
the Emperor, considering Guǎng Píng to be in the north
and incurring many border expenses,
transferred Xiàn to be Xī Píng Wáng,
dividing eight counties of Rǔ Nán to form his principality.
When the Emperor passed away,
his dying edict re-enfeoffed Xiàn as Chén Wáng,
with the commandery of Huái Yáng as his domain,
and he proceeded to his principality that year.
He died after thirty-seven years on the throne,
and his son Sī Wáng Jūn succeeded him.
After Jūn ascended,
he frequently acted unlawfully,
even performing the Son of Heaven's grand archery ceremony.
He was secretly malicious
and fond of legalistic matters.
If any principality chancellor (èr qiān shí) disagreed with him,
he would secretly harm them.
He hated and resented King Jìng's consort Lǐ Yí and others.
In the eleventh year of Yǒng Yuán,
he instigated the guest assassin Kuí Jiǔ
to murder Lǐ Yí's family members.
Officials captured Kuí Jiǔ
and imprisoned him in the Cháng Píng prison.
Jūn wanted to sever his testimony,
so he again hired assassins to murder Kuí Jiǔ.
When the matter was exposed,
officials reported it,
and Jūn was punished by having the three counties of Xī Huá, Xiàng, and Xīn Yáng removed from his domain.
In the twelfth year,
Jūn's six younger brothers were enfeoffed as lieutenants.
Later, Jūn took a woman, Lǐ Ráo, who had left the imperial concubines' quarters, as his lesser wife,
and was again punished by having the three counties of Yǔ, Yí Lù, and Fú Gōu removed from his domain.
In the seventh year of Yǒng Chū,
King Jìng's grandson Ān Guó was enfeoffed as Gēng Tíng Hóu.
Jūn died after twenty-one years on the throne.
His son, King Huái, Sǒng, succeeded him.
He died after two years on the throne.
He had no son,
and the state was abolished.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
Chóng, the son of King Jìng, Ānshòu Tínghóu, was enfeoffed as King Chén.
This was King Qǐng.
He died after five years on the throne.
His son, King Xiào, Chéng, succeeded him.
After Chéng died,
his son, King Mǐn, Chǒng, succeeded him.
In the second year of Xīpíng,
the Chancellor of the State, Shī Qiān, submitted a memorial accusing the former Chancellor, Wèi Yīn, of jointly offering sacrifices to heavenly spirits with Chǒng,
hoping for things not to be desired.
The crime amounted to "unfilial and unrighteous" (búdào).
The relevant authorities proposed sending an envoy to investigate.
At that time, King Bóhǎi, Kuī, had just been executed,
and Emperor Líng could not bear to apply the law again.
He decreed that Yīn and Qiān be transported in caged carts to the North Temple Imperial Prison,
and ordered the Palace Regular Attendant Wáng Pú
to conduct a joint investigation with the President of the Masters of Writing and the Imperial Censor.
Yīn confessed to jointly sacrificing to Huáng-Lǎo Jūn with the king,
seeking only long life and blessings,
with no other illicit hopes.
Pú and others reported that Yīn's duty was to correct,
yet his actions were improper,
and Qiān falsely accused his king,
slandering him with "unfilial and unrighteous" (búdào).
Both were sentenced to death.
An imperial edict pardoned Chǒng, stopping the investigation.
Chǒng was skilled in crossbow shooting,
hitting the target ten times out of ten,
and all shots landed in the same spot.
In the middle of Zhōngpíng,
the Yellow Turban rebels rose.
All commanderies and counties [gǒng] walled themselves in and fled,
but Chǒng had several thousand powerful crossbows
and deployed troops at Dūtíng.
The people of the state had long heard of the king's excellent archery skills
and dared not rebel.
Thus, Chén alone remained intact,
and over one hundred thousand people took refuge there.
At the beginning of Emperor Xiàn's reign,
righteous armies arose.
Chǒng led his forces to garrison Yángxià
and proclaimed himself Grand General Who Aids the Hàn.
The Chancellor of the State, Luò Jùn of Kuàijī, had long commanded prestige and benevolence.
At that time, there was widespread famine,
and many people from neighboring commanderies sought refuge with him.
Jùn emptied his assets to provide relief,
allowing everyone to survive.
Later, Yuán Shù sought grain from Chén, but Jùn refused him.
Shù was enraged
and sent an assassin to deceitfully kill Jùn and Chǒng.
Chén was consequently ruined.
At this time, the various states no longer received revenue or salaries,
and were often plundered.
They ate every other day,
and many died and were left in ditches.
It is said that many wives and concubines were abducted by the soldiers from Dānlíng or Wūhuán.
Gōng, the King Jìng of Péngchéng,
was granted the title King Língshòu in the ninth year of Yǒngpíng.
In the fifteenth year,
he was enfeoffed as King Jùlù.
In the third year of Jiànchū,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as King Jiānglíng,
and Nánjùn was renamed as his state.
In the second year of Yuánhé,
the Three Excellencies reported that Jiānglíng was directly south of the capital
and unsuitable for enfeoffment.
So, he was transferred to be King Liù'ān,
and Lújiāng Commandery became his state.
When Emperor Sù died,
his will decreed that Gōng be transferred and enfeoffed as King Péngchéng,
to reside in Chǔ Commandery.
That year, he proceeded to his state.
Gōng was honest, dignified, and respected,
and his actions were orderly.
Officials and common people loved and respected him.
In the sixth year of Yǒngchū,
Gōng's son, Ānú, was enfeoffed as Zhúyì Hóu.
In the third year of Yuánchū,
Gōng became angry with his son, Pú, over a matter,
and Pú committed suicide.
The Chancellor of the State, Zhào Mù, reported the situation
and then falsely accused Gōng of performing "evil words" (èyán) during sacrifices,
a crime amounting to high treason and "unfilial and unrighteous" (búdào).
The relevant authorities proposed his execution.
Gōng submitted a memorial defending himself.
The court, knowing his long-standing reputation for integrity,
ordered an investigation.
No evidence was found,
and Mù was imprisoned.
He was later pardoned from the death penalty.
Gōng died after forty-six years on the throne.
His son, King Kǎo, Dào, succeeded him.
In the fifth year of Yuánchū,
three of Dào's younger brothers were enfeoffed as Xiānghóu,
and Gōng's grandson, Shùn, was enfeoffed as Dōng'ān Tínghóu.
Dào died after twenty-eight years on the throne.
His son, King Qǐng, Dìng, succeeded him.
In the first year of Běnchū,
Dìng's nine brothers were all enfeoffed as Tínghóu.
Dìng died after four years on the throne.
His son, King Xiào, Hé, succeeded him.
Hé was exceptionally filial.
When his grand empress dowager died,
he observed mourning at the tomb site,
and his self-mortification exceeded the proper rites.
The Grand Tutor and Chancellor reported this.
Emperor Huán decreed that an envoy be sent with beef and wine to welcome the king back to his palace.
Hé respected the virtuous and loved to bestow favors.
The people of the state loved him.
In the middle of Chūpíng,
when there was great chaos in the world,
Hé was attacked by the bandit Chāng Wù.
He fled to Dōng'ē
and later managed to return to his state.
He died after sixty-four years on the throne.
His grandson, Zhī, succeeded him.
After seven years on the throne,
Wèi received the abdication,
and Zhī was made Chóngdé Hóu.
Dǎng, the King Jìng of Lèchéng,
was granted the title King Chóngxī in the ninth year of Yǒngpíng.
In the fifteenth year, he was enfeoffed as King Lèchéng.
Dǎng was intelligent and wise,
skilled in historical writings,
and enjoyed correcting texts.
He was the same age as Emperor Sù
and they were particularly close and affectionate.
In the fourth year of Jiànchū,
eight counties were added to Lèchéng State: Yóu and Guānjīn from Qīnghé;
Dōngguāng and Chéngpíng from Bóhǎi;
and Zhōngshuǐ, Ráoyáng, Ānpíng, and Nánshēnzé from Zhuōjùn.
After the Emperor died,
he proceeded to his state that same year.
Dǎng was cruel and harsh and did not abide by the laws and regulations.
It was an old prohibition that palace women, when married out,
could not be sent to the various states.
There was a former Yè Tíng entertainer, Āi Zhì,
who was married to a man named Zhāng Chū.
Dǎng summoned Āi Zhì into the palace and had intercourse with her.
Chū intended to memorialize about this.
Dǎng, in fear,
secretly bribed Āi Zhì's elder sister, Jiāo, to kill Chū.
When the matter was discovered,
Dǎng then strangled three of his palace attendants
to silence them.
He also took Lǐ Yǔshēng, a maidservant of the late King Jiǎn of Zhōngshān, as a concubine.
In the seventh year of Yǒngyuán,
the Chancellor of the State impeached him.
Emperor Hé decreed that the counties of Dōngguāng and Quē be removed from his state.
He died after twenty-five years on the throne.
His son, King Āi, Chóng, succeeded him.
He died after two months on the throne.
He had no son,
and the state was abolished.
The next year,
Emperor Hé enfeoffed Chóng's elder brother, Xiūhóu Xún, as King Lèchéng.
This was King Lí.
He died after fifteen years on the throne.
His son, King Yǐn, Bīn, succeeded him.
He died after eight years on the throne.
He had no son,
and the state was abolished.
The next year,
Cháng, the son of King Huì of Jìběi, was again established as a successor to King Lèchéng.
After Cháng arrived in his state for several months,
he became arrogant, licentious, and lawless.
His offenses accumulated to the point that
the Inspector of Jì Province and the Chancellor of the State impeached Cháng, stating his crimes amounted to "unfilial and unrighteous" (búdào).
Emperor Ān decreed,
"Cháng, despite his prominent position,
has indulged his heart in wantonness.
Knowing the great importance of ancestral temples
and the solemn rites of succession,
he did not consider the reverence due
nor the solemn caution required.
Instead, he dared to arbitrarily diminish the sacrificial animals
and failed to prepare the offerings adequately.
He treated the Grand Matriarch with disrespect
and did not heed her teachings.
His comings and goings were disorderly,
and a licentious atmosphere pervaded his household.
He took others' wives
and lavished gifts on maidservants and concubines.
He beat officials and commoners,
acting tyrannically and self-servingly.
His transgressions are immense,
and most shameful.
I have reviewed the deliberations on the eight categories of crimes,
but I cannot bear to apply the full rigor of the law.
Therefore, Cháng's peerage is demoted to Línhú Hóu.
I lack the sagely wisdom
to have prevented this disorder in succession.
Failing to bring comfort to the Grand Matriarch,
I am filled with endless lamentation."
In the first year of Yánguāng,
Gē was made the successor to Jìngwáng of Héjiān, as the son of Xiàowáng of Héjiān.
As Lèchéng had been abolished,
the state was renamed Ānpíng.
This was Ānpíng Xiàowáng.
He died after reigning for thirty years.
His son Xù succeeded him.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng,
when the Yellow Turban rebels rose,
he was kidnapped and held hostage,
imprisoned in Guǎngzōng.
After the rebellion was suppressed, he was restored to his state.
In the autumn of that year,
he was executed for being unprincipled.
After reigning for thirty-four years,
his state was abolished.
Xiàpī Huìwáng Yǎn
was enfeoffed in the fifteenth year of Yǒngpíng.
Yǎn was handsome,
and when Sùzōng ascended the throne,
he was always at his side.
At the beginning of Jiànchū, when he came of age,
an imperial edict bestowed upon Yǎn's teachers and subordinates gold and silk, each in varying amounts.
In the fourth year,
Línhuái Commandery and seventeen counties from Jiǔjiāng—Zhōnglí, Dāngtú, Dōngchéng, Lìyáng, and Quánjiāo—were added to the state of Xiàpī.
When the emperor died,
he proceeded to his state that same year.
Later, Yǎn became mentally disturbed,
and Crown Prince Áng was deposed for his offenses.
All of the concubines vied to have their sons established as heir,
repeatedly submitting memorials accusing each other.
Hé Dì took pity on them
and sent Péngchéng Jìngwáng Gōng to Xiàpī to determine the proper succession based on legitimacy,
establishing his son Chéng as Crown Prince.
Yǎn died after reigning for fifty-four years.
His son Zhēnwáng Chéng succeeded him.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn,
Chéng's two elder brothers and two grandsons of Huìwáng were all enfeoffed as列hóu.
Chéng died after reigning for two years.
His son Mǐnwáng Yì succeeded him.
In the first year of Yángjiā,
eight of Yì's younger brothers were enfeoffed as xiāng-hóu and tíng-hóu.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng,
Yì encountered the Yellow Turbans
and fled his state.
After the rebellion was suppressed, he was restored to his state,
but died a few months later.
He reigned for fifty-seven years,
and was ninety years old.
His son Āiwáng Yí succeeded him,
but died a few months later.
He had no son,
and in the eleventh year of Jiàn'ān, the state was abolished.
Liáng Jiéwáng Chàng
was enfeoffed as Rǔnánwáng in the fifteenth year of Yǒngpíng.
His mother, Yin Guìrén, was favored,
and Chàng was especially loved and favored;
the revenue from his territory was double that of other states.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
following the intentions of the late emperor,
he bestowed generous rewards and favors.
In the second year of Jiànchū,
Chàng's maternal uncle Yīn Táng was enfeoffed as Xīlínghóu.
In the fourth year,
he was moved to become Liángwáng,
with Yǎn and Nínglíng from Chénliú,
and Bó, Dānfù, Jǐshì, and Chéngwǔ from Jìyīn,
a total of six counties,
added to the state of Liáng.
When the emperor died,
he proceeded to his state that same year.
Chàng was intelligent and clever,
but as a youth, he was arrogant
and somewhat disregarded the laws.
After returning to his state,
he frequently had bad dreams.
His subordinate Biàn Jì claimed to be able to command the Liù Dīng [six celestial generals]
and was skilled at interpreting dreams,
so Chàng often had him perform divinations.
Furthermore, Chàng's wet nurse Wáng Lǐ and others,
on this basis, claimed to be able to see ghosts and spirits.
They then together observed the qi [vital energy]
and offered sacrifices to seek blessings.
Jì and the others flattered him,
saying that the spirits had declared that the king would become the Son of Heaven.
Chàng was pleased in his heart
and assented to them.
In the fifth year of Yǒngyuán,
Liáng Xiàng, the Provincial Inspector of Yùzhōu, impeached Chàng for being unprincipled.
When interrogated,
he refused to confess.
The officials requested that Chàng be summoned to the Imperial Prison of the Grand Judge,
but Hé Dì did not permit it.
The officials repeatedly memorialized, requesting that Chàng's state be abolished
and he be exiled to Jiǔzhēn.
The emperor could not bear to,
but merely curtailed the two counties of Chéngwǔ and Dānfù.
Chàng was ashamed and fearful,
and submitted a memorial of apology, saying:
"I, your subject, am by nature mad and foolish.
Born in the deep palace,
raised by my wet nurse and tutors,
I believed and was misled by the words of those around me.
Upon returning to my state,
I did not know how to guard against prohibitions.
My subordinates and attendants sought personal gain from my wealth,
misleading me, your subject Chàng.
I, your subject Chàng, saw nothing clearly,
and made promises with them,
unaware that I was falling into a capital offense,
leading to this investigation.
My flesh trembles and my heart palpitates;
I regret deeply that it is too late.
I thought I would immediately face a public execution,
my soul leaving my body,
destined for the Yellow Springs.
Unexpectedly, Your Majesty's sagely virtue,
bending the law and showing fairness,
did not listen to the officials,
and graciously granted me a pardon.
I have trembled for months,
not daring to feel at ease.
Thinking above that I have betrayed the late emperor and caused Your Majesty to be sullied throughout the realm on my account,
I truly have no breath to breathe,
my bones and muscles are not connected.
I, your subject Chàng, know that such a great pardon cannot be obtained a second time.
I swear to restrain myself and my family,
not daring to again act out of line in my comings and goings,
not daring to again make any wanton expenditures.
As my revenue is abundant,
I beg to keep only five counties for sustenance: Suīyáng, Gǔshú, Yú, Méng, and Nínglíng,
and return the remaining four counties I oversee.
I, your subject Chàng, have thirty-seven minor wives;
those without children I wish to return to their original families.
I shall select and retain two hundred obedient slaves and maids.
All others received—tiger guards, official cavalry, and various artisans, musicians, servants, slaves, weapons, and stable horses—I shall return to their original departments.
I, your subject Chàng, being a close relative by blood,
have disrupted the sacred transformation [of the empire]
and sullied the clear current [of governance].
Having been allowed to live,
I truly have no heart or face to live viciously again in a grand palace,
eat from a large state,
deploy officials,
or store treasures.
I beg Your Majesty to bestow greater grace,
open the door for my self-reproach,
grant me the path to minor goodness,
so that all under Heaven may know that I have received grace,
escaped death and embraced life,
and am somewhat able to repent.
I keep the imperial edict detailing the offenses against me, as memorialized by the high officials, always before me,
reading it day and night.
I am but a petty person,
greedy to witness this bright era,
and cannot immediately take my own life.
I only beg Your Majesty to pity me,
and grant me a brief moment of respite.
If this is not granted,
I truly have no face to live long;
when I descend to the Yellow Springs,
I will have no way to face the late emperor.
This truly is my sincere heart.
I wish to return more of what I received,
but fear that Your Majesty's grace will not permit it.
The amount I propose to keep
is ample for me, your subject Chàng."
The imperial reply stated:
"We consider the king to be our closest kin,
possessing excellent purity and goodness.
It was his tutors and chancellors who were not good,
unable to guard against evil,
leading to these numerous complaints from the officials.
Now the king deeply reflects and repents of his faults,
sincerely taking responsibility,
which deeply grieves Us.
The intention was not from the king;
the fault lies with those petty individuals.
If one can subdue oneself and return to propriety for a single day,
all under Heaven will return to benevolence.
May the king be at peace and calm his mind,
and continue to lead with virtuous conduct.
Does the Yì [Jīng] not say: 'One humility brings four benefits.
If there are minor complaints,
it will ultimately be auspicious'?
Eat well and take care of yourself."
Chàng firmly declined,
submitting memorials several times,
but he was ultimately not permitted.
He died after reigning for twenty-seven years.
His son Gōngwáng Jiān succeeded him.
In the sixteenth year of Yǒngyuán,
two of Jiān's younger brothers were enfeoffed as xiāng-hóu and tíng-hóu.
Jiān died after reigning for twenty-six years.
His son Huáiwáng Kuāng succeeded him.
In the second year of Yǒngjiàn,
seven of Kuāng's brothers were enfeoffed as xiāng-hóu and tíng-hóu.
Kuāng (匡) reigned for eleven years and then passed away.
He had no sons.
Emperor Shùn (順帝) enfeoffed Kuāng's (匡) younger brother, Chéng (成), the Marquis of Xiàoyángtíng (孝陽亭), as the King of Liáng (梁王).
This was King Yí (夷王).
He reigned for twenty-nine years and then passed away.
His son, Jìng Wáng Yuán (敬王元), succeeded him.
He reigned for sixteen years and then passed away.
His son Mí (彌) succeeded him.
After forty years of his reign,
Wèi (魏) received the abdication,
and he was made the Marquis of Chóngdé (崇德侯).
Huáiyáng Qǐng Wáng Bǐng (淮陽頃王昞)
was enfeoffed as the King of Chángshān (常山王) in the fifteenth year of Yǒngpíng (永平).
In the fourth year of Jiànchū (建初),
he was moved to become the King of Huáiyáng (淮陽王),
with Xīn'ān (新安) and Xīhuá (西華) from Rǔnán (汝南) added to the Huáiyáng (淮陽) kingdom.
He reigned for sixteen years and then passed away.
Before a successor could be established,
in the second year of Yǒngyuán (永元),
Emperor Hé (和帝) re-established Bǐng's (昞) youngest son, Cè (側), as the King of Chángshān (常山王),
to uphold Bǐng's (昞) lineage.
This was King Shāng (殤王).
He reigned for thirteen years and then passed away.
Neither father nor son had yet gone to their fiefdom,
and both were buried in the capital.
Cè (側) had no sons.
In that same month, his elder brother Fáng's (防) son, Hóu Zhāng (侯章), was established as the King of Chángshān (常山王).
Emperor Hé (和帝) pitied Zhāng (章) for being orphaned young,
and frequently bestowed rewards upon him.
In the first year of Yánpíng (延平), he went to his fiefdom.
He reigned for twenty-five years and then passed away.
This was King Jìng (靖王).
His son, Qǐng Wáng Yí (頃王儀), succeeded him.
In the second year of Yǒngjiàn (永建),
two of Yí's (儀) elder brothers were enfeoffed as Marquis of Tíng (亭侯).
Yí (儀) reigned for seventeen years and then passed away.
His son, Jié Wáng Bào (節王豹), succeeded him.
In the first year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
four of Bào's (豹) elder brothers were enfeoffed as Marquis of Tíng (亭侯).
Bào (豹) reigned for eight years and then passed away.
His son Gǎo (暠) succeeded him.
In the thirty-second year [of his reign],
he encountered the Huángjīn (黃巾) bandits,
fled his state,
and in the eleventh year of Jiàn'ān (建安), the kingdom was abolished.
Jìyīn Dào Wáng Cháng (濟陰悼王長)
was enfeoffed in the fifteenth year of Yǒngpíng (永平).
In the fourth year of Jiànchū (建初),
Líhú (離狐) from Dōngjùn (東郡) and Chángyuán (長垣) from Chénliú (陳留) were added to the Jìyīn (濟陰) kingdom.
After thirteen years of his reign,
he passed away in the capital.
He had no sons,
and the kingdom was abolished.
The discourse says: Yàn Zǐ (晏子) said,
"When human life is abundant and its use is beneficial,
then one rectifies virtue to broaden it,
which is called 'broadening benefit'."
This means that human nature requires moderation to rectify its virtue,
just as cloth needs width to complete its measure.
Emperor Míng (明帝) enfeoffed his sons,
but their annual revenue did not exceed twenty million,
and Empress Mǎ (馬后) spoke on their behalf but could not obtain more.
How virtuous!
Was it merely frugality?
He knew that pride and nobility are insatiable,
and desires are hard to limit.
Therefore, few of the nobles in the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng) came to disaster or ruin.
The eulogy says: Xiàomíng (孝明) passed down his lineage,
securing eight states as his bastions.
Chén Jìng (陳敬) was solemn and serious,
Péngchéng (彭城) had profound virtue.
Xiàpī (下邳) suffered illness,
Liáng Jié (梁節) was misled by evil.
Three vassal states were young in age,
their factions only wild and perverse.
Biographies of Lǐ Xún (李恂), Chén Chán (陳禪), Páng Càn (龐參), Chén Qiáo (陳喬), Liezhuan 41
Lǐ Xún (李恂), courtesy name Shúyīng (叔英),
was a native of Línjìng (臨涇) in Āndìng (安定).
In his youth, he studied the *Hán Shī* (韓詩),
teaching hundreds of students regularly.
The Grand Administrator, Lǐ Hóng (李鴻) of Yǐngchuān (潁川), invited him to serve as Gōngcáo (功曹).
Before he could arrive,
the province appointed him as a Cóngshì (從事).
Coincidentally, Hóng (鴻) passed away.
Xún (恂) did not respond to the provincial appointment,
but instead escorted Hóng's (鴻) coffin back to his hometown.
After the burial,
he stayed to build the tomb and mound,
observing mourning for three years.
He was appointed to Sītú Huán Yú's (司徒桓虞) office.
Later, he was appointed Shìyùshǐ (侍御史),
bearing the imperial insignia on an envoy mission to Yōuzhōu (幽州),
proclaiming imperial benevolence,
and comforting and pacifying the Northern Dí (北狄).
Everywhere he went, he sketched and copied the mountains, rivers, military farms, and settlements into over a hundred scrolls,
all of which he sealed and presented to the throne.
Sùzōng (肅宗) praised him.
He was appointed Cìshǐ (刺史) of Yǎnzhōu (兗州).
He led his subordinates with integrity and frugality,
always sitting on a sheepskin,
and using a cloth quilt.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Zhāngyè (張掖),
where he gained a reputation for authority and seriousness.
At that time, General-in-Chief Dòu Xiàn (竇憲) led troops and garrisoned Wǔwēi (武威).
All prefectures and commanderies, near and far, in the empire presented gifts and paid respects.
Xún (恂) upheld public duty without partiality,
and was impeached and dismissed by Xiàn (憲).
Later, he was again summoned and appointed Yèzhě (謁者),
holding the imperial insignia and serving as Deputy Colonel of the Western Regions (Xīyù Fù Xiàowèi).
The Western Regions (Xīyù) were wealthy
and rich in treasures.
The royal hostages from various states, as well as the supervising envoys and merchants (Jiǎhú),
often sent Xún (恂) slaves, Wǎn (宛) horses, gold, silver, incense, and woolen blankets,
but he accepted none of them.
The Northern Xiōngnú (北匈奴) frequently cut off communication with Chēshī (車師) and Yīwú (伊吾) in the Western Regions (Xīyù),
preventing envoys from passing west of Lǒngshā (隴沙).
Xún (恂) offered rewards [for enemy heads],
and subsequently beheaded the barbarian leader,
hanging his head at the camp gate.
From then on, the roads were clear and safe,
and his authority and benevolence were equally effective.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi (武威).
Later, he was dismissed due to an incident,
and walked back to his hometown,
living in seclusion in the mountains and marshes,
building a hut of grass,
and supporting himself solely by weaving mats with his students.
At that time, the Western Qiāng (西羌) rebelled.
Xún (恂), while at a farmhouse,
was captured by them.
The Qiāng (羌), having long heard of his reputation,
released him.
Xún (恂) then went to Luòyáng (洛陽) to offer thanks.
At that time, it was a famine year.
Sīkōng Zhāng Mǐn (司空張敏) and Sītú Lǔ Gōng (司徒魯恭), among others, each sent their sons to offer him provisions,
but he accepted none of them.
He moved to live below Xīn'ān Pass (新安關),
gathering acorns to sustain himself.
He died at the age of ninety-six.
Chén Chán (陳禪), courtesy name Jìshān (紀山),
was a native of Ānhàn (安漢) in Bājùn (巴郡).
He served as Gōngcáo (功曹) in the commandery,
commending the good and dismissing the wicked,
and was feared by the people of the state.
He was investigated as Xiàolián (孝廉),
and the province appointed him as Zhìzhōng Cóngshì (治中從事).
At that time, the Cìshǐ (刺史) was accused of accepting bribes.
Chán (禪) was to transmit the investigation,
carrying nothing but
only funeral garments and implements.
When he arrived,
he was flogged countless times,
and all five tortures were applied.
Chán's (禪) spirit remained composed,
his words and replies unchanged,
and the case was eventually dismissed.
General of Chariots and Cavalry Dèng Zhì (車騎將軍鄧騭) heard of his reputation and appointed him,
promoting him as Màocái (茂才).
At that time, the Mányí (蠻夷) in Hànzhōng (漢中) rebelled,
and Chán (禪) was appointed Grand Administrator of Hànzhōng (漢中).
The barbarian bandits, having long heard of his fame,
immediately surrendered.
He was promoted to Zuǒ Féngyì (左馮翊),
and then entered the court to be appointed Jiànyì Dàfū (諫議大夫).
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
the king of the Shàn kingdom of the Southwestern Yí
offered music and illusionists.
They could breathe fire,
disarticulate themselves,
and swap the heads of oxen and horses.
The next year, at the New Year's court assembly,
they performed in the courtyard.
Emperor Ān and his ministers watched together,
and were greatly amazed.
Chán Dú rose from his seat, raised his hands, and said loudly:
"In the past, Qí and Lǔ had the Jiágǔ conference.
Qí performed a dwarf's music,
and Zhòngní executed them.
He also said: 'Banish the music of Zhèng,
and keep away from sycophantic people.'
The court of an emperor
is not suitable for displaying the skills of barbarians."
Shàngshū Chén Zhōng impeached and memorialized against Chán, saying:
"In ancient times, the music of joy and harmony was danced in the hall,
while the music of the four barbarians was displayed at the gate.
Thus, the Shī Jīng says, 'With Yǎ and Nán,
Zhū and Lí were appointed.'
Now, the Shàn kingdom has crossed the shifting sands
and traversed precipitous passes,
traveling ten thousand Lǐ to present tribute.
This is not the music of Zhèng or Wèi,
nor is it comparable to sycophantic people.
Yet Chán publicly slandered court policies.
I request that Chán be impeached and imprisoned."
An edict was issued not to arrest him,
but to demote him to Xuántú Hòuchéng Zhàngwèi.
The edict stated,
"Dare anyone not go to their post,
and the names of their wife, children, and followers shall be reported."
After Chán left,
many in the court defended him.
At that time, the Northern Xiōngnú invaded Liáodōng,
so Chán was posthumously appointed Liáodōng Tàishǒu.
The Hú feared his might and power,
and retreated several hundred Lǐ.
Chán did not deploy troops,
but merely sent officials and soldiers to enlighten and comfort them.
The Chányú returned to the commandery with the envoys.
Chán observed rites at the school,
and expounded on righteousness to move and transform them.
The Chányú was won over and submitted,
leaving behind precious goods from among the Hú before departing.
When Dèng Zhì was executed and deposed,
Chán was dismissed as a former subordinate.
He again became Chēqí Jiāngjūn Yán Xiǎn's Chángshǐ.
When Emperor Shùn ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Sīlì Xiàowèi.
The next year,
he died in office.
His son, Chéng,
had a pure reputation,
and his official position reached Hànzhōng Tàishǒu.
Chán's great-grandson, Bǎo,
was also resolute and strong, possessing Chán's demeanor.
He served as Zhōu Biéjià Cóngshì,
and made a name for himself in the province and locality.
Páng Cān, courtesy name Zhòngdá,
was a native of Gōushì, Hénán.
Initially, he served in the commandery
without much renown.
Hénán Yǐn Páng Fèn saw him and was impressed,
recommending him as Xiàolián.
He was appointed Zuǒxiào Lìng.
Due to a legal transgression, he was sentenced to forced labor at Ruòlú.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
the Xiānlíng Qiāng of Liángzhōu rebelled.
Chēqí Jiāngjūn Dèng Zhì was dispatched to suppress them.
Cān, while a convict, had his son Jùn submit a memorial saying:
"At present, the displaced people of Xīzhōu are restless,
and levies are unceasing.
Floods do not abate,
and the land's fertility is not restored.
Furthermore, there is a large army,
and people are exhausted by distant garrisons.
Agricultural labor is consumed by transportation,
and resources are depleted by levies.
Fields cannot be cultivated,
and crops cannot be harvested.
People are impoverished and distressed,
with no hope for the coming autumn.
The people's strength is exhausted,
and they can no longer endure.
Your humble servant believes that transporting grain for ten thousand Lǐ
to reach the Qiāng and Róng
is not as good as gathering troops and nurturing the populace,
waiting for them to become weary.
Chēqí Jiāngjūn Zhì should temporarily withdraw his army,
and leave Zhēngxī Xiàowèi Rèn Shàng to supervise the soldiers and people of Liángzhōu,
relocating them to Sānfǔ.
Suspend corvée labor to assist them in their time,
and stop burdensome taxes to increase their wealth.
Allow men to cultivate,
and women to weave.
Then, accumulate elite forces,
and seize the moment when the enemy is lax and discouraged.
Strike when they are not expecting it,
and attack when they are unprepared.
Then the vengeance of the border people will be exacted,
and the shame of defeat will be avenged."
After the memorial was submitted,
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Fán Zhǔn also submitted a memorial recommending Cān, saying:
"Your humble servant has heard that a hundred common birds
are not equal to one eagle.
In the past, Emperor Xiàowén understood Fèng Táng's words
and pardoned Wèi Shàng's crime,
making him a border defender.
The Xiōngnú dared not move south.
Indeed, for one minister
to resolve a major difficulty in a region,
it is because the selection and appointment were correct.
Your humble servant respectfully observes that the former Zuǒxiào Lìng, Páng Cān of Hénán,
possesses unfathomable courage and wisdom,
is outstanding and extraordinary,
with great talent and military strategy,
possessing the demeanor of Wèi Shàng.
Previously, due to a minor legal transgression,
he was sentenced to forced labor for a period.
Now, the Qiāng Róng are a menace,
and a large army is stationed in the west.
Your humble servant believes that a person like Cān
should be in the ranks.
May Your enlightened Majesty adopt the practice of former generations,
consider the achievements of Wèi Shàng,
grant Cān a pardon from his sentence,
and make him a vanguard of the army.
He will surely achieve results
and enhance national prestige."
Empress Dowager Dèng accepted his words,
immediately promoted Cān from among the convicts,
summoned him to be appointed Yèzhě,
and sent him west to supervise the various armies stationed in Sānfǔ,
while recalling Dèng Zhì.
In the fourth year,
the Qiāng raiders became increasingly formidable,
military expenses grew daily,
and there were successive years of poor harvests,
with grain prices exceeding ten thousand coins per shí.
Páng Cān submitted a memorial to Dèng Zhì, saying:
“In recent years, the Qiāng raiders have particularly afflicted Lǒngyòu,
and the burdens of corvée and taxes have grown daily,
with the government owing the people tens of billions.
Now, the common people are again being conscripted,
grain and silk are being appropriated,
and goods are being sold off
to meet the demands of officials.
Externally, we injure the Qiāng barbarians;
internally, we exhaust the populace with levies.
Consequently, provisions are transported over a thousand lǐ,
sent far to Wǔdū and Xījùn.
The roads are rugged and perilous,
and difficulties and hardships are myriad.
If they travel quickly, they are harmed by banditry;
if they advance slowly, the grain is gradually depleted.
Provisions are scattered across the wilderness during transport,
and oxen and horses die in the mountains and marshes.
When the county government is insufficient,
it borrows from the people.
The people are already impoverished;
from whom shall we seek aid?
Nominally, we save Jīnchéng,
but in reality, we exhaust Sānfǔ.
Once Sānfǔ is exhausted,
it will in turn become a disaster for Jīnchéng.
I, Cān, have repeatedly said before that we ought to abandon the Xīyù,
but I was ridiculed by the literati and gentry of Xīzhōu.
Now, we greedily cling to barren land,
and compassionately care for people who are not our subjects.
We deploy troops in the wilds of Yīwú,
and worry about those beyond the three clans,
which indeed led to the defeat of Liángzhōu,
and chaos that continues to this day.
Indeed, expanding territory that brings no peace
is of no benefit to strength;
having much land that is not cultivated,
how can it alleviate hunger and destitution!
Therefore, those who govern a state well
focus on nurturing their internal populace,
and do not seek external gains;
they strive to enrich their people,
and do not covet vast territories.
The mountains and plains of Sānfǔ are vast and distant,
its people sparse,
and many of the old county seats and walled cities
are habitable.
Now, it is fitting to relocate those border commanderies that cannot sustain themselves
to reside among the imperial mausoleums,
and to garrison and cultivate the old counties.
Isolated cities and cut-off commanderies should be provisionally relocated;
the distant costs of transportation
should be reduced by concentrating them nearby;
the frequent corvée duties
should be suspended to give people rest.
This is the best of the best solutions.”
Dèng Zhì and the high-ranking ministers, considering the insufficiency of national resources,
wished to follow Páng Cān’s proposal,
but as many disagreed,
they stopped.
Páng Cān was appointed Administrator of Hànyáng.
A man from the commandery, Rèn Táng,
possessed extraordinary integrity,
living as a recluse and teaching.
When Páng Cān arrived,
he first called upon him.
Rèn Táng did not speak to him,
but merely placed a large bunch of scallions
and a bowl of water
in front of the screen at his door,
and embracing his grandson, prostrated himself beneath the doorway.
The Chief Clerk reported this, deeming it arrogant.
Páng Cān pondered its subtle meaning,
and after a long while said:
“Rèn Táng intends to enlighten the Administrator.
The water
means he wishes me to be pure.
Pulling up a large bunch of scallions
means he wishes me to strike down powerful clans.
Embracing a child at the doorway
means he wishes me to open the gate and show compassion to orphans.”
Thereupon, he sighed and returned.
While in office,
Páng Cān indeed suppressed the strong and aided the weak,
gaining the people’s favor through his benevolent governance.
In the first year of Yuánchū,
he was promoted to Colonel Protector of the Qiāng.
The rebellious Qiāng cherished his kindness and trust.
The following year,
the Qiāng tribes, including the Shāodāng clan, led by Hào Duō, all surrendered,
and for the first time were able to return to Dūlìngjū,
opening the road to Héxī.
At that time, the Xīanlíng Qiāng chieftain usurped the title of Běidì.
An imperial edict ordered Páng Cān to lead the surrendered Qiāng and seven thousand Hú from Huángzhōng Yìcóng,
and meet the General Who Conquers the West, Sīmǎ Jūn, at Běidì to attack him.
On the way, Páng Cān was defeated by the Qiāng.
Having missed the appointed time,
he feigned illness and led his troops back.
He was charged with feigning illness, summoned, and imprisoned.
Mǎ Róng, a Scholar-Official in the Imperial Library, submitted a memorial requesting his release, saying:
“I humbly observe that the Western戎 have rebelled,
raiding and plundering five provinces.
Your Majesty pities the suffering of the common people,
and grieves over the loss of livelihoods for the masses,
exhausting the imperial treasury to supply the army.
In the past, King Xuān of Zhōu faced the Xiǎnyǔn invading Hàogǎo and Fāng;
Emperor Xiàowén faced the Xiongnú also raiding Shàngjùn.
Yet King Xuān established the achievement of a middle restoration,
and Emperor Wén earned the title of Tàizōng.
This was not solely because both rulers possessed bright and discerning qualities,
but also because their defenders had the assistance of roaring tigers.
Thus, Nán Zhòng’s glorious deeds
are recorded in the Odes of Zhōu;
Yàfū’s valiant spirit
is inscribed in the annals of Hàn.
I secretly observe that the former Colonel Protector of the Qiāng, Páng Cān,
is fully equipped with civil and military talents,
and his wisdom and strategy are profound and far-reaching.
He possesses both righteous courage and decisive integrity,
and also a broad erudition and deep foresight.
Furthermore, Liáng Jǐn, the General Who Crosses the Liao,
formerly commanded the Xīyù,
toiling for several years,
and then remained in Sānfǔ,
where his meritorious services were established.
While stationed on the northern border,
the Chányú surrendered.
Now they are both imprisoned,
caught in the net of the law.
In the past, Xún Línfù suffered a defeat at Bì,
but the Marquis of Jìn reinstated him;
Mèng Míngshì lost his army at Xiáo,
but the Count of Qín did not dismiss him from his office.
Thus, Duke Jǐng of Jìn annexed the territory of the Chìdí,
and Duke Mù of Qín eventually became hegemon of the Xīróng.
It is fitting to consider these two rulers from afar,
and allow Páng Cān and Liáng Jǐn to be granted clemency.
This would truly benefit our diplomatic efforts,
and assist Your Sacred Transformation.”
Upon the submission of the memorial,
Páng Cān and others were pardoned.
Later, Páng Cān was appointed Administrator of Liáodōng.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn,
he was promoted to General Who Crosses the Liao.
In the fourth year,
he entered the court as Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Yú Xǔ, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, recommended Páng Cān
as possessing the capacity for a prime minister,
and (during Emperor Shùn’s reign) he was appointed Grand Commandant
and concurrently acted as Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
At this time, among the Three Excellencies,
Páng Cān was known for his loyalty and integrity,
but was repeatedly slandered and ruined by those around the emperor.
Because his appointments displeased the emperor,
the Colonel Director of the Retainers, acting on the emperor’s sentiments, investigated him.
It was then time for the gathering of the Mào Cái and Xiào Lián candidates.
Páng Cān, having been impeached,
claimed illness and could not attend.
Duàn Gōng of Guǎnghàn, a Senior Clerk in charge of annual accounts, seized the opportunity to memorialize, saying:
“I humbly observe that travelers on the roads,
farmers, and weaving women,
all say, ‘Grand Commandant Páng Cān,
has exhausted his loyalty and fulfilled his duties.
Merely because of his uprightness, he could not bend his heart,
standing alone amidst a group of villains,
and placing himself in a position to be slandered.’
I still hoped that during Your Majesty’s reign,
he would enjoy safety.
But again, slanderers and sycophants are harming and destroying the loyal and upright.
This is a great prohibition of heaven and earth,
and the ultimate warning for a ruler.
In the past, when Bái Qǐ was granted death,
the feudal lords toasted each other in congratulation;
when Jì Zǐ returned,
the people of Lǔ rejoiced at his relief from difficulty.
Indeed, a state flourishes through its worthy men,
and a ruler finds peace through his loyal subjects.
Now, the whole empire rejoices that Your Majesty possesses such loyal and worthy men.
I wish that you would always favor and entrust them,
to secure the state.”
Upon the submission of the memorial,
an imperial edict immediately dispatched a Small Yellow Gate official to examine Páng Cān’s illness,
and the Imperial Physicians delivered mutton and wine.
Later, Cān’s wife, out of jealousy, threw his former wife’s son
into a well and killed him.
Cān had long been on bad terms with the Luòyáng Prefect, Zhù Liáng.
Liáng, hearing of this,
led his officials and soldiers into the Grand Commandant’s residence to investigate the matter and establish the facts.
He then memorialized Cān’s crimes,
who was subsequently dismissed from office due to inauspicious portents.
The relevant authorities, however, felt that Liáng had not first reported the matter to the throne,
and had instead abruptly humiliated a prime minister.
He was therefore imprisoned in the imperial gaol.
Liáng had won the hearts of the common people;
the officials and commoners of Luòyáng stood at the palace gate requesting to atone for his crime,
with several tens of millions of people appearing daily.
The emperor then pardoned his punishment.
In the fourth year of Yángjiā,
Cān was again appointed Grand Commandant.
In the first year of Yǒnghé,
he was dismissed due to prolonged illness,
and died at home.
Chén Guī, courtesy name Shúzhēn,
was a native of Xuànshì in Shàngdǎng.
His family had for generations served as border generals,
so he was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and was renowned in the northern provinces.
Guī had great ambition from a young age.
During the Yǒngjiàn period,
he was recommended as xiàolián,
and after five promotions, became the Administrator of Wǔyuán.
In the fifth year of Yǒnghé,
he was appointed Colonel Protector of the Xiongnú.
At that time, the Left Wing of the Southern Xiongnú rebelled.
Guī, believing the Chányú was unable to control his subordinates,
outwardly compliant but inwardly rebellious,
promptly ordered him to commit suicide.
For this, he was summoned, imprisoned, and dismissed.
Later, after two more promotions,
he was appointed Prefect of Jīngzhào.
At that time, many powerful and influential families in Sānfǔ
often wronged the common people.
Upon Guī’s arrival,
he sternly enforced the law
and resolved all the grievances of those who had been wronged,
much to the great satisfaction of the entire commandery.
Coincidentally, the Qiāng and Hú barbarians encroached upon the border,
killing chief officials
and plundering the populace.
Emperor Huán, knowing that Guī was intimately familiar with border customs due to his family background,
appointed him General Waging the Expedition Beyond the Borders.
Before Guī departed,
he submitted a memorial which said:
“Your servant Guī, having received grace for generations,
has galloped across the frontiers.
Even if I were to exert myself like a hawk or a hound,
and die exhausted in the land of the Húlǔ,
my soul and bones not returning,
but instead offered as sustenance to foxes,
it would still be insufficient to repay the immense debt
and reciprocate a ten thousandth of Your Majesty’s kindness.
Your servant is extremely dull and incompetent,
lacking even the utility of a lead knife for a single cut.
Yet I have excessively received national grace,
enjoying both honor and superior rank.
From the day I was born to the day I die,
I shall forever fear not being able to repay it.
I have heard that when the Three Luminaries deviate from their course,
scholars are promoted to prime ministers;
when barbarians are disrespectful,
common soldiers are elevated to generals.
Your servant possesses no talent, either civil or military,
yet I am undeservingly burdened with the responsibility of an ‘eagle’s soaring’ general.
Upward, I am ashamed before the enlightened court;
downward, I fear being a useless eater.
Even if I were to sacrifice my body,
it would be of no avail.
Currently, the western frontier is desolate and barren.
People live on horseback,
their livelihood being hunting.
Men lack the benefits of cultivation,
and women lack the abundance of weaving.
They guard the passes and keep watch,
risking their lives against weapons.
When an emergency is heard, they advance rapidly,
departing with no thought of return.
In recent years,
the Xiongnú have repeatedly attacked commanderies and counties,
slaughtering chief officials
and humiliating and plundering the good and the humble.
Warriors’ bodies cover the desert,
and residents’ heads are tied to saddles.
Sometimes an entire nation closes its doors,
its whole population wiped out,
with orphans and widows
wailing in empty cities.
The wilderness has no green grass,
and houses are empty as hanging chime-stones.
Although they possess life,
they are effectively like withered and rotten things.
In previous years, Bīngzhōu suffered from floods and rain,
with disasters and insect pests arising alternately.
Crops were devastated and ruined,
and rent and corvée were left unfulfilled.
The elderly feared they would not live out the year,
and the young and strong feared hardship and calamity.
Your Majesty regards the common people as Your children,
and the populace regards Your Majesty as their father.
How can Your Majesty not daily vex Your spirit
and bestow the grace of comfort and succor?
Emperor Táng Yáo personally relinquished his son to cede the throne to Yú Shùn,
wishing for the people to encounter a sagacious ruler,
not to meet a wicked lord.
Thus, when Gǔ Gōng took up his staff,
his people increased fivefold;
when King Wén was Lord of the West,
the empire submitted to him.
[一０] How could this be achieved by merely conveying gold and precious treasures
to benefit the people?
Recently, Emperor Xiàowén was moved by the words of a single woman
and abolished the law of corporal punishment.
[一一] He embodied virtue and practiced benevolence,
becoming a worthy ruler of the Hàn.
Your Majesty has succeeded to the restoration’s lineage,
inheriting the achievements of Guāngwǔ.
Although you preside over the court and administer governance,
your sagacious intentions have not yet been fully applied.
Furthermore, unworthy provincial governors and prefects,
some of whom come from among the palace eunuchs,
fear displeasing Your Majesty’s will
and merely seek immediate gain.
The cries of suffering
invite disaster,
and the fierce Húlǔ barbarians
exploit weakness and seize opportunities.
To allow the granaries to fall into the mouths of wolves and jackals,
and for public achievements to yield no results,
is all due to disloyal generals and commanders
and the gathering of scoundrels.
The former Inspector of Liángzhōu, Zhù Liáng,
upon his initial appointment to the province,
extensively investigated and punished wrongdoing.
Nearly half of the administrators and prefects
were demoted or dismissed.
His administration did not last long,
yet its effects were remarkable.
He truly deserved special commendation
to encourage meritorious service.
[Therefore,] reform the appointment of provincial governors and prefects,
and dismiss treacherous and cruel officials.
Furthermore, it is advisable to re-select the Colonels Protector of the Xiongnú, Wūhuán, and Qiāng,
to carefully choose those with both civil and military talents,
and to instruct them in laws and regulations.
Abolish the rent and corvée for this year in Bīng and Liáng provinces,
grant clemency to criminals and slaves,
and sweep away all corruption.
Then good officials will know the blessings of public service,
and evil ones will realize the calamity of selfish gain.
The Hú horses will then not dare to spy on the Great Wall,
and there will be no worries of border watchtowers.”
The Emperor, awakened,
then re-selected the Inspectors of Yōu and Jǐng provinces,
and from the commandery administrators and commandants downwards,
extensively reformed and replaced many officials.
He issued an edict
stating: “For General Chén,
abolish one year’s rent and taxes in Bīng and Liáng,
to be granted to the officials and common people.”
Once Guī took office,
the provincial and commandery officials trembled with fear.
The Xiānbēi dared not approach the border,
and expenditures were reduced,
saving hundreds of millions annually.
[一二]
Grand General Liáng Jì had long harbored a grudge against Guī.
He slandered him, claiming he undermined national prestige,
sought personal glory,
and was not feared by the Húlǔ.
Guī was summoned back,
and subsequently requested to retire to his home.
He was later recalled to serve as a Minister.
As Jì’s tyranny worsened daily,
Guī submitted a memorial detailing his crimes
and requesting his execution.
The Emperor did not heed it.
Knowing he would surely be harmed by Jì,
he starved himself for seven days and died.
The Hú barbarians of the Western Regions,
and the common people of Bīng and Liáng,
all mourned for him
and offered sacrifices at his tomb.
Qiáo Xuán 字 Gōngzǔ,
was a native of Suīyáng, Liángguó.
His seventh-generation ancestor, Rén,
studied with Dài Dé from the same commandery,
and authored forty-nine chapters of commentaries on the Lǐjì,
which were known as
“Mr. Qiáo’s Learning.”
During the reign of Emperor Chéng, he served as Dàhónglú.
His grandfather, Jī,
was the Administrator of Guǎnglíng.
His father, Sù,
was the Administrator of Dōnglái.
Xuán began his career as a Xiàn Gōngcáo.
At that time, Zhōu Jǐng, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, was touring Liángguó.
Xuán visited Jǐng,
prostrated himself, and reported the crimes of Chén Xiàng Yáng Chāng,
begging to be appointed as a Bùchén Cóngshì
to thoroughly investigate his corruption.
Jǐng admired Xuán’s determination
and appointed him, then sent him off.
Upon arrival, Xuán
arrested all of Chāng’s retainers
and thoroughly investigated their crimes.
Chāng had long been favored by Dàjiāngjūn Liáng Jì,
who sent a urgent dispatch to rescue him.
Jǐng, acting on instructions, summoned Xuán.
Xuán returned the dispatch unopened
and pressed the investigation even harder.
Chāng was summoned in a caged cart,
and Xuán became famous because of this.
He was recommended as Xiàolián
and appointed as Luòyáng Zuǒwèi.
At that time, Liáng Bùyí was the Hénán Yǐn.
Xuán, having official business that required him to report to the prefecture for an audience,
was ashamed to be humiliated by him,
and resigned his office to return to his hometown.
Later, after four promotions, he became the Prime Minister of Qí,
but was sentenced to penal servitude as a chéngdàn for an offense.
After his sentence was completed,
he was summoned
and promoted twice to become the Administrator of Shànggǔ,
and then the Administrator of Hànyáng.
At that time, Huángfǔ Zhēn, the Magistrate of Shàngguī, was guilty of corruption.
Xuán arrested him, interrogated him, shaved his head, and flogged him.
He died in Jìshì,
and the entire commandery was shaken.
A man from the commandery, Jiāng Qí of Shàngguī,
lived in reclusion, upholding his principles,
and his fame reached Xīzhōu.
Xuán summoned him to be an official,
but he claimed illness and did not take the position.
Xuán was enraged
and ordered the Dūyóu, Yǐn Yì, to force him to come,
saying:
“If Qí does not come,
quickly marry off his mother!”
Yì strongly protested but could not succeed,
so he hurriedly went to explain the situation to Qí.
Qí steadfastly lay down and refused to get up.
The gentry and officials within the commandery also rushed to remonstrate,
and Xuán finally relented.
At the time, this was somewhat criticized.
Later, he resigned due to illness,
was again summoned by gōngchē to be Sītú Zhǎngshǐ,
and then appointed Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng.
Towards the end of Emperor Huán’s reign,
the Xiānbēi, Southern Xiōngnú, and Gāogōulí successor Bó Gù all rebelled
and raided the borders.
The four ministries recommended Xuán to be Dùliáo Jiāngjūn,
granting him the yellow battle-axe.
Upon arriving at his post, Xuán
rested his troops and nurtured his soldiers,
and then commanded his generals to defend and attack the Húlǔ and Bó Gù, among others.
They were all defeated, scattered, and fled.
He served for three years,
and the border regions became peaceful.
At the beginning of Emperor Líng’s reign,
he was summoned to the capital to be Hénán Yǐn,
then transferred to Shàofǔ, and Dàhónglú.
In the third year of Jiànníng,
he was promoted to Sīkōng,
then transferred to Sītú.
He had a long-standing rift with Chén Qiú, the Administrator of Nányáng,
but when he was in a public position,
he recommended Qiú for Tíngwèi.
Believing that the state was weak
and estimating that his strength would be of no use,
Xuán claimed illness and submitted a memorial,
citing numerous disasters as a self-impeachment.
He was subsequently dismissed by imperial edict.
After a year or so,
he was appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
At that time, Gài Shēng, a Tàizhōng Dàfū, had old favors with the Emperor.
Previously, as Administrator of Nányáng,
he had embezzled hundreds of millions or more.
Xuán memorialized for Shēng’s dismissal and perpetual ban from office,
and confiscation of his wealth.
The Emperor did not comply,
but instead promoted Shēng to Shìzhōng.
Xuán claimed illness and resigned,
and was appointed Guānglù Dàfū.
In the first year of Guānghé,
he was promoted to Tàiwèi.
After several months,
he was again dismissed due to illness,
appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū,
and went to seek medical treatment in his village residence.
Xuán’s young son, ten years old,
was playing alone by the gate
when suddenly three men with staffs kidnapped him.
They entered the house, went up to the tower,
and demanded money from Xuán.
Xuán refused to give it.
After a short while,
Yáng Qiú, the Sīlì Xiàowèi, along with the Hénán Yǐn and the Luòyáng Lìng, surrounded Xuán’s house.
Qiú and the others feared that they might kill his son
and were reluctant to press.
Xuán glared and shouted:
“These villains are outrageous!
How can I, Xuán, let loose a national bandit for the life of one son?!”
He urged the soldiers to advance.
Thereupon, they attacked,
and Xuán’s son also died.
Xuán then went to the imperial court to apologize
and requested that an imperial edict be issued to the whole empire:
“Whenever there are kidnappers holding hostages,
they should all be killed together,
and not be redeemed with money and treasures,
thereby opening up a path for villainy.”
The imperial edict approved his proposal.
From the time of Emperor Ān onwards,
laws and prohibitions had gradually become lax,
and kidnappings and hostage-takings in the capital
did not spare the powerful and noble.
From then on, such incidents completely ceased.
Xuán died in the sixth year of Guānghé,
at the age of seventy-five.
Xuán was by nature rigid and impetuous, lacking broad vision,
yet he was humble and treated scholars respectfully,
and none of his sons, younger brothers, or close relatives held high office.
When he died,
his family had no property,
and there was no place to house his coffin.
He was praised for this at the time.
Initially,
when Cáo Cāo was obscure
and unknown to others,
he once visited Xuán.
Xuán saw him and was struck by his uniqueness,
saying to him:
“Today, the world is about to be in chaos.
To bring peace to the common people,
that task might rest with you!”
Cāo was always grateful for his recognition.
Later, whenever he passed by Xuán’s tomb,
he would feel sorrowful and offer sacrifices.
He personally wrote a eulogy for him, saying:
“The late Grand Commandant, Duke Qiáo,
possessed admirable virtue and lofty conduct,
with universal love and broad magnanimity.
The state remembers his enlightened teachings,
and scholars recall his excellent strategies.
His spirit has receded into obscurity,
alas, how distant!
I, Cāo, in my youth,
was privileged to enter his hall,
and particularly with my dull disposition,
was accepted by this gentleman.
All increases in honor and prestige
came from his encouragement and assistance,
just as Zhòngní praised Yán Yuān,
and Lǐ Shēng deeply admired Jiǎ Fù.
A scholar dies for his bosom friend;
I cherish this and will never forget it.
I also remember his casual and solemn words: ‘After my death,
if you pass by my road,
do not fail to pour a measure of wine and offer a single chicken as a libation.
If your carriage passes by more than three paces,
do not complain of a stomachache.’
Although these were playful words at the time,
if not for the profound affection of a close friend,
how could he have uttered such words?
Remembering the past and looking back,
my heart is filled with sorrow.
Obeying the imperial command for an eastern campaign,
I am encamped near his hometown.
Looking north towards his revered land,
my heart is with his tomb.
I have prepared a meager offering;
may the Duke accept it!”
Xuán’s son, Yǔ,
rose to the office of Administrator of Rènchéng.
A commentary states: Rèn Táng and Jiāng Qí,
were known throughout their generations for their integrity.
They fashioned a jar for a window and declined high appointments;
were they not reclusive gentlemen of Hàn Yáng?
Páng Cān personally observed the rites for seeking out the worthy,
hence the people delighted in his governance.
Qiáo Xuán, however, asserted the might of a regional lord,
and the multitude lost their affection for him.
How could this be due to a lack of power?
Surely, there was a proper way.
If one allows that way to be forgotten,
then brute force will prevail.
A proverb says:
"The commander of three armies may be seized,
but the will of a common man cannot be taken."
Zǐ Gòng said:
"Better to lose a thousand pieces of gold
than to lose the heart of a scholar."
In the past, Duàn Gān Mù climbed over a wall to avoid the summons of Wén Hóu,
and Xiè Liǔ closed his gate, refusing to admit the request of Mù Gōng.
The noble must sometimes yield,
and the humble also have their day.
A eulogy says: Old man Lǐ diligently toiled,
content with hunger, declining offerings.
Chán hid himself for his lord,
unwavering until death.
Guī practiced border merits,
Cān rose from the ranks.
Lord Qiáo discerned the times,
a foreseer of heroic eras.
Collation Notes, page 1684, line 10: 州辟治中從事 (Zhōu pì zhìzhōng cóngshì). Note: Jíjiě (集解) quotes Qián Dàxīn's (錢大昕) saying,
that Zhāng Huái (章懷) avoided the Taboo of Táng (唐諱),
so whenever the character
"治" (zhì)
appeared, it was sometimes changed to
sometimes to
"化" (huà),
and sometimes to
"持" (chí).
Thus, the character
"治中" (zhìzhōng)
here must have also been changed,
and later Song (宋) collators changed it back.
Page 1684, line 13: 夷賊素聞其聲 (Yí zéi sù wén qí shēng). Note: The Jí (汲) and Diàn (殿) editions
have the character
"名" (míng)
before
"聲" (shēng).
Page 1685, line 7: 韎任朱離 (Mèi Rèn Zhū Lí). Note: Jíjiě (集解) quotes Qián Dàxīn's (錢大昕) saying,
that there must be missing text before and after this phrase,
and it is unlikely that the Shī (詩, Classic of Poetry) contains this expression.
Page 1685, line 15: 手足異處 (Shǒuzú yì chù). Jiānwù (刊誤) states that
"手" (shǒu)
should be
"首" (shǒu).
My comment: The Shǐjì (史記) Kǒngzǐ Shìjiā (孔子世家) also uses
"手足異處" (shǒuzú yì chù),
but the Gǔliáng Zhuàn (穀梁傳) uses
"首足異門而出" (shǒuzú yì mén ér chū).
It is probable that Mr. Liú (劉氏) based his statement on the Gǔliáng Zhuàn.
Page 1686, line 3: 毛詩無韎任朱離之文 (Máo Shī wú Mèi Rèn Zhū Lí zhī wén). Note: Jíjiě (集解) quotes Huáng Shān's (黃山) saying,
that Xián's (賢) annotation quotes Xuē Jūn's (薛君) Hàn Shī (韓詩) commentary,
which does not mention
"韎任朱離" (Mèi Rèn Zhū Lí).
This indicates that Hàn Shī (韓詩) also lacks this phrase,
not just Máo Shī (毛詩).
The current statement "Máo Shī (毛詩) has none"
means the character
"毛" (máo)
was likely a mistaken alteration by later generations.
The note does not refer to Máo Zhuàn (毛傳),
so it would certainly not abandon Hàn (韓) to consider Máo (毛).
Page 1686, line 6: 縣度者山名也 (Xiándù zhě shān míng yě). Note: The Qián Shū (前書) Xīyù Zhuàn (西域傳) has
"山名也" (shān míng yě)
as
"石山也" (shí shān yě).
This is an error.
The Zhāng Dì Jì Zhù (章帝紀注) quotes it as
"石山也" (shí shān yě),
which is not erroneous.
Page 1686, line 6: 去陽關五千八百八十里 (Qù Yángguān wǔqiān bābǎi bāshí lǐ). Note: The Qián Shū (前書)
has
"八十八里" (bāshíbā lǐ)
instead of "八十里" (bāshí lǐ).
Page 1689, line 10: 始復得還都令居 (Shǐ fù dé huándū lìng jū). Note: Jíjiě (集解) quotes Huáng Shān's (黃山) saying,
that the Tōngjiàn (通鑑)
has
"治" (zhì)
for "都" (dū),
this was changed to avoid the Táng (唐) taboo.
Page 1691, line 1: (順帝時)以為太尉 ((Shùndì shí) yǐwéi Tàiwèi). Shěn Qīnhán (沈欽韓) stated that there are events from Yǒngjiàn (永建) first year above it,
so the three characters
"順帝時" (Shùndì shí)
are redundant text.
Now deleted accordingly.
Page 1691, line 5: 夫國以賢化 (Fú guó yǐ xián huà). Jíjiě (集解) quotes Huì Dòng's (惠棟) saying,
that
"化" (huà)
should be
"治" (zhì).
Note: This was also changed by Zhāng Huái (章懷) to avoid a taboo.
Page 1691, line 9: 言其來歸何 (Yán qí lái guī hé). Jiānwù (刊誤) states that
"言其" (yán qí)
should be
"其言" (qí yán).
Note: The current edition of Gōngyáng Zhuàn (公羊傳) has
"其言" (qí yán).
Page 1691, line 13: 良字邵平 (Liáng zì Shàopíng). Note: Jíjiě (集解) quotes Huì Dòng's (惠棟) saying,
that the Chángshā Qíjiù Zhuàn (長沙耆舊傳) has
"字邵卿" (zì Shàoqīng),
and the Shuǐjīng Zhù (水經注) also has
"邵卿" (Shàoqīng).
Zhāng Huái's (章懷) note is incorrect.
Page 1692, line 8: (至)臣【至】頑駑 ((Zhì) chén [zhì] wánnú). Corrected based on Jiānwù (刊誤).
Page 1692, line 10: 上慙聖(朝)【明】(Shàng cán shèng [míng]). Corrected based on Jí (汲) and Diàn (殿) editions.
Page 1694, line 4: 乃推授舜【授舜】則天下得其利而丹朱病 (Nǎi tuī shòu Shùn [shòu Shùn] zé tiānxià dé qí lì ér Dānzhū bìng). Jiānwù (刊誤) states that according to the original text of Shǐjì (史記),
the two characters
"授舜" (shòu Shùn)
are also present.
Now added accordingly.
Page 1695, line 1: 七世祖仁從同郡戴德學 (Qī shì zǔ Rén cóng tóngjùn Dài Dé xué). Note:
"戴德" (Dài Dé)
should be
"戴聖" (Dài Shèng).
Jíjiě (集解) quotes Zhū Yízūn's (朱彝尊) saying,
that according to the Qián Shū (前書) Rúlín Zhuàn (儒林傳),

The statement here of
"戴德" (Dài Dé)
is probably incorrect.
Page 1695, line 2: 成帝時為大鴻臚 (Chéngdì shí wéi Dà Hónglú). Note: Jíjiě (集解) quotes Hóng Liàngjí's (洪亮吉) saying,
that according to the Qián Shū (前書) Bǎiguān Biǎo (百官表),
it was in the first year of Píng Dì's (平帝) Yuánshǐ (元始) reign that Dà Hónglú (大鴻臚) Qiáo Rén (橋仁) was mentioned.
Therefore, the statement
"成帝時" (Chéngdì shí)
is incorrect.
Page 1695, line 3: 陳相羊昌 (Chén xiàng Yáng Chāng). Note: Jíjiě (集解) quotes Hé Zhuó's (何焯) saying,

"羊" (Yáng)
in old transcriptions of Guǎngchuān Shū Bá (廣川書跋) was
"芊" (Qiān).
Page 1696, line 14: 玄以光和六年卒時年七十五 (Xuán yǐ Guānghé liù nián zú shí nián qīshíwǔ). Jíjiě (集解) quotes Huì Dòng's (惠棟) saying,
that the Qiáo Gōng Miào Bēi (橋公廟碑) states:
"In the fifth month of the seventh year, on the day Jiǎyín, [he] passed away in the capital as Grandee Remonstrant."
Both steles of Lord Qiáo (橋公) state Guānghé (光和) seventh year,
so the biography is probably mistaken.
It also quotes Hóu Kāng's (侯康) saying,
that Xuán (玄) died at the age of seventy-five,
and Cài Bójiē's (蔡伯喈) Xī Dǐng Míng (西鼎銘) records Xuán (玄) saying in Guānghé (光和) first year:
"My old age is seventy."
Then he truly died in the sixth year,
and the biography is not mistaken.
My comment: The seventh year of Guānghé (光和) was changed to Zhōngpíng (中平) in the twelfth month, on the day Jǐsì.
If based on the Qiáo Gōng Miào Bēi (橋公廟碑),
then it should be written as
"中平元年" (Zhōngpíng yuánnián).

Biographies of Cuī Yīn, Chapter 42 (His son Cuī Yuàn, his grandson Cuī Shí).
Cuī Yīn, courtesy name Tíngbó,
was a native of Ānpíng, Zhuójùn.
His great-great-grandfather, Cháo,
served as a Registrar of Yōuzhōu (幽州 Cóngshì) during the reign of Emperor Zhāo (昭帝),
advising the Inspector not to communicate with the King of Yān Lài (燕剌王).
When the King of Lài (剌王) was defeated, [he] was promoted to Imperial Censor.
He begot Shū,
who served as Administrator for four commanderies,
and was reputed to be capable wherever he served.
Shū Xiǎozǐ Zhuàn,
during Wáng Mǎng's time, served as Jùn Wénxué (Scholar of the Commandery).
He was summoned to Gōngchē for his mastery of the classics.
Tàibǎo Zhēn Fēng recommended him as Bùbīng Xiàowèi (Commander of Infantry).
Zhuàn declined, saying:
"I have heard that when attacking a state, one does not consult benevolent men;
when engaging in battle formations, one does not consult scholars.
What is the purpose of this appointment reaching me?"
Thereupon, he threw down his seal of office and returned home.
Mǎng disliked those who did not align with him,
often harming them through legal means.
At that time, Zhuàn's elder brother, Fā, enjoyed Mǎng's favor due to his flattery and cunning,
reaching the position of Dà Sīkōng (Grand Minister of Works).
His mother, Shī Shì, was knowledgeable in classical studies and the sayings of the hundred schools.
Mǎng showered her with special honors,
granting her the title Yìchéng Fūrén (Lady of Righteous Accomplishment),
a gold seal and purple ribbon,
an ornate carriage with vermilion hubs,
making her prominent in the New Dynasty.
Later, Zhuàn was appointed Jiànxīn Dàyǐn (Grand Administrator of Jiànxīn).
Zhuàn had no choice but
to sigh, saying:
"I was born in an era of misfortune,
encountering a ruler like Jiāo and Yì.
Above, I have an elderly mother;
below, I have brothers.
How can I alone preserve my integrity and endanger those who gave me life?"
So he traveled alone by carriage to his post.
He feigned illness and did not attend to official business,
not visiting the counties for three years.
Mémén Yuàn Ní Chǎng remonstrated with him.
Zhuàn then reluctantly arose to conduct the spring inspection.
In every county he visited,
prisons were filled to the brim.
Zhuàn wept, saying:
"Alas!
When punishments are unjust,
people are trapped in pitfalls.
What crimes have all these people committed
to come to this!"
He then rectified their cases,
releasing over two thousand people.
The clerks and officials prostrated themselves, admonishing him:
"The court is in its initial administration,
and the Zhōu Mù (Provincial Governor) is severe and strict.
To pardon errors and redress wrongs is indeed the heart of a benevolent person;
however, by acting alone as a gentleman,
you might have regrets!"
Zhuàn said:
"Zhū Wéngōng did not exchange his own life for that of one man,
and gentlemen called him one who understood destiny.
If killing one Dàyǐn could redeem two thousand people,
that would be my wish."
Thereupon, he feigned illness and left.
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
many in the court recommended him.
The Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ (Inspector of Yōuzhōu) also nominated Zhuàn as "Xiánliáng" (Worthy and Upright).
Zhuàn, feeling ashamed before the Hàn court because his family had received Mǎng's false favors,
declined the appointment and returned home, not taking office.
He lived as a guest in Xíngyáng,
closing his gate and contemplating in seclusion.
He authored sixty-four chapters of the Zhōuyì Lín,
using it for divining good and ill fortune,
and many of his predictions were verified.
Before his death, he composed a fu (rhapsody) to lament himself,
titled Wèizhì (Consoling the Will).
Its words were: How splendid were the ancients who met their opportune times,
beautiful were the eras of Yī [Yǐn] and Fù [Yuè]!
They matched the pure quality of compasses and squares,
surpassing Bān [Shū] and Chuí [who could craft] and regulating them.
They aligned with the true standards of levels and plumb lines,
sharing the profound stratagems that cut through metal.
How could they ride the heavenly path in a prosperous age,
transcending a thousand years to leave behind their achievements?
Was it the
utmost extent of cultivating virtue,
or was it where Heaven bestowed its blessing?
The six handles of power were controlled by the domestic faction,
the royal order was brittle and overbearing.
Lí and Gòng rose in arrogance and tyranny,
Yì and Zhuó became mad and rampant.
Seeing the arrogant and treacherous
seizing the opportunity,
they secretly usurped the divine instruments of all affairs.
Thinking to assist and support them to preserve themselves,
they also wailed and responded with sighs.
Alas, the three matters burdened me,
forcing me with heavenly might.
How could I not have the slight integrity of Xióng Liáo?
I lament that my life was destroyed and ruined.
I aspire to the noble spirit of the enlightened,
yet I fear the censure of the
Grand Odes.
Thereupon, I folded my wings and committed my fate,
receiving the seal to guard in the northeast.
I regretted meeting closure without withdrawing,
deviating from the lofty
path of Shímén.
I flaunted my beauty at Fùguān,
transgressing Kǒng [Zǐ]'s warning against seductive appearances.
I admire the common people's awakening and repentance,
longing for the path followed by the white colt.
Thus,
I feigned illness and repeatedly returned [home],
after three years, my request was granted.
Lightly and leisurely, I departed and fled far away,
seeking secluded refuge in lofty mountains.
Quietly contemplating the
profound and subtle,
I traversed the hidden depths of the Six Classics.
The Emperor issued a second decree to continue my compassion,
showing favor towards the Jiànwǔ reign.
The comet swept with lightning speed,
clearing the lands of the six directions.
Sagely virtue spread far and wide,
the common people rejoiced and danced.
The four gates were opened to broadly invite,
and the Yōu Mù
recommended me.
When divisions were set and plans decided,
how could it be said that an old and rustic man would be honored?
So I unharnessed my carriage and tethered my horses,
cutting off the worldly pursuit of advancement.
I sighed at the
completion of the spring rites,
closing my humble gate and sweeping my path.
Leisurely and content, I pass my days,
preserving my nature and fulfilling my years.
I value the return of my body
to wholeness,
hoping not to bring shame upon my ancestors.
Zhuàn gave birth to Yì,
who, due to illness, remained hidden and did not serve.
Yì gave birth to Yīn,
who at thirteen could master the Shī, Yì, and Chūnqiū.
He was widely learned and possessed great talent,
thoroughly understanding ancient and modern commentaries and the sayings of the hundred schools,
and was skilled in writing.
In his youth, he studied at the Tàixué (Imperial University),
being equally famous as Bān Gù and Fù Yì during their time.
He always devoted himself to classical texts,
not yet having time for official advancement.
People at the time sometimes criticized him for being too profound and reclusive,
fearing that his later reputation would not match reality.
Yīn imitated Yáng Xióng's Jiěcháo (Dispelling Ridicule),
writing Dázhǐ (Reaching the Core) in response.
Its words were:
"It blossoms with its flowers,
in autumn, it harvests its fruits.
Having a beginning and an end,
thereupon, its true essence is established.
Now, you store the Six Classics in your chest,
deeply embrace the Daoist arts,
travel through generations,
and speak
with lofty wisdom daily.
You look down to plumb the depths of the profound abyss,
look up to explore the distant nine heavens,
exhaust the ultimate subtleties in the obscure,
and fathom the hidden and boundless source.
Yet, you do not walk
below in the courts of Qīng and Xiàng,
nor ascend above to the gates of Wáng and Gōng.
When advancing, you do not form factions to praise yourself;
when retreating, you do not defile yourself with common people.
You uniquely take morality as your teacher and friend,
aligning with the
true essence of the past,
holding to your principles and standing alone,
not flocking with other scholars.
Indeed, tall trees have no shade alone,
a single tree does not make a forest.
According to the fitness of the times,
the Dao values following the ordinary.
At this time, the Supreme [Ruler]
governs the world with heavenly virtue,
instituting Wáng Liáo and appointing officials;
he comes to the Yōng and Pàn schools to expand Confucianism,
clearing the way for carriages and caps to honor the worthy;
he leads with profound virtue to encourage loyalty
and filial piety,
promoting grand transformation to sharpen benevolence and righteousness;
he selects keen instruments from good materials,
seeking Mòyé swords among the wise.
Not to seize this opportunity to climb the steps of the Terrace,
peek into the purple
palace gate,
occupy a high carriage,
and gaze at the vermilion gates,
while desiring a thousand li but not taking the first step,
I am indeed puzzled by this.
Therefore, when a hero seizes this opportunity,
it is like
an escaped bird flying to a deep forest,
or gnats rushing towards a great swamp.
Why remain silent and long sunken in obscurity?"
When Heaven and Earth were first ordered,
the imperial order emerged like threads.
Imperial annals were then established,
transmitting and ordering the succession of eras,
and the rise and fall of the Three Dynasties.
In ancient times, Dàtíng was revered,
but Hèxū is hardly known.
The era of simplicity became scattered and fragmented,
and people became conflicted and perverse.
When Gāoxīn descended,
their aspirations diverged.
The Way has no constant measure,
it expands and contracts with the times.
Losing benevolence is wrong,
gaining righteousness is right.
A *jūnzǐ* adapts to changes,
each carefully considering their path.
Thus, some scholars cover their eyes and dive into the depths,
or wash their ears and dwell in the mountains;
some
plow in the fields and barely have enough to eat,
or live on roots and suffer from constant hunger;
some are repeatedly invited but do not come,
〔一０〕while others are repeatedly dismissed but do not leave;
〔一一〕some brazenly seek
advancement,
while others observe expressions and then act;
〔一二〕some, as laborers, inspire dreams in kings and nobles,
〔一三〕while others, as fishermen, provide omens through sacred turtles.
〔一四〕When chaos
blocks the roads,
and tyranny spreads widely,
〔一五〕people suffer from distress and confusion,
and rulers worry and seek counsel.
〔一六〕Branches hang and vines intertwine,
the high and low seek each other out.
〔一七〕It is
then that worthy people offer their help,
rescuing the world from disaster,
〔一八〕traversing difficult paths to engage with society,
responding to the urgency of the moment.
〔一九〕In the past, Yáo harbored sorrow and Gāoyáo advised;
Gāozǔ sighed and
Zǐfáng deliberated;
〔二０〕calamities were not dispersed, and Cáo, Jiàng rose up;
〔二一〕knots were not untied, and Chén Píng weighed options.
〔二二〕When their strategies aligned with the Way,
they subdued chaos and quelled conflict.
Then they would engrave dark jade tablets,
and record their illustrious deeds,
〔二三〕inscribing them on the forges of Kūn Wú,
〔二四〕and carving them on the bells of Jǐng and Xiāng.
〔二五〕When there was work to be done,
they would lift their skirts and wet their feet,
not even bothering about their caps.
〔二六〕If people were drowning and not saved,
that would be unbenevolent.
When there was nothing to do,
they would adjust their cap strings and straighten their lapels,
walking with orderly steps.
〔二七〕If virtue and deference were not
cultivated,
that would be disloyal.
Therefore, in times of danger, they saved society;
in peaceful times, they upheld propriety.
They acted with public spirit,
not for their personal gain.
They united differences,
harmonizing the myriad varieties of things.
They unified the disparate in measure,
and melted them in a single furnace.
All beings obtained their proper order,
and myriad achievements were consolidated.
Every household had means to enjoy
harmony,
and every person had means to excel.
Weapons were stored away and ritual vessels were displayed,
the Six Canons were laid out and the Nine Punishments were abolished.
Thus, the masses were helped,
and led onto the path of
peace and ease.
Even with the strategies of Lìmù,
the sternness of Shàngfù,
if Yī and Gāoyáo are not discussed,
what need is there for Fàn and Cài?
When a grand mansion is built, the lush trees flourish;
when a distant
search for sustenance exists, good horses are tethered;
when hidden tasks are completed, the Water Constellation is stored away;
when the harvest work is finished, the Dàhuǒ constellation enters.
At such times,
reclusive scholars are as numerous as mountains,
and learners flow like rivers.
Their robes cover the heavens,
and their caps float like clouds.
This is like the forests of Héngyáng,
and the foothills of Dàiyīn.
〔一０〕Felling trees of a *xún* or *bào* girth is not considered rare,
planting those of an *gǒng*
or *bǎ* girth is not counted.
〔一一〕Limitless and vast,
each also has his gains.
〔一二〕They pick its flowers,
I gather its fruits.
To put it aside is to store it,
it is what I have
learned.
〔一三〕Therefore, to advance and act according to the Way,
is not to refuse to hold the *guī* tablet and bear the Pillar of State office;
〔一四〕to return to stillness according to principle,
is to be content with coarse food and feel at peace with wild herbs.
To boast and sell oneself,
to hoist a banner to make oneself known,
is not the treasure of Suí and Hé.
To flaunt one's wisdom to dazzle the world,
and thereby seek emolument,
is not the Way of Zhòngní.
To associate without regard for ethics,
solely for one's own benefit,
to compete relentlessly,
and befriend for profit.
You laugh at my stagnation,
and I too find fault with your relentless striving.
The ancients have principles, and I do not diminish them;
there are crooked paths, and I do not follow them.
Good or bad rests with me,
let the world judge as it will.
I shall naturally follow my innate
disposition,
reciting the lofty teachings of the ancient sages;
chanting the pure winds of peace,
and practicing the ultimate conformity in the world.
I fear my own defiled virtue,
