and diligently cultivate my hundred *mǔ* lest they are
not weeded.
I will tether my horse and walk peacefully,
awaiting what fate has in store.
In the past, Kǒngzǐ asserted his authority at Jiágǔ,
〔一０〕Yàn Yīng displayed courage before Cuī
Zhù;
〔一一〕Cáo Guì demonstrated integrity at Kēméng,
〔一二〕Biàn Yán achieved victory against a powerful
foe;
〔一三〕Fàn Lǐ established his position at Kuàijī,
〔一四〕Wǔ Yuán accomplished great deeds at
Bójǔ;
〔一五〕Lǔ Lián used eloquent words to repel Yān,
〔一六〕Bāo Xū, with a single plea, saved Chǔ;
〔一七〕Táng Jū, with his gray hair, enlightened Qín,
〔一八〕Gān Luó, with his childlike teeth, rendered service to
Zhào;
〔一九〕Yuán Shuāi showed his honesty at Húpiàn,
〔二０〕Xuān Mèng received virtue with a bundle of dried meat;
〔二一〕Wú Zhá established trust by an old tree,
〔二二〕Zhǎn Jì showed his
constancy toward a woman at the gate;
〔二三〕Yán Huí demonstrated benevolence while measuring spokes,
Chéng Yīng displayed righteousness concerning Zhào Wǔ.
〔二四〕I am truly unable to enumerate virtues among these,
but I secretly admire what the ancients have described."
In the Yuánhé era,
Sùzōng first began to restore ancient rites,
and made an inspection tour of the Fangyùe.
Yīn presented "Four Inspection Tour Eulogies" to praise Hàn's virtue,
the language was very elegant and beautiful,
but the text is too long, so it is not included here.
The Emperor was genuinely fond of literature.
After seeing Yīn's eulogy,
he (帝) often sighed in admiration,
and said to the *shìzhōng*, Dòu Xiàn:
"Do you know Cuī Yīn?"
He replied:
"Bān Gù has often spoken of him to your servant,
but I have not yet met him."
The Emperor said:
"You love Bān Gù but neglect Cuī Yīn,
this is like Lord Yè's love of dragons.
Please try to invite him to meet me."
Thus, Yīn called upon Xiàn.
Xiàn put on his sandals and met him at the gate,
smiling, he said to Yīn:
"Tíngbó,
I have received an imperial decree to associate with you,
how can you treat me lightly?"
Then he bowed and led him in as an honored guest.
Not long after,
the Emperor visited Xiàn's residence.
At that time, Yīn happened to be with Xiàn.
The Emperor heard of it and wished to summon and meet him.
Xiàn advised against it,
believing it was inappropriate to meet with a commoner.
The Emperor understood and said:
"I can have Yīn by my side morning and evening,
why must it be here?"
He was about to appoint him to office, but then the Emperor passed away.
Dòu Tàihòu 臨cháo,
Xiàn, as a powerful relative by marriage, issued edicts from the inner court.
Yǐn presented a letter to admonish him, saying: "I have heard that for those who are superficially acquainted to speak profoundly
is foolish;
for those in a humble position to aspire to a noble one
is deluded;
and for those who are not yet trusted to offer loyal advice
is to invite slander.
All three
are improper,
yet some people still tread this path
because they wish to offer their humble service,
their indignation overflowing and unstoppable.
I secretly observe that you possess a pure and virtuous nature,
and embody a noble
disposition,
with beautiful intentions and rigorous aspirations,
possessing the character of an esteemed worthy.
I, Yǐn, am fortunate enough to serve in a humble office,
and rank among the officials in the rear,
and therefore I offer my sincere thoughts,
daring to present a word of advice.
As your prestige rises,
and all officials observe your conduct,
living in a prosperous age like that of Yáo and Shùn,
and holding a prominent position in a glorious era,
how can you not strive day and night
to uphold public acclaim,
to magnify the virtues of Shēn Bó
and achieve the accomplishments of Zhōu Shào?
An adage says:
'Do not worry about lacking a position;
worry about how you stand.'
In the past, Féng Yěwáng held office as an imperial relative
and was praised
as a worthy minister.
More recently, Yīn Wèiwèi curbed himself and adhered to ritual propriety,
ultimately receiving great blessings.
The Tán clan's lineage
was not without honor;
the Yáng Píng
clan
was not without prosperity.
They accumulated marquisates and held generalships,
established the celestial pivot,
and wielded the Dipper's handle.
What caused them to be criticized in their time
and leave behind faults for posterity?
What
was it?
It was because they were full but did not moderate,
their position was ample but their benevolence insufficient.
From the rise of the Hàn dynasty
until the reigns of Āi and Píng,
among twenty maternal relatives,
only four
managed to preserve their clan and protect themselves.
The Shū Jīng says:
'Take warning from the Yīn dynasty.'
How can one not be cautious!
Since the restoration,
those within secured themselves with loyalty and integrity,
and those outside maintained themselves with laws and regulations,
ultimately enjoying and transmitting the state's prosperity,
and bequeathing blessings to the present.
The radiance of humble virtue
is praised in the Zhōu Yì;
a position of overflowing abundance
is cautioned against by the Daoists.
Thus, a gentleman fears more as his blessings grow,
and becomes more respectful as his rank rises.
Observe the distant and examine the near,
looking up and down for
principles;
inscribe them on your desk and staff,
and engrave them on your basins and tubs.
Be diligent and cautious,
without weariness or negligence.
If you do this,
then a hundred blessings will be yours,
and prosperity will flow endlessly."
When Xiàn became Chējì Jiāngjūn,
he appointed Yǐn as a clerk.
Xiàn's mansion was important and prestigious,
and its thirty clerks
were all former cǐshǐ or officials of two thousand shí;
only Yǐn, as a young commoner,
was promoted among them.
Xiàn was arrogant and abusive of his power,
and Yǐn repeatedly admonished him.
When Xiàn went out to attack the Xiongnú,
there were even more unlawful acts on the roads.
Yǐn, as the chief clerk,
submitted dozens of memorials
pointing out his faults.
Xiàn could not tolerate him,
gradually distanced himself,
and then, observing Yǐn's superior talent,
sent him out to be the Magistrate of Chángcén.
Yǐn, feeling that he was being sent far away
and was dissatisfied,
did not take office and returned home.
In the fourth year of Yǒngyuán,
he died at home.
His collected works, including poems, rhapsodies, inscriptions, eulogies, letters, records, memorials, Qī Yī, wedding addresses, and admonitions against drunkenness, totaled twenty-one pieces.
His middle son was Yuàn.
Yuàn, courtesy name Zǐyù,
was orphaned early,
and was determined and fond of learning,
fully capable of transmitting his father's legacy.
At eighteen,
he went to the capital,
and followed Shìzhōng Jiǎ Kuí to clarify the great principles.
Kuí treated him well,
and Yuàn stayed to study,
subsequently mastering astronomy, calendrical calculations, Jīng Fáng's commentary on the Yì, and the Lìurì Qīfēn.
All scholars esteemed him.
He was particularly close friends with Fúfēng Mǎ Róng and Nányáng Zhāng Héng.
Initially,
Yuàn's elder brother Zhāng was killed by someone from the province,
and Yuàn avenged him with his own hand,
then became a fugitive.
He met with an amnesty
and returned home.
His family was poor,
and his brothers lived together for several decades,
which influenced the local community.
At over forty years old,
he first became a commandery official.
Due to an incident, he was imprisoned in Fāgān, Dōng Jùn.
The prison clerk was good at observing etiquette,
and when Yuàn was interrogated,
he would always ask about ritual explanations.
His dedication to learning was such that
even in adversity, he would pursue it.
Later, after the incident was resolved, he returned home
and was appointed by the Dùliáo Jiāngjūn Dèng Zūn.
Not long after,
Zūn was executed,
and Yuàn was dismissed and returned home.
Later, he was again appointed to the mansion of Chējì Jiāngjūn Yán Xiǎn.
At that time, Yán Tàihòu was acting as regent,
and Xiǎn was involved in governing affairs.
Previously, Emperor Ān had deposed the crown prince as Jìyīn Wáng,
and installed Běixiāng Hóu as his heir.
Yuàn, believing that the marquis's enthronement was not legitimate,
knew that Xiǎn would fail,
and wanted to persuade him to depose and enthrone,
but Xiǎn was drunk daily
and could not be seen.
So he said to the Chief Clerk Chén Chán:
"The Middle Regular Attendants Jiāng Jīng, Chén Dá, and others
used their favoritism to delude the late emperor,
causing him to depose the legitimate heir
and establish a distant and inferior relative.
The young emperor, upon ascending the throne,
fell ill in the ancestral temple,
a sign like that of Zhōu Bó,
which is seen again here.
Now I wish to seek an audience with the Chief Clerk and you,
to persuade the General to inform the Empress Dowager,
to arrest Jiāng Jīng and the others,
depose the young emperor,
and enthrone the King of Jìyīn.
This will surely accord with the will of Heaven above
and meet the hopes of the people below.
The merits of Yī and Huò
will be established without leaving your seats,
and then the General's brothers will transmit the imperial succession endlessly.
If you resist and disobey the will of Heaven,
and leave the divine regalia vacant for too long,
then you will be punished as though guilty of the chief wickedness, despite your innocence.
This is what is called the confluence of fortune and misfortune,
the time to distinguish merit."
Chán hesitated and dared not follow.
Coincidentally, Běixiāng Hóu died,
and Sūn Chéng enthroned the King of Jìyīn,
who became Emperor Shùn.
Yán Xiǎn and his brothers were all executed,
and Yuàn was implicated and dismissed.
His student Sū Qí fully knew Yuàn's plan
and wanted to memorialize the situation,
but Yuàn heard and immediately stopped him.
At that time, Chén Chán was Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and he summoned Yuàn and said:
"Just let Qí submit the memorial,
and I, Chán, will vouch for it."
Yuàn said:
"This is like the whispered words of children and concubines;
I wish, sir, that you would not mention it again."
He then resigned and returned home,
no longer responding to calls from the province or commandery.
After a long time,
the Grand General Liáng Shāng first established his staff headquarters,
and again appointed Yuán as the chief clerk.
He believed that he had twice served as an official for the imperial relatives,
but had been unjustly dismissed.
Therefore, he firmly declined, citing illness.
During that year, he was recommended as an outstanding talent (màocái)
and was promoted to Magistrate of Jí (Jí Lìng).
While in office, he frequently offered practical suggestions,
and opened several hundred qǐng of rice fields for the people.
He served for seven years,
and the common people sang his praises.
In the early years of Hàn'ān,
the Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dà Sī nóng) Hú Guǎng and the Palace Secretary (Shǎofǔ) Dòu Zhāng jointly recommended Yuán as a scholar of profound virtue and great learning,
who had left his mark in administration,
and ought not to remain long in a low position.
Consequently, he was promoted to Administrator of Jìběi (Jìběi Xiàng).
At that time, Lǐ Gù was the Administrator of Tàishān (Tàishān Tàishǒu),
and admired Yuán's elegance in writing.
He sent a letter expressing his utmost respect and courtesy.
After more than a year,
the Grand Master of Light (Guānglù Dàfū) Dù Qiáo served as one of the Eight Envoys,
touring the commanderies and kingdoms.
He impeached Yuán for corruption,
and he was summoned to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
Yuán submitted a petition to defend himself,
and was cleared and released.
He then fell ill and died,
at the age of sixty-six.
At his deathbed,
he looked at his son Shí and said:
"Man receives the qi of Heaven and Earth to be born,
and when his end comes,
his spirit returns to Heaven,
and his bones return to Earth.
What place cannot contain one's physical form?
Do not return to the hometown.
As for the funerary gifts,
and the offerings of sheep and pigs,
not a single one is to be accepted."
Shí honored his father's last wish,
and thus buried him in Luòyáng.
Yuán excelled in literary composition,
especially in writing letters, records, admonitions (zhēn), and inscriptions (míng).
His published works include rhapsodies (fù), stelae (bēi), inscriptions (míng), admonitions (zhēn), eulogies (sòng), Qī Sū,
Nányáng Wénxué Guānzhì, laments (tàncí), petitions to local deities (yíshè wén), repentant prayers (huǐqí), works on cursive script (cǎoshū yì), and seven-character poems (qīyán),
totaling fifty-seven pieces.
His Nányáng Wénxué Guānzhì was renowned in later generations,
and all who were skilled in writing considered themselves not as good.
Yuán loved scholars,
and enjoyed entertaining guests.
He lavishly prepared food and drink,
indulging in rich flavors,
without regard for his remaining property.
Yet, he usually ate plain vegetables and vegetable soup.
His family had no reserves of even a dān or shí of grain,
and he was considered pure by his contemporaries.
Shí, whose courtesy name was Zǐzhēn,
also had the name Tái,
and courtesy name Yuánshǐ.
When young, he was quiet and calm,
and fond of classics.
After his father's death,
he lived in seclusion by the tomb.
After completing the mourning period,
the Three Excellencies (Sān Gōng) all invited him to serve,
but he declined all of them.
In the early years of Emperor Huán,
an imperial edict commanded the high ministers, grandees, and commanderies to recommend filial and upright gentlemen who acted independently.
Shí was recommended by his commandery,
and summoned to the imperial coach (Gōngchē),
but due to illness, he could not present his policy ideas.
He was appointed as a Gentleman (Láng).
He was clear about the principles of government,
and had more than enough administrative talent.
He discussed several tens of current practical matters,
which he titled Zhènglùn.
His points were incisive and relevant to the times,
and his words were eloquent and precise.
His contemporaries praised him.
Zhòngcháng Tǒng said:
"For any ruler,
it is advisable to copy one edition
and keep it by their seat."
Its text says:
Jī's instructions brought prosperity to Yīn and Zhōu.
As for the succeeding rulers,
who wished to achieve the功 of a middle revival,
how could they not rely on the strategies of wise and virtuous men?
The reason why the world
is often not well governed
is that rulers, after long periods of peace,
allow customs to gradually decay without realizing it,
and policies to steadily decline without changing them.
Accustomed to chaos and secure in danger,
they are oblivious
and do not see it themselves.
Some are addicted to desires,
and disregard the myriad affairs of state;
some are deaf to admonitions and advice,
disliking falsehoods but ignoring truths;
some hesitate at crossroads,
not knowing which path
to follow;
some trusted assistants,
remain silent to protect their positions;
or distant ministers,
whose words are dismissed due to their low status.
Hence, the royal authority is loose and corrupted above,
while wise scholars are frustrated
and suppressed below.
Alas!
When the people are in distress,
they all again think of the rescue of a middle revival.
Moreover, the methods for saving the age and rescuing the world,
must they necessarily embody Yáo and tread in the steps of Shùn to bring order?
The goal is to mend
what is broken,
to prop up what is leaning,
to cut and adapt according to the situation,
and merely to place this generation in a state of peace and tranquility.
Therefore, the sages, holding power,
established regulations according to the times,
and the differences in their steps
each had their own setup.
They did not force people to do what they could not,
nor did they abandon urgent needs to pursue what they had heard.
Indeed, Kǒngzǐ's replies to Yè Gōng
on how to attract distant people,
to Āi Gōng on how to govern people,
and to Jǐng Gōng on how to regulate rituals,
were not contradictory,
but addressed different urgent tasks.
Thus, rulers who received the mandate
always created
new institutions;
and enlightened rulers (zhǔ) of a middle revival
also rectified the errors of their time.
In ancient times, Pángēng sympathized with Yīn,
moved the capital and changed the people;
when Zhōu Mù had shortcomings,
Fǔ Hóu rectified the punishments.
Common
people are constrained by texts and bound by ancient ways,
not understanding expedient measures and regulations.
They marvel at what they have heard,
and ignore what they see.
How can one discuss the great affairs of the state with them?
Therefore, those who speak on affairs,
even if their words
accord with sagely virtue,
are always criticized and suppressed.
Why?
Because the ignorant scholars are blind to the exigencies of the time,
accustomed to what they have seen,
and do not know how to enjoy success,
let alone consider its beginnings.
They merely
say, "Follow the old regulations."
As for the enlightened ones, some are proud of their reputation and jealous of talent,
ashamed if policies are not their own;
they wield their pens and unleash words
to undermine the proposals.
The few cannot overcome the many,
and thus
they are rejected
and dismissed.
Even if Jì and Qì were alive again,
they would still be in distress.
This is why Jiǎ Shēng was ostracized by Jiàng and Guàn,
and Qū Zǐ vented his profound indignation.
Considering
Emperor Wén's sagacity,
Jiǎ Shēng's wisdom,
and Jiàng and Guàn's loyalty,
yet such troubles arose,
how much more so for others!
It is appropriate to impose heavy rewards and severe punishments to control them,
and to clearly establish laws and methods to restrain them.
Except for those of supreme virtue,
strictness brings order,
while leniency leads to chaos.
How can this be proven
to be so?
Recently, Emperor Xiàoxuān was clear about the way of a ruler,
and precise in the principles of governance.
Thus, he enforced severe punishments and strict laws,
breaking the courage of villains and deviants.
The realm within the four seas was clean and solemn,
and the world was orderly.
His achievements were offered in the ancestral temple,
and he was honored with the title Zhōngzōng.
His calculations proved effective,
surpassing Emperor Xiàowén.
However, when Emperor Yuán ascended the throne,
he widely adopted lenient policies,
ultimately failed,
his authority and power were gradually lost,
and he became the lord who laid the foundation for disaster in the Hàn dynasty.
The successes and failures of governance
can be seen here.
Formerly, Kǒngzǐ composed the Chūnqiū,
praising Qí Huán,
extolling Jìn Wén,
and lamenting the achievements of Guǎn Zhòng.
How could he not appreciate the ways of Wén and Wǔ?
It was truly the principle of adapting to circumstances and remedying defects.
Therefore, the sage
can change with the times,
but common scholars stubbornly refuse to adapt,
thinking that the covenant of knotted ropes
can restore order to the chaos of Qín,
and the shield and axe dance
is
sufficient to lift the siege of Píngchéng.
Indeed, the laws of governing a state
are similar to managing one's body:
when healthy, one nourishes it;
when ill, one attacks the illness.
Now, punishments
are the medicine and stone for treating disorder;
moral education
is the
nourishment for promoting peace.
To eliminate evil with moral education
is like treating an illness with rich food;
to bring peace with punishments
is like providing nourishment with medicine and stone.
Currently, we inherit
the decay of a hundred kings
and encounter an era of tribulation.
For several generations,
policies have been overly lenient,
the charioteer has abandoned his reins,
the horses have shed their bits,
the four steeds run wild,
and the imperial road
is dangerously inclined.
We are about to rein in and harness them to save the situation;
how can we have time to sound the imperial bells
and perfect the rhythm?
Formerly, Gāozǔ ordered Xiāo Hé to formulate the laws of the Jiǔzhāng,
which
included the order of exterminating three generations of a family,
tattooing, cutting off the nose, severing toes, cutting off the tongue, and decapitation.
Therefore, these were called the five punishments.
Although Wéndì abolished physical mutilation,
those who deserved nose-cutting were lashed
three hundred times;
those who deserved to have their left foot severed were lashed five hundred times;
those who deserved to have their right foot severed [had their heads displayed publicly].
Those who had their right foot severed often died,
and those who were lashed also frequently died.
Though there was a name for
lighter punishments,
in reality, it was killing.
At this time,
the people all wished for the restoration of physical mutilation.
In the first year of Jǐngdì's reign,
an edict was issued saying:
“ 【The addition of】 lashing is
no different from a severe crime;
if one is fortunate enough not to die,
one cannot be 【a person】 (among people).”
Then new laws were enacted,
reducing the number of lashes and lightening the blows.
From then on,
those who were lashed could survive.
From this, it can be said that
Wéndì actually increased the severity of punishments,
not lightened them;
he achieved peace through severity,
not through leniency.
If you are determined to implement such words,
you must thoroughly establish their
foundation,
making the ruler emulate the Five Sovereigns and follow the Three Kings.
Sweep away the customs of the fallen Qín,
adhere to the ways of the ancient sages,
reject policies that merely preserve the status quo,
tread the path of examining antiquity,
restore the five ranks of nobility,
and establish the well-field system.
Then, select Jì Qì as assistants,
Yī Lǚ as advisors,
let music play and the phoenix dance,
strike stones and a hundred
beasts dance.
If not,
then there will only be more burdens.
Subsequently, he was invited by Grand Commandant Yuán Tāng and General-in-Chief Liáng Jì's residences,
but declined both.
Grand Minister of Agriculture Yáng Fù and Palace Assistant He Bào submitted memorials recommending Shí, stating his talent, beauty, and high ability,
making him suitable for the court.
He was summoned and appointed Counselor,
then promoted to Chief Clerk for General-in-Chief Jì,
and together with Biān Sháo, Yán Dǔ, and others, he worked on texts at the Eastern Lodge.
He was sent out as Administrator of Wǔyuán.
The land of Wǔyuán was suitable for hemp and ramie,
but the local customs did not include weaving and spinning.
The people had no clothes in winter,
piled up fine grass and slept in it,
and when they saw officials, they wore grass and came out.
Upon Shí's arrival at the post,
he sold off stored provisions
and had tools for spinning, weaving, and reeling hemp made to teach them.
The people were thus relieved from the cold and hardship.
At this time, the Hú barbarians repeatedly invaded Yúnzhōng and Shuòfāng,
killing and plundering officials and commoners.
In one year, there were up to nine urgent military dispatches.
Shí disciplined his soldiers and horses,
and strictly maintained the signal fires.
The barbarians dared not trespass,
and he was always considered the best at the frontier.
Due to illness, he was recalled,
appointed Counselor,
and again collaborated with various scholars and erudites to collectively revise the Five Classics.
When Liáng Jì was executed,
Shí, as his former subordinate, was dismissed from office
and banned from holding office for several years.
At that time, the Xiānbēi repeatedly violated the frontier.
An imperial edict ordered the Three Excellencies to recommend brave, capable, and strategic individuals.
Minister of Works Huáng Qióng recommended Shí,
who was appointed Administrator of Liáodōng.
While traveling,
his mother, Lady Liú, fell ill and passed away.
He submitted a memorial requesting to return home to bury her and observe mourning.
His mother possessed the virtues of a maternal model,
and was well-read in books and historical accounts.
Initially,
when Shí was in Wǔyuán,
she often instructed him in the policies of governing the people.
Shí's good achievements
were aided by his mother.
After completing the mourning period,
he was summoned and appointed Palace Attendant.
Shí, seeing that the world was in turmoil and disorder,
claimed illness and did not attend to affairs,
and was dismissed and returned home after several months.
Initially,
when Shí's father died,
he sold his fields and houses,
built a tomb,
and erected a stele with a eulogy.
After the burial,
his assets were exhausted.
Due to poverty,
he made a living by brewing and selling alcohol.
Many people at the time criticized [him for this],
but Shí never changed.
He also only took enough to get by,
not accumulating surplus.
When he became an official,
serving in various border prefectures,
he became even poorer.
He died of illness during the Jiànníng era.
His family had only four bare walls,
with nothing for his funeral.
Court Architect Yáng Cì, Grand Coachman Yuán Féng, and Palace Assistant Duàn Jiǒng provided the coffin and burial necessities,
and Grand Herald Yuán Wěi erected a stele praising his virtues.
His writings, including steles, treatises, admonitions, inscriptions, replies, seven-character poems, temple inscriptions, essays, memorials, records, and letters, totaled fifteen篇 (piān).
Shí’s elder cousin, Liè,
had a great reputation in the northern provinces,
and successively held positions as Commander of Commanderies and Nine Ministers.
During the reign of Emperor Líng,
the Hóngdū Mén was opened, and offices and aristocratic titles were sold,
from high-ranking officials and provincial governors down to those with yellow sashes, each with a different price.
The wealthy would pay in advance,
while the poor would pay double after assuming office,
or they would seek connections through eunuchs or wet nurses to gain advancement.
At this time, though Duàn Jiǒng, Fán Líng, Zhāng Wēn and others had achieved meritorious service and fame,
they all first paid money and goods before ascending to public office.
At the time, Liè, through his foster mother, paid five million (coins),
and became Sītú.
On the day of his appointment,
the Son of Heaven presided from the imperial carriage,
and all officials were present.
The Emperor looked at his favored attendants and said,
"I regret not being a little more stingy; it could have reached ten million!"
Empress Chéng, who was nearby, responded,
"Cui Gōng is a renowned scholar from Jìzhōu,
how could he possibly buy an office?
Thanks to me he got this,
and he doesn't even know how good it is!"
Thereupon, Liè’s reputation declined.
After a long time, he felt uneasy,
and leisurely asked his son, Jūn,
"How do I fare as one of the Three Ducal Ministers,
in the opinion of those who discuss such things?"
Jūn replied,
"Your Excellency had a brilliant reputation in your youth,
and successively held positions as Ministers and Commanders;
commentators did not say you were unworthy of being a Three Ducal Minister;
but now that you have ascended to that position,
the world is disappointed."
Liè asked,
"Why is that?"
Jūn replied,
"Commentators dislike your 'smell of copper'."
Liè became angry,
and raised his staff to strike him.
Jūn, then a Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng,
wearing military attire,
and adorned with a hornbill feather,
fled in a panic.
Liè cursed,
"You dead soldier!
Your father strikes you and you run,
is that filial?"
Jūn replied,
"When Shùn served his father,
he received small blows,
but fled from large blows;
that was not unfilial."
Liè felt ashamed and stopped.
Liè was later appointed Tàiwèi.
Jūn, while young, befriended heroes,
gained a reputation,
and became the Grand Administrator of Xīhé.
At the beginning of Emperor Xiàndì’s reign,
Jūn and Yuán Shào both raised troops in Shāndōng.
Dǒng Zhuó, because of this, arrested Liè and imprisoned him in Méiyù,
fettering him
with iron chains.
After Zhuó was executed,
Liè was appointed Chéngmén Xiàowèi.
When Lǐ Jué entered Cháng'ān,
he was killed by mutinous soldiers.
Liè possessed literary talent,
and wrote four pieces of poetry, prose, admonitions, and eulogies.
Commentary says: The Cuī clan had fine talents for generations,
and moreover, they were deeply immersed in classical texts,
thus becoming a school of Confucian scholars and literary figures.
Yīn and Yuàn, though they first dedicated themselves to powerful relatives,
were able to conclude their lives by maintaining integrity,
so their ultimate intention differed from those who sought quick advancement!
Lǐ Gù,
a man of lofty purity,
was a neighbor of Yuàn in a bordering commandery,
and presented gifts to establish friendship.
From this, we know that Dù Qiáo’s impeachment
was likely an error.
Shí’s political treatises,
which discussed the order and disorder of his time,
could not be surpassed even by the likes of Cháo Cuò.
Eulogy says: The Cuī were literary masters,
for generations, they carried on the art of writing.
Jiàn Shīn, ashamed of purity,
crushed his ambition to seek favor.
Forever the long promontory,
on the shady side of Liáo.
If one does not have a righteous path,
why sink into the mud?
Yuàn did not speak of emolument,
yet also suffered unjust disgrace.
Zǐ Zhēn’s arguments,
awakened the ignorant populace.
Biographies of Zhōu, Huáng, Xú, Jiāng, Shēntú, Chapter 43
The Yì says:
"The way of the noble person,
sometimes to emerge, sometimes to withdraw,
sometimes to be silent, sometimes to speak."
Kǒngzǐ praised
"Qú Bóyù: when the state has the Way, he serves;
when the state lacks the Way, he can roll it up and hold it to his breast."
However, the matter of serving or withdrawing
is how the noble person preserves their integrity.
Therefore, when they act,
they wet their feet and cover themselves in dust,
offering themselves to serve the times;
and when they cease,
they dwell in poverty and eat beans,
concealing their talents to keep them from a misguided state.
Mǐn Zhòngshú of Tàiyuán,
was known as a man of integrity,
even Zhōu Dǎng, in his purity,
considered himself inferior to him.
Dǎng saw him eating beans and drinking water,
and offered him raw garlic,
which he accepted but did not eat.
During the Jiànwǔ period,
he was summoned by Sītú Hóu Bà.
Upon arrival,
Bà did not discuss government affairs,
but merely tired him out.
Zhòngshú lamented,
"Initially, when I received the auspicious summons,
I was both happy and apprehensive;
now that I have seen Your Excellency,
both happiness and apprehension are gone.
If you deem Zhòngshú unworthy of being consulted,
you should not have summoned him.
To summon and not consult
is to fail to utilize a person."
Thereupon, he resigned,
submitted his impeachment, and departed.
He was later summoned as a Bóshì,
but did not go.
He lived as a guest in Ānyì.
Old, ill, and poor,
he could not afford meat,
and bought one slice of pig liver daily.
The butcher sometimes refused to give it to him.
The Magistrate of Ānyì heard this,
and ordered officials to always provide it.
Zhòngshú, surprised, asked about it,
and when he learned the reason,
he sighed,
"How can Mǐn Zhòngshú burden Ānyì for his mere stomach?"
Thereupon, he left,
and lived as a guest in Pèi.
He died of old age.
Xún Rèn, of the same commandery as Zhòngshú,
courtesy name Jūndà,
also cultivated a pure and upright character in his youth.
He had wealth of ten million,
but when his father Yuè died,
he distributed it all among his relatives.
He lived in seclusion in the mountains and marshes,
seeking to fulfill his aspirations.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng’s reign,
the Xiongnú invaded his home county, Guǎngwǔ.
Hearing of Rèn's reputation and integrity,
they agreed not to enter the Xún clan's village.
Emperor Guāngwǔ summoned him,
but he did not come due to illness.
At the beginning of the Yǒngpíng era,
Wáng Cāng of Dōngpíng became Grand General of Cavalry,
and opened his eastern residence to invite talented individuals.
Rèn was summoned and responded.
Later, during an imperial audience,
Emperor Xiǎnzōng joked with him,
"The late Emperor summoned you, but you did not come;
the Grand General of Cavalry summoned you, and you came.
Why is that?"
He replied,
"The late Emperor upheld virtue to bestow kindness upon his subordinates,
thus your servant could afford not to come.
The Grand General of Cavalry enforces the law to control his subordinates,
thus your servant dared not not come."
A little over a month later,
he was dismissed and returned home,
where he died.
During the reign of Huán Dì,
Wèi Huán from Ānyáng,
whose courtesy name was Zhòngyīng,
was also repeatedly summoned.
His fellow villagers encouraged him to go.
Huán said:
“Seeking official emoluments and advancement
is for the purpose of carrying out one’s ambitions.
Now, there are thousands of women in the imperial harem;
can they be reduced?
There are ten thousand horses in the stables;
can they be decreased?
The powerful and influential are all on the left and right;
can they be removed?”
Everyone replied:
“No.”
Huán then sighed regretfully:
“If I, Huán, were to go and die there,
what would it avail my sons!”
Thereupon, he retired and did not emerge.
Such men as these two or three,
may be said to understand the principle of action and withdrawal,
and to act according to the opportune moment.
Indeed,
how could it merely be a matter of withering away and making do?
They surely adapted to the times and examined themselves,
to accomplish their Way.
Therefore, I have listed their distinguished conduct,
and recorded them separately.
Zhōu Xiè, whose courtesy name was Yànzǔ,
was from Ānchéng, Rǔnán.
He was a descendant of Yān, the clerk of the Judicial Bureau.
Xiè was born with a receding chin and a flat nose bridge,
his ugly appearance was startling.
His mother wished to
abandon him, but his father did not allow it,
saying:
“I have heard that many sages and worthies have unusual appearances.
The one who will bring glory to our clan
will be this child.”
Thus, he was raised.
When he was first in childhood,
he already knew modesty and humility;
at the age of ten, he attended school,
and could comprehend the Shī and Lùn;
when he grew up,
he specialized in the Lǐ and Yì.
He did not read books not by the sages,
nor did he cultivate the habit of exchanging felicitations.
His ancestors had a thatched hut built by the water’s edge,
below which were pond fields,
where he constantly worked diligently to support himself.
If he did not personally farm or fish,
he would not eat.
Few of his fellow villagers or clan members ever saw him.
He was nominated as Xiàolián, Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng,
and specially summoned,
but he always declined on grounds of illness.
In the second year of Yán'guāng,
Ān Dì invited Xiè and
Féng Liáng from Nányáng with offerings of black and red silk and lambskin;
each of the two commanderies sent an Assistant and a Clerk to deliver the courtesies.
His clan members again urged him, saying:
“Cultivating virtue and establishing conduct
is for the benefit of the state.
From our ancestors’ time,
merit and favor have been passed down;
why do you alone guard the ponds of Dōnggāng?”
Xiè said:
“Since I cannot live hidden in caves,
following the footsteps of Qǐ Jì,
yet I am conspicuously not far from my parents’ state,
this is truly to stir the mud and raise the waves,
joining their current.
He who cultivates the Way,
measures the time and then acts.
If one acts not at the right time,
how can one be successful!”
Thereupon, he traveled by carriage to Yángchéng in Yǐngchuān,
sent a student to deliver his respects,
and then declined on grounds of illness and returned.
Liáng also traveled while ill to a nearby county,
delivered his respects, and returned.
An imperial decree informed the two commanderies
to provide lamb and wine annually for their convalescence.
Liáng’s courtesy name was Jūnláng.
He came from a humble background,
and in his youth, served as a county clerk.
At the age of thirty,
he became an assistant to the commandant.
When he received an official document to welcome the Inspector,
he was filled with emotion on the road,
ashamed to be in menial service,
and consequently smashed his carriage, killed his horse,
tore up his clothes and hat,
then fled to Jiānwéi,
where he studied under Dù Fǔ.
His wife and children searched for him,
but his tracks were completely lost.
Later, when a damaged carriage and dead horse were found in the grass,
with decayed clothes,
it was believed he had been killed by tigers, wolves, or bandits,
and a funeral was held with mourning rites.
After about ten years,
he finally returned to his hometown.
His ambition and conduct were lofty and disciplined;
he did not move against propriety.
He treated his wife and children as if they were lord and minister,
and his fellow villagers regarded him as a model.
Both Xiè and Liáng died in their seventies.
Huáng Xiàn, whose courtesy name was Shúdù,
was from Shènyáng, Rǔnán.
His family was poor and humble;
his father was a cattle doctor.
Xún Shú from Yǐngchuān came to Shènyáng
and met Xiàn at an inn.
Xiàn was then fourteen years old.
Shú was awe-struck and found him extraordinary,
bowed and spoke with him,
and could not leave for an entire day.
He said to Xiàn:
“You,
are my teacher and model.”
Afterwards, he went to Yuán Làng’s
residence,
before he could even offer greetings,
Làng preemptively asked:
“Does your state have a Yán Zǐ;
do you know him?”
Làng said:
“Have you seen my Shúdù?”
At that time,
Dài Liáng, of the same commandery, was arrogant due to his high talent,
yet when he saw Xiàn, he never failed to compose his expression respectfully,
and when he returned,
he would be absent-minded as if he had lost something.
His mother asked:
“Have you come back from that cattle doctor’s son again?”
He replied:
“Before Liáng met Shúdù,
he did not think himself inferior;
but having seen the man,
one looks up and he is ahead,
then suddenly he is behind,
truly difficult to fathom.”
Chén Fān and Zhōu Jǔ, also of the same commandery, often said to each other:
“If we do not see Huáng Shēng for a month or so,
the sprouts of vulgarity and meanness reappear in our hearts.”
When Fān became one of the Three Ducal Ministers,
he sighed from the imperial court:
“If Shúdù were alive,
I would not dare to wear the official seal first.”
When Grand Administrator Wáng Gōng was in the commandery,
he courteously promoted the virtuous and eminent,
and made many concessions to attract them,
but ultimately could not compel Xiàn.
Guō Línzōng, in his youth, traveled to Rǔnán,
first visited Yuán Làng,
but left without staying overnight;
he then went to Xiàn,
and only returned after several days.
Someone asked Línzōng about this.
Línzōng said:
“Fènggāo’s capacity,
is like an overflowing stream,
though clear, it is easy to draw from.
Shúdù is like a vast, boundless reservoir of a thousand qǐng,
clarified, it does not become clearer;
muddied, it does not become muddier,
it cannot be measured.”
Xiàn was first recommended as Xiàolián,
and also invited to the ducal government.
His friends urged him to enter officialdom,
and Xiàn did not refuse,
temporarily going to the capital and then returning,
ultimately achieving nothing.
He died at the age of forty-eight,
and the world called him
“Zhēngjūn” (Invited Gentleman).
A commentary states: Huáng Xiàn’s words and style
are nowhere transmitted,
yet gentlemen and scholars who met him
were all impressed by his profoundness
and shed their own faults and meanness.
Was it perhaps because his Way was complete and his nature perfect,
so that he was praised without specific virtues?
My great-grandfather, Marquis Mù,
believed that Xiàn was calm and yielding in his conduct,
and profound, resembling the Way;
his depth and shallowness could not be discerned,
nor could his clarity or turbidity be discussed.
If he had studied under Confucius,
he would probably have been close to him!
Thus, he once wrote a treatise on this.
Xú Zhì
was a native of Nánchāng, Yùzhāng.
His family was poor,
and he constantly cultivated his own fields,
never eating unless it was by his own labor.
He was modest, frugal, righteous, and yielding.
Wherever he lived, people admired his virtue.
He was repeatedly invited to serve in ducal administrations,
but he refused to take office.
At that time, Chén Fān was the Grand Administrator,
and he courteously invited Xú Zhì to be appointed as Gōngcáo.
Xú Zhì could not decline,
so he paid his respects and then withdrew.
Chén Fān, while in the commandery, did not receive guests,
but for Xú Zhì alone, he specially set up a couch;
when Xú Zhì left, he would hang it up.
Later, he was recommended as "One Possessing the Way"
and was appointed Grand Administrator of Tàiyuán,
but he accepted neither.
In the second year of Yánxī,
Chén Fān, the Shàngshū Lìng, and Hú Guǎng, the Púyè, submitted a memorial recommending Xú Zhì and others, saying:
“Your humble servants have heard that good people are the order of heaven and earth,
and the foundation of governance.
The Shī Jīng says: ‘
So grand were the many officers, born in this royal domain.’
Heaven has produced outstanding talents,
for Your Majesty’s sake.
They ought to assist and guide this enlightened age,
and support the great enterprise.
We humbly observe that the recluse scholars Xú Zhì of Yùzhāng, Jiāng Hóng of Péngchéng, Yuán Hóng of Rǔnán,
Wéi Zhù of Jīngzhào,
and Lǐ Tán of Yǐngchuān
all possess pure and complete virtue,
renowned among the people.
If they were promoted to the San Shi (Three Ministers),
to assist in the Emperor’s work,
they would surely be able to widely proclaim great virtues
and add luster to the brightening day.”
Therefore, Emperor Huán sent an Ānchē Xuánxūn
and all the appropriate rites to summon them,
but none arrived.
The Emperor then asked Chén Fān,
“Among Xú Zhì, Yuán Hóng, and Wéi Zhù, who is superior?”
Chén Fān replied,
“Yuán Hóng was born into a ducal family,
and gradually learned the Way.
Wéi Zhù grew up in the custom of rites and righteousness in Sānfǔ,
who is, as it is said, one who straightens without support,
and carves without chiseling.
As for Xú Zhì,
he comes from the humble and lowly region south of the Jiāng,
yet he stands out as an eminent figure,
and ought to be considered first.”
Xú Zhì was once invited by Grand Commandant Huáng Qióng,
but did not accept.
When Huáng Qióng died and was to be buried,
Xú Zhì carried provisions and traveled on foot to Jiāngxià to attend,
offering a simple sacrifice of chicken and wine,
wept, and then left,
without disclosing his name.
At that time, among the dozens of famous scholars from all quarters, such as Guō Línzōng,
who were present,
upon hearing of this, suspected it might be Xú Zhì.
They then selected Máo Róng, who was eloquent, to pursue him with light cavalry.
When he caught up on the road,
Máo Róng prepared a meal for him,
and they discussed farming matters together.
When it was time to part,
Xú Zhì said to Máo Róng,
“Please tell Guō Línzōng for me,
‘A great tree is about to fall,
it cannot be secured by a single rope.
Why are you bustling about, finding no peace?’”
Later, when Guō Línzōng was in mourning for his mother,
Xú Zhì went to offer condolences,
placed a bundle of fresh straw in front of the mourning hut, and left.
Everyone was surprised,
not knowing the reason.
Guō Línzōng said,
“This must be the noble scholar Xú Rúzi from the southern region.
Does not the Shī Jīng say,
‘A bundle of fresh straw,
the person is like jade.’
I am not virtuous enough to merit this.”
At the beginning of Emperor Líng’s reign,
he wanted to summon Xú Zhì with a púlún carriage,
but he passed away at that time,
at the age of seventy-two.
His son, Xú Yìn, courtesy name Jìdēng,
was diligent in filial piety and fraternal duty, and also lived as a recluse, refusing to serve.
Grand Administrator Huà Xīn courteously invited him for an audience,
but he resolutely feigned illness and did not go.
Towards the end of the Hàn dynasty, when bandits were rampant,
they all respected Xú Yìn’s rites and conduct,
and mutually agreed and ordered
not to violate his village.
He died during the Jiàn'ān period.
Lǐ Tán, courtesy name Yún,
was orphaned young.
His stepmother was cruel,
but Lǐ Tán served her with even greater diligence,
and was praised and emulated by the villagers.
He cared for his parents and practiced the Way,
never taking office throughout his life.
Jiāng Hóng, courtesy name Bóhuái,
was a native of Guǎngqī, Péngchéng.
His family was a renowned lineage for generations.
Jiāng Hóng and his two younger brothers, Zhònghǎi and Jìjiāng,
were all famous for their filial piety.
Their brotherly love was profound and natural;
they always slept and rose together.
When they each married,
the brothers were so attached to each other
that they could not sleep separately.
Since it was necessary to establish heirs,
they would take turns going to their wives’ chambers.
Jiāng Hóng was broadly learned in the Wǔ Jīng
and also understood the stars and weft texts.
Over three thousand scholars came from afar to study with him.
Various dukes competed to appoint him,
but he declined them all.
His two younger brothers also had similar reputations
and did not respond to summons or invitations.
People of the time admired them.
Jiāng Hóng once visited the commandery with Jìjiāng.
At night, they encountered robbers on the road
who intended to kill them.
The Jiāng brothers competed to die for each other,
whereupon the robbers released both,
only plundering their clothes and money.
When they arrived in the commandery,
seeing Jiāng Hóng without clothes,
people asked in surprise the reason.
Jiāng Hóng made up another excuse,
never mentioning the robbers.
The robbers heard of this and were moved to repentance.
Later, they went to the hermitage
to seek an audience with the summoned gentleman.
Jiāng Hóng met with them,
and they all kowtowed, apologizing,
and returned the plundered items.
Jiāng Hóng did not accept them,
but entertained them with food and drink and sent them away.
Later, he was summoned together with Xú Zhì,
but did not arrive.
Emperor Huán then sent an order to Péngchéng to have a painter draw his likeness.
Jiāng Hóng lay down in a dark place,
covered his face with a quilt,
saying he suffered from dizziness
and did not wish to be exposed to the wind.
The painter ultimately could not see him.
The Zhōngchángshì Cáo Jié and others monopolized court affairs,
having recently executed Grand Tutor Chén Fān and General-in-Chief Dòu Wǔ.
Wishing to gain favor by showing respect for the virtuous,
to appease public sentiment,
they memorialized to summon Jiāng Hóng as Grand Administrator.
Upon receiving the edict,
Jiāng Hóng privately told his friends,
“I have gained substance from nothing,
thus borrowing a reputation.
Even when the government is clear and aboveboard,
one should still firmly adhere to one’s original aspirations,
how much more so now that power rests with eunuchs?
What is there to do?”
So he concealed himself and fled,
drifting far away to the seashore.
He was summoned again with xuánxūn,
but did not accept.
He was then appointed Tài Zhōng Dàfū,
and when the imperial edict arrived at his door,
Jiāng Hóng had his family reply
that he had been “long sick and seeing a doctor.”
Then he dressed in humble clothes and traveled incognito,
hiding in the area of Qīngzhōu,
earning a living by fortune-telling.
When the summons was finally rescinded,
his family still did not know his whereabouts,
and it was years before he returned.
At the age of seventy-seven,
he died at home in the second year of Xīpíng.
His disciple Liú Cāo of Chénliú,
admiring Jiāng Hóng’s virtue,
together carved a stone eulogy for him.
Shēntú Pán, courtesy name Zǐlóng,
was a native of Wàihuáng, Chénliú.
At the age of nine, he lost his father,
and his grief and emaciation exceeded proper bounds.
After the period of mourning,
he abstained from alcohol and meat for over ten years.
On every death anniversary,
he would fast for three days.
In the same commandery, a woman named Yù (玉) from Gōu (緱) District avenged her father,
killing a member of her husband's clan.
The officials arrested Yù (玉) and reported her to Liáng Pèi (梁配), the magistrate of Wàihuáng (外黃).
Pèi (配) intended to sentence Yù (玉) to death.
Shēntú Pán (申屠蟠) was then fifteen years old
and a student.
He stepped forward and remonstrated, saying:
"Yù (玉)'s (玉) integrity and righteousness
are enough to inspire the shameless,
and to stir those who endure humiliation.
Even if she had not encountered an enlightened age,
she should still have her grave and dwelling marked with banners.
How much more so in a time of clear judgment,
should she not be shown mercy and compassion!"
Pèi (配) approved of his words
and therefore deliberated, obtaining a reduced sentence short of death.
The people of the district praised and admired him.
His family was poor,
so he worked as a lacquer artisan.
Guō Línzōng (郭林宗) saw him and considered him extraordinary.
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) of the same commandery deeply respected Pán (蟠).
When he was summoned by the province,
he declined, saying:
"Shēntú Pán (申屠蟠) is endowed with profound and subtle spirit;
his nature is keen and his mind perceptive.
In mourning his parents, he observed the rites fully,
almost to the point of self-destruction.
Such noble conduct and admirable righteousness
are rarely achieved by others.
Content in poverty and joyful in obscurity,
he savors the Dao and guards his true self,
unaffected by changes in circumstances,
and unswayed in his principles by poverty or success.
Compared to myself, Yōng (邕),
he is senior in age,
and superior in virtue."
Later, the commandery summoned him to be chief clerk,
but he did not go.
He then lived in seclusion, diligently studying,
thoroughly mastering the Five Classics,
and also clearly understanding the diagrams and apocrypha.
He had earlier studied at the Imperial Academy with Wáng Zǐjū (王子居) of Jìyīn (濟陰).
When Zǐjū (子居) was about to die,
he entrusted his body to Pán (蟠).
Pán (蟠) then personally pushed the wheeled carriage,
escorting the funeral back to his hometown.
He encountered a Sīlì Cóngshì (司隸從事) (Supervisor of the Capital Region) between the Hé (河) and Gǒng (鞏) rivers.
The Cóngshì (從事) (Supervisor) admired his righteousness
and offered him a sealed travel permit for protection and escort.
Pán (蟠) refused to accept it,
throwing the permit to the ground and leaving.
After the matter was concluded, he returned to his studies.
He was summoned by the Grand Commandant Huáng Qióng (黃瓊),
but did not accept.
When Qióng (瓊) died,
and was to be buried in Jiāngxià (江夏),
six or seven thousand renowned figures from all directions gathered at his tent,
conversing and discussing among themselves,
but none surpassed Pán (蟠).
Only one student from Nánjùn (南郡) exchanged words with him.
After they parted,
he grasped Pán (蟠)'s (蟠) hand and said:
"You will either be recruited or summoned;
we shall meet again in the capital."
Pán (蟠) indignantly flushed and said:
"Initially, I thought you were someone I could talk to.
How could you be one of those who advocate for wealth and honor?"
Thereupon, he shook off his hand and left,
never speaking to him again.
He was twice nominated as "possessing the Way,"
but did not accept.
Earlier, wandering scholars in the capital, such as Fàn Pāng (范滂) of Rǔnán (汝南), had criticized court politics,
and from the grandees and ministers downwards, all lowered themselves and showed deference to them.
Imperial Academy students vied to emulate their style,
believing that literature was about to flourish and reclusive scholars would again be employed.
Pán (蟠) alone sighed, saying:
"In ancient times, during the Warring States period,
reclusive scholars debated freely,
and the kings of various states
even went so far as to sweep the path and clear the way for them.
Eventually, there was the disaster of burying scholars alive and burning books;
this is what is meant by the present situation."
He then withdrew completely to the area between Liáng (梁) and Dàng (碭),
building a house by a tree,
and living like a common laborer.
After two years,
Pāng (滂) and others indeed suffered from the "Proscription of Partisans,"
with hundreds dying or being punished.
Pán (蟠) alone remained steadfast and free from suspicion.
Later, Pán (蟠)'s (蟠) friend Fēng Yōng (馮雍) of Chénjùn (陳郡) was imprisoned for an offense.
The Governor of Yùzhōu (豫州), Huáng Wǎn (黃琬), intended to execute him.
Someone urged Pán (蟠) to save Yōng (雍),
but Pán (蟠) refused to go,
saying:
"If Huáng Zǐyǎn (黃子琰) (Huáng Wǎn's courtesy name) acts on my behalf,
Yōng (雍) may not be found guilty.
If he doesn't heed my words,
what good would it do to go,
even if I were to go?"
Wǎn (琬) heard of this
and consequently pardoned Yōng (雍).
General-in-Chief Hé Jìn (何進) repeatedly summoned Pán (蟠) but he did not appear.
Jìn (進) was determined to secure his presence,
Yáng Zhèn (楊震), whose courtesy name was Bóqǐ (伯起),
was a native of Huáyīn (華陰), Hóngnóng (弘農).
His eighth generation ancestor, Xǐ (喜),
had rendered meritorious service during Emperor Gāozǔ's (高祖) time
and was enfeoffed as Chìquán Hóu (赤泉侯).
His great-grandfather, Chǎng (敞),
served as Chancellor during Emperor Zhāodì's (昭帝) time
and was enfeoffed as Ānpíng Hóu (安平侯).
His father, Bǎo (寶),
studied the Ouyáng (歐陽) version of the *Shàngshū* (尚書).
During the reigns of Emperors Āi (哀) and Píng (平),
he lived in seclusion and taught.
In the second year of the regency (Jūshè (居攝), 7 AD),
he was summoned along with the two Gǒng (龔)s and Jiǎng Xǔ (蔣詡),
but he fled and disappeared,
his whereabouts unknown.
Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武) highly esteemed his integrity.
In the Jiànwǔ (建武) era,
he was specially summoned by imperial carriage,
but due to old age and illness, he did not go
and died at home.
At that time, an imperial edict dispatched envoys to greatly renovate the residence of the Empress Dowager's mother.
The Palace Attendants Fán Fēng 樊豐 and Zhōu Guǎng 周廣, Xiè Yùn 謝惲, and others incited each other,
shaking the imperial court.
Zhèn 震 again submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your servant has heard that in ancient times, after nine years of farming, there must be three years' worth of reserves.
Therefore, when Yáo 堯 encountered the great flood,
people did not show starvation.
Your servant humbly reflects that at present, disasters are erupting,
growing increasingly severe.
The common people are destitute
and cannot sustain themselves.
Compounding this are locusts,
and Qiāng 羌 and lǔ 虜 bandits' plundering.
The three frontiers are greatly disturbed,
and the campaigns of war have not ceased to this day.
Military equipment and provisions can no longer be supplied.
The Grand Minister of Agriculture’s treasury is depleted,
which is surely not a time of peace and tranquility for the state.
Your servant humbly observes the imperial edict to construct a residence for the Empress Dowager's mother inside the Jīnchéngmén 津城門,
combining two into one,
connecting hamlets and extending across streets.
It is carved, repaired, and adorned,
exhausting all ingenious craftsmanship.
Now it is high summer, the earth phase is ascendant,
yet mountains are being attacked and stones quarried.
The Grand Superintendent of Works, the Left Workshop, and the detached commanderies' construction sections number several tens of places,
constantly pressing each other forward,
incurring immense costs.
Zhōu Guǎng 周廣 and Xiè Yùn’s 謝惲 brothers,
who are not related to the state by intimate or distant ties,
rely on favored and treacherous individuals,
sharing power and authority with Fán Fēng 樊豐, Wáng Yǒng 王永, and others.
They entrust their requests to provinces and commanderies,
swaying high ministers.
The chief ministers, when appointing officials,
anticipate their intentions,
recruiting corrupt individuals from within the seas.
They accept bribes,
even allowing those who were corruptly imprisoned and abandoned by society to regain prominent positions.
Black and white are mixed,
the clear and the turbid share the same source.
The whole empire is in an uproar,
everyone saying that wealth flows upwards,
bringing ridicule upon the court.
Your servant has heard a teacher say: 'What the superior takes,
if wealth is exhausted, there will be resentment;
if strength is exhausted, there will be rebellion.'
Resentful and rebellious people
cannot be used again.
Therefore it is said: 'If the common people are insufficient,
with whom can the ruler be sufficient?'
May Your Majesty consider this.”
Fán Fēng 樊豐, Xiè Yùn 謝惲, and others, seeing Zhèn 震 repeatedly offering blunt admonitions that were not heeded,
and having no scruples,
then fraudulently issued an imperial edict
to requisition money and grain from the Minister of Agriculture, and laborers and timber from the Grand Superintendent of Works,
each building their own residences, gardens, and viewing pavilions,
incurring countless expenses.
Zhèn 震, because of an earthquake,
again submitted a memorial, saying:
“Your servant has received grace to be counted among the highest officials,
yet cannot uphold and propagate political transformation
nor harmonize yin and yang.
Last year, on the fourth day of the twelfth month,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
Your servant has heard a teacher say: 'Earth is the essence of yin,
and should be quiet and receptive to yang.'
That it now shakes
indicates the ascendance of the yin principle.
That day was wùchén 戊辰,
all three elements being earth,
positioned in the central palace.
This is an omen of favored court officials and close officials being ascendant in holding power and managing affairs.
Your servant humbly reflects that Your Majesty, seeing the unsettled frontiers,
personally practices frugality.
The palace walls and roofs are leaning,
merely propped up,
with no new constructions,
wishing to let all, near and far, know the clear current of political transformation
and the majesty of the capital city.
Yet close and favored ministers
have not yet cultivated the firmness of 'cutting metal,'
are arrogant and exceed the law,
requesting many laborers
to lavishly build residences,
and selling their influence and power.
The roads are filled with clamor,
heard and seen by the multitude.
The anomaly of the earthquake,
close to the city,
was likely caused by this.
Moreover, there was no lingering snow in winter,
and no rain in early spring.
All officials are anxious,
yet renovations do not cease.
This is truly a sign that causes drought.
The *Shū* 書 says: 'The arrogant and unprincipled make themselves appear glorious;
ministers should not wield authority and power, nor live in luxury.'
May Your Majesty exert the virtue of heaven’s steadfastness,
discard arrogant and extravagant ministers,
to silence the mouths of slanderers,
and accept the warning from August Heaven,
not allowing power and authority to long remain with those below.”
The memorials Zhèn 震 submitted, one after another,
became increasingly urgent and direct.
The Emperor was already displeased with him,
and Fán Fēng 樊豐 and others all glared with indignation and resentment,
but because he was a famous scholar,
they dared not harm him.
Soon after, a man from Héjiān 河閒, Zhào Téng 趙騰, went to the palace gate to submit a memorial,
pointing out successes and failures.
The Emperor grew angry
and had him arrested and interrogated in the imperial prison,
convicting him of "deceiving the superior and being disloyal."
Zhèn 震 again submitted a memorial to save him, saying:
“Your servant has heard that in the eras of Yáo 堯 and Shùn 舜,
admonition drums and slander posts
were set up in the court;
wise kings of Yīn 殷 and Zhōu 周,
when common people complained and reviled,
would instead cultivate their own virtue.
This was to achieve clear understanding,
to open up avenues for direct speech,
to widely gather opinions from humble folk,
and to fully understand the sentiments of the lowest classes.
Now, Zhào Téng's 趙騰 crime is for incitement, denunciation, and slanderous speech,
which differs from physically committing a crime.
I beg for leniency,
to spare Téng's 騰 life,
to encourage words from woodcutters and commoners.”
The Emperor did not heed him,
and Téng 騰 ultimately met his end, his corpse displayed in the marketplace.
It happened that in the spring of the third year,
the Emperor made an eastern tour to Dàizōng 岱宗.
Fán Fēng 樊豐 and others, taking advantage of the imperial carriage being away,
competed to build and renovate residences.
Zhèn’s 震 subordinate clerk Gāo Shū 高舒 summoned the Grand Superintendent of Works’ registrars to audit this,
and discovered the imperial edicts fraudulently issued by Fán Fēng 樊豐 and others.
He fully reported it,
intending to present it upon the Emperor's return from the tour.
Fán Fēng 樊豐 and others, hearing this,
were terrified.
Just then, the Grand Astrologer reported a celestial anomaly where stars moved retrogradely.
They then jointly slandered Zhèn 震, saying:
“Since Zhào Téng's 趙騰 death,
he has harbored deep resentment;
moreover, he was a former subordinate of the Dèng 鄧 clan,
and holds grudges.”
When the imperial carriage returned,
and immediately visited the Imperial Academy,
envoys were sent that night to confiscate Zhèn’s 震 Grand Commandant seal and sash.
Thereupon, his gate was closed to visitors.
Fán Fēng 樊豐 and others, still bearing ill will,
then requested Grand General Gěng Bǎo 耿寶 to memorialize that Zhèn 震, as a high minister, did not accept his guilt,
and harbored resentment and discontent.
An imperial edict was issued, ordering him to return to his home commandery.
As Zhèn 震 traveled to Jīyáng Tíng 几陽亭 west of the city,
he spoke with emotion to his sons and disciples, saying:
“Death is the common fate of a scholar.
I received grace to reside in a high office,
yet I was angered by the treachery and cunning of wicked ministers and could not execute them;
I detested the beloved concubines who caused disorder and could not restrain them.
What face do I have to again see the sun and moon!
On the day of my death,
make a coffin of miscellaneous wood,
a single cloth blanket just enough to cover my form.
Do not return to my ancestral tomb,
and do not set up sacrifices.”
He then drank poison and died,
at the age of over seventy.
The Administrator of Hóngnóng 弘農, Yí Liáng 移良,
following the instructions of Fán Fēng 樊豐 and others,
dispatched officials to Xiá Xiàn 陝縣 to detain Zhèn’s 震 funeral,
leaving the coffin exposed by the roadside,
and punished Zhèn’s 震 sons, making them carry official documents in his place.
People on the road all shed tears for him.
More than a year later,
Shùn Dì ascended the throne,
Fán Fēng, Zhōu Guǎng, and others were executed.
Zhèn's students, Yú Fàng and Chén Yì, went to the palace gate to petition for Zhèn's case.
The imperial court universally praised his loyalty,
and an edict was issued to appoint his two sons as imperial gentlemen.
A gift of a million coins was bestowed,
and he was ceremoniously reburied in Huá Yīn Tóng Tíng.
People from far and near all attended.
About ten days before the reburial,
a large bird, over a *zhang* tall,
gathered before Zhèn's coffin,
bowing and crying mournfully,
with tears wetting the ground.
After the burial was complete,
it flew away.
The commandery reported the details.
At that time, there were continuous calamities and anomalies.
The emperor was moved by Zhèn's injustice,
and an edict was issued, which stated:
"The late Grand Commandant Zhèn,
was upright and virtuous,
and helped rectify the government of his time.
Yet, 'green flies stained the pure white,'
sharing this fate in the provinces.
Heaven sent down its wrath,
and disasters repeatedly occurred.
You divined with tortoise shells and yarrow stalks,
and it was all due to Zhèn.
My own lack of virtue
has caused these calamities to manifest.
Mountains collapse and pillars break –
I am truly in danger!
Now, I send the Grand Administrator's Aide with medium-level sacrificial offerings to worship him.
If his soul has consciousness,
may he perhaps accept and enjoy them."
At this, people of the time erected a stone bird effigy at his tomb.
When Zhèn was slandered,
Gāo Shū also incurred guilt,
and was sentenced to a reduced penalty.
When Zhèn's case was vindicated,
Shū was appointed Palace Censor,
and rose to be Inspector of Jīng Zhōu.
Zhèn had five sons.
The eldest son was Mù,
who served as Chancellor of Fù Bō.
Mù's grandson, Qí,
was a Palace Attendant during the reign of Líng Dì.
The emperor once casually asked Qí,
"How do I compare to Huán Dì?"
He replied,
"Your Majesty compared to Huán Dì,
is like Yú Shùn comparing his virtue to Táng Yáo."
The emperor was displeased and said,
"You are obstinate,
truly a descendant of Yáng Zhèn.
After your death, a great bird will surely appear again."
He was sent out to be Grand Administrator of Rǔ Nán.
After the emperor's death,
he re-entered the court as Palace Attendant and Commandant of the Guards.
He followed Xiàn Dì during the westward migration,
and rendered meritorious service.
When Lǐ Jué coerced the emperor to return to his camp,
Qí, together with Palace Attendant Zhōng Yáo, enticed Jué's subordinates Sòng Yè and Yáng Áng to rebel against Jué.
Jué was thus isolated and weakened,
and the emperor was then able to move east.
Later, when the capital was moved to Xǔ,
Qí's son Liàng was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Yáng Chéng Tíng.
Zhèn's youngest son was Fèng.
Fèng's son was Fū,
who was earnest in his aspirations and broadly learned.
Commentators believed he could perpetuate his family's legacy.
Fū died young.
His son, Zhòng,
also inherited the ancestral profession.
As Palace Usher, he followed Xiàn Dì into the pass,
and successively rose to Censor-in-chief.
When the emperor returned east,
he fled by night across the river.
Zhòng led all the officials to follow on foot to Tài Yáng,
and was appointed Palace Attendant.
In the second year of Jiàn'ān,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Nù Tíng for his previous merits.
Zhèn's middle son was Bǐng.
Bǐng, courtesy name Shú Jié,
inherited his father's profession in his youth,
and was also learned in the Jīng's school of the *Yì*.
He was broadly versed in books and commentaries,
and often lived in reclusion, teaching.
At over forty years old,
he responded to an invitation from the Minister of Works,
and was appointed Palace Censor.
He was frequently sent out as Inspector of the four provinces of Yù, Jīng, Xú, and Yǎn,
and then promoted to Chancellor of Rèn Chéng.
From the time he served as Inspector and official of two thousand *shi*,
he received his stipend daily,
and surplus emoluments did not enter his private household.
A former subordinate brought a million coins as a gift,
but Bǐng closed his door and refused to accept it.
He was praised for his integrity.
When Huán Dì ascended the throne,
Bǐng was summoned to the court for his clear understanding of the *Shàng Shū* to give lectures,
and was appointed Grand Master of the Palace and Left Commandant of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant and Imperial Secretary.
At that time, the emperor made incognito visits,
privately visiting the residence of Liáng Yìn, Grand Administrator of Hé Nán.
On that day, a great wind uprooted trees,
and it was dark at midday.
Bǐng then submitted a memorial remonstrating, saying:
"Your servant has heard that auspicious signs arise from virtue,
and calamities respond to deeds.
The *Zhuàn* says: 'Calamity and fortune have no gate,
they are invited by people themselves.'
Heaven does not speak,
but warns through calamities and anomalies.
Thus, Confucius would certainly change his demeanor at violent thunder and fierce winds.
The *Shī* says: 'Revere the majesty of Heaven,
do not dare to rush about.'
The sovereign is the most honored;
his comings and goings have a constant order,
he travels with imperial escorts and stops in quiet chambers.
Unless it is for affairs of the ancestral temple or suburban sacrifices,
then the imperial banner is not unfurled.
Thus the *Shī* speaks of 'from the suburban sacrifice to the ancestral temple,'
and the *Yì* says 'the king arrives at the ancestral temple,
to offer filial sacrifices.'
If even a feudal lord visiting a minister's house
was warned against in the *Chūn Qiū*,
how much more so to go out for private amusements in the ritual robes of the former kings!
This brings disorder to seniority and inferiority,
and causes the ranks and authority to be without order.
The imperial guards protect an empty palace,
the official seal is entrusted to concubines.
Should there be an extraordinary change,
or a plot like that of Rèn Zhāng,
you would disappoint the former emperors above,
and regret would be too late below.
Your servant's family has received grace for generations,
and I am privileged to be among those who speak to the emperor.
Furthermore, with my meager learning,
I am employed in imperial lectures.
I have been particularly favored with compassion and recognition,
and seen by the sun and moon.
With such heavy grace and light life,
righteousness compels a scholar to die.
How dare I shy away from breaking my back
and merely present my foolishness."
The emperor did not accept it.
Bǐng requested retirement due to illness,
and was sent out as Right Protector of Fú Fēng.
Grand Commandant Huáng Qióng regretted his departure from the court,
and memorialized that Bǐng was suitable for giving lectures in the imperial tent,
and should not be transferred externally.
He was retained and appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness.
At this time, General-in-Chief Liáng Jì wielded power,
and Bǐng claimed illness.
Six years later,
after Jì was executed,
Bǐng was then appointed Grand Coachman,
and promoted to Grand Minister of Ceremonies.
In the third year of Yán Xī,
Lǐ Yún, Magistrate of Bái Mǎ, incurred guilt for his remonstrance.
Bǐng argued for him but could not succeed,
and was dismissed from office for this,
returning to his hometown.
In the winter of that year,
he was again summoned and appointed Grand Administrator of Hé Nán.
Previously, Shàn Chāo's younger brother Kuāng, a Regular Palace Attendant,
was Grand Administrator of Jì Yīn.
He was impeached by Inspector Dì Wǔ Zhǒng for corruption.
In his desperation,
he bribed a retainer, Rèn Fāng, to assassinate Wèi Yǔ, an aide in Yǎn Zhōu.
The incident is detailed in Zhǒng's biography.
When Fāng was captured,
he was imprisoned in Luò Yáng.
Kuāng feared that Bǐng would investigate the matter thoroughly,
so he secretly arranged for Fāng and others to escape from prison.
The Imperial Secretary summoned Bǐng and reproached him.
Bǐng replied:
"The *Chūn Qiū* did not punish Lǐ Bǐ, yet Lǔ had many thieves.
Fāng and the others are despicable,
but the crime originated with Shàn Kuāng.
To assassinate an official enforcing the law,
harm a minister serving the public,
and then allow them to escape,
thus leniently releasing guilty individuals,
these arch-criminals and great villains
will ultimately harm the state.
I request that Shàn Kuāng be brought in a caged cart for examination and verification of this matter,
then the traces of treachery
can certainly be immediately found."
However, Bǐng was ultimately sentenced to penal labor at the Left School,
and released due to a long drought.
That day there was a solar eclipse.
The Grand Administrator of Tài shān, Huángfǔ Guī, and others petitioned, stating that Bǐng was loyal and upright,
and should not be suppressed and left unused for long.
An imperial edict summoned Bǐng and the hermit Wéi Zhù to the imperial carriage office.
Both men claimed illness and did not arrive.
The relevant authorities impeached both Bǐng and Zhù for great disrespect,
requesting that they be handed over to their respective jurisdictions to clarify their crimes.
Shàngshū Lìng Zhōu Jǐng and Shàngshū Biān Sháo debated and reported:
"Bǐng, as a Confucian scholar and lecturer,
has always been humble;
Zhù lives in reclusion practicing righteousness,
making humility his principle.
Their failure to appear after being summoned
is indeed contrary to the emperor's eager anticipation,
yet their reluctance to serve
is sufficient to curb the trend of opportunistic advancement.
In the age of an enlightened monarch,
there must be ministers who are not summoned.
The sagely court, in its magnanimous nurturing,
should employ a gentle and accommodating approach.
They should be informed at their respective residences,
and made to understand the court's gracious intentions.
If they still do not arrive,
their punishment should be thoroughly discussed."
Consequently, they were summoned again,
and then they arrived,
and Bǐng was appointed Tài Cháng.
In the winter of the fifth year,
he replaced Liú Jǔ as Tài Wèi.
At this time, the eunuchs were extremely powerful,
appointing their relatives and protégés to official positions,
filling the entire empire.
They competed in greed and debauchery,
causing lament and resentment throughout the court and the populace.
Bǐng, along with Sī Kōng Zhōu Jǐng, submitted a memorial, stating:
"Many internal and external officials
are not suitable for their positions.
Those who have been summoned recently
were all specially appointed without examination,
leading to rampant theft and wanton behavior,
and a multitude of grievances and lawsuits.
According to old regulations,
the relatives and protégés of inner court officials were not allowed to hold positions of power,
yet now their kin and retainers are extensively placed in various offices.
Some are young and mediocre individuals,
presiding over and governing prefectures and commanderies,
causing anger and distress among all,
and widespread sorrow and suffering.
It is advisable to adhere to the old regulations,
dismiss the greedy and cruel,
and block the source of calamities and slanders.
We request that the Sīlì Xiàowèi, the Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí, the Èr Qiān Shí, the Chéngmén Wǔyíng Xiàowèi, and the Běijūn Zhōng Hóu
each thoroughly investigate their respective departments.
Those who should be dismissed
should be reported with their circumstances.
If the Sān Fǔ discover any omissions in their incorruptible inspections,
they should follow up with additional reports."
The emperor agreed.
Thereupon, Bǐng itemized and impeached over fifty people, including shepherds and governors like Xiōngnú Zhōngláng Jiàng Yān Yuàn, Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Liàng, and Liáodōng Tài shǒu Sūn Xuān.
Some died, some were dismissed,
and the whole empire was awestruck.
At that time, many accountants from commanderies and kingdoms were retained and appointed as Láng.
Bǐng submitted a memorial, stating that there were over seven hundred Láng in the three offices,
the treasury was empty,
and those living off state funds were numerous.
Meanwhile, corrupt governors and chancellors
desired to exploit the state for their own benefit,
washing away their dirt and defilement.
It is advisable to stop arbitrary appointments
to curb the root of covetousness.
From then until the end of Huán Dì's reign,
no accountants were retained and appointed.
In the seventh year,
the emperor made a southern tour of the imperial mausoleums,
and specifically decreed that Bǐng should accompany him.
Zhāng Biāo, the Grand Administrator of Nányáng, had received old favors from the emperor when he was still obscure.
As the imperial carriage was approaching,
he took advantage by making levies,
diverting much into his private coffers.
Upon hearing this, Bǐng
issued a letter rebuking the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu,
and appended the details to the report submitted to the Gōng Fǔ.
When the entourage arrived in Nányáng,
the emperor's attendants engaged in corrupt practices,
and many appointments and dismissals were made by imperial edict.
Bǐng again submitted a memorial, advising:
"Your servant has heard that the former kings established states
and regulated officials in accordance with Heaven.
The accumulated stars in the Tàiwēi constellation are named 'Láng positions,'
serving as guards in the palace and governing the people outside.
Gāotáo cautioned Yú
regarding the appointment of officials.
Recently, appointments have been made along the roadsides,
bestowing favor upon mere servants;
titles are obtained through bribery,
and thereby morality is corrupted.
This is why common people discuss it in the alleys,
and the white steed flees far away.
The serene court,
far and wide, is no longer respected.
It is advisable to cut off the compassion that one cannot bear to relinquish
to block the path of covetous desires."
Thereupon, the imperial edicts concerning appointments stopped.
At that time, Hóu Lǎn, a Zhōng Cháng Shì, had a younger brother, Cān, who was the Cìshǐ of Yìzhōu.
He had accumulated many crimes of corruption
and tyrannized the entire province.
The following year,
Bǐng impeached Cān,
who was then summoned in a cage-cart to the Tíng Wèi.
Cān, in fear,
committed suicide on the way.
Bǐng then impeached Lǎn and Zhōng Cháng Shì Jù Yuàn, saying:
"Your servant observes that according to the old state regulations,
the office of eunuchs
was originally to serve and attend in the palace,
to manage the closing and opening of doors and guard the night.
Yet now, they improperly receive excessive favor,
wielding political power.
Those who flatter them to gain favor
are then publicly recommended through them
to repay private kindness;
those who offend them
are certainly targeted with accusations
to unleash their fierce anger.
They imitate kings and dukes in their homes,
their wealth rivals that of the state.
Their food is of the finest delicacies,
their servants and concubines fill their silken quarters.
Even Jì Shì's usurpation in Lǔ
and Ráng Hóu's dominance in Qín,
how could they surpass this!
Regarding Zhōng Cháng Shì Hóu Lǎn's brother, Cān,
he was greedy, cruel, and a prime evildoer,
bringing ruin upon himself.
Lǎn, knowing the severity of his brother's crimes,
must surely harbor doubts about himself.
Your servant foolishly believes he should no longer be seen as a close confidant.
In ancient times, Duke Yì punished Bǐng Chù's father
and took Yán Zhí's wife,
yet he made both men serve in his carriage,
which eventually led to the disaster in Zhú Zhōng.
The Spring and Autumn Annals recorded this
as a supreme warning.
Indeed, when Zhèng Zhān came, the state was in chaos;
when the four villains were banished, the multitude was appeased.
Viewed in this light,
how can such a person be kept close?
Lǎn should be immediately banished
and cast to wolves and tigers.
Such a person
should not be pardoned by grace.
I request that he be dismissed from office and sent back to his home commandery."
When the memorial was submitted,
the Shàngshū summoned Bǐng's retainers and asked:
"The Gōng Fǔ holds an external office,
yet it impeaches close officials.
Is there any precedent in classical Han institutions?"
Bǐng's retainer replied:
"In the Spring and Autumn period, Zhào Yāng, with the troops of Jìnyáng,
drove away the wicked at the ruler's side.
The commentaries say: 'To eliminate the ruler's evil,
one acts according to one's strength.'
Dèng Tōng was lax and disrespectful;
Shēntú Jiā summoned Dèng Tōng and reprimanded him,
and Emperor Wén then pleaded on his behalf.
In the Han dynasty, according to historical precedents,
the Sān Gōng had jurisdiction over everything."
The Shàngshū could not refute this.
The emperor, having no choice,
eventually dismissed Lǎn from office
and reduced Yuàn's fief.
Whenever there were gains or losses in the court,
he would always offer loyal remonstrances,
and many were adopted.
Bǐng was by nature abstinent from alcohol,
and having lost his wife early,
he never remarried.
Wherever he served, he was known for his purity and integrity.
He once calmly said:
"I have three things I am not deluded by:
alcohol,
sex,
and wealth."
He passed away in the eighth year,
at the age of seventy-four.
He was granted a burial plot near the imperial mausoleum.
His son was Cì.
Cì, courtesy name Bóxiàn.
In his youth, he transmitted the family learning,
and was devoted to broad knowledge.
He often retired to live in seclusion,
teaching disciples,
and did not respond to invitations for official positions from provinces and commanderies.
Later, he was recruited to the household of Grand General Liáng Jì,
which was not to his liking.
He was appointed as the Magistrate of Chéncāng,
