but did not take up the post due to illness.
Summoned by gōngchē (imperial carriage), he did not arrive,
repeatedly declining the appointments of the Three Dukes.
Later, as a high-ranking official under the Sīkōng,
he was promoted twice to Shìzhōng and Yuèjì Xiàowèi.
At the beginning of Jiànníng,
when Emperor Líng was to receive instruction,
an edict ordered the Tàifù and the Three Dukes to select someone well-versed in the chapters and sentences of the Shàngshū by Huán Jūn, who had a long-standing distinguished reputation.
The Three Dukes recommended Cì,
and he then served as lecturer in the Huáguāng Diàn.
He was promoted to Shàofǔ and Guānglùxūn.
In the first year of Xīpíng,
when a green serpent was seen on the imperial seat,
the Emperor asked Cì about it.
Cì submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that harmonious qi brings auspiciousness,
and discordant qi brings disaster.
Auspicious omens are met with the Five Blessings,
and inauspicious omens are met with the Six Extremes.
Good fortune does not come groundlessly,
nor does disaster arise without cause.
When a king has something in his thoughts,
or something in his intentions,
though not yet expressed in his appearance,
the Five Planets shift because of it,
and yin and yang alter their regular course for it.
Viewing it thus,
how can Heaven and man
not correspond?
The Shàngshū says: 'Heaven is as one with man,
lending me a day.'
This is a clear proof.
If the imperial ultimate is not established,
then there will be calamities of snakes and dragons.
The Shī (Classic of Poetry) says: 'Both vipers and serpents
are omens concerning women.'
Therefore, in the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals), two serpents fought at the Zhèng Gate,
and Duke Zhāo was almost ruined by women;
King Kāng rose late one morning,
and the Guān Jū (ode) was composed upon observing the omen.
Indeed, if female influence prevails, slanderers prosper;
if slanderers prosper, bribery becomes rampant.
Therefore, Yīn Tāng used this to warn himself,
and ultimately overcame the disaster of severe drought.
May Your Majesty contemplate the Way of Heavenly Strength,
distinguish between internal and external proprieties,
uphold the system of Emperor Yǐ,
receive the blessings of the Supreme Good Fortune,
restrain the power of Huángfǔ,
and cut off affection for enchanting consorts.
Then the serpent omen can be dispelled,
and auspicious signs will immediately respond.
The affairs of Yīn Wù and Sòng Jǐng
are very clear."
[一一]
In the second year,
he replaced Táng Zhēn as Sīkōng,
but was dismissed due to calamities and strange phenomena.
He was again appointed Guānglù Dàfū,
with a stipend of two thousand shí.
In the fifth year,
he replaced Yuán Wěi as Sītú.
At this time, appointments and promotions in the court
were often not in due order,
and the Emperor enjoyed making incognito trips,
traveling to the outer imperial gardens.
Cì again submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that Heaven gave birth to the myriad people,
who could not govern themselves,
thus it established rulers and chiefs to shepherd them.
Therefore, Táng Yú were diligent and cautious,
and King Wén of Zhōu was busy day and night without leisure,
carefully selecting officials,
so that talented individuals were in office.
Performance was evaluated every three years,
to observe their achievements.
But now, those appointed and employed have no other virtue,
only influence.
They are repeatedly promoted within days,
while those who uphold integrity
remain unshifted for years.
Labor and ease are not distinguished,
good and evil flow together.
The poem 'Běi Shān'
was composed as a lesson for this.
Furthermore, I hear Your Majesty frequently makes incognito trips to the imperial gardens,
observing the displays of hawks and dogs,
indulging in extreme pleasure and aimless wandering.
Government affairs decline daily,
and great transformation is hindered.
Your Majesty disregards the diligent endeavors of the Two Ancestors,
and does not emulate the splendid examples of the Five Sovereigns.
Yet you wish for great peace.
This is like trying to straighten a shadow by bending the gnomon,
or walking backward and seeking to catch up with those ahead.
It is fitting to cease frivolous entertainments,
to remember the importance of selecting officials,
to cut off the favor of arbitrary appointments,
and to be cautious about the sequence of promotions,
so that ugly women do not lament 'four near-misses,'
and those near and far do not harbor sounds of resentment.
I have received exceptionally special grace,
and am undeservedly entrusted with the role of a mentor.
I dare not equate myself with ordinary officials,
to close my mouth and avoid blame.
Therefore, I respectfully hand-wrote this secret memorial."
Later, he was dismissed from his post for associating with members of the proscribed faction.
He was again appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū).
In the first year of Guānghé (光和) [178 CE],
a rainbow appeared in broad daylight in front of Jiādé Hall (Jiādé Diàn).
The emperor, disturbed by this,
summoned Cì (Cì) and Counselor Cài Yōng (Cài Yōng), among others, to the Chóngdé (Chóngdé) office within the Jīnshāng (Jīnshāng) Gate.
He ordered the Palace Regular Attendants Cáo Jié (Cáo Jié) and Wáng Fǔ (Wáng Fǔ) to question them about the auspicious or inauspicious meaning of the anomaly.
Cì (Cì) looked up at the sky and sighed,
saying to Jié (Jié) and the others:
“Every time I read the biography of Zhāng Yǔ (Zhāng Yǔ),
I am never without indignation and sighs.
He could neither exhaust his loyalty and feelings
to speak plainly about what was essential,
but instead focused on his younger son
and begged for the return of his son-in-law.
That Zhū Yóu (Zhū Yóu) wanted to obtain the imperial 'horse-slaying sword' to deal with him
was indeed appropriate.
I, with my meager learning,
fill the last ranks of my former teachers.
For generations I have received favor,
but have been unable to repay the country.
Now, I am impertinently facing a great inquiry,
and I shall not stop until I die.”
Then he wrote his reply, saying:
“Your servant has heard from the Classics and commentaries
that some obtain spiritual aid and prosper,
while others obtain spiritual aid and perish.
When the state is peaceful and enlightened,
it observes its virtue;
when it is perverse, chaotic, and benighted,
it observes its calamities.
Now, the aura in front of the palace,
manifesting as a rainbow,
is all born of evil and perversity,
an irregular omen,
what the poets called the ‘bow-worm’ (dīdōng).
In the Yìjīng's (Yìjīng) Zhōngfú (Zhōngfú) hexagram, it says: ‘The comparison to a rainbow,
is one who lacks virtue but seeks intimacy through beauty.’
At present, there are many favored sycophants within,
and incompetent petty officials are employed externally.
Both high and low are resentful,
and clamor fills the roads.
This is why disasters and anomalies are repeatedly seen,
with prior warnings clearly given.
Now a rainbow appears again;
it can be said to be severe indeed.
According to the Chūnqiū Chèn (Chūnqiū Chèn) [Spring and Autumn Annals Prophetic Text], it states: ‘When Heaven casts down a rainbow,
the world resents,
and the land within the seas is in chaos.’
Moreover, the four hundred year period [of the Hàn dynasty]
is also drawing near.
〔一０〕Formerly, when a rainbow pierced Niúshān (Niúshān),
Guǎn Zhòng (Guǎn Zhòng) advised Duke Huán (Huán Gōng) not to approach his concubines' quarters.
〔一一〕The Yìjīng (Yìjīng) says: ‘Heaven displays images,
revealing good and ill fortune; the sages take these as their guide.’
〔一二〕Now, concubines, favored individuals, eunuchs, and the like
together control the national court,
deceiving the emperor.
Moreover, beneath the Hóngdū (Hóngdū) Gate,
they gather groups of mean individuals,
fabricating prose and essays,
and gaining favor at the time with their minor skills of 'worm-script' (chóngzhuàn).
〔一三〕Like Huāndōu (Huāndōu) and Gònggōng (Gònggōng) who recommended each other,
〔一四〕within a month or so,
all were promoted.
Lè Sōng (Lè Sōng) held the position of Constant Attendant (chángbó),
and Rèn Zhī (Rèn Zhī) served as Master of Remonstrance (nàyán).
Xī Jiǎn (Xī Jiǎn) and Liáng Hú (Liáng Hú), both with their servile natures
and flattering eloquence,
each received abundant titles and unprecedented favors,
while gentlemen of integrity
are left to hide in the fields,
reciting the words of Yáo (Yáo) and Shùn (Shùn),
and embodying conduct that transcends the common world.
They are abandoned in ditches and gullies,
never sought out.
Caps and shoes are inverted,
mountains and valleys swap places.
〔一五〕Following the evil intentions of petty men,
and complying with the ignorant's private desires,
they do not remember the compositions of Bǎn (Bǎn) and Dàng (Dàng) [poems in the Shījīng criticizing corrupt officials],
or the warnings of the viper and lizard [referring to poisonous creatures/evil omens].
〔一六〕There has never been a danger
more perilous than today.
〔一七〕Fortunately, August Heaven has displayed omens to admonish us.
The Zhōu Shū (Zhōu Shū) states: ‘When the Son of Heaven sees an anomaly, he cultivates virtue;
when a feudal lord sees an anomaly, he cultivates governance;
when a high minister or grandee sees an anomaly, he cultivates his duties;
when a scholar or commoner sees an anomaly, he cultivates himself.’
May Your Majesty heed the warnings of the classics,
and plan the way to change and restoration.
〔一八〕Expel and distance sycophantic and cunning ministers,
and swiftly summon worthy scholars who 'cry like cranes' [i.e., live in seclusion].
Internally, be close to Zhāng Zhòng (Zhāng Zhòng) [referring to loyal ministers],
and externally, employ Shān Fǔ (Shān Fǔ) [referring to capable officials].
〔一九〕Cut off short messages [i.e., petty communications from favorites],
and stop aimless excursions.
Focus your thoughts on all matters of government,
and dare not be idle or neglectful.
May Heaven then restore its awe,
and all calamities can be averted.
This old servant has excessively received the responsibility of a tutor [shīfù],
and repeatedly enjoyed the grace of special favor.
How dare I cherish my declining years
and not exhaust my sincere heart!”
〔二０〕When the memorial was presented,
it greatly offended Cáo Jié (Cáo Jié) and the others.
Cài Yōng (Cài Yōng) was convicted for his direct criticism and exiled to Shuòfāng (Shuòfāng).
Cì (Cì), due to the favor shown to him as a tutor,
was spared punishment.
That winter,
during the Bìyōng (Bìyōng) ceremony,
Cì (Cì) was invited to serve as Sānlǎo (Sānlǎo).
He was again appointed Director of the Imperial Household (Shàofǔ) and Superintendent of the Imperial Household (Guānglù Xūn),
then replaced Liú Hé (Liú Hé) as Minister of Works (Sītú).
The emperor wished to build the Bìguī Língkūn Yuàn (Bìguī Língkūn Yuàn) garden.
Cì (Cì) again submitted a memorial in remonstrance, saying:
“I secretly hear that envoys have been dispatched
to survey and measure the fields of people south of the city,
intending to make them into a garden.
In ancient times, when the former kings established hunting parks,
they were just large enough for the 'three drives' ritual.
Firewood, fodder, and grazing
were all available there.
The system of the former emperors
opened the Hóngchí (Hóngchí) lake on the left
and built Shànglín (Shànglín) on the right,
neither extravagant nor frugal,
to accord with propriety.
Now, it is presumptuously planned
to take land in the city suburbs
for a garden,
destroying fertile land,
abandoning cultivated fields,
driving away residents,
and raising birds and beasts.
This is surely not
the meaning of 'protecting the infant.'
At present, there are already five or six imperial gardens outside the city,
which can satisfy desires
and align with the four seasons.
It is fitting to consider the modest palace of Yu (Yǔ) the Great
and the simple terrace of Tàizōng (Tàizōng),
to comfort the toiling common people.”
When the memorial was presented,
the emperor wished to stop,
and consulted with Palace Attendant Rèn Zhī (Rèn Zhī) and Palace Regular Attendant Lè Sōng (Lè Sōng).
Sōng (Sōng) and the others said:
“Of old, King Wén's (Wén Wáng) park was a hundred *lǐ* (lǐ),
and people thought it small;
King Xuān (Xuān) of Qí's (Qí) was five *lǐ* (lǐ),
and people thought it large.
If it is shared with the common people now,
it will not harm governance.”
The emperor was pleased
and proceeded to order the construction of the garden.
Four years later
Cì (Cì) was dismissed due to illness.
Not long after,
he was appointed Grand Protector (Tàicháng).
An edict bestowed upon Cì (Cì) a set of imperial robes,
along with the cap, headband, and ribbon he wore,
a jade vase, a leather belt,
and a gold-inlaid hook pendant.
In the winter of the fifth year,
he was again appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
In the first year of Zhōngpíng (Zhōngpíng) [184 CE],
when the Yellow Turban rebels rose,
Cì (Cì) was summoned to a meeting at the imperial secretariat,
where he gave sharp remonstrances that displeased the emperor.
Consequently, he was dismissed due to the bandits and rebels.
Formerly, the Yellow Turban chieftains Zhāng Jiǎo and others practiced heterodox ways,
claiming to be Great Sages
to deceive and mislead the common people.
People from all over the empire, carrying their children on their backs, flocked to them.
Cì was at that time the Sītú.
He summoned his clerk Liú Táo and said:
"Zhāng Jiǎo and his ilk, having been pardoned, show no remorse,
but rather are gradually spreading more.
If we now order the commanderies and districts to arrest and suppress them,
I fear it will cause further disturbance
and quickly exacerbate the problem.
I propose to strictly instruct the Cìshǐ and the Two-Thousand-Picul officials
to identify the displaced people
and escort each back to their native commandery,
thereby weakening their party.
Then, we can execute their leaders.
This way, we can pacify them without effort.
What do you think?"
Táo replied:
"This is what Sūnzi called 'subduing the enemy without fighting,'
a technique for victory in the ancestral temple."
Cì then submitted a memorial presenting this idea.
However, he was dismissed from his post,
and the matter remained in the imperial archives.
Later, the Emperor moved to the Nángōng,
reviewed old records,
and found Cì's memorial on Zhāng Jiǎo and the previous Imperial Lecturer's annotations.
He then understood and was enlightened,
issuing an edict to enfeoff Cì as Marquis of Línjìn,
with an estate of one thousand five hundred households.
Initially,
Cì, along with Tàiwèi Liú Kuān and Sīkōng Zhāng Jì,
had all served as Imperial Lecturers.
Feeling it was inappropriate for him alone to receive the enfeoffment and reward,
he submitted a memorial wishing to share the households and estate with Kuān and Jì.
The Emperor praised and sighed with admiration,
and again enfeoffed Kuān and Jì's son,
appointing Cì as Shàngshūlìng.
After several days, he was appointed Tíngwèi.
Cì, believing himself not to be a legal scholar,
said:
"The three queens achieved success,
only Yin relied on the people,
Gāoyáo was not involved.
This is probably out of reluctance."
He then firmly declined,
and retired to his residence as a Tèjìn.
In the ninth month of the second year,
he again replaced Zhāng Wēn as Sīkōng.
He passed away that month.
The Son of Heaven wore plain clothes,
did not hold court for three days,
and granted a coffin made of Catalpa wood from the Dōngyuán, funeral vestments,
three million coins,
and five hundred rolls of cloth.
The imperial decree stated:
"The late Sīkōng, Marquis of Línjìn, Cì,
was a man of distinguished talent like Huàshān,
with nine virtues perfectly complete.
For three generations, he served as prime minister,
assisting the state with loyalty.
When We first ascended the throne,
he imparted the Dao in Our private chambers,
thus leading Us to achieve great deeds
and ascend to the grand path.
His功 as a teacher and model
was manifest both within and without,
and his efforts in the duties of all officials
were also diligent and painstaking.
Seven times he served as a high official,
holding special posts and serving as Tèjìn.
Five times he ascended to the highest ministerial positions,
suppressing difficulties and bringing peace.
Though he received the feudal grant,
his merits have not yet been fully rewarded.
Now that this wise man has withered,
whom shall We consult and plan with!
We are deeply afraid.
Rituals establish different ranks,
and things have their attire and insignia.
We now order the Zuǒzhōnglángjiàng Guō Yí to hold the imperial insignia and posthumously grant him the rank of Tèjìn,
and posthumously bestow upon him the seal and sash of Sīkōng Píqíjīangjūn."
At the time of the funeral,
the Shìyùshǐ also held the imperial insignia to escort the funeral procession.
Ten Lántáilìshǐ dispatched feather-forest cavalry and light chariots with armored guards,
with drum and wind ensembles leading and following.
It was also ordered that the officials belonging to the Píqíjīangjūn and the Sīkōng's imperial carriage
escort the procession to the ancestral tomb.
The Gōngqīng and those below them attended the funeral.
His posthumous title was Wénlièhóu.
At the small anniversary of his death,
they again gathered.
His son Biāo succeeded him.
Biāo, courtesy name Wénxiān,
studied the family scholarship from a young age.
He was first nominated as Xiàolián,
then by the province as Màocái,
and invited to serve in the Duke's residence,
but he declined all of them.
During the Xīpíng era,
due to his extensive knowledge of ancient texts,
he was summoned by imperial carriage and appointed Yìláng,
then promoted to Shìzhōng and Jīngzhàoyǐn.
During the Guānghé era,
the Huángménlìng Wáng Fǔ had his disciples illegally corner and exploit government assets worth over seventy million.
Biāo exposed his misdeeds
and reported them to the Sīlì.
Sīlìxiàowèi Yáng Qiú then memorialized for Wáng Fǔ's execution,
and everyone in the empire was pleased.
He was recalled to serve as Shìzhōng and Wǔguānzhōnglángjiàng,
then promoted to Yǐngchuān and Nányáng Tàishǒu,
and again appointed Shìzhōng,
and three times promoted to Yǒnglèshǎofǔ, Tàipú, and Wèiwèi.
In the sixth year of Zhōngpíng,
he replaced Dǒng Zhuó as Sīkōng.
That winter,
he replaced Huáng Wǎn as Sītú.
The following year,
troops rose in Guāndōng.
Dǒng Zhuó was afraid
and wanted to move the capital to avoid this difficulty.
He then convened a grand assembly of high officials and discussed, saying:
“Gāozǔ established his capital in Guānzhōng for eleven generations.
Guāngwǔ resided in Luòyáng,
and it has also been ten generations until now.
According to Shí Bāo’s prophecy,
it is advisable to move the capital to Cháng’ān
to accord with the will of Heaven and man.”
None of the officials dared to speak.
Biāo said:
“Moving the capital and changing the system
is a matter of great importance to the empire.
Therefore, when Pán Gēng moved five times,
the people of Yīn all complained.
In the past, Guānzhōng suffered from Wáng Mǎng’s rebellion,
palaces were burned and destroyed,
and the common people were in dire straits;
barely one in a hundred survived.
When Guāngwǔ received the Mandate of Heaven,
he re-established the capital in Luòyì.
Today, the empire is at peace,
the common people are happy and secure.
Mínggōng has established a sagely ruler
and brought great glory to the Hàn dynasty’s mandate.
To abandon the ancestral temples
and forsake the imperial tombs without cause
will surely alarm the common people,
and there will inevitably be widespread chaos.
Shí Bāo’s chamber prophecy
is a book of demonic falsehoods;
how can it be trusted?”
Zhuó said:
“Guānzhōng is fertile and rich;
that is how Qín was able to conquer the six states.
Moreover, timber is readily available from Lǒngyòu,
and transport is very easy.
And below Dùlíng’s southern mountains, there are thousands of Wǔdì’s old tile kilns;
if we combine our efforts to build them,
it can be accomplished in a single day.
Why should we consult the common people?
If anyone hesitates,
I will drive them with a large army;
they can be made to go to the Canghai Sea!”
Biāo said:
“To stir up the empire is very easy,
but to bring it peace is very difficult.
I hope Mínggōng will consider this.”
Zhuó’s expression changed, and he said:
“Are you trying to thwart the national plan?”
Tàiwèi Huáng Wǎn said:
“This is a matter of great importance to the state;
should Yánggōng’s words not be considered?”
Zhuó did not respond.
Sīkōng Xún Shuǎng, seeing Zhuó’s resolute intent,
feared harm to Biāo and others.
He then spoke calmly, saying:
“Does Xiàngguó truly enjoy this?
The troops from Shāndōng have risen,
and they cannot be suppressed in a single day.
Therefore, we should relocate to plan our strategy;
this is the established practice of Qín and Hàn.”
Zhuó’s anger slightly subsided.
Shuǎng privately told Biāo:
“If you gentlemen insist on arguing without ceasing,
disaster will surely befall you.
That is why I did not do so.”
After the deliberation concluded,
Zhuó ordered Sīlì Xiàowèi Xuān Bō to impeach and dismiss Biāo and others based on omens of disaster.
They went to the palace gate to apologize
and were immediately appointed Guānglù Dàfū.
Ten-plus days later,
he was promoted to Dàhónglú.
He followed into the passes,
and was successively transferred to Shǎofǔ, then Tàicháng,
and was dismissed due to illness.
He was again appointed Jīngzhàoyǐn, then Guānglù Xūn,
and then again promoted to Guānglù Dàfū.
In the autumn of the third year,
he replaced Chúnyú Jiā as Sīkōng
and was dismissed due to an earthquake.
He was again appointed Tàicháng.
In the first year of Xīngpíng,
he replaced Zhū Jùn as Tàiwèi
and concurrently managed the affairs of the Shàngshū.
During the chaos of Lǐ Quē and Guō Sì,
Biāo devoted himself to protecting the emperor,
enduring hardships amidst danger,
and nearly escaping harm.
The details are in the biography of Dǒng Zhuó.
When the imperial carriage returned to Luòyáng,
he again served as Shàngshūlìng.
In the first year of Jiàn’ān,
he followed the emperor to the Eastern Capital, Xǔ.
At that time, the Son of Heaven had newly relocated,
and a grand assembly of high officials was held.
Cáo Cāo, the Cìshǐ of Yǎozhōu, ascended the hall
and, seeing Biāo’s displeased expression,
feared that he would be plotted against there.
Before the banquet could begin,
he feigned illness and went to the latrine,
then left and returned to his camp.
Biāo was dismissed due to illness.
At that time, Yuán Shù usurped power and caused chaos.
Cáo Cāo used Biāo’s marital ties with Yuán Shù as a pretext,
falsely accusing him of intending to depose and replace the emperor.
He submitted a memorial to have him arrested and imprisoned,
impeaching him for high treason.
Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng Kǒng Róng heard of this,
and without waiting to put on his court robes,
went to see Cáo Cāo and said:
“Yánggōng’s family has enjoyed four generations of pure virtue,
admired throughout the realm.
The Book of Zhōu states that sons and brothers are not to be held accountable for each other’s crimes,
much less to attribute Yuán Shì’s guilt to Yánggōng.
The Yì Jīng says, ‘Accumulated goodness brings abundant blessings’—
is that merely to deceive people?”
Cáo Cāo said:
“This is the will of the state.”
Kǒng Róng said:
“Even if King Chéng were to kill Shàogōng,
could the Duke of Zhōu claim ignorance?
Today, all the officials
look up to Mínggōng
because of your intelligence, benevolence, and wisdom,
assisting the Hàn court,
promoting the upright and correcting the wrong,
thereby achieving harmony and prosperity.
Now, if you wantonly kill the innocent,
then among those who observe and listen throughout the realm,
who will not lose heart?
Kǒng Róng is but a man from the state of Lǔ;
tomorrow I shall simply shake off my robes and leave,
never again to attend court!”
Cáo Cāo had no choice
but to order Biāo’s release.
In the fourth year,
he was again appointed Tàicháng,
and was dismissed in the tenth year.
In the eleventh year,
all who had been enfeoffed through imperial grace were stripped of their titles.
Biāo, seeing that the Hàn dynasty’s mandate was nearing its end,
then claimed a leg ailment and ceased to walk,
for ten years.
Later, his son Xiū was killed by Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo saw Biāo and asked:
“Why are you so thin, Gōng?”
He replied:
“I am ashamed that I do not possess the foresight of Jì Rìdī,
yet I still cherish the love of an old cow licking its calf.”
Cáo Cāo’s expression changed because of this.
Xiū, courtesy name Dézǔ,
was fond of learning
and possessed outstanding talent.
He served as the Zhǔbù to Chancellor Cáo Cāo,
and wielded influence within the Cáo clan.
When Cáo Cāo had pacified Hànzhōng
and wished to proceed to attack Liú Bèi but could not advance,
yet found it difficult to achieve success if he merely held his ground,
the Hùjūn did not know whether to advance or retreat.
Cáo Cāo then issued an order,
saying only
“chicken ribs.”
That was all.
The outer camp could not understand it,
but Xiū alone said:
“Chicken ribs—
eating them yields little,
but to discard them would be a pity.
The Chancellor’s plan to return is settled.”
He then ordered the outer sentries to gradually prepare for a retreat.
Cáo Cāo consequently withdrew his army.
Xiū’s decisive insight
was often of this nature.
Xiū also once went out,
and anticipating that Cáo Cāo would ask about outside affairs,
he prepared a memo of answers in advance
and instructed his servant:
“If an order is issued,
pass it on in sequence.”
It indeed happened as he predicted.
This occurred three times,
and Cáo Cāo, surprised by his speed,
had him investigated.
Upon learning the situation,
he began to be wary of Xiū.
Moreover, as Xiū was the nephew of Yuán Shù,
he feared future trouble,
and thus used an incident to kill him.
Xiū’s writings, including fù, sòng, bēi, zàn, shī, āicí, biǎo, jì, and shū, totaled fifteen pieces.
When Emperor Wén of Wèi (Wèi Wéndì) received the abdication,
he wished to appoint Yáng Biāo as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
First, he sent an envoy to express his intent.
Yáng Biāo declined, saying:
“I, Biāo, have served as one of the Three Ducal Ministers (Sān Gōng) of Hàn,
and during a time of upheaval and chaos,
I was unable to provide any assistance.
Now in my old age and afflicted by illness,
how can I assist a newly established court?”
So he firmly declined.
Instead, he was appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū),
and granted a desk, a staff, and robes.
During court assemblies, he was summoned for an audience,
and permitted to wear a plain cloth tunic and a deer-skin cap,
entering with a staff,
and treated with the courtesy due to a guest.
At the age of eighty-four,
he died at home in the sixth year of Huángchū (Huángchū liù nián).
From Yáng Zhèn to Yáng Biāo,
four generations held the position of Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
Their virtues and achievements were passed down,
and it is said that they, along with the Yuán clan, were a renowned family in the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng).
A commentary says: Confucius (Kǒngzǐ) stated,
“If one does not uphold when in danger,
nor support when falling,
then of what use will that assistant be?”
Indeed, the responsibility of bearing a heavy burden
cannot be undertaken lightly,
and a high position
carries grave concerns and profound duties.
During the period between Yánxī and Guānghé (Yán-Guāng zhī jiān),
Yáng Zhèn served as the prime minister (shàngxiàng),
standing firm and upright against corrupt power,
prioritizing public welfare over personal fame.
He can be said to have possessed the integrity of a royal minister (wángchén),
and understood the true nature of his responsibilities.
Thus, his descendants accumulated virtue through generations,
succeeding one another as prime ministers.
Truly, it is said,
“The family that accumulates good deeds
will surely have an abundance of blessings.”
Compared to the Wéi and Píng families of earlier times,
they were insignificant.
A eulogy says: The Yáng clan accumulated virtue,
for generations serving as pillars of the state (zhùguó).
Yáng Zhèn feared the "four knowings" (sì zhī),
and held to casting off the "three confusions" (sān huò).
Yáng Cì also concealed nothing,
Yáng Biāo was truly unwavering.
Though Yáng Xiū was talented,
he altered our pure principles.
Biography of the Eight Princes of Emperor Zhāng (Zhāngdì Bāwáng Zhuàn), Forty-Fifth Chapter.
Emperor Xiàozhāng (Xiàozhāng Huángdì) had eight sons: Consort Sòng (Sòng Guìrén) gave birth to Qīnghé Xiàowáng Qìng;
Consort Liáng (Liáng Guìrén) gave birth to Emperor Hé (Hé Dì);
Consort Shēn (Shēn Guìrén) gave birth to Jìběi Huìwáng Shòu;
Héjiān Xiàowáng Kāi;
the mothers of these four princes are not recorded.
Qiānchéng Zhēnwáng Kàng
was enfeoffed in the fourth year of Jiànchū (Jiànchū sì nián).
When Emperor Hé (Hé Dì) ascended the throne,
because Kàng was his eldest brother,
he was greatly honored and treated with deference.
He died after fifteen years on the throne.
His son Chǒng succeeded him,
also named Fúhú.
In the seventh year of Yǒngyuán (Yǒngyuán qī nián),
the state's name was changed to Luò'ān.
He died after twenty-eight years on the throne,
and was known as King Yí.
Both father and son died in the capital,
and were buried in Luòyáng.
His son Hóng succeeded him.
When Emperor Ān (Ān Dì) died,
Hóng first went to his state.
Hóng gave birth to Emperor Zhì (Zhì Dì).
When Emperor Zhì (Zhì Dì) was enthroned,
Empress Dowager Liáng (Liáng Tàihòu) issued an edict
stating that the land of the Luò'ān state was low and damp,
and its tax revenue meager;
so Hóng was re-enfeoffed as Bóhǎi Wáng.
He died after twenty-six years on the throne,
and was known as King Xiào.
He had no son.
The Empress Dowager (tàihòu) appointed Lǐwú Hóu Kuī, Emperor Huán’s (Huán Dì) younger brother, as Bóhǎi Wáng,
to offer sacrifices to Hóng.
In the eighth year of Yánxī (Yánxī bā nián),
Kuī plotted treason.
The officials requested that he be deposed.
The Emperor could not bear to,
and so demoted him to Yǐngtáo Wáng,
granting him one county as his fief.
Kuī later sought to have his state restored through the Central Regular Attendant (Zhōng Chángshì) Wáng Fǔ,
promising a bribe of fifty million cash.
As the Emperor was dying,
he left a will to restore Kuī as Bóhǎi Wáng.
Kuī knew it was not Wáng Fǔ’s (Fǔ) merit,
and refused to return the promised money.
Wáng Fǔ (Fǔ) was enraged,
and secretly sought out his faults.
Initially,
when Emperor Líng (Líng Dì) was brought to the throne,
rumors circulated that Kuī resented not being enthroned and wished to intercept the imperial decree.
Meanwhile, the Central Regular Attendant (Zhōng Chángshì) Zhèng Sà
and the Central Eunuch (Zhōng Huángmén) Dǒng Téng
were both chivalrous and frivolous,
and frequently interacted with Kuī.
Wáng Fǔ (Fǔ) investigated and
concluded that there was illicit activity.
He secretly reported this to the Colonel Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi) Duàn Jiǒng.
In the first year of Xīpíng (Xīpíng yuán nián),
Zhèng Sà (Sà) was arrested and sent to the North Temple Prison (Běisì Yù).
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng) Lián Zhōng was instructed to falsely accuse Zhèng Sà (Sà) and others of plotting to bring Kuī to the throne,
an act of great rebellion and unrighteousness.
An edict was then issued to the Inspector of Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu Cìshǐ) to arrest Kuī and investigate the facts.
Also, the Grand Minister of Dependencies (Dà Hónglú) was dispatched with an imperial staff, along with the Director of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng) and the Commandant of Justice (Tíngwèi), to Bóhǎi,
to pressure Kuī.
Kuī committed suicide.
His eleven concubines,
seventy children,
and twenty-four female performers
all died in prison.
His tutors and chancellors (fù, xiàng) and those below them
were all executed
for disloyalty in assisting and guiding the prince.
Kuī's state was abolished after twenty-five years.
The common people all pitied him.
Píngchūn Dàowáng Quán
was enfeoffed in the fourth year of Jiànchū (Jiànchū sì nián).
He died that same year,
and was buried in the capital.
He had no son,
and his state was abolished.
Qīnghé Xiàowáng Qìng,
whose mother was Consort Sòng (Sòng Guìrén).
Consort Sòng (Guìrén) was
an eighth-generation descendant of Sòng Chāng,
from Pínglíng in Fúfēng.
Her father, Yáng,
was known in his village for his reverence and filial piety,
and did not respond to calls from the commandery or province.
Yáng's aunt was the maternal grandmother of Empress Mǎ (Mǎ Hòu) of Illustrious Virtue (Míngdé).
Empress Mǎ (Mǎ Hòu) heard that Yáng's two daughters were both talented and beautiful,
so she welcomed them and had them trained.
Towards the end of Yǒngpíng (Yǒngpíng mò),
they were selected to enter the Crown Prince's palace (Tàizǐ Gōng),
and were greatly favored.
When Emperor Sù (Sù Zōng) ascended the throne,
both became Consorts (Guìrén).
In the third year of Jiànchū (Jiànchū sān nián),
the elder Consort (Dà Guìrén) gave birth to Qìng,
and the following year he was established as the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
Yáng was summoned to be a Gentleman Consultant (Yìláng),
and granted generous rewards.
Consort Sòng (Guìrén) was skilled in human affairs
and served at the Chánglè Palace (Chánglè Gōng),
personally preparing and serving meals,
which the Empress Dowager (tàihòu) pitied.
After the Empress Dowager (tàihòu) died,
Empress Dòu (Dòu Huánghòu) became greatly favored.
Because Consort Sòng’s (Guìrén) sisters were also favored,
and Qìng was the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ),
she secretly disliked them.
She conspired with her mother, Lady Bìyáng (Bìyáng Zhǔ), to frame the Sòng clan.
Externally, she ordered her brothers to seek out their minor faults;
internally, she had her attendants spy on their mistakes.
Later, at the Yètíng Gate (Yètíng Mén), she intercepted a letter from Consort Sòng (Guìrén),
which said,
“I am ill and crave a live rabbit,
so I have asked my family to find one.”
Empress Dòu (Dòu) then falsely accused her of wanting to practice witchcraft and curses,
using the rabbit as a charm to ward off evil.
With day and night slander,
Consort Sòng (Guìrén) and her son gradually fell out of favor.
Qìng moved out to live in the Chénglù Guān.
Several months later,
Empress Dòu (竇后) subtly influenced the Director of the Yètíng (掖庭令) to falsely impeach him concerning the previous matters,
requesting a thorough verification.
In the seventh year,
the emperor (帝) therefore deposed Crown Prince Qìng (慶) and established Imperial Crown Prince Zhā (ザ).
Zhā
was the son of Consort Liáng (梁貴人).
An imperial edict was then issued, stating:
"The Imperial Crown Prince possesses a character that is lost and unpredictable.
From infancy
to the present, this has become increasingly evident.
Fearing he might inherit the vicious temperament of his mother,
he is unfit to serve the ancestral temple
and be the lord of all under heaven.
Great righteousness may necessitate destroying kinship,
how much more so demotion!
Therefore, Qìng is now deposed as the Prince of Qīnghé (清河王).
Imperial Prince Zhā, fostered by the empress (皇后),
receiving instruction from her bosom,
has developed a good nature,
and will become a capable vessel.
Indeed, between a concubine's son and a kind mother,
there can still be lifelong affection;
how could this compare to the rectitude and clarity between a principal empress and her charge!
Therefore, Zhā is now made the Imperial Crown Prince."
The sisters of the consort were then sent out and placed in the Bǐngshè (丙舍).
The lesser eunuch Cài Lún (蔡倫) was ordered to investigate the matter thoroughly;
all were induced to fabricate their stories according to the subtle imperial directive,
and they were then transported to the Bàoshì (暴室).
The two consorts simultaneously drank poison and committed suicide.
The emperor (帝) still grieved for them
and ordered the Director of the Yètíng (掖庭令) to bury them in Fánzhuójù (樊濯聚).
Thereupon, Yáng (楊) was dismissed and returned to her home commandery.
The commandery and county authorities then seized and imprisoned her again based on the incident.
Yáng's (楊) friends, including Zhāng Jùn (張峻) of Shānyáng (山陽), former magistrate of Huái (懷), and Liú Jūn (劉均) of Pèiguó (沛國), Left Fēngyì (左馮翊), rushed to her defense and intervened,
enabling her to be acquitted.
Yáng (楊), disheartened and gaunt,
died at home.
Though Qìng (慶) was young at the time,
he knew to avoid suspicion and fear misfortune,
daring not to mention the Sòng (宋) family.
The emperor (帝) pitied him even more
and ordered the empress (皇后) to ensure his clothing was equal to that of the crown prince (太子).
The crown prince (太子) was especially fond of Qìng (慶);
when inside, they shared a room,
and when outside, they rode in the same carriage.
When the crown prince (太子) ascended the throne,
known as Emperor Hé (和帝),
he treated Qìng (慶) with even greater generosity,
surpassing all other princes.
They often discussed private matters together.
Later, as Qìng (慶) grew older,
he moved to live separately in the Bǐngshè (丙舍).
In the fourth year of Yǒngyuán (永元),
the emperor (帝) moved to the Zhāngdé Diàn (章德殿) in the Northern Palace
and lectured at the Báihǔ Guān (白虎觀).
Qìng (慶) was allowed to enter and stay overnight.
When the emperor (帝) was about to punish the Dòu (竇) family,
he wanted to obtain records of the imperial relatives.
Fearing his attendants would not dare to retrieve them,
he ordered Qìng (慶) to secretly ask the Prince of Qiānchéng (千乘王) for them,
and to bring them in alone at night.
He also ordered Qìng (慶) to relay a message to the Palace Regular Attendant Zhèng Zhòng (鄭衆) to seek out historical precedents.
After General-in-Chief Dòu Xiàn (竇憲) was executed,
Qìng (慶) moved to live in a mansion,
and was granted three hundred slaves,
carriages, horses, money, silk, curtains, precious jewels, and cherished playthings, filling his residence.
He also bestowed money and silk, varying in amounts, to his Grand Tutor (中傅) and all below him, down to his left and right attendants.
Qìng (慶) often suffered from illness,
and sometimes felt unwell.
The emperor (帝) inquired about his health morning and evening,
providing food and medicine,
showing exceptionally comprehensive concern.
Qìng (慶) was cautious and respectfully filial.
Considering his deposition,
he was particularly fearful of trouble and careful with laws.
Each time he paid respects at the imperial mausoleum and ancestral temple,
he would prepare his attire rigorously in the middle of the night,
waiting in his official robes and cap until dawn.
He strictly ordered his officials
not to compete with the carriages of other princes.
He constantly felt regret over the deficiencies in his consort mother's funeral rites,
and often harbored secret resentment.
During the four seasonal festivals and the Làyin (伏臘) sacrifices,
he would always offer sacrifices in his private chamber.
After the Dòu (竇) family was punished,
he first allowed his wet nurse to offer remote sacrifices from north of the city.
When Empress Dowager Dòu (竇太后) passed away,
Qìng (慶) requested to visit her tomb to express his grief.
The emperor (帝) permitted it
and ordered the Grand Provisioner (太官) to provide sacrificial items for the four seasons.
Qìng (慶) shed tears and said:
"Though I could not provide for her during her life,
I can finally offer sacrifices,
and my private wish is fulfilled."
He wanted to build a shrine,
but feared the suspicion of equating himself with the respectful and gentle Empress Liáng (恭懷梁后),
so he dared not speak of it.
He often wept to his attendants,
considering it a lifelong regret.
Later, he memorialized that his maternal grandmother Wáng (王) was old
and suffering from illness due to grief,
with no medicine in her remote area.
He wished to request her to come to Luòyáng (洛陽) for treatment.
Thereupon, an edict ordered the Sòng (宋) family to all return to the capital.
Qìng's (慶) maternal uncles Yǎn (衍), Jùn (俊), Gài (蓋), Xiān (暹), and others were all made Láng (郎).
In the fifteenth year,
officials, citing the solar eclipse as a sign of excessive Yin (陰盛),
memorialized to send the princes and marquises to their feudal states.
An edict stated:
"The anomaly of Jiǎzǐ (甲子)
is a responsibility resting on one person.
The princes are young,
having left their parents early.
They have nurtured each other since coming of age,
always with the sorrow of 'Liáoé' (蓼莪) and 'Kǎifēng' (凱風).
This partiality and kindness,
I know, is not according to state regulations,
but they must still remain."
By winter,
when accompanying the sacrifices at Zhāng Líng (章陵),
an edict granted each prince forty Yǔlín (羽林) cavalry.
Later, the Grand Tutor (中傅) Wèi Xīn (衞訢) privately embezzled over ten million.
An edict ordered an investigation
and also reprimanded Qìng (慶) for not reporting it.
Qìng (慶) said:
"Xīn (訢), with the esteemed position of a teacher,
was selected by Your Sacred Court.
I, your foolish servant, only knew to follow his words and obey his commands,
and did not extensively investigate him."
The emperor (帝) praised his reply
and bestowed all of Xīn's (訢) ill-gotten wealth upon Qìng (慶).
When the emperor (帝) passed away,
Qìng (慶) wept bitterly in the front hall,
vomiting several liters of blood,
which then caused him to fall ill.
The following year,
the princes went to their feudal states.
Empress Dowager Dèng (鄧太后) specifically allowed the Prince of Qīnghé (清河王) to appoint a Grand Commandant (中尉) and a Grand Administrator (內史),
and bestowed various items, all taken from the emperor's personal use.
Sòng Yǎn (宋衍) and others were all made Grand Masters of Qīnghé (清河中大夫).
When Qìng (慶) arrived in his state,
he issued an order:
"I, the lonely one, was born in the deep palace
and grew up in the court,
relying on the enlightened sovereign
to achieve all without effort.
Due to my meager fortune,
I was separated from my parents early.
Now, encountering great sorrow,
my heart is filled with grief and emotion.
Having received the grace of a great state,
my duty is merely to assist the imperial family.
Having just left the capital,
my heart is filled with solitary worry,
striving day and night,
unsure of what to establish.
Indeed, I have heard that wisdom does not govern alone,
but must rely on the wise and virtuous.
Now, my officials all hold important positions,
and both successes and failures are shared.
I sincerely hope you will uphold the imperial decrees and admonitions,
and avoid remorse and blame below.
You must scrutinize and correct injustices,
clearly observe regulations and prohibitions,
and prevent me, the solitary one, from incurring the sin of negligence."
Empress Dowager Dèng (鄧太后), considering the infant Emperor Shāng (殤帝)
and fearing unforeseen circumstances,
kept Qìng's (慶) eldest son, Yòu (祐), and his legal mother, Gěng Jī (耿姬), to live in the Qīnghé mansion.
By autumn,
the emperor (帝) passed away,
and Yòu (祐) was established as the successor,
known as Emperor Ān (安帝).
The empress dowager (太后) sent a Central Yellow Gate (中黃門) to send Gěng Jī (耿姬) back to her state.
The emperor's (帝) birth mother was Zǔo Jī (左姬),
courtesy name Xiǎo'é (小娥).
Her elder sister's courtesy name was Dà'é (大娥).
They were from Jiànwéi (犍為).
Initially,
their paternal uncle Shèng (聖) was executed for making seditious prophecies,
and their family property was confiscated.
The two sisters entered the Yètíng (掖庭) when they were several years old.
As they grew up,
both possessed talent and beauty.
Xiǎo'é (小娥) was skilled in historical writings and enjoyed prose and poetry.
Emperor Hé (和帝) bestowed palace women upon the princes,
and thus she entered the Qīnghé mansion.
Qìng (慶) first heard of her beauty,
and rewarded her wet nurse to obtain her.
Later, his favor and affection for her reached their peak,
unrivaled by his other concubines.
The sisters all died
and were buried in the capital.
Qìng stood for twenty-five years,
then returned to his state.
That year, he fell gravely ill,
and said to Sòng Yǎn and others:
"Qīnghé is meager and thin.
I wish to beg for my bones to be buried next to the tomb of a noble person, merely for the coffin to be lowered.
The great benevolence of the court
should still provide a memorial hall,
so that mother and son can eat together,
and our souls have something to rely on and shelter in.
What regret would there be in death?"
Then he submitted a memorial to the Empress Dowager, saying:
"Your servant's homeland is low and damp;
I wish to beg for my bones
to be laid next to the noble person in Fán Zhuó.
Though deceased, I will not decay.
Now, while my mouth and eyes can still speak and see,
I presumptuously make this request.
My life hangs by a thread;
I beg for your pity and compassion."
Soon after, he passed away,
at the age of twenty-nine.
The Sīkōng was dispatched, bearing a staff of authority, along with the Zōngzhèng, to offer condolences and sacrifices.
Also, the Chánglè Yèzhě Púshè and two Zhōng Yèzhě were sent to assist in guarding the funeral arrangements.
He was granted a dragon banner with nine streamers,
and a hundred Hǔbēn,
with rites comparable to those of Dōnghǎi Gōng Wáng.
The Empress Dowager ordered a Yètíng Chéng to escort Zǔo Jī's coffin,
and she was interred with the king in Guǎngqiū.
His son Mǐn Wáng Hǔwēi succeeded him.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
the Empress Dowager enfeoffed Sòng Yǎn as Shèngxiāng Hóu.
Qīnghé was divided into two states,
and Qìng's younger son Chángbǎo was enfeoffed as Guǎngchuān Wáng.
His eleven daughters were all made Xiāng Gōngzhǔ,
with stipends and territories.
The following year,
Chángbǎo passed away
without sons,
and the state was abolished.
Hǔwēi ruled for three years and passed away,
also without sons.
Empress Dowager Dèng re-established Lè'ān Wáng Chǒng's son Yánpíng as Qīnghé Wáng,
who became Gōng Wáng.
When the Empress Dowager passed away,
the relevant officials memorialized, saying:
"Qīnghé Xiào Wáng, with his utmost virtue and pure essence,
nurtured the sagely emperor
who received the Mandate of Heaven and upheld the imperial succession,
serving as the master of the suburban altars and ancestral temples.
Since the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
Gāo Huángdì honored his father as Tàishàng Huáng,
and Xuān Dì referred to his father as Huángkǎo,
arranging the generations
and establishing ancestral estates.
The principle of [Dà]zōng
must not forget the old precedents.
It is fitting to bestow upon him the honorable title of Xiàodé Huáng,
his empress mother, Zǔo Shì, as Xiàodé Hòu,
and Xiàodé Huáng's mother, Sòng Guìrén, be posthumously titled Jìngyǐn Hòu."
Accordingly, a notification and sacrifice were made at the Gāo Miào,
and the Sītú, bearing a staff of authority, along with the Dà Hónglú, were sent with a written decree and seal cords to Qīnghé,
to posthumously bestow the honorable titles.
Furthermore, a Zhōng Chángshì was dispatched to offer the Grand Sacrifice,
and the Hùlǐyí Shìzhōng Líu Zhēn and others, as well as members of the imperial clan and various marquises, all attended the ceremony.
His mausoleum was honored as Gānlíng,
his temple as Zhāomiào,
and a令 and a丞 were appointed,
with armed chariots for protection and perimeter defense,
comparable to Chānglíng.
Guǎngchuān was again incorporated into the Qīnghé state.
Gěng Jī was honored as Gānlíng Dà Guìrén.
Also, his younger sister Shìnán was enfeoffed as Nèiyáng Cháng Gōngzhǔ,
Biéde as Wǔyīn Cháng Gōngzhǔ,
Jǐucháng as Púyáng Cháng Gōngzhǔ,
and Zhídé as Píngshì Cháng Gōngzhǔ.
The other seven princesses all died young,
and thus could not have their ranks advanced.
Posthumous gifts of seals and ribbons were given to Jìngyǐn Hòu's younger sister Xiǎo Guìrén,
and Sòng Yáng was posthumously enfeoffed and titled Dāngyáng Mù Hóu.
Yáng's four sons were all made marquises,
each with a stipend of five thousand households.
More than ten members of the Sòng clan served as ministers, commanders, palace attendants, grand masters, imperial attendants, and palace scribes.
Xiàodé Hòu's two half-brothers, Cì and Dáshēng,
and her nine nephews,
all served as Lángzhōng in the Qīnghé state.
Gěng Guìrén was
the granddaughter of Móupíng Hóu Shū.
Guìrén's elder brother, Bǎo,
inherited the title of Móupíng Hóu.
Because the Emperor considered Bǎo his legitimate maternal uncle,
he was treated with exceptional favor and affection,
and his position reached that of Dà Jiàngjūn.
His deeds are already recorded in the biography of Gěng Shū.
[Yánpíng] ruled for thirty-five years and passed away.
His son Suàn succeeded him.
When Chōng Dì passed away,
Suàn was summoned to the capital
to discuss his succession.
At that time, Dà Jiàngjūn Liáng Jì and Empress Dowager Liáng established Zhì Dì,
and Suàn was dismissed and returned to his state.
Suàn was a person of serious demeanor,
whose every action was measured,
and among the court officials, including Tàiwèi Lí Gù, none did not hold him in high regard.
Initially,
Zhōng Chángshì Cáo Téng paid a visit to Suàn,
but Suàn did not treat him with proper courtesy,
and the eunuchs consequently bore ill will towards him.
When the emperor passed away,
all the high officials publicly advocated for establishing Suàn,
but Cáo Téng persuaded Liáng Jì not to agree,
and consequently, Huán Dì was established.
The details are found in Lí Gù's biography.
Suàn thus incurred disfavor.
In the first year of Jiànhé,
Líu Wén from Gānlíng colluded with the demonic bandit Líu Wěi from Nánjùn,
spreading rumors that the King of Qīnghé was to rule as Son of Heaven,
intending to collectively enthrone Suàn.
When the matter was discovered,
Wén and others kidnapped Xiè Hào, the Administrator of Qīnghé,
and brought him to the Sīmǎ Mén of the royal palace,
saying:
"We shall enthrone the King as Son of Heaven,
and Hào as Duke."
Hào refused,
cursing them,
whereupon Wén stabbed and killed Hào.
Consequently, Wén and Wěi were apprehended and executed.
The relevant officials then impeached Suàn,
who was demoted to Wèishì Hóu,
exiled to Guìyáng,
and committed suicide.
After three years of his rule,
the state was abolished.
Liáng Jì disliked the name Qīnghé,
so the following year,
he changed it to Gānlíng.
Empress Dowager Liáng established Ānpíng Xiào Wáng Jīng Hóu Lí as Gānlíng Wáng,
to maintain the sacrifices to Xiàodé Huáng,
who became Wēi Wáng.
Lí ruled for twenty-five years and passed away.
His son Zhēn Wáng Dìng succeeded him.
Dìng ruled for four years and passed away.
His son Xiàn Wáng Zhōng succeeded him.
When the Yellow Turban rebellion broke out,
Zhōng was captured by the people of his state,
but was later released.
Líng Dì, out of familial affection,
decreed the restoration of Zhōng's state.
Zhōng ruled for thirteen years and passed away.
His heir was killed by the Yellow Turbans.
In the eleventh year of Jiàn'ān,
due to having no heir,
the state was abolished.
Jìběi Huì Wáng Shòu,
whose mother was Shēn Guìrén,
was from Yǐngchuān,
and her family had served as officials receiving two thousand dàn of grain for generations.
Guìrén entered the Yètíng at the age of thirteen.
Shòu was enfeoffed in the second year of Yǒngyuán,
and Tàishān Commandery was divided to form his state.
Hé Dì followed the precedents of Sù Zōng,
keeping all his brothers in the capital,
and showing them deep favor and affection.
When officials requested that the various kings be sent to their fiefs,
he could not bear to allow it.
It was only when the emperor passed away
that they proceeded to their states.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng enfeoffed Shòu's maternal uncle, Shēn Zhuǎn, as Xīntíng Hóu.
Shòu ruled for thirty-one years and passed away.
From Yǒngchū onwards,
due to rebellions by the Róng and Dí,
the state's resources were insufficient.
When a newly enfeoffed king died,
the funeral money was reduced to ten million [cash],
and ten thousand bolts of cloth.
When a successor king died,
it was five million [cash],
and five thousand bolts of cloth.
At that time, Shòu was the most revered and closely related,
so he was specially granted thirty million [cash] in funeral money,
and thirty thousand bolts of cloth.
His son Jié Wáng Dēng succeeded him.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
Dēng's five younger brothers were enfeoffed as Xiāng Hóu,
each separately receiving a stipend from the Tàishān district.
Dēng ruled for fifteen years and passed away.
His son Āi Wáng Duō succeeded him.
Duō ruled for three years and passed away,
without sons.
In the fourth year of Yǒnghé,
Zhànxiāng Hóu Ānguó was established as Jìběi Wáng,
who became Lí Wáng.
Ān-guó-lì ((ten)) [seven] years, passed away.
His son, Xiào-wáng Cì, succeeded.
In the first year of Běnchū,
Cì's younger brother, Měng, was enfeoffed as Tíng-hóu.
Cì lost his father at the age of nine
and was extremely filial.
In the first year of Jiànhé,
Empress Dowager Liáng issued an edict saying:
"Jìběi-wáng Cì, though young, has presided over his fief,
personally practiced filial piety,
mourned his father with profound grief,
and withered away beyond the customary rites.
He has lived in a straw hut with an earthen mat,
wearing sackcloth and relying on a staff,
his head uncombed and unwashed,
his body covered in sores and swellings.
Twenty-eight months have passed since his period of deep mourning,
and among all the states facing such sorrow,
none have been heard to act in this manner.
The imperial court greatly commends this.
Does not the Shū-jīng say: 'By virtue, his goodness is displayed.'
And the Shī-jīng says: 'A filial son is inexhaustible;
forever will his kind be bestowed.'
Now, Cì's fief is increased by five thousand households,
expanding his territory,
to comfort the toils of this compassionate filial son."
Cì ruled for [ten] seventeen years and passed away.
His son Luán succeeded.
When Luán passed away,
his son Zhèng succeeded.
When Zhèng passed away,
he had no son.
In the eleventh year of Jiàn'ān,
the state was abolished.
Héjiān Xiào-wáng Kāi,
was enfeoffed in the second year of Yǒngyuán.
Lèchéng, Bóhǎi, and Zhuójùn were partitioned to form his state.
In the first year of Yánpíng, he went to his state.
Kāi diligently followed the laws and regulations,
and the officials and people respected him.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
Empress Dowager Dèng enfeoffed Kāi's son Yì as Píngyuán-wáng,
to oversee the ancestral sacrifices of Huái-wáng Shèng;
and his son Dé as Ānpíng-wáng,
to oversee the ancestral sacrifices of Lèchéng-wáng Dǎng.
Kāi ruled for forty-two years and passed away.
His son, Huì-wáng Zhèng, succeeded.
Zhèng was obstinate
and did not obey the laws and statutes.
Emperor Shùn, noting that Shěn Jǐng of Wú-jùn, a Palace Attendant Censor, was praised for his strong capabilities,
thus promoted him to Minister of Héjiān.
When Jǐng arrived at the state and sought an audience with the king,
the king was not dressed properly and
sat sprawled on the palace hall.
The court attendants announced the ritual bows,
but Jǐng stood still and did not perform the rites.
He asked where the king was.
The Royal Guard said:
"Is this not the king?"
Jǐng said:
"If the king is not properly dressed,
how is he different from a common person!
I am here to meet the king,
not to meet someone who is without礼!"
The king was ashamed and changed his clothes,
after which Jǐng bowed.
He then went out and stood outside the palace gate,
and summoned the King's Grand Tutor to rebuke him, saying:
"When I departed from the capital,
Your Majesty personally received the imperial edict,
stating that the king was disrespectful, and thus ordered me to supervise him.
You gentlemen receive your noble ranks and salaries in vain,
without any duty of instruction and guidance."
He then submitted a memorial to punish them.
The imperial edict admonished Zhèng and reprimanded the Grand Tutor.
Jǐng then arrested various villains, investigated their crimes,
executed dozens of the most wicked,
and released over a hundred people from wrongful imprisonment.
Zhèng subsequently reformed his conduct
and repented his faults, cultivating himself.
In the first year of Yángjiā,
Zhèng's thirteen younger brothers were all enfeoffed as Tíng-hóu.
Zhèng ruled for ten years and passed away.
His son, Zhēn-wáng Jiàn, succeeded.
Jiàn ruled for ten years and passed away.
His son, Ān-wáng Lì, succeeded.
Lì ruled for twenty-eight years and passed away.
His son, Gāi, succeeded.
Gāi ruled for forty-one years.
When the Wei dynasty received the abdication,
he was made Chóngdé-hóu.
Lǐwú-hóu Yì,
in the sixth year of Yuánchū, Empress Dowager Dèng summoned the sons of the Kings of Jìběi and Héjiān to the capital.
She found Yì to have a remarkably beautiful appearance,
and thus made him the successor of Píngyuán Huái-wáng.
He remained in the capital.
A little over a year later,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
Emperor Ān's wet nurse, Wáng Shèng, along with the Eunuch Attendant Jiāng Jīng and others, slandered Dèng Zhì's brothers and Yì,
claiming they plotted disloyalty with the Grand Master Zhào Wáng,
coveting the imperial throne
and harboring great treasonous intentions.
Yì was demoted to Dūxiāng-hóu
and sent back to Héjiān.
Yì then dismissed his guests
and lived in seclusion behind closed doors.
In the fifth year of Yǒngjiàn,
his father, Kāi, submitted a memorial,
requesting to partition Lǐwú County to enfeoff Yì,
and Emperor Shùn agreed.
Yì died,
and his son Zhì succeeded,
who was established by Grand General Liáng Jì,
becoming Emperor Huán.
Empress Dowager Liáng issued an edict to posthumously honor Héjiān Xiào-wáng as Xiàomù Huáng,
and his wife Lady Zhào as Xiàomù Hòu.
Their temple was named Qīng-miào,
and their mausoleum was named Lèchéng-líng.
The former Marquis of Lǐwú was honored as Xiàochóng Huáng,
his temple named Liè-miào,
and his mausoleum named Bólíng.
Both were provided with Administrators (lìng) and Assistant Administrators (chéng),
and the Grand Minister of Works (Sītú) was dispatched with an imperial credential to present the imperial rescript and seals,
offering sacrifices with a grand animal (tài-láo).
In the second year of Jiànhé,
Emperor's ((elder brother)) [younger brother] Dūxiāng-hóu Shuò was re-enfeoffed as Píngyuán-wáng,
remaining in Bólíng,
to oversee Yì's ancestral sacrifices.
Yì's wife Lady Mǎ was honored as Xiàochóng Bóyuán Guìrén,
and the three counties of Liángxiāng and Gù'ān in Zhuójùn,
and Lǐwú in Héjiān, were designated as her bath and food tax fiefs (tāngmù-yì).
Shuò was fond of alcohol
and committed many transgressions.
The Emperor ordered Lady Mǎ Guìrén to manage the affairs of the king's household.
In the eleventh year of Jiàn'ān,
the state was abolished.
Jiědú Tíng-hóu Shú,
was enfeoffed as the son of Héjiān Xiào-wáng.
When Shú died,
his son ((Cháng)) [Cháng] succeeded.
When ((Cháng)) [Cháng] died,
his son Hóng succeeded,
who was established by Grand General Dòu Wǔ,
becoming Emperor Líng.
In the first year of Jiànníng,
Empress Dowager Dòu issued an edict to posthumously honor her imperial ancestor Shú as Xiàoyuán Huáng,
and his wife Lady Xià as Xiàoyuán Hòu.
Their mausoleum was named Dūnlíng,
and their temple was named Jìng-miào.
Her imperial father Cháng was honored as Xiàorén Huáng,
and his wife Lady Dǒng as Shènyuán Guìrén.
Their mausoleum was named Shènlíng,
and their temple was named Huàn-miào.
Both were provided with Administrators (lìng) and Assistant Administrators (chéng).
The Grand Minister of Works (Sītú) was dispatched with an imperial credential to Héjiān to present the imperial rescript and seals,
offering sacrifices with a grand animal (tài-láo).
Regularly, at the turn of the seasons, a Eunuch Attendant was dispatched with an imperial credential to Héjiān to perform sacrifices.
In the third year of Xīpíng,
an envoy was sent to appoint Kāng, the son of Héjiān Ān-wáng Lì, as Jìnán-wáng,
to oversee the ancestral sacrifices of Xiàorén Huáng.
When Kāng passed away,
his son Yūn succeeded.
In the twelfth year of Jiàn'ān,
he was killed by the Yellow Turban bandits.
His son Kāi succeeded.
After ruling for thirteen years,
when the Wei dynasty received the abdication,
he was made Chóngdé-hóu.
Chéngyáng Huái-wáng Shú,
was enfeoffed in the second year of Yǒngyuán, with Jìyīn partitioned to form his state.
He ruled for five years and passed away,
buried in the capital.
He had no son,
so the state was abolished,
and Jìyīn was rejoined.
Guǎngzōng Shāng-wáng Wànsùi,
was enfeoffed in the fifth year of Yǒngyuán,
with Jùlù partitioned to form his state.
He passed away in the same year,
buried in the capital.
He had no son,
so the state was abolished,
and Jùlù was rejoined.
Píngyuán Huái-wáng Shèng,
was the eldest son of Emperor Hé.
His mother's clan is not recorded.
He suffered from a chronic illness in his youth.
He was enfeoffed in the first year of Yánpíng.
He ruled for eight years and passed away,
buried in the capital.
He had no son,
so Empress Dowager Dèng established Dé, the son of Lè'ān Yí-wáng Chǒng, as Píngyuán-wáng,
to oversee Shèng's ancestral sacrifices,
thus he became Āi-wáng.
Dé Lì reigned for six years and then passed away.
He had no sons.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
the Empress Dowager again enthroned Yì, Marquis of Dūxiāng and son of Kāi, Prince of Héjiān, as the heir to the Prince of Píngyuán.
Emperor Ān deposed him,
and the princedom was abolished.
The eulogy states: The tradition records that Wú Zǐ Yímèi
was deeply virtuous and magnanimous,
and that those who possessed the state of Wú
must be his descendants.
Emperor Zhāng, as an elder,
acted with generosity and sincerity.
Those who continued the sacrifices to the Hàn imperial house
were all his descendants.
How true are the words of the ancients!
The encomium says: Zhāng's blessings continue without end,
and the main lineage flows with grace.
Zhì was an eminent grandson,
and Ān was also a blessed son.
Héjiān had abundant fortune;
Huán and Líng succeeded to the sacrifices.
Jìběi was without arrogance,
and the imperial favor was ample.
Píngyuán suffered from chronic illness;
three princes passed away in court.
The numerous descendants,
some flourished like flowers, some like sprouts.
Biography of Zhāng, Wáng, Zhǒng, Chén, Liezhuan 46
Zhāng Hào, courtesy name Shūmíng,
was from Wǔyáng, Jiànwéi.
His sixth-generation ancestor, Liáng,
served as Tutor to the Crown Prince during Emperor Gāo's reign,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Liú.
Hào studied in the capital when young.
In the Yǒngyuán era,
he returned to serve in the commanderies and prefectures,
and was appointed to the staff of Grand General Dèng Zhì.
He was promoted five times to Shàngshū Púyè,
holding the position for eight years,
before being sent out as Chancellor of Péngchéng.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
he was summoned and appointed Tíngwèi.
Although Hào was not a legal expert,
he devoted himself to criminal judgments,
often debating and correcting difficult cases with the Shàngshū,
and his detailed and appropriate opinions were often adopted.
At that time, Emperor Ān deposed the Crown Prince, making him Prince of Jìyīn.
Hào, along with Tàicháng Huán Yān and Tàipú Lái Lì, argued against it in court,
but could not succeed.
The matter is fully detailed in Lái Lì's biography.
Afterwards, he submitted a memorial which stated:
"In the past, the traitorous minister Jiāng Chōng
fabricated slander and rebellion,
which led to Lì Yuán raising troops,
ultimately resulting in disaster and calamity.
Later, a single word from the three elders of Húguān
awakened the Emperor,
but though he regretted his past mistakes,
how could it be timely then!
Now the Crown Prince is just beginning his tenth year;
he has not yet seen the meaning of the nine virtues from his 保傅 (Bǎofù, protectors and tutors).
It is fitting to select worthy assistants
to perfect his sacred nature."
The memorial was submitted but not heeded.
When Emperor Shùn ascended the throne,
Hào was appointed Sīkōng.
During his tenure, he recommended and promoted many individuals,
and the empire praised his promotion of scholars.
At that time, Zhào Téng of Qīnghé submitted a memorial on natural disasters,
satirizing the imperial court.
The memorial was sent down to the relevant authorities,
and Téng was arrested and interrogated.
Over eighty people implicated as his associates
were all to be subjected to severe punishment for defamation.
Hào submitted a memorial in remonstrance, stating:
"I have heard that Yáo and Shùn erected drums for remonstrance,
the Three Kings planted 'slander trees' (trees where criticisms could be posted),
the Spring and Autumn Annals recorded good and bad deeds,
and enlightened rulers did not punish commoners for their words.
Although Téng and others infringed upon the ruler and violated the law,
their words were originally intended to express loyalty and offer upright counsel.
If they are to be executed,
the world will seal its lips,
blocking the source of remonstrance and debate,
which is not the way to manifest virtue and show it to future generations."
The Emperor then understood,
reducing Téng's death sentence by one degree,
and the rest were sent to Sīkòu (Minister of Justice).
Four years later,
he was dismissed from office due to disharmony between yin and yang.
In the first year of Yángjiā,
he was again appointed Tíngwèi.
He died in office that year
at the age of eighty-three.
An envoy was sent to mourn and offer sacrifices,
and he was granted burial land in Hénán County.
His son was Gāng.
Gāng, courtesy name Wénjì.
He was proficient in classical studies from a young age.
Although he was a son of a nobleman,
he maintained the integrity of a commoner.
He was recommended as Xiaolián but did not accept the position. The Sītú appointed him to a high-ranking post as 【Shì】 Yùshǐ (Palace Censor).
The Sītú appointed him to a high-ranking post as Yùshǐ.
At that time, Emperor Shùn indulged the eunuchs,
causing alarm among the discerning.
Gāng was often moved with indignation,
and sighed with emotion, saying:
"Filth and wickedness fill the court;
if I cannot exert myself and risk my life to sweep away the nation's troubles,
I do not wish to live."
He then retired and submitted a memorial, stating:
"The Shī says: 'Neither deviating nor forgetting,
they follow the old statutes.'
Looking back at the initial flourishing of the great Hàn,
and the era of restoration,
Emperors Wén and Míng,
their virtuous transformation was especially profound.
Observing their governance,
it is easy to follow and easy to see;
it was merely about being respectful, frugal, and upholding integrity,
disciplining oneself and valuing virtue.
The Zhongguān Chángshì (palace attendants) were never more than two,
and the rewards for favored close associates barely amounted to a few catties of gold.
They cherished expenditures and valued people,
hence families were self-sufficient and people were content.
The Yi and Di barbarians, hearing that China was prosperous and wealthy,
trusted in its morality,
which caused their treacherous schemes to naturally dissipate and a harmonious atmosphere to resonate.
However, in recent times,
the old canons have not been followed.
Unworthy commoners without merit all have official titles and ranks.
They are enriched and indulged, and then harmed,
which is not loving people, valuing instruments,
or complying with heaven and following the Dao.
I humbly wish Your Majesty would spare a little of your sagely thought,
diminish those around you,
to serve the will of Heaven."
The memorial was submitted but not heeded.
In the first year of Hàn'ān,
eight envoys were selected and dispatched to inspect local customs.
All were aged scholars of renown,
many having held prominent positions.
Only Gāng was young,
and his official rank was the lowest.
While others received their orders and departed for their assigned regions,
Gāng alone buried his carriage wheels at the Dūtíng (capital pavilion) in Luòyáng,
saying:
"When wolves and jackals block the road,
why ask about foxes and badgers!"
He then presented a memorial, saying:
"Grand General Jì,
and Hénán Yǐn Bùyí,
relying on the support of their maternal relatives,
bearing the nation's profound grace,
with the qualifications of commoners,
hold the important office of Āhéng (Chief Minister).
They are unable to spread the five teachings
or assist the sun and moon,
but instead exclusively act as great wild boars and long serpents,
indulging their greed and rapacity,
delighting in wealth,
unrestrainedly indulging their desires,
cultivating many sycophants,
to harm the loyal and good.
This is truly unforgivable by heavenly wrath,
and punishment should not be avoided.
I respectfully list fifteen instances of their disloyal hearts,
which are all things that臣子 (chénzǐ, loyal subjects) grind their teeth over."
The memorial reached the emperor,
and the capital was shaken.
At that time, Jì's sister was the Empress,
and her imperial favor was flourishing.
Jì's and Liáng's relatives filled the court.
Although the Emperor knew Gāng's words were direct, he ultimately could not bear to use them.
At that time, the bandit Zhāng Yīng (張嬰) and his followers from Guǎnglíng (廣陵) numbered several tens of thousands.
They killed governors (cìshǐ 刺史) and officials receiving two thousand dàn (èrqiānshí 二千石) of salary,
plundering and causing chaos between Yáng (揚) and Xú (徐) provinces.
This continued for over ten years,
and the imperial court was unable to suppress them.
Jì (冀) then subtly suggested to the Secretariat (Shàngshū 尚書)
that Gāng (綱) be made the Administrator of Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu 廣陵太守),
intending to use this matter to implicate him.
Previous prefects (jùnshǒu 郡守) dispatched
often requested more soldiers and horses,
but Gāng (綱) alone requested to proceed with a single carriage.
Upon arrival,
he brought only about ten officers and soldiers,
and went directly to Yīng's (嬰) encampment.
He comforted and reassured them,
seeking to meet with the elders
to convey the emperor's benevolence.
Yīng (嬰) was initially greatly surprised.
Upon seeing Gāng's (綱) sincerity and trustworthiness,
he came out to pay respects.
Gāng (綱) invited him to sit in the seat of honor
and asked about their grievances and hardships.
He then explained to them, saying:
"The former officials receiving two thousand dàn (èrqiānshí 二千石) often indulged in greed and tyranny,
thus causing you all to harbor resentment and gather together.
Indeed, those officials were guilty,
but what you have done is also not righteous.
Now, the benevolent and sagacious emperor
wishes to subdue rebels with civil virtues.
Therefore, he has sent me, the Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守),
hoping to honor you with ranks and stipends,
and not wishing to inflict punishment upon you.
Now is truly the time to turn misfortune into fortune.
If you hear what is righteous but do not submit,
and the Son of Heaven becomes furiously enraged,
and the great armies of Jīng (荊), Yáng (楊), Yǎn (兗), and Yù (豫) gather like clouds,
would you not be in danger?
If you do not assess your strength against ours,
you are not discerning;
to reject good and embrace evil
is not wise;
to abandon what is compliant and follow what is rebellious
is not loyal;
to cut off your lineage and descendants
is not filial;
to turn your back on righteousness and follow wickedness
is not upright;
to see what is righteous but not act upon it
is not brave. These six points are the keys to success or failure,
and the source of benefit or harm.
You should ponder them deeply."
Yīng (嬰), upon hearing this,
wept
and said:
"We, ignorant people from a desolate borderland,
are unable to communicate directly with the imperial court.
Unable to endure oppression and injustice,
we consequently gathered together to eke out a living,
like fish swimming in a pot,
gasping for breath for a brief moment.
Now that I have heard the words of Your Honor (Míngfǔ 明府),
it is truly the dawn of a new life for Yīng (嬰) and his followers.
Having already fallen into unrighteousness,
we genuinely fear that on the day we lay down our arms,
we will not escape the slaughter of our families."
Gāng (綱) swore an oath with them by heaven and earth,
and pledged by the sun and moon.
Yīng (嬰) was deeply moved and awakened,
and then took leave to return to his camp.
The next day,
he led over ten thousand of his subordinates, along with their wives and children, to surrender, bound by their own hands.
Gāng (綱) then entered Yīng's (嬰) encampment with a single carriage.
He held a grand gathering,
set out wine for enjoyment,
and dispersed Yīng's (嬰) followers,
allowing them to go wherever they wished;
he personally helped them choose residences
and surveyed their fields;
for those among their sons and younger brothers who wished to be officials,
he invited and appointed them all.
The people were pleased and submitted,
and the southern provinces were peaceful.
The imperial court considered rewarding Gāng's (綱) merits with a title,
but Liáng Jì (梁冀) obstructed it,
and so it was stopped.
The emperor praised Gāng (綱) and wished to summon him for promotion,
but Yīng (嬰) and others submitted a memorial requesting him to stay,
which was granted.
Gāng (綱) served in the commandery for one year
and died at the age of forty-six.
Countless common people, old and young, supported each other
as they went to the prefectural office to mourn.
From the time Gāng (綱) fell ill,
officials and commoners alike offered sacrifices and prayed for blessings,
all saying,
"A thousand autumns and ten thousand years,
when shall we see such a lord again?"
Zhāng Yīng (張嬰) and over five hundred others put on mourning attire and observed the funeral rites,
escorting his coffin to Jiānwéi (犍為),
where they carried soil to build his tomb.
An imperial edict stated:
"The former Administrator of Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu 廣陵太守), Zhāng Gāng (張綱),
a scion of a great minister,
received the tally to govern affairs,
rectified himself and guided his subordinates,
and promulgated virtue and trustworthiness,
causing the surrender and submission of the formidable bandit Zhāng Yīng (張嬰) and his ten thousand men.
He ended the conflict of war,
and alleviated the distress of the common people.
Before he could attain a prominent rank,
he unfortunately died early.
Yīng (嬰) and others, wearing mourning clothes and carrying staffs,
mourned as if for their own parents.
朕 (zhèn) is deeply saddened by this!"
Gāng's (綱) son, Xù (續), was appointed as a Gentleman of the Palace (Lángzhōng 郎中)
and given one million coins.
Wáng Gōng (王龔), courtesy name Bózōng (伯宗),
was from Gāopíng (高平), Shānyáng (山陽).
His family had been a prominent clan for generations.
He was initially recommended as Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián 孝廉),
and gradually promoted to Governor of Qīngzhōu (Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ 青州刺史).
He impeached and brought to justice several corrupt officials receiving two thousand dàn (èrqiānshí 二千石) of salary.
Emperor Ān (Ān Dì 安帝) praised him,
and summoned him to be appointed as a Minister (Shàngshū 尚書).
In the first year of Jiànguāng (建光)
he was promoted to Colonel Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi 司隸校尉).
The next year, he was transferred to Administrator of Rǔnán (Rǔnán Tàishǒu 汝南太守).
His governance favored mildness and harmony.
He appreciated talent and valued scholars,
introducing Húang Xiàn (黃憲) and Chén Fān (陳蕃) from his commandery.
Although Xiàn (憲) remained unyielding,
Fān (蕃) eventually took office.
Fān (蕃) had a high and clear temperament.
When he first arrived,
Gōng (龔) did not immediately summon him for an audience,
so Fān (蕃) left a note excusing himself due to illness and departed.
Gōng (龔) was angry
and ordered his name to be removed from the register.
The Commissioner of Merit (Gōngcáo 功曹), Yuán Làng (袁閬), requested an audience
and said:
"I have heard it said in the traditions, 'An official who has not been recognized by his lord
dares not stand in the court.'
Since Fān (蕃) has been invited due to his virtue,
it is improper for him to withdraw due to a breach of etiquette."
Gōng (龔) changed his demeanor and apologized, saying:
"This is my fault."
He then treated him generously again.
From then on, all rising notable scholars pledged their loyalty to him.
Làng (閬), courtesy name Fènggāo (奉高),
repeatedly declined invitations from ducal mansions,
and did not cultivate eccentric conduct,
yet achieved renown at that time.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn (永建),
Gōng (龔) was summoned to be Grand Coachman (Tàipú 太僕),
then transferred to Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常).
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Minister of Works (Sīkōng 司空),
but was dismissed due to an earthquake.
In the first year of Yǒnghé (136 CE),
he was appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
In his position, he was respectful and cautious.
Unless it was for public affairs,
he did not communicate with the provincial and commandery secretariats.
Those he appointed
were all respected elders from within the empire.
Wáng Gōng deeply detested the eunuchs' monopolization of power,
and his ambition was to set things right.
So, he submitted a memorial describing the situation in extreme terms,
requesting their dismissal and expulsion.
The Yellow Gates (Huángmén) were afraid.
Each had their retainers falsely accuse Wáng Gōng of crimes.
Shùn Dì ordered him to quickly verify the facts himself.
His former subordinate, Lǐ Gù, was then an attendant official (cóngshì zhōngláng) to the General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn), Liáng Shāng.
So, he wrote a letter to Liáng Shāng, saying:
"This morning, I heard that an imperial order was issued for Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Wáng Gōng to verify the facts himself.
I do not know the depth or nature of the matter.
Wáng Gōng maintains strict discipline and upholds integrity,
is devoted to learning and literature,
does not seek ill-gotten gains,
and does not act improperly.
But because of his firm and unyielding principles,
he has gone against common customs and alienated the masses,
and has been maliciously framed and slandered by sycophants.
When people hear of this,
none fail to sigh in alarm.
The Three Ducal Ministers (Sān Gōng) are highly esteemed,
embodying heaven's principles and serving as the ultimate standard.
There has never been a precedent for them to appear in court to plead their grievances.
If even minor grievances
are immediately brought for resolution,
then according to old statutes, unless there was a major crime,
there would be no intensive questioning.
Wáng Gōng is calm and inwardly discerning,
and should not be subjected to unreasonable treatment.
Should any other change occur,
the imperial court would acquire the name of harming the worthy,
and the multitude of officials would lose their duty to protect him.
In the past, when Jiàng Hóu (Zhōu Bó) was accused,
Yuán Àng explained away his fault.
When Wèi Shàng incurred offense,
Féng Táng pleaded his innocence.
The rulers of the time praised them
and they were recorded in histories and biographies.
Now, General, you rely on the Emperor (Zhìzūn) internally
and wield the reins of state externally.
Your words carry weight and your credibility is established;
your commands are met with no dissent.
You ought to present a memorial to rescue him
and save Wáng Gōng from his difficulties.
The saying goes: 'When a good man is in distress,
the hungry cannot wait for a meal.'
This is that very time."
Liáng Shāng immediately reported this to the Emperor,
and the matter was then resolved.
Wáng Gōng was in office for five years.
Due to old age and illness, he requested to retire,
and died at home.
His son was Wáng Chàng.
The commentary says: Zhāng Hào and Wáng Gōng
were known as distinguished (tuī) scholars.
Their inclination to promote and attract the good,
and to clearly recommend people,
was the sentiment of benevolent people.
When scholars advance, the world utilizes their talents;
when the worthy are employed, people offer their abilities.
When abilities are offered, their merits are indeed great;
when talents are utilized, their governance also extends throughout the empire.
The benefits are immense,
yet no one prioritizes this.
Is it not like 'breaking a branch for an elder' (zhézhe) where 'not doing it is the difficulty'?
In the past, Liǔxià Huì was suppressed by Zāng Wén,
while Chúnyú Cháng was praised by Fāng Jìn.
