Therefore, those who establish virtue are easily overlooked due to their humble obscurity,
while those who achieve prominence are easily promoted due to their noble path.
Thus, the gatekeeper (Chén Mén) had the duty of guarding the pass,
but the official at the pillar (Zhù Xià) did not have the anxieties of a high-ranking minister.
Wáng Chàng's courtesy name was Shūmào.
From a young age, he was praised for his integrity and honesty,
and did not engage in factionalism.
Initially nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián) candidate,
he declined due to illness.
General-in-Chief (Dà Jiāngjūn) Liáng Shāng specifically appointed him as an Outstanding Talent (Màocái).
He was successively promoted four times to Prefect of the Masters of Writing (Shàngshū Lìng),
then transferred out to become Chancellor of Qí (Qí Xiāng).
He was summoned to be appointed Colonel Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi),
then transferred to be Administrator of Yúyáng (Yúyáng Tàishǒu).
In every place he served, he was praised for his strictness and clarity.
He was removed from office for an incident.
At this time, many governmental affairs were handled by the Masters of Writing (Shàngshū).
Huán Dì specially decreed to the Three Ducal Ministers (Sān Gōng)
to select able and worthy officials.
Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Chén Fān recommended Wáng Chàng as upright, impartial, and just,
with an unyielding demeanor.
Because of this, he again became a Master of Writing (Shàngshū).
Soon after, he was appointed Administrator of Nányáng (Nányáng Tàishǒu).
Previous administrators (èr qiān dàn) were intimidated by the imperial relatives in the capital region,
and many did not fulfill their duties.
Wáng Chàng deeply resented this.
Upon arrival, he vigorously displayed his power and might.
Any powerful factions (háodǎng) that had committed misdeeds
were all investigated and exposed.
A general amnesty was declared,
and the cases were dropped.
Wáng Chàng deeply regretted this.
He then established new regulations:
those who had accepted bribes of twenty million (cash) or more and did not voluntarily confess
had all their property confiscated.
If they concealed it,
he ordered officials to demolish their houses, cut down their trees,
fill their wells, and flatten their stoves.
The powerful local gentry were greatly shaken.
The meritorious official (gōngcáo) Zhāng Chǎng submitted a memorial to admonish him, saying:
"The Five Teachings (Wǔ Jiào) emphasize leniency,
recorded in the classics.
Tāng removed the 'three-sided net' (sān miàn),
and the eight directions returned to benevolence.
King Wǔ entered Yīn (Shāng),
first abolishing the 'roasting pillar' (páogé) punishment.
Gāozǔ learned from Qín,
establishing only the 'three-chapter law' (sān zhāng zhī fǎ).
Emperor Xiàowén was moved by one Tí Yíng,
and abolished mutilating punishments.
Zhuó Mào, Wén Wēng, Zhào Fù and their like
all detested harshness and severity,
and strove to promote warmth and generosity.
The governance of benevolent and worthy people
has been passed down to later generations.
Indeed, a wise ruler
allows 'fish that can swallow a boat' (tūn zhōu zhī yú) to escape the net,
and then the three luminaries (sān guāng) shine brightly above,
and people are pleased below.
Though it may sound roundabout,
its effects are very direct.
Demolishing houses and cutting down trees
will be considered severe and harsh.
Though you wish to punish evil,
it will be difficult to gain widespread positive renown.
With your Lordship's (Míngfǔ) supreme intelligence
and the brilliance of the sun and moon,
if you implement benevolent and gracious governance,
the whole empire will change its view.
It would truly be as easy as 'breaking a branch' (zhézhe),
and not as difficult as 'carrying a mountain' (jiā shān).
This commandery is an old capital, a domain (hóudiàn) state.
The imperial gardens and ancestral temples originated from Zhānglíng.
The three empresses were born in Xīnyě.
Men and women are steeped in moral education,
and the common people look up to your virtuous influence.
Since the restoration (Zhōngxīng),
meritorious officials and prime ministers
have flourished for generations.
I foolishly believe that being diligently strict with punishment
is not as good as practicing benevolence;
and zealously seeking out wickedness
is not as good as treating the worthy with礼 (lǐ).
When Shùn appointed Gāoyáo,
the unbenevolent kept their distance.
When Suí Huì governed,
the thieves of Jìn fled to Qín.
When the people of Yú and Ruì entered the border,
a yielding heart spontaneously arose.
Transformation lies in virtue,
not in the use of punishment."
Wáng Chàng deeply accepted Zhāng Chǎng's admonition.
He then promoted lenient governance,
was cautious with punishments and simplified penalties,
and moral education was thus put into practice.
Many powerful families in the commandery competed in extravagance and luxury.
Wáng Chàng always wore plain clothes and a leather mat,
and his carriages and horses were worn out,
to correct this custom.
Liú Biǎo, who was seventeen at the time and from the same commandery,
studied under Wáng Chàng.
He offered admonishment, saying:
"Indeed, extravagance should not transgress those above,
and frugality should not oppress those below.
Following the Way and observing the rites (lǐ),
the noble should position themselves between 'allowable' and 'not allowable.'
Qú Bóyù was ashamed to be the only gentleman.
Your Lordship (Fǔjūn) does not aspire to the clear teachings of Confucius (Kǒng Shèng),
but rather admires the lesser conduct of Bó Yí and Shú Qí (Yí Qí).
Is this not to conspicuously exalt yourself in the world?"
Wáng Chàng said:
"In ancient times, Gōngyí Xiū, when in Lǔ,
pulled up his garden mallows
and sent away his weaving wife.
Sūn Shú'áo, when serving as Chancellor of Chǔ,
had his son wear a fur cloak and cut firewood.
Indeed, few are those who err by being too frugal.
Those who hear the conduct of Bó Yí
become incorruptible if greedy,
and resolute if timid.
Even if I am unworthy,
I dare to emulate their legacy."
Later, he was summoned to be the Colonel of the Changlè Garrison.
In the first year of Jiànníng (168 CE),
he was promoted to Sīkōng.
Several months later,
he was dismissed due to floods.
The following year,
he died at home.
His son, Qiān,
was the Chief Clerk to the Grand General Hé Jìn.
Qiān's son, Càn,
was famous for his literary talent.
Zhǒng Gǎo, courtesy name Jǐngbó,
was a native of Luòyáng, Hénán.
He was a descendant of Zhòngshān Fǔ.
His father was the Prefect of Dìngtáo,
and had 30 million in wealth.
When his father died,
Gǎo distributed all of it to relieve his impoverished clan members and villagers.
He did not associate
with those who sought fame and profit.
Initially, he served as a Clerk in the county yamen.
At that time, Wáng Chén, the nephew of Tián Xīn, the Administrator of Hénán,
was known for his ability to judge people.
Xīn said to him:
"Today I must recommend six Filial and Incorrupt,
and I have received many letters of recommendation from imperial relatives.
I should not disregard them.
I wish to personally select one distinguished scholar to repay the state;
you help me find him."
The next day,
Chén was seeing off a guest at Dàyáng Guō
when he saw Gǎo from a distance,
and was impressed by him.
Returning, he reported to Xīn, saying:
"The Administrator has found a Filial and Incorrupt;
he is a Clerk from Luòyáng's yamen."
Xīn laughed and said:
"He should be an obscure recluse from the mountains and marshes.
(((Close)) [Nǎi] Is he a Luòyáng official?"
Chén replied:
"The mountains and marshes do not necessarily have extraordinary individuals,
and extraordinary individuals are not necessarily in the mountains and marshes."
Xīn immediately summoned Gǎo to the courtyard,
and questioned him about his duties.
Gǎo's replies were orderly,
and Xīn was greatly impressed.
He summoned him to be appointed Chief Clerk,
and subsequently recommended him as Filial and Incorrupt.
He was invited to the Grand Commandant's Residence
and recommended as a High Talent.
At the end of the reign of Emperor Shùn,
he served as Imperial Censor.
At that time, the eight envoys sent out, including Dù Qiáo, Grand Master of Guanglù, and Zhōu Jǔ,
made many impeachments.
However, Grand General Liáng Jì and various eunuchs interceded for each other,
and all the cases were suppressed.
Gǎo, considering that his duty was to impeach and investigate,
and being determined to expose evil and wrongdoing,
again impeached the Prefect of Shǔjùn, Liú Xuān, and others, who had been accused by the eight envoys. Their crimes were manifest,
and they ought to be executed.

He also memorialized, requesting an imperial edict for the four offices to list and recommend relatives of high officials and those with close ties who were Governors or Administrators (two thousand *shí*), especially those who were corrupt and incompetent,
to be dismissed and investigated for their crimes.
The Emperor then agreed.
Gǎo was promoted to oversee the Crown Prince at Chéngguāng Palace.
The Palace Regular Attendant Gāo Fàn, alone in a chariot, came from the palace to greet the Crown Prince.
At that time, Grand Tutor Dù Qiáo and others were hesitant to follow,
confused and not knowing what to do.
Gǎo then drew his sword and stood before the chariot,
saying:
"The Crown Prince is the nation's heir,
and human lives depend on him.
Now, the Regular Attendant comes without an imperial edict;
how can we know he is not a traitor?
Today, there is only death."
Fàn was put to shame and could not respond,
so he rushed to report it.
When the imperial edict arrived in reply,
the Crown Prince was then able to leave.
When the imperial edict arrived in reply,
Qiáo withdrew and sighed,
ashamed of his indecision in the face of the situation, while Gǎo was clear-headed.
The Emperor also commended his steadfastness,
and praised him repeatedly for a long time.
He was sent out as Inspector of Yìzhōu.
Gǎo was always magnanimous
and fond of accomplishing deeds and establishing achievements.
In his three years in office,
he proclaimed benevolence to distant barbarians
and enlightened diverse customs.
The various tribes in the Mín Mountains all submitted to Han virtue.
The kingdoms of Báiláng, Pánmù, Tángzōu, Qióng, and Bó,
had been cut off since the death of the previous Inspector, Zhū Fǔ.
When Gǎo arrived,
he again encouraged their submission and conversion.
At that time, the Administrator of Yǒngchāng cast a golden snake with patterns
and offered it to Liáng Jì.
Gǎo exposed and arrested him,
and sent a fast-relay memorial to the throne.
However, the two Grand Offices were timid
and dared not investigate the matter,
and Jì consequently harbored resentment towards Gǎo.
It happened that Fú Zhí of Bājùn gathered several hundred people,
proclaiming himself
"Heavenly King."
Gǎo and Administrator Yīng Chéng attacked and captured him,
but failed,
and many officials and common people were wounded.
Jì used this to frame them,
and transmitted orders to arrest Gǎo and Chéng.
Grand Commandant Lǐ Gù submitted a memorial to save them, saying:
"Your servant humbly hears that the injuries sustained during the capture
were not the intention of Gǎo and Chéng.
It was actually because the county officials feared the law and punishment,
and pursued them too relentlessly,
leading to this misfortune.
Recently, bandits have risen in groups,
and are still rampant everywhere.
Gǎo and Chéng were the first to expose major evildoers,
but are now suffering punishment together.
Your servant fears that this will discourage the enthusiasm of the prefectures and counties to expose wrongdoing,
and they will instead collude to conceal it,
no longer doing their utmost."
Empress Dowager Liáng reviewed the memorial,
and then pardoned Gǎo and Chéng's crimes,
only dismissing them from office.
Later, when the Qiāng in Liángzhōu rebelled,
Gǎo was appointed Inspector of Liángzhōu,
and he gained the great affection of the people.
When he was summoned to be transferred,
officials and common people went to the palace to request that he remain.
The Empress Dowager sighed, saying:
"I have never heard of an Inspector who won the hearts of the people like this."
So she granted the request.
Gǎo remained for another year,
then was transferred to be Administrator of Hànyáng.
The nomadic men and women escorted him to the border of Hànyáng,
and Gǎo bid them farewell,
unable to ride in his carriage for a thousand *lǐ*.
Upon arriving in the commandery,
he transformed the Qiāng and Hú,
prohibiting plunder.
He was transferred to be the Colonel-Protector of the Xiongnú.
At that time, the Wūhuán in Liáodōng rebelled,
so he was again transferred to be Administrator of Liáodōng.
The Wūhuán, upon hearing of him, submitted immediately,
greeting and bowing to him at the border.
He was dismissed and returned home due to an incident.
Later, the Supervisor of the Masters of Writing recommended Gǎo as virtuous and upright,
but he did not respond.
He was summoned to be appointed Counselor,
then transferred to be Administrator of Nánjùn,
and entered the court as a Minister of the Imperial Household.
When the Xiongnú happened to invade Bìng and Liáng provinces,
Emperor Huán promoted Gǎo to be General Who Crosses the Liao.
Upon arriving at his camp,
Gǎo first proclaimed benevolence and trustworthiness,
enticing the various Hú to surrender.
Only those who did not submit
were then attacked.
Any Qiāng captives who had been seized and held as hostages in commanderies and counties previously
were all sent back.
He sincerely appeased them,
and rewards and punishments were clearly defined.
Consequently, the Qiāng Hú, Kūcí, Shāchē, Wūsūn, and others all came to submit.
Gǎo then removed the beacon fires
and abolished the watchtowers,
and the border regions were peaceful and without incident.
He entered the court as Grand Minister of Agriculture.
In the fourth year of Yánxī (161 CE),
he was promoted to Grand Tutor.
He recommended and advanced renowned ministers such as Qiáo Xuán and Huángfǔ Guī,
who were deemed competent as chief ministers.
He served for three years
and died at the age of sixty-one.
The border people of Bìng and Liáng provinces all mourned for him.
When the Xiongnú heard of Gǎo's death,
the entire nation grieved for him.
Whenever the Chányú came to court to offer congratulations,
upon seeing his tomb,
he would weep and offer sacrifices.
He had two sons: Dài
and Fú.
Dài's courtesy name was Gōngzǔ.
He was fond of learning and cultivated his aspirations.
He was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt and Flourishing Talent,
and invited to serve in the public offices,
but he did not accept any.
He was specially summoned by the Imperial Courier,
but died of illness.
Initially,
Zhǒng Dài and Lǐ Gù's son, Lǐ Xiè, were simultaneously summoned as Advisors on Policy.
When Lǐ Xiè heard of Zhǒng Dài's death,
he was deeply grieved,
and thus submitted a memorial requesting that Zhǒng Dài be honored with additional rites.
He stated:
"Your servant has heard that when benevolence and righteousness flourish, then morality thrives;
when morality thrives, then governance and transformation are clear;
when governance and transformation are clear, then the myriad people are at peace.
I respectfully observe that the late retired scholar Zhǒng Dài
was pure, harmonious, and understood principles,
delighting in poetry and books.
Wealth and honor could not sway his thoughts,
nor could the myriad things disturb his heart.
His allotted lifespan was not long,
and he suddenly passed away.
Had he not lingered and been slow to advance,
those of his generation would all be high officials by now.
In ancient times, after a worthy sage died,
there was the custom of posthumous promotion.
The Rites of Zhōu honored great virtues
with epitaphs and eulogies.
Yet Zhǒng Dài, in life, had no honor of official seals and ribbons,
and in death, no posthumous official title.
Although he did not establish loyalty or render service,
he was chosen by the emperor's grace,
and was universally esteemed far and wide.
He ought to receive a special reward."
The court ultimately could not comply.
Zhǒng Fú had the courtesy name Yǐngbó.
Initially, he served as an Aide to the Grand Administrator of the Capital Region,
then was appointed Prefect of Wǎn.
At that time, officials of Nányáng Commandery were fond of using their days off
to roam the market streets,
which caused distress to the common people.
Zhǒng Fú, when he encountered them,
would invariably dismount from his carriage and formally greet them,
to shame their hearts.
From then on, none dared to go out.
He had a reputation for good governance,
and was successively promoted to Grand Master of Guanglu.
In the first year of Chūpíng (190 CE),
he replaced Xún Shuǎng as Minister of Works.
The following year,
due to an earthquake, he was dismissed from office by imperial decree,
and again served as Grand Astrologer.
During the rebellion of Lǐ Què and Guō Sì,
Cháng'ān city fell into chaos.
Many officials fled to avoid the brunt of the fighting.
Zhǒng Fú brandished his sword and declared:
"As a high minister of the state,
I cannot stop the war and eliminate the villains,
which has led to the fierce bandits' weapons pointing towards the palace.
Where do you wish to go?"
He then fought and died.
His son was Zhǒng Shào.
Zhǒng Shào's courtesy name was Shēnfǔ.
He was well-known in his youth.
At the end of Zhōngpíng (c. 189 CE),
he became an Advisor on Policy.
When Grand General Hé Jìn was about to execute the eunuchs,
he summoned the Provincial Governor of Bìngzhōu, Dǒng Zhuó.
When Dǒng Zhuó reached Miǎnchí,
Hé Jìn's resolve became more hesitant,
and he dispatched Zhǒng Shào to convey an imperial decree ordering him to stop.
Dǒng Zhuó did not comply
and continued his advance to Hénán.
Zhǒng Shào met him and welcomed him,
and then reasoned with him to return his troops.
Dǒng Zhuó suspected treachery,
and ordered his soldiers to threaten Zhǒng Shào with weapons.
Zhǒng Shào, enraged,
proclaimed the imperial decree and shouted at them loudly,
whereupon the soldiers scattered.
He then stepped forward to confront and rebuke Dǒng Zhuó.
Dǒng Zhuó, finding himself in the wrong,
then returned his troops to Xīyángtíng.
After Hé Jìn's defeat,
Emperor Xiàn ascended the throne,
and Zhǒng Shào was appointed Attendant at the Palace.
Dǒng Zhuó, having seized power,
disliked Zhǒng Shào's strong will,
and thus demoted him to Advisor on Policy
and sent him out as Inspector of Yì and Liáng Provinces.
Coincidentally, his father Zhǒng Fú died in battle,
and he ultimately did not take up the post.
After the mourning period ended,
he was summoned to be Minister Steward and Grand Herald,
but he declined both appointments.
He said:
"In the past, my late father sacrificed himself for the state.
As a subject and son,
I cannot eliminate the villains and avenge his death.
How can I face the enlightened ruler in court?"
Thus, he joined Mǎ Téng, Hán Suì, and the Left Commander of the Gentlemen of the Household Liú Fàn, and Advisor on Policy Mǎ Yǔ, to attack Lǐ Què and Guō Sì,
to avenge his father.
He fought Guō Sì below Chángpíngguān,
but his army was defeated,
and Zhǒng Shào and the others all died.
Mǎ Téng then returned to Liángzhōu.
Chén Qiú, courtesy name Bózhēn,
was a native of Huáipǔ, Xiàpī.
His family was famous for generations.
His father, Chén Wěi,
was Grand Administrator of Guǎnghàn.
Chén Qiú studied Confucianism in his youth
and was skilled in laws and regulations.
During the Yángjiā era (132-135 CE),
he was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt,
and gradually promoted to Prefect of Fányáng.
At that time, the Grand Administrator of Wèijùn hinted to the counties to submit bribes.
Chén Qiú did not give any,
and the Grand Administrator, enraged, flogged the Supervising Secretary,
intending to have him expel Chén Qiú.
The Supervising Secretary refused,
saying:
"Of the fifteen cities in Wèijùn,
only Fányáng has distinct governance.
If I now receive orders to expel him,
it will surely lead to discussion throughout the empire."
The Grand Administrator then stopped.
Chén Qiú was again appointed to a ducal office,
recommended as High Class,
and appointed Palace Assistant Imperial Censor.
At this time,
the cunning bandits Lǐ Yán and others in Guìyáng gathered to plunder,
running rampant in the Jīng Province area.
The provincial and commandery authorities were weak
and unable to suppress them.
Grand Commandant Yáng Bǐng recommended Chén Qiú as Grand Administrator of Línglíng.
Upon Chén Qiú's arrival,
he devised strategies,
and within a month,
the bandits dispersed.
However, the provincial troops led by Zhū Gài and others rebelled,
and, with the Guìyáng bandit Hú Lán and tens of thousands of men, turned to attack Línglíng.
Línglíng was low-lying and wet,
with a city wall constructed of wood,
making it indefensible.
The commandery was terrified.
The clerks and officials suggested sending their families away to avoid disaster.
Chén Qiú angrily said:
"As Grand Administrator, holding the state's tiger tally,
and entrusted with authority over a region,
how can I consider my wife and children and undermine the state's prestige?
Anyone who speaks of this again will be executed!"
He then brought all the elderly and weak officials and commoners inside,
and together they defended the city.
They bent large timbers into bows,
feathered spears into arrows,
and used mechanisms to launch them,
shooting over a thousand paces,
killing and wounding many.
The bandits then diverted a stream to flood the city.
Chén Qiú immediately, from within, used the terrain to reverse the flow and flood the bandits instead.
They resisted each other for more than ten days,
and the city could not be taken.
Coincidentally, Commander of the Gentlemen of the Household Dù Shàng arrived with relief troops.
Chén Qiú recruited soldiers,
and together with Dù Shàng, they defeated and beheaded Zhū Gài and others.
He was awarded 500,000 cash,
and one of his sons was appointed a Gentleman.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Wèijùn.
He was summoned and appointed Grand Artisan,
to construct Emperor Huán's imperial tomb.
He saved over a myriad in expenses.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Nányáng,
but because he impeached and exposed powerful local families,
he was slandered by influential households,
and summoned to the Court of the Imperial Censor to be charged.
Due to a general amnesty,
he returned home.
(*Fù*) Chēng was appointed as *Tíngwèi*.
In the first year of Xīpíng,
Empress Dowager Dòu passed away.
The Empress Dowager had previously been relocated to the Yúntái terrace in the Southern Palace.
The eunuchs, harboring long-standing resentment against the Dòu clan,
therefore used a clothes-cart to carry the Empress Dowager's corpse,
and left it in a market stall south of the city for several days.
The *Zhōngchángshì* Cáo Jié and Wáng Fǔ wanted to inter her with the rites of a *guìrén*.
The Emperor said:
"The Empress Dowager personally established me [on the throne],
allowing me to inherit the great enterprise.
The *Shī* says: 'No virtue goes unrewarded,
no word goes unanswered.'
How can she be laid to rest as a *guìrén*?"
Thereupon, funeral rites were initiated and completed.
When it was time for the burial,
Jié and others again wished to bury the Empress Dowager separately,
and to have Consort Féng accompany and be interred with the Emperor.
An edict ordered the *gōngqīng* to gather in a large assembly at the imperial court,
and commanded *Zhōngchángshì* Zhào Zhōng to oversee the deliberations.
The *Tàiwèi* Lǐ Xián was ill at the time,
but supported himself to rise,
and ground pepper to take with him,
saying to his wife and children:
"If the Empress Dowager cannot be interred with Emperor Huán,
I will not return alive."
Once the deliberations began,
there were several hundred people present.
They all looked to the *zhōngguān*,
and for a long time no one dared to speak first.
Zhào Zhōng said:
"The discussion should be settled now."
He wondered why the *gōngqīng* and those below them were all looking at each other.
Qiú said:
"The Empress Dowager, with her abundant virtue and good family background,
presided over the world as mother.
It is fitting for her to be interred with the late Emperor;
there is no doubt about this."
Zhōng smiled and said:
"Tíngwèi Chén should write this down immediately."
Qiú immediately put forth the proposal, saying:
"The Empress Dowager, from her time in the *jiāofáng*,
possessed the virtue of intelligent maternal bearing.
Encountering an unfortunate era,
she supported and established a sagacious and enlightened ruler,
thereby continuing the ancestral temple,
her meritorious achievements are extremely great.
When the late Emperor passed away,
she then encountered a great tribulation,
and was moved to an empty palace,
unfortunately passing away early.
Although her family was found guilty,
the matter did not concern the Empress Dowager herself.
If she were to be buried separately now,
it would truly disappoint the hopes of the world.
Furthermore, Consort Féng's tomb has been opened,
her bones exposed,
her body mingled with robbers' corpses,
her spirit defiled,
and she rendered no service to the state.
How can it be proper for her to be interred with the Most Exalted?"
Zhōng reviewed Qiú's proposal,
his expression changed as he looked up and down,
and he sneered at Qiú, saying:
"Tíngwèi Chén's proposal is very bold!"
Qiú said:
"As the Chén and Dòu clans were wronged,
and the Empress Dowager was unjustly confined,
I have always felt heartbroken,
and the world has expressed indignation and lament.
To speak of it today,
and then return to suffer punishment,
is my long-cherished wish."
The *gōngqīng* and those below,
all followed Qiú's proposal.
Lǐ Xián initially dared not speak first,
but seeing Qiú's righteous words,
he then spoke loudly, saying:
"I originally thought it should be so,
it truly aligns with my intention."
All those present felt ashamed for him.
Cáo Jié and Wáng Fǔ again argued,
believing that the Lǐang Empress's family had committed evil and rebellious acts,
and she was buried separately at Yìlíng.
Emperor Wǔ had deposed Empress Wèi,
and instead had Lady Lǐ interred with him.
Now, the Dòu clan's crime is deep,
how can she be buried with the late Emperor?
Lǐ Xián then went to the palace gate and submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly reflect that Empress Dòu of Zhāngdé cruelly harmed Gōnghuái,
and Empress Yán of Ānsī's family committed evil and rebellious acts.
Yet, Emperor Hé had no discussion of a separate burial,
and the court of Emperor Shùn had no document of demotion.
As for Empress Wèi,
she was personally deposed by Emperor Xiàowǔ,
and cannot be used as a comparison.
Now, the Empress Dowager Chánglè holds the exalted title,
has personally presided over state affairs,
and nurtured the world.
Furthermore, she supported and established a sagacious and enlightened ruler,
glorifying the imperial succession.
The Empress Dowager regarded Your Majesty as her son,
how can Your Majesty not regard the Empress Dowager as your mother?
A son does not depose his mother,
a subject does not demote his lord.
It is fitting for her to be buried with Emperor Xuān at Xuānlíng,
fully in accordance with the old system."
The Emperor reviewed the memorial,
and said to Cáo Jié and others:
"Although the Dòu clan acted improperly,
the Empress Dowager has shown virtue towards me,
and it is not proper to demote her."
Jié and others had nothing more to say,
and thus the resolution was settled.
Xián's *zì* was Yuánzhēn,
and he was from Rǔnán.
Having served repeatedly in prefectures and commanderies,
he was known for his integrity and competence;
in court, he was pure and loyal,
and the powerful favorites feared him.
Six years later,
Qiú was promoted to *Sīkōng*,
but was dismissed due to an earthquake.
He was appointed *Guānglù Dàfū*,
and then again served as *Tíngwèi* and *Tàicháng*.
In the first year of Guānghé,
he was promoted to *Tàiwèi*,
but after several months,
was dismissed due to a solar eclipse.
He was again appointed *Guānglù Dàfū*.
The following year,
he became *Yǒnglè Shàofǔ*.
He then secretly conspired with *Sītú* Líu Hé from Héjiān to execute the eunuchs.
Originally,
Hé's elder brother, *Shìzhōng* Shū,
had conspired with *Dàjiāngjūn* Dòu Wǔ and both died,
hence Hé and Qiú became allies.
Before the plan could be launched,
Qiú again wrote to persuade Hé, saying:
"You come from the imperial clan,
and hold a position among the highest ministers.
The world looks up to you,
and you are a pillar of the state.
How can you simply conform and acquiesce without objection?
Now, Cáo Jié and others act wantonly and cause harm,
yet they have been by the Emperor's side for a long time.
Furthermore, your brother, *Shìzhōng*, suffered harm from Jié and others,
which Empress Dowager Yǒnglè is personally aware of.
You can now memorialize to transfer *Wèiwèi* Yáng Qiú to *Sīlì Xiàowèi*,
and then successively arrest and execute Jié and others.
With governance emanating from the sagacious ruler,
the world will be at peace,
and you can await it with folded arms."
Furthermore, *Shàngshū* Líu Nà, who had offended the eunuchs due to his uprightness,
was exiled to become *Bùbīng Xiàowèi*.
He also strongly urged Hé.
Hé said:
"The wicked eunuchs have many ears and eyes.
I fear that before the matter can be realized,
we will suffer its calamity first."
Nà said:
"You are a pillar of the state.
If you do not support it when it is in peril,
what use is that prime minister?"
Hé assented,
and also conspired with Yáng Qiú.
Qiú's concubine [or younger wife] was
the daughter of Chéng Huáng.
Huáng served in the palace,
and was known as Chéng Dàrén.
Jié and others somewhat heard of the plot,
so they heavily bribed Huáng,
and also threatened him.
Huáng, intimidated and pressured,
reported Qiú's plot to Jié.
Jié then jointly reported to the Emperor, saying:
"Hé and others constantly communicate with the feudal states,
harboring evil intentions.
They frequently invoke the influence of Yǒnglè,
and have indiscriminately accepted bribes.
*Bùbīng Xiàowèi* Líu Nà, *Yǒnglè Shàofǔ* Chén Qiú, and *Wèiwèi* Yáng Qiú have communicated through letters
and conspired in an unlawful plot."
The Emperor was greatly enraged,
and ordered Hé's dismissal.
Hé, along with Qiú, Líu Nà, and Yáng Qiú, were all imprisoned and died.
Qiú was sixty-two years old at the time.
His son, Yǔ,
was *Wú Jùn Tàishǒu*;
Yǔ's younger brother, Cóng,
was *Rǔyīn Tàishǒu*;
his nephew, Guī,
was *Pèixiāng*;
Guī's son, Dēng,
was *Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu*: all were renowned.
A eulogy states: When the heir apparent faced slander,
Zhāng Qīng had a request.
Gǒng Jiū was glib and flattering,
and considered straightforwardness a flaw.
The two (Dù Gēn and Chéng Yìshì) were excessively upright,
burying carriages and filling in wells.
Zhǒng Gōng started from obscurity,
and wielded authority upon assuming office.
Chén Qiú held exclusive sway in discussions,
while Huán Sī followed suit.
Biographies of Dù, Luán, Liú, Lǐ, Liú, Xiè, Chapter 47
Dù Gēn, courtesy name Bójīn,
was a native of Dìnglíng, Yǐngchuān.
His father, Ān,
courtesy name Bóyí,
had ambition and integrity from a young age.
At thirteen, he entered the Imperial Academy,
and was known as a "child prodigy."
The noble relatives in the capital admired his reputation,
some sending him letters.
Ān did not open them,
but stored them all in a wall niche.
Later, when noble relatives and their retainers were investigated and arrested,
Ān opened the niche and took out the letters,
their seals intact as before.
He thus avoided trouble,
and people of the time esteemed him.
He rose to the position of Grand Administrator of Bājùn,
and his administration was highly regarded.
Gēn's nature was upright and steadfast,
and he was fond of speaking out directly.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (107 CE),
he was recommended as Xiaolián
and became a Lángzhōng.
At that time, Empress Héxī Dèng was presiding over the court,
and power resided with her maternal relatives.
Gēn believed that Emperor Ān was of age
and should personally manage state affairs.
So, with other Láng, he submitted a memorial of direct remonstrance.
The Empress Dowager was furious,
arrested Gēn and others,
ordered them to be put into silk sacks,
and beaten to death in the palace hall.
The law enforcement officers, knowing Gēn's reputation,
privately told the executioners not to exert full force.
Afterwards, he was carried out of the city,
and Gēn revived.
The Empress Dowager sent people to inspect,
so Gēn feigned death.
Three days later,
maggots appeared in his eyes.
He then escaped,
and became a servant in a wine shop in the mountains of Yíichéng.
After fifteen years,
the wine shop owner, realizing his virtue,
treated him with great respect.
When the Dèng clan was overthrown,
everyone around spoke of the loyalty of Gēn and the others.
The emperor, believing Gēn to be dead,
issued an edict proclaiming it throughout the empire
and sought out his descendants.
Gēn then returned to his hometown,
was summoned by Gōngchē,
and appointed Shìyùshǐ.
Initially,
Chéng Yìshì, an official from Píngyuán Commandery, also advised the Empress Dowager to return power to the emperor.
He was convicted and punished.
He was summoned along with Gēn
and promoted to Shàngshū Láng,
both being accepted and employed.
Someone asked Gēn,
"When you encountered that disaster,
the whole world sympathized,
and you had many acquaintances.
Why did you suffer so much?"
Gēn replied,
"Moving among the common people is not a place where one can disappear without a trace.
If I were accidentally exposed,
disaster would befall my close friends and relatives,
so I did not do that."
During Emperor Shùn's reign,
he was gradually promoted to Grand Administrator of Jìyīn.
He resigned from office and returned home,
dying at seventy-eight.
Yìshì, courtesy name Jìmíng,
was fond of learning in his youth
and deeply understood Daoist arts.
In Yánguāng (122-125 CE),
the palace regular attendant Fán Fēng and the emperor's wet nurse Wáng Shèng together slandered the crown prince,
who was deposed as King of Jìyīn.
Yìshì repeatedly submitted memorials pleading for him
and also exposed the deceitful actions of Fán Fēng and Wáng Shèng.
The emperor did not heed him,
and Fēng and others framed him with serious charges,
imprisoning him and sentencing him to death.
An imperial edict remitted his punishment to dismissal from office and return to his home commandery.
When the King of Jìyīn ascended the throne,
who was Emperor Shùn,
Sīkōng Zhāng Hào invited him to serve.
Hào, recognizing Yìshì's previous advocacy for the deposed crown prince,
recommended him as Yìláng.
Yìshì, feeling his contribution was not prominent,
was ashamed to accept the position
and impeached himself to return home.
The Three Ducal Ministers repeatedly invited him,
but he did not respond.
Shàngshū Púyè Yú Xǔ greatly esteemed him
and wished to involve him in court politics.
So he submitted a memorial recommending him,
and he was summoned and appointed Yìláng.
Later, Shàngshū Lìng Zuǒ Xióng and Púyè Guō Qián again recommended him as Shàngshū.
In court, his demeanor was upright,
and all officials respected him.
Luán Bā, courtesy name Shúyuán,
was a native of Nèihuáng, Wèijùn.
[He loved the Way.]
In Emperor Shùn's time,
he was assigned to the Yètíng as a eunuch official,
and appointed Huángmén Lìng,
which was not to his liking.
His nature was honest and straightforward,
and he had extensively studied the classics.
Although he was a palace official,
he did not associate with the other regular attendants.
Later, when the yang energy flowed freely (an auspicious omen),
he memorialized requesting to retire.
He was promoted to Lángzhōng
and advanced through four positions to Grand Administrator of Guìyáng.
As the commandery was located in the southern frontier
and not well-versed in cultural traditions,
he established regulations for marriage and mourning rites for the officials and common people,
and founded schools
to encourage learning.
Even minor clerks and low-ranking officials
were required to study and read.
They were tested and evaluated,
and promoted according to their abilities.
His governance was clear and discerning.
After serving for seven years,
he requested retirement due to illness.
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Gù recommended Bā's administrative achievements,
and he was summoned and appointed Yìláng,
acting Guānglù Dàfū,
and, with Dù Qiáo, Zhōu Jǔ, and eight others, toured the provinces and commanderies.
After Bā returned from his mission to Xúzhōu,
he was twice promoted to Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng.
The commandery's territory had many mountains, rivers, and ghostly apparitions.
Common people often spent their wealth on prayers and sacrifices.
Bā, having always practiced Daoist arts,
could command ghosts and spirits.
He thus completely destroyed the shrines and altars,
and eliminated mischievous shamans.
Consequently, the strange phenomena disappeared on their own.
At first, the common people were somewhat afraid,
but in the end, they all found peace.
He was transferred to Pèi Xiàng.
He achieved merit wherever he served
and was summoned and appointed Shàngshū.
At that time, the emperor passed away,
and the construction of the Xiànlíng mausoleum began.
Around the mausoleum, there were some tombs of common people.
The officials in charge wanted to encroach upon and destroy them.
Bā repeatedly submitted urgent memorials remonstrating against it.
At that time, Empress Dowager Liáng was presiding over the court,
and she issued an edict questioning Bā, saying:
"The late emperor passed away some days ago.
The selection of the mausoleum grounds
is intended to be economical and restrained.
The total area of the burial grounds
is merely twenty qǐng.
Yet Bā falsely claims that the officials in charge are destroying people's tombs.
Since the matter is not true,
it was ignored and not reported to the lower levels.
Yet Bā stubbornly persists in his foolishness
and again submits slanderous memorials.
To recklessly indulge in such wild and ignorant talk
is utterly intolerable."
Bā was imprisoned,
convicted,
and banned from holding office, returning home.
More than twenty years later,
Emperor Líng ascended the throne.
General-in-Chief Dòu Wǔ and Grand Mentor Chén Fān assisted in governing,
and Bā was summoned and appointed Yìláng.
Fān and Wǔ were executed,
and Bā, as their associate,
was again demoted to Grand Administrator of Yǒngchāng.
He impeached himself for his service,
declining due to illness and not taking up the post.
He submitted an extremely forceful memorial,
arguing the innocence of Chén and Dòu.
The emperor was enraged,
issued an edict severely reprimanding him,
and had him arrested and handed over to the Tíngwèi.
Bā committed suicide.
His son, Hè,
rose to the position of Grand Administrator of Yúnzhōng.
Liú Táo, courtesy name Zǐqí,
also known as Wěi,
was a native of Yǐngyīn in Yǐngchuān,
a descendant of Jìběi Zhēnwáng Bó.
Táo was a man of integrity,
not attending to minor details.
The friends he associated with
were always those with similar ideals.
If their preferences differed,
he would not seek their company for wealth or status;
if their dispositions were compatible,
he would not change his mind due to poverty or humble circumstances.
His kinsman, Liú Kǎi,
was renowned for his refined virtue,
and particularly esteemed Táo.
At that time, Grand General Liáng Jì held exclusive power at court,
and Emperor Huán had no son.
Years of famine followed one another,
and omens of disaster frequently appeared.
Táo, then studying at the Imperial Academy,
submitted a memorial on affairs, saying: "Your subject has heard that without Heaven and Earth, man cannot live;
without man, Heaven and Earth cannot be spiritual.
Therefore, without man, the Emperor cannot be established;
without the Emperor, man cannot be at peace.
Indeed, Heaven and the Emperor,
the Emperor and man,
are like head and foot,
mutually dependent for their functioning.
I humbly submit that Your Majesty, with abundant years and flourishing virtue,
reigns supreme under Heaven,
inheriting the blessings of eternal existence,
following an unchanging system.
Your eyes do not witness the events of Míngtiáo,
Your ears do not hear the sound of the 'cracked chariot' (bēng chē).
Heavenly disasters do not afflict Your skin and flesh;
earthquakes and eclipses do not immediately harm Your sacred body.
Thus, You disregard the errors of the three luminaries [sun, moon, stars]
and treat lightly the wrath of High Heaven.
I humbly recall that Gāozǔ's rise
began as a commoner.
He picked up the tatters of the tyrannical
Qín,
chased the lost deer of the fallen Zhōu,
united the scattered and supported the injured,
and successfully established the imperial enterprise.
His accomplishments were manifest,
his diligence was supreme.
His blessings and legacy flowed down
to
Your Majesty.
Your Majesty, however, is unable to further illuminate the path of Your illustrious ancestors,
and instead ignores Gāozǔ's diligence.
You presumptuously lend out the instruments of power,
and entrust the reins of the state,
allowing a multitude of villains and former convicts
to mow down the common people,
exhausting all under Heaven,
and spreading tyranny far and wide.
Therefore, Heaven sends numerous anomalies
to warn Your Majesty.
Your Majesty remains unaware,
and instead allows tigers and leopards to make their dens
in the fields of fawns,
and jackals to suckle in the spring parks.
How can this be the intention of Táng consulting Yǔ and Jì,
or Yì presiding over the imperial affairs of Yú,
discussing matters and assigning lands to the myriad people?
Moreover,
now
governors and chief officials,
from top to bottom, compete against each other;
greedy officials like 'great boars and long snakes' [fēngshǐ chángshé]
devour the realm;
the wealthy become the aggrieved souls of the poor,
the poor and starving become hungry and cold
ghosts;
high-ranking families are entangled in the guilt of Dōngguān,
and prosperous households are caught in the crimes of rebellion;
the dead are mourned in their graves,
the living are distressed in court and countryside.
This is what your foolish subject laments, sighs over, and reflects upon at length.
Furthermore, when Qín was about to fall,
those who offered upright counsel were executed,
while flatterers were rewarded.
Loyal words were confined to loyal tongues,
and the fate
of the state came from slanderous mouths.
The eunuch Zhào Lè enjoyed himself in Xiányáng,
and Zhào Gāo was given charge of the imperial stables.
Power departed from oneself without awareness,
and authority left the body without concern.
Ancient and modern
are judged by the same standard,
success and failure follow the same course.
I wish Your Majesty would look back at the downfall of the mighty Qín,
and examine closely the changes during the reigns of Āi and Píng.
The gains and losses are clear,
and fortune and misfortune are evident.
May you restore [the state]
to save it from the desolation of Yí and Lì.
I humbly observe that the former Inspector of Jìzhōu, Zhū Mù of Nányáng,
and the former Colonel of Wūhuán, my fellow countryman Lǐ Yīng,
both walked upright and were pure
and just,
of towering integrity, surpassing the mundane.
Mù, when previously in Jìzhōu,
upheld the law and acted fairly,
crushing corrupt factions
and sweeping clean a thousand leagues.
Yīng successively served as governor,
setting an example for his subordinates with his upright conduct.
When he took charge of the army,
his prestige spread throughout the northern frontiers.
These are truly excellent assistants for the restoration of the dynasty,
and pillars of the state.
They should be recalled to the central court
to assist the imperial house,
to align with the seven
luminaries above,
and to bring stability to the myriad states below.
Your subject dares to voice untimely opinions in a court where plain speech is taboo,
like ice and frost seeing the sun,
they are bound to melt away.
Your subject initially grieved over the lamentable state
of the world;
now the world also grieves over your subject's foolishness and delusion."
At that time, someone submitted a memorial arguing that the people's poverty
was caused by cheap and lightweight money,
and suggested recasting larger coins.
The matter was referred to the four ministries, all officials, and scholars fluent in speech from the Imperial Academy.
Táo submitted his opinion, saying: "Enlightened kings, receiving Heaven's mandate, govern all things,
and guide the actions of men.
When they accomplish great deeds, the multitudes rejoice in their work;
when they raise armies, the soldiers delight in their campaigns.
Therefore, in the Spiritual Terrace [Língtái] there were people who came
on their own accord,
and in the martial campaigns there were men who sang 'Fú Zǎo' [ode to diligence].
All actions were appropriate for the times,
and moved in accordance with the human way.
I humbly read the edict on coining money
and the discussions on adjusting the weight.
Enquiring deeply into subtle matters,
not overlooking the poor and humble,
is why this humble person, who eats coarse food,
is mistakenly given this opportunity.
Observing phenomena and nurturing creation,
respectfully assigning the people their seasons,
ensures men do not neglect their fields,
and women do not leave their looms.
Thus, the way of ruler and subject flourishes,
and the teaching of the kingly path is understood.
From this
it can be said,
food is truly the treasure of a nation,
the most precious thing for the common people.
I humbly observe that in recent years,
good crops have been consumed by locusts and grubs,
and looms are empty
due to public and private demands.
What is urgent is the daily meal,
what is feared is the lack of provisions.
How can this be attributed to the thickness or thinness of money,
or the lightness or heaviness of a 'zhū' or 'liǎng'?
Even
if today sand and pebbles turned into Nánjīn gold,
and tiles and stones transformed into Hétián jade,
if the common people have nothing to drink when thirsty,
and nothing to eat when hungry,
even the pure virtue of Huángxī,
or the civilization of Táng and Yú,
would still be unable to protect what is within the palace walls.
Indeed, people can go a hundred years without money,
but cannot endure hunger for a single day.
Therefore, food is of utmost urgency.
The debaters do not grasp the fundamental importance of agriculture,
and instead talk much about the convenience of minting.
Some wish to take advantage of this to commit fraud
and exploit the nation's wealth.
When the nation's wealth is about to be exhausted,
those who take it will compete,
and the origin of minting [more coins] thus arises.
Indeed, if ten thousand people minted,
and one person seized,
it would still not be enough;
how much more so now, if one person mints,
and ten thousand people seize
it?
Even if yin and yang were used as charcoal,
and all creation as copper,
and unfeeding the people
and making them not hungry,
it would still not be enough to satisfy insatiable demands."
Now, for the people to be prosperous and wealth to abound,
the key lies in stopping forced labor and prohibiting expropriation.
Then the common people will be content without toil.
Your Majesty's sagely virtue,
pities the suffering and distress within the seas,
and grieves over the
hardships of the world.
You wish to mint coins to unify currency and remedy its弊 (corrupt practices),
but this is like raising fish in a boiling cauldron,
or nesting birds atop a blazing fire.
Water and wood are originally where fish and birds are born,
yet,
if used unseasonably,
they will surely lead to scorching and ruin.
I wish Your Majesty would ease the prohibitions on thin coinage and melting,
postpone discussions on smelting and casting,
listen to the laments of the common folk,
inquire about the worries of the
roadside elders,
and observe the bright patterns of the three luminaries,
and the branching flows of mountains and rivers.
Then the hearts of all under Heaven,
and the great affairs of the state,
will all be clearly seen,
without
any remaining confusion.
The sounds of hunger and toil
are more severe than these songs.
Is this why the awakening to the sorrow of a common woman's lament over Lǔ
begins here?
Seeing the meaning of the "White Colt" (Bái Jù) poem,
I pace back and forth,
agitated,
unable to sleep soundly.
I humbly reflect that at present the land is vast yet cannot be cultivated,
and the people are numerous yet have nothing to eat.
Petty men scramble forward,
holding positions of national power,
soaring like eagles
over the world,
greedy for satiety like cormorants,
devouring flesh and bone,
gnawing insatiably.
I sincerely fear that suddenly there might be exhausted laborers and impoverished artisans,
rising up from among the
earthen walls,
tossing aside their axes and baring their arms,
ascending high and shouting far,
causing the sorrowful and resentful people
to respond like gathering clouds,
the eight directions to collapse,
and the Central Plain to scatter like fish.
Even a square-inch
coin,
how could it be of any help!
The danger is like lifting a cauldron big enough for a whole ox,
suspended by a slender, withered strand.
This is why poets look back with concern,
and shed tears
for it.
Later, Táo (陶) was recommended as a Xiàolián (孝廉)
and appointed as the magistrate of Shùnyáng (順陽).
The county had many treacherous and cunning individuals.
When Táo arrived at the official post,
he publicly announced recruitment for officials and commoners with strength and bravery,
who were willing to trade death for life,
without distinction of being fugitives or criminals.
Thereupon, more than ten swift sword-wielding bravoes, such as Guò Yàn (過晏),
all came to enlist.
Táo held them accountable for their past transgressions,
demanding future performance,
and had each gather their close young men,
obtaining several hundred people,
all armed and awaiting orders.
Then he investigated criminal activities,
uncovering them as if by divine power.
He was dismissed due to illness,
and the officials and commoners missed him and sang about him, saying:
"The town is indeed unhappy,
missing our Lord Liú (劉).
When will he return,
to bring peace to these common people?"
Táo was skilled in the Shàngshū (尚書) and Chūnqiū (春秋),
and provided commentaries for them.
He collated the Shàngshū
of the Three Schools and the Old Text (Gǔwén),
correcting over seven hundred textual errors,
and named it Zhōngwén Shàngshū (中文尚書).
Shortly thereafter,
he was appointed Shìyùshǐ (侍御史).
Emperor Líng (靈帝) had long heard of his reputation
and frequently invited and received him.
At that time, Zhāng Jiǎo (張角) of Jùlù (鉅鹿) falsely claimed to follow the Great Way,
deceiving and bewitching the common people.
Táo, along with Fèngchē Dūwèi (奉車都尉) Yuè Sōng (樂松) and Yìláng (議郎) Yuán Gòng (袁貢), jointly submitted a memorial about this,
saying:
"A sagely king uses the ears and eyes of all under Heaven as his own hearing and seeing,
thus he can hear and see everything.
Now Zhāng Jiǎo's followers are countless.
Previously, Sītú (司徒) Yáng Cì (楊賜) submitted a memorial asking for an imperial edict,
strictly ordering the provinces and commanderies
to protect and escort migrants.
However, Yáng Cì left his post,
and they were no longer pursued or arrested.
They only met with an amnesty,
but their plot did not disband.
Private rumors from all directions
say that Zhāng Jiǎo and his ilk secretly entered the capital,
spying on court affairs,
with 'bird voices and beast hearts,'
secretly plotting together.
The provinces and commanderies are wary and avoid the topic,
only secretly exchanging information,
none willing to make it public.
It is advisable to issue a clear edict,
heavily reward those who capture Zhāng Jiǎo and his group,
and grant them land as a prize.
Anyone daring to conceal them
shall be punished with the same crime."
The Emperor was utterly unaware,
and instead ordered Táo to arrange the Chūnqiū (春秋) statutes in order.
The next year,
Zhāng Jiǎo rebelled,
and the whole country was in turmoil.
The Emperor remembered Táo's words,
ennobled him as Hóu (侯) of Zhōnglíng Xiāng (中陵鄉),
and thrice promoted him to Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令).
As his former subordinates had been promoted to Shàngshū (尚書),
it was difficult for him to rank alongside them,
so he requested to be a casual official,
and was appointed Shìzhōng (侍中).
Because of his frequent frank remonstrances,
he was feared by powerful officials,
and was transferred to be Jīngzhào Yǐn (京兆尹).
Upon arriving at his post,
he was expected to contribute ten million (qiānwàn) in funds for palace repairs.
Táo was already pure and poor,
and felt ashamed to buy his position with money,
so he claimed illness and did not attend to governance.
The Emperor had long valued Táo's talent,
pardoned his offense,
and summoned him to be appointed Jiàn yì Dàfū (諫議大夫).
At that time, the empire grew more perilous by the day,
with bandits and rebels flourishing.
Táo worried that the situation would collapse into chaos,
and again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that those whose affairs are urgent cannot speak calmly,
and those whose hearts are in pain cannot speak slowly.
I secretly observe that the empire first encountered the chaos of Zhāng Jiǎo,
and later suffered the banditry of Biān Zhāng.
Every time the urgent warnings of the feather-message arrived,
my heart burned within,
and my four limbs trembled in alarm.
Now, the rebellious tribes of the Western Qiāng
have privately appointed their own generals and commanders,
most of whom were officials under Duàn Jiǒng,
skilled and practiced in battle formations,
knowledgeable about mountains and rivers,
and employing myriad deceptions.
Your servant has always feared that they would lightly venture out to Hédōng and Féngyì,
assaulting the rear of the western army,
and advancing east to Hángǔ Pass,
occupying the heights and overlooking the plains.
Now they have indeed attacked Hédōng,
and I fear they will then turn and charge like wild boars towards Shàngjīng.
If this happens, the southern route will be cut off,
the cavalry army will be isolated,
the Guāndōng region will lose heart,
and the four quarters will be shaken.
If we command, they will not come;
if we call, they will not answer.
Even if we had the strategies of Tián Dān and Chén Píng,
their plans would be useless.
Your servant previously sent a swift messenger to offer advice,
urgently suggesting to stop the levies and tributes from various commanderies,
hoping it might still bring stability.
The matter was passed to the responsible officials,
and has been delayed until now,
with no one bothering to inquire about it.
Now the people of the three commanderies have all fled,
moving south out of Wǔguān,
and north to Húgǔ Valley,
scattering like melting ice or wind-blown dust,
fearing only to be left behind.
Of those who remain, there are still only thirteen or fourteen percent.
Military officers, soldiers, and common folk watch each other in sorrow and distress.
The people have a hundred hearts to flee and die,
but not one plan to advance and fight for life.
The western bandits are advancing,
a咫尺 from our camp.
The barbarian cavalry are spread out,
and have already reached the imperial tombs.
General Zhāng Wēn
is naturally brave and resolute,
yet the responsible officials press him day and night,
leaving no rear guard for the army.
If by chance they suffer a defeat,
the disaster will be beyond salvation.
Your servant knows that his words are often unwelcome,
but he cannot restrain himself from speaking,
believing that if the state is secure, his servant will share in its blessings;
if the state is in peril, his servant will also be among the first to perish.
I respectfully present again eight urgent matters for the present situation,
begging a moment of your time
to deeply consider and accept them."
Regarding these eight matters,
they generally stated that the great chaos in the empire
was all due to the eunuchs.
The eunuchs, seeing their situation become urgent,
jointly slandered Táo, saying:
"When the affair of Zhāng Jiǎo first broke out,
the imperial edict showed both majesty and grace.
Since then,
everyone has reformed.
Now the four quarters are peaceful,
yet Táo denounces the sacred administration,
speaking only of evil omens and misfortunes.
If the prefectures and commanderies have not reported anything,
how can Táo know?
We suspect Táo is colluding with the rebels."
Thereupon, Táo was arrested
and imprisoned in the Huángmén Běisì Yù (Northern Prison of the Yellow Gate),
with interrogation and torture intensifying daily.
Táo knew he was doomed to die,
and said to the envoy:
"What did the imperial court enfeoff your servant as before?
Now I am suffering from wicked slander.
I regret not being of the same caliber as Yī and Lǚ,
but instead being counted among the Three Benevolent Ones."
He then held his breath and died.
There was no one in the empire who did not mourn him.
Táo authored several hundred thousand words,
and also wrote Qī Yào Lùn, Kuāng Lǎozi, Fǎn Hán Fēi, Fù Mèng Kē,
as well as memorials discussing current beneficial policies, regulations, rhapsodies, petitions, letters, records, and debates on doubts,
totaling over a hundred pieces.
At that time, the Sītú (Minister of Works), Chén Dān of Dōnghǎi,
also died unjustly in prison with Táo.
Dān was praised for his loyalty and integrity,
and had held positions among the Three Excellencies.
In the fifth year of Guānghé,
an imperial edict commanded the high officials to report, based on rumors, any governors or two-thousand-piculs officials who were harming the people.
At that time, Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) Xǔ Kuí and Sīkōng (Minister of Education) Zhāng Jì catered to the wishes of the inner palace officials,
and accepted bribes.
Although the eunuchs' disciples and guests were corrupt and defiled,
they dared not question them.
Instead, they falsely impeached twenty-six upright and benevolent officials from distant small commanderies.
Officials and commoners went to the palace gate to complain.
Dān and Yìláng (Palace Attendant) Cáo Cāo submitted a memorial, saying:
"The officials nominated by the high officials
mostly favor their own partisans,
which is like releasing owls and jailing phoenixes."
Their words were loyal and incisive.
The emperor reproached Xǔ Kuí and Zhāng Jì because of this,
and consequently, all those who had been summoned due to rumors were appointed Yìláng.
The eunuchs resented this,
and thus falsely accused Dān, leading to his death in prison.
Lǐ Yún, courtesy name Xíngzǔ,
was a native of Gānlíng.
He was fond of learning
and skilled in Yīnyáng.
He was first nominated as Xiàolián (Filial and Incorrupt),
and twice promoted to Bái Mǎ Lìng (Magistrate of Báimǎ).
In the second year of Yánxī of Emperor Huán,
Grand General Liáng Jì was executed.
The five Regular Palace Attendants, including Dān Chāo, were all enfeoffed as marquises due to their meritorious service in executing Jì,
and they monopolized the power of selection and appointment.
Moreover, a common woman from the Yètíng, Lady Bó, was made Empress.
Within a few months,
four members of the Empress's family were enfeoffed,
and rewards amounted to millions.
At this time, the earth frequently trembled and cracked,
and numerous calamities descended repeatedly.
Lǐ Yún was by nature upright,
and worried that the state was nearing peril,
he could not bear it in his heart.
So, he openly submitted a memorial,
and sent copies to the three highest officials,
saying:
"Your servant has heard that the Empress is the mother of all under Heaven,
her virtue matching the Earth's spirit.
If the right person is found, then the five clans will all be prepared;
if the wrong person is found, then the earth will shake the palace.
In recent years, the natural disasters and anomalies
can be said to be numerous,
and the warnings from August Heaven
can be said to be extreme.
Since Emperor Gāozǔ received the mandate,
it has been three hundred and sixty-four years.
The reign of a monarch has a cycle;
there should be a 'Yellow Essence' appearing as a substitute.
The surnames are Chén, Xiàng, Yú, Tián, Xǔ.
These people should not be allowed to hold the offices of Grand Commandant or Grand Mentor, which command troops.
Every action is of utmost importance,
and one cannot but be careful.
The distribution of merits and awards
should correspond to the reality of the achievement.
Although Liáng Jì held exclusive power and control,
and his tyranny spread throughout the empire,
he has now been punished for his crimes,
which is merely like summoning a family retainer and strangling him.
Yet, trusted advisors were arbitrarily enfeoffed with ten thousand households or more.
If Emperor Gāozǔ were to hear of this,
would he not disapprove?
Would the generals in the northwest
not become disheartened?
Confucius said: 'The Emperor (Dì)
is the one who discerns (dì).'
Now, official positions are in disarray,
petty men ingratiate themselves to advance,
bribery is openly practiced,
governance and moral transformation decline daily,
and appointments are made without imperial review or discretion.
Is this because the Emperor does not wish to discern?"
The Emperor, receiving the memorial, was furious and trembled.
He ordered the relevant authorities to arrest Lǐ Yún,
and decreed that the Minister of the Imperial Household, escorted by guards with spears and halberds, send him to the Northern Prison of the Yellow Gates,
and ordered the Regular Palace Attendant Guǎn Bà, along with the Censor and Grand Judge, to jointly investigate him.
At that time, Dù Zhòng, a Registrar of the Five Bureaus from Hóngnóng, lamented that Lǐ Yún had been penalized for his loyal remonstrance,
and submitted a memorial wishing to die on the same day as Lǐ Yún.
The Emperor grew even angrier,
and consequently sent him also to the Grand Judge.
The Grand Herald Chén Fān submitted a memorial to rescue Lǐ Yún, saying:
"Although Lǐ Yún's words
showed ignorance of taboos
and went against the imperial will,
his intention was solely to be loyal to the state.
In the past, Emperor Gāozǔ tolerated Zhōu Chāng's straightforward remonstrance,
and Emperor Chéng pardoned Zhū Yún for pulling the reins of his carriage.
If Lǐ Yún is killed today,
your servant fears that the criticism of 'gouging out one's own heart' will be discussed again in the world.
Therefore, I dare to provoke the dragon's scales
and presumptuously plead for him."
〔一０〕The Grand Master of Ceremonies Yáng Bǐng, the Mayor of Luòyáng Mù Máo, and the Gentleman Shàngguān Zī all submitted memorials requesting for Lǐ Yún.
The Emperor was greatly vexed.
The relevant authorities then reported that this constituted "great irreverence."
An edict sharply reprimanded Chén Fān and Yáng Bǐng,
dismissing them to return to their hometowns;
Mù Máo and Shàngguān Zī were demoted two ranks.
At that time, the Emperor was at the Zhuólóng Pond.
Guǎn Bà presented the matters concerning Lǐ Yún and the others.
Guǎn Bà deceptively said:
"Lǐ Yún is an ignorant scholar from the wilderness,
and Dù Zhòng is a petty official from a commandery;
their actions stem from madness and foolishness,
and do not warrant severe punishment."
The Emperor said to Guǎn Bà:
"'The Emperor does not wish to discern'—what kind of words are these,
that a Regular Palace Attendant wishes to pardon them?"
He then instructed a lesser Yellow Gate attendant to approve the memorial [for punishment].
Lǐ Yún and Dù Zhòng both died in prison.
Later, Jìzhōu Inspector Jiǎ Cóng, while on his inspection tour,
passed by and offered sacrifices at Lǐ Yún's tomb,
and had a stone tablet inscribed to mark it.
The论 (Commentary) says: In the Rites, there are five types of remonstrance,
and veiled criticism is superior.
If one uses objects to express feelings,
and embeds meaning within writing,
so that the speaker is blameless,
and the listener is sufficiently warned,
the value lies in the meaning being conveyed and the words being followed,
and the reason returns to righteousness.
Why should one be so aggressive and confrontational towards the superior,
to flaunt oneself and achieve fame?
Lǐ Yún, a commoner,
did not understand the principle of preserving his life.
Thus, he openly remonstrated with the Emperor
and issued a proclamation to the three highest officials,
even to the point of not caring about facing execution.
This is indeed not the 'madness' of the ancients!
For to remonstrate without first gaining trust
is to be taken as slandering oneself;
thus, those who counsel understand its difficulty.
Liú Yú, courtesy name Jìjié,
was a native of Guǎnglín.
His great-grandfather was the King Jìng of Guǎnglín.
His father, Biàn,
was the Administrator of Qīnghé.
Liú Yú was fond of classical studies in his youth,
and was particularly skilled in prognostication, astronomy, and calendrical calculations.
He did not accept invitations from the commanderies and provinces.
In the eighth year of Yánxī,
Grand Commandant Yáng Bǐng recommended him as a "Worthy and Upright" scholar.
Upon reaching the capital,
he submitted a memorial discussing affairs, saying:
"Your servant Liú Yú considers himself a humble and unrefined person from the eastern land,
yet, as a descendant of Fēngpèi,
I have been granted exemption from corvée,
and am not required to serve in the military.
The late Grand Commandant Yáng Bǐng, knowing that your servant secretly studies
the classics,
unworthily put me forward for prominent recommendation,
sincerely hoping that my foolish straightforwardness
might offer one in ten thousand improvements.
However, Yáng Bǐng's loyal counsel was not realized,
and his life ended like morning dew.
Your servant, in my humble position,
hears
songs and ballads,
tales of arrogant officials and oppressive governance,
and the laments of people near and far.
I am secretly filled with bitterness and sorrow,
weeping tears of blood.
Fortunately, I have been summoned and recorded,
prepared to answer Your Majesty's questions,
and to pour out
my utmost feelings,
daring not to be evasive.
I sincerely wish Your Majesty would take a moment to reflect,
and examine the affairs of the present and past:
Why do people sigh and lament?
Why does Heaven cause commotions
and changes?
People eagerly establish heirs,
to succeed to the lineage and inherit titles,
some begging for children from distant relatives,
others buying children from the marketplace.
This largely deviates from the principle of founding a state and establishing a family.
All of them must adorn themselves with ornaments and lavishly
eat in empty palaces,
exhausting their spirit,
and fostering six kinds of illnesses.
This is a cost to the state,
and a harm to life.
Moreover, the nature of Heaven and Earth,
the proper order of Yin and Yang—
if their ways are separated and cut off,
then floods and droughts will occur together.
The Odes say:
'Five days is the appointed time,
six days and still no meeting.'
Complaints of lonely women gave rise to songs,
recorded by Zhòng Ní (Confucius).
How much more so when from youth to old age,
women are hidden away and perish their lives!
Furthermore, Regular Palace Attendants and Yellow Gate attendants
also extensively marry wives.
The atmosphere of resentment and poison
coalesces into portents of disaster.
There are words circulating among passers-by:
'Officials forcibly abduct women,
take them and then release them,'
causing mutual fear and panic.
Who would not be fully aware of this?
There is no reason for such slander to arise groundlessly.
Zōu Yǎn, a common man,
and the common woman of the Jí family,
still caused extraordinary events like city walls collapsing and frost falling in summer;
how much more so when groups of people are filled with resentment?
Can there be no repercussions?
Severe punishments
and strict laws
are used to enforce.
People who are innocent are unjustly imprisoned,
and people who own land have it unjustly taken away.
Provincial and commandery officials,
each investigate cases themselves,
and evil deeds
Bribery
all becomes bait for officials.
The people are all resentful and disheartened,
rising up to join bandit gangs.
The authorities then raise troops
to punish their crimes.
Impoverished people
sometimes sell their own heads
to claim rewards.
Fathers and elder brothers take turns in mutilating themselves,
while wives and children are forced to witness their families torn apart.
Reduced to such destitution,
and then punished in this way,
how can it not be painful!
The roads are scorched,
and thus violence runs rampant,
nothing is spared.
Currently, the Sāngōng are in office,
all broadly accomplished in the Dào and arts,
and each rectifies themselves,
yet none offers correction or benefit.
This is
not because they lack wisdom,
but because they fear death and punishment.
I humbly suggest that Your Majesty appoint seven ministers
to broaden the channels of remonstrance,
and open the books of the Dōngxù and Jīnténg historians,
to follow the paths to prosperity taken by Yáo,
Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ.
Keep away treacherous and wicked people,
and banish the music of Zhèng and Wèi.
Then governance will achieve peace and harmony,
and virtue will evoke auspicious winds.
I, your subject,
sincerely offer my feelings.
My words may not be worth adopting,
and I fear that by offending,
I will be arrested, imprisoned, and agitated.
When the Emperor died,
the Grand General Dòu Wǔ wanted to execute a large number of eunuchs.
He then invited Yú to be Shìzhōng,
and also appointed Shìzhōng Yǐn Xūn as Shàngshūlìng,
to jointly plan the scheme.
When Dòu Wǔ was defeated,
Yú and Xūn were both executed.
The events are in Dòu Wǔ's biography.
Xūn, courtesy name Bóyuán,
was a native of Hénán.
His paternal grand-uncle Mù was Tàiwèi,
and Mù's grandson Sòng was Sītú.
Xūn was a man of firm resolve and upright character.
When he was young, whenever he read books
and encountered the deeds of loyal ministers and righteous gentlemen,
he never failed to throw down the book and sigh in admiration.
He believed his conduct did not conform to the times,
and did not respond to invitations from prefectures, commanderies, or public offices.
During the reign of Huán Dì,
he was summoned for his sagacity
and successively rose to Shàngshūlìng.
In the Yánxī era,
when Grand General Liáng Jì was executed,
the Emperor summoned Xūn to distribute the various official posts.
He demonstrated excellent strategies,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yíyáng Xiāng.
Púyè Huò Xǔ,
Shàngshū Zhāng Jìng, Ōuyáng Cān, Lǐ Wěi, Yú Fàng, and Zhōu Yǒng
were all enfeoffed as Tínghóu.
Xūn later moved up twice to a Jiǔqīng position,
but was dismissed due to illness,
and then appointed Shìzhōng.
Eight years later,
Zhōngchángshì Jù Yuàn, Zuǒ Guàn, and others were dismissed for their crimes,
and their enfeoffments were revoked.
Consequently, Xūn's and others' ranks were also demoted.
After Yú was executed,
the eunuchs burned all of his memorials,
claiming them to be false rumors.
His son, Wǎn,
inherited Yú's learning,
was skilled in astrological prognostication,
and could describe ominous portents.
He was recommended as a fāngzhèng,
but did not take office.
Xiè Bì, courtesy name Fǔxuān,
was a native of Wǔyáng in Dōngjùn.
He was honest, upright, and just,
and was regarded as a master by his hometown.
In the second year of Jiànníng,
an imperial edict called for sagacious scholars.
Bì, along with Chén Dūn of Dōnghǎi and Gōngsūn Dù of Xuántú, all submitted policy recommendations,
and were all appointed Lángzhōng.
At that time, a green snake appeared in the front palace,
and strong winds uprooted trees.
The Emperor ordered the Gōngqīng and below to state their opinions on the gains and losses.
Bì submitted a sealed memorial, saying: I have heard that harmonious qi responds to virtue,
and ominous portents arise from misgovernance.
When Heaven sends down warnings,
the ruler should reflect on his transgressions.
If the path of governance is flawed,
then corrupt
ministers bear the punishment.
Now, snakes
are born of yin qi;
scales
are symbols of weapons and armor.
The Hóngfàn commentary says:
“When the extreme is weak,
then there will be the evil of snakes
and dragons.”
Moreover, when Yínghuò (Mars) guards Kàng and
lingers without departing,
the law indicates that close ministers are plotting rebellion,
originating from the Emperor's immediate surroundings.
I do not know who Your Majesty's trusted confidants are,
those with whom you relax
within the curtains.
It is advisable to quickly dismiss them
to avert Heaven's warning.
I have also heard
“Only the viper, only the snake,
is a feminine omen.”
I humbly
believe that the Empress Dowager made the decision within the palace
to support and establish the sagacious and enlightened ruler.
The classics say:
“Fathers, sons, and brothers,
their crimes do not implicate each other.”
The execution of the Dòu clan,
how can it be right to extend the blame to the Empress
Dowager?
Isolated in the empty palace,
her sorrow moves Heaven's heart.
If she were to suffer an illness from the mist and dew (i.e., cold and dampness),
what face would Your Majesty have to meet the world?
In the past, King Xiāng of Zhōu failed
to respectfully serve his mother,
and the Róng and Dí consequently invaded.
Emperor Xiàohé did not sever his kindness towards Empress Dòu,
and previous generations considered this a fine example.
The Rites say: “One who becomes a person's
successor becomes their child.”
Now, considering Huán Dì as your father,
how can you not consider the Empress Dowager as your mother?
The Yuánshénqì says:
“When the Son of Heaven practices filial piety,
the Four Barbarians become peaceful
and harmonious.”
Currently, the borders are shrinking daily,
and military conflicts are erupting like swarms of bees.
Other than filial piety,
how can this be remedied!
I wish Your Majesty would look up to emulate the flourishing transformation of Yǒuyú,
and look
down to recall the sentiment of Kāifēng (a poem) comforting one's mother.
When a mother is favored privately,
she enjoys great enfeoffment.
Strong winds, rain, and hail
also stem from this.
Furthermore, the late Grand Tutor Chén Fán,
who assisted Your Majesty as a prime minister,
diligently served the royal house,
working day and night
without slackening,
yet was entrapped by a group of wicked individuals
and was annihilated overnight.
Such extreme cruelty and injustice
shocked the world,
and his disciples and former subordinates
were all exiled and prohibited from office.
Chén Fán himself has
passed away,
and no amount of people can redeem him!
It is fitting to return his family members
and lift the ban.
The high ministers (Tái Zǎi) are vital instruments,
upon whom the nation's destiny depends.
Among the current four Gōng,
only Sīkōng
Liú Chǒng is steadfastly virtuous.
The rest are people who hold office without doing anything and have brought about calamities,
and they are surely destined for the misfortune of breaking their feet and overturning their cauldrons (i.e., failure and disaster).
They should be dismissed,
taking advantage of these portents of disaster.
Summon the former Sīkōng Wáng Chàng
and Chánglè Shǎofǔ Lǐ Yīng
to govern,
so that disasters and calamities may be averted
and the nation's destiny be eternal.
I, your subject, am ignorant and obscure from the mountains and swamps,
not yet comprehending
the national code.
The policy states:
“Do not hide anything.”
How dare I not express my foolishness,
forgetting all taboos and fears.
I humbly request Your Majesty to decide on the punishments.
Cáo Jié's adopted son, Cáo Shào, a Zhōng Chángshì, was the Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn.
He resented Bì deeply,
and so, on some other charge, arrested, tortured, and interrogated him.
Bì died in prison.
People of the time mourned and grieved for him.
In the second year of Chūpíng,
Zhào Qiān, the Sīlì Xiàowèi, pleaded Bì's loyalty and integrity,
and sought to avenge his grievances.
Thereupon, Shào was arrested and executed.
A eulogy states: Dèng Bùmíng did not avoid [calamity].
Liáng Bùsǔn did not harm Líng.
Heartfelt were Luán and Dù,
their remonstrances inspired by their words.
When the Yellow Bandits were rampant,
Zǐqí had foresight.
His military strategies were truly excellent,
and Yú also agreed with his aspirations.
Bì defied the eunuchs' sentiments,
and Yún offended the taboos of the time.
They achieved benevolence and sacrificed themselves,
sharing the same path but different circumstances.
Biography of Yú, Fù, Gài, Zāng (Liezhuan 48)
Yú Xǔ, courtesy name Shēngqīng,
was a native of Wǔpíng, Chénguó.
His grandfather, Jīng,
was a prison official in the commandery and county.
He handled cases fairly according to the law,
striving for leniency and forgiveness.
Every winter, when he submitted the case records,
he would always shed tears as he followed them.
He once said:
"Yú Gōng of Dōnghǎi served as the gatekeeper of his village,
and his son Dìngguó eventually became Chancellor.
I have judged cases for sixty years.
Although I am not as good as Yú Gōng,
I am probably close!
Why should my descendants not become Nine Ministers?"
Thus, he named Xǔ Shēngqīng.
At the age of twelve, Xǔ
could understand the Shàngshū.
He was orphaned early
and cared for his grandmother with filial piety.
The county recommended him as a filial grandson,
and the state chancellor was impressed by him,
wishing to appoint him as an official.
Xǔ declined, saying:
"My grandmother is ninety years old,
and cannot be cared for without me."
The chancellor then stopped.
Later, his grandmother passed away.
After the mourning period,
he was invited to the office of Grand Commandant Lǐ Xiū
and appointed Lángzhōng.
In the fourth year of Yǒngchū,
the Qiāng and Hú rebelled,
devastating Bìng and Liáng [provinces].
General-in-chief Dèng Zhì believed that military expenses were high,
and resources were insufficient.
He wished to abandon Liángzhōu
and concentrate forces on the northern border.
So, he convened the high officials for a discussion.
Zhì said:
"It is like a torn garment;
sacrificing one part to patch another still leaves something whole.
If we do not do this,
we will lose both."
All the deliberators agreed.
When Xǔ heard this,
he explained to Lǐ Xiū:
"I have heard that the high officials have decided to abandon Liángzhōu.
In my humble opinion,
I do not see its convenience.
The former emperor opened up and expanded our territory,
toiling to establish it later.
But now, fearing a small expense,
we propose to abandon it.
Once Liángzhōu is abandoned,
the Sānfǔ will become the frontier;
if Sānfǔ becomes the frontier,
then the imperial tombs will be exposed.
This is an extreme impropriety.
It is said:
'Guānxī produces generals,
and Guāndōng produces chancellors.'
Observing their martial skills and bravery,
they indeed surpass other provinces.
The reason the Qiāng and Hú dare not invade and occupy Sānfǔ
to become a threat to our heartland
is because Liángzhōu is behind them.
The reason its natives push forward with sharp weapons,
without thoughts of retreating,
is because they are subjects of Hàn.
If we abandon their territory
and relocate their people,
being attached to their land and reluctant to move,
they will surely develop rebellious intentions.
If powerful heroes gather,
sweeping eastward,
even if Bēn and Yù were soldiers,
and Tàigōng were a general,
I fear they would not be sufficient to defend against them.
The debaters liken it to patching a garment, which still leaves something whole;
I fear it would be like a spreading ulcer that invades without limit.
Abandoning it is not a good plan."
Xiū said:
"My thoughts did not reach this far.
Without your words,
the affairs of the state would almost be ruined.
What, then, should the plan be?"
Xǔ said:
"Currently, the land of Liáng is disturbed,
and the people are unsettled.
I secretly worry about sudden and extraordinary changes.
