It would be truly appropriate to order the Four Bureaus and Nine Ministers
to each invite several people from that province,
and all the sons and younger brothers of its governors, administrators, magistrates, and chiefs should be appointed to vacant posts.
Outwardly, this encourages and rewards
their merits and diligence;
inwardly, it restrains them
and prevents their wicked schemes."
Xiū praised his words
and reconvened the Four Bureaus;
all followed Xǔ's suggestion.
Thereupon, eminent figures from Xīzhōu were appointed as clerks and subordinates,
and the sons and younger brothers of governors, administrators, and chief officials were appointed as Láng,
to appease them.
Dèng Zhì and his brothers, because Xǔ had disagreed with their proposal,
were consequently displeased
and sought to harm Xǔ through legal means.
Later, Níng Jì and other bandits from Cháogē, numbering several thousand, attacked and killed chief officials,
and were entrenched for years.
The province and commandery could not suppress them.
So, Xǔ was made the Magistrate of Cháogē.
His old friends all consoled Xǔ, saying:
"To be sent to Cháogē, how unlucky!"
Xǔ laughed and said:
"Not to seek what is easy,
not to avoid what is difficult,
is the duty of a minister.
Without encountering tangled roots and gnarly knots,
how can one distinguish a sharp tool?"
Upon his arrival,
he paid his respects to Mǎ Léng, the Grand Administrator of Hénèi.
Léng encouraged him, saying:
"You are a scholar;
you should be strategizing in the imperial court.
Why are you in Cháogē instead?"
Xǔ said:
"On the day of my initial appointment,
all the officials came to condole and encourage me.
They deemed me deceptive,
knowing that I could do nothing.
Cháogē
is the border region of Hán and Wèi,
backed by Tàiháng [mountains] and
facing the Yellow River.
It is a hundred *lǐ* from Áocāng,
and tens of thousands of people from Qīng and Jì have fled there.
The bandits do not know to open granaries to attract followers,
seize weapons from armories,
guard Chénggāo,
and cut off the empire's right arm.
These are not to be worried about.
Currently, their numbers are newly strong,
making it difficult to contend with them head-on.
Warfare does not disdain expediency.
I only ask for a wide berth in strategy,
without any restrictions."
Upon taking office,
he established three categories of regulations to recruit brave men.
From clerks down, each recommended those they knew.
Those who committed robbery and plunder were the top category;
those who injured people or committed theft were next;
those wearing mourning clothes and not attending to family business were the lowest.
He gathered over a hundred men.
Xǔ held a feast for them,
pardoned all their crimes,
and sent them into the bandit ranks,
enticing them to plunder.
Then, he ambushed them,
killing several hundred bandits.
He also secretly dispatched poor people who could sew,
to work as tailors for the bandits.
They stitched the hems of their garments with colored thread as a distinguishing mark.
When any appeared in the markets,
officials would immediately capture them.
The bandits were thereby alarmed and dispersed,
all praising his divine wisdom.
He was promoted to Magistrate of Huái.
Later, the Qiāng people plundered Wǔdū.
Empress Dowager Dèng, considering Yú Xǔ to possess the strategies of a general,
appointed him Administrator of Wǔdū.
She granted him an audience in Jiādé Diàn,
and bestowed generous rewards.
The Qiāng then led several thousand men
to intercept Yú Xǔ at Chénshí and Xiáogǔ.
Yú Xǔ immediately halted his army and did not advance,
but publicly announced that he had submitted a memorial requesting more troops,
and would set out once they arrived.
When the Qiāng heard this,
they divided their forces to raid neighboring counties.
Yú Xǔ, taking advantage of their scattered troops,
advanced day and night,
covering over a hundred *lǐ* a day.
He ordered his officers and men to each make two cooking stoves,
doubling the number each day.
The Qiāng did not dare to approach.
Someone asked,
“Sūn Bìn reduced his stoves, but you increased yours.
Military strategy dictates marching no more than thirty *lǐ* a day
to guard against the unexpected,
yet today you travel almost two hundred *lǐ*.
Why?”
Yú Xǔ replied,
“The barbarians are numerous,
and our troops are few.
If we march slowly, they can easily overtake us;
if we advance quickly, they will not expect it.
When the barbarians see our stoves increasing daily,
they will surely believe that the provincial troops are coming to meet us.
With many troops moving quickly,
they will surely be afraid to pursue me.
Sūn Bìn showed weakness;
I now show strength.
The circumstances are different, that is why.”
Upon reaching the commandery,
his troops numbered less than three thousand,
while the Qiāng numbered over ten thousand.
They besieged Chìtíng for several tens of days.
Yú Xǔ then ordered his army
to refrain from firing strong crossbows,
but secretly to fire small crossbows.
The Qiāng believed the arrows were weak
and could not reach,
so they combined their forces and attacked urgently.
Yú Xǔ then had twenty strong crossbows shoot at a single man,
and none missed their mark.
The Qiāng were greatly alarmed
and retreated.
Yú Xǔ then led an sally from the city and attacked,
inflicting many casualties.
The next day, he arrayed all his troops,
ordering them to exit the East Guōmén
and enter the North
Guōmén,
exchanging clothes,
and circling several times.
The Qiāng did not know their true numbers
and became mutually agitated with fear.
Yú Xǔ calculated that the bandits would retreat,
so he secretly dispatched over five hundred men to set an ambush in the shallow waters,
awaiting their escape route.
The barbarians indeed fled in great panic,
and were ambushed and attacked,
suffering a great defeat.
Many were captured and slain.
The bandits were thus scattered and defeated,
fleeing south into Yìzhōu.
Yú Xǔ then surveyed the terrain,
built 180 garrisons and stockades,
recalled the displaced,
and provided relief to the poor.
The commandery then became stable.
Previously, the transport route was arduous and perilous,
with no passage for boats or carriages.
Donkeys and horses carried loads,
and five units of goods were hired to transport one.
Yú Xǔ then personally led his officers and men
to survey the rivers and valleys.
From Jū to Xiàbiàn,
for several tens of *lǐ*,
he had stones burned and trees cut,
opening a canal for boats.
He used the hire fees for human labor to employ workers.
Thus, water transport became smooth and profitable,
saving over forty million (cash) annually.
When Yú Xǔ first arrived in the commandery,
households barely exceeded ten thousand.
After pacifying and gathering the remnants
and recalling the scattered,
within two or three years,
they increased to over forty thousand households.
Salt and rice became abundant and cheap,
ten times more so than before.
He was dismissed due to a legal offense.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn (126 CE),
he replaced Chén Chán as Commandant of the Capital.
Within a few months,
he impeached Grand Tutor Féng Shí, Grand Commandant Liú Xī, and Central Regular Attendants Chéng Huáng, Chén Bǐng, Mèng Shēng, Lǐ Rùn, and others.
All officials watched him cautiously,
calling him harsh and severe.
The Three Ducal Ministers impeached Yú Xǔ, alleging he unjustly detained many innocents in midsummer,
causing distress to the officials and people.
Yú Xǔ submitted a memorial defending himself, saying:
“Laws and prohibitions are the dikes of custom;
punishments are the reins of men.
Now, provinces say they trust the commanderies,
and commanderies say they trust the counties,
mutually delegating responsibilities from afar.
The common people are resentful and impoverished,
considering indulgence to be sagely
and loyalty to be foolish.
The crimes I have exposed
are not few.
The two high offices fear being impeached by me,
and thus maliciously accuse me.
I shall follow Shǐ Yú in death,
and make my remonstrance with my corpse.”
Emperor Shùn reviewed his memorial,
and consequently dismissed Grand Minister of Works Táo Dūn.
At that time, Central Regular Attendant Zhāng Fáng wielded special power,
often making requests and receiving bribes.
Yú Xǔ would invariably investigate him,
but his reports were repeatedly suppressed and not acted upon.
Yú Xǔ, unable to bear his indignation,
then voluntarily reported himself to the Court of Judicial Review,
and submitted a memorial stating:
“In the past, Emperor Xiào'ān employed Fán Fēng,
who then disrupted the legitimate succession,
almost destroying the state.
Now, Zhāng Fáng again manipulates power,
and the nation's disaster will soon arrive again.
Your servant cannot bear to serve in the same court as Fáng.
I humbly report myself for detention to make this known,
lest your servant follow in Yáng Zhèn’s footsteps.”
When the memorial was presented,
Zhāng Fáng wept and complained to the emperor.
Yú Xǔ was convicted and sentenced to forced labor at the Left Bureau.
Zhāng Fáng was determined to harm him.
Within two days,
he was interrogated and examined in four prisons.
The prison officials advised Yú Xǔ to commit suicide.
Yú Xǔ said,
“I would rather fall beneath the executioner's blade to demonstrate [my innocence] to those far and near.”
The eunuchs Sūn Chéng and Zhāng Xián and others, knowing Yú Xǔ was punished for his loyalty,
then together presented a memorial requesting an audience.
Sūn Chéng said:
“When Your Majesty and your servants first undertook this enterprise,
you always detested treacherous officials,
knowing they would subvert the state.
Now that you are on the throne, you again act for yourself.
How is this different from the former emperor?
Commandant of the Capital Yú Xǔ was utterly loyal to Your Majesty,
yet he is now detained;
Regular Attendant Zhāng Fáng’s crimes of corruption are clear and evident,
yet he falsely accuses the loyal and good.
Now, a 'guest star' guards the Yǔlín,
which portends treacherous officials in the palace.
It is fitting to immediately arrest Zhāng Fáng and send him to prison
to avert this celestial omen.
Issue an edict to release Yú Xǔ
and restore his official seal and ribbons.”
At this time, Zhāng Fáng was standing behind the emperor.
Sūn Chéng then shouted at Zhāng Fáng, saying,
“Treacherous official Zhāng Fáng,
why do you not descend from the hall!”
Zhāng Fáng had no choice
and hurried to the eastern annex.
Sūn Chéng said,
“Your Majesty, quickly arrest Zhāng Fáng,
and do not let him seek favors from the Empress Dowager.”
The emperor questioned the various Imperial Secretaries.
Imperial Secretary Jiǎ Lǎng, who was always friendly with Zhāng Fáng,
attested to Yú Xǔ's guilt.
The emperor was doubtful
and said to Sūn Chéng,
“You may leave for now;
I will consider this.”
Thereupon, Yú Xǔ’s son, Yǐ, and over a hundred disciples
raised banners and awaited the carriage of Central Regular Attendant Gāo Fàn.
They kowtowed until their heads bled,
pleading his wrongful situation.
Gāo Fàn then entered and reported it.
Zhāng Fáng was sentenced to exile to the frontier,
Jiǎ Lǎng and six others either died or were dismissed.
Yú Xǔ was pardoned and released that very day.
Sūn Chéng again submitted a memorial, presenting Yú Xǔ's great achievements,
his words very urgent and impassioned.
The emperor was moved and enlightened,
and again summoned him to be appointed Counselor.
A few days later, he was promoted to Chief Imperial Secretary.
At that time, chief officials and officials receiving a salary of two thousand *dàn* who heard cases of common people being fined and punished would have them pay a redemption fee.
This was
called "righteous money" (Yìqián),
ostensibly to be stored for the poor,
but the governors and magistrates used it to amass wealth.
Xǔ (Xǔ) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Since the first year of Yuánnián (Yuánnián),
impoverished common people have repeatedly reported that chief officials have taken millions [of cash] or more,
and such complaints are endless.
Officials and commoners have been fined and punished to the tune of tens of millions,
yet the Three Excellencies (Sāngōng) and regional inspectors (Cìshǐ) have rarely impeached anyone.
I recall that during the Yǒngpíng (Yǒngpíng) and Zhānghé (Zhānghé) eras,
commanderies and counties used money for soldiers and porters to lend to the poor,
and the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) investigated the matter,
resulting in the dismissal of all commandery, county, and prefecture officials.
Now, we should follow previous precedents
and abolish these temporary regulations."
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued, referencing Xǔ's (Xǔ) memorial,
sternly reprimanding the commanderies and counties.
Fines and redemptions ceased from this point.
Previously, the Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) of Níngyáng (Níngyáng) had gone to the palace gate
to complain about the injustice of his county magistrate (xiànlìng),
but his plea remained unheeded for six or seven years.
The Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) then submitted a memorial, saying:
"I am Your Majesty's son,
and Your Majesty is my father.
I have submitted a hundred memorials,
yet none have been heeded.
How can I not go north to the Xiongnu Chányú (Chányú) to voice my grievances?"
The Emperor was greatly angered,
held the memorial, and showed it to the Grand Secretaries (Shàngshū).
The Grand Secretaries (Shàngshū) then impeached him for high treason.
Xǔ (Xǔ) refuted this, saying:
"What the Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) complained about
was an injustice to his lord and father;
that a hundred submissions failed to reach [the Emperor]
was the fault of the officials in charge.
A foolish and simple person
is not worth executing extensively."
The Emperor accepted Xǔ's (Xǔ) words,
and he was merely flogged.
Xǔ (Xǔ) then said to the Grand Secretaries (Shàngshū):
"If a common person has a grievance,
and travels a thousand *lǐ* (lǐ) or more,
cutting his hair and carving his flesh,
to present his case at the palace gate,
and it is not addressed,
how is that the righteousness of your subordinates?
What kinship do you have with corrupt chief officials,
and what enmity do you have with the aggrieved person?"
Those who heard him were all ashamed.
Xǔ (Xǔ) also memorialized:
"Court Gentlemen (Táiláng) hold prominent positions,
a common stepping stone in official careers.
Now, some commanderies have seven or eight,
while some provinces have none.
It is fitting that they be evenly distributed,
to satisfy the expectations of all under Heaven."
And many of his memorials and proposals
were adopted.
Xǔ (Xǔ) enjoyed impeaching and exposing wrongdoing,
showing no deference,
and repeatedly offended powerful relatives and influential families with this,
consequently being censured and investigated nine times,
and suffering punishment three times.
Yet his upright and steadfast nature
remained unyielding until old age.
At the beginning of the Yǒnghé (Yǒnghé) era,
he was promoted to Minister of the Grand Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng),
but was dismissed from office due to a public matter.
The imperial court esteemed his loyalty
and summoned him again,
but he died soon after.
On his deathbed,
he said to his son Gōng (Gōng):
"I served my lord with integrity
and acted without shame.
My only regret is that when I was the magistrate of Cháogē (Cháogē), I killed several hundred bandits,
and how could there not have been some innocent among them?
Since then, for over twenty years,
my family has not added a single member.
This is how I incurred the wrath of Heaven."
Gōng (Gōng) possessed outstanding talent,
and his highest office was Administrator of Shàngdǎng (Shàngdǎng).
Fù Xiè (Fù Xiè), courtesy name Nánróng (Nánróng),
was a native of Língzhōu (Língzhōu), Běidì (Běidì).
His original courtesy name was Yòuqǐ (Yòuqǐ),
but admiring Nánróng (Nánróng) who "thrice repeated the white *guī*",
he changed his courtesy name.
He was eight *chǐ* tall and possessed an imposing presence.
In his youth, he studied under Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Liú Kuān (Liú Kuān).
He was twice nominated as Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián).
When he heard that the commander he had nominated had died,
he
resigned his office to observe mourning.
Later, he became Protector-General's Chief Clerk (Hùjūn Sīmǎ)
and joined Left General of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household (Zuǒ Zhōngláng Jiāng) Huángfǔ Sōng (Huángfǔ Sōng) in suppressing the rebel Zhāng Jiǎo (Zhāng Jiǎo).
Xiè (Xiè) had always detested eunuchs.
Having set out,
he then submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that the calamities under Heaven
do not arise from external sources,
but all originate internally.
Therefore, when Yú Shùn (Yú Shùn) ascended the throne,
he first eliminated the Four Felons,
and only then employed the Sixteen Ministers.
It is clear that if evil people are not removed,
good people have no means to advance.
Now, Zhāng Jiǎo (Zhāng Jiǎo) has risen in Zhào (Zhào) and Wèi (Wèi),
and the Yellow Turbans (Huángjīn) are in turmoil across six provinces.
These are all troubles that erupted within the inner chambers,
yet their disaster extends to the four seas.
I have received military command,
bearing the imperial charge to punish the wicked,
and upon arriving in Yǐngchuān (Yǐngchuān),
my battles have been without fail.
Although the Yellow Turbans (Huángjīn) are mighty,
they are not cause for worry in the imperial court.
What I fear
is like controlling a flood without addressing its source,
where the downstream currents only grow wider.
Your Majesty's benevolence, virtue, and magnanimity
lead you to tolerate much,
hence eunuchs wield power,
and loyal officials cannot advance.
Even if Zhāng Jiǎo (Zhāng Jiǎo) were to be utterly destroyed
and the Yellow Turbans (Huángjīn) to change their ways,
my worries
would only deepen.
Why is this?
For wicked and righteous people cannot coexist in the same state,
just as ice and charcoal cannot be in the same vessel.
Knowing that the merits of righteous people become manifest,
and the omens of their own peril appear,
they will all use clever words and elaborate arguments
to collectively foster falsehood.
A filial son can be doubted by repeated visits,
and a tiger in the market is believed by three men.
If the truth and falsehood are not carefully distinguished,
loyal officials will again face the execution at Dùyóu (Dùyóu).
Your Majesty should reflect on Yú Shùn's (Yú Shùn) act of punishing the Four Felons,
and swiftly carry out the execution and banishment of slandering flatterers.
Then good people will be eager to advance,
and treacherous villains will naturally cease.
I have heard that a loyal minister serving his lord
is like a filial son serving his father.
When a son serves his father,
how can he not express his full feelings?
Even if I were to suffer the punishment of the axe and hatchet,
should Your Majesty heed my words even slightly,
it would be a blessing for the state."
When the memorial was presented,
the eunuch Zhào Zhōng (Zhào Zhōng) saw it and became furious.
When Zhāng Jiǎo (Zhāng Jiǎo) was defeated,
Xiè (Xiè)'s numerous merits warranted enfeoffment,
but Zhōng (Zhōng) slandered him.
Emperor Líng (Língdì) still remembered Xiè's (Xiè) words,
and so he was spared punishment,
but ultimately he was not enfeoffed,
and was made Commandant of Āndìng (Āndìng).
He was relieved of duty due to illness.
Later, he was appointed Yìláng.
It happened that the Western Qiāng revolted,
Biān Zhāng and Hán Suí caused disturbances in Lǒngyòu,
conscripting troops from all under Heaven,
with endless labor and taxes.
Sītú Cuī Liè believed that Lǐangzhōu should be [⿱𠫓廾]abandoned.
An imperial edict summoned the gōngqīng and all officials,
and Liè adamantly adhered to his original proposal.
Xiè sternly said:
“Execute the Sītú,
then all under Heaven will be at peace.”
Shàngshūláng Yáng Zàn impeached Xiè for publicly insulting a high official.
The emperor questioned Xiè about this.
Xiè replied:
“In ancient times, Màodún was extremely rebellious,
and Fán Kuài, as a supreme general,
wished to lead a hundred thousand troops to march through the Xiōngnú territory.
His indignation and desire to fight
did not violate the duty of a subject,
it was merely a question of whether his plan should be followed or not.
Yet Jì Bù said, ‘Kuài should be executed.’
Now, Lǐangzhōu is a vital region for all under Heaven,
a frontier defense for the state.
When Gāozǔ first rose,
he sent Lì Shāng to separately pacify Lǒngyòu;
Shìzōng expanded the borders,
establishing four commanderies,
which strategists considered cutting off the right arm of the Xiōngnú.
Now, the administration of the regional inspector has been discordant,
causing an entire province to rebel,
and the whole country is in turmoil,
His Majesty cannot rest peacefully.
Liè, as prime minister,
does not contemplate policies to suppress it for the benefit of the state,
but instead wishes to abandon a vast territory of ten thousand *lǐ*.
I am secretly perplexed by this.
If these barbarian invaders, who wear clothes opening to the left, were to occupy this land,
with strong soldiers and sturdy armor,
they would use it to cause further chaos.
This would be the gravest concern for all under Heaven,
a deep worry for the altars of soil and grain.
If Liè does not know this,
it is extreme ignorance;
if he knows and deliberately says it,
it is disloyalty.”
The emperor followed Xiè's counsel.
From then on, the imperial court respected his uprightness,
and whenever there was a vacancy among the gōngqīng,
he was the one everyone suggested.
After a while,
Zhào Zhōng became Chēqí Jiāngjūn.
The emperor commanded Zhōng to assess the merits of suppressing the Yellow Turbans.
Zhífengwú Zhēn Jǔ and others said to Zhōng:
“Fù Nánróng (Fù Xiè) was formerly in the Eastern Army,
had merits but was not enfeoffed,
hence all under Heaven is disappointed.
Now that the general personally bears a heavy responsibility,
you should advance the worthy and redress wrongs,
to satisfy the public.”
Zhōng accepted their words
and sent his younger brother, Chéngmén Xiàowèi Yán, to convey his regards.
Yán said to Xiè:
“If Nánróng would only slightly defer to my Chángshì (Zhào Zhōng),
a marquisate of ten thousand households would not be difficult to obtain.”
Xiè sternly refused him, saying:
“To be recognized or not,
is fate;
for merits not to be acknowledged,
is the times.
Would Fù Xiè seek private rewards!”
Zhōng harbored even greater resentment,
but fearing Xiè's reputation,
dared not harm him.
Powerful nobles also largely resented him,
which is why he could not remain
and was sent out as Hànyáng Tàishǒu.
Initially,
the former commander of the commandery, Fàn Jīn, was skilled at discerning people
and recommended Xiè as Xiaolián.
When Jīn later served as Hànyáng Tàishǒu,
he handed over his duties to Xiè,
exchanged the imperial tallies, and departed.
His hometown honored this.
Jīn's courtesy name was Wényuān,
and he was a native of Nányáng.
Xiè was good at caring for people,
and the rebellious Qiāng were touched by his benevolence and transforming influence,
all coming to surrender and attach themselves to him.
He then widely opened up military agricultural colonies
and established over forty camps.
At that time, Cìshǐ Gěng Bǐ entrusted the administration to Zhìzhōng Chéng Qiú.
Qiú engaged in illicit gains,
and the literati resented him.
In the fourth year of Zhōngpíng (187 CE),
Bǐ led the troops of six commanderies to suppress the Jīnchéng bandits Wáng Guó and Hán Suí.
Xiè knew that Bǐ had lost popular support
and would certainly fail,
so he admonished him:
“The general has governed for only a short time,
and the people are not yet familiar with your directives.
Confucius said: ‘To lead people into battle without training them
is called [⿱𠫓廾]abandoning them.’
Now, leading untrained men,
crossing the barrier of Dàlǒng,
will result in ten dangers out of ten endeavors.
Moreover, when the bandits hear that a large army is approaching,
they will certainly become united.
The frontier soldiers are mostly brave,
their vanguard is hard to resist,
and a newly assembled force
lacks harmony between superiors and subordinates.
Should an internal change occur,
it would be too late to regret.
It would be better to rest the army and cultivate virtue,
clearly administering rewards and punishments.
If the bandits are given a respite,
they will surely think us timid,
and the various evil factions will contend,
their division is certain.
Then, leading trained men
to suppress divided bandits,
success can be awaited with ease.
Now, not pursuing the advantage of absolute safety,
but instead heading towards certain disaster,
I secretly find it unacceptable for the general.”
Bǐ did not listen.
When they reached Dídào,
there indeed were rebels,
who first killed Chéng Qiú,
then harmed Bǐ.
The rebels then advanced and besieged Hànyáng.
With few soldiers and exhausted provisions in the city,
Xiè still held firm.
At that time, several thousand Hú cavalry from Běi[dì] accompanied the rebels in attacking the commandery.
They all cherished Xiè’s kindness from long ago,
and collectively kowtowed outside the city,
asking to escort Xiè back to his hometown.
His son, Gàn, aged thirteen,
was with him in the official residence.
Knowing Xiè’s unyielding nature
and noble righteousness,
he feared his father would be unable to compromise his will to escape.
He stepped forward to admonish him:
“The state is in chaos,
thus causing adults (like you) to be unwelcome at court.
Now all under Heaven has rebelled,
and our troops are insufficient for self-defense.
The Qiāng and Hú from our native region
have previously received your benevolence,
and wish for you to abandon the commandery and return.
Please be sure to agree to this.
Then, slowly return to your hometown,
muster and inspire righteous followers,
and assist those who possess the Way,
to save all under Heaven.”
Before he finished speaking,
Xiè sighed with emotion
and called Gàn by his pet name:
“Biéchéng,
do you think I must die?
Indeed, ‘a sage achieves the ultimate principle,
one of lesser virtue upholds principle.’
Moreover, even with the tyranny of Yīn Zhòu,
Bó Yí refused to eat the millet of Zhōu and died,
and Kǒng Ní praised his worthiness.
Now the court is not as tyrannical as Yīn Zhòu,
and is my virtue truly inferior to Bó Yí?
The world is in chaos, I cannot cultivate a magnificent will,
and yet holding office and receiving emoluments, I would wish to evade its difficulties?
Where would I go?
I must die here.
You have talent and wisdom,
strive diligently, strive diligently.
My Zhǔbù Yáng Huì
is my Chéng Yīng.”
Gàn choked with sobs and could speak no more,
and all those around them wept.
Wáng Guó sent the former Jǐuquán Tàishǒu Huáng Yǎn to persuade Xiè, saying:
“The outcome of success and failure
is already clear.
One who rises first
can achieve the deeds of a hegemon king,
and below, accomplish the merits of Yī and Lǚ.
All under Heaven no longer belongs to Hàn.
Would the Prefect (Fù Xiè) be willing to be a teacher for us?”
Xiè grasped his sword and roared at Yǎn:
“You, a minister who received an imperial tally,
are instead speaking for rebels!”
He then waved to his attendants to advance the troops
and died in battle.
He was posthumously honored as Zhuàngjié Hóu.
Gàn became famous
and rose to the position of Fúfēng Tàishǒu.
Gài Xūn, courtesy name Yuángù,
was a man from Guǎngzhì, Dūnhuáng.
His family for generations had held offices of two thousand shí.
Initially nominated as xiàolián,
he served as the Chief Scribe of Hànyáng.
At that time, the Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi, relying on his power and influence,
indulged in greed and tyranny.
Sū Zhènghé, a functionary from Wǔdū, investigated and established his guilt.
Liáng Hú, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, fearing the imperial relatives,
wished to kill Zhènghé to absolve himself of fault,
so he consulted Xūn.
Xūn had long harbored enmity towards Zhènghé,
and some advised Xūn to use this opportunity to take revenge.
Xūn said:
“Absolutely not.
To plot and kill an innocent person
is not loyalty;
to take advantage of someone’s danger
is not benevolence.”
He then advised Hú, saying:
“If one tethers an eagle and feeds it, desiring its ferocity,
and then, when it becomes fierce, slaughters it,
what use will it be?”
Hú followed his advice.
Zhènghé, delighted at his reprieve,
went to Xūn to offer thanks.
Xūn refused to see him,
saying:
“I planned for Inspector Liáng,
not for Sū Zhènghé.”
His resentment remained as before.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng (184 CE),
the Qiāng and Hú tribes of Běidì, along with Biān Zhāng and others, rebelled and raided Lǒngyòu.
The Inspector, Zuǒ Chāng, taking advantage of the military campaign, embezzled tens of millions.
Xūn strongly remonstrated,
but Chāng, enraged,
ordered Xūn to separately garrison Āyáng to resist the enemy’s vanguard,
intending to use the military situation to find fault with him.
However, Xūn repeatedly achieved military successes.
Biān Zhāng and others then attacked Jīnchéng,
killing the Administrator Chén Yì.
Xūn urged Chāng to go to their aid,
but he did not comply.
Biān Zhāng and others advanced and besieged Chāng in Jì.
Chāng, fearful, summoned Xūn.
Xūn had initially been garrisoned at Āyáng with his functionaries Xīn Zēng and Kǒng Cháng.
When Chāng’s summons arrived,
Zēng and others were hesitant and unwilling to go.
Xūn angrily said:
“In the past, Zhuāng Jiǎ was late,
and Ráng Jū drew his sword.
Are today’s functionaries
more important than the ancient’s army supervisors?”
Zēng and others, fearing, followed him.
Xūn immediately led his troops to rescue Chāng.
Upon arrival,
he reproached Biān Zhāng and others,
accusing them of treason.
They all said:
“If Inspector Zuǒ had followed your advice earlier,
and brought troops against us,
we might have been able to reform ourselves.
But now our crimes are too heavy,
and we cannot surrender.”
So they lifted the siege and departed.
Chāng was dismissed for embezzlement and summoned,
and Sòng Xiāo of Fúfēng replaced him.
Xiāo was troubled by the many rebels
and said to Xūn:
“Liángzhōu lacks scholarship,
which is why rebellions frequently occur.
Now I wish to extensively copy the Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety),
and have every household study it,
hoping it might make people understand righteousness.”
Xūn advised:
“In ancient times, Tài Gōng was enfeoffed in Qí,
yet Cuī Zhù murdered his lord;
Bó Qín was made marquis of Lǔ,
yet Qìng Fù usurped the throne.
Were these two states lacking scholars?
Now, instead of urgently seeking methods to quell the troubles,
you are hastily undertaking an extraordinary measure.
This will not only incur resentment throughout the province
but also become a laughingstock for the imperial court.
I do not think this is advisable.”
Xiāo did not listen
and proceeded to implement it.
Indeed, he received an imperial edict of reprimand,
and was dismissed for his arrogance and frivolity.
At that time, the rebellious Qiāng besieged Xià Yù, the Colonel Protector of the Qiāng, at Xùguān.
Xūn, with combined forces from the province and commanderies, went to rescue Yù.
When they reached Húpán,
they were defeated by the Qiāng.
Xūn rallied his remaining troops, about a hundred men,
and formed a “fish-scale” formation.
The elite Qiāng cavalry attacked them fiercely from both sides,
and many soldiers died.
Xūn suffered three wounds,
but stood firm and unmoving,
then pointed to a wooden marker
and said:
“My corpse shall surely lie here.”
Diān Wú, a Qiāng of the Gōujiù tribe,
who had always been treated kindly by Xūn,
then used his troops to shield the crowd, saying:
“Chief Scribe Gài is a worthy man;
those among you who kill him will be committing a crime against Heaven.”
Xūn looked up and cursed him, saying:
“You dead rebel,
what do you know?
Come quickly and kill me!”
The others looked at each other in astonishment.
Diān Wú dismounted and offered his horse to Xūn,
but Xūn refused to mount,
and thus was captured by the rebels.
The Qiāng and Róng admired his righteousness and bravery,
dared not harm him,
and sent him back to Hànyáng.
Later, Inspector Yáng Yōng immediately memorialized to have Xūn appointed as the Grand Administrator of Hànyáng.
At that time, people were suffering from famine,
resorting to cannibalism.
Xūn distributed grain to them,
[一０]first taking out his own family’s provisions to set an example for the populace,
saving over a thousand lives.
Later, he left office
and was summoned to be appointed as Colonel Exterminating the Barbarians.
Emperor Líng summoned him
and asked:
“Why is the empire suffering and rebelling to such an extent?”
Xūn replied:
“It is due to the disturbance caused by the children of favored ministers.”
At that time, Jiǎn Shuò, the Palace Eunuch and Colonel of the Upper Army, was present.
The Emperor glanced at Shuò,
who, startled,
did not know how to respond,
and harbored resentment towards Xūn because of this.
The Emperor then said to Xūn:
“I have already arrayed troops at Pínglèguān,
and disbursed a large amount of treasures from the imperial stores to entice the soldiers.
What do you think?”
Xūn replied:
“Your servant has heard that ‘the former kings displayed virtue, not military might.’
Now, the rebels are far away, yet you set up a formation nearby;
this is insufficient to manifest courage and resolve,
and will only tarnish the military.”
The Emperor said:
“Excellent.
I regret not meeting you sooner;
my courtiers have never uttered such words.”
Xūn, at that time, served alongside Liú Yú, the宗正 (Imperial Clan Court Administrator), and Yuán Shào, the Colonel of the Auxiliary Army, in charge of the imperial guards.
Xūn said to Yú and Shào:
“I have repeatedly met with His Majesty,
and His Majesty is very intelligent,
but he is merely obstructed by those around him.
If we collectively unite our strength to execute the favored sycophants,
and then recruit and promote outstanding talents
to revive the Hàn dynasty,
achieving success and then retiring,
would that not be splendid!”
Yú and Shào also had similar intentions,
and so they allied with each other.
Before they could act,
Zhāng Wēn, the Colonel Director of Retainers, nominated Xūn to be the Administrator of Jīngzhào.
The Emperor was just about to further engage Xūn,
but Jiǎn Shuò and others, fearing him,
all advised following Wēn’s recommendation,
and so he was appointed Administrator of Jīngzhào.
At that time, Yáng Dǎng, the Prefect of Cháng’ān,
whose father was a Regular Palace Attendant,
relied on his influence and indulged in corruption.
Xūn investigated and uncovered over ten million in embezzled funds.
The imperial relatives all pleaded on his behalf,
but Xūn did not listen,
reporting the matter in detail,
and implicating Dǎng’s father.
An imperial edict ordered a thorough investigation,
and his authority shook the capital.
At that time, Gāo Wàng, a Little Yellow Gate from Jīngzhào, served as the Supervisor of Imperial Medicine
and was favored by the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince, through Jiǎn Shuò, had requested that Wàng’s son be recommended as xiàolián,
but Xūn refused to comply.
Someone said:
“The Crown Prince is the Deputy Lord,
and Wàng is his favorite;
Shuò is the Emperor’s favored minister,
yet you oppose them.
This is what is called ‘three resentments make a den’.”
Xūn said:
“Selecting the worthy is to repay the nation.
If they are not worthy, I will not nominate them.
What regret would I have even if I die!”
Although Xūn was in an outer post,
whenever there were secret military or national affairs,
the Emperor would often personally write edicts to inquire of him.
He repeatedly bestowed rewards,
and was greatly trusted and favored,
ranking above other court officials.
When the emperor died,
Dǒng Zhuó deposed the young emperor [Shàodì],
and killed Empress Dowager Hé [Hé Tàihòu].
Gài Xūn wrote to Dǒng Zhuó, saying:
“In the past, Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng wielded power to accomplish great deeds,
yet one can still feel a chill at their actions.
You, sir, are a petty scoundrel,
how can you hope to succeed in this?
Those who offer congratulations are at the gate,
while those who offer condolences are in their homes.
Can you not be careful? ”
Dǒng Zhuó received the letter
and was greatly awed by him.
He summoned Gài Xūn to be an Advisor [Yìláng].
At that time, General of the Left Huángfǔ Sōng [Huángfǔ Sōng] had 30,000 elite troops stationed in Fúfēng.
Gài Xūn secretly sought to ally with him,
intending to attack Dǒng Zhuó.
Coincidentally, Huángfǔ Sōng was also summoned,
and Gài Xūn, considering his forces too weak to act independently,
returned to the capital with them.
From the high officials [gōngqīng] downwards,
none failed to humble themselves before Dǒng Zhuó.
Only Gài Xūn offered a long bow, maintaining proper禮 [lǐ],
and all who witnessed it turned pale.
Dǒng Zhuó asked Minister of Works Wáng Yǔn [Wáng Yǔn],
“I want to appoint an efficient Colonel-Director of Retainers [Sīlì Xiàowèi],
who would be suitable? ”
Wáng Yǔn replied,
“Only Gài Jīngzhào [Gài Jīngzhào] would do. ”
Dǒng Zhuó said,
“This man has more than enough intelligence and wisdom,
but he cannot be entrusted with a powerful position. ”
Instead, he made him Colonel of the Agile Cavalry [Yuèqí Xiàowèi].
Dǒng Zhuó also did not want him to command the imperial guard [jìnbīng] for long,
so he sent him out again as Administrator of Yǐngchuān [Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu].
Before he could reach the commandery,
he was summoned back to the capital.
At that time, Zhū Jùn [Zhū Jùn], the Magistrate of Hénán [Hénán Yǐn], was discussing military affairs with Dǒng Zhuó.
Dǒng Zhuó interrupted Zhū Jùn, saying,
“I have fought a hundred battles and won a hundred victories;
my decisions are made in my heart.
You need not speak idly,
lest you defile my sword. ”
Gài Xūn said,
“In ancient times, Wǔ Dīng [Wǔ Dīng], despite his wisdom,
still sought advice and remonstrance.
How much more so for one like you,
who wishes to silence others? ”
Dǒng Zhuó said,
“I was just joking. ”
Gài Xūn said,
“I have never heard that angry words can be considered a joke. ”
Dǒng Zhuó then apologized to Zhū Jùn.
Although Gài Xūn was unyielding and upright,
he was internally weary of Dǒng Zhuó
and discontent.
He developed a carbuncle on his back and died [zú]
at the age of fifty-one.
His will forbade accepting Dǒng Zhuó's funeral contributions.
Dǒng Zhuó, wishing to appear magnanimous,
issued a memorial granting him secret burial objects from the Eastern Park [Dōngyuán Mìqì] as funeral gifts,
and sent him off according to ritual.
He was buried in Ānlíng.
His son, Gài Shùn [Gài Shùn],
rose to the post of Administrator of Yǒngyáng [Yǒngyáng Tàishǒu].
Zāng Hóng [Zāng Hóng], courtesy name Zǐyuán [Zǐyuán],
was a native of Shèyáng in Guǎnglíng.
His father, Zāng Mín [Zāng Mín],
had a talent for administration.
In the first year of Xīpíng,
the bandit leader Xǔ Zhāo [Xǔ Zhāo] from Kuàijī [Kuàijī] raised an army in Gòuzhāng,
styling himself
“Grand General” [Dà Jiāngjūn],
and established his father, Xǔ Shēng [Xǔ Shēng], as the King of Yuè [Yuèwáng].
They attacked and captured cities,
their numbers reaching tens of thousands.
They appointed Zāng Mín as Inspector of Yángzhōu [Yángzhōu Cìshǐ].
Zāng Mín, leading Chén Yín [Chén Yín], the Administrator of Dānyáng, attacked Xǔ Zhāo
and defeated him.
Xǔ Zhāo then regrouped and continued to cause great trouble.
Zāng Mín and others advanced,
fighting continuously for three years,
and pacified the rebellion,
capturing Xǔ Zhāo and his son
and beheading several thousand people.
Zāng Mín was then promoted to Colonel-Protector of the Southern Xiongnu [Shǐ Xióngnú Zhōnglángjiàng].
When Zāng Hóng was fifteen,
due to his father's merits, he was appointed a Youth Cavalier [Tóngzǐ Láng]
and became famous at the Imperial University [Tàixué].
Zāng Hóng had a magnificent physique
and an extraordinary appearance.
He was nominated as Filial and Incorrupt [Xiàolián]
and appointed Chief of Jíqiū.
At the end of Zhōngpíng,
he resigned his office and returned home.
Administrator Zhāng Chāo [Zhāng Chāo] invited him to be his Chief Clerk [Gōngcáo].
At that time, Dǒng Zhuó assassinated the emperor [shìdì],
endangering the imperial altars [shèjì].
Zāng Hóng persuaded Zhāng Chāo, saying,
“Your Excellency's family has received imperial favor for generations,
and your brothers all hold important commanderies.
Now the imperial house is in peril,
and the treacherous minister [zéichén] glares like a tiger.
This is truly the time for loyal men [yìshì] to pledge their lives.
Currently, your commandery's borders are intact,
and the officials and people are prosperous.
If we beat the drums of war,
we can raise twenty thousand men.
With these, to punish and eliminate the national traitor [guózéi]
and initiate a righteous cause [chàngyì] for all under Heaven,
would that not be appropriate? ”
Zhāng Chāo agreed with his words
and went west with Zāng Hóng to Chénliú,
to discuss matters with his elder brother Zhāng Miǎo [Zhāng Miǎo].
Zhāng Miǎo first said to Zhāng Chāo,
“I heard that when you became Administrator of the commandery,
you entrusted affairs to Zāng Hóng.
What kind of man is Zāng Hóng? ”
Zhāng Chāo replied,
“Zāng Hóng is a unique scholar within the seas [hǎinèi qíshì];
his talent, strategy, wisdom, and calculations are incomparable to mine. ”
Zhāng Miǎo immediately invited Zāng Hóng to speak
and was greatly impressed by him.
He then sent him to see Liú Dài [Liú Dài], Inspector of Yǎnzhōu [Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ],
and Kǒng Zhòu [Kǒng Zhòu], Inspector of Yùzhōu [Yùzhōu Cìshǐ],
and they all became friendly.
Zhāng Miǎo had already made plans,
and when Zhāng Chāo arrived,
they finalized their discussions
and held a grand meeting with all the regional governors and administrators [mùshǒu] in Suānzǎo.
They set up an altar [tánchǎng]
and were about to swear an oath.
However, they deferred to each other,
no one daring to be the first to ascend.
They all pushed Zāng Hóng forward.
Zāng Hóng then adjusted his robes, ascended the altar,
took the blood [cāoxiě], and swore the oath, saying:
“The Han dynasty is unfortunate,
the imperial order [huánggāng] has lost its unity.
The treacherous minister Dǒng Zhuó [Dǒng Zhuó],
has seized the opportunity to wreak havoc,
bringing disaster upon His Majesty [Zhìzūn]
and poisoning the populace.
We greatly fear the ruin of the altars of soil and grain [shèjì]
and the overthrow of the four seas.
Inspector Dài [Dài] of Yǎnzhōu [Yǎnzhōu], Inspector Zhòu [Zhòu] of Yùzhōu [Yùzhōu], Administrator Miǎo [Miǎo] of Chénliú, Administrator Mào [Mào] of Dōngjùn,
Administrator Chāo [Chāo] of Guǎnglíng, and others,
have gathered a righteous army [yìbīng]
to jointly confront the national calamity.
All of us, our allies,
are united in heart and strength,
to fulfill our duty as subjects.
Even if we must lose our heads and lives,
we shall have no second thoughts.
Should anyone violate this oath,
may their life be forfeit,
and may they leave no descendants.
Heaven and Earth [Huángtiān Hòutǔ],
and the bright spirits of our ancestors [Zǔzōng Mínglíng],
bear witness to this! ”
Zāng Hóng's words and demeanor were resolute and inspiring,
and all who heard him
were moved and roused.
After this,
however, all the armies harbored suspicions,
none daring to advance first,
which led to the depletion of provisions [liángchǔ]
and the dispersal of the troops.
At that time, Gōngsūn Zàn [Gōngsūn Zàn], Colonel Who Attacks the Lù [Tǎolǔ Xiàowèi], had a rift with Grand Marshal Liú Yú [Liú Yú].
Zhāng Chāo then sent Zāng Hóng to Liú Yú
to jointly plan against the difficulty.
When he reached Héjiān, he encountered fighting between Yōu and Jì provinces,
which obstructed his route.
He consequently took refuge with Yuán Shào [Yuán Shào].
Yuán Shào saw Zāng Hóng
and was greatly impressed by him,
forming a friendship with him
and appointing Zāng Hóng as Inspector of Qīngzhōu [Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ].
The previous Inspector, Jiāo Hé [Jiāo Hé], was fond of establishing a false reputation
and skilled in pure conversation [qīngtán].
At that time, Yellow Turban [Huángjīn] bandits were erupting everywhere,
but Qīng Province was prosperous,
and its military forces were still numerous.
Jiāo Hé wished to go west with his allies to the capital,
but before he could depart,
the bandits had already sacked cities.
Jiāo Hé did not manage military alerts;
instead, he merely sat with shamans and scribes [wūshǐ],
performing sacrifices and prayers to all the gods.
He also feared that the bandits would cross when the river froze,
so he ordered many "ice-trap pills" [xiànbīngwán] to be made
and thrown into the river.
Consequently, his troops dispersed,
and Jiāo Hé also died of illness.
Zāng Hóng gathered and pacified the scattered and rebellious people,
and the common folk were again at peace.
After serving for two years,
Yuán Shào, fearing his ability,
transferred him to be the Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn,
with his seat at Dōngwǔyáng.
At that time, Cáo Cāo was besieging Zhāng Chāo at Yōngqiū,
who was in great peril.
Zhāng Chāo told his officers:
"Today's situation,
only Zāng Hóng will surely come to my rescue."
Someone said:
"Yuán Shào and Cáo Cāo are currently in good terms,
and Hóng is employed by Shào.
He probably cannot break off good relations and travel far to come,
exchanging blessings for disaster."
Zhāng Chāo said:
"Zǐyuán is a righteous man of the realm,
and will ultimately not betray his foundation.
Perhaps he is being controlled by a powerful force
and cannot reach us."
When Zāng Hóng first heard of Zhāng Chāo's siege,
he wept barefoot,
and mustered his troops,
preparing to go to his aid.
Believing his forces were weak,
he requested troops from Yuán Shào,
but Shào ultimately did not listen to him.
Zhāng Chāo's city subsequently fell,
and the Zhāng clan was exterminated.
Zāng Hóng therefore resented Yuán Shào,
and completely ceased communication with him.
Yuán Shào raised an army and besieged him,
but for a year could not take the city.
He sent Chén Lín, a man from Zāng Hóng's county, with a letter to admonish Zāng Hóng,
showing him the consequences,
and reproaching him with kindness and duty.
Zāng Hóng replied:
"I have received
the esteemed letter,
narrating misfortune and fortune,
addressing both public and private matters with utmost earnestness.
With your talent,
thoroughly versed in classics and records,
how could you be ignorant of the great Way,
or fail to understand my
aspirations?
Therefore, I refrained from
responding at all,
hoping you would remotely fathom my narrow heart
and roughly understand my humble nature.
Now I have again received your message,
citing numerous examples.
Although I
wished not to reply,
my righteous indignation compels me to speak.
Must I return the blade?
Each time I ascend the city wall and face the troops,
observing the banners and drums of the master,
gazing at the tents and canopies,
I am moved by the camaraderie of old friends.
As I touch the bowstring and grasp an arrow,
I cannot help but feel tears stream down my face.
Why is this?
I believe that in assisting my master,
I have nothing to regret;
and my master's treatment of me
surpassed all others.
At the beginning
of my appointment,
our aspirations were united for a great cause:
to sweep away rebels and enemies,
and together uphold the royal house.
How could I have expected that my home province would be invaded,
its Grand Administrator encounter distress,
my request for troops be rejected,
and my departure be restrained,
leading to my former lord,
Zhāng Chāo, being utterly destroyed?
My meager integrity,
unable to be fulfilled,
how can I preserve the way of friendship
and further tarnish my reputation for loyalty and filial piety?
Therefore,
I suppress my grief and wield my spear,
wiping away tears as I sever ties.
If the master had shown a little of the ancient spirit of loyalty and forgiveness—
welcoming those who come and
restraining those who depart—
then I
would have upheld the resolve of Jì Zhá,
and there would be no battle today.
Because of a message,
I was not granted leniency for my transgression,
but instead suffered the disaster of annihilation.
When Lǚ Fèngxiān came to defect after attacking Zhuó,
he did not receive troops.
What was his crime
in asking to leave,
that he was again cut down and stabbed?
When Liú Zǐhuáng served as envoy past his appointed time,
he was denied permission to resign.
Fearing his lord and missing his kin,
he used a deception to seek return.
He could be said to have a heart for loyalty and filial piety,
without harming the Way of the Hegemon.
Yet he too was left a corpse beneath the banners,
not granted any exemption.
Those who seek advancement are honored;
those who oppose are executed.
This is the master's gain,
not the wish
of wandering scholars.
Therefore, learning from the lessons of predecessors,
I will defend this isolated city to the death.
Also, a gentleman does not
defect to an enemy state.
Righteousness may lead to ruin.
In the past, Yàn Yīng did not yield his will to sharp blades,
and the Southern Historian did not distort his writing to preserve his life.
Thus, their images were transmitted,
and their names endure for posterity.
Moreover, I hold a fortified city,
command the strength of scholars and commoners,
distribute three years' worth of stores as one year's provisions,
relieving the distressed and assisting the lacking,
to please the world.
How could I think
of building a house and returning to farming?
I only fear that when the autumn wind stirs up dust,
Bóguī's horse head turns south,
Zhāng Yáng and Fēiyàn's combined forces cause trouble,
the northern frontier will
report urgent danger,
and your trusted aides will present memorials begging to return.
My master should learn from the example of Cáo [Cāo] and his kind,
turn back his banners and withdraw his troops.
Why should he long maintain his fierce anger,
and display
his might beneath my city?
He established his foundation from the Green Forest,
and eventually soared like a dragon to receive the Mandate,
restoring the imperial enterprise.
If one can assist the lord in promoting civilization,
what is there to dislike?
Moreover, I personally received an imperial rescript
and served with him!
in Cháng'ān.
You say that I will die and my name will perish;
I also laugh that you will live and die without renown.
Though our origins were the same, our paths diverge at the end.
Strive, strive!
What more
can be said!"
Yuán Shào saw Zāng Hóng's letter,
knew he had no intention of surrendering,
and increased his troops for an urgent assault.
Inside the city, provisions were exhausted,
and there was no outside relief.
Zāng Hóng, judging himself inescapable,
called his officers and men and said:
"Yuán Shào is lawless,
plotting treachery,
and moreover did not rescue Hóng's Grand Administrator.
For the sake of great righteousness,
Hóng cannot but die.
I fear that you gentlemen have done nothing wrong,
yet are caught in this calamity.
You may leave with your wives and children
before the city falls."
The officers and men all wept and said:
"Our Lord and the Yuán clan
originally had no enmity.
Now, for the sake of the Grand Administrator,
you have brought yourself into danger and distress.
How can we, your subordinates, bear to abandon our Lord and leave?"
At first, they even dug for rats,
tendons, and horns.
Later, having nothing left to eat,
the Chief Clerk reported three dòu of rice in the inner kitchen,
and requested to make some gruel.
Zāng Hóng said:
"How can I enjoy this alone?"
He had thin gruel made
and distributed it throughout the army.
He also killed his beloved concubine,
and fed her to the soldiers.
The soldiers all shed tears,
unable to look up.
Seventy or eighty men and women died leaning against each other,
none defecting.
The city fell,
and Zāng Hóng 臧洪 was captured alive.
Yuán Shào 袁紹 erected a splendid tent
and convened all his generals to see Zāng Hóng 臧洪.
He said to him:
“Zāng Hóng 臧洪, how could you betray me to such an extent!
Are you submitting today?”
Zāng Hóng 臧洪 squatted on the ground, glaring, and said:
“The Yuán 袁 clan served the Hàn 漢,
with four generations holding five ducal positions,
which can be called having received great favor.
Now the imperial house is weak,
yet you have no intention of supporting it,
but instead wish to seize the opportunity
to desire what is beyond your hopes,
killing many loyal and good men
to establish your treacherous authority.
I personally saw the general call Zhāng Chénliú 張陳留 his elder brother;
then my lord Zāng Hóng 臧洪 should also be his younger brother.
Yet you could not unite your efforts
to eliminate harm for the state,
but instead sat idly with your army
watching others be massacred.
I regret that my strength is insufficient
to wield a blade and avenge the world;
how can I speak of submitting?”
Yuán Shào 袁紹 originally loved Zāng Hóng 臧洪,
intending to make him submit and then pardon him.
Seeing his vehement refusal,
knowing he would ultimately not be used,
he ordered him to be killed.
Chén Róng 陳容, a native of Zāng Hóng’s 臧洪邑 district,
had been a scholar in his youth,
and was fond of and admired Zāng Hóng 臧洪.
He followed him to become the Administrator of Dōngjùn 東郡.
Before the city fell,
Zāng Hóng 臧洪 had sent him to Yuán Shào 袁紹.
At that time, Chén Róng 陳容 was present
and, seeing Zāng Hóng 臧洪 about to die,
he stood up and said to Yuán Shào 袁紹:
“The general is undertaking a great enterprise,
wishing to eliminate tyranny for the world,
yet you first execute the loyal and righteous.
How can this accord with Heaven’s will?
Zāng Hóng 臧洪 took up arms as a commandery governor;
how can you kill him!”
Yuán Shào 袁紹 was ashamed,
and had someone drag him out,
saying:
“You are not Zāng Hóng’s 臧洪’s associate;
why do you needlessly act like this?”
Chén Róng 陳容 looked back and said:
“Benevolence and righteousness do not have a fixed abode;
to tread by them makes one a jūnzi 君子,
to turn against them makes one a xiǎorén 小人.
Today, I would rather die on the same day as Zāng Hóng 臧洪
than live on the same day as the general.”
Thereupon, he too was killed.
Among those seated with Yuán Shào 袁紹,
none did not sigh,
whispering to each other:
“How can two brave martyrs be executed in one day!”
Previously, Zāng Hóng 臧洪 had dispatched two of his Sīmǎ 司馬 to go out
and seek aid from Lǚ Bù 呂布.
By the time they returned,
the city had already fallen,
and they both rushed to the enemy and died.
The commentary says: During the siege of Yōngqiū 雍丘,
Zāng Hóng’s 臧洪’s righteous indignation was truly grand!
One can imagine him walking barefoot and wailing,
donning his armor and requesting to take up arms;
it is indeed pitiable.
As for the choices of heroes and magnates,
are they different from the heart that upholds righteousness?
If they are those who conspire and form alliances,
harboring deceitful calculations to compete with each other,
it is merely for where benefit and power lie.
Moreover, when the isolated city was already in peril,
Cáo Cāo 曹操 and Yuán Shào 袁紹 were at peace.
Zāng Hóng 臧洪 merely pointed to external alliances
to relieve the imminent danger.
An army driven by rage and resentment
is avoided by military strategists.
He can be said to have harbored the resolve of weeping for Qín 秦,
but preserving Jīng 荊 is unheard of.
A eulogy states: The Xiānlíng [tribes] disturbed the borders;
Dèng, Cuī [and others] pacified Liáng.
Xǔ and Xiè made plans,
and again fully secured the Jīnfāng region.
Gài Xūn resisted Dǒng [Zhúo],
and in the end was truly unyielding.
With noble aspirations and exceptional integrity,
though his strength failed, his will prevailed.

Biography of Zhāng Héng, Forty-ninth.
Zhāng Héng, courtesy name Píngzǐ,
was a native of Xī'è, Nányáng.
His family had long been a prominent clan.
His grandfather, Kān,
was the Grand Administrator of Shǔjùn.
Zhāng Héng was skilled at writing in his youth,
traveled through the Sānfǔ,
and then entered the capital,
observing the Imperial Academy.
He thus became proficient in the Wǔjīng [Five Classics]
and mastered the Liùyì [Six Arts].
Although his talent surpassed his contemporaries,
he had no arrogant or conceited disposition.
He was always composed and tranquil,
disliking association with common people.
During the Yǒngyuán era,
he was recommended as Xiàolián but did not accept,
and was repeatedly invited to serve in the Duke's offices but did not take up the posts.
At that time, the world had enjoyed peace for a long time,
and from kings and marquises downwards,
no one failed to be extravagant.
Zhāng Héng then emulated Bān Gù's Liǎng Dū,
composing the Èrjīng Fù,
thereby offering subtle admonition.
He pondered and compiled it meticulously,
taking ten years to complete it.
The text is extensive, so it is not included here.
Grand General Dèng Zhì admired his talent,
but Zhāng Héng did not respond to repeated summons.
Zhāng Héng was skilled in mechanical arts,
and especially devoted his thoughts to astronomy, Yīnyáng, and calendrical calculations.
He often indulged in the profound classics,
and said to Cuī Yuàn:
“I have observed the Tàixuán,
and only then did I realize that Zǐyún's profound understanding of numbers was truly exceptional,
and it is comparable to the Wǔjīng,
not merely a genre of biographies.
It makes it difficult for people to discuss the matters of Yīnyáng;
it is a book for the Hàn dynasty that obtained the empire for two hundred years.
After another two hundred years,
will it perhaps come to an end?
Thus, the number of authors [who achieve this]
must be prominent in one generation;
this is a constant omen.
When the Hàn dynasty reaches four hundred years,
the Xuán will flourish!”
Ān Dì had long heard of Zhāng Héng’s skill in scholarship,
and by special imperial summons via gōngchē, he was appointed as Lángzhōng,
and then twice promoted to Tàishǐ Lìng.
He then thoroughly researched Yīnyáng,
perfectly elucidating the precision of the celestial sphere,
created the Húntiān Yí [armillary sphere],
and wrote the Língxiàn and Suànwǎng Lùn,
which explained things with great detail and clarity.
At the beginning of Shùn Dì's reign,
he was transferred again,
and returned to being Tàishǐ Lìng.
Zhāng Héng did not seek fame in his time;
the official posts he held
he would occupy for years without moving.
After leaving his historical post,
he returned after five years.
Then he set up a guest interview [qìngwèn]
and composed Yìngjiān to express his aspirations, saying:
“Then one would act in the evening.
Establish merits and achieve deeds,
thus illuminating a virtuous reputation.
Therefore, Yī Yǐn thought of making the ruler like Yáo and Shùn,
so that the people would live in the era of Táng and Yú.
How could those be empty words
only?
They must have been for the sake of manifesting their inherent integrity.
Jiù Dān and Wū Xián
truly guarded the royal house.
Shēn Bó and Fán Zhòng
truly served the Zhōu state.
They wore ceremonial robes and
held court,
their jade tablet serving as a good omen.

In the first year of Yángjiā,

Inside, there was a central pillar (dūzhù),
with eight channels running along its sides,
which operated a mechanism.
Outside, there were eight dragons,
each holding a bronze ball in its mouth.
Below them were toads,
with open mouths to receive the balls.
Its ingenious gear mechanism
was entirely concealed within the *zūn*,
covered closely and seamlessly.
If an earthquake occurred,
the *zūn* would vibrate, causing a dragon's mechanism to activate and release its ball,
which the toad would then catch.
The resonating sound would alert
the attendant, who would then know.
Even if only one dragon's mechanism activated,
the other seven heads would not move.
By identifying its direction,
the location of the earthquake would be known.
When verified with actual events,
it matched perfectly, as if by divine power.
Among records in historical texts,
nothing like it had existed before.
Once, a dragon's mechanism activated, but no earthquake was felt in the capital.

In the beginning of YǒngHé,
Héng was appointed as the Chancellor of HéJiān.
At that time, the king of the state was arrogant and extravagant,
not abiding by the classics and laws;
furthermore, there were many powerful magnates
who together engaged in lawless behavior.
Upon arriving at his post,
Héng established strict authority,
rectified laws and regulations,
secretly learned the names of the treacherous factions,
and arrested them all at once.
All levels of society became orderly,
and his administration was called well-governed.
After three years in office,
he submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
and was summoned to be appointed as ShàngShū.
He was sixty-two years old,
and passed away in the fourth year of YǒngHé.
He authored *ZhōuGuān XùnGǔ*,
which CuīYuàn believed was no different from other scholars' works.
He also wished to complete KǒngZǐ's *Yì* commentary on the deficient *Tuàn* and *Xiàng*,
but ultimately could not finish it.
His works include *Shī*, *Fù*, *Míng*, *QīYán*, *LíngXiàn*, *YìngXián*, *QīBiàn*, *XúnGào*, and *XuánTú*, totaling thirty-two chapters.
During the Yǒngchū reign,
Liú Zhēn (劉珍), the Yèzhě Púshè (謁者僕射), Liú Táotú (劉騊駼), the Jiàoshūláng (校書郎), and others composed at the Dōngguān (東觀),
compiling the Hànjì (漢記).
They then settled the Hàn (漢) imperial rites.
They submitted a memorial requesting Héng (衡) to participate in the discussion of these matters.
But they all died before this could happen,
and Héng (衡) often sighed
wishing to complete it.
When he became a Shìzhōng (侍中),
he submitted a memorial requesting permission to exclusively manage affairs at the Dōngguān (東觀),
collecting scattered writings
and exerting all his strength to mend and supplement them.
He also listed more than ten instances where Sīmǎ Qiān (司馬遷) and Bān Gù’s (班固) works did not align with classical texts.
He further believed that Wáng Mǎng’s (王莽) main biography should only record his usurpation,
and as for the chronological years
and records of disasters and auspicious signs,
these should be made into the Yuánhòu Běnjì (元后本紀).
He also believed that Gēngshǐ (更始) held the throne
with no dissenting expectations from the people,
and Guāngwǔ (光武) initially served as his general,
only later assuming the true imperial position.
Therefore, the reign title of Gēngshǐ (更始) should be established at the beginning of Guāngwǔ’s (光武) reign.
His memorials were submitted multiple times,
but ultimately not heeded.
Later writings,
being mostly undetailed in their sources,
were lamented by people of the time.
A commentary states: Cuī Yuàn (崔瑗) praised Píngzǐ (平子) saying:
“His knowledge of numerology exhausted heaven and earth;
his creations emulated the transformations of nature.”
Can such an achievement truly be spoken of!
His scope enveloped the two primal forces;
heaven and earth held no secrets from his spirit.
He governed the mechanisms of emotion and matter;
no living being could match his wisdom.
Hence,
his profound thoughts were of the highest caliber among men.
The Records say:
“Virtue leads one upward;
art leads one downward.”
Measuring this thought,
how could it be mere art?
What virtue would it diminish!
A eulogy states: The principles of the Three Powers are interconnected,
but human intellect is often obscured.
Near, it deduces shapes and calculations;
far, it extracts profound mysteries.
Without profound foresight,
who could make things clear?
Biography of Mǎ Róng (馬融), Chapter 50 Part 1
Mǎ Róng (馬融), courtesy name Jìcháng (季長),
was a native of Máolíng (茂陵) in Fúfēng (扶風),
and the son of Yán (嚴), the Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng (將作大匠).
He had a beautiful appearance and eloquent speech,
possessing outstanding talent.
Initially,
Zhì Xún (摯恂) of Jīngzhào (京兆) taught Confucianism,
living as a recluse in the Nánshān (南山),
refusing imperial summons.
His reputation was great in Guānxī (關西).
Róng (融) studied with him,
gaining extensive knowledge of the classics.
Xún (恂) marvelled at Róng’s (融) talent
and gave him his daughter in marriage.
In the second year of Yǒngchū (永初) (108 CE),
Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍) Dèng Zhì (鄧騭) heard of Róng’s (融) fame
and summoned him to be a Shèrén (舍人).
This was not to his liking,
so he did not respond to the summons
and lived as a guest in the borderlands of Wǔdū (武都) and Hànyáng (漢陽) in Liángzhōu (涼州).
It happened that the Qiāng (羌) barbarians rose up,
the border regions were disturbed,
and grain prices soared.
West of the passes,
dead bodies littered the roads.
Róng (融), being hungry and distressed,
regretted his decision and sighed,
saying to his friend:
“The ancients said: ‘Holding the map of the world in one’s left hand,
and cutting one’s throat with the right,
a fool would not do it.’
The reason for this is
that life is more precious than the world.
Now, to destroy one’s invaluable body
for the petty shame of a common custom
is probably not what Lǎozhuāng (老莊) would call for.”
Therefore, he went to respond to Zhì’s (騭) summons.
In the fourth year (110 CE),
he was appointed Jiàoshūlángzhōng (校書郎中),
and went to the Dōngguān (東觀) to supervise and edit secret archives.
At this time, Empress Dèng (鄧) was regent,
and Zhì (騭) and his brothers assisted in governance.
But common scholars and worldly gentlemen
believed that civil virtues should be promoted
and military achievements abolished.
Thus, the rites of imperial hunts were suspended,
and the methods of warfare abandoned.
Consequently, cunning bandits rampaged,
taking advantage of this lack of preparedness.
Róng (融) was moved,
believing that the ways of civil and military affairs
should not be discarded by sages,
and that none of the Five Talents (五才) should be abolished.
In the second year of Yuánchū (元初) (115 CE),
he presented the Guǎngchéng Sòng (廣成頌)
as a remonstrance.

Cài Yōng, courtesy name Bójiē,
was a native of Yǔ, Chénliú.
His sixth-generation ancestor, Xūn,
was fond of Huánglǎo teachings,
and served as Méi Lìng during the reign of Píng Dì.
At the beginning of Wáng Mǎng’s reign,
he was offered the position of Yānrong Liánshuài.
Xūn, facing the seal and ribbon, sighed to the heavens, saying:
“My name is inscribed in the register of the Hàn house,
and I shall die loyal to its rightful rule.
In the past, Zēngzǐ did not accept the gifts of Jì Sūn,
how much less can I serve two dynasties?”
Thereupon, he took his family,
and fled into the deep mountains,
refusing to serve the new dynasty along with Bào Xuān, Zhuó Mào, and others.
His father, Léng,
also had a clean and upright conduct,
and was posthumously named Zhēndìng Gōng.
Yōng was profoundly filial by nature.
His mother was constantly ill for three years,
and Yōng, except for seasonal changes in temperature,
never loosened his collar or belt,
and did not sleep for seventy days.
After his mother died,
he built a hut beside her tomb,
conducting himself with propriety in all his actions.
A rabbit became tame and settled near his dwelling,
and also a tree grew with intertwined branches.
People from far and near marveled at this,
and many came to observe it.
He lived with his uncle and cousins,
and for three generations, they did not divide their property.
The local community highly regarded their righteousness.
In his youth, he was broadly learned,
and studied under Tàifù Hú Guǎng.
He was fond of literary works, mathematics, and astronomy,
and was exceptionally skilled in musicology.
During the reign of Huán Dì,
Zhōngchángshì Xú Huáng, Zuǒ Guàn, and other five marquises were arrogant and unrestrained.
Hearing that Yōng was skilled at playing the *qín*,
they reported it to the Son of Heaven,
who ordered the Chénliú Tàishǒu to urgently dispatch him.
Yōng had no choice,
but when he reached Yǎnshī,
he feigned illness and returned home.
He lived in leisure, contemplating antiquity,
and did not associate with the people of his time.
He was moved by the *Kènàn* of Dōngfāng 【Shuò】 and the likes of Yáng Xióng, Bān Gù, and Cuī Yīn, who posed questions to express themselves,
and by pondering various opinions,
approving what was right and correcting what was wrong,
he wrote *Shìhuì* to admonish and encourage.

Cài Yōng believed that the classics had been distant from the sages for too long,
that many characters were erroneous,
and that vulgar scholars had misinterpreted them,
misleading later students.
In the fourth year of Xīpíng,

he, along with the Central Colonel-Protector of the Five Bureaus Tángxī Diǎn, Grand Master of Guanglu Yáng Cì, Counselor Remonstrant Mǎ Rìdī, *Yìláng* Zhāng Xùn, Hán Shuō, and Grand Astrologer Dān Yáng,
memorialized to request the correct standardization of the characters of the Six Classics.
Emperor Líng agreed.
Cài Yōng then personally inscribed (the text) in [cinnabar] on steles,
and had artisans carve them and erect them outside the gate of the Imperial Academy.
Thereafter, later Confucian scholars and students
all used them for correction.

numbered over a thousand carriages daily,
filling the streets.

and prohibitions became even stricter,
making selection and appointment difficult.
The two provinces of Yōu and Jì
had long had vacancies that were not filled.
Cài Yōng submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly observe that the old territories of Yōu and Jì,
which produce armored horses,
have in recent years suffered from military famine,
gradually becoming desolate and depleted.
Now the common people are scattered,
a thousand *lǐ* are desolate,
positions have been vacant for a long time,
and officials and commoners are eagerly awaiting appointments,
yet the three high offices' selections
remain undecided for over a month.
Your servant has been perplexed by this matter,
and those who discuss it say, 'to avoid the three mutuals.'
Eleven provinces have prohibitions,
so only two provinces can be drawn upon.
Moreover, the gentry from these two provinces
are sometimes further restricted by age and tenure,
causing hesitation and delay,
thus missing opportunities for action.
I foolishly believe that the prohibition of the 'three mutuals'
is a minor restriction.
If we simply reinforce it with imperial majesty
and clarify its decrees,
would those in office not be cautious and fearful?
Why then should we deliberately establish the 'three mutuals'
and create obstacles for ourselves?
In the past, Hán Ānguó rose from a commoner,
Zhū Mǎchén came from humble origins,
both were appointed due to their talent,
and returned to govern their native lands.
Furthermore, Zhāng Chǎng, despite being an outlaw,
was promoted to govern a crucial province.
Would they then have considered observing the 'three mutuals'
and subsequently minor regulations?
The Three Dukes clearly know the importance of the two provinces,
and that appointments should be made quickly.
They should override the prohibitions and select the capable,
to remedy the current ills;
yet they disregard the righteousness of remonstrating officials,
merely avoiding trivial penalties,
delaying selections,
and thereby losing suitable people.
Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would follow the example of previous emperors,
abolish recent prohibitions,
and for those provincial governors whose abilities can be replaced,
do not restrict them by tenure or the 'three mutuals,'
to choose the appropriate ones."
The memorial was submitted but not acted upon.
Initially,
the Emperor was fond of learning.
He personally composed fifty chapters of the Huángxī Piān,
and consequently invited various scholars capable of writing essays and rhapsodies.
Initially, he mostly recruited them for their classical scholarship.
Later, those who excelled in writing letters and in bird-and-seal script
were all summoned and invited,
eventually reaching several tens of people.
The Attendants-in-Ordinary and Libationers, Yuè Sōng and Jiǎ Hù,
mostly brought in those who were unprincipled and sought power,
and they were all stationed at the Hóngdū Gate.
They delighted in presenting minor local matters and village affairs,
and the Emperor was greatly pleased with them,
granting them positions of unusual prominence.
Furthermore, dozens of market traders and common people
who claimed to be filial sons to Xuānlíng
were also recruited,
all appointed as Lángzhōng and Taìzǐ Shèrén.
At that time, there were frequent thunderstorms and strong winds,
damaging trees and uprooting wood,
as well as earthquakes, hailstorms, and locust plagues.
Moreover, the Xiānbēi violated the borders,
and military levies and taxes burdened the people.
In the seventh month of the sixth year,
an imperial edict attributed the fault to himself,
advising all ministers to each present their essential policies for implementation.
Yōng submitted a sealed memorial, stating:
Calamitous omens
arrive in accordance with the phenomena.
The repeated thunderbolts
are probably caused by an excessive number of executions and punishments.
Wind is the command of Heaven,
intended to instruct people.
Indeed,
those who serve the Lord-on-High reverently
will naturally harbor abundant blessings;
those who show respect in the ancestral temples
will manifest the presence of ghosts and spirits.
The great affairs of the state
must prioritize sacrificial
rites,
which the Son of Heaven himself ought to diligently attend to.
Since I served in the government
and was appointed to wear the scarlet robe,
I have participated in the welcoming of qi at the five suburban altars,
but the imperial carriage rarely attended.
The reverence due at the four
seasons
was repeatedly entrusted to the relevant officials.
Although there were dispensations,
it was still considered a neglectful omission.
Therefore, August Heaven was displeased,
manifesting these various anomalies.
The Hóngfàn commentary says:
"When government
is perverse and virtue is concealed,
the wind will unroof houses and break trees."
Kūn represents the way of the earth;
the Yì Jīng calls it "peaceful and firm."
When yin energy is resentfully abundant,
what should be still becomes agitated,
which portends a rebellion
from below.
If power is not with the sovereign,
hail will damage things;
if government is harsh and tyrannical,
tigers and wolves will devour people;
if greed harms the people,
locusts will damage crops.
On the twenty-eighth day of the sixth
month,
Tàibái and the Moon approached each other,
which is an ill omen for military affairs.
The Xiānbēi have violated the frontier;
their origin is distant.
The current deployment of troops
does not appear to be advantageous.
Above, it violates astronomical phenomena;
below, it contradicts human affairs.
It is truly imperative to widely consult various opinions
and adopt what is secure.
Overwhelmed by indignation,
I respectfully present seven matters that should be implemented, listed
below:
Bumper Harvest.
Sacrifices in the pure temples,
recalling past filial piety and respect,
and supporting the elderly in the Bìyōng
to demonstrate ritual transformation to the people,
these are all great undertakings of emperors
and practices reverently upheld by ancestors.
However,
officials repeatedly cite mourning by vassal states,
births within the palace,
and minor impurities of clerks and soldiers
as frequent reasons for prohibitions.
I have observed that the fasting and purification for the southern suburban sacrifice
have never been abandoned,
but for other sacrifices,
they invariably raise differing opinions.
How can the southern suburban sacrifice be humble and other sacrifices esteemed?
The imperial edict of Emperor Xiàoyuán states:
"Among the utmost respects in rites,
none is more important than
sacrifices,
which are to be personally conducted with utmost sincerity
to achieve solemn reverence."
Moreover, the old regulations of Yuánhé
reiterated earlier ordinances.
Previous imperial edicts
expressed heartfelt
compassion.
But in recent times,
the Grand Astrologer has been relied upon instead.
Forgetting the greatness of ritual reverence
and relying on books of taboos,
they adhere to minor prohibitions
to the detriment of major rites.
According to the rites,
if a wife
or concubine gives birth,
one should not enter the side chambers during fasting,
but there is no text stating that the sacrifice should be abandoned.
What is meant by "if there is a death in the palace,
one does not sacrifice for three months"
refers to scholars and common people
who live in cramped quarters,
sharing the same space;
how can it refer to the vast imperial residence
and the multitude of servants?
From now on, the regulations for fasting should revert to the old precedents,
to respond to the anomalies of wind
and thunder calamities.
And also widely seek out what is right and wrong.
Furthermore, due to the calamitous omens,
hidden talents should be brought forth,
and the selection of virtuous, upright, honest, and sagely individuals should be emphasized,
so that courageous remonstrances
never cease
at court.
Since Your Majesty assumed personal governance,
calamitous omens have occurred annually,
yet no special decree for broad selection has been heard.
It is truly imperative to reflect upon and revive old practices,
so that loyal
ministers can express their frank opinions,
thereby resolving the Yì Zhuàn's
statement: "When government is perverse and virtue is concealed."
Three matters: Indeed, the way to seek out worthy individuals
is not necessarily uniform;
some are distinguished by their virtue,
others are lauded for their words.
Recently,
those who serve at court
have never been rewarded for their loyalty
and trustworthiness;
instead, they are constantly punished for slanderous accusations,
thus causing everyone below to keep silent,
and no one dares to present upright opinions.
Lángzhōng Zhāng Wén
alone previously dared to speak frankly,
and the sagely ear accepted it,
holding the Three Departments accountable.
Ministers and subjects were openly pleased,
and the common people rejoiced.
I, your humble servant, believe it appropriate to promote Wén to a senior position
to encourage loyalty and outspokenness,
to proclaim this throughout the land,
and to broadly open up the path of governance.
Xǐ, Inspector of Yìzhōu Páng Zhī, and Inspector of Liángzhōu Liú Qián
each possess a heart devoted to public duty and abhorring corruption.
The abuses rectified by Xǐ and others
were particularly numerous and effective.
The rest were all corrupt
and ineffective,
unable to perform their duties.
Some harbored guilt and flaws,
sharing the same failings as their subordinates.
The net of the law was loosely cast,
and no one reported or investigated each other,
and the central government offices also remained silent.
An imperial edict in the fifth year
proposed sending out eight envoys,
and also ordered the Three Dukes to report on popular grievances.
At that time, those who upheld public duty were delighted and achieved their aspirations,
while the corrupt and perverse were anxious
and lost color.
It is unclear why this proposal
was shelved.
Formerly, Liú Xiàng reported:
"Indeed, those who cling to hesitant plans
open the door to all kinds of wrongdoings;
those who foster indecisive thoughts
者，
來讒邪之口． ”
今始聞善政，
旋復變易，
足令海內測度朝政．
宜追定八使，
糾舉
非法，
