At that time, strange portents appeared frequently,
alarming and disturbing people.
In July of that year,
an imperial edict summoned Yōng with Guānglù Dàfū Yáng Cì, Jiànyì Dàfū Mǎ Rìdī, Yìláng Zhāng Huá, and Tàishǐ Lìng Shàn Yáng to Jīnshāngmén,
and led them into Chóngdé Diàn.
The Zhōngchángshì Cáo Jié and Wáng Fǔ were instructed to question them about the calamities and strange phenomena, and what measures should be taken to avert and alter them.
Yōng responded with all his heart,
his account being recorded in the Wǔxíng and Tiānwén Zhì.
Furthermore, a special edict asked:
"Recently, disasters and changes have arisen repeatedly,
but their causes are unknown.
The imperial court is anxious,
bearing fear in its heart.
Although we frequently consult the high officials and gentry,
hoping to hear loyal words,
each keeps silent,
none willing to speak their mind fully.
Because Yōng's scholarship is profound,
we specifically and privately seek your counsel.
You should openly disclose what is lost and gained,
and point out the essentials of governance,
without hesitation
or self-imposed reticence.
Present your detailed response on governance
sealed in a black bag."
Yōng replied:
"I humbly believe Your Majesty possesses sagely virtue and profound understanding,
deeply lamenting the calamities and misfortunes.
You praise my humble learning
and specially deign to inquire,
which I, a mere ant, cannot possibly live up to.
This is truly a moment to pour out one's heart and soul, even risking one's life.
How can I, by fearing trouble and avoiding harm,
prevent Your Majesty from hearing the utmost warnings!
I humbly reflect on these various strange occurrences;
they are all portents of a nation's demise.
Heaven, towards the great Hàn,
is unceasingly diligent,
thus repeatedly sending forth omens and changes
to act as a rebuke,
wishing to awaken the sovereign
to change from danger to peace.
Now, the emergence of calamities
is not elsewhere,
but far off, within the palace gates,
and near, within the government offices.
The warning they provide
can be said to be most urgent.
The falling rainbow and the hen transforming [into a rooster]
are all caused by women meddling in politics.
Formerly, the wet nurse Zhào Ráo,
was honored above all others;
while alive, her wealth equaled that of the imperial treasury,
and upon her death, her tomb surpassed imperial mausoleums.
Her two sons received enfeoffment,
and her brothers governed commanderies.
This was followed by the Yǒnglè Ménshǐ Huò Yù,
who relied on her influence to establish herself,
and also engaged in treachery.
Now, rumors abound on the streets,
again speaking of a certain Chéng Dàrén,
whose reputation suggests
she will become a national calamity.
It is advisable to build high defenses,
clearly establish prohibitions,
and deeply reflect on Zhào and Huò
as the most serious warnings.
Now Your Majesty's sagely intention is diligent,
wishing to discern the righteous from the wicked.
However, it is heard that Tàiwèi Zhāng Hào
was promoted by Yù;
Guānglùxūn, whose surname is Zhāng,
is known for being greedy and corrupt.
Furthermore, Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi Zhào Xuán
and Túnqí Xiàowèi Gài Shēng
have both enjoyed timely favor,
and are overflowing with honor and wealth.
It is advisable to consider the fault of small-minded men in positions of power,
and reflect on the blessing of withdrawing and giving way to the worthy.
I humbly observe that Tíngwèi Guō Xǐ
is pure, honest, and mature;
Guānglù Dàfū Qiáo Xuán
is intelligent, insightful, and upright;
and the late Tàiwèi Liú Chǒng
was loyal, honest, and upheld righteousness:
all are suitable to be strategists and should be frequently consulted.
Prime ministers and high officials are
the sovereign's four limbs;
[一０] when entrusting responsibilities and expecting results,
their merits and demerits are already clear.
It is inappropriate to listen to minor officials
and discredit high officials.
[一一] Furthermore, the productions of the Shàngfāng artisans
and the prose and poetry of the Hóngdū [Ménxué],
should perhaps be curtailed for a time
to show a state of worry.
The *Shī Jīng* says: 'Fearing the wrath of Heaven,
one dares not indulge in amusement.'
Heaven's warnings truly cannot be trifled with.
The Xiaolián recommended by the Prime Minister's office
are the highest selection of scholars.
Recently, because appointments were not made carefully,
the Sāngōng were severely rebuked;
yet now, candidates are being chosen and promoted based on minor literary achievements,
opening the door to personal influence
and violating the regulations of enlightened kings.
The masses are displeased,
but none dare to speak of it.
[一二] I wish Your Majesty would endure and abolish this,
and consider the myriad affairs of state,
to respond to Heaven's expectations.
Since the sagely court has disciplined itself,
those close to the emperor should also follow suit.
When people restrain themselves,
to block misfortunes and warnings,
then the Way of Heaven will diminish fullness,
and ghosts and spirits will bless the humble.
I, with my foolish straightforwardness,
am moved to forget myself,
daring to infringe taboos,
and have written this detailed reply by hand.
For if the communication between sovereign and minister is not kept secret,
the former risks leaked words,
and the latter risks personal ruin.
[一三] I pray that this memorial be kept confidential,
so that no loyal official
suffers resentment from treacherous enemies."
When the memorial was submitted,
the emperor read it and sighed.
He then rose to change his clothes.
Cáo Jié secretly peeked at it from behind,
and fully disclosed its contents to those around him,
thus the matter was leaked.
All those whom Yōng had criticized and dismissed
cast sidelong glances, plotting revenge.
Initially,
Cài Yōng and Sītú Liú Hé had always been at odds.
His paternal uncle, Wèiwèi Zhì,
was also at odds with Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng Yáng Qiú.
Yáng Qiú was the son-in-law of Zhōng Chángshì Chéng Huáng.
Chéng Huáng then sent someone to submit a flying memorial, accusing Cài Yōng and Zhì of repeatedly entreating Liú Hé with private matters.
When Liú Hé did not comply,
Cài Yōng harbored resentment
and intended to harm him.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was sent to the Shàngshū,
summoning Cài Yōng to explain the situation.
Cài Yōng submitted a memorial, presenting his case:
"Your servant was summoned
and questioned about Dàhónglú Liú Hé previously serving as Jìyīn Tàishǒu,
about Your servant's subordinate Zhāng Wǎn taking a hundred days of leave,
about Liú Hé, as Sīlì,
again entrusting Lǐ Qí, an official from Hénèi Jùn, to be a zhōu shūzuǒ,
and about protecting the former Hénán Yǐn Yáng Zhì and Shìyùshǐ Húmǔ Bān,
and about Liú Hé's refusal to use them leading to resentment.
Your servant, upon being summoned for interrogation, was terrified,
his liver and gall turning to mud,
not knowing where his death sentence lay.
Secretly, upon examining the matter,
it was indeed related to Wǎn and Qí,
but not involving Zhì and Bān.
Generally, giving leave to minor officials
is not a cause for deep hatred.
As Your servant is related by marriage to Zhì,
how would I dare to assist a private faction?
If Your servant's father and son wished to harm and frame each other,
they would clearly state it to the imperial court
and fully explain the origins of their resentment.
With no private matters involved,
and yet slanderous letters are circulated,
it would be appropriate to cross-reference Your servant's statement with Liú Hé's.
Your servant, having received special commendation for his scholarship,
served in the secret archive,
holding a brush before Your Majesty,
his name and appearance
briefly touching Your Majesty's heart.
In July of this year,
Your servant was summoned to the Jīnshāngmén,
questioned about calamities and anomalies,
and presented with an edict conveying Your Majesty's will,
inducing Your servant to speak.
Your servant is truly foolish and reckless,
knowing only loyalty and utmost devotion,
risking his life and forgetting his body,
not considering future harm,
and thus criticized the Gōngqīng,
even extending to favored ministers.
This was truly to answer Your Majesty's questions from above,
to avert calamities and anomalies,
and to devise a plan for Your Majesty's peace and stability.
Your Majesty does not remember the loyal minister's honest words,
which should have been protected,
but when slander suddenly arrived,
immediately harbored suspicion and doubt.
How can a devoted official
be tolerated?
Each time an imperial edict is issued,
all officials submit sealed memorials,
wishing to reform governance and reflect on transgressions,
to avert misfortune and bring about auspiciousness,
yet those who speak do not receive the blessing of being heeded,
but are instead immediately subjected to the disaster of being framed and destroyed.
Now everyone is silent,
taking Your servant as a warning.
Who would dare to be loyal and filial to Your Majesty?
Your servant's paternal uncle Zhì
has been repeatedly promoted
to a high position.
Your servant has been favored
and frequently consulted.
Those who speak ill intend to use this to frame Your servant's father and son,
to destroy Your servant's family,
not to expose villains
and benefit the state.
Your servant is forty-six years old,
an orphan without kin,
fortunate to be called a loyal minister;
death would bring him more than enough honor.
I fear that Your Majesty will no longer hear true words after this.
Your servant's foolishness and recklessness
naturally bring about misfortune,
but as for the previous statements,
Zhì did not hear them,
yet old and white-haired,
he is unjustly implicated
and will be destroyed along with Your servant,
falling into a pit.
This is truly unjust and painful.
Once Your servant enters prison,
he will be tormented by torture,
forced to sign a confession.
How can his true feelings ever be heard again?
With death approaching,
I presumptuously present myself.
I pray that I alone bear the guilt and punishment,
and that Zhì not be implicated.
Then, the day of my death
will be the year of my rebirth.
I only wish Your Majesty would eat well
and take care of yourself for the sake of the myriad common people."
Thereupon, Cài Yōng and Zhì were imprisoned in Luòyáng.
They were accused of using public office for personal vendettas,
plotting to harm a high official,
and of great disrespect,
deserving execution in the marketplace.
When the matter was reported,
Zhōng Chángshì Lǚ Qiáng, pitying Cài Yōng's innocence,
pleaded for him.
The Emperor also reconsidered his memorial,
and an edict was issued to commute his death sentence by one degree,
and he and his family were shaved, shackled, and exiled to Shuòfāng,
not to be pardoned by any amnesty.
Yáng Qiú sent assassins to intercept Cài Yōng on the road,
but the assassins were moved by Cài Yōng's righteousness and none would carry out the act.
Yáng Qiú then bribed the chief of Cài Yōng's local administration to poison him,
but the bribed official instead warned Cài Yōng of the plot,
so he always managed to escape.
He lived in Ānyáng Xiàn, Wǔyuán.
Earlier, when Cài Yōng was at Dōngguān,
he collaborated with Lú Zhí, Hán Shuō, and others to compile and supplement the Hòuhàn Jì.
However, he encountered trouble and was forced to wander,
so he could not finish it.
Consequently, he submitted a memorial explaining himself,
presenting ten intentions for his writings,
classifying the headings,
and attaching them to the memorial.
The Emperor admired his great talent,
and coincidentally, there was a great amnesty the following year,
and Cài Yōng was also pardoned and returned to his home commandery.
From his exile until his return,
it was a total of nine months.
As he was about to return,
Wǔyuán Tàishǒu Wáng Zhì gave him a farewell feast.
When the wine was flowing freely,
Wáng Zhì rose to dance and urged Cài Yōng to join,
but Cài Yōng did not reciprocate.
Wáng Zhì was
the younger brother of Zhōng Chángshì Wáng Fǔ,
and had always been arrogant and proud.
Ashamed before his guests,
he cursed Cài Yōng, saying:
"How dare you slight me!"
Cài Yōng brushed his sleeves and left.
Wáng Zhì bore a grudge
and secretly reported that Cài Yōng harbored resentment about his imprisonment and exile,
and slandered the imperial court.
The favored eunuchs hated him.
Fearing that he would not escape punishment,
Cài Yōng fled to Jiānghǎi,
hiding far away in Wú and Huì.
He often sought refuge with the Yáng clan of Tàishān.
After twelve years,
he was in Wú.
A man from Wú was burning a tung tree to cook with.
Cài Yōng heard the sound of the burning fire
and recognized it as good wood.
He then requested it and fashioned it into a qín.
Indeed, it produced beautiful music,
but its tail was still scorched,
so people at the time named it
"Jiāowěi Qín" (Scorched-Tail Qín).
Earlier,
when Cài Yōng was in Chénliú,
a neighbor invited him for food and drink.
By the time he arrived, the guests were already in high spirits.
A guest was playing the qín behind a screen.
Cài Yōng, reaching the gate, secretly listened,
and said:
"Alas!
I was invited with music, yet there is murderous intent.
Why?"
He then turned back.
The messenger told the host:
"Mr. Cài came just now,
but turned back at the gate."
Cài Yōng was always revered by the local community,
so the host immediately chased after him and asked the reason.
Cài Yōng explained everything,
and everyone was astonished.
The qín player said:
"As I was playing just now,
I saw a mantis facing a cicada,
the cicada about to leave but not yet flown,
and the mantis moved back and forth.
My heart was startled,
only fearing that the mantis would miss it.
Could this have been murderous intent manifested in the sound?"
Cài Yōng smiled knowingly and said:
"That is enough to account for it."
In the sixth year of Zhōngpíng,
Emperor Líng (Líng Dì) passed away.
Dǒng Zhuó became Sīkōng (Minister of Works).
Hearing of Cài Yōng's (Cài Yōng) high reputation,
he invited him.
Cài Yōng (Yōng) feigned illness and did not comply.
Dǒng Zhuó (Zhuó) was greatly enraged,
and cursed, saying:
"My power can wipe out entire clans.
If Cài Yōng (Cài Yōng) continues to be arrogant and stubborn,
he won't last long."
He also strictly ordered the commanderies and states to send Cài Yōng (Yōng) to his mansion.
Cài Yōng (Yōng) had no choice
but to go.
He was appointed Jìjiǔ (Libationer)
and was greatly respected.
He was recommended as a High Talent (Gāodì),
appointed Shìyùshǐ (Attending Imperial Censor),
then transferred to Chíshū Yùshǐ (Imperial Censor Holding Letters),
and promoted to Shàngshū (Minister).
Within three days,
he had served in three high offices (sān tái).
He was promoted to Bājùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Bā Commandery),
but was retained as Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant).
In the first year of Chūpíng,
he was appointed Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng (General of the Left Palace Guard),
followed Emperor Xiàn (Xiàn Dì) in moving the capital to Cháng'ān,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Gāoyáng Township (Gāoyáng Xiāng Hóu).
Dǒng Zhuó's (Dǒng Zhuó) guests and military retainers (bù qǔ) debated wanting to elevate Dǒng Zhuó (Zhuó) to be comparable to Tàigōng (Grand Duke),
calling him Shàngfù (Grand Tutor).
Dǒng Zhuó (Zhuó) consulted Cài Yōng (Yōng) about this.
Cài Yōng (Yōng) said:
"Tàigōng assisted Zhōu
and received the mandate to destroy Shāng,
hence that unique title was specially for him.
Currently, your illustrious lord's (míng gōng) awe-inspiring virtue
is indeed grand and towering.
However, to compare it to Shàngfù,
my humble opinion is that it is not yet appropriate.
It would be advisable to wait until the area east of the passes (Guāndōng) is pacified,
and the imperial carriage (chē jià) returns to the old capital,
then discuss it."
Dǒng Zhuó (Zhuó) followed his advice.
In the sixth month of the second year (Chūpíng),
there was an earthquake.
Dǒng Zhuó (Zhuó) asked Cài Yōng (Yōng) about it.
Cài Yōng (Yōng) replied:
"Earthquakes
are caused by the excessive growth of Yin (yīn shèng) encroaching upon Yang (yáng),
and by subordinates overstepping their bounds.
Last spring, when performing the suburban sacrifice to Heaven (jiāo tiān),
you, Duke (gōng), personally led the imperial carriage (chē jià),
riding in a golden-flowered (jīnhuá) green canopy (qīnggài) carriage,
with painted claws on both wheel covers.
Both near and far considered it improper."
Dǒng Zhuó (Zhuó) thereupon changed to riding a black canopy (zàogài) carriage.
Dǒng Zhuó (Zhuó) valued Cài Yōng's (Cài Yōng) talent and learning,
and treated him generously.
Whenever there was a gathering or banquet,
he would order Cài Yōng (Yōng) to play the qín (qín) and commend the proceedings.
Cài Yōng (Yōng) also always tried to offer corrections and benefits.
However, Dǒng Zhuó (Zhuó) mostly acted on his own stubborn will,
and Cài Yōng (Yōng) regretted that his words were rarely followed.
He said to his younger cousin Gǔ (Gǔ):
"Duke Dǒng's (Dǒng Gōng) nature is stubborn and he persists in his errors,
he will ultimately be difficult to save.
I wish to flee east to Yǎnzhoū.
If the road is too distant to reach,
I could at least hide in Shāndōng to await developments.
What do you think?"
Gǔ (Gǔ) said:
"Your appearance is different from ordinary people;
whenever you travel, observers gather in crowds.
To hide yourself with this,
would it not be difficult?"
Cài Yōng (Yōng) then stopped his plan.
When Dǒng Zhuó (Zhuó) was executed,
Cài Yōng (Yōng) was at the residence of Sītú (Minister of Education) Wáng Yǔn (Wáng Yǔn).
He unexpectedly spoke of it with a sigh,
and his expression changed.
Wáng Yǔn (Yǔn) angrily rebuked him, saying:
"Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) was a great traitor to the state,
who almost overthrew the Hàn dynasty (Hàn Shì).
As a minister of the king,
you should share in the indignation,
yet you cherish his private favor,
and forget the greater principle!
Now that Heaven has punished the guilty,
and you instead grieve for him,
is this not joining in rebellion?"
He immediately had him arrested and sent to the Tíngwèi (Grand Judge) for punishment.
Cài Yōng (Yōng) presented a petition, apologizing,
and begged to be branded on the face and have his feet amputated (qíng shǒu yuè zú),
so that he could continue to complete the Hàn History (Hàn Shǐ).
Many scholars and officials (shìdàfū) pleaded for him,
but could not succeed.
Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) Mǎ Rìdī (Mǎ Rìdī) rushed to Wáng Yǔn (Yǔn) and said:
"Bójiē is an unparalleled talent of his age,
highly knowledgeable in Hàn (Hàn) affairs.
He should continue to complete the Later History (Hòushǐ),
which would be a great classic for a generation.
Moreover, his loyalty and filial piety are well-known,
and the crime he is accused of is groundless.
To execute him, would it not disappoint the hopes of the people?"
Wáng Yǔn (Yǔn) said:
"In the past, Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì) did not kill Sīmǎ Qiān (Sīmǎ Qiān),
which led to the creation of slanderous writings
that circulated for later generations.
Currently, the imperial destiny (guózào) is in decline,
the sacred implements (shénqì) are not secure,
and we cannot allow a sycophantic minister to hold a brush beside the young emperor (yòuzhǔ).
This would not benefit the emperor's (shèng dé) virtue,
and would furthermore cause our faction to suffer calumny and criticism."
Mǎ Rìdī (Rìdī) withdrew and told others:
"Will Duke Wáng (Wáng Gōng) not last long in this world?
Good people
are the pillars of the state;
creative works
are the classics of the state.
To destroy pillars and abandon classics,
how can it last long?"
Cài Yōng (Yōng) then died in prison.
Wáng Yǔn (Yǔn) regretted it
and wished to stop it, but it was too late.
He was sixty-one at the time.
The gentry (jìnshēn) and scholars (zhūrú) all wept.
Zhèng Xuán (Zhèng Xuán) of Běihǎi (Běihǎi) heard of it and sighed:
"Hàn (Hàn) affairs of this era,
who will set them right!"
In Yǎnzhoū and Chénliú, everyone painted his portrait and composed eulogies.
His compilations of Hàn (Hàn) affairs
were not recorded to continue the Later History (Hòushǐ).
He merely composed the Líng Jì (Record of Emperor Líng) and Shí Yì (Ten Principles),
and supplemented forty-two chapters of various Biographies (Lièzhuàn).
Due to the chaos caused by Lǐ Jué (Lǐ Jué),
most were lost and no longer exist.

His collected works, including poems (shī), rhapsodies (fù), steles (bēi), eulogies (lěi), inscriptions (míng), praises (zàn), linked pearls (liánzhū), admonitions (zhēn), laments (diào), discourses and discussions (lùn yì), independent judgments (dúdàn), encouragements to study (quàn xué), explanations and admonitions (shì huì), music (yuè), women's instructions (nǚ xùn), seal script manuals (zhuàn yì), sacrificial prayers (zhùwén), memorials and reports (zhāng biǎo), and correspondence (shūjì),
totaling one hundred and four chapters,
were transmitted to later generations.
The commentary states: The emotions stirred by a relationship
are what a noble person (shì) cannot forget.
The ultimate turn of fate
is what all living beings deeply grieve.
When Bójiē was bound with fetters (qián niǔ)
and exiled to remote regions (yōuyì),
looking up at the sun and moon yet seeing no light,
facing the wind and dust yet unable to pass through,
how could his feelings be conveyed to those who enjoyed peace and security?
When he shed his prisoner's clothes
and fled to the lands of Ōu and Yuè,
hiding in boats in rivers and valleys,
not knowing how far he was,
and walking swiftly through deep forests,
still fearing discovery,
he only wished to turn his head north towards his old home (jiù qiū)
and return his bones to his ancestral tomb (xiān lǒng).
Could that even be achieved?
When Dǒng Zhuó (Dǒng Zhuó) suddenly entered the court,
the invitation first arrived,
clearly an unjust entanglement,
yet he was promoted three times in a few days.
His guidance and advice were presented,
and the tyrannical excesses were repeatedly corrected.
He utilized the initial renown of a fellow person (tóng rén),
and gained the later fortune of the northern elder (běi sǒu).
Among those who celebrated his good fortune,
how could there be no one with such feelings?
When a gentleman (jūnzǐ) judges a crime,
he might still refrain from acting,
let alone when state law is applied in haste,
without prior deliberation,
and in a moment of emotional change of countenance,
the punishment is the same as that for an evil faction?
The administrator then retrospectively blamed Zǐcháng (Sīmǎ Qiān) for his slanderous writings circulating later,
and on this basis carried out the execution.
No such legal precedent has ever been heard of.
The eulogy says: Jìcháng (Cài Yōng) was from the Qī clan,
his talent was extensive, his emotions extravagant.
He excelled in literary classics,
and was delighted by music and artistry.
Cài Yōng (Yōng) truly yearned for tranquility,
his mind keen, his words ornate.
He spoke out against Jīn (Jīn) and Shāng,
traveling south and moving north.
He relied on Liáng (Liáng) and harbored Dǒng (Dǒng),
his reputation defiled, his body destroyed.
Zuǒ Zhōu Huáng Lièzhuàn (Biography of Zuǒ Zhōu Huáng), Chapter Fifty-One.
Zuǒ Xióng (Zuǒ Xióng), courtesy name Bóháo,
was a native of Nièyáng, Nányáng Commandery.
During Emperor Ān's (Ān Dì) reign,
he was recommended as Xiàolián (Filial and Incorrupt),
and gradually promoted to Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (Inspector of Jì Province).
The province had many powerful clans
who liked to seek favors,
but Zuǒ Xióng (Xióng) always closed his door and did not associate with them.
He impeached greedy and corrupt officials holding two thousand dàn (èr qiān dàn),
without any reservations or taboos.
In the early years of Yǒngjiàn,
Gōngchē summoned [him] to be appointed Yìláng.
At that time, Shùndì had just ascended the throne,
ministers were lax,
and the court had many administrative deficiencies.
Xióng repeatedly spoke on affairs of state,
his words being profound and incisive.
Shàngshū Púyè Yú Xǔ, recognizing Xióng's loyal and public-spirited integrity,
submitted a memorial recommending him, saying:
"I observe that currently, among the Gōngqīng and below,
many mostly fold their arms in silence,
considering the cultivation of favors as wisdom,
and giving their all as foolishness.
They even warn each other, saying: 'White jade cannot be created [by oneself];
being complacent often brings future blessings.'
I respectfully observe that Yìláng Zuǒ Xióng
has repeatedly submitted confidential memorials,
even citing Your Majesty's personal experience of hardship and adversity
as a warning,
truly possessing the loyal and upright integrity of a royal minister
and the style of Zhōu Gōng strategizing for Chéngwáng.
He should be promoted to an official position of 'throat and tongue' (i.e., a speaking role),
and he will surely bring benefits of correction and assistance."
Because of this, Xióng was appointed Shàngshū,
and was twice promoted to Shàngshūlìng.
He submitted a memorial detailing his views, saying:
"To Dà Yǔ,
what was valued was knowing people.
'To bring peace to the people is benevolence;
the common people will cherish it.'
When Bó (feudal lords) were enfeoffed and Hou (marquises) established,
replacing positions and governing the people directly,
the people became harmonious and peaceful,
and courtesy and deference
flourished.
Therefore, the Shī Jīng says:
'Thick are the clouds, dark and deep;
the rain falls in heavy drops.
It rains on our public fields,
and reaches our private ones.'
When Yōu and Lì were muddled and chaotic,
they did not
govern themselves;
Bāoyàn used her power,
and the seven sons advanced their faction.
The worthy and the foolish were confused,
and deep valleys became hills.
Thus, its poem says:
'The four states have no government,
and do not use their
good officials.'
It also says:
'Alas for the people of today,
why are they like vipers?'
This means people fear officials as they would vipers.
After the fall of the Zōngzhōu,
the Six States were annexed by Qín,
scholars were buried
alive, and classics destroyed.
The five ranks were abolished,
and commanderies and counties were re-established.
Counties had Lìng and Zhǎng,
and commanderies had Shǒu and Wèi.
The 'shi-wu' system spied on each other,
and the people were like wild boars.
When the great Hàn
received the Mandate,
although it did not restore the ancient ways,
it was able to cautiously select all officials,
remove harshness, remedy defects,
and joyfully overcome difficulties,
comforting and guiding them.
By the time of Wén and Jǐng,
the empire was prosperous and well-governed.
This was truly due to their profound tranquility and gentle leniency,
and their careful selection of officials.
Later, when Xuāndì,
who rose from humble origins,
investigated names and realities,
and understood what afflicted the times,
he would personally summon and interview
Cǐshǐ and Shǒuxiàng,
examining their words and deeds,
and ensuring reliable rewards and certain punishments.
The emperor then sighed, saying:
'The reason why the people are peaceful and without resentment
is that the government is fair and the officials are good.
Those who share
this with me,
are they not the good èrqiānshí!'
He believed that if officials were frequently changed,
those below would not be secure in their work;
if they remained long in their positions,
the people would obey their teachings.
For those
who achieved good governance,
he would commend them with imperial letters,
increase their rank, and bestow gold,
or grant them titles up to Guānnèihóu.
If a Gōngqīng position became vacant, they would be used in order.
Thus, officials excelled in their
duties,
and people were secure in their work.
Good officials in the Hàn dynasty
were most abundant at this time,
and thus they were able to bring auspicious omens of submission
and achieve the accomplishment of a middle resurgence.
Moving without constancy,
each harboring a temporary mindset,
not considering the long term.
They call killing innocent people 'awe-inspiring,'
and accumulating wealth and acting decisively 'talented.'
They consider self-governance and bringing peace to the people as inferior
and weak,
and upholding laws and following principles as inflexible.
Punishments like shaving heads and tattooing faces
arise from trivial resentments;
the disaster of corpses lying about
is caused by moods of joy and anger.
They regard the people as enemies,
and tax
them like wolves and tigers.
The supervising officials look at each other's backs,
sharing the same illness;
they do not report wrongs when seen,
nor investigate evils when heard.
They observe governance at roadside stations,
and demand results
within a month.
They do not praise virtue when speaking of good,
nor base evaluation of merit on facts.
Those who are boastful and exaggerated gain renown,
while those who are strict and disciplined incur slander.
Some use their crimes to achieve high status,
or make a show of themselves to seek fame.
Regional governors do not scrutinize;
they compete to appoint and summon,
leap and rise,
exceeding their proper ranks.
Some are impeached, captured, and investigated,
but escape
punishment.
Meeting with amnesties and giving bribes,
they are once again cleared.
Crimson and purple are the same color,
the clear and the turbid are not distinguished.
This allows treacherous and corrupt individuals
to lightly regard their comings and goings,
appointments and dismissals are
like flowing water,
vacancies numbering in the hundreds.
Local officials and departmental clerks,
their duties are demanding, but their salaries meager.
Carriages, horses, and clothing
all come from the people.
The honest take just enough,
the greedy fill their homes.
Special
selections and arbitrary levies
are numerous and incessant.
Sending off and welcoming creates burdensome expenses,
harming governance and injuring the people.
The harmonious qi is not yet spread,
calamities and misfortunes do not disappear;
all faults lie here.
Today's 'ink
sashes' (i.e., local officials),
are like the feudal lords of old.
They are appointed titles in the royal court,
and their carriages and robes are fixed,
but they are equated with commoners.
They betray commands and evade responsibilities.
This is not how to uphold the constitution and clarify
principles,
or to benefit and nurture the masses.
Your foolish subject believes that for Shǒuxiàng and Zhǎnglì
who have shown clear effectiveness in benevolence and harmony,
their ranks should be increased in situ,
and they should not be moved.
They should not be allowed to leave office
unless for the mourning of parents.
Those who do not follow the laws and prohibitions,
and do not obey royal commands,
should be permanently barred from office,
they should not be reinstated.
If someone is impeached,
and absconds
without submitting to the law,
their family should be relocated to a border commandery,
to deter others in the future.
Local and departmental officials who deal directly with the people
should all be upright scholars capable of governance,
Considering,
〔一二〕if their official salaries were increased,
and officials served a full year in their posts,
only then would the prime minister's office, provinces, and commanderies be permitted to nominate and appoint them.
If this were done,
the paths of power and favoritism would be blocked,
the roots of falsehood and hypocrisy would be severed,
the burden of sending
and greeting officials would be lightened,
and the sources of exaction and taxation would cease.
Officials who followed principles
would be able to accomplish their reforms;
the people throughout the land
would each settle in their places.
This would emulate the path of the restorations of
Wén and Xuān,
〔一三〕shining brightly and leaving a legacy
that would endure for eternity.
The Emperor was moved by his words,
and ordered the relevant departments
to verify their truthfulness
and consider their implementation.
However, the proposals of Xióng
were all clear and insightful regarding governance,
but because the eunuchs usurped power,
they could ultimately not be adopted.
From then on, selections and replacements alternated frequently,
magistrates changed monthly,
and the welcoming of the new and sending off of the old
caused endless toil and disruption.
Sometimes official bureaus were empty and vacant,
with no one to handle affairs,
and whenever a selection department was busy,
officials would even flee.
In the third year of Yǒngjiàn,
the capital (Jīngshī) and Hànfáng experienced earthquakes and ground fissures,
and springs of water gushed forth.
In the fourth year,
Sī and Jì again suffered great floods.
Xióng analyzed these calamities and anomalies,
believing they were omens of insubordination among the common people,
and again submitted a memorial stating:
"It is advisable to make secret preparations,
to await unforeseen events."
Soon after, widespread banditry erupted in Qīng, Jì, and Yáng Zhōu,
and within a few years,
the entire realm was in turmoil.
Afterward, a general amnesty was declared across the empire;
although the bandits mostly dispersed,
the officials remained unprepared,
and the remnants of the rebels and fugitives
rose again within a few months.
Xióng and Púshè Guō Qián jointly submitted a memorial,
believing
"Banditry has plagued us for years,
and more than half have died.
When one person breaks the law,
their entire clan flees en masse.
It is advisable, while they are still few,
to allow them to repent and reform.
If they report their accomplices,
they should be pardoned;
those who can execute or capture them
should be clearly rewarded."
The memorial was submitted,
but both were disregarded.
He also memorialized again:
"It is advisable to promote classical learning
and renovate the Tàixué."
The Emperor complied.
In the first year of Yángjiā,
the Tàixué was newly completed,
and an imperial edict commanded that those who passed the examination on the classics be appointed as students (dìzǐ),
increasing the A and B categories,
with ten individuals in each.
One hundred thirty-eight esteemed scholars aged sixty and above from the capital (Jīngshī) and commanderies and kingdoms were appointed as Láng, Shèrén, or Zhū Wángguó Láng.
Xióng also memorialized again:
"Xiàolián from the commanderies and kingdoms
are the gòngshì of ancient times;
when they go out, they govern the people
and spread harmonious customs and teachings.
If they are like 'facing a wall' (ignorant),
they will be useless.
Confucius said, 'At forty, one is free from doubt,'
and the rites speak of 'being strong in service.'
I request that from now on, no Xiàolián under forty
be nominated for examination.
They should all first go to the gōngfǔ;
students (zhūshēng) should be tested on their family traditions (jiāfǎ),
and clerical officials (wénlì) on their memorials and reports (jiānzòu).
These should be copied and sent to Duānmén,
to verify their merits and weaknesses,
to observe unusual abilities,
and to improve customs.
Those who do not comply with regulations
should have their crimes punished according to law.
However, those with outstanding talent and extraordinary conduct
may naturally be exempt from age restrictions."
The Emperor complied,
and this was then promulgated to the commanderies and kingdoms.
The next year,
there was a Xiàolián from Guǎnglíng named Xú Shú,
who was not yet old enough for selection.
A bureaucrat (Táiláng) doubted and questioned him.
He replied:
"The imperial edict states, 'If there are those like Yán Huí or Zǐ Qí,
they are not restricted by age.'
Therefore, my home commandery selected me for this position."
The bureaucrat could not refute him.
Xióng questioned him, saying:
"Formerly, Yán Huí heard one thing and understood ten.
How many things has Xiàolián understood from one?"
Xú Shú had no reply,
and was then sent back to his commandery.
Thereupon, Jìyīn Tàishǒu Hú Guǎng and more than ten others were all dismissed for erroneous nominations,
while only Rǔnán Chén Fān, Yǐngchuān Lǐ Yīng, Xiàpī Chén Qiú, and more than thirty others were appointed Lángzhōng.
From then on, governors (mùshǒu) were fearful and cautious,
none daring to nominate lightly.
Until Yǒngxǐ,
the selections and examinations were fair and just,
and many capable individuals were found.
Xióng also memorialized to summon renowned scholars from across the realm to be Bóshì,
and to make sons and younger brothers of high officials (gōngqīng) into students (zhūshēng).
Those with integrity and ambition
had their salaries increased.
Rǔnán Xiè Lián
and Hénán Zhào Jiàn,
though only twelve years old,
were each able to master the classics,
and Xióng memorialized for both to be appointed Tóngzǐ Láng.
Thereupon, those carrying books to study
gathered like clouds in the capital (Jīngshī).
Initially,
the Emperor was deposed and made Jìyīn Wáng.
His wet nurse, Sòng É, and the eunuch Sūn Chéng and others together deliberated on establishing the Emperor.
Later, because É had previously been involved in the plot,
the Emperor enfeoffed her as Shānyáng Jūn,
with a fief of five thousand households.
He also enfeoffed the son of the Grand General Liáng Shāng, Jì, as Xiāngyì Hóu.
Xióng submitted a memorial, saying:
“Indeed, carving up land and enfeoffing marquises
is a matter greatly esteemed by the royal system.
Gāo Huángdì made a covenant:
‘Those not of the Liú clan shall not be made kings,
and those without merit shall not be made marquises.’
Xiào'ān Huángdì enfeoffed Jiāng Jīng, Wáng Shèng, and others,
which subsequently led to the anomaly of an earthquake.
In the second year of Yǒngjiàn,
when merit for a secret plot was enfeoffed,
there was also the變 (change) of a solar eclipse.
Those skilled in numerology
all attributed the blame to the enfeoffments.
Currently, Qīngzhōu is suffering from famine,
bandits have not ceased,
and the people are in dire straits,
seeking rations and loans from above.
Your Majesty diligently labors and contemplates,
making the relief of the people your duty.
It is appropriate to follow ancient laws,
to be tranquil and practice non-action,
to seek Heaven’s will,
and to dispel calamities and anomalies.
It is truly inappropriate to retrospectively reward small favors
and thereby violate the great code.”
The Emperor did not listen.
Xióng again remonstrated, saying:
“I have heard that no ruler does not favor loyalty and uprightness and abhor slander and flattery.
However, throughout the ages,
none have failed to be punished for loyalty and uprightness,
while slanderers and flatterers have enjoyed favor.
This is because it is difficult to heed loyalty
and easy to follow flattery.
Indeed, punishment
is what human nature deeply abhors;
honors and favors
are what human nature deeply desires.
Therefore, in these times, few act loyally,
while many practice flattery.
Thus, rulers frequently hear their praises,
rarely know their faults,
and remain deluded and unaware,
leading to danger and ruin.
I humbly observe the imperial edict considering the old virtue and past favor of the imperial wet nurse,
desiring to bestow a special prominent reward.
According to the precedents of the Shàngshū,
there is no system for enfeoffing wet nurses with noble ranks or fiefs.
Only Wáng Shèng, the imperial wet nurse during the previous Emperor’s time, was made Yěwáng Jūn.
Shèng caused the disaster of treacherous slander, deposition, and establishment,
and while alive, she was reviled by all under Heaven;
after death, she was celebrated by all within the seas.
Jié and Zhòu, though noble as Sons of Heaven,
were disdained by common servants who would be ashamed to be compared to them,
because they were without righteousness.
Yí and Qí, though lowly commoners,
were sought after by kings and marquises who vied to associate with them,
because they possessed virtue.
Now, the imperial wet nurse personally practices frugality and moderation,
leading her subordinates by example,
and all officials and common people
are inspired by her conduct.
If she is now to share the same noble title as Wáng Shèng,
I fear it would go against her fundamental principles
and disappoint her usual wishes.
I, your foolish servant, believe that the human heart,
in principle, is not far removed from this;
what causes unease
is the same throughout ancient and modern times.
The hundred surnames have been deeply admonished by the disaster of Wáng Shèng’s downfall,
where the lives of the populace
were as precarious as piled eggs.
They constantly fear that such things might recur in this age.
The thought of trepidation
has not left their minds;
words of fear
have not ceased from their mouths.
I beg that, as previously suggested,
tens of millions of cash be annually given to support the imperial wet nurse.
Internally, this would be sufficient to fully express the joy of kindness and affection,
and externally, it would not be regarded as strange by officials and commoners.
As for Liáng Jì’s enfeoffment,
it is not an urgent matter.
It would be appropriate to postpone it past this period of disaster and misfortune,
and then calmly deliberate its propriety.”
At that time, there was another earthquake and the anomaly of Mt. Gōushì collapsing.
Xióng again submitted a memorial, saying:
“The previous Emperor enfeoffed Yěwáng Jūn, and there was an earthquake in Hànyáng.
Now Shānyáng Jūn is enfeoffed and the capital again experiences a tremor.
Power residing exclusively with women
is an even greater calamity.
My previous foolish words stated that enfeoffment is a matter of utmost importance;
a king may privately bestow wealth upon individuals,
but not official positions.
It is fitting to revert the imperial wet nurse’s enfeoffment
to quell the calamities and anomalies.
Now that Jì has already humbly declined,
Shānyáng Jūn should also uphold her original integrity.”
Xióng’s words were frequently earnest and direct.
É also felt fearful and declined,
but the Emperor was so deeply attached that he could not desist,
and ultimately enfeoffed her.
Later, the imperial wet nurse subsequently lost her title due to improper association.
At this time, the Grand Minister of Agriculture, Liú Jù, was reprimanded for his official duties,
summoned to the Imperial Secretariat,
and urged to hasten his steps by repeated shouts,
and also beaten with rods.
Xióng submitted a report, saying:
“The Nine Ministers hold positions second to the Three Excellencies,
and their rank is among the great ministers.
In their conduct, they observe the decorum of wearing jade pendants;
in their movements, they maintain the etiquette of the academy.
It was Xiàomíng Huángdì who first introduced beatings and punishments,
all of which are not in accordance with ancient precedents.”
The Emperor followed and changed this,
and thereafter, the Nine Ministers were no longer subjected to beatings.
From the time Xióng took charge of the Nàyán,
he rectified and disciplined many things.
Whenever there were memorials or official proposals,
the imperial court considered them precedents.
He was promoted to Sīlì Xiàowèi.
Initially,
Xióng recommended Zhōu Jǔ to be a Shàngshū.
Jǔ proved competent in his duties,
and all who discussed him praised him.
When Xióng was Sīlì,
he again recommended the former Inspector of Jìzhōu, Féng Zhí, as a general,
but Zhí had once been convicted of corruption.
Jǔ impeached Xióng on this ground.
Xióng was pleased and said:
“I once served Féng Zhí’s father and was also friendly with Zhí himself.
Now Xuānguāng impeaches me on this,
which is truly an act like that of Hán Jué.”
Because of this, all under Heaven respected him.
The next year, he was dismissed due to a legal issue.
Later, he again became a Shàngshū.
He died in the third year of Yǒnghé.
Zhōu Jǔ, courtesy name Xuānguāng,
was a native of Rǔyáng, Rǔnán,
and the son of the Administrator of Chénliú, Fáng.
Fáng is mentioned in the RúLín Zhuàn.
Jǔ was short and plain in appearance,
but extensively learned and widely read,
revered by scholars.
Thus, a saying circulated in the capital about him:
“The Five Classics, vertical and horizontal, are Zhōu Xuānguāng.”
In the fourth year of Yánguāng,
he was appointed to the staff of the Sītú, Lǐ Hé.
At that time, the eunuch Sūn Chéng and others had established Shùndì,
and exterminated the Yán clan.
The Deliberative Counselor Chén Chán believed that Empress Dowager Yán had no maternal affection for the Emperor,
and suggested she should be moved to a separate residence
and forbidden from court audiences.
All the deliberating ministers agreed that this was appropriate.
Jǔ said to Hé:
“Formerly, Zhèng Wǔjiāng plotted to kill Yángōng,
and Yángōng swore to her in the Yellow Springs.
Qín Shǐhuáng resented his mother for her misconduct,
and kept her isolated for a long time,
but later, moved by the words of Yǐngkǎoshū and Máocāo,
he resumed his filial duties.
Historical records praise this.
Now that the Yán clan has just been punished,
the Empress Dowager is confined in a detached palace.
If she were to fall ill from sorrow and grief,
and something unexpected were to happen one day,
how would the Emperor command the world?
If Chán’s proposal is followed,
later generations will attribute blame to you, my lord.
It is advisable to secretly memorialize the court,
ordering them to attend to the Empress Dowager,
and urging the assembled officials
to conduct court audiences as before,
to satisfy Heaven’s heart
and respond to the people’s expectations.”
Hé immediately submitted a memorial explaining this.
In the first month of the next year,
the Emperor then paid homage at the Eastern Palace,
and the Empress Dowager was thereby put at ease.
Later, Zhū Chāng
, the Minor Prefect of Chánglè, replaced Hé as Sītú
, and Jǔ was appointed as an official.
At that time, Sūn Chéng and others, for bringing a memorial into the palace and vying for credit,
angered the Emperor.
They were all exiled to distant counties,
and an imperial edict ordered the Magistrate of Luòyáng to expedite their departure.
Jǔ advised Zhū Chāng, saying:
“When the court was in distress in the west,
if not for Sūn Chéng and others, how could it have been established?
Even the achievements of Hán, Péng, Wú, and Jiǎ,
how could they surpass this!
Now, forgetting their great virtues,
and recording their minor transgressions,
if they were to die prematurely on the road,
the Emperor would incur the reproach of killing loyal ministers.
Before they depart,
you should memorialize urgently.”
Chāng said:
“The imperial edict is now angered,
and the two Shàngshū have already reported on this matter.
If I alone memorialize on this,
I will certainly invite blame and punishment.”
Jǔ said:
“Your Excellency is over eighty years old,
and holds the position of a Tái fǔ.
If you do not exhaust your loyalty to serve the nation at this time,
and instead cherish your life and seek comfort in favor,
what do you hope to achieve?
Even if your salary and position are preserved,
you will certainly fall into the reproach of being a sycophant.
If you admonish and are punished,
you will still have the name of a loyal and steadfast person.
If my words are not worth adopting,
please allow me to resign from this point.”
Chāng then submitted a memorial of remonstrance,
and the Emperor indeed followed it.
Jǔ was later recommended as Màocái,
and became the Magistrate of Píngqiū.
He submitted memorials discussing the gains and losses of the current era,
and his words were very incisive and upright.
Shàngshū Guō Qián, Yīng Hè, and others sighed upon seeing them,
and jointly submitted a memorial praising Jǔ’s loyalty and uprightness,
desiring the Emperor to place the memorial by his seat,
to serve as a regulation and warning.
Jǔ was gradually promoted to Cìshǐ of Bìngzhōu.
In the commandery of Tàiyuán,
the old custom was that because Jiè Zǐtuī was burned to death,
there was a taboo against using fire on “dragon taboos” days.
When it came to the month of his death,
everyone said that the spirits were displeased with the lighting of fires.
Therefore, the gentry and common people every winter would observe a month of Cold Food,
not daring to light fires for cooking.
The old and young could not endure it,
and many died each year.
When Jǔ arrived at the province,
he wrote a condolence letter and placed it in Jiè Zǐtuī’s temple,
stating that extinguishing fires in the deep winter
harmed the lives of the people,
and was not the intention of a worthy person.
He used this to explain to the ignorant people,
encouraging them to return to warm food.
Thereupon, the public’s confusion gradually dissipated,
and the custom was considerably reformed.
He was transferred to be the Inspector of Jìzhōu.
In the third year of Yángjiā
(128 CE), Zuo Xióng, the Colonel Director of Retainers, recommended him,
and he was summoned and appointed Minister.
He and the Palace Assistant, Huáng Qióng, worked in harmony to assist in governance.
His reputation was great in the court,
and those around him feared him.
That year, Hénán and the Sānfǔ suffered a great drought;
the five grains were damaged by the disaster.
The Son of Heaven personally sat in the open air in the east wing of Dèyángdiàn to pray for rain.
He also ordered the Director of Retainers and Hénán to offer sacrifices to the River God, famous mountains, and great marshes.
The imperial edict stated that Jǔ’s talent and learning were profound and superior,
and specially issued a policy question, saying:
"I, being without virtue,
have reverently received the three successions.
Rising early and sleeping late,
I strive to harmonize with the great central principle.
For some years now,
drought disasters have frequently occurred;
the crops are parched and withered,
and the people's food is scarce.
The five moral duties are not taught,
and the royal benevolence has not flowed.
All officials are idly eating (holding positions without doing work),
occupying positions that are not theirs.
When should they be demoted or dismissed?
What are the signs of transformation and restoration?
How will their effects be manifested?
Discuss and answer in detail,
hiding nothing."
Jǔ replied, saying:
"Your servant has heard the Yì Jīng states, 'Heaven is honored, Earth is humble;
thus Qían and Kūn are established.'
When the two primal forces interact,
all things are born.
Among all things,
humans are the most noble.
Therefore, the sages govern them as rulers,
and perfect them through transformation,
following the suitability of the four seasons,
and adapting to the harmony of yīn and yáng,
so that marriages of men and women do not exceed their proper time.
They envelop them with benevolence and grace,
guide them with virtuous teachings,
show them omens of disaster,
and instruct them with auspicious signs.
This was how the former sages received Qían and nurtured creation at the beginning.
If yīn and yáng are obstructed and separated,
then the two energies are blocked and choked;
if the two energies are blocked and choked,
then people and things will not prosper;
if people and things do not prosper,
then wind and rain will be untimely;
if wind and rain are untimely,
then floods and droughts will become disasters.
Your Majesty occupies the position of Táng and Yú,
but has not implemented the policies of Yáo and Shùn.
Recently, the laws of Emperor Wén and Emperor Guāngwǔ have been abolished,
and the extravagant desires of the fallen Qín dynasty are followed.
Internally, there are accumulated resentful women;
externally, there are unmarried men.
Now, the imperial lineage is not thriving,
and the Eastern Palace has not been established.
This is caused by harming harmony, going against reason,
and severing human relations.
It is not only Your Majesty who performs this;
the eunuchs,
too, abuse their power and influence,
intimidate good families,
take their daughters and confine them,
to the extent that some grow old and die without a spouse,
which is contrary to the will of Heaven.
In the past, King Wǔ, upon entering Yīn,
released the women from the 'slanted palace';
Chéng Tāng, when afflicted by disaster,
exercised self-restraint in six matters;
Duke Xī of Lǔ, encountering drought,
reprimanded himself and prayed for rain:
all used their sincerity to turn misfortune into blessings.
Since the drought began,
it has lasted for years.
I have not heard of Your Majesty's effective reforms,
only the futile labor of the exalted one exposing himself to wind and dust,
which truly is of no benefit.
Moreover, you have ordered the prefectures and commanderies to pray to the spirits for rain.
In the past, Qí suffered a great drought,
and Duke Jǐng wanted to sacrifice to the River God.
Yàn Zǐ remonstrated, saying: 'This is not permissible.
The River God has water as his city-state,
and fish and turtles as his common people.
If the water is depleted and the fish wither,
would he not wish for rain?
He himself is unable to bring it.'
What Your Majesty does
only pursues its superficiality,
not seeking its reality.
It is like climbing a tree to seek fish,
or walking backward to go forward.
Truly, it is appropriate to cultivate trustworthiness and reform governance,
exalt the Way and transform confusion,
release the unused women from the imperial harem,
redress the wrongful cases of the empire,
and abolish the heavy expenses of the Grand Provisioner.
As for the five moral duties not being taught,
the blame lies with the Minister of Education.
Those who occupy positions that are not theirs
should be immediately dismissed.
I, your servant, was promoted from outside the provinces to oversee matters of state;
my learning is shallow and my wisdom limited,
insufficient to answer.
The Yì Chuán says: 'The yang responds to Heaven,
without delay.'
Thereupon, Jǔ, together with the Director of the Palace Library Chéng Yìshì and Palace Assistant Huáng Qióng, were summoned for an audience,
and questioned about gains and losses.
Jǔ and the others all replied that it was appropriate to be cautious in appointing officials,
to remove and dismiss the corrupt,
to distance oneself from sycophants and the depraved,
to follow the frugality of Emperor Wén,
and to honor the teachings of Emperor Xiàomíng,
then timely rain would surely come.
The Emperor asked:
"Who among the hundred officials are corrupt, sycophantic, and depraved?"
Jǔ alone replied:
"Your servant comes from a lower prefecture,
and was exceptionally appointed to confidential matters,
insufficient to distinguish among all officials.
are loyal and steadfast;
those who flatter and blindly conform
are sycophantic and depraved.
The Minister of Education has been in office for six years,
and I have not heard any loyal words or unique strategies from him.
This is my foolish thought."
Thereafter, the Minister of Education Liú Qí was dismissed due to an incident,
and Jǔ was promoted to Colonel Director of Retainers.
In the first year of Yǒnghé
(136 CE), numerous disasters and strange phenomena appeared.
The palace felt ill omens from them.
An edict summoned the Dukes, Ministers, officials receiving two thousand dàn, and Ministers to Xiǎnqīndiàn,
and asked:
"Many who speak on affairs of state say that
in the past, Duke Zhōu governed as regent for the Son of Heaven.
When he died,
King Chéng wished to bury him with the rites of a Duke,
and Heaven showed anomalies.
When he was re-buried with the rites of a Son of Heaven,
there was a corresponding change in the wind.
The Marquis of Běixiāng personally served as Son of Heaven, yet was buried with the rites of a King.
Therefore, there have been numerous disasters and strange phenomena.
It is fitting to add a respectful posthumous title
and rank him in the ancestral temple."
Many among the assembled officials discussed and thought it appropriate to follow the imperial edict.
Jǔ alone replied:
"In the past, Duke Zhōu had the response of 'requesting the mandate,'
and achieved the merits of great peace,
thus August Heaven moved its might
to manifest his sagely virtue.
The Marquis of Běixiāng was not of the legitimate lineage to begin with,
established by treacherous ministers.
He was on the throne for less than a year,
and his regnal name was not changed.
August Heaven did not protect him,
and his great mandate ended prematurely in obscurity.
The Chūnqiū does not record the death of Prince Měng as 'beng' (death of an emperor),
nor the burial of Zǐ Yě of Lǔ.
Now, the Marquis of Běixiāng has no other meritorious virtues.
To bury him with the rites of a King
is already grand for his circumstances.
It is not appropriate to bestow a posthumous title.
The coming of disasters and misfortunes
is not due to this."
Thereupon, Minister of Education Huáng Shàng, Grand Minister of Ceremonies Huán Yān, and seventy other individuals agreed with Jǔ’s opinion,
and the Emperor followed it.
Shàng, courtesy name Bóhé,
was from Nánjùn.
In his youth, he successively held prominent positions,
and was also known for his administrative abilities.
Zhōu Jǔ was promoted to Grand Administrator of Shǔjùn,
but was dismissed for an offense.
Grand General Liáng Shāng recommended him as Attendant-in-ordinary,
and greatly respected him.
In the third month of the sixth year, on the Shangsi Day,
Liáng Shāng hosted a grand gathering of guests,
feasting at the Luòshuǐ River.
Zhōu Jǔ claimed illness and did not attend.
Liáng Shāng and his close associates drank heartily and were extremely joyful.
When the drinking ended and the entertainers stopped,
they continued with a song of sorrow.
Those who heard it among the attendees
all covered their faces and wept.
Grand Coachman Zhāng Zhǒng was also present at the time,
and upon returning,
he told Zhōu Jǔ about the matter.
Zhōu Jǔ sighed and said,
"This is what is called joy and sorrow at the wrong time,
it is not appropriate.
Disaster will surely befall him!"
Liáng Shāng indeed died that autumn.
When Liáng Shāng was critically ill,
the Emperor personally visited him
and asked for his dying words.
He replied,
"When a person is about to die,
their words are good.
My Attendant-in-ordinary Zhōu Jǔ
is pure, upright, and loyal,
and can be entrusted with heavy responsibilities."
Because of this, Zhōu Jǔ was appointed Remonstrance Official.
At that time, there were consecutive disasters and anomalies,
and the Emperor recalled Liáng Shāng's words.
He summoned Zhōu Jǔ to the Xiǎnqīn Hall
and questioned him about the omens and calamities.
Zhōu Jǔ replied,
"When Your Majesty first ascended the throne,
you followed and upheld the old institutions,
promoting transformation and bringing about good governance,
and those near and far were reverent.
In recent years,
there has been a gradual deviation from before.
The court has many favorites,
and stipends are not granted based on virtue.
Observing heaven and examining people,
comparing the present with the past,
it is truly a cause for alarm.
The *Shūjīng* says: 'When the transgressions are frequent, then the prolonged drought is severe.'
If transgressions are excessive and without measure,
then words are not followed, and those below are not upright;
if the *yáng* has nothing to restrain it,
then those above are disturbed and those below are exhausted.
It is advisable to secretly and strictly command the commanderies and prefectures
to investigate powerful clans and great villains,
and to capture and punish them in a timely manner."
Thereafter, cunning bandits such as Zhōu Shēng and Xú Fèng rose up everywhere in the Jiānghuái region,
just as Zhōu Jǔ had stated.
At that time, an imperial edict dispatched eight envoys to inspect local customs,
all of whom were selected for their established prestige.
Zhōu Jǔ was then appointed Imperial Household Grandee.

Imperial Household Grandee Dù Qiáo, acting Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments Zhōu Xǔ, former Governor of Qīngzhōu Fēng Xiàn, Minister Luán Bā, Palace Assistant Imperial Censor Zhāng Gāng, Governor of Yǎnzhōu Guō Zūn, and Chief Clerk of the Grand Commandant Liú Bān were all appointed acting Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments,
and divided among themselves to travel throughout the empire.
For governors and officials with salaries of two thousand *dàn* with clear evidence of corruption,
reports were sent quickly by post horse;
for those of *mòshòu* rank and below,
they were immediately arrested.
For those who were pure, loyal, benevolent, and beneficial,
and were beloved by the common people,
and deserved to be distinguished,
all their deeds were reported.
Thereupon, the eight envoys were all appointed at the same time,
and the empire called them
"The Eight Talents."
Zhōu Jǔ then impeached the corrupt and cunning,
and recommended the public-spirited and upright,
and the court praised him.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Hénèi,
and then summoned to be Grand Minister of the Court.
When Empress Dowager Liáng assumed regency,
she issued an edict stating that since Emperor Shāng had died young,
his ancestral tablet's position in the temple should be below that of Emperor Shùn.
Grand Herald Mǎ Fǎng memorialized that it should be as the imperial edict stated,
but Remonstrance Official Lǚ Bó believed that it should follow the order of *zhāomù*,
with Emperor Shāng first,
and then Emperor Shùn.
The edict was sent to the high ministers.
Zhōu Jǔ deliberated, saying,
"In the *Chūnqiū* period, Duke Mǐn of Lǔ had no son,
and his half-brother Duke Xī succeeded him.
Duke Xī's son, Duke Wén, then placed Duke Xī above Duke Mǐn.
Confucius criticized this,
and the *Chūnqiū* records: 'There was a service in the Grand Temple,
Duke Xī was elevated.'
The commentary says: 'This was a reversal of the ancestral order.'
When Duke Dìng corrected the order,
the classic states 'offering sacrifices to the former dukes in order,'
which became a law for ten thousand generations.
Now Emperor Shāng is earlier,
and in terms of rank, is the father;
Emperor Shùn is later,
and in terms of kinship, is the son.
The principle of 'first and last' cannot be changed,
and the order of *zhāomù* cannot be confused.
Lǚ Bó's argument is correct."
The Empress Dowager issued an edict adopting his view.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies,
but then had to leave office due to the mourning for his mother.
Later, he was appointed Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments.
He died in Jiànhé 3rd year (149 CE).
The court considered Zhōu Jǔ to be pure, just, honest,
and had intended to make him a prime minister,
and deeply lamented his passing.
An edict was then issued to the Grand Master of Ceremonies and the Grand Administrator of Rǔnán, saying,
"In former ages,
seekers of worthy men were as if thirsty,
sealing tombs and bowing at gates,
to glorify the virtuous and wise.
Thus Gōngshū was eulogized,
and Wēngguī received an account,
thereby illuminating loyalty, inspiring customs,
and serving as a model for future generations.
The late Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments Zhōu Jǔ
had a nature comparable to Bó Yí and Shū Qí,
and his loyalty surpassed Súi Hé and Guǎn Zhòng.
Previously appointed as a prefect and administrator,
and later returning as an imperial counselor,
in and out of the capital,
he achieved admirable accomplishments,
and in the inner court, he had a reputation for discretion and tranquility.
I recorded his merits,
thereby elevating him to the Nine Ministers.
I was just about to use him to regulate all officials,
and to wisely assist in the three major affairs of state,
but he did not live to his destined end,
thus thwarting our long-term plans.
The court mourns and grieves for him,
truly with sorrow.
Does not the *Shījīng* say: 'Swiftly he performed his military exploits,
thereby bestowing upon you blessings.'
Therefore, let all officials from Grand Master down attend the mourning on the day of his funeral.
An additional sum of one hundred thousand coins is granted,
to honor his integrity of 'humble and unadorned' conduct."
His son was Xié.
Xié, courtesy name Jùshèng,
in his youth favored profound emptiness,
and was appointed a gentleman based on his father's rank,
but he resigned and returned home.
His father's former subordinate, Zhào Kuí of Hénán, became a regional commander,
and lowered himself to extend courtesy,
showing respect to Xié.
Xié was ashamed to return the favor,
and so he closed his gate and isolated himself.
Later, the Grand Administrator recommended him as *xiàolián*,
but he again left due to illness.
At that time, Liáng Jì was powerful and prosperous,
and none dared to refuse his summons,
but Xié was summoned three times,
and ultimately could not be compelled.
Later, he was recommended as *xiánliáng fāngzhèng*,
but did not respond.
Again, he was summoned by the public carriage,
with elaborate ceremonies, but he firmly declined, citing illness and infirmity.
He often lived in seclusion, hiding himself,
admiring the tranquility of Lǎo Dān,
cutting off all human contact.
Thorns grew in his alley,
for more than ten years.
It was not until Yánxī 2nd year (159 CE)
that he opened his gate to receive guests,
engaging in discussions and joyful banquets.
That autumn, Liáng Jì was executed,
and at the end of the year, Xié died,
at the age of fifty.
Cài Yōng considered him to have known his destiny.
From Xié's great-grandfather Yáng to Xié's grandson Xún,
six generations in one lineage
were all well-known.
Huáng Qióng, courtesy name Shìyīng,
was a native of Ānlù in Jiāngxià.
He was the son of Huáng Xiāng, Grand Administrator of Wèijùn.
Huáng Xiāng is mentioned in the "Biographies of Literati."
Huáng Qióng was initially appointed Palace Gentleman of the Heir Apparent based on his father's rank,
but declined, citing illness, and did not take the position.
He experienced the mourning for his father,
and after the mourning period concluded,
all five bureaus of government invited him,
but he refused for consecutive years.
During the Yǒngjiàn era,
many high officials recommended Qióng.
Thereupon, he, along with Hé Chún of Kuàijī and Yáng Hòu of Guǎnghàn, were summoned by gōngchē.
When Qióng reached Lúnshì,
he pleaded illness and did not proceed.
The authorities impeached him for disrespect,
but an imperial edict ordered the county to comfort and dismiss him with due ceremony,
so he could not refuse.
Previously, many hermits summoned and invited did not live up to expectations.
Lǐ Gù had always admired Qióng,
so he sent him a letter in advance saying:
"I heard you have already crossed the Yī and Luò rivers,
and are currently near Wàansuì Pavilion.
Is it that you are gradually engaging in affairs,
or will you comply with the imperial command?
A gentleman considers Bó Yí narrow-minded,
and Liǔxià Huì irreverent,
hence the saying goes: 'Neither Bó Yí nor Liǔxià Huì,
(it is) between appropriateness and impropriety.'
This is what the wise and virtuous value in their conduct.
If you truly wish to pillow on mountains and dwell in valleys,
emulating Cháo and Yóu,
then this would be acceptable;
but if you are to assist in governance and benefit the people,
now is the time.
Since the beginning of mankind,
good governance has been rare and chaotic customs abundant.
If one must wait for a ruler like Yáo or Shùn,
then ambitious scholars would never have their opportunity.
I often hear the saying: 'The towering are easily broken,
the pure are easily stained.'
The 'Songs of Yangchun' [highbrow music]
have few who can harmonize with them,
and under a great reputation,
it is truly difficult to live up to it.
Recently, Fan Jūn of Lǔyáng, when first summoned and arriving,
the court set up altars and mats,
treating him as if he were a divine being.
Although there were no great differences,
his words and actions were beyond reproach.
Yet slander spread,
and his reputation quickly diminished.
Is this not because public expectation was too high,
and his fame too great?
In recent times, among the scholars summoned and invited,
Hú Yuán'ān, Xuē Mèngcháng, Zhū Zhōngzhāo, Gù Jìhóng, and others,
their achievements were not commendable.
Therefore, common opinion says that hermits merely steal empty fame.
I hope, Sir, that you will uphold this far-reaching plan,
so that the multitude will admire and submit,
and thoroughly wipe away this statement."
When Qióng arrived,
he was immediately appointed Yìláng,
and gradually promoted to Shàngshū Púyè.
Originally,
Qióng followed his father in the imperial court,
becoming familiar with established practices.
Later, when he held office,
he was thoroughly practiced in official affairs.
When debating in the imperial hall,
no one could resist or usurp him.
At that time, there were continuous natural disasters and anomalies.
Qióng submitted a memorial to Emperor Shùn, saying:
"Since recently,
the hexagram positions have been disordered,
cold and heat have interfered with each other,
hazy mists have risen,
the sun has been dim, and the moon scattered.
Examining the will of Heaven,
it is probably not for naught.
Your Majesty should open the stone chamber,
consult the Hélúo diagrams,
and externally command the historians
to thoroughly list the disasters and anomalies from the beginning of the Hàn dynasty up to before Yǒngjiàn,
and from Yǒngjiàn until today,
and determine which period had more.
Also, dispatch close ministers and scholars to examine government affairs,
frequently consult with high officials,
and investigate successes and failures.
All those without merit or virtue
should be dismissed.
I previously made some statements about disasters and misfortunes,
and also recommended Guanglù Dàfū Fán Yīng, Tàizhōng Dàfū Xuē Bāo, as well as Hé Chún of Kuàijī and Yáng Hòu of Guǎnghàn,
but my recommendations have not yet received Your Majesty's attention.
I humbly observe that hermits Huáng Cuò of Bājùn and Rèn Táng of Hànyáng,
both of whom are elderly,
have the ambition of the 'Seven Authors.'
They should be further invited and brought in,
to assist in promoting great transformation."
Thereupon, an edict summoned Cuò and others by gōngchē.
In the third year [of Yǒngjiàn],
there was a great drought.
Qióng again submitted a memorial, saying:
"Formerly, when Duke Xī of Lǔ encountered a drought,
he attributed it to six shortcomings of his own,
personally practicing frugality,
closing off private petitions from women,
(punishing) thirteen slanderers and sycophants,
executing nine who collected taxes from the people and accepted bribes,
and withdrawing from the southern suburb.
Heaven immediately sent a great rain.
Today, Your Majesty should also reflect on government affairs,
make necessary reductions,
strive for simplicity and frugality,
to satisfy the people.
Let the Imperial Workshops and Imperial Treasury
cease extravagant expenses.
Clearly instruct close ministers
to abide by laws and regulations,
and if anyone does not change,
show them Your likes and dislikes.
Frequently meet with high officials,
invite and admit scholars,
consult them on governance and transformation,
and let them point out successes and failures.
Furthermore, prisoners are still accumulated,
many dying,
which is also sufficient to disturb harmony,
and bring down disasters and drought.
If Your Majesty changes what is detrimental and follows what is good,
and selects and employs excellent counsel,
then disasters will dissipate and blessings will arrive."
After the memorial was presented,
he was granted an audience in the Déyáng Hall,
and the Zhong Chángshì was ordered to pass Qióng's memorial to the responsible officials for implementation.
Since the Emperor's accession,
the ceremony of personally tilling the imperial fields had not been performed.
Qióng believed that such a great national ceremony should not be abandoned for long,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"From ancient times, sagely emperors and enlightened kings
all respectfully observed bright sacrifices,
to increase blessings and auspiciousness,
and thus they personally performed the rites at the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
and personally undertook the toil of tilling the imperial fields,
to set an example for the multitude,
and encourage agricultural labor.
In ancient times, King Xuān of Zhōu did not till the thousand mu,
and Zǐ Wén Gōng considered it a great reproach.
Consequently, there was the difficulty with the Qiāngróng,
ultimately damaging his reputation for a middle revival.
I humbly observe that Your Majesty follows the grand enterprise of studying antiquity,
embodies reverence to respond to Heaven,
complies with the seasons to honor the origin,
cherishes and appeases all spirits,
is exposed to dust on the roads morning and night,
and listens to various government affairs day and night to care for the people.
Though the Odes praise Chéng Tāng for his untiring diligence,
and the History lauds King Wén for having no leisure to eat,
Your Majesty's efforts truly cannot be surpassed.
Now, the temple sacrifices have just concluded,
and the rituals for praying for grain and purified fasting
are near, scheduled for tomorrow.
I fear that those around Your Majesty
are unwilling to frequently disturb Your sacred person,
believing that the rite of personal plowing
can be abandoned.
I have heard that the former kings established statutes,
and there was a specific day for tilling the imperial fields.
The Sītú would issue warnings,
and the Sīkōng would clear the altar.
Five days before,
there would be a response from the harmonious winds,
the King would go to the fasting palace,
offer libations and load the plow.
This truly showed its importance.
Since the guǐsì day,
the wind has remained from the northwest,
and sweet rain has not gathered,
and coldness still persists.
You did not personally attend the welcoming of spring in the eastern suburb.
The ceremony for the first farmer
is what Your Majesty should personally undertake,
to welcome the harmonious qi,
and bring timely winds.
The Yì says: 'The gentleman strives unceasingly.'
This is the way."
The memorial was presented,
and the Emperor followed it.
Shortly thereafter,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Lìng.
Qióng believed that the previous selection of Xiàolián by Zuǒ Xióng,
which exclusively used Confucian scholars and literary officials,
still omitted something in the principle of selecting talents.
So he proposed adding filial piety and those capable of governing as four categories,
and this measure was eventually implemented.
Furthermore, Xióng had previously proposed that officials to be recommended should first be tested in the public office,
and then re-tested at the Duānmén.
Later, Shàngshū Zhāng Shèng proposed abolishing this policy.
Qióng again submitted a memorial, saying:
"The institution of re-testing
is to clarify the pure and the turbid,
and verify the empty and the excessive,
and should not be reformed."
The Emperor then stopped (the reform).
He was sent out as the Grand Administrator of Wèijùn,
and gradually promoted to Tàicháng.
During the Hépíng era,
he was selected to serve as an imperial lecturer in the Forbidden Palace.

he was transferred to Sīkōng
