He submitted a memorial, remonstrating, saying:
"Your servant has heard that Heaven strives to make its *qì* strong,
and the ruler strives to make his governance powerful.
This is why a king, dwelling on high and holding himself up,
must not be insecure;
and treading on danger and relying on strength,
must not be without support.
If one holds oneself up insecurely, one will fall;
if one relies on strength without support, one will be in peril.
Therefore, when the sage ascends to a high position and occupies the supreme office,
he takes virtue and righteousness as his head;
when traversing peril and treading on precipices,
he takes worthy men as his strength.
Táng Yáo took virtuous transformation as his crown and diadem,
and Jì and Xiè as his sinews and strength.
High, he grew ever more exalted;
active, he grew ever more secure.
This is why the former sages were able to long preserve the myriad states,
and protect their altars of soil and grain.
In the past, Gāo Huángdì responded to Heaven and followed the people,
wielded his sword and became king,
swept away Qín and Xiàng,
changed the mandate and established new institutions,
and bestowed virtue and continued his blessings.
It was not until Āi and Píng
that the imperial Way lost its guiding principles,
and corrupt governance grew daily more chaotic,
thus allowing treacherous sycophants to fill the court,
and imperial relatives to act arbitrarily.
What was crowned was not crowned with benevolence and righteousness,
and what was relied upon was not supported by worthy assistants,
ultimately leading to collapse,
and the extinguishing of the Hàn legacy.
The celestial order was overturned and the people and spirits were desolate.
Fortunately, the august Heaven bestowed its mandate,
and the fiery virtue shone again.
Guāng Wǔ, with his sacred martial prowess naturally endowed by Heaven,
continued the succession and founded the enterprise,
establishing his foundation upon ice that was melting,
and setting his feet in a forest of thorny brambles.
He promoted the worthy from among the ignorant masses,
and achieved great deeds in a formless age.
He upheld rites and righteousness amidst contention,
and followed the Way and transformation amidst chaos and separation.
Thus, he traversed heights without falling,
and relied on strength in danger without stumbling,
restoring the great lineage,
initiating a revival,
extending his brilliance to the eight cardinal directions,
and leaving an endless name.
However, in the middle period,
this glorious enterprise gradually declined.
Your Majesty, initially from a vassal state,
then ascended to the imperial throne;
the world wiped its eyes,
expecting to see great peace.
But since your ascension,
there has been no superior governance.
The various Liángs wield power,
eunuchs fill the court,
they are repeatedly enfeoffed and accumulated in office,
swaying the court.
The selection of ministers, commanders, governors, and prefects,
all originates from their gates.
Treasures of feathers, fur, teeth, hides, bright pearls, and southern gold,
overflow their chambers,
their wealth rivals that of princely mansions,
their power overturns Heaven and Earth.
Those who speak of this are surely exterminated;
those who attach themselves to them are surely honored.
Loyal subjects, fearing death, seal their mouths,
and all people, terrified of disaster, become tongue-tied,
blocking Your Majesty's keen ears and eyes,
making you a deaf and blind ruler.
Thus, the former Grand Commandant Lǐ Gù and Dù Qiáo,
loyal in their direct speech,
virtuous in assisting governance,
considered the nation above their own lives,
and met their demise as their reward,
yet for discussing state affairs,
they were cruelly annihilated.
The worthy and the foolish alike felt profound pain,
and within the seas, sorrow and fear arose.
Furthermore, the former Prefect of Báimǎ, Lǐ Yún,
pointed out that the crimes and filth of the eunuchs deserved execution,
all based on the hearts of the multitude,
to rescue the accumulation of dangers.
Dù Zhòng of Hóngnóng,
knowing that Yún's words should be acted upon,
feared that Yún would suffer for his loyalty,
and therefore submitted a memorial explaining his reasoning,
begging to die on the same day,
in order to awaken the state,
hoping Yún might be spared.
But Yún was innocent,
and Zhòng was also implicated and executed.
The world felt especially grieved,
and resentment grew stronger.
Therefore, people in court and country
regarded loyalty as a taboo.
In ancient times, when Zhào killed Míng Dú,
Kǒngzǐ turned back from the river.
If nests are overturned and eggs broken,
then the phoenix will not soar;
if sacrificial animals are disemboweled and fetuses killed,
then the *qílín* will not arrive.
Indeed, things of a kind attract each other,
and reason makes it so.
The Imperial Secretary Zhōu Yǒng,
formerly Prefect of Pèi,
had long served Liáng Jì,
and relied on his power and influence.
When he was implicated in an incident and deserved punishment,
he was instead promoted to a prefectural post.
Seeing that Jì was about to decline,
he then feigned denouncement to show loyalty,
and through a cunning scheme,
also obtained a marquisate.
Moreover, the Palace Yellow Gate Xié and his wicked associates,
formed factions.
From the time Jì rose to prominence,
they were intimate allies,
plotting day and night,
jointly contriving treacherous schemes.
When Jì was about to be executed,
having no trick left to employ,
they again reported his wickedness,
to claim titles and rewards.
Your Majesty did not thoroughly investigate,
nor carefully distinguish between true and false,
but instead simultaneously enfeoffed them alongside loyal subjects,
making scarlet and purple share the same color,
and white and black mixed and trampled,
which is like casting gold and jade among sand and gravel,
and smashing jade scepters and discs in mud.
When the four quarters hear of this,
none are not indignant and sighing.
In ancient times, Zēngzǐ was supremely filial,
yet his kind mother threw the shuttle;
Bó Qí was supremely worthy,
yet ended up in exile.
〔一０〕Indeed, when slanders and flattery elevate,
there is no one, however high, who cannot be raised;
when partisan factions suppress,
there is no one, however deep, who cannot be submerged.
Can you not investigate?
Your servant is utterly dull and inept,
yet has continuously received national grace,
my person is light but my position is heavy,
my diligence does not make up for my faults,
but I fear that if I die eternally,
my offenses will become even deeper.
I dare, on my dying day,
to express words that are not taboo,
hoping that there may be one in ten thousand,
and I will have no regrets in the Three Springs."
〔一一〕He died that year,
at the age of seventy-nine.
He was posthumously granted the title of General of Chariots and Cavalry,
and given the posthumous name Zhōng Hóu.
His grandson was Wǎn.
Wǎn's courtesy name was Zǐyǎn.
He lost his father when young.
Early on, he was eloquent and intelligent.
His grandfather, Qióng,
initially served as the Administrator of Wèijùn.
In the first month of the first year of Jiànhé, there was a solar eclipse.
The capital did not see it, but Qióng reported it.
The Empress Dowager issued an edict asking about the extent of the eclipse.
Qióng pondered how to answer, but did not know how to describe it.
Wǎn, seven years old,
was nearby,
and said:
"Why not say that the remainder of the solar eclipse
is like the beginning of the moon?"
Qióng was greatly astonished,
and immediately used his words to respond to the edict,
and deeply cherished and loved him.
Later, Qióng became Grand Minister of Works (Sītú).
Wǎn, as a grandson, was appointed Youth Gentleman (Tóngzǐ Láng),
but declined due to illness and did not take the post,
becoming famous in the capital.
At that time, the Grand Minister over the Masses (Sīkōng), Shèng Yǔn, was ill.
Qióng sent Wǎn to inquire about his health.
It happened that Jiāngxià had reported a matter concerning barbarian bandits to the vice-prefecture.
Yǔn opened the letter and read it.
He jokingly said to Wǎn:
"Jiāngxià is a great state,
but it has many barbarians and few scholars."
Wǎn bowed and replied:
"It is the responsibility of the Grand Minister over the Masses
when barbarians disrupt China."
Then he flicked his sleeves and left.
Yǔn was greatly impressed by him.
He was slightly promoted to Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng.
At that time, Chén Fán was Guānglù Xūn,
and he deeply respected and treated him well,
often discussing affairs with him.
According to the old system,
the Guānglù would recommend officials from the Three Bureaus,
designating those with high achievement, long service, and exceptional talent and virtue as Màocái Sìxíng.
At that time, many sons of powerful and wealthy families gained recommendations through personal connections,
while the poor and principled were overlooked due to their impoverished state and humble positions.
The capital had a folk rhyme about this:
"If you wish for the unable,
it's the Guānglù Màocái."
Thereupon, Wǎn and Fán, with one mind,
prominently employed principled scholars.
Liú Chún of Píngyuán, Zhū Shān of Hédōng, Yīn Cān of Shǔjùn, and others were all recommended for their talent and conduct.
Fán and Wǎn were then slandered and harmed by the officials from powerful and wealthy families.
The matter was sent down to Yùshǐ
Chéng Wáng Chàng and Shìyùshǐ Diāo Wěi.
Wěi and Chàng had long esteemed Fán and Wǎn,
and did not pursue the matter.
But those around them again trapped them with the charge of forming a clique.
Chàng was demoted to Yìláng and Fán was dismissed from office.
Wǎn and Wěi were both banished from officialdom.
Wěi’s courtesy name was Zǐróng,
and he was from Péngchéng.
Later, when Chén Fán was summoned,
many who spoke on affairs pleaded for Wěi,
so he was again appointed Yìláng,
and promoted to Shàngshū.
In court, he showed integrity and straightforwardness,
and was later appointed xiāng of Lǔ and Dōnghǎi Commanderies.
He was firm and resolute by nature,
with clear strategy,
and was praised as divine wherever he served.
He always disciplined himself by laws and regulations,
and his family members never saw him behave negligently.
Wǎn was dismissed for almost twenty years.
Towards the end of the Guānghé era,
Tàiwèi Yáng Cì submitted a memorial recommending Wǎn as having the talent to restore order amidst chaos.
Consequently, he was summoned and appointed Yìláng,
promoted to Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and then transferred to Shìzhōng.
In the early Zhōngpíng era,
he was sent out as Yòufúfēng,
then summoned and appointed Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng, Shàofǔ, and Tàipú.
He also served as Yùzhōu Mù.
At that time, bandits were rampant,
and the provincial territory was ravaged.
Wǎn suppressed and pacified them,
and his prestige greatly spread.
His administrative achievements became a model for the empire,
and he was enfeoffed as Guānnèihóu.
When Dǒng Zhuó took power,
he respected Wǎn as a famous minister,
summoned him as Sītú,
promoted him to Tàiwèi,
and re-enfeoffed him as Yángquán Xiānghóu.
Dǒng Zhuó proposed moving the capital to Cháng'ān.
Wǎn and Sītú Yáng Biāo jointly remonstrated, but were not heeded.
Wǎn retired and argued against the proposal, saying:
"In the past, the Duke of Zhōu established Luòyì to bring peace to the Jī house,
and Guāngwǔ chose the Eastern Capital to prosper the Hàn dynasty.
This was initiated by Heaven and
settled by the spirits.
Since the great enterprise is already established,
how can we recklessly move it,
thereby diminishing the hopes of the entire realm?"
People at the time feared Dǒng Zhuó's violent rage,
believing Wǎn would surely come to harm,
and strongly advised him.
Wǎn replied:
"In the past, when Bái Gōng caused rebellion in Chǔ,
Qū Lú advanced through blades;
when Cuī Zhù assassinated his ruler in Qí,
Yàn Yīng did not fear his oath.
Although I am not virtuous,
I sincerely admire the integrity of ancient people."
Wǎn was eventually dismissed due to this.
Dǒng Zhuó still respected his reputation for virtue and his old family background,
and dared not harm him.
Later, he and Yáng Biāo were jointly appointed Guānglù Dàfū.
When the capital was moved to the Western Capital,
he was transferred to Sīlì Xiàowèi.
He conspired with Sītú Wáng Yǔn to execute Dǒng Zhuó.
When Dǒng Zhuó's generals Lǐ Quē and Guō Sì attacked and broke into Cháng'ān,
they consequently arrested Wǎn, imprisoned him, and he died there,
at the age of fifty-two.
The discourse says: In ancient times, feudal lords annually presented scholars.
Promoting the worthy brought the highest rewards,
while the unworthy were demoted in rank and territory.
They were raised to Sīmǎ,
their talents debated,
and only after their assessment was settled were they given office,
and only after taking office were they given emoluments.
Thus, the ruler obtained the right people,
officials were encouraged in their conduct,
and the state's important affairs were managed.
This practice has a long history.
In the early Hàn dynasty, edicts called for the recommendation of Xiánliáng and Fāngzhèng,
and prefectures and commanderies investigated Xiàolián and Xiùcái.
This was also a method of presenting scholars.
After the restoration, categories such as Dūnpǔ, Yǒudào, Xiánnéng, Zhíyán, Dúxíng, Gāojié, Zhìzhí, Qīngbái, and Dūnhòu were added.
With the path to honor broadened,
it became difficult to control expectations.
From then on, those who stole fame and feigned virtue
gradually became rampant competitors.
Requests and appeals from powerful families and noble officials
flourished.
Since Zuǒ Xióng took charge of affairs,
limiting age and testing talent,
although there were some imperfections,
it was indeed adapting to the needs of the time.
However, Yáng Qióng, Hú Guǎng, Zhāng Héng, Cuī Yuàn, and their ilk,
were stuck in old methods,
contradicting each other.
Those who adhered to names overlooked their shortcomings,
while those who calculated results highlighted their effectiveness.
Therefore, when Xióng was Shàngshū,
the empire dared not arbitrarily select officials.
For over ten years,
it was praised as having selected the right people.
Was this not also evidence of effectiveness?
When Emperor Shùn, though young and weak,
first took back power and issued edicts himself,
entrusting capable people,
scholars were thus able to dedicate themselves,
and the empire looked up to his demeanor with eager anticipation.
Consequently, he prepared black and red silks, jade, and bolts of cloth
to invite Fán Yīng of Nányáng.
The Son of Heaven descended from his private chamber,
set up an altar and mat,
and the Shàngshū led him in,
to inquire about gains and losses.
He was eager to promote the worthy
and humble himself with ritual.
Thereupon, reclusive scholars and humble commoners,
forgetting their confined scholarship,
wiped their headscarves and donned coarse clothes,
hoping for the invitation of the imperial carriage.
Thus, Yīng was able to emulate his example,
and all talented and virtuous individuals served.
Such as Lǐ Gù and Zhōu Jǔ, whose profound strategies were deep;
Zuǒ Xióng and Yáng Qióng, whose governance was upright and firm;
Huán Yān and Yáng Hòu, who advanced through Confucian scholarship;
Cuī Yuàn and Mǎ Róng, who were distinguished by their literary works;
Wú Yòu, Sū Zhāng, Chóng Gǎo, and Luán Bā, excellent administrators of the people;
Páng Cān and Yú Xǔ, great strategists as generals;
Wáng Gōng and Zhāng Hào, who humbly promoted scholars;
Zhāng Gāng and Dù Qiáo, who corrected wrongs with upright principles;
Láng Yǐ, whose Yin-Yang theories were meticulous;
Zhāng Héng, whose mechanical arts were exceptionally brilliant:
the scholars of the Eastern Capital
were abundant in this era.
If the court had accepted their lofty plans,
if their wisdom and strength had been vigorously utilized,
if the inner chambers had tolerated their frank words,
and if all actions had followed their established models,
then the achievements of Emperors Wǔ and Xuān
would not have been far off!
The Shījīng says:
"There is none who does not have a beginning,
few are those who have a good end."
This is indeed regrettable!
By the time of Emperor Huán,
great virtues emerged one after another.
Chén Fán and Yáng Bǐng were praised as worthy ministers in court;
Huángfǔ, Zhāng, and Duàn were renowned as famous generals when serving outside;
Wáng Chàng and Lǐ Yīng repaired the imperial shortcomings;
Zhū Mù and Liú Táo offered advice and corrected the times;
Guō Yǒudào praised and discerned human character;
Chén Zhònggōng spread the Dao in his rural home.
As for other profound Confucians and far-sighted strategists,
those with noble hearts and pure conduct,
who stirred up the prevailing trends,
they are too numerous to mention.
Yet this Dao was not invigorated,
civil and military affairs declined.
Those in court suffered execution for righteous discourse,
and those who withdrew from affairs faced disaster due to party proscriptions.
Although the previous cart broke,
the incoming one was still accelerating.
That it tilted but did not fall,
that it cracked but did not collapse,
was it not due to the efforts of benevolent gentlemen?
Alas!
The encomium says: Xióng acted as Nàyán,
like the Eight Worthies of antiquity.
Elevating them by category,
rising from the lower borders.
Entering court to manage state affairs,
together they alleviated disaster and gloom.
Qióng's name was known early,
repeatedly reporting national flaws.
Wǎn also showed early brilliance,
his position reached his aspirations.
Xún, Hán, Zhōng, Chén Biographies, Chapter Fifty-two.
Xún Shú 字 Jìhé,
a native of Yǐngyīn, Yǐngchuān,
was an eleventh-generation descendant of Xún Qīng.
In his youth, he possessed noble conduct,
was extensively learned, but disliked textual exegesis.
He was often criticized by common scholars,
but people in his hometown praised him for his discerning judgment of people.
During the reign of Emperor Ān,
he was summoned and appointed as Lángzhōng.
Later, he was twice promoted to become the Magistrate of Dāngtú.
He resigned from office and returned to his hometown.
Contemporary famous worthies such as Lǐ Gù and Lǐ Yīng all regarded him as their teacher and master.
When Empress Dowager Liáng took charge of the government,
there were changes like a solar eclipse and an earthquake.
An edict was issued for dukes and ministers to recommend worthy and upright individuals.
Guānglùxūn Dù Qiáo and Shàofǔ Fáng Zhí recommended Shú to submit a policy proposal.
He satirized and criticized the powerful favorites,
which made him resented by the Grand General Liáng Jì.
He was sent out to become the Chancellor of Lánglíng Hóu.
He managed affairs with clarity and reason,
and was called a "Divine Lord."
After a short while,
he resigned and returned,
living in seclusion and nurturing his aspirations.
Each time his property increased,
he would use it to support his clan and close friends.
He died at the age of sixty-seven
in the third year of Jiànhé.
Lǐ Yīng, who was then Shàngshū,
personally requested leave for a teacher's mourning.
Both counties erected shrines for him.
He had eight sons: Jiǎn,
Gǔn,
Jìng,
Táo,
Wāng,
Shuǎng,
Sù,
Zhuān.
All of them were famous,
and people at the time called
them the "Eight Dragons."
Originally,
the old village of the Xún clan was named Xīháo.
The Magistrate of Yǐngyīn, Yuàn Kāng of Bóhǎi, considered that ancient Gāoyáng Shì had eight talented sons,
and now the Xún clan also had eight sons,
so he renamed their village Gāoyáng Lǐ.
Jìng had extremely virtuous conduct,
did not serve in office,

In the ninth year of Yánxī,

Fire on earth,

Ritual and righteousness.

The Hàn dynasty inherited the Qín dynasty's laws,

People of later generations,

Winter
and summer clothes,

to support useless
women.

After submitting the memorial,
he immediately left his official post.
Later, he was caught in the Dǎnggù (Proscription of Partisans),
and lived in seclusion by the sea,
then fled south to the banks of the Hàn River.
For over ten years,
he engaged in writing,
and thus came to be known as a great scholar.
When the partisan ban was lifted,
the Five Departments simultaneously invited him.
Sīkōng Yuán Féng recommended him as a man of the Way,
but he did not respond.
When Yuán Féng died,
he observed mourning rites for three years,
which in his time often became a common custom.
At that time, many people did not wear mourning clothes for their wives;
even during deep mourning for relatives, there were still those who made condolence calls or inquired about illnesses,
and also privately bestowed posthumous titles upon their lords, fathers, and various famous scholars.
In all these cases, he cited major principles
and corrected them according to the classics.
Although not everything was changed,
there were considerable reforms.
Later, he was summoned by public coaches to serve as a Retainer in the General-in-Chief Hé Jìn’s (何進) administration.
Hé Jìn (何進) feared he might not come,
so he welcomed and recommended him as a Palace Attendant.
When Hé Jìn (何進) was defeated, the imperial summons ceased.
When Emperor Xiàn (獻帝) ascended the throne,
Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) assisted in governing,
and summoned him again.
Shuǎng (爽) wanted to flee,
but the officials held him tightly,
preventing him from leaving.
So he went and was appointed as the Chancellor of Píngyuán (平原相).
When he arrived at Wǎnlíng (宛陵),
he was again recalled to serve as the Grand Master of Ceremonies.
After serving for three days,
he was promoted to Minister of Works.
From the time Shuǎng (爽) was first summoned to his ascension to the highest ministerial ranks,
ninety-five days had passed.
He then followed the relocation of the capital to Cháng’ān (長安).
Shuǎng (爽) saw that Dǒng Zhuó’s (董卓) cruelty and violence were growing excessively,
and would surely endanger the state.
He recruited and appointed talented and strategic individuals,
intending to plot against Dǒng Zhuó (董卓).
He also colluded with Minister of the Masses Wáng Yǔn (王允) and Dǒng Zhuó’s (董卓) Chief Clerk Hé Yóng (何顒) and others for an internal conspiracy.
He unfortunately died of illness,
aged sixty-three.
He authored *Lǐ Zhuàn* (禮傳), *Yì Zhuàn* (易傳), *Shī Zhuàn* (詩傳), *Shàngshū Zhèngjīng* (尚書正經), and *Chūnqiū Tiáolì* (春秋條例).
He also compiled a collection of the successes and failures of Hàn (漢) affairs that could serve as lessons,
which he called *Hànyǔ* (漢語).
He also wrote *Gōngyáng Wèn* (公羊問) and *Biàn Chèn* (辯讖),
along with other treatises,
titled *Xīnshū* (新書).
There were altogether over one hundred chapters,
but many are now lost or incomplete.
His nephews, Yuè (悅) and Yù (彧), were both renowned.
Yù (彧) has his own biography.
A commentary states: Xún Shuǎng (荀爽), Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄), and Shēntú Pán (申屠蟠) were all reclusive scholars known for their Confucian conduct.
They were repeatedly summoned but consistently declined due to illness.
However, when Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) was in power,
he again respectfully summoned them.
Pán (蟠) and Xuán (玄) ultimately did not yield, thereby preserving their integrity.
Shuǎng (爽), though already white-haired,
alone went.
In less than ten *xún* (旬), he attained the rank of a high minister.
One might suspect that his actions deviated from the proper course,
but I privately ponder his circumstances,
believing that a gentleman’s decision to serve or retire is a weighty matter.
In peaceful times, he promotes the Dao to realize his aspirations;
in times of decline, he adapts his actions to rectify the era.
Was Xún Gōng’s (荀公) eagerness to exert himself
an instance of adapting his actions?
Otherwise,
why would he forsake auspicious uprightness and tread upon a tiger’s tail?
Considering his humble words regarding the proposal to move the capital,
which saved Yáng (楊) and Huáng (黃) from disaster,
and his subsequent secret plot against the Dǒng (董) family,
which nearly restored the national destiny—
this is what is called
“great straightness seems bent,”
the Dao is indeed circuitous.
Yuè (悅), courtesy name Zhòngyù (仲豫), was the son of Jiǎn (儉).
Jiǎn (儉) died young.
When Yuè (悅) was twelve,
he could explain the *Chūnqiū* (春秋).
His family was poor and lacked books.
Whenever he went among people,
he could recite and memorize most of the texts
he saw at a single glance.
He was by nature calm and quiet,
and of handsome appearance,
especially fond of writing.
During Emperor Líng’s (靈帝) reign, eunuchs held power,
and many scholars withdrew to live in reclusion.
Yuè (悅) therefore feigned illness and lived in seclusion.
People at the time did not recognize him,
though his cousin Yù (彧) particularly held him in high regard.
Initially, he was invited to the residence of General Who Guards the East, Cáo Cāo (曹操).
He was promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
Emperor Xiàn (獻帝) was quite fond of literature.
Yuè (悅), Yù (彧), and Minister of the Privy Purse Kǒng Róng (孔融) attended the emperor in the palace,
discussing matters morning and evening.
He was successively promoted to Palace Librarian and Palace Attendant.
At that time, political power had shifted to the Cáo (曹) family,
and the Son of Heaven merely maintained his composure.
Yuè (悅) was devoted to offering counsel,
but his advice was not utilized.
So he wrote the five chapters of *Shēnjiàn* (申鑒).
His arguments
comprehensively revealed the principles of governance.
After completing it, he presented it.
Its general outline states:
The foundation of the Dao
is nothing but benevolence and righteousness.
The Five Canons order it,
and all other texts elaborate on it.
It is sung,
played on strings, and danced to.
Past precedents
are already clear,
and it is further reiterated later.
Therefore, the sage kings of antiquity,
in regard to benevolence and righteousness,
simply emphasized and repeated them.
Then governance would proceed.
If customs are chaotic, the Dao becomes desolate;
even Heaven and Earth cannot preserve their nature.
If laws are destroyed, the world declines;
even the ruler cannot maintain his
standard.
If norms are transgressed, ritual is lost;
even the sage cannot preserve his Dao.
If systems fail, desires run rampant;
even the four quarters cannot satisfy their demands.
These
are called the four afflictions.
Rewards and punishments unite the law.
These are called the five principles of governance.
If people do not fear death,
they cannot be deterred by punishment.
If people do not enjoy life,
they cannot be encouraged to do good.
Even if Qì (契) promulgated the five teachings,
and Gāoyáo (臯陶) served as Minister of Justice,
governance would not
be effective.
Therefore, those in authority must first enrich the people’s wealth to stabilize their resolve.
The emperor personally plows the imperial field,
the empress cultivates silkworms in the palace,
there are no idlers in the state,
no abandoned
occupations in the countryside.
Wealth is not squandered,
effort is not idly expended,
to provide for human affairs.
This is called nurturing life.
Good and bad.
Good and evil are determined by merits and demerits.
Praise and blame are proven by verification.
Listen to words and hold them accountable to deeds,
name and examine reality,
without being misled by deceit,
to cleanse the hearts of the multitude.
Thus,
no affair will be unverified,
no thing will be irrelevant,
no good will be unmanifested,
no evil will be unexposed,
no wickedness or strangeness will exist in customs,

The common people, high and low, seeing that their interests
depend on themselves,

and carefully cultivate their conduct.
Internally, they will not be misguided,
and externally, they will have no divergent desires.
Then the people’s will will be calm.
This is called rectifying customs.
Gentlemen are guided by sentiment,
commoners by punishment.
Honor and disgrace
are the essence of rewards and punishments.
Therefore, ritual teaching, honor, and disgrace
are applied to gentlemen
to transform
their sentiments;
shackles and flogging

A gentleman will not commit an act that brings disgrace,

A commoner does not fear punishment,
how much less
disgrace!
If education is abandoned,
ordinary people will fall into the realm of commoners;

This
is called manifesting transformation.
The nature of commoners is:
when lax, they become arrogant;
when arrogant, they become wanton;
when wanton, they become resentful;
when resentful, they rebel.
When in danger, they plot rebellion;
when secure, they indulge in desires.
Without strong authority,
there is no way to deter them.
Therefore, those in authority
must have military preparations
to guard against unforeseen events
and to suppress bandits and tyranny.
In peaceful times, these are entrusted to internal governance;
when there are affairs, they are used
in military campaigns.
This is called wielding awe.
They merely love their wealth.
If rewards are granted arbitrarily, goodness will not be encouraged.
Not to punish arbitrarily,
is not to pity the people;
if punishments are carried out arbitrarily, evil will not be deterred.
Rewards that do not encourage

punishments that do not deter are called indulging evil.
If those in authority can avoid hindering their subordinates from doing good,
and avoid indulging their subordinates in doing evil,

This is called
unifying the laws.
When applying them,
do not meddle in affairs,
but let them naturally resolve themselves.
Without strictness, order will be achieved;

with folded hands and humble deference,

This is called
the method of governance.
Rites.

Defying Heaven brings misfortune;

Moreover, in ancient times, when the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords had important matters,

Events became the Chūnqiū,

Every act of the sovereign was recorded;
goodness and evil,
success and failure,

Down to scholars and commoners,
if there was anything exceptionally outstanding,

Some wished to be famous but could not;

Gains and losses for a single day,

Good people are encouraged by this,

It is appropriate for the present age to fully establish historical officials,

The Emperor loved classics and books.

Its preface states:

established the Imperial Ultimate,
ordered Heaven and Earth,

The former kings greatly expanded this grand enterprise,

And their descendants,

The establishment of classics has five aims: first, to convey the Dao and righteousness;
second, to clarify laws and regulations;
third, to connect ancient and modern times;
fourth, to record meritorious deeds;
fifth, to highlight the virtuous and capable.
Thus, the interaction between Heaven and humanity,

Generations have continued their path,

Reductions and additions, fullness and emptiness,

Though good and bad differ,

The Hàn dynasty, for four hundred and six years,
restored order from chaos,
unified by military might and flourished through culture.
Ever mindful of the great legacy of their ancestors,

His Sacred Majesty, with serene contemplation,
cared deeply for culture and writings,
looking forward and back,
succeeding and continuing what came before,
expounding and honoring the great Way,

Thus, old books were compiled,
to narrate the Hàngjì.
Before the restoration of the dynasty,
the records of the successes and failures of enlightened rulers and worthy officials

Hán Sháo, courtesy name Zhònghuáng,
was a native of Wǔyáng, Yǐngchuān.
In his youth, he served in the commandery,
and was later summoned to the Sītú's mansion.
At that time, Gōngsūn Jǔ, a bandit from Tàishān, had falsely claimed a title for years,

many consequently incurring legal penalties.
The Shàngshū selected clerks from the three ministries who were capable of managing difficult affairs,
and thus appointed Sháo as the Chief of Yíng.
When the bandits heard of his virtue,
they warned each other not to enter the territory of Yíng.
Many other counties suffered from banditry,
and farming and sericulture were abandoned;
a great number of people flowed into his county seeking clothes and provisions.
Sháo pitied their hunger and distress,
and thus opened the granaries to relieve them,
providing for over ten thousand households.
The officials in charge strongly argued against it.
Sháo said:
"To save people from dying in ditches
and suffer punishment for it, I would enter the earth smiling."
The Grand Administrator, who had long known of Sháo's reputation for virtue,
ultimately did not punish him for this.
He died of illness while in office.
Lǐ Yīng, Chén Shí, Dù Mì, Xún Shú, and others from the same commandery erected a stele and eulogy for him.
His son, Róng,
courtesy name Yuáncháng.
In his youth, he was articulate and reasoned but did not pursue pedantic textual scholarship.
His reputation was very great,
and he was summoned by all five ministries.
At the beginning of Emperor Xiàn's reign,
he reached the position of Grand Coachman.
He died at the age of seventy.
Zhōng Hào, courtesy name Jìmíng,
was a native of Chángshè, Yǐngchuān.
He belonged to a prominent local family
known for generations for their expertise in law.
Hào was famous in his youth for his steadfast conduct;
the public ministries repeatedly invited him,
but as his two elder brothers had not yet entered officialdom,
he withdrew and lived in seclusion in Mìshān,
teaching poetry and law to over a thousand disciples.
Chén Shí, from the same commandery,
was younger than Hào,
but Hào befriended him.
Hào served as Administrator of Merit for the commandery,
and was concurrently summoned by the Sītú's mansion.
Upon his departure,
the Grand Administrator asked:
"Who can replace you?"
Hào replied:
"If your enlightened office truly wishes to find the right person,
Chén Shí, the head of Xīmén Pavilion, would be suitable."
When Shí heard this,
he said:
"Lord Zhōng seems not to discern people well;
I wonder why he alone recognizes me?"
After a short while, Hào impeached himself and left.
He was repeatedly invited by public ministries nine times,
and summoned to serve as Rectifier of the Grand Judge, Erudite, and Chief of Línglǜ,
but he declined all these appointments.
At that time, Hào and Xún Shú were both respected and admired by scholars and officials.
Lǐ Yīng often sighed and said:
"Lord Xún's pure discernment is difficult to emulate,
Lord Zhōng's supreme virtue is worthy of being a teacher."
Hào’s elder brother’s son, Jǐn’s mother,
was Yīng’s aunt.
Jǐn loved learning and admired the ancients,
possessing a retiring and yielding character.
He was the same age as Yīng,
and both had significant reputations.
Yīng’s grandfather, Grand Commandant Xiū,
often said:
“Jǐn resembles my family’s nature:
if the state has the Way, he will not be neglected;
if the state lacks the Way, he will escape punishment and death.”
He also gave Yīng’s younger sister to Jǐn in marriage.
Jǐn was appointed to provincial and prefectural offices,
but he never bent his will.
Yīng said to him:
“Mèngzǐ believed that ‘a person without a sense of right and wrong
is not a human.’
Why do you not align yourself with Mèng Kē?”
Jǐn often reported Yīng’s words to Hào.
Hào said:
“In the past, Guó Wǔzǐ enjoyed pointing out others’ faults,
which led to resentment.
Ultimately, to preserve oneself and one’s family,
your way is more valuable.”
The principles and teachings he embraced
were often of this kind.
At sixty-nine,
he died at home.
The various scholars eulogized him, saying:
“Of Línlǜ, with excellent virtue,
he did not dwell where rites were lacking.
Delighting in these poems and books,
he plucked the zither, enjoying antiquity.
Five times summoned by the province,
nine times invited by the court,
he hesitated before the royal command,
and spent his remaining years at ease.”
Hào’s grandson, Yáo,
was Commandant of the Capital in the Jiàn’ān era.
Chén Shí, courtesy name Zhònggōng,
was a native of Xǔ in Yǐngchuān.
He came from humble origins.
From childhood,
even in play,
he was deferred to by his peers.
In his youth, he became a county clerk,
often serving as a menial laborer.
Later, he became a deputy in the Capital Pavilion.
Yet he was ambitious and loved learning,
reading while sitting or standing.
The county magistrate, Dèng Shào, tried speaking with him
and was impressed,
allowing him to study at the Imperial Academy.
Later, the magistrate again summoned him to be an official,
but he instead sought refuge in the Yángchéng mountains.
At that time, there was a murderer,
and a county official named Yáng suspected Shí.
The county then arrested and imprisoned him,
but torture yielded no evidence,
and he was subsequently released.
When he became Inspector,
he secretly entrusted the magistrate of Xǔ
to formally summon official Yáng.
Those who heard of it, far and near,
all sighed in admiration.
His family was poor,
and he again became the Western Gate Pavilion Chief for the commandery,
soon transferring to Chief of Merit Records.
At that time, Regular Attendant Hóu Lǎn requested Grand Administrator Gāo Lún to employ an official.
Lún instructed him to appoint a Literary Clerk.
Shí knew he was not the right person,
so he carried the official document and requested an audience.
He said:
“This person should not be employed,
but Regular Attendant Hóu cannot be disobeyed.
I ask to be appointed to an external post,
so as not to tarnish your bright virtue.”
Lún agreed.
Thereupon, the local community found his appointment strange,
but Shí said nothing.
Lún was later summoned to be a Grand Master of Scribes,
and the gentry and officials of the commandery accompanied him to the coaching inn in Lúnshì.
Lún told the crowd:
“Previously, I employed an official at Regular Attendant Hóu’s request.
Master Chén secretly brought the instruction back
and had himself appointed to an outside post.
I hear that some critics disparaged him for this.
This fault lay with me, for fearing and being intimidated by the powerful.
Master Chén can be said to be one who ‘attributes good to his superior
and faults to himself.’”
Shí steadfastly took the blame himself.
Those who heard this then sighed in admiration,
and from then on, the world respected his virtue.
Grand Minister of Works Huáng Qióng appointed him to manage difficult cases,
making him the Magistrate of Wénxǐ.
Within a month or so,
he resigned due to a year-long mourning period.
He was again twice promoted to be the Magistrate of Tàiqiū.
He cultivated virtue and maintained tranquility,
and the common people were at peace.
When people from neighboring counties sought refuge and attached themselves to him,
Shí would always instruct and explain,
sending each back to their original official post or circuit.
The officials, fearing disputes,
requested permission to prohibit them.
Shí said:
“Lawsuits are for seeking justice.
If we prohibit them, how can justice be expressed?
Do not place any restrictions.”
The circuit officials heard this and sighed, saying:
“If Master Chén speaks like this,
how could anyone bear resentment towards him?”
And indeed, there were no lawsuits.
When the Grand Administrator of Pèi collected taxes unlawfully,
and Shí resigned his seal and left,
the officials and people longed for him.
Later, when the partisans were arrested,
Shí was also implicated.
Many others fled to escape,
but Shí said:
“If I do not go to prison,
the crowd will have no one to rely on.”
He then requested to be imprisoned.
He was released during an amnesty.
At the beginning of Emperor Líng’s reign,
Grand General Dòu Wǔ appointed him to his staff.
At that time, Regular Attendant Zhāng Ràng’s power overshadowed the world.
When Ràng’s father died,
and was buried in Yǐngchuān,
though the entire commandery attended,
no famous scholars went.
Ràng was deeply ashamed of this,
but Shí alone offered condolences.
Later, when partisans were again purged,
Ràng, grateful to Shí,
spared and pardoned many.
When Shí was in his village,
he treated people fairly.
If there were disputes,
he would always seek to judge and rectify them,
explaining right and wrong,
and no one left with resentment.
It even came to the point where people would exclaim:
“Rather be subjected to criminal punishment
than be criticized by Master Chén.”
At a time of famine and hardship,
a thief entered his house one night,
stopping on the beam.
Shí secretly saw him,
then rose, adjusted his attire,
called his children and grandchildren,
and with a solemn expression, instructed them, saying:
“One must strive to better oneself.
A bad person is not necessarily evil by nature;
it is habit that forms their character,
leading them to this point.
The gentleman on the beam is an example of this!”
The thief was greatly startled,
threw himself to the ground,
and kowtowed, confessing his crime.
Shí slowly explained to him:
“Looking at your appearance,
you do not seem like a bad person.
You should deeply restrain yourself and return to goodness.
However, this must be due to poverty.”
He ordered two bolts of silk to be given to him.
From then on, there were no more thefts in the entire county.
Grand Commandant Yáng Cì and Grand Minister of Education Chén Dān,
whenever they were appointed to high official positions,
all their subordinates would congratulate them.
Cì and others often sighed that Shí had not yet reached a high position,
and felt ashamed to have preceded him.
When the partisan prohibitions began to be lifted,
Grand General Hé Jìn and Grand Minister of Education Yuán Wěi sent people to urge Shí,
wishing to specially recommend him for an unconventional appointment.
Shí then declined to the envoy, saying:
“I have long cut off ties with worldly affairs,
and am merely preparing my funeral attire to await my end.”
Whenever the Three Excellencies had a vacancy,
discussions always pointed to him.
He was repeatedly summoned,
but he never rose,
closing his door and hanging up his carriage,
living a life of quiet retirement.
In the fourth year of Zhōngpíng,
at the age of eighty-four,
he died at home.
Hé Jìn sent an envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices.
Over thirty thousand people from across the realm attended,
and hundreds wore mourning clothes.
Together, they carved a stone and erected a stele,
bestowing on him the posthumous title of Master Wénfàn.
He had six sons,
Jì and Chén being the most virtuous.
Chén Jì,
whose courtesy name was Yuánfāng, was also known for his supreme virtue.
The brothers were filial and supportive,
and their household was harmonious.
Later generations of scholars all admired their conduct.
When the Partisan Prohibitions struck,
he vented his frustration by writing a book of tens of thousands of words,
titled *Chén Zǐ*.
When the party prohibitions were lifted,
the four high offices all summoned him,
but he would not yield or accept any position.
When he experienced the sorrow of his father's death,
whenever his grief peaked,
he would cough up blood and lose consciousness.
Although the mourning period was over,
his accumulated sorrow and emaciation
nearly consumed his life.
The Inspector of Yùzhōu, admiring his ultimate conduct,
memorialized the Grand Chancellor (Shàngshū)
to depict him in paintings throughout a hundred cities
to encourage good customs.
When Dǒng Zhuó entered Luòyáng,
he ordered Chén Jì to be appointed as Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng at home.
Having no choice,
he went to the capital,
and was promoted to Shìzhōng.
He was sent out as the Chancellor (Xiàng) of Píngyuán.
He went to visit Dǒng Zhuó,
who at the time wished to move the capital to Cháng'ān.
He then said to Chén Jì:
"The three commanderies (sānfǔ) are spacious and open,
with险固 on four sides.
The land is fertile and beautiful,
known as the 'landlocked sea' (lùhǎi).
Now that the troops east of the pass (guāndōng) have risen,
I fear Luòyáng cannot be occupied for long.
Cháng'ān still has palaces,
so what do you think of moving west now?"
Chén Jì replied:
"When the world is governed by the Way,
its security lies in the Four Barbarians (sìyí).
It is fitting to cultivate virtuous governance
to win over those who are not attached.
Relocating the Emperor (Zhìzūn)
is truly the last resort.
I humbly suggest that you, my lord, should entrust matters to the high officials (gōngqīng)
and focus your energy on external affairs.
If anyone disobeys your commands,
then suppress them with military might.
Now the troops east of the pass have risen,
and the people are suffering unbearable hardships.
If you humbly distance yourself from court politics
and lead an army to suppress them,
then the people suffering in misery
might perhaps be saved.
If you wish to move the Emperor (wànshèng) to secure your own safety,
you will face the danger of a stacked-egg and
the peril of towering cliffs."
Dǒng Zhuó was greatly displeased,
but he respected Chén Jì's reputation and conduct,
and said nothing more.
At that time, there was a discussion about making him Sītú,
but Chén Jì saw that chaos was about to erupt.
He did not bother to prepare
and immediately went to his commandery.
An imperial edict (xǐshū) was sent to posthumously appoint him Tàipú,
and he was also summoned to be Shàngshūlìng.
In the beginning of Jiàn'ān,
Yuán Shào was Tàiwèi
and offered the position to Chén Jì;
Chén Jì did not accept,
and was appointed Dàhónglú.
At the age of seventy-one,
he died in office.
His son, Chén Qún,
became Sīkōng of Wèi.
The world believed that dukes (gōng) were ashamed before ministers (qīng),
and ministers were ashamed before elders (zhǎng).
His younger brother, Chén Chén,
whose courtesy name was Jìfāng,
shared the same virtue and conduct as Chén Jì.
Father and sons all achieved high renown,
and were known at the time as the "Three Gentlemen" (sānjūn).
Whenever the chief minister's office (zǎifǔ) invited and summoned them,
they were always simultaneously honored with appointments,
like flocks of geese.
Those of that era all considered it an honor.
Chén Chén died young.
Commentary states: Since the middle period of the Hàn dynasty,
eunuchs were arbitrary and abusive,
and so it became the custom to value those who withdrew from society, upheld integrity, and spoke out.
If a scholar did not speak of these things,
then even ordinary folk and herdsmen would shout at him.
Thus, the more muddled the government of the time,
the more prevalent this trend became.
Only the principles of advance and retreat of Master Chén
were surely measurable.
Firmly established in virtue, he was not violated by things;
content in benevolence, he did not separate from the masses.
His conduct was perfected in his person, and his Way instructed the world,
thus fierce evil could not seize him with power,
nor could kings and dukes flaunt their nobility before him.
This is why imperial teachings failed above,
yet customs remained pure below.
Eulogy says: The two Lǐs were teachers of purity,
Lord Chén was a friend to the brilliant.
Hán Sháo assumed office,
Yíng Kòu harbored the Way.
Tàiqiū was profound and vast,
modeling our ethical norms.
Even his deep path
made the superficial pure.
When the foundation of fortune was established,
there was splendor by the Yǐng River.
The two Fāngs inherited the pattern,
and the eight Cís followed in their dust.
Biography of Lǐ and Dù, Chapter 53.
Lǐ Gù,
whose courtesy name was Zǐjiān, was a native of Nánzhèng, Hànzhōng,
and the son of Sītú Lǐ Hé.
Lǐ Hé is in the biographies of Diviners (fāngshù zhuàn).
Lǐ Gù had an extraordinary appearance,
with a "tripod horn" (dǐngjiǎo) and "hidden rhinoceros" (nìxī) features,
and "turtle patterns" (guīwén) on his feet.
In youth, he loved learning
and often traveled on foot to seek teachers,
not deterred by thousands of miles.
He thoroughly studied the classics (fénjí)
and befriended heroes and worthies.
Many ambitious scholars from all directions
admired his character and came to study.
The capital residents all sighed, saying:
"This one is another Master Lǐ!"
The Sīlì Commandery and Yìzhōu both ordered the commanderies to recommend him as Xiàolián,
and he was invited as a clerk (yuàn) for Sīkōng,
but he did not accept any of these.
In the second year of Yángjiā,
there were unusual occurrences: earthquakes, landslides, and fires.
The high officials (gōngqīng) recommended Lǐ Gù to answer the imperial edict (duìcè).
The edict also specifically asked about the current abuses of the era
and what was appropriate for governance.
Lǐ Gù replied:
"These are all related to Heaven's will
and manifest in accomplished affairs.
Indeed, transformation is achieved through duties,
and offices are managed by the able.
In ancient times, those who advanced
had virtue and destiny;
now,
those who advance
rely only on wealth and power.
I humbly hear that the imperial edict aims for broad leniency
and detests severity and cruelty.
Yet now, many chief magistrates (zhǎnglì) who achieve fame through killing
are sure to be
promoted and rewarded;
those who maintain leniency and harmony without partisan support
are frequently dismissed.
Thus, the customs of purity and generosity are not promulgated,
and the corrupt and superficial customs are not reformed.
Even with numerous punishments and heavy
prohibitions,
how can there be any benefit?
The former Emperor Xiào'ān disrupted old regulations,
enfeoffing his wet nurse (āmǔ) with titles,
and consequently created chaos and depravity,
allowing Fán Fēng and his ilk to seize power and act wantonly,
usurping the emperor's authority,
and altering the legitimate succession,
even causing the sacred person (shènggōng) to be distressed
and personally experience such hardship.
Having escaped from dire straits,
and ascending the throne with great fortune,
the world
looked forward eagerly
to a virtuous administration.
After accumulated decay,
it is easy to achieve a revitalization (zhōngxīng),
and truly one should earnestly contemplate good ways.
Yet some commentators still say
that current
affairs
are again like those of the past.
Your servant, from the mountains and wilds,
feels pain in his heart and breast.
Indeed, since the rise of Hàn,
over three hundred years,
sages and worthies have succeeded each other,
eighteen
rulers.
Was there no affection for wet nurses?
Did they forget the favor of noble titles?
However, out of reverence for Heaven's majesty above,
and consulting the classics below,
they knew it was not righteous
and therefore did not enfeoff them."
Now, Sòng Āmǔ,
though she has the great merit of diligence and circumspection,
a mere increase in rewards
would be sufficient to compensate for her arduous work;
as for partitioning land to establish a state,
it truly deviates from the old
precedent.
I hear that Āmǔ is humble in nature,
and will surely show deference,
so Your Majesty should allow her to decline the offer of a state,
thus achieving the blessing of universal peace.
Knowing when to restrain oneself
prevents downfall.
The late emperor favored Yán Shì,
granting titles too quickly,
hence her suffering calamity
in no time at all.
Lǎozi said:
"What advances
sharply,
retreats swiftly."
Now, Liáng Shì, as a relative in the imperial consort's family,
is not subject to ministerial duties according to ritual,
so honoring her with a high noble rank
might still be acceptable.
But her sons and younger brothers,
and followers,
are all showered with glory and prominence,
which was hardly the case in the precedents of Yǒngpíng and Jiànchū.
It was not like this.
It is fitting to order Bùbīng Xiàowèi Jì and the various Shìzhōng to return to their positions in the Huángmén,
to remove power from the maternal relatives,
and return governance to the state.
Would this not be excellent?
However, the Zhōng Chángshì, being by the emperor's side day and night,
have influence and power that shakes the world.
Their sons and younger brothers receive official salaries,
without any limit.
Although they outwardly feign humility and silence,
not interfering with the prefectures and commanderies,
yet
flattering and deceitful people
advance and are promoted simply by their reputation.
Now, a permanent prohibition can be established for them,
treating them the same as other inner court officials.
Formerly, Guǎntáo Gōngzhǔ sought an official position for her son,
but Míngdì did not permit it,
instead granting her ten million coins.
The reason for lightly giving generous gifts
but heavily valuing humble positions
is that officials
lacking talent
harm the common people.
I secretly hear that Chángshuǐ Sīmǎ Wǔ Xuān and
Kāiyáng Chéngmén Hòu Yáng Dí, among others,
without other merits or virtues,
were appointed directly
to substantial posts upon their initial assignment.
Although this is a small error,
it gradually corrupts the old regulations.
The laws and regulations of the former sages
should be firmly upheld;
if governance and teaching falter even once,
they will not recover for a hundred years.
The Shī says:
"Shàngdì is perverse,
the people below are all afflicted."
This censures Zhōu Wáng for changing the ancestral laws and regulations,
thereby causing the common people to all fall ill.
The primal qi
circulates evenly through the four seasons.
The Shàngshū receive and issue imperial decrees,
distributing governance throughout the realm.
Their power is exalted, their authority weighty,
and responsibility falls upon them.
If their minds are not impartial,
calamities and misfortunes will surely arise.
It is truly appropriate to carefully select the right persons
to assist in the sagely governance.
Now, those who govern the world with Your Majesty
are, externally, the Gōngqīng and Shàngshū,
and internally, the Cháng
shì and Huángmén.
This is like matters within one household,
the affairs of one family:
if peaceful, they share in its blessings and good fortune;
if perilous, they share in its calamities and ruin.
The Cìshǐ and Èrqiānshí,
outwardly supervise
their duties,
and inwardly receive the laws.
If the gnomon is crooked, its shadow will certainly be askew;
if the source is clear, the stream will certainly be pure.
Just like striking the root of a tree,
all its branches move.
The Zhōu Sòng says:
"Just shake it,
and none will not tremble and quake."
This speaks of action within
that echoes externally.
From this,
how can the edicts
and commands
of this court be allowed to falter?
If a crack is opened,
wicked people's hearts will stir;
if contention for profit is even momentarily initiated,
the path of benevolence and righteousness will be blocked.
Punishments will no longer be able to restrain,
and moral guidance
will gradually deteriorate.
This is the discipline of the world,
the urgent task of the present.
Your Majesty should open the stone chamber,
display the maps and books,
summon an assembly of scholars,
and inquire about
successes and failures,
pointing out anomalies and changes,
to seek the will of Heaven.
If their words contain sound reason,
they should be immediately implemented,
and those individuals prominently promoted,
to recognize the capable.
Thus, the sagely hearing will
daily gain insights,
and loyal ministers will fully express what they know.
Furthermore, it is appropriate to dismiss the eunuchs,
and remove their excessive power,
setting only two Chángshì,
who are upright and virtuous,
to serve
by your side;
and five Xiǎo Huángmén,
who are talented, intelligent, and refined,
to serve in the palace.
If this is done,
then critics will be silenced,
and an era of peace can be achieved.
The reason why
I dare to present my foolish and blind views,
and audaciously make myself heard,
is perhaps that August Heaven wishes for this humble minister to awaken Your Majesty.
Your Majesty should carefully examine my words,
and mercifully pardon my death.
He went out to be the Magistrate of Luò [luò] in Guǎnghàn [guǎng hàn],
and when he reached Báishuǐguān [bái shuǐ guān],
he relinquished his official seal and sash,
returned to Hànzhōng [hàn zhōng],
and kept his doors shut, not engaging in human affairs.
Within a year,
Liáng Shāng [liáng shāng] invited him to be a Chief Clerk.
Shāng [shāng], as the emperor's father-in-law, assisted in governance,
but was gentle and self-restrained,
unable to rectify or regulate anything.
Disasters and anomalies frequently appeared,
and the power of subordinates grew heavier day by day.
Gù [gù] earnestly wished that Shāng [shāng] would first rectify moral transformation
and retire from his high position.
So, he presented a memorial, saying:
“The Spring and Autumn Annals praises Yí Fù [yí fù] for opening the path of righteousness
and condemns Wú Hài [wú hài] for closing the gate of profit.
If the path of righteousness is closed, then the gate of profit opens;
if the gate of profit opens, then the path of righteousness is closed.
Previously, Emperor Xiào'ān [xiào ān] internally relied on Bó Róng [bó róng], Fán Fēng [fán fēng], and the like,
and externally entrusted affairs to Zhōu Guǎng [zhōu guǎng], Xiè Yùn [xiè yùn], and their ilk.
They opened their doors to receive bribes
and appointed people out of order,
causing the empire to be in chaos,
with sounds of resentment filling the roads.
When the court was first established,
it largely maintained purity and tranquility,
but not many years passed
before it gradually declined again.
Those who advanced by partisan connections
received promotions daily,
while those who adhered to the good Way even unto death
were stranded in poverty,
and there was no method to change these corrupt practices and establish virtue.
Furthermore, since His Majesty ascended the throne,
more than ten years have passed,
yet a sacred heir has not been established,
which the populace below eagerly awaits.
It is advisable to command the Central Palace to widely select consorts and concubines,
and also to choose humble and low-born women suitable for childbearing,
to be presented to the Supreme One,
to assist in accordance with Heaven’s will.
If there is a prince,
the mother should nurse him herself,
and not entrust him to wet nurses or shamans,
to avoid the calamity of Fēi Yàn [fēi yàn].
Your Excellency, the Illustrious General, your prestige is high and your position prominent;
you ought to be concerned for the empire,
promote humility and frugality,
and set an example for the myriad regions.
However, you are newly constructing ancestral halls,
with expenditures reaching hundreds of millions,
which is not to display your illustrious virtue
or to promote purity and frugality.
In recent years,
disasters and anomalies have frequently appeared;
recently there has been no rain,
but a persistent, oppressive gloom.
Within the palace,
there may be hidden conspiracies.
Confucius said: ‘The wise see changes and contemplate punishment;
the foolish see anomalies and avoid naming them.’
The Way of Heaven is impartial;
it should be revered and feared.
Moreover, recently there was a total lunar eclipse beside the Duānmén [duān mén] gate.
The moon
is the embodiment of the great ministers.
[一０]For one who climbs too high, there is danger;
for one who is too full, there is overflow;
when the moon waxes, it wanes;
when the sun is at its zenith, it declines.
[一一]These four
are the natural order.
The heart of Heaven and Earth
blesses humility and detests excess.
[一二]Therefore, the wise and accomplished, having achieved success, retreat from their positions,
[一三]preserving their reputation and prolonging their lives,
free from the worries of fear and urgency.
[一四]If the royal order is truly rectified,

Your Excellency will follow the lofty example of Bó Chéng [bó chéng],

[一五]How can this be compared to those common imperial relatives who indulge in glory and cling to their positions!
I am a madman, of the lowest stupidity,
not understanding the greater scheme of things.
Yet, I am moved by the ancient saying of repaying even a single meal,
[一六]how much more so when I have received your kindness and cannot fail to give my utmost!”
Shāng [shāng] could not make use of his advice.
In the Yǒnghé [yǒng hé] era,
bandits arose in Jīngzhōu [jīng zhōu],
and for a full year, they remained unsubdued.
So, Gù [gù] was appointed as the Inspector of Jīngzhōu [jīng zhōu].
Upon his arrival,
Gù [gù] sent officials to tour the region and express his condolences,
pardoned the previous offenses of the bandits,
and started anew with them.
Thereupon, the bandit leaders, Xià Mì [xià mì] and others, gathered their main followers, numbering over six hundred,
bound themselves, and surrendered.
Gù [gù] pardoned all of them,
sent them back,
and had them recruit others,
displaying his authority and laws.
Within half a year,
the remaining groups all surrendered,
and the province was peaceful and orderly.
He then memorialized that the Administrator of Nányáng [nán yáng], Gāo Cì [gāo cì], and others were corrupt.
Cì [cì] and others, fearing punishment,
then jointly heavily bribed the Grand General Liáng Jì [liáng jì].
Jì [jì] sent out a thousand-mile dispatch,
but Gù [gù] pursued the matter even more urgently.
Jì [jì] then ordered Gù [gù] to be transferred as the Administrator of Tàishān [tài shān].
At that time, bandits in Tàishān [tài shān] had been gathered for years,
and the county troops, usually a thousand men,
were unable to control them in pursuit and suppression.
Upon Gù's [gù] arrival,
he dismissed them all to return to farming,
only selecting and retaining over a hundred men skilled in combat,
and attracted them with kindness and trust.
Before a year had passed,
the bandits were all quelled and dispersed.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Works.
He presented a memorial discussing affairs, saying:
“I have heard that the pure essence of qi [qì] becomes spirit,
and the pure among men become worthies.
Those who nourish the self value refining the spirit,
and those who pacify the nation follow the Way of accumulating worthies.
In the past, when Qín [qín] planned to attack Chǔ [chǔ],
Wángsūn Yǔ [wáng sūn yǔ] set up altars at the western gate,
displaying the names of famous ministers.
The Qín [qín] envoy was startled,
and consequently, the troops were pacified.
Wèi Wénhóu [wèi wén hóu] took Bǔ Zǐxià [bǔ zǐ xià] as his teacher,
friended Tián Zǐfāng [tián zǐ fāng],
and bowed to Duàn Gànmù [duàn gàn mù].
Thus, many distinguished individuals eagerly came,
and his fame surpassed that of Qí Huán [qí huán].
The people of Qín [qín] dared not spy on the troops in Xīhé [xī hé].
This is indeed a sign of accumulating worthies.
Your Majesty, rising from chaos like a dragon,
first ascended to the great position,
invited Fán Yīng [fán yīng] of Nányáng [nán yáng], Huáng Qióng [huáng qióng] of Jiāngxià [jiāng xià], Yáng Hòu [yáng hòu] of Guǎnghàn [guǎng hàn], and Hè Chún [hè chún] of Kuàijī [kuài jī],
and your edicts praised them,
treating them with the rank of grandee.
Because of this, reclusive scholars from mountain caves,
and men of wisdom and skill,
brushed off their caps and shook their robes,
eager to be employed.
The four seas rejoiced,
and submitted to your sacred virtue.
Hòu [hòu] and others, while in office,
though without extraordinary achievements,
were diligent and hardworking day and night,
with their hearts set on worrying for the nation.
When I was previously in Jīngzhōu [jīng zhōu],
I heard that Hòu [hòu], Chún [chún], and others were dismissed due to illness and returned home.
I was truly saddened,
and felt it a pity for the times.
One day at court,
I saw that all the attendant-counsellors were young,
with not a single elder scholar or great man to consult,
which is truly lamentable.
It is advisable to recall Hòu [hòu] and others,
to meet the expectations of the multitude.
Qióng [qióng] has long been an Erudite Counsellor,
for nearly ten years.
Everyone wonders why he was initially highly esteemed
but is now stagnant.
Zhōu Jǔ [zhōu jǔ], Grand Master of Guanglu,
possesses high and upright talent and strategy,
and ought to be among the regular chamberlains,
to be consulted for his opinions.
Dù Qiáo [dù qiáo], Attendant Counsellor,
is profound in learning and upright in conduct,
a worthy minister of this age.
He has long claimed illness,
but he should be ordered to rise.”
He further recommended Yáng Lún [yáng lún] of Chénliú [chén liú],
Yǐn Cún [yǐn cún] of Hénán [hé nán] Commandery, Wáng Yùn [wáng yùn] of Dōngpíng [dōng píng], Hé Lín [hé lín] of Chénguó [chén guó],
Fáng Zhí [fáng zhí] of Qīnghé [qīng hé], and others.
On that day, an imperial edict was issued to summon Lún [lún], Hòu [hòu], and others,
and Qióng [qióng], Jǔ [jǔ] were promoted.
Gù [gù] was appointed Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Previously, Zhōu Jǔ and eight other envoys had inspected the empire,
and impeached and reported many officials.
Among these were all relatives of eunuchs,
who then pleaded on their behalf.
The emperor issued an edict ordering that they not be investigated.
Also, previously, the Three Excellencies were responsible for selecting clerical officials,
and the Grand Master of Ceremonies tested the Masters of Writing.
At that time, all were directly appointed,
no longer requiring selection or examination.
Gù then, with Court Commandant Wú Xióng, submitted a memorial,
arguing that those impeached by the eight envoys
should be immediately punished,
and that appointments and placements
should be returned to the proper authorities.
The emperor was moved by their words,
and subsequently dismissed the provincial governors and two-thousand-bushel officials impeached by the eight envoys.
From then on, direct appointments became rare,
and the Three Excellencies were sternly reprimanded,
with strict orders for closer scrutiny.
The court acclaimed this as good.
Then, he again, with Grand Master of Ceremonies Liú Xuān, submitted a memorial, stating:
"Recently, the selection of provincial governors and administrators
has often resulted in unsuitable individuals,
who then act without principles
and oppress the common people.
It is also advisable to cease leisurely excursions
and focus entirely on state affairs."
The emperor accepted their words,
and thereupon issued an edict commanding that if any provincial governor or administrator (or lower)
was impeached by the various prefectures for misgovernance
or lacking benevolence towards the people,
they would be dismissed from their current office.
As for those guilty of grave corruption and serious crimes,
they were to be arrested and sent to the imperial prison.
When Emperor Chōng ascended the throne,
Gù was made Grand Commandant,
and participated in recording matters of the Masters of Writing with Liáng Jì.
The following year, the emperor died.
Empress Dowager Liáng, fearing that the widespread banditry in Yáng and Xú Provinces
might cause alarm and lead to chaos,
had a Regular Attendant eunuch instruct Gù and others,
wishing to await the arrival of the summoned princes and marquises before announcing the mourning.
Gù replied:
"Although the emperor was young,
he was still the father of the empire.
Now that he has passed away,
it moves both heaven and earth.
How can subjects then conspire to conceal it?
In the past, when Emperor Qín died at Shāqiū,
Hú Hài and Zhào Gāo concealed the news and did not announce it,
ultimately harming Fúsū
and leading to the downfall of the dynasty.
More recently, when the Marquis of Běixiāng died,
Empress Yán's brothers and Jiāng Jīng and others also conspired to conceal it,
which led to Sūn Chéng's act of personally slaying them.
This is a great taboo in the empire,
the most impermissible of things."
The empress dowager followed his advice
and announced the mourning that very evening.
Gù, believing that Qīnghé Wáng Suàn was older and virtuous,
wished to establish him as emperor.
He said to Liáng Jì:
"Now, in establishing an emperor,
it is fitting to choose one who is of mature age, intelligent, virtuous,
and capable of personally handling government affairs.
I wish for the general to carefully consider this great plan,
observing Zhōu and Huò's establishment of Wén and Xuān,
and heeding Dèng and Yán's exploitation of the young and weak."
Jì did not comply,
but instead established Zǐ Zuǎn, the son of the Prince of Lè'ān,
who was eight years old.
This was Emperor Zhì.
At this time, Emperor Chōng was to be buried north of the imperial tomb,
so Gù debated, saying:
"Currently, bandits are rampant everywhere,
and military expenses have doubled.
The construction of Xiàn Líng is new,
and levies are numerous.
The emperor is still young;
a tomb can be built within the Xiàn Líng precinct,
following the system of Kāng Líng,
thereby reducing labor and costs by one-third."
His proposal was then adopted.
At that time, the empress dowager, having successively faced misfortunes,
entrusted matters to the chief ministers.
Whatever Gù rectified,
she invariably adopted,
and all the palace eunuchs were dismissed.
The whole empire hoped for lasting peace,
but Liáng Jì was suspicious and tyrannical,
always jealous and resentful of Gù.
Originally,
during Emperor Shùn's reign, many official appointments were not made in proper order.
When Gù took office,
he impeached and dismissed over a hundred people.
These individuals, being resentful,
and hoping to curry favor with Jì,
together composed a 'flying memorial'
falsely accusing Gù, stating:
"Your servant has heard that if a ruler does not study antiquity,
he cannot receive Heaven's mandate;
if a subject does not recount the past,
he cannot serve his ruler.
After Yáo's demise,
Shùn mourned for three years,
seeing Yáo on the wall when he sat,
and seeing Yáo in his soup when he ate.
This is what is meant by 'pursuing filial piety'
and not losing the conduct of a subject or son.
Grand Commandant Lǐ Gù,
under the guise of public duty, pursues private interests;
under the cloak of righteousness, he commits evil;
he alienates close relatives
and promotes his own faction.
As for those he recommends and promotes,
they are all his disciples;
and those he summons and appoints
are none other than his old acquaintances.
Some are wealthy individuals bribing him,
others are his sons-in-law or marriage relatives.
Those listed in the official documents amount to forty-nine people.
Moreover, he widely selects merchants and peddlers
to fill clerical positions;
he recruits fine horses,
having them presented and tested at his window.
His comings and goings are extravagant and excessive,
his carriages dazzling in the sun.
When the Great Emperor was in his coffin,
passersby wiped away tears,
but Gù alone powdered his face,
stroked his hair, struck poses,
strutted and swaggered,
leisurely taking frivolous steps,
without the slightest sorrow or grief.
While the imperial tomb is unfinished,
he defies and alters old policies,
claiming credit for successes
and shifting blame to the ruler.
He expels close ministers,
preventing them from attending the funeral procession,
acting with tyrannical authority;
no one is more excessive than Gù.
Your servant has heard that the position of a chief minister
is truly to harmonize yin and yang.
If the celestial mechanism is unbalanced,
and bandits and rebels arise,
the responsibility lies with the Grand Commandant.
Since Gù assumed office,
the Southeast has been rebellious;
several prefectures in two provinces,
a thousand li of desolation,
the common people suffering grievous harm,
and the great transforming influence in decline.
Yet he criticizes the former emperor
and recklessly indulges his arrogance.
While alive, he showed no loyalty in court remonstrance,
and after death, he spreads slanderous remarks.
No son's crime is greater than bringing shame upon his father;
no subject's wickedness is deeper than slandering his ruler.
Gù's faults and transgressions
warrant execution."
When the memorial was submitted,
Jì reported it to the empress dowager,
asking her to send the matter down for investigation.
The empress dowager did not agree,
and he was spared.
Jì feared the emperor's intelligence,
thinking he would become a future threat,
so he ordered his attendants to administer poison.
The emperor suffered greatly from distress,
and asked for Gù to be summoned urgently.
Gù entered,
came forward and asked:
"Your Majesty, what is the cause of your illness?"
The emperor could still speak,
saying:
"I ate a cake;
now my stomach is stuffy.
If I can have water, I might still live."
Jì was also at his side,
saying:
"I fear he will vomit;
he must not drink water."
Before he finished speaking, the emperor died.
Gù knelt over the corpse, wailing,
and recommended investigation of the imperial physician.
Jì, fearing the matter would be exposed,
greatly detested him for this.
Because a discussion arose about establishing an heir,
Gù steadfastly brought in the Grand Minister over the Masses, Hú Guǎng, and the Minister of Works, Zhào Jiè.
He first sent a letter to Jì, saying:
"The empire is unfortunate,
again encountering great sorrow.
The Empress Dowager, with her sagely virtue, presides over the court,
managing all affairs of state.
The Illustrious General embodies loyalty and filial piety,
and his worries are for the altars of soil and grain.
Yet in recent years,
the imperial line has been cut off three times.
Now an emperor must be established,
a most crucial matter for the empire.
I sincerely know that the Empress Dowager is deeply concerned,
and the General is troubled,
carefully selecting the right person,
striving to secure a sagely and enlightened one.
However, my humble feelings are deeply attached,
and I secretly harbor a concern.
Looking back at the old precedents for dethronement and establishment from former generations,
and observing recent events concerning the succession to the throne,
it has never failed that the advice of the high officials was sought,
and the opinions of the multitude were widely gathered,
so that it might accord with the will of Heaven above,
and meet the expectations of the people below.
Moreover, since Yǒngchū,
state affairs have often been erroneous.
Earthquakes have struck palace temples,
and comets have traversed the sky.
Truly, these are days for the General to apply his feelings.
The Classic says: 'To give the empire to someone is easy,
to find the right person for the empire is difficult.'
In the past, the establishment of Chāngyì resulted in
increasing chaos and disorder.
Huò Guāng, distressed and ashamed, burst out in anger,
regretting it to the point of breaking bones.
Had it not been for the loyalty and courage of Bólù and
the resolute action of Yánnián,
the sacrifices of the Great Hàn
would nearly have been overthrown.
This is of the utmost concern and importance,
how can it not be thoroughly considered!
Among the myriad affairs of the world,
only this is the greatest.
The rise or fall of the state
rests on this single decision."
When Jì received the letter,
he then summoned the Three Ducal Ministers, the two thousand-picul officials in the central government, and the various marquises for a great deliberation on who should be established.
Gù, Guǎng, Jiè, and the Grand Herald Dù Qiáo all believed that Qīnghé Wáng Suàn was known for his clear virtue,
and was also the most senior and closely related,
and thus ought to be established as heir.
Earlier, Líwú Hóu Zhì was to marry Jì's younger sister;
he was then in the capital.
Jì wanted to establish him.
Since the public opinions differed,
Jì was resentful and displeased,
but had no means to overrule them.
The Palace Regular Attendant Cáo Téng and others heard of this and went by night to persuade Jì, saying:
"General, your family for generations has had intimate ties with the imperial consort's family,
wielding control over all state affairs.
Your guests and retainers are rampant,
and there have been many transgressions.
Qīnghé Wáng is strict and upright;
if he is indeed established,
then the General will not escape misfortune for long.
It would be better to establish Líwú Hóu;
wealth and honor can then be long preserved."
Jì assented to their words.
The next day, the high officials reconvened.
Jì's demeanor was fierce,
and his words were sharp and aggressive.
From Hú Guǎng and Zhào Jiè downwards,
none failed to be awed and intimidated by him.
They all said:
"Only the will of the Grand General matters."
But Gù alone, with Dù Qiáo, firmly upheld the original proposal.
Jì loudly exclaimed:
"Adjourn the meeting!"
Gù, since his intention was not followed,
still hoped that public sentiment could prevail,
and again wrote a letter to urge Jì.
Jì became even more enraged,
and then persuaded the Empress Dowager to first dismiss Gù from office,
and ultimately established Líwú Hóu,
who became Huán Dì.
More than a year later,
Liú Wén from Gānlíng and Liú Wěi from Wèijùn each plotted to establish Suàn as the Son of Heaven.
Liáng Jì then falsely accused Gù of conspiring with Wén and Wěi in seditious talk,
and imprisoned him.
His protégé, Wáng Diào of Bóhǎi, appeared in shackles and submitted a memorial,
attesting to Gù's injustice.
Zhào Chéng and dozens of others from Hénèi also demanded to wear the axe and chopper to the palace gate to present their appeal.
The Empress Dowager understood his innocence,
and thus pardoned him.
When he was released from prison,
the entire capital and market hailed him with "Long Live!"
Jì heard of this and was greatly alarmed,
fearing that Gù's reputation and virtue would eventually harm him.
He then reiterated the former accusation in a memorial,
and consequently executed him.
He was fifty-four years old at the time.
Before his death,
he wrote a letter to Hú Guǎng and Zhào Jiè, saying:
"Gù received great favor from the state,
and therefore exerted himself completely,
disregarding death,
desiring to uphold the imperial house,
and make it comparable to Wén and Xuān.
How could I have imagined that in one morning the Liáng clan would be deluded,
and you, gentlemen, would yield to them,
turning what was auspicious into calamity,
and success into failure?
The decline of the Hàn house
begins from this point.
You, gentlemen, received great emoluments from the ruler;
when things fell, you did not support them;
you overturned great affairs.
Later good historians,
how could they be partial?
My body is already gone;
in righteousness, I have achieved my goal;
what more can be said!"
Guǎng and Jiè received the letter with grief and shame,
both sighing deeply and shedding tears.
The commanderies and prefectures arrested Gù's two sons, Jī and Zī, in Yǎnchéng,
and both died in prison.
His youngest son, Xiè, managed to escape and went into exile.
Jì then enfeoffed Guǎng and Jiè, but exposed Gù's corpse at the crossroads,
ordering that anyone who dared to mourn him would be punished.
Gù's disciple, Guō Liàng of Rǔnán,
who had just reached adolescence,
was studying in Luòyáng.
He then, holding a banner and axe in his left hand,
and an axe and chopper in his right,
went to the palace gate and submitted a memorial,
begging for Gù's body to be collected.
This was not granted.
He then went to mourn and weep,
laying out his case before it,
and then remained to keep watch over the body.
The pavilion chief of Xiàmén shouted at him, saying:
"The two Lords, Lǐ and Dù, as high ministers,
failed to secure the ruler and offer loyal advice,
but instead caused groundless trouble.
What kind of worthless fellow are you,
to publicly defy the imperial edict,
and test the authorities?"
Liàng replied:
"I, Liàng, was born embodying yin and yang,
wearing Heaven and treading Earth.
Moved by righteousness,
how could I care for my life,
why should I be intimidated by death?"
The pavilion chief sighed, saying:
"Living in a lawless world,
Heaven is high, one dares not but stoop;
Earth is thick, one dares not but walk carefully.
One's ears and eyes should only listen and see appropriately,
one's mouth cannot speak recklessly."
The Empress Dowager heard of this and did not punish him.
Dǒng Bān from Nányáng also went to weep for Gù,
and remained by the corpse, unwilling to leave.
The Empress Dowager took pity on them, and then permitted the body to be shrouded, coffined, and returned for burial.
These two thereby gained renown,
and the Three Ducal Ministers all offered them appointments.
Bān then disappeared,
and his whereabouts became unknown.
Gù's collected works, including memorials, tables, submissions, deliberations, edicts, policy responses, records, and inscriptions, totaled eleven pieces.
His disciples Zhào Chéng and others grieved endlessly,
and then jointly compiled Gù's words and deeds into a volume on his virtuous conduct.
Xiè, whose courtesy name was Dégōng.
