Initially,
after Gù had been dismissed by imperial edict,
knowing he could not escape misfortune,
he sent his three sons back to their hometown.
At that time, Xiè was thirteen years old.
His elder sister, Wénjī, was the wife of Zhào Bóyīng from the same commandery,
and she was virtuous and intelligent.
When she saw her two elder brothers return,
she fully understood the root of the matter.
Silently, she grieved alone and said:
"The Lǐ clan is doomed!
Since Tài Gōng,
they have accumulated virtue and benevolence.
How can they encounter this?"
Secretly, she conspired with her two elder brothers to hide Xiè in advance,
claiming they were returning to the capital.
Everyone believed them.
Soon after, trouble arose,
and the commandery authorities were sent to apprehend Gù's three sons.
The two elder brothers were harmed.
Wénjī then told Wáng Chéng, a former student of her father:
"You uphold righteousness, following my late father,
and possess the integrity of ancient people.
Now I entrust you with this orphan of six *chǐ*.
The survival or destruction of the Lǐ clan
rests with you."
Chéng was moved by her righteousness,
and so he took Xiè and traveled downstream along the Jiāng River,
entering the territory of Xúzhōu.
He instructed Xiè to change his name and surname and work as an assistant in a wine shop,
while Chéng himself sold divinations in the market.
Each pretended to be a different person,
secretly maintaining contact.
Xiè received his education from him.
The wine shop owner found him unusual,
suspecting he was no ordinary person,
and gave his daughter to Xiè in marriage.
Xiè devoted himself to the study of the Classics.
After more than ten years,
Liáng Jì was executed, and portents of disaster appeared repeatedly.
The following year,
the imperial historians submitted a memorial stating that an imperial amnesty was appropriate,
and that the descendants of loyal ministers who had died unjustly should be preserved and recorded.
Thereupon, a great amnesty was granted to all under Heaven,
and Gù's descendants were also sought.
Xiè then told the wine shop owner the full story.
The wine shop owner provided him with a cart and generous provisions for his departure,
all of which Xiè refused.
He then returned to his hometown
and observed mourning rites.
When the sister and brother met,
their grief moved bystanders.
Later, she admonished Xiè, saying:
"Your late father was upright and honest,
a loyal minister to Hàn,
but he encountered a chaotic court,
and Liáng Jì acted tyrannically,
causing our ancestral sacrifices to be almost cut off.
Now you are fortunate enough to have been saved;
is this not Heaven's will?
You should avoid all people,
do not associate thoughtlessly,
and be careful not to utter a single word against the Liáng clan.
Speaking against the Liáng clan would implicate the emperor,
and disaster would strike again heavily.
You must only take the blame yourself."
Xiè respectfully followed her instruction.
Later, Wáng Chéng died.
Xiè buried him with proper rites,
and, moved by his former kindness,
he would set up a place for an honored guest and offer sacrifices to him every four seasons.
He was invited by the province and commanderies,
and summoned by the four ducal offices,
but he accepted none of them.
Later, he was summoned and appointed as Yìláng.
While in office,
he maintained integrity and uprightness,
and among those he associated with, he always overlooked their shortcomings and focused on their strengths,
delighting in helping others achieve success.
At that time, Xún Shuǎng and Jiǎ Biāo of Yǐngchuān,
though both renowned, were not on good terms.
Xiè associated with both men,
showing no partiality,
and the world praised his fairness and impartiality.
During the reign of Emperor Líng, he was appointed Administrator of Ānpíng.
Before this, Wáng Xù of Ānpíng had been captured by the bandit Zhāng Jiǎo.
The state ransomed the king, and he was returned.
The court debated restoring his kingdom.
Xiè submitted a memorial, stating:
"Xù had no good governance in his kingdom,
was captured by a demonic bandit,
and failed in his duty as a vassal,
bringing disgrace to the sacred court.
He should not have his kingdom restored."
At the time, the opinions of the debaters differed,
but Xù eventually returned to his fief.
For slandering the imperial clan, Xiè
was sent to labor in Zuǒxiào.
Before a year was out,
the king was indeed executed for unfilial conduct.
Thereupon, Xiè was appointed Yìláng.
A saying circulated in the capital:
"The father would not establish an emperor,
the son would not establish a king."
He was promoted to Hénán Yǐn.
At that time, officials were appointed through bribery.
An imperial edict was again arbitrarily issued to raise three hundred million cash,
to fill the Xīyuán treasury.
Xiè submitted a memorial remonstrating against it,
with profound and urgent words.
The emperor then stopped the order.
Before this, Zhēn Shào of Yǐngchuān had flattered and attached himself to Liáng Jì,
and became Magistrate of Yè.
A contemporary of his had incurred Jì's displeasure
and fled to Shào.
Shào pretended to shelter him but secretly reported him to Jì.
Jì immediately arrested and killed him.
Shào was due for promotion to Commander,
but his mother died.
Shào buried her body temporarily in a horse shed,
first accepted the enfeoffment,
and then announced the mourning.
When Shào returned to Luòyáng,
Xiè encountered him on the road.
He ordered his soldiers to push Shào's carriage into a ditch,
whipped him profusely,
and wrote in large characters on a piece of silk attached to his back:
"Flattering the powerful to betray a friend,
greedy for office to bury one's mother."
He then fully memorialized his conduct.
Shào was consequently dismissed and banned from office for life.
Xiè died after two years in office.
People at the time, moved by his family's loyalty and uprightness through generations,
all grieved and lamented his passing.
Dù Qiáo, whose courtesy name was Shúróng,
was a native of Línlǜ in Hénèi.
In his youth, he was a scholar,
was nominated as Xiàolián,
and was invited to the office of Sītú Yáng Zhèn.
He was gradually promoted to Administrator of Nánjùn,
then transferred to Administrator of Dōnghǎi,
and upon entering the capital, was appointed Shìzhōng.
In the first year of Hàn'ān,
Qiáo was appointed Superintending Grand Master of the Palace
and dispatched to inspect Yǎanzhōu.
He memorialized that Lǐ Gù, the Administrator of Tàishān, had the best governance in the empire;
and that Liáng Ràng, the Administrator of Chénliú, Fàn Gōng, the Administrator of Jìyīn, and Cuī Yuàn, the Chancellor of Jìběi, had committed embezzlement of over ten million.
Ràng was the youngest uncle of Grand General Liáng Jì,
and Gōng and Yuàn were both favored by Jì.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince,
then promoted to Grand Minister of Agriculture.
At that time, five of Liáng Jì's younger relatives and the Palace Regular Attendants were all enfeoffed without merit.
Qiáo submitted a memorial of remonstrance, saying:
"Your Majesty, you rose from a vassal lord,
ascended to the throne like a dragon,
and the hearts of Heaven and men are turned towards you;
the myriad states rely upon you.
Instead of urgently honoring the loyal and virtuous,
you first grant enfeoffments to your close attendants,
harming goodness and damaging virtue,
and encouraging sycophancy.
I have heard that ancient enlightened rulers
always based rewards and punishments on merit and demerit;
while the benighted rulers of later ages
dispensed punishments and rewards each according to their private interests.
Now, the Liáng family,
and the minor offspring of eunuchs,
are all wearing the insignia of unmerited rank,
and partitioning the lands of meritorious ministers.
The extent of this deviation and impropriety
cannot be fully expressed!
For merit to go unrewarded
causes good deeds to lose their appeal;
for treachery to go unpunished
allows wickedness to run rampant.
Thus, when axes of punishment are displayed, people feel no awe;
when ranks are conferred, people feel no encouragement.
If this path is pursued,
it will not only harm governance
and lead to disorder,
but also result in the destruction of the self and the ruin of the state.
How can one not be cautious!?"
The memorial was submitted but not heeded.
Zhǒng Gǎo, the Inspector of Yìzhōu, impeached Liú Jūnshì, the Administrator of Yǒngchāng, for presenting a golden snake to Liáng Jì.
The matter came to light,
and the snake was transferred to the Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Jì asked Qiáo to borrow it for viewing,
but Qiáo refused to give it,
and Jì began to resent him.
He was successively promoted to Grand Minister of the Court.
At that time, Jì's youngest daughter died,
and he ordered the dukes and ministers to attend the funeral.
Qiáo alone did not go,
and Jì again held a grudge against him.
He was promoted to Guānglùxūn.
In the first year of Jiànhé [147 CE],
he replaced Hú Guǎng as Tàiwèi.
When Huán Dì was about to take Liáng Jì’s sister as his empress,
Jì wanted her to be welcomed with lavish gifts.
Qiáo Jù insisted on adhering to the old rites
and would not consent.
Jì also urged Qiáo to appoint Sǐ Gōng as Shàngshū,
but Qiáo, seeing that Gōng’s misdeeds were clearly evident,
refused to employ him.
Because of this, he daily incurred Jì’s displeasure.
Before this, Lǐ Gù had been deposed,
and spirits, both inside and outside the court, were low.
All the officials stood on tiptoe,
but only Qiáo, with a serious demeanor, would not yield.
Because of this, the whole country sighed in admiration,
and the court and populace looked up to him.
He was in office for several months
when he was dismissed due to an earthquake.
The eunuchs Táng Héng and Zuǒ Guàn, among others, then jointly slandered him to the emperor, saying:
“When Your Majesty was about to ascend the throne previously,
Qiáo and Lǐ Gù strongly objected, saying that Your Majesty was unfit to serve the Hàn imperial ancestral rites.”
The emperor also resented him.
When the incident involving Qīnghé Wáng Suàn arose,
Liáng Jì then prompted the relevant authorities to impeach Qiáo and Lǐ Gù for colluding with Liú Wěi and others,
requesting their arrest and prosecution.
However, Empress Dowager Liáng had always known Qiáo’s loyalty,
and merely dismissed him from office.
Jì grew even angrier,
and sent someone to threaten Qiáo, saying:
“Act promptly as advised,
and your wife and children may be spared.”
Qiáo refused.
The next day, Jì sent cavalry to his gate,
and hearing no sound of weeping,
he reported him and had him arrested and imprisoned.
He died in prison.
His wife and children returned to their home commandery.
His body, along with Lǐ Gù’s, was exposed in public north of the city,
and his family and old friends dared not look upon it.
Yáng Kuāng of Chénliú, a former subordinate of Qiáo, heard of this,
wept bitterly, and traveled day and night to Luòyáng.
He then donned an old red headscarf,
posing as a gate officer of Xiàmén Tíng,
to guard the corpses,
driving away flies and insects.
After twelve days,
a Dūguān Cóngshì arrested him and reported it.
Empress Dowager Liáng admired his righteousness and did not punish him.
Kuāng then, carrying an axe and chopping block, went to the imperial palace to submit a memorial,
and also begged for the bones of the two gentlemen, Lǐ and Dù.
The Empress Dowager granted his request.
He performed the funeral rites and shrouded them,
and sent Qiáo’s coffin back home.
He performed the burial rites and observed mourning,
then lived in seclusion and did not serve in office.
Kuāng was initially fond of learning,
and often taught disciples in the great marsh of Wàihuáng.
He was appointed Qí Zhǎng.
His administration showed extraordinary achievements,
and he was promoted to Píngyuán Lìng.
At that time, the Guóxiàng was Xú Zēng,
who was the elder brother of the Zhōng Chángshì Huáng.
Kuāng was ashamed to work with him
and feigned illness, saying he was herding pigs.
Commentary says: As for those called benevolent people,
their Dao is grand!
In their words and actions,
how could they merely seek fame and personal comfort?
They aim to establish the principles of engagement and disengagement,
to rectify the customs of the world,
to ensure that life is preserved through reason,
and death is aligned with righteousness.
If one acts solely for righteousness, one harms life;
if solely for life, one diminishes righteousness;
if solely for others, one harms wisdom;
if solely for oneself, one impairs benevolence.
If righteousness outweighs life,
it is permissible to sacrifice life;
if life outweighs righteousness,
it is permissible to preserve life.
Above, the ruler lost the way of a monarch through cruelty and obscurity;
below, the minister exhausted his loyalty and integrity through steadfastness.
When a minister’s integrity is exhausted and he dies for it,
it is to sacrifice oneself to achieve benevolence,
not to withdraw in order to seek life and harm benevolence.
During the period of Shùn and Huán,
the imperial succession was severed three times,
the empress dowager held regency,
and treacherous ministers eyed the throne.
Lǐ Gù held his position with gravity,
contending for great righteousness,
firm and unyielding.
〔一０〕How could he not know that upholding integrity invites disaster,
yet he was ashamed of the injury to his responsibility from collapse and failure?
〔一一〕Observing his righteous pronouncements
and the letter he left to Liáng Jì,
though his plans failed and strategies miscarried,
he still clung to them and could not stop.
How profound!
The heart for the state!
He regarded Hú Guǎng and Zhào Jiè
as mere dung.
A Eulogy says: Lǐ and Dù held office,
united in heart and strength.
They brought order to the lords Wén and Xuān,
and resisted with the passion of Yī and Jì.
When the Dao was lost and the times were dark,
they ultimately met their tragic end.
They were like Zhào Gū,
whose rectitude was preserved by the world.
Biography of Wú, Yán, Shǐ, Lú, Zhào, Chapter 54
Wú Yòu, courtesy name Jìyīng,
was a native of Chénliú Zhǎngyuán.
His father, Huī,
served as Nánhǎi Tàishǒu.
When Yòu was twelve,
he accompanied his father to the official post.
Huī intended to scrape green bamboo slips to copy scriptures.
Yòu advised him, saying:
“Now, your excellency has crossed the Five Ridges,
far away on the coast.
The customs here are indeed unsophisticated,
but in the past, there were many rare treasures,
which made the state above suspicious,
and those in power below covetous.
If this book were completed,
it would involve both.
馬 Yuán was slandered because of coix seeds,
and Wáng Yáng gained a name with a clothing bag.
The space between suspicion and certainty
is truly what the former sages were cautious about.”
Huī then stopped,
and stroked his head, saying:
“The Wú clan will never lack a Jìzǐ.”
When he reached twenty,
he lost his father,
and had no home or possessions,
yet he refused any assistance or gifts.
He often herded pigs in the Zhǎngyuán marsh,
reciting scriptures while walking.
He met an old friend of his father’s,
who said to him:
“You are the son of a two-thousand-shi official, yet you engage in a lowly occupation yourself.
Even if you are shameless,
what about your late father?”
Yòu merely bowed in apology,
maintaining his resolve as before.
Later, he was recommended as Xiàolián.
As he was about to depart,
the commandery held a farewell ceremony.
Yòu crossed the altar and chatted happily for a long time with the junior clerk Yōngqiū Huáng Zhēn,
befriending him before parting.
The Gōngcáo, deeming Yòu arrogant,
requested his dismissal.
The Tàishǒu said:
“Wú Jìyīng has the discernment to know people.
You must not speak of this yet.”
Zhēn was later also recommended as Xiàolián,
and appointed Xīncài Zhǎng,
and was praised by his generation for his integrity.
At that time, Gōngshā Mù came to study at the Imperial Academy [Tàixué]
but lacked provisions.
So he disguised himself as a hired laborer,
and worked for Yòu grinding grain.
Yòu talked with him and was greatly astonished,
and they then formed a friendship amidst the mortar and pestle.
Yòu, owing to his outstanding conduct as Grand Master of Splendor, was promoted to the position of Intendant (xiāng) of Jiāodōng Commandery.
At that time, Dài Hóng, from Jìběi, served as a county assistant (xiànchéng),
and Hóng, then sixteen,
stayed with him in the assistant's quarters.
Whenever Yòu walked in the gardens,
he often heard sounds of reciting and chanting.
He was impressed and treated Dài Hóng generously,
even befriending him.
Dài Hóng eventually became a Confucian master,
renowned throughout Dōngxià,
and rose to the post of Administrator (tàishǒu) of Jiǔquán.
Yòu's administration was characterized by benevolence and simplicity,
leading the people by personal example.
When people had disputes,
he would close his doors and blame himself,
then resolve their conflicts
by explaining the principles of the Way to them.
Sometimes he would personally visit villages
to mediate and reconcile them.
From then on,
disputes and quarrels greatly diminished,
and officials and commoners held him in awe and dared not deceive him.
A village elder (sèfū) named Sūn Xìng privately levied money from the people,
bought clothes with it, and presented them to his father.
When his father received them, he angrily said:
"With a lord like this,
how can you bear to deceive him!"
He urged his son to return and confess his crime.
Sūn Xìng, ashamed and afraid,
went to the prefect's residence, holding the clothes, and confessed.
Yòu dismissed his attendants and asked him the reason.
Sūn Xìng fully recounted his father's words.
Yòu said:
"You, as an official (yuàn), incurred the disgraceful name
of defiling the harvest (huòyàn) for the sake of your parent.
This is what is meant by 'by observing one's faults, one knows the person.' "
He sent Sūn Xìng home to thank his father
and returned the clothes to him as a gift.
Furthermore, a man from Ānqiū named Wúqiū Zhǎng was walking in the market with his mother
when they encountered a drunken man who insulted his mother.
Zhǎng killed the man and fled.
Ānqiū officials tracked him to Jiāodōng and apprehended him.
Yòu summoned Zhǎng and said:
"Your mother was insulted,
which is a disgrace to human sentiment.
However, a filial son, though enraged, must consider the difficulties,
and act so as not to burden his parents.
Now, if you indulge your anger, abandoning your parents,
and kill someone in broad daylight,
to pardon you would be unjust,
but to punish you is unbearable.
What shall be done?"
Zhǎng bound himself with shackles
and said:
"The state has established laws,
and I, a prisoner, have violated them.
Although your enlightened prefect (míngfǔ) shows pity and compassion,
your grace has no place to be bestowed."
Yòu asked Zhǎng if he had a wife and children.
He replied:
"I have a wife but no children yet."
Immediately, Yòu transferred Zhǎng's wife from Ānqiū for apprehension.
When his wife arrived,
he removed Zhǎng's shackles and cangue
and allowed them to stay together in the prison.
His wife subsequently became pregnant.
When winter ended, the executions were carried out.
Zhǎng tearfully said to his mother:
"I have failed you and deserve to die.
How can I repay Lord Wú?"
Then he bit his finger and swallowed it,
speaking with blood in his mouth:
"If my wife bears a son,
name him 'Wúshēng.'
Tell him that I, at the point of death, swallowed my finger as a vow,
entrusting my son to repay Lord Wú."
He then put his head in the noose and died.
Yòu served in Jiāodōng for nine years,
then was promoted to Intendant (xiāng) of Qí.
The General-in-Chief (dàjiāngjūn) Liáng Jì memorialized to appoint him as Chief Clerk (chángshǐ).
When Liáng Jì falsely impeached Grand Commandant (tàiwèi) Lǐ Gù,
Yòu heard of it and requested an audience,
arguing with Liáng Jì about the matter,
but he was not heeded.
At that time, Mǎ Róng from Fúfēng was present,
drafting the memorial for Liáng Jì.
Yòu then said to Mǎ Róng:
"Lǐ Gōng's crime
is formed by your hand.
Once Lǐ Gōng is executed,
how will you face the people of the world?"
Liáng Jì angrily stood up and went into his room.
Yòu also left directly.
Liáng Jì's route meant Yòu was appointed Intendant (xiāng) of Héxián,
but Yòu resigned and returned home,
never again serving in office.
He personally irrigated his garden vegetables
and taught the classics.
He died at the age of ninety-eight.
His eldest son, Fèng,
rose to the position of Administrator (tàishǒu) of Lèlàng.
His youngest son, Kǎi, was Magistrate (lìng) of Xīnxī.
Fèng's son, Féng,
was Intendant (xiāng) of Dòngyáng Commandery.
All
were renowned in their time.
Yán Dǔ, courtesy name Shújīān,
was a man from Chóu, Nányáng.
In his youth, he studied the Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn under Táng Xīdiǎn of Yǐngchuān.
Within ten days, he could recite it,
and Táng Xīdiǎn held him in deep respect.
He also studied under Mǎ Róng,
becoming extensively versed in the classics, commentaries, and the writings of the hundred schools,
and was able to compose essays,
gaining fame in the capital.
He was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián)
and became Intendant (xiāng) of Píngyáng Commandery.
Upon taking office,
he had Gōng Suì's tomb memorialized,
erected a stele, performed sacrifices,
and promoted his descendants from the fields.
Due to the death of his teacher, he resigned from office and rushed to the funeral.
The five bureaus all invited him but he did not accept.
Emperor Huán summoned him as an Erudite (bóshì),
appointed him Grand Master of Remonstrance (yìláng),
and he worked with Zhū Mù and Biān Sháo on compiling works at the Dōng Guān library.
He gradually rose to become Palace Attendant (shìzhōng).
The Emperor frequently questioned him on political affairs,
and Dǔ would respond with subtle words and confidential advice,
always adhering to principles and righteousness.
He was promoted to Left Protector of the Capital (zuǒfēngyì),
and then transferred to Metropolitan Commandant (jīngzhàoyǐn).
His administration was broad and benevolent,
showing concern for the common people,
and he promoted virtuous elders
to participate in governance.
The commandery was filled with joy and affection,
and the Sān Fǔ region sighed in admiration.
Earlier, Biān Fèng of Chénliú had been Metropolitan Commandant (jīngzhàoyǐn),
and also had a reputation for ability.
The people of the commandery had a saying about him:
"Before, there were Zhào, Zhāng, and the three Wángs;
later, there were the two lords, Biān and Yán."
At that time, a prince was ill,
and the commanderies and counties were ordered to provide precious medicines.
The General-in-Chief (dàjiāngjūn) Liáng Jì sent a guest with a letter to Jīngzhào
and also a consignment of ox gallstones (niúhuáng).
Dǔ opened the letter and arrested the guest,
saying:
"The General-in-Chief is related to the imperial family through marriage,
and the prince is ill.
He should present medical prescriptions.
How can he send a guest a thousand li to seek profit?"
He then executed him.
Liáng Jì was ashamed and could not speak,
while the officials in charge tried to find fault with Yán Dǔ at Liáng Jì's implicit instruction.
Dǔ, claiming illness, resigned and returned home,
teaching in his family's neighborhood.
People at the time sometimes doubted the precedence of Rén and Xiào,
so Dǔ debated it, saying:
“Observing the arguments about Rén and Xiào,
they are紛然 (fēnrán) divergent,
mutually citing classical texts,
and successively drawing on factual evidence;
they can be called solid arguments.
Indeed, these two virtues stem from the same source,
and comprehensively lead all good conduct.
It is not a matter of a few ounces of differing weight,
nor a fixed order of precedence.
However, if one wishes to broadly distinguish them,
and give them names based on their substance,
then xiào lies in serving one’s parents,
while rén is extended to all beings.
Extending to all beings results in功濟於時 (gōng jì yú shí) – merit benefiting the times;
serving one’s parents results in virtue returning to oneself.
When it returns to oneself, the scope of action is small;
when it benefits the times, the merit is great.
Judging from this,
rén is then far-reaching.
Nevertheless, things can emerge subtly and become manifest,
and events can originate obscurely and become clear.
Taking examples close to the body:
the ears have the function of hearing and receiving,
the eyes have the clarity of observing and seeing,
the feet have the toil of reaching far,
and the hands have the merit of embellishing and guarding.
Though the merit is manifested externally,
what fundamentally causes it is the heart/mind.
Taking examples from distant objects:
the growth of plants
begins with sprouts,
and ends with widespread proliferation;
branches and leaves are luxuriant and sprawling,
blooming flowers are abundant and profuse.
Though the extremities are flourishing and dense,
what causes it is the root.
The rén person's possession of xiào
is like the four limbs having the heart and abdomen,
or branches and leaves having the root and trunk.
The sages understood this,
hence they said: ‘
Indeed, xiào is the constant principle of Heaven,
the rightness of Earth,
and the conduct of humanity.’
‘The jūnzi devotes himself to the root;
when the root is established, the Dào is born.
Xiào and tì,
are they not the root of rén?’
However, it is difficult to embody the entire great substance,
and human nature tends towards partiality,
hence what is applied differs,
and few actions encompass both.
If one must compare their superiority or inferiority,
then rén is considered great for its luxuriant and sprawling branches and leaves,
and xiào is considered primary for being the heart and body, the root and trunk.
There can be no dispute about this.
Some say that placing xiào before rén
does not accord with Zhòngní’s ordering of Huí and Cān’s intentions.
[一０]This is because it is believed that rén and xiào arise from the same essence;
for those who fully embody them,
they are used interchangeably as appellations,
as in the case of Yú Shùn and Yán Huí.
[一一]If they are embodied partially,
then each has its specific category,
as in the case of Gōng Liú and Zēng Cān.
[一二]Indeed, Zēng and Mǐn considered xiào and tì to be the ultimate virtues,
[一三]while Guǎn Zhòng considered the nine alliances to be the merit of rén.
[一四]Never has there been a discussion of virtue that does not prioritize Huí and Cān,
nor an evaluation of merit that does not highly esteem Yí Wú.
From this perspective,
each follows its own appellation.”
The former Prefect of Yuèxī, Lǐ Wéndé, had always been friendly with Dǔ.
At that time, he was in the capital
and said to the gōngqīng:
“Yán Shūjiān possesses the talent of a king's assistant,
why should he be confined to a position a thousand lǐ away?”
He wished to introduce him.
When Dǔ heard this,
he wrote a letter to stop Wéndé, saying:
“Indeed, the decline of the Dào
is what is called fate.
Rumors say you wish to help me return to the Dōngguān;
though your invitation is sincere,
it is something I dare not accept.
I have often combed my hair at dawn,
sitting in the guest hall.
In the morning, I recite the Yì of Xī and Wén,
the Shū of Yú and Xià,
study the rituals of Gōng Dàn,
and read the Chūnqiū of Zhòngní.
In the evening, I stroll leisurely on the inner steps,
chanting poetry from the southern veranda.
The various works of the hundred schools,
I pick up when I am free.
How vast they are, filling my ears!
How brilliant they are, overflowing my eyes!
How abundant and joyful is my solitary pleasure!
At such times,
I am unaware of Heaven being a canopy,
or Earth being a carriage;
unaware that there are people in the world,
or that I have a body.
Even Jiàn Lí striking the zhú
as if no one were around,
or Gāo Fèng reading
unaware of a violent storm,
[一０]compared to me,
are not enough to describe it.
Moreover, since my coming of age,
[一一]as a minister I have not fallen into disloyalty,
as a son I have not fallen into unfilial conduct;
in dealing with superiors I do not fawn,
in dealing with inferiors I do not demean.
[一二]If I die adhering to this,
and meet my ancestors below,
I will not be ashamed.
[一三]If one does not stop such a person with goodness,
I fear it would be like teaching Yì how to shoot.
[一四]Be careful not to lose its foundation,
and thereby twist one's life.”
Later, he was implicated in the party persecutions and forbidden from office.
In the first year of Yǒngkāng,
he died at home.
The local people depicted his image in the temple of Qū Yuán.
Dǔ’s discussions and explanations of the classics
corrected many points,
and later scholars like Fú Qián considered them balanced and fair.
His collected works, including poems, treatises, inscriptions, letters, responses to inquiries, memorials, and edicts,
totaled twenty volumes.
Shǐ Bì, courtesy name Gōngqiān,
was a native of Kǎochéng, Chénliú.
His father, Chǎng,
rose to the positions of Shàngshū and Prefect during Emperor Shùn’s reign due to his glibness.
Bì was devoted to study from a young age,
gathering hundreds of students.
He served in the commandery and prefecture,
was appointed to the ducal establishment,
and was promoted to Běijūn Zhōnghòu.
At this time, the Emperor Huán's (Huán Dì) younger brother, the Prince of Bóhǎi (Bóhǎi Wáng), Lǐ, had always behaved in a dangerous and perverse manner,
being arrogant and lawless in many ways.
Bì was afraid that his arrogance and rebelliousness would lead to disorder,
so he submitted a sealed memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that for emperors and kings regarding their relatives,
even if their love is profound,
they must show them their authority;
even if their status is noble,
they must restrain them with proper limits.
If this is done,
the way of harmony will flourish,
and the kindness of kinship will endure.
In the past, King Xiāng of Zhōu (Zhōu Xiāng Wáng) indulged Duke Zhāo (Zhāo Gōng),
and Emperor Jǐng of Hàn (Hàn Jǐng Huángdì) spoiled King Xiào of Liáng (Liáng Xiào Wáng);
and as the two younger brothers rose in favor,
they eventually became arrogant,
leading to the disaster of upheaval in Zhōu (Zhōu),
and the 'Yuán Àng (Yuán Àng) Incident' in Hàn (Hàn).
I secretly hear that the Prince of Bóhǎi (Bóhǎi Wáng), Lǐ,
relies on his close kinship,
trusts in his partial affection,
neglects the etiquette of serving his superior,
and harbors ambitions of usurpation and arrogance.
Externally, he gathers unscrupulous and reckless individuals;
internally, he indulges in wine and entertainment,
coming and going unpredictably.
Those he associates with
are all boastful and unprincipled,
some being the abandoned sons of powerful families,
or disgraced officials of the court.
There will surely be a calamity like that of Yáng Shèng (Yáng Shèng) and Wǔ Bèi (Wǔ Bèi).
The provincial authorities dare not investigate or impeach him,
and his tutors and chancellors are unable to correct and assist him.
Your Majesty, out of profound brotherly affection,
cannot bear to cut him off.
I fear that this will continue to spread,
and the harm will grow immensely.
I beg that my memorial be made public,
announced to all officials,
so that I may openly state his faults in the clear court,
and then Your Majesty can instruct the dukes and ministers to fairly determine his punishment according to the law.
When the law is decided and the guilt established,
then Your Majesty may issue a reluctant decree.
Only after your servants firmly insist,
then may you grant a small concession.
If this is done,
then the sagely court will not suffer the criticism of harming a relative,
and Bóhǎi (Bóhǎi) will have the blessing of enjoying his state.
Otherwise,
I fear that a great imprisonment will arise,
and envoys will be seen one after another on the road.
My duty is to command the imperial guard,
to guard against unusual events,
yet I have presumptuously concerned myself with a vassal state,
and infringed upon a close relative.
My crime is not worthy of pardon.
Unable to suppress my indignation,
I respectfully risk death to report this."
The Emperor, considering the close kinship,
could not bear to act on this matter.
Later, Lǐ was indeed implicated in a rebellion plot,
and demoted to be the Prince of Yǐngtáo (Yǐngtáo Wáng).
Bì was promoted to Shàngshū (Shàngshū) and
sent out to be the Chancellor of Píngyuán (Píngyuán Xiàng).
At that time, an imperial edict was issued to round up 'partisans'.
The number of those implicated by reports from various commanderies and states reached several hundred,
but Bì alone reported none.
Imperial edicts repeatedly and sharply reprimanded the prefectures and commanderies,
flogging and shaving the heads of subordinate officials.
An inspector, having been delegated to investigate, said reproachfully:
"The imperial edict condemns 'partisans',
and its intent is earnest and compassionate.
Of the six commanderies in Qīngzhōu (Qīngzhōu),
five have partisans.
In the nearby state of Gānlíng (Gānlíng),
both the northern and southern districts were investigated.
What reason is there for Píngyuán (Píngyuán) alone to have none?"
Bì said:
"The former kings demarcated the world,
drawing boundaries and dividing territories.
The lands and waters differ,
and customs vary.
Other commanderies may have them,
but Píngyuán (Píngyuán) simply does not.
How can they be compared?
If I were to anticipate the wishes of my superiors,
falsely incriminate good people,
inflict excessive punishments,
and act against reason,
then every household in Píngyuán (Píngyuán)
could be labeled as partisans.
As for me, the Chancellor, I can only die;
I cannot do such a thing."
and immediately arrested the commandery officials and sent them to prison,
reporting Bì on the way.
It so happened that the partisan prohibition was lifted,
and Bì used his salary to redeem his fault and was spared,
The inspector was furious,
Bì's governance was characterized by special suppression of the powerful and oppressive,
while for minor offenders among the common people,
he was largely lenient.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Hédōng (Hédōng Tàishǒu).
An edict was issued requiring the recommendation of Xiàolián (Xiàolián).
Bì knew that many powerful figures would make requests,
so he preemptively ordered a halt to receiving letters from family members.
The Cóngchángshì (Cóngchángshì) Hóu Lǎn (Hóu Lǎn) indeed sent a scholar with a letter to make a request,
and also asked for a temporary exemption from salt taxes.
For many days, he could not gain an audience.
The scholar then sought an audience with Bì under another pretext,
and thereby delivered Lǎn's (Lǎn) letter.
Bì was greatly angered, saying:
"As Grand Administrator, I bear a heavy responsibility;
I should select worthy individuals to serve the nation.
Who are you to be so deceptive and disrespectful!"
He ordered his attendants to drag him out,
and flogged him several hundred times.
Over ten officials, including the Prefect of the Commandery and clerks, all remonstrated in the court,
but Bì did not respond.
He then sent the scholar to Ānyì (Ānyì) Prison,
and had him interrogated and killed that very day.
Hóu Lǎn (Hóu Lǎn) bore a deep grudge,
and falsely submitted a flying memorial to the Sīlì (Sīlì),
slandering Bì for defamation.
Bì was summoned in a caged cart.
No officials dared to approach him,
only the former Xiàolián (Xiàolián) Péi Yú (Péi Yú) accompanied him to the area between Xiáo (Xiáo) and Miǎn (Miǎn),
and loudly declared by the roadside:
"My lord has curbed oppressive officials,
and selected virtues to repay the nation.
If he is to be punished for this,
it will be enough to leave his name in history.
I hope you will not worry or fear."
Bì said:
"'Who says the wild herb (tú) is bitter,
its sweetness is like shepherd's purse (jì).'
In ancient times, people would cut their throats,
and not regret dying nine times."
When he was delivered to the imperial prison of Tíngwèi (Tíngwèi),
the officials and common people of Píngyuán (Píngyuán) rushed to the imperial palace to plead his case.
Moreover, the former Xiàolián (Xiàolián) Wèi Shào (Wèi Shào) disguised himself, changing his clothes,
pretending to be a household servant,
and looked after Bì.
Bì was then falsely accused,
and his case was to be executed in the market.
Shào (Shào), along with people from the commandery, sold the commandery's official residences,
and bribed Hóu Lǎn (Hóu Lǎn),
obtaining a one-degree reduction in the death penalty,
and was sentenced to penal servitude in the Zuǒxiào (Zuǒxiào).
Some people at the time mocked, saying:
"Píngyuán (Píngyuán) traded bribes to save their lord,
isn't that foolish!"
Táoqiū Hóng (Táoqiū Hóng) said:
"In the past, when King Wén (Wén Wáng) was imprisoned in Yǒulǐ (Yǒulǐ),
Hóng (Hóng) and Sǎn (Sǎn) brought forth gold.
Shǐ Bì (Shǐ Bì) suffered misfortune,
and righteous men offered treasure.
What is there to doubt?"
Thereupon, the discussions ceased.
After his sentence was completed, he returned to his rural home,
claiming illness and closing his door, not going out.
He was repeatedly recommended by dukes and ministers.
The Yìláng (Yìláng) Hé Xiū (Hé Xiū) also argued that Bì possessed the talent to manage the state,
and should ascend to the position of prime minister.
He was summoned and appointed Yìláng (Yìláng).
Hóu Lǎn (Hóu Lǎn) and others resented him.
During the Guānghé (Guānghé) era,
he was sent out as Chancellor of Péngchéng (Péngchéng Xiàng),
but died of illness.
Péi Yú (Péi Yú) rose to the position of Shàngshū (Shàngshū).
A commentary says: Indeed, those with a stern and resolute nature
are rarely gentle and forgiving;
those who are benevolent and gentle by nature
often lack integrity and straightforwardness.
Wú Jìyīng (Wú Jìyīng) looked at people with fear of harming them,
and spoke with earnestness,
resembling a scholar;
yet he harbored indignation and was stirred to action,
curbing and conceding against corrupt power.
How courageous he was!
Benevolent in cherishing things,
righteous in retreating himself—
he was a gentleman!
The saying goes:
"Those who save a thousand people will have their descendants enfeoffed."
Shǐ Bì (Shǐ Bì) confronted tyrannical officials,
ultimately preserving the partisans of Píngyuán (Píngyuán),
yet his later descendants did not achieve greatness.
This cannot be discussed in the usual way.
Lú Zhí 字 Zǐgàn,
a man from Zhuō County, Zhuō Commandery.
He was eight *chǐ* and two *cùn* tall,
and his voice was like a bell.
When young, he and Zhèng Xuán both served Mǎ Róng,
and he was able to master ancient and modern scholarship.
He enjoyed meticulous research and did not cling to chapter-and-verse interpretations.
Mǎ Róng was a powerful maternal relative,
and often had female entertainers and singers performing before him.
Lú Zhí attended lectures for years,
never once turning his gaze.
Mǎ Róng respected him for this.
When his studies were complete, he took his leave and returned home,
closing his doors to teach.
He was by nature firm and resolute, possessing great integrity,
and always harbored the ambition to save the world.
He disliked *cí* and *fù* (rhapsodies),
and could drink one *shí* of wine.
At that time, the Empress's father, the Grand General Dòu Wǔ, supported and enthroned Emperor Líng,
and first took charge of government affairs.
The court debated bestowing further titles and honors.
Although Lú Zhí was a commoner,
knowing that Dòu Wǔ had always had a good reputation,
he presented a memorial to advise him, saying:
"Your servant has heard of the widow who neglected her loom,
and the grief of the woman in the painted room leaning against the pillar;
deep worry and far-reaching thoughts are the sentiments of a *jūnzǐ*.
Indeed, a scholar establishes friendships through contention,
and righteousness values mutual instruction.
The *Shū* states, 'consult the common people,'
and the *Shī* sings, 'inquire of the woodcutters.'
Your servant has recited the books of the former kings for a long time,
how dare I withhold my 'blind words'!
Now, your Excellency's position in the Han court
is like that of Dàn and Shì in the Zhōu house,
establishing a sagely ruler,
on whom the four seas depend.
Commentators believe your son's merit
in this regard is profound.
The world gathers its eyes to see,
and cups its ears to listen,
believing that, judging by previous events,
there will be a felicitous destiny of 'auspicious wind.'
Examining the meaning of the *Chūnqiū*,
when a queen has no heir,
a close relative of senior standing is chosen.
If their age is equal, virtue decides;
if their virtue is equal, then divination decides.
[一０]Now, successors are chosen from the same clan,
by unrolling maps and examining genealogies,
and enthroned in sequence.
What merit is there in this?
How can one presumptuously claim heavenly achievements as one's own power!
[一一]One should decline great rewards
to preserve one's reputation.
Moreover, in recent generations, the imperial lineage has not been strong,
[一二]still seeking heirs from outside;
this can be called perilous.
And the four directions are not yet peaceful,
bandits lie in wait for opportunities.
Héng Yuè and Bó Jié
[一三]especially have many villains and thieves.
There will soon be the change of Chǔ people threatening Bǐ,
and the Yǐn family establishing a court.
[一四]It is fitting to follow ancient rites,
to establish officials for the sons of the imperial clan,
to summon beloved sons of kings and marquises,
and worthy talents from the imperial house,
to externally promote the principle of instruction and guidance,
and internally quell the desire for greed and gain.
Select those with good abilities,
and bestow titles upon them according to their usefulness.
This is the way to strengthen the trunk and weaken the branches."
[一五]Dòu Wǔ ultimately did not adopt his advice.
The commanderies and provinces repeatedly summoned him,
but Lú Zhí did not accept.
During the Jiànníng era,
he was summoned to be a *bóshì*,
and only then did he begin his official career.
In the fourth year of Xīpíng,
the Man people of Jiǔjiāng rebelled.
The four government offices selected Lú Zhí for his combined civil and military talent,
and appointed him Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng.
The Man bandits submitted.
He left office due to illness.
He authored *Shàngshū Zhāngjù* and *Sān Lǐ Jiěgǔ*.
At that time, the imperial academy's stone classics were first erected
to standardize the texts of the Five Classics.
Lú Zhí then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant, when young, followed the erudite scholar, the former Grand Administrator of Nánjùn, Mǎ Róng, to study ancient scholarship,
and quite knows that the present-day *Lǐjì* contains many errors.
pointed out inaccuracies and errors.
Dare to offer my humble and superficial efforts,
and provided explanations and commentaries for them.
However, my family is poor,
and lacks the means to provide for copying and submitting them.
Your servant previously, regarding the *Zhōulǐ* and other classics,
and together go to the Dōngguān,
and use official provisions and resources,
to wholeheartedly devote ourselves to meticulous research,
to compile the *Shàngshū Zhāngjù*,
and examine the errors and correct portions of the *Lǐjì*,
so as to finalize the sacred canons,
and correct the inscriptions on the steles.
The ancient script, *kēdòu*,
is close to the original reality,
but it is suppressed by popular custom,
and relegated to 'minor learning.'
Since the Central Revival,
erudite scholars such as Bān Gù, Jiǎ Kuí, and Zhèng Xīng and his son
all highly valued it.
Now, the *Máoshī*, *Zuǒshì*, and *Zhōulǐ* each have their own commentaries,
and their rise and fall are mutually reflective.
It is fitting to establish *bóshì* for them,
to create academic offices,
to assist future generations,
and to expand the sagely intention."
Coincidentally, the Nányí rebelled.
Because Lú Zhí had served in Jiǔjiāng and had shown kindness and trustworthiness,
he was appointed Grand Administrator of Lújiāng.
Lú Zhí deeply understood the appropriateness of governance,
endeavoring to maintain purity and tranquility,
and merely upholding the grand principles.
More than a year later,
he was again summoned and appointed as a Yìláng.
He, along with Jiànyì Dàfū Mǎ Rìdī, Yìláng Cài Yōng, Yáng Biāo, Hán Shuō, and others, were all in the Dōngguān,
collating the five classics, records, and commentaries of the Zhōngshū,
and continuing the Hànjì.
The emperor considered this not an urgent matter,
and transferred him to serve as Shìzhōng,
then promoted him to Shàngshū.
In the first year of Guānghé (178 CE),
there was an unusual solar eclipse.
Zhí submitted a memorial remonstrating, saying:
"Your servant has heard the Wǔxíng Zhuàn (Treatise on the Five Elements) states: 'When the sun is obscured and the moon appears, it is called tiǎo;
the king and marquises are leisurely.'
This means that the ruler's governance is lax and slow,
hence the sun is eclipsed and obscured.
The Chūnqiū Zhuàn (Spring and Autumn Annals Commentary) says: 'The Son of Heaven avoids his position for a time,'
meaning the obscuration does not exceed a short period.
But recently, the solar eclipse lasted from sì (9-11 AM) past wǔ (11 AM-1 PM),
and after the eclipse,
clouds and fog obscured the sky.
In recent years, there have been earthquakes,
and comets and meteors have appeared alternately.
Your servant has heard that the Hàn dynasty follows the virtue of fire,
and its transformation should be broad and enlightened.
Recently, favoring beauty and believing slander,
and holding extreme jealousies,
is like fire fearing water.
Observing this year's omens,
all indicate the yang losing and the yin encroaching.
To dispel and ward off disaster and misfortune,
there should be a proper way.
I respectfully present eight brief proposals: first, employ the good;
second, pardon the proscribed;
third, ward off epidemics;
fourth, guard against bandits;
fifth, cultivate conduct;
sixth, follow Yáo;
seventh, govern subordinates;
eighth, distribute wealth.
Regarding 'employing the good,'
it is fitting to order the commanderies and prefectures to rigorously nominate worthy and good men,
appoint them according to their suitability,
and hold them accountable for their selections.
Regarding 'pardoning the proscribed,'
all those involved in the 'Party Proscriptions'
were mostly not guilty of crimes;
they can be granted amnesty and pardon,
and those wronged can be rehabilitated.
Regarding 'warding off epidemics,'
the family members of Empress Sòng
were all innocently left as corpses,
unable to be collected and buried.
The arrival of epidemics
is all due to this.
It is fitting to order their collection and burial
to pacify the wandering souls.
Regarding 'guarding against bandits,'
the families of the marquises and kings
have had their taxes and levies reduced,
leading to sorrow, poverty, and thoughts of rebellion,
which will inevitably lead to unrest.
It is fitting to ensure they have sufficient provisions
to prevent future troubles.
Regarding 'cultivating conduct,'
men of the Way should be summoned,
such as Zhèng Xuán and his like,
to expound the Hóngfàn (Great Plan)
and ward off disasters and calamities.
Regarding 'following Yáo,'
at present, commandery governors and inspectors are frequently transferred monthly.
It is fitting to follow the system of promotion and demotion,
to make their abilities clear.
Even if not for nine years,
they should serve for a full three years.
Regarding 'governing subordinates,'
this refers to those who seek rank through solicitation;
this should be strictly prohibited.
〔一０〕As for promotions and appointments,
the responsible officials should be held accountable.
Regarding 'distributing wealth,'
the Son of Heaven, by principle,
should not have private accumulations.
It is fitting to promote great endeavors
and eliminate minor extravagances."
〔一一〕The emperor did not heed him.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng (184 CE),
the Yellow Turban rebels rose.
The four ministries recommended Zhí,
who was appointed Běi Zhōnglángjiàng,
and given the credential (jié).
He served as deputy to Hù Wūhuán Zhōnglángjiàng Zōng Yuán,
leading the five corps of the Northern Army,
and dispatched troops from all commanderies in the realm to suppress them.
He repeatedly engaged and defeated the rebel leader Zhāng Jiǎo,
killing and capturing over ten thousand men.
Jiǎo and others fled and took refuge in Guǎngzōng.
Zhí built a siege, dug tunnels,
and constructed cloud ladders,
on the verge of capturing them.
The emperor sent Xiǎohuángmén Zuǒ Fēng to the army to observe the rebel situation.
Someone advised Zhí to bribe Fēng,
but Zhí refused.
Fēng returned and reported to the emperor, saying:
"The Guǎngzōng rebels are easy to defeat.
Lú Zhōngláng is merely holding his ground and resting his troops,
waiting for Heaven's punishment."
The emperor was enraged,
and thereupon had Zhí brought back in a cage cart,
reducing his death penalty by one degree.
When the Chējì Jiāngjūn Huángfǔ Sōng subsequently pacified the Yellow Turbans,
he highly praised Zhí's military strategies,
saying Sōng had utilized Zhí's plans and counsel
to achieve his success.
In that same year, Zhí was reinstated as Shàngshū.
When the emperor died,
Dàjiāngjūn Hé Jìn plotted to execute the eunuchs,
and thus summoned the Bìngzhōu Mù Dǒng Zhuó,
to intimidate the empress dowager.
Zhí knew Dǒng Zhuó was fierce and difficult to control,
and would inevitably cause future trouble,
so he strongly advised against it.
Hé Jìn did not listen.
When Dǒng Zhuó arrived,
he indeed oppressed the imperial court.
He then convened all officials in the court hall,
to discuss deposing and installing an emperor.
None of the officials dared to speak,
but Zhí alone strongly opposed it.
Dǒng Zhuó angrily dismissed the meeting
and intended to execute Zhí.
The account is in Dǒng Zhuó's biography.
Zhí had always been good friends with Cài Yōng.
When Cài Yōng was previously exiled to Shuòfāng,
Zhí was the only one to memorialize asking for his return.
Cài Yōng was at that time close to Dǒng Zhuó,
so he went to plead for Zhí.
Also, Yìláng Péng Bó remonstrated with Dǒng Zhuó, saying:
"Lú Shàngshū is a great Confucian scholar renowned throughout the realm,
a man of high hopes.
If you harm him first,
the world will be shocked and terrified."
Dǒng Zhuó then stopped,
and merely dismissed Zhí from office.
Zhí, citing old age and illness, requested to return home,
fearing he would not escape misfortune.
He then took a secret route, exiting through Huànyuán.
Dǒng Zhuó indeed sent men to pursue him,
but they reached Huái
and failed to catch him.
He then lived in seclusion in Shànggǔ,
avoiding social interaction.
Yúán Shào, the Jìzhōu Mù, invited him to be his military advisor.
He died in the third year of Chūpíng (192 CE).
Before his death,
he instructed his son Jiǎn to bury him in an earthen pit,
without a coffin,
with only a single piece of silk covering his body.
He authored a total of six pieces, including steles, dirges, memorials, and records.
During the Jiàn'ān period (196-220 CE),
Cáo Cāo, while campaigning north to Liǔchéng,
passed through Zhuōjùn.
He told the governor and magistrate:
"The late Běi Zhōnglángjiàng Lú Zhí's
name is renowned throughout the realm,
his scholarship is that of a Confucian patriarch,
a model for scholars,
and a pillar of the state.
When King Wǔ entered Yīn,
he enfeoffed Shāng Róng's neighborhood.
When Zhèng lost Zǐchǎn,
Zhòngní wept.
When I arrived in this province,
I admired his lingering influence.
According to the principles of the Chūnqiū,
the descendants of worthy men
deserve special rites.
Immediately send the prefectural assistant to clear his tomb,
provide for his descendants,
and offer a modest libation,
to honor his virtue."
His son, Yù,
was well-known.
A commentary says: "Wind and frost distinguish the nature of grasses and trees;
peril and chaos reveal the integrity of the upright and good.
Thus, Lú Gōng's heart can be known.
When troubles arise within,
and thunder startles the ears,
even men like Bēn, Yù, Jīng, and Zhū
cannot avoid hesitation and acting out of character.
Did Zhí, drawing his white blade beneath the strict palace gates,
pursuing the emperor between the river fords,
pushing through spears and blades,
rushing towards mutilation and death,
plan this beforehand?
For a gentleman, loyalty and righteousness
are essential even in haste,
and indispensable even in distress."
Zhào Qí 字 Bīnqīng,
was a native of Chánglíng, Jīngzhào.
His original name was Jiā.
He was born in the Censorate (Yùshǐ Tái),
and thus was styled Táicīng.
Later, when avoiding disaster,
he changed his name himself,
to show he did not forget his homeland.
As a youth, Qí was knowledgeable in the Classics
and possessed talent and skill.
He married the elder sister of Mǎ Róng from Fúfēng.
Mǎ Róng was a powerful family through his maternal relatives,
and Qí often disdained him,
refusing to meet with him.
He served in commanderies and counties,
and was feared for his integrity, straightforwardness, and hatred of evil.
When he was over thirty years old,
he suffered from a severe illness,
confined to bed for seven years.
Fearing that his end was near,
he made a will instructing his elder brother's son, saying:
"A great man, born into this world,
if in reclusion, has not the integrity of Jī Shān;
if in office, has not the achievements of Yī and Lǚ.
Heaven does not favor me,
what more can I say!
You may erect a round stone in front of my tomb,
and engrave on it: '
In Hàn there was a recluse, surnamed Zhào, personal name Jiā.
He had ambition but no opportune time.
Alas, what fate!'"
Afterwards, he recovered from his illness.
In the second year of Yǒngxīng (154 CE),
he was summoned as a clerk (yuàn) by the Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
He argued that officials of two thousand *dàn* salary should be allowed to resign their posts to perform mourning rites for their parents,
and the imperial court adopted his suggestion.
Afterwards, he was summoned by the Great General Liáng Jì.
He presented a policy on advantages and disadvantages and seeking worthy individuals,
but Jì did not accept it.
He was recommended for his administrative ability
and became the Prefect of Píshì.
At that time, Liú Yòu, the Grand Administrator of Hédōng, left his post,
and the brother of the Central Regular Attendant (Zhōngchángshì) Zuǒ Guàn, Shèng, replaced him.
Qí was ashamed and disgusted by eunuchs,
and immediately returned west that very day.
Yán Dǔ, the Administrator of Jīngzhào, again appointed him Chief Clerk (Gōngcáo).
Previously, the brother of the Central Regular Attendant (Zhōngchángshì) Táng Héng, Xuán, was the Commander of the Tiger Teeth Guard (Hǔyá Dūwèi) of Jīngzhào.
The people of the commandery, because Xuán's advancement was not due to virtue,
all treated him with contempt and disdain.
Qí and his cousin Xí also frequently criticized him,
which Xuán deeply resented.
In the first year of Yánxī (158 CE),
Xuán became the Administrator of Jīngzhào.
Qí feared that disaster would strike,
so he and his nephew Jiǎn fled to avoid him.
Xuán indeed arrested Qí's family and clan relatives,
implicated them with severe laws,
and killed them all.
Qí then fled in all directions,
across the Jiāng, Huái, the sea, and Tài Shān,
leaving no place unvisited.
He hid his name,
selling cakes in the marketplace of Běihǎi.
At that time, Sūn Sōng of Ānqīu, who was over twenty years old,
saw Qí in the market.
Perceiving him to be no ordinary man,
he stopped his carriage and called him to ride together.
Qí was frightened and lost color.
Sōng then lowered the curtain
and ordered his riders to clear the way for passersby.
He secretly asked Qí, saying:
"Looking at you, you are no cake seller,
and when asked, your expression changed.
If you don't have a grave enmity,
then are you a fugitive?
I am Sūn Bīnshí of Běihǎi.
My household numbers a hundred mouths,
and I am capable of helping you."
Qí had long heard of Sōng's reputation,
and immediately told him the truth,
then went home with him.
Sōng first entered and reported to his mother, saying:
"On my outing,
I found a friend to die for."
He welcomed Qí up to the main hall,
and entertained him with great joy.
He hid Qí in a hidden wall for several years,
during which Qí composed twenty-three chapters of "Songs of Hardship and Difficulty" (Ètún Gē).
Later, all the Táng family members died out,
and he came out due to an amnesty.
The Three Ducal Ministries (Sānfǔ) heard of him,
and simultaneously summoned him.
Nine years later,
he responded to the summons of Hú Guǎng, the Minister of the Masses (Sītú).
At that time, the Southern Xiōngnú, Wūhuán, and Xiānbēi rebelled.
The dukes and ministers recommended Qí,
and he was promoted to Governor (Cìshǐ) of Bìngzhōu.
Qí intended to submit a policy for guarding the frontier,
but before he could,
he was dismissed due to factional entanglements.
He then compiled his ideas into "Discourse on Resisting Bandits" (Yùkòu Lùn).
In the early years of Emperor Líng,
he again suffered from the "Prohibition on Factions" (Dǎnggù) for over ten years.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng (184 CE),
uprisings occurred in all directions.
An imperial edict commanded the selection of former governors (cìshǐ) and officials of two thousand *dàn* salary who possessed civil and military talents,
and Qí was summoned and appointed Gentleman Consultant (Yìláng).
General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn) Zhāng Wēn went west to pacify Guānzhōng,
and requested Qí to fill the post of Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ),
with a separate garrison in Āndìng.
The Great General Hé Jìn recommended him as Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng.
On his way to Xiāngwǔ,
Qí and several newly appointed Grand Administrators were captured by the bandits Biān Zhāng and others.
The bandits wanted to coerce him into becoming their leader,
but Qí managed to escape through deceptive words
and eventually returned to Cháng'ān.
When Emperor Xiàn moved west to the capital,
Qí was again appointed Gentleman Consultant (Yìláng),
and gradually promoted to Grand Coachman (Tàipú).
When Lǐ Jué monopolized power,
he sent Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Mǎ Rìdī to pacify the empire,
with Qí as his deputy.
When Rìdī arrived in Luòyáng,
he memorialized to separately dispatch Qí to proclaim the imperial decrees.
Wherever he went in the commanderies and counties,
the common people rejoiced, saying:
"Today we finally see the envoy's carriage again."
At this time, Yuán Shào and Cáo Cāo were contending with Gōngsūn Zàn for Jìzhōu.
Shào and Cāo, hearing of Qí's arrival,
both personally led troops several hundred *lǐ* to welcome him.
Qí deeply expounded the Son of Heaven's grace and virtue,
and the way to cease warfare and bring peace to the people.
He also sent a letter to Gōngsūn Zàn,
explaining the advantages and disadvantages.
Shào and the others each withdrew their troops,
and all promised Qí to meet in Luòyáng
to welcome the imperial carriage.
Qí traveled south to Chénliú,
and contracted a severe illness.
Two years passed,
and those who had promised did not arrive.
In the first year of Xīngpíng (194 CE),
an imperial edict summoned Qí.
At that time, the Emperor was about to return to Luòyáng,
and had first dispatched General of the Guards (Wèijiāngjūn) Dǒng Chéng to repair the palaces.
Qí said to Chéng:
"Now, the realm is fragmented.
Only Jīngzhōu has vast territory and strategic advantages,
connecting to Bā and Shǔ in the west,
and bordering Jiāozhǐ in the south.
Its harvests are uniquely abundant,
and its soldiers are relatively intact.
Although Qí is pressed by old age,
he still aspires to repay the state.
I wish to personally ride an ox-cart
south to persuade Liú Biǎo.
He could be made to personally lead troops to guard the imperial court,
and together with the General, act with one heart and one strength,
to jointly assist the royal house.
This is a policy for bringing peace to the ruler and saving the people."
Chéng immediately memorialized to dispatch Qí as an envoy to Jīngzhōu,
to supervise grain and provisions.
When Qí arrived,
Liú Biǎo immediately dispatched troops to Luòyáng to assist in repairing the palaces,
and military supplies flowed continuously,
without interruption.
At that time, Sūn Sōng also resided with Liú Biǎo,
but Liú Biǎo did not treat him with respect.
Qí then praised Sōng's consistent integrity and fierce character,
and together they memorialized for Sōng to be appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Qīngzhōu.
Qí, being old and ill,
remained in Jīngzhōu.
Cáo Cāo, then Minister of Works (Sīkōng), recommended him to replace himself.
Huán Diǎn, the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Guānglùxūn), and Kǒng Róng, the Minister Steward (Shàofǔ), submitted memorials recommending him.
Thereupon, Qí was appointed Grand Messenger (Tàicháng) while remaining where he was.
He was over ninety years old
and died in the sixth year of Jiàn'ān (201 CE).
He had previously built his own tomb,
depicting the four images of Jì Zhá, Zǐchǎn, Yàn Yīng, and Shú Xiàng occupying the guest seats,
and also drawing his own image in the host seat,
all with praises written for them.
He instructed his sons, saying:
"On the day I die,
gather sand in the tomb to make a bed,
spread a bamboo mat and white clothes,
lay my hair loose on it,
cover me with a single quilt,
and immediately lower me that day.
Once lowered, immediately cover it."
Qí wrote many works,
most notably "Annotations to the Chapters and Sentences of Mencius" (Mèngzǐ Zhāngjù) and "Records of Decisions of the Three Auxiliaries" (Sānfǔ Juélù) which were transmitted at that time.
The encomium says: Wú Wēng was kind and loving;
Yì Gān was resolute and unyielding.
Yán and Shǐ befriended people;
their gentle manner fostered kindness.
Liáng Shǐ displayed punishments;
conspiratorial factions secretly ceased.
Zǐ Gàn possessed multiple talents;
with scholarly robes, he oversaw the army.
Bīn Qīng went beyond the borders;
solely demonstrating the court's might.
Biographies of Huángfǔ, Zhāng, and Duàn, Chapter Fifty-Five
Huángfǔ Guī, courtesy name Wēimíng,
was a native of Cháonà, Āndìng.
His grandfather, Léng,
was Dùliáo Jiāngjūn.
His father, Qí,
was Fúfēng Dūwèi.
In the sixth year of Yǒnghé
(141 CE), the Western Qiāng greatly plundered Sānfǔ,
and besieged Āndìng.
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Mǎ Xián led the troops from various commanderies to attack them,
but could not overcome them.
Although Guī was still a commoner,
he saw that Xián neglected military affairs,
and, realizing he would certainly be defeated,
he submitted a memorial detailing the situation.
Soon after, Xián was indeed defeated by the Qiāng.
The commandery administrator, knowing Guī possessed military strategy,
appointed him Gōngcáo,
and ordered him to lead eight hundred armored soldiers
to engage the Qiāng.
He cut off several heads,
and the bandits subsequently retreated.
Guī was promoted to Shàngjì Yuàn.
Subsequently, the Qiāng forces united in large numbers,
attacking and burning Lǒngxī.
The imperial court was troubled by this.
Guī then submitted a memorial requesting to offer his services,
saying:
"In recent years,
I have repeatedly presented proposals of expediency.
Before the Qiāng-Róng moved,
I predicted their rebellion.
When Mǎ Xián first set out,
I knew he would surely be defeated.
My words, though perhaps mistakenly,
can be verified.
I often reflect that Xián and his like have commanded troops for four years
without achieving success.
The expenses of maintaining the army are nearly a hundred billion,
taken from common people
and diverted to corrupt officials.
Thus, people by the rivers and lakes
have formed groups of bandits.
Qīng and Xú are suffering from famine,
with people carrying their children and scattering.
The Qiāng-Róng's rebellion and defection
did not arise in times of peace,
but rather from the border generals' failure in pacification and control.
If they act aggressively while in a stable position,
then the ruler is violated and oppressed.
If they merely compete for small gains,
then great harm results.
With a slight victory, they falsely exaggerate the number of heads taken;
when the army is defeated, they conceal it and say nothing.
Soldiers are exhausted and resentful,
suffering at the hands of cunning officials.
When advancing, they cannot fight boldly to achieve merit;
when retreating, they cannot be well-fed and warm to preserve their lives.
They starve to death in ditches,
their bones exposed in the Central Plains.
One only sees the imperial army march out,
but hears no sound of its victorious return.
Chieftains weep blood,
fear and alarm giving rise to rebellion.
This is why peace cannot last long,
and defeat extends for years.
This is what causes me to clasp my hands to my heart and sigh repeatedly.
I request to be granted two camps and two commanderies,
with five thousand idle, 'eating-in-place' soldiers,
to strike when they least expect it,
and to coordinate with Hùqiāng Xiàowèi Zhào Chōng.
The land and valleys
I am familiar with;
the military tactics and opportune moments
I have experienced.
This can be achieved without bothering with an inch-square seal
or a foot of silk as a reward.
At best, it can eliminate calamity;
at worst, it can secure surrender.
If it is believed that I am too young and my office too humble
to be of use,
then consider that all defeated generals
were not lacking in high office
or advanced age.
I am overcome by my utmost sincerity
and present myself even unto death."
At that time, the emperor was unable to employ him.
During the reign of Chōng Zhì,
Empress Dowager Liáng presided over the court.
Guī was recommended as Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng.
In his response, he said: "I respectfully consider that Emperor Xiàoshùn,
when he first diligently administered the imperial government,
disciplined and regulated the four directions,
and almost achieved peace.
Later, he encountered corrupt and deceitful individuals,
whose authority was divided among intimate attendants.
They hoarded wealth
and horses,
and their frivolous activities were known.
Moreover, taking advantage of favored courtiers,
they accepted bribes and sold offices,
lightly employing guests and retainers,
whose numbers intertwined among them.
The empire was in turmoil,
following chaos as if returning home.
Therefore, whenever there were campaigns,
few were not defeated and wounded,
and both officials and common people were exhausted,
with superiors and subordinates utterly impoverished.
I am in Guānxī
and have secretly listened to the rumors.
I have not heard that the state has any priorities,
but rather that all power and influence
belong to those with influence.
Your Majesty possesses the virtues of heaven and earth,
and is intelligent, wise, and profoundly virtuous.
At the beginning of your regency,
you promoted loyal and upright individuals,
and corrected many
other principles
of governance.
Near and far, all rejoiced,
hoping to see great peace.
However, after the earthquake,
the fog was white and turbid,
the sun and moon lacked brilliance,
drought demons wreaked
havoc,
great bandits roamed freely,
blood stained the fields red,
and the common people were in unrest.
Repeated heavenly warnings
were probably caused by the excessive power of treacherous ministers.
Those Chángshì who are particularly
ill-behaved
should be immediately dismissed and banished.
Sweep away the wicked factions,
confiscate their ill-gotten gains,
to appease the bitter grievances
and respond to the warnings from Heaven.
Today, though your title is noble,
it is truly fitting to cultivate humility further,
supplemented by Confucian principles,
to eliminate unnecessary entertainments and trivial matters,
and to cut back on useless
ornaments for palaces and mansions.
Indeed, the ruler is the boat,
and the people are the water.
The ministers are those who ride in the boat,
and Your Majesty's brothers, the generals, are those who steer the oars.
If you can align your will and exert all
your strength
to ferry the masses across,
this is what is called fortune.
If, however, you become negligent,
you will sink into the waves.
How can one not be cautious!
Indeed, if virtue does not match one's emoluments,
it is like digging away the foundation of a wall
to increase its height.
How can this be the way to measure one's strength, assess one's merits, and ensure security?
All those old rascals, drunkards, and pleasure-seekers
who listen to evil words
and speak flattering
words,
who delight in leisure and extravagance,
and instigate unrighteousness,
should also be demoted and expelled
to punish their unruly behavior.
Let Jì and others deeply consider the blessings of employing worthy people
and the burdens of losing them.
Furthermore,
those in office who consume without working,
Shàngshū who neglect their duties,
and supervising officials who are indecisive,
none of whom are willing to investigate and rectify,
cause Your Majesty to exclusively hear flattering words
and not to know what happens beyond your windows.
I sincerely know that flattery brings blessings,
and deep words invite calamity.
How dare I conceal my true feelings to avoid punishment and blame!
I grew up in a remote border region
and rarely visited the purple court.
In my fear and trembling, I lost
my composure,
and have not expressed my whole heart."
At that time, the bandit Shū Sūn Wú Jì from Tài Shān was causing disturbances in the commanderies and counties.
The Colonel, Zōng Zī, had been campaigning against him but had not yet subdued him.
A special summons was issued for Guī,
and he was appointed Administrator of Tài Shān.
When Guī arrived at his post,
he extensively implemented strategies,
and the bandits were all pacified.
In the autumn of the fourth year of Yán Xī [159 CE],
the rebellious Qiāng, Lǐng Wú and others, along with another branch of the Xiān Líng, plundered Guān Zhōng,
and the Protector of the Qiāng, Duàn Jiǒng, was recalled as a result.
Later, the various Xiān Líng tribes became unruly,
and overran military camps and fortified villages.
Guī had always been familiar with Qiāng affairs
and was determined to exert himself.
He then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Since Your subject received his appointment,
he has dedicated his humble efforts.
He truly relied on the clear-sighted bravery of the Inspector of Yǎn Zhōu, Qiān Hào,
and the trustworthiness and integrity of the Colonel, Zōng Zī,
to execute his duties
and fortunately avoid blame or praise.
Now that the cunning bandits are almost eliminated,
and Tài Shān is mostly pacified,
I again hear that all the various Qiāng tribes have rebelled.
Your subject grew up in Bīn Qí,
is fifty-nine years old,
and in the past, as a commandery official,
twice encountered rebellious Qiāng.
When planning these matters,
his words sometimes hit the mark.
Your subject has always suffered from a chronic illness,
and fears that his remaining years are few,
and he will not be able to repay Your great kindness.
I wish to request a nominal official post,
to serve as a lone envoy with a single carriage,
to visit and console the Sān Fǔ region,
to proclaim the nation's power and benevolence,
and with my knowledge of the terrain and military situation,
to assist the various armies.
Your subject has lived in remote and perilous circumstances,
observing the commandery generals,
for several decades now.
From Niǎo Shǔ to Dōng Dài,
their ailment is one and the same.
To strenuously seek out fierce enemies
is not as good as having peace and order;
to diligently study Wú and Sūn [military texts]
is not as good as upholding the law.
The previous changes are not long past,
and Your subject is truly distressed by them.
Therefore, I overstep my bounds
to express my humble thoughts."
By winter,
the Qiāng had indeed united in large numbers,
causing concern at court.
The Three Excellencies recommended Guī as Colonel,
to hold the imperial insignia and supervise the troops west of the passes,
to campaign against Lǐng Wú and others.
He defeated them,
beheading eight hundred people.
The various Xiān Líng Qiāng tribes admired Guī's authority and trustworthiness,
and encouraged each other to surrender, numbering over a hundred thousand.
The following year,
Guī then mobilized their cavalry to jointly attack Lǒng Yòu,
but the roads were cut off,
and a great plague broke out in the army,
killing three or four tenths of the men.
Guī personally entered the thatched huts,
inspecting his officers and soldiers.
The entire army was moved and pleased.
The Eastern Qiāng then sent envoys to beg for surrender,
and Liáng Zhōu was reconnected.
Previously, the Administrator of Ān Dìng, Sūn Jùn, had been grossly corrupt;
the Commander of the Dependent State, Lǐ Xī, and the Supervising Army Censor, Zhāng Bǐng, had killed many surrendering Qiāng;
and the Inspector of Liáng Zhōu, Guō Hóng, and the Administrator of Hàn Yáng, Zhào Xī, were both old and weak and unfit for duty,
yet all relied on powerful and influential figures,
disregarding the law.
When Guī arrived at the provincial border,
he meticulously itemized and impeached their crimes,
resulting in some being dismissed and others executed.
When the Qiāng people heard of this,
they immediately turned to good.
The great chieftains of the Shěn Dǐ, Diān Chāng and Jī Tián, and over a hundred thousand people,
again came to Guī to surrender.
Guī had served for several years,
held the imperial insignia as a general,
commanded troops, achieved merit,
and returned to supervise his homeland.
He had no other private favors,
but rather impeached many.
He also strongly detested eunuchs
and refused to associate with them.
Thus, both the court and the provinces harbored resentment,
and conspired to falsely accuse Guī of bribing the Qiāng tribes
to make them feign surrender.
Imperial edicts rebuking him followed one after another.
Guī feared he would not escape punishment,
and submitted a memorial to defend himself, saying:
"In the autumn of the fourth year,
the barbarian hordes were rebellious and unruly,
starting from Xī Zhōu,
invading as far as Jīng Yáng.
The old capital was terrified,
and the court looked west with apprehension.
The enlightened edict, not considering Your subject's foolishness and weakness,
urgently dispatched the army to proceed.
Fortunately, relying on Your majestic power,
the nation's destiny was revived.
The various Qiāng tribes,
great and small, bowed their heads.
I then issued dispatches to the military commanderies
to inquire about executing or accepting surrenders.
The expenses saved
exceeded one hundred million.
Believing it to be the duty of a loyal minister,
I dared not speak of my toil,
and thus was ashamed to mention my humble achievements in a single word.
However, comparing this to previous events,
I hope to be free from fault and regret.
Previously, when I entered the provincial border,
I first impeached the Administrator Sūn Jùn,
and next the Commander of the Dependent State Lǐ Xī and the Supervising Army Censor Zhāng Bǐng.
Upon returning the army south,
I again impeached the Inspector of Liáng Zhōu Guō Hóng and the Administrator of Hàn Yáng Zhào Xī,
detailing their transgressions and evils,
and enforced capital punishment.
Of these five officials,
their factions filled half the country.
As for the other officials,
down to the lowest clerks,
those implicated
numbered over a hundred more.
Officials sought to avenge their general's grievances;
sons wished to restore their father's honor.
They carried gifts and rode carriages,
and brought provisions and walked on foot,
colluding with powerful families,
competing to spread slander and calumny,
saying that Your subject privately repaid the various Qiāng
and thanked them with money and goods.
If Your subject used his private wealth,
then his family would have nothing;
if the goods came from official funds,
then the official records would be easy to check.
Even if Your subject were foolish and confused,
and it were true as they say,
previous generations still presented the Xiongnú with palace ladies
and pacified the Wū Sūn with princesses.
to appease the rebellious Qiāng.
Then, what crime could such talent and strategy of a loyal minister,
so valued by military strategists,
possibly have committed,
that would be disloyal or unreasonable?
Since Yǒng Chū,
not a few generals have been dispatched,
five armies have been destroyed,
costing enormous sums.
Some, upon returning their armies intact,
reported their achievements to powerful families,
Now Your subject has returned to supervise his homeland,
investigated and impeached various commanderies,
severed ties and estranged relatives,
and disgraced old acquaintances.
It is therefore natural
that he should be subject to widespread slander and secret harm.
Although Your subject is defiled and has no reputation for integrity,
now facing ruin,
his shame and pain are truly profound.
The saying goes, 'A dying deer does not choose its cry.'
I respectfully make this brief and rash submission."
In the winter of that year,
he was recalled and appointed Counsellor.
His achievements merited enfeoffment.
However, the palace eunuchs Xú Huáng and Zuǒ Kuài wished to extort goods from him,
and repeatedly sent guests to inquire about his merits.
Guī steadfastly refused to respond.
Huáng and his associates were enraged
and implicated him in previous matters,
handing him over to the authorities.
His subordinates wished to levy contributions to thank them,
but Guī swore not to allow it.
Consequently, for the reason that the remaining bandits were not entirely wiped out,
he was imprisoned by the Grand Judge
and sentenced to be exiled to the Left Workshop.
The various Excellencies and over three hundred Grand Students, including Zhāng Fèng, went to the palace gate to plead for him.
A general amnesty was issued,
and he returned home.
Huángfǔ Guī was appointed Colonel Who Crosses the Liao.
After several months in camp,
he submitted a memorial recommending Colonel Zhāng Huàn to replace him.
He said:
"I have heard that people have no constant customs,
but governance has its periods of order and chaos;
troops have no inherent strength or weakness,
but generals have their abilities and incapacities.
I humbly observe that Colonel Zhāng Huàn
possesses both talent and strategy in abundance.
He is fit to be the chief commander
and fulfill the popular expectation.
If it is still believed that your foolish servant is suitable for military affairs,
I request a superfluous office
to serve as Huàn's deputy."
The imperial court agreed to this,
and appointed Zhāng Huàn to replace Huángfǔ Guī as Colonel Who Crosses the Liao,
while Huángfǔ Guī was made Envoy and Colonel of the Xiongnú.
When Huàn was promoted to Grand Minister of Agriculture,
Huángfǔ Guī again replaced him as Colonel Who Crosses the Liao.
Huángfǔ Guī was a person of many schemes and calculations.
Believing himself to have held high positions for a long time,
he wished to withdraw and avoid further promotion.
He repeatedly pleaded illness,
but was not granted permission.
It so happened that his friend, Wáng Mín, the Administrator of Shàngjùn, was returning from a funeral.
Huángfǔ Guī, dressed in mourning white, crossed the border
and went to Xiàtíng to meet him.
He then secretly ordered a guest to inform Hú Fāng, the Inspector of Bīngzhōu,
saying that Huángfǔ Guī had ventured far from the army camp,
publicly violating regulations and laws,
and should be immediately impeached.
Hú Fāng said:
"Wēimíng wishes to avoid promotion and leave his official career,
that is why he is provoking me!
I should cherish talent for the imperial court;
how could I carry out this man's scheme?"
Thus, he made no inquiry.
When the incident of the Factionalists erupted on a large scale,
many famous and virtuous people throughout the realm were implicated and arrested.
Although Huángfǔ Guī was a renowned general,
his long-standing reputation was not high.
Considering himself a hero and outstanding figure from Xīzhōu,
he was ashamed not to be involved.
So he first submitted a self-impeachment, saying:
