"Your servant previously recommended the former Grand Minister of Agriculture, Zhāng Huàn,
which constitutes associating with the Faction.
Moreover, when your servant was deliberating on being sentenced to the Left School,
students like Zhāng Fèng submitted memorials to defend your servant,
which means your servant was supported by Faction members.
Your servant ought to be punished for this."
The imperial court knew the truth but did not question him,
and people at the time considered Huángfǔ Guī virtuous.
He held office for several years,
and the northern borders were pacified and subservient.
In the first year of Yǒngkāng (167 CE),
he was summoned to be a Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
That summer, there was a solar eclipse,
and an imperial edict commanded high officials to recommend worthy and upright individuals,
and to inquire about successes and failures.
Huángfǔ Guī responded:
"Heaven's relationship with a king
is like a lord's with his minister,
or a father's with his son.
It warns with calamities and portents,
and leads to blessings and good omens.
In the eight years of Your Majesty's reign,
three major judicial cases have been concluded,
one internal favorite removed,
and two external officials executed.
Yet calamities and anomalies still appear,
and public sentiment is not yet at ease.
This is probably because in the advancement and retreat of the worthy and the foolish,
and the application of prestige and punishment,
there have been instances contrary to reason.
Former Grand Commandants Chén Fān and Liú Jǔ,
whose loyal counsel was exalted by the age,
are now dismissed and dwell in common alleys;
Liú Yòu, Féng Gǔn,
Zhào Diǎn, and Yǐn Xūn,
upright but often resented,
have been banished to their homes;
Lǐ Yīng, Wáng Chàng, and Kǒng Yì,
who kept themselves pure and adhered to ritual,
never attained the rank of chief minister.
As for the misfortune of the Factionalists,
it arose without cause,
oppressing the worthy and harming the good,
and even innocent people suffered.
Now, to initiate benevolent governance
is as easy as turning one's hand,
yet all the ministers are silent,
fearing past harm,
looking at each other,
none daring to speak truthfully.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will temporarily suspend your divine wisdom,
and tolerate blunt and straightforward speech.
Then former transgressions can be averted,
and future blessings will surely descend."
After the memorial was presented,
it was not heeded.
Huángfǔ Guī was transferred to be Administrator of Hóngnóng,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Shòuchéng Tíng,
with an income of two hundred households.
He declined the enfeoffment and did not accept it.
He was twice transferred to be Commander of the Qiāng.
In the third year of Xīpíng (174 CE),
he was recalled due to illness.
Before he arrived,
he died in Gǔchéng at the age of seventy-one.

His writings, including rhapsodies (fù), inscriptions (míng), steles (bēi), eulogies (zàn), prayers (dǎowén), laments (diào), memorials (zhāngbiǎo), edicts (jiàolìng), letters (shū), manifestos (xí), and notes (jiànjì),
totaled twenty-seven篇.
A commentary states: Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) said,
"If one speaks without shame,
then it will be difficult to act accordingly."
Examining Huángfǔ Guī's words,
his heart felt no shame!
Indeed, when he scrutinized himself, he sought office;
when he saw the worthy, he resigned his position.
Thus, seeking office was not considered greed,
and resigning a position was not for the sake of humility;
praising himself did not imply boasting,
and yielding to others involved no fear.
Therefore, he was able to achieve meritorious deeds against the Róng and Dí,
and preserve his person for the state.
Zhāng Huàn, courtesy name Ránmíng,
was from Dūnhuáng Yuánquán.
His father, Zhāng Dūn,
was Administrator of Hànyáng.
Zhāng Huàn traveled through the Sānfǔ in his youth,
studying under Grand Commandant Zhū Kǒng,
and learned the Ōuyáng version of the Shàngshū.
Initially,
Móu Shì's commentary had flowery and verbose language, totaling over four hundred and fifty thousand characters.
Zhāng Huàn reduced it to ninety thousand characters.
Later, he was appointed to the staff of Grand General Liáng Jì.
He then submitted a memorial to Emperor Huán,
presenting his commentary.
An imperial edict ordered it to be deposited at the Dōngguān Library.
He left office due to illness,
and was later again recommended as worthy and upright.
He placed first in the policy examination
and was promoted to be a Palace Aide.
In the first year of Yǒngshòu (155 CE),
he was transferred to be Commandant of the Dependent State of Āndìng.
Upon first arriving at his post,
the Southern Xiongnú Left Yùjiān Táiqí, and Qú Qú Bódé,
along with over seven thousand others, raided Měijì.
The Eastern Qiāng also rose up in response.
Zhāng Huàn's encampment only had about two hundred men.
Upon hearing the news, he immediately ordered his troops out.
His military officers, believing their strength to be insufficient,
knocked their heads and vehemently tried to stop him.
Zhāng Huàn did not listen,
and instead advanced to garrison Chángchéng.
He gathered soldiers
and sent General Wáng Wèi to entice the Eastern Qiāng,
then occupied Guīcí,
preventing the Southern Xiongnú from communicating with the Eastern Qiāng.
The various chieftains then led their people to make peace with Zhāng Huàn,
and together they attacked Yùjiān and others,
defeating them in successive battles.
Bódé was terrified
and surrendered with his followers,
bringing peace to the commandery.
The Qiāng chieftains were grateful for Zhāng Huàn's benevolence and virtue.
They presented twenty horses,
and the Xiānlíng chieftain further sent eight gold bells.
Zhāng Huàn accepted them all,
but then summoned his chief clerk before the various Qiāng,
and poured wine on the ground, saying:
"Even if the horses were as numerous as sheep,
I would not take them into my stable;
even if the gold were as abundant as grain,
I would not take it into my bosom."
He returned all the gold and horses.
The Qiāng were by nature greedy but valued upright officials.
Previously, eight commandants had been fond of wealth,
causing them much trouble.
When Zhāng Huàn rectified himself and remained pure,
his authority and transformative influence became widely effective.
He was transferred to be Envoy and Colonel of the Xiongnú.
At that time, the Xiūtú Gè
and the Shuòfāng Wūhuán simultaneously rebelled,
burning the gate of the Colonel Who Crosses the Liao's headquarters.
They withdrew and encamped at Chìkēng,
their smoke and fires visible from afar.
The troops were greatly alarmed,
each wishing to flee.
Zhāng Huàn sat calmly within his tent,
lecturing and reciting with his disciples as if nothing was amiss,
and the soldiers gradually calmed down.
He then secretly enticed the Wūhuán and made a covert alliance with them,
subsequently causing them to decapitate the Xiūtú Gè chieftain
and attack and defeat his followers.
All the various Hú then surrendered.
In the first year of Yánxī
the Xiānbēi invaded the border.
Huàn led the Southern Chányú to attack them,
beheading several hundred.
The following year,
Liáng Jì was executed,
and Huàn, as a former subordinate, was dismissed from office and subjected to lifelong prohibition from holding office.
Huàn was a close friend of Huángfǔ Guī.
After Huàn was banned,
all his former acquaintances dared not speak on his behalf.
Only Guī recommended him repeatedly, seven times in total.
After four years at home,
he was again appointed Administrator of Wǔwēi.
He equalized the labor services and taxes,
and rallied those who had scattered and fled.
and Hēxī was thereby preserved.
The local customs had many taboos;
all children born in the second or fifth month, or those born in the same month as their parents,
were killed.
Huàn enlightened them with principles of righteousness,
and strictly applied rewards and punishments.
The customs were consequently changed,
and the common people erected shrines for him during his lifetime.
He was selected for his exceptional abilities
and promoted to Commander of Dùliáo.
Within several years,
Yōu and Bìng were pacified.
In the spring of the ninth year,
he was summoned and appointed Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng).
When the Xiānbēi heard that Huàn had left,
that summer,
they consequently rallied and allied with the Southern Xiōngnú and Wūhuán, invading the frontier through several routes.
Some had five or six thousand cavalry,
others three or four thousand cavalry,
and they plundered the nine commanderies along the border,
killing and kidnapping common people.
In the autumn,
the Xiānbēi again led eight or nine thousand cavalry to invade the frontier,
enticing the Eastern Qiāng to form an alliance with them through oaths.
Thereupon, the Shěndī of Shàngjùn and the Xiānlíng and other tribes of Āndìng jointly attacked Wǔwēi and Zhāngyè,
causing great distress along the border.
The imperial court considered this a serious concern,
and again appointed Huàn as Colonel Protector of the Xiōngnú (Hùxiōngnú Zhōnglángjiàng).
With the rank of a Nine Ministers (Jiǔqīng), he was given superintendence over the three provinces of Yōu, Bìng, and Liáng, as well as the two camps of Dùliáo and Wūhuán.
He also inspected the capabilities of the Provincial Governors (Cìshǐ) and officials receiving two thousand dàn of salary,
and was given very generous rewards.
When the Xiōngnú and Wūhuán heard of Huàn's arrival,
they consequently led their people back and surrendered,
totaling two hundred thousand individuals.
Huàn only executed the principal offenders;
the rest he comforted and accepted.
Only the Xiānbēi withdrew beyond the frontier.
In the spring of the first year of Yǒngkāng,
the Eastern Qiāng and Xiānlíng, with five or six thousand cavalry, attacked Guānzhōng,
besieged Duìyǔ,
and plundered Yúnyáng.
That summer,
they again attacked and destroyed two camps,
killing over a thousand people.
In the winter,
Qiāng Ānwěi and Mōbiē, among others,
coerced their kinsmen to again raid the Sānfǔ region.
Huàn dispatched his Sīmǎ Yǐn Duān and Dǒng Zhuó to jointly attack them,
greatly defeating them.
He beheaded their chieftains and leaders,
capturing over ten thousand heads and captives.
The three provinces were pacified.
He deserved a peerage for his meritorious service,
but Huàn did not flatter the eunuchs,
so the reward was not bestowed.
He was only granted two hundred thousand cash
and one member of his household was appointed as a Gentleman (Láng).
He declined both and did not accept,
instead wishing to move his household to Huáyīn, Hóngnóng.
According to old regulations, border people were not allowed to move inland.
Only Huàn, due to his accomplishments, was specially permitted,
and thus he became a person of Hóngnóng.
In the first year of Jiànníng,
he returned with his troops.
At that time, Empress Dowager Dòu was regent.
Grand General Dòu Wǔ and Grand Tutor Chén Fān conspired to eliminate the eunuchs.
When the plot was exposed,
the Central Regular Attendant (Zhōng Chángshì) Cáo Jié and others initiated a rebellion in the palace.
As Huàn had just been summoned and
was unaware of the original plot,
they forged an imperial edict ordering Huàn and the Palace Steward (Shǎofǔ) Zhōu Jìng to lead five battalions of soldiers to surround Dòu Wǔ.
Dòu Wǔ committed suicide,
and Chén Fān was consequently killed.
Huàn was promoted to Palace Steward (Shǎofǔ),
then again appointed Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng),
and enfeoffed as a marquis for his achievements.
Huàn deeply resented being used by Cáo Jié.
He submitted a memorial firmly declining
and returned the seal and sash,
ultimately refusing to accept.
The following summer,
a green snake appeared in front of the imperial carriage pavilion,
and there were also strong winds, heavy rain, and hail.
Thunderbolts uprooted trees.
An edict commanded all officials to state the meaning of these omens.
Huàn submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that wind is a symbol of commands,
and living things communicate through vital energy.
Wood is born from fire,
and they depend on each other for illumination.
Snakes can coil and extend,
matching dragons in their soaring and hibernating.
When they arrive in harmony, they are auspicious signs;
when they arrive in opposition, they are calamities and misfortunes.
When yin energy becomes dominant,
it condenses into hail.
Therefore, Grand General Dòu Wǔ and Grand Tutor Chén Fān,
one dedicated to stabilizing the state,
the other upright and unyielding,
were previously overcome by slander
and both executed.
The realm has been silent,
but people harbor shock and indignation.
In antiquity, when Duke of Zhōu was not buried with proper rites,
Heaven showed its might.
Now, Dòu Wǔ and Chén Fān were loyal and upright,
but have not yet been clearly exonerated.
The arrival of these ominous phenomena
is all for this reason.
It is imperative to quickly rebury them
and move their families back.
All those implicated and subjected to lifelong prohibition
should be universally pardoned.
Furthermore, although the Empress Dowager resides in Nánjū,
she is not treated with warmth and courtesy,
and no court official speaks out,
causing disappointment far and wide.
One should consider the great principle of filial return. "
The Son of Heaven deeply accepted Huàn's words,
and consulted the regular attendants of the Yellow Gates.
His entourage all disliked it,
and the Emperor was unable to follow his own inclination.
Huàn was transferred to Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
Together with the Secretaries (Shàngshū) Liú Měng, Diāo Wěi, and Wèi Liáng, he jointly recommended Wáng Chàng and Lǐ Yīng as suitable candidates for the Three Dukes.
However, Cáo Jié and others intensely resented their words,
and consequently issued an edict sharply reprimanding them.
Huàn and the others imprisoned themselves at the Court of the Imperial Censor (Tíngwèi),
and were only released after several days,
all redeeming their offenses with three months' salary.
Wáng Yù, the Colonel Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi),
came from the eunuch faction.
He wanted to use his favor to influence the high officials,
seeking recommendations.
All officials feared him
and none refused him,
except Huàn, who alone rejected him.
Wáng Yù was angered,
and thus implicated him in the crime of factionalism,
subjecting him to lifelong prohibition and sending him back to his rural home.
Huàn previously served as Dùliáo Jiāngjūn,
and contended with Duàn Gǒng in attacking the Qiāng,
but they were not on good terms.
When Gǒng became Sīlì Xiàowèi,
he wished to pursue Huàn back to Dūnhuáng
and harm him.
Huàn was worried and afraid,
and presented a memorial to Gǒng, saying:
“This humble person is unenlightened,
and has offended the provincial governor.
From a thousand *lǐ* away, I entrust my life,
and in feeling, return to you.
Your Excellency is benevolent and honest,
and perceives my hardships.
Before I could return,
I again received your official letter.
The imperial edict is clear,
and I have already copied and presented it,
but the provincial deadline is pressing,
and the commanderies and counties are panicked and fearful,
eagerly waiting
and expectantly awaiting their fate.
My parents’ decaying bones,
and their lonely souls are entrusted to me.
If I receive your pity and compassion,
a single act of kindness,
then your favor will flow to the Yellow Springs,
extending to the netherworld,
which Huàn’s life or death cannot repay.
To exert no effort, not even a hair’s worth of labor,
yet desire others to serve like mountains,
this is why Chúnyú Kūn slapped his thigh, looked up to the sky, and laughed.
I truly know my words will be ridiculed,
yet I cannot be without hope.
Why?
Decaying bones are of no benefit to others,
yet King Wén buried them;
a dead horse is no longer useful,
yet King Zhāo of Yān treasured it.
To follow the virtues of Wén and Zhāo,
is that not great?
It is the common human sentiment
that when wronged, one calls out to Heaven;
when destitute, one beats one’s heart.
Now, calling to Heaven is unheard,
beating my heart is useless;
I am truly heartbroken.
Born in the same sacred age,
yet alone I am considered an outcast.
A lonely and humble person
has nowhere to appeal.
If you do not pity me,
I will become fish and meat.
My heart yearns eastward,
I have nothing more to say.”
Though Gǒng was stern and fierce,
he read the letter and pitied him,
and in the end could not bear to harm him.
At that time, many of those subjected to the "party prohibitions" could not remain quiet,
some died, some were exiled.
Huàn shut his doors and did not go out,
supporting a thousand disciples.
He wrote a commentary on the Shàngshū in over three hundred thousand characters.
From a young age, Huàn had firm aspirations and principles.
He once said to his friends:
“A true man living in this world
should establish meritorious service for the nation on its borders.”
When he became a general,
he indeed achieved fame and merit.
Dǒng Zhuó admired him,
and had his elder brother send him a hundred bolts of silk.
Huàn detested Dǒng Zhuó’s character,
and refused to accept them.
He died in the fourth year of Guānghé,
aged seventy-eight.
His last will said:
“Throughout my career,
I have held high positions ten times,
but could not blend in with the world
and was resented by slanderers and villains.
Success and failure are fate,
constancy is the norm.
However, the earth is dark and deep,
with no prospect of dawn,
and to be wrapped in silk floss
and sealed with nails
is something I do not like.
Fortunately, there is a ready grave,
so I can die in the morning and be buried in the evening.
Place my body on a spiritual couch,
with just a simple headscarf.
Not extravagant like King Wén of Jìn,
nor frugal like Wáng Sūn,
following my feelings and wishes,
there should be no blame or regret.”
His sons followed his wishes.
In Wǔwēi, many established shrines for him,
which were passed down through generations.
He authored twenty-four pieces, including inscriptions, eulogies, letters, teachings, admonitions, records, memorials, and policy responses.
His eldest son, Zhī,
courtesy name Bóyīng,
was the most famous.
Zhī and his younger brother Chǎng,
courtesy name Wénshū,
were both skilled in *cǎoshū*,
and are still praised for it today.
Initially,
when Huàn was the Administrator of Wǔwēi,
his wife was pregnant
and dreamt of wearing Huàn’s seal and ribbon, ascending a tower and singing.
She consulted a diviner,
who said:
“She will certainly give birth to a son,
who will again govern this land,
and his fate will end in this way.”
Later, she gave birth to a son named Měng.
During the Jiàn’ān era, he became Administrator of Wǔwēi.
He killed the Inspector Hándān Shāng,
and the provincial army besieged him closely.
Měng, ashamed to be captured,
then climbed a tower, set himself on fire, and died,
which exactly fulfilled the divination.
A commentary says: Since the enfeoffment of Cháoxiāng,
the power of the eunuchs flourished for decades.
They were tyrannical and arbitrary for several decades,
and within the four seas,
everyone gnashed their teeth in full indignation,
wishing to turn their weapons against their clan.
Chén Fān and Dòu Wǔ rose up righteously and planned a conspiracy,
assembling talented and discerning men from all over the realm,
which was widely known.
Yet Zhāng Huàn was deceived by a youngster,
and raised his halberd to cut off the loyal and valiant.
Although bitterness and poison were in his heart,
he resigned his official title and apologized for his fault.
The Shī says:
“He sobs his tears,
but what avails his sighing!”
Duàn Gǒng, courtesy name Jìmíng,
was a native of Gūzāng, Wǔwēi.
His ancestor was Duàn from Zhèng Gòngshū,
and he was the grandnephew of Huì Zōng, the Protector-General of the Western Regions.
From a young age, Gǒng was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and enjoyed *yóuxiá*,
lightly valuing wealth.
As an adult, he restrained himself and devoted himself to classical studies.
Initially recommended as a *Xiàolián*,
he served as Xiànlíng Yuánchéng and Yánglíng Lìng,
demonstrating capable governance wherever he served.
He was promoted to Liáodōng Shǔguó Dūwèi.
At that time, the Xiānbēi invaded the frontier,
and Gǒng immediately led his troops to rush to confront them.
However, fearing that the raiders would be alarmed and flee,
he sent a messenger on horseback to pretend to carry an imperial edict recalling Gǒng.
Gǒng feigned retreat on the road,
and secretly set up an ambush on the return path.
The barbarians believed it to be true,
and entered to pursue Gǒng.
Gǒng then launched a major offensive,
slaughtering and capturing all of them.
He was punished with a severe penalty for forging an imperial edict,
but due to his merits, he was pardoned from the criminal punishment.
After the punishment,
he was summoned and appointed Yìláng.
At that time, bandits Dōngguō Dòu and Gōngsūn Jǔ from Tàishān and Lángyá, among others, gathered three thousand men,
destroying commanderies and counties.
Troops were dispatched to suppress them,
but for years they failed.
In the second year of Yǒngshòu,
Emperor Huán ordered the Grand Ministers to select a general who possessed both civil and military talents.
Sītú Yǐn Sòng recommended Gǒng,
and he was appointed Zhōnglángjiàng.
He attacked Dòu and Jǔ,
greatly defeating and beheading them,
capturing over ten thousand heads.
The remaining factions surrendered and dispersed.
Gǒng was enfeoffed as a Marquis,
granted five hundred thousand *qián*,
and one of his sons was appointed Lángzhōng.
In the second year of Yánxī,
he was promoted to Hùqiāng Xiàowèi.
At this time, eight Qiāng tribes, including Shāodāng, Shāohé, Dāngjiān, and Lèjiě,
raided Lǒngxī and Jīnchéng forts.
Gǒng led his troops and twelve thousand cavalry of loyal Qiāng from Huángzhōng out of Huánggǔ,
and defeated them.
He pursued and attacked them as they crossed south of the river,
sending his officers Tián Yàn and Xià Yù to recruit vanguards,
who pulled themselves across with ropes.
They fought again at Luótíng,
and greatly defeated them,
beheading over two thousand of their chiefs and others.
They captured over ten thousand captives,
and all the barbarians fled.
The following spring,
the Yúqiāng (餘羌) again, with the great chieftain Shāohé (燒何), plundered Zhāngyè (張掖),
attacked and captured Jùlùwù (鉅鹿塢),
killed officers and people of the dependent state,
and also recruited over a thousand allied settlements of their own kind.
They combined forces and rushed to Gěng (熲)'s army at dawn.
Gěng (熲) dismounted and fought a great battle.
By midday,
his sword was broken and arrows exhausted,
and the barbarians also retreated.
Gěng (熲) pursued them,
fighting and marching,
attacking day and night.
They cut meat and ate snow,
for over forty days,
until they reached the Jīshíshān (積石山) at the source of the river,
having traveled more than two thousand *lǐ* (里) outside the frontier.
They beheaded Shāohé (燒何), the great chieftain,
and captured over five thousand heads.
They also divided their troops to attack the Shíchéng Qiāng (石城羌),
beheading or drowning sixteen hundred people.
Over ninety members of the Shāodāng (燒當) tribe went to Gěng (熲) and surrendered.
Furthermore, various Qiāng (羌) tribes gathered at Báishí (白石);
Gěng (熲) again advanced and attacked them,
capturing over three thousand heads.
In winter,
the Lèjiě (勒姐) and Língwú (零吾) tribes besieged Yǔnjiē (允街),
killing and kidnapping officers and people.
Gěng (熲) broke through the encampment to rescue them,
beheading and capturing several hundred people.
In the winter of the fourth year,
the Shěndī (沈氐) of Shàngjùn (上郡) and the Láojiě (牢姐) and Wūwú (烏吾) and other Qiāng (羌) tribes of Lǒngxī (隴西) jointly plundered Bìng (并) and Liáng (涼) two *zhōu* (州).
Gěng (熲) led the Righteous Volunteers from Huángzhōng (湟中) to suppress them.
Guō Hóng (郭閎), the Inspector of Liángzhōu (涼州), coveted joint credit for the achievement,
and deliberately held back Gěng (熲)'s army,
preventing it from advancing.
The Righteous Volunteers, having been on campaign for a long time,
yearned for their homes,
and all rebelled.
Guō Hóng (郭閎) blamed Gěng (熲),
who was summoned and imprisoned,
and sent to perform labor at the Zuǒxiào (左校).
The Qiāng (羌) then became rampant,
overrunning and destroying camps and stockades,
recruiting and forming alliances,
and raiding various commanderies.
Consequently, officers and common people, numbering in the thousands, stood at the palace gate to plead for Gěng (熲).
The imperial court learned that Gěng (熲) had been falsely accused by Guō Hóng (郭閎),
and issued an edict inquiring about the situation.
Gěng (熲) merely apologized for his faults,
not daring to speak of the injustice,
and was praised in the capital as a worthy man.
He was released from his penal servitude,
and again appointed to the post of Yìláng (議郎),
then promoted to Inspector of Bìngzhōu (并州).
At that time, the Diānnà (滇那) and other Qiāng (羌) tribes, five or six thousand strong, plundered Wǔwēi (武威), Zhāngyè (張掖), and Jiǔquán (酒泉),
burning people's homes.
In the sixth year,
the raiding force grew even stronger,
and Liángzhōu (涼州) was almost lost.
In winter,
Gěng (熲) was again appointed Colonel Protector of the Qiāng (護羌校尉),
traveling by post-horse to assume his office.
The following spring,
Fēnglù (封僇), Liángduō (良多), Diānnà (滇那), and other Qiāng (羌)
chieftains, three hundred fifty-five in number, leading three thousand settlements, went to Gěng (熲) and surrendered.
The Dāngjiān (當煎) and Lèjiě (勒姐) tribes, however, still remained entrenched.
In winter,
Gěng (熲) led over ten thousand men to attack and defeat them,
beheading their chieftains,
and capturing over four thousand heads.
In the spring of the eighth year,
Gěng (熲) again attacked the Lèjiě (勒姐) tribe,
beheading over four hundred,
and receiving the surrender of over two thousand people.
In summer,
he advanced his army to attack the Dāngjiān (當煎) tribe in Huángzhōng (湟中).
Gěng (熲)'s army was defeated
and besieged for three days.
Using the strategy of the recluse Fán Zhìzhāng (樊志張),
he secretly moved his troops out at night,
then beat drums and returned to battle,
utterly defeating them,
capturing several thousand heads.
Gěng (熲) then pursued them relentlessly,
moving back and forth through valleys and mountains.
From spring to autumn,
there was not a day without battle.
The barbarians eventually became starved, exhausted, and scattered,
plundering the area north of Wǔwēi (武威).
Gěng (熲) completely defeated the Western Qiāng (西羌),
beheading twenty-three thousand,
capturing tens of thousands of people alive,
and eight million horses, cattle, and sheep.
Over ten thousand settlements surrendered.
Gěng (熲) was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dūxiāng (都鄉),
with five hundred households.
In the first year of Yǒngkāng (永康),
the Dāngjiān (當煎) and other tribes again rebelled,
gathering over four thousand people,
intending to attack Wǔwēi (武威).
Gěng (熲) again pursued and attacked them at Luánniǎo (鸞鳥),
utterly defeating them,
killing their leaders,
and beheading over three thousand.
The Western Qiāng (西羌) were pacified thereafter.
As for the Eastern Qiāng (東羌), such as the Xiānlíng (先零),
ever since they defeated and killed the General who Conquers the West (征西將軍) Mǎ Xián (馬賢),
the imperial court had been unable to suppress them,
and they frequently raided and disturbed the Three Commanderies (三輔).
Later, General who Crosses the Liao River (度遼將軍) Huángfǔ Guī (皇甫規) and Colonel-Director of Retainers (中郎將) Zhāng Huàn (張奐) recruited them for successive years,
but they rebelled again after surrendering.
Emperor Huán (桓帝) issued an edict asking Gěng (熲):
"The Xiānlíng (先零) Eastern Qiāng (東羌) have committed evil and rebelled,
yet Huángfǔ Guī (皇甫規) and Zhāng Huàn (張奐), each commanding strong forces,
have not pacified them in time.
I wish for Gěng (熲) to transfer troops to the east to suppress them,
but am unsure if it is appropriate.
Please consider strategies and plans."
Gěng (熲) then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your subject humbly observes that although the Xiānlíng (先零) Eastern Qiāng (東羌) have frequently rebelled,
those who surrendered to Huángfǔ Guī (皇甫規)
already number some twenty thousand settlements.
The good and evil are already separated,
and the remaining bandits are few.
Zhāng Huàn (張奐) hesitates and does not advance for a long time
because he must be concerned about external separation and internal collusion,
and that the army's advance will surely alarm them.
Moreover, from winter to spring,
they have been gathered and not dispersed.
Their people and livestock are weary and emaciated.
This is a situation of self-destruction.
It would be better to simply recruit those who surrender
and defeat the strong enemy while sitting idle.
Your subject believes that these wolf-cubs have wild hearts
and are difficult to appease with kindness.
Although they submit when their power is exhausted,
they will stir again once the troops leave.
Only with long spears threatening their sides
and white blades at their necks will they be subdued.
It is estimated that the remaining Eastern tribes number over thirty thousand settlements.
They live close to the frontier,
and the roads have no dangerous defiles.
They do not have the strategic advantage of Yān (燕), Qí (齊), Qín (秦), and Zhào (趙) with their vertical and horizontal alliances,
yet they have long troubled Bìng (并) and Liáng (涼),
repeatedly invaded the Three Commanderies (三輔),
and Xīhé (西河) and Shàngjùn (上郡)
have already had their populations moved inward.
Āndìng (安定) and Běidì (北地) are again on the verge of being endangered.
From Yúnzhōng (雲中) and Wǔyuán (五原)
west to Hànyáng (漢陽), a distance of over two thousand *lǐ* (里),
the Xiōngnú (匈奴) and various Qiāng (羌) tribes
share their lands.
This is like a festering ulcer,
lodged beneath the ribs.
If it is not exterminated,
it will grow and spread.
If we now use five thousand cavalry,
ten thousand infantry,
and three thousand chariots,
in three winters and two summers,
it will be sufficient to break and pacify them.
There is no need to worry about the expense, which would be five point four billion *qián* (錢).
If this is done,
then
the various Qiāng (羌) can be utterly destroyed,
the Xiōngnú (匈奴) will be long subdued,
and the internally relocated commanderies and counties
can return to their native lands.
Your subject humbly calculates that in the Yǒngchū (永初) period,
the various Qiāng (羌) rebelled
for fourteen years,
costing two hundred forty billion;
at the end of the Yǒnghé (永和) period,
it lasted for another seven years,
costing over eighty billion.
The expenditure was such,
yet they were not completely exterminated.
The remaining evils rise again,
causing harm at this time.
If we do not temporarily exhaust the people now,
there will be no lasting peace.
Your subject, though dull and weak,
humbly awaits your command."
The Emperor consented
and allowed everything as submitted.
In the spring of the first year of Jiànníng,
Gěng led more than ten thousand troops,
carrying fifteen days' rations,
straight from Péngyáng to Gāopíng,
and fought various Xiānlíng tribes at Féngyìshān.
The barbarian army was strong,
and Gěng's troops were afraid.
Gěng then ordered his army to display sharp arrowheads and blades,
long spears in three rows,
flanked by strong crossbows,
and light cavalry arrayed as left and right wings.
Tears streaming, he angrily addressed his officers and soldiers:
"Now we are thousands of *lǐ* from home.
Advance and our task will be accomplished;
flee and we will surely all die.
Strive together for glory!"
He then let out a great shout,
and all the troops responded by charging forward.
Gěng galloped on horseback alongside them,
attacking them suddenly.
The barbarian host was utterly routed,
more than eight thousand heads were cut off,
and two hundred and eighty thousand head of cattle, horses, and sheep were captured.
At that time, Empress Dowager Dòu was regent,
and issued an edict saying:
"The Xiānlíng Dōngqiāng have been a menace for years.
Gěng previously presented a memorial,
desiring to utterly annihilate them.
He traversed frost and snow,
marched day and night,
personally endured arrows and stones,
and inspired his officers and soldiers.
Before even ten days had passed,
the fierce rabble was routed and broken,
with piles of bodies and countless captives,
and immeasurable plunder.
He has wiped away a century of arrears,
and comforted the spirits of loyal generals.
His merits are outstanding,
and We greatly commend him.
When the Dōngqiāng are completely pacified,
all merits and diligence will be recorded together.
For now, We bestow upon Gěng two hundred thousand cash,
and appoint one person from his household as Lángzhōng."
An imperial order was given to the Central Treasury to allocate gold, cash, and colored silks,
to augment military expenses.
Gěng was appointed Qiāng Jiāngjūn.
In summer,
Gěng again pursued the Qiāng out of Qiáomén,
reaching the upper reaches of Zǒumǎshuǐ.
Soon he heard that the barbarians were in Shēyánzé,
so he led light troops, marching continuously,
over two hundred *lǐ* in one day and one night,
and attacked and defeated the bandits at dawn.
The remaining barbarians fled towards Luòchuān,
and again gathered their forces.
Gěng then dispatched Cavalry Sīmǎ Tián Yàn with five thousand men to emerge from their east,
and acting Sīmǎ Xià Yù with two thousand men to circle to their west.
The Qiāng divided six or seven thousand men to attack and besiege Yàn and his troops.
Yàn and his troops fought them,
and the Qiāng scattered and fled.
Gěng advanced rapidly,
and together with Yàn and his troops pursued them to the upper reaches of Língxiānshuǐ.
Gěng's soldiers were hungry and thirsty,
so he ordered his troops to push forward and seize the water,
and the barbarians again scattered and fled.
Gěng then kept close to them,
fighting and advancing,
reaching Língwǔgǔ.
Gěng then donned his armor and was the first to ascend,
and no soldier dared to lag behind.
The Qiāng were then utterly defeated,
throwing away their weapons and fleeing.
He pursued them for three days and three nights,
until all the soldiers had severely calloused feet.
Upon reaching Jīngyáng,
the remaining four thousand barbarian settlements
all scattered and entered the mountains and valleys of Hànyáng.
At that time, Zhāng Huàn submitted a memorial stating:
"Although the Dōngqiāng have been defeated,
it is difficult to eliminate all the remaining tribes.
Gěng is impulsive and reckless,
and I fear he cannot always avoid defeat.
It would be advisable to pacify them with benevolence for now,
so as to avoid future regret."
An imperial edict was sent to Gěng.
Gěng again submitted a memorial, stating:
"I have always known that although the Dōngqiāng are numerous,
they are weak and easily controlled,
which is why I repeatedly presented my humble thoughts,
and devised a plan for eternal peace.
However, Zhōnglángjiàng Zhāng Huàn
claimed that the barbarians were strong and difficult to defeat,
and that it was advisable to use conciliation.
The sagely court, with its clear discernment,
believed and accepted my blind words,
thus my plan was put into action,
and Huàn's scheme was not used.
The situation was contradictory,
and so he harbored suspicion and resentment.
He believed the accusations of the rebellious Qiāng,
embellished his words,
saying that my troops had repeatedly suffered setbacks,
and also said that the Qiāng were all born of the same breath,
and could not be utterly exterminated,
that the mountains and valleys were vast,
and could not be emptied,
and that blood flowing and defiling the fields
would harm harmony and bring disaster.
I humbly reflect that in the time of Zhōu and Qín,
the Róng and Dí were a menace,
and since the restoration,
the Qiāng bandits have been most prevalent.
If not utterly exterminated,
even if they surrendered, they would rebel again.
Now the mixed tribes of Xiānlíng
have repeatedly turned rebellious,
attacking and capturing counties and towns,
plundering people and goods,
digging up graves and exposing corpses,
bringing calamity upon both the living and the dead.
Heaven is greatly enraged,
and lends its hand to execute judgment.
In the past, when Xíng was without the Way,
the state of Wèi attacked it,
and when the army was launched, it rained.
I mobilized troops in summer,
and repeatedly received timely sweet rain,
the year was bountiful,
and no one suffered disease.
Looking up, it indicates Heaven's will,
not disaster or harm;
looking down, it examines human affairs,
the multitude is harmonious, and the army is victorious.
From Qiáomén westward,
and Luòchuān eastward,
the former official counties and towns
are connected to each other,
not deep, perilous, or inaccessible regions.
Chariots and cavalry can travel safely,
there should be no setbacks.
Now, Huàn, as a Han official,
holding a military post,
stationed troops for two years,
could not pacify the bandits,
yet idly seeks to cultivate letters and sheathe weapons,
and invite fierce enemies to surrender.
His grandiloquent empty words
are presumptuous and without evidence.
Why do I say this?
In the past, when Xiānlíng caused trouble,
Zhào Chōngguó moved them to live inland;
when Jiāndāng brought chaos to the border,
Mǎ Yuán relocated them to Sānfǔ.
They initially submitted but eventually rebelled,
and remain a thorn to this day.
〔一０〕Therefore, men of foresight
considered it a deep concern.
Now the households in the surrounding commanderies are few,
and have been repeatedly harmed and poisoned by the Qiāng,
yet he desires to let the surrendered barbarians live mixed among them.
This is like planting thorny brambles in fertile fields,
or raising vipers in one's house.
Therefore, I, your servant, wielding the might of the Great Hàn,
establish a long-term strategy,
desiring to sever their roots,
and prevent them from regenerating.
〔一一〕The original plan estimated three years of expenditure,
using fifty-four *yì*,
but now only one year has passed,
and less than half has been consumed,
while the remaining bandits and embers
are approaching annihilation.
〔一二〕I, your servant, constantly obey imperial edicts,
the army is not to be managed internally.
〔一三〕I wish to uphold these words,
and let me handle this alone.
I will assess the situation as appropriate,
and not miss any expedient opportunities."
In the second year,
an imperial edict ordered the court attendant Féng Chán to persuade the scattered Qiāng in Hànyáng to surrender.
Duan Jiǒng believed that it was spring planting season,
and the common people were spread across the fields.
Although the Qiāng had temporarily surrendered,
the government had no provisions,
and they would certainly become bandits again.
It would be better to take advantage of their weakness and dispatch troops;
they would certainly be annihilated.
In summer,
Jiǒng personally advanced his camp,
about forty or fifty *lǐ* from Fántíng Mountain, where the Qiāng were encamped.
He sent Tián Yàn and Xià Yù with five thousand men to occupy the mountain.
The Qiāng attacked them with all their forces,
and shouted loudly, asking:
"Are Tián Yàn and Xià Yù here?
Where are all the Yi-Cong Qiāng from Huángzhōng?
Today we wish to decide life and death!"
The army was afraid,
but Yàn and others encouraged the soldiers,
and they fought a desperate battle,
and subsequently defeated them.
The Qiāng forces disintegrated
and fled east,
regrouping in Shèhǔ Valley.
They divided their troops to guard the upper and lower gates of the various valleys.
Jiǒng planned to annihilate them in one swift action,
not wishing to let them scatter and flee again.
He then sent a thousand men to Xīxiàn to build a wooden palisade,
twenty *bù* wide
and forty *lǐ* long,
to block them.
He separately dispatched Yàn, Yù, and others with seven thousand men
to secretly ascend Xīshān at night,
to build a camp and dig trenches,
about one *lǐ* from the barbarians.
He also sent Sīmǎ Zhāng Kǎi and others with three thousand men to ascend Dōngshān.
The barbarians then discovered this
and attacked Yàn and the others,
dividing their forces to cut off the water supply route.
Jiǒng personally led infantry and cavalry to attack by the water.
The Qiāng retreated,
and he then, with Kǎi and others, clamped them between the east and west mountains,
unleashed his troops, and defeated them.
The Qiāng were again routed and scattered.
Jiǒng pursued them into the deep mountains and valleys, all the way to the upper and lower gates of the valley,
defeating them everywhere.
He decapitated their leaders and subordinates, totaling nineteen thousand heads.
He captured an incalculable number of cattle, horses, donkeys, mules, felt cloaks, tents, and other items.
The four thousand people persuaded to surrender by Féng Chán and others
were distributed among the three commanderies of Āndìng, Hànyáng, and Lǒngxī.
Thus, the Eastern Qiāng were completely pacified.
In total, there were one hundred and eighty battles,
thirty-eight thousand six hundred and odd heads were taken,
and four hundred and twenty-seven thousand five hundred and odd cattle, horses, sheep, mules, donkeys, and camels were captured.
The expenditure was forty-four hundred million (4.4 billion),
and over four hundred soldiers died.
He was again enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīnfēng County,
with ten thousand households.
Jiǒng was benevolent in his military campaigns;
for sick soldiers,
he personally visited them
and dressed their wounds with his own hands.
He was on the border for over ten years,
never sleeping on a mat for a single day.
He shared the hardships with his officers and men,
which is why they were all willing to fight to the death.
In the spring of the third year,
he was summoned back to the capital,
leading over fifty thousand Qin-Hú infantry and cavalry,
as well as thousand-li "blood-sweating" horses,
and over ten thousand captives.
An imperial edict sent the Grand Minister of Ceremonies with a *jié* to comfort and reward him at Gǎo.
Upon the army's arrival,
he was appointed Sīzhōng.
He was then transferred to Zhíjīn Wú and Hénán Yǐn.
When there was a theft at the tomb of Consort Féng,
he was demoted to Jiànyì Dàfū,
and later promoted twice to Sīlì Xiàowèi.
Jiǒng bowed to the eunuchs' will,
thus preserving his wealth and status.
He then allied with the palace attendant Wáng Fǔ,
wrongfully executing palace attendants Zhèng Sà, Dǒng Téng, and others,
and was granted an additional four thousand households,
making a total of fourteen thousand households.
The following year,
he replaced Lǐ Xián as Tàiwèi,
but fell ill and was dismissed that winter.
He returned to Sīlì Xiàowèi.
After several years,
he was transferred to Yǐngchuān Grand Administrator,
then summoned and appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū.
In the second year of Guānghé,
he again replaced Qiáo Xuán as Tàiwèi.
After holding the position for just over a month,
he impeached himself due to a solar eclipse.
The relevant authorities presented his case,
and an imperial edict ordered the collection of his seals and ribbons,
and he was brought before the Tíngwèi.
At that time, Sīlì Xiàowèi Yáng Qiú impeached and executed Wáng Fǔ,
and also implicated Jiǒng.
He was interrogated in prison
and subsequently drank poison and died.
His family was exiled to the frontier.
Later, the palace attendant Lǚ Qiáng submitted a memorial,
posthumously arguing for Jiǒng's achievements.
Emperor Líng then decreed that Jiǒng's wife and children should return to their native commandery.
Initially,
Jiǒng, along with Huángfǔ Wēimíng and Zhāng Ránmíng,
were all renowned and distinguished,
and were known in the capital as
"The Three Míng of Liángzhōu."
The eulogy states: Shānxī has many fierce ones,
"The Three Míng"
followed in their footsteps.
Barbarian cavalry entangled,
dust stirred the Hé and Tóng.
Guī and Huàn judiciously strategized,
swiftly curbing the violent and fierce.
Scholars and military men shared ambitions,
accommodating each other.
Duàn pursued the two Dí,
tying horses and suspending blades.
In chaos and assault,
the valleys quieted, the mountains emptied.
Biography of Chén Wáng, Chapter 56
Chén Fán, courtesy name Zhòngjǔ,
was a native of Píngyú, Rǔnán.
His grandfather was the Grand Administrator of Hédōng.
When Fán was fifteen,
he once stayed alone in a room,
while his courtyard was overgrown and dirty.
His father's friend, Xuē Qín from the same commandery, came to visit him
and said to Fán:
"Young man, why do you not sweep and clean to await guests?"
Fán replied:
"A true man living in the world
should sweep away all evil under Heaven;
what's the point of just one room?"
Qín knew he had an ambition to purify the world
and greatly admired him.
He first served in the commandery,
was nominated as Xiàolián,
and appointed Lángzhōng.
He suffered his mother's death
and resigned from office to observe mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
the inspector Zhōu Jǐng invited him as Biéjià Cóngshì,
but he left after disagreeing through remonstrance.
Later, he was invited by the public administration to be nominated as Fāngzhèng,
but he declined all offers.
Tàiwèi Lǐ Gù recommended him,
and he was summoned and appointed Yìláng,
then twice promoted to Lè'ān Grand Administrator.
At that time, Lǐ Yīng was the Inspector of Qīngzhōu,
known for his authoritative governance.
All subordinate counties, hearing of his reputation,
withdrew themselves,
but Fán alone remained due to his clean administration.
A man from the commandery, Zhōu Qiú,
was a noble and pure scholar.
Previous commandery administrators had invited him, but he never accepted,
only Fán was able to attract him.
He addressed him by his courtesy name rather than his personal name,
and specially prepared a couch for him;
when he left, it was hung up.
Qiú's courtesy name was Mèngyù,
a native of Línjì,
with a good reputation.
There was a commoner, Zhào Xuān, who, after burying his parents,
did not close the burial tunnel,
but lived inside it,
observing mourning for over twenty years.
The local community praised his filial piety,
and the province and commandery repeatedly invited him with ceremonies.
The commandery recommended him to Fán.
Fán met with him
and asked about his wife and children.
It turned out Xuān's five sons were all born during the mourning period.
Fán was greatly enraged and said:
"The sages established rites,
the virtuous humble themselves to observe them,
the unworthy strive to reach them.
Moreover, sacrifices should not be too frequent,
because they easily become defiled.
How much more so to sleep and reside in a tomb,
and give birth there,
deceiving the times and misleading the masses,
and defiling ghosts and spirits?"
Thereupon, he had him punished for his crime.
Grand General Liáng Jì (梁冀) wielded power that awed the whole empire.
At that time, he frequently sent letters to Fān (蕃),
requesting favors.
Fān (蕃) would not grant them.
Once, an envoy pretended to seek an audience,
enraging Fān (蕃),
who had him flogged to death.
As a consequence, he was demoted to Commandant of Xiūwǔ (脩武令).
Gradually, he was promoted
and appointed Shàngshū (尚書).
At that time, mountain bandits in Línglíng (零陵) and Guìyáng (桂陽) were causing harm.
The ducal ministers discussed sending an expedition to suppress them.
An imperial edict was also issued to the provinces and commanderies,
allowing all of them to recommend Xiàolián (孝廉) and Màocái (茂才).
Fān (蕃) submitted a memorial refuting this, saying:
“In ancient times, when Gāozǔ (高祖) founded the empire,
all regions rested from their burdens,
and he nurtured the common people
as if they were his own infants.
Now, the people of these two commanderies
are also Your Majesty’s infants.
To allow these infants to cause harm,
is it not because the local officials are greedy and tyrannical,
causing them to be so?
It is fitting to strictly instruct the Three Ducal Offices
to secretly investigate the regional governors, administrators, and commandants.
If any among them govern in discord
and oppress the common people,
they should be immediately impeached.
Instead, select honest and virtuous people who are devoted to public service,
and who can proclaim laws and show compassion and benevolence.
Then, there will be no need for the imperial army,
and the bandits will be suppressed.
Furthermore, there are over two thousand junior officials in the Three Bureaus,
and the number of subordinate officials in the Three Ducal Offices exceeds the limit and has not been reduced.
One should simply choose the good and appoint them,
and dismiss the bad.
Why bother with a blanket edict
to widen the path of requests and favoritism!”
Because of this, he offended those around the emperor,
and was therefore sent out to be the Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng (豫章).
He was naturally upright and strict,
and did not entertain guests.
Scholars and common people alike feared his lofty character.
When he was summoned to be Shàngshūlìng (尚書令),
those who sent him off did not go beyond the city gate.
He was promoted to Dàhónglú (大鴻臚).
At that time, Lǐ Yún (李雲), the Commandant of Báimǎ (白馬), presented a memorial of remonstrance,
enraging Emperor Huán (桓帝),
who ordered him to be executed.
Fān (蕃) submitted a memorial to save Yún (雲),
and was consequently dismissed and returned to his hometown.
He was again summoned and appointed Yìláng (議郎),
and after several days, promoted to Guānglùxūn (光祿勳).
At that time, rewards and honors exceeded regulations,
and the imperial consorts and favorites were excessively numerous.
Fān (蕃) then submitted a memorial of remonstrance, saying:
“Your servant has heard that those who serve the ancestral altars and land
do so for the ancestral altars and land;
those who serve the monarch
do so for favor and pleasure.
Now, your servant has received grace from the sagely court,
and holds a position among the Nine Ministers.
If I see wrongdoing and do not remonstrate,
then I am seeking favor and pleasure.
The feudal lords above symbolize the four constellations and the twenty-eight mansions,
shining brightly in the heavens,
and below correspond to partitioned territories,
serving as screens for the imperial court.
Gāozǔ (高祖) decreed that no one without meritorious service should be enfeoffed as a marquis.
Yet, I hear of pursuing and recording the minor merits of Dèng Wànshì's (鄧萬世) father, Zūn (遵), the Administrator of Hénán (河南尹),
and re-enfeoffing the ancestors of Huáng Jùn (黃儁), the Shàngshūlìng (尚書令), with a title that had been abolished.
Close retainers are granted fiefs unjustly,
and imperial attendants receive rewards without merit.
Appointments are made without considering suitability,
and territories are granted without recording their achievements.
It has reached a point where within a single family,
there are several marquises.
Thus, the celestial phenomena lose their order,
and Yin and Yang fall out of sequence,
crops fail to grow,
and the people are not at peace.
Your servant knows that the enfeoffments have already been carried out,
and speaking of them now is too late.
I sincerely wish Your Majesty would stop from this point forward.
Furthermore, in recent years, harvests
have been diminished by five or six tenths.
Tens of thousands of people are hungry and cold,
unable to make a living.
Yet, there are thousands of palace women,
eating meat and wearing fine silk,
their cosmetics
beyond measure.
A vulgar proverb says,
‘Bandits do not pass through the gates of a family with five daughters,’
meaning daughters impoverish a family.
How then can the women in the imperial harem
not impoverish the nation?
Thus, when the entire palace was married off, the empire was transformed;
when the women of Chǔ (楚) grieved, the western palace suffered disaster.
Moreover, gathering them without intimacy
will inevitably lead to feelings of sorrow and grief,
and cause misfortunes of flood and drought.
Prisons are for prohibiting evil and transgressions;
offices are for assigning talent to manage affairs.
If the law is unfair,
and officials are ill-chosen,
then the Way of the King is flawed.
Yet, the consensus of opinion throughout the empire
is that imprisonments arise from grievances,
and ranks are achieved through bribery.
If there were no foul smell,
then flies would not swarm.
Your Majesty should seek out successes and failures,
and choose to follow loyalty and goodness.
Delegate the selection of officials
to the Shàngshū (尚書) and the Three Ducal Offices,
so that praise, blame, punishment, and reward
each have their proper recipients.
Would this not be truly fortunate!”
The emperor somewhat accepted his words,
and released over five hundred palace women.
However, Jùn (儁) was only granted the title of Guānnèihóu (關內侯),
while Wànshì (萬世) received Nánxiānghóu (南鄉侯).
In the sixth year of Yánxī (延熹)
the imperial carriage went to Guǎngchéng (廣成) for a hunt.
Fān (蕃) submitted a memorial of remonstrance, saying:
“Your servant has heard that when a monarch engages in activities in the imperial parks,
it is only in the western suburbs during mid-autumn,
following the season to practice military skills,
and killing game for sacrifices
to demonstrate filial piety and reverence.
If one deviates from this,
it is considered unrestrained indulgence.
Thus, Gāotáo (皐陶) warned Shùn (舜), ‘Do not teach extravagant leisure,’
and Duke of Zhōu (周公) warned King Chéng (成王), ‘Do not indulge in hunting.’
Even Yú Shùn (虞舜) and King Chéng (成王) had these warnings;
how much more so for one whose virtue does not equal these two rulers!
During times of peace and stability,
one should still exercise moderation,
let alone in the present age,
which faces the calamity of the ‘three empties’!
The fields are empty,
the court is empty,
and the granaries are empty.
These are called the ‘three empties.’
Moreover, military conflicts have not ceased,
and the four directions are scattered.
This is the time for Your Majesty to be anxious and worn out,
sitting up until dawn.
How can it be appropriate to unfurl banners and display military might,
indulging in the spectacle of carriages and horses!
Furthermore, last autumn
had abundant rain, and the people had just planted wheat.
Now, they miss the time for encouraging planting,
and instead are forced into tasks of driving game and clearing roads.
This is not the intent of a wise and sagely ruler who cares for the people.
Qí Jǐnggōng (齊景公) wished to view the sea,
and went to Lángyá (琅邪).
Yànzǐ (晏子) explained to him how the common people hated to hear the sound of banners, carriages, and horses,
and how they would frown and raise their brows in discontent.
Jǐnggōng (景公) therefore did not proceed.
When King Mù (穆) of Zhōu (周) desired to extend the tracks of his carriages and horses,
Jìgōng Mófù (祭公謀父) recited the poem of Qízhāo (祈招) to him,
to stop his inclination.
Truly, they abhorred the harm of extravagant leisure.”
The memorial was submitted but not accepted.
From the time Fān (蕃) became Guānglùxūn (光祿勳),
he shared the responsibility of official selection with Huáng Wǎn (黃琬), the Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng (五官中郎將).
They did not favor the powerful and wealthy,
and were therefore slandered by the attendants of powerful families,
and consequently dismissed and returned home.
Soon after,
he was summoned to be Shàng Púyè (尚僕射),
then transferred to Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫).
In the eighth year,
he succeeded Yáng Bǐng (楊秉) as Tàiwèi (太尉).
Fān (蕃) declined, saying:
“ ‘Without error or forgetfulness,
following the old statutes,’
your servant is not as good as Hú Guǎng (胡廣), the Tàicháng (太常).
‘To regulate the seven administrations and instruct in the five virtues,’
your servant is not as good as Wáng Chàng (王暢), the Yìláng (議郎).
‘Intelligent and perceptive,
with both civil and military talents,’
your servant is not as good as Lǐ Yīng (李膺), the Shǔ Xíngtú (薥刑徒).”
The emperor did not permit it.
The Regular Palace Attendants Sū Kāng (蘇康) and Guǎn Bà (管霸) were again appointed to positions,
and thereupon they began to frame loyal and good officials,
flattering each other.
The Grand Minister of Agriculture, Liú Yòu (劉祐), the Court Commandant, Féng Gǔn (馮緄),
and the Administrator of Hénán (河南), Lǐ Yīng (李膺),
all incurred displeasure,
and were condemned by them.
Fān (蕃), during a court assembly,
resolutely argued on behalf of Yīng (膺) and others,
requesting that they be pardoned and reinstated,
and promoted to official positions.
His words were earnest and repeated,
sincere and heartfelt.
The Emperor did not listen,
and rose in tears.
At this time, the Minor Palace Attendant Zhào Jīn (趙津) and the great scoundrel Zhāng Fàn (張氾) from Nányáng (南陽),
served the eunuchs,
and, emboldened by their influence, violated the law.
Liú Lí (劉𬘩), the Administrator of Tàiyuán (太原), and Chéng Xiāo (成瑨), the Administrator of Nányáng (南陽), investigated their crimes,
and despite an imperial amnesty,
they both ultimately investigated and executed them.
The eunuchs harbored resentment and anger,
and the relevant authorities, following imperial instructions,
thereupon memorialized that Lí (𬘩) and Xiāo (瑨) deserved to be executed in the marketplace.
Furthermore, Zhái Chāo (翟超), the Administrator of Shānyáng (山陽),
confiscated the property of the Regular Palace Attendant Hóu Lǎn (侯覽);
Huáng Fú (黃浮), the Chancellor of Dōnghǎi (東海),
executed Xú Xuān (徐宣), the Prefect of Xiàpī (下邳).
Chāo (超) and Fú (浮) were both sentenced to have their heads shaved and wear iron collars,
and transported to labor in the Zuǒxiào (左校).
Fān (蕃), along with the Minister of Works, Liú Jǔ (劉矩), and the Grand Commandant, Liú Mào (劉茂), jointly pleaded for Lí (𬘩), Xiāo (瑨), Chāo (超), Fú (浮), and others.
The Emperor was displeased.
The relevant authorities impeached them,
and Jǔ (矩) and Mào (茂) dared not speak again.
Fān (蕃) then alone submitted a memorial, saying:
"I have heard that Duke Huán (桓) of Qí (齊), in establishing his hegemony,
focused on internal governance;
and in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* concerning Lǔ (魯),
even small transgressions were recorded.
It is appropriate to first rectify oneself,
and then extend it to others.
Now, bandits are outside,
a sickness of the four limbs;
internal governance is not in order,
a disease of the heart and belly.
I cannot sleep,
nor eat my fill,
truly worried that those around Your Majesty grow closer each day,
while loyal words become estranged,
internal troubles accumulate,
and external difficulties deepen.
Your Majesty, you rose from among the marquises,
inheriting the celestial throne.
Even a small family with a million cash in assets,
its descendants would still be ashamed to lose their ancestral estate,
how much more so when one possesses the whole world,
having received it from the former emperor,
and yet wishes to be lax and neglectful?
If you truly do not care for yourself,
should you not at least recall the hardships with which the former emperor acquired it?
Previously, the five clans of the Liáng (梁) family
poisoned the entire realm;
Heaven enlightened Your Majesty's sagely mind,
and you seized and executed them.
The world's opinion
hoped that peace would follow.
The lesson is not far off;
the overturned carriage is as if it happened yesterday,
yet the power of the close attendants
again incites and forms factions.
The Minor Palace Attendant Zhào Jīn (趙津) and the great scoundrel Zhāng Fàn (張氾) and others
indulge in greed and tyranny,
flattering those around Your Majesty.
The former Administrator of Tàiyuán (太原), Liú Lí (劉𬘩), and the Administrator of Nányáng (南陽), Chéng Xiāo (成瑨),
investigated and executed them.
Although it is said that they should not have been executed after an amnesty,
considering their sincere intentions,
it was to remove evil.
As for Your Majesty,
what exactly causes your indignation?
Yet petty individuals prevail,
confusing the sagely hearing,
thus causing celestial wrath to be aroused because of them.
To inflict punishment already
would have been excessive,
how much more so to apply a heavy penalty, ordering them to face the executioner's blade!
Furthermore, the former Administrator of Shānyáng (山陽), Zhái Chāo (翟超), and the Chancellor of Dōnghǎi (東海), Huáng Fú (黃浮),
upheld public duty without bending,
hating evil as an enemy.
Chāo (超) confiscated Hóu Lǎn's (侯覽) property,
and Fú (浮) executed Xú Xuān (徐宣) for his crimes.
Both suffered criminal sentences
and did not receive pardon.
Lǎn's (覽) reckless behavior meant that the confiscation of his wealth was already fortunate;
Xuān (宣) committed offenses and transgressions,
and his death was more than deserved.
In the past, Chancellor Shēntú Jiā (申屠嘉) summoned and reprimanded Dèng Tōng (鄧通),
and the Prefect of Luòyáng (洛陽), Dǒng Xuān (董宣), humiliated a princess,
yet Emperor Wén (文) granted him an audience and offered apologies,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武) bestowed heavy rewards.
We have never heard of these two officials being executed for exceeding their authority.
But now, the group of petty men around Your Majesty,
fearing harm to their faction,
falsely accuse each other,
leading to these punishments.
Hearing these words from your minister,
they will surely complain again.
Your Majesty should deeply consider cutting off the source of close attendants participating in government affairs,
and bring in the matters of the Grand Secretariat and the court,
allowing the Grandees and high officials
to hold court once every five days,
selecting the pure and upright,
and dismissing the sycophantic and wicked.
If this is done, Heaven will be harmonious above,
Earth will be peaceful below,
and auspicious omens and portents
will not be far away!
Although Your Majesty may detest your minister's words,
any ruler must exert himself.
I dare to present this even if it means death."
The Emperor grew even angrier upon receiving the memorial
and ultimately accepted none of it.
Among the court and the common people, none did not resent this.
The eunuchs, from this time, hated Fān (蕃) even more intensely,
and any appointments or memorials he presented
were immediately rejected with imperial edicts.
Many, from his Chief Clerk downwards, were even condemned to punishment.
However, because Fān (蕃) was a renowned minister,
they dared not harm him directly.
Lí (𬘩), whose courtesy name was Wénlǐ (文理),
was from Gāotáng (高唐).
Xiāo (瑨), whose courtesy name was Yòupíng (幼平),
was from Shǎn (陝).
Both were celebrated for their scholarship,
and in their positions, they dared to speak frankly,
engaging in many disputes,
and were well-known at the time.
Both died in prison.
In the ninth year,
Lǐ Yīng and others were imprisoned and interrogated for their involvement in the "Partisan Prohibitions."
Chén Fán thereupon submitted a strongly worded memorial, saying:
“I have heard that enlightened rulers
entrust their hearts to their assistants;
while rulers of doomed states
are loath to hear direct criticism.
Thus, though Tāng and Wǔ were sages,
they rose to power with the help of Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng;
while Jié and Zhòu were deluded,
and perished through losing worthy men.
From this, it can be said that
the ruler is the head,
and the ministers are the limbs,
mutually dependent as one body,
together creating good or ill.
I humbly observe that former Colonel Director of Retainers Lǐ Yīng, Grand Coachman Dù Mì, and Grand Commandant’s Clerk Fàn Pāng, among others,
maintained their integrity without blemish,
and were utterly devoted to the state.
Because their loyalty went against Your Majesty's will,
they were unjustly subjected to interrogation and investigation,
some confined and isolated,
others dying or being exiled to inappropriate places.
To block the mouths of all under Heaven,
and to deafen and blind the people of an entire generation,
how is this different
from Qín’s burning of books and burying of scholars alive?
In the past, when King Wǔ conquered Yīn,
he honored the virtuous and sealed the tombs;
now Your Majesty governs,
and first executes loyal and worthy individuals.
Why are good people treated so harshly?
Why are bad people treated so favorably?
Indeed, slander appears to be factual,
and artful words are like a reed pipe’s sounds,
making those who listen confused,
and those who see them bewildered.
The manifestation of fortune or misfortune
depends on discerning goodness;
the turning point of success or failure
lies in evaluating words.
The ruler of men
governs the affairs of Heaven and Earth,
holds the reins of the four seas;
his actions cannot deviate from sacred laws,
his advances and retreats cannot depart from the rules of the Way.
When erroneous words escape his mouth,
chaos reaches the eight directions;
how much more so when innocent people are shaved and imprisoned,
and the blameless are executed in the marketplace!
In ancient times, when Yǔ was inspecting the southern regions of Cāngwú,
he saw someone being executed in the marketplace,
alighted from his carriage, and wept, saying: ‘If the myriad regions have sins,
the fault lies with me alone!’
Thus, his rise was vigorous.
Moreover, Qīngzhōu and Xúzhōu are suffering from severe drought,
the five grains are damaged,
the people are migrating and displaced,
and even eating wild beans is insufficient.
Yet palace women accumulate in the inner chambers,
state expenses are squandered on fine silks,
and imperial relatives and private households
are greedy for wealth and accept bribes.
This is what is called ‘salary leaving the public office,
and governance residing with the grandees.’
In the past, at the end of the Spring and Autumn period,
the virtue of Zhōu waned;
for several decades, there were no calamities or misfortunes,
because Heaven was [protecting] them.
Heaven's concern for Hàn
is unendingly profound
[一０], hence it diligently manifests portents
to awaken Your Majesty.
Eliminating omens of disaster and removing calamities
truly lies in cultivating virtue.
As your minister, I hold a position among the Three Excellencies,
with deep anxieties and heavy responsibilities;
I dare not merely enjoy my salary and cherish my life,
sitting idly by and watching success or failure unfold.
If I am honored with your acceptance,
even if my body were to be torn apart,
my head and limbs exiting through different gates,
I would have no regrets.”
[一一]The Emperor found his words too sharp,
and used the pretext that Chén Fán had improperly appointed his subordinates
to dismiss him from office.
In the first year of Yǒngkāng,
the Emperor passed away.
Empress Dòu assumed regency,
and issued an edict saying:
“Indeed, the people establish a ruler
to shepherd them;
he must have worthy assistants
to solidify the royal enterprise.
Former Grand Commandant Chén Fán
is loyal, pure, direct, and brilliant.
Therefore, let Chén Fán be appointed Grand Tutor,
and supervise the affairs of the Imperial Secretariat.”
At this time, the state had just suffered a great loss,
and the heir to the throne had not yet been established.
The Imperial Secretaries, fearing the powerful official,
feigned illness and did not attend court.
Chén Fán reprimanded them in a letter, saying:
“The ancients established their integrity,
serving the deceased as if they were alive.
Now the imperial succession is not yet settled,
and state affairs worsen daily;
how can you gentlemen abandon the bitterness of hardship,
and rest idly in your beds?
This is not righteous,
how can it be benevolent!”
The Imperial Secretaries were terrified,
and all rose to attend to their duties.
When Emperor Líng ascended the throne,
Empress Dowager Dòu again issued a gracious edict to Chén Fán, saying:
“Indeed, praising merit encourages goodness,
and highlighting righteousness inspires customs.
No virtue goes unrewarded;
this is praised in the Great Odes.
Grand Tutor Chén Fán
assisted the late emperor,
serving inside and outside the court for many years.
His virtues of loyalty and filial piety
surpass those of the present court;
his integrity in direct remonstrance
grows ever stronger with his white hair.
Now, Chén Fán is enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāoyáng Township,
with an estate of three hundred households.”
Chén Fán submitted a memorial declining, saying:
“The envoy arrived at my humble dwelling,
and presented the seal and ribbon of Marquis of Gāoyáng Township.
My heart is truly grieved,
and I do not know how to handle this.
I have heard that yielding
is the adornment of a person,
and the manifestation of virtue,
yet I dare not falsely claim this as my renown.
I humbly consider that grants of land and enfeoffment
are for meritorious deeds.
I have reflected upon myself,
and in all my previous positions,
I have had no other extraordinary abilities;
whether it was appropriate or not, I received a salary.
Although I do not possess conduct of pure integrity,
I secretly admire the saying, ‘A noble person does not obtain it by improper means,
nor does he keep it.’
If I were to accept the title without yielding,
and hide my face to take it,
it would cause the August Heaven to be enraged,
and disaster to flow down upon the common people.
What refuge
would there be for my own person?
I merely consider that Your Majesty pities my old age,
and cautions me against taking what is not rightfully mine.”
Empress Dowager Dòu did not permit it,
and Chén Fán again firmly declined.
His memorials were submitted ten times in total,
and he ultimately did not accept the enfeoffment.
Initially,
Huán Dì wanted to establish the favored Lady Tián as empress.
Chén Fán, on account of the Tián clan's humble origins
and the Dòu clan being a good family,
contended very strongly for the latter.
The Emperor, having no other choice,
then established Empress Dòu.
When the Empress assumed regency,
she entrusted affairs to Chén Fán.
Chén Fán and the Empress's father, Grand General Dòu Wǔ,
were united in heart and devoted their full strength,
recruiting and employing famous worthies,
jointly participating in governance.
The scholars of the realm
all craned their necks, longing for an era of great peace.
However, the Emperor's wet nurse, Zhào Ráo,
was constantly by the Empress Dowager's side.
The Central Regular Attendants Cáo Jié, Wáng Fǔ, and others colluded with her,
flattering and serving the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager believed them,
and frequently issued imperial edicts,
bestowing seals and appointments,
such that their relatives
often indulged in greed and cruelty.
Chén Fán always detested this
and was determined to execute the eunuchs.
Coincidentally, Dòu Wǔ also had such a plan.
Chén Fán, considering that he had already earned popular support and the Empress Dowager's favor,
was convinced that his aspirations could be realized.
So he first submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that if words are not direct and actions are not upright,
then one deceives Heaven and betrays men.
If one speaks critically and expresses one's full thoughts,
then the numerous villains will cast sideways glances,
and disaster will strike without delay.
Between these two,
your servant would rather incur disaster
than dare to deceive Heaven.
Currently, the capital is in an uproar,
the roads are filled with clamor,
saying that Hóu Lǎn, Cáo Jié, Gōngchéng Xīn, Wáng Fǔ, Zhèng Bǐ, and others, along with Madam Zhào and the various imperial women, are together bringing chaos to the empire.
Those who follow them are promoted,
while those who oppose them are slandered and harmed.
At present, the court officials
are like wood ear fungi in a river,
drifting east and west,
greedy for salaries and fearing harm.
When Your Majesty first assumed power,
you executed criminals in accordance with Heaven's will,
and Sū Kāng and Guǎn Bà both suffered their due punishment.
At that time, Heaven and Earth were clear and bright,
and men and spirits rejoiced.
How can you, a few months later, again let those around you run rampant?
There are no greater primary evildoers and great villains than these.
If they are not immediately executed,
they will surely cause rebellion and chaos,
endangering the state.
Their calamity would be immeasurable.
I pray that my memorial be published and shown to those around you,
and also let all the villains in the realm know that your servant detests them."
The Empress Dowager did not accept it.
Those in court who heard of it were all terrified.
Chén Fán then plotted with Dòu Wǔ;
the details are in the biography of Dòu Wǔ.
When the plot was exposed,
Cáo Jié and others forged an imperial edict to execute Dòu Wǔ and his associates.
Chén Fán was over seventy years old at the time.
Hearing that the disaster had broken out,
he led his subordinates and eighty or so students,
all drawing their blades,
and charged into the Chéngmíng Gate,
bareing his arms and shouting,
"The Grand General is loyal in defending the state!
The eunuchs are rebellious!
How can you say the Dòu clan is immoral?"
Wáng Fǔ happened to come out
and encountered Chén Fán.
Upon hearing his words,
he rebuked Chén Fán, saying:
"The late Emperor has just passed away,
and his tomb is not yet completed.
What merit does Dòu Wǔ have
to have his brothers, father, and son,
three marquises from one family?
Furthermore, he took many palace women from the Yèting,
made music, and held banquets.
Within a few months,
his wealth amounted to hundreds of millions.
For a great minister to be like this,
is this what you call morality?
You are the pillar of the state,
yet you bend and collude with factions.
Where else would you seek traitors?"
Then he ordered Chén Fán's arrest.
Chén Fán drew his sword and shouted at Wáng Fǔ.
Wáng Fǔ's soldiers dared not approach.
So he added more men, surrounding Chén Fán dozens deep,
and then seized Chén Fán and sent him to the Yellow Gate Northern Prison.
The Yellow Gate attendants
trampled Chén Fán, saying,
"You old devil!
Can you still reduce our staff numbers
or deprive us of our allowances?"
He was killed that very day.
His family was exiled to Bǐjǐng.
His clan members, disciples, and former officials were all dismissed and barred from holding office.
Chén Fán's friend Zhū Zhèn of Chénliú,
who was then the magistrate of Zhì,
heard of it and resigned his post to mourn him.
He collected and buried Chén Fán's body
and hid his son, Yì, in the Gānlíng region.
When the matter was discovered, he was imprisoned,
and his entire family was shackled.
Zhū Zhèn endured torture,
swearing to die rather than speak,
thus Yì was spared.
Later, when the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out,
a general amnesty was granted to the partisans.
Yì was then recalled
and served as Grand Administrator of Lǔ.
Zhū Zhèn, whose courtesy name was Bóhòu,
initially served as a provincial attendant.
He impeached Shàn Kuāng, the Grand Administrator of Jìyīn, for corruption,
and also implicated Kuāng's brother, the Central Regular Attendant and General of Chariots and Cavalry, Chāo.
Huán Dì had Shàn Kuāng arrested and sent to the Court of Judicial Review,
thereby admonishing Chāo.
Chāo went to the prison to apologize.
The Three Excellencies had a saying:
"Carriages like chicken roosts, horses like dogs,
hating evil like the wind is Zhū Bóhòu."
Commentary: In the eras of Huán and Líng,
people like Chén Fán
were all able to establish a reputation and moral influence,
and argue against the benighted customs.
But they operated in a dangerous environment,
contending with criminal and corrupt men in the same court,
eventually meeting with disaster and destruction.
It was not that they could not keep their character pure
and avoid the defiling fog.
Pity that the scholars of the age considered distancing oneself from society as lofty,
and thus human relationships offered no mutual solace.
They considered retreating from the world as unrighteous,
thus they repeatedly retired but did not depart;
they took benevolence as their responsibility,
and though the path was distant, they grew more resolute.
When they encountered an opportune moment,
they collaborated with Dòu Wǔ,
believing it to be a once-in-a-myriad-ages opportunity.
How awe-inspiring were the endeavors of Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng!
Though their work did not reach completion,
their trustworthiness and integrity were sufficient to rally the people's hearts.
The Hàn dynasty was in chaos but did not perish
for over a hundred years,
thanks to the efforts of several such gentlemen.
Wáng Yǔn, whose courtesy name was Zǐshī,
was from Qí, Tàiyuán.
His family had served in various prefectures and commanderies for generations, holding high official positions.
Guō Línzōng, from the same commandery, once met Wáng Yǔn and was impressed by him,
saying:
"Master Wáng travels a thousand *lǐ* in a day;
he is a talent for assisting a king."
Then they established a friendship.
At nineteen,
he became a commandery official.
At that time, Jìn Yáng Zhào Jīn, a Little Yellow Gate, was corrupt and tyrannical,
a great menace to the entire county.
Wáng Yǔn hunted him down and killed him.
However, Zhào Jīn's brothers flattered the eunuchs
and used their connections to slander Wáng Yǔn.
Huán Dì was furious
and summoned the Grand Administrator Liú Yí,
who was subsequently imprisoned and died.
Wáng Yǔn escorted his funeral back to Píngyuán,
completing the three-year mourning period
before returning home.
He returned to official service.
There was a man from the commandery named Lù Fó,
who, though lacking a good reputation in his youth,
was summoned by the Grand Administrator Wáng Qiú to be appointed an official.
Wáng Yǔn firmly argued against this,
which angered Wáng Qiú,
who arrested Wáng Yǔn, intending to kill him.
Dèng Shèng, the Inspector, heard of it and swiftly dispatched an envoy to appoint Wáng Yǔn as an Assistant Administrator.
Wáng Yǔn became famous from this,
while Lù Fó was consequently dismissed.
Wáng Yǔn, from a young age, loved great principles,
and was ambitious to achieve meritorious deeds.
He constantly recited classics and commentaries,
and practiced riding and archery day and night.
The Three Ducal Ministers all summoned him,
and he was made Attendant Censor (shìyùshǐ) for his high standing with the Minister of Works (Sītú).
In the first year of the Zhōngpíng era (184 CE),
the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out,
and he was specially selected and appointed Inspector of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu cìshǐ).
He invited Xún Shuǎng and Kǒng Róng, among others, to be his subordinates (cóngshì),
and memorialized the throne to lift the proscription on the Partisan Faction.
He attacked the separate commanders of the Yellow Turbans,
greatly defeating them.
Along with the Left Colonel of the Household (Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng) Huángfǔ Sōng and the Right Colonel of the Household (Yòu Zhōnglángjiàng) Zhū Suì, he received the surrender of hundreds of thousands.
Among the rebels, he found letters and memorials from the guests and retainers of the Palace Regular Attendant (Zhōng Chángshì) Zhāng Ràng,
communicating with the Yellow Turbans.
Wáng Yǔn fully exposed their treachery,
reporting the details to the throne.
Emperor Líng was angered and rebuked Zhāng Ràng,
but Ràng kowtowed and offered apologies,
and ultimately could not be punished.
However, Zhāng Ràng harbored resentment and anger,
and used this matter to implicate Wáng Yǔn.
The following year,
Wáng Yǔn was consequently arrested and imprisoned.
Meeting with a general amnesty,
he was reinstated as Inspector.
Within ten days,
he was again arrested for another offense.
The Minister of Works (Sītú) Yáng Cì, knowing Wáng Yǔn's usual high character,
did not wish him to suffer further humiliation,
so he sent a retainer to express his sympathy, saying:
"You, because of the matter concerning Zhāng Ràng,
have been summoned twice within a month.
Evil and malevolence are hard to fathom;
it is best for you to make a deep plan."
Also, his subordinates (cóngshì) who were known for their resolute spirit,
all wept as they offered him a potion.
Wáng Yǔn sternly declared:
"As a subject,
having offended my lord,
I ought to suffer the great execution to apologize to the world.
How can I seek death by taking a potion of milk?"
He threw down the cup and rose,
going out to enter the caged cart.
Upon arriving at the Court of the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi),
