those around him all urged his case forward,
and no court official failed to sigh in sorrow.
The General-in-Chief (Dàjiāngjūn) Hé Jìn, the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Yuán Wěi, and the Minister of Works (Sītú) Yáng Cì jointly submitted a memorial pleading on his behalf, saying:
"If one looks inward and listens attentively,
loyal ministers will exhaust their sincerity;
if one is lenient towards the virtuous and sympathetic towards the capable,
righteous scholars will sharpen their principles.
This is why Emperor Xiàowén adopted Fēng Táng's counsel,
and Duke Dào of Jìn pardoned Wèi Jiàng's offense.
Wáng Yǔn received his commission through special selection,
punishing the rebellious and pacifying the obedient.
Not even a full month had passed,
and the provincial borders were cleared and peaceful.
We were just about to list his meritorious service
and request rewards,
yet he is to suffer great execution
for an impropriety in serving.
The fault is light, but the punishment is heavy,
which damages public expectation.
We, your ministers, holding the positions of prime ministers,
dare not remain silent.
We sincerely believe that Wáng Yǔn should be heard under the three槐 (guāi) trees,
to make manifest his loyal and steadfast heart."
When the memorial was presented,
he was allowed to have his sentence reduced from death.
In the winter of that year, there was a great amnesty,
but Wáng Yǔn alone was not pardoned.
The Three Ducal Ministers all spoke up for him again.
It was not until the following year
that he was finally released.
At this time, the eunuchs were tyrannical,
and one could be killed for merely incurring their displeasure.
Wáng Yǔn feared he would not escape,
so he changed his name and surname,
and moved secretly between Hénèi and Chénliú.
When the emperor died,
he rushed to the capital to mourn.
At that time, the General-in-Chief (Dàjiāngjūn) Hé Jìn wished to execute the eunuchs,
and summoned Wáng Yǔn to discuss the matter,
requesting him to serve as Attendant Colonel (cóngshì zhōngláng),
and later promoted him to Administrator of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn).
When Emperor Xiàndì ascended the throne,
he was appointed Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú),
and twice promoted to acting President of the Imperial Secretariat (shǒushàngshūlìng).
In the first year of the Chūpíng era (190 CE),
he replaced Yáng Biāo as Minister of Works (Sītú),
retaining his position as President of the Imperial Secretariat (shàngshūlìng).
When Dǒng Zhuó moved the capital to Guānzhōng,
Wáng Yǔn collected all the essential maps, records, secret documents, and apocryphal texts from the Lántái and Shíshì archives to take with him.
Upon arriving in Cháng'ān,
he meticulously sorted and submitted them all.
He also gathered all the old precedents of the Hàn dynasty that were still applicable,
and submitted them to the throne.
The classics and texts were thus preserved,
and Wáng Yǔn was instrumental in this.
At that time, Dǒng Zhuó was still in Luòyáng,
and all matters of court administration, great and small,
were entrusted to Wáng Yǔn.
Wáng Yǔn concealed his true feelings and bent his will,
always humoring and deferring to him.
Dǒng Zhuó also trusted him completely,
never becoming suspicious,
thus Wáng Yǔn was able to support the imperial house amidst chaos and danger.
Both officials and ruler, internal and external,
all relied upon him.
Wáng Yǔn saw that Dǒng Zhuó's evil was deepening,
and signs of usurpation had already appeared,
so he secretly plotted with the Colonel Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi) Huáng Wǎn and the President of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū) Zhèng Gōngyè to kill him.
He then memorialized to appoint Yáng Zàn, Protector of the Qiāng (Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi), to act as General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn),
and Shìsūn Ruì, Bearer of the Gilded Mace (Zhí Jīnwú), as Administrator of Nányáng (Nányáng Tàishǒu),
both to lead troops out through the Wǔguān Pass,
ostensibly to attack Yuán Shù,
but in reality intending to divide their forces to conquer Dǒng Zhuó,
and then bring the Son of Heaven back to Luòyáng.
Dǒng Zhuó became suspicious and detained them.
Wáng Yǔn then brought Shìsūn Ruì into the court as Palace Assistant (Púyè)
and Yáng Zàn as President of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū).
In the second year (191 CE),
Dǒng Zhuó returned to Cháng'ān,
and in recognition of Wáng Yǔn's achievements in entering the pass,
he enfeoffed Wáng Yǔn as Marquis of Wēn (Wēn Hóu),
with a stipend of five thousand households.
Wáng Yǔn firmly declined to accept.
Shìsūn Ruì persuaded Wáng Yǔn, saying:
"To maintain humility and simplicity
depends on the timing.
You and Grand Preceptor Dǒng are both in high positions and were both enfeoffed,
but if you alone insist on your noble principles,
is this the way to harmonize with the times?"
Wáng Yǔn heeded his words,
and accepted two thousand households.
In the spring of the third year (192 CE),
there was continuous rain for over sixty days.
Wáng Yǔn, Shìsūn Ruì, and Yáng Zàn ascended a platform to pray for clear weather,
and renewed their previous plot.
Shìsūn Ruì said:
"Since the end of last year,
the sun has not shone,
heavy rains have accumulated,
the moon has encroached upon the 'enforcers,'
and comets have repeatedly appeared.
It is overcast by day and clear by night,
with mist and fog invading everywhere.
This indicates that the time for action is imminent,
and those who act from within will prevail.
The opportunity cannot be missed;
you must plan for it."
Wáng Yǔn affirmed his words,
and then secretly allied with Dǒng Zhuó's general Lǚ Bù,
making him an inside accomplice.
When Dǒng Zhuó entered for the New Year's congratulations,
Lǚ Bù took the opportunity to assassinate him.
The details are found in Dǒng Zhuó's biography.
Wáng Yǔn initially considered pardoning Dǒng Zhuó's troops,
and Lǚ Bù also repeatedly urged him to do so.
But then he doubted, saying:
"These people are innocent;
they merely followed their master.
If we now brand them as evil rebels but then specially pardon them,
it will only make them suspicious of us;
it is not the way to put them at ease."
Lǚ Bù also wanted to distribute Dǒng Zhuó's wealth to the ducal ministers and generals,
but Wáng Yǔn again refused.
Moreover, he had always held Lǚ Bù in low regard,
treating him as a mere swordsman.
Lǚ Bù, on his part, felt entitled due to his achievements,
often boasting about them,
and having lost his expectations,
gradually became discontent.
Wáng Yǔn's nature was rigid and disliked evil.
Initially, fearing Dǒng Zhuó, who was like a jackal or wolf,
he humbled himself to plot against him.
Once Dǒng Zhuó was eliminated,
he believed there would be no more troubles.
But in interactions,
he often lacked a gentle and amiable demeanor,
upholding righteousness and gravity,
and not adapting to expedient measures.
Therefore, his subordinates were not very devoted to him.
Most of Dǒng Zhuó's generals and officers, and those in positions of power, were from Liángzhōu.
Wáng Yǔn proposed to disband their armies.
Someone advised Wáng Yǔn, saying:
"The people of Liángzhōu have always dreaded the Yuán clan and feared Guāndōng.
If we suddenly disband their troops (in Guāndōng)
now, then everyone will certainly feel unsafe.
We can appoint Huángfǔ Yìzhēn as general,
have him take command of their forces,
and then have them remain in Shǎn to pacify them,
while gradually communicating with Guāndōng
to observe the changing situation."
Wáng Yǔn said:
"No.
Those in Guāndōng who have raised righteous armies
are all our allies.
If we now guard strategic passes and garrison Shǎn,
though it might pacify Liángzhōu,
it would greatly arouse suspicion in Guāndōng,
which is unacceptable."
At that time, the common people spread rumors
that all the people of Liángzhōu were to be executed,
which caused them to fear one another.
Those who were in Guānzhōng
all took up arms to defend themselves.
They said to each other:
"Dīng Yànsī and Cài Bójiē were executed simply for being close to Duke Dǒng,
and now we are implicated.
Since they will not pardon us,
and wish to disband our armies,
if we disband our armies today,
tomorrow we will again be treated like fish and meat."
Dǒng Zhuó's subordinate generals, Lǐ Quē, Guō Sì, and others, who were previously leading troops in Guāndōng,
felt uneasy,
so they conspired to rebel
and besieged Cháng'ān.
When the city fell,
Lǚ Bù fled.
Lǚ Bù halted his horse outside the Qīngsuǒ Gate,
and called out to Wáng Yǔn, saying:
"My lord, can you leave?"
Wáng Yǔn said:
"If, by the grace of the altars of soil and grain,
I could bring peace to the state,
that would be my wish.
If I cannot achieve that,
then I shall dedicate my life to dying for it.
The court is young,
and relies on me alone;
to shirk danger and escape with my life
is something I cannot bear.
Please convey my earnest apologies to the lords of Guāndōng,
and urge them to diligently keep the state in mind."
Initially,
Wáng Yǔn appointed Sòng Yì, from his home commandery, as Left Fēngyì,
and Wáng Hóng as Right Fúfēng.
At this time, the population of Sānfǔ was flourishing,
and its military provisions and resources were abundant.
Lǐ Quē and the others wanted to immediately kill Wáng Yǔn,
but feared trouble from the two commanderies,
so they first summoned Sòng Yì and Wáng Hóng.
Wáng Hóng sent an envoy to Sòng Yì, saying:
"Guō Sì and Lǐ Quē have not yet harmed Duke Wáng because we two are outside.
If we answer the summons today,
tomorrow our clans will all be exterminated.
What strategy should we adopt?"
Sòng Yì replied:
"Although fortune and misfortune are hard to predict,
the emperor's command cannot be avoided."
Wáng Hóng said:
"Righteous armies are rising like a boiling cauldron
because of Dǒng Zhuó,
let alone his partisans!
If we raise troops to jointly attack the wicked people by the ruler's side,
Shāndōng will surely respond.
This is a plan to turn misfortune into fortune."
Sòng Yì did not agree.
Wáng Hóng could not act alone,
so they both answered the summons
and were imprisoned in the Court of the Commandant of Justice.
Lǐ Quē then arrested Wáng Yǔn, Sòng Yì, and Wáng Hóng,
and killed them all.
Wáng Yǔn was fifty-six years old at the time.
His eldest son, Gài, who was a Palace Attendant, his second sons, Jǐng and Dìng, and more than ten other relatives were all executed.
Only his nephews, Chén and Líng, managed to escape and return to their hometowns.
The Son of Heaven was moved to sorrow,
and the common people lost heart.
No one dared to collect Wáng Yǔn's body,
except for his former subordinate, Zhào Jiǎn, the Magistrate of Pínglíng,
who resigned his office to arrange the funeral.
Wáng Hóng, courtesy name Chángwén,
was strong and spirited in his youth,
Initially, he served as Governor of Hóngnóng,
and investigated those in the commandery who had purchased official titles from eunuchs.
Although some held positions of two thousand *shí*,
he had them all flogged, investigated, arrested,
and subsequently killed several tens of people,
which spread his prestige to neighboring regions.
and not bothered by minor conduct.
When Wáng Hóng was imprisoned,
Hú Zhǒng pressured and hastened his execution.
As Wáng Hóng faced death, he cursed
and said:
"Sòng Yì is a mere pedant,
unfit to discuss grand strategies.
Hú Zhǒng delights in the misfortunes of others,
and misfortune will soon befall him."
Afterwards, Hú Zhǒng would often see Wáng Hóng striking him with a staff in his sleep,
and consequently fell ill,
dying a few days later.
Later, when the capital was moved to Xǔ,
the Emperor, remembering Wáng Yǔn's loyalty and integrity,
ordered his reburial.
He sent the Commandant-Lieutenant of the Tiger Guards with a memorial to mourn and offer sacrifices,
bestowed secret objects from the Eastern Park,
granted him his original official seal and ribbon,
and sent him back to his home commandery.
His grandson, Hēi, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Ānlè Tíng,
with a stipend of three hundred households.
Shìsūn Ruì, courtesy name Jūncè,
was from Fúfēng and
possessed considerable talent and strategy.
Shìsūn Ruì attributed the merit of punishing Dǒng Zhuó entirely to Wáng Yǔn,
and thus did not seek enfeeoffment,
which is how he avoided calamity.
Later, he became the Three Elders of the State and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness.
Whenever there was a vacancy among the Three Excellencies,
Yáng Biāo and Huángfǔ Sōng both deferred to Shìsūn Ruì.
In the second year of Xīngpíng (195 CE),
he accompanied the emperor on his eastward journey
and was killed by rebellious soldiers.
Zhào Jiǎn, courtesy name Shūmào,
was from Chánglíng,
and by nature upright and resourceful.
In the middle of Chūpíng,
he served as a Minister of the Imperial Secretariat
and was in charge of appointments.
Dǒng Zhuó repeatedly tried to make private appointments,
but Zhào Jiǎn always firmly refused to listen,
speaking with strong and stern words and demeanor.
Dǒng Zhuó, enraged,
summoned him to be killed.
Everyone else was terrified,
but Zhào Jiǎn's expression and manner remained unchanged.
Dǒng Zhuó regretted it,
apologized, and released him.
During the turmoil in Cháng'ān,
he found refuge in Jīngzhōu,
where Liú Biǎo treated him with great courtesy.
When Cáo Cāo pacified Jīngzhōu,
he invited Zhào Jiǎn to serve,
and clasping Zhào Jiǎn's hand, said:
"I regret meeting you so late."
He eventually died as Chief Clerk to Chancellor Zhōng Yáo.
A commentary says: Although scholars establish themselves through righteousness,
they also succeed through strategy.
If Wáng Yǔn had promoted Dǒng Zhuó and given him power,
and waited for an opportunity to expose his crimes,
at that time,
the emperor would have been immediately relieved.
Yet, he ultimately did not allow suspicion or resentment to become a cause for conflict,
for the wise are fundamentally rooted in sincere loyalty and righteousness.
Therefore, promoting Dǒng Zhuó was not a deviation from righteousness,
sharing power was not a reckless usurpation,
and waiting for an opportunity was not cunning deception.
When his plan succeeded and his intentions were fulfilled,
the achievement was attributed to righteousness.
A eulogy says: Chén Fán lived in a humble abode,
determined to rectify the celestial order.
Though human plans were meticulously laid,
the hidden destiny was not yet due.
Observing the desolation and ruin,
how could it not be said to have perished?
Zǐshī planned in difficulty,
concealing his true intentions and sacrificing himself.
His efforts eradicated the prime villain,
but his body was destroyed by the remaining evildoers.
Times have their rise and fall,
and affairs have their successes and failures.
Kǒngzǐ曰:
“Xìng xiāngjìn yě,
xí xiāngyuǎn yě.”
Yán shì'è zhī běn tóng,
ér qiān rǎn zhī tú yì yě.
Fú kèyì zé xíng bù sì,
qiānwù zé qí zhì liú.
Shìyǐ shèngrén dǎorén lǐxìng,
cáiyì dàngyì,
shèn qí suǒ yǔ,
jié qí suǒ piān.
Suī qíngpǐn wànqū,
zhìwén yìshù,
zhìyú táowù zhènsú,
qí dào yī yě.
Shú mò jiāozá,
wángdào língquē,
ér yóu jiǎrén yǐ xiàojǐ,
píngyì yǐ jìgōng.
Jǔ zhōng yú lǐ,
zé qiángliáng chuìqì;
piànyán wéizhèng,
zé sī tái jiěqíng.
Gài qiánzhé zhī yíchén,
yǒu zú qiú zhě.
Bàdé jì shuāi,
jūzhà méngqǐ.
Qiángzhě yǐ juéshèng wéi xióng,
ruòzhě yǐ zhàliè shòuqū.
Zhì yǒu huà bàncè ér wàn wànjīn,
kāi yīshuō ér cì chēnruì.
Huò qǐ túbù ér shì zhíguī,
jiě cǎoyī yǐ shēng qīngxiàng.
Shì zhī shìqiǎo chíchù,
yǐ yàonéng diàolì zhě,
bùqī ér jǐngcóng yǐ.
Zì shì àishàng xiāngduó,
yǔ shí huíbiàn,
qí fēng bùkě liú,
qí bì bùnéng fǎn.
Jí Hànzǔ zhàngjiàn,
wǔfū xīng,
xiànlìng kuānsā,
wénlǐ jiǎnkuò,
xùyú sìháo zhī liè,
rén huái língshàng zhī xīn,
qīngsǐ zhòngqì,
yuànhuì bìchóu,
lìngxíng sítíng,
quányí pǐshù,
rènxía zhī fāng,
chéng qí sú yǐ.
Zì Wǔdì yǐhòu,
chóngshàng rúxué,
huáijīng xiéshù,
suǒzài wùhuì.
Zhì yǒu Shíqú fēnzhēng zhī lùn,
dǎngyú fá yì zhī shuō,
shǒuwén zhī tú,
shèngyú shí yǐ.
Zhì Wáng Mǎng zhuānwěi,
zhōngyú cuànguó.
Zhōngyì zhī liú,
chǐjiàn yīngfú,
suìnǎi rónghuá qiūhè,
gānzú kūgǎo.
Suī Zhōngxīng zài yùn,
Hàndé chóngkāi,
ér bǎoshēn huáifāng,
mí xiāngmùxí,
qùjiù zhī jié,
zhòngyú shí yǐ.
Dài Huán Líng zhī jiān,
zhǔ huāng zhèngmiù,
guómìng wěiyú yānsì,
shìzǐ xiū yǔ wéiwǔ.
Gù pǐfū kàngfèn,
chǔshì héngyì,
suìnǎi jīyáng míngshēng,
hùxiāng dífú,
pǐnhé gōngqīng,
cáilíang zhízhèng,
xìngzhí zhī fēng,
yú sī xíng yǐ.
Fú shànghǎo zé xià bìshèn,
jiǎowǎng gù zhíbìguò,
qí lǐ rán yǐ.
Ruò Fàn Pāng, Zhāng Jiǎn zhī tú,
qīngxīn jì'è,
zhōng xiàn dǎngyì,
bù qí rán hū?
Chū,
Huán Dì wéi Líwú Hóu,
shòuxué yú Gānlíng Zhōu Fú.
Jí jí dìwèi,
zhuófú wéi Shàngshū.
Shí tóngjùn Hénán Yǐn Fáng Zhí yǒumíng dāngcháo.
Xiāngrén wèi zhī yáo yuē:
“Tiānxià guījǔ Fáng Bówǔ,
yīn shī huòyìn Zhōu Zhòngjìn.”
Èr jiā bīnkè,
hùxiāng jīchuǎi,
suì gè shù péngtú,
jiànchéng yóuxì,
yóushì Gānlíng yǒu nán běibù,
dǎnguī zhī yì,
zìcǐ shǐ yǐ.
Hòu Rǔnán Tàishǒu Zōng Zī rèn Gōngcáo Fàn Pāng.
Nányáng Tàishǒu Chéng Gǒng yì wěi Gōngcáo Cén Zhì.
Èr jùn yòu wèi yáo yuē:
“Rǔnán Tàishǒu Fàn Mèngbó,
Nányáng Zōng Zī zhǔ huànuò.
Nányáng Tàishǒu Cén Gōngxiào,
Hóngnóng Chéng Gǒng dàn zuòxiào.”
Yīncǐ liúyán zhuǎnrù Tàixué,
zhūshēng sānmàn yú rén,
Guō Línzōng, Jiǎ Wěijié wéi qí guān,
bìng yǔ Lǐ Yīng, Chén Fān, Wáng Chàng gèng xiāng bāozhòng.
Xuézhōng yǔ yuē:
“Tiānxià mókǎi Lǐ Yuánlǐ,
bùwèi qiángyù Chén Zhòngjǔ,
Tiānxià Jùnxiù Wáng Shūmào.”
Yòu Bóhǎi gōngzú Jìn Jiē,
Fúfēng Wèi Qíqīng,
bìng wēiyán shēnlùn,
bù yǐn háoqiáng.
Zì gōngqīng yǐxià,
mòbù wèi qí biǎnyì,
xǐlǚ dàomén.
Shí Hénèi Zhāng Chéng shànshuō fēngjiǎo,
tuīzhān dāngshè,
suì jiàozǐ shārén.
Lǐ Yīng wéi Hénán Yǐn,
dūcù shōubǔ,
jì'ér féng yòu huòmiǎn,
Yīng yù huáifènjí,
jìng ànshā zhī.
Chū,
Chéng yǐ fāngjì jiāotōng huànguān,
Dì yì pō suì qí zhān.
Chéng dìzǐ Láo Xiū yīn shàngshū wūgào Yīng děng yǎng Tàixué yóushì,
jiāojié zhūjùn shēngtú,
gèng xiāng qūchí,
gòng wéi bùdǎng,
fěixiàn cháotíng,
yílùan fēngsú.
Yúshì Tiānzǐ zhènnù,
bānxià jùnguó,
dàibǔ dǎngrén,
bùgào tiānxià,
shǐ tóngfènjí,
suì shōuzhí Yīng děng.
Qí cí suǒ liánjí Chén Shí zhī tú èrbǎi yú rén,
huò yǒu táodùn bùhuò,
jiē xuánjīn gòumù.
Shǐzhě sìchū,
xiāngwàng yú dào.
Míngnián,
Shàngshū Huò Xǔ, Chéngmén Xiàowèi Dòu Wǔ bìng biǎo wèi qǐng,
Dì yì shāojiě,
nǎi jiē shèguī tiánlǐ,
jìngù zhōngshēn.
Ér dǎngrén zhī míng,
yóu shū wángfǔ.
From this point on,
the upright were dismissed and banished,
while crooked and wicked factions flourished.
Those in the realm who admired such integrity
began to collectively extol one another,
assigning titles
to the eminent scholars of the world.
The highest were called
"Sān Jūn" (Three Lords),
next were the
"Bā Jùn" (Eight Talents),
then the
"Bā Gù" (Eight Guides),
followed by the
"Bā Jí" (Eight Reachers),
and finally the
"Bā Chú" (Eight Stewards).
This was
like the ancient
"Bā Yuán" (Eight Primes)
and "Bā Kǎi" (Eight Excellents).
Dòu Wǔ, Liú Shú, and Chén Fān were the
"Sān Jūn."
"Jūn"
signifies those revered by an entire generation.
Lǐ Yīng, Xún Yì, Dù Mì, Wáng Chàng, Liú Yòu, Wèi Lǎng, Zhào Diǎn, and Zhū Yù were the
"Bā Jùn."
"Jùn"
refers to the elites among men.
Guō Línzōng, Zōng Cí, Bā Sù, Xià Fú, Fàn Pāng, Yǐn Xūn, Cài Yǎn, and Yáng Zhì were the
"Bā Gù."
"Gù"
describes those capable of inspiring others through their virtuous conduct.
Zhāng Jiǎn, Cén Zhì, Liú Biǎo, Chén Xiáng, Kǒng Yù, Yuàn Kāng, Bó (fū) Bīn, and Zhái Chāo were the
"Bā Jí."
"Jí"
indicates those who could guide others to follow their example.
Dù Shàng, Zhāng Miǎo, Wáng Kǎo, Liú Rú, Húmǔ Bān, Qín Zhōu, Fān Xiàng, and Wáng Zhāng were the
"Bā Chú."
"Chú"
denotes those who could rescue people with their wealth.
Later, Zhāng Jiǎn's fellow townsman, Zhū Bìng,
acting on the intentions of the Regular Palace Attendant Hóu Lǎn,
submitted a memorial accusing Jiǎn and twenty-four others from his hometown of secretly designating titles for themselves,
forming a faction,
and plotting to endanger the state.
He named Jiǎn, Bó Bīn, Chǔ Fèng, Zhāng Sù, Xuē Lán, Féng Xǐ, Wèi Xuán, and Xú Gān as the
"Bā Jùn";
Tián Lín, Zhāng Yǐn, Liú Biǎo, Xuē Yù, Wáng Fǎng, Liú Zhī, Xuān Jìng, and Gōng Xùgōng as the
"Bā Gù";
Zhū Kǎi, Tián Pán, Shū Dān, Xuē Dūn, Sòng Bù, Táng Lóng, Yíng Zī, and Xuān Bǎo as the
"Bā Jí."
He claimed they carved stone tablets and erected altars,
forming a faction,
with Jiǎn as their leader.
Emperor Líng issued an edict to publish the charges and arrest Jiǎn and the others.

The Grand Chief Eunuch Cáo Jié then hinted to the officials to memorialize for the arrest of over a hundred people from the former faction, including the former Minister of Works Yú Fàng, Grand Coachman Dù Mì, Prefect of Chánglè Lǐ Yīng, Colonel Director of Retainers Zhū Yù, Administrator of Yǐngchuān Bā Sù, Chancellor of Pèi Xún Yì, Administrator of Hénèi Wèi Lǎng, Administrator of Shānyáng Zhái Chāo, Chancellor of Rènchéng Liú Rú, and Assistant to the Grand Commandant Fàn Pāng.
All died in prison.
Others had either died earlier and were not implicated,
or escaped by fleeing into exile.
From this time on, those who harbored resentment or grudges
used these events to entrap and harm others.
Even trivial animosities
were indiscriminately included in the "faction."
Moreover, provincial and commandery officials, following orders,
even implicated those who had never been associated,
causing them to suffer calamity.
Six or seven hundred people died, were exiled, dismissed, or prohibited from office.
In the fifth year of Xīpíng (176 CE),
Cáo Luán, the Administrator of Yǒngchāng, submitted a memorial vigorously pleading for the faction members,
his words being very direct and sharp.
The Emperor, upon reading the memorial, was greatly enraged,
and immediately ordered the Director of Retainers and Yìzhōu province to arrest Luán in a caged cart,
send him to Huáilǐ prison, and torture him to death.
Then, an edict was again issued to the provinces and commanderies to further investigate the students, former subordinates, fathers, sons, and brothers of the faction members.
Those in office
were dismissed and prohibited from holding future office,
extending even to the five degrees of kinship.
In the second year of Guānghé (179 CE),
Hé Hǎi, the Chief of Shànglù,
memorialized:
"According to the rites,
paternal cousins who live separately and have different property
have already lightened ties of kindness and duty,
and their allegiance is distant and minimal.
Yet now, faction members are prohibited even to the five degrees of kinship,
which not only contradicts the established teachings
but also deviates from regular law."
The Emperor read it and understood.
The prohibitions on faction members, from paternal cousins downwards,
were all lifted.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng (184 CE),
the Yellow Turban rebels rose.
The Regular Palace Attendant Lǚ Qiáng said to the Emperor:
"The prohibitions on faction members have accumulated for a long time,
and public sentiment is widely resentful.
If they are not pardoned soon,
they might easily conspire with Zhāng Jiǎo,
and the rebellion will become vast,
making regret useless."
The Emperor feared his words,
and so issued a great amnesty to the faction members,
allowing those who had been executed or exiled to return to their former commanderies.
Thereafter, the Yellow Turbans grew strong,
the court and the countryside disintegrated,
and the moral order and cultural institutions were swept away.
In general, the faction affair began in Gānlíng and Rǔnán,
culminated with Lǐ Yīng and Zhāng Jiǎn,
and plunged the realm into misery
for over twenty years.
All those implicated
were good scholars of the world.
The thirty-five people known as the Sān Jūn, Bā Jùn, etc.,
whose names and deeds are extant,
are all recorded in this chapter.
Chén Fān, Dòu Wǔ, Wáng Chàng, Liú Biǎo, Dù Shàng, and Guō Línzōng have separate biographies.
Xún Yì is appended to the biography of his ancestor, Shú.
Zhāng Miǎo is appended to the biography of Lǚ Bù.
Húmǔ Bān is appended to the biography of Yuán Shào.
Wáng Kǎo, courtesy name Wénzǔ,
was from Shòuzhāng, Dōngpíng,
and was the Inspector of Jìzhōu.
Qín Zhōu, courtesy name Píngwáng,
was from Píngqiū, Chénliú,
and was the Chancellor of Běihǎi.
Fān Xiàng, courtesy name Jiājǐng,
was from Lǔguó,
and was a Gentleman.
Wáng Zhāng, courtesy name Bóyí,
was from Qǔchéng, Dōnglái,
and was a Minor Prefect.
Their positions and conduct were not particularly prominent.
Zhái Chāo,
Administrator of Shānyáng,
his deeds are mentioned in the biography of Chén Fān,
but his courtesy name and specific commandery are not detailed.
Zhū Yù,
from Pèi,
died in prison along with Dù Mì and others.
Only Zhào Diǎn's name appears without further details.
Liú Shú, courtesy name Zhòngchéng,
was from Lèchéng, Héjiān.
His grandfather, Chēng,
was the Colonel Director of Retainers.
Shú, in his youth, studied and mastered the Five Classics.
He then lived in seclusion,
establishing a private academy to lecture,
with often several hundred students.
Provincial and commandery officials offered invitations,
and the Five Offices repeatedly summoned him,
but he did not accept.
In the second year of Yǒngxīng (154 CE),
the Minister of Works Zhǒng Gǎo recommended Shú as "worthy and upright,"
but he declined due to illness.
Emperor Huán, hearing of Shú's high reputation,
severely rebuked the provincial and commandery officials,
ordering them to bring Shú, even if ill, to the capital.
Shú had no choice but to go to Luòyáng.
His policy response was judged the best in the realm,
and he was appointed Gentleman Consultant.
He also presented an analysis of the successes and failures of contemporary governance,
and interpretations of auspicious and inauspicious portents,
all of which proved effective.
He was twice promoted to Minister of the Secretariat,
offering loyal advice and suggestions,
which were greatly beneficial.
He was again twice promoted to Palace Attendant and Commander of the Tiger Guards.
He submitted a memorial suggesting the dismissal of eunuchs,
his words very direct and sharp.
Though the Emperor could not adopt it,
he did not punish him.
Because Shú was a worthy member of the imperial clan,
the Emperor showed him special respect and deference.
Whenever there was a doubtful matter,
he would secretly consult Shú.
When Emperor Líng ascended the throne,
the eunuchs slandered Shú, accusing him of conspiring with Dòu Wǔ and others.
He was imprisoned and committed suicide.
Lǐ Yīng, courtesy name Yuánlǐ,
was from Xiāngchéng, Yǐngchuān.
His grandfather, Xiū,
was the Grand Commandant during Emperor Ān's reign.
His father, Yì,
was the Chancellor of Zhàoguó.
Yīng was by nature aloof and arrogant,
and did not associate with many people,
only regarding Xún Shú and Chén Shí from his own commandery as teachers and friends.
Initially recommended as Xiàolián,
he was appointed by Sītú Hú Guǎng.
He was recommended as Gāodì,
and was twice promoted to Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
The governors and magistrates feared his awe-inspiring clarity;
many resigned their posts at the mere mention of his arrival.
He was later summoned again,
and was twice promoted to Yúyáng Tàishǒu.
Soon after, he was transferred to Shǔjùn Tàishǒu,
but he begged off the appointment because his mother was old.
He was then transferred to Hù Wūhuán Xiàowèi.
The Xiānbēi frequently encroached upon the frontier,
but Lǐ Yīng often braved arrows and stones,
and each time routed them,
making the barbarians greatly fearful and intimidated.
He was dismissed from office due to a public matter,
and returned to reside in Lúnshì,
where he taught up to a thousand students.
Fán Líng from Nányáng sought to become his disciple,
but Lǐ Yīng politely refused.
Fán Líng later, by flattering the eunuchs,
rose to the position of Tàiwèi,
and was scorned by men of integrity.
Xún Shuǎng once visited Lǐ Yīng,
and even drove his carriage for him.
When he returned,
he joyfully said,
"Today I had the honor of driving for Master Lǐ!"
Such was the admiration he commanded.
In the second year of Yǒngshòu,
the Xiānbēi raided Yúnzhōng.
Emperor Huán, hearing of Lǐ Yīng's abilities,
again summoned him to be Dùliáo Jiāngjūn.
Before this, the Qiāng barbarians, along with Shūlè and Qiūcí,
frequently attacked and plundered Zhāngyè, Jiǔquán, and Yúnzhōng Commanderies,
and the populace suffered repeatedly from their depredations.
From the time Lǐ Yīng arrived at the frontier,
they all submitted in awe at his mere reputation,
and all the men and women they had previously plundered
were sent back to the border.
Thereafter,
his fame spread throughout distant regions.
In the second year of Yánxī, he was summoned,
and was twice promoted to Hénán Yǐn.
At that time, Yáng Yuánqún, a prominent figure from Wǎnlíng, was dismissed from Běihǎi Jùn,
his crimes of corruption were widely known,
and the privy chambers in the commandery office were exquisitely crafted,
so he loaded them up and took them home.
Lǐ Yīng submitted a memorial intending to investigate his crimes,
but Yáng Yuánqún bribed the eunuchs,
and Lǐ Yīng was instead implicated and sentenced to penal labor at the Zuǒxiào.
Earlier,
Lǐ Yīng, along with Tíngwèi Féng Gǔn and Dàsīnóng Liú Yòu, shared the same resolve
to expose and punish corrupt favorites.
Féng Gǔn and Liú Yòu had also been implicated and sentenced to penal labor at that time.
Sīlì Xiàowèi Yīng Fèng submitted a memorial defending Lǐ Yīng and the others, saying:
"In the past, when the people of Qín observed the treasures of Chǔ,
Zhāo Xīxù responded by presenting the virtuous.
When King Huì of Liáng showed off his luminous night-pearl,
King Wēi of Qí responded by presenting his four ministers.
Indeed, loyal and virtuous generals
are the heart and backbone of the state.
I humbly observe that among the penal laborers at the Zuǒxiào are the former Tíngwèi Féng Gǔn, Dàsīnóng Liú Yòu, and Hénán Yǐn Lǐ Yīng.
They upheld the law without bending,
executed and impeached corrupt officials,
and enforced justice,
for which the common people praised them.
In ancient times, Jìsūn Xíngfù, though a father, defied his lord's command
and expelled Jǔ Pú;
his merit was one-twentieth of Shùn's.
Now, Lǐ Yīng and the others cast themselves against the powerful and oppressive,
exerting their full strength to bring them to justice.
Yet Your Majesty neither listened to nor investigated,
but instead readily accepted slanderous accusations,
thereby causing loyal ministers to share the same fault as arch-villains.
From spring to winter,
they have not received your leniency or pardon.
People near and far who observe and hear of this
sigh in lament.
Indeed, the essence of governance
is to remember merits and forget shortcomings.
Thus, Emperor Wǔ spared Ānguó Shǎo Jì among the prisoners,
and Emperor Xuān summoned Zhāng Chǎng even after he became a fugitive.
Féng Gǔn previously campaigned against the Mánjīng,
achieving merits equal to Yǐn Jífǔ.
Liú Yòu frequently oversaw inspections,
displaying integrity that would not swallow dirt.
Lǐ Yīng established his authority in Yōu and Bìng,
and left behind affection when he was Dùliáo.
Now the three borders are stirring restlessly,
and the royal armies have not yet been mustered.
The Yì Jīng says: 'Thunder and rain cause release;
the noble person pardons faults and forgives crimes.'
I beg you to pardon Lǐ Yīng and the others,
to prepare for unforeseen circumstances."
When the memorial was presented,
their sentences were all remitted.
He was twice promoted,
and again appointed Sīlì Xiàowèi.
At that time, Zhāng Ràng's younger brother, Shuò, was the Magistrate of Yěwáng;
he was greedy, cruel, and lawless,
even killing pregnant women.
Hearing of Lǐ Yīng's severe authority,
he feared punishment and fled back to the capital,
hiding in his elder brother Zhāng Ràng's residence,
concealed within a hollow pillar.
Lǐ Yīng learned of his whereabouts,
led his officers and soldiers, broke open the pillar to seize Shuò,
and delivered him to the Luòyáng Prison.
After completing the interrogation,
he immediately executed him.
Zhāng Ràng appealed to the Emperor, claiming injustice.
The Emperor summoned Lǐ Yīng to the palace,
and personally presided over the imperial audience,
questioning him as to why he executed Shuò without first requesting permission.
Lǐ Yīng replied:
"In the past, Duke Wén of Jìn apprehended Duke Chéng of Wèi and brought him back to the capital,
which the Chūnqiū approved.
The Rites say that if a ducal relative commits a crime,
even if it is said they should be pardoned,
the officials upholding the law do not comply.
In ancient times, Zhòngní served as Sīkòu of Lǔ,
and executed Shǎozhèng Mǎo within seven days.
Now, I have been in office for a full ten days,
and privately feared being at fault for delay,
not expecting to be accused of acting too swiftly.
I truly know my guilt and responsibility,
and will not shrink from death.
I only beg to be granted five more days,
to exterminate the arch-villains,
after which I will willingly submit to the cauldron;
this is my lifelong wish."
The Emperor had no further words,
and, looking at Zhāng Ràng, said,
"This is your brother's crime.
What fault does the Sīlì have?"
Then he dismissed Lǐ Yīng.
Thereafter, all the Huángmén Chángshì bowed and held their breath,
not daring to leave the palace during their days off.
The Emperor, wondering at the reason, asked them.
They all kowtowed and wept, saying,
"We fear Colonel Lǐ."
At that time, the imperial court was daily in disarray,
and the rules and regulations were decaying.
Lǐ Yīng alone maintained upright conduct,
and elevated himself through his reputation.
Those scholars who were received by him
were said to have 'ascended the Dragon Gate.'
When the Calamity of Partisan Prohibitions occurred,
Lǐ Yīng and the others were to be investigated and scrutinized.
The case went through the Sānfǔ,
but Tàiwèi Chén Fán rejected it.
He said:
"Those now being investigated,
are all men praised throughout the land,
ministers who worried for the state and were loyal to the public.
Such men should be pardoned for ten generations;
how can they be arrested and tortured when their crimes are not even clear?"
He refused to sign the document.
The Emperor grew even angrier,
and consequently had Lǐ Yīng and the others imprisoned in the Huángmén Běisì Yù.
Lǐ Yīng and the others implicated many sons and younger brothers of eunuchs,
which greatly frightened the eunuchs.
They requested the Emperor to grant a general amnesty due to the opportune time.
Thereupon, a great amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
Lǐ Yīng was pardoned and returned to his hometown,
residing in the mountains of Yángchéng.
All the gentry of the realm highly regarded his principles,
and considered the court defiled.
When Chén Fān (陳蕃) was dismissed from the position of Grand Commandant,
the court and the populace turned their attention to Yīng (膺).
Xún Shuǎng (荀爽) feared that his high reputation would bring disaster,
and wished him to humble himself to preserve himself in an era of turmoil.
He wrote a letter to Yīng, saying:
"It has been long since I last stood in your presence,
and I have not heard your kind instructions.
Gazing upon the distant mountains,
I feel each day is a year.
I know that the straight path is not tolerated in these times,
so I delight in mountains and waters,
and have made my home in Yángchéng (陽城).
The path is near and smooth,
and I should have visited immediately,
but I am ill and unable,
thus failing in my reverence.
Recently I heard that the Heavenly Emperor is greatly angered,
demoting and expelling eminent ministers.
Both men and spirits conspire,
believing that the Son of Heaven should emulate the Zhēngguān (貞觀) era's twenty-fifth year,
and benefit from seeing great men.
Yet, it is not said that at the first dawn of the Yi (夷) hexagram,
though bright, it has not yet fully melted,
the rainbow's brilliance rises,
and those who are [𠫓廾] (gǒng) and compliant attain accord.
Presently, the qi of heaven and earth is closed,
and great men are at a standstill.
The wise see danger
and cast it far away to avoid harm.
Though it may disappoint public expectations,
it aligns with one's private desires.
I imagine you are quite pleased,
and hold no regret.
I hope you can ease your mind from worldly affairs,
and rest behind your humble gate,
〔一０〕allowing things to rise or fall as they may,
and adapting to the times."
Shortly after,
the Emperor passed away.
Chén Fān (陳蕃) became Grand Tutor,
and together with the General-in-Chief Dòu Wǔ (竇武), they wielded power in the court.
They conspired to execute the eunuchs,
and thus appointed renowned scholars from across the empire.
Yīng (膺) was appointed Chief of Chánglè (長樂) Lesser Palace.
After the defeat of Chén (陳) and Dòu (竇),
Yīng (膺) and others were again dismissed.
Later, when Zhāng Jiǎn's (張儉) affair arose,
and the "factionalists" were rounded up and arrested,
his fellow villagers said to Yīng (膺):
"You should leave."
He replied:
"To not shrink from difficulty in affairs,
and not evade punishment for crimes,
is the integrity of a minister.
I am already sixty years old;
life and death are ordained by fate.
Where would I go if I left?"
He then went to the imperial prison.
He died under torture,
his wife and children were exiled to the frontier,
and his disciples, former subordinates, and their fathers and elder brothers
were all proscribed.
At that time, Jǐng Yì (景毅) of Shǔjùn (蜀郡), a Censor, had a son named Gù (顧) who was a disciple of Yīng (膺),
but had not yet been formally registered,
thus escaping condemnation.
Yì (毅) then indignantly declared:
"I originally believed Yīng (膺) to be worthy,
and sent my son to study under him.
How can I let him escape merely by omission from the register,
and live in peace alone!"
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial to resign and returned home.
People of the time admired his righteousness.
Yīng (膺)'s son, Zǎn (瓚),
reached the position of Chancellor of Dōngpíng (東平).
Initially,
when Cáo Cāo (曹操) was still obscure,
Zǎn (瓚) recognized his talent.
When he was about to die,
he said to his sons Xuān (宣) and others:
"The times will soon be in chaos;
among the heroes of the realm, none surpasses Cáo Cāo (曹操).
Zhāng Mèngzhuó (張孟卓) is a good friend of mine,
and Yuán Běnchū (袁本chū) is your maternal relative.
Even so, do not rely on them;
you must return to the Cáo (曹) clan."
His sons followed his advice,
and all escaped the turmoil of the era.
Dù Mì (杜密), courtesy name Zhōufǔ (周甫),
was from Yǐngchuān Yángchéng (潁川陽城).
He was solemn and substantial by nature,
and in his youth had the ambition to rectify society.
He was recruited by the Grand Minister of Works Hú Guǎng (胡廣),
and gradually promoted to Grand Administrator of Dàijùn (代郡).
Recalled,
he was successively promoted three times to Grand Administrator of Tàishān (太山) and Minister of Běihǎi (北ihǎi).
Whenever eunuchs' sons and younger brothers served as magistrates or chiefs and committed wicked deeds,
he would arrest and prosecute them.
During a spring inspection, he arrived at Gāomì (高密) county,
and saw Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) serving as a local official.
Recognizing his extraordinary talent,
he immediately summoned him to serve in a commandery post,
and then sent him to further his studies.
Later, Mì (密) resigned from office and returned home.
Whenever he visited a Grand Administrator or Magistrate,
he would make many recommendations.
Liú Shèng (劉勝) of the same commandery,
also returned to his hometown from Shǔjùn (蜀郡),
closed his door, swept his tracks clean,
and did not interfere in any affairs.
Grand Administrator Wáng Yù (王昱) said to Mì (密):
"Liú Jìlíng (劉季陵) is a man of integrity and high principles,
and many high officials recommend him."
Mì (密) knew Yù (昱) was trying to provoke him,
and replied:
"Liú Shèng (劉勝), though holding the rank of Grand Master
and treated as an honored guest,
knows good deeds but does not recommend them,
hears of evil but says nothing,
concealing his feelings and being protective of himself,
like a silent cicada.
This is a transgressor.
Now, I reveal virtuous men of integrity and practical action,
and correct those who deviate from the Way and lose their integrity,
enabling your enlightened prefecture to administer rewards and punishments justly,
and let your good name spread.
Is this not a tiny contribution?"
Yù (昱) felt ashamed and convinced,
and treated him with even greater respect.
Later, Emperor Huán (桓) summoned him to be appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
then promoted him to Administrator of Hénán (河南),
and transferred him to Grand Coachman.
When the proscription of factionalists arose,
he was dismissed and returned to his home commandery,
and was implicated along with Lǐ Yīng (李膺).
Their reputations and conduct were comparable,
thus people of the time also referred to them
as "Lǐ Dù (李杜)."
Later, when Grand Tutor Chén Fān (陳蕃) assisted in government,
he again became Grand Coachman.
The following year,
he was summoned due to the factionalists' affair
and committed suicide.
Liú Yòu (劉祐), courtesy name Bózǔ (伯祖),
was from Ānguó (安國), Zhōngshān (中山).
Ānguó (安國) later became part of Bólíng (博陵).
Yòu (祐) was initially recommended as Filial and Incorrupt,
and appointed Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
He was well-versed in precedents
and skilled in persuasive writing.
Whenever there were memorials or discussions,
he responded without impediment,
and was respected by his colleagues.
He was appointed Magistrate of Rènchéng (任城),
and Yǎnzhōu (兗州) recommended him as outstandingly capable.
He was promoted to Inspector of Yángzhōu (揚州).
At this time, Liáng Mín (梁旻), Grand Administrator of Kuàijī (會稽),
was the younger cousin of the General-in-Chief Jì (冀).
Yòu (祐) impeached him for his crimes,
and Mín (旻) was summoned for investigation.
Yòu (祐) was again promoted to Grand Administrator of Hédōng (河東).
At that time, many county magistrates and chiefs were sons or younger brothers of palace eunuchs,
and the common people suffered greatly from them.
When Yòu (祐) arrived,
he dismissed the powerful and influential,
and justly resolved grievances.
His administration became a model for the Three Rivers region.
He was promoted twice more.
In the fourth year of Yánxī (延熹)
he was appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
then sent out to be Administrator of Hénán (河南),
and transferred to Colonel Director of Retainers.
At that time, sons of powerful and noble families, who had been dismissed from provincial and commandery posts and returned to the capital,
would change their carriages and attire upon reaching the border,
and conceal their wealth,
wielding great influence in the court.
He was appointed Minister of the Imperial Clan,
and three times transferred to Grand Minister of Agriculture.
At that time, the Regular Palace Attendants Sū Kāng (蘇康) and Guǎn Bà (管霸) held power within the palace,
and seized good fields, choice estates,
mountains, forests, and lakes throughout the empire.
The common people were impoverished,
and the provinces and commanderies were filled with resentment.
Yòu (祐) issued letters to all localities,
confiscating these properties according to regulations.
Emperor Huán (桓) was greatly enraged,
and ordered Yòu (祐) to be sentenced to the Left Bureau.
Later, he was pardoned and released.
He served as one of the Three Ministers again,
but each time he resigned due to illness,
begging for his bones to be returned to his fields and home.
An imperial edict appointed him Zhōngsàn Dàfū,
and he then sealed his gates and cut off all traces.
Whenever there was a vacancy among the Sān Gōng,
the imperial court always thought of Yòu,
but due to slander and calumny, he was not employed.
Yán Dǔ wrote him a letter saying:
"In antiquity, Tàibó yielded three times,
and people praised him despite having no virtue to claim.
Yánlíng (Jì Zhá) waved his hand in refusal,
and Huáxià looked up to his integrity.
You, sir, embrace the 'can be rolled up' (i.e., retreat when times are bad) principle of Qú Shì,
and embody the 'like a fool' demeanor of Níng Zǐ.
Subtle, profound, and universally penetrating,
empty yet never overflowing;
you disregard the brightness of the three luminaries (sun, moon, stars),
not yet having the leisure to concern yourself with the affairs of the world.
How excellent you are!"
At the beginning of Emperor Líng's reign,
Chén Fān assisted in governance
and made Yòu Hénán Yǐn.
When Fān was defeated,
Yòu was dismissed and returned home,
where he died.
The next year,
there was a great purge of the Dǎng Rén,
but fortunately, he was not affected by the disaster.
Wèi Lǎng, courtesy name Shàoyīng,
was a native of Shàngyú, Kuàijī.
In his youth, he was a county official.
When his elder brother was killed by a fellow villager,
Lǎng, in broad daylight, wielded a blade to avenge him within the county,
and then became a fugitive, arriving in Chén Guó.
He studied Chūnqiū Túwěi with Doctor Xì Zhòngxìn,
and also went to the Imperial Academy to receive instruction in the Wǔ Jīng.
The elders of the capital, such as Lǐ Yīng and his followers, vied to learn from him.
He was first appointed to the Sītú's mansion,
then twice promoted to Péngchéng Lìng.
At that time, the sons and younger brothers of the eunuchs served as Guó Xiàng,
often acting unlawfully.
Lǎng and they frequently presented memorials against each other.
The favored officials became indignant and resentful,
wishing to harm him.
Coincidentally, bandits arose in Jiǔzhēn,
so they jointly recommended Lǎng as Jiǔzhēn Dūwèi.
Upon arriving at his post,
he encouraged his officials and soldiers,
attacked and defeated the bandits,
beheading two thousand.
Emperor Huán praised his achievements
and summoned him to be appointed Yìláng.
Shortly thereafter,
he was promoted to Shàngshū.
He repeatedly presented beneficial proposals,
which brought about improvements.
He was sent out as Hénèi Tàishǒu,
and his governance was praised among the Sān Hé (three commanderies around the Yellow River).
Shàngshū Lìng Chén Fān recommended Lǎng as publicly loyal, honest, and straightforward,
suitable for confidential matters,
and he was again summoned to be Shàngshū.
Coincidentally, he was implicated in the Dǎng (factional) debate
and was dismissed and returned home.
Lǎng was severe and dignified by nature,
keeping his gate shut and maintaining strict rules;
his family members never saw him appear lax.
Later, Dòu Wǔ and others were executed,
and Lǎng was urgently summoned as a member of the Dǎng.
He traveled to Niúzhǔ,
and committed suicide.
He wrote several books,
known as Wèi Zǐ Yún.
Xià Fù, courtesy name Zǐzhì,
was a native of Yǔ, Chénliú.
In his youth, he was a scholar,
straightforward in speech and conduct.
The Gāo clan and Cài clan in the same county were both wealthy and prosperous,
and the people of the commandery feared and served them.
Only Fù, though his gate was nearby, did not associate with them.
Because of this, he was hated by the powerful clans.
At the beginning of Emperor Huán's reign,
he was recommended for his straightforward speech,
but did not take office.
Although Fù did not associate with the eunuchs of the time,
his reputation was feared by the Zhongguān (eunuchs).
Thus, along with Fàn Pāng, Zhāng Jiǎn, and others, he was falsely accused.
An imperial edict was sent to the prefectures and commanderies,
ordering their arrest as Dǎngkuí (leaders of the faction).
When Jiǎn and the others became fugitives,
every place they passed through
was subjected to arrests and investigations,
Fù then stamped his foot and sighed:
"The calamity I brought upon myself
has wrongfully implicated good people.
resulting in their implication being spread throughout the empire.
but disaster befalls tens of thousands of families.
Why should I live?"
He then cut his beard, disguised himself,
and entered the Línlǜ Mountains,
concealing his name,
and worked as a laborer for a blacksmith.
He personally endured smoke and charcoal,
his appearance became disfigured and emaciated.
For two or three years,
no one recognized him.
Later, Fù's younger brother Jìng,
riding in a carriage
and carrying silk,
sought him in Nièyáng market.
He met Fù but did not recognize him.
Hearing his voice,
he then realized it was him and bowed.
Fù avoided him and did not speak.
Jìng followed him to an inn
and spent the night together.
In the middle of the night, Fù secretly called Jìng and said:
"Because I upheld the Dao and detested evil,
I was framed by the powerful eunuchs.
I merely thought of barely preserving myself
to protect my life.
Why do you seek me with goods,
thereby drawing misfortune upon me?"
The next morning,
they parted ways.
He died before the Dǎng ban was lifted.
Zōng Cí, courtesy name Xiàochū,
was a native of Ānzhòng, Nányáng.
He was recommended as Xiàolián,
was invited to the Gōngfǔ nine times,
and was summoned as a 'man of the Dao,'
but did not accept.
Later, he became Xiūwǔ Lìng.
At that time, the Tàishǒu came from a powerful and influential family,
and frequently took bribes.
Cí then resigned his office and left.
He was summoned to be appointed Yìláng,
but before he arrived,
he died from illness on the road.
All the scholars of Nányáng greatly valued his righteous conduct.
Bā Sù, courtesy name Gōngzǔ,
was a native of Gāochéng, Bóhǎi.
He was first investigated as Xiàolián,
and successively served as Shèn Lìng and Bèiqiū Zhǎng.
In both cases, he resigned due to illness, believing the Jùnshǒu was not the right person.
He was invited to the Gōngfǔ,
and gradually promoted to Yìláng.
He conspired with Dòu Wǔ, Chén Fān, and others to execute the eunuchs.
Wǔ and the others were killed,
and Sù was also imprisoned due to the Dǎng ban.
Zhōng Chángshì Cáo Jié later learned of his plot
and arrested him.
Sù drove himself to the county office.
The Xiàn Lìng saw Sù,
entered his private chambers, removed his seal and ribbons, and wanted to leave with him.
Sù said:
"As a minister,
if one has a plan, one dares not hide it; if one has committed a crime, one does not flee punishment.
Since I did not hide my plan,
how could I dare to flee my punishment?"
He was then killed.
The Cìshǐ Jiǎ Cóng carved a stone inscription to record this.
Fàn Pāng, courtesy name Mèngbó,
was a native of Zhēngqiāng, Rǔnán.
In his youth, he cultivated a pure and upright character,
which was respected by his prefecture and village.
He was recommended as Xiàolián and Guānglù Sìxíng.
At that time, Jì Zhōu suffered from famine,
and bandits rose everywhere.
Therefore, Pāng was appointed Qīngzhào Shǐ
to investigate.
Pāng mounted his carriage and grasped the reins,
filled with the lofty ambition of bringing order to the world.
Upon reaching the provincial border,
the local administrators, knowing their own corruption,
resigned their seals and ribbons at the mere sight of him.
His impeachments
all satisfied public opinion.
He was promoted to Guānglù Xūn Zhǔshì.
At that time, Chén Fān was Guānglù Xūn.
Pāng, holding the official tablet, went to Fān,
but Fān did not stop him.
Pāng felt resentment,
threw down his tablet, resigned his office, and left.
Guō Línzōng heard of this and reproached Fān, saying:
"Should a man like Fàn Mèngbó
be treated with mere official etiquette?
Now you have solidified his reputation for principled resignation;
will you not bring upon yourself the criticism of being ungenerous?"
Fān then apologized.
He was again summoned by Tàiwèi Huáng Qióng.
Later, an edict ordered the officials of the Sānfǔ to report rumors.
Pāng submitted a memorial denouncing more than twenty powerful and influential figures among the Cìshǐ and Èrqiānshí.
The Shàngshū rebuked Pāng for impeaching too many people,
suspecting private motives.
Pāng replied,
"Among those I have accused,
none are not greedy, corrupt, treacherous, or violent,
and deeply harmful to the people.
How could I otherwise stain my writing tablet [with their names]?
Recently, the deadline for submissions was pressing,
so I first reported those who were urgent.
Those I am still unsure about
I will further investigate and verify.
I have heard that when farmers remove weeds,
the good grains will surely flourish;
when loyal officials eliminate traitors,
the royal way will become clear.
If my words contain any duplicity,
I am willing to suffer public execution."
The officials could not refute him.
Pāng, seeing that the times were difficult
and knowing his intentions would not be carried out,
then resigned his post and left.
The Tàishǒu Zōng Zī had heard of his reputation,
and requested him to serve as Gōngcáo,
entrusting him with administrative affairs.
While Pāng was in office,
he was strict, upright, and abhorred evil.
Anyone whose conduct violated filial piety or fraternal duty,
or deviated from benevolence and righteousness,
he would remove all traces of and expel,
not allowing them to share the court.
He prominently recommended those of extraordinary integrity
and elevated the obscure and humble.
Pāng's maternal nephew, Lǐ Sòng of Xīpíng,
was a descendant of a princely clan,
but was shunned by his local community.
Zhōngchángshì Táng Héng pleaded with Zī on Sòng's behalf,
and Zī appointed him as an official.
Pāng, deeming him unsuitable,
ignored the appointment and did not summon him.
Zī became angry
and had the clerk Zhū Líng beaten.
Líng looked up and said,
"Fàn Pāng's clear judgment
is like a sharp blade cutting through rotten wood.
Today, I would rather be beaten to death
than defy Pāng."
Zī then stopped.
Among the common people in the commandery,
none failed to harbor resentment,
and they labeled those whom Pāng employed
as the "Fàn Party."
Later, Láo Xiū falsely accused people of forming cliques,
and Pāng was imprisoned in the Huángmén Běisì Prison.
The prison guard said to him,
"All those who are imprisoned offer sacrifices to Gāotáo."
Pāng said,
"Gāotáo was a worthy man,
an upright official of ancient times.
If he knows Pāng is innocent,
he will surely present the case to the Emperor;
if Pāng is guilty,
what good would sacrificing to him do?"
The crowd consequently stopped as well.
When the prison guards were about to inflict torture,
Pāng, seeing that many fellow prisoners were ailing,
requested to go first to the torture rack,
and thus contended with Yuán Zhōng, a fellow native of the same commandery, to endure the painful torment.
Emperor Huán sent Zhōngchángshì Wáng Fǔ to interrogate them in order,
and Pāng and the others were all put in three cangues and their heads covered with sacks,
exposed at the foot of the steps.
The other prisoners came forward first,
some answering, some not.
Pāng and Zhōng advanced out of order from behind.
Wáng Fǔ questioned them, saying,
"As subjects,
you do not only show loyalty to the state,
but instead form factions,
praise each other,
criticize the court,
and fabricate groundless charges.
What do all your conspiracies
intend to achieve?
Answer honestly,
without concealment."
Pāng replied,
"I have heard the words of Zhòngní,
'See good as if you cannot reach it;
see evil as if you are touching boiling water.'
We wished to make those who love good share in its purity,
and those who hate evil share in its defilement.
We thought this was what the royal government desired to hear,
not realizing it would instead be considered a faction."
Fǔ said,
"You elevate each other,
acting as lips and teeth for one another.
If there is anyone not aligned with you,
you reject and exclude them upon sight.
What is the meaning of this?"
Pāng then, with indignation, looked up to heaven and said,
"In ancient times, those who followed good
sought much fortune for themselves;
today, those who follow good
are plunged into great execution.
On the day of my death,
I wish to be buried near Shǒuyángshān,
so that above, I do not fail the August Heaven,
and below, I am not ashamed before Yí and Qí."
Fǔ, filled with pity, changed his demeanor.
They were then able to have their shackles removed.
After Pāng's case was resolved,
he returned south.
When he first departed the capital,
thousands of carriages of scholar-officials from Rǔnán and Nányáng came to welcome him.
His fellow prisoners, the villagers Yīn Táo and Huáng Mù,
also escaped and returned with him,
and they both attended to Pāng,
responding to guests.
Pāng looked at Táo and the others and said,
"By accompanying me now,
you are compounding my misfortune."
He then fled back to his hometown.
Initially,
when Pāng and others were imprisoned,
Shàngshū Huò Xū pleaded on their behalf.
When they were acquitted
and arrived at the capital,
they visited Xū but did not thank him.
Someone reproached Pāng for this.
He replied,
"In the past, Shū Xiàng was implicated,
and Qí Xī saved him.
We have not heard of Yángshé expressing gratitude,
nor Qí Lǎo displaying self-praise."
He said nothing further.
In the second year of Jiànníng (169 AD),
a great purge of the Party Members was carried out,
and an imperial edict was issued for the swift arrest of Pāng and others.
Dūyóu Wú Dǎo arrived at the county,
clutched the imperial edict,
closed himself in the courier station,
and cried on his bed.
Pāng heard of this
and said,
"It must be for me."
He immediately went to the prison himself.
The county magistrate Guō Yī was greatly alarmed,
came out, removed his seal and sash,
and urged Pāng to flee with him.
He said,
"The world is vast!
Why must you stay here?"
Pāng said,
"If Pāng dies, then the disaster will be averted.
How dare I burden you with my crime,
and also cause my aged mother to wander!"
His mother came to bid him farewell.
Pāng said to his mother,
"Zhòng Bó is filial and respectful,
enough to provide for you.
Pāng will follow Lord Lóngshū to the Yellow Springs;
the living and the dead will each find their proper place.
Only, my dear mother, please suppress this unbearable affection
and do not increase your sorrow."
His mother said,
"Now that you can be named alongside Lǐ and Dù,
what regret is there in dying?
Having already achieved a good name,
can one also seek a long life?
Can both be obtained?"
Pāng knelt to receive her instruction,
bowed twice, and took his leave.
He turned to his son and said,
"If I were to tell you to do evil,
evil cannot be done;
if I tell you to do good,
then I would not be doing evil."
Those who heard this on the road
were all moved to tears.
He was thirty-three years old at the time.
The eulogy states: Lǐ Yīng distinguished himself and rose from the midst of filth and danger,
embodying righteousness and creating a trend,
thereby inspiring the common people,
spurring moral conduct to shame the powerful,
and establishing integrity and esteem to revive the noble and influential,
causing the scholars of the world to be roused and moved,
to surge and follow him,
even to the point of being deeply imprisoned, having their families destroyed, and yet not regretting it,
such that sons accepted their death and mothers rejoiced in their righteousness.
How magnificent!
The Master said:
"Is the Way to be abandoned?
It is fate!"
Yǐn Xūn
, courtesy name Bóyuán, was a native of Gǒng
in Hénán. His family for generations had been officials.
His uncle Mù was the Sītú,
his elder brother Sòng was the Tàiwèi,
and many of his relatives held high positions.
Yet Xūn alone maintained a pure character,
not relying on his family's influence to look down on others.
The province and commanderies repeatedly summoned him;
he was recommended as Xiàolián,
and after three promotions, became the Magistrate of Hándān.
His administration achieved extraordinary results.
Later, he was designated Gāodì
and after five promotions, became Shàngshūlìng.
When Emperor Huán executed the Grand General Liáng Jì,
Xūn participated in planning the great strategy
and was enfeoffed as Dūxiānghóu.
He was promoted to Rǔnán Premier.
He submitted a memorial requesting the lifting of the partisan proscription against Fàn Pāng, Yuán Zhōng, and others.
Soon after, he was summoned and appointed Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng
and then transferred to Dàsīnóng.
Because of Dòu Wǔ's affairs,
he was imprisoned and committed suicide.
Cài Yǎn
, courtesy name Mèngxǐ, was a native of Xiàng
in Rǔnán. In his youth, he mastered the classics and lectured on them,
transforming his hometown with ritual and deference.
When there were disputes in his hometown,
people would go to Yǎn for resolution.
His settlements
were always accepted without complaint.
He was recommended as Xiàolián
and gradually promoted to Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Zhōngchángshì Jù Yuàn entrusted his younger brother Gōng to recommend a Màocái,
but Yǎn did not accept.
Instead, he arrested and investigated the messenger who delivered the letter.
He also impeached Cáo Dǐng
, the Rǐnán Xiàng, for embezzling ten million.
Dǐng was the younger brother of Zhōngchángshì Téng.
Téng had Grand General Liáng Jì write a letter to intercede for him,
but Yǎn did not respond.
Dǐng was ultimately sentenced to penal labor at the Zuǒxiào.
Yǎn was then summoned and appointed Yìláng and Fújiélìng.
Liáng Jì heard of Yǎn's virtue
and invited him for a meeting,
but Yǎn declined, feigning illness, and did not go.
Jì resented him for this.
At that time, Nányáng Premier Chéng Gā and others were brought to the Tíngwèi for investigating eunuchs.
Yǎn and Yìláng Liú Yú submitted a memorial to save them,
speaking very sharply and sternly.
As a result, he was dismissed from office and returned home,
closing his door and not going out.
When Emperor Líng ascended the throne,
he was again appointed Yìláng,
but he died of illness soon after.
Yáng Zhì
, courtesy name Sìzǔ, was a native of Liángfù
in Tàishān. His family was a prominent clan for generations.
Zhì in his youth was pure, upright, learned, and of good conduct.
He was recommended as Xiàolián
and appointed to the staff of Tàiwèi Lǐ Gù.
He was designated Gāodì
and appointed Shìyùshǐ.
When Gù was executed,
Zhì, as his former subordinate, was proscribed for several years.
He was again designated Gāodì
and promoted a second time to Jìzhōu Cìshǐ.
He impeached and investigated corrupt officials,
and order was restored wherever he served.
He was again promoted twice to Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng and Chéngmén Xiàowèi,
and a third time to Shàngshūlìng.
At that time, Tàiwèi Zhāng Hào, Sītú Fán Líng, Dàhónglú Guō Fáng, Tàipú Cáo Líng, and Dàsīnóng Féng Fāng were all intermarried with and secretly connected to the eunuchs,
publicly engaging in bribery.
Zhì memorialized to dismiss them all,
but his plea was not accepted.
He recommended the former Tàiwèi Liú Chǒng, Sīlì Xiàowèi Xǔ Bīng, Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Xī, Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Gōng, and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Páng Ài as being clear and upright in public service,
and recommended them for promotion.
The Emperor praised him
and appointed Zhì as Hénányǐn.
He received his salary daily,
and often ate dry rice and vegetables,
controlling the powerful and influential.
The capital feared him.
When the partisan proscriptions arose,
he was dismissed from office and proscribed,
and died at home.
Zhāng Jiǎn
, courtesy name Yuánjié, was a native of Gāopíng
in Shānyáng, a descendant of Zhào King Zhāng Ěr.
His father Chéng
was the Jiāngxià Premier.
Jiǎn was initially recommended as Màocái,
but, deeming the Cìshǐ an unsuitable person,
he feigned illness and did not take office.
In the eighth year of Yánxī,
Premier Zhái Chāo invited him to serve as Dōngbù Dūyóu.
At that time, Zhōngchángshì Hóu Lǎn's family resided east of Fáng,
tyrannizing the populace,
and engaging in unlawful activities.
Jiǎn impeached Lǎn and his mother for their crimes,
requesting their execution.
Lǎn blocked all memorials and reports,
preventing them from being submitted,
thus creating an enmity.
A fellow townsman, Zhū Bìng,
who was naturally obsequious and corrupt,
had been slighted by Jiǎn.
Bìng harbored resentment
and consequently submitted a memorial accusing Jiǎn and twenty-four others from the same commandery of forming a clique.
Thereupon, an edict was issued to pursue and arrest them.
Jiǎn managed to escape,
distressed and fleeing,
knocking on doors seeking refuge.
None failed to admire his reputation and conduct,
and they would break up their families to shelter him.
Later, he drifted to Dōnglái
and stayed at Lǐ Dú's house.
Máo Qīn
, the Magistrate of Wàihuáng, arrived at the door with his troops. Dú led Qīn in and said,
"Zhāng Jiǎn is famous throughout the world,
and his flight is not due to his own fault.
Even if Jiǎn could be captured,
would you really have the heart to seize him?"
Qīn then rose and patted Dú, saying,
"Qú Bóyù was ashamed to be a gentleman alone;
how can you monopolize benevolence and righteousness?"
Dú replied,
"Although I am fond of righteousness,
the imperial court today contains half of it."
Qīn sighed and departed.
Dú then arranged for Jiǎn to escape beyond the frontier,
and thus he was spared.
In the places he passed through,
those who suffered severe punishment numbered in the tens;
their relatives were all wiped out,
and commanderies and counties were ruined because of this.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng,
the partisan proscription was lifted,
and he returned to his hometown.
The Grand General and the Three Excellencies all invited him,
and he was also recommended as Dūnpǔ.
The imperial carriage specifically summoned him,
and he was appointed Shàofǔ from his home,
but he did not accept any of these.
At the beginning of Emperor Xiàn's reign,
the common people suffered from famine,
but Jiǎn's financial situation was relatively comfortable.
He then exhausted his wealth
and shared it with his village,
saving hundreds of people.
At the beginning of Jiàn'ān,
he was summoned to be Wèiwèi,
and reluctantly took office.
Jiǎn saw that the virtue of the Cáo clan was already emerging,
so he closed his doors and 'hung up his carriage' [retired],
no longer participating in government affairs.
A little over a year later, he died in Xǔ.
He was eighty-four years old.
A commentary says: In the past, Wèi Qí escaped death,
and Yú Qīng resigned his seal;
Jì Bù fled,
and Zhū Jiā willingly accepted punishment.
But Zhāng Jiǎn, incurring the wrath of the reigning monarch,
wandered and sought refuge,
and those who heard of his plight throughout the world
all pitied his grand aspirations
and competed to shelter him.
Indeed, dozens or hundreds abandoned their cities, relinquished their titles, ruined their families, and sacrificed their lives
for him.
How virtuous!
However, Jiǎn, with a mere palm,
wished to block the Jiāng and Hé rivers alone,
ultimately inviting the great turmoil of illness.
Many saw that he did not know his own measure.
Cén Zhì
, courtesy name Gōngxiào, was a native of Jíyáng
in Nányáng. His father Yù
was the Nánjùn Premier
and was executed for greed.
Zhì was young and not yet well-known.
He went to visit Zōng Cí
from the same commandery. Cí was then being summoned for his wisdom,
and his gate was full of guests.
Deeming Zhì not to be from a good family,
he refused to see him.
Zhì remained at his gate for several days
before finally being admitted.
Cí conversed with him,
was greatly surprised by his talent,
and consequently took him to Luòyáng
where he then attended the Imperial Academy to study.
Hǎo Zhì (晊) had high talent.
Guō Línzōng (郭林zōng), Zhū Gōngshū (朱公叔) and others were all his friends.
Lǐ Yīng (李膺) and Wáng Chàng (王暢) praised him as having the capacity to govern the state.
Although he lived among the common people,
he was filled with the noble ambition to rectify the world.
When the Grand Administrator Chéng Gǒng (成瓚) of Hóngnóng (弘農) took office,
he desired to establish his authority.
Hearing of Hǎo Zhì’s (晊) high reputation,
he invited him to be the Chief Clerk (gōngcáo).
He also appointed Zhāng Mù (張牧) as the Central Officer in charge of bandits (zhōngzéicáo lì).
Chéng Gǒng (瓚) trusted Hǎo Zhì (晊) and Zhāng Mù (牧) wholeheartedly.
They commended the good and corrected the wrong,
肅清朝府 (sùqīng cháofǔ) making the government administration肃清 (sùqīng) pure and clear.
In Wǎn (宛) there was a rich merchant, Zhāng Fàn (張汎),
a relative of Emperor Huán’s (桓帝) beautiful concubine.
He was skilled at carving and crafting precious objects.
He often bribed court eunuchs,
thereby obtaining prominent positions.
Relying on his skills and cunning,
he wielded power arbitrarily.
Hǎo Zhì (晊) and Zhāng Mù (牧) urged Chéng Gǒng (瓚) to arrest Zhāng Fàn (汎) and his associates.
Soon after, they encountered a general amnesty,
but Hǎo Zhì (晊) ultimately executed him.
He also rounded up Zhāng Fàn’s (汎) clan and retainers,
killing over two hundred people.
Only then did he submit a memorial to the throne.
Thereupon, the Palace Regular Attendant Hóu Lǎn (侯覽) had Zhāng Fàn’s (汎) wife submit a petition pleading his innocence.
The Emperor was greatly enraged.
He summoned Chéng Gǒng (瓚),
who died in prison.
Hǎo Zhì (晊) and Zhāng Mù (牧) fled and hid in the region between Qí (齊) and Lǔ (魯).
They were released during a general amnesty.
Later, when the provinces and commanderies conducted recommendations,
and the three highest ministries repeatedly invited them to serve,
they both declined.
When Lǐ (李) and Dù (杜) were executed,
they fled again,
and reportedly died in the mountains of Jiāngxià (江夏).
Chén Xiáng (陳翔), courtesy name Zǐlín (子麟),
was from Shàolíng (邵陵), Rǔnán (汝南).
His grandfather, Zhēn (珍),
was the Colonel Director of Retainers (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
Chén Xiáng (翔) was famous in his youth
for his good connections.
He was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián).
Grand Commandant Zhōu Jǐng (周景) invited him and recommended him as a High Talent (gāodì).
He was appointed Palace Remonstrance Official (Shìyùshǐ).
At that time, during the New Year’s Day audience,
Grand General Liáng Jì (梁冀) appeared disrespectful.
Chén Xiáng (翔) memorialized that Liáng Jì (冀) was presumptuous and disrespectful due to his high status,
and requested his arrest and punishment.
People at the time found this extraordinary.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Dìngxiāng (定襄),
then summoned to be an Attendant Counselor (Yìláng),
and later promoted to Inspector of Yángzhōu (揚州).
He impeached Wáng Yǒng (王永), the Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng (豫章), for communicating with court eunuchs,
and Xú Cān (徐參), the Grand Administrator of Wú County (吳郡), for corruption in office.
Both were summoned to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
Xú Cān (參)
was the younger brother of the Palace Regular Attendant Huáng (璜).
As a result, his prestige greatly increased.
He was again summoned to be an Attendant Counselor (Yìláng),
and appointed Imperial Palace Grandee (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
Implicated in the Party Prohibitions, he was interrogated in the Prison of the Northern Division of the Yellow Gate,
but was acquitted due to lack of evidence,
and died at home.
Kǒng Yù (孔昱), courtesy name Yuánshì (元世),
was from Lǔ (魯) in Lǔ Prefecture (魯國).
His seventh-generation ancestor, Bà (霸),
served as a Nine Ministers (Jiǔ Qīng) during Emperor Chéng’s (成帝) reign and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Bāochéng (褒成侯).
From Bà (霸) to Yù (昱),
titles and positions were passed down in the family.
There were fifty-three of them who served as high ministers, grand administrators, or inspectors,
and seven were enfeoffed as marquis.
Kǒng Yù (昱) studied his family’s scholarship in his youth.
Grand General Liáng Jì (梁冀) invited him to serve,
but he did not respond.
The Grand Commandant recommended him as an Upright and Forthright (fāngzhèng) scholar,
but his policy proposals were not accepted,
so he resigned due to illness.
Later, he was implicated in the Party Prohibitions and banned from office.
When Emperor Líng (靈帝) ascended the throne,
he was summoned by the public carriage to be appointed Attendant Counselor (Yìláng),
and then appointed Magistrate of Luòyáng (洛陽).
Due to the death of his teacher,
he resigned from office
and died at home.
Yuàn Kāng (苑康), courtesy name Zhòngzhēn (仲真),
was from Chónghé (重合), Bóhǎi (勃海).
In his youth, he studied at the Imperial Academy
and was close friends with Guō Línzōng (郭林宗).
He was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián),
and twice promoted to Magistrate of Yǐngyīn (潁陰),
where he showed capability.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Tàishān (太山).
Many powerful families within the commandery were lawless.
When Yuàn Kāng (康) arrived,
he displayed fierce anger
and issued strict orders.
No one dared to transgress.
Lands and houses previously seized from people were all immediately returned.
At that time, Zhāng Jiǎn (張儉) of Shānyáng (山陽) killed the mother of the Regular Attendant Hóu Lǎn (侯覽).
He investigated Zhāng Jiǎn’s (儉) clan and retainers,
some of whom fled and hid in the Tàishān (太山) region.
Yuàn Kāng (康), who had always detested the eunuchs,
took this opportunity to thoroughly pursue and apprehend them all,
leaving none uncaptured.
Hóu Lǎn (覽) bore him great resentment.
He falsely accused Yuàn Kāng (康), the Inspector of Yǎnzōu (兗州) Dìwǔ Zhǒng (第五種), and the Commandant Hú Jiā (壺嘉) of fabricating reports of bandit surrenders.
Yuàn Kāng (康) was summoned to the Grand Judge’s (Tíngwèi) prison,
his death sentence was commuted by one degree,
and he was exiled to Rìnnán (日南).
The people of Yǐngyīn (潁陰) and Yáng Zhì (羊陟) of Tàishān (太山) went to the imperial palace to plead on his behalf.
He was then pardoned and returned to his home commandery,
and died at home.
Zhāng Bù (張璵), courtesy name Wényǒu (文有),
was from Xiáqiū (瑕丘), Shānyáng (山陽).
In his youth, he was a student,
poor but of pure ambition,
and would not accept favors from his hometown.
He was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián),
and repeatedly invited by the ducal ministries,
but he declined all.
He established a study hall to teach,
and several hundred people often came from distant places.
During Emperor Huán’s (桓帝) reign,
he was summoned to be an academician,
but he declined.
When Emperor Líng (靈帝) ascended the throne,
Grand Commandant Huáng Qióng (黃瓊) recommended him as an Upright and Forthright (fāngzhèng) scholar.
His policy proposals were timely and appropriate.
He was twice promoted to Attendant Counselor (Yìláng),
and appointed Magistrate of Méng (蒙).
Because the Grand Administrator was not a suitable person,
he resigned from office.
His family had no property,
and his children left home wearing the same clothes.
At the age of eighty,
he died at home.
Liú Rú (劉儒), courtesy name Shúlín (叔林),
was from Yángpíng (陽平), Dōng Commandery (東郡).
Guō Línzōng (郭林宗) often said that Liú Rú (儒) was slow of speech but sharp of mind,
and possessed the quality of a jade tablet of authority.
He was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián),
recommended as a High Talent (gāodì),
and three times promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
During Emperor Huán’s (桓帝) reign,
there were frequent disasters and anomalies.
The Emperor issued an edict widely seeking frank advice.
Liú Rú (儒) submitted a sealed memorial of ten articles,
speaking frankly about successes and failures.
His words were very loyal and earnest.
The Emperor could not accept them,
and sent him out to be the Chancellor of Rènchéng (任城).
After a while,
he was summoned to be an Attendant Counselor (Yìláng).
During Dòu Wǔ’s (竇武) affair,
he was imprisoned and committed suicide.
Jiǎ Biāo (賈彪), courtesy name Wěijié (偉節),
was from Dìnglíng (定陵), Yǐngchuān (潁川).
In his youth, he traveled to the capital.
He was high-minded and fervent,
and was as famous as Xún Shuǎng (荀爽) from the same commandery.
Initially, he served in the province and commandery.
He was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián),
and appointed Magistrate of Xīnxī (新息).
The common people were poor and distressed,
and many did not raise their children.
Jiǎ Biāo (彪) strictly regulated this,
making it a crime equivalent to murder.
There was a bandit who robbed and harmed people south of the city,
and a woman who killed her child north of the city.
Jiǎ Biāo (彪) went out to investigate the cases,
but his clerks wanted to go south.
Jiǎ Biāo (彪) angrily said:
“Bandits harming people
is common sense,
but a mother and child killing each other
is against Heaven and violates the Way!”
He then drove his carriage northward
to investigate that crime.
When the bandits south of the city heard of this,
they also bound themselves and surrendered.
Within a few years,
thousands of people raised their children.
All said,
“Chief Jiǎ’s (賈父) achievement,”
and if a boy was born, he was named
“Jiǎ Zǐ (賈子),”
and if a girl was born, she was named
“Jiǎ Nǚ (賈女).”
In the ninth year of Yánxī [166 CE],
the partisan proscription began.
Tàiwèi Chén Fān argued against it but could not succeed.
The court officials felt a chill in their hearts,
and no one dared to speak again.
Biāo (Jiǎ Biāo) said to his comrades:
“If I do not go west,
this great disaster will not be resolved.”
So he entered Luòyáng
and persuaded the Chéngmén Xiàowèi Dòu Wǔ and the Shàngshū Huò Xù.
Wǔ and others pleaded for them,
and Huán Dì consequently granted a general amnesty to the partisans.
Lǐ Yīng was released
and said:
“My escape from this
was due to Jiǎ Shēng’s (Jiǎ Biāo's) plan.”
Earlier, Cén Zhì had fled due to the partisan proscription,
and many friends and relatives harbored him,
but Biāo alone closed his gate and did not admit him.
At the time, people looked to him with expectation.
Biāo said:
“The saying goes, ‘Act according to the times,
and do not implicate later generations.’
Gōng Xiào (Cén Zhì) provoked conflict by pressuring the sovereign,
bringing this calamity upon himself.
Since I could not wield a spear to confront him,
how could I, on the contrary, shelter and conceal him?”
Thereupon, everyone submitted to his judiciousness.
Due to the partisan proscription,
he eventually died at home.
Originally,
Biāo had three brothers,
all with high reputations,
but Biāo was the most outstanding.
Thus, the world called them:
“The three tigers of the Jiǎ clan,
Wěijié (Jiǎ Biāo) is the fiercest.”
Hé Yǒng, courtesy name Bóqiú,
was a native of Xiāngxiāng, Nányáng.
In his youth, he studied in Luòyáng.
Although Yǒng was a latecomer,
Guō Línzōng, Jiǎ Wěijié, and others befriended him,
and he became famous in the Tàixué.
His friend Yú Wěigāo had a father's vendetta yet to be avenged,
and was gravely ill, nearing his end.
Yǒng went to visit him,
and Wěigāo wept as he recounted his story.
Yǒng was moved by his righteousness,
avenged him,
and poured wine on his tomb with his head.
When Chén Fān and Lǐ Yīng were defeated,
Yǒng, being on good terms with Fān and Yīng,
was consequently framed by the eunuchs.
He changed his name
and fled to hide in Rǔnán.
Wherever he went, he befriended the local gentry and heroes,
and gained renown in the regions of Jīng and Yù.
Yuán Shào admired him
and secretly exchanged visits with him,
forming a bond of mutual support.
At this time, the partisan proscription arose,
and many throughout the land suffered from its calamity.
Yǒng often secretly entered Luòyáng
to consult and plan with Shào.
For those who were in dire straits and imprisoned,
he sought aid and rescue
to relieve their suffering.
For those who were about to be arrested,
he devised various stratagems
to enable them to escape and hide,
and many were completely saved.
When the partisan proscription was lifted,
Yǒng was appointed to the Sīkōng Office.
Whenever the Three Offices held a meeting,
everyone deferred to Yǒng’s leadership.
He was successively promoted.
When Dǒng Zhuó held power,
he compelled Yǒng to become his Zhǎngshǐ.
Yǒng feigned illness and did not accept the post,
but instead conspired with Sīkōng Xún Shuǎng, Sītú Wáng Yǔn, and others against Zhuó.
It happened that Shuǎng died,
and Yǒng was implicated by Zhuó in another matter,
dying of grief and indignation.
Earlier,
when Yǒng saw Cáo Cāo,
he exclaimed:
“The Hàn dynasty is about to perish;
the one who will bring peace to the world must be this man.”
Cāo esteemed him for this.
He once said,
“Xún Yù of Yǐngchuān
is an instrument for a king's aide.”
When Yù became Shàngshū Lìng,
he sent someone west to welcome his uncle Shuǎng,
and also brought Yǒng’s body,
burying it beside Shuǎng’s tomb.
Eulogy: The Wèi river is made turbid by the Jīng,
jade is made pure by pebbles.
The natures of things are distinct,
likes and dislikes follow their form.
Orchids and stinking herbs cannot coexist,
waxing and waning constantly incline.
I only regret that fragrant ointment,
is burned to light a lamp.
Biography of Guō Fú Xǔ, Chapter Fifty-Eight
Guō Tài, courtesy name Línzōng,
was a native of Jièxiū, Tàiyuán.
