His family was poor and humble for generations.
He became an orphan early,
and his mother wanted to make him serve in the county court.
Línzōng said:
“How can a great man engage in the service of a petty official?”
So he declined.
He went to study with Qū Bóyàn in Chénggāo,
and after three years, he completed his studies,
thoroughly understanding the ancient books.
He was good at discussion
and had a beautiful voice and manner.
He then traveled to Luòyáng.
He first met Hénán Yǐn Lǐ Yīng,
who greatly admired him
and befriended him.
Thereupon, his fame shook the capital.
Later, when he returned to his hometown,
scholars in official attire saw him off to the river,
with thousands of carriages.
Línzōng alone crossed the river in the same boat as Lǐ Yīng.
The many guests watched them,
thinking they were immortals.
Sītú Huáng Qióng summoned him,
and Tàicháng Zhào Diǎn recommended him as a man of virtue.
Someone advised Línzōng to enter official service,
to which he replied:
“At night, I observe the celestial phenomena;
by day, I examine human affairs.
What Heaven rejects
cannot be supported.”
So he did not respond to any summons.
He was discerning in recognizing people
and enjoyed encouraging and instructing scholars.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
with a majestic appearance,
dressed in loose robes and wide belts,
traveling throughout the commanderies and states.
Once, while traveling between Chén and Liáng, he encountered rain,
and one corner of his headcloth became askew.
People at the time deliberately folded one corner of their headcloths,
calling it
“Línzōng's headcloth.”
Such was the admiration he commanded.
Someone asked Fàn Pāng of Rǔnán:
“What kind of person is Guō Línzōng?”
Pāng replied:
“In reclusion, he does not abandon his kin;
in integrity, he does not cut himself off from the world.
The Son of Heaven cannot command him as a subject,
nor can the feudal lords befriend him.
I know nothing else.”
Later, he suffered the sorrow of his mother's death
and was praised for his extreme filial piety.
Although Línzōng was skilled in human relations,
he did not engage in dangerous words or sharp criticisms,
thus the eunuchs who controlled the government could not harm him.
When the partisan proscription arose,
many famous scholars suffered its harm,
but only Línzōng and Yuán Hóng of Rǔnán escaped.
He then closed his gate and taught,
with thousands of disciples.
In the first year of Jiànníng [168 CE],
Tàifù Chén Fān and Dàjiàngjūn Dòu Wǔ were harmed by the eunuchs.
Línzōng wept for them in the wilderness,
grief-stricken.
Afterwards, he sighed:
“‘When the men depart,
the state is ruined.’
‘See where the crow alights,
not knowing on whose roof’
it will land.”
The following spring,
he died at home,
at the age of forty-two.
Over a thousand scholars from all directions
came to attend his funeral.
His comrades jointly carved a stone and erected a stele,
with Cài Yōng composing the inscription.
Afterwards, he said to Lú Zhí of Zhuó Jùn:
“I have written many stele inscriptions,
all of which cause me some shame,
but only for Guō Yǒudào do I feel no shame.”
His recognition and promotion of scholars
were always as he assessed them.
Later, those who enjoyed such matters
sometimes added to and exaggerated them,
hence many flowery and unsubstantiated phrases,
also resembling books of divination.
Now, I record those cases where his predictions were clearly effective,
at the end of this chapter.
Zuǒ Yuán
was a native of Chénliú.
He was a student of the commandery,
but committed an offense and was expelled.
Línzōng once met him on the road,
and offered him wine and food to comfort him.
He said:
“In the past, Yán Zhuōjù was a great bandit of Liángfǔ,
and Duàn Gānmù was a great horse-trader of the state of Jìn,
yet they eventually became loyal ministers of Qí
and famous worthies of Wèi.
Qú Yuàn and Yán Huí still could not be without fault,
how much more so the rest?
Be careful not to harbor resentment,
but rather blame yourself.”
Yuán accepted his words and left.
Some people criticized Línzōng for not cutting off ties with evil people.
He replied:
“If people are not benevolent,
and you hate them too much,
it leads to chaos.”
Later, Yuán suddenly nursed a grudge again,
and gathered followers intending to retaliate against the students.
On that day, Línzōng was at the academy,
and Yuán, ashamed of his previous words,
therefore stopped and left.
Later, when the matter was exposed,
everyone admired and submitted to him.
Máo Róng, courtesy name Jìwěi,
was a native of Chénliú.
When he was over forty years old,
he was plowing in the fields.
At that time, he and his peers were sheltering from the rain under a tree.
Everyone else sat sprawled out facing each other,
but Róng alone sat upright and was even more respectful.
Línzōng, passing by, saw him and found him extraordinary,
so he spoke with him,
and then asked to stay overnight.
The next morning,
Róng killed a chicken to prepare a meal.
Línzōng thought it was prepared for him,
but it was actually served to his mother.
He himself ate coarse vegetables with his guest.
Línzōng rose and bowed, saying:
“You are truly worthy!”
Then he encouraged him to study,
and he eventually achieved virtue.
Mèng Mǐn, courtesy name Shúdá,
was a native of the Yáng clan of Jùlù.
He resided as a guest in Tàiyuán.
He was carrying a rice steamer, and it fell to the ground.
He did not look back and left.
Línzōng saw this and asked his reason.
He replied:
“The steamer is already broken,
what good is looking at it?”
Línzōng found him extraordinary because of this,
and then encouraged him to travel and study.
Ten years later, he became famous,
and all Three Dukes invited him,
but he did not yield.
Yǔ Chéng, courtesy name Shìyóu,
was a native of Yānlíng, Yǐngchuān.
When young, he served in the county court as a gatekeeper.
Línzōng saw and promoted him,
encouraging him to travel and study for an official position,
so he became a servant for various students.
Later, he was able to lecture and discuss.
Considering his humble origins,
he always took a lower seat.
Students and erudites all came to him to check their understanding and ask questions,
thus, in the academy, the lower seat became honorable.
Later, he was invited to serve but did not rise,
and was called
“Zhēngjūn.”
Sòng Guǒ, courtesy name Zhòngyǐ,
was a native of Fúfēng.
His nature was light-hearted and fierce,
and he loved to seek revenge on people,
which was detested by the commandery and county.
Línzōng then instructed him in righteous ways,
and warned him of disaster and ruin.
Guǒ felt remorse,
bowed his head and confessed his faults,
and then reformed himself.
Later, he became known for his fierce integrity,
was invited to a ducal office,
and served as Attendant Censor and Governor of Bīngzhōu,
bringing transformation wherever he went.
Jiǎ Shú, courtesy name Zǐhòu,
was a fellow villager of Línzōng.
Although his family had held high positions for generations,
his nature was dangerous and harmful,
and the villagers suffered from him.
When Línzōng was in mourning for his mother,
Shú came to offer condolences.
Soon after, Sūn Wēizhí of Jùlù also arrived.
Wēizhí found it strange that Línzōng, being a worthy man, accepted condolences from an evil person,
and, feeling puzzled, did not enter but left.
Línzōng pursued him and apologized, saying:
“Jiǎ Zǐhòu is indeed of vicious character,
but he has cleansed his heart and turned towards goodness.
Confucius did not reject the people of Hùxiāng,
therefore I allowed him to enter.”
Shú heard this,
reformed his faults and disciplined himself,
and eventually became a good man.
When there were troubles or misfortunes in the village,
Shú would always exert himself to help,
and was praised by the people of the district.
Shǐ Shūbīn
was a native of Chénliú.
In his youth, he had a great reputation.
Línzōng saw him and told others:
“A wall with a high top and a low foundation,
even if gained, will surely be lost.”
Later, he indeed ruined his reputation due to biased and twisted discussions.
Huáng Yǔn, courtesy name Zǐ'ài,
was a native of Jìyīn.
He was known for his outstanding talent.
Línzōng saw him and said:
“You have extraordinary talent,
enough to become a great vessel.
However, I fear that you will not firmly uphold the Way,
and will lose it.”
Later, Sītú Yuán Wěi wanted to arrange a marriage for his niece.
He saw Yǔn and sighed:
“To have a son-in-law like this is enough.”
Yǔn heard this and dismissed his wife, Lady Xiàhóu.
The wife said to her mother-in-law:
“Now I am about to be divorced,
and will bid a long farewell to the Huáng family.
I beg to gather my relatives for a meeting,
to express the feelings of parting.”
Thereupon, a large gathering of over three hundred guests assembled.
The wife sat in the middle,
rolled up her sleeves, and enumerated fifteen hidden and foul misdeeds of Yǔn.
Having finished speaking,
she boarded a carriage and left.
Yǔn was consequently disgraced at that time.
Xiè Zhēn, courtesy name Zǐwēi,
was a native of Shàolíng, Rǔnán.
He and Biān Ràng of Chénliú were both good at discussion,
and both had great reputations.
Whenever they visited Línzōng together,
it was never less than several days and nights.
Línzōng said to his disciples:
“These two have abundant talent,
but neither enters the Way,
what a pity!”
Later, Zhēn did not adhere to minor conduct,
and was scorned by his contemporaries.
Ràng, for lightly insulting Cáo Cāo,
was killed by Cāo.
Wáng Róu, courtesy name Shúyōu,
and his younger brother Zé,
courtesy name Jìdào,
were natives of Jìnyáng County, in the same commandery as Línzōng.
The brothers, as young children, visited Línzōng together,
to inquire about what talents and conduct were appropriate for them.
Línzōng said:
“Shúyōu should become prominent through official advancement,
and Jìdào should become accomplished through classical studies.
However, if they deviate from their path and change their pursuits,
they will not achieve it.”
Later, it turned out as he had said:
Róu became Protector of the Xiongnu and Colonel,
and Zé became Administrator of Dàijùn.
He also recognized Zhāng Xiàozhòng among herders,
knew Fàn Tèzǔ from his postal service duties,
and summoned Gōngzǐ and Xǔ Wěikāng, who were both butchers,
and Sīmǎ Zǐwēi, whom he promoted from the ranks of soldiers.
And sixty others, including Guō Chángxìn, Wáng Chángwén, Hán Wénbù, Lǐ Zǐzhèng, Cáo Zǐyuán of the same commandery, Zhōu Kāngzǐ of Dìngxiāng, Wáng Jìrán of Xīhé, Qiū Jìzhì of Yúnzhōng, Hǎo Lǐzhēn,
all became famous.
A commentary says: Zhuāng Zhōu said,
“Human nature is more treacherous than mountains and rivers,
because their movements can be known,
but hidden obstacles are difficult to ascertain.”
Therefore, deep and profound natures
are deceptive in their emotions and appearances;
the discernment of
“the sagacious”
was difficult even for the Sage Emperors.
Yet Línzōng, whether with the refined or the common, lost none.
Could it be that his enlightened nature had a special guiding principle?
Nevertheless, humble in words and cautious in conduct,
he ultimately flourished in times of obscurity,
and gently and kindly guided
so that scholars yearned to achieve fame.
Even the followers of Mò and Mèng
could not surpass him.
Fú Róng
Whǐmíng, was a man from Jùnyí,
Chénliú.
As a youth he served as a Dūguān official,
but ashamed of it,
he resigned and left.
Later, he studied at the Imperial Academy,
and served Lǐ Yīng, the Shǎofǔ, as his teacher.
Lǐ Yīng was lofty and simple in character.
Whenever he met Fú Róng,
he would dismiss other guests
to listen to his discussions.
Fú Róng, with his head wrapped in a cloth and his sleeves rolled up,
spoke eloquently like clouds,
and Lǐ Yīng would often cup his hands and sigh in admiration.
When Guō Línzōng first arrived in the capital,
at the time few people knew him.
Fú Róng, upon seeing him, admired him greatly,
and thus introduced him to Lǐ Yīng,
whereupon he became known.
At that time, Jìn Wénjīng from Hánzhōng and Huáng Zǐ'ài from Liángguó,
both relying on their talent and wisdom,
flaunted themselves in the capital,
feigning illness and not receiving anyone.
Good-natured scholar-officials in Luòyáng,
hearing of their reputation,
would sit at their gates inquiring after their health,
yet still could not see them.
Those recommended or summoned by the Sāngōng
would always inquire about them,
and based on their praise or criticism,
decided who to promote or dismiss.
Fú Róng discerned that they were not genuine,
so he went to the Imperial Academy
and met Lǐ Yīng, saying:
"These two men have no known conduct,
yet they present themselves as heroes,
leading the high officials to inquire about their health,
and royal ministers to sit at their gates.
I fear that their minor tricks will undermine righteousness
and their empty reputations will deviate from reality.
It is particularly appropriate to investigate this."
Lǐ Yīng agreed.
From then on, the reputation of the two men gradually declined,
and their followers diminished.
Within a few days,
they fled in shame and regret.
Later, they indeed became frivolous individuals,
and were both dismissed due to crimes.
Fú Róng's reputation grew even more.
He received invitations and respectful requests from the provinces and commanderies,
was recommended as Xiàolián,
and repeatedly summoned by the public offices,
but he did not accept any of them.
The Grand Administrator Fēng Dài was renowned,
and upon taking office,
invited Fú Róng to meet him.
Fú Róng went once,
and recommended Fàn Rǎn, Hán Zhuó, and Kǒng Zhòu, three gentlemen from the commandery,
and then excused himself due to illness, severing ties.
Later, when the Factional Prohibitions occurred,
he was also implicated and banned from office.
When his wife died,
he was too poor to afford a funeral.
The villagers wanted to provide a coffin and funeral clothes for him,
but Fú Róng refused to accept.
He said:
"In ancient times, the deceased
were buried in the wilderness.
Only a wife and children can fulfill one's will;
just bury her in the earth, that is all."
Tián Shèng,
courtesy name Zhòngxiàng,
from the same commandery as Fú Róng,
shared a liking with Guō Línzōng,
and was also known for recognizing talent.
He lived a life of leisure, never taking office,
and both died of old age.
Xǔ Shào,
courtesy name Zǐjiāng, was a man from Píngyú,
Rǔnán.
In his youth, he upheld a strict sense of integrity,
was fond of human character assessment,
and recognized many talents.
Figures like Fán Zǐzhāo and Hé Yángshì
all gained fame in the world.
Therefore, when people spoke of selecting worthy individuals,
they all mentioned Xǔ and Guō.
Initially, he served as the Gōngcáo of the commandery.
The Grand Administrator Xú Qióu greatly respected him.
Everyone in the office, hearing that Zǐjiāng was an official,
changed their conduct and adorned their actions.
Yuán Shào,
a powerful and chivalrous member of a ducal family from the same commandery,
returned from his post as the Prefect of Púyáng
with a very grand retinue.
When he was about to enter the commandery's borders,
he dismissed his guests,
saying: "How can Xǔ Zǐjiāng see my lavish carriage and attire?"
Thus, he returned home in a single carriage.
Xǔ Shào once visited Yǐngchuān,
where he frequently associated with respected elders,
but he never called on Chén Shí.
Also, when Chén Fán returned for his wife's funeral,
all the villagers came,
but Xǔ Shào alone did not go.
Someone asked him the reason,
and Xǔ Shào replied:
"Tàichéng's path is broad;
if broad, it is difficult to encompass everyone.
Zhòngjǔ's character is severe;
if severe, it has few connections.
Therefore, I did not visit them."
Such was his extensive judgment.
When Cáo Cāo was still obscure,
he often humbly offered generous gifts,
seeking Xǔ Shào's assessment of him.
Xǔ Shào despised him and refused to respond.
Cáo Cāo then seized an opportunity to threaten Xǔ Shào.
Xǔ Shào, having no choice,
said:
"You are an able villain in a peaceful world,
and a hero in a chaotic age."
Cáo Cāo was greatly pleased and left.
Xǔ Shào's paternal grand-uncle Jìng,
Jìng's son Xùn,
and Xùn's son Xiàng
all became Sāngōng.
Xiàng, by being skilled at flattering the eunuchs,
thereby achieved the position of Táisī and was enfeoffed as a Marquis.
He repeatedly sent invitations to Xǔ Shào.
Xǔ Shào detested his despicable conduct
and never called on him.
Lǐ Kuí, a man from Xǔ Shào's district,
was brave, upright, and high-spirited.
Xǔ Shào initially thought well of him,
but later found fault with him.
He also had disagreements with his cousin Jìng,
and public opinion at the time therefore thought less of him.
Initially,
Xǔ Shào and Jìng both had high reputations,
and enjoyed discussing and evaluating people in their hometown.
Each month they would change their classifications,
thus a custom arose in Rǔnán
called "Yuèdàn Píng"
(Monthly Evaluations).
Sīkōng Yáng Biāo summoned him,
and recommended him as Fāngzhèng and Dūnpiáo.
He was also summoned by the court,
but he accepted none of these.
Someone advised Xǔ Shào to take office,
to which he replied:
"At present, the way of the petty man prevails,
and the royal house is about to fall into chaos.
I wish to escape to Huáihǎi
to save my family, old and young."
So he went south to Guǎnglíng.
The Inspector of Xúzhōu, Táo Qiān, treated him very generously.
Xǔ Shào felt uneasy,
and told his followers:
"Táo Gōngzǔ outwardly seeks fame,
but inwardly is not genuine.
Although he treats me well,
his favor will inevitably wane.
It is better to leave him."
So he went to join the Inspector of Yángzhōu, Liú Yáo, at Qū'ā.
Afterwards, Táo Qiān indeed arrested many exiled scholars.
When Sūn Cè pacified Wú,
Xǔ Shào and Liú Yáo fled south to Yùzhāng and died,
at the age of forty-six.
His elder brother Qián was also famous;
the people of Rǔnán called the Abyss of Píngyú "two dragons."
Eulogy says: Línzōng cherished his talents,
his discernment was profound in evaluation.
Early he circulated widely,
always speaking of the way of the times.
Fú Róng discerned truth,
Zǐjiāng knew human character.
They upheld integrity and cherished shame,
and both were hesitant.
Biography of Dòu and Hé, Chapter 59.
Dòu Wǔ,
courtesy name Yóupíng, was a man from Pínglíng,
Fúfēng, and a great-great-grandson of Dài Hóu Róng of Ānfēng.
His father, Fèng,
was the Grand Administrator of Dìngxiāng.
In his youth, Dòu Wǔ was known for his virtuous conduct and scholarship.
He often taught in the Great Marsh,
not involving himself in current affairs,
and his reputation was prominent west of the pass.
In the eighth year of Yánxī,
his eldest daughter was chosen to enter the Yètíng.
Emperor Huán considered her a guìrén,
and he was appointed Wǔ Lángzhōng.
That winter,
the guìrén was made empress.
Wǔ was promoted to Yuèqí Xiàowèi,
enfeoffed as the Marquis of Huáilǐ,
with five thousand households.
The winter of the next year,
he was appointed Chéngmén Xiàowèi.
In office, he frequently invited renowned scholars,
maintained personal integrity, hated evil,
and accepted no gifts or bribes.
His wife and children had barely enough food and clothing.
At this time, Qiāng and Mán tribes raided and caused difficulties;
the harvest was poor, and the people starved.
Wǔ took the rewards and grants from the two palaces
and distributed them all to the students of the Tàixué,
and also transported provisions and food on the roads
to distribute to the poor.
His nephew Shào
was Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng,
naturally careless, extravagant, and simple.
Wǔ frequently admonished and warned him sternly,
but he still did not grasp it.
So Wǔ submitted a memorial requesting Shào's dismissal from his post,
and also blamed himself for failing to instruct him,
stating that he should be punished first.
From this, Shào became more disciplined,
and no one, great or small, dared to transgress.
At that time, national governance suffered many failings;
inner palace officials monopolized favor.
Lǐ Yīng, Dù Mì, and others were interrogated and arrested for the "Partisan Prohibition" incident.
In the first year of Yǒngkāng,
he submitted a memorial advising, saying:
"I have heard that enlightened rulers do not shrink from critical words,
to probe the truth of hidden matters;
and loyal ministers do not fear the peril of remonstrance,
to express fully the myriad affairs.
This is why ruler and minister prosper together,
and their fame spreads for a hundred generations.
I am fortunate to have encountered an era of brilliant enlightenment,
and met the transforming influence of civil and military virtues.
How dare I cling to my salary, escape blame,
and not exhaust my sincerity!
Your Majesty, having first come from a feudal state,
ascended the sacred throne,
and the world was at ease and joyful,
believing that a restoration was at hand.
Since your enthronement,
I have not heard of any good governance.
Although Liáng, Sūn, Kòu, and Dèng may have been punished and exterminated,
the Chángshì and Huángmén officials continue to cause calamity and oppression,
deceiving and misleading Your Majesty,
competing in their cunning and treachery,
arbitrarily creating regulations,
and falsely ennobling unworthy individuals.
Court affairs daily decline,
and treacherous ministers daily grow stronger.
Reflecting on the Western capital's indulgence of the Wáng clan,
with sycophants holding power,
ultimately led to the loss of the empire.
If now we do not consider the errors of previous events,
and again follow the path of the overturned carriage,
I fear the calamity of the Second Emperor
will surely recur,
and the treachery of Zhào Gāo
will come in the morning or evening.
Recently, the treacherous minister Láo Xiū
fabricated the 'Partisan Prohibition' charges,
and consequently arrested and interrogated former Sīlì Xiàowèi Lǐ Yīng, Tàipú Dù Mì, Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Chén Xiáng, Tàiwèi Yuán Fàn Pāng, and others,
implicating hundreds of people,
who have been detained for a long time,
with no evidence of wrongdoing.
I believe Yīng and the others upheld loyalty and integrity,
intending to manage the imperial house.
These are truly Your Majesty's assistants like Jì, Kuí, Yī, and Lǚ.
Yet they have been falsely slandered and framed by treacherous ministers and villainous sons,
causing chilling despair throughout the empire,
and disappointment across the seas.
I implore Your Majesty to pay attention and clarify the situation,
and promptly release them,
to satisfy the yearning hearts of both men and spirits.
I have heard that ancient enlightened rulers
must have worthy assistants
to perfect the path of governance.
Currently, the close ministers in the Censorate,
Shàngshū Lìng Chén Fān,
Púyè Hú Guǎng,
Shàngshū Zhū Yù, Xún Gǔn,
Líu Yòu, Wèi Lǎng, Líu Jǔ, Yǐn Xūn, and others,
are all loyal gentlemen of the state,
and excellent assistants of the court.
The Shàngshū Láng Zhāng Líng, Guī Hào, Yuàn Kāng, Yáng Qiáo, Biān Sháo, Dài Huī, and others,
are accomplished in both literary skill and moral integrity,
and are clear and discerning in national laws.
In both internal and external offices,
many talents are arrayed.
Yet Your Majesty entrusts power to close attendants,
exclusively establishing gluttons for power,
who govern prefectures and commanderies externally,
and internally manage the innermost core.
It is appropriate to successively demote and dismiss them,
investigate their crimes and punish them,
suppress and seize the enfeoffments of eunuchs who deceive the state,
investigate their baseless slanders and crimes of deception,
trust loyal and good people,
impartially judge right and wrong,
so that the praise and criticism of the upright and the perverse
each receive their due,
cherish the officials appointed by heaven,
and only bestow positions upon the worthy.
If this is done,
signs of misfortune can be dispelled,
and heavenly blessings can be awaited.
Recently, there have been sightings of auspicious grain, spirit ganoderma, and a yellow dragon.
However, auspicious omens arise only from worthy gentlemen,
and blessings truly come from good people.
When there is virtue, it is an auspicious omen;
without virtue, it is a disaster.
What Your Majesty is doing
is not in accordance with Heaven's will,
and should not be celebrated."
After the memorial was presented,
he then, citing illness, requested to return his seals of Chéngmén Xiàowèi and Marquis of Huáilǐ.
The Emperor did not permit it,
but an imperial edict was issued to pardon Lǐ Yīng, Dù Mì, and others.
From the prisons of Huángmén Běisì, Ruòlú, and Dūnèi,
all prisoners whose crimes were minor were released.
That winter, the Emperor died
without an heir.
Wǔ summoned the Shìyùshǐ Líu Shū from Héjiān,
and consulted him about worthy princes and marquises in his kingdom.
Shū recommended Jǐedú Tínghóu Hóng.
Wǔ entered and reported this to the Empress Dowager,
and consequently Hóng was summoned and enthroned,
becoming Emperor Líng.
Wǔ was appointed Dà Jiāngjūn,
and always resided within the forbidden palace.
After the Emperor was enthroned,
his merit for determining the succession was discussed,
and Wǔ was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Wénxǐ;
his son Jī was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wèiyáng
and appointed Shìzhōng;
his nephew Shào was enfeoffed as Marquis of Hù
and promoted to Bùbīng Xiàowèi;
Shào's younger brother Jìng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīxiāng
and appointed Shìzhōng,
overseeing the Yǔlín Zuǒqí.
Once Wǔ assisted in court governance,
he constantly harbored the intention of punishing and eliminating the eunuchs.
Tàifù Chén Fān also had long planned this.
At that time, they met together in the court hall.
Fān privately said to Wǔ:
"The Zhōng Chángshì Cáo Jié, Wáng Fǔ, and others
have manipulated state power since the previous emperor's time,
corrupting and bringing chaos throughout the empire.
The common people are agitated,
attributing blame to them.
If Jié and the others are not executed now,
it will be difficult to deal with them later."
Wǔ deeply agreed with this.
Fān was greatly pleased,
and pushed his mat with his hand and stood up.
Wǔ then recruited his like-minded colleague Yǐn Xūn as Shàngshū Lìng,
Líu Yú as Shìzhōng,
Féng Xù as Túují Xiàowèi;
he also summoned renowned scholars who had been dismissed from across the empire: former Sīlì Lǐ Yīng, Zōngzhèng Líu Měng, Tàipú Dù Mì, Lújiāng Tàishǒu Zhū Yù, and others,
to serve at court;
he invited former Yuèsuí Tàishǒu Xún Yì to be Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
and appointed Chén Shí of Yǐngchuān as his subordinate: together they devised plans.
Thus, the heroic and outstanding talents of the empire,
knowing his intentions,
all craned their necks and stood on tiptoe,
eager to exert their wisdom and strength.
In the fifth month, there was a solar eclipse.
Chén Fán again said to Dòu Wǔ:
“Formerly, Xiāo Wàngzhī was troubled by one Shí Xiǎn;
more recently, Li, Dù, and other gentlemen had misfortune extend to their wives and children.
How much more so now, with dozens of Shí Xiǎn-like individuals!
I, Fán, at the age of eighty,
wish to eliminate this harm for the general.
Now, you can take advantage of the solar eclipse
to dismiss the eunuchs,
thereby averting the celestial anomaly.
Also, Zhào Fūrén and the female court scribes
are disrupting the empress dowager morning and night;
it is urgent that they be removed and cut off.
Only the general must consider this.”
Dòu Wǔ then reported to the empress dowager, saying:
“According to precedent,
the Yellow Gates and Regular Attendants should merely attend to matters within the palace,
manage the gates,
and oversee the property of the adjacent offices.
Now, however, they are made to participate in governance and hold heavy authority,
their relatives are widely distributed,
and they specialize in greed and tyranny.
The unrest throughout the empire
is precisely due to this.
They ought all to be executed and abolished
to purify the court.”
The empress dowager said:
“Since the Hàn, this has been the custom for generations.
Only those who are guilty should be executed;
how can all of them be abolished?”
At that time, the Central Regular Attendant Guǎn Bà was rather talented and strategic,
exercising exclusive control within the palace.
Dòu Wǔ first requested the execution of Guǎn Bà and Central Regular Attendant Sū Kāng and others,
and they indeed died.
Dòu Wǔ repeatedly requested the execution of Cáo Jié and others,
but the empress dowager hesitated and could not bear it,
so the matter was not pursued for a long time.
By the eighth month,
the Great White (Venus) appeared in the west.
Liú Yú, who was skilled in celestial observations,
considered it ominous
and submitted a memorial to the empress dowager, saying:
“The Great White has violated the left shaft of Fáng (Scorpio),
and the General's Star has entered Tàiwēi (Leo).
The prognostication is that the palace gates will be closed,
generals and prime ministers will be inauspicious,
and treacherous individuals will be beside the ruler.
I ask that you urgently guard against this.”
He also wrote to Dòu Wǔ and Chén Fán,
stating that the disordered celestial bodies
were inauspicious for high officials
and that a grand plan should be decisively acted upon quickly.
Dòu Wǔ and Chén Fán received the letter and were about to act.
Thereupon, they appointed Zhū Jū as Controller of the Capital,
Liú Yòu as Intendant of Hénán,
and Yú Qí as Prefect of Luòyáng.
Dòu Wǔ then memorialized to dismiss the Prefect of the Yellow Gates, Wèi Biāo,
and replaced him with Shān Bīng, a Lesser Yellow Gate close to him.
He had Shān Bīng memorialize against Zhèng Sāi, the Prefect of Chánglè who was notoriously cunning and wicked,
sending him to the Northern Prison.
Chén Fán said to Dòu Wǔ:
“This fellow should be immediately arrested and killed;
why bother with an investigation?”
Dòu Wǔ did not agree,
and ordered Shān Bīng to jointly interrogate Zhèng Sāi with Yǐn Xūn and Palace Remonstrant Zhù Hé,
whose testimony implicated Cáo Jié and Wáng Fǔ.
Yǐn Xūn and Shān Bīng immediately memorialized to arrest Cáo Jié and others,
and sent Liú Yú to present the memorial internally.
At that time, Dòu Wǔ was staying outside the palace at his residence.
The officials in charge of the Central Secretariat had already informed Zhū Yǔ, the Wǔguān Scribe of Chánglè.
Zhū Yǔ secretly opened Dòu Wǔ's memorial
and cursed, saying:
“Those middle officials who are unrestrained can be executed,
but what crime have we committed
that we should all be exterminated?”
Thereupon, he shouted loudly:
“Chén Fán and Dòu Wǔ have memorialized to the empress dowager to depose the emperor;
this is high treason!”
He then summoned seventeen strong and brave trusted attendants of Chánglè, such as Gòng Pǔ and Zhāng Liàng, that night,
and they drank blood together and swore to execute Dòu Wǔ and the others.
Cáo Jié heard this,
started up in alarm,
and reported to the emperor, saying:
“There is great commotion outside;
please come to the Déyáng Front Hall.”
He ordered the emperor to draw his sword and leap about,
and had his wet nurse Zhào Ráo and others guard him on either side.
He seized the imperial credentials
and closed all forbidden gates.
He summoned the officials of the Secretariat
and, threatening them with drawn swords,
made them draft imperial edicts.
He appointed Wáng Fǔ as Prefect of the Yellow Gates,
and sent him with imperial credentials to the Northern Prison to arrest Yǐn Xūn and Shān Bīng.
Shān Bīng was suspicious
and refused the edict,
so Wáng Fǔ killed him with a spear.
He then killed Yǐn Xūn
and released Zhèng Sāi.
Returning, they jointly coerced the empress dowager
and seized the imperial seals and documents.
He ordered the Central Attendants to guard the Southern Palace,
closed the gates,
and cut off the secret passages.
He sent Zhèng Sāi and others with imperial credentials,
along with Palace Remonstrants and Attendants, to arrest Dòu Wǔ and others.
Dòu Wǔ refused the edict,
raced into the Infantry Camp,
and with Shào, shot and killed the envoys.
He summoned thousands of soldiers from the Northern Army's Five Divisions to encamp below the Capital Pavilion,
and told the soldiers:
“The Yellow Gates and Regular Attendants have rebelled!
Those who exert themselves will be enfeoffed as marquises and heavily rewarded.”
An edict was issued appointing Zhōu Jìng, the Prefect of the Lesser Treasury, as acting General of Chariots and Cavalry,
with imperial credentials,
to lead five divisions of soldiers with the Protector of the Southern Xiongnú, Zhāng Huàn, to suppress Dòu Wǔ.
When the night watch ended,
Wáng Fǔ led over a thousand men from the Tiger Guards, Feathered Forest Guards, Mounted Archery Escort, Commanders, and Sword and Halberd Warriors,
and encamped outside the Zhuquè Side Gate,
joining Zhāng Huàn and the others.
The next morning, the entire army arrayed below the palace gate,
facing Dòu Wǔ.
Wáng Fǔ's forces gradually grew stronger.
He ordered his soldiers to shout loudly to Dòu Wǔ's army:
“Dòu Wǔ has rebelled!
You are all imperial guards,
whose duty is to guard the palace.
Why are you following a rebel?
Those who surrender first will be rewarded!”
The camp officials had always feared and obeyed the middle officials.
Therefore, Dòu Wǔ's army gradually surrendered to Wáng Fǔ.
From dawn until mealtime,
almost all the soldiers had surrendered.
Dòu Wǔ and Shào fled.
The various armies pursued and surrounded them.
They both committed suicide,
and their heads were displayed at the Capital Pavilion in Luòyáng.
Their relatives, guests, and in-laws were arrested
and all executed.
Liú Yú and Féng Shù
also had their clans exterminated.
Dòu Wǔ's family members were exiled to Rìnán,
and the empress dowager was moved to Yúntái Palace.
At this time,
the villainous scoundrels achieved their aims,
and all literati and officials lost their spirit.
Hú Téng of Guìyáng, a clerk in Dòu Wǔ's office,
had studied under Dòu Wǔ since youth.
He alone performed the funeral rites and mourning,
and was consequently subjected to lifelong prohibition from office.
Dòu Fǔ, Dòu Wǔ's grandson,
was two years old at the time
and escaped to safety.
When the matter became known,
Cáo Jié and others vigorously pursued him.
Hú Téng and the clerk Zhāng Chǎng of Nányáng
jointly hid Dòu Fǔ in the Línglíng region,
falsely claiming he had died.
Hú Téng adopted him as his own son
and arranged for him to marry.
Later, he was nominated as Filial and Incorrupt from Guìyáng.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, heard of him and invited him to serve,
making him an Administrator,
and allowed him to revert to the Dòu surname,
reporting the matter to the emperor.
Coincidentally, Liú Biǎo died,
and Cáo Cāo pacified Jīngzhōu.
Dòu Fǔ and his clansmen relocated to Yè,
and he was invited to the Prime Minister's office.
He participated in the campaign against Mǎ Chāo
and was struck by a stray arrow and died.
Initially,
when Dòu Wǔ's mother gave birth to Dòu Wǔ,
she also gave birth to a snake,
which was released into the forest.
Later, when his mother died,
and before her burial,
a large snake emerged from the dense undergrowth,
went directly to the mourning site,
struck the coffin with its head,
its tears and blood flowing.
It bowed and writhed,
as if weeping in sorrow,
and then left after a moment.
At the time, people knew this was an auspicious omen for the Dòu clan.
Téng, courtesy name Zǐshēng.
Initially,
when Emperor Huán made an imperial tour to Nányáng,
he appointed Téng as Supervisor of the Imperial Escort.
The vehicles and cavalry of the dukes, ministers, and imperial relatives numbered in the tens of thousands.
The levies and labor demanded
were immeasurable.
Téng submitted a memorial, stating:
“The Son of Heaven has no outside;
wherever the imperial carriage is present,
that immediately becomes the capital.
I request that the Inspector of Jīngzhōu be ranked with the Commandant of Sīlì,
and I, myself, be equivalent to a Supervisor of the Bureau of State Affairs.”
The Emperor consented.
From then on, there was an atmosphere of solemnity,
and no one dared to make unauthorized requests or desires.
Téng gained renown for this.
After the Dǎnggù (Proscription of Partisans) was lifted,
he rose to the position of Grand Minister of the Court.
Zhāng Chǎng was
the younger brother of Grand Commandant Wēn.
Hé Jìn, courtesy name Suí gāo,
was a native of Wǎn in Nányáng.
His paternal half-sister was selected to enter the imperial harem as a Guìrén (Honored Lady),
and was favored by Emperor Líng.
Jìn was appointed Lángzhōng (Gentleman),
then successively promoted to Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng (Colonel of the Tiger-Bannered Elite),
and later posted as Administrator of Yǐngchuān.
In the third year of Guānghé,
the Guìrén was established as Empress.
Jìn was summoned to the capital
and appointed Shìzhōng (Attendant at Court), Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng (Grand Master of Works), and Hénán Yǐn (Governor of Hénán).
In the first year of Zhōngpíng,
when the Yellow Turban rebels, Zhāng Jiǎo and others, rose up,
Jìn was appointed Grand General,
and commanded the troops of the Left and Right Yǔlín (Feathered Forest) and the Five Battalions to encamp at Dūtíng,
repairing weapons and equipment,
to suppress the capital.
When Mǎ Yuányì, another faction of Zhāng Jiǎo’s party, plotted an uprising in Luòyáng,
Jìn uncovered their conspiracy
and was ennobled as Shènhóu (Marquis of Shèn) for his merit.
In the fourth year,
several thousand bandits in Xíngyáng rose up,
attacking and burning commanderies and counties,
and killing the magistrate of Zhōngmóu County.
An imperial edict ordered Jìn’s younger brother, Miáo, the Governor of Hénán, to attack them.
Miáo defeated the bandits
and returned after pacifying the region.
An imperial edict dispatched an envoy to meet him at Chénggāo,
and he was appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry)
and ennobled as Jìyánghóu (Marquis of Jìyáng).
In the fifth year,
as chaos increasingly spread throughout the land,
observers of atmospheric phenomena believed that the capital would experience a great war,
and blood would flow in both palaces.
The Grand General's Commandant, Xǔ Liáng, and Acting Commandant, Wǔ Dàng, advised Jìn, saying:
“The Grand Duke’s Six Strategies contains instructions for the Son of Heaven commanding troops,
which can overawe the four directions.”
Jìn thought this was a good idea
and reported it to the Emperor.
Thereupon, an imperial edict ordered Jìn to greatly mobilize troops from the four directions
and conduct military exercises below the Pínglèguān (Pavilion of Peaceful Joy).
A large altar was erected,
on which a twelve-layered, five-colored ornate canopy,
ten zhàng high, was placed.
To the northeast of the altar was a small altar,
on which a nine-layered ornate canopy,
nine zhàng high, was placed.
Infantry
and tens of thousands of cavalry were arrayed,
forming camps and battle formations.
The Son of Heaven personally came to review the army,
stationed under the large ornate canopy.
Jìn was stationed under the small ornate canopy.
After the ceremony,
the Emperor personally donned armor and mounted his warhorse,
proclaiming
“Supreme General,”
and circled the formation three times before returning.
An imperial edict ordered Jìn to lead all the troops to encamp below the pavilion.
At this time, eight Colonels of the Western Garden were established.
Jiǎn Shuò, a Xiǎohuángmén (Junior Palace Attendant), was made Colonel of the Upper Army;
Yuán Shào, Colonel of the Tiger-Bannered Elite, was made Colonel of the Central Army;
Bào Hóng, Commandant of Cavalry, was made Colonel of the Lower Army;
Cáo Cāo, a Counselor, was made Colonel Overseeing the Army;
Zhào Róng was made Assistant Colonel of the Army;
Chúnyú Qióng was made Deputy Colonel of the Army;
and there were also Colonels of the Left and Right.
The Emperor, considering Jiǎn Shuò to be strong and possessing military strategy,
particularly trusted and relied on him,
making him the Marshal,
supervising everyone from the Commandant of Sīlì downwards,
and even the Grand General was subordinate to him.
Although Shuò commanded troops in the palace,
he still feared and was jealous of Jìn.
So he conspired with the other regular attendants to persuade the Emperor to send Jìn west to attack Biān Zhāng and Hán Suì.
The Emperor consented,
granting him one hundred chariots and
the axes of the Tiger-Bannered Elite.
Jìn secretly knew of their plot,
so he submitted a memorial requesting to send Yuán Shào east to attack the troops of Xú and Yǎn provinces.
He stated that he would undertake military affairs
only after Shào returned,
thus delaying the departure date.
Initially,
Empress Hé gave birth to Imperial Prince Biàn,
and Consort Wáng gave birth to Imperial Prince Xié.
The ministers requested the establishment of a Crown Prince.
The Emperor considered Biàn to be frivolous and lacking in dignity,
unfit to be a ruler.
However, the Empress was favored,
and Jìn also held significant power,
so he procrastinated in making a decision.
In the sixth year,
the Emperor fell gravely ill
and entrusted Xié to Jiǎn Shuò.
Shuò, having received the Emperor's dying instruction,
and having always been disdainful and jealous of Jìn and his brothers,
when the Emperor died,
Shuò was then in the inner palace
and wished to first execute Jìn and enthrone Xié.
When Jìn entered from outside,
Shuò’s Commandant, Pān Yǐn, who had long been an old friend of Jìn,
met him and winked at him.
Jìn was startled,
raced back to his camp via a side path,
and led his troops to encamp at the residence of the hundred commanderies.
He then claimed illness and did not enter the palace.
Shuò’s plot failed.
Imperial Prince Biàn then ascended the throne.
Empress Dowager Hé presided over the court.
Jìn, along with Grand Tutor Yuán Wěi, assisted in government
and recorded matters of the Grand Minister of the Court.
Jìn had long known that the eunuchs were universally detested.
Additionally, he resented Jiǎn Shuò for plotting against him.
Upon holding court power,
he secretly planned to execute them.
Yuán Shào also had long harbored this intention.
He used Jìn’s close associate, Zhāng Jīn, to persuade him, saying:
“The power of the Palace Attendants has been great for a long time,
and they collude with Empress Dowager Chánglè for illicit gain.
The General should select virtuous and capable individuals anew,
bring order to the empire,
and eliminate this menace to the state.”
Jìn agreed with his words.
Furthermore, because the Yuán clan had enjoyed favor and prominence for generations,
and were respected throughout the land,
and Shào was skilled at nurturing retainers
and capable of employing heroes and outstanding individuals;
his younger cousin, Yù, Colonel of the Tiger-Bannered Elite, also valued chivalry and spirit.
Therefore, Jìn treated them both generously.
He also broadly recruited intelligent and resourceful individuals such as Féng Jì, Hé Yǒng, and Xún Yōu,
and made them his trusted confidants.
Jiǎn Shuò felt insecure and uneasy.
He wrote to Zhào Zhōng and other Regular Attendants, saying:
“The Grand General and his brothers now hold the reins of government and exclusively control the court.
They are now conspiring with the partisans throughout the empire to execute the former Emperor's close attendants
and eradicate us.
It is only because I command the palace guard troops
that they are hesitant for now.
We should now jointly close the inner gate
and swiftly arrest and execute them.”
Guō Shèng, a Regular Attendant,
was from the same commandery as Jìn.
When the Empress Dowager and Jìn gained favor and prominence,
Shèng had been instrumental.
Therefore, Shèng was a trusted confidant of the Hé family.
He then discussed with Zhào Zhōng and others
and did not follow Shuò’s plan,
but instead showed his letter to Jìn.
Jìn then ordered the Head of the Yellow Gates to arrest Shuò
and execute him,
subsequently taking command of his stationed troops.
Yuán Shào (袁紹) again persuaded Jìn (進), saying:
"Previously, Dòu Wǔ (竇武) wished to execute the imperial favorites but was instead harmed by them.
This was because his words were leaked,
and the Five Garrisons and all the officials feared and obeyed the eunuchs.
Now, the General-in-Chief already holds the great authority of an imperial maternal uncle,
and his brothers all command elite troops.
His subordinate officers and officials are all outstanding and renowned gentlemen,
willing to exert their utmost effort and lives.
The matter is within your grasp;
this is a time blessed by Heaven.
The General-in-Chief should once and for all eliminate this scourge for the empire,
and his name will be passed down through later generations.
Even Shēn Bó (申伯) of Zhōu (周)
is not worth mentioning!
Now, the Great Deceased Emperor is in the front palace.
The General-in-Chief should receive an edict to command the palace guards,
and should not lightly enter or exit the imperial palace."
Jìn (進) very much agreed with this,
so he feigned illness and did not attend the mourning,
nor did he escort the funeral procession to the imperial tomb.
Thereupon, he and Shào (紹) finalized their plans
and reported their strategy to the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager did not listen,
saying:
"Eunuchs have commanded the Forbidden Palace
from ancient times until now;
it is a custom of the Hàn (漢) house
and cannot be abolished.
Moreover, the late emperor has just departed from the world.
How can I, a mere woman, personally work with gentlemen?"
Jìn (進) found it difficult to go against the Empress Dowager's wishes,
and moreover, only wanted to execute those among them who were excessively unrestrained.
Shào (紹) believed that the eunuchs were close to the Supreme One,
issuing commands for ingress and egress,
and if they were not all abolished now,
they would certainly become a future problem.
However, the Empress Dowager's mother, Wǔyáng Jūn (舞陽君), and Miáo (苗) had repeatedly received bribes and gifts from the various eunuchs.
Knowing that Jìn (進) wanted to execute them,
they repeatedly reported to the Empress Dowager,
shielding the eunuchs.
They also said:
"The General-in-Chief is monopolizing power, arbitrarily killing those around the emperor,
seizing authority and weakening the imperial house."
The Empress Dowager suspected this to be true.
The eunuchs in the palace had been there for decades,
ennobled as marquises and favored with high status,
solidifying their influence inside and out.
Jìn (進), newly entrusted with this heavy responsibility,
had always respected and feared them.
Although outwardly he gained a great reputation, inwardly he could not make a decisive move,
so the matter remained unresolved for a long time.
Shào (紹) and others again devised a plan,
to summon many fierce generals from the four directions and various prominent figures,
and have them lead their troops towards the capital city,
to coerce the Empress Dowager.
Jìn (進) agreed.
The Chief Clerk, Chén Lín (陳琳), entered to remonstrate, saying:
"The Yì (易) says 'to pursue a deer without a guide,'
and the proverb says 'to catch a sparrow by covering one's eyes.'
Even a tiny creature cannot be deceived to achieve one's goal,
let alone a great matter of the state;
how can it be established by deceit?
Now, the General-in-Chief commands imperial majesty,
holds military power,
soaring like a dragon and striding like a tiger;
success or failure rests in your mind.
This is like blowing a great furnace to burn away a hair.
To go against principle but conform to the Way
is what Heaven and man follow.
Yet you abandon and release a sharp weapon,
and instead summon external aid.
When large armies gather,
the strong become dominant.
This is what is called holding a shield and spear upside down,
giving control to others.
Success will surely not be achieved,
but only lead to chaos."
Jìn (進) did not listen.
Thereupon, he summoned Dǒng Zhuó (董卓), the former General of the Vanguard, from the west to encamp in the Shànglín Yuàn (上林苑) of Guānzhōng (關中).
He also sent his clerk, Wáng Kuāng (王匡) of Tàishān (太山), to the east to dispatch the strong crossbowmen of his commandery.
He also summoned Qiáo Mào (橋瑁), the Administrator of Dōngjùn (東郡), to encamp at Chénggāo (城皐),
and had Dīng Yuán (丁原), the Commandant of Martial Might, burn Mèngjīn (孟津),
with the fires lighting up the city.
All of them made the extermination of the eunuchs their stated purpose.
The Empress Dowager still did not comply.
Miáo (苗) said to Jìn (進):
"We came together from Nányáng (南陽),
both poor and lowly,
and relied on the inner court to achieve wealth and nobility.
Affairs of state
are not so easy!
Spilled water cannot be collected.
You should deeply reflect on this,
and moreover, maintain harmony with the inner court."
Jìn's (進) resolve became even more hesitant.
Shào (紹), fearing Jìn (進) might change his plan,
coerced him, saying:
"The conspiracy is already formed,
the situation is already exposed.
Delaying the matter will lead to complications.
What more do you, General-in-Chief, wish to wait for,
instead of deciding early?"
Jìn (進) thereupon appointed Shào (紹) as the Administrator of Affairs of the Masters of Writing,
granting him a credential of authority,
with full power to judge and decide;
and Wáng Yǔn (王允), an attendant to the central secretaries, as the Intendant of Hénán (河南).
Shào (紹) had Lùoyáng (洛陽) security officers secretly observe the eunuchs,
and urged Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) and others to hasten their advance by relay post,
intending to move troops to Pínglèguān (平樂觀).
The Empress Dowager then became frightened
and dismissed all the Regular Attendants and Palace Attendants,
sending them back to their residences,
retaining only those Jìn (進) personally trusted
to guard the palace.
All the Regular Attendants and Palace Attendants went to Jìn (進) to apologize,
awaiting his arrangements.
Jìn (進) said to them:
"The world is in turmoil,
precisely because of you gentlemen.
Now Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) is almost here.
Why do you gentlemen not each return to your fiefs early?"
Yuán Shào (袁紹) urged Jìn (進) to make a decision then and there,
even repeatedly.
Jìn (進) did not agree.
Shào (紹) also wrote letters to all the commanderies and states,
falsely proclaiming Jìn's (進) intention,
to have them arrest and prosecute the relatives of the eunuchs.
Jìn's (進) plot had been brewing for days,
and it had somewhat leaked.
The eunuchs, fearing, contemplated a counter-move.
Zhāng Ràng's (張讓) daughter-in-law
was the Empress Dowager's sister.
Ràng (讓) bowed his head to his daughter-in-law, saying:
"This old servant has incurred offense
and ought to return to a private home with my daughter-in-law.
However, having received favor for generations,
I am now about to leave the palace far behind.
My heart is full of reluctance.
I wish to enter service one more time,
to briefly behold the countenances of the Empress Dowager and His Majesty,
and then withdraw to the ditches and valleys;
then I will die without regret."
The daughter-in-law spoke to Wǔyáng Jūn (舞陽君),
who reported it to the Empress Dowager,
and so an edict was issued for all the Regular Attendants to resume their duties.
In the eighth month,
Jìn (進) entered the Chánglè (長樂) Palace to see the Empress Dowager,
requesting the execution of all Regular Attendants and below,
and the selection of officials from the Three Departments to guard the eunuchs' residences.
The eunuchs said to one another:
"The General-in-Chief feigned illness and did not attend the mourning,
nor did he escort the funeral.
Now he suddenly enters the palace. What is his intention?
Will the Dòu (竇) family's affair
happen again?"
Moreover, Zhāng Ràng (張讓) and others sent people to secretly listen,
and they heard all these words.
Thereupon, they, led by Regular Attendants Duàn Guī (段珪) and Bì Lán (畢嵐) and several dozens of others,
carrying weapons, secretly entered through a side gate,
and lay in ambush within the palace.
When Jìn (進) came out,
they then falsely announced an edict from the Empress Dowager to summon Jìn (進).
Upon entering and sitting in the palace gatehouse,
Ràng (讓) and others interrogated Jìn (進), saying:
"The world is in chaos;
it is not solely our fault.
The late emperor and the Empress Dowager once had a disagreement,
almost leading to ruin.
We wept and resolved the matter,
each contributing millions from our family wealth as gifts,
to please His Majesty's heart.
We only wished to rely on your family.
Now you intend to exterminate our entire clan;
is this not excessive?
You say the inner court is corrupt.
Who among the high officials and below is loyal and pure?"
At this, Qú Mù (渠穆), the Supervisor of the Imperial Workshops, drew his sword and killed Jìn (進) in front of the Jiādé (嘉德) Hall.
Ràng (讓), Guī (珪), and others forged an edict,
appointing the former Grand Commandant Fán Líng (樊陵) as Administrator of Affairs of the Masters of Writing,
and Xǔ Xiàng (許相), the Minor Treasurer, as Intendant of Hénán (河南).
The Masters of Writing received the imperial tablet
and suspected it,
saying:
"We request the General-in-Chief to come out and discuss this."
A palace attendant threw Jìn's (進) head to the Masters of Writing,
saying:
"Hé Jìn (何進) conspired to rebel
and has already been executed."
Hé Jìn’s subordinates Wú Kuāng and Zhāng Zhāng,
whom he had always favored,
upon hearing from outside that Jìn had been assassinated,
desired to lead troops into the palace.
The palace gates were shut.
Yuán Shù and Kuāng together hacked and attacked them.
The middle yellow gatekeepers held weapons and guarded the gates.
As dusk fell,
Shù then burned the Nángōng Jiǔlóngmén and the east and west palaces,
intending to intimidate Ràng and the others into coming out.
Ràng and the others entered and reported to the Empress Dowager,
saying, "The Grand General's troops have rebelled,
burned the palace,
and attacked the secretariat gates."
They then led the Empress Dowager, the Son of Heaven, and the Prince of Chénliú,
and also kidnapped the internal officials and attendants,
and fled through a covered walkway to the Běigōng.
Shàngshū Lú Zhí held a spear by a window of the covered walkway,
looking up and reprimanding Duàn Guī.
Duàn Guī and the others were afraid,
and so released the Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager jumped from the walkway and escaped.
Yuán Shào, with his uncle Wěi, issued a false edict to summon Fán Líng and Xǔ Xiàng,
and executed them.
Miáo and Shào then led their troops and encamped below the Zhūquè Què,
captured Zhào Zhōng and others,
and executed them.
Wú Kuāng and others had long resented Hé Miáo for not being of one mind with Jìn,
and further suspected him of conspiring with the eunuchs,
so they ordered the army, saying:
"The one who killed the Grand General is none other than the General of Chariots and Cavalry.
Can the officers and soldiers avenge him?"
Jìn had always been benevolent and kind,
and all the officers and soldiers wept, saying,
"We are willing to die!"
Kuāng then led his troops with Dǒng Zhuó's brother, the Fèngchē Dūwèi Mín, and attacked and killed Miáo,
exposing his corpse in the imperial park.
Shào then closed the Běigōng gates,
marshaled his troops, and hunted down the eunuchs,
killing them all, regardless of age.
Some clean-shaven men were mistakenly killed,
until they revealed their true identities and were then spared.
Over two thousand people [died].
Shào then advanced his troops and forced their way into the palace,
some even climbing onto the roofs of the Duānmén,
to attack the interior of the palace.
Zhāng Ràng, Duàn Guī and the others, cornered and desperate,
then took the Emperor and the Prince of Chénliú, with dozens of others, and walked out of the Gǔmén,
fleeing to Xiǎopíngjīn.
The grandees and ministers all went out to the Pínglè Guān,
but none could follow the Emperor.
Only Shàngshū Lú Zhí rode through the night to the river,
and Wáng Yǔn dispatched the Hénán Zhōngbù Yuàn Mǐn Gòng to follow Zhí.
When Gòng arrived,
he personally drew his sword and killed several men;
the rest jumped into the river and died.
The next day,
the grandees, ministers, and all officials then welcomed the Son of Heaven back to the palace.
Gòng was appointed Lángzhōng
and enfeoffed as Dūtíng Hóu.
Dǒng Zhuó then deposed the Emperor,
and further coerced and killed the Empress Dowager,
and killed Wǔyáng Jūn.
The Hé clan thus perished,
and the Hàn dynasty also fell into disarray from this point.
A commentary says: Dòu Wǔ and Hé Jìn, relying on their status as maternal uncles,
held the power of regency.
Internally, they relied on the authority of the Empress Dowager presiding over the court;
externally, they welcomed the momentum of the heroes rising like a wind.
Yet, in the end, their affairs were ruined by eunuchs,
their bodies died, and their achievements crumbled,
becoming a sorrow for the world.
Was it perhaps that their wisdom was insufficient, but their power excessive?
The tradition says:
"Heaven has long intended to depose Shāng;
you, my lord, shall restore it."
This is why Sòng Xiānggōng was defeated at Hóng.
A eulogy says: Wǔ's birth omen was a snake;
Jìn was originally a butcher.
Only their sister and daughter
brought them into the purple chambers (palace).
The emperor above was muddled, and those below were favored,
people and spirits were moved to resentment.
They were about to correct evil and wickedness,
to fulfill the people's wishes.
But the Dao was blocked,
and the era fell into dire straits.
Biography of Zhèng, Kǒng, Xún, Lieh-chuan 60
Zhèng Tài, courtesy name Gōngyè,
was from Kāifēng, Hénán,
and a great-grandson of Sīnóng Zhòng.
In his youth, he possessed talent and strategy.
At the end of Emperor Líng's reign,
knowing that the world was about to fall into chaos,
he secretly befriended powerful heroes.
His family was rich in wealth,
owning four hundred qǐng of land,
yet his provisions were always insufficient.
His reputation was known east of the mountains.
Initially, he was nominated as Xiàolián,
and invited by the three ducal offices,
and summoned by public carriage,
but he accepted none of them.
When Grand General Hé Jìn became regent,
he summoned and employed famous scholars,
appointing Gōngyè as Shàngshū Shìláng,
and later promoting him to Shìyùshǐ.
When Jìn was about to execute the eunuch officials,
he wanted to summon the Governor of Bīngzhōu, Dǒng Zhuó, for assistance.
Gōngyè said to Jìn:
"Dǒng Zhuó is strong, cruel, and without righteousness,
his ambition insatiable.
If you entrust him with court administration,
and assign him important affairs,
he will indulge his wicked desires
and surely endanger the court.
Your Excellency, with your weighty status as a close relative,
and holding the power of a regent,
should act decisively on your own will
to execute the guilty.
Indeed, you should not rely on Zhuó for aid.
Moreover, delays breed changes,
and the lesson of Yīn is not far away."
He also presented several urgent matters of the time.
Jìn was unable to use his advice,
so he resigned his office and left.
He said to Xún Yōu of Yǐngchuān:
"Hé Gōng is not an easy person to assist."
Jìn was eventually harmed and killed,
and Zhuó indeed caused chaos.
Gōngyè and others, along with Palace Attendant Wǔ Qióng and Zhuó’s Chief Clerk Hé Yóng, all advised Zhuó
to make Yuán Shào the Grand Administrator of Bóhǎi
to prevent the plans of the rebels in Shāndōng.
When the righteous army rose,
Zhuó then gathered the imperial ministers to discuss,
and greatly mobilized troops to suppress them.
None of the officials dared to defy his will.
Gōngyè feared that the multitude of troops would make him more arrogant,
and that his fierce strength would be difficult to control,
so he alone said:
"Governing lies in virtue,
not in numbers."
Zhuó was displeased
and said,
"According to your words,
are soldiers useless then?"
Gōngyè was afraid,
and thus deceptively replied:
"It's not that I mean they are useless;
I just think that Shāndōng does not need such a large army.
If there is any disbelief,
allow me to briefly explain the main points to you, Illustrious Sir.
Currently, Shāndōng has conspired together,
provinces and commanderies are linked,
and the people are agitated,
so they are not weak.
However, since Guāngwǔ,
there has been no alarm in the Central Plains,
the people have been at ease,
and have forgotten warfare for a long time.
Zhòngní said: 'Not instructing people in warfare
is called abandoning them.'
Although their numbers are great,
they cannot cause harm.
This is the first reason.
Illustrious Sir comes from Xīzhōu,
served as a national general in his youth,
is skilled in military affairs,
has often been on battlefields,
and his name shakes the present age.
People hold him in awe and submission.
This is the second reason.
Yuán Běnchū is a son of an imperial minister,
born in the capital.
Zhāng Mèngzhuó is an elder from Dōngpíng,
who does not even peek out of his hall while sitting.
Kǒng Gōngxù
engages in pure talk and high discourse,
able to bring the dry to life and blow life into the dead.
None of them possess military talent,
or the drive of fierce power;
facing the enemy and deciding battles,
they are not your match, Sir.
This is the third reason.
The scholars of Shāndōng are naturally lacking in bravery and fierceness.
They do not possess the courage of Mèng Bēn,
the swiftness of Qìng Jì,
the defense of Liáochéng,
or the strategies of Liáng and Píng,
to be entrusted with a detached force
and be held accountable for success.
This is the fourth reason.
Even if such people existed,
their ranks would be disordered,
and no royal titles would be granted.
If they rely on numbers and boast of their strength,
they will each form separate
camps to observe success or failure,
unwilling to be of one heart and mind,
and advance or retreat together.
This is the fifth reason.
The commanderies of Guānxī
are quite accustomed to military affairs.
Since recent times,
they have often fought against the Qiāng.
Even women still carry halberds and wield spears,
with bows strung and arrows in quivers,
to face those who fight recklessly!
Their victory is certain.
This is the sixth reason.
Furthermore, among the strong and brave of the world,
those whom the people fear
are the people of Bìng and Liáng,
as well as the Xiōngnú, Túgē, Huángzhōng righteous followers, and the eight tribes of the Xīqiāng,
as your claws and fangs,
like driving tigers and rhinoceroses to attack dogs and sheep.
This is the seventh reason.
Moreover, Illustrious Sir's generals and commanders
are all close relatives and trusted confidants,
who have been together for a long time,
with deep affection and trust,
trustworthy in their loyalty,
and reliable in their wisdom.
Using such a solid force
is like a fierce wind sweeping withered leaves.
This is the eighth reason.
Indeed, in battle there are three ways to perish:
those who attack order with chaos perish,
those who attack righteousness with wickedness perish,
and those who attack obedience with rebellion perish.
Now, Illustrious Sir governs the state justly and fairly,
exterminating the eunuchs,
thus establishing loyalty and righteousness.
With these three virtues,
countering those three ways to perish,
carrying out a punitive expedition by imperial command,
who dares to resist him!
This is the ninth reason.
Zhèng Xuán of Dōngzhōu is learned in ancient and modern times,
and models for all gentlemen.
If those generals were to consult their plans,
they would surely know the strengths and weaknesses.
Moreover, Yān, Zhào, Qí, and Liáng were not without prosperity,
yet they were eventually destroyed by Qín;
Wú, Chǔ, and the Seven States were not without numbers,
yet they were ultimately defeated at Xíngyáng.
and excellent trusted aides,
how could they support their plans
and create chaos to prolong the enemy?
It will not be so.
This is the tenth reason.
If what I have presented has even a little merit,
there is no need to conscript soldiers and alarm the world,
causing people burdened by corvée to gather and commit evil,
abandoning virtue and relying on numbers,
thereby diminishing your own prestige."
Zhuó was then pleased,
appointed Gōngyè as a general,
and made him command all armies to attack Guāndōng.
Someone advised Zhuó, saying:
"Zhèng Gōngyè's wisdom and strategy surpass others,
but he is conspiring with external enemies.
Now, to provide him with soldiers and horses,
and let him join his confederates,
I secretly fear for you, Illustrious Sir."
Zhuó then recalled his troops,
and kept him as an Imperial Gentleman.
After Zhuó moved the capital to Cháng'ān,
the world was plagued by famine and chaos,
and many officials did not meet their end naturally.
However, Gōngyè had surplus wealth in his family,
and daily invited guests for grand gatherings with music and entertainment,
providing aid and rescue to many.
He then conspired with Hé Yóng and Xún Yōu to kill Zhuó.
The plot was leaked,
Yóng and others were arrested,
but Gōngyè escaped through Wǔguān and fled
east to Yuán Shù.
Shù appointed him as Inspector of Yángzhōu.
He died on the way
before reaching his post,
at the age of forty-one.
Kǒng Róng, courtesy name Wénjǔ,
was a native of Lǔguó,
and a twentieth-generation descendant of Kǒngzǐ.
His seventh-generation ancestor, Bà,
was a teacher to Emperor Yuán,
and rose to the position of Palace Attendant.
His father, Zhòu,
was the Commander of Tàishān.
Kǒng Róng, when young, possessed extraordinary talent.
At the age of ten,
he accompanied his father to the capital.
At that time, Lǐ Yīng,
the Prefect of Hénán, held himself with an air of solemnity and self-importance,
not casually receiving scholar-guests.
He had issued an order to those outside that unless one was a famous person of the time or belonged to a family with whom his own had long-standing connections,
they were not to be announced.
Kǒng Róng wished to observe Lǐ Yīng,
so he went to Yīng's gate.
He told the gatekeeper:
"I am a junior member of a family connected to Lǐ Jūn for generations."
The gatekeeper reported this.
Lǐ Yīng invited Kǒng Róng in
and asked:
"Did your esteemed ancestors ever have favors or old connections with me?"
Kǒng Róng said:
"Indeed.
My ancestor, Kǒng Fūzǐ, and your ancestor, Lǐ Lǎojūn, shared the same virtue and righteousness,
and were teachers and friends to each other.
Therefore, Róng and you are connected families for generations."
All those seated present could not help but sigh in admiration.
Chén Wěi, a Tàizhōng Dàfū, arrived later.
Those present informed Wěi of the incident.
Wěi said:
"When a person is intelligent and sharp in youth,
they are not necessarily extraordinary when grown up."
Kǒng Róng retorted instantly:
"From what you say,
might it be that you yourself were not intelligent in your youth?"
Lǐ Yīng laughed heartily and said:
"Your esteemed self will surely become a great talent!"
At the age of thirteen,
Kǒng Róng's father passed away.
His grief and emaciation were excessive, beyond what was proper for mourning.
He had to be supported to rise.
The people of the prefecture praised his filial piety.
He had a nature that loved learning,
extensively reading and widely surveying many texts.
Zhāng Jiǎn of Shānyáng was resented by Hóu Lǎn, a Zhōng Chángshì.
Hóu Lǎn published a memorial and sent it to the prefectures and commanderies,
listing Zhāng Jiǎn as wanted for arrest.
Zhāng Jiǎn had an old connection with Kǒng Róng's elder brother, Kǒng Bāo,
so he fled to Kǒng Bāo,
but did not find him.
At that time, Kǒng Róng was sixteen years old.
Zhāng Jiǎn considered him too young and did not confide in him.
Kǒng Róng saw his distressed look
and said:
"Although my brother is away,
can I not take charge for you alone?"
He then let him stay and sheltered him.
Later, the matter was exposed.
The Guóxiàng and others secretly went to capture Zhāng Jiǎn.
Zhāng Jiǎn managed to escape,
but Kǒng Bāo and Kǒng Róng were both arrested and sent to prison.
The two did not know the charge.
Kǒng Róng said:
"It was Róng who harbored and sheltered him,
so I should be charged."
Kǒng Bāo said:
"He came seeking me;
it is not my brother's fault.
I beg to suffer the crime."
The official asked their mother.
The mother said:
"Household matters are managed by the eldest.
I should bear the guilt."
The entire family contended to die for each other.
The commandery and county were perplexed and could not decide,
so they reported the case to the throne for judgment.
The imperial decree ultimately sentenced Kǒng Bāo.
Kǒng Róng thereby gained fame,
achieving renown alongside Táoqiū Hóng of Píngyuán and Biān Ràng of Chénliú.
Though invited by the prefectures and commanderies,
he did not accept any positions.
He was appointed to the staff of Sītú Yáng Cì.
At that time, Yáng Cì was investigating and exposing corrupt officials,
intending to demote and dismiss them. Kǒng Róng frequently brought up the relatives of court eunuchs.
The Shàngshū, fearing pressure from inside the court,
summoned Kǒng Róng, the Yuánshǔ, and reproached him.
Kǒng Róng stated the crimes and evils
without bending or yielding in his words.
Hénán Yǐn Hé Jìn was about to be promoted to Dàjiāngjūn.
Yáng Cì sent Kǒng Róng to present a congratulatory card to Hé Jìn.
He was not admitted in a timely manner,
so Kǒng Róng immediately snatched back the card and returned to the office,
then threw down his resignation and left.
The officials in Hénán felt disgraced by this
and privately sent swordsmen to pursue and kill Kǒng Róng.
A guest spoke to Hé Jìn, saying:
"Kǒng Wénjǔ has a great reputation.
If the General creates an enemy of this man,
then the scholars from all four directions will stretch their necks and leave.
It would be better to treat him with courtesy;
this can demonstrate your broad-mindedness to the world."
Hé Jìn agreed.
After he was appointed, he invited Kǒng Róng to his staff,
recommended him as a Gāodì,
and he became Shìyùshǐ.
Being at odds with Zhào Shè, the Zhōngchéng,
Kǒng Róng pleaded illness and returned home.
Later, he was appointed Yuán to the Sīkōng,
and then made Zhōngjūnhóu.
Within three days of taking office,
he was promoted to Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiāng.
When Dǒng Zhuó was deposing and establishing emperors,
Kǒng Róng would always offer correcting and righteous words
during discussions and responses.
Because he defied Dǒng Zhuó's will,
he was transferred to Yìláng.
At that time, the Yellow Turbans were plundering several provinces,
and Běihǎi was the most heavily attacked by the rebels.
Dǒng Zhuó then subtly influenced the Three Ducal Ministries to collectively recommend Kǒng Róng as Běihǎi Xiàng.
Upon arriving in the commandery, Kǒng Róng
gathered scholars and common people,
raised troops and trained in martial arts,
dispatched urgent proclamations and flying letters,
seeking advice from the provinces and commanderies.
The rebels Zhāng Ráo and others, a multitude of 200,000, returned from Jìzhōu.
Kǒng Róng met them in battle,
but was defeated by Zhāng Ráo,
and so he gathered his scattered troops and defended Zhūxū County.
He gradually reassembled officials and people who had been misled by the Yellow Turbans, some 40,000 men and women,
re-established towns and cities,
set up schools,
promoted Confucian scholarship,
and recommended worthy and talented individuals such as Zhèng Xuán, Péng Qiú, and Bǐng Yuán.
Locals from the commandery, Zhēn Zǐrán and Lín Xiàocún, who were famous but died early,
Kǒng Róng regretted not having met them,
so he ordered that they be honored with sacrificial offerings at the county shrine.
As for others, even if they had but a single good quality,
he treated them all with respect.
For those from the commandery who died without heirs and traveling scholars from other regions who passed away,
he provided coffins and interred them.
At that time, the Yellow Turbans again came to invade and harass.
Kǒng Róng then moved his garrison to Dūchāng,
where he was besieged by the rebel Guǎn Hài.
Kǒng Róng, in dire straits,
dispatched Tàishǐ Cí of Dōnglái to seek aid from Liú Bèi, the Píngyuán Xiàng.
Liú Bèi was astonished and said:
"Kǒng Běihǎi actually knows that there is a Liú Bèi in the world?"
He immediately dispatched 3,000 soldiers to rescue him,
whereupon the rebels dispersed and fled.
At that time, Yuán Shào and Cáo Cāo were both powerful,
but Kǒng Róng did not ally with either.
Zuǒ Chéngzǔ,
claiming to have a strategic plan,
urged Kǒng Róng to form alliances.
Kǒng Róng knew that Yuán Shào and Cáo Cāo ultimately intended to usurp the Hàn dynasty,
and did not wish to associate with them,
so he became angry and killed Zuǒ Chéngzǔ.
Kǒng Róng was proud of his lofty spirit
and aspired to quell the troubles,
but his talent was insufficient and his ambitions too grand,
achieving no success in the end.
After six years in the commandery,
Liú Bèi petitioned to have him appointed as Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān (196 CE),
he was attacked by Yuán Tán.
From spring to summer,
only a few hundred soldiers remained.
Arrows fell like rain,
and spears and halberds clashed at close quarters.
Kǒng Róng leaned on his desk and read,
conversing and laughing as usual.
The city fell that night,
so he fled to Dōngshān,
and his wife and children were captured by Yuán Tán.
When Emperor Xiàn moved the capital to Xǔ,
Kǒng Róng was summoned to be Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng,
then promoted to Shǎofǔ.
Whenever there were court assemblies and discussions,
Kǒng Róng would always present his upright views and settle opinions,
while the Gōngqīng and Dàfū merely put their names down.
Initially,
Grand Tutor Mǎ Rìdī was dispatched on a mission to Shāndōng,
When he reached Huáinán,
he repeatedly showed inclination towards Yuán Shù.
Yuán Shù treated him with contempt,
and thus seized his credentials (imperial staff).
He requested to leave but was not permitted,
and Yuán Shù then tried to force him to become a military commander.
Mǎ Rìdī deeply resented this,
and consequently vomited blood and died.
When his coffin was returned,
the court deliberated on whether to grant him special honors.
Róng alone argued:
"Mǎ Rìdī, with the esteemed position of a Grandee,
wielding the imperial staff as an envoy,
carrying the imperial mandate to directly supervise,
and pacify the Eastern regions,
instead obsequiously flattered a treacherous minister,
and was led by him.
When memorials and proclamations were signed and used,
he consistently placed his name first.
He allied with inferiors and deceived superiors,
serving his lord with treachery.
Formerly, Guó Zuǒ faced the Jìn army without yielding.
Yí Liáo faced a drawn blade with an unperturbed expression.
How can a high minister of the imperial court
use being threatened as an excuse!
Furthermore, Yuán Shù's usurpation and rebellion
was not a matter of a single day or night;
Mǎ Rìdī followed him,
associating with him for over a year.
According to Hàn law, anyone associating with a criminal for three days or more
is presumed to be aware of their intentions.
In the Spring and Autumn Annals, when Lǔ Shūsūn Décén died,
because he did not expose Xiāng Zhòng's crimes,
he was censured by not having his death recorded with a specific day.
The people of Zhèng, in punishing the chaos caused by Yōu Gōng,
hacked apart Zǐ Jiā's coffin.
〔一０〕The sagely emperor, out of compassion for an old minister,
has not yet seen fit to investigate this matter further,
it is inappropriate to grant him special honors."
The court agreed with him.
At that time, many commentators wished to restore corporal punishments.
Róng then proposed:
"In ancient times, when customs were simple and robust,
good and bad were not distinguished,
officials were upright and punishments were fair,
and government had no faults.
When the common people committed crimes,
they all brought it upon themselves.
In later generations, morals declined,
customs and transformations were corrupted and chaotic,
government disturbed their customs,
and laws harmed the people.
Thus it is said: 'When the ruler loses his Way,
the people have long been scattered.'
To now wish to regulate them with ancient punishments,
and cast them into mutilating punishments,
is not what is meant by adapting to the times.
Zhòu cut open the shins of those crossing the ford in the morning;
the world called him without the Way.
In the lands of the Nine Provinces,
there are eighteen hundred lords.
If each of them were to amputate one person,
then there would always be eighteen hundred Zhòu's below.
To seek peaceful customs,
that would not be achievable.
Moreover, those who have suffered punishment,
their thoughts do not dwell on life,
their will is set on death,
most tend towards evil,
and none return to rectitude.
Sùshā brought chaos to Qí;
Yī Lì brought disaster to Sòng;
Zhào Gāo and Yīng Bù
became great scourges of their age.
This cannot stop people from committing wrongdoing,
it merely suffices to prevent people from returning to goodness.
Even one as loyal as Yù Quán,
〔一０〕as trustworthy as Biàn Hé,
〔一一〕as wise as Sūn Bìn,
〔一二〕as wronged as Xiàng Bó,
〔一三〕as talented as Shǐ Qiān,
〔一四〕as accomplished as Zǐ Zhèng,
〔一五〕once subjected to the knife and saw,
will be disdained for the rest of their lives.
〔一六〕This means that Tài Jiǎ's reflection on his faults,
〔一七〕Mù Gōng's dominance over Qín,
〔一八〕Nán Suī's skeletal appearance,
Wèi Wǔ's initial feast,
〔一九〕Chén Tāng's establishment of reliance,
〔二０〕Wèi Shàng's defense of the border,
〔二一〕all would have no further application.
The Hàn (dynasty) opened the path for changing from evil,
it was all for this purpose.
Therefore, a ruler of enlightened virtue,
considers deeply and thoroughly,
curtailing the disadvantages and embracing the advantages,
and does not carelessly reform his policies."
The court approved of this,
and ultimately did not change it.
At this time, Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, failed to provide official tribute,
and committed many acts of usurpation and deceit.
He even performed sacrifices to Heaven and Earth in the suburbs,
and presumptuously made claims to the imperial carriage.
An imperial edict was issued to publicize these matters.
Róng submitted a memorial, stating:
"I humbly hear that Liú Biǎo, who holds the post of Governor of Jīngzhōu, is rebellious and unrestrained,
his actions are lawless,
even performing suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
and imitating the rituals of the altars of land and grain.
Although his depravity and usurpation are extreme,
and his crimes are unforgivable,
regarding the national prestige,
it would be advisable to temporarily conceal it.
Why so?
The Ten Thousand Chariots (the Emperor) is of utmost importance,
the Son of Heaven is supremely revered.
His person is sacred,
the state is a divine vessel.
The distance between the imperial steps is vast,
the boundaries of status and position are absolute,
just as Heaven cannot be ascended by steps,
and the sun and moon cannot be surpassed.
Whenever a petty minister
is said to aspire to it,
if this is made manifest in all directions,
it is not the way to suppress evil sprouts.
I foolishly believe that even with grave offenses,
it is imperative to endure them in secret.
Jiǎ Yì's saying 'to throw at a rat but fear damaging the vessel,'
probably refers to this situation.
Therefore, when Qí's army advanced to Chǔ,
they only demanded the 'bāomáo' grass.
When the royal army was defeated,
they did not record the Jìn people (as victors).
Previously, Yuán Shù's crimes were exposed;
now, if Liú Biǎo's matters are again publicized,
it is like making a lame ewe desire to spy on a high bank,
and a natural barrier can be ascended.
〔一０〕Upon investigation, Liú Biǎo is arrogant and overbearing,
has arbitrarily executed marquises,
obstructed imperial edicts,
stolen and withheld tribute baskets,
〔一一〕summoned chief villains
to protect himself,
and is entirely devoted to a group of rebels,
becoming the primary gathering place for them.
〔一二〕The Gào Dǐng is in the ancestral temple,
what could be more manifest (than his crime)!
〔一三〕Like mulberries falling and tiles crumbling,
his downfall is apparent.
〔一四〕Your humble servant foolishly believes it is advisable to conceal the matter of the suburban sacrifices,
to uphold national prestige."
In the fifth year,
Nányáng Wáng Fèng and Dōnghǎi Wáng Zhī died.
