The Emperor was grieved by their premature deaths,
and wished to establish quarterly sacrifices for them.
He consulted Róng about this.
Róng replied:
"Your sacred benevolence is profound and harmonious,
and at this time, your thoughts are deeply stirred,
mourning the spirits of the two princes,
and issuing an edict of sorrow and compassion,
to examine previous precedents,
and rectify the ritual system.
I humbly observe past affairs:
The former Liáng Huái Wáng, Línjiāng Mǐn Wáng, Qí Āi Wáng, and Línhuái Huái Wáng all died without heirs.
Their younger brothers, born of the same mother,
who became the four Emperors Jǐng, Wǔ, Zhāo, and Míng,
were not known to have established sacrifices for them in previous reigns.
If such measures were adopted temporarily,
they were not recorded in biographies or annals.
Your humble servant foolishly believes that for those who died young,
Your sacred compassion mourns them,
and the rites should be similar to those for adults,
and those given posthumous titles,
should fittingly demonstrate imperial grace.
Once the sacrificial rites are concluded,
they should then be discontinued.
As for a limit of one year (for sacrifices),
it does not accord with ritual propriety,
and also violates the established practices of previous emperors,
which I dare not decide upon."
Initially,
when Cáo Cāo attacked and massacred Yèchéng,
many of Yuán’s clan’s women and children were violated,
and Cāo’s son, Pī, secretly took Yuán Xī’s wife, Zhēn Shì.
Róng then wrote a letter to Cāo,
stating
“King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
and bestowed Dájǐ upon Duke of Zhōu.”
Cāo did not understand,
and later asked from which classic this came.
He replied:
“Judging by current standards,
it must be what one would imagine.”
Later, when Cāo campaigned against the Wūhuán,
he again mocked him, saying:
“The Great General campaigns far away,
desolate beyond the seas.
In ancient times, the Sùshèn did not present kúshǐ (arrow shafts of prickly ash),
and the Dīnglíng stole Sū Wǔ’s cattle and sheep;
these cases can be considered together.”
At that time, there was famine and military campaigns were underway,
and Cāo memorialized to institute a prohibition on alcohol.
Róng repeatedly wrote to dispute this,
using many insulting and disrespectful words.
Seeing that Cāo’s cunning and deceit were increasingly evident,
he often found it unbearable,
and thus his words became unrestrained and biased,
often leading to discord.
He also once memorialized that the ancient system of the royal domain should be followed,
where within a thousand *lǐ* of the capital,
feudal lords should not be enfeoffed.
Cāo suspected that his proposed arguments were becoming increasingly extensive,
and feared him even more.
However, because Róng’s reputation was renowned throughout the empire,
he outwardly tolerated him,
but secretly harbored resentment against his upright critiques,
fearing they would obstruct his great enterprise.
Xī Lǜ of Shānyáng,
perceiving Cāo’s intentions,
used a minor legal infraction to memorialize for Róng’s dismissal from office.
Then, openly revealing their animosity,
Cāo deliberately wrote a letter to provoke and encourage Róng, saying:
“I have heard that in the courts of Táng and Yú,
there were ministers who yielded to others,
which is why *lín* and *fèng* appeared and songs of praise were composed.
In later generations, when virtue declined,
there were still those who sacrificed their lives for their lord,
and ruined their families for the state.
But when it came to its extreme,
a grudge as small as an angry stare must be avenged,
and a kindness of a single meal must be repaid.
Thus, Cháo Cuò, thinking of the state,
met with disaster from Yuán Àng;
[一０]Qū Píng, mourning Chǔ,
suffered slander from Jiāo and Lán;
[一一]Péng Chǒng’s upheaval and chaos
originated from Zhū Fú;
[一二]Dèng Yǔ’s prestige diminished,
owing to Zōng and Féng.
[一三]From this, it can be said that
joy, anger, resentment, and love,
are the causes of misfortune and fortune;
how can one not be careful!
[一四]In ancient times, Lián and Lìn, ministers of a small state,
were still able to defer to each other;
[一五]Kòu and Jiǎ, mere common soldiers,
bent their will and fostered good relations;
Guāngwǔ did not question Bóshēng’s resentment;
the Marquis of Qí did not suspect the captured archer of the hook.
[一六]Indeed, how could one who holds great principles
be entangled by trivial matters!
I heard that the two gentlemen formerly had a fair application of the law,
and considering this a small disagreement,
[一七]they should restore their old friendship;
but resentment has gradually accumulated,
and they intend to harm each other.
Hearing this, I was dismayed,
and rose in the middle of the night.
[一八]When the state moved eastward,
Wénjǔ greatly praised Hóngyù, saying his reputation and reality matched,
that he was thoroughly versed in classical studies,
surpassing Zhèng Xuán,
and also understood Sīmǎ’s military methods.
[一九]Hóngyù also praised Wénjǔ as exceptionally free-spirited and widely learned.
It is truly strange that your current relationship contradicts your initial one.
Although I and Wénjǔ are not old friends,
nor do I owe any kindness to Hóngyù,
yet I wish for people to praise each other,
and do not enjoy people harming each other.
Therefore, I earnestly desire to foster harmony and good relations.
I also know that the two gentlemen have been provoked by petty individuals.
As a subject,
I cannot promote moral transformation throughout the realm,
nor can I, in retirement, establish virtue and harmonize people.
However, in nurturing soldiers,
sacrificing myself for the state,
and eliminating those who pursue empty fame and associate for profit,
I have more than enough achievements.”
Róng replied:
“Thank you for your humble letter and instruction,
informing me of my shortcomings.
Róng and Hóngyù are from neighboring prefectures,
and I knew him earliest.
Although I once spoke of his merits and virtues,
desiring to deepen his personal favor
and his trustworthiness to the state,
I did not seek to cover his faults or conceal his evils,
hoping that if he committed a crime, he would not be punished.
When I was dismissed from office earlier,
I joyfully accepted it.
In ancient times, Zhào Xuānzǐ promoted Hán Jué in the morning,
and in the evening was killed by him,
yet he rejoiced and sought congratulations.
How much less, then, should I, without his accomplishments,
dare to violate the fairness of public office!
I am not Zhōng of the Three Ministers,
nor is my wisdom like Cháo Cuò’s;
usurping a position was my fault,
and being pardoned from punishment is my fortune.
To have my lingering remarks heard afar
is indeed a cause for shame and fear.
Zhū, Péng, Kòu, and Jiǎ were
stalwart men of their age;
their love and hatred clashed,
and they could cause anxiety for the state.
As for the weak and inferior,
they are like insects gnawing at each other;
they merely bring harm upon themselves,
and truly achieve nothing.
Marquis of Jìn praised his ministers for striving for great things,
but Shī Kuàng believed that inner contention was better.
My nature is gentle,
and I do no harm to others.
Even if I endured the humiliation of passing under someone’s crotch,
or the disgrace at Yúcì,
I would not consider it a degradation to myself,
but merely like the passing of a mosquito or gnat.
Zǐchǎn said that people’s hearts are not alike;
[一０]some, who are arrogant,
wish to take victory as their glory,
and do not consider that the people of Sòng treated guests from all corners of the world
and did not wish for their great furnace to let the wine turn sour.
[一一]As for *qūgǔ* or *jùhù*,
they are sturdy but have no opening;
they should simply be condemned for their uselessness.
[一二]As for other matters, I respectfully follow your strict instructions,
and dare not let them fall by the wayside.
Xī was a former subordinate,
promoted by Róng.
Zhào Shuāi’s promotion of Xì Hú
[一三]did not diminish Gōngshú’s elevation of his subordinates.
[一四]I know you share this love,
and your teaching truly strikes home.
[一五]Even Yìbó’s jealousy
could not be entertained,
[一六]how much less should I rely on old friendships
and wish to distance myself from worthy officials!
[一七]I will immediately lay bare my heart,
and restore our friendship as before.
Your sincere and profound words
I shall recite for the rest of my life.”
After more than a year,
he was again appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance.
His nature was tolerant and had few taboos,
he loved scholars,
and enjoyed attracting and benefiting promising juniors.
When he retired to a leisurely position,
guests filled his gate daily.
He often sighed:
“My seats are always full of guests,
and the wine jar is never empty;
I have no worries then.”
He had always been good friends with Cài Yōng.
After Yōng’s death,
there was a *Hǔbēnsì* (imperial guardsman) who resembled Yōng in appearance.
Whenever Róng was in his cups,
he would invite him to sit with him,
saying:
“Though the old, experienced man is gone,
there is still an exemplary model.”
When Róng heard of others’ good qualities,
it was as if they originated from himself.
If their words were worth adopting,
he would certainly elaborate and develop them,
tell them their shortcomings to their face,
but praise their strengths behind their back.
He recommended and promoted worthy scholars,
encouraging many to advance.
If he knew of something good but had not spoken of it,
he considered it his own fault.
Thus, all the heroes and outstanding talents throughout the realm trusted and submitted to him.
Cáo Cāo, having accumulated resentment and jealousy,
and Xī Lǜ further fabricating his crimes,
then ordered Prime Minister's Army Advisor Jìjiǔ Lù Cuì
to falsely accuse Kǒng Róng in a memorial, saying:
"Shàofǔ Kǒng Róng,
formerly in Běihǎi,
seeing the imperial house in disquiet,
gathered followers,
wishing to plot rebellion,
saying, 'I am a descendant of a great sage,
but was extinguished by Sòng.
As for those who possess the empire,
why must it be 'Mǎo Jīn Dāo'?'
And when speaking with Sūn Quán's envoy,
he slandered the imperial court.
Moreover, Róng, as a 'Jiǔliè',
did not observe court etiquette,
wearing a simple turban and moving about discreetly,
rudely intruding upon the palace.
Furthermore, previously, he and the commoner Ní Héng indulged in discussions,
saying, 'Between father and son,
what kind of intimacy should there be?
Considering their original intention,
it is truly born of desire.
Between son and mother,
what is there again?
It is like an object entrusted to a container,
once taken out, they are separated.'
Subsequently, he and Héng praised each other.
Héng said to Róng, 'Zhòngní never died.'
Róng replied, 'Yán Huí has been reborn.'
This is greatly rebellious and unfilial,
and warrants the severest punishment."
When the memorial was presented,
Kǒng Róng was imprisoned and executed in the marketplace.
He was fifty-six years old at the time.
His wife and children were all executed.
Initially,
his daughter was seven years old,
and his son nine years old;
because of their youth and weakness, they were spared,
and entrusted to another household.
The two children were playing 'yì' (a board game),
when Róng was arrested, but they did not move.
Those around them asked,
"Your father has been seized, yet you do not rise,
why?"
They replied:
"How can a nest be destroyed and the eggs not break?"
The host had some leftover meat broth,
and the boy, being thirsty, drank it.
The girl said:
"Given today's calamity,
how can we live long?
What use is it to know the taste of meat?"
Her brother stopped crying.
Someone reported this to Cáo Cāo,
who then had them all killed.
When the executioners arrived,
the girl said to her brother:
"If the dead have knowledge,
to be able to see our parents,
would that not be our greatest wish!"
Then they stretched their necks to receive the execution,
their expressions unchanged;
everyone was grieved.
Initially,
Zhī Xí Yuánshēng from Jīngzhào,
was close to Róng,
and often warned Róng about his bluntness.
When Róng was killed,
no one in Xǔ was brave enough to collect his body,
but Xí went and caressed the corpse, saying:
"Wénjǔ died for me,
why should I live?"
Cáo Cāo heard this and was furious,
intending to arrest Xí and kill him,
but later Xí was pardoned and released.
Emperor Wén of Wèi deeply admired Róng's literary style,
often sighing and saying:
"He is a peer of Yáng and Bān."
He offered rewards of gold and silk
to anyone in the empire who submitted Róng's writings.
His works included poems, eulogies, epitaphs, discourses, 'liùyán' pieces, policy essays, memorials, proclamations, edicts, and letters, totaling twenty-five pieces.
Emperor Wén, considering Xí to possess the integrity of Luán Bù,
appointed him Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
The discourse states: Formerly, Grand Master Remonstrant Zhèng Chāng said:
"Where there are fierce beasts in the mountains,
the 'líhuò' (wild herbs) are left ungathered."
Therefore, Kǒng Fù, with his stern countenance,
would not tolerate plots of regicide and cruelty;
Píng Zhòng, standing in court,
had the hope of alleviating Qí's woes from bandits.
As for Wénjǔ's noble aspirations and straightforward nature,
they were enough to stir righteous indignation and offend powerful hearts.
Thus, the traces of shifting the cauldron,
the matter was separated from the living person;
the plan for an alternate succession,
its opportunity was revealed after his death.
Indeed, a stern spirit and upright nature,
will break rather than bend.
How can one be yielding and compromising,
and thus prolong one's life?
Resolutely and
spotlessly pure,
they can be compared to fine jade and autumn frost in quality.
Gōu Yù, courtesy name Wénruò,
was from Yǐngyīn, Yǐngchuān.
He was the grandson of Lánglíng Magistrate Shú.
His father, Gǔn,
was the Grand Administrator of Jǐnán.
Gǔn, fearing and being wary of the eunuchs,
had Yù marry the daughter of the Regular Palace Attendant Táng Héng.
Because Yù had talent and renown from a young age,
he was thus spared from criticism.
Hé Yóng, known for discerning people, from Nányáng,
saw Yù and was impressed,
saying:
"He is a talent for a king's aide."
In the sixth year of Zhōngpíng (189 CE),
he was nominated as Xiàolián,
and twice promoted to Magistrate of Kàngfù.
During the chaos of Dǒng Zhuó,
he resigned his office and returned to his hometown.
His fellow townsman Hán Róng, at the time, was leading over a thousand clansmen,
seeking refuge in the western mountains of Mì.
Yù said to the elders:
"Yǐngchuān
is a land of four battles.
When there is upheaval in the world,
it is always the focus of military attack.
Although Mì is slightly fortified,
it is insufficient to withstand great calamity;
it is advisable to avoid it quickly."
Many villagers, attached to their homeland, could not bear to leave.
At that time, Hán Fù, the Governor of Jìzhōu and a fellow native of the commandery, sent cavalry to welcome them,
so Yù alone led his clan to follow Fù.
Those who remained were later largely killed or plundered by Dǒng Zhuó's general Lǐ Jué.
By the time Yù arrived in Jìzhōu,
Yuán Shào had already usurped Fù's position,
and Shào treated Yù with the courtesy due to an honored guest.
Yù was discerning and insightful,
and seeing the collapse and chaos of the Hàn dynasty,
he always harbored the ambition to assist in restoration.
At that time, Cáo Cāo was in Dōngjùn,
and Yù heard that Cāo possessed great strategy,
and judged that Shào would ultimately not be able to achieve great success.
In the second year of Chūpíng (191 CE),
he left Shào and joined Cāo.
Cāo was greatly pleased after speaking with him,
saying:
"You are my Zǐfáng!"
He appointed him Fènwǔ Sīmǎ;
he was twenty-nine years old at the time.
The following year,
he was again appointed Cāo's Zhèndōng Sīmǎ.
In the first year of Xīngpíng (194 CE),
Cāo attacked Táo Qiān in the east,
and ordered Yù to guard Zhènchéng,
entrusting him with remaining affairs.
At that time, Zhāng Miǎo and Chén Gōng rebelled against Cāo with Yǎnzōu,
and secretly welcomed Lǚ Bù.
Once Bù arrived,
all the cities responded to him.
Miǎo then sent someone to deceive Yù,
saying:
"General Lǚ has come to assist Lord Cáo in attacking Táo Qiān;
it is advisable to quickly supply military provisions."
Yù knew that Miǎo had rebelled,
and immediately marshaled troops to prepare defenses,
thus Miǎo's plan failed.
Guō Gòng, the Inspector of Yùzhōu, led tens of thousands of soldiers and arrived outside the city,
requesting to see Yù.
Yù was about to go,
but Xiàhóu Dūn, the Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn, and others stopped him,
saying:
"How do you know Gòng is not conspiring with Lǚ Bù,
and lightly wish to see him?
Now you are the commander of a province;
going would surely be dangerous."
Yù replied:
"Gòng and Miǎo are not old associates.
His swift arrival now means
his plans are surely not yet decided.
While he is still hesitating,
it is advisable to persuade him in good time.
Even if he does not join us,
we can make him remain neutral.
If we first show suspicion,
he will become angry and finalize his plans;
it is better to go."
When Gòng saw that Yù showed no fear,
he knew the city could not be attacked,
and thus withdrew.
Yù then sent Chéng Yù to persuade Fàn and Dōng'ē,
to strengthen their defenses,
and ultimately preserved the three cities to await Cāo.
In the second year,
Táo Qiān died.
Cāo wanted to immediately seize Xúzhōu,
then return and pacify Lǚ Bù.
Xùn advised, saying:
“In the past, Gāozǔ secured Guānzhōng,
and Guāngwǔ held Hénèi.
Both deeply rooted and solidified their foundations,
thereby controlling the world.
Advancing, they could defeat enemies;
retreating, they had sufficient strength to hold firm.
Thus, even when they encountered difficulties and defeats,
they ultimately accomplished their great undertakings.
You, General, originally initiated your enterprise in Yǎnzhōu,
and were thus able to pacify Shāndōng.
This is truly a vital strategic location in the world,
and your Guānzhōng and Hénèi.
If you do not first pacify it,
where will your foundation be placed?
You should swiftly dispatch forces to attack Chén Gōng,
preventing the bandits from looking west,
and in the interim, harvest the ripe wheat,
conserve provisions,
to support a single decisive action.
Then Lǚ Bù will be easily defeated.
Now, to abandon this and go east,
I do not see the benefit.
If you leave too many troops, your strength will not be sufficient against the enemy;
if you leave too few troops, your rear will not be secure.
Lǚ Bù will take advantage of the emptiness to raid and create chaos,
shaking people's hearts.
Even if a few cities might remain intact,
the rest will no longer be yours.
Then where will you, General, return?
Moreover, when you previously attacked Xúzhōu,
your authority and punishment were truly implemented.
Their sons and younger brothers, remembering the shame of their fathers and elder brothers,
will surely each defend themselves.
Even if you can defeat them,
they cannot be secured.
If they, out of fear, form alliances
and act as a united front,
fortifying their walls and clearing the fields
to await you, General,
you will attack them without success,
and plunder without gain.
Within ten days,
your army of a hundred thousand will be self-defeated before even fighting.
Indeed, things inherently involve giving up one to take another,
to weigh the temporary situation.
I hope, General, you will consider this.”
Cāo then extensively harvested the ripe wheat,
and again fought with Lǚ Bù.
Lǚ Bù was defeated and fled,
and Cāo then divided his forces to pacify the various counties.
Yǎnzhōu was thus pacified.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān,
Emperor Xiàn returned from Hédōng to Luòyáng.
Cāo debated whether to welcome the imperial carriage
and move the capital to Xǔ.
Many thought that Shāndōng was not yet pacified, and that
Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng, emboldened by their achievements, were acting recklessly
and could not be quickly brought under control.
Xùn then advised Cāo, saying:
“In the past, Duke Wén of Jìn received King Xiāng of Zhōu,
and the feudal lords followed him.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn wore mourning white for Emperor Yì,
and the world submitted to him.
Since the Son of Heaven has been cast into the dust,
you, General, were the first to raise an army of righteousness.
Merely because Shāndōng was in turmoil,
you have not had time to travel far to assist.
Although you have resisted difficulties externally,
your heart has always been with the imperial house.
Now the imperial carriage has turned back,
but the Eastern Capital is overgrown with weeds.
Righteous scholars have a desire to restore the foundation,
and the common people harbor sorrow for the past.
If you can indeed at this time welcome the sovereign and follow the people's wishes,
that is a great compliance.
If you uphold absolute impartiality to subdue the world,
that is a great strategy.
If you uphold grand righteousness to attract heroes,
that is a great virtue.
Though there may be rebels in the four directions,
what can they do?
Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng,
why worry about them?
If you do not decide this promptly,
allowing powerful figures to harbor ambitions,
then even if you later consider it,
it will be too late.”
Cāo followed his advice.
When the emperor settled in Xǔ,
Xùn was appointed Shìzhōng,
and served as Shàngshūlìng.
Whenever Cāo went on campaigns,
all matters of military and state
were planned with Xùn.
Xùn also recommended to Cāo his nephew Yōu, a man of strategic counsel,
as well as Zhōng Yáo, Guō Jiā,
Chén Qún, Dù Xí,
Sīmǎ Yì, Xì Zhìcái, and others.
All praised his recommendations.
Only Yán Xiàng, who was made governor of Yángzhōu,
and Wéi Kāng, who was made governor of Liángzhōu,
later suffered defeat.
Yuán Shào, having annexed the lands north of the Yellow River,
became arrogant.
When Cāo was defeated by Zhāng Xiù,
Shào's letter to Cāo was extremely condescending.
Cāo was enraged
and wanted to attack him first,
but worried that his strength was insufficient.
He consulted Xùn.
Xùn estimated that although Shào was strong,
he would ultimately be controlled by Cāo.
He then advised Cāo to first capture Lǚ Bù,
and then plan for Shào.
Cāo followed his advice.
In the third year,
Lǚ Bù was captured,
and Xúzhōu was pacified.
In the fifth year,
Yuán Shào led a large army to attack Xǔ.
Cāo confronted him.
Shào's armored forces were very strong,
and all the deliberators were filled with fear.
The Prefect of the Palace Grand Library, Kǒng Róng, said to Xùn:
“Yuán Shào has vast territory and strong armies.
Tián Fēng and Xǔ Yōu, men of intelligence and strategy, plan for him.
Shěn Péi and Féng Jì, loyal and devoted officials, manage his affairs.
Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu, whose bravery is unmatched in the three armies,
command his troops.
Is he perhaps difficult to overcome?”
Xùn said:
“Although Shào's army is numerous, its discipline is lax.
Tián Fēng is rigid and offends his superiors.
Xǔ Yōu is greedy and not upright.
Shěn Péi is autocratic and lacks strategy.
Féng Jì is resolute but self-willed.
Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu have but the courage of common men,
and can be captured in a single battle.”
Later, everything unfolded as Xùn had planned,
as recorded in the Biography of Yuán Shào.
Cāo held Guāndù,
and fought continuously with Shào.
Although victorious, his army's provisions were almost exhausted.
He wrote to Xùn to discuss,
wanting to return to Xǔ to draw Shào's army.
Xùn replied:
“Although our provisions are scarce now,
it is not as dire as when Chǔ and Hàn were between Xíngyáng and Chénggāo.
At that time, neither Liú Bāng nor Xiàng Yǔ were willing to retreat first,
believing that the first to retreat would lose their advantage.
You, Duke, with one-tenth of the enemy's forces,
have drawn a line and defended it,
gripping his throat and preventing him from advancing,
for half a year now.
His situation is evident, and his strength is exhausted;
there will surely be a change.
This is the time to use a surprise strategy;
it must not be missed.”
Cāo followed his advice,
then fortified his walls and held firm.
He then used surprise tactics to defeat Shào,
who retreated and fled.
Xùn was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wàansuì Pavilion,
with a thousand households in his fief.
In the sixth year,
Cāo considered that Shào, having just been defeated,
could not pose a threat,
and only wanted to leave troops to guard against him,
while he himself wished to campaign south against Liú Biǎo.
He asked Xùn for advice.
Xùn replied:
“Shào has just been defeated,
and his troops are fearful of disturbance.
If you do not take this opportunity to pacify him,
but instead wish to send forces far to Jiānghàn,
if Shào gathers his scattered forces
and takes advantage of the emptiness to strike,
then your cause, Duke, will be lost.”
Cāo then stopped.
In the ninth year [of Jiàn'ān],
Cáo Cāo captured Yè,
and personally assumed the title of Governor of Jìzhōu.
There were those who suggested that Cáo Cāo should re-establish the Nine Provinces,
believing that if Jìzhōu's jurisdiction was sufficiently expanded,
then the world would be easily subdued.
Cáo Cāo was about to follow this advice.
Xún Yù said:
"If we now follow the ancient system,
it would mean that Jìzhōu's jurisdiction
would encompass all the lands of Hédōng, Fēngyì, Fúfēng, Xīhé, Yōu, and Bìng.
When Your Excellency previously massacred Yèchéng,
the whole empire was shocked and terrified,
each fearing that they would not be able to preserve their territories
and retain their armed forces.
If one area is now invaded,
they will certainly believe that they will be dispossessed in turn.
People's hearts are easily swayed,
and if a sudden change occurs,
the empire cannot yet be secured.
I wish Your Excellency would first pacify Héběi,
and then restore the old capital,
proceeding south to Chǔ Yǐng,
to demand the unpaid royal tribute.
When all under Heaven know Your Excellency's intentions,
then everyone will feel secure.
Only after the empire is completely settled
should the ancient system be discussed.
This is a long-term benefit for the state."
Cáo Cāo replied:
"Had it not been for your remonstrance,
I would have lost much!"
Thus, the discussion about the Nine Provinces was shelved.
In the twelfth year,
Cáo Cāo submitted a memorial to the throne, praising Xún Yù, saying:
"Formerly, Yuán Shào rebelled,
massing troops at Guāndù.
At that time, with our forces outnumbered and provisions scarce,
I contemplated returning to Xǔ.
However, Shàngshū Lìng Xún Yù strongly proposed the advantage of holding our ground,
and broadly expanded the strategy of further advance,
stirring my heart
and changing my foolish thoughts.
We fortified our camp and held firm,
laying an ambush for his supplies.
Thus, we crushed the great bandit,
saving the perilous situation and bringing peace.
After Shào was defeated,
my own provisions were also exhausted.
I was about to abandon the plan for Héběi
and change to a strategy for Jīngnán.
Xún Yù again thoroughly explained the pros and cons,
causing me to change my decision.
Thus, we were able to turn our banners back to Jìzhōu,
and pacify the four provinces.
Had I retreated from Guāndù then,
Shào would certainly have advanced boldly.
The enemy, encouraged by their advantage, would have doubled their strength,
while my troops, disheartened, would have lost morale.
There would have been a certainty of defeat,
with no chance of victory.
Again, had I marched south against Liú Biǎo,
abandoning Yǎn and Yù,
my hungry army would have advanced deep,
crossing the Jiāng and Miǎn rivers.
Not only would victory be difficult to achieve,
but we would also have lost our base.
Yet Xún Yù proposed these two strategies,
turning peril into preservation,
and misfortune into blessing.
His plans were extraordinary, and his merits unique,
surpassing my own.
This is why the former sage emperors valued the merit of strategic direction,
and lightly rewarded the achievement of actual capture.
〔一０〕The ancients esteemed the counsel within the strategist's tent,
and considered lesser the power of direct assault.
〔一一〕Considering his achievements and effectiveness,
he is worthy of a high title.
But the world has not understood his true circumstances,
and what he has received does not match his merits.
〔一二〕I truly lament this.
I beg that the matter be re-examined,
and his fiefdom and households be increased."
〔一三〕Xún Yù deeply declined the offer.
Cáo Cāo admonished him, saying:
"Formerly, Jiè Zǐtuī said: 'Stealing another's wealth
is still called theft.'
〔一四〕How much more so your ingenious plans, which lifted us from peril,
and upon which hinged the rise and fall of states—
can you claim sole possession of them?
〔一五〕Although I admire Lǔ Lián's noble conduct,
〔一六〕should one adhere to the principle of a virtuous person who acts according to circumstances?"
〔一七〕Thereupon, his fiefdom was increased by a thousand households,
making a total of two thousand households, including the previous grant.
Cáo Cāo also wanted to appoint him to a senior official position,
〔一八〕but Xún Yù had Xún Yōu earnestly decline on his behalf,
repeatedly, a dozen times,
before it was dropped.
When Cáo Cāo was about to attack Liú Biǎo,
he asked Xún Yù for his strategy.
Xún Yù said:
"Now the Central Plains are pacified,
Jīng and Hàn know their doom is near.
You can make a feint towards Wǎn and Yè, while secretly advancing lightly,
to catch them off guard."
Cáo Cāo followed his advice.
Coincidentally, Liú Biǎo died of illness.
〔一九〕
In the seventeenth year,
Dǒng Zhāo and others
wished to jointly promote Cáo Cāo to the rank of Duke of a State,
with the Nine Bestowments fully granted,
and secretly consulted Xún Yù about it.
Xún Yù said:
"Cáo Gōng originally raised an army of righteousness
to support and revitalize the Hàn dynasty.
Although his achievements and merits are vast and prominent,
he still upholds the principle of loyalty and integrity.
A virtuous person loves others with virtue;
this (proposal) is inappropriate."
The matter was subsequently dropped.
Cáo Cāo was displeased.
When he was about to campaign south against Sūn Quán,
he submitted a memorial requesting Xún Yù to visit his army at Qiáo,
and then, through the memorial, kept Xún Yù, saying:
"I have heard that in ancient times, when generals were dispatched,
supervisory authority was placed above them,
and second-in-command duties were established below them. This was to uphold the dignity of the state's mandate
and ensure that plans were rarely flawed.
As I am now about to cross the river [Jiāng]
to execute the mandate and punish the offenders,
there should be a grand envoy to respectfully convey the royal command.
The combined use of civil and military officials
has existed since ancient times.
Xún Yù, the Commissioner with Credentials, Attendant at the Imperial Gate, Keeper of the Imperial Secretariat, and Marquis of Wànsuì Tíng,
is a [revered] minister of the state,
whose virtue permeates the Central Plains.
Since he has arrived at the stopping place for the army,
it is expedient for him to advance with me
to proclaim the state's mandate
and awe and appease the vile barbarians.
Military protocol prioritizes speed,
and I could not request permission beforehand.
I have therefore retained Xún Yù
to serve in this important capacity."
The memorial was presented,
and the Emperor approved it.
Thus, Xún Yù was appointed Attendant at the Imperial Gate, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,
with credentials,
to participate in the Prime Minister's military affairs.
Upon reaching Rúxū,
Xún Yù fell ill and remained in Shòuchūn.
Cáo Cāo sent him a food box.
When he opened it and looked inside,
it was empty.
Thereupon, he took poison and died.
He was fifty years old at the time.
The Emperor grieved and lamented his death,
and for an entire day, halted banquets and entertainment for him.
He was posthumously given the title of Jìng Hóu.
The following year,
Cáo Cāo indeed declared himself Duke of Wèi.
A commentary says: Since the relocation of the Emperor to the Western Capital,
the lands east of the mountains erupted in turmoil,
and the fate of the empire hung by a thread.
Master Xún then crossed the Hé and Jì rivers,
travelling with difficulty to follow the Cáo clan.
Observing his decisive actions,
his proposed policies,
and his advocacy of the clear royal strategy
to address the national crisis,
how can it be said that he merely used the chaos to feign righteousness
and pursue a plan contrary to the correct path?
Truly, he took benevolence as his own responsibility,
aiming to relieve the people in their urgent distress.
Yet, his opposition to Dǒng Zhāo's proposal
led to his untimely demise.
Was this not fate?
Those who speak of Master Xún in the world
may sometimes err in their judgment of his successes and failures.
I have always believed that for those of middling virtue and below,
the Way cannot be expected to be perfectly complete;
their calculations of wisdom may have oversights,
and the beginning does not necessarily require the end.
This is a principle that cannot be fully challenged.
Consider the wisdom of Wèi Cì,
whose single counsel led to the ruin of two states.
He was not lacking in benevolence, nor did he desire such an outcome;
it is simply that where there is complete preservation, there must also be loss.
This is also an instance where merit cannot be comprehensive.
At a time when fate was arduous and difficult,
without heroic talent, none could save those drowning.
When achievements are great and power is strong,
the imperial regalia naturally shifts.
〔一０〕This is another instance where timing and principle cannot coexist.
Perhaps one should simply take the return to righteousness as the goal,
which is also the meaning of sacrificing oneself to achieve benevolence.
An encomium states: Gōngyè [Kong Rong] was lauded as a hero,
his excellent reputation soaring.
At times, he was pressured by cunning power,
lavishing gold on his colleagues and friends.
Běihǎi's [Kong Rong's] temperament was carefree,
but his expressions of sentiment were cut short.
The common people of Yuè [South China] were easily alarmed,
and his lone voice found few echoes.
With a straight rein, where could he safely return?
Who could assist his lofty plans?
As for Yù [Xún Yù] having Bì [Xún Yù],
he sincerely felt the nation's distress.
His accomplishments aligned with a change of fortune,
his actions were suspected but his heart was one.
Biographies of Huángfǔ Sōng and Zhū Jùn, Chapter Sixty-one
Huángfǔ Sōng, courtesy name Yìzhēn,
was a native of Cháonà, Āndìng Commandery.
He was the elder nephew of the General Who Crosses the Liao, Guī [Huángfǔ Guī].
His father, Jié,
was the Administrator of Yànmén.
Sōng, in his youth, possessed aspirations and integrity in both civil and martial arts,
enjoyed poetry and books,
and practiced archery and horsemanship.
Initially, he was nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt and a Flourishing Talent.
Grand Commandant Chén Fán and Grand General Dòu Wǔ repeatedly invited him,
but he did not accept either offer.
Emperor Líng later summoned him by public carriage to be an Imperial Consultant,
and he was promoted to Administrator of Běidì.
Initially,
Zhāng Jiǎo of Jùlù called himself
"Great Teacher of Virtuous Peace,"
worshipped the doctrines of Huáng-Lǎo,
and raised disciples.
They would kneel and bow, confessing their faults,
and use charmed water and incantations to treat illnesses.
Many of the sick recovered,
and the common people believed in and followed him.
Jiǎo then sent eight disciples to various regions,
to spread his virtuous teachings and transform the world,
deceiving and misleading others.
Within more than ten years,
his followers numbered several hundred thousand,
connecting commanderies and kingdoms.
From the people of Qīng, Xú, Yōu, Jì, Jīng, Yáng, Yǎn, and Yù — eight provinces
— none failed to respond.
They then established thirty-six "Fāng."
A "Fāng" was like a general's title.
A large "Fāng" had over ten thousand people,
a small "Fāng" had six or seven thousand,
each with its own leader.
Rumors circulated:
"The Blue Heaven is dead,
the Yellow Heaven is to rise.
When the year is Jiǎzǐ,
the world will be greatly auspicious."
They wrote "Jiǎzǐ"
characters in white earth
on the gates of temples in the capital and on official buildings in the provinces and commanderies.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng (184 CE),
the great "Fāng" leader Mǎ Yuányì and others first gathered tens of thousands of people from Jīng and Yáng,
planning to launch the uprising in Yè.
Yuányì frequently traveled to the capital,
using the Palace Regular Attendants Fēng Xǔ and Xú Fèng as internal collaborators,
agreeing to rise simultaneously inside and outside on the fifth day of the third month.
Before they could begin the rebellion,
Zhāng Jiǎo's disciple Táng Zhōu of Jìnán submitted a memorial to expose them.
Consequently, Yuányì was torn apart by chariots in Luòyáng.
Emperor Líng sent Zhōu's memorial to the Three Excellencies and the Minister of Works,
and ordered the Chief of the Hooked Spades, Zhōu Bīn, to lead the clerks from the three ministries
to investigate palace guards and commoners involved in Jiǎo's doctrine.
Over a thousand people were executed.
He then interrogated those in Jì Province
and pursued and arrested Jiǎo and his followers.
Jiǎo and his followers, knowing their plot was revealed,
hurriedly ordered all "Fāng" leaders day and night
to rise simultaneously.
All wore yellow turbans as their distinctive sign,
which is why people at the time called them
"Yellow Turbans,"
and also "Moth Bandits."
They sacrificed people to Heaven.
Jiǎo called himself
"General of Heavenly Peace,"
Jiǎo's younger brother Bǎo called himself
"General of Earthly Peace,"
and Bǎo's younger brother Liáng called himself
"General of Human Peace."
Wherever they went, they burned official buildings,
plundered and raided towns and villages.
The provinces and commanderies lost their strongholds,
and many chief officials fled.
Within ten days,
the whole world responded,
and the capital was shaken.
An imperial edict ordered provinces and commanderies to repair defenses,
and train troops and weaponry.
At Hángǔ, Dàgǔ, Guǎngchéng, Yīquè, Huànyuán, Xuánmén, Mèngjīn, Xiǎopíngjīn, and other passes,
Grand Commandants were appointed.
The emperor summoned his ministers for a council.
Sōng suggested lifting the ban on partisans,
and distributing more of the money from the internal treasury and horses from the Western Garden stables
to the soldiers.
The emperor followed his advice.
Thereupon, elite troops from across the empire were mobilized,
and commanders were widely selected.
Sōng was appointed Left Colonel of the Household,
bearing the imperial credential.
Together with Right Colonel of the Household Zhū Jùn,
they mobilized riders from the Five Schools and Three Rivers, as well as recruited brave elites,
totaling over forty thousand men.
Sōng and Jùn each commanded an army,
and together they attacked the Yǐngchuān Yellow Turbans.
Jùn had previously fought the bandit Bō Cái
and was defeated.
Sōng then advanced to hold Chángshè.
Bō Cái led his large army to besiege the city.
Sōng's troops were few,
and all the soldiers were afraid.
He then gathered his military officers and said:
"In warfare, there are unexpected stratagems;
it's not about numerical superiority or inferiority.
Now, the bandits have set up camps relying on grass,
which makes them vulnerable to wind and fire.
If we use fire at night,
they will certainly be greatly alarmed and confused.
If I lead the troops out to attack them,
and they are surrounded from all four sides,
the accomplishment of Tián Dān can be achieved."
That evening, a strong wind arose.
Sōng then ordered his soldiers to tie bundles of reeds and mount the city walls,
and sent elite warriors to sneak out beyond the encirclement.
They set fire and shouted loudly,
while those on the city walls raised torches in response.
Sōng then beat the drums and charged their formation.
The bandits were alarmed, fell into disorder, and fled.
Coincidentally, Emperor Líng had dispatched Cavalry Commandant Cáo Cāo with troops, who arrived just then.
Sōng, Cáo Cāo, and Zhū Jùn joined forces and fought again,
greatly defeating them,
and beheading tens of thousands of enemy soldiers.
Sōng was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng.
Sōng and Jùn took advantage of their victory to pursue and attack the Rǔnán and Chén Kingdom Yellow Turbans.
They chased Bō Cái to Yángdí
and attacked Péng Tuō in Xīhuá,
defeating them both.
The remaining bandits surrendered or dispersed,
and the three commanderies were all pacified.
They then advanced to attack Bǔ Jǐ, the Yellow Turban leader of Dōng Commandery, at Cāngtíng.
Bǔ Jǐ was captured alive,
and over seven thousand heads were taken.
At that time, Northern Colonel of the Household Lú Zhí and Eastern Colonel of the Household Dǒng Zhuó had attacked Zhāng Jiǎo,
but returned without success.
An imperial edict then ordered Sōng to advance and attack him.
Sōng fought Jiǎo's younger brother Liáng at Guǎngzōng.
Liáng's forces were elite and brave,
and Sōng could not overcome them.
The next day,
he closed his camp and rested his soldiers,
to observe their movements.
Knowing that the bandits' resolve was somewhat slackening,
he secretly ordered his troops to prepare at night.
At cockcrow, they charged into their formation.
They fought until dusk,
greatly defeating them.
Liáng was killed,
thirty thousand heads were taken,
and about fifty thousand people died by drowning in the river.
Over thirty thousand carts of supplies were burned,
and all their women and children were captured;
the number of captives was very large.
Jiǎo had already died of illness,
so his coffin was opened, his corpse desecrated,
and his head sent to the capital.
Sōng then, with the Administrator of Jùlù, Guō Diǎn of Féngyì, attacked Jiǎo's younger brother Bǎo at Xiàqǔyáng,
and also killed him.
Over one hundred thousand heads were taken,
and a Jingguan (mound of enemy heads) was built south of the city.
Sōng was immediately appointed General of the Left Chariots and Cavalry,
and concurrently Governor of Jì Province,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Huáilǐ,
with fiefs in the two counties of Huáilǐ and Měiyáng,
totaling eight thousand households.
As the Yellow Turbans had already been pacified,
the reign title was changed to Zhōngpíng.
Huángfǔ Sōng memorialized, requesting a year's land tax from Jìzhōu
to provide for the famine-stricken people.
The emperor granted his request.
The common people sang:
"The world is in great chaos, the markets are ruins;
Mothers cannot protect their children, wives lose their husbands.
Thanks to Huángfǔ, we are once again at peace."
Huángfǔ Sōng showed warmth and sympathy to his soldiers,
and was greatly loved by the populace.
Whenever his army halted its march,
he would wait until the encampment's tents were set up
before he would take his own lodging.
Only after all the soldiers had eaten
did he taste his own food.
If an official accepted bribes for some matter,
Huángfǔ Sōng would instead give them money and goods.
The officials would be filled with shame,
some even to the point of suicide.
After Huángfǔ Sōng crushed the Yellow Turbans,
his prestige shook the world.
However, court politics grew increasingly chaotic,
and the land within the seas became impoverished and exhausted.
Therefore, Yán Zhōng of Hànyáng, the Magistrate of Xìndū, tried to persuade Huángfǔ Sōng, saying:
"What is hard to gain and easy to lose
is opportunity;
what arrives without a moment's delay
is the critical moment.
Thus, the sage acts in accordance with the times,
and the wise seize the critical moment to act.
Now, General, you have encountered a rare opportunity,
and are treading upon a perilous critical moment.
Yet you do not grasp the opportunity,
and when faced with the moment, you do not act.
How then will you preserve your great reputation?"
Huángfǔ Sōng said:
"What do you mean?"
Yán Zhōng replied:
"Heaven's Way shows no favoritism;
the people support the able.
Now, General, you received your axe of authority in late spring,
and achieved your success in late winter.
Your troops move like spirits,
your plans require no second thought.
Crushing the strong is easier than snapping a dry twig,
melting the firm is quicker than hot water melting snow.
Within a month or so,
your divine army swept through like lightning,
burying corpses and carving stones,
facing south to report victory.
Your awe and virtue shook the imperial court,
and your renown spread beyond the seas.
Even the campaigns of Tāng and Wǔ
did not surpass yours, General.
Now you have established merits that cannot be rewarded,
and embody virtues that transcend ordinary men.
Yet you face north to a mediocre ruler;
how can you seek peace?"
Huángfǔ Sōng said:
"Morning and night I am devoted to public duty,
my heart never forgets loyalty.
Why would I not be at peace?"
Yán Zhōng said:
"Not so.
In the past, Hán Xìn could not endure the humiliation of a single meal
and established a three-way division of power.
When the sharp sword was already at his throat,
he then uttered a lament of bitter regret.
This was because the critical moment was lost and his plans went awry.
Now, the emperor's power is weaker than that of Liú and Xiàng,
while your authority, General, is greater than that of Huáin Yīn.
A mere gesture from you is enough to stir winds and clouds,
a shout can summon thunder and lightning.
Suddenly rise up with vigor,
take advantage of the peril to overthrow the decaying order,
bestow great favor to pacify those who first submit,
and display military might to rule those who later yield.
Summon the warriors of Jìfāng,
mobilize the armies of seven zhōu.
Let feathered urgent dispatches race ahead,
and the grand army's rumble follow behind.
Cross the flowing Zhānghé,
water your horses at Mèngjīn.
Punish the crimes of the eunuchs,
eliminate the accumulated evils of the villains.
Even a young child could be made to clench a fist and exert strength,
a woman could be made to lift her skirt and obey orders,
let alone stirring up troops as fierce as bears and tigers,
and taking advantage of a swift gale!
Once your great achievement is accomplished,
and the world has submitted,
then you can invoke the Supreme Emperor,
and display the mandate of Heaven.
Unify the six directions,
face south and proclaim yourself ruler.
Transfer the precious regalia to the rising power,
overthrow the fallen Hàn.
This is truly the ultimate convergence of divine opportunity,
a propitious time for a swift uprising.
For what is already rotten cannot be carved,
and a decaying age is hard to assist.
If you wish to assist a hard-to-assist court,
and carve a rotten, decaying piece of wood,
it is like rolling a ball uphill,
or rowing against the wind.
How can it be called easy?
Moreover, now the eunuchs gather in crowds,
their wickedness as numerous as a marketplace.
Imperial commands are not obeyed,
power resides with the trusted retainers.
Under a dim-witted ruler,
it is difficult to remain for long.
For unrewarded achievements,
slanderers cast sidelong glances.
If you do not plan early,
regret will be too late."
Huángfǔ Sōng said with apprehension:
"Extraordinary plans
are not applied to ordinary circumstances.
To conceive such a great undertaking
is not something a mediocre talent can achieve.
The Yellow Turbans were a minor nuisance,
not enemies like Qín or Xiàng.
What is newly formed is easily dispersed;
it is difficult to achieve a great enterprise with them.
Furthermore, people have not forgotten their lord,
and Heaven does not aid rebels.
If I were to falsely create unhoped-for achievements
to hasten imminent disaster,
how would that compare to dedicating loyalty to the imperial court
and maintaining my duty as a minister?
Although there might be much slander,
it would be nothing more than being dismissed and exiled.
I would still have a good name,
and my death would not be in vain.
Such rebellious talk
I dare not hear."
Yán Zhōng knew his plan would not be used,
and so he fled.
Later, Biān Zhāng and Hán Suí caused rebellion in Lǒngyòu.
The following spring,
an imperial edict ordered Huángfǔ Sōng to return and garrison Cháng'ān
to protect the imperial tombs.
Biān Zhāng and others then again invaded Sānfǔ,
and Huángfǔ Sōng was ordered to suppress them.
Initially,
when Huángfǔ Sōng was suppressing Zhāng Jiǎo,
he passed through Yè.
Seeing that the residence of the Cáo Chángshì Zhào Zhōng exceeded regulations,
he memorialized to have it confiscated.
Also, the Cáo Chángshì Zhāng Ràng secretly asked for fifty million cash,
but Huángfǔ Sōng refused him.
These two consequently bore grudges,
and memorialized that Huángfǔ Sōng fought continuously without merit
and incurred great expenses.
That autumn, he was recalled,
his seal and sash as Zǔo Chējì Jiāngjūn were collected,
and six thousand households were reduced from his fief.
He was re-enfeoffed as Dūxiāng Hóu,
with two thousand households.
In the fifth year,
the bandits from Liángzhōu, Wáng Guó, besieged Chéncāng.
Sōng was again appointed Left General,
and was made supervisor of Former General Dǒng Zhuó.
Each was to lead twenty thousand men to resist them.
Dǒng Zhuó wanted to advance quickly to Chéncāng,
but Sōng did not agree.
Dǒng Zhuó said:
"A wise person does not miss an opportunity;
a brave person does not hesitate in making a decision.
If we rescue it quickly, the city will be preserved;
if we do not rescue it, the city will fall.
The situation of preservation or destruction
rests on this."
Sōng said:
"Not so.
A hundred victories in a hundred battles
are not as good as subduing the enemy's army without fighting.
Therefore, first make yourself invincible,
then wait for the enemy to become vulnerable.
Invincibility lies with us;
vulnerability lies with the enemy.
If their defense is insufficient,
our attack will be more than enough.
Those who have more than enough move above the nine heavens;
those who have insufficient sink below the nine earths.
Now, although Chéncāng is small,
its city defenses are strong and prepared;
it is not a trap of the nine earths.
Although Wáng Guó is strong,
he is attacking where we are not rescuing,
which is not the advantage of the nine heavens.
Indeed, if the advantage is not of the nine heavens,
the attacker suffers harm;
if the trap is not of the nine earths,
the defender is not dislodged.
Wáng Guó has now fallen into a position of suffering harm,
while Chéncāng holds an unassailable city.
I can achieve complete victory
without bothering the troops or mobilizing the multitude.
What need is there to rescue it?"
So, he did not listen.
Wáng Guó besieged Chéncāng
from winter until spring,
for over eighty days.
The city's defenses were strong and firm,
and he ultimately could not take it.
The bandit forces were exhausted and weakened,
and indeed dispersed on their own.
Sōng advanced his troops and attacked them.
Dǒng Zhuó said:
"No.
The art of war states:
Do not press desperate foes;
do not pursue a retreating army.
Now, if we pursue Wáng Guó,
it is pressing a retreating army
and pursuing desperate foes.
Even a trapped beast will fight;
wasps and scorpions are venomous,
let alone a large army!"
Sōng said:
"Not so.
Previously, I did not attack
to avoid their sharpness.
Now, I attack them
to await their decline.
The army I am attacking is exhausted,
not a retreating multitude.
Wáng Guó's forces are about to flee,
having no will to fight.
To strike chaos with order is not pursuing desperate foes."
So he alone advanced and attacked them,
making Dǒng Zhuó the rear guard.
They fought continuously and utterly defeated them,
beheading over ten thousand.
Wáng Guó fled and died.
Dǒng Zhuó was greatly ashamed and resentful,
and from then on, he resented Sōng.
The following year,
Dǒng Zhuó was appointed Governor of Bìngzhōu,
and an imperial edict ordered him to hand over his troops to Sōng.
Dǒng Zhuó did not comply.
Sōng's nephew, Lì,
who was then in the army,
persuaded Sōng, saying:
"The court has lost its way,
and the empire is in dire straits.
Only you and Dǒng Zhuó can stabilize the danger and right the downfall.
Now, a rift of resentment has formed,
and the situation does not allow for both to exist.
Dǒng Zhuó was ordered to hand over his troops,
yet he submitted a memorial requesting to keep them;
this is defying an imperial order.
Moreover, seeing the chaos in the capital,
he hesitates to advance;
this is harboring treacherous intentions.
Furthermore, he is brutal and unkind,
and his officers and soldiers are not loyal to him.
You, sir, are now the marshal;
you should wield the national might to punish him.
This would uphold loyalty and righteousness above,
and eliminate a scourge below.
This is the work of Huán Gōng and Wén Gōng."
Sōng said:
"While acting without orders is a crime,
executing without orders also incurs blame.
It is better to openly memorialize the matter
and let the court decide."
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial to inform the emperor.
The emperor reprimanded Dǒng Zhuó,
who then held even more resentment towards Sōng.
Later, when Dǒng Zhuó gained control of the government,
in the first year of Chūpíng,
he summoned Sōng to be Colonel of the City Gates,
intending to kill him.
As Sōng was about to depart,
Chief Clerk Liáng Yǎn persuaded him, saying:
"The Han dynasty is weak,
and eunuchs are disrupting the court.
Although Dǒng Zhuó executed them,
he could not be entirely loyal to the state.
Instead, he plundered the capital
and deposed and enthroned at will.
Now, summoning the general
means great danger or misfortune at worst,
and humiliation at best.
Dǒng Zhuó is now in Luòyáng,
and the Son of Heaven has moved west.
With your forces,
thirty thousand elite soldiers,
you could welcome the Venerable One,
receive orders to punish the rebel,
issue commands throughout the land,
and summon troops from various commanders.
The Yuán clan would press him from the east,
and you, General, would pressure him from the west.
This would be trapping a bird in a cage."
Sōng did not comply
and proceeded to the summons.
The officials, following Dǒng Zhuó's intent,
memorialized to have Sōng handed over to the authorities,
intending to execute him.
Sōng's son, Jiānshòu, had always been on good terms with Dǒng Zhuó.
He fled from Cháng'ān to Luòyáng
and sought refuge with Dǒng Zhuó.
Dǒng Zhuó was holding a joyful banquet when
Jiānshòu went straight forward to reproach him,
accusing him with great righteousness,
kowtowing and shedding tears.
Those seated were moved
and all left their seats to plead for Sōng.
Dǒng Zhuó then rose,
pulled Jiānshòu to sit with him,
ordered Sōng's release from prison,
and reappointed Sōng as Gentleman-Consultant,
later promoting him to Imperial Censor.
When Dǒng Zhuó returned to Cháng'ān,
the high officials and various civil and military officers welcomed him along the road.
Dǒng Zhuó instructed the Imperial Censor and those below to bow, intending to humiliate Sōng.
Afterward, he clasped hands with Sōng and said:
"Yìzhēn, are you well?"
Sōng smiled and thanked him,
and Dǒng Zhuó then reconciled.
When Dǒng Zhuó was executed,
Sōng was made General Who Conquers the West,
and later promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry.
In the autumn of that year,
he was appointed Grand Commandant.
In winter,
he was dismissed due to a falling star.
He was again appointed Grand Master of Splendid Happiness
and promoted to Grand Minister of the Court.
Soon after, Lǐ Jué caused chaos,
and Sōng also died of illness.
He was posthumously granted the seal and ribbon of General of Agile Cavalry,
and one person from his family was appointed Gentleman.
Sōng was a person who was cautious, diligent, and loving.
He submitted over five hundred memorials and remonstrances that were beneficial,
all of which he personally wrote down and then destroyed the drafts,
not letting them be known outside.
He also humbled himself before scholars,
and there were no lingering guests at his gate.
People of his time all praised and attached themselves to him.
Jiānshòu also gained renown
and was later appointed Court Attendant.
He declined the appointment
and died of illness.
Zhū Jùn 朱儁, whose courtesy name was Gōngwěi 公偉,
was a native of Shàngyú 上虞 in Kuàijī 會稽.
He was orphaned young,
and his mother used to deal in silk as a profession.
Jùn 朱儁 gained a reputation for his filial piety and care,
serving as a junior clerk in the county office.
He loved righteousness and made light of wealth;
the people of his hometown respected him.
At that time, Zhōu Guī 周規, from the same commandery, was invited to serve in a ducal office.
When he was about to depart,
he borrowed a million cash from the commandery treasury
to cover the expenses for his caps and headcloths.
Later, he was suddenly pressed for repayment,
but Guī's 周規's family was poor and could not afford it.
So Jùn 朱儁 secretly took his mother's silk
to settle the debt for Guī 周規.
His mother, having lost her livelihood,
was deeply resentful and reproached him.
Jùn 朱儁 said,
"A small loss now will lead to great gain later.
Being poor at first and rich afterward
is a natural principle."
Dù Shàng 度尚 of Shānyáng 山陽, the former county magistrate, saw this and was struck by him.
He recommended Jùn 朱儁 to the Administrator Wéi Yì 韋毅,
and Jùn 朱儁 gradually held various commandery positions.
Later, Administrator Yǐn Duān 尹端 appointed Jùn 朱儁 as his Chief Clerk.
In the second year of Xīpíng 熹平 (173 CE),
Duān 尹端 was impeached for his failure in suppressing the bandit Xǔ Zhāo 許昭,
and was reported to the province.
His crime warranted public execution.
Jùn 朱儁 then disguised himself in plain clothes and traveled incognito,
carrying several hundred catties of gold to the capital.
He bribed the officials in charge of memorials,
and thus managed to revise and finalize the provincial report,
allowing Duān 尹端 to be sentenced to penal labor at the Left Workshop.
Duān 尹端 was pleased by his reduced sentence but did not know the reason,
and Jùn 朱儁 never mentioned it.
Later, Administrator Xú Guī 徐珪 nominated Jùn 朱儁 as Filial and Incorrupt,
and he was twice promoted to be Magistrate of Lánlíng 蘭陵.
His administration showed extraordinary ability,
and he was praised in a memorial by the Chancellor of Dōnghǎi 東海.
Coincidentally, many bandits arose together in the Jiāozhǐ 交阯 region,
and the governors and administrators were weak and unable to suppress them.
Moreover, the Jiāozhǐ 交阯 bandit Liáng Lóng 梁龍 and over ten thousand others,
along with Kǒng Zhī 孔芝, the Administrator of Nánhǎi 南海, rebelled,
attacking and destroying commanderies and counties.
In the first year of Guānghé 光和 (178 CE),
Jùn 朱儁 was immediately appointed as the Inspector of Jiāozhǐ 交阯.
He was ordered to pass through his home commandery to recruit household soldiers and gather those already mobilized,
totaling five thousand men.
They advanced along two routes.
Upon reaching the provincial border,
he kept his armor concealed and did not advance,
but first sent envoys to the commanderies
to observe the bandits' situation,
and to proclaim his authority and virtue,
thereby shaking their morale.
Afterward, he advanced with the troops from the seven commanderies and pressed upon them.
He then beheaded Liáng Lóng 梁龍,
and tens of thousands surrendered.
Within ten days or a month, the region was entirely pacified.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dūtíng 都亭,
with fifteen hundred households,
and was bestowed fifty catties of gold.
He was summoned to be a Grand Master Remonstrant.
When the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out,
many high-ranking officials recommended Jùn 朱儁 for his talents and strategies.
He was appointed as Right Commander of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household,
holding the imperial insignia,
and, with the Left Commander of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household Huángfǔ Sōng 皇甫嵩, suppressed the bandits in Yǐngchuān 潁川, Rǔnán 汝南, and Chénguó 陳國.
They completely crushed and pacified them.
Sōng 皇甫嵩 then memorialized the facts,
attributing the credit to Jùn 朱儁.
Thereupon, Jùn 朱儁 was further enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīxiāng 西鄉
and promoted to General Who Guards Against Bandits.
At that time, Zhāng Mánchéng 張曼成 of Nányáng 南陽, a Yellow Turban leader, raised an army,
proclaiming himself
"Envoy of the Divine Master."
His followers numbered tens of thousands.
He killed Chǔ Gòng 褚貢, the Administrator of the commandery,
and encamped below Wǎn 宛 for over a hundred days.
Later, Administrator Qín Xié 秦頡 attacked and killed Mánchéng 張曼成,
but the bandits then chose Zhào Hóng 趙弘 as their leader.
Their numbers swelled,
eventually reaching over a hundred thousand,
and they occupied Wǎnchéng 宛城.
Jùn 朱儁, along with Xú Qiú 徐璆, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu 荊州, and Qín Xié 秦頡, combined their forces of eighteen thousand men and besieged Hóng 趙弘.
From June to August, they failed to capture the city.
The relevant authorities proposed to recall Jùn 朱儁.
Sīkōng 司空 Zhāng Wēn 張溫 submitted a memorial, stating:
"In the past, Qín 秦 employed Bái Qǐ 白起,
and Yān 燕 relied on Yuè Yì 樂毅;
both took years and months
to defeat their enemies.
Jùn 朱儁 suppressed Yǐngchuān 潁川
with success,
then led his army south.
His strategies are already in place.
Replacing a general in the midst of battle
is something military strategists forbid.
It is appropriate to give him more time
and demand his success."
Emperor Líng 靈帝 then ceased the recall.
Jùn 朱儁 then launched an urgent attack on Hóng 趙弘
and beheaded him.
The remaining bandit leader Hán Zhōng 韓忠 again occupied Wǎn 宛 and resisted Jùn 朱儁.
Jùn's 朱儁's forces were few and could not match them.
So he constructed an encircling encampment and built ramparts,
raising earthen mounds to overlook the city.
He then sounded drums to attack its southwest,
and the bandits all rushed their forces there.
Jùn 朱儁 personally led five thousand elite soldiers
to ambush their northeast,
and entered the city by scaling the walls.
Zhōng 韓忠 then retreated to a small fort,
terrified and begging for surrender.
Sīmǎ 司馬 Zhāng Chāo 張超, Xú Qiú 徐璆, and Qín Xié 秦頡 all wanted to accept it.
Jùn 朱儁 said,
"There are situations in warfare that appear similar but are fundamentally different.
In the past, during the time of Qín 秦 and Xiàng Yǔ 項羽,
the people had no fixed lord,
so rewards were given to those who joined to encourage others to come.
Now, the entire realm is unified;
only the Yellow Turbans have risen in rebellion.
Accepting their surrender will not encourage goodness,
but suppressing them is enough to punish evil.
If we accept them now,
it will further embolden rebellious intentions.
If the bandits profit, they will advance and fight;
if they are at a disadvantage, they will beg for surrender.
Letting the enemy grow stronger and prolonging the rebellion
is not a good plan."
Thereupon, he pressed the attack,
fighting continuously but failing to conquer.
Jùn 朱儁 climbed an earthen mound and looked down,
then turned to Zhāng Chāo 張超 and said,
"I understand now.
The bandits' outer encirclement is now tightly sealed,
and their inner camp is under severe pressure.
They beg for surrender, but it is not accepted;
they want to break out, but cannot.
This is why they are fighting to the death.
If ten thousand men are united in spirit,
they are still unstoppable,
let alone a hundred thousand!
This is extremely dangerous.
It is better to lift the siege
and consolidate our forces inside the city.
When Zhōng 韓忠 sees the siege lifted,
he will certainly sally forth.
Once he sallies forth, their resolve will disperse;
that is the way to easily defeat them."
Soon after, the siege was lifted,
and Zhōng 韓忠 indeed sallied out to fight.
Jùn 朱儁 then attacked him,
utterly routing him.
He pursued the fleeing enemy for several tens of *lǐ* 里,
beheading over ten thousand.
Zhōng 韓忠 and others then surrendered.
However, Qín Xié 秦頡, harboring accumulated resentment against Zhōng 韓忠,
killed him.
The remaining followers, fearing for their safety,
again chose Sūn Xià 孫夏 as their leader,
and returned to encamp in Wǎn 宛.
Jùn 朱儁 immediately attacked them.
Xià 孫夏 fled,
and Jùn 朱儁 pursued him to Jīngshān 精山 in Xī'è 西鄂,
where he again defeated them.
He again beheaded over ten thousand,
and the bandits then dispersed.
In the spring of the next year,
an envoy was dispatched with the imperial insignia to appoint Jùn 朱儁 as Right General of Cavalry and Chariots.
He returned to the capital with his victorious army
and was made Grand Master of Guanglu.
His enfeoffment was increased by five thousand households,
and he was newly enfeoffed as the Marquis of Qiántáng 錢塘,
and granted the additional title of Special Advanced.
He left office due to his mother's mourning.
After the period of mourning,
he was reappointed as Grand Architect,
then transferred to Privy Treasurer and Grand Coachman.
After the Yellow Turban bandits,

there were also the likes of Hēishān 黑山, Huánglóng 黃龍, Báibō 白波, Zuǒxiào 左校, Guō Dàxián 郭大賢, Yú Dī Gēn 于氐根, Qīngniújǐao 青牛角, Zhāng Báijí 張白騎, Liú Shí 劉石, Zuǒzī Zhàngbā 左髭丈八, Pínghàn 平漢, Dàjì 大計, Sīlì 司隸, Yuànzāi 掾哉,
Léigōng 雷公, Fúyún 浮雲, Fēiyàn 飛燕, Báiquè 白雀, Yáng Fèng 楊鳳, Yú Dú 于毒, Wǔlù 五鹿, Lǐ Dàmù 李大目, Bái Rào 白繞, Qí Gù 畦固, Kǔsào 苦唒.
They all arose in the valleys
and were countless.
The loudest among them were called Léigōng 雷公 (Thunder Duke),
those who rode white horses were Zhāng Báijí 張白騎 (Zhang the White Rider),
the nimble ones were called Fēiyàn 飛燕 (Flying Swallow),
those with many beards were nicknamed Yú Dī Gēn 于氐根,
and those with large eyes were Dàmù 大目 (Big Eyes).
Such titles
each had a reason.
The larger groups numbered twenty to thirty thousand,
and the smaller ones six to seven thousand.
The bandit chieftain Zhāng Yàn, a man from Chángshān,
was swift, brave, and agile.
Thus, the army nicknamed him "Flying Swallow" (Fēiyàn).
He was skilled at winning the hearts of his soldiers.
He then connected with bandits from the mountains and valleys of Zhōngshān, Chángshān, Zhàojùn, Shàngdǎng, and Hénèi.
Their forces reached a million,
and they were called the "Black Mountain Bandits" (Hēishān Zéi).
All the commanderies and counties north of the Yellow River suffered their depredations,
and the imperial court was unable to suppress them.
Yàn then sent envoys to the capital,
presenting a memorial to request surrender.
Consequently, Yàn was appointed General of the Household for Pacifying Disturbances (Píngnàn Zhōnglángjiāng),
and was put in charge of all affairs in the mountain valleys north of the Yellow River.
Each year, he was allowed to recommend one *xiàolián* and one *jìlì*.
Later, Yàn gradually encroached upon Hénèi,
approaching the capital.
Thereupon, Jùn was appointed Grand Administrator of Hénèi (Hénèi Tàishǒu),
and, leading his family troops, attacked and repelled them.
Thereafter, many of the bandits were pacified by Yuán Shào;
the details are in Shào's biography.
Jùn was again appointed Grand Master of Guanglu (Guānglù Dàfū),
then transferred to General of Agile Cavalry (Túnqí Jiāngjūn),
and soon after appointed Colonel of the City Gates (Chéngmén Xiàowèi) and Administrator of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn).
At that time, Dǒng Zhuó dominated the government.
As Jùn was an experienced general,
Zhuó outwardly treated him with great intimacy but secretly harbored jealousy.
When the Guāndōng forces grew strong,
Zhuó became afraid
and repeatedly invited high-ranking officials to a meeting
to discuss moving the capital to Cháng'ān.
Jùn always opposed this.
Although Zhuó disliked Jùn for disagreeing with him,
he coveted Jùn's great reputation.
Thus, he submitted a memorial to promote Jùn to Grand Coachman (Tàipú),
to serve as his deputy.
When the envoy came to appoint him,
Jùn declined and refused to accept.
He then said:
"If the state moves west,
it will surely abandon the hopes of the empire
and create strife east of the mountains.
I do not see how this can be beneficial."
The envoy questioned him, saying:
"You were summoned to receive an appointment, but you refused it.
You were not asked about the relocation, yet you presented your views on it.
What is the reason for this?"
Jùn replied:
"Deputy Prime Minister (Fù Xiàngguó) is not a position I am capable of holding;
the plan to move the capital
is not an urgent matter.
To decline what I am not capable of,
and to speak on what is not urgent,
is fitting for your servant."
The envoy said:
"Regarding the matter of moving the capital,
I have not heard of the plan.
Even if it has not yet been revealed,
how could you have received such information?"
Jùn replied:
"Prime Minister Dǒng Zhuó himself told your servant all about it;
that is how I knew."
The envoy could not refute him,
and thus he remained without the deputy position.
Later, when Zhuó entered the passes,
he left Jùn to guard Luòyáng.
However, Jùn secretly conspired with the generals east of the mountains to provide an internal response.
Afterwards, fearing an attack from Zhuó,
he abandoned his post and fled to Jīngzhōu.
Zhuó appointed Yáng Yì of Hóngnóng as Administrator of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn)
to guard Luòyáng.
When Jùn heard this,
he again advanced his troops back to Luòyáng,
and Yì fled.
As Hénán was devastated and had no resources,
Jùn then encamped in Zhōngmóu to the east,
sending letters to the provinces and commanderies,
requesting troops to attack Zhuó.
Táo Qiān, the Inspector of Xúzhōu, sent three thousand elite soldiers.
Other provinces and commanderies also provided some aid,
and Qiān then nominated Jùn to act as General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn).
When Dǒng Zhuó heard of this,
he dispatched his generals Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì, and tens of thousands of others to encamp in Hénán and resist Jùn.
Jùn met them in battle
but was defeated by Jué and Sì.
Jùn knew he was no match,
and remained below the passes, not daring to advance further.
After Dǒng Zhuó was executed
and Jué and Sì caused chaos,
Jùn was still in Zhōngmóu at that time.
Táo Qiān considered Jùn a renowned official
with numerous military achievements,
who could be entrusted with important affairs.
Thus, he and other prominent figures jointly nominated Jùn as Grand Tutor (Tàishī),
and then issued a proclamation to the provincial governors,
to jointly attack Lǐ Jué and others,
and welcome the Emperor.
He then presented a letter to Jùn, saying:
"Táo Qiān, Inspector of Xúzhōu; Zhōu Qián, former Inspector of Yángzhōu; Yīn Dé, Chancellor of Lángyé; Liú Kuí, Chancellor of Dōnghǎi;

Jí Lián, Chancellor of Péngchéng; Kǒng Róng, Chancellor of Běihǎi; Yuán Zhōng, Chancellor of Pèi; Yīng Shào, Grand Administrator of Tàishān; Xú Qiú, Grand Administrator of Rǔnán; Fú Qián, former Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng; Dr. Zhèng Xuán, and others,
dare to address the General of Chariots and Cavalry and Administrator of Hénán's headquarters:
The state has already suffered Dǒng Zhuó's calamity,
compounded by the disaster caused by Lǐ Jué and Guō Sì.
The young Emperor is held captive,
loyal and good officials are ruined and oppressed,
Cháng'ān is cut off,
and we know not what fortune or misfortune prevails.
Therefore, all officials and upright scholars
with discernment
are filled with worry and fear,
believing that without wise, sagacious, and heroic men,
how can these disasters and chaos be overcome?
Since the raising of troops three years ago,
until now,
provinces and commanderies have merely watched each other,
achieving no valiant attacks,
but instead engaging in private disputes
and mutual suspicion.
We, Qiān and others, have all consulted together
to discuss eliminating the national calamity.
All agreed: 'General, Marquis,
you are both civil and martial,
emerging in response to destiny.
All noble gentlemen,
without exception, look up to you with eagerness.'
Therefore, we have spurred each other on,
selected the finest and bravest,
capable of deep penetration,
to advance directly to Xiányáng.
They carry ample provisions,
sufficient for half a year.
We respectfully entrust them, with one heart,
to the Grand Marshal."
Coincidentally, Lǐ Jué, using the counsel of Grand Commandant Zhōu Zhōng and Minister of Works Jiǎ Xǔ,
summoned Jùn to court.
All the military officers feared entering the passes
and wanted to respond to Táo Qiān and the others.
Jùn said:
"When a lord summons a minister,
righteousness dictates no delay,
let alone an imperial edict!
Moreover, Jué and Sì are mere youngsters,
and Fán Chóu an ordinary fellow,
without great far-reaching strategies.
Furthermore, their powers are evenly matched,
so conflict and trouble are bound to arise.
If I take advantage of their discord,
great things can be accomplished."
Thus, he declined Qiān's proposal and responded to Jué's summons,
again becoming Grand Coachman (Tàipú).
Qiān and the others then disbanded.
In the fourth year of Chūpíng (193 CE),
he replaced Zhōu Zhōng as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi)
and oversaw the affairs of the Masters of Writing.
In the autumn of the following year,
he was dismissed due to a solar eclipse,
and again appointed to act as General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn),
holding the *jié* and garrisoning Guāndōng.
Before he could depart,
Lǐ Jué killed Fán Chóu,
and Guō Sì became suspicious himself,
attacking Jué.
Cháng'ān was in chaos,
so Jùn remained and did not set out,
staying to be appointed Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng).
Emperor Xiàn decreed Jùn, Grand Commandant Yáng Biāo, and over ten others to persuade Guō Sì
to reconcile with Lǐ Jué.
Sì refused,
and consequently held Jùn and others as hostages.
Jùn, being inherently resolute, fell ill and died that very day.
His son, Hào,
also possessed talent and integrity,
and rose to the position of Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng Tàishǒu).
The discussion says: Huángfǔ Sōng and Zhū Jùn were both endowed with the strategy of a supreme general,
receiving their command in a time of emergency.
When their mission was accomplished and their armies victorious,
their prestige resounded throughout the world.
When they encountered a weak ruler in distress,
and savage bandits running rampant,
this was truly the opportune moment for Yè Gōng to cast off his sleeve
and for Zhái Yì to rally his troops.
Therefore, Liáng Yǎn offered counsel,
and the eastern regions of the mountains formed an alliance.
But they abandoned the great cause of defying Heaven
and stuck to the petty integrity of common men.
In the end, they were miserably trapped in the tiger's mouth,
and became a laughingstock to the wise.
Was it Heaven's will to prolong this chaos?
How terrible that their wisdom and courage did not last to the end!
The former historian Huá Jiào of Píngyuán, Jìn,
stated that his father, Grand Master of Guanglu, Biǎo,
often spoke of his grandfather, Grand Commandant of Wèi, Xīn,
who said,
"People of the time spoke of Huángfǔ Sōng's lack of boastfulness:
in the battles of Rǔ and Yù,
he attributed the success to Zhū Jùn;
in the victory over Zhāng Jiǎo,
he credited Lú Zhí.
He amassed fame and counsel
without claiming it for himself.
Indeed, fame and achievement
are things highly valued by the world.
If one can truly avoid contending for what the world values most highly,
then resentment and calamity will not run deep."
For a man like Duke Huángfǔ to respond to danger and chaos,
and yet be able to ultimately preserve himself whole,
is his attainment not indeed precious?
Therefore, Yán Zǐ desired to prioritize not boasting of one's good deeds,
and this is also an essential principle for conducting oneself!
A eulogy says: The yellow evil erupted,
Sōng then wielded his axe.
Who rallied the troops?
He did not dwell on, nor boast of, his deeds.
Jùn swiftly moved through Chén and Yǐng,
also pacifying Yuè.
His words expressed the solemn royal command,
but both encountered difficulties.
Biography of Dǒng Zhuó, Chapter 62
Dǒng Zhuó, courtesy name Zhòngyǐng,
was a native of Líntáo, Lǒngxī.
He was by nature fierce and bold, but also cunning.
In his youth, he often traveled among the Qiāng,
and forged strong ties with all their powerful chieftains.
Later, he returned to farm in the countryside.
When powerful chieftains came to visit him,
Dǒng Zhuó would slaughter his ox
to feast and entertain them.
The chieftains were moved by his sincerity,
and upon returning, they collected over a thousand head of various livestock and gave them to him.
From this, he became known as a strong and chivalrous man.
He served as a military aide in the province,
often guarding the frontier outposts.
Dǒng Zhuó possessed extraordinary physical strength,
carrying two quivers at his sides,
galloping and shooting left and right,
and was feared by the Qiāng and Hú.
Towards the end of Emperor Huán's reign,
he was appointed a Yǔlín Láng (Imperial Guard) from among the "good families" of the six commanderies,
and served as Sīmǎ (Military Administrator) under Zhonglang General Zhāng Huàn,
jointly attacking the rebellious Qiāng of Hànyáng.
They defeated them,
and he was appointed Lángzhōng (Gentleman),
and granted nine thousand bolts of silk.
Dǒng Zhuó said,
"The doer is oneself,
the owner is the soldier."
He then distributed all of it to his officers and soldiers,
keeping nothing for himself.
He was gradually promoted to Wùjǐ Xiàowèi (Commander of the Western Regions),
but was dismissed due to an incident.
Later, he became the Inspector of Bìngzhōu,
and the Grand Administrator of Hédōng.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng (184 CE),
he was appointed Dōng Zhōngláng Jiāng (Central Inspector of the East),
bearing a ceremonial staff,
to replace Lú Zhí in attacking Zhāng Jiǎo at Xiàqǔyáng.
His army was defeated, and he was found guilty.
That winter,
the Xiānlíng Qiāng of Běidì and bandits from Fāohǎn and Héguān rebelled.
They jointly established Běigōng Bóyù and Lǐ Wénhóu, two Yìcóng Hú (Righteous Allied Hu) from Huángzhōng, as generals,
and killed Líng Zhēng, the Protector of the Qiāng.
Bóyù and others then abducted Biān Zhāng and Hán Suì from Jīnchéng,
making them solely responsible for military and political affairs.
They jointly killed Chén Yì, the Grand Administrator of Jīnchéng,
and attacked and burned down prefectures and commanderies.
The following spring,
they led tens of thousands of cavalry to invade Sānfǔ,
threatening the imperial tombs,
under the pretext of executing the eunuchs.
An imperial edict appointed Dǒng Zhuó as Zhōngláng Jiāng (Central Inspector),
to assist the General of the Left Chariots and Cavalry, Huángfǔ Sōng, in suppressing them.
Huángfǔ Sōng returned without achieving success and was dismissed,
while Biān Zhāng, Hán Suì, and others grew greatly in power.
The court again appointed Sīkōng (Minister of Works) Zhāng Wēn as General of Chariots and Cavalry,
granting him a ceremonial staff,
with Zhífú Wú (Commander of the Imperial Guards) Yuán Pāng as his deputy.
Dǒng Zhuó was appointed Pòlǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Breaks the Barbarians),
and along with Dàngkòu Jiāngjūn (General Who Suppresses Bandits) Zhōu Shèn, they were both under Zhāng Wēn's command.
Bringing together the infantry and cavalry from various commanderies, numbering over one hundred thousand,
they camped at Měiyáng
to protect the imperial tombs.
Zhāng and Suì also advanced their troops to Měiyáng.
Zhāng Wēn and Dǒng Zhuó engaged them in battle,
but were always unsuccessful.
In the eleventh month,
a meteor like fire appeared at night,
its light stretching over ten *zhàng*,
illuminating the camps of Zhāng and Suì.
Donkeys and horses all cried out.
The rebels considered it an ill omen,
and wished to return to Jīnchéng.
Dǒng Zhuó was pleased when he heard this.
The next day,
he joined forces with Bào Hóng, the Right Fúfēng, and others to attack,
utterly defeating them,
beheading several thousand.
Zhāng and Suì fled to Yúzhōng.
Zhāng Wēn then dispatched Zhōu Shèn with thirty thousand men to pursue and attack them.
Zhāng Wēn's Military Advisor, Sūn Jiān,
advised Zhōu Shèn, saying,
"The rebels have no grain in their city;
they must transport provisions from outside.
I wish to take ten thousand men to cut off their supply route.
If the General follows with the main army,
the rebels will surely be in distress and dare not fight.
If they flee into the Qiāng territory,
