and we unite our strength to attack them,
then Liángzhōu can be pacified."
Zhōu Shèn did not heed him,
and led his army to besiege Yúzhōng city.
But Zhāng and Suì divided their forces and camped in Kuíyuánxiá,
in turn cutting off Zhōu Shèn's supply route.
Zhōu Shèn was afraid,
and abandoned his heavy wagons and retreated.
At that time, Zhāng Wēn also sent Dǒng Zhuó with thirty thousand soldiers to attack the Xiānlíng Qiāng.
Dǒng Zhuó was surrounded by the Qiāng and Hú
north of Wàngyuán,
his food supplies were exhausted,
and he was in a desperate situation, unable to advance or retreat.
He then falsely set up a dam in the river he was crossing,
pretending to fish,
while secretly crossing his army under the dam.
By the time the rebels pursued him,
the water released by the dam was already deep,
making it impossible to cross.
At that time, the other armies were defeated and retreated,
only Dǒng Zhuó returned with his forces intact,
camping at Fúfēng.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Tái Township,
with a thousand households.
In the spring of the third year,
an envoy bearing a ceremonial staff was sent to Cháng'ān to appoint Zhāng Wēn as Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant).
This was the first time a Sāngōng (Three Excellencies) was appointed while outside the capital,
beginning with Zhāng Wēn.
That winter,
Zhāng Wēn was recalled to the capital.
Hán Suì then killed Biān Zhāng, Bóyù, and Wénhóu,
and with over one hundred thousand soldiers,
advanced to besiege Lǒngxī.
The Grand Administrator, Lǐ Xiāngrú, rebelled,
and allied with Hán Suì,
jointly killing Gěng Bǐ, the Inspector of Liángzhōu.
And Gěng Bǐ's Military Administrator, Mǎ Téng of Fúfēng,
also raised troops and rebelled.
Furthermore, Wáng Guó of Hànyáng,
styled himself
"General Who Gathers the Multitude,"
all allied with Hán Suì.
They jointly acclaimed Wáng Guó as their leader,
and entrusted him with command of all their forces,
to raid and plunder Sānfǔ.
In the fifth year,
they besieged Chéncāng.
Dǒng Zhuó was then appointed Qián Jiāngjūn (General of the Vanguard),
and with Zuǒ Jiāngjūn (General of the Left) Huángfǔ Sōng, they attacked and defeated them.
Hán Suì and others again jointly deposed Wáng Guó,
and abducted Yán Zhōng of Hànyáng, former Prefect of Xìndū,
making him oversee all their divisions.
Yán Zhōng, ashamed to be coerced by the multitude,
fell ill and died from indignation.
Hán Suì and others gradually vied for power,
killing each other,
and their various divisions dispersed.
Six years later,
Dǒng Zhuó was summoned to be Minister of the Privy Purse (Shǎofǔ),
but he refused to take up the post.
He submitted a memorial saying:
“The righteous volunteers from Huángzhōng and the Qín Hú soldiers under my command all came to me and said: 'The provisions are not fully paid,
and our grants and allowances are cut off,
our wives and children are starving and freezing.'
They pulled on my carriage,
preventing me from moving.
The Qiāng Hú are like emaciated dogs,
I cannot control them,
so I can only humor them and comfort them.
When their numbers increase, I will report again.”
The imperial court could not control him
and was rather concerned.
When Emperor Líng fell ill,
an imperial edict appointed Dǒng Zhuó as Governor of Bìngzhōu,
ordering him to transfer his troops to Huángfǔ Sōng.
Dǒng Zhuó again submitted a memorial, saying:
“I have neither old wisdom
nor great achievements in my youth,
but Heaven's grace has been mistakenly bestowed upon me,
allowing me to command the army for ten years.
The soldiers, young and old, have been close to me for a long time,
cherishing the kindness of my nurturing,
and are willing to fight for me for a single day.
I beg to lead them to the northern regions
to exert our strength on the frontier.”
Thereupon, he stationed his troops in Hédōng
to observe the changing situation.
When the Emperor passed away,
Grand General Hé Jìn and Colonel Director of Retainers Yuán Shào plotted to eliminate the eunuchs,
but the Empress Dowager did not permit it.
So they secretly summoned Dǒng Zhuó to lead his troops into the capital
to threaten the Empress Dowager.
Upon receiving the summons, Dǒng
immediately set out.
He also submitted a memorial
saying:
“The Palace Regular Attendant Zhāng Ràng and others have secretly enjoyed favor and received寵,
corrupting the entire realm.
I have heard that to stop boiling water,
nothing is better than removing the firewood;
an ulcer, though painful,
is better than an internal festering.
In the past, Zhào Yǎng raised the army of Jìnyáng
to drive out the wicked people beside the ruler.
Now I shall sound the drums and bells into Luòyáng,
and request to arrest Zhāng Ràng and others
to cleanse the corruption.”
Before Dǒng Zhuó arrived, Hé Jìn was defeated.
Colonel of the Tiger Swift Cavalry Yuán Shù then burned the Southern Palace,
intending to attack the eunuchs.
However, the Palace Regular Attendant Duàn Guī and others
abducted the Young Emperor and the Prince of Chénliú, fleeing by night to Xiǎopíngjīn.
Dǒng Zhuó saw the fire from afar,
led his troops and advanced quickly,
arriving at the west of the city before dawn.
Hearing that the Young Emperor was at Běimáng,
he went to escort him.
When the Emperor saw Dǒng Zhuó leading his soldiers approaching,
he was terrified and wept.
Dǒng Zhuó spoke with him,
but he could not respond;
when Dǒng Zhuó spoke with the Prince of Chénliú,
the conversation turned to the chaos and disaster.
Dǒng Zhuó considered the Prince to be worthy,
and he was also raised by Empress Dowager Dǒng.
Dǒng Zhuó himself felt he was of the same clan as the Empress Dowager,
so he had the intention of deposing and establishing.
Initially,
when Dǒng Zhuó entered the capital,
he had no more than three thousand infantry and cavalry.
Feeling his troops were too few,
and fearing he would not be obeyed by those near and far,
every four or five days he would secretly lead his army out to nearby camps at night,
and then return the next morning with a grand display of banners and drums,
making it seem as if more western troops had arrived.
No one in Luòyáng knew the truth.
Soon after, all the troops previously led by Hé Jìn and his brother Hé Miáo returned to Dǒng Zhuó.
Dǒng Zhuó also sent Lǚ Bù to kill Administrator of the Capital (Zhí Jīnwú) Dīng Yuán and absorb his forces.
Dǒng Zhuó's army greatly increased.
He then subtly urged the imperial court to dismiss Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Liú Hóng and replace him with himself.
Subsequently, he convened a meeting to discuss the deposition and establishment of an emperor.
At a grand gathering of officials,
Dǒng Zhuó raised his head and said:
“The greatest are Heaven and Earth,
and next are ruler and minister, which constitute governance.
The Emperor is dim and weak,
unfit to serve the ancestral temple
and be the master of the world.
Now, I wish to follow the precedents of Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng,
and establish the Prince of Chénliú instead.
What do you think?”
None of the high officials down to the lower ranks dared to respond.
Dǒng Zhuó again declared:
“In the past, Huò Guāng made his decision,
and Yán Nián brandished his sword.
Anyone who dares to obstruct this grand discussion
shall be dealt with according to military law.”
All those seated trembled.
Only Grand Master of Ceremonies (Shàngshū) Lú Zhí said:
“In the past, Tàijiǎ, upon ascending the throne, was not enlightened;
Chāngyì's transgressions amounted to over a thousand.
Thus, there were acts of deposition and establishment.
The current Emperor is young,
and his conduct is without fault.
This is not comparable to those previous cases.”
Dǒng Zhuó was greatly enraged
and dismissed the assembly.
The next day, he again gathered the officials in the Chóngdé Front Hall,
and then coerced the Empress Dowager
to issue an edict deposing the Young Emperor.
He said:
“The Emperor, during mourning,
showed no filial piety,
and his demeanor was unlike a ruler.
He is now deposed as the King of Hóngnóng.”
Then the Prince of Chénliú was enthroned,
who became Emperor Xiàn.
He also ordered the Empress Dowager
to pressure Empress Dowager Yǒnglè
until she died of sorrow,
reversing the proper rites between mother-in-law and daughter-in-law,
and showing no filial devotion.
She was moved to Yǒng'ān Palace,
and subsequently assassinated.
Dǒng Zhuó was promoted to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
concurrently serving as General of the Van (Qián Jiāngjūn),
and was granted the imperial ensigns of a General with Imperial Authority (Jié), the imperial carriage with axe and battle-axe (fǔyuè), and the Tiger Swift cavalry,
and was further enfeoffed as Marquis of Méi.
Dǒng Zhuó then, along with Minister of the Masses (Sītú) Huáng Wǎn and Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Yáng Biāo,
both carrying axes and sacrificial knives, went to the palace gate to submit a memorial,
posthumously rehabilitating Chén Fān, Dòu Wǔ, and other partisans,
to satisfy popular expectations.
Thereupon, all their former titles and ranks were restored,
and their descendants were promoted.
Soon after, Dǒng Zhuó was promoted to Chancellor (Xiàngguó),
allowed to enter court without hurrying,
and wear his sword and shoes into the hall.
His mother was enfeoffed as Lady of Chíyáng,
and an official (chéng) was appointed to administer her household.
At this time, the residences of nobles and relatives in Luòyáng were numerous and visible everywhere,
and their gold, silk, and property
were amassed in every household.
Dǒng Zhuó allowed his soldiers to run wild,
raiding their homes,
sexually assaulting women,
and plundering their possessions,
which he called
“searching for provisions.”
People were terrified and panicked,
uncertain if they would live to see the next day.
When Empress Hé was buried,
and the Wén Mausoleum was opened,
Dǒng Zhuó took all the treasures from the tomb.
He also raped princesses
and seized palace women as wives,
inflicting cruel punishments and arbitrary penalties;
a mere glance could mean death.
Neither internal nor external officials could feel secure.
Dǒng Zhuó once sent his army to Yángchéng.
At that time, people were gathered at a communal festival.
He ordered them all to be beheaded,
loaded their carts with their belongings,
and their women,
tying the heads to the carriage shafts,
singing and shouting as they returned.
He also destroyed the Wǔzhū coins
and minted smaller coins instead,
taking all the bronze figures, bells, pedestals, flying beasts, and bronze horses from Luòyáng and Cháng'ān
to use for casting.
Consequently, currency became cheap and goods expensive,
with a stone of grain costing tens of thousands.
Moreover, the coins had no rims or inscriptions,
making them inconvenient for use.
People at the time believed that Qín Shǐhuáng had seen giants in Líntáo
and then cast bronze figures.
Dǒng Zhuó,
a native of Líntáo,
now destroyed them.
Though the creation and destruction differed,
their cruelty and brutality were similar.
Zhúo had long heard that everyone in the empire suffered from the eunuchs who had murdered loyal and good men.
When he was in power,
though he acted without principle,
he still suppressed his nature and feigned emotion,
promoting and employing many scholars.
He appointed Zhōu Bì (周珌) of Hànyáng (漢陽) as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), Wǔ Qióng (伍瓊) of Rúnán (汝南) as Imperial Attendant (Shìzhōng),
Zhèng Gōngyè (鄭公業) as Minister (Shàngshū),
and Hé Yǒng (何顒) as Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ), among others.
He made the reclusive scholar Xún Shuǎng (荀爽) Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Those who had been implicated in the Dǎnggù (黨錮) proscriptions, such as Chén Jì (陳紀) and Hán Róng (韓融),
were all made high officials (lièqīng).
Many reclusive scholars
were prominently promoted.
He made Hán Fú (韓馥) of Minister (Shàngshū) the Inspector of Jìzhōu (冀州 Cìshǐ),
Liú Dài (劉岱) of Imperial Attendant (Shìzhōng) the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (兗州 Cìshǐ),
Kǒng Zhòu (孔伷) of Chénliú (陳留) the Inspector of Yùzhōu (豫州 Cìshǐ),
and Zhāng Zī (張咨) of Yǐngchuān (潁川) the Administrator of Nányáng (Nányáng Tàishǒu).
Those whom Zhúo personally favored
were not placed in prominent positions,
but merely as commanders and officers.
In the first year of Chūpíng (初平) (190 CE),
when Fú and the others arrived at their posts,
they, along with more than ten others like Yuán Shào (袁紹),
each raised righteous armies,
formed an alliance to attack Zhúo,
while Wǔ Qióng and Zhōu Bì secretly served as their internal leaders.
Initially,
at the end of Emperor Língdì’s (靈帝) reign,
remnant Yellow Turbans, such as Guō Tài (郭太) and others, rose again in Báibō Gǔ (白波谷) in Xīhé (西河).
They then plundered Tàiyuán (太原)
and subsequently defeated Hédōng (河東).
The common people relocated to Sānfǔ (三輔),
and were called
“Báibō Zéi (白波賊)” (White Wave Bandits),
numbering over one hundred thousand.
Zhúo sent Colonel Niú Fǔ (牛輔) to attack them,
but he could not repel them.
When Zhúo heard that an army had risen in the east,
he was afraid,
so he poisoned the King of Hóngnóng (弘農 Wáng),
intending to move the capital to Cháng'ān (長安).
During a discussion with the high officials (gōngqīng),
Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Huáng Wǎn (黃琬) and Minister of Education (Sītú) Yáng Biāo (楊彪) argued in court but could not succeed,
and Wǔ Qióng and Zhōu Bì also strongly remonstrated against it.
Zhúo then became enraged and said:
“When Zhúo first entered the court,
these two men advised me to employ good scholars,
so I followed them.
But when you gentlemen arrived at your posts,
you raised armies to attack me.
These two gentlemen betrayed Zhúo;
how can Zhúo fail them!”
He then executed Qióng and Bì.
Biāo and Wǎn, trembling with fear,
went to Zhúo and apologized, saying:
“We insignificant people are merely nostalgic for the old ways;
we do not wish to obstruct state affairs.
Please consider our lack of foresight our crime.”
After Zhúo had killed Qióng and Bì,
he soon regretted it,
so he memorialized the court to appoint Biāo and Wǎn as Grand Masters of Remonstrance (Guānglù Dàfū).
Thereupon, he moved the Son of Heaven to the western capital.
Initially,
Cháng'ān had suffered from the Chìméi (赤眉) rebellion,
and its palaces, temples, and official residences were burned to nothing.
At this time, only the Grand Ancestral Temple (Gāomiào) and the Jingzhào Prefecture (Jīngzhào Fǔ) building remained,
so they temporarily resided there.
Later, they moved to the Wèiyāng Palace (Wèiyāng Gōng).
Thereupon, Zhúo moved all the people of Luòyáng (洛陽), numbering several million, to Cháng'ān.
The infantry and cavalry drove and pressed them,
trampling over each other.
Starvation, banditry, and plunder
left piled corpses filling the roads.
Zhúo himself was stationed in the Bìguī Yuàn (畢圭苑) garden,
and he burned all the palaces, temples, official residences, and private homes.
Within two hundred *lǐ* (里), nothing was left.
He also sent Lǚ Bù (呂布) to excavate the imperial mausoleums
and the tombs of high officials and below,
collecting their treasures.
At that time, Sūn Jiān (孫堅), the Administrator of Chángshā (Chángshā Tàishǒu), also led troops from the various commanderies of Yùzhōu to attack Zhúo.
Zhúo first sent generals Xú Róng (徐榮) and Lǐ Méng (李蒙) to plunder in all directions.
Róng encountered Jiān at Liáng (梁),
fought with him,
defeated Jiān,
and captured Lǐ Mín (李旻), the Administrator of Yǐngchuān (Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu), alive,
and boiled him.
All the righteous soldiers captured by Zhúo
were wrapped in cloth,
stood on their heads,
and killed by having hot oil poured over them.
At that time, Wáng Kuāng (王匡), the Administrator of Hénèi (Hénèi Tàishǒu),
stationed troops at Héyáng Jīn (河陽津),
intending to attack Zhúo.
Zhúo sent decoy troops to challenge them,
while secretly sending elite soldiers to cross the river north of Xiǎopíng Jīn (小平津),
defeating them,
with almost all of them killed.
The next year,
Sūn Jiān gathered his scattered soldiers
and advanced to Yángrén (陽人) in Liáng Xiàn (梁縣).
Zhúo sent generals Hú Zhěn (胡軫) and Lǚ Bù to attack him.
Bù and Zhěn did not get along,
and the army itself was alarmed and terrified,
with the soldiers scattered and chaotic.
Jiān pursued and attacked them,
and Zhěn and Bù were defeated and fled.
Zhúo sent general Lǐ Què (李傕) to Jiān to seek peace,
but Jiān refused to accept it
and advanced to Dàgǔ (大谷),
ninety *lǐ* (里) from Luòyáng.
Zhúo himself came out and fought Jiān among the imperial tombs.
Zhúo was defeated and fled,
retreating to Mǐnchí (黽池),
and gathered troops in Shǎn (陝).
Jiān advanced to the Xuānyáng (宣陽) city gate of Luòyáng
and again attacked Lǚ Bù.
Bù was again defeated and fled.
Jiān then cleared the ancestral temples,
filled and leveled the imperial tombs,
and dispatched troops out of Hángǔ Guān (函谷關),
to the area between Xīn'ān (新安) and Mǐnchí,
to cut off Zhúo’s retreat.
Zhúo said to Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ) Liú Ài (劉艾):
“The generals east of the pass have been defeated many times;
they are incapable.
Only Sūn Jiān is a little bit reckless;
all generals should be cautious of him.”
He then ordered Colonel-Protector of the East (Dōng Zhōnglángjiàng) Dǒng Yuè (董越) to garrison Mǐnchí,
Colonel (Zhōnglángjiàng) Duàn Wēi (段煨) to garrison Huàyīn (華陰),
Colonel Niú Fǔ to garrison Ānyì (安邑),
and the remaining Colonels and Commandants (Xiàowèi) to be stationed in various counties,
to defend against the forces east of the mountains.
Zhúo implicitly instructed the court to have Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglùxūn) Xuān Fán (宣璠)
bear the imperial insignia and appoint Zhúo as Grand Preceptor (Tàishī),
a rank above that of the feudal kings.
He then returned to Cháng'ān.
All officials greeted him on the road, bowing.
Zhúo then presumptuously imitated imperial carriages and attire,
riding in a golden-wheeled, green-canopied carriage,
with dragon-claw paintings on both sides of the wheels.
People at the time called it
“Gānmó Chē (竿摩車)” (Pole-Rubbing Carriage),
meaning that his attire was close to that of the Son of Heaven.
He made his brother Mín (旻) Left General (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Hù (Hù Hóu).
His nephew Huáng (璜) became Imperial Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Commandant of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Xiàowèi).
Both were in charge of military affairs.
Thereupon, his relatives, both internal and external,
all held high positions.
Even his descendants who were still children
—the boys were all enfeoffed as marquises,
and the girls were made Ladies of Districts (Yì Jūn).
He frequently held banquets and feasts with the hundreds of officials,
indulging in excessive pleasure.
He then built a camp in the east of Cháng'ān city to reside in.
He also built a fortress in Méi (郿),
seven *zhàng* (丈) high and thick,
called
“Wànsuì Wǔ (萬歲塢)” (Ten Thousand Year Fortress).
He stored enough grain for thirty years.
He said of himself:
“If I succeed,
I will dominate the world;
if I do not succeed,
guarding this will be enough to live out my old age.”
He once went to Méi to inspect the fortress.
High officials and others bade him farewell outside the Héngmén (橫門) gate.
Zhúo set up tents and offered drinks and food.
He lured several hundred rebels from Běidì (北地) into surrendering
and killed them at the banquet.
First, their tongues were cut out,
then their hands and feet were chopped off,
then their eyes were gouged out,
and they were boiled in a pot.
Before they could die,
they writhed between the [cup and] tables.
Those present trembled,
losing their spoons and chopsticks,
while Zhúo ate and drank as usual.
Any generals who spoke carelessly
were executed before him.
He also gradually executed the old aristocratic families in Guānzhōng (關中),
implicating them in rebellion.
At that time, the Grand Astrologer observed the celestial phenomena
and said that a high minister would be executed.
Therefore, Dǒng Zhuó sent someone to falsely accuse the Commandant of the Guards, Zhāng Wēn, of colluding with Yuán Shù.
Then he had Zhāng Wēn flogged in the marketplace
and killed him,
to avert the celestial omen.
Previously, Zhāng Wēn had led troops to garrison Měiyáng,
and Dǒng Zhuó, having fought unsuccessfully against Biān Zhāng and others,
was summoned by Zhāng Wēn but did not respond to the order in a timely manner.
When he finally arrived, his words during the audience were disrespectful.
At that time, Sūn Jiān was Zhāng Wēn’s Staff Officer [cānjūn],
and he urged Zhāng Wēn to deploy troops and execute Dǒng Zhuó.
Zhāng Wēn said:
"Dǒng Zhuó has a fearsome reputation;
we are still relying on him to march west."
Sūn Jiān said:
"My Lord, you personally command the imperial army,
and your prestige shakes the world.
Why rely on Dǒng Zhuó and depend on him?
I have heard that the renowned generals of old,
wielding their battle-axes before the masses,
never failed to execute someone to display their might and authority.
Thus, Ráng Jū executed Zhuāng Jiǎ,
and Wèi Jiàng executed Yáng Gān.
If you let him go now,
you will diminish your own prestige.
What good will regret do later?"
Zhāng Wēn could not follow this advice,
but Dǒng Zhuó still harbored resentment and hatred,
and thus Zhāng Wēn met his misfortune.
Zhāng Wēn, courtesy name Bóshèn,
had a good reputation from a young age,
and had successively risen to the ranks of high officials.
He was also secretly conspiring with the Minister of Works [sītú] Wáng Yǔn to eliminate Dǒng Zhuó,
but the plot had not yet been launched when he was harmed.
The Colonel of Yueqi [yuèqí xiàowèi], Wǔ Fú of Rǔnán,
enraged by Dǒng Zhuó's savagery and cruelty,
resolved to kill him with his own hands.
He then went to see Dǒng Zhuó in court attire, with a dagger concealed in his sash.
After Wǔ Fú finished speaking and took his leave,
Dǒng Zhuó rose to escort him to the door of the chamber,
and placed his hand on Wǔ Fú's back.
Wǔ Fú then drew his knife and stabbed him,
but missed.
Dǒng Zhuó struggled and managed to escape,
urgently shouting for his attendants to seize and kill Wǔ Fú,
and loudly cursed,
saying:
"The rascal wants to rebel!"
Wǔ Fú loudly declared:
"I only regret that I couldn't tear this wicked villain limb from limb in the marketplace
to appease Heaven and Earth!"
Before he finished speaking, he died.
At that time, Wáng Yǔn, along with Lǚ Bù and the Palace Aide to the Imperial Censors [púyè] Shìsūn Ruì, plotted to kill Dǒng Zhuó.
Someone wrote
the character "Lǚ"
on a piece of cloth,
carried it on his back, and walked through the marketplace,
singing:
"Bù!
Someone reported this to Dǒng Zhuó,
but Dǒng Zhuó did not understand.
In the fourth month of the third year,
the Emperor, having just recovered from an illness,
held a grand assembly at Wèiyáng Palace.
Dǒng Zhuó, in court attire, ascended his carriage.
Soon after, his horse bolted and fell into the mud.
He returned inside to change his clothes.
His young wife tried to stop him,
but Dǒng Zhuó did not listen
and proceeded.
He arrayed soldiers along both sides of the road,
from his fortress to the palace,
infantry on the left and cavalry on the right,
guarding the entire perimeter,
and ordered Lǚ Bù and others to protect the front and rear.
Wáng Yǔn then secretly presented a memorial about the matter with Shìsūn Ruì,
and had Shìsūn Ruì personally write an imperial edict to Lǚ Bù.
He ordered the Commandant of Cavalry [qí dūwèi] Lǐ Sù
and more than ten brave warriors loyal to Lǚ Bù
to pretend to be palace guards and wait for Dǒng Zhuó inside the North Yè Gate.
As Dǒng Zhuó was about to arrive,
his horse balked and refused to move.
He felt strange and fearful, and wanted to turn back.
Lǚ Bù urged him to advance,
and so he entered the gate.
Lǐ Sù stabbed him with a halberd,
but Dǒng Zhuó was wearing armor, so it did not penetrate.
He was wounded in the arm and fell from his carriage.
He looked back and cried loudly:
"Where is Lǚ Bù?"
Lǚ Bù replied:
"There is an imperial edict to punish the traitorous minister!"
Dǒng Zhuó cursed loudly:
"You miserable dog, how dare you do this?!"
Lǚ Bù, at his cue, held his spear and stabbed Dǒng Zhuó,
then ordered soldiers to cut him down.
The Chief Clerk [zhǔbù] Tián Yí
and Dǒng Zhuó’s personal attendants rushed forward to his corpse,
but Lǚ Bù killed them too.
An edict of amnesty was swiftly dispatched
to the palace and throughout the capital.
All the soldiers shouted "Long live the Emperor!",
and the common people sang and danced in the streets.
Men and women in Cháng’ān sold their pearls, jade, and fine clothes to buy wine and meat to celebrate,
filling the streets and markets.
Huángfǔ Sōng was ordered to attack Dǒng Zhuó’s younger brother Dǒng Mín at Méiwù,
killing his mother, wife, and children,
utterly exterminating his clan.
Dǒng Zhuó’s corpse was then displayed in the marketplace.
As it was the beginning of summer,
Dǒng Zhuó, who was extremely fat,
had his fat flow onto the ground.
The officer guarding the corpse lit a fire and placed it in Dǒng Zhuó’s navel,
which glowed brightly until dawn,
lasting for several days.
The retainers of the Yuán family also gathered the corpses of the Dǒng clan,
burned them to ashes, and scattered them on the road.
The valuable treasures in the fortress included twenty to thirty thousand catties of gold,
eighty to ninety thousand catties of silver,
and countless silks, brocades, damasks, gauzes, fine plain silks, and rare curiosities,
piled up like mountains.
Initially,
Dǒng Zhuó had entrusted Niú Fǔ, his son-in-law,
whom he deeply trusted,
with troops to garrison Shǎn.
Niú Fǔ then dispatched his colonels [xiàowèi] Lǐ Què, Guō Sì, and Zhāng Jì
with tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry
to defeat Zhū Jùn, the Grand Administrator of Hénán [Hénán Yǐn], at Zhōngmóu.
Consequently, they plundered the various counties of Chénliú and Yǐngchuān,
killing and kidnapping men and women,
leaving no survivors in their path.
Lǚ Bù then ordered Lǐ Sù, with an imperial edict, to go to Shǎn to attack Niú Fǔ and his cohorts.
Niú Fǔ and his cohorts engaged Lǐ Sù in battle,
and Lǐ Sù was defeated and fled to Hóngnóng,
where Lǚ Bù executed him.
Afterwards, there was a sudden panic in Niú Fǔ's camp for no reason.
Niú Fǔ, frightened,
took gold and treasures and fled over the city wall.
His attendants, coveting his wealth,
beheaded Niú Fǔ
and sent his head to Cháng’ān.
Jué, Sì and others, because Wáng Yǔn and Lǚ Bù had killed Dǒng Zhuó,
were furious with the people of Bìngzhōu.
Several hundred men and women from Bìngzhōu who were in the army
were all executed.
After Niú Fǔ was defeated,
the masses had no one to rely on
and wanted to scatter.
Jué and the others were afraid,
so they first sent an envoy to Cháng'ān
to beg for a pardon.
Wáng Yǔn thought that one could not grant a second pardon in a single year,
and refused it.
Jué and the others grew even more worried and fearful,
not knowing what to do.
Jiǎ Xǔ, a man from Wǔwēi, was then in Jué's army.
He advised them,
saying:
“I hear that in Cháng'ān there is a discussion to execute all the people from Liángzhōu.
If you gentlemen disperse the army and travel alone,
then a single Tíngzhǎng will be able to bind you.
It would be better to lead your forces west
to attack Cháng'ān
and avenge Duke Dǒng.
If the matter succeeds,
you can uphold the state and bring order to all under Heaven;
if it does not succeed,
fleeing will not be too late.”
Jué and the others agreed with him,
and they said to each other:
“The capital will not pardon us;
we must decide this with our lives.
If we attack Cháng'ān and conquer it,
then we will gain all under Heaven;
if we do not conquer it,
we will plunder the women and wealth of Sānfǔ,
return west to our hometowns,
and still be able to prolong our lives.”
The masses thought this was right.
Thereupon, they swore an oath together,
led several thousand troops,
and marched west day and night.
Wáng Yǔn heard of this,
and dispatched Dǒng Zhuó's former generals Hú Zhěn and Xú Róng to attack them at Xīnfēng.
Róng died in battle,
and Zhěn surrendered with his troops.
Jué gathered soldiers along the way.
By the time they reached Cháng'ān,
they numbered over one hundred thousand,
and joined with Dǒng Zhuó's former部曲 Fán Chóu, Lǐ Méng and others,
to besiege Cháng'ān.
The city walls were high and could not be attacked.
After defending for eight days,
an old soldier in Lǚ Bù's army rebelled from within
and allowed Jué's troops to enter.
The city fell,
and the soldiers were unleashed to plunder and pillage;
over ten thousand people died.
They killed Wèi Wèi Zhǒng Fú and others.
Lǚ Bù was defeated and fled.
Wáng Yǔn escorted the Son of Heaven to the tower of the Xuānpíng city gate.
Thereupon, a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
Lǐ Jué, Guō Sì, Fán Chóu and others were all made generals.
They then surrounded the gate tower,
and together presented a memorial requesting Sītú Wáng Yǔn to come out,
asking,
“What crime did the Tài shī commit?”
Yǔn, in dire straits, descended,
and was killed a few days later.
Jué and others buried Dǒng Zhuó in Méi,
and also collected the ashes of Dǒng's family members who had been burned,
collecting them into one coffin for burial.
On the day of the burial,
there was a great storm,
thunder struck Dǒng Zhuó's tomb,
and flowing water entered the burial chamber,
floating away his coffin.
Jué was further promoted to Chēqí Jiāngjūn,
established a fu,
held the post of Sīlì Xiàowèi,
and was granted jiǎjié.
Sì was made Hòujiāngjūn,
Chóu Ròujiāngjūn,
Zhāng Jì Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn,
and all were enfeoffed as Lièhóu.
Jué, Sì, and Chóu jointly managed the affairs of the court.
Jì was stationed outside at Hóngnóng.
Jiǎ Xǔ was made Zuǒ Fēngyì,
and they intended to enfeoff him.
Xǔ said:
“This was a plan to save our lives;
what merit is there in it!”
He firmly declined and they stopped.
Instead, he was made Shàngshū Diǎnxuǎn.
The following year, in summer,
there was heavy rain day and night for over twenty days,
which drowned common people,
and the wind was like winter.
The Emperor sent Yùshǐ Péi Mào to investigate the imperial prisons,
releasing over two hundred detainees.
Among them were those unjustly imprisoned by Jué.
Jué feared Mào would pardon them,
so he memorialized that Mào had unauthorizedly released prisoners,
suspecting a treacherous motive,
and requested his arrest.
An imperial edict stated:
“Calamities and anomalies have repeatedly descended,
and continuous rain causes harm.
The envoy carries out his mission to proclaim grace and favor,
to release those with minor offenses,
hoping to align with the will of Heaven.
Should we seek to undo grievances and then punish them again?
Do not question this at all.”
Previously,
when Dǒng Zhuó entered the pass,
he sought out Hán Suì and Mǎ Téng to jointly plan against Shāndōng.
Suì and Téng, seeing that the world was in chaos,
also wanted to rely on Dǒng Zhuó to raise an army.
In the first year of Xīngpíng,
Mǎ Téng came from Lǒngyòu to pay respects at court,
and then advanced to encamp at Bàqiáo.
At that time, Téng privately had a request for Jué,
but was not granted it and became angry.
So he, along with Shìzhōng Mǎ Yǔ, Yòuzhōnglángjiàng Liú Fàn,
former Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Zhǒng Shào, and Zhōnglángjiàng Dù Bǐng,
combined their forces to attack Jué,
but for days the battle remained undecided.
Hán Suì heard of this,
and led his troops, intending to mediate between Téng and Jué,
but then reunited with Téng.
Jué sent his nephew Lì, along with Guō Sì and Fán Chóu, to battle Téng and others below Chángpíngguān.
Suì and Téng were defeated,
with over ten thousand heads cut off;
Zhǒng Shào, Liú Fàn and others all died.
Suì and Téng fled back to Liángzhōu,
and Chóu and others pursued them.
Hán Suì sent someone to speak to Chóu, saying:
“The world's reversals are unpredictable.
We are from the same region;
although we have a minor disagreement now,
we must eventually be in great harmony.
I wish to have a word with you.”
Thereupon, they rode their horses side by side, linking arms,
and laughed and talked for a long time.
When the army returned,
Lì told Jué:
“Fán and Hán rode side by side, laughing and talking;
I don't know what they said,
but their affection seemed very close.”
Thereupon, Jué and Chóu began to suspect each other.
Still, Chóu and Guō Sì were granted the right to establish a fu,
and combined with the Sāngōng to form the Liùfǔ,
all participating in selections.
At that time, banditry in Cháng'ān was unrestrained;
daylight kidnappings and looting occurred.
Jué, Sì, and Chóu then divided the city into three parts,
each guarding their respective areas,
yet they still could not control it,
and their sons and younger brothers ran rampant,
violently oppressing the common people.
At this time, one hú of grain cost five hundred thousand [coins],
and beans and wheat two hundred thousand.
People ate each other,
white bones piled up,
and foul smells filled the roads.
The Emperor sent Shìyùshǐ Hóu Wèn
to take rice and beans from the Tàicāng to make gruel for the hungry,
but after a day, the number of deaths did not decrease.
The Emperor suspected that the relief distribution was not real,
so he personally inspected it himself before his imperial presence.
Having learned that it was not true,
he sent Shìzhōng Liú Ài to admonish the responsible officials.
Thereupon, the Shàngshūlìng and others below went to the court to apologize,
and memorialized to arrest Hóu Wèn for investigation.
An imperial edict stated:
“I cannot bear to subject Wèn to legal process;
he may be flogged fifty times.”
Thereafter, many more people were saved.
The following spring,
Guō Mó assassinated Fán Chóu at a gathering.
Consequently, the various generals became mutually suspicious,
and Guō Mó and Guō Sì once again marshaled their troops and attacked each other.
Yáng Dìng, the General of the Pacifying West,
was formerly a divisional commander under Dǒng Zhuó.
Fearing Guō Mó’s cruelty,
he conspired with Guō Sì to welcome the Son of Heaven to their camp.
Guō Mó, aware of their plan,
immediately ordered his nephew, Xiān,
to lead several thousand men to surround the palace.
He used three carriages to welcome the Son of Heaven and the Empress.
Grand Commandant Yáng Biāo said to Xiān,
“Throughout ancient and modern times, no emperor
has ever resided in a minister’s house.
When you gentlemen undertake an action,
you should align with the will of Heaven.
How can you act like this!”
Xiān replied,
“The General’s decision is firm.”
Thereupon, the Emperor proceeded to Guō Mó’s camp,
and Yáng Biāo and others followed on foot.
Disorderly soldiers entered the palace,
plundering palace women and valuables.
Guō Mó also moved the gold and silk from the imperial treasury, and the imperial carriages, vessels, and robes,
and then set fire to the palaces, official residences, and private dwellings, burning everything completely.
The Emperor sent Yáng Biāo, Grand Minister of Works Zhāng Xǐ, and more than ten others to mediate between Guō Mó and Guō Sì.
Guō Sì did not comply,
and consequently held the high officials hostage.
Yáng Biāo said to Guō Sì,
“General, you are a discerning person in worldly affairs.
How can you allow the ruler and his ministers to be divided and fight?
One person seizes the Son of Heaven,
and another takes the high officials hostage.
Is this permissible?”
Guō Sì became enraged
and wanted to personally slay Yáng Biāo.
Yáng Biāo said,
“You still do not respect the state,
why should I seek to live?”
Many attendants pleaded,
and Guō Sì then stopped.
He then led his troops to attack Guō Mó.
Arrows reached the Emperor’s presence
and also pierced Guō Mó’s ear.
Guō Mó’s general Yáng Fèng, originally a White Wave bandit leader,
then led troops to rescue Guō Mó,
and Guō Sì’s forces then retreated.
On that day,
Guō Mó again moved the Emperor to his northern redoubt,
accompanied only by the Empress and Consort Sòng.
Guō Mó had a colonel guard the gates,
isolating the interior from the exterior.
Soon after, he again wished to move the Emperor to Chíyáng, to Huángbái City,
causing the ruler and ministers to be terrified.
Grand Minister of the Masses Zhào Wēn earnestly reasoned with him,
and he then stopped.
An imperial edict dispatched the Palace Usher and Commandant Huángfǔ Lì to mediate between Guō Mó and Guō Sì.
Lì first reasoned with Guō Sì,
who immediately obeyed.
He then went to Guō Mó,
but Guō Mó would not listen.
He said,
“Guō Duō [Guō Sì],
is merely a horse-thief and barbarian.
How dare he presume to be my equal!
He must be executed.
Sir, look at my strategy, officers, and men,
are they enough to deal with Guō Duō or not?
Guō Duō also holds high officials hostage.
His actions are like this,
and yet you simply want to support him!”
Guō Sì’s other name was Duō.
Lì said,
“Now Guō Sì holds high officials hostage,
while you, General, coerce the ruler.
Which is more serious?”
Guō Mó became enraged,
scolded and dismissed Lì,
and then ordered the Tiger Guard Wáng Chāng to pursue and kill him.
Wáng Chāng feigned inability to catch him,
and Lì was able to escape.
Guō Mó then appointed himself Grand Marshal.
He and Guō Sì attacked each other for months,
with tens of thousands of dead.
Zhāng Jì came from Shǎn to reconcile the two,
and still wished to move the Emperor temporarily to Hóngnóng.
The Emperor also longed for the old capital,
and thus sent envoys to earnestly request Guō Mó to allow him to return east.
After ten pleas, he consented.
The imperial carriage departed that very day.
Lǐ Guō encamped at Cáoyáng.
He appointed Zhāng Jì as General of Agile Cavalry,
and he returned to encamp at Shǎn.
Guō Sì was promoted to General of Chariots and Cavalry,
Yáng Dìng to General of the Rear,
and Yáng Fèng to General Who Inspires Righteousness.
He also appointed Dǒng Chéng, formerly a divisional commander under Niú Fǔ, as General Who Pacifies and Collects.
Guō Sì and others escorted the imperial carriage.
Guō Sì then again wished to coerce the Emperor to Méi,
but Yáng Dìng, Yáng Fèng, and Dǒng Chéng would not allow it.
Guō Sì feared a change of events,
and so he withdrew his troops and returned to Lǐ Guō.
The imperial carriage advanced to Huáyīn.
Duàn Wēi, the General Who Brings Peace and Order, then prepared imperial robes, carriages, and supplies for the high officials and below,
and invited the Emperor to his camp.
Initially,
Yáng Dìng and Duàn Wēi had a rift,
so Yáng Dìng falsely accused Duàn Wēi of rebellion
and attacked his camp,
but could not take it for over ten days.
Yet Duàn Wēi continued to provide imperial meals
and supply the needs of all officials,
showing no disloyalty.
Lǐ Guō and Guō Sì, having regretted letting the Son of Heaven go east,
then came to rescue Duàn Wēi,
and took the opportunity to seize the Emperor and return west.
Yáng Dìng was intercepted by Guō Sì
and fled to Jīngzhōu.
Meanwhile, Zhāng Jì and Yáng Fèng and Dǒng Chéng were not getting along,
so Zhāng Jì instead allied with Lǐ Guō and Guō Sì
and together pursued the imperial carriage.
They fought a great battle in the eastern gully of Hóngnóng.
Dǒng Chéng and Yáng Fèng’s army was defeated,
and countless officials and soldiers died.
All their women, baggage,
imperial articles, tallies, and archives
were almost entirely plundered.
Jǔ Jùn, the Commandant of Shooting Guards, was wounded and fell from his horse.
Lǐ Guō said to his attendants,
“Can he still be kept alive?”
Jǔ Jùn cursed him, saying,
“You villains are rebellious
and coerce the Son of Heaven!
Rebellious ministers and traitorous sons,
there has never been anyone like you!”
Lǐ Guō had him killed.
The Son of Heaven then openly encamped at Cáoyáng.
Dǒng Chéng and Yáng Fèng then cunningly made peace with Lǐ Guō and others,
but secretly sent secret envoys to Hédōng,
inviting the former White Wave leaders Lǐ Lè, Hán Xiān, Hú Cái, and the Right Worthy King Qù Bēi of the Southern Xiōngnú.
They all led several thousand cavalry to come
and together with Dǒng Chéng and Yáng Fèng attacked Lǐ Guō and others,
decisively defeating them,
beheading several thousand.
The imperial carriage was then able to advance.
Dǒng Chéng and Lǐ Lè protected the Emperor on his left and right,
while Hú Cái, Yáng Fèng, Hán Xiān, and Qù Bēi formed the rear guard.
Lǐ Guō and others came to fight again,
and Yáng Fèng and his allies were utterly defeated,
with more dead than at the eastern gully.
From the eastern gully, the fighting continued for forty lǐ,
before they finally reached Shǎn,
where they established a camp to defend themselves.
At that time, among the remnants of the defeated forces,
the Tiger Guards and Feathered Forest Guards numbered less than a hundred,
and all were disloyal.
Dǒng Chéng and Yáng Fèng and others secretly planned that night to cross the river,
sending Lǐ Lè ahead to prepare boats
and light a fire as a signal.
The Emperor walked out of the camp
and approached the river, intending to cross.
The bank was over ten zhàng high,
so they used silk ropes to lower him down.
Others either crawled along the riverbank
or threw themselves down from above,
resulting in many deaths and injuries,
no longer recognizing each other.
Those who scrambled for the boats
could not be controlled.
Dǒng Chéng struck them with a spear,
and severed fingers in the boats could be scooped up by the handful.
Those who successfully crossed were only the Empress, Consort Sòng,
Yáng Biāo, Dǒng Chéng, and the Empress’s father, the Commandant of the Gilded Plumes, Fú Wán, and a few dozen others.
All the palace women were plundered by Lǐ Guō’s soldiers,
and many died from freezing or drowning.
Having arrived at Dàyáng,
they stayed in people’s houses,
and then proceeded to Lǐ Lè’s camp.
The officials were starving.
Zhāng Yáng, the Grand Administrator of Hénèi,
sent several thousand people to carry rice and provisions.
The Emperor then rode in an ox-cart
and made Ānyì his provisional capital.
Wáng Yì, the Grand Administrator of Hédōng, offered cotton and silk,
which were all distributed to the high officials and below.
Wáng Yì was enfeoffed as a Marquis,
Hú Cái was appointed General Who Conquers the East,
and Zhāng Yáng was appointed General Who Pacifies the State,
all granted imperial credentials and authorized to establish their own offices.
The various petty chieftains in the walled camps
competed to seek appointments and titles.
There were not enough seals to carve,
so they even used awls to scratch them.
Some brought wine and meat to feast with the Son of Heaven.
The Emperor also sent Grand Messenger Hán Róng to Hóngnóng
to make peace with Lǐ Guō, Guō Sì, and others.
Lǐ Guō then released the high officials and all other officials,
and returned a good number of palace women
and imperial carriages, vessels, and robes.
Initially,
when the Emperor entered the pass,
the households of Sānfǔ still numbered several hundred thousand.
After Guō Sì and Lǐ Quē attacked each other,
and the Son of Heaven returned east,
Cháng'ān city was empty for over forty days.
The strong scattered,
and the weak cannibalized each other.
Within two or three years,
there were no longer any human traces in Guānzhōng.
In the spring of Jiàn'ān元年 (196 CE),
the generals contended for power.
Hán Xiān then attacked Dǒng Chéng.
Chéng fled to Zhāng Yáng.
Zhāng Yáng then ordered Dǒng Chéng to first repair the Luò Palace.
In the seventh month,
the Emperor returned to Luòyáng
and resided in Yáng'ān Palace.
Zhāng Yáng considered this his achievement,
and thus named
the palace
“Yáng.”
He then said to the generals:
“The Son of Heaven should be shared by all under Heaven.
The court has its own high officials and ministers.
I, Yáng, should go out and guard against external dangers.
What business do I have in the capital? ”
He then returned to Yěwáng.
Yáng Fèng also left to garrison Liáng.
Zhāng Yáng was appointed Dà Sīmǎ,
Yáng Fèng as Chējì Jiāngjūn,
and Hán Xiān as Dà Jiāngjūn,
also holding the post of Sīlì Xiàowèi.
All were granted jǐe and yuè.
Hán Xiān and Dǒng Chéng both remained to guard the palace.
Hán Xiān, priding himself on his achievements, became arrogant and wanton,
interfering with government affairs.
Dǒng Chéng was troubled by this
and secretly summoned the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu, Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo then came to the palace gate to offer tribute,
providing for the high officials and ministers below.
He then impeached Hán Xiān and Zhāng Yáng for their crimes.
Hán Xiān, fearing execution,
fled alone on horseback to Yáng Fèng.
The Emperor, considering Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng had meritorious service in assisting the imperial carriage,
decreed that they should not be questioned at all.
Thereupon, more than ten people, including Wèi Jiāngjūn Dǒng Chéng and Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Fú Wán, were enfeoffed as列侯 (Liehou).
Jǔ Jùn was posthumously granted the title of Hóngnóng Tàishǒu.
Cáo Cāo, seeing Luòyáng was ruined and desolate,
then moved the Emperor to Xǔ.
Yáng Fèng and Hán Xiān tried to intercept the imperial carriage,
but failed.
Cáo Cāo attacked them,
and Fèng and Xiān fled to Yuán Shù,
then wreaked havoc between Yáng and Xú.
The next year,
Zuǒ Jiāngjūn Liú Bèi lured Fèng and beheaded him.
Xiān, afraid,
fled back to Bìngzhōu,
but was killed by someone on the way.
Hú Cái and Lǐ Lè remained in Hédōng.
Hú Cái was killed by his enemies,
and Lǐ Lè died of illness.
Zhāng Jì, suffering from hunger,
went south to Nányáng,
attacked Ráng,
and died in battle.
Guō Sì was killed by his general Wǔ Xí.
In Jiàn'ān三年 (198 CE),
Yèzhě Púshè Péi Mào was sent to summon the Guānzhōng generals, such as Duàn Wēi, to attack Lǐ Quē,
exterminating his three clans.
Duàn Wēi was appointed Ānnán Jiāngjūn
and enfeoffed as Wènxiāng Hóu.
In Jiàn'ān四年 (199 CE),
Zhāng Yáng was killed by his general Yáng Chǒu.
Dǒng Chéng was appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn
and granted permission to establish a government office.
After the capital was moved to Xǔ,
power returned to the Cáo clan.
The Son of Heaven merely managed his own affairs,
and the hundred officials merely filled their posts.
The Emperor, resenting Cáo Cāo's exclusive and oppressive power,
secretly issued an edict to Dǒng Chéng,
ordering him to gather righteous men from all under Heaven to jointly execute Cáo Cāo.
Dǒng Chéng then conspired with Liú Bèi.
Before they could act,
Liú Bèi went on a campaign.
Dǒng Chéng then conspired with Piān Jiāngjūn Wáng Fú, Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi Zhǒng Jí, and Yìláng Wú Shuò.
The plot was discovered,
and Chéng, Fú, Jí, and Shuò were all executed by Cáo Cāo.
Hán Suì and Mǎ Téng returned to Liángzhōu,
and then engaged in mutual warfare.
They then descended from Lǒng and occupied Guānzhōng.
As Cáo Cāo was busy with Héběi,
fearing they would take advantage of the opportunity to cause trouble,
in Jiàn'ān七年 (202 CE),
he appointed Mǎ Téng as Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn
and Hán Suì as Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,
both granted permission to establish government offices.
Later, Duàn Wēi was summoned to be Dà Hónglú,
and died of illness.
Mǎ Téng was again summoned to be Wèi Wèi
and enfeoffed as Huáilǐ Hóu.
Mǎ Téng then answered the summons,
but left his son Mǎ Chāo to command his troops.
In Jiàn'ān十六年 (211 CE),
Mǎ Chāo and Hán Suì raised an army in Guānzhōng and rebelled against Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo defeated them,
and Hán Suì and Mǎ Chāo fled.
Mǎ Téng was implicated and his three clans were exterminated.
Mǎ Chāo attacked and killed the Inspector of Liángzhōu, Wéi Kāng,
and again occupied Lǒngyòu.
In Jiàn'ān十九年 (214 CE),
Yáng Fù from Tiānshuǐ defeated Mǎ Chāo.
Mǎ Chāo fled to Hànzhōng
and surrendered to Liú Bèi.
Hán Suì fled into the Qiāng territory of Jīnchéng
and was killed by his subordinates.
Initially,
Zōng Jiàn, a native of Lǒngxī, was in Fāohǎn
and called himself
“Héshǒu Pínghàn Wáng” (King who Pacified Han at the Head of the River),
appointing various officials for some thirty years.
Cáo Cāo then sent Xiàhóu Yuān to attack Zōng Jiàn,
beheaded him,
and thus Liángzhōu was completely pacified.
A critique says: Dǒng Zhuó initially had a fierce and ferocious nature,
and because he encountered a collapsing and disintegrating situation,
he was able to trample upon the moral order
and tear apart the imperial domain.
Indeed, with a nature that would gouge livers and chop off feet,
the multitude of living beings was not enough to satisfy his pleasure.
However, he still tried to win over the gentry
and was wary of being robbed and usurped;
there was still a way of thievery.
When the remnant bandits took advantage of the situation,
overturning mountains and oceans,
the fire of Kūngāng
ignited from this point,
and the chapter of desolation
reached its extreme here.
Alas,
it is difficult for humans to be born!
〔一０〕How unkind are Heaven and Earth!
〔一一〕
The eulogy says: The cycle of a hundred six years came,
Guò and Bō brought disaster.
Dǒng Zhuó's wickedness reached the heavens,
violating the Three Powers.
All under Heaven boiled and erupted,
the imperial capital turned to smoke and dust.
Though disrespect reached its peak,
the lingering miasma spread.
Arrows extended to the imperial carriage,
war ensnared the elephant of Wèi.
The imperial domain tottered and overturned,
humans and gods were tossed about.
Biographies of Liú Yú, Gōngsūn Zàn, Táo Qiān, Chapter Sixty-Three
Liú Yú, courtesy name Bó'ān,
was from Tán, Dōnghǎi.
His grandfather, Jiā,
was Guānglù Xūn.
Liú Yú was initially nominated as Xiaolian,
and gradually promoted to Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ.
The people and barbarians were moved by his virtuous governance.
From the Xiānbēi, Wūhuán, Fúyú, and Wèimò,
all paid tribute according to the seasons,
none daring to disturb the borders.
The common people sang his praises.
He left office due to public affairs.
At the beginning of Zhōngpíng,
when the Yellow Turbans rebelled,
attacking and capturing various commanderies in Jìzhōu,
Liú Yú was appointed Gānlíng Xiāng,
pacifying the desolate and remaining areas,
and leading by example with frugality and simplicity.
He was promoted to Zōngzhèng.
Later, the General of Chēqí, Zhāng Wēn, campaigned against the rebels Biān Zhāng and others.
He dispatched three thousand swift cavalry from the Wūhuán of Yōuzhōu,
but their provisions were in arrears,
and they all defected and returned to their native lands.
The former Chancellor of Zhōngshān, Zhāng Chún, privately said to the former Administrator of Tàishān, Zhāng Jǔ:
“Now that the Wūhuán have defected,
they all wish to cause trouble.
Rebels have risen in Liángzhōu,
and the imperial court cannot suppress them.
Furthermore, a woman in Luòyáng gave birth to a two-headed child.
This signifies the decline and end of the Hàn dynasty’s mandate,
and is an omen that there will be two rulers in the world.
If you and I lead the Wūhuán multitude to raise an army,
we might be able to achieve a great undertaking.”
Zhāng Jǔ assented to this.
In the fourth year [of the Zhōngpíng era],
Zhāng Chún and others thereupon allied with the Wūhuán chiefs,
attacked the area beneath Jì,
burned down cities and fortifications,
and captured and plundered the populace.
They killed Jī Chóu, the Commandant Protector of the Wūhuán, Liú Zhèng, the Administrator of Yòuběipíng, Yáng Zhōng, the Administrator of Liáodōng, and others.
Their forces reached over ten myriad,
and they encamped at Féirú.
Zhāng Jǔ proclaimed himself
“Son of Heaven,”
and Zhāng Chún proclaimed himself
“General Mitian, Prince of Āndìng.”
They issued letters to the various commanderies and prefectures,
saying that Zhāng Jǔ was to replace the Hàn,
ordering the Son of Heaven to abdicate,
and instructing the dukes and ministers to welcome him.
Zhāng Chún also sent Wūhuán King Qiào and others
with fifty thousand infantry and cavalry
into Qīng and Jì provinces,
attacking and breaking Qīnghé and Píngyuán,
and killing officials and commoners.
The imperial court considered Yú’s prestige and trustworthiness to be long-established,
and his benevolence accumulated in the north.
The following year,
he was again appointed Governor of Yōuzhōu.
When Yú arrived at Jì,
he dismissed the garrison troops
and diligently spread benevolence and trust.
He sent envoys to inform King Qiào and others of the imperial court’s generous grace
and to open a path to goodwill.
He also set up rewards for the capture of Zhāng Jǔ and Zhāng Chún.
Zhāng Jǔ and Zhāng Chún fled beyond the frontier,
and the rest surrendered and dispersed.
Zhāng Chún was killed by his retainer Wáng Zhèng,
who sent his head to Yú.
Emperor Líng sent an envoy to appoint him Grand Commandant [on the spot]
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Róngqiū.
When Dǒng Zhuó took power,
he sent an envoy to confer upon Yú the title of Grand Minister of War [Dà Sīmǎ]
and further enfeoffed him as Marquis of Xiāngbēn.
In the first year of Chūpíng,
he was again summoned to replace Yuán Kuí as Grand Tutor.
The roads were obstructed,
and the imperial mandate ultimately could not reach him.
The former Yōuzhōu department was responsible for communicating with the wild territories beyond the frontier,
and its expenses were very large.
Annually, over two hundred million [cash] were regularly allocated from the taxes and levies of Qīng and Jì [provinces]
to cover these expenses.
At that time, communication was cut off everywhere,
and supplies could not arrive.
However, Yú strove to maintain a lenient administration,
encouraged and supervised agricultural planting,
opened up the profitable Hu markets in Shànggǔ,
and facilitated the abundant salt and iron production in Yúyáng.
The people were pleased, and the harvests were good,
with grain selling for thirty cash per shí.
Over a million people, both gentry and commoners, from Qīng and Xú who fled the disaster of the Yellow Turbans and sought refuge with Yú,
were all received, cared for, and treated with compassion.
He settled them and established livelihoods for them,
and the displaced people forgot their wanderings.
Although Yú was a high-ranking minister,
he was by nature frugal,
wearing worn-out clothes and straw sandals,
and his meals never had more than one meat dish.
None of the powerful and outstanding figures, near or far, who had previously been extravagant,
failed to change their conduct and pledge their allegiance to him.
Initially,
an imperial edict ordered Gōngsūn Zàn to campaign against the Wūhuán,
and he was to be subject to Yú’s command.
However, Gōngsūn Zàn merely sought to gather followers to strengthen himself,
and he allowed his subordinates to act freely,
often harassing the populace.
Yú, on the other hand, governed with benevolence and love,
concerned with benefiting the people and things.
Because of this, he and Gōngsūn Zàn gradually became at odds.
In the second year,
Hán Fù, the Inspector of Jìzhōu, Yuán Shào, the Administrator of Bóhǎi, and other generals east of the mountains deliberated,
considering the imperial court to be young and vulnerable,
pressured by Dǒng Zhuó,
and separated by distant passes,
unsure if it still existed.
They regarded Yú as an elder of the imperial clan
and wished to enthrone him as ruler.
So they sent Zhāng Qí, the former Administrator of Lèlàng, and others with their proposal,
to offer Yú the honorable title.
When Yú saw Zhāng Qí and the others,
he sternly rebuked them, saying:
“Now the world is in chaos,
and the emperor is in distress.
I have received great grace,
yet I have been unable to clear the national shame.
You gentlemen, each holding your own provinces and commanderies,
should unite your efforts
and wholeheartedly serve the royal house.
Instead, you are plotting rebellion
to disgrace and mislead each other!”
He firmly refused them.
Hán Fù and others again requested Yú to take charge of the affairs of the Secretariat [Shàngshū]
and to confer enfeoffments and appointments by imperial decree,
but he again refused.
He then arrested and executed the envoys.
Thereupon, he selected his aide, Tián Chóu of Yòuběipíng, and the Administrator, Xiānyú Yín,
to travel through dangerous and secluded paths,
bearing a mission to Cháng’ān.
Emperor Xiàn, desiring to return east,
was greatly pleased to see Tián Chóu and others.
At that time, Yú’s son, Yú Hé, was a Household Gentleman.
Taking advantage of this, Emperor Xiàn sent Yú Hé to secretly leave through Wǔguān
to inform Yú to bring troops to escort him.
The route passed through Nányáng.
When the General of the Rear, Yuán Shù, heard of this situation,
he detained Yú Hé
and made him report to Yú to send troops to go west together.
Yú then sent several thousand cavalry to Yú Hé to escort the Son of Heaven,
but Yuán Shù ultimately did not release him.
Initially,
Gōngsūn Zàn knew Yuán Shù’s deception
and strongly advised Yú against sending troops.
Yú did not listen.
Gōngsūn Zàn then secretly persuaded Yuán Shù to seize Yú Hé
and take his troops.
From then on, the enmity between Yú and Gōngsūn Zàn deepened.
Yú Hé soon escaped from Yuán Shù and returned north,
but was again detained by Yuán Shào.
Gōngsūn Zàn had been repeatedly defeated by Yuán Shào,
yet he continued to attack him without cease.
Yú was troubled by Gōngsūn Zàn’s warmongering
and feared that if he achieved his ambitions, he would be uncontrollable.
Therefore, he firmly forbade him to act
and gradually curtailed his provisions and allowances.
Gōngsūn Zàn was angry,
repeatedly violating Yú’s commands,
and also infringing upon the common people.
The rewards and gifts Yú bestowed upon the Hú barbarians
were often plundered by Gōngsūn Zàn.
Unable to stop him,
Yú sent express messengers to present a memorial denouncing Gōngsūn Zàn’s crimes of violence and plunder.
Gōngsūn Zàn also memorialized that Yú’s provisions were insufficient.
The two memorials flew back and forth,
each denouncing the other,
and the imperial court merely prevaricated.
Gōngsūn Zàn then built a fortified camp [jīng] at Jì City to guard against Yú.
Yú repeatedly summoned Gōngsūn Zàn,
who always claimed illness and did not respond.
Yú then secretly plotted to campaign against him
and informed Wèi Yōu of Yòuběipíng, his East Bureau Aide.
Wèi Yōu said:
“Now the people of the world look to you,
Sir, as their leader.
Counsellors and strong enforcers
are indispensable.
Gōngsūn Zàn’s literary and martial talents are reliable.
Although he has minor faults,
he should certainly be tolerated.”
Yú then stopped.
After a short while, Yóu died,
but the accumulated resentment did not cease.
In the winter of the fourth year,
he personally led the various garrison troops, a force of one hundred thousand men, to attack Gōngsūn Zàn.
As he was about to depart,
the Aide from Dàijùn, Chéng Xù, removed his helmet and stepped forward, saying:
“Although Gōngsūn Zàn has committed wrongs,
his crime has not yet been formally established.
If you, Illustrious Sir, do not first inform and enlighten him to allow him to change his ways,
but instead wage war within the household,
it will not benefit the state.
Furthermore, victory and defeat are hard to guarantee.
It is better to station the troops
and confront him with military might.
Zàn will surely regret his errors and beg for forgiveness.
This is what is called 'subduing people without fighting.' ”
Yú, considering that Xù was obstructing the discussion at a critical moment,
therefore had him beheaded as an example.
He then instructed his soldiers, saying:
“Do not harm any other person;
only kill Bóguī.”
At that time, there was a provincial Aide named Gōngsūn Jì,
whom Zàn treated generously due to their shared surname.
Jì learned of Yú’s plan and reported it to Zàn that night.
Zàn's troops were then scattered abroad,
and in his haste, fearing he could not escape,
he dug a tunnel from the eastern wall, intending to flee.
Yú’s troops were not skilled in combat,
and furthermore, they cherished people’s dwellings,
being ordered not to burn them.
They fiercely attacked and besieged the city but could not take it.
Zàn then selected and recruited several hundred elite warriors,
and using the wind, set fire
and charged straight into them.
Yú was then utterly defeated,
and with his officials, fled north to Jūyōng Xiàn.
Zàn pursued and attacked him.
After three days, the city fell,
and he captured Yú and his wife and children, returning to Jì.
He still made Yú oversee the provincial documents.
It happened that the Son of Heaven sent an envoy, Duàn Xùn, to increase Yú’s enfeoffment,
and supervise the affairs of six provinces;
he appointed Zàn as General of the Vanguard,
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Yì,
and granted him the Imperial Insignia to supervise Yōu, Bìng, Qīng, and Jì.
Zàn then falsely accused Yú of having previously conspired with Yuán Shào and others to claim the title of emperor,
and coerced Xù into beheading Yú in the Jì marketplace.
Before sitting down, he swore, saying:
“If Yú is destined to be the Son of Heaven,
then Heaven will send wind and rain to save him.”
At that time, the drought was severe and intense,
and he was then executed.
His head was sent to the capital, but
his former subordinate Wěi Dūn intercepted Yú’s head on the road and brought it back for burial.
Zàn then recommended Xù to be the Inspector of Yōuzhōu.
Yú, having gained the support of the populace through his benevolence and generosity,
was beloved throughout the northern provinces.
The old residents and common folk
all mourned him deeply.
Initially,
Yú maintained a simple and frugal conduct;
if his cap was worn out, he would not change it,
but would mend its holes.
However, when he was killed,
Zàn’s soldiers searched his inner chambers,
and his wife and concubines were dressed in silk damask
and adorned with rich ornaments.
People at the time found this suspicious.
Hé later avenged Zàn from Yuán Shào.
Gōngsūn Zàn, courtesy name Bóguī,
was a native of Lìngzhī, Liáoxī.
His family had held positions of two thousand *shí* for generations.
Because Zàn's mother was of humble origin,
he became a minor official in the commandery.
He was handsome in appearance,
had a loud voice,
and was eloquent and discerning in his speech.
The Grand Administrator admired his talent
and gave him his daughter in marriage.
Later, he studied with Lú Zhí of Zhuōjùn in the Gōushì Mountains,
and had a general understanding of books and histories.
He was appointed as a Chief Clerk of Merit.
When Grand Administrator Liú Jūn was implicated in a matter and summoned in a caged cart,
the official regulations prohibited subordinates from being close to him.
Zàn then changed his appearance and attire,
falsely claiming to be a servant,
personally carrying his provisions,
and driving the cart to Luòyáng.
When the Grand Administrator was to be exiled to Rìnán,
Zàn prepared pork and wine on Běimáng mountain,
offered sacrifices to his ancestors,
and poured a libation, praying:
“Formerly a son,
now a minister,
I am about to go to Rìnán.
Rìnán has much miasma,
and I fear I may not return.
I shall then bid a long farewell to these tombs.”
He was filled with sorrow and wept,
bowing twice before departing.
All who witnessed it sighed in admiration.
After he set off,
he received a pardon on the way.
Zàn returned to the commandery,
was nominated as Filial and Incorrupt,
and appointed as Chief of the Liaodong Protectorate.
Once, while traveling beyond the frontier with a few dozen horsemen,
he suddenly encountered several hundred Xiānbēi cavalry.
Zàn retreated into an empty pavilion,
and instructed his followers, saying:
“If we do not charge them now,
we will all die.”
He then personally wielded a double-bladed spear,
charged out and attacked the bandits,
killing and wounding several dozen men.
Half of Zàn's retinue also perished,
but he managed to escape.
During the Zhōngpíng era,
Zàn was appointed to supervise the Wūhuán cavalry,
and the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Zhāng Wēn, was campaigning against the bandits in Liángzhōu.
It happened that the Wūhuán rebelled,
and together with the bandit Zhāng Chún and others, attacked Jìzhōng.
Zàn led his forces to pursue and suppress Chún and his group, achieving merit,
and was promoted to Cavalry Commandant.
Zhāng Chún again rebelled with the Hu, Qiūlìjū and others, raiding Yúyáng, Héjiān, and Bóhǎi,
entering Píngyuán,
and killing and abducting many.
Zàn pursued and fought them at Shímén in the Protectorate,
and the barbarians were utterly defeated.
They abandoned their wives and children and fled across the frontier,
and all the men and women they had abducted were recovered.
Zàn penetrated deeply without reinforcements,
and in turn was besieged by Qiūlìjū and others at Guǎnzǐchéng in Liáoxī
for over two hundred days.
When provisions ran out, they ate their horses;
when horses ran out, they ate their crossbows and shields.
They fought fiercely but could not prevail.
So, he bade farewell to his officers and soldiers,
and they each dispersed to return.
At that time, there was much rain and snow,
and fifteen or sixteen out of every hundred died in the ditches.
The barbarians were also hungry and exhausted,
and fled far away to Liǔchéng.
An imperial edict appointed Zàn as Colonel Who Subdues the Barbarians,
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Dūtíng,
and he again concurrently held the post of Chief of the Protectorate.
His duty was to command the army
and connect with the border invaders.
Whenever he heard of an alarm,
Zàn would immediately grow fierce and angry,
as if going to confront a sworn enemy,
chasing after the dust trails,
sometimes continuing with night battles.
The barbarians recognized Zàn’s voice
and feared his bravery;
none dared to resist or offend him.
Zàn often rode with several dozen skilled archers,
all mounted on white horses,
forming his left and right wings.
He called himself
“The White Horse Righteous Followers.”
The Wūhuán would warn each other,
“Avoid the Chief of the White Horses.”
They even drew Zàn’s image,
rode their horses and shot at it,
and those who hit it all shouted “Long live!”
From then on, the barbarians
fled far beyond the frontier.
Zàn was determined to wipe out the Wūhuán,
but Liú Yú wished to attract them through kindness and trust,
which caused a conflict between him and Yú.
In the second year of Chūpíng,
three hundred thousand Yellow Turban rebels from Qīng and Xú entered the Bóhǎi region,
intending to join forces with the Black Mountain bandits.
Zàn led twenty thousand infantry and cavalry,
and attacked them in the south of Dōngguāng,
greatly defeating them,
beheading over thirty thousand.
The bandits abandoned their baggage carts, tens of thousands of them,
and fled across the river.
Zàn attacked them while half were still crossing,
and the bandits were again utterly defeated.
Tens of thousands died,
their blood staining the water red.
He captured over seventy thousand prisoners,
and the number of carts, armor, and valuables was incalculable.
His prestige greatly shook the land.
He was appointed General Who Rouses Martial Might,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Jì.
Gōngsūn Zàn, having already advised Liú Yú to send troops to Yuán Shù,
and fearing that Shù would know of his resentment,
therefore sent his younger cousin, Yuè, leading over a thousand cavalry, to Shù to form a bond.
Shù sent Yuè to follow his general Sūn Jiān
to attack Yuán Shào’s general Zhōu Xīn.
Yuè was struck by a stray arrow and died.
Gōngsūn Zàn was enraged at Yuán Shào because of this,
and consequently marched his army to encamp at Pánhé,
intending to take revenge on Shào.
He then submitted a memorial stating:
“Your subject has heard that since the time of Huángxī,
the way of sovereign and minister has been established.
Rites are displayed to guide people,
and punishments are set up to restrain violence.
Now, the General of Chariots and Cavalry, Yuán Shào,
claims to follow the path of his ancestors,
and his rank and responsibilities are weighty and esteemed.
Yet his nature is inherently licentious and chaotic,
and his disposition and conduct are frivolous and shallow.
Previously, as the Minister over the Masses,
he served during a time when the state faced many difficulties.
The Empress Dowager was acting as regent,
and the Hé family assisted the court.
Shào was unable to elevate the upright and displace the crooked,
but instead devoted himself to flattery and evil,
attracting lawless individuals,
misleading the state and its altars of soil and grain,
to the extent that Dīng Yuán burned Méngjīn,
and Dǒng Zhuó initiated the rebellion.
This is Shào’s first crime.
Dǒng Zhuó, having acted without禮(lǐ),
held the emperor hostage.
Shào was unable to devise strategies
to save his sovereign and father,
but instead cast aside his credentials and seals,
fleeing and absconding.
He disgraced his rank and mandate,
and betrayed his sovereign.
This is Shào’s second crime.
As the Administrator of Bóhǎi,
Shào should have attacked Dǒng Zhuó,
but instead he secretly selected warhorses
without informing his father and elder brothers,
which led to the entire household of the Grand Tutor
perishing in succession.
He was inhumane and unfilial.
This is Shào’s third crime.
Shào, having raised an army,
traversed two years,
not caring for the state’s difficulties,
but widely enriching himself.
He drew upon vast amounts of provisions,
exclusively for non-urgent matters,
cruelly extorting without method,
and torturing the common people.
The pain and resentment he caused
caused everyone to sigh in grief.
This is Shào’s fourth crime.
He oppressed Hán Fù
and secretly seized his province,
fraudulently carving gold and jade
to make seals,
and whenever he issued something,
he would seal it in a black bag
and declare it a decree.
In the past, the usurper Wáng Mǎng was extravagant and presumptuous,
gradually seizing the throne.
Observing Shào’s imitation,
he will surely use it to incite chaos.
This is Shào’s fifth crime.
Shào ordered astrologers to observe auspicious and ominous signs,
bribed them with money and goods,
shared food and drink with them,
set dates for meetings,
and attacked and plundered commanderies and counties.
How can this be something a high minister should do?
This is Shào’s sixth crime.
Shào and the former Commandant of Tiger-Tooth, Liú Xūn,
were the first to raise an army together.
Xūn surrendered to Zhāng Yáng
and achieved repeated meritorious deeds,
but due to a minor grievance, Shào unjustly inflicted cruel harm upon him.
He trusted slanderous and wicked individuals
to facilitate his lawlessness.
This is Shào’s seventh crime.
The former Administrator of Shànggǔ, Gāo Yān,
and the former Chancellor of Gānlíng, Yáo Gòng,
were both subjected by Shào to greedy
[一０] and unwarranted demands for money.
When the money was not fully supplied,
both men lost their lives.
This is Shào’s eighth crime.
According to the principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
a son gains honor through his mother.
[一一] Shào’s birth mother was a maidservant,
her status was truly humble and lowly,
yet he occupies a high and important position,
enjoying abundant fortune.
He has the ambition to advance improperly
but no desire to retreat honorably.
This is Shào’s ninth crime.
Moreover, the Administrator of Chángshā, Sūn Jiān,
previously serving as the Inspector of Yùzhōu,
was able to drive away Dǒng Zhuó
and clear the imperial tombs and temples.
His loyalty and diligence to the royal house
were of the greatest merit.
Shào sent a minor general to usurp his position,
cut off Jiān’s supplies,
preventing him from advancing deeper,
and thereby allowing Dǒng Zhuó to avoid execution for a long time.
This is Shào’s tenth crime.
In the past, when the Zhōu dynasty’s government was weak,
the royal way declined,
the Son of Heaven moved,
and the feudal lords rebelled.
Therefore, Duke Huán of Qí established the alliance at Kē [Tíng]
[一二] and Duke Wén of Jìn held the assembly at Jiàntǔ,
[一三] attacking Jīngchǔ to ensure the tribute of reeds,
[一四] and executing Cáo and Wèi to make clear their lack of proper conduct.
[一五] Though your subject is insignificant,
and his name is not among the ancient sages,
[一六] he has received imperial grace
and bears a heavy responsibility.
His duty is to wield the axe of punishment,
to carry out the imperial decree and punish the wicked.
[一七] I shall, together with the generals and commandery administrators, attack Shào and his ilk.
If this great undertaking is victorious,
and the culprits are captured,
[一八] I hope to continue the loyal and sincere achievements of Dukes Huán and Wén.”
Thereupon, he raised an army and attacked Shào.
Consequently, all the cities in Jìzhōu revolted and joined Gōngsūn Zàn.
Shào was frightened,
and so he gave the seal and ribbon of the Administrator of Bóhǎi, which he wore, to Gōngsūn Zàn’s younger cousin Fàn,
sending him to the commandery,
hoping to form a bond with him.
However, Fàn subsequently betrayed Shào
and led the Bóhǎi troops to assist Gōngsūn Zàn.
Gōngsūn Zàn then personally appointed his generals as Inspectors of the three provinces of Qīng, Jì, and Yǎn,
and also appointed administrators and magistrates for all commanderies and counties.
He engaged Shào in a great battle at Jièqiáo.
Gōngsūn Zàn’s army was defeated and returned to Jì.
Shào sent his general Cuī Jùyè with tens of thousands of troops to besiege Gù’ān, but failed to take it.
They withdrew their forces and returned south.
Gōngsūn Zàn led thirty thousand infantry and cavalry to pursue and attack them at Jùmǎ Shuǐ,
thoroughly defeating their forces.
Seven or eight thousand people died.
He pressed on southward,
capturing commanderies and counties,
and finally reached Píngyuán.
He then sent his Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Tián Kǎi, to occupy the territory of Qí.
Shào again sent tens of thousands of troops to fight Kǎi for two years.
Provisions were exhausted,
and the soldiers were weary and distressed.
They plundered the common people in turn,
and there was no green grass in the fields.
Shào then sent his son Tán to be the Inspector of Qīngzhōu.
Kǎi fought him
but was defeated and retreated.
In this year,
Gōngsūn Zàn defeated and captured Liú Yú,
taking full possession of Yōuzhōu,
and his fierce ambition grew even stronger.
Before this, there was a children’s rhyme that said:
“The south end of Yān,
the north edge of Zhào,
the middle does not meet, large as a grindstone,
only in this place can one avoid the world.”
Gōngsūn Zàn thought that this place referred to him,
and so he moved his headquarters there.
He then extensively repaired his camps and fortresses,
with dozens of towers and observatories,
overlooking the Yìhé,
and connecting to Liáohǎi.
Liú Yú’s subordinate, Xiānyú Fǔ of Yúyáng, and others,
gathered and led provincial troops,
wishing to jointly take revenge on Gōngsūn Zàn.
Fǔ, knowing that Yán Róu of Yānguó had always been benevolent and trustworthy,
appointed him as the Wūhuán Sīmǎ.
Yán Róu recruited and enticed tens of thousands of Hú and Hàn people,
and fought Gōngsūn Zàn’s appointed Administrator of Yúyáng, Zōu Dān, north of Lù,
beheading Dān and over four thousand others.
Qìao, the Wūhuán King, moved by Liú Yú’s kindness and virtue,
led his tribesmen and over seven thousand Xiānbēi cavalry,
together with Fǔ, to welcome Liú Yú’s son Hé in the south.
They joined forces with Yuán Shào’s general Qū Yì, with a total of one hundred thousand troops,
and jointly attacked Gōngsūn Zàn.
In the second year of Xīngpíng
they defeated Gōngsūn Zàn at Bāoqiu,
beheading over twenty thousand people.
Gōngsūn Zàn then fortified Yìjīng,
opened up military agricultural colonies,
and gradually became self-sufficient.
After a standoff of over a year,
Qū Yì’s army ran out of provisions,
and his soldiers were hungry and exhausted.
The remaining several thousand troops retreated.
Gōngsūn Zàn intercepted and defeated them,
seizing all their baggage and heavy equipment.
At that time, there was drought and locusts, and grain was expensive;
the people ate each other.
Gōngsūn Zàn 瓚, relying on his talent and strength,
did not care for the common people.
He remembered wrongs and forgot kindness,
and would certainly take revenge for the slightest grievance.
For worthy gentlemen in the commanderies and districts whose names were above his,
he would certainly harm them by legal means.
He often said,
"Those in official attire all believe that their wealth and honor come from their positions and duties,
and do not thank others for favors."
Therefore, those he favored and cherished
were mostly merchants, peddlers, and common youths.
Wherever he went, he was oppressive and violent,
and the common people resented him.
Thereupon, Dài Jùn 代郡, Guǎngyáng 廣陽, Shànggǔ 上谷, and Yòuběipíng 右北平 each killed the chief officials appointed by Gōngsūn Zàn,
and reunited their forces with Wú Fǔ 輔 and Wàn Hé 和.
Gōngsūn Zàn, fearing the extraordinary,
then resided in Gāojīng 高京,
making his gates of iron.
He dismissed his attendants,
and no man aged seven or older was allowed to enter Yì Mén 易門.
He was exclusively attended by his concubines.
His documents and records were all pulled up by a well-pulley.
He ordered women to practice speaking in loud voices,
so that they could be heard several hundred paces away,
to transmit his orders and decrees.
He alienated his guests
and had no one he trusted intimately;
thus, his strategists and fierce generals
gradually dispersed.
From then on,
he rarely engaged in offensive warfare.
Someone asked him the reason.
Gōngsūn Zàn said,
"In the past, I drove the rebellious Hú 胡 people beyond the frontier,
and swept away the Huángjīn 黃巾 at Mèngjīn 孟津.
At that time,
I thought the world could be settled with a wave of the hand.
But now,
when military conflict is just beginning,
I see this is not something I can decide.
It is better to cease hostilities and diligently farm,
to relieve the lean years.
The Art of War says a hundred towers cannot be attacked.
Now, my numerous camp towers extend a thousand *lǐ* 里,
and I have accumulated three million *hú* 斛 of grain.
This food is enough to await any change in the world."
In the third year of Jiàn'ān 建安 (198 CE),
Yuán Shào 袁紹 again launched a major attack on Gōngsūn Zàn.
Gōngsūn Zàn sent his son, Gōngsūn Xù 續, to request aid from the various chiefs of Hēishān 黑山,
while he himself intended to lead his elite cavalry straight out,
along the western hills, to cut off Yuán Shào's rear.
His Chief Clerk, Guān Jìng 關靖, admonished him, saying,
"Currently, among the General's officers and soldiers,
none do not harbor thoughts of collapse.
The reason they can still hold together
is out of concern for their old and young,
and because they rely on the General as their leader.
If we hold firm for an extended period,
perhaps Yuán Shào can be made to retreat on his own.
If you abandon them and go out,
with no one to hold the fort,
the danger to Yì Jīng 易京
can be expected immediately."
Gōngsūn Zàn then stopped.
Yuán Shào gradually pressed his attack,
and Gōngsūn Zàn's forces diminished daily.
He then retreated
and built three layers of camps to secure himself.
In the spring of the fourth year (199 CE),
Zhāng Yàn 張燕, the chief of the Hēishān bandits, and Gōngsūn Xù led an army of one hundred thousand,
coming in three routes to rescue Gōngsūn Zàn.
Before they arrived,
Gōngsūn Zàn secretly sent a messenger carrying a letter to Gōngsūn Xù, saying,
"At the end of the Zhōu 周 dynasty, during the chaos and destruction,
corpses covered the ground.
Judging by imagination,
it was still not as bad as this.
I did not expect to personally face its brunt today.
Yuán's attack
is like ghosts and gods.
Ladders and assault vehicles dance on my towers,
drums and horns sound from underground.
With days dwindling and months pressing,
I have no leisure to rest.
Birds harass returning people,
and dammed water floods high places.
You must smash your head against Zhāng Yàn
and hasten to report the urgency.
The bond between father and son is nature's way;
it acts without words.
Moreover, prepare five thousand iron cavalry in the northern wetlands,
light a fire as a signal,
and I will come out from within,
displaying my might and valor,
to stake my life here.
Otherwise,
after my demise,
though the world is vast,
there will be no place for your feet."
Yuán Shào's scouts obtained the letter,
and at the appointed time, they lit fires.
Gōngsūn Zàn thought the rescue had arrived,
and immediately went out to battle.
Yuán Shào set an ambush,
and Gōngsūn Zàn was utterly defeated,
returning to defend the small inner city.
Concluding that he could not survive,
he had all his sisters, wives, and children hanged,
and then set himself on fire.
