Yuán Shào's troops rushed up to the platform, decapitated him.
Guān Jìng, seeing Gōngsūn Zàn's defeat,
sighed with regret, saying,
"If I had not stopped the General from going out himself earlier,
it might not have failed.
I have heard that a gentleman who leads someone into danger
must share their hardship.
How can I live alone?"
Thereupon, he galloped his horse towards Yuán Shào's army and died.
Gōngsūn Xù was killed by the Túcáo 屠各.
Tián Kǎi 田揩 died fighting Yuán Shào.
Xiānyú Fǔ 鮮于輔 led his followers to defect to Cáo Cāo 曹操.
Cáo Cāo appointed Xiānyú Fǔ as Dùliáo Jiāngjūn 度遼將軍 [General Who Crosses Liao]
and enfeoffed him as Dūtíng Hóu 都亭侯 [Marquis of a Capital Pavilion].
Yán Róu 閻柔 led his troops to join Cáo Cāo in attacking the Wūhuán 烏桓.
He was appointed Hù Wūhuán Xiàowèi 護烏桓校尉 [Protector of the Wūhuán]
and enfeoffed as Guānnèi Hóu 關內侯 [Marquis Within the Passes].
Zhāng Yàn, having been defeated by Yuán Shào,
saw his followers gradually disperse.
When Cáo Cāo was about to pacify Jì Zhōu 冀州,
Zhāng Yàn led his followers to Yè 鄴 to surrender,
and was appointed Píngběi Jiāngjūn 平北將軍 [General Who Pacifies the North]
and enfeoffed as Ānguó Tínghóu 安國亭侯 [Marquis of Ānguó Pavilion].
A commentary says: From the scions of imperial clans, kings, and dukes,
all grew up in luxury
and knew nothing of farming.
As for those who could strictly conduct themselves and discipline their bodies,
standing out from the crowd,
perhaps none have been heard of.
Liú Yú 劉虞 upheld the Way and sought renown,
governing himself with loyalty and generosity.
How splendid he was,
a noble scion of the Jì Hàn 季漢 (Later Hàn) dynasty!
If Liú Yú and Gōngsūn Zàn had no discord,
shared sentiment and joined forces,
gathered and united people,
secured the abundance of Yān 燕 and Jì 薊,
repaired their armies and displayed their might,
to face the fissures among the warlords,
setting aside celestial fate
and striving for human achievement,
then the glorious deeds of antiquity
would not have been far off!
Táo Qiān 陶謙, courtesy name Gōngzǔ 恭祖,
was a native of Dānyáng 丹陽.
In his youth, he was a scholar.
He served in various commanderies and prefectures,
and after four promotions, became the Sīmǎ 司馬 (Military Advisor) for Chējì Jiāngjūn 車騎將軍 [General of Chariots and Cavalry] Zhāng Wēn 張溫,
going west to suppress Biān Zhāng 邊章.
At that time, the Huángjīn 黃巾 uprising occurred in Xú Zhōu 徐州.
Táo Qiān was appointed Xú Zhōu Cìshǐ 徐州刺史 [Inspector of Xú Province].
He attacked the Huángjīn,
routing them with a great defeat,
and the region became peaceful.
Although Dǒng Zhuó 董卓 had been executed at that time,
Lǐ Jué 李傕 and Guō Sì 郭汜 caused chaos in Guānzhōng 關中.
At this time, communications in all directions were cut off,
but Táo Qiān regularly sent emissaries on secret routes
to offer tribute to Xī Jīng 西京 (the Western Capital, Cháng'ān 長安).
An imperial edict promoted him to Xú Zhōu Mù 徐州牧 [Governor of Xú Province],
added the title Āndōng Jiāngjūn 安東將軍 [General Who Pacifies the East],
and enfeoffed him as Lìyáng Hóu 溧陽侯 [Marquis of Lìyáng].
At this time, the people of Xú Fāng 徐方 were prosperous,
and grain harvests were abundant.
Many refugees returned to his jurisdiction.
However, Táo Qiān entrusted people unwisely,
and his administration of laws and government was disordered.
His Biéjià Cóngshì 別駕從事 [Special Advisor], Zhào Yù 趙昱,
was a renowned scholar,
but because of his loyalty and uprightness, he was alienated
and sent out to be Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu 廣陵太守 [Administrator of Guǎnglíng].
Cáo Hóng 曹宏 and other sycophantic small-minded people
were greatly trusted and appointed by Táo Qiān,
and many good people suffered harm because of them.
From this, chaos gradually grew.
Yán Xuān 閻宣 from Xiàpī 下邳 called himself
"Son of Heaven."
Táo Qiān initially allied with him,
but later killed him and absorbed his followers.
Initially,
Cáo Sōng (曹嵩), Cáo Cāo's (曹操) father, sought refuge in Lángyá (琅邪).
At that time, Táo Qiān's (陶謙) subordinate general was guarding Yīnpíng (陰平).
The soldiers coveted Cáo Sōng's (曹嵩) wealth and treasures,
and so attacked and killed him.
In the fourth year of Chūpíng (初平) (193 CE),
Cáo Cāo (曹操) attacked Táo Qiān (陶謙),
and defeated him at Péngchéng (彭城) and Fùyáng (傅陽).
Táo Qiān (陶謙) retreated to defend Tán (郯).
Cáo Cāo (曹操) attacked Tán (郯) but could not conquer it,
so he returned.
On his way, he captured Lǜlǜ (慮), Jūlíng (雎陵), and Xiàqiū (夏丘),
slaughtering all of them.
In total, hundreds of thousands of men and women were killed,
not even chickens and dogs were spared.
The Sìshuǐ (泗水) River stopped flowing because of the corpses.
From then on, the five county towns and strongholds
were completely devoid of human traces.
Earlier, the Sānfǔ (三輔) region suffered from Lǐ Jué's (李傕) rebellion,
and all the displaced people who sought refuge with Táo Qiān (陶謙) were annihilated.
In the first year of Xīngpíng (興平) (194 CE),
Cáo Cāo (曹操) attacked Táo Qiān (陶謙) again,
conquering and pacifying various counties in Lángyá (琅邪) and Dōnghǎi (東海).
Táo Qiān (陶謙) was afraid he would not escape,
and wanted to flee back to Dānyáng (丹陽).
Coincidentally, Zhāng Miǎo (張邈) welcomed Lǚ Bù (呂布) to occupy Yǎnzhōu (兗州),
so Cáo Cāo (曹操) returned to attack Lǚ Bù (呂布).
That year,
Táo Qiān (陶謙) fell ill and died.
Initially,
Zá Róng (笮融), a man from the same commandery,
gathered several hundred people
and went to rely on Táo Qiān (陶謙).
Táo Qiān (陶謙) made him supervise the transport of grain from Guǎnglíng (廣陵), Xiàpī (下邳), and Péngchéng (彭城).
He then cut off the supplies from the three commanderies,
and erected a large Buddhist temple (fútú sì 浮屠寺).
At the top, golden plates were stacked,
at the bottom, there was a multi-storied building.
Moreover, the halls and pavilions extended all around,
able to accommodate about three thousand people.
He made gold-painted statues,
and clothed them in brocade and colorful silks.
Whenever the Buddha was bathed,
he would prepare many meals and drinks,
spreading mats along the roads.
Those who came to eat or watch amounted to over ten thousand people.
When Cáo Cāo (曹操) attacked Táo Qiān (陶謙),
Xúfāng (徐方) became unstable.
Zá Róng (笮融) then led ten thousand men and women and three thousand horses to Guǎnglíng (廣陵).
Zhào Yù (趙昱), the Administrator of Guǎnglíng (廣陵), treated him with guest courtesies.
Zá Róng (笮融) coveted Guǎnglíng's (廣陵) resources and goods,
so he took advantage of a drunken moment to kill Zhào Yù (趙昱),
letting his soldiers plunder extensively.
He then crossed the river
and fled south to Yùzhāng (豫章),
killing the Administrator Zhū Hào (朱皓),
and occupying his city.
Later, he was defeated by Liú Yáo (劉繇), the Inspector of Yángzhōu (楊州).
He fled into the mountains
and was killed by someone.
Zhào Yù (趙昱), courtesy name Yuándá (元達),
was from Lángyá (琅邪).
He was pure-minded and detested evil,
devoting himself secretly to study.
Even close friends rarely saw him.
He was a man whose ears would not listen to impropriety,
and whose eyes would not gaze at what was wrong.
Tàipú (太僕) Zhǒng Fú (种拂) recommended him as "Rectitude."
The encomium says: Xiāngbēn (襄賁) strove for virtue,
a bulwark north of Yān (燕).
His benevolence reached the common people,
his loyalty defended the state.
Bóguī (伯珪) was crude and wild,
his martial talent swift and fierce.
Yú Hǎo (虞好) had no end,
Shào's (紹) power was hard to match.
Xúfāng (徐方) was devastated and depleted,
truly Táo Qiān (陶謙) was the obstruction.
Biographies of Yuán Shào (袁紹) and Liú Biǎo (劉表), Part One, Chapter Sixty-Four (Yuán Shào's son, Yuán Tán 袁譚)
Yuán Shào (袁紹), courtesy name Běnchū (本初),
was from Rǔyáng (汝陽), Rǔnán (汝南).
He was the grandson of Sītú (司徒) Yuán Tāng (湯).
His father, Yuán Chéng (成),
was the Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng (五官中郎將).
Yuán Shào (紹) was strong, healthy, and good at making connections.
From Dàjiāngjūn (大將軍) Liáng Jì (梁冀) downwards, no one failed to befriend him.
Yuán Shào (袁紹) served as a gentleman (láng 郎) in his youth,
and was appointed Magistrate of Púyáng (濮陽).
He left office due to his mother's mourning.
After the three-year mourning period was complete,
he was deeply moved by his childhood orphanhood,
and observed his father's mourning rites again.
After the mourning period ended,
he moved to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Yuán Shào (袁紹) had a handsome appearance and an imposing demeanor.
He cherished scholars and cultivated his reputation.
Having come from a family that served as ministers of state for generations (lěishì Táisī 累世台司),
he was the destination for many guests.
Moreover, he was humble and polite (qīngxīn zhéjié 傾心折節),
so everyone vied to visit his court.
Scholars, regardless of their status,
treated him with equal deference.
Their carriages, whether ornate or simple,
filled and crowded the streets and lanes.
However, the inner court officials all disliked him.
Zhào Zhōng (趙忠), the Zhōngchángshì (中常侍), said within the palace:
“Yuán Běnchū (袁本初) deliberately builds his reputation
and likes to gather dare-to-die warriors.
I don't know what this boy ultimately wants to do.”
His uncle, Tàifù (太傅) Yuán Kuí (隗), heard this and summoned Yuán Shào (袁紹),
reprimanding him with Zhào Zhōng's (趙忠) words.
But Yuán Shào (袁紹) never changed.
Later, he was recruited as an aide (yuán 掾) by Dàjiāngjūn (大將jūn) Hé Jìn (何進),
and served as Shìyùshǐ (侍御史) and Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng (虎賁中郎將).
In the fifth year of Zhōngpíng (中平) (188 CE),
the Xīyuán Bāxiàowèi (西園八校尉) were first established,
and Yuán Shào (紹) was made Zuǒjūn Xiàowèi (佐軍校尉).
When Emperor Líng (靈帝) died,
Yuán Shào (紹) advised Hé Jìn (何進) to summon Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) and other armies
to pressure the Empress Dowager into executing all the eunuchs, and transferred Yuán Shào (紹) to Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉).
The details are already in the biography of Hé Jìn (何進).
When Dǒng Zhuó (卓) led his troops to the capital,
Bào Xìn (鮑信), the Qí Dūwèi (騎都尉) of Tàishān (泰山), advised Yuán Shào (紹) saying:
“Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) commands a strong army
and harbors sinister intentions.
If we don't act quickly now,
we will surely be controlled by him.
While he has just arrived and is tired,
we can attack him and capture him.”
Yuán Shào (紹) feared Dǒng Zhuó (卓)
and dared not act.
Soon after,
Dǒng Zhuó (卓) discussed deposing the emperor and establishing a new one,
saying to Yuán Shào (紹):
“The ruler of the empire
should be wise and enlightened.
Whenever I think of Emperor Líng (靈帝),
it fills me with anger and bitterness.
Dǒng Hóu (董侯) seems suitable;
we should enthrone him now.”
Yuán Shào (紹) replied:
“The current emperor is in the prime of his youth,
and no misdeeds of his have been proclaimed throughout the empire.
If you disregard propriety and act on your own desires,
deposing the legitimate heir and enthroning a collateral one,
I fear public opinion will not be at ease.”
Dǒng Zhuó (卓) slammed his sword and shouted at Yuán Shào (紹):
“You mere boy, how dare you!
Are not the affairs of the empire
in my hands?
If I wish to do it,
who dares not to obey!”
Yuán Shào (紹) cunningly replied:
“This is a major affair of the state;
please allow me to discuss it with the Tàifù (太傅).”
Dǒng Zhuó (卓) then said
“The Liú (劉) clan is not worthy of being spared.”
Yuán Shào (紹) retorted angrily:
“Among the valiant men of the world,
how can there be only Duke Dǒng (董公)!”
He then drew his sword, gave a long bow, and left directly.
He hung his official seal at the Shàngdōngmén (上東門)
and fled to Jìzhōu (冀州).
Dǒng Zhuó (董卓) offered a reward for Yuán Shào's (紹) capture.
At that time, Zhōu Bì (周珌), Shìzhōng (侍中), and Wǔ Qióng (伍瓊), Chéngmén Xiàowèi (城門校尉), were trusted and favored by Dǒng Zhuó (卓).
Wǔ Qióng (瓊) and others secretly spoke to Dǒng Zhuó (卓) on behalf of Yuán Shào (紹), saying:
“The matter of deposing and establishing an emperor is a great affair,
not something an ordinary person can comprehend.
Yuán Shào (袁紹) did not understand the gravity of the situation and fled in fear,
he has no other intentions.
If you urgently seek his capture now,
the situation will surely lead to trouble.
The Yuán (袁) clan has extended kindness for four generations,
and their retainers and former officials are all over the empire.
If he gathers heroes to assemble a multitude,
and brave men rise because of him,
then Shāndōng (山東) will not belong to you, Duke.
It would be better to pardon him,
and appoint him as an Administrator of a commandery.
Yuán Shào (紹) will be happy to be forgiven,
and there will surely be no trouble.”
Dǒng Zhuó (卓) thought this was reasonable,
and so he dispatched an envoy to appoint Yuán Shào (紹) as the Administrator of Bóhǎi (勃海),
and enfeoffed him as Hóu of Dāngxiāng (邟鄉侯).
Yuán Shào (紹) still claimed to concurrently hold the office of Sīlì (司隸).
In the first year of Chūpíng,
Yuán Shào then raised an army in Bóhǎi.
He, along with his younger cousin, the General of the Rear Yuán Shù, the Inspector of Jìzhōu Hán Fú,

the Inspector of Yùzhōu Kǒng Zhòu, the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu Liú Dài, the Administrator of Chénliú Zhāng Miǎo, the Administrator of Guǎnglíng Zhāng Chāo, the Administrator of Hénèi Wáng Kuāng, the Administrator of Shānyáng Yuán Yí, the Administrator of Dōngjùn Qiáo Mào,
and the Chancellor of Jìběi Bào Xìn, simultaneously rose in rebellion.
Each had several tens of thousands of troops,
ostensibly to punish Dǒng Zhuó.
Yuán Shào and Wáng Kuāng were stationed in Hénèi,
Kǒng Zhòu in Yǐngchuān,
Hán Fú in Yè,
and the remaining armies were all stationed in Suānzǎo.
They formed an alliance
and remotely nominated Yuán Shào as their leader.
Yuán Shào styled himself General of Chariots and Cavalry
and concurrently held the position of Colonel-Director of Retainers.
When Dǒng Zhuó heard that Yuán Shào had risen in arms east of the mountains,
he executed Yuán Shào's uncle, Yuán Kuí,
and all of his clan members who were in the capital,
exterminating them completely.

Dǒng Zhuó then dispatched the Grand Messenger Hán Róng, the Minor Supervisor Yīn Xún, the Bearer of the Golden Insignia Húmǔ Bān, the Grand Builder Wú Xún, and the Colonel of Agile Cavalry Wáng Guī to try to persuade Yuán Shào and the other commanders to disband their forces.
Yuán Shào ordered Wáng Kuāng to kill Húmǔ Bān, Wáng Guī, Wú Xún and others.
Yuán Shù also captured and killed Yīn Xún.
Only Hán Róng was spared due to his prominent virtue.
At this time, many heroes had attached themselves to Yuán Shào,
and also, deeply affected by the calamity that befell his family,
everyone wished to avenge him.
Commanderies and provinces rose in swarms,
all acting in the name of the Yuán clan.
Hán Fú, seeing that public sentiment leaned towards Yuán Shào,
was jealous that he was gaining followers
and feared that Yuán Shào would plot against him.
He often sent his subordinates to guard Yuán Shào's gate,
not allowing him to send out troops.
Qiáo Mào then falsely composed a letter from the Three Excellencies,
which he transmitted by post to the various provinces and commanderies,
recounting Dǒng Zhuó's misdeeds
and the critical danger faced by the Son of Heaven.
It called upon righteous armies to come forth
to relieve the nation's distress.
Hán Fú thereupon allowed Yuán Shào to raise an army.
He then consulted his subordinates, saying:
"Should we assist the Yuán clan,
or assist the Dǒng clan?"
His Chief Clerk, Liú Huì, indignantly said:
"We raise an army for the nation;
why ask about Yuán or Dǒng?"
Hán Fú still harbored deep suspicions of Yuán Shào,
and frequently reduced the military rations,
hoping to cause his forces to disperse.
The following year,
Hán Fú's general, Qū Yì, rebelled.
Hán Fú fought him and suffered a defeat.
Yuán Shào, already resentful of Hán Fú,
then allied himself with Qū Yì.
Yuán Shào's retainer, Féng Jì, said to Yuán Shào:
"To undertake a great enterprise,
one cannot establish oneself
without occupying a province.
Now Jìzhōu is strong and rich,
but Hán Fú is a mediocre talent.
You can secretly urge Gōngsūn Zàn to lead his troops south.
Hán Fú, hearing this, will surely be frightened.
Also send eloquent speakers to lay out the advantages and disadvantages for him.
Hán Fú, pressed by the urgency,
can surely be made to yield his position."
Yuán Shào agreed with this,
became closer to Féng Jì,
and immediately wrote a letter to Gōngsūn Zàn.
Gōngsūn Zàn then led his troops and arrived,
outwardly claiming to punish Dǒng Zhuó,
but secretly plotting to attack Hán Fú.
Yuán Shào then sent his maternal nephew Gāo Gàn of Chénliú, and Xún Chén of Yǐngchuān, and others
to persuade Hán Fú, saying:
"Gōngsūn Zàn is coming south on the crest of victory,
and the various commanderies are responding to him.
General of Chariots Yuán is leading his army eastward,
and his intentions are unfathomable.
I secretly fear for your generalship."
Hán Fú, alarmed,
said:
"If that is the case, what should I do?"
Xún Chén said:
"Do you assess yourself as benevolent and tolerant, capable of gathering the multitude,
and to whom the world is attached,
compared to the Yuán clan?"
Hán Fú said:
"No, I am not."
"In times of crisis, do you make decisive judgments, with wisdom and courage surpassing others,
again, compared to the Yuán clan?"
Hán Fú said:
"No, I am not."
"Has your family spread kindness and virtue throughout the generations,
with the world receiving its benefits,
again, compared to the Yuán clan?"
Hán Fú said:
"No, I am not."
Xún Chén said:
"Though Bóhǎi is a commandery,
in reality, it is a province.
Now, General, with three inferior qualities,
if you long remain in this position,
the Yuán clan, a hero of this age,
will surely not place themselves below you.
Moreover, Gōngsūn Zàn leads the troops of Yān and Dài,
and their vanguard is irresistible.
Jìzhōu is a vital resource for the empire.
If the two armies combine their strength,
and fighting erupts beneath the city walls,
ruin and death can be expected immediately.
Furthermore, the Yuán clan are old acquaintances of the General,
and are also allies.
The best plan now
is to yield Jìzhōu to the Yuán clan.
They will surely treat the General with great honor,
and Gōngsūn Zàn will no longer be able to contend with them.
In this way, the General will have the reputation of yielding to the worthy,
and his person will be as secure as Mount Tài.
I beg you not to hesitate."
Hán Fú, whose nature was always timid,
then agreed to his plan.
Hán Fú's Chief Scribe Gěng Wǔ, Assistant Inspector Mǐn Chún, and Cavalry Commander Jǔ Shòu heard of this and remonstrated, saying:
"Although Jìzhōu is humble,
it has a million armed men,
and enough grain for ten years.
Yuán Shào is a solitary guest with a impoverished army,
dependent on us for his survival.
He is like an infant in the palm of one's hand;
if we cut off its milk,
it can be starved to death immediately.
How can you wish to give the province to him?"
Hán Fú said:
"I am an old subordinate of the Yuán clan,
and my talent is not equal to Běnchū's (Yuán Shào's courtesy name).
To measure one's virtue and yield is what the ancients valued.
Why are you gentlemen alone distressed?"
Before this,
Hán Fú's subordinates Zhào Fú and Chéng Huàn, with ten thousand strong crossbowmen, were stationed at Mèngjīn.
Hearing of this,
they led their troops back swiftly
and requested to resist Yuán Shào,
but Hán Fú again refused to listen.
He then relinquished his position,
moved to the former residence of the Regular Palace Attendant Zhào Zhōng,
and sent his son with his seal and sash to yield to Yuán Shào.
Yuán Shào then took over as Inspector of Jìzhōu,
and acting under imperial authority, appointed Hán Fú as General Who Rouses Awe,
but gave him no command.
He invited Jǔ Shòu to be Assistant Inspector,
and then said to Jǔ Shòu:
"Now traitorous ministers cause chaos,
and the imperial court has moved.
My family has received favors for generations;
I am determined to exert all my strength and life
to restore the Hàn dynasty.
However, Qí Huán could not achieve hegemony without Yí Wú,
and Gōujiàn could not preserve his state without Fàn Lǐ.
Now I wish to work together with you wholeheartedly
to stabilize the nation.
How shall we rescue and assist it?"
Jǔ Shòu stepped forward and said:
"General, you entered court in your youth,
and your name spread throughout the land.
At the time of the deposition and establishment,
your loyalty and righteousness stirred,
you fled alone on horseback,
causing Dǒng Zhuó to be apprehensive.
Crossing the river and heading north,
Bóhǎi submitted to you.
Controlling the troops of one commandery,
gathering the forces of Jìzhōu,
your prestige dominates north of the Yellow River,
and your name is renowned throughout the empire.
If you lead your army eastward,
the Yellow Turban rebels can be swept away;
turning back to attack Heishān,
Zhāng Yàn can be eliminated;
redirecting your forces northward,
Gōngsūn Zàn will surely be captured;
intimidating the Róng and Dí,
the Xiōngnú will be immediately pacified.
Dominating the north of the Yellow River,
uniting the lands of the four provinces,
gathering heroes,
commanding a million troops,
welcoming the Emperor from Cháng'ān,
restoring the ancestral temple in Luòyì,
issuing commands to the world,
and punishing those who do not submit.
With this, who can resist you in contending for supremacy!
Within a few years,
this achievement will not be difficult."
Yuán Shào said happily:
"This is my very thought!"
He immediately memorialized to appoint Jǔ Shòu as General Who Rouses Martial Might,
and made him supervise all the generals.
Shěn Péi of Wèijùn,
Tián Fēng of Jùlù,
both had been unable to achieve their ambitions under Hán Fù due to their uprightness.
Shào then appointed Fēng as his chief clerk (biéjià)
and Péi as administrator (zhìzhōng),
and greatly valued and employed them.
Hán Fù, harboring suspicion and fear,
resigned from Shào and sought to leave,
going to rely on Zhāng Miǎo.
Later, Shào sent an envoy to Zhāng Miǎo
to discuss some matters,
and they conversed in whispers.
Hán Fù was present at the time,
and, thinking he was being plotted against,
shortly thereafter,
went to the latrine and committed suicide.
That winter,
Gōngsūn Zàn heavily defeated the Yellow Turban rebels
and returned to garrison Pánhé,
his might shaking the region north of the Yellow River.
There was no city in Jìzhōu that did not respond to him by simply hearing of his name.
Shào then personally attacked him.
Gōngsūn Zàn had thirty thousand troops,
arranged in a square formation,
with ten thousand elite cavalry
flanking the army on both sides,
their vanguard being extremely sharp.
Shào first ordered Qū Yì to lead eight hundred elite soldiers
and one thousand powerful crossbows
to serve as the vanguard.
Gōngsūn Zàn, underestimating their small numbers,
let loose his cavalry to charge them.
Qū Yì's soldiers hid behind their shields,
and all fired at once.
Gōngsūn Zàn's army suffered a great defeat,
and they beheaded Yán Gāng, the Inspector (cìshǐ) of Jìzhōu whom Gōngsūn Zàn had appointed,
capturing over a thousand armored heads.
Qū Yì pursued them to Jièqiáo,
where Gōngsūn Zàn gathered his forces and fought again.
Qū Yì again defeated him,
and then reached Gōngsūn Zàn's camp,
pulling down his main banner (yámén).
The rest of his forces all fled.
Shào was ten li or more behind.
Hearing that Gōngsūn Zàn had been defeated,
he dismounted and rested his horses,
with only several dozen strong crossbows
and about a hundred great halberd-wielding guards protecting his tent.
Over two thousand of Gōngsūn Zàn's scattered cavalry suddenly arrived,
surrounding Shào several layers deep,
and arrows rained down.
Tián Fēng helped Shào
retreat into an empty ruined wall.
Shào took off his helmet and threw it to the ground,
saying:
"A true man should fight to the death at the front,
how can he instead flee between walls?"
He quickly ordered all the crossbows to fire continuously,
wounding many of Gōngsūn Zàn's cavalry.
The enemy did not know it was Shào,
and gradually retreated.
At that moment, Qū Yì arrived to meet him,
and the cavalry dispersed and retreated.
In the third year,
Gōngsūn Zàn again sent troops to Lóngcòu to challenge Shào,
and Shào again attacked and defeated them.
Gōngsūn Zàn then returned to Yōuzhōu,
not daring to sally forth again.
In the early fourth year,
the Son of Heaven sent Grand Coachman (tàipú) Zhào Qí to reconcile the Guāndōng region,
ordering each to cease hostilities.
Gōngsūn Zàn therefore wrote a letter to Shào, saying:
"Grand Coachman Zhào, with the virtues of Zhōu Gōng and Shào Gōng,
has been entrusted with a mission to come and levy,
to proclaim the grace of the court,
and to show harmony and friendship.
It is like the clouds parting to reveal the sun,
what joy could be greater?
In the past, Jiǎ Fù and Kòu Xún contended and sought to harm each other,
but upon meeting Emperor Shìzǔ who resolved their conflict,
they then rode in the same carriage together.
Once the hostility was resolved,
people of the time praised them.
I, a humble man from the frontier,
can share this good fortune with the general.
This is truly the general's [favor],
and also Zàn's wish."
Shào then led his army south.
On the third day of the third month (Shangsi Festival),
he hosted a grand gathering of guests and followers at Bólàojīn.
He heard that troops in Wèijùn had rebelled,
and along with tens of thousands of Black Mountain bandits like Gāndú, they had jointly overthrown Yèchéng,
killing the commandery administrator.
Guests at the banquet whose families were in Yèchéng
all turned pale with worry and fear,
some even stood up and wept.
Shào's expression remained calm
and did not change his usual demeanor.
Among the bandits was Táo Shēng,
who called himself
"General Pacifying Hàn,"
and alone rebelled against the other bandits.
He led his followers over the western city wall and entered,
closed the government office gate,
prepared carriages,
loaded Shào's family and all the officials and gentry in the province,
personally protected them,
and sent them to Chìqiū.
When Shào returned,
he then garrisoned Chìqiū,
and appointed Táo Shēng as Colonel of Illustrious Righteousness (Jiànyì Zhōnglángjiàng).
In the sixth month,
Shào then led his army out,
entering the Cāngyán Valley entrance of Lùcháng Shān in Cháogē,
to suppress Gāndú.
After besieging them for five days,
he defeated them,
beheading Gāndú and over ten thousand of his followers.
Shào then followed the mountains northward,
advancing to attack the various bandits like Zuǒzī Zhàngbā,
all of whom he beheaded.
He also attacked Liú Shí, Qīngniújiǎo, Huánglóng, Zuǒxiào, Guō Dàxián, Lǐ Dàmù, Yúdīgēn, and others, again beheading tens of thousands,
and slaughtered all their encampments.
He then fought the Black Mountain bandit Zhāng Yàn and the four camps of Túcāo and the Yànmén Wūhuán at Chángshān.
Zhāng Yàn had tens of thousands of elite soldiers
and several thousand cavalry.
After fighting for more than ten days,
although Zhāng Yàn's troops suffered many dead and wounded,
Shào's army was also exhausted,
and so they each retreated.
Qū Yì, relying on his achievements,
became arrogant and undisciplined.
Shào summoned and killed him,
and absorbed his forces.
In the second year of Xīngpíng,
Shào was appointed General of the Right (Yòu Jiāngjūn).
That winter,
the imperial carriage was pursued by Lǐ Què and others at Cáoyáng.
Jū Shòu advised Shào, saying:
"The general's family has served as prime ministers for generations,
and has consistently displayed loyalty and righteousness.
Now the imperial court is in exile,
the ancestral temples are ruined.
Observing the various commanderies and provinces,
although they outwardly claim to raise righteous armies,
inwardly they are plotting against each other,
none have the intention of worrying for the altars of soil and grain and caring for the people.
Moreover, now that your province and city are generally settled,
your army is strong and your soldiers are loyal.
If you welcome the great imperial carriage from the west,
and immediately establish the capital at Yè,
you can hold the Son of Heaven hostage to command the feudal lords.
With soldiers and horses, you can suppress those who defy the court,
who could resist you?"
Shào was about to follow his plan.
Guō Tú and Chúnyú Qióng of Yǐngchuān said:
"The Hàn dynasty has been in decline
for a long time now.
To wish to revive it now,
is it not difficult?
Furthermore, heroes are rising simultaneously,
each occupying provinces and commanderies.
They gather followers and crowds,
moving in tens of thousands.
This is what is called 'Qín lost its deer,
and whoever gets it first becomes king.'
If we welcome the Son of Heaven now,
we will constantly have to report to him.
To follow him would diminish our authority,
to disobey him would be to resist an imperial order.
This is not a good plan."
Jū Shòu said:
"To welcome the court now
is right in terms of righteousness,
and appropriate for the times.
If we do not decide early,
there will surely be someone who precedes us.
Indeed, power should not miss its opportune moment,
and achievements should not dislike speed.
I hope you will consider this."
As the establishment of the emperor was not Shào's original intention,
he ultimately could not follow it.
Yuán Shào had three sons: Tán, courtesy name Xiǎnsī;
Xī, courtesy name Xiǎnyōng;
Shàng, courtesy name Xiǎnfǔ.
Tán was the eldest and intelligent,
Shàng was the youngest and handsome.
Yuán Shào’s second wife, Lady Liú, was favored,
and she particularly loved Shàng,
frequently praising him to Yuán Shào.
Yuán Shào also admired his appearance
and wished to make him his successor.
So he made Tán succeed his elder brother
and sent him out as the Intendant of Qīngzhōu.
Jǔ Shòu remonstrated, saying:
“It is said that when ten thousand people chase a rabbit,
and one person catches it,
the greedy ones all stop,
because the shares are settled.
Moreover, to appoint based on age if wisdom is equal,
or by divination if virtue is equal,
is an ancient system.
I wish Your Majesty would reflect on the warnings of success and failure from previous generations,
and consider the principle of ‘shares settled when chasing a rabbit.’
If this is not changed,
calamity will begin here.”
Yuán Shào said:
“I want my sons to each command a province,
to observe their capabilities.”
Thereupon, he made his second son Xī the Intendant of Yōuzhōu,
and his nephew Gāo Gàn the Intendant of Bīngzhōu.
In the first year of Jiàn’ān (196 CE),
Cáo Cāo welcomed the Son of Heaven to the capital Xǔ.
An imperial edict was then issued to Yuán Shào,
reproaching him for having vast territory and numerous troops yet unilaterally forming factions,
and not deploying forces to support the emperor but merely attacking each other.
Yuán Shào submitted a memorial, saying: “Your subject has heard that in ancient times there were those whose sorrowful sighs caused frost to fall,
and whose mournful cries made city walls collapse.
Whenever I read such accounts,
I believed them to be true;
but now, comparing them to the present situation,
I
realize they were fictitious.
Why?
Your subject rose to serve the state,
ruined his family to achieve his purpose,
yet despite holding loyalty, he incurred suspicion;
holding faith, he met doubt.
Day and night I sigh continuously,
my liver ripped apart, weeping
blood,
yet there has been no response of collapsing city walls or falling frost.
Thus, how could Zōu Yǎn and Xī Fù have truly moved heaven and earth?
Righteousness,
so I disbanded my forces and fled,
devising a plan beyond the river.
At that time, Zhuó was eager to gather foreign aid,
recruiting and pleasing heroes.
Thus, he immediately appointed your subject to Bóhǎi
and bestowed military
titles.
So there was not the slightest animosity between your subject and Zhuó.
If I had merely wanted to muddle through and stir up trouble,
to illicitly seek glory and profit,
then I could have advanced to usurp
high office,
and retreated without fear of domestic trouble.
However, your subject foolishly adhered to his principles,
with no ambition to seize power.
Thus, I gathered heroes,
raised an army of a million,
watered horses at Mèngjīn,
and
swore an oath by blood at Zhānghé.
At that time, the former Intendant of Jìzhōu, Hán Fù, harbored treasonous intentions,
wishing to monopolize power,
cutting off your subject’s military supplies,
preventing me from continuing my advance,
which led the crafty bandits to unleash their
venom,
bringing harm to my entire family,
young and old, high and low,
all executed on the same day.
Even birds and beasts,
still know how to cry out.
The reason your subject utterly disregarded sorrow,
outwardly showing no
hidden grief,
was truly because loyalty and filial piety,
two paths that cannot coexist;
considering private matters and personal feelings
would prevent the completion of great achievements.
This is also the second proof of your foolish subject’s sacrificing his family for the state.
The cunning enemy, knowing their doom,
thus Hán Fù harbored fear,
apologized for his faults and surrendered his territory;
Zhāng Yáng and Hēishān simultaneously begged for surrender.
Your subject then, acting by imperial mandate,
stealthily compared himself to Dòu Róng,
appointing the Discussant
Cáo Cāo as acting Intendant of Yǎnzhōu.
At that time, Gōngsūn Zàn’s army swept south,
plundering the northern border.
Your subject immediately sped forth, rolling up the land like a mat,
engaging Zàn in battle.
By
heaven’s might,
every battle was a victory.
Your subject, a descendant of a ducal clan,
grew up in the capital,
somewhat familiar with ceremonial rites,
but not accustomed to warfare;
moreover, from my great-grandfather, our former minister,
onwards,
our family has served as assistants for generations,
all serving with civil virtue and utmost loyalty,
thus escaping punishment.
Your subject did not contend with Zàn for military power,
nor vie for battlefield achievements.
Truly
because treacherous ministers should not go unpunished,
as condemned by the Spring and Autumn Annals;
if it truly benefits the state,
I will devote myself without doubt.
Therefore, I braved frost and snow,
not fearing toil,
truly hoping for a
single victory,
to establish a lifelong achievement.
The altars of soil and grain still unsettled,
your subject is truly ashamed of this.
The Grand Coachman Zhào Qí came bearing an imperial command,
proclaiming Your Majesty’s benevolent and magnanimous grace,
clearing away petty grievances,
and renewing all below.
On the day the edict was received,
I led my army southward.
This is the third proof of your subject’s awe of heavenly might
and his不敢怠慢之三驗也．
列．
However, provincial and commandery governors and administrators
vie to steal fame,
harboring dual loyalties,
lingering and looking on,
all granted fiefs and jades,
straddling provinces and connecting commanderies.
This is why far and near are suspicious,
and opinions are confused.
Your subject has heard that in times of peace,
those with high virtue are esteemed;
in times of crisis,
those with great achievements are richly rewarded.
Your Majesty has been displaced
from your rightful place,
Luòyì lacks sacrifices,
the world grieves,
and brave scholars are indignant.
This is why loyal ministers willingly lay down their lives,
their flesh and bones torn apart, without regret,
because
they are moved by righteousness.
Now, rewards are given to the undeserving,
thereby alienating the virtuous;
loyal achievements are obstructed and rejected,
thereby creating doubt in the public’s expectations.
Is this the farsighted plan of Your Majesty’s trusted advisors?
Or is it due to the perverse words of slanderers and wicked individuals?
Your subject’s rank is a Marquess of Guānní,
his position a salary of two thousand shi.
Your subject has already enjoyed
these extraordinary favors and profound kindness,
how dare I covet
greater honors,
hoping for the command of a vermilion bow and black arrows?
I am truly saddened that assistant commanders and officers,
whose diligence is unrecorded,
who serve the state with utmost loyalty,
are instead blamed for serious faults.
This is
why Méng Tián wept bitterly in the frontier prison,
and Bái Qǐ sighed at Dùyóu.
The Grand Tutor Rìdī, holding the position of Imperial Tutor,
was entrusted with the eastern expedition,
yet
he disrupted the imperial mandate,
favored and employed the wrong people;
all those he promoted
were scorned by the public.
Yet, Your Majesty accepted his plans
and made him chief strategist,
causing your subject’s blood relatives,
his brothers,
to become enemies,
engaging in battle,
causing strife to intensify.
Although your subject wishes to lay down his armor and throw away his weapons,
circumstances compel him otherwise.
I truly fear that Your Majesty’s wisdom, as bright as the sun and moon,
something not illuminated,
the hearing of the four senses something not heard.
I beg that my memorial be sent down,
to be consulted among the assembled wise,
and let the Sān Huái and Jiǔ Jí
deliberate on my crimes and transgressions.
If
my current exercise of authority is considered a fault,
then Huán and Wén ought to have been utterly destroyed;
if not chastising the thief is deemed virtuous by the masses,
then Zhào Dùn might have escaped the ignominy of having his regicide recorded.
Indeed.
Though I am a humble person,
my resolve guards a single principle.
If I could make clear my original intention,
without shaming the late emperor,
then to lay my head before a curved knife,
or pull up my clothes and step into a cauldron,
would be my
desire.
I only wish that Your Majesty would extend the impartiality of the turtledove,
put an end to theories of wickedness and flattery,
and not allow your foolish minister to carry resentment to the three springs.
Thereupon, Shào was appointed Tàiwèi,
and enfeoffed as Yè Hóu.
At that time, Cáo Cāo appointed himself Dà Jiàngjūn,
and Shào felt it shameful to be beneath him,
so he falsely memorialized to decline the appointment.
Cāo was greatly alarmed,
and then yielded the position to Shào.
Two years later,
he sent the Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng Kǒng Róng, holding a staff of authority, to appoint Shào Dà Jiàngjūn,
bestowing upon him bows, arrows, a staff of authority, and an axe,
and a hundred húbēns,
also supervising the four provinces of Jì, Qīng, Yōu, and Bìng.
Only then did he accept it.
Whenever Shào received imperial edicts,
he was troubled by anything inconvenient for himself,
and therefore wished to move the Son of Heaven closer to him,
sending someone to persuade Cāo that Xǔxià was low-lying
and damp,
and Luòyáng was ruined,
suggesting it was appropriate to move the capital to Zhēnchéng,
to achieve complete stability.
Cāo refused him.
Tián Fēng advised Shào, saying:
"The plan to move the capital,
since it could not be followed,
you should quickly plan to seize Xǔ,
welcome the Son of Heaven,
act with his edicts as your mandate,
and echo your call throughout the realm.
This is the best strategy.
Otherwise,
you will ultimately be captured by others,
and though you repent, it will be useless."
Shào did not follow.
In the spring of the fourth year,
he attacked Gōngsūn Zàn,
and thus pacified Yōutǔ.
The details are in Zàn's biography.
After Shào had annexed the territory of the four provinces,
with hundreds of thousands of troops,
his arrogant heart grew even stronger,
and his tribute and offerings became rare and simple.
The Chief Clerk Gěng Bāo secretly memorialized to Shào, saying:
"The Red Virtue has decayed completely,
and Yuán is of the Yellow Lineage.
It is appropriate to conform to heaven's will,
and follow the people's hearts."
Shào showed Bāo's memorial to his military staff and subordinates.
The deliberators believed Bāo's words were demonic and absurd, and he ought to be executed.
Shào knew that the sentiments of the masses were not in agreement,
and had no choice but to kill Bāo to suppress his trace.
Thereupon, he selected 100,000 elite soldiers,
and 10,000 cavalry,
intending to march out and attack Xǔ,
with Shěn Pèi and Féng Jì overseeing military affairs,
Tián Fēng, Xún Chén, and Xǔ Yōu from Nányáng as strategists,
and Yán Liáng and Wén Chǒu as commanders.
Jū Shòu came forward and advised, saying:
"Recently, when attacking Gōngsūn,
the army was out for years,
the people are exhausted and impoverished,
the granaries have no reserves,
and taxes and levies are currently heavy.
This is a profound worry for the state.
It is appropriate to first send envoys to present our victory to the Son of Heaven,
and allow the farmers and people to rest.
If we cannot get through,
then memorialize that Cáo Cāo has blocked our royal road,
and then advance and station troops at Líyáng,
gradually build up forces in Hénán,
build more boats,
repair weapons and equipment,
and dispatch elite cavalry,
to raid his borders,
so that he cannot be at peace,
while we take advantage of his exhaustion.
In this way, we can settle the matter while sitting."
Guō Tú and Shěn Pèi said:
"The military classics state that
for a force ten times the enemy, besiege; five times, attack;
if equal, then one can fight.
Now, with your sagely martial prowess,
and the strong forces of Héshuò,
to attack Cáo Cāo,
the situation is like turning over one's hand.
If we do not seize the moment,
it will be difficult to plan later."
Shòu said:
"Indeed, to suppress chaos and punish the tyrannical
is called an army of righteousness;
to rely on numbers and presumptuous strength
is called an arrogant army.
The righteous are invincible,
the arrogant are first destroyed.
Cáo Cāo welcomed the Son of Heaven,
and established the palace in Xǔdū.
Now to move the army southwards,
is contrary to righteousness.
Moreover, the strategy for victory in the ancestral temple
does not lie in strength or weakness.
Cáo Cāo's laws are already implemented,
his soldiers are well-trained,
he is not like Gōngsūn Zàn, who passively endured a siege.
Now, to abandon the [secure] method for lasting peace,
and raise an army without a just cause,
I secretly fear for you."
Tú and others said:
"Wǔ Wáng's campaign against Zhòu
was not considered unrighteous;
how much less so is an army dispatched against Cáo Cāo,
to be called without a just cause!
Furthermore, your army is elite and brave,
your officers and men are eager to fight,
and if you do not seize the moment to establish the great enterprise,
it is what is meant by 'Heaven grants, but one does not take,
and instead receives calamity.'
This is why Yuè became hegemon,
and Wú was destroyed.
The strategy of the supervisor of the army
lies in firmness,
not in discerning timely changes and subtle opportunities."
Shào adopted Tú's words.
Tú and others then slandered Jū Shòu, saying:
"Shòu oversees both internal and external affairs,
his prestige shakes the three armies.
If he becomes increasingly powerful,
how can he be controlled?
For a minister and lord to be alike flourishes,
but for a lord and minister to be alike perishes.
This is what Huáng Shí warned against.
Moreover, when commanding the army externally,
one should not know internal affairs."
Shào then divided Shòu's command into three chief governorships,
making Shòu, Guō Tú, and Chún Yú Qióng each lead one army.
This had not yet been put into effect.
In the fifth year,
the General of the Left Liú Bèi killed the Inspector of Xú Province Chē Zhòu,
occupied Pèi, and rebelled against Cáo Cāo.
Cāo was alarmed,
and personally led a campaign against Bèi.
Tián Fēng advised Shào, saying:
"The one who contends with you for the realm
is Cáo Cāo.
Cāo is now attacking Liú Bèi in the east,
his army engaged and not easily disengaged,
if you now lead your army to assault his rear,
you can settle the matter in one stroke.
Troops move by opportune moments,
and this is that time."
Shào declined, citing his son's illness,
and did not proceed.
Fēng struck the ground with his staff, saying:
"Alas,
the opportunity is gone!
To encounter such a rare opportunity,
and lose the chance due to a child's illness,
what a pity!"
Shào heard this and was enraged,
and from then on, he distanced himself from him.

In former years, beating drums, he marched north,
to attack Gōngsūn Zàn.
Gōngsūn Zàn was strong, defiant, and rebellious,
resisting the siege for a year.
Cāo, seeing that he had not yet been defeated,
secretly
exchanged letters,
wishing to enlist the aid of the King's army,
to launch a surprise attack,
thus leading his troops to the river,
crossing north on square boats.
It so happened that his messenger was discovered,
and Zàn was also defeated and killed,
which caused
his ambitions to be thwarted,
and his plan to fail.
He stationed his troops at Áocāng,
using the river as a stronghold,
now desiring to wield a mantis's axe,
to resist a heavy chariot's tracks.
The
Mùfǔ, upholding the might and power of Hàn,
parries attacks across the universe,
with a million long halberds,
and a thousand hordes of barbarian cavalry,
rousing the soldiers like Zhōnghuáng, Yù, and Huò,
unleashing the power
of good bows and strong crossbows.
Bīngzhōu crosses the Tàiháng Mountains,
Qīngzhōu crosses the Jì and Luò rivers.
The main army will cross the Yellow River to confront him in front,
and Jīngzhōu will descend upon Wǎn and Yè to pinch him
from behind.
[一０] With thunderous steps like a tiger,
they will all gather at the enemy's court,
like raising a blazing fire to burn flying thistles,
[一一] or overturning the vast sea and pouring in sparks,
[一二] what could possibly not be
annihilated?
This disaster
arose from this.
This is the season for loyal ministers to lay down their lives,
and for valiant warriors to achieve great deeds.
How can we not strive earnestly?
Then he first sent Yán Liáng to attack Cáo Cāo's detached general Liú Yán at Báimǎ.
Shào himself led troops to Líyáng.
Jǔ Shòu, before departing,
gathered his clan members,
and distributed his assets to them.
He said:
"If our power remains, our prestige will be universally applied;
if our power perishes, I cannot even preserve myself.
Alas!"
His younger brother Zōng said:
"Cáo Cāo's soldiers and horses are no match;
why are you afraid, sir?"
Shòu said:
"Given Cáo Yánzhōu's clear strategies,
and his holding the Son of Heaven as a resource,
although I defeated Bóguī,
our forces are truly exhausted,
and our lord is arrogant and our generals are .
The defeat and ruin of the army
lies in this campaign.
Yáng Xióng said: 'The Six States were ignorant,
and were weakened by Yíng.'
Is this not what is happening now?"
Cáo Cāo then rescued Liú Yán,
attacked Yán Liáng and beheaded him.
Shào then crossed the river,
encamping south of Yánjīn.
Jǔ Shòu sighed as he approached the boat:
"The superior fills his ambitions,
the inferior strives for achievements;
the vast Yellow River,
shall I cross it?"
Then he retreated due to illness.
Shào did not permit it and resented him for it,
reassessing his command,
and assigning it to Guō Tú.
Shào sent Liú Bèi and Wén Chǒu to challenge,
but Cáo Cāo again defeated them,
beheading Wén Chǒu.
In two battles, two generals were captured,
shaking Shào's army greatly.
Cāo returned to station his troops at Guāndù,
while Shào advanced to secure Yángwǔ.
Jǔ Shòu again advised Shào, saying:
"The northern army, though numerous,
is not as robust and resolute as the southern army;
the southern army has less grain,
and its supplies are not as good as the north's.
The south benefits from a swift battle,
the north profits from a prolonged campaign.
It is advisable to proceed slowly and endure,
prolonging it for months and days."
Shào did not follow.
The continuous camps gradually moved forward,
increasingly pressing upon Guāndù,
then joined battle.
Cāo's army was at a disadvantage,
and returned to strengthen its fortifications.
Shào erected high watchtowers,
built earthen mounds,
and shot into the camp.
All [the soldiers in the camp] moved under shields.
Cāo then deployed stone-throwing chariots to attack Shào's towers,
all of which were destroyed.
The army called them
"Thunderbolt Chariots".
Shào built tunnels to ambush Cāo,
but Cāo always built long defenses inside to resist them.
He also sent elite troops to raid Shào's supply wagons,
heavily defeating them,
and burning all their grain and provisions.
After a standoff of over a hundred days,
the people of Hénán were exhausted,
and many defected to Shào.
Shào sent Chúnyú Qióng and others with over ten thousand troops to the north to welcome grain supplies.
Jǔ Shòu advised Shào that Jiǎng Qí could be sent to form a separate supporting army on the flank,
to cut off Cáo Cāo's raids.
Shào did not follow.
Xǔ Yōu stepped forward and said:
"Cáo Cāo's troops are few and he has committed all his forces to resist us.
The remaining defenses in Xǔ are surely empty and weak.
If we dispatch light troops,
moving swiftly to launch a surprise attack,
if Xǔ is captured, Cāo will be captured.
If he has not yet collapsed,
we can make him run back and forth,
and defeat him for sure."
Shào again could not use this advice.
It so happened that Yōu's family committed a crime,
and Shěn Pèi arrested and imprisoned them.
Yōu, feeling frustrated,
then defected to Cáo Cāo,
and advised him to launch a surprise attack on Chúnyú Qióng and others.
Qióng and others were at that time camped at Wūcháo,
forty *lǐ* from Shào's army.
Cāo personally led five thousand infantry and cavalry,
attacking and defeating Qióng and others that night,
beheading all of them.
Initially,
when Shào heard that Cāo was attacking Qióng,
he said to his eldest son, Tán:
"Even if Cāo defeats Qióng,
I will capture his camp,
and he will have nowhere to return to."
So he sent Gāo Lǎn and Zhāng Hé and others to attack Cāo's camp,
but they could not capture it.
The two generals, hearing that Qióng and others were defeated,
then defected to Cāo.
Thereupon, Shào's army was alarmed and disturbed,
and utterly collapsed.
Shào, with Tán and others, with headbands and on horseback,
crossed the river with eight hundred cavalry,
reaching the north bank of Líyáng,
entering the camp of his general Jiǎng Yìqú.
Upon reaching the tent,
he grasped his hand and said:
"I entrust my life to you."
Yìqú moved away from his tent to make space for him.
He issued orders.
When the crowd heard Shào was there,
they gradually reassembled.
The remaining troops feigned surrender,
but Cáo Cāo buried all of them alive,
killing eighty thousand people in total.
Jǔ Shòu was captured by Cāo's army,
and then cried out:
"Shòu will not surrender!
I was captured!"
Cāo saw Shòu and said:
"Our fates were different,
thus we were separated,
I never thought we would meet today!"
Shòu replied:
"Jìzhōu made a mistake,
bringing about its own defeat.
Shòu's strength and wisdom are both exhausted,
it is fitting that I am captured."
Cāo said:
"Běncū was without strategy,
and did not employ your plans.
Now chaos has long persisted,
the state is not yet settled,
and I am just about to plan with you."
Shòu said:
"My uncle, mother, and brother's lives hang on the Yuán clan.
If I receive your mercy,
a quick death would be a blessing."
Cāo sighed and said:
"If I had gained you earlier,
the world would not be a concern."
Then he pardoned him and treated him generously.
Shòu soon plotted to return to the Yuán clan,
so he was executed.
Yuán Shào was outwardly generous, elegant, and possessed a sense of decorum.
His joys and sorrows were not expressed on his face,
but his nature was proud, stubborn, and self-important.
He was poor at adopting good advice,
hence he came to ruin.
When the army returned,
someone said to Tián Fēng:
"You will certainly be highly regarded."
Tián Fēng said:
"His Lordship is outwardly generous but inwardly jealous.
He did not appreciate my loyalty,
and I repeatedly opposed him with frank words.
If he had won and was happy,
he surely would have forgiven me.
But since we lost and he feels resentment,
his inner jealousy will manifest.
If the army had been successful in its expedition,
I would have been spared.
Now that we have been defeated,
I do not expect to live."
When Yuán Shào returned,
he said:
"I did not follow Tián Fēng's advice,
and indeed I have become a laughingstock."
He then killed him.
In the defeat at Guāndù,
Shěn Pèi's two sons were captured by Cáo Cāo.
Méng Dài had a rift with Shěn Pèi,
and through Jiǎng Qí, he spoke to Yuán Shào, saying:
"Shěn Pèi wields sole authority in his position,
his clan is large and his troops are strong.
Moreover, his two sons are in the south,
so he must harbor rebellious intentions."
Guō Tú and Xīn Píng also concurred.
Yuán Shào then appointed Méng Dài as Inspector of the Army
to replace Shěn Pèi in guarding Yè.
Commander of the Guards Féng Jì was not on good terms with Shěn Pèi.
When Yuán Shào questioned him about it,
Féng Jì replied:
"Shěn Pèi is by nature strong and upright.
In all his words and actions,
he emulates the integrity of ancient people.
He would not consider his two sons being in the south as a reason for disloyalty.
Your Lordship should not doubt him."
Yuán Shào said:
"Do you not bear him ill will?"
Féng Jì said:
"What we previously contended over was personal sentiment;
what I am now presenting is a matter of state."
Yuán Shào said,
"Excellent."
He then did not dismiss Shěn Pèi,
and Shěn Pèi and Féng Jì subsequently became more amicable.
Many cities and towns in Jìzhōu revolted,
and Yuán Shào again attacked and pacified them.
After the defeat of his army, he fell ill.
In the summer of the seventh year,
he passed away.
Before a successor could be established,
Féng Jì and Shěn Pèi had long been criticized by Yuán Tán for their extravagance and arrogance.
Xīn Píng and Guō Tú were both close to Yuán Tán and had a rift with Shěn Pèi and Féng Jì.
The multitude, seeing Yuán Tán as the eldest,
wished to enthrone him.
Shěn Pèi and others feared that if Yuán Tán were enthroned, Xīn Píng and others would cause harm.
Therefore, they forged Yuán Shào's dying command
and enthroned Yuán Shàng as the successor.
Biography of Yuán Shào and Liú Biǎo, Volume 64, Part 2 (Yuán Shào's son, Yuán Tán)
Yuán Tán proclaimed himself General of Agile Cavalry
and led his army out to Líyáng.
Yuán Shàng gave him few soldiers,
and sent Féng Jì to accompany him.
Yuán Tán requested more troops,
but Shěn Pèi and others again deliberated and decided not to grant them.
Yuán Tán was enraged
and killed Féng Jì.
Cáo Cāo crossed the river and attacked Yuán Tán.
Yuán Tán reported the urgency to Yuán Shàng.
Yuán Shàng then left Shěn Pèi to guard Yè
and personally led forces to assist Yuán Tán,
confronting Cáo Cāo at Líyáng.
From the ninth month to the second month of the following year,
a great battle was fought beneath the city walls.
Yuán Tán and Yuán Shàng were defeated and retreated.
Cáo Cāo was about to besiege them,
but they fled back to Yè by night.
Cáo Cāo advanced,
but Yuán Shàng launched a counter-attack and defeated Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo's army returned to Xǔ.
Yuán Tán said to Yuán Shàng:
"My armor was not good,
which is why I was previously defeated by Cáo Cāo.
Now Cáo Cāo's army has retreated,
and his men yearn to return home.
Before they have crossed the river,
if we send out troops to ambush them,
we can cause a great rout.
This strategy must not be missed."
Yuán Shàng was suspicious and did not agree.
He neither increased the troops
nor replaced the armor.
Yuán Tán was greatly enraged.
Guō Tú and Xīn Píng then said to Yuán Tán:
"That the late lord placed you, the general, as the younger brother,
was all engineered by Shěn Pèi."
Yuán Tán assented to this.
He then led his troops to attack Yuán Shàng,
fighting at the outer gate.
Yuán Tán was defeated
and led his troops back to Nánpí.
Wáng Xiū, the Assistant Administrator, led officials and common people from Qīngzhōu to rescue Yuán Tán.
When Yuán Tán returned and wanted to attack Yuán Shàng again,
he asked Wáng Xiū:
"What strategy should I adopt?"
Wáng Xiū said:
"Brothers
are like the left and right hands.
It's like a person about to fight who cuts off their right hand
and says, 'I will surely defeat you.'
Is such a thing acceptable?
If brothers do not love each other,
then who in the world will love them?
There are slanderers sowing discord between them,
seeking temporary advantage.
I beg you to plug your ears and not listen to them.
If you execute a few sycophants
and restore mutual affection,
so as to resist the four directions,
you can move unhindered throughout the world."
Yuán Tán did not follow this advice.
Yuán Shàng again personally led an attack on Yuán Tán.
Yuán Tán was heavily defeated
and entrenched himself within the city, defending it steadfastly.
Yuán Shàng's siege was urgent.
Yuán Tán fled to Píngyuán,
and dispatched Xīn Pí of Yǐngchuān to Cáo Cāo to request aid.
Liú Biǎo sent a letter admonishing Yuán Tán, saying: "Heaven sends down calamities;
disasters flow abundantly.
Initially, we allied with different clans,
eventually forming a common alliance.
This caused the royal house to tremble
and the moral order to collapse.
Therefore, discerning
scholars
all feel profound pain,
grieving that people cannot bear with one another in these times.
Nevertheless, I and the Grand Duke [Yuán Shào]
shared the same aspiration and goal.
Although Chǔ and Wèi are far apart,
and mountains and rivers separate us,
we exerted our efforts and put our hearts into it,
together assisting the royal house,
so that no alien clans would interfere with our alliance,
and different kinds would not break our good relations.
This is what I and the Grand Duke
achieved with unwavering resolve.
Our great work was not yet finished when
the Grand Duke passed away.
His worthy heir inherited the succession
to continue the grand enterprise.
He proclaimed the virtues of his successive generations
and took up the greatly manifest
throne,
crushing the formidable enemy at Yè Dū
and displaying magnificent achievements in the northern lands.
He secured his territory
and glared like a tiger beyond the river.
All our allies
eagerly attached themselves to him.
How
is it that green flies now buzz around the banner,
and sycophants roam within the two camps,
causing limbs and bones to divide into two bodies,
and chest and back to sever into separate entities?
When I first heard this news,
I
thought it was not true.
When I heard the confirmed news,
I then knew that the wrath of Èbó and Shíshěn had already formed,
and the plan to turn kin into foes had been decided.
Banners and pennants clash in the Central Plains,
and corpses pile up beneath the city walls.
Hearing this, I choke with sobs,
feeling as if I exist and yet do not exist.
In the past, from the Three Sovereigns and Five Hegemons
down to the Warring States period,
ministers murdered their lords,
fathers killed their sons,
brothers massacred each other,
and relatives exterminated one another—
these things indeed happened at times.
However, some wished to establish a royal enterprise,
others wished to achieve hegemonic accomplishments.
These were all what is called 'taking by force
and holding by righteousness,'
seeking wealth and power for a generation.
There has never been anyone who estranged
his kin, severing his very roots,
and was able to endure for a long time."
The resentment of Yóu in Qí,
was not as great as the indignation of Tàigōng in Cáo;
the minister Chéngyè of Xuānzǐ,
was not as great as a Rénjūn succeeding to the succession.
Furthermore, a gentleman
avoids misfortune and does not go to an enemy state,
and when relations are broken, he does not utter harsh words.
How much more so to forget the hatred of one's ancestors,
abandon the affection of relatives,
and become a warning for ten thousand generations,
leaving behind a disgrace for allies!
Even the southern barbarians, eastern Yi, western Rong, and northern Di will have words of reproach,
how much more so our own kind,
who would not feel heartbroken!
Going [there],
without the integrity of humility and obedience,
a Rénjūn should humble his ambition and disgrace his person,
making it his duty to accomplish the matter.
After the matter is settled,
let the world judge its right and wrong,
would this not
also be a noble act?
Now, the Rénjūn is hated by the Fūrén,
not as much as Zhèng Zhuāng was by Jiāngshì;
the suspicion among brothers,
not as much as Chónghuá was by Xiàng’áo.
Yet Duke Zhuāng eventually enjoyed the pleasure of the great tunnel,
and Xiàng’áo ultimately received the enfeoffment of Yǒubí.
I wish you would cast aside all illnesses,
recall the old righteousness,
and once again be mother and son, brothers, as
at first.
Now, having marshalled the soldiers and horses,
they stand gazing expectantly.
Cáo Cāo then returned to relieve Tán,
arriving at Líyáng in the tenth month.
Shàng heard that Cāo had crossed the river,
so he released Píngyuán and returned to Yè.
Shàng's generals Lǚ Kuàng and Gāo Xiáng rebelled and surrendered to the Cáo clan,
and Tán secretly engraved a general's seal again,
to falsely present to Kuàng and Xiáng.
Cāo knew Tán's deception,
so he had his son Zhěng marry Tán's daughter to appease him,
and withdrew his army.
In the third month of the ninth year,
Shàng ordered Shěn Pèi to guard Yè,
and again attacked Tán at Píngyuán.
Pèi presented a letter to Tán, saying:
“Pèi has heard that good medicine tastes bitter but is beneficial for illness,
and loyal words grate on the ear but are convenient for action.
May the Jiāngjūn temper his heart and suppress his anger,
and eventually reflect on my foolish words.
Indeed, according to the righteousness of the Chūnqiū,
the ruler of a state dies for the altars of soil and grain,
and a loyal minister dies for his lord's command.
If one plots to endanger the ancestral temple,
and disrupt the state,
then relatives and strangers are treated the same.
Thus, Zhōugōng shed tears to conceal the executions of Guǎn and Cài,
and Jì Yǒu sobbed while carrying out the execution of Shúyá.
Why?
Because righteousness is weighty and human life is light,
and the matter could not be helped.
Formerly, the late Lord deposed the Jiāngjūn to continue the line of your virtuous elder brother,
and established our Jiāngjūn as the legitimate heir.
This was announced to the Zǔlíng above,
and recorded in the genealogical registers below.
Throughout the land, far and near,
who does not fully know this!
How could the villainous minister Guō Tú,
wantonly draw legs on a snake,
speak crooked words and flatter,
and cause discord among noble relatives?
It has even caused the Jiāngjūn to forget the benevolence of filial piety and brotherly love,
following the footsteps of È and Shěn,
letting loose soldiers to plunder and raid,
massacring cities and killing officials.
The wronged souls suffer in the underworld,
and the wounded are covered in grass and thorns.
Furthermore, you plotted to seize Yè Chéng,
promising rewards to the Qín Hú,
their wealth, goods, and women,
already having been allotted.
You also said: 'Although I have an aged mother,
just ensure her body remains intact.'
Those who heard these words,
all lamented in their hearts and shed tears,
causing the Tàifūrén to be distressed, sorrowful, and indignant,
and the lord and ministers of our province to be restless in sleep and sigh with sorrow.
If we sincerely remained silent and listened to your plans,
then we would fear violating the Chūnqiū's principle of dying for one's command,
bringing unpredictable calamity upon the Tàifūrén,
and harming the unparalleled legacy of the late Lord.
Our Jiāngjūn could not decline the command,
leading to the battle of Guǎntáo.
I humbly believe the Jiāngjūn's utmost filial piety was manifest,
evident from his youth,
and his brotherly affection,
was born of nature.
It was distinguished by his intelligence,
and practiced with quick understanding.
He examined the actions of past and present,
observed the signs of rise and fall,
held glorious wealth as lightly as dung and soil,
and valued reputation and position as highly as hills and mountains.
How could he suddenly become lost and fall,
abandoning the conduct of a sage and worthy,
accumulating resentment and indulging in anger,
bringing about the disaster of a ruined family!
We crane our necks in anticipation,
awaiting enemies,
abandoning our benevolent mother to the teeth of tigers and wolves,
to satisfy a momentary ambition,
is this not tragic!
If Heaven should enlighten your noble heart,
change your plans and thoughts,
then our Jiāngjūn would prostrate himself, weeping bitterly, before your lap,
and Pèi and others would also personally lay down their bodies to receive the punishment of axe and chisel.
If you still do not repent,
disaster will surely befall you.
I hope you will carefully consider what is auspicious and what is inauspicious,
and grant us a choice between going and staying.”
Tán did not accept it.
Cáo Cāo consequently advanced to attack Yè,
Shěn Pèi's general Féng Lǐ acted as an inside collaborator,
opening a sally port to let in over three hundred Cāo soldiers.
Pèi discovered it,
and from the city wall, he struck the gate with large stones,
closing the gate.
All who had entered died.
Cāo then dug a trench around the city,
forty *lǐ* in circumference.
At first, he made it shallow,
making it appear as if it could be crossed.
Pèi saw it from a distance,
laughed, and did not go out to contend for advantage.
Cāo deepened it overnight,
to a width and depth of two *zhàng*,
diverting the Zhāng Shuǐ to flood it.
From the fifth month to the eighth month,
more than half of the people in the city died of starvation.
Shàng heard that Yè was in urgent straits,
and with over ten thousand generals and men, he returned to relieve the city.
Cāo attacked and defeated them.
Shàng fled and set up camp along Qǔzhāng,
Cāo again surrounded him.
Before the encirclement was complete,
Shàng was afraid,
and sent Yīn Kuí and Chén Lín to seek surrender.
[Cáo Cāo] did not listen.
Shàng fled back to Lánkǒu,
Cāo advanced again,
and quickly besieged him.
Shàng's general Mǎ Yán and others surrendered on the battlefield,
and the army was greatly routed.
Shàng fled to Zhōngshān.
[Cáo Cāo] collected all their baggage and supplies,
obtaining Shàng's seals, ribbons, credentials, battle-axes, and clothing.
He displayed these to those in the city,
and the morale in the city collapsed.
Shěn Pèi commanded his soldiers, saying:
"Hold firm and fight to the death!
Cáo Jūn is exhausted.
Yōuzhōu is about to arrive,
why worry about having no lord!"
Cāo went out to inspect the siege,
and Pèi ambushed him with crossbows, shooting at him.
He almost hit him.
[Shěn Pèi] appointed his elder brother's son, Róng, as the Commandant of the East Gate.
Róng opened the gate at night to let in Cāo Bīng,
and Pèi resisted the fight within the city.
[They] captured Pèi alive.
Cāo said to Pèi:
"When I recently inspected the siege,
why were there so many crossbows?"
Pèi replied:
"I only regret that there were too few."
Cāo said:
"You are loyal to the Yuán clan,
and thus could not have done otherwise."
He intended to spare him.
Pèi's spirit was heroic and unyielding,
and he never softened his words.
All who saw him sighed in admiration,
so he was executed.
[Cáo Cāo] spared Shàng's mother, wife, and children,
and returned their treasures.
Gāo Gàn surrendered with Bìngzhōu,
and was reinstated as Cìshǐ.
When Cáo Cāo besieged Yè,
Tán again turned against him,
and consequently seized Gānlíng, Ānpíng, Bóhǎi, and Héjiān.
He attacked Shàng at Zhōngshān.
Shàng was defeated,
and fled to Gù’ān to join Xī.
Tán collected all his forces,
and returned to garrison Lóngcòu.
In the twelfth month,
Cáo Cāo attacked Tán,
encamping before his gate.
Tán fled during the night
and camped by the Qīnghé River.
In the first month of the following year,
Cáo Cāo fiercely attacked him.
Tán wanted to sally forth and fight,
but his army was routed before it could even assemble.
Tán, with dishevelled hair, galloped wildly,
and the pursuers, judging him to be no ordinary man,
rushed to capture him.
Tán fell from his horse,
and looking back, said:
"Hey!
You who pass me,
I can make you rich and noble."
Before he could finish speaking,
his head had already fallen to the ground.
Thereupon, Guō Tú and others were executed,
and their wives and children slaughtered.
Xī and Shàng were attacked by their generals Jiāo Chù and Zhāng Nán,
and fled to the Wūhuán of Liáoxī.
Chù declared himself Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ,
and led the grand administrators and prefects of various commanderies to turn their backs on Yuán and align with Cáo,
deploying several tens of thousands of troops.
They slaughtered a white horse for an oath,
and issued an order saying:
"Those who disobey shall be executed!"
None of the multitude dared to look up,
and each in turn drank the blood.
When it came to Hán Héng, the Biejia of Dàijùn,
he said:
"I have received great kindness from Yuán Gōng, father and son.
Now that they are broken and ruined,
my wisdom cannot save them,
and my courage cannot die for them.
This is a deficiency in righteousness.
As for facing north and serving the Cáo
that is something I cannot do!"
Everyone present turned pale for Héng.
Chù said:
"Indeed, in undertaking a great endeavor,
one must establish great righteousness.
Whether the affair succeeds or fails
does not depend on one person.
Héng's resolve can be fulfilled,
to encourage loyalty to one's lord."
Cáo Cāo heard of Héng's integrity,
and greatly esteemed him.
He repeatedly summoned him, but Héng did not come,
and died at home.
Gāo Gàn rebelled again,
arrested the Grand Administrator of Shàngdǎng,
and raised an army to defend Húkǒuguān Pass.
In the eleventh year,
Cáo Cāo personally campaigned against Gàn.
Gàn then left his general to guard the city,
and personally went to the Xiōngnú to seek aid.
Failing to obtain it,
he fled alone with a few horsemen,
intending to flee south to Jīngzhōu.
The Dūwèi of Shàngluò captured and executed him.
In the twelfth year,
Cáo Cāo campaigned in Liáoxī,
and attacked the Wūhuán.
Shàng and Xī, along with the Wūhuán, confronted Cáo's army,
were defeated and fled.
They then, with several thousand personal guards, fled to Gōngsūn Kāng in Liáodōng.
Shàng, possessing courage and strength, had previously plotted with Xī, saying:
"Now that we have reached Liáodōng,
Kāng will surely meet us.
I will personally strike him for you, my elder brother,
and moreover seize his commandery.
We can still expand our territory."
Kāng also secretly intended to capture Shàng to gain merit.
So he first placed elite warriors in the stable,
and then invited Shàng and Xī.
Xī was suspicious and did not want to enter,
but Shàng urged him forcefully,
so they entered together.
Before they could sit down,
Kāng shouted to his hidden troops to seize them,
and made them sit on the frozen ground.
Shàng said to Kāng:
"Before death,
the cold is unbearable.
Could we share a mat?"
Kāng said:
"Your head will soon travel ten thousand *lǐ*;
what need is there for a mat!"
Thereupon, he beheaded them and sent their heads away.
Kāng,
was a native of Liáodōng.
His father was Dù.
He initially avoided official service and became a minor official in Xuántù,
gradually rising through the ranks.
In the first year of Chūpíng,
he returned to become the administrator of his home commandery.
While in office, he dared to kill and punish,
executing and exterminating over a hundred prominent local families with whom he had old grudges.
He then attacked Gāogōulí to the east,
and the Wūhuán to the west,
establishing his might along the coast.
At that time, the imperial court was in chaos,
and Dù, relying on his distant location,
secretly harbored ambitions.
Coincidentally, in Xiāngpíng, a large stone over ten feet tall appeared spontaneously,
with three small stones at its base serving as feet.
Dù considered this an auspicious omen for himself.
In the first year of Chūpíng,
he then divided Liáodōng into Liáoxī and Zhōngliáo commanderies,
establishing grand administrators for both.
He crossed the sea to take control of various counties in Dōnglái,
became Yíngzhōu Cìshǐ,
declared himself Marquis of Liáodōng and Pastor of Píngzhōu,
and posthumously enfeoffed his father Yán as Marquis of Jiànyì.
He erected temples to the two founding emperors of Hàn.
Acting on his own authority, he set up altars at the south of Xiāngpíng city,
performed suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
cultivated imperial fields, drilled troops,
and rode in a carriage adorned with phoenixes, nine pennants, yak-tail streamers, and feather plumes.
In the ninth year of Jiàn'ān,
Sīkōng Cáo Cāo memorialized to appoint him as Fènwēi Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Yǒngníng Xiāng.
When Dù died,
Kāng succeeded him,
and thus continued to hold the territory of Liáo.
Liú Biǎo, courtesy name Jǐngshēng,
was a native of Gāopíng, Shānyáng,
and a descendant of Rǔ Gōng Wáng.
He was over eight feet tall,
with a gentle and imposing appearance.
Together with Zhāng Jiǎn and others from his commandery, he was criticized and denounced,
and they were known as
"The Eight Guides."
An imperial edict ordered the arrest of the Party Members,
but Biǎo fled and escaped.
When the Party Prohibitions were lifted,
he was appointed as an aide to Dàjiāngjūn Hé Jìn.
In the first year of Chūpíng,
Sūn Jiān, Grand Administrator of Chángshā, killed Wáng Ruì, the Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
An imperial edict appointed Biǎo as Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
At that time, bandit groups from noble families in Jiāngnán were rampant,
and Yuán Shù also blocked the way with his troops, encamped at Lǔyáng.
Biǎo was unable to reach his post.
So he entered Yíchéng alone on horseback,
and invited Kuǎi Yuè from Nánjùn and Cài Mào from Xiāngyáng to plan with him.
Biǎo said to Yuè:
"Though the noble bandits are strong, the populace does not adhere to them.
If Yuán Shù takes advantage of this,
disaster will surely come.
I wish to raise an army,
but I fear it cannot be assembled.
What strategy do you propose?"
He replied:
"Those who govern in peace prioritize benevolence and righteousness;
those who govern in chaos prioritize power and stratagem.
Troops are not about quantity,
but about securing the right people.
Yuán Shù is arrogant and lacks strategy,
and the noble bandits are mostly greedy and tyrannical.
I have some whom I have nurtured.
If we send people to show them benefits,
they will surely come with their followers.
If you punish the lawless,
and employ their talents,
your prestige and virtue will be established,
and people will come carrying their infants on their backs.
With an assembled army and popular support,
holding Jiānglíng in the south
and defending Xiāngyáng in the north,
the eight commanderies of Jīngzhōu
can be settled by merely issuing a proclamation.
Even if Gōnglù arrives,
he will be able to do nothing."
Biǎo said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he had Yuè dispatch people to entice the leaders of the noble bandits.
Fifteen men came,
all of whom he executed and seized their followers.
Only Zhāng Hǔ and Chén Zuò, bandits from Jiāngxià, held troops and occupied Xiāngyáng city.
Biǎo sent Yuè and Páng Jì to persuade them,
and they surrendered.
Jiāngnán was entirely pacified.
Upon hearing of Biǎo's prestige, many of the grand administrators and prefects
relinquished their seals and left.
Biǎo then organized his forces in Xiāngyáng,
observing the changing times.
Yuán Shù and his older cousin Shào had a rift.
Shào, moreover, had allied with Biǎo,
so Shù, together with Sūn Jiān, formed an alliance and attacked Biǎo.
Biǎo was defeated,
and Jiān then besieged Xiāngyáng.
At that time, Biǎo’s general Huáng Zǔ arrived with reinforcements.
Jiān was struck and killed by a stray arrow,
and the rest of his troops retreated.
When Lǐ Quē and others entered Cháng'ān,
in winter,
Biǎo sent an envoy to offer tribute.
Quē appointed Biǎo as General Who Guards the South and Governor of Jīngzhōu,
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Chéngwǔ,
granted him insignia of authority,
taking him as his supporter.
In the first year of Jiàn'ān,
General of Agile Cavalry Zhāng Jì fled from Guānzhōng to Nányáng,
and consequently attacked Rángchéng,
where he was struck by a flying arrow and died.
All of Jīngzhōu’s officials and subordinates offered congratulations.
Biǎo said:
“Jì came in desperation,
and the host was impolite,
leading to a confrontation.
This was not the intention of this governor.
This governor accepts condolences, not congratulations.”
He sent someone to gather their troops,
and the troops, hearing this, were pleased,
and subsequently all submitted.
In the third year,
Zhāng Xiàn, the Administrator of Chángshā, led the three commanderies of Línglíng and Guìyáng in rebellion against Biǎo.
Biǎo dispatched troops to attack and besiege them,
defeated Xiàn,
and pacified the region.
Thus, his territory expanded,
bordering the Five Ridges to the south,
and occupying the Hàn River region to the north,
with an area of several thousand *lǐ*,
and over a hundred thousand armored soldiers.
Initially,
the people of Jīngzhōu were inclined to disorder,
and furthermore, the four directions were shaken and disturbed,
with bandits inciting each other,
causing turmoil everywhere.
Biǎo’s methods of recruitment and inducement were effective,
his awe and compassion were both well-received,
and even cunning veteran bandits began to serve him.
The region was pacified for thousands of *lǐ*,
and everyone, great and small, was pleased and submitted to him.
Scholars from Guānxī, Yǎn, and Yù who came to him numbered perhaps a thousand.
Biǎo comforted and provided for them,
and they all found full support.
He then established schools,
extensively seeking out Confucian scholars.
Qímǔ Kǎi, Sòng Zhōng, and others
compiled and established the *zhāngjù* commentaries for the Five Classics,
which were later known as the “Later Definitive Version.”
He loved his people and nurtured his scholars,
calmly maintaining his own security.
When Cáo Cāo and Yuán Shào were in a stalemate at Guāndù,
Shào sent someone to request assistance.
Biǎo promised it,
but did not go,
nor did he aid Cáo Cāo,
instead wishing to observe the changes in the world.
Hán Sōng of Nányáng, an Acting Colonel,
and Liú Xiān, a Provisional Aide, persuaded Biǎo,
saying:
“Now, heroes are contending,
and two powerful figures are locked in a struggle.
The weight of the Son of Heaven rests with the General.
If you wish to achieve something,
you can rise and take advantage of their exhaustion;
if not,
you should certainly choose whom to follow.
How can you, with a hundred thousand armored soldiers,
merely sit and watch their success or failure,
unable to aid those who seek assistance,
and unwilling to submit to the worthy?
These two resentments will surely converge on the General,
and I fear you will not be able to remain neutral.
Cáo Cāo is skilled in warfare,
and many worthy and talented individuals have submitted to him.
His power will surely overcome Yuán Shào,
and then he will move his troops towards Jiānghàn.
I fear the General will not be able to resist.
The best plan now
is to offer Jīngzhōu to Cáo Cāo.
Cāo will surely greatly respect the General,
and you will long enjoy good fortune,
passing it down to your descendants.
This is a perfectly safe strategy.”
Kuǎi Yuè also advised him similarly.
Biǎo hesitated and could not make a decision,
so he sent Sōng to see Cāo,
to observe the true situation.
He said to Sōng:
“Today, the world’s fate is still uncertain,
and Cáo Cāo holds the Son of Heaven in Xǔ.
You observe his weaknesses for me.”
Sōng replied:
“I observe Cáo Gōng’s brilliance,
and he will surely achieve his ambitions in the world.
If the General wishes to submit to him,
sending me is acceptable;
but if you still hesitate,
when I arrive at the capital,
the Son of Heaven may grant me an office.
If I cannot decline the appointment,
then I will become a minister of the Son of Heaven,
and merely a former subordinate of the General.
I will serve my new lord as a lord,
and no longer die for the General.
Please give this serious thought.”
Biǎo thought he was reluctant to go,
and forced him.
Upon reaching Xǔ,
Sōng was indeed appointed Palace Attendant and Administrator of Línglíng.
When he returned,
he highly praised the court and Cáo Cāo’s virtues,
and advised Biǎo to send his son to serve at court.
Biǎo was greatly angered,
believing he harbored disloyal intentions,
deployed soldiers, insulted Sōng,
