and was about to execute him.
Sōng showed no change in expression,
and calmly recounted his words before departing.
Biǎo’s wife, Lady Cài, knowing Sōng’s wisdom,
advised him to stop.
Biǎo was still angry,
so he interrogated and killed those who had accompanied Sōng.
Realizing there was no other intent,
he merely imprisoned Sōng.
In the sixth year,
Liú Bèi fled from Yuán Shào to Jīngzhōu.
Biǎo treated him generously and formed an alliance but could not employ him.
In the thirteenth year,
Cáo Cāo personally led an expedition against Biǎo.
Before he arrived,
in the eighth month,
Biǎo died of a carbuncle on his back.
He had been in Jīngzhōu for nearly twenty years,
and his family had no surplus savings.
He had two sons: Qí,
and Cóng.
Biǎo initially favored Qí greatly because he resembled him in appearance.
Later, he arranged for Cóng to marry the niece of his second wife, Lady Cài.
Lady Cài then loved Cóng and disliked Qí,
and daily words of slander and praise reached Biǎo.
Biǎo indulged his second wife’s favoritism,
always believing and accepting her words.
Furthermore, his wife’s younger brother Cài Mào and his nephew Zhāng Yǔn both enjoyed Biǎo’s favor,
and were also on good terms with Cóng.
Qí, however, was uneasy.
He once consulted Zhūgě Liàng of Lángyá for advice on how to secure his position.
Liàng initially did not respond.
Later, they ascended a tall building together,
and Qí then had the ladder removed,
saying to Liàng:
“Today, we are not reaching heaven above,
nor touching earth below.
Words spoken from your mouth enter my ear.
Can you speak now?”
Liàng said:
“Have you not seen that Shēn Shēng was endangered while staying within,
while Chóng'ěr was safe while dwelling outside?”
Qí was enlightened by this,
and secretly planned to leave.
At that time, Huáng Zǔ, Biǎo’s general and Administrator of Jiāngxià, was killed by Sūn Quán.
Qí then requested to take up his post.
When Liú Biǎo
became gravely ill, Liú Qí
returned to visit him.
He was known for his filial piety. Liú Yǔn and others feared that if he saw Liú Biǎo, father and son would be moved by emotion,
and there might be an intention to entrust the succession.
So they said to Liú Qí:
“The General ordered you to govern Jiāngxià,
a position of extreme importance.
If you abandon your troops and come now,
you will surely incur his reprimand and anger.
This would hurt your parent’s feelings
and gravely worsen his illness,
which is not the way of filial piety and reverence.”
Thus, they blocked him outside the door,
preventing him from seeing Liú Biǎo.
Liú Qí departed in tears,
and many people heard of it and were saddened.
Consequently, Liú Cóng was made the successor.
Liú Cóng gave the Marquis’s seal to Liú Qí.
Liú Qí was enraged,
threw it to the ground,
and intended to seize the opportunity of the funeral to cause trouble.
Just then, Cáo Cāo’s army arrived at Xīnyě,
and Liú Qí fled south of the river.
Kuǎi Yuè, Hán Sōng, and Fù Xùn, clerk of the Eastern Section, among others, persuaded Liú Cóng to surrender.
Liú Cóng said:
“Now, if we and all of you hold the entire territory of Chǔ
and maintain our late lord’s enterprise,
observing the situation in the world,
what is there that is not permissible?”
Fù Xùn said:
“There is a general principle for rebellion and submission,
and a fixed situation for strength and weakness.
For a subject to resist his sovereign is a rebellious path;
for the newly established Chǔ to resist the Central Plains
is certainly perilous;
for Liú Bèi to contend with Cáo Gōng
is inappropriate.
All three are disadvantages.
To attempt to resist the vanguard of the imperial army
with these
is a path to certain destruction.
General, how do you compare yourself to Liú Bèi?”
Liú Cóng said:
“I am not as good.”
Fù Xùn said:
“If indeed Liú Bèi is insufficient to resist Cáo Gōng,
then even the entirety of Chǔ cannot save itself.
If indeed Liú Bèi is sufficient to resist Cáo Gōng,
then Bèi will not be subservient to the General.
May the General not hesitate.”
When Cáo Cāo’s army arrived at Xiāngyáng,
Liú Cóng offered the entire province in surrender,
and Liú Bèi fled to Xiàkǒu.
Cáo Cāo appointed Liú Cóng as the Inspector of Qīngzhōu
and enfeoffed him as a 列侯 (lièhóu).
Kuǎi Yuè and fifteen others were enfeoffed as marquises.
Cáo Cāo then released Hán Sōng from imprisonment,
and because of Hán Sōng's high reputation,
he treated him with great courtesy,
ordering him to assess the merits and demerits of the people of the province,
all of whom he promoted and employed.
Hán Sōng was appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies,
and treated with the courtesies due to a friend.
Kuǎi Yuè was appointed Minister of the Imperial Household,
and Liú Xiān was appointed Minister of the Imperial Secretariat.
Initially,
when Liú Biǎo formed an alliance with Yuán Shào,
Dèng Yì, an Attendant Official and Aide, remonstrated against it but was not heeded.
Dèng Yì retired due to illness
and did not serve throughout Liú Biǎo’s lifetime.
Cáo Cāo appointed him Attendant Official.
Many others reached high offices.
Later, Cáo Cāo was defeated at Chìbì,
and Liú Bèi nominated Liú Qí as Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
He died the following year.
The commentary states: Yuán Shào initially gained popularity through his chivalrous and heroic conduct,
and subsequently harbored ambitions of hegemony.
Throughout the realm, those who raised armies and banners
all claimed to act in his name.
When it came to confronting the enemy on the battlefield,
brave warriors vied for their lives;
when it came to deep strategy and grand proposals,
wise scholars were devoted to him.
How magnificent
were the resources he commanded!
Hán Fēi said:
“Being obstinately rigid and unharmonious,
stubbornly erring and fond of victory,
making the legitimate son light and the concubine’s son heavy –
these are called signs of downfall.”
Liú Biǎo’s path did not exceed this,
yet he wished to passively seize the mandate of heaven
and emulate the division of the realm into three,
much like a wooden puppet compared to a human.
The eulogy says: Shào had a magnanimous and refined disposition,
and Biǎo was also a worthy gentleman.
They asserted their might north of the Hé River
and strengthened themselves in the southern Xià region.
Their Han war-junks arrayed like fish,
their Jì horses gathered like clouds.
They plotted to seize the imperial throne,
and offered sacrifices to Heaven and Earth.
They claimed the work of Heaven,
and also relied on human wisdom.
Arrogant and strong, yet achieving little,
what hope can there be in idle talk?
They turned to the favored concubine,
their persons decayed and their enterprises lost.
Biographies of Liú Yān, Yuán Shù, and Lǚ Bù, Chapter Sixty-Five
Liú Yān, courtesy name Jūnláng,
was a native of Jìnglín, Jiāngxià,
and a descendant of Prince Gōng of Lǔ.
During Emperor Sùzōng’s reign,
his family moved to Jìnglín.
Liú Yān served in various prefecture and commandery posts in his youth,
and as a member of the imperial clan, he was appointed Court Gentleman.
He resigned from office and resided on Yángchéng Mountain,
diligently studying and teaching.
He was recommended as “贤良方正” (xiánliáng fāngzhèng) (worthy and upright),
and gradually promoted to Administrator of Nányáng, Court Architect, and Grand Master of Ceremonies.
At that time, Emperor Líng’s governance was in decline,
and bandits plagued all directions.
Liú Yān believed that the authority of Inspectors was too weak,
not only making them unable to suppress the unrest,
but also that using unsuitable people
only increased violence and chaos.
Therefore, he proposed replacing Inspectors with Pastors,
to pacify and stabilize the regions,
and to select upright high officials
to fill these positions.
Liú Yān secretly sought to be appointed to Jiāozhǐ,
to avoid the troubles of the time.
Before his proposal could be implemented,
it happened that Xī Jiǎn, the Inspector of Yìzhōu, was causing much trouble in his administration,
and rumors spread far and wide.
Moreover, Zhāng Yì, the Inspector of Bìngzhōu, and Gěng Bǐ, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, were both killed by bandits.
Therefore, Liú Yān’s proposal was adopted.
Liú Yān was sent out as Envoy Supervising the Army,
concurrently serving as Pastor of Yìzhōu;
Huáng Wǎn, the Grand Coachman, was made Pastor of Yùzhōu;
and Liú Yú, the Court Architect, was made Pastor of Yōuzhōu.
All held their positions with their original official ranks.
The importance of provincial appointments
began from this time.
At this time, Mǎ Xiāng, a bandit in Yìzhōu,
also proclaimed himself “Yellow Turban,”
gathering several thousand exhausted laborers.
He first killed the Prefect of Miánzhú,
then advanced to attack Luòxiàn,
killing Xī Jiǎn.
He then attacked Shǔjùn and Jiànwéi.
Within ten days or a month,
he devastated three commanderies.
Mǎ Xiāng declared himself “Son of Heaven,”
and his followers reached over a hundred thousand people.
He dispatched troops to attack Bājùn,
killing the Administrator Zhào Bù.
Jiǎ Lóng, an official of the province,
who had previously led several hundred soldiers in Jiànwéi,
then rallied officials and common people to attack Mǎ Xiāng.
He defeated him,
and Jiǎ Lóng then sent officers and soldiers to welcome Liú Yān.
Upon Liú Yān’s arrival,
he appointed Jiǎ Lóng as Commandant
and moved his residence to Miánzhú.
Jiǎ Lóng
pacified and received those who had defected,
focusing on benevolence and generosity,
but secretly harbored other plans.
Zhāng Lǔ of Pèi,
whose mother was beautiful
and also practiced occult arts,
frequented Liú Yān’s home.
Liú Yān then appointed Zhāng Lǔ as Commandant Supervising Righteousness
and, together with Zhāng Xiū, a Commandant of a Separate Command, led troops to ambush and kill Sū Gù, the Administrator of Hánzhōng.
They cut off Xié Valley
and killed the imperial envoy.
After Zhāng Lǔ gained Hánzhōng,
he then killed Zhāng Xiū and absorbed his followers.
Yān wished to establish a fearsome reputation and aggrandize himself,
so he fabricated other reasons
to kill over ten local powerful and influential figures.
The gentry and common people all resented him.
In the second year of Chūpíng (191 CE),
Rèn Qí, the Administrator of Jiànwéi, and Jiǎ Lóng both rebelled
and attacked Yān.
Yān defeated them
and killed them all.
From this point, his ambition gradually grew,
and he consequently manufactured over a thousand imperial carriages and chariots.
Yān had four sons:
Fàn was Left Central Cavalier,
Dàn was Rectifier of Records,
Zhāng was Chariot-and-Cavalry Commandant,
and they were all with Emperor Xiàn in Cháng'ān.
Only Mào, a Separate Command司馬, remained with Yān in Yìzhōu.
The imperial court sent Zhāng to reason with Yān,
but Yān kept Zhāng and did not send him back.
In the first year of Xīngpíng (194 CE),
General Who Conquers the West Mǎ Téng conspired with Fàn to execute Lǐ Jué.
Yān sent five thousand of his soldiers to assist them.
They were defeated,
and Fàn and Dàn were both killed.
Yān grieved for his two sons,
and then a celestial fire burned his city-fortress, carriages, and chariots,
spreading to the common people's homes.
His residential compound was completely destroyed.
Thereupon, he moved to Chéngdū
and then died of a carbuncle on his back.
The high officials of the province, Zhào Wěi and others, were fond of Zhāng's gentle and benevolent nature,
so they established him as the Inspector.
The imperial edict subsequently appointed Zhāng as Supervising Military Envoy
and Governor of Yìzhōu,
and Wěi as Central Cavalier Who Conquers the East.
Previously, Liú Biǎo, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, had memorialized that Yān was presumptuously imitating imperial carriages, regalia, and ceremonial utensils.
Wěi, because of this, then garrisoned troops in Qú to prepare for Liú Biǎo.
Initially,
tens of thousands of households from Nányáng and Sānfǔ had flowed into Yìzhōu.
Yān gathered them all to form a multitude
named
"Eastern Soldiers" (Dōngzhōubīng).
Zhāng was soft and lenient by nature, lacking military prowess.
The Eastern Soldiers were abusive and tyrannical, causing distress to the people,
and he could not restrain them.
Many of the old gentry were alienated and resentful.
When Zhào Wěi was in Bāzhōng,
he greatly won the hearts of the people.
Zhāng entrusted him with power.
Wěi, seeing that popular sentiment was not united,
secretly allied with the powerful families in the province.
In the fifth year of Jiàn'ān (200 CE),
they returned together to attack Zhāng.
Shǔjùn, Guǎnghàn, and Jiànwéi all responded to their call.
The Eastern Soldiers, fearing extermination,
then united their hearts and strength
and fought desperately for Zhāng.
They consequently defeated the rebels
and advanced to attack Wěi at Jiāngzhōu,
where they executed him.
Zhāng Lǔ, seeing Zhāng's weakness and incompetence,
no longer obeyed him.
Zhāng was angered
and killed Lǔ's mother and younger brother.
He then dispatched his generals Páng Xī and others to attack Lǔ,
but they were repeatedly defeated.
Many of Lǔ's subordinate units were in Bātǔ,
so Xī was appointed Administrator of Bājùn.
Lǔ subsequently seized it
and thus became powerful in Bāhàn.
In the thirteenth year (208 CE),
Cáo Cāo personally led an expedition against Jīngzhōu.
Zhāng then sent an envoy to pay his respects.
Cáo Cāo bestowed upon Zhāng the title of General Who Spreads Awe,
and his elder brother Mào the title of General Who Suppresses Bandits.
Zhāng then sent his Secretary to the Inspector, Zhāng Sōng, to visit Cáo Cāo,
but Cáo Cāo did not receive him with courtesy.
Sōng returned with resentment
and advised Zhāng to sever ties with the Cáo clan
and ally with Liú Bèi.
Zhāng followed this advice.
In the sixteenth year (211 CE),
Zhāng heard that Cáo Cāo was about to dispatch troops to Hànzhōng to attack Zhāng Lǔ.
He harbored internal fears,
and Sōng again persuaded Zhāng to welcome Liú Bèi to resist Cáo Cāo.
Zhāng immediately dispatched Fǎ Zhèng with troops to welcome Liú Bèi.
Zhāng's Chief Clerk from Bāxī, Huáng Quán, advised him, saying:
"Liú Bèi has a reputation for ruthlessness.
If you treat him as a subordinate,
he will not be satisfied.
If you treat him as a guest,
one state cannot accommodate two masters.
This is not a path to security."
Wang Lěi, a Secretary from Guǎnghàn, hung himself upside down at the provincial gate to remonstrate.
Zhāng accepted none of it.
Liú Bèi hastened from Jiānglíng to Fúchéng.
Zhāng led tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry to meet with Liú Bèi.
Zhāng Sōng urged Liú Bèi to ambush Zhāng at the meeting,
but Liú Bèi could not bear to do so.
The following year,
Liú Bèi garrisoned his troops at Jiāmén.
Sōng's elder brother, Zhāng Sù, the Administrator of Guǎnghàn, feared that disaster would befall him,
so he reported Sōng's scheme to Zhāng.
Sōng was arrested and executed,
and orders were given to the various passes and garrisons not to allow further passage.
Liú Bèi was greatly angered
and turned his troops back to attack Zhāng,
winning battles everywhere.
In the nineteenth year (214 CE),
he advanced to besiege Chéngdū.
For several tens of days,
the city had thirty thousand elite soldiers
and enough grain for a year,
and the officials and people all wished to resist the fight.
Zhāng said:
"My father and I have been in this province for over twenty years,
without bestowing kindness or virtue upon the common people.
And for three years of warfare,
those whose flesh and fat lie in the wild fields
did so because of me.
How can I bear to be at peace!"
Thereupon, he opened the city gates and surrendered.
None of his subordinates failed to weep.
Liú Bèi relocated Zhāng to Gōng'ān,
returned his treasures,
and he later died of illness.
The following year,
Cáo Cāo defeated Zhāng Lǔ
and pacified Hànzhōng.
Lǔ's courtesy name was Gōngqí.
Initially,
his grandfather Líng,
during Emperor Shùn's reign, sojourned in Shǔ,
studying the Way in the Crane-Call Mountains.
He created talismans and writings
to delude the common people.
Those who received his Way would each offer five dǒu of rice,
hence he was called
"Rice Thief" (Mǐzéi).
Líng passed it to his son Héng,
Héng passed it to Lǔ,
and Lǔ then proclaimed himself
"Master-Lord" (Shī Jūn).
Those who came to learn from him
were initially called
"Ghost Soldiers" (Guǐzú),
and later known as
"Libationers" (Jìjiǔ).
Each Libationer led a multitude.
Those with a large multitude were called
"Head of Reason" (Lǐtóu).
All were judged by sincerity and trustworthiness,
and deception was not permitted.
If one was ill, one only needed to confess one's faults.
All the Libationers erected righteous lodges along the roads,
similar to post stations,
and provided rice and meat for travelers.
Eaters would take only what their stomachs required.
If they took too much, the ghosts would sicken them.
Those who violated the law were first granted three pardons,
and then punished.
No chief officials were appointed;
the Libationers served as rulers,
and both the Han and non-Han people trusted and followed them.
The imperial court could not suppress them,
so they eventually appointed Lǔ as Central Cavalier Who Suppresses Barbarians
and Administrator of Hànníng,
allowing him to present tributes.
During the chaos of Hán Suì and Mǎ Chāo,
tens of thousands of households from Guānxī fled to Lǔ.
At that time, someone found a jade seal in the ground,
and Lǔ's subordinates wished to honor Lǔ as King of Hànníng.
Lǔ's Chief Clerk, Yán Pǔ, advised him, saying:
"The people of Hánchuān number over a hundred thousand households,
with dangerous and fortified terrain on all four sides,
and abundant wealth and fertile land.
If you support the Son of Heaven,
you will be like Huán and Wén.
Next, you could be like Dòu Róng,
and not lose wealth and nobility.
Now, you are administering and appointing officials under imperial authority,
and your power is sufficient to make decisive judgments.
Hasty declaration of a royal title
will certainly be the precursor to disaster."
Lǔ followed this advice.
Zhāng Lǔ had been in Hánchuān for nearly thirty years.
When he heard that Cáo Cāo was campaigning against him,
and had reached Yángpíng,
he wanted to surrender Hànzhōng.
His younger brother, Zhāng Wèi, disagreed,
and led tens of thousands of troops
to resist at the pass and hold it firmly.
Cáo Cāo defeated Zhāng Wèi
and executed him.
Zhāng Lǔ heard that Yángpíng had fallen,
and was about to prostrate himself in surrender.
Yán Pǔ advised him, saying:
"If you go now in this urgent situation,
your merit will be light.
It's better to temporarily rely on Bāzhōng,
and then offer your allegiance;
your merit will surely be greater."
So he fled to Nánshān.
His attendants wanted to burn all his treasures and warehouses.
Zhāng Lǔ said:
"My original intention was to submit to the state;
that intention has not yet been realized.
My fleeing today
is to avoid the sharp edge of the attack,
not out of ill will."
So he sealed up his stores and left.
Cáo Cāo entered Nánzhèng
and greatly commended him.
Also, because Zhāng Lǔ had initially shown good intentions,
he sent someone to comfort and reassure him.
Zhāng Lǔ immediately went out with his family to meet him,
was appointed General who Guards the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn),
enfeoffed as Marquis of Làngzhōng,
with an estate of ten thousand households,
and was about to return to the Central Plain
where he would be treated with the etiquette due to a guest.
Zhāng Lǔ's five sons and Yán Pǔ and others were all enfeoffed as various marquises.
When Zhāng Lǔ died,
his posthumous title was Yuánhóu.
His son, Zhāng Fù, succeeded him.
The commentary says: Liú Yān, seeing that the times were difficult,
first sought a place to survive and then perish,
hoping to act upon seeing an opportunity.
When land is vast, a proud and arrogant heart arises;
when wealth accumulates, a presumptuous and extravagant spirit is indulged.
This is indeed an inevitable stage for ordinary people.
Liú Zhāng was able to close his borders and nurture his strength,
guarding his territory and planning ahead.
He could have still adapted to the changing times,
but he abruptly surrendered his strategic assets,
passively accepting banishment.
This is what is meant by "a sheep's quality with a tiger's skin,"
terrified upon seeing a jackal.
Alas!
Yuán Shù, courtesy name Gōnglù,
was a man from Rǔyáng, Rǔnán.
He was the son of Sìkōng Yuán Fēng.
In his youth, he was known for his chivalry,
often flying eagles and chasing dogs with other noble sons,
but later he somewhat reformed himself.
He was nominated as Xiàolián,
and was successively promoted to Governor of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn) and Colonel of the Imperial Guard (Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng).
At that time, Dǒng Zhuó intended to depose and enthrone an emperor,
and appointed Yuán Shù as General of the Rear (Hòujiāngjūn).
Yuán Shù, fearing Dǒng Zhuó's calamity,
fled to Nányáng.
Coincidentally, Sūn Jiān, the Administrator of Chángshā, killed Zhāng Zī, the Administrator of Nányáng,
and led his troops to join Yuán Shù.
Liú Biǎo recommended Yuán Shù as Administrator of Nányáng,
and Yuán Shù, in turn, recommended Sūn Jiān as Inspector of Yùzhōu,
dispatching him to lead the troops of Jīng and Yù
to defeat Dǒng Zhuó at Yángrén.
Yuán Shù's cousin, Yuán Shào, while Sūn Jiān was still campaigning against Dǒng Zhuó
far away,
sent his general Zhōu Xīn of Kuàijī to seize Yùzhōu from Sūn Jiān.
Yuán Shù was enraged
and attacked Zhōu Xīn, driving him away.
Yuán Shào proposed to enthrone Liú Yú as emperor.
Yuán Shù, who liked to indulge himself,
was reluctant to enthrone an upright ruler,
and used public righteousness as an excuse not to agree.
This accumulated resentment eventually led to a rift.
They then each sought foreign allies
to plot against each other.
Yuán Shù allied with Gōngsūn Zàn,
while Yuán Shào connected with Liú Biǎo.
Many heroes and magnates sided with Yuán Shào.
Yuán Shù angrily said:
"These commoners don't follow me,
but follow my family slave?!"
He also wrote to Gōngsūn Zàn,
saying that Yuán Shào was not a son of the Yuán family.
Yuán Shào heard this and was furious.
In the third year of Chúpíng (192 CE),
Yuán Shù sent Sūn Jiān to attack Liú Biǎo at Xiāngyáng,
and Sūn Jiān died in battle.
Gōngsūn Zàn had Liú Bèi join Yuán Shù in a conspiracy to jointly pressure Yuán Shào.
Yuán Shào met with Cáo Cāo to attack them,
and they were all defeated.
In the fourth year (193 CE),
Yuán Shù led his army into Chénliú,
encamping at Fēngqiū.
The remaining bandits of the Hēishān and the Xiongnú's Yúfúluó and others assisted Yuán Shù,
fighting Cáo Cāo at Kuāngtíng,
where they suffered a great defeat.
Yuán Shù retreated to defend Yōngqiū,
and then led his remaining troops to flee to Jiǔjiāng,
killed Chén Wēn, the Inspector of Yángzhōu, and appointed himself to that position,
also claiming to be the Count of Xúzhōu.
Lǐ Què entered Cháng'ān
and wanted to ally with Yuán Shù for support,
so he appointed him General of the Left (Zuǒjiāngjūn),
granted him the Imperial Mace (jiǎjié),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Yángzhái.
Initially,
when Yuán Shù was in Nányáng,
the population still numbered several hundred thousand,
but he did not uphold laws and regulations,
relying on plunder for resources,
and was insatiably extravagant and unrestrained.
The common people suffered from this.
He also came across a prophecy book in his youth,
which said:
"He who replaces the Hàn shall be Gāofù (high in the road)."
He claimed that his courtesy name (Gōnglù) matched this.
Furthermore, believing the Yuán clan originated from Chén as descendants of Shùn,
and that yellow would replace red in the cycle of virtues,
he harbored thoughts of usurpation and rebellion.
He also heard that Sūn Jiān had obtained the Imperial Seal,
and so he detained Sūn Jiān's wife and seized it.
In the winter of the second year of Xīngpíng (195 CE),
the Son of Heaven was wandering,
defeated at Cáoyáng.
Yuán Shù gathered his subordinates for a grand meeting,
and then said to them:
"Now the land is in turmoil,
and the Liú clan is weak.
My family has served as prime ministers for four generations,
and the common people look to us.
I wish to respond to Heaven and comply with the people;
what do you gentlemen think?"
None dared to respond.
His chief clerk, Yán Xiàng, stepped forward and said:
"In antiquity, the Zhōu dynasty, from Hòujì to King Wén,
accumulated virtue and merit,
possessing two-thirds of the world,
yet still served the Yīn.
Although your distinguished lord's family has prospered for generations,
how does it compare to the flourishing of Zhōu?
Although the Hàn dynasty is weak,
it has not reached the decadence of Yīn Zhòu."
Yuán Shù remained silent
and sent for Zhāng Fàn.
Zhāng Fàn declined due to illness,
sending his younger brother, Zhāng Chéng, to respond instead.
Yuán Shù asked:
"In ancient times, when the Zhōu house declined,
there were the hegemonies of Duke Huán and Duke Wén;
when Qín lost its governance,
Hàn followed and utilized it.
Now, I, with the vastness of my territory
and the multitude of my scholars,
wish to seek fortune like Duke Huán of Qí
and emulate Emperor Gāozǔ.
Is this permissible?"
Zhāng Chéng replied:
"It lies in virtue, not in multitude.
If one can use virtue to align with the desires of the whole world,
even if called a commoner,
one can be a hegemon or a king.
If one is excessively arrogant and unrestrained,
acting against the times,
whom the multitude detests,
who can raise him up?"
Yuán Shù was displeased.
After Sūn Jiān died,
his son Sūn Cè again took control of his troops.
Yuán Shù sent them to attack Liú Yáo, the Inspector of Yángzhōu.
They defeated him,
and Sūn Cè consequently occupied Jiāngdōng.
Sūn Cè heard that Yuán Shù intended to usurp the imperial title,
so he wrote a letter of remonstrance, saying:
"Dǒng Zhuó was without principle,
oppressing the royal house,
bringing calamity upon the Empress Dowager,
and violence to Hóngnóng.
The Son of Heaven was exiled,
the palaces and ancestral temples burned down.
This is why the heroes were enraged
and rose up together in a mighty surge.
Once the chief villain was dead,
the young sovereign looked east,
and so he sent royal envoys to convey his commands,
to proclaim the grace of the court,
to cease military action and cultivate civil virtues,
and to make a new start.
However, Héběi harbors different plans with the Hēishān bandits,
Cáo Cāo's poison has spread to Dōngxú,
Liú Biǎo has usurped and caused chaos in Nánjīng,
Gōngsūn has rebelled in Shuòběi,
Zhèng Lǐ obstructs with troops,
Xuándé contends for supremacy;
thus, we have not yet been able to obey the mandate
to sheath our bows and stack our spears.
It is expected that you, sir, would share the same aspirations as the state,
yet you neglect this
and completely harbor the ambition to seize power for yourself.
I fear this is not what the people within the seas aspire to.
When Chéng Tāng campaigned against Jié,
he declared, 'Yǒuxià has many sins.'
When Wǔ Wáng attacked Zhòu,
he said, 'Yīn has grievous punishments.'
These two kings,
though possessing sagely virtue,
if the times had not seen the error of a wayward path,
would have had no means to press and seize power.
Now, the present sovereign has done no evil to the world,
but merely as a young child is coerced by powerful ministers,
which is different from the times of Tāng and Wǔ.
Moreover, I hear the young sovereign is intelligent and astute,
possessing virtues developed early.
Though the world has not yet received his grace,
all hearts turn to him.
If you assist him and bring about his rise,
then the merits of Dàn and Shì
would be what all under heaven hope for.
You, sir, have inherited your position for five generations,
〔一０〕serving as prime ministers of Hàn.
The height of your honor and favor
is unparalleled.
It is fitting for you to show loyalty and maintain integrity
to repay the royal house.
Many people of our time are confused by prophecies and diagrams,
erroneously citing unrelated texts,
and merely consider pleasing the ruler as virtue,
disregarding the plans for success or failure.
This is something greatly cautioned against throughout history;
should it not be carefully considered?
Loyal words grate on the ear,
dissenting opinions incur hatred,
〔一一〕but if it benefits your esteemed sagacity,
I dare not decline. "
Yuán Shù did not accept it,
and Sūn Cè consequently broke off relations with him.
In the second year of Jiàn'ān,
using the auspicious prophecy from Zhāng Jiǒng of Hénèi,
Yuán Shù indeed usurped the imperial title,
calling himself
"Zhòngjiā."
He appointed the Grand Administrator of Jiǔjiāng as the Governor of Huáinán,
established dukes, ministers, and all officials,
and offered sacrifices to Heaven and Earth in the suburbs.
He then sent an envoy to inform Lǚ Bù of his usurpation
and also sought Lǚ Bù's daughter in marriage for his son.
Lǚ Bù detained Yuán Shù's envoy and sent him to Xǔ.
Yuán Shù was greatly enraged,
and sent his generals Zhāng Xūn and Qiáo Ruí to attack Lǚ Bù,
but they were soundly defeated and returned.
Yuán Shù then led his troops to attack Chénguó,
luring and killing King Chǒng and his Chancellor Luò Jùn.
Cáo Cāo then personally campaigned against him.
Yuán Shù was greatly alarmed upon hearing this,
and immediately fled across the Huái River,
leaving Zhāng Xūn and Qiáo Ruí at Qíyáng
to resist Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo defeated them and beheaded Qiáo Ruí,
while Zhāng Xūn retreated.
Yuán Shù's army was weakened,
his major general dead,
and public sentiment was disloyal and rebellious.
Furthermore, there was a drought and a famine year,
the soldiers and people suffered from cold and hunger;
those between the Jiāng and Huái rivers were almost completely eaten by each other.
At that time, Shū Zhòngyīng was Yuán Shù's Chancellor of Pèi.
Yuán Shù gave him 100,000 *hú* of rice for military provisions,
but Shū Zhòngyīng distributed it all to the starving people.
Yuán Shù was enraged upon hearing this
and arrayed his troops, intending to execute him.
Shū Zhòngyīng said:
"I knew I would surely die,
so I did it anyway.
It is better to save the common people from dire suffering
with the life of one man."
Yuán Shù dismounted and pulled him, saying:
"Zhòngyīng,
do you alone wish to enjoy a great reputation throughout the world,
and not share it with me?"
Although Yuán Shù valued reputation and admired the unusual,
his innate character was arrogant and self-indulgent,
exalting himself and looking down upon others.
When he usurped the false title,
his extravagance and luxury grew even worse;
his several hundred concubines and maids
all wore fine silk,
and gorged on rich food,
while those below them were hungry and distressed,
and none were cared for.
Consequently, his resources were completely exhausted,
and he could not maintain himself.
In the summer of the fourth year,
he burned his palaces
and fled to his subordinates Chén Jiǎn and Léi Bó in the mountains.
Again he was repelled by Chén Jiǎn and the others,
and thus fell into great distress and poverty,
his soldiers dispersed and fled.
Full of worry and depression, not knowing what to do,
he then offered the imperial title to Yuán Shào,
saying:
"The mandate has departed from the Hàn imperial house for a long time;
the world is divided,
and governance rests within powerful clans.
Heroes contend for supremacy,
carving up territories.
This is no different from the Seven Warring States at the end of Zhōu,
only the strong will annex them.
The Yuán clan is destined to become king,
the auspicious signs are clearly manifest.
Now you, sir, possess four provinces
and a million households.
In terms of strength, none can rival your greatness;
in terms of position, none can compare in loftiness.
Although Cáo Cāo wishes to support the fading and encourage the weak,
how can he continue a broken destiny
or revive what has already perished!
I respectfully offer the great mandate;
may you, sir, bring it to prosperity."
Yuán Shào tacitly approved of his plan.
Yuán Shù then wanted to go north to Qīngzhōu to join Yuán Tán.
Cáo Cāo sent Liú Bèi to intercept him,
preventing him from passing.
He then fled back to Shòuchūn.
In the sixth month,
he arrived at Jiāngtíng.
Sitting on a reed mat, he sighed, saying:
"Has Yuán Shù come to this!"
He then fell ill from indignation and depression,
vomited blood, and died.
His wife and children depended on his former subordinate Liú Xūn, the Grand Administrator of Lújiāng.
When Sūn Cè defeated Liú Xūn,
they were again taken in and cared for.
Yuán Shù's daughter entered Sūn Quán's palace,
and his son Yuán Yào served as a Palace Gentleman in Wú.
Commentary says: The verification of Heaven's mandate
can be seen,
but cannot be spoken.
However, those who receive great fortune in general
return to sincerity and compliance!
Indeed, if affairs are not in accordance,
even with strong power and extensive schemes,
one cannot obtain it.
If one schemes for unattainable things,
they daily lose loyalty and sincerity,
and deceptions and lies arise spontaneously.
How much more so if one merely acts recklessly,
is that not deceiving Heaven?
Even if one feigns auspicious signs and usurps titles,
where will one ultimately be accommodated?
Lǚ Bù, courtesy name Fèngxiān,
was a man from Jiǔyuán, Wǔyuán.
He served Bīngzhōu with his excellent archery and horsemanship.
Dīng Yuán, the Inspector, made him Commandant of Cavalry,
(Dīng Yuán) garrisoned at Hénèi,
appointed Lǚ Bù as his Chief Clerk,
and greatly favored and trusted him.
When Emperor Líng died,
Dīng Yuán received Hè Jìn's summons
and led troops to Luòyáng,
becoming Commandant of the Gilded Cavalry.
Coincidentally, Hè Jìn was defeated,
and Dǒng Zhuó enticed Lǚ Bù to kill Dīng Yuán and annex his troops.
Zhuó made Bù a Cavalry Commandant,
swearing to be father and son,
and loved and trusted him greatly.
He was gradually promoted to Colonel of the Guards,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng.
Zhuó, knowing his own savagery and capriciousness,
was always suspicious and fearful.
He always kept Bù by his side for protection when moving about.
Once, Bù slightly displeased Zhuó,
and Zhuó drew a hand-halberd and threw it at him.
Bù, agile with his fists, managed to dodge it,
then composed himself and apologized,
and Zhuó's anger also subsided.
From then on, Bù secretly resented Zhuó.
Zhuó also made Bù guard his private chambers,
while he himself had a secret affair with a maidservant,
which made him even more uneasy.
So Bù went to see Minister of Works Wáng Yǔn,
and recounted how Zhuó had almost killed him.
At that time, Yǔn and Acting Grandee Secretary Shìsūn Ruì were secretly plotting to execute Zhuó.
Yǔn then informed Bù,
and had him act as an inside agent.
Bù said:
"What about the father-son relationship?"
Yǔn replied:
"Your surname is Lǚ;
you are not related by blood.
Now you are worried about death and have no time for anything else,
what talk is there of father and son?
At the moment he threw the halberd,
was there any father-son affection?"
Bù then agreed,
and so assassinated Zhuó at the gate.
The details are already recorded in Zhuó's biography.
Yǔn appointed Bù as General of Valiant Might,
granted him the Staff of Authority,
gave him the honors of the Three Ducal Ministers,
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Wēn.
As Yǔn did not pardon the people of Liángzhōu,
Zhuó's generals Lǐ Jué and others consequently banded together
and returned to attack Cháng'ān.
Bù fought with Jué,
was defeated,
and so took several hundred cavalry,
tied Zhuó's head to his saddle,
and fled through Wǔguān,
making for Nányáng.
Yuán Shù treated him very well.
Bù, relying on his feat of killing Zhuó,
believed he had rendered a service to the Yuán clan,
and thus allowed his soldiers to plunder freely.
Shù was troubled by this.
Bù felt uneasy
and again left to join Zhāng Yáng in Hénèi.
At this time, Lǐ Jué and others were urgently offering bounties for Bù,
and all the generals under Yáng wanted to kill him.
Bù was afraid
and said to Yáng:
"You and I are from the same region.
If I am killed now,
the reward may not be great.
It would be better to sell Bù alive;
you could gain great titles and favors from Jué and the others."
Yáng thought this was a good idea.
After a while,
Bù managed to escape and went to Yuán Shào.
Shào and Bù attacked Zhāng Yàn in Chángshān.
Yàn had over ten thousand elite soldiers
and several thousand cavalry.
Bù always rode a good horse,
named Chìtù,
capable of galloping over city walls and flying over moats.
With his brave generals Chéng Lián and Wèi Yuè and several dozens of cavalry, he charged into Yàn's formations,
sometimes three or four times a day,
each time beheading enemies before emerging.
After more than ten days of continuous fighting,
they finally defeated Yàn's army.
Bù, emboldened by his success,
again asked Shào for more troops.
Shào refused,
and Bù's officers and soldiers were often unruly,
which troubled Shào.
Bù felt uneasy,
and so asked to return to Luòyáng.
Shào permitted it,
and acting on imperial authority, made him Governor of Sīlì,
sending brave warriors to escort Bù, but secretly ordering them to kill him.
Bù suspected their plot against him,
and so had someone play the zither inside his tent,
while he secretly slipped away.
Troops were raised in the middle of the night,
but Bù had already fled.
Shào heard of this,
feared trouble,
and dispatched a pursuit,
but no one dared approach him,
so he eventually returned to Zhāng Yáng.
On his way through Chénliú,
the Administrator Zhāng Miǎo sent an envoy to welcome him,
treating him very courteously,
and at their farewell, they clasped arms and swore an oath.
Miǎo, courtesy name Mèngzhuó,
was from Dōngpíng,
and was known for his chivalry in his youth.
He was initially appointed to the Ducal Office
and gradually promoted to Administrator of Chénliú.
During the chaos of Dǒng Zhuó,
he and Cáo Cāo together raised an army of righteousness.
When Yuán Shào became the alliance leader,
he displayed arrogance,
and Miǎo righteously reprimanded him.
Shào resented Miǎo
and also heard of his closeness to Bù,
so he ordered Cáo Cāo to kill Miǎo.
Cāo did not comply,
but Miǎo felt uneasy in his heart.
In the first year of Xīngpíng (194 CE),
Cáo Cāo marched east to attack Táo Qiān,
leaving his general Chén Gōng of Wǔyáng to garrison Dōngjùn.
Gōng then persuaded Miǎo, saying:
"Today the world is in disarray,
and heroes are rising everywhere.
You command a hundred thousand troops,
holding a strategically vital territory.
By gripping your sword and looking around,
you are well enough to be a hero,
yet you are constrained by others.
Is this not ignoble?
Now the provincial army is campaigning in the east,
leaving this area empty.
Lǚ Bù is a valiant warrior,
excellent in battle, unmatched.
Welcome him to jointly hold Yǎnzhōu,
observe the situation in the world,
and await opportunities to adapt to changing circumstances.
This too is a way to dominate for a time."
Miǎo followed his advice,
and so, with his younger brother Chāo and Gōng and others, welcomed Bù to be Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
occupying Púyáng,
and all the commanderies and counties responded to him.
Cáo Cāo heard of this and led his army to attack Bù.
After repeated battles,
they were deadlocked for over a hundred days.
At this time, there was drought and locusts, and grain was scarce,
so the people resorted to cannibalism.
Bù moved his garrison to Shānyáng.
After two years,
Cáo Cāo recaptured all the cities
and defeated Bù at Jùyě.
Bù fled east to Liú Bèi.
Miǎo went to Yuán Shù for help,
leaving Chāo to command his family and garrison Yōngqiū.
Cāo besieged Chāo for several months,
massacred them,
and exterminated his three clans.
Miǎo had not yet reached Shòuchūn
when he was harmed by his own soldiers.
At that time, Liú Bèi
governed Xúzhōu, residing in Xiàpī,
and was contending with Yuán Shù along the Huái River.
Shù wished to incite Lǚ Bù to attack Liú Bèi,
and so he wrote a letter to Bù, saying:
“When Shù raised an army to approach the imperial court,
I was unable to utterly defeat Dǒng Zhuó.
General, you executed Zhuó,
avenging Shù’s humiliation;
this is your first great achievement.
In the past, Jīn Yuánhxiū came south to Fēngqiū,
and was defeated by Cáo Cāo.
General, you attacked him,
allowing Shù to regain prominence far and wide;
this is your second great achievement.
Since Shù was born,
I have never heard of Liú Bèi in the world;
yet Bèi dared to raise an army and fight against Shù.
By relying on the General’s might and prestige,
I was able to defeat Bèi;
this is your third great achievement.
General, you have rendered these three great services to Shù;
though Shù is not talented,
I shall serve you with my life.
General, you have been engaged in warfare for years,
and your military provisions are severely lacking.
I am now sending two hundred thousand hú of rice.
Not only will it not stop here,
but more will be continuously delivered.
All your needs, whether great or small, are at my command.”
Bù was greatly pleased upon receiving the letter,
and immediately led his troops to attack Xiàpī,
capturing Bèi’s wife and children.
Bèi was defeated and fled to Haǐxī,
where he suffered from hunger and hardship,
and requested to surrender to Bù.
Bù, also enraged that Shù had not sent further provisions,
prepared carriages and horses to welcome Bèi,
appointed him as the Inspector of Yùzhōu,
and sent him to garrison Xiǎopèi.
Bù proclaimed himself the Governor of Xúzhōu.
Shù, fearing that Bù would harm him,
sought a marriage alliance for his son,
which Bù again agreed to.
Shù sent his generals Jì Líng and others, with thirty thousand infantry and cavalry, to attack Bèi.
Bèi sought help from Bù.
His generals said to Bù:
“General, you have always wanted to kill Liú Bèi;
now you can let Shù do it for you.”
Bù said:
“No.
If Shù defeats Bèi,
he will then link up with Tàishān in the north,
and I will be trapped within Shù’s encirclement.
I cannot but save him.”
So he led more than a thousand infantry and cavalry,
and galloped to their aid.
When Líng and others heard of Bù’s arrival,
they all withdrew their troops and stopped.
Bù encamped outside Pèi City,
sent someone to invite Bèi,
and also invited Líng and others to a feast with him.
Bù said to Líng:
“Xuándé
is my younger brother.
He is being harassed by you gentlemen,
so I have come to save him.
My nature is not to enjoy fighting,
but rather to resolve conflicts.”
He then ordered a military officer to plant a halberd at the camp gate,
and Bù drew his bow and looked around, saying:
“Gentlemen, watch me shoot the small crescent moon of this halberd.
If I hit it, you should all withdraw your troops;
if I miss, you may stay and fight to the death.”
Bù immediately fired an arrow,
hitting the crescent moon of the halberd precisely.
Líng and the others were all astonished,
saying,
“General, your divine might!”
The next day, they held another joyful gathering,
and then each dispersed.
Yuán Shù sent Hán Yìn to inform Bù of his imperial proclamation,
and thereby requested to fetch his bride.
Bù sent his daughter with him.
Pèi Chancellor Chén Guī feared that if Shù and Bù completed the marriage alliance,
Xú and Yáng Provinces would combine,
creating endless trouble.
Therefore, he went to persuade Bù, saying:
“Cáo Gōng welcomed the Son of Heaven,
and assisted in governing the state.
General, you should cooperate with him in strategy,
and together preserve the great plan.
Now, if you form a marriage alliance with Yuán Shù,
you will certainly incur the name of unrighteousness,
and face the danger of a stack of eggs.”
Bù had also long resented Shù,
but his daughter was already on her way.
So he recalled her, broke off the marriage,
arrested Yìn and sent him to Xǔ,
where Cáo Cāo executed him.
Chén Guī wanted to send his son Dēng to see Cáo Cāo,
but Bù steadfastly refused.
Coincidentally, an envoy arrived,
appointing Bù as General of the Left.
Bù was greatly pleased,
and immediately allowed Dēng to go,
and also ordered him to present a memorial of thanks.
When Dēng met Cáo Cāo,
he then presented his views on Bù, saying he was brave but lacked foresight,
and was capricious in his alliances.
He advised to deal with him early.
Cāo said:
“Bù has the heart of a wolf cub, wild and untamed;
indeed, it is difficult to keep him long.
No one but you could discern his true nature.”
Immediately, he increased Guī’s rank to two thousand shí,
and appointed Dēng as the Administrator of Guǎnglíng.
Before parting,
Cāo held Dēng’s hand and said:
“The affairs of the East
are entrusted to you.”
He ordered him to secretly gather his forces,
to act as an internal confederate.
Originally, Bù had asked Dēng to request the Xúzhōu Governorship,
but did not get it.
When Dēng returned,
Bù was angry,
drew his halberd and chopped the desk, saying:
“Your father advised me to cooperate with Cáo Cāo,
and break off the marriage with Gōnglù.
Now I have gained nothing of what I sought,
yet you father and son are both prominent and important.
I have simply been sold out by you.”
Dēng showed no change of expression,
and slowly replied:
“When Dēng saw Cáo Gōng,
I said that keeping the General is like keeping a tiger.
One must feed it its fill of meat,
for if it is not full, it will bite people.
The Duke said: ‘Your words are not quite right.
It is more like keeping a hawk:
when hungry, it is useful;
when full, it will fly away.’
That is what he said.”
Bù’s anger then subsided.
Yuán Shù was enraged that Bù had killed Hán Yìn,
and sent his great generals Zhāng Xūn, Qiáo Ruí, and others, allied with Hán Xiān and Yáng Fèng,
with tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry,
to attack Bù along seven routes.
Bù at that time had three thousand soldiers
and four hundred horses,
and feared he would not be able to contend.
He said to Chén Guī:
“Now Shù’s army has arrived;
this is your doing.
What is to be done?”
Guī said:
“Xiān and Fèng, and Shù,
are but a hastily assembled force.
Their plans are not firmly established,
and they cannot support each other.
Your son Dēng compared them to a string of chickens;
they cannot roost together
and can be separated immediately.”
Bù used Guī’s plan,
and wrote to Xiān and Fèng, saying:
“You two generals personally escorted the imperial carriage,
and I personally killed Dǒng Zhuó.
We all established great reputations,
which should be recorded in history.
Now Yuán Shù is rebelling;
we should jointly punish him.
Why do you return with the bandit to attack me?
We should now unite our strength to defeat Shù,
eliminate a scourge for the state,
and establish meritorious deeds in the world.
This opportunity must not be missed.”
He also promised that if they defeated Shù’s army,
he would give them all the military supplies.
Xiān and Fèng were greatly pleased,
and so they jointly attacked Xūn and others at Xiàpī,
utterly defeating them.
They captured Qiáo Ruí alive,
and the remaining forces scattered and fled.
Almost all who were killed, wounded, or drowned perished.
At that time, Zāng Bà (臧霸) and others from Tài Shān (太山) attacked and broke through Jǔ Chéng (莒城).
Lǚ Bù (呂布) promised wealth and goods to ally with them,
but before they could be sent,
Bù then went himself to request them.
His commanding general, Gāo Shùn (高順), advised against it,
saying:
"General, your awe-inspiring reputation is widely known;
you are feared far and wide.
What is there that you cannot obtain,
that you should go yourself to seek bribes?
If by any chance you fail,
would that not be a loss of face?"
Bù did not listen.
When he arrived at Jǔ (莒),
Bà (霸) and the others could not fathom his intention in coming,
so they held their ground and resisted him.
He returned with no gains.
Shùn (順) was a man of integrity and dignity,
spoke little,
and managed his troops in an orderly fashion.
Every battle he fought, he was victorious.
Bù (布) was by nature irresolute and fickle;
his actions were inconsistent.
Shùn (順) often advised him, saying:
"General, in your actions,
you are unwilling to think things through carefully.
When there are sudden gains or losses,
you always say it was a mistake.
How can mistakes be countless?"
Bù (布) knew he was loyal but could not follow his advice.
In the third year of Jiàn'ān (建安) (198 CE),
Bù (布) again sided with Yuán Shù (袁術).
He sent Shùn (順) to attack Liú Bèi (劉備) at Pèi (沛),
and defeated him.
Cáo Cāo (曹操) sent Xiàhóu Dūn (夏侯惇) to rescue Bèi (備).
He was defeated by Shùn (順).
Cāo (操) then personally led an attack against Bù (布),
arriving before Xiàpí (下邳) city.
He sent Bù (布) a letter,
explaining the advantages and disadvantages.
Bù (布) wanted to surrender,
but Chén Gōng (陳宮) and others, considering themselves guilty before Cāo (操),
strongly thwarted his plan,
and said to Bù (布):
"Cáo Gōng (曹公) has come from afar;
his strength cannot last long.
If the General takes his cavalry and infantry to encamp outside,
Gōng (宮) will lead the remaining troops to close ranks and defend within.
If he attacks the General,
Gōng (宮) will lead his forces to attack his rear;
if he only attacks the city,
then the General can provide relief from outside.
In no more than ten days or a month,
their army's provisions will be exhausted,
and we can attack and defeat them."
Bù (布) agreed.
Bù's (布) wife said:
"In the past, the Cáo (曹) family treated Gōng Tái (公臺) like a baby,
yet he still abandoned them and came to us.
Now, General, your generosity to Gōng Tái (公臺) does not exceed that of the Cáo (曹) family,
yet you want to entrust the entire city,
abandon your wife and children,
and go out alone with an isolated army?
If, by any chance, something unexpected happens,
how could your concubine remain your wife?"
Bù (布) then stopped.
However, he secretly sent someone to seek help from Yuán Shù (袁術),
and personally led over a thousand cavalry out.
He was defeated in battle and fled back,
securing the city and daring not to go out.
Shù (術) also could not rescue him.
Cáo Cāo (曹操) besieged him,
damming the Yí (沂) and Sì (泗) rivers to flood his city.
After three months,
those above and below were disunited.
His general Hóu Chéng (侯成) had a guest herd his famous horses,
but the guest rode them away in rebellion.
Chéng (成) pursued the guest and recovered the horses.
The generals collectively offered congratulations to Chéng (成) with ceremony.
Chéng (成) divided wine and meat,
and first went to Bù (布) and said:
"Thanks to the General's divine power,
I recovered my lost horses.
All the generals are congratulating me,
but have not yet dared to taste the wine and meat,
so I present them to you first."
Bù (布) angrily said:
"I forbade wine, yet you all brewed it.
Are you trying to conspire against me through wine?"
Chéng (成) was enraged and frightened,
so he, along with the other generals, seized Chén Gōng (陳宮) and Gāo Shùn (高順),
and led their troops to surrender.
Bù (布) and his subordinates ascended the Bái Mén Lóu (白門樓).
The besieging troops pressed hard;
he ordered his attendants to take his head to Cāo (操).
His attendants could not bear to,
and instead surrendered.
Bù (布) saw Cāo (操) and said:
"From this day forward,
the world is settled."
Cāo (操) said:
"Why do you say so?"
Bù (布) said:
"Your Excellency's concern is merely Bù (布).
Now I am subdued.
If you let Bù (布) command the cavalry,
and Your Excellency commands the infantry,
the world will not be difficult to settle."
He then looked at Liú Bèi (劉備) and said:
"Xuándé (玄德),
you are an honored guest seated there,
while I am a captured slave.
My ropes are bound tightly.
Can you not say a word for me?"
Cāo (操) laughed and said:
"When binding a tiger, one must bind it tightly."
He then ordered Bù's (布) ropes to be loosened.
Liú Bèi (劉備) said:
"No.
Does Your Excellency not remember Lǚ Bù's (呂布) dealings with Dīng Jiànyáng (丁建陽) and Dǒng Tài Shī (董太師)?"
Cāo (操) nodded.
Bù (布) glared at Bèi (備) and said:
"Big-eared fellow is the most untrustworthy!"
Cāo (操) said to Chén Gōng (陳宮):
"Gōng Tái (公臺) always considered himself overly wise;
what do you think now?"
Gōng (宮) pointed at Bù (布) and said:
"This fellow would not follow Gōng's (宮) words,
which is why it has come to this.
If he had listened,
it would be immeasurable what could have been achieved."
Cāo (操) again said:
"What about your elderly mother?"
Gōng (宮) said:
"My elderly mother's fate is with Your Excellency,
not with Gōng (宮).
A ruler who governs the world with filial piety
does not harm another's parents."
Cāo (操) further said:
"What about your wife and children?"
Gōng (宮) said:
"I have heard that a hegemon king
does not cut off another's lineage."
He firmly requested to face execution,
and then walked out without looking back.
Cāo (操) wept for him.
Bù (布), along with Gōng (宮) and Shùn (順), were all hanged,
and their heads were displayed in Xǔ Shì (許市).
The eulogy says: Why act as a mediocre shepherd,
hoping for future blessings?
How can one speak of bearing burdens?
The territory falls, the body is driven out.
Shù (術) was already greedy,
Bù (布) was also faithless.
Biographies of Upright Officials, Chapter 66
Initially,
Guāngwǔ grew up among the common people,
and was quite discerning of truth and falsehood.
He saw the hardships of farming
and the suffering of the people.
When the empire was settled,
he prioritized peace and tranquility,
abolishing Wáng Mǎng's numerous and strict laws,
and restoring the lenient laws of the Hàn dynasty.
He himself wore plain coarse silk,
without elaborate colors,
his ears did not listen to the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
and his hands did not hold precious jewels.
There were no private favorites in his palace,
nor partial favors among his attendants.
In Jiànwǔ thirteenth year,
a foreign country offered a famous horse
that could travel a thousand *lǐ* a day,
and also presented a precious sword
worth a hundred gold pieces.
An imperial edict commanded that the horse be used to pull a drum carriage,
and the sword be bestowed upon a knight.
He reduced the officials of the Shanglín Imperial Park,
and abolished the practice of chariot racing, hunting, and fowling.
His handwritten letters bestowed upon various states
were all a single sheet with ten lines,
finely written and coherent.
The spirit of diligence and frugality
prevailed from the top down.
He frequently invited high ministers, dukes, and colonels,
to be seated at the imperial court.
He widely sought out the people's sufferings
and listened to popular ballads.
Thus, both within and outside the court, there was no idleness,
and the common people enjoyed peace and rest.
All who governed territories
competed to excel in their offices.
For example, Dù Shī, who governed Nányáng,
was known as
"Mother Dù."
Rèn Yán and Xī Guāng transformed the customs of the border regions;
these were their most outstanding achievements.
Furthermore, people like Dìwǔ Lún and Sòng Jūn
were also worthy of praise.
However, during the period between Jiànwǔ and Yǒngpíng,
official affairs were harsh and strict,
and governors and chiefs were frequently replaced
due to rumors and single accusations.
Therefore, Zhū Fú repeatedly submitted admonishing memorials,
critically criticizing the severe government,
and Zhōnglí Yì and others also earnestly remonstrated,
speaking as elders,
but they could not succeed.
Therefore, the splendor of the Restoration
was perhaps not fully realized.
After Zhāng and Hé,
those with good achievements
were often numerous.
For example, Lǔ Gōng, Wú Yòu, Liú Kuān, and the four elders of Yǐngchuān,
all, with benevolence, trust, and sincerity,
made people not dare to deceive;
Wáng Táng and Chén Chǒng entrusted virtuous and capable individuals,
and their duties were naturally managed well:
these all could inspire people and effect change.
Biān Fèng and Yán Dǔ successively served as Jīngzhàoyǐn,
and people of their time compared them to the Zhào and Zhāng of former generations.
Also, Wáng Huàn and Rèn Jùn, in their capacity as Luòyáng prefects,
brought hidden crimes to light,
and officials were honest and restrained.
However, their guidance of virtue and regulation of rituals
were somewhat lacking,
yet they were still good and capable officials of their time.
Now, I have compiled various notable accounts and deeds
to form the chapter on model officials.
Wèi Sà, courtesy name Zǐchǎn,
was from Xiūwǔ, Hénèi.
His family was poor, but he loved learning.
When he followed his teacher, he had no provisions,
and often worked as a laborer to support himself.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
he served in the commandery and successively as a provincial administrator.
In Jiànwǔ second year,
he was summoned to the residence of Grand Minister over the Masses Dèng Yǔ.
He was recommended for his ability to handle difficult cases,
and appointed as Palace Assistant Imperial Censor,
then Prefect of Xiāngchéng.
His administration gained renown,
and he was promoted to Grand Administrator of Guìyáng.
The commandery bordered Jiāozhōu,
and was somewhat influenced by its customs,
being ignorant of proper rituals.
When Sà arrived,
he established schools for education
and set up marriage rites.
Within a year,
the local customs were transformed.
Before this, the three counties of Hánkūang, Zhēnyáng, and Qǔjiāng
were former territories of Yuè.
Emperor Wǔ pacified them
and brought them under Guìyáng Commandery.
The people lived in deep mountains
and along valleys,
accustomed to their local customs,
and did not pay land tax.
Those far from the commandery
were sometimes a thousand *lǐ* away.
When officials traveled there,
they would always conscript people to ferry them by boat,
which was called
"relay service."
Every time an official went out,
several families were burdened by the labor service,
and the common people suffered greatly from it.
Sà then cut through mountains to open a road more than five hundred *lǐ* long,
established relay stations,
and set up post-houses.
Consequently, the labor service was reduced, people rested,
and corrupt officials were eliminated.
Displaced people gradually returned,
and gradually formed settlements,
making them pay rent and taxes,
just like ordinary citizens.
Furthermore, Lěiyáng County produced iron and stone,
and commoners from other commanderies often gathered there
to privately smelt and cast iron,
thus attracting fugitives,
leading to many illicit activities and banditry.
Sà then requested to establish an official iron agency,
and abolished private smelting,
increasing annual revenue by over five million.
He admonished and cared for the people's affairs,
and governed as if it were his own household;
all his policies
were appropriate to the circumstances.
After ten years in office,
the commandery was well-governed.
In the twenty-fifth year,
he was recalled.
Guāngwǔ intended to make him Lesser Minister of the Treasury,
but Sà happened to be ill
and unable to prostrate himself,
so he was ordered to return home as Grand Administrator of Guìyáng,
awaiting a future imperial edict.
Two years later,
he journeyed to the court despite his illness,
declaring his severe condition,
and then his seal and ribbon were collected,
and he was granted 100,000 cash.
He later died at home.
Cí Chōng of Nányáng succeeded Sà as Grand Administrator of Guìyáng.
He also governed well,
teaching the people to plant mulberry, ramie, and other fibrous plants,
and encouraging them to raise silkworms and weave sandals,
whereby the people benefited.
Rèn Yán, courtesy name Chángsūn,
was from Wǎn, Nányáng.
At the age of twelve,
he became a student
and studied in Cháng'ān,
mastering the *Shī* (Odes), *Yì* (Changes), and *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals),
gaining fame at the Imperial Academy.
He was known among the students as
"Saint Child Rèn."
During a tumultuous period,
he fled from war to Lǒngxī.
At that time, Kuí Xiāo had already occupied four commanderies,
and sent envoys to invite Yán,
but Yán did not accept.
In Gēngshǐ first year,
Yán was appointed assistant to the Grand Minister over the Masses,
and then Grand Commandant of Kuàijī.
He was nineteen years old at the time,
and those who welcomed him were surprised by his youth.
Upon his arrival,
he was calm and inactive,
only sending gifts to worship Jì Zǐ of Yánlíng first.
At that time, the empire had just been settled,
and roads were not yet clear.
Those who had fled to Jiāngnán to escape the chaos had not yet returned to the central plains,
and Kuàijī was quite famous for its many scholars.
When Yán arrived,
he invited all highly virtuous individuals like Dǒng Zǐyí and Yán Zǐlíng,
treating them with the respect due to teachers and friends.
For poor clerks and officials,
he would distribute his salary to relieve them.
He reduced the number of soldiers
and ordered them to cultivate public lands
to assist the poor and needy.
Whenever he inspected counties,
he would encourage dutiful sons
and dine with them.
In Wú there was a man named Lóngqiū Chāng,
who lived in seclusion in Tàimò,
his will unyielding to humiliation.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
the Four Regents and Three Ducal Ministers repeatedly invited him,
but he did not go.
A clerk requested that he be summoned.
Yán said:
"Master Lóngqiū embodies virtue and practices righteousness,
possessing the integrity of Yuán Xiàn and Bó Yí.
Even if the Area Commander were to sweep his gate,
he would still fear bringing him shame,
so summoning him is impossible."
He sent the Gōngcáo to present his respects,
compose letters,
and send medicines,
with officials and envoys constantly on the road.
After a full year,
Chāng finally rode a litter to the government office gate,
wishing to die first and be recorded.
Yán repeatedly declined and yielded,
and then appointed him as Jìjiǔ of the Yìcáo.
Chāng soon fell ill and died,
and Yán personally attended the funeral,
not holding court for three days.
Because of this, the worthy gentlemen and officials in the commandery vied to serve there.
In the early Jiànwǔ period,
Yán submitted a memorial requesting to retire,
wishing to return to pay homage at the imperial court.
An edict summoned him to be the Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn.
Guāngwǔ granted him an audience,
bestowed horses and various silks,
and ordered his wife and children to remain in Luòyáng.
The custom in Jiǔzhēn was to live by hunting,
not knowing ox-plowing.
The people often bought grain from Jiāozhǐ,
and frequently suffered from scarcity.
Yán then ordered the casting of farming tools
and taught them to clear and cultivate land.
The cultivated fields expanded year by year,
and the hundred surnames became well-supplied.
Moreover, the Luòyuè people had no marriage rites or laws;
each indulged in licentious preferences,
without proper spouses or partners,
ignorant of the nature of father-son relationships
and the Way of husband and wife.
Yán then sent letters to the subordinate counties,
ordering that all men aged twenty to fifty
and women aged fifteen to forty
be matched according to their age.
For those who were poor and lacked betrothal gifts,
he ordered the chief officials and below to each reduce their salaries to provide relief and assistance.
More than two thousand people were married at the same time.
That year, the wind and rain were in season,
and the grain harvests were abundant.
Those who bore children
then first learned about their lineage.
They all said:
"The one who enabled us to have these children
is Lord Rèn."
Many named their children
"Rèn."
Thereupon, the barbarian tribes beyond the borders, such as Yèláng, admired his righteousness and guarded the passes,
and Yán then stopped and dismissed the scouts and garrison soldiers.
Initially,
during the reign of Emperor Píng,
Xī Guāng of Hànzhōng served as Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ,
teaching and guiding the local people and barbarians,
gradually instilling礼义(lǐyì) (rites and righteousness),
and his civilizing influence was comparable to Yán's.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
he closed the borders and resisted.
In the early Jiànwǔ period,
he sent envoys to offer tribute
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yánshuǐ.
The influence of the Southern culture
began with these two Grand Administrators.
Yán held office for four years,
and was summoned to Luòyáng,
but due to illness, he delayed his departure,
and was demoted to Magistrate of Suīyáng.
The officials and people of Jiǔzhēn spontaneously erected a temple for him.
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi,
and the Emperor personally granted him an audience,
admonishing him, saying:
"Serve your superiors well,
and do not lose your good reputation."
Yán replied:
"I have heard that a loyal minister is not self-serving,
and a self-serving minister is not loyal.
To uphold righteousness and serve the public
is the duty of a minister.
If superiors and subordinates blindly concur,
it is not a blessing for Your Majesty.
To 'serve superiors well,'
I dare not obey this edict."
The Emperor sighed, saying:
"Your words are right."
After arriving in Wǔwēi,
at that time, the Administrator of Military Affairs, Tián Gàn,
was a prominent local magnate,
and his sons, younger brothers, and retainers committed violent acts.
Yán arrested Gàn and imprisoned him,
and five or six of his sons, younger brothers, and retainers were executed.
Gàn's youngest son, Shàng, then gathered several hundred unruly individuals,
proclaimed himself a general,
and attacked the commandery at night.
Yán immediately dispatched troops and defeated them.
From then on, his prestige spread throughout the region,
and officials and common people lived in peace.
The commandery's north faced the Xiongnú,
and its south bordered the Qiāng,
and the people feared raids and plunder,
many abandoning their fields.
Upon Yán's arrival,
he selected and gathered a thousand skilled warriors,
clearly stipulating rewards and punishments,
and ordered them to lead mixed barbarian cavalry, Xūtú and Huángshí, to garrison strategic points.
If there was an emergency,
they were to counterattack and pursue the raiders.
Many of the barbarians were wounded or killed,
and they eventually dared not venture out again.
Héxī had historically suffered from little rainfall,
so he established water management officials,
repaired irrigation channels,
and all benefited from this.
He also established commandery schools,
ordering all sons and grandsons of clerks and officials
to attend school and receive instruction,
exempting them from corvée labor.
Once they mastered the classics,
he promoted them prominently.
The commandery then produced refined scholars.
Later, he was implicated and demoted to Magistrate of Zhàolíng
for executing Qiāng without prior reporting.
Upon the ascension of Emperor Xiǎnzōng,
he was appointed Grand Administrator of Yǐngchuān.
In the second year of Yǒngpíng,
he was summoned to a gathering at the Bìyōng,
and subsequently made Grand Administrator of Hénèi.
He served for nine years,
then died of illness.
His youngest son, Kǎi,
rose to the rank of Tàicháng.
Wáng Jǐng, courtesy name Zhòngtōng,
was a native of Lèwàng Lùhán.
His eighth-generation ancestor, Zhòng,
was originally from Bùqí, Lángyé.
He was fond of Taoist arts
and skilled in astronomy.
When the Lǚ family caused chaos,
Qí'áiwáng Xiāng plotted to raise troops
and frequently consulted Zhòng.
When Jìběi Wáng Xīngjū rebelled,
he wanted to entrust military command to Zhòng.
Fearing disaster would strike him,
Zhòng then fled by sea eastward to the mountains of Lèwàng,
and settled there.
His father, Hóng,
served as the Three Elders of the commandery.
When Gēngshǐ failed,
the local man Wáng Diào killed the Grand Administrator Liú Xiàn,
and proclaimed himself Grand General and Grand Administrator of Lèwàng.
In the sixth year of Jiànwǔ,
Guāngwǔ dispatched Grand Administrator Wáng Zūn to lead troops to attack him.
Upon reaching Liáodōng,
Hóng and the commandery's Registrar of Legal Cases, Yáng Yì, among others, jointly killed Diào and welcomed Zūn.
All were enfeoffed as marquises,
but Hóng alone declined the peerage.
The Emperor admired his integrity and summoned him,
but he fell ill and died on the way.
Jǐng studied the Yì (Book of Changes) in his youth,
then widely delved into numerous books,
and was also fond of astronomy and numerology,
deeply skilled in many arts.
He was appointed to the office of Sīkōng Fú Gōng.
At that time, someone recommended Jǐng as capable of water management,
and Emperor Xiǎnzōng issued an edict for him to work with the Palace Attendant, Wáng Wú, to repair and dredge the Jùnyí Canal.
Wú adopted Jǐng's method for water flow,
and the water no longer caused harm.
Initially,
during the reign of Emperor Píng,
the Yellow River and the Biàn River burst their banks,
but repairs could not be carried out in time.
In the tenth year of Jiànwǔ,
Zhāng Sì, the magistrate of Yángwǔ, submitted a memorial stating:
"The river has been breached for a long time,
and with each passing day, it causes more damage.
The Jì Canal has flooded several dozens of counties.
The cost of repairs
would not be difficult to manage.
It is fitting to repair the dikes
to bring peace to the common people."
When the memorial was submitted,
Emperor Guāngwǔ immediately dispatched troops.
While the river project was being prepared,
Lè Jùn, the magistrate of Jùnyí, again submitted a memorial, saying:
"In the past, during the Yuánguāng era,
the population was flourishing,
and people cultivated land along the dikes.
Yet, when the Húzi River breached,
it remained unblocked
for over twenty years.
Now, households are scarce,
and arable land is abundant.
Even if it is not repaired,
the trouble is still manageable.
Moreover, we have just suffered from warfare,
and are now undertaking forced labor.
Grievances and toil are already abundant,
and the people cannot bear such demands.
It is advisable to wait until peace is restored,
and then reconsider this matter."
When Emperor Guāngwǔ received this, he stopped the project.
Later, the Biàn Canal encroached eastward,
widening day by day.
The old locations of the sluice gates
were all within the river.
The people of Yǎn and Yù complained,
believing that the government was undertaking other projects
instead of prioritizing the people's urgent needs.
In the twelfth year of Yǒngpíng,
there was a discussion about repairing the Biàn Canal.
Jǐng was summoned
and questioned about the proper methods for water control.
Jǐng presented the advantages and disadvantages,
responding articulately.
The emperor praised him.
Also, because he had successfully repaired Jùnyí in the past,
he was granted the Shānhǎi Jīng, the Héqú Shū,
the Yǔ Gòng Tú,
and money, silks, and clothing.
In the summer,
several hundred thousand troops were dispatched,
and Jǐng, along with Wáng Wú, was sent to repair the canal and build dikes,
from Xíngyáng eastward to the mouth of the Qīanchéng Sea,
a distance of over a thousand *lǐ*.
Jǐng then surveyed the terrain,
cut through mountains and hills,
broke through rocks and dams,
straightened channels and ravines,
blocked strategic points,
and cleared away blockages.
He set up a water gate every ten *lǐ*,
allowing the water to circulate and flow into each other,
thereby eliminating the problem of breaches and leaks.
Although Jǐng simplified the labor and expenses,
they still amounted to hundreds of millions.
The following summer,
the canal was completed.
The emperor personally inspected it,
and issued an edict for the riverside commanderies and kingdoms to appoint river dike officials,
following the old system of the Western Capital.
Jǐng became famous as a result.
Wáng Wú and all the other assistants and clerks were promoted one rank.
Jǐng was promoted three times to Shìyùshǐ.
In the fifteenth year,
he accompanied the emperor on his eastern inspection tour.
When they reached Wúyán,
the emperor praised his accomplishments,
appointed him Héqú Yèzhě,
and bestowed upon him a carriage, horses, silk, and money.
In the seventh year of Jiànchū,
he was promoted to Xúzhōu Cìshǐ.
Previously, Dù Dǔ of Dùlíng had submitted a "Lùndū Fù"
proposing that the imperial carriage return to Cháng'ān.
When the elders heard it,
they were all moved by nostalgia for their homeland,
and all looked westward with longing.
Jǐng, fearing that people would be confused due to the established palaces and temples,
and coincidentally there were auspicious signs such as divine sparrows at the time,
composed the "Jīnrén Lùn"
to eulogize the beauty of Luòyì
and the harmony between heaven and man.
His prose was worth adopting.
The following year,
he was promoted to Lújiāng Tàishǒu.
Previously, the common people did not know how to use ox-drawn plows,
resulting in fertile land but constant food shortages.
Within the commandery, there were paddy fields at Quèpí
established by Sūn Shú'áo, Prime Minister of Chǔ.
Jǐng then led the officials and people
to repair the desolate and abandoned areas,
and taught them to use plow farming.
As a result, the cultivated land more than doubled,
and the region became prosperous.
He then inscribed a stone tablet with an oath,
to inform the people of the permanent regulations.
He also instructed them in sericulture and weaving,
establishing regulations that were
posted in the villages and communities.
Lújiāng transmitted his written words.
He died in office.
Initially,
Jǐng believed that what was recorded in the Six Classics
all involved divination,
and that actions and conduct
should be subjected to the *shīguī*.
However, the various books were mixed and confused,
with auspicious and inauspicious signs contradicting each other.
Therefore, he compiled the writings on various numerological arts,
taboos for tombs and residences,
and *kānyú* and date-selection,
selecting those suitable for practical use,
and compiled them into a work called "Dàyǎn Xuánjī."
Qín Péng, courtesy name Bóu Píng,
was from Máolíng, Fúfēng.
Since the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
his family had held successive official positions.
His sixth-generation ancestor, Xí,
served as Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
Along with five other relatives, he held the rank of two thousand *dàn* at the same time.
Therefore, the Three Fǔ region called them
"the Ten Thousand *Dàn* Qín Clan."
Péng's younger sister,
during Emperor Xiǎnzōng's reign, entered the court as a *Guìrén*,
and was favored.
In the seventh year of Yǒngpíng,
because Péng was the elder brother of the *Guìrén*,
he was promoted to Kāiyáng Chéngmén Hòu along with the minor marquises of the four prominent clans.
In the fifteenth year,
he was appointed Jì Dūwèi,
and served as deputy to Fùmǎ Dūwèi Gěng Bǐng in the northern campaign against the Xiongnú.
In the first year of Jiànchū,
he was promoted to Shānyáng Tàishǒu.
He instructed people with ritual,
and did not rely on severe punishments.
He esteemed Confucian elegance,
and earnestly clarified the principles of education.
During the spring and autumn sacrificial archery ceremonies,
he always observed the rituals of ascending, descending, bowing, and yielding.
He established four admonitions for people,
to regulate the rituals between the six kin and between elders and juniors.
Those who followed his teachings
were promoted to Xiāng Sānlǎo,
and he regularly presented them with wine and meat in the eighth month to encourage them.
If an official made a mistake,
they were dismissed,
without being subjected to shame or disgrace.
The common people cherished him,
and none dared to deceive or transgress.
He initiated several thousand *qǐng* of paddy fields.
During the farming months,
he personally measured the *qǐng* and *mǔ*,
distinguished between fertile and barren land,
classified them into three grades,
and established written registers for each,
which were stored in the villages and counties.
Consequently, corrupt officials were restrained,
with no room for deceit.
Péng then submitted a memorial,
suggesting that all under heaven should adopt this uniform system.
An imperial edict ordered that the regulations he had established
be distributed to the Three Offices
and also sent down to the provinces and commanderies.
He served for six years,
then was transferred to Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
There were continuous auspicious omens such as phoenixes, *qílín*, auspicious grains, and sweet dew,
which gathered in his commandery.
Emperor Sùzōng, during his inspection tours,
visited Yǐngchuān twice,
and each time bestowed money and grain,
showing exceptional favor.
He died in the second year of Zhānghé.
Péng's younger brothers, Dūn and Bāo,
both served as Shèshēng Xiàowèi.
Wáng Huàn
Zì Zhìzǐ was a native of Guǎnghàn’s Qī district.
His father, Shùn,
was the Grand Administrator of Āndìng.
Huàn, in his youth, was fond of chivalry
and valued strength and spirit.
He frequently associated with reckless youths.
Later, he changed his ways,
devoting himself to Confucian studies,
mastering the Shàngshū,
and reading the laws and ordinances,
roughly grasping their main points.
He served as the Chief Scribe for Grand Administrator Chén Chǒng.
In his duties, he made decisive judgments
and did not avoid the powerful and wealthy.
Chǒng’s reputation greatly spread,
and he was promoted to Grand Minister of Agriculture.
Emperor Hé asked him:
“How did you govern in your commandery?”
Chǒng bowed his head and replied:
“Your subject relied on the Chief Scribe Wáng Huàn to select the worthy and choose the capable,
and on the Chief Clerk Tán Xiǎn to pick up omissions and fill gaps.
Your subject merely promulgated imperial edicts.”
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
Huàn thereby gained fame.
The province nominated him as ‘Flourishing Talent,’
and he was appointed Magistrate of Wēn.
The county had many cunning and wicked people,
who had long been a nuisance to the populace.
Huàn, using strategies, pursued and attacked them,
executing them all.
The area became peaceful and orderly;
merchants slept exposed on the roads.
Those who herded cattle
would just say they entrusted them to Zhìzǐ,
and no one would ever trespass.
After three years in Wēn,
he was promoted to Inspector of Yǎnzōu.
He disciplined and rectified the commanderies in his department,
and his prestigious authority became widely known.
Later, he was impeached for an investigation into seditious talk that proved false.
After more than a year,
he was summoned and appointed Imperial Household Remonstrant.
In the fifteenth year of Yǒngyuán,
he accompanied the Emperor on a southern tour,
and upon return, became Magistrate of Luòyáng.
He conducted himself with fairness and uprightness,
achieving the appropriate balance of leniency and strictness.
Regarding long-standing grievances and lawsuits,
which previous administrations had failed to resolve,
and which were difficult to settle by law or reason,
he invariably thoroughly investigated the facts and deceptions,
dispelling all doubts.
He was also capable of uncovering hidden treachery through clever stratagems.
The capital praised him,
believing Huàn had divine foresight.
In the first year of Yuánxīng,
he died of illness.
The common people in the markets were all filled with lamentation.
Men and women, young and old, all banded together to contribute,
offering thousands of sacrifices and libations.
When Huàn’s coffin traveled west,
passing through Hóngnóng,
the common folk all set out platters and tables on the road.
Officials asked for the reason,
and they all said: “Normally, when we carried rice to Luòyáng,
we were plundered by the soldiers
and always lost half.
Since Lord Wáng took office,
we have not been wronged or violated,
so we have come to repay his kindness.”
His governance and transformative influence on the people were truly like this.
The people cherished his virtue
and erected a shrine for him west of Ānyáng Pavilion.
Every meal, they would play string instruments and sing as they offered sacrifices to him.
In the second year of Yǒngchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng issued an edict saying:
“Loyal and good officials
are how the state is governed.
They are sought with great diligence,
but few are found.
Hence Confucius said, ‘Talent is hard to find, is it not!’
In the past, the Grand Minister of Agriculture Zhū Yì
and the Right Protector Yǐn Wēngguī,
whose administrative achievements were outstanding and distinctive,
and whose good names were widely renowned,
were admired and pitied by Emperor Xiàoxuān,
who bestowed upon their sons one hundred catties of gold.
