The former Magistrate of Luòyáng, Wáng Huàn,
upheld a pure and upright character
and trod the path of the 'Lamb's Gown' (integrity).
He devoted his heart to public service,
striving to benefit the people.
His accomplishments were not yet complete,
when unfortunately, he died young.
The common people remember him with fondness
and erected a shrine for him.
If not for the utmost loyalty and love,
who could be like this!
Now, let Huàn’s son, Shí, be appointed a Gentleman,
to encourage diligence and effort.”
During the Yánxī era,
Emperor Huán, in his devotion to the Yellow Emperor and Lǎozi’s teachings,
ordered the destruction of all other local shrines.
Only by special imperial edict was the temple of the late Grand Tutor Zhuó Mào preserved in Mì County,
and Wáng Huàn’s shrine was kept in Luòyáng.
Tán Xiǎn later also became famous,
serving as Inspector of Yùzhōu during Emperor Ān’s reign.
At that time, the empire suffered from famine,
and people competed to become bandits.
In his province, nearly ten thousand people were arrested.
Xiǎn, pitying their destitution
and self-incrimination,
would often pardon them,
then impeach himself.
An imperial edict ordered no action to be taken.
Later, he rose to the position of Chánglè Guard Commander.
Since Huàn’s death,
consecutive edicts commanded the Three Excellencies to specifically select a Magistrate for Luòyáng,
but none proved competent.
During the Yǒnghé era,
Rèn Jùn Zì Shúgāo of Bóhǎi, a renowned magistrate for difficult areas, was appointed to the post.
Jùn promoted and employed civil and military officials,
all of whom fully exercised their abilities.
He rigorously investigated and eliminated bandits and criminals,
giving them no room to turn back.
In a year, the number of resolved lawsuits
did not exceed a few tens.
His formidable authority was more severe than Huàn’s,
but his administrative principles were inferior.
Jùn
eventually died as Grand Administrator of Tàishān.
Xǔ Jīng Zì Shàozhāng
was a native of Kuàijī’s Yángxiàn county.
His grandfather, Wǔ,
was recommended as ‘Filial and Incorrupt’ by Grand Administrator Dìwǔ Lún.
Wǔ, seeing that his two younger brothers, Yàn and Pǔ, had not yet achieved prominence,
wished to help them make a name for themselves.
So he requested:
“Ritual dictates the principle of division and separation,
and families have the custom of living apart.”
Thereupon, they jointly divided their property into three parts.
Wǔ himself took the fertile fields, spacious houses, and the strongest slaves,
while what his two younger brothers received was altogether inferior and meager.
The local people all praised the younger brothers for their humility and deference, and scorned Wǔ for his greed.
Because of this, Yàn and the others all obtained official appointments.
Then Wǔ assembled his relatives
and wept, saying:
“As an elder brother, I was unworthy,
stealing reputation and usurping position.
My two younger brothers are older,
but have not yet enjoyed honors or emoluments.
Therefore, I sought to divide the property
and brought great ridicule upon myself.
Now, the property I managed has increased
threefold compared to before,
and I shall hand it all over to my two younger brothers,
keeping nothing.”
At this, the entire commandery was greatly impressed,
and he was praised far and wide.
He rose to the position of Lesser Prefect of Chánglè.
Jīng, while young, served as a commandery official.
His nephew, Shì, once avenged a wrong by killing someone.
The aggrieved parties, armed with weapons, attacked him.
When Jīng heard of it,
he went out to meet the attackers
and knelt, saying:
“Shì previously acted improperly and offended you.
The fault lies entirely with Jīng for failing to instruct him.
Since his father died young,
he is the sole heir.
If the deceased’s line were to be extinguished, it would be a tragedy.
I beg you to kill me in his stead.”
The aggrieved family helped Jīng up
and said:
“Xǔ Yuàn is praised as worthy in the commandery;
how dare we harm you?”
They then left.
Jīng’s reputation grew even more prominent.
Grand Administrator Huáng Jīng nominated him as ‘Filial and Incorrupt.’
During the reign of Emperor Hé,
Jīng was gradually promoted to Grand Administrator of Guìyáng.
The commandery bordered the southern regions,
where customs were fragile and undeveloped,
and people were unfamiliar with learning and righteousness.
Jīng established systems for mourning rites and marriages,
making them understand the prohibitions of propriety.
Once, during a spring inspection, he arrived at Lèiyáng County.
There was a man named Jiǎng Jūn,
whose brothers were quarreling over property,
mutually accusing each other in lawsuits.
Jīng sighed to them, saying:
"I bear a heavy responsibility for the state,
but moral education is not being implemented;
the fault lies with the Grand Administrator."
Then he turned to his clerks and ordered them to memorialize the situation,
requesting to be sent to the Court of the Commandant of Justice (Tíngwèi).
The Jūn brothers were moved to repentance,
each begging to receive punishment.
He served for twelve years,
and the elders sang his praises.
Due to illness, he submitted his resignation,
was summoned and appointed Counsellor Remonstrant (Jiànyì Dàfū),
and died in office.
The people of Guìyáng erected a temple and a stele for him.
Jīng's grandson, Qí,
served as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) during the reign of Emperor Líng.
Mèng Cháng, courtesy name Bózhōu,
was a native of Shàngyú, Kuàijī.
His ancestors for three generations served as commandery officials,
all upholding their integrity and dying in times of difficulty.
Cháng cultivated his conduct from a young age,
and served the commandery as Clerk of the Household (Hùcáo Shǐ).
In Shàngyú, there was a widow who was extremely filial in caring for her mother-in-law.
When the mother-in-law died of old age,
her husband's younger sister, who harbored resentment beforehand,
falsely accused the wife of being weary of providing care
and poisoning her mother,
and brought the case before the county court.
The commandery did not investigate further
and consequently concluded her guilt.
Cháng had already known about the injustice,
and fully explained it to the Grand Administrator,
but the Grand Administrator would not address it.
Cháng wept sorrowfully at the outer gate,
then resigned due to illness and left.
The wife ultimately died unjustly.
After this, the commandery suffered two consecutive years of drought,
and prayers yielded no results.
Later, when Grand Administrator Yīn Dān arrived in office,
he inquired about the cause.
Cháng went to the yamen and fully recounted the widow's wrongful accusation.
He then said:
"In the past, the filial woman of Dōnghǎi,
moved Heaven and caused a drought.
Yú Gōng's single word
brought timely sweet rain.
It is fitting to execute the accuser
to appease the wronged spirit,
so that hidden injustices may be redressed,
and timely rain can be hoped for."
Dān agreed,
and immediately executed the accuser and offered sacrifices at the widow's tomb.
Heaven responded with a pouring rain,
and the grain harvest was abundant.
Later, Cháng was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt (Xiàolián) candidate,
then presented as a Flourishing Talent (Màocái),
and appointed Magistrate of Xú.
The province and commandery memorialized his competence,
and he was promoted to Grand Administrator of Hépǔ.
The commandery did not produce grain,
but the sea yielded pearls and treasures.
Bordering Jiāozhǐ,
they regularly engaged in trade,
bartering for provisions.
Previously, the local officials were mostly corrupt and greedy,
deceiving people to procure them,
without knowing any limit,
so the pearls gradually migrated to the Jiāozhǐ Commandery area.
Consequently, merchants ceased to come,
and the people had no resources,
with the poor starving to death on the roads.
When Cháng arrived in office,
he reformed the previous abuses
and sought what benefited the people and eliminated their suffering.
Before even a year had passed,
the pearls that had left returned,
and the common people all resumed their occupations,
and goods circulated freely.
He was praised as divine.
Due to illness, he submitted his resignation,
and was summoned to return.
Officials and common people clung to his carriage, begging him to stay.
Since Cháng could not proceed,
he took a boat with local villagers and fled by night.
He lived in seclusion in a remote swamp,
personally working as a hired laborer.
People from neighboring counties, admiring his virtue,
came to reside near him, numbering over a hundred families.
During the reign of Emperor Huán,
Yáng Qiáo, a Minister (Shàngshū) from the same commandery, memorialized to recommend Cháng, saying:
"I have submitted seven memorials previously regarding the former Grand Administrator of Hépǔ, Mèng Cháng,
but my status is low and my words carry little weight,
so they have never been noticed.
My earnest efforts have been in vain.
Cháng is benevolent and upholds righteousness,
enjoys morality and virtue,
his pure conduct surpasses the ordinary,
and his abilities are exceptional.
When he previously served as a local official,
he transformed customs and reformed governance,
causing the pearls that had left to return,
and the starving people to be saved.
Moreover, the South Sea is rich in treasures,
and wealth is easily accumulated.
Within one's grasp,
the value can exceed double gold.
Yet Cháng, single-handedly, resigned due to illness,
personally tilled the fields,
concealing his reputation and hiding his talents,
not flaunting his brilliance.
He is truly a beautiful and useful feather,
not merely hair on the belly and back.
Yet he languishes in the wilderness,
unreached by good appointments.
The treasure of the imperial court
is discarded in ditches.
Furthermore, years have an end,
and the evening of life is approaching,
and his loyalty and integrity
will be forever missed by this sagacious era.
I am truly saddened,
and privately shed tears.
Indeed, things become precious when they come from afar,
and scholars are valued for being rare.
A gnarled and decayed piece of wood,
if used by a ruler of ten thousand chariots,
is merely tolerated by those around it.
When a king selects talent,
he should elevate those whom the multitude values.
I, with my limited capacity,
serve day and night at Your Majesty's side.
I wish to establish a humble principle
and dare not be partial to my native place.
I am secretly moved by Qín Xī,
who sacrificed himself to advance a worthy person."
Cháng was ultimately not employed.
At seventy years old,
he died at home.
Dìwǔ Fǎng, courtesy name Zhòngmóu,
was a native of Chánglíng, Jīngzhào.
He was a grandnephew of Sīkōng Lún.
He was an orphan and poor in his youth,
often working as a hired laborer to support his elder brother and sister-in-law.
Whenever he had leisure,
he would study literature.
He served the commandery as Chief Clerk (Gōngcáo),
was assessed as Filial and Incorrupt,
and appointed Magistrate of Xīndū.
His administration was fair and his reforms effective.
Within three years,
neighboring counties submitted to him,
and the population increased tenfold.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Zhāngyè.
During a famine year,
grain cost several thousand cash per shí.
Fǎng then opened the granaries to distribute provisions to alleviate the distress.
Officials feared reprimand
and vied to memorialize.
Fǎng said:
"If we wait for a reply from above,
it will be to harm the people.
The Grand Administrator is happy to save the common people with his own person!"
So he distributed grain to the people.
Emperor Shùn bestowed an imperial rescript praising him.
Because of this,
the entire commandery was saved.
After more than a year,
both officials and common people were prosperous,
and there were no bandits or thieves in the territory.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Nányáng,
then left office.
He was appointed Colonel Protector of the Qiāng (Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi),
and the border regions submitted to his authority and trustworthiness.
He died in office.
Liú Jǔ, courtesy name Shūfāng,
was a native of Xiāo, Pèiguó.
His uncle, Guāng,
served as Minister over the Masses (Sītú) during the reign of Emperor Shùn.
Jǔ had high principles from a young age.
Because his uncle Liáo had not yet obtained an official position,
he refused appointments from the province and commandery.
Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Zhū Chǒng and Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Huán Yān praised his resolve and righteousness.
Therefore, his uncle Liáo was invited by these high-ranking officials
and appointed Counsellor (Yìláng).
Only then did Jǔ accept the recommendation as Filial and Incorrupt.
He was slightly promoted to be the Magistrate of Yōngqiū.
He transformed the people with propriety and humility.
Those who lacked filial piety and righteousness
were all moved to repent and reform themselves.
When the people had disputes,
Jǔ would often summon them before him,
pull their ears, and admonish them,
saying that anger could be endured,
but the county office should not be entered.
He would send them home to reconsider.
The litigants, moved by this,
would each cease their dispute and depart.
Those who found lost items on the road
all diligently sought out their owners.
He served in the county for four years
before resigning due to his mother's mourning.
Later, Grand Commandant Hú Guǎng recommended Jǔ as a "Worthy and Upright" scholar,
and he was promoted four times to be Shàngshū Lìng.
Jǔ was naturally straightforward
and unable to accommodate himself to the powerful and influential.
Because of this, he incurred the displeasure of the General-in-Chief Liáng Jì,
and was sent out as the Administrator of Chángshān,
from which he resigned due to illness.
At that time, Sūn Zhǐ, Liáng Jì's wife's elder brother, was the Administrator of Pèi.
Jǔ feared that he would be harmed,
and dared not return to his hometown,
so he stayed at a friend's house in Péngchéng.
After more than a year,
Liáng Jì's anger somewhat subsided,
and the matter ceased.
He was appointed Congshì Zhōngláng,
then again served as Shàngshū Lìng,
and was promoted to Zōngzhèng and Tàicháng.
In the fourth year of Yánxī,
he replaced Huáng Qióng as Tàiwèi.
Huáng Qióng again served as Sīkōng.
Jǔ, Qióng, and Sītú Zhǒng Gǎo wholeheartedly assisted in governance,
and were renowned as "worthy ministers."
At that time, there were continuous calamities and anomalies.
The Sīlì Xiàowèi impeached the Three Excellencies.
Shàngshū Zhū Mù submitted a memorial,
praising Jǔ and others as good assistants,
and speaking of the righteousness of Yīn Tāng and Gāozōng not punishing their subordinates.
The Emperor did not heed it,
and they were eventually dismissed due to the rebellion of the southern barbarians.
Later, he was again appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū.
At the beginning of Emperor Líng's reign,
he replaced Zhōu Jǐng as Tàiwèi.
Jǔ twice served as one of the Three Excellencies,
and all those he recommended and summoned were renowned scholars and virtuous elders.
He did not associate with the provincial and commandery administrations.
He offered gentle and subtle remonstrances,
many of which were heeded and adopted.
He was again dismissed due to a solar eclipse.
Thereupon, he requested to retire due to old age,
and died at home.
Liú Chǒng, courtesy name Zǔróng,
was a native of Móupíng, Dōnglái.
He was a descendant of Qí Dàohuì Wáng.
Dàohuì Wáng's son, Xiàowáng Jiānglǘ,
had a younger son who was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Móupíng.
His descendants made their home there.
His father, Pī,
was widely learned,
and known as a "thorough scholar."
Chǒng received his father's instruction from a young age.
He was recommended as Xiàolián for his clear understanding of the classics
and was appointed Magistrate of Dōngpínglíng.
He was loved by officials and common people for his benevolence and kindness.
When his mother fell ill,
he resigned from office and left.
The common people lined the roads to send him off, blocking the way,
so his carriage could not advance.
He then fled in simple attire.
Later, he was promoted four times to be the Administrator of Yùzhāng,
and then promoted three times to be the Administrator of Kuàijī.
The mountain people were simple and honest;
some had white hair but had never entered the market.
They were quite disturbed by the officials.
Chǒng simplified and abolished troublesome regulations,
and prohibited and investigated illegal acts.
The commandery was greatly transformed.
He was summoned to be Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng.
In Shānyīn County, there were five or six old men,
with shaggy eyebrows and white hair,
who emerged from the valleys of Ruòyé Mountain.
Each brought a hundred coins to send Chǒng off.
Chǒng comforted them, saying:
"Why do the elders trouble yourselves so?"
They replied:
"We, humble folk of the mountain valleys,
have never seen the commandery court.
When other administrators were in office, officials would continuously demand things from the people,
until late at night,
sometimes dogs would bark all night,
and the people could not rest peacefully.
Since the enlightened lord took office,
dogs do not bark at night,
and the people do not see officials.
We, old as we are, have encountered a sage ruler.
Now we hear you are about to leave us,
so we have come to support ourselves and send you off."
Chǒng said:
"How can my governance compare to what you say?
Thank you for your hard work, elders!"
He selected one large coin from them and accepted it.
He was transferred to be Zōngzhèng and Dàhónglú.
In the fourth year of Yánxī,
he replaced Huáng Qióng as Sīkōng.
He was dismissed due to cloudy weather obstructing the sun's warmth.
Soon after,
he was appointed Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng,
and again served as Zōngzhèng.
In the first year of Jiànníng,
he replaced Wáng Chàng as Sīkōng,
and was frequently promoted to Sītú and Tàiwèi.
In the second year,
he was dismissed by imperial decree due to a solar eclipse,
and returned to his hometown.
Chǒng successively governed two commanderies,
and repeatedly rose to high ministerial positions,
yet he was frugal and simple,
with no accumulated wealth at home.
Once, when he was leaving the capital,
he wanted to rest at a courier station.
The station official stopped him,
saying:
"We are tidying up and sweeping
to await Lord Liú,
you cannot stay here."
Chǒng left without a word.
People at the time praised him as a gentleman.
He died at home from old age and illness.
His younger brother, Fāng,
rose to the post of Administrator of Shānyáng.
Fāng had two sons: Dài, courtesy name Gōngshān,
and Yáo, courtesy name Zhènglǐ.
The brothers were equally renowned.
When Dǒng Zhuó entered Luòyáng,
Dài, from being a Shìzhōng, was sent out to be the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
He was humble and cherished the people,
and was supported by the scholars.
In the third year of Chūpíng,
the Yellow Turban rebels from Qīngzhōu entered Yǎnzhōu,
killed Zhèng Suí, the Administrator of Rènchéng,
and then moved into Dōngpíng.
Dài attacked them
and died in battle.
During the Xīngpíng period,
Yáo served as the Governor of Yángzhōu and Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn.
At that time, Yuán Shù occupied Huáinán,
so Yáo moved to Qū'ā.
During a period of turmoil and chaos in the central plains,
many scholars and friends fled south.
Yáo welcomed and took them in,
sharing their hardships and pleasures,
and thus gained a great reputation.
Yuán Shù sent Sūn Cè to attack and defeat Yáo.
He then fled to Yùzhāng
and died of illness.
Qiú Lǎn (仇覽), styled Jìzhì (季智),
also named Xiāng (香),
was a native of Kǎochéng (考城) in Chénliú (陳留).
In his youth, he was a quiet and silent scholar,
unknown to his fellow villagers.
At forty years old,
the county summoned him to be an official.
He was chosen to be the Chief of Pú (蒲亭長).
He encouraged people to engage in productive work,
and established regulations for them.
Even for fruits and vegetables, limits were set;
chickens and pigs had their numbers specified.
Once farm work was completed,
he would order the younger generation to gather
and return to the academies for study.
Those who were frivolous and indulged in idleness
were all assigned to cultivate fields and mulberry trees,
and severe penalties were strictly enforced.
He personally assisted with funerals
and provided relief to the poor and widowed.
Within a year, his great civilizing influence was acclaimed.
When Lǎn (覽) first arrived at the pavilion,
there was a man named Chén Yuán (陳元),
who lived alone with his mother.
His mother went to Lǎn (覽) to accuse Yuán (元) of unfilial conduct.
Lǎn (覽) was astonished and said:
"I recently passed by his home;
his dwelling was tidy,
and his farming was done in season.
This is not a bad person;
it must be that the civilizing influence has not yet reached him.
Mother, you have kept your widowhood and raised your orphan,
toiled your body into old age.
How can you indulge your anger for a single day
and wish to bring your son to unrighteousness?"
The mother heard this and was moved to repentance,
weeping as she left.
Lǎn (覽) then personally went to Yuán's (元) home,
drank with the mother and son,
and expounded on human ethics and filial piety,
illustrating with words of fortune and misfortune.
Yuán (元) eventually became a filial son.
The local community made a proverb for this, saying:
"Where are our parents? They are in our courtyard!
He transforms us, like the owlet feeding its mother."
At that time, the Prefect of Kǎochéng (考城), Wáng Huàn (王渙) from Hénèi (河內),
whose governance was known for its strictness and severity,
heard that Lǎn (覽) civilized people with virtue.
He appointed him as Clerk (主簿).
He said to Lǎn (覽):
"Clerk, hearing of Chén Yuán's (陳元) transgression,
you did not punish but civilized him.
Do you not have a bit of the ambition of a hawk or falcon?"
Lǎn (覽) replied:
"To be a hawk or falcon
is not as good as being a phoenix."
Huàn (渙) apologized and sent him off, saying:
"Thorns are not where phoenixes perch;
a hundred *lǐ* is hardly the path for a great worthy.
Today, those at the Imperial Academy who drag long robes
and spread their fame
are all behind you, Clerk.
I give you one month's salary as a travel fund;
strive to accomplish your noble conduct."
Lǎn (覽) entered the Imperial Academy.
At that time, among the students, Fú Róng (符融) from the same commandery had a high reputation.
He lived next to Lǎn (覽),
and his room was full of guests.
Lǎn (覽) always kept to himself,
and did not speak with Róng (融).
Róng (融) observed his demeanor,
and felt uniquely impressed by him.
So he said:
"You and I are from the same commandery
and our rooms share a wall.
Now in the capital, heroes gather from all four directions,
and it is a time for ambitious men to form connections.
Although we are dedicated to classical studies,
why are you so stubbornly reclusive?"
Lǎn (覽) then sternly said:
"The Son of Heaven established the Imperial Academy,
how could it merely be for people to engage in idle talk within it!"
He gave a high bow and left,
never speaking with him again.
Later, Róng (融) told this to Guō Línzōng (郭林宗).
Línzōng (林宗) then went with Róng (融), carrying calling cards, to visit his room,
and then asked to stay overnight.
Línzōng (林宗) sighed in admiration and
stepped down from the bed to bow to him.
After Lǎn (覽) finished his studies and returned to his hometown,
both the province and commandery invited him,
but he declined all due to illness.
Even when at leisure at home,
he always maintained his conduct with propriety.
If his wife or children made a mistake,
he would immediately remove his cap and blame himself.
His wife and children would apologize in the courtyard,
and only after Lǎn (覽) put his cap back on,
would they dare to ascend to the hall.
His family never saw any difference in his expressions of joy or anger.
Later, he was summoned as an "Upright Scholar" (方正),
but he fell ill and died.
All three of his sons had literary and historical talents;
his youngest son, Xuán (玄),
was the most renowned.
Tóng Huī (童恢), styled Hànzōng (漢宗),
was a native of Gūmù (姑幕) in Lángyé (琅邪).
His father, Zhòngyù (仲玉),
encountered a period of famine and desolation.
He spent his family fortune to provide relief,
and hundreds of his clan and villagers were saved thanks to him.
Zhòngyù (仲玉) died young.
Huī (恢) served as an official in the province and commandery in his youth.
Sītú Yáng Cì (司徒楊賜) heard of his impartial and honest enforcement of the law,
and thus appointed him.
When Cì (賜) was impeached and about to be dismissed,
all the subordinates submitted their calling cards and left.
Huī (恢) alone went to the imperial court to argue on his behalf.
When Cì (賜) was cleared,
all the subordinates returned to the office,
but Huī (恢) departed with his staff.
Because of this, commentators praised him.
He was again appointed to a ducal office,
and made Prefect of Bùqí (不其).
If any officials or common people violated prohibitions or laws,
he would immediately explain the situation to them.
If officials performed their duties well,
or people performed good deeds,
he would reward them with wine and food,
to encourage them.
Farming, weaving, planting, and harvesting
all had regulations.
The entire region was peaceful and quiet;
for consecutive years, there were no prisoners in the jails.
People from neighboring counties migrated to him, drawn by his civilizing influence,
relocating over twenty thousand households.
The people were once harmed by tigers,
so he set up traps to catch them,
capturing two tigers alive.
Huī (恢) heard and came out,
cursing the tigers, saying:
"Heaven gives birth to all things,
but only humans are noble.
Tigers and wolves should eat livestock,
yet you brutally harm people.
According to the king's law, those who kill are put to death;
those who injure are judged by law.
If you are the one who killed,
you should hang your heads and confess your crime;
if you know yourselves to be innocent,
you should roar and proclaim your grievance."
One tiger lowered its head and closed its eyes,
appearing as if terrified, and was immediately killed.
The other looked at Huī (恢) and roared,
leaping and struggling,
so he ordered it to be released.
Officials and common people sang praises for him.
Qīngzhōu (青州) recommended him as "Exceptionally Distinguished,"
and he was promoted to Grand Administrator of Dānyáng (丹陽),
but he died suddenly from an illness.
His younger brother, Yì (翊), styled Hànwén (漢文),
was more renowned than Huī (恢).
The ducal offices first appointed him.
Yì (翊) pretended to be mute and refused to serve,
but when Huī (恢) received his appointment,
he then accepted the title of "Filial and Incorrupt" (孝廉)
and was made Chief of Xūchāng (須昌).
His governance was uniquely effective,
and the officials and common people erected a monument in his honor while he was still alive.
When he heard that his elder brother (referring to Huī (恢), though 'jǔ' here is ambiguous and sometimes means his elder brother as in the character '兄') was about to have a funeral,
he resigned from office and returned.
Later, he was recommended as "Flourishing Talent" (茂才),
but did not accept.
He died at home.
Eulogy says: Governance fears harshness,
order thrives on gentleness.
Extend loyalty to all,
and all afflictions will naturally disappear.
When one man understands the truth,
a thousand households play their lutes.
Their virtuous love we cherish,
forever carrying on the legacy of these worthies.
Biographies of Strict Officials, Chapter 67
The Hàn dynasty inherited the lingering ferocity of the Warring States period,
and there were many powerful and unruly people.
Those who engrossed and annexed properties overran the towns and cities;
those who were fierce and robust lorded over their villages and neighborhoods.
Furthermore, magistrates and governors were distant,
and the population was vast.
Therefore, the duty of governing the people
focused entirely on awe-inspiring decisive action,
exterminating criminals and evildoers,
acting first and reporting afterwards.
They gave full vent to their stern and resolute nature,
establishing an unyielding authority.
They defied the multitude and acted on their own judgment,
demonstrating their unfathomable wisdom.
As for those who were unjustly implicated
and swept up in the wrath of those in power,
how could their number ever be fully told?
Hence, piles of bones filled wells,
and blood flowed for ten *lǐ*.
This led Wēnshū to be known as an official with the ferocity of a tiger,
and Yánnián to receive the name of a butcher—
how could this be false?
As for their skill in thwarting powerful and influential individuals,
crushing high officials,
and shattering their heads without a second thought,
that was indeed a formidable sight.
Since the Zhongxīng era,
the legal network gradually tightened,
and the number of officials who severely harmed others
was fewer compared to previous generations.
However, eunuchs and their relatives
oppressed and abused the world.
This even led Yáng Qiú to dismember Wáng Fǔ’s corpse,
and Zhāng Jiǎn to excavate Cáo Jié’s tomb.
Such incidents,
though they satisfied public indignation,
were also extremely cruel!
Jiǎn was well-known,
so he is appended to the biography of the Dǎng Rén.
Dǒng Xuān, courtesy name Shàopíng,
was a native of Yǔ, Chénliú.
Initially, he was invited by Sītú Hóu Bà,
recommended as a man of high distinction,
and successively promoted to Běihǎi Xiàng.
Upon arriving at his post,
he appointed Gōngsūn Dān, a powerful local magnate, as Wǔguān Yuán.
Dān had recently built a new residence,
and a diviner predicted that someone would die there.
Dān then ordered his son to kill a passerby,
place the body inside the house,
to ward off the misfortune.
Xuān learned of this,
immediately arrested Dān and his son, and killed them.
Dān’s clan relatives and associates, numbering over thirty,
took up weapons and went to the magistrate’s office,
crying out and shouting their grievances.
Xuān, remembering that Dān had previously attached himself to Wáng Mǎng,
feared that he might conspire with pirates.
So he arrested them all and imprisoned them in a severe jail,
ordering his subordinate scribe, Shuǐqiū Cén, to kill them all.
Qīngzhōu province, considering this an excessive abuse,
impeached Xuān and questioned Cén.
Xuān was summoned to the Tíngwèi.
While in prison,
he recited texts day and night,
showing no sign of worry.
When it was time for his execution,
his subordinates prepared a meal to send him off.
Xuān, however, sternly said:
"Dǒng Xuān has never eaten another's food in his life,
much less when facing death!"
He then got into the cart and left.
At that time, nine other prisoners were to be executed with him,
and Xuān's turn was next.
Guāngwǔ sent a swift envoy on horseback to specifically pardon Xuān's execution,
and ordered him back to prison.
The envoy was dispatched to question Xuān about killing many innocent people.
Xuān fully explained the situation,
saying that Shuǐqiū Cén had acted on his orders,
and the guilt was not his.
He requested to be killed and Cén saved.
The envoy reported this,
and an imperial edict demoted Xuān to Huái Magistrate,
and ordered Qīngzhōu not to prosecute Cén.
Cén later rose to the position of Sīlì Xiàowèi.
Later, when the fierce bandit Xià Xǐ and others plundered Jiāngxià commandery,
Xuān was appointed Jiāngxià Tàishǒu.
Upon reaching the border,
he sent a letter saying:
"The imperial court considers the Tàishǒu capable of capturing cunning bandits,
hence this humble appointment.
Now, with troops arrayed at the border,
upon receipt of this dispatch,
you would do well to consider how to secure your own safety."
Xǐ and the others, hearing this,
were terrified
and immediately surrendered and dispersed.
The Empress’s relative, the Yīn clan, held the position of Jùn Dūwèi.
Xuān treated them with disrespect
and was dismissed for it.
Later, he was specially summoned to serve as Luòyáng Lìng.
At that time, Húyáng Gōngzhǔ’s servant killed someone in broad daylight,
and then hid in the princess’s residence,
so the officials could not apprehend him.
When the princess traveled out,
with her servant riding alongside her carriage,
Xuān waited for her at Xiàmén Tíng.
He stopped her carriage, struck her horses,
drew a line on the ground with his knife,
and loudly enumerated the princess's faults,
shouting for the servant to get out of the carriage.
He then seized and killed him.
The princess immediately returned to the palace to complain to the Emperor.
The Emperor was furious,
summoned Xuān,
and wanted to flog him to death.
Xuān kowtowed and said:
"I beg to utter one word before I die."
The Emperor said:
"What do you wish to say?"
Xuān replied:
"Your Majesty’s sagely virtue has restored the dynasty,
yet you indulge a servant in killing an innocent person.
How will you govern the world then?
I do not need a flogging;
I request to take my own life."
He then struck his head against a pillar,
blood flowing over his face.
The Emperor ordered a junior eunuch to hold him
and make Xuān kowtow and apologize to the princess.
Xuān refused.
When forced to bow,
Xuān braced himself with both hands on the ground,
absolutely refusing to yield.
The princess said:
"When Wénshū was a commoner,
he harbored fugitives and hid those who had committed capital crimes,
and officials dared not approach his gate.
Now that he is the Son of Heaven,
can his authority not even enforce a single command?"
The Emperor smiled and said:
"The Son of Heaven is not the same as a commoner."
He then ordered the "Strong-Necked Magistrate" to leave.
He was given thirty thousand coins,
which Xuān distributed entirely among his subordinates.
From then on, he confronted powerful and influential figures,
and none failed to tremble.
The capital called him
"Crouching Tiger."
A song about him went:
"The drums do not beat for Dǒng Shàopíng."
He served in the county for five years.
At seventy-four,
he died in office.
An imperial edict sent an envoy to inspect his residence,
who found only a cloth blanket covering his corpse,
his wife and children weeping,
a few *hú* of barley, and one dilapidated cart.
The Emperor was saddened by this and
said:
"Dǒng Xuān was incorruptible;
I only knew it upon his death!"
Because Xuān had once been a two-thousand-piculs official,
he was granted an ái seal and ribbon,
and buried with the rites of a grandee.
His son, Bìng, was appointed Lángzhōng,
and later served as Qí Xiàng.
Fán Yè, courtesy name Zhònghuá,
was a native of Xīnyě, Nányáng.
He had been an old acquaintance of Guāngwǔ in his youth.
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
he was summoned to serve as Shìyùshǐ,
promoted to Hédōng Dūwèi,
and granted an audience at Yúntái.
Earlier,
when Guāngwǔ was a commoner,
he was once detained on a matter in Xīnyě.
Yè, then a market official,
gave him a basket of pastries.
The Emperor gratefully remembered this,
and subsequently bestowed upon Yè imperial food
and imperial carriage attire.
He then playfully said:
"A basket of pastries for a Dūwèi,
how about that?"
Yè bowed his head in thanks and declined.
Upon arriving at the commandery,
he executed powerful local magnates like Mǎ Shìkuāng.
Bandits were cleared,
and officials and common people feared him.
After several years,
he was promoted to Yángzhōu Mù,
teaching the people methods for farming, planting trees, and managing their households.
After serving for over ten years,
he was demoted to Zhǐ Magistrate due to a legal transgression.
After Wěi Xiāo was destroyed,
Lǒngyòu became unsettled.
Thus, Fán Yè was appointed Grand Administrator of Tiānshuǐ.
His administration was severe and fierce,
fond of Shēn Bùhài and Hán Fēi's legalist principles,
and he made immediate judgments on good and evil.
Those who violated his prohibitions
rarely left prison alive.
Officials, commoners, Qiāng, and Hú feared him.
Nothing was picked up from the roads.
Travelers, arriving at night,
would gather their clothes and luggage by the roadside,
saying,
"We entrust this to Lord Fán."
Liángzhōu sang a song about him, saying:
"Wandering sons often suffer poverty,
industrious sons are enriched by heaven.
I'd rather face a tiger's den,
than enter the Yì Fǔ Temple.
A loud laugh ensures certain death,
anger might spare one.
Alas, our Lord Fán Fǔ,
how can we encounter him again!"
He served for fourteen years
and died in office.
During the Yǒngpíng reign,
Xiǎnzōng recalled Fán Yè's administrative abilities when he was in Tiānshuǐ,
believing that no one after him could compare.
An imperial edict granted his family a million cash.
His son, Fán Róng,
was exceptionally talented,
fond of Huáng Lǎo Daoism,
and refused to become an official.
Lǐ Zhāng, whose courtesy name was Dìgōng,
was from Huái, Hénèi.
For five generations, his family held positions of two thousand Dàn.
Lǐ Zhāng studied Yán Shì Chūnqiū,
was a clear and effective teacher of the classics,
and served as an official in various provinces and commanderies.
When Guāngwǔ was Grand Marshal,
pacifying Héběi,
he summoned Lǐ Zhāng and appointed him as a subordinate in the Eastern Bureau,
often accompanying him on campaigns.
Upon Guāngwǔ's ascension to the throne,
he appointed Lǐ Zhāng as Magistrate of Yángpíng.
At that time, powerful local magnates in Zhào and Wèi often gathered their forces.
Zhào Gāng, a prominent clan leader from Qīnghé, thus built a fortified encampment within the county's borders,
equipped armor and weapons,
and was a menace to the locality.
When Lǐ Zhāng arrived,
he arranged a banquet
and invited Zhào Gāng.
Zhào Gāng, wearing an ornamented sword
and feather robes, came with over a hundred followers.
Lǐ Zhāng feasted and drank with him.
After a while,
he personally drew his sword and
executed Zhào Gāng.
His hidden troops also killed all of Zhào Gāng's followers.
He then swiftly rode to the fortified encampment,
launched a surprise attack, and destroyed it.
The officials and commoners then found peace.
He was promoted to Grand Administrator of Qiānchéng.
For executing bandits and thieves excessively,
he was summoned to prison and dismissed.
Within a year, he was appointed Palace Investigating Censor,
and then transferred out to be Grand Administrator of Lángyé.
At that time, Xià Chángsī and other prominent clan leaders from Ānqiū, Běihǎi, rebelled,
imprisoned the Grand Administrator Chǔ Xìng,
and occupied the city of Yínglíng.
When Lǐ Zhāng heard this,
he immediately dispatched a thousand soldiers
and rushed to attack them.
A clerk (or official) stopped Lǐ Zhāng, saying:
"A two thousand Dàn official must not leave his jurisdiction,
nor may he mobilize troops."
Lǐ Zhāng, gripping his sword, angrily said:
"These rebellious scoundrels are behaving outrageously,
imprisoning and abducting the Grand Administrator!
How can this be tolerated!
If I die for suppressing bandits,
I shall have no regrets!"
He then led his troops to the foot of Ānqiū city,
recruited brave men to burn the city gates,
fought Xià Chángsī,
beheaded him,
captured over three hundred heads,
and returned with over five hundred cattle and horses.
Chǔ Xìng returned to the commandery,
reported the situation to the Emperor,
and distributed all the spoils to reward the officials and soldiers.
Later, he was impeached for inaccurate assessments of people's land for taxation.
Because Lǐ Zhāng had rendered meritorious service,
he was merely judged by the Minister of Justice.
After more than a month, he was released from punishment and returned home.
He was later summoned again,
but died of illness.
Zhōu Yù, whose courtesy name was Wéntōng,
was from Xú, Xiàpī.
He was a sharp and unmerciful man,
fond of Hán Fēi's methods.
In his youth, he was a clerk in the Grand Judge's office.
During the Yǒngpíng reign,
he was appointed Magistrate of Nánxíngtáng.
Upon arriving at his post,
he instructed his officials, saying:
"The court does not deem me unworthy,
and has made me shepherd the common people.
By nature, I am an enemy of cunning officials,
and my ambition is to eliminate powerful bandits.
Let us not test each other!"
He then executed several dozen of the most egregious offenders in the county,
which greatly alarmed the officials and commoners.
He was promoted to Magistrate of Bó Píng.
He arrested and interrogated corrupt individuals;
none left prison alive.
Due to his fearsome reputation, he was promoted to Chancellor of Qí.
He was also quite severe and cruel,
relying exclusively on penal law.
However, he was skilled at drafting legal documents and regulations,
serving as a model for the province.
Later, for killing an innocent person,
he was demoted again to Magistrate of Bó Píng.
During the Jiànchū reign,
he became Grand Administrator of Bóhǎi.
Whenever an imperial amnesty arrived in the commandery,
he would conceal it and not announce it.
He would first send envoys to the subordinate counties to clear all criminal cases,
and only then would he release the imperial edict.
For this, he was summoned to the Grand Judge's office
and dismissed to return home.
He was honest and incorruptible, without personal wealth,
often making bricks to support himself.
Sùzōng heard of this and pitied him,
reappointing him as a Gentleman,
and then twice promoted him to Chancellor of Shàolíng Marquisate.
The county clerks, fearing his strictness and clarity,
wished to undermine his authority.
So, one morning, they took a dead person, cut off their hands and feet,
and placed them at the temple gate.
Zhōu Yù heard of it,
went to the side of the dead person,
as if conversing with the dead.
He secretly observed their mouth and eyes for rice husks.
Then he secretly asked the gatekeeper:
"Who carried straw into the city?"
The gatekeeper replied:
"Only the county clerk."
He then asked his attendants:
"Did anyone outside suspect me of speaking with the dead?"
They replied:
"The county clerk suspected you."
So, he arrested the county clerk and interrogated him,
who fully confessed,
"I did not kill anyone,
but took a dead person from the roadside."
After this, no one dared to deceive him.
He was summoned and appointed Magistrate of Luòyáng.
Upon arriving at his post,
he first asked for the names of the prominent clans.
His officials listed the powerful magnates in the neighborhoods in response.
He sternly and angrily said:
"I asked about noble relatives like the Mǎ and Dòu families.
How could I know these vegetable-selling peddlers?"
Thereupon, his subordinate officials, understanding his intentions,
eagerly sought to be incisive and decisive in their actions.
The noble relatives became circumspect,
and the capital was thoroughly purified.
Dòu Dú, brother of the Empress and a Yellow Gate Attendant, returned from the palace.
At night, he stopped at Zhǐjiān Pavilion.
The pavilion head, Huò Yán, stopped Dòu Dú.
Dòu Dú's servant disputed with him.
Huò Yán then drew his sword and pointed it at Dòu Dú,
cursing him freely.
Dòu Dú reported this incident to the Emperor.
An edict summoned the Commander of the Metropolitan Police and the Prefect of Hénán to the Department of State Affairs for censure and interrogation.
Armed guards were sent to arrest Huò Yán and deliver him to the Grand Judge's imperial prison.
He was released after several days.
The Emperor knew that Zhōu Yù upheld the law and detested corruption,
and did not curry favor with the noble relatives.
However, his severity and cruelty were excessive,
and he was often impeached by the appropriate authorities.
After eight years,
he was dismissed from office.
Later, he became Palace Assistant Imperial Censor.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne,
Grand Tutor Dèng Biāo memorialized that Zhōu Yù had been excessively cruel in his post,
and was unsuitable to manage the affairs of the capital.
He was dismissed and returned to his hometown.
Later, when the Dòu clan became powerful and prominent,
Dòu Dú and his brothers wielded authority.
All who had incurred their slightest displeasure or old grudges were brought down.
Zhōu Yù thought he would not escape unharmed,
so he barred his gate and remained isolated,
awaiting his misfortune.
However, because Dòu Dú and his brothers were just,
and the animosity had a clear origin,
they ultimately dared not harm him.
In the fifth year of Yǒngyuán,
he was again summoned to serve as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Although the Zhū Dòu had been executed,
Héyáng Hóu Guī was still in court.
He detested him,
and so submitted a memorial saying:
“Your servant has heard that when Zāng Wénzhòng served his lord,
if he saw someone who treated his lord with courtesy,
he served them as a filial son would care for his parents;
if he saw someone who treated his lord with disrespect,
he executed them as a hawk or falcon hunts sparrows.
Examining Héyáng Hóu Guī,
he originally came from a frivolous background,
his ambition lay in perversity,
he had no classical learning,
yet he presumptuously set up a lecture hall,
externally recruiting Confucian scholars,
but actually gathering rogues and villains.
He lightly regards heavenly majesty,
and insults the imperial house.
Moreover, he fabricated books on imperial tours and the Fēng Shàn sacrifices,
deceiving the masses with impropriety.
He ought to be put to death,
yet those in charge pursue private interests,
not considering the welfare of the state.
Though a trickle of water is small,
it can eventually form rivers;
though a spark is tiny,
it can ultimately set a field ablaze.
Walking on frost is a gradual process;
how can one not reform and rectify?
It is fitting to recall Lǚ Chǎn's exclusive usurpation and rebellion,
and forever remember Wáng Mǎng's treachery and usurpation,
to secure the plans for the state,
and dispel the confusion of the myriad people.”
It happened that Guī returned to his fief,
and he was promoted to Sīlì Xiàowèi.
In the summer of the sixth year, there was a drought.
The imperial carriage personally visited Luòyáng to review prisoners.
Two people were tortured and produced maggots.
He was demoted to Zuǒ Zhuǎn Qí Dūwèi.
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng.
In the ninth year,
he died in office.
Huáng Chāng, courtesy name Shèngzhēn,
was a native of Yúyáo, Kuàijī.
His family was originally humble.
Living near the academy,
he often saw students performing the rites of the academy,
and consequently developed a liking for it,
thus engaging in classical studies.
He also understood and practiced legal texts,
and served the commandery as Juécáo.
The inspector, while on tour,
saw Chāng,
and greatly admired him,
appointing him as an attendant.
Later, he was appointed Wǎnlìng.
His administration favored severity and strictness,
and he delighted in exposing hidden evil.
There was a person who stole his carriage canopy.
Chāng initially said nothing,
but later secretly dispatched trusted retainers to the household of the door guard's criminal clerk to seize it,
and arrested everyone in his household,
executing them all at once.
The great families were terrified,
all proclaiming his divine sagacity.
The imperial court recognized his ability,
and promoted him to Shǔjùn Tàishǒu.
The former Prefect, Lǐ Gēn, was old and often made perverse rulings,
causing the common people to suffer injustice.
When Chāng arrived,
there were over seven hundred officials and commoners lodging complaints.
He judged and settled all of them,
and none failed to obtain justice.
He secretly apprehended a bandit leader,
and coerced him into listing the names and residences of the violent and powerful people in all the counties.
Then he dispatched men to surround and attack them,
leaving no one behind.
Long-standing evildoers and great villains
all fled to other territories.
Originally,
when Chāng was a clerk in the province,
his wife returned home to visit her family,
encountered bandits, was captured,
and subsequently drifted to Shǔ to become another man's wife.
Her son committed a crime,
and so she went to Chāng to plead her case.
Chāng suspected the mother was not like the people of Shǔ,
and so asked about her origins.
She replied:
“Your servant is originally Dài Cìgōng's daughter from Yúyáo, Kuàijī,
and the wife of the provincial clerk Huáng Chāng.
I once returned home,
was captured by bandits,
and thus came to this place.”
Chāng was surprised,
called her forward and said:
“How do you recognize Huáng Chāng?”
She replied:
“Chāng has a black mole on the sole of his left foot,
and he always said he would become a Two-Thousand-Picul official.”
Chāng then revealed his foot to her.
They then embraced each other, weeping with sorrow,
and were reunited as husband and wife.
After serving for four years,
he was recalled,
and twice promoted to Chén Xiāng.
There was a Pēng family in the county, formerly powerful and unrestrained,
who had built a grand residence
with a tall building overlooking the road.
Whenever Chāng traveled through the county,
women of the Pēng family would ascend the building to watch.
Chāng was displeased,
and consequently ordered them arrested and imprisoned,
and had them executed after an investigation.
He was again promoted to Hénèi Tàishǒu,
and then again promoted to Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
In the fifth year of Yǒnghé,
he was summoned and appointed Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng.
In the first year of Hàn'ān,
he was advanced to Dà Sīnóng,
then demoted to Tàizhōng Dàfū,
and died in office.
Yáng Qiú, courtesy name Fāngzhèng,
was a native of Quánzhōu, Yúyáng.
His family had been a great gentry family for generations.
Qiú was skilled in swordsmanship
and practiced archery and horsemanship.
His nature was stern and severe,
and he favored the teachings of Shēn Bùhài and Hán Fēi.
A commandery official insulted his mother.
Qiú gathered several tens of youths,
killed the official,
and exterminated his family,
thereby becoming renowned.
He was first nominated as Xiàolián,
and appointed Shàngshū Shìláng.
He was familiar with precedents and established practices,
and his memorials and proposals
were always highly esteemed and trusted by the court.
He was posted out as Gāotáng Lìng,
but was dismissed due to excessive harshness in governance.
The commandery governor arrested and impeached him,
but he was pardoned during an amnesty.
He was invited to the residence of Sītú Liú Chǒng,
and was recommended as a High Talent.
Bandits rose in Jiǔjiāng,
and could not be suppressed for months.
The three highest offices recommended Qiú as having talent for managing villains,
and he was appointed Jiǔjiāng Tàishǒu.
Upon Qiú's arrival,
he devised strategies,
and the vicious bandits were annihilated.
He arrested and executed all the corrupt officials in the commandery.
He was promoted to Píngyuán Xiāng.
He issued an edict saying:
“I previously served as Gāotáng Lìng,
and intended to eliminate corruption and villainy,
but was unjustly impeached by your noble commandery.
In the past, Duke Huán released Guǎn Zhòng from the enmity of shooting the hook,
and Emperor Gāozǔ pardoned Jì Bù for the crime of being a fugitive.
Though I lack virtue,
how dare I forget the former righteousness?
Moreover, the division between ruler and subject is fixed,
so how can one harbor past grudges!
Now I shall pardon past transgressions,
expecting future good conduct.
If, after receiving this instruction, one does not reform one's villainous ways,
there will be no further tolerance.”
Everyone in the commandery feared and submitted to him.
At that time, there was a great drought across the land.
Sīkōng Zhāng Hào submitted a memorial listing harsh, cruel, and greedy long-term officials,
and all were dismissed.
Qiú was dismissed due to his severity and harshness,
summoned to the Tíngwèi,
and was about to be removed from office.
Emperor Líng, considering Qiú's achievements during his time in Jiǔjiāng,
appointed him Yìláng.
He was promoted to Grand Architect,
but was condemned for an offense.
After a short while,
he was appointed Grand Secretariat.
He memorialized to abolish the Hóngdū Academy of Literature,
saying:

“I humbly understand there is an imperial edict instructing the Central Imperial Workshop to depict and laud thirty-two individuals, including Yuè Sōng and Jiāng Lǎn of the Hóngdū Academy of Literature,
to encourage scholars.
Your servant has heard the proverb which says: ‘When the lord acts, it must be recorded.
If it is recorded but not according to the law,
what will later generations observe!’
Upon investigation, Yuè Sōng, Jiāng Lǎn, and others all came from humble and obscure backgrounds,
insignificant persons
who relied on powerful relatives,
attached themselves to influential magnates,
bowed their brows and watched their every move,
to achieve advancement in a bright era.
Some presented one rhapsody,
others filled a scroll with bird-script,
and yet they were promoted to Lángzhōng,
and their figures were depicted in painting.
There are also those whose brushes never touched the page,
whose words did not reflect their hearts,
who used others to write on their behalf,
practicing a hundred kinds of deceit and falsehood,
all of whom received special favor,
shedding their murky origins.
Therefore, discerning people cover their mouths,
and the world laments.
Your servant has heard that the purpose of establishing images
is to illustrate encouragement and warning,
to make the ruler keenly aware of gains and losses.
It has never been heard that lowly individuals,
who fraudulently compose eulogies,
could presumptuously usurp imperial offices,
and have their images hung on plain silk.
Currently, the Grand Academy and the Eastern Lodge are sufficient to proclaim and illuminate the sagely transformation.
I wish to abolish the selection of Hóngdū,
to eliminate the world’s censure.”
His memorial was submitted but not heeded.
At that time, the Central Regular Attendants Wáng Fǔ and Cáo Jié and others were wicked and wielded power oppressively,
stirring up trouble inside and out.
Yáng Qiú often slapped his thigh and expressed his indignation, saying:
“If Yáng Qiú were Sīlì,
how could these fellows be tolerated?”
In Guānghé second year (179 CE),
he was promoted to Commandant of the Capital.
Wáng Fǔ was on leave at his residence.
Yáng Qiú went to the imperial court to offer thanks,
and memorialized for the arrest of Wáng Fǔ and the Central Regular Attendants Chúnyú Dēng, Yuán Shè, Fēng Bá,
Central Yellow Gate Liú Yì, Minor Yellow Gate Páng Xùn, Zhū Yǔ, Qí Shèng, etc.,
as well as their sons and younger brothers who served as administrators or magistrates,
who were treacherous and indulged in wanton behavior,
their crimes deserving of extermination of their clans.
The Grand Commandant Duàn Jiǒng fawned over and attached himself to corrupt favorites,
and should also be executed.
Thereupon, Wáng Fǔ, Duàn Jiǒng, and others were all arrested and sent to Luòyáng prison,
along with Wáng Fǔ’s son Wáng Méng, the Yonglè Prefect, and Wáng Jí, the Administrator of Pèi.
Yáng Qiú personally supervised the interrogation of Wáng Fǔ and others,
applying all five extreme tortures.
Wáng Méng said to Yáng Qiú:
“Since father and son are to be executed,
please spare my old father some of this torture.”
Yáng Qiú said:
“Your crimes are monstrous,
and even death cannot atone for them,
yet you still ask for mercy?”
Wáng Méng then cursed, saying:
“You previously served my father and me like a slave.
How dare a slave turn against his master!
Today you torment me,
but retribution will soon reach you!”
Yáng Qiú ordered dirt to be used to gag Wáng Méng,
and whipping and beating ensued,
both father and son died under the rods.
Duàn Jiǒng also committed suicide.
Wáng Fǔ’s corpse was then stretched and exposed at Xiàchéng Gate,
with a large sign proclaiming
“Traitorous Minister Wáng Fǔ.”
All his property was confiscated,
and his wife and children were exiled to Bǐjǐng.
After Yáng Qiú executed Wáng Fǔ,
he intended to next impeach Cáo Jié and others,
so he instructed the Central Capital Officials saying:
“First eliminate the great villains,
then we will investigate the powerful and influential.”
When the powerful families heard this,
none dared to breathe.
All luxurious items
were sealed away,
none dared to display them.
The capital was struck with fear.
At that time, Empress Shùn’s noble consort Yú was buried.
When the hundred officials returned from the funeral,
Cáo Jié saw Wáng Fǔ’s corpse exposed by the roadside,
and sadly wiped away tears, saying:
“We imperial attendants can devour each other,
but why should dogs be allowed to lick their juices?”
He told the other attendants,
“Let us all go in together now,
and not pass by our residences.”
Cáo Jié went straight into the palace,
and reported to the Emperor, saying:
“Yáng Qiú is a naturally cruel and violent official.
Previously, the Three Excellencies memorialized for his dismissal,
but due to his minor merit in Jiǔjiāng,
he was again promoted and appointed.
Such a flawed person,
who loves to act recklessly,
should not be allowed to remain as Sīlì,
to unleash his cruelty.”
The Emperor then transferred Yáng Qiú to Commandant of the Guards.
At that time, Yáng Qiú was out to pay respects at the imperial mausoleum.
Cáo Jié instructed the Grand Secretariat to summon and appoint him,
allowing no delay for even a foot and an inch.
Yáng Qiú was summoned urgently,
and requested an audience with the Emperor,
kowtowing and saying:
“Your servant has no noble conduct,
but has undeservedly received the responsibility of a hawk or dog.
Although I previously investigated and executed Wáng Fǔ and Duàn Jiǒng,
that was merely removing some foxes and badgers,
not enough to declare to the world.
I beg your Majesty to grant me one month,
and I will surely make the jackals, wolves, owls, and vultures
each receive their just punishment.”
He kowtowed until his head bled.
Those in the palace hall shouted:
“Is the Commandant of the Guards defying the imperial edict?!”
This happened two or three times,
before he finally accepted the appointment.
That winter,
the Minister of Works Liú Hé and Yáng Qiú discussed arresting Zhāng Ràng and Cáo Jié.
Cáo Jié and others learned of this,
and jointly slandered Liú Hé and others to the Emperor.
The details are already in the biography of Chén Qiú.
Thereupon, Yáng Qiú was arrested and sent to Luòyáng prison,
executed,
and his wife and children were exiled to the frontier.
Wáng Jí was
a native of Jùnyí, Chénliú,
and the adopted son of the Central Regular Attendant Wáng Fǔ.
Wáng Fǔ is in the Biography of Eunuchs.
Wáng Jí was fond of reciting classics and commentaries in his youth,
and delighted in fame,
but his nature was cruel and ruthless.
Because his father held power and favor,
at the age of twenty-plus,
he became the Administrator of Pèi.
He was knowledgeable in governance,
capable of judging and discerning difficult cases,
exposing hidden treachery,
often surpassing common opinion.
He ordered the counties within his commandery to each report corrupt officials and powerful individuals who had committed minor offenses involving wine and meat as bribes,
and even if decades had passed, they were still demoted and disgraced,
their names recorded in the register.
He specifically selected fierce and decisive officials
to punish illegal acts.
If anyone gave birth to a child and did not raise it,
he would immediately execute the parents,
and bury them together in a thorny pit.
Whenever someone was killed, their corpse was exposed on a cart,
according to the nature of their crime,
and paraded through the affiliated counties.
If it rotted in summer,
then their bones were strung together with rope,
and paraded throughout the entire commandery before stopping,
which terrified those who saw it.
In his five years in office,
he killed over ten thousand people in total.
Other brutal and vicious tortures
were innumerable.
The commandery was filled with dread,
no one dared to feel safe.
When Yáng Qiú impeached Wáng Fǔ,
Wáng Jí was arrested,
and died in Luòyáng prison.
Discussion: In ancient times, people were simple and honest,
and good and evil were easily distinguished.
It reached the point where clothes and caps were prescribed,
and clothing colors differentiated,
and no one dared transgress.
In later, decadent ages, integrity diminished,
and superiors and subordinates deceived each other.
Virtue and righteousness were insufficient to reconcile them,
and moral guidance could not deter wrongdoing.
Consequently, severe punishments and brutal executions were employed,
and rules were subsequently enforced.
Harsh and severe officials were appointed
to violently manage evildoers,
relying on the impartial righteousness of those who abhorred wickedness
to carry out their cruel and oppressive desires.
The so-called "cruelly capable" officials of the Hàn era
were certainly well-known.
They were all distinguished by their daring, astute, and quick-witted nature,
cleverly attaching themselves to legal principles,
sweeping through like a harsh frost,
with their prestige and renown clamorously resounding.
How different they were in their skill and lack thereof
from those officials who stubbornly adhered to the Dao!
Therefore, Yán Jūn scorned the methods of Huáng Bà,
and those close to Mì Rén laughed at Zhuó Mào's governance.
Though severity had reached its extreme,
it still often failed to prevail.
Yet Zhū Yì never inflicted flogging or humiliation upon others,
and Yuán Ān never interrogated anyone for corruption,
but cunning evildoers restrained themselves,
and people did not cheat or offend.
Why was this?
It is because when deterrent laws are employed,
actions of mere evasion arise;
〔一０〕when benevolence and trustworthiness are deeply embraced,
the sentiment of being influenced and transformed becomes evident.
〔一一〕Those who merely evade will commit crimes when strictness relaxes;
those who are influenced will remember and cherish even after the person is gone.
〔一二〕If we apply this from a single region to the entire realm,
could the proliferation of lawsuits and punishments
be something we would seek?
Eulogy: When the Great Dao had departed,
punishment and ritual became shallow.
People became scattered,
and deceit and trickery began to sprout.
Dispensing with killing stems from benevolence,
and showing leniency is not cruelty.
Though ultimate violence may prevail,
the fundamental principles are often neglected.
Biography of Eunuchs, Chapter 68
The Yì Jīng says:
"Heaven displays its images,
and the sages emulate them."
The four stars of the eunuchs
are beside the imperial position;
thus, the Zhōu Lǐ also established officials
to fill their numbers.
The gatekeepers guarded the prohibitions of the inner gate,
and the court attendants managed the rules of the women's palace.
It also says,
"There are five officials who preside over the King's inner court."
The Yuè Lìng states:
"In mid-winter,
the eunuch-overseer is ordered to inspect the gates and alleys,
and carefully manage the private chambers."
In the Xiǎo Yǎ of the Shī Jīng,
there is also the chapter "Xiàng Bó" criticizing slander.
However, the presence of eunuchs in the imperial court
has a long history.
Is it because their bodies are not whole,
and their emotions and will are entirely devoted and good,
that they can communicate with those within the palace,
and are easy to employ and nurture?
Nevertheless, later generations continued this,
and their talents and responsibilities gradually expanded.
Among the capable ones,
Bó Diāo and Guǎn Sū rendered meritorious service to Chǔ and Jìn;
Jǐng Jiān and Miáo Xián achieved distinction in Qín and Zhào.
But when they became corrupt,
Shù Diāo brought chaos to Qí,
and Yī Lì brought disaster to Sòng.
When the Hàn dynasty arose,
it largely adopted the Qín system,
establishing the office of Zhōng Cháng Shì.
However, they also appointed scholars
to join their ranks,
all wearing silver hat-ornaments and left-side mink tails,
serving in the palace chambers.
When Empress Gāo assumed regency,
she appointed Zhāng Qīng as Grand Attendant (dà yè zhě),
who entered and exited her private chambers,
receiving and proclaiming imperial edicts.
During Emperor Wén's reign,
there were Zhào Tán and Běi Gōng Bó Zǐ,
who were quite favored.
As for Emperor Wǔ,
he also loved Lǐ Yán Nián.
The Emperor often feasted in the rear palace,
or secretly visited detached palaces,
hence important state affairs requiring submission
were often handled by eunuchs.
By the time of Emperor Yuán,
Shǐ Yóu served as Huáng Mén Lìng,
devoting his heart to offering loyal advice,
which brought some benefits.
Later, Hóng Gōng and Shí Xiǎn advanced through flattery and treachery,
eventually leading to the disasters involving Xiāo and Zhōu,
thus defiling the imperial virtue.
At the beginning of the Restoration (Zhōng Xīng),
all eunuch officials were exclusively eunuchs,
no longer mixing in other scholars.
During the Yǒng Píng era,
a fixed number of positions was first established:
four Zhōng Cháng Shì,
and ten Xiǎo Huáng Mén.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne, he was young and weak,
and Dòu Xiàn and his brothers monopolized all power and authority.
Officials inside and outside the court
had no way to directly approach the emperor,
and those who stayed with him
were only the eunuchs.
Thus, Zhèng Zhòng gained exclusive power to scheme within the forbidden palace,
eventually eliminating the great villain,
and subsequently enjoying enfeoffment with land,
and being promoted to the position of a palace minister.
From then on, the power of inner court officials (eunuchs) began to flourish.
From Emperor Míng onwards,
up to the Yán Píng era,
their delegated authority gradually increased,
and their numbers slightly grew.
The Zhōng Cháng Shì reached ten individuals,
and the Xiǎo Huáng Mén twenty,
now wearing golden hat-ornaments and right-side mink tails,
also holding positions as court ministers.
When Empress Déng presided over the government as a female ruler,
and myriad state affairs were complex and distant,
court officials and national deliberations
had no way to participate in decisions behind the screens.
Issuing edicts and proclaiming orders
could not go beyond the private chambers of the empress,
and she had no choice but to rely on castrated men,
entrusting them with the fate of the nation.
They held royal titles in their hands,
and pronounced imperial laws with their mouths,
no longer merely serving in the imperial women's quarters
or managing household affairs.
Later, Sūn Chéng established the merit of appointing Emperor Shùn,
and Cáo Téng participated in devising strategies for establishing Emperor Huán.
This was followed by the five marquises conspiring together,
and Liáng Jì being given the axe (executed).
Their actions were based on justice,
and their favor was secured in the emperor's heart.
Thus, both those inside and outside the court obeyed,
and superiors and subordinates held their breath.
Some praised them for achievements like Yī Yǐn and Huò Qùbìng,
saying they were no less than those of old;
others said that the plans of Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng
were revived in their time.
Although there were occasionally loyal and public-spirited individuals,
they were ultimately rejected and expelled.
Their actions could move mountains and seas,
and their breath could change frost and dew.
If one catered to their wishes and sought their favor,
their three clans would be glorified;
if one was straightforward and opposed their will,
their five clans would be destroyed.
The Hàn dynasty's governance and discipline were in great disorder.
As for those with tall caps and long swords,
who wore crimson and carried gold,
they filled the palace chambers;
those who were enfeoffed with land and given tiger tallies,
who sat facing south and ruled over others,
numbered perhaps in the tens.
Their administrative offices, mansions, and villas
were arrayed throughout the capital and provinces;
their sons, younger brothers, and dependents
accounted for more than half the population of the prefectures and states.
Piles of southern gold, Hébǎo jewels, bīngwán silk, and wùhú gauze
filled their treasure houses;
the pleasures of qiángyuán beauties,侍兒 attendants, gētóng singers, and wǔnǚ dancers
fully equipped their luxurious chambers.
Dogs and horses were adorned with carved patterns,
and structures of earth and wood were covered with crimson embroidery.
All of them exploited the common people,
competing to indulge their extravagant desires.
They conspired to harm sagacious and virtuous people,
and exclusively promoted their own factions.
Those who mutually supported and promoted each other,
and attached themselves to the powerful,
all corrupted their bodies and defiled their descendants
to flaunt their advancement.
Sharing in corruption and helping each other,
their followers thus multiplied,
and the affairs that ruined the state and corrupted the government
cannot be fully enumerated.
Consequently, the whole empire groaned in agony,
men of ambition lived in impoverished obscurity,
bandits and rebels seized opportunities,
and disturbed the central plains.
Although loyal and good men harbored indignation,
and sometimes rose up,
their words brought calamity,
and they were soon annihilated.
Therefore, a large-scale investigation of "hooked parties" was again conducted,
and accusations spread to implicate others.
〔一０〕All those called virtuous gentlemen
could not escape suffering from calamity and poison.
Dòu Wǔ and Hé Jìn,
though their positions were exalted and they were close relatives of the imperial family,
rode on the widespread resentment of the nine provinces
and rallied the power and influence of heroes,
〔一一〕yet due to their indecision and hesitation,
they met with ruin.
Was this not the extreme of fate!
Although Yuán Shào acted ruthlessly
and swept them away completely,
to replace chaos with tyranny
was of no avail!
〔一二〕Since Cáo Téng persuaded Liáng Jì,
resulting in the establishment of a weak and ignorant emperor,
〔一三〕Wèi Wǔ took advantage of this,
and thus relocated the imperial altars.
〔一四〕The saying,
"The sovereign who begins with this
will surely end with this,"
is indeed true!
〔一五〕
Zhèng Zhòng, courtesy name Jìchǎn,
was a man from Chōu, Nányáng.
He was cautious, quick-witted, and insightful.
During the Yǒngpíng reign,
he first served in the Crown Prince's household.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
he was appointed Assistant Yellow Gate,
and promoted to Regular Palace Attendant.
At the beginning of Hédì's reign,
he was further appointed Gōudùn Lìng.
At that time, Empress Dowager Dòu held power,
and her brother, General-in-Chief Dòu Xiàn, and others all usurped authority.
Officials, high and low, all attached themselves to them,
but Zhòng alone remained loyal to the imperial house,
and did not curry favor with the powerful factions.
The emperor deeply trusted him.
When Xiàn and his brothers planned to rebel,
Zhòng was the first to plot their extermination,
and for his merit was promoted to Grand Chief Guardian.
When merits were evaluated and rewards distributed,
he always declined much and accepted little,
thus he was always consulted in deliberations.
The use of power by court eunuchs
began with Zhòng.
In the fourteenth year,
the emperor, remembering Zhòng's excellent service,
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Chāoxiāng,
with an income of one thousand five hundred households.
In the first year of Yǒngchū,
Empress Dowager Héxī increased his income by three hundred households.
He died in the first year of Yuánchū,
and his adopted son Hóng succeeded him.
After Hóng's death,
his son Ān succeeded him.
Later, the marquisate was abolished.
In the second year of Yánxī, during Huándì's reign,
Zhòng's great-grandson, Shí Chóu, was granted the title of Marquis within the Passes.
Cài Lún, courtesy name Jìngzhòng,
was a man from Guìyáng.
At the end of Yǒngpíng, he began serving in the imperial household,
and during Jiànchū,
he became a Junior Yellow Gate.
When Hédì ascended the throne,
he was transferred to Regular Palace Attendant,
and participated in confidential court affairs.
Lún possessed talent and learning,
and was diligent and cautious.
He often risked offending the emperor
to correct his errors.
Whenever he had a day off,
he would close his door, refuse guests,
and expose himself to the elements in the countryside.
Later, he was promoted to Supervisor of the Imperial Manufactories.
In the ninth year of Yǒngyuán,
he supervised the manufacture of secret swords and various instruments,
all of which were exquisitely crafted and sturdy,
setting a standard for later generations.
From ancient times, written documents were mostly compiled on bamboo slips;
those using woven silk were called "paper".
Silk was expensive and slips were heavy,
neither being convenient for people.
Lún then conceived the idea
of using tree bark, hemp waste, worn-out cloth, and fishing nets to make paper.
In the first year of Yuánxīng, he presented it to the emperor,
who praised his skill,
and from then on, everyone adopted it,
thus the world universally called it
"Marquis Cài's paper."
In the first year of Yuánchū,
Empress Dowager Dèng, because Lún had served in the palace for a long time,
enfeoffed him as Marquis of Lóngtíng,
with an income of three hundred households.
Later, he became Grand Coachman of Chánglè.
In the fourth year,
the emperor, finding that the texts of classics and commentaries contained many errors,
selected erudite scholars and palace attendants such as Liú Zhēn and erudites and good historians to go to Dōngguān,
where they collated the texts according to their respective family traditions,
and ordered Lún to supervise the matter.
Lún had initially acted on the instructions of Empress Dowager Dòu,
falsely implicating Empress Āndì's grandmother, Consort Sòng.
When the empress dowager died,
Āndì began to personally handle all state affairs,
and ordered Lún to report himself to the Grand Judge.
Lún, ashamed to suffer such humiliation,
bathed, straightened his clothes and cap,
drank poison, and died.
The marquisate was abolished.
Sūn Chéng, courtesy name Zhìqīng,
was a man from Xīnchéng, Zhuōjùn.
During Āndì's reign,
he was a Middle Yellow Gate,
serving in Chánglè Palace.
At that time, Empress Dowager Dèng governed the court,
and the emperor did not personally attend to state affairs.
Junior Yellow Gate Lǐ Rùn and the emperor's wet nurse Wáng Shèng often slandered the empress dowager's brother, Commandant of the Capital Wǔ Kūi, and others,
saying they intended to depose the emperor
and establish the Prince of Píngyuán (Dé) Yì.
The emperor was often angry and afraid.
When the empress dowager died,
he then executed the Dèng clan and deposed the Prince of Píngyuán,
enfeoffing Rùn as Marquis of Yōngxiāng;
also Junior Yellow Gate Jiāng Jīng, who advanced through flattery,
had initially welcomed the emperor to his residence,
and for this merit was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūxiāng,
each with an income of three hundred households.
Rùn and Jīng were both promoted to Regular Palace Attendant,
Jiāng Jīng also serving as Grand Chief Guardian.
Together with Regular Palace Attendant Fán Fēng, Yellow Gate Director Liú Ān, Gōudùn Lìng Chén Dá, and Wáng Shèng and her daughter Bórong, they stirred up trouble inside and outside the court,
competing in extravagance and cruelty.
Moreover, the emperor's maternal uncle, General-in-Chief Gěng Bǎo, and the empress's brother, Grand Master of Ceremonies Yán Xiǎn, colluded with each other,
and falsely killed Grand Commandant Yáng Zhèn,
and deposed the Crown Prince, making him Prince of Jìyīn.
The following year, the emperor died,
and the Marquis of Běixiāng was established as emperor.
Xiǎn and his faction then monopolized the court and contended for power,
and instigated officials to memorialize for the execution of Fán Fēng,
the deposition of Gěng Bǎo and Wáng Shèng,
and all their partisans were put to death or exiled.
In the tenth month,
Běixiāng Hóu fell gravely ill.
Chéng said to Cháng Xīngqú, the Administrator of the Guests of the Prince of Jìyīn:
"The Prince, by his legitimate lineage,
originally committed no fault,
but the late emperor, swayed by slander,
eventually deposed him.
If Běixiāng does not recover from his illness,
let us together eliminate Jiāng Jīng and Yán Xiǎn,
and the matter can be accomplished."
Qú and the others assented.
Furthermore, the Zhonghuángmén, Wáng Kāng of Nányáng,
had previously been an clerk in the Crown Prince's palace.
Since the Crown Prince's deposition,
he had always felt sorrow and indignation.
Also, Wáng Guó of Jīngzhào, the Chánglè Tàiguān Céng,
all attached themselves to and agreed with Chéng.
By the twenty-seventh day,
Běixiāng Hóu passed away.
Yán Xiǎn reported to the Empress Dowager,
to summon various princes to select one as the imperial successor.
Before they arrived,
on the second day of the eleventh month,
Chéng, along with Wáng Kāng and eighteen others, gathered to plot beneath the Western Bell,
all dressed in plain clothes, taking an oath.
On the night of the fourth day,
Chéng and the others met together atop the Chóngdé Palace,
then entered through the Zhāngtái Gate.
At that time, Jiāng Jīng, Liú Ān, Lǐ Rùn, Chén Dá, and others were all seated beneath the Shěngmén.
Chéng and Wáng Kāng went together and beheaded Jīng, Ān, and Dá.
As Lǐ Rùn's power and influence had long been respected within the Shěng,
they wished to make him their leader,
and so they raised their blades and threatened Rùn, saying:
"Today we are to enthrone the Prince of Jìyīn;
do not waver."
Rùn said:
"Yes."
Thereupon, they helped Rùn up,
and together they went beneath the Western Bell to welcome the Prince of Jìyīn and enthrone him.
This was Shùn Dì.
He summoned the Shàngshū Lìng, Púyè, and others below them,
who followed his imperial carriage to Nángōng Yúntái.
Chéng and the others remained guarding the Shěngmén,
blocking off the inside and outside.
Yán Xiǎn was in the Forbidden Palace at the time,
anxious and not knowing what to do.
The Xiǎohuángmén, Fán Dēng, persuaded Xiǎn to dispatch troops.
With an edict from the Empress Dowager, he summoned the Yuèqí Jiàowèi, Féng Shī, and the Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiāng, Yán Chóng,
to garrison at Shuòpíng Gate,
to resist Chéng and the others.
He lured Shī into the Shěng,
and the Empress Dowager had him presented with a seal,
saying:
"Whoever can seize the Prince of Jìyīn will be enfeoffed as a Wànhù Hóu;
whoever can seize Lǐ Rùn will be a Wǔqiānhù Hóu."
Xiǎn, considering the small number of troops Shī commanded,
sent him with Dēng to gather officers and soldiers outside the Zuǒyì Gate.
Shī then fought and killed Dēng,
and returned to his camp to defend it.
Xiǎn's younger brother, the Wèiwèi, Yán Jǐng, hastily returned from the Shěng to the outer headquarters,
gathered troops, and reached Shèngdé Gate.
Chéng sent for the various Shàngshū to apprehend Jǐng.
Shàngshū Guō Zhèn was ill in bed at the time,
but upon hearing this,
he immediately led the imperial guards on duty out of the Nánzhǐchē Gate.
He encountered Jǐng, who was followed by officers and soldiers.
Drawing a white blade,
he shouted:
"No unauthorized military interference!"
Zhèn immediately got out of his chariot,
and at that moment, read out an imperial decree to him.
Jǐng said:
"What kind of decree?"
He then struck at Zhèn,
but missed.
Zhèn drew his sword and struck Jǐng, knocking him from his chariot.
His attendants used halberds to stab him in the chest,
and thus captured him.
He was sent to the Tíngwèi prison,
and died that very night.
The next morning,
an order was issued for the Shìyùshǐ to arrest Xiǎn and the others and send them to prison.
Thus, the situation was settled.
An edict was issued, which stated:
"To commend merits and reward good deeds
is a universal principle throughout antiquity and the present.

Therefore, the Zhōngchángshì, the Chánglè Tàipú Jiāng Jīng, the Huángmén Lìng Liú Ān, and the Gōudùn Lìng Chén Dá, along with the former Chēqí Jiāngjūn Yán Xiǎn and his brothers, conspired in evil and rebellion,
disrupting the world.

The Zhōnghuángmén Sūn Chéng, Wáng Kāng, the Chánglè Tàiguān Céng Wáng Guó, the Zhōnghuángmén Huáng Lóng, Péng Kǎi, Méng Shū, Lǐ Jiàn, Wáng Chéng, Zhāng Xián, Shǐ Fàn, Mǎ Guó, Wáng Dào, Lǐ Yuán, Yáng Tuó,
Chén Yǔ, Zhào Fēng, Lǐ Gāng, Wèi Měng, Miáo Guāng, and others,
filled with loyal indignation, rose up,
