and united their strength and conspired,
thereby eliminating the chief evildoers,
and stabilizing the royal house.
Does not the Book of Songs say: 'No word unspoken goes unreturned;
no good deed unrewarded'?
Chéng was the chief plotter,
Kāng and Guó assisted him.
Therefore, Chéng is enfeoffed as Fúyáng Hóu,
with a stipend of ten thousand households;
Kāng as Huáróng Hóu,
Guó as Lì Hóu,
each with nine thousand households;
Huáng Lóng as Xiāngnán Hóu,
five thousand households;
Péng Kǎi as Xīpíngchāng Hóu,
Méng Shū as Zhōnglú Hóu,
Lǐ Jiàn as Fùyáng Hóu,
each with four thousand two hundred households;
Wáng Chéng as Guǎngzōng Hóu,
Zhāng Xián as Zhù'ā Hóu,
Shǐ Fàn as Línjǔ Hóu,
Mǎ Guó as Guǎngpíng Hóu,
Wáng Dào as Fànxiàn Hóu,
Lǐ Yuán as Bāoxìn Hóu,
Yáng Tuó as Shāndū Hóu,
Chén Yǔ as Xiàjùn Hóu,
Zhào Fēng as Xīxiàn Hóu,
Lǐ Gāng as Zhījiāng Hóu,
each with four thousand households;
Wèi Měng as Yílíng Hóu,
two thousand households;
Miáo Guāng as Dōng'ā Hóu,
one thousand households."
These were the nineteen marquises.
In addition, carriages, horses, gold, silver, money, and silk were bestowed, each in varying amounts.
Lǐ Rùn was not enfeoffed because he was not involved in the conspiracy beforehand.
Thereupon, Chéng was promoted and appointed Qíjì Dūwèi.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn,
Chéng, along with Zhāng Xián, Méng Shū, Mǎ Guó, and others, defended Yú Xǔ, the Sīlì Xiàowèi, against accusations,
carrying a memorial and entering the imperial presence,
and reprimanding those around them.
The Emperor was enraged,
and consequently dismissed Chéng from his office.
He then sent all nineteen marquises to their respective states.
Later, Chéng's enfeoffment was transferred to Yíchéng Hóu.
After Chéng arrived at his state,
he felt resentment and discontent,
so he returned his seal and ribbon, and his tally and bamboo slips,
and fled back to the capital,
to the mountains.
An imperial edict was issued to seek him out,
and he was restored to his former noble rank and territory.
He was granted a chariot, horses, and clothing,
and sent back to his state.
In the third year,
the Emperor, remembering the merits of Chéng and the others,
summoned them all back to the capital.
Chéng, Wáng Dào, and Lǐ Yuán were all appointed Qíjì Dūwèi,
while the rest were all granted audiences at court.
In the first year of Yángjiā,
Chéng fell gravely ill,
and was immediately appointed Fèngchē Dūwèi,
with the special rank of Tèjìn.
Upon his death,
the Wǔguān [Zhōng]lángjiāng was sent to posthumously bestow upon him the seal and ribbon of Chēqí Jiāngjūn,
and he was granted the posthumous title Gāng Hóu.
A Shìyùshǐ held the imperial staff to supervise the funeral arrangements.
The imperial chariot proceeded to the Beìbù Wèi relay station,
to view the Chēqí.
On his deathbed, Chéng
left a will in a memorial,
to transmit his marquisate to his younger brother, Měi.
The Emperor granted this,
but divided Chéng's portion in half,
enfeoffing Chéng's adopted son, Shòu, as Fúyáng Hóu.
Later, an imperial edict recognized minor merits,
and enfeoffed Xīngqú as Gāowàng Tínghóu.
In the fourth year,
an edict was issued that adopted sons of eunuchs were all permitted to be heirs,
inheriting their titles and ranks,
and this was formally established in law.
Wáng Kāng, Wáng Guó, Péng Kǎi, Wáng Chéng, Zhào Fēng, and Wèi Měng, six individuals, all died early.
Huáng Lóng, Yáng Tuó, Méng Shū, Lǐ Jiàn, Zhāng Xián, Shǐ Fàn, Wáng Dào, Lǐ Yuán, and Lǐ Gāng, nine individuals, along with the Āmǔ, Shānyáng Jūn Sòng É, engaged in mutual bribery,
seeking higher offices and increased stipends,
and also falsely accused the Zhōngchángshì Cáo Téng, Méng Bēn, and others.
In the second year of Yǒnghé,
this was discovered,
and they were all sent to their states,
with their rent reduced by a quarter.
Sòng É was stripped of her title and returned to her rural dwelling.
Only Mǎ Guó, Chén Yǔ, and Miáo Guāng preserved their enfeoffments.
Initially,

when the Emperor was deposed, the Supervisor of the Crown Prince's household, the Xiǎohuángmén Jí Jiàn, the Fù Gāo Fàn, the Chángqiū Zhǎng Zhào Xī, the Céng Liáng Hè, and the Yàocháng Xià Zhēn, all suffered punishment without fault.
Jiàn and the others were banished to Shuòfāng.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
they were all promoted to Zhōngchángshì.
Fàn was convicted of corruption,
and his death sentence was commuted by one degree.
Later, Jiàn was enfeoffed as Dōngxiāng Hóu,
with three hundred households.
Hè Qīngjiǎn was humble and sincere.
He rose to the position of dàchángqiū.
During the Yángjiā reign,
an imperial edict ordered the Nine Ministers to recommend brave and fierce men.
Hè alone recommended no one.
The emperor summoned him and asked for the reason.
He replied:
"Your servant was born in humble circumstances
and grew up in the imperial palace.
I have neither the discernment to know people
nor have I ever associated with scholars.
In the past, Wèi Yāng was introduced by Jǐng Jiàn,
and those with foresight knew he would not last.
If I were to recommend someone now,
it would be a disgrace, not an honor."
He steadfastly declined.
After he died,
the emperor remembered Hè's loyalty
and enfeoffed his adopted son as Dūxiāng Hóu,
with three hundred households.
Cáo Téng, courtesy name Jìxīng,
was a man from Qiáo, Pèiguó.
During Emperor Ān's reign,
he was appointed Huángmén Cóngguān.
When Emperor Shùn was still the crown prince,
Empress Dowager Dèng, seeing Téng was young, cautious, and sincere,
ordered him to attend the Crown Prince's studies,
and he was particularly favored and loved.
When the emperor ascended the throne,
Téng became a Xiǎohuángmén
and was promoted to Zhōngchángshì.
When Emperor Huán was enthroned,
Téng, along with Chánglè Tàipú Zhōu Fǔ and seven others,
were all enfeoffed as Tínghóu
for their meritorious service in establishing the new emperor.
Téng became Fèitíng Hóu,
was promoted to Dàchángqiū,
and was given the honorary rank of Tèjìn.
Téng served in the palace for over thirty years,
serving four emperors,
and never once made a mistake.
Those he promoted
were all famous people from within the empire,
such as Yú Fàng and Biān Sháo from Chénliú, Yán Gù and Zhāng Wēn from Nányáng, Zhāng Huàn from Hóngnóng, and Tángxī Diǎn from Yǐngchuān.
At that time, the Prefect of Shǔjùn, through his administrative clerk, gave a bribe to Téng.
Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhǒng Gǎo searched and found the letter at Xiégǔguān,
then reported the Prefect to the throne,
and also impeached Téng,
requesting that the case be handed over to the Tíngwèi for judgment.
The emperor said:
"The letter came from outside;
it is not Téng's fault."
Thus, Gǎo's memorial was shelved.
Téng bore no ill will;
he often praised Gǎo as a capable official,
and people at the time admired him.
When Téng died,
his adopted son Sōng succeeded him.
Later, Zhǒng Gǎo became Sītú,
and he told his guests:
"My current position as a minister
is all due to Cáo Chángshì's influence."
During Emperor Líng's reign, Sōng bribed palace officials and paid one hundred million coins to the Xīyuán,
thus he reached the position of Tàiwèi.
When his son Cāo raised an army,
Sōng refused to follow him,
and instead fled with his younger son Jí to Lángyá to avoid the chaos,
where they were killed by Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Táo Qiān.
Shàn Chāo was
from Hénán;
Xú Huáng was
from Liángchéng, Xiàpī;
Jù Yuàn was
from Yuánchéng, Wèijùn;
Zuǒ Kuàng was
from Píngyīn, Hénán;
Táng Héng was
from Yǎn, Yǐngchuān.
At the beginning of Emperor Huán's reign,
Chāo, Huáng, and Yuàn were Zhōngchángshì,
while Kuàng and Héng were Xiǎohuángmén Shǐ.
Initially,
Liáng Jì's two younger sisters became empresses to Emperors Shùn and Huán.
Jì succeeded his father Shāng as Dàjiāngjūn,
and for two generations, the Liáng clan held great power,
their authority shaking the entire empire.
After Jì had Tàiwèi Lǐ Gù, Dù Qiáo, and others executed,
his arrogance and tyranny grew even worse.
The empress, relying on her influence, was jealous and unrestrained,
poisoning many.
Everyone, high and low, was silenced,
and no one dared to speak.
The emperor, long intimidated and fearful,
constantly harbored resentment,
but fearing exposure,
dared not plot.
In the second year of Yánxī (159 CE),
the empress died.
The emperor, on going to the toilet,
alone called Héng and asked:
"Who among my attendants and the outside officials are on bad terms?"
Héng replied:
"Shàn Chāo and Zuǒ Kuàng previously went to Hénán Yǐn Bùyí,
and their courtesy was somewhat lacking.
Bùyí arrested their brothers and sent them to the Luòyáng prison.
The two of them went to his gate to apologize
before they were released.
Xú Huáng and Jù Yuàn often privately resented and detested the arrogance of the outside officials,
but dared not speak of it."
Thereupon, the emperor called Chāo and Kuàng into the room
and said:
"General Liáng and his brothers have monopolized the court,
coercing both inside and outside the palace.
From the dukes and ministers downwards, all follow their dictates.
Now I wish to execute them.
What do the Chángshì think?"
Chāo and the others replied:
"They are truly national traitors,
and should have been executed long ago.
We servants are weak and incompetent,
and do not know what Your Majesty's true intention is."
The emperor said:
"If that is truly the case,
the Chángshì should secretly plan it."
They replied:
"Planning it is not difficult,
but we only fear Your Majesty may hesitate again."
The emperor said:
"These treacherous ministers are coercing the state;
they deserve their punishment.
Why should I hesitate?"
Thereupon, he summoned Huáng, Yuàn, and the other five men,
and their plan was settled.
The emperor bit Chāo's arm until it bled as an oath.
Then an edict was issued to arrest Jì and his relatives and partisans, and all were executed.
Kuàng and Héng were promoted to Zhōngchángshì.
Chāo was enfeoffed as Xīnfēng Hóu,
with twenty thousand households;
Huáng as Wǔyuán Hóu,
Yuàn as Dōngwǔyáng Hóu,
each with fifteen thousand households,
and each granted fifteen million coins.
Kuàng as Shàngcài Hóu,
Héng as Rǔyáng Hóu,
each with thirteen thousand households,
and each granted thirteen million coins.
The five men were enfeoffed on the same day,
hence they were commonly referred to
as "The Five Marquises."
Eight other Xiǎohuángmén, including Liú Pǔ and Zhào Zhōng, were also enfeoffed as Xiānghóu.
From then on, power shifted to the eunuchs,
and the court grew increasingly chaotic.
When Chāo fell ill,
the emperor sent an envoy to bestow upon him the title of Chējì Jiāngjūn.
He died the following year,
and was granted secret artifacts from the Eastern Park,
jade ornaments for his coffin,
and posthumously awarded the seal and ribbon of a Hóu Jiāngjūn.
An envoy was dispatched to manage his funeral.
At the burial,
five battalions of cavalry were dispatched,
(a general and) an Attending Imperial Censor supervised the funeral,
and the Grand Architect constructed his tomb.
Thereafter, the other four marquises became even more arrogant,
and the people of the empire had a saying about them:
"Zuǒ turns the heavens,
Jù sits alone,
Xú lies like a tiger,
Táng sways on two sides."
They all vied to build mansions,
with magnificent multistoried towers,
exhausting all craftsmanship.
Gold, silver, and fine fabrics
were used to adorn their dogs and horses.
They took many beautiful women from good families as concubines,
all adorned with precious and extravagant decorations,
rivaling palace ladies.
Their attendants all rode ox-carts while following in rows of cavalry.
They also adopted their distant relatives,
or adopted people of different surnames,
or bought servants as sons,
all to pass down the state and inherit their titles.
Their brothers and in-laws all governed provinces and commanded commanderies,
extorting the common people,
no different from bandits.
Chāo's younger brother Ān was Hédōng Tàishǒu,
his nephew Kuāng was Jìyīn Tàishǒu,
Huáng's younger brother Shèng was Hénèi Tàishǒu,
Kuàng's younger brother Mǐn was Chénliú Tàishǒu,
Yuàn's elder brother Gōng was Pèi Xiàng,
all of whom were scourges in their respective localities.
Huáng's elder brother's son, Xuān, became the Magistrate of Xiàpī.
His tyranny was particularly severe.
Previously, he had sought the daughter of Lǐ Guǎng of Xiàpī, former Grand Administrator of Rǔnán, but could not obtain her.
Upon arriving at the county,
he immediately led his officers and soldiers to Guǎng's home,
took his daughter away,
and cruelly shot her to death,
burying her within a temple.
At that time, Xiàpī County was under Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Huáng Fú of Rǔnán was the Grand Administrator of Dōnghǎi.
Someone reported Xuān.
Fú then arrested Xuān's family members,
torturing all of them, regardless of age.
His subordinates and clerks strongly remonstrated.
Fú said:
"Xú Xuān is a national villain.
If I kill him today,
even if I am executed for it tomorrow,
I will be able to rest in peace."
He then prosecuted Xuān's crimes, executed him in the marketplace,
and exposed his corpse to show the common people.
The entire commandery was shocked and terrified.
Huáng then reported his grievances to the Emperor.
The Emperor was greatly angered.
Fú was punished with a shaved head and an iron collar,
and was sent to labor at the Right Prison.
The relatives and retainers of the Five Marquises committed widespread atrocities throughout the empire.
The people could no longer endure it,
and rose up as bandits and rebels.
Seven years later,
Héng died.
He was also posthumously granted the title of General of Chariots and Cavalry,
following the precedent of Chāo.
When Huáng died,
he was given a funerary gift of money and silk,
and bestowed with land for a tomb.
The following year,
Sīlì Xiàowèi Hán Yǎn consequently impeached Wǎn for his evil deeds,
and also his elder brother, Tàipú Nánxiāng Hóu Chēng, for soliciting favors from provinces and commanderies,
accumulating wealth through corrupt means,
and allowing his retainers to act wantonly,
infringing upon officials and common people.
Wǎn and Chēng both committed suicide.
Yǎn further impeached Yuàn's elder brother, Pèi Xiàng Gōng, for his crimes of embezzlement,
and summoned him to the Grand Judge.
Yuàn went to prison to offer an apology,
and surrendered his seal and sash as Marquis of Dōngwǔ.
An imperial edict demoted him to Dūxiāng Hóu,
and he died at home.
Those who inherited the titles of Chāo, Huáng, and Héng,
were all demoted to Xiānghóu.
Their annual rent income was all three million.
Their sons and younger brothers who had been enfeoffed
all had their titles and lands confiscated.
Liú Pǔ and others were demoted to Guānnèi Hóu.
Hóu Lǎn was
a native of Fángdōng, Shānyáng.
At the beginning of Emperor Huán's reign, he became a Zhōng Chángshì.
He rose through flattery and cunning,
abused his power, and was greedy and unrestrained,
accepting countless bribes and gifts.
During the Yánxī reign,
there were successive years of military campaigns,
and the treasury was empty.
So, the salaries of all officials and the taxes of kings and marquises
were temporarily withheld.
Lǎn also offered five thousand bolts of silk
and was granted the title of Guānnèi Hóu.
He also claimed credit for his role in plotting the execution of Liáng Jì,
and was promoted to Gāoxiāng Hóu.
The family of Xiǎo Huángmén Duàn Guī was in Jìyīn.
He and Lǎn jointly established agricultural enterprises
near the border of Jìběi.
Their servants and retainers infringed upon the common people,
robbing travelers.
Jìběi Xiàng Téng Yán summarily arrested them all,
killed dozens of people,
and displayed their corpses at crossroads.
Lǎn and Guī were greatly resentful
and reported the matter to the Emperor.
Yán was punished for killing too many innocent people,
summoned to the Grand Judge,
and dismissed.
Yán's courtesy name was Bóxíng,
a native of Běihǎi.
Later, he became Jīngzhào Yǐn,
and was renowned for his governance.
He was popularly called a venerable elder.
Having achieved this, Lǎn and his ilk became even more unrestrained.
Lǎn's elder brother Cān was Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
Whenever there were wealthy people,
he would falsely accuse them of high treason,
exterminating them all,
and confiscating their property.
The accumulated sum amounted to billions.
Tàiwèi Yáng Bǐng impeached Cān,
who was summoned in a caged cart
and committed suicide on the way.
Jīngzhào Yǐn Yuán Féng inspected Cān's three hundred-plus carriages at a post station,
all filled with gold, silver, brocade, silk, and precious curiosities,
innumerable.
Lǎn was dismissed because of this,
but was quickly reinstated to his post.
In the second year of Jiànníng,
he returned home for his mother's funeral
and erected a lavish tomb.
Dūyóu Zhāng Jiǎn then impeached Lǎn for his greed, extravagance, and wantonness,
stating that he had previously requested and seized three hundred and eighty-one private residences
and one hundred and eighteen qǐng of land.
He had built sixteen residential complexes,
all with tall buildings, ponds, and gardens,
with halls and pavilions visible from afar,
decorated with brocades, paintings, and vermilion lacquer,
their scale grand and profound,
usurping the style of the imperial palace.
He also prematurely built his own tomb,
with a stone coffin and twin gate towers,
a high portico one hundred feet tall,
destroying people's homes
and excavating graves.
He abducted good people,
kidnapped wives and children,
and committed various other crimes and misdeeds,
requesting his execution.
However, Lǎn guarded and intercepted
the memorial, so it was never submitted.
Jiǎn then broke into Lǎn's tomb and residence,
confiscating his assets,
and fully stated his crimes.
He also impeached Lǎn's mother for associating with retainers during her lifetime
and disrupting commanderies and states.
Again, the memorial was not presented to the Emperor.
Lǎn then falsely accused Jiǎn of being part of a faction,
along with the former Chánglè Shàofǔ Lǐ Yīng and Tàipú Dù Mì,
and had them all exterminated.
He then replaced Cáo Jié as Chánglè Tàipú.
In the first year of Xīpíng,
the relevant authorities impeached Lǎn for his monopolization of power, arrogance, and extravagance,
decreed the confiscation of his seal and sash,
and he committed suicide.
All his partisans were dismissed.
Cáo Jié, courtesy name Hànfēng,
was a native of Xīnyě, Nányáng.
His ancestral home was Wèijùn,
and his family had held positions of two thousand shí for generations.
At the beginning of Emperor Shùn's reign, he was promoted to Xiǎo Huángmén from a Xīyuán Cavalryman.
During Emperor Huán's time,
he was promoted to Zhōng Chángshì
and Fèngchē Dūwèi.
In the first year of Jiànníng,
he held the ceremonial staff and led one thousand Zhōng Huángmén, Hǔbēn, and Yǔlín troops
to the north to welcome Emperor Líng,
accompanying him into the palace.
Upon his enthronement,
for his role in establishing the new emperor, he was enfeoffed as Cháng'ān Xiānghóu,
with six hundred households.
At that time, Empress Dowager Dòu held court.
Her father, Grand General Dòu Wǔ, conspired with Grand Tutor Chén Fān to eliminate the palace eunuchs.
Jié, along with Chánglè Wǔguān Shǐ Zhū Yǔ, subordinate officials Gòng Pǔ and Zhāng Liàng,
Zhōng Huángmén Wáng Zūn, Chánglè Yèzhě Téng Shì, and seventeen others,
jointly forged an imperial edict to appoint Chánglè Shíjìan Wáng Fǔ as Huángmén Lìng,
leading troops to execute Wǔ and Fān, etc.
The details are fully recorded in the biographies of Fān and Wǔ.
Jié was promoted to Chánglè Wèiwèi
and enfeoffed as Yùyáng Hóu,
with an increase of three thousand households in his territory.
Fǔ was promoted to Zhōng Chángshì,
retaining his position as Huángmén Lìng.
Yǔ was enfeoffed as Dūxiāng Hóu,
with one thousand five hundred households.
Pǔ, Liàng, and five others each received three hundred households.
The remaining eleven were all made Guānnèi Hóu,
receiving an annual rent of two thousand hú.
Earlier, Yǔ and others secretly prayed to Heaven in the Míngtáng, saying:
"The Dòu clan is without principle.
We ask Heaven to assist the Emperor in executing them,
so that the matter may succeed
and the empire may find peace."
After Wǔ and others were executed,
an imperial edict ordered the Grand Provisioner to provide offerings for the altars,
and bestowed fifty million cash upon Yǔ,
with others receiving varying amounts.
Later, he was further enfeoffed as Huáróng Hóu.
Two individuals:
When Jié was severely ill,
an imperial edict appointed him General of Chariots and Cavalry.
After a while, he recovered from his illness,
returned his seal and sash,
was dismissed,
and resumed his position as Zhōng Chángshì,
with the special honor of Tèjìn,
and a salary equivalent to Zhōng Èrqiān Shí.
Soon after, he was transferred to Dà Chángqiū.
In the first year of Xīpíng [172 CE],
Empress Dowager Dòu died.
Someone wrote on the Zhūquè Gate,
saying,
"The world is in great chaos.
Cáo Jié and Wáng Fǔ have secretly murdered the Empress Dowager.
The Chángshì Hóu Lǎn has killed many partisans.
The Gōngqīng all enjoy their salaries in vain,
without anyone speaking truthfully."
Thereupon, an edict ordered Sīlì Xiàowèi Liú Měng to pursue and arrest them,
convening a meeting every ten days.
Měng considered the libelous writing truthful
and was unwilling to make urgent arrests.
After more than a month,
the perpetrators' names had not been established.
Měng was demoted and transferred to be an Jiànyì Dàfū.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Duàn Jiǒng replaced Měng.
He then sent out forces in all four directions to pursue and arrest,
including students from the Imperial Academy.
More than a thousand people were imprisoned.
Jié and others held an unending grudge against Měng.
They had Jiǒng impeach Měng on other charges,
and he was sentenced to hard labor at the Zuǒxiào.
Many court officials spoke up on his behalf,
so he was released from punishment
and re-summoned to court via the Gōngchē system.
Jié then, with Wáng Fǔ and others, falsely accused Emperor Huán's younger brother, Bóhǎi Wáng Kuī, of plotting rebellion,
and he was executed.
Twelve people were enfeoffed for their meritorious service.
Fǔ was enfeoffed as Guànjūn Hóu.
Jié also had his stipend increased by 4,600 households,
making a total of 7,600 households previously.
His father, elder brothers, sons, and younger brothers all became Gōngqīng, column commanders, governors, prefects, and magistrates,
spreading throughout the empire.
Jié's younger brother, Pòshí, was Yuèqí Xiàowèi.
The wife of a five-hundred-man officer in the Yuèqí camp was beautiful.
Pòshí demanded her from him.
The five-hundred-man officer dared not refuse,
but his wife resolutely refused to go
and then committed suicide.
Their depravity, violence, and lawlessness
were often of this kind.
In the second year of Guānghé [179 CE],
Sīlì Xiàowèi Yáng Qiú impeached and executed Wáng Fǔ and his son, Chánglè Shàofǔ Méng, and Pèi Xiàng Jí.
They all died in prison.
At that time, there were continuous natural disasters and anomalies.
Lángzhōng Shěn Zhōng from Liáng, believing these were caused by the evil deeds of Zhū Yǔ and others,
submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your subject has heard that if a state is governed by the worthy, it is stable;
if it loses the worthy, it is imperiled.
Thus, Shùn had five able ministers, and the empire was well-governed.
Tāng appointed Yī Yǐn, and the inhumane were banished.
At the beginning of Your Majesty's reign,
you were not yet able to manage all affairs of state.
The Empress Dowager, mindful of nurturing you,
temporarily assumed regency.
Hence, the Zhōng Chángshì Sū Kāng and Guǎn Bà were promptly executed.
Tàifù Chén Fān and Dà Jiāngjūn Dòu Wǔ investigated their accomplices,
intending to purify court politics.
Huáróng Hóu Zhū Yǔ, knowing his deeds were exposed
and disaster would befall him,
then instigated a rebellious plot,
causing disorder in the royal household,
storming and trampling the palace gates,
seizing the imperial seals and ribbons,
coercing Your Majesty,
gathering officials,
and alienating the affection between flesh and blood, mother and son.
Consequently, Fān, Wǔ, and Yǐn Xūn were executed.
Then they jointly partitioned the cities and altars,
bestowing honors upon themselves.
Their fathers, sons, and brothers received great honors,
and those they were close to were placed in provinces and commanderies,
some ascending to the Nine Ranks,
some holding the Three Ministries.
They did not consider the responsibility that comes with high salaries and esteemed positions,
but instead pursued private interests,
amassed great wealth,
and renovated their mansions,
connecting entire neighborhoods.
They stole imperial water to fish,
and their carriages, horses, clothing, and playthings rivaled those of the imperial family.
All the Gōngqīng held their tongues and swallowed their words,
none daring to speak.
Provincial governors and commandery administrators followed their directives,
summoning and electing officials,
releasing the worthy and appointing the foolish.
Therefore, locusts arose,
and barbarian invaders appeared.
Heaven's wrath accumulated,
for more than ten years.
Thus, there were frequent solar eclipses above
and earthquakes below,
serving as warnings to the sovereign,
wishing him to awaken
and eradicate the unscrupulous.
In ancient times, Gāozōng, because of the omen of the pheasant's crow,
achieved the success of a restoration.
Recently, the deities enlightened Your Majesty,
unleashing a mighty wrath.
Thus, Wáng Fǔ and his sons were immediately beheaded.
Men and women in the streets all praised it,
as if they had avenged their parents.
It is truly strange that Your Majesty tolerates such traitorous subjects
and does not completely eradicate them.
In the past, Qín trusted Zhào Gāo,
thereby endangering its state.
Wú employed a criminal,
and its ruler met with disaster.
Duke Yú, embracing his treasure and leading his horse,
and Duke Zhāo of Lǔ, being driven out to Gānhóu,
met with destruction and disgrace because they did not employ Gōng Zhīqí and Zǐ Jiājū.
Now, with an act of undeserved kindness,
you pardon those deserving of annihilation.
If their treacherous plot succeeds,
what regret will be enough!
Your subject has been a Láng for fifteen years,
all that I have heard and seen.
What Yǔ has done
is truly something that August Heaven will not again forgive.
I wish Your Majesty would take a moment to listen,
carefully consider my memorial,
and sweep away these vile individuals,
to respond to Heaven's wrath.
If, when tested against Yǔ,
anything I have said proves untrue,
I am willing to suffer the punishment of the boiling cauldron,
and my wife and children shall all be exiled,
to close the path of false speech."
The memorial was not acted upon.
Jié then took the position of Shàngshū Lìng.
Four years later,
he died
and was posthumously granted the title of Chējì Jiāngjūn.
Later, Yǔ also died of illness.
Both adopted sons to transmit their lineages.
Shěn Zhōng, courtesy name Gōngchéng,
was appointed to the Gōngfǔ
after the eunuchs were punished.
Lǚ Qiáng, courtesy name Hànshèng,
was from Chénggāo, Hénán.
While young, he became a Xiǎo Huángmén as a eunuch,
and was twice promoted to Zhōng Chángshì.
He was honest and devoted to public service.
During Emperor Líng's reign,
eunuchs were routinely enfeoffed,
and Qiáng was made Dūxiāng Hóu.
Qiáng earnestly declined,
firmly refusing to accept it,
and the Emperor eventually allowed it.
He then submitted a memorial detailing his views: "Your subject has heard that regional lords symbolize the four sevens,
and below, they cleave the royal land. Gāozǔ strictly decreed that only those with merit could be enfeoffed,
thereby emphasizing the heavenly rank and clarifying warnings.
I have
heard that Zhōng Chángshì Cáo Jié, Wáng Fǔ, Zhāng Ràng, and others,
as well as Shìzhōng Xǔ Xiāng,
were all enfeoffed as marquises.
Jié and the other eunuchs have meager blessings,
low status, and mean character.
They flatter and
cater to the sovereign,
using flattery and treachery to gain favor,
poisoning people,
and envying the loyal and good.
They have caused the disaster of Zhào Gāo,
yet have not suffered the punishment of being torn apart.
They obscure the clarity of the court
and form their private factions.
Yet Your Majesty is unaware,
and arbitrarily bestows upon them fiefs,
establishing states and founding households.
Such petty men are being used.
Moreover, their families are also involved,
with heavy gold and
purple robes,
successively becoming supporters.
Having received great imperial grace,
they do not remember their ancestors,
nor cultivate their virtue,
but instead associate with evil factions
and conspire with the multitude of flatterers below.
Your
Majesty may consider their talents insignificant,
yet they receive special favors.
Furthermore, positions are granted improperly,
and the worthy are not promoted.
Those who enjoy salaries without working and those who are privately favored
are always promoted.
When Yin and Yang are out of harmony,
crops are barren,
and people are not well.
All these stem from this.
Your subject truly knows that the enfeoffments have already taken place,
and speaking now is too late.
The reason I risk death to present my humble
loyalty
is truly that I wish Your Majesty to correct the existing errors
and stop here."
Those who were once noble but are now lowly
are due to the excessive number of taxes levied,
to satisfy the imperial court.
They dare not wear clothes in the cold,
nor eat when hungry.
The people suffer such distress,
yet no one
pities them.
The palace women are useless,
filling the rear palace;
even if the whole empire were to exert its utmost in farming and sericulture,
it would still be unable to provide for them.
In the past, when the Chu women were sorrowful,
disaster befell the Western Palace.
How much more so
when they are accumulated year-round,
how could there be no worries or grievances!
Heaven gives birth to the myriad people,
and establishes rulers to shepherd them.
When the ruler's Way is obtained,
the people support him as parents,
and look up to him as the sun and moon.
Even if there are taxes and levies from time to time,
they still hope for his benevolent grace and favor.
The Yìjīng says:
"By delighting them, one employs the people,
and the people forget their toil;
by delighting them, one confronts
difficulty,
and the people forget their death."
The Crown Prince, the Vice-Ruler,
should recite and ponder these words;
those who face south and govern the state
should put these matters into practice.
How could they entertain thoughts of attachment and reluctance?
Moreover, Hékàn is distant and remote,
and the Jǐedú [River] has just been cut off.
Yet the people's labor and resources are being exhausted,
with no visible benefit.
Furthermore, currently the four
surnames of favored relatives by marriage,
and the eunuchs and imperial relatives without merit or virtue,
have erected residences,
numbering in the tens of thousands.
Multi-storied buildings are connected,
with red paint and white plaster,
and carved
decorations,
too numerous to describe individually.
Funerals exceed regulations,
their luxury and splendor go beyond propriety.
They compete to imitate each other,
none willing to correct or oppose this.
The Gǔliáng Zhuàn says:
"When wealth is exhausted,
there is resentment;
when strength is exhausted, there is dissatisfaction."
Shīzǐ says:
"The ruler is like a basin,
the people are like water;
if the basin is square, the water is square;
if the basin is round, the water is round."
The influence of superiors
on subordinates
is like wind bending grass.
Now, superiors do not practice frugality to eliminate extravagance,
while subordinates indulge in the vice of desire.
This leads to birds and beasts consuming the people's delicacies,
and wood and earth wearing the people's
silk.
In the past, Shī Kuàng advised Jìn Pínggōng, saying:
"If beams and pillars wear embroidery,
the people will have no coarse clothing;
if the ponds have
fine wine, scholars will die of thirst;
if horses are fed millet,
the people
will have hunger in their faces.
Close ministers dare not admonish,
and distant ministers cannot express themselves freely."
This is what is meant.
Cherishing the Way yet misled by the state,
and speaking with earnestness and bluntness,
criticizing and disparaging noble ministers,
and mocking and scolding eunuchs.
Your Majesty did not keep his words secret,
allowing them to be exposed.
The multitude of villains craned their necks,
greasing
their lips and wiping their tongues,
eager to devour him.
They fabricated baseless accusations.
Your Majesty accepted the slanders,
and inflicted severe punishment upon Yōng,
his family exiled,
old and young separated and scattered.
How could this not be betraying a loyal minister!
Now all ministers take Yōng as a warning,
fearing unpredictable calamity above,
and the harm of swordsmen below.
I know the court will
no longer hear loyal words.
Thus, the former Grand Commandant Duàn Jiǒng,
whose martial valor surpassed the world,
was skilled in frontier affairs.
He served in the military from youth,
and completed his meritorious deeds with white hair.
He served two
rulers,
his achievements and renown uniquely brilliant.
Your Majesty had already honored him,
and he ascended to the position of a Grand Minister,
yet he was falsely accused and coerced by Sīlì Xiàowèi Yáng Qiú.
His own person perished,
and his wife and children were scattered far away.
The empire was sorrowful,
and meritorious ministers were disappointed.
It would be appropriate to summon Yōng and reassign him,
and return Jiǒng's family.
Then the path of loyalty and integrity would open,
and the grievances of the multitude would be quelled
thereby.
At that time, the Emperor had many private hoards,
collecting treasures from across the empire.
Whenever commanderies and states made offerings,
they were first delivered to the Central Office,
named
"guidance fee."
Qiáng presented a memorial, admonishing:
The treasures of the commanderies,
the Central Imperial Treasury accumulating silks from across the empire,
the Western Garden taking deposits from the Minister of Agriculture,
the Central Store gathering horses from the Minister of the Imperial Stud,
and the offices to which these were transported
always had
guidance fees.
Levies were extensive and the people were impoverished,
expenses were many and offerings few.
Corrupt officials profited from this,
and the common people suffered its ill effects.
Moreover, sycophantic ministers
liked to offer their private possessions,
and those who tolerated
flattery and indulged
themselves advanced by this means.
to succeed.
If there is nothing to investigate,
then it should be handed over to the Department of State Affairs.
If the Department of State Affairs impeach,
it should be submitted to the Commandant of Justice,
to investigate the truth,
and carry out punishment.
Now, however,
only the Department of State Affairs is relied upon,
or they are ordered to use.
If so,
the Three Ducal Ministers would be free from the burden of selection,
and the Department of State Affairs would also not be held accountable.
With no one to assign responsibility or reward,
who would be willing to exert themselves for
nothing?
to be found wanting,
then it should not be illuminated.
I wish Your Majesty would carefully consider my words,
and not hold me accountable for recording faults and being found wanting.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng,
when the Yellow Turban rebels arose,
the Emperor asked Qiáng what should be done.
Qiáng wished to first execute the corrupt individuals around him,
greatly pardon the Partisan Prohibitions victims,
and evaluate the capabilities of the Inspectors and Two-Thousand-Picul officials.
The Emperor accepted this,
and thus first pardoned the Partisan Prohibitions victims.
Thereupon, all the Regular Palace Attendants sought to resign,
and also recalled their relatives, sons, and younger brothers who were in the commanderies and states.
The Central Regular Palace Attendants Zhào Zhōng, Xià Yùn, and others then conspired against Qiáng,
saying,
"He discusses court affairs with the Partisan Prohibitions victims,
and frequently reads the biography of Huò Guāng.
Qiáng's brothers are all corrupt and defiled wherever they are."
The Emperor was displeased,
and sent a Central Yellow Gate official with soldiers to summon Qiáng.
When Qiáng heard the Emperor's summons,
he angrily said:
"When I die,
chaos will arise.
A man wishes to be utterly loyal to the state,
how can he face a prison official!"
He then committed suicide.
Zhōng and Yùn again slandered him, saying:
"Qiáng was summoned, but before knowing what he was asked,
he went outside to hide himself among the grass,
proving his treachery."
Consequently, his relatives were arrested,
and their property confiscated.
At that time, the five eunuchs Dīng Sù (濟陰丁肅), Xú Yǎn (下邳徐衍), Guō Dān (南陽郭耽), Lǐ Xún (汝陽李巡), and Zhào Yòu (北海趙祐) were called "pure and loyal."
They all resided in their native villages,
and did not contend for power.
Lǐ Xún observed that when the various Erudites tested candidates for the Grades A and B,
they disputed over who was superior or inferior,
and accused each other,
even to the point of giving bribes to determine the characters in the Lántái (蘭臺) lacquer-script classics,
to make them conform to their private texts.
He then reported this to the emperor,
and together with other scholars, carved the texts of the Five Classics onto stone.
Thereupon, an edict commanded Cài Yōng (蔡邕) and others to rectify their texts.
After this, the Five Classics were standardized,
and disputes ceased.
Zhào Yòu was widely learned and well-read,
and distinguished himself in writing and collating books;
the scholars praised him.
Moreover, Wú Kàng (甘陵吳伉), a Lesser Yellow Gate,
was skilled in interpreting wind direction,
was widely knowledgeable, and had a reputation for public service.
Knowing he would not be employed,
he often feigned illness and returned to his temple lodging,
calmly nurturing his aspirations.
Zhāng Ràng (張讓)
was from Yǐngchuān (潁川);
Zhào Zhōng (趙忠)
was from Ānpíng (安平).
When young, they both served in the imperial secretariat.
During Emperor Huán's (桓帝) reign, they became Lesser Yellow Gates.
Zhào Zhōng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dūxiāng (都鄉侯) for his功in executing Liáng Jì (梁冀).
In the eighth year of Yánxī (延熹),
he was demoted to Marquis of Guānnèi (關內侯),
and received a thousand hú (斛) of grain tax from his native county.
During Emperor Líng's (靈帝) reign,
Zhāng Ràng and Zhào Zhōng were both promoted to Regular Palace Attendants,
enfeoffed as marquises,
and collaborated with Cáo Jié (曹節) and Wáng Fǔ (王甫) among others.
After Cáo Jié's death,
Zhào Zhōng became the Grand Steward of the Empress's Household.
Zhāng Ràng had a supervising slave who managed his household affairs,
engaging in bribery and corruption,
with his power and influence widely known.
Mèng Tuó (扶風人孟佗) from Fúfēng (扶風),
who was exceedingly wealthy,
befriended this slave,
sparing no expense in presenting gifts,
holding nothing back.
The slave was grateful and
asked Mèng Tuó:
"What do you desire, sir?
I am capable of arranging it."
Mèng Tuó replied:
"I only wish for you and your associates to bow to me once."
At that time, guests seeking an audience with Zhāng Ràng
often numbered several hundreds or thousands of carriages.
When Mèng Tuó went to Zhāng Ràng's residence,
he arrived late
and could not enter.
The supervising slave then led all the "head-cleaners" (黃門) to greet and bow to him on the road,
and together they lifted his carriage to enter the gate.
All the guests were astonished,
thinking Mèng Tuó was on very good terms with Zhāng Ràng,
and all vied to bribe him with treasures and curiosities.
Mèng Tuó distributed these as gifts to Zhāng Ràng,
who was greatly pleased,
and consequently appointed Mèng Tuó as the Inspector of Liángzhōu (涼州刺史).

At this time, Zhāng Ràng, Zhào Zhōng, and Xià Yùn (夏惲), Guō Shèng (郭勝), Sūn Zhāng (孫璋), Bì Lán (畢嵐), Lì Sōng (栗嵩), Duàn Guī (段珪), Gāo Wàng (高望), Zhāng Gōng (張恭), Hán Kuī (韓悝), Sòng Diǎn (宋典) — these twelve individuals
were all Regular Palace Attendants,
enfeoffed as marquises and highly favored.
Their fathers, elder brothers, sons, and younger brothers were stationed throughout the prefectures and commanderies,
wherever they were, they were greedy and cruel,
and were a blight upon the people.
When the Yellow Turbans arose,
bandits were rampant.
Zhāng Jūn (中山張鈞) from Zhōngshān (中山), a Gentleman of the Interior, submitted a memorial stating:
"I humbly believe that the reason Zhāng Jiǎo (張角) was able to raise an army and cause rebellion,
and why tens of thousands of people gladly joined him,
is entirely because the Ten Regular Attendants extensively appointed their fathers, elder brothers, in-laws, and guests to positions in the prefectures and commanderies,
where they illicitly monopolized wealth and profit,
and plundered the common people.
The people's grievances had no channel for redress,
thus they plotted rebellion
and gathered as bandits.
It is fitting to execute the Ten Regular Attendants,
hang their heads in the southern suburbs,
to apologize to the common people.
Furthermore, by sending envoys to declare this throughout the empire,
there will be no need for troops,
and the great bandits will naturally dissipate."
The Emperor showed Zhāng Jūn's memorial to Zhāng Ràng and others.
They all removed their caps, went barefoot, kowtowed,
and begged to be sent to the Luòyáng (洛陽) imperial prison,
and offered all their family wealth to aid military expenses.
An edict commanded them all to resume their caps and shoes and continue their duties as before.
The Emperor angrily said to Zhāng Jūn:
"This is truly a madman!
Among the Ten Regular Attendants, could there not be a single good person?"
Zhāng Jūn submitted another memorial,
similar to the previous one,
but it was suppressed and not responded to.
An edict ordered the Minister of Justice and the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor to investigate those who preached Zhāng Jiǎo's doctrine.
The Imperial Censor, acting on the instructions of Zhāng Ràng and others,
then falsely accused Zhāng Jūn of studying the Yellow Turban doctrine,
arrested him, and he died in prison from torture.
However, Zhāng Ràng and others were actually deeply involved in communicating with Zhāng Jiǎo.
Later, the Regular Palace Attendants Fēng Xù (封諝) and Xú Fèng (徐奉) were individually exposed and executed.
The Emperor, in anger, questioned Zhāng Ràng and others, saying:
"You always claimed that the Partisans wanted to rebel,
and had them all imprisoned,
or some even executed.
Now the Partisans are serving the state,
while you, on the contrary, communicate with Zhāng Jiǎo.
Are you not worthy of execution?"
They all kowtowed and said:
"This was the doing of the late Regular Palace Attendants Wáng Fǔ (王甫) and Hóu Lǎn (侯覽)."
The Emperor then stopped.
The following year,
the Southern Palace suffered a fire.
Zhāng Ràng, Zhào Zhōng, and others persuaded the Emperor to levy a tax of ten cash per mú (畝) of land throughout the empire,
to repair the palace buildings.
Timber and ornamental stones were requisitioned from the commanderies of Tàiyuán (太原), Hédōng (河東), and Díidào (狄道).
Whenever these materials were transported from the provinces and commanderies to the capital,
the Yellow Gate Regular Attendants would always criticize them as substandard,
then forcibly buy them at a low price,
paying only one-tenth of their value.
They would then resell them to other eunuchs,
who would not immediately accept them either,
so the timber accumulated and rotted,
and the palace buildings remained unfinished for years.
Inspectors and Grand Administrators further imposed private levies,
and the common people groaned in distress.
All requisitions commanded by edict
were handled by the messengers of the Western Garden, who secretly gave orders,
and were called
"Imperial Envoys,"
intimidating the provinces and commanderies
and receiving many bribes.
Inspectors, officials of two thousand dàns (二千石), and those promoted as Abundant Talents (茂才) and Filial and Incorrupt (孝廉)
were all demanded to pay money for military aid and palace repair;
large commanderies paid up to twenty or thirty million,
while others paid varying amounts.
Those appointed to official positions
first had to go to the Western Garden to negotiate a price,
and only then were they allowed to depart.
Some who could not pay the full amount
even committed suicide.
Those who maintained their integrity
begged not to take office,
but were all forced to go.
At that time, Sīmǎ Zhí (河內司馬直) from Hénèi (河內), the newly appointed Grand Administrator of Jùlù (鉅鹿),
because of his reputation for integrity, had his demanded payment reduced by three million.
When Sīmǎ Zhí received the edict,
he said with sorrow:
"To be the parent of the people,
and yet to exploit them
to satisfy current demands,
I cannot bear it."
He pleaded illness,
but was not granted leave.
Upon reaching Mèngjīn (孟津),
he submitted a memorial vehemently criticizing the errors of the age
and the warnings of disaster and ruin from ancient and modern times,
then swallowed poison and committed suicide.
When his memorial was presented,
the Emperor temporarily stopped the palace repair funds.
He also constructed the Hall of Ten Thousand Gold (萬金堂) in the Western Garden,
and had the gold, cash, silk, and cloth from the Minister of Finance
piled up therein.
He also returned to Héjiān (河閒) to buy fields and residences,
and built mansions and towers.
The Emperor was originally from a marquis's family
and had been poor in his youth.
He often lamented that Emperor Huán (桓帝) could not manage a household,
so he accumulated private wealth,
and also deposited tens of millions of cash with the Lesser Yellow Gates and Regular Attendants.
He often said:
"Regular Attendant Zhāng (張常侍) is my father,
Regular Attendant Zhào (趙常侍) is my mother."
The eunuchs, having their way,
feared nothing,
and all built grand residences,
emulating imperial palaces.
The Emperor often ascended the terrace of Marquis Yǒng'ān (永安侯臺).
The eunuchs, fearing he would see their residences,
then had the palace attendant Shàng Dàn (尚但) remonstrate, saying:
"The Son of Heaven should not ascend to high places;
ascending to high places causes the common people to scatter."
From then on, he dared not ascend terraces and pavilions again.
The following year,
he then ordered Gōudùn Lìng Sòng Diǎn to repair the Jade Hall of the Southern Palace.
He also ordered Yètíng Lìng Bì Lán to cast four bronze figures to be placed in front of the Cānglóng and Xuánwǔ Gates.
He further cast four bells,
each capable of holding two thousand hú,
and hung them in the Jade Hall and in front of the Yúntái Palace.
He also cast a Tiānlù and a Há,
which spouted water onto the east side of the bridge outside the Píngmén Gate,
diverting the water into the palace.
He also made a fānchē and a kèwū,
placed them on the west side of the bridge,
and used them to sprinkle water on the roads of the northern and southern suburbs,
thereby saving the common people the expense of sprinkling the roads.
He also cast sīchūwénqián,
which all had four grooves.
Those who recognized the signs privately said that the extravagance and tyranny were already excessive,
and the form foreshadowed it:
once these coins were made,
they would surely "go away in four directions."
When the capital fell into great chaos,
the coins indeed spread throughout the four seas.
Again, Zhōng was appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn,
but was dismissed after a little over a hundred days.
In the sixth year,
the emperor died.
Zhōngjūn Xiàowèi Yuán Shào persuaded Dàjiāngjūn Hé Jìn
to execute the court eunuchs to please the empire.
The plot was leaked,
and Ràng and Zhōng and others consequently entered the palace to see Jìn,
and together they killed Jìn.
Yuán Shào, however, commanded his troops to execute Zhōng,
and captured all eunuchs, young and old, and had them all beheaded.
Ràng and several tens of others took the emperor hostage and fled to the Héshàng.
When the pursuit became urgent,
Ràng and the others wept bitterly and said goodbye, saying:
"We ministers are utterly destroyed,
and the empire is in chaos.
Your Majesty, please take care of yourself!"
They all threw themselves into the river and died.
A commentary states: From ancient times, those who lost great enterprises and broke the ancestral sacrifices
had reasons for their gradual decline.
The three dynasties brought disaster upon themselves through favored concubines;
the Yíng clan brought calamity through extravagance and cruelty;
the Western Capital lost its dynastic power due to external relatives;
and the Eastern Capital saw its state overturned by eunuchs.
The coming of success or failure
has long been pondered by ancient historians.
As for the troubles arising from eunuchs,
their general outline can still be explained.
Why is this?
The ugly ones who have undergone castration,
by their nature, lack the completeness of a whole life;
their reputation and honor cannot shine through their family lineage,
and their flesh and skin cannot be passed on to future generations.
To infer their feelings, one cannot discern their shortcomings,
and in their actions, it is easy to gain trust.
Furthermore, they gradually become involved in court affairs,
and acquire some knowledge of official matters.
Therefore, young rulers rely on their careful and old-fashioned mediocrity,
and empresses dowager depend on their orders concerning ingress and egress.
When consulted, there is no suspicion or apprehension in their minds,
and in intimacy, there is a pleasing demeanor.
There are also those who are loyal, honest, and upright,
harboring methods to correct evil;
or those with quick wit and eloquent responses,
disguising cunning to disrupt the truth;
or those who borrow reputations of integrity and goodness,
and recommend themselves in advance.
It is not merely that they indulge in evil deeds
and are limited to tyrannical behavior.
However, truth and falsehood coexist,
and feelings and appearances diverge,
thus they are able to confuse and mislead the ignorant young,
and muddle their sight and hearing.
This also has its reasons.
As deceitful gains proliferated,
and their factions expanded daily,
loyal ministers who argued against them
would surely reveal the gaps in their prior words,
and closest relatives who expressed indignation
would only open up opportunities for their usurpation.
[一０] This is why loyal and virtuous individuals were outwitted,
and the altars of soil and grain became ruins.
The Yìjīng says:
"Tread on frost, and hard ice will come."
It means that what it comes from has been there for a long time.
Now, tracing its origins,
how could it be a matter of one morning or one evening!
[一一]
A eulogy states: If appointments are misused, there is no small fault;
if excessively used, it leads to transgression.
How much more so for those of lowly office,
who deeply involve themselves in the affairs of state.
They manipulate texts with cunning guile,
dispensing favor and wielding power.
Causing harm to families and ruining states,
how could their outcomes be different!
Rúlín Lièzhuàn, Volume 69, Part 1
In the time of Wáng Mǎng and Gēngshǐ,
the empire was in disarray,
rites and music were shattered,
and classical texts were scattered and incomplete.
When Guāngwǔ rose again to restore the dynasty,
he loved the classics and their principles.
Before he even alighted from his carriage,
he first sought out refined scholars,
collected missing texts,
and patched together omissions and errors.
Previously, many scholars from all directions carried books and diagrams,
and hid in forests and swamps.
From then on, none failed to carry and embrace their volumes of classics,
gathering like clouds in the capital.
Fàn Shēng, Chén Yuán, Zhèng Xīng, Dù Lín, Wèi Hóng, Liú Kūn, Huán Róng, and others
arrived one after another.
Thereupon, Five Classics Academicians were established,
each teaching according to their family tradition.
For the Yìjīng, there were the Shī, Mèng, Liángqiū, and Jīng schools;
for the Shàngshū, the Ouyáng, Major Xiàhóu, and Minor Xiàhóu schools;
for the Shījīng, the Qí, Lǔ, and Hán schools;
for the Lǐjīng, Major Dài and Minor Dài;
for the Chūnqiū, the Yán and Yǎn schools.
In total, there were fourteen academicians,
all supervised in order by the Tàicháng.
In the fifth year of Jiànwǔ,
the Imperial Academy was renovated and built,
following classical models.
The forms of biāndòu and gānqī [ritual vessels and dance implements]
were fully displayed,
and those wearing square collars and practicing proper steps
gathered abundantly within it.
In the first year of Zhōngyuán,
the Sānyōng [three educational institutions] were first established.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he personally performed its rites.
The Son of Heaven first wore the tōngtiān crown,
garments depicting the sun and moon,
prepared the imperial carriage with all its ritual objects,
and held a grand procession to clear the way.
He sat in the Míngtáng to hold court with the various princes,
ascended the Língtái to observe the clouds and celestial phenomena,
performed the stripping and cutting ceremony at the Bìyōng,
and honored and nourished the Sānlǎo and Wǔgēng.
After the banquet and archery ceremony were concluded,
the Emperor sat upright and personally lectured,
while various scholars held their classics and raised questions and difficulties before him.
Those wearing caps, sashes, and formal attire,
who gathered around the Qiáo Mén gate to watch and listen, were said to number in the millions.
Afterwards, separate school buildings were also established for the descendants of meritorious officials and the younger relatives of the Four Surnames,
and highly capable individuals were selected to instruct them.
Even the guards of the Qímén and Yǔlín were all ordered to understand the chapters and sentences of the Xiàojīng,
and the Xiongnu also sent their sons to study.
How grand and numerous!
How vast and profound!
It flourished greatly during the Yǒngpíng era!
During the Jiànchū reign,
a grand assembly of scholars was held at Báihǔguān,
where they examined and clarified agreements and disagreements.
It concluded after several months.
Sùzōng personally attended, presiding over the discussions
like in the Shíqú Pavilion precedent.
He commanded his historians
to compile the debates into a comprehensive treatise.
He also issued an edict for talented students to study the Gǔwén Shàngshū, Máoshī, Gǔliáng Commentary, and Zuǒshì Chūnqiū.
Although no official academic posts were established for them,
they were all promoted to high-ranking jiǎngláng [lecturers],
serving in nearby government offices.
This was to recruit those who had been overlooked
and broadly preserve various schools of thought.
Xiàohé also frequently visited Dōngguān [Eastern Pavilion],
perusing the vast collection of books.
When Empress Déng took over the regency,
scholars became rather lax.
At that time, Fán Zhǔn and Xú Fáng both emphasized the importance of diligent study,
and also stated that many in scholarly positions were not suited for them.
Thereupon, an imperial edict commanded the gōngqīng [high officials] to carefully select the best candidates.
Láng [gentlemen] from the three bureaus who were proficient in classical studies
were all eligible for recommendation and appointment.
From the time Āndì assumed power,
he showed little regard for arts and letters.
The bóshì [academicians] leaned on their seats without lecturing,
their associates looked at each other with idleness and laxity,
the school buildings fell into disrepair,
turning into vegetable gardens,
and shepherd boys and firewood gatherers
even cut firewood beneath them.
Shùndì was moved by Dié Pú's words
and therefore renovated the academic buildings,
constructing a total of 240 rooms
and 1850 chambers.
Those who passed the examination in classics and were placed in the lower ranks were appointed as disciples,
and the number of students in the Jiǎ and Yǐ divisions was increased by ten each.
Elderly scholars from the commanderies and kingdoms were all appointed as láng or shèrén [secretaries].
In the first year of Běnchū (146 CE),
Empress Dowager Liáng issued an edict which said:
"From the dàjiāngjūn [general-in-chief] down to officials of 600 dàn,
all shall send their sons to study.
Each year, they shall be entertained once during the month of the archery ritual.
Let this be the regular practice."
From then on, the number of traveling students greatly increased,
reaching over 30,000 students.
However, the interpretation of textual passages gradually became superficial,
and many valued ostentation and extravagance,
so the scholarly ethos indeed declined.
After the Dǎng People were purged,
many renowned and virtuous individuals were implicated, exiled, or dismissed.
Later, disputes escalated into bitter quarrels,
with people accusing each other.
Some also privately bribed officials with gold and goods
to fix the characters in the Lántái lacquer-written classics
to match their own private interpretations.
In the fourth year of Xīpíng (175 CE),
Língdì therefore commanded scholars to officially establish the correct text of the Five Classics,
which were then carved onto stone tablets.
They used the three calligraphic styles—gǔwén, zhuàn, and lì—for mutual verification,
and erected them at the academy gate,
so that all under Heaven could take them as standards.
Initially,
when Guāngwǔ returned to Luòyáng,
the classical texts and secret archives he transported weighed over 2000 liǎng.
From then on,
they increased threefold compared to before.
When Dǒng Zhuó relocated the capital,
officials and common people were in turmoil.
The collections of classics and documents from Bìyōng, Dōngguān, Lántái, Shíshì, Xuānmíng, and Hóngdū
were fiercely plundered and dispersed.
Silk scrolls and illustrated books,
if large, were sewn into curtains or canopies;
if small, they were made into corded bags.
Of what Wáng Yǔn collected and transported westward,
there were only about 70 carts,
and due to the difficult and distant journey,
half of them were again lost.
Later, during the chaos in Cháng'ān,
everything was burned and destroyed at once,
nothing was left.
The scholars in the Eastern Hàn were so numerous
that it is difficult to record them all in detail.
Now, only those who were proficient in the classics and prominent scholars are recorded
to form the "Rú Lín Piān" [Treatise on Scholars].
Those who have their own biographies
are not included here.
However, if it is necessary to record the names of teachers and their successors
as evidence,
they are included.
The previous book states: Tián Hé transmitted the Yì to Dīng Kuān.
Dīng Kuān transmitted it to Tián Wángsūn.
Wángsūn transmitted it to Shī Chóu of Pèi, Méng Xǐ of Dōnghǎi, and Liángqiū Hè of Lángyá.
Hence, the Yì had the schools of Shī, Méng, and Liángqiū.
Also, Jīng Fáng of Dōngjùn received the Yì from Jiāo Yánshòu of Liángguó,
forming the Jīng family school.
There was also Fèi Zhí of Dōnglái,
who transmitted the Yì
to Wáng Héng of Lángyá,
forming the Fèi family school.
It was originally based on ancient characters
and known as the Gǔwén Yì.
Additionally, Gāo Xiàng of Pèi transmitted the Yì
to his son Gāo Kāng and Wú Jiāngyǒng of Lánlíng,
forming the Gāo family school.
The four schools of Shī, Méng, Liángqiū, and Jīng were all granted doctoral positions.
The Fèi and Gāo schools did not receive official recognition.
Liú Kūn, courtesy name Huángōng,
was a native of Dōnghūn, Chénliú,
and a descendant of King Xiào of Liáng.
In his youth, he practiced the Róng Lǐ [rites].
During the reign of Píngdì,
he received the Shī family Yì from Dài Bīn of Pèi.
He could play the elegant qín [zither]
and understood the melody of the Qīngjué [clear horn].
During Wáng Mǎng's era,
he continuously taught over 500 disciples.
During the spring and autumn archery rituals,
he always prepared the ceremonial arrangements,
using plain wooden gourds and leaves for sacrificial vessels,
and mulberry bows with Artemisia arrows
to shoot
at the "rabbit head" target.
Whenever a ceremony was performed,
the county magistrate would lead his subordinates to observe it.
Wáng Mǎng, believing Kūn was gathering too many followers
and privately performing grand rituals,
which showed a presumption of imperial authority,
imprisoned Kūn and his family in the prison of Wàihuáng.
Soon after Wáng Mǎng's defeat, he was released.
Afterwards, when the world descended into great chaos,
Kūn sought refuge in Mount Fùdú in Hénán.
In the fifth year of Jiànwǔ (29 CE),
he was recommended as xiàolián [filial and incorruptible],
but he did not take office.
He then fled
and taught in Jiānglíng.
Guāngwǔ heard of him
and immediately appointed him as Jiānglíng lìng [magistrate of Jiānglíng].
At that time, the county suffered continuous fire disasters year after year.
Kūn would always face the fire and kowtow,
often succeeding in bringing rain and stopping the wind.
He was summoned and appointed yìláng [counselor],
then successively promoted to shìzhōng [palace attendant] and Hóngnóng tàishǒu [Administrator of Hóngnóng].
Before this, the postal roads in Xiáo and Mǐn suffered many tiger attacks,
making travel impossible.
Kūn governed for three years,
and his benevolent influence spread widely,
causing all the tigers to carry their young across the river.
The Emperor heard of this and marveled.
In the twenty-second year (46 CE),
he was summoned to replace Dù Lín as Guānglùxūn [Minister of the Household].
The Emperor asked Kūn in an edict:
"Previously in Jiānglíng, you turned the wind and extinguished fires,
and later as Administrator of Hóngnóng,
the tigers crossed the river northwards.
What benevolent policies did you implement to achieve these things?"
Kūn replied:
"It was merely by chance."
Those around him all laughed at his simple and taciturn nature.
The Emperor sighed and said:
"These are indeed the words of a man of virtue."
He then ordered it to be recorded in the official documents.
He then commanded Kūn to teach the Crown Prince and over fifty other kings and minor marquises.
In the twenty-seventh year (51 CE),
he was appointed Qídūwèi [Colonel of Cavalry].
In the thirtieth year (54 CE),
he requested to retire due to old age.
An edict granted him a residence in Luòyáng
and allowed him to retain his salary of 1000 dàn for the rest of his life.
He died in the second year of Zhōngyuán (57 CE).
His son, Liú Yì,
courtesy name Jūn Wén,
inherited Kūn's profession,
and his disciples also flourished.
During the Yǒngpíng reign,
he served as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ [Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince].
During the Jiànchū reign,
he was successively promoted to Zōngzhèng [Minister of the Imperial Clan],
and died in office,
thus the family continuously held the position of Zōngzhèng.
Wā Dān 窪丹, courtesy name Zǐyù 子玉,
was a native of Yùyáng 育陽 in Nányáng 南陽.
His family traditionally transmitted the *Mèng Shì Yì* 孟氏易.
During the time of Wáng Mǎng 王莽,
he often avoided worldly affairs to teach,
devoting himself to study and not entering officialdom.
His disciples numbered several hundred.
In the early Jiànwǔ 建武 era,
he became a Bóshì 博士 (Erudite).
He was gradually promoted,
and in the eleventh year,
he became Dàhónglú 大鴻臚 (Grand Herald).
He authored seven chapters of *Yì Tōnglùn* 易通論 (Comprehensive Discourses on the Changes),
which the world called *Wā Jūn Tōng* 洼君通.
Dān's 丹 scholarship was profound and thorough in its meaning,
and masters of the *Yì* 易 (Book of Changes) honored him,
calling him a "Great Ru 儒 (Confucian scholar)."
In the seventeenth year,
he died in office
at the age of seventy.
At that time, Hóu Yáng Hóng 觟陽鴻 of Zhōngshān 中山,
courtesy name Mèngsūn 孟孫,
also taught the *Mèng Shì Yì* 孟氏易,
and was renowned.
In the Yǒngpíng 永平 era, he became Shàofǔ 少府 (Minor Treasurer).
Rèn Ān 任安, courtesy name Dìngzǔ 定祖,
was a native of Miánzhú 綿竹 in Guǎnghàn 廣漢.
As a youth, he traveled to the Tàixué 太學 (Imperial Academy),
where he received the *Mèng Shì Yì* 孟氏易,
and also mastered several other Classics.
He also studied Túcèn 圖讖 (Prognostic Charts and Apocrypha) from Yáng Hòu 楊厚 of the same commandery,
mastering its techniques.
Contemporaries said of him:
"If you wish to know Zhònghuán 仲桓, ask Rèn Ān 任安."
They also said:
"Living in the present but acting according to the ancients is Rèn Dìngzǔ 任定祖."
After finishing his studies,
he returned home to teach,
and students came from afar.
Initially, he served in the commandery and province.
Later, the Tàiwèi 太尉 (Grand Commandant) twice invited him,
appointing him Bóshì 博士 (Erudite) and
summoning him by Gōngchē 公車 (Public Carriage),
but he always declined, citing illness.
The Provincial Governor Liú Yān 劉焉 memorialized recommending him,
but at that time, the royal roads were blocked,
so the imperial edict never reached him.
At seventy-nine,
in the seventh year of Jiàn'ān 建安,
he died at home.
Yáng Zhèng 楊政, courtesy name Zǐxíng 子行,
was a native of Jīngzhào 京兆.
As a youth, he loved learning.
He received the *Liángqiū Yì* 梁丘易 from Fàn Shēng 范升 of Dàijùn 代郡,
and was skilled at expounding the Classics.
The capital had a saying about him:
"Expounding the Classics with clarity is Yáng Zǐxíng 楊子行."
He taught several hundred people.
Fàn Shēng 范升 was once accused by his divorced wife
and imprisoned.
Zhèng 楊政 then bared his torso,
pierced his ear with an arrow,
and carrying Shēng's 范升 son, hid by the roadside.
Waiting for the imperial carriage,
he held a memorial, kowtowed, and loudly declared:
"Fàn Shēng 范升 has married three times,
and has only one son,
who is now just three years old.
His orphanhood is pitiable!"
The Wǔqí Hǔbēn 武騎虎賁 (Cavalry and Tiger Guards), fearing for the imperial carriage,
raised their bows and shot at him,
but he still refused to leave.
The Máotóu 旄頭 (Lance Bearers) then poked Zhèng 楊政 with their halberds,
wounding him,
but Zhèng 楊政 still did not retreat.
His mournful weeping and pleading touched the emperor's heart.
The emperor, touched,
issued an edict, saying:
"Grant Yáng Shēng's 楊生 teacher [his freedom]!"
Immediately, Shēng 范升 was released by imperial decree.
Zhèng 楊政 thus became famous.
He was a heavy drinker
and disregarded minor conventions,
being bold and assertive,
yet deeply devoted to righteousness.
At that time, Liáng Sōng 梁松, the emperor's son-in-law,
and Yīn Jiù 陰就, the empress's younger brother,
both admired his reputation
and requested his friendship.
Whenever Zhèng 楊政 discussed matters with them,
he was always earnest and direct,
never yielding.
Once, he visited Mǎ Wǔ 馬武, Marquis of Yángxū 楊虛.
Mǎ Wǔ 馬武 found it difficult to see Zhèng 楊政,
claiming illness and not rising for him.
Zhèng 楊政 entered the room,
went straight to the bed, pushed Mǎ Wǔ 馬武,
grabbed his arm, and rebuked him, saying:
"You have received the nation's grace,
and hold a position as a regional assistant.
Instead of seeking worthy men to repay this special favor,
you arrogantly treat the world's heroes with disdain.
This is not the way to cultivate oneself.
Move now, and a knife will enter your ribs!"
Mǎ Wǔ's 馬武 sons and attendants were all greatly alarmed,
thinking he was being robbed.
They armed themselves and surrounded him,
but Zhèng's 楊政 expression remained calm.
Coincidentally, Yīn Jiù 陰就 arrived,
rebuked Mǎ Wǔ 馬武,
and ordered him to befriend Zhèng 楊政.
His upright and self-willed character
was always like this.
In the Jiànchū 建初 era,
he rose to the position of Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng 左中郎將 (Left Palace Assistant).
Zhāng Xīng 張興, courtesy name Jūnshàng 君上,
was a native of Yānlíng 鄢陵 in Yǐngchuān 潁川.
He studied and taught the *Liángqiū Yì* 梁丘易.
In the Jiànwǔ 建武 era,
he was nominated as Xiàolián 孝廉 (Filial and Incorrupt) and became a Láng 郎 (Gentleman),
but he left, citing illness,
and returned to gather disciples.
Later, he was invited to the retinue of Sītú 司徒 (Minister of Works) Féng Qín 馮勤.
Féng Qín 馮勤 recommended him as Xiàolián 孝廉,
and he was gradually promoted to Bóshì 博士 (Erudite).
In the early Yǒngpíng 永平 era,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng Jìjiǔ 侍中祭酒 (Libationer of the Palace Attendants).
In the tenth year,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shàofù 太子少傅 (Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent).
Xiǎnzōng 顯宗 often consulted him on classical scholarship.
Subsequently, his reputation became widely known,
and disciples came from afar,
with records showing nearly ten thousand,
making him the patriarch of the Liángqiū 梁丘 school.
In the fourteenth year,
he died in office.
His son, Fáng 魴,
inherited Xīng's 張興 profession
and rose to the position of Zhāngyè Shǔguó Dūwèi 張掖屬國都尉 (Commander of the Dependent State of Zhāngyè).
Dài Píng 戴憑, courtesy name Cìzhòng 次仲,
was a native of Píngyú 平輿 in Rǔnán 汝南.
He studied the *Jīng Shì Yì* 京氏易.
At sixteen,
the commandery nominated him as Míngjīng 明經 (Scholar of Classics),
and he was summoned for examination as a Bóshì 博士 (Erudite),
then appointed Lángzhōng 郎中 (Gentleman of the Palace).
At that time, an imperial edict summoned the Gōngqīng 公卿 (Dukes and Ministers) for a grand assembly.
All the officials took their seats,
but Píng 戴憑 stood alone.
Guāngwǔ 光武 (Emperor Guangwu) asked his reason.
Píng 戴憑 replied:
"The Bóshì 博士 (Erudites) expound the Classics, but none are as good as I,
yet they are seated above me.
Therefore, I cannot take a seat."
The emperor immediately summoned him to the imperial hall
and ordered him to debate with the other scholars.
Píng 戴憑 offered many explanations.
The emperor praised him
and appointed him Shìzhōng 侍中 (Palace Attendant),
often granting him audiences to ask about gains and losses.
The emperor said to Píng 戴憑:
"As a Shìzhōng 侍中 (Palace Attendant), you should correct and supplement national policies.
Do not conceal anything."
Píng 戴憑 replied:
"Your Majesty is stern."
The emperor said:
"Why am I stern?"
Píng 戴憑 replied:
"I humbly observe that the former Tàiwèi 太尉 (Grand Commandant)'s Xīcáoyuàn 西曹掾 (Chief Clerk of the Western Department), Jiǎng Zūn 蔣遵,
was pure, brilliant, loyal, and filial,
with learning that encompassed ancient and modern times.
Your Majesty listened to superficial accusations,
which resulted in his imprisonment.
The world considers this to be sternness."
The emperor angrily said:
"Do you, son of Rǔnán 汝南, wish to form a faction again?"
Píng 戴憑 left
and bound himself at the Tíngwèi 廷尉 (Minister of Justice).
An edict was issued to release him.
Later, he was again granted an audience.
Píng 戴憑 apologized, saying:
"Your servant does not possess the integrity of a straightforward speaker,
but has uttered foolish words.
Unable to remonstrate by sacrificing my life,
I have clung to life and merely existed,
which truly shames me before the holy court."
The emperor immediately ordered the Shàngshū 尚書 (Minister of the Imperial Secretariat) to lift Zūn's 蔣遵 imprisonment
and appointed Píng 戴憑 Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiàng 虎賁中郎將 (Commander of the Tiger Guards),
while also retaining his position as Shìzhōng 侍中 (Palace Attendant).
On the New Year's Day court audience,
all officials were assembled.
The Emperor commanded his ministers who were skilled in expounding the classics to challenge each other.
If the meaning was unclear,
their seats would be taken away and given to those who were clear.
Píng consequently occupied over fifty seats.
Thus, the capital had a saying:
"When expounding the classics, Dài Shìzhōng is never stumped."
He served for eighteen years,
and died in office.
An imperial edict granted him a tǐ zǐqì from Dōngyuán,
and 200,000 qián.
At that time, Wèi Mǎn, whose courtesy name was Shúyá, from Nányáng,
also studied Jīng's Yì
and taught it.
During the Yǒngpíng era,
he reached the position of Hóngnóng Tàishǒu.
Sūn Qī, whose courtesy name was Zhòngyù,
was from Chéngwǔ, Jìyīn.
When young, he was a scholar,
studying Jīng's Yì and Gǔwén Shàngshū.
His family was poor,
but he was extremely filial to his mother.
He herded pigs in a large marsh,
to support her.
Distant people who came to study under him
all carried their classics by the dike to follow him.
The villages were transformed by his benevolence and humility.
When the Huángjīn bandits arose,
passing by Qī's villages,
they agreed not to trespass on "Mr. Sūn's" dwelling.
The commandery nominated him as Fāngzhèng,
and sent an official with sheep and wine to invite Qī,
but Qī drove his pigs into the grass without a backward glance.
Sītú Huáng Wǎn specially invited him,
but he did not go,
and died at home.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
Fàn Shēng transmitted Mèng's Yì,
teaching it to Yáng Zhèng.
Chén Yuán and Zhèng Zhòng both transmitted Fèi's Yì,
and later Mǎ Róng also wrote a commentary for it.
Róng taught Zhèng Xuán,
Xuán wrote an Yì Zhù.
Xún Shuǎng also wrote an Yì Chuán.
From then on, Fèi's school flourished,
while Jīng's school gradually declined.
The Former Han History states: Fú Shēng of Jìnán
transmitted the Shàngshū,
teaching it to Zhāng Shēng of Jìnán and Ōuyáng Shēng of Qiāncéng.
Ōuyáng Shēng taught Ér Kuān of the same commandery.
Kuān taught Ōuyáng Shēng's son.
It was passed down through generations
to his great-grandson Ōuyáng Gāo,
forming the Ōuyáng school of Shàngshū.
Zhāng Shēng taught Xiàhóu Dūwèi.
Dūwèi taught his clansman Shǐchāng.
Shǐchāng transmitted it to his clansman Shèng,
forming the Dàxiàhóu school.
Shèng transmitted it to his elder cousin's son Jiàn.
Jiàn separately formed the Xiǎoxiahóu school. All three families established Bóshì.
Furthermore, Kǒng Ānguó of Lǔ transmitted the Gǔwén Shàngshū to Dūwèi Cháo.
Cháo taught Yōng Tán of Jiāodōng,
forming the Gǔwén school of Shàngshū,
but it was not established.
Ōuyáng Xī, whose courtesy name was Zhèngsī,
was from Qiāncéng, Lè'ān.
From Ōuyáng Shēng, who transmitted Fú Shēng's Shàngshū,
to Xī, eight generations,
all served as Bóshì.
After Xī transmitted the lineage,
he was humble and fond of modesty.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
he was Chángshè Zǎi.
When Gēngshǐ was established,
he was Yuánwǔ Lìng.
When Shìzǔ pacified Hébĕi,
he arrived at Yuánwǔ
and saw Xī diligently governing the county,
and promoted him to Hénán Dūwèi,
later acting as Tàishǒu.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was first made Hénán Yǐn,
and enfeoffed as Bèiyáng Hóu.
In the fifth year of Jiànwǔ,
he was dismissed from office due to a matter.
The following year,
he was appointed Yángzhōu Mù,
and then promoted to Rǔnán Tàishǒu.
He promoted and employed worthy talents,
and his governance was noted for its extraordinary achievements.
In the ninth year,
he was re-enfeoffed as Yè Hóu.
While Xī was in the commandery,
he taught several hundred people.
After serving for nine years,
he was summoned to be Dàsītú.
He was imprisoned after a thousand myriad zāngzuì in Rǔnán were discovered.
More than a thousand scholars pleaded for Xī outside the palace gate,
some even shaved their heads.
Lǐ Zhèn of Píngyuán,
seventeen years old,
heard that the judgment was imminent,
rushed to the capital,
and when he reached Huòjiā county in Hénèi,
he bound himself
and submitted a memorial requesting to die in Xī's place.
He said:
"I humbly observe that my teacher, Dàsītú Ōuyáng Xī,
whose learning is that of a Confucian patriarch,
an eight-generation Bóshì,
is to suffer severe punishment due to a fault of embezzlement.
Xī's family is small, and his son is young,
unable to transmit his learning.
After his death,
it will be permanently lost and cut off.
This will make Your Majesty subject to the criticism of having killed a worthy,
and below, it will cause scholars to lose the benefits of a teacher.
I beg to be executed in place of Xī's life."
The memorial was presented,
but Xī had already died in prison.
Xī's Aide, Chén Yuán, submitted a memorial to posthumously vindicate him,
speaking with great earnestness.
The Emperor then bestowed a coffin,
granted an official seal and sash,
and a funeral gift of three thousand rolls of silk.
His son Fù inherited.
After Fù died
without a son,
the fief was abolished.
Cáo Zēng, whose courtesy name was Bóshān, from Jìyīn,
received the Shàngshū from Xī.
He had three thousand disciples
and reached the position of Jiànyì Dàfū.
His son Zhǐ,
Hénán Yǐn,
transmitted his father's teaching and lectured.
Also, Chén Yǎn,
whose courtesy name was Shúmíng, from Chénliú,
also received Ōuyáng's Shàngshū from Sītú Dīng Hóng,
and served as Qí Zhǎng.
Móu Cháng, whose courtesy name was Jūngāo,
was from Línjì, Lè'ān.
His ancestors were enfeoffed in Móu.
At the end of the Spring and Autumn period,
the state was extinguished,
and they adopted the surname.
Cháng studied Ōuyáng's Shàngshū in his youth
and did not serve during Wáng Mǎng's era.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Dàsīkōng Hóng
specially invited him,
appointed him Bóshì,
and he was gradually promoted to Hénèi Tàishǒu.
He was dismissed for inaccurate land reclamation reports.
From the time Cháng was a Bóshì and while he was in Hénèi,
there were always over a thousand scholars attending his lectures,
with ten thousand registered over time.
He authored Shàngshū Zhāngjù,
all based on the Ōuyáng school,
which the common people called Móu's Zhāngjù.
He was again summoned to be Zhōngsàn Dàfū,
granted a year's leave,
and died at home.
His son Yū,
also taught as a recluse,
with a thousand disciples.
Sùzōng heard of him and summoned him,
intending to make him a Bóshì,
but he died on the way.
Sòng Dēng, whose courtesy name was Shúyáng,
was from Cháng'ān, Jīngzhào.
His father Yóu
was Tàiwèi.
Dēng transmitted Ōuyáng's Shàngshū in his youth,
teaching several thousand people.
He served as Rǔyīn Lìng.
His governance was renowned for its clarity and competence,
and he was called
"Divine Father."
He was promoted to Zhào Xiàng,
and then entered the court as Shàngshū Púyè.
Shùndì, recognizing Dēng's clear understanding of rituals and music,
sent him with a jǐe to supervise the Tàixué,
where he memorialized to establish the codes and regulations.
He was then appointed Shìzhōng.
He repeatedly submitted sealed memorials,
restraining powerful officials,
and consequently was sent out as Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu.
In the markets, there were no two prices;
on the roads, nothing was picked up.
He was dismissed due to illness,
and died at home.
The people of Rǔyīn enshrined him in local temples.
Zhāng Xùn
zì Zǐjùn, was a native of Dìngtáo, Jìyīn.
In his youth, he traveled to the Imperial Academy [tài xué]
and was able to recite the *Spring and Autumn Annals with Zuǒ Commentary* [Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn].
He taught the *Book of Documents* [Shàngshū] in the style of Dà Xiàhóu.
He was appointed to a ducal [gōng fǔ] office,
promoted to an eminent position,
and appointed Consultant [yì láng].
He and Cài Yōng jointly presented a petition to standardize the characters of the Six Classics [Liù Jīng].
He was promoted to Imperial Attendant [shì zhōng],
managing the Secretarial Bureau [mì shū jìn shǔ],
and was much appreciated and admired.
He took the opportunity to air his views on the advantages and disadvantages of government policies,
and the court praised him for it.
He was transferred to become Administrator [tài shǒu] of Dānyáng,
where his governance was benevolent.
In the seventh year of Guānghé (184 CE),
he was summoned and appointed Minister of the Imperial Household [shàng shū],
then moved to become Grand Minister of Agriculture [dà sī nóng].
In the middle of Chūpíng (190-193 CE),
he died in office.
Yǐn Mǐn
zì Yòujì, was a native of Dǔyáng, Nányáng.
In his youth, he was a student of the classics [zhū shēng].
Initially, he studied the *Book of Documents* [Shàngshū] in the Ouyáng [Ōuyáng] school,
then later received the ancient text [gǔ wén] tradition,
and was also proficient in the *Mao Commentary on the Book of Odes* [Máoshī], *Gǔliáng Commentary* [Gǔliáng], and *Zuǒ Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals* [Zuǒshì Chūnqiū].
In the second year of Jiànwǔ (26 CE),
he submitted a memorial explaining methods to avert disaster through the *Great Plan* [Hóngfàn].
At that time, Emperor Shìzǔ [Shìzǔ] was just beginning to establish the empire,
and had no leisure for such matters,
so he ordered Mǐn to await orders at the Public Carriages [gōng chē],
