appointed him Gentleman [láng zhōng],
and assigned him to the Grand Minister of Works's [dà sī kōng] office.
The Emperor, seeing Mǐn's extensive knowledge of classics and records,
ordered him to collate the prognostic charts [tú chèn],
and to remove the entries and classifications made by Cuī Fā [Cuī Fā] for Wáng Mǎng [Wáng Mǎng].
Mǐn replied:
"The prognostic charts are not the work of sages;
they contain many vulgar and corrupt characters,
and resemble common sayings,
which I fear might mislead later generations."
The Emperor did not accept this.
Mǐn then added to a missing phrase, saying:
"The ruler without a mouth [jūn wú kǒu]
shall aid Hàn [wéi Hàn fǔ]."
The Emperor saw it and found it strange,
so he summoned Mǐn and asked him the reason.
Mǐn replied:
"I saw that previous people had added to and subtracted from the charts and documents,
and daring to presume beyond my measure,
I secretly hoped for a chance."
The Emperor strongly disapproved of this,
and although he did not punish him eventually,
Mǐn was subsequently held back because of this.
He was a close friend of Bān Biāo [Bān Biāo];
whenever they met,
they would often forget to eat until dusk,
and not sleep until midnight,
considering themselves like Zhōng Qí [Zhōng Qí] and Bó Yá [Bó Yá], or Zhuāng Zhōu [Zhuāng Zhōu] and Huì Shī [Huì Shī] in their mutual understanding.
Later, he was transferred three times, becoming Magistrate [lìng] of Chánglíng.
In the fifth year of Yǒngpíng (62 CE),
an imperial edict ordered the arrest of the man Zhōu Lǜ [Zhōu Lǜ].
Lǜ was well-known
and on good terms with Mǐn;
Mǐn was implicated, arrested, and dismissed from office.
When he was released,
he sighed:
"The deaf and mute [yīn lóng zhī tú]
are truly the men of the Dao [dào] in this world;
why do I, being too discerning, encounter such misfortune?"
In the eleventh year (68 CE),
he was appointed Gentleman [láng zhōng],
then promoted to Grand Master of Remonstrance [jiàn yì dà fū].
He died at home.
Zhōu Fáng
zì Wěigōng, was a native of Rǔyáng, Rǔnán.
His father, Yáng [Yáng],
was orphaned and humble in his youth;
he often managed an inn,
providing for travelers,
but accepting no payment in return.
When Fáng was sixteen,
he served as a minor official in the commandery [jùn].
When Emperor Shìzǔ [Shìzǔ] toured Rǔnán,
he summoned the subordinate officials [yuàn shǐ] to test their knowledge of the classics;
Fáng was particularly adept at recitation,
and was appointed Protector-Assistant [shǒu chéng].
Fáng, being not yet capped,
petitioned to resign.
He became a student of Gài Yù [Gài Yù], Inspector [cì shǐ] of Xúzhōu,
and received the ancient text *Book of Documents* [gǔ wén Shàngshū].
His classical learning was profound,
so he was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt [xiào lián]
and appointed Gentleman [láng zhōng].
He compiled *Miscellaneous Records of the Book of Documents* [Shàngshū Zájì] in thirty-two chapters,
totaling four hundred thousand characters.
Grand Commandant [tài wèi] Zhāng Yǔ [Zhāng Yǔ] recommended him to be appointed Erudite [bó shì],
and he was gradually promoted to Administrator [tài shǒu] of Chénliú,
but was dismissed due to legal issues.
He died at home
at the age of seventy-eight.
His son Jǔ [Jǔ]
has his own biography.
Kǒng Xī
zì Zhònghé, was a native of Lǔ, Lǔguó.
From Ānguó [Ānguó] downwards,
his family hereditarily transmitted the ancient text *Book of Documents* [gǔ wén Shàngshū] and the *Mao Commentary on the Book of Odes* [Máoshī].
His great-grandfather, Zǐjiàn [Zǐjiàn],
traveled to Cháng'ān in his youth
and was good friends with Cuī Zhuàn [Cuī Zhuàn].
When Zhuàn served Wáng Mǎng [Wáng Mǎng] as Grand Governor of Jiànxīn [Jiànxīn Dàyǐn],
he once urged Zǐjiàn to take office.
Zǐjiàn replied:
"I have the heart of a commoner,
while you have the ambition for robes and crowns;
each following his own preference,
is that not well!
Since our paths diverge,
I ask to take my leave from this point."
Thereupon, he returned home
and died there.
Xī, together with Cuī Zhuàn and Sūn Yīn, once again became good friends.
They frequently visited the Imperial Academy together,
studying the Spring and Autumn Annals.
As they read about the events during the time of King Fūchā of Wú,
Xī put down his book and sighed, saying:
“If it is like this,
it is like the saying, ‘One who fails to draw a dragon instead draws a dog.’”
Yīn said:
“Indeed.
In the past, when Emperor Xiàowǔ first became Son of Heaven,
he was only eighteen years old.
He reverently believed in the sagely Way,
and took the former kings as his models.
Within five or six years,
he was hailed as surpassing [Emperors] Wén and Jǐng.
But afterwards, he indulged himself,
forgetting the good deeds he had done before.”
Xī said:
“Historical accounts and traditions contain many such instances!”
Liáng Yù, a student from a neighboring room, interjected and harmonized, saying:
“If that is the case,
is Emperor Wǔ also a dog?”
Xī and Yīn remained silent and did not reply.
Yù became angry and resentful of them.
He secretly submitted a memorial accusing Yīn and Xī of slandering the former emperor
and criticizing the current age.
The matter was handed down to the relevant authorities.
Yīn went to the officials to be interrogated.
Xī, as the officials were about to arrest him,
feared execution.
So he submitted a memorial to Sùzōng, defending himself, saying:
“My foolish opinion
is that all talk of slander
refers to falsely accusing someone of something that did not actually happen.
As for Emperor Xiàowǔ,
the good and bad of his governance
are clearly recorded in the Hàn History,
as plain as the sun and moon.
This is merely speaking plainly about actual historical facts and traditions,
not baseless slander.
If an emperor does good,
then all the good in the world flows to him;
if he does not do good,
then all the evil in the world likewise gathers around him.
These are all things that lead to such outcomes,
and thus cannot be attributed to the execution of others.
Moreover, since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
your governance and teachings have not been amiss,
and your benevolence and grace have increased,
as is evident to all under Heaven.
How then could your servants alone criticize and satirize?
Even if what was criticized were indeed true,
then it should naturally lead to correction and reform;
if it is inappropriate,
it should still be tolerated and accommodated.
What crime is there in that?
Your Majesty does not consider the broader perspective,
nor plan deeply for yourself,
but merely gives vent to private resentment
to satisfy your feelings.
Even if your servants are punished and
die, so be it.
But the people of the world
will surely look askance and change their minds,
using this matter to discern Your Majesty’s heart.
From now on,
if they see anything untoward,
they will never speak of it again.
The reason your servant does not cherish his life
and still dares to speak frankly
is truly out of deep concern for this great enterprise of Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty does not cherish it yourself,
then what dependence do your servants have?
Duke Huán of Qí personally publicized the faults of his late lord
to inspire Guǎn Zhòng,
after which his ministers were able to fully express their minds.
Now Your Majesty wishes to obscure historical facts
regarding Emperor Wǔ of ten generations ago.
Is this not different from Duke Huán?
Your servant fears that the relevant authorities may suddenly contrive a case,
leading to resentment and injustice,
without being able to defend oneself,
and that later commentators
will take it upon themselves to make comparisons with Your Majesty.
How can this be covered up by your descendants later?
I respectfully await grave punishment before the palace gate.”
The Emperor initially had no intention of faulting Xī and others.
When the memorial was presented,
he immediately issued an edict not to investigate.
He appointed Xī as Lántái Lìngshǐ.
In the spring of the second year of Yuánhé,
the Emperor made an eastern inspection tour.
Upon his return, he passed through Lǔ
and visited Quèlǐ.
He offered a grand sacrifice (tàiláo) to Kǒngzǐ and his seventy-two disciples,
performed the music of the Six Dynasties,
and convened a great gathering of sixty-three males of the Kǒng clan aged twenty and above.
He ordered scholars to lecture and discuss the Analects (Yǔ).
Xī then presented himself to apologize.
The Emperor said:
“Does this gathering today
bring honor to your clan?”
He replied:
“Your servant has heard that enlightened kings and sagely rulers
all respect teachers and value the Way.
Now Your Majesty personally condescends, with your myriad chariots,
to grace our humble village.
This is indeed to honor the former master [Kǒngzǐ]
and add splendor to your sagely virtue.
As for honor,
it is not something your servant dares to claim.”
The Emperor laughed heartily and said:
“If not a descendant of a sage,
how could one utter such words!”
He then appointed Xī as Lángzhōng,
bestowed money and silk upon Bāochéng Hóu Sǔn and the Kǒng clan’s men and women,
and ordered Xī to return to the capital with him,
assigning him to collate books at the Dōngguān.
In winter,
he was appointed Magistrate of Línjìn.
Cuī Yīn consulted his family’s diviner
and said it was inauspicious.
He stopped Xī, saying:
“Why don't you decline?”
Xī said:
“Learning is not for others,
and official service does not choose its post.
Auspiciousness and inauspiciousness come from oneself;
how can they depend on divination?”
He served in the county for three years
and died in office.
His dying wish was to be buried immediately.
His two sons, Zhǎngyàn and Jìyàn,
were both just over ten years old.
Xǔ Jūnrán, the Magistrate of Púbǎn, urged them to return to Lǔ.
They replied:
“If we carry the coffin and return now,
we would violate our father’s dying wish;
if we abandon the grave and leave,
our hearts cannot bear it.”
So they remained in Huáyīn.
Zhǎngyàn was fond of textual studies,
and Jìyàn maintained the family’s livelihood,
with several hundred disciples.
In the first year of Yángguāng,
there was a great hailstorm in Héxī,
with hailstones as large as dippers.
Emperor Ān issued an edict for men of the Daoist arts to fully explain the omens of calamity,
so Jìyàn was summoned to meet him at Déyáng Diàn.
The Emperor personally asked him the reason.
He replied:
“These are all signs of Yīn overpowering Yáng.
Currently, favored officials wield power,
and the empress dowager’s faction is strong.
Your Majesty should cultivate sagely virtue
and be mindful of these two things.”
The Emperor remained silent,
and his attendants all disliked it.
He was nominated as a Xiàolián
but did not accept the appointment.
Three years later,
at the age of forty-seven,
he died at home.
Initially,
during Emperor Píng’s reign, Wáng Mǎng held power.
He enfeoffed Kǒng Jūn, a descendant of Kǒngzǐ, as Bāochéng Hóu,
and posthumously honored Kǒngzǐ as Bāochéng Xuānnī.
When Mǎng was defeated,
the state was lost.
In the thirteenth year of Jiànwǔ,
Shìzǔ re-enfeoffed Kǒng Zhì, Jūn’s son, as Bāochéng Hóu.
When Zhì died,
his son Sǔn succeeded.
In the fourth year of Yǒngyuán,
he was transferred and enfeoffed as Bāotíng Hóu.
When Sǔn died,
his son Yào succeeded.
When Yào died,
his son Wán succeeded.
The succession continued through generations
until the beginning of Emperor Xiàn’s reign,
when the lineage was severed.
Yáng Lún, courtesy name Zhònglǐ,
was from Dōnghūn, Chénliú.
As a youth, he was a student
and studied under the Grand Administrator Dīng Hóng,
learning the Old Text Book of Documents (Gǔwén Shàngshū).
He served as a Wénxué Yuàn in the commandery.
He served under several generals,
but his aspirations diverged from the times.
Unable to handle worldly affairs,
he resigned from office
and no longer responded to invitations from provinces and commanderies.
He lectured and taught in a large marsh,
and his disciples numbered over a thousand.
In the Yuánchū period,
the commandery respectfully invited him,
the Three Excellencies all summoned him,
and he was summoned by Gōngchē.
He declined all due to illness and did not take up the posts.
Later, he was appointed Bóshì
and Fù to Qīnghé Wáng.
That year,
Āndì died.
Lún immediately [⿱𠫓廾] his office and rushed to mourn,
wailing incessantly beneath the palace gate.
Empress Dowager Yán dismissed him from office for his arbitrary actions,
and he was convicted.
When Shùndì ascended the throne,
an edict pardoned Lún's sentence,
and he was allowed to remain to observe the mourning period at Gōnglíng.
When the mourning period ended,
he was summoned and appointed Shìzhōng.
At this time, Rèn Jiā, the magistrate of Shàolíng, was corrupt in office,
but was transferred to be the Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi.
Later, the authorities reported that Jiā had embezzled ten million [coins],
and he was summoned for investigation by the Tíngwèi.
More than a hundred generals, ministers, and high officials were implicated.
Lún then submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that in the Chūnqiū, evil is punished at its root.
When the root is punished, evil disappears. Just as when one shakes a fur coat by its collar,
if the collar is straight, the fur will lie flat.
Now, Rèn Jiā's crimes are rampant,
yet he has not been punished with execution.
Instead, with his defiled body,
he was reassigned to govern a large commandery.
Unless those who promoted him are investigated and held accountable,
it will be impossible to suppress the seeds of treachery.
In the past, Zhāng Dié, the magistrate of Húlù, Sī Xián, the magistrate of Xiāo, Liú Fú, the Inspector of Xúzhōu, and others,
their污秽 was clear,
and they all suffered their due punishment.
But the officials who act like jackals and wolves are still not eradicated today.
Is this not because the superiors who promoted them were not punished?
When Qí Wēi Bā ruled in the past,
he executed five corrupt ministers
and also those who promoted them,
to quell public criticism.
Not to act when action is required
is what Huáng Shí warned against.
The reason why a sagely king listens to the words of a common man or woman
is like dust added to Sōngdài,
or mist gathering over Huáihǎi.
Although it may not bring immediate benefit,
it does no harm.
I beg Your Majesty to give this your careful consideration."
When the memorial was presented to the Emperor,
the authorities considered Lún's words too blunt,
and his language not humble or compliant,
so they dismissed it.
The Shàngshū reported that Lún had pried into secret matters
and agitated for what he considered righteousness.
He was convicted of disrespect
and sentenced to serve as a 'ghost faggot-gatherer'.
An edict stated that because Lún had repeatedly offered loyal advice,
he was specially pardoned
and allowed to return to his home village.
In Yángjiā Èrnián,
he was summoned and appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū.
Dàjiāngjūn Liáng Shāng made him his Chángshǐ.
Because his remonstrances were not accepted,
he was appointed Fù to Chángshān Wáng.
He fell ill and did not take office.
An imperial edict ordered the Sīlì to urge his departure.
Lún then remained in Cháogē, Hénèi,
and reported his illness,
saying:
"I would rather die one foot from here
than go one inch north.
I would not change my mind even if my neck were severed,
nor would I regret it if I were torn into nine pieces.
The resolve of a common man
is stronger than three armies.
Thus, I dare to offer this excuse."
The Emperor then issued an edict, saying:
"Lún has risen from obscurity to high position,
favored with the post of a princely tutor.
Yet he delays the king's command,
arbitrarily stops on the road,
claims illness to do as he pleases,
and indulges his unyielding will."
He was then summoned to the Tíngwèi,
but an edict pardoned his offense.
Lún was summoned three times in total,
each time his blunt remonstrances were not accepted.
After returning home,
he closed his door to teach,
cutting himself off from social interaction.
When the Gōngchē summoned him again,
he modestly declined to go,
and died at home.
During the *Zhōngxīng* era,
Móu Róng of Běihǎi studied the Greater Xiàhóu *Shàngshū*;
Wáng Liáng of Dōnghǎi studied the Lesser Xiàhóu *Shàngshū*;
Huán Róng of Pèiguó studied the Ōuyáng *Shàngshū*.
Róng's family transmitted and taught it through generations,
becoming most prominent in the Eastern Hàn.
Dù Lín of Fúfēng transmitted the Ancient Text *Shàngshū*.
Jiǎ Kuí, from the same commandery as Lín, wrote a commentary for it;
Mǎ Róng wrote a *zhuàn* (commentary/biography);
Zhèng Xuán annotated it,
from which the Ancient Text *Shàngshū* became renowned in the world.

Here, the character
is missing,
now supplemented.
Page 2558, line 1: Zhāng Xùn. Note: The *Jíjiě* cites Huì Dòng’s explanation,
stating that
“馴” (*xùn*)
is also written as
which are interchangeable in ancient texts.
Page 2560, line 6: Kǒng Xī, courtesy name Zhònghé. Note: The *Jíjiě* cites Huì Dòng’s explanation,
stating that *Liáncóngzǐ* writes
“Zǐhé”.

Page 2560, line 6: “世傳古文尚書毛詩” (*shì chuán gǔwén Shàngshū Máo Shī*, “The Ancient Text *Shàngshū* and *Máo Shī* were transmitted through generations”). Note: The *Jíjiě* cites Lǐ Liángqiú’s explanation,
stating that Ānguó is not known to have received the *Máo Shī*,
and “毛詩” (*Máo Shī*)
is probably
an error for “魯詩” (*Lǔ Shī*).
Page 2560, line 11: “所謂畫龍不成反為狗者” (*suǒwèi huà lóng bù chéng fǎn wèi gǒu zhě*, “what is called failing to draw a dragon and instead drawing a dog”). Note: *Kānwù* states that
the character “龍” (*lóng*)
is an error for
the character “虎” (*hǔ*).
The supplementary note cites Wáng Mào’s explanation,
stating that during the Táng dynasty, to avoid
the character “虎” (*hǔ*),
was changed
to
“龍” (*lóng*),
which is not an error.
Page 2561, line 4: “天下所具也” (*tiānxià suǒ jù yě*, “what the world possesses”). Note: The *Jíjiě* states that Yuán Hóng’s *Jì* writes
“天下所共見也” (*tiānxià suǒ gòng jiàn yě*, “what the world commonly sees”).
Page 2562, line 11: “命儒者講論【語】” (*mìng rúzhě jiǎnglùn [yǔ]*, “ordered scholars to discuss and deliberate”). Note: *Jiàobǔ* cites Qián Dàzhāo’s explanation,
stating that the Mǐn edition
has the character
after “論” (*lùn*).
*Jiàobǔ* states that the Mǐn edition is correct,
and all other editions are missing one character.
Now supplemented accordingly.
Page 2563, line 9: “年四十七終於家” (*nián sìshíqī zhōng yú jiā*, “died at home at forty-seven years old”). Note: The *Jíjiě* cites Huì Dòng’s explanation,
stating that *Liáncóngzǐ* says he was forty-nine,
and died on the *dīngchǒu* day of the eleventh month in the third year of *Yán’guāng*.
Page 2563, line 10: “追謚孔子為襃成宣尼” (*zhuī shì Kǒngzǐ wèi Bāochéng Xuānní*, “posthumously conferred Kǒngzǐ the title of Bāochéng Xuānní”). Note: *Kānwù* states that this text is missing
the character “公” (*gōng*).

Page 2563, line 11: “建武十三年世祖復封均子志為襃成侯” (*Jiànwǔ shísān nián Shìzǔ fù fēng Jūn zi Zhì wèi Bāochéng Hóu*, “In the thirteenth year of *Jiànwǔ*, Emperor Shìzǔ again enfeoffed Jūn’s son Zhì as Marquis of Bāochéng”). Note: The *Jíjiě* cites Hóng Liàngjí’s explanation,
stating that the *Jì* records it as the fourth month of the fourteenth year,
and the note cites *Gǔjīn Zhù*,
saying that Zhì was the Magistrate of Mì at the time.
This mention of
“十三年” (*shísān nián*, “thirteenth year”)
seems to be an error.
Page 2564, line 2: Yáng Lún, courtesy name Zhònglǐ. Note: The *Jíjiě* cites Hóng Yíxuān’s explanation,
stating that Yáng Zhèn’s biography says
“Zhèn recommended clear-minded scholars such as Yáng Lún of Chénliú.”
Lǐ’s note says,
“His courtesy name was Zhòngyuán.
Xiè Chéng’s book recommended five people including Yáng Zhòngyuán,
each appointed Academician from their household.”
This differs from his courtesy name Zhònglǐ.
Also note:
“楊” (*Yáng*)
was originally a corrupted character
“揚” (*Yáng*),
corrected directly.
Biography of Ruists, Volume 69, Part Two.
The former book states that Shēn Gōng of Lǔ received the *Shī* from Fúqiū Bó,
and composed commentaries for it,
which became the *Lǔ Shī*;
Yuán Gùshēng of Qí also transmitted the *Shī*,
which became the *Qí Shī*;
Hán Yīng of Yàn also transmitted the *Shī*,
which became the *Hán Shī*: all three schools established academicians.
Máo Cháng of Zhào transmitted the *Shī*,
which became the *Máo Shī*,
but was not yet established.
Gāo Xǔ, courtesy name Jìhuí,
was a man from Píngyuán Bān.
His great-grandfather Jiā
taught the *Lǔ Shī* to Emperor Yuán,
and served as Grand Administrator of Shànggǔ.
His father Róng
began studying Jiā's teachings in his youth,
and during the *Āi-Píng* era, served as Grand Master of Guanglu.
Xǔ, by virtue of his father's appointment, became a Lángzhōng.
His family passed down the Lǔ Shī.
He was known for his integrity and upright conduct.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
father and son claimed blindness,
fled,
and did not serve in Wáng Mǎng's reign.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
Dà Sīkōng Sòng Hóng recommended Xǔ.
He was summoned to be a Láng,
and then appointed Prefect of Fúlǐ.
He left office,
and was later summoned to be a Bóshì.
In the eleventh year of Jiànwǔ,
he was appointed Dà Sīnóng.
In court, he was praised for his uprightness.
In the thirteenth year,
he died in office,
and was granted money and burial land.
Bāo Xián, courtesy name Zǐliáng,
was a native of Qǔ'ē, Kuàijī.
When young, he was a student of the Classics,
studying in Cháng'ān,
and served Bóshì Yòushī Xìjūn as his teacher,
learning the Lǔ Shī and the Lúnyǔ.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
he returned to his hometown,
and in the area of Dōnghǎi, he was captured by the Chìméi rebels,
and thus was held in captivity.
For more than ten days,
Xián recited the Classics morning and night as if undisturbed.
The rebels found him unusual and released him.
Thereupon, he stayed in Dōnghǎi,
established a private academy, and lectured.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he then returned to his hometown.
The Grand Administrator Huáng Dǎng appointed him Hùcáoshǐ,
wanting to summon Xián to instruct his son.
Xián said,
"According to the Rites, students come to learn,
but there is no going out to teach."
Dǎng then sent his son to become Xián's disciple.
He was nominated as Xiàolián,
and appointed Lángzhōng.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
he entered the palace to instruct the Crown Prince in the Lúnyǔ,
and also composed its chapters and sentences.
He was appointed Jiànyì Dàfū, Shìzhōng, and Yòu Zhōnglángjiāng.
In the fifth year of Yǒngpíng,
he was promoted to Dà Hónglú.
Whenever he had an audience,
he was granted a stool and a staff,
and when entering the screen, he did not rush;
when presenting matters, he was not called by name.
If there were doubts in the Classics and commentaries,
the Xiǎohuángmén would be sent to his residence to inquire immediately.
Xiǎnzōng, due to Xián's kindness as a teacher and mentor,
and his consistent simplicity and hardship,
often specially bestowed upon him rare treasures, fine playthings, and bolts of silk.
His salary was increased beyond that of other Qīng,
and Xián distributed all of it among his poor students.
When his illness became severe,
the Emperor personally drove his carriage to visit him.
In the eighth year,
at the age of seventy-two,
he died in office.
His son, Fú,
was appointed Lángzhōng,
and also entered the palace to instruct Hédì in the Lúnyǔ.
Wèi Yìng, courtesy name Jūnbó,
was a native of Rènchéng.
When young, he loved learning.
At the beginning of Jiànwǔ,
he went to a Bóshì to receive instruction,
studying the Lǔ Shī.
He studied diligently behind closed doors,
not associating with colleagues or factions,
and was praised in Jīngshī.
Later, he returned to serve as a county official,
was nominated for Míngjīng,
and appointed Jìyīn Wáng Wénxué.
He resigned due to illness,
and taught in the mountains and marshes,
with hundreds of disciples constantly.
At the beginning of Yǒngpíng,
he became a Bóshì,
and was twice promoted to Shìzhōng.
In the thirteenth year,
he was promoted to Dà Hónglú.
In the eighteenth year,
he was appointed Guānglù Dàfū.
In the fourth year of Jiànchū,
he was appointed Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiāng,
and ordered to enter the palace to instruct Qiānchéng Wáng Kàng.
Yìng's knowledge of the Classics was clear, and his conduct was exemplary.
Disciples came from distant places,
with thousands registered.
Sùzōng greatly esteemed him,
frequently granted him audiences,
discussed difficulties before him,
and specially bestowed rewards.
At that time, the scholars of Jīngshī gathered at Báihǔ Guān
to discuss the similarities and differences of the Wǔ Jīng.
Yìng was appointed to specifically manage the questions and answers.
Shìzhōng Chúnyú Gōng presented this,
and the Emperor personally presided and issued decrees,
following the precedent of Shíqú.
The following year,
he was sent out as Grand Administrator of Shàngdǎng,
then summoned and appointed Qí Dūwèi,
and died in office.
Fú Gōng, courtesy name Shúqí,
was a native of Dōngwǔ, Lángyá,
and the elder nephew of Sītú Zhàn.
Zhàn's younger brother, Àn,
courtesy name Zhìwén,
was renowned for his clear understanding of the Qí Shī.
He revised and standardized the chapters and sentences,
and wrote nine chapters of explanations.
He rose to the position of Guānglùxūn,
but had no son,
so he adopted Gōng as his heir.
Gōng was filial by nature,
and served his stepmother with great care.
When young, he inherited Àn's scholarship,
and was appointed Láng due to his position.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
he was appointed Prefect of Jù.
He served for thirteen years,
and was known for his benevolent governance and impartiality.
Qīngzhōu recommended him as exceptionally outstanding,
and he ranked first in the Tàicháng's Classics examination.
He was appointed Bóshì,
and promoted to Grand Administrator of Chángshān.
He vigorously promoted schools,
and taught without ceasing,
which led to many in the northern provinces adopting the Fú family's scholarship.
In the second year of Yǒngpíng,
he succeeded Liáng Sōng as Tàipú.
In the fourth year,
the Emperor personally visited Píyōng,
and during the ritual ceremony, appointed Gōng as Sīkōng.
Scholars considered this an honor.
Initially,
his father Àn's chapters and sentences were numerous and verbose.
Gōng therefore reduced the superfluous words,
standardizing it to two hundred thousand characters.
He served for nine years,
and then requested to retire due to illness,
and an imperial edict granted him a salary of one thousand shí until the end of his life.
In the fifteenth year,
when the Emperor made a tour to Lángyá,
he was granted an audience with the same honors as a Sāngōng.
In the winter of the second year of Jiànchū,
Sùzōng held a banquet,
and appointed Gōng as Sānlǎo.
At ninety years old,
he died in the first year of Yuánhé,
and was granted burial near Xiǎnjié Líng.
His son, Shòu,
rose to the position of Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn.
Rèn Mò, courtesy name Shúběn,
was a native of Fán, Shǔjùn.
When young, he studied the Qí Shī,
traveled to Jīngshī,
and taught for over ten years.
His friend Dǒng Fèngdé died of illness in Luòyáng.
Mò then personally pushed a deer cart,
transporting Fèngdé's coffin to his burial site,
and thereby became known.
He served as Jùn Gōngcáo,
but resigned due to illness.
Later, while rushing to his teacher's funeral,
he died on the way.
On his deathbed,
he instructed his nephew Zào, saying:
"You must bring my body to my teacher's gate,
so that if I have consciousness after death,
my soul will not be ashamed;
if I have no consciousness,
it is merely to return to the earth."
Zào followed his wishes.
Jǐng Luán (景鸞), courtesy name Hàn Bó (漢伯),
was a native of Zǐtóng (梓潼), Guǎnghàn (廣漢).
In his youth, he followed a teacher to study the classics,
traveling through seven prefectures.
He was skilled in interpreting the *Qí Shī* (齊詩) and *Shī Shì Yì* (施氏易),
and also received instruction in the *Hé Luò Tú Wěi* (河洛圖緯).
He wrote an explanation of the *Yì* (易說) and an interpretation of the *Shī* (詩解).
His phrasing and sentences incorporated elements from the *Hé Luò* (河洛),
grouping them by category,
and named it *Jiāo Jí* (交集).
He also compiled the *Lǐ Nèi Wài Jì* (禮內外記),
titled *Lǐ Lüè* (禮略).
He furthermore copied various works on *fēng jué* (風角),
listing their divinations and verifications,
and wrote the *Xīng Dào* (興道) in one chapter.
He also composed chapter and verse interpretations for the *Yuè Lìng* (月令).
All his writings amounted to more than 500,000 words.
He repeatedly submitted memorials to present methods for alleviating disasters.
He declined appointments from the prefectures and commanderies.
He died of old age.
Xuē Hàn (薛漢), courtesy name Gōng Zǐ (公子),
was a native of Huái Yáng (淮陽).
His family had generations of expertise in the *Hán Shī* (韓詩),
and father and son were famous for their chapter and verse interpretations.
Hàn (漢) in his youth inherited his father's profession,
and was particularly skilled at explaining disasters, anomalies, prophecies, and apocrypha.
He regularly taught several hundred students.
At the beginning of the Jiànwǔ (建武) era,
he became a *Bóshì* (博士) (Erudite),
and was ordered to collate and verify the diagrams and apocrypha.
Among the contemporary interpreters of the *Shī* (詩),
Hàn (漢) was considered the foremost.
During the Yǒngpíng (永平) era,
he served as the Grand Administrator of Qiānchéng (千乘),
where his administration showed unusual achievements.
Later, he became implicated in the affairs of Chǔ (楚)
and died in prison.
His most famous disciples were Dù Fǔ (杜撫) of Jiànwéi (犍為), Tán Tái Jìng Bó (澹臺敬伯) of Kuàijī (會稽), and Hán Bó Gāo (韓伯高) of Jùlù (鉅鹿).
Dù Fǔ (杜撫), courtesy name Shú Hé (叔和),
was a native of Wǔyáng (武陽), Jiànwéi (犍為).
He had high talent in his youth.
He studied under Xuē Hàn (薛漢),
and codified the chapter and verse interpretations of the *Hán Shī* (韓詩).
Later, he returned to his hometown to teach.
He was calm and content with his principles,
and all his actions were in accordance with ritual.
He had over a thousand disciples.
Later, he was recruited by Piàojì Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍) (General of Cavalry), Prince Cāng (蒼) of Dōngpíng (東平).
When Cāng (蒼) went to his fief,
all his clerks and officials were appointed to royal positions.
Before a year had passed,
they all impeached themselves and returned home.
At that time, Fǔ (撫) was a *Dàfū* (大夫) (Grandee);
he could not bear to leave.
When Cāng (蒼) heard of this,
he bestowed upon him carriages, horses, and valuables, and sent him away.
He was recruited by the office of the Tàiwèi (太尉) (Grand Commandant).
During the Jiànchū (建初) era,
he served as the Gōngchē Lìng (公車令) (Prefect of the Palace Coach Office).
He died in office after several months.
His interpretations of the *Shī* (詩) were succinct in their titles and clear in their meanings.
Scholars passed them down,
referring to them as "Lord Dù's (杜君) method."
Shào Xún (召馴), courtesy name Bó Chūn (伯春),
was a native of Shòuchūn (壽春), Jiǔjiāng (九江).
His great-grandfather, Xìn Chén (信臣),
served as Shǎofǔ (少府) (Privy Treasurer) during the reign of Emperor Yuán (元).
His father served as the Prefect of Juǎn (卷令) during the Jiànwǔ (建武) era,
and was unrestrained and unconventional, not bothered by minor details.
Xún (馴) in his youth studied the *Hán Shī* (韓詩),
and was extensively versed in books and traditions.
He was known for his aspirations and righteousness,
and his hometown referred to him as
"the virtuous and gentle Shào Bó Chūn (召伯春)."
He successively served in prefectures and commanderies,
and was recruited by the office of the Sītú (司徒) (Minister of Works).
In the first year of Jiànchū (建初),
he was gradually promoted to Qí Dūwèi (騎都尉) (Colonel of Cavalry),
and lectured to Emperor Sùzōng (肅宗).
He was appointed Zuǒ Zhōng Láng Jiāng (左中郎將) (Left Commander of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household),
and entered to instruct the various princes.
The emperor praised his scholarly righteousness,
and his favor and honor were exceptionally high.
He was appointed Grand Administrator of Chénliú (陳留),
and was gifted swords, money, and valuables.
In the second year of Yuánhé (元和),
he became Hénán Yǐn (河南尹) (Prefect of Hénán).
In the second year of Zhānghé (章和),
he replaced Rèn Kuí (任隗) as Guānglù Xún (光祿勳) (Grand Master of Ceremonies).
He died in office,
and was granted a tomb and burial plot accompanying the imperial mausoleum.
His grandson, Xiū (休),
reached the position of Cìshǐ (刺史) (Inspector) of Qīngzhōu (青州).
Yáng Rén (楊仁), courtesy name Wén Yì (文義),
was a native of Lángzhōng (閬中), Bājùn (巴郡).
During the Jiànwǔ (建wǔ) era,
he went to a teacher to study the *Hán Shī* (韓詩).
After several years, he returned
and lived quietly, teaching.
He served in the commandery as Gōngcáo (功曹) (Clerk of Merit),
was nominated as *Xiàolián* (孝廉) (Filial and Incorrupt),
and appointed as a *Láng* (郎) (Gentleman).
The Tàicháng (太常) (Grand Master of Ceremonies) recommended Rén (仁) as a *Bóshì* (博士) (Erudite) in the classics.
Rén (仁) considered himself not yet fifty,
and thus not compliant with the old regulations.
He submitted a petition to the court to decline the selection.
Emperor Xiǎozōng (顯宗) issued a special edict appointing him Běigōng Wèishì Lìng (北宮衞士令) (Prefect of the Northern Palace Guards).
He was granted an audience
and asked about current political affairs.
Rén (仁) replied that the priority should be leniency and harmony, appointing the worthy,
and suppressing and demoting the arrogant and privileged.
He also presented twelve matters of immediate benefit,
all of which were urgent issues of the time.
The emperor praised him
and bestowed upon him silk and money.
When the emperor died,
the various Mǎ (馬) clans were powerful and prosperous,
each vying to enter the palace.
Rén (仁), donned in armor and holding a halberd,
strictly commanded the gate guards,
and none dared to advance lightly.
After Sùzōng (肅宗) ascended the throne,
the various Mǎ (馬) clans jointly slandered Rén (仁) as harsh and severe.
The emperor, knowing his loyalty,
esteemed him even more,
and appointed him Prefect of Shífāng (什邡).
He governed with leniency and benevolence,
encouraging and instructing his clerks, officials, and disciples,
all of whom he compelled to pursue studies.
Those who were thoroughly enlightened in classical arts
he promoted to the right-hand posts (higher positions),
or recommended to the court.
Because of this, scholarly righteousness greatly flourished.
Over a thousand *qǐng* (頃) of land were reclaimed.
He left office to mourn his elder brother.
Later, he was recruited by the office of Sītú Huán Yú (司徒桓虞).
There was a clerk named Sòng Zhāng (宋章),
who was greedy, extravagant, and lawless.
Rén (仁) never spoke with him or sat at the same table,
and people of the time respected his integrity.
Later, he became Prefect of Lángzhōng (閬中),
and died in office.
Zhào Yè (趙曄), courtesy name Cháng Jūn (長君),
was a native of Shānyīn (山陰), Kuàijī (會稽).
In his youth, he once served as a county official.
When he was ordered to carry a summons to welcome a *Dūyóu* (督郵) (Inspector),
Yè (曄) was ashamed of the servile duty
and drove away his carriage and horses.
He arrived at Zīzhōng (資中), Jiànwéi (犍為),
and went to Dù Fǔ (杜撫) to study the *Hán Shī* (韓詩),
mastering its methods.
For twenty years,
he cut off communication and did not return,
and his family held a funeral and wore mourning clothes for him.
After Fǔ (撫) died, Yè (曄) returned.
The prefecture summoned him to serve as a Cóngshì (從事) (Supervisor),
but he declined.
He was recommended as a person of the Dao.
He died at home.
Yè (曄) authored *Wú Yuè Chūnqiū* (吳越春秋) and *Shī Xì Lì Shén Yuān* (詩細歷神淵).
When Cài Yōng (蔡邕) arrived in Kuàijī (會稽),
he read *Shī Xì* (詩細) and sighed in admiration,
believing it to be superior to *Lùn Héng* (論衡).
When Yōng (邕) returned to the capital,
he propagated it,
and scholars all recited and studied it.
At that time, Zhāng Kuāng (張匡) of Shānyáng (山陽),
courtesy name Wén Tōng (文通),
also studied the *Hán Shī* (韓詩)
and wrote chapter and verse interpretations.
Later, he was recommended as a person of the Dao,
and was summoned by the *Bóshì* (博士) (Erudites),
but he declined.
He died at home.
Wèi Hóng (衞宏), courtesy name Jìng Zhòng (敬仲),
was a native of Dōnghǎi (東海).
In his youth, he and Zhèng Xìng (鄭興) of Hénán (河南) both loved ancient learning.
Initially,
Xiè Màn Qīng (謝曼卿) of Jiǔjiāng (九江) was skilled in the *Máo Shī* (毛詩)
and wrote its commentaries.
Hóng (宏) studied under Màn Qīng (曼卿),
and subsequently wrote the *Máo Shī Xù* (毛詩序) (Preface to the Máo Shī),
which skillfully captured the essence of the *Fēng* (風) and *Yǎ* (雅) sections,
and is still transmitted to this day.
Later, he further studied the Ancient Text *Shàngshū* (尚書) under Dà Sīkōng Dù Lín (大司空杜林) (Grand Minister of Works Dù Lín),
and wrote its commentaries.
At that time, Xú Xún (徐巡) of Jìnán (濟南) was Hóng's (宏) student.
Later, Xú Xún (徐巡) studied under Lín (林),
and also became prominent through Confucianism.
From this, ancient learning greatly flourished.
Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武) appointed him Yìláng (議郎) (Gentleman Consultant).
Hóng (宏) wrote *Hàn Jiù Yí* (漢舊儀) in four chapters,
which recorded miscellaneous affairs of the Western Capital;
he also authored seven pieces of *fù* (賦), *sòng* (頌), and *lěi* (誄),
all of which are transmitted to this day.
After the Restoration,
Zhèng Zhòng (鄭衆) and Jiǎ Kuí (賈逵) transmitted the *Máo Shī* (毛詩).
Later, Mǎ Róng (馬融) wrote the *Máo Shī Chuán* (毛詩傳) (Commentary on the Máo Shī),
and Zhèng Xuán (鄭玄) wrote the *Máo Shī Jiàn* (毛詩箋) (Notes on the Máo Shī).
The previous book records that Gāo Tángshēng of Lǔ,
when the Hàn dynasty arose, transmitted the seventeen chapters of the *Lǐ*.
Later, Xiāo Fèn of Xiáqiū passed it on to Hòu Cāng of the same commandery.
Cāng passed it on to Dài Dé of Liáng, as well as Dài Dé's nephew, Shèng, and Qìng Pǔ of Pèi.
Thereupon, Dài Dé produced the *Dà Dài Lǐ*,
Shèng produced the *Xiǎo Dài Lǐ*,
and Pǔ produced the *Qìng Shì Lǐ*.
All three schools established Erudites (Bóshì).
The fifty-six chapters of the ancient *Lǐ* classics and the six chapters of the *Zhōu Guān* classics presented by Kǒng Ānguó
were transmitted in previous generations,
but did not have an established school (míngjiā).
After the restoration (Zhōngxīng),
there were also Dà Dài and Xiǎo Dài Erudites.
Although the transmission never ceased,
none of them achieved prominence in the scholarly world (Rú Lín).
During the Jiànwǔ era,
Cáo Chōng studied the Qìng school,
transmitting it to his son Bāo.
He then compiled the *Hàn Lǐ*;
this is recorded in Bāo's biography.
Dǒng Jūn, courtesy name Wénbó,
was a native of Zīzhōng, Jiànwéi.
He studied the Qìng school of *Lǐ*.
He served Dàhónglú Wáng Lín.
During the Yuánshǐ era,
he was recommended as "Mingjing" (one who understands the classics),
and was promoted to Lǐnxī Lìng.
He resigned due to illness.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
he was recommended as "Xiaolian" (filial and incorruptible),
and was appointed to the Sītú's office.
Jūn was broadly conversant with antiquity and modernity,
and frequently offered counsel on governance.
In the early Yǒngpíng era,
he became an Erudite.
At that time, when the sacrifices at the Five Altars (Wǔ Jiāo) were being initiated,
as well as the rituals and music for the Ancestral Temple,
and the ceremonial attire,
Jūn was always asked to participate in the discussions.
Many of his suggestions were adopted,
and he was hailed by his contemporaries as a "thorough scholar" (Tōng Rú).
He was successively promoted to Wǔguān Zhōngláng Jiàng,
and consistently taught over a hundred students.
Later, he was demoted to Qí Dūwèi for an offense.
At over seventy years old,
he died at home.
During the restoration (Zhōngxīng),
Zhèng Zhòng transmitted the *Zhōu Guān Jīng*.
Later, Mǎ Róng composed the *Zhōu Guān Zhuàn*,
which he taught to Zhèng Xuán.
Xuán wrote the *Zhōu Guān Zhù*.
Xuán originally studied the Xiǎo Dài Lǐ,
but later collated it with the ancient classics,
adopting what he considered superior;
thus, his became known as the Zhèng school.
Xuán also annotated the forty-nine chapters of the *Lǐ Jì* transmitted by Xiǎo Dài,
combining them into the Three Rites (Sān Lǐ).
The previous book records that Húmǔ Zǐdū of Qí transmitted the *Gōngyáng Chūnqiū*,
teaching it to Yíng Gōng of Dōngpíng.
Yíng Gōng taught it to Mèng Qīng of Dōnghǎi.
Mèng Qīng taught it to Suī Mèng of Lǔ.
Suī Mèng taught it to Yán Péngzǔ of Dōnghǎi and Yán Ānlè of Lǔ.
Péngzǔ established the Yán school of *Chūnqiū*,
and Ānlè established the Yán school of *Chūnqiū*.
Also, Jiāng Gōng of Xiáqiū transmitted the *Gǔliáng Chūnqiū*.
All three schools established Erudites.
Jiǎ Yì, Grand Tutor (Tàifù) of Liáng, wrote explanatory notes for the *Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū Zhuàn*,
teaching it to Guàn Gōng of Zhào.
Dīng Gōng, courtesy name Zǐrán,
was a native of Dōngmín, Shānyáng.
He studied the *Gōngyáng Yán Shì Chūnqiū*.
Gōng's scholarship was profound and brilliant,
and he regularly taught several hundred students.
He declined invitations from the provinces and commanderies.
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
he served as Jiànyì Dàfū and Erudite,
and was enfeoffed as Guānnèi Hóu.
In the eleventh year,
he was promoted to Shǎofǔ.
Thousands of students from distant lands
were registered,
and he was recognized by his contemporaries as a "Great Scholar" (Dà Rú).
Tàicháng Lóu Wàng, Shìzhōng Chéng Gōng, Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi Fán Chuò (鯈), and others all received instruction from Gōng.
In the twentieth year,
he was appointed Shìzhōng Jìjiǔ and Qí Dūwèi.
Together with Shìzhōng Liú Kūn, he was constantly at the side of Guāngwǔ,
who consulted them on every matter.
He died in office.
Zhōu Zé, courtesy name Zhìdū,
was a native of Ānqiū, Běihǎi.
In his youth, he studied the *Gōngyáng Yán Shì Chūnqiū*.
He lived in seclusion and taught,
with hundreds of disciples constantly attending him.
Towards the end of the Jiànwǔ era,
he was appointed to the Dà Sīmǎ's office,
and served as Yìcáo Jìjiǔ.
After several months,
he was summoned to be tested for an Erudite position.
In the first year of Zhōngyuán,
he was promoted to Mǐnchí Lìng.
He was dedicated to public service and self-restrained,
showing compassion to orphans and the weak.
Officials and common people loved and respected him.
In the fifth year of Yǒngpíng,
he was promoted to Yòuzhōngláng Jiàng.
In the tenth year,
he was appointed Tàicháng.
Zé was decisive and outspoken,
frequently arguing based on evidence.
Later, Liáo Xìn, Governor (Tàishǒu) of Běidì,
was imprisoned for corruption and filth,
and his property was confiscated.
Xiǎnzōng distributed Xìn's seized assets to various incorruptible officials.
Only Zé, along with Guānglùxūn Sūn Kān and Dà Sīnóng Cháng Chōng, received special grants.
At that time, the capital rejoiced,
and all officials in positions of power exhorted themselves to greater effort.
Kān, courtesy name Zǐzhì,
was a native of Gōushì, Hénán.
He was well-versed in classical studies,
had strong integrity,
was pure, upright, and steadfast.
He loved scholars and officials,
yet never took even a single hair from anyone.
He conducted himself with integrity, principles, and righteous courage.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
when wars erupted everywhere,
his elderly and weak clan members were safe in the military encampment.
Kān often fought fiercely against the enemy,
without any hesitation,
and was wounded many times.
His clan relied on him,
and the commandery admired his righteousness and courage.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
he served in commanderies and counties.
He was fair, just, and incorruptible.
His salary did not reach his wife and children,
but was all used to entertain guests.
When he became a senior official,
he left a mark wherever he served,
and was respected and admired by officials and common people.
He delighted in making clear distinctions and decisions.
Once, as a county magistrate,
when he went to an audience at the prefecture,
he walked slowly.
The gate warden reprimanded Kān's carriage official.
Kān immediately removed his seal and sash and left,
not returning to his post.
Later, he again served as Zuǒ Fēngyì,
but was dismissed for being too harsh and impatient with his subordinates,
as impeached by the Sīlì Xiàowèi.
After several months,
he was summoned to be Shìyùshǐ,
and was twice promoted to Shàngshū Lìng.
In the eleventh year of Yǒngpíng,
he was appointed Guānglùxūn.
Kān was pure and incorruptible,
and decisive in governance,
frequently speaking frankly,
and many of his suggestions were accepted.
In the eighteenth year,
he requested retirement due to illness,
and became Shìzhōng Qí Dūwèi.
He died in office.
Kān's conduct was similar to Zé's,
thus the capital nicknamed them
"The Two Zhì."
In the twelfth year,
Zé temporarily administered the affairs of Sītú,
as if he were the actual holder of the office.
Zé was by nature informal,
neglecting ceremony,
and somewhat failed to meet the expectations of a prime minister.
After several months,
he reverted to Tàicháng.
He was pure and conscientious in his duties,
showing utmost reverence to the ancestral temples.
He often lay ill in the purification palace.
His wife, pitying Zé's old age and illness,
peeped in to ask about his suffering.
Zé was greatly enraged,
accusing his wife of violating the purification taboos,
and consequently had her arrested and sent to the imperial prison to confess her crime.
Contemporaries suspected he was being theatrically extreme.
People at the time made a saying about this:
"Born into an unfortunate life,
to be the wife of a Tàicháng,
three hundred and sixty days in a year,
three hundred and fifty-nine days of purification."
In the eighteenth year,
he was appointed Shìzhōng Qí Dūwèi.
Later, he repeatedly served as Sānlǎo and Wǔgēng.
He retired during the Jiànchū era,
and died at home.
Zhōng Xīng (鍾興), courtesy name Cìwén (次文),
was a native of Rǔyáng (汝陽), Rǔnán (汝南).
In his youth, he studied Master Yán’s (嚴氏) Chunqiu (春秋) under Dīng Gōng (丁恭), the Lesser Minister of Agriculture.
Gōng (恭) recommended Xīng (興) for his profound scholarship and conduct.
Guāngwǔ (光武) summoned him for an audience,
questioning him on classical doctrines.
His responses were very clear.
The Emperor praised him,
appointed him as a Lángzhōng (郎中),
and he gradually rose to be a Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng (左中郎將).
An imperial edict commanded him to standardize the chapters and sentences of the Chunqiu (春秋),
removing redundancies,
to teach them to the Crown Prince.
He also had members of the imperial clan and various marquises study the chapters and sentences under Xīng (興).
He was enfeoffed as a Guānnèi Hóu (關內侯).
Xīng (興) felt he had rendered no service
and dared not accept the title.
The Emperor said:
"To educate and instruct the Crown Prince and the various kings and marquises, is that not a great service?"
Xīng (興) replied:
"My teacher is Dīng Gōng (丁恭)."
Thereupon, Gōng (恭) was again enfeoffed,
but Xīng (興) firmly declined to accept the title,
and died in office.
Zhēn Yǔ (甄宇), courtesy name Chángwén (長文),
was a native of Ānqiū (安丘), Běihǎi (北海).
He was pure, tranquil, and had few desires.
He specialized in Master Yán’s (嚴氏) Chunqiu (春秋)
and regularly taught several hundred students.
During the Jiànwǔ (建武) era,
he served as a Zhōu Cóngshì (州從事),
was summoned and appointed Bóshì (博士),
and gradually promoted to Tàizǐ Shàofù (太子少傅),
dying in office.
He passed on his scholarship to his son Pǔ (普),
and Pǔ (普) passed it on to his son Chéng (承).
Chéng (承) was especially devoted to his studies,
never attending to family affairs,
and regularly lectured to several hundred students.
Other scholars, seeing that Chéng (承) had continued the family scholarship for three generations,
all submitted to him.
In the Jiànchū (建初) era,
he was nominated as Xiàolián (孝廉),
and died while serving as Liáng Xiàng (梁相).
His descendants continued the scholarship without interruption.
Lóu Wàng (樓望), courtesy name Cìzǐ (次子),
was a native of Yōngqiū (雍丘), Chénliú (陳留).
In his youth, he specialized in Master Yán’s (嚴氏) Chunqiu (春秋).
His conduct was pure and unblemished,
earning him praise in his hometown.
In the Jiànwǔ (建武) era,
Xǔ (栩), the Prince Xié (節王) of Zhào (趙),
heard of his high reputation,
and sent an envoy with jade and silk to invite him to be his teacher,
but Wàng (望) did not accept.
Later, he served as a Jùn Gōngcáo (郡功曹).
In the early Yǒngpíng (永平) era,
he became a Shìzhōng (侍中) and Yuèqí Xiàowèi (越騎校尉),
lecturing inside the palace.
In the sixteenth year,
he was promoted to Dà Sīnóng (大司農).
In the eighteenth year,
he succeeded Zhōu Zé (周澤) as Tàicháng (太常).
In the fifth year of Jiànchū (建chū),
he was demoted to Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫) for an offense,
and later became Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng (左中郎將).
He lectured tirelessly,
and was known to his generation as a Rúzōng (儒宗, revered Confucian scholar);
over nine thousand students were registered under him.
At the age of eighty,
in the twelfth year of Yǒngyuán (永yuán),
he died in office.
Several thousand students attended his funeral,
which Confucians regarded as an honor.
Chéng Zēng (程曾), courtesy name Xiùshēng (秀升),
was a native of Nánchāng (南昌), Yùzhāng (豫章).
He received his education in Cháng'ān (長安),
specializing in Master Yán’s (嚴氏) Chunqiu (春秋)
for over ten years,
then returned home to lecture.
Several hundred people, including Gù Fèng (顧奉) of Kuàijī (會稽), often resided at his gate.
He authored over a hundred works,
all of which were comprehensive discussions of difficulties in the Five Classics;
he also wrote chapters and sentences for the Mencius (孟子).
In the third year of Jiànchū (建chū),
he was nominated as Xiàolián (孝廉),
promoted to Hǎixī Lìng (海西令),
and died in office.
Zhāng Xuán (張玄), courtesy name Jūnxià (君夏),
was a native of Héyáng (河陽), Hénèi (河內).
In his youth, he specialized in Master Yán’s (顏氏) Chunqiu (春秋),
and was also conversant with the methods of several other schools.
In the early Jiànwǔ (建wǔ) era,
he was nominated for his clear understanding of the classics,
appointed Hóngnóng Wénxué (弘農文學),
and promoted to Chéncāng Xiànchéng (陳倉縣丞).
He was pure and without desires,
dedicating himself entirely to the classics.
When he was lecturing and discussing,
he would sometimes not eat for a whole day.
When someone posed a difficult question,
he would always present the explanations of several schools,
allowing the questioner to choose the one they found most acceptable.
All scholars acknowledged his extensive knowledge;
over a thousand students were registered under him.
When Xuán (玄) first became a Xiànchéng (縣丞),
he once went to the prefecture to report on his official duties,
but did not know where the official office was.
An official reported it and reproached him at the gate.
At that time, Xú Yè (徐業) of Lángyá (琅邪), who was the Yòu Fúfēng (右扶風),
was also a great scholar.
Hearing of Xuán's (玄) students,
he tried to meet him.
After speaking with him,
he exclaimed in great surprise:
"Meeting you today
has truly enlightened me!"
He then invited him to ascend the hall,
and questioned him until the end of the day.
Later, Xuán (玄) left office,
was nominated as Xiàolián (孝廉),
and appointed as a Láng (郎).
When the position of Master Yán’s (顏氏) Bóshì (博士) became vacant,
Xuán (玄) ranked first in the examination,
and was appointed Bóshì (博士).
After several months,
students reported that Xuán (玄) also expounded on Master Yán’s (嚴氏) and Míng’s (冥氏) doctrines,
and was therefore unsuitable to be exclusively Master Yán’s (顏氏) Bóshì (博士).
Guāngwǔ (光武) ordered him to return to his former post,
but he died before being reassigned.
Lǐ Yù (李育), courtesy name Yuánchūn (元春),
was a native of Qī (漆), Fúfēng (扶風).
In his youth, he specialized in Gōngyáng (公羊) Chunqiu (春秋).
He pondered deeply and with concentrated focus,
widely read books and commentaries,
and became renowned in the Imperial Academy.
He was highly esteemed by Bān Gù (班固) of the same commandery.
Gù (固) submitted a memorial recommending Yù (育) to Cāng (蒼), the Prince of Dōngpíng (東平), who was the General of Agile Cavalry.
Consequently, the noble and powerful families in the capital vied to associate with him.
When he was invited by provinces and commanderies,
Yù (育) would arrive
and then feign illness and leave.
He often sought refuge in other places to lecture,
with several hundred disciples.
He was somewhat conversant with ancient learning.
He once read the Zuǒshì Zhuàn (左氏傳),
and although he enjoyed its literary style,
he believed it did not grasp the profound meaning of the Sage,
and that previous scholars like Chén Yuán (陳元) and Fàn Shēng (范升) merely criticized each other,
often citing prognostications and omens,
without relying on reasoned principles.
Therefore, he wrote "Forty-one Difficulties in the Meaning of the Zuǒshì" (難左氏義四十一事).
In the first year of Jiànchū (建chū),
Wèi Wèi (衛尉) Mǎ Liáo (馬廖) recommended Yù (育) for his uprightness,
and he was made a Yìláng (議郎).
Later, he was appointed Bóshì (博士).
In the fourth year,
an edict commanded him to debate the Five Classics with other scholars at the Bái Hǔ Guān (白虎觀).
Yù (育) challenged Jiǎ Kuí (賈逵) with the meaning of Gōngyáng (公羊),
and their exchanges were all well-reasoned and evidenced,
making him the most learned scholar.
He was twice promoted to Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令).
When the Mǎ (馬) clan fell from power,
Yù (育) was implicated for having been recommended by them and dismissed to return home.
After more than a year, he was again summoned,
and twice promoted to Shìzhōng (侍中),
dying in office.
Hé Xiū (何休), courtesy name Shàogōng (邵公),
was a native of Fán (樊), Rènchéng (任城).
His father, Bào (豹), was Shàofù (少府).
Xiū (休) was simple and taciturn,
yet had a refined mind,
and meticulously studied the Six Classics.
No contemporary scholar could match him.
By imperial edict, as the son of a high-ranking minister, he was appointed Lángzhōng (郎中),
but this was not to his liking,
so he resigned due to illness and left.
He did not serve in provincial or commandery offices.
His every action was in accordance with propriety.
The Grand Tutor Chén Fān (陳蕃) invited him
and he participated in government affairs.
When Fān (蕃) was defeated,
Xiū (休) was implicated and ostracized,
whereupon he wrote the Chūnqiū Gōngyáng Jiěgǔ (春秋公羊解詁).
He concentrated his thoughts and did not peek out of his door
for seventeen years.
He also annotated and expounded on the Xiaojing (孝經), Lunyu (論語), and Fēngjiǎo Qīfēn (風角七分),
all of which integrated the classics and historical records,
differing from common interpretations.
Furthermore, he refuted over six hundred historical events of the Han (漢) dynasty using the Chunqiu (春秋),
brilliantly capturing the original meaning of Gōngyáng (公羊).
Xiū (休) was skilled in calendrical calculations.
With his teacher, Bóshì (博士) Yáng Bì (羊弼),
he continued Lǐ Yù’s (李育) ideas to critique the two other commentaries,
writing Gōngyáng Mòshǒu (公羊墨守),
Zuǒshì Gāohuang (左氏膏肓), and Gǔliáng Fèijí (穀梁廢疾).
The party prohibitions were lifted,
and he was again appointed Sītú.
The nobles all stated that Xiū’s Daoist methods were profound and clear,
and that he was suitable to attend the imperial court.
The favored officials were displeased with this,
so he was appointed Yìláng.
He frequently presented loyal remonstrances.
He was twice promoted to Jiànlì Dàfū.
At fifty-four years old,
he died in Guānghé fifth year.
Fú Qián, courtesy name Zǐshèn,
was initially named Chóng,
then Zhī,
and later changed to Qián.
He was a native of Xíngyáng, Hénán.
From a young age, he established his aspirations through purity and hardship,
and entered the Imperial Academy to study.
He possessed refined talent,
was skilled at writing essays and treatises,
and composed the Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Zhuàn Jiě,
which has been in circulation ever since.
He also used the Zuǒzhuàn to refute Hér Xiū’s sixty points of contention regarding Hàn affairs.
He was recommended as Xiàolián,
and gradually promoted.
At the end of Zhōngpíng,
he was appointed Jíujiāng Tàishǒu.
After being dismissed,
he encountered turmoil while traveling,
and died of illness.
His writings included fù, bēi, lěi, shūjì, liánzhū, and Jiǔfèn,
totaling over ten chapters.
Yǐng Róng, courtesy name Zǐyán,
was a native of Chángpíng, Chénguó.
He was broadly learned and widely conversant,
skilled in the Chūnqiū Zuǒshì,
and studied under Tàiwèi Yáng Cì.
The commandery recommended him as Xiàolián,
the province appointed him,
and the gōngchē summoned him,
but he declined them all.
During the Chūpíng era,
he fled the chaos to Jīngzhōu,
where he gathered over a thousand disciples.
Liú Biǎo wanted to make him Wǔlíng Tàishǒu,
but he refused to take office.
He wrote Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Tiáolì, comprising over fifty thousand words,
and died during the Jiàn'ān era.
Xiè Gāi, courtesy name Wényí,
was a native of Zhānglíng, Nányáng.
He was skilled at illuminating the Chūnqiū Zuǒshì,
and was a renowned Confucian scholar of his time,
with several hundreds of thousands of disciples.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
Yuè Xiáng from Hédōng listed dozens of obscure and difficult passages from the Zuǒshì to ask him about.
Gāi thoroughly explained them all,
and it was named Xièshì Shì,
circulating in the world.
He served as Gōngchē Sīmǎ Lìng,
but because his parents were old,
he feigned illness and resigned.
He wished to return to his hometown,
but at the time the Jīngzhōu route was blocked,
preventing him from leaving.
Shàofǔ Kǒng Róng submitted a memorial recommending him, saying:
“Your servant has heard that when Gāozǔ founded the dynasty,
generals Hán and Péng campaigned against rebels,
while Líng Jiǎ and Shūsūn Tōng presented arguments on poetry and history.
When Guāngwǔ brought about the restoration,
Wú and Gěng assisted him,
while Fàn Shēng and Wèi Hóng compiled and narrated ancient works.
Thus, he was able to employ both civil and military strengths,
and establish a long-lasting plan.
Your Majesty’s sagely virtue is revered and clear,
matching the two ancestors.
Toil, humility, and hardship have marked your reign;
only after three years did joy arrive.
Now, the Grand Mentor is soaring like an eagle,
Fāng Shū is flying high like a hawk,
the imperial army is swift as lightning,
and the multitude of villains has been crushed and annihilated.
It is time to put away bows and lay down drums,
and thus fitting to obtain renowned Confucian scholars
to manage the rites and records.
I humbly observe that the former Gōngchē Sīmǎ Lìng Xiè Gāi
embodies the excellent character of Zēng and Shǐ,
and possesses the literary scholarship of Shāng and Yǎn.
He is broadly conversant in all arts,
and has thoroughly examined antiquity and modernity.
When things arise, he responds;
when matters occur, he is not perplexed.
He is pure and upright, of extraordinary conduct,
and ardently delights in Daoist teachings.
Searching far and wide,
few can rival him.
As for the giant bone emerging from Wú,
the hawk landing in Chén’s courtyard,
the yellow snake entering the bedchamber,
and the boar with two heads—
If one is not broadly learned,
one cannot discern their origins.
Jùn Bùyí resolved matters before the Northern Palace Gate,
Hàhóu Shèng elucidated the portents of Chángyīn,
and thereafter the court officials increasingly valued Confucian learning.
Now, Gāi truly stands out and ranks among these predecessors.
He resigned from office
due to his parents' old age and illness, wishing to return home,
but the roads are treacherous and blocked,
making it impossible for him to reach his destination.
To allow such a talented person to embrace simplicity and flee,
crossing mountains and rivers,
and sinking into Jīng-Chǔ,
is what is called ‘going and not returning.’
Later, should we need to offer music to lure Yóu Yú,
or carve images to seek Fù Yuè,
would that not be troublesome?
Your ignorant servant believes that he should be traced and located,
and summoned back.
The people of Chǔ tried to stop Sūn Qīng from leaving the state,
and the Hàn court pursued Kuāng Héng in Píngyuán.
They honored Confucianism and valued learning,
regretting the loss of worthy men.”
After the memorial was submitted,
an imperial edict immediately summoned him back,
and appointed him Yìláng.
He died of old age.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
Zhèng Xìng and Chén Yuán transmitted the Chūnqiū Zuǒshì scholarship.
At that time, Shàngshū Lìng Hán Xīn submitted a memorial,
wishing to establish a博士 for the Zuǒshì.
Fàn Shēng and Xīn debated this unresolved issue.
Chén Yuán submitted a memorial advocating for the Zuǒshì,
and consequently Lǐ Fēng of Wèijùn was made the Zuǒshì Bóshì.
Later, a number of obstinate Confucian scholars repeatedly argued against this in court.
When Fēng died,
Guāngwǔ was reluctant to go against public opinion again,
and consequently did not fill the position.
Xǔ Shèn, courtesy name Shúzhòng,
was a native of Shàolíng, Rǔnán.
His nature was pure and earnest;
from a young age, he was broadly learned in the classics.
Mǎ Róng always held him in high regard.
People of the time had a saying about him:
“No one rivals Xǔ Shúzhòng in the Five Classics.”
He served as Jùn Gōngcáo,
was recommended as Xiàolián,
and was twice promoted to be Xiáo Zhǎng.
He died at home.
Initially,
Shèn, seeing the varying interpretations and criticisms of the Five Classics,
therefore compiled Wǔjīng Yìyì,
and also wrote Shuōwén Jiězì in fourteen chapters,
both of which have been passed down to the present day.
Cài Xuán, courtesy name Shúlíng,
was a native of Nándùn, Rǔnán.
He was proficient in the Five Classics,
and constantly had a thousand disciples,
with sixteen thousand registered students.
He declined summonses and appointments.
Shùn Dì issued a special edict summoning and appointing him Yìláng.
He lectured on the similarities and differences of the Five Classics,
which greatly pleased the emperor.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng,
then sent out to be Hóngnóng Tàishǒu,
and died in office.
A discourse says: From the middle of Guāngwǔ's [reign] onwards,
the weapons of war were gradually put away,
and attention was solely devoted to classical studies.
From then on, this trend became deeply ingrained in society.
Those who wore scholar's robes,
spoke of the former kings,
roamed the academies (xiángxù),
and gathered in private
schools (shú),
had spread throughout the regions (bāngyù).
As for the places where classical scholars resided,
it was not uncommon for people to travel thousands of miles;
refined dwellings were temporarily erected,
and provisions often amounted to hundreds or thousands.
Those esteemed for their reputation and high principles, who opened their doors to accept students,
had rosters exceeding ten thousand people.
All of them specialized in transmitting the teachings of their ancestors,
without any error or admixture.
Some even engaged in disputes in the royal court,
formed factions in their private villages,
elaborated on their rules and regulations,
and delved into obscure texts
to align them with their own school's doctrine.
Therefore, Yáng Xióng said:
"Today's scholars
not only adorn it with eloquence,
but also embroider its sash and pouch."
Indeed, the principles of books are not two,
and the meaning ultimately has a common source.
Yet, scholars of great learning
do not deviate from their chosen path.
Thus, accomplished individuals (tōngrén) disdain their obstinacy.
This is also what Yáng Xióng called
"the clamorous learning,
each adhering to their own master."
Moreover, if one observes those who achieve fame and high honors,
few are ultimately able to reach great heights,
yet their adherence to tradition is such.
However, what they discuss is benevolence and righteousness (rényì),
and what they transmit are the sagely methods.
Therefore, people understood the principles of ruler and minister, father and son,
and families knew the path to abandon evil and return to righteousness.
From the time of Huán and Líng,
the imperial way became flawed and corrupt,
the court's discipline declined daily,
and national rifts frequently opened.
From those of average intelligence downwards,
none failed to perceive this collapse and disintegration.
Yet powerful and influential ministers
restrained their schemes of usurpation and theft,
and valiant and outstanding individuals
submitted to the opinions of humble scholars,
because people recited the words of the former kings,
and the populace feared the consequences of rebellion and submission.
Take, for instance, Zhāng Wēn and Huángfǔ Sōng;
their achievements secured half the empire,
and their renown spread beyond the four seas.
With a mere glance or gesture,
the imperial destiny could have been shifted.
Yet they still bowed before the incompetent ruler,
and humbly obeyed the urgent imperial edicts,
dispersing their assembled troops
and submitting to restrictions,
without any regret.
It was not until the [dynasty's] decline reached its extreme,
and the mandate of Heaven and men was exhausted,
that the heroes seized their opportunity,
and the inherited virtue of the age ended its reign.
Tracing the causes of this decline and decay,
that it was able to last for so many years,
was this not the effect of learning?
Therefore, the former masters, in establishing their classic texts,
praised and encouraged the merits of scholars
most sincerely and earnestly.
Not to follow the Spring and Autumn Annals
is even compared to murder and rebellion –
surely there is a deep intention behind this!
A eulogy says: This culture has not yet declined,
and each has their inheritors.
Paths diverge and branches separate,
specialized schools rise in parallel.
Minute distinctions and broad outlines meet differently,
openness and obstruction challenge each other.
If a thousand years pass without such works being made,
who will clarify the original source?
Biographies of Literary Figures, Chapter 70, Part 1
Dù Dǔ, courtesy name Jìyǎ,
was a native of Dùlíng in Jīngzhào.
His great-grandfather, Yánnián,
served as Grandee Secretary (Yùshǐ Dàfū) during Emperor Xuān's reign.
Dǔ was widely learned in his youth,
but disregarded minor details,
and was not held in high esteem by his fellow villagers.
Residing in Měiyáng,
he associated with the Měiyáng Magistrate,
often asking for favors,
but failing,
they became somewhat resentful of each other.
The Magistrate grew angry,
arrested Dǔ, and sent him to the capital.
It so happened that the Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ) Wú Hàn had died,
and Guāngwǔ ordered all scholars to write a eulogy for him.
Dǔ, from prison, composed a eulogy,
whose language was the most superior.
The Emperor admired it,
bestowing silk and pardoning him.
Dǔ believed that Guānzhōng, with its mountains and rivers forming a strategic barrier,
was the former capital of the previous emperors,
and it was inappropriate to relocate the capital to Luòyì.
So he submitted a memorial on the Capital Rhapsody (Lùndūfù), saying: Your servant has heard that to know and then know again
is to know profoundly.
What your servant wishes to speak of,
Your Majesty already knows,
thus I shall only outline the general points,
not daring to fully present them.
In the past, Pángēng (Bāngēng) left extravagance,
practicing frugality in Bó (Bó);
the prosperity of Chéng Zhōu
was then established in central Luò (Luò).
Capitals were established according to the times,
not always in the same place.
The considerations of sages
may have superiority or inferiority;
the postures of hegemons and kings
clearly differ.
The strategies for governing a state
lead to the same goal through different methods;
some avoid barriers
and seek ease
and accessibility;
some rely on mountains and rivers,
swallowing the Six States;
some, rich and noble, yearn to return,
disregarding impending attacks;
some strike at emptiness and weakness,
emerging from Shǔ Hàn;
the imperial carriage of that day
was strategized by a single soldier;
some, though knowing, do not follow,
long residing in barren lands.
[一０]Your servant dares not assert any specific point.
I humbly observe that Sīmǎ Xiāngrú and Yáng Zǐyún composed rhapsodies (cífù) to subtly admonish the emperor.
Your servant sincerely admires them,
and has respectfully composed one piece of writing,
named "On the Capital" (Lùndū),
which I reverently seal and present herewith.
He closed the gate,
