Yì, seeing that Xiǎozōng was not earnest in seeking worthy people, and many scholars were in reclusion, thus wrote Seven Excitations as a satire.
During the Jiànchū reign, Sùzōng extensively summoned men of literature,
and appointed Yì as Lántái Lìngshǐ,
then promoted him to Lángzhōng.
He was entrusted with compiling and editing books together with Bān Gù and Jiǎ Kuí.
Yì reflected on the splendid achievements and virtues of Emperor Xiàomíng,
for whom no temple eulogy had yet been erected.
So, following the style of the Qīng Miào, he composed ten chapters of the Xiǎozōng Sòng and presented them.
From this, his literary elegance became renowned at court.
Mǎ Fáng, the General of Chariots and Cavalry, a respected imperial maternal relative,
invited Yì to be his Jūn Sīmǎ,
treating him with the courtesy due to a teacher and friend.
When the Mǎ clan fell,
Yì was dismissed from office and returned home.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán, Dòu Xiàn, the General of Chariots and Cavalry, again invited Yì to be his Zhǔjìshì,
and Cuī Yīn to be his Zhǔbù.
When Xiàn was promoted to Grand General,
he again appointed Yì as Sīmǎ,
and Bān Gù as Zhōnghùjūn.
The literary brilliance of Xiàn's administration
was preeminent in its time.
Yì died young,
leaving behind twenty-eight pieces of work, including poems, rhapsodies, laments, eulogies,祝文 (zhùwén), Seven Excitations, and 連珠 (liánzhū).
Huáng Xiāng, courtesy name Wénqiáng,
was a native of Ānlù, Jiāngxià.
At the age of nine,
he lost his mother,
and was so consumed by grief and emaciation
that he almost did not survive the mourning period.
The people of his village acclaimed his extreme filial piety.
At twelve,
Liú Hù, the Grand Administrator, heard of him and summoned him,
appointing him as a Xiàozǐ (Filial Son) in his retinue,
and held him in great affection and respect.
Huáng Xiāng's family was poor,
with no servants inside,
so he personally undertook hard labor,
devoting himself wholeheartedly to his father's support.
He then extensively studied the classics,
delving deeply into various arts and techniques.
He was skilled in writing,
and the capital called him
"The unparalleled youth from Jiāngxià."
He was first appointed Lángzhōng.
In the first year of Yuánhé,
Sùzōng ordered Huáng Xiāng to go to the Dōngguān
to read books he had not yet seen.
Huáng Xiāng later requested leave.
When he returned to the capital,
at a time when King Qiānchéng had been crowned,
the Emperor held a gathering at the Zhōngshān Residence.
He then ordered Huáng Xiāng to come before the hall,
and turning to the various kings, said:
"This
is 'The unparalleled youth from Jiāngxià.'"
All those present
could not but look at him anew.
Later, he was summoned to the Ānfú Diàn to discuss political affairs,
and was appointed Shàngshū Láng.
He frequently pointed out advantages and disadvantages,
and his rewards and grants increased.
He often stayed overnight alone at the government office,
never leaving the imperial chambers day or night,
and the Emperor, hearing of this, approved.
In the fourth year of Yǒngyuán,
he was appointed Zuǒ Chéng.
His merits were full and he was due for promotion,
but Emperor Hé kept him,
increasing his rank.
In the sixth year,
he was successively promoted to Shàngshū Lìng.
Later, he was appointed Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn.
Huáng Xiāng submitted a memorial declining the appointment, saying:
"Your servant, an humble and lowly person from Jiānghuái,
a foolish and insignificant young man,
has no academic learning or practical ability
worth recording.
I encountered an era of great peace,
and thanks to the lingering blessings of my ancestors,
I, at a young age, was especially favored with an invitation to serve,
and through successive ranks and appointments,
I reached the highest offices.
Yet I have achieved not a single small accomplishment.
To repay this grace and serve unto death,
I honestly did not expect to suddenly receive an unexpected honor,
a distinguished appointment to a nearby prefecture,
a position of honor a thousand li away.
Your servant has heard that offices should be bestowed according to ability,
so that no duties are neglected;
and titles granted based on merit,
so that the worthy and the foolish are appropriately placed.
Your servant Huáng Xiāng is an insignificant person;
as a youth, I was merely a student.
To govern a prefecture and administer politics
is truly beyond my capabilities.
I genuinely fear that, due to my dullness,
I would unfairly occupy Your Sacred Grace.
Moreover, the position of head of the privy council
is of utmost importance,
and it is also not a position Your servant Huáng Xiāng should long hold.
Upon receiving the imperial edict, I was startled and dismayed,
not knowing how to proceed.
Your servant Huáng Xiāng is in his prime,
just suitable for general duties.
I humbly request your remaining grace,
to be kept as a supernumerary official,
and granted a minor supervisory position,
entrusting me with the tedious affairs of the palace and official residences,
to fulfill Your servant Huáng Xiāng's humble aspiration,
which would truly be my dying wish,
and the greatest honor for my dust and ashes."
The Emperor also valued Huáng Xiāng's competence,
and his long familiarity with old affairs,
so he kept him as Shàngshū Lìng,
increased his rank by two thousand dàn (shí),
and bestowed upon him three hundred thousand coins.
Thereafter, he managed the crucial affairs of state,
and was greatly trusted and esteemed.
Huáng Xiāng also diligently handled all matters,
worrying about public affairs as if they were his own family's.
In the twelfth year,
Dōngpíng and Qīnghé reported omens and said that Qīng Zhòngliáo and others,
who were implicated, numbered nearly a thousand people.
Huáng Xiāng investigated and categorized the cases based on the memorials,
saving many lives.
Whenever there was a doubtful case in a commandery or kingdom,
he always sought to apply lighter penalties,
cherishing human lives,
and always striving to relieve suffering.
He was also knowledgeable about frontier affairs,
and could appropriately assess military administration,
making all arrangements suitable.
The Emperor, knowing his dedication and diligence,
frequently bestowed favor and rewards upon him.
When he was ill, the Emperor would inquire about him
and grant him medicine.
During his tenure, he recommended and advanced many people,
and received extremely lavish favor and treatment.
Critics, however, ridiculed him for being overly privileged.
In the first year of Yánpíng,
he was transferred to be Grand Administrator of Wèijùn.
The prefecture traditionally had inner and outer garden fields,
which were usually shared with people for planting,
yielding several thousand hú of grain annually.
Huáng Xiāng said:
"The field decree states 'merchants do not farm,'
and the royal regulations state 'officials do not plow.'
Those who 'cut ice and eat salaries' [i.e., officials]
should not compete with the common people for profit."
So, he distributed all the fields to the people,
ordering them to cultivate them.
At that time, there was a flood and a famine year,
so he distributed his salary and received rewards to assist the poor.
Thereupon, wealthy families each contributed righteous grain
to help the officials provide relief and loans,
and the displaced people were saved.
Later, he was dismissed from office due to matters related to floods.
Several months later,
he died at home.
He authored five pieces of work: rhapsodies, memorials, petitions, letters, and decrees.
His son, Qióng,
has his own biography.
Liú Yì,
was the son of Jìng Wáng of Běihǎi.
Initially enfeoffed as the Marquis of Píngwàng,
in the Yǒngyuán reign period,
he was stripped of his peerage for an offense.
Yì was known from a young age for his literary talent and eloquence.
In the first year of Yuánchū (114 CE),
he presented the *Hàndé Lùn* and *Xiàn Lùn*, twelve chapters in total.
At that time, Liú Zhēn, Dèng Dān, Yǐn Duì, and Mǎ Róng jointly submitted a memorial praising his excellence.
Ān Dì commended him,
bestowed 30,000 coins,
and appointed him Yìláng.
Lǐ Yóu, courtesy name Bórén,
was a native of Luò, Guǎnghàn.
He became prominent in his youth for his literary works.
During the Hè Dì's reign,
the attendant Jiǎ Kuí recommended Yóu, stating he possessed the style of Xiāngrú and Yáng Xióng.
He was summoned to the Dōngguān,
received an imperial edict to compose rhapsodies,
and was appointed Lántái Lìngshǐ.
He was gradually promoted.
During Ān Dì's reign, he served as Jiànyì Dàfū,
and received an imperial edict to compile the *Hàn Jì* together with Yèzhě Púshè Liú Zhēn and others.
Later, when the emperor deposed the Crown Prince to be the Prince of Jìyīn,
Yóu submitted a memorial to admonish and argue against it.
When Shùn Dì ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Lè'ān Xiàng.
He died at the age of eighty-three.
His collected works, including poems, rhapsodies, inscriptions, elegies, eulogies, *Qī Tàn*, and *Āi Diǎn*, totaled twenty-eight chapters.
Lǐ Shèng, from the same commandery as Yóu,
also possessed literary talent,
served as Dōngguān Láng,
and authored dozens of chapters of rhapsodies, elegies, eulogies, and treatises.
Sū Shùn,
courtesy name Xiàoshān,
was a native of Bālíng, Jīngzhào.
During the Hè and Ān reign periods, he was known for his talent and scholarship.
He was fond of the art of nourishing life
Only late in life did he enter officialdom,
appointed Lángzhōng,
and died in office.
His collected works, including rhapsodies, treatises, elegies, lamentations, and miscellaneous essays, totaled sixteen chapters.
At that time, the Sānfǔ had many scholars.
Cáo Zhòngbóshī of Fúfēng also possessed talent and scholarship,
and authored four chapters of elegies, letters, and treatises.
There was also Cáo Shuò,
whose origin is unknown,
who composed four chapters of *Hàn Sòng*.
Liú Zhēn, courtesy name Qiūsūn,
also named Bǎo,
was a native of Càiyáng, Nányáng.
He was fond of learning in his youth.
In the Yǒngchū reign period,
he served as Yèzhě Púshè.
Empress Dowager Dèng issued an edict instructing him, along with the proofreader Liú Táotú, Mǎ Róng, and the Five Classics scholars,
to collate and standardize the Five Classics, various philosophical works, biographies, and the hundred schools of arts and methods at the Dōngguān,
to rectify omissions and errors,
and to correct the text.
In the first year of Yǒngníng (120 CE),
the Empress Dowager again ordered Zhēn and Táotú to compile the biographies of famous ministers since the Jiànwǔ era.
He was promoted to Shìzhōng and Yuèqí Xiàowèi.
In the fourth year of Yánguāng (125 CE),
he was appointed Zōngzhèng.
The following year,
he was transferred to Wèiwèi,
and died in office.
He authored elegies, eulogies, and *Lián Zhū*, totaling seven chapters.
He also compiled *Shìmíng* in thirty chapters,
to explain the names of myriad things.
Gě Gōng, courtesy name Yuánfǔ,
was a native of Nínglíng, Liángguó.
During Hè Dì's reign,
he was renowned for his skill in writing and record-keeping.
He was by nature bold and heroic,
with extraordinary strength.
During Ān Dì's Yǒngchū reign period,
he was recommended as Xiàolián,
and served as Tàiguān Céng.
He submitted four proposals for expedients,
and was appointed Dàngyīn Lìng.
He was invited to the Tàiwèi's residence,
but did not accept due to illness.
The province recommended him as Màocái,
and he served as Línfén Lìng.
In both counties,
he achieved commendable results.
He authored essays, rhapsodies, steles, elegies, and records, totaling twelve chapters.
Wáng Yì, courtesy name Shūshī,
was a native of Yíchéng, Nánjùn.
In the Yuánchū reign period,
he was recommended as a chief clerk for merit review (*shàngjìlì*),
and served as Jiàoshū Láng.
During Shùn Dì's reign,
he served as Shìzhōng.
His *Chǔcí Zhāngjù* circulated widely.
His rhapsodies, elegies, letters, treatises, and miscellaneous essays totaled twenty-one chapters.
He also composed one hundred twenty-three chapters of *Hàn Shī*.
His son, Yánshòu,
courtesy name Wénkǎo,
possessed outstanding talent.
In his youth, he traveled to Lǔguó,
and composed the *Língguāng Diàn Fù*.
Later, Cài Yōng also began to compose this rhapsody,
but had not finished it.
When he saw what Yánshòu had composed,
he greatly admired it,
and thus laid down his brush.
He once had a strange dream,
which he found ominous,
and so he composed the *Mèng Fù* to encourage himself.
Later, he drowned,
at the age of just over twenty.
Cuī Qí, courtesy name Zǐwěi,
was a native of Ānpíng, Zhuójùn,
and a clansman of Yuàn, the Xiàng of Jìběi.
In his youth, he traveled to the capital to study,
and was known for his literary works and broad knowledge.
Initially recommended as Xiàolián,
he became a Láng.
Liáng Jì, the Yǐn of Hénán, heard of his talent,
and invited him to associate.
Jì's conduct was often unruly;
Qí repeatedly cited examples of success and failure from ancient and modern times to warn him,
but Jì could not accept it.
So he composed the *Wàiqī Zhēn*.
Its text states:
Wáng Yàn rose,
Queen Jiāng removed her hairpin.
Duke Huán of Qí delighted in music,
but Lady Wèi kept silent.
All assisted their lords with propriety,
supported their rulers with benevolence,
promoted talent and advanced goodness,
and preserved themselves through righteousness.
The search for [a mate],
the crowing of the hen at dawn.
Monopolizing power and exclusive favor,
exalting oneself and obscuring others.
Overriding elders and old friends,
corrupting and exploiting close relatives.
Equal to the empress, rivaling the legitimate heir,
licentious women brought ruin upon Chén.
Non-virtuous ones are exalted,
even serving as Sītú.
Bearing titles and riding in carriages,
feasting in famous cities.
The poets criticize them,
their virtue not
revered.
Violent Xīn deluded by women,
rejecting counsel and isolating himself.
unleashing poison upon the innocent.
disemboweling pregnant women.
Heaven's
wrath and Earth's indignation,
human plots and ghostly schemes.
On the dim morning of Jiǎzǐ,
bodies and heads were separated.
later a human ghoul.
ancestral temples burned.
Mòxī ruined Xià,
Bāosì destroyed Zhōu,
Dájǐ brought down Yīn,
Zhào Líng died at Shāqiū.
Qī Jī became a "human pig",
Lǚ
clan thus failed.
Empress Chén practiced witchcraft,
and eventually died in exile.
Huò desired to poison her son,
and she herself was deposed.
Capable,
yet you defied Heaven and man.
Calamity arises from a lack of virtue,
fortune from cautious timing.
The sun does not always stay at its zenith,
the moon, when full, wanes.
Those who follow the Dao are secure,
those who rely on power are in peril.
This humble minister, attending to relatives,
dares to present this counsel.
Qí, feeling that his words were not heeded,
became disheartened,
and again wrote the *Bái Hú Fù* to express his remonstrance.
Liáng Jì saw it,
and summoned Qí, asking:
"Within and without the court, the hundred officials
each have their designated duties.
The world is in such a state,
but is it solely the fault of us individuals?
Why are your criticisms so excessive?"
Qí replied:
"In the past, Guǎn Zhòng, as prime minister of Qí,
was pleased to hear words of criticism and remonstrance.
Xiāo Hé, assisting the Hàn dynasty,
even established officials to record faults.
Now, General, your family has been grand counselors for generations,
assuming responsibilities equal to Yī Yǐn and the Duke of Zhōu,
yet your virtuous governance is unheard of.
The common people are in distress.
You fail to gather the upright and good
to avert disaster and ruin,
but instead wish to gag the mouths of scholars
and obstruct the ruler's hearing.
Will this cause black and yellow to change colors,
or deer and horses to swap forms?"
Jì had no answer,
and thus sent Qí home.
Later, he was appointed Magistrate of Línjì,
but he dared not take up the post,
and laid down his seal and ribbon, departing.
Jì then secretly ordered assassins to kill him.
The assassin saw Qí plowing in the fields,
with a scroll of writings in his bosom,
and whenever he rested, he would lie down and chant from it.
The assassin pitied his aspirations,
and told Qí the truth,
saying:
"The General ordered me to apprehend you.
But now that I see you are a man of worth,
my heart feels unbearable.
You should flee quickly,
and I too will disappear from here."
Qí managed to escape,
but Jì later eventually captured and killed him.
His collected works, comprising *fù*, *sòng*, *míng*, *lěi*, *zhēn*, *diào*, *lùn*, *jiǔ zī*, and *qī yán*,
totaled fifteen篇 (piān).
Biān Sháo, courtesy name Xiàoxiān,
was a native of Jùnyí, Chénliú.
He was famous for his literary compositions
and taught hundreds of students.
He was eloquent,
and once, during the day, he feigned sleep.
His disciples secretly mocked him, saying:
"Biān Xiàoxiān,
pot-bellied.
Too lazy to read books,
only wants to sleep."
Sháo secretly heard it,
and immediately responded:
"Biān is the surname,
Xiào is the courtesy name.
Pot-bellied?
A repository for the Five Classics!
Only wants to sleep?
I'm pondering the Classics' affairs!
In slumber, I commune with the Duke of Zhōu in dreams;
in stillness, I share the same mind with Kǒngzǐ.
To mock a teacher,
from what canon or record does this come?"
The mockers were greatly ashamed.
Such was the quick wit of Sháo.
During the reign of Emperor Huán,
he served as the Administrator of Línyǐnghóu.
He was summoned and appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū,
and worked at the Dōngguān Library.
He was again promoted to Běidì Tàishǒu,
and then appointed Shàngshūlìng.
Later, he served as the Administrator of Chén,
and died in office.
He authored fifteen works including poems, eulogies, steles, inscriptions, memorials, and strategies.

Correction Notes, page 2595, line 12: 即日車駕策由一卒 (On that day, the imperial carriage was driven by a single soldier). Comment: The 校補 (jiàobǔ, collation supplement) states that it is proposed the character
即 (jí, immediately)
should have the character
或 (huò, or)
above it.
If Emperor Gāo did not come out of Shǔhàn and immediately establish his capital in Guānzhōng,
then the two phrases are separate matters.
Page 2597, line 6: 言順斗建及北極之星運轉而行也 (It means it moves in accordance with the rotation of the constellation Dǒujiàn and the North Pole Star). Comment: The Diànběn edition reads
「言順斗建及斗極北星運轉而行也」 (It means it moves in accordance with the rotation of the constellation Dǒujiàn and the North Pole Star).
Page 2599, line 11: (乘)【漂】昆崙 (to [float] across Kūnlún). Changed according to the Diànběn edition.
Comment: The 校補 (jiàobǔ) states that the Diànběn edition's note
乘 (chéng, to ride)
is written as
漂 (piāo, to float),
which matches the Wénxuǎn.
The Qiánshū (Former Book) reads
票 (piào, to float).
Page 2602, line 8: 攠亦靡字也音摩 (Mí is also the character mí, pronounced mó). Comment: The Jíbén edition reads
「攠亦摩字也，
音靡」 (Mí is also the character mó, pronounced mí).
The Diànběn edition reads
「攠亦摩字，
音摩」 (Mí is also the character mó, pronounced mó).
Page 2604, line 5: 大王居岐 (King Dà lived in Qí). Comment:
岐 (Qí)
was originally mistakenly written as
歧 (Qí),
and has been directly corrected.
Page 2604, line 12: 鐇（推）【椎】也 (Fán is [a pestle]). Changed according to the Diànběn edition.
Page 2605, line 9: 今流俗比地之良沃者為贍者也 (Nowadays, the common custom is to compare fertile land to a rich person). Comment: In the Jíbén and Diànběn editions,
比 (bǐ, to compare)
is written as
北 (běi, north).
The Kānwù (Correction of Errors) states that in the text,
北 (běi)
should be
以 (yǐ, to use),
and an extra character
者 (zhě, one who)
was added.
Page 2606, line 14: 呼池 (Hūchí). Comment: The Jíbén and Diànběn editions read
「滹沱」 (Hūtúo).
Page 2611, line 6: 奕世載德 (Virtue carried through generations). Comment:
奕 (Yì)
was originally mistakenly written as
弈 (Yì),
and has been directly corrected.
Page 2611, line 9: 爾尚明保【予】 (You should still clearly protect [me]). Supplemented according to the Diànběn and Jíjiěběn editions.
Page 2612, line 13: 二事謂事不專一也 (「Two affairs」 means affairs are not singular). Comment: The character
事 (shì, affair)
in
「二事」 (èrshì, two affairs)
was originally mistakenly written as
十 (shí, ten),
and has been directly corrected.
Page 2613, line 4: （毛）【韓】詩曰密勿從事 (The [Hán] Shījing says: "Diligently perform your duties"). Changed according to the Diànběn edition.
Page 2614, line 2: 遂博學經典 (Then he extensively studied the classics). Comment: The 校補 (jiàobǔ) states that there must be missing text above this sentence,
as "devotedly serving and nourishing" must be followed by his father's affairs,
so that the service and nourishment have a context,
and also something to rely on,
to then be able to extensively study the classics.
Page 2614, line 11: 連階累任 (Successive promotions and multiple appointments). Comment:
階 (jiē, steps)
was originally mistakenly written as
偕 (jiē, together),
and has been directly corrected according to the Jíbén and Diànběn editions.
Page 2615, line 3: 謝承書 (Xiè Chéngshū). Comment:
承 (Chéng)
was originally mistakenly written as
丞 (Chéng),
and has been directly corrected according to the Jíbén edition.
Page 2615, line 8: 賜醫藥 (granted medicine). Comment:
醫 (yī, medicine)
was originally written as
毉 (yī),
and has been directly changed according to the Jíbén and Diànběn editions.
Page 2615, line 9: 田令商者不農 (Those who engage in trade through agricultural decrees do not farm). Comment: Qián Dàzhāo said that the character
田 (tián, field)
is probably wrong,
and might be the character
甲 (jiǎ, armor).
The 校補 (jiàobǔ) states that Qián's observation is very accurate.
The Qiánshū Zhuànshù Jǐngjì says
「匪怠匪荒，
務在農桑，
著于甲令，
民用寧康」 (Neither lazy nor neglectful,
focused on agriculture and sericulture,
recorded in the first decrees,
the people thereby live in peace and prosperity).
Yán's note states:
「甲令即景紀令甲也． 」 (Jiǎlìng is the first decree of Jǐngjì).
Page 2618, line 2: 凡十二篇 (a total of twelve chapters). Comment: The Jíbén edition reads
「二十篇」 (twenty chapters).
Page 2619, line 8: 事瞽叟謙讓恭儉 (served Gǔsǒu with humility, yielding, respect, and frugality). Comment: In the Jíbén and Diànběn editions,
儉 (jiǎn, frugality)
is written as
敬 (jìng, reverence).
Page 2620, line 2: 番為司徒 (Fān served as Sītú). Comment:
為 (wéi, to be)
should be
唯 (wéi, only) according to the Shījīng.
Page 2621, line 13: 湯伐之遂死於南巢 (Tāng attacked him, and he then died in Náncháo). Comment: The Diànběn edition reads
「湯遂放桀於南巢」 (Tāng then exiled Jié to Náncháo).
Page 2622, line 14: 乃設書過之吏 (Then officials were appointed to record transgressions). Comment: The Kānwù (Correction of Errors) states that
吏 (lì, official)
should be
史 (shǐ, historian/scribe).
Page 2623, line 2: 伊尹【周】公 (Yī Yǐn and the Duke of Zhōu). The 校補 (jiàobǔ) states that the character
周 (Zhōu)
is clearly missing before
公 (Gōng).
Zhāng Sēnkǎi's correction notes, however, state that the character
旦 (Dàn)
is missing after
公 (Gōng).
Now, we follow the 校補 (jiàobǔ) and add the character
【周】 (Zhōu).
Page 2623, line 8: 七言 (seven-character poem). Comment: The Jíjiě (Collected Explanations) quotes Wáng Bǔ's explanation,
stating that the Yùlǎn, Chūxuèjì, and Yìwénlèijù all quote Cuī Qí's Qījuān in six places,
namely in Liú Jùn's Biànmìnglùn, Cáo Zhí's Wáng Zhòngxuān Lěi, and Wáng Kāngjū's Fǎnzāoyǐnshī note in the Wénxuǎn,
all quoting it as
「七蠲」 (Qījuān).
Only the text here reads
「七言」 (Qīyán).
Perhaps it is an error due to the similar pronunciation of yán and juān?
It should follow juān.
Biography of Literati, Chapter 70, Part 2:
Zhāng Shēng, courtesy name Yànzhēn,
was a native of Wèishì, Chénliú, and a grandson of Fùpínghóu.
Shēng was fond of learning from a young age,
and read widely,
but he was unrestrained by his temperament.
With those whose intentions aligned with his,
he would wholeheartedly form friendships,
regardless of their poverty or low status.
If someone's aspirations did not match his,
even if they were kings, dukes, or great officials,
he would never yield to them.
He often sighed and said:
「Life and death are determined by fate,
wealth and honor are in Heaven's hands.
If someone truly understands me,
they can be close even if they are from Hú or Yuè;
but if we do not understand each other,
what good is it to follow the crowd? 」
He served the commandery as a chief clerk,
and due to his ability, was appointed Magistrate of Wàihuáng.

At the time, guests filled the hall,

The Bureau Secretaries Kǒng Róng and Wáng Lǎng both paid him formal calls.

I have secretly observed the Clerk Biān Ràng of Chénliú;

As a child, he was orphaned early,

But when he went to school in his hut,

Upon first delving into the various classics,
he understood their meaning upon sight.
Those who taught him could not answer his questions,

His mind is clear and his nature is perceptive;

He does not act contrary to禮 (lǐ),

If he had lived in the time of Zhòngní,

His rank and position

Much of his writing has been lost.
Lì Yán, courtesy name Wénshèng,
was a Fányáng man,
a descendant of Lì Yìjī.
Lì Yán had literary talent,
understood music,
and was quick and articulate in speech,
many admired his ability to reason.
During the reign of Emperor Líng,
he was summoned by provinces and commanderies,
but he did not accept any of these appointments.
He had ambition and spirit,
and composed two poems, saying:
A thousand-mile steed.
Soaring and surpassing, stirring no dust as it gallops,
who can suddenly pursue it?
Are the wise and foolish of constant kind?
Their nature is endowed with purity or turbidity.
The wealthy and noble have a human record,
the poor and humble have no
heavenly record.
If success or failure is indeed due to oneself,
a man of ambition does not consult diviners.
Chén Píng idled in his village,
Hán Xìn fished at the bend of the river.
Ultimately, they became ministers
of the realm,
enjoying a salary of ten thousand measures.
Their virtuous reputation flows for a thousand years,
their achievements and fame are weighty as mountains.
Substance and refinement are valued by the Dao,
meeting the right time brings praise.
Jiàng and Guàn, when serving as ministers,
considered Yì’s proposals as exalting superficiality.
The worthy talent was suppressed and not used,
sent far away to the sands of Jīngnán.
Holding a jade disc, riding a dragon-steed,
but not encountering Yuè or Hé.
How can Kǒng Zhòngní be found,
to arrange the four subjects for the world!
Later, Lì Yán suffered from a wind-illness, leading to confusion.
He was extremely filial by nature.
During the mourning period for his mother,
his illness severely flared up.
His wife died in shock shortly after childbirth.
His wife's family sued him,
and he was arrested and imprisoned.
Lì Yán was too ill to defend himself,
and in the sixth year of Xīpíng,
he died in prison,
at the age of twenty-eight.
Lú Zhí, the Minister of Personnel, composed a eulogy and praise for him,
to illuminate his excellent virtue.
Hóu Jǐn, courtesy name Zǐyú,
was a Dūnhuáng man.
He was orphaned and poor in his youth,
and lived with his clansmen.
He was naturally diligent in study,
always taking on odd jobs for sustenance,
and would return in the evening to gather firewood and read.
He always disciplined himself with禮 (lǐ),
remaining alone in his room
as if in the presence of esteemed guests.
Provinces and commanderies repeatedly summoned him,
and there were imperial summons by public carriage,
but he feigned illness and did not arrive.
He wrote “A Discourse on Rectifying the Age” to criticize contemporary society.
He then moved into the mountains,
and engaged in deep thought and writing.
Because he was not recognized by the world,
he wrote “Answering the Guest’s Difficulties” to express his feelings.
He also compiled events from the Zhongxing period onward based on the Hàndàijì,
creating thirty chapters of “Biographies of Imperial Virtue,”
which circulated in the world.
His other miscellaneous writings, numbering several tens of chapters,
were mostly lost.
The people of Xīhé respected his talent but dared not call him by name,
all referring to him as “Lord Hóu.”
Gāo Biāo, courtesy name Yìfāng,
was a native of Wú Jùn, Wúxī.
His family was originally poor,
but by Biāo's time, he became a student
and studied at the Imperial Academy.
He had refined talent but was slow of speech.
Once, he followed Mǎ Róng, wishing to inquire about profound principles,
but Mǎ Róng was ill and could not be seen.
So he folded his calling card and sent a letter to Mǎ Róng, saying:
“I have long admired your reputation,
for many years now.
Therefore, I did not wait for an intermediary to visit the door of a great gentleman,
hoping to catch a glimpse of your brilliance,
to fulfill my heartfelt desire.
I did not expect to encounter your illness,
keeping you confined and unable to open your door.
In ancient times, Zhōu Gōng Dàn, whose father was Wén and brother was Wǔ,
was appointed a high-ranking official
to govern Huáxià,
yet he would wring out his hair while washing and spit out his food
to welcome commoners.
Thus, the Zhōu Way prospered,
and the world submitted to its virtue.
That you now recuperate from your illness and are arrogant towards scholars
is certainly proper.”
Mǎ Róng, upon reading the letter, was ashamed,
apologized, and returned the card,
but Biāo left without looking back.
Later, the commandery nominated him as Xiàolián.
He ranked first in the classics examination,
and was appointed Lángzhōng.
He proofread books at the Dōngguān,
and frequently submitted fu, song, and remarkable essays,
using them to offer remonstrance based on current events.
Emperor Líng was struck by this.
At that time, Wǔyǒng of Jīngzhào was Dūjūn Yùshǐ
and was dispatched to supervise Yōuzhōu.
All the officials gathered in a grand assembly
to bid him farewell at the Chánglè Guān.
Cài Yōng, a Yìláng, and others all composed poems,
but Biāo alone wrote a zhēn, saying:
“When civil and military virtues were about to decline,
an eminent minister was employed.
To straighten our imperial order,
and control the disloyal.
Gentlemen of old,
when going to war, forgot themselves.
They showed their decisiveness and bravery,
and were esteemed for their might.
Lǚ Shàng at seventy,
had spirit that surpassed three armies.
Poets sang of him,
like an eagle, like a falcon.
Heaven has Tàiyī,
five generals, and three gates;
Earth has nine transformations,
hills, mountains, and rivers;
Man has strategies,
six wonders, and five deceptions:
Combining these three matters,
when planning, consult.
Do not say 'I am capable,'
but strive to seek the worthy,
the bravery of Huáinán,
is respected throughout the wild.
[一０]Zhōu Gōng, a great sage,
Shí Què, a pure minister,
used prestige to overcome affection,
used righteousness to destroy family ties.
[一一]Do not say the times are perilous,
and fail to rectify your own person.
Do not say there are no worthy people,
and fail to recognize your true self.
Forget wealth, abandon nobility,
then blessings and emoluments will endure.
To bend the way and form alliances,
will result in nothing commendable.
[一二]The lofty principles of previous dukes,
are truly worthy of eternal adherence.
Keep these admonitions,
to spur you throughout your life.”
Cài Yōng and others greatly admired his writing,
considering it unsurpassed.
Later, he was promoted to Wàihuáng Lìng.
The emperor ordered his colleagues to see him off,
and held a farewell banquet at Shàngdōng Mén.
An imperial edict commanded the Dōngguān to paint Biāo’s portrait to encourage scholars.
Upon arriving at his post, Biāo
governed with virtue and submitted a memorial recommending Shēntú Pán and others from the county.
He
died of illness while in office.
Many of his writings are lost.
His son, Dài,
was also renowned.
Zhāng Chāo, courtesy name Zǐbìng,
was a native of Héjiān, Mò,
and a descendant of Liú Hóu Liáng.
He possessed literary talent.
During Emperor Líng's reign,
he followed Chēqí Jiāngjūn Zhū Jùn in suppressing the Huáng Jīn,
serving as Biébù Sīmǎ.
He authored fu, song, stele inscriptions, recommendations, manifestos, letters, petitions, and satires,
totaling nineteen pieces.
Zhāng Chāo was also skilled in cursive script,
surpassing his contemporaries in its excellence,
and it was widely transmitted in his time.
Ní Héng, courtesy name Zhèngpíng,
was a native of Píngyuán, Bān.
In his youth, he possessed talent and eloquence,
but was proud and arrogant,
fond of mocking the times and belittling others.
During the Xīngpíng era,
he sought refuge in Jīng Zhōu.
In the early Jiàn'ān era,
he came to sojourn in Xǔxià.
When he first arrived in Yǐngchuān,
he secretly carried a calling card,
but then had no one to present it to,
until the characters on the card faded away.
At this time, Xǔdū was newly established,
and worthy scholars and officials gathered from all directions.
Someone asked Ní Héng:
“Why do you not follow Chén Chángwén or Sīmǎ Bódá?”
He replied:
“How could I follow butchers and peddlers!”
Again, he was asked:
“What about Xún Wénruò and Zhào Zhìcháng?”
Ní Héng said:
“Wénruò can be borrowed for mourning visits,
and Zhìcháng can be made to supervise the welcoming of guests.”
He only praised Kǒng Róng of Lǔ Guó and Yáng Xiū of Hóngnóng.
He often said:
“The elder is Kǒng Wénjǔ,
the younger is Yáng Dézǔ.
The rest are mere nobodies,
not worth mentioning.”
Kǒng Róng also deeply admired his talent.
Ní Héng was just coming of age,
while Róng was forty years old,
and they consequently became close friends.
Kǒng Róng submitted a memorial recommending him, saying:
"Your servant has heard that when the great floods overflowed,
the Emperor desired to bring order,
seeking far and wide in all directions,
to recruit the worthy and outstanding.
In the past, Emperor Xiàowǔ inherited the throne,
intending to expand his ancestral enterprise,
he consulted widely to find those who could assist him,
and numerous scholars responded and arrived.
Your Majesty is sagacious and wise,
inheriting the foundation of the enterprise,
encountering difficult times,
working diligently day by day.
It is like the mountains sending down spirits,
extraordinary men emerging in unison.
Your servant has secretly observed the recluse Ní Héng of Píngyuán,
aged twenty-four,
whose courtesy name is Zhèngpíng.
He possesses a pure and honest character,
and brilliant, outstanding talent.
From his first foray into literature and art,
he ascended the hall and glimpsed the profound.
Whatever his eyes once saw,
he could recite it by mouth;
whatever his ears casually heard,
he would not forget it in his heart.
His nature is in harmony with the Dao,
and his thoughts are as if divine.
Gōng Hóngyáng's hidden calculations,
Jīn Ānshì's silent memory—
if measured against Héng,
they are truly nothing to marvel at.
He is loyal, resolute, and upright,
his aspirations like frost and snow.
He is startled by good as if it were a surprise,
and hates evil as if it were an enemy.
Rèn Zuò's noble conduct,
Shǐ Yú's strict integrity—
Héng hardly falls short of them.
Many common birds
are not equal to one osprey.
〔一０〕If Héng were to stand in court,
there would surely be something remarkable to behold.
His swift debates and soaring rhetoric,
his overflowing and gushing energy,
would resolve doubts and untie knots,
more than sufficient for confronting adversaries.
In the past, Jiǎ Yí sought to be appointed an envoy to a dependent state,
feigning to restrain the Chányú;
〔一一〕Zhōng Jūn wished to use a long rope
to drag the powerful Yuè king back.
〔一二〕Their youthful fervor
was admired by previous generations.
Recently, Lù Cuì and Yán Xiàng
were also promoted to court officials due to their extraordinary talents;
Héng is fit to be compared with them.
If he could leap like a dragon into the heavenly path,
spread his wings in the Milky Way,
proclaim his voice in the Purple Palace,
and cast his light like a rainbow,
it would be enough to illuminate the many scholars in the nearby offices
and enhance the solemn dignity of the Four Gates.
〔一三〕The vast music of Jūntiān
must have wondrous and beautiful spectacles;
〔一四〕the imperial household and palace
must possess extraordinary treasures.
Men like Héng
are rare and hard to find.
Jīchǔ and Yáng Ā,
dancers of supreme beauty,
are coveted by those who manage the stage;
〔一五〕Feitù and Yàoniǎo,
steeds of peerless speed,
are eagerly sought by Bó Lè and Wáng Liáng.
〔一六〕Your servants, in their humble capacities,
how could they not report this?"
Kǒng Róng, deeply admiring Héng's talent,
frequently praised him to Cáo Cāo.
Cāo wanted to meet him,
but Héng, who had always looked down upon and disliked Cāo,
claimed to be suffering from a mad sickness
and refused to go,
often making outrageous remarks.
Cāo harbored resentment,
but because of Héng's talent and reputation,
he did not want to kill him.
Hearing that Héng was skilled at drumming,
Cāo summoned him to be a drum official.
On a grand gathering of guests,
he ordered the drum officials to perform and demonstrate their rhythms.
Those officials who had passed
were all ordered to take off their old clothes
and change into uniforms of 'cénmóu' and 'dājiǎo'.
When it was Héng's turn,
Héng performed the 'Yúyáng sān zhuā',
stepping forward with a unique demeanor.
His performance was moving and grand,
and all who listened were deeply stirred.
Héng advanced to Cāo's front and stopped.
An official rebuked him, saying:
"Why hasn't the drum official changed his attire?
How dare you advance so presumptuously?"
Héng replied:
"Yes."
Thereupon, he first removed his underwear,
then stripped off his other clothes,
standing naked.
Slowly, he took the 'cénmóu' and 'dājiǎo' and put them on.
When finished,
he again performed the 'sān zhuā' and departed,
without a trace of shame on his face.
Cāo laughed and said:
"I intended to humiliate Héng,
but Héng has instead humiliated me."
Kǒng Róng then withdrew and reproached him, saying:
"Zhèngpíng, a man of great refinement,
should you really act like this?"
Then he conveyed Cāo's sincere desire.
Héng agreed to go.
Róng again met Cāo,
explaining that Héng was suffering from a 'mad sickness'
and now sought to apologize personally.
Cāo was pleased,
and ordered his gatekeepers to admit any visitors immediately,
waiting for a very long time.
Héng then put on a plain single robe and a loose turban,
holding a three-foot staff.
He sat at the main camp gate
and furiously cursed, beating the ground with his staff.
An officer reported: "There is a mad scholar outside,
sitting at the camp gate,
speaking rebelliously.
I request permission to arrest him and punish him for his crime."
Cāo was enraged and said to Róng:
"That boy Ní Héng
is like a sparrow or a mouse to me, I could kill him easily.
However, this man has always had an undeserved reputation,
and people near and far would say I cannot tolerate him.
Now I will send him to Liú Biǎo,
let's see what happens."
So, he dispatched riders to send him away.
On the eve of his departure,
everyone prepared a farewell feast for him.
They first set up the feast south of the city,
then warned each other:
"Ní Héng is abusive and ill-mannered.
Now, when he arrives later,
we should all remain seated to disrespect him."
When Héng arrived,
no one among the crowd would stand up.
Héng sat down and wailed loudly.
The crowd asked him why.
Héng said:
"Those who sit are tombs,
those who lie are corpses.
Between corpses and tombs,
how can one not be sad!"
Liú Biǎo and the literati of Jīngzhōu had long admired his talent and reputation,
and treated him with great respect as a guest.
In literary compositions and discussions,
nothing was settled without Héng.
Biǎo once drafted a memorial with various literati,
all exerting their utmost talent and thought.
At that time, Héng was out.
When he returned and saw it,
before he had even finished reviewing it,
he tore it up and threw it to the ground.
Biǎo was astonished and appalled.
Héng then asked for writing brushes and paper.
In a moment, he completed a new one,
whose words and meaning were remarkable.
Biǎo was greatly pleased
and esteemed him even more.
Later, Héng again treated Biǎo with disrespect.
Biǎo felt ashamed that he could not tolerate him,
and knowing that Huáng Zǔ, the Administrator of Jiāngxià, was short-tempered,
he therefore sent Héng to him.
Zǔ also treated him well.
Héng wrote documents for him,
and for matters of urgency or leisure, detail or brevity,
each was appropriately handled.
Zǔ held his hand and said:
"Scholar,
this perfectly captures my intention,
it is exactly what I wished to say in my heart."
Zǔ Zhǎngzǐ
Shè, serving as the Grand Administrator of Zhānglíng,
was especially skilled at discerning character,
and once he and Hénɡ traveled together.
They read an inscription composed by Cài Yōnɡ.
Shè admired its wording,
and later regretted not having copied it down.
Hénɡ said,
"Though I only glanced at it once,
I can still remember it.
Only two characters where the stone is chipped are unclear to me."
Then he wrote it out.
Shè swiftly sent someone to copy the inscription and return to check it.
It was exactly as Hénɡ had written,
and everyone was filled with admiration.
At that time, Shè hosted a grand gathering of guests.
Someone presented a parrot,
and Shè raised his goblet to Hénɡ, saying,
"I wish for you, Sir, to compose a rhapsody for it,
to entertain our esteemed guests."
Hénɡ [lǎn] seized a brush and composed it,
without a single revision,
and its rhetoric was exceedingly beautiful.
Later, Huáng Zǔ was on a mèngchōng ship,
hosting a grand gathering of guests,
but Hénɡ spoke disrespectfully.
Zǔ was embarrassed,
and therefore reprimanded him.
Hénɡ stared back intensely and said,
"You dead fellow!
What did you just say?"
Zǔ was furious,
and ordered five hundred soldiers to come out,
intending to flog him.
Hénɡ then cursed loudly.
Zǔ was enraged
and ordered him killed.
Zǔ's Chief Clerk had long disliked Hénɡ,
and immediately killed him.
Shè rushed barefoot to save him,
but it was too late.
Zǔ also regretted it,
and therefore provided a generous coffin and burial.
Hénɡ was twenty-six years old at the time.
Many of his writings are said to have been lost.
The encomium states: When emotions and aspirations are stirred,
poetic verses become valuable.
To reveal the heart and present its form,
is neither to carve nor to embellish.
Diverse forms share a common essence,
same sound, different spirit.
Their words offer a beautiful model,
forever monitoring extravagance and waste.
Biographies of Singular Conduct, Chapter 71.
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Rather than failing to attain the Mean,
one should certainly be an ardent or a scrupulous person!"
He also said,
"The ardent are progressive,
while the scrupulous have things they will not do."
This is perhaps falling short of the path of perfect completeness,
and choosing one of the extreme ends.
However, if there are things one will not do,
there will also be things one will certainly do;
since it speaks of being progressive,
there will also be things one will not take on.
Thus,
dispositions are still divergent,
and actions lead to different outcomes.
In the middle ages, many individuals of singular integrity
were able to establish their fame and standing.
Indeed, there were many.
Some had wills as strong as metal and stone,
and were able to resist the powerful and oppressive.
Some had intentions as severe as winter frost,
and yet were content with small kindnesses.
There were also those who formed friendships and alliances,
sharing a common heart in obscurity and prominence;
they trod the path of righteousness through danger,
treating life and death as equal in their principles.
Although their actions were not perfectly rounded,
their conduct and character were truly worthy of remembrance.
However, their circumstances and traces are too varied and complex,
making it difficult to classify them.
Single phrases with unique nuances
are insufficient for differentiation.
If omitted, some deeds might be left out;
if included, the sequence of narratives would lack coherence.
Because their names and forms may differ,
but their integrity and conduct are all exceptional,
they are collectively compiled into the chapter on Singular Conduct.
This is to supplement missing texts,
and record omitted aspirations, that is all.
Qiáo Xuán, courtesy name Jūnhuáng,
was from Làngzhōng, Bājùn.
In his youth, he loved learning
and was skilled at explaining the Yì and Chūnqiū.
He served in the province and commandery.
In the second year of Yǒngshǐ of Emperor Chéng (9 BCE),
there was a solar eclipse,
and an edict was issued to recommend one person each who was honest, modest, and virtuous.
The province recommended Xuán.
He went to the gōngchē,
and his policy response received high marks.
He was appointed Yìláng.
The Emperor had just established the Qímén,
and frequently made incognito tours.
He made Zhào Fēiyàn empress,
who monopolized favor and was jealous,
and many imperial princes died prematurely.
Xuán submitted a memorial admonishing, saying:
"Your servant has heard that a king, receiving Mandate from Heaven,
inherits the ancestral lineage and reigns supreme,
and that nothing is more urgent for preserving his enterprise and extending his prosperity
than having an heir.
Thus, the Yì has the meaning of 'correcting decay,'
and the Shī Yǒng extols the blessing of numerous descendants.
Now, Your Majesty's sacred heir is not yet established,
and the empire looks on in anticipation.
Yet, you do not consider the plans for the altars of soil and grain,
but exclusively focus on incognito tours,
bestowing favor and using those who lead you astray,
and yielding to what is improper.
I secretly heard that imperial princes born in the inner palace are not raised.
When your servant heard this, I was greatly distressed,
my heart aching and wounded.
I secretly harbor worry for the state,
not forgetting for a moment.
If the guards are not maintained,
then unexpected troubles will arise.
Should there be a drunken madman,
quarreling in the streets,
there would be no dignity or decorum,
and how would he recognize the distinction between high and low?
This would be like barbarians rising up beneath the chariot wheels,
and rebellion erupting from within.
I wish Your Majesty would remember the extreme importance of Heaven,
cherish your precious body,
bestow favor equally on many women,
and preserve endless blessings.
This would be the great fortune of the empire."
At that time, there were frequent omens and calamities,
and Xuán invariably presented his analysis of their changes.
Since his advice was not heeded,
he remained a lángguān for a long time.
Later, he was promoted to Tàichángchéng,
but resigned due to his brother's mourning period.
In the first year of Yuánshǐ of Emperor Píng (1 CE),
there was a solar eclipse,
and an edict was again issued for high officials to recommend honest and outspoken individuals.
Dàhónglú Zuǒ Xián recommended Xuán to the gōngchē to answer policy questions.
He was again appointed Yìláng,
and promoted to Zhōngsàndàfū.
In the fourth year (4 CE),
eight individuals who were intelligent, understood governance, and could transform customs were selected.
At that time, Xuán was also recommended
to serve as a Xiùyī Shǐzhě,
holding the imperial credential,
and, with Tàipú Wáng Yùn and others, they were to tour the empire separately,
observing customs,
and at each place they went, they had the authority to mete out punishments and rewards.
Before the mission was completed,
Wáng Mǎng assumed regency.
Xuán then released his envoy's carriage,
changed his name,
and secretly returned home,
thus going into reclusion.
Later, Gōngsūn Shù usurped the title in Shǔ,
and repeatedly invited him, but he would not go.
Shù then sent an envoy with complete formalities to summon him;
if Xuán refused to come,
he was to be given poison.
The Grand Administrator then personally brought the imperial rescript to Xuán's dwelling,
saying,
"Your high principles are already renowned,
and the court is considering you.
It is truly inappropriate to refuse again,
and bring disaster upon yourself."
Xuán looked up to heaven and sighed, saying,
"Táng Yáo was a great sage,
yet Xǔ Yóu was ashamed to serve.
Zhōu Wǔ possessed ultimate virtue,
yet Bó Yí chose to starve.
Who were they?
And who am I?
To preserve my resolve and uphold my lofty principles,
what regret would there be in death!"
Thereupon, he took the poison.
Xuán's son, Yīng, cried blood and kowtowed to the Grand Administrator, saying,
"Currently, the state has a formidable enemy to the east,
and troops are deployed in all directions.
State expenditures and military provisions are sometimes insufficient.
I wish to offer ten million of my family's money
to redeem my father's life."
The Grand Administrator pleaded for him,
and Shù granted permission.
Xuán then hid in the countryside
for the duration of Shù's reign.
At that time, for years there had been war,
and no one was able to pursue scholarship.
Xuán alone instructed his sons to diligently study the Classics and historical records.
In the eleventh year of Jiànwǔ, he died.
The next year,
the empire was pacified,
and Xuán’s younger brother, Qìng, presented a memorial at the imperial court to state his case.
Guāngwǔ praised him,
and issued an edict to Xuán’s home commandery, ordering that he be sacrificed to with a Zhōngláo offering,
and commanded that the local authorities return money to Xuán’s family.
At that time, there was also Fèi Yí of Jiànwéi,
who refused to serve Shù.
He painted his body black to appear leprous,
feigning madness to avoid service,
and retreated to hide in the mountains and wilds for over ten years.
After Shù was defeated,
he served as the Grand Administrator of Hépǔ.
Yīng was skilled at explaining the *Yì*,
which he taught to Xiǎnzōng,
and became the Commandant of the Northern Palace Guards.
Lǐ Yè, courtesy name Jùyóu,
was a native of Zǐtóng, Guǎnghàn.
In his youth, he had firm ambitions and principles,
and was independent and distinguished.
He studied the Lǔ school of the *Shī* (Classic of Poetry),
learning from Erudite Xǔ Huǎng.
During the Yuánshǐ era,
he was recommended as a Mingjīng (scholar of the Classics),
and appointed as a Lang (Gentleman).
When Wáng Mǎng assumed regency,
Yè resigned his office due to illness,
shut his door, and did not respond to invitations from the commandery or provinces.
Grand Administrator Liú Xián forcibly summoned him,
but Yè arrived at the gate in a litter, feigning illness.
Xián was enraged,
and issued an order saying:
“A worthy man does not avoid danger.
It is like shooting a crossbow in the marketplace;
those with thin fates die first.
I heard of Yè’s reputation,
and therefore wished to govern with him,
but instead he uses illness as an excuse?”
He ordered Yè to be sent to prison to "recover from his illness,"
intending to kill him.
A guest spoke to Xián, saying:
“Zhào killed Míng Dú, and Kǒngzǐ crossed the river and departed.
I have never heard of seeking worthy men by threatening them with prison.”
Xián then released him,
and subsequently recommended him as a Fāngzhèng (Upright and Frank).
Wáng Mǎng appointed Yè as a Jiǔshì (Officer in charge of wine),
but he did not report to office due to illness.
He then disappeared, exiting the valley,
and completely concealed his name and tracks,
for the remainder of Wáng Mǎng’s reign.
When Gōngsūn Shù usurped the throne,
having long heard of Yè’s virtue,
he summoned him,
wanting to appoint him as an Erudite,
but Yè adamantly refused due to illness.
After several years,
Shù was ashamed that he could not secure his service,
so he sent Grand Minister of the Court for Dependencies Yǐn Róng with poisoned wine, bearing an imperial decree to coerce Yè: if he would rise,
he would receive the position of a Duke or Marquis; if he would not,
he would be granted the medicine.
Róng explained the purport, saying:
“Today, the empire is in disarray.
Who knows right from wrong?
Why should you, with your insignificant self,
test yourself against an unfathomable abyss?
The court admires your renowned virtue,
and has kept an office vacant for you,
for seven years now.
For all four seasons, rare delicacies have been sent,
not forgetting you, our lord.
You should respond to your appreciative sovereign above,
and for your descendants below,
your body and name both complete—
would this not be excellent?
If you do not rise for several years now,
suspicion will turn to hostility,
and calamity will immediately befall you.
This is not a wise plan.”
Yè then sighed, saying:
“One does not enter a perilous state,
nor reside in a chaotic state.
For one who is personally committing evil,
righteousness dictates one does not follow.
A gentleman, seeing danger, gives his life.
Why then tempt me with high positions and heavy bait?”
Róng saw that Yè’s resolve was unyielding,
and again said:
“You should call your family to discuss it.”
Yè said:
“A man’s decision is made in his heart long ago.
What is the need for a wife and children?”
He then drank the poison and died.
Shù heard of Yè’s death,
was greatly astonished,
and also ashamed to bear the name of having killed a worthy man.
He then sent an envoy to offer condolences and sacrifices,
and bestowed a funerary gift of a hundred bolts of silk.
Yè’s son, Huī, fled and refused the gift.
When Shǔ was pacified,
Guāngwǔ issued an edict to commend his village gate,
and the records of Yìbù documented his noble integrity
and depicted his image.
Previously,
during Emperor Píng’s reign,
Wáng Hào of Shǔjùn was the Magistrate of Měiyáng,
and Wáng Jiā was a Lang.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
they both resigned their offices and returned west.
When Gōngsūn Shù declared himself Emperor,
he sent envoys to summon Hào and Jiā.
Fearing they would not come,
he first imprisoned their wives and children.
The envoy said to Jiā:
“Hurry and prepare,
and your wife and children can be spared.”
He replied:
“Even dogs and horses recognize their master,
how much more so humans!”
Wáng Hào first slit his own throat,
and gave his head to the envoy.
Shù was enraged,
and then executed Hào’s family.
Wáng Jiā heard this and sighed:
“Too late!”
He then faced the envoy, fell on his sword, and died.
At this time, Rèn Yǒng of Jiànwéi
and Fěng Xìn, Yè’s fellow commandery man,
were both fond of learning and widely knowledgeable of antiquity.
Gōngsūn Shù repeatedly summoned them,
treating them with high positions,
but they both feigned blindness to avoid the world’s difficulties.
Yǒng’s wife committed adultery in front of him,
but he concealed his feelings and said nothing;
seeing his child fall into a well,
he endured and did not save him.
Xìn’s maidservant also committed adultery in front of Xìn.
When they heard of Shù’s execution,
they both washed themselves and looked again, saying:
“The world is finally peaceful,
and our eyes are now clear.”
The adulterers committed suicide.
Guāngwǔ heard of this and summoned them,
but they both fell ill and died.
Liú Mào, courtesy name Zǐwèi,
was a native of Jìnyáng, Tàiyuán.
He was orphaned young,
and lived alone, attending to his mother.
His family was poor,
so he used his physical strength to provide for her,
and his filial piety was renowned in his hometown.
When he grew up,
he was able to study the *Lǐjīng* (Classic of Rites),
and taught several hundred people.
During Emperor Āi’s reign,
he was investigated as a Xiàolián (Filial and Incorrupt),
and twice promoted to Commandant of Wǔyuán Subordinate State.
He resigned his office due to his mother’s mourning.
After the mourning period, he became the Magistrate of Jǔyáng.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
Mào resigned his office,
and avoided the world, teaching in the Hóngnóng mountains.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
he returned
and became an Aide in the commandery government.
At that time, the Chìméi bandits, over two hundred thousand strong, attacked the commandery and counties,
killing magistrates and government officials.
Mào carried Grand Administrator Sūn Fú, climbing over a wall and hiding in a hollow cave,
thus escaping.
That evening,
they both fled to Méng county.
By day they hid,
by night they sought food.
After over a hundred days,
the bandits left,
and they were able to return to the government seat.
The next year,
an imperial edict sought righteous men throughout the empire.
Fú spoke of Mào, saying:
“Previously, I was attacked by the Chìméi,
and officials and commoners were in chaos,
fleeing to the mountains.
I was surrounded by the bandits,
my life hanging by a thread,
but relied on Mào who carried me over the city wall
to safety in Méng county.
Mào and his brother braved the weapons and blades,
climbed mountains to carry food,
and I and my wife were able to escape death.
His integrity and righteousness are especially high.
He should be commended and promoted,
to encourage other righteous men.”
The imperial edict immediately summoned Mào and appointed him as a Yìláng (Consultant Gentleman),
then promoted him to Zōngzhèngcéng (Assistant in the Court of the Imperial Clan).
Later, he was appointed as a Shìzhōng (Attendant at Court),
and died in office.
During the [Yánpíng] reign (of Yuánchū),
hundreds of Xiānbēi cavalry plundered Yúyáng.
The Grand Administrator, Zhāng Xiǎn, led his officers and men in pursuit beyond the frontier.
From afar, they saw the smoke and fires of the enemy camp,
and quickly advanced towards them.
The Chief of Military Affairs, Yán Shòu, feared an ambush
and strenuously advised against it,
but Zhāng Xiǎn did not listen.
Zhāng Xiǎn pressed them to advance.
Yán Shòu, having no choice,
went forward to battle.
The ambush was sprung,
and Yán Shòu suffered ten wounds
and died on the battlefield.
Zhāng Xiǎn drew his sword and pursued the scattered soldiers,
but could not control them.
The barbarians shot and wounded Zhāng Xiǎn.
The Chief Clerk, Wèi Fú, and the Administrator of Merit, Xú Xián, rushed to his side.
Zhāng Xiǎn then fell from his horse.
Wèi Fú shielded him with his body,
and the barbarians killed them both.
The imperial court grieved at the integrity of Yán Shòu and the others,
and an imperial edict praised them,
lavishly bestowing rewards.
One son from each family was appointed as a Lángzhōng.
In the second year of Yǒngchū,
the formidable bandits Bì Háo and others entered Píngyuán territory.
The county magistrate, Liú Xióng, led officers and men to pursue them by boat.
Upon reaching the Yàncì River,
they engaged the bandits in battle.
Liú Xióng was defeated.
They seized Liú Xióng
and stabbed him with a spear.
At that time, a minor official, Suǒ Fǔ,
came forward, kowtowed, and pleaded for mercy,
offering to die in Liú Xióng's place.
Bì Háo and the others released Liú Xióng and stabbed Suǒ Fǔ,
who died instantly, the spear piercing his heart and coming out his back.
The Grand Administrator of Dōngjùn captured Bì Háo and the others,
and fully reported the incident.
An imperial edict lamented his death,
bestowing two hundred thousand coins
and appointing his father, Fèng, as a Lángzhōng.
Wēn Xù, courtesy name Zìfáng,
was a native of Qí in Tàiyuán.
He served as a Commandery Supervisor.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the Cavalry Commandant, Gōng Lǐshù,
led troops to pacify the northern provinces.
Upon arriving in Tàiyuán,
he extensively sought out heroes and distinguished personages,
consulting them on strategy.
Gōng Lǐshù saw Wēn Xù and admired his exceptional qualities,
and submitted a memorial recommending him.
Thereupon, Wēn Xù was summoned to serve as a Shìyùshǐ.
He was promoted to Commandant of Wǔlíng,
but was dismissed due to illness.
Six years later,
he was appointed as an Yèzhě,
and then promoted to Protector of the Qiāng.
Wēn Xù was on an inspection tour when he reached Xiāngwǔ,
where he was seized and held captive by Gǒu Yǔ, a separate general of Wěi Xiāo.
Gǒu Yǔ said to Wēn Xù:
"If you would join me in might and power,
the world could be ours to conquer."
Wēn Xù replied:
"Having received a heavy responsibility from the state,
it is my duty to die for it.
It would be unrighteous to covet life and betray such grace."
Gǒu Yǔ and others tried again to persuade him with explanations.
Wēn Xù, who had always possessed courage and strength,
became furious
and shouted at Gǒu Yǔ and the others:
"How dare you barbarians coerce a Han general!"
He then used his staff to strike and kill several people.
The bandits contended to kill him.
Gǒu Yǔ stopped them, saying:
"This righteous gentleman will die for his integrity.
He may be granted a sword."
Wēn Xù received the sword,
held his beard in his mouth,
and looked left and right, saying:
"Since I am to be coerced and killed by bandits,
let not my beard be defiled by the soil."
He then fell on his sword and died.
Wēn Xù's Chief Clerk, Hán Zūn, and Supervisor, Wáng Zhōng, carried his body home for burial.
Guāngwǔ heard of it and felt pity,
ordering Wáng Zhōng to escort the coffin to Luòyáng,
granting land near the city for his tomb,
and bestowing a thousand *hú* of grain and five hundred bolts of silk.
Three of his sons were appointed as Lángzhōng.
His eldest son, Shòu,
after completing his mourning, served as the Chancellor of Zōupíng Hóu.
He dreamt that Wēn Xù told him:
"Long a guest, I yearn for my homeland."
Shòu immediately resigned from his post,
submitting a memorial requesting to retire and be buried with his family.
The Emperor granted his request,
and so he returned to the old family grave.
Péng Xiū, courtesy name Zǐyáng,
was a native of Pílíng in Kuàijī.
When he was fifteen,
his father, who was a commandery official,
received leave
and was returning home with Péng Xiū.
On the way, they were ambushed by bandits.
Péng Xiū, in desperation,
drew his belt knife and confronted the bandit leader, saying:
"If a father is humiliated, his son dies.
Do you not fear death?"
The bandits said to each other:
"This young boy is a righteous man;
we should not press him."
They then apologized and left.
His fellow villagers praised his name.
Later, he served the commandery as Gōngcáo.
At that time, the Western Commandant, Zǎi Cháo, was acting as Grand Administrator.
For a minor offense, he arrested a prison official from Wú County
and intended to kill him.
The Chief Clerk, Zhōnglí Yì, vehemently remonstrated.
Zǎi Cháo was enraged
and ordered Zhōnglí Yì to be arrested and bound,
intending to prosecute him.
None of the other officials dared to remonstrate.
Péng Xiū pushed open the gate and walked straight in,
bowing in the courtyard,
and said:
"My lord has unleashed thunder upon the Chief Clerk.
I beg to hear his fault."
Zǎi Cháo said:
"He received instructions three days ago but failed to implement them.
To disregard an order is disloyal.
Is this not a fault?"
Péng Xiū then bowed and said:
"In ancient times, Rèn Zuò directly admonished Duke Wén,
and Zhū Yún grasped and broke the palace railing.
If not for a worthy ruler,
how could there be loyal ministers?
Today, I congratulate my lord for being a worthy ruler,
and the Chief Clerk for being a loyal minister."
Zǎi Cháo then pardoned Zhōnglí Yì
and commuted the prison official's sentence.
Later, the province appointed him as a Supervisor.
At that time, hundreds of bandits, including Zhāng Zǐlín, were causing unrest.
The commandery reported to the province
and requested Péng Xiū to serve as Magistrate of Wú.
Péng Xiū went out with the Grand Administrator to suppress the bandits.
When the bandits saw their carriages and horses,
they shot at them competitively,
and flying arrows rained down.
Péng Xiū shielded the Grand Administrator
and was struck and killed by a stray arrow,
but the Grand Administrator survived.
The bandits, who had long heard of his kindness and trustworthiness,
immediately killed the crossbowman who shot Péng Xiū,
and all the others surrendered and dispersed.
They said:
"We surrender for the sake of Lord Péng,
not for the Grand Administrator."
Suǒ Lúfàng, courtesy name Jūnyáng,
was a native of Dōngjùn.
He taught the Book of Documents to over a thousand people.
Initially, he was appointed as a Clerk in the Commandery's Gatehouse.
During the Gēngshǐ reign,
an imperial envoy was inspecting the commanderies and states.
The Grand Administrator had committed an offense
and was to be executed.
Suǒ Lúfàng stepped forward and said:
"The reason the world suffered under the Wáng clan
and pledges allegiance to the August Han
is truly due to its sagely government's benevolence and compassion.
Yet, wherever the imperial carriage passes,
no grace has been heard of.
The Grand Administrator is to be punished,
and I truly dare not speak,
but I fear that the world will be panicked
and each person will conceive doubts and rebellion.
Indeed, it is better to employ those who have erred than those who have achieved merit.
I wish to die in place of the Grand Administrator's life."
He then advanced to face execution.
The envoy, moved by his righteousness,
pardoned him,
whereby his name became prominent.
In the sixth year of Jiànwǔ,
he was summoned to serve as Magistrate of Luòyáng,
where his governance was noted for its ability.
He requested leave due to illness,
and was transferred to Jiànyì Dàfū,
where he frequently offered loyal advice.
Later, he left office due to illness.
At the end of Jiànwǔ,
he was again summoned but did not rise.
Guāngwǔ sent people to convey him
to see him at the Yúntái in Nángōng,
bestowed two thousand *hú* of grain,
and sent him home,
appointing his son as a Prince's Attendant.
He died at home.
Zhōu Jiā 周嘉, courtesy name Huìwén 惠文,
was from Ānchéng 安城, Rǔnán 汝南.
His great-great-grandfather, Yàn 燕,
served as the Commandant of Justice (juécáoyuán 決曹掾) for the commandery during the reign of Emperor Xuān 宣帝.
The Grand Administrator (tàishǒu 太守) wanted to wrongly execute a man.
Yàn 燕 admonished him, but was not heeded.
So the prisoner was killed, and Yàn 燕 was dismissed.
The prisoner's family went to the palace gate and cried out their grievance.
An imperial edict was issued, sending an envoy to review the case.
Yàn 燕 met the Grand Administrator and said:
"I wish to carefully prepare the documents,
listing my name on all of them.
Your Excellency only needs to say that you were ill at the time."
He then went out and said to the other officials:
"When you are questioned,
you must all ascribe the blame to me.
If even one word implicates Your Excellency,
I will stab myself with my sword."
The envoy then arrested Yàn 燕 and imprisoned him.
He was repeatedly beaten and tortured,
but his words showed no sign of yielding.
When he was about to be subjected to castration (cánshì 蠶室),
he sighed and said:
"I am a descendant of King Píng 平王,
and a great-grandson of Zhèng Gōng 正公.
How can I, as a remnant from blades and saws, face my ancestors?"
Thereupon, he refused to eat and died.
Yàn 燕 had five sons,
all of whom rose to the positions of Regional Inspector (cìshǐ 刺史) and Grand Administrator (tàishǒu 太守).
Jiā 嘉 served the commandery as Chief Clerk (zhǔbù 主簿).
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's 王莽 reign,
a band of bandits entered Rǔyáng 城 汝陽 city.
Jiā 嘉 followed Grand Administrator Hé Chǎng 何敞 in suppressing the bandits.
Chǎng 何敞 was struck by a stray arrow.
The commandery troops fled north,
and the bandits surrounded them in dozens of layers,
with naked blades clashing.
Jiā 嘉 then embraced Chǎng 何敞,
shielding him with his body.
He then shouted at the bandits:
"You are all common people.
Having become bandits is already rebellious;
how can you further harm your lord?
I, Jiā 嘉, ask to die to redeem my lord's life."
Thereupon, he looked up to heaven and cried aloud.
The bandits then looked at each other,
saying:
"This is a righteous man!"
They provided him with a cart and horses,
and sent him away.
Later, Grand Administrator Kòu Xún 寇恂 recommended him as a Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián 孝廉).
He was appointed Palace Attendant (shàngshū shìláng 尚書侍郎).
Emperor Guāngwǔ 光武 summoned him for an audience,
and asked him about the incident where he encountered danger.
Jiā 嘉 replied:
"The Grand Administrator was wounded,
his life hanging by a thread in the bandits' hands.
I was truly cowardly and timid,
unable to die in the crisis."
The Emperor said:
"This is an honorable man."
An edict ordered Jiā 嘉 to marry a princess,
but Jiā 嘉 claimed severe illness,
unwilling to accept.
He was gradually promoted to Grand Administrator of Línglíng 零陵.
He served for seven years,
then passed away.
The people of Línglíng 零陵 praised his enduring kindness,
and the officials and common people erected a shrine for him.
Jiā's 嘉 cousin, Chàng 暢,
courtesy name Bó Chí 伯持,
was kind and compassionate by nature.
He served as Administrator of Hénán (hénányǐn 河南尹).
In the second year of Yǒngchū 永初 (108 CE),
there was a severe summer drought.
Prayers for rain went unanswered for a long time.
Chàng 暢 then collected and buried the skeletons of more than ten thousand strangers who had died by the city of Luòchéng 洛城.
Immediately, a heavy rain fell,
and the year brought a rich harvest.
He rose to the position of Minister of the Imperial Household (guānglùxūn 光祿勳).
Fàn Shì 范式, courtesy name Jùqīng 巨卿,
was from Jīnxiāng 金鄉, Shānyáng 山陽.
He was also named Fàn 氾.
As a youth, he traveled to the Imperial Academy (tàixué 太學),
and while a student,
became friends with Zhāng Shào 張劭 from Rǔnán 汝南.
Shào's 劭 courtesy name was Yuánbó 元伯.
The two both announced their return to their hometowns.
Shì 范式 said to Yuánbó 元伯:
"Two years from now, I will return,
and will pass by to pay my respects to your parents,
and see your child."
They then set a specific date.
When the appointed date approached,
Yuánbó 元伯 told his mother everything,
and asked to prepare a feast to await him.
His mother said:
"After two years of separation,
you made this promise from a thousand miles away.
Why are you so certain he will keep his word?"
He replied:
"Jùqīng 巨卿 is a trustworthy man;
he will certainly not break his promise."
His mother said:
"If that is so,
I shall brew wine for you."
On that day,
Jùqīng 巨卿 indeed arrived.
He ascended the hall, paid his respects, drank,
and they parted in joy.
Shì 范式 served as County Merit Officer (gōngcáo 功曹).
Later, Yuánbó 元伯 fell gravely ill.
Zhì Jūnzhāng 郅君章 and Yīn Zǐzhēng 殷子徵, from the same commandery, visited him day and night.
As Yuánbó 元伯 was dying,
he sighed and said:
"I regret not seeing my friend in death!"
Zǐzhēng 殷子徵 said:
"Jūnzhāng 君章 and I have dedicated ourselves to you.
If we are not friends in death,
then who else do you seek?"
Yuánbó 元伯 said:
"You two are merely friends in life.
Fàn Jùqīng 范巨卿 of Shānyáng 山陽,
he is what I call a friend in death."
Soon after, he passed away.
Shì 范式 suddenly dreamt that Yuánbó 元伯, in a black cap with dangling tassels and straw sandals, called out:
"Jùqīng 巨卿,
I died on a certain day,
and will be buried at that time,
returning eternally to the Yellow Springs.
If you have not forgotten me,
how can you not come?"
Shì 范式 woke up startled,
sighed in sorrow, and wept.
He told the Grand Administrator everything,
requesting permission to rush to the funeral.
Although the Grand Administrator did not believe it in his heart, he was reluctant to deny his sentiment,
so he granted permission.
Shì 范式 then put on the attire of a friend,
timed his arrival for the burial day,
and rushed to attend.
Before Shì 范式 arrived,
the funeral procession had already started.
When they reached the burial pit,
and were about to inter the coffin,
the coffin refused to move forward.
His mother stroked it and said:
"Yuánbó 元伯,
are you perhaps waiting for someone?"
So they halted the coffin for a time.
Then they saw a plain carriage and white horse,
with someone crying aloud, approaching.
His mother looked and said:
"That must be Fàn Jùqīng 范巨卿!"
When Jùqīng 巨卿 arrived,
he knocked on the coffin and said:
"Go now, Yuánbó 元伯!
The paths of life and death are different;
from this moment, we bid eternal farewell."
A thousand people gathered for the funeral,
all shed tears.
Shì 范式 then took hold of the coffin rope and pulled,
and the coffin then moved forward.
Shì 范式 stayed by the tomb,
tending to the grave and planting trees,
and only then departed.
Later, he went to the capital,
and studied at the Imperial Academy.
At that time, Chén Píngzǐ 陳平子 from Chángshā 長沙, also a student there,
had not yet met Shì 范式.
Píngzǐ 陳平子 fell ill and was about to die.
He said to his wife:
"I have heard that Fàn Jùqīng 范巨卿 of Shānyáng 山陽
is a man of integrity,
and one can entrust their death to him.
After my death,
simply bury my body in front of Jùqīng's 巨卿 residence."
He then tore a piece of silk for a letter,
to be given to Jùqīng 巨卿.
After he died,
his wife followed his instructions.
At that time, Shì 范式 had just returned from an outing.
He saw the letter and the burial,
and was deeply moved.
He bowed and wept before the tomb,
considering him a friend in death.
He then took care of Píngzǐ's 陳平子 wife and children,
personally escorting the funeral to Línxiāng 臨湘.
When they were four or five *lǐ* 里 away,
he placed a plain silk letter on the coffin,
wept his farewell, and departed.
His brothers heard of this,
searched for him but did not see him again.
The Chief Clerk (shàngjìyuànshǐ 上計掾史) from Chángshā 長沙 went to the capital,
submitting a memorial detailing Shì's 范式 conduct.
All three chief ministries (sānfǔ 三府) invited him,
but he did not respond.
He was nominated as a *Mào cái* (茂才) by the prefecture,
and was four times promoted, eventually becoming the *Cìshǐ* (刺史) of Jīngzhōu (荊州).
His friend, Kǒng Sōng (孔嵩) from Nányáng (南陽),
was poor and his parents were old.
So he changed his name
and became a street guard in Ālǐ (阿里) street, Xīnyě (新野) county.
Shì (式) was inspecting the district and arrived in Xīnyě (新野).
The county selected Kǒng Sōng (孔嵩) to be the mounted escort to welcome Shì (式).
Shì (式) saw him and recognized him.
He called out to Kǒng Sōng (孔嵩)
and, holding his arm, said:
"Are you not Kǒng Zhòngshān (孔仲山)?"
Kǒng Sōng (孔嵩) sighed in response,
and they spoke of their past lives.
Shì (式) said:
"In the past, you and I both wore long robes,
and roamed the imperial academy.
I received the grace of the state,
and reached the position of a provincial governor,
yet you, cherishing the Dao, have hidden yourself,
and remain among the ranks of common soldiers.
Is this not regrettable!"
Kǒng Sōng (孔嵩) replied:
"Hóu Yíng (侯嬴) long adhered to his humble profession,
and Chén Mén (晨門) freely pursued his ambition as a gatekeeper.
If a gentleman wishes to reside among the Jiǔ Yí (九夷),
he does not worry about its squalor.
Poverty is fitting for a scholar;
how can it be considered ignoble!"
Shì (式) ordered the county to replace Kǒng Sōng (孔嵩).
Kǒng Sōng (孔嵩) thought his prior employment was not yet finished,
and refused to leave.
While Kǒng Sōng (孔嵩) was in Ālǐ (阿里),
he conducted himself uprightly and acted rigorously.
The young people on the street all submitted to his instruction and transformation.
He was then appointed to a government office.
When he traveled to the capital,
he lodged overnight at Xiàtíng (下亭) station.
Thieves stole his horse.
Upon inquiring and realizing it was Kǒng Sōng (孔嵩),
they admonished each other, saying:
"Kǒng Zhòngshān (孔仲山) is a good man;
how can he be robbed!"
Thereupon, they returned the horse and apologized to him.
Kǒng Sōng (孔嵩) rose to the position of *Tàishǒu* (太守) of Nánhǎi (南海).
Shì (式) was later promoted to *Tàishǒu* (太守) of Lújiāng (廬江).
He had a reputation for authority
and died in office.
Lǐ Shàn (李善), whose *zì* (字) was Cìsūn (次孫),
was a native of Yùyáng (淯陽), Nányáng (南陽).
Originally, he was a servant of Lǐ Yuán (李元) from the same county.
During an epidemic in the Jiànwǔ (建武) era,
Lǐ Yuán's (李元) family successively died,
leaving only an orphaned child, Xù (續), who was only a few tens of days old,
but possessed tens of millions in wealth.
All the slaves privately conspired,
planning to murder Xù (續)
and divide his property.
Lǐ Shàn (李善) was deeply saddened for the Lǐ (李) clan but was powerless to stop them.
So he secretly carried Xù (續) and fled,
hiding in the border area of Xiáqiū (瑕丘), Shānyáng (山陽).
He personally fed and raised him,
suckling him with his own milk,
placing him in dry spots and occupying the wet ones himself,
enduring all sorts of hardships.
Even though Xù (續) was in his infancy,
Lǐ Shàn (李善) served him as if he were an elder,
always kneeling to report and seek permission for any matter
before acting.
The villagers were moved by his conduct
and all followed his example in cultivating righteousness.
When Xù (續) was ten years old,
Lǐ Shàn (李善) returned with him to their home county
and restored the family's former estate.
He reported the slaves to the chief magistrate,
who had them all arrested and executed.
At that time, Zhōnglí Yì (鍾離意) was the magistrate of Xiáqiū (瑕丘).
He submitted a memorial recommending Lǐ Shàn's (李善) conduct.
Emperor Guāngwǔ (光武) issued an edict appointing both Lǐ Shàn (李善) and Xù (續) as *Tàizǐ Shèrén* (太子舍人).
Lǐ Shàn (李善),
during Emperor Xiǎnzōng's (顯宗) reign, was appointed to a government office.
Because of his ability to manage difficult affairs,
he was twice promoted, becoming *Tàishǒu* (太守) of Rìnán (日南).
When traveling from the capital to his post,
he passed through Yùyáng (淯陽)
and visited Lǐ Yuán's (李元) tomb.
Not yet a *lǐ* (里) away,
he removed his court robes,
took a hoe, and cleared the weeds.
When he bowed at the tomb,
he wept bitterly,
personally cooked the food,
and arranged the tripod and cutting board to perform the sacrifice.
He wept and said:
"My lord and lady,
Shàn (善) is here."
He expressed his profound grief
and only left after several days.
Upon arriving at his post,
he governed with love and benevolence,
attracting foreign peoples.
He was promoted to *Tàishǒu* (太守) of Jiǔjiāng (九江),
but fell ill and died on the way
before reaching his post.
Xù (續) rose to the position of *Xiāng* (相) of Héjiān (河閒).
Wáng Tún (王忳), whose *zì* (字) was Shàolín (少林),
was a native of Xīndū (新都), Guǎnghàn (廣漢).
Wáng Tún (王忳) once went to the capital,
and in an empty house, he saw a scholar critically ill.
He approached him and looked at him.
The scholar said to Wáng Tún (王忳):
"I was supposed to go to Luòyáng (洛陽),
but I fell ill,
and my life is but a moment away.
Underneath my bed are ten *jīn* (斤) of gold.
I wish to give it to you as a gift,
and after I die, please bury my bones."
He died before Wáng Tún (王忳) could ask his name.
Wáng Tún (王忳) immediately sold one *jīn* (斤) of gold
to arrange his funeral.
He placed the remaining gold under the coffin,
and no one knew about it.
Several years later, he returned home.
The county appointed Wáng Tún (王忳) as the *Tíngzhǎng* (亭長) of Dàdù (大度) post.
On the day he first arrived,
a horse galloped into the post and stopped.
That day,
a strong wind blew a silk-embroidered quilt,
which then fell in front of Wáng Tún (王忳).
He immediately reported it to the county,
and the county returned it to Wáng Tún (王忳).
Later, Wáng Tún (王忳) rode the horse to Luòxiàn (雒縣).
The horse suddenly bolted,
pulling Wáng Tún (王忳) into another dwelling.
The owner saw him and joyfully exclaimed:
"Now the thief has been caught!"
He asked Wáng Tún (王忳) how he got the horse.
Wáng Tún (王忳) fully explained the situation,
including the embroidered quilt.
The owner was thoughtful for a long time,
then said:
"The quilt was carried away by a whirlwind, and the horse also went missing.
What hidden virtue do you possess to have obtained these two items?"
Wáng Tún (王忳) recalled the matter of burying the scholar
and then recounted it,
also describing the scholar's appearance and the place where the gold was buried.
The owner was greatly astonished and cried out:
"That was my son!
His surname was Jīn (金) and given name Yàn (彥).
He went to the capital earlier,
and I didn't know where he was.
Who would have thought that you buried him!
This great kindness has long gone unrewarded;
Heaven is using this to manifest your virtue!"
Wáng Tún (王忳) returned the quilt and horse to him.
Yàn's (彥) father would not accept them,
and also generously offered gifts to Wáng Tún (王忳).
Wáng Tún (王忳) declined and left.
At that time, Yàn's (彥) father was a *Cóngshì* (從事) of the prefecture.
He then informed the magistrate of Xīndū (新都),
granted Wáng Tún (王忳) leave,
and personally went with him to collect Yàn's (彥) remains,
finding all the remaining gold still there.
