Wáng Tún (王忳) became renowned because of this.
He served as the Administrator of Merits in the commandery,
and as an Attendant Official in the provincial government.
He was recommended as a Mào cái,
and appointed as the Magistrate of Méi.
Upon arriving at his post,
he reached Lái Tíng.
The head of the post-station said:
"There is a ghost in this station,
which has repeatedly killed passing travelers,
so you cannot stay here."
Tún said:
"Benevolence overcomes evil,
and virtue removes misfortune.
Why should I avoid a ghost?"
He immediately entered the station and stayed overnight.
In the middle of the night, he heard the voice of a woman crying out her grievance.
Tún chanted:
"What injustice have you suffered?
Can you come forward and seek justice?"
The woman said:
"I have no clothes,
and dare not approach."
Tún then threw his clothes to her.
The woman then came forward and complained, saying:
"My husband was the Magistrate of Fú.
On his way to his post, he stayed overnight at this station.
The station head, being unscrupulous,
murdered my family of more than ten people,
buried them under the building,
and seized all our valuables."
Tún asked the station head's name.
The woman said:
"He is the current patrolman at the gate."
Tún asked:
"Why do you repeatedly kill passing travelers?"
She replied:
"I cannot plead my case in broad daylight.
Every night I express my grievance,
but the travelers always sleep and do not respond.
Overwhelmed by anger and resentment,
I killed them."
Tún said:
"I will administer justice for this wrong for you.
Do not kill good and innocent people again."
Thereupon, she placed the clothes on the ground,
and suddenly disappeared.
The next morning, he summoned the patrolman and questioned him.
He fully confessed his crime,
and was immediately arrested and imprisoned.
Over ten accomplices also confessed their guilt.
Officials were dispatched to send her remains back to her hometown.
From then on, the post-station became peaceful and safe.
Zhāng Wǔ was
a native of Yóuquán in Wú Jùn.
His father, Yè,
was a subordinate clerk in the commandery government.
When he was escorting the Grand Administrator's wife and children back to their hometown,
they reached Hénèi Tíng,
where bandits robbed them at night.
Yè fought the bandits and died,
and his body was lost.
Wǔ was young at the time,
and too young to have known his father.
Later, he went to the Imperial Academy to study.
At every festival,
he would always carry a sword left by his father,
and offer sacrifices at the place where he died,
crying before returning.
The Grand Administrator, Dìwǔ Lún, praised his conduct
and recommended him as a Xiàolián.
He suffered from excessive grief during his mother's mourning,
lamenting that his father's soul had not returned,
and consequently died from overwhelming sorrow.
Líng Xù, styled Zhìchū,
was a native of Wú in Kuàijī.
His family had been a prominent clan for generations.
His grandfather, Hóng,
styled Zǐchūn,
served as Shàngshū Lìng during the Jiànwǔ era.
He was handsome,
and liked to wear single garments made of Yuè cloth.
Guāngwǔ saw them and liked them,
and from then on, he regularly ordered the Kuàijī Commandery to present Yuè cloth.
Xù was orphaned young.
He served as the Household Clerk in the commandery.
At that time, the year was barren and the people were starving.
Grand Administrator Yǐn Xīng ordered Xù to distribute gruel to the people at the city station.
Xù carefully inspected all the people,
and questioned them by name.
When the task was completed,
Xīng asked how many had been fed.
Xù then verbally reported over six hundred people,
distinguishing all their surnames and given names,
without any error.
Xīng was surprised by this.
When the Inspector toured the region,
he met Xù
and appointed him as Bìjià Cóngshì.
He left due to illness,
and returned to serve as the Commandery Gate Subordinate.
At this time, King Yīng of Chǔ plotted rebellion,
secretly making a list of virtuous scholars throughout the empire.
When the Chǔ affair was discovered,
Xiǎnzōng obtained the record,
which contained Yǐn Xīng's name.
Xīng was then summoned to the廷Wèi prison.
Xù, along with Chief Clerk Liáng Hóng, Administrator of Merits Clerk Sì Xūn, and over five hundred other clerks and subordinates, went to the imperial prison in Luòyáng to be interrogated.
Most of the officials could not endure the pain
and died.
Only Xù, Hóng, and Xūn, after being tortured with the five poisons,
their flesh wasted away,
still maintained their original statements.
Xù's mother traveled far to the capital
to inquire about news.
The prison affairs were particularly urgent,
and there was no way for her to communicate with Xù.
His mother simply prepared food
and entrusted it to the gate guard to deliver to him.
Although Xù was subjected to severe torture,
his words and expression remained resolute,
and he never changed his demeanor.
Only when faced with food did he weep bitterly,
unable to control himself.
The envoy was puzzled and asked him the reason.
Xù said:
"My mother has come, but I cannot see her,
that is why I weep."
The envoy was greatly angered,
thinking that the gate guard had conveyed messages,
and summoned him for investigation.
Xù said:
"When I ate the soup from the meal,
I recognized that my mother had prepared it herself,
so I knew she had come.
No one told me."
The envoy asked:
"How do you know it was made by your mother?"
Xù said:
"My mother always cuts meat into square shapes,
and cuts spring onions to a length of one inch.
This is how I knew."
The envoy inquired among the guest houses,
and indeed Xù's mother had arrived.
Thereupon, he secretly admired him,
and submitted a memorial explaining Xù's conduct.
The Emperor immediately pardoned Xīng and the others,
allowing them to return to their hometowns,
but they were forbidden from holding office for life.
Xù died from old age and illness.
His eldest son, Chóu,
was the Grand Administrator of Guǎnglín,
and was renowned for his governance.
His second son, Féng,
was the Grand Administrator of Yuè'ān.
His youngest son, Bāo,
was diligent and fond of learning,
not aspiring to fame and honor.
He was repeatedly summoned but did not take office.
Bāo's son, Kāng,
has already been mentioned in the previous biography.
Dài Fēng, styled Píngzhòng,
was a native of Gāng in Jìběi.
At fifteen,
he went to the Imperial Academy
and studied under Shēn Jūn of Dōnghǎi, who was the Magistrate of Mào.
When Shēn Jūn died,
he escorted the coffin to Dōnghǎi.
The route happened to pass by his home.
His parents, expecting Fēng to return,
had arranged a marriage for him in advance.
Fēng briefly visited to pay respects to his parents,
but did not stay overnight and left.
He returned to the capital to complete his studies.
At that time, his fellow student Shí Jìngpíng died of a fever.
Fēng cared for him, arranged his funeral,
bought a small coffin with the provisions he had brought,
and escorted the body home.
When the family re-interred the body,
they found all of Jìngpíng's writings and belongings from his lifetime inside the coffin.
They were greatly surprised.
Later, Fēng encountered bandits.
All his valuables were plundered,
except for seven bolts of fine silk.
The bandits did not know where they were.
Fēng then pursued them and gave the silk to them,
saying:
"I know you gentlemen are in need,
so I am sending this to you as a gift."
The bandits were astonished and said:
"This is a virtuous man!"
They returned all his belongings.
Later, he was nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate.
He served as a principal clerk in the Court of the Imperial Household (Guānglù Zhǔshì).
Upon the death of his paternal uncle, he resigned from office.
An imperial edict sought virtuous, upright, and outspoken gentlemen,
who possessed supreme conduct and could avert disasters and suppress anomalies.
The three highest ministers (Gōngqīng) and various commandery governors (Jùnshǒu) each nominated one person.
The commandery and the Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng) both nominated Fēng.
He was summoned by the imperial carriage (Gōngchē),
had an audience with the emperor,
and his policy response was ranked first.
He was promoted to Gentleman Consultant (Yìláng).
He was transferred to become the magistrate of Xīhuá.
At that time, there was a locust plague in Rǔ and Yǐng commanderies,
but it uniquely did not enter the borders of Xīhuá.
At that time, an imperial inspector (Dūyóu) was touring the counties.
Locusts suddenly arrived in great numbers.
The inspector left that very day,
and the locusts also completely disappeared.
The entire region considered it a wonder.
That year, there was a great drought.
Fēng prayed and pleaded but received no relief.
So he piled up firewood and sat upon it to immolate himself.
As the fire started, a heavy rain suddenly arrived.
Thereupon, people from far and near praised and submitted to him.
He was transferred to become the administrator of Zhōngshān.
At that time, there were over four hundred prisoners in the various counties,
whose cases had already been finalized
and were due for execution.
Fēng pitied them
and sent them all home,
agreeing on a specific return date.
None of them failed to return.
An imperial edict praised this.
In the twelfth year of Yǒngyuán (100 CE),
he was summoned to be appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
He died in office.
Lǐ Chōng, courtesy name Dàxùn,
was a native of Chénliú.
His family was poor,
and six brothers shared food and passed clothes among themselves.
His wife secretly said to Chōng,
“Our present poverty is such
that it is difficult to maintain peace for long.
I have private property,
and I wish to consider a separation.”
Chōng feigned a response to her, saying,
“If you wish to live separately,
we should brew wine and prepare a feast,
invite our neighbors and relatives,
and discuss the matter together.”
His wife followed Chōng’s suggestion and prepared wine and entertained guests.
Chōng, in the middle of the gathering, knelt forward and reported to his mother, saying,
“This woman is ill-behaved
and has taught me to separate from my mother and brothers.
Her crime warrants dismissal.”
Then he reprimanded his wife
and drove her out the door.
His wife left, weeping silently.
Those present were astonished and awestruck,
and subsequently dispersed.
Later, Chōng suffered the loss of his mother
and observed mourning by her tomb.
When someone stole trees from her tomb,
Chōng personally killed him with his own hand.
After the mourning period ended,
he established a private academy (jīngshè) to teach.
The grand administrator (Tàishǒu) Lǔ Píng asked him to be appointed Chief Clerk (Gōngcáo),
but he did not accept.
Píng was angered,
and so he seized Chōng and threw him into a ditch.
Then he was demoted and appointed Chief of the County Post Station (Xiàn Dūtíngzhǎng).
Having no alternative,
he undertook this public service.
Later, Emperor Hé summoned him by imperial carriage,
but he did not go.
During the Yánpíng reign (106 CE),
an edict ordered the highest ministers, the two-thousand-pic officials (Zhōng Èrqiān Shí), and others, each to recommend reclusive scholars and great Confucians,
seeking those of high conduct,
to encourage future generations.
Chōng was specifically summoned to be a Erudite (Bóshì).
At that time, Lǔ Píng was also an Erudite.
Whenever they met,
Píng often praised and submitted to him.
Chōng was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
The Grand General Dèng Zhì, a powerful relative by marriage, swayed the times,
and bowed to no one.
Because of Chōng’s lofty integrity,
he always treated him with humility and respect.
Once, he held a banquet and invited Chōng.
The hall was filled with guests.
When the wine was flowing,
Zhì knelt and said,
“Fortunately, I am related to the empress (jiāofáng),
and my position is that of a supreme general.
My headquarters (mùfǔ) has just been established,
and I wish to recruit extraordinary talents from across the realm
to compensate for my deficiencies.
I only ask that all of you extensively seek out such individuals.”
Chōng then spoke of reclusive gentlemen throughout the land who cherished the Dao.
Many of his suggestions were not agreeable.
Zhì wanted to cut him off
and offered him meat to eat.
Chōng tossed the meat to the ground and said,
“A speaker (shuōshì) should still find meat delicious!”
Then he went out
and left directly.
Zhì was greatly disappointed in him.
Zhāng Mèngjǔ of Rǔnán, who was present, went to reprove Chōng, saying,
“Today I heard that your discussion with General Dèng on recommending gentlemen was not concluded.
You were provoked and directly rebuked him,
without acting with moderation.
The blame for your words
is not something that will bring glory to your descendants.”
Chōng replied,
“A great man living in the world
values acting according to his will.
How can one plan far ahead for one’s descendants!”
Because of this, he was disapproved of by the powerful relatives.
He was transferred to Lieutenant-General of the Palace Guard (Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiàng).
At the age of eighty-eight,
he became one of the Three Elders of the state (Guó Sānlǎo).
Emperor Ān often granted him special audiences
and bestowed upon him a small table (jǐ) and a staff (zhàng).
He died at home.
Móu Róng, courtesy name Yùgōng,
was a native of Shàolíng, Rǔnán.
He became an orphan in his youth.
The four brothers
all shared their property and livelihood.
When they each married wives,
the women then sought separation,
and there were also frequent quarrels.
Róng was deeply indignant and sighed.
So he closed the door and flogged himself, saying,
“Móu Róng,
you cultivate your conduct and act with prudence,
learning the methods of the sages,
intending to rectify customs.
How can you fail to govern your own family!”
His younger brothers and their wives heard this
and all kowtowed to apologize.
They then changed their ways to be harmonious and affectionate.
He served as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) in the county.
At that time, the county magistrate was impeached and investigated.
All the clerks were fearful and falsely accused themselves,
but Róng alone provided evidence for the truth of the matter.
He was severely beaten and tortured,
to the point that maggots grew on his body.
He was then successively transferred to five different prisons,
enduring over four years.
The magistrate eventually managed to clear himself.
The Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) Liáng Zhàn of Lǒngxī summoned him to be Clerk of the Judiciary (Juécáo Shǐ).
At the beginning of Emperor Ān’s reign,
Zhàn died in office.
Róng escorted the funeral procession back to Lǒngxī.
After the initial burial,
it happened that the Western Qiāng rebelled.
Zhàn’s wife and children all fled to other commanderies to escape the chaos,
but Róng alone remained and did not leave.
He built a tomb mound for him,
then secretly dug a cave next to the well,
hiding there by day
and carrying earth at night.
By the time the rebels were pacified, the tomb mound was already erected.
Zhàn’s wife and children thought Róng had died;
when they returned and saw him, they were greatly astonished.
People in Guānxī all praised and spread his story,
and collectively offered him carriages, horses, clothes, and funds.
Róng refused them and returned to his hometown.
He was invited to serve in the public administration (gōngfǔ),
and was nominated as especially outstanding.
He was transferred to be the magistrate of Zhōngmóu.
The county was near the capital,
and there were many powerful and influential families.
When Róng arrived,
he executed over a hundred corrupt officials and those who invoked the names of powerful relatives and retainers.
His prestige and reputation consequently spread.
He died in office.
Chén Chóng, courtesy name Jǐnggōng,
was a native of Yīchūn, Yùzhāng.
In his youth, he was friends with Léi Yì from the same commandery.
They both studied the Lǔ Recension of the Odes (Lǔ Shī) and Yán Shì Chūnqiū.
The grand administrator (Tàishǒu) Zhāng Yún nominated Chóng as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate.
Chóng yielded the nomination to Yì,
writing over ten letters back and forth,
but Yún did not agree.
The next year, Yì was nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate,
and Chóng and he both served in the Bureau of Gentlemen (Lángshǔ).
There was a bureaucrat in the same office who owed several hundred thousand (cash) in interest-bearing loans.
The creditor came daily to demand payment,
and resorted to constant deceitful pleas.
Chén Zhòng then secretly repaid the loan on his behalf.
The bureaucrat later found out and profusely thanked him.
Chén Zhòng said,
"It wasn't I who did it;
there must be someone with the same name."
He ultimately did not mention the favor.
Another bureaucrat from the same dormitory had taken leave to visit his parents
and mistakenly took a neighbor's trousers with him.
The owner suspected Chén Zhòng had taken them.
Chén Zhòng did not explain himself,
but bought new trousers to compensate the owner.
Later, when the bureaucrat on leave returned,
he returned the trousers to the owner,
and the truth of the matter became clear.
Later, Chén Zhòng and Léi Yì were both appointed Shàngshū Láng.
Léi Yì took the blame for a contemporary,
and was consequently demoted and dismissed.
Chén Zhòng, seeing Léi Yì leave,
also resigned due to illness.
Later, he was recommended as Màocái
and appointed Xiàyáng Lìng.
His administration showed extraordinary transformative power,
and he was highly praised.
He was slated for promotion to Huìjī Tàishǒu,
but resigned due to his sister's mourning.
Later, he was recruited by the Sītú's office
and appointed Shìyùshǐ.
He died in office.
Léi Yì, courtesy name Zhònggōng,
was a native of Póyáng in Yùzhāng.
Initially, he served as a Gōngcáo in the commandery.
He [嘗] always promoted good people,
without boasting of his accomplishments.
Léi Yì once saved a person from a death sentence.
The grateful person later thanked him with two catties of gold.
Léi Yì refused it.
The owner of the gold, waiting for Léi Yì to be absent,
secretly threw the gold onto the ceiling beams.
Later, when Léi Yì renovated his house,
he found it.
The owner of the gold had already died,
so there was no one to return it to.
Léi Yì then handed it over to the county office.
Later, he was recommended as Xiàolián
and appointed Shàngshū Shìláng.
A fellow bureaucrat was implicated in a case and was to be sentenced to penal labor.
Léi Yì secretly submitted a memorial taking the blame for him,
and was consequently sentenced by the Sīkòu.
The fellow bureaucrat in the same department, realizing this,
resigned his position and reported himself,
begging to redeem Léi Yì's crime.
Emperor Shùn decreed that both be pardoned from punishment.
Léi Yì returned,
was recommended as Màocái,
but yielded the position to Chén Zhòng.
The Cìshǐ would not permit it.
Léi Yì then feigned madness, let his hair down, and ran away,
refusing the appointment.
The villagers made a saying about them:
"Lacquer and glue claim to be strong,
but they are not as good as Léi and Chén."
The Three Ducal Ministries simultaneously recruited both men.
Léi Yì then served as Shǒu Guàn Yèzhě.
He was dispatched with a staff of authority to inspect the customs of the commanderies and kingdoms,
and seventy Tàishǒu and Lìngzhǎng were disciplined.
He was subsequently appointed Shìyùshǐ,
then Nándùn Lìng.
He died in office.
His son, Shòu,
rose to the rank of Cāngwú Tàishǒu.
Fàn Rǎn, courtesy name Shǐyún,
was a native of Wàihuáng in Chénliú.
When young, he was a minor county official.
At eighteen,
he was ordered to receive the Dūyóu.
Fàn Rǎn was ashamed of this,
and so he fled.
He arrived in Nányáng
and studied under Fán Yīng.
He then traveled through Sānfǔ,
studying the classics with Mǎ Róng.
After several years, he returned.
Fàn Rǎn delighted in defying the times and distancing himself from popular customs,
engaging in eccentric behavior.
He always admired the conduct of Liáng Bólúan and Mǐn Zhòngshū.
He was close friends with Lǐ Gù of Hànzhōng and Wáng Huàn of Hénèi,
but disdained Jiǎ Wěijié and Guō Línzōng.
Wáng Huàn later became Kǎochéng Lìng,
with his jurisdiction bordering Wàihuáng.
He repeatedly sent letters inviting Fàn Rǎn,
but Fàn Rǎn did not come.
When Wáng Huàn was transferred to Hànyáng Tàishǒu,
and was about to depart,
Fàn Rǎn and his younger brother Xié walked and carried wheat beer,
setting up an altar by the roadside to wait for him.
Fàn Rǎn saw Wáng Huàn's carriages and entourage streaming by,
and so did not make himself known,
but only debated with his brother on the road.
Wáng Huàn recognized his voice,
immediately dismounted and greeted him respectfully.
Wáng Huàn said,
"We are in a hurry on the road,
not a place to express [契] our long separation.
We can go to the next pavilion to rest for the night
and then part."
Fàn Rǎn said,
"When you were previously in Kǎochéng,
I wanted to follow you,
but my humble status prevented me from associating with distinguished friends.
Now you are traveling a thousand *lǐ* away,
and we have no definite time to meet again.
Therefore, I made this light journey to await you,
to bid you farewell.
If I were to pursue you,
I would incur the criticism of seeking favor with the powerful."
He then stood up, announced his departure,
brushed his clothes, and left.
Wáng Huàn watched, unable to catch up,
and Fàn Rǎn walked away without looking back.
During Emperor Huán's reign,
Fàn Rǎn was made Láiwú Zhǎng.
He encountered his mother's mourning
and did not report to office.
Later, he was recruited by the Tàiwèi's office.
Because of his obstinacy and inability to conform to custom,
he always wore *wéi* (rough leather) in court (as a symbol of his integrity).
Those who debated desired to appoint him Shìyùshǐ.
He consequently fled and hid himself between Liáng and Pèi,
traveling on foot in worn clothes,
and selling divination in the market.
During the proscription of partisans,
he then pushed a deer cart,
carrying his wife and children,
gathering scraps to support himself,
sometimes lodging in guest houses,
sometimes staying under tree shades.
After more than ten years of this,
he built a thatched hut and lived there.
His dwelling was simple and humble.
Sometimes his food ran out,
but he remained composed in his poverty,
his speech and appearance unchanged.
The villagers sang of him, saying:
"Dust grows in the steamer for Fàn Shǐyún,
fish grow in the cauldron for Fàn Láiwú."
When the partisan proscription was lifted,
he was recruited by the Three Ducal Ministries,
and he answered the Sīkōng's summons.
At that time, the Western Qiāng had rebelled,
and the Yellow Turbans were causing trouble.
A decree forbade officials of the various ministries from wantonly leaving their posts.
Fàn Rǎn was the first to impeach himself and retire.
An imperial edict specifically pardoned him and did not punish him.
He was again recruited by the Tàiwèi's office,
but did not go due to illness.
In the second year of Zhōngpíng (185 CE),
at the age of seventy-four,
he died at home.
On his deathbed, he left a will instructing his son, saying:
"I was born in a dark age,
and lived amidst extravagant customs.
Since I could not rectify the age and save the times while alive,
how can I bear to be the same as the world in death!
As soon as my breath stops, prepare me for burial.
Dress me in ordinary clothes,
enough to cover my form.
The coffin should be large enough to encompass my body.
As soon as the burial preparations are complete, dig the grave.
As soon as the grave is dug, bury me.
For the offering in the Mingtang,
use dry rice and cold water.
As for food and drink,
do not place anything elaborate.
The height of the tomb mound
should be just enough to conceal me.
Those who truly understand my heart are Lǐ Zǐjiān and Wáng Zǐbǐng.
Now they are both gone.
The arrangements are up to you.
Do not let the villagers or relatives add anything more."
Thereupon, the Three Ducal Ministries each sent clerks to mourn him.
General-in-chief Hé Jìn sent a letter to the Chénliú Tàishǒu,
repeatedly discussing and conferring a posthumous title.
All agreed he should be titled Zhēnjié Xiānshēng.
More than two thousand people attended his funeral.
The Cìshǐ and Jùnshǒu each erected a stele and marked his tomb.
Dài Jiù
字 Jǐngchéng, from Shàngyú, Kuàijī.
He served in the commandery as Cāngcáo Yuàn.
Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Ōuyáng Cān impeached Grand Administrator Chéng Gōngfú for corruption,
and sent his subordinate Cóngshì Xuē Ān to investigate the warehouse accounts.
Dài Jiù was arrested and imprisoned in Qiántáng County.
He was held captive and tortured,
subjected to all five types of brutal punishment.
Dài Jiù spoke with indignation and integrity,
his countenance showing no change.
They also heated a short-handled axe
and made Dài Jiù hold it under his armpits.
Dài Jiù told the jailers:
“Make sure the axe is thoroughly heated;
do not let it cool.”
Whenever he was subjected to harsh torture,
he would stop eating and refuse to swallow.
When his flesh was charred and fell to the ground,
he would pick it up and eat it.
The officials in charge, having exhausted their cruelest methods
with no further means,
then made Dài Jiù lie under an overturned boat
and fumigated him with horse dung.
After one night and two days,
everyone thought he was dead.
When they lifted the boat to look,
Dài Jiù was just opening his eyes and loudly cursing:
“Why didn’t you add more fuel,
and instead let it extinguish!”
They then burned the ground again
and used large needles to pierce his fingernails,
making him grasp soil.
All his fingernails fell off.
The officials reported the situation to Xuē Ān.
Ān summoned Dài Jiù to see him,
and said:
“The Grand Administrator’s crimes and corruption are rampant.
I have received orders to investigate and verify.
Why do you resist and defend him with your own flesh and blood?”
Dài Jiù, sitting on the ground, replied:
“The Grand Administrator received his credentials as a high minister;
he should repay the state with his life.
Although you bear a commission,
you should properly redress this injustice and wrong.
How can you falsely accuse loyal and good men,
forcefully interrogate and rationalize,
and make a subject slander his lord,
or a son testify against his father!
Xuē Ān, you are foolish and
obstinately act without righteousness.
On the day I die under torture,
I shall report it to Heaven
and, with a host of ghosts, kill you in the pavilion.
If I am spared with my life,
I will personally dismember you with a blade!”
Ān deeply admired his resolute integrity,
and immediately unfettered him.
He then had a pleasant conversation with him,
reported Dài Jiù’s words,
and cleared up the commandery's affairs.
Fú was summoned back to the capital
and dismissed to his hometown.
Grand Administrator Liú Chǒng recommended Dài Jiù as Xiàolián,
who then served as Guānglù Zhǔshì
before dying of illness.
Zhào Bāo,
字 Wēiháo, from Dōngwǔchéng, Gānlíng.
His elder cousin, Zhōng,
was a Zhōngchángshì.
Bāo deeply felt ashamed that his family had a powerful eunuch by name,
and did not associate with Zhōng.
He first served in the province and commandery,
was recommended as Xiàolián,
and twice promoted to Gǔanglíng Lìng.
After three years in office,
his administration and governance were clear and upright.
The commandery reported his achievements,
and he was promoted to Liáoxī Tàishǒu.
He was strict and dignified,
his reputation shaking the border regions.
The year after he took office,
he sent envoys to welcome his mother, wife, and children.
Just as they were about to arrive in the commandery,
they passed through Liǔchéng
and encountered over ten thousand Xiānbēi entering the pass to raid and plunder.
Bāo’s mother, wife, and children were consequently seized as hostages
and used to attack the commandery.
Bāo led twenty thousand infantry and cavalry
and arrayed them against the bandits.
The bandits brought out his mother and showed her to Bāo.
Bāo cried out mournfully to his mother, saying:
“Your son is unworthy;
I wished to serve you daily with my meager salary,
but unexpectedly brought disaster upon you, mother.
Formerly, I was your son;
now, I am a minister of the King.
Righteousness dictates I cannot consider private affections
and destroy my loyalty and integrity.
I can only die ten thousand deaths,
unable to atone for my sin.”
His mother, from afar, said:
“Wēiháo,
everyone has their fate.
How can you look back
and compromise loyalty and righteousness!
In the past, Wáng Líng’s mother faced the Hàn envoy and fell upon her sword
to solidify her resolve.
You should strive to do the same.”
Bāo immediately advanced to battle.
The bandits were utterly crushed,
and his mother and wife were both killed by them.
After Bāo completed his mother's funeral rites,
he requested leave to return home for her burial.
Emperor Líng sent an imperial edict of condolence
and enfeoffed him as Shū Hóu.
After Bāo completed the burial,
he said to the villagers:
“To receive emoluments and avoid danger
is not loyal;
to kill one’s mother to preserve righteousness
is not filial.
If this is the case,
what face do I have to stand in this world!”
Thereupon, he vomited blood and died.
Xiàng Xǔ,
字 Fǔxīng, from Cháogē, Hénèi,
a descendant of Xiàng Cháng.
In his youth, he was a scholar,
with a unique and unconventional nature.
He constantly read the Lǎozi,
appearing to be a follower of the Dao.
He also seemed like a mad scholar,
fond of letting his hair down
and wearing a crimson silk headscarf.
He often sat on a wooden bedboard north of the stove.
After a long period of this,
the board showed indentations from his knees, ankles, and toes.
He disliked talking but enjoyed long whistling.
When guests approached,
he would often prostrate himself and avoid looking.
He had disciples,
named
“Yán Yuān,”
“Zǐgòng,”
“Jì Lù,”
and
“Rǎn Yǒu,”
among others.
Sometimes, he would ride a donkey into the market
and beg from people.
Sometimes, he would invite all the beggars to come home and stay the night,
providing them with food and wine.
People of his time could not fathom him.
The commandery respectfully invited him to serve,
recommending him as Xiàolián, Xiánliáng Fāngzhèng, and Yǒudào.
The ducal palaces also invited him,
but he never accepted any appointment.
He was also summoned along with Jiāng Hōng of the city
and Wéi Zhù of Jīngzhào,
but Xǔ did not respond.
Later, he was specially summoned
and accepted,
being appointed Zhào Xiàng.
When he took office,
people at the time thought he would surely shed his plain lifestyle for frugality,
but Xǔ instead rode in a brightly decorated carriage
and drove fine horses.
The world suspected his initial behavior was a pretense.
Upon arriving at his post,
he barely looked at official documents;
weeds grew in his residence.
He was summoned and appointed Shìzhōng.
Whenever there was a major court affair,
he would speak boldly and with a righteous expression,
and all officials feared him.
When Zhāng Jiǎo rebelled,
Xǔ submitted a memorial offering advice,
which somewhat criticized those around the emperor,
and did not wish for the state to raise an army.
Instead, he suggested sending a general to the bank of the Yellow River to face north and read the Xiàojīng,
and the rebels would naturally be annihilated.
Zhōngchángshì Zhāng Ràng slandered Xǔ,
saying he did not want the state to appoint generals and deploy troops,
suspecting he was of the same mind as Zhāng Jiǎo
and intended to act as an inside supporter.
He was arrested and sent to the Huángmén Běisì prison,
where he was killed.
Liàng Fǔ 字 Hànrú,
was a native of Xīndū, Guǎnghàn.
He served in the commandery as Wǔguān Yuàn.
At that time, there was a great drought in summer.
The Grand Administrator personally went out to pray to the mountains and rivers,
but after several days, no rain descended.
Fǔ then exposed himself in the courtyard,
and with emotion, he swore:
"As a limb and vital organ [of the administration],
I am unable to offer counsel and loyalty,
recommend the worthy and dismiss the wicked,
harmonize Yin and Yang,
and comply with the will of Heaven.
This has led to the separation of Heaven and Earth,
the scorching and withering of all things,
and the people’s silent suffering,
with no one to whom to appeal.
The blame for all of this rests entirely with me.
Now, the Grand Administrator of the commandery has changed his attire and taken responsibility,
praying for blessings for the people,
with sincerity and earnestness,
yet there has been no response.
I now dare to pray myself:
if it does not rain by midday,
I beg to use my body to atone for this impropriety."
Thereupon, he piled up firewood and gathered straw to encircle himself,
and lit a fire nearby,
intending to immolate himself.
the sky became dark with clouds,
and in an instant, a pouring rain fell,
drenching the entire commandery.
The world praised his utmost sincerity for this.
Liú Yì 字 Zǐxiàng,
was a native of Yǐngyīn, Yǐngchuān.
His family was wealthy,
and he often gave generously without claiming credit for his beneficence.
Once, while traveling in the Rǔnán region,
he met Zhāng Jìlǐ of Chén Prefecture, who was traveling far to attend his teacher’s funeral.
He encountered freezing ice and his cart broke down,
leaving him stranded on the road.
Yì saw him and said:
"You are diligent in observing rites and upholding righteousness;
your journey should be completed quickly."
He immediately got off his own carriage and gave it to Zhāng Jìlǐ,
without revealing his name,
and rode away on his horse.
Jìlǐ suspected he was Zǐxiàng,
and later deliberately went to Yǐngyīn
to return the borrowed carriage.
Yì closed his gate and declined the visit,
refusing to meet him.
He often upheld his principles and feigned illness,
never bending to offers of official appointments.
When Zhǒng Fú of Hénán arrived at the commandery,
he invited Yì to be Gōngcáo.
Yì, considering Fú to be the son of a prominent figure,
then rose to the occasion.
Fú, seeing that he chose his time to serve,
respected and trusted him greatly.
Huáng Gāng of Yángdí, relying on the power of Fú Rén Chéng,
sought to claim mountains and lakes for his own cultivation.
Fú summoned Yì and asked:
"The Chéng clan is powerful and prominent,
and they are close to the Emperor.
If I do not listen, I fear their resentment;
if I grant their request, I will deprive the people of their benefits.
What should be done?"
Yì replied:
"Famous mountains and great lakes are not to be enfeoffed,
for they belong to the people.
If you listen to him, enlightened sir,
you will be tainted with the name of being obsequious to flatterers.
If you incur misfortune for this,
your worthy sons Shēn and Fǔ
will not feel alone."
Fú followed Yì's words
and did not grant the request.
He then nominated Yì as Xiàolián,
but Yì did not accept.
Later, when the Yellow Turban Rebellion broke out,
and the commanderies and prefectures suffered from famine,
Yì helped and supplied hundreds of those in need,
providing them with food.
For the poor in his clan and village,
if they died, he provided for their burials;
if they were widows or single, he helped arrange their marriages.
When Emperor Xiàn moved the capital to Xī Jīng,
Yì was appointed as Shàngjì Yuàn.
At that time, bandits and thieves arose,
and roads were cut off,
so few envoys and couriers reached their destinations.
Yì traveled by night and rested by day,
eventually reaching Cháng'ān.
An imperial edict praised his loyalty and diligence,
and he was specially appointed Yìláng,
then promoted to Chénliú Tàishǒu.
Yì distributed the precious items and treasures he possessed,
keeping only his carriage and horse,
and rode east to return home.
Several hundred *lǐ* outside the pass,
he saw an official who had died by the roadside.
Yì exchanged his horse for a coffin,
and took off his clothes to shroud the body.
He then encountered an old acquaintance suffering from hunger and distress on the road,
and could not bear to abandon him.
He consequently slaughtered his own ox,
to relieve their hardship.
Everyone tried to stop him,
but Yì said:
"To see someone dying and not rescue them
is not the act of a noble-minded person."
They then all starved to death together.
Wáng Liè 字 Yànfāng,
was a native of Tàiyuán.
In his youth, he studied under Chén Shí,
and was renowned for his righteous conduct.
There was a cattle thief in his hometown;
the owner caught him,
and the thief begged for forgiveness, saying:
"I am willing to accept punishment,
but I beg that Wáng Yànfāng not know of this."
Liè heard of this and sent someone to apologize to him,
and gave him a piece of cloth.
Someone asked him the reason,
and Liè said:
"The thief feared that I would hear of his misdeed,
which means he has a sense of shame for wrongdoing.
Since he harbors shame for wrongdoing,
he will surely be able to reform himself,
so I used this to encourage him."
Later, an old man lost a sword on the road;
a passerby saw it and guarded it.
By evening,
the old man returned
and found his sword.
He was surprised and asked the man's name,
then reported the matter to Liè.
Liè had him investigated,
and it turned out to be the former cattle thief.
Whenever there were disputes over right and wrong,
people would go to Liè to seek judgment.
Some would turn back on the road,
or return upon seeing his cottage.
Such was his power to move people through virtue.
He was nominated as Xiàolián,
and invited by all three principal offices,
but he accepted none.
During the chaos of the Yellow Turbans and Dǒng Zhuó,
he sought refuge in Liáodōng,
where the local people respected and honored him.
The Grand Administrator Gōngsūn Dù treated him with the courtesy due to a younger brother,
and sought his advice on governance.
He wanted to make him Chángshǐ,
but Liè deliberately defiled himself by pretending to be a merchant
to avoid the appointment.
Cáo Cāo heard of Liè's high reputation
and sent for him, but he did not come.
In the 24th year of Jiàn'ān [219 CE],
he died in Liáodōng,
at the age of seventy-eight.
Eulogy: Steady in conduct and never deviating,
unwavering in the face of righteousness.
Such was his unyielding purity,
decisive in action and cultivating virtue.
Biographies of Esoteric Arts, Volume 72, Part 1
Zhòngní praised the *Yì* for having four aspects of the way of the *jūnzǐ*:
it is said,
"Diviners value its predictions."
Prediction,
is how the former kings settled fortunes and misfortunes,
resolved doubts,
offered silent aid to the gods,
and thus knew future events.
As for the study of *yīn-yáng* and astronomical calculations,
they are frequently seen in ancient records.
However, sacred scriptures and strange documents,
jade slips and golden ropes,
locked away in the abode of bright spirits,
sealed on jade altars,
are not to be spied upon.
As for the writings of the Hé and Luò rivers,
the diagrams of the turtle and dragon,
Jīzǐ’s methods,
Shī Kuàng’s books,
the sections on *wěihòu*,
and the talismans of *qiánjué*,
all serve to explore the profound mysteries,
verify human affairs,
and are sometimes accessible.
Furthermore, its branches include the arts of *fēngjiǎo*, *dùnjiǎ*, *qīzhèng*, *yuánqì*, *liùrì qīfēn*, *féngzhān*, *rìzhě*, *tǐngzhuān*, *xūyú*, and *gūxū*,
[一０] as well as observing clouds and examining vital energies,
predicting auspicious and ominous events,
which at times also prove effective in practice.
[一一] Yet this Way is obscure and distant,
recondite and difficult to fathom;
thus, the sages did not speak of strange spirits,
and rarely discussed nature and destiny.
[一二] Some initiated the lesser points but suppressed the main ones,
[一三] or used indirect language to illustrate their meaning,
[一四] as the saying goes:
"The people can be made to follow it,
but cannot be made to understand it."
[一五]
From the time of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn, who was quite fond of *fāngshù*,
scholars throughout the land who cherished the arts and ways,
all came forward, filled with enthusiasm,
flocking to him.
Later, Wáng Mǎng deceitfully used omens and mandates,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ particularly trusted prophetic sayings;
those scholars who sought to align with the times,
all galloped forth, delving deeply,
vying to speak of them.
Thus, Wáng Liáng and Sūn Xián were famed for their accordance with *túlù*,
and ascended to high positions;
Zhèng Xīng and Jiǎ Kuí gained renown by echoing these beliefs;
Huán Tán and Yǐn Mǐn perished for their dissent.
From then on, the practice of "inner learning" became common,
valuing strange writings,
esteeming unusual numbers,
and was not lacking at the time.
Therefore, enlightened scholars and great students,
indignant at its fraudulence and irregularity,
passionately submitted memorials,
arguing that it should be hidden and rejected.
Zǐcháng also said:
"Observing the books of *yīn-yáng* makes people constrained and full of taboos."
This is presumably why.
Indeed, when things are biased,
they cannot be without flaws;
though called the Great Way,
its obstacles may be the same.
If the fault of *Shī* is foolishness,
and the fault of *Shū* is falsehood,
then the fault of *shùshù*
reaches the point of deceiving the common people?
If one is gentle and sincere without being foolish,
this one is profound in *Shī*;
if one is clear-sighted and far-reaching without being false,
this one is profound in *Shū*;
if one thoroughly understands numbers and discerns changes without deceiving the common people,
this one is profound in *shùshù*.
Therefore it is said:
"If it is not the right person,
the Way will not travel in vain."
It is likely that many lose their grasp of its essence,
making rather partial choices and rejections,
and even being excessively extravagant or misleading is also a fault.
In the middle ages, Zhāng Héng was a master of *yīn-yáng*,
Láng Yǐ was most meticulous in predicting omens,
and others were also prominent masters.
Among their followers, there were also refined talents and great virtues,
who did not necessarily embody the ultimate art and skill.
Now, we generally focus on their particular strengths in predicting changes,
which can greatly supplement current affairs,
and so they are included in this table.
Rèn Wéngōng
was a native of Lángzhōng, Bājùn.
His father, Wénsūn,
was clear and knowledgeable about celestial observations and the secret essentials of *fēngjiǎo*.
Wéngōng, in his youth, cultivated his father's arts,
and was appointed by the prefecture as an aide.
During the reign of Emperor Āi,
there was a report that the Grand Administrator of Yuèkuí intended to rebel.
The Inspector was greatly alarmed
and sent Wéngōng and five other aides to inspect the commandery,
secretly observing the true situation.
They stayed together in a post-house.
At that time, a sudden violent storm arrived.
Wéngōng urgently rushed to tell the other aides to leave quickly,
saying there would be a rebellious incident to harm people.
He then quickly drove away.
The other aides had not yet departed
when the commandery indeed sent soldiers to kill them,
but Wéngōng alone escaped.
Later, he became an Aide for Judicial Affairs.
At that time, there was a great drought.
He reported to the Inspector, saying:
"On the first day of the fifth month,
there will be a great flood.
Its change has already arrived
and cannot be prevented or rescued.
It is advisable to order the officials and people to prepare for it in advance."
The Inspector did not listen.
Wéngōng alone stored large boats.
Some common people, hearing of it,
made some preparations.
When that day arrived, the drought was severe.
Wéngōng urgently ordered quick loading
and sent someone to inform the Inspector.
The Inspector laughed at him.
As noon approached,
clouds gathered in the north.
In a moment, there was a heavy rain.
By the *bū* hour (late afternoon),
the Jiān River surged more than ten *zhàng* high,
destroying houses
and harming several thousand people.
Wéngōng consequently became famous for his divinatory arts.
He was appointed as a Clerk for the Minister of Works.
When Emperor Píng ascended the throne,
he feigned illness and returned home.
After Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
Wéngōng calculated the numbers,
knowing that great chaos was coming.
He then ordered his family members to carry burdens of a hundred *jīn*
and run around the house
dozens of times a day.
People at the time did not know his reason.
Later, military bandits rose simultaneously.
Few of those who fled were able to escape on their own.
Only Wéngōng, both old and young, carried provisions and walked swiftly,
all managing to escape unharmed.
They then fled to Zǐgōng Shān,
and for more than ten years, they were not affected by warfare.
During Gōngsūn Shù’s time,
the Wǔdān stone in Shǔ broke.
Wéngōng said:
"Alas!
A wise man from Xīzhōu will die,
and I am the one it concerns."
From then on, he often gathered his children and grandchildren,
serving wine and food.
Three months later, he indeed died.
Thus, the region of Yì Bù had a saying about him:
"Rèn Wéngōng,
wisdom unparalleled."
Guō Xiàn, courtesy name Zǐhéng,
was a native of Sòng, Rǔnán.
In his youth, he studied under Wáng Zhòngzǐ of Dōnghǎi.
At that time, Wáng Mǎng was Grand Minister of War
and summoned Zhòngzǐ.
Zhòngzǐ wanted to go.
Xiàn remonstrated, saying:
"According to ritual, there is coming to learn,
but no principle of going to teach.
Now, you humble the Way and fear the powerful,
which I privately disapprove of."
Zhòngzǐ said:
"Grandee Wáng is extremely influential,
I dare not defy him."
Xiàn said:
"We are currently in the midst of lecturing;
let's finish our task first."
Zhòngzǐ followed his advice,
and went only when it was late in the day.
Mǎng asked:
"Why have you come so late?"
Zhòngzǐ honestly replied with Xiàn’s words.
Mǎng secretly found this remarkable.
Later, when Mǎng usurped the throne,
he appointed Xiàn as a Langzhong
and bestowed clothes upon him.
Xiàn received the clothes, burned them,
and fled to the coast of Dōnghǎi.
Mǎng was deeply enraged and resentful, sought him out, but did not know his whereabouts.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he sought virtuous men throughout the empire.
He then summoned Guō Xiàn and appointed him as a Bóshì.
After two more promotions,
in the seventh year of Jiànwǔ,
he replaced Zhāng Kān as Guānglùxūn.
He accompanied the emperor to the southern suburbs for a sacrifice.
While Xiàn was in office,
he suddenly turned to the northeast
and spit out three mouthfuls of wine.
The officer of the law impeached him for irreverence.
An imperial edict asked for the reason.
Xiàn replied,
"The state of Qí has caught fire;
I am therefore suppressing it with this."
Later, Qí indeed reported a fire disaster,
on the same day as the suburban sacrifice.
In the eighth year,
the imperial carriage was going west to campaign against Wěi Xiāo.
Xiàn remonstrated, saying,
"The empire has only just been settled;
the imperial carriage should not be moved yet."
Xiàn then stood in front of the carriage, drew his sword, and cut the carriage traces.
The emperor did not heed him
and proceeded to Lǒng.
Afterwards, a rebellion broke out in Yǐngchuān,
so the imperial carriage turned back and returned.
The emperor sighed, saying,
"I regret not having listened to Zǐháng's words."
At that time, the Xiōngnú repeatedly violated the frontier.
The emperor was troubled by this
and summoned all his officials for a court deliberation.
Xiàn believed that the empire was exhausted
and it was not advisable to mobilize the masses.
His remonstrances were not accepted.
He then prostrated himself, claiming to be dizzy and faint,
and said nothing further.
The emperor ordered two palace attendants to help him down from the hall,
but Xiàn did not bow either.
The emperor said,
"I often heard 'Guān Dōng's upright Guō Zǐháng,'
and it is indeed not an empty reputation."
Xiàn then resigned due to illness
and died at home.
Xǔ Yáng, courtesy name Wěijūn,
was a native of Píngyú, Rǔnán.
In his youth, he was fond of occult arts and calculations.
When Wáng Mǎng assisted in government,
he was summoned to be a Láng,
and gradually promoted to Jǐuquán Dūwèi.
When Mǎng usurped the throne,
Yáng changed his name and became a shaman-physician,
fleeing and hiding in other regions.
When Mǎng was defeated,
he then returned to his hometown.
In Rǔnán, there was an old Hóngxì Pí.
During the reign of Emperor Chéng,
Chancellor Zhái Fāngjìn memorialized to have it destroyed.
In the Jiànwǔ era,
the Grand Administrator Dèng Chén wanted to restore its function.
Hearing that Yáng understood water veins,
he summoned him to discuss it.
Yáng said,
"Formerly, Emperor Chéng used Fāngjìn's words,
and soon after, he dreamed he ascended to heaven,
where the Heavenly Emperor angrily said, 'Why did you destroy my Zhuólóng Yuān?'
Thereafter, the people lost its benefit,
and many suffered from hunger and distress.
At that time, there was a folk song that went: 'The one who destroyed our embankment is Zhái Zǐwēi;
he gave us large beans,
and cooked our large taro.
When it turns over,
the embankment will be restored.'
Formerly, Dà Yǔ channeled the Jiāng and dredged the Hé to benefit the world.
Now, your excellency is reviving a neglected enterprise,
enriching the state and bringing peace to the people.
The words of the children's rhyme
will find their verification in this.
I sincerely wish to dedicate my life to this effort."
Chén was greatly pleased,
and thereupon appointed Yáng as Dūshuǐ Yuàn,
entrusting him with the matter.
Yáng, based on the contours and terrain,
built dikes over four hundred *lǐ*,
which were completed after several years.
The common people benefited from it,
and for successive years there were great harvests.
Initially,
the powerful and prominent families, taking advantage of the embankment project,
competed to unfairly assess the local land.
Yáng did not listen to any of them.
Consequently, they jointly slandered Yáng, claiming he accepted bribes.
Chén then arrested Yáng and put him in prison,
but his shackles always unbound themselves.
The prison officials were afraid
and promptly reported it to Chén.
Chén exclaimed in surprise,
"It is indeed a wrongful accusation!
The Grand Administrator heard that loyalty and trustworthiness can move spirits.
Is this its manifestation now!"
He immediately released Yáng that night
and sent him home.
At that time, the sky was very dark and gloomy,
but there seemed to be a fiery light illuminating his path.
People at the time found this extraordinary.
Later, he died of illness.
Chén established a temple for Yáng in the [palace] courtyard,
where his likeness was painted.
The common people, remembering his achievements,
all offered sacrifices to him.
Gāo Huò, courtesy name Jìnggōng,
was a native of Xīnxī, Rǔnán.
He had a broad, square face and a prominent forehead.
In his youth, he traveled to the capital to study
and had an old acquaintance with Guāngwǔ.
He studied under Sītú Ōuyáng Shè.
When Shè was imprisoned and about to be sentenced,
Huò put on an iron helmet
and carried a chopping axe,
going to the imperial court to plead for Shè.
Although the emperor did not pardon him,
he granted Huò an audience.
He said to him,
"Jìnggōng,
I wish to employ you as an official;
you should change your usual nature."
Huò replied,
"My nature was received from my parents;
it cannot be changed for Your Majesty."
He then left and resigned.
The Sān Gōng competed to invite him, but he did not respond.
Later, Grand Administrator Bào Yù invited Huò.
When Huò arrived at the gate,
Yù ordered his Zhǔbù to go meet him.
The Zhǔbù, however, only sent a cavalry officer to welcome him.
When Huò heard this,
he immediately left.
Yù sent someone to pursue and invite Huò,
who looked back and said,
"My lord, you are simply being deceived by your Zhǔbù;
it's not worth talking to you."
He then did not stay.
At that time, there was a great drought in the commandery.
Huò had always been skilled in astronomy,
understood Dùnjiǎ,
and could command ghosts and spirits.
Yù personally went to ask how to bring rain.
Huò said,
"Immediately dismiss the Dūyóu of the three departments.
Your excellency should then go out to the north,
and when you reach the thirtieth *lǐ* pavilion,
rain can be brought."
Yù followed this advice,
and indeed there was heavy rain.
Whenever he traveled through a county,
he would always bow at their village gate.
Huò then fled far away to Jiāngnán
and died in Shíchéng.
The people of Shíchéng remembered him
and collectively established a shrine for him.
Wáng Qiáo
was a man from Hédōng.
During the reign of Emperor Xiǎnzōng,
he served as the magistrate of Yè.
Wáng Qiáo possessed divine arts.
On the first and fifteenth day of each month,
he would always travel from his county to the imperial court for an audience.
The Emperor was surprised by his frequent arrivals
without seeing any carriages or retinue.
He secretly ordered the Grand Astrologer to observe him.
The Grand Astrologer reported that just before Wáng Qiáo arrived,
a pair of wild ducks would fly in from the southeast.
Thereupon, waiting for the ducks to arrive,
they cast a net and caught them,
but only found one shoe.
The Emperor then commanded the Directorate for Imperial Manufactories to examine it,
and it turned out to be the shoe bestowed upon an official of the Department of the Imperial Secretariat over the past four years.
Whenever it was time for court,
the drums at Yè's gates would beat by themselves,
and the sound would be heard throughout the capital.
Later, a jade coffin descended before his hall.
Officials and commoners pushed and shoved it,
but it would not budge.
Wáng Qiáo said,
"Is the Heavenly Emperor summoning me alone?"
He then bathed, dressed, and lay down inside it,
and the lid immediately covered him.
The next morning, he was buried to the east of the city,
and the earth itself formed a mound.
That night,
all the oxen in the county were sweating and gasping for breath,
but no one knew why.
The common people then erected a temple for him,
calling it the Shrine of Lord Yè (Yè Jūn Cí).
Governors and administrators would always pay their respects first whenever they took up their posts.
Officials and commoners who prayed
always received a response.
If anyone violated
its sanctity, it would immediately cause misfortune.
The Emperor then had his drum brought
and placed it under the Capital Pavilion (Dū Tíng),
but it made no sound thereafter.
Some say this was indeed the ancient immortal, Prince Qiáo (Wángzǐ Qiáo).
Xiè Yíwú, courtesy name Yáoqīng,
was a man from Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
When young, he served as a county official,
studying wind divination and prognostication.
The Grand Administrator, Dìwǔ Lún, promoted him to Supervising Secretary (Dūyóu).
At that time, the magistrate of Wūchéng had a hidden offense,
and Dìwǔ Lún sent Xiè Yíwú to arrest him and investigate his crime.
When Xiè Yíwú arrived at the county,
he found no evidence,
but merely looked at the official residence, knelt, and wept, then returned.
The entire county was astonished,
not knowing what he had done.
Upon his return,
he reported to Dìwǔ Lún, saying,
"I secretly used prognostication
and knew that the magistrate was destined to die.
It would be within thirty days,
and no more than sixty days at most.
His wandering soul was merely borrowing a breath,
and he was not to be subjected to punishment,
so I did not arrest him."
Dìwǔ Lún listened to his words,
and after more than a month,
an express rider indeed brought the magistrate's seal and ribbon,
reporting his sudden death.
Dìwǔ Lún therefore held him in even greater respect and trust.
He was nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt,
and served as the magistrate of Shòuzhāng,
gradually rising to become Inspector of Jīngzhōu,
then Grand Administrator of Jùlù.
Wherever he served, he cherished and nurtured the people,
achieving good results.
When Dìwǔ Lún became Minister of Works (Sītú),
he ordered Bān Gù to write an essay recommending Xiè Yíwú, saying:
"I have heard that when Yáo appointed Jì and Qì,
governance flourished and brought great peace;
when Shùn employed Gāoyáo,
governance achieved harmony and prosperity.
Even though the Yin and Zhōu dynasties had rulers like Gāozōng, Chāng, and Fā,
they still relied on the strategies of Fù Yuè and Lǚ Wàng,
thus they were able to magnificently complete their undertakings
and truly align with the Great Middle.
I humbly observe the Grand Administrator of Jùlù, Xiè Yíwú from Kuàijī,
who hails from the eastern region,
where the soil is muddy,
yet his heroic demeanor is distinctively unique,
extraordinary and outstanding.
His talents encompass the four branches,
his conduct embodies the nine virtues.
His benevolence is sufficient to save the age,
his knowledge encompasses all things.
Furthermore, in his youth, he embraced classical refinement,
mastering the Six Classics,
investigating and examining celestial measures,
comprehensively comparing diagrams and records,
exploring the profundities of the sages,
observing changes and verifying omens,
knowing Heaven and understanding Earth,
in accord with divine harmony.
He relies on his virtue and integrity
to manage royal affairs.
Formerly, as a subordinate official,
he served with me,
displaying loyal and resolute conduct,
embodying the integrity of Shǐ Yú,
supervising my strict principles,
encouraging my timidity,
whereby I was able to avoid transgression,
truly relying on his merits.
When he was selected to serve as a magistrate,
his benevolence spread throughout the hundred-li region,
bringing forth increasingly extraordinary blessings,
his transformative influence like that of a spirit.
He then governed Jīngzhōu,
his authority extending throughout the states.
Upholding the law and governing,
he possessed the style of Zhōu and Shào;
living frugally and adhering to simplicity,
he inherited the integrity of Gōng Yí.
In seeking out merits and evaluating abilities,
he is a model for external administration;
in listening to reputation and examining reality,
he is the foremost among the nine feudal lords.
Transferred to govern Jùlù,
his administration brought harmony to the times.
His virtuous capacity and strategic foresight
are comparable to Yī, Lǚ, Guǎn, and Yàn;
in elucidating profound doctrines,
he is on par with Shǐ Sū and Jīng Fáng.
Although diligently engaged in public service,
his body is present while his heart is hidden,
not sacrificing his name for reputation,
nor striving for favor,
but rather embracing a spirit of humility and retreat,
emulating the aspirations of Jīshān.
Compared to the sages of antiquity,
he indeed has a place;
among those chosen today,
he stands transcendently apart from the mundane.
He is truly the great tortoise shell of the state,
the ridgepole of the Great Hàn.
He ought to be promoted
to a position among the Three Dukes,
so that above, the three luminaries follow their orbits in the celestial charts,
and below, the five human relationships are all taught in auspicious times,
〔一０〕surely bringing the blessings of excellent omens and flourishing prosperity,
not merely observing laws and fulfilling duties.
I, with my dullness and ineptitude,
my abilities not matching my position,
〔一一〕have long occupied a salaried post without performing,
waking nightly with apprehension as if facing danger.
〔一二〕I wish to beg for my bones (retirement),
and that Xiè Yíwú be appointed instead,
so that above, the brilliance of the Seven Luminaries may be glorified,
and below, the hopes of all under heaven may be satisfied,
thereby allowing this humble servant to avert fault and avoid regret."
Later, for conducting his spring inspection tour in a simple cart
with only two officials,
the Inspector of Jìzhōu reported that his conduct was not commensurate with his rank,
which was detrimental to the national code.
He was demoted to magistrate of Xiàpī.
He had previously predicted his death day,
and indeed died as scheduled.
He instructed his sons, saying,
"At the end of the Hàn dynasty, there will be chaos,
and certainly the disaster of graves being dug up and remains exposed."
He had himself buried in a hanging coffin without raising a mound.
At that time, Guō Fèng of Bóhǎi, a court erudite, also liked *túchèn* (prophetic texts),
was skilled at explaining anomalies,
and divining good and ill fortune.
He knew his death date in advance,
and instructed his disciples to buy a coffin and burial supplies.
On that day, he died.
Yáng Yóu, courtesy name Āihóu,
was a man from Chéngdū, Shǔjùn.
In his youth, he studied the *Yìjīng*,
as well as the Seven Regulators, primordial *qì*, wind, and cloud prognostication.
He served as a literary clerk in the commandery.
At that time, a large bird gathered at night on the Kùlóu constellation.
The Grand Administrator, Lián Fàn, asked Yáng Yóu about it.
Yáng Yóu replied,
"This omen indicates there will be a small skirmish within the commandery,
but it will cause no harm."
More than twenty days later,
the Man barbarians of Guǎngróu County rebelled,
killing and injuring officials.
The commandery dispatched troops from its arsenal to attack them.
Later, wind blew a *xuēbǔ* (fruit),
and the Grand Administrator asked Yáng Yóu about it.
Yáng Yóu replied,
"Soon there will be someone offering tree fruit,
yellow and red in color."
Shortly thereafter,
the Chief Clerk presented several bundles of tangerines.
Yóu once drank with someone.
He instructed his charioteer, saying:
"If the wine has been served three times,
prepare the carriage immediately."
Soon after, he hastened away.
Later, a fight occurred at the host's house, resulting in a death.
People asked Yóu how he knew.
Yóu replied:
"Earlier, there was a fight between doves on a tree in the temple grounds.
This is a sign of soldiers or bandits."
His predictions were often accurate.
He authored more than ten chapters of writings,
titled Qí Píng.
He died at home.
Lǐ Nán, courtesy name Xiàoshān,
was a native of Jùróng in Dānyáng.
In his youth, he was diligent in study
and was skilled in interpreting wind patterns (fēngjiǎo).
During the Yǒngyuán reign of Emperor Hé,
Grand Administrator Mǎ Léng was summoned for a banditry case,
and was to report to the Grand Judge (Tíngwèi).
The officials and common people were uneasy,
but Nán alone called on him to offer congratulations.
Léng harbored resentment,
and said to him:
"This Grand Administrator is without virtue,
and is now about to be punished.
Why do you, on the contrary, congratulate me?"
Nán said:
"This morning there was a favorable wind.
Tomorrow at noon, there should be good news,
which is why I came to offer congratulations."
The next day,
Léng waited and watched as the day grew late,
thinking there was no sign;
but towards evening,
an express messenger arrived carrying an imperial edict that pardoned and suspended Léng's case.
Nán asked about the reason for his delay.
The messenger said:
"Just now, when crossing the Pǔlǐ ferry at Wǎnlíng,
my horse sprained its foot,
which is why I could not be quick."
Léng then admired him.
Later, he was recommended as "Having the Way" (yǒudào)
and was invited to the ducal household (gōngfǔ),
but being ill, he did not go,
and died at home.
Nán's daughter also understood the family's techniques.
She was married to a man from Yóuquán County.
One morning, as she went to the kitchen,
a sudden violent wind arose.
The woman immediately went up to the hall and asked her mother-in-law to return home,
to bid farewell to her parents.
Her mother-in-law would not permit it,
so she knelt and wept, saying:
"My family's inherited art teaches that
when a strong wind suddenly rises,
first blowing the chimney and the well,
this misfortune is for the woman cooking,
an omen that your servant will die."
She then stated the day of her death.
So she was allowed to return home,
and she died of illness as predicted.
Lǐ Hé, courtesy name Mèngjié,
was a native of Nánzhèng in Hànzhōng.
His father, Jié,
was renowned for his Confucian scholarship
and rose to the post of Erudite (Bóshì).
Hé followed his father's profession,
studied at the Imperial Academy (Tàixué),
and mastered the Five Classics.
He was skilled in the divination of the Yellow River and Luò River (Héluò) and celestial phenomena (fēngxīng).
Outwardly simple and unadorned,
people did not recognize his abilities.
The county summoned him to be appointed as a gate guard (mùmén hòulì).
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne,
he dispatched envoys,
all in plain clothes and traveling alone,
each to the various provinces and commanderies,
to observe and collect folk songs.
Two envoys were to go to the Yì Province,
and they stayed at Hé's guard station.
It was a summer evening, and they were sitting outdoors.
Hé, looking up at the sky,
asked:
"When you two gentlemen left the capital,
did you know that the imperial court had dispatched two envoys?"
The two men were silent,
and looked at each other in astonishment, saying:
"We did not hear of it."
They asked how he knew.
Hé pointed to the stars and said:
"There are two envoy stars moving towards the Yì Province sector;
that is how I know."
Three years later,
one of the envoys was appointed Grand Administrator of Hànzhōng.
Hé was still a subordinate official.
The Grand Administrator admired his hidden virtue
and appointed him as Household Registrar (Hùcáo Shǐ).
At that time, Grand General Dòu Xiàn took a wife,
and all commanderies and kingdoms under heaven sent gifts and congratulations.
The commandery also dispatched an envoy.
Hé advised, saying:
"Grand General Dòu, related by marriage to the imperial family,
does not cultivate propriety and virtue,
but wields power arbitrarily and is arrogant and unrestrained.
The calamity of ruin and destruction can be awaited on tiptoe.
I wish that Your Excellency would be wholeheartedly devoted to the imperial house
and not associate with him."
The Grand Administrator insisted on sending the envoy.
Hé could not stop him
and requested to go himself.
Permission was granted.
Hé then stayed in various places
to observe the changes.
He traveled to Fúfēng,
where Dòu Xiàn had committed suicide in his fief,
and all his associates were executed.
All who had associated with Dòu Xiàn
were dismissed from office,
except the Grand Administrator of Hànzhōng, who was not involved.
Within a year, Hé was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt (xiàolián),
was promoted five times to Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng),
and was again appointed Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng).
In the fourth year of Yuánchū,
he replaced Yuán Chǎng as Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
He frequently submitted memorials on gains and losses
and displayed the integrity of a loyal minister.
He held office for four years,
but was dismissed for a petitioning and soliciting incident.
When Emperor Ān died,
and the Marquis of Běixiāng was enthroned,
he was again appointed Minister of Education (Sītú).
When the Marquis of Běixiāng fell ill,
Hé secretly conspired with the Grand Steward (Shǎofǔ) Táo Fàn of Hénán and the Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi) Zhào Zhí to enthrone Emperor Shùn.
However, Sūn Chéng and others had already accomplished the deed,
so Hé's achievement was not evident.
The next year,
on account of the illness of officials and common people
and repeated disasters and anomalies,
he was granted an edict of dismissal.
Zhái Pú, Grand Architect (Jiāngzuò Dàjiàng), memorialized that Hé
"secretly planned great strategies
to stabilize the nation."
Thereupon, his contribution to the secret plot was recorded,
and Hé was enfeoffed as Marquis of Shèdū.
He declined and did not accept.
He died at home at over eighty years old.
His disciple, Féng Zhòu of Shàngdǎng, was the only one to wear mourning clothes
and observe three years of mourning in his heart (xīnsāng).
People at the time found this unusual.
Zhòu, courtesy name Shìwēi,
was a descendant of Fèng Shì.
He always admired the conduct of Zhōu Bókuàng and Mǐn Zhòngshū,
living in seclusion in mountains and marshes,
not responding to summons or invitations.
Hé's son, Gù,
has already been mentioned in a previous biography.
His disciple, Lì,
courtesy name Jìzǐ.
He was pure, upright, and principled,
broadly learned and skilled in making friends,
associating with Zhèng Xuán, Chén Jì, and others.
He served as the Chief of Xīnchéng,
governing with a preference for non-action.
He also enjoyed esoteric arts (fāngshù).
At that time, there was a drought throughout the realm,
but his county alone received rain.
He rose to the official position of Commandant of Chariots (Fèngchē Dūwèi).
Duàn Yì
with the courtesy name Yuánzhāng, was from Xīndū
in Guǎnghàn. He studied the Yìjīng
and understood fē̄ngjiǎo.
At that time, if there were scholars who came to him,
even if they had not yet arrived,
he would always know their names in advance.
He once told a ferry guard,
“On a certain day, two scholars
carrying burdens will inquire about my residence.
Please be kind enough to tell them.”
Later, it turned out exactly as he said.
Another scholar came to study,
and after several years,
he felt he had grasped the essentials of the art
and bade farewell to return to his hometown.
Yì prepared a medicinal paste for him,
and also sealed a letter in a bamboo tube,
telling the scholar,
“Open this if you have an emergency.”
When the scholar reached Jiāměng,
he had a dispute with an official over crossing the river,
and the ferry official struck and broke the head of one of his attendants.
The scholar opened the tube and found the letter,
which said, “Upon reaching Jiāměng,
if you quarrel with an official and someone's head is broken,
use this paste to treat it.”
The scholar followed his words,
and the injured person immediately recovered.
The scholar was filled with admiration
and returned to complete his studies.
Yì then lived in seclusion, hiding his tracks,
and died at home.
Liáo Fú
with the courtesy name Wénqǐ, was from Píngyú
in Rǔnán. He studied the Hán Shī and the Ōuyáng Shàngshū,
and often taught hundreds of students.
His father served as the Administrator of Běidì,
and during the Yǒngchū era,
was imprisoned and died for the Qīang people's encroachment on the commandery.
Fú felt deeply that his father had lost his life due to the law,
and was wary of becoming an official.
After the mourning period ended, he sighed and said,
“Lǎozi said, ‘Which is dearer, fame or life?’
How could I pursue fame?”
Thus, he completely gave up his ambition for worldly affairs.
He focused intensely on the classics,
especially mastering astronomy, chènwěi,
fē̄ngjiǎo, and tuībù arts.
He did not respond to invitations from the provincial and commandery administrations or ducal mansions.
When consulted about calamities and anomalies,
he also offered no response.
Fú foresaw a famine
and gathered several thousand hú of grain,
which he entirely distributed to his relatives and in-laws.
He also collected and buried those who died in the plague and could not be buried by their families.
He always lived by his ancestors' tombs
and never entered the city.
The Administrator, Yè Huàn,
was formerly a student
who studied under Fú.
Later, when he was appointed to the commandery,
before his arrival,
he first sent an official to perform the rites of a disciple.
He also wanted to promote Fú's sons and nephews,
but Fú firmly refused.
At that time, people therefore called him "Mr. Běiguō."
He died at home
at the age of eighty.
His two sons,
Mèngjǔ and Wěijǔ,
were both famous.
Shé Xiàng
with the courtesy name Bóshì, was from Luò
in Guǎnghàn. His ancestor Zhāng Jiāng
was enfeoffed as Marquis Shé.
His great-grandson, Guó, became the Administrator of Yùlín,
and moved to Guǎnghàn,
thus taking Shé as his family name.
Guó begot Xiàng.
Guó had two hundred million in wealth
and eight hundred household servants.
Xiàng was benevolent from a young age,
not killing insects
or breaking budding sprouts.
He could comprehend the Jīng Shì Yì
and favored the teachings of Huáng-Lǎo.
When Guó died,
Xiàng was moved by the principle that "great accumulation leads to great loss."
So he distributed his gold, silk, and assets
to relatives and strangers alike.
Someone advised Xiàng,
“You have three sons and two daughters,
and grandchildren filling your presence.
You should increase your family's property;
why are you exhausting yourself by squandering it?”
Xiàng replied,
“Dòu Zǐwén once said, ‘I am escaping calamity,
not avoiding wealth.’
My family has accumulated wealth for a long time;
the misfortune of over-fullness
is what Daoists shun.
Now the world is declining,
and my sons are not talented.
To be rich without benevolence
is considered misfortune.
When a wall is cracked yet built high,
its collapse will surely be swift.”
When wise people heard this, they all admired him.
He knew the day of his death beforehand
and invited guests and relatives for a meal to bid farewell,
then suddenly passed away.
He was eighty-four years old at the time.
His family had no surplus assets,
and his sons were weak and inferior, just as he had predicted.
Fán Yīng
with the courtesy name Jìqí, was from Lǔyáng
in Nányáng. In his youth, he received instruction in Sānfǔ,
studied the Jīng Shì Yì,
and was also proficient in the Wǔjīng.
He was also skilled in fē̄ngjiǎo, xīngsuàn, Hélúo Qīwěi,
and deducing calamities and anomalies.
He lived in seclusion on the southern side of Húshān,
and students came from all directions to receive his teachings.
He did not respond to successive invitations from the provincial and commandery authorities;
nor did he accept nominations from high officials for xíanliáng fāngzhèng or yǒudào.
Once, a violent wind arose from the west.
Yīng told his students,
“The fire in Chéngdū is very fierce.”
Then he took a mouthful of water and gargled facing west,
and instructed them to record the date and time.
Later, a guest came from the region of Shǔ
and said,
“On that day, there was a great fire,
and suddenly a black cloud rose from the east.
In a moment, there was heavy rain,
and the fire was then extinguished.”
Thereupon, the whole world praised his art.
At the beginning of Emperor Ān's reign,
he was summoned to be a bóshì.
In the first year of Jiànguāng,
an imperial edict was again issued via gōngchē, bestowing a written instruction,
summoning Yīng and his fellow commandery residents Kǒng Qiáo,
Lǐ Bǐng,
Běihǎi's Láng Zōng,
Chénliú's Yáng Lún,
and Dōngpíng's Wáng Fǔ, six people in total.
Only Láng Zōng and Yáng Lún reached Luòyáng;
Yīng and the other four did not arrive.
In the second year of Yǒngjiàn,
Emperor Shùn issued a written instruction with full ceremonial courtesies,
sending black and crimson silk as a summons,
but he again firmly declined, claiming severe illness.
An edict was then issued severely reprimanding the commandery and county,
ordering them to bring him by carriage.
Yīng had no choice but
to come to the capital.
He claimed illness and refused to rise.
He was then forcibly carried into the palace,
but still would not yield to the rites.
The emperor was angered
and said to Yīng,
“I can give you life,
and I can take your life;
I can ennoble you,
and I can humble you;
I can enrich you,
and I can impoverish you.
Why do you disrespect my command?”
Yīng replied,
“Your subject receives his destiny from Heaven.
To live out one's full life
is Heaven's will;
to die before one's destined time
is also Heaven's will.
How can Your Majesty give me life?
How can Your Majesty take my life?
Your subject regards a tyrannical ruler as an enemy;
I would not even stand in his court,
so how can I be ennobled?
Even when I am among commoners,
within a humble dwelling,
I am calmly content,
and would not exchange it for the dignity of ten thousand chariots.
How then can I be humbled?
How can Your Majesty ennoble me?
How can Your Majesty humble me?
Your subject would not accept an emolument not in accordance with ritual,
even if it were ten thousand zhōng of grain;
if I can fulfill my aspirations,
even a simple meal will not displease me.
How can Your Majesty enrich me?
How can Your Majesty impoverish me?”
The emperor could not make him yield,
but respected his reputation,
and ordered him to be sent to the Grand Physician to recuperate,
with monthly provisions of lamb and wine.
In the third month of the fourth year,
the Son of Heaven then set up an altar and mat for Fán Yīng,
ordering the Gōngchē Lìng to guide him,
the Shàngshū to usher him,
and bestowed upon him a kneeling mat and staff.
He was treated with the禮 (lǐ) of a master and tutor,
and consulted on successes and failures.
Fán Yīng did not dare to decline,
and was appointed Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng.
A few months later,
Fán Yīng claimed severe illness.
An edict appointed him Guānglù Dàfū,
and granted him leave to return home.
It ordered that a thousand hú of grain be sent from his locality,
and a bull and
three hú of wine be delivered every eighth month.
Should he unfortunately pass away,
he was to be sacrificed to with a zhōngláo (an intermediate sacrifice).
Fán Yīng declined the position and did not accept it.
An imperial edict advised him to not refuse.
When Fán Yīng first received the imperial summons,
everyone thought he would surely not compromise his principles.
But when he later responded,
he offered no extraordinary plans or profound strategies,
which talkers deemed a disappointment.
Initially,
Zhāng Kǎi of Hénán was summoned together with Fán Yīng.
Afterwards, he said to Fán Yīng:
"There are two paths in the world:
to enter service or to remain in reclusion.
I previously thought that by entering service,
you could assist this ruler
and save these people.
However, you, with your humble status,
first angered the lord of ten thousand chariots;
yet when you enjoyed rank and emolument,
no methods of rectifying or saving were heard from you.
You have no basis for either advancing or retreating."
Fán Yīng was skilled in divination techniques.
Whenever there were calamities or anomalies in the court,
an edict would immediately be issued to inquire about the effects of changes and reversals.
Much of what he said proved true.
Originally,
Fán Yīng wrote commentaries on the Yì,
which the world called Fán Shì Xué,
and taught using diagrams and prophecies.
Chén Shí of Yǐngchuān studied under Fán Yīng in his youth.
Once, when he was ill,
his wife sent a maid to inquire after him with a bow.
Fán Yīng got off his bed and returned the bow.
Chén Shí was surprised and asked him about it.
Fán Yīng said:
"A wife is
qí (equal);
together they serve the ancestral sacrifices.
There is no礼 (lǐ) in which one does not respond."
Such was his reverence and caution.
He died at home
at over seventy years of age.
His grandson, Líng,
during Emperor Líng's reign, flattered eunuchs and became Sītú.
Xì Xún of Chénjùn studied and transmitted Fán Yīng's craft,
and rose to the official position of Shìzhōng.
The commentary states: The character of those whom the Hàn dynasty called "famous scholars"
can be known.
Although their taking up or forsaking office
at times lacked purity,
in refining their emotions and cultivating their appearance,
relying on the Dao and arts,
to achieve their reputation and standing,
they were not capable of understanding the ways of the world
or promoting current affairs.
When Fán Yīng and Yáng Hòu were summoned,
the court treated them as if they were divine,
yet in the end, nothing extraordinary happened.
Fán Yīng's reputation was the highest,
but his censure was the most severe.
Lǐ Gù, Zhū Mù, and others believed that hermits merely stole empty fame
without any benefit to practical use,
hence the reason for this.
Nevertheless, later generations admired them to achieve fame,
and rulers of the age honored them to gain adherents.
If we consider their uselessness as precisely their usefulness,
then their usefulness might sometimes turn into uselessness.
Why do I say this?
Indeed, brilliant literary works
may sometimes diverge from their purpose;
and the fundamentals of rites and music
may be neglected at the extremities.
Yet, when they mold gentry
and refine hearts and natures,
causing people to follow them unknowingly,
is this not because the Dao is vast and its application evident,
and the divergence merely a few traces?
