But some people ignore the untrodden path,
disregard the merit of uselessness,
and even scoff at profound arts,
belittling the nation's glory,
believing that cunning and deception can save what is ruined,
and that literary regulations are sufficient to achieve peace and stability.
They believe wisdom is exhausted in suspicion and scrutiny,
and the Dao is fulfilled in laws and decrees.
Even if this were to save ten thousand generations,
it would be no different from the Yí and Dí (barbarians).
Mèng Kē (Mencius) said:
"I have heard of changing the Yí into Xìa,
but not of changing Xìa into Yí."
How much more so when there are still things unaccomplished!
Biographies of Fangshù, Part Two, Chapter 72.
Tán Bù, courtesy name Zǐchǎn,
was a native of Nánchāng, Yùzhāng.
In his youth, he traveled to the Imperial Academy,
studying the Jīng Shì Yì, Hán Shī, and Yán Shì Chūnqiū,
and was particularly fond of disaster omens and stellar divination.
Later, he returned to his hometown,
teaching regularly over a hundred people.
In the seventh year of Yuánchū,
a ganoderma mushroom grew in the commandery.
The Grand Administrator, Liú Zhī, wanted to report it,
and asked Tán Bù about it.
Tán Bù replied:
"At present, the imperial relatives are powerful and prosperous,
while the yang principle is weak.
How can this be an auspicious omen?"
Liú Zhī then stopped.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
a woman in Nánchāng gave birth to four children.
Liú Zhī again asked Tán Bù about the implications of this anomaly.
Tán Bù believed that there would be military conflict in the capital,
and the disaster would arise within the palace walls.
By the fourth year of Yánguāng,
the Zhonghuángmén Sūn Chéng led soldiers in the palace,
executing the Empress's brother, Chēqí Jiāngjūn Yán Xiǎn, and others,
and enthroning the King of Jìyīn as the Son of Heaven,
which indeed matched his prediction.
In the fifth year of Yǒngjiàn,
he was recommended as Xiàolián,
and appointed Lángzhōng.
At this time, a white rainbow pierced the sun.
Tán Bù then submitted three proposals for opportune measures,
explaining their ominous signs.
After his memorial was presented,
he resigned from office.
He authored twenty-eight chapters,
titled Tán Zǐ.
He died at home.
Gōngshā Mù, courtesy name Wén Yì,
was a native of Jiāodōng, Běihǎi.
His family was poor and humble.
From childhood, he disliked playing games.
As an adult, he studied the Hán Shī and Gōngyáng Chūnqiū,
and was particularly keen on the arts of calculation and astronomy from Hélùo.
He lived in Jiànchéng Mountain,
building a hut amidst the forests and ravines,
sleeping alone without companionship.
Once, during a violent storm with thunder,
a voice from outside called Mù three times.
Mù did not respond.
A moment later,
the caller entered through the window.
Its voice and form were very strange,
but Mù recited scriptures as usual.
Ultimately, there were no other strange or demonic occurrences,
which people at the time found remarkable.
Later, he retired to Dōnglái Mountain,
and scholars came from afar to study with him.
There was a rich man, Wáng Zhòng,
who had accumulated thousands of gold.
He said to Mù:
"In today's world,
one makes connections through wealth.
I will give you a million as capital,
what do you say?"
Mù replied:
"Your intention is generous.
However, wealth and nobility are determined by Heaven;
obtaining them is a matter of fate.
To seek position with wealth,
I cannot bear to do."
Later, he was nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate.
Because of his excellent record, he was made a Zhǔshì.
He was promoted to Xiàng of Zēng.
At that time, Liú Chǎng, Marquis of Zēng,
a descendant of Gōng Wáng of Dōnghǎi,
did many unlawful things.
He deposed his legitimate son and established a concubine's son,
acting arrogantly and unrestrainedly.
When Mù arrived at his post,
he requested an audience and said:
"On the day I was first appointed,
the capital city all said to me, 'Zēng has an evil marquis,'
and pitied the minor Xiàng.
How did the enlightened Marquis come to acquire such a terrible reputation?
Fortunately inheriting the lineage of your ancestors,
and holding the important position of feudal lord,
you do not act with fear and trembling,
but violate laws and regulations.
Therefore, the imperial court sent me to be your assistant.
I hope you will reform your past and cultivate your future,
to seek much fortune for yourself."
Thereupon, he reported and confiscated the official and private land that Chǎng had encroached upon,
deposed his concubine's son,
and reinstated the legitimate heir.
When his attendants and retainers committed crimes,
he had them all arrested and interrogated.
He then earnestly admonished Chǎng.
Chǎng wept and apologized,
and mostly followed his recommendations.
He was promoted to Prefect of Hóngnóng.
Within the county borders, there were cutworms eating the crops,
and the common people were terrified.
Mù then set up an altar and prayed, saying:
"If the common people have faults,
the sin is due to Mù.
I beg to offer myself as a sacrifice."
Thereupon, there was a heavy rain.
When it cleared, the cutworms disappeared by themselves,
and the common people called him divine and enlightened.
In the first year of Yǒngshòu,
there were continuous rains and great floods,
and all areas east of Sānfǔ were submerged.
Mù was clear and knowledgeable about astronomical observations.
He therefore forewarned the common people to move to higher ground,
so the people of Hóngnóng alone were spared from harm.
He was promoted to Commandant of the Dependent State of Liáodōng,
and was good at winning the hearts of officials and people.
He died in office at the age of sixty-six.
All six of his sons were well-known.
Xǔ Màn was
a person from Píngyú, Rǔnán.
His grandfather, Jùn,
courtesy name Jìshān,
was skilled in the art of divination,
and had many prominent verifications.
People of his time compared him to Jīng Fáng of previous generations.
He himself said that when he was young, he suffered from a severe illness,
which did not heal for three years.
He then went to Tài Shān to request a decree (from heaven),
and on his way, he met the Taoist priest Zhāng Jùjūn,
who imparted to him the art of divination.
His work, Yìlín,
is still circulated in the world today.
Màn learned Jùn's teachings from a young age.
During the reign of Huán Dì,
Féng Gǔn, Administrator of Lǒngxī, had just been appointed to the commandery.
When he opened his sash box,
two red snakes ran out, dividing to the north and south.
Gǔn ordered Màn to divine it.
When the hexagram was formed,
Màn said:
"After three years,
you will become a frontier general.
Your office will have an 'east' in its name,
and you will travel three thousand *lǐ* to the northeast.
After another five years,
you will again become a grand general,
and campaign in the south."
In the first year of Yánxī,
Gǔn was appointed Administrator of Liáodōng,
to suppress the Xiānbēi.
By the fifth year,
he was again appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn,
to attack the Wǔlíng Mán rebels,
all of which happened as predicted.
Many other instances were similar to this.
Zhào Yàn was
a person from Lángyá.
From a young age, he possessed scholarly arts.
In the third year of Yánxī,
Láo Bǐng, a bandit from Lángyá, and Shúsūn Wújì, a bandit from Tàishān, killed the Commandant,
attacked and took over dependent counties of Lángyá,
and harmed officials and common people.
The imperial court appointed Zōng Zī of Nányáng as Tǎokòu Zhōnglángjiāng,
wielding the ceremonial axe and leading troops,
to oversee the joint suppression of Wújì by the provinces and commanderies.
Yàn presented the method of "isolated and void,"
stating that since the bandit encampment was in Jǔ,
and Jǔ had five *yáng* locations,
it was advisable to dispatch troops from the five *yáng* commanderies,
to strike the "void" from "isolation" and attack them.
Zī fully reported the situation,
and an imperial edict dispatched the five *yáng* troops.
Yàn used the Dùnjiǎ technique,
instructing them on the opportune time to advance troops.
In one battle, they defeated the bandits,
burning their encampments and fortifications.
The two provinces of Xú and Yǎn were pacified at once.
Fán Zhìzhāng was
a person from Nánzhèng, Hànzhōng.
He was broadly learned and widely versed,
but lived in seclusion and did not serve in office.
He once traveled to Lǒngxī.
At that time, Duàn Gǔn, the Pòqiāng Jiāngjūn, was campaigning against the Western Qiāng,
and requested to meet Zhìzhāng.
That evening,
Gǔn's army was surrounded by the Qiāng in several layers.
He was consequently kept in the army camp,
unable to leave for three days.
At night, he said to Gǔn:
"There are no more Qiāng in the southeast corner.
You should seize the opportunity to lead out from the void,
stop a hundred *lǐ* away,
then return with the army to attack them.
You can achieve a complete victory."
Gǔn followed his advice,
and indeed defeated the bandits.
Thereupon, he reported the situation in a memorial.
He also said that this person possessed the wisdom of Zǐ Shèn, Jiāo, and Dǒng,
and should assist the sagely court,
consulting him on unusual matters.
An imperial edict was then issued to specially summon him,
but he passed away due to illness.
Shàn Yáng, courtesy name Wǔxuān,
was a person from Húlù, Shānyáng.
He established himself through solitary and austere means,
and was skilled in understanding celestial phenomena and computational arts.
He was nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate,
and gradually rose to Grand Astrologer,
and Shìzhōng.
He was appointed Administrator of Hànzhōng,
but was dismissed for official matters.
Later, he was appointed Shàngshū,
and died in office.
Initially,
at the end of Xīpíng,
a yellow dragon appeared in Qiáo.
Qiáo Xuán, Grand Master of Guanglu, asked Yáng:
"What omen is this?"
Yáng said:
"A king will rise in that state.
Within fifty years,
the dragon will appear again.
This is its fulfillment."
Yīn Dēng of Wèijùn secretly recorded this.
In the spring of the twenty-fifth year of Jiàn'ān,
a yellow dragon reappeared in Qiáo.
That winter,
Wèi received the abdication.
Hán Yuè, courtesy name Shúrú,
was a person from Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
He was broadly versed in the Five Classics,
and particularly skilled in the study of apocryphal texts.
He was nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate.
He was good friends with Cài Yōng, a Counselor.
He frequently presented memorials on disasters and anomalies,
as well as submitting *fù*, *sòng*, and *liánzhū*.
He gradually rose to Shìzhōng.
In the tenth month of the first year of Guānghé,
Yuè reported to Líng Dì,
saying that on the last day of the month, there would certainly be an eclipse,
and asked for all officials to prepare solemnly.
The Emperor followed his advice,
and it happened exactly as he said.
In the second month of the second year of Zhōngpíng,
he again submitted a sealed memorial,
predicting a disaster in the palace on a certain date.
On that day, a great fire occurred in the Southern Palace.
Yuè was promoted to Administrator of Jiāngxià,
but was dismissed for official matters.
At the age of seventy,
he died at home.
Dǒng Fú, courtesy name Mào'ān,
was a person from Miánzhú, Guǎnghàn.
As a youth, he traveled to the Imperial Academy,
and was as famous as Rèn Ān, his fellow townsman.
Both served Yáng Hòu of the same commandery,
studying apocryphal texts.
Upon returning home, he lectured and taught,
and disciples came from afar.
He was invited by the Three Dukes' residences ten times,
and summoned by imperial carriage three times.
He was twice nominated as "Wise and Upright," "Erudite," and "Possessor of the Way,"
but he always claimed illness and did not take office.
During Emperor Líng’s reign,
Great General Hé Jìn recommended Dǒng Fú,
who was summoned and appointed Palace Attendant.
He was greatly esteemed.
Dǒng Fú privately told Grand Commandant Liú Yān,
“The capital is about to fall into chaos.
The celestial omens for Yìzhōu indicate the presence of an Emperor.”
Liú Yān believed him,
and consequently requested to be appointed Governor of Yìzhōu,
while Dǒng Fú also became Commandant of the Dependent State of Shǔjùn.
Together, they entered Shǔ.
One year after they left,
the Emperor passed away,
and the world fell into great disorder.
Dǒng Fú then resigned his office and returned home.
He died at the age of eighty-two.
Later, Liú Bèi declared himself Emperor in Shǔ,
all just as Dǒng Fú had predicted.
Zhūgě Liàng, Chancellor of Shǔ, asked Qín Mì of Guǎnghàn about
the strengths of Dǒng Fú and Rèn Ān.
Qín Mì said,
“Dǒng Fú praises the slightest good
and condemns the smallest evil.
Rèn Ān remembers people’s good deeds
and forgets their faults.”
So it was said.
Guō Yù
was a native of Luò in Guǎnghàn.
Originally,
there was an old man of unknown origin
who often fished in the Fúshǔi,
and was thus called Fú Wēng.
He begged for food among people.
Whenever he saw someone with an illness,
he would sometimes apply acupuncture and moxibustion,
and it would always be effective immediately.
He then wrote the *Zhēnjīng* (Acupuncture Classic) and *Zhěnmàifǎ* (Pulse Diagnosis Method), which were passed down to the world.
His disciple Chéng Gāo sought him out for many years,
until Fú Wēng finally taught him.
Chéng Gāo also lived in reclusion and did not serve in office.
Guō Yù studied under Chéng Gāo when he was young,
learning the diagnostic arts of the six subtle conditions
and the methods of Yin and Yang, hidden and manifest.
During Emperor Hé’s reign,
he served as Assistant Imperial Physician,
and had many effective treatments.
The Emperor was amazed by him.
He then tested him by having a favored minister with beautiful wrists and a woman sit together behind a curtain.
He had Guō Yù diagnose one hand from each,
and asked about their ailments.
Guō Yù said,
“The left is Yang, the right is Yin.
The pulses show male and female,
appearing as if from different people.
I am suspicious of the reason.”
The Emperor sighed and praised him.
Guō Yù was benevolent and not boastful.
Even for the poor, lowly, and servants,
he would devote all his heart and effort.
However, when treating nobles,
sometimes they would not be cured.
The Emperor then ordered a noble to dress plainly and change their location.
With one needle, the illness was cured.
He summoned Guō Yù and questioned him about the situation.
Guō Yù replied,
“The meaning of 'medicine' is 'intent'.
The skin and muscle texture are extremely subtle;
one must skillfully adapt to the Qi.
In the application of needles and stones,
a hairsbreadth difference can lead to divergence.
The spirit resides at the juncture of the heart and hands,
which can be understood but not expressed in words.
Now, a noble person occupies a high and revered position above me,
and I, as a minister, attend to them with fear and trepidation.
In such treatments,
there are four difficulties: acting on one’s own will and not trusting the minister is
the first difficulty;
not being careful with one’s body is
the second difficulty;
one’s bones and joints not being strong,
making it impossible to apply medicine, is
the third difficulty;
loving ease and disliking labor is
the fourth difficulty.
Acupuncture has its precise measurements,
and sometimes there are breaks or leaks.
Coupled with a fearful heart,
and the intention to be cautious,
my intent cannot even be fully expressed,
how can it reach the illness?
This is why they are not cured.”
The Emperor approved of his answer.
He died of old age in office.
Huà Tuó, courtesy name Yuánhuà,
was from Qiáo in Pèiguó,
and also known as Fū.
He traveled and studied in Xútǔ,
mastering several classics.
He understood the art of preserving health,
and though nearly a hundred years old, still had a youthful appearance.
People at the time considered him an immortal.
Chén Guī, Chancellor of Pèi, recommended him as *Xiàolián*,
and Grand Commandant Huáng Wǎn summoned him,
but he declined both.
He was skilled in prescriptions and medicines.
His concoctions never exceeded a few ingredients,
and he knew the exact measurements by heart,
without needing scales.
Acupuncture and moxibustion never required more than a few points.
If the illness was deep-seated internally,
beyond the reach of needles and medicine,
he would first have the patient drink a dose of *Máféisǎn* mixed with wine.
Once intoxicated and unconscious,
he would then incise and open the abdomen or back,
and cut out accumulated masses.
If it was in the intestines and stomach,
he would sever, rinse, and cleanse them,
removing the diseased filth.
Afterward, he would stitch it up
and apply a miraculous salve.
In four or five days, the wound would heal,
and within a month, they would be completely recovered.
Once, Huà Tuó was traveling
and saw a person suffering from a blocked throat.
He said to him,
“Just now, at the corner of the road, there was a person selling pancakes.
Their water fern pickle was very sour.
You can drink three *shēng* of it,
and the illness will surely depart.”
The man did as Huà Tuó said,
and immediately vomited up a snake.
He then hung it on his carriage and waited for Huà Tuó.
At that time, Huà Tuó’s young children were playing at the gate.
They saw the man approaching
and said to each other,
“There’s something by the guest’s carriage;
it must be someone who has met our father.”
When the guest arrived,
they looked towards the north wall
and saw dozens of snakes hanging,
and then realized his extraordinary ability.
Another time, a commandery governor was severely ill for a long time.
Huà Tuó believed that intense anger would cure him.
So he accepted a lot of money from him but did not perform the treatment.
Soon after, he left
and also left a letter scolding him.
The governor indeed became furious
and ordered men to pursue and kill Huà Tuó.
They failed to catch him.
Due to his anger,
he vomited several *shēng* of black blood and recovered.
There was another patient
who came to Huà Tuó seeking treatment.
Huà Tuó said,
“Your illness is deeply rooted;
you should have your abdomen opened.
However, your lifespan will not exceed ten years,
and this illness cannot kill you.”
The patient could not bear the suffering
and insisted on having it removed.
So Huà Tuó performed the treatment,
and he was cured immediately.
Ten years later, he indeed died.
Chén Dēng, Administrator of Guǎnglíng, suddenly suffered from vexation and fullness in his chest,
a red face,
and loss of appetite.
Huà Tuó felt his pulse
and said,
“Your Excellency’s stomach has worms,
which are about to form an internal abscess.
This is caused by raw and bloody foods.”
He immediately prepared two *shēng* of decoction.
After two doses,
in a short while,
the patient vomited about three *shēng* of worms,
with red heads and squirming bodies.
Half of them were still like raw fish slices,
and his suffering immediately ceased.
Huà Tuó said,
“This illness will recur after three *jī* (a three-year cycle).
If you encounter a good doctor, you can be saved.”
When the time came, Chén Dēng’s illness recurred.
Huà Tuó was not present at the time,
and so he died.
Cáo Cāo heard of him and summoned Huà Tuó,
who always stayed by his side.
Cáo Cāo had long suffered from headaches and dizziness.
Huà Tuó applied acupuncture,
and he was cured immediately.
There was a General Lǐ
whose wife fell ill.
He called Huà Tuó to examine her pulse.
Huà Tuó said:
"You injured yourself, but the fetus is not gone."
The general said that he had indeed injured himself in leisure,
and the fetus had already passed.
Huà Tuó said:
"According to the pulse,
the fetus has not passed."
The general thought otherwise.
After his wife felt slightly better for over a hundred days, she moved again,
so he called Huà Tuó again.
Huà Tuó said:
"The pulse condition is as before.
These are twins;
the first one passed,
with much blood,
so the second child could not come out.
Since that fetus is already dead,
the blood vessels will not return,
and it must be dried and attached to the mother's spine."
He then applied needles
and also ordered a decoction to be taken.
The woman then wanted to give birth but couldn't.
Huà Tuó said:
"The dead fetus is dry and shriveled;
it cannot come out on its own."
He sent someone to retrieve it,
and indeed, a dead fetus was obtained,
its human form recognizable,
but its color was already black.
Huà Tuó's extraordinary skills
were all of this kind.
He was by nature ill-tempered and hard to please,
and he was ashamed to be seen as a physician.
Also, he was away from home and longed to return,
so he went to Cáo Cāo to ask to go home and fetch medical prescriptions.
He then feigned his wife's illness
and did not return after the appointed time.
Cáo Cāo repeatedly wrote to summon him,
and also ordered the commanderies and counties to send him forth,
but Huà Tuó, relying on his skill, was weary of the matter
and still refused to come.
Cáo Cāo was furious
and sent someone to investigate him,
learning that his wife's illness was a pretense.
So he had Huà Tuó arrested, imprisoned, and interrogated,
and through torture, he confessed.
Xún Yù pleaded, saying:
"Huà Tuó's medical arts are truly excellent,
and human lives depend on him;
he should be fully pardoned."
Cáo Cāo did not comply,
and ultimately killed him.
Before his death, Huà Tuó
gave a scroll of writings to the prison guard,
saying:
"This can save people's lives."
The guard, fearing the law, dared not accept it.
Huà Tuó did not force it on him
and asked for fire to burn it.
Previously,
an army officer named Lǐ Chéng suffered from a severe cough
and could not sleep day or night.
Huà Tuó considered it intestinal worms
and gave him two *qián* of powder to take.
He immediately vomited two *shēng* of pus and blood,
and from this, he gradually recovered.
Huà Tuó then warned him, saying:
"Eighteen years from now,
the illness will recur.
If you do not get this medicine,
it cannot be cured."
He also gave him some more powder.
Five or six years later,
a villager similar to Lǐ Chéng fell ill first
and urgently requested the medicine.
Lǐ Chéng, out of compassion, gave it to him.
He then specifically went to Qiáo to ask Huà Tuó for more,
but it happened that Huà Tuó was just being arrested,
and he couldn't bear to speak of it.
Eighteen years later,
Lǐ Chéng's illness recurred,
and without the medicine, he died.
Wú Pǔ from Guǎnglíng and Fán Ā from Péngchéng both studied under Huà Tuó.
Wú Pǔ followed Huà Tuó's treatments
and saved many lives.
Huà Tuó told Wú Pǔ:
"The human body needs to exercise,
but it should not be overexerted.
Movement allows the *gǔ qì* to dissipate,
blood circulation to flow,
and illness not to arise.
It is like a door hinge,
which never decays.
This is why the immortals of antiquity performed *dǎo yǐn* exercises,
like the 'bear's hang' and 'owl's gaze,'
stretching and flexing their bodies,
moving all their joints,
to seek longevity.
I have a technique
called the 'Five Animal Frolics': the first is the tiger,
the second is the deer,
the third is the bear,
the fourth is the ape,
the fifth is the bird.
It also eliminates illness,
and benefits the limbs,
serving as a *dǎo yǐn* exercise.
If one feels unwell,
one gets up and performs one animal frolic,
feels pleased and sweats,
then applies powder,
and the body feels light and nimble, and one desires food."
Wú Pǔ practiced this,
and at over ninety years old,
his ears and eyes were sharp,
and his teeth were strong and firm.
Fán Ā was skilled in acupuncture.
All physicians generally said that one should not rashly needle the back and chest cavity,
and that needling should not exceed four *fēn*,
but Fán Ā would needle the back by one or two *cùn*,
and the *Jù Quē* in the chest cavity by five or six *cùn*,
and all illnesses were cured.
Fán Ā asked Huà Tuó for prescriptions that could be taken to benefit people.
Huà Tuó gave him the "Lacquered Leaf Green Powder":
one *dòu* of lacquered leaf powder,
fourteen *liǎng* of green,
using this as the ratio.
He said that long-term use
removes the three worms,
benefits the five *zàng* organs,
lightens the body,
and prevents hair from turning white.
Fán Ā followed his advice
and lived for over a hundred years.
Lacquered leaves are found everywhere.
Green grows between Fēng, Pèi, Péngchéng, and Cháo Gē.
In the Hàn era, there were many men of unusual arts.
Although it is said they are not orthodox,
there are also things that cannot be denied.
Therefore, I have selected the best among them and listed them at the end of the biography:
Léng Shòu Guāng, Táng Yú, and Lǔ Nǚ Shēng, these three
were all contemporaries of Huà Tuó.
Léng Shòu Guāng was about one hundred fifty or sixty years old.
He practiced the method of Yǒng Chéng Gōng for women,
often bending his neck and breathing like a crane.
His hair and beard were all white,
but his complexion and skin were like when he was thirty or forty.
He died in Jiānglíng.
Táng Yú lived in the villages of Chì Méi and Zhāng Bù.
If one were to encounter them,
he died in Bùqí County, in his hometown.
Lǔ Nǚ Shēng often spoke of events during the reign of Xiǎn Zōng
with great clarity,
leading discussants to suspect he was a contemporary.
After Dǒng Zhuó's rebellion,
his whereabouts were unknown.
Xú Dēng,
a person from Mǐnzhōng,
was originally a woman who
transformed into a man.
He was skilled in sorcery.
Also, Zhào Bǐng,
courtesy name Gōng Ā,
a person from Dōngyáng,
was able to perform Yuè-style magic.
At that time, due to military unrest,
a great epidemic broke out.
The two met above the Wū Shāng stream,
then made a pact,
and together used their arts to treat illnesses.
Each said to the other:
"Now that we share the same aspirations,
let us each test our abilities."
Xú Dēng then enchanted the stream.
The water stopped flowing.
Zhào Bǐng, in turn, enchanted a withered tree,
and the tree immediately sprouted.
The two looked at each other and smiled,
and together they pursued their path.
Xú Dēng was older,
so Zhào Bǐng served him as a master.
They valued simplicity and frugality,
and when honoring spirits, they used only flowing water from the east as libation
and dried mulberry bark as dried meat.
They simply performed incantations and enchantments,
and all those they treated were cured.
Later, after Hòu Dēng passed away,
Bǐng Dōng entered Zhāng'ān.
The common people did not yet know of him.
Bǐng then intentionally ascended a thatched hut,
and set a *dǐng* on a *wú* wood to cook.
The owner, seeing this, was startled and frightened.
Bǐng smiled and did not respond.
Soon after, the cooking was done,
and the hut was undamaged and unchanged.
Another time, he sought passage across water,
but the boatmen would not cooperate.
Bǐng then spread an umbrella, sat within it,
let out a long whistle, summoned the wind,
and crossed the turbulent currents.
Thereupon, the common people revered him as a spirit,
and his followers were like people returning home.
The magistrate of Zhāng'ān, disliking his deceiving the masses,
arrested and killed him.
People built a memorial shrine for him in Yǒngkāng,
and to this day, mosquitoes and gnats cannot enter it.
Fèi Chángfáng
was a man from Rǔnán.
He once served as a market official (*shìyuàn*).
In the market, there was an old man selling medicine,
who hung a gourd at the head of his stall.
And when the market closed,
he would always leap into the gourd.
The market people did not see this,
only Chángfáng, from an upper floor, observed it.
He found it extraordinary,
and so went to repeatedly bow and present wine and dried meat.
The old man, knowing that Chángfáng understood his spiritual nature,
said to him:
"You may come again tomorrow."
Chángfáng returned to the old man the next morning,
and the old man then went with him into the gourd.
They saw only a magnificent jade hall,
with fine wine and sweet delicacies overflowing within it.
After they finished drinking together, they came out.
The old man enjoined him not to tell anyone.
Later, the old man waited on an upper floor and said to Chángfáng:
"I am an immortal.
I was blamed for a transgression,
and now that the matter is concluded, I must depart.
Can you follow me?
Downstairs there is a little wine,
which I give to you as a farewell."
Chángfáng sent someone to fetch it,
but they could not lift it.
He then ordered ten people to carry it,
but they still could not lift it.
The old man heard this,
laughed, and came downstairs,
and with one finger lifted it and went upstairs.
The vessel looked to be about one *shēng* in size,
yet the two of them drank from it all day without it being exhausted.
Chángfáng then wished to seek the Way,
but worried about his family.
The old man then cut a green bamboo,
measured it to be the same height as Chángfáng,
and told him to hang it behind his house.
When his family saw it,
it was Chángfáng's form,
and they thought he had hanged himself,
so everyone, great and small, cried out in alarm,
and then buried him.
Chángfáng stood beside them,
but no one saw him.
Thereupon, he followed the old man into the deep mountains,
treading through thorns among a multitude of tigers.
The old man left him to stay alone,
and Chángfáng was not afraid.
He also lay in an empty room,
with a decaying rope suspending a ten-thousand-*jīn* stone above his heart.
Many snakes competed to gnaw at the rope, nearly breaking it,
but Chángfáng did not move either.
When the old man returned,
he stroked him and said:
"You are teachable."
He then made him eat excrement.
In the excrement were three worms,
and the stench was especially foul.
Chángfáng felt repulsed by it.
The old man said:
"You were on the verge of attaining the Way,
but regretfully, you could not succeed at this.
What a pity!"
Chángfáng bid farewell to return home.
The old man gave him a bamboo staff,
saying:
"Ride this wherever you wish to go,
and it will take you there automatically.
Once you arrive,
you can throw the staff into Gě Pí."
He also made him a talisman,
saying:
"With this, you can command the ghosts and spirits on earth."
Chángfáng rode the staff,
and in a moment arrived home.
He thought he had only been away from home for a few days,
but it had already been more than ten years.
He then threw the staff into the pond,
and looking back, it was a dragon.
His family, believing he had long been dead,
did not believe him.
Chángfáng said:
"What was buried that day
was only a bamboo staff."
So they opened the tomb and split the coffin,
and the staff was still there.
He then became capable of healing all illnesses,
flogging a hundred ghosts,
and driving and employing the *Shè Gōng* (Earth God).
Sometimes, while sitting with others,
he would become angry by himself.
When people asked him the reason,
he said:
"I am punishing ghosts and spirits who have violated the law."
In Rǔnán, year after year, there was always a demon
that would falsely assume the official robes of a grand administrator,
and go to the prefecture gate to beat the drum.
The commandery suffered from this.
At this time, the demon happened to come,
and met Chángfáng paying respects to the prefectural lord.
Terrified, it could not retreat,
and so came forward, removed its clothes and official hat,
kowtowed, and begged for its life.
Chángfáng scolded it, saying:
"Right here in the central courtyard, resume your original form!"
Immediately, it turned into an old turtle,
as large as a cartwheel,
with a neck a *zhàng* long.
Chángfáng then ordered it to confess its crime to the grand administrator,
and gave it a written instruction,
to transmit to the Lord of Gě Pí.
The demon kowtowed and wept,
held the instruction and planted it by the pond,
wrapped its neck around it, and died.
Later, the Lord of Dōnghǎi came to visit the Lord of Gě Pí,
and then seduced his lady.
Thereupon, Chángfáng impeached and imprisoned him for three years,
and there was a great drought in Dōnghǎi.
Chángfáng went to the seashore,
and saw the people praying for rain.
So he said to them:
"The Lord of Dōnghǎi has committed a crime;
I previously imprisoned him in Gě Pí.
Now I am about to release him to make rain."
Thereupon, rain immediately poured down.
Chángfáng once walked with someone
and saw a scholar wearing a yellow turban and a fur coat,
riding a horse without a saddle.
The scholar dismounted and kowtowed.
Chángfáng said:
"Return its horse,
and your death penalty will be pardoned."
The person asked the reason,
and Chángfáng said:
"This is a wild cat (*lí*),
it stole the *Shè Gōng*'s horse."
Another time, while entertaining guests,
he sent someone to Wǎn market for fermented fish (*zhǎ*).
In a moment, he returned,
and then they ate.
Sometimes, within a single day,
people saw him in several places a thousand *lǐ* away.
Later, he lost his talisman,
and was killed by a multitude of ghosts.
Jì Zǐxùn,
his origin is unknown.
During the Jiàn'ān reign,
he was a guest in Wǎnjù, Jìyīn.
He possessed miraculous and extraordinary powers.
He once held a neighbor's baby,
and intentionally let it slip from his hand, falling to the ground and dying.
Its parents cried out in alarm, resentment, and pain,
unbearably to hear,
but Zǐxùn only apologized for the mistake,
and offered no other explanation,
so they buried the child.
More than a month later,
Zǐxùn returned with the child in his arms.
The parents were greatly frightened,
saying:
"Life and death are different paths.
Although we miss our child,
we beg you not to let us see him again."
The child recognized its parents,
laughed joyfully,
and wanted to go to them.
The mother unconsciously reached out and took him,
and it was indeed her real child.
Though greatly delighted,
they still had doubts in their hearts,
so they secretly opened and inspected the dead child,
but saw only clothes and bedding.
Only then did they believe.
Thereupon, Zǐxùn's name spread to the capital,
and all the literati and officials looked up to him and admired him.
Later, he drove a donkey cart
and went with his disciples to Xǔxià.
Passing through Xíngyáng,
they stayed at a host's inn.
Suddenly, the donkey he was driving stiffened and died.
Maggots streamed out.
The host quickly reported this.
Zǐxùn said,
"Is that so?"
He sat calmly and ate his meal.
After finishing,
he slowly went out and tapped the donkey with his staff.
The donkey immediately roused itself,
walked as before,
and they continued on their way.
Those who followed to watch were always in the thousands.
Upon arriving in the capital,
those who awaited him, from high officials down,
numbered several hundred sitting at his gatherings,
all of whom he provided with wine and dried meat,
which never ran out throughout the day.
Later, he disappeared,
and his whereabouts became unknown.
On the day he first departed,
only white clouds were seen rising,
from dawn till dusk,
in dozens of places like this.
At that time, there was an old man of a hundred years
who said he had seen Zǐxùn selling medicine in the market of Kuàijī when he was a child,
and his appearance was no different from then.
Later, people saw him again in Dōngbàchéng, Cháng'ān.
He was with an old man, both stroking a bronze figure,
and they said to each other,
"We just saw this being cast,
and it has been nearly five hundred years."
He glanced at the people who saw him and departed,
still driving the same donkey cart he used to ride.
Those who saw him called out,
"Jì Xiānsheng, wait a moment!"
He responded while walking alongside them.
He seemed slow,
but even a galloping horse could not catch up.
With that, he vanished.
Liú Gēn was
a native of Yǐngchuān.
He lived in seclusion in Sōngshān.
Many enthusiasts came from afar
to learn the Dao from Gēn.
The Grand Administrator, Shǐ Qí, considered Gēn a fraud
and had him arrested and brought to the commandery,
accusing him,
"What magic do you possess
to deceive and mislead the common people?
If you truly have divine power,
you can display a verifiable feat.
Otherwise,
you will die immediately."
Gēn said,
"I truly have no other special ability;
I can only make people see ghosts."
Qí said,
"Quickly summon them,
so the Grand Administrator can see with his own eyes;
then it will be clear."
Gēn then looked left and whistled.
A moment later,
dozens of Qí's deceased fathers, grandfathers, and close relatives
all appeared before him, bound with their hands behind their backs.
They bowed their heads to Gēn and said,
"This little child is rude;
he deserves myriad deaths."
They turned and reprimanded Qí, saying,
"As a son,
you cannot benefit your ancestors,
but instead bring shame and disgrace upon the spirits of the deceased!
Bow your head and apologize for us."
Qí was terrified, saddened,
and prostrated himself until his head bled,
asking to accept his punishment.
Gēn remained silent and did not respond.
Suddenly, they all disappeared,
and their whereabouts became unknown.
Zuǒ Cí, courtesy name Yuánfàng,
was a native of Lújiāng.
From a young age, he possessed spiritual powers.
Once, he was seated with Sīkōng Cáo Cāo.
Cáo Cāo casually looked at the guests and said,
"Today's grand gathering is almost complete with delicacies,
but we are only missing the perch from Sōngjiāng in Wú."
Yuánfàng, from his seat below, replied,
"That can be obtained."
He then asked for a copper basin filled with water
and fished in the basin with a bamboo rod and bait.
In a short while, he pulled out a perch.
Cáo Cāo clapped his hands and laughed loudly,
and all the guests were astonished.
Cáo Cāo said,
"One fish is not enough for the entire banquet;
can you get another?"
Yuánfàng then re-baited his hook and lowered it.
Soon, he pulled out another one.
Both were over three feet long,
fresh and appealing.
Cáo Cāo had them sliced and served right before his eyes,
enough for all the guests.
Cáo Cāo then said,
"Now that we have the fish,
I regret that we lack fresh ginger from Shǔ."
Yuánfàng said,
"That can also be obtained."
Cáo Cāo, fearing he would get it from nearby,
said,
"I previously sent someone to Shǔ to buy silk brocade;
you can instruct my messenger to buy two additional bolts."
A moment later,
the ginger returned,
and he also received a report from Cáo Cāo's messenger.
Later, Cáo Cāo's messenger returned from Shǔ,
and when questioned about the additional brocade and the exact time and date,
it matched perfectly, like a tally.
Later, Cáo Cāo went out to the near suburbs,
accompanied by about a hundred officials and scholars.
Cí brought one shēng of wine
and one jīn of dried meat
and personally poured and distributed it.
All the officials were drunk and full.
Cáo Cāo found this strange
and sent people to investigate the reason.
Upon inspecting the various stoves,
all the wine and dried meat were gone.
Cáo Cāo was displeased
and ordered Cí to be arrested at the banquet to be executed.
Cí then retreated into the wall
and suddenly disappeared.
Someone saw him in the marketplace,
and they tried to capture him again.
But all the market people transformed themselves to look like Cí,
so it was impossible to tell who he was.
Later, people encountered Cí on the peak of Yángchéng Shān.
They pursued him again,
and he ran into a flock of sheep.
Cáo Cāo knew he could not be caught
and ordered them to tell him among the sheep,
"I will not kill you anymore;
I was just testing your magic."
Suddenly, an old ram bent its two front knees,
stood upright like a person, and said,
"Is it so urgent?"
Then everyone rushed towards it,
but hundreds of sheep in the flock all transformed into old rams,
all bending their front knees and standing upright,
saying,
"Is it so urgent?"
Thus, it was impossible to seize him.
Jì Zǐxūn
was from an unknown commandery or county.
Everyone said he was several hundred years old
and walked among people.
One day, he suddenly said he would die at noon.
His host gave him a kudzu cloth robe,
which Zǐxūn put on before lying down properly.
At noon, he indeed died.
Shàng Chénggōng
was a native of Mìxiàn.
In his early days, he traveled for a long time and did not return.
Later, he came back
and told his family,
"I have already attained immortality."
Then he bid his family farewell and left.
His family saw his steps becoming higher and higher,
and after a long time, he disappeared into the clouds.
Chén Shí and Hán Sháo both witnessed this event.
Xiè Núgū and Zhāng Diāo
were also from unknown commanderies or states.
They could all make themselves invisible
and enter and exit without using doors or windows.
Núgū could change the form of objects
to deceive and delude people.
Also, in Hénán, there was Qū Shèngqīng,
who was skilled at writing talismans with cinnabar
to suppress and command ghosts and spirits.
There was also Biān Mángyì,
who also communicated with ghostly beings.
Initially,
during the reign of Huán Dì there was a Marquis of Shòuguāng
who could impeach a hundred ghosts and numerous sprites,
making them bind themselves and reveal their forms.
There was a woman in his village afflicted by a sprite.
The marquis impeached it for her,
and a large snake several *zhàng* long
was found dead outside her gate.
There was also a divine tree
which would kill anyone who stopped beneath it,
and birds that flew over it would inevitably fall.
The marquis impeached it again,
and the tree withered and shed its leaves in mid-summer,
revealing a large snake seven or eight *zhàng* long,
hanging dead among its branches.
The emperor heard of this and summoned him.
Then he tested him, asking:
"After midnight beneath my palace hall,
there are often several people in crimson robes with disheveled hair,
carrying fire and accompanying each other.
Can you impeach them?"
The marquis said:
"These are minor anomalies;
they are easily dispelled."
The emperor covertly had three men impersonate them.
The marquis impeached the three men,
and they immediately collapsed to the ground, breathless.
The emperor was greatly alarmed and said:
"They are not sprites;
I was merely testing you."
He revived them, and they woke up.
Gān Shǐ, Dōngguō Yánnián,
and Fēng Jūndá were three
*fāngshì* (practitioners of occult arts).
They could all practice the art of Róngchéng for managing women,
some by drinking urine,
some by hanging themselves upside down.
They cherished and conserved their vital essence,
avoiding extreme looking or loud speaking.
Gān Shǐ, Yuánfàng, and Yánnián were all recruited by Cāo,
who inquired about their arts and practiced them.
Jūndá was known as
"Master Qīngniú."
All these few people
were over a hundred or even two hundred years old.
Wáng Zhēn and Hǎo Mèngjié
were both from Shàngdǎng.
Wáng Zhēn was nearly a hundred years old,
but his face had a radiant glow,
appearing to be not yet fifty.
He himself said:
"I have traveled extensively, ascending the Five Sacred Mountains and famous peaks,
and I can practice all the methods of *tāixī* (embryonic breathing) and *tāishí* (embryonic feeding).
I gargle and swallow the spring beneath my tongue,
and I do not abstain from sexual activity."
Mèngjié could hold a date pit in his mouth,
and go without food for five to ten years.
He could also hold his breath indefinitely,
his body not moving,
appearing like a dead person,
for up to a hundred days or half a year.
He also had a family.
He was honest, careful, and did not speak idly,
like a virtuous gentleman.
Cáo Cāo made him lead all the other *fāngshì*.
Wáng Hépíng of Běihǎi
was fond of Daoist arts,
and believed he would become an immortal.
Sūn Yǒng of Jìnán served him from a young age,
following him to the capital.
When Hépíng fell ill and died,
Yǒng buried him in Dōngtáo.
There were over a hundred scrolls of books
and several bags of medicine,
all of which he buried with him.
Later, his disciple Xià Róng said that Hépíng had undergone *shījiě* (liberation by means of a corpse),
and Yǒng regretted not taking his precious books and immortal medicine.
An encomium states: Rare are the subtle rewards revealed,
difficult are the clear omens to verify.
If one does not delve into the profound and distant,
how can one be moved by spiritual efficacy?
Should there be any errors or shifts,
they would truly deviate from the abstruse and profound.

The Qúnfǔlù (羣輔錄) states that Mùzhī (穆之) had five sons,
all with excellent reputations.
The capital called them
「公沙五龍 (Gōngshā wǔ lóng),
天下無雙 (tiānxià wúshuāng)」.

and the common people mistakenly use the character 密 (mì) (dense, secret).
Page 2735, line 1, 郭玉者廣漢雒人也 (Guō Yù zhě Guǎnghàn Luò rén yě). I note: the collected commentaries cite Huì Dòng's (惠棟)說 (shuō),

Drawing out fish over three chi long from a copper basin filled with water is also illogical.

Biographies of Reclusive Scholars, Chapter 73.
The *Yì*
states: "The significance of the time of *Dùn* [Retreat] is truly great!"
It also says:
"Not serving kings or lords,
but holding one's own affairs in high esteem."
Therefore, when Yáo
was praised for following Heaven, he did not bend to the loftiness of Yǐngyáng;
when Wǔ
achieved the utmost beauty, he fully preserved the purity of Gūzhú.
From this time onward,
the refined and unrestrained [spirit] became ever more abundant.
The path of permanent withdrawal did not differ,
but the reasons for being moved to it were not singular.
Some concealed themselves to pursue their ambitions,
some avoided [worldly affairs] to preserve their integrity,
some quieted themselves to calm their impetuosity,
some departed from danger to secure their safety,
some sullied themselves with vulgarity to stir their ambition,
or some criticized worldly things to stimulate their purity.
However, observing their willingness to live contentedly in the fields and furrows,
or to become gaunt and haggard by rivers and seas,
how could it be that they necessarily enjoyed the fish and birds or delighted in the forests and grasses?
It was also merely due to their natural disposition.
Thus, there were guests who endured shame,
repeatedly dismissed yet not leaving their state;
〔一０〕there were those who demonstrated integrity by plunging into the sea,
whose resolve could not be swayed by a thousand chariots.
〔一一〕If they were forced to change their choices to come or go,
then they could not act on their own.
〔一二〕Although they may have been obstinate, somewhat like those seeking fame,
〔一三〕yet they shed themselves from the dust and clamor,
and naturally removed themselves from the mundane world,
how different they were from those who adorned themselves with cleverness and cunning to chase fleeting profits!
Xún Qīng
had a saying: "When one's will and resolve are cultivated, one disdains wealth and nobility;
when virtue and righteousness are valued, one holds kings and dukes lightly."
〔一四〕
When the Hàn dynasty was in decline,
and Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
the scholars were deeply moved by righteous indignation.
At that time, those who tore their caps and broke their ceremonial robes,
and left hand in hand,
were simply too numerous to count.
Yáng Xióng
said: "The swan flies high into the dark,
what can the fowler grasp?"
He meant their far removal from calamity.
Guāngwǔ
sought out recluses with earnestness, as if he could not reach them quickly enough;
the banners and simple carriages sent to invite them
were seen one after another in the mountains.
Such as Xuē Fāng and Péng Méng, who were invited but refused to come;
Yán Guāng, Zhōu Dǎng, and Wáng Bà came but could not be swayed.
All [these] individuals fulfilled their [aspirations],
and men of high resolve cherished benevolence.
This indeed is what is meant by
"raising the reclusive people, and the hearts of the world return."
Sùzōng
also treated Zhèng Jūn with禮 and invited Gāo Fèng,
to complete their integrity.
Thereafter, imperial virtue gradually declined,
and wicked individuals held sway at court.
Chaste hermits remained upright and resolute,
ashamed to be ranked with ministers;
they even indignantly resisted without regard [for consequences],
often losing their balanced conduct.
We include those who utterly rejected the dust of the world and did not return,
likening them to the authors [of these deeds],
and list them in this chapter.
The two elders of Yěwáng
— it is unknown where they were from.
Initially,
Guāngwǔ
was at odds with Gēngshǐ.
At that time, Guānzhōng was in turmoil.
He sent the former general Dèng Yǔ to the west, accompanying him on the road.
Upon his return,
he hunted in Yěwáng
and on the road encountered and caught two old men.
Guāngwǔ asked:
"Where do the captured animals go?"
They both raised their hands and pointed west,
saying:
"There are many tigers here.
When this subject catches animals,
the tigers also catch this subject.
Great King, do not go there."
Guāngwǔ said:
"If one is prepared,
what harm can tigers do?"
The elders said:
"How mistaken you are, Great King!
In ancient times, Tāng
captured Jié at Míngtiáo, and built a great city at Bó;
King Wǔ also captured Zhòu at Mùyě,
and built a great city at Jiáěrú.
Those two kings,
their preparations were not shallow.
Therefore, those who capture others,
others will also capture them.
Even if one is prepared,
how can one be careless?"
Guāngwǔ understood their meaning,
and looking at those around him, said:
"These are recluses."
He intended to employ them,
but they declined and departed,
their whereabouts unknown.
Xiàng Cháng, courtesy name Zǐpíng,
was a native of Cháogē in Hénèi.
He lived in seclusion and did not serve in office,
his nature valued moderation and harmony,
and he enjoyed understanding Lǎo and Yì.
Poor and without provisions,
good-hearted people would send him gifts of food,
which he accepted only until he had enough, returning the rest.
Wáng Mǎng's Grand Minister of Works, Wáng Yì, invited him,
and he arrived after several years.
Wáng Yì wanted to recommend him to Mǎng,
but he firmly declined, so Wáng Yì stopped.
He lived secretly in his home.
When reading the *Yì* to the *Sǔn* and *Yì* hexagrams,
he sighed deeply and said:
"I already know that wealth is not as good as poverty,
and nobility is not as good as lowliness;
but I do not yet know what death is like compared to life."
During the Jiànwǔ era,
after his children were married,
he instructed that he would no longer be concerned with family affairs,
as if he were dead.
Thereupon, he indulged his inclinations,
and with his like-minded friend, Qín Qìng of Běihǎi,
they traveled together to the Five Sacred Mountains and other famous mountains,
and his ultimate fate is unknown.
Péng Méng, courtesy name Zǐkāng,
was a native of Dūchāng in Běihǎi.
His family was poor,
so he served the county as a *tíngzhǎng*.
At that time, the commandant passed through his *tíng*.
Méng waited to greet and pay respects,
but then threw down his shield and sighed:
"How can a great man serve others as an役?"
So he left for Cháng'ān to study,
and mastered the *Chūnqiū Jīng*.
At that time, Wáng Mǎng killed his son Yǔ.
Méng said to his friends:
"The three cardinal guides are severed!
If we do not leave,
calamity will reach us."
He immediately took off his cap and hung it on the east gate of Dūchéng,
returned home,
took his family, crossed the sea,
and became a sojourner in Liáodōng.
Méng was deeply learned in Yin and Yang,
and knew that Mǎng would fail.
After a while,
he went to the market with a broken pot on his head,
crying:
"New! New!"
Then he went into hiding.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
he went to Láo Shān in Lángyá,
cultivating his aspirations and practicing the Dao;
everyone was transformed by his virtue.
The Administrator of Běihǎi had long heard of his lofty character
and sent an official with a formal invitation and gifts,
but Méng did not respond.
The Administrator held a grudge and sent officers to arrest him.
The officers knocked their heads on the ground and said:
"Zǐkāng is a great sage,
known throughout the world.
Wherever he resides,
people respect him as a father.
If we go, we will certainly not capture him,
but only bring disgrace upon ourselves."
The Administrator was angry,
arrested and imprisoned them,
and dispatched other officers.
When they arrived at Láo Shān,
people indeed rallied together with weapons and crossbows to defend him,
the officers were wounded and bled,
and fled back.
Later, an imperial edict summoned Méng,
but he feigned old age and confusion,
losing his way and not knowing east from west.
He told the envoy:
"The court summons me
because I might be beneficial to governance.
Yet I do not even know which direction I am facing,
how can I save the times?"
He then mounted his carriage and returned.
Despite repeated summons, he did not come,
and died of old age.
Initially,
Méng and his fellow provincials Xú Fáng of the same commandery, Lǐ Zǐyún of Píngyuán, and Wáng Jūngōng were good friends.
All understood Yin-Yang principles,
but their conduct was both virtuous and corrupt.
Fáng and Zǐyún each had a thousand disciples,
while Jūngōng, facing chaos, alone did not leave;
he became a cattle broker to hide himself.
People at the time commented on him, saying:
"Wáng Jūngōng, who withdraws from the world behind a wall to the east."
Zhōu Dǎng, courtesy name Bókuàng,
was a native of Guǎngwǔ in Tàiyuán.
His family owned a thousand pieces of gold.
Orphaned young,
he was raised by his clansmen,
who treated him unfairly,
and when he grew up,
they did not return his property.
Dǎng went to the local county to sue,
and the magistrate then returned his property.
Afterward, he distributed it among his clan,
completely emancipating his slaves and maidservants,
and then went to Cháng'ān to study.
Earlier,
a village official had publicly insulted Dǎng,
and Dǎng harbored a grudge for a long time.
Later, when reading the Spring and Autumn Annals,
he heard about the principle of revenge,
so he stopped his studies and returned,
sending word to the village official,
setting a date for a duel.
When their blades met,
Dǎng was wounded by the village official
and in distress.
The village official admired his righteousness,
carried him home and nursed him,
and after several days he revived,
then awoke and left.
From then on, he disciplined himself and cultivated his will,
and the province and localities praised his integrity.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he feigned illness and kept his gate shut.
Afterward, when bandits raged everywhere,
destroying commanderies and counties,
they only reached Guǎngwǔ,
passing by the city without entering.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
he was summoned as an Imperial Counselor,
but resigned due to illness,
and then took his wife and children to live in Mǐnchí.
He was summoned again,
and having no choice,
he put on a short cloth tunic
and a coarse bark-fiber headband,
waiting to be seen by the Grand Secretariat.
When Guāngwǔ granted him an audience,
Dǎng prostrated but did not pay respects,
stating his desire to maintain his resolve,
and the Emperor permitted it.
Academician Fàn Shēng submitted a memorial criticizing Dǎng, saying:
"Your servant has heard that Yáo did not need Xǔ Yóu and Cháo Fù
to establish his dominion over All-under-Heaven;
Zhōu did not wait for Bó Yí and Shú Qí
for the Kingly Way to be achieved.
I humbly observe that Zhōu Dǎng of Tàiyuán, Wáng Liáng of Dōnghǎi, Wáng Chéng of Shānyáng, and others
have received abundant favor,
and only after three invitations by envoys
would they condescend to ride in the carriage.
And upon being granted an audience in the imperial court,
Dǎng did not submit according to ritual,
but prostrated without paying respects,
arrogant and fierce,
all departing at the same time.
Dǎng and his ilk cannot expound righteousness in letters,
nor die for their lord in battle.
They fish for illustrious fame,
hoping to attain the position of the Three Ducal Ministers.
Your servant wishes to sit below the Cloud Terrace
and test their methods for governing the nation.
If they do not match your servant's words,
they should be punished for the crime of falsehood and deceit.
Yet they dare to privately steal false fame,
boast to the superior, and seek high positions—
all are greatly disrespectful."
When the memorial was submitted,
the Son of Heaven showed it to the Grandees and Ministers.
An edict said:
"Since ancient times, enlightened kings and sagely rulers have always had subjects who were unwilling to serve.
Bó Yí and Shú Qí did not eat Zhōu millet,
and Zhōu Dǎng of Tàiyuán does not accept Our emolument;
each has his own aspirations.
Let him be granted forty bolts of silk."
Dǎng then lived in seclusion in Mǐnchí,
authored two volumes of books, and then died.
The local people esteemed him and offered sacrifices to him.
Earlier,
Dǎng, along with Tán Xián Bóshēng of the same commandery and Yīn Mó Jūncháng of Yànmén,
all upheld their principles and did not serve during Wáng Mǎng's reign.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
they were summoned but none arrived.
Wáng Bà, courtesy name Rúzhòng,
was a native of Guǎngwǔ in Tàiyuán.
From a young age, he had a pure character.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he cast off his cap and belt,
and broke off ties with officialdom.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
he was summoned and arrived at the Grand Secretariat,
bowing and stating his name,
but not addressing himself as a subject.
The officials in charge asked the reason.
Bà said:
"The Son of Heaven has those he does not treat as subjects,
and feudal lords have those he does not treat as friends."
The Grand Minister of Works, Hóu Bà, yielded his position to Wáng Bà.
Yán Yáng disparaged him, saying:
"Tàiyuán has a customary faction,
and Rúzhòng largely shares their ways."
So he stopped.
He returned home due to illness.
He lived in seclusion, upholding his principles,
in a thatched cottage with a simple door.
Repeatedly summoned, he did not come,
and died of old age.
Yán Guāng, courtesy name Zǐlíng,
also named Zūn,
was a native of Yúyáo in Kuàijī.
From a young age, he had a high reputation
and studied with Guāngwǔ.
When Guāngwǔ ascended the throne,
Yán Guāng changed his name,
and hid himself, not to be seen.
The Emperor, missing his worthy friend,
ordered him to be sought out by his appearance.
Later, Qí Commandery reported:
"There is a man
fishing in the marshes, wearing a sheepskin cloak."
The Emperor suspected it was Guāng,
so he prepared an anché (a comfortable carriage) and black and crimson silks,
and sent an envoy to invite him.
After three visits, he finally arrived.
He was housed in the Northern Army barracks,
provided with a bed and bedding,
and the Grand Provisioner supplied his meals morning and evening.
The Grand Minister of Works Hóu Bà, who had been an old friend of Guāng,
sent an envoy with a letter.
The envoy then said to Guāng:
"His Excellency heard of your arrival,
and in his eagerness wished to visit immediately,
but being constrained by his official duties,
he could not.
He hopes that as evening approaches,
you might condescend to speak."
Guāng did not reply,
but threw a slip of wood to him
and dictated, saying:
"To my friend Jūnfáng: Your position has reached the pinnacle,
which is very good.
If you embrace benevolence and assist righteousness, All-under-Heaven will rejoice;
if you flatter and follow mandates, your head will be severed."
Bà received the letter
and sealed it to present to the Emperor.
The Emperor laughed and said:
"That crazy fellow is true to his old ways!"
That very day, the imperial carriage went to his lodging.
Guāng lay down and did not get up.
The Emperor went to his bed
and stroked Guāng's belly, saying:
"Alas, alas, Zǐlíng,
can you not help me govern?"
Guāng again feigned sleep and did not respond.
After a long while,
he opened his eyes and stared intently,
saying:
"In ancient times, Emperor Yáo cultivated virtue,
and Cháo Fù washed his ears.
A scholar naturally has his aspirations;
why must you press me so?"
The Emperor said:
"Zǐlíng,
can I truly not make you submit?"
Thereupon, he got into his carriage, sighed, and left.
Later, he invited Guāng in again,
and they discussed the Way and old times,
facing each other for several days.
The Emperor casually asked Guāng:
"How am I compared to old times?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty has improved somewhat compared to the past."
Then they lay down together,
and Guāng placed his foot on the Emperor's belly.
The next day,
the Grand Astrologer reported that a guest star had gravely intruded upon the Imperial Seat.
The Emperor laughed and said:
"It was merely My old friend Yán Zǐlíng sleeping with Me."
He was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance,
but he refused to comply,
and instead went to cultivate land on Fùchūn Shān.
Later generations named the place where he fished Yánlíng Lài.
In the seventeenth year of Jiànwǔ,
he was again specially summoned,
but he did not come.
At the age of eighty,
he died at home.
The emperor was saddened and cherished him,
and issued an edict to the prefectures and counties to bestow a million coins and a thousand *hú* of grain.
Jǐng Dān, whose courtesy name was Dàchūn,
was from Méi in Fúfēng.
In his youth, he studied at the Grand Academy,
mastered the Five Classics,
and was skilled in discussion.
Thus, a saying circulated in the capital about him:
"The Five Classics, though intricate, are mastered by Jǐng Dàchūn."
His nature was pure and noble,
and he never sent a formal calling card to visit others.
Towards the end of Jiànwǔ,
Prince Fǔ of Pèi and four other princes resided in the Northern Palace.
All were fond of guests
and repeatedly sent invitations to Dān,
but could not persuade him to come.
Yīn Jiù, the Marquis of Xìnyáng,
who was the younger brother of Empress Guāngliè,
and was honored and prosperous due to his status as an imperial relative,
then cunningly told the five princes
that he needed ten million coins
and promised he could bring Dān,
but secretly sent men to waylay and coerce him.
Dān had no choice,
and when he arrived,
Jiù intentionally set out a meal of wheat rice and scallion leaves for him.
Dān pushed it away,
saying:
"I came to visit you because I heard you, Marquis, could provide delicious food.
How can it be so meager?"
When a lavish meal was set out instead,
he ate.
When Jiù rose,
his attendants brought forth a sedan chair.
Dān laughed and said:
"I heard that Jié drove people as chariots;
is this it?"
Everyone in the room turned pale.
Jiù had no choice but to order the sedan chair removed.
From then on, he lived in seclusion, detached from worldly affairs,
and died of old age.
Liáng Hóng, whose courtesy name was Bólán,
was from Pínglíng in Fúfēng.
His father, Ràng,
was Commander of the City Gates during Wáng Mǎng's time,
ennobled as Earl Xiūyuǎn,
and appointed to serve the descendants of Shàohào.
He settled in Běidì and died there.
Hóng was still young,
and because he lived in a chaotic era,
he simply rolled up a mat and buried him.
Later, he studied at the Grand Academy.
Though his family was poor, he upheld high moral principles
and was widely read, understanding everything,
but he did not focus on textual exegesis.
After finishing his studies,
he herded pigs in the Shànglín Park.
He once accidentally caused a fire that spread to another's dwelling.
Hóng then sought out the owner whose property had burned,
asked about his losses,
and compensated him entirely with his pigs.
The owner still thought it was too little.
Hóng said:
"I have no other wealth;
I am willing to work for you as your servant."
The owner agreed.
He then labored diligently,
without slackening from morning till night.
The elders of the neighboring households, seeing that Hóng was no ordinary man,
collectively admonished the owner
and praised Hóng as a man of virtue.
Only then did the owner begin to respect him differently
and returned all his pigs.
Hóng refused to accept them and departed,
returning to his hometown.
Powerful families admired his noble integrity
and many wished to give him their daughters in marriage,
but Hóng refused them all and remained unmarried.
There was a daughter of the Mèng family in the same county,
who was stout, ugly, and dark-skinned,
and could lift a stone mortar.
She was selective in choosing a spouse and remained unmarried
until she was thirty.
Her parents asked her the reason.
The daughter said:
"I wish to marry a man as virtuous as Liáng Bólán."
Hóng heard of this and sought her hand in marriage.
The daughter requested to make clothes of coarse cloth and hemp sandals,
and to weave baskets and spin thread.
When she married,
she initially entered the home in elaborate attire.
For seven days, Hóng did not speak to her.
His wife then knelt beneath the bed and pleaded, saying:
"I have heard that my husband possesses high integrity
and has rejected several women.
I, too, have been proud and rejected several men.
Now that I am chosen,
how dare I not beg for forgiveness?"
Hóng said:
"I desire a person dressed in simple furs and coarse cloth,
who can accompany me in hiding in the deep mountains.
But now you wear fine silk,
and apply powder and makeup;
is this what Hóng desires?"
His wife said:
"I merely wished to observe your aspirations.
I have my own attire for reclusive living."
She then changed to a simple bun,
wore coarse cloth,
and came forward to perform her duties.
Hóng was greatly pleased and said:
"This is truly Liáng Hóng's wife!
She can serve me!"
He gave her the courtesy name Déyào,
and her personal name was Mèng Guāng.
After living there for a while,
his wife said:
"I have often heard that my husband wishes to live in seclusion and avoid trouble.
Why are you silent now?
Are you perhaps considering bowing down to compromise?"
Hóng said:
"Indeed."
So they together entered the Bàlíng Mountains,
taking up farming and weaving as their occupation,
reciting poetry and scriptures,
and playing the *qín* to amuse themselves.
They admired the noble recluses of past generations,
and Hóng composed eulogies for twenty-four such individuals from the time of the Four Hoaries onwards.
He then traveled east beyond the pass,
passed through the capital,
and composed the "Song of Five Sighs," saying:
"Ascend that Běimáng,
Alas!
Look upon the imperial capital,
Alas!
The palaces are towering,
Alas!
The people toil so hard,
Alas!
Far, far, it is endless,
Alas!"
Sùzōng heard this and disapproved,
and sought Hóng but could not find him.
He then changed his surname to Yùnqī,
his personal name to Yào,
and his courtesy name to Hóuguāng,
and lived with his wife between Qí and Lǔ.
After a while,
they again departed for Wú.
As they were about to leave,
he composed a poem, saying:
"Leaving the old land, I journey afar,
To gather distantly in the southeast.
My heart is sorrowful and weary,
My will drifts up and down.
I wish to take the reins and gallop forth,
But I detest my generation for their slanders.
They eagerly promote the crooked and discard the straight,
All prioritize the sycophantic, fawning.
Firmly without shame, I stand alone,
Hoping other provinces still honor the worthy.
Leisurely I wander and roam,
Following Zhòngní's circuits.
If by chance I see one who pleases me,
I will abandon my carriage and take to the boat.
I pass by Jì Zhá at Yánlíng,
And seek Lǔ Lián at the sea's edge.
Though my appearance is not observed,
May the spirits grant me peace.
It is the last month of spring, flowers abound,
The wheat, full of grain, is now in bloom.
Alas, the prime of time passes quickly,
I grieve that fragrance daily decays.
I lament my heart's failure to attain,
Long entangled, how can it find rest?
My mouth is clamorous with my reproaches,
Alas, who, in this state of anxiety, will stay?"
He then went to Wú,
relying on the magnate Gāo Bótōng,
living under a eaves,
working as a hired pounder of grain.
Each time he returned,
his wife would prepare food for him,
not daring to look up at Hóng in front of him,
holding the tray to her eyebrows.
Bótōng observed this and found it extraordinary,
saying:
“This laborer can make his wife respect him so much;
he is no ordinary man.”
Thereupon, he lodged him in his own home.
Hóng secluded himself and wrote more than ten chapters of books.
When he was ill and near death,
he told his host:
“In the past, Jìzǐ of Yánlíng buried his son between Yíng and Bó,
and did not return to his hometown.
Be sure not to let my son carry my coffin back to our native place.”
When he died,
Bótōng and others sought a burial place for him beside the tomb of Wú Yàolí.
They all said:
“Yàolí was a brave warrior,
and Bólúan was pure and lofty;
they can be close to each other.”
After the burial,
his wife and children returned to Fúfēng.
Initially,
Hóng’s friend Gāo Huī from Jīngzhào,
who had been fond of Lǎozi since youth,
lived in seclusion in Huáyīn Shān.
When Hóng traveled east and thought of Huī,
he wrote a poem saying:
“Birds chirp, chirping, awaiting their friend;
I think of Gāozi, my heart filled with longing;
Thinking of Huī, I gather here.”
The two never saw each other again.
Huī was also lofty and unyielding,
never taking office throughout his life.
Gāo Fèng, courtesy name Wéntōng,
was a native of Yè, Nányáng.
In his youth, he was a scholar;
his family made a living from farming,
but he devoted himself to diligent recitation and study,
day and night without ceasing.
One time his wife went to the fields,
spreading wheat to dry in the courtyard,
and told Fèng to guard the chickens.
At that time, there was a sudden downpour,
but Fèng held a pole and recited classics,
unaware that the rainwater was washing away the wheat.
When his wife returned and asked in surprise,
Fèng only then realized it.
Thereafter, he became a famous Confucian scholar,
and taught his profession in Xītáng Shān.
When neighbors had a dispute over property,
they came to blows with weapons,
Fèng went to mediate,
but they would not stop.
He then took off his head covering and kowtowed,
earnestly pleading:
“Benevolence, righteousness, humility, and deference—
how can you forsake them!”
Thereupon, the disputants were moved,
threw down their weapons, and apologized.
When Fèng was old,
his resolve remained unflagging,
and his reputation became widely known.
The Grand Administrator repeatedly summoned and invited him,
and fearing he could not refuse,
he claimed he was originally from a family of shamans,
and should not be an official,
and also fraudulently litigated with his widowed sister-in-law over land,
thus he did not take office.
In the Jiànchū period,
the Grand Master of Works Rèn Kuí recommended Fèng for his straightforward speech,
but upon arriving at the imperial carriage,
he feigned illness and fled home.
He distributed all his property
to his orphaned nephews.
He lived in seclusion, fishing and angling,
and died at home.
The论 (commentary) says: My late great officer, Xuānhóu,
once, in the leisure time from lecturing on the Way,
devoted himself to the chapters about recluses.
When he reached the biography of Gāo Wéntōng,
he paused, deeply moved,
considering him a true recluse,
and thereupon wrote a commentary on his deeds, saying:
“In ancient times, reclusion
was highly esteemed.
Yǐngyáng washed his ears,
ashamed to hear of abdication;
Gūzhú endured long hunger,
ashamed to eat the millet of Zhōu.
Some lived in high places to avoid worldly conduct,
others resented worldly things to refine their sentiments.
Though their paths diverged,
their going and staying were one.
As for such a man,
his ambition soared above the blue clouds,
while his body was hidden in the mud and filth.
Even the name in his heart was not yet manifest,
how much less any resentment or burdens!
Is he not far removed from those who cast their bodies into deep sands
or played their lutes facing the sun?!”
Tái Tóng, courtesy name Xiàowēi,
was a native of Yè, Wèijùn.
He lived in seclusion in Wǔ'ān Shān,
making a cave his dwelling,
and earning his living by gathering herbs.
In the Jiànchū period,
the province summoned him, but he did not respond.
When the Inspector toured the commandery,
he sent his subordinate to pay a visit.
Tóng went to express his thanks, feigning illness.
The Inspector then held the ceremonial gift and met Tóng, saying:
“Xiàowēi, living like this,
is very hard,
how do you manage?”
Tóng replied:
“Tóng is fortunate to preserve his life till the end,
and nourish his spirit and harmony.
As for your esteemed lord, proclaiming imperial edicts,
and being vigilant about various matters day and night,
is that not harder?”
Thereupon he left,
and lived in seclusion,
never to be seen again.
Hán Kāng, courtesy name Bóxiū,
also named Tiánxiū,
was a native of Bālíng, Jīngzhào.
His family was a prominent lineage for generations.
He often gathered medicinal herbs in famous mountains,
and sold them in the Cháng'ān market,
never haggling over prices,
for more than thirty years.
At one time, a woman bought medicine from Kāng,
and Kāng stuck to his price.
The woman angrily said:
“Are you Hán Bóxiū?
And yet you don't haggle?”
Kāng sighed, saying:
“I originally wanted to avoid fame,
but now even a young woman knows about me.
What use is medicine?”
Thereupon he fled into Bālíng Shān.
The Erudites and imperial carriages repeatedly summoned him, but he did not come.
Emperor Huán then prepared the ritual gifts of dark silk and red silk,
and invited him with an imperial carriage.
The envoy, following the imperial edict, went to Kāng;
Kāng had no choice but
to agree.
He declined the imperial carriage,
and rode his own simple cart,
departing before the envoy at dawn.
When they arrived at a post station,
the postmaster, knowing that Hán Zhēngjūn was about to pass,
was mobilizing men and oxen to repair the road and bridge.
When he saw Kāng in his simple cart and head-covering,
he thought he was a farmer,
and made him give up his oxen.
Kāng immediately unharnessed them and gave them to him.
A moment later,
the envoy arrived,
and the old man whose oxen had been taken was indeed the summoned worthy.
The envoy wanted to impeach the postmaster for execution.
Kāng said:
“This old man willingly gave them,
what crime has the postmaster committed!”
And so it stopped.
Kāng then fled [mid-route]
and lived out his years.
Jiǎo Shèn, courtesy name Zhòngyàn,
was a native of Màolíng, Fúfēng.
In his youth, he was fond of Huáng-Lǎo (Huang-Lao Daoism),
and lived in seclusion in mountain valleys,
making a cave his dwelling,
admiring the Daoist longevity techniques of Sōng and Qiáo.
He was a fellow countryman and contemporary of Mǎ Róng and Sū Zhāng;
Róng was famous for his talent and erudition,
Zhāng was known for his integrity and uprightness,
yet both deferred to Shèn.
Rǔnán’s Wú Cāng
deeply respected him, and so sent a letter to observe his aspirations, saying:
"Zhòngyàn, my dear sir: You diligently reside in reclusion.
Though I ride the clouds and you tread the mud,
our resting places are different,
yet whenever the west wind blows,
how can I not sigh!
I have heard the words of Huáng and Lǎo:
to ascend into the void and enter the depths,
to hide oneself and flee far away,
and also to govern the state and nourish the people,
applying oneself to governance.
As for ascending mountains and leaving no trace,
the spirits do not bear witness to it,
and humans do not see its proof.
I wish, sir, that you would follow what is possible.
What are your thoughts on this?
In ancient times, Yī Yǐn did not conceal his Way while awaiting a sovereign like Yáo or Shùn.
Nowadays, the age is enlightened,
the four seas are open and vast.
Cháo and Xǔ would not act reclusively on Jī Shān,
and Yí and Qí would regret entering Shǒuyáng.
If you, my dear sir, can truly ride dragons and play with phoenixes,
soaring and frolicking among the clouds,
then you are not someone whom foxes, rabbits, swallows, or sparrows would dare to scheme against."
Shèn did not reply.
He was over seventy years old
and still refused to marry.
Later, he suddenly returned home,
declared the day of his death himself,
and indeed died on the appointed day.
Later, some people saw Shèn in Dūnhuáng,
which is why earlier generations found him extraordinary,
some even saying he was an immortal.
Shèn’s fellow commandery man, Mǎ Yáo,
lived as a recluse on Qīan Shān,
taking care of rabbits as his occupation.
The customs of the place where he lived were transformed,
and the common people admired him,
calling him Mr. Mǎ Mù.
Dài Liáng, courtesy name Shūluán,
was a native of Rǔnán, Shènyáng.
His great-grandfather, Zūn,
courtesy name Zǐgāo,
served as a Grandee Remonstrant
during Emperor Píng’s reign.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he feigned illness and returned to his hometown.
His family was wealthy,
and he enjoyed giving to others,
upholding a chivalrous spirit.
He often had three or four hundred retainers.
People at the time had a saying about him:
"The great magnate east of the pass is Dài Zǐgāo."
Liáng had an unconventional character in his youth.
His mother liked the braying of donkeys,
and Liáng often imitated it to entertain her.
When his mother died,
his elder brother Bólúan lived in a mourning hut, drinking congee,
never acting contrary to ritual.
Liáng alone ate meat and drank wine,
crying only when sorrow truly struck,
yet both of them showed signs of emaciation from grief.
Someone asked Liáng:
"Is your observance of mourning
in accordance with ritual?"
Liáng replied:
"Yes.
Ritual is for restraining excessive emotions;
if emotions are not excessive,
what is there to discuss about ritual!
If delicious food tastes bland,
then it naturally results in the reality of an emaciated appearance.
If there is no flavor in the mouth,
then eating it is permissible."
Debaters could not refute him.
Liáng’s talent was both eminent and profound,
and his discussions favored the unconventional,
often startling common society.
Xiè Jìxiào, from the same commandery, asked him:
"Who do you consider yourself comparable to in the world?"
Liáng replied:
"If I were Zhòngní born in Eastern Lǔ,
or Dà Yǔ emerging from Western Qiāng,
walking alone in the world,
who would be my match!"
He was recommended as Xiaòlián
but did not accept the position.
He was twice summoned by the Sīkōng office,
but did not arrive for a whole year.
When the province and commandery pressed him,
he then made an excuse to flee and proceed to the office,
taking his entire family with him.
After setting out on the road,
he then escaped into the mountains of Jiāngxià.
He lived a life of leisure, avoiding official service,
and died of old age.
In the beginning,
Liáng had five daughters who were all virtuous.
Whenever there was a proposal for marriage,
he would readily agree to give them away,
sending them off with coarse skirts and cloth blankets,
bamboo baskets and wooden clogs.
His five daughters were able to follow his teachings,
and all possessed the demeanor of recluses.
Fǎ Zhēn, courtesy name Gāoqīng,
was a man from Fúfēng, Méi,
and the son of Xióng, the Grand Administrator of Nánjùn.
He was fond of learning but had no fixed home.
He was widely versed in both inner and outer texts and classics,
becoming a great Confucian scholar in Guānxī.
Disciples from distant places came to him,
including several hundred people like Fàn Rǎn from Chénliú.
He was by nature tranquil and had few desires,
not involving himself in worldly affairs.
The Grand Administrator invited him for an audience,
and Zhēn then went to pay his respects wearing a simple cloth headscarf.
The Grand Administrator said:
"Although Duke Āi of Lǔ was unworthy,
Zhòngní acknowledged him as his sovereign.
I, the Grand Administrator, am humble and shallow,
but I wish to prevail upon you to serve as Gongcáo,
to bring glory and assistance to the imperial court.
What do you think?"
Zhēn replied:
"Because your illustrious office treats me with courtesy,
I dare to consider myself among your humble guests.
If you wish to treat me as an official,
Zhēn will be north of the northern mountain,
and south of the southern mountain."
The Grand Administrator was startled,
and dared not speak again.
He was summoned by the ducal office
and recommended as Xiánliáng,
but he did not accept any of these.
Tián Ruò, from the same commandery, recommended Zhēn, saying:
"The recluse Fǎ Zhēn
embodies the four virtues,
his learning penetrates the profound classics,
he dwells in quiet tranquility,
forgetting sorrow in his joy.
He will follow the lofty path of Lǎo Zǐ,
and will not be swayed by official robes.
Your subject wishes that the sacred court would bestow a high official position upon him,
