for he will surely be able to sing the songs of the pure temple,
and bring forth the phoenix of auspicious omen."
When Emperor Shùn was on a western tour,
Ruò again recommended him.
The emperor sincerely wished to secure his service,
summoning him four times in total.
Zhēn said:
"Since I cannot conceal my form and distance myself from the world,
how can I drink the water of ear-washing (like Xǔ Yóu)?"
Thereupon, he deeply secluded himself,
ultimately refusing to yield.
His friend Guō Zhèng praised him, saying:
"Fǎ Zhēn’s name can be heard,
but his person is difficult to see.
He flees fame, but fame follows him;
he avoids fame, but fame pursues him.
He can be called a teacher for a hundred generations!"
Thereupon, they together carved a stone inscription to praise him,
calling him Mr. Xuándé.
He was eighty-nine years old,
and in the fifth year of Zhōngpíng (188 CE),
he died of old age.
The old man of Hànyīn
— his origin is unknown.
During the Yánxī reign of Emperor Huán,
he traveled to Jìnglǐng,
passed through Yúnmèng,
and approached the Miǎn River.
The common people all came to watch,
but an old man alone continued plowing without stopping.
Zhāng Wēn of Nányáng, a Shàngshū Láng, found this unusual
and sent someone to ask:
"Everyone has come to watch;
why does the old man alone not stop?"
The old man smiled but did not answer.
Wēn descended a hundred paces from the road
and spoke with him himself.
The old man said:
"I am but a rustic,
I do not understand such words.
May I ask whether the Son of Heaven is established when the world is in chaos,
or when it is in order?
Is the Son of Heaven established to be the father of all under Heaven,
or is all under Heaven exploited to serve the Son of Heaven?
In ancient times, when sage kings governed the world,
they lived in thatched huts with rafters of mulberry,
yet the myriad people were at peace.
Now your ruler
exhausts the people for his own indulgence,
traveling for pleasure without restraint.
I am ashamed for you,
how can you bear to let people watch him?"
Wēn was greatly ashamed.
He asked for his name,
but the old man did not tell him and departed.
The old man of Chénliú
— his origin is unknown.
During the reign of Emperor Huán,
the Affair of the Partisan Prohibitions arose.
Zhāng Shēng of Chénliú, who was the Prefect of Wàihuáng,
resigned his office and returned to his hometown.
On the road, he met a friend,
and they sat together on the grass to talk.
Shēng said:
"I have heard that when Zhào killed Míngdú,
Zhòngní turned back from the river;
when nests are overturned and abysses drained,
dragons and phoenixes depart and do not arrive.
Now eunuchs daily cause chaos,
entrapping and harming the loyal and good.
Will the worthy men and gentlemen then leave the court?
Indeed, if virtue is not established,
and people have no support,
will not even their lives be endangered?
What can be done?"
Thereupon, they embraced and wept.
An old man hastened past them,
planted his staff,
and sighed, saying:
"Alas!
Why do you two grandees weep so sorrowfully?
Indeed, dragons do not hide their scales,
and phoenixes do not conceal their feathers.
If the nets are hung high,
where will they go to escape?
Even weeping, what can it avail?"
The two wanted to speak with him,
but he did not look back and departed,
and no one knew his end.
Páng Gōng
was a native of Xiāngyáng in Nánjùn.
He resided south of Mt. Xiàn,
and never entered a city or government office.
His wife and he respected each other as guests.
Liú Biǎo, the Inspector of Jīng Province, repeatedly invited him,
but could not compel him,
so he went to visit him.
He said:
"Among preserving oneself,
what is better than preserving all under Heaven?"
Páng Gōng smiled and said:
"Swans and wild geese nest on high trees,
and at dusk find their roost;
turtles and alligators burrow in deep abysses,
and at evening find their dwelling.
Indeed, whether one comes or goes, acts or stops,
is also a person's nest or burrow.
Each merely finds their own roost and dwelling,
the world is not what one preserves."
Thereupon, he released his plow on the ridge,
and his wife and children weeded in front.
Liú Biǎo pointed and asked:
"Sir, you suffer to live in the fields and refuse official salary;
what will you leave your descendants in later generations?"
Páng Gōng said:
"Everyone in the world leaves them danger;
I alone leave them peace.
Although what is left is different,
it is not that nothing is left."
Liú Biǎo sighed and departed.
Later, he took his wife and children to ascend Mt. Lùmén,
and gathered herbs, never to return.
Eulogy says: Rivers and seas vanish into obscurity,
mountains and forests are for long departure.
Their distant nature is sparse like the wind,
their free spirit is above the clouds.
Their Way achieves perfect emptiness,
their affairs diverge from worldly wrongs.
Biographies of Exemplary Women, Chapter Seventy-Four
The words of the Shī and Shū concerning female virtue are esteemed.
As for worthy consorts who assist the state ruler's governance,
wise women who uphold the Way of the family,
lofty scholars who propagate a pure and clear spirit,
and chaste women who illuminate a bright and unsullied integrity,
their admirable beauty is not distinct,
yet worldly records often omit them.
Therefore, from the Restoration onwards,
summarizing their accomplished deeds,
we have compiled this chapter on exemplary women.
As for Empress Mǎ, Empress Dèng, and Empress Liáng, they are separately seen in previous records.
Liáng Yì and Lǐ Jī are each appended to their family biographies.
Such cases
are not included here.
The rest are merely arranged by those whose talents and conduct are especially outstanding,
not necessarily focusing on a single virtue.
Bāo Xuān's wife from Bóhǎi
was a daughter of the Huán clan,
courtesy name Shàojūn.
Xuān once studied under Shàojūn's father.
Her father admired his integrity and austerity,
and so gave his daughter to him as wife,
sending a very generous dowry and gifts.
Xuān was displeased
and said to his wife:
"Shàojūn was born to wealth and indulgence,
accustomed to fine adornments,
while I am truly poor and humble;
I dare not accept such ceremony."
His wife said:
"My lord, seeing that you cultivate virtue and uphold frugality,
has therefore allowed this humble concubine to attend to your needs.
Having received and served a gentleman,
I shall obey only your commands."
Xuān smiled and said:
"If you can be like this,
that is my wish."
His wife then returned all the attendant garments and ornaments,
changed into a coarse cloth skirt,
and together with Xuān pulled a deer-cart back to their hometown.
After completing the ritual bows to her mother-in-law,
she carried a jar to draw water.
She practiced the virtues of a wife,
and her hometown praised her.
Xuān, during the reign of Emperor Āi, rose to the position of Sīlì Xiàowèi.
His son Yǒng,
at the beginning of the Restoration, served as the Grand Administrator of Lǔ Commandery.
Yǒng's son Yù casually asked Shàojūn:
"Does your ladyship still remember the time you pulled the deer-cart?"
She replied:
"My late mother-in-law had a saying:
'When prosperous, do not forget ruin;
when safe, do not forget danger.'
How could I dare to forget?"
Yǒng and Yù have already been seen in previous biographies.
The wife of Wáng Bà
of Tàiyuán, her maiden name is unknown.
Bà, while young, established a high moral character.
During the time of Guāngwǔ Dì,
he was repeatedly summoned to serve but refused.
Bà has already been noted in the Biographies of Reclusive Scholars.
His wife also had beautiful aspirations and conduct.
Initially,
Bà was friends with Línghú Zǐbó from the same commandery.
Later, Zǐbó became the Chancellor of Chǔ,
and his son became the Administrator of Meritorious Deeds for the commandery.
Zǐbó then ordered his son to deliver a letter to Bà,
with carriages, horses, and attendants,
dignified and elegant.
Bà's son was at that time plowing in the field.
Hearing that guests had arrived,
he dropped his plow and returned.
Upon seeing Línghú Zǐ,
he was embarrassed and ashamed, unable to look up.
Bà looked at him,
with a look of shame,
and after the guest left, he lay down for a long time and did not get up.
His wife, puzzled, asked him the reason.
At first, he refused to tell,
but after his wife begged him to confess,
he then said:
"Zǐbó and I have always been unequally matched.
Just now I saw his son, whose attire was splendid,
and whose every movement was appropriate.
But my son, with disheveled hair and crooked teeth,
does not know proper etiquette.
Seeing the guest, he showed embarrassment.
The affection between father and son is deep,
so I couldn't help but lose myself in thought."
His wife said:
"My lord, you cultivated a pure character in your youth,
not caring for glory or emoluments.
Now, how does Zǐbó's nobility compare to your eminence?
Why should you forget your original aspirations and feel ashamed of your child?"
Bà sat up with a laugh and said:
"You are right!"
Thus, they lived out their lives together in reclusion.
The wife of Jiāng Shī
of Guǎnghàn was the daughter of Páng Shèng from the same commandery.
Shī served his mother with utmost filial piety,
and his wife was especially devoted in her obedience.
His mother liked to drink river water,
and the river was six or seven *lǐ* from their home.
His wife would always go against the current to fetch water.
Later, caught in a storm,
she could not return in time.
His mother was thirsty,
so Shī scolded her and sent her away.
His wife then stayed with a neighbor,
spinning day and night.
She bought delicacies,
and had the neighbor's mother covertly give them to her mother-in-law.
This continued for a long time.
Her mother-in-law, surprised, asked the neighbor's mother,
who told her everything.
The mother-in-law, moved and ashamed, called her back,
and treated her with even greater kindness and care.
Later, their son drowned while fetching water from afar.
The wife, fearing her mother-in-law's grief,
dared not speak of it,
but claimed he was away studying.
Her mother-in-law loved sliced fish (kuài),
and could not eat alone.
The couple often worked hard to provide *kuài*,
and invited the neighbor's mother to share it.
Suddenly, a spring gushed forth beside their house,
tasting like river water.
Every morning, two carp would emerge,
which were always used to provide meals for the two mothers.
When the Chìméi rebels passed through Shī's village,
they put away their weapons and passed through,
saying:
"Disturbing a great filial son will surely provoke ghosts and spirits."
It was a year of famine at the time.
The rebels then left rice and meat for Shī.
He accepted it and buried it.
The entire village was thus protected.
In the third year of Yǒngpíng,
a *xiàolián* was nominated.
Xiǎnzōng issued an edict saying:
"The greatly filial should enter court.
All those nominated shall be judged fairly."
From then on, they were all appointed as Lángzhōng.
Shī was subsequently appointed as the Magistrate of Jiāngyáng
and died in office.
Where he governed,
the local people erected a shrine for him.
The wife of Zhōu Yù of Pèijùn
was the daughter of Zhào Xiào from the same commandery,
with the courtesy name Ā.
In her youth, she learned proper etiquette and training,
and was skilled in the way of women.
However, Yù was arrogant, licentious, and fickle,
often behaving improperly.
Yù's father, Wěi, said to Ā:
"My daughter-in-law, you are the daughter of a virtuous man,
and should guide your husband with principle.
If Yù does not change,
it will be your fault."
Ā bowed and accepted the command.
She withdrew and said to her attendants:
"I do not possess the conduct of Fán Jī or Wèi Jī,
which is why my lord reproaches me.
If I speak and am not heeded,
my lord will surely say I did not obey his instruction,
and then the fault will be mine.
But if I speak and am heeded,
then the son will be disobeying his father and following his wife,
and the fault will be his.
To live like this,
what joy is there?"
So she committed suicide.
None were not saddened by it.
The wife of Cáo Shìshú of Fúfēng
was the daughter of Bān Biāo from the same commandery,
named Zhāo,
with the courtesy name Huìbān,
also known as Jī.
She was broadly learned and highly talented.
Shìshú died young.
She possessed moral integrity and proper conduct.
Her brother Gù was compiling the Hàn Shū,
but died before completing the Eight Tables and the Treatise on Astronomy.
Hé Dì then ordered Zhāo to go to the Zàngshūgé in the Dōngguān to complete it.
The Emperor often summoned her to the palace,
instructing the Empress and other noble ladies to learn from her,
calling her Dàjiā.
Whenever rare tribute items were presented,
the Emperor would command Dàjiā to compose *fù* and encomiums.
When Empress Dowager Dèng governed from behind the curtain,
she was consulted on matters of state.
Due to her diligent service,
her son Chéng was specially enfeoffed as a Guānnèi Hóu,
and rose to the position of Chancellor of Qí.
At that time, when the Hàn Shū was first released,
many could not fully comprehend it.
Mǎ Róng from the same commandery knelt below the pavilion
to receive instruction from Zhāo.
Later, an edict also commanded Róng's elder brother Xù to continue Zhāo's work and complete it.
In the Yǒngchū era,
the Empress Dowager's elder brother, Grand General Dèng Zhì, mourned his mother,
and submitted a memorial requesting to resign his post.
The Empress Dowager did not wish to grant it,
and consulted Zhāo.
Zhāo then submitted a memorial, saying:
"I humbly consider Your Majesty, the Empress Dowager,
to embody the beauty of great virtue,
and to uphold the governance of Táng and Yú.
You open the four gates and receive advice from all four directions,
gathering the blind words of commoners,
and accepting the counsel of woodcutters.
I, Zhāo, though foolish and decrepit,
live in this illustrious age,
and dare not fail to lay bare my heart and liver,
to offer one in ten thousand of my thoughts.
I have heard that among the virtues of humility and deference,
none is greater.
Thus, the ancient texts praise it,
and gods bestow blessings.
In ancient times, Yí and Qí left their state,
and the world admired their integrity and nobility.
Tàibó abandoned Bīn,
and Kǒngzǐ called it 'three acts of deference.'
This is how their excellent virtues were illuminated
and their names glorified for posterity.
The Lúnyǔ says: 'If one can govern a state with courtesy and deference,
what difficulty is there in engaging in government?'
From this, it can be said
that the sincerity of deference
leads to far-reaching results.
Now, the four maternal uncles deeply uphold loyalty and filial piety,
and withdraw themselves.
Yet because the border regions are not yet pacified,
you refuse to permit them.
If even a slight imperfection should occur after today,
I truly fear that the reputation for deference cannot be regained.
As I have been granted this opportunity,
I dare, at the risk of death, to exhaust my foolish sentiments.
I know my words are not worth adopting,
but they show the sincere heart of an insect or ant."
The Empress Dowager followed her advice and permitted it.
Thereupon, Zhì and the others each returned to their private residences.
She wrote seven chapters of "Admonitions for Women,"
which aided in domestic instruction.
Its preface states: "I, a humble and ignorant person,
am not quick by nature.
I received the remaining favor of my late father,
and relied on the standard teachings of my mother and teachers.
At the age of fourteen,
I took up the broom at Cáo."
Shì,
for over forty years until now.
Trembling with fear,
constantly dreading dismissal and disgrace,
thereby increasing my parents’ shame,
and adding to the burdens of my kin, both within and without.
From dawn
to dusk, I toiled with a heavy heart,
diligently, without complaining of weariness.
From this day forward,
I finally know liberation.
My nature is dull and stubborn,
my teaching and guidance lacking.
I constantly feared that Zǐgǔ would bring disgrace upon the
court.
The Sacred Grace was bestowed unexpectedly,
generously granting me the golden-purple insignia.
This was truly beyond what a humble person like myself could have hoped for.
My son is now capable of planning for himself,
and I no longer worry
about him.
However, I grieve that my daughters are about to be married,
yet they have not gradually received instruction and guidance,
nor have they heard of the rules of womanhood.
I fear they will lose face in other families,
and bring shame upon our clan.
Now, my illness is in a state of
stagnation,
and my life is uncertain.
Thinking of you, my children, in this way,
I am always filled with sorrow.
I have informally written Seven Chapters of Admonitions for Women.
I wish that each of you, my daughters, would copy one set,
so that it may be of some benefit,
and
assist your person.
Go forth,
and diligently strive!
Weakness
means being humble before others.
Playing with tiles and bricks
demonstrates a habit of labor,
meaning being diligent in duties.
Announcing to the ancestors in a fast
shows that one should continue the ancestral sacrifices.
These three
are surely the constant principles of women,
the canonical teachings of ritual and law.
Being humble, yielding, respectful, and reverent,
putting others before oneself,
if one has done good, not claiming credit,
if one has done wrong, not shirking responsibility,
enduring humiliation and
defilement,
always as if in fear,
this is called being humble and subservient.
Sleeping late and rising early,
not fearing day or night,
attending to personal duties,
not refusing difficult or easy tasks,
completing
all that is undertaken,
keeping one's handiwork tidy,
this is called diligence.
Maintaining a proper demeanor and upright conduct
in serving one's husband,
keeping oneself pure and tranquil,
not being fond of frivolous laughter,
making clean and orderly food and
drink
to offer to the ancestors,
this is called continuing the ancestral sacrifices.
If these three are prepared,
yet one fears that one's good name will not be heard,
or that dismissal and disgrace will befall one,
I have not
seen it.
If these three are lost,
how can one's good name be heard,
or dismissal and disgrace be kept far away!
Regarding the importance of the relationship between men and women,
the Shī has recorded the meaning of Guān Jū.
From this, it can be said
that it must not be taken lightly.
If the husband is not virtuous,
then he has no means to manage his wife;
if the wife is not
virtuous,
then she has no means to serve her husband.
If the husband does not manage his wife,
then his dignity and decorum are neglected;
if the wife does not serve her husband,
then righteousness and principle fall into disuse.
As for these two matters,
their
function is one.
Observing the gentlemen of today,
they only know that wives must be managed,
and that dignity must be maintained.
Therefore, they instruct their sons
and restrain them with books and traditions,
but they completely ignore that husbands must be served,
and that ritual and righteousness must be preserved.
To only teach sons and not daughters,
is this not to be biased in the matter of what applies to both
sexes?
According to the Lǐ,
at eight years old, one begins to be taught writing;
by fifteen, one reaches the age of study.
Why can we not follow this as a model?
for beauty.
Therefore, a rustic saying goes:
"To bear a son is like having a wolf,
one still fears it will be ;
to bear a daughter is like having a mouse,
one still fears it will become a tiger."
So, for self-cultivation, nothing is better than reverence;
for avoiding the strong, nothing is better than submission.
Therefore, it is said that the way of reverence and submission
is the great ritual for women.
Reverence is nothing else;
it means enduring continuously.
Submission is nothing else;
it means being tolerant
and generous.
One who endures continuously
knows when to stop and be content.
One who is tolerant and generous
values humility.
The affection between husband and wife
should not be separated throughout life.
Intimacy within the chambers
eventually
leads to familiarity and disrespect.
Once familiarity and disrespect arise,
excessive words follow.
Once excessive words follow,
unrestrained indulgence is sure to occur.
Once unrestrained indulgence occurs,
then the heart of disrespecting the husband arises.
This comes from not knowing when to stop and be content.
Matters have right and wrong,
words have truth and falsehood.
The one who is in the right cannot but contend,
the one who is in the wrong cannot but dispute.
Once disputes and contentions
are engaged,
then acts of anger will follow.
This comes from not valuing humility.
If disrespect for the husband is not restrained,
scolding and reprimand will follow;
if anger does not cease,
physical
punishment will follow.
For those who are husband and wife,
righteousness creates harmony and intimacy,
and kindness brings about good union.
If physical punishment is carried out,
what righteousness remains?
If scolding and reprimand are proclaimed,
what kindness
exists?
If both kindness and righteousness are abandoned,
husband and wife will separate.
Women's Conduct, Chapter Four: A woman has four types of conduct:
first, wifely virtue (fùdé);
second, wifely speech (fùyán);
third, wifely appearance (fùróng);
fourth, wifely work (fùgōng).
Wifely virtue, as it is called,
does not necessarily mean extraordinary talent or intelligence;
wifely speech
does not necessarily mean eloquent or clever words;
wifely appearance
does not necessarily mean exceptional beauty;
wifely work
does not necessarily mean skill
surpassing others.
Being quiet and leisurely, chaste and tranquil,
observing decorum and being orderly,
having a sense of shame in one's conduct,
and having rules for one's actions and stillness,
this is called wifely virtue.
Choosing words before speaking,
not uttering malicious language,
speaking only at the appropriate time,
so as not to displease others,
this is called wifely speech.
Washing away dirt and grime,
keeping clothes fresh and clean,
bathing at the proper times,
so the body is not defiled or shamed,
this is called wifely
容。
To be wholeheartedly devoted to spinning and weaving,
not fond of jesting and laughing,
to prepare wine and food neatly,
in order to serve guests,
this is called "woman's work" (fùgōng).
These four are
the great virtues of women,
and must
not be lacking.
However, to do them is very easy;
it merely lies in having the intention.
The ancients had a saying:
"Is benevolence far away?
If I desire benevolence,
then benevolence will arrive."
This is what it means.
逃,
a husband is indeed indispensable.
If one's conduct violates the gods (shénqí),
Heaven will punish them;
if there are faults in ritual and righteousness (lǐyì),
the husband will look down upon them.
Therefore, the "Woman's Constitution" (Nǚxiàn) says:
"To gain the favor of one
person [the husband]
is called eternal completion;
to lose the favor of one person [the husband]
is called eternal termination."
From this,
one must seek to win the husband's heart.
However, what is sought
is not
flattery, fawning, or illicit intimacy.
Indeed, nothing is better than being devoted and proper (zhuānxīn zhèngsè).
To maintain ritual and righteousness in purity,
to have no improper listening,
no lewd looking,
no flirtatious appearance when going out,
no neglected adornment when staying in,
no gathering with groups of companions,
no peeking out the door—
this is what is meant by being devoted and proper.
If, however, one's actions are frivolous and reckless,
one's seeing and hearing are narrow and superficial,
at home one lets one's hair become dishevelled
and body become unkempt,
and when going out, one acts coquettishly and puts on airs,
saying what one ought not to say,
and looking at what one ought not to see—
this is called being unable to be devoted and proper.
How can the hearts of one's father-in-law (jiù) and mother-in-law (gū) be lost?
Some things are broken by affection (ēn) itself,
and some are ruined by righteousness (yì) itself.
Even if the husband expresses love,
if the parents-in-law express disapproval,
this is what is called being ruined by righteousness itself.
So, what should be done about the hearts of the parents-in-law?
Indeed, nothing is better than unconditional compliance (qūcóng).
If the mother-in-law says something is not so, and it is correct,
one should
certainly obey;
if the mother-in-law says something is so, and it is incorrect,
one should still comply with her command.
One must not contradict her on right and wrong,
or argue over what is crooked or straight.
This is what is called unconditional compliance.
Therefore,
the "Woman's Constitution" (Nǚxiàn) says:
"A wife is like an echo;
how can she not be appreciated?"
From this,
whether I am good or bad, praised or slandered,
depends entirely on my sisters-in-law (shūmèi).
The hearts of the sisters-in-law
must also not be lost.
Everyone knows that sisters-in-law must not be
lost,
but cannot harmonize with them to seek intimacy—
how deluded they are!
Unless one is a sage,
few can be without faults.
Therefore, Yán Zǐ (顏子) was valued for his ability to reform,
and Zhòngní (仲尼) praised him
for not repeating his mistakes.
How much more so for women!
Even with the conduct of virtuous women
and intelligent, wise natures,
can they be perfect?
Therefore, if the family is harmonious, slander is concealed;
if internal and external relations are estranged, evil is spread.
This is an inevitable outcome.
The "Yì" (易) says:
"If two people are of one mind,
their sharpness can cut metal.
Words from a united heart
smell like orchids."
This is what it means.
Elder sisters-in-law (sǎomèi)
are equal in status but revered,
distant in affection yet close in righteousness.
If one is a virtuous and humble person,
then one can rely on righteousness to
deepen affection,
and uphold kindness to form alliances,
making excellent virtues conspicuous,
and faults and transgressions hidden.
Parents-in-law will praise her goodness,
and the husband will commend her beauty.
Her reputation will shine in the neighborhood,
and her auspicious light will extend to her own parents.
But if one is foolish and ignorant,
towards an elder sister-in-law (sǎo), one takes advantage of her name to elevate oneself;
towards a younger sister-in-law (mèi), one becomes arrogant and overbearing due to favor.
Once arrogance and overbearingness are displayed,
how can there be harmony?
Once kindness and righteousness are estranged,
how can praise arrive?
Thus, beauty is hidden and faults are publicized,
the mother-in-law is angry and the husband is resentful.
Slander and criticism spread inside and out,
disgrace
accumulates upon oneself,
further shaming one's parents,
and increasing the burden on one's husband.
This is the root of honor and disgrace,
and the foundation of fame and ignominy.
How can one not be careful?
Therefore, to win the hearts of sisters-in-law,
nothing is better than humility and compliance.
Humility is the handle of virtue,
and compliance is the conduct of a wife.
These two
are sufficient
to achieve harmony.
The "Shī" (詩) says:
"There, no one dislikes you;
here, no one detests you."
This is what it means.
Bān Zhāo's (班昭) younger sister, Cáo Fēngshēng (曹豐生),
also possessed talent and wisdom.
She wrote a book to challenge her,
and its words are worth reading.
Zhāo (昭) died at over seventy years old.
The empress dowager (huángtàihòu) wore plain clothes and mourned,
and dispatched an envoy to supervise the funeral arrangements.

Her collected works, including rhapsodies (fù), eulogies (sòng), inscriptions (míng), elegies (lěi), questions (wèn), annotations (zhù), laments (āicí), letters (shū), treatises (lùn), memorials to the throne (shàngshū), and last testaments (yí lìng),
totaled sixteen chapters.
Her daughter-in-law, Dīng (丁) née, compiled them,
and also composed an encomium for the great mistress (dàjiā).
The wife of Lè Yángzǐ (樂羊子) of Hénán (河南)
is not known by her maiden name.
Yángzǐ (羊子) once walked on the road
and found a cake of gold that had been lost.
He returned and gave it to his wife.
His wife said:
"I have heard that a person of integrity does not drink from a 'thief's spring' (dàoquán zhī shuǐ),
and an honest person does not accept 'begging food' (jiēlāi zhī shí).
How much more so to pick up something lost to seek profit,
thereby sullying one's conduct!"
Yángzǐ (羊zǐ) was greatly ashamed,
so he threw the gold away in the wilderness
and went far away to seek a teacher and study.
After a year, he returned home.
His wife knelt and asked him why.
Yángzǐ (羊zǐ) said:
"I have been away for a long time and missed you;
there is nothing else special."
His wife then took a knife, approached the loom, and said:
"This fabric is born from silkworm cocoons,
and completed on the loom.
Each [thread]
accumulates to an inch.
If the accumulation of inches does not stop,
it will eventually become a roll of cloth.
Now, if you were to cut this fabric,
you would abandon successful completion
and waste time and months.
You, my husband, are accumulating learning,
and should daily understand what you are lacking,
to achieve excellent virtue.
If you return halfway,
how is that different from cutting this fabric?"
Yángzǐ (羊zǐ) was moved by her words,
returned to complete his studies,
and consequently did not return for seven years.
His wife always diligently took care of her mother-in-law,
and also sent provisions to Yángzǐ (羊zǐ) from afar.
Once, a chicken from another household mistakenly entered the garden.
The mother-in-law secretly killed and ate it.
The wife, facing the chicken meat, refused to eat and wept.
The mother-in-law asked her the reason, puzzled.
The wife said:
“I grieve for my own poverty,
which forces us to eat another’s meat.”
The mother-in-law ultimately threw it away.
Later, a robber intended to violate the wife,
so he first seized her mother-in-law.
The wife heard,
grasped a knife and came out.
The robber said:
“If you put down your knife and follow me, you can be spared.
If you do not follow me,
I will kill your mother-in-law.”
The wife looked up to heaven and sighed,
raised the knife, slit her own throat, and died.
The robber also did not kill her mother-in-law.
The Grand Administrator, Tàishǒu, heard of it,
and immediately arrested and executed the robber.
He also bestowed silk upon the wife
and buried her with ritual honors,
giving her the title
“Chaste and Righteous” (Zhēnyì).
The wife of Chéng Wénjù of Hànzhōng
was the elder sister of Lǐ Fǎ from the same commandery,
courtesy name Mùjiāng.
She had two sons,
and his previous wife had four sons.
Wénjù was the Magistrate of Ānzhòng,
and died in office.
The four sons, considering their mother was not their birth mother,
their resentment and defamation grew daily.
However, Mùjiāng was kind, loving, gentle, and benevolent,
and her care and upbringing of them became even more profound.
Her provisions of clothing and food were double that given to her own children.
Someone once said to the mother:
“The four sons are extremely unfilial,
why don’t you live separately to distance yourself from them?”
She replied:
“I am guiding them with righteousness,
so that they may reform themselves.”
When Xīng, the eldest son of the former wife, fell gravely ill,
the mother felt natural compassion,
personally prepared medicines and meals,
and her kindness and affection were profound.
After a long illness, Xīng recovered.
Thereupon, he called his three younger brothers and said:
“Our stepmother is kind and benevolent,
this comes from a heavenly disposition.
We brothers, ignorant of her grace and nurture,
have hearts like beasts.
Though her motherly virtue grows ever greater,
our transgressions and wickedness are already deep!”
Then he took his three younger brothers to the prison in Nánzhèng,
presented the mother’s virtue,
described his own faults,
and begged for punishment.
The county reported this to the commandery.
The Grand Administrator (Jùnshǒu) distinguished the mother,
exempted the family from corvée labor,
discharged the four sons,
and allowed them to reform.
Thereafter, their education and guidance became more enlightened,
and they all became good gentlemen.
Mùjiāng died at over eighty years old.
Before her death, she admonished her sons, saying:
“My younger brother Bóduó
is a wise and accomplished scholar.
His arguments for simple burial
are of profound righteousness.
And the instructions he left before his death
are the law of sages.
I order you to follow them,
do not conform to common customs,
and thus increase my burden.”
Her sons dutifully carried out her wishes.
The filial daughter Cáo É
was from Shàngyú, Kuàijī.
Her father Xū,
was skilled in stringed instruments and singing,
and served as a shaman.
On the fifth day of the fifth month of Hàn'ān second year (143 CE),
while performing a ritual (welcoming) in the county river against the surging waves to welcome a deity,
he drowned and his body was not recovered.
Cáo É, at fourteen years old,
cried along the river,
day and night without ceasing,
for seventeen days,
then she threw herself into the river and died.
In Yuánjiā first year (151 CE),
the County Magistrate Dù Shàng reburied Cáo É by the roadside south of the river
and erected a stele for her.
The wife of Xǔ Shēng of Wú
was a daughter of the Lü family,
courtesy name Róng.
Shēng was a gambler in his youth,
and did not manage his conduct.
Róng often personally worked diligently at family affairs
to support her mother-in-law.
She frequently urged Shēng to study,
and whenever he did something wrong,
she would weep and offer counsel.
Róng’s father, accumulating anger and resentment towards Shēng,
called Róng, wanting to remarry her.
Róng sighed and said:
“Given my destiny,
it is unrighteous to leave him!”
She ultimately refused to return.
Shēng was moved and spurred himself on,
then sought a teacher and studied far away,
eventually achieving fame.
Soon, he was appointed by his home province,
but on his way to Shòuchūn,
he was harmed by robbers on the road.
The Inspector, Cǐshǐ, Yǐn Yào, captured the robbers.
Róng was accompanying the funeral procession on the road.
Hearing this, she went to the provincial capital
to request permission to personally avenge her husband.
Yào granted it.
Róng then personally cut off their heads
to offer sacrifice to Shēng’s spirit.
Later, the commandery suffered from bandits.
The bandits intended to violate her.
Róng climbed over a wall and fled.
The bandits drew their swords and pursued her.
The bandit said:
“If you follow me, you live.
If you don't follow me, you die.”
Róng said:
“It is unrighteous to allow my body to be disgraced by bandits!”
Then she killed them.
On that day, a fierce wind and heavy rain,
with thunder and lightning, made the sky dark.
The bandits, frightened, kowtowed and apologized,
then buried her.
The wife of Yuán Kuí of Rǔnán
was a daughter of Mǎ Róng of Fúfēng.
Her courtesy name was Lún.
Kuí has already been mentioned in a previous biography.
Lún was talented and articulate in her youth.
Mǎ Róng’s family was wealthy and prominent for generations,
and her dowry was very rich.
When they first completed the wedding ceremony,
Kuí asked her:
“A wife serves with broom and dustpan only,
why such excessive extravagance in your adornments?”
She replied:
“My loving parents bestowed this out of affection;
I dared not disobey their command.
If my lord wishes to emulate the lofty integrity of Bào Xuān and Liáng Hóng,
I too would request to follow the example of Shǎojūn and Mèng Guāng.”
Kuí also said:
“A younger brother marrying before an elder brother
is considered a laughingstock by the world.
Now, my elder sister is not yet married,
is it permissible for me to marry first?”
She replied:
“My elder sister has lofty conduct and extraordinary talent,
but has not yet met a worthy match.
She is not like your humble servant,
who merely settled for what was available.”
He then asked:
“Lord of Nánjùn (referring to her father, Mǎ Róng) has profound learning and deep understanding of the Dao,
and his writing is the pinnacle of literary composition.
Yet, in every office he held,
he was invariably criticized for his covetousness of wealth.
Why is this?”
She replied:
“Confucius, a great sage,
could not escape the defamation of Wǔ Shū;
Zǐlù, though most virtuous,
still faced the slander of Bóláo.
That my family head (father) suffered this
is indeed to be expected.”
Kuí was silent and unable to refute her,
and those listening outside the curtain were ashamed.
As Kuí was favored and esteemed at that time,
Lún also became famous in the world.
She died at over sixty years old.
Lún’s younger sister Zhī
also possessed talent and righteousness.
She lost her parents and elders early in life and was deeply moved,
thus she composed the “Shēnqíng Fù” (Rhapsody on Expressing Feelings).
Páng Yù's mother, from Jiǔquán,
was a daughter of the Zhào clan,
with the courtesy name É.
Her father was killed by a man from the same county,
and É's three brothers,
all fell ill and died at that time.
Her enemy rejoiced and congratulated himself,
thinking no one would avenge her.
É secretly harbored resentment,
and thus stealthily prepared a knife and weapon.
She often waited for the enemy's family in a covered carriage.
For over ten years, she could not find him.
Later, she encountered him at the Dūtíng [pavilion]
and stabbed him to death.
She then went to the county office to surrender.
She said:
"My father's enemy has been avenged;
please execute me."
The Chángyǐn, Jiāyì, of Fú Lù county, out of admiration,
took off his official seal and sash, wanting to flee with her.
É refused to go.
She said:
"To die for a satisfied grievance is
my clear destiny;
to judge crimes and manage prisons is
your normal duty.
How dare I, for a moment, cling to life
and violate public law!"
Later, she was pardoned and released.
The province and commandery honored her village gate.
Tàicháng Zhāng Huàn admired and praised her,
gifting her with a bolt of silk.
The wife of Liú Chángqīng of Pèi [commandery]
was the daughter of Huán Luán from the same commandery.
Huán Luán has already been mentioned in a previous biography.
She bore one son, and Chángqīng died when the boy was five years old.
The wife carefully avoided suspicion
and refused to return to her parental home.
When her son was fifteen,
he too died prematurely.
The wife, fearing she might not escape remarriage,
then deliberately cut her own ear to swear her vow.
The women of the clan sympathized with her
and collectively said:
"Your family truly has no other intentions;
even if there were,
you could still express your sincerity through your aunts and sisters.
Why value righteousness so much and hold your life so lightly!"
She replied:
"In the past, my ancestor, the Wǔ Gēng,
studied to become a Confucian master,
and was honored as an imperial tutor.
Since the Wǔ Gēng,
this has continued through generations without interruption.
Men have been distinguished by loyalty and filial piety,
women renowned for their chastity and obedience.
The 'Book of Poetry' says: 'Do not disgrace your ancestors,
but cultivate your virtue.'
Therefore, I mutilated myself in advance
to clarify my resolve."
Wáng Jí, the Xiàng of Pèi, reported her lofty conduct,
honored her household,
and designated it as
"The Righteous Huán Lineage."
Whenever there was a sacrifice in the county, her family would receive sacrificial meat.
The wife of Huángfǔ Guī of Āndìng [commandery],
whose clan name is unknown.
Guī initially lost his wife,
and later married her.
The wife was skilled in writing
and could write in grass script.
She often drafted letters for Guī,
and people marveled at her skill.
When Guī died,
his wife was still in the prime of her life,
and beautiful.
Later, Dǒng Zhuó, as Xiàngguó,
heard of her reputation
and sought to marry her, sending a hundred carriages,
twenty horses,
and countless slaves, money, and silks filling the road.
The wife then, lightly dressed, went to Dǒng Zhuó's gate,
knelt, and pleaded her case,
her words filled with deep sorrow.
Dǒng Zhuó ordered his attendant slaves and servants to draw their swords and surround her,
and said:
"My authority and teachings
are meant to make the whole world succumb.
How can they not apply to one woman!"
The wife knew she could not escape,
and immediately stood up and cursed Dǒng Zhuó, saying:
"You are of Qiāng-Hú descent;
is causing havoc throughout the world still not enough for you?!
My ancestors
have upheld pure virtue for generations.
The Huángfǔ clan possessed both literary and martial talents,
and were loyal subjects of Hàn.
Were your parents not his subordinate officials and servants?
How dare you attempt to commit an impropriety against your lord's wife!"
Dǒng Zhuó then pulled a carriage into the courtyard,
tied her head to the shaft,
and whipped her mercilessly.
The wife said to the men holding the whips:
"Why aren't you hitting harder?
Please finish quickly as a kindness."
She died beneath the carriage.
Later generations depicted her in paintings
and called her
"Lǐ Zōng" (Pillar of Propriety).
Thus it is said.
The wife of Yīn Yú of Nányáng,
was a daughter of Xún Shuǎng of Yǐngchuān,
named Cǎi,
with the courtesy name Nǚxún.
She was intelligent and talented in arts.
At seventeen,
she married into the Yīn clan.
At nineteen, she bore a daughter,
and Yú died.
Cǎi was still young and beautiful,
and constantly worried about being pressured by her family,
so she defended herself very resolutely.
Later, Guō Yì of the same commandery lost his wife,
and Xún Shuǎng promised Cǎi to him.
He then falsely claimed to be gravely ill
and summoned Cǎi.
Having no choice but to return,
she hid a blade and swore her vow.
Xún Shuǎng ordered a maid to seize her blade,
and had her held and put into a carriage.
Still worried she might be provoked to indignation,
he gave strict orders for her escort.
When the woman arrived at the Guō family's home,
she feigned an expression of joy,
and said to those around her:
"I originally vowed to share a grave with the Yīn clan,
but could not escape the coercion,
and so I have come to this.
My original intention unfulfilled,
what can be done?"
She then ordered four lamps to be lit,
adorned herself lavishly,
and invited Yì to meet her.
They conversed,
her words flowing without interruption.
Yì, feeling respect and awe,
thus dared not force her,
and left at dawn.
Cǎi then instructed her attendants to prepare a bath.
Once in the room, she closed the door,
and temporarily dismissed her maids.
She wrote on the door with powder:
"My body returns to Yīn."
Before the character for
"Yīn" was complete,
fearing someone might come,
she hanged herself with her sash.
Her attendants, playing, did not take it seriously.
When they checked,
she was already dead.
People of the time grieved for her.
The wife of Shèng Dào of Jiànwéi,
was a daughter of the Zhào clan from the same commandery,
with the courtesy name Yuánjiāng.
In the fifth year of Jiàn'ān,
the Yìbù region was in turmoil.
Shèng Dào gathered a multitude and raised troops.
The enterprise failed,
and the couple was arrested and imprisoned,
destined for death.
In the middle of the night, Yuánjiāng told Shèng Dào:
"The law has its fixed punishments;
there is no hope of survival.
You must quickly escape,
establish a household [elsewhere],
while I remain in prison
to take the blame for you."
Shèng Dào hesitated and did not comply.
Yuánjiāng then removed Shèng Dào's shackles
and prepared food and money for him.
Their son Xiáng, who was five years old at the time,
was made to be carried by Shèng Dào as he fled.
Yuánjiāng took Shèng Dào's place during the night watch,
answering questions without error.
When she estimated that Shèng Dào was far away,
she then told the truth to the officials
and was immediately killed.
Shèng Dào and his son later returned due to a general amnesty.
Shèng Dào was moved by her righteousness,
and never married again in his lifetime.
The filial daughter, Shū Xiān-Xióng,
was a native of Jiānwéi.
Her father, Ní Hé,
became the County Commandant's assistant (gōngcáo) at the beginning of the Yǒngjiàn era.
The county magistrate sent Ní Hé to deliver an official dispatch (xí) and pay respects to the Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Bā Jùn.
While traveling by boat, he fell into a rapid and drowned.
His body was never recovered.
Xióng was deeply saddened, filled with resentment and pain,
weeping day and night.
She had no desire to live,
and constantly contemplated drowning herself.
She had two children, a boy and a girl,
both only a few years old.
Xióng then made a pouch for each,
filled with pearls and rings, and tied them to her children,
often saying words of farewell.
Her family constantly kept watch over her,
but after about a hundred days, they gradually became less vigilant.
Xióng then took a small boat,
and at the spot where her father fell, she cried piteously,
then threw herself into the water and died.
Her younger brother, Xián,
that evening dreamed that Xióng told him:
"Six days from now,
I will emerge together with Father."
On the appointed day, he waited for them,
and indeed, they emerged holding each other,
floating on the river.
The commandery and county reported this to the emperor,
and a stele was erected for Xióng,
with her image carved upon it.
The wife of Dǒng Sì of Chénliú
was the daughter of Cài Yōng from the same commandery.
Her personal name was Yǎn,
and her courtesy name was Wénjī.
She was learned, eloquent,
and also highly skilled in music.
She married Wèi Zhòngdào of Hédōng.
After her husband died and she had no children,
she returned to her family home.
During the Xīngpíng era,
the world fell into chaos and turmoil.
Wénjī was captured by Hú (nomadic) cavalry
and became the possession of the Zǔo Xián-Wáng of the Southern Xiōngnú.
She stayed among the Hú for twelve years,
giving birth to two sons.
Cáo Cāo had always been friendly with Yōng
and grieved that he had no heir.
So he sent envoys with gold and jade to ransom her,
and then remarried her to Sì.
Sì was a Commandant of Agricultural Garrisons (Túntián Dūwèi),
but he committed a crime for which he was to be executed.
Wénjī went to Cáo Cāo to plead for him.
At that time, high-ranking officials (gōngqīng), famous scholars (míngshì), and envoys from distant places filled the hall.
Cāo said to his guests:
"Cài Bójiē's daughter is outside;
I shall let you see her now."
When Wénjī entered,
with disheveled hair and bare feet,
she kowtowed and begged for her husband's pardon.
Her voice and words were clear and eloquent,
and her plea was profoundly mournful.
Everyone present changed their expression in sympathy.
Cāo said:
"I truly pity you,
but the written verdict has already been issued,
what can be done?"
Wénjī replied:
"My Lord has ten thousand horses
and an army of brave warriors like a forest.
Why begrudge one swift horse
and not save a life at death's door?"
Cāo was moved by her words,
and thereupon retracted Sì's death sentence.
As it was cold then,
he bestowed upon her a headscarf, shoes, and socks.
Cāo then asked:
"I hear that your family formerly possessed many books;
do you still remember them?"
Wénjī replied:
"My late father once had about four thousand scrolls of books.
In the chaos and suffering,
none survived.
What I can now recite and remember
is merely over four hundred chapters."
Cāo said:
"I shall now have ten scribes come to you to copy them down."
Wénjī replied:
"I have heard that concerning the separation of men and women,
ritual forbids personal instruction.
I beg you to provide paper and brushes,
and I will write it down, whether in regular script (zhēn) or cursive (cǎo), as you command."
Thereupon, she transcribed the books and sent them,
with no omissions or errors.
Later, she was saddened by the chaos and separation,
and recalled her sorrow and indignation,
composing two chapters of poetry.
The lyrics are as follows: In the late Hán, power was lost,
Dǒng Zhuó disrupted the cosmic order.
Desiring to usurp and assassinate,
he first harmed the virtuous and good.
He forced the migration to the old capital,
seizing the emperor to strengthen himself.
Righteous armies rose throughout the land,
wishing to jointly punish the ominous one.
Dǒng Zhuó's troops came eastward,
golden armor gleaming in the sunlight.
The people of the plains were weak and fragile,
the invading soldiers were all Hú and Qiāng.
They hunted
in the wilds, besieged cities and towns,
everywhere they went was broken and ruined.
They slaughtered without leaving a single survivor,
corpses piled up against each other.
Men's heads hung by the horses' flanks,
women were loaded behind the horses.
They drove
westward into the Pass,
the winding road treacherous and difficult.
Looking back, it was vast and dim,
my heart and lungs utterly ravaged.
Ten thousands were captured,
not allowed to gather together.
Some had
their kin with them,
wanting to speak but daring not.
If they showed the slightest discontent,
they were immediately told, "We will kill the surrendered captives!"
"We shall surely use our sharp blades,
we will not let you live!"
How could one
value life,
unable to endure their curses?
Some were immediately beaten with clubs and staffs,
the poisonous pain striking them down together.
In the morning, they cried and walked;
at night, they grieved and moaned as they sat.
Wanting to die but unable
to,
wanting to live but finding no way.
What fault had the azure heavens,
to suffer such misfortune and calamity!
The borderlands and the Huá (Central Plains) are different,
the people's customs lack righteousness and reason.
The places have much frost and snow,
Hú winds rise in spring and summer.
Fluttering, they blow my clothes;
rustling, they enter my ears.
Feeling the times, I think of my parents,
my sorrowful sighs are endless.
When a visitor came from outside,
I heard
of them and was always joyful.
I welcomed and asked for news,
but they were never from my hometown.
By chance, my wish was granted,
my kin came to welcome me.
I was able to free myself,
but I had to
abandon my sons.
Heavenly bonds connect hearts,
thinking of separation with no meeting date.
Living and dead forever parted,
I could not bear to bid them farewell.
My sons embraced my neck,
asking, "Mother, where
are you going?"
"People say mother is leaving,
will you ever return?"
"Mother was always kind and compassionate,
why are you suddenly not loving?"
"We are not yet grown,
why do you not care
for us!"
Seeing this, my inner organs collapsed,
I became delirious and deranged.
Wailing, I caressed them with my hands,
about to depart, I hesitated again.
And there were companions of the same time,
seeing me off and bidding
farewell.
Envying that I alone could return,
their mournful cries tore through me.
The horses stopped, hesitating;
the chariots would not turn their wheels.
Onlookers all sighed;
passersby also wept mournfully.
Leaving, leaving, cutting off emotional attachment,
traveling quickly, day by day further away.
Three thousand li, so vast,
when will we meet again?
Thinking of my children born from my womb,
my chest and heart were shattered.
Already
zhì jiārén jìn,
yòu fù wú zhōngwài.
Chéngguō wéi shānlín,
tíngyǔ shēng jīng'ài.
Báigǔ bùzhī shuí,
cónghéng mò fùgài.
Chūmén
wú rénshēng,
cháiláng háo qiě fèi.
Qióngqióng duì gūjǐng,
dátzhà mí gānfèi.
Dēng gāo yuǎn tiàowàng,
húnshén hū fēishì.
Yǎnrúo shòu
mìngjìn,
pángrén xiāng kuāndà.
Wèi fù qiáng shìxī,
suī shēng hé liáolài!
Tuōmìng yú xīnrén,
jiéxīn zì xùlì.
Liúlí chéng bǐ
jiàn,
cháng kǒng fù juānfèi.
Rénshēng jǐhé shí,
huái yōu zhōng niánsuì!
Gǔ miǎo xī lù mànmàn,
juàn dōnggù xī dàn bēitàn.
Míng dāng qǐn xī bùnéng ān,
jī dāng shí xī bùnéng cān,
cháng liútì xī zì
bù gān,
bó zhìjié xī niàn sǐnán,
suī gǒuhuó xī wú xíngyán.
Wéi bǐ fāng xī yuǎn yángjīng,
yīqì níng xī xuě xià líng.
Shāmò
yōng xī chén míngmíng,
yǒu cǎomù xī chūn bù róng.
Rén sì qín xī shí chòuxīng,
yán dōulí xī zhuàng yǎotíng.
Suì yù mù xī shí
mài zhēng,
yè yōucháng xī jìnmén.
Bùnéng mèi xī qǐ píngyíng,
dēng húdiàn xī lín guǎngtíng.
Xuányún hé xī yì yuèxīng,
běifēng
lì xī sù línglíng.
Hújiā dòng xī biānmǎ míng,
gūyàn guī xī shēng yīngyīng.
Yuèrén xìng xī tán qínzhēng,
yīn xiānghé xī bēi qiě
qīng.
Xīn tǔ sī xī xiōng fènyíng,
yù shūqì xī kǒng bǐ jīng,
hán āi yàn xī tì zhānjǐng.
Jiā jì yíng xī dāng guīníng,
lín chánglù
xī juān suǒshēng.
Ér hū mǔ xī háo shīshēng,
wǒ yǎněr xī bùrěn tīng.
Zhuī chí wǒ xī zǒu qióngqióng,
dùn fù qǐ xī huǐ yánxíng.
Huán gù zhī xī pò rénqíng,
xīn dájué xī sǐ fù shēng.
Zàn yuē: Duān cāo yǒu zōng,
yōuxián yǒu róng.
Qū míng fēngliè,
zhāo wǒ guǎntóng.
Dōngyí Lièzhuàn dìqīshíwǔ
Wáng Zhì yún:
"Dōngfāng yuē Yí."
Yí zhě,
dǐ yě,
yán rén ér hàoshēng,
wànwù dǐdì ér chū.
Gù tiānxìng róushùn,
yì yǐ dào yù,
zhì yǒu Jūnzǐ, Bùsǐzhīguó yān.
Yí yǒu jiǔ zhǒng,
yuē Quǎnyí,
Yúyí,
Fāngyí,
Huángyí,
Báiyí,
Chìyí,
Xuányí,
Fēngyí,
Yángyí.
Gù Kǒngzǐ yù jū Jiǔyí yě.
Xī Yáo mìng Xī Zhòng zhái Yúyí,
yuē Yánggǔ,
gài rì zhī suǒchū yě.
Xià Hòushì Tàikāng shīdé,
Yírén shǐ pàn.
Zì Shàokāng yǐhòu,
shì fú wánghuà,
suì bīn yú wángmén,
xiàn qí lèwǔ.
Jié wéi bàolüè,
zhū Yí nèiqīn,
Yīn Tāng gémìng,
fá ér dìng zhī.
Zhìyú Zhòng Dīng,
Lányí zuòkòu.
Zì shì huò fú huò pàn,
sānbǎi yú nián.
Wǔ Yǐ shuāibì,
Dōngyí shèng,
suì fēnqiān Huái, Dài,
jiàn jū zhōngtǔ.
Jí Wǔ Wáng miè Zhòu,
Sùshèn lái xiàn shígǔ, hǔshǐ.
Guǎn, Cài pàn Zhōu,
nǎi zhāoyòu Yídí,
Zhōu Gōng zhēng zhī,
suì dìng Dōngyí.
Kāng Wáng zhī shí,
Sùshèn fù zhì.
Hòu Xúyí jiànhào,
nǎi shuài Jiǔyí yǐ fá Zōng Zhōu,
xī zhì Héshàng.
Mù Wáng wèi qí fāngchì,
nǎi fēn dōngfāng zhūhóu,
mìng Xú Yǎnwáng zhǔ zhī.
Yǎnwáng chǔ Huángchí dōng,
dìfāng wǔbǎi lǐ,
xíng rényì,
lùdì ér cháo zhě sānshíyǒuliù guó.
Mù Wáng hòu dé Jìlù zhī chéng,
nǎi shǐ Zàofù yù yǐ gào Chǔ,
lìng fá Xú,
yīrì ér zhì.
Yúshì Chǔ Wénwáng dà jǔbīng ér miè zhī.
Yǎnwáng rén ér wúquán,
bùrěn dòu qí rén,
gù zhì yú bài.
Nǎi běi zǒu Péngchéng Wǔyuánxiàn Dōngshān xià,
bǎixìng suí zhī zhě yǐ wànshù,
yīncí míng qí shān wèi Xúshān.
Lì Wáng wú dào,
Huáiyí rùkòu,
wáng mìng Guó Zhòng zhēng zhī,
bù kè,
Xuān Wáng fù mìng Shào Gōng fá ér píng zhī.
Jí Yōu Wáng yínluàn,
Sìyí jiāoqīn,
zhì Qí Huán xiū bà,
ráng ér què yān.
Jí Chǔ Líng huì Shēn,
yì lái yù méng.
Hòu Yuè qiān Lángyé,
yǔ gòng zhēngzhàn,
suì língbào Zhūxià,
qīnmìe xiǎobāng.
Qín bìng Liùguó,
qí Huái, Sì Yí jiē sàn wèi mínhù.
Chén Shè qǐbīng,
tiānxià bēngkuì,
Yànrén Wèi Mǎn bìdì Cháoxiǎn,
yīn wáng qí guó.
Bǎi yǒuyú suì,
Wǔdì miè zhī,
yúshì Dōngyí shǐ tōng shàngjīng.
Wáng Mǎng cuànwèi,
Mòrén kòubiān.
Jiànwǔ zhī chū,
fù lái cháogòng.
Shí Liáodōng Tàishǒu Jì Róng wēizhè Běifāng,
shēng xíng hǎibiǎo,
yúshì Huì, Mò, Wō, Hán wànlǐ cháoxiàn,
gù Zhāng, Hé yǐhòu,
shǐ pìngtōng liúcháng.
Dài Yǒngchū duōnán,
shǐ rù kòuchāo;
Huán, Líng shīzhèng,
jiàn zī màn yān.
Zì Zhōngxīng zhīhòu,
Sìyí láibīn,
suī shí yǒu guāipàn,
ér shǐyì bùjué,
gù guósú fēngtǔ,
kě dé lüèjì.
Dōngyí shuài jiē tǔzhù,
xǐ yǐnjiǔ gēwǔ,
huò guānbian yī jǐn,
qìyòng zǔdòu.
Suǒwèi Zhōngguó shīlǐ,
qiúzǐ Sìyí zhě yě.
Fán Mán, Yí, Róng, Dí zǒngmíng Sìyí zhě,
yóu Gōng, Hóu, Bó, Zǐ, Nán jiē hào Zhūhóu yún.
Fúyúguó,
zài Xuántú běi qiānlǐ.
Nán yǔ Gāogōulí,
dōng yǔ Yìlóu,
xī yǔ Xiānbēi jiē,
běi yǒu Ruòshuǐ.
Dìfāng èrqiānlǐ,
běn Huìdì yě.
Initially,
the king of the Běiyí Suǒlí Kingdom was traveling,
when his serving girl became pregnant in the rear.
When the king returned,
he wanted to kill her.
The serving girl said:
"Previously, I saw a vapor in the sky,
as large as a hen's egg,
which descended upon me,
and thus I became pregnant."
The king imprisoned her,
and later she gave birth to a boy.
The king ordered him to be placed in a pigsty;
the pigs breathed upon him with their mouths,
and he did not die.
He was then moved to a stable,
and the horses also did the same.
The king considered it divine,
and thus allowed his mother to raise him,
naming him Dōngmíng.
When Dōngmíng grew up, he was skilled at archery.
The king feared his fierceness,
and again wanted to kill him.
Dōngmíng fled,
traveling south to the Yǎnshuǐ River.
He struck the water with his bow;
fish and turtles all gathered and floated on the water.
Dōngmíng rode on them and was able to cross,
and thus arrived in Fúyú and became its king.
In the region of the Dōngyí,
it was the most level and open,
and the soil was suitable for the five grains.
It produced famous horses, red jade, and sable-like beasts,
and large pearls like sour dates.
They used circular palisades as their cities,
and had palaces, storehouses, and prisons.
Their people were large, strong, and brave, yet cautious and honest,
and did not engage in banditry or raids.
They used bows, arrows, swords, and spears as weapons.
They named their officials after the six domestic animals,
having Mǎjiā, Niújiā, and Gǒujiā.
Their settlements were all presided over by the various Jiā.
For eating and drinking, they used stands and vessels.
During assemblies, they bowed over their wine cups, washed them,
and made bows and concessions while ascending and descending.
They sacrificed to Heaven in the twelfth lunar month,
holding a grand assembly for several consecutive days,
with eating, drinking, singing, and dancing.
It was called
"Yínggǔ".
At this time, legal cases were suspended,
and prisoners were released.
When there were military matters, they also sacrificed to Heaven,
killing a cow,
and divined its fortune (auspicious or inauspicious) from its hoofs.
Travelers, day or night,
enjoyed singing and chanting,
their voices never ceasing.
Their customs involved severe and harsh punishments;
those executed had their family members confiscated as slaves.
For theft, one was fined twelve times the stolen amount.
Both men and women committing adultery were killed.
They especially punished vicious and jealous women;
after killing them,
their bodies were abandoned on a mountain.
If a brother died, his younger brother married his widow.
When someone died, there was an outer coffin but no inner coffin.
People were sacrificed and buried with the dead,
often numbering in the hundreds.
Their kings were buried in jade caskets.
The Hàn Cháo always prepared jade caskets in advance and entrusted them to Xuántú Jùn.
When a king died, they would retrieve one for burial.
During the Jiànwǔ period,
all the Dōngyí states came to offer tribute and seek audience.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the king of Fúyú sent an envoy to present tribute.
Emperor Guāngwǔ richly reciprocated,
and thereafter emissaries were exchanged annually.
By the fifth year of Yǒngchū under Emperor Ān,
the king of Fúyú for the first time led seven or eight thousand infantry and cavalry to raid Lèlàng,
killing and injuring officials and common people.
Later, they again returned to allegiance.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
he then sent his heir Wèiqíutái to the imperial court to present tribute.
The Son of Heaven bestowed upon Wèiqíutái a seal and ribbon, and silks.
In the first year of Yǒnghé under Emperor Shùn,
their king came to the capital for an audience;
the Emperor staged "Yellow Gate" drum and wind music performances and horn-butting wrestling for his farewell.
In the fourth year of Yánxī under Emperor Huán,
they sent envoys to offer imperial congratulations and tribute.
In the first year of Yǒngkāng,
King Fūtái led over twenty thousand men to raid Xuántú.
The Administrator of Xuántú, Gōngsūn Yù, attacked and defeated them,
beheading over a thousand.
By the third year of Xīpíng under Emperor Líng,
they again presented a memorial and tribute.
Fúyú originally belonged to Xuántú.
During the time of Emperor Xiàn,
its king requested to be subordinate to Liáodōng, it is said.
Yìlóu,
was the ancient Sùshèn state.
It was located over a thousand *lǐ* northeast of Fúyú,
bordered the great sea to the east,
and adjoined Běiwòjǔ to the south.
Its northern extent was unknown.
The land was mostly mountainous and treacherous.
Their physical appearance was similar to that of Fúyú people,
but their languages were different.
They had five grains and hemp cloth,
and produced red jade and fine sable.
They had no single ruler;
each settlement had its own elder.
They lived amidst mountains and forests.
The climate was extremely cold,
and they habitually lived in pits (cave dwellings),
valuing depth.
Large households even reached nine ladders deep.
They liked to raise pigs,
ate their meat,
and wore their hides.
In winter, they smeared pig fat on their bodies,
several *fēn* thick,
to ward off wind and cold.
In summer, they went naked,
using a foot-long piece of cloth to cover their front and back.
Their people were smelly, dirty, and unkempt.
They built latrines in the center,
and lived circularly around them.
Since the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
they were vassals of Fúyú.
Although their population was small,
they were mostly brave and strong.
Living in treacherous mountains,
and skilled at archery,
their shots could pierce a person's eye.
Their bows were four *chǐ* long,
with the power of a crossbow.
Their arrows were made of *hú* wood,
one *chǐ* and eight *cùn* long,
with blue stone arrowheads.
All arrowheads were poisoned,
and a hit person would die immediately.
They were adept at using boats,
and enjoyed raiding and plundering.
Neighboring states feared them as a menace,
yet ultimately could not subdue them.
The Dōngyí and Fúyú, for their eating and drinking, all used stands and vessels.
Only Yìlóu alone did not,
their laws and customs being the most undisciplined.
Gāogōulí
is a thousand *lǐ* east of Liáodōng.
To its south are Cháoxiǎn and Huìmò,
to its east Wòjū,
and to its north Fúyú.
Its territory spans two thousand *lǐ*,
with many great mountains and deep valleys,
where people reside in accordance with the terrain.
There is little farmland,
and diligent labor is insufficient to sustain themselves,
hence their custom of frugality in food and drink,
and their fondness for building palaces and houses.
The Eastern Yí傳people traditionally consider them a separate branch of Fúyú,
thus their language and customs are mostly similar,
but they kneel and bow dragging one leg,
and all their walking steps are a run.
There are five clans in total:
the Xiāonú-bù,
Jué’nǔ-bù,
Shùnnú-bù,
Guànnú-bù,
and Guìlóu-bù.
Originally, the Xiāonú-bù was the ruling clan,
but they gradually weakened,
and later the Guìlóu-bù replaced them.
Their officials include:
Xiàngjiā, Duìlú, Pèizhě, Gǔzōudàjiā,
Zhǔbù, Yōutái, Shǐzhě, and Báiyīxiānrén.
When Emperor Wǔ destroyed Cháoxiǎn,
he established Gāogōulí as a county
and made it subordinate to Xuántú Commandery,
bestowing drums, wind instruments, and entertainers.
Their customs are licentious;
they all enjoy being clean and delighted,
and at night, men and women often gather in groups for singing and dancing.
They like to sacrifice to ghosts and spirits, to the gods of land and grain, and to the star Línxīng.
In the tenth month, they hold a great festival to worship Heaven,
named
“Dōngméng”.
East of their country is a large cave,
called the abode of the Guǐshén spirits,
which they also welcome and sacrifice to in the tenth month.
At public gatherings, their clothing is all brocade and embroidery,
adorned with gold and silver.
The Dàjiā and Zhǔbù all wear *zé*,
similar to a ceremonial cap but without a back;
the Xiǎojiā wear *zhéfēng*,
shaped like a *biàn* cap.
They have no prisons;
if there is a crime,
all the *jiā* discuss and execute the offender,
confiscating their wife and children as slaves.
For marriage, they all go to the wife's family;
after children are born and grow up,
they are then brought back.
Then, preparations for the funeral are gradually arranged.
Gold, silver, and valuables are exhausted for lavish burials,
stones are piled up for the mound,
and pines and cypresses are also planted.
Their people are fierce and impulsive,
possess great strength,
are skilled in warfare,
and are fond of raiding.
Wòjū and Dōnghuì are all subordinate to them.
Gōulí is also called Mò (耳).
There is a separate branch
that lives by small rivers,
hence they are called Xiǎoshuǐmò.
They produce excellent bows,
which are the so-called
“Mò bows”.
In the early years of Wáng Mǎng,
Gōulí soldiers were conscripted to attack the Xiōngnú.
The people did not wish to go,
but were forcibly dispatched,
and they all fled beyond the frontier to become bandits.
Tián Tán, the Grand Administrator of Liáoxī, pursued and attacked them,
and died in battle.
Wáng Mǎng ordered his general Yán Yóu to attack them,
lured Gōulí Hóu Zōu into the frontier,
beheaded him,
and sent his head to Cháng’ān.
Wáng Mǎng was greatly pleased,
and renamed the King of Gāogōulí to Hòugōulí Hóu.
Thereupon, the Mò people's raids on the frontier became even more severe.
In the eighth year of Jiànwǔ,
Gāogōulí sent envoys to pay tribute,
and Emperor Guāngwǔ restored their royal title.
In the winter of the twenty-third year,
over ten thousand people from the Cánzhīluò clan of Gōulí, led by Dàjiā Dài Shēng and others,
came to Lèlàng to submit.
In the spring of the twenty-fifth year,
Gōulí raided Yòuběipíng, Yúyáng, Shànggǔ, and Tàiyuán,
but Jì Róng, the Grand Administrator of Liáodōng, attracted them with kindness and trust,
and they all returned to loyalty to the frontier.
Later, King Gōng of Gōulí was born with his eyes open and able to see.
The people of the country cherished him,
and when he grew up, he was brave and strong,
frequently violating the border.
In the spring of the first year of Yuánxīng of Emperor Hé,
he again entered Liáodōng,
raiding six counties.
Grand Administrator Gěng Kuí attacked and defeated them,
beheading their chieftain.
In the fifth year of Yǒngchū of Emperor Ān,
Gōng sent envoys to offer tribute
and requested to be subordinate to Xuántú.
In the fifth year of Yuánchū,
he again, with the Huìmò, raided Xuántú
and attacked Huálì City.
In the spring of the first year of Jiànguāng,
Féng Huàn, Inspector of Yōuzhōu, Yáo Guāng, Grand Administrator of Xuántú, Cài Fěng, Grand Administrator of Liáodōng, and others led troops out of the frontier to attack them,
capturing and beheading the Huìmò chieftain,
and seizing weapons, horses, and valuables.
Gōng then sent his heir, Suìchéng, leading over two thousand men to meet Yáo Guāng and others,
sending envoys to feign surrender.
Yáo Guāng and others believed him,
and Suìchéng then occupied strategic positions to block the main army,
while secretly sending three thousand men to attack Xuántú and Liáodōng,
burning cities and walls,
and killing or wounding over two thousand people.
Thereupon, over three thousand cavalry from Guǎngyáng, Yúyáng, Yòuběipíng, and Zhuójùn dependent states were dispatched to rescue them,
but the Mò people had already departed.
In the summer,
he again, with over eight thousand Xiānbēi from Liáodōng, attacked Liáoduì,
killing and abducting officials and people.
Cài Fěng and others pursued and attacked them at Xīnchāng,
and were killed in battle.
The Merit Officer Gěng Hào, the Military Officer Yuán Lóng Duān, and the Military Horse Officer Gōngsūn Pú defended Cài Fěng with their lives,
all perishing in the battle array,
with over a hundred dead.
In the autumn,
Gōng then led several thousand cavalry from Mǎhán and Huìmò to besiege Xuántú.
King Wèi Qiútái of Fúyú sent his son, Wèi Qiútái, leading over twenty thousand men,
who joined forces with the provincial and commandery troops to attack and defeat them,
beheading over five hundred.
That year, Gōng died,
and his son Suìchéng was enthroned.
Yáo Guāng reported that he wished to take advantage of the funeral to dispatch troops and attack them,
and all those who debated thought it permissible.
Shàngshū Chén Zhōng said:
“Gōng was previously unruly and cunning,
and Yáo Guāng could not subdue him.
To attack him after his death
is not righteous.
It is proper to send condolences and inquiries,
and then reproach him for his former crimes,
pardoning him without further punishment,
to gain his future goodwill.”
Emperor Ān followed this.
The next year,
Suìchéng returned the Han captives
and went to Xuántú to surrender.
An imperial edict stated:
“Suìchéng and others were unruly and monstrous,
deserving to be cut up and minced to show the common people,
but fortunately, they have met with a pardon edict
and begged for forgiveness and surrendered.
The Xiānbēi and Huìmò have raided for years,
abducting common people,
often by the thousands,
but have only sent dozens or hundreds of people back,
which is not the heart of seeking assimilation.
From now on,
those who do not fight with the county officials but voluntarily approach and send back captives
shall all be given redemption money:
forty bolts of silk per adult,
and half for minors.”
Suìchéng died,
and his son Bógù was enthroned.
Thereafter, the Huìmò submitted,
and there was little trouble on the eastern frontier.
In the first year of Yángjiā of Emperor Shùn,
six agricultural colonies were established in Xuántú Commandery.
During the reigns of Zhì and Huán,
they again violated Xi’ānpíng in Liáodōng,
killed the Prefect of Dàifāng,
and plundered the wife and children of the Grand Administrator of Lèlàng.
In the second year of Jiànníng,
Gěng Lín, the Grand Administrator of Xuántú, attacked them,
beheading several hundred,
and Bógù surrendered,
requesting to be subordinate to Xuántú.
Dōng Wòjū is to the east of the Gàimǎ Dàshān Mountains in Gāogōulí.
To its east, it borders the great sea.
To the north, it borders Yìlóu and Fúyú.
To the south, it borders Huì Mò.
Its land is narrow from east to west
and long from north to south,
approximately a thousand *lǐ* square.
The soil is fertile and beautiful.
With mountains at its back and facing the sea,
it is suitable for the five grains
and skilled in cultivation.
It has settlements with chiefs.
The people are naturally straightforward, strong, and brave,
adept at wielding spears in foot combat.
Their language, eating and drinking habits, dwelling places, and clothing are similar to Gāogōulí.
For their burials,
they construct a large wooden coffin-chamber
more than ten *zhàng* long,
opening one end as a door.
The newly deceased are first temporarily buried.
When the flesh and skin are completely gone,
the bones are then taken and placed inside the coffin-chamber.
All family members share one coffin-chamber.
They carve wood to resemble ancestral tablets,
the number of which corresponds to the deceased.
When Wǔdì destroyed Cháoxiǎn,
he made the land of Wòjū into Xuántú Jùn.
Later, it was invaded by the Yí Mò,
and the commandery was moved to the northwest of Gāogōulí.
Wòjū was then made into a county,
subordinate to the Dōngbù Dūwèi of Lèlàng.
When Guāngwǔ abolished the Dūwèi office,
their chiefs were all subsequently enfeoffed
as Wòjū Hóu.
Their land was cramped and small,
situated between large states,
and thus they became subjects of Gāogōulí.
Gāogōulí then appointed a *dàrén* from among them as an envoy
to supervise and lead them.
They were charged with taxes,
sable furs, cloth, fish, salt,
and foodstuffs from the sea.
Beautiful women were sent to be servants and concubines.
There is also Běi Wòjū,
also named Zhìgōulóu,
more than eight hundred *lǐ* from Nán Wòjū.
Its customs are all the same as the south.
Its southern border adjoins Yìlóu.
The Yìlóu people are fond of sailing boats to plunder,
and Běi Wòjū fears them.
Every summer, they hide in caves.
Until winter, when the water routes are impassable,
they then descend to live in their settlements.
Their elders say
that they once found a cloth garment in the sea,
its shape like the clothing of people of the central plains,
but its two sleeves were three *zhàng* long.
Also, they saw a person on a broken boat by the shore,
who had another face on the crown of his head.
They could not communicate with him,
and he died without eating.
They also say there is a kingdom of women in the sea,
without men.
Some transmit that their country has a divine well,
and whoever gazes into it will give birth to a child.
Huì borders Gāogōulí and Wòjū to the north,
Jīnhán to the south,
reaches the great sea to the east,
and Lèlàng to the west.
Huì, Wòjū, and Gāogōulí
were originally all lands of Cháoxiǎn.
In ancient times, Wǔwáng enfeoffed Jīzǐ in Cháoxiǎn.
Jīzǐ taught them etiquette, righteousness, agriculture, and sericulture,
and also instituted the Eight Articles of Instruction.
His people never stole from each other
and had no need to lock their doors.
Women were chaste and trustworthy.
Food and drink were served in *biāndòu* vessels.
After more than forty generations,
reaching Lord Zhǔn of Cháoxiǎn,
who styled himself King.
During the great chaos at the beginning of Hàn,
tens of thousands of people from Yān, Qí, and Zhào went there to seek refuge.
A man from Yān, Wèi Mǎn, defeated Zhǔn and became King of Cháoxiǎn himself.
The kingdom was passed down to his grandson Yòuqú.
In the first year of Yuánsuò,
Lord Nánlǘ of Huì and others rebelled against Yòuqú,
leading two hundred eighty thousand people to pledge allegiance to Liáodōng.
Wǔdì made their land into Cānghǎi Jùn,
but it was abolished after several years.
In the third year of Yuánfēng,
Cháoxiǎn was destroyed,
and Lèlàng, Líntún, Xuántú, and Zhēnfān four commanderies were established.
In the fifth year of Shǐyuán under Zhāodì,
Líntún and Zhēnfān were abolished,
and their territories merged into Lèlàng and Xuántú.
Xuántú was again moved to reside in Gāogōulí.
From the Dāndān Dàlǐng Mountains eastward,
Wòjū and Huì Mò were all subordinate to Lèlàng.
Later, due to the vastness of the territory,
the seven counties in the eastern part were again separated
and the Lèlàng Dōngbù Dūwèi was established.
After they pledged allegiance,
customs gradually became less pure,
and laws and prohibitions also progressively increased,
reaching more than sixty articles.
In the sixth year of Jiànwǔ,
the Dūwèi office was abolished,
and the eastern territories were abandoned.
All their chiefs were enfeoffed as Xiànhóu,
and they all offered seasonal tribute and congratulations.
There were no great kings or chiefs.
Their officials included *hóu*, *yìjūn*, and *sānlǎo*.
The elders call themselves of the same lineage as Gāogōulí,
and their language, laws, and customs are generally similar.
Their people are simple-minded,
have few desires,
and do not beg.
Both men and women wear curved-collar clothing.
Their custom respects mountains and rivers.
Mountains and rivers each have their tribal boundaries,
and they must not arbitrarily interfere with each other.
Those of the same surname do not intermarry.
They have many taboos.
In cases of illness or death,
they immediately abandon their old homes
and build new dwellings.
They know how to plant hemp,
raise silkworms,
and make cotton cloth.
They understand how to observe stars and constellations
to predict whether the year will be abundant or scarce.
They regularly perform sacrifices to Heaven in the tenth month,
drinking, singing, and dancing day and night,
naming it
"Wǔtiān."
They also worship tigers as gods.
If settlements invade each other,
they punish each other,
demanding captives, cattle, or horses,
naming it
"Zétuò."
Those who kill must pay with their lives.
There are few bandits.
They can fight on foot,
making spears three *zhàng* long,
which are sometimes wielded by several people together.
The Lèlàng *bógōng* (a type of bow) comes from their land.
There are also many spotted leopards,
and small horses that can pass under fruit trees.
Striped fish come from the sea.
Whenever envoys come, they offer these.
There are three types of Hán: one is Mǎhán,
two is Jīnhán,
and three is Biànchén.
Mǎhán is in the west,
with fifty-four states.
Its north borders Lèlàng,
and its south borders Wō.
Jīnhán is in the east,
with twelve states.
Its north borders Huì Mò.
Biànchén is to the south of Jīnhán,
also with twelve states.
Its south also borders Wō.
In total, there are seventy-eight states,
among which Bǎijì is one state.
The large ones have over ten thousand households,
the small ones several thousand families.
They are all located between mountains and the sea.
The land combined is over four thousand *lǐ* square.
The sea limits them from east to west.
They are all the ancient kingdom of Chén.
Mǎhán is the largest.
They jointly established one of their own as Chén Wáng,
whose capital was Mùzhī Guó,
ruling all the land of the Three Hán.
Their kings were all originally Mǎhán people.
The Mǎhán people knew how to cultivate fields and raise silkworms,
making cotton cloth.
They produced large chestnuts, like pears.
There were long-tailed chickens,
with tails five feet long.
Their settlements were mixed,
and they had no city walls or outer walls.
They made earthen chambers,
shaped like tombs,
with the entrance at the top.
They did not know how to kneel or bow.
There was no distinction between old and young, or male and female.
They did not value gold, precious jewels, brocades, or rugs,
and did not know how to ride oxen or horses.
They only prized stringed pearls,
which they used to adorn their clothes,
and also hung from their necks and dangled from their ears.
Most of them had their hair tied in a topknot and exposed (魁頭露紒),
wearing cloth robes and straw sandals.
Their people were strong and brave.
When young men built houses or performed strenuous labor,
they would thread a rope through the skin of their backs,
and hang a large log from it,
shouting to show their strength.
They regularly sacrificed to ghosts and spirits in the fifth month when the fields were finished,
drinking and feasting day and night,
gathering in groups to sing and dance.
Their dances often involved dozens of people tapping the ground in unison to keep time.
In the tenth month, when the agricultural work was complete,
they did the same again.
Each state and settlement appointed one person to preside over the sacrifices to the heavenly spirits,
who was called
"Tiānjūn."
They also erected a Sūtú,
setting up a large wooden post from which bells and drums were hung,
to serve the ghosts and spirits.
Their southern border was close to Wō,
and some of them also had tattooed bodies.
The Chénhán,
whose elders said they were fugitives from Qín,
fleeing forced labor,
who came to Hán territory.
Mǎhán ceded its eastern borderland to them.
They called a state a "bāng,"
a bow an "hú,"
a bandit a "kòu,"
serving wine "xíngshāng,"
and addressing each other as "tú."
This was similar to the Qín language,
so some called them Qínhán.
They had city walls, fences, and houses.
Each of the small separate settlements
had its own chief (qúshuài).
The largest were called Chénzhì,
next were Jiǎncè,
next Fánzhǐ,
next Shāxī,
and next Yìjiè.
Their land was fertile and beautiful,
suitable for the five grains.
They knew how to raise silkworms and cultivate mulberry,
making pongee and cloth.
They rode oxen and horses.
Marriages were conducted with propriety.
Travelers yielded the road to each other.
The state produced iron,
and Wèi, Wō, and Mǎhán all purchased it from them.
All trade
used iron as currency.
It was their custom to enjoy singing, dancing, drinking, and playing the zither.
When children were born, they wanted their heads to be flat,
so they all pressed them with stones.
Biànchén and Chénhán lived mixed together,
their city walls and clothing were the same,
but their language and customs were different.
Their people were all tall,
with beautiful hair,
and clean clothing.
Their laws were strict and severe.
Their country was near Wō,
so many of them had tattooed bodies.
Initially,
King Jǔn of Cháoxiǎn was defeated by Wèimǎn,
so he led his remaining several thousand followers into the sea,
attacked Mǎhán,
defeated it,
and established himself as King of Hán.
Later, Jǔn's lineage died out,
and the Mǎhán people again established themselves as King of Chén.
In the twentieth year of Jiànwǔ,
Sūmǎtí and others from the Hán people and the Liánsī people went to Lèláng to offer tribute.
Guāngwǔ enfeoffed Sūmǎtí as Hán Liánsī Yìjūn,
making him subject to Lèláng Prefecture,
to pay homage seasonally.
Towards the end of Emperor Líng's reign,
Hán and Wèi both flourished,
