and the commanderies and prefectures could not control them.
The common people suffered from chaos,
and many became refugees fleeing into Hán.
West of Mǎhán,
there was the state of Zhōuhú on an island in the sea.
Its people were short,
with shaved heads,
wearing leather clothes,
covering the upper body but not the lower.
They liked to raise cattle and pigs.
They traveled by boat,
trading in Hán territory.
Wō was in the great sea southeast of Hán,
dwelling by mountains.
There were over a hundred states in total.
Since Emperor Wǔ destroyed Cháoxiǎn,
about thirty states communicated with Hán through envoys,
each state calling itself a king,
and passing down their traditions for generations.
The Great King of Wō resided in the Yémádái state.
The frontier of Lèláng Prefecture
was 12,000 *lǐ* from their state,
and 7,000 *lǐ* from their northwestern border, Gūxiéhán state.
Their land was generally east of Kuàijī Dōngyě,
and close to Zhūyá and Dān'ěr,
thus their laws and customs were often similar.
The soil was suitable for rice, millet, hemp, ramie, silkworms, and mulberries,
and they knew how to weave and spin to make pongee and cloth.
They produced white pearls and green jade.
Their mountains had cinnabar soil.
The climate was mild,
and edible vegetables grew in winter and summer.
There were no cattle, horses, tigers, leopards, sheep, or magpies.
Their weapons included spears, shields, and wooden bows,
with bamboo arrows, some tipped with bone.
Men all tattooed their faces and bodies,
using the size and placement of the tattoos to distinguish social ranks.
Men's clothing consisted of horizontal strips of fabric tied and joined together.
Women wore their hair loose and tied in a knot,
their clothes were like single blankets,
worn by passing the head through.
They all smeared their bodies with cinnabar,
like the Chinese use powder.
They had city walls, fences, and houses.
Parents and siblings lived in separate places,
only gathering together without distinction between men and women.
They ate with their hands,
but used *biān* and *dòu* vessels.
It was customary to go barefoot,
and squatting was considered respectful.
Their people were fond of wine.
Many lived long lives,
with many reaching over a hundred years.
The country had many women;
important men all had four or five wives,
the rest had two or three.
Women were not licentious or jealous.
Also, it was not customary to steal,
and there were few disputes.
Those who violated the law had their wives and children enslaved,
and for serious offenses, their entire family was exterminated.
After a death, the body was kept for over ten days;
family members wept
and abstained from wine and food,
while others of their kind gathered to sing and dance for entertainment.
They used bone scorching for divination,
to determine good and bad fortune.
When traveling across the sea,
they assigned one person to not comb their hair, wash,
eat meat,
or go near women.
This person was called
"Chíchuāi."
If the journey was smooth and auspicious,
they were rewarded with valuables;
if they fell ill or suffered harm,
it was believed that the Chíchuāi had not been diligent,
and they would then kill him.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ Zhōngyuán,
the Wōnúnú state offered tribute and paid homage,
their envoy claiming to be a Dàfū,
from the southernmost border of Wō country.
Guāngwǔ bestowed upon him an imperial seal and ribbon.
In the first year of Yǒngchū during Emperor Ān's reign,
King Shuàishēng of Wō country and others presented 160 living captives,
requesting an audience.
Between the reigns of Huán and Líng,
Wō country was in great chaos,
with mutual attacks and conflicts,
and for years there was no ruler.
There was a woman named Bīmǐhū,
who was elderly and unmarried,
serving the way of ghosts and spirits,
and capable of enchanting the masses with sorcery.
Thus, they collectively established her as queen.
She had a thousand female attendants,
few of whom were ever seen;
only one man served her food and drink,
and conveyed messages.
Her residential palace, watchtowers, and city fences
were all guarded by armed men.
Her laws and customs were strict and severe.
East of the kingdom of Nǚwáng, crossing the sea for over a thousand *lǐ*, one reaches the kingdom of Jūnú.
Although all are of the Wō race,
they are not subject to the Nǚwáng.
South of the kingdom of Nǚwáng for four thousand *lǐ* is the kingdom of Zhūrú,
where people are three to four *chǐ* tall.
From Zhūrú, sailing southeast for one year,
one reaches Luǒguó and Hēichǐguó.
The extent of reports from envoys
ends here.
Overseas from Kuàijī there are the Dōngtí people,
divided into more than twenty states.
There are also Yízhōu and Chánzhōu.
Tradition says that Qín Shǐhuáng dispatched the *fāngshì* Xú Fú with several thousand boys and girls into the sea
to seek the immortals of Pénglái, but failed to find them.
Xú Fú, fearing execution, dared not return,
and consequently settled on this island.
Generations succeeded one another,
numbering tens of thousands of families.
Their people sometimes came to market in Kuàijī.
There were people from the Dōngyě county of Kuàijī who went to sea, encountered a storm,
and drifted to Chánzhōu.
The locations are extremely distant,
making travel impossible.
A commentary says: In ancient times, Jīzǐ, avoiding the decline of the Yīn dynasty,
fled to Cháoxiǎn.
Initially, the customs of his country were unheard of,
but when he implemented the eight articles of agreement,
making people aware of prohibitions,
there were no lewd acts or banditry in the settlements,
and doors were not locked at night.
He changed their stubborn and crude customs,
and adopted lenient laws.
This continued for several hundred or even a thousand years.
Therefore, the Eastern Yí are generally known for their gentleness and prudence as their prevailing custom,
different from the peoples of the three other directions.
If governance is effective,
then morality and righteousness exist.
Kǒng Ní harbored resentment,
believing that one could dwell among the Jiǔ Yí.
Some doubted its crudeness.
The Master said:
"If a *jūnzǐ* dwells there,
how can there be crudeness!"
This also certainly had its reasons.
Afterward, they established communication with merchants,
and gradually interacted with the superior states.
However, the Yān man Wèi Mǎn disrupted and corrupted their customs,
whereupon they became debased and different.
Lǎo Zǐ said:
"The more laws and edicts multiply,
the more bandits there are."
If Jīzǐ, simplifying legal clauses, relied on trust and righteousness,
he indeed grasped the origin of the laws made by the sagely and virtuous!
An encomium says: Dwelling in this Yúyí,
it is called Yánggǔ.
Nesting in mountains, lurking in seas,
their domain encompasses nine clans.
At the end of Yíng (Qín), chaos reigned,
and Yān people avoided the calamity.
Mingling Chinese (Huá) with their crude origins,
they then communicated with the mighty Hàn.
Distant and remote interpreters,
some followed, some rebelled.
Biography of the Southern Mán and Southwestern Yí, Chapter 76
In ancient times, Gāoxīnshì suffered from the incursions of the Quǎnrong.
The Emperor was troubled by their violent aggressions,
and military expeditions failed to overcome them.
He then sought and recruited throughout the realm,
proclaiming that whoever could obtain the head of General Wú of the Quǎnrong
would be rewarded with a thousand *yì* of gold,
ten thousand households,
and also his young daughter as a wife.
At that time, the Emperor owned a dog
whose fur was five-colored,
named Pánhù.
After the decree was issued,
Pánhù indeed carried a human head and presented it below the palace gate.
The courtiers were astonished and examined it,
and it was indeed the head of General Wú.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
but considered that Pánhù could not be given his daughter as a wife,
nor was there a way to bestow a title or fief,
and he discussed how to reward him but did not know what was appropriate.
The daughter heard of this,
and believed that since the Emperor had issued a decree,
its trustworthiness could not be violated,
and therefore requested to go.
The Emperor, having no choice,
then married his daughter to Pánhù.
Pánhù, having obtained the daughter,
carried her and ran into the Southern Mountains,
stopping in a stone chamber.
The place was precipitous and remote,
with no human tracks.
Thereupon, the daughter removed her clothes,
made a servant's knot in her hair,
and wore a single-legged garment.
The Emperor, filled with sorrow and longing,
sent envoys to search for her,
but they invariably encountered storms and thunderous darkness,
and the envoys could not proceed.
After three years,
she gave birth to twelve children,
six boys and six girls.
After Pánhù died,
they consequently married among themselves.
They wove and spun tree bark,
dyed it with grass fruits,
favored five-colored clothing,
and their garments all had tail-like shapes.
Their mother later returned,
and reported the situation to the Emperor.
Thereupon, he sent for and brought the children.
Their clothes were striped and varied,
their language unintelligible,
they liked to go into mountains and valleys,
and disliked open plains.
The Emperor respected their wishes
and bestowed upon them famous mountains and vast marshes.
Their descendants proliferated,
and they were called Mányí.
Outwardly foolish but inwardly cunning,
they cherished their homeland and ancient customs.
Because their ancestor had rendered meritorious service
and their mother was the Emperor's daughter,
they engaged in farming and trading,
without passes or permits for barriers,
or taxes and levies.
They had local rulers and chiefs,
all of whom were granted seals and ribbons,
and wore otter-skin caps.
The principal chiefs were called *jīngfū*,
and they called each other *yāngtú*.
These are the Mán of Chángshā and Wǔlíng today.
During the time of Táng and Yú,
treaties and pledges were made with them,
hence they were called *yāofú* (pledged subjects).
During the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
they gradually became a border threat.
By the Zhōu era,
their factions grew increasingly powerful.
When Xuānwáng brought about a revitalization,
he ordered Fāng Shū to lead a southern expedition against the Mán territory,
which the poets referred to as
"the Mán Jīng coming to submit."
It also says:
"Foolish Mán Jīng,
you make the great state your enemy."
This shows that
their factions were numerous and widespread,
and thus they resisted all the Xià states.
When Píngwáng moved east,
the Mán then violently encroached upon the superior states.
When Jìn Wénhóu assisted in governance,
he led Cài Gònghóu to attack and defeat them.
By the time of Chǔ Wǔwáng,
the Mán and the son of Luō together defeated the Chǔ army,
killing their general Qū Xiá.
When Zhuāngwáng first ascended the throne,
the people were hungry and the army weak,
and they were again raided by them.
After the Chǔ army was reinvigorated,
they then submitted,
and from then on belonged to Chǔ.
In the Battle of Yānlíng,
the Mán joined Gōngwáng's forces to attack Jìn.
When Wú Qǐ served as prime minister to Dàowáng,
he subjugated the Mán and Yuè to the south,
thus possessing Dòngtíng and Cāngwú.
Qín Zhāowáng sent Bái Qǐ to attack Chǔ,
seizing the Mányí territory,
and first established Qiánzhōng Commandery.
When the Hàn dynasty arose,
it was renamed Wǔlíng.
Annually, adult males were required to pay one bolt of cloth,
and young males two *zhàng*,
which was called *cóngbù*.
Although they sometimes acted as bandits,
they were not a major concern for the commanderies and kingdoms.
During the restoration of
Guāngwǔ, the Mán-Yí (barbarians) of Wǔlíng became particularly numerous and powerful.
In the 23rd year of Jiànwǔ (47 CE),
Jīngfū Xiāng Dānchéng and others, relying on their perilous strongholds,
greatly plundered the commanderies and counties.
Liú Shàng, the General of Wǔwēi, was dispatched, raising over ten thousand soldiers from Nánjùn, Chángshā, and Wǔlíng.
They sailed up the Yuánshǔi River into Wǔxī to attack them.
Shàng, underestimating the enemy, advanced into dangerous terrain.
The mountains were deep, and the waters swift;
the boats could not proceed upstream.
The Mán (barbarians) knew that Shàng's provisions were scarce and that he had advanced far,
and also that he was unfamiliar with the paths.
So they massed and held their strongholds.
Shàng, running out of food, led his forces back.
The Mán (barbarians) ambushed and fought them along the route.
Shàng's army was utterly defeated,
and all were overwhelmed and captured.
In the 24th year (48 CE),
Xiāng Dānchéng and others descended to attack Lín Yuán.
Yèzhě Lǐ Sōng and Zhōngshān Tàishǒu Mǎ Chéng were dispatched to attack them,
but could not overcome them.
In the spring of the following year (49 CE),
Fúbō Jiāngjūn Mǎ Yuán, Zhōnglángjiāng Liú Kuāng, Mǎ Wǔ, Sūn Yǒng, and others
led troops to Lín Yuán
and defeated them.
Dānchéng and others, suffering from hunger and distress, begged to surrender.
As Mǎ Yuán unfortunately died of illness,
Yèzhě Zōng Jūn listened and accepted all their surrenders.
Officials were appointed for them,
and the various Mán (barbarians) were thus pacified.
In the 1st year of Jiànchū (76 CE) of Sùzōng,
Chén Cóng and others, Mán (barbarians) from Lǐzhōng in Wǔlíng, rebelled,
entering the Mán (barbarian) territory of Língyáng.
That winter,
the Wǔlǐ Jīngfū Mán (barbarians) of Língyáng, acting for the commandery, attacked and defeated Chén Cóng,
and Chén Cóng and his followers all surrendered.
In the winter of the 3rd year (78 CE),
Tán Érjiàn and others, Mán (barbarians) from Lóuzhōng, rebelled again,
attacking and burning parts of Língyáng, Zuòtáng, and Chánlíng.
In the spring of the following year (79 CE),
troops were raised from seven commanderies in Jīngzhōu, as well as from Rǔnán and Yǐngchuān (including)
They defended Língyáng,
and four thousand Mán Jīngfū (barbarian leaders) from Chōngzhōng and Wǔlǐ who had not rebelled were recruited
to attack the rebels in Lǐzhōng.
In the spring of the 5th year (80 CE),
Tán Érjiàn and others requested to surrender,
but this was not granted.
The commandery then advanced its troops and fought them at Hóngxià,
greatly defeating them.
Tán Érjiàn's head was cut off,
and the rest fled back to Lóuzhōng,
then sent another request to surrender,
which was then accepted.
Thereupon, the garrison troops in Wǔlíng were dismissed,
and rewards were distributed according to merit.
In the winter of the 4th year of Yǒngyuán (92 CE) of Hédi,
Tán Róng and others, Mán (barbarians) from Lóuzhōng and Lǐzhōng, rebelled.
They burned postal stations,
killed and plundered officials and common people.
The commandery troops attacked, defeated, and pacified them.
In the 2nd year of Yuánchū (115 CE) of Āndì,
the Lǐzhōng Mán (barbarians), feeling that the levies and taxes imposed by the commanderies and counties were unfair,
harbored resentment.
They consequently gathered over two thousand people from various tribes in Chōngzhōng
and attacked cities and killed senior officials.
The province and commandery recruited six contingents of Wǔlǐ Mán (barbarian) troops to pursue and defeat them,
and they all dispersed and surrendered.
The chieftains of Wǔlǐ and the six contingents were given gold and silk according to their varying ranks.
In the autumn of the following year (116 CE),
four thousand Mán (barbarians) from Lóuzhōng and Lǐzhōng became brigands.
Furthermore, Yáng Sūn, Chén Tāng, and others, over a thousand Mán (barbarians) from Línglíng,
wore red turbans,
called themselves generals,
burned official buildings,
and plundered the common people.
The province and commandery recruited "good Mán" (barbarians) to suppress and pacify them.
In the 1st year of Yǒnghé (136 CE) of Shùndì,
the Tàishǒu of Wǔlíng submitted a memorial,
stating that since the Mán-Yí (barbarians) had submitted,
they could be treated like Hàn people
and their rent and taxes increased.
All the deliberators thought it acceptable.
Shàngshūlìng Yú Xǔ alone memorialized, saying:
"Since ancient times, sagely kings have not made subjects of foreign customs.
It is not that their virtue could not reach them,
or their might could not be applied,
but because they knew their bestial hearts were greedy
and difficult to govern with ritual.
Therefore, they were restrained and appeased;
if they submitted, they were accepted without opposition;
if they rebelled, they were repulsed but not pursued.
The old system of the former emperors,
regarding the amount of tribute and tax,
has a long history.
Now, to arbitrarily increase it
will certainly lead to resentment and rebellion.
Considering what is gained,
it will not compensate for what is spent,
and there will certainly be regret later."
The Emperor did not heed him.
That winter, the Mán (barbarians) from Lǐzhōng and Lóuzhōng indeed disputed the tribute cloth, which was not according to the old agreement,
and consequently killed local officials,
and their entire tribes rebelled.
In the spring of the following year (137 CE),
twenty thousand Mán (barbarians) besieged Chōngchéng,
and eight thousand raided Yídào.
Wǔlíng Tàishǒu Lǐ Jìn was dispatched to attack and defeat them,
beheading several hundred,
and the rest all surrendered.
Lǐ Jìn then selected competent officials
who gained their trust and goodwill.
After nine years in the commandery,
Empress Dowager Liáng took charge of the court,
and issued an edict to increase Lǐ Jìn's rank by two thousand dàn and
granted him two hundred thousand coins.
In the autumn of the 1st year of Yuánjiā (151 CE) of Huándì,
Zhān Shān and others, over four thousand Mán (barbarians) from Wǔlíng, rebelled,
detained the county magistrate,
and gathered in the deep mountains.
By the 1st year of Yǒngxīng (153 CE),
Tàishǒu Yīng Fèng, using kindness and trust, enticed them,
and they all surrendered and dispersed.
In the eleventh month of the 3rd year of Yǒngshòu (157 CE),
the Chángshā Mán (barbarians) rebelled,
garrisoning Yìyáng.
By the autumn of the 3rd year of Yánxī (160 CE),
they plundered the commandery's borders,
their numbers reaching over ten thousand,
killing and wounding senior officials.
Furthermore, the Línglíng Mán (barbarians) entered Chángshā.
That winter,
over six thousand Mán (barbarians) from Wǔlíng raided Jiānglíng.
Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Dù, Yèzhě Mǎ Mù, and Nánjùn Tàishǒu Lǐ Sù all fled.
Lǐ Sù's Zhǔbù Hú Shuǎng stopped his horse and admonished him, saying:
"The Mán-Yí (barbarians) saw that the commandery had no preparations,
and so dared to advance by taking advantage of the opportunity.
My lord is a high official of the state,
with a thousand li of connected cities.
Raising the banner and beating the drum
would summon ten thousand people immediately.
How can you abandon the heavy responsibility of your office
and become a fugitive?"
Lǐ Sù drew his blade towards Hú Shuǎng, saying:
"Clerk, hurry and leave!
The Tàishǒu is in dire straits now;
how can there be time for such advice?"
Hú Shuǎng held onto the horse and stubbornly admonished him.
Lǐ Sù then killed Hú Shuǎng and fled.
The Emperor, hearing of this,
summoned Lǐ Sù to be executed in the market,
reduced Liú Dù and Mǎ Mù's punishment by one degree from death,
restored Hú Shuǎng's family and clan,
and appointed one person from his family as a Láng (gentleman-in-waiting).
Thereupon, Dù Shàng, the Right Commandant, was appointed Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
to suppress the Chángshā rebels,
and he pacified them.
Chējì Jiāngjūn Féng Gǔn was also dispatched to suppress the Wǔlíng Mán (barbarians),
and they all surrendered and dispersed.
When the army returned,
the rebels again raided Guìyáng.
Tàishǒu Liáo Xī fled.
The Wǔlíng Mán (barbarians) also attacked their commandery again.
Tàishǒu Chén Fèng led officials and people to attack and defeat them,
beheading over three thousand,
with over two thousand surrendering.
By the 3rd year of Zhōngpíng (186 CE) of Língdì,
the Wǔlíng Mán (barbarians) rebelled again,
raiding the commandery's borders.
The province and commandery attacked and defeated them.
The Lǐjì (Book of Rites) states:
"To the south are called Mán,
tattooed-forehead and crossed-feet."
Their custom is for men and women to bathe together in the same stream,
hence they are called Jiāozhǐ (crossed-feet).
To their west is the kingdom of man-eaters.
When they bear their first child, they immediately butcher and eat it,
calling it "suitable for the younger brother."
If the taste is good,
they present it to their lord,
and the lord is pleased and rewards the father.
If they take a beautiful wife,
they yield her to their elder brother.
The Wūhǔ people are such today.
South of Jiāozhǐ is the state of Yuèshāng.
When Zhōu Gōng acted as regent for six years,
he established rites and composed music.
The world was at peace.
Yuèshāng, by means of three interpreters, presented a white pheasant.
They said:
"The roads are long and distant,
and the mountains and rivers are steep and deep.
Our language and envoys cannot communicate,
therefore we have used multiple interpreters to come to court."
King Chéng referred this to Zhōu Gōng.
Zhōu Gōng said:
"If virtue is not extended to them,
then a gentleman does not accept their tribute.
If governance is not applied to them,
then a gentleman does not treat their people as subjects.
How can I receive this gift!"
Their envoy requested, saying:
"I received orders from the elders
of my country, who said: 'It has been a long time
since Heaven has sent fierce winds, thunder, and rain.
Perhaps there is a sage in the Central Plains?
If so, why not go and pay him homage.' "
Zhōu Gōng then returned it to the King,
citing the divine achievements of the former kings,
and offered it in the ancestral temple.
When the virtue of Zhōu eventually declined,
these contacts gradually ceased.
When the Viscount of Chǔ established hegemony,
the Bǎiyuè paid tribute.
When Qín unified All-under-Heaven,
it awed and subdued the southern barbarians,
and first opened up the lands beyond the mountain ranges,
establishing Nánhǎi, Guìlín, and Xiàngjùn commanderies.
When Hàn arose,
Wèi Tuó established himself as King of Nányuè,
and passed down the kingdom for five generations.
Until the fifth year of Yuándǐng in the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
it was finally滅之,
and nine commanderies were established,
with the Inspector of Jiāozhǐ overseeing them.
The two commanderies of Zhūyá and Dān'ěr were on an island in the sea,
a thousand *lǐ* from east to west,
and five hundred *lǐ* from north to south.
Their chiefs esteemed long ears,
and all pierced them and hung weights,
so they dangled three inches below their shoulders.
At the end of Emperor Wǔ's reign,
Sūn Xìng of Kuàijī, the Administrator of Zhūyá, demanded wide cloth as tribute.
The barbarians could not endure the imposition,
and consequently attacked the commandery and killed Xìng.
Xìng's son, Bào Hé, led loyal men and again defeated them.
He personally took charge of the commandery's affairs,
and suppressed the remaining factions.
It took several years to pacify them.
Bào dispatched an envoy to return the seal and ribbon,
and submitted a memorial reporting the situation.
An imperial edict immediately appointed Bào as Administrator of Zhūyá.
His authority and governance were widely effective,
and tribute arrived annually.
The Central Plains coveted their precious bribes,
and gradually encroached upon and insulted them,
hence they rebelled every few years.
In the third year of Chūyuán during Emperor Yuán's reign,
they were finally abolished.
The commandery had been established for a total of sixty-five years.
When Wáng Mǎng assisted in governance,
in the second year of Yuánshǐ,
the state of Huángzhī, south of Rìnán, came to present a rhinoceros.
In all the territories under Jiāozhǐ's jurisdiction,
although commanderies and counties were established,
their languages were all different,
requiring multiple interpreters to communicate.
The people were like birds and beasts,
with no distinction between old and young.
They tied their hair in a topknot and went barefoot,
wearing cloth passed through a hole in the head.
Later, many criminals from the Central Plains were relocated,
and made to live among them.
Only then did they gradually learn to speak,
and slowly acquired manners and culture.
During the Guāngwǔ Restoration,
Xī Guāng served in Jiāozhǐ,
and Rèn Yán guarded Jiǔzhēn.
Thereupon, they taught them farming,
established a system for caps and shoes,
first set up matchmakers,
and began to understand marriage,
established schools,
and guided them in rites and righteousness.
In the twelfth year of Jiànwǔ,
Zhāng Yóu, a chieftain of the barbarians outside the borders of Jiǔzhēn,
led his people to admire and embrace the culture and submit,
and was enfeoffed as the Lord of Guīhàn Ward.
The next year,
barbarians from outside the borders of Nányuè presented white pheasants and white rabbits.
By the sixteenth year,
Zhēng Cè, a woman from Jiāozhǐ, and her younger sister Zhēng È rebelled,
and attacked the commandery.
Zhēng Cè was
the daughter of a Luò general from Mílìng county.
She was married to Shī Suǒ of Zhūréng,
and was very courageous.
Sū Dìng, the Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, restrained her with law,
and Cè was indignant,
hence she rebelled.
Thereupon, the barbarian communities of Jiǔzhēn, Rìnán, and Hépǔ all responded to her,
and they seized a total of sixty-five cities,
proclaiming themselves king.
The Inspector of Jiāozhǐ and the various Administrators could barely defend themselves.
Emperor Guāngwǔ then issued an edict to Chángshā, Hépǔ, and Jiāozhǐ to prepare chariots and boats,
repair roads and bridges,
clear blocked streams,
and store grain.
In the eighteenth year,
he dispatched Fúbō General Mǎ Yuán and Lóuchuán General Duàn Zhì,
to mobilize over ten thousand soldiers from Chángshā, Guìyáng, Línglíng, and Cāngwú to suppress them.
The next year, in the fourth month of summer,
Mǎ Yuán defeated Jiāozhǐ,
beheaded Zhēng Cè and Zhēng È,
and the rest surrendered and dispersed.
He advanced to attack the bandits such as Dū Yáng in Jiǔzhēn,
defeated and pacified them.
He relocated over three hundred households of their chiefs to Línglíng.
Thereupon, all the lands south of the mountain ranges were pacified.
In the first year of Yuánhé during Emperor Sùzōng's reign,
the barbarian chieftain Jiū Bù Shì Rén
from outside the borders of Rìnán presented a live rhinoceros and a white pheasant.
In the twelfth year of Yǒngyuán during Emperor Hé's reign, in the fourth month of summer,
over two thousand barbarians from Rìnán and Xiànglín plundered the common people,
and burned official buildings.
The commanderies and counties dispatched troops to attack,
beheading their chiefs,
and the remaining forces then surrendered.
Thereupon, an Army Commander and Chief Clerk of Xiànglín was established,
to prevent such troubles.
In the first year of Yǒngchū during Emperor Ān's reign,
the Yèláng barbarians from outside the borders of Jiǔzhēn offered their entire territory for submission,
opening up a border of one thousand eight hundred forty *lǐ*.
In the second year of Yuánchū,
the Cāngwú barbarians rebelled,
and the next year,
they enticed several thousand barbarian and Han people from Yùlín and Hépǔ to attack Cāngwú Commandery.
Empress Dowager Dèng dispatched Imperial Censor Rèn Zhuó
with an imperial edict to pardon them,
and the bandits all surrendered and dispersed.
In the first year of Yán'guāng,
barbarians from outside the borders of Jiǔzhēn offered tribute and submitted.
In the third year,
barbarians from outside the borders of Rìnán again came and submitted.
In the sixth year of Yǒngjiàn during Emperor Shùn's reign,
King Biàn of Yèdiáo, from outside the borders of Rìnán, sent envoys to offer tribute,
and the Emperor bestowed upon Biàn a gold seal and purple ribbon.
In the second year of Yǒnghé,
several thousand men from the external barbarian tribes of Rìnán and Xiànglín, led by Qūlián and others, attacked Xiànglín County,
burned the city temple,
and killed the chief official.
The Inspector of Jiāozhǐ, Fán Yǎn, dispatched over ten thousand troops from the two commanderies of Jiāozhǐ and Jiǔzhēn to rescue it.
The soldiers, tired of the distant campaign,
rebelled,
and attacked his headquarters.
Although the two commanderies defeated the rebels,
the strength of the bandits grew.
At that time, the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor, Jiǎ Chāng, was on a mission in Rìnán,
and immediately joined forces with the provincial and commandery authorities to suppress them.
They were unsuccessful,
and consequently came under attack.
They were besieged for over a year, and their troops and grain supplies ran out,
which concerned the Emperor.
The following year,
he summoned the high ministers, all officials, and the subordinate officials of the Four Bureaus,
and asked for their strategies.
All proposed dispatching a great general,
and mobilizing forty thousand troops from Jīng, Yáng, Yǎn, and Yù provinces to go there.
The Major of the General-in-Chief's staff, Lǐ Gù, rebutted:
"If Jīng and Yáng were peaceful,
dispatching them would be acceptable.
But now, bandits in these two provinces are organized and rampant,
the barbarians in Wǔlíng and Nánjùn are not yet settled,
and Chángshā and Guìyáng have frequently been levied.
If they are disturbed again,
it will surely create further trouble.
This is the first reason why it is not feasible.
Furthermore, if the people of Yǎn and Yù are suddenly levied,
sent thousands of *lǐ* away,
with no return date,
and the imperial edict urges them on,
it will inevitably lead to rebellion and desertion.
This is the second reason why it is not feasible.
The southern climate is warm and humid,
and there is also malaria,
causing four or five out of ten to die.
This is the third reason why it is not feasible.
After traveling thousands of *lǐ*,
the officers and soldiers will be exhausted.
By the time they reach Lǐngnán,
they will no longer be fit for combat.
This is the fourth reason why it is not feasible.
A military march covers thirty *lǐ* per day,
and Rìnán is over nine thousand *lǐ* away.
It would take three hundred days to arrive.
Calculating five *shēng* of provisions per person,
sixty thousand *hú* of rice would be needed,
not counting food for generals, officials, donkeys, and horses.
Just for carrying armor and getting themselves there,
the expense would be like this.
This is the fifth reason why it is not feasible.
Even if the army reaches the destination,
the casualties will surely be numerous.
They would not be sufficient to resist the enemy,
and more would have to be dispatched.
This is like cutting out the heart and abdomen to mend the limbs.
This is the sixth reason why it is not feasible.
Jiǔzhēn and Rìnán are a thousand *lǐ* apart;
mobilizing their own officials and people
is already unbearable,
let alone inflicting hardship on the troops of four provinces
to face the difficulties of thousands of *lǐ*!
This is the seventh reason why it is not feasible.
Previously, Colonel Yǐn Jiù attacked the rebellious Qiāng in Yìzhōu.
A proverb in Yìzhōu said: 'The barbarians coming is still tolerable;
Yǐn coming kills us.'
Later, when Yǐn Jiù was recalled,
he handed over his troops to Inspector Zhāng Qiáo.
Zhāng Qiáo, relying on his generals and officials,
within a month,
completely defeated the bandits.
This demonstrates the ineffectiveness of dispatching generals
and the reliability of commanderies and provinces.
It is advisable to select individuals with courage, strategy, benevolence, and compassion who are capable of leadership,
appointing them as Inspectors and Grand Administrators,
and having them all reside in Jiāozhǐ.
Currently, Rìnán lacks troops and grain,
insufficient for defense
and unable to fight.
Its officials and people should all be relocated north to rely on Jiāozhǐ.
After peace is restored,
they can be ordered to return to their homes.
Furthermore, recruit barbarians,
and make them fight each other,
transferring gold and silk
as their resources.
Those who can sow dissension and bring the heads of leaders
should be promised rewards of ennoblement and territorial grants.
The former Inspector of Bìngzhōu, Zhù Liáng of Chángshā,
is known for his bravery and decisiveness.
Also, Zhāng Qiáo of Nányáng
previously achieved success in defeating barbarians in Yìzhōu.
Both can be employed.
In the past, Emperor Tàizōng personally promoted Wèi Shàng to Governor of Yúnzhōng,
and Emperor Āi immediately appointed Gōng Shè as Grand Administrator of Tàishān.
It is appropriate to immediately appoint Zhù Liáng and others,
and send them directly to their posts."
The Four Bureaus all agreed with Lǐ Gù's proposal.
Zhù Liáng was immediately appointed Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn,
and Zhāng Qiáo was appointed Inspector of Jiāozhǐ.
Upon Zhāng Qiáo's arrival,
he openly showed compassion and enticed them,
and all submitted and dispersed.
Zhù Liáng arrived in Jiǔzhēn,
entered the bandit territory with a single carriage,
devised strategies,
and attracted them with his authority and trustworthiness.
Tens of thousands surrendered,
all building administrative offices for Zhù Liáng.
Thus, the region beyond the ridge was pacified again.
In the first year of Jiànkāng,
over a thousand barbarians from Rìnán again attacked and burned counties and towns,
then incited Jiǔzhēn,
and allied with them.
The Inspector of Jiāozhǐ, Xià Fāng of Jiǔjiāng, offered clemency and enticed them,
and the bandits all surrendered.
At that time, Empress Dowager Liáng was regent.
Admiring Xià Fāng's achievements,
she promoted him to Grand Administrator of Guìyáng.
In the third year of Yǒngshòu, during Emperor Huán's reign,
the Magistrate of Jūfēng was excessively greedy and cruel.
The people of the county, Zhū Dá and others, along with the barbarians, gathered together,
attacked and killed the magistrate.
Their numbers reached four or five thousand.
They advanced and attacked Jiǔzhēn,
and the Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn, Ér Shì, died in battle.
An imperial edict granted six hundred thousand cash,
and appointed his two sons as Lang.
The Commandant of Jiǔzhēn, Wèi Lǎng, was dispatched to suppress and defeat them,
beheading two thousand.
However, the bandit leaders still occupied Rìnán,
and their strength grew.
In the third year of Yánxī,
an imperial edict re-appointed Xià Fāng as Inspector of Jiāozhǐ.
Xià Fāng's authority and benevolence were well-known,
and when the long-standing bandits of Rìnán heard of it,
over twenty thousand people came together to surrender to Xià Fāng.
In the third year of Jiànníng, during Emperor Líng's reign,
the Grand Administrator of Yùlín, Gǔ Yǒng, by kindness and trustworthiness, attracted over a hundred thousand Wūhǔ people to surrender and become imperial subjects.
All received caps and sashes,
and seven counties were established for them.
In the twelfth month of winter in the second year of Xīpíng,
foreign states from beyond the borders of Rìnán brought tribute through multiple interpreters.
In the first year of Guānghé,
the Wūhǔ barbarians of Jiāozhǐ and Hépǔ rebelled,
enticed Jiǔzhēn and Rìnán,
amassing tens of thousands of people,
and attacked and captured commanderies and counties.
In the fourth year,
Inspector Zhū Jùn defeated them.
In the sixth year,
foreign states from beyond the borders of Rìnán again came to present tribute.
The Mán of Bā Jùn and Nán Jùn
originally had five surnames: Bā shì,
Fán shì,
Tán
shì,
Xiāng shì,
Zhèng shì.
All originated from Wǔluò Zhōnglí Shān.
This mountain had two caves, one red and one black.
The sons of Bā shì were born in the red cave;
the sons of the four other surnames were all born in the black cave.
Before there was a ruler,
they all served ghosts and spirits.
So they jointly threw swords into a stone cave,
agreeing that whoever could hit the target
would be honored as their ruler.
Wùxiàng, son of Bā shì, alone hit it,
and the crowd all marveled.
Then they ordered each to ride an earthen boat,
agreeing that whoever's boat could float
would be made ruler.
The boats of the other surnames all sank,
only Wùxiàng's alone floated.
They then jointly established him,
and he was known as Lǐn Jūn.
He then rode an earthen boat
from Yí Shuǐ to Yányáng.
A divine woman of Yán Shuǐ
said to Lǐn Jūn:
"This land is vast,
producing fish and salt.
I wish you would stay and live together with me."
Lǐn Jūn did not agree.
The Yán God would come every evening to stay the night,
and in the morning transform into an insect,
flying in a swarm with many other insects,
obscuring the sunlight,
making heaven and earth dim and dark.
After more than ten days,
Lǐn Jūn [sì]
seized the opportunity and shot and killed her,
whereupon the sky cleared.
Lǐn Jūn then ruled Yí Chéng,
and the four other surnames all became his subjects.
When Lǐn Jūn died,
his spirit for generations became a white tiger.
As Bā shì believed the tiger drank human blood,
they sacrificed humans to it.
When Qín Huì Wáng annexed Bā Zhōng,
he made Bā shì the MánYí ruler,
who for generations married Qín women.
Their people's rank was comparable to Bùgēng,
and those who committed crimes could have them pardoned by their rank.
Their ruler annually paid a tax of two thousand and sixteen coins,
and every three years an additional voluntary tax of one thousand eight hundred coins.
Each household among their people paid eight zhàng and two chǐ of jīng cloth,
and thirty shé of chicken feathers.
When Hàn rose,
Nán Jùn Tàishǒu Jìn Qiáng requested to continue the Qín era practices.
By Jiànwǔ twenty-three years (47 CE),
the Mán of Pǔ Shān in Nán Jùn, led by Léi Qiān and others, first rebelled,
plundering the common people.
Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn Liú Shàng was sent with over ten thousand men to suppress and defeat them,
relocating seven thousand odd people of their kind to the Jiāngxià region.
Today's Miǎn Zhōng Mán are these people.
In Hé Dì Yǒngyuán thirteen years (101 CE),
the Wū Mán, led by Xǔ Shèng and others,
resented the unfair collection of taxes by the commandery,
harboring grievances,
and thus gathered and rebelled.
The following summer,
an envoy was dispatched to supervise the troops of Jīng Zhōu's various commanderies, over ten thousand men, to suppress them.
Shèng and his followers relied on their difficult and narrow terrain,
and were not defeated for a long time.
The various armies then divided their routes and advanced simultaneously,
some attacking from Bā Jùn and Yúfù along several routes.
The Mán then scattered and fled,
their chieftains were executed,
and they were pursued in victory,
decisively defeating Shèng and his followers.
Shèng and his followers begged for surrender,
and were again all relocated to Jiāngxià.
In Líng Dì Jiànníng two years (169 CE),
the Jiāngxià Mán rebelled,
and the province and commandery suppressed them.
In Guānghé three years (180 CE),
the Jiāngxià Mán rebelled again,
connecting with the Lújiāng bandit Huáng Ráng.
Over one hundred thousand people
attacked and took four counties,
causing trouble for several years.
Lújiāng Tàishǒu Lù Kāng suppressed and defeated them,
and the rest all surrendered and dispersed.
The Bǎnshǔn MánYí:
During Qín Zhāoxiāng Wáng's time, there was a white tiger
which often roamed the borders of Qín, Shǔ, Bā, and Hàn with a pack of tigers,
injuring over a thousand people.
Zhāo Wáng then heavily rewarded anyone in the state who could kill the tiger,
promising a fief of ten thousand households
and a hundred yì of gold.
At that time, there was an Yí man from Lángzhōng, Bā Jùn,
who could make crossbows of white bamboo.
He ascended a tower and shot the white tiger dead.
Zhāo Wáng commended him,
but because he was an Yí man,
did not wish to grant him a full enfeoffment.
Instead, he carved an oath on stone,
exempting the Yí people's qǐng of land from rent,
and ten wives from being counted.
Those who injured others would be punished by law,
and those who killed others could redeem death with tán money.
The oath stated:
"If Qín offends Yí,
it shall surrender a pair of yellow dragons;
if Yí offends Qín,
it shall surrender a goblet of clear wine."
The Yí people were content with this.
When Gāozǔ became King of Hàn,
he mustered the Yí people to return and attack the Three Qín.
Once the Qín territory was settled,
he sent them back to Bā Zhōng,
restoring the seven surnames of their chieftains: Luó, Piáo, Dū, È, Dù, Xī, Gōng.
They were exempt from paying rent and taxes,
while other households annually paid cōng money,
forty (coins) per person.
They were known for generations as the Bǎnshǔn MánYí.
In Lángzhōng, there is the Yú Shuǐ,
and its people mostly lived along its banks.
They were naturally strong and brave,
and initially served as the Hàn vanguard,
often breaking enemy formations.
Their custom was to enjoy singing and dancing.
Gāozǔ watched them
and said:
"This is the song of Wǔ Wáng's campaign against Zhòu."
He then ordered musicians to learn it,
which is what is called the Bā Yú Dance.
Thus, for generations, they remained obedient.
As for the Central Revival [period],
the commandery governors often led them in military expeditions.
During the reign of Huán Dì,
the Bǎnshǔ frequently rebelled.
Zhào Wēn, the Grand Administrator of Shǔjùn Commandery, subdued them with kindness and trust.
In the second year of Guānghé (180 CE) of Líng Dì's reign,
the Bǎnshǔ of Bājùn Commandery rebelled again,
raiding and plundering the three Shǔ commanderies and the various commanderies in Hànzhōng.
Líng Dì sent Xiāo Yuàn, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief, to supervise the Yìzhōu troops and suppress them.
For years, he could not overcome them.
The Emperor desired to raise a large army,
so he asked the accounting officials of Yìzhōu,
questioning them about strategies for the punitive expedition.
Chéng Bāo, the chief accounting official from Hànzhōng, replied:
"The Bǎnshǔ, comprising seven clans,
earned merit by shooting and killing a white tiger,
and their ancestors were acknowledged as righteous people.
These people are brave and fierce,
skilled in warfare.
Previously, in the Yǒngchū era,
when the Qiāng entered Hánzhōu,
and the commanderies and counties were devastated,
it was the Bǎnshǔ who rescued them.
The Qiāng were almost entirely defeated and killed,
hence they were called 'divine troops'.
The Qiāng people feared and dreaded them,
spreading the word among their kin
not to go south again.
By the second year of Jiànhé,
when the Qiāng invaded greatly again,
it truly relied on the Bǎnshǔ to repeatedly crush and defeat them.
The former General of Chariots and Cavalry, Féng Gǔn, campaigned south against Wǔlíng;
although he received the sharp elite troops of Dānyáng,
he also relied on the Bǎnshǔ to achieve his success.
Recently, when Yìzhōujùn Commandery was in turmoil,
Grand Administrator Lǐ Yǒng also used the Bǎnshǔ to suppress and pacify it.
Their loyalty and merit are like this;
they originally had no malicious intent.
However, the chief officials and local gentry levied excessively heavy taxes,
and their servants were flogged and beaten
more severely than slaves.
There were even cases of selling wives and children,
or even going so far as to cut their own throats.
Although they appealed their grievances to the provinces and commanderies,
the regional governors and commandery administrators did not handle them fairly.
The imperial court was distant,
and they could not make themselves heard.
They harbored resentment, called out to Heaven,
and beat their chests in the desolate valleys.
They suffered from oppressive taxes and corvée labor,
and endured cruel punishments.
Thus, the villages gathered together,
leading to their rebellion and defiance.
They did not have a mastermind usurping a title
to plot treachery.
If now we merely select enlightened and capable regional governors and commandery administrators,
they will naturally be pacified and settled,
without needing a punitive expedition."
The Emperor followed his words
and sent Grand Administrator Cáo Qiān to proclaim an imperial edict granting them amnesty,
and they all immediately surrendered.
By the fifth year of Zhōngpíng,
when the Yellow Turban bandits arose in Bājùn Commandery,
the Bǎnshǔ barbarians consequently rebelled again,
raiding and plundering cities and towns.
Zhào Jǐn, the Major of the Separate Division of the Upper Army of the Western Garden, was sent to suppress and pacify them.
The southwestern Yí were
outside the borders of Shǔjùn Commandery.
There was the kingdom of Yèláng,
which bordered Jiāozhǐ to the east.
To the west was the kingdom of Diān,
and to the north was the kingdom of Qióngdū.
Each established its own ruler.
Their people all wore coiled topknots and garments fastened on the left,
living in settlements and villages,
and were capable of farming.
Beyond them, there were also the various settlements of Kuí and Kūnmíng.
To the extreme west was Tóngshī,
and to the northeast was Yèyú,
covering an area of several thousand *lǐ*.
They had no rulers,
braided their hair,
and migrated erratically with their livestock.
Northeast of Kuí was the kingdom of Zuòdū,
and northeast of that was the kingdom of Rǎnmáng.
Some were settled,
while others migrated with their livestock.
Northeast of Rǎnmáng was the kingdom of Báimǎ,
which was of the Dī ethnicity.
These three kingdoms also had rulers.
Regarding Yèláng,
initially, a woman was washing clothes in the Dùnshǔi River.
Three-jointed large bamboo floated into her feet.
Hearing a crying sound within,
she split open the bamboo and looked,
finding a baby boy.
She took him home and raised him.
When he grew up,
he possessed talent and martial prowess,
and established himself as the Marquis of Yèláng,
taking 'Zhú' (Bamboo) as his surname.
In the sixth year of Yuándǐng (111 BCE) of Wǔ Dì's reign,
the southern Yí were pacified,
and Zāngkē Commandery was established.
The Marquis of Yèláng came to surrender,
and the Son of Heaven bestowed upon his king an imperial seal and ribbon.
Later, he was killed.
The Yí and Láo all considered the Bamboo King not born of flesh and blood,
greatly revering him,
and requested that an heir be established for him.
Bà, the Grand Administrator of Zāngkē, reported this,
and the Son of Heaven then enfeoffed his three sons as marquises.
When they died,
they were sacrificed to alongside their father.
Today, in Yèláng County, the shrine to the Three Lords of the Bamboo King exists.
Originally,
during the reign of Qǐngxiāng Wáng of Chǔ,
General Zhuāng Háo was sent from the Yuánshuǐ River to attack Yèláng.
The army reached Qiělán,
where they scuttled their boats on the bank and fought on foot.
After subduing Yèláng,
he remained and ruled in Diānchí.
Because Qiělán had the place where the boats were scuttled,
its name was changed to Zāngkē.
Zāngkē is a land of frequent rain and floods.
The local customs favor shamans, spirits, and taboos.
There is little livestock
and no silkworm cultivation,
hence its commandery is the poorest.
Jùdīng County has the *guàngláng* tree,
which can be used for food,
and the common people rely on it.
During the time of Gōngsūn Shù,
the powerful clans Lóng, Fù, Yǐn, and Dǒng,
together with Xiè Xiān, the Registrar of the commandery, defended the borders for Han.
They then sent envoys from Pānyú via river to offer tribute.
Guāngwǔ commended them
and bestowed additional rewards.
During the reign of Huán Dì,
Yǐn Zhēn, a native of the commandery, considered himself born in a wild frontier
and ignorant of rites and righteousness.
So, he studied classics, commentaries, diagrams, and prophecies with Xǔ Shèn and Yīng Fèng from Rǔnán.
After completing his studies,
he returned to his hometown and taught,
whereupon learning first began in the southern regions.
Zhēn's highest official position was Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
The King of Diān
was a descendant of Zhuāng Qiáo.
In the second year of Yuánfēng (109 BCE),
Wǔ Dì pacified it,
making its land into Yìzhōujùn Commandery,
and allotted several counties from Zāngkē and Yuèkuí to it.
A few years later,
the land of Kūnmíng was also incorporated,
all belonging to this commandery.
There is a lake
with a circumference of over two hundred *lǐ*.
The source of the water is deep and wide,
but the end becomes shallow and narrow,
appearing to flow in reverse,
hence it is called Diānchí.
The river valley is flat and open,
producing many parrots and peacocks.
It is rich in salt ponds, fields, and fisheries,
and abundant in gold, silver, and livestock.
The local people are powerful and wealthy.
Those who hold official positions are all wealthy for generations.
When Wáng Mǎng's government was in chaos,
the Yí chieftains Dòngcán and Ruòdòu of Yìzhōujùn Commandery raised troops and killed the commandery administrator.
The Gūfù Yí people of Yuèkuí, led by Dàmóu, also rebelled,
killing and plundering officials and people.
Mǎng sent Lián Dān, the General Who Establishes Peace,
to mobilize officials and people from Bā and Shǔ, and transfer over one hundred thousand soldiers and laborers to attack them.
Officials and soldiers suffered from hunger and disease,
and for years could not overcome them and returned.
Wén Qí of Guǎnghàn was appointed Grand Administrator.
He constructed reservoirs,
opened up irrigation channels,
and reclaimed over two thousand *qǐng* of farmland.
He led and exhorted his troops and cavalry,
repaired fortifications,
and brought together the various Yí,
winning their harmony greatly.
When Gōngsūn Shù seized the land of Yì,
Qí firmly defended the strategic passes.
Shù detained his wife and children,
promising him enfeoffment as a marquis,
but Qí still did not surrender.
Hearing that Guāngwǔ had ascended the throne,
he secretly sent an envoy to report his situation.
After Shǔ was pacified,
he was summoned to be the General Who Guards the Distant,
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Chéngyì.
He died on the way.
An edict commanded the construction of a memorial hall for him,
and the people of the commandery erected a temple to sacrifice to him.
In the eighteenth year of Jiànwǔ,
the Yí leader Dòngcán, along with the various tribes of Gūfù, Yèyú, Nángdòng, Liánrán, Diānchí, Jiàn (Líng), and Kūnmíng, rebelled
and killed the chief officials.
Fán Shèng, the Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu, fought them and was defeated,
retreating to defend Zhūtí.
In the nineteenth year,
Liú Shàng, the General of Wǔwēi, and others were dispatched to mobilize people from Guǎnghàn, Jiànwéi, Shǔjùn, and the Yí of Zhūtí,
amounting to thirteen thousand men, to attack them.
Shàng's army then crossed the Lúshuǐ
and entered the borders of Yìzhōu.
When the various Yí heard that a large army was approaching,
they all abandoned their strongholds and fled.
Shàng captured their weak and infirm, as well as their grain and livestock.
In the twentieth year,
he advanced his troops and fought Dòngcán and others in successive battles for several months,
defeating them all.
In the first month of the following year,
he pursued them to Bùwéi,
beheading the leader Dòngcán.
In total, more than seven thousand heads and captives were taken,
five thousand seven hundred live captives were obtained,
three thousand horses,
and over thirty thousand cattle and sheep.
All the various Yí were pacified.
During the Yuánhé era of Sùzōng,
Wáng Zhuī served as the Grand Administrator of Shǔjùn.
His governance and reforms were particularly extraordinary,
and four divine horses appeared from the Diānchí River.
Sweet dew fell,
white crows were seen.
He began to establish schools
and gradually changed their customs.
In the fifth year of Xīpíng of Emperor Líng,
the various Yí rebelled
and seized the Grand Administrator Yōng Zhì.
Zhū Guī, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief, was sent to suppress them,
but could not succeed.
The court deliberated, believing that since the commandery was on the frontier,
the Mányí were prone to rebellion,
and it would be an arduous and distant expedition for the army.
It would be better to abandon it.
Lǐ Yǒng of Bājùn, an aide to the Grand Commandant, proposed a plan for suppression.
Consequently, Yǒng was appointed Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu,
and together with Páng Zhī, the Inspector, he mobilized the Bǎnshùn Mán to attack, defeat, and pacify them,
and retrieved Yōng Zhì.
After Yǒng's death,
the Yí people rebelled again.
Jǐng Yì of Guǎnghàn was appointed Grand Administrator,
and he suppressed and pacified them.
When Yì first arrived at the commandery,
a *hú* of rice cost ten thousand cash.
Gradually, through his benevolence and kindness,
within a few years,
the price of rice dropped to several tens.
The Āiláo Yí's
ancestor was a woman named Shāyī,
who lived on Láoshān.
She once caught fish in the water
and touched a sunken log, as if she was moved,
thus becoming pregnant.
After ten months,
she gave birth to ten sons.
Later, the sunken log transformed into a dragon
and emerged from the water.
Shāyī suddenly heard the dragon say:
"You bore sons for me,
where are they all now?"
Nine sons saw the dragon and fled in fear.
Only the youngest son could not leave;
he turned his back to the dragon and sat down.
The dragon then licked him.
His mother spoke in a bird language,
calling 'back' *jiǔ*,
and 'sit' *lóng*.
Thus, she named her son Jiǔlóng.
When he grew up,
his elder brothers considered Jiǔlóng clever for being licked by their father,
and together they chose him as their king.
Later, at the foot of Láoshān, a husband and wife
again gave birth to ten daughters.
Jiǔlóng and his brothers all married them as wives,
and gradually they multiplied.
The people of this tribe all carved and painted their bodies,
resembling dragon patterns,
and their clothes all had tails.
When Jiǔlóng died,
his line succeeded him for generations.
They were divided and small kings were appointed,
residing in various settlements,
scattered throughout the valleys.
This remote and wild region,
with its deep and treacherous mountains and rivers,
had, since the dawn of humanity,
never communicated with the Central Plains.
In the twenty-third year of Jiànwǔ,
their king Xiánlì dispatched troops on raft boats,
sailing south along the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
to attack Lùduō, an Yí tribe attached to the frontier.
The Lùduō people were weak
and were captured.
Thereupon, thunder roared and rain poured heavily,
a south wind arose,
the water flowed upstream,
surging over two hundred *lǐ*.
The raft boats sank,
and several thousand of the Āiláo people
drowned.
Xiánlì again sent six of his kings with ten thousand men to attack Lùduō.
The King of Lùduō fought them
and killed their six kings.
The elders of Āiláo collectively buried the six kings,
but at night tigers again dug up their bodies and ate them.
The remaining troops were terrified and withdrew.
Xiánlì was panicked
and said to his elders:
"We have entered the frontier regions,
which has been our custom since ancient times.
Now, when we attack Lùduō,
we are invariably met with divine punishment.
Does the Central Plains perhaps have a sage emperor?
Heaven assists him,
how manifest this is!"
In the twenty-seventh year,
Xiánlì and others then led their people, two thousand seven hundred and seventy households,
and seventeen thousand six hundred and fifty-nine individuals,
to surrender to Zhèng Hóng, the Grand Administrator of Yuèkuì,
requesting to be incorporated into the interior.
Guāngwǔ enfeoffed Xiánlì and others as lords.
From then on, they came to pay tribute annually.
In the twelfth year of Yǒngpíng,
Liǔmào, the King of Āiláo, sent his son to lead his people to be incorporated into the interior.
There were seventy-seven people who claimed to be kings of settlements,
fifty-one thousand eight hundred and ninety households,
and five hundred fifty-three thousand seven hundred and eleven individuals.
This was seven thousand *lǐ* southwest of Luòyáng.
Xiǎnzōng established Āiláo and Bónán counties in their territory,
and detached six counties under the Western Chief Commandant of Yìzhōu Commandery,
combining them to form Yǒngchāng Commandery.
They first opened the Bónán Mountain
and crossed the Láncāng River,
which travelers found arduous.
The song goes:
"The Han's virtue is vast,
opening up those who do not submit.
Crossing Bónán,
passing Lánjīn.
Crossing Láncāng,
we become others' (laborers)."
The Āiláo people all pierced their noses and wore large ear ornaments.
Their leaders called themselves kings,
and their ear ornaments hung three *cùn* below their shoulders.
Commoners' ornaments only reached their shoulders.
The land was fertile and beautiful,
suitable for the five grains and sericulture.
They knew how to dye, embroider,
and make felted woolen fabrics,
stacked silks,
and fine *lán'gān* cloth,
woven with patterns like brocade.
There was a Wútóng wood flower
which was spun into cloth,
five *chǐ* wide,
pure white and resistant to dirt.
It was first used to cover the deceased,
and then worn.
Their bamboo internodes were one *zhàng* apart,
named Púzhú bamboo.
They produced copper, iron, lead, tin, gold, silver, luminous pearls,
amber,
crystal, lapis lazuli, *kēchóng*, river pearls,
peacocks, kingfishers, rhinoceros, elephants, orangutans, and *mò* beasts.
Yúnnán County had two divine deer
that could eat poisonous herbs.
Previously,
Zhèng Chún (鄭純) of Guǎnghàn (廣漢), the Western Commandant (Xībù Dūwèi 西部都尉), governed with integrity and purity.
His transforming influence spread among the Yí (夷) and Mó (貊) peoples.
Their rulers and elders were moved by admiration,
and all offered local treasures
to praise his virtues.
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ 天子) commended him
and immediately appointed him as the Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Yǒngchāng (永昌).
Chún (純) made an agreement with the Āiláo (哀牢) Yí (夷) people:
the local magnates would annually contribute two pieces of "cloth-pierced-head" clothing
and one Hú (斛) of salt
as a regular tax,
which the Yí (夷) people found acceptable.
Chún (純), from being Commandant (Dūwèi 都尉) to Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守),
died in office after ten years.
In the first year of Jiànchū (建初) (76 CE),
Lèiláo (類牢), the King of Āiláo (哀牢), had a dispute with a local magistrate (shǒu lìng 守令).
He then killed the magistrate and rebelled,
attacking Xiétáng (巂唐) city.
The Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守), Wáng Xún (王尋), fled to Diéyú (楪榆).
Over three thousand Āiláo (哀牢) people attacked Bónán (博南),
burning people's houses.
Sùzōng (肅宗) conscripted nine thousand Yí (夷) and Hàn (漢) people from Yuècuí (越巂), Yìzhōu (益州), and Yǒngchāng (永昌) to suppress them.
In the spring of the following year,
Lǔ Chéng (鹵承) and others from the Kūnmíng (昆明) Yí (夷) tribe of Xiélóng (邪龍) county
responded to the recruitment.
They led their tribesmen and the soldiers from various commanderies to attack Lèiláo (類牢) at Bónán (博南),
decisively defeating and beheading him.
His head was sent to Luòyáng (洛陽).
Lǔ Chéng (鹵承) was rewarded with ten thousand bolts of silk
and enfeoffed as Bòlǔ Bàngyì Hóu (破虜傍邑侯).
In the sixth year of Yǒngyuán (永元) (94 CE),
Mòyán (莫延), king of the Dūnrěnyǐ (敦忍乙) tribe outside the commandery's frontiers (jùn jiǎo wài 郡徼外), admired righteousness
and sent envoys and interpreters to offer rhinoceroses and elephants.
In the ninth year (97 CE),
the Mán (蠻) outside the frontiers (jiǎo wài 徼外) and Yōngyóudiào (雍由調), the king of the Shàn (撣) Kingdom,
sent multiple interpreters to present precious treasures of their land.
Emperor Hé (Hé Dì 和帝) bestowed upon him a gold seal and a purple ribbon.
Lesser chieftains were all granted seals, ribbons, money, and silk.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (永初) (107 CE),
Lùlèi (陸類) and others, a tribe of Jiāojiǎo (僬僥) Yí (夷) from outside the frontiers (jiǎo wài 徼外), numbering over three thousand individuals, brought their entire tribe to pledge allegiance internally,
offering elephant tusks, water buffalo, and yak.
In the first year of Yǒngníng (永寧) (120 CE),
Yōngyóudiào (雍由調), the king of the Shàn (撣) Kingdom, again sent envoys to the imperial court to offer congratulations,
presenting musicians and conjurers
who could transform, breathe fire,
dismember themselves,
and exchange the heads of oxen and horses.
They were also skilled at juggling balls,
even up to a thousand.
They claimed, "We are people from the west of the sea."
The west of the sea is Dàqín (大秦).
The Shàn (撣) Kingdom communicates with Dàqín (大秦) to its southwest.
At the New Year's assembly (Yuán huì 元會) the following year,
Emperor Ān (Ān Dì 安帝) arranged for music in the court.
Yōngyóudiào (雍由調) was enfeoffed as Hàn Dàdūwèi (漢大都尉)
and granted a seal, a ribbon, gold, silver, and colored silk, each according to a specified grade.
The Qióngdū (邛都) Yí (夷)
were originally brought under control by Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì 武帝),
who established Qióngdū (邛都) county.
Not long after, the land sank and became a marsh,
thus it was named Qióngchí (邛池).
The people of the south called it Qiónghé (邛河).
Later, they rebelled again.
In the sixth year of Yuándǐng (元鼎) (111 BCE),
Hàn (漢) troops attacked them from the Yuècuí (越巂) River
and established Yuècuí (越巂) Commandery.
Its land was a flat plain,
with rice fields.
On Yútóng (禺同) Mountain in Qīnglíng (青蛉) county, there were jade chickens and golden horses,
whose brilliant forms occasionally appeared.
The local customs were characterized by much wandering
and a fondness for singing,
largely similar to Zāngkē (牂柯).
The powerful chieftains were unruly
and difficult to control.
During Wáng Mǎng's (王莽) reign,
Méi Gēn (枚根), the Administrator (jùnshǒu 郡守), recruited Cháng Guì (長貴) from Qióng (邛)
to serve as a military commander (jūnhóu 軍候).
In the second year of Gēngshǐ (Gēngshǐ 二年) (24 CE),
Cháng Guì (長貴) led his tribesmen to attack and kill Méi Gēn (枚根),
establishing himself as King of Qiónggǔ (Qiónggǔ Wáng 邛穀王)
and managing the affairs of the Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守).
He also surrendered to Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述).
After Shù (述) was defeated,
Guāngwǔ (Guāngwǔ 光武) enfeoffed Cháng Guì (長貴) as King of Qiónggǔ (Qiónggǔ Wáng 邛穀王).
In the fourteenth year of Jiànwǔ (Jiànwǔ 十四年) (38 CE),
Cháng Guì (長貴) sent an envoy to present a three-year report.
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ 天子) immediately bestowed upon him the seal and ribbon of the Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Yuècuí (越巂).
In the nineteenth year (43 CE),
Liú Shàng (劉尚), the General of Wǔwēi (Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn 武威將軍), attacked the Yí (夷) of Yìzhōu (益州),
his route passing through Yuècuí (越巂).
Cháng Guì (長貴), hearing of this,
suspected that once Shàng (尚) had pacified the southern border,
his authority and laws would certainly be enforced,
and he himself would no longer be able to act unrestrainedly.
So he gathered troops and established camps,
summoning various chieftains.
He brewed much poisonous wine,
intending first to treat the army
and then ambush Shàng (尚).
Shàng (尚), aware of his plot,
immediately divided his troops and first occupied Qióngdū (邛都),
then ambushed and executed Cháng Guì (長貴),
relocating his family to Chéngdū (成都).
In the first year of Yǒngpíng (永平) (58 CE),
the Gūfù (姑復) Yí (夷) again rebelled.
The Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Yìzhōu (益州) dispatched troops, defeated them,
and beheaded their chieftain,
sending his head to the capital.
Later, Zhāng Xī (張翕) of Bājùn (巴郡) became Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守).
His governance was clear and peaceful,
and he earned the harmony of the Yí (夷) people.
He served in the commandery for seventeen years
before he died.
The Yí (夷) people loved and missed him
as if they had lost their parents.
Over two hundred Sūqí (蘇祈) elders
carried oxen and sheep to attend his funeral
all the way to Xī's (翕) hometown of Ānhàn (安漢),
where they erected a grave and offered sacrifices.
An imperial edict commended him,
and a memorial shrine was built for him.
In the third year of Yuánchū (元初) of Emperor Ān (Ān Dì 安帝) (116 CE),
eight tribes from outside the commandery's frontiers (jùn jiǎo wài 郡徼外), including the Dàyáng (大羊) tribe,
with thirty-one thousand households
and one hundred sixty-seven thousand six hundred twenty individuals,
admired righteousness and pledged allegiance internally.
At that time, the commandery and counties imposed frequent and burdensome levies.
Five years later (121 CE),
Fēng Lí (封離) and others from the Dàniú (大牛) tribe of Juǎnyí (卷夷) rebelled,
killing the magistrate (lìng 令) of Suìjiǔ (遂久).
The following year (122 CE),
the Yí (夷) of Yǒngchāng (永昌), Yìzhōu (益州), and Shǔjùn (蜀郡) all rebelled in response.
Their numbers reached over one hundred thousand.
They destroyed more than twenty counties,
killed chief officials,
burned towns and cities,
plundered the common people,
leaving piles of bones,
and making a thousand Lǐ (里) uninhabited.
An imperial edict ordered Zhāng Qiáo (張喬), the Inspector (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Yìzhōu (益州), to select capable subordinates to suppress them.
Qiáo (喬) then dispatched his subordinate Yáng Sǒng (楊竦) to lead troops to Diéyú (楪榆) to attack them.
As the rebels were formidable, he did not dare to advance immediately.
First, he issued imperial edicts to inform the three commanderies,
secretly recruiting warriors
and offering generous rewards.
Then he advanced his army and fought Fēng Lí (封離) and others,
decisively defeating them,
beheading over thirty thousand,
capturing one thousand five hundred living individuals,
and seizing over forty million in valuables,
all of which were used to reward the soldiers.
Fēng Lí (封離) and others were terrified.
They beheaded their co-conspirator chieftains
and went to Sǒng (竦) to beg for surrender.
Sǒng (竦) graciously accepted and comforted them.
The remaining thirty-six tribes all came to surrender and submit.
Sǒng (竦) then reported ninety corrupt officials who had encroached upon the Mányí (蠻夷),
all of whom had their death sentences commuted.
While the provincial government was still discussing the merits and before they could report to the throne,
Sǒng (竦) unfortunately died from illness.
Zhāng Qiáo (張喬) deeply mourned him,
so he carved a stone inscription
and commissioned a portrait of him.
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ 天子), recognizing Zhāng Xī's (張翕) enduring affection,
appointed his son Tuān (湍) as Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守).
The Yí (夷) people were delighted
and welcomed him along the road.
They said,
"The young master's appearance resembles our late Administrator (fǔjūn 府君)."
Later, Tuān (湍) somewhat lost their trust,
and some wished to rebel.
But the Yí (夷) elders explained to each other,
"We should do this for the sake of the former Administrator (fǔjūn 府君)."
Thus, peace was maintained.
Later, between Shùn (順) and Huán (桓) (126-168 CE),
Féng Hào (馮顥) of Guǎnghàn (廣漢) served as Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守),
and it is said that his governance produced many extraordinary achievements.
The Zuòdū (莋都) Yí (夷)
were brought under control by Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì 武帝),
who established Zuòdū (莋都) county.
Their people all wore their hair loose and their robes with the left lapel over the right.
Their speech was often fond of analogies.
Their dwelling places were largely similar to the Wénshān (汶山) Yí (夷).
The land produced miraculous elixirs for longevity,
and it was where the immortal Shān Tú (山圖) resided.
In the sixth year of Yuándǐng (元鼎) (111 BCE),
it was made Shěnlí (沈黎) Commandery.
By the fourth year of Tiānhàn (天漢) (97 BCE),
it was merged with Shǔ (蜀) to form the Western Region (Xībù 西部),
and two Commandants (Dūwèi 都尉) were established.
One resided at Máoniú (旄牛),
overseeing the Yí (夷) outside the frontiers (jiǎo wài 徼外).
The other resided at Qīngyī (青衣), overseeing the Hàn (漢) people.
During the Yǒngpíng reign,
Zhū Fǔ (朱輔) of Liángguó (梁國), the Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州),
was fond of achieving meritorious deeds and fame,
and was magnanimous and possessed great strategies.
Having been in the province for several years,
he proclaimed the virtue of the Hàn (漢),
and awed and pacified the distant barbarians.
From Wénshān (汶山) westward,
regions which were not reached by previous generations,
and where the imperial calendar had not yet been applied,
the Báiláng (白狼), Pánmù (槃木), Tángzōu (唐菆), and over a hundred other states,
with over one million three hundred thousand households,
and more than six million people,
all brought tributes,
and declared themselves subjects and servants.
Fǔ (輔) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant heard the Shī (詩) say: 'To that diverging road they went,
where the barbarians were transformed.'
The commentary says: 'Although the Qí (岐) road was remote,
people did not find it distant.'
The poet's chant
was taken as a verification.
Now the King of Báiláng (白狼), Tángzōu (唐菆), and others, admiring the transformation and returning to righteousness,
have composed three poems.
Their path crosses the great Qiónglái (邛來) mountains and the Línggāo (零高) slopes,
which are precipitous, perilous, and rugged,
a hundred times more so than the Qí (岐) road.
Yet they carry their old and young,
as if returning to a benevolent mother.
The language of the distant barbarians
is difficult to accurately render in meaning and expression.
Their plants are of different species,
and their birds and beasts of distinct kinds.
There is Tián Gōng (田恭), a clerk from Jiānwéi (犍為) Commandery, who is familiar and intimate with them,
and quite understands their speech.
Your servant has accordingly ordered him to inquire into their customs
and translate their words.
I now dispatch the Attendant Official Lǐ Líng (李陵) with Gōng (恭) to escort them to the capital,
and also present their pleasure songs.
In ancient times, the sagely emperors
danced to the music of the four barbarians;
what is presented now,
may perhaps serve as one of those."
The Emperor praised this,
and the matter was sent to the imperial historiographers,
who recorded their songs.
The 'Song of the Distant Barbarians' Joyful in Virtue' says: "Great Hàn (漢) has good governance,
(堤官隗搆.)
Its will accords with Heaven's.
(魏冒踰糟.)
Officials translate fairly,
(罔驛劉脾.)
No one comes unwillingly.
(旁莫支留.)
Hearing of its influence, we are transformed,
(微衣隨旅.)
What we see is marvelous.
(知唐桑艾.)
Much silk and cloth are bestowed,
(邪毗_ョD)
Sweet and delicious wine and food.
(推潭僕遠.)
Joyful music and flying meat
(拓拒蘇便.)
are fully provided in abundance.
(局後仍離.)
We, the Mányí (蠻夷), are poor and meager,
(僂讓龍洞.)
With nothing to repay in return.
(莫支度由.)
May the Lord live long,
(陽雒僧鱗.)
And his descendants prosper.
(莫穉角存.)"
The 'Song of the Distant Barbarians' Admiring Virtue' says:
"Where the Mányí (蠻夷) dwell,
(僂讓皮尼.)
Is the region of the setting sun.
(且交陵悟.)
Admiring righteousness, we turn towards transformation,
(繩動隨旅.)
And return to the Lord of the rising sun.
(路旦揀雒.)
His sagely virtue and profound grace
(聖德渡諾.)
Enrich the people.
(魏菌度洗.)
In winter there is much frost and snow,
(綜邪流藩.)
In summer much gentle rain.
(莋邪尋螺.)
The cold and warmth
are timely and fitting,
(藐潯瀘灕.)
The people of the tribes are numerous and prosperous.
Treading through dangers and overcoming perils,
(辟危歸險.)
We do not consider ten thousand *lǐ* (里) far.
(莫受萬柳.)
Abandoning our customs, we return to virtue,
(術疊附德.)
Our hearts turn to a benevolent mother.
(仍路孳摸.)"
The 'Song of the Distant Barbarians' Cherishing Virtue' says:
"Beyond the wild frontiers,
(荒服之儀.)
The land is barren and poor.
(犂籍憐憐.)
We eat meat and wear skins,
(阻蘇邪犁.)
Not seeing salt or grain.
(莫碭麤沐.)
Officials translate and spread the news,
(罔譯傳微.)
That the Great Hàn (漢) is peaceful and joyful.
(是漢夜拒.)
Carrying and supporting, we return to benevolence,
(蹤優路仁.)
Daring to brave dangers and narrow passes.
(雷折險龍.)
High mountains
are steep and rugged,
(倫狼藏幢.)
We climb cliffs and roll stones.
(扶路側祿.)
Breaking through forests, we leave our homes,
(息落服淫.)
And arrive at Luò (洛) after a hundred sleeps.
(理歷髭雒.)
Fathers and sons are bestowed together,
(捕茝菌毗.)
Embracing silks.
(懷匹漏.)
We spread the word to our kin,
(傳室呼敕.)
Forever wishing to be subjects and servants.
(陵陽臣僕.)"
At the beginning of Sùzōng's (肅宗) reign,
Fǔ (輔) was dismissed from office due to a matter.
At that time, the residences of the commandery commander and government offices were all carved and decorated,
with paintings of mountain spirits, sea deities, strange birds, and exotic beasts,
to dazzle and impress,
and the barbarians became even more awed and fearful.
In the twelfth year of Yǒngyuán (永元) of Emperor Hé (和),
Tángzēng (唐繒) and other kings of the Báiláng (白狼) and Lóubó (樓薄) Mányí (蠻夷) beyond the Máoniú (旄牛) frontier,
then led their people, one hundred seventy thousand strong,
to return to righteousness and pledge allegiance.
An imperial edict bestowed them with gold seals and purple ribbons,
and the minor chieftains received money and silks, each according to their rank.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (永初) of Emperor Ān (安),
the Sānxiāng (三襄) tribes of Shǔjùn (蜀郡) and the Wūyǎn (汙衍) tribes from beyond the frontier, totaling over three thousand people, rebelled,
attacking Cánlíng (蠶陵) city
and killing its chief magistrate.
In the second year,
Lìng Tián (令田), the chieftain of the Qīngyī (青衣) Dao barbarians,
along with thirty-one thousand people from three tribes beyond the frontier,
brought gold and yak-tail plumes,
and their entire territory pledged allegiance.
Emperor Ān (安) increased Lìng Tián's (令田) title to Fèngtōng Yìjūn (奉通邑君).
In the spring of the second year of Yán'guāng (延光),
the Máoniú (旄牛) barbarians rebelled,
attacked Língguān (零關),
and killed the chief magistrate.
Zhāng Qiáo (張喬), the Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州), and the Western Commandery Commandant defeated them.
Thereupon, a Shǔjùn (蜀郡) Dependent State Commandant was established,
administering four counties as a Grand Administrator.
In the second year of Yǒngshòu (永壽) of Emperor Huán (桓),
the Shǔjùn (蜀郡) barbarians rebelled,
killing and plundering officials and common people.
In the second year of Yánxī (延熹),
the Sānxiāng (三襄) barbarians of Shǔjùn (蜀郡) raided Cánlíng (蠶陵),
killing the chief magistrate.
In the fourth year,
the barbarians of Jiānwéi (犍為) Dependent State raided the commandery border.
Shān Yù (山昱), the Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州), defeated them,
beheading one thousand four hundred,
and the rest dispersed.
During Emperor Líng's (靈) time,
the Shǔjùn (蜀郡) Dependent State
was made Hànjiā (漢嘉) Commandery.
The Rǎn-Máng Yí
were pacified by Emperor Wǔ.
In the sixth year of Yuán-Dǐng (111 BCE),
it was established as Wèn-Shān Jùn.
By the third year of Dì-Jié (67 BCE),
due to the heavy levies imposed by the prefecture,
Emperor Xuān therefore abolished and merged it into Shǔ Jùn as Běi-Bù Dū-Wèi.
In its mountains dwell the six Yí, seven Qiāng, and nine Dǐ,
each with their own tribes.
Their kings and marquises mostly understand written documents,
and their laws are severe.
They honor women
and favor the maternal clan.
When someone dies, their corpse is cremated.
The climate is mostly cold;
even in high summer, ice does not melt,
thus the Yí people avoid the cold in winter,
entering Shǔ to work as laborers,
and in summer they flee the heat,
returning to their settlements.
They all live in the mountains,
piling stones to make houses,
some reaching over ten *zhàng* in height,
called Qióng-Lóng.
Also, the soil is barren and saline,
producing no grain, millet, hemp, or beans,
relying solely on wheat for sustenance,
but it is suitable for animal husbandry.
They have *máo-niú* (yak),
which are hornless,
also called *tóng-niú*,
their meat weighs a thousand *jīn*,
and their hair can be made into felt.
Famous horses are produced there.
There are *líng-yáng* (antelopes),
which can cure poisons.
There are also deer that eat medicinal herbs;
for a doe that is pregnant,
the feces in its intestines also cure toxic diseases.
They also have five-horned sheep, musk, light-haired *jiē*-chickens, and *shēng-shēng* (rhino-like beasts).
Their people can make felt from yak hair, patterned blankets (*bān-jì*), green woolen fabrics (*qīng-dùn*), felted cloth (*pī-duō*), and sheepskin robes (*yáng-suō*), and the like.
There are especially many kinds of medicinal herbs.
The land has saline earth,
which is used as salt;
deer, sheep, cattle, and horses that eat it all become fat.
To their west are also the Sān-Hé and Pán-Yú Lǔ,
to the north are the Huáng-Shí, Běi-Dì, and Lú-Shuǐ Hú,
whose territory is considered beyond the frontier.
During the reign of Emperor Líng,
Shǔ Jùn Běi-Bù was again divided to form Wèn-Shān Jùn.
The Bái-Mǎ Dǐ
were, in the sixth year of Emperor Wǔ's Yuán-Dǐng era (111 BCE),
part of Guǎng-Hàn Xī-Bù was detached
and combined to form Wǔ-Dū.
The land is rugged and perilous,
with hemp fields,
producing famous horses, cattle, sheep, lacquer, and honey.
The Dǐ people are brave, reckless, and daring,
greedy for goods and keen on profit.
They live in Hé-Chí,
also called Qiú-Chí,
an area of one hundred *qǐng*,
with sheer cliffs on all four sides.
They frequently raided the borders;
when the prefectures and counties attacked them,
they would rely on their strongholds for defense.
In the third year of Yuán-Fēng (108 BCE),
the Dǐ people rebelled;
troops were sent to defeat them,
and they were relocated to Jiǔ-Quán Jùn.
In the first year of Emperor Zhāo's Yuán-Fèng era (80 BCE),
the Dǐ people rebelled again.
Zhí-Jīn-Wú Mǎ Shì-Jiàn,
Lóng-Hóu Hán Zēng, and Dà-Hóng-Lú Tián Guǎng-Míng were dispatched,
leading troops from Sān-Fǔ and Tài-Cháng to suppress and defeat them.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped and caused chaos,
the Dǐ people also rebelled.
In the early Jiàn-Wǔ era (c. 25 CE),
the Dǐ all submitted to Lǒng and Shǔ.
When Kuí Xiāo was annihilated,
their chieftains then turned away from Gōng-Sūn Shù and surrendered to Han.
Mǎ Yuán, the Administrator of Lǒng-Xī, petitioned to reinstate their kings, marquises, lords, and chiefs,
and they were granted seals and ribbons.
Later, Kuí Xiāo's former subordinate Kuí Mào rebelled,
killing the Administrator of Wǔ-Dū.
Qí Zhōng-Liú, a great chieftain of the Dǐ, was respected and trusted by his kind,
and he brought the various chieftains under his sway.
He joined with the prefectural assistant Kǒng Fèn to attack Mào,
defeating and beheading him.
Later, they also occasionally engaged in raiding and banditry,
and the prefectures and counties attacked and defeated them.
Discussion: The Han dynasty's campaigns against the Róng and Dí,
engaging in distant border affairs,
began and ended with the imperial enterprise.
As for those instances where borders were lost,
and armies were defeated and generals perished,
it was not infrequent.
Ultimately, they were able to open up the territories of the four Yí,
and bring different customs into submission.
As for the spread of civilizing influence
and the renown that circulated,
it nearly reached where the sun rises and sets.
What is recorded in the *Shān-Jīng* and *Shuǐ-Zhì*
also briefly mentions them.
Although submission and rebellion were not constant,
and imperial benevolence was sometimes distant,
when its transforming influence took effect,
then those with hanging ears and tattooed feet,
those who lived like beasts and spoke like birds,
all without exception abandoned their tribes,
turned their faces and pleaded for officials,
crossing seas and barriers,
bringing multiple interpreters to submit.
Therefore, those recorded as Zhōng-Láng and Xiào-Wèi,
and counted among the Dū-Hù and Bù-Shǒu,
numbered in the millions.
Moreover, the spiritual creatures hidden in mountains and seas,
and the rare treasures submerged in sand or dwelling on land,
all manifested in wondrous beauty,
adorning the imperial palaces and tents.
Furthermore, the tributes of *cóng-jiā*, fire fleece, tamed birds, and sealed beasts
were accumulated in the imperial treasury;
the skills of Yí songs, Bā dances, and diverse melodies and rhythms
were performed publicly.
Is it that the way of pacification
must necessarily stop here?
However, it can be said that it reached far.
Although the Mán Yí reside in rugged valleys,
they generally live on fixed land,
extending through the regions of Jīng and Jiāo,
and spreading beyond Bā and Yōng;
their number is immeasurable.
However, their ferocity, bravery, cunning, and calculative nature
are inferior to those of the Qiāng and Dí,
thus the harm from their depredations
cannot be profound.
The southwestern frontier
is particularly weak in this regard.
Thus, the defense of Yǒng-Chāng,
which began remotely,
opening up land and settling people,
continues to be achieved today.
