Eulogy: The myriad Mán live in confusion,
occupying those distant frontiers.
With tattooed bodies and grass clothing,
they rely on deep and precipitous terrain.
There are also separate Yí,
stationed beyond Shǔ.
Their settlements are scattered,
and their paths winding and branched.
When transforming influence arrived and was trusted,
they changed their attire and offered treasures.
Thus Yǒng-Chāng was established,
incorporating millions into the imperial register.
Biography of the Western Qiāng, Chapter Seventy-Seven
The origins of the Xī Qiāng
stem from Sān Miáo,
a branch of the Jiāng clan.
Their territory was near Nán Yuè.
When Shùn banished the Four Villains,
he resettled them at Sān Wēi.
This is the Qiāng land southwest of Héguān.
Bordering Cì Zhī
and extending to the headwaters of the Hé,
it stretches for a thousand *lǐ*.
Cì Zhī
is what Yǔ Gòng called Xī Zhī.
To the south, they bordered the Mányí beyond the frontiers of Shǔ and Hàn;
to the northwest, they bordered the various states of Shànshàn and Chēshī.
Their habitations were not fixed;
they followed water and pasture.
The land yielded few grains,
so they subsisted on livestock farming.
Their customs regarding clans were unsettled;
sometimes they used the father's given name and mother's surname as a clan designation.
After twelve generations,
they intermarried.
If a father died, his stepmother became a wife;
if an elder brother died, his wife was taken in.
Thus, their state had no widows or
unattached people, and their population flourished.
They did not establish rulers or ministers,
nor did they have a supreme leader.
The strong would divide into separate clans and become chieftains;
the weak would become dependents of others.
They constantly raided and brutalized each other,
with strength being the measure of supremacy.
A killer paid with death;
there were no other prohibitions.
Their soldiers were formidable in mountain valleys
but weaker on flat ground.
They could not sustain prolonged battles
but were fierce in initial charges.
Death in battle was considered auspicious,
while death from illness was deemed inauspicious.
They could endure hardship and cold
like wild animals.
Even women giving birth
did not avoid wind and snow.
Their nature was resolute, strong, and brave,
having inherited the *jīn* (metal) element energy of the West.
When royal governance was sound, they submitted;
when moral education failed, they became bandits and rebels.
In ancient times, when Xià Hòu Shì Tài Kāng lost his state,
the Four Barbarians rebelled.
When Hòu Xiāng ascended the throne,
he campaigned against the Quǎnyí.
Only after seven years did they come to submit.
When Hòu Xiè ruled,
he first bestowed ranks and titles,
and from then on, they obeyed.
During Hòu Jié's chaotic reign,
the Quǎnyí settled between Bīn and Qí.
When Chéng Tāng rose to power,
he attacked and repelled them.
When the Yīn dynasty was in decline,
all the barbarians rebelled.
During Wǔ Dīng's reign,
he campaigned against the Xī Róng and Guǐ Fāng,
conquering them after three years.
Hence, his poem says:
"From those Dī and Qiāng,
none dared not come and pay homage."
When Wǔ Yǐ was tyrannical,
the Quǎnróng raided the borders.
Zhōu Gǔ Gōng crossed Mount Liáng and sought refuge beneath Mount Qí.
His son, Jì Lì,
then attacked the Xīluò Guǐ Róng.
During Tài Dīng's time,
Jì Lì again attacked the Yàn Jīng Róng,
but the Róng people severely defeated the Zhōu army.
Two years later,
the Zhōu people conquered the Yúwú Róng.
Thereupon, Tài Dīng appointed Jì Lì as Shepherd.
From then on,
he successively attacked the Shǐ Hū and Yì Tú Róng,
conquering them all.
When Wén Wáng became the Lord of the West,
he faced the threat of the Kūn Yí in the west
and the difficulty of the Xiǎnyǔn in the north.
He then repelled and garrisoned against the Róng and Dí,
and all submitted.
He led the Xī Róng
to campaign against Yīn's rebellious states in service to Zhòu.
When Wǔ Wáng attacked Shāng,
the Qiāng and Máozài led their armies to gather at Mùyě.
During Mù Wáng's time,
the Róng and Dí did not pay tribute.
The king then campaigned west against the Quǎnróng,
capturing their five kings,
and also obtained four white deer
and four white wolves.
The king then moved the Róng to Tàiyuán.
When Yí Wáng declined and weakened,
the distant tribute states did not come to court.
He then ordered Bì Gōng to lead six armies to attack the Tàiyuán Róng.
Upon reaching Yú Quán,
they captured a thousand horses.
Lì Wáng was without principle,
and the Róng and Dí raided.
They then entered Quǎn Qiū
and killed Qin Zhòng's clan.
The king ordered a campaign against the Róng,
but it was unsuccessful.
Four years after Xuān Wáng ascended the throne,
he sent Qín Zhòng to attack the Róng,
but Qín Zhòng was killed by the Róng.
The king then summoned Qín Zhòng's son, Zhuāng Gōng,
and gave him seven thousand soldiers
to attack and defeat the Róng,
which caused them to retreat slightly.
Twenty-seven years later,
the king dispatched troops to attack the Tàiyuán Róng,
but was unsuccessful.
Five years later,
the king attacked the Tiáo Róng and Bēn Róng,
and the royal army suffered a defeat.
Two years later,
the Jìn people defeated the Běi Róng at Fénxí,
and the Róng people destroyed the city of Jiāng Hóu.
The next year,
the king campaigned against the Shēn Róng
and defeated them.
Ten years later,
Yōu Wáng ordered Bó Shì to attack the Liù Jì Róng.
The army was defeated,
and Bó Shì died there.
In that same year,
the Róng besieged Quǎn Qiū
and captured Qín Xiāng Gōng's elder paternal uncle.
At that time, Yōu Wáng was dissolute and tyrannical,
and the Four Barbarians frequently invaded.
He then deposed Empress Shēn and enthroned Bāo Sì.
Márquís Shēn was enraged,
and allied with the Róng to attack Zhōu,
killing Yōu Wáng at Mount Lí.
Zhōu then moved east to Luòyì.
Qín Xiāng Gōng attacked the Róng and saved Zhōu.
Two years later,
Márquís Xíng severely defeated the Běi Róng.
Towards the end of Píng Wáng's reign,
Zhōu declined,
and the Róng pressed upon the various Chinese states.
From west of Mount Lǒng,
and reaching to the Yī and Luò rivers,
there were Róng everywhere.
Thus, at the headwaters of the Wèi River, there were the Dí, Lí, Guī, and Jì Róng.
North of the Jīng River, there were the Yìqú Róng.
In Luò Chuān, there were the Dàlì Róng.
South of the Wèi River, there were the Lí Róng.
Between the Yī and Luò rivers, there were the Yáng Jù and Quán Gāo Róng.
West of the headwaters of the Yǐng River, there were the Mán Shì Róng.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
they dwelled among the Central States
and entered into covenants and alliances with the various Chinese states.
Lǔ Zhuāng Gōng attacked Qín and took the Guī and Jì Róng.
More than ten years later,
Jìn extinguished the Lí Róng.
At this time,
the Yī and Luò Róng were strong,
invading Cáo and Lǔ to the east.
Nineteen years later,
they entered the royal capital.
Thereupon, Qín and Jìn attacked the Róng to save Zhōu.
Two years later,
they again raided the capital,
and Qí Huán Gōng summoned the feudal lords to garrison Zhōu.
Nine years later,
the Lùhún Róng moved from Guā Zhōu to Yī Chuān.
The Yǔn Xìng Róng moved to the confluence of the Wèi River,
extending east to Huànyuán.
Those residing north of the mountains in Hénán were called the Yīn Róng.
The Yīn Róng population then greatly increased.
〔一０〕Jìn Wén Gōng desired to establish his hegemony,
so he bribed the Róng and Dí to open a path
to assist the royal house.
Qín Mù Gōng gained the Róng man Yóu Yú
and consequently became hegemon of the Xī Róng,
expanding his territory by a thousand *lǐ*.
〔一一〕During Jìn Dào Gōng's time,
he again sent Wèi Jiàng to make peace with the various Róng,
and re-established his hegemony.
〔一二〕At this time, Chǔ and Jìn were powerful,
subduing the various Róng.
The Lùhún, Yī, Luò, and Yīn Róng served Jìn,
while the Mán Shì followed Chǔ.
Later, the Lùhún rebelled against Jìn,
and Jìn ordered Xún Wú to destroy them.
〔一三〕Forty-four years later,
Chǔ captured the Mán Shì and imprisoned all their people.
At this time, the Yìqú and Dàlì were the strongest;
they built dozens of walled cities,
all proclaiming themselves kings.
In the eighth year of King Zhēn of Zhōu,
Duke Lì of Qín annihilated the Dàlì,
and seized their territory.
Zhào also destroyed the Dài Róng,
which was the Běiróng.
Hán and Wèi again jointly and gradually absorbed the Yī, Luò, and Yīnróng,
and eliminated them.
Those who escaped
fled west, crossing the Qiān and Lǒng rivers.
From then on, the Central Plains had no Róng invaders,
except for the remaining Yìqú.
In the twenty-fifth year of King Zhēn,
Qín attacked Yìqú
and captured its king.
Fourteen years later,
Yìqú invaded Qín as far as Wèiyīn.
About a hundred years later,
Yìqú defeated the Qín army at Luò.
Four years later,
there was chaos in the state of Yìqú.
King Huì of Qín dispatched Shùzhǎng Cāo to lead an army to pacify it,
and Yìqú then submitted to Qín.
Eight years later,
Qín attacked Yìqú
and took Yùzhì.
Two years later,
Yìqú defeated the Qín army at Lǐbó.
The next year,
Qín attacked Yìqú
and took twenty-five cities in Túxìng.
When King Zhāo ascended the throne,
the King of Yìqú paid homage to Qín
and then had an affair with King Zhāo's mother, Empress Dowager Xuān,
and they had two sons.
In the forty-third year of King Nǎn,
Empress Dowager Xuān lured and killed the King of Yìqú in the Gānquán Palace,
and then raised an army to eliminate Yìqú,
establishing Lǒngxī, Běidì, and Shàngjùn prefectures.
The Róng originally had no rulers.
At the end of the Xià Hòushì dynasty and during the Shāng and Zhōu periods,
some followed marquises and counts in campaigns and earned merits,
whereupon the Son of Heaven granted them titles
to serve as frontier vassals.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
the Lùhún and Mánshì Róng called themselves "zi" (viscount);
during the Warring States period,
the Dàlì and Yìqú called themselves "wang" (king).
When they declined and fell,
the remaining tribes all reverted to being chieftains.
A Qiāng man named Wúyì Yuánjiàn
was captured by Qín during the time of Duke Lì of Qín
and made a slave.
It is not known what branch of Róng Yuánjiàn belonged to.
Later, he managed to escape,
but the Qín people pursued him relentlessly,
so he hid in a cave and escaped.
The Qiāng people say that when Yuánjiàn first hid in the cave,
the Qín people set it on fire.
There was an apparition like a tiger
that shielded him from the fire,
allowing him to survive.
After he came out,
he encountered a woman whose nose had been cut off in the wilderness,
and they became husband and wife.
The woman was ashamed of her appearance
and covered her face with her hair.
The Qiāng people adopted this as a custom.
They then both fled into the area between the Sānhé.
When the various Qiāng saw that Yuánjiàn had survived being burned,
they were amazed by his divinity
and collectively feared and served him,
electing him as their chieftain.
The area between the Hé and Huáng rivers had little grain
but many birds and beasts,
so they made hunting their occupation.
Yuánjiàn taught them farming and animal husbandry,
and he was consequently respected and trusted.
The number of people settling in his encampments and following him increased daily.
The Qiāng people called slaves "wúyì,"
and because Yuánjiàn had once been a slave,
they named him after that.
His descendants were chieftains for generations.
When Yuánjiàn's great-grandson Rěn was alive,
Duke Xiàn of Qín had just ascended the throne
and wished to restore the achievements of Duke Mù,
so he led his army to the source of the Wèi River
and annihilated the Dí Róng.
Rěn's younger paternal uncle, Áng, fearing the might of Qín,
led his people to attach themselves to a settlement and move south,
traveling several thousand li west of the Cìzhī River bend,
severing contact with the majority of the Qiāng
and no longer communicating.
Later, his descendants separated,
each forming their own tribes,
going wherever they pleased.
Some became the Máoniú tribe,
which are the Yuèsuī Qiāng;
some became the Báimǎ tribe,
which are the Guǎnghàn Qiāng;
some became the Cānláng tribe,
which are the Wǔdū Qiāng.
Rěn and his younger brother Wǔ alone remained in the Huángzhong
and both married many wives.
Rěn had nine sons, forming nine tribes;
Wǔ had seventeen sons, forming seventeen tribes.
The flourishing of the Qiāng
began from this point.
When Rěn's son Yán ascended,
King Xiào of Qín was powerful
and subjugated the Qiāng Róng.
King Xiào sent his crown prince Sī to lead ninety-two Róng and Dí states to pay homage to King Xiǎn of Zhōu.
Yán was exceptionally brave,
so the Qiāng later called his descendants the Yán tribe.
During the time of Qín Shǐhuáng,
he focused on unifying the six states
and dealing with the feudal lords,
so his army did not move west.
Therefore, the tribes were able to thrive.
After Qín annexed all under heaven,
Měng Tián was dispatched to lead an army to seize territory,
driving out the various Róng to the west,
and repelling the various Dí to the north.
He built the Great Wall to demarcate the border,
and the various Qiāng no longer crossed south.
When the Hàn dynasty rose,
Mòdún of Xiōngnú was powerful,
defeating the Dōnghú,
driving away the Yuèzhī,
and intimidating all the barbarians,
subjugating the various Qiāng.
During the reign of Emperor Jǐng,
Liú Hé of the Yán tribe led his people to request to guard the Lǒngxī pass.
Thereupon, Liú Hé and others were resettled in Dídao and Āngù,
extending to Líntáo, Dīdào, and Qiāngdào counties.
When Emperor Wǔ campaigned against the Four Barbarians,
opening up vast territories,
he repelled the Xiōngnú to the north
and drove out the various Qiāng to the west.
He then crossed the Hé and Huáng rivers
and built the Lìngjū pass.
He first opened up Hexi,
establishing four commanderies,
opening the road to Yùmén,
and cutting off the Qiāng and Hú,
preventing interaction between north and south.
Thus, barriers, passes, watchtowers, and signal fires extended several thousand li beyond the Great Wall.
At this time, the Xiānlíng Qiāng and the Fēngyǎng Láojiě tribe resolved their enmity and formed an alliance,
communicating with the Xiōngnú.
They combined their forces of over one hundred thousand
and jointly attacked Lìngjū and Āngù,
then besieged Fáohǎn.
Hàn dispatched General Lǐ Xī and Commandant of the Household Xú Zìwéi to lead an army of one hundred thousand men to defeat and pacify them.
The Protector of the Qiāng Commander was first established,
holding a scepter and overseeing them.
The Qiāng then left the Huángzhong
and settled around the Xīhǎi and Yánchí lakes.
Hàn then built passes using the mountains,
and the Hexi region became vacant.
People were gradually relocated to populate it.
When it reached the time of Emperor Xuān,
he dispatched Grand Master of Remonstrance Yìqú Ānguó
to observe the various Qiāng tribes.
Their Xiānlíng leaders stated:
"We wish to cross the Huángshuǐ river
and occupy uncultivated lands for pasturage."
Ānguó reported the matter to the throne,
but the General of the Rear, Zhào Chōngguó, deemed it inadvisable.
Later, by virtue of their previous statement,
they eventually crossed the Huángshuǐ,
and the commanderies and counties were unable to stop them.
By the third year of Yuánkāng,
the Xiānlíng, together with other Qiāng tribes, swore a great oath,
intending to raid the border.
When the Emperor heard this,
he again sent Ānguó with troops to observe them.
Upon Ānguó's arrival,
he summoned over forty Xiānlíng leaders and executed them.
He then unleashed his troops to attack their tribe,
beheading over a thousand.
At this, the various Qiāng were resentful and angry,
and consequently raided Jīnchéng.
Zhào Chōngguó was then dispatched with other generals, leading sixty thousand troops, to defeat and pacify them.
It was then that Shāodāng, the thirteenth-generation descendant of Yán, rose to prominence.
During the reign of Emperor Yuán,
the Guòjiě and six other Qiāng tribes raided Lǒngxī.
The General of the Right, Féng Fèngshì, was sent to defeat and pacify them.
From Yuán Jiàn's tribe, five generations passed until Yán.
Yán was the most valorous and robust,
and thereafter his tribe was named after him.
Thirteen generations later, Shāodāng appeared.
He was again valorous and robust,
and his descendants subsequently adopted Shāodāng as their tribal name.
For several decades after the submission of the Guòjiě Qiāng,
the four barbarian tribes were compliant,
and the frontier regions were peaceful.
When Wáng Mǎng assumed regency,
wishing to display his might and virtue,
he used "cherishing the distant" as a pretext.
He ordered interpreters to convey his intentions to the various Qiāng,
compelling them to jointly offer the land of Xīhǎi.
Initially, it was established as a commandery,
and five counties were constructed.
Border watchtowers and signal fires stretched as far as the eye could see.
Diānliáng
was the great-great-grandson of Shāodāng.
At that time, towards the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
the four barbarian tribes encroached inward.
When Mǎng was defeated,
the various Qiāng returned to occupy Xīhǎi and became raiders.
During the period of Gèngshǐ and Chìméi,
the Qiāng became even more unrestrained,
raiding Jīnchéng and Lǒngxī.
Although Kuí Xiāo commanded troops, he could not suppress them.
Instead, he appeased and conciliated them,
and then mobilized their forces to resist the Hàn.
In the ninth year of Jiànwǔ,
Kuí Xiāo died.
Bān Biāo, a clerk of the Minister of Works, submitted a memorial, stating:
"Now the commandery of Liángzhōu all have surrendered Qiāng.
The Qiāng and Hú, with unbound hair and garments buttoned on the left,
live intermingled with Hàn people.
Their customs are different,
and their languages are mutually unintelligible.
They are frequently encroached upon and plundered by petty officials and cunning individuals,
leading to their desperate rage and misery,
thus causing rebellion.
Indeed, all barbarian incursions and disturbances
are caused by this.
The old system in Yìzhōu Commandery had the Commander of Barbarian Cavalry (Mányí Jì Dūwèi),
in Yōuzhōu Commandery the Commandant Overseeing the Wūhuán (Lǐng Wūhuán Xiàowèi),
and in Liángzhōu Commandery the Protector of the Qiāng (Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi).
All held imperial credentials and were responsible for protection,
resolving their grievances,
making annual tours,
and inquiring about their sufferings.
Furthermore, frequent envoys were dispatched to communicate movements,
making the Qiāng and other barbarians beyond the frontier the eyes and ears of officials,
allowing the provinces and commanderies to be prepared.
It is fitting now to revert to the old system
to clearly demonstrate deterrent power."
Emperor Guāngwǔ adopted this,
immediately appointing Niú Hán as Protector of the Qiāng,
holding imperial credentials as before.
Upon Hán's death, the position was abolished.
In the tenth year,
the Xiānlíng leaders formed alliances with various tribes,
again raiding Jīnchéng and Lǒngxī.
Central Household Commander Lái Xī and others were sent to attack them,
achieving a great victory.
The details are provided in Xī's biography.
In the summer of the eleventh year,
the Xiānlíng tribe again raided Líntáo.
Mǎ Yuán, the Administrator of Lǒngxī, defeated and pacified them.
Later, all submitted,
and were resettled in the three commanderies of Tiānshuǐ, Lǒngxī, and Fúfēng.
The following year,
the Cānláng Qiāng of Wǔdū rebelled.
Yuán again defeated and pacified them.
The details are provided in Yuán's biography.
From Shāodāng to Diānliáng,
they resided generation after generation north of the river in Dàyǔn Gǔ.
Their tribe was small and its people poor.
However, the Xiānlíng and Bēinǎn were both strong and wealthy,
and frequently encroached upon them.
Diānliáng and his father had long endured insults and oppression,
and were angered.
Yet, they had always commanded trust and loyalty within their tribe.
Therefore, they gathered their dependent clans and various other tribes,
then entered through Dàyú,
and launched a surprise attack on the Xiānlíng and Bēinǎn.
They greatly defeated them,
killing three thousand people,
plundering their wealth and livestock,
and seizing their land in Dàyú.
From this, they began to grow strong.
Diān Wú, Diānliáng's son, succeeded him.
In the first year of Zhōngyuán,
the Cānláng Qiāng of Wǔdū rebelled,
killing and plundering officials and civilians.
The Administrator fought them but was defeated.
Liú Xū, the Administrator of Lǒngxī, dispatched Assistant Xīn Dū and Supervisor-of-the-Army Clerk Lǐ Bāo,
leading five thousand men to Wǔdū.
They fought the Qiāng,
beheaded their chieftain,
and captured over a thousand heads.
At that time, the Wǔdū forces also defeated them again,
beheading over a thousand,
and the rest all surrendered.
At this time, Diān Wú's dependent clans grew stronger,
and he constantly dominated the various Qiāng tribes.
Whenever they wished to raid the border,
Diān Wú would instruct them in strategy,
acting as their chief leader.
In the autumn of the second year,
Diān Wú of the Shāodāng Qiāng, along with his younger brother Diān Àn, led five thousand infantry and cavalry to raid the Lǒngxī fortifications.
Liú Xū sent troops to attack them at Fáohǎn,
but could not defeat them.
They also fought at Yǔnjiē,
and were defeated by the Qiāng,
losing over five hundred men.
Thereupon, all the Qiāng guarding the fortifications again banded together to raid.
Usher Zhāng Hóng was sent to lead the troops of various commanderies to attack them.
They fought at Yǔnwú and Tánggǔ,
and the army was defeated.
Hóng and Tián Sà, the Chief Clerk of Lǒngxī, were both lost.
Furthermore, the Tiānshuǐ forces were defeated by the Láojiě tribe at Báishí,
with over a thousand dead.
At this time, there was a woman among the Shāohé leaders named Bǐtóngqián,
over a hundred years old,
who was very wise and resourceful.
She was trusted and respected by her tribesmen,
who all sought her advice.
When they were attacked by the Lúshuǐ Hú,
Bǐtóngqián led her people to seek refuge with the commanderies and counties.
However, some of her tribesmen committed crimes, and the Chief of Línqiāng arrested Bǐtóngqián
and executed six or seven hundred of her people.
Emperor Xiǎnzōng took pity on them
and issued an edict saying:
"In ancient times, Duke Huán attacked the Róng but showed no benevolence or kindness,
hence the 'Spring and Autumn Annals' disparaged him as 'the man of Qí'.
Now the state lacks virtue,
and its grace does not reach the distant.
What sin have the weak and helpless committed
to deserve collective execution?
The brutality of Chángpíng
is not the achievement of an emperor;
the fault lies with administrators and chief officials who arbitrarily inflicted massacres.
For those of Bǐtóngqián's people who are still alive,
wherever they are, provide medical care and sustenance,
and allow them to summon their tribesmen.
If they wish to return to their ancestral lands,
generously send them back.
If smaller tribes surrender themselves,
wishing to contribute,
all their crimes shall be pardoned.
If anyone has rebellious intentions and is captured by officials,
and their case has not yet been decided in court,
all such individuals shall be granted to those who have rendered meritorious service."
In the first year of Yǒngpíng,
Dòu Gù, the Commandant of Cavalry, and Mǎ Wǔ, the General who Captures Barbarians, were again dispatched to attack Diānwú at Xīhán.
They inflicted a great defeat upon him.
The details are already recorded in the biography of Mǎ Wǔ and others.
Diānwú retreated far away,
and the rest all dispersed and surrendered.
Seven thousand households were moved and settled in Sānfǔ.
Dòu Lín, an Attendant, was appointed as the Protector-General of the Qiāng,
residing in Dídao.
Dòu Lín was trusted by the various Qiāng tribes,
and Diān'àn then went to Dòu Lín to surrender.
Dòu Lín was deceived by his subordinate officials,
who falsely reported to the emperor that Diān'àn was a great chieftain.
He was granted the title of Guīyì Hóu by imperial decree,
and given the additional title of Grand Commandant of Hàn.
The following year,
Diānwú surrendered again,
and Dòu Lín again reported him as the foremost chieftain,
bringing him to the imperial court for an audience.
The emperor found it strange to have two chieftains of the same tribe
and doubted the truth of the matter.
He questioned Dòu Lín about it.
Dòu Lín, in a difficult position,
then falsely replied:
"Diān'àn is Diānwú;
the pronunciation in Lǒngxī is merely incorrect."
The emperor thoroughly investigated and discovered the truth,
and angrily dismissed Dòu Lín from office.
At that time, the Inspector of Liángzhōu also reported Dòu Lín's offenses,
so he was imprisoned and died.
Guō Xiāng, an Attendant, temporarily took over the duties of the Protector-General.
Upon arriving in Lǒngxī,
he heard that the Qiāng in Liángzhōu were numerous and powerful.
He returned to the imperial court,
and was punished for his crime.
Thereupon, the office of Protector-General was again abolished.
Diānwú's son, Dōngwú, succeeded him.
Because his father had surrendered to Hàn,
he moved to reside within the frontier,
acting cautiously and maintaining peace.
However, his younger brothers Míwú and others repeatedly engaged in banditry.
In the first year of Jiànchū, during Sùzōng's reign,
an official of Ānyí County kidnapped a woman of the Bēinán Qiāng tribe.
The official was killed by her husband.
Zōng Yán, the Prefect of Ānyí, pursued them outside the frontier.
The tribesmen, fearing execution,
jointly killed Zōng Yán,
and allied with the Lèjiě and Wúliáng tribes to become bandits.
Sūn Chún, the Administrator of Lǒngxī, dispatched Lǐ Mù, an Administrator, along with troops from Jīnchéng to assemble at Héluó Gǔ.
They fought against the Bēinán and others,
beheading and capturing several hundred people.
Wú Táng, the former General who Crossed the Liao River, was again appointed as Protector-General of the Qiāng,
residing in Ānyí.
In the summer of the second year,
Míwú gathered his forces with various tribes,
intending to rebel and leave the frontier.
Hǎo Chóng, the Administrator of Jīnchéng, pursued them.
They fought at Lì Gǔ,
where Hǎo Chóng's army was greatly defeated.
Hǎo Chóng escaped with light cavalry,
and over two thousand men died.
Thereupon, all the tribes and the Lúshuǐ Hú of the dependent states responded to the call,
and Wú Táng was unable to control them.
He was summoned and dismissed from office.
Fù Yù, the Administrator of Wǔwēi, succeeded him as Protector-General,
relocating his residence to Línqiāng.
Míwú, along with Bùqiáo and other chieftains of the Fēngyǎng tribe, totaling over fifty thousand people, jointly raided Lǒngxī and Hànyáng.
Thereupon, Mǎ Fáng, the Acting General of Agile Cavalry,
and Gěng Gōng, the Commandant of Chángshuǐ, were dispatched as his deputy,
to suppress and defeat them.
Consequently, the Línzhōu, Suǒxī, Míwú, and other tribes all surrendered.
Mǎ Fáng then built the city of Suǒxī,
moving the Southern Commandant of Lǒngxī to garrison it,
and restored all the observation posts.
By the third year of Yuánhé,
Míwú again rebelled with his younger brother Hàowú and various other tribes.
In autumn,
Hàowú first made a minor incursion into the Lǒngxī border.
Lǐ Zhāng, the Chief of Beacon Supervisors of the commandery, pursued him,
capturing Hàowú alive
and bringing him to the commandery.
Hàowú said:
"Killing me alone
will not harm the Qiāng.
If I can truly return alive,
I will certainly have all the troops withdrawn
and no longer violate the frontier."
Zhāng Yū, the Administrator of Lǒngxī, used his discretion to release him.
The Qiāng then disbanded,
each returning to their former lands.
Míwú retreated to Guīyìchéng, north of the Yellow River.
Fù Yù did not want to lose trust and attack him,
so he recruited men to fight the various Qiāng and Hú.
The Qiāng and Hú refused,
and then rebelled again, leaving the frontier,
seeking refuge with Míwú.
In the first year of Zhānghé,
Fù Yù requested the dispatch of five thousand men each from Lǒngxī, Zhāngyè, and Jiǔquán.
The administrators of the various commanderies would lead them.
Fù Yù himself would lead five thousand men from Hànyáng and Jīnchéng,
totaling twenty thousand troops.
He set a date with the various commanderies to attack them,
ordering the Lǒngxī troops to occupy the area south of the Yellow River,
and the Zhāngyè and Jiǔquán troops to block their west.
Before the forces could unite,
Fù Yù's army advanced alone.
Míwú heard of this,
and moved his encampment away.
Fù Yù selected three thousand elite cavalry to pursue him relentlessly.
At night, they reached Sāndōu Gǔ, south of Jiànwēi,
a few li from the barbarians.
He intended to attack them at dawn,
and did not set up defenses.
Míwú then ambushed with three hundred men,
attacking Fù Yù's camp at night.
The camp was alarmed and scattered,
Fù Yù dismounted and fought hand-to-hand,
killing over ten men before he died.
Eight hundred and eighty men died.
When the troops from the various commanderies arrived,
the Qiāng had already withdrawn.
Fù Yù
was from Běidì.
At the beginning of Xiǎnzōng's reign,
he was the Prefect of Línqiāng,
and with Mǎ Wǔ, the General who Captures Barbarians, and others, he attacked the Qiāng Diānwú,
his achievements surpassing all other armies.
When he was in Wǔwēi,
his prestige was heard even by the Xiongnú.
He received emoluments for several decades,
but spent all his salary and provisions on assisting friends and acquaintances.
His wife and children were not exempt from fetching water and grinding grain.
Sùzōng issued an edict posthumously commending him.
His son, Yì, was enfeoffed as Míngjìn Hóu,
with seven hundred households.
Zhāng Yū, the Administrator of Lǒngxī, succeeded him as Protector-General,
leading ten thousand men to garrison Línqiāng.
After Míwú killed Fù Yù,
he became accustomed to the spoils from the border.
In the first year of Zhānghé,
he again entered the Jīnchéng frontier with seven thousand foot and cavalry from various tribes.
Zhāng Yū dispatched Sīmǎ Fáng, an Administrator, leading over a thousand cavalry and troops from Jīnchéng, to battle at Mùchéng Gǔ.
Míwú's forces were defeated and fled.
Through an interpreter, he sought to surrender,
and Zhāng Yū accepted him.
Míwú then brought his tribesmen to Línqiāng County.
Zhāng Yū set up a grand military assembly,
and put poison in the wine.
When the Qiāng became drunk,
Zhāng Yū personally attacked them,
and his ambushers rose up,
executing over eight hundred chieftains and prominent figures.
He beheaded Míwú and four others,
offering their heads as sacrifice at Fù Yù's tomb.
He then released his troops to attack those in the mountains and valleys,
beheading over four hundred people
and capturing over two thousand alive.
Míwú's son, Mítáng, and his tribesmen wept and wailed towards the frontier.
They allied with Shāohé, Dāngjiān, Dāngtián, and others,
exchanging their children and gold and silver as betrothal gifts with various tribes,
resolving old feuds and exchanging hostages.
They led five thousand men to raid the Lǒngxī frontier.
Kòu Xū, the Administrator, fought with them at Báishí.
Mítáng was at a disadvantage
and withdrew to Dà Yú Gǔ and Xiǎo Yú Gǔ.
Northwards, he summoned the various Hú tribes of the dependent states,
gathering his affiliated settlements.
His tribal forces grew strong and numerous,
and Zhāng Yū was unable to suppress them.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
Zhāng Yū was summoned and dismissed due to his actions.
Dèng Xùn, the Administrator of Zhāngyè, was appointed as Protector-General in his place.
Dèng Xùn gradually used rewards and bribes to sow discord among them,
and thus the various tribes somewhat eased their activities.
Dōngwú Zǐdōng Hào Lì.
At this time, Hào Wú led his people to surrender.
Commandant Dèng Xùn sent troops to attack Mítáng;
Mítáng left Dàyúgǔ and Xiǎoyúgǔ,
and moved to live in Pōyángǔ.
In the fourth year of Yongyuán of Emperor Hé,
Xùn died of illness.
Ní Shàng, the Administrator of Shǔjùn, replaced him as commandant.
Shàng saw that his predecessors had repeatedly campaigned without success,
and wished to subdue them with civil virtue.
So he sent an envoy to summon Mítáng,
and had him return to live in Dàyúgǔ and Xiǎoyúgǔ.
After Mítáng had returned,
he sent his paternal grandmother, Bēiquē, to Shàng.
Shàng personally escorted her to the frontier,
set up a farewell feast for her,
and ordered interpreter Tián Sǐ and five others to guard and escort her to the encampment.
Mítáng then rebelled,
and together with various tribes, brutally slaughtered Sǐ and the others,
swore a blood oath,
and again raided Jīnchéngsài.
In the fifth year,
Shàng was summoned (for official duties) and dismissed.
Guàn Yǒu, the Commander of Jūyán, replaced him as commandant.
Yǒu considered Mítáng difficult to win over with virtue,
and that he would eventually rebel.
So he sent envoys to sow discord among the various tribes,
enticing them with wealth.
Thus, they dispersed.
Yǒu then sent troops out of the frontier,
attacked Mítáng at Dàyúgǔ and Xiǎoyúgǔ,
captured over eight hundred heads and captives,
and collected tens of thousands of hú of wheat.
He then built fortresses along the Fēngliú Dàhé,
made large rafts,
and constructed a river bridge,
intending to cross troops to attack Mítáng.
Mítáng then led his tribe far away to rely on the bends of the Cìzhī Hé.
By the eighth year,
Yǒu died of illness.
Shǐ Chōng, the Administrator of Hànyáng, replaced him as commandant.
When Chōng arrived,
he immediately dispatched Qiāng and Hú from Huángzhōng to go out of the frontier and attack Mítáng.
However, the Qiāng met and defeated Chōng's troops,
killing several hundred people.
The next year,
Chōng was summoned (for official duties).
Wú Zhǐ, the Administrator of Dàijùn, replaced him as commandant.
That autumn,
Mítáng led eight thousand men to raid Lǒngxī,
killing several hundred people.
Taking advantage of his victory, he advanced deeply,
coercing the various Qiāng tribes within the frontier to join him in banditry.
All the Qiāng tribes again responded to him,
gathering thirty thousand infantry and cavalry,
attacked and defeated the Lǒngxī troops,
and killed the Grand Chief of Dàxià.
Liú Shàng, acting General Who Attacks the West, and Zhào Dài, Deputy Colonel of the Agile Cavalry, were dispatched
to lead the Five Battalions of the Northern Army, the Liyáng and Yōng Battalions, the elite archers of the Sānfǔ, and thirty thousand frontier soldiers, Qiāng, and Hú to suppress them.
Shàng was stationed at Díyáng,
and Dài was stationed at Páohǎn.
Shàng sent his Sīmǎ, Kòu Xū, to oversee the troops of the various commanderies,
converging from all four directions.
Mítáng, fearing,
fled with his old and weak into the south of Líntáo.
Shàng and others pursued him to Gāoshān.
Mítáng, desperate,
led his elite and strong forces in a great battle.
Xū beheaded over a thousand captives
and captured over ten thousand head of cattle, horses, and sheep.
Mítáng withdrew.
The Han troops also suffered many dead and wounded,
and could not pursue further.
So they returned within the frontier.
The next year,
Shàng and Dài were both summoned, imprisoned,
and dismissed for cowardice.
Wáng Xìn, the Palace Attendant, commanded Shàng's camp and was stationed at Páohǎn.
Gěng Tán, the Palace Attendant, commanded Dài's camp and was stationed at Báishí.
Tán then offered rewards,
and many tribes came to submit.
Mítáng, afraid,
then requested to surrender.
Xìn and Tán then accepted his surrender and withdrew their troops,
sending Mítáng to the imperial court.
The remaining tribes, numbering less than two thousand,
were hungry and unable to sustain themselves,
so they moved into Jīnchéng.
Emperor Hé ordered Mítáng to lead his people back to Dàyúgǔ and Xiǎoyúgǔ.
Mítáng believed that since Han had built a river bridge,
troops would come unpredictably,
and his former land was no longer habitable.
He declined, citing that his people were starving
and unwilling to move far.
Wú Zhǐ and others then generously bestowed Mítáng with gold and silk,
ordering him to buy grain and livestock
and urging him to go out of the frontier.
His people became more suspicious and alarmed.
In the twelfth year,
he again rebelled,
coercing the various Hú of Huángzhōng
to raid and then depart.
Wáng Xìn, Gěng Tán, and Wú Zhǐ were all summoned (for official duties).
Zhōu Wěi, the Administrator of Jiǔquán, replaced him as commandant.
The next year,
Mítáng returned to the bends of the Cìzhī Hé.
Initially,
the Lěijiě tribe had attached themselves to Han.
Mítáng resented this,
and consequently attacked and killed their chiefs.
From this, he became an enemy of the various tribes,
and his allies became increasingly scarce.
That autumn,
Mítáng again led troops towards the frontier.
Zhōu Wěi, together with Hóu Bà, the Administrator of Jīnchéng,
and the troops of various commanderies, the subordinate state's Yuèzhī Hú of Huángzhōng, and the Láojiě Qiāng of Lǒngxī,
assembled thirty thousand men.
They went out of the frontier to Yǔnchuān
and fought Mítáng.
Zhōu Wěi returned to his camp and defended himself,
only Hóu Bà's troops broke the enemy formation,
beheading over four hundred.
The Qiāng forces suffered injuries,
and their people disintegrated.
Over six thousand surrendered,
and were relocated to Hànyáng, Āndìng, and Lǒngxī.
Mítáng then weakened,
his people numbering less than a thousand.
He traveled far beyond the source of the Cìzhī Hé,
relying on the Fāqiāng for habitation.
The next year,
Zhōu Wěi was summoned (for official duties) for cowardice.
Hóu Bà replaced him as commandant.
The surrendered Qiāng of Āndìng, Shāohézhǒng, coerced several hundred Qiāng to rebel.
The commandery troops attacked and annihilated them,
confiscating all the weak and vulnerable as slaves.
At that time, Xīhǎi and the areas around Dàyúgǔ and Xiǎoyúgǔ were free from Qiāng raids.
Cáo Fèng, the Chancellor of Yúmí, submitted a memorial:
"The Xīróng causing harm
was a problem for previous generations.
I cannot recount ancient history,
but let me speak of recent events.
Since Jiànwǔ,
those who broke the law
have always started with the Shāodāng tribe.
The reason for this is
that they live in Dàyúgǔ and Xiǎoyúgǔ,
where the land is fertile and beautiful,
and also close to the interior of the frontier,
making it easy for various tribes to cause trouble,
and difficult to attack.
To the south, they gained Zhōngcún to expand their numbers,
to the north, they were blocked by the Dàhé, using it as a stronghold.
They also had the benefits of fish and salt from Xīhǎi,
and along the mountains and by the water,
they expanded their fields and livestock.
Thus, they were able to become strong
and always dominated the other tribes,
relying on their power and bravery,
enticing Qiāng and Hú.
Now they are in decline and distress,
their allies are ruined and discouraged,
their relatives have split and rebelled.
The remaining effective soldiers are no more than several hundred,
fleeing and hiding,
relying far away on the Fāqiāng.
I, your humble servant, believe that it is opportune at this time
to re-establish the commanderies and counties of Xīhǎi,
to fortify the two Yú valleys,
to widely establish military agricultural colonies,
to block the paths of interaction for the Qiāng and Hú,
and to cut off the source of the cunning and avarice of the barbarians.
Moreover, by cultivating grain and enriching the frontier,
the burden of transportation can be reduced,
and the state can be free from worries in the west."
Thereupon, Fèng was appointed Commander of the Western District of Jīnchéng,
and was to lead relocated soldiers to garrison Lóngqí.
Later, Shàngguān Hóng, the Chief Prefect of Jīnchéng, proposed establishing twenty-seven military agricultural colonies for Guīyì and Jiànwēi,
and Hóu Bà again proposed establishing five military agricultural colonies for Dōnghán and Xīhán,
and adding two for Liú and Fēng.
The Emperor approved all of them.
Garrisons were arrayed along the river,
totaling thirty-four.
Their work was almost complete.
By the middle of Yǒngchū,
the various Qiāng rebelled,
and so they were abolished.
Mítáng lost his people
and died of illness.
He had one son who came to surrender, with a household of less than several tens.
Dōnghào Zǐ Mánú was installed.
He first surrendered with his father,
and resided in Āndìng.
At that time, the surrendered Qiāng were scattered across various commanderies and counties,
all subjected to corvée labor by local officials and powerful families,
accumulating resentment and grievances.
In the summer of Yǒngchū 1st year (107 CE) of Emperor Ān,
the Court Attendant with Cavalry, Wáng Hóng, was dispatched to raise several hundred thousand Qiāng cavalry from Jīnchéng, Lǒngxī, and Hànyáng to conquer the Western Regions.
Hóng pressed for their immediate departure.
The various Qiāng feared a distant deployment from which they would not return,
and many scattered and rebelled
when they reached Jiǔquán.
Each commandery dispatched troops to intercept them,
sometimes destroying their homes.
Thereupon, the great chieftains of the Lèjiě and Dāngjiān tribes, Dōng'àn and others, became even more alarmed,
and simultaneously fled in disarray.
Mánú and his brothers, along with their people, subsequently departed west out of the frontier pass.
Diānlíng, a separate branch of the Xiānlíng, and various Zhōng Qiāng tribes, engaged in extensive banditry and looting,
cutting off the Lǒng Road.
At that time, the Qiāng had been under Han rule for a long time,
and no longer possessed weapons or armor.
Some carried bamboo poles or wooden branches in place of spears and halberds,
some carried planks and tables as shields,
and some held bronze mirrors to symbolize weapons.
The commanderies and counties were fearful and weak, unable to control them.
In winter,
Chariot and Cavalry General Dèng Zhì was dispatched,
with the Colonel of the Campaign against the West, Rèn Shàng, as his deputy,
leading the Five Garrisons and troops from Sānhé, Sānfǔ, Rǔnán, Nányáng, Yǐngchuān, Tàiyuán, and Shàngdǎng, totaling 50,000 men,
to garrison Hànyáng.
In the spring of the following year,
before the troops from the various commanderies could arrive,
several thousand Zhōng Qiāng first defeated Zhì's army west of Jì,
killing over a thousand people.
Colonel Hóu Bà was summoned and dismissed due to the rebellion of the Qiāng,
and Duàn Xǐ, the Protector General of the Western Regions, was appointed to replace him as Colonel.
That winter,
Zhì sent Rèn Shàng and the Attendant Official, Sīmǎ Jūn, to lead troops from various commanderies to battle several tens of thousands of Diānlíng and others at Píngxiāng.
Shàng's army was utterly defeated,
with over 8,000 dead.
Thereupon, Diānlíng and others proclaimed themselves
"Sons of Heaven"
in Běidì,
recruiting various mixed tribes from Wǔdū, Cānláng, Shàngjùn, and Xīhé.
Their forces grew greatly,
attacking Zhào and Wèi to the east,
and entering Yìzhōu to the south,
killing Dǒng Bǐng, the Administrator of Hànzhōng,
then raiding and looting the Sānfǔ,
and cutting off the Lǒng Road.
Grain in the various counties of Huángzhōng cost ten thousand cash per shí,
and countless common people died.
The court was unable to control them,
and transport difficulties became severe.
Consequently, an edict ordered Zhì to return his army,
leaving Rèn Shàng to garrison Hànyáng
to coordinate all armies.
Due to the Empress Dowager Dèng,
the court welcomed and appointed Zhì as Grand General,
and enfeoffed Rèn Shàng as Marquis of Lètíng,
with an income fief of three hundred households.
In the spring of the 3rd year,
Court Attendant with Cavalry Rèn Rén was again dispatched to supervise the garrisoned troops of various commanderies to rescue the Sānfǔ.
Rén was always unsuccessful in battle,
and the Qiāng, emboldened by victory, repeatedly defeated the Han army.
The Dāngjiān and Lèjiě tribes attacked and captured Pòqiāng County,
and the Zhōng Qiāng also captured Líntáo County,
taking the Southern Commander of Lǒngxī alive.
In the spring of the following year,
Diānlíng sent men to raid Bāozhōng,
burning post stations
and extensively plundering the populace.
Thereupon, Zhèng Qín, the Administrator of Hànzhōng, moved his garrison to Bāozhōng.
The army had been campaigning for a long time without success,
and agricultural production was neglected.
Thus, an edict ordered Rèn Shàng to lead his officials and soldiers back to garrison Cháng'ān,
dismissing the officials and soldiers from Nányáng, Yǐngchuān, and Rǔnán.
The Hǔyá Commander of Jīngzhào was stationed in Cháng'ān,
and the Fúfēng Commander in Yōng,
following the old precedents of the Sānfǔ Commanders of the Western Capital.
At this time, the Qiāng again attacked Bāozhōng.
Zhèng Qín wanted to engage them.
His Chief Clerk, Duàn Chóng, advised against it,
believing that since the "barbarians" were victorious,
their vanguard was irresistible,
and it was advisable to hold firm and await them.
Qín did not follow,
and went out to battle,
suffering a great defeat,
with over 3,000 dead.
Duàn Chóng and his subordinates, Wáng Zōng and Yuán Zhǎn, protected Qín with their bodies,
and died with him.
Thereupon, Jīnchéng Commandery was moved to Xiāngwǔ.
Rèn Rén suffered repeated defeats,
and his soldiers were undisciplined.
He was summoned in a caged cart to the judicial prison of the Court of the Imperial Censor and died.
Duàn Xǐ died of illness,
and the former Colonel Hóu Bà was again appointed to replace him,
subsequently moving his residence to Zhāngyè.
In the spring of the 5th year,
Rèn Shàng was dismissed for lack of merit.
The Qiāng then invaded Hédōng,
reaching Hénèi.
The common people panicked,
many fleeing south across the Yellow River.
Zhū Chǒng, the Chief of the Northern Army, was sent to lead the Five Garrisons to garrison Mèngjīn.
An edict ordered Wèijùn, Zhàoguó, Chángshān, and Zhōngshān to build 616 walled strongholds and watchtowers.
As the Qiāng became increasingly powerful,
many of the Administrators (two-thousand-shi rank), Prefects, and Chiefs were from interior commanderies,
having no intention to defend or fight,
and all vied to request relocation of their commanderies and counties to avoid the banditry.
The court complied,
thus moving Lǒngxī to Xiāngwǔ,
Āndìng to Měiyáng,
Běidì to Chíyáng,
and Shàngjùn to Yá.
The common people were attached to their land
and unwilling to leave their old homes.
So, their crops were cut down,
their houses dismantled,
their camps leveled,
and their stores destroyed.
At that time, there were continuous droughts, locusts, and famine,
and people were driven, abducted, and plundered,
scattered and separated,
dying along the roads.
Some abandoned the elderly and weak,
some became servants and concubines for others,
losing more than half their numbers.
Rèn Shàng was again appointed Imperial Household Grandee,
and attacked the various Qiāng at Yángtóu Mountain in Shàngdǎng,
defeating them.
Over 200 of the surrendered were lured and killed.
The Mèngjīn garrison was then disbanded.
That autumn,
Dù Qí of Hànyáng and his brother Jìgòng, along with Wáng Xìn and others from the same commandery, conspired with the Qiāng,
gathered a multitude, and entered Shàngguī city.
Qí proclaimed himself General who Pacifies Han.
Thereupon, an edict offered a reward: whoever obtained Qí's head
would be enfeoffed as a ranked marquis and
granted one million cash.
Qiāng or Hú who beheaded Qí would be given one hundred catties of gold
and two hundred catties of silver.
Zhào Bó, the Administrator of Hànyáng, sent assassin Dù Xí to assassinate Qí.
Xí was enfeoffed as Marquis who Suppresses Treachery
and granted one million cash.
However, Dù Jìgòng, Wáng Xìn, and others led their forces to occupy Chūquán camp.
Imperial Household Grandee Táng Xǐ led troops from various commanderies to attack and defeat them,
beheading over 600 of Wáng Xìn and others,
confiscating 500 wives and children,
and seizing over 100 million in gold, silver, and silk.
Dù Jìgòng fled to Diānlíng.
In the 6th year,
Rèn Shàng was again summoned and dismissed.
Diānlíng died,
and his son Língchāng was installed in his place.
Being still young,
Lángmò, of the same tribe, advised him.
He appointed Dù Jìgòng as general,
residing separately in Dīngxī City.
In the summer of the 7th year,
Court Attendant with Cavalry Mǎ Xián and Hóu Bà launched a surprise attack on Língchāng's separate division, the Láojiāng, in Āndìng,
capturing a thousand people,
and obtaining over 20,000 donkeys, mules, camels, horses, cattle, and sheep,
which were distributed to the captors.
In the spring of the first year of Yuánchū,
troops were dispatched to garrison Hénèi,
and thirty-three strategically important valleys and passes
were fortified with earthworks and walls,
and signal drums were set up.
Língchāng sent troops to raid Yōngchéng.
Hàoduō, together with the great chieftains of Dāngjiān and Lèjiě, coerced various tribes
and divided their forces to plunder Wǔdū and Hànzhōng.
The Bǎnshǔnmán of Bājùn led troops to rescue them.
Chéngxìn, the Wǔguān Yuàn of Hànzhōng, led brave warriors and, together with the Mán, attacked and defeated them.
Hàoduō retreated,
then cut off the Lǒngdào road,
and conspired with Língchāng.
Hóu Bà and Mǎ Xián led officials and commoners from Huángzhōng, as well as surrendered Qiāng and Hú, to Fúhǎn to attack them,
beheading over two hundred.
Pí Yáng, the Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu, attacked the Qiāng at Dídao,
suffering a great defeat,
with over eight hundred dead.
Yáng was summoned and dismissed for this.
Hóu Bà died of illness.
Páng Cān, the Tàishǒu of Hànyáng, succeeded him as Xiàowèi.
Cān attracted and enticed them with kindness and trust.
In the spring of the second year,
Hàoduō and others led over seven thousand people to Cān to surrender,
and were sent to the imperial court.
Hàoduō was bestowed with a marquis's seal and ribbon and sent away.
Cān deceived them into returning to live in Lìngjū,
thus opening up the Hexī Road.
However, Língchāng's tribes again divided to raid Yìzhōu.
Zhōnglángjiàng Yǐn Jiù was sent with Nányáng troops,
and then mobilized garrison troops from various commanderies in Yìbù to attack Língchāng's faction, Lǚ Shūdū, and others.
By autumn,
Chén Xǐng and Luó Héng of Shǔ responded to the call,
assassinating Shūdū,
and both were enfeoffed as marquises and rewarded with money.
Túnqí Xiàowèi Bān Xióng was also stationed in Sānfǔ.
Sīmǎ Jūn, the Zuǒ Fēngyì, was sent to act as Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,
commanding Yòu Fúfēng Zhòngguāng, Āndìng Tàishǒu Dù Huī, Běidì Tàishǒu Shèng Bāo, Jīngzhào Hǔyá Dūwèi Gěng Pǔ, Yòu Fúfēng Dūwèi Huángfǔ Qí, and others,
totaling over eight thousand men.
Páng Cān also led over seven thousand Qiāng and Hú soldiers.
They divided their forces with Jūn and advanced north to attack Língchāng.
Cān's army reached east of Yǒngshì,
and was defeated by Dù Jìgòng,
whereupon he retreated.
Jūn and others advanced alone,
attacked and captured Dīngxī Chéng,
achieving a great victory and spoils.
Dù Xiùgòng led his forces in a feigned retreat.
Jūn ordered Guāng, Huī, Bāo, and others to collect the Qiāng's grain. Guāng and others disregarded Jūn's orders,
scattering their troops and penetrating deep,
whereupon the Qiāng set an ambush and attacked them.
Jūn was in the city,
angry but did not rescue them.
Guāng and others were all lost,
with over three thousand dead.
Jūn then sent them back,
and was summoned and committed suicide.
Páng Cān was found guilty for failing to meet the deadline and suffering a military defeat.
Mǎ Xián was appointed to act as Xiàowèi in his place.
Later, Rèn Shàng was sent as Zhōnglángjiàng,
leading three thousand five hundred Yǔlín and Tíqí and sons of the Five Garrisons,
to replace Bān Xióng in Sānfǔ.
As Shàng was about to depart,
Yú Xǔ, a native of Huáilìng, advised Shàng, saying:
"Your Excellency has repeatedly received imperial orders to suppress bandits.
The garrison troops in the three provinces number over two hundred thousand,
neglecting farming and sericulture,
and suffering from arduous labor,
yet no achievements have been made,
and the costs and labor increase daily.
If this expedition is not successful,
I truly fear for Your Excellency."
Shàng said:
"I have been worried and anxious for a long time,
not knowing what to do."
Xǔ said:
"Military strategy dictates that the weak do not attack the strong, and those on foot do not pursue those who fly.
This is the natural course of events.
Now the barbarians are all cavalry,
traveling hundreds of li a day.
They arrive like wind and rain,
and depart like a snapped bowstring.
To pursue them on foot,
the situation is that they cannot be caught up with,
which is why there has been prolonged and fruitless effort.
My plan for Your Excellency is
none other than to dismiss the troops from the various commanderies,
and order each to contribute several thousand coins.
Twenty men should collectively buy one horse.
If this is done,
armor can be discarded,
and light cavalry can be used.
With a force of ten thousand cavalry,
to pursue several thousand barbarians,
tailing and enveloping them,
their path will naturally be exhausted.
This will be convenient for the men and beneficial for the task,
and a great achievement will be established."
Shàng was greatly pleased,
and immediately submitted a memorial adopting his plan.
Light cavalry were then dispatched to raid Dù Jìgòng at Dīngxī Chéng,
beheading over four hundred
and capturing several thousand cattle, horses, and sheep.
The following summer,
Dèng Zūn, the Dùliáo Jiāngjūn, led Nán Chányú and the Zuǒ Lùlí Wáng Xūshěn with ten thousand cavalry
to attack Língchāng at Língzhōu,
beheading over eight hundred,
and enfeoffing Xūshěn as Pòlǔ Hóu,
with a golden seal and purple ribbon,
and various rewards of gold and silk.
Rèn Shàng sent troops to defeat the Xiānlíng Qiāng at Dīngxī Chéng.
In autumn,
five hundred watchtowers were built along the northern border of Fēngyì.
Rèn Shàng also sent his acting Sīmǎ to recruit assault troops
to attack Língchāng in Běidì,
killing his wife and children,
capturing twenty thousand cattle, horses, and sheep,
burning his encampments,
beheading over seven hundred,
and obtaining documents of his usurped titles and the seals and ribbons of generals he had captured.
In the spring of the fourth year,
Shàng sent five men, including Yúguǐ of the Dāngtián Qiāng tribe, to assassinate Dù Jìgòng,
and enfeoffed Yúguǐ as Pòqiāng Hóu.
That summer,
Yǐn Jiù was summoned and punished for failing to pacify Yìzhōu.
Zhāng Qiáo, the Cìshǐ of Yìzhōu, took command of Yǐn Jiù's garrison.
He attracted and enticed the rebellious Qiāng,
who gradually surrendered and dispersed.
In autumn,
Rèn Shàng again recruited Hàofēng of the Xiàogōng tribe to assassinate Língchāng,
and enfeoffed Hàofēng as Qiāng Wáng.
In winter,
Rèn Shàng led troops from various commanderies and advanced with Mǎ Xián into Běidì to attack Lángmò.
Xián arrived first at Qīngshí'àn in Āndìng,
where Lángmò counter-attacked and defeated him.
When Shàng's army arrived at Gāopíng,
they combined forces and advanced together.
Lángmò and others retreated.
They then moved their camp to press him,
and at Běidì,
they held out for over sixty days.
They fought at Fùpíng Hér,
and greatly defeated him,
beheading five thousand,
and recovering over one thousand captured men and women,
and over one hundred thousand cattle, horses, donkeys, sheep, and camels.
Lángmò fled.
Then, eleven thousand people of the Qiánrén tribe from Xīhé surrendered to Dèng Zūn.
In the fifth year,
Dèng Zūn recruited Diāohé and others of the Quánwú tribe from Shàngjùn to assassinate Lángmò.
Diāohé was rewarded as Qiāng Hóu,
and Zūn was enfeoffed as Wǔyáng Hóu,
with three thousand households.
Because Zūn was the Empress Dowager's younger cousin,
his爵封优大 was generous and grand.
Rèn Shàng contended with Zūn for credit,
and also falsely inflated the number of enemy heads,
accepted bribes and violated the law,
embezzling over ten million.
He was summoned in a caged cart and executed in the marketplace,
and his fields, houses, slaves, and property were confiscated.
Since the deaths of Língchāng and Lángmò,
the various Qiāng tribes disintegrated,
and Sānfǔ and Yìzhōu were free from further banditry and alarm.
For over ten years since the Qiāng rebellion,
wars were continuous and the armies weary,
with no moment of peace.
Military expenses,
transportation, and supplies
cost over two hundred forty billion,
and the state treasury was depleted.
This extended to the inner commanderies,
and countless border residents died,
leading to the exhaustion of Bìng and Liáng provinces.
In the spring of the sixth year,
the Lèjiě tribe and the Hàoliáng and other Qiāng tribes from Lǒngxī conspired to rebel.
Mǎ Xián preemptively attacked them at Āngù,
beheading Hàoliáng and several hundred tribesmen.
They all surrendered and dispersed.
In the spring of the first year of Yǒngníng,
over five thousand people of the Shěndī Qiāng tribe from Shàngjùn again raided Zhāngyè.
That summer,
Mǎ Xián led ten thousand men to attack them.
They were initially defeated in battle,
with hundreds killed.
They fought again the next day,
and defeated them,
beheading one thousand eight hundred,
capturing over a thousand prisoners,
and tens of thousands of horses, cattle, and sheep.
The remaining barbarians all surrendered.
At that time, the great chieftain Jīwǔ and others of the Dāngjiān tribe,
knowing that Mǎ Xián's troops were in Zhāngyè,
took advantage of the emptiness to raid Jīnchéng.
Mǎ Xián returned with his army, pursued them out of the pass,
beheaded several thousand, and returned.
The Shāodāng and Shāohé tribes, hearing of Mǎ Xián's army's return,
led over three thousand men to again raid Zhāngyè,
killing a senior official.
Earlier,
the great chieftains Lú Cōng and Rěnlíang, of the same tribe as Jīwǔ, with over a thousand households, had remained separately in Yǔnjiē,
and were ambivalent in their loyalties.
In the spring of the first year of Jiànguāng,
Mǎ Xián led troops to summon Lú Cōng and beheaded him.
He then released his troops to attack their tribesmen,
capturing over two thousand heads and prisoners,
and plundering one hundred thousand horses, cattle, and sheep.
Rěnlíang and others all fled out of the pass.
An imperial edict enfeoffed Mǎ Xián as the Marquis of Āntíng,
with a fief of one thousand households.
Rěnlíang and others, considering Mánú and his brothers as the rightful hereditary leaders of the Shāodāng,
and that Mǎ Xián's pacification and support were inadequate,
harbored resentment.
In the autumn,
they consequently allied themselves and together coerced and led three thousand tribal infantry and cavalry to raid Huángzhōng,
attacking the counties of Jīnchéng.
Mǎ Xián led the Xiānlíng tribe to engage them,
fighting at Mùyuàn.
His army was defeated,
with over four hundred killed.
Mánú and others also defeated the Wǔwēi and Zhāngyè commandery troops at Língjū,
and then coerced and led over four thousand households of the Xiānlíng and Shěndī tribes
to flee west along the mountains,
raiding Wǔwēi.
Mǎ Xián pursued them to Luánniǎo,
and called them to surrender.
Several thousand tribesmen surrendered,
and Mánú returned south to Huángzhōng.
In the spring of the first year of Yán'guāng,
Mǎ Xián pursued them to Huángzhōng.
Mánú went out of the pass and crossed the river.
Mǎ Xián again pursued, attacked, and defeated them.
The tribes dispersed and fled,
going to the Inspector of Liángzhōu, Zōng Hàn, to surrender.
Mánú and others were isolated, weak, hungry, and distressed.
In the winter of that year,
they led over three thousand households to surrender to the Administrator of Hànyáng, Gěng Zhǒng.
Emperor Ān granted them golden seals and purple sashes,
and bestowed gold, silver, and colored silks in varying amounts.
In this year,
the Qiánrén Qiāng tribe and the Hú from Shàngjùn rebelled,
attacking Gǔluóchéng.
General Dùliáo, Gěng Kuí, led the commandery troops and Wūhuán cavalry to engage and defeat them.
In the autumn of the third year,
Lǒngxī Commandery began to return to Dídào.
Mánú's younger brother, Xīkǔ, was established.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn under Emperor Shùn,
the Zhōng Qiāng of Lǒngxī rebelled.
Colonel Mǎ Xián led over seven thousand men to attack them,
fighting at Líntáo,
beheading over a thousand.
They all led their tribesmen to surrender.
Mǎ Xián was further enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dūxiāng.
From then on, Liángzhōu was peaceful.
By the fourth year,
Minister Púyè, Yú Xǔ, submitted a memorial stating:
"I have heard that descendants show filial piety by serving their ancestors,
and rulers demonstrate enlightenment by bringing peace to their people.
This is why Gāozōng and Zhōu Xuān could be compared with Tāng and Wǔ.
The Yǒngzhōu region described in the Yǔgòng
has the best land.
Moreover, it has a thousand li of fertile plains,
with abundant grain harvests,
and also the salt ponds of Qiūcí, which benefit the people.
The water and grass are lush,
the land is suitable for pasturage,
horses and cattle form continuous lines,
and flocks of sheep block the roads.
To the north, it is blocked by mountains and rivers,
and controls strategic strongholds.
Irrigation relies on canals,
and water mills grind grain for river transport.
The effort required is minimal,
yet military provisions are ample.
Therefore, Emperor Xiàowǔ and Emperor Guāngwǔ built Shuòfāng,
opened Xīhé,
and established Shàngjùn,
all for these reasons.
However, it suffered from unwarranted disasters,
with the various Qiāng tribes causing internal collapse,
and commanderies and counties experiencing war and desolation for over twenty years.
To abandon the richness of fertile land,
and lose natural resources,
cannot be called advantageous;
to leave the obstructions of rivers and mountains,
and guard indefensible places,
is difficult to secure.
Now the three commanderies are not yet restored,
and the imperial tombs are exposed to the outside.
Yet the dukes and ministers are weak and timid,
only concerned with their own safety,
raising difficulties and objections,
only calculating expenses,
and not planning for peace.
It is fitting to display your sagely virtue,
and consider what is best to implement."
After the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor then restored the three commanderies.
He dispatched Usher Guō Huáng to supervise and urge the relocated people,
each to return to their former counties,
repair city walls,
and establish watchtowers and stations.
Thereafter, rivers were diverted and canals deepened for military agricultural colonies,
saving an estimated one hundred million per year in costs for the inner commanderies.
Consequently, Āndìng, Běidì, Shàngjùn, and Lǒngxī, Jīnchéng were ordered to constantly store grain and millet,
enough for several years.
Mǎ Xián, because Xīkǔ and his brothers had repeatedly rebelled,
imprisoned hostages at Língjū.
That winter,
Mǎ Xián was summoned and dismissed due to an offense.
Hán Hào, Administrator of Yòufúfēng, replaced him as Colonel.
The next year,
Xīkǔ went to Hán Hào, stating his desire to return to his former lands,
but Hán Hào again refused to send him.
Consequently, the military agricultural colonies were relocated to Huángzhōng,
placed between the two rivers,
to pressure the various Qiāng tribes.
Hán Hào was again summoned and dismissed.
Mǎ Xù, Administrator of Zhāngyè, replaced him as Colonel.
The Qiāng tribes between the two rivers, feeling that the military agricultural colonies were too close,
feared they would inevitably be targeted.
They then resolved their feuds and swore alliances,
each preparing themselves.
Mǎ Xù wished to first show kindness and trust,
so he memorialized to move the military agricultural colonies back to Huángzhōng.
The Qiāng tribes' anxieties then settled.
By the first year of Yángjiā,
because the Huángzhōng region was vast,
five more military agricultural divisions were added,
making a total of ten divisions.
In the summer of the second year,
the Southern Commandant of Lǒngxī was re-established as per the old system.
In the third year,
Liángfēng and others of the Zhōng Qiāng again raided Lǒngxī and Hànyáng.
An imperial edict appointed former Colonel Mǎ Xián as Usher,
to pacify and comfort the various tribes.
Mǎ Xù dispatched troops to attack Liángfēng,
beheading several hundred.
In the fourth year,
Mǎ Xián also mobilized officials and soldiers from Lǒngxī, and Qiāng and Hú troops, to attack and kill Liángfēng,
beheading one thousand eight hundred,
and capturing over fifty thousand horses, cattle, and sheep.
Liángfēng's relatives all went to [Mǎ] Xián to surrender.
Mǎ Xián further attacked the Zhōng Qiāng chieftain Qiěchāng.
Qiěchāng and others led over one hundred thousand people from various tribes to the Inspector of Liángzhōu to surrender.
In the first year of Yǒnghé,
Mǎ Xù was promoted to General Dùliáo,
and Mǎ Xián again replaced him as Colonel.
Initially,
the Báimǎ Qiāng of Wǔdū Sàishàng attacked and destroyed the garrison officials,
rebelling for consecutive years.
In the spring of the second year,
the Commandant of the Guǎnghàn Dependent State defeated them,
beheading over six hundred.
Mǎ Xián also attacked and beheaded their chieftains Jīzhǐlěizǔ and others, numbering three hundred.
Thereupon, the area west of Lǒng was again pacified.
The next winter,
Nàlí and others from the Shāodāng tribe, with over three thousand cavalry, raided the Jīnchéng frontier.
Mǎ Xián led troops to engage them,
beheading over four hundred,
and capturing one thousand four hundred horses.
Nàlí and others again recruited Qiāng and Hú from the west,
killing and injuring officials and common people.
In the fourth year,
Mǎ Xián led the Righteous Auxiliaries from Huángzhōng and over ten thousand Qiāng and Hú cavalry to ambush Nà Lí and others.
They were decapitated.
Over 1,200 heads were captured, along with prisoners,
and over 100,000 horses, mules, and sheep were seized.
Mǎ Xián was summoned and appointed Grand Administrator of Hóngnóng.
Lái Jī was appointed Inspector of Bìngzhōu.
Liú Bǐng was appointed Inspector of Liángzhōu.
All assumed their respective posts.
Grand General Liáng Shāng said to Lái Jī and the others:
"The Róng and Dí are 'wildly submissive' (huāng fú),
the Mán and Yí are 'submissive by obligation' (yào fú),
meaning their nature is erratic and inconstant.
Therefore, the method of governance
also has no fixed rules.
Adapt to circumstances,
and largely follow their customs.
Now, you three gentlemen are by nature intolerant of evil,
and wish to clearly distinguish right from wrong.
Confucius said: 'If a man is not benevolent,
and you detest him excessively,
it leads to disorder.'
How much more so with the Róng and Dí!
You must strive to pacify the Qiāng and Hú,
prevent their major offenses,
and tolerate their minor transgressions."
Lái Jī and the others were naturally cruel and harsh,
and thus could not comply.
Upon arriving at their provinces,
they caused much unrest.
In the summer of the fifth year,
the Qiāng tribes of Qiě Dòng, Fù Nán, and others rebelled,
attacking Jīnchéng.
Together with the mixed Qiāng and Hú from Xīsài and Huángzhōng, they heavily plundered the Sānfǔ region,
killing many senior officials.
Lái Jī and Liú Bǐng were both recalled from their posts.
Thereupon, troops from the capital region, nearby commanderies, and various provinces were dispatched to suppress them.
Mǎ Xián was appointed General Who Conquers the West.
Gěng Shū, a Cavalry Commandant, was made his deputy.
They led the Left and Right Yǔlín, the Five School officers, and troops from various provinces and commanderies, totaling 100,000 men, to garrison Hànyáng.
Furthermore, three hundred strongholds (wùbì) were built in Fúfēng, Hànyáng, and Lǒngdào,
where garrisoned troops were stationed
to protect and gather the common people.
Qiě Dòng separately dispatched his tribesmen to raid Wǔdū,
burn Lǒngguān Pass,
and plunder the imperial stud farms.
In the spring of the sixth year,
Mǎ Xián led five or six thousand cavalry to attack them.
Upon reaching Shègūshān,
Mǎ Xián's army was defeated,
and Mǎ Xián and his two sons all died in battle.
Emperor Shùn, pitying them,
bestowed three thousand bolts of cloth
and one thousand hú of grain.
Mǎ Xián's grandson, Mǎ Guāng, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔyáng Tíng,
with an annual rent income of one million (coins).
An Attendant Imperial Censor was sent to supervise the General Who Conquers the West's camp troops
and to care for the dead and wounded.
At this, the Eastern and Western Qiāng greatly united.
The Gǒng Táng tribe, with over three thousand cavalry, plundered Lǒngxī,
also burning imperial gardens and tombs,
and pillaging Guānzhōng.
They killed and injured senior officials.
Rèn Yūn, the Magistrate of Héyáng, pursued them
and died in battle.
A Commandant of the Household, Páng Jùn, was sent to recruit 1,500 brave warriors to garrison Měiyáng,
as reinforcements for Liángzhōu.
Zhào Chōng, the Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi, pursued and attacked the Gǒng Táng Qiāng,
beheading over four hundred
and capturing over 18,000 horses, cattle, sheep, and donkeys.
Over two thousand Qiāng surrendered.
An edict ordered Zhào Chōng to command the troops of the four commanderies west of the river as a military governor (jié dù).
Over a thousand of the Hǎn tribe Qiāng raided Běidì.
Jiǎ Fú, the Grand Administrator of Běidì, and Zhào Chōng attacked them,
but were unsuccessful.
In the autumn,
eight or nine thousand cavalry from various tribes raided Wǔwēi,
and the Liáng province was shaken with fear.
Therefore, the people of Āndìng were again moved to reside in Fúfēng,
and those of Běidì to Féngyì.

Zhāng Qiáo, acting General of Chariots and Cavalry and Bearer of the Golden Mace, was sent to lead the Left and Right Yǔlín, the Five School officers, and troops from Hénèi, Nányáng, and Rǔnán, totaling 15,000 men, to garrison the Sānfǔ.
In the first year of Hàn'ān,
Zhào Chōng was appointed Protector of the Qiāng.
Zhào Chōng appeased and attracted the rebellious Qiāng,
and the Hǎn tribe, with over five thousand households, surrendered to Zhào Chōng.
Thereupon, Zhāng Qiáo's garrisoned army was disbanded.
Only three thousand households of the Shāo Hé tribe remained in the northern border of Cān.
In the summer of the third year,
Zhào Chōng and Zhāng Gòng, the Grand Administrator of Hànyáng, ambushed them,
beheading 1,500
and capturing 180,000 cattle, sheep, and donkeys.
In the winter,
Zhào Chōng attacked various tribes,
beheading over four thousand.
An edict appointed one of Zhào Chōng's sons as a gentleman (láng).
Zhào Chōng again pursued and attacked at Āyáng,
beheading eight hundred.
Thereupon, over thirty thousand households of various tribes, in succession, surrendered to the Inspector of Liángzhōu.
In the spring of the first year of Jiànkāng,
Mǎ Xuán, the Protector of the Qiāng's aide, was enticed by various Qiāng
and led the Qiāng masses to flee outside the frontier.
Wèi Yáo, the acting Protector of the Qiāng, pursued Mǎ Xuán and others,
beheading over eight hundred
and capturing over 200,000 cattle, horses, and sheep.
Zhào Chōng again pursued the rebellious Qiāng to Yīnhé in Jiànwēi.
Before his army had fully crossed the river,
over six hundred surrendered Hú under his command rebelled and fled.
Zhào Chōng led several hundred men in pursuit,
encountered a Qiāng ambush,
and died in battle.
Although Zhào Chōng died,
he had achieved many victories and captures previously,
and the Qiāng were consequently weakened.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā,
Zhào Chōng's son, Zhào Kǎi, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yìyáng Tíng.
Zhāng Gòng, the Grand Administrator of Hànyáng, was appointed to replace him as Protector (of the Qiāng).
Liáng Bìng, the Left Administrator of Féngyì, gradually attracted them with kindness and trust.
Thereupon, over fifty thousand households of Línán, Húnú, and other tribes surrendered to Liáng Bìng,
and Lǒngyòu was pacified again.
Liáng Bìng
was a clansman of Grand General Liáng Jì.
He was enfeoffed as Marquis of Hù,
with a fief of two thousand households.
From the Qiāng rebellion in Yǒnghé
until this year,
a period of over ten years,
expenses amounted to over eighty billion (coins).
Many generals embezzled military provisions
and enriched themselves privately.
They all bribed the imperial entourage with precious treasures and goods.
Both high and low were dissolute,
neglecting military affairs.
Those soldiers who did not die a natural death,
their bones lay scattered across the fields.
In the second year of Jiànhé of Emperor Huán,
the Bái Mǎ Qiāng raided Guǎnghàn Dependent State
and killed senior officials.
At this time, the Western Qiāng and the Hú of Huángzhōng rebelled again and became bandits.
The Inspector of Yìzhōu led the Bǎnshùn Mán to attack and defeat them,
beheading or bringing to surrender two hundred thousand people.
In the first year of Yǒngshòu,
Protector Zhāng Gòng died.
Fèngwǔ Fǎng, the former Grand Administrator of Nányáng, was appointed to replace him as Protector.
He possessed great authority and benevolence,
and the western frontier was peaceful.
In the second year of Yánxī,
Fèngwǔ Fǎng died.
Duàn Jiǒng, a Commandant of the Household, was appointed to replace him as Protector.
At this time, the eight Shāo Dāng tribes raided Lǒngyòu.
Duàn Jiǒng attacked and decisively defeated them.
In the fourth year,
Líng Wú, together with Xiānlíng and the Shěndī and Láojiě tribes from Shàngjùn, combined forces to raid Bìng, Liáng, and the Sānfǔ.
At this time, Duàn Jiǒng was recalled due to an offense,
and Hú Hóng, the Chancellor of Jìnán, was appointed to replace him as Protector.
Hú Hóng lacked prestige and strategy,
and the Qiāng consequently became unruly,
overrunning and destroying camps and strongholds.
The banditry grew rampant.
Huángfǔ Guī, a Commandant of the Household, attacked and defeated them.
In the fifth year,
the Shěndī tribes again raided Zhāngyè and Jiǔquán.
Huángfǔ Guī summoned them,
and they all surrendered.
The details are fully recorded in Huángfǔ Guī's biography.
The Niǎo Wú tribe again raided Hànyáng.
Troops from Lǒngxī, Jīnchéng, and other commanderies jointly attacked and defeated them,
and they all returned and submitted.
By winter,
Diānnà and five or six thousand others again attacked Wǔwēi, Zhāngyè, and Jiǔquán,
burning people's homes.
In the sixth year,
Sūn Qiāng, the Grand Administrator of Lǒngxī, attacked and defeated them,
beheading or drowning over three thousand people.
Hú Hóng fell ill,
and Duàn Jiǒng was again appointed Protector.
In the first year of Yǒngkāng,
Ānwěi and other Eastern Qiāng coerced their tribesmen to repeatedly raid the Sānfǔ.
Zhāng Huàn, a Commandant of the Household, pursued, defeated, and beheaded them.
The details are fully recorded in Zhāng Huàn's biography.
The Dāngjiān Qiāng raided Wǔwēi.
Duàn Jiǒng, General Who Breaks the Qiāng, again defeated and annihilated them,
and the rest all surrendered and dispersed.
The details are fully recorded in Duàn Jiǒng's biography.
In the third year of Jiànníng of Emperor Líng,
the Shāo Dāng Qiāng sent envoys to offer tribute.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng,
the Xiānlíng tribe of the surrendered Qiāng from Běidì, taking advantage of the great Yellow Turban rebellion,
rebelled with the Huángzhōng Qiāng and the Righteous Auxiliary Hú, Běigōng Bóyù and others,
and raided Lǒngyòu.
The details are fully recorded in Dǒng Zhuó's biography.
In the first year of Xīngpíng,
the surrendered Qiāng of Féngyì rebelled
and raided various counties.
Guō Sì and Fán Chóu attacked and defeated them,
beheading several thousand.
From Ái Jiàn onwards,
his descendants branched into a total of 150 kinds.
Of these, nine kinds were west of the source of the Cìzhī River,
and north of the borders of Shǔ and Hàn.
Previous histories do not record their population.
Only the Cānláng were in Wǔdū,
with several thousand fighting men.
Fifty-two of these kinds declined,
unable to stand on their own,
and scattered into attached settlements,
or were completely extinguished without heirs,
or migrated far away.
Of the remaining eighty-nine kinds,
only the Zhōng were the strongest,
with over 100,000 fighting men.
The larger of the others had over 10,000 people,
the smaller ones several thousand people.
They mutually plundered each other,
their strength and weakness constantly changing.
It is estimated that during the reign of Shùndì, their combined fighting men could have reached 200,000.
The Fā Qiāng and Tángmáo, among others, were so remote
that they never had any contact.
The Máoniú and Báimǎ Qiāng were in Shǔ and Hàn.
Their different tribal names
cannot all be recorded or known.
In the 13th year of Jiànwǔ,
the Báimǎ Qiāng chieftains Lóu Dēng and others from outside the Gǔanghàn frontier led over 5,000 households of their people to submit.
Guāngwǔ enfeoffed Lóu Dēng as Guīyì Jūnzhǎng.
By the 6th year of Yǒngyuán during Hédì's reign,
the Dàzāngyí tribal Qiāng chieftains Zàotóu and others from outside the Shǔjùn frontier led over 500,000 people of their tribe to submit.
Zàotóu was appointed Yìjūnzhǎng
and granted a seal and ribbon.
By the 1st year of Yǒngchū during Āndì's reign,
the Qiāng Lóng Qiáo and five other tribes, totaling 17,280 people, from outside the Shǔjùn frontier submitted.
The following year,
the Qiāng Bóshēn and seven other tribes, totaling 36,900 people, from outside the Shǔjùn frontier again brought their land and submitted.
In winter,
the Cānláng tribal Qiāng, 2,400 people, from outside the Gǔanghàn frontier again came to submit.
In the 2nd year of Jiànhé during Huándì's reign,
over 1,000 Báimǎ Qiāng raided the commandery dependent on Gǔanghàn,
killed the chief officials,
and the Yìzhōu Cìshǐ led the Bǎnbùn Mán to attack and defeat them.
The Yuèzhī Hú in Huángzhōng
were a branch of the former Dàyuèzhī;
they previously lived in the lands of Zhāngyè and Jiǔquán.
The Yuèzhī King was killed by Móudún of the Xiōngnú,
and the remaining tribes scattered,
crossing the Cōng Líng to the west.
The weaker among them moved south into the mountains,
settling among the various Qiāng,
and consequently intermarried with them.
When the General of Agile Cavalry Huò Qùbìng defeated the Xiōngnú
and captured the lands of Xīhé,
opening up Huángzhōng,
the Yuèzhī then came to surrender
and lived interspersed with the Hàn people.
Although they were attached to the county administration,
they played both sides.
When fighting with Hàn troops,
they acted according to the strength or weakness of the situation.
Their clothing, food, and language were roughly the same as the Qiāng;
they also used their father's given name and mother's surname as their tribal designation.
They had seven major tribes,
with a combined total of over 9,000 fighting men,
distributed in Huángzhōng and Lìngjū.
Another several hundred households were in Zhāngyè,
known as Yìcóng Hú.
In the 1st year of Zhōngpíng,
they rebelled with Běigōng Bóyù and others,
killed the Protector-General of the Qiāng Líng Zhēng and the Administrator of Jīnchéng Chén Yì,
and consequently plundered and caused chaos in Lǒngyòu.
A commentary states: The troubles with the Qiāng and Róng
have been ongoing since the Sān Dài (Three Dynasties).
During the Hàn dynasty, when compared to the Xiongnu,
they were rather few and weak.
However, after the Restoration (Zhōngxīng),
border difficulties gradually escalated.
The court's policies lost their harmony of appeasement,
and the Róng commanders broke their promises.
Those who had submitted internally
were either oppressed by powerful local magnates
or forced into servitude as slaves.
When the frontier was peaceful,
they harbored resentment and thought of mischief;
when the drums of war briefly sounded,
they quickly donned their quivers and scattered like startled birds.
Thus, during the Yǒngchū period,
various tribes rose up like swarms of bees.
They settled their old feuds
and formed solemn alliances,
recruiting mountain chieftains,
and gathering together through mutual calls.
They fashioned wood into weapons
and carried firewood as shields.
