Their chariots and horses stirred up dust,
rampaging across the Sānfǔ region.
They established their own names and systems,
acting wantonly in Běidì.
To the east, they encroached upon the suburbs of Zhào and Wèi;
to the south, they entered the borders of Hàn and Shǔ.
They blockaded Huángzhōng,
cut off the Lǒng Dào (Long Road),
burned imperial tombs (língyuán),
plundered cities,
inflicting continuous devastation,
with urgent reports arriving daily.
The people of Bìng and Liáng provinces
were especially ravaged and killed.
The strong and brave sacrificed themselves on the battlefield,
while women were bound and taken captive.
Graves were dug up, and corpses exposed,
with both the living and the dead suffering terribly.
Since the Western Róng began their rebellion,
never had they so domineeringly challenged the superior state with such intensity.
Héxī, as a female ruler governing personally,
lacked external prestige.
The court deliberations feared the loss of military strength,
preferring temporary peace.
Some argued that the border prefectures were difficult to assist
and should be abandoned;
others feared that the "gangrene" would spread and fester,
with no end in sight.
Strategists wavered,
and brave warriors hesitated.
Consequently, the people from the four commanderies of Xīhé were relocated
and settled among the counties of Guān Yòu.
Their houses were pulled down and trees felled,
to cut off their attachment to their homeland;
their wealth and stores were burned and destroyed,
to prevent thoughts of returning.
Thereupon, generals such as Dèng Zhì, Rèn Shàng, Mǎ Xián, Huángfǔ Guī, and Zhāng Huàn
competed to propose grand strategies
and successively received orders to launch punitive expeditions.
They conscripted troops and assembled forces
to exploit their weaknesses.
They galloped east and west,
rushing to the rescue of various fronts,
shaking the borders of several provinces,
and depleting thousands of gold daily.
This included increasing taxes on the populace,
borrowing provisions from feudal lords,
drawing upon precious gold, silver, silk, and brocade,
and levying stores of grain, salt, and iron.
The expenses for bribes, rewards,
transport, and labor
amounted to tens of millions, before and after.
Sometimes, they captured and killed chieftains,
destroyed affiliated tribes,
and had captives filling the roads,
with cattle and sheep covering the mountains.
However, before the military reports could detail the gains and losses,
the signs of disloyalty and rebellion were already evident.
Thus, the gains did not compensate for the losses,
and the achievements were not half the effort.
The armies were exposed to the elements,
for years without decisive victory.
Officials were exhausted,
and valiant men died in frustration.
Duàn Jiǒng took charge of affairs,
exclusively managing military responsibilities.
He relied on the fierce nature of the people from Xīshānlǐ,
and was skilled in the customs and dispositions of the Róng.
He fully exerted his military prowess and exhausted his elite forces to carry out his task.
He donned armor and led the advance,
personally facing death in a hundred battles.
He endured ice and snow,
traversing paths of a thousand twists and turns.
He initially annihilated the Western tribes
and ultimately pacified the Eastern bandits.
As for those slaughtered in direct assaults
or scattered in hot pursuit,
their heads severed and rolling down ten-thousand-foot mountains,
their bodies dismembered on towering cliffs,
they were countless.
Those who managed to crawl through grass and rocks,
and escape from the spearheads and arrows,
were less than one or two in a hundred.
Yet Zhāng Huàn highly praised
"the Róng and Dí, born of the same vital energy,
should not be utterly exterminated.
Shedding blood to pollute the fields harms harmony and invites ill omens."
How circuitous these words are!
Although the Qiāng were an external threat,
they were truly a deep internal ailment.
If not attacked at the root,
it would be like nurturing a chronic disease in the heart and belly.
Alas, the enemies were almost pacified,
but the Hàn dynasty's fate also declined.
Alas!
In ancient times, the former kings wisely managed the Nine Regions,
distinguishing between the royal domain and the wilderness.
Knowing that the Yí and Mò had different natures
and were difficult to govern by moral principles,
they therefore kept the various Huá tribes distant,
lightened their tribute duties,
and only required essential verbal agreements.
The methods of the two Hàn dynasties in governing the Róng
had lost their original principle.
Why so?
When Xiānlíng invaded the border,
Zhào Chōngguó moved them to the interior;
when Dāngjiān became a bandit,
Mǎ Wényuān relocated them to the Sānfǔ.
They coveted the temporary peace it brought,
and trusted their feigned submission,
considering only day-to-day expediency
and forgetting long-term strategies for governing the world.
How could this be the action of those who discern the subtle?
Thus, Wēizǐ wept at the ivory chopsticks,
and Xīnyǒu sighed deeply at the Yīchuān.
An encomium says: The element metal is of rigid energy,
giving birth to the Western Qiāng.
The Dǐ chieftains split into different tribes,
and thus became mighty and strong.
They ravaged Lǒngběi,
and presumptuously usurped power in Jīngyáng.
The court was exhausted by internal deliberations,
and the army wearied by external resistance.
Biography of the Western Regions, Chapter 78
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ,
the Western Regions became internally subservient,
comprising thirty-six states.
The Han court appointed envoys and commandants to administer and protect them.
Emperor Xuān changed the title to Protector-General (dūhù).
Emperor Yuán then established the two commandants of Wù and Jǐ,
who cultivated fields at the former royal court of Chēshī.
During the reigns of Emperors Āi and Píng,
these states were self-divided into fifty-five states.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he degraded and changed the titles of marquises and kings.
As a result, the Western Regions resented and rebelled,
severing ties with the Central Plains,
and again became subjects of the Xiōngnú.
The Xiōngnú collected heavy and harsh taxes,
which the various states could not bear.
In the Jiànwǔ era,
they all sent envoys to seek internal allegiance,
requesting the establishment of a Protector-General.
Guāngwǔ, believing that the empire had just been settled
and had no time for external affairs,
ultimately did not grant permission.
At a time when the Xiōngnú were weak,
Xián, King of Shāchē, exterminated various states.
After Xián's death,
they again attacked each other.
Xiǎoyuǎn, Jīngjué, Rónglú, and Qiěmò were annexed by Shànshàn.
Qúlè and Píshān were subjugated by Yútián,
which possessed all their territories.
Yùlì, Dānhuán, Gūhú, and Wūtānzīlí were destroyed by Chēshī.
Later, these states were all re-established.
During the Yǒngpíng era,
the Northern Captives (Běilǔ) coerced the various states to jointly invade the commanderies and counties of Héxī,
causing city gates to be closed during the day.
In the sixteenth year,
Emperor Míng ordered his generals
to campaign north against the Xiōngnú,
capturing the land of Yīwúlú,
where he established the Commandant of Yíhé to cultivate fields.
Thus, communication with the Western Regions was re-established,
and Yútián and other states all sent sons to serve at court.
The Western Regions, after sixty-five years of severance,
were thus reconnected.
The following year,
a Protector-General and Commandants of Wù and Jǐ were first established.
When Emperor Míng died,
Yānqí and Gūzī
attacked and overran the Protector-General Chén Mù,
annihilating all his forces.
The Xiōngnú and Chēshī besieged the Commandants of Wù and Jǐ.
In the spring of the first year of Jiànchū,
Duàn Péng, Administrator of Jiǔquán, heavily defeated Chēshī at Jiāohé City.
Emperor Zhāng, not wishing to exhaust the Central Plains to deal with the barbarians,
recalled the Commandants of Wù and Jǐ
and did not send another Protector-General.
In the second year,
the military agricultural settlements at Yīwú were again abolished,
whereupon the Xiōngnú sent troops to guard the Yīwú territory.
At that time, Bān Chāo, a military commander (jūnsīmǎ), remained in Yútián,
pacifying and rallying the various states.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán of Emperor Hé,
Grand General Dòu Xiàn heavily defeated the Xiōngnú.
In the second year,
Xiàn then dispatched Vice-Commandant Yán Pán with over two thousand cavalry to ambush Yīwú,
defeating them.
In the third year,
Bān Chāo finally pacified the Western Regions,
and was consequently made Protector-General (dūhù),
residing in Gūzī.
Commandants of Wù and Jǐ were re-established,
leading five hundred soldiers,
residing in Gāochāng Wall of Chēshī's former department.
A Commander (hóu) of the Wù department was also established,
residing in the Commander's city of Chēshī's latter department,
five hundred lǐ apart.
In the sixth year,
Bān Chāo again attacked and defeated Yānqí,
whereupon over fifty states all submitted hostages and became internally subservient.
Even distant states like Tiáozhī and Ānxī, as far as forty thousand lǐ to the seashore,
all offered tribute through multiple interpreters.
In the ninth year,
Bān Chāo dispatched his subordinate Gān Yīng to reach the Western Sea and return.
These were places unheard of by previous generations,
and not detailed in the Shānjīng.
None failed to describe their customs and geography,
and transmit their rare and strange things.
Thereupon, distant states like Méngqí and Dōulè all came to submit,
sending envoys to offer tribute.
When Emperor Xiàohé passed away,
the Western Regions revolted.
In the first year of Yǒngchū of Emperor Ān,
they repeatedly attacked and besieged the Protector-General Rèn Shàng, Duàn Xǐ, and others.
The imperial court, considering the region dangerous and distant,
and difficult to reinforce,
decreed the abolition of the Protector-General.
From this point, the Western Regions were [abandoned].
The Northern Xiōngnú immediately reasserted control over the various states,
and together they raided the borders for over ten years.
Cáo Zōng, Administrator of Dūnhuáng, distressed by their depredations,
in the sixth year of Yuánchū,
requested to dispatch Provisional Chief Clerk Suǒ Bān,
leading over a thousand men to garrison Yīwú to recruit and pacify them.
Thereupon, the former King of Chēshī and the King of Shànshàn surrendered.
After several months,
the Northern Xiōngnú again led the latter King of Chēshī to jointly attack and defeat Suǒ Bān and his group,
then drove away the former King.
Shànshàn, being hard-pressed,
sought aid from Cáo Zōng.
Zōng therefore requested to dispatch troops to attack the Xiōngnú,
to avenge the humiliation of Suǒ Bān,
and further intended to recover the Western Regions.
Empress Dowager Dèng did not permit it,
but only ordered the establishment of a Vice-Commandant for the Protection of the Western Regions,
residing in Dūnhuáng,
and reorganized three hundred camp soldiers,
merely to maintain loose control.
Thereafter, the Northern Captives frequently allied with Chēshī to invade Héxī,
which the imperial court could not prohibit.
The discussants therefore wished to close the Yùmén and Yángguān passes
to eliminate this trouble.
In the second year of Yánguāng,
Zhāng Dāng (張璫), the Administrator of Dūnhuáng (敦煌), submitted a memorial proposing three strategies.
He opined
that "the northern barbarian Hūyǎn Wáng (呼衍王) constantly moves between Púlèi (蒲類) and Qínhǎi (秦海),
unilaterally controlling the Western Regions,
and together they commit acts of banditry and raiding.
Now, if we gather more than two thousand officers and soldiers from the commandery dependent on Jiǔquán (酒泉) at Kūnlún (昆侖) Pass,
first attack Hūyǎn Wáng (呼衍王)
to sever his roots,
and then dispatch five thousand Shànshàn (鄯善) troops to threaten the Rear Division of Chēshī (車師),
this is the best strategy.
If we cannot send out troops,
we can appoint an Army Sīmǎ (司馬)
with five hundred officers and soldiers,
with the four commanderies supplying them with oxen for plowing and grain,
to station them at Liǔzhōng (柳中).
This is the medium strategy.
If this also cannot be done,
then it is advisable to abandon Jiāohé (交河) city,
gather Shànshàn (鄯善) and others, and make them all enter the pass.
This is the inferior strategy."
The imperial court deliberated on his proposal.
Shàngshū (尚書) Chén Zhōng (陳忠) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant has heard that among the incursions of the eight barbarian tribes,
none is more severe than that of the northern barbarians.
When the Hàn (漢) dynasty rose,
Gāozǔ (高祖) was distressed by the siege of Píngchéng (平城),
and Tàizōng (太宗) suffered the humiliation of having to make offerings.
Therefore, Xiàowǔ (孝武), in his wrath,
deeply considered a long-term plan,
and ordered the dispatch of valiant ministers,
to cross rivers and traverse deserts,
utterly defeating the barbarian court.
During these campaigns,
the common people perished north of Lángwàng (狼望),
and wealth and goods were squandered in the valleys of Lúshān (盧山).
The treasuries were depleted,
the looms empty,
even counting up to boats and carriages,
and extending to the six types of livestock.
Why would this not cause distress?
It was due to long-term considerations.
Thus, the four commanderies west of the river were established
to cut off the Southern Qiāng (羌),
and the thirty-six states were incorporated,
severing the right arm of the Xiōngnú (匈奴).
For this reason, the Chányú (單于) became isolated,
scurrying away and hiding far off.
By the reigns of Xuān (宣) and Yuán (元),
they were fully prepared to be vassal states.
[一０] The frontier passes were not closed,
and urgent dispatches were not sent.
From this, we can see
that the Róng (戎) and Dí (狄) can be subdued by might,
but are difficult to assimilate through familiarity.
The Western Regions have been attached to us for a long time,
and have frequently looked eastward and knocked on our gates,
which is proof that they are not happy with the Xiōngnú (匈奴) and yearn for the Hàn (漢).
Now the northern barbarians have already defeated Chēshī (車師),
and their power will inevitably lead them to attack Shànshàn (鄯善) to the south.
If we abandon them and do not rescue them,
then all the states will follow suit.
If that happens,
the barbarians' wealth and resources will increase,
their courage and power will grow,
[一一] they will impose their authority on the Southern Qiāng (羌),
and ally with them.
If this happens,
the four commanderies west of the river will be in danger.
Once Héxī (河西) is in danger,
we will have no choice but to rescue it,
which will lead to a hundredfold more campaigns
and an incalculable expenditure of resources.
Those who propose abandoning them only consider the great distance of the Western Regions,
and worry about the trouble and expense,
failing to see the painstaking efforts and toil of our ancestors.
At present, the means of defense on the border are not refined,
and the military preparations within the commanderies are not in order.
Dūnhuáng (敦煌) is isolated and in danger,
and has sent a distant plea for help.
If we do not provide assistance,
internally we will have nothing to comfort and reassure our officials and people,
and externally we will have nothing to awe and demonstrate to the hundred barbarian tribes.
To shrink the state and reduce territory
is clearly forbidden by the classics.
[一二] Your servant believes that a Xiàowèi (校尉) should be established in Dūnhuáng (敦煌),
and based on past practice, increase the garrison troops in the four commanderies,
to pacify the various states to the west.
This would be sufficient to deter enemies from afar,
and strike fear into the Xiōngnú (匈奴)."
[一三] The Emperor accepted this,
and appointed Bān Yǒng (班勇) [一四] as the Chángshǐ (長史) of the Western Regions,
leading five hundred banished convicts to be soldiers,
to be stationed in Liǔzhōng (柳中) to the west.
Bān Yǒng (班勇) then defeated and pacified Chēshī (車師).
From Jiànwǔ (建武) to Yánguāng (延光),
the Western Regions were severed and reconnected three times.
In the second year of Yǒngjiàn (永建) of Emperor Shùn (順),
Bān Yǒng (班勇) again attacked and subdued Yānqí (焉耆).
Thereupon, Qiūcí (龜茲), Shūlè (疏勒), Yútián (于窴), Shāchē (莎車), and seventeen other states all came to submit,
but Wūsūn (烏孫) and the states west of the Cōnglǐng (葱嶺) were then cut off.
In the sixth year,
the Emperor, considering that Yīwú (伊吾) was an old fertile land
close to the Western Regions,
and the Xiōngnú (匈奴) used it as a resource
for their raids and violence,
again ordered the establishment of military agricultural colonies as in the Yǒngyuán (永元) period,
and appointed one Yīwú Sīmǎ (伊吾司馬).
From Yángjiā (陽嘉) onwards,
the imperial authority gradually diminished,
and the various states became arrogant and unruly,
attacking each other.
In the second year of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
Chángshǐ (長史) Wáng Jìng (王敬) was killed by Yútián (于窴).
In the first year of Yǒngxīng (永興),
the King of Chēshī (車師) Rear again rebelled and attacked the garrison camp.
Although there were some who surrendered,
[一五] none were ever disciplined or reformed,
and from then on, a sense of neglect and laxity gradually set in.
Bān Gù (班固) recorded the geography, customs, and people of the various states
in detail in the former book.
Now, I have compiled an account of events after Jiànwǔ (建武) that differ from earlier ones,
to form the "Treatise on the Western Regions" (Xīyù Zhuàn 西域傳),
all based on the records made by Bān Yǒng (班勇) at the end of Emperor Ān's (安) reign.
The states of the Western Regions that were subject to the interior
stretched six thousand li (里) from east to west,
and more than a thousand li (里) from north to south,
bounded on the east by Yùmén (玉門) and Yángguān (陽關),
and on the west by Cōnglǐng (葱嶺).
To their northeast, they bordered the Xiōngnú (匈奴) and Wūsūn (烏孫).
There are great mountains to the north and south,
with a river in the center.
Its southern mountain extends eastward to Jīnchéng (金城),
connecting with the Hàn (漢)'s southern mountains.
The river has two sources:
one flows eastward from Cōnglǐng (葱嶺),
and one flows northward from the southern mountains of Yútián (于窴),
joining the Cōnglǐng (葱嶺) river,
and flowing eastward into Púchānghǎi (蒲昌海).
Púchānghǎi (蒲昌海) is also called Yánzé (鹽澤),
and is over three hundred li (里) from Yùmén (玉門).
From Dūnhuáng (敦煌), going west out of Yùmén (玉門) and Yángguān (陽關),
crossing Shànshàn (鄯善),
northward to Yīwú (伊吾) is over a thousand li (里).
From Yīwú (伊吾), northward to the Gāochāngbì (高昌壁) of Chēshī (車師) Front Division is one thousand two hundred li (里).
From Gāochāngbì (高昌壁), northward to Jīnmǎnchéng (金滿城) of the Rear Division is five hundred li (里).
These are the gateways to the Western Regions,
which is why the Wùjǐ Xiàowèi (戊己校尉) were alternately stationed there.
The land of Yīwú (伊吾) is suitable for the five grains, mulberry, hemp, and grapes.
To its north is also Liǔzhōng (柳中),
both being fertile lands.
Therefore, the Hàn (漢) often contended with the Xiōngnú (匈奴) over Chēshī (車師) and Yīwú (伊吾),
in order to control the Western Regions.
From Shànshàn (鄯善), crossing Cōnglǐng (葱嶺) to the states further west,
there are two routes.
Following the northern side of the southern mountains,
skirting the river westward
to Shāchē (莎車),
is the Southern Route.
The Southern Route, crossing Cōnglǐng (葱嶺) to the west,
leads to the states of Dàyuèzhī (大月氏) and Ānxī (安息).
From the court of the Front King of Chēshī (車師), following the northern mountains,
skirting the river westward to Shūlè (疏勒),
is the Northern Route.
The Northern Route, crossing Cōnglǐng (葱嶺) to the west,
leads to Dàyuān (大宛), Kāngjū (康居), and Yǎncài (奄蔡).
Going out of Yùmén (玉門),
passing through Shànshàn (鄯善), Qiěmò (且末), and Jīngjué (精絕) for over three thousand li (里) to Jūmí (拘彌).
The state of Jūmí (拘彌) is located in Níngmí (寧彌) city,
four thousand nine hundred li (里) from Liǔzhōng (柳zhōng), where the Chángshǐ (長史) resided,
and twelve thousand eight hundred li (里) from Luòyáng (洛陽).
It controlled two thousand one hundred seventy-three households,
with a population of seven thousand two hundred fifty-one,
and one thousand seven hundred sixty able-bodied soldiers.
In the fourth year of Yǒngjiàn (永建) of Emperor Shùn (順),
Fàng Qián (放前), the King of Yútián (于窴), killed Xīng (興), the King of Jūmí (拘彌),
and installed his own son as the King of Jūmí (拘彌),
and sent envoys to pay tribute to Hàn (漢).
Xú Yóu (徐由), the Administrator of Dūnhuáng (敦煌), memorialized requesting to attack them,
but the Emperor pardoned Yútián (于窴)'s crime,
ordering them to return the state of Jūmí (拘彌).
Fàng Qián (放前) refused.
In the first year of Yángjiā (陽嘉),
Xú Yóu (徐由) dispatched Chén Pán (臣槃), the King of Shūlè (疏勒), with twenty thousand men to attack Yútián (于窴).
They defeated them,
beheading several hundred,
and Fàng Qián (放前)'s troops plundered greatly.
A kinsman of Xīng (興), Chéng Guó (成國), was installed as King of Jūmí (拘彌) and they returned.
By the fourth year of Xīpíng (熹平) of Emperor Líng (靈),
Ān Guó (安國), the King of Yútián (于窴), attacked Jūmí (拘彌),
heavily defeating them,
killing their king.
The number of dead was very large.
The Wùjǐ Xiàowèi (戊己校尉) and the Chángshǐ (長史) of the Western Regions each dispatched troops to assist in installing Dìng Xīng (定興), a royal scion of Jūmí (拘彌), as king.
At that time, the population barely numbered a thousand.
The state bordered Yútián (于窴) to the west, at a distance of three hundred ninety li (里).
The kingdom of Yútián
is located in the Western Regions, five thousand three hundred *lǐ* from the residence of the Chief Clerk,
and eleven thousand seven hundred *lǐ* from Luòyáng.
It has thirty-two thousand households
and eighty-three thousand people,
with over thirty thousand soldiers.
At the end of the Jiànwǔ reign,
Xián, the king of Shāchē, grew powerful
and attacked and annexed Yútián,
relocating its king, Yú Lín, to be king of Líguī.
During the Yǒngpíng reign of Emperor Míng,
Xiūmòbà, a general from Yútián, rebelled against Shāchē
and declared himself king of Yútián.
After Xiūmòbà died,
his nephew Guǎngdé was enthroned,
and later he destroyed Shāchē,
making his kingdom even more prosperous.
The thirteen kingdoms from Jīngjué northwest to Shūlè all submitted to him.
And the king of Shànshàn also began to grow powerful.
From then on, of the southern route east of the Cōnglǐng Mountains,
only these two kingdoms were large.
In the sixth year of Yǒngjiàn of Emperor Shùn,
Fàngqián, the king of Yútián, sent a princely hostage to the imperial court to offer tribute.
In the first year of Yuánjiā,
Zhào Píng, the Chief Clerk, died of an ulcer in Yútián.
Píng's son went to escort the coffin
and passed through Jūmí.
Chéngguó, the king of Jūmí, had long held a grudge against Jiàn, the king of Yútián,
so he told Píng's son:
"The king of Yútián ordered a Hu physician to put poison in the wound,
which is why he died."
Píng's son believed him,
and when he returned through the pass,
he reported it to Mǎ Dá, the Administrator of Dūnhuáng.
The following year,
Wáng Jìng was appointed Chief Clerk in his place.
Dá ordered Jìng to discreetly investigate the matter.
Jìng first stopped in Jūmí,
where Chéngguó again said:
"The people of Yútián want me to be their king.
Now you can use this crime to execute Jiàn,
and Yútián will surely submit."
Jìng, coveting fame for his achievements,
and swayed by Chéngguó's words,
proceeded to Yútián,
set up a banquet and invited Jiàn,
but secretly plotted against him.
Someone informed Jiàn of Jìng's plot,
but Jiàn did not believe it,
saying:
"I am innocent.
Why would Chief Clerk Wáng want to kill me?"
The next morning,
Jiàn, accompanied by several dozen officials, went to Jìng.
After they were seated,
Jiàn rose to offer wine.
Jìng shouted at his attendants to seize him.
However, his officers and soldiers had no intention of killing Jiàn,
and Jiàn's officials all managed to flee.
At that time, Qín Mù, the Chief Clerk of Chéngguó, was accompanying Jìng at the gathering.
He drew his knife and said:
"The important matter is decided;
why hesitate further?"
He then stepped forward and beheaded Jiàn.
The marquises and generals of Yútián, such as Shūbó, then gathered their forces and attacked Jìng.
Jìng held up Jiàn's head, climbed a tower, and announced:
"The Son of Heaven ordered me to execute Jiàn!"
The marquises and generals of Yútián then set fire to the camp,
burning and killing the officers and soldiers,
climbed the tower, beheaded Jìng,
and hung his head in the marketplace.
Shūbó wanted to enthrone himself as king,
but the people of the kingdom killed him
and enthroned Ānguó, Jiàn's son.
When Mǎ Dá heard of this,
he wanted to lead the troops from various commanderies beyond the pass to attack Yútián.
However, Emperor Huán did not permit it,
recalled Dá,
and replaced him with Sòng Liàng as Administrator of Dūnhuáng.
When Liàng arrived,
he encouraged Yútián
to behead Shūbó themselves.
At that time, a month had already passed since Shūbó's death.
So they cut off the head of a dead person and sent it to Dūnhuáng,
without explaining the circumstances.
Liàng later realized their deception
but ultimately could not send troops.
Yútián, relying on this, became arrogant.
From Yútián, through Píshān,
one reaches Xīyè, Zǐhé, and Dérě.
The kingdom of Xīyè is also called Piāoshā.
It is fourteen thousand four hundred *lǐ* from Luòyáng.
It has two thousand five hundred households,
over ten thousand people,
and three thousand soldiers.
Its land produces white grass
which is poisonous.
The people of the kingdom boil it to make medicine
and apply it to arrowheads.
Whoever is struck by them dies instantly.
The *Hàn Shū* mistakenly states that Xīyè and Zǐhé are one kingdom,
but now they each have their own king.
The kingdom of Zǐhé is located in the Hūjiān Valley.
It is one thousand *lǐ* from Shūlè.
It has three hundred and fifty households,
four thousand people,
and one thousand soldiers.
The kingdom of Dérě has over one hundred households,
six hundred and seventy people,
and three hundred and fifty soldiers.
It is three thousand five hundred and thirty *lǐ* east of the Chief Clerk's residence
and twelve thousand one hundred and fifty *lǐ* from Luòyáng,
adjoining Zǐhé.
Their customs are all the same.
From Píshān southwest, through Wūchá,
crossing Xuándù,
and passing through Jìbīn,
after more than sixty days' journey, one reaches the kingdom of Wūyìshānlí,
which spans several thousand *lǐ* and was at that time renamed Páichí.
Then, southwest by horse for over a hundred days, one reaches Tiáozhī.
The city of the kingdom of Tiáozhī
is situated on a mountain,
with a circumference of over forty *lǐ*.
It borders the Western Sea.
The seawater curves around its south and northeast sides,
cutting off access on three sides.
Only the northwest corner connects to a land route.
The land is hot and humid,
producing lions, rhinoceroses, "sealed oxen" (presumably a type of bovine), peacocks, and large birds.
The eggs of the large birds are as big as jars.
Turning north and then east,
after another sixty days' journey by horse, one reaches Ānxī.
Later, Ānxī subjugated Tiáozhī
and appointed a grand general
to oversee its many small cities.
The kingdom of Ānxī is located in the city of Héjiù.
It is twenty-five thousand *lǐ* from Luòyáng.
It borders Kāngjū to the north
and Wūyìshānlí to the south.
It spans several thousand *lǐ*,
has several hundred small cities,
and its population and military strength are the most abundant.
Its eastern border city, Mùlù,
is called "Little Ānxī"
and is twenty thousand *lǐ* from Luòyáng.
In the first year of Zhānghé of Emperor Zhāng,
it sent envoys to offer a lion and a *fúbá*.
The *fúbá* resembles a *lín* but has no horn.
In the ninth year of Yǒngyuán of Emperor Hé,
Dūhù Bān Chāo sent Gān Yīng as an envoy to Dàqín.
He reached Tiáozhī
and stood by the great sea, wanting to cross it.
However, the boatmen on the western border of Ānxī told Yīng:
"The sea is vast.
Those who travel across it, if they encounter favorable winds, can cross in three months.
But if they encounter adverse winds,
some take two years.
Therefore, those who enter the sea all carry three years' provisions.
The sea often makes people long for their homeland and yearn to return,
and many die."
Yīng heard this and stopped.
In the thirteenth year,
Mǎnqū, the king of Ānxī, again presented a lion and a large bird from Tiáozhī,
which at that time was called an "Ānxī sparrow."
From Ānxī, going west three thousand four hundred *lǐ*, one reaches the kingdom of Āmán.
From Āmán, going west three thousand six hundred *lǐ*, one reaches the kingdom of Sībīn.
From Sībīn, going south across a river,
and then southwest to the kingdom of Yúluó, nine hundred and sixty *lǐ*, marks the westernmost boundary of Ānxī.
This marks the western border of Ānxī.
From here, going south by sea,
one reaches Dàqín.
Its land abounds in rare and exotic treasures from west of the sea.
The kingdom of Dàqín is also called Líqián.
Because it is west of the sea, it is also called the "Western Sea Kingdom."
It spans several thousand *lǐ*
and has over four hundred cities.
Dozens of smaller kingdoms are subject to it.
Its city walls are made of stone.
Post stations are regularly established,
all plastered and whitewashed.
It has pine, cypress, and various other trees and a hundred kinds of grasses.
The people are diligent in farming
and widely cultivate silkworms and mulberries.
They all shave their heads and wear embroidered clothes,
riding in covered, white-canopied small carts,
beating drums when coming and going,
and raising flags and banners.
The cities and towns where they reside,
have a circumference of over a hundred *lǐ*.
Within the cities are five palaces,
each ten *lǐ* apart.
The palace buildings all have crystal pillars,
and their tableware is also made of the same.
Their king tours one palace each day,
attending to affairs for five days before completing a full circuit.
He always has one person carry a satchel accompanying the king's carriage.
If anyone has matters to present,
they immediately throw a written submission into the satchel.
When the king arrives at a palace, he opens and examines them,
settling what is wrong and what is right.
Each has its own official departments and documents.
Thirty-six generals are appointed,
all of whom deliberate on state affairs.
Their kings are not hereditary;
instead, the worthy are selected and installed.
If there are disasters or unusual phenomena in the country, or unseasonable wind and rain,
they are immediately deposed and replaced.
Those who are deposed accept their demotion without resentment.
Their people are all tall, upright, and just,
resembling the Central Plain,
hence it is called Dàqín.
The land is rich in gold, silver, and precious treasures,
such as luminous jade discs, moon-bright pearls, terrifying rooster rhinoceros horn,
coral, amber, *liúlí*, *lánggān*, cinnabar, and azure-green jade.
They embroider with gold thread,
weaving golden carpets and brocades of various colors.
They make gold paint and fire-proof cloth.
They also have fine cloth,
which some say is made from water-sheep wool,
or from wild silkworm cocoons.
They blend various incense,
and boil its juice to make *sūhé*.
All the rare and exotic treasures from foreign lands originate here.
They use gold and silver as currency;
ten silver coins are equivalent to one gold coin.
They trade with Ānxī and Tiānzhú in the sea,
profiting ten-fold.
Their people are honest and straightforward;
there are no two prices in the market.
Grain and food are always cheap,
and the country's resources are abundant.
When envoys from neighboring countries reach their border,
they ride post-carriages to the king's capital.
Upon arrival, they are given gold coins.
Their king always wished to establish diplomatic relations with Hàn,
but Ānxī wanted to trade Hàn silks and brocades with them,
so they obstructed Dàqín from reaching Hàn directly.
It was not until the 9th year of Yánxī of Emperor Huán,
that Āndūn, the King of Dàqín, sent envoys who offered ivory, rhinoceros horn, and tortoiseshell from beyond the borders of Rìnán,
and only then was a connection finally made.
The tributes they presented
contained nothing truly rare or exotic,
leading to suspicion that the accounts were exaggerated.
Some say that to the west of their country there are Ruòshuǐ and Liúshā,
near the dwelling place of Xīwángmǔ,
almost at the setting sun.
The *Hànshū* says,
"Traveling west from Tiáozhī for over two hundred days,
one approaches the setting sun,"
which differs from the current text.
All Hàn envoys in previous generations returned from Wūyì,
none ever reached Tiáozhī.
It also states,
"Traveling from Ānxī by land, circling north of the sea, one exits the western sea to reach Dàqín.
The population is continuous,
with a relay station every ten *lǐ*,
and a post station every thirty *lǐ*.
There are never any bandits or alarms of marauders.
However, the roads are full of fierce tigers and lions,
obstructing travelers.
If a group is fewer than a hundred people,
carrying weapons,
they are inevitably eaten by them."
It further says,
"There are flying bridges several hundred *lǐ* long, which can cross the north of the sea."
The various unusual jade, stones, and other items produced in these countries
are often too strange and unsubstantiated,
so they are not recorded here.
The country of Dàyuèzhī
resides in Lánshì Chéng,
bordering Ānxī to the west, a journey of forty-nine days.
It is six thousand five hundred and thirty-seven *lǐ* east of where the Chángshǐ resides,
and sixteen thousand three hundred and seventy *lǐ* from Luòyáng.
It has one hundred thousand households,
four hundred thousand mouths,
and over one hundred thousand soldiers.
Initially,
Yuèzhī was conquered by the Xiōngnú,
and consequently migrated to Dàxià.
Their country was divided into Xiūmì, Shuāngmí, Guìshuāng, Dùn, and Dūmì,
a total of five *xīhóu* principalities.
Over a hundred years later,
Qiūjiùquè, the *xīhóu* of Guìshuāng, attacked and annihilated the other four *xīhóu*,
establishing himself as king,
with the kingdom named Guìshuāng.
He invaded Ānxī,
and took the land of Gāofù.
He also subjugated Púdá and Jìbīn,
taking possession of their entire countries.
Qiūjiùquè died at over eighty years old.
His son, Yángāozhēn, succeeded him as king.
He further conquered Tiānzhú,
appointing a general to oversee it.
From this time onward, Yuèzhī
became the wealthiest and most powerful.
All countries referred to its ruler as the King of Guìshuāng.
Hàn, however, retained its original name,
calling it Dàyuèzhī.
The country of Gāofù is southwest of Dàyuèzhī,
and is also a large country.
Its customs are similar to Tiānzhú,
but it is weaker
and easily subdued.
They are skilled in commerce
and internally wealthy.
Its allegiance is not constant;
when the three countries of Tiānzhú, Jìbīn, and Ānxī are strong, they control it,
and when they are weak, they lose it.
It never belonged to Yuèzhī.
The *Hànshū* considered it one of the five *xīhóu* principalities,
which is not accurate.
Later, it belonged to Ānxī.
When Yuèzhī defeated Ānxī,
they finally acquired Gāofù.
The country of Tiānzhú, also named Shēndú,
is several thousand *lǐ* southeast of Yuèzhī.
Its customs are similar to Yuèzhī,
but it is low-lying, damp, and hot.
The country borders a great river.
They fight mounted on elephants.
Its people are weaker than those of Yuèzhī,
and practice the Fútú (Buddhist) way,
not engaging in killing,
which has become their custom.
From Yuèzhī and Gāofù countries westward,
south to the Western Sea,
and east to the country of Pánqǐ,
all are lands of Shēndú.
Shēndú has several hundred separate cities,
each with a chief.
It has dozens of separate states,
each with a king.
Although each has minor differences,
they are all known as Shēndú.
At that time, they all belonged to Yuèzhī.
Yuèzhī killed their kings and appointed generals,
ordering them to govern the people.
The land produces elephants, rhinoceroses, tortoiseshell, gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, and tin.
It communicates with Dàqín to the west
and possesses Dàqín's precious goods.
It also has fine cloth, good carpets,
various incenses, rock candy, black pepper, ginger, and black salt.
During the reign of Emperor Hé,
they frequently sent envoys with tribute,
but later, when the Western Regions rebelled,
ties were severed.
During the 2nd and 4th years of Yánxī of Emperor Huán,
they repeatedly came to offer tribute from beyond the borders of Rìnán.
It is popularly said that Emperor Míng dreamed of a golden man,
tall and large,
with light emanating from his head.
He asked his officials about it.
Someone said:
"In the west, there is a god
named Fó (Buddha),
whose form is sixteen feet tall and golden-colored."
The Emperor then sent envoys to Tiānzhú to inquire about the Fó (Buddhist) teachings,
and consequently had his image painted in the Central Plain.
Chǔ Wáng Yīng was the first to believe in its teachings,
and consequently, some people in the Central Plain began to follow its way.
Later, Emperor Huán, who was fond of deities,
frequently offered sacrifices to Fútú (Buddha) and Lǎozǐ.
The common people gradually adopted these practices,
and later it became increasingly popular.
The country of Dōnglí resides in Shāqí Chéng,
more than three thousand *lǐ* southeast of Tiānzhú,
and is a large country.
Its climate and types of goods are similar to Tiānzhú.
It has dozens of separate cities,
all claiming kingship.
Dàyuèzhī attacked it
and consequently subjugated it.
Both men and women are eight feet tall,
but timid and weak.
They ride elephants and camels
to travel between neighboring countries.
When there are invaders,
they fight mounted on elephants.
The country of Lìyì belongs to Kāngjū.
It produces famous horses, cattle, sheep, grapes, and various fruits.
Its soil and water are excellent,
hence its grape wine is particularly renowned.
The state of Yán
was north of Yāncài, belonging to Kāngjū,
and exported rat furs as tribute.
The state of Yāncài changed its name to Ālánliáo,
its capital was in Dìchéng,
and it belonged to Kāngjū.
The climate was mild,
with many zhēnsōng pines and white grasses.
The customs and clothing of the people were the same as those of Kāngjū.
From the state of Shāchē, one went west through Púlí and Wúlèi to the Great Yuèzhī;
to the east, it was 10,950 lǐ from Luòyáng.
During Wáng Măng's rebellion, the Xiongnú Chányú
encroached upon the Western Regions.
Only Yán, the King of Shāchē, was the strongest
and refused to submit.
During the time of Emperor Yuán,
he had served as a hostage prince,
grown up in the capital,
admired and enjoyed the Central Plains,
and also participated in its codes and laws.
He often instructed his sons
that they should always serve the Hàn imperial house
and never betray it.
In the fifth year of Tiānfèng
(25 CE), Yán died,
posthumously named King Zhōngwǔ.
His son, Kāng, succeeded him.
At the beginning of Emperor Guāngwǔ's reign,
Kāng led neighboring states to resist the Xiongnú,
protecting over a thousand people, including the wives and children of the former Protector-General and his officials and soldiers.
He dispatched a letter to Héxī,
inquiring about the situation in the Central Plains,
expressing his longing for the Hàn imperial house.
In the fifth year of Jiànwǔ (29 CE),
Dòu Róng, the Grand General of Héxī, acting on imperial authority, enfeoffed Kāng as King Hàn Shāchē Jiàngōng Huáidé and Grand Commandant of the Western Regions.
All fifty-five states submitted to him.
In the ninth year (33 CE),
Kāng died,
posthumously named King Xuānchéng.
His younger brother Xián succeeded him.
Xián attacked and defeated the states of Jūmí and Xīyè,
killed their kings,
and installed Kāng's two sons as the kings of Jūmí and Xīyè respectively.
In the fourteenth year (38 CE),
Xián and Ān, the King of Shànshàn, jointly sent envoys to the imperial court to offer tribute.
From then on, the Western Regions began to have communication with Hàn.
All the states east of the Cōnglíng mountains submitted to Xián.
In the seventeenth year (41 CE),
Xián again sent envoys to offer tribute
and requested a Protector-General.
The Son of Heaven consulted Grand Minister of Works Dòu Róng,
who believed that Xián's father, sons, and brothers had pledged to serve Hàn,
and their sincerity was profound,
so it was fitting to grant him a title and position to stabilize the region.
The Emperor then, through his envoy,
bestowed upon Xián the seal and sash of the Protector-General of the Western Regions,
as well as chariots, banners, gold, and brocade.
Péi Zūn, the Administrator of Dūnhuáng, submitted a memorial, saying:
"Barbarians should not be entrusted with great power,
as it would also disappoint the other states."
An imperial edict ordered the return of the Protector-General's seal and sash,
and instead bestowed upon Xián the seal and sash of a Hàn Grand General.
His envoy refused to exchange them,
so Zūn forcibly seized them.
From this, Xián began to bear resentment.
However, he still falsely claimed to be the Grand Protector-General,
sending letters to various states,
and all states submitted to him,
styling Xián as Chányú.
Xián gradually became arrogant and overbearing,
heavily demanding taxes,
and frequently attacking the states of Qiūcí and others,
which caused the states great distress and fear.
In the winter of the twenty-first year (45 CE),
the former king of Chēshī, Shànshàn, Yānqí, and eighteen other states collectively sent their sons to serve at court
and offered their treasures.
When they were granted an audience,
they all wept and prostrated themselves,
wishing for a Protector-General.
The Son of Heaven, considering that the Central Plains had only recently been pacified
and the northern borders were still unsubdued,
returned all their hostage princes
and generously rewarded them.
At this time, Xián, relying on his military strength,
wished to annex the Western Regions,
and his attacks became even more frequent.
The states, hearing that no Protector-General was dispatched
and that their hostage princes had all returned,
became greatly worried and fearful.
They then sent a dispatch to the Administrator of Dūnhuáng,
requesting to keep the hostage princes to show Shāchē,
stating that if the hostage princes were kept,
a Protector-General would soon be dispatched,
hoping to temporarily halt Xián's aggression.
Péi Zūn reported the situation,
and the Son of Heaven consented.
In the twenty-second year (46 CE),
Xián, knowing that no Protector-General would arrive,
then sent a letter to Ān, the King of Shànshàn,
ordering him to cut off the road to Hàn.
Ān did not accept and killed his envoy.
Xián was furious
and dispatched troops to attack Shànshàn.
Ān engaged in battle,
but his army was defeated
and he fled into the mountains.
Xián killed and captured over a thousand people before leaving.
That winter,
Xián again attacked and killed the King of Qiūcí,
and then annexed his state.
The hostage princes from Shànshàn, Yānqí, and other states had been detained in Dūnhuáng for a long time,
were distressed and homesick,
and all fled back.
The King of Shànshàn submitted a memorial,
wishing to again send his son to serve at court
and once more requesting a Protector-General.
If no Protector-General was dispatched,
they would indeed be compelled to submit to the Xiongnú.
The Son of Heaven replied:
"Currently, our great army and envoys are unable to set out.
If the various states find their strength lacking,
they are free to go east, west, north, or south as they please."
Thereupon, Shànshàn and Chēshī again submitted to the Xiongnú,
and Xián became even more overbearing.
The King of Guīsài, considering his state distant,
then killed Xián's envoy.
Xián attacked and destroyed his state,
installing a nobleman from that state, Sìjiān, as King of Guīsài.
Xián also installed his own son, Zéluó, as King of Qiūcí.
As Zéluó was young,
Xián divided Qiūcí into the state of Wūlěi,
transferred Sìjiān to be King of Wūlěi,
and again appointed a nobleman as King of Guīsài.
After several years,
the people of Qiūcí collectively killed Zéluó and Sìjiān,
and sent envoys to the Xiongnú,
requesting them to install a new king.
The Xiongnú installed Shēndú, a nobleman from Qiūcí, as King of Qiūcí,
and Qiūcí thus belonged to the Xiongnú.
Xián, considering the tribute from Dàyuān to be too little,
personally led tens of thousands of soldiers from various states to attack Dàyuān.
Yánliú, the King of Dàyuān, met them and surrendered.
Xián then returned to his state,
transferring Qiáosàidí, the King of Jūmí, to be King of Dàyuān.
But Kāngjū frequently attacked him.
Qiáosàidí stayed in the state for over a year,
then fled back.
Xián again made him King of Jūmí,
and sent Yánliú back to Dàyuān,
ordering him to contribute tribute as before.
Xián also transferred Yúlí, the King of Yútián, to be King of Líguī,
and installed his younger brother Wèishì as King of Yútián.
Over a year later,
Xián suspected that the various states intended to rebel.
He summoned Wèishì and the kings of Jūmí, Gūmò, and Zǐhé,
and killed them all.
He no longer appointed kings,
but merely sent generals to garrison their states.
Róng, the son of Wèishì, fled and surrendered to Hàn,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis Shǒujié.
Jūndé, a Shāchē general in Yútián, was tyrannical,
and the common people suffered from him.
In the third year of Emperor Míng's Yǒngpíng era (60 CE),
Dūmò, a prominent figure, went out of the city
and saw a wild boar,
intending to shoot it.
The boar then spoke, saying:
"Do not shoot me,
I will kill Jūndé for you."
Dūmò then, with his brothers, killed Jūndé.
Then another prominent figure, Xiūmòbà, together with the Hàn Chinese Hán Róng and others, killed Dūmò and his brothers,
and established himself as King of Yútián.
He then, with the people of Jūmí, attacked and killed the Shāchē general stationed in Píshān,
and led his troops back.
Thereupon, Xián sent his crown prince and prime minister,
leading twenty thousand soldiers from various states to attack Xiūmòbà.
Bà met them and engaged in battle,
and the Shāchē army was defeated and fled,
with over ten thousand killed.
Xián again raised tens of thousands from various states,
and personally led them to attack Xiūmòbà.
Bà again defeated them,
slaying more than half,
and Xián barely escaped back to his state.
Xiūmòbà advanced and besieged Shāchē,
but died from an arrow wound,
and the army then withdrew.
The chancellor Sū Yú Lēi (蘇榆勒) and others of the kingdom of Yútián (于窴) jointly established Guǎngdé (廣德), the nephew of Xiūmò Bà (休莫霸), as king.
The Xiōngnú (匈奴) and various kingdoms of Qiūcí (龜茲) jointly attacked Shāchē (莎車),
but could not take it.
Guǎngdé (廣德), taking advantage of Shāchē's (莎車) distress,
sent his younger brother, the Fǔguó Hóu (輔國侯) Rén (仁), to lead troops to attack Xián (賢).
Xián (賢), having been repeatedly attacked by armies,
then sent envoys to make peace with Guǎngdé (廣德).
Previously, Guǎngdé's (廣德) father had been detained in Shāchē (莎車) for several years.
Thereupon, Xián (賢) returned his father [to him]
and gave his daughter to him as wife,
forming a bond of brotherhood.
Guǎngdé (廣德) then withdrew his troops.
The following year,
the chancellor Qiěyùn (且運) and others of Shāchē (莎車),
troubled by Xián's (賢) arrogance and cruelty,
secretly plotted to revolt and surrender the city to Yútián (于窴).
King Guǎngdé (廣德) of Yútián (于窴) then led 30,000 troops from various kingdoms to attack Shāchē (莎車).
Xián (賢) defended the city
and sent an envoy to say to Guǎngdé (廣德):
"I returned your father to you,
and gave you my daughter as wife.
Why have you come to attack me?"
Guǎngdé (廣德) replied:
"Your Majesty
is my father-in-law.
We have not seen each other for a long time.
I wish for each of us to bring two people and meet outside the city to conclude an alliance."
Xián (賢) consulted Qiěyùn (且運) about this.
Qiěyùn (且運) said:
"Guǎngdé (廣德) is your son-in-law, a close relative.
You should go out to meet him."
Xián (賢) then went out lightly,
and Guǎngdé (廣德) seized Xián (賢).
Qiěyùn (且運) and others then let in the Yútián (于窴) army,
captured Xián's (賢) wife and children, and annexed his kingdom.
Xián (賢) was taken back in chains
and killed more than a year later.
When the Xiōngnú (匈奴) heard that Guǎngdé (廣德) had destroyed Shāchē (莎車),
they sent five generals to mobilize more than 30,000 troops from Yānqí (焉耆), Wèilí (尉黎), Qiūcí (龜茲), and fifteen other kingdoms to besiege Yútián (于窴).
Guǎngdé (廣德) begged for surrender,
offering his crown prince as a hostage,
and promised an annual tribute of fine silk and cotton.
In winter,
the Xiōngnú (匈nú) again sent troops and established Xián's (賢) hostage son Bùjūzhēng (不居徵) as King of Shāchē (莎車).
Guǎngdé (廣德) again attacked and killed him,
and established his younger brother Qílí (齊黎) as King of Shāchē (莎車).
This was in the third year of Yuánhé (元和) of Emperor Zhāng (章帝).
At that time, Chángshǐ (長史) Bān Chāo (班超) mobilized troops from various kingdoms to attack Shāchē (莎車),
severely defeating them.
From this, Shāchē (莎車) finally surrendered to Hàn (漢).
The details are already recorded in the biography of Bān Chāo (班超).
Shāchē (莎車) is northeast of Shūlè (疏勒).
The kingdom of Shūlè (疏勒) is five thousand *lǐ* (里) from the residence of the Chángshǐ (長史),
and ten thousand three hundred *lǐ* (里) from Luòyáng (洛陽).
It has 21,000 households,
and more than 30,000 able-bodied soldiers.
In the sixteenth year of Yǒngpíng (永平) of Emperor Míng (明帝),
King Jiàn (建) of Qiūcí (龜茲) attacked and killed King Chéng (成) of Shūlè (疏勒),
and established himself, Dōutí (兜題), the Zǔo Hóu (左侯) of Qiūcí (龜茲), as King of Shūlè (疏勒).
In winter,
Hàn (漢) sent Jūn Sīmǎ (軍司馬) Bān Chāo (班超) to seize and bind Dōutí (兜題),
and established Zhōng (忠), the nephew of Chéng (成), as King of Shūlè (疏勒).
Later, Zhōng (忠) rebelled.
Chāo (超) attacked and beheaded him.
The details are already recorded in Chāo's (超) biography.
In the Yuánchū (元初) period of Emperor Ān (安帝),
King Ānguó (安國) of Shūlè (疏勒) moved his maternal uncle Chén Pán (臣磐), who had committed a crime,
to Yuèzhī (月氏).
The King of Yuèzhī (月氏) held him in high regard.
Later, Ānguó (安國) died
without a son.
His mother governed the state
and, together with the people, established Yífù (遺腹), Chén Pán's (臣磐) half-brother's son, as King of Shūlè (疏勒).
Chén Pán (臣磐) heard of this
and petitioned the King of Yuèzhī (月氏), saying:
"Ānguó (安國) died without a son,
and his clan is weak.
If the mother's clan is established,
I am Yífù's (遺腹) paternal uncle.
I ought to be king."
Yuèzhī (月氏) then sent troops to escort him back to Shūlè (疏勒).
The people of the kingdom had always respected and loved Chén Pán (臣磐),
and also feared Yuèzhī (月氏).
They immediately seized Yífù's (遺腹) seal and ribbon,
welcomed Chén Pán (臣磐) and established him as king,
and made Yífù (遺腹) the Hóu (侯) of Pánchéng (磐城).
Later, Shāchē (莎車) repeatedly revolted against Yútián (于窴)
and belonged to Shūlè (疏勒).
Shūlè (疏勒) thus became strong,
and was able to be an enemy state to Qiūcí (龜茲) and Yútián (于窴).
In the second year of Yǒngjiàn (永建) of Emperor Shùn (順帝),
Chén Pán (臣磐) sent envoys with tribute.
The Emperor appointed Chén Pán (臣磐) as Dà Dūwèi (大都尉) of Hàn (漢),
and his nephew Chén Xūn (臣勳) as Shǒuguó Sīmǎ (守國司馬).
In the fifth year,
Chén Pán (臣磐) sent his son as a hostage, who, along with envoys from Dàyuān (大宛) and Shāchē (莎車), arrived at the imperial court to offer tribute.
In the second year of Yángjiā (陽嘉),
Chén Pán (臣磐) again offered a lion and a zebu.
In the first year of Jiànníng (建寧) of Emperor Líng (靈帝),
King Yú (于) of Shūlè (疏勒), the Dà Dūwèi (大都尉) of Hàn (漢), was shot and killed during a hunt by his youngest paternal uncle, Hédé (和得).
Hédé (和得) then established himself as king.
In the third year,
Mèng Tuó (孟佗), the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Liángzhōu (涼州), sent his subordinate Rèn Shè (任涉) to lead five hundred soldiers from Dūnhuáng (敦煌),
together with Wù Sīmǎ (戊司馬) Cáo Kuān (曹寬) and Xīyù Chángshǐ (西域長史) Zhāng Yàn (張晏),
leading the front and rear divisions of Yānqí (焉耆), Qiūcí (龜茲), and Chēshī (車師),
totaling more than 30,000 people,
to attack Shūlè (疏勒).
They attacked Zhēnzhōng Chéng (楨中城),
but after more than forty days could not take it,
and withdrew.
Thereafter, the kings of Shūlè (疏勒) repeatedly killed each other,
and the imperial court was also unable to stop it.
Northeast through Wèitóu (尉頭), Wēnsù (溫宿), Gūmò (姑墨), and Qiūcí (龜茲) to Yānqí (焉耆).
The King of Yānqí (焉耆) resides in Nánhé Chéng (南河城).
It is eight hundred *lǐ* (里) north of the residence of the Chángshǐ (長史),
and eight thousand two hundred *lǐ* (里) east of Luòyáng (洛陽).
It has fifteen thousand households,
fifty-two thousand people,
and more than twenty thousand able-bodied soldiers.
The kingdom is surrounded by large mountains on all four sides,
connected to Qiūcí (龜茲),
with treacherous terrain that is easy to defend.
There is a sea (lake) whose waters curve into the four mountains,
encircling its city for more than thirty *lǐ* (里).
At the end of Yǒngpíng (永平),
Yānqí (焉耆) and Qiūcí (龜茲) jointly attacked and annihilated Dūhù (都護) Chén Mù (陳睦) and Fù Xiàowèi (副校尉) Guō Xún (郭恂),
killing more than two thousand officials and soldiers.
In the sixth year of Yǒngyuán (永元),
Dūhù (都護) Bān Chāo (班超) mobilized troops from various kingdoms to attack Yānqí (焉耆), Wēixū (危須), Wèilí (尉黎), and Shānguó (山國).
He then beheaded the kings of Yānqí (焉耆) and Wèilí (尉黎),
and sent their heads to the capital,
where they were displayed at the residence for barbarians.
Chāo (超) then established Yuán Mèng (元孟), the Zuǒ Hóu (左侯) of Yānqí (焉耆), as king.
Wèilí (尉黎), Wēixū (危須), and Shānguó (山國) all established new kings.
In the time of Emperor Ān (安帝),
the Western Regions revolted.
In the Yánguāng (延光) period,
Chāo's (超) son Yǒng (勇) became the Xīyù Chángshǐ (西域長史)
and again attacked and pacified the various kingdoms.
Yuán Mèng (元孟), along with Wèilí (尉黎) and Wēixū (危須), did not surrender.
In the second year of Yǒngjiàn (永建),
Yǒng (勇) and Dūnhuáng Tàishǒu (敦煌太守) Zhāng Lǎng (張朗) defeated them.
Yuán Mèng (元孟) then sent his son to the imperial court to offer tribute.
The kingdom of Púlèi (蒲類) is located in Xīshūyú Gǔ (西疏榆谷) in Tiānshān (天山).
It is one thousand two hundred ninety *lǐ* (里) southeast of the residence of the Chángshǐ (長史),
and ten thousand four hundred ninety *lǐ* (里) from Luòyáng (洛陽).
It has more than eight hundred households,
more than two thousand people,
and more than seven hundred able-bodied soldiers.
They live in tents,
follow water and grass,
and are somewhat knowledgeable in farming.
They have cattle, horses, camels, and sheep.
They can make bows and arrows.
The kingdom produces good horses.
Púlèi (蒲類) was originally a large kingdom.
Previously, when the Western Regions belonged to the Xiōngnú (匈nú),
its king offended the Chányú (單于).
The Chányú (單于) was enraged
and moved more than six thousand people from Púlèi (蒲類)
into the À'è Dì (阿惡地) of the Xiōngnú (匈nú) Right Department,
and thus it was called the kingdom of À'è (阿惡).
It is more than ninety days' horse travel south of Chēshī (車師) Rear Department.
The population is poor and weak,
having fled into the mountains and valleys.
Therefore, it remained a kingdom.
The kingdom of Yízhī (移支) is located in Púlèi (蒲類) territory.
It has more than one thousand households,
more than three thousand people,
and more than one thousand able-bodied soldiers.
Its people are brave and fierce in battle,
engaging in raiding and plunder.
They all wear their hair loose,
follow their livestock and water and grass,
and do not know how to farm.
All their products are the same as Púlèi (蒲類).
The kingdom of Dōngqiěmí (東且彌) is eight hundred *lǐ* (里) east of the residence of the Chángshǐ (長史),
and nine thousand two hundred fifty *lǐ* (里) from Luòyáng (洛陽).
It has more than three thousand households,
more than five thousand people,
and more than two thousand able-bodied soldiers.
They live in tents,
follow water and grass,
and practice some farming.
Their products are also the same as Púlèi (蒲類).
Their dwelling places are not fixed.
The former King of Chēshī (車師) resided in Jiāohé Chéng (交河城).
The river divides and flows around the city,
hence it is called Jiāohé (交河) (Confluence).
It is eighty *lǐ* (里) from Liǔzhōng (柳中), the residence of the Chángshǐ (長史),
and nine thousand one hundred twenty *lǐ* (里) east of Luòyáng (洛陽).
It has more than fifteen hundred households,
more than four thousand people,
and two thousand able-bodied soldiers.
The king of Hòubù (Rear Division) resided in Wùtúgǔ,
five hundred *lǐ* from the residence of the Chángshǐ,
and nine thousand six hundred and twenty *lǐ* from Luòyáng.
He commanded over four thousand households,
over fifteen thousand people,
and over three thousand trained soldiers.
The Qiánbù (Front Division) and Hòubù, as well as Dōngqiěmí, Bēilù, Púleì, and Yízhī,
were known as the Six Kingdoms of Chēshī.
They bordered the Xiōngnú to the north.
Qiánbù communicated with Yānqí via the northern route to the west,
while Hòubù communicated with Wūsūn to the west.
In the 21st year of Jiànwǔ,
Chēshī, along with Shànshàn and Yānqí, sent their sons to serve as hostages.
Guāngwǔ sent them back,
whereupon Chēshī submitted to the Xiōngnú.
In the 16th year of Yǒngpíng of Emperor Míng,
the Hàn captured Yīwúlú
and opened up the Western Regions,
and Chēshī began to resubmit to the interior.
The Xiōngnú sent troops to attack them,
and they again surrendered to the Northern Barbarians.
In the 2nd year of Yǒngyuán of Emperor Hé,
Grand General Dòu Xiàn defeated the Northern Xiōngnú.
Chēshī was greatly intimidated,
and the kings of Qiánbù and Hòubù each sent their sons to offer tribute and serve as hostages,
and were all bestowed with seals, sashes, gold, and silk.
In the 8th year,
the Wùjǐ Jiàowèi Suǒ Yūn wanted to depose Zhuódī, the King of Hòubù,
and install Pòlǔ Hóu Xìzhì.
Zhuódī was enraged that the former king, Wèibēidà, had betrayed him,
and consequently counterattacked Wèibēidà,
capturing his wife and children.
The following year,
the Hàn dispatched the Jiàngbīng Chángshǐ Wáng Lín,
who mobilized over twenty thousand troops from the six commanderies of Liángzhōu and from the Qiāng and Hú tribes,
to attack Zhuódī.
Over a thousand enemy heads and captives were taken.
Zhuódī fled to the Northern Xiōngnú,
and the Hàn army pursued him,
beheading him.
Nóngqí, Zhuódī's younger brother, was installed as king.
In the 1st year of Yǒngníng,
the King of Hòubù, Jūn Jiù, and his mother, Shāmá, revolted
and killed the Sīmǎ of Hòubù and the Dūnhuáng Xíngshì.
In the 4th year of Yánguāng of Emperor Ān,
Chángshǐ Bān Yǒng attacked Jūn Jiù,
inflicting a great defeat
and beheading him.
In the 1st year of Yǒngjiàn of Emperor Shùn,
Bān Yǒng led Jiātènnú, the son of the former King Nóngqí, and Bāhuá and others,
mobilizing elite troops to attack Hūyǎn Wáng of the Northern Barbarians,
and defeated him.
Bān Yǒng then memorialized to install Jiātènnú as King of Hòubù,
and Bāhuá as the pro-Hàn marquis of Hòubù.
In the summer of the 3rd year of Yángjiā,
the Sīmǎ of Chēshī Hòubù led Jiātènnú and others, numbering fifteen hundred men,
to surprise attack the Northern Xiōngnú in Chāngwúlù Gǔ.
They destroyed their encampments,
beheaded several hundred people,
and captured the Xiānyú's mother, her younger sister, and several hundred women,
over a hundred thousand head of cattle and sheep,
over a thousand carts,
and a great many weapons and other articles.
In the spring of the 4th year,
Hūyǎn Wáng of the Northern Xiōngnú led troops to invade Hòubù.
The Emperor considered the Six Kingdoms of Chēshī to be close to the Northern Barbarians
and serving as a barrier for the Western Regions,
so he ordered the Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng to mobilize troops from various kingdoms,
as well as the guards of Yùmén Pass and the Sīmǎ of Yīwú,
to gather six thousand three hundred cavalry to rescue them,
and to ambush the Northern Barbarians at Lè Shān.
The Hàn army was unsuccessful.
In the autumn,
Hūyǎn Wáng again led two thousand men to attack Hòubù
and defeated them.
In the 1st year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Huán,
Hūyǎn Wáng led over three thousand cavalry to raid Yīwú.
Máo Kǎi, the Sīmǎ of Yīwú, dispatched five hundred officials and soldiers to battle Hūyǎn Wáng east of Púlèihǎi,
but they were all annihilated.
Hūyǎn Wáng then attacked the garrison city of Yīwú.
In the summer,
the Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng, Sīmǎ Dá, was dispatched to lead over four thousand officials and soldiers from Dūnhuáng, Jiǔquán, and Zhāngyè Commandery Dependencies to relieve them.
They exited the pass and reached Púlèihǎi.
Hūyǎn Wáng heard of this and withdrew,
and the Hàn army returned without achieving anything.
In the 1st year of Yǒngxīng,
Āluōduō, the King of Chēshī Hòubù, and Yán Hào, the Wùbù Hóu, were at odds with each other.
Āluōduō became furious and revolted,
attacking and besieging the Hàn military agricultural colony at Qiěgùchéng,
killing and wounding officials and soldiers.
Tànzhē, the Hòubù Hóu, led the remaining people to revolt against Āluōduō and surrender to the Hàn officials.
Āluōduō, being pressed hard,
fled with his mother, wife, and children, accompanied by over a hundred cavalry, to the Northern Xiōngnú.
Sòng Liàng, the Grand Administrator of Dūnhuáng, memorialized to install Bēijūn, the hostage son of the former King Jūn Jiù of Hòubù, as King of Hòubù.
Later, Āluōduō returned from the Xiōngnú
and contended with Bēijūn for the kingdom,
gathering some of his countrymen.
Yán Xiáng, the Wùjiàowèi, feared that he might attract the Northern Barbarians
and cause chaos in the Western Regions,
so he issued a trustworthy proclamation,
promising to reinstate him as king.
Āluōduō then went to Yán Xiáng and surrendered.
Thereupon, the seals and sashes bestowed upon Bēijūn were confiscated,
and Āluōduō was reinstated as king.
Bēijūn was then taken back to Dūnhuáng,
and three hundred households from Hòubù were separately assigned to his service,
and he was to collect their taxes.
The term "household" (*zhàng*)
is similar to "number of households" (*hù shù*) in China.
A commentary states: The accounts of the climate and customs of the Western Regions
were unknown in ancient times.
In the Hàn era, Zhāng Qiān harbored strategies for distant lands,
and Bān Chāo was fired with the ambition of a marquis,
ultimately achieving meritorious service in the distant west
and bringing the foreign regions into submission.
From those subdued by military might
to those enticed by wealth and gifts,
there were none who did not offer exotic treasures,
present beloved hostages,
and, with bared heads and crawling on elbows,
face east to pay homage to the Son of Heaven.
Therefore, officials of Wùjǐ were established
to divide their responsibilities;
commanders of the Dūhù were appointed
to collectively manage their authority.
Those who submitted early were rewarded with crates of gold and bestowed with tortoise sashes;
those who submitted later had their heads tied and were sacrificed at the northern palace gate.
Military agricultural colonies were established in fertile lands,
and post stations were set up along strategic routes.
Orders were dispatched swiftly by relay,
without interruption for months;
merchant Hú and traders
arrived daily at the frontier passes.
Later, Gān Yīng reached Tiáozhī and traversed Ānxī,
overlooking the Western Sea to gaze upon Dàqín,
a distance of over forty thousand *lǐ* from Yùmén and Yángguān.
Nothing was left unexplored.
As for the superiority or inferiority of their customs, character, and intelligence,
the different categories of products they yielded,
the sources and barriers of their rivers and mountain ranges,
the connections and separations of their climate, cold and hot,
the paths of scaling mountains, building plank roads through valleys, and traversing sand with ropes,
and regions of body heat, headache, wind disasters, and ghost calamities,
all were meticulously described in detail,
and their root causes thoroughly investigated.
As for the divine transformations of Buddhism,
which originated in Tiāndú,
none of the records from the two Hàn dynasties mention it.
Zhāng Qiān merely noted that the land was mostly hot and humid,
and that people fought mounted on elephants.
Although Bān Yǒng listed their worship of the Buddha (*fú tú*)
and their abstinence from killing,
there is no record of the profound texts and excellent laws that guided and enlightened them.
What I heard from later accounts is that
that country is as rich as the Central Plains,
with harmonious energy like a jade candle,
where spiritual sages gather
and virtuous and eminent figures are born.
Its divine signs and strange phenomena
are beyond human reason,
and its clear and evident miracles
are truly otherworldly.
But Zhāng Qiān and Bān Chāo heard nothing of this.
Was it that its doctrine was closed in their time,
and its destiny only revealed in later generations?
If not,
why such extensive misrepresentation?
The Hàn began with Chǔ Yīng who first vigorously observed fasts and sacrifices;
Emperor Huán also adorned the *huágài*.
Was it that the subtle meaning was not yet translated,
and they simply regarded it as divine?
Examining its teachings of purifying the mind and releasing burdens,
and its doctrine of simultaneously abandoning both existence and non-existence,
it belongs to the lineage of Daoist texts.
Moreover, it loves benevolence and abhors killing,
eliminating evil and promoting good,
which is why many wise and distinguished gentlemen appreciate its teachings.
However, it tends towards grandiosity and exaggeration,
with endless wonders and paradoxes.
〔一０〕Even the eloquence of Zōu Yǎn discussing heaven
and Zhuāng Zhōu's discourse on the snail's horns
〔一一〕are not enough to encompass a fraction of it.
Furthermore, the appearance and disappearance of spirits
and the continuous cycle of retribution are
like enlightenment that leads to confusion,
thus many enlightened people are perplexed by it.
〔一二〕Indeed, there are various ways to guide the populace,
and different situations lead to different approaches.
If one takes what leads to the same goal
and sets aside doubtful theories,
then the great Dao will be understood.
Eulogy: Far indeed are the Western Hú,
a region beyond heaven.
Their land produces splendid treasures,
but their people are debauched and superficial.
They do not follow Chinese rites,
nor do they possess classic writings.
If not for the subtle divine path,
what would they care for, what would they be restrained by?
Biography of the Southern Xiongnú, Chapter 79 (The Former Hàn History directly refers to the Xiongnú biography
without specifying North or South.
The current designation of "Southern"
clarifies that it refers to those who emerged from the North.
As the Southern Chányú were particularly inclined towards Han culture,
we highlight those who aligned themselves with it and place them at the beginning.
The Dōngguān Jì refers to it as "Biography of the Southern Xiongnú Chányú,"
but Fàn Yè later removed the two characters
"Chányú"
Bǐ, the Luòshīzhú Tī Chányú of the Southern Xiongnú,
was the grandson of Hūhánxié Chányú
and the son of Wūzhūliú Ruòdī Chányú.
After Hūhánxié,
his sons succeeded him in order.
When Bǐ's paternal uncle, Xiào Chányú Yú, was on the throne,
Bǐ was appointed Yòu Àojiàn Rìzhú Wáng,
leading the southern border region and the Wūhuán.
In the early Jiànwǔ era,
Péng Chǒng rebelled in Yúyáng.
The Chányú allied with him,
and subsequently supported Lú Fāng,
sending him to reside in Wǔyuán.
In the early years of Guāngwǔ's reign,
he was still pacifying Zhūxià
and had no time for foreign affairs.
By the sixth year,
he finally dispatched Guīdé Hóu Liú Sà as an envoy to the Xiongnú.
The Xiongnú also sent envoys to offer tribute.
Hàn, in turn, sent Zhōnglángjiàng Hán Tǒng to reciprocate,
presenting gifts of gold and silks,
to restore their former good relations.
However, the Chányú grew arrogant,
comparing himself to Mòdú,
and spoke rudely and disrespectfully to the envoy.
The Emperor treated him as before.
Initially,
diplomatic missions were constant,
but the Xiongnú frequently invaded the northern border with Lú Fāng.
In the ninth year,
Dàsīmǎ Wú Hàn and others were sent to attack them.
After a year, no success was achieved,
and the Xiongnú grew stronger,
their raids and depredations increasing daily.
In the thirteenth year,
they invaded Hédōng,
which the prefectures and commanderies could not prevent.
Consequently, the border inhabitants of Yōu and Bìng were gradually relocated to east of Chángshān Guān and Jūyōng Guān,
and the Xiongnú's left wing then moved into the pass.
The court was troubled by this,
and increased the number of border troops by several thousand,
extensively built watchtowers,
and repaired the beacon fires.
When the Xiongnú heard that Hàn was seeking Lú Fāng,
coveting wealth,
they sent Fāng back to surrender,
hoping to receive a reward.
However, Fāng claimed his return as his own achievement,
not mentioning he was sent by the Xiongnú.
The Chányú was also ashamed to reveal his scheme,
so the reward was not given.
Because of this, he harbored deep resentment,
and his invasions became even more severe.
In the twentieth year,
they reached Shàngdǎng, Fúfēng, and Tiānshuǐ.
In the winter of the twenty-first year,
they again raided Shànggǔ and Zhōngshān,
killing, capturing, and plundering a great many people.
The northern border had no more peaceful years.
Originally,
the Chányú's younger brother, Yòu Gǔlí Wáng Yī Tú Zhīyáshī,
was next in line to become Zuǒxián Wáng.
The Zuǒxián Wáng was the heir apparent to the Chányú.
The Chányú wished to pass the throne to his son,
and so he killed Zhīyáshī.
Zhīyáshī was
the son of Wáng Zhāojūn.
Zhāojūn, whose courtesy name was Qiáng,
was from Nánjùn.
Originally,
during Emperor Yuán's reign,
she was selected from a good family to enter the Yèting.
At that time, when Hūhánxié came to court,
the Emperor commanded that five palace women be bestowed upon him.
Zhāojūn had been in the palace for several years
without being summoned by the Emperor.
Filled with sorrow and resentment,
she requested the Yèting令 to allow her to go.
At the grand farewell assembly for Hūhánxié,
the Emperor summoned the five women to show them to him.
Zhāojūn, with her beautiful countenance and elegant adornments,
illuminated the Hàn palace.
Glancing at her reflection, she lingered,
moving those around her to admiration.
The Emperor was greatly astonished upon seeing her,
and intended to keep her,
but found it difficult to go back on his word.
So, she was given to the Xiongnú.
She bore two sons.
When Hūhánxié died,
his previous Yānzhī's son succeeded him
and wanted to marry her.
Zhāojūn submitted a memorial requesting to return home.
Emperor Chéng commanded her to follow Xiongnú customs,
and so she became the Yānzhī of the subsequent Chányú.
Bǐ, seeing Zhīyáshī executed,
uttered words of resentment, saying:
"Speaking of brothers,
the Yòu Gǔlí Wáng should be next to ascend;
speaking of sons,
I am the eldest son of the former Chányú,
and I should ascend."
Thus, he harbored suspicion and fear,
and his attendance at court assemblies became infrequent.
The Chányú suspected him,
and sent two Gǔdōuhóu to supervise Bǐ's troops.
In the twenty-second year,
Chányú Yú died.
His son, Zuǒxián Wáng Wūdádī Hóu, was enthroned as Chányú.
He also died,
and his younger brother, Zuǒxián Wáng Púnú, was enthroned as Chányú.
Bǐ was not enthroned,
which filled him with resentment.
Moreover, the Xiongnú suffered from successive years of drought and locusts,
leaving thousands of li of land barren,
with all vegetation withered.
People and livestock suffered from hunger and plague,
and more than half died.
The Chányú feared that Hàn would take advantage of their weakness,
so he sent an envoy to Yúyáng to seek peace and alliance.
Thereupon, Zhōnglángjiàng Lǐ Mào was dispatched to reciprocate.
Meanwhile, Bǐ secretly sent the Han man Guō Héng with a map of the Xiongnú territory.
In the twenty-third year,
he went to the Grand Administrator of Xīhé to request surrender.
The two Gǔdōuhóu somewhat perceived his intentions.
During the fifth month dragon sacrifice,
they informed the Chányú,
saying that Àojiàn Rìsuì had long intended to cause trouble,
and if he was not executed,
the country would be thrown into chaos.
At that time, Bǐ's younger brother, Jiànjiāng Wáng, was in the Chányú's tent.
Hearing this,
he rushed to inform Bǐ.
Bǐ, in fear,
gathered the four or five tens of thousands of people from the eight southern tribes under his command.
He waited for the two Gǔdōuhóu to return,
intending to kill them.
The Gǔdōuhóu, approaching,
learned of his plot,
and all fled on light cavalry,
reporting to the Chányú.
The Chányú sent ten thousand cavalry to attack him,
but seeing Bǐ's forces were strong,
they dared not advance and returned.
In the spring of the twenty-fourth year,
the adults of the eight tribes collectively deliberated and enthroned Bǐ as Hūhánxié Chányú,
because his great-grandfather had relied on Hàn and found peace,
so he wished to adopt that title.
Thereupon, he approached the Wǔyuán pass,
wishing to eternally be a protective screen,
defending against the northern barbarians.
The Emperor adopted the proposal of Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng Gěng Guó,
and permitted it.
That winter,
Bǐ enthroned himself as Hūhánxié Chányú.
In the spring of the twenty-fifth year,
he sent his younger brother, Zuǒxián Wáng Mò, with over ten thousand troops to attack the Northern Chányú's younger brother, Àojiàn Zuǒxián Wáng,
capturing him alive.
He also defeated the Northern Chányú's camp,
capturing over ten thousand people in total,
seven thousand horses, and ten thousand cattle and sheep.
The Northern Chányú was terrified
and retreated a thousand li.
Originally,
the Emperor had created war chariots
that could be drawn by several oxen,
with towers and turrets built on top,
placed on the frontier passes
to repel the Xiongnú.
Those who saw them at the time sometimes said to each other:
"The prophecy says that in the ninth generation of Hàn, the northern barbarians' territory will retreat a thousand li.
Does it refer to this?"
And now,
the territory was indeed expanded.
The Northern Àojiàn Gǔdōuhóu and Yòu Gǔdōuhóu led over thirty thousand people to submit to the Southern Chányú.
The Southern Chányú again sent an envoy to the imperial court,
offering tribute and proclaiming himself a vassal,
presenting national treasures,
requesting an envoy for supervision,
sending a princely hostage,
and renewing the old covenant.
In the 26th year,
Duan Chēn, a zhonglángjiàng,
and Wáng Yù, a fùxiàowèi, were dispatched as envoys to the Southern Chányú.
His court was established
eighty lǐ west of the Wǔyuán frontier fortress.
The Chányú then welcomed the envoys.
The envoys said:
"The Chányú must prostrate himself and receive the imperial edict."
The Chányú looked around for a moment,
then prostrated himself, declaring himself a subject.
After the prostration,
he ordered an interpreter to explain to the envoys:
"The Chányú has just ascended,
and is truly ashamed before his attendants.
May the envoys not humiliate him in front of the multitude."
When the Gǔdōuhóu and others saw this,
they all wept.
When Chēn and the others returned with their report,
an imperial edict permitted the Southern Chányú to reside in Yúnzhōng.
He sent an envoy to submit a memorial,
offering two camels
and ten patterned horses.
In the summer,
the Northern Lǔ’s Yùjiān Zuǒxiánwáng, whom the Southern Chányú had captured, along with his followers and five Southern Gǔdōuhóu, a total of more than thirty thousand people, rebelled and returned.
They went over three hundred lǐ from the Northern Court,
and together established Yùjiān Zuǒxiánwáng as Chányú.
More than a month later,
they attacked each other.
All five Gǔdōuhóu died,
and the Zuǒxiánwáng subsequently committed suicide.
The sons of the various Gǔdōuhóu each took up arms and defended themselves.
In the autumn,
the Southern Chányú sent his son to serve at court,
presenting a memorial at the palace gates.
An imperial edict bestowed upon the Chányú a cap and sash, clothing, a golden seal, a lǜwā sash,
an ānchē with a feather canopy,
a huázǎo-decorated four-horse carriage,
a precious sword and bow and arrows,
three black ensigns,
two fùmǎ (imperial horses),
gold, brocade, silk, and cloth totaling ten thousand bolts,
ten thousand catties of floss,
musical instruments, drum carriages,
qǐjǐ (decorated halberds) and armed soldiers,
and provisions and miscellaneous items.
Furthermore, twenty-five thousand hù of Hédōng rice provisions
and thirty-six thousand head of cattle and sheep were transported
to supply them.
A zhonglángjiàng was ordered to appoint an ānjí yuàn (or zhíshǐ) [史] to lead fifty zhúxíng,
armed with weapons and crossbows, to follow wherever the Chányú resided,
to participate in legal disputes,
and to observe movements.
At the end of each year, the Chányú would send a memorial
and send a hostage prince to court.
A cóngshì of the zhonglángjiàng would lead him to the palace gates.
The Hàn sent a yèzhě to escort the former hostage prince back to the Chányú’s court,
meeting on the road.
After the New Year’s court audience
and the completion of the sacrifices at the imperial mausoleum and ancestral temple,
the Hàn then dispatched an envoy to the Chányú,
ordering a yèzhě to escort him,
bestowing a thousand bolts of colorful silk,
four pieces of brocade,
ten catties of gold,
imperial sauces from the Tàiguān (Grand Provider’s Office), and oranges, tangerines, longans, and lychees.
The Chányú’s mother, the various yānzhī, the Chányú’s sons, and the deserving Zuǒxiánwáng, Yòuxiánwáng, Zuǒgǔlǐwáng, Yòugǔlǐwáng, and Gǔdōuhóu
were given a total of fourteen thousand pieces of silk and colorful fabrics.
This became a regular practice annually.
According to Xiongnú custom,
there were three dragon sacrifices each year,
always on the wù days of the first, fifth, and ninth months, to sacrifice to the gods of heaven.
After the Southern Chányú had submitted,
he also sacrificed to the Hàn Emperor,
and thereby gathered the various tribes
to deliberate on state affairs,
and enjoyed horse racing and camel racing.
His great ministers, in order of nobility, were the Zuǒxiánwáng,
followed by the Zuǒgǔlǐwáng,
then the Yòuxiánwáng,
then the Yòugǔlǐwáng;
these were called the Four Horns.
Next were the Zuǒrìzhúwáng and Yòurìzhúwáng,
then the Zuǒwēnyútuódīwáng and Yòuwēnyútuódīwáng,
then the Zuǒjiānjiàngwáng and Yòujiānjiàngwáng;
these were the Six Horns: all were sons and younger brothers of the Chányú,
and were next in line to become Chányú.
Ministers of different surnames included the Zuǒgǔdōuhóu and Yòugǔdōuhóu,
followed by the Zuǒshīzhúgǔdōuhóu and Yòushīzhúgǔdōuhóu.
The remaining official titles, such as Rìzhú, Qiejū, and Dānghù,
were ranked according to their power and influence, and the size of their tribal groups.
The Chányú’s surname was Xūliántí.
Among the different surnames were the Hūyǎn, Xūbǔ, Qiūlín, and Lán clans,
these four surnames
were prominent families within the country
and regularly intermarried with the Chányú.
The Hūyǎn clan was on the left,
and the Lán and Xūbǔ clans were on the right,
responsible for deciding judgments and hearing lawsuits,
determining the severity [of cases],
and orally reporting to the Chányú,
without written documents or ledgers.
In winter,
the sons of the five Gǔdōuhóu who had previously rebelled again led their three thousand followers to return to the Southern tribes.
The Northern Chányú sent cavalry to pursue and attack them.
They captured all their followers.
The Southern Chányú sent troops to resist them,
but was unsuccessful in the engagement.
Thereupon, an edict again ordered the Chányú to relocate to Měijì in Xīhé.
Accordingly, Zhonglángjiàng Duàn Chēn and Fùxiàowèi Wáng Yù were left in Xīhé to protect him,
