and official bureaus, cóngshì, and yuànshǐ were established for him.
The Xīhé Chángshǐ was ordered to lead two thousand cavalry each year,
and five hundred zhúxíng,
to assist the zhonglángjiàng in guarding the Chányú,
garrisoning in winter and disbanding in summer.
This became a regular practice thereafter,
and all eight frontier commanderies were restored.
After the Southern Chányú resided in Xīhé,
he also arranged and established various tribal kings,
to assist in defense.
Hánshì Gǔdōuhóu was stationed in Běidì,
the Yòuxiánwáng in Shuòfāng,
Dāngyú Gǔdōuhóu in Wǔyuán,
Hūyǎn Gǔdōuhóu in Yúnzhōng,
Lángshì Gǔdōuhóu in Dìngxiāng,
the Zuǒnán Jiāngjūn in Yànmén,
and Lìjí Gǔdōuhóu in Dàijùn.
All commanded their tribal groups to serve as scouts and lookouts for the commanderies and counties.
The Northern Chányú was alarmed
and partially returned the Hàn people he had plundered,
to show goodwill.
Whenever raiding soldiers reached the territory of the Southern tribes,
they would pass by watchtowers
and apologize, saying:
"We only attacked the fugitive Yùjiān Rìzhú;
we dared not violate the Hàn people."
In the 27th year,
the Northern Xiongnú finally sent an envoy to Wǔwēi to request peace and kinship.
The Son of Heaven summoned the gōngqīng for a court deliberation,
but no decision was reached.
The Imperial Crown Prince said:
"The Southern Chányú has newly submitted.
The Northern Lǔ are fearful of being attacked,
hence they lend an ear [to offers],
vying to return to righteousness.
Now, if we are unable to send troops
and instead communicate with the Northern Lǔ,
I fear the Southern Chányú will harbor ulterior motives,
and those Northern Lǔ who would surrender will no longer come."
The Emperor agreed,
and informed the Wǔwēi Tàishǒu not to receive their envoy.
In the 28th year,
the Northern Xiongnú again sent an envoy to the palace,
offering horses and furs,
again requesting peace and kinship,
and also asking for music,
and requesting to lead the Hú guests from the various Western Regions states to present themselves together.
The Emperor sent down the matter to the Three Excellencies for deliberation on the appropriate response.
Sītú Yuàn Bān Biāo memorialized, saying: "Your subject has heard that Emperor Xiàoxuān instructed the frontier guardians and commanders, saying:
'The Xiongnú is a great nation,
full of tricks and deceit.
If contact is made with understanding of their true intentions,
then enemies are repulsed and forces are broken;
if responses
fall into their calculations,
then one will instead be lightly deceived.'
Now the Northern Xiongnú see the Southern Chányú has submitted,
and fearing plots against their state,
they repeatedly beg for peace and kinship,
and also drive cattle and horses from afar
to trade with Hàn,
and send important princes [as envoys],
making many contributions.
These are all outward displays of wealth and strength,
intended to deceive us.
Your subject sees that their offerings become heavier,
knowing their state
is increasingly empty; their requests for kinship become more frequent,
and their fear becomes greater.
However, since we have not yet been able to assist the South,
it is also not appropriate to sever ties with the North.
According to the principle of loose rein (jīmí),
there is no礼 that is not reciprocated.
It is suggested that we could give generous rewards,
roughly equivalent to their offerings,
and clearly instruct them regarding the actions of Hūhánxié and Zhìzhī in previous generations.
To cultivate peace and kinship,
thereby assisting oneself and pacifying the state –
this counsel is most profound,
and the Chányú should laud it.
In the past,
the Xiongnú frequently faced chaos.
Hūhánxié and Zhìzhī were in a state of
enmity and conflict with each other.
Both received the benevolent protection of Emperor Xiàoxuān,
and thus each sent a hostage prince, declaring themselves vassals and guarding the frontier.
Later, Zhìzhī became enraged and violent,
cutting himself off from the imperial grace,
while Hū
Hán's relatives,
their loyalty and filial piety were profoundly manifested.
When Hàn destroyed Zhìzhī,
they then secured their state and transmitted their succession,
with sons and grandsons following one another.
Now the Southern Chányú has brought his multitude southward,
presenting himself at the
frontier and surrendering his life.
He considers himself Hūhán's legitimate eldest son,
and that by order he should be established,
but he has been seized and deprived of his position,
and they have become suspicious and turned their backs on each other.
Repeatedly he has requested soldiers and generals,
to return and sweep the Northern Court,
with plans
and schemes in a flurry,
stopping at nothing.
Only, I consider these words not to be listened to solely,
and also because the Northern Chányú has for years made contributions,
and desires to cultivate peace and kinship,
therefore I have refused and have not
granted it,
intending to fulfill the Chányú's loyalty and filial piety.
Hàn holds authority and trustworthiness,
commanding all nations;
wherever the sun and moon shine,
all are its subjects.
Regarding diverse customs and a hundred barbarian tribes,
there is
no distinction of closeness or remoteness;
those who submit are praised and rewarded,
those who rebel are punished,
the consequences of good and evil are
Hūhán and Zhìzhī.
Now the Chányú wishes to cultivate peace and kinship,
his sincerity
has already reached us.
What objection is there that you wish to lead the various Xīyù states to come together to present themselves and have an audience?
If the Xīyù states belong to the Xiōngnú,
how is that different from belonging to Hàn?
The Chányú has repeatedly been involved in military strife,
his country is depleted;
the tribute items are merely for the sake of courtesy,
why must horses and furs be offered?
Now five hundred bolts of assorted silk,
one bow and quiver and arrow bag,
and four quivers of arrows
are dispatched
to the Chányú.
Also, to the Zuǒ Gǔdū Hóu and Yòu Gǔlí Wáng who offered horses, four hundred bolts of assorted silk each are bestowed,
and one cavalry sword each.
The Chányú previously said that the yú, sè, and kōnghóu given to Hūhánxié during the
former emperor's time were all damaged,
and he wished for them to be [re-]made and bestowed.
Considering that the Chányú's state is not yet stable,
and he is currently exerting military prowess,
with
war and conquest as his priority,
the use of yú and sè is not as good as good bows and sharp swords,
therefore they have not yet been sent.
I do not begrudge small items to the Chányú,
whatever is convenient and desired,
send an envoy
to inform me."
The Chányú Bǐ died after reigning for nine years.
Zhōnglángjiàng Duàn Chēn led troops to mourn,
offering sacrifices of wine and rice,
and assigned soldiers to guard him.
Bǐ's younger brother, Zuǒ Xián Wáng Mò, was established.
The emperor sent an envoy with a sealed letter to soothe and comfort him,
bestowing upon him the seal and sash,
and presenting him with a cap and headscarf,
three sets of crimson single robes,
one child's dagger and one braided belt each,
and also four thousand bolts of silk fabric,
ordering them to be rewarded to the various kings and Gǔdū Hóu and those below.
Thereafter, when a Chányú died,
mourning, sacrifices, comforting, and bestowals became the norm.
Qiūfúyóudī Chányú Mò
was established in the first year of Zhōngyuán,
and died in one year.
His younger brother Hàn was established.
Yīfáwūlǜdī Chányú Hàn
was established in the second year of Zhōngyuán.
In the second year of Yǒngpíng,
Hùyúqiū of the Northern Xiōngnú led over a thousand people to surrender.
The Southern Chányú Hàn died after reigning for two years.
Chányú Bǐ's son Shì was established.
Tóngshīzhúhóudī Chányú Shì
was established in the second year of Yǒngpíng.
In the winter of the fifth year,
six or seven thousand Northern Xiōngnú cavalry entered Wǔyuán Pass,
then plundered Yúnzhōng as far as Yuányáng.
The Southern Chányú attacked and repelled them.
Xīhé Zhǎngshǐ Mǎ Xiāng rushed to rescue,
and the captives then withdrew.
Chányú Shì died after reigning for four years.
Chányú Mò's son Sū was established,
who was Qiūchúchēlīndī Chányú.
After a few months he also died.
Chányú Shì's younger brother Cháng was established.
Húxiéshīzhúhóudī Chányú Cháng
was established in the sixth year of Yǒngpíng.
At that time, the Northern Xiōngnú were still strong,
repeatedly raiding the borders,
which caused concern in the court.
Coincidentally, the Northern Chányú desired to establish a market,
and sent envoys to seek peace and kinship.
Xiǎnzōng hoped that they would establish contact
and no longer raid.
So he granted it.
In the eighth year,
he sent Yuèqí Sīmǎ Zhèng Zhòng on a northern mission to respond to the summons.
However, the Southern Xūbǔ Gǔdū Hóu and others, knowing that Hàn was exchanging envoys with the Northern captives,
harbored suspicion and resentment and desired to rebel.
They secretly used the Northern envoy
to ask them to send troops to welcome them.
When Zhèng Zhòng left the pass,
he suspected something was amiss.
He waited and indeed found Xūbǔ's envoy.
He then reported that a new great general should be appointed
to prevent communication between the two captive groups.
Because of this, the Dùliáo Camp was first established,
with Zhōnglángjiàng Wú Táng acting as Dùliáo Jiāngjūn.
Fù Xiàowèi Lái Miáo, Zuǒ Xiàowèi Yán Zhāng, and Yòu Xiàowèi Zhāng Guó led the Lìyáng Hǔyá Camp soldiers to garrison at Wǔyuán Mánbǎi.
Additionally, Qí Dūwèi Qín Péng was sent to lead troops to garrison at Měijì.
In the autumn of that year,
the Northern captives indeed sent two thousand cavalry to scout Shuòfāng,
and made leather boats,
intending to cross to welcome the Southern rebels.
However, seeing that Hàn was prepared,
they withdrew.
They repeatedly plundered and raided the border commanderies,
burning down cities and towns,
killing and seizing many people,
causing the city gates of Héxī to be closed during the day.
The emperor was distressed by this.
In the sixteenth year,
he then greatly dispatched border troops,
sending various generals out of the pass in four routes,
to campaign against the Xiōngnú in the north.
The Southern Chányú sent Zuǒ Xián Wáng Xìn to follow Tàipú Jì Róng and Wú Táng out from Shuòfāng Gāoquē,
to attack Gāolín Wēnyúdú Wáng at Zhuóxié Mountain.
When the captives heard of the Hàn army's arrival,
they all crossed the desert and departed.
Róng and Táng were dismissed for not reaching Zhuóxié Mountain.
Qí Dūwèi Lái Miáo acted as Dùliáo Jiāngjūn.
That year,
the Northern Xiōngnú entered Yúnzhōng,
and then reached Yúyáng.
Tàishǒu Lián Fàn attacked and repelled them.
An edict ordered envoy Gāo Hóng to mobilize troops from three commanderies to pursue them,
but nothing was gained.
In the first year of Jiànchū,
Lái Miáo was promoted to Jìyīn Tàishǒu.
Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn Gěng Bǐng acted as Dùliáo Jiāngjūn.
At that time, Gāolín Wēnyúdú Wáng again led his multitude back to reside at Zhuóxié Mountain.
The Southern Chányú, hearing of this,
sent light cavalry with border commandery troops and Wūhuán soldiers out of the pass to attack him,
beheading several hundred and
receiving three or four thousand surrenders.
That year,
the South suffered from locusts,
and there was a great famine.
Sùzōng provided food to over thirty thousand poor people.
In the seventh year,
Gěng Bǐng was promoted to Zhí Jīnwú.
Zhāngyè Tàishǒu Dèng Hóng acted as Dùliáo Jiāngjūn.
In the eighth year,
Sānmùlóuzī Dàrén Jīliúsī and others of the Northern Xiōngnú led thirty-eight thousand people, twenty thousand horses, and over one hundred thousand cattle and sheep
to surrender at Wǔyuán Pass.
In the first year of Yuánhé,
Wǔwēi Tàishǒu Mèng Yún reported that the Northern Chányú again wished to establish a market with officials and people.
An imperial edict allowed Yún to send envoys to welcome, console, and accept them.
The Northern Chányú then sent Dàqiěqú Yīmòzī Wáng and others,
driving over ten thousand head of cattle and horses to trade with Hàn merchants.
Some of the kings and elders arrived earlier,
and the local commanderies and counties set up official residences for them,
rewarding and treating them well.
The Southern Chányú, hearing this,
sent light cavalry out to Shàngjùn,
to intercept and capture people,
and plunder cattle and horses,
driving them back into the pass.
In the first month of the second year,
Chēlì, Zhuóbīng, and other elders of the Northern Xiōngnú fled into the pass,
a total of seventy-three people.
At this time, the Northern captives were in decline,
their factions and multitudes were scattered and rebellious.
The South attacked them from the front,
the Dīnglíng plundered them from the rear,
the Xiānbēi attacked their left,
and Xīyù invaded their right.
They could no longer sustain themselves,
and thus withdrew far away.
Chányú Cháng died after reigning for twenty-three years.
Chányú Hàn's son Xuān was established.
Yī Túyúyǘ Dī Chányú Xuān
was enthroned in the second year of Yuánhé.
That year,
the Chányú dispatched over a thousand soldiers to hunt as far as Zhuóxié Shān.
They unexpectedly encountered King Wēnyúdú of the Northern Lǔ
and engaged in battle,
capturing his head and returning.
In winter,
Mèng Yún submitted a memorial, saying:
"The Northern Lǔ previously entered into a 'peace and kinship' agreement,
but the Southern tribes again went to plunder them.
The Northern Chányú believes that the Hàn is deceiving him
and is plotting to invade the frontier.
It would be appropriate to return the captives taken by the Southern tribes
to appease their intentions."
Sùzōng followed the advice of Tàipú Yuán Ān
and permitted it.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued, stating:
"The enmity of the Xiǎnyǔn and Xūnzhōu towards the Middle Kingdom
has a long history.
Though there were 'peace and kinship' agreements in the past,
they ultimately had no effect whatsoever.
The people of these barren lands
were repeatedly afflicted by suffering,
with fathers fighting in the front
and sons dying in the rear.
Young women were seized at the frontier forts,
and orphaned children cried on the roads.
Old mothers and widowed wives offered empty sacrifices,
shedding tears
and longing for the return of their souls from beyond the desert.
How sorrowful this was!
The proverb says: 'The reason why rivers and seas can nourish all streams
is because they position themselves below them.'
To yield a little
is nothing to be concerned about.
Moreover, now that the relationship between our emperor and the Xiongnú is established,
the declarations are compliant and the agreements clear,
and tributes have arrived repeatedly,
how can we violate trust and incur blame ourselves?
Let Dùliáo and Lǐng Zhōnglángjiàng Páng Fèn be commanded to pay double to the Southern tribes for the captives they obtained,
to return them to the Northern Lǔ.
As for the Southern tribes who decapitated or captured enemies,
they shall be rewarded according to their achievements as per the usual regulations."
Thereupon, the Southern Chányú again ordered Àodī Rìzhú Wáng Shīzi to lead several thousand light cavalry out of the frontier to ambush the Northern Lǔ,
and they again captured and killed a thousand people.
The Northern Lǔ populace believed that the Southern tribes were favored by the Hàn,
and also heard that thousands of defectors arrived each year.
In the first year of Zhānghé,
the Xiānbēi entered the left territory and attacked the Northern Xiongnú,
greatly defeating them,
beheading Yōuliú Chányú,
and taking his Xiongnú hide before returning.
The Northern Court fell into great chaos.
Fifty-eight tribes, including Qūlán, Chǔbēi, and Húdūxū,
totaling two hundred thousand people,
with eight thousand able-bodied soldiers,
came to Yúnzhōng, Wǔyuán, Shuòfāng, and Běidì to surrender.
Chányú Xuān died after three years on the throne.
Chányú Zhǎng's younger brother, Túntúhé, was enthroned.
Xiūlán Shīzhúhóudī Chányú Túntúhé
was enthroned in the second year of Zhānghé.
At this time, the Northern Lǔ were in great disarray,
and moreover suffered from famine and locusts.
Defectors arrived continuously.
The Southern Chányú intended to annex the Northern Court.
Then Sùzōng died,
and Empress Dowager Dòu presided over the court.
In the seventh month of that year,
the Chányú submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your servant's family has received countless favors
for generations.
Emperor Xiàozhāng, with his sagely and far-sighted wisdom,
desired to bring about our success,
and thus ordered the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi to attack the Northern Lǔ,
beheading their Chányú
and destroying their state.
Now, Xūqú and others, who recently surrendered, came to your servant and said: 'In the third month of last year, we departed from the Lǔ court.
The Northern Chányú, having been severely defeated by the Southern troops,
and also fearing the Dīnglìng and Xiānbēi,
fled far away
and took refuge west of the Ānhóu River.
In the first month of this year,
the Gǔdōuhóu and others jointly enthroned the Chányú's paternal half-brother, the Right Xiánwáng, as Chányú.
As for that person, due to brothers contending for the throne,
they have all dispersed.'
Your servant and the various kings, Gǔdōuhóu, and newly surrendered chieftains discussed strategies,
and all said that it is advisable to take advantage of the Northern Lǔ's internal strife
and dispatch troops to attack them,
defeating the North to unite with the South,
and merge into one state,
so that the Hàn imperial house may forever be free from northern concerns.
Moreover, on the eighth day of this month,
the recently surrendered Right Xū Rìzhú Xiāntáng came from afar from the Lǔ court to your servant,
saying that many Northern Lǔ tribes wish to turn to us,
but are ashamed to initiate it themselves,
which is why none have arrived yet.
If we dispatch troops to attack swiftly,
there will surely be a response.
If we do not go this year,
we fear they will unite again.
Your servant humbly reflects that since my late father submitted to the Hàn,
we have been covered and borne by its grace,
with strong frontier defenses and clear watchtowers,
and protected by large armies,
for forty years.
Your servants were born and raised in Hàn territory,
eating what we are given,
and receiving annual rewards
amounting to hundreds of millions.
Though we rest in peace with folded hands,
we are ashamed to have no means of repayment.
I wish to dispatch the elite troops from my state, from the various old Hú tribes, and from the newly surrendered,
and send Zuǒ Gǔlí Wáng Shīzi and Zuǒ Hūyán Rìzhú Wáng Xūzī with ten thousand cavalry out from Shuòfāng,
and Zuǒ Xiánwáng Ānguó and Yòu Dàqújú Wáng Jiāolèsū with ten thousand cavalry out from Jūyán.
They are to meet in the Lǔ territory in the twelfth month.
Your servant will lead the remaining ten thousand soldiers to garrison Wǔyuán and the Shuòfāng frontier
for defense.
Your servant is inherently foolish and shallow,
and my forces are few and weak,
insufficient to defend against internal and external threats.
I request that Zhí Jīnwú Gěng Bǐng, Dùliáo Jiāngjūn Dèng Hóng, and the Tàishǒu of Xīhé, Yúnzhōng, Wǔyuán, Shuòfāng, and Shàngjùn be dispatched to combine their forces and advance north.
Let the Tàishǒu of Běidì and Āndìng each garrison strategic points.
I hope that through the awe-inspiring power of the Sacred Emperor,
we can pacify them in one swift action.
The success or failure of your servant's state
rests on this year.
I have already ordered the various tribes to prepare their troops and horses,
and after the dragon sacrifice in the ninth month,
they will all assemble by the river.
May Your Majesty graciously consider and examine this!"
The Empress Dowager showed it to Gěng Bǐng.
Bǐng submitted a memorial, saying:
"In the past, Emperor Wǔ alone dominated the world,
wishing to make the Xiongnú his subjects,
but as the opportune moment had not arrived,
the undertaking was unsuccessful.
In the era of Emperor Xuān,
Hūhán happened to surrender,
and thus the frontier people gained peace,
the interior and exterior became one,
and the people rested for over sixty years.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
he changed their titles,
causing endless depletion and disturbance,
whereupon the Chányú rebelled.
When Guāngwǔ received the Mandate,
he again embraced and accepted them,
and the devastated commanderies along the frontier were able to be restored.
The Wūhuán and Xiānbēi were all coerced into allegiance,
and his authority suppressed the Four Barbarians;
such was its effectiveness.
Now, fortunately, heaven has provided this opportunity,
with the Northern Lǔ divided by internal strife.
Using barbarians to attack barbarians is a benefit to the state,
and should be granted."
Bǐng then personally stated
that he had received grace and it was his duty to risk his life to serve.
The Empress Dowager agreed.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
Bǐng was appointed as Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn,
and with Chējì Jiāngjūn Dòu Xiàn, he led eight thousand cavalry,
along with the Dùliáo forces and thirty thousand cavalry from the Southern Chányú's army,
to advance from Shuòfāng to attack the Northern Lǔ,
greatly defeating them.
The Northern Chányú fled,
and over two hundred thousand heads and captives were taken.
The details of this event are fully recorded in the biography of Dòu Xiàn.
In the second year, spring,
Dèng Hóng was promoted to Dà Hónglú.
Huángfǔ Léng, the Grand Administrator of Dìngxiāng, was appointed acting Commander Pro tem of the Dùliáo Army.
The Southern Chányú again submitted a memorial requesting to exterminate the Northern Court.
Thereupon, the Left Gǔlí Wáng, Shīzi, and others were dispatched, leading eight thousand cavalry from the left and right divisions out through Jīlù Sài.
Zhōnglángjiāng Gěng Tán sent an attendant to supervise them.
Upon reaching Zhuóxié Shān,
they left their baggage train
and divided into two divisions,
each leading light troops to attack from two routes.
The left division went north past Xī Hǎi to Héyún Běi.
The right division circled west from the Xiōngnú Hé River around Tiānshān,
and crossed the Gānwēi Hé River to the south.
The two armies met,
and at night surrounded the Northern Chányú.
The Chányú was greatly alarmed,
and led over a thousand elite soldiers to engage in battle.
The Chányú was wounded,
fell from his horse but remounted,
and fled with several tens of light cavalry,
barely escaping.
His jade seal was captured,
and his Yānshī and five men and women were taken.
Over eight thousand heads were cut off,
and several thousand people were captured alive before they returned.
At this time, the southern region continually achieved victories and received surrenders,
and its followers were most numerous,
with thirty-four thousand households,
two hundred thirty-seven thousand three hundred people,
and fifty thousand one hundred seventy able-bodied soldiers.
Therefore, the Zhōnglángjiāng in charge of affairs was provided with two attendants.
Gěng Tán, seeing that there were many new surrenderers,
memorialized to increase the number of attendants to twelve.
In the third year,
the Northern Chányú was again defeated by Right Xiàowèi Gěng Kuí,
and fled to an unknown location.
His younger brother, Right Gǔlí Wáng Yúchújiān, declared himself Chányú.
He led the Right Wēnyújiān Wáng and Gǔdōu Hóu, and thousands of others,
and stopped at Púlèi Hǎi,
sending envoys to establish friendly relations at the frontier.
Dàjiāngjūn Dòu Xiàn memorialized,
proposing to recognize Yúchújiān as the Northern Chányú,
and the court agreed.
In the fourth year,
Gěng Kuí was dispatched to formally present the seal and ribbon,
and four jade swords and
one four-horse carriage with feather canopy were bestowed.
Zhōnglángjiāng Rèn Shàng was sent with the imperial insignia to garrison and protect Yīwú,
following the precedent of the Southern Chányú.
They were about to assist in the return to the Northern Court,
when Dòu Xiàn was executed.
In the fifth year,
Yúchújiān rebelled and returned north.
The Emperor dispatched Jiāngbīng Chángshǐ Wáng Fǔ with over a thousand cavalry to pursue him with Rèn Shàng, entice him back, and then execute him,
destroying his followers.
Chányú Túhé, who had been stationed at Túhé, died in the sixth year of his reign.
Chányú Xuān’s younger brother Ānguó was enthroned.
Chányú Ānguó
was enthroned in the fifth year of Yǒngyuán.
Ānguó was initially the Left Xián Wáng but had no reputation.
Left Gǔlí Wáng Shīzi was always brave, cunning, and knowledgeable.
Both the former Chányú Xuān and Túhé admired his decisive spirit,
and thus frequently sent him to lead troops out of the frontier
to ambush the Northern Court.
Upon his return, he received rewards,
and the Son of Heaven also granted him special favors.
Therefore, everyone in the state respected Shīzi
and did not support Ānguó.
Ānguó, because of this, resented Shīzi
and wanted to kill him.
The newly surrendered Hú, who were originally outside the frontier,
had frequently been driven off and plundered by Shīzi,
and all resented him greatly.
Ānguó, taking advantage of this, entrusted his plans to the surrenderers
and conspired with them.
After Ānguó was enthroned as Chányú,
Shīzi, in turn, became Left Xián Wáng.
Realizing that the Chányú and the new surrenderers were plotting,
he moved to reside separately within the Wǔyuán boundary.
Whenever the Chányú held important meetings to discuss affairs,
Shīzi would always claim illness and not attend.
Huángfǔ Léng knew this
and also protected him, not sending him.
The Chányú's indignation grew even stronger.
In the sixth year, spring,
Huángfǔ Léng was dismissed.
Zhū Huī, the Zhí Jīnwú, was appointed acting Commander Pro tem of the Dùliáo Army.
At this time, the Chányú and Zhōnglángjiāng Dù Chóng were not on good terms,
so he memorialized to accuse Chóng.
Chóng implicitly instructed the Grand Administrator of Xīhé to block the Chányú's memorial,
so it could not be heard directly.
Instead, Chóng and Zhū Huī jointly memorialized:
"The Southern Chányú Ānguó is alienated from the old Hú and
close to the new surrenderers.
He wants to kill Left Xián Wáng Shīzi and Left Tái Jūqú Liú Lì and others.
Moreover, the surrenderers from the right division are plotting to coerce Ānguó
and raise an army to rebel.
We request that Xīhé, Shàngjùn, and Āndìng be put on alert."
Emperor Hé submitted the matter to the grand ministers for deliberation.
All believed that
"the barbarians are fickle,
and though difficult to predict,
a large army assembled will certainly not dare to stir.
Currently, it is fitting to dispatch an envoy with strategy to the Chányú's court
to join forces with Dù Chóng, Zhū Huī, and the Grand Administrator of Xīhé,
to observe their movements.
If there are no other changes,
Chóng and others can be ordered to meet Ānguó with his surrounding ministers,
and hold them accountable for their divisions' violent acts that harm the frontier,
and jointly punish the guilty.
If they do not comply,
let a provisional strategy be implemented.
After the matter is concluded,
simply bestow customary gifts,
which will also be sufficient to deter all barbarians."
The Emperor agreed.
Thereupon, Huī and Chóng indeed raised troops and advanced to his court.
Ānguó heard of the Han army's arrival at night,
was greatly alarmed,
abandoned his tent, and left.
He then raised an army and, with the newly surrendered, intended to execute Shīzi.
Shīzi, having prior knowledge,
led all his households into Màn Bǎi Chéng.
Ānguó pursued him to the city wall,
but the gate was closed, and he could not enter.
Zhū Huī sent an official to explain and mediate,
but Ānguó did not listen.
Since the city could not be taken,
he led his troops to garrison Wǔyuán.
Chóng and Huī then dispatched cavalry from various commanderies to pursue him urgently.
Everyone was greatly terrified.
Ānguó's uncle, Gǔdōu Hóu Xǐ, and others feared they would also be executed,
so they killed Ānguó.
Ānguó reigned for one year.
Shīzi, the son of Chányú Shì, was enthroned.
Tíngdúshīzhúhóudī Chányú Shīzi
was enthroned in the sixth year of Yǒngyuán.
Five or six hundred surrendered Hú attacked Shīzi at night.
Ānjí Yuàn Wáng Tián led his guards and fought them,
defeating them.
Thereupon, the newly surrendered Hú were alarmed,
and over two hundred thousand people from fifteen divisions all rebelled,
coercing Fēng Hóu, son of former Chányú Túhé and Áo Rìzhú Wáng, to become Chányú.
They then killed officials and civilians,
burned postal stations and tents,
and, taking their chariots and baggage, headed towards Shuòfāng,
intending to cross north of the desert.

Thereupon, acting Chēqí Jiāngjūn Dèng Hóng, Yuèqí Xiàowèi Féng Zhù, and acting Dùliáo Jiāngjūn Zhū Huī were dispatched, leading the left and right Yǔlín, the Five Bureaus of the Northern Army, troops from commanderies and kingdoms, and frontier troops.
Wūhuán Xiàowèi Rèn Shàng led the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi,
a total of forty thousand men, to attack them.
At this time, the Southern Chányú and Zhōnglángjiāng Dù Chóng were garrisoned at Mùshī Chéng.
Fēng Hóu led over ten thousand cavalry to besiege them,
but had not yet taken it.
In winter,
Dèng Hóng and others arrived at Měijì.
Fēng Hóu then crossed the pass on ice
and headed towards Mǎnyí Gǔ.
The Southern Chányú dispatched his son leading ten thousand cavalry,
and Dù Chóng's four thousand cavalry,
to pursue and attack Fēng Hóu with Dèng Hóng and others at Dàchéng Sài.
Over three thousand heads were cut off,
and over ten thousand captives and surrenderers were taken.
Féng Zhù again divided his troops to pursue and attack their separate divisions,
cutting off over four thousand heads.
Rèn Shàng led the Xiānbēi Dà Dūhù Sūbáhuī
and the Wūhuán Dàrén Wùkē with eight thousand cavalry
to intercept and attack Fēng Hóu at Mǎnyí Gǔ,
and again greatly defeated him.
In total, over seventeen thousand heads were cut off.
Fēng Hóu then led his followers out of the frontier,
and the Han army could not pursue him.
In the seventh year, first month,
the army returned.
Féng Zhù (馮柱) kept the Hǔyá Camp (虎牙營) stationed in Wǔyuán (五原).
He dismissed the Xiānbēi (鮮卑), Wūhuán (烏桓), Qiāng (羌), and Hú (胡) soldiers.
He enfeoffed Sū Bákuài (蘇拔廆) as the Shàizhong Wáng (率衆王),
and also bestowed gold and silk upon him.
Dèng Hóng (鄧鴻) returned to the capital.
He was charged with lingering and losing an advantage,
imprisoned, and died.
Later, the Emperor learned that Zhū Huī (朱徽) and Dù Chóng (杜崇) had failed to maintain harmony with the Hú (胡),
and also forbade them from submitting memorials,
which led to the rebellion.
They were all summoned, imprisoned, and died.
The Grand Administrator of Yànmén (鴈門), Páng Fèn (龐奮), was appointed acting General Wielding the Liao (度遼將軍).
Péng Hóu (逢侯) divided his forces outside the frontier into two parts.
He personally led the right wing and camped at the foot of Zhuóxié Mountain (涿邪山),
while the left wing camped northwest of Shuòfāng (朔方),
several hundred *lǐ* (里) apart.
In the winter of the eighth year [of Yǒngyuán (永元)],
the Hú (胡) of the left wing, suspecting each other, rebelled,
and returned into the Shuòfāng (朔方) frontier.
Páng Fèn (龐奮) welcomed, received, comforted, and assimilated them.
Their 4,000 able-bodied soldiers
and over 10,000 weak and young surrendered.
They were distributed among the various northern border commanderies.
The Southern Chányú (單于) wished to interrogate his Right Wēnyúdú Wáng (右溫禺犢王), Wūjūzhàn (烏居戰),
who had initially conspired with Ān Guó (安國).
Wūjūzhàn (烏居戰) then
led several thousand men and rebelled again,
fleeing to the mountain valleys outside the frontier,
causing harm to officials and common people.
In the autumn,
Páng Fèn (龐奮), Féng Zhù (馮柱), and the troops from various commanderies attacked Wūjūzhàn (烏居戰).
His followers surrendered.
Thereupon, Wūjūzhàn's (烏居戰) followers and all those who had returned and surrendered, over 20,000 people, were resettled in Āndìng (安定) and Běidì (北地).
Féng Zhù (馮柱) returned [to the capital]
and was promoted to Grand Architect.
Péng Hóu's (逢侯) followers suffered from hunger and poverty,
and were also attacked by the Xiānbēi (鮮卑).
Having nowhere to go,
those who fled into the frontier came in an unbroken stream.
Chányú (單于) Shīzi (師子) died after reigning for four years.
The son of Chányú (單于) Cháng (長), Bù (ブ), was enthroned.
The Wànshì Shīzhú Dī Chányú (萬氏尸逐鞮單于), Bù (ブ),
was enthroned in the tenth year of Yǒngyuán (永元).
In the twelfth year,
Páng Fèn (龐奮) was promoted to Governor of Hénán (河南尹),
and Wáng Biāo (王彪), Grand Administrator of Shuòfāng (朔方), was appointed acting General Wielding the Liao (度遼將軍).
The Southern Chányú (單于) sent troops to attack Péng Hóu (逢侯) year after year,
capturing many.
The number of people recovered and brought back alive totaled thousands, both before and after,
and Péng Hóu (逢侯) became increasingly distressed.
In the sixteenth year,
the Northern Chányú (單于) sent envoys to the imperial court to offer tribute,
wishing for peace and marriage alliances,
and to restore the old treaty of Hūhánxié (呼韓邪).
Emperor Hé (和帝), deeming their old rites incomplete,
did not grant his request,
but generously bestowed rewards
and did not reply to his envoy.
In the first year of Yuánxīng (元興),
he again sent envoys to Dūnhuáng (敦煌) to offer tribute,
claiming that his state was poor and unable to fully observe the rites,
and requested a grand envoy,
promising to send a son to serve at court.
At that time, Empress Dowager Dèng (鄧太后) was regent.
She also did not reply to his envoy,
only adding to the gifts.
In the summer of the third year
of Yǒngchū (永初),
Hán Cóng (韓琮), a Hàn (漢) man, accompanied the Southern Chányú (單于) to court.
Upon his return,
he told the Southern Chányú (單于):
"East of the passes, there are floods,
and the people are dying of starvation.
They can be attacked."
The Chányú (單于) believed his words
and then raised troops and rebelled,
attacking the Commandant-in-Chief Gěng Zhǒng (耿种) at Měijì (美稷).
In the autumn,
Wáng Biāo (王彪) died.
In the winter,
the acting General of Chariots and Cavalry, Hé Xī (何熙), and the Deputy Commandant-in-Chief, Páng Xióng (龐雄), were sent to attack him.
In the spring of the fourth year,
Bù (ブ) sent over a thousand cavalry to raid Chángshān (常山) and Zhōngshān (中山).
Liáng Jǐn (梁慬), the Colonel of the Western Regions, was appointed acting General Wielding the Liao (度遼將軍),
and together with Gěng Kuí (耿夔), Grand Administrator of Liáodōng (遼東), defeated them.
The details are fully recorded in the biographies of Jǐn (慬) and Kuí (夔).
When the Chányú (單于) saw all the armies advancing,
he was greatly terrified
and turned to rebuke Hán Cóng (韓琮), saying:
"You said the Hàn (漢) people were all dead.
Who are these people now?"
He then sent an envoy to beg for surrender,
which was granted.
The Chányú (單于), bareheaded and barefoot,
bowed before Páng Xióng (龐雄) and others,
confessing his capital offense.
Thereupon, he was pardoned
and treated as before.
He returned the Hàn (漢) men and women he had plundered, as well as those captured by the Qiāng (羌) and resold into the Xiōngnú (匈奴), totaling over 10,000 people.
In the fifth year,
Liáng Jǐn (梁慬) was dismissed,
and Gěng Kuí (耿夔), Grand Administrator of Yúnzhōng (雲中), was appointed acting General Wielding the Liao (度遼將軍).
In the first year of Yuánchū (元初),
Kuí (夔) was dismissed,
and Dèng Zūn (鄧遵), Colonel of Wūhuán (烏桓), was appointed General Wielding the Liao (度遼將軍).
Zūn (遵) was
the Empress Dowager's younger cousin,
and thus he was first made a true General.
In the fourth year,
Péng Hóu (逢侯) was defeated by the Xiānbēi (鮮卑),
his followers scattered,
all returning to the northern barbarians.
In the spring of the fifth year,
Péng Hóu (逢侯) and over a hundred cavalrymen returned,
going to the Shuòfāng (朔方) frontier to surrender.
Dèng Zūn (鄧遵) memorialized to resettle Péng Hóu (逢侯) in Yǐngchuān (潁川) Commandery.
In the first year of Jiànguāng (建光),
Dèng Zūn (鄧遵) was dismissed,
and Gěng Kuí (耿夔) again replaced him as General Wielding the Liao (度遼將軍).
At that time, the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) were raiding the borders.
Kuí (夔) and Wēnyúdú Wáng (溫禺犢王) Hūyóuhuī (呼尤徽), leading the newly surrendered, repeatedly went out of the frontier for years,
to attack the Xiānbēi (鮮卑).
Upon their return,
they were again ordered to be stationed in strategic locations.
However, Gěng Kuí's (耿夔) levies were troublesome and severe,
and all the newly surrendered nursed grievances and plotted rebellion.
Chányú (單于) Bù (ブ) died after reigning for twenty-seven years.
His younger brother, Bá (拔), was enthroned.
Gěng Kuí (耿夔) was again dismissed,
and Fǎ Dù (法度), Grand Administrator of Tàiyuán (太原), replaced him as General.
Wūjīhóu Shīzhú Dī Chányú (烏稽侯尸逐鞮單于) Bá (拔)
was enthroned in the third year of Yánguāng (延光).
In the summer,
Ā Zú (阿族) and other leaders of a newly surrendered tribe rebelled,
coercing Hūyóuhuī (呼尤徽) to leave with them.
Hūyóuhuī (呼尤徽) said:
"I am old,
and have received the grace of the Hàn (漢) court.
I would rather die than follow you!"
The crowd wanted to kill him,
but some saved him,
and he escaped.
Ā Zú (阿族) and others then fled with their wives, children, and baggage train.
The Commandant-in-Chief Mǎ Yì (馬翼) sent troops and Hú (胡) cavalry to pursue and attack them,
defeating them.
Almost all were beheaded or threw themselves into the river and died.
Over 10,000 horses, cattle, and sheep were captured.
In the winter,
Fǎ Dù (法度) died.
In the fourth year,
Fù Zhòng (傅衆), Grand Administrator of Hànyáng (漢陽), replaced him as General.
That winter,
Fù Zhòng (傅衆) also died.
In the first year of Yǒngjiàn (永建),
Páng Cān (龐參), Grand Administrator of Liáodōng (遼東), replaced him as General.
Previously, many of the frontier fortifications west of Shuòfāng (朔方) had not been repaired,
and the Xiānbēi (鮮卑) consequently frequently raided the southern regions,
killing Jiànjiāng Wáng (漸將王).
The Chányú (單于), worried and fearful,
memorialized to request the repair of the frontier fortifications.
Emperor Shùn (順帝) agreed.
Thus, the Liyáng (黎陽) garrison troops were sent to be stationed on the northern border of Zhōngshān (中山),
and troops in the various border commanderies were increased,
stationed in rows below the frontier,
and trained in battle and archery.
Chányú (單于) Bá (拔) died after reigning for four years.
His younger brother, Xiūlì (休利), was enthroned.
Qùtèruò Shīzhú Jiù Chányú (去特若尸逐就單于) Xiūlì (休利)
was enthroned in the third year of Yǒngjiàn (永建).
In the fourth year,
Páng Cān (龐參) was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies,
and Sòng Hàn (宋漢), Chancellor of Dōngpíng (東平), replaced him as General Wielding the Liao (度遼將軍).
In the second year of Yángjiā (陽嘉),
Hàn (漢) was promoted to Grand Coachman,
and Gěng Yè (耿曄), Colonel of Wūhuán (烏桓), replaced him as General Wielding the Liao (度遼將軍).
In the first year of Yǒnghé (永和),
Yè (曄) was summoned due to illness,
and Mǎ Xù (馬續), Colonel Protector of the Qiāng (護羌校尉), replaced him as General Wielding the Liao (度遼將軍).
In the summer of the fifth year,
the Left Judròong Wáng Wúsī and Chēniǔ of the Southern Xiōngnú rebelled.
They led over three thousand cavalry to raid Xīhé,
then again enticed the Right Xiánwáng,
and with seven or eight thousand cavalry, besieged Měijì,
killing the Chief Clerks of Shuòfāng and Dàijùn.
Mǎ Xù, along with the Colonel-Director Láng Liáng Bìng and the Wūhuán Commandant Wáng Yuán, mobilized frontier troops and Wūhuán, Xiānbēi, Qiānghú totaling over twenty thousand men,
and launched a surprise attack, defeating them.
Wúsī and others then re-formed their camps,
attacking and capturing cities and towns.
The Son of Heaven sent envoys to reprimand the Chányú,
explaining to him the principles of benevolence and righteousness,
and ordering him to persuade the rebels to surrender.
The Chányú, who had not been involved in the conspiracy,
removed his cap and left his tent,
going to Bìng to apologize.
Bìng was recalled due to illness,
and Chén Guī, the Administrator of Wǔyuán, replaced him as Colonel-Director.
Guī believed that the Chányú was inherently unable to control his subordinates,
and pressured him.
The Chányú and his younger brother, the Left Xiánwáng, both committed suicide.
Chányú Xiūlì had reigned for thirteen years.
Guī also wanted to move the Chányú's close relatives to the inner commanderies,
which made the surrendered ones even more suspicious.
Guī was imprisoned for this and dismissed.
The Grand General Liáng Shāng, seeing that the Qiānghú had recently revolted,
and their forces had just united,
believed it would be difficult to subdue them by force.
He thought it appropriate to use persuasion to induce surrender,
and therefore submitted a memorial, saying:
“The Xiōngnú have raided and rebelled,
knowing full well their extreme guilt.
Like cornered birds and trapped beasts,
they all seek to save their lives.
How much more so with their numerous and flourishing kind,
who cannot be entirely wiped out.
Currently, transportation costs increase daily,
the three armies are weary and suffering,
and emptying the interior to supply the exterior is
not beneficial to the Middle Kingdom.
I have secretly observed that the General Who Crosses the Desert, Mǎ Xù, has always had strategic insight,
and has long been in charge of the frontier.
He deeply understands military essentials,
and every time I receive a letter from Xù,
his plans align with mine.
It is advisable to order Xù to dig deep trenches and build high walls,
to attract surrenders with benevolence and trust,
to announce rewards,
and to make their terms clear.
If this is done,
then the wicked kind can be subdued,
and the state will be at peace.”
The Emperor agreed,
and thus issued an edict to Xù to persuade the rebellious captives to surrender.
Shāng also sent a letter to Xù and others, saying:
“The Middle Kingdom has been peaceful,
and has forgotten war for a long time.
Good cavalry engaging in open fields,
clashing weapons and exchanging arrows,
deciding victory in the moment,
are the strengths of the Róng Dí,
and the weaknesses of the Middle Kingdom.
Strong crossbowmen on the city walls,
and firmly fortified camps,
waiting for their decline,
are the strengths of the Middle Kingdom,
and the weaknesses of the Róng Dí.
It is advisable to first employ our strengths,
to observe their changes,
to offer bounties and open up rewards,
to announce opportunities for repentance,
and not to covet small achievements,
thereby disrupting grand strategies.”
Xù and all the commanderies complied.
Thereupon, over thirteen thousand people from the Right Xiánwáng's division, including Yìdī, surrendered to Xù.
In the autumn,
Jùlóng Wúsī and others established Jùlóng Wáng Chēniǔ as Chányú.
They drew in the Wūhuán from the east,
and gathered Qiāng Róng and various Hú totaling tens of thousands from the west,
attacking and breaking the Hǔyá Camp of Jīngzhào,
killing the Commandant of Shàngjùn and the Army Sīmǎ,
and then raiding and plundering the four provinces of Bìng, Liáng, Yōu, and Jì.
Therefore, the seat of Xīhé was moved to Líshí,
Shàngjùn to Xiàyáng,
and Shuòfāng to Wǔyuán.
In winter,
the Colonel-Director Zhāng Dān was sent to lead the Wūhuán of Yōuzhōu and the troops from various commandery camps,
to attack the rebellious Chēniǔ and others.
They fought at Mǎyì,
beheading three thousand enemies
and capturing a great number of prisoners, weapons, cattle, and sheep.
Chēniǔ and others, along with the various chieftains and Gǔdōuhóu, begged for surrender,
but Wúsī still led his troops and the Wūhuán to raid and plunder.
In the spring of the sixth year,
Mǎ Xù led five thousand Xiānbēi cavalry to Gǔchéng and attacked them,
beheading several hundred.
Zhāng Dān was brave and sharp,
and good at comforting his soldiers,
so all in his army fought with loyalty.
He then used ropes to suspend men,
ascending to the Tiānshān Mountains,
and greatly defeated the Wūhuán,
beheading all their chieftains,
recovering Hàn citizens,
and capturing their livestock and wealth.
In summer,
Mǎ Xù was again dismissed,
and the Commandant of the City Gates, Wú Wǔ, replaced him as general.
In the autumn of the first year of Hàn'ān,
Wúsī, along with Àodī Táiqí and Jūqú Bódé, again plundered Bìng Province.
Hūlánruòshīzhújiù Chányú Dōulóuchǔ had been in the capital earlier,
and was enthroned in the second year of Hàn'ān.
The Son of Heaven presided from the imperial carriage,
and the Grand Master of Ceremonies, holding the imperial credential, bestowed the imperial seal and ribbon,
then led him up to the palace hall.
He was granted a green canopy, a four-horse chariot, a drum chariot, a comfortable chariot, a mounted attendant, a jade-ornamented sword, and various items,
and given two thousand bolts of colored silk and cloth.
The Chányú's Yānzhī and others were given golden brocade and various mixed ornaments,
and two carriages with outriders.
An acting Colonel-Director was sent with imperial credentials to escort the Chányú back to the Southern Court.
An edict ordered the Grand Minister of Ceremonies and the Grand Master of Ceremonies, along with the hostage princes from various states, to hold
a farewell gathering outside the Guǎngyáng city gate,
to feast and bestow gifts, with music,
wrestling, and various entertainments.
Emperor Shùn personally visited the Hútáo Palace to observe it.
In winter,
Colonel-Director Mǎ Shí recruited assassins to kill Jùlóng Wúsī,
and sent his head to Luòyáng.
In the first year of Jiànkāng,
the remaining rebels were attacked,
and twelve hundred heads were taken.
Over seven hundred thousand Wūhuán surrendered to Shí,
their wagons, cattle, and sheep were countless.
Chányú Dōulóuchǔ died after reigning for five years.
Yīlíngshīzhújiù Chányú Jūchē'ér
was enthroned in the first year of Jiànhé.
By the first year of Yǒngshòu,
the Xiōngnú Left Àodī Táiqí and Jūqú Bódé rebelled again,
raiding Měijì and Āndìng.
Zhāng Huàn, the Commandant of the Dependent State, defeated and made them surrender.
The details are already in Huàn's biography.
In the first year of Yánxī,
all the Southern Chányú's divisions rebelled,
and together with the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi, raided the nine frontier commanderies.
Zhāng Huàn was appointed Colonel-Director of the North to suppress them,
and all the Chányú's divisions surrendered.
Huàn, believing the Chányú was unable to govern state affairs,
detained him,
and memorialized to enthrone the Left Gǔlìwáng.
Emperor Huán issued an edict saying:
“The Spring and Autumn Annals emphasize
upholding righteousness. Jūchē'ér wholeheartedly turned towards civilization,
what crime has he committed to be deposed?
Let him be sent back to his court.”
Chányú Jūchē'ér died after reigning for twenty-five years,
and his son [Name Unknown] was enthroned.
Tútèruòshīzhújiù Chányú [Name Unknown]
was enthroned in the first year of Xīpíng.
In the sixth year,
the Chányú, along with Colonel-Director Zāng Mín, went out from Yànmén to attack the Xiānbēi Bùshíhuái,
and returned after a great defeat.
That year,
the Chányú died,
and his son Hūzhēng was enthroned.
Chányú Hūzhēng
was enthroned in the first year
of Guānghé.
In the second year,
Colonel-Director Zhāng Xiū and the Chányú were not on good terms,
and Xiū, without authorization, executed him,
and enthroned the Right Xiánwáng Qiāngqú as Chányú.
Because Xiū had not sought prior permission and had executed him without authorization,
he was summoned in a caged cart to the Court of Judicial Review to face charges.
Chányú Qiāngqú
was enthroned in the second year of Guānghé.
In the fourth year of Zhōngpíng,
the former Administrator of Zhōngshān, Zhāng Chún, rebelled,
and then led the Xiānbēi to raid the frontier commanderies.
Emperor Líng issued an edict to mobilize Southern Xiōngnú troops,
to be assigned to the Governor of Yōuzhōu, Liú Yú, to suppress them.
The Chányú sent the Left Xiánwáng to lead cavalry to Yōuzhōu.
The people of the state feared that the Chányú would repeatedly send out troops,
so in the fifth year,
the Right Division, along with Xiūzhuó and various Hú like Báimǎtóng, totaling over one hundred thousand people, rebelled
and attacked and killed the Chányú.
Chányú Qiāngqú had reigned for ten years,
and his son, the Right Xiánwáng Yúfúluó, was enthroned.
He was brought before the Chán Yú Shīzhúhóu Yúfúluó,
who was enthroned in the 5th year of Zhōngpíng (188 CE).
His countrymen, who had killed his father, then rebelled.
They jointly enthroned Xūbǔ Gǔdūhóu as Chán Yú,
while Yúfúluó went to the imperial court to plead his case.
It happened that Emperor Líng died,
and great chaos broke out in the realm.
The Chán Yú, with several thousand cavalry, joined forces with the Báibō bandits to plunder the commanderies of Hénèi.
At that time, the common people all gathered together for protection,
so their plundering brought no profit,
and his troops were consequently battered and wounded.
He wished to return to his country,
but his countrymen would not receive him,
so he remained in Hédōng.
Xūbǔ Gǔdūhóu died after one year as Chán Yú,
and the Southern Court then left the position vacant,
using an elder king to manage the affairs of the state.
Chán Yú Yúfúluó died after seven years on the throne,
and his younger brother Hūchúquán was enthroned.
Chán Yú Hūchúquán
was enthroned in the 2nd year of Xīngpíng (195 CE).
Because his elder brother had been driven out
and could not return to his country,
he was repeatedly raided by the Xiānbēi.
In the 1st year of Jiàn'ān (196 CE),
Emperor Xiàn returned east from Cháng'ān.
The Right Worthy King, Qùbēi, and the Báibō bandit chief, Hán Xiān,
among others, guarded the Son of Heaven
and repelled Lǐ Jué and Guō Sì.
When the imperial carriage returned to Luòyáng
and then moved to Xǔ,
he then returned to his country.
In the 21st year (216 CE),
the Chán Yú came to court.
Cáo Cāo consequently detained him in Yè,
and sent Qùbēi back to oversee his country.
Discussion: At the beginning of the Hàn dynasty, when facing Mòdú's ferocity and cunning,
and his strong and flourishing tribe,
Emperor Gāozǔ's might extended over the four seas,
yet he was trapped in the siege of Píngchéng.
Emperor Tàizōng, with his governance close to a state of no punishments,
did not avenge the shame of that humiliation.
It was only when Emperor Xiàowǔ frequently initiated border strategies,
and had aspirations concerning the Xiongnú,
that he grandly appointed generals.
Military banners stretched like stars,
sentinels were arrayed in the imperial suburbs,
and signal fires reached Gānquán.
Yet the whistling arrows still raised dust,
entering and exiting the imperial domain,
until military strength was exhausted,
and only imperial resources were used,
for many years to repel them.
Although the bandits were significantly defeated,
the exhaustion of Hàn was almost equal.
Emperor Xuān was faced with a divided barbarian court,
and Hūhánxié came to submit.
He then wisely adopted a policy of appeasement,
and made them a border guard,
removing the alerts from the passes and fortresses,
and resting the soldiers and common people.
With imperial chariots and robes,
bells tolled and drums sounded over the Qīngwèi River,
[一０]he faced south to hold court with the Chán Yú,
and for over sixty years, [一 一]there was no trace of a single horse in Shuò and Yì.
Later, Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne with arrogance,
stirring up the Róng and Yí.
[一二]This was followed by the chaos of Gēngshǐ,
and the Central Plains were fragmented.
[一三]From then on, the Xiongnú achieved their desires,
their wolfish hearts revived,
taking advantage of the interval to invade and plunder,
spreading harm to the bordering regions.
At the beginning of the restoration,
the old good relations were renewed.
[一四]Emissaries followed one another,
and gold and silk filled the roads.
[一五]But the Chán Yú grew increasingly arrogant and tyrannical,
and internal violence deepened.
[一六]Emperor Shìzǔ, being occupied with affairs in Zhūhuá,
did not have time for matters beyond the deserts.
[一七]He endured the humiliation and considered the difficulty,
merely responding with thanks.
[一八]Consequently, he moved the people of Yōu and Bìng,
and increased the border garrisons.
[一九]When Guāndōng was gradually pacified,
and Lǒng and Shǔ were cleared,
his fierce warriors and resolute generals
all stamped their feet and brandished their arms,
eagerly speaking of the deeds of Wèi and Huò.
[二０]But the Emperor was weary of war,
and quietly cultivated civil governance,
not granting their wishes.
[二一]Afterward, when the Xiongnú contended for the throne,
the Rìzhú came to submit,
wishing to renew the good relations with Hūhán,
to resist the onslaught of the Northern Dí,
[二二]to serve as a vassal and declare allegiance,
and forever be an outer bulwark.
The Son of Heaven gathered all counsel
and peacefully accepted it.
[二三]He then issued an edict to the responsible officials to open the northern frontiers,
select fertile land,
and settle them according to water and grass resources.
He dispatched envoys from the Central Regular Army,
who imposed laws and regulations upon them.
They regulated their clothing,
provided cultural artifacts,
added the seal and ribbon of office,
and rectified the title of Chán Yú.
Thus, the Xiongnú were divided,
and for the first time, there were Southern and Northern Courts.
Their enmity deepened,
and they mutually sought opportunities,
drawing bows and raising spears,
watching for dust clouds,
gathering like clouds and scattering like birds,
attacking each other.
There was no year of peace
from their collapses and injuries,
yet the Hàn borderlands remained tranquil.
[二四]Later, expeditions were also launched,
combining forces for thorough eradication.
Dòu Xiàn and Gěng Kuí, among others, were ordered
to advance simultaneously,
all employing bravery and cunning,
setting up ingenious strategies,
converging from different routes,
ultimately sweeping through their lairs,
pursuing the fleeing Northern Barbarians
[二五]for over three thousand *lǐ*.
[二六]They then destroyed the Dragon Shrine,
burned felt tents,
buried the ten-horned sacrificial objects,
and shackled the Yānzhī.
[二七]Their achievements were engraved on stone,
and they returned with shouts of triumph.
[二八]The Chán Yú was awe-struck and held his breath,
fleeing in felt cloaks to the land of Wūsūn,
and the Mòběi region was emptied.
[二九]If at that time, taking advantage of the situation
and its emptiness, the Southern captives had been returned to Yīnshān,
and the Wést [river] had been returned to the interior,
[三０]thus upholding Emperor Guāngwǔ's expedient strategy
and preventing the future chaos of the Róng and Jié barbarians,
[三一]Gěng Guó's calculations would not have erred in his time,
[三二]and Yuán Ān's proposal would have been followed by later kings,
[三三]straightforward and righteous,
how grand that would have been!
[三四]But Dòu Xiàn boasted of his three victories,
disregarding the long-term plan for the world.
He was unruly and unethical,
monopolizing power and favor.
[三五]He then re-established the Northern Barbarians,
restoring them to their former court,
[三六]extending favor and protecting both sides,
for his private benefit,
[三七]disregarding divine justice,
and thereby planting a great problem.
Reflecting on past records,
how deep is this regret and indignation!
[三八]Thereafter, statecraft lost its direction,
allegiance became inconsistent,
and the resulting affliction
is beyond simple words!
[三九]Down to later generations,
it was treated as a common custom,
ultimately leading to the engulfment of the sacred land
and the ruin of the imperial capital.
Alas!
A difference of a thousand *lǐ*
begins from a hair's breadth;
the source of gains and losses
will remain for a hundred generations, unforgotten.
Eulogy says: When the Xiongnú divided,
urgent reports became rare.
But their wild ambitions are hard to repent,
and ultimately, they were still in turmoil.
Biography of the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi, Chapter 80.
The Wūhuán
were originally Dōnghú.
In the early Hàn dynasty,
Mòdùn of the Xiōngnú destroyed their state.
The remnants of their kind sought refuge on Mount Wūhuán,
and thus took it as their name.
Their customs involved skilled archery from horseback.
They hunted birds and beasts for their livelihood.
They grazed their livestock following water and grass,
having no fixed abode.
They used felt tents (qiónglú) as their dwellings,
opening to the east, facing the sun.
They ate meat and drank milk (lào),
and wore clothes made of felt and fur (máocuì).
They valued the young and despised the old,
their nature was fierce and simple.
In anger, they would kill their fathers and elder brothers,
but would never harm their mothers,
because mothers had relatives (zúlèi),
whereas fathers and elder brothers had no one to avenge them.
Those who were brave, strong, and capable of settling disputes and quarrels
were elected as Dàrén (chieftains),
with no hereditary succession.
Each settlement had its own minor leader (xiǎoshuài).
Several hundred or a thousand settlements formed a single tribe (yībù).
When a Dàrén issued a summons,
they would carve wood as a token of trust.
Although they had no writing,
the tribal members dared not disobey.
Their clan names (shìxìng) were not constant;
they adopted the names of the strong and capable Dàrén as their surnames.
Below the Dàrén,
each person raised livestock and managed their own property,
not performing labor service for others.
For marriage, they first abducted the woman and expressed their affection,
sometimes for half a year or a hundred days,
and then sent cattle, horses, and sheep
as betrothal gifts (pìnbì).
The groom would return to the wife's home with her.
At the wife's home, regardless of seniority,
he would bow to them daily,
but would not bow to his own parents.
He would serve as a servant to his wife's family
for one or two years.
Then the wife's family would generously send off the daughter,
providing for all living arrangements and property.
Their custom was to marry one's stepmother
and take over a widow,
who, upon death, would return to her former husband.
They consulted women for strategy and planning;
only matters of fighting and warfare were decided by the men themselves.
Fathers and sons, men and women, sat facing each other in a squatting position.
They considered a shaved head (kūntóu) to be convenient.
Women would only grow their hair when they were about to marry.
They would divide it into buns (jì),
wear 'hook fasteners' (gōujué),
decorated with gold and jade (jīnbì),
similar to the 'net-cap' (guǒ) and 'trembling hairpins' (bùyáo) of Zhōngguó.
Women could embroider patterns onto leather (cìwéi wénxiù)
and weave felt rugs (lúhé).
Men could make bows, arrows, saddles, and bridles,
and forge gold and iron into weapons.
Their land was suitable for millet (jì) and Dōngqiáng.
Dōngqiáng resembled tumbleweed (péngcǎo),
its seeds were like millet,
and it ripened in the tenth month.
They observed the pregnancy and birth of birds and beasts
to distinguish the four seasons.
Their custom valued dying in battle.
They embalmed the body in a coffin,
and there was sorrowful weeping.
But at the burial, they would sing and dance to send off the deceased.
They would fatten a dog,
lead it with a colorful rope,
and also take the clothing and belongings of the deceased's horse.
All were burned and sent along,
saying that they were entrusting them to the dog
to protect the spirit of the deceased on its journey to Chìshān.
Chìshān was several thousand lǐ northwest of Liáodōng,
just as the souls of the dead in Zhōngguó return to Mount Dài.
They revered ghosts and spirits,
and sacrificed to heaven, earth, sun, moon, stars, mountains, rivers, and earlier Dàrén who had famous names.
Sacrifices involved cattle and sheep,
which were all burned afterward.
Their laws stated: those who disobeyed the Dàrén's words
were punishable by death.
If someone committed robbery or murder,
the tribe was ordered to avenge themselves.
If it didn't stop,
they would report it to the Dàrén,
who would allow them to offer horses, cattle, or sheep to redeem the death.
Killing one's own father or elder brother was not a crime.
If someone deserted or rebelled and was captured by a Dàrén,
the settlements were not allowed to harbor them;
they were all exiled to the lands of Yōngkuáng,
in the middle of the desert.
That land had many vipers,
located southwest of the Dīnglìng
and northeast of Wūsūn.
After the Wūhuán were defeated by Mòdùn,
their populace became isolated and weak.
They were constantly subjugated to the Xiōngnú,
annually paying tribute of cattle, horses, sheep, and furs.
If they failed to provide these on time,
their wives and children would be confiscated.
When Emperor Wǔ sent the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn) Huò Qùbìng to defeat the western territory of the Xiōngnú,
he relocated the Wūhuán outside the passes of the five commanderies: Shànggǔ, Yúyáng, Yòuběipíng, Liáoxī, and Liáodōng,
to act as scouts for Hàn to monitor the movements of the Xiōngnú.
Their Dàrén visited the court once a year.
It was then that the Protector of the Wūhuán (Hù Wūhuán Xiàowèi) was first established,
with a rank of two thousand dàn (shí),
who, holding a banner of authority (jié), supervised them,
preventing them from communicating with the Xiōngnú.
During Emperor Zhāo's reign,
the Wūhuán gradually grew stronger.
They then plundered the tombs of the Xiōngnú Chányú
to avenge the grievance caused by Mòdùn.
The Xiōngnú were greatly enraged,
and consequently attacked and defeated the Wūhuán to the east.
The Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn) Huò Guāng heard of this,
and therefore sent the General Who Crosses the Liao (Dùliáo Jiāngjūn) Fàn Míngyǒu with twenty thousand cavalry out of Liáodōng to intercept the Xiōngnú,
but the barbarians had already retreated.
Míngyǒu, taking advantage of the Wūhuán's recent defeat,
proceeded to attack them,
beheading over six thousand,
capturing the heads of their three kings before returning.
Because of this, the Wūhuán again raided Yōuzhōu,
but Míngyǒu consistently defeated them.
During Emperor Xuān's reign,
they gradually settled near the passes and surrendered.
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne
and wished to attack the Xiōngnú,
he raised an army of twelve divisions,
and sent Yán Yóu, the General of the Eastern Region (Dōngyù Jiāngjūn), to lead Wūhuán and Dīnglìng troops to garrison Dàijùn,
holding their wives and children as hostages in the commanderies and counties.
The Wūhuán were unaccustomed to the climate and terrain,
and feared a prolonged garrison without rest.
They repeatedly requested leave to depart.
Wáng Mǎng refused to send them away,
so they deserted and rebelled,
returning to engage in banditry.
All the commanderies then killed their hostages,
which created enmity between them and Wáng Mǎng.
The Xiōngnú then enticed their powerful leaders (háoshuài) to become officials,
and the rest were restrained (jīmí) and brought under their control.
In the early years of Guāngwǔ's reign,
the Wūhuán allied with the Xiōngnú to form bandit groups,
and the area east of Dàijùn suffered particularly.
They resided close to the passes;
they would depart their felt tents in the morning
and arrive at cities and towns by evening.
The common people of the five commanderies
each suffered their harm,
to the extent that commanderies and counties were damaged,
and the populace fled.
Those among them who lived outside the pass of Shànggǔ in Bái Shān
were the strongest and wealthiest.
In the twenty-first year of Jiànwǔ (45 CE),
the General Who Quells Waves (Fúbō Jiāngjūn) Mǎ Yuán was dispatched with three thousand cavalry to attack them by surprise from Wǔruǎn Guān.
The Wūhuán, anticipating this,
all gathered and fled.
Mǎ Yuán pursued and beheaded a hundred, then returned.
The Wūhuán then attacked Mǎ Yuán's rear,
so Mǎ Yuán hastened back day and night.
By the time he entered the pass,
over a thousand horses had died.
In the twenty-second year (46 CE),
the Xiōngnú state was in chaos.
The Wūhuán took advantage of their weakness and defeated them.
The Xiōngnú then migrated north several thousand lǐ.
The land south of the desert (Mònán) became empty,
so the Emperor bribed the Wūhuán with silk.
In the twenty-fifth year (49 CE),
Hǎo Dàn and nine hundred twenty-two other Dàrén of the Liáoxī Wūhuán led their people to submit,
coming to the imperial court to offer tribute,
presenting male and female slaves, cattle, horses, bows, and skins of tigers, leopards, and sables.
At this time, the four barbarians came to court to offer congratulations,
arriving in continuous streams.
The Son of Heaven then commanded a grand assembly for feasting and entertainment,
bestowing precious treasures upon them.
Some Wūhuán desired to remain and serve as guards.
Thereupon, their chiefs were enfeoffed as marquises, kings, lords, and commanders, eighty-one in total.
All resided within the frontier,
distributed among the various commanderies along the border.
They were ordered to attract and bring in their kinsmen,
and were provided with clothing and food.
They then served as scouts for Hàn,
assisting in attacking the Xiōngnú and Xiānbēi.
At that time, Bān Biāo, a clerk of the Sìtú, submitted a memorial, stating:
“The Wūhuán are by nature quick-witted and crafty,
and are fond of being bandits and thieves.
If they are long left unchecked without a unified leader,
they will certainly again plunder the residents.
To simply entrust them to the officials responsible for surrendered barbarians
is, I fear, not enough to control them.
Your servant humbly believes that it would be advisable to re-establish a Wūhuán Xiàowèi.
This would truly be beneficial for their consolidation
and would alleviate the state’s frontier concerns.”
The Emperor followed his advice.
Thus, a Xiàowèi was first re-established at Shànggǔ Níngchéng,
with an encampment and yámen opened.
He also took charge of the Xiānbēi,
rewarding and bestowing gifts upon their hostages,
and engaging in periodic border markets.
During the reigns of Míng, Zhāng, and Hé,
the frontier remained secure and peaceful.
In the summer of Yǒngchū third year during Emperor Ān’s reign,
the Wūhuán of Yúyáng and the Hú of Yòuběipíng, over a thousand strong, raided Dàijùn and Shànggǔ.
In autumn,
Wú Hé (Yǔn), king of the Yànmén Wūhuán, leading his people,
along with the Xiānbēi chief Qiū Lún and others,
and the Gǔdū Hóu of the Southern Xiōngnú,
totaling seven thousand cavalry, raided Wǔyuán.
They fought the Grand Administrator at Jiǔyuán Gāoqú Gǔ.
The Hàn army suffered a great defeat,
and the commandery’s chief official was killed.
Thereupon, the Hàn sent Chēqí Jiāngjūn Hé Xī and Dùliáo Jiāngjūn Liáng Jǐn, among others, to attack them.
They thoroughly defeated them.
Wú Hé begged for surrender,
and the Xiānbēi fled back beyond the frontier.
Thereafter, the Wūhuán gradually became 친附 again,
and their chief Róng Zhūhuī was appointed Qīnhàn Dūwèi.
In the winter of Yángjiā fourth year during Emperor Shùn’s reign,
the Wūhuán raided Yúnzhōng,
intercepting over a thousand carts and oxen belonging to merchants on the road.
Dùliáo Jiāngjūn Gěng Yè led over two thousand men to pursue and attack them,
but was unsuccessful.
They then fought again at Shānán,
beheading five hundred.
The Wūhuán then besieged Yè at Lánchí Chéng.
Thereupon, two thousand picked archers and
one thousand men from the Dùliáo garrison
were dispatched and assigned to the Shàngjùn garrison
to suppress the Wūhuán,
who then retreated.
In Yǒnghé fifth year,
the Wūhuán chiefs Ā Jiān and Qiāng Qú, among others, along with Jùlóng Wúsī of the Southern Xiōngnú’s Left Faction, rebelled.
Zhōnglángjiāng Zhāng Dān attacked, defeated, and executed them.
The remaining forces all surrendered.
During the Yǒngshòu era of Emperor Huán,
the Shuòfāng Wūhuán rebelled alongside the Xiūzhù Túrgé.
Zhōnglángjiāng Zhāng Huàn attacked and pacified them.
In the summer of Yánxī ninth year,
the Wūhuán, together with the Xiānbēi and Southern Xiōngnú, again raided the nine border commanderies,
all rebelling.
Zhāng Huàn attacked them,
and they all fled beyond the frontier.
In the early years of Emperor Líng’s reign,
among the Wūhuán chiefs, Nánlóu of Shànggǔ
had over nine thousand households.
Qiūlìjū of Liáoxī
had over five thousand households.
Both claimed the title of King.
Also, Sūpúyán of Liáodōng
had over one thousand households,
claiming the title of Qiàowáng.
Wūyán of Yòuběipíng
had over eight hundred households,
claiming the title of Hánlǔ Wáng. All were brave, strong, and resourceful.
In Zhōngpíng fourth year,
Zhāng Chún, former Grand Administrator of Zhōngshān, rebelled,
joining Qiūlìjū’s forces.
He styled himself Mítiān Āndìng Wáng,
and subsequently became the supreme commander of the Wūhuán in various commanderies,
raiding Qīng, Xú, Yōu, and Jì four provinces.
In the fifth year,
Liú Yú was appointed Governor of Yōuzhōu.
Yú offered a bounty for Chún’s head,
and the northern provinces were then pacified.
In the early Chūpíng era of Emperor Xiàn,
Qiūlìjū died.
His son Lóubān was young,
so his cousin Tàdùn, who possessed military strategy,
succeeded him,
taking overall command of the three commanderies.
Everyone obeyed his orders.
In the early Jiàn’ān era,
Yuán Shào, Governor of Jìzhōu, and Gōngsūn Zàn, the Former General, were locked in an indecisive struggle.
Tàdùn sent an envoy to Shào to request alliance and kinship,
and then dispatched troops to assist in attacking Zàn,
defeating him.
Shào falsely issued an imperial edict bestowing upon Tàdùn, Nánlóu, Sūpúyán, Wūyán, and others
the seals and cords of a Chányú.
Later, Nánlóu and Sūpúyán led their tribes to support Lóubān as Chányú,
while Tàdùn became King.
However, Tàdùn still held control of strategy.
Yán Róu of Guǎngyáng,
who as a youth had been captured among the Wūhuán and Xiānbēi,
was trusted by their people.
Róu then, relying on the Xiānbēi forces,
killed Xíng Jǔ, the Wūhuán Xiàowèi, and took his place.
Yuán Shào then showed favor and comfort to Róu
to pacify the northern border.
When Shào’s son Shàng was defeated,
he fled to Tàdùn.
At that time, over a hundred thousand households of officials and commoners from Yōu and Jì fled to the Wūhuán.
Shàng wished to rely on their military strength
to again scheme for the Central Plains.
Coincidentally, Cáo Cāo pacified Hébĕi.
Yán Róu led the Xiānbēi and Wūhuán to surrender.
Cāo immediately appointed Róu as Xiàowèi.
In Jiàn’ān twelfth year,
Cáo Cāo personally led an expedition against the Wūhuán,
severely defeating Tàdùn at Liǔchéng,
and beheading him.
Over two hundred thousand heads and captives were taken.
Yuán Shàng, Lóubān, Wūyán, and others all fled to Liáodōng.
Gōng Kāng, Grand Administrator of Liáodōng, beheaded and sent them.
The remaining forces, over ten thousand households,
were all moved to reside in the Central Plains.
The Xiānbēi
were also a branch of the Dōnghú.
They separately settled by Xiānbēi Shān,
hence their name.
Their language and customs were the same as the Wūhuán.
Only in marriage did they first shave their heads.
In the third month of spring, they held a grand assembly by the Ráulè Shuǐ,
and after drinking and feasting,
they would then pair up.
Also, their wild animals, different from those in the Central Plains,
included wild horses, gazelles, and jiǎoduān oxen.
They used the horns of the latter to make bows,
which were commonly called jiǎoduān bows.
They also had sable, badger, and ermine,
whose furs were soft and supple,
hence they were renowned throughout the world for making fine fur robes.
In the early Hàn,
they were also defeated by Mòdú,
and were banished far to beyond the Liáodōng frontier,
adjoining the Wūhuán.
They had never communicated with the Central Plains.
In the early years of Guāngwǔ,
the Xiōngnú were strong and prosperous.
They led the Xiānbēi and Wūhuán to raid and plunder the northern frontier,
killing and abducting officials and commoners,
leaving no peaceful year.
In Jiànwǔ twenty-first year,
the Xiānbēi and Xiōngnú entered Liáodōng.
Jì Róng, Grand Administrator of Liáodōng, attacked and defeated them,
nearly annihilating them.
The details are fully recorded in Róng’s biography,
and they were thus intimidated.
When the Southern Chányú submitted to Hàn,
the Northern Barbarians became isolated and weak.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the Xiānbēi first established diplomatic relations.
Thereafter, Pīanhé and other Dūhùs came to Jì Róng seeking to prove their merit.
They were then ordered to attack the Left Yīyùzī Faction of the Northern Xiōngnú,
beheading over two thousand.
Thereafter, Pīanhé continuously led troops to attack the Northern Barbarians year after year,
always returning with severed heads to Liáodōng to receive rewards.
In the thirtieth year,
the Xiānbēi chiefs Yúqiúfēn and Mǎntóu, among others, led their people to the imperial court to offer congratulations,
admiring the righteousness and attaching themselves to the interior.
The Emperor enfeoffed Yúqiúfēn as King
and Mǎntóu as Marquis.
At that time, Xīnzhìfēn and others from the Wūhuán of Chìshān in Yúyáng frequently raided Shànggǔ.
In Yǒngpíng first year,
Jì Róng again bribed Pīanhé to attack Xīnzhìfēn,
defeating and beheading him.
Thereupon, all the Xiānbēi chiefs came to submit,
and all went to Liáodōng to receive rewards.
Qīng and Xú two provinces provided two hundred seventy million cash annually as a regular payment.
During the reigns of Míng and Zhāng,
the frontier remained secure and peaceful.
In the Yǒngyuán reign of Emperor Hé,
Grand General Dòu Xiàn dispatched the Right Commandant, Gěng Kuí, to defeat the Xiōngnú.
The Northern Chányú fled,
and the Xiānbēi consequently migrated and occupied their territory.
Of the remaining Xiōngnú tribes who stayed behind, there were still over ten myriad households,
all calling themselves Xiānbēi.
From this, the Xiānbēi gradually became powerful.
In the ninth year,
the Liáodōng Xiānbēi attacked Féirú County.
The Grand Administrator, Jì Cān, was imprisoned and
died in jail for his incompetence.
In the thirteenth year,
the Liáodōng Xiānbēi raided Yòuběipíng,
and then entered Yúyáng.
The Grand Administrator of Yúyáng defeated them.
In the first year of Yánpíng,
the Xiānbēi again raided Yúyáng.
The Grand Administrator, Zhāng Xiǎn, led several hundred men out of the frontier to pursue them.
The Cavalry Clerk, Yán Shòu, remonstrated, saying:
"The path ahead is treacherous and obstructed.
The enemy's strength is hard to gauge.
It would be advisable to first establish a camp
and then send light cavalry to scout them out."
Xiǎn was exceedingly eager,
and angrily wanted to execute him.
He then advanced his troops.
They encountered an enemy ambush,
and all the soldiers fled.
Only Shòu fought with all his might,
sustaining ten wounds on his body,
killing several men with his own hands before dying.
Xiǎn was hit by a stray arrow.
The Chief Clerk, Wèi Fú, and the Record Keeper, Xú Xián, both threw themselves towards Xiǎn,
and all perished on the battlefield.
Empress Dowager Dèng issued a decree praising and lamenting them,
awarding Xiǎn six hundred thousand coins
and appointing two members of his family as gentlemen-in-waiting.
Shòu, Fú, and Xián each received one hundred thousand coins,
and one son from each was appointed as a gentleman-in-waiting.
In the Yǒngchū reign of Emperor Ān,
Yān Yáng, a Xiānbēi chieftain, came to the palace to offer congratulations to the court.
Empress Dowager Dèng bestowed upon Yān Yáng a royal seal and ribbon,
and a red carriage with three horses,
ordering him to reside below Huánchéng, where the Wūhuán Colonel resided,
to open a market for the Hú (barbarians),
and consequently built guest houses for the northern and southern tribes.
One hundred and twenty Xiānbēi settlements
each sent a hostage.
Thereafter, some surrendered and some rebelled,
constantly attacking each other with the Xiōngnú and Wūhuán.
In the autumn of the second year of Yuánchū,
the Liáodōng Xiānbēi besieged Wúlǜ County.
The provinces and commanderies combined their forces and fortified their positions, clearing the land.
The Xiānbēi gained nothing.
They attacked the Fúlí camp
and killed the chief official.
In the fourth year,
Lián Xiū and other Liáoxī Xiānbēi burned the frontier gates,
raiding the common people.
Yú Zhìjū and other Wūhuán chieftains, who had a long-standing grudge against Lián Xiū,
joined the commandery troops in an attack,
greatly defeating them,
beheading over one thousand three hundred people,
and capturing all their captives, cattle, horses, and valuables.
In the autumn of the fifth year,
over ten thousand Xiānbēi cavalry from Dàijùn broke through the frontier and raided,
dividing to attack cities and towns,
burning government offices,
and killing chief officials before leaving.
Then, armored soldiers from the frontier and the Liyáng garrison troops were mobilized
and stationed in Shànggǔ to guard against them.
In the winter,
the Xiānbēi entered Shànggǔ
and attacked Jūyōng Pass.
Again, soldiers from various frontier commanderies, Liyáng garrison troops, and twenty thousand skilled archers, both infantry and cavalry, were mobilized
and stationed at strategic points.
In the autumn of the sixth year,
the Xiānbēi entered Mǎchéng Pass,
killing the chief official.
General Dèng Zūn of Dùliáo mobilized three thousand skilled archers,
and the Colonel-Director Mǎ Xù led the Southern Chányú,
who met with the forces from Liáoxī and Yòuběipíng.
They went beyond the frontier to pursue and attack the Xiānbēi,
greatly defeating them,
capturing many captives, cattle, sheep, and valuables.
Three thousand more skilled archers
and three thousand horses were dispatched
to the Dùliáo camp for garrison duty.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
Wū Lún and Qízhìjiān, Xiānbēi chieftains from Liáoxī, led their followers to Dèng Zūn and surrendered,
offering tribute.
An imperial edict enfeoffed Wū Lún as the King Who Leads the Masses,
and Qízhìjiān as the Marquis Who Leads the Masses,
bestowing upon them colored silks according to their ranks.
In the autumn of the first year of Jiànguāng,
Qízhìjiān rebelled again,
raiding Jūyōng.
The Grand Administrator of Yúnzhōng, Chéng Yán, attacked them.
His army was defeated.
The Record Keeper, Yáng Mù, protected Yán with his body,
and both died in battle.
The Xiānbēi then besieged Colonel of the Wūhuán, Xú Cháng, at Mǎchéng.
General Gěng Kuí of Dùliáo and the Inspector of Yōuzhōu, Páng Cān, mobilized armored soldiers from Guǎngyáng, Yúyáng, and Zhuōjùn,
dividing into two routes to rescue him.
Cháng managed to sneak out at night,
joined forces with Kuí and others, and advanced together,
attacking the enemy's siege
and relieving it.
Having repeatedly killed commandery administrators, the Xiānbēi's
courage and ambition grew,
and their archers numbered tens of thousands of cavalry.
In the winter of the first year of Yánguāng,
they again raided Yànmén and Dìngxiāng,
then attacked Tàiyuán,
plundering and killing common people.
In the winter of the second year,
Qízhìjiān personally led over ten thousand cavalry into Dōnglǐnghòu,
dividing into several routes,
attacking the Southern Xiōngnú at Mànbǎi.
The King of Àojiàn Rìzhú died in battle,
and over one thousand people were killed.
In the autumn of the third year,
they again raided Gāoliǔ,
defeating the Southern Xiōngnú
and killing the King of Jiānjiàng.
In the autumn of the first year of Yǒngjiàn of Emperor Shùn,
the Xiānbēi chieftain Qízhìjiān raided Dàijùn.
The Grand Administrator, Lǐ Chāo, died in battle.
In the spring of the following year,
Colonel-Director Zhāng Guó dispatched an attendant to lead over ten thousand Southern Chányú infantry and cavalry out of the frontier,
defeating them,
and capturing over two thousand types of their heavy baggage.
At that time, over six thousand Liáodōng Xiānbēi cavalry also raided Liáodōng and Xuántú.
Wūhuán Colonel Gěng Yè mobilized troops from various frontier commanderies and the Wūhuán King Who Leads the Masses to go out of the frontier and attack them,
beheading several hundred people,
and capturing a great number of their captives, cattle, horses, and goods.
