The Xiānbēi then led thirty thousand of their tribesmen to Liáodōng to surrender.
In the third year
and fourth year,
the Xiānbēi repeatedly raided Yúyáng and Shuòfāng.
In the autumn of the sixth year,
Gěng Yè dispatched a Sīmǎ to lead several thousand Hú soldiers
out of the frontier to attack and defeat them.
In the winter,
the Grand Administrator of Yúyáng again dispatched Wūhuán troops to attack them,
beheading eight hundred people
and capturing cattle, horses, and captives.
Fúshù Guāngyǒngjiàn, a Wūhuán chieftain, was brave and strong.
Whenever he fought the Xiānbēi,
he would always break the enemy's lines.
An imperial edict bestowed upon him the title of
"Lord Who Leads the Masses."
In the winter of the first year of Yángjiā,
Gěng Yè dispatched Róng Zhūguī, the Wūhuán Captain Who Cherishes Hàn, and Duōguī and other kings and marquises who led their masses,
to go out of the frontier to raid and attack the Xiānbēi,
making great kills and captures before returning.
Duōguī and those below him were granted the titles of King Who Leads the Masses, Marquis, and Chief,
and were bestowed colored silks according to their ranks.
Later, the Xiānbēi raided Liáodōng Shǔguó.
Therefore, Gěng Yè moved his garrison to Wúlǜchéng in Liáodōng to defend against them.
In the spring of the second year,
Xiōngnú Colonel-Director Zhào Chóu dispatched an attendant to lead Fūshěn and other Gǔdūhóu of the Southern Xiōngnú
out of the frontier to attack the Xiānbēi,
defeating them,
and making many kills and captures.
An imperial edict bestowed upon Fūshěn a golden seal with purple ribbon and silks according to their ranks.
In the autumn,
the Xiānbēi broke through the frontier into Mǎchéng.
The Grand Administrator of Dàijùn attacked them,
but could not overcome them.
Later, Qízhìjiān died,
and Xiānbēi raids and plunder became less frequent.
During the reign of Huán Dì,
the Xiānbēi, Tánshíhuái,
his father, Tóulùhóu, had initially served in the Xiongnú army for three years.
His wife, at home, gave birth to a child.
When Tóulùhóu returned,
he found it strange and wanted to kill the child.
His wife said that once, while walking in broad daylight, she heard a clap of thunder.
She looked up at the sky and hail entered her mouth.
She consequently swallowed it,
then became pregnant,
and after ten months gave birth.
“This child must be extraordinary;
furthermore, it is fitting to let him grow up and observe him.”
Tóulùhóu did not listen,
and abandoned him.
His wife secretly told the household steward to take him in and raise him,
naming him Tánshíhuái.
At fourteen or fifteen years old,
he was brave, robust, and possessed great strategy.
When adults from other tribes plundered his maternal relatives’ cattle and sheep,
Tánshíhuái, riding alone, pursued and attacked them.
He was unstoppable wherever he went,
and recovered all that had been lost.
Because of this, the tribes feared and submitted to him.
He then established laws and prohibitions,
judged fairly between right and wrong,
and no one dared to violate them.
Thus, they elected him as their adult leader.
Tánshíhuái then established his court at Dànhànshān, by the Chuòqiú River,
more than three hundred *lǐ* north of Gāoliǔ.
His military forces were very strong,
and the adults of the eastern and western tribes all submitted to him.
Consequently, he plundered the border regions to the south,
resisted the Dīnglíng to the north,
repelled the Fúyú to the east,
and attacked the Wūsūn to the west.
He occupied all the former Xiongnú territories,
stretching over fourteen thousand *lǐ* from east to west,
and seven thousand *lǐ* from north to south,
encompassing mountains, rivers, marshes, and salt lakes.
In the autumn of the second year of Yǒngshòu,
Tánshíhuái led three or four thousand cavalry to raid Yúnzhōng.
In the first year of Yánxī,
the Xiānbēi raided the northern frontier.
In winter,
Zhāng Huàn, the Commandant of the Xiongnú, led the Southern Chányú to sally forth and attack them,
beheading two hundred.
In the second year,
they again entered Yànmén,
killed several hundred people,
and left after extensive plundering.
In the summer of the sixth year,
over a thousand cavalry raided Liáodōng Commandery Dependent State.
In the summer of the ninth year,
they then divided tens of thousands of cavalry to enter the nine commanderies along the border,
killing and plundering officials and common people alike.
Thereupon, Zhāng Huàn was again dispatched to attack them,
and the Xiānbēi then withdrew beyond the frontier.
The imperial court had long suffered from this,
but was unable to control them.
So, they sent an envoy with an imperial seal and ribbon to enfeoff Tánshíhuái as a King,
hoping to establish harmonious relations.
Tánshíhuái refused to accept,
and his raids and plundering became even more severe.
He then divided his territory into three sections:
from Yòuběipíng eastward to Liáodōng,
bordering Fúyú and Huì-Mò, comprising over twenty settlements, was the Eastern Section;
from Yòuběipíng westward to Shànggǔ, comprising over ten settlements, was the Central Section;
from Shànggǔ westward to Dūnhuáng and Wūsūn, comprising over twenty settlements, was the Western Section.
Each was assigned an adult leader to govern it,
all subordinate to Tánshíhuái.
When Líng Dì ascended the throne,
the commanderies along the borders of Yōu, Bìng, and Liáng provinces were raided by the Xiānbēi every year,
with countless killings and abductions.
In the winter of the third year of Xīpíng,
the Xiānbēi entered Běidì.
The Grand Administrator, Xià Yù, led the Xiūzhù Túgè to pursue and defeat them.
Yù was promoted to Colonel Protector of the Wúhuán.
In the fifth year,
the Xiānbēi raided Yōuzhōu.
In the summer of the sixth year,
the Xiānbēi raided the three frontiers.
In autumn,
Xià Yù reported:
“The Xiānbēi have raided the border
over thirty times since spring.
I request to mobilize troops from the various commanderies of Yōuzhōu to sally forth and attack them.
In one winter and two springs,
we will surely be able to capture and eliminate them.”
The imperial court had not yet approved.
Previously, Tián Yàn, the Colonel Protector of the Qiāng, had been pardoned from a criminal sentence for a previous offense.
Desiring to make meritorious achievements to prove himself,
he requested the Palace Regular Attendant Wáng Fǔ to secure him a generalship.
Fǔ used this opportunity to propose sending troops to join forces with Yù in attacking the bandits.
The Emperor then appointed Yàn as Commandant Who Destroys the Xiānbēi.
Many high officials disagreed,
so all officials were summoned to discuss the matter in the imperial hall.
Councillor Cài Yōng argued:
The *Shū* warns against the crafty Xià,
the *Yì* speaks of attacking Guǐfāng.
The Zhōu dynasty had campaigns against the Xiǎnyǔn and Mán-Jīng,
and the Hàn dynasty had the affairs of Tiányán and Hànhǎi.
Expeditions against
different kinds of people
have long existed.
However, times differ,
and situations may or may not be suitable.
Therefore, strategies have their successes and failures,
and affairs have their achievements and setbacks;
they cannot be treated uniformly.
When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn
drained the wealth of the empire,
within several decades,
both the government and the people were exhausted.
He then initiated profits from salt, iron, and liquor monopolies,
and imposed heavy taxes through the *gàomín* system.
The people could not
endure their lot
and rose up as bandits.
The region east of the passes was in turmoil,
and roads were impassable.
Envoys with embroidered robes and direct authority
were sent out in droves, wielding axes.
Later, he awoke
to the realization,
and then ceased military actions and disbanded the laborers,
even enfeoffing the Chancellor as Marquis of Rich People.
Therefore, Zhǔfù Yàn said:
“Indeed, those who strive for victory in war
and exhaust military affairs
have never failed to regret
it.”
Even with Shìzōng’s (Emperor Wǔ) divine martial prowess,
his excellent and fierce generals and chancellors,
and abundant financial resources,
where he expanded his territory far and wide,
he still had regrets.
How much more so now, when both human and financial resources are
lacking,
and affairs are inferior to past times!
Furthermore, the border defenses are not
strict, and there are many loopholes in the prohibitions.
Fine gold and good iron
all belong to the bandits.
Hàn people who have fled
become their strategists,
making their weapons sharper and horses swifter
than those of the Xiongnú.
In the past, Duàn
Qióng, a good general,
skilled in military affairs and warfare,
still took over ten years
to deal with the Western Qiāng.
Now, the talents and strategies of Yù and Yàn
may not surpass Qióng’s,
and the Xiānbēi population
is no weaker than
in former times.
Yet, they vainly estimate two years
and promise success.
If misfortune escalates and war drags on,
how can it be stopped midway?
We would have to continually conscript more people
and endlessly transport supplies,
which would
deplete all of China
and concentrate our strength on the barbarians.
The troubles on the frontier
are like itching and scratching of the limbs;
the difficulties within China
are like carbuncles on the back.
At present,
we cannot even suppress bandits in the commanderies and counties,
how much less can these despicable barbarians be subdued!
If the Way has been lost,
how can we argue over comings and goings with insect-like, (cor. by Jia Gongyan: "crafty") cunning bandits?
Even if we somehow defeat them,
how can they be completely annihilated?
And for this, should
the imperial court skip meals?
In the past, Huáinán Wáng Ān advised against attacking Yuè, saying:
“The Son of Heaven’s army
is for punitive expeditions, not for battles (where equals contend).
This means no one dares to resist it.
If the Yuè people, embracing death, resist
even the lowest servants and porters,
and one of them returns unprepared,
even if we obtain the head of the King of Yuè,
it would still be a shame for the Great Hàn.”
Now, we wish to replace our good people
with despicable barbarians,
and humble imperial prestige before foreign barbarians.
Even if things go as they say,
it is still perilous,
let alone if gains and losses cannot be measured!
In the past, when Zhūyá Commandery rebelled, Emperor Yuán
Emperor Yuán [Yuán Dì] adopted Jiǎ Juānzhī’s [Jiǎ Juānzhī] words
and issued an edict which stated:
“Zhūyá [Zhūyá] has rebelled.
Now, some discussants say it can be attacked,
while others say it should be abandoned.
Day and night, I reflect on this.
I am ashamed that my prestige
is not effective,
and so I wish to punish them;
but considering the changes of the times,
I also worry about the myriad people.
Between the starvation of the myriad people and the failure to punish distant barbarians,
which is the greater concern?
The sacrifices to the ancestral temples [zōngmiào]
are sometimes incomplete even in years of famine,
how much more so when avoiding the shame of not engaging!
Now Guāndōng [Guāndōng] is in great distress,
unable to support itself,
and we would furthermore have to deploy troops,
which would not merely exhaust the people.
Therefore, let the Zhūyá [Zhūyá] Commandery [Jùn] be abolished.”
This was how Emperor Yuán [Yuán Dì] expressed his virtuous decree.
Indeed, to commiserate with the people and relieve their urgent needs,
even if a commandery or county has been established,
it should still be abandoned,
let alone
territory beyond the frontier barriers [zhàngsài],
which has never been inhabited by our people!
As for the art of defending the borders,
Lǐ Mù [Lǐ Mù] excelled in its strategy;
as for the discourse on protecting the frontier,
Yán Yóu [Yán Yóu] emphasized its essentials.
Their legacy remains,
and their writings are fully preserved.
By following the policies of these two men,
and adhering to the regulations of the former emperors,
your minister says it would be acceptable.
In the Guānghé [Guānghé] era,
Tǔfā Shíhuái [Tǔfā Shíhuái] died,
at the age of forty-five.
His son Hélián [Hélián] succeeded him.
Hélián’s [Hélián] talent and strength were inferior to his father's,
and he also frequently engaged in raids.
His nature was greedy and lecherous,
and his administration of law was unfair,
so half of his people rebelled.
Later, he led an attack on Běidì [Běidì],
and a skilled crossbowman from that region
shot Hélián [Hélián],
who died immediately.
His son Qiānmàn [Qiānmàn] was young,
so his nephew Kuítóu [Kuítóu] succeeded him.
Later, when Qiānmàn [Qiānmàn] grew up,
he contended with Kuítóu [Kuítóu] for the state,
and the populace scattered.
Kuítóu [Kuítóu] died,
and his younger brother Bùdùgēn [Bùdùgēn] succeeded him.
Since Tǔfā Shíhuái [Tǔfā Shíhuái],
the various chieftains [dàrén] have successively inherited the position.
Commentary states: The savagery of the Four Barbarians [Sì Yí]
saw their power waxing and waning.
The Xiōngnú [Xiōngnú] were rampant during the flourishing Hàn [Hàn] dynasty,
and the Xīqiāng [Xīqiāng] were fierce during the Restoration.
Between the Líng [Líng] and Xiàn [Xiàn] emperors,
the two barbarian groups alternately flourished.
Shíhuái [Shíhuái] was valiant and fierce,
possessing all the territory of the Chányú [Chányú];
Tàdùn [Tàdùn] was cruel and tyrannical,
openly occupying the lands of Liáoxī [Liáoxī].
Their encroachment upon China [Zhōngguó],
and the troubles they inflicted upon the living,
meant no era knew peace.
However, superior strategies for control
were unheard of throughout the ages;
the policies of Zhōu [Zhōu] and Hàn [Hàn]
were merely of middle or lower effectiveness.
Could this be due to Heaven's [Tiān] hidden destiny,
leading to such a state?

On Lǜlì [Lǜlì]: The Lǜzhǔn [Lǜzhǔn] and Hòuqì [Hòuqì].
The ancients discussed numbers,
saying:
"Things are born, and then there are images;
images, and then there is growth;
growth, and then there are numbers."
Thus, when Heaven and Earth first took shape,
and humans and things were established,
the matters of calculation arose.
Records say that Dàrǎo [Dàrǎo] created the Jiǎzǐ [Jiǎzǐ] cycle,
and Lìshǒu [Lìshǒu] created numbers.
Once these two were established,
they were used to compare the sundial [rìbiǎo] [rìbiǎo]
and to manage all affairs.
Indeed, one, ten, hundred, thousand, and myriad
are used in common;
pitch-pipes [lǜ], measures of length [dù], capacity [liàng], and weight [héng], and calendars [lì]
are used for specific purposes.
Therefore, when bodies have length,
they are measured by a ruler;
when things have quantity,
they are received by measures of capacity;
when measures have weight,
they are balanced by scales;
when sounds have pitch,
they are harmonized by pitch-pipes [lǜlǚ];

and subtle changes

During the reign of Xiàowǔ [Xiàowǔ], music was rectified,

By the Yuánshǐ [Yuánshǐ] period,
those who were extensively knowledgeable about bells and pitch-pipes [zhōnglǜ] were summoned,
their meanings were examined,
Xīhé [Xīhé] Liú Xīn [Liú Xīn] took charge of drafting memorials,
and Bān Gù [Bān Gù], the former historian, adopted them as a monograph.

These are the origin of sounds and energies,
and the correct forms of the five notes.
Therefore, each
The others operate in sequence,

The 'Lǐyùn [Lǐyùn] Pian' [Piān] says: 'The five notes, six pitch-pipes, and twelve pipes [guǎn] reciprocally serve as Gōng [Gōng]',
this is what is meant.
By dividing the days of a cycle using the sixty pitch-pipes,
Huángzhōng [Huángzhōng] begins at the winter solstice,
and returns at the winter solstice,
and predictions of yin [yīn] and yang [yáng], cold and heat, wind and rain arise.
By this, all sounds can be controlled,
and their highness and lowness examined;
unless they are sounds of plants and wood,

Jīng Fáng [Jīng Fáng] also said:
"Bamboo sounds cannot be precisely regulated,
therefore a zhǔn [zhǔn] (pitch standard) was made to fix the numbers.
The shape of the zhǔn [zhǔn] is like a sè [sè],
ten feet long with thirteen strings,
the space between frets is nine feet,
corresponding to the nine inches of the Huángzhōng [Huángzhōng] pitch-pipe;
the central string
has markings below it dividing inches,
to indicate the clear and turbid sections of the sixty pitch-pipes."
Jīng Fáng's [Jīng Fáng] words on pitch-pipes are more detailed than those memorialized by Xīn [Xīn],
and his method was implemented by the historians [shǐguān] [shǐguān]
and used by the observatory department [hòubù].
The text is too extensive to be fully recorded.
Therefore, its essentials are summarized
to continue the previous monograph.
The art of pitch-pipes states: yang [yáng] takes a circle as its form,
its nature is movement.
Yin [yīn] takes a square as its division,
its nature is stillness.
The moving ones are counted by three,
the still ones are counted by two.
To generate yin [yīn] from yang [yáng],
double it;
to generate yang [yáng] from yin [yīn],
quadruple it: all are three parts making one.
Yang [yáng] generating yin [yīn] is called 'lower generation',
yin [yīn] generating yang [yáng] is called 'upper generation'.
Upper generation must not exceed the turbidness of Huángzhōng [Huángzhōng],
lower generation must not reach the clearness of Huángzhōng [Huángzhōng].
All follow the principle of 'three heaven, two earth',
round cover, square base,
six pairs supporting odd numbers.
Huángzhōng [Huángzhōng] is
the head of the pitch-pipes [lǜlǚ],
and generates the eleven other pitch-pipes.
In their mutual generation,
all are divided into three parts, and then augmented or diminished.
Therefore, of the twelve pitch-pipes,
one obtains one hundred seventy-seven thousand one hundred forty-seven,
which is the actual number of Huángzhōng [Huángzhōng].
Then, multiplying by two and reducing by three,
this is the actual number of Línzhōng [Línzhōng] generated downwards.
Then, multiplying by four and reducing by three,
this is the actual number of Tàicù [Tàicù] generated upwards.
By extrapolating this upwards and downwards,
the actual numbers of the sixty pitch-pipes are determined.
Dividing by nine and then by three,
one obtains nineteen thousand six hundred eighty-three as the modulus.
For pitch-pipes, it is inches;
for the zhǔn [zhǔn], it is feet.
If it is not a whole number, multiply by ten,
the result is fen [fēn].
If it is still not a whole number, multiply by ten again,
the result is xiǎofēn [xiǎofēn].
The remainder corrects its strength and weakness.
Cutting tubes to make pitch-pipes,
blowing them to test sounds,
and arranging them to align with energies [qì],
is the foundation of the Dao [Dào].
Practitioners of the art consider their sounds subtle and their physical nature difficult to discern,
their fractions unclear,
therefore they made the zhǔn [zhǔn] to replace them.
The sound of the zhǔn [zhǔn]
is clear, bright, and easy to understand,
and its divisions in inches are also coarser.
However, strings vary in their looseness and tightness, clarity and turbidity,
so without the tubes, there is no way to correct them.
By harmonizing its central string
so that it matches Huángzhōng [Huángzhōng],
and then following the markings to find the other pitch-pipes,
none will fail to correspond exactly to the numbers.
The subtlety of musical sounds,
can be understood by those who synthesize them.
In Yuánhé first year (806 CE),
the Daìzhào Hòu Zhōnglǜ Yīnrǒng submitted a memorial, saying:
"The officials lack anyone who understands the sixty lǜ well enough to calibrate sounds.
Therefore, Daìzhào Yán Chóng fully taught the calibration methods to his son, Xuān,
and Xuān mastered them.
I wish for Xuān to be summoned and appointed to the Xuéguān,
to be in charge of tuning musical instruments."
The imperial edict stated:
"If Chóng's son truly understands the lǜ,
can distinguish their families,
and harmonize their sounds,
he shall be thoroughly tested.
He must not rely on his father's learning,
mistaking deafness for hearing.
Sounds are subtle and intricate;
if only one person knows, none other will understand;
if only one person believes it's correct, none other will discern it.
If he can play the lǜ incorrectly,
yet still identify all twelve lǜ without a single error,
only then can he truly be said to have inherited Chóng's learning."
Tàishǐ Chéng Hóng tested the twelve lǜ;
two were correct,
four were incorrect,
and for six, Xuān did not know what lǜ they were.
Xuān was consequently dismissed.
Since then, no lǜ master has been able to calibrate strings accurately,
and the Hòubù has never seen such skill again.
In Xīpíng sixth year (177 CE),
the Dōngguān summoned the officials in charge of lǜ, including Tàizǐ Shèrén Zhāng Guāng, to inquire about the intention of the zhǔn (pitch standard).
Zhāng Guāng and others did not know,
so they returned to examine old records
and found the instrument.
Its form and construction were as described in the Fáng Shū,
but they still could not determine the tension of its strings.
The sounds could not be written down to make them clear to people,
those who knew desired to teach but had no means,
and those who understood by heart comprehended but had no master.
Thus, the ability of historians to distinguish clear and浊 (turbid) tones was completely lost.
What could be transmitted
was only the general constants and the method of hòu qì (observing the qi).
The five notes originate from Yīn and Yáng,
divided into twelve lǜ,
which in turn generate sixty.
All these are used to record the Dǒu qì
and correspond to various phenomena.
Heaven responds with celestial phenomena,
and Earth responds with sounds,
which are the lǜ.
When Yīn and Yáng are in harmony, celestial phenomena appear;
when the lǜ qì responds, the ashes scatter.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven would always, on the days of the winter and summer solstices, proceed to the Qiándiàn,
assemble scholars skilled in the eight disciplines,
arrange the eight musical instruments,
listen to the musical harmonies,
measure the length of the sundial shadow,
observe the zhǒnglǜ (bell pitches),
weigh the tǔtàn (earth and charcoal),
and observe Yīn and Yáng.
At the winter solstice, when the Yáng qì responds,
the musical harmony is clear,
the shadow is at its longest,
the Huángzhōng note is pure,
and the tǔtàn is light, causing the balance to tilt upwards.
At the summer solstice, when the Yīn qì responds,
the musical harmony is turbid,
the shadow is at its shortest,
the Ruíbīn note is pure,
and the tǔtàn is heavy, causing the balance to tilt downwards.
Advancing or retreating within five days before or after,
each of the eight scholars reported their observations,
and the Tàishǐ sealed and presented them.
If they corresponded, it was harmonious;
if not, it was considered an omen.
The method for hòu qì involved
constructing a three-layered chamber,
with its doors closed
and cracks thoroughly sealed,
and densely draped with scarlet curtains.
Inside the chamber, wooden tables were used,
one for each lǜ,
lower on the inside and higher on the outside,
arranged according to their directions.
A lǜ tube was placed on each table,
with reeds' pith ash covering its inner end.
They then observed according to the calendar.
When the qì arrived, the ash moved.
If the ash was moved by the qì, it would scatter;
if moved by humans or wind, it would gather.
In the Diànzhōnghòu, twelve jade lǜ tubes were used.
Only at the two solstices were observations made at the Língtái,
using sixty bamboo lǜ tubes.
The observation days followed the calendar.
Lǜlì Zhōng Jiǎ Kuí's Treatise on the Calendar,
Yǒngyuán's Treatise on the Calendar, Yánguāng's Treatise on the Calendar, Hàn'ān's Treatise on the Calendar, Xīpíng's Treatise on the Calendar, Treatise on Lunar Eclipses.
From Tàichū first year (104 BCE), the Sāntǒng Calendar was first adopted.
After it had been in use for over a hundred years,
the calendar gradually fell behind the heavens,
the new moon (朔, shuò) preceded the calendar,
sometimes the new moon fell on the last day of the month (晦, huì),
and sometimes the moon was seen on the new moon day.
Examining its movements, the sun seemed to recede rather than advance,
and the moon to advance rather than recede.
In Jiànwǔ eighth year (32 CE),
Tàipú Zhū Fú and Tàizhōng Dàfū Xǔ Shú, among others, repeatedly submitted memorials,
stating that the calendar's new moon was incorrect
and should be reformed.
At that time, the observed discrepancy in degrees was still minor,
and the emperor, believing the empire had only recently been settled,
did not have time to rectify it.
By Yǒngpíng fifth year (62 CE),
the official calendar recorded a lunar eclipse on the sixteenth day of the seventh month.
Daìzhào Yáng Cén observed that lunar eclipses at the time often occurred earlier than predicted by the calendar.
He immediately used a shortened calculation to determine the day,
and then submitted a memorial
saying:
"The moon should eclipse on the fifteenth day,
and the official calendar is incorrect."
An imperial edict commanded Yáng Cén to observe
and compare with the official calendar.
From July
through November,
there were five occurrences of xuán (first quarter) and wàng (full moon).
The official calendar was wrong in all cases,
while Yáng Cén was correct in all.
On the Gēngyǐn day,
an imperial edict commanded Yáng Cén to record the xuán, wàng, and lunar eclipse times for the officials,
and further commanded Daìzhào Zhāng Shèng, Jǐng Fáng, Bào Yè, and others to compare with Yáng Cén using the Sìfēn method.
After more than a year,
Zhāng Shèng and others were correct in six more instances than Yáng Cén.
On the Bǐngzǐ day of the eleventh month of the twelfth year (70 CE),
an imperial edict commanded Zhāng Shèng and Jǐng Fáng to replace Yáng Cén in recording the xuán, wàng, and lunar eclipse times.
The Sìfēn method
thus began to be partially implemented.
At this time, Zhāng Shèng and others were not yet able to clearly define the calendar's epoch
or comprehensively calibrate the degree divisions,
so they only used its predictions for xuán and wàng.
Formerly,
in the ninth year (of the Jiànchū reign, 84 CE),
Dǒng Méng (董萌), a Probationer of the Grand Historian, submitted a memorial stating that the calendar was incorrect.
The matter was referred to the Sāngōng (三公) and Tàicháng (太常) and those knowledgeable in calendrical matters for a joint discussion.
By the fourth month of the tenth year,
no one was able to provide clear evidence.
By the second year of Yuánhé (元和, 85 CE),
the Tàichū (太初) calendar had become increasingly distant from the heavens,
and the perceived differences in the lodging degrees of the sun and moon grew.
Observers all knew that on the winter solstice, the sun was in Dǒu (斗) at twenty-one degrees,
and had not yet reached five degrees before Qiānniú (牽牛),
yet it was assumed to be the middle star of Qiānniú.
Subsequently, the heavens were three-quarters of a day [behind the calendar],
and the new and full moons, and the first and last quarters were one day off.
The lodging degrees were off by five degrees.
Emperor Zhāng (章) knew of these errors
and questioned the court astronomers.
Although they knew of the discrepancies,
they could not change them.
Therefore, he summoned Biān Xīn (編訢) and Lǐ Fàn (李梵), who specialized in calendrical calculations, to comprehensively review its state.
On the jiǎyín (甲寅) day of the second month,
an imperial edict was issued, which stated:
“I have heard that the ancient sage kings,
by anticipating heaven, did not violate heaven,
and by following heaven, respected the heavenly seasons.
The Hétú (河圖) states: ‘When the nine reds converge, prosperity will flourish;
for ten generations it will shine,
and in the eleventh, it will rise.’
It also says: ‘In the age of the nine names,
the emperor practices virtue,
and curtails harsh governance.’
I, with my lack of virtue,
have inherited this great enterprise,
and day and night I am reverent and fearful,
not daring to relax.
As a mere youth,
entrusted at the end of a cycle,
how can I continue to make it flourish,
magnify the ancestors,
and save the common people?
The Shàngshū Xuánjīqián (尚書琁璣鈐) states: ‘It recounts the age of Yáo (堯),
and imitates the culture of Táng (唐).’
The Dìmìngyàn (帝命驗) says: ‘Comply with Yáo (堯)'s esteemed virtue,
and establish the astronomical images for the appointed time.’
Moreover, the steps of the Three (三) and Five (五) were vastly different in their merits and shortcomings,
how much more so for one so ignorant and crude [as I],
unable to withstand [the burden].
Although I wish to follow them,
I have no means to do so.
Each time I see the charts and records,
my heart is filled with shame.
Since some time past,
governance has not been effective,
yin and yang are out of harmony,
calamities and anomalies have not ceased,
and pestilential qi
has spread, harming cattle,
and the fundamental agriculture is not sown.
Indeed, the omens of good and ill fortune,
the responses of the Five Matters,
all rest with me.
Truly, there are shortcomings.
How shall I remedy them?
The Shū (書) says: ‘Only the former kings rectified their affairs.’
It also says: ‘In the second month of the year,
he made a tour of inspection to the east,
arriving at Dàizōng (岱宗),
where he offered sacrifice by burning wood,
and performed graded sacrifices to the mountains and rivers.
Then he met the eastern lords,
and harmonized the seasons and months, and rectified the days.’
Our ancestor Yáo (堯), at Dàizōng (岱宗),
standardized weights and measures,
and examined them by means of the armillary sphere and horizontal tube,
to rectify the celestial phenomena,
which would perhaps be beneficial.
The Chūnqiū Bǎogāntú (春秋保乾圖) says: ‘Every three hundred years, the Dǒu (斗) calendar changes its constitution.’
The court astronomers use the Tàichū (太初) method of Dèng Píng (鄧平),
which has an excess fraction of one,
placing it within the realm of three hundred years,
where the orbital calculations gradually err,
and become increasingly fallacious.
The xuánjī (琁璣) is incorrect,
and the astronomical observations are not verified.
On the winter solstice, the sun is in Dǒu (斗) at twenty-one degrees,
but the calendar considers it to be the middle star of Qiānniú (牽牛).
One day before Lìchūn (立春),
is the Lìchūn (立春) day according to the Sīfēn (四分) system.
To use this for judging cases and imposing capital punishment,
it is already contrary to the qi;
to use it to harmonize the full moon and conform to the meaning of the times,
is indeed far off.
Now, we shall adopt the Sīfēn (四分) method,
to follow Yáo (堯),
and to conform to the text of Confucius' (孔聖) reverence for Heaven.
I hope that the hundred lords and the people
will collectively and respectfully receive this,
and perchance attain universal harmony,
to manifest the lasting accomplishments of my ancestors.”
Thereupon, the Sīfēn (四分) calendar was put into effect.
However, Xīn (訢) and Fàn (梵) still believed that the first month of the year (元首) should begin with a large month (thirty days),
wishing to make the first and last quarters of the moon (弦望) coincide,
so that the imperial decrees would have fixed dates.
But in nineteen years, seven intercalary months could not be achieved,
and the new and full moons (晦朔) lost their accuracy.
Before it had been in use for a full year,
Emperor Zhāng (章) again had a sagely thought,
examining it against the classics and apocrypha.

He dispatched the Left Central Supervisor (Zǔo Zhōnglángjiàng) Jiǎ Kuí (賈逵) to question calendrical experts Wèi Chéng (衞承), Lǐ Chóng (李崇), Assistant to the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi zhǔ) Liáng Yú (梁鮪), Aide to the Minister of Works (Sītú yuán) Yán Xù (嚴勗), Palace Attendant (Tàizǐ shèrén) Xú Zhèn (徐震), Senior Member (Gōngchéng) of Jùlù (鉅鹿) Sū Tǒng (蘇統), and Xīn (訢) and Fàn (梵) and eight others.
They believed that the month should begin with a small month (twenty-nine days),
based on the Spring and Autumn Annals where the new moon (朔) is recorded, but not the last day of the lunar month (晦).
This implies that the new moon must involve both brightness and obscurity,
and if there is no new moon, it must be within that month.
If it begins with a large month,
then there would be two new moons in one month,
and no new moon in the next month,
which means brightness cannot be guaranteed.
Fàn (梵) and others believed it should begin with a large month,
but without textual verification,
they merely wanted to make the full moon (望) coincide with the sixteenth day,
the moon setting at dusk,
and the last day of the lunar month (晦) simply disappearing.
Furthermore, the last day of the lunar month (晦) should coincide with the conjunction (合同),
and not be on a different day.
Moreover, the Emperor understood Xīn (訢) and Fàn (梵)'s narrow views,
and ordered that the already promulgated calendar should not be restricted,
and that the month in which the beginning of the celestial cycle (tiānyuán) started
should be small.
This was established,
and the calendrical calculations of the following years were thus corrected.
During the Yǒngyuán (永元) reign (89-105 CE),
the court astronomers were again ordered to observe the first and last quarters (弦望) using the Jiǔdào (九道) method,
and no discrepancies were found.
Jiǎ Kuí (賈逵) compiled and summarized these accounts,
allowing later scholars to make balanced judgments,
which is why they are recorded in detail here.
Jiǎ Kuí (賈逵) argued:
“In the Tàichū (太初) calendar, the winter solstice sun was at the beginning of Qiānniú (牽牛),
which is the middle star of Qiānniú (牽牛).
In ancient times, during the reigns of Huángdì (黃帝), Xià (夏), Yīn (殷), Zhōu (周), and Lǔ (魯), the winter solstice sun was in Jiànxīng (建星),
which is today’s Dǒu (斗) star.
The Tàichū (太初) calendar placed Dǒu (斗) at twenty-six degrees and 385/385 parts,
and Qiānniú (牽牛) at eight degrees.
According to the annotations of the court astronomers in charge of current affairs,
the winter and summer solstices consistently fall short of the Tàichū (太初) calendar by five degrees.
The winter solstice sun is in Dǒu (斗) at twenty-one and a quarter degrees.
The Shíshì Xīngjīng (石氏星經) states: ‘The ecliptic circle passes through the beginning of Qiānniú (牽牛), directly at Dǒu (斗) twenty degrees,
and twenty-five degrees from the pole.’
On the celestial equator,
it is Dǒu (斗) twenty-one degrees.
The Sīfēn (四分) method corresponds to the celestial degrees observed in current affairs.
The Shàngshū Kǎolíngyào (尚書考靈曜) states: ‘Dǒu (斗) twenty-two degrees,
without remainder, the winter solstice is where Qiānniú (牽牛) begins.’
Furthermore, Biān Xīn (編訢) and others based their argument on the current position
being five degrees before the middle star of Qiānniú (牽牛),
which is Dǒu (斗) twenty-one and a quarter,
close to the Kǎolíngyào (考靈曜),
thus clarifying the matter.
In the eighth month of the second year of Yuánhé (元和, 85 CE),
an imperial edict stated: ‘The stone (astronomical stone) must not be deviated from,’
ordering two observations,
and the one with the greater calculation result was to be submitted.
From the second year of Yuánhé (元和) to the first year of Yǒngyuán (永元, 89 CE),
Grand Historian Xuán (玄) and others observed that in these five years, the daily motion of the sun and the winter solstice were at Dǒu (斗) twenty-one and a quarter degrees,
which matched the ancient calendar’s Jiànxīng (建星) and the Kǎolíngyào (考靈曜)’s solar position,
and the stellar distances were all in accordance with the Shíshì (石氏) traditions.
Other methods that placed the winter solstice sun at the beginning of Qiānniú (牽牛)
were consequently rejected.”
Kuí lùn yuē:
"Yǐ Tàichū Lì kǎo Hàn Yuán jìn Tàichū Yuánnián rì (suò) [shí] èrshísān shì,
qí shíqī dé suò,
sì dé huì,

yǐ Xīn Lì shíliù dé suò,
qī dé èr rì,

yǐ Xīn Lì shíqī dé suò,

Yòu yǐ Xīn Lì shàng kǎo Chūnqiū zhōng yǒu rì suò zhě èrshísì shì,
shī bù zhōng zhě èrshísān shì.
Tiāndào cēncī bù qí,
bì yǒu yú,
yú yòu yǒu chángduǎn,
bù kěyǐ děng qí.
Zhì lì zhě fāng yǐ qīshíliù suì duàn zhī,

Shàng zhōng duō chén jiào."

Kuí lùn yuē:

Jù guān zhù tiāndù wéi fēnshuài,
yǐ qí shùfǎ shàng kǎo Jiànwǔ yǐlái yuèshí fán sānshíbā shì,
chà mì jìn,
yǒu yì,
(xuān) [yí] kèshì shàng."
We note that the imperial historians historically possessed the "Nine Paths Method" (Jiǔdàoshù),
but it had been abandoned and neglected.
During the Xīpíng (熹平) era,
Zōng Zhěng (宗整) of Liángguó (梁國), a former calendar official (zhìlìláng), submitted the Nine Paths Method (Jiǔdàoshù).
An imperial edict was sent to the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ),
who compared it with the old methods,
and found them to correspond.
Féng Xùn (馮恂), a retainer (shèrén) to the Crown Prince's Household (Tàizǐ), was assigned to review and calibrate it.
Xùn (恂) also devised his own Nine Paths Method (Jiǔdàoshù),
adjusting its divisions.
When calibrated alongside Zhěng's (整) method,
it proved to be slightly closer (to the truth).
The Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐlìng) Yáng (颺) submitted Xùn's (恂) method for use in conjunction with the crescent (xián) and full (wàng) moons.
However, the added time still fluctuated before and after the celestial phenomena,
sometimes by more than ten degrees.
In the fourteenth year of Yǒngyuán (永元) (102 CE),
Huò Róng (霍融), an attendant (dàizhào) in the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ) office, reported:
"The official clepsydra's (lòukè) rate varies by one *kè* (刻) every nine days,
which does not correspond to the heavens.
Sometimes the error reaches two and a half *kè* (刻),
making it less precise than the Xià (夏) calendar."
An imperial edict was sent to the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng),
ordering the imperial historians to use instruments to calibrate the heavens with Róng (融),
and to measure the distances (of celestial bodies).
The Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐlìng) Shū (舒), Chéng (承), Fàn (梵), and others responded:
"We find that the official clepsydra (lòufǎ) currently in use is the 'Sixth Division of the Permanent Clepsydra Regulation' (Jiǎdìliùchángfúlòupǐn),
issued in the twelfth month of the *yǐyǒu* (乙酉) day of the third year of Emperor Xiàoxuān (孝宣) (71 BCE),
and put into effect by imperial edict on the *rénwǔ* (壬午) day of the second month of the tenth year of Jiànwǔ (建武) (34 CE).
The clepsydra's (lòukè) count is based on the varying length of the day,
with a rate of increase or decrease of one *kè* (刻) for every two and four-tenths degrees of north-south movement of the sun.
Each *qì* (氣) lasts fifteen days,
and the sun's distance from the celestial pole varies.
Now, the official clepsydra (lòushǔai) rate shifts one *kè* (刻) every nine days,
not adjusting with the sun's advance or retreat.
The Xià (夏) calendar's clepsydra (lòu) adjusts its length according to the sun's north-south movement,
making it more precise than the official clepsydra (lòu) and
clearly fit for implementation."
In the eleventh month of the *jiǎyín* (甲寅) day of that year (102 CE),
an imperial edict stated:
"Proclaim to the Minister of Works (Sītú) and the Grand Minister of Agriculture (Sīkōng): The clepsydra (lòu) is used to regulate time divisions
and determine dusk and dawn.
The length of dusk and dawn
originates from the sun's distance from the celestial pole.
The sun's path is circular,
and cannot be calculated by fixed rates.
It should be based on instrumental measurements
and verified against gnomon shadows (guǐjǐng).
Currently, the official clepsydra (lòu) uses fixed rates to divide dusk and dawn,
increasing or decreasing one *kè* (刻) every nine days,
which deviates from the truth,
resulting in overly coarse or fine divisions to match the method.
The attendant (dàizhào) in the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ) office, Huò Róng (霍融), reported
that it does not correspond to the heavens.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) and imperial historians (shǐguān) operated instruments and drew water,
finding the official clepsydra (lòu) to deviate from the heavens by up to three *kè* (刻).
When using gnomon shadows (guǐjǐng) to determine *kè* (刻),
there were few discrepancies,
and its precision was confirmed.
We now issue the gnomon shadow (guǐjǐng) clepsydra (lòukè) with forty-eight arrows (jiàn).
The officials responsible for implementation in government offices should use this.
When the accountants (jìlì) arrive,
distribute the forty-eight arrows (jiàn)."
The text is extensive,
so we excerpt the positions of the sun for the twenty-four *qì* (氣),
along with the distance of the ecliptic (huángdào) from the celestial pole, the gnomon shadows (guǐjǐng), the clepsydra (lòukè), and the *kè* (刻) of the culminating stars at dusk and dawn.
When the Tàichū (太初) calendar (lì) began,
its conception started in Yuánfēng (元封),
and its establishment was initiated in Yuánfèng (元鳳).
After a cumulative period of one hundred and thirty years,
its rightness and wrongness were finally clear.
When the "Four-Part Calendar" (Sìfēnlì) was adopted,
it was also during Jiànwǔ (建武),
implemented in Yuánhé (元和),
and continued until Yǒngyuán (永元).
After more than seventy years,
then the instruments and methods were fully established,
and observations had a standard.
Celestial matters are profound and subtle,
and thus difficult.
Since the Restoration (Zhōngxīng),
the prognostic charts (túchèn) have leaked,
and both the *Kǎolíngyào* (考靈曜) and *Mìnglìxù* (命曆序) both have a *jiǎyín* (甲寅) epoch.
Its origin is one hundred and fourteen years after the *gēngshēn* (庚申) epoch of the Four-Part Calendar (Sìfēnlì),
with a two-day discrepancy in the new moon (shuò).
Scholars in the private sector (cǎozé) revised it,
believing they had attained correctness.
And after the Tàichū (太初) calendar, celestial movement was considered faster (tīanjí),
and those who revised it said:
"Every one hundred and forty-four years, the Grand Year (Tàisuì) advances by one *chén* (辰).
Every one hundred and seventy-one years, sixty-three parts of the new moon (shuòyú) should be discarded,
and one thousand one hundred and ninety-seven *zhōngyú* (中餘) should be discarded,
then it can proceed regularly."
From the first year of Tàichū (太初) (104 BCE) to the eleventh year of Yǒngpíng (永平) (68 CE), which is one hundred and seventy-one years,
the parts should have been discarded but were not,
thus making the discrepancies even greater.
These two schools constantly held onto their methods,
hoping for their implementation.
Whenever there was a dispute,
the numerous officials would convene,
and the various scholars would exert their intellect.
Their discussions were systematic,
benefiting those who possessed extensive knowledge and understanding.
Therefore, these were recorded in detail.
In the second year of Yán'guāng of Emperor Ān,
the chamberlain Zhòng Jiézhě Dǎn Sòng argued for the use of the Jiǎyín Yuán (calendar),
while Hénán Liáng Fēng argued for reverting to the Tàichū (calendar).
Shàngshū Láng Zhāng Héng and Zhōu Xīng, both skilled in calendrical calculations,
challenged Sòng and Fēng with numerous difficulties.
Some did not respond,
others spoke erroneously.
Héng and Xīng jointly examined the ceremonial records,
comparing past and present,
and concluded that the Jiǔdào method was the most accurate.
An imperial edict was issued to the high ministers for detailed deliberation.
Tàiwèi Kǎi and others presented the deliberation of Shìzhōng Shī Yán and others:
"The Tàichū calendar is ahead of the heavens,
by one degree per day;
the quarter and full moons are out of alignment,
the new moon appears in the west at dusk,
and eclipses do not correspond with celestial phenomena.
The Yuánhé calendar adopted the Sìfēn method,
and although Sìfēn is more accurate than Tàichū,
it is also incorrect.
Neither can be used.
The Jiǎyín Yuán calendar corresponds with the heavens
and aligns with the prognostications,
so it should be implemented."
Bóshì Huáng Guǎng and Dàxíng Lìng Rèn Qiān deliberated,
agreeing with the Jiǔdào.
Hénán Yǐn Zhǐ, Tàizǐ Shèrén Lǐ Hóng, and forty other individuals deliberated:
"If the Jiǎyín Yuán calendar is adopted immediately,
it must remove 114 years from Yuánmìng Bāo's 'Heaven and Earth Opened, Qílín Obtained,'
and when calculating the intercalary months, the six 'zhí' days,
or the new moon, full moon, first quarter, and last quarter,
and the twenty-four solar terms' stellar positions, are often inconsistent.
If Jiǔdào is used for the new moon,
months having three big (30-day) and two small (29-day) months consecutively
are all distant from reality.
The Yuánhé calendar was changed
to correspond with the text in Bǎogān Tú, 'Every three hundred years, the Dǒulì calendar changes its constitution.'
The Sìfēn calendar originated from prognostications,
and is the most accurate;
it should not be changed."
Kǎi and eighty-four others deliberated,
preferring to follow Tàichū.
Shàngshū Lìng Zhōng submitted a memorial:
"All who advocate for Tàichū
have no other supporting evidence,
but merely use the longevity of Emperor Shìzōng's reign and his expansion of territory by expelling barbarians as their reason.
Some also say that when Emperor Xiàozhāng changed to Sìfēn,
disasters and anomalies intensified suddenly,
without any favorable responses.
I humbly observe that when sagely kings arose,
each adopted different calendrical systems
to connect the three successions.
When the Hàn ancestor received the mandate,
he followed the Qín's system,
making the tenth month the start of the year,
and intercalary months always placed at the end of the year.
This did not scrutinize earlier generations
and deviated from the imperial canons.
Emperor Tàizōng diligently reformed,
whereupon the Three Orders were made even,
yellow dragons arrived,
penalties and prisons were set right,
and the Five Virtues were made complete.
At the time of Emperors Āi and Píng,
though they all followed Tàichū,
calamities repeatedly occurred,
and misfortunes were numerous.
The deliberators do not analyze existing data,
seeking truth and reality,
but broadly cite baseless claims,
attributing blessings to Tàichū
and faults to Sìfēn.
The Tàichū calendar was established by many wise men,
and its right and wrong have already been settled.
Yǒngpíng did not scrutinize it,
and again reformed its quarter and full moons.
Sìfēn has errors,
and cannot be implemented.
The phoenix in Yuánhé should not have flown and gathered in response to the calendar.
If one praises previous creations,
then their benefits are [displayed];
if one criticizes later changes,
then their blessings are concealed.
Such biased arguments are revealed and cannot be considered correct.
Your subject again repeatedly challenged Héng and Xīng,
believing that the Wǔjì Lùn's calculation of planetary motion
was closer to reality compared to other methods at the time,
yet it still did not scrutinize antiquity.
And when Xiàng Zǐxīn sought to align it with the Spring and Autumn Annals,
he arbitrarily cut off years,
reducing Xià and increasing Zhōu,
and when examined against historical records,
it showed discrepancies of several hundreds.
When comparing the two calendars,
after 6156 years,
Tàichū has one extra day.
The winter solstice should be at Dòu (Sagittarius),
but it says it is at Qiānniú (Aquila).
Its inaccuracies are so [obvious] that it cannot be used again,
manifestly so.
This is commonly seen by historians,
not just Héng and Xīng.
Previously, Jiǔdào was considered accurate and close,
but now the deliberators find it flawed;
and the Jiǎyín Yuán also has many errors,
none of which can be adopted as correct.
Of old, Zhòngní respected the name 'Jiǎmǎ'
to uphold the righteousness of the ruler.
How much more so for the celestial calendrical numbers,
which cannot be based on doubt and emptiness,
to replace right with wrong."
The emperor accepted his words,
and thus [shelved] the matter of calendar reform.
In the second year of Hàn'ān during the reign of Shùndì,
Shàngshū Shìláng Biān Sháo presented a memorial, saying:
"The world weakens when calculations are flawed,
and the Way flourishes when constants are obtained.
When calculations are flawed, things decline;
when constants are obtained, the state prospers.
Xiàowǔ Huángdì, expressing his sage wisdom,
took the winter solstice on the Jiǎzǐ day of the new moon in the eleventh month of the seventh year of Yuánfēng
and commanded Tàishǐ Lìng Sīmǎ Qiān and Zhìlì Dèng Píng and others to re-establish Tàichū,
change the reign era and the beginning of the month,
implement the proper calendar of Xià,
and use 'Qián Zuó Dù's' forty-three parts out of eighty as the daily motion calculation.
He set up observations at the Qīngtái Terrace,
verified the six anomalies,
and meticulously assessed the results.
The Tàichū calendar was the best.
Afterward, Liú Xīn, deeply investigating its intricacies,
verified it with the 'Chūnqiū,'
and consulted the 'Yì Dào.'
Using the 'Hétú Dì Lǎn Xī' and 'Luòshū Qián Yào Dù,' he expanded the nine paths,
advancing or retreating sixty-three parts every one hundred seventy-one years,
and advancing by one position every one hundred forty-four years.
This corresponded with Heaven
with few errors or omissions.
From Tàichū to the eleventh year of Yǒngpíng,
a total of one hundred seventy-one years had passed.
The remaining sixty-three parts for advancement or retreat
were unknown to the calendar makers.
Calculations showed that the new and full moons did not correspond in twelve degrees,
allowing proponents of obsolete methods to propagate their theories.
By the second year of Yuánhé,
the accumulated small remainder gradually became excessive,
and the extra parts steadily increased,
causing the moon to be seen before the new or full moon.
Xiàozhāng Huángdì, based on 'Bǎo Qián Tú's' 'three hundred years, the Dǒu calendar changes its system,'
adopted the Sifen (Four-Part) calendar.
He changed Tàibái's return to Jiǎzǐ to Guǐhài,
drawing astronomical calculations
to match current observations.
Furthermore, setting Gēngshēn as the beginning of the era
lacked clear documentation;
it was attributed to the year of the capture of the Qílín,
but this did not align with the year of Dān'è in the 'Gǎnjīng Fú.'
Successive imperial scribes
developed customary doubts,
few being able to delve deeply and reach far;
examining the new and full moons is sufficient to understand this."
The imperial edict was sent to the Sāngōng and all officials for discussion.
Tàishǐ Lìng Yú Gōng and Zhìlì Zōng Xīn and others deliberated, stating:
"The foundation of establishing a calendar
must first be the establishment of the epoch.
Once the epoch is correct, then the daily motion calculation is determined.
Once the calculation is determined, then the circumference of the heavens is measured to determine the solstices and equinoxes.
If these three are in place,
then a calendar can be perfected.
The epoch of the Zhòngjì of the Sifen calendar
began in the third year of Hòuyuán during the reign of Xiàowén Huángdì,
which was a Gēngchén year.
Counting back forty-five years,
to an Yǐwèi year, that was
the first year of the Hàn dynasty's founding.
Counting back another two hundred seventy-five years,
to a Gēngshēn year, that was
when Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) captured the Qílín.
Two million seven hundred sixty thousand years,
tracing upwards,
again yields a Gēngshēn year.
Year by year, successive,
tracing from bottom to top,
its adherence is not mistaken.
This is the clear documentation in the diagrams and prophecies of the Sifen calendar's epoch.
The first year of Tàichū was a Dīngchǒu year.
Tracing back to its ultimate epoch,
it should be a Gēngxū year,
yet it claims to be a Bǐngzǐ year,
stating that it leaps one position every one hundred forty-four years,
with a total of nine hundred ninety-three leaps,
and an empty cycle of eighty-two full years with a remainder,
to reach Bǐngzǐ.
Examining the years that leap,
on the Jiǎzǐ day of the new moon at the winter solstice in the eleventh month of the Heavenly epoch,
both sun and moon leap.
The sun travels one degree,
accumulating three hundred sixty-five and one-quarter degrees to complete one circuit of the heavens,
which is called a year.
A year starts from one 'chén' (position);
the sun cannot make an empty circuit of the heavens,
so a year cannot leap 'chén.'
Examining the one hundred seventy-one years, two 'bù' and one 'zhāng,'
with a small remainder of sixty-three,
these are natural numbers.
Numbers originate from the most minute 'miǎo huò,'
forming 'háo máo,'
and 'liàng máo' accumulates
to form 'fēncùn.'
Once the two luminaries are set,
the sun and moon begin to separate.
Initially, they generate divisions,
and these divisions accumulate to form degrees.
The sun travels one degree, completing a circuit in one year.
Therefore, calendar makers
each devise their own degree methods,
some using nine hundred forty,
others eighty-one.
Methods have fine and coarse distinctions,
which give rise to two categories,
but their ultimate aim is one.
The daily motion calculation
is the fractional motion of the sun.
The sun descends to bring light,
moving with a constant rhythm.
The scope of the daily motion calculation is vast and endless;
even a slight increase or decrease of 'háo máo'
results in a difference of a thousand 'lǐ.'
From this perspective,
there is no reason for numbers to have intentions of loss or abandonment.
Now, to remedy the errors of flatness,
to break the law and deduct divisions,
we fear it would harm the Great Way.
In calculating the motion of the sun and moon,
the final numbers are different.
The four 'zhāng' cannot result in a remainder of one at the new moon.
Although it is said that the nine paths are used to advance and retreat in calculations,

Moreover, the method of checking the calendar,

Now, if we use the method of removing sixty-three parts for the calendar,
and check the twenty solar changes

since the first year of Zhānghé,

When comparing calculations,
the Sifen calendar still yields more
and is also more convenient and accurate.
Xiàozhāng Huángdì's calendar calculations were accurate and correct;

corresponded with Heaven,
and cannot be surpassed.
The 'Wényào Gōu' states:
'Gāoxīn received the mandate;

From antiquity to the present,

rectify all doubts,
secretly preserve them in the imperial library,

Guāngwǔ Huángdì repeatedly issued imperial edicts,

Xiàomíng Huángdì verified its truth,

Three sages ruled in succession,

believed and verified it,

Its epoch traces back to the opening of heaven and earth,

It should be in accordance with the precedent of the Jiǎyín imperial edict."
The memorial was approved.
In the fourth year of Xīpíng during the reign of Língdì,

On the Yǐmǎo day,

The Hàn dynasty succeeded Qín,

The Tàichū

Astronomers

The Yuánmìngbāo and Qiánzáodù both state that from the creation of the world to the capture of the Qilin was two million seven hundred and sixty thousand years.

years.

Therefore,

And Guāng and Huàng's calendar takes the Kǎolíngyào

The Tàichū Lì (太初曆) often erred in predicting lunar eclipses.
The Sìfēn Lì (四分曆) was based on the Tàichū Lì (太初曆) methods.
It took the *guǐsì* year of Hépíng (河平) as its epoch,
and was implemented for five years.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán (永元)
(90 CE), the heavens showed an eclipse in the intercalary seventh month,
but the calendar predicted it for the eighth month.
On the twelfth day of the first month of its second year (91 CE),
Méng Gōngchéng Zōng Gàn (蒙公乘宗紺) submitted a memorial, stating:
"On the sixteenth of this month, there will be a lunar eclipse,
but the calendar predicts it for the second month."
On the appointed date, it occurred as Gàn (紺) had stated.
The Grand Astrologer, Xún (巡), reported that Gàn (紺)'s method was beneficial for official use,
and he was appointed as a Gentleman Attendant.
In the *jiǎchén* year (92 CE),
an imperial edict decreed the adoption of Gàn (紺)'s method.
It was implemented for fifty-six years.
By the first year of Běnchū (本初)
(146 CE), the heavens showed an eclipse in the twelfth month,
but the calendar predicted it for the first month of the following year.
From this point, discrepancies began to appear.
By the third year of Xīpíng (熹平)
(174 CE), within twenty-nine years,
there were sixteen instances where the calendar's prediction of an eclipse was earlier than the actual event.
Liú Hóng (劉洪), the Grand Administrator of Chángshān (常山), submitted his work, the Qīyào Shù (七曜術).

In the *jiǎchén* year (174 CE), an imperial edict ordered it to be assigned to the Grand Astrologer, the Bureau Chief Liú Gù (劉固), and the Palace Attendant Fény Xún (馮恂), among others, to test its efficacy.
Then, the Bāyuán Shù (八元術) was created.
Gù (固) and others developed a lunar eclipse method,
which was also considered.
Gù (固)'s method was the same as the Qīyào Shù (七曜術).
Regarding the errors in lunar eclipse predictions,
they all agreed that in the *jǐwèi* year (179 CE), the eclipse should occur in the fourth month.
Xún (恂)'s method predicted the third month,
and the official calendar predicted the fifth month.
The Grand Astrologer assessed them,
stating that at the time of implementation, the best one should be used.
In the *dīngsì* year (177 CE),
an imperial edict approved it.
In its fourth year (178 CE),
Gàn (紺)'s grandson, Chéng (誠), submitted a memorial, stating:

it should be revised.
This year, in the twelfth month, there will be an eclipse,
but the official calendar predicts it for the first month of the following year."
On the appointed date, it occurred as he had stated.
Chéng (誠) was appointed as a Palace Attendant.
In the *bǐngshēn* year (178 CE),
an imperial edict permitted the implementation of Chéng (誠)'s method.
In the second year of Guānghé (光和), the *jǐwèi* year (179 CE),

concluding that the third month was closer,
and the fourth month was farther.
Chéng (誠) predicted the fourth month.
A memorial was submitted to abolish Chéng (誠)'s method
and to adopt Xún (恂)'s method.
In its third year (180 CE),

Zhěng (整)'s memorial was submitted to the Grand Astrologer,

and the fourth month was farther.
Eclipses should be verified by observation,
without considerations of 'closer' or 'farther.'
An imperial edict was sent down to the Grand Minister of Ceremonies, stating:
"Carefully examine the annotations and records,
impartially deliberate on the essence of the methods,
and verify their accuracy and inaccuracy."

The Grand Minister of Ceremonies, Jiù Dān (就耽), selected the Attendant Counselor Hán Yuè (韓說), the Erudite Cài Jiào (蔡較), the Gǔchéng Mén Hóu (穀城門候) Liú Hóng (劉洪), and the Right Bureau Chief Chén Diào (陳調) at the Grand Minister of Ceremonies' office
to re-examine the annotations and records,
and to impartially deliberate on the difficult questions.
Xún (恂) and Chéng (誠) each presented their arguments.
Xún (恂)'s method used 5,640 months with 961 eclipses as its rule.
After removing the components
and simply adding the hanging method,
it calculated 327 eclipses from the time of Jiànwǔ (建武) (25 CE) onward.
Of these, 327 eclipses were correctly predicted,
but fifteen were incorrect.
According to the official annotations,
98 eclipses were observed in the heavens,
corresponding to both methods,
with a discrepancy of 2,100.
Chéng (誠)'s method used 135 months with 23 eclipses as its rule.
After multiplication and division to complete the months,
41 were subtracted from the period before Jiànkāng (建康) (144 CE),
and 35 were subtracted from the period since Jiànkāng (建康),
because none of them had eclipses.
Xún (恂)'s method altered the old rules,
and Chéng (誠)'s method further subtracted and reduced.
Comparing their strengths and weaknesses,
neither surpassed the other.
Each cited books and *wěi* (緯) texts to prove their own points,
but their writings lacked essential meaning,
merely seeking to catch up with celestial phenomena.
Regarding the methods for the sun and moon:
the sun follows the ecliptic,
and the moon follows the nine paths.
According to the equatorial armillary sphere,
at the winter solstice, the sun's distance from the pole is 115 degrees.
When it enters its mansion,
the equator is at 11 in Dòu (斗),
while the ecliptic is at 19 in Dòu (斗).
Comparing the two armillary spheres,
the movements of the sun and moon
have differences in their curves and straight lines,
which cause advancements and retreats.
Therefore, when the moon moves through Jǐng (井) and Niú (牛),
it is above 14 degrees.
When it is in Jiǎo (角) and Lóu (婁),
it is above 12 degrees.
None of these conform to the rates of motion.
From this, it can be said:
a method is not revised unless there is a discrepancy,
and it is not used unless it is verified.
The way of heaven is subtle and profound,
its measurements are difficult to determine,
there are many methods,
and calendars are not uniform.
Without verification, one cannot know if it is correct;
without discrepancies, one cannot know its errors.
Only when there is an error should it be revised;
only when it is correct should it be used.
This is what is meant by "holding fast to the Mean."
Currently, Chéng (誠)'s method has not yet shown any erroneous discrepancies,
and Xún (恂)'s method has not yet shown any unique accuracy.
To revise an un-erring method without verification
is to take future verification as correctness.
Chéng (誠)'s method, with 135 months and 23 eclipses,
its texts are in the records,
studied by scholars,
implemented for a long time,
and maintained by officials.
It has governed the sun and moon,
proven robust and without transgression.
It is trusted in astronomy,
transmitted but not created.
Xún (恂) has long been in the observation department,
with a careful mind and good intentions,
capable of measuring instruments and degrees,
establishing methods and calculations.
Calculating forward and checking backward,
it also corresponds to observed eclipses.
However, to harmonize the calendar and rectify the records,
reverently following the August Heaven,
it is proper to adhere to old regulations,
as per the imperial edicts of *jiǎchén* (甲辰) and *bǐngshēn* (丙申),
taking observed eclipses as the standard.
It is now appropriate to implement Chéng (誠)'s method,
and abandon Xún (恂)'s method.
The Historians should evaluate it,
and if it is verified later,
then its method should be implemented
to scrutinize the methods and calculations
and to conform to revisions.
Dān (耽) submitted the deliberation of Yuè (說) and others,
and an imperial edict approved it.
Xún (恂), Zhěng (整), and Chéng (誠) each submitted further memorials.
Xún (恂) argued that Chéng (誠)'s method should not be implemented,
and Zhěng (整) argued that Xún (恂)'s method should not be abandoned again.
Being criticized by Hóng (洪)'s deliberation,
the matter was sent down to the Yǒng'ān Tái (永安臺) for re-verification,
which found that none of it was as Xún (恂) and Chéng (誠) had stated.
An impeachment memorial accused them of deceit.
An imperial edict was issued,
stating that Xún (恂) and Chéng (誠) each had to redeem their offenses with two months' service,
and Zhěng (整) was sentenced to two months of service as a Zǔocáo (左校).
Consequently, Hóng (洪) and others were employed, and Chéng (誠)'s method was implemented.
In the second year of Guanghé (179 CE),
Wànnián gōngchéng Wáng Hàn submitted a commentary on lunar eclipses.
From the first year of Zhānghé (87 CE) to this year, a total of ninety-three years have passed,
encompassing one hundred and ninety-six eclipses.
He identified a discrepancy in the first year of Hépíng (28 BCE) of the official calendar,
taking Jǐsì as the epoch.
The matter was sent down to Tàishǐlìng Xiū,
who reported:
"Two items in Hán's commentary do not correspond to observed eclipses,
and twenty-nine items that should be treated as different are treated as the same."
The Shàngshū summoned Gǔchéng Ménhoú Liú Hóng.
An imperial edict stated:
"Previously, Lángzhōng Féng Guāng and Sītú Yuán Chén Huǎng each advocated for a calendar,
and Guìláng Cài Yōng jointly supplemented their work.
Now, Hóng, you are to go to Xiū,
and together with Hàn,
deduce the epoch and calculate the divisions,
to verify the lunar eclipses.
If the Jǐsì epoch is truly precise and close,
and has a reliable tradition,
then Hóng should learn from Hàn.
If not,
then report back."
Hóng reported:
"By deducing Hàn's Jǐsì epoch,
it corresponds to the Yǐmǎo epoch of the Kǎolíng Yàozhān méng year,
which intersects with Guāng and Huǎng's Jiǎyín epoch.
In retrospect, the calendar created for heaven,
which calculates the movements of the three luminaries,
is now found to be imprecise.
Confucius's commentary, in one instance, showed two different aspects,
clarifying that the rise and fall of calendars
follow the dictates of Heaven.
The Jiǎyín calendar was effective in Confucius's time;
the Jǐsì calendar was used by Zhuānxū and Qin,
and when the Hàn dynasty arose, it was initially adopted,
and not changed.
By the Yuánfēng (110-105 BCE) period, it was found to be too broad and inaccurate,
so the Tàichū calendar was adopted instead,
fulfilling the period of three hundred years for constitutional change.
Although the Jiǎyín and Jǐsì prophecies have texts,
their precise year counts are omitted,
which is why scholars each transmit what they have heard,
but when it comes to calculation and verification,
none can obtain its correctness.
The Jiǎyín epoch has the first day of the first month of the celestial year (Tiānzhèng), Jiǎzǐ shòudàn dōngzhì,
and the rise of the seven luminaries begins at the beginning of Niú.
The Yǐmǎo epoch has the first day of the first month of the human year (Rénzhèng), Jǐsì shòudàn lìchūn,
with the three luminaries gathered within five degrees of Tiānmiào.
Calculating the two epochs,
the difference in the remaining intercalary days is three of one hundred and fifty-two parts,
the new moon (朔) is three hundred and four,
and the remaining days for the central solar terms are twenty-nine.
Since it is difficult to reconcile these to verify their reliability,
Hàn does not explain,
but merely says that the ancients had books.
When Hàn's completed commentary is compared with the official implementation,
the methods differ in twenty-nine items,
and two items do not correspond to observed eclipses.
Examining Hàn's study,
he saw the Jǐsì epoch,
saying that the court did not hear of it,
not knowing that the sages alone possess the principle of rise and fall,
and that the scribes of history possess secret methods that conform to Heaven.
Jiǎyín and Jǐsì were
previously implemented,
but their later effects were found to be discordant and were no longer used.
Hépíng was imprecise,
and the scribes of history have already abandoned it,
yet Hàn uses past events to dispute,
which is probably not his intention.
Even if there is a traditional method,
it is as if there were none.
Furthermore, the calculation is not precise.
His explanation of the bùng numbers
is commonly known to calendrical specialists,
and there is nothing to adopt from it."
Hàn was sent back to his hometown.
Section on Calendar Systems
In ancient times, when the sages created the calendar,
they observed the movements of the xuánjī,
the courses of the three luminaries,
the expansion and contraction of the Dào,
the lengths of shadows,
the constellations indicated by the handle of the Dipper,
and the mansions traversed by the Azure Dragon.
They combined and varied these elements,
interweaving their numbers,
and thus formulated their methods.
When Heaven moves,
it completes a revolution in one day and one night;
the stars follow Heaven westward,
while the sun moves eastward, against Heaven's rotation.
The path that the sun traverses, completing a revolution,
forms degrees in the sky,
and days in the calendar.
It is housed among the constellations,
ending in the twenty-eight mansions;
it is received by the Jiǎyǐ cycle,
ending in sixty days.
The sun and moon push each other;
the sun is slow, the moon is fast.
When they are at the same place,
it is called conjunction (héshuò).
When the slow one precedes and the fast one follows,
with one near and three far,
it is called crescent or half-moon (xián).
When they are opposite each other,
dividing the middle of Heaven,
it is called full moon (wàng).
When the fast one overtakes the slow one,
and its light is entirely covered, its body hidden,
it is called last day of the month (huì).
The joining and separation of huì and shuò,
and the shifting of the Dipper's pointer to a new辰 (chén),
is called a month (yuè).
The movement of the sun and moon
brings winter and summer;
between winter and summer,
there are spring and autumn.
Therefore, when the sun travels through the northern path, it is called winter;
through the western path, it is called spring;
through the southern path, it is called summer;
and through the eastern path, it is called autumn.
When the sun's path expands southward,
moving further from the pole,
its shadow becomes longer;
when it reaches its furthest and longest extent,
winter arrives.
When the sun's path contracts northward,
moving closer to the pole,
its shadow becomes shorter;
when it reaches its closest and shortest extent,
summer arrives.
Between the two solstices,
the path is balanced and the shadow is upright,
marking the spring and autumn equinoxes.
When the sun completes its cycle in the sky,
undergoing one cold and one hot period,
the four seasons are fully formed,
and all myriad things undergo change.
Shètí (Jupiter) shifts its position,
and the Azure Dragon moves its mansion,
this is called a year (suì).
The beginning of the year is the solstice (zhì);
the beginning of the month is the new moon (shuò).
When the solstice and new moon fall on the same day, it is called a zhāng;
when they both fall on the first day (of a sexagenary cycle), it is called a bù;
when a bù ends in sixty days, it is called a jì;
when the year and new moon also recur (to the same starting point), it is called a yuán.
Therefore, the sun fills it (with days),
the moon interpolates it (with intercalary months),
the seasons divide it,
the year completes its cycle,
the zhāng illuminates it,
the bù organizes it,
the jì records it,
and the yuán originates it.
Then, even if there are myriad changes,
and variations without definite pattern,
all are connected to this and derive their correctness from it.
The Gí (celestial axis) is erected in the center,
the Dào operates outside it.
The xuánhéng (armillary sphere) tracks the sun,
to observe the [fā] (expansion) and liǎn (contraction),
and thus the guāngdào (ecliptic) is produced.
A kǒnghú (perforated clepsydra) serves as the water clock,
and a fújiàn (floating arrow) marks the divisions.
The dripping of the clepsydra measures the intervals,
to examine the culminations of the stars,
and thus the hūnmíng (dusk and dawn) are produced.
The sun has its guāngdào,
the moon has its jiǔháng (nine courses).
When the jiǔháng enter and exit, intersections are produced.
At the new moon, it meets; at the full moon, it aligns.
Approaching the intersection,
eclipses and occultations are produced.
The moon has its huìshuò (obscurity and newness),
the stars have their héjiàn (conjunctions and visibility).
The moon has its xiánwàng (crescent and full),
the stars have their liúní (stationary and retrograde motions).
Their return to unity,
is how bùshù (astronomical calculations) are produced.
Jīn (Venus) and Shuǐ (Mercury) follow the yang,
before and after the sun.
When swift, they precede the sun,
then become stationary,
stationary then retrograde,
retrograde diverging from the sun.
Diverging then swift,
swift competing with the sun,
competing again preceding the sun.
Swift, direct, retrograde motions,
thus chénxī (morning and evening appearances) are produced.
The sun, moon, and Wǔwěi (five planets) each have a termination and an origin,
and thus the Qīyuán (seven luminaries) are produced.
Visibility and invisibility have their days,
stationary and direct motions have their degrees,
and thus shuàishù (ratio and numbers) are produced.
When differences are made uniform,
and amounts are equalized,
then huìzhōng (conjunctions at the end of cycles) are produced.
To extend and expand it,
to touch and lengthen it,
to explore the abstruse and search the hidden,
to plumb the depths and reach the distant,
there is no darkness, seclusion, or concealment,
that is not understood by its essence.
Thus, yin and yang have their divisions,
and cold and heat have their seasons.
Heaven and earth are truly observed,
the sun and moon are truly bright.
As for the auspicious techniques opening the way,
and the pure radiance of celestial light,
Chóng and Lí were at the forefront of this.
Receiving the command of the sage emperor like august heaven,
they superintended the celestial phenomena and the three luminaries,
to instruct the people in their affairs.
They established intercalary months and fixed the times,
to complete the year's achievements,
Xī and Hé were glorious in this.
Taking their models from Jīn (metal) and Huǒ (fire),
they revolutionized and created systems,
managed the calendar and clarified the times,
responding to heaven and complying with the people.
Tāng and Wǔ were flourishing in this.
But when the king's virtue declined,
unprincipled rulers brought chaos from above,
and stubborn and ignorant historians erred from below.
During the time of Xiàhòu,
Xī and Hé indulged in drunkenness,
neglecting the times and disrupting the days,
Yǐn then punished them.
Zhòu committed lewdness and cruelty,
losing his jiǎzǐ (cyclical dates),
Wǔwáng then executed him.
Those who could make it true and clear,
their rise was vigorous;
those who perverted and ruined it,
their demise was sudden.
How magnificent, like regulating the principles of heaven and earth,
and the grand accomplishments of emperors and kings!
Therefore, the sage treasures it,
and the noble person diligently practices it.
Indeed, the calendar possesses six virtues of the sage: those who base it on fundamental qi value its substance,
those who integrate numbers value its patterns,
those who examine categories value its images,
those who undertake affairs value its timing,
those who divine the past value its source,
and those who know the future value its flow.
Great undertakings are recorded,
good and bad fortune are produced,
therefore, when a noble person is about to embark on something,
they consult it and proceed accordingly,
receiving the mandate without daring to disobey it.
As for utilizing heaven and following earth,
measuring the times and disseminating teachings,
promulgating them in the Míngtáng,
to serve as the standard for the people,
nothing is greater than the Yuèlìng.
The great duties of emperors and kings are fully provided,
and all the capable affairs of the world are completed.
Beyond this,
there are only various taboos and arbitrary prohibitions,
which the noble person may not necessarily understand.
Dǒu (the Dipper) is at twenty-one degrees,
furthest from the celestial pole.
When the sun is there, it is the winter solstice,
and all things begin to grow.
Therefore, the lǜ (musical scale) begins with Huángzhōng,
the calendar begins with the winter solstice,
the month begins with Jiànzǐ,
and the time is midnight.
In the forty-fifth year after Hàn Gāohuángdì received the mandate,
Yang was in Shàngzhāng,
Yin was in Zhíxú.
In the eleventh month of winter, on the jiǎzǐ day, at midnight, at the new moon, it was the winter solstice.
The numbers for the sun, moon, and intercalary accumulations all began from this point.
Establishing the yuán (epoch) and zhèngshuò (first new moon),
it was called the Hàn Lì.
Furthermore, adding two yuán earlier,
the yuán for lunar eclipses and the five planets,
all commenced from there.
The production of calendrical calculations
requires setting up a yí (gnomon) and biǎo (sundial post),
to measure the sun's shadow.
A longer shadow means the sun is farther,
this is the beginning of celestial degrees.
The sun starts from this point,
completes a circuit for a year.
However, its shadow does not return to its original state.
After one thousand four hundred and sixty-one days over four circuits,
the shadow returns to its initial position,
this is the completion of the sun's motion.
Dividing the total days by the circuits,
we get three hundred and sixty-five and one-quarter degrees,
as the number of days in a year.
The sun travels one degree per day,
which is also a celestial degree.
Observing the sun and moon both starting from the same degree,
the sun travels nineteen circuits,
and the moon travels two hundred and fifty-four circuits,
before they meet again at the starting point.
This is the completion of the moon's motion.
Dividing the moon's circuits by the sun's circuits,
we get the number of circuits in a year.
Subtracting one circuit of the sun,
the remainder is seven-nineteenths of a circuit,
which is the number of circuits the moon travels beyond, and the sun travels.
This is the year's months.
Dividing the year's days by this,
gives the number of days in a month.
When the remaining fractions of the month accumulate to the required amount,
one month is gained,
when a month is complete, the year becomes [dà] (long).
The month (long) shifts through the four seasons,
therefore twelve zhōngqì (major solar terms) are set to fix the month's position.
A month with a new moon but no zhōngqì is an intercalary month.
The beginning of a zhōngqì [is called] jiéqì (minor solar term),
together with the zhōngqì, they form the Èrshísì Qì (twenty-four solar terms).
Dividing the year's days by this,
gives the number of days for one qì (solar term).
When its fractions accumulate to form a day, it is called mò (lapse).
Combining the fractions of the annual solar terms,
according to the method, it becomes the annual mò.
The mò fractions are distributed at the end of the zhōngqì,
the zhōngqì ends at the winter solstice.
When the fractions of the winter solstice accumulate according to the method to form one day,
it completes in four years.
Months combine to form intercalary months,
seven intercalary months complete the cycle,
making nineteen years,
which is called a zhāng.
When the initial fractions of a zhāng are exhausted,
and four such cycles are completed,
it is called a bù.
Multiplying by the number of days in a year,
gives the number of days in a bù.
Named by jiǎzǐ,
it returns to its beginning after twenty cycles,
therefore twenty bù constitute a jì.
The year of the jì, Qīnglóng, does not end,
after three completed years, it returns to Qīnglóng as the yuán.

The generation of the number of lunar eclipses
is recorded as the number of total lunar eclipses.
On average, twenty-three eclipses bring it back to a total eclipse.
The number of months is one hundred thirty-five.
Dividing the rates by each other,
one eclipse occurs every five and twenty-three twentieths of a month.
Dividing this into the months of one year,
it is found that there are fifty-five/five hundred thirteenths of a second eclipse in a year.
Taking the fraction to its denominator,

Inverting them,

The method for calculating entry into a bù cycle is as follows: Subtract the shàngyuán from the yuánfǎ;
divide the remainder by the jìfǎ.
The resulting number starts from Tiānjì;
what falls outside the calculation is the jì entered.
If it is less than the jìfǎ,
that is the number of years entered in the jì.
Divide it by the bùfǎ.
The resulting number starts from jiǎzǐ bù;
what falls outside the calculation
is named according to the entry jìsuì.
What falls within the calculation
is the location of the Tàisuì for the year sought.
To calculate the bùhuì year of entry for a lunar eclipse: Subtract the shàngyuán from the yuánhuì.
Divide the remainder by the bùhuì.
Multiply the result by twenty-seven.
If it reaches sixty, remove it.
Divide the remainder by twenty.
The resulting number starts from Tiānjì;
what falls outside the calculation
is the jì entered.
If it is less than twenty,
the number starts from jiǎzǐ bù;
what falls outside the calculation
is the bùhuì entered.
If the initial value is less than the bùhuì,
it is the number of years entered in the bùhuì.
Each is named according to the jìsuì entered.
What falls within the calculation
is the location of the Tàisuì for the year sought.
