To calculate the Tiānzhèng method:
Set the entered bù year minus one.
Multiply it by the zhāngyuè.
If it reaches the zhāngfǎ, one is obtained,
named jīyuè.
If less, it is the rùnyú.
If it is twelve or more,
that year has an intercalary month.
To calculate the Tiānzhèng shuòrì:
Set the entered bù jīyuè.
Multiply it by the bùrì.
If it reaches the bùyuè, one is obtained,
named jīrì.
If less, it is the xiǎoyú.
Remove sixty from the jīrì.
The remainder is the dàyú.
Name it according to the entered bù name.
Beyond the completion of the calculation,
it is the eleventh month shuòrì of Tiānzhèng of the previous year.
If the xiǎoyú is four hundred forty-one or more,
that month is long.
To find the next month's shuò,
add twenty-nine to the dàyú
and four hundred ninety-nine to the xiǎoyú.
If the xiǎoyú reaches the bùyuè, one is obtained.
Add it to the dàyú.
Name it as before.
One method:
Multiply the dàyú by the year.
Subtract the zhōutiān multiplied by the rùnyú.
If the remainder reaches the bùyuè,
then it is the Tiānzhèng shuòrì.
To calculate the twenty-four qi (solar terms) method: Set the entered bù year minus one.
Multiply it by the rìyú.
If it reaches the zhōngfǎ, one is obtained,
named dàyú.
If less, it is the xiǎoyú.
If the dàyú reaches sixty, remove it.
The remainder is named according to the bù name.
Beyond the completion of the calculation,
it is the day of the winter solstice of the previous year.
To find the next qi,
add fifteen to the dàyú
and seven to the xiǎoyú.
After dividing, name it as before;
this is the day of Xiǎohán.
To determine the location of the intercalary month:
Subtract the rùnyú from the zhāngfǎ.
Multiply the remainder by twelve.
If it reaches the zhāngrùn number, one is obtained.
If it is four or more, one is also counted.
Starting from the eleventh month of the previous year,
beyond the completion of the calculation,
it is the intercalary month.
Alternatively, advance or retreat,
determining it by the zhōngqì.
To calculate the day of xián (first quarter) and wàng (full moon):
Using the numbers for the month's shuò, dàyú and xiǎoyú,
add seven to the dàyú
and three hundred fifty-nine and three-quarters to the xiǎoyú.
If the xiǎoyú reaches the bùyuè, one is obtained.
Add it to the dàyú.
Name the dàyú according to the method.
This gives the shàngxián.
Adding again gives the wàng.
Next, the xiàxián.
Then the next month's shuò.
If the xián and wàng xiǎoyú are two hundred sixty or less,
multiply it by one hundred kè.
If it reaches the bùyuè, one kè is obtained.
If less, the half of the night leakage for the nearest solar term
is taken as the day for calculation.
To calculate the mòmiè method:
Set the entered bù year minus one.
Multiply it by the mòshù.
If it reaches the rìfǎ, one is obtained,
named jīmò.
The remainder is the mòyú.
Multiply the jīmò by the tōngfǎ.
If it reaches the mòfǎ, one is obtained,
named dàyú.
The remainder is the xiǎoyú.
If the dàyú reaches sixty, remove it.
The remainder is named according to the bù name.
Beyond the completion of the calculation,
it is the day of mò before the winter solstice of the previous year.
To find the next mò,
add sixty-nine to the dàyú
and four to the xiǎoyú.
If the xiǎoyú reaches the mòfǎ,
it goes to the dàyú.
Name it as before.
If there is no fraction, it is miè.
The generation of the Five Planets' calculations
is individually recorded by day,
and is aligned with the degrees of the celestial circuit to form a ratio.
Multiply the *zhāng* method by the *zhōu* ratio to obtain the [monthly] method.
Multiply the *zhāng* month by the daily ratio,
as per the monthly method,
to get the accumulated month and the monthly remainder.
Multiply the [day] of the month by the accumulated [month],
to get the greater and lesser remainders of the new moon.
Multiply it to obtain the daily remainder for entering the month.
Multiply the daily method by the *zhōu* ratio to obtain the daily degree method.
Use the [Zhou] ratio to subtract the daily ratio.
Multiply the remainder by the celestial circuit.
As per the daily degree method,
this is the [accumulated] degree and the degree remainder.
When the daily ratios are aligned and taken,
Then the Five Planets complete their cycles,
like the number of the *bù*,
connecting with the *yuán*.

To calculate the methods for the Five Planets:
Take the years from the *shàngyuán* to the desired year.
Multiply this by the *zhōu* ratio.
For every full daily ratio, one is obtained,
called "accumulated conjunction";
the remainder is called the conjunction remainder.
Divide the [conjunction] remainder by the *zhōu* ratio.
If it does not divide, retreat the year.
If nothing is obtained,
the planet is in conjunction in that year.
One conjunction means the previous year,
two conjunctions mean two years prior.
For Vēnus (金, Jīn) and Mercūry (水, Shuǐ), an odd accumulated conjunction means morning,
and an even one means evening.
For that which does not reach a full *zhōu* ratio, subtract it in reverse.
The remainder is the degree fraction.
To calculate the planetary conjunction month:
Multiply the accumulated months by the accumulated conjunction to get a small accumulation.
Also multiply the monthly remainder by the accumulated conjunction.
For every full monthly method, one is obtained,
[taken] from the small accumulation as the accumulated month;
the remainder is the monthly remainder.
When the accumulated month reaches the *jì* month, subtract it.
The remainder is the month for entering the *jì*.
Each time, multiply by the *zhāng* intercalary cycle.
For every full *zhāng* month, one is obtained as an intercalary month;
the remainder is the intercalary remainder.
Subtract the intercalary month from the month for entering the *jì*.
Divide the remainder by twelve.
The remainder is the number of months for entering the year,
starting from the first month of the *tiānzhèng*,
beyond calculation,
which is the month of the planetary conjunction.
If the intercalary [remainder] is 224 or more, up to 231, the planet is in conjunction in an intercalary month.
Intercalary months may advance or retreat,
governed by the new moon.
To calculate the day of the new moon:
Multiply the *bù* day by the month for entering the *jì*.
For every full *bù* month, one is obtained as an accumulated day.
The remainder is the lesser remainder.
When the accumulated day reaches sixty, subtract it.
The remainder is the greater remainder,
designated by the *jiǎzǐ*.
Beyond calculation,
this is the day of the new moon of the planetary conjunction month.
To calculate the day of the lunar ingress:
Multiply the remainder of the month by the Bù (蔀) days.
Multiply the small remainder of the new moon by its monthly coefficient.
Add these together.
Divide by four thousand four hundred sixty-five.
For every full day's coefficient obtained,
this is the day of the lunar ingress.
The remainder is the day's remainder.
Designate the day of the lunar ingress by jiǎzǐ (甲子).
Beyond calculation,
this is the day of the planetary conjunction.
To calculate the degree of conjunction:
Multiply the circumference of the heavens by the degree minutes.
For every full day's degree coefficient obtained, this is the accumulated degree.
The remainder is the degree remainder.
Designate the degree by Dǒu (斗) twenty-one and a quarter.
Beyond calculation,
this is the degree where the planetary conjunction occurs.
One method:
Add one to the decremented year.
Subtract this from the beginning of the epoch (shàngyuán, 上元).
If it reaches eighty, remove it.
Multiply the remainder by the number of disappearances.
For every full day's coefficient obtained,
this is the great remainder.
The remainder is the small remainder.
Designate the great remainder by jiǎzǐ (甲子).
Then, this is the day of the planetary conjunction and the winter solstice (dōngzhì, 冬至) of the celestial prime of the year.
Multiply the small remainder by the circumference ratio.
And add the degree remainder.
If the remainder fills the day's degree coefficient, add it to the degrees.
This is the number of days after the winter solstice (dōngzhì, 冬至) when the planetary conjunction occurs.
Designate it by the winter solstice (dōngzhì, 冬至).
To find the month of a subsequent conjunction:
Add the accumulated month of conjunction to the ingress year-month.
Add the month remainder to the month remainder.
For every full monthly coefficient obtained,
add it to the ingress year-month.
If the ingress year-month reaches twelve, remove it.
Account for leap months.
Designate the remainder as before.
Beyond calculation,
this is the month of the subsequent conjunction.
For Jīn (金) and Shuǐ (水): adding morning gives evening,
adding evening gives morning.
To find the new moon day:
Add the great and small remainders to the current result.
If the month remainder results in one month,
then add twenty-nine to the great remainder,
and four hundred ninety-nine to the small remainder.
If the small embellishment fills a Bù (蔀) month, add one
to the great remainder.
Designate the great remainder as before.
To find the day of lunar ingress:
Add the day remainder of the lunar ingress to the current result.
For every full day's degree coefficient obtained,
add it to the day.
If the small remainder of the new moon of the previous conjunction month does not fill its void fraction,
add one day for nothing.
If the day fills, first remove twenty-nine.
If the small remainder of the new moon of the subsequent conjunction month does not fill four hundred ninety-nine,
then subtract one day.
Designate the remainder as before.
To find the degree of conjunction:
Add the accumulated degree and degree remainder to the current result.
For every full day's degree coefficient obtained, add it to the degrees.
Designate it as before.
Crossing Dǒu (斗) is removed according to the circumference ratio.
For Mù (木):
When it is in morning occultation,
it is sixteen days and seven thousand three hundred twenty and a half parts.
It travels two degrees and thirteen thousand eight hundred eleven parts.
It is thirteen-odd degrees behind the sun,
and appears in the east.
When it appears direct,
the sun travels eleven parts of fifty-eight degree parts.
In fifty-eight days, it travels eleven degrees.
When it is faint,
the sun travels nine parts.
In fifty-eight days, it travels nine degrees.
It remains stationary,
for twenty-five days.
It retrogrades,
the sun travels one part of seven degree parts.
In eighty-four days, it retrogrades twelve degrees.
It remains stationary again,
for twenty-five days.
It resumes direct motion,
in fifty-eight days, it travels nine degrees.
Then, in another fifty-eight days, it travels eleven degrees.

The ecliptic's distance from the pole,
the generation of sun's shadow,
is based on instruments and gnomons.
The generation of water clock divisions [kè],
uses the difference in distance from the pole multiplied by the difference in solar terms.
If the distance difference is one kè,
it is used to increase or decrease each other.
The generation of dawn and dusk,
multiply the celestial dù by the day kè of the water clock,
subtract
the night kè, divide by two hundred to make one,
this is the fixed dù.
Subtract this from the celestial dù,
the remainder is dawn;
add one fixed dù for dusk.
Its remainder is quartered.
According to the method, it is "minor" (shǎo).
Two is "half" (bàn),
three is "major" (tài).
If it does not divide evenly,
it is tripled.
According to the method, it is "strong" (qiáng);
if the remainder is half of the divisor or more, it also counts as "strong".
Three "strong" make a "minor" (shǎo),
four "minor" make a dù.
Two "strong" make a "minor weak" (shǎo ruò).
Also, use the remaining dù of the sun as "minor strong",
and add it to each.
The central star is determined by the sun's position.
The sun's movement completes a cycle in four years.
Take the requested year's remaining *èrshísì qì* (二十四氣) and multiply by four.
Following the method, determine *shǎo* (少) and *dà* (大).
If there's a remainder,
multiply by three.
Following the method, determine *qiáng* (強) and *ruò* (弱).
Subtract this from the *jiéqì hūnmíng* (節氣昬明) central star,
and each is thereby determined.
*Qiáng* (強) means
positive;
*ruò* (弱) means
negative.
When *qiáng* (強) and *ruò* (弱) are subtracted from each other,
same signs are subtracted,
different signs are added.
Adding *shǎo* (少) to *qiáng* (強) makes it *ruò* (弱);
subtracting *shǎo* (少) from *ruò* (弱) makes it *qiáng* (強).
From the *Shàngyuán* (上元) when *Tàisuì* (太歲) was in *Gēngchén* (庚辰)
until the third year of *Xīpíng* (熹平),
when *suì* (歲) was in *Jiǎyín* (甲寅),
there have been 9,455 years accumulated.
A commentary states: The *Yì* (易) has the *Tàijí* (太極),
which gives rise to the *Liǎngyí* (兩儀).
The division of the *Liǎngyí* (兩儀) is ancient;
then came *Huángxī* (皇犧).
When *Huángxī* (皇犧) possessed the world,
there were no written records or calculations.
As eras passed,
reaching *Huángdì* (黃帝),
he displayed and promulgated writings.
*Zhònglí* (重黎) recorded and annotated,
images corresponded to famous writings,
beginning and end verified each other.
Standards and measurements traced back to the origin,
and then calendrical calculations were established.
Heaven is hard to trust,
which is why from the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns (五、三) until today,
each has had revisions and new creations,
not universally applicable.
Thus, *Huángdì* (黃帝) created the calendar,
with its *yuán* (元) starting in *Xīnmǎo* (辛卯).
*Zhuānxū* (顓頊) used *Yǐmǎo* (乙卯).
*Yú* (虞) used *Wùwǔ* (戊午).
*Xià* (夏) used *Bǐngyín* (丙寅).
*Yīn* (殷) used *Jiǎyín* (甲寅).
*Zhōu* (周) used *Dīngsì* (丁巳).
*Lǔ* (魯) used *Gēngzǐ* (庚子).
The Hàn (漢) dynasty rose, inheriting from the Qín (秦),
initially using *Yǐmǎo* (乙卯).
By the *Yuánfēng* (元封) era of Emperor Wǔ (武),
it no longer aligned with Heaven.
So, astrologers were assembled to create the *Tàichū Lì* (太初曆),
with its *yuán* (元) in *Dīngchǒu* (丁丑).
During the time of Wáng Mǎng (王莽),
Líu Xīn (劉歆) created the *Sāntǒng* (三統),
tracing back thirty-one *yuán* (元) before *Tàichū* (太初),
arriving at the year *Gēngxū* (庚戌) when the five planets converged,
which he took as the *Shàngyuán* (上元).
The *Tàichū Lì* (太初曆) by the *Yuánhé* (元和) era of Emperor Zhāng (章)
again became imprecise.
Capable astrologers were summoned to examine and compare various calendars,
to determine the new moon and verify the origin.
Tracing back to the forty-fifth year of Hàn (漢), the year *Gēngchén* (庚辰),
and adjusting the new moon by one day,
it then aligned with Heaven.
This was taken as the *Sìfēn Lì* (四分曆) *yuán* (元).
Adding 605 *yuán* (元) and one *jì* (紀),
it reaches *Gēngshēn* (庚shen).
There is a proximity to the *wěi* (緯) (apocryphal texts),
but the *suì* (歲) does not correspond to *shètí* (攝提) (Jupiter's position).
This allowed calendar experts to open their discussions,
but its *yuán* (元) rarely matched the *wěi* (緯).
If it did match, it might not be obtained from Heaven.
However, the rise and fall of calendars
are judged by their precision,
and thus are not solely dependent on the *yuán* (元).
In the first year of *Guānghé* (光和),
Counsellor Cài Yōng (蔡邕) and Gentleman Líu Hóng (劉洪) supplemented and continued the Treatise on Harmonics and Calendars (*Lǜlì Zhì*, 律曆志).
Cài Yōng (蔡邕) was skilled in writing,
and in the clear and turbid tones of the pitch-pipes (*zhōnglǜ*, 鍾律).
Líu Hóng (劉洪) was skilled in calculation,
and in expounding on the three luminaries (*sānguāng*, 三光).
Now, examining their work,
their ideas are broadly comprehensive,
and their mathematical methods are generally presented.
Therefore, they are compiled into upper and lower parts,
continuing the previous treatise,
to complete a single family's work.

Commentary: Lǐ Ruì's (李銳) explanation cited in the *Jíjiě*
states that these equatorial degrees are the stellar distances of the *Tàichū* (太初) method as seen in the *Sāntǒngshù* (三統術).
They have been continuously used from the Hàn (漢) dynasty onwards.
It was not until the Dàyǎnshù (大衍術) of the Táng (唐) dynasty that the four mansions Bì (畢), Zī (觜), Shēn (參), and Guǐ (鬼) were changed.
The Later Hàn (後漢) adopted the Sìfēn (四分) method
but did not revise the measurements,
so the degrees of these two mansions should not differ from the *Sāntǒngshù* (三統術).
The current text's "危十六" (*wēishíliù*) and "壁十" (*bìshí*)
are incorrect due to their relation to the ecliptic degrees in the following text.

Page 3079, line 2: zhàng (丈).
After "zhàng" (丈),
the original text had the four characters
"sì cùn èr fēn" (四寸二分).
The jíjiě (集解) quotes Lǐ Ruì's (李銳) explanation,
stating that upon investigation, Zǔ Chōngzhī's (祖沖之) method for the shadow length at the two solstices is consistent with this.
The shadow lengths for the qi (氣) before and after these solstices
are obtained by adding the shadow lengths before and after these solstices in pairs
and then taking half.
For example, according to this method, the shadow length for Dàxuě (大雪) is one zhàng (丈) two chǐ (尺) five cùn (寸) six fēn (分),
and for Xiǎohán (小寒) it is two chǐ (尺) three cùn (寸).
Adding them and halving them
yields Zǔ Chōngzhī's (祖沖之) method for Dàxuě (大雪) and Xiǎohán (小寒) shadow lengths, which is one zhàng (丈) two chǐ (尺) four cùn (寸) three fēn (分).
Upon re-examining this text,
only the Lìdōng (立冬) qi (氣) does not match.
According to Zǔ Chōngzhī (祖沖之), the sìfēnzhì (四分志) states that the mid-shadow length for Lìdōng (立冬) is one zhàng (丈),
and for Lìchūn (立春) it is nine chǐ (尺) six cùn (寸).
Adding them and halving them
yields nine chǐ (尺) eight cùn (寸),
which perfectly matches Zǔ Chōngzhī's (祖沖之) method for Lìchūn (立春) and Lìdōng (立冬) shadow lengths.
Therefore, the text's shadow length for Lìdōng (立冬), one zhàng (丈) four cùn (寸) two fēn (分),
is an erroneous addition of the four characters
"sì cùn èr fēn" (四寸二分).
It has now been directly deleted.

Rites and Ceremonies: New Moon, Beginning of Spring, Five Offerings, Imperial Tomb Visit, Capping, Evening Sacrifice, Plowing, Gāoméi (高禖) Sacrifice, Care for the Elderly, First Silkworms, Purification Rites.
Indeed, dignified deportment
is what distinguishes ruler and minister,
and orders the six kin.
If a ruler lacks the dignity of a ruler,
and a minister lacks the decorum of a minister,
then superiors will be negligent and inferiors will usurp their place—
this is called great disorder.
When great disorder arises,
all living beings suffer its calamities;
how can one not be cautious?
Therefore, records of the enforcement of dignified deportment
are made into the Treatise on Rites and Ceremonies.
Regarding the rites of dignified deportment:
on the first day of each month,
the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ, 太史) presents the calendar for that month;
the officials in charge (Yǒusī, 有司), the Attendant Censors (Shìláng, 侍郎), and the Palace Secretaries (Shàngshū, 尚書) observe and read the decree,
and uphold and execute its policies.
Two days before and after the new moon,
sheep and wine are brought to the altars of the local earth god (shè, 社) to sacrifice to the sun.
If there is an anomaly in the sun,
a sheep is slaughtered to offer to the earth god (shè, 社),
to avert the solar anomaly.
Those performing the rites wear long caps,
black single garments,
crimson collars and sleeves [edged] with green,
and crimson trousers,
to perform the ceremony
as per established practice.
On the day of the Beginning of Spring (Lìchūn, 立春),
before five *kè* (刻) of the night watch have passed,
all officials in the capital wear green robes.
Officials from commanderies, kingdoms, counties, and circuits, down to the lowest-ranking *dǒushí lìngshǐ* (斗食令史), all wear green headcloths,
erect green banners,
and place clay oxen and plowing figures outside their gates,
to show the common people,
until the Beginning of Summer (Lìxià, 立夏).
Only military officials do not follow this practice.
On the day of the Beginning of Spring (Lìchūn, 立chūn),
a broad edict is issued, stating:
“An imperial edict to the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng, 三公): as spring begins and the eastern work (farming) commences,
respect the beginning and be cautious of small matters;
let all actions follow this.
For crimes not punishable by death,
do not investigate or try them for now;
all must await the autumn harvest.
Dismiss the corrupt and cruel,
promote the gentle and good,
and appoint those who should be employed
as per established practice.”
On the first *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) or *bǐngzǐ* (丙子) day of the first month,
sacrifices are made at the Southern Suburb (Nánjiāo, 南郊).
After the rites,
they proceed to the Northern Suburb (Běijiāo, 北郊),
the Bright Hall (Míngtáng, 明堂),
the Supreme Ancestor's Temple (Gāomiào, 高廟),
and the Temple of Shìzǔ (世祖).
These are called the Five Offerings (Wǔgòng, 五供).
After the Five Offerings (Wǔgòng, 五供),
they proceed to visit the imperial tombs (shànglíng, 上陵) in sequence.
The Western Capital (Xīdū, 西都) formerly had the practice of visiting imperial tombs.
For the ceremonies in the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū, 東都),
all officials, women from the four noble families, princesses, grandees of the imperial princes,
envoys and princely attendants from foreign nations, and comptrollers from commanderies and kingdoms gather at the imperial tombs.
When the daytime clepsydra reaches its mark,
the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Dàhónglú, 大鴻臚) arranges the nine ranks of guests,
who stand in front of the sleeping hall.
When the bell rings,
the Ushers (Yèzhě, 謁者) manage the rites and lead the guests,
and the assembled officials take their positions as prescribed.
The emperor's carriage descends from the east wing,
the Grand Master of Rituals (Tàicháng, 太常) leads the procession out,
faces west and bows,
then turns and ascends the eastern steps (zuòjiē, 阼階),
and bows to the spirit seats.
He retires and sits in the east wing,
facing west.
The Palace Attendants (Shìzhōng, 侍中), Palace Secretaries (Shàngshū, 尚書), and attendants at the steps (bìzhě, 陛者) all stand behind the spirit seats.
The dukes, ministers, and assembled officials pay respects to the spirit seats.
The Grand Provisioner (Tàiguān, 太官) presents food,
and the Grand Master of Rituals (Tàicháng, 太常) has music played for the food offering (shíjǔ, 食舉),
performing the dances of Wénshǐ (文始) and the Five Phases (Wǔxíng, 五行).
When the music ends,
and the assembled officials have received and finished the bestowed food,
the comptrollers from the commanderies and kingdoms advance in sequence,
standing before the spirit portal to report the grain prices in their respective commanderies [and kingdoms],
the sufferings of the people,
wishing the spirits to know their movements and conditions.
A filial son serves his parents with complete decorum,
with a heart of reverence and love.
This is thoroughly in accordance with the rites.
Finally, after personally visiting the tombs,
the comptrollers are dispatched and given belts and ornaments.
In the eighth month, during the *zhòu* (酎) offering,
there is also a visit to the imperial tombs (shànglíng, 上陵),
and the rites are similar.
In general, for fasting (zhāi, 齋):
for Heaven and Earth, seven days;
for ancestral temples, mountains, and rivers, five days;
for minor sacrifices, three days.
If there is defilement within the fasting period,
the fasting is suspended,
and the deputy (fùcuì, 副倅) performs the rites.
One day before fasting,
if there is defilement or a calamity,
the fasting and sacrifice are performed as prescribed.
For a great mourning,
only for the sacrifices to Heaven and the suburban altars (tiānojiāo, 天郊) does one proceed with fasting even if wearing mourning ropes;
for sacrifices to Earth and below, one fasts only after one hundred days,
as per established practice.
The first *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) or *bǐngzǐ* (丙子) day of the first month is an auspicious day,
suitable for the capping ceremony (jiāyuánfú, 加元服).
The ceremony follows the capping rites.
The emperor first wears a black cloth "Progressing Sage" (jìnxián, 進賢) cap,
next the "Sparrow's Beak" (juébàn, 爵弁) cap,
next the "Martial Cap" (wǔbàn, 武弁),
and next the "Reaching Heaven" (tōngtiān, 通天) cap.
After the capping,
all proceed to the Temple of Gāozǔ (高祖廟) to pay respects according to the rites.
Princes and dukes and those below them
only wear the "Progressing Sage" (jìnxián, 進賢) cap for their first capping.
In the first month,
for the suburban sacrifice to Heaven,
the animals were sacrificed in the evening.
Eighteen *kè* after the beginning of the fifth *kè* before the end of daylight,
and eight *kè* after the beginning of the fifth *kè* before the end of night,
the cooked offerings were presented.
The Grand Supplicator (Tàizhù) escorted [the offerings],
then turned back.
All proceeded to the pyre site.
The Chief Sacrificer (Zǎizhù) raised fire to burn the firewood.
When the fire ignited,
the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) bowed twice.
He rose.
The officers-in-charge (Yǒusī) announced that the ritual was complete.
For the Evening Sacrifices (Xīshēng) at the Míngtáng, the Five Suburbs (Wǔjiāo), the Ancestral Temples (Zōngmiào), the Grand Altar of Land and Grain (Tàishèjì), and the Six Zōng (Liùzōng),
all were performed eighteen *kè* after the beginning of the fifth *kè* before the end of daylight,
and eight *kè* after the beginning of the fifth *kè* before the end of night.
The cooked offerings were presented,
the spirits were escorted away,
and then [the participants] returned.
The officers-in-charge (Yǒusī) announced that the ritual was complete.
For the burning sacrifice (Fánliáo) to the Six Zōng (Liùzōng),
when the fire burned brightly,
the officers-in-charge (Yǒusī) announced that the ritual was complete.
In the first month, cultivation began.
When the water clock reached its highest point and began to descend,
the officials-in-charge (Zhíshì) announced the sacrifice to the First Farmer (Xiānnóng),
which had already been offered.
At the time of plowing,
the officers-in-charge (Yǒusī) requested to proceed with the ceremony.
They went to the plowing position.
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ), the Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng), the Nine Ministers (Jiǔqīng), the feudal lords (Zhūhóu), and all the officials (Bǎiguān) plowed in sequence.
When the diligent farmers (Lìtián) had finished sowing and harrowing,
the officers-in-charge (Yǒusī) announced that the ritual was complete.
The seasonal ordinance for this month stated:
"The Grand Administrators (Shǒuxiàng) of the commanderies (Jùn) and kingdoms (Guó) shall all encourage the people to begin plowing,
according to the established rites.
All travels and entries/exits shall be accompanied by the ringing of bells,
and the playing of music.
If there are disasters or misfortunes,
or other special circumstances,
such as requesting rain or stopping rain,
bells shall not be rung,
nor shall music be played."
In the middle month of spring,
a sacrifice to Gāoméi (Gāoméi Cí) was established south of the city,
with a single animal as offering.
In the third month of the second year of the Yǒngpíng (Yǒngpíng) reign of Emperor Míng (Míngdì),
the Emperor (Shàng) first led his officials to personally attend to the Three Elders (Sānlǎo) and Five Supervisors (Wǔgēng) at the Pìyōng.
The Grand Archery Ceremony (Dàshè Dàlǐ) was performed.
The commanderies (Jùn), counties (Xiàn), and districts (Dào) held village drinking ceremonies (Xiāngyǐnjǐu) at schools,
all sacrificing to the Sacred Teachers Duke Zhōu (Zhōugōng) and Kǒngzǐ,
using dogs as sacrificial animals.
Thereupon, the rituals and music for the Seven Suburbs (Qījiāo) and the meaning of the Three Yōng (Sānyōng) were complete.
The ceremony for attending to the Three Elders (Sānlǎo) and Five Supervisors (Wǔgēng) involved:
First, selecting an auspicious day.
The Minister of Education (Sītú) would present names of former Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng) who served as Grand Tutors (Tàifù) or Lecturers (Jiǎngshī).
One person with outstanding virtue, conduct, and advanced age would be chosen as an Elder (Lǎo),
and another, next in line, as a Supervisor (Gēng).
They all wore large, unlined robes of fine ramie (Dūzhù Dàpáo Dānyī),
with a black-edged collar and sleeves on their inner garment (Zhōngyī),
a 'Recommending the Worthy' (Jìnxián) cap,
and a king-staff (Wángzhàng).
The Five Supervisors (Wǔgēng) also dressed similarly,
but without staffs.
They all observed a fast in the lecture hall of the Grand Academy (Tàixué Jiǎngtáng).
On that day,
the Emperor's chariot (Chéngyú) would first arrive at the ritual hall of the Pìyōng (Pìyōng Lǐdiàn).
The Emperor (Yù) would sit in the east wing.
Envoys were dispatched with comfortable carriages (Ānchē) to welcome the Three Elders (Sānlǎo) and Five Supervisors (Wǔgēng).
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) would welcome them at the screen-gate (Ménpíng),
exchanging greetings.
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) proceeded from the eastern steps (Zuòjiē),
while the Three Elders (Sānlǎo) ascended from the guest steps (Bīnjiē).
Upon reaching the steps,
the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) bowed as per ritual.
The Three Elders (Sānlǎo) ascended,
facing east.
The Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng) set up their mats,
the Nine Ministers (Jiǔqīng) adjusted their shoes.
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) personally bared his arm to cut the sacrificial animal,
holding the sauce to offer food,
and holding the goblet to offer drink.
The *Zhùgěng* (a type of offering) was placed in front,
and the *Zhùyì* (another type of offering) was placed behind.
The Five Supervisors (Wǔgēng) faced south.
The Ducal Ministers (Gōng) advanced with the ritual offerings,
also in a similar manner.
The next day, all went to the Imperial Palace (Quē) to express gratitude,
because they had been accorded such a greatly honored and distinguished reception.
In this month,
the Empress (Huánghòu) led the wives of the Ducal Ministers (Gōngqīng) and feudal lords (Zhūhóu) in sericulture (Cánsī).
A sacrifice was made to the First Silkworm Goddess (Xiāncán),
with the rite of the 'Lesser Sacrifice' (Shǎoláo).
On the Shàngsì (Shàngsì) day of this month,
officials and commoners (Guānmín) all purified themselves by bathing in the eastward-flowing water,
calling it 'great purification' (Dàjié), which meant washing away old grime and ailments.
Purification (Jié)
refers to the spreading forth of Yang energy,
all things having emerged,
and thus being purified.

Rituals for the establishment of summer (Lìxià), requesting rain (Qǐngyǔ), audience with the Crown Prince (Bàihuángtàizǐ), audience with kings and dukes (Bàiwánggōng), peach charms (Táoyìn), yellow suburban sacrifice (Huángjiāo), establishment of autumn (Lìqiū), chūliú (Chūliú) ritual, household sacrifice to stars (Ànhù Cíxīng), establishment of winter (Lìdōng), winter solstice (Dōngzhì), Làyī (Làyī) festival, Grand Exorcism (Dànuó), clay ox (Tǔniú), dispatching palace guards (Qiǎnwèishì), and court assemblies (Cháohuì).
On the day of the Establishment of Summer (Lìxià),
five *kè* before the end of night,
all officials in the capital (Jīngdū) wore red,
changing to yellow in late summer,
for the suburban sacrifice (Jiāo).
The ritual involved a single offering,
and a sacrifice to the Stove God (Jìzào).
From the Establishment of Spring (Lìchūn) until the Establishment of Autumn (Lìqiū),
commandery (Jùn) and kingdom (Guó) officials reported on rainfall.
If it was scarce,
the prefectures (Fǔ), commanderies (Jùn), and counties (Xiàn) would each clean their Altars of Land and Grain (Shèjì).
If there was a drought,
the Ducal Ministers (Gōngqīng) and officials-in-charge (Guānzhǎng) would successively perform the *yú* ritual (Yúlǐ) to pray for rain.
They would close all Yang places (Zhūyáng),
wear black,
raise clay dragons,
and set up clay figures with two rows of child dancers (Wǔtóng Èryì).
This was changed every seven days, as per established practice.
They would reverse, bind the Altar of Land (Shè) with red ropes,
and beat red drums.
Prayers and thanksgiving sacrifices (Dǎosài) were offered with the 'Lesser Sacrifice' (Shǎoláo) as per ritual.
The ceremony for an audience with the Crown Prince (Bàihuángtàizǐ):
All officials (Bǎiguān) assembled.
Once positions were set, the herald (Yèzhě) led the Crown Prince (Huángtàizǐ) to stand below the Imperial Throne (Yùzuò Diànxià),
facing north.
The Minister of Works (Sīkōng) stood northwest of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ),
facing east.
After the imperial edict (Cèshū) was read,
the Palace Regular Attendant (Zhōngchángshì) held the Crown Prince's seal and ribbon (Huángtàizǐ Xǐshòu) and handed it to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ), facing east.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) bowed twice,
and thrice kowtowed.
The herald (Yèzhě) announced: "Your servant [name] (Chén Mǒu), the Crown Prince (Huángtàizǐ)..."
The Inner Herald (Zhōng Yèzhě) declared the imperial command (Zhì) saying,
"Granted."
The Three Ducal Ministers (Sāngōng) ascended the steps to the main hall,
offering congratulations and wishing ten thousand years.
Thereupon, a general amnesty (Dàshè Tiānxià) was declared.
After the offerings and bestowals (Gōngcì) and rituals were complete,
the assembly dispersed.
The ceremony for an audience with the feudal kings and dukes (Bài Zhūhóu Wánggōng):
The Stone Officials (Shíguān) assembled.
Once positions were set, the herald (Yèzhě) led the Superintendent of the Imperial Household (Guānglùxūn) forward.
The herald (Yèzhě) led the one to be appointed forward,
who would sit prostrate below the hall.
The Superintendent of the Imperial Household (Guānglùxūn) came forward,
bowed once,
raised his hand and said:
"An imperial edict (Zhìzhào) commands that so-and-so (Mǒu) be appointed as so-and-so (Mǒu)."
After the imperial edict (Cèshū) was read,
the herald (Yèzhě) declared: "Your servant [name] (Chén Mǒu) bows twice."
The Secretary of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshūláng) handed the seal, stamp, and ribbon (Xǐ Yìnshòu) to the Imperial Censor (Shìyùshǐ).
The Imperial Censor (Shìyùshǐ) came forward,
faced east,
and handed over the seal, stamp, and ribbon (Xǐ Yìnshòu).
The king or duke (Wánggōng) bowed twice and kowtowed thrice.
The herald (Zàn Yèzhě) said:
"King [name] (Mǒu Wáng Chén Mǒu) has been newly enfeoffed;
Duke [name] (Mǒu Gōng Mǒu) has been newly appointed.
Offer thanks."
The Inner Herald (Zhōng Yèzhě) replied: "Respectfully accepts thanks."
The herald (Zànzhě) stood and said:
"The Emperor (Huángdì) rises for the duke."
They reseated themselves.
The recipient of the edict bowed in thanks.
He rose and returned to his position.
After the offerings and bestowals (Gōngcì) and rituals were complete,
the assembly dispersed.
In the middle month of summer,
all myriad things are flourishing.
On the summer solstice,
Yīn energy begins to sprout,
fearing that things might not fully thrive.
Its ritual: red ropes are used to tie together pungent vegetables,
and a large bell is adorned with mugwort.
A peachwood seal, six cùn long
and three cùn square,
is inscribed with characters in five colors according to the proper method,
and placed on doors and windows.
Generations substitute with whatever they value as decoration.
The Xiàhóu Shì, associating with the Metal element,
made rush reeds,
symbolizing the intermingling of energy.
The Yīn people, associating with the Water element,
used a snail's head,
being careful about its closure and obstruction,
making it like a snail.
The Zhōu people, associating with the Wood element,
used peachwood for a change,
symbolizing the mutual change of energies.
The Hàn dynasty used both,
hence on the fifth day of the fifth month,
red ropes and five-colored seals were used as door decorations,
to ward off evil qì.
On the summer solstice,
it was forbidden to light large fires,
stop charcoal smelting and casting,
and completely cease all saltpeter refining.
This continued until the beginning of autumn,
following the customary practice.
On this day, wells were dredged and water was changed.
It is said that on the winter solstice,
fire was drilled and changed.
Eighteen days before the beginning of autumn,
a suburban sacrifice was offered to Huángdì.
On this day, before the fifth kě of the night clepsydra had ended,
all officials in the capital wore yellow.
At the beginning of autumn,
they welcomed the qì in the yellow suburbs,
played music with the Gōng mode of Huángzhōng,
sang Dì Lín,
wore ceremonial caps, held shields and battle-axes,
and danced the Yúnqiáo and Yùmìng,
to nurture and instruct the season.
On the day of the beginning of autumn,
before the fifth kě of the night clepsydra had ended,
all officials in the capital wore white,
with black collars and bordered inner garments,
welcoming the qì in the white suburbs.
After the ceremony,
they all wore crimson
until the beginning of winter.
On the day of the beginning of autumn,
after the ceremony in the white suburbs,
they began to display military might,
slaughtering sacrificial animals at the east gate of the suburbs,
to offer them to the imperial tombs and ancestral temples.
The ritual: the imperial carriage rode in a war chariot,
drawn by white horses with red manes,
and the emperor personally held a crossbow to shoot the sacrificial animal.
The sacrificial animal was a fawn.
The Tàizǎi Lìng and one Yèzhě each
loaded it onto a hunting cart,
and galloped to deliver it to the imperial tombs and ancestral temples.
Then the imperial carriage returned to the palace,
and envoys were dispatched with bundles of silk to bestow upon military officials.
Military officials practiced military drills,
trained in battle formations and the ritual of slaughtering animals,
which was called Chúliú.
Soldiers and officials all practiced Sūn Wú's sixty-four military formations,
named Chéngzhī.
At the beginning of spring,
envoys were dispatched with bundles of silk to bestow upon civil officials.
The ritual of Chúliú: a sacrifice was offered to the Xīanyú.
After the officiant announced that the Xīanyú sacrifice was completed,
when the fresh meat was being cooked,
the supervisor made an announcement,
then retreated to shoot the animal.
When the hunting cart arrived,
the supervisor announced that the ritual was completed.
In the middle month of autumn,
all counties and districts checked households and enumerated the people.
Those aged seventy years or older at the beginning of the year
were bestowed with the royal staff,
and fed with gruel.
For those aged eighty and ninety,
there were additional ritual gifts.
The royal staff was nine chǐ long,
adorned at the tip with a dove.
The dove
is a bird that does not choke.
This was to wish that the elderly would not choke.
In this month,
the Lǎorén Xīng was sacrificed at the Lǎorén Temple in the southern suburbs of the capital.
In the last month of autumn,
a sacrifice was offered to the stars at the Xīnxīng Temple on the southern suburban altar in the city.
On the day of the beginning of winter,
before the fifth kě of the night clepsydra had ended,
all officials in the capital wore black,
welcoming the qì in the black suburbs.
After the ceremony,
they all wore crimson
until the winter solstice, when all affairs ceased.
Around the winter solstice,
the gentleman settled his body and calmed his mind,
all officials ceased their affairs,
did not attend to governance,
and only resumed matters after selecting an auspicious day.
On the day when affairs ceased,
before the fifth kě of the night clepsydra had ended,
all officials in the capital wore crimson
until the beginning of spring.
For all five seasonal changes of attire,
those in charge always performed them one day before or after the designated time.
On the winter solstice and summer solstice,
when the lengths of the Yīn and Yáng shadows reach their extremes,
is where subtle qì is born.
Therefore, eight capable scholars were employed,
some playing the Yu instrument to the Huángzhōng pitch;
some striking the Huángzhōng bell;
some measuring shadows and their lengths,
weighing the lightness and heaviness of water,
one shēng of water
weighs thirteen liǎng heavier in winter;
some striking the Huángzhōng qìng;
some playing the Huángzhōng sè,
with nine chǐ between the bridges,
twenty-five strings,
the Gōng note in the middle,
and Shāng, Zhǐ, Jué, Yǔ on its left and right;
some striking the Huángzhōng drum.
Three days beforehand,
the Tàishǐ announced it.
On the day itself,
in summer, the four first months (of the seasons),
in winter, the four middle months (of the seasons),
their qì arrives.
When the *qì* first arrives at the fifth *kè*,
the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐ Lìng) and the eight accomplished scholars (Bā Neng zhī Shì)
take their seats in the west side-hall of the Duānmén. The Grand Musician (Dàyǔ) arranges the musical instruments,
red in summer and black in winter,
arrayed in front of the front hall, westward from the east.
The bell is at the end.
The Palace Guard (Shǒugōng) sets up mats to the south of the instruments,
facing north with the east side as superior.
Zhèngdé's mat is placed,
facing west to the south of the drums.
The gnomon (guǐyí) is placed to the northeast.
At the third *kè*,
the Central Yellow Gate (Zhōng Huángmén) holding weapons,
leads the Grand Astrologer and the eight accomplished scholars in through the Duānmén,
to take their positions.
At the second *kè*,
the Attendants-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng), Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū), Imperial Censors (Yùshǐ), and Palace Attendants (Yèzhě) all ascend the steps.
At the first *kè*,
the imperial carriage (chéngyú) personally arrives at the balcony,
and the emperor sits calmly to listen.
The Grand Astrologer advances,
kneeling facing north beneath the eaves of the balcony.
He raises his hands and says:
"The eight accomplished scholars are ready.
Please proceed with the ceremony."
The edict says:
"Granted."
The Grand Astrologer bows his head to the ground and says:
"Understood."
He stands up and retreats a little,
then looks at Zhèngdé and orders:
"You may proceed with the ceremony."
Zhèngdé says:
"Understood."
They all turn and return to their positions.
Zhèngdé stands,
and orders the eight accomplished scholars:
"Proceed in order,
tuning the notes with the *yú*."
The eight accomplished scholars say:
"Understood."
Each of the five notes is played thirty times, forming a movement (quē).
Zhèngdé says:
"Combine the five musical modes (wǔyīn lǜ)."
First, one sings,
then the five notes play simultaneously,
for twenty-five movements,
all tuned with the *yú*.
When finished,
Zhèngdé says:
"Let each of the eight accomplished scholars state their affairs."
Each of the eight accomplished scholars writes their statement on a tablet.
The text reads:
"Your servant [name] states that
on the [number] day of this month, on the *jiǎyǐ* day, it is the Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì).
The note of Huángzhōng is harmonious,
the ruler's way (jūndào) is attained,
and filial piety (xiàodào) is praised."
There is one tablet each for the *shāng* (officials),
*jué* (people),
*zhǐ* (affairs),
*yǔ* (things).
If not, the Grand Astrologer is summoned to write on each tablet,
sealed in a black bag (zàonáng),
and sent to the west steps (xī bì).
Kneeling, it is handed to the Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū),
who places it facing the balcony,
bowing his head to the ground facing north,
and then bows as he presents the sealed memorial (fēngshì).
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat hands it to the Attendant-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng) or Regular Attendant (Chángshì) who receives it,
and reports the news.
This is regulated by the banner (fānhuī) and tally (jié) of the Lesser Yellow Gate (Xiǎo Huángmén).
The Grand Astrologer advances and declares
the ceremony (lǐ) is complete.
The edict says:
"Granted."
The Grand Astrologer advances and bows his head to the ground, saying:
"Understood."
The Grand Astrologer orders the eight accomplished scholars to proceed to the Grand Provisioner (Tàiguān) to receive rewards.
Those on the steps (bì zhě) withdraw in order.
The ceremony for the Summer Solstice (Xiàzhì) is also like this.
In the month of late winter (jìdōng),
when the stars revolve and the year ends,
and yin and yang intersect,
farmers are rewarded with the grand Làyàn feast.
One day before the Làyàn,
a grand Exorcism (Dà Nuó) is held,
called "Chasing Away Epidemics" (Zhuí Yì).
The ceremony is as follows: youths are selected from among the sons of the Central Yellow Gate (Zhōng Huángmén), aged ten to twelve,
one hundred and twenty of them, to be the exorcist boys (zhuìzǐ).
They all wear red headbands (chìzé) and black uniforms (zàozhì),
and carry large drums (dàtáo).
The Fāngxiāngshì (Exorcist in Chief) has four golden eyes,
is covered in bearskin,
wears a dark tunic and red skirt,
and carries a spear and shield.
The twelve beasts have fur, clothes, and horns.
The Central Yellow Gate directs them,
and the Assistant Chief of Retainers (Rǒngcóng Púyè) leads them,
to chase evil ghosts out of the forbidden palace.
When the night clepsydra's (yèlòu) water rises,
the court officials assemble.

The Attendants-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng), Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū), Imperial Censors (Yùshǐ), Palace Attendants (Yèzhě), Tiger Guards (Hǔbēn), and Feathered Forest Cadets (Yǔlín Lángjiàng) are on duty,
all wearing red headbands and guarding the steps.
The imperial carriage (chéngyú) proceeds to the front hall.
The Chief of the Yellow Gates (Huángmén Lìng) reports:
"The exorcist boys are ready.
Please proceed with chasing away epidemics."
Then the Central Yellow Gate takes the lead,
and the exorcist boys respond in chorus,
saying:
"Jiǎzuò eats ,
Féiwèi eats tigers,
Xióngbó eats demons,
Téngjiǎn eats misfortune,
Lǎnzū eats blame,
Bóqí eats dreams,
Qiángliáng and Zǔmíng together eat the executed and parasites,
Wěisuí eats *guān*,
Cuòduàn eats *jù*,
Qióngqí and Ténggēn together eat *gǔ* (poisonous vermin).
All these twelve gods are ordered to pursue the wicked and凶
burn your bodies,
tear your bones,
disjoint your flesh,
and pull out your lungs and intestines.
If you do not leave quickly,
you will become food for those who come after!"
Then the Fāngxiāngshì and the twelve beasts perform.
They shout and cheer,
making three rounds through the front and back palaces.
Holding torches,
they send the epidemic out through the Duānmén.
Outside the gate, the imperial cavalry (zōuqí) relay the torches out of the palace.
Outside the Sīmǎ Què Mén, the riders of the five camps (wǔyíng qíshì) relay the fire and discard it into the Luòshui river.
All government offices, after appointing a wooden-faced beast capable of acting as a Nuó master,
set up peach figures (táogěng), *yùléi*,
and reed matting (wěijiāo).
Then the officials on duty withdraw.
Reed halberds (wěijǐ) and peach staffs (táozhàng) are bestowed upon the dukes (gōng), ministers (qīng), generals (jiāngjūn), special marquises (tèhóu), and other marquises.
In this month,
six clay oxen (tǔniú) are set up in the *chǒu* direction outside the city walls of the national capital, commanderies, and counties,
to see off the great cold.
The ceremony for feasting and dispatching former palace guards (gù wèishì) is:
all officials assemble,
and when positions are taken, the Palace Attendant (Yèzhě) holding a tally (jié) leads the former palace guards in through the Duānmén.
The Palace Guard Cavalry Commander (Wèisīmǎ) holding a banner (fān) and gong (zhēng) escorts their procession.
When they are in position,
the Imperial Censor Attendant (Shì Yùshǐ) holding a tally (jié) expresses comfort and solicitude,
inquiring about their hardships with imperial grace,
and receives their memorials (zhāngzòu) and desired statements.
After the feast,
music is performed as a reward,
and they watch horn wrestling (jiǎodǐ).
When the music ends, they are dismissed,
and encouraged in agriculture and sericulture (nóngsāng).
At the beginning of each year (zhēngyuè),
a grand court audience (dàcháo) is held to receive congratulations.
The ceremony is: seven *kè* before the end of the night clepsydra's water,
the bell rings,
and congratulations are received.
Regarding the tribute (zhì):
dukes (gōng) and marquises (hóu) present jade disks (bì);
Ministers of Two Thousand Piculs (zhōng èrqiānshí) and Two Thousand Piculs (èrqiānshí) present lambs (gāo);
One Thousand Piculs (qiānshí) and Six Hundred Piculs (liùbǎishí) present geese (yàn);
Four Hundred Piculs (sìbǎishí) and below present pheasants (zhì).
All officials congratulate for the New Year.
Officials of Two Thousand Piculs and above ascend the hall and proclaim "Long Live!" (wànsuì).
They raise their cups before the imperial seat.
The Minister of Works (Sīkōng) offers soup (gēng),
and the Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng) offers rice (fàn),
and the "Music for Serving Food" (Shí Jǔ zhī Yuè) is played.
All officials receive a bestowed banquet (xīyàn xiǎng),
and grand music is performed.
Each new moon,
only on the first day of the tenth month is the old custom (gùshì) followed,
which was the month when Gāozǔ established Qín,
and the beginning of the first year.
Rites and ceremonies for great funerals, the death of feudal kings (zhūhóuwáng), enfeoffed marquises (lièhóu), noble persons (guìrén), and princesses (gōngzhǔ).
When the emperor was unwell,
the Grand Physicians-in-Chief and their assistants, along with medical practitioners,
would prepare and administer suitable medicines.
The supervisor of imperial tasting, trusted close officials, the Regular Palace Attendants, and the Junior Yellow Gates all tasted the medicine first,
with a twelve-fold excess.
The Dukes and Ministers, and court officials inquired about his health without interruption.
The Grand Commandant requested permission for the Southern Suburban Sacrifice;
the Minister over the Masses and the Minister of Works requested permission for the Ancestral Temple sacrifices;
and sacrifices were made to the Five Sacred Mountains, the Four Great Rivers, and all other deities,
all praying for blessings.
During illness,
the Dukes and Ministers again observed the proper rites.
In times of military alert,
the fierce tiger guards, the feather forest guards, and the gentlemen of the palace all kept strict vigil.
The palace and government offices were all on alert.
The Five Battalions of the Northern Army surrounded the palace with deployed troops.
The Prefect of the Yellow Gates, the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat, the Imperial Censor, and the ushers patrolled day and night.
The Three Excellencies reported on the color and condition of the emperor's hands, feet, and skin, as prescribed by ritual.
The Empress, Crown Prince, and Imperial Princes wept and leaped in mourning, as prescribed by ritual.
The bathing was conducted as prescribed by ritual.
The Prefect of the Imperial Storehouses, also serving as the Eastern Park Craftsman, brought women attendants.
Yellow floss silk, figured silk, gold embroidery, and jade burial coverings were used according to precedent.
Rice and containing pearls and jade in the mouth were performed as prescribed by ritual.
Ice was placed around the body as prescribed by ritual.
All officials wept below the palace hall.
On that night,
bamboo tallies were dispatched to inform the commanderies, kingdoms ruled by officials of two thousand *shí*, and kings.
Upon arrival of the bamboo tallies,
all prostrated themselves, wept, and expressed their deepest sorrow.
The minor shrouding was performed as prescribed by ritual.
The Eastern Park Craftsman and the Prefect of Manufacturing presented the secret instruments of the Eastern Park.
The outer coffin was painted red with patterns of dragons and serpents.
The funerary hearse was carved with images of the sun, moon, birds, turtles, dragons, tigers, continuous *bì* discs, and crescent moons.
The cypress outer coffin and catalpa inner coffin were made according to precedent.
The grand shrouding was performed between the two pillars.
The Five Officials, the left and right fierce tiger guards, and the five generals of the feather forest guards,
each led their respective divisions,
wielding fierce tiger halberds,
and were stationed at the ends of the palace hall, at the side wings of the main gate and the steps.
The Central Yellow Gates held weapons on the palace hall.
At nightfall,
the officials entered.
At daytime, when the water clock marked the hour,
the Grand Herald arranged the nine categories of guests,
who stood below the hall accordingly.
The ushers led the kings to stand below the hall,
facing west, with their superiors to the north.
Imperial clan members, various kings, and minor marquises of the four prominent clans were behind them,
facing west, with their superiors to the north.
The Master of Ceremonies led the Three Excellencies to their positions,
below the hall, facing north.
The Specially Advanced officials were next, followed by officials of the middle two thousand *shí* rank.
The enfeoffed marquises were next, followed by officials of the two thousand *shí* rank.
Officials of six hundred *shí* and the Erudites were behind them.
All officials attending as companions stood in double rows,
ascending westward.
When positions were settled,
the Grand Herald announced that all was ready.
The ushers reported it.
The Empress faced east.
The noble consorts, princesses, and imperial clan women stood behind her in order.
The Crown Prince and Imperial Princes were to the east,
facing west.
The younger Imperial Princes were set back to the south,
facing north. All prostrated themselves and wept.
The Grand Herald led the weeping,
and all officials wept.
The Three Excellencies ascended from the eastern steps,
placing the *guī* and *zhāng* jade tablets and other items inside the catalpa inner coffin.
Close officials assisted according to precedent.
The heir wept and leaped in mourning as prescribed by ritual.
The Eastern Park Craftsman and the warriors lowered the nails and cross-pieces,
cutting off the *yá* (tooth-like projections).
The Grand Master of Ceremonies presented the Grand Sacrifice of a whole ox.
The Supervisor of Food from the Grand Provisioner, the Central Yellow Gates, and the Supervisor of Imperial Meals presented their offerings in sequence.
Those performing duties acted according to ritual.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies and the Grand Herald led the weeping as prescribed.
The Three Excellencies presented the Imperial Edict of Succession from the *Shàngshū*.
The Crown Prince immediately ascended the Son of Heaven's throne before the coffin,
requesting that the Crown Prince assume the imperial throne,
and the Empress become the Empress Dowager.
This was approved.
All officials exited.
They re-entered in auspicious attire for the assembly, as prescribed.
The Grand Commandant ascended from the eastern steps,
prostrating himself to the north of the imperial seat by the coffin.
After reading the edict,
he knelt, facing east, and presented the Imperial Seal and ribbon to the Crown Prince,
who then assumed the imperial throne.
The Central Yellow Gates, in charge of weapons, presented the jade-handled sword, the *Suíhóu* pearl, and the dragon-slaying precious sword to the Grand Commandant,
who then announced it to all officials.
All officials prostrated themselves and shouted "Long live!"
Sometimes a great amnesty was granted throughout the empire.
Envoys were dispatched to issue an edict to open the city gates and palace gates,
and to dismiss the garrison troops.
The officials and all civil servants dispersed,
and entered to put on mourning attire as prescribed by ritual.
The military officials wore their military uniforms.
The Three Excellencies
and the Grand Master of Ceremonies observed the rituals.
According to precedent: all officials met for mourning once every five days.

Former officials, those of two thousand *shí* rank, Inspectors, and the Chief Clerks and Scribes for the annual reports from commanderies and kingdoms in the capital region, all met once every five days.
Officials and common people throughout the empire observed mourning for three days.
Two days before the burial,
all mourned in the morning and evening.
After the burial,
mourning attire was removed.
There were no prohibitions on marriage or sacrificial offerings.
Junior clerks and below
wore plain caps and headcloths,
with mourning bands no wider than three inches,
mourning in the courtyard.
Military officers wore plain headcloths and large caps.
The Grand Minister of Agriculture disbursed cash and grain,
providing the equivalent of six *zhàng* of cloth.
For the burial,
deep mourning lasted fifteen days,
light mourning fourteen days,
and minimal mourning seven days,
after which mourning attire was removed.

Provincial Inspectors, officials of two thousand *shí* rank, and enfeoffed marquises in their territories, as well as marquises of the Passes, and chief officials of the imperial clan, would submit memorials via the postal service.
Kings would send one *dàfū* to submit memorials.
Mourning officials requested postal relays with publicly posted reports,
and this was approved.
The hearse was made of wood,
nine *chǐ* high,
and wide enough for eight *lì* (carts),
wrapped in reed mats.
The canopy and mourning curtains for the gate were all made of bamboo mats.
All carts had their auxiliary side panels removed,
and were fitted with coarse cloth and simple wheels.
All runners wore plain headcloths.
The Grand Coachman drove a four-wheeled carriage with a long pole as the guest carriage,
with a canopy of coarse silk.
Twenty Central Yellow Gates and twenty fierce tiger guards each held ropes.
The Minister of Works selected the earth and dug the burial pit.
The Grand Astrologer divined the day.
Two ushers,
the Palace Usher Director and the Deputy Palace Usher, directed the work,
using an oiled figured silk tent to cover the pit.
Square stones were used to construct the *huángcháng tícuò biànfáng* as prescribed by ritual.
The imperial carriage,
Tài Pú (太僕) directs.
Fāng Xiàng Shì (方相氏) with four golden eyes,
covered in bear skin,
wearing a dark top and red skirt,
holding a spear and raising a shield,
stands on a four-horse chariot as the vanguard.
The banner's design,
three rèn (仞) long,
with twelve streamers,
trailing on the ground,
depicts the sun, moon, and a rising dragon,
with the inscription on the funereal banner reading
"Coffer of the Son of Heaven."
Two Yè Zhě (謁者) stand on six-horse chariots as the next in line.
The grand imperial procession for Gān Quán (甘泉) consists of official carriages and retinue,
including the Jīn Gēn Róng Chē (金根容車) (golden-rooted ceremonial carriage),
and the Lán Tái Fǎ Jià (蘭臺法駕) (Orchid Terrace standard carriage).
The funeral adornments for Dà Háng (大行) (the deceased emperor) are like those of the Jīn Gēn Chē (金根車).
The emperor attends the sending-off procession according to ritual.
Tài Cháng (太常) presents the memorial for the offering.
At the twentieth mark of the night clepsydra,
Tài Wèi (太尉) puts on a long cap,
wears fasting robes,
rides in a high chariot,
and stops at the gate outside the palace hall.
When the envoy arrives,
standing facing south,
Tài Wèi (太尉) advances, prostrates, bows, and receives the edict.
Tài Wèi (太尉) proceeds to the southern suburb.
Before the ninth mark is fully spent,
Dà Hóng Lú (大鴻臚) arranges the nine guests to stand in order,
the assembled officials enter their positions,
and Tài Wèi (太尉) performs the ritual.
All officers in charge wear long caps
and fasting robes.
Tài Zhù Lìng (太祝令) kneels and reads the eulogistic decree,
Tài Wèi (太尉) bows twice and prostrates his head.
The ritual official announces the completion of affairs.
Tài Wèi (太尉) respectfully holds the eulogistic decree,
returns to the Duān Mén (端門) (Front Gate) of the palace.
Tài Cháng (太常) performs the ancestral offering.
Zhōng Huáng Mén Shàng Yī (中黃門尚衣) (Chief of the Central Yellow Gate for Imperial Robes) respectfully places the robes on the Róng Gēn Chē (容根車).
The Dōng Yuán Wǔ Shì (東園武士) (Eastern Garden Warriors) carry Dà Háng (大行).
Sī Tú (司徒) (Minister of Education) walks backward and stands before the carriage.
The ritual official leads Tài Wèi (太尉) to his position,
the Dà Háng (大行) carriage is slightly south of west,
facing east to respectfully present the eulogistic decree,
Tài Shǐ Lìng (太史令) (Grand Astrologer) respectfully holds the mournful decree and stands behind.
Tài Cháng (太常) kneels and says
"Advance,"
the emperor advances.
Tài Wèi (太尉) reads the eulogistic decree,
and stores it in a golden casket.
The emperor's subsequent decrees are stored in the ancestral temple.
Tài Shǐ (太史) respectfully carries the mournful decree in a reed basket to the mausoleum.
Tài Wèi (太尉) turns and returns to his official position,
bows twice and stands (crying).
Tài Cháng (太常) kneels and says
"Weep,"
Dà Hóng Lú (大鴻臚) transmits the call to weep,
fifteen times raising their voices,
then stops weeping.
Tài Cháng (太常) performs the sending-off offering, all according to ritual.
The request to weep and stop weeping is as prescribed.
When the clepsydra indicates noon,
permission is requested to depart.
Sī Tú (司徒) and Hé Nán Yǐn (河南尹) (Magistrate of Hénán) first lead the turning of the carriage,
Tài Cháng (太常) kneels and says
"Please bow in farewell."
The carriage is adorned with white ropes and interwoven silk cords,
thirty zhàng (丈) long,
seven cùn (寸) in diameter for pulling,
in six rows,
with fifty people per row.
There are three hundred people in total, including sons and younger brothers of dukes and ministers,
all wearing plain headbands and wěi mào guān (委貌冠) (ceremonial caps),
and plain skirts.
Three hundred Xiào Wèi (校尉) (commanders),
all wearing red headbands without caps,
with crimson single robes,
holding banners and streamers.
Hòu Sī Mǎ Chéng (候司馬丞) acts as the head of the procession,
all holding gags in their mouths.
Sixty Yǔ Lín Gū Ér (羽林孤兒) (Orphans of the Feathered Forest Guard) and Bā Yú Zhuó Gē Zhě (巴俞擢歌者) (Bā-Yú selected singers),
form six rows.
Eight Duó Sī Mǎ (鐸司馬) (Bell Officers)
hold bells and lead the way.
Dà Hóng Lú (大鴻臚) arranges the nine guests,
who stand by the eastern side of the mausoleum's south Xìan Mén (羨門) (main gate),
facing north;
the feudal lords, kings, and grand masters by the western side of the road,
facing north, with the superior positions to the east;
the Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí (中二千石), Èr Qiān Shí (二千石), and Liè Hóu (列侯) (marquises) stand directly east of the nine guests,
facing north, with the superior positions to the west.
The emperor, under a white cloth canopy and plain curtain,
flanking the eastern side of the Xìan Dào (羨道) (spirit path),
faces west according to ritual.
The Róng Chē (容車) (ceremonial carriage) with its curtained seat is on the western side of the Xìan Dào (羨道),
facing south,
the carriage is directly opposite the seat,
facing south,
Zhōng Huáng Mén Shàng Yī (中黃門尚衣) respectfully brings the robes to the curtained seat.
The carriage moves slightly forward,
Tài Zhù (太祝) (Grand Invoker) presents the sweet wine offering according to ritual.
Sī Tú (司徒) kneels and says
"The imperial carriage requests to halt,"
Tài Shǐ Lìng (太史令) from the south of the carriage,
facing north, reads the mournful decree,
Zhǎng Gù (掌故) (archivist) is behind,
having already wept in sorrow.
Tài Cháng (太常) kneels and says
"Weep,"
Dà Hóng Lú (大鴻臚) transmits the call to weep as prescribed.
Sī Tú (司徒) kneels and says
"Please proceed to the lower position,"
the Dōng Yuán Wǔ Shì (東園武士) respectfully help dismount the carriage.
Sī Tú (司徒) kneels and says
"Please proceed to the lower chamber,"
the Dū Dǎo (都導) (Chief Guide) and Dōng Yuán Wǔ Shì (東園武士) respectfully guide the carriage into the chamber.
Sī Tú (司徒) and Tài Shǐ Lìng (太史令) respectfully hold the eulogistic and mournful decrees.
The Wǔshì 武士 of the Eastern Park (Dōngyuán 東園) brought down the spirit objects.
Eight sāo 筲 (bamboo rice containers),
each holding three shēng 升,
one of panicled millet (shǔ 黍),
one of foxtail millet (jì 稷),
one of wheat (mài 麥),
one of broomcorn millet (liáng 粱),
one of rice (dào 稻),
one of hemp seeds (má 麻),
one of soybeans (shú 菽),
and one of adzuki beans (xiǎodòu 小豆).
Three wèng 甕 (jars),
each holding three shēng 升,
one of vinegar (xī 醯),
one of mincemeat (hǎi 醢),
and one of finely chopped meat (xiè 屑).
Malt candy made from millet (shǔyí 黍飴).
Carried on a wooden frame (mùhéng 木桁),
covered with coarse cloth (shūbù 疏布).
Two wǔ 甒 (small jars),
each holding three shēng 升,
one of sweet wine (lǐ 醴),
and one of wine (jiǔ 酒).
Carried on a wooden frame (mùhéng 木桁),
covered with fine cloth (gōngbù 功布).
One pottery lamp (wǎdēng 瓦鐙).
Four red arrows (tóngshǐ 彤矢),
with protruding and rounded shaft ends (xuānzhōuzhōng 軒輖中),
and also short feathering (duǎnwèi 短衞).
Four red arrows (tóngshǐ 彤矢),
with bone tips (gǔ 骨),
and short feathering (duǎnwèi 短衞).
One red bow (tónggōng 彤弓).
Eight zhī 巵 (goblets),
eight móu 牟 (cups),
eight dòu 豆 (pedestal bowls),
eight biān 籩 (bamboo containers),
and eight square wine pots (xíngfāng jiǔhú 形方酒壺).
One set of pání 槃匜 (basin and ewer).
One staff (zhàng 杖) and one armrest (jǐ 几) each.
One parasol (gài 蓋).
Sixteen zhòng 鍾 (bells),
without stands (wúju 無虡).
Four bó 鎛 (large bells),
without stands (wúju 無虡).
Sixteen qìng 磬 (stone chimes),
without stands (wúju 無虡).
One xūn 壎 (ocarina),
four xiāo 簫 (vertical flutes),
one shēng 笙 (mouth organ),
one chí 箎 (horizontal flute),
one zhù 柷 (wooden percussion instrument),
one yù 敔 (tiger-shaped percussion instrument),
six sè 瑟 (zithers),
one qín 琴 (guqin),
one yú 竽 (large mouth organ),
one zhú 筑 (plucked string instrument),
and one kǎnhóu 坎侯 (target).
One shield (gàn 干) and one dagger-axe (gē 戈) each.
One rope (zuó 笮).
One armor (jiǎ 甲).
One helmet (zhòu 冑).
[一０]Nine funeral carts (wǎnichē 輓車).
Thirty-six straw effigies of horses (chúlíng 芻靈).
[一一]Two pottery stoves (wǎzào 瓦竈).
Two pottery cauldrons (wǎfǔ 瓦釜).
One pottery steamer (wǎzèng 瓦甑).
Twelve pottery tripods (wǎdǐng 瓦鼎),
each holding five shēng 升.
One gourd ladle (páosháo 匏勺),
holding one shēng 升.
Nine pottery tables (wǎ'àn 瓦案).
Sixteen large pottery cups (wǎdàbēi 瓦大杯),
each holding three shēng 升.
Twenty small pottery cups (wǎxiǎobēi 瓦小杯),
each holding two shēng 升.
Ten pottery rice plates (wǎfànpán 瓦飯槃).
Two pottery wine vessels (wǎjiǔzūn 瓦酒樽),
each holding five dòu 斗.
Two gourd ladles (páosháo 匏勺),
each holding one shēng 升.
When the offering of the sacrificial robes (jìfúyī 祭服衣) was completed,
the Eastern Park artisan (Dōngyuán jiàng 東園匠) said,
"It is permitted to weep,"
and all who were in the chamber wept.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常) and Grand Herald (Dàhónglú 大鴻臚) requested that the weeping cease, [ku 哭] as was customary.
The Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒) said,
"The hundred officials have completed their duties,
your servant requests dismissal,"
and all who had entered the chamber bowed twice,
exited,
and returned to their positions.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常) led the Emperor (Huángdì 皇帝) to the offering position.
The Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒) knelt and said,
"Please present the offerings."
The Attendant (Shìzhōng 侍中) held the hóngdòng 鴻洞 (funerary shaft).
The offering of the guī 珪 (jade tablet) was fourteen cùn 寸 long,
placed on a purple cloth (zǐjīn 紫巾),
three cùn 寸 wide and long respectively,
made of red silk (tíjié 緹𩹉),
with a red border (chìxūn zhōuyuán 赤纁周緣);
the offering of silks (zèngbì 贈幣) included
three black (xuán 玄) and two crimson (xūn 纁),
each twelve cùn 寸 long,
and the full width of the fabric (guǎngchōngfú 廣充幅).
The Emperor (Huángdì 皇帝) knelt forward,
approached the door of the side chamber (xiàndàofánghù 羨道房戶) of the spirit path,
faced west,
placed the offerings by hand,
and dropped them into the hóngdòng 鴻洞 (funerary shaft)
three times.
The Eastern Park artisan (Dōngyuán jiàng 東園匠) then sealed and placed them into the burial chamber.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常) knelt and said,
"The Emperor (Huángdì 皇帝) respectfully bows twice,
please weep."
The Grand Herald (Dàhónglú 大鴻臚) transmitted the weeping, as was customary.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常) knelt and said,
"The offering ceremony is complete."
The Emperor (Huángdì 皇帝) quickly returned to his position.
The rónggēnchē 容根車 carried the ceremonial robes (róngyī 容衣).
The Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒) proceeded to the side palace (biàndiàn 便殿),
and all the accompanying cavalry dismounted under the jade canopy (yùzhàng 玉帳) of the róngchē 容車.
The Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒) knelt and said,
"Please proceed to the tent."
He guided the ascent.
The Director of Imperial Wardrobe (Shàngyī 尚衣) presented the robes,
and in sequence presented the utensils and clothing,
storing them in the side palace (biàndiàn 便殿).
The Grand Invoker (Tàizhù 太祝) presented the sweet wine (lǐ 醴) offering.
The entire descent [into the tomb]
took ten kè 刻 (marks on a clepsydra).
When the ceremony was complete,
the Minister of Works (Sīkōng 司空) led his subordinates to restore the earth.
The Emperor (Huángdì 皇帝), Empress (Huánghòu 皇后), and those below them all removed their coarse mourning clothes (cūfú 麤服),
and wore large red (dàhóng 大紅) garments.
They returned to the palace (huángōng 反宮), entered the mourning hut (fǎnlú 反廬),
and established the spirit tablet (lìzhǔ 立主) as prescribed by ritual.
The mulberry wood spirit tablet (sāngmùzhǔ 桑木主) was twelve cùn 寸 long,
and did not bear the posthumous title.
When the Yú 虞 ceremony was completed,
the spirit tablet was interred at the ancestral temple (fùyúmiào 祔於廟),
as prescribed by ritual.

On the day prior to the imperial carriage's (dàjià 大駕) procession, the roaming caps (yóuguān 游冠) and robes (yī 衣) in all the palaces (zhūgōng 諸宮) and halls (zhūdiàn 諸殿) were all auspicious attire (jí fú 吉服) and attended the assembly as prescribed by ritual.
The mourning attire of the Emperor's (Huángdì 皇帝) close ministers (jìnchén 近臣) was as prescribed by ritual.
After removing the large red (dàhóng 大紅) garments,
they wore small red (xiǎohóng 小紅) garments,
and a cap (liàn’guān 練冠) of eleven shēng 升 of unbleached cloth (dūbù 都布).
After removing the small red (xiǎohóng 小紅) garments,
they wore fine cloth (xiān 纖).
After removing the fine cloth (xiān 纖),
they wore yellow-brown (liúhuáng 留黃) garments,
and a regular cap (chángguān 常冠).
Close ministers (jìnchén 近臣) and officials of two thousand dàn 擔 of grain income (èrqiānshí 二千石) and below all wore yellow-brown caps (liúhuáng guān 留黃冠).
All other officials (bǎiguān 百官) wore black (zào 皁) garments.
Each time the mourning attire was changed,
they proceeded from weeping to the imperial tomb (línghuì 陵會) as prescribed by ritual.
Sacrifices were made with a single animal (tèshēng 特牲),
but no fur, blood, or head were presented.
The Minister of Education (Sītú 司徒) and Superintendent of the Imperial Household (Guānglùxūn 光祿勳) prepared three cups of wine (sānjué 三爵) as prescribed by ritual.
When a Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihuángtàihòu 太皇太后) or Empress Dowager (Huángtàihòu 皇太后) passed away,
the Minister of Works (Sīkōng 司空) announced the posthumous title (gàoshì 告謚) with a single animal (tèshēng 特牲) at the ancestral temple (zǔmiào 祖廟) as prescribed by ritual.
The Grand Coachman of Chánglè (Chánglè tàipú 長樂太僕), the Privy Treasurer (Shàofǔ 少府), and the Grand Chief Steward (Dàchángqiū 大長秋) were in charge of the funeral affairs (sāngshì 喪事).
The Three Excellencies (Sāngōng 三公) upheld the regulations (zhìdù 制度),
and all others followed the ritual ceremonies (lǐyí 禮儀).
For joint burial (hézàng 合葬): the spirit path (xiàndào 羨道) was opened,
the Emperor (Huángdì 皇帝) visited the side chamber (biànfáng 便房),
the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常) guided him to the spirit path (xiàndào 羨道),
where he left his staff.
The Palace Attendant (Zhōngchángshì 中常侍) received it.
Upon arriving before the coffin (jiùqián 柩前),
he paid respects,
prostrated himself, and wept, stopping as prescribed by ritual.
After bidding farewell,
the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng 太常) guided him out.
The Palace Attendant (Zhōngchángshì 中常侍) handed him his staff.
He ascended his carriage and returned to the palace (guīgōng 歸宮).
After this,
the Yú 虞 ceremony and the establishment of the spirit tablet (lìzhǔ 立主) were performed as prescribed by ritual.
All sacrificial robes (jìfú 祭服) from suburban and ancestral temples (jiāomiào 郊廟) were brought down to the side chamber (biànfáng 便房).
One set of court robes (cháofú 朝服) for each of the five seasons (wǔshí 五時) was placed in the imperial tomb (língqǐn 陵寢).
The rest, including informal attire (yànfú 宴服), were sealed in chests (jiéssì 篋笥),
and stored in the rear chambers (hòugéshì 後閤室) of the palace halls.
When vassal kings (zhūhóuwáng), marquises (lièhóu), newly enfeoffed nobles (shǐfēng guìrén), or princesses (gōngzhǔ) passed away,
all were commanded to be bestowed with seals (yìnxǐ) and jade burial suits (yùxiá) with silver threads;
great nobles (dà guìrén) and senior princesses (cháng gōngzhǔ) received copper threads.
Vassal kings (zhūhóuwáng), nobles (guìrén), princesses (gōngzhǔ), dukes (gōng), generals (jiāngjūn), and specially advanced officials (tèjìn) were all granted implements,
twenty-four items from the imperial household.
Envoys managed the funeral,
constructing the burial chamber,
with cypress outer coffins (bǎi guǒ),
and all officials attended the send-off,
as per established practice.
Vassal kings (zhūhóuwáng), princesses (gōngzhǔ), and nobles (guìrén) all had camphorwood coffins (zhāng guān),
painted bright vermilion,
with cloud patterns.
Dukes (gōng) and specially advanced officials (tèjìn) had camphorwood coffins (zhāng guān) with black lacquer.
Officials holding two thousand stone (èrqiānshí) or less had lacquered outer coffins (kǎnhóu qī).
For court officials (cháochén) of two thousand stone (èrqiānshí) and generals (jiāngjūn),
envoys offered condolences and sacrifices.
For two thousand stone (èrqiānshí) and six hundred stone (liùbǎishí) officials in commanderies (jùn) and kingdoms (guó) down to those with yellow seals (huángshòu),
all were granted common carriages (chángchē) and relay oxen (yìniú) for the funerary offerings.
It was proper that from chief clerks (zuǒshǐ) upwards,
the great shrouding was performed in court robes.
When the ruler (jūn) personally offered condolences or dispatched an envoy,
the host removed the mourning headband (miǎn dié) and put away the staff (qù zhàng), looking towards the horse's head (wàngmǎshǒu) as per ritual.
Removing the mourning headband (miǎn dié) and putting away the staff (qù zhàng)
was because one dared not face the venerable one in mourning attire.
From kings (wáng), princesses (zhǔ), and nobles (guìrén) down to chief clerks (zuǒshǐ),
the escorting carriages, cavalry, and accompanying officials and soldiers
each followed their respective official ranks.
The adornments for the hearse included a canopy (gài),
a dragon's head and fish's tail,
embroidered cloth walls (huábù qiáng),
crimson borders (xūn shàng zhōu),
intertwined front and back,
and curtains and valances (wéisháng) with cloud patterns.
Officials of two thousand stone (èrqiānshí) and above had a baggage wagon (zī),
with a green dragon (qīnglóng) on the left and a white tiger (báihǔ) on the right,
and a vermilion bird (zhūniǎo) and a black tortoise (xuánwǔ);
dukes (gōng) and marquises (hóu) and above added reclining deer (yǐlù) and crouching bears (fúxióng).
For officials of one thousand stone (qiānshí) and below,
there were black cloth walls and canopies (zī bù gài qiáng),
and only fish and dragon heads and tails.
For officials of two hundred stone (èrbǎishí) and those with yellow seals (huángshòu) down to hermits (chǔshì),
all used reed mats (diànxí) for walls and canopies.
Their principal wives (zhèngfēi), secondary wives (fūrén), and wives (qī) all followed the same regulations.
For vassal kings (zhūhóowáng),
the Grand Tutor (fù), Chancellor (xiàng), Commandant (zhōngwèi), and Grand Administrator (nèishǐ) managed the funeral affairs.
The Grand Herald (dàhónglú) proposed the posthumous title (shì).
The Son of Heaven's (tiānzǐ) envoy bestowed jade discs (bì) and silk (bó),
and the posthumous title (shì) was announced on an auspicious day, as per ritual.
When descending the tumulus (líng),
the assembled officials offered libations (yì) and wore coarse clothing (cūfú) as prescribed,
and the host observed the rites.
An encomium states: Though great rites are simple,
magnificent ceremonies are yet inclusive.
Heaven is honored, Earth is lowly;
the ruler is dignified, the ministers reverent.
Plainness and refinement adapt and transform,
grief and respect follow in turn.
The fundamental order is thus established,
and the family and state then prosper.
Collation Notes, page 3142, line 10: 【Guǎng】 two and a half cùn. According to Lú's (盧) collation, it
matches the Tōngdiǎn (通典).
Page 3142, line 10: (請) 諸衣衿斂之 (Please) gather all collars. Lú (盧) said the character
"qǐng" (請)
is superfluous.
It is now deleted accordingly.
Page 3142, line 11: 諸侯飯以珠唅以 (珠)【璧】(Princes eat with pearls and mouth with (pearls) 【bì】) - corrected according to Lú's (盧) collation.
Commentary: Lú (盧) changed it based on the citation in the Lǐ Tán Gōng Zhèng Yì (禮檀弓正義), and
Qián Dàzhāo (錢大昭) also said it should be
Page 3143, line 10: 兵官戎 (Military officers of the army) - Commentary: Lú (盧) said these three characters are superfluous,
and are not in the Tōngdiǎn (通典).
The Jíjiě (集解) cites Huáng Shān's (黃山) explanation,
stating that these three characters, as written, are incomprehensible, and
when combined with the following
"Sān Gōng Tàicháng" (三公太常)
as text,
the phrasing is also not coherent.
Why would the note involve chariots, instruments, and armored soldiers?
It is known that this text must have errors or omissions.
Page 3144, line 1: 及因郵奉奏 (And then through post to present memorials) - Commentary: The Jíjiě (集解) cites Huáng Shān's (黃山) explanation,
stating that
"jí" (及)
is a graphic error for
meaning that all were allowed not to send people to present memorials.
Page 3144, line 3: Wéndì (文帝)遗诏文 (Emperor Wen's posthumous edict text) - Commentary: Lú (盧) collated the latter
"wén" (文)
character to
"yòu" (又).
Page 3144, line 5: 紅者 【小】祥大祥以紅為領緣【也】(Red ones. 【Xiǎo】xiáng and Dàxiáng use red as collar trim 【also】) - Corrected "zhōng" (中)
to "xiǎo" (小)
according to Lú's (盧) collation.
The character "yě" (也)
is supplemented according to Huì Dòng's (惠棟) explanation.
Page 3144, line 5: 纖
"zhě" (者)
dǎn (禫) also. In total, thirty-six days before releasing 【mourning clothes】 - supplemented according to Huì Dòng's (惠棟) explanation cited in the Jíjiě (集解).
