Sacrifices: Guāngwǔ (光武) ascends the throne and announces to Heaven; Jiao (郊) sacrifices; Fēngshàn (封禪).
The way of sacrifices has existed since the birth of mankind.
Jackals and otters know how to offer sacrifices,
how much more so humans!
Therefore, humans' knowledge of this reaches the point of contemplation,
just like the natural instinct of jackals and otters.
However, ancient times were simpler and later ages were more ornamented.
Since ancient times, the collective sacrifices performed by kings and nobles,
up to Wáng Mǎng (王莽),
are already recorded in the Hànshū Jiāosì Zhì (漢書郊祀志).
Therefore, this "Jìsì Zhì" (祭祀志) now only lists those that have been practiced and used since the Zhongxing (中興) era.
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
Guāngwǔ ascended the throne in Guō,
and erected an altar and encampment on the sunny side of Guō.
He offered sacrifices and prayers to Heaven and Earth,
adopting the precedent of the suburban sacrifice from the Yuánshǐ era.
The six Zōng and all the deities were included,
but he did not yet associate an ancestor with them.
Heaven and Earth shared one calf;
other sacrificial animals were still few.
His proclamation stated:
"August Heaven Supreme Lord,
Sovereign Earthly Spirits,
have looked upon me and bestowed your mandate,
assigning Xiù to the common people,
to be the parent of the people.
Xiù dares not accept this.
However, the multitude of subordinates and all officials,
without prior consultation, spoke with one voice.
All said that Wáng Mǎng usurped, murdered, and stole the throne.
Xiù, filled with indignation, raised an army of righteousness,
defeated Wáng Yì's million-strong forces at Kūnyáng,
and executed the bandits Wáng Láng, Tóngmǎ, Chìméi, and Qīngdú.
He has pacified the realm,
and the whole country has received grace.
This accords with the will of Heaven above,
and is what the common people below desire.
The prophecies state: 'Liú Xiù raises an army to capture the lawless,
the 'Mǎo Jīn' cultivates virtue to become the Son of Heaven.'
Xiù still firmly declined,
even a second time,
even a third time.
The subordinates said: 'The great mandate of August Heaven
must not be delayed.'
How dare I not respectfully accept?"
In the first month of the second year,
the suburban sacrificial ground was first established seven *lǐ* south of Luòyáng city,
following the precedent of Guō.
It adopted the practices from the Yuánshǐ era.
A circular altar with eight terraces was built,
and in the center, a double altar was also constructed,
where Heaven and Earth were placed at its top,
all facing south,
with the west as the place of honor.
On the outer altar were the positions for the Five Emperors.
The position of the Azure Emperor was in the *jiǎyín* direction,
the position of the Red Emperor was in the *bǐngsì* direction,
the position of the Yellow Emperor was in the *dīngwèi* direction,
the position of the White Emperor was in the *gēngshēn* direction,
and the position of the Black Emperor was in the *rén hài* direction.
Outside that was an enclosure wall.
The double encampment was entirely purple,
to symbolize the Purple Palace;
it had four thoroughfares serving as gates.
The Sun and Moon were within the central encampment's southern path,
the Sun in the east,
the Moon in the west,
the Big Dipper in the west of the northern path,
all having separate positions,
not among the ranks of other deities.
There were eight terraces;
each terrace had fifty-eight libations (*juàn*),
totaling four hundred sixty-four libations.
For the terraces of the Five Emperors,
each emperor had seventy-two libations,
totaling three hundred sixty libations.
The four gates of the central encampment
had fifty-four gods per gate,
totaling two hundred sixteen gods.
The four gates of the outer encampment
had one hundred eight gods per gate,
totaling four hundred thirty-two gods.
All faced inward toward the encampment.
The four gates of the central encampment
had four *fēng* gods per gate.
The four gates of the outer encampment
had four *fēng* gods per gate,
totaling thirty-two gods.
In all, there were one thousand five hundred fourteen gods.
The "encampment" (*yíng*) here refers to the enclosure wall (*wéi*).
*Fēng* refers to
building up earth.
The gods facing away from the central encampment
were the Five Planets,
and the gods of the Five Officials of the central constellations, and those belonging to the Five Peaks.
The gods facing away from the outer encampment
were the twenty-eight constellations of the outer stars,
and those belonging to the Duke of Thunder, the First Farmer, the Earl of Wind, the Master of Rain, the Four Seas, the Four Rivers, famous mountains, and great rivers.
By the fifth month of the seventh year,
an edict was issued to the Three Dukes, stating:
"The Hàn dynasty should offer suburban sacrifice to Yáo.
You, along with the ministers, grand masters, and erudites, should discuss this."
At that time, the Palace Censor Dù Lín submitted a memorial,
opining that
"the Hàn arose not through inheriting from Yáo,
which differs from the suitable practices of the Yīn and Zhōu.
Moreover, the old system included Emperor Gāo in the sacrifice.
Since military forces are currently engaged outside,
it is permissible to follow the precedent of the suburban sacrifice from the first year."
The Emperor adopted his suggestion.
The details are found in Lín's biography.
After Lǒng and Shǔ were pacified,
the suburban sacrifice was expanded.
Emperor Gāo was included in the offering,
his position being on the central altar,
facing west with the north as the place of honor.
Heaven, Earth, Emperor Gāo, and the Yellow Emperor each used one calf.
The Azure Emperor and the Red Emperor shared one calf.
The White Emperor and the Black Emperor shared one calf.
In total, six calves were used.
The Sun, Moon, and Big Dipper shared one ox.
The gods of the four encampments shared four oxen.
In total, five oxen were used.
The music performed included Qīngyáng, Zhūmíng, Xīhào, and Xuánmíng,
as well as the dances Yúnqiáo and Yù Mìng.
For the four gates of the central encampment,
eighteen mats were used per gate.
For the four gates of the outer encampment,
thirty-six mats were used per gate.
In total, two hundred sixteen mats were used,
all made of *guǎndiàn*,
with an average of three gods per mat.
The Sun, Moon, and Big Dipper had no terraces, enclosures, or libations.
After sending off the gods,
the sacrificial meat was burned and placed in the *sì* direction south of the altar.
In the second month of the thirtieti year of Jiànwǔ,
the officials presented a memorial, stating that
after thirty years on the throne,
it was appropriate to perform the *fēngshàn* sacrifice on Mount Tài.
The imperial edict stated:
"Thirty years on the throne,
the people are full of resentment.
Whom do I deceive?
Do I deceive Heaven?
Could Mount Tài be inferior to Lín Fàng?
Why should I defile the records of seventy-two generations!
Duke Huán wanted to perform *fēng*,
but Guǎn Zhòng opposed him.
If commanderies and counties send officials from afar to offer congratulations
and greatly extol false virtues,
they shall certainly be punished with *kūn* (shaving of hair),
and additionally ordered to establish military agricultural colonies."
From then on, the officials dared not speak again.
In the third month,
the Emperor visited Lǔ,
passed Mount Tài,
and instructed the Grand Administrator to offer sacrifices to the mountain and Mount Liángfù, in accordance with the edict concerning his passage.
At that time, the Commandant of the Tiger-Guards, Liáng Sōng and others, debated:
"The records state: 'When Qí is about to perform an affair at Mount Tài,
it first performs an affair at Pèilín.'
This is presumably the ritual for feudal lords.
The Yellow River and sacred peaks are regarded as equivalent to dukes and marquises;
it is the king who offers sacrifice to them.
It is fitting that there should be no gradual progression of immediate affairs,
and Pèilín should not be sacrificed to."
In the first month of the thirty-second year,
the Emperor fasted,
and at night read the *Hétú Huìchāngfú*,
which said:
"The ninth of the Red Liú
shall meet its destiny at Dàizōng.
If one is not cautious in its use,
what benefit is there in succession?
If one truly uses it well,
deceit and falsehood will not sprout."
Moved by this text,
he then ordered Sōng and others to re-examine and search for the *Hé Luò Chènwén* that spoke of the *fēngshàn* of the ninth generation.
Sōng and others presented their findings in a memorial,
and then he consented.
Initially,
Emperor Xiàowǔ desired to seek immortals.
Influenced by the words of *fāngshì* (occultists) that the Yellow Emperor became an immortal after performing *fēngshàn*,
he thus wished to perform *fēngshàn*.
The *fēngshàn* was not a regular ceremony,
and people at the time did not know how to perform it.
In the first year of Yuánfēng,
the Emperor, following the words of the *fāngshì*, had *fēngshàn* implements made
and showed them to the various Confucians.
Many said they did not conform to ancient practices,
so he dismissed the Confucians and did not use them.
In the third month,
the Emperor traveled east to Mount Tài,
and then erected a stone on the summit of Mount Tài.
He then toured east along the coast,
seeking immortals,
but saw none and returned.
In the fourth month,
he performed the *fēng* sacrifice on Mount Tài.
Fearing that what he had done might not be correct,
he kept the matter secret.
The details are found in the "Treatise on Sacrifices" of the *Hàn Shū*.
The Emperor approved the memorial of Liáng Sōng and others.
He then sought precedents for the Fēngshàn ceremony from the Yuánfēng era,
to discuss what was used for the Fēngshàn ceremony.
The relevant officials memorialized that a square stone should be double-stacked and placed in the altar.
Each (stone) was five *chǐ* square,
one *chǐ* thick.
A jade tablet with an inscription was to be used and hidden within the square stone.
The tablet was five *cùn* thick,
one *chǐ* three *cùn* long,
and five *cùn* wide.
It had a jade clasp.
Additionally, ten stone clasps were to be used,
arranged beside the stone,
three each on the east and west,
and two each on the north and south.
All were three *chǐ* long,
one *chǐ* wide,
and seven *cùn* thick.
In each clasp, three places were carved,
four *cùn* deep,
five *cùn* square,
with covers.
The clasps were adorned with five bands of gold filigree,
using mercury mixed with gold to make the paste.
The royal seal was one square *cùn* and two *fēn*;
another (seal) was five *cùn* square.
At the four corners of the square stone, there were also buttressing stones,
all double-stacked.
Each was one *zhàng* long,
one *chǐ* thick,
and two *chǐ* wide.
All these were on the circular altar.
Below it, eighteen buttressing stones were used.
All were three *chǐ* high,
one *chǐ* thick,
and two *chǐ* wide,
like small steles,
erected around the altar,
three paces away from the altar.
Below the buttressing stones, all had stone pedestals,
entering the ground by four *chǐ*.
Furthermore, a stone stele was to be used,
nine *chǐ* high,
three *chǐ* five *cùn* wide,
and one *chǐ* two *cùn* thick.
It was erected in the Bǐng Dì direction of the altar,
more than three *zhàng* away from the altar,
for carving an inscription.
The Emperor, because the work with stone was difficult
and he also wished to complete the *fēng* sacrifice by the second month,
therefore issued an edict to Liáng Sōng, wishing to use the old *fēng*-stone's empty clasps
and merely add a seal.
Liáng Sōng submitted a memorial arguing against this,
believing that
"The rite of Dēngfēng
announces achievements to Huángtiān,
and is transmitted endlessly to posterity,
for the myriad people.
Receiving the reverence due to Heaven,
it should especially be clearly displayed.
Offering auspicious signs of diagrams and writings,
it should especially be prominent.
Now, if we rely on the old *fēng* (stone),
and furtively place the jade tablet beneath the old stone,
I fear this does not accord with the principle of a renewed Mandate.
Having received the Mandate and brought about a restoration,
it should be especially distinct,
in order to manifest Heaven's will."
Thereupon, (he) ordered Tàishān Jùn and Lǔ to hasten the stone masons,
to obtain intact bluestone.
There was no need to insist on five colors.
At that time, because the seal carvers were unable to carve the jade tablet,
(they) wished to use red lacquer to write on it;
but by chance, someone capable of carving jade was found,
and so the inscription was carved.
The inscription was secretly carved inside the square stone,
so as to contain the jade tablet.
In the second month,
the Emperor arrived at Fènggāo.
He dispatched a Palace Censor (shìyùshǐ) and a Director of the Imperial Archives (Lántái Lìngshǐ)
to lead workers to the mountain to carve a stone inscription.
The text read:
"On the second month of the thirty-second year of Jiànwǔ,
the Emperor made an eastern inspection tour,
arriving at Dàizōng.
He performed the Chái sacrifice,
offering to the mountains and rivers in their proper order,
and to all the deities,
and then had an audience with the Empress of the East (Dōnghòu).
His accompanying ministers included Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Xī, and Grandee of Special Advance (Tèjìn) and Marquis of Gāomì Yǔ, acting as Grand Minister of Works (Sītú), among others.
The descendants of the Two Kings, guests of Hàn, were in office.
The Marquis of Bāochéng, a descendant of Kǒngzǐ,
was ranked after the Empress of the East.
Twelve vassal kings (fānwáng)
all came to assist in the sacrifices.
The Hétú Chìfú Fú says: 'Liú Xiù raises troops to apprehend the lawless;
the four barbarian tribes gather like clouds in the dragon-fighting field;
at the junction of four and seven, fire is sovereign.'
The Hétú Huìchāng Fú says: 'The Red Emperor (Chìdì), in his ninth generation,
inspects and finds the mean;
when governance is peaceful, he performs the Fēng sacrifice.
Truly in accordance with the imperial Dao and Kǒngjù,
then celestial omens appear,
and terrestrial auspicious signs arise.
The ninth descendant of Emperor Liú
meets his destiny at Dàizōng;
if he truly employs it well,
treachery and deceit will not sprout.
When the virtue of the Red Hàn flourishes,
and the ninth generation experiences great prosperity,
inspecting Dài is always appropriate.
Heaven and Earth assist the ninth,
upholding the constant principles.
Hàn will greatly prosper;
the Dao resides in the ruler of the ninth generation.
Perform the Fēng sacrifice on Tài Shān,
carve a stone to record it,
and the Shàn sacrifice at Liángfù,
then retire to reflect on the five.'
The Hétú Hégǔ Piān says: 'The outstanding one of Emperor Liú,
the generation of the nine names,
the Emperor practices virtue,
and performs the Fēng sacrifice, carving his reign.'
The Hétú Tíliú Yǔ says: 'The Emperor of the ninth generation,
enlightened and sagely,
holds the balance and resists,
the nine provinces are peaceful,
and the world is given.'
The Luòshū Zhēnyào Dù says: 'The red has three virtues,
prospering for nine generations,
meeting to cultivate the talismans,
conforming to the imperial junction,
diligently performing the Fēng sacrifice.'
The Xiàojīng Gōumìng Jué says: 'Whom shall I follow?
The Red Liú employs the imperial virtue,
establishes filial piety thrice,
cultivates nine times,
devoting himself to performing the Fēng sacrifice on Tàiqīng.'
The Hétú and Luòshū mandate the successors,
transmitted by the classics and prognostication texts.
In ancient times, Emperor Yáo,
intelligent and discerning, subtle and profound,
abdicated in favor of Shùn, his non-lineal successor,
whose descendants then grasped the mechanism of power.
Wáng Mǎng, as the family of the maternal empress,
wielded the power of the three ministers (sānsī) forming a tripod of authority, acting as prime minister (zhǒngzǎi).
He relied on the righteousness of Zhōugōng and Huò Guāng in assisting a minor ruler and returning governance to him,
and thus committed usurpation and rebellion,
usurping the title and establishing himself.
The ancestral temples (zōngmiào) were destroyed,
the altars of soil and grain (shèjì) were lost,
and there was no blood sacrifice for
eighteen years.
The three provinces of Yáng, Xú, and Qīng initiated rebellion,
weapons and armor ran rampant,
extending to Jīngzhōu.
Heroes combined and annexed territories,
with fortified settlements every hundred *lǐ*,
frequently usurping titles.
The northern barbarians (běiyí) caused havoc,
for a thousand *lǐ* there was no smoke,
no sound of chickens crowing or dogs barking.
Heaven looked upon the Emperor,
who, as a commoner, received the mandate to restore the dynasty,
raising troops at the age of twenty-eight,
(then) successively punishing and suppressing,
for more than ten years,
the offenders were thus apprehended.
The common people could dwell in their fields
and live peacefully in their homes.
Writing was unified,
chariot tracks were unified,
and human relations were unified.
Wherever boats and carriages could reach,
wherever human footprints extended,
none failed to render service.
He built the Míngtáng,
established the Pìyōng,
erected the Língtái,
and set up schools (xiángxù).
He unified the pitch-pipes (lǜ), measures (dù), capacities (liàng), and weights (héng).
He rectified the Five Rites (wǔlǐ):
five jades,
three silks,
two animals,
one corpse,
returning to the old regulations.
He has been on the throne for thirty-two years,
and is sixty-two years old.
He has been diligent and cautious day by day,
not daring to be idle or at ease,
traversing dangers and overcoming perils,
personally inspecting the common people,
reverently solemn towards the deities,
benevolently comforting the aged,
governing the populace in accordance with ancient ways,
wise, impartial, and understanding.
The Emperor sincerely heeds the authentic texts of the Hétú and Luòshū.
On this day Xīnmǎo of this month,
he performed the Chái sacrifice,
and ascended Tài Shān for the Fēng sacrifice.
On Jiǎwǔ,
he performed the Shàn sacrifice at Liángyīn.
Thus receiving auspicious omens,
for the sake of the myriad people,
to forever unify this universe,
and transmit it to future generations.
All officials and accompanying ministers,
commanders of commanderies (jùnshǒu) and imperial preceptors (shīyǐn),
all receive blessings and good fortune,
eternal and without end.
Qín Prime Minister (Xiàng) Lǐ Sī burned the *Shī* and *Shū*,
music collapsed, and ritual was destroyed.
Before the first year of Jiànwǔ,
documents were scattered and lost,
the old regulations were incomplete,
unable to clarify the classics,
explaining obscure points with eighty-one volumes,
what was clear was taken as verification,
and another ten volumes
were all unclear.
Zǐgòng wished to do away with the sacrificial lamb offered at the beginning of the month.
Kǒngzǐ said: 'Cì,
you cherish the lamb,
I cherish the ritual.'
Should there be a sage in the future,
he will correct the errors
and record them on stone."
On the twenty-second day, Xīnmǎo morning,
a pyre sacrifice was offered to Heaven south of Tài Shān.
All the deities followed,
and the music was like that of the southern suburban sacrifice.
All the kings (zhūwáng), the two dukes (èrgōng) who were descendants of former kings, and the Marquis of Bāochéng, a descendant of Kǒngzǐ,
all assisted in the sacrificial duties.
When the ceremonies were completed,
they prepared to ascend for the Fēng sacrifice.
Someone said:
"Although Tài Shān has already received offerings in the Chái sacrifice,
now that we are personally ascending to announce achievements,
a ritual sacrifice is appropriate."
Thereupon, the usher (yèzhě) was ordered to offer a single special animal sacrifice at the usual place of worship for Tài Shān,
to announce the sacrifice to Tài Shān,
following the precedents of personal plowing, the Chūliú sacrifice, the Xīancí, the Xiānnóng, and the Xiānyú sacrifices.
At mealtime, the imperial carriage ascended the mountain.
After noon, the Emperor arrived at the mountain top, changed clothes,
and in the early afternoon, took his place at the altar,
facing north.
The various ministers arranged themselves in order behind him,
ascending from the west,
and all took their places on the altar.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshūlìng) presented the jade tablet (yùdié) and its seal-cover (jiǎn).
The Emperor personally sealed it with a seal one *cùn* and two *fēn* in size.
After this was completed,
the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) ordered someone to open the stone on the altar.
After the Director of the Imperial Secretariat had stored the jade tablet,
the stone was replaced and covered.
The Director of the Imperial Secretariat then sealed the stone cover with a five-*cùn* seal.
When the rites were finished,
the Emperor bowed twice,
and the ministers exclaimed "Long live!"
He ordered men to erect the carved stone tablet,
and then returned down the road.
On the twenty-fifth day, Jiǎwǔ,
the Shàn sacrifice was performed,
offering to Earth at Liángyīn,
with Empress Gāo as co-sacrificant.
The mountains, rivers, and all deities followed,
following the precedents of the northern suburban sacrifice in the Yuánshǐ era.
In the fourth month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
The thirty-second year of Jiànwǔ was designated the first year of Jiànwǔ Zhōngyuán.
Bó and Fènggāo, and Yíngwù were exempted from paying their annual rent and fodder for the first year.
On an auspicious day, the jade tablet text was carved, placed in a letter-box, and stored in a golden casket.
It was sealed with a royal seal.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
the Grand Commandant was dispatched to perform the duty
of making a special announcement at the Gāomiào temple.
The Grand Commandant presented the casket and made the announcement at Gāomiào,
storing it in a stone chamber on the west wall of the temple chamber, below the main chamber where the high spirit tablet was kept.
Sacrifices were offered at the Northern Suburban Altar, the Míngtáng, the Bìyōng, the Língtái, for welcoming the seasonal qi, and additional sacrifices were made to the Six Zōng and Lǎozǐ.
This year, the Northern Suburban Altar was first established.
The Míngtáng,
the Bìyōng, and
the Língtái were not yet in use.
Empress Lǚ Tàihòu was moved to the imperial garden.
The Emperor conferred the honored title of Gāo Huánghòu upon Empress Bó Tàihòu,
to be paired with the earth in the suburban sacrifice at Gāomiào.
The details are recorded in the annals of Guāngwǔ.
The Northern Suburban Altar was located four lǐ north of Luòyáng city,
and consisted of a square platform with four steps.
In the first month of the thirty-third year, on the day Xīnwèi,
the suburban sacrifice was performed.
Separate sacrifices were offered to the Earth Deities,
whose positions faced south, with the west being superior.
Empress Gāo was paired,
facing west, with the north being superior.
All were on the altar.
The local deities and all other gods were to partake in the sacrifice,
all below the altar,
following the precedents of the Yuánshǐ era.
Mount Zhōngyuè was in the wèi direction,
and the Four Yuè were each in the land of their respective direction's first earthly branch.
These were within the inner enclosure.
The Sea was in the east;
the Four Dú (Rivers) were Hé in the west,
Jǐ in the north,
Huái in the east,
and Jiāng in the south.
Other mountains and rivers were each in their respective directions,
all within the outer enclosure.
Libations on the four steps and seals for the gods at the gates of the inner and outer enclosures were performed as at the Southern Suburban Altar.
For the Earth Deities and Empress Gāo, one calf each was used.
For the Five Yuè, one ox was shared.
For the Sea and the Four Dú, one ox was shared.
For all other gods, two oxen were shared.
Music was played also as at the Southern Suburban Altar.
After sending off the gods,
the sacrificial meats and contents were buried north of the altar.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
in the first month of the second year of Yǒngpíng, on the day Xīnwèi,
sacrifices were first offered to the Five Emperors at the Míngtáng,
with Emperor Guāngwǔ as their counterpart.
The Five Emperors were seated in the hall,
each in their respective direction.
The Yellow Emperor was in the wèi direction,
all positions were as at the Southern Suburban Altar.
Emperor Guāngwǔ's position was slightly retreated south of the Green Emperor,
facing west.
For each, one calf was sacrificed,
and music was played as at the Southern Suburban Altar.
Upon completion of the rites,
they ascended the Língtái
to observe the clouds and atmospheric phenomena.
To welcome the seasonal qi,
the omens of the Five Suburbs were observed.
Since the Yǒngpíng era,
based on the Lǐchèn and the seasonal colors of the Míngyuèlìng for welcoming the qi at the Five Suburbs,
they adopted the precedents of the Yuánshǐ era,
observing omens at the Five Suburbs in the four directions of Luòyáng.
The central omen was in the wèi direction.
All altars were three chǐ high,
with no steps of different levels.
On the day of Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring),
spring was welcomed at the Eastern Suburban Altar,
sacrificing to the Green Emperor and Gōumáng.
The carriages, banners, and attire were all green.
The Qīngyáng song was sung,
and the eight-row dance of Yúnqiáo was performed.
Officials from the Grand Tutor and Minister of Education downwards were granted silk in varying amounts.
On the day of Lìxià (Beginning of Summer),
summer was welcomed at the Southern Suburban Altar,
sacrificing to the Red Emperor and Zhùróng.
The carriages, banners, and attire were all red.
The Zhūmíng song was sung,
and the eight-row dance of Yúnqiáo was performed.
Eighteen days before Lìqiū (Beginning of Autumn),
the Yellow Spirit was welcomed at the central omen site,
sacrificing to the Yellow Emperor and Hòutǔ.
The carriages, banners, and attire were all yellow.
The Zhūmíng song was sung,
and the eight-row dances of Yúnqiáo and Yùmìng were performed.
On the day of Lìqiū,
autumn was welcomed at the Western Suburban Altar,
sacrificing to the White Emperor and Rùshōu.
The carriages, banners, and attire were all white.
The Xīhào song was sung,
and the eight-row dance of Yùmìng was performed.
The Herald was to first offer a special single sacrifice to the former hunters at the altar.
When a ritual was performed,
the Son of Heaven entered the park to shoot game,
which was then used to sacrifice at the ancestral temples,
named Chūliú.
The details are in the Lǐyí Zhì.
On the day of Lìdōng (Beginning of Winter),
winter was welcomed at the Northern Suburban Altar,
sacrificing to the Black Emperor and Xuánmíng.
The carriages, banners, and attire were all black.
The Xuánmíng song was sung,
and the eight-row dance of Yùmìng was performed.
When Emperor Zhāng ascended the throne,
in the first month of the second year of Yuánhé,
an edict stated:
"Of the mountains, rivers, and hundred gods,
not all those who should receive sacrifices have been acknowledged.
Let there be discussions to add and revise the communal sacrifices that ought to be offered."
In the second month,
the Emperor made an eastern tour of inspection.
Upon approaching Mount Tài,
he dispatched an envoy to offer a grand sacrifice to Emperor Yáo at the Língtái in Chéngyáng, Jìyīn.
When the Emperor arrived at Mount Tài,
he restored Emperor Guāngwǔ's altar and omen-site south of the mountain.
On the day Xīnwèi,
the faggot sacrifice was offered to Heaven, Earth, and all gods, as was customary.
On the day Rénshēn,
the Five Emperors were worshipped at the Míngtáng built by Emperor Xiàowǔ at Wénshàng,
with Emperor Guāngwǔ as their counterpart,
following the rites of the Luòyáng Míngtáng.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
new announcements and sacrifices were made to Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, Shìzōng, Zhōngzōng, Shìzǔ, and Xiǎnzōng at the Míngtáng,
each with a grand sacrifice.
Upon completion of the rites,
he then granted an audience to the Eastern Empress.
Feasts and rewards were given to the kings, marquises, and all officials.
During his tour of the commanderies and kingdoms,
he visited Lǔ,
and offered sacrifices to Prince Gōng of Dōnghǎi,
as well as to Kǒngzǐ and his seventy-two disciples.
In the fourth month,
he returned to the capital.
On the day Gēngshēn,
an announcement of his return was made,
and sacrifices were offered to Gāomiào and Shìzǔ,
each with a special ox.
He also composed poems for the twelve gates of the Língtái,
which were recited during the sacrifices of their respective months.
Emperor Hé made no additions or alterations.
When Emperor Ān ascended the throne,
in the sixth year of Yuánchū,
based on the Ouyáng family's interpretation of the Book of Documents,
it was held that the Six Zōng
were in the center of Heaven and Earth and the four directions, serving as the patriarchs of above, below, and the four directions.
Following the precedents of the Yuánshǐ era,
the interpretation that the Six Zōng were the qi of the Six Sons, namely the sun, moon, Lord of Thunder, Count of Wind, mountains, and marshes, was deemed incorrect.
In the third month, on the day Gēngchén,
the Six Zōng were first re-established
and sacrificed to in the xu-hài region northwest of Luòyáng,
the rites being comparable to those of the Grand Altar of the Earth.
In the third year of Yánguāng,
the Emperor made an eastern tour of inspection,
arrived at Mount Tài,
performed the faggot sacrifice,
and sacrificed at the Míngtáng at Wénshàng,
following the precedents of the second year of Yuánhé.
When Emperor Shùn ascended the throne,
he maintained the customary sacrifices.
Huán Dì ascended the throne for eighteen years.
He was fond of matters concerning immortals.
In the eighth year of Yánxī,
he first sent the Central Regular Attendant to Chén Guó, Kǔ Xiàn to sacrifice to Lǎozi.
In the ninth year,
he personally sacrificed to Lǎozi at Zhuólóng.
A patterned rug was used for the altar,
decorated with pure gold inlaid vessels,
and a seat with a grand canopy was set up,
using the music for suburban sacrifices to Heaven.
Collating notes, page 3178, line 7: "The Son of Heaven obtains the rites of the Spirit Terrace" - according to the Hànxuétáng compiled edition, "rites" (禮) includes the text supplemented by Wén Jiā.

"It means that teachings and decrees are issued from its upper part, called the Spirit Terrace."

"distinguished" (異)
is written as

Page 3179, line 7: "the Grand Ancestral Temple of Lǔ is like the Qīngmiào of Zhōu" (明魯之太廟猶周清廟也) / "hall" (堂) - changed according to the Diànběn edition.

the character
"hall" (堂)
is supernumerary after

and the character

Both are corrected according to the Sòngběn edition.
Page 3179, line 8: "The Son of Heaven enters the Eastern Academy at dawn." Commentary: In the Jíbén and Diànběn editions,

is written as

Page 3179, line 11: "met the son of the Nine Marquises." Commentary: The current text of Cài Yōngjí lacks the character

and

"plan" (猷).
The commentary to Wáng Róng's Qūshuǐ Shī Xù in Wénxuǎn quotes Cài Yōng's Yuèlìng Lùn as stating

Page 3179, line 12: "the southeast is called a gate, the northwest is called a smaller gate" (東南稱門西北稱闈) / "gate" (門) - changed according to Lú's collation.

Page 3179, line 15: "Then seats for the Three Elders and Five Seniors were set up there, meaning that teaching began with caring for the elderly, starting from the east as the year begins. Also, in spring and summer, one learns military skills." (遂設三老五更之席位焉言教學始之於養老由東方歲始也又春夏學干戈) - supplemented according to the Diànběn edition.

to

Commentary: Huáng Shān said that Wǔ Dì's ritual songs originally had a separate chapter "Dìlín" for sacrificing to the Central Huáng Dì. Wáng Mǎng began the sacrifices of welcoming the qi at the five suburbs, and the central altar for welcoming the qi sacrificed to Huáng Dì, not singing "Dìlín" but "Zhūmíng", which probably had a different intention. Míng Dì did not perceive this and ignorantly continued it.
The explanation is detailed in Jíjiě.
Page 3182, line 9: "sing 'Xīhào'." Jíjiě quotes Qián Dàxīn's explanation,
stating that the Míng Dì Jì commentary quotes this passage as singing "Báicáng".
Comparing this with "Qīngyáng", "Zhūmíng", and "Xuánmíng" in the context,
then "Báicáng" is correct.
Commentary: Huáng Shān said that "Qīngyáng", "Zhūmíng", "Xīhào", and "Xuánmíng" were originally Wǔ Dì's suburban ritual songs, fully recorded in the Qián Shū Lǐyuè Zhì.
Wáng Mǎng cited the text "autumn is called Báicáng" from Éryǎ
and changed "Xīhào" to "Báicáng". The Later Hàn continued this, but this text specifically uses its original name according to Bān Zhì.
The explanation is detailed in Jíjiě.
Page 3182, line 16: "The hall steps have eight levels." (堂階八等) / "eight" (八) - changed according to Lú's collation.
Commentary: Jíjiě quotes Huì Dòng's explanation,
stating that Shàngshū Dàchuán records "eight levels".
Page 3183, line 2: "The hall steps have seven levels." (堂階七等) / "seven" (七) - changed according to Lú's collation.
Commentary: Jíjiě quotes Huì Dòng's explanation,
stating that Shàngshū Dàchuán records "seven levels".
Page 3183, line 2: "seven red carts." Commentary: "seven" (七) was originally a mistaken "ten" (十),
and has been corrected directly based on the Jíbén and Diànběn editions.
Page 3183, line 6: "the first month of Yuánhé second year." Commentary: Jíjiě quotes Qián Dàxīn's explanation,

Page 3183, line 9: "because the sun, moon, and stars are what the people look up to." (以日月星辰民所瞻仰也) - supplemented according to the Jíbén and Diànběn editions.
Page 3183, line 10: "Hence, sacrifices were made to them." Commentary: "yíng" (禜) was originally a mistaken "róng" (榮),
and has been corrected directly;
the same applies below.

Commentary: Tōngdiǎn and Tōngzhì both use "rites" (禮).
Page 3184, line 14: "the deliberation is inappropriate for sacrifice" (議不當祭) / "not" (不) - deleted according to Lú's collation.

Commentary: Zhāng Sēnkǎi's collation notes state that the following text also says "sacrificing to ancestors", so the character "rites" (禮) is incorrect and should be changed.
Also, commentary: "yīn" (禋) was originally a mistaken "rites" (禮),

Page 3186, line 5: "tours of inspection completed in one year." Commentary: "one" (一) was originally a mistaken "ten thousand" (萬),

Page 3186, line 8: "did not announce when departing" (去時不告) / "auspicious" (吉) - changed according to the Jíbén and Diànběn editions.

Page 3187, line 10: "six is the middle of the earth numbers." (六是地數之中) - supplemented according to Lú's collation.

None of the editions have corrected this.
Now it is changed according to Lú's collation.
Sacrifices to the ancestral temples, altars of soil and grain, numinous stars, first farmer, and welcoming spring.
In the first month of the second year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
a high temple (gāomiào) was established in Luòyáng.
At the four seasonal *xiá* sacrifices,
Emperor Gāo (Gāo Dì) was designated Tàizǔ,
Emperor Wén (Wén Dì) as Tàizōng,
and Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì) as Shìzōng,
as before.
For other emperors, the four seasonal sacrifices were held in the first month for spring,
the fourth month for summer,
the seventh month for autumn,
and the tenth month for winter, plus the *là* sacrifice,
making five sacrifices in a year.
In the first month of the third year,
a ancestral temple (qīnmào) was established in Luòyáng
to sacrifice to his father, Nándùn Jūn, and his ancestors up to Chōnglíng Jiéhóu.
At that time, bandits had not yet been pacified,
and the focus was on military campaigns,
so the sacrificial rituals had not yet been fully instituted.
It was not until the nineteenth year,
when the bandits had been suppressed,
and military affairs had relatively ceased,
that Zhāng Chún, the Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiàng, and Zhū Fú, the Tàipú, submitted a memorial arguing:
“According to the Rites,
a son serving the main ancestral line
should reduce his private kin’s status.
The institution of rites
distinguishes between what is bestowed and what is naturally acquired.
Therefore, the four present ancestral temples (qīnmào) should be abolished.
Emperor Xiàoxuān, as a grandson succeeding to an ancestor,
established a temple for his father in Fèngmíng,
called the Huángkǎo Miào,
where only officials participated in the sacrifice.
We request that the relevant authorities discuss which of the four former emperors’ temples should replace the current ancestral temples, and also the matter of the Huángkǎo Miào.”
This was submitted to the Gōngqīng, Bóshì, and Yìláng.
Dàsītú Shè and others deliberated:
“It is appropriate to honor those who are to be replaced,
and establish temples for Emperor Píng, Emperor Āi, Emperor Chéng, and Emperor Yuán,
to replace the current ancestral temples.
For brothers and lesser kin,
let the relevant officials conduct the sacrifices.
It is appropriate to establish a Huángkǎo Miào for Nándùn Jūn,
sacrificing up to Chōnglíng Jiéhóu,
with officials attending the sacrifices.”
At the time, there were differing opinions,
which were not resolved.
The Emperor approved the deliberation of Shè and others,
and issued an edict stating:
“Since the location of the ancestral temples (zōngmiào) has not yet been determined,
for now, let the *xiá* sacrifice be performed at the high temple (gāomiào).
As for Chéng, Āi, and Píng, let their sacrifices be temporarily conducted at the old high temple (gāomiào) in Cháng’ān.
As for Nányáng Chōnglíng, let the seasonal sacrifices each be temporarily performed at the old garden temple (yuánmiào).
For garden temples far from the Taìshǒu’s administrative seat,
let the local Lìngzhǎng act as Taìshǒu and attend the sacrifices.
Only Emperor Xiàoxuān had meritorious virtue,
so he shall be granted the esteemed title Zhōngzōng.”
Thereupon, at the Luòyáng high temple (gāomiào), additional seasonal sacrifices were offered to Xiàoxuān and Xiàoyuán,
making a total of five emperors.
At the western temple, the spirits of the three emperors Chéng, Āi, and Píng
were sacrificed to seasonally at the old high temple (gāomiào).
The Jīngzhàoyǐn attended the sacrifices at the eastern temple,
with clothing, chariots, and attendants as per the Tàicháng’s rites for sacrificing at mausoleum temples.
Nándùn Jūn and his ancestors up to Jiéhóu
all had their sacrifices performed at their respective garden temples (yuánmiào).
Nándùn Jūn was called the Huángkǎo Miào,
the Jùlù Dūwèi was called the Huángzǔkǎo Miào,
the Yùlín Tàishǒu was called the Huángzēngzǔkǎo Miào,
and Jiéhóu was called the Huánggāozǔkǎo Miào,
with officials from their respective commanderies and counties attending the sacrifices.
In the twenty-sixth year,
an edict inquired of Zhāng Chún
how many years the *dì* and *xiá* rites had not been performed.
Chún reported:
“According to the Rites,
a *xiá* sacrifice is performed every three years,
and a *dì* sacrifice every five years.
The spirit tablets of destroyed temples
are placed at the Tàizǔ’s temple;
the spirit tablets of existing temples
are all ascended to share meals with the Tàizǔ;
the grand sacrifices (*yīnjì*) are performed twice every five years.
According to the old system,
a *xiá* sacrifice was performed every three years,
with the spirit tablets of destroyed temples sharing meals at the high temple (gāomiào),
but those of existing temples never combined.
In the fifth year of Yuánshǐ,
the *dì* rite was first performed.
The father was *zhāo*,
facing south;
the son was *mù*,
facing north.
Father and son did not sit together,
but the grandson followed the grandfather.
*Dì* means to clarify (*dì*).
It clarifies the *zhāo-mù* order
and the principles of seniority and inferiority.
In the fourth month of summer, the *yáng* energy is above,
and the *yīn* energy is below,
thus establishing the principles of seniority and inferiority.
*Xiá* is in the tenth month of winter,
when the five grains are ripe,
thus kinship gathers for food and drink.
The ancestral temples (zǔzōngmiào) not yet being fixed,
they were temporarily combined for sacrifice.
Now is the time to fix them.”
This account is in Chún’s biography.
The Emperor found it difficult to re-establish temples,
and thus made the combined sacrifice at the high temple (gāomiào) a permanent practice.
Later, during the time of the three-year winter *xiá* and five-year summer *dì* sacrifices,
they merely offered sacrifices to the spirit tablets of destroyed temples,
which was called the *yīn* sacrifice.
Tàizǔ faced east,
Emperors Huì, Wén, Wǔ, and Yuán were *zhāo*,
and Emperors Jǐng and Xuān were *mù*.
Emperors Huì, Jǐng, and Zhāo were not sacrificed to during non-*yīn* sacrifice times.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ passed away,
Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
and because Emperor Guāngwǔ restored order and revived the dynasty,
a new temple was built for him,
with the esteemed title Shìzǔ Miào.
Because Emperor Yuán was *mù* to Guāngwǔ,
though not of the main lineage,
his temple was not destroyed.
This then became the norm.
When Emperor Míng was nearing his end, he issued a testamentary edict,
stating that he should follow the frugal example of not establishing a temple or an inner shrine (qǐnmiào).
His spirit tablet (zhǔ) was to be interred in the changing room (gēngyī) of the temple of Emperor Shìzǔ.
When Emperor Xiàozhāng ascended the throne,
he dared not violate this.
As the changing room (gēngyī) had a slight distinction,
he conferred the honorary title of Xiǎnzōng Miào,
offering sacrifices in a separate shrine within the changing room (gēngyī),
and performing combined sacrifices four times a year at the temple of Emperor Shìzǔ.
The account is in the chapter on the annals (Zhāng Jì).
When Emperor Zhāng was nearing his demise,
he issued a testamentary edict not to establish a temple or an inner shrine (qǐnmiào),
and that his temple should follow the precedent of the previous emperor.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne, he dared not violate this,
and conferred the honorary title of Sùzōng.
Later emperors, in accepting their veneration,
all interred their spirit tablets (zhǔ) in the temple of Emperor Shìzǔ.
As they accumulated, there was no distinction,
and thereafter Xiǎnzōng merely became the designation for the imperial tomb.
During the Yǒngyuán era,
Emperor Hé posthumously honored his mother, Consort Liáng, as Empress Gōnghuái,
and her tomb [was called Xīlíng].
Because Empress Dòu was enshrined with Emperor Zhāng,
When Emperor Hé died,
he was conferred the honorary title of Mùzōng.
Emperor Shāng died after a little over three hundred days,
and Empress Dowager Dèng governed as regent.
Because he was still an infant (yīnghái),
he was not listed in the temple,
and was merely worshipped at his tomb and inner shrine.
Emperor Ān, as the son of King Xiào of Qīnghé, ascended the throne.
In the first year of Jiànguāng,
he posthumously honored his grandmother, Consort Sòng, as Empress Jìngyǐn,
and her tomb was called Jìngběilíng.
She was also worshipped at her tomb and inner shrine,
with the Grand Herald (Tàicháng) presiding, similar to Xīlíng.
He posthumously honored his father, King Xiào of Qīnghé, as Emperor Xiàodé,
and his mother as Empress Xiàodé.
The King of Qīnghé, as his successor, merely offered sacrifices.
Because Emperor Ān harmed ministers with slander
and deposed the Crown Prince,
when he died,
there was no memorial submitted for conferring a temple name (zōng).
Later, because there had been no destruction [of a temple] since the Jiànwǔ era,
regular sacrifices were continued,
and his tomb name (línghào) was used to refer to him as Gōngzōng.
When Emperor Shùn ascended the throne,
he posthumously honored his mother as Empress Gōngmǐn,
and her tomb was called Gōngběilíng.
She was worshipped at her tomb and inner shrine,
similar to Jìngběilíng.
When Emperor Shùn died,
he was conferred the honorary title of Jìngzōng.
Emperors Chōng and Zhì both died young,
and Empress Dowager Liáng governed as regent.
Following the precedent of Emperor Shāng,
they were worshipped at their tombs and inner shrines.
After all ancestral temple ceremonies,
the Three Excellencies (Sāngōng) would divide the sacrifices among themselves.
Emperor Huán, as Lǐwú Hóu, a grandson of King Xiào of Héjiān, ascended the throne,
and also posthumously honored his ancestors;
the kingdom provided the sacrifices.
The account is in the biography of the Eight Kings of Zhānghé.
When the emperor died,
he was conferred the honorary title of Wēizōng,
and had no heir.
Emperor Líng, as Xièdú Hóu, a great-grandson of King Xiào of Héjiān, ascended the throne,
and also posthumously honored his ancestors.
The account is in the biography of the Eight Kings of Zhānghé.
During Emperor Líng's time,
the imperial capital annually sacrificed to five spirit tablets (zhǔ) in the Gāomiào temple,
seven spirit tablets (zhǔ) in the temple of Emperor Shìzǔ,
three tombs of young emperors,
and three tombs of posthumously honored empresses.
In total, eighteen grand sacrificial animals (tàiláo) were used,
all with secondary offerings.
Therefore, after the three spirit tablets (zhǔ) of the Gāomiào temple were personally destroyed,
sacrifices were offered only in years of grand sacrifices (yīnjì).
When Emperor Líng died,
Emperor Xiàn ascended the throne.
During the Chūpíng era,
Xiàngguó Dǒng Zhuó, Zuǒzhōnglángjiàng Cài Yōng, and others argued that from Emperor Hé onwards,
their merits and virtues were not extraordinary,
and they had committed transgressions;
they ought not to be granted temple names (zōng).
Additionally, the three empresses who were posthumously honored but were not of the main lineage
were all requested to be abolished.
The sacrifices offered four times a year were for
one ancestor and two Zōng in Gāomiào,
and four recent emperors,
making a total of seven emperors.
In antiquity, tomb sacrifices were not performed.
The Hàn imperial tombs all had garden shrines (yuánqǐn),
following the practice of Qín.
Commentators believed that in ancient ancestral temples, the temple (miào) was built first,
and then the inner shrine (qǐn),
symbolizing a human dwelling having a court in front
and private quarters at the back.
The Yuèlìng states,
"First offer to the inner shrine and temple (qǐnmiào)."
The Shī (Book of Poetry) states,
"The inner shrine and temple (qǐnmiào) are splendid,"
indicating their interconnectedness.
The temple (miào) was for storing spirit tablets (zhǔ) and for seasonal sacrifices.
The inner shrine (qǐn) contained clothes, hats, chairs, staffs, and other items symbolizing the living,
for offering new things.
Qín first established inner shrines (qǐn)
next to the tombs.
Hàn followed this practice without change,
hence the term "inner shrine hall" (qǐndiàn) on tombs,
with items for daily life, clothing, symbolizing a living person.
This was the original meaning of the ancient inner shrine (qǐn).
Since the Jiànwǔ era,
the imperial tombs west of the pass (Guānxī) became increasingly distant in time,
and only special animal sacrifices were offered seasonally;
when the emperor personally visited Cháng'ān to pay respects at the various tombs,
then grand animal sacrifices (tàiláo) were offered.
From the Luòyáng imperial tombs up to Emperor Líng's time,
sacrifices were offered on the last day and the fifteenth day of the lunar month, the twenty-four solar terms, Fúlà (summer and winter sacrifices), and the four seasons.
On temple days, food was presented.
The Grand Provisioner (Tàiguān) sent supplies,
and the park director (yuánlìng) and food supervisor (shíjiān) oversaw them.
The palace staff at the imperial tombs would arrange bedding and pillows according to the water clock,
prepare washing water,
and display ceremonial implements.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
the Grand Altar of Land and Grain (Tàishèjì) was established in Luòyáng,
to the right of the ancestral temple.
It was a square altar,
without a roof,
having only walls and a gate.
In the second and eighth months, and at Lày (winter sacrifice),
sacrifices were offered three times a year,
all with grand sacrificial animals (tàiláo),
performed by the appropriate officials.
The Xiàojīng Yuánshénqì states:
"Shè is
the lord of the land.
Jì is
the chief of the five grains."
The Lǐjì and Guóyǔ both state that the son of Gònggōng Shì was named Jùlóng,
who served as the official for Hòutǔ,
and was able to pacify the nine lands;
thus, he was worshipped as Shè.
The son of Lièshān Shì was named Zhù,
who was able to plant a hundred grains and cultivate them;
from Xià onwards, he was worshipped as Jì.
By the Yīn dynasty, Zhù had become remote,
and Qì, during Yáo's time, was appointed Hòujì,
also planting a hundred grains;
thus, Zhù was abolished,
and Qì was worshipped as Jì.
The Grand Minister of Agriculture (Dàsīnóng), Zhèng Xuán, said that
in antiquity, officials who performed great deeds
were enshrined and shared sacrifices with the gods.
Thus, Jùlóng was enshrined with Shè,
and Qì was enshrined with Jì.
Commanderies and counties established Shèjì altars.
Grand Administrators (Tàishǒu), magistrates (lìng), and chiefs (zhǎng) attended the sacrifices,
using sheep and pigs as sacrificial animals.
Only the seats of prefectures had Shè but no Jì,
because of their official capacity.
In antiquity, when armies marched and pacified, they carried the spirit tablet of Shè,
but not of Jì.
The state also had the sacrifices of the Five Spirits (Wǔsì),
managed by the appropriate officials,
and their rituals were simpler than those for Shèjì.
Eight years after the founding of Hàn,
it was said that when Zhōu rose, a city established the worship of Hòujì.
Thereupon, Emperor Gāo ordered all under heaven to establish shrines for Língxīng.
It is said that Hòujì was worshipped, but called Língxīng,
because Hòujì was also enshrined with the stars.
According to old accounts,
the star refers to the Celestial Field star.
Another account says
the Dragon's left horn is the Celestial Field official,
governing grains.
Sacrifices were offered on the Rénchén day at the appropriate position.
Rén represents water,
and Chén represents the dragon, fitting their category.
Grand sacrificial animals (tàiláo) were used,
and county magistrates (lìng) and chiefs (zhǎng) attended the sacrifices.
Sixteen young boys were used as dancers.
The dances symbolized agricultural teaching,
first representing clearing,
then plowing and sowing, weeding, driving away birds, harvesting, and pounding and winnowing,
symbolizing their labor.
Counties and cities regularly offered sacrifices to Xiānnóng on the Yǐwèi day at the Yǐ location,
to Fēngbó on the Bǐngxū day at the Xū location,
and to Yǔshī on the Jǐchǒu day at the Chǒu location,
using sheep and pigs.
On the day of Lìchūn,
everyone wore blue banners and headcloths,
welcoming spring outside the eastern wall of the city.
A young boy was ordered to wear a blue scarf,
and blue clothes,
and to be waiting in the fields outside the eastern wall.
When those welcoming spring arrived,
he would emerge from the fields.
Then, those welcoming him would bow and return,
without offering sacrifice.
For the three seasons, there was no welcoming ceremony.
The discussion states: Zāng Wénzhòng sacrificed to Yuánjū,
but Kǒngzǐ considered it ignorant.
The "Jiaosì Zhì" in the Hànshū details that from Qín to Wáng Mǎng,
some sacrificial rites were not performed,
and instances like Yuánjū were numerous.
When Shìzǔ revived the dynasty,
he abolished extraordinary practices,
and restored the old sacrifices.
Compared to previous affairs, it was vastly different.
I once heard Confucian sayings:
The Sānhuáng had no written language,
and governed by tying knots.
It was only from the Wǔdì that written characters existed.
By the time of the Sānwáng,
customs had become elaborate and ornate,
and deceit and falsehood gradually arose.
Only then did seals appear to check emergent treachery.
However, there were still no vessels of gold, jade, silver, or bronze.
From the time of the Shànghuáng,
those who performed the Fēng sacrifice on Tài Shān,
up to the Zhōu dynasty, numbered seventy-two generations.
Fēng refers to
piling earth to form an altar,
burning wood to sacrifice and report to Heaven,
marking successful achievements generation after generation.
This is what the Lǐjì refers to as
"ascending to Heaven from a famous mountain."
Changing the dynasty meant changing the Fēng sacrifice,
marking the beginning of a new era,
and indicating that it was not inherited.
Kings of successive generations, when on inspection tours,
would merely repair the altar for sacrifice.
From Qín Shǐhuáng and Xiàowǔ Dì,
their performance of the Fēng sacrifice on Tài Shān
originated from their fondness for immortals and belief in the words of alchemists,
creating the practice of stone tablets and sealed inscriptions.
This is what I have heard.
Although the Way of Heaven is indeed difficult to fathom and know,
its general principles still have a fundamental essence.
The Way of Heaven is simple and sincere,
economical and not extravagant.
Therefore, for sacrificial animals (had) [used] wooden tablets,
and vessels of pottery and gourds.
There was hardly any need for the complexities of sealed inscriptions,
nor for difficult-to-carve stones.
Moreover, only a change of dynasty warranted a Fēng sacrifice,
which is why it is called Dàizōng.
Xià Kāng and Zhōu Xuān,
who revived their dynasties after decline,
are not known to have altered the Fēng sacrifice.
Shìzǔ wished to follow Xiàowǔ's former Fēng sacrifice,
which was truly continuing the way of his ancestors.
But Liáng Sōng strongly argued,
insisting it must be changed.
Then, after the Fēng sacrifice was performed,
before any blessings were received,
Sōng was eventually executed.
Although the crime was his own,
it was perhaps also due to the fault of slandering the gods.
Furthermore, the reason why emperors could be greatly renowned by later generations
truly lay in their virtue benefiting the people,
not, it is said, in the Fēng sacrifice.
Among those who speak of Heaven and Earth, none is greater than the Yìjīng.
The Yìjīng has no image of "six zōng" in the center.
If it is truly believed to be revered by Heaven, Earth, and the four directions,
this is of utmost greatness.
But to liken it to the Tàishè
is again to be misguided,
making it difficult to consider sincere!
Eulogy says: [For] Heaven and Earth, the suburban sacrifices;
for ancestral temples, the offerings and sacrifices.
All ranks are without [distinguishing] patterns,
and mountains and rivers are completely regulated.
Excess leads to national disorder;
the canons are the imperial records.
Beginning from the utmost reverence,
who established their origin?
Collation Notes, page 3193, line 9: 下公卿博士議郎 (xià gōngqīng bóshì yìláng) – According to Lú Wénchāo (盧文chāo), there should be the character

below.
Page 3195, line 7: 名曰 (míng yuē) (惟) [堆]俎 (duīzǔ) – According to Lú’s (盧) collation,

was changed to
帷 (wéi).
Sūn Xīngyǎn (孫星衍) collated the Hàn Jiù Yí (漢舊儀) as
堆 (duī).
Now, it is changed according to Sūn’s (孫) collation.
Page 3195, line 8: 各配其左 (gè pèi qí zuǒ) – According to the Diànběn (殿本),
左 (zuǒ)
is written as
祖 (zǔ).
Page 3195, line 9: 復位 (fùwèi) (而) 皇帝上堂盥 (huángdì shàng táng guàn) – Deleted according to Lú’s (盧) collation.
Page 3195, line 12: 即更衣 (jí gēng yī) [巾] (jīn) – Changed according to Sūn’s (孫) collation of Hàn Jiù Yí (漢舊儀).
Page 3196, line 3: 公卿奏議世祖廟登歌八佾舞 (gōngqīng zòuyì Shìzǔ miào dēnggē bāyì wǔ) (功) 名 (míng) – Deleted according to Lú’s (盧) collation.
Page 3196, line 8: 元命包曰緣天地之所雜樂為之文典 (Yuán Mìng Bāo yuē yuán tiāndì zhī suǒ zá yuè wéizhī wéndiǎn) – According to Lú Wénchāo (盧文chāo), there is a mistake in 文 (wén).
According to Yùlǎn (御覽) 566, it cites:

Page 3196, line 8: 文王之時 (Wénwáng zhī shí) – According to Lú (盧),

Page 3196, line 9: (樞) [琁]機鈐曰 (xuánjīqián yuē) – According to Qián Dàxīn (錢大昕),
樞 (shū)
should be
琁 (xuán).

Lǐ Shàn’s (李善) commentary to Wénxuǎn Dōngdū Fù (文選東都賦) cites it as

Page 3196, line 11: 依書文始五行武德昭真修之舞 (yī shū wén shǐ wǔxíng wǔdé zhāozhēnxiū zhī wǔ) – According to Lú’s (盧) collation, the three characters

Page 3196, line 12: (勿) 進武德舞歌詩曰 (jìn Wǔdé wǔ gē shī yuē) – Lú (盧) said that the character

is likely redundant.
Now, it is deleted accordingly.
Page 3196, line 14: 進武德之舞如故 (jìn Wǔdé zhī wǔ rú gù) – According to Lú (盧), there seems to be missing text.
Below
故 (gù),
the character

Page 3197, line 2: 陵 [曰西陵] (líng yuē Xīlíng) – Jíjiě (集解) cites Qián Dàxīn’s (錢大昕) statement,

Page 3197, line 4: 以尚嬰 (yǐ shàng yīng) (孫) [孩] (hái) – Changed according to Lú’s (盧) collation.
According to Yuán Jì (袁紀), it is written as

Page 3198, line 7: 不當與世 (bù dàng yǔ shì) (祖) [宗] (zōng) 廟盛德之舞同名 (miào shèngdé zhī wǔ tóngmíng) – Changed according to Lú’s (盧) collation.
According to Lú (盧),

Page 3198, line 13: 昭哉來御慎其祖武 (zhāozāi lái yù shèn qí zǔwǔ) – According to the Diànběn (殿本) text verification, Háng Shìjùn (杭世駿) stated,

is written as

According to the Hǎiyuángé (海原閣) edition of Cài Zhōngláng Jí (蔡中郎集), not only are these two sentences absent,
but also the passage from

to
不應為宗 (bù yīng wéi zōng)
