Five types of conduct: disrespect,
excessive rain,
inauspicious clothing,
chicken omens,
green blight,
houses collapsing spontaneously,
rumors,
drought,
ballads,
and wolves eating people.
The theories of the Five Elements and their corresponding omens are recorded in detail in the Treatise on the Five Elements in the Hànshū.
Therefore, Yìng Shào, Grand Administrator of Tàishān, Dǒng Bā, Attendant Censor, and Qiáo Zhōu, Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary,
all compiled records of calamitous anomalies since Jiànwǔ.
They are now combined and discussed
to continue the previous treatise.
The Treatise on the Five Elements states:
"If hunting is not completed,
food and drink are not offered,
comings and goings are not regulated,
the people's farming season is taken away,
or there are treacherous schemes,
then wood will not bend or straighten."
This means that wood loses its natural properties and becomes a disaster.
It also states:
"Disrespect in demeanor
is called irreverence.
Its fault is madness,
its punishment is constant rain,
its extreme is evil.
The explanation says: when energies harm each other, it is called "hài" (harm).
In the first year of Jiànwǔ,
the Chìméi bandits' leaders Fán Chóng, Féng Ān, and others jointly established Liú Pénzǐ as Emperor.
However, Chóng and the others treated him like a child,
doing everything as they pleased,
and never showing him any care or respect.
Later, on the first day of the new year,
when the emperor and his officials were about to feast together,
after sitting down, before the wine and food were served,
the officials began to rise one after another,
creating chaos that could not be disciplined.
At that time, Grand Minister of Agriculture Yáng Yīn, drawing his sword, angrily said:
"Children's games are not even this bad!"
Afterward, they were defeated and destroyed,
and Chóng, Ān, and the others were all executed.
Only Yīn became a Marquis within the Pass [guānnèi hóu]
and died of old age.
When Emperor Guāngwǔ passed away,
Liú Jīng, Prince of Shānyáng, cried without sorrow,
and sent a flying letter to the Prince of Dōnghǎi,
encouraging him to rebel.
During the reign of Emperor Zhāng,
Dòu Huánghòu’s brother, Dòu Xiàn, due to the Empress’s great favor with the Emperor,
was feared by all.
Dòu Xiàn then forcibly demanded to seize the lands of Princess Qìnshuǐ Zhǎng,
who, fearing Dòu Xiàn,
gave them to him.
Dòu Xiàn then treated her with contempt.
Later, when the Emperor visited the Princess’s land,
he noticed this
and questioned Dòu Xiàn.
Dòu Xiàn again reported that he had merely borrowed them.
Out of consideration for the Empress,
the Emperor merely admonished him
and did not punish him for his crime.
Later, after Emperor Zhāng passed away,
Empress Dowager Dòu acted as regent,
and Dòu Xiàn held military and state secrets.
Loyal and upright officials who opposed Dòu Xiàn
were often harmed by him.
Thereafter, Dòu Xiàn and his brothers were all executed.
During the reign of Emperor Huán,
Liáng Jì held political power.
His brothers, noble and prosperous, acted wantonly.
They enjoyed excessively fast driving.
Even upon returning home,
they would still gallop into the gates.
The common people called this
“the Liáng family’s household-destroying gallop.”
Later, they were indeed annihilated.
In the tenth,
thirteenth,
fourteenth,
and fifteenth years of Yǒngyuán of Emperor Hé’s reign,
there were continuous heavy rains that damaged the crops.
In the fourth year of Yuánchū of Emperor Ān’s reign, in autumn,
ten commanderies and kingdoms suffered continuous heavy rains that damaged the crops.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
thirty-three commanderies and kingdoms suffered continuous heavy rains that damaged the crops.
In the first year of Jiànguāng,
the capital and twenty-nine commanderies and kingdoms suffered continuous heavy rains that damaged the crops.
At this time, the Qiāng rebellion had long been ongoing and unpacified.
The common people were stationed for defense
and could not escape their sorrow and hardship.
In the first year of Yánguāng,
twenty-seven commanderies and kingdoms suffered continuous heavy rains that damaged the crops.
In the second year,
five commanderies and kingdoms suffered continuous rains that damaged the crops.
In the fourth year of Yǒngjiàn of Emperor Shùn’s reign,
the Sīlì, Jīng, Yù, Yǎn, and Jì provinces suffered continuous heavy rains that damaged the crops.
In the sixth year,
Jì Zhōu suffered continuous heavy rains that damaged the crops.
In the summer of the second year of Yánxī of Emperor Huán’s reign,
there was continuous rain for over fifty days.
At this time,
the General-in-Chief, Liáng Jì, held political power
and plotted to murder Xuān, the mother of the Emperor’s favored Lady Dèng Guìrén.
Liáng Jì also arbitrarily killed the Court Counselor Bǐng Zūn.
The Emperor wished to execute Liáng Jì,
but feared that his long-held power,
strong influence,
and possible defiance
would harm officials and common people.
He secretly discussed a plan with trusted attendants and regular palace attendants such as Dān Chāo.
In the eighth month of that year,
Liáng Jì finally admitted his guilt and was executed.
In the summer of the first year of Jiànníng of Emperor Líng’s reign,
there was continuous rain for over sixty days.
At this time, the General-in-Chief, Dòu Wǔ, plotted to stage a coup and abolish the palace eunuchs.
In the ninth month of that year,
Zhū Yǔ, the Wǔguān Historian of Chánglè, and others, together with the Regular Palace Attendant Cáo Jié, raised troops.
They first executed Dòu Wǔ,
fought outside the palace gate,
and Dòu Wǔ fled in defeat.
They pursued and beheaded Dòu Wǔ and his brothers,
with several hundred people dying.
In the summer of the first year of Xīpíng,
there was continuous rain for over seventy days.
At this time, the Palace Attendant Cáo Jié and others
jointly falsely accused Lǐ, the King of Bóhǎi, of rebellion.
In the tenth month, Lǐ was executed.
In the summer of the sixth year of Zhōngpíng,
there was continuous rain for over eighty days.
At this time, Emperor Líng had newly abandoned his ministers.
The deceased Emperor was still in his coffin.
The General-in-Chief Hé Jìn, with Yuan Shào, the Adjutant Military Commandant, and others, plotted to execute and depose the palace eunuchs.
After the funeral rites were completed,
the Regular Palace Attendant Zhāng Ràng and others jointly killed Hé Jìn.
There was battle in the capital,
and thousands died.
Dozens of the Gēngshǐ generals who passed through Luòyáng
all wore turbans and embroidered women’s robes with wide sleeves.
At the time, wise people saw this
and considered the attire inappropriate,
a harbinger of personal disaster.
They then fled to the border commanderies to avoid it.
This was a clothing omen.
Thereafter, Gēngshǐ was indeed killed by the Chìméi.
During the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Huán,
women in the capital adopted "sorrowful eyebrows," "teardrops," "fallen horse's mane" hairstyles, "crooked waist" gaits, and "toothache smiles."
So-called "sorrowful eyebrows"
were thin and curved.
"Teardrops"
involved lightly wiping below the eyes,
as if having cried.
"Fallen horse's mane" hairstyles
were worn to one side.
"Crooked waist" gaits
meant the feet were not directly beneath the body.
"Toothache smiles"
were like a toothache,
without genuine happiness.
These trends originated from the household of the General-in-Chief Liáng Jì.
The capital eagerly adopted them,
and all of China imitated them.
This was a near clothing omen.
Liáng Jì, for two generations, served as commander-in-chief,
was related by marriage to the imperial family,
and wielded immense power and influence,
which would endanger the state.
Heaven’s warning seemed to say: Troops will come to arrest them,
women will be sorrowful,
frowning and weeping,
officials and soldiers will drag them roughly,
breaking their waists and spines,
causing their hairpins to tilt,
and though they might force a smile,
it will have no real flavor.
By the second year of Yánxī,
their entire clan was executed.
During Yánxī,
after Liáng Jì was executed,
headwear in the capital became short at the front and long at the back,
and clothing became short at the top and long at the bottom.
At this time, the Regular Palace Attendants Dān Chāo, Zuǒ Kuàng, Xú Huáng, Jù Yuàn, and Táng Héng were by the Emperor’s side,
indulging in their wickedness.
The people of the realm grumbled: "One General-in-Chief dies,
five General-in-Chiefs appear."
Households had several marquises,
sons and younger brothers were distributed throughout provinces and commanderies.
Guests and retainers scrambled and soared.
Short at the top and long at the bottom
shared the same omen as Liáng Jì.
By the eighth year,
Emperor Huán, in response to the anomaly of a solar eclipse,
appointed former Minister of Works Hán Yín as Colonel Director of Retainers,
who then systematically eliminated them,
and the capital became rectified and pure.
During Yánxī,
elderly men in the capital all wore wooden clogs;
newly married women
even made straps decorated with painted lacquer in five colors.
This was a clothing omen.
By the ninth year,
the factional persecutions began.
Those involved were sent to the North Imperial Prison.
At that time, in fear and confusion,
unable to believe in Heaven’s mandate,
many fled and did not submit to interrogation.
Their nine familial relations were imprisoned,
and wherever they went,
old and young women alike were subjected to shackles and fetters,
which corresponded to the image of wooden clogs.
During the Jiànníng era of Emperor Líng,
elderly men in the capital all used reed square baskets as utensils;
even commoners did so.
At that time, discerning people secretly said: "Reed square baskets
are the judgment boxes of commanderies and kingdoms.
Now that they are prized and used,
this means all people under heaven will be judged for crimes by judicial officials."
By the amnesty edict of the third year of Guānghé, Guǐchǒu,
officials and commoners imprisoned due to factional prohibitions were pardoned.
If the text was unclear,
others with similar doubtful cases were judged.
Thus, all commanderies involved in factionalism submitted judgments to the Grand Judge,
and everyone's names were put into square baskets.
Emperor Líng was fond of "Hu" (foreign) clothing, "Hu" tents, "Hu" beds, "Hu" sitting styles, "Hu" food, "Hu" kongsang, "Hu" flutes, and "Hu" dances.
Nobles and imperial relatives in the capital all competed to adopt these.
This was a clothing omen.
Thereafter, Dǒng Zhuó commanded many "Hu" troops,
filling the streets,
looting the palace,
and desecrating imperial tombs.
Emperor Língdì, in the Western Garden of the palace, harnessed four white donkeys.
He personally held the reins
and drove them around,
finding great joy in this.
Consequently, the dukes, ministers, nobility, and imperial relatives all began to imitate him,
even riding in covered carts (zīpíng) as if they were cavalry escorts.
They competed to seize them,
and their prices rivaled those of horses.
The Yì says:
"From time to time, one rides six dragons to rule Heaven."
Among those that traverse the heavens, none are like dragons;
among those that traverse the earth, none are like horses.
The Shī says:
"The four stallions are mighty and strong,
carrying this regular attire."
"The sandalwood chariot gleams brightly,
the four stallions are stout."
Now, donkeys are used to carry heavy loads and travel long distances,
up and down mountains and valleys.
They are merely for the use of common folk.
How can an emperor or a gentleman harness and ride them?
Donkeys are dull creatures,
yet now they are valued.
It is as if Heaven's will says: The state will soon be in great chaos,
the wise and the foolish will be inverted,
and all those in power will be like donkeys.
Subsequently, Dǒng Zhuó tyrannized the imperial house,
drawing in many border people to fill the central court.
Barbarians and people of different ethnicities
trampled upon Zhōngguó.
During the Xīpíng era,
within the province, people wore dog-caps and sashes,
finding it amusing.
One dog suddenly appeared,
running into the gate of the Sītú's mansion.
Those who saw it
were all astonished and perplexed.
Jīng Fáng's Yìzhuàn says:
"If the ruler is not upright,
and the ministers desire to usurp,
the omen is a dog wearing a cap appearing."
Later, Emperor Língdì favored and employed his close attendants and younger relatives,
the guests of Yǒnglè and the petty officials of Hóngdū.
They mutually promoted each other,
and dukes, ministers, provincial governors, and prefects
were all of this type, standing shoulder to shoulder.
He also sent imperial censors to the Western [Dǐ] to sell official positions.
Marquises of Guānnèi who paid five million [coins]
were given gold and purple (symbols of high rank).
Those who went to the imperial court to submit memorials to apply for magistrate or chief positions
had the price determined by the quality of the county,
whether it was rich or poor.
The powerful were as greedy as jackals and tigers;
the weak were almost inhuman.
These were truly "dogs wearing caps."
The Sītú was the ancient chancellor,
who unified the governance of the state.
Heaven's warning was as if to say: Many chancellors are not the right people,
they merely occupy their positions and consume their salaries without accomplishment,
unable to uphold righteousness and maintain authority,
but rather follow intentions and yield to wishes.
Those currently in office are all like dogs,
hence the dog ran into their gate.
Emperor Língdì frequently played games in the Western Garden.
He ordered imperial concubines and palace women to act as innkeepers,
while he himself dressed as a merchant.
When he arrived at an inn,
the palace women would offer wine and food,
and they would eat and drink together as a form of amusement.
This was an omen of deviant attire.
After this, the world fell into great chaos.
During Emperor Xiàndì's Jiàn'ān era,
men's clothing
favored long torsos with very short lower garments,
while women favored long skirts with very short upper garments.
At the time, Mò Sì, an official from Yìzhōu, considered this an omen of deviant attire,
meaning that the yang lacked a lower part and the yin lacked an upper part,
and the world was not yet destined for peace.
After this,
great chaos ensued.
In the first year of Emperor Língdì's Guānghé era,
a hen in the Nángōng Shìzhōng Temple was about to transform into a rooster.
All the feathers on its body resembled those of a rooster,
but its comb had not yet changed.
An imperial edict was issued to ask Yìláng Cài Yōng about this.
Cài Yōng replied:
"If the appearance is irreverent,
there will be a chicken omen (jīhuò).
In the first year of Emperor Xuāndì's Huánglóng era,
a hen in the Wèiyāng Palace transformed into a rooster,
but it did not crow and had no spurs.
In that year, Emperor Yuándì first ascended the throne
and established Empress Wáng.
By the first year of Chūyuán,
a hen in the residence of the chancellor's clerk transformed into a rooster,
with comb, spurs, and crowing like a general.
In that year, the empress's father, Jìn, was made Marquis of Píngyáng,
and his daughter was established as empress.
When Emperor Āidì passed away,
the empress regent assumed power,
and Wáng Mǎng, being her nephew, was made Grand Marshal,
which led to chaos.
I humbly deduce
that the head
is the sovereign,
the symbol of the monarch.
Now, the chicken's body has changed,
but it has not reached the head,
and the higher authorities are aware of it.
This is an omen that something will happen but will not be fully realized.
If the response is not precise,
and the government makes no reforms,
and the comb eventually forms,
the calamity will be even greater."
After this, Zhāng Jiǎo rebelled, calling himself the Yellow Turban,
and subsequently caused widespread destruction.
The four quarters were exhausted by levies and corvée,
and many rebelled.
The emperor did not reform the government,
which eventually led to great chaos throughout the land.
In the fourth month of the second year of Emperor Huándì's Yǒngxīng era, on the day bǐngwǔ,
a green qi appeared at night beneath the wall of the Guānglùxūn's official residence.
Upon inspection,
one jade hook (gōu) and one jade ring (jué) were found.
The hook was seven cùn and two fēn long,
the jué was five cùn and four fēn in circumference,
and both were carved.
This was a green omen (qīngxiáng).
Jade is
a type of metal.
Seven cùn and two fēn
are numbers associated with shang (metal).
Five cùn and four fēn
are numbers associated with zhǐ (fire).
Shang represents ministers,
and zhǐ represents affairs.
This indicates that ministers who make decisions are not solemn,
and calamity will ensue.
At this time, Liáng Jì held power and was autocratic.
Four years later,
the Liáng clan was exterminated.
In the fifth year of Yánxī,
the gate of the Imperial Academy (Tàixué) spontaneously collapsed.
Xiāng Kǎi believed that the Imperial Academy was a place for doubt and residence,
and its gate collapsing spontaneously meant that
cultural virtue would be lost,
and education would be abandoned.
After this, the world indeed fell into destruction and chaos.
In the tenth month of the first year of Yǒngkāng, on the day rénxū,
the inner house of the Píngchéng Gate in Nángōng spontaneously collapsed.
Metal suppresses wood,
so wood moved.
In the twelfth month of that year,
the imperial carriage passed away (the emperor died).
In the first year of Emperor Língdì's Guānghé era,
the inner house of the Nángōng Píngchéng Gate, the Wǔkù house, and the outer eastern wall house all collapsed one after another.
Cài Yōng replied:
"The Píngchéng Gate
is the gate of upright yang,
connected to the palace.
The imperial carriage for suburban sacrifices passes through it,
making it the most revered of gates.
The Wǔkù
is where forbidden weapons are stored.
The Eastern Wall
is the outer barrier of the armory.
The Yìzhuàn says: 'When petty individuals are in high positions,
superiors and subordinates alike are perverse,
the omen is the collapse of the inner city gate.'
Qiántán Bā says: 'If palace tiles fall spontaneously,
the feudal lords will powerfully oppress the ruler.'
These are all the faults of petty individuals in prominent positions disrupting the law."
After this, the Yellow Turban bandits first arose in the east,
and the weapons in the armory were greatly stirred (used).
Empress's paternal elder brother Hé Jìn was Grand General;
her maternal younger brother Miáo was General of Cavalry and Chariots.
Both brothers were noble and powerful,
and both commanded troops in the capital.
Later, Hé Jìn wanted to execute and depose the eunuchs,
but he was killed by the Permanent Attendant Zhāng Ràng, Duàn Guī, and others.
Soldiers fought at the palace gates,
slaughtering each other,
and great military uprisings occurred throughout the land.
In the second month of the third year [of Zhōngpíng],
the veranda where the imperial carriage stopped at the Public Mansion spontaneously collapsed,
over thirty bays north and south.
In the second month, on the day guǐhài, of the second year of Zhōngpíng,
the upper house outside the Guǎngyáng city gate spontaneously collapsed.
In the third month of the second year of Emperor Xiàndì's Chūpíng era,
the house outside the Xuānpíng Gate in Cháng'ān spontaneously collapsed without cause.
By the summer of the third year,
Sītú Wáng Yǔn sent the Commandant Lǚ Bù to kill Grand Tutor Dǒng Zhuó,
exterminating his three clans.
In the tenth month of the first year of Xīngpíng [192 AD],
the city gates of Cháng'ān spontaneously collapsed without cause.
By the spring of the second year,
Lǐ Quē and Guō Sì were fighting in Cháng'ān.
Lǐ Quē coerced and kidnapped the Son of Heaven,
moving him to Lǐ Quē's camp.
He burned down all the palaces, city gates, government offices, and private dwellings,
and unleashed his soldiers to raid and plunder the grandees and below.
In winter,
the Son of Heaven returned east to Luòyáng.
Lǐ Quē and Guō Sì pursued and caught up with him at Cáoyáng,
plundering the imperial carriage and baggage train,
and killing dozens of people, including Grand Master of Ceremonies Dèng Yuān, Grand Judge Xuān Fán, and Lesser Treasury Minister Tián Bīn.
The Wǔxíng Zhuàn says:
"If one is fond of attacking and warring,
disregards the common people,
adorns city walls,
and invades border regions,
then Metal will not follow its nature (of 'from 革' meaning 'changes')."
This means Metal loses its nature and becomes a calamity.
It also says:
"If words are not heeded,
this is called '不' (disobedience).
Its fault is 'jiàn' (transgression),
its punishment is constant heat,
and its extreme manifestation is sorrow.
At such times there are ominous poems,
〔一０〕at such times there are afflictions from shelled insects,
〔一一〕at such times there are dog calamities,
〔一二〕at such times there are ailments of the mouth and tongue,
〔一三〕at such times there are white misfortunes and white auspicious signs,
when Wood subdues Metal."
Jièchóng (shelled insects),
Liú Xīn's biography considers to be máochóng (hairy insects).
Yì means
to govern.
In the eleventh month of the first year of Yǒngchū of Emperor Ān [107 AD],
the people spread rumors and frightened each other.
The common people of the Sìlì, Bìng, and Jì Provinces migrated.
At this time, Empress Dowager Dèng held exclusive power.
It is the Way for women to be submissive,
thus the Rítu
command of "upon husband's death, follow the son."
Now she monopolized
affairs,
this is disobedience and transgression.
In the summer of the
fifth year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Shìzǔ [29 AD],
there was a drought.
Jīng Fáng's biography says:
"If virtue is desired but not used,
this is called zhāng (spreading),
its calamity is barrenness,
its drought has dark clouds but no rain,
changing to red due to four yin.
If the multitude emerges past its time,
this is called guǎng (spreading wide),
its drought produces nothing.
If both high and low are obscured,
this is called gé (separation),
its drought has the sky red for three months,
at times with hail killing flying birds.
If the superior seeks a consort by climbing [in rank],
this is called jiàn (transgression),
its drought has three months of great warmth without clouds.
If the ruler builds high platforms and mansions,
this is called fàn (offence),
yin invades yang,
its drought kills the roots of all things,
and there are fire calamities.
If ordinary officials overstep their bounds,
this is called jiàn (transgression),
its drought causes plants in marshes to wither,
and to be damaged by fire."
At this time, those who were transgressive and rebellious in the empire had not yet been fully punished,
and armies often overstayed their time.
In the summer of the second year of Zhānghé of Emperor Zhāng [88 AD],
there was a drought.
At this time, after Emperor Zhāng's death,
Empress Dowager Dòu's brothers were in power, extravagant and transgressive.
In the autumn of the sixth year of Yǒngyuán of Emperor Hé [94 AD],
the capital suffered a drought.
At this time, there were wrongfully imprisoned individuals in Luòyáng.
Emperor Hé visited the temples of Luòyáng,
reviewed the prisoners,
and redressed the wrongly accused.
He collected orders and sent them to prison to be punished.
Before he returned to the palace,
a torrential rain fell.
In the summer of the
sixth year of Yǒngchū of Emperor Ān [112 AD],
there was a drought.
In the summer of the seventh year,
there was a drought.
In the summer of the first year of Yuánchū [114 AD],
there was a drought.
In the summer of the second year,
there was a drought.
In the summer of the sixth year,
there was a drought.
In the summer of the third year of Yǒngjiàn of Emperor Shùn [128 AD],
there was a drought.
In the summer of the fifth year,
there was a drought.
In the summer of the second year of Yángjiā [133 AD],
there was a drought.
At this time, Lǐ Gù offered advice,
attributing it to extravagance and transgression.
In the summer of the first year of Yǒngxī of Emperor Chōng [145 AD],
there was a drought.
At this time, Emperor Chōng died young.
Grand Commandant Lǐ Gù advised the Empress Dowager and her brother Liáng Jì to establish a worthy successor,
choosing an older, virtuous person.
The empire would rely on this,
and their achievements would be immortal.
If a child was chosen, it was unknowable,
and if he later turned out to be bad,
regret would be too late.
At that time, the Empress Dowager and Liáng Jì were greedy to enthrone a child
to prolong their own exclusive power,
and thus enthroned Emperor Zhì,
who was eight years old.
This was not using virtue.
In the summer of the first year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Huán [151 AD],
there was a drought.
At this time, Liáng Jì held power,
and his wife and children were all enfeoffed,
their favor exceeding proper bounds.
In the sixth month of the first year of Yánxī [158 AD],
there was a drought.
In the summer of the fifth year of Xīpíng of Emperor Líng [176 AD],
there was a drought.
In the summer of the sixth year,
there was a drought.
In the summer of the fifth year of Guānghé [182 AD],
there was a drought.
In the summer of the sixth year,
there was a drought.
At this time, the Chamberlains and Palace Attendants transgressively wielded power and influence.
In the autumn of the first year of Xīngpíng of Emperor Xiàn [194 AD],
Cháng'ān suffered a drought.
At this time, Lǐ Quē and Guō Sì monopolized power and acted unrestrainedly.
During Gēngshǐ's reign,
there was a children's rhyme in Nányáng:
"Harmony or disharmony,
lies with the Chìméi.
To get or not to get,
lies north of the Yellow River."
At this time, Gēngshǐ was in Cháng'ān,
and Emperor Shìzǔ was the Grand Marshal, pacifying the area north of the Yellow River.
Gēngshǐ's ministers all transgressively monopolized power,
hence the ominous rhyme appeared.
Later, Gēngshǐ was indeed killed by the Chìméi;
this was Gēngshǐ's disharmony lying with the Chìméi.
Emperor Shìzǔ rose from north of the Yellow River.
In the sixth year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Shìzǔ [30 AD],
a children's rhyme in Shǔ said:
"Yellow ox, white belly,
Wǔzhū coins shall return."
At this time, Gōngsūn Shù usurped the imperial title in Shǔ.
People secretly said that Wáng Mǎng called himself "Yellow,"
and Gōngsūn Shù wanted to succeed him,
hence he called himself "White."
Wǔzhū coins
were the currency of the Hàn dynasty,
indicating they would definitely return.
Gōngsūn Shù was subsequently annihilated.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
a children's rhyme in Tiānshuǐ said:
"Go out Wúmén,
look at Tíqún.
See a lame man,
saying he wants to ascend to heaven;
if heaven can be ascended,
how can there be people on earth!"
At this time, Kuí Xiāo had just raised troops in Tiānshuǐ.
Later, his ambitions gradually grew,
wanting to become the Son of Heaven,
and he was subsequently destroyed.
Kuí Xiāo had been lame since childhood due to illness.
Wúmén
is the name of a city gate in Jì's outer wall.
Tíqún
is the name of a mountain.
At the end of the reign of Emperor Shùn,
a children's rhyme in Jīngdū went:
"Straight as a bowstring,
dies by the roadside.
Crooked as a hook,
is granted a marquisate."
Examining this, when Emperor Shùn passed away,
Emperor Zhì had a short reign.
The Grand General Liáng Jì, greedy for power, established a young and inexperienced ruler,
taking it as his own achievement.
He monopolized the state's commands and edicts,
to satisfy his personal desires.
The Grand Commandant Lǐ Gù believed that Prince Yǎ of Qīnghé was naturally intelligent,
devoted to poetry and fond of ritual,
and furthermore a close relative.
To establish the elder would be proper,
to appoint the virtuous would be secure.
However, Jì presented a proposal to the Empress Dowager,
which led to Gù's removal from office.
He then summoned the Marquis of Líwú,
who thereupon ascended to the supreme position.
On that very day, Gù was secretly killed in prison,
his body exposed on the road.

Meanwhile, Grand Commandant Hú Guǎng was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānlè Xiāng, Minister over the Masses Zhào Jiè as the Marquis of Chútíng, and Minister of Works Yuán Tāng as the Marquis of Ānguó Tíng.
At the beginning of Emperor Huán's reign,
a children's rhyme across the land went:
"The small wheat is green, the large wheat is withered.
Who will harvest it? The wife and the mother-in-law.
Where is the husband? West, striking the Hú.
The officials buy horses,
you prepare the carriages.
Please, for all of you, I'll drum a 'lónghú'."
Examining this, in the Yuánjiā period, the various Qiāng tribes of Liángzhōu all rebelled simultaneously,
entering Shǔ and Hàn to the south,
pillaging Sānfǔ to the east,
and extending to Bìng and Jì.
This caused great harm to the people.
Generals were commanded to lead armies,
but they were always defeated in every battle.
As Zhōngguó sent out more armored soldiers,
much wheat was abandoned,
and only women were left to harvest it.
"Officials buy horses,
you prepare the carriages"
refers to the heavy levies and conscriptions imposed even on those with official ranks.
"Please, for all of you, I'll drum a 'lónghú'"
means they dared not speak publicly,
but whispered privately.
At the beginning of Emperor Huán's reign,
a children's rhyme in Jīngdū went:
"Crow on the city wall,
its tail hangs down.
The father is an official,
the son is a soldier.
One soldier dies,
a hundred chariots.
Chariots in sequence,
enter Hèjiān.
Hèjiān's beautiful women are skilled at counting money,
with money they build rooms, with gold they build halls.
On the stones, they grind yellow millet, discontent.
Beneath the beams is a suspended drum,
I want to strike it, but the ministers are angry."
Examining this, all these refer to the government's greed.
"Crow on the city wall,
its tail hangs down"
means holding a high position and enjoying benefits alone,
not sharing with those below;
it refers to the ruler accumulating much wealth.
"The father is an official,
the son is a soldier"
means that when the barbarians are about to rebel,
the father is already a military official, and his son is also sent as a soldier to attack them.
"One soldier dies,
a hundred chariots"
means that after one person was sent to suppress the Hú and died,
a hundred chariots were again dispatched.
"Chariots in sequence,
enter Hèjiān"
means that the emperor was about to die,
and the imperial carriages entered Hèjiān in sequence to welcome Emperor Líng.
"Hèjiān's beautiful women are skilled at counting money,
with money they build rooms, with gold they build halls"
means that after Emperor Líng ascended the throne,
his mother, Empress Dowager Yǒnglè, was fond of accumulating gold to build halls.
"On the stones, they grind yellow millet, discontent"
means that although Yǒnglè accumulated gold and money,
she was always discontent and felt it was not enough,
so she made people grind yellow millet and eat it.
"Beneath the beams is a suspended drum,
I want to strike it, but the ministers are angry"
means that Yǒnglè taught Emperor Líng
to sell offices for money,
appointing unworthy people.
Loyal and sincere gentlemen of the realm resented this,
wanting to strike the suspended drum to seek an audience,
but the ministers who were in charge of the drum
also flattered and complied,
becoming angry and stopping me.
At the beginning of Emperor Huán's reign,
a children's rhyme in Jīngdū went:
"Yóupíng sells seals, and there is indeed Píng,
not avoiding powerful gentry or great clans."
Examining this, towards the end of the Yánxī period,
Empress Déng committed suicide due to a condemnation.
Dòu Guìrén was then appointed to replace her.
Her father, whose courtesy name was Yóupíng,
was named Wǔ and was appointed Colonel of the City Gate.
When the Empress Dowager took charge of the government,
he became Grand General.
He joined forces with Grand Tutor Chén Fān,
devoting their efforts to establishing virtue.
Those who received official seals
were all the right people,
and the powerful gentry and great clans
all lost hope.
At the end of Emperor Huán's reign,
a children's rhyme in Jīngdū went:
"In one qǐng of cogon grass field there is a well,
its four sides are slender and cannot be straightened.
Chew and chew again,
this year is still acceptable, next year will be disastrous."
Examining this, the Yì says:
"Pulling up cogon grass by its roots,
for its kind,
undertaking it brings good fortune."
Cogon grass symbolizes worthy gentlemen.
The well
represents the law.
At that time, the Central Regular Attendants Guǎn Bà and Sū Kāng intensely disliked the brilliant and wise men within the seas,
and together with the Superintendent of the Imperial Household of Chánglè Liú Xiāo, Grand Master of Ceremonies Xǔ Yǒng, Minister of Personnel Liǔ Fēn,
Xún Mù, Shǐ Tóng,
and Intendant of the Capital Táng Zhēn, among others,
they acted as their mouthpieces.
Láo Chuān of Hénèi presented a memorial to the court:
"Rǔ, Yǐng, and Nányáng,
they merely seek empty reputations and monopolize power and influence.
Gānlíng has two parts, north and south,
and Sānfǔ is especially severe."
Because of this, the Yellow Gate and Northern Temple were ordered to investigate,
and they were first seen to be abandoned.
"One qǐng of cogon grass field"
means that there were many worthy gentlemen.
"In it there is a well"
means that even in distress,
they did not deviate from their principles.
"Its four sides are slender and cannot be straightened"
means that wickedness was rampant
and could not be rectified.
"Chew and chew again"
refers to the words used to urge drinking in Jīngdū.
It means that those who ate meat were contemptible,
not caring about state affairs,
but only indulging in banquets, drinking, singing, and shouting.
"This year is still acceptable"
means only that they were proscribed.
"Next year will be disastrous"
refers to the execution of Chén and Dòu,
which caused great ruin throughout the land.
At the end of Emperor Huán's reign,
a children's rhyme in Jīngdū went:
"How long and winding the small white-canopied carriage!
Hèjiān comes to make harmony,
Hèjiān comes to make harmony!"
Examining this, Jiědú Tíng belonged to Ráoyáng County in Hèjiān.
Not long after, Emperor Huán died,
and the envoy and the Marquis of Jiědú both came from Hèjiān in white-canopied carriages.
Yányán
describes their multitude.
At this time, Censor Liú Shū suggested establishing Emperor Líng.
Shū was appointed Palace Attendant.
The Central Regular Attendant Hóu Lǎn feared his closeness
would surely harm himself.
He proposed appointing Shū as Grand Administrator of Tàishān,
and then ordered the Intendant of the Capital to press for his execution.
The court lacked
wise and experienced officials.
Remembering Shū's effectiveness,
they promoted and appointed his younger brother Hé,
who reached the position of Minister over the Masses.
This was the "making harmony."
At the end of Emperor Líng's reign,
a children's rhyme in Jīngdū went:
"Marquis not marquis,
King not king,
a thousand chariots and ten thousand riders ascend Běimáng."
Examining this, in the sixth year of Zhōngpíng,
the Marquis Shǐ ascended to the supreme position.
Emperor Xiàn had not yet received a noble title.
He was seized by dozens of people, including the Central Regular Attendant Duàn Guī.
The grandees and all officials followed behind them.
After reaching Héshàng,
they were able to return.
This is what "marquis not marquis, king not king, ascending Běimáng" refers to.
In the middle of the Zhōngpíng period of Emperor Líng,
a song was sung in the capital:
“Enjoying the world of joy, Dǒng Táo,
roaming the four city walls, Dǒng Táo,
receiving heavenly grace, Dǒng Táo,
wearing gold and purple, Dǒng Táo,
going to give thanks, Dǒng Táo,
arranging chariots and cavalry, Dǒng Táo,
about to depart, Dǒng Táo,
bidding farewell to the court, Dǒng Táo,
exiting the west gate, Dǒng Táo,
gazing at the palace, Dǒng Táo,
looking at the capital city, Dǒng Táo,
day and night breaking away, Dǒng Táo,
heart utterly broken, Dǒng Táo.”
Upon examination,
"Dǒng"
refers to Dǒng Zhuó.
It means that although he was tyrannical
and indulged in his cruelty,
he would eventually flee and hide,
leading to the extermination of his clan.
At the beginning of Emperor Xiàn's reign,
a children's rhyme in the capital went:
“A thousand li of grass,
how verdant it is.
Ten days, a divination,
cannot live.”
Upon examination, "a thousand li of grass" forms Dǒng (董),
and "ten days, a divination" forms Zhuó (卓).
Normally, when breaking down characters,
one always starts from the top,
combining and separating the left and right parts.
There is no instance of starting from the bottom.
The fact that these two characters are like this
suggests the will of Heaven, as if to say: Zhuó (卓) rises from the bottom to oppress the top,
meaning a subject overthrows his ruler.
“How verdant”
describes the appearance of his overbearing power.
“Cannot live”
also means he would quickly perish.
In the early Jiàn'ān period,
a children's rhyme in Jīngzhōu went:
“After eight or nine years, it will begin to decline;
by the thirteenth year, nothing will be left.”
This meant that since the restoration of the dynasty,
Jīngzhōu had been free from turmoil.
When Liú Biǎo became governor,
the people again enjoyed prosperity,
and this situation lasted for eight or nine years.
“Will begin to decline”
refers to the impending death of Liú Biǎo's wife
and the downfall of his various generals.
“By the thirteenth year, nothing will be left”
means that in the thirteenth year, Liú Biǎo would also die,
and the people would have to move to Jìzhōu.
In the tenth month of the first year of Yángjiā of Emperor Shùn,
wolves in Púyīn, Wàngdū, killed ninety-seven children.
At that time, Lǐ Gù, in his policy recommendations,
cited Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn, saying:
“When the ruler is without the Way,
harm will reach the people.
Go to the deep mountains to save oneself.
That omen is wolves eating people.”
If Your Majesty awakens,
and seeks out the reclusive and the hidden,
then the wolf calamity will cease.
In the Jiànníng period of Emperor Líng,
dozens of wolves entered the south gate of Jìnyáng city and bit people.
The Two Calamities of the Five Phases: Fire, Plant Omen, Feathered Insect Calamity, Sheep Misfortune.
The Wǔ Xíng Zhuàn says:
“To abandon laws,
banish meritorious ministers,
kill the crown prince,
and take a concubine as wife,
then fire will not rise upwards.”
This means fire loses its nature and becomes a disaster.
It also says:
“To not see clearly,
this is called being unwise.
Its fault is indulgence,
its punishment is constant warmth,
its extreme is illness.
Then there are plant omens,
〔一０〕then there is the calamity of wingless insects,
〔一一〕then there is the misfortune of sheep, 〔一二〕then there are red calamities and red auspicious signs,
and only water restrains fire.”
Luó Chóng (蠃蟲),
Liú Xīn's biography considers it a feathered insect.
In the Jiànwǔ period,
Péng Chǒng, the Administrator of Yúyáng, was summoned.
When the imperial edict arrived,
the next day there was a fire in Lù Xiàn.
The disaster started inside the city,
flew outside the city walls,
burned over a thousand households,
and killed people.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Zhuàn says:
“If the ruler is not frugal,
and the people are not restrained,
fierce fires will repeatedly erupt,
burning palaces and residences.”
Confucian scholars say fire, with its brightness, is a virtue and governs rites.
At that time, Péng Chǒng had a rift with Zhū Fú, the Governor of Yōuzhōu.
He suspected Zhū Fú was slandering him,
and thus became suspicious.
His wife persuaded him not to answer the summons,
so he rebelled and attacked Zhū Fú,
and was eventually executed and his clan exterminated.
On the Dīngsì day of the twelfth month of the eighth year of Yǒngyuán of Emperor Hé,
there was a fire in the Xuānshì Hall of the Southern Palace.
At this time, Emperor Hé was residing in the Northern Palace,
and Empress Dowager Dòu was in the Southern Palace.
The following year,
Empress Dowager Dòu passed away.
On the Jǐhài day of the eighth month of the thirteenth year,
there was a fire at the Shèngzhuàn Gatehouse of the Northern Palace.
At this time, Emperor Hé favored Lady Dèng,
while Empress Yīn's favor waned, and she harbored resentment.
The emperor had intentions of deposing her.
The following year,
it was discovered that Empress Yīn was involved in practicing false doctrines,
so she was deposed and relocated to Tónggōng,
where she died of grief.
Lady Dèng was established as empress.
On the Xīnyǒu day of the sixth month of the fifteenth year,
the south city gate of Chénggù, Hànzhōng, suffered a disaster.
This was an omen that Emperor Xiàohé's lineage would be cut off.
Two years later,
the imperial carriage departed (meaning the emperor died),
and Emperor Shāng and the Prince of Píngyuán both died young,
ending Emperor Hé's line.
Emperor Ān.
On the Jiǎyín day of the fourth month of the second year of Yǒngchū,
a fire broke out in Āyáng city, Hànyáng,
burning and killing three thousand five hundred and seventy people.
Before this, Emperor Hé had passed away,
leaving two imperial sons.
The elder imperial son was Shèng,
but Empress Dèng, coveting Emperor Shāng's youth,
wished to raise and establish him herself.
In the first year of Yánpíng,
Emperor Shāng died.
Shèng had a mild illness, but it was not serious.
All the ministers wanted to establish him,
but the Empress Dowager, having previously not established Shèng,
instead established the son of the Prince of Qīnghé,
who was Emperor Ān.
Sīkōng Zhōu Zhāng and others were not satisfied,
and conspired to execute the Dèng clan,
depose the Empress Dowager and Emperor Ān,
and instead establish Shèng.
In the eleventh month of the first year,
the plot was discovered,
and Zhōu Zhāng and others were executed.
Afterwards, the rebellious Qiāng in Liángzhōu caused great harm.
The various commanderies of Liángzhōu relocated their administrations to the borders of Féngyì and Fúfēng.
After the Empress Dowager passed away,
the Dèng clan was executed.
On the Wùzǐ day of the third month of the fourth year,
Dùlíng Garden caught fire.
On the Rénxū day of the second month of the fourth year of Yuánchū,
the Imperial Armory caught fire.
At this time, the Qiāng rebelled,
causing great banditry and harm.
Troops from across the empire were dispatched to attack and resist them,
which continued for over ten years without cessation.
The empire was weary and suffering from military service.
On the Wùzǐ day of the eighth month of the first year of Yángguāng,
the ancestral temple of Yánglíng Garden caught fire.
Any disaster that occurs at an imperial tomb
is an omen that the Crown Prince will be deposed.
As if to say: one should not depose the Crown Prince and thus harm oneself,
just as fire should not harm the ancestral temple's chambers.
The following year,
the emperor, due to slanderous words, deposed the Crown Prince, making him the King of Jìnyīn.
Two years later,
the imperial carriage departed (the emperor died).
Nineteen people, including the Central Eunuch Sūn Chéng, raised troops in the palace,
executed the treacherous ministers,
and established the King of Jìnyīn.
On the Yǐchǒu day of the seventh month of autumn in the fourth year,
the gate tower of Yúyáng city suffered a disaster.
On the Dīngyǒu day of the seventh month of the third year of Yǒngjiàn of Emperor Shùn,
the ancestral temple of Màolíng Garden suffered a disaster.
In the first year of Yángjiā,
the side corridors of Gōnglíng suffered a disaster,
and the Eastern and Western Governorates (Mòfǔ) caught fire.
Grand Commandant Lǐ Gù believed this was caused by extravagance and excess.
At the initial construction of the tomb,
disaster reached the dry bones,
and they planned to widely expand and further adorn it.
Moreover, the emperor wanted to build new palaces
and add terraces and towers,
hence the fire started at the Mòfǔ,
burning timber.
In the first year of Yǒnghé (136 CE), in the tenth month, on the day Dīngwèi,
Chéngfú Diàn caught fire.
Before this, Empress Sòng É, whose honorary title was Āmǔ (mother), had been enfeoffed as Shānyáng Jūn.
The Empress's father, Liáng Shāng, was originally a national marquis,
and Liáng Shāng's enfeoffment was further greatly increased.
Shāng's eldest son, Jì, was due to inherit Shāng's title.
As Shāng was still alive,
Jì was additionally enfeoffed as Xiāngyì Hóu.
The Empress's mother was posthumously granted the title Kāifēng Jūn. All these actions were excessive and contrary to propriety.
In the first year of Hàn'ān (142 CE), in the third month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
197 households, including Liú Hàn in Luòyáng, were consumed by fire.
Four years later,
the imperial carriage departed three times (i.e., three emperors died in succession).
It was not until the first year of Jiànhé (147 CE) that the position of sovereign was settled.
In the second year of Jiànhé (148 CE) of Emperor Huán, in the fifth month, on the day Guǐchǒu,
Déyáng Diàn in the Northern Palace's Yètíng caught fire,
as did the Zuǒyèmén (Left Side Gate).
Before this, Liáng Jì, the elder brother of Empress Dowager Liáng, indulged in treachery and injustice.
Because Grand Commandant Lǐ Gù and Dù Qiáo were upright,
fearing they would obstruct his schemes,
he had people falsely accuse Lǐ Gù and Dù Qiáo, leading to their execution and extermination.
After this, Empress Dowager Liáng passed away,
and the Liáng clan was exterminated.
In the fourth year of Yánxī (161 CE), in the first month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
Jiādé Diàn in the Southern Palace caught fire.
On the day Wùzǐ,
Bǐngshǔ caught fire.
In the second month, on the day Rénchén,
the Imperial Armory caught fire.
In the fifth month, on the day Dīngmǎo,
Chángshòu Mén of Yuán Líng caught fire.
Before this, Empress Bó, due to a person of humble origin gaining favor,
was granted the title Guìrén (Honorable Lady),
and became Empress.
The Emperor enfeoffed her mother Xuān as Cháng'ān Jūn,
and granted titles to her brothers.
Their favoritism and elevation were immense,
and many undeserving individuals were also enfeoffed.
In the spring of the previous year,
Lǐ Yún, the Magistrate of Báimǎ, died for his outspoken remonstrance.
At this point, a comet cleared the Xīn (Heart) and Wěi (Tail) constellations,
and fires occurred consecutively.
In the fifth year (162 CE), in the first month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Bǐngshǔ in the Southern Palace caught fire.
In the fourth month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
the Eastern Que of Gōng Běi Líng caught fire.
On the day Wùchén,
Hǔbēn Yèmén caught fire.
In the fifth month,
Kāng Líng Yuánqǐn caught fire.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Chánglù Shǔ of Zhōngzàng Fǔ caught fire.
In the seventh month, on the day Jǐwèi,
the interior of Chéngshàn Tà in the Southern Palace caught fire.
In the sixth year (163 CE), in the fourth month, on the day Xīnhài,
Kāng Líng Dōngshǔ caught fire.
In the seventh month, on the day Jiǎshēn,
Píng Líng Yuánqǐn caught fire.
In the eighth year (165 CE), in the second month, on the day Jǐyǒu,
Jiādé Shǔ, Huánglóng Diàn, and Qiānqiū Wànsuì Diàn in the Southern Palace all caught fire.
In the fourth month, on the day Jiǎyín,
Ān Líng Yuánqǐn caught fire.
In the intercalary month,
Chángqiū Diàn, Héhuān Diàn Hòugōudùn, and Yètíng Shuòpíng Shǔ in the Southern Palace all caught fire.
In the eleventh month, on the day Rénzǐ,
the western pavilion of Déyáng Qiándiàn and Huángmén Běisì caught fire,
killing people.
In the ninth year (166 CE), in the third month, on the day Guǐsì,
at night, firelight moved about in the capital,
and the people were alarmed and agitated.
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Xīpíng (175 CE) of Emperor Líng,
Yán Líng Yuán suffered a calamity.
In the intercalary month of the fourth year of Guānghé (181 CE), on the day Xīnyǒu,
Yǒngxiàng Shǔ of Běigōng Dōngyètíng suffered a calamity.
In the fifth month of the fifth year (182 CE), on the day Gēngshēn,
Yǒnglè Tàihòu Gōngshǔ, inside the entrance to the northwest of Déyáng Qiándiàn, caught fire.
In the second month of the second year of Zhōngpíng (185 CE), on the day Jǐyǒu,
Yúntái in the Southern Palace suffered a calamity.
On the day Gēngxū,
Yuèchéng Mén suffered a calamity,
extending to the Northern Què,
and burning across the road to the west, consuming Jiādé Diàn and Héhuān Diàn.
Upon investigation, the calamity at Yúntái originated from above;
hundreds of rafters and decorated beams
ignited simultaneously,
as if from suspended decorative lanterns.
On that day, it was completely burned,
and extended to Báihǔ, Wēixīng Mén, Shàngshū, Fújīe, and Lántái.
Now, Yúntái
was built by the Zhōu family,
and it was where maps, books, magical texts, rare treasures, and strange curiosities were all stored.
Jīng Fáng's Commentary on the Yì says:
"If the ruler does not contemplate the Way,
the omen is fire burning the palace."
At this time, the Yellow Turbans stirred up evil,
disrupting the normal order of heaven.
Seven provinces and twenty-eight commanderies simultaneously rose up.
Generals were appointed and armies dispatched.
Although some were captured,
Wǎn, Guǎngzōng, and Qǔyáng had not yet been subdued.
The war began across the sea,
looms hung empty,
and more than half the common people had died or been injured.
Yet Emperor Líng still did not restrain himself and restore propriety.
His tyranny and extravagance became increasingly severe.
He created rain-cloths one foot and one inch long,
his cavalry galloped like lightning,
officials were chosen inappropriately,
His inner favorites at Hóngdū
were all granted titles and ranks.
The capital had a saying for this:
"This year is the year of the feudal lords."
Heaven's warning was as if to say: "Rewarding the corrupt and punishing the virtuous,
what is the use of old traditions?"
Therefore, it burned down its platform gates and secret archives.
Three years later,
Emperor Líng died suddenly.
This was followed by the chaos of Dǒng Zhuó,
and fires burned for three days without ceasing,
turning the capital into ruins.
In the eighth month of the first year of Chūpíng (190 CE) of Emperor Xiàn,
Bàqiáo suffered a calamity.
Three years later,
Dǒng Zhuó was killed.
Concerning the common omen of persistent warmth,
the Book of Hàn considers winter warmth to be its response.
Since the restoration (Eastern Hàn),
there have also been warm winters,
but the records do not mention them.
In the third year of Yuánchū (116 CE) of Emperor Ān,
there were unusual melons growing together from a single stem,
eight melons on one pedicel.
At the time, they were considered auspicious melons.
Some believed that melons, by extending outwards,
bearing fruit away from the main stem,
symbolized women associating with outsiders.
At this time, Empress Yán had just been enthroned.
Later, Empress Yán, together with her maternal relatives like Gěng Bǎo, slandered the Crown Prince,
who was deposed as Jìyīn Wáng.
They then welcomed the son of the Jìběi prince and established him as heir.
This was a plant omen.
In the ninth year of Yánxī (166 CE) of Emperor Huán,
some bamboo and cypress leaves in the offices of Luòyáng city were damaged.
The divination said:
"The Son of Heaven will suffer misfortune."
In the third year of Xīpíng (174 CE) of Emperor Líng,
in a separate workshop on the right side of the school grounds, there were two Chinese toon trees,
both about four feet tall.
One of them suddenly grew overnight,
growing more than ten feet tall,
with a circumference of one *wéi*,
and resembled a Hu (foreign) person,
with head, eyes, sideburns, and hair all complete.
Jīng Fáng's Commentary on the Yì says:
"When the King's virtue declines,

In the tenth month of the fifth year (176 CE), on the day Rénwǔ,
the locust trees behind the palace where the emperor resided,

In the summer of the first year of Zhōngpíng (184 CE),

Jìyáng and Chángyuán in Chénliú,

Its stems were soft and swollen, as large as fingers,
resembling the shapes of doves, sparrows, dragons, snakes, birds, and beasts,
with five colors corresponding to their shapes,
and feathers, heads, eyes, feet, and wings all complete.
This was a recent plant omen.
In this year, the Yellow Turban rebels first rose.
Empress's brother Hé Jìn,

Later, Zhū Miáo was enfeoffed as Jìyáng Hóu.
Hé Jìn and Zhū Miáo then wielded great power,
controlling the reins of the state.
The Hàn dynasty consequently weakened,

During the Zhōngpíng era,
in a hollow tree six or seven *lǐ* northwest of Cháng'ān city,

In the ninth month of the first year of Xīngpíng (194 CE) of Emperor Xiàn,

In the third year of Yán'guāng of Emperor Ān, the second month, on the day Wùzǐ,
a large five-colored bird gathered on the terrace in Jǐnán.
In the tenth month,

At the time, it was taken to be a Fènghuáng.
Some considered the Fènghuáng to be a manifestation of the bright Yang,
and therefore, if there was not an enlightened ruler,
it would hide and not be seen.
In general, large five-colored birds resembling the Fènghuáng
are often an omen of disaster from feathered creatures.
At this time, Emperor Ān believed the slanderous words of the Palace Attendants Fán Fēng and Jiāng Jīng, his wet nurse Wáng Shèng, and his maternal relative Gěng Bǎo, among others.
He dismissed Grand Commandant Yáng Zhèn
and demoted the Crown Prince to Prince of Jìyīn.
This was a misfortune of impropriety.
At the end of Emperor Zhāng's reign,
the Fènghuáng was reported to have been seen 149 times.
At the time, the upright official Hé Chǎng thought that feathered creatures resembling the Fènghuáng,
soaring around palace roofs,
were not properly investigated.
Reporters believed that when Emperor Zhāng subsequently died,
this was the verification.
Upon examination, during the reigns of Emperor Xuān and Emperor Míng,
flocks of five-colored birds flew around palace roofs.
Jiǎ Kuí believed this to be a sign of barbarian surrender.
The emperors had many good policies;
although there were shortcomings,
they did not reach the point of extreme decline.
In their later years, 200,000 barbarians surrendered.
This was its verification.
During the time of the emperor,
the Qiāng and Hú rebelled externally,

It was a time of feathered omens.

At this time, the political situation was in decline,

In the fourth year of Guānghé of Emperor Líng, in autumn,
a large five-colored bird was seen in Xīnchéng,

At this time, Emperor Líng neglected government affairs,

In the middle of the eighth month of the third year of Zhōngpíng,
there were over ten thousand sparrows on Huáilíng.
First, they cried out extremely sadly,

By the sixth year,
Emperor Líng died.
General-in-Chief Hé Jìn, due to internal favorites and external flatterers,

However, the Empress Dowager was hesitant,

When Jìn left the palace,
he was killed inside the provincial office.
As a result, the authorities cleansed and massacred,
and none of those who enjoyed high salaries and respected positions survived.
Now, a mausoleum (líng)
is a symbol of high grandeur.
The heavenly warning was as if to say: "Those who harbor official salaries and respected positions,
will turn and harm each other to their own destruction."
In the third year of Jiànhé of Emperor Huán, in autumn, the seventh month,

At this time, Empress Dowager Liáng was regent,

The world felt their injustice.
Afterward, the Liáng clan was exterminated.

The *Wǔxíng Zhuàn* says:
"If one neglects ancestral temples,

abolishes ancestral rites,
and goes against the timing of Heaven,
then water will not moisten downwards."
This means water loses its nature and becomes a disaster.
It also says:
"If listening is not discerning,
this is called lack of deliberation.
Its fault is urgency,
its punishment is constant cold,
its extreme is poverty.
At times, there are drum omens,
at times, there are fish calamities,
at times, there are pig misfortunes,
at times, there are ear diseases,
at times, there are black scourges and black omens,
only fire affects water."
Fish calamities,

When there is such water,
rain kills people,

the sky turns yellow.
If there is famine but no loss,
this is called 'excessive.'
Its water kills people.
If one obstructs the virtuous,
this is called 'madness.'
Its water flows and kills people,
and after the water recedes, the earth produces insects.
If one holds people in prison without release,
this is called 'pursuing wrongdoing.'
Its water kills people with cold.
If one pursues executions without release,
this is called 'unreasonable.'
Its water prevents the harvest of the five grains.
If one fails greatly without release,
this is called 'all Yin.'
Its water flows into cities and towns,
and frost falls, killing crops."

seven provinces suffered from locusts.
Before this, the Xiānbēi had violated the frontier more than thirty times.
This year, Hù Wūhuán Xiàowèi Xià Yù, Pò Xiānbēi Zhōnglángjiāng Tián Yàn, and Shǐ Xiōngnú Zhōnglángjiāng Zāng Mín, leading the Nán Chányú and his subordinates,
departed simultaneously via three routes to campaign against the Xiānbēi.
The Dàsīnóng’s funds were insufficient,
so he heavily levied the commanderies and kingdoms
to provide military provisions.
The three generals achieved nothing,
and less than half of their troops returned.
In the first year of Guānghé, an imperial edict posed a question:
“Locusts have persisted for consecutive years, even surviving until winter.
Where lies the fault for this?”
Cài Yōng replied:
“Your servant has heard that the Yì Zhuàn says: ‘When great undertakings are carried out at the wrong time,
Heaven sends down disaster,
and the fault for this is the coming of locusts.’
The Hétú Mìzhēng Piān says: ‘If the emperor is greedy, then government is tyrannical and officials are cruel.
If cruel, then punishments are severe and execution is certain,
which brings forth locusts.’
Locusts
are caused by greed and harshness.”
At this time, all officials relocated their offices,
and all privately offered gifts to the Xīyuán to make it their office.
In the first year of Xīngpíng during the reign of Emperor Xiàn, summer,
there was a great locust infestation.
At this time, the world was in great chaos.
In the fifth month of Jiàn'ān 2 (197 CE),
there were locusts.
Correction note, page 3305, line 10: In the summer, fifth month, xīn (mǎo) [hài], a suburban sacrifice was performed. Changed based on the Jíben and Diànběn editions.
Page 3306, line 12: East of Dōngjùn was damaged by water. Annotation:
"Dōng"
was originally corrupted to
"lái",
now directly corrected.
Page 3306, line 13: The residence of the Dūwèi of Hóngnóng (zhé) [xī] was swept away and destroyed by water. Changed based on the Jíjiěběn edition.
Annotation: The jiàobǔ states that this is corrected based on the Yīnyì of the Dìlǐ Zhì in the Qiánshū.
Furthermore, the jiàobǔ quotes Qián Dàzhāo's remarks,
stating that in the Qián Zhì, Hóngnóng had Xī county,
and in the Xù Zhì, Xī belonged to Nányáng.
However, the Qián Zhì does not mention a Dūwèi in Hóngnóng,
nor does it mention the Dūwèi's residence under Xī,
and in Jiànwǔ 6 (30 CE), all Dūwèi of the commanderies had already been abolished,
so Hóngnóng should not have been the sole exception.
Moreover, the Běnjì merely states
"that summer there were continuous rains and floods,"
and there is no record of the imperial carriage personally inspecting the floods.
It is suspected that the Gǔjīn Zhù is mistaken.
Further annotation:
"Suǒ"
was originally corrupted to
"yí",
now directly corrected.
Page 3306, line 15: In Jiànwǔ 8 (32 CE), the commanderies and states experienced major floods one after another. Annotation: In the Jíben and Diànběn editions,
"bǐ"
is consistently written as
"qī".
Page 3307, line 1: His method was transmitted to Yǒugēn. Annotation:
"Gēn"
is likely a corruption of
"Hàn",
however, all editions write it as
"gēn".
The Jùzhēnběn Dōngguān Jì also writes it as
"gēn".
Only Yán Kějiūn's compilation of Quán Hòuhàn Wén writes it as
"Hàn",
probably a change made by Mr. Yán based on his own judgment.
Page 3307, line 1: Therefore, the six clans of the Yīn clan were divided for Bóqín. Annotation: In the Zuǒ Zhuàn,
"shì"
is written as
"mín".
The jiàobǔ states that
"Yīn shì"
contrasted with
"Huáixìng"
below,
is certainly a difference in transmitted editions.
Page 3307, line 4: There were no households seeking profit in the villages. Annotation:
"Yíng"
was originally corrupted to
"guǎn",
now directly corrected.
Page 3307, line 5: Retrospectively observe the past laws. Annotation:
"Guān"
was originally corrupted to
"jí",
now directly corrected.
Page 3307, line 5: Therefore, they all perpetually enjoyed the blessings of peace and tranquility. Annotation:
"Yǐ jiē"
was originally inverted,
now directly rectified.
Page 3307, line 6: This was also how they dispersed their quarrels. Annotation:
"Jiù"
is suspected to be a corruption of
"shù".
Page 3307, line 8: The intentions of (niǔ) [jū] náo. Corrected based on Hé Zhuó's collation.
Page 3307, line 8: Stretching endlessly. Annotation: The jiàobǔ states that based on the text,
"zú"
should be
"dìng".
Page 3307, line 9: Allowing them to again flourish and spread unhindered. Annotation:
"Lìng"
was originally corrupted to
"hé",
now directly corrected.
Page 3307, line 10: Dispersed and displaced from their homes. Annotation:
"Xǐ"
was originally corrupted to
"cóng",
now directly corrected.
Page 3307, line 11: Stating that natures do not harm each other. Annotation:
"Xiāng"
was originally corrupted to
"yòng",
now directly corrected.
Page 3307, line 16: Still rectify and avert disasters. In the Diànběn edition,
"zhèng"
is written as
"zhèng".
Annotation: The two characters (正 and 政) are interchangeable.
Page 3308, line 4: The water (ér) [yǔ] killed people. The jiàobǔ states that when compared with the Qián Zhì,
"ér"
is a corruption of
"yǔ",
which has not been corrected in any edition.
Now corrected accordingly.
Page 3309, line 6: Thirty-seven commanderies and states experienced major floods. Annotation: The jiàobǔ states that in the Jì,
"dàshuǐ"
is written as
"yǔshuǐ".
Page 3309, line 10: Did not establish Crown Prince Shèng. Annotation: Zhāng Sēnkǎi's correction notes state that Imperial Prince Shèng was never a Crown Prince,
the character
"tài"
is superfluous, and the same error occurs in the Dàfēng section of the next volume.
Page 3309, line 12: Jealous and hostile towards the worthy. Annotation:
"Dù"
was originally corrupted to
"zhì",
now directly corrected based on the Jíben and Diànběn editions.
Page 3309, line 15: The capital and forty commanderies and states experienced (yǒu) [dà] floods. The jiàobǔ states that
"yǒu"
is a corruption of
"dà",
which can be proven by the Běnjì,
and all editions have failed to correct it.
Now corrected accordingly.
Page 3309, line 15: Jiā collected and buried the bones of those who died away from home. The Jíjiě quotes Huì Dòng's remarks,
stating that according to Fàn Shū's Zhuō Jiā Zhuàn,
it was Jiā's younger brother Chàng,
and the annotation was based on Sīmǎ Shū.
Annotation: The jiàobǔ states that upon detailed examination of this annotation,
it is in fact a concise summary of the text from Zhōu Jiā Zhuàn, an independent biography in this book.
The character
"Jiā"
above
"shōuzàng"
was likely originally the character
"yīn",
later arbitrarily changed by someone who had not seen the original biography.
Since it is a concise summary,
it is not necessarily required to specify who did the collecting and burying.
Mr. Huì's supplementary note, based on the doubt of this one character,
then stated that the annotation was based on Sīmǎ Shū.
However, the annotation first cites the Běnjì,
which is Fàn Shū's Běnjì;
then cites Zhōu Jiā Zhuàn,
and does not differentiate it,
meaning it is the original biography.
Page 3310, line 9: The (lín) [liú] water turned into blood [and did not flow].
"Lín"
is written as
"liú" in the Jíben and Diànběn editions.
Now corrected accordingly.
Furthermore, the Jíjiě quotes Huì Dòng's remarks,
stating that
after
"xuè",
the two characters
"bù liú"
are missing.
Now supplemented accordingly.
Page 3310, line 10: The divination says, "Crying blood on the roads, crossing over the reeds, where can one reside?" Annotation:
"Zhān"
is written as
"míng" in the Diànběn edition.
"Hé"
is written as
"hé" in the Jíben edition.
The jiàobǔ states that
"shè sū yú hé yǐ chù"
is also an erroneous passage and cannot be forced to make sense.
Page 3310, line 13: Killed [qiān] more than a thousand people. Changed based on the Jíben and Diànběn editions.
Page 3311, line 4: Over [shí] tens of thousands of households were harmed and swept away. The jiàobǔ quotes Qián Dàzhāo's remarks,
stating that both the Zhū Mù Zhuàn and Huán Dì Jì mention tens of thousands of households,
so
"qiān"
should be
"shí".
Now corrected accordingly.
Page 3311, line 4: Embracing and containing the waters. Annotation:
"Huái"
was originally corrupted to
"huài",
now directly corrected.
Page 3311, line 7: Tàibái (Venus) traversed the sky. Annotation:
"Jīng"
was originally corrupted to
"jué",
now directly corrected based on the Jíben and Diànběn editions.
Page 3311, line 8: Bandits were mostly pacified [mín]. The jiàobǔ states that according to the text,
after
"píng",
there should be the character
"mín",
or perhaps the Tang people removed it to avoid a taboo.
Now supplemented accordingly.
Page 3311, line 13: The [Hé] water in Jìběi became clear. The Jíjiě quotes Qián Dàxīn's remarks stating that
after
"Jìběi",
the character
"Hé"
is missing.
“‘The Ji-Yīn, Dōng-Jùn, and Jǐ-Běi rivers run clear.’”
This
indicates
that four characters are also missing above “Jǐ-Běi”.
Now, upon examination: The records in the Jì and Zhì
may differ.
The character
“Hé”
is clearly missing
below “Jǐ-Běi”;
it has now been added.
Page 3312, Line 7: “In the fourth year, in summer, three rivers in the commanderies and kingdoms.” Annotation: The Jiàobǔ states that the Jì has
“seven great floods.”
Page 3312, Line 9: “In the fifth year of Zhōng-Píng, six rivers in the commanderies and kingdoms had great floods.” Annotation: The Jíjiě cites Huì-Dòng’s explanation,
stating that the Dìjì has
“seven great floods.”

Page 3313, Line 8: “In the fifth year of Yǒng-Yuán of Emperor Hé, in the sixth month, three commanderies and kingdoms had hailstones as large as chicken eggs.” Annotation: The Jùzhēn-Běn Dōngguān Jì has
“commandery and kingdoms had great hailstones,
as large as goose eggs.”
Page 3313, Line 11: “Within the bedroom.” Annotation:
“Rèn”
was originally written
“Rèn” (任);
it has been directly changed according to the Jí-Běn and Diàn-Běn.
Page 3313, Line 11: “Dispensed but not widely.” Annotation:
“Bó”
was originally mistaken for
“Chuán”;
it has been directly corrected.
Page 3313, Line 11: “The essence of Yin congealed and was (destroyed) [formed].” Changed according to the Jí-Běn and Diàn-Běn.
Page 3313, Line 12: “Suppressing the worthy and not promoting them.” Annotation:
“Yáng”
was originally mistaken for
“Yì”;
it has been directly corrected.
Page 3314, Line 3: “In the third year, hailstones.” Annotation: The Jíjiě cites Huì-Dòng’s explanation,
stating that the Jì has
“the capital and forty-one commanderies and kingdoms had rain and hail.”
Page 3314, Line 5: “As large as basins and cups.” Annotation: The Jíjiě cites Huì-Dòng’s explanation,
stating that
“yú-bēi”
is written
