Page 3314, Line 8: “In the Biography of Yǐn-Mǐn: In this year, Hexī had great hailstones as large as buckets. Emperor Ān saw Kǒng Jì-Yàn and asked him the reason.” Annotation: The Jíjiě cites Qián Dà-Xīn’s explanation,
stating that Jì-Yàn’s affair is now in the Biography of Kǒng Xī,
or Sīmǎ Biāo’s book attached Jì-Yàn to the Biography of Yǐn-Mǐn.
The Jiàobǔ states that this note citing Jì-Yàn’s affair
is also clearly from Fàn Shū’s Biography of Kǒng Xī,
and thus it was mistakenly recorded because Yǐn-Mǐn was in the same column of the Rúlín Zhuàn.
Page 3314, Line 11: “In the fifth year of Yǒng-Jiàn of Emperor Shùn, twelve commanderies and kingdoms had hailstones.” Annotation: In the Jí-Běn and Diàn-Běn,
“five”
is written
“three.”
Page 3315, Line 8: “In the seventh year of Jiàn-Wǔ of Emperor Guāng-Wǔ, Liáo-Dōng had winter thunder.” Annotation: In the Jí-Běn and Diàn-Běn,
“seven”
is written
“ten.”
Page 3315, Line 10: “Stones (with) [and] thunder falling together.” Changed according to the Jí-Běn and Diàn-Běn.
Page 3315, Line 11: “Therefore, it was (long) [constant].” Changed according to the Jí-Běn and Diàn-Běn.
Page 3315, Line 14: “Pity the young and orphans.” Annotation:
“Xù”
was originally mistaken for
“Shuài”;
it has been directly corrected according to the Jí-Běn and Diàn-Běn.

Page 3316, Line 9: “In the fourth year of Yán-Guāng, nineteen commanderies and kingdoms had winter thunder. At this time, the Empress Dowager held regency.” Annotation: Empress Hé-Xī died in the first year of Jiàn-Guāng;
how could it be said that the Empress Dowager held regency again in the fourth year of Yán-Guāng?
“Shì shí”
is probably a mistake for
“xiān shì.”
Page 3316, Line 13: “Dōng-Lái had winter thunder.” Annotation: In the Jí-Běn and Diàn-Běn,
“dōng”
is written
“dà.”
Page 3317, Line 4: “Mountains (perished) [earth] collapsed.” Changed according to the Jí-Běn and Diàn-Běn.

Page 3318, Line 2: “In the twenty-eighth year, in the third month, eighty commanderies and kingdoms had locusts.” Annotation: The Jiàobǔ states that in Emperor Guāng-Wǔ’s time, there were ninety-three commanderies and kingdoms.
If eighty had locusts,
the locusts would have almost covered the entire nation.
In the late Huán and Líng eras, there were no such strange disasters,
let alone in the flourishing time of the restoration,
how could such a thing be appropriate?
“Bā-shí”
is probably a
mis-inverted
“shí-bā.”
Page 3319, Line 5: “At this time, Liáng-Jì held power without foresight.” Annotation: The Jiàobǔ states that
“xiàn”
is probably a mistake for
“lǜ.”
Page 3319, Line 10: “The calamity of not listening keenly.” Annotation: In the Jí-Běn and Diàn-Běn,
“huò”
is written
“guò.”
Page 3320, Line 3: “(Residing) [bending] the province and storing separately.” Changed according to the Jí-Běn and Diàn-Běn.
Line 5: “Four earthquakes, mountains collapsing, ground collapsing, great winds uprooting trees, locusts, cattle plague.”
The Wǔxíng Zhuàn says:
“If palaces are built,
terraces and pavilions are adorned,
lewdness is practiced internally,
relatives are offended,
and fathers and elder brothers are insulted,
then the harvest will fail.”
This means that the earth loses its nature and becomes a disaster.
It also says:
“If thoughts are not tolerant,
this is called unholy.
Its calamity is a dense mist,
its punishment is constant wind,
and its extreme is ill-fated short life.
At times, there are omens of oily nights,
at times, there are floral blights,
at times, there are cattle misfortunes,
at times, there are ailments of the heart and abdomen,
at times, there are yellow ominous signs and yellow auspicious signs,
only metal, water, wood, and fire harm the earth.”
“Huá-niè,”
Liú Xīn interprets it as the blight of insect pests,
meaning a type of locust.
In the ninth month of the twenty-second year of Jiàn-Wǔ of Shì-Zǔ,
forty-two commanderies and kingdoms had earthquakes,
Nán-Yáng being particularly severe,
with the ground cracking and crushing people to death.
Afterwards, the Wǔ-Xī Man-Yí rebelled,
causing harm as bandits,
reaching Nán-Jùn,
mobilizing troops from various commanderies in Jīng-Zhōu,
and sending General Wǔ-Wēi Liú Shàng to attack them.
He was besieged by the Yi,
and more troops were dispatched to assist him,
but Shàng was eventually lost to them.
In the third month, jiǎ-(shēn) [yín], of the first year of Jiàn-Chū of Emperor Zhāng,
Shān-Yáng and Dōng-Píng had earthquakes.
In the sixth month, bǐng-chén, of the fourth year of Yǒng-Yuán of Emperor Hé,
thirteen commanderies and kingdoms had earthquakes.
The Chūn-Qiū Hàn Hán Zī says:
“If the empress is powerful,
and ministers control decrees,
then the earth will shake and crack,
rebellions will rise,
and mountains will collapse and sink.”
At this time, Empress Dowager Dòu held regency,
and her brother Dòu Xiàn monopolized power;
they would thus suffer calamity.
Five days later,
an imperial edict ordered the seizure of Xiàn’s seals and ribbons,
and his brothers were sent to their fiefs,
where they were forced to commit suicide.
In the second month, wù-wǔ, of the fifth year,
Lǒng-Xī had an earthquake.
The Ru school says that people are those who settle the earth,
and when it is about to move greatly,
great tremors will occur.
In the ninth month,
the Xiongnu Chányú Yú-Chú-(Nán)-Jiān rebelled,
and envoys were sent to mobilize border commandery troops to suppress him.
In the ninth month, guǐ-mǎo, of the seventh year,
the capital had an earthquake.
The Ru school says that eunuchs have no yang to bestow,
like women.
At this time, Emperor Hé plotted with the Palace Regular Attendant Zhèng Zhòng to seize power from the Dòu clan;
he valued him,
and thus appointed him.
And he favored the Regular Attendant Cài Lún,
and the two began to wield power together.
In the third month, gēng-chén, of the ninth year,
Lǒng-Xī had an earthquake.
In the intercalary month,
the Qiāng beyond the frontier attacked the frontier,
killing and plundering officials and common people,
and General Zhēng-Xī Liú Shàng was sent to attack them.
In the first year of Yǒng-Chū of Emperor Ān,
eighteen commanderies and kingdoms had earthquakes.
Lǐ Gù said:
“Earth is Yin;
by law, it should be calm.
Now it oversteps the duty of Yin
and monopolizes the governance of Yang,
therefore it responds with tremors.”
At this time, Empress Dowager Dèng held regency and monopolized affairs.
Until the middle of Jiàn-Guāng,
when the Empress Dowager died,
Emperor Ān was then able to control governance.
Consequently, Yin-related factions all prevailed,
and the Western Qiāng disrupted Xià,
for more than ten years.
In the second year,
twelve commanderies and kingdoms had earthquakes.
In the twelfth month, xīn-yǒu, of the third year,
nine commanderies and kingdoms had earthquakes.
In the third month, guǐ-sì, of the fourth year,
four commanderies and kingdoms had earthquakes.
In the first month, bǐng-xū, of the fifth year,
ten commanderies and kingdoms had earthquakes.
In the seventh year, in the first month, on the day rén-yín,
in the second month, on the day bǐng-wǔ,
eighteen commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the first year of Yuánchū,
fifteen commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the second year, in the eleventh month, on the day gēng-shēn,
ten commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the third year, in the second month,
ten commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the eleventh month, on the day guǐ-mǎo,
nine commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the fourth year,
thirteen commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the fifth year,
fourteen commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the sixth year, in the second month, on the day yǐ-sì,
the capital and forty-two commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In some places, the earth cracked open,
water gushed forth,
and city walls, outer walls, and people's houses were destroyed,
crushing people.
In winter,
eight commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the first year of Yǒngníng,
twenty-three commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the first year of Jiànguāng, in the ninth month, on the day jǐ-chǒu,
thirty-five commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In some places, the earth cracked open,
destroying city walls, outer walls, and houses,
crushing and killing people.
At this time, Àn Dì was unable to see clearly;
he believed the slanderous words of palace women and his foster mother, Shèng, etc.,
and ruined the household of Empress Dowager Dèng.
Thereupon, he exclusively listened to and trusted Shèng and the eunuchs.
The Central Regular Attendants Jiāng Jīng and Fán Fēng, among others, all gained power.
In the first year of Yán'guāng, in the seventh month, on the day guǐ-mǎo,
the capital and thirteen commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the ninth month, on the day wù-shēn,
twenty-seven commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the second year,
the capital and thirty-two commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
In the third year,
the capital and twenty-three commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
At this time, Grand Commandant Yáng Zhèn was dismissed due to slander,
and the Crown Prince was deposed.
In the fourth year, in the eleventh month, on the day dīng-sì,
the capital and sixteen commanderies and states experienced earthquakes.
At this time, Àn Dì had already collapsed.
Empress Dowager Yán acted as regent.
Her brothers, Yán Xiǎn and others, all held power,
and then banished Àn Dì's son.
They further summoned princes from various states.
Before they arrived,
the Central Yellow Gates then executed Xiǎn and his brothers.
In Shùn Dì's Yǒngjiàn third year, in the first month, on the day bǐng-zǐ,
the capital and Hànyáng experienced earthquakes.
In Hànyáng, houses were destroyed and people were killed,
and the earth cracked open, with water gushing out.
At this time, Shùn Dì's foster mother, Sòng É, and the Central Regular Attendant Zhāng Fǎng, among others, held power.
In Yángjiā second year, in the fourth month, on the day jǐ-hài,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
At this time, Sòng É was conferred the title of Shānyáng Jūn.
In the fourth year, in the twelfth month, on the day jiǎ-yín,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
In Yǒnghé second year, in the fourth month, on the day bǐng-shēn,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
At this time, Sòng É plotted treachery and deception.
In the fifth month, the matter was discovered.
Her official seals and sashes were confiscated,
and she was sent back to her hometown.
In the eleventh month, on the day dīng-mǎo,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
At this time, Grand Commandant Wáng Gōng, seeing that the Central Regular Attendant Zhāng Fǎng and others were monopolizing state power,
wished to present a memorial to have them executed.
At that time, a relative of Gōng from the same clan, citing Yáng Zhèn's actions, advised him against it and he stopped.
In the third year, in the second month, on the day yǐ-hài,
the capital, Jīnchéng, and Lǒngxī experienced earthquakes and cracks.
Many city walls, outer walls, and houses were destroyed,
crushing and killing people.
In the intercalary month, on the day jǐ-yǒu,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
In the tenth month,
more than two thousand Qīng Xiāng cavalry entered the Jīnchéng Pass,
causing harm to Liángzhōu.
In the fourth year, in the third month, on the day yǐ-hài,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
In the fifth year, in the second month, on the day wù-shēn,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
In Jiànkāng first year, in the first month,
six commanderies in the Liángzhōu region
experienced earthquakes.
From the ninth month of the previous year until the fourth month,
there were a total of one hundred and eighty earthquakes.
Mountains and valleys cracked open,
destroying city temples,
and harming people and things.
In the third month,
Commander Zhào Chōng, who protected the Qiāng, was killed by rebellious Hú.
In the ninth month, on the day bǐng-wǔ,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
At this time, Shùn Dì collapsed.
Empress Dowager Liáng acted as regent.
Wishing to build a mausoleum for Shùn Dì,
its scale and luxury were excessive,
destroying many graves of officials and common people.
Minister Luán Bā remonstrated against the matter.
The Empress Dowager was enraged.
On the day guǐ-mǎo,
an imperial edict ordered Bā's arrest and imprisonment.
She intended to kill him.
On the day bǐng-wǔ, an earthquake occurred.
Thereupon, the Empress Dowager released Bā,
and demoted him to commoner status.
In Huán Dì's Jiànhé first year, in the fourth month, on the day gēng-yín,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
In the ninth month, on the day dīng-mǎo,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
At this time, Empress Dowager Liáng acted as regent,
and her brother Jì held power.
By Hépíng first year,
the Empress Dowager collapsed.
However, Jì still wielded government and monopolized affairs.
By Yánxī second year,
he was then executed and exterminated.
In the third year, in the ninth month, on the day jǐ-mǎo,
an earthquake occurred.
On the day gēng-yín, it shook again.
In Yuánjiā first year, in the eleventh month, on the day xīn-sì,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
In the second year, in the first month, on the day bǐng-chén,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
In the tenth month, on the day yǐ-hài,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
In Yǒngxīng second year, in the second month, on the day guǐ-mǎo,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
In Yǒngshòu second year, in the twelfth month,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
In Yánxī fourth year,

Five elements, five portents: shooting omens, dragon and snake anomalies, horse calamities, human ailments, human transformations, the dead returning to life, epidemics, and falling rainbows.
The Wǔxíng Zhuàn (五行傳) says:
"If the sovereign is not supreme,
this is called not being established.
Its fault is dimness,
its punishment is perpetual overcast,
its extreme is weakness.
At such times there are shooting omens,
at such times there are dragon and snake anomalies,
at such times there are horse calamities,
at such times there are ailments where common people strike down superiors,
at such times the sun and moon travel erratically,
and the stars move retrogradely."
Huáng (皇)
is the ruler.
Jí (極)
is the center.
Mào (眊)
is obscurity.
The explanation says: This is an affliction of Heaven.
Not mentioning the affliction of Heaven
is a deferential expression for the most revered.
In the Chūnqiū (春秋),
"the king's army suffered a major defeat,"
using self-defeat as the expression.
Perpetual overcast: there are no records of this since the Zhongxing (中興) period.
During the Guānghé (光和) period of Língdì (靈帝),
a man from Luòyáng (雒陽) named Yèlóng (夜龍) shot at the Northern Palace Gate with a bow and arrow at night.
Officials arrested and interrogated him.
He stated:
"I was poor and in debt,
with no means of livelihood,
so I bought a bow and arrows to shoot."
This was a recent shooting omen.
Afterwards, General of Chariots and Cavalry Hé Miáo (何苗),
and his brother, Grand General Jìn (進), suspected each other after their troops returned,
and they attacked each other
and fought below the palace gate.
Miáo (苗) died, and his army was defeated,
killing several thousand people.
The imperial palace and inner chambers in Luòyáng (雒陽) were completely burned.
In the third year of Yánguāng (延光) of Āndì (安帝),
Jǐnán (濟南) reported a yellow dragon seen in Lìchéng (歷城),
and Lángxié (琅邪) reported a yellow dragon seen in Zhū (諸).
At this time, Āndì (安帝) listened to slander
and dismissed Grand Commandant Yáng Zhèn (楊震),
and Zhèn (震) committed suicide.
Furthermore, the emperor had only one son,
whom he made crown prince,
but he believed slander and deposed him.
This was the sovereign not being central,
thus there were dragon anomalies.
At this time, many flatterers were employed,
so this was considered an auspicious omen.
In the first month of the following year,
Dōngjùn (東郡) again reported two yellow dragons seen in Púyáng (濮陽).
In the seventh year of Yánxī (延熹) of Huándì (桓帝), sixth month, rénzǐ (壬子) day,
a dragon died on the mountain in Yěwáng (野王), Hénèi (河內),
its length several tens of zhàng.
Xiāng Kǎi (襄楷) believed that a dragon is an auspicious omen for emperors and kings,
and the Yì (易) discusses great men.
During the Tiānfèng (天鳳) period,
a dead dragon was found in Huángshān Gōng (黃山宮).
The Han army executed Wáng Mǎng (王莽), and Shìzǔ (世祖) revived [the dynasty].
This was a sign of dynastic change.
By the twenty-fifth year of Jiàn'ān (建安),
Wèi Wéndì (魏文帝) supplanted the Han.
In the first year of Yǒngkāng (永康), eighth month,
Bājùn (巴郡) reported a yellow dragon seen.
At that time, the official Fù Jiān (傅堅) believed the prefecture intended to report it,
and secretly stated that it was just a joke by a footman
and should not be reported.
The Grand Administrator did not listen.
I once heard Jiān (堅) say:
"At that time, the people, due to the heat,
wanted to go bathing in a pond.
Seeing the pond water was murky,
they jokingly scared each other, 'There's a yellow dragon in here,'
and the story spread among people.
Hearing that the prefecture wanted to treat it as a good omen,
I therefore said it."
At that time, the historians recorded it in the Imperial Annals.
During the reign of Huándì (桓帝), the government was in decline and deficient,
yet many auspicious omens were reported everywhere;
they were all of this kind.
Moreover, previous Confucians said: If an auspicious omen appears at an inappropriate time,
then it becomes a malevolent anomaly,
and the people's rumors of a dragon being born
are all dragon anomalies.
In the first year of Xīpíng (熹平), fourth month, jiǎwǔ (甲午) day,
a green snake was seen on the imperial seat.
At this time, Língdì (靈帝) entrusted power to eunuchs,
and the royal house was weak.
In the second year of Gēngshǐ (更始), second month,
[he] departed from Luòyáng (雒陽),
intending to enter Cháng'ān (長安).
Sīzhí (司直) Lǐ Sōng (李松) led the way.
The carriage bolted,
colliding with the iron pillar gate of the Northern Palace,
and all three horses died.
This was a horse calamity.
At that time, Gēngshǐ (更始) had lost the Way
and was about to perish.
In the fifth year of Yánxī (延熹) of Huándì (桓帝), fourth month,
startled horses and runaway elephants rushed into the palace.
This was a recent horse calamity.
At this time, Huándì's (桓帝) government was in decline and deficient.
In the first year of Guānghé (光hé),
the horse of Sītú Chángshǐ (司徒長史) Féng Xún (馮巡) gave birth to a human.
Jīng Fáng's (京房) Yì Zhuàn (易傳) says:
"If the emperor is lost,
and feudal lords attack each other,
the omen is a horse giving birth to a human."
Later, Féng Xún (馮巡) was transferred to be the Minister of Gānlíng (甘陵).
When the Yellow Turban Rebellion first broke out, [he] was massacred by them,
and the state also faced enemies from all sides.
Afterwards, the commanderies and prefectures east of the pass each raised righteous armies,
eventually attacking each other,
the Son of Heaven moved west,
and imperial rule was cut off.
Its prognostication is the same as Jīng Fáng's (京房).
During the Guānghé (光hé) period,
a horse belonging to a resident near the Xīqiáo (西橋) bridge in Luòyáng (雒陽) bolted
and then bit a person to death.
At this time, high officials and ministers, as well as those on the left and right, were frequently executed.
In the first year of Yǒngchū (永初) of Āndì (安帝), eleventh month, wùzǐ (戊子) day,
people began to run in fright,
abandoning their belongings
and leaving their homes.
In the third year of Jiànníng (建寧) of Língdì (靈帝), spring,
a woman in Hénèi (河內) ate her husband,
and a man in Hénán (河南) ate his wife.
In the second year of Xīpíng (熹平), sixth month,
people in Luòyáng (雒陽) spread rumors that there was a yellow man inside the east wall of the Hǔbēn Sì (虎賁寺).
His appearance, beard, and eyebrows were quite distinct.
Tens of thousands of spectators,
all from within the provincial capital, came out,
and the roads were blocked.
By the first year of Zhōngpíng (中平), second month,
Zhāng Jiǎo (張角) and his brothers raised an army in Jìzhōu (冀州),
calling themselves Yellow Heaven.
Thirty-six regions,
all four directions sent harmonious responses.
Generals and commanders were spread like stars,
officials and soldiers submitted to them,
and taking advantage of their weariness and hunger,
they led and overcame them.
In the first year of Guānghé, on the *rénwǔ* day of the fifth month,
a certain man in white clothes wished to enter Déyángmén.
He stated,
"I am Liáng Bóxià,
and I have been instructed to ascend the hall to become the Son of Heaven."
The Central Eunuchs Huán Xián and others called for the gate official, the *Púyè*,
intending to seize and bind the man.
Before the official arrived,
the man suddenly ran away a moment later,
and could not be found.
His name was unknown.
At that time, Cài Yōng recalled that during Emperor Chéng's reign, a man named Wáng Bāo, clad in crimson, entered the palace,
and went to the front hall's unusual chamber,
saying,
"The Celestial Emperor has ordered me to reside here."
Later, Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne.
Now, this incident is similar to, yet different from, the one during Emperor Chéng's time.
The attire is different,
and he was detected before entering Yúnlóngmén.
His claim to be Liáng Bóxià
was a rather trivial statement.
Comparing the past with the present,
there will likely be a foolish and cunning person
who attempts a plot like the Wáng clan's,
but the matter will not succeed.
Afterwards, Zhāng Jiǎo claimed to be the Yellow Heaven and instigated a rebellion,
which was ultimately crushed.
In the second year,
outside the Upper West Gate of Luòyáng, a woman gave birth to a child
with two heads,
sharing different shoulders and a common torso,
both facing forward.
It was considered inauspicious,
so it was abandoned after birth.
From then on,
the imperial court was in chaos,
governance was controlled by private households,
and there was no distinction between high and low—
an omen of two heads.
Later, Dǒng Zhuó executed the Empress Dowager,
imposing on her the charge of unfilial conduct,
and deposed the Son of Heaven,
later harming him again.
Since the beginning of the Hàn dynasty,
no calamity had surpassed this.
In the fourth year,
Zhāng Bó, a man from Wèijùn, presented an iron plough to the Tàiguān.
Bó submitted a memorial in the study hall, by the mountain dwelling, behind the palace,
where a house collapsed with a loud clamor.
The Emperor had him seized and interrogated.
He stated,
"I suddenly lost awareness."
In the first year of Zhōngpíng, on the *rénshēn* day of the sixth month,
Liú Cāng, a man from Luòyáng residing outside the Upper West Gate,
had a son born to his wife
with two heads sharing one body.
During Emperor Líng's reign,
the mother of the Huáng clan in Jiāngxià,
while bathing, transformed into a soft-shelled turtle
and entered a deep abyss.
Afterwards, she occasionally emerged and was seen.
She had initially worn a silver hairpin while bathing,
and when she was seen,
it was still on her head.
In the *Chūpíng* period of Emperor Xiàn's reign,
a man named Huán from Chángshā
died.
After being coffined for over a month,
his mother heard a sound from within the coffin.
She opened it,
and he revived.
The divination stated:
"Extreme Yin becomes Yang,
the lower rises to the upper."
Thereafter, Cáo Gōng rose from a common scholar.
In the second month of the fourth year of Jiàn'ān,
Lǐ É, a woman from Chōngxiàn in Wǔlíng,
over sixty years old,
died.
She was interred in a cypress wood coffin from her home,
buried several *lǐ* outside the city.
Fourteen days later,
a traveler heard sounds from her tomb
and immediately informed her family.
The family went, heard the sounds,
and promptly unearthed her,
whereupon she revived.
In the seventh year,
in Yuèsuī, a man transformed into a woman.
At that time, Zhōu Qún memorialized that
there had been a similar anomaly during Emperor Āi's reign,
indicating an impending change of dynasty.
By the twenty-fifth year,
Emperor Xiàn was enfeoffed in Shānyáng.
During the Jiàn'ān period,
a woman gave birth to a male child
with two heads sharing one body.
In the fourth month of summer in the sixth year of Yuánchū of Emperor Ān's reign,
Kuàijī suffered a great plague.
In the winter of the fourth year of Yán'guāng,
the capital suffered a great plague.
In the first month of the first year of Yuánjiā of Emperor Huán's reign,
the capital suffered a great plague.
In the second month,
Jiǔjiāng and Lújiāng also suffered plagues.
In the first month of the fourth year of Yánxī,
there was a great plague.
In the third month of the fourth year of Jiànníng of Emperor Líng's reign,
there was a great plague.
In the first month of the second year of Xīpíng,
there was a great plague.
In the spring of the second year of Guānghé,
there was a great plague.
In the second month of the fifth year,
there was a great plague.
In the first month of the second year of Zhōngpíng,
there was a great plague.
In the twenty-second year of Jiàn'ān of Emperor Xiàn's reign,
there was a great plague.
In the sixth month of the first year of Guānghé of Emperor Líng's reign, on the *dīngchǒu* day,
a black *qì* fell in the eastern courtyard of Wēnmíngdiàn in the Northern Palace.
It was black like a carriage canopy,
then surged and unfurled,
its body five-colored,
with a head,
and a body over ten *zhàng* long,
its form resembling a dragon.
The Emperor questioned Cài Yōng,
who replied:
"This is what is called a 'celestial falling *ní*'.
Since its feet and tail are not seen,
it cannot be called a dragon.
The *Yì Zhuàn* says: 'The *ní* is compared to something without virtue,
which attracts by its color.'
The *Qiántán Bā* says: 'When a rainbow appears,
the empress or concubines secretly coerce the ruler.'
It also says: 'When five colors arrive alternately,
shining upon the palace halls,
there will be military affairs.'
The *Yǎnkǒng Tú* says: 'If the Son of Heaven suffers from external military troubles,
and his internal authority is seized,
and his ministers are disloyal,
then a celestial *ní* will fall.'
An anomaly does not arise in vain,
nor does divination speak idly."
Previously, Empress Hé was established.
Whenever the Empress observed a fast,
she was supposed to visit the ancestral temple,
but there was always an anomaly preventing her visit.
In the first year of Zhōngpíng,
the Yellow Turban rebels, Zhāng Jiǎo and others, established thirty-six divisions,
raised an army, and burned commanderies and kingdoms.
In the seven provinces east of the mountains, everywhere responded to Jiǎo.
Troops were dispatched externally to suppress Jiǎo and others,
while internally, the Empress's two elder brothers were made great generals to command the troops.
That year,
the Emperor passed away,
the Empress assumed regency,
and her two elder brothers wielded power.
They censured and reproached the Emperor's mother, Empress Yǒnglè,
ordering her to commit suicide.
Secretly, they called for the Provincial Governor of Bìngzhōu, Dǒng Zhuó, wishing to collectively execute the eunuchs.
The eunuchs preemptively killed Great General Jìn.
Troops attacked each other,
and the capital's roads were blocked by combatants.
The Empress Dowager and her son were then deposed by Grand Commandant Zhuó and others,
and all died.
The ruin of the empire,
with warfare first arising in the palace and court,
then extending throughout the land,
lasting for twenty or thirty years,
its calamity originated from the Hé family.

Five elements and six solar eclipses; the sun embraced; the sun red and without light; the sun with a yellow halo; the sun black in the middle; a rainbow piercing the sun; a lunar eclipse not in its proper month.
Guāngwǔ Dì
Jìanwǔ, second year, first month, jiǎzǐ shuò,
there was a solar eclipse.
It occurred at the eighth degree of the Wēi (危) mansion.
The discourse on solar eclipses states:
"The sun
is the essence of the great yang,
an emblem of the monarch.
When the monarch's dao is deficient,
it is overcome by the yin,
hence the eclipse.
An eclipse
means the yang is not victorious."
Its various divinations,
the Hànshū Wǔxíng Zhì certainly records them.
The Rú (Confucian) explanation states that if the regional lords wield excessive power,
then the omen mostly corresponds to the state in which the sun resides.
If various celestial phenomena follow it,
then it mostly concerns matters of the king.
If the monarch reforms and cultivates his virtue,
then calamities and harms are removed.
At this time, Shìzǔ had just risen,
and the banditry and chaos in the world were not yet pacified.
Xū (虛) and Wēi (危)
belong to Qí (齊).
The bandit Zhāng Bù (張步) held troops and occupied Qí (齊).
The Emperor sent Fú Lóng (伏隆) to persuade Bù (步),
who promised to surrender,
but then rebelled again and declared himself king.
He was not defeated until the fifth year.
Third year, fifth month, yǐmǎo huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the fourteenth degree of the Liǔ (柳) mansion.
Liǔ (柳)
is Hénán (河南).
At that time, Shìzǔ was in Luòyáng (雒陽).
The Chìméi (赤眉) rebel Fán Chóng (樊崇) plotted rebellion.
In the seventh month, it was discovered,
and all were executed.
Sixth year, ninth month, bǐngyín huì,
there was a solar eclipse.
The imperial historians did not observe it,
but the commanderies reported it.
It occurred at the eighth degree of the Wěi (尾) mansion.
Seventh year, third month, guǐhài huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the fifth degree of the Bì (畢) mansion.
Bì (畢) signifies border troops.
In autumn,
Wēi Xiāo (隗囂) rebelled,
invading Āndìng (安定).
In winter,
the Grand Administrators of Shuòfāng (朔方) and Yúnzhōng (雲中), appointed by Lú Fāng (盧芳), each surrendered their commanderies.
Sixteenth year, third month, xīchǒu huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the seventh degree of the Mǎo (昴) mansion.
Mǎo (昴) signifies judicial matters.
At that time, the Grand Administrators of various commanderies were implicated in inaccurate land surveys.
Shìzǔ was enraged,
killing more than ten people,
and only then deeply regretted it.
Seventeenth year, second month, yǐwèi huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the ninth degree of the Wèi (胃) mansion.
Wèi (胃) signifies granaries.
At that time, the various commanderies had just been charged with new rents,
and the world was worried and fearful.
This was interpreted as related to grain,
hence the omen was shown.
Some say: Wèi (胃)
is the official in charge of provisions.
In the tenth month of that year,
Empress Guō (郭) was deposed,
and the imperial edict stated,
"She cannot attend to the provisions."
Twenty-second year, fifth month, yǐwèi huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the seventh degree of the Liǔ (柳) mansion,
which is the metropolitan mansion.
Liǔ (柳) signifies the imperial granaries,
for sacrificial grain.
It is near the Yúguǐ (輿鬼) mansion,
which signifies the ancestral temples.
In the nineteenth year,
officials proposed to establish four temples near the emperor for sacrifices.
There was an imperial edict
stating, "The location of the temples is not yet decided;
for now, let us perform the joint sacrifice at the Gāomiào (高廟)."
By this time, three years had passed,
and no temples had been established.
There was a negligent and lazy attitude,
and a deficiency in serving the ancestors,
hence the omen was shown.
Twenty-fifth year, third month, wùshēn huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the fifteenth degree of the Bì (畢) mansion.
Bì (畢) signifies border troops.
In the tenth month of that winter,
because the Mán (蠻) barbarians of Wǔxī (武谿) were causing harm,
Fúbō Jiāngjūn Mǎ Yuàn (伏波將軍馬援) led troops to attack them.
Twenty-ninth year, second month, dīngsì shuò,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the fifth degree of the Dōngbì (東壁) mansion.
Dōngbì (東壁) signifies literature,
also known as the mouth of Jūzī (娵訾).
Before this, the imperial princes and kings each recruited scholars of literature and discourse.
Last year,
someone submitted a memorial:
"Among those hosted by the kings,
some are mixed true and false,
and descendants of those who received punishments,
it would be appropriate to differentiate them."
Thereupon, the Emperor was angered,
and issued an edict to arrest the kings' guests.
All were subjected to harsh laws,
and many died.
Shìzǔ had not established clear prohibitions early enough;
the governance at that time was excessively severe,
hence Heaven showed the omen.
Shìzǔ then repented,
and sent envoys to redress all those who had been unjustly wronged.
Thirty-first year, fifth month, guǐyǒu huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the fifth degree of the Liǔ (柳) mansion,
which is the metropolitan mansion.
From the omen shown in the twenty-first year until this time, ten years had passed.
Two years later,
the imperial carriage departed (the emperor passed away).
Zhōngyuán (中元), first year, eleventh month, jiǎzǐ huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the twentieth degree of the Dǒu (斗) mansion.
Dǒu (斗) signifies temples,
and presides over titles and emoluments.
The Rú (Confucian) explanation states that jiǎzǐ (甲子) in the eleventh month
is the day of the reigning king,
and also corresponds to Xīngjì (星紀),
which presides over titles and emoluments,
so its divination is significant.
Míng Dì (明帝) Yǒngpíng (永平), third year, eighth month, rénshēn huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the second degree of the Dī (氐) mansion.
Dī (氐) signifies the imperial palace.
At this time, Míng Dì (明帝) was building the Northern Palace.
Eighth year, tenth month,
rén'yín huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
which was total,
at the eleventh degree of the Dǒu (斗) mansion.
Dǒu (斗) signifies Wú (吳).
Guǎnglíng (廣陵) astrologically belongs to Wú (吳).
Two years later,
Wáng Jīng (王荊) of Guǎnglíng (廣陵) committed suicide due to plotting rebellion.
Thirteenth year, tenth month,
jiǎchén huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the seventeenth degree of the Wěi (尾) mansion.
Sixteenth year, fifth month, wùwǔ huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the fifteenth degree of the Liǔ (柳) mansion.
The Rú (Confucian) explanation states that wùwǔ (戊午) in the fifth month
is like jiǎzǐ (甲子) in the eleventh month,
and also the mansion is in the capital,
so its divination is significant.
Two years later,
the imperial carriage departed (the emperor passed away).
Eighteenth year, eleventh month, jiǎchén huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the twenty-first degree of the Dǒu (斗) mansion.
At this time, Míng Dì (明帝) had already passed away,
and Empress Mǎ (馬) controlled titles and emoluments,
hence the yang was not victorious.
Zhāng Dì (章帝) Jìanchū (建初), fifth year, second month, gēngchén shuò,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the eighth degree of the Dōngbì (東壁) mansion.
The precedent is in the twenty-ninth year of Jìanwǔ (建武).
At this time, various officials debated the classics,
and many denounced and slandered each other.
Sixth year, sixth month, xīnwèi huì,
there was a solar eclipse,
at the sixth degree of the Yì (翼) mansion.
Yì (翼) presides over distant guests.
In winter,
Wáng Cāng (王蒼) of Dōngpíng (東平) and others came to pay homage.
In the first month of the following year,
Cāng (蒼) died.
(Yuán) [Zhāng] Hé (章和), first year, eighth month, yǐwèi huì,
there was a solar eclipse.
The imperial historians did not observe it,
but other officials reported it.
The sun was at the fourth degree of the Dī (氐) mansion.
Hé Dì (和帝) Yǒngyuán (永元), second year, second month, rénwǔ,
there was a solar eclipse.
The imperial historians did not observe it,
but Zhuō Jùn (涿郡) reported it.
The sun was at the eighth degree of the Kuí (奎) mansion.
In the fourth year, in the sixth month, on the *wùxū* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in the *Qīxīng* (Seven Stars) lunar mansion, at two degrees,
which governs clothing.
It also said that it was near Xuānyuán,
in the left corner,
which represents the empress dowager's clan.
On the nineteenth day of this month,
the Emperor dismissed the officials of the Empress Dowager's brothers, Dòu Xiàn and others,
and sent them to their respective fiefs.
He selected Yán Néng as chancellor,
who was then cornered in his state and committed suicide.
In the seventh year, in the fourth month, on the *xīnhài* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Zīxī* (Beak and Snout),
which represents *bǎolǚ*,
and governs collection and storage.
Confucian scholars said that *Bǎolǚ* is an omen concerning the imperial palace,
and *shōuliǎn* (collection and storage) is an omen of greed and jealousy.
In this year, Dèng Guìrén first entered the palace.
In the following year, in the third month,
Empress Yīn was established.
Dèng Guìrén enjoyed imperial favor,
and Empress Yīn became jealous of her.
The empress was subsequently deposed.
Another account says it was about to enter *Shēn* (Orion).
*Shēn* and *Fá* (Punishment) represent cutting and slaughter.
In the following year, in the seventh month,
Féng Zhù, the Commandant of Elite Cavalry, captured and beheaded Wēnyúdú Wáng Wūjūzhàn of the Xiongnu.
In the twelfth year, in the autumn, in the seventh month, on the *xīnhài* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Yì* (Wings), at eight degrees,
which is the mansion of Jīngzhōu.
In the following year, in winter,
the Man and Yi people of Nánjùn rebelled and became bandits.
In the fifteenth year, in the fourth month, on the *jiǎzǐ* last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in Dōngjǐng (Eastern Well), at twenty-two degrees.
Dōngjǐng
is the mansion that governs wine and food.
The duty of a woman
is to be without fault and without impropriety;
wine and food are her concern.
In the previous winter,
Empress Dèng was established.
She had a masculine disposition
and participated in external affairs;
thus, Heaven showed this omen.
In this year, there were floods,
and the rains damaged the crops.
In the first year of Ān Dì's Yǒngchū era, on the second day of the third month, *guǐyǒu*,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Wèi* (Stomach), at two degrees.
*Wèi* governs granaries.
At this time, Empress Dowager Dèng held exclusive power.
In the previous year, great floods damaged the crops,
and the granaries were empty.
In the fifth year, in the first month, on the *gēngchén* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Xū* (Emptiness), at eight degrees.
The first month
is the proper day for the ruler to administer affairs.
*Xū*
means "empty".
At this time, Empress Dowager Dèng was regent,
and Emperor Ān was unable to conduct affairs.
Neither was in their proper place,
as if the ruler's position was empty.
Therefore, in the first month, the *yáng* could not overcome the *yīn*,
showing an omen.
Thus, the *yīn* prematurely overcame the *yáng*,
and therefore the Yi and Di peoples simultaneously became bandits and caused harm,
and the western border commanderies all became desolate.
In the seventh year, in the fourth month, on the *bǐngshēn* last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in Dōngjǐng (Eastern Well), at one degree.
In the first year of Yuánchū, in the tenth month, on the *wùzǐ* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Wěi* (Tail), at ten degrees.
*Wěi* represents the inner palace,
the palace of succession.
At this time, the Emperor greatly favored Yán Guìrén,
and was about to establish her as empress.
Therefore, an unfavorable sign was shown,
foretelling disaster for the succession.
In the following year, in the fourth month,
she was indeed established as empress.
The empress then colluded with Jiāng Jīng, Gěng Bǎo, and others to falsely accuse the Crown Prince and have him deposed.
In the second year, in the ninth month, on the *rénwǔ* last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Xīn* (Heart), at four degrees.
*Xīn* represents the ruler,
clearly indicating that the position would be lost for a long time.
In the third year, on the second day of the third month, *xīnhài*,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Lóu* (Bond), at five degrees.
The court astrologers did not observe it,
but Liáodōng reported it.
In the fourth year, in the second month, on the *yǐsì* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Kuí* (Legs), at nine degrees.
The court astrologers did not observe it,
but seven commanderies reported it.
*Kuí* governs the armory and weapons.
On the eighteenth day of that month, *rénxū*,
the armory caught fire,
burning weapons.
In the fifth year, in the eighth month, on the *bǐngshēn* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Yì* (Wings), at eighteen degrees.
The court astrologers did not observe it,
but Zhāngyè reported it.
In the sixth year, in the twelfth month, on the *wùwǔ* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse,
almost total,
and the earth was as if in twilight.
It was in *Xūnǚ* (Maiden), at eleven degrees,
which bodes ill for the empress.
Two years later, in the third month,
Empress Dowager Dèng passed away.
In the first year of Yǒngníng, in the seventh month, on the *yǐyǒu* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Zhāng* (Extended Net), at fifteen degrees.
The court astrologers did not observe it,
but Jiǔquán reported it.
In the third year of Yánguāng, in the ninth month, on the *gēngshēn* last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Dǐ* (Root), at fifteen degrees.
*Dǐ* represents the palace.
The palace
means the central palace.
At this time, the Emperor listened to the slanderous words of the Palace Attendants Jiāng Jīng, Fán Fēng, and the wet nurse Wáng Shèng, and others,
and deposed the Crown Prince.
In the fourth year, in the third month, on the *wùwǔ* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Wèi* (Stomach), at twelve degrees.
Lǒngxī, Jiǔquán, and Shuòfāng each reported the phenomenon,
but the court astrologers were unaware.
In the second year of Shùn Dì's Yǒngjiàn era, in the seventh month, on the *jiǎxū* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Yì* (Wings), at nine degrees.
In the fourth year of Yángjiā, in the intercalary month, on the *dīnghài* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Jiǎo* (Horn), at five degrees.
The court astrologers did not observe it,
but Línglíng reported it.
In the third year of Yǒnghé, in the twelfth month, on the *wùxū* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Xūnǚ* (Maiden), at eleven degrees.
The court astrologers did not observe it,
but Kuàijī reported it.
In the following year,
the Palace Attendants Zhāng Kuí and others plotted to slander the empress's father, Liáng Shāng, intending to cause rebellion.
After investigation,
Zhāng Kuí and others were executed.
In the fifth year, in the fifth month, on the *jǐchǒu* last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in Dōngjǐng (Eastern Well), at thirty-three degrees.
Dōngjǐng
is the mansion of Sānfǔ.
It was also near Yúguǐ (Ghost Cart),
and Yúguǐ represents the ancestral temple.
That autumn,
the Western Qiāng became bandits,
reaching the imperial tombs in Sānfǔ.
In the sixth year, in the ninth month, on the *xīnhài* last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Wěi* (Tail), at eleven degrees.
*Wěi* governs the inner palace,
the palace of succession.
This was considered an omen that the succession would not flourish.
In the first year of Huán Dì's Jiànhé era, in the first month, on the *xīnhài* first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Yíngshì* (Encampment), at three degrees.
The court astrologers did not observe it,
but the commanderies and states reported it.
At this time, Empress Dowager Liáng was regent.
In the third year, in the fourth month, on the *dīngmǎo* last day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in Dōngjǐng (Eastern Well), at twenty-three degrees.
This is analogous to the fifteenth year of Yǒngyuán.
Dōngjǐng governs law.
Empress Dowager Liáng also listened to her brother, Jì, who unjustly killed high officials,
thereby violating heavenly law.
In the following year,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
In the second year of Yuánjiā, on the second day of the seventh month, *gēngchén*,
there was a solar eclipse.
It was in *Yì* (Wings), at four degrees.
The court astrologers did not observe it,
but Guǎnglíng reported it.
*Yì* governs music and entertainment.
At this time, the Emperor was excessively fond of music.
On the *dīngmǎo* day, the first day of the ninth month of the second year of Yǒngxīng,
there was a solar eclipse,
at five degrees in the constellation Jǐao (角).
Jǐao,
is the mansion of Zhèng.
In the eleventh month,
bandits rose up en masse in Tài-Shān,
robbing and killing senior officials.
Tài-Shān, in astronomy, belongs to Zhèng.
On the *gēngchén* day, the last day of the intercalary month of the third year of Yǒngshòu,
there was a solar eclipse,
at two degrees in the constellation Qīxīng (七星).
The historians did not observe it,
but commanderies and kingdoms reported it.
An example occurred in the fourth year of Yǒngyuán.
Two years later,
Empress Liáng (梁皇后) passed away,
and the Jì (冀) brothers were executed.
On the *jiǎxū* day, the last day of the fifth month of the first year of Yánxī,
there was a solar eclipse,
at seven degrees in the constellation Liǔ (柳),
which is the mansion of the capital.
On the *bǐngshēn* day, the last day of the first month of the eighth year,
there was a solar eclipse,
at thirteen degrees in the constellation Yíngshì (營室).
In Yíngshì,
is the symbol of the empress.
In the *guǐhài* month (癸亥) of its second month,
Empress Dèng (鄧皇后) was implicated in drunkenness,
and the emperor sent her to the bào shì,
ordering her to commit suicide,
and her family members were executed.
The same happened when Empress Dà Lǚ (呂太后) passed away.
On the *xīnmǎo* day, the first day of the first month of the ninth year,
there was a solar eclipse,
at three degrees in the constellation Yíngshì.
The historians did not observe it,
but commanderies and kingdoms reported it.
Gǔ Yǒng (谷永) believed that the respected figures of the three courts were displeased by it.
In the following year,
the imperial carriage departed (the emperor died).
On the *rénzǐ* day, the last day of the fifth month of the first year of Yǒngkāng,
there was a solar eclipse,
at one degree in the constellation Yúguǐ (輿鬼).
Confucian scholars said that *rénzǐ* is the day of pure water,
and the yang could not overcome it,
so there would be water damage.
In its eighth month,
there were great floods in six provinces,
and Bó-Hǎi (勃海) overflowed.
On the *dīngwèi* day, the first day of the fifth month of the first year of Jiànníng of Emperor Líng,
there was a solar eclipse.
In the winter, on the *jiǎchén* day, the last day of the tenth month,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *wùxū* day, the last day of the tenth month of the second year,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Right Fúfēng (右扶風) reported it.
On the *bǐngyín* day, the last day of the third month of the third year,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Chancellor of Liáng (梁相) reported it.
On the *xīnyǒu* day, the first day of the third month of the fourth year,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *guǐyǒu* day, the last day of the twelfth month of the second year of Xīpíng,
there was a solar eclipse,
at two degrees in the constellation Xū (虛).
At this time, the Permanent Attendants Cáojíe (曹節) and Wángfǔ (王甫) monopolized power.
On the *guǐchǒu* day, the first day of the tenth month of the sixth year,
there was a solar eclipse,
and the Chancellor of Zhào (趙相) reported it.
On the *xīnhài* day, the first day of the second month of the first year of Guānghé,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day, the last day of the tenth month,
there was a solar eclipse,
at four degrees in the constellation Jī (箕).
Jī signifies disputes and gossip in the empress's palace.
In this month,
the emperor, listening to slander, deposed Empress Sòng (宋皇后).
On the *jiǎxū* day, the first day of the fourth month of the second year,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *gēngyín* day, the first day of the ninth month of the fourth year,
there was a solar eclipse,
at six degrees in the constellation Jǐao.
On the *rénchén* day, the last day of the fifth month of the third year of Zhōngpíng,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day, the first day of the fourth month of the sixth year,
there was a solar eclipse.
In that month, after ten days,
the imperial carriage departed (the emperor died).
On the *jiǎyín* day, the first day of the first month of the fourth year of Chūpíng of Emperor Xiàn,
there was a solar eclipse,
at four degrees in the constellation Yíngshì.
At this time, Lǐjué (李傕) and Guōsì (郭汜) monopolized the government.
On the *yǐsì* day, the last day of the sixth month of the first year of Xīngpíng,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *gēngwǔ* day, the first day of the ninth month of the fifth year of Jiàn'ān,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *dīngmǎo* day, the first day of the second month of the sixth year,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *guǐwèi* day, the first day of the tenth month of the thirteenth year,
there was a solar eclipse,
at twelve degrees in the constellation Wěi (尾).
On the *yǐsì* day, the first day of the second month of the fifteenth year,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *gēngyín* day, the last day of the sixth month of the seventeenth year,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *jǐhài* day, the first day of the fifth month of the twenty-first year,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *rénzǐ* day, the last day of the second month of the twenty-fourth year,
there was a solar eclipse.
In total, during the twelve generations of the Restoration of the Hàn,
over one hundred and ninety-six years,
there were seventy-two solar eclipses: thirty-two on the first day of the month (*shuò*),
thirty-seven on the last day (*huì*),
and three on the second day of the month.
On the *bǐngyín* day of the fourth month of the seventh year of Jiànwǔ of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
there was a solar halo,
a white rainbow pierced the halo,
at eight degrees in the constellation Bì (畢).
Bì signifies border troops.
In autumn,
Wěixiāo (隗囂) rebelled,
invading Āndìng.
The annotation directly states, "It is an ear (珥)."
Mèng Kāng (孟康) said:
"A ring is like a ring."
Sòng Jūn (宋均) said:
"A yellow qi embraces the sun,
meaning auxiliary ministers offer loyalty."
During the time of Emperor Líng,
the sun often appeared in the east,
pure red like blood,
without light,
and only cast a shadow when two *zhàng* (two丈) high.
And when it entered the west,
two *zhàng* (二丈) from the ground,
it was also like this.
Its prognostication said,
if one is not reverent in serving Heaven,
then the sun and moon will be red.
At this time, the moon, upon rising and setting, was two or three *zhàng* (二三丈) from the ground,
and was often red like blood.
On the *jǐsì* day of the second month of the fourth year of Guānghé,
a yellow qi embraced the sun,
with a yellow-white ear (珥) on its surface.
On the *bǐngshēn* day of the third month of the fourth year of Zhōngpíng,
a black qi as large as a melon
was in the sun.
In the first month of the fifth year,
the sun's color was reddish-yellow,
with a black qi within it like a flying magpie,
which only dissipated after several months.
On the *yǐwèi* day of the second month of the sixth year,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
On the *rénchén* day of the second month of the first year of Chūpíng of Emperor Xiàn,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
On the *rénxū* day of the twelfth month of the third year of Yǒngshòu of Emperor Huán,
there was a lunar eclipse not in its proper month.
On the *xīnsì* day of the first month of the eighth year of Yánxī,
there was a lunar eclipse not in its proper month.
An encomium states: when the Supreme Ultimate is established,
the five matters are set right.
Punishments and misfortunes enter as calamities;
rebellion and disorder increasingly interfere.
Fire descends, water surges;
wood is weak, metal is sour.
How can omens be groundless?
Their essence is observed.

The new moon for the sixth month of the eleventh year was jǐhài (己亥),

Present calculations show that the new moon for the seventh month of that year was wùchén (戊辰),
which was the last day of the sixth month, dawn or night, according to the contemporary calendar,
so a solar eclipse could not have been seen.
Also, the new moon for the twelfth month of that year was dīngyǒu (丁酉),
so xīnhài (辛亥) was also not a new moon day.
Present calculations show that the new moon for this month was bǐngshēn (丙申),
which was the last day of the eleventh month according to the contemporary calendar,
and a solar eclipse could have been seen.
The Gǔjīnzhu (古今注) is mistaken here.

Note on the annotation style of this book:
identical date names are not re-annotated.
However, here it quotes
the phrase "zhūhóu xiāng gōng" (諸侯相攻),
while later, under the Bǐngshēn (丙申) new moon in the eighth month of Yuánchū (元初) 5th year, it quotes

The same date having different prognoses

Current annotation: The Jiàobǔ (校補) states that Qián (錢) considered the phrase
"yídí nèi rǎng" (夷狄內攘) quoted in a later annotation to be a variant of
"yídí nèi qīn" (夷狄內侵),
but his explanation is also incorrect.
This is because the divination record for the Bǐngshēn (丙申) day from Qiántánbā (潛潭巴) cited in the annotation
originally lacked
the five characters "yídí nèi qīn hàn" (夷狄內侵旱).
The explanation will be detailed later.
On page 3364, line 1: "yuánchū yuán nián shí yuè wù zǐ shuò rì yǒu shí zhī" (元初元年十月戊子朔日有蝕之). The Jíjiě (集解) quotes Huì Dòng's (惠棟) remark,
stating that the Běnjì (本紀) records a solar eclipse on a Guǐyǒu (癸酉) new moon in the third month.
Current annotation: The new moon in the third month of Yuánchū (元初) 1st year occurred on a Rénxū (壬戌) day,
with no solar eclipse.
The Jì (紀) is mistaken.
On page 3364, line 4: "cí bì chéng xióng" (雌必成雄). Annotation: The Jíjiě (集解) quotes Qián Dàxīn's (錢大昕) remark,

"bì chéng xióng,
yǒu yōu" (必成雄，有憂).
On page 3364, line 7: "sì nián èr yuè yǐ (hài) [sì] shuò" (四年二月乙（亥）【巳】朔). The Jíjiě (集解) quotes Hóng Liàngjí's (洪亮吉) remark,
stating that according to Ānjì (安紀) it is "yǐsì" (乙巳),
and it later mentions Dīngyǒu (丁酉) and Rénxū (壬戌),
so the date characters should follow the Běnjì (本紀).
It also quotes Zhōu Shòuchāng's (周壽昌) remark,
stating that it later says,
"on the eighteenth day of that month, a Rénxū (壬戌) day,
the military arsenal caught fire" (其月十八日壬戌，武庫火),
which is consistent with the Jì (紀).
From the Yǐsì (乙巳) new moon to the Rénxū (壬戌) day is exactly eighteen days.
If it were an Yǐhài (乙亥) new moon,
then there could not be a Rénxū (壬戌) day later.
It should follow the Běnjì (本紀).
Current annotation: Calculations show that the new moon in the second month of that year was on an Yǐsì (乙巳) day,
and a solar eclipse was visible.
Hóng (洪) and Zhōu's (周) explanations are correct,
and we now adopt this correction.
Further annotation: Liú Zhù (劉注) quotes from the Chūnqiū Huì Qiántánbā (春秋諱潛潭巴) regarding
"yǐhài" (乙亥), and so on,
which sufficiently proves that the original text seen indeed read
"yǐhài" (乙亥).

If there were the character

On page 3364, line 11: "qiántánbā yuē bǐng shēn shí yídí nèi rǎng" (潛潭巴曰丙申蝕夷狄內攘). Annotation: The Jiàobǔ (校補) states that the Zhànjīng (占經) has it as

Qián Dàxīn (錢大昕) inadvertently forgot that

Commanderies and States: 1 Hénán,
Hénèi, Hédōng, Hóngnóng, Jīngzhào, Féngyì, Fúfēng, Right Sīlì.
The Hàn Shū Dìlǐ Zhì records the origins and history of all prefectures and counties under heaven,
as well as strange mountains and rivers,
and the origins of customs,
to the utmost.
Now, we only record the changes in prefectures and counties since the restoration,
and the place names of campaigns that coincide in the Chūnqiū and the Three Histories,
to form the Jùnguó Zhì (Treatise on Commanderies and States).
All county names in the previous treatise
that are not included here
were merged and abolished by Emperor Shìzǔ.
Those not in the former but present now
were established later.
All county names written first
are where the commandery administered.

The Geography Treatise of the Hàn Shū inherited thirty-six commanderies from Qín,
with several hundred counties and districts.
Later, they were gradually divided,
until the time of Emperor Xiàopíng,
there were a total of one hundred and three commanderies and states,
and one thousand five hundred and eighty-seven counties, districts, routes, and marquisates.
When Shìzǔ revived the dynasty,
only because there were too many officials and burdens,
he ordered mergers and reductions,
abolishing ten commanderies and states,
and over four hundred counties, districts, routes, and marquisates.
By Emperor Míng, one commandery was established;
by Emperor Zhāng, two commanderies and states were established;
by Emperor Hé, three were established;
Emperor Ān further ordered six tributary states to be separately administered like commanderies;
moreover, the abolished counties were gradually re-established.
By Emperor Xiàoshùn,
there were a total of one hundred and five commanderies and states,
and one thousand one hundred and eighty counties, districts, routes, and marquisates,
with a population of nine million six hundred ninety-eight thousand six hundred and thirty households,
and forty-nine million one hundred fifty thousand two hundred and twenty mouths.
An encomium states: The multitudes were at peace, and their descendants prospered;
governance was harmonious, dividing the regions.
侯 Hóu were dismissed and appointed to ranks;
the people had no fixed ruler.
Titles were adopted and shifted,
divisions of fiefs were entangled.
Briefly, some additions and deletions have been made,
largely confirming earlier accounts.
Collation Notes, page 3506, line 8: 錫 Xī. Annotation: In the former record, it is written as
「鍚 Yáng」.
Yīng Shào said it is pronounced Yáng.
Wáng Xiānqiān’s supplementary note states that Yīng Shào was a person from the Later Hàn dynasty;
at that time, this county still existed,
so Yīng Shào’s pronunciation must not be wrong.
It should be considered correct to write it as
「鍚 Yáng」.
The same applies to page
Page 3506, line 12: 有唐公（防 Fáng）【房 Fáng】祠. The collected explanations cite Qián Dàxīn’s remark,
stating that
「防 Fáng」
should be written as
「房 Fáng」.
Hàn people’s clerical script
「房 Fáng」
was sometimes written as
「𠂝 Fáng」,
which was then corrupted to Páng.
Now revised accordingly.
Page 3506, line 14: 至于錫 Xī 穴. Annotation: In the Zuǒ Zhuàn,
「錫 Xī」
is written as
「鍚 Yáng」.
Page 3507, line 2: 初平 Chūpíng 【元 Yuán】年. Huì Dòng’s supplementary note states that there was no sixth year of Chūpíng,
and it should follow the Huáyáng Guó Zhì in writing
「初平元年 Chūpíng Yuánnián」.
Now revised accordingly.
Page 3507, line 2: 趙穎 Zhào Yǐng 分巴為二郡. In the Sānguó Zhì, Liú Yān’s biography,
「趙穎 Zhào Yǐng」
is written as
「趙韙 Zhào Wěi」.
Zhāng Sēnkǎi’s collation note states: Based on Shěn Yuè’s citation of Qióu Zhōu’s Bā Jì yuánwén and the Tōngjiàn, all record it as
「韙 Wěi」.
It is suspected that the character
「穎 Yǐng」
is incorrect.
Page 3507, line 2: 故郡以墊江為治安漢以下為永寧郡. Annotation: Qián Dàxīn’s textual research on discrepancies states: According to the Huáyáng Guó Zhì,
Zhào Yǐng suggested that everything above Diànjiāng be Bājùn,
with its seat of governance in Ānhàn. From Jiāngzhōu to Línjiāng would be Yǒngníngjùn.
This means Ānhàn and Diànjiāng were both within Bājùn,
and Ānhàn was even the commandery seat.
Yǐng was from Ānhàn,
so he wished to transfer the name of Bājùn to Ānhàn.
This text seems to have an error.
Page 3507, line 3: 劉 (Chuò)【Zhāng】分巴. Revised according to the diànběn (Palace Edition).
Annotation: The diànběn also has instances of
「綽 Chuò」.
Therefore, Qi Zhàonán’s textual research states that
「劉綽 Liú Chuò」
should be
「劉璋 Liú Zhāng」.
Zhāng divided Bā into Bādōng and Bāxī commanderies;
this can be verified in the Shǔ Zhì.
Page 3507, line 8: 則膏 (Huī)【Zé】鮮芳. Revised according to the Jíběn (Ji Edition) and diànběn.
Page 3507, line 10: 山有大小石城 (勢者). Deleted according to Huì Dòng’s remark cited in the collected explanations.
Page 3507, line 12: 左傳文十【六 Liù】年. Supplemented according to the diànběn’s textual research.
Page 3507, line 15: 從枳南入折丹涪水本與楚商於之地接. The diànběn
has the character
「水 Shuǐ」,
「陵 Líng」
before
and lacks the character
「與 Yǔ」.
「本 Běn」

Qi Zhàonán’s textual research states: Xī and Dānshuǐ are both county names,
bordering Fúlíng.
The note should say,
「從枳南入析、丹水、涪陵，與商於之地接 Cóng Zhǐ nán rù Xī, Dānshuǐ, Fúlíng, yǔ Shāngyú zhī dì jiē (From south of Zhǐ, enter Xī, Dānshuǐ, Fúlíng, bordering the land of Shāngyú).」
「析 Xī」
was corrupted to
「折 Zhé」,
and
「丹涪陵水 Dān Fúlíng Shuǐ」
had its characters inverted, making it incomprehensible.
Now, upon examination: The collected explanations cite Mǎ Yǔlóng’s remark,
stating that Xī and Dānshuǐ counties belong to Nányángjùn,
bordering Shāngyú,
but they are separated from Fúlíng by a great distance north and south,
nor can one enter them from south of Zhǐ.
Shāngyú never belonged to Chǔ.
Now, examining the Huáyáng Guó Zhì,
Fúlíng is the southern commandery of Bā.
Entering from south of Zhǐ county,
and sailing upstream on the Fúshuǐ river,
Qín’s Sīmǎ Cuò used this route to take Qiánzhōng.
According to this,
it is suspected that in the note,
「折 Zhé」
should be
「泝 Sù」,
「丹 Dān」
should be
「舟 Zhōu」,
and
「商於 Shāngyú」
should be changed to
「黔中 Qiánzhōng」,
for the geography to fit.
Page 3507, line 15: 漢時赤 (Tián)【Jiǎ】軍. The collected explanations cite Huì Dòng’s remark,
stating that
「赤田 Chìtián」
should follow the Huáyáng Guó Zhì in being written as
「赤甲 Chìjiǎ」.
Now revised accordingly.
Page 3508, line 7: (Zhōu) Cìshǐ Zhì. Qi Zhàonán’s textual research in the diànběn states that the seat of governance for various prefectural governors (cìshǐ) typically lacks the character
「州 Zhōu」.
Thus, this character
「州 Zhōu」
is redundant.
Now deleted accordingly.
Page 3508, line 7: 什邡 Shífāng. Annotation: In the former record, it is written as
「汁方 Zhīfāng」.
The Gōngchén Biǎo (Table of Meritorious Officials) writes it as
「汁防 Zhīfáng」.
The Jìn Zhì (History of Jìn) again writes it as
「什方 Shífāng」.
Various editions are inconsistent.
Page 3508, line 9: 水通巴 (Hàn). The collected explanations cite Huì Dòng’s remark,
stating: According to the Huáyáng Guó Zhì, the water flows to Bā.
The note has a redundant character
「漢 Hàn」.
Now deleted accordingly.
Page 3509, line 2: 汶江道 Wènjiāng Dào. Annotation: The former record lacks the character
「道 Dào」.
Page 3509, line 2: 八陵 Bālíng. Annotation: The collected explanations cite Qián Dàxīn’s remark,
stating that the former record has Cánlíng,
not Bālíng.
The Jìn Zhì also writes it as
「蠶陵 Cánlíng」.
It also cites Huì Dòng’s remark,
stating that Emperor Líng established Wènshānjùn by combining Wènjiāng, Cánlíng, and Guǎngróu counties.
「八陵 Bālíng」
should be written as
「蠶陵 Cánlíng」.
Page 3509, line 2: 緜虒道 Miánsī Dào. Annotation: The former record lacks the character
「道 Dào」.
Page 3510, line 1: 有魚 (Qì)【Fú】津. The collected explanations cite Qián Dàzhāo’s remark,
stating that
「泣 Qì」
should be
「涪 Fú」.
In Wú Hàn’s biography, Hàn battled Gōngsūn Shù’s generals Wèi Dǎng and Gōngsūn Yǒng at Yúfújīn.
The note states it is in Nán’ān county,
bordering the Great River to the north.
The Shǔ Dū Fù note writes it as
「魚符津 Yúfújīn」;
Fú and Fú (涪 and 符) are similar in sound.
Now revised accordingly.
Page 3510, line 2: (Hè)【Fú】節. The collected explanations cite Qián Dàxīn’s remark,
stating that the former record has Fú,
not Hèjié.
It is suspected that
「荷 Hè」
is a corruption of
「符 Fú」,
and the character
「節 Jié」
is redundant.
Now, upon examination: Fújié Zhǎng Wáng Shì
is mentioned in the Shǔ Zhì, Yáng Xì’s biography,
indicating that Dōng Hàn changed the name to Fújié,
and Shǔ of the Sānguó period followed it.
The character
「節 Jié」
should therefore not be a redundant text. Hè and Fú, however, are graphically similar and thus corrupted.
Now the character
「荷 Hè」
is revised,
but the character
「節 Jié」
is not deleted.
Page 3510, line 5: 縣之南有五屼山一山而五里在越巂界. Annotation: The collected explanations cite Huì Dòng’s remark,
stating that the current Shǔ Dū Fù note says,
「一山有五重，在縣南 (One mountain has five layers, located south of the county).」
Page 3510, line 9: 有【蜀 Shǔ】王 (Yuè)【Bīng】蘭. The collected explanations cite Huì Dòng’s remark,
stating that the Jiāng Shuǐ Zhù (Commentary on the River) says,
「縣有蜀王兵蘭 (The county has the Shǔ King’s Binglán).」
Lán and Lán (蘭 and 闌) are anciently interchangeable.
Now supplemented and revised according to Huì Dòng’s remark.
Note: *Huáyáng Guózhì* also states
"Jídào has the old Shǔ King's soldier's-orchids."
Page 3510, line 9. Lǐ Bīng burned the cliff, which has five colors: red and white reflecting in the water, and black and yellow. Note:
The character
"所" (suǒ)
is likely missing before
"燒" (shāo).
The current *Huáyáng Guózhì* reads:
"Its cliffs were so steep that they could not be chiseled,
so he piled up firewood and burned them.
Therefore, the cliffs at that place are red, white, and five-colored."
It also states:
"The cliff that Lǐ Bīng burned has five colors:
red and white reflecting in the water, and black and yellow."
Page 3510, line 11. There is Fāng [Shān] Lán temple. *Jíjiě* cites Huì Dòng's explanation,
stating that various editions omitted the character
"山" (shān).
It is now supplemented accordingly.
Page 3511, line 1. Jìnchéng. Note: The *qiánzhì* (former gazetteer) reads
"Jìnsāng,"
and the *Shuǐjīng Yèyúshuǐ Zhù* also reads
"Jìnsāng."
Page 3511, line 2. There is (Shěn) [Yuán] water. Changed according to Wáng Xiānqiān's explanation.
