According to notes, the Jùzhēn (聚珍) edition of the Dōngguān Hànjì (東觀漢記) also has
“三” (sān).
Page 3534, line 1, regarding “永嘉【元】年” (Yǒngjiā 【yuán】 nián). The collected explanations cite Hé Zhuō’s (何焯) remark
that there was no second year of Yǒngjiā (永嘉),
so “二” (èr)
should be
“元” (yuán).
This change is adopted now.
Page 3534, line 8, regarding “口四千八百六十九萬七百八十九” (kǒu sìqiān bābǎi liùshíjiǔ wàn qībǎi bāshíjiǔ). According to Zhāng Sēnkǎi’s (張森楷) collation notes, during the reign of Emperor Hé (和帝),
the population was over 53 million,
and households were just over 9.2 million.
Here, households are already over 9.6 million,
but the population is only over 40 million,
which is actually less.
This is clearly unreasonable.
It is suspected that
“四” (sì)
is a corruption of
The population figure for Emperor Shùn (順帝) below is similar.
Official Ranks: One Grand Tutor, Grand Commandant, Minister of Education, Minister of Works, General.
At the beginning of the Hàn (漢) dynasty, having inherited a period of great chaos,
military affairs were not yet settled,
and laws and regulations were nascent,
largely following the Qín (秦) system,
which later generations continued.
It was not until Emperor Jǐng (景帝) that, moved by the difficulties of Wú (吳) and Chǔ (楚),
he began to suppress and diminish the power of the feudal lords.
By the time of Emperor Wǔ (武帝),
many reforms were made,
but they led to extravagance and expansion,
and the people suffered from scarcity.
Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) (Guāngwǔdì (光武帝)) initiated a restoration,
emphasizing frugality,
consolidating offices and streamlining functions,
reducing expenditures by hundreds of millions.
This allowed for the repair of deficiencies.
While he was alive, he did not change this,
and the entire realm followed his example,
bringing peace and joy to the Central Plains.
In ancient times, the Duke of Zhōu (周公) established the Offices of Zhōu (周官),
clearly defining responsibilities,
with laws and regulations supporting one another.
Even when the royal house declined,
it was able to endure for a long time.
The surviving records of this
allow us to observe the utmost virtue of the Zhōu (周) dynasty in governing the people,
and also provide a beneficial model for future endeavors,
which is perhaps inexhaustible.
Therefore, Wáng Lóng (王隆), the magistrate of Xīnjí (新汲), compiled the Xiǎoxué Hànguānpiān (小學漢官篇),
but its various explanations were incomplete and lacked thoroughness.
Only Bān Gù (班固) wrote the Bǎiguān Gōngqīng Biǎo (百官公卿表),
recording the origins and evolution of official positions established by the Hàn (漢) dynasty following the Qín (秦),
up to Wáng Mǎng (王莽),
which was somewhat orderly.
However, it primarily detailed the extravagant and expansive affairs of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武),
and the division of duties was not fully comprehensive.
The system of frugality established by Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖)
should serve as the permanent standard.
Therefore, based on his official records,
the division of duties is roughly annotated
to form the Bǎiguān Zhì (百官志, Treatise on Official Ranks).
The origins of official establishments
and those eliminated during the Restoration
that cannot be traced again
are already in the Hànshū Bǎiguān Biǎo (漢書百官表, Table of Officials in the Book of Han),
and are not fully recounted here.
Grand Tutor (Tàifù (太傅)),
one person, a Senior Excellency.
The original note states: Responsible for guiding with goodness, without fixed duties.
Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) appointed Zhuó Mào (卓茂) as Grand Tutor.
Upon his death,
the office was abolished.
Subsequently, whenever an emperor first ascended the throne,
a Grand Tutor was appointed to oversee the affairs of the Masters of Writing (Shàngshū (尚書)).
Upon his death,
the office was abolished.
Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi (太尉)),
one person, an Excellency.
The original note states: Responsible for military affairs and merit assessments throughout the realm.
At the end of each year, he would report on the best and worst performances and administer rewards and punishments.
For suburban sacrifices,
he oversaw the secondary offerings.
For grand funerals, he announced the posthumous title at the southern suburb.
Whenever there were major creations or serious doubts in the state,
he would consult and deliberate with the Minister of Education (Sītú (司徒)) and the Minister of Works (Sīkōng (司空)).
If the state had shortcomings,
he would remonstrate jointly with the two Excellencies.
Upon Emperor Shìzǔ’s (世祖) accession,
he served as Grand Marshal (Dàsīmǎ (大司馬)).
In the 27th year of Jiànwǔ (建wǔ) (51 CE),
the title was changed to Grand Commandant.
Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ (長史)), one person, of a thousand *shí* (石) salary.
The original note states: In charge of all departmental affairs.
Attendants and Clerks (Yuánshǐ shǔ (掾史屬)), twenty-four persons.
The original note states: According to old Hàn (漢) annotations, the clerks of the Western and Eastern Bureaus (Xī Cáo Yuán (西曹掾), Dōng Cáo Yuán (東曹掾)) were equivalent to 400 *shí* (石),
other clerks were equivalent to 300 *shí* (石),
and attendants were equivalent to 200 *shí* (石).
Therefore, they were called "Excellency’s Bureau Clerks" (Gōngfǔ Yuán (公府掾)),
equivalent to the three-times-appointed "primordial scholars" (yuánshì (元士)) of antiquity.
Alternatively, it is said that
at the beginning of the Hàn (漢) dynasty, clerks and attendants were appointed by recommendation and
their names submitted to the emperor,
hence their rank and salary were comparable to appointed officials.
Those not reported
were 100 *shí* (石) attendants.
Later, all were appointed and dismissed by the officials themselves,
hence they were collectively referred to as 100 *shí* (石).
The Western Bureau (Xī Cáo (西曹)) was in charge of the appointment and use of government clerks.
The Eastern Bureau (Dōng Cáo (東曹)) was in charge of the promotion and dismissal of 2,000 *shí* (石) chief officials and military officers.
The Household Bureau (Hù Cáo (戶曹)) was in charge of household registers, sacrifices, agriculture, and sericulture.
The Memorial Bureau (Zòu Cáo (奏曹)) was in charge of memorials and deliberations.
The Litigation Bureau (Cí Cáo (辭曹)) was in charge of litigation.
The Law Bureau (Fǎ Cáo (法曹)) was in charge of postal relays and regulations.
The Military Transport Bureau (Wèi Cáo (尉曹)) was in charge of transportation of soldiers and laborers.
The Bandit Bureau (Zéi Cáo (賊曹)) was in charge of banditry.
The Judgment Bureau (Jué Cáo (決曹)) was in charge of criminal law.
The Military Bureau (Bīng Cáo (兵曹)) was in charge of military affairs.
The Treasury Bureau (Jīn Cáo (金曹)) was in charge of currency, salt, and iron affairs.
The Granary Bureau (Cāng Cáo (倉曹)) was in charge of granary affairs.
The Yellow Pavilion (Huáng Gé (黃閤)) Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù (主簿)) recorded and reviewed various matters.
Secretaries (Lìngshǐ (令史)) and Imperial Attendants (Yùshǔ (御屬)), twenty-three persons.
The original note states: According to old Hàn (漢) annotations, the public secretaries were 100 *shí* (石).
Since the Restoration,
the annotations do not specify the *shí* (石) amount.
The Imperial Attendants were responsible for driving the Excellency’s carriage.
The Secretaries Below the Pavilion (Gé Xià Lìngshǐ (閤下令史)) were responsible for ceremonial matters below the pavilion.
The Record-keeping Secretary (Jìshì Lìngshǐ (記室令史)) was responsible for presenting memorials, reports, and official correspondence.
The Gate Secretary (Mén Lìngshǐ (門令史)) was responsible for the gate of the government office.
The other Secretaries
each managed the documents of their respective bureaus.
Minister of Education (Sītú (司徒)),
one person, an Excellency.
The original note states: Responsible for the affairs of the people.
He deliberated on the systems
as well as matters of nurturing life and sending off the dead.
and established the standards
for teaching the people filial piety, brotherly submission, humility, and frugality,
For all assessments of the people's affairs throughout the realm,
at the end of each year, he would report on the best and worst performances and administer rewards and punishments.
For suburban sacrifices,
he was responsible for inspecting the sacrificial animals and the ritual washing.
For grand funerals, he was responsible for the reverent placement of the coffin.
Whenever there were major doubts or important matters in the state,
he consulted with the Grand Commandant.
Upon Emperor Shìzǔ’s (世祖) accession,
he served as Grand Minister of Education (Dàsītú (大司徒)).
In the 27th year of Jiànwǔ (建wǔ) (51 CE),
the character
“大” (dà)
was removed.
Attendants and Clerks (Yuánshǔ (掾屬)), thirty-one persons.
Secretaries and Imperial Attendants, thirty-six persons.
The original note states: Upon Emperor Shìzǔ’s (世祖) accession,
following the precedent of Emperor Wǔ (武帝),
a Commissioner of Rectification (Sīzhí (司直)) was established,
residing in the Prime Minister's (Chéngxiàng (丞相)) office,
to assist in supervising and recording affairs in all provinces.
This office was abolished in the 18th year of Jiànwǔ (建wǔ) (42 CE).
The Sīkōng
consists of one official.
The original commentary states: [He] is in charge of matters concerning water and soil.
Whenever cities are constructed, towns established, ditches and channels dredged, or dikes and embankments repaired,
he discusses their advantages
and oversees their completion.
Whenever there are achievements in water and soil projects across the four directions,
at the end of the year, he presents a report of their merits and demerits, and rewards and punishments are administered accordingly.
For matters concerning suburban sacrifices,
he is in charge of cleaning musical instruments;
during a grand funeral, he is in charge of leading officers and soldiers in restoring earth (to the grave).
Whenever the state has major construction projects or grave doubts,
he offers remonstrance and advice,
together with the Tàiwèi.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was made Dà Sīkōng.
In Jiànwǔ twenty-seventh year,
the character
"Dà" (大) was removed.
One Zhǎngshǐ
was subordinate to him, with a salary of one thousand shí.
There were twenty-nine Yuánshǔ.
There were forty-two Lìngshǐ and Yùshǔ.
Jiāngjūn
were not permanently established.
The original commentary states: [They] are in charge of punitive expeditions against rebels.
There are four ranks comparable to a Gōng: the first is Dà Jiāngjūn,
the second is Piàojì Jiāngjūn,
the third is Chējì Jiāngjūn,
and the fourth is Wèi Jiāngjūn.
There were also Qián, Hòu, Zuǒ, and Yòu Jiāngjūn.
Initially,
Wǔdì, seeing Wèi Qīng's numerous successful military campaigns,
appointed him Dà Jiāngjūn,
wishing to honor and favor him.
Considering that in ancient times, the only highly esteemed officials were the Sān Gōng,
and all generals originated from Qín and Jìn,
being considered a ministerial title,
he therefore established the official title of Dà Sīmǎ to crown him.
Subsequently, Huò Guāng, Wáng Fèng, and others were all treated similarly.
In Suīhé first year of Chéngdì,
the seal and ribbon of Dà Sīmǎ were bestowed,
and the general's office was abolished.
When Shìzǔ restored the dynasty,
Wú Hàn, as Dà Jiāngjūn, was made Dà Sīmǎ;
Jǐng Dān was made Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn,
whose rank was below that of the Gōng;
and the Qián, Hòu, Zuǒ, Yòu, and other miscellaneous-titled generals were numerous,
all primarily leading punitive expeditions,
and were all dismissed once the mission was accomplished.
When Míngdì first ascended the throne,
because his younger brother, Dōngpíng Wáng Cāng, possessed outstanding talent,
he was appointed Piàojì Jiāngjūn;
due to his status as a king,
his rank was above that of the Gōng,
but he was dismissed several years later.
When Zhāngdì ascended the throne,
the Xī Qiāng rebelled,
so his maternal uncle Mǎ Fáng was appointed acting Chējì Jiāngjūn to lead an expedition against them,
and was dismissed upon his return.
When Hédì ascended the throne,
his maternal uncle Dòu Xiàn was appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn
to lead an expedition against the Xiōngnú,
his rank being below that of the Gōng;
upon his return, having again achieved merit,
he was promoted to Dà Jiāngjūn,
his rank being above that of the Gōng;
he was again sent to campaign against the Xī Qiāng,
and upon his return, he was dismissed from office
and relieved of his command.
When Āndì ascended the throne,
the Xī Qiāng raided and caused disturbances,
so his maternal uncle Dèng Zhì was again appointed Chējì Jiāngjūn to lead an expedition against them,
and upon his return, he was promoted to Dà Jiāngjūn,
his rank being the same as Xiàn's,
and he was dismissed several years later.
From the time Āndì's administration began to decline and become deficient,
his maternal cousin Gěng Bǎo was first appointed Dà Jiāngjūn,
and regularly resided in the capital.
When Shùndì ascended the throne,
the Empress's father, elder brother, and younger brothers successively became Dà Jiāngjūn,
like the Sān Gōng.
There was one Zhǎngshǐ and one Sīmǎ,
each with a salary of one thousand shí.
The original commentary states: The Sīmǎ is in charge of military affairs,
like the Tàiwèi.
There were two Cóngshì Zhōngláng,
with a salary of six hundred shí.
The original commentary states: Their duty is to participate in strategic discussions.
There were twenty-nine Yuánshǔ.
There were thirty-one Lìngshǐ and Yùshǔ.
The original commentary states: These are all staff positions within the headquarters.
Additionally, thirty imperial cavalrymen
and drum and wind instrument players were bestowed.
Their commanders all had Bùqǔ.
The Dà Jiāngjūn's camp had five Bù;
each Bù had one Xiàowèi,
ranking equivalent to two thousand shí;
each Bù also had one Jūn Sīmǎ,
ranking equivalent to one thousand shí.
Below each Bù were Qǔ;
each Qǔ had one Jūnhóu,
ranking equivalent to six hundred shí.
Below each Qǔ were [Tún];
each [Tún] had one [Tún]zhǎng,
ranking equivalent to two hundred shí.
For those camps that did not have a Xiàowèi Bù,
there was only one Jūn Sīmǎ.
There were also Jūn Jiǎ Sīmǎ and Jiǎhóu,
all serving as deputies.
Those separately established camps and their subordinates were called Biébù Sīmǎ,
and the number of their soldiers varied according to contemporary needs.
The gates had Mén Hóu.
Other generals,
appointed for punitive expeditions,
had no fixed staff positions,
but also had Bùqǔ, Sīmǎ, and Jūnhóu to command troops.
Each department had one Zhí Lì Bùjí
who was generally in charge of camp affairs.
The Bīngcáo Yuánshǐ were in charge of military affairs and weaponry.
The Bǐngjiǎ Yuánshǐ were in charge of provisions, leave, prohibitions, and administration.
Additionally, Wài Cì and Cì Jiān were established,
in charge of criminal law.
Míngdì first established the Dùliáo Jiāngjūn,
to guard against the Nán Chányú's followers, who had recently surrendered but were disloyal;
subsequently, there were often disturbances,
so it became a permanent garrison.
Hundred Officials: Two Tàicháng, Guānglùxūn, Wèiwèi, Tàipú, Tíngwèi, Dàhónglú.
Tàicháng,
one Qīng,
ranking as Zhōng Èrqiān Shí.
The original commentary states: [He] is in charge of rites and sacrifices.
For every sacrifice,
he first presents the rituals;
and during the actual performance,
he always prompts the Son of Heaven.
Whenever Bóshì are selected and tested,
he reports on their ability.
For grand archery ceremonies, elderly care rituals, and grand funerals,
he presents all the rituals.
On the last day of each month,
he inspects the imperial tombs and ancestral temples.
One Céng,
ranking equivalent to one thousand shí.
The original commentary states: [He] is in charge of all rituals and minor sacrificial matters,
and oversees all departmental affairs.
The Yuánshǐ of these departments
are staffed according to their duties,
and this is true for all Qīng.
One Tàishǐ Lìng,
with a salary of six hundred shí.
The original commentary states: [He] is in charge of celestial phenomena and astronomical calendars.
At the end of each year,
he presents the calendar for the new year.
For all state sacrifices, funerals, and marriages,
he is in charge of presenting auspicious days and seasonal taboos.
Whenever the state experiences auspicious omens or calamities,
he is in charge of recording them.
One Céng.
One Míngtáng and Língtái Céng,
with a salary of two hundred shí.
The original commentary states: The two Céng
are in charge of guarding the Míngtáng and Língtái.
The Língtái is in charge of observing the sun, moon, stars, and atmospheric phenomena,
all subordinate to the Tàishǐ.
One Bóshì Jìjiǔ,
with a salary of six hundred shí.
Originally a Púyè,
during the restoration, he was transferred to Jìjiǔ.
Fourteen Bóshì,
ranking equivalent to six hundred shí.
The original commentary states: Fours for Yì,
from the Shī, Mèng, Liángqiū, and Jīng clans.
Threes for Shàngshū,
from the Ōuyáng, Dà Xiàhóu, and Xiǎo Xiàhóu clans.
Threes for Shī,
from the Lǔ, Qí, and Hán clans.
Twos for Lǐ,
from the Dà Dài and Xiǎo Dài clans.
Twos for Chūnqiū,
from the Gōngyáng Yán and Yán clans.
They are in charge of teaching disciples.
Whenever the state has doubtful matters,
they are in charge of accepting inquiries and providing answers.
Originally four hundred shí,
Xuāndì increased their rank.
One Tàizhù Lìng,
with a salary of six hundred shí.
The original commentary states: For all state sacrifices,
he is in charge of reading the prayer,

One Céng.
The original commentary states: [He] is in charge of praying to minor deities.

The original commentary states: They are in charge of sacrificial vessels like cauldrons (dǐng), tripods (zǔ), and other food preparation items.

The Grand Musician (Dà Yǔyuè) has one director (lìng),

The Gāomiào Temple has one director (lìng),
