The original commentary states: There is no fixed number of positions.
They are in charge of the emperor's steeds.
The Commandant of Cavalry (Jì Dūwèi)
has a salary equivalent to 2000 dàn of grain.
The original commentary states: There is no fixed number of positions.
Originally, they supervised the Feathered Forest Cavalry (yǔlín jí).
The Grand Master of Glorious Emolument (Guānglù Dàfū)
has a salary equivalent to 2000 dàn of grain.
The original commentary states: There is no fixed number of positions.
All Grand Masters (dàfū) and Counsellors (yìláng) are generally in charge of consultation and answering questions,
having no regular duties,
but only carrying out imperial edicts.
For the mourning of the heirs of all kingdoms,
the Grand Master of Glorious Emolument (Guānglù Dàfū) is in charge of offering condolences.
The Grand Master of the Center (Tàizhōng Dàfū)
has a salary equivalent to 1000 dàn of grain.
The original commentary states: There is no fixed number of positions.
The Grand Master of Dispersed Leisure (Zhōngsàn Dàfū)
has a salary equivalent to 600 dàn of grain.
The original commentary states: There is no fixed number of positions.
The Grand Master of Admonishment (Jiànyì Dàfū)
has a salary equivalent to 600 dàn of grain.
The original commentary states: There is no fixed number of positions.
The Counsellor (Yìláng)
has a salary equivalent to 600 dàn of grain.
The original commentary states: There is no fixed number of positions.
The Palace Assistant of Ushers (Yèzhě Pūshè) has one official,
whose salary is equivalent to 1000 dàn of grain.
The original commentary states: They serve as the head of the Usher Bureau (yèzhě tái),
supervising the ushers (yèzhě).
When the Son of Heaven goes out,
they lead the procession.
In ancient times, martial arts were highly valued,
and there was an official in charge of archery to supervise and record it,
hence the name "Palace Assistant" (pūshè).
There are five Permanent Palace Attendant Ushers (Chángshì Yèzhě),
whose salaries are equivalent to 600 dàn of grain.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of seasonal decorum and majesty in the palace hall.
There are thirty Ushers (Yèzhě).
The Ushers on Duty (Gěishì Yèzhě)
have a salary of 400 dàn of grain.
The Junior Ushers (Guàn Yèzhě Lángzhōng)
have a salary equivalent to 300 dàn of grain.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of assisting guests and receiving petitions,
and submitting memorials and responding to inquiries.
For the mourning of generals and grand masters and below,
they are in charge of sending condolences.
Originally there were seventy officials,
but during the Restoration (Zhōngxīng) there were only thirty.
Initially serving as Junior Ushers (guàn yèzhě),
after a full year they become Ushers on Duty (gěishì yèzhě).
The Commandant of the Palace Guard (Wèiwèi)
has one minister (qīng),
whose salary is equivalent to 2000 dàn of grain.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of the palace guards at the palace gates,
and patrolling within the palace.
There is one assistant (chéng),
whose salary is equivalent to 1000 dàn of grain.
The Gōngchē Sīmǎ Lìng (Public Coach Marshal Director) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of the southern gate of the palace,
receiving all memorials from officials and commoners,
tributes from the four directions,
and those summoned to the public coach (gōngchē).
A Chéng (Assistant) and a Wèi (Captain) each have one person.
The original commentary states: The Chéng is selected for their understanding of taboos,
and is in charge of identifying illegal acts.
The Wèi is in charge of the troops guarding the palace gate and enforcing prohibitions,
and guarding against unusual occurrences.
The Nángōng Wèishì Lìng (Southern Palace Guard Director) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of the Southern Palace Guards.
A Chéng has one person.
The Běigōng Wèishì Lìng (Northern Palace Guard Director) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of the Northern Palace Guards.
A Chéng has one person.
The Zuǒyòu Dūhòu (Left and Right Capital Inspectors) each have one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of sword-and-halberd bearers,
patrolling the palace,
and cases where the Son of Heaven orders an arrest or investigation.
A Chéng each has one person.
For the palace gates (gōngyèmén),
each gate has one Sīmǎ (Marshal),
ranking equivalent to 1,000 dàn.
The original commentary states: The Nángōng Nántún Sīmǎ (Southern Palace Southern Garrison Marshal)
is in charge of the Píngchéng Gate;
the Běigōngmén Cānglóng Sīmǎ (Northern Palace Gate Azure Dragon Marshal)
is in charge of the Eastern Gate;
the Xuánwǔ Sīmǎ (Dark Warrior Marshal)
is in charge of the Xuánwǔ Gate;
the Běitún Sīmǎ (Northern Garrison Marshal)
is in charge of the Northern Gate;
the Běigōng Zhūquè Sīmǎ (Northern Palace Vermilion Bird Marshal)
is in charge of the Southern Side Gate;
the Dōngmíng Sīmǎ (Eastern Brightness Marshal)
is in charge of the Eastern Gate;
the Shuòpíng Sīmǎ (Northern Peace Marshal)
is in charge of the Northern Gate:
there are seven gates in total.
All those residing within the palace
have their household registers (kǒují) recorded with the gate they belong to.
The palace names, consisting of two characters,
are used for iron seals and tally slips.
One checks and verifies the tally slips before entering.
If outsiders need to enter for business,
the palace's (gōng) [official's] (guān) Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk) issues sealed passes.
Those with official ranks, when entering or exiting, have their ranks announced by their charioteers.
The Tàipú (Grand Coachman)
has one Qīng (Minister),
with a salary of 2,000 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of carriages and horses.
Whenever the Son of Heaven goes out,
they report on the preparation of the imperial carriage and the use of the imperial retinue.
For grand processions, they personally drive the carriage.
A Chéng has one person,
ranking equivalent to 1,000 dàn.
The Kǎogōng Lìng (Director of Arts and Crafts) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of manufacturing weapons like bows, crossbows, swords, armor, and similar items.
Once completed, these are transferred by the Zhí Jīn Wǔ (Bearer of the Golden Halberd) into the military arsenal,
and they also oversee the weaving of ribbons and other various crafts.
The Zuǒyòu Chéng (Left and Right Assistants) each have one person.
The Chēfǔ Lìng (Director of the Imperial Chariots) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of the imperial carriages and other vehicles.
A Chéng has one person.
The Wèiyāng Jiù Lìng (Wèiyāng Stables Director) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of the imperial horses and all other horses in the stables.
The Chánglè Jiù Chéng (Chánglè Stables Assistant) has one person.
The Tíngwèi (Grand Judge)
has one Qīng (Minister),
with a salary of 2,000 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of impartially hearing cases,
and presenting rulings according to what is appropriate.
All doubtful cases from commanderies and kingdoms,
are to be ruled upon and reported back.
The Zhèng Jiān (Chief Supervisor) and Zuǒ Jiān (Left Supervisor) each have one person.
The Zuǒpíng (Left Administrator) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of impartially resolving cases in imperial prisons.
The Right is subordinate to the Tíngwèi.
The original commentary states: From Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) onwards,
twenty-six central imperial prisons (zhōngdūguānyù) were established,
each with its own director and chief. During the restoration by Shìzǔ (Guāngwǔdì), all were abolished,
leaving only the Tíngwèi and the imperial prison in Luòyáng.
The Dàhónglú (Grand Herald)
has one Qīng (Minister),
with a salary of 2,000 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of the feudal lords (zhūhóu) and the barbarian tribes (mányí) from the four directions who pledge allegiance.
During sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
they lead and guide,
requesting the performance of rites.
Once approved,
they issue orders to the various departments.
When kings enter the court,
they are to be welcomed at the suburban altars,
and the Dàhónglú manages their ceremonies.
And when commanderies and kingdoms submit their annual reports (shàngjì),
and people from the four directions come,
they also fall under their jurisdiction.
When imperial princes are enfeoffed as kings,
they assist in presenting the seals and ribbons.
And when feudal lords, their heirs, and foreign tribes from the four directions are enfeoffed,
the Dàhónglú summons them to be enfeoffed before the imperial platform.
When a king dies, they send condolences,
and enfeoff the king's heir.
A Chéng has one person,
ranking equivalent to 1,000 dàn.
The Dàxíng Lìng (Director of Grand Ceremonies) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of the various imperial gentlemen (zhūláng).
A Chéng has one person.
There are forty-seven Zhìlǐ Láng (Ritual Gentlemen).
These are subordinate to the Dàhónglú.
The original commentary states: Succeeding from Qín, there was the Diǎnshǔguó (Superintendent of the Household for Dependencies),
who specifically managed the tributary barbarians from the four directions and hostage princes.
During Emperor Chéng's (Chéngdì) reign, this office was abolished and merged into the Dàhónglú.
During the restoration (Zhōngxīng), the Yìguān (Post Station Official) and Biéhuǒ (Separate Fire) directors and assistants,
as well as the commandery lodge directors and assistants, were abolished,
leaving only the Láng (Gentlemen) to manage the commandery lodges.
The Hundred Officials: Three Departments: Zōngzhèng, Dàsīnóng, Shǎofǔ.
The Zōngzhèng (Court of the Imperial Clan)
has one Qīng (Minister),
with a salary of 2,000 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of recording the order of legitimate and illegitimate children of the imperial lineage,
and the closeness or distance of kinship among all imperial clan members.
Each year, commanderies and kingdoms, based on their annual reports, submit registers of imperial clan members.
If anyone commits a crime warranting punishment of shaving the head or more severe,
it is first reported to the Zōngzhèng,
the Zōngzhèng reports it to the emperor,
and then the decision is made.
A Chéng has one person,
ranking equivalent to 1,000 dàn.
For the various princesses (zhūgōngzhǔ),
each princess's household has one Jiālìng (Household Director),
with a salary of 600 dàn.
A Chéng has one person,
with a salary of 300 dàn.
The original commentary states: The remaining subordinate officials vary in number.
These are subordinate to the Zōngzhèng.
The original commentary states: During the restoration, the Dū Sīkōng (Metropolitan Minister of Works) director and assistant were abolished.
The Dàsīnóng (Grand Minister of Agriculture)
has one Qīng (Minister),
with a salary of 2,000 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of all money, grain, gold, silk, and other currencies.
Commanderies and kingdoms submit monthly money and grain accounts on the first day of each season.
Outstanding arrears are to be detailed separately.
For frontier commanderies whose officials request provisions,
supplies are provided;
reducing surplus and increasing deficiency,
to ensure sufficient supply.
A Chéng has one person,
ranking equivalent to 1,000 dàn.
A Bù Chéng (Department Assistant) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: The Bù Chéng is in charge of the treasury.
The Tàicāng Lìng (Grand Granary Director) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of receiving grain transported by commanderies and kingdoms.
A Chéng has one person.
The Píngzhǔn Lìng (Director of Standardization) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of knowing commodity prices,
and overseeing dyeing [fabrics] and making colors.
A Chéng has one person.
The Dǎoguān Lìng (Director of Selection Officials) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of pounding imperial rice [for fine grain],
and making dried rations.
Dǎo [in Dǎoguān]
means to select.
A Chéng has one person.
Other offices like the Yúnshū (Equalization and Transport) were all abolished.
The Shǎofǔ (Privy Treasury)
has one Qīng (Minister),
with a salary of 2,000 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of all items for imperial use,
including clothing, precious goods, and delicacies.
A Chéng has one person,
ranking equivalent to 1,000 dàn.
The Tàiyī Lìng (Grand Physician Director) has one person,
with a salary of 600 dàn.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of all physicians.
A Yào Chéng (Medicine Assistant) and a Fāng Chéng (Prescription Assistant) each have one person.
The original commentary states: The Yào Chéng is in charge of medicines.
The Fāng Chéng is in charge of medical prescriptions.
The Grand Provisioner (Tàiguān Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: Responsible for imperial food and drink.
Left Assistant (Zuǒchéng), Sweet Assistant (Gānchéng), Soup Official Assistant (Tāngguānchéng), and Fruit Assistant (Guǒchéng), one person each.
Original annotation: The Left Assistant is in charge of food and drink.
The Sweet Assistant is in charge of meal utensils.
The Soup Official Assistant is in charge of wine.
The Fruit Assistant is in charge of fruit.
The Palace Guardian (Shǒugōng Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: In charge of imperial paper, brushes, and ink,
as well as various supplies for the Secretariat (Shàngshū) and sealing clay.
An Assistant (Chéng) one person.
The Director of the Shànglín Imperial Park (Shànglínyuàn Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: In charge of birds and beasts in the park.
If there were commoners living there,
he was in charge of all of them.
Captured beasts were sent to the Grand Provisioner (Tàiguān).
An Assistant (Chéng) and a Commandant (Wèi), one person each.
The Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
equivalent to 2000 *shí*.
Original annotation: No fixed number.
Responsible for attending the emperor,
advising on various matters,
consulting and responding.
When the imperial carriage (fǎjià) went out,
one knowledgeable person would participate as a co-driver,
the rest would ride on horseback behind the imperial carriage.
Originally there was a Palace Attendant Supervisor (Púyè) one person,
which in the restoration (Zhōngxīng) was changed to Libationer (Jìjiǔ),
sometimes appointed, sometimes not.
The Regular Palace Attendant (Zhōngchángshì),
Original annotation: Eunuchs,
no fixed number.
Later their rank was increased to be equivalent to 2000 *shí*.
Responsible for attending the emperor,
accompanying him into the inner palace,
advising on various internal matters,
consulting, responding, and serving.
The Yellow Gate Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng),
Original annotation: No fixed number.
Responsible for attending the emperor,
serving within the palace,
and communicating between the inner and outer courts.
When kings of various states had an audience in the main hall,
he would lead the kings to their seats.
The Minor Yellow Gate (Xiǎohuángmén),
[Original annotation]: Eunuchs,
no fixed number.
Responsible for attending the emperor,
receiving matters from the Secretariat (Shàngshū).
When the emperor was in the inner palace,
he would communicate between the inner and outer courts,
and handle various matters concerning the empress (Zhōnggōng) and below.
When princesses and royal consorts had illnesses or distress,
he would be sent to inquire.
The Director of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: Eunuch.
In charge of the eunuchs within the directorate.
An Assistant (Chéng) and a Follower Assistant (Cóngchéng), one person each.
Original annotation: Eunuchs.
The Follower Assistant is in charge of accompanying the emperor when entering and exiting.
The Directors of the Yellow Gate Office (Huángmén Shǔzhǎng), the Painting Chamber Office (Huàshì Shǔzhǎng), and the Jade Hall Office (Yùtáng Shǔzhǎng), one person each.
Directors of the Bǐng Office (Bǐngshǔzhǎng) seven people.
All 400 *shí*,
with a yellow ribbon.
Original annotation: Eunuchs.
Each in charge of a separate area within the inner palace.
The Yellow Gate Following Palace Attendant Supervisor (Zhōnghuángmén Núcóng Púyè) one person,
Original annotation: Eunuch.
In charge of the Yellow Gate Following Palace Attendants.
When at the palace, they would guard overnight,
and stand watch at the gates;
when accompanying the emperor outside, they would ride on horseback,
flanking the imperial carriage.
The Yellow Gate Palace Attendant (Zhōnghuángmén),
equivalent to 100 *shí*.
Original annotation: Eunuchs,
no fixed number.
Later increased to be equivalent to 300 *shí*.
Responsible for serving within the forbidden palace.
The Director of the Yètíng (Yètíng Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: Eunuch.
In charge of noble ladies and selected women in the rear palace.
The Left Assistant (Zuǒchéng), Right Assistant (Yòuchéng), and Violent Chamber Assistant (Bàoshì Chéng), one person each.
Original annotation: Eunuchs.
The Violent Chamber Assistant is in charge of women in the palace who are ill,
who are treated in this chamber;
if the empress or noble ladies commit crimes,
they are also held in this chamber.
The Director of the Eternal Alley (Yǒngxiàng Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: Eunuch.
In charge of palace maids for service.
An Assistant (Chéng) one person.
Original annotation: Eunuch.
The Director of the Imperial Wardrobe (Yùfǔ Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: Eunuch.
In charge of palace maids making internal clothes, mending, and washing them.
An Assistant (Chéng) and a Weaving Chamber Assistant (Zhīshì Chéng), one person each.
Original annotation: Eunuch.
The Director of Sacrifices (Císì Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: In charge of various small sacrifices within the palace.
An Assistant (Chéng) one person.
Original annotation: Eunuch.
The Director of the Hook Shield (Gōudùn Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: Eunuch.
In charge of various nearby pools, parks, and pleasure grounds.
An Assistant (Chéng) and an Eternal Peace Assistant (Yǒng'ān Chéng), one person each,
Original annotation: Eunuch.
Yǒng'ān
is the name of a small separate palace northeast of the North Palace (Běigōng),
with a garden view.
The Park Assistant (Yuànzhōng Chéng), Fruit Assistant (Guǒchéng), Hóngchí Assistant (Hóngchí Chéng), and South Park Assistant (Nányuán Chéng), one person each,
Original annotation: The Park Assistant is in charge of the detached palaces within the park.
The Fruit Assistant is in charge of the orchards.
Hóngchí
is the name of a pool,
twenty *lǐ* east of Luòyáng.
The South Park (Nányuán) is south of the Luò River.
The Supervisor of the Dragon Washing Pond (Zhuólóng Jiān)
and the Supervisor of Zhí Lǐ (Zhílǐ Jiān), one person each,
Original annotation: Zhuólóng is also a garden name,
near the North Palace (Běigōng).
Zhílǐ is also a garden name,
at the southwest corner of the city of Luòyáng.
The Director of the Inner Treasury (Zhōngcángfǔ Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: In charge of internal silks, gold, silver, and various goods.
An Assistant (Chéng) one person.
The Director of the Inner Service (Nèizhě Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: In charge of arranging various personal items in the palace.
The Left Assistant (Zuǒchéng) and Right Assistant (Yòuchéng), one person each.
The Director of the Imperial Workshops (Shàngfāng Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: In charge of the handcrafting of imperial swords and other fine artifacts.
An Assistant (Chéng) one person.
The Director of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng) one person,
Original annotation: Inherited from what the Qín (Qín) established.
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì) used eunuchs,
changing it to Director of the Central Secretariat and Palace Ushers (Zhōngshū Yèzhě Lìng).
Emperor Chéng (Chéngdì) used scholars,
restoring the original title.
In charge of all selections and appointments, as well as submitting documents and various matters to the bureaus of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Cáo).
The Palace Attendant Supervisor of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Púyè) one person,
Original annotation: In charge of matters of the Secretariat (Shàngshū).
If the Director (Lìng) is absent, he submits various matters.
Six Secretaries (Shàngshū),
Original annotation: Emperor Chéng (Chéngdì) first appointed four Secretaries (Shàngshū),
divided into four bureaus (cáo):
The Secretary of the Regular Palace Attendant Bureau (Chángshì Cáo Shàngshū) was in charge of matters concerning the high officials;
The Secretary of the Two Thousand *Shí* Bureau (Èrqiānshí Cáo Shàngshū) was in charge of matters concerning officials of 2000 *shí* in commanderies and states;
The Secretary of the People's Bureau (Mín Cáo Shàngshū) was in charge of memorials from all officials;
The Secretary of the Guest Bureau (Kè Cáo Shàngshū) was in charge of matters concerning foreign countries and barbarians.
Emperor Shìzǔ (Shìzǔ) followed this system.
Later, the Two Thousand *Shí* Bureau (Èrqiānshí Cáo) was divided,
and the Guest Bureau (Kè Cáo) was also divided into the Southern Chief Guest Bureau (Nán Zhǔkè Cáo) and Northern Chief Guest Bureau (Běi Zhǔkè Cáo),
making a total of six bureaus.
The Left Assistant (Zuǒchéng) and Right Assistant (Yòuchéng), one person each,
Original annotation: In charge of recording documents and deadlines.
The Left Assistant (Zuǒchéng) is in charge of memorials and reports from officials and commoners, as well as the attendants and clerks.
The Right Assistant (Yòuchéng) temporarily holds the seal and ribbon,
and is in charge of paper, brushes, ink, and various financial supplies and stores.
Original annotation: Each bureau (cáo) has six people,
in charge of drafting documents.
Original annotation: Each bureau (cáo) has three,
in charge of writing.
Later, three more were added to the busy bureaus,
making a total of twenty-one.
The Fújié Lìng (符節令) [Director of Tallies and Credentials] had one incumbent,
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: [He was] the head of the Fújié Tái (符節臺) [Bureau of Tallies and Credentials],
managing matters concerning tallies and credentials.
Whenever envoys were dispatched, he was in charge of issuing their credentials.
There were four Shàng Fúxǐ Lángzhōng (尚符璽郎中) [Gentlemen-in-Waiting for Tallies and Seals].
The original commentary states: Formerly there were two individuals within the court,
in charge of the imperial seals and half of the tiger tallies and bamboo tallies.
The Fújié Lìngshǐ (符節令史) [Clerk of the Tallies and Credentials Bureau]
had a salary of two hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: [He was] in charge of writing.
The Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞) [Imperial Censor-in-Chief] had one incumbent,
with a salary of one thousand shí (石).
The original commentary states: He was the aide to the Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫) [Grand Imperial Censor].
Formerly, a separate censor supervised the imperial censors within the palace,
secretly reporting illegal activities.
When the Yùshǐ Dàfū (御史大夫) was transferred to become Sīkōng (司空) [Minister of Works],
he remained separately within the court,
serving as the head of the Yùshǐ Tái (御史臺) [Censorate].
Later, he was again subordinated to the Shàofǔ (少府) [Privy Treasury].
There were two Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ (治書侍御史) [Censors for Managing Documents],
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: [They were] in charge of selecting those skilled in law for these positions.
For all difficult cases and doubtful matters in the empire,
they were in charge of determining right and wrong according to the law.
There were fifteen Shìyùshǐ (侍御史) [Attendant Censors],
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: [They were] in charge of observing and reporting illegal activities,
receiving memorials from the Gōngqīng (公卿) [Dukes and Ministers] and various officials,
and impeaching those who committed errors or transgressions.
Whenever there were sacrifices in the suburbs and ancestral temples, grand court assemblies, or grand enfeoffments and appointments,
two or one person would supervise the ceremonies and deportment.
If there were errors or transgressions, they would impeach and memorialize.
The Lántái Lìngshǐ (蘭臺令史) [Clerk of the Orchid Terrace]
had a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: [He was] in charge of memorials and stamping official documents.
The above were subordinated to the Shàofǔ (少府).
The original commentary states: The officials whose duties fell under the Shàofǔ (少府)
were, starting from Tàiyī (太醫) [Imperial Physician] and Shànglín (上林) [Imperial Park], a total of four offices.
From the Shìzhōng (侍中) [Palace Attendant] to the Yùshǐ (御史) [Imperial Censor],
all were formally subordinate to it.
Following the Qín (秦) dynasty,
all taxes from mountains, marshes, dikes, and ponds
were called Jìnqián (禁錢) [Prohibited Funds]
and belonged to the Shàofǔ (少府).
Shìzǔ (世祖) changed this to be subordinate to the Sīnóng (司農) [Minister of Agriculture].
Kǎogōng (考工) [Director of Works] was transferred to the Tàipú (太僕) [Grand Coachman].
Dūshuǐ (都水) [Director of Waterways] was subordinated to the prefectures and commanderies.
In the early reign of Xiàowǔ Dì (孝武帝), the Shuǐhéng Dūwèi (水衡都尉) [Commander of Water and Balance] was first established,
with a rank equivalent to two thousand shí (石).
He was separately in charge of the Shànglín Yuàn (上林苑) [Upper Forest Park] and its detached palaces for imperial rest.
Shìzǔ (世祖) abolished this position,
and its duties were combined with the Shàofǔ (少府).
On the day of the Lìqiū Chúliú (立秋貙劉) [Autumnal Equinox sacrificial hunt],
the Shuǐhéng Dūwèi (水衡都尉) was temporarily re-established,
and abolished once the event was concluded.
The Shàofǔ (少府) originally had six Chéng (丞) [Aides],
five of which were abolished.
Also abolished were the Tāngguān (湯官) [Director of Baths] and Zhīshì (織室) Lìng (令) [Director of the Weaving Office],
and Chéng (丞) [Aides] were appointed instead.
Furthermore, the Shànglín Shíchí Jiān (上林十池監) [Supervisors of Ten Ponds in the Upper Forest],
Pāorén Zhǎng Chéng (胞人長丞) [Chief Aide of the Kitchen Staff],
Huànzhě (宦者) [Eunuchs], Kūntái (昆臺) [Kun Terrace],
and Cìfēi (佽飛) [Swift Flight]
three Lìng (令) [Directors],
and twenty-one Chéng (丞) [Aides] were abolished.
Also abolished were over twenty Lìng (令), Zhǎng (長), Chéng (丞), and Wèi (尉) [Directors, Chiefs, Aides, and Commanders] of the Shuǐhéng (水衡) subordinate offices.
From Zhānghé (章和) onwards,
the number of court officials gradually increased,

adding the Chángyào (嘗藥) [Director of Medicinal Tasters], Tàiguān (太官) [Grand Provisioner], Yùzhě (御者) [Director of Imperial Chariots], Gōudùn (鉤盾) [Director of Shield Hooks], Shàngfāng (尚方) [Director of Imperial Manufactories], Kǎogōng (考工) [Director of Works], and Biézuò Jiān (別作監) [Supervisor of Separate Workshops],
all with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
Eunuchs held these positions,
serving as acting deputies.
Some were abolished,
hence only the original offices are recorded.
One Hundred Officials: Four Zhíjīnwú (執金吾), Tàizǐ Tàifù (太子太傅), Dàchángqiū (大長秋), Tàizǐ Shàofù (太子少傅), Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng (將作大匠), Chéngmén Xiàowèi (城門校尉), Běijūn Zhōnghòu (北軍中候), Sīlì Xiàowèi (司隸校尉).
The Zhíjīnwú (執金吾) [Bearers of the Gilded Mace] had one incumbent,
with a salary equivalent to two thousand shí (石).
The original commentary states: [He was] in charge of patrolling outside the palace to guard against unusual events like fires or floods.
Three times a month, he would patrol outside the palace,
and also manage weapons.
Wú (吾) is like Yù (禦) [to guard/protect].
There was one Chéng (丞) [Aide],
with a salary equivalent to one thousand shí (石).
There were two hundred Tíqí (緹騎) [Red-Clad Cavalry].
The original commentary states: They had no official rank,
but received provisions like officials.
The Wǔkù Lìng (武庫令) [Director of the Imperial Armory] had one incumbent,
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: [He was] in charge of weapons.
There was one Chéng (丞) [Aide].
The above were subordinated to the Zhíjīnwú (執金吾).

The original commentary states: Originally there were three officials: Shìdào (式道), Zuǒ Zhōnghòu (左中候), and Yòu Zhōnghòu (右中候) [Director of Clearance, Left Central Commander, and Right Central Commander],
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
When the imperial carriage went out,
they were in charge of clearing the path ahead.
Upon return, they held banners until the palace gate,
and only then would the palace gate open.
During the restoration (Eastern Hàn), there was only one person,
and this position was not always established.
Whenever the emperor went out,
a Láng (郎) [Gentleman] would temporarily serve as Shìdào Hòu (式道候) [Commander for Clearance].
Once the matter was concluded,
he was no longer subordinate to the Zhíjīnwú (執金吾).

Also abolished were the Zhōnglěi (中壘) [Commander of the Central Ramparts], Sìhù (寺互) [Director of Temples and Gates], Dūchuán (都船) Lìng (令) [Director of Boats], Chéng (丞) [Aides], Wèi (尉) [Commanders], and the Zuǒyòu Jīngfǔ Dūwèi (左右京輔都尉) [Left and Right Commanders for the Capital and Auxiliary Districts].
The Tàizǐ Tàifù (太子太傅) [Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince] had one incumbent,
with a salary equivalent to two thousand shí (石).
The original commentary states: His duty was to assist and guide the Crown Prince.
His status was like that of a teacher,
and he did not command subordinate officials.
The Tàichángqiū (太長秋) [Grand Chief Steward] had one incumbent,
with a salary of two thousand shí (石).
The original commentary states: Following the Qín (秦) system, he was the Jiàngxíng (將行) [Chief of Attendants],
a eunuch.
Jǐng Dì (景帝) changed this to Dàchángqiū (大長秋),
sometimes filled by literati.
During the restoration (Eastern Hàn), eunuchs were commonly used.
His duty was to convey the orders of the Central Palace (Empress).
He managed all gifts and provisions for imperial relatives,
and facilitated visits for imperial relatives who wished to see the Empress.
When the Empress left the palace, he would accompany her.
There was one Chéng (丞) [Aide],
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: A eunuch.
The Zhōnggōng Pú (中宮僕) [Attendant for the Central Palace] had one incumbent,
with a salary of one thousand shí (石).
The original commentary states: A eunuch.
In charge of driving the imperial carriage.
The original commentary states: The Tàipú (太僕) [Grand Coachman]
had a rank of two thousand shí (石).
During the restoration (Eastern Hàn), the character
"Tài" (太) was removed,
and the rank was reduced by one thousand shí (石),
making him subordinate to the Chángqiū (長秋).
The Zhōnggōng Yèzhě Lìng (中宮謁者令) [Director of Palace Ushers for the Central Palace] had one incumbent,
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: A eunuch.
There were three Zhōnggōng Yèzhě (中宮謁者) [Palace Ushers for the Central Palace],
with a salary of four hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: Eunuchs.
In charge of reporting within the palace.
There were five Zhōnggōng Shàngshū (中宮尚書) [Secretaries for the Central Palace],
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: Eunuchs.
In charge of internal palace documents.
The Zhōnggōng Sīfǔ Lìng (中宮私府令) [Director of the Private Treasury for the Central Palace] had one incumbent,
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: A eunuch.
In charge of storing currency, silks, and various items within the palace,
and overseeing the tailoring, mending, and washing of clothes and quilts.
There was one Chéng (丞) [Aide].
The original commentary states: A eunuch.
The Zhōnggōng Yǒngxiàng Lìng (中宮永巷令) [Director of the Inner Lane for the Central Palace] had one incumbent,
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: A eunuch.
In charge of palace women.
There was one Chéng (丞) [Aide].
The original commentary states: A eunuch.
The Zhōnggōng Huángmén Nùcóng Púyè (中宮黃門ヌ從僕射) [Chief of Yellow Gate Attendants for the Central Palace] had one incumbent,
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: A eunuch.
In charge of the palace's yellow gate attendants.
The Zhōnggōng Shǔ Lìng (中宮署令) [Director of the Palace Office for the Central Palace] had one incumbent,
with a salary of six hundred shí (石).
The original commentary states: A eunuch.
In charge of keeping the official records for the Son of Heaven within the palace.
There were six Nǚqí (女騎) [Female Riders],
and one Chéng (丞) [Aide] and one Fùdào Chéng (復道丞) [Aide for Covered Walkways] each.
The original commentary states: Eunuchs.
The Fùdào Chéng (復道丞) was in charge of the inner elevated walkways.
One Chief of Medicines of the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng yàozhǎng),
salary of four hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: a eunuch.
These belong to the Grand Chief of the Autumn Palace (Dà Chángqiū).
Original commentary says: Following the Qín [dynasty],
there was one Chamberlain for the Empress (Zhānshì),
whose position was above the Chief of the Autumn Palace (Chángqiū),
also a eunuch,
in charge of all the offices within the palace.
Emperor Chéng abolished this office,
transferring its duties to the Chief of the Autumn Palace (Chángqiū).
After this, when the Empress was to make a formal procession (fǎjià chū),
the eunuch officials (Zhōngyè, Zhōnghuànzhě zhí lì) would temporarily assume the duties of the Chamberlain for the Empress (Zhānshì) to serve as escorts (fèngyǐn),
until the procession concluded.
After the eunuchs were punished,
the Minister of the Palace (Shàngshū) would select one official with concurrent duties to serve as escort.
For the Chángxìn and Chánglè palaces,
one Palace Intendant (Shǎofǔ) was established,
with duties similar to the Chief of the Autumn Palace (Chángqiū),
and all other officials were named after the palace,
with their numbers and ranks similar to those in the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng).
Original commentary says: The emperor's grandmother was called the Chángxìn Palace,
hence there was a Chángxìn Palace Intendant (Chángxìn Shǎofǔ)
and a Chánglè Palace Intendant (Chánglè Shǎofǔ),
whose positions were above the Chief of the Autumn Palace (Chángqiū),
and whose officials were all eunuchs,
with ranks similar to those in the Central Palace (Zhōnggōng).
The Chánglè Palace also had a Commandant of the Guard (Wèiwèi)
and a Grand Coachman (Pú wéi Tàipú),
both with a salary of two thousand *dàn* of grain,
above the Palace Intendant (Shǎofǔ).
These were abolished upon the death of the empress dowager and
not permanently established.
One Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàofù),
salary of two thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: Also responsible for assisting and guiding,
entirely overseeing the Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) subordinate officials.
One Director of the Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Affairs (Tàizǐ Shuàigēnglìng),
salary of one thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of the regular duties of the Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) officials (shùzǐ, shèrén),
duties similar to the Palace Intendant (Guānglù).
Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Officials (Tàizǐ Shùzǐ),
salary of four hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: No fixed number,
like the Gentlemen of the Three Bureaus (sānshǔ zhōngláng).
Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Attendants (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
salary of two hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: No fixed number,
on regular duty for night guard,
like the Gentlemen of the Three Bureaus (sānshǔ lángzhōng).
One Chief Administrator of the Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Household (Tàizǐ Jiālìng),
salary of one thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of granaries and provisions,
duties similar to the Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng) and Palace Intendant (Shǎofǔ).
One Director of the Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Granary (Tàizǐ Cānglìng),
salary of six hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of granaries.
One Director of the Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Provisions (Tàizǐ Shíguānlìng),
salary of six hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of provisions.
One Grand Coachman of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Pú),
salary of one thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of chariots and horses,
duties similar to the Grand Coachman (Tàipú).
One Chief of the Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Stables (Tàizǐ Jiùzhǎng),
salary of four hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of chariots and horses.
Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Gate Grandee (Tàizǐ Méndàfū),
salary of six hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: Old commentary says duties similar to a Commandant (Lángjiàng).
Formerly there were Left and Right Household Generals (Zuǒyòu Hùjiàng),
separately in charge of the Left and Right Household Gentlemen (Zuǒyòu Hùzhíláng),
but these were abolished since the Jiànwǔ era.
Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Central Retainers (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ),
salary of six hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: Five members,
duties similar to a Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Equerry (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ),
comparable to six hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: Old commentary says sixteen members,
duties similar to an Usher (Yèzhě).
When the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ) goes out,
those on duty serve as escorts and uphold the decorum in front.
One Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Central Shield Bearer (Tàizǐ Zhōngdùn),
salary of four hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of palace guards and patrols.
One Heir Apparent's (Tàizǐ) Chief of Guards (Tàizǐ Wèishutài),
salary of four hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of gate guards.
These belong to the Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shàofù).
Original commentary says: Generally, when the emperor first ascends the throne
and has no Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ),
all subordinate officials are dismissed,
except for the Attendants (Shèrén) who are not dismissed,
but placed under the Palace Intendant (Shǎofǔ).
One Grand Master of Works (Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng),
salary of two thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: Following the Qín [dynasty],
called Chief of Works (Jiàngzuò Shǎofǔ),
Emperor Jǐng changed it to Grand Master of Works (Jiàngzuò Dàjiàng).
Responsible for the construction and repair of ancestral temples, imperial sleeping quarters (lùqǐn), palaces, and imperial tombs,
and also planting paulownia and catalpa trees along the roadside.
One Assistant (Chéng),
salary of six hundred *dàn* of grain.
One Director of the Left Workshop (Zuǒxiàolìng),
salary of six hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of left artisans.
One Assistant (Chéng).
One Director of the Right Workshop (Yòuxiàolìng),
salary of six hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of right artisans.
One Assistant (Chéng).
One Commandant of the City Gates (Chéngmén Xiàowèi),
comparable to two thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of the twelve city gates of Luòyáng.
One Army Commander (Sīmǎ),
salary of one thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of soldiers.
One Gate Guard (Ménhòu) for each city gate,
salary of six hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: The twelve gates of Luòyáng city are:
the one due south is called Píngchéngmén Gate,
the North Palace Gate (Běigōngmén),
which belongs to the Commandant of the Guard (Wèiwèi).
The others are: Upper West Gate (Shàngxīmén),
Yōngmén Gate,
Guǎngyángmén Gate,
Jīnmén Gate,
Xiǎoyuànmén Gate,
Kāiyángmén Gate,
Hāomén Gate,
Central East Gate (Zhōngdōngmén),
Upper East Gate (Shàngdōngmén),
Gǔmén Gate,
Xiàmén Gate,
these are all twelve gates.
One Central Aide of the Northern Army (Běijūn Zhōnghòu),
salary of six hundred *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of supervising the Five Battalions (wǔyíng).
One Commandant of Garrison Cavalry (Túnqí Xiàowèi),
comparable to two thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of palace guard soldiers.
One Army Commander (Sīmǎ),
salary of one thousand *dàn* of grain.
One Commandant of Valiant Cavalry (Yuèqí Xiàowèi),
comparable to two thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of palace guard soldiers.
One Army Commander (Sīmǎ),
salary of one thousand *dàn* of grain.
One Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi),
comparable to two thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of palace guard soldiers.
One Army Commander (Sīmǎ),
salary of one thousand *dàn* of grain.
One Commandant of Chángshuǐ (Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi),
comparable to two thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of palace guard soldiers.
One Army Commander (Sīmǎ) and one Commander of Barbarian Cavalry (Húqí Sīmǎ) each,
salary of one thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of palace guards,
specifically the Wūhuán cavalry.
One Commandant of Archers (Shèshēng Xiàowèi),
comparable to two thousand *dàn* of grain.
Original commentary says: In charge of palace guard soldiers.
One Army Commander (Sīmǎ),
salary of one thousand *dàn* of grain.
The Grand Minister of Justice (Sīlì Xiàowèi) is one person,
ranked at two thousand dàn of grain.
The original commentary states: Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武帝) first established this office,
holding a jǐe (節) [an imperial credential],
responsible for investigating and impeaching all officials below a certain rank,
as well as those in the capital and nearby commanderies who violated the law.
Emperor Yuán (元帝) removed the jǐe,
Emperor Chéng (成帝) abolished the office,
but it was re-established during the Jiànwǔ (建武) period,
also governing one province (zhōu).
There are twelve Assistants (Cóngshì Shǐ).
The original commentary states: The Commissioner for Capital Affairs (Dūguān Cóngshì)
is mainly responsible for investigating and impeaching officials who violate the law.
The Commissioner for Merits (Gōngcáo Cóngshì)
is mainly responsible for provincial selections, appointments, and various general affairs.
The Commissioner Accompanying the Chariot (Biéjià Cóngshì)
serves as an escort when the Grand Minister of Justice (Xiàowèi) makes an inspection tour,
and records various affairs.
The Commissioner for Records (Bùcáo Cóngshì)
is mainly responsible for financial and grain records.
If there are military matters,
then a Commissioner for Military Affairs (Bīngcáo Cóngshì) is appointed,
mainly responsible for military affairs.
The remaining Commissioners for Departmental Commanderies and Kingdoms (Bù Jùnguó Cóngshì),
one for each commandery and kingdom,
are mainly responsible for overseeing documents,
and investigating illegal activities.
All are appointed and dismissed by the province itself,
hence they are collectively referred to as being of one hundred dàn.
There are twenty-five Acting Assistants (Jiǎzuǒ).
The original commentary states: The Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) records affairs below the imperial palace gates [i.e., general administrative matters],
and reviews documents.
The Gate Superintendent (Méntíngzhǎng) is in charge of provincial administration.
The Clerk to the Commissioner for Merits (Mén Gōngcáo Shūzuǒ) is in charge of selections and appointments.
The Master of the Classic of Filial Piety (Xiàojīng Shī) is in charge of supervising examinations on the classics.
The Master of the Monthly Ordinances (Yuèlìng Shī) is in charge of seasonal festivals and sacrifices.
The Master of Laws and Ordinances (Lǜlìng Shī) is in charge of legal administration.
The Clerk to the Commissioner for Records (Bùcáo Shūzuǒ) is in charge of records.
The remaining Clerks for Capital Affairs (Dūguān Shūzuǒ) and for each commandery and kingdom,
each have one Clerk in Charge of the Commandery (Diǎnjùn Shūzuǒ),
each primarily responsible for the documents of one commandery.
They are appointed from among commandery officials,
and replaced annually.
The Grand Minister of Justice (Sīlì) governs seven commanderies.
The Metropolitan Prefect of Hénán (Hénán Yǐn) is one person,
in charge of the capital,
and specially invited to court.
The Metropolitan Prefect of Jīngzhào (Jīngzhào Yǐn), the Prefect of Zuǒ Fēngyì (Zuǒ Fēngyì), and the Prefect of Yòu Fúfēng (Yòu Fúfēng) are three persons.
When the Hàn (漢) dynasty initially had its capital at Cháng'ān (長安),
all were ranked at an intermediate two thousand dàn,
and called the Sānfǔ (三輔) [Three Auxiliaries].
During the revival, the capital was moved to Luòyáng (洛陽),
and the commandery of Hénán (Hénán Jùn) was made an independent prefecture (yǐn).
As the Sānfǔ (三輔) was where the imperial mausoleums and temples were located,
their titles were not changed,
only their rank was reduced.
The remaining three commanderies are Hóngnóng (Hóngnóng), Hénèi (Hénèi), and Hédōng (Hédōng).
The establishment of the Prefect (yǐn),
the Administrator (Fēngyì), the Commander (Fúfēng), and the Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) and Aide (Chéng) at their original posts
is detailed in the "Treatise on Geography."
Collation Note, page 3605, line 6, "No rank or stipend for officials." Note:
"吏" (lì) [official]
was originally a mistake for
"史" (shǐ) [scribe],
directly corrected based on the Jí (汲) and Diàn (殿) editions.

Page 3606, line 1, "[Holders of Halberds (Chí Jǐ)] five hundred twenty people." Supplemented based on the citation from Yīng Shào's (應劭) Hàn Guān Yí (漢官儀) in the "Department of Official Establishment" (Shè Guān Bù) of Běitáng Shūchāo (北堂書鈔).
Note: Five hundred (wǔbǎi) is equivalent to five hundred (wǔbǎi).
The "Collected Explanations" (Jíjiě) cites Lǐ Zǔmáo's (李祖楙) explanation,
stating that Gǔ Jīn Zhù (古今注) says five hundred (wǔbǎi) refers to "the head of a wu (伍) [group of five]."
"Five men are called a wu (伍),
the head of five is called a bó (伯),
also called a hùbó (戶伯) [householder's elder]."
It is also noted that the commentary to the "Biography of Eunuchs" (Huànzhě Zhuàn Zhù) cites Wéi Zhāo's (韋昭) Biàn Shì Míng (辨釋名),
saying the meaning of five hundred (wǔbǎi) differs from Gǔ Jīn Zhù (古今注).
Page 3608, line 9, "Staff of twelve officials." Note: In the Jí (汲) and Diàn (殿) editions,
"十二" (shí'èr) [twelve]
is written as
"十三" (shísān) [thirteen],
which is the same in Sūn Jí Hàn Guān (孫輯漢官).

Page 3608, line 10, "The Superintendent of the Crown Prince's Household (Tàizǐ Shuàigēng Lìng) whose duties resemble those of the Minister of the Imperial Household (Guānglù)." Note: The Imperial Readings of the Taiping Era (Yùlǎn) Volume 247 cites it as
"The Superintendent of the Crown Prince's Household (Shuàigēng Lìng) ranks at one thousand dàn,
takes turns with the Royal Tutor (Shùzǐ) and Gentleman-in-Waiting (Shèrén),
his duties resemble those of the Minister of the Imperial Household (Guānglùxūn),
he is in charge of the prohibitions at the palace gates,
and the garrison guards (Lángjiàng) and soldiers (Túnwèi Zhī Shì)."
The collation note states that the text used by Yùlǎn (御覽) here is different.
Tōngdiǎn (通典) also writes
"similar to the Minister of the Imperial Household (Guānglùxūn),"
adding the character
"勳" (xūn).
Page 3609, line 9, "Crown Prince's Groom (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ)." Note: Jíjiě (集解) cites Lǐ Zǔmáo's (李祖楙) explanation,
stating that in Qián Shū (前書)
"洗" (xǐ) [wash]
is written as
"先" (xiān) [foremost].
Page 3609, line 9, "When the Crown Prince goes out, the one on duty leads the ceremonial procession." Note: In Yùlǎn (御覽) Volume 246,
"者" (zhě) [one]
is written as
"一人" (yīrén) [one person]
two characters.
Page 3610, line 4, "Plant chestnut, lacquer, catalpa, paulownia." Note: The Jí (汲) and Diàn (殿) editions read
"Plant chestnut, elm, paulownia, catalpa."
Page 3610, line 5, "Ling (機) [machine] (璣) [celestial sphere]." Corrected based on the Jí (汲) and Diàn (殿) editions.
Page 3610, line 5, "Today (民) [people] (人) [person] say wútóng is correct." Zhāng Sēnkǎi's (張森楷) collation note states that
"民" (mín) [people]
should be
"人" (rén) [person],
suspecting it to be a later alteration of the Táng (唐) edition which resulted in an error,
as evidenced by the continued use of
"今人" (jīnrén) [modern people] in the following text.
Note: Zhāng's (張) explanation is correct,
and is now used for correction.
Page 3610, line 11, "(右) [right] (石) [stone] storehouse." Corrected based on Qián Zhì (前志).
Page 3611, line 1, "Hàomén (秏門) Gate." Note: Yùlǎn (御覽) 183 cites Lǐ Yóu's (李尤) Máochéngmén Míng (旄城門銘) as
"Máomén (旄門) Gate."
Shěn Jiābén (沈家本) states that the gate should not be named Hàomén (秏),
and Máomén (旄) is correct.
Page 3611, line 6, "Therefore it is carved in red (丹) (漆) [lacquer]." Supplemented based on Huì Dòng's (惠棟) explanation cited in Jíjiě (集解).
Page 3611, line 9, "Position for the last month of the season (Jìyuè Wèi)." Note:
"未" (wèi) [not yet/branch symbol]
was originally an error for
"木" (mù) [wood],
directly corrected.
Page 3611, line 12, "Hàomén (秏門) Gate faces the last month of the season (Jìyuè), position in Chén (辰)." Note: Yùlǎn (御覽) 183 cites it as
"Máomén (旄門) Gate faces the last month of the season (Jìyuè), its position is in Chén (辰)."
Page 3611, line 13, "Central East is at the middle month of the season (Zhòngyuè), position is Mǎo (卯)." Note: Yùlǎn (御覽) cites it as
"East is at the middle month of the season (Zhòngyuè), its position is Mǎo (卯)."
Page 3612, line 8, "Blue Turban (Qīngjīn) (右) [right] (左) [left] Commander (Xiàowèi)." Jíjiě (集解) cites Huì Dòng's (惠棟) explanation,
stating that
"右" (yòu) [right]
should be
"左" (zuǒ) [left].
The Blue Turban Left Commander (Qīngjīn Zuǒ Xiàowèi) was established in the ninth year of Jiànwǔ (建武),
and changed in the fifteenth year.
Now corrected accordingly.
Page 3613, line 1, "The stables are near Chángshuǐ (長水) (胡) [beard] (故) [old] hence it is named." Corrected based on the Jí (汲) and Diàn (殿) editions.
Page 3613, line 1, "Chángshuǐ (長水) is probably the name of a small stream within Guānzhōng (關中) (蓋) [cover] (關) [pass]." Jíjiě (集解) cites Huì Dòng's (惠棟) explanation,
stating that Shěn Yuē (沈約) cites Biàn Shì Míng (辨釋名) as "is probably the name of a small stream within Guānzhōng (關中)."
Wáng Xiānqiān (王先謙) states that Wéi's (韋) commentary
"中" (zhōng) [middle]
is missing the character
"關" (guān) [pass] above it.
Now supplemented accordingly.

All officials, five provinces and commanderies, counties and townships, postal stations and villages, the Commissioner for the Southern Xiongnu (Xiōngnú Zhōngláng Jiàng), the Commissioner for the Wūhuán (Wūhuán Xiàowèi), the Commissioner for the Qiāng (Hù Qiāng Xiàowèi), kingdoms (Wángguó) like Sòng (Sòng) and Wèi (Wèi), Marquises (Lièhóu), Marquises of the Imperial Domain (Guānnèi Hóu), and four barbarian states.
All officials received stipends from
the twelve outer provinces,
each province (zhōu) having one Inspector (Cìshǐ),
ranked at six hundred dàn.
The original commentary states: Qín (秦) had Censor-Inspectors (Jiān Yùshǐ)
who supervised various commanderies.
When Hàn (漢) arose, this was abolished,
and only clerks of the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng Shǐ) were dispatched to inspect various provinces,
without a permanent office.
Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武帝) first established thirteen Inspectors (Cìshǐ),
ranked at six hundred dàn.
Emperor Chéng (成帝) changed them to Governors (Mù),
ranked at two thousand dàn.
In the eighteenth year of Jiànwǔ (建wǔ),
they were again made Inspectors (Cìshǐ),
twelve persons, each governing one province,
with one province belonging to the Grand Minister of Justice (Sīlì Xiàowèi).
The Inspectors (Cìshǐ) of all provinces regularly toured their subordinate commanderies and kingdoms in the eighth month,
recorded prisoners,
and evaluated performance.
Initially, at the end of each year, they would proceed to the capital to report on affairs;
during the revival, they merely relied on the accounting officials (jìlì).
All had Assistants (Cóngshì Shǐ) and Acting Assistants (Jiǎzuǒ).
The original commentary states: Their duties were generally similar to those of the Grand Minister of Justice (Sīlì),
without a Commissioner for Capital Affairs (Dūguān Cóngshì),
and their Commissioner for Merits (Gōngcáo Cóngshì) was called Commissioner for General Administration (Zhìzhōng Cóngshì).
Yùzhōu (豫州) province governed six commanderies and kingdoms,
Jìzhōu (冀州) province nine,
Yǎnzhōu (兗州) province eight,
Xúzhōu (徐州) province five,
Qīngzhōu (青州) province six,
Jīngzhōu (荊州) province seven,
Yángzhōu (揚州) province six,
Yìzhōu (益州) province twelve,
Liángzhōu (涼州) province twelve,
Bìngzhōu (并州) province nine,
Yōuzhōu (幽州) province eleven,
Jiāozhōu (交州) province seven,
totaling ninety-eight.
Among these, twenty-seven were Chancellors for Kingdoms (Wángguó Xiàng),
and seventy-one were Grand Administrators for Commanderies (Jùn Tàishǒu).
There were also Commandants of Dependent States (Shǔguó Dūwèi).
Dependent states (Shǔguó) were established by partitioning distant counties from commanderies,
similar to a slightly smaller commandery,
and named after their original commandery.
Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) consolidated and abolished over four hundred commanderies and counties;
later generations gradually increased them again.
All commanderies supervised by a zhōu are designated as the imperial capital (Jīngdū).
One Yǐn is appointed,
with a salary of two thousand dàn of grain,
and one chéng.
For each commandery (jùn), one tàishǒu is appointed,
with a salary of two thousand dàn of grain,
and one chéng.
For commanderies situated on the border as garrisons,
the chéng serves as a zhǎngshǐ.
The xiàng of a kingdom (wángguó) is also like this.
For each dependent state (shǔguó), one dūwèi is appointed,
ranking equivalent to two thousand dàn,
and one chéng.
The original commentary states: All commanderies and kingdoms are responsible for governing the people,
promoting the worthy and encouraging merit,
and settling disputes and investigating wrongdoing.
They regularly travel to the counties under their jurisdiction in spring,
encouraging the people in agriculture and sericulture,
and providing relief to the destitute.
In autumn and winter, they dispatch harm-free officials to investigate prisoners,
to make their judgments and laws equitable,
and to assess and grade their performance.
At the end of the year, they send officials to present their annual reports.
They also recommend xiàolián,
one person for every two hundred thousand households in a commandery.
[One wěi]
was in charge of military prohibitions,
and guarding against bandits.
During Jǐngdì’s reign, the name was changed to dūwèi.
Wǔdì further established one dūwèi for each of the Sānfǔ,
to inspect ingress and egress.
Border commanderies established agricultural dūwèi,
who were in charge of garrison farms and grain cultivation.
They also established shǔguó dūwèi,
who were in charge of surrendered barbarians (mányí).
In the Zhongxing period, in the sixth year of Jiànwǔ,
all commandery dūwèi were abolished,
and their duties were merged with those of the tàishǒu,
eliminating the need for the dūshì duty.
The pass dūwèi were abolished.
Only border commanderies sometimes had dūwèi and shǔguó dūwèi,
who gradually had some counties divided under them,
governing the people like a commandery.
As Āndì found that the Qiāng had violated the law,
and the Sānfǔ had guards for the imperial mausoleums,
he re-established the Yòufúfēng dūwèi
and the Jīngzhào Hǔyá dūwèi.
All of them established various caó yuánshǐ.
The original commentary states: The various caó were generally like the caó of the ducal administrations,
without the Dōngcáo and Xīcáo.
There was a gōngcáoshǐ,
in charge of selecting and assigning meritorious service.
There was a wǔguānyuán,
who managed the gōngcáo and other caó affairs.
For supervising dependent counties,
there were five bùdūyóu
and one cáoyuán.
At the main gate, there was one tíngzhǎng.
The zhǔjìshìshǐ
was in charge of recording documents
and urging timely meetings.
There was no lìshǐ.
Under the palace gate (gěxià) and in all caó, there were shūzuǒ,
who were responsible for managing documents.
Subordinate officials:
For each county (xiàn), city (yì), and circuit (dào),
the larger ones appointed one lìng,
with a salary of one thousand dàn;
the next in size appointed a zhǎng,
with a salary of four hundred dàn;
the smaller ones appointed a zhǎng,
with a salary of three hundred dàn;
the xiàng of a marquisate (hóuguó)
had the same salary rank.
The original commentary states: All are responsible for governing the people,
manifesting goodness and encouraging righteousness,
prohibiting wrongdoing and punishing evil,
settling disputes and suppressing brigandage,
caring for the people's seasonal affairs,
and collecting assessments in autumn and winter,
and submitting annual reports to their respective commanderies and kingdoms.
Any county (xiàn) that primarily governs barbarians (mányí) is called a dào.
The revenue-producing estates (tāngmù) granted to princesses are called (guó) [yì].
A county with over ten thousand households is designated a lìng;
those with fewer are designated a zhǎng.
Marquisates are designated a xiàng.
These are all Qín system regulations.
Each has one chéng.
Larger counties have two wěi,
smaller counties have one.
The original commentary states: The chéng manages documents
and oversees granaries and prisons.
The wěi is in charge of bandits.
Whenever a banditry occurs
and the main culprits are not immediately identified,
they must investigate and search,
and examine the treacherous and lawless,
to uncover the clues.
Each appoints various caó yuánshǐ.
The original commentary states: The various caó are generally like the commandery officials;
the wǔguān serve as tíngyuán,
supervising the five bù in the xiāng.
In spring and summer, they serve as quànnóngyuán;
in autumn and winter, they serve as zhìdùyuán.
Xiāng established yǒuzhì, sānlǎo, and yóujiǎo.
The original commentary states: The yǒuzhì
are appointed by the commandery,
with a salary of one hundred dàn,
and are in charge of the people of one xiāng;
for smaller xiāng,
the county appoints one sèfū.
All are responsible for knowing the good and bad deeds of the people,
the order of corvée labor,
the wealth and poverty of the people,
and the amount of taxes to be levied,
to ensure fair grading.
The sānlǎo are in charge of moral education.
Whenever there are filial sons and obedient grandsons,
chaste women and righteous wives,
those who forgo wealth to save from calamity,
and scholars who serve as models for the people,
their gates are all marked with plaques
to promote good conduct.
The yóujiǎo are in charge of patrolling,
and suppressing and investigating wrongdoing and banditry.
There are also xiāngzuǒ,
subordinate to the xiāng,
in charge of the people and collecting taxes.
Tíng have a tíngzhǎng,
to suppress bandits.
The original commentary states: The tíngzhǎng
is in charge of seeking and apprehending bandits,
and takes orders from the dūwèi.
Lǐ have a lǐkuí;
the people are organized into shíwǔ,
reporting good and bad deeds.
The original commentary states: The lǐkuí manages one lǐ of one hundred households.
Shí manage ten households,
wǔ manage five households,
to supervise each other.
When people have good or bad deeds,
they report them to the supervising official.
Border counties have zhàngsàiwèi.
The original commentary states: They are in charge of prohibiting and guarding against Qiāng and Yí from violating the border passes.
For commanderies that have salt officials (yánguān), iron officials (tiěguān), craft officials (gōngguān), or water conservancy officials (dūshuǐguān),
lìng, zhǎng, and chéng are appointed according to the scale of the matter,
their ranks are all the same as those of counties and dào,
without separate staff,
they are given equally to the existing officials.
The original commentary states: All commanderies and counties that produce a lot of salt establish yánguān,
in charge of salt taxes.
Those that produce a lot of iron establish tiěguān,
in charge of smelting and casting.
Those with many craftsmen establish gōngguān,
in charge of craft taxes and goods.
Those with many ponds and fishing benefits establish shuǐguān,
in charge of water regulation and collecting fishing taxes.
The officials of the various counties in the locality are uniformly assigned to these positions,
officials are appointed according to the specific tasks,
not necessarily having the full complement of county officials.
One shǐxiōngnúzhōnglángjiàng is appointed,
ranking equivalent to two thousand dàn.
The original commentary states: In charge of guarding the Southern Chányú.
Two cóngshì are appointed,
with additional ones appointed as needed for specific matters,
and yuán are appointed as needed.
The same applies to the appointments of hùqiāng and wūhuánxiàowèi.
One hùwūhuánxiàowèi is appointed,
ranking equivalent to two thousand dàn.
The original commentary states: In charge of the Wūhuán Hu.
One hùqiāngxiàowèi is appointed,
ranking equivalent to two thousand dàn.
The original commentary states: In charge of the Western Qiāng.
When imperial sons are enfeoffed as kings,
their commanderies become kingdoms (guó),
each appointing one fù
and one xiàng,
both with a salary of two thousand dàn.
The original commentary states: The fù is in charge of guiding the king towards goodness,
and is treated with the禮 (lǐ) of a teacher,
not as a subordinate.
The xiàng is like a tàishǒu.
There is a zhǎngshǐ,
like a commandery chéng.
In the early Hán dynasty, kings were established,
following the system of kings established by Xiàng Yǔ.
Their territories were vast,
some extending for a thousand *lǐ*.
Furthermore, their official titles were: *Fù* was *Tàifù*,
*Xiāng* was *Chéngxiàng*.
There were also *Yùshǐ Dàfū* and various *Qīng*,
all ranked at two thousand *shí*.
All their official positions were like those of the imperial court.
The imperial court only appointed the *Chéngxiàng* for them;
their *Yùshǐ Dàfū* and below were all appointed by themselves.
By the time of Emperor Jǐng,
the seven states of Wú and Chǔ, relying on the size of their states,
then rebelled,
almost imperiling the Hán house.
After they were suppressed and eliminated,
Emperor Jǐng, learning from this,
then ordered that the kings were not allowed to govern the people.
He ordered the *Nèishǐ* to primarily govern the people.
The *Chéngxiàng* was renamed *Xiāng*.
The offices of *Yùshǐ Dàfū*, *Tíngwèi*, *Shàofǔ*, *Zōngzhèng*, and *Bóshì* were abolished.
Emperor Wǔ changed the names of Hán *Nèishǐ*, *Zhōngwèi*, and *Lángzhōnglìng*.
But the kingdoms remained as before.
All their officials were appointed by the imperial court,
and they were not allowed to appoint their own.
By the time of Emperor Chéng, the *Nèishǐ*'s role in governing the people was abolished.
Instead, the *Xiāng* was ordered to govern the people,
and the *Tàifù* was simply called *Fù*.
One *Zhōngwèi*,
ranked at two thousand *shí*.
The original note says: Their duties were like those of a Commandery *Dūwèi*,
in charge of bandits and thieves.
One *Lángzhōnglìng*,
one *Pú*.
Both ranked at one thousand *shí*.
The original note says: The *Lángzhōnglìng* was in charge of the kings' *Dàfū* and *Lángzhōng* who guarded the palace.
The office was like that of the *Guānglùxūn*.
Since the *Shàofǔ* was abolished,
all its duties were combined with this office.
The *Pú* was in charge of chariots and driving,
like the *Tàipú*.
The original note says *Tàipú*,
ranked at two thousand *shí*.
Emperor Wǔ changed it,
simply calling it *Pú*,
and also reduced all their ranks.
*Zhìshū*,
ranked at six hundred *shí*.
The original note says: *Zhìshū* was originally the *Shàngshū* renamed.
*Dàfū*,
ranked at six hundred *shí*.
The original note says: There was no fixed number of them.
They were in charge of presenting the king's envoys to the capital,
presenting jade *bì* to congratulate the New Year,
and sending envoys to other states.
Originally, they all carried *jié*,
but later the *jié* were removed.
*Yèzhě*,
ranked at four hundred *shí*.
The original note says: In charge of wearing the long cap.
Originally, there were sixteen members,
later reduced.
*Lǐyuèlìng*.
The original note says: In charge of musicians.
*Wèishìzhǎng*.
The original note says: In charge of guardsmen.
*Yīgōngzhǎng*.
The original note says: In charge of medicine.
*Yǒngxiàngzhǎng*.
The original note says: A eunuch,
in charge of palace maids and servants.
*Císìzhǎng*.
The original note says: In charge of sacrifices.
All ranked at four hundred *shí*.
*Lángzhōng*,
two hundred *shí*.
The original note says: No fixed number of them.
Wèi Gōng, Sòng Gōng.
The original note says: In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Jī Cháng, a descendant of Zhōu, was enfeoffed as Zhōu Chéngxīu Gōng;
in the fifth year,
Kǒng Ān, a descendant of Yīn, was enfeoffed as Yīn Shàojiā Gōng.
In the thirteenth year,
Cháng was renamed Wèi Gōng,
and Ān was renamed Sòng Gōng,
to be guests of Hán,
ranking above the Three Excellencies.
*Lièhóu*,
the county they ate from became a marquisate.
The original note says: Following the Qín's twenty ranks of nobility,
they were *Chèhóu*,
with gold seals and purple ribbons,
bestowed to reward meritorious service.
Those with great merit ate from counties,
those with less ate from townships or villages.
They could command the officials and people of their fief.
Later, to avoid Emperor Wǔ's personal name,
they were called *Lièhóu*.
In the second year of Yuánsuò, Emperor Wǔ,
ordered that the kings could "extend their benevolence" (tuī ēn) to divide land among their many sons.
The state enfeoffed them,
and they also became *Lièhóu*.
Old *Lièhóu* who attended court in Cháng'ān,
their rank was next to the Three Excellencies.
Since the Mid-Hán restoration,
only those granted the rank of *Tèjìn* for their merit and virtue,
ranked next to the *Chējì Jiāngjūn*;
those granted the rank of *Cháohóu*,
ranked next to the Five Colonels;
those granted the rank of *Cíhóu*,
ranked next to the *Dàfū*.
The rest, who were relatives or descendants of princesses, maintaining ancestral graves in the capital,
also attended court from time to time,
ranking below *Bóshì* and *Yìláng*.
Enfeoffed kings received *máo tǔ* (a bundle of earth with grass),
which they took back to establish altars of the land and grain;
this was the proper ritual.
*Liètǔ*, *Tèjìn*, and *Cháohóu* presented jade *bì* to congratulate the New Year.
Each state had one *Xiāng*,
their rank was like that of the original county.
The original note says: In charge of governing the people,
like a *Lìng* or *Zhǎng*,
but not subject to the marquis.
They only submitted taxes to the marquis,
limited by the number of households.
For their household officials,
they appointed one *Jiāchéng* and one *Shùzǐ* each.
The original note says: In charge of serving the marquis,
and managing household affairs.
*Lièhóu* originally had *Xíngrén*, *Xǐmǎ*, and *Méndàfū*,
a total of five officials.
Since the Mid-Hán restoration,
those with fiefs of a thousand households or more appointed one *Jiāchéng* and one *Shùzǐ* each.
Those with less than a thousand households did not appoint a *Jiāchéng*.
And *Xíngrén*, *Xǐmǎ*, and *Méndàfū* were all abolished.
*Guānnèihóu*,
following Qín's nineteenth rank of nobility,
were *Guānnèihóu*.
They had no land,
their income was based in the county where they resided.
The amount of people's rent,
each had a limited number of households.
Kings of the Four Barbarian tribes,
Chiefs of various kings,
*Guīyìhóu*,
*Yìjūn*,
*Yìzhǎng*,
all had a *Chéng*,
ranked like a commandery or county.
Salary regulations for all officials:
*Dàjiāngjūn* and the Three Excellencies' salary,
three hundred fifty *hú* per month.
Two thousand *shí* (medium) salary,
one hundred eighty *hú* per month.
Two thousand *shí* salary,
one hundred twenty *hú* per month.
Compared to two thousand *shí* salary,
one hundred *hú* per month.
One thousand *shí* salary,
eighty *hú* per month.
Six hundred *shí* salary,
seventy *hú* per month.
Compared to six hundred *shí* salary,
fifty *hú* per month.
Four hundred *shí* salary,
forty-five *hú* per month.
Compared to four hundred *shí* salary,
forty *hú* per month.
Three hundred *shí* salary,
forty *hú* per month.
Compared to three hundred *shí* salary,
thirty-seven *hú* per month.
Two hundred *shí* salary,
thirty *hú* per month.
Compared to two hundred *shí* salary,
twenty-seven *hú* per month.
One hundred *shí* salary,
sixteen *hú* per month.
*Dòushí* salary,
eleven *hú* per month.
*Zuǒshǐ* salary,
eight *hú* per month.
All recipients of salaries,
received half in cash and half in grain.
An encomium states: The Imperial Way is profound and silent;
the chief commanders cultivate virtue.
They govern the many with few,
and succeed by dividing responsibilities.
They neither appoint nor supervise,
having neither arrogance nor error.
They follow these principles as teachers,
bringing peace to the people and stability to the state.
Collated notes, page 3617, line 5: 外十二州 (wài shí'èr zhōu) (Twelve outer provinces/circuits). Note: The Jíběn and Diànběn editions
after the character 十 (shí)
have the character
有 (yǒu).
Page 3617, line 10: 省察治政 (shěngchá zhìzhèng) (Inspect and govern). Note: In the former table, Yán's annotation
cites 治政 (zhìzhèng)
as 治狀 (zhìzhuàng).
Sūn Xīngyǎn's compiled edition is the same.
Sūn says the annotation to the Guāngwǔ Jì (Annals of Guāngwǔ)
cites 治狀 (zhìzhuàng)
as 政教 (zhèngjiào).
Page 3617, line 12: 喜則任賞 (xǐ zé rèn shǎng) (When pleased, they bestow rewards). Note: In the former table, Yán's annotation
cites 任 (rèn)
as 淫 (yín).
Sūn's compiled edition is the same.
Page 3617, line 12: 煩擾苛暴 (fánrǎo kēbào) (Harassment, harshness, and tyranny). Note: In the former table, Yán's annotation
cites 苛 (kē)
as 刻 (kè).
The annotation in the Tōngdiǎn is the same.
Page 3617, line 12: 剝戮黎元 (bōlù líyuán) (Exploiting and slaughtering the common people). Note: In the former table, Yán's annotation
cites 戮 (lù)
as 截 (jié).
The annotation in the Tōngdiǎn is the same.
Page 3618, line 1: 怙恃榮勢 (hùshì róngshì) (Relying on glory and power). Note: In the former table, Yán's annotation
cites 怙恃 (hùshì)
as 恃怙 (shìhù).
Sūn's compiled edition is the same.
The annotation in the Tōngdiǎn is the same.
Page 3618, line 2: 比諸持板揖不拜 (bǐ zhū chí bǎn yī bù bài) (Compared to those holding tablets, bowing but not prostrating). Note: Sūn says
after the character 諸 (zhū)
there should be missing text.
Page 3618, line 7: 東安南 (Dōng'ānnán). Note: The Jíjiě (Collected Explanations) quotes Qián Dàxīn,
who says there is no verifiable Dōng'ānnán Commandery.
The Qín Zhōng Jì (Records of Central Qín) states that in the fifth year of Zhōngpíng, Nán'ān Commandery was established by dividing Hàn yáng.
The Jìn Zhì (Records of Jìn) states that Nán'ān Commandery governed the three counties of Dào, Xīnxīng, and Zhōngtáo.
It is suspected that this text originally read
南安 (Nán'ān)
and the character
東 (Dōng)
was an extraneous addition.
Page 3618, line 8: 凡十三【郡】 (fán shísān [jùn]) (A total of thirteen commanderies). Supplemented according to the Jíběn and Diànběn editions.
Page 3618, line 9: 凡十四【郡】 (fán shísì [jùn]) (A total of fourteen commanderies). Supplemented according to the Jíběn and Diànběn editions.
Page 3619, line 16: 雖不頓革 (suī bù dùn gé) (Although not completely reformed). Note:
頓 (dùn)
was originally erroneously written as
(tún);
it has been directly corrected.
Page 3620, line 7: 夫聖主御世 (fū shèngzhǔ yùshì) (Now, a sage lord governs the world). Note:
主 (zhǔ)
was originally written as
王 (wáng);
it has been directly corrected based on the Jíběn and Diànběn editions.

Page 3621, line 4: 凡州所監都為京都置尹一人 (fán zhōu suǒ jiān dōu wèi Jīngdū zhì yǐn yī rén) (For all prefectures supervised, an Administrator was appointed for the capital). The Jíjiě quotes Qián Dàxīn,

Huángshān's collation and supplement, however, states that

is a corruption of the character
郡 (jùn),
meaning that if any commandery became the capital, an Administrator was appointed, which was the practice during both the Former and Later Hàn dynasties.

This means that the *pú* (僕) of a kingdom was initially also called *Tàipú* (太僕),

Page 3629, line 8, “本注曰掌冠長冠本員十六人後減” (Běn zhù yuē zhǎng guān chángguān běnyuán shíliù rén hòu jiǎn): Jíjiě (集解) cites Qián Dàxīn’s (錢大昕) explanation,
stating that this sentence is suspected to have omissions and errors.
In the Hàn (漢) dynasty, the *yèzhě* (謁者) was in charge of guest reception, assisting in affairs, and presenting memorials and replies to queries.
Therefore, the duties of the *yèzhě* (謁者) in a kingdom should also have been similar.
Some say that *zhǎng guān* (掌官) and *chángguān* (長冠) were separate officials,
like *lǐyuè zhǎng* (禮樂長) or *wèishì zhǎng* (衞士長),
in which case the number of personnel could not have been so many.
The *Jiàobǔ* (校補) refers to the *Yúfú Zhì* (輿服志) which states

should be
“常” (cháng).
Now I comment: All instances of
“本注曰” (běn zhù yuē) and so on
are used to explain their duties.
Changing
“掌” (zhǎng)
to
“常” (cháng)
does not conform to the established pattern,
and the *Jiàobǔ’s* (校補) explanation
is also not convincing.
