On carriages and attire (輿服), there are: the jade carriage (*yùlù* 玉輅), imperial carriage (*chéngyú* 乘輿), gold-root carriage (*jīngēn* 金根), comfortable carriage (*ānchē* 安車), standing carriage (*lìchē* 立車), farming carriage (*gēngchē* 耕車), war chariot (*róngchē* 戎車), hunting carriage (*lièchē* 獵車), curtained carriage (*píngchē* 軿車), blue-canopy carriage (*qīnggàichē* 青蓋車), green carriage (*lǜchē* 綠車), black-canopy carriage (*zàogàichē* 皁蓋車), lady’s comfortable carriage (*fūrén ānchē* 夫人安車), grand imperial procession (*dàjià* 大駕), ceremonial imperial procession (*fǎjià* 法駕), small imperial procession (*xiǎojià* 小駕), light carriage (*qīngchē* 輕車), major envoy carriage (*dàshǐchē* 大使車), minor envoy carriage (*xiǎoshǐchē* 小使車), transport carriage (*zàichē* 載車), escort carriage (*dǎocóngchē* 導從車), and carriage and horse ornaments (*chēmǎshì* 車馬飾).
The *Shū* (書) says:
“Clearly test by merit,
carriages and clothes by achievement.”
It means that in ancient times, the sages brought about great benefits for the world,
and eliminated great harms for the world.
They personally engaged in these affairs,
and endured their hardships.
They worried and toiled,
not avoiding cold or heat,
so that the people and creatures of the world
could each live securely in their nature and life,
without the calamity of premature death or violent oppression.
Therefore, the people of the world
respected and loved them
as if they were their own parents;
they emulated and nourished them
as if looking up to the sun and moon.
Those who loved them desired their longevity,
did not shirk from labor,
and together built palaces,
raising beams and supporting roofs,
to shelter them,
desiring their longevity.
Those who respected them desired their dignity and solemnity,
did not shirk from toil and trouble,
and together built carriages, wheels, banners, and emblems,
to dignify them.
This is the utmost of love,
and the extreme of respect.
If one’s heart is truly loving and respectful,
even if the recompense is extreme,
the sentiment is still not fully expressed.
Some would sacrifice their lives for them,
fully expressing their sentiment;
others would worship them for generations,
making known their accomplishments.
Thus, their brilliant renown endures as long as heaven and earth.
Later sages,
knowing that those who deeply and greatly worry about the people
will certainly enjoy their happiness;
and those who diligently show benevolence and nurture creatures so they do not perish prematurely
will certainly receive their blessings.
Therefore, they established rituals to regulate them,
so that the superior benevolent ones could succeed Heaven and manage all things,
without boasting of their accomplishments,
and the people and creatures would be peaceful and content,
as if it happened naturally,
without knowing whom to thank.
Lǎozi (老子) said:
“The sage is not benevolent,
treating the common people as straw dogs.”
This is what is meant.
Now, the rise of ritual attire
served to recognize merit and distinguish virtue,
to honor benevolence and esteem the worthy.
Therefore, rituals honor the esteemed and value the noble;
one must not transgress these boundaries,
this is what ritual is for.
One who is not the proper person must not wear the proper attire,
this is to follow ritual.
When ritual is followed, there is order between the high and the low;
those with lesser virtue withdraw,
those with abundant virtue are adorned.
Thus, the sages, occupying the position of the Son of Heaven,
wore garments adorned with jade tassels and deep borders (suìyán),
with designs of sun, moon, and ascending dragons,
rode in a “mountain carriage” (shānchē) with golden axle caps,
beneath a yellow canopy with a left-side banner (zuǒdáo),
all to match their virtue
and display their achievements.
The benevolent and worthy who assist the sage,
enfeoffed with territories and governing the people,
wore garments with fǔfú embroidery,
and rode in carriages with descending dragons (lùchē),
all to make manifest their benevolence
and glorify their capabilities.
By the late period,
the sages did not attain their positions,
and the worthy were hidden away.
As a result, the Son of Heaven became weak and powerless,
and the feudal lords became a threat.
At this time, people esteemed each other by rank,
reviled each other for wealth,
and bribed each other for profit;
the rituals of the world were in chaos.
When Zhōu Yí Wáng descended the hall to welcome the feudal lords,
this was the Son of Heaven's loss of ritual,
the beginning of his weakness.
From then on, feudal lords played palace music and feasted,
sacrificed with white bulls,
struck jade qìngs,
had red shields with metal ornaments (xī),
and wore mǐan caps while performing the Dàwǔ dance.
Great officers had raised gatehouses, planted trees in their courtyards, and had earth mounds for libations (fǎndiàn);
they wore embroidered fǔfú and crimson inner garments,
used carved food vessels (gǔi), and wore crimson chin straps (zhūhóng);
these were instances of great officers usurping the rituals of feudal lords.
The Shī (Classic of Poetry) criticized,
“That son of a b*tch,
his attire does not match him,”
lamenting the corruption of customs.
The Yì (Classic of Changes) ridiculed,
“Carrying a load while riding in a carriage,
inviting bandits,”
meaning that when a petty person rides in a gentleman's vehicle,
bandits think of seizing it.
From then on, the ritual system was in great disarray,
and weapons of war arose in unison;
there was no law between high and low,
and feudal lords' retainers
used carved rafters and painted beams (zǎojǐ).
When it reached the Warring States period,
extravagance and usurpation grew even more rampant;
ritual texts were abolished and destroyed,
likely because they contained words harmful to themselves.
People competed to adorn themselves with strange and beautiful attire,
embellished with carriages and horses,
ornate rugs and jade bridles,
ivory bits and golden saddles (jīn'àn),
to boast over one another.
They fought for the profit of a chisel or a knife,
killing people as if mowing grass,
and their ancestral temples were also swiftly annihilated.
Glory and profit were all that mattered to them;
even death brought no regret.
When Qín unified the world,
it appropriated their carriages and attire;
the best were selected for imperial use,
and the next best were bestowed upon officials.
When Hàn arose,
literature was lacking,
and the era was also in its initial stages,
inheriting the Qín system.
Later, it was gradually revised and refined,
drawing upon the Six Classics,
approaching elegance and correctness.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If there be any who continues the Zhōu,
they will follow the righteousness of Xià,
ride in the carriage of Yīn,
wear the mǐan cap of Zhōu,
and find their music in Sháowǔ."
Therefore, I have compiled this account of carriages and attire and set it down in a chapter,
to observe the meaning of ancient and modern gains and losses.
In high antiquity, the sages,
seeing a rolling tumbleweed, first learned to make a wheel.
Wheels could carry loads,
and thus, by observing things, they came to know how to create,
and further made carriages.
Carriages and wheels supported each other,
moving endlessly,
carrying heavy loads and reaching distant places;
the world benefited from them.
Later sages observed the heavens,
watching the Dipper revolve;
with its square bowl (kuí) and curved handle (sháo),
they took the constellations Lóng and Jiǎo as the Emperor's chariot.
Thereupon, they curved the shafts,
hitched oxen and harnessed horses,
ascended dangerous paths, faced difficulties,
and surveyed the eight directions.
Thus, in the Yì, Zhèn (Thunder) riding Qián (Heaven)
is called Dàzhuàng (Great Vigor),
meaning no instrument could surpass it.
From then on,
generations added to its embellishments.
When Xī Zhòng served as the Director of Carriages for Xià,
he established its banners and pennants,
and for the noble and the humble, the high and the low,
each had their own grades.
The Zhōu house was fully equipped,
officials had six positions,
and the hundred artisans comprised one of them.
Among the artifacts for which many artisans exerted their skill,
carriages were the most numerous.
Therefore, the materials were prepared in due season,
and all six types of timber were excellent.
The carriage body was square, symbolizing the earth;
the canopy was round, symbolizing heaven;
thirty spokes symbolized the sun and moon;
twenty-eight ribs of the canopy bow symbolized the constellations.
The dragon banner (lóngqí) had nine streamers (jiǔliú),
seven rèn (measures) high, level with the front crossbar (zhěn),
symbolizing Dàhuǒ (Antares);
the bird banner (niǎoyú) had seven streamers,
five rèn high, level with the pole-end (jiào),
symbolizing Qúnhuǒ (the Hyades);
〔一０〕the bear banner (xióngqí) had six streamers,
five rèn high, level with the shoulder (jiān),
symbolizing Cān (Orion) and Fá (Theta Orionis);
〔一一〕the turtle banner (guīzhào) had four streamers,
four rèn high, level with the head (shǒu),
symbolizing Yíngshì (Pegasus-Andromeda);
〔一二〕the bow banner (hú jīng wǎng shǐ) with its crooked arrow,
symbolized the celestial bow (Hú): 〔一三〕These were the banners established by feudal lords and those below them.
〔一四〕
The Son of Heaven’s jade carriage (yùlù),
was adorned with jade,
with twelve layers of metal ornaments (xīfányīng),
displaying the Great Banner (Tàicháng),
with twelve streamers,
nine rèn long, dragging on the ground,
depicting the sun, moon, and ascending dragons,
symbolizing the brightness of heaven.
From Yí Wáng onward,
the Zhōu house declined and weakened,
and feudal lords began to use grand carriages (dàlù).
When Qín unified the world,
it reviewed the rituals of the Three Dynasties.
Some say that the Yīn used the Ruìshān carriage,
which had golden axle caps.
Hàn inherited the Qín system,
and the Emperor rode in the imperial carriage (chéngyú),
which is what Kǒngzǐ referred to as riding in the carriage of Yīn.
The imperial carriage (chéngyú), gold-axle-cap carriage (jīngēn), comfort carriage (ānchē), and standing carriage (lìchē)
all had wheels with vermillion stripes and double teeth (zhūbān chóngyá),
two hubs and two linchpins,
gold foil with entwined dragons,
for the carriage frame and pole-ends,
a patterned tiger crouching on the armrest (shì),
dragon heads holding the yoke,
good-fortune pipes (jíyángtǒng) on the left and right,
luan-birds standing on the crossbar (héng),
painted shafts,
a feathered canopy with ornate tassels (huázǎo),
displaying a grand banner (dàqí),
with twelve streamers,
painted with the sun, moon, and ascending dragons.
They were drawn by six horses,
with ivory bits and carved metal ornaments (lòuxī),
golden bridle-ornaments (jīnwǎn) on the forehead-straps,
adorned with pheasant tails,
vermillion harness-ornaments and bridle-tassels,
red felt and velvet stirrup-leathers,
with twelve layers of gold ornamentation.
A left-side banner (zuǒdáo) made of yak tail,
was placed on the yoke of the left outside horse,
as large as a dou measure.
〔一０〕This was the Virtue Carriage (déchē).
The Five Seasons Carriages (wǔshíchē),
both comfort and standing types, were also all like this,
each matching the color of its direction,
and the horses likewise.
For white horses,
their manes and tails were dyed red to be red manes.
The emperor's personal carriage was drawn by six horses,
while all others were drawn by four.
The one following behind was the secondary carriage.
〔一一〕
The plowing carriage
had all its decorations like these.
There were three types of canopies.
One was called the Zhīchē (芝車, "Spirit Car"),
which contained a quiver for plows and spades,
and was ridden by the sovereign when personally plowing.
The war chariot
had all its decorations like these.
It was adorned with spears, banners, golden drums, feathered fan-shaped banners,
and a quiver for helmets, armor, and crossbows.
The hunting chariot
had all its decorations like these.
It had heavy felloes and wrapped wheels,
with intertwined dragons coiled around them.
One was called the Xīzhūchē (闟豬車, "Boar-hunting Car"),
ridden by the sovereign when personally participating in hunts.
The Fǎjià (法駕, ceremonial carriage) of the Tàihuángtàihòu (太皇太后) and Huángtàihòu (皇太后)
all used the Jīngēn (金根, "Golden Root") carriage,
with a Jiāoluòzhàngshang (交絡帳裳, cross-netted curtain and skirt).
For non-Fǎjià (法駕),
they rode a zǐjìpíngchē (紫罽軿車, purple felt enclosed carriage),
with cloud patterns painted on the axle,
and the wǔmò (五末, five ends)
and the gài zǎo (蓋蚤, canopy's "feet") gilded.
There was a right and left *fēi* (騑, outrigger horse),
harnessing three horses.
Chánggōngzhǔ (長公主) rode a chìjìpíngchē (赤罽軿車, red felt enclosed carriage).
Dàguìrén (大貴人), Guìrén (貴人), Gōngzhǔ (公主), Wángfēi (王妃), and Fēngjūn (封君) rode yóuhuàpíngchē (油畫軿車, painted enclosed carriages).
Dàguìrén (大貴人) had an additional jiéhuàzhōu (節畫輈, section-painted axle).
All of them had only a right *fēi* (騑).
Huángtàizǐ (皇太子) and Huángzǐ (皇子) all rode Ānchē (安車, comfortable carriages),
with vermilion banded wheels,
a green canopy,
golden decorative "feet",
black patterns,
painted side screens with patterned axles,
and gilded wǔmò (五末).
When a Huángzǐ (皇子) was enfeoffed as a Wáng (王),
he was granted permission to ride this,
hence it was called the Wáng Qīnggàichē (王青蓋車, "King's Green Canopy Carriage").
Huángsūn (皇孫) followed in a lǜchē (綠車, green carriage).
All had right and left *fēi* (騑),
harnessing three horses.
Gōng (公) and Lièhóu (列侯) rode Ānchē (安車),
with vermilion banded wheels,
deer-shaped armrests,
crouching-bear footrests,
a black silk canopy,
black side screens,
and a right *fēi* (騑).
Zhōng'èrqiānshí (中二千石) and Èrqiānshí (二千石) all had black canopies
and two vermilion side screens.
Those of Qiānshí (千石) and Liùbǎishí (六百石) had
a vermilion left side screen.
The side screen was six *chǐ* long,
eight *cùn* wide at the bottom curve,
one *chǐ* and two *cùn* wide at the top,
with nine patterns,
twelve beginnings (divisions),
and the rear tapering by one *cùn*,
like the crescent moon,
showing that one dared not be full of oneself.
In the fifth year of the Zhōngyuán (中元) era of Jǐngdì (景帝),
an edict first allowed officials of Liùbǎishí (六百石) and above to use carriage side screens,
obtain bronze wǔmò (五末),
and have *jíyángtǒng* (吉陽筩, auspicious sun tubes) on their yokes.
Zhōng'èrqiānshí (中二千石) and above had a right *fēi* (騑).
Sānbǎishí (三百石) and above had black cloth canopies.
Qiānshí (千石) and above had black silk covers for their canopies.
Èrbǎishí (二百石) and below had white cloth canopies.
All had sìwéigāngyī (四維杠衣, four-cornered pole coverings).
Merchants were not allowed to ride horse-drawn carriages.
Except for officials, the poles were painted red;
all others were painted with green clouds.
The wives of Gōng (公), Lièhóu (列侯), Zhōng'èrqiānshí (中二千石), and Èrqiānshí (二千石),
when attending court or the silkworm ceremony,
each rode her husband's Ānchē (安車),
with a right *fēi* (騑),
and an added Jiāoluòwéishang (交絡帷裳, cross-netted curtain and skirt),
all in black.
When not for public assemblies,
they were not allowed to ride the court carriages,
but could ride a qībùzīpíngchē (漆布輜軿車, lacquered cloth baggage and enclosed carriage)
with bronze wǔmò (五末).
For the Shèngyú Dàjià (乘輿大駕, Emperor's Grand Imperial Procession),
the Gōng (公) and Qīng (卿) led the way,
the Tàipú (太僕) drove,
and the Dàjiàngjūn (大將軍) rode as assistant.
There were eighty-one attached carriages,
preparing for a thousand chariots and ten thousand cavalry.
When performing sacrifices to Heaven in the suburbs in the Western Capital,
Gānquán (甘泉) prepared it.
The officials had their registry for it,
named Gānquán Lǔbù (甘泉鹵簿).
In the Eastern Capital, only for Dàháng (大行, great funeral procession) was the Dàjià (大駕) used.
For Dàjià (大駕),
the Tàipú (太僕) inspected the driving;
for Fǎjià (法駕),
the Huángménlìng (黃門令) inspected the driving.
For the Shèngyú Fǎjià (乘輿法駕, Emperor's Ceremonial Imperial Procession),
the Gōng (公) and Qīng (卿) were not included in the *lǔbù* (鹵簿) registry.
The Hénányǐn (河南尹), Zhíjīnwú (執金吾), and Luòyánglìng (雒陽令) led the way,
the Fèngchēláng (奉車郎) drove,
and the Shìzhōng (侍中) rode as assistant.
There were thirty-four or sixteen attached carriages.
In the vanguard were nine *yóu* (斿, pennants) and cloud banners,
phoenix *xī* (闟, banners) and halberds,
leather-sided carriages and *luánqí* (鸞旗, phoenix banners),
all carried by Dàfū (大夫).
*Luánqí* (鸞旗) were
woven with feathers and yak tails,
arranged and tied alongside the banners.
Some common people called them *jīqiào* (雞翹, chicken plumes),
which was incorrect.
Behind were golden *zhēng* (鉦, gongs) and yellow *yuè* (鉞, axes),
and the Huángméngǔchē (黃門鼓車, Yellow Gate drum carriages).
In ancient times, feudal lords had nine auxiliary chariots.
Qín (秦) destroyed the Nine States,
absorbing their chariots and attire,
thus the Dàjià (大駕) had eighty-one attached carriages,
and the Fǎjià (法駕) had half of that.
All attached carriages had black canopies and red *yǎn* (𩹉, panels),
vermilion side screens,
and quivers for *gē* (戈, dagger-axes), spears, and crossbows,
ridden by the Shàngshū (尚書) and Yùshǐ (御史).
The very last carriage had a leopard tail hung,
and everything before the leopard tail was arranged according to the central bureaus.
When performing sacrifices to Heaven in the suburbs, the Fǎjià (法駕) was used.
For sacrifices to Earth and in the Míngtáng (明堂), it was reduced by one-third.
For sacrifices to the ancestral temple, it was even more reduced,
called Xiǎojià (小駕, "Small Procession").
Each time the emperor went out,
the Tàipú (太僕) presented the *lǔbù* (鹵簿) for the imperial procession,
with the Zhōngchángshì (中常侍) and Xiǎohuángmén (小黃門) as deputies;
the Shàngshū (尚書) in charge, with the Láng (郎) and Lìshǐ (令史) as deputies;
the Shìyùshǐ (侍御史),
with the Láimtáilìshǐ (蘭臺令史) as deputies.
All held the registry,
to supervise and maintain order among the carriages and cavalry,
which was called Hùjià (護駕, "Protecting the Imperial Procession").
In spring and autumn, when ascending the imperial tombs,
it was even more reduced than the Xiǎojià (小駕);
only one Zhíshì Shàngshū (直事尚書) followed,
while the rest, from Lìng (令) downwards,
all went ahead and returned later.
The Qīngchē (輕車, light chariot)
was an ancient war chariot.
It had open vermilion wheels and body,
no curtain or canopy,
and was fitted with spears, halberds, banners, pennants,
and crossbows.
It was stored in the Wǔkù (武庫, Imperial Armory).
When the Dàjià (大駕) or Fǎjià (法駕) went out,
the Shèshēng Xiàowèi (射聲校尉) and Sīmǎlì (司馬吏) rode it,
following the attached carriages in order,
as part of the *lǔbù* (鹵簿) registry.
All chariots had spears and halberds;
their decorative banners, pennants, and flags were all in five colors,
their system followed the *Zhōulǐ* (周禮).
Sūn Bīng (孫兵) of Wú (吳) stated in his *Bīngfǎ* (兵法):
"Those with curtains and canopies
are called Wǔgāngchē (武剛車, 'Martial Strong Chariots')."
Wǔgāngchē (武剛車)
served as the vanguard.
They also served as attached carriages and light chariots,
forming the rearguard.
For the Dàshǐchē (大使車, carriage of a Grand Envoy),
one stood to ride,
harnessing four horses,
with a red curtain.
For those holding a *jié* (節, imperial credential),

there was a double escort: two Zéicáochē (賊曹車, carriages of the Registrar of Criminals), two Fǔchē (斧車, axe carriages), two Dūchē (督車, carriages of the Supervisor), two Gōngcáochē (功曹車, carriages of the Registrar of Merits);
one Dàchē (大車, large carriage),
with twelve Wǔbó (伍伯) carrying crossbows;
four Pìchē (辟車, carriages for opening the way);
and four Zòngchē (從車, accompanying carriages).
Without a *jié* (節),
there was a single escort,
reduced by half.
The Xiǎoshǐchē (小使車, carriage of a Minor Envoy)
was not for standing to ride,
had a *fēi* (騑),
a red mudguard,
and a double crimson curtain.
The escort had no Fǔchē (斧車).
The Jìnxiǎoshǐchē (近小使車, carriage of a Close Minor Envoy)
was a lányú (蘭輿, orchid carriage) with red hubs,
a white canopy and red curtain.
It was followed by forty *zōuqí* (騶騎, mounted attendants).
This refers to the carriages ridden by those
who were dispatched to pursue and apprehend, or to conduct investigations.
All envoys' chariots had vermilion, patterned wheels,
with four spokes,
and red crossbars and yokes.
When they saw off funerals,
below the white chalk line,
they sprinkled their chariots and then returned.
Gōng, Qīng, Zhōng’èrqiānshí, and Èrqiānshí,
when going to the suburban altars, ancestral temples, Míngtáng, or sacrificial mausoleums,
or for legal proceedings,
all used large chariots,
stood to ride,
and were drawn by four horses.
For other outings,
they rode in ānchē.
Dàxíng rode in a chariot
whose ornamentation was like that of the Jīngēnchē,
with added interwoven jade-disk strings at the four corners,
golden dragon heads grasping jade disks,
hanging five-colored
pheasant feather tassels at the front and back,
a canopy and skirt painted with cloud patterns,
and patterned, curved front screens,
and long suspended streamers, etc.
The Tàipú drove,
harnessing six bùshīmǎ.
Bùshīmǎ
were pure white dappled horses,
whose bodies were branded with black medicine to create tiger patterns.
After descending,
the horses were sold off,
and the chariot was stored in a secret palace north of the city;
neither was allowed to enter the city gate.
When needed,
the Tàipú and Kǎogōng would then bring it in, decorate, and repair it.
Rites for auspicious and inauspicious occasions did not interfere with each other.
From Gōng and Qīng down to the xiàn Sānbǎishízhǎng leading their retinues,
they had five officials from the ménxià, a Zéicáo, and a Dúdàozéigōngcáo,
all wearing swords,
with three chariots leading;
the Zhǔbù and Zhǔjì
had two chariots following.
Xiànlìng and above
added an axe-chariot to the lead.
When Gōng rode in an ānchē,
they would have standing riders on both sides of the chariot.
The Cháng’ān and Luòyáng magistrates and those of capital counties in princely states added armed chariots in front and behind.
Tíngzhǎng
had a right outrigger horse
and drove with two horses.
For qiānwǔbó with suǒnǔchē,
Gōng had eight men,
Zhōng’èrqiānshí, Èrqiānshí, and Liùbǎishí all had four men,
and from Sìbǎishí down to Èrbǎishí all had two men.
Huángshòu officials
were wǔguānwǔbó;
wénguān were bìchē.
The língxià, shìgé, ménlán, bùshǔ, and jiēlǐzǒuzú
all had prescribed ranks and duties,
their numbers varying according to what they managed.
Relay horses were stationed every thirty lǐ,
and the soldiers all wore red turbans and crimson leggings.
In ancient times, when an army marched out,
all the shī and lǚ followed;
the Qín dynasty reduced their numbers,
retaining only the names of shī and lǚ.
From Gōng down to Èrqiānshí,
there were four qílì;
from Qiānshí down to Sānbǎishí,
and xiànzhǎng had two,
all wearing swords,
carrying qǐjǐ in the front ranks,
and bearing bows and nine quivers.
For the ceremonial chariots of Zhūhóuwáng,
their officials, from fùxiàng downwards,
all prepared lǔbù,
similar to the mounted officials in the capital,
with drawn bows and quivers,
escorting their comings and goings in a regulated manner.
Lièhóu
had jiāchéng and shùzǐ leading their retinues.
If they attended plowing sacrifices,
the presiding county would temporarily provide bìchē and splendid soldiers
to complete their regalia.
Once the escort duties were finished,
all borrowed personnel were dismissed.
The designs of various chariots: for the imperial carriage,
there were reclining dragons and crouching tigers,
painted poles,
dragon-head and luán-bird yokes,
double-toothed patterned wheels,
and soaring dragon flying screens.
For the Huáng Tàizǐ and Zhūhóuwáng,
there were reclining tigers and crouching deer,
painted poles and screens,
Jíyáng tubes,
vermilion patterned wheels,
deer-pattern flying screens,
and qífán with nine streamers and descending dragons.
For Gōng and Lièhóu,
there were reclining deer and crouching bears,
black screens,
vermilion patterned wheels,
deer-pattern flying screens,
and nine streamers with descending dragons.
For Qīng,
there were two vermilion screens,
and five streamers with descending dragons.
From Èrqiānshí downwards, each followed their rank and grade.
For all chariots with screens and above,
the yokes all had Jíyáng tubes.
The designs of various horses: for the imperial carriage,
there were golden (màn) [xiàng] square forehead ornaments,
pheasant feather decorated bits,
dragon patterns,
foamy soaring dragons,
red sweat-wipers,
blue two wings,
and tails.
For fùmǎ,
there were red ear tassels on the left and right,
flying bird ornaments,
and red chest-bands.
The Huáng Tàizǐ might also have similar.
For Wáng, Gōng, and Lièhóu,
there were carved (xīyì) [xīwén] manes,
vermilion bits and vermilion deer,
vermilion patterns,
crimson sweat-wipers,
and blue wings and tails.
From Qīng downwards, those with outrigger horses
had dark red sweat-wipers,
blue wings and tails,
and dānglú (yì) [wén] manes,
applicable to all ranks.
From Zhōng’èrqiānshí upwards, and envoys,
had outrigger horse carriages.

Imperial carriages and robes: Miǎnguān, Chángguān, Wěimàoguān, Píbìanguān, Juébìanguān, Tōngtiānguān, Yuǎnyóuguān, Gāoshānguān, Jìnxiánguān, Fǎguān, Wǔguān, Jiànhuáguān, Fāngshānguān, Qiǎoshìguān, Quèfēiguān, Quèdíguān, Fánkuàiguān, Shùshìguān, Héguan, Zé, Pèi, Dāo, Yìn, Huángchìshòu, Chìshòu, Lǜshòu, Zǐshòu, Qīngshòu, Hēishòu, Huángshòu, Qīnggānlún, and robes for empresses and noblewomen.
In high antiquity, people lived in caves and dwelt in the wilderness,
clothed in fur and covered with skins,
without established systems.
Later generations of Sages replaced them with silk and hemp,
observed the patterns of pheasants and kingfishers [huīdié],
and the colors of flowers and blossoms,
then dyed silks to imitate them,
first creating the five colors,
to complete their attire.
Seeing that birds and beasts had designs of crowns, horns, and beards,
they then made crowns, ceremonial hats, tassels, and pendants [yīngruí]
as head ornaments.
In total there were twelve chapters.
Therefore, the Yì says:
"When Páoqīshì ruled the world,
he looked up to observe the images in the sky,
looked down to observe the patterns on the earth,
observed the markings of birds and beasts,
and the suitability of the land,
taking inspiration from near at hand,
and from distant objects,
and thus first created the Eight Trigrams,
to communicate the virtues of the divine and enlightened,
and to categorize the natures of all things."
Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn brought order to the world by merely letting their robes hang down,
which was probably derived from Qiánluò.
Qiánluò has patterns,
hence the upper garment was black,
and the lower garment yellow.
The sun, moon, and stars,
mountains, dragons, and splendid insects [huáchóng],
were embroidered into huì, zōngyí,
water grasses, fire, powdered rice,
fǔfú, and fine embroidery,
using the five colors for patterns and applying them to the five colors to make robes.
The Son of Heaven wore all the patterns;
Gōng, from mountains downwards;
Hóubó, from splendid insects downwards;
Zǐnán, from water grasses and fire downwards;
Qīng Dàfū, from powdered rice downwards.
By the Zhōu dynasty, changes were made,
using the three luminaries as qífán.
When the King sacrificed to the Emperor on High,
he wore a large fur robe and a ceremonial cap;
Gōng, Hóu, Qīng, and Dàfū wore robes with nine patterns or fewer.
The Qín, rising from the Warring States period to the position of Son of Heaven,
abolished ritual studies,
and the robes for suburban sacrifices were all dark black.
The Hàn inherited the Qín precedents.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
establishing the capital in the center of the earth,
he first renovated the Sānyōng
and properly established the seven suburban altars.
Xiǎozōng then completed the great work,
first wearing the liúmiǎn
and robes with patterns,
red sandals and embroidered shoes,
to sacrifice to Heaven and Earth,
and to nourish the Sānlǎo and Wǔgēng at the Sānyōng;
at that time, great peace was achieved.
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ), the Three Dukes (Sāngōng), the Nine Ministers (Jiǔqīng), the Marquis of Special Advance (Tèjìn Hóu), and the Marquis Attending Sacrifices (Shìcí Hóu)
all sacrificed to Heaven and Earth (Tiāndì) and the Bright Hall (Míngtáng).
They all wore a feathered crown (liúmiǎn),
with upper garments of dark-blue and lower garments of crimson.
The Imperial carriage was fully adorned
with the twelve imperial symbols of the sun, moon, and stars.
The Three Dukes and the various Marquises (Zhūhóu) used the nine symbols of mountains and dragons.
The Nine Ministers and those below them used the seven symbols of splendid insects.
All were furnished with five colors.
They wore a large jade pendant (dàpèi),
red shoes (chìxì) with embroidered toe-caps (qú lǚ),
to attend the great sacrifices.
All officials performing duties
wore a long cap (chángguān),
and all wore solemn attire (zhīfú).

For the Five Sacred Mountains (Wǔyuè), Four Great Rivers (Sìdú), mountains and rivers (shānchuān), ancestral temples (zōngmiào), altars of land and grain (shèjì), and all other officially sanctioned sacrifices,
they all wore dark-blue (jūn xuán) and a long cap.
For the Five Suburban Sacrifices (Wǔjiāo), they each wore the color appropriate to their direction.
Officials not performing duties
each wore their usual cap and dark-blue attire when accompanying.
The crown (miǎnguān)
had hanging tassels (chuíliú).
The front and back of the crown were deep and extended.
It had jade streamers (yùzǎo).
In the second year of Yongpíng (Yǒngpíng) of Emperor Xiàomíng (Xiàomíng Huángdì)
an edict was first issued ordering officials to consult the Zhōuguān (Zhōuguān), the Lǐjì (Lǐjì), and the Gāotáo (Gāotáo) chapter of the Shàngshū (Shàngshū).
The attire for the Imperial carriage followed the theories of Ouyáng (Ouyáng) clan.
For the Dukes and Ministers downwards, it followed the theories of the elder and younger Xiàhóu (Xiàhóu) clans.
All crowns were seven cǔn wide
and one chǐ two cǔn long.
They were round in front and square in back,
with vermilion and green lining (zhūlǜxiáng),
dark-blue on top.
In front, it hung down four cǔn,
and in back, three cǔn.
Twelve tassels (shí'èr liú) were suspended, made of white jade beads.
Their cords (zǔyīng) were of the same color as their sashes (shòu).
The Three Dukes and the various Marquises had seven tassels,
with blue jade beads.
The Ministers (Qīng) and Grand Masters (Dàfū) had five tassels,
with black jade beads.
All had tassels in front but not in back.
Their cords were of the same color as their sashes,
with yellow silk floss (tǒuhuáng) hanging at the sides.
For sacrifices to Heaven and Earth (Tiāndì) in the suburbs,
ancestral sacrifices (zōngcí),
and the Bright Hall (Míngtáng),
these crowns were worn.
The garments (yīshang) and jade pendants (yùpèi) were fully adorned with symbols and colors.
The Imperial carriage's garments were embroidered (cìxiù).
For Dukes (Gōng), Marquises (Hóu), Nine Ministers (Jiǔqīng), and those below, they were woven.
This was said to be presented by Chénliú (Chénliú) and Xiāngyì (Xiāngyì).
The long cap (chángguān),
also called the ritual cap (zhāiguān),
was seven cǔn high
and three cǔn wide.
It was made of tightly lacquered silk (cùqīlǐ).
Its shape was like a board,
with a bamboo frame (zhúxiáng).
Originally,
when Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) was of humble status,
he made it from bamboo skin.
It was called the Liú (Liú) family cap,
a Chu (Chǔ) style cap.
The common people called it the magpie-tail cap (quèwěiguān),
which is incorrect.
For sacrifices to ancestral temples (zōngmiào) and other sacrifices, this cap was worn.
All wore dark-blue (jūn xuán) attire,
with crimson-edged collars and sleeves as inner garments.
They wore crimson trousers (jiàngkuò),
showing their sincere devotion to the deities.
For the Five Suburban Sacrifices (Wǔjiāo), the attire, cap, and trousers were each of their respective colors.
This cap was created by Gāozǔ,
hence it was used as sacrificial attire,
showing the utmost respect.
The dignified cap (wēimàoguān) and the leather cap (píbìanguān) were of the same design.
They were seven cǔn long
and four cǔn high.
Their shape was like an inverted cup,
high and wide in front,
low and pointed in back.
This is what was called the Wú Zhuī (Wú Zhuī) of Xià (Xià)
and the Zhāngfǔ (Zhāngfǔ) of Yīn (Yīn).
The dignified cap (wēimàoguān) was made of dark-blue silk (zàojuàn),
and the leather cap (píbìanguān) was made of deerskin.
When performing the grand archery ceremony (dàshè lǐ) at the Bìyōng (Bìyōng),
the Dukes, Ministers, Marquises, and Grand Masters who performed the rites
wore the dignified cap (wēimàoguān)
and black formal attire (xuánduān) with plain lower garments (sùshang).
Those performing duties wore the leather cap (píbìanguān),
black hemp garments (zīmáyī),
with dark-blue collars and sleeves,
and plain lower garments.
This is what was called the leather cap and plain pleated skirt (píbìan sùjī).
The sparrow cap (juébiàn)
was also called a crown (miǎn).
It was eight cǔn wide
and one chǐ two cǔn long.
It resembled the shape of a sparrow,
smaller in front and larger in back.
The top was covered with silk resembling the color of a sparrow's head.
It had a band to hold the hairpin (shōuchí jī).
This is what was called the Xià (Xià) band (xiàshōu) and the Yīn (Yīn) hairpin (yīnxǔ).
For sacrifices to Heaven and Earth (Tiāndì), the Five Suburban Sacrifices (Wǔjiāo), and the Bright Hall (Míngtáng),
the Cloud Peak (Yúnqiáo) dancers and musicians wore it.
The Lǐjì (Lǐjì) states:
"With vermilion shields and jade battle-axes (zhūgānyùqī),
one dances the Great Xià (Dàxià) wearing a crown."
This is what it refers to.
The Heaven-Connecting Cap (tōngtiānguān) was nine cǔn high,
standing upright.
The top slightly receded,
then dropped straight down to form an iron curved beam (tiějiǎnjuànliáng).
In front, there was a mountain-like ornament (shān).
An extended tube (zhǎntǒng) formed a 'shù' ornament.
This was usually worn by the Imperial carriage.
The formal garments (fúyī)
were of the deep garment (shēnyī) style,
with a robe (páo).
The color varied according to the five seasons.
Regarding the robe,
some say that Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng) held King Chéng (Chéng Wáng) while at ease,
hence the use of robes.
The Lǐjì (Lǐjì) states:
"Confucius (Kǒngzǐ) wore a robe with ample sleeves (féngyì zhī yī)."
Its sleeves
were gathered and sewn wide.
It is similar to today's robes.
Today, even the lowest-ranking minor officials (jiàngèngxiǎoshǐ)
all wear robes of a standard design,
unlined garments (dānyī),
and inner garments with dark-blue collars and sleeves (zàoyuán lǐngxiù zhōngyī),
which are considered court attire.
The Far-Roaming Cap (yuǎnyóuguān)
was made like the Heaven-Connecting Cap (tōngtiānguān),
with an extended tube (zhǎntǒng) crossing in front,
but without the mountain-like ornament or the 'shù' ornament.
It was worn by the various princes (zhūwáng).
The High Mountain Cap (gāoshānguān),
also called the Side-Slanting Cap (cèzhù),
was made like the Heaven-Connecting Cap (tōngtiānguān),
[but] the top did not recede,
it stood straight up,
without the mountain-like ornament, 'shù' ornament, or extended tube.
It was worn by central and local officials, heralds (yèzhě), and palace attendants (púshè).
Grand Tutor Hú Guǎng (Hú Guǎng) said:
"The High Mountain Cap (gāoshānguān)
was probably the cap of the King of Qí (Qí Wáng).
When Qín (Qín) destroyed Qí,
it bestowed its ruler's cap upon close officials and heralds to wear."
The Cap of Advance of Worthies (jìnxiánguān)
was an ancient black cloth cap (zībùguān).
It was worn by cultured scholars (wénrú).
It was seven cǔn high in front
and three cǔn high in back,
and eight cǔn long.
Dukes and Marquises had three beams (sānliáng).
Officials from two thousand shí (èrqiānshí) downwards, including Academicians (Bóshì), had two beams (liǎngliáng).
From Academicians downwards to minor officials (xiǎoshǐ) and private students (sīxué dìzǐ),
all had one beam (yīliáng).
Members of the Imperial clan of Liú (Liú Shì) also had two-beamed caps,
indicating their elevated status.
The Law Cap (fǎguān),
also called the Rear Pillar Cap (zhùhòu),
was five cǔn high.
It used silk for the extended tube,
and an iron pillar roll (tiězhùjuǎn).
It was worn by law enforcement officials,
such as Imperial Censors (shìyùshǐ), and the Chief and Assistant Justice (tíngwèizhèngjiānpíng).
Some called it the Xièzhì (Xièzhì) Cap.
The Xièzhì (Xièzhì) was a mythical sheep
capable of discerning right from wrong.
The King of Chǔ (Chǔ Wáng) once obtained one,
hence it was used as a cap.
Hú Guǎng (Hú Guǎng) said:
"The Zuǒshì Zhuàn (Zuǒshì Zhuàn) of the Chūnqiū (Chūnqiū) mentions someone 'wearing a southern cap and bound' (nánguān ér zhí).
That was a Chu (Chǔ) cap.
When Qín (Qín) destroyed Chǔ,
it bestowed its ruler's attire upon close law enforcement officials and Imperial Censors (yùshǐ) to wear."
The Wǔguān (Military Cap),
also called Wǔbiàn Dàguān (Great Military Cap),
was worn by all military officials.
The Shìzhōng and Zhōngchángshì (Central Regular Attendants) added a golden *dāng* (ornament),
with cicadas forming the pattern,
and mink tails as decoration.
It was called
"Zhào Huìwénguān" (Cap of King Huìwén of Zhào).
Hú Guǎng said:
"King Wǔlíng of Zhào adopted Hu (nomadic) clothing,
decorating his head with golden *dāng*,
and inserting a mink tail in front,
marking a noble position.
When Qín conquered Zhào,
it bestowed the cap of the Zhào ruler upon its close ministers."
During the Jiànwǔ era,
when the Xiongnú became internally subordinate,
Shìzǔ (Emperor Guāngwǔ) bestowed clothing upon the Southern Chányú,
including the Huìwénguān of a Zhōngchángshì,
and the ceremonial dagger of a Zhōnghuángmén (Eunuch) youth.
The Jiànhuáguān (Constructed Flower Cap)
had an iron column-like coil,
strung with nine large copper beads.
Its design resembled a *lùlù* (filigree deer).
A record states:
"Those who understand Heaven wear the *shù* cap;
those who understand Earth wear *qú* shoes."
The *Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn* (Zuo Commentary to the Spring and Autumn Annals) states:
"Zhèng Zǐzāng loved the *yù* (snipe) cap."
It was round in front,
and this is probably it.
Performers of the *yùmìng* dance music for the ceremonies of Heaven, Earth, the Five Suburbs, and the Míngtáng wore it.
The Fāngshānguān (Square Mountain Cap)
resembled the Jìnxián (Cap for Advancing the Worthy),
and was made of five-colored gauze.
Performers of the *dàyǔ*, Bāyì (Eight-Row Dance), Four Seasons, and Five Elements music wore it during ancestral sacrifices and court audiences.
Their caps and robes were each of the color corresponding to their cardinal direction when they danced.
The Qiǎoshìguān (Artisan's Cap)
was seven *cùn* high in the front,
connected at the waist in the back,
and stood straight up.
It was not worn regularly,
but only during the suburban sacrifice to Heaven,
when four attending officials of the Huángmén (Eunuchs) wore it.
They were in the imperial procession,
behind the imperial chariot,
to represent the four eunuch stars.
The Quèfēiguān (Repelling Evil Cap)
was similar in design to the Chángguān (Long Cap),
but shorter at the bottom.
Palace gate officials and *púyè* (chamberlains) wore it.
They carried red banners,
with green wings and swallow tails.
All *púyè*'s banners were like this.
The Quèdíguān (Repelling Enemy Cap)
was four *cùn* high in front,
four *cùn* long overall,
and three *cùn* high in back.
Its design resembled the Jìnxián,
and guardsmen wore it.
The Fánkuàiguān (Cap of Fán Kuài)
was the cap Fán Kuài wore in haste
when entering Xiàng Yǔ's army.
It was nine *cùn* wide,
seven *cùn* high,
and extended four *cùn* in front and back.
Its design resembled a *miǎn* (ceremonial crown).
Guardsmen of the Sīmǎ (Minister of War) palace gate wore it.
Some say
Fán Kuài always carried an iron shield.
Hearing that Xiàng Yǔ intended to kill the King of Hàn,
Kuài tore his clothes to wrap the shield,
and wearing it as a cap, entered the army camp,
standing beside the King of Hàn,
and looking at Xiàng Yǔ.
The Shùshìguān (Cap of Diviners)
was round in front,
a Wú (state) design,
with four staggered and undulating layers.
King Wǔlíng of Zhào liked to wear it.
It is not used today,
but the official records contain its illustration.
All caps had tassels (*yīngruí*).
Officials and military officers all had shortened tassels,
hanging five *cùn*.
The Wǔguān (Military Cap),
popularly called Dàguān (Great Cap),
had a circular tassel without *ruí* (pendants),
used a green cord as a border,
and added two *hé* (pheasant) tails,
standing upright on the left and right,
thus called the Hégūan (Pheasant Cap).

The Wǔguān, the Left and Right Hǔbēn (Tiger Troopers), Yǔlín (Feathered Forest), the Wǔ Zhōnglángjiàng (Five Central Colonels), and the Left and Right Yǔlín Jiān (Superintendents of the Feathered Forest) all wore the Hégūan,
with single garments of gauze.
The Hǔbēnjiàng (Tiger Trooper Generals) wore tiger-patterned trousers,
and carried swords and daggers with white tiger patterns.
All Hǔbēn Wǔqí (Tiger Trooper Cavalry) wore Hégūan,
and tiger-patterned single garments.
Xiāngyì annually presented woven tiger patterns.
The *hé* (pheasant)
is a courageous pheasant.
When they fight, they do not stop until one dies.
Therefore, King Wǔlíng of Zhào used it to honor warriors,
and Qín adopted it.
When Emperor Ān established the Crown Prince,
the Crown Prince paid respects at the temple of Gāozǔ (Emperor Gāo) and Shìzǔ (Emperor Guāngwǔ).
The Mén Dàfū (Gate Grandees) attending
wore the two-beam Jìnxián cap;
the Xǐmǎ (Master of Horses) wore the Gāoshān (High Mountain) cap.
After the temple ceremony,
Shìyùshǐ Rèn Fāng submitted a memorial requesting that when not accompanying the emperor,
they all wear the one-beam cap,
and that it should not be their regular attire.
The matter was sent to the relevant department.
Shàngshū Chén Zhōng submitted a memorial:
"The Mén Dàfū's duties are like those of a Jiàndàfū (Grandee Remonstrant),
and the Xǐmǎ's duties are like those of an Yèzhě (Usher).
Therefore, they all wear their respective attire;
this is an old practice of the former emperors.
Fāng's words can be set aside."
The memorial was approved.
The Yèzhě
was anciently also called Xǐmǎ.
In ancient times, there were caps but no *zé* (headcloths).
When they were worn,
they were placed on the head with a *kuǐ* (inner cap),
which secured the object.
Therefore, the *Shī* (Book of Odes) says
"There is a *kuǐ* for the *biàn* cap,"
which refers to this.
During the Three Dynasties,
laws and regulations became increasingly clear.
Down to the Warring States period,
both civil and military practices were used.
Qín dominated the feudal lords,
and added a crimson *pà* (headband) to the headdress of its military generals
to distinguish rank.
Later, it gradually became *yántí* (forehead band).
When Hàn arose,
it continued the *yán* (forehead) part,
but removed the *luǒ* (bun-cover),
added a *jīn* (cloth) connecting the *tí* (band),
and covered the back.
Today's mourning *zé* is of this design.
It was named *zé*.
The *zé*
means *zé* (strictness, dignity),
meaning the head is strictly dignified.
It was not until Emperor Xiàowén that the *yántí* was raised,
extended to form "ears,"
and the *jīn* was elevated to form a "roof."
The back was brought together and tied.
All officials and commoners, regardless of rank, wore it.
Civil officials had long "ears,"
and military officials had short "ears,"
matching their caps.
The Shàngshū (Minister of State) had a *zé* with a tie
three *cùn* square,
named Nàyán (Receiving Words),
to show loyalty and integrity,
and to highlight their close position.
When welcoming the *qì* (energies) in the Five Suburbs,
each wore the color appropriate to its direction,
following the ceremonial robes.
All officials in black robes wore green *zé* in spring,
stopping on Lìxià (Beginning of Summer),
to assist the subtle *qì* and follow the season,
honoring that direction.
Military officials always wore red *zé*,
to enhance their authority.
Uncapped youths wore *zé* without a "roof,"
to show they were not yet adults.
Young children entering school wore *zé* with a curled roof,
to show they were still young,
and not yet far from home.
Mourning *zé* had the *luǒ* part reversed,
returning to the original rite.
The number of *shēng* (tiers) was like that of the cap,
accompanying the cap.
For a one-year mourning period, the "ears" began with a tie,
and the plain *zé* was also like this.
The weight of rites had regulations,
and changes and removals were gradual,
this being *wén* (refinement).
In ancient times, rulers and ministers wore jade pendants,
with distinctions in rank;
they wore fù (aprons) above,
with differences for noble and humble.
The pèi (jade pendant)
was used to manifest virtue,
being at the core of one's attire.
The fù (apron)
was used to manage affairs,
being for the reverence of ritual.
Thus, rituals had their specific degrees,
and the system of solemn deportment
was common to the Sān Dài (Three Dynasties).
When the Wǔ Bà (Five Hegemons) rose in succession,
and military conflicts were ceaseless,
the pèi was not a weapon,
and the fù was not a military banner.
Thereupon, the fù and pèi were removed,
but their suì (strings for pendants) were retained
to serve as an outer adornment.
Therefore, the Shī (Odes) says,
"The glistening suì of the pèi,"
this is what it refers to.
Once the fù and pèi were abolished,
Qín then used colored cords to connect to the suì,
brightly adorning the exterior,
intertwined and joined together.
Hence, it was called shòu (seal cord).
Hàn inherited the Qín system,
using it without alteration,
and thus added to it the ornament of a double seal and a dagger.
When it came to Xiàomíng Huángdì,
he then established the dà pèi (great pendant),
with chōngyá and a pair of yǔhuáng,
all made of white jade.
The imperial carriage's cords were adorned with white pearls,
while gōngqīng and zhūhóu used colored silk.
Their [jade] resembled the miǎnliú (imperial crown with fringes),
and was for sacrificial attire.
Regarding the pèi dāo (dagger),
for the imperial carriage, it was gold all over with mink inlay,
half with shark scales,
gold lacquer inlay,
a realgar-colored sheath,
and a five-colored wool felt lining with floral patterns.
For zhūhóu wáng, it was gold inlay,
with a ring hilt and half shark scales,
and a black sheath.
For gōngqīng and all bǎiguān, they were entirely black,
without half shark scales.
Xiǎohuángmén had realgar-colored sheaths,
Zhōnghuángmén had vermilion sheaths,
all tóngzǐ had tiger claw patterns,
hǔbēn had yellow sheaths with tiger patterns,
their jiàng had white tiger patterns,
all using white pearls and shark skin as mouth decorations.
Those for the imperial carriage
added a emerald mountain
with ribbons wrapped around its side.
The pèi shuāng yìn (double seal)
was one cùn and two fēn long,
and six fēn square.
For the imperial carriage, zhūhóu wáng, gōng, and lièhóu, they were made of white jade.
From zhòng èr qiān shí down to sì bǎi shí, all used black rhinoceros horn.
From èr bǎi shí down to private school disciples, all used ivory.
At the top, silk cords were joined.
For the imperial carriage, a string threaded with white pearls,
and a red wool felt ruí (tassel).
From zhūhóu wáng down, a silk cord with a red silk ruí,
the strings and cords matching the material of their respective seals.
The engraved inscription read:
"In the first month, the gāngmǎo is already determined,
the spiritual shū (peg) points in four directions,
red, green, white, yellow,
these four colors are appropriate.
The Emperor commands Zhùróng,
to instruct Kuí Lóng,
let all epidemics and illnesses,
not dare to contend with me.
On the auspicious day of yánmǎo,
the Emperor commands Kuí to transform,
be cautious in your full submission,
transform this spiritual shū.
Already correct and straight,
already angled and square,
let all epidemics and illnesses,
not dare to contend with me."
There were sixty-six characters in total.
The imperial carriage wore a huángchì shòu (yellow and red seal cord),
with four colors:
yellow, red, (dark red) blue [dark red],
a solid yellow guī (tablet),
one zhàng,
nine chǐ, and nine cùn long,
with five hundred shǒu (strands).
Zhūhóu wáng wore a chì shòu (red seal cord),
with four colors:
red, yellow, blue, dark red,
a solid red guī,
two zhàng and one chǐ long,
with three hundred shǒu.
Tàihuáng Tàihòu and Huáng Tàihòu's
shòu were all the same as for the imperial carriage;
Huánghòu also followed this.
Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ and Tiānzǐ Guìrén had shòu the same as zhūhóu wáng,
this was an added distinction.
Zhūguó Guìrén and Xiàngguó all wore lǜ shòu (green seal cords),
with three colors:
green, purple, dark red,
a solid green guī,
two zhàng and one chǐ long,
with two hundred and forty shǒu.
Gōng, Hóu, and Jiāngjūn wore zǐ shòu (purple seal cords),
with two colors:
purple, white,
a solid purple guī,
one zhàng and seven chǐ long,
with one hundred and eighty shǒu.
Gōngzhǔ and Fēngjūn wore zǐ shòu.
Jiǔ Qīng, Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí, and Èr Qiān Shí wore qīng shòu (blue seal cords),
with three colors:
blue, white, red,
a solid blue guī,
one zhàng and seven chǐ long,
with one hundred and twenty shǒu.
From the qīng shòu upwards,
the xiè were all three chǐ and two cùn long,
with the same colors as the shòu but half the number of shǒu.
The xiè
was the ancient pèi suì.
The pèi and shòu met and received each other,
hence it was called xiè.
From the zǐ shòu upwards,
a jade ring and buckle could be placed between the xiè and shòu.
Qiān Shí and Liù Bǎi Shí wore hēi shòu (black seal cords),
with three colors:
blue, red, dark red,
a solid blue guī,
one zhàng and six chǐ long,
with eighty shǒu.
Sì Bǎi Shí and Sān Bǎi Shí had the same length.
Sì Bǎi Shí, Sān Bǎi Shí, and Èr Bǎi Shí wore huáng shòu (yellow seal cords),
[one color],
a solid yellow guī,
(one color) one zhàng and five chǐ long,
with sixty shǒu.
From the hēi shòu downwards,
the xiè shòu were all three chǐ long,
with the same colors as the shòu but half the number of shǒu.
Bǎi Shí wore qīnggàn (luán) [shòu] (blue and dark red [cord]),
one color,
twisted and interwoven [guī],
one zhàng and two chǐ long.
In general, first, single spun threads were combined to form one xì (strand),
four xì formed one fú (bundle),
five fú formed one shǒu (head),
five shǒu formed one wén (pattern),
and the solid wén cǎi (patterned color) formed one guī.
Those with many shǒu had fine xì,
those with few had coarse xì,
all were one chǐ and six cùn wide.
Tàihuáng Tàihòu and Huáng Tàihòu wore temple attire,
dark red above and black below,
silk-reeling robes,
blue above and pale blue below,
all in the style of deep robes,
with concealed collars and sleeve edges trimmed with ribbons.
They wore jiǎn máo dài (cut hair bun)
and zān'ěr (hairpins and earrings).
The ěr (earrings)
were ear pendants with hanging pearls.
The zān (hairpin) used mào as its tí (ornamental part),
one chǐ long,
the end formed a huáshèng (ornamental hairpiece),
with a fènghuáng jué (phoenix sparrow) on top,
using emeralds for its feathers,
with white pearls below,
and hanging golden niè (tweezer-like ornaments).
One was horizontally pinned on each side
to secure the dài knot.
All zān'ěr were of the same design,
but their tí had different ranks.
The empress's attire for visiting the ancestral temple:
a dark blue upper garment and a black lower garment.
For sericulture:
a green upper garment and a light blue lower garment,
all in the *shēnyī* style,
with concealed collar and sleeve edges bound with cords.
She wore a *jiǎjié*,
a *bùyáo*,
and *zāněr*.
The *bùyáo* was made of gold for the mountain theme,
strung with white pearls to intertwine like cinnamon branches,
with one *jué* and nine *huá*,
and six beasts: bears, tigers, red bears, *tiānlù*, *pìxié*, and the *nánshān fēngdàtè*,
which is what the *Shī*
refers to as "the *fùjī* with six *jiā*".
All *jué* and beasts were made of kingfisher feathers.
With a gold theme,
encircled by white pearl pendants,
and decorated with kingfisher feathers for the *huá* clouds.
The attire of noble ladies assisting in sericulture:
entirely light blue, upper and lower garments,
in the *shēnyī* style.
They wore a *dàjié*,
a *mòmào*,
and also *zāněr*.
The attire for *zhǎnggōngzhǔ* at gatherings:
she added a *bùyáo*.
*Gōngzhǔ* wore a *dàjié*,
all had *zāněr*,
and the garments were of the same style.
From *gōngzhǔ* and *fēngjūn* upwards, all wore *dài shòu*,
using colored cords for the sash,
each according to the color of their *shòu*.
A gold *pìxié*
formed the buckle of the belt,
adorned with white pearls.
The wives of *gōng*, *qīng*, *lièhóu*, *zhōng'èrqiānshí*, and *èrqiānshí*:
a dark blue silk hairnet,
a gold dragon head holding a white pearl,
a fish-whisker hairpin,
one *chǐ* long,
forming the *zāněr*.
Those entering the temple to assist in sacrifices wore black silk upper and lower garments;
those assisting in sericulture wore light blue silk upper and lower garments,
all in the *shēnyī* style,
with borders.
From the wives of *èrqiānshí* upwards to the empress,
all used the sericulture attire as court dress.
*Gōngzhǔ*, noble ladies, *fēi*, and above,
for marriages, could wear brocade, damask, gauze, and silk,
in twelve colors,
with double-bordered robes.
*Tèjìn*, *lièhóu*, and above wore brocade and silk,
in twelve colors.
Six hundred *shí* and above wore heavy plain silk,
in nine colors,
with red, purple, and dark blue prohibited.
Three hundred *shí* and above wore five colors:
green, crimson, yellow, red, and emerald green.
Two hundred *shí* and above wore four colors:
green, yellow, red, and emerald green.
Merchants
wore only pale yellow and light blue.
*Gōng*, *lièhóu*, and below all had single-bordered sleeves
and wore embroidered patterns for sacrificial attire.
From the empress downwards,
all were forbidden from wearing the ancient ornate *guī*, *sān*, and *guīyuán jiāshàng* garments.
During the *Jiànwǔ* and *Yǒngpíng* eras, these were strictly prohibited;
during the *Jiànchū* and *Yǒngyuán* eras, they were again partly reinstated.
Consequently, the world could not establish a consistent regulation for their tailoring,
and so they were eventually completely abolished.
Regarding all caps, clothes, and other attire:
*liúmiǎn*, *chángguān*, *wěimào*, *píbàn*, *juébàn*, *jiànhuá*, *fāngshān*, *qiǎoshì*,
embroidered garments,
red sandals,
*fúqū* shoes,
and large pendants
were all for sacrificial attire;
the rest were all for everyday court wear.
Only the *chángguān*
was used by the *yèzhě* of various kingdoms as regular court attire.
For ancestral temples and below,
all sacrifices were attended wearing *chángguān*,
black silk robes and single garments,
an inner garment with crimson-bordered collar and sleeves,
and crimson *kù[mò]*.
The five suburbs followed their respective colors.
A eulogy says: Carriages and palanquins each had their proper use;
banners and flags occupied different positions.
Caps and robes were made beautiful,
with pendants adorning jade seals.
Respectfully showing sentiment,
the revered bowed their desires.
Who boasted of splendid patterns,
if not those of magnificence and intricacy?
Collation Notes, page 3661, line 8: "遂作冠冕纓蕤" (suì zuò guān miǎn yīng ruí). Note: The Jíjiě (集解) quotes Huì Dòng's (惠棟) saying,
